courses.title: Prosthetics & Orthotics

options: Evaluate swallowing and consider alternative stabilization
Add chin support to the collar
Continue the orthosis without any modification
Switch immediately to a soft collar
questions.explanation: Dysphagia in a patient wearing a rigid cervical collar warrants formal evaluation of the swallowing mechanism, since collar-related anterior neck pressure can impair swallowing, and an alternative method of cervical stabilization should be considered if the current device is unsafe. Simply continuing without modification risks aspiration. Immediately discontinuing stabilization without addressing spinal safety would be inappropriate if instability still requires support.
questions.question: A patient with a Miami J collar develops dysphagia. What is the MOST appropriate next step?

options: Ankle inversion strap or pad with a plantarflexion stop
Free-motion ankle joint with no stops
questions.question: A stroke patient with equinovarus deformity bears weight primarily on the lateral border of the foot during stance. Which AFO feature is most important to control this deformity?
questions.explanation: Equinovarus deformity is best managed with an AFO that includes a plantarflexion stop to control excess plantarflexion and an inversion strap or pad to control the inversion component. A free-motion ankle would fail to control the abnormal posture during stance and swing. Attaching the orthosis to an orthopedic shoe further enhances control.

options: Reducing step length on sound side
Prolonging stance time on prosthetic side
Loading the prosthetic toe in late stance
questions.question: A transtibial amputee using an energy-storing prosthetic foot is undergoing gait training. What focus is MOST important for efficient push-off?
questions.explanation: Energy-storing feet depend on adequate loading of the forefoot keel during terminal stance to compress and then release stored energy at push-off. Without sufficient toe loading, the energy return mechanism is underutilized regardless of cadence or stance duration. Gait training should therefore emphasize progressing weight fully onto the prosthetic forefoot before swing.

options: Collar use prevents chronic pain development
Extended collar use promotes faster recovery
Collars are mandatory for all whiplash cases
Early mobilization without collar shows better outcomes
Six months of collar use is required
questions.question: A patient with whiplash injury asks about current evidence regarding cervical collar use. What should the physiotherapist explain?
questions.explanation: Current evidence in whiplash management favors early active mobilization over prolonged collar immobilization, as extended rigid bracing has been associated with worse functional outcomes and slower recovery. This contrasts with older practice that assumed extended immobilization was protective. Educating patients on this evidence helps reduce unnecessary prolonged collar dependence.

questions.question: A patient with knee disarticulation is compared to a transfemoral amputee for prosthetic fitting. What is the MAIN challenge specific to this level?
questions.explanation: Knee disarticulation preserves a long residual limb with excellent end-bearing capacity and good suspension, but the prosthetic knee joint must be placed distally to match the natural knee, often creating a visibly longer thigh segment when seated. This asymmetry in knee center height compared to the sound side is the defining bilateral cosmetic and mechanical challenge. Suspension and muscle control are actually advantages at this amputation level.

questions.question: A patient recovering from cervical spine fusion continues wearing a collar postoperatively. What is the PRIMARY purpose at this stage?
questions.explanation: Postoperative collar use after cervical fusion provides supplemental external support during the vulnerable healing period before solid bony fusion has occurred, reducing stress on the surgical construct. It does not replace internal fixation or guarantee fusion success, both of which depend on biological healing and surgical technique. The collar's role is protective and temporary.
options: Providing stability during healing before fusion
Enhancing the cosmetic appearance of the neck
Replacing the need for internal fixation hardware
Direct rigid immobilization of the vertebral segments
Complete elimination of paraspinal muscle activity
Surgical-level fixation of the facet joints
Elevation of intra-abdominal pressure to unload the spine
questions.question: A patient with acute low back pain from a lumbar strain, without instability, is prescribed a flexible lumbosacral support. What is the primary physiological mechanism by which this device relieves symptoms?
questions.explanation: Flexible lumbosacral corsets and binders elevate intra-abdominal pressure, which unloads the spine and supporting structures while also providing kinesthetic feedback and warmth, rather than truly restricting motion to a significant degree. This differs from rigid orthoses, which provide more direct mechanical motion restriction. Flexible supports are chosen when pain relief and postural feedback are the main goals rather than rigid immobilization.

Proper cane height is generally set to equal the distance from the heel base to the upper border of the greater trochanter, positioning the elbow in slight flexion during use. Incorrect height compromises the mechanical advantage and safety of the device. This measurement standard applies broadly across single-point cane prescriptions.
questions.question: What is the recommended total height of a properly fitted single-point cane, measured from the floor?
options: From the base of the heel to the anterior superior iliac spine
From the base of the heel to the xiphoid process
From the base of the heel to the umbilicus
From the base of the heel to the upper border of the greater trochanter
From the base of the heel to the iliac crest

questions.question: A physiotherapist is training a paraplegic patient in reciprocal ambulation using a Louisiana State University reciprocating gait orthosis (RGO) with two crutches. What gait pattern is this orthosis specifically designed to facilitate?
questions.explanation: The LSU RGO uses a cam mechanism and thrust-bearing hip joints to prevent simultaneous bilateral hip flexion, enabling reciprocal extension of the contralateral hip during a step, which supports a four-point reciprocal gait pattern using two crutches. This differs from the swing-through pattern often used with simpler HKAFOs lacking reciprocal hip coupling. Training must be tailored specifically to the orthosis's mechanical design to maximize gait efficiency.

options: It eliminates the need for any transfer technique modification
It functions identically to a soft lumbar binder in all respects
It provides complete triplanar motion control equal to a custom body jacket
It fully restricts lateral bending but allows unrestricted flexion
It controls flexion only and does not limit lateral or rotary trunk movements
questions.question: A physiotherapist is coordinating transfer training with a patient using a Jewett hyperextension brace. What functional limitation of this brace type should inform expectations during transfer practice?
questions.explanation: The Jewett brace, like the CASH orthosis, uses a three-point pressure system that prevents flexion only, without limiting lateral or rotary trunk movements, unlike a custom-molded body jacket that offers more comprehensive triplanar control. Understanding this limitation helps the physiotherapist anticipate which movements remain unrestricted during functional transfer training. This knowledge also informs safety counseling regarding activities that involve twisting or side bending.

questions.question: A patient asks why a rigid cervical collar was chosen over a soft collar. What is the PRIMARY indication?
questions.explanation: A rigid cervical collar provides genuine structural restriction of cervical motion, which is necessary when actual spinal stability is a concern, whereas a soft collar functions mainly as a kinesthetic reminder to limit voluntary movement without true mechanical restriction. Cosmetic appearance, cost, and comfort are not the deciding clinical factors. The level of true motion control needed determines the appropriate collar type.
options: Superior comfort compared to rigid types
Need for structural motion limitation, not reminder
Generally lower cost of the device

questions.question: A physiotherapist is fitting axillary crutches for a patient. Which measurement approach is correct for determining crutch length?
questions.explanation: Axillary crutch length should approximate the distance from the anterior axillary fold to the bottom of the heel, adding 3 to 5 cm, or alternatively to a point six inches anterolateral to the foot. Improper crutch length increases the risk of axillary nerve compression injury, sometimes called crutch palsy, if the patient leans excessively on the crutch tops. Correct measurement is therefore both a functional and safety consideration.
options: Distance from the sternal notch to the floor, measured in a relaxed standing posture
Distance from the top of the shoulder to the floor, with no further adjustment made
Distance from the greater trochanter to the floor, without any additional correction
Distance from the anterior axillary fold to the heel plus 3 to 5 cm, or to a point 6 inches anterolateral to the foot
Distance from the umbilicus to the floor, measured with the patient standing upright

questions.explanation: Although a longer stretching time will reduce a contracture more rapidly, the risk of skin breakdown increases steadily with wearing duration, requiring the clinician to balance these competing factors when designing a wearing schedule. Distributing pressure over a larger surface area, when possible, is better tolerated than a small focused pressure point. This balance is central to safe dynamic orthosis prescription.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is developing an individualized wearing schedule for a dynamic finger orthosis being used to stretch an IP joint flexion contracture. What tissue tolerance principle should guide session duration?
options: Shorter sessions always produce faster contracture correction
Wearing schedule is irrelevant once the orthosis is correctly fabricated
Duration has no relationship to either correction speed or skin risk
Longer stretching duration increases contracture correction speed but also increases skin breakdown risk
Skin breakdown risk decreases as wearing duration increases

questions.explanation: An adductor roll results from incomplete pulling of proximal thigh soft tissue into a suction socket, compressing tissue between the socket brim and pelvis. Choke syndrome instead refers to distal residual limb swelling from a socket that is too tight at mid-thigh. Correct donning technique or socket modification resolves an adductor roll.
questions.question: A transfemoral prosthesis user develops a painful compression of soft tissue in the medial groin between the proximal socket and pelvis. What is this complication called?
Which cervical orthosis is named for its three points of body attachment: sternum, occiput, and mandible?
questions.explanation: The SOMI (sternal-occipital-mandibular immobilizer) is named for its three attachment points and provides good flexion control while lacking posterior thoracic support, making it useful for bedridden patients. The Minerva, by comparison, is a total-contact device offering broader triplanar control. Understanding the naming convention helps clarify each device's mechanical design.

options: The lower thigh and calf bands and the hip joint
The rigid upper thigh band entirely
The stirrup and sole plate entirely
The bail lock knee mechanism entirely
The ankle joint and footplate entirely
questions.explanation: The Scott-Craig orthosis eliminates the lower thigh and calf bands and the hip joint typical of a standard HKAFO, which facilitates donning and doffing and reduces overall weight. This design relies instead on rigid connections and a bail-type knee lock along with a rigid ankle stirrup set in slight dorsiflexion. Recognizing these design features helps the therapist anticipate the specific don/doff training needed for this orthosis.
questions.question: A physiotherapist working with a spinal cord injury patient using a Scott-Craig orthosis for standing and ambulation should recognize that this design specifically eliminates which components compared to a standard HKAFO?
Which thoracolumbosacral orthosis is a rigid metal anterior frame shaped like a cross, generally better tolerated than the Jewett brace for similar indications?
questions.explanation: The CASH orthosis is a cross-shaped anterior metal frame that is generally easier to don and doff and better tolerated than the Jewett brace, though both share the same three-point hyperextension mechanism. The Taylor and Knight-Taylor braces instead use posterior uprights and axillary straps for flexion-extension or added lateral control. Selection depends on the desired directional control and patient tolerance.

questions.question: Which suspension liner mechanism for a transtibial prosthesis relies on a metal pin at the distal end that inserts into a locking mechanism within the socket?
questions.explanation: Gel liners function as both interface and suspension by using a distal pin that inserts into a locking mechanism in the socket, or alternatively a Velcro lanyard strap through a socket slot. This anchoring creates friction and suction between liner and limb that maintains suspension. This differs from strap or sleeve suspension systems, which rely purely on external encirclement rather than a locking mechanism.
options: Suction valve suspension without a liner
Waist belt with anterior fork strap
Silicone or elastomeric gel liner with locking pin

questions.explanation: Because an insensate limb cannot provide protective sensory feedback about pressure or rubbing, the socket must be carefully contoured to distribute load evenly and avoid any focal high-pressure areas that could cause unnoticed skin breakdown. Rigid walls or minimal padding would increase the risk of localized pressure injury. Pressure management takes priority over suspension security or visualization in this population.
questions.question: A patient with peripheral neuropathy and an insensate residual limb needs a new prosthetic socket. What modification is MOST important?
options: Rigid socket walls for added proprioception
Careful pressure distribution avoiding focal stress
Minimal padding to reduce overall bulk

questions.question: A physiotherapist is assessing a patient with bilateral upper limb amputation for early functional independence. What device might be introduced early to assist feeding and grooming before definitive prosthetic fitting?
questions.explanation: Providing a utensil cuff that attaches to a residual arm allows early restoration of feeding and tooth brushing function in bilateral upper limb amputees, prior to definitive prosthetic fitting. Early restoration of any ADL function is emphasized given the profound functional impact of bilateral loss. Physiotherapists and occupational therapists collaborate closely in this early rehabilitation phase.
options: A wheeled walker for upper limb support
A utensil cuff attached to the residual arm
A definitive myoelectric prosthesis on both sides immediately
A cervical collar for postural support
A halo vest for trunk stabilization
Incorporation of wrist flexion units to permit midline activities
Complete avoidance of prosthetic fitting until adulthood
Exclusive use of cosmetic passive hands bilaterally
Avoidance of any wrist rotator units
questions.explanation: In bilateral upper limb amputation, wrist flexion units, particularly on the dominant side, permit midline activities such as shirt buttoning, belt buckling, and toileting, while wrist rotator units further assist bilateral prosthetic function. Special toileting techniques and independence training are also emphasized in this population. Early prosthetic fitting, even with temporary devices, is prioritized in bilateral cases.
questions.question: Which special component consideration is emphasized for the dominant residual limb in a patient with bilateral upper limb amputation?
For a knee disarticulation amputee, which prosthetic knee design is most favored to maintain symmetric knee centers with the sound limb?
questions.explanation: Because the knee disarticulation residual limb is long, a four-bar or polycentric knee allows the mechanical knee center to be placed to better match the sound-side anatomical knee center. This preserves cosmesis and biomechanical symmetry despite the long residual limb. Single-axis knees would place the mechanical joint too distally for good cosmesis.

questions.question: A physiotherapist is progressing a new transtibial amputee through gait training in the parallel bars. What should be mastered before progressing to ambulation with a gait aid outside the bars?
questions.explanation: Gait training begins with weight shifting and balance activities in the parallel bars before progressing to ambulation with or without gait aids. Mastery of these foundational skills reduces fall risk as the patient advances to more complex tasks such as uneven terrain or stairs. Skipping this progression increases the risk of instability during early prosthetic use.

options: A rigid shank is typically used together with a rocker sole to maintain functional propulsion
A rigid shank is used only as a permanent alternative and is never combined with a rocker sole
The two modifications cannot be used on the same shoe under any circumstance
A rigid shank has no relevance to hallux rigidus management
A rocker sole eliminates any need to ever consider a rigid shank
questions.explanation: An extended rigid shank must be used in conjunction with a rocker sole, since the rigid shank alone would stiffen the midfoot and forefoot in a way that impedes normal propulsion unless the rocker sole compensates by facilitating forward roll-through. This combined approach is specifically relevant to conditions such as symptomatic hallux rigidus. Recognizing this pairing helps the physiotherapist understand why these two modifications are frequently prescribed together rather than as isolated alternatives.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is assessing a patient's need for a rocker sole versus an extended rigid shank for hallux rigidus management. What is the relationship between these two modifications when both are indicated?

options: Suction suspension is contraindicated in all patients under any circumstance
Suction suspension eliminates the need for any socket at all
Suction suspension is more expensive than every alternative regardless of stage
Suction suspension cannot be used with any type of prosthetic knee
Suction suspension requires a stable residual limb volume, which is not yet present during early rapid shrinkage
questions.explanation: Suction suspension requires a stable residual limb volume and is therefore a poor option for a preparatory prosthesis during a period of expected rapid limb shrinkage. Simpler suspension systems that better accommodate volume change, such as hard sockets with sock ply adjustment, are more appropriate during this early phase. Once the limb has matured, suction suspension can be reconsidered for the definitive prosthesis if appropriate.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is asked to help a patient understand why a suction socket suspension is not recommended for their initial preparatory transfemoral prosthesis. What is the primary reason?
Which finding was noted regarding maximal mouth opening in patients wearing rigid cervical collars such as the Philadelphia or Miami J?
options: An increased inter-incisor distance improving airway access
Complete inability to open the mouth in all patients
No measurable change in mouth opening
A reduced inter-incisor distance that could complicate emergency airway management
Increased risk of temporomandibular joint dislocation only
questions.explanation: Studies found that some patients wearing hard cervical collars exhibited a reduced inter-incisor distance, which could obstruct visualization of the glottis during emergency intubation. Clinicians are advised to maintain manual stabilization while removing the anterior shell if emergent intubation is required. This finding underscores the airway management implications of rigid collar use.

The blucher-type opening allows a wide opening for easy foot insertion and greater midfoot adjustability because the lace stay is not directly attached to the vamp. The bal-type (Balmoral) throat, in contrast, attaches the lace stay directly to the vamp, offering less accessibility. This distinction is particularly relevant when selecting shoes for patients using an AFO or with reduced hand dexterity.
questions.question: Which shoe opening style provides the widest opening for easy foot insertion because the lace stay is not directly fastened to the vamp?

questions.explanation: When descending stairs, the reverse pattern from ascending is used: the weaker limb plus the cane lead the movement, followed by the stronger leg. When ascending, the stronger leg advances first. This distinction, often summarized as 'up with the good, down with the bad,' is a fundamental patient safety teaching point in stair training.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is training a patient with hemiplegia to descend stairs using a single-point cane. What sequence should be taught?
options: Advance the weaker leg alone first without the cane
Advance the cane alone first, then both legs simultaneously
Advance the cane and the weaker leg together first, followed by the stronger leg
Advance the stronger leg and cane simultaneously, then the weaker leg
Advance the stronger leg first, followed by the cane and weaker leg

questions.question: A physiotherapist is conducting a home safety assessment prior to discharging a patient who will use a rolling (wheeled) walker. What specific safety feature should be verified as functional?
options: The presence of a cup holder attachment
The color of the walker frame
The height of the walker exceeding the patient's shoulder
Hand brakes, especially if the walker is a four-wheeled model with a seat
The absence of any adjustable height settings
questions.explanation: Four-wheeled walkers used for fatigue management, sometimes fitted with a seat for rest periods, should ideally include functional hand brakes, since uncontrolled rolling introduces its own fall risk. Verifying this safety feature is an important part of predischarge equipment assessment. This is distinct from cosmetic features, which do not affect functional safety.

Soft cervical collars are made of foam and cannot provide true structural support; they function mainly by providing warmth, psychological reassurance, and a kinesthetic reminder to limit cervical motion. Rigid collars such as the Philadelphia or Miami J instead provide measurable motion restriction through more rigid molded shells. This limits soft collar use to mild muscular spasm or minor soft-tissue injury.
questions.question: Which cervical orthosis category, unlike a rigid collar, cannot provide structural support but instead offers warmth and kinesthetic reminders to limit motion?
A patient with a short transfemoral residual limb requires socket modification for adequate stability. What change is MOST important?
options: Addition of a simple hip joint
Proximal extension with a shoulder cap or spica
questions.explanation: A very short transfemoral residual limb has insufficient length and leverage for stable socket suspension and control, requiring the socket to be extended proximally, sometimes incorporating a pelvic or spica-type extension, to capture more surface area for stability. Reducing trim lines or adding distal flexibility would worsen control in this scenario. Proximal extension compensates directly for the short lever arm.

questions.question: What is the primary function of the toe box within the anterior portion of a shoe upper?
options: To attach the outer sole to the last
To protect the toes from trauma and maintain shoe appearance
To provide the primary shock-absorbing function of the shoe
To anchor the eyelets for the shoe laces
questions.explanation: The toe box, part of the vamp, is a reinforced structure that protects the toes against trauma and preserves the shape of the shoe front. Shock absorption instead is primarily a function of the sole materials. The lace stay, not the toe box, houses the eyelets.

A Thomas heel is a flat heel modified with a medial extension that supports a weakened longitudinal arch. A standard flat heel lacks this medial extension and offers only general support. This modification is a targeted correction rather than a general shock-absorbing feature.
questions.question: Which shoe heel modification has a medial extension used to support a weak longitudinal foot arch?

A patient in a cervicothoracic orthosis complains of increasing head elevation, cervical extension, and limited chin tuck resulting in swallowing difficulty. Which orthosis is most associated with this complication?
questions.explanation: The Minerva brace has been reported to cause dysphagia with risk of aspiration pneumonia due to head elevation, slight cervical extension, and limited chin tuck that interfere with normal swallowing mechanics. This complication highlights the need to monitor for feeding and swallowing difficulty in patients wearing rigid cervicothoracic orthoses. Similar but milder swallowing changes have also been observed with other rigid cervical devices.

options: Prolonged hip flexion and abduction positioning
Prone lying for short supervised periods
questions.question: A physiotherapist is planning postoperative positioning for a patient with a transfemoral amputation to prevent contracture. Which positioning error should be specifically avoided?
questions.explanation: Muscle imbalance and postoperative positioning for comfort can lead to hip flexion and abduction contractures in transfemoral amputees, making prolonged flexed, abducted positioning a pattern to avoid. Encouraging prone lying and active range-of-motion exercises, along with early mobilization, helps prevent this complication. Preventing contracture is critical, since a significant flexion contracture can render a patient a poor prosthetic candidate.

questions.question: A patient with active rheumatoid arthritis of the wrist is prescribed a resting hand splint. What is the PRIMARY purpose at this stage?
questions.explanation: During active inflammation, a resting hand splint maintains the wrist and fingers in an anti-deformity position to protect inflamed joints and prevent the progression of deformities such as ulnar drift. It is not intended to correct deformities that have already developed or to strengthen muscles. Protective positioning during the inflammatory phase is the central goal.

questions.question: A physiotherapist is working with a patient recovering from cervical spine surgery who has been fitted with a Philadelphia collar. The patient reports increasing sweating and skin irritation under the collar. What is an appropriate first-line action?
questions.explanation: Constant collar wear can increase local skin temperature and perspiration, predisposing to maceration and breakdown, so keeping the skin clean, dry, and cool while inspecting pressure-prone areas such as the occiput, mandible, clavicles, and ears is an appropriate first-line action. Tightening the collar further would likely worsen shear and pressure-related skin injury rather than help. Any concerning skin findings should prompt communication with the prescribing physician or orthotist rather than unilateral discontinuation.
options: Ensure the skin is kept clean, dry, and cool, and inspect for early breakdown at pressure-prone areas
Advise the patient to avoid any skin inspection to prevent irritation
Increase collar tightness to reduce movement of the skin
Apply an occlusive dressing directly under the entire collar
Immediately discontinue the collar without medical consultation

questions.explanation: A quick-disconnect wrist unit is chosen primarily for convenience, allowing the user to rapidly swap terminal devices for different tasks, such as switching from a hook to a recreational attachment. This is unrelated to cosmesis, weight, or grip strength. The functional benefit is task-specific adaptability.
questions.question: A patient using a quick-disconnect wrist unit asks why this was selected over a standard friction wrist. What should the physiotherapist explain?
options: It reduces overall prosthesis weight greatly
It increases grip force of the hand
It allows fast interchange of terminal devices
It eliminates the need for any wrist rotation
Weight-activated stance control or offset knee
questions.explanation: Patients with weak quadriceps cannot reliably control knee stability through muscular effort alone, so mechanical stance-control features such as weight-activated friction brakes or geometrically offset knee axes provide passive safety during loading. Free-motion or simple friction knees rely more on voluntary control, which this patient lacks. A permanently locked knee sacrifices swing-phase function unnecessarily.
questions.question: A patient with quadriceps weakness requires a transfemoral prosthetic knee unit. Which design feature provides the MOST appropriate stance stability?

questions.explanation: Body-powered prostheses function through a harness and Bowden cable system that converts shoulder flexion and scapular abduction into mechanical cable excursion, which operates the terminal device or elbow. This is distinct from myoelectric systems, which use electrical muscle signals. Understanding this principle helps patients learn efficient harness movements.
questions.question: A physiotherapist explains the biomechanical principle of body-powered prosthetic control to a new transhumeral amputee. Which statement is MOST accurate?
options: Voice commands trigger component movement directly
Shoulder and scapular motion generates cable tension
Residual limb rotation alone controls positioning
Electrical signals activate terminal device motors
Weight shifting alone activates control mechanisms
The overall weight of the cosmetic shell
The knee alignment relative to the trochanter-knee-ankle (TKA) reference line
The color match of the socket liner
The brand of the prosthetic socks used
The prosthetic foot's cosmetic covering material
questions.explanation: Knee buckling at initial contact can result from excessive heel lever or from incorrect prosthetic knee alignment relative to the trochanter-knee-ankle (TKA) reference line, both of which affect stability during loading response. Realigning the TKA relationship addresses malalignment-related buckling, while heel stiffness adjustment addresses lever-related causes. Weak hip extensors are also a contributing factor requiring gait training and strengthening.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is treating a transfemoral amputee whose knee buckles at initial contact. Besides checking heel stiffness, what prosthetic alignment factor should be reviewed?

options: Expandable wall prosthesis with a flexible inner liner
questions.explanation: The expandable wall prosthesis uses a flexible silicone or elastomer inner wall with a rigid outer frame, allowing the bulbous residual limb to slide in easily while remaining strong. This design suits active or obese patients and those with upper limb impairment. Window sockets, by contrast, weaken the socket structure and are less cosmetic.
questions.question: A patient with a Syme amputation has a very bulbous residual limb requiring easy donning. Which prosthetic design is most appropriate?

options: Simple free-swinging knee with no resistance control
questions.explanation: Hydraulic or pneumatic knee units provide swing or combined swing-and-stance phase control that adapts to changing cadence, making them suitable for K3 and K4 level individuals with variable walking speeds. Simpler knees such as the single-axis constant-friction design only support a single fixed cadence. Matching knee complexity to activity level avoids both under- and over-prescription.
questions.question: Which category of prosthetic knee is generally reserved for K3 and K4 level individuals who frequently change walking cadence?

options: Fully replacing the function of the anterior cruciate ligament
Immobilizing the knee completely in full extension
Providing prophylactic protection during contact sports only
Unloading the affected medial tibiofemoral compartment
questions.explanation: An unloader-type knee orthosis is designed to shift load away from an arthritic compartment, in this case the medial tibiofemoral compartment, rather than to fully immobilize the joint or address ligamentous or patellofemoral issues. This class of orthosis is distinguished from prophylactic and patellofemoral orthoses, which serve different biomechanical purposes. Recognizing this distinction allows the physiotherapist to correctly interpret the treatment goal behind the prescription.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is assessing a patient with a knee orthosis prescribed for medial compartment osteoarthritis. What is the primary intended biomechanical function of this orthosis category?

options: Apply powder directly onto the skin
Provide replacement padding for alternating use
Cover the collar with plastic wrap
Discontinue the device against medical advice
questions.explanation: Increased perspiration under a cervical orthosis is managed by providing replacement or interchangeable padding so the patient can alternate pieces, allowing proper drying and hygiene while maintaining required immobilization. Loosening the collar would reduce its therapeutic effectiveness. Maintaining stabilization while addressing moisture management is the appropriate clinical balance.
questions.question: A patient using a cervical orthosis develops increased perspiration and skin irritation. What intervention is MOST appropriate?

questions.explanation: For a short residual limb with poor medial-lateral prosthetic control despite adequate socket fit, accepting the limitation or adding a hip joint is a recognized option to improve stability. This reflects the mechanical challenge posed by a shortened lever arm at the transfemoral level. Collaborative discussion between physiotherapist and prosthetist is essential when standard adjustments are insufficient.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is asked to help a patient with a short transfemoral residual limb who has poor medial-lateral prosthetic control despite good socket fit. What should be considered as an additional prosthetic option?
options: Adding a hip joint for additional stability
Switching to a soft cervical collar
Prescribing a bilateral standard walker permanently

questions.question: What is the recommended immobilization position for the metacarpophalangeal joints when splinting the hand to prevent contracture, in order to preserve collateral ligament length?
questions.explanation: The MCP joints should be immobilized in flexion to maintain collateral ligament length, while the interphalangeal joints are positioned in extension. This combined positioning prevents the classic intrinsic-minus contracture pattern. Failure to follow this anatomical principle risks permanent loss of hand function.

questions.question: Which flexible spinal support is specifically noted to place the diaphragm in a superior position, assisting diaphragmatic expansion in patients with paralysis and respiratory insufficiency?
questions.explanation: The lumbosacral corset, in addition to providing pain relief and postural support, elevates the diaphragm to a superior position, assisting diaphragmatic expansion in patients with paralysis and respiratory insufficiency. This respiratory benefit is a secondary but clinically important function distinct from its motion-restriction role. Sacroiliac belts, in contrast, target pelvic rather than respiratory mechanics.

options: Excessive socket flexion or a soft heel
questions.question: During gait training, a transtibial prosthesis user shows early knee flexion immediately after heel strike. What is the MOST likely cause?
questions.explanation: Early stance knee flexion in a transtibial amputee is typically due to excessive initial socket flexion or a heel cushion that compresses too quickly, creating a flexion moment at the knee. This causes the patient to feel unstable just after heel strike. Adjusting socket alignment or heel stiffness usually resolves the deviation.

options: An opponens bar for thumb positioning
questions.question: A patient with median nerve injury needs an orthosis to support thumb function. Which component is MOST critical?
questions.explanation: Median nerve injury impairs thenar muscle function, particularly opposition, so the orthosis must include an opponens bar that positions the thumb in opposition to support pinch and grasp activities. The other listed components address different nerve distributions or deformities not characteristic of median nerve loss. Restoring opposition is the defining orthotic priority for this nerve injury.

options: Elimination of any wrist motion at all times
Continued activation of long flexor and extensor tendons for finger control
Complete immobilization of all finger joints permanently
Total restriction of any hand use during daily activities
Full immobilization of the elbow joint
questions.explanation: Static hand-finger orthoses for rheumatoid MCP subluxation and ulnar drift are designed to control or prevent subluxation while still allowing long flexor and extensor tendons to activate finger control, preserving functional use of the hand. Total immobilization would be excessive and counterproductive to hand function. This balance between stability and mobility is central to orthotic management in progressive inflammatory conditions.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is caring for a patient with rheumatoid arthritis who has MCP subluxation with ulnar drift. What functional feature should a prescribed static hand-finger orthosis preserve?

questions.explanation: Extrinsic residual limb pain is caused by a mismatch between the socket and the residual limb, such as with volume changes or malalignment, unlike intrinsic pain which arises from changes or complications within the limb tissue itself, such as bony overgrowth or neuroma. Distinguishing extrinsic from intrinsic causes directs whether socket modification or medical/surgical management is the appropriate next step. Malalignment of the prosthesis can also create abnormal extrinsic pressure patterns.
options: Bony overgrowth at the distal limb
questions.question: Which cause of extrinsic residual limb pain arises specifically from a mismatch between the socket and the shape or volume of the residual limb?

questions.explanation: Body-powered prosthetic limbs use control cables to translate movements such as scapular abduction, shoulder depression, and humeral flexion into activation of the terminal device or elbow. Dual-control cable systems allow the same cable to sequentially control both elbow flexion and terminal device opening in transhumeral prostheses. Harnessing provides the anchor point but does not itself transmit the controlling motion.
questions.question: Which upper limb prosthesis component links shoulder and humeral movements, such as scapular abduction, to activation of the terminal device or elbow?

questions.explanation: Dynamic response, or energy-storing, feet incorporate elastic spring-like elements that compress during loading and return energy at push-off, benefiting active users in running or jumping activities. Objective evidence for metabolic efficiency gains is mixed and mostly evident at faster walking speeds. These feet are typically reserved for K3-K4 activity level individuals.
questions.question: Which term describes prosthetic feet that store energy during limb loading and mid-stance and return it during push-off, benefiting individuals involved in running and jumping activities?

options: The need for frequent foot replacement due to rapid growth favoring cost-effective options
The elimination of any need for socket adjustments over time
The avoidance of any dynamic response foot at any age
The requirement for microprocessor-controlled components exclusively
The mandatory use of suction suspension in all pediatric cases
questions.explanation: Because children require frequent foot changes due to rapid growth, cost-effective options such as the SACH foot are often preferred for pediatric prescriptions despite the availability of more advanced designs. As the child matures and activity level increases, upgrading to more sophisticated components can be considered. This reflects a practical balance between cost, growth, and functional need in pediatric prosthetics.
questions.question: Which pediatric-specific consideration influences the choice of a prosthetic foot for a growing child with an amputation?
Which factor determines the appropriate Medicare functional classification (K-level) assigned to a lower limb prosthesis user?
questions.explanation: The Medicare K-code hierarchy classifies patients from K0 (no ambulation potential) to K4 (high-activity users exceeding basic ambulation) based on functional and mobility potential. This classification then limits which prosthetic components can be justified for use. Age or brand are not part of the classification criteria.
options: The manufacturer of the prosthetic components
The individual's mobility potential and expected activity level
The total cost of the prosthetic components
The type of amputation surgical technique used

questions.explanation: A vertical shock pylon contains a compressible element that absorbs axial impact loading during heel strike and stance, reducing the jarring transmitted to the residual limb and improving walking economy. This impact absorption indirectly lowers the metabolic cost of ambulation. It is not primarily designed for rotation, height adjustment, or appearance.
options: Absorbs impact and reduces oxygen cost
questions.question: A physiotherapist explains the function of a vertical shock pylon to an active prosthesis user. What is its PRIMARY purpose?
A physiotherapist assessing a patient with a new AFO for equinovarus following stroke notes persistent lateral weight bearing during stance despite the orthosis. What should be checked first?
questions.explanation: Persistent lateral weight bearing despite an AFO suggests inadequate control of the inversion component, warranting a check of the inversion strap or pad application and the plantarflexion stop setting, which should be adjusted just before triggering ankle clonus if present. If these components are correctly applied yet control remains inadequate, referral back to the orthotist for reassessment is appropriate. This systematic check ensures the orthosis is functioning as prescribed before considering other interventions.
options: Whether the patient has increased cardiovascular endurance
Whether the contralateral limb has adequate strength only
Whether the patient can tolerate a rocker sole modification
Whether the patient's shoes are a fashionable style
Whether the inversion strap or pad is properly applied and the plantarflexion stop is correctly set

questions.question: A physiotherapist explains the function of a thoracic extension added to a lumbosacral orthosis. What should be stated?
questions.explanation: Adding a thoracic extension to a lumbosacral orthosis lengthens the lever arm of the device upward, allowing it to control motion at lower thoracic spinal segments that a standard lumbosacral design would not adequately address. This is a functional modification rather than a cosmetic or comfort feature. Extending control to the appropriate spinal level is the clinical rationale.
options: It provides attachment for head support
It extends motion control to lower thoracic segments
It reduces the overall orthosis weight

questions.explanation: During emergency intubation in a patient with suspected cervical injury, the anterior portion of the collar is removed to allow airway access while a team member maintains manual in-line cervical stabilization to prevent spinal movement. Leaving the entire collar on would obstruct the airway, while removing it without manual support risks spinal injury. This combined approach balances airway access with spinal protection.
questions.question: A patient with a cervical collar requires emergency intubation. What is the MOST appropriate management approach?
options: Attempt intubation without removing any collar part
Remove the anterior shell, maintain manual stabilization
Refuse intubation to keep the collar intact
Remove the entire collar without any stabilization
Keep the collar fully intact throughout intubation

questions.question: A physiotherapist is advising a patient with an AFO about permissible footwear changes. What is the key requirement when switching between different pairs of shoes?
options: Maintaining a constant heel height to preserve the intended dynamic alignment
Selecting shoes only in a single specific brand
Selecting shoes with progressively higher heels over time
Ensuring each new shoe pair has a different sole material weekly
questions.explanation: Patients using an orthosis that fits inside the shoe are generally permitted to exchange shoes as long as a constant heel height is maintained, since altering heel height would change the intended dynamic alignment of the device. This is a practical and frequently overlooked patient education point. Failure to maintain consistent heel height can lead to unexpected gait deviations despite a properly fabricated orthosis.

questions.question: A patient with a stable lower cervical fracture is using a rigid collar at home. What instruction is MOST important?
options: The collar can be removed during showering
The collar guarantees no further injury
A looser fit improves comfort without issue
Wear the device continuously as prescribed
Exercise is contraindicated while wearing collar
questions.explanation: For a stable fracture managed conservatively, continuous wear as prescribed, including during sleep, is essential to maintain adequate immobilization throughout the healing period, since intermittent removal undermines fracture stability. Loosening the fit for comfort would compromise its mechanical effectiveness. Patient education on strict compliance is therefore the most critical instruction.

questions.question: What has research shown regarding gait characteristics of patients wearing a halo vest?
options: Stride length increases while stride time decreases
Stride length decreases and stride time increases, slowing gait speed
Arm swing increases due to compensatory strategies
Pelvic girdle motion increases relative to the trunk
Gait speed is unaffected by halo vest wear
questions.explanation: Patients wearing a halo vest show decreased stride length and increased stride time, resulting in slower gait speed, along with reduced motion between the shoulder and pelvic girdles and the trunk, reducing arm swing. These changes represent compensatory strategies for impaired balance caused by the device. This has direct implications for fall-prevention education prior to discharge.

questions.question: A patient asks why a Boston brace was prescribed for their adolescent scoliosis. What is the PRIMARY indication?
options: Thoracic curves exclusively in all cases
Thoracolumbar and lumbar curves in growing patients
questions.explanation: The Boston brace is a symmetric, prefabricated TLSO commonly used for thoracolumbar and lumbar curves in skeletally immature adolescent patients within a moderate Cobb angle range, aiming to prevent curve progression during growth. It is less effective for high thoracic curves or in skeletally mature adults. Matching curve location and patient growth potential to brace type guides appropriate prescription.

While external knee control from a KAFO, KO, or AFO can improve limb stability during early stance, a knee extensor strengthening exercise program is important since orthotic interventions may otherwise promote muscle disuse. This combined approach addresses both immediate functional stability and long-term muscle recovery. Neglecting the strengthening component risks prolonging dependence on the orthosis.
options: Exclusive focus on upper extremity strengthening
A knee extensor strengthening program to counteract muscle disuse from orthotic use
Isolated core stability training with no limb-specific component
Avoidance of any strengthening exercise while wearing the orthosis
Complete rest of the limb until nerve recovery is complete
questions.question: A physiotherapist is treating a patient with peripheral nerve injury causing early stance-phase knee instability. Besides external orthotic support, what specific exercise focus is recommended to prevent further problems?

options: Apply antiperspirant directly to the limb
Discontinue use of the gel liner
Provide a spare liner for alternating use
questions.question: A patient using a gel liner reports excessive sweating that loosens prosthetic fit by midday. What is the MOST appropriate intervention?
questions.explanation: Excessive perspiration with a gel liner is best managed by providing a second liner so the patient can alternate between a dry and a sweaty liner during the day, allowing proper drying and hygiene without interrupting prosthetic use. Stopping liner use or drastically reducing wear time would compromise function unnecessarily. Antiperspirant application is not a standard or reliable clinical solution.

questions.question: A physiotherapist is assisting a patient in log-rolling while wearing a rigid cervical collar to inspect the skin. What precaution must be maintained throughout the procedure?
questions.explanation: When removing or applying a portion of the collar to inspect the skin, such as during log rolling, the clinician must maintain proper neck alignment throughout to prevent injury to the cervical spine. This requires coordinated technique, often with one clinician maintaining manual stabilization while another manages the collar. This precaution is critical regardless of how routine the skin check may seem.
options: The patient should actively rotate the neck during the roll to ease inspection
Only the posterior shell needs to be considered; anterior alignment is irrelevant
Proper neck alignment must be maintained while temporarily removing portions of the collar
The collar should be fully removed and left off during the entire roll
Neck alignment is not a concern once the collar has been applied once

questions.question: Which shoe modification is specifically indicated for a fixed equinus foot position or to reduce strain on the Achilles tendon?
questions.explanation: A heel-only elevation accommodates a fixed equinus position or reduces strain on the Achilles tendon, whereas a full heel-to-ball buildup (shoe lift) is more appropriate to compensate for overall limb-length discrepancy. Choosing the correct type of elevation avoids pushing the foot out of the shoe or worsening biomechanical instability. Buildups greater than one inch generally require a high-top shoe or AFO for added ankle stability.
options: Full-length shoe lift from heel to ball

questions.question: Which socket design captures the ischial tuberosity within the socket walls rather than resting it on the posterior brim?
questions.explanation: The ischial containment socket extends the trim lines proximally and contours the medial wall to capture the ischial tuberosity inside the socket, improving mediolateral pelvic stability. The quadrilateral socket instead bears weight on the ischium at the posterior brim. This distinction guides selection for transfemoral prosthetic users.

options: It significantly lowers prosthesis purchase cost
It eliminates the need for volume accommodation
It allows easier donning than other systems
Continuous vacuum reduces pistoning and improves fit
It is compatible with all socket designs
questions.explanation: Vacuum-assisted suspension maintains a continuous negative pressure between the liner and socket, which actively reduces pistoning, the up-and-down limb movement within the socket during gait, and helps maintain an intimate, stable fit throughout the day. This differs from passive suspension methods that cannot adapt to volume fluctuations as effectively. Donning ease and cost are not the primary clinical advantages.
questions.question: A patient with a vacuum-assisted socket suspension system asks about its main biomechanical benefit. What should the physiotherapist explain?

questions.explanation: Approximately half of total cervical rotation occurs at the atlantoaxial (C1-2) joint, where the atlas rotates around the odontoid process in the absence of an intervening disc. The atlanto-occipital joint instead predominantly permits flexion and extension (nodding). Understanding this segmental distribution guides expectations for cervical orthosis motion control at different levels.
questions.question: At which cervical spinal segment does the majority of axial rotation of the cervical spine occur?

questions.explanation: Crutches are most commonly prescribed to decrease loading in cases of muscle weakness or joint pain, allowing a greater degree of weight-bearing restriction than a cane, which offers comparatively modest load reduction. Selecting the correct gait aid depends on the required degree of offloading as well as the patient's upper extremity strength and coordination. This principle guides appropriate device selection following lower limb surgery with specific weight-bearing restrictions.
options: Axillary or Lofstrand crutches, used with a non-weight-bearing or partial weight-bearing gait pattern
A single-point cane on the unaffected side
No assistive device, relying on protective stepping alone
questions.question: A physiotherapist is helping select a walking aid for a patient recovering from lower limb surgery who has good upper extremity strength but needs to significantly offload one limb. Which gait aid provides the greatest degree of load reduction?

questions.explanation: Both CASH and Jewett braces provide three-point extension control of the thoracolumbar spine, but the CASH brace uses a simpler anterior frame without posterior uprights, making it easier to don independently, which can be the deciding factor when patient preference and ease of application matter. Lateral bending control and lordosis enhancement are not features either brace primarily provides. The functional difference is mainly in donning convenience.
options: Patient preference for an anterior-only frame
A requirement for lateral bending control
A need for additional cervical support
A need for thoracic extension restriction
A need for greater lordosis enhancement
questions.question: A patient asks why a CASH brace was selected instead of a Jewett brace. What is the MOST likely reason?

questions.explanation: The Knight brace is essentially a chairback brace with added lateral uprights that pass over the iliac crests, providing additional control of lateral trunk motion. Careful fitting is required to avoid pressure over the iliac crests from these lateral bars. This modification distinguishes it from the simpler flexion-extension-only chairback design.
questions.question: Which rigid lumbosacral orthosis adds lateral uprights to a chairback brace design to further limit coronal plane motion?

questions.explanation: A posterior offset knee joint provides mechanical stance-phase stability by placing the knee axis posterior to the anatomical joint while still allowing knee flexion during swing, making it appropriate when spasticity or contracture is absent. Locking knee joints instead eliminate all knee motion, which may be unnecessarily restrictive if adequate stance control can be achieved with an offset design. Careful patient-specific assessment determines which knee joint feature is most appropriate.
options: Fixed rigid knee joint with no motion
questions.question: A physiotherapist is fitting a patient for a KAFO due to weak knee extensors with buckling into flexion, but without significant spasticity or contracture. Which knee joint feature would most directly address stance-phase stability while still allowing swing-phase flexion?

options: Louisiana State University reciprocating gait orthosis
questions.explanation: The LSU reciprocating gait orthosis uses a cam and thrust-bearing hip joints to prevent bilateral simultaneous hip flexion, permitting reciprocal extension of the contralateral hip during a step, allowing a four-point gait pattern with crutches. The Scott-Craig orthosis, by contrast, does not include hip joints at all. This mechanism specifically targets a functional walking pattern in paraplegic patients.
questions.question: Which orthosis uses a cam mechanism and thrust-bearing hip joints to prevent simultaneous bilateral hip flexion, enabling a reciprocal gait pattern in paraplegia?

questions.explanation: Low-temperature thermoplastics soften with mild heat, such as from a heat gun, allowing easy shaping and remolding without requiring specialized high-temperature ovens. Carbon fiber and metal components instead offer strength and durability but limited chairside adjustability. Material selection depends on the balance between adjustability and structural demand.
questions.question: Which upper limb orthotic material softens with heat application and can be repeatedly remolded, making it suitable for adjustable clinic fabrication?

options: Ankle invertors of the sound limb only
questions.explanation: Hip abductor strength is particularly important for lateral stability during prosthetic stance phase, and weakness in this muscle group is a recognized cause of lateral trunk bending over the prosthesis during gait. Alongside hip extensors and flexors, this muscle group should be specifically targeted in a preprosthetic strengthening program. Addressing this early can help prevent later gait deviations related to hip abductor weakness.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is reviewing a patient's exercise program prior to prosthetic fitting for a transfemoral amputation. Which specific hip muscle group deserves particular strengthening focus to support future prosthetic stance-phase stability?

A physiotherapist notices a patient's orthotic alignment appears clinically acceptable immediately after fitting, but the patient continues to report discomfort after several days of use. What principle explains this discrepancy?
questions.explanation: Even under ideal circumstances, orthotic alignment cannot be completely evaluated until the patient has had time to walk in and accommodate to the device, allowing compensatory muscle strategies and symptoms to stabilize. This explains why initial fitting satisfaction does not guarantee long-term comfort. Scheduled follow-up assessment is therefore essential rather than relying solely on the initial fitting visit.
options: Orthotic alignment is always perfect immediately after fitting, needing no follow-up review
Patient-reported discomfort after fitting is never a clinically relevant finding to consider
Compensatory muscle strategies around the orthosis stabilize instantly upon initial donning
True alignment cannot be judged until the patient has walked in and accommodated to the device
Orthotic alignment only matters at the very first fitting appointment and never afterward
Rigid rocker sole with carbon fiber or spring steel sole shank
questions.explanation: For a more active individual with a transmetatarsal amputation, options such as carbon fiber or spring steel sole shanks, rocker soles, or a short AFO better substitute for the lost anterior lever arm needed for effective push-off. A soft accommodative insole alone is adequate only for less active individuals limited to level-surface ambulation. Selecting the correct modification depends on the patient's expected activity demands.
questions.question: A patient with a partial foot amputation at the transmetatarsal level has an active lifestyle. Which orthotic modification best substitutes for the lost anterior foot lever arm?

options: It distributes weight equally across three points
It provides adjustment at three locations for growth
It creates three separate motion control zones
It applies one corrective force opposed by two counterforces
It enables triplanar motion through three joints
questions.question: A patient asks how the three-point pressure system biomechanically affects spinal correction. What should the physiotherapist explain?
questions.explanation: The three-point pressure principle works by applying a single corrective force at the apex of a deformity while two opposing counterforces act above and below it, generating a stable bending moment that resists the unwanted curve or motion. This is the core mechanism behind many spinal orthoses for conditions like kyphosis or scoliosis. It is unrelated to growth adjustment or triplanar joint motion.

questions.question: What is the maximum medial flare typically recommended before requiring the addition of a buttress for adequate control?
questions.explanation: Medial flares exceeding one-half inch (1.2 cm) risk causing the patient to trip with the opposite foot, and lateral flares exceeding this amount require an added buttress for adequate control. This guideline balances the corrective benefit of a flare against the practical risk of tripping. Excessive flares without a buttress compromise safety rather than improve stability.

questions.question: Which upper limb orthotic design maintains the first web space between the thumb and fingers to preserve gross grasp?
questions.explanation: The C-bar maintains the web space between the thumb and other fingers, preventing web space contracture and preserving both gross grasp and fine pinch. The opponens bar instead positions the thumb opposite the fingers for prehension. Both features are commonly combined in a short opponens orthosis.

Vertical shock absorbers cushion impact loading between the socket and pylon and may reduce oxygen consumption during ambulation. Transverse rotators instead reduce axial torque rather than vertical impact. Endoskeletal designs allow these add-on components more readily than exoskeletal designs.
options: Extra limb socks for volume control
questions.question: A physiatrist wants to reduce oxygen consumption and cushion impact loading in an active endoskeletal transtibial prosthesis user. Which component addition is most appropriate?

questions.explanation: Type II odontoid fractures managed non-operatively typically require either a rigid cervical collar or, for higher stability needs, a halo vest, both of which provide adequate immobilization across the unstable C1-C2 segment. A soft collar or activity restriction alone provides insufficient control for this fracture pattern. A thoracic orthosis does not address the cervical level of injury.
options: A rigid cervical collar or halo vest
questions.question: A patient with a stable odontoid fracture Type II is treated conservatively. Which device is MOST commonly used?

options: Fit under the occiput and mandible with trim lines
The color chosen for the collar
The time of day it is worn
The brand name of the device
The patient's hair length or style
questions.explanation: Effective cervical motion control depends on how intimately the orthosis contacts bony landmarks such as the occiput and mandible, along with properly contoured trim lines that maximize leverage against motion. Superficial factors like color or brand have no biomechanical relevance. Precise fit at these contact points is the determining factor for control.
questions.question: A patient asks what most affects motion control with a cervical orthosis. What factor should the physiotherapist identify?

questions.explanation: Deep pin penetration through the outer table of the skull can allow bacteria to track intracranially, presenting with signs such as intracranial abscess or new-onset seizures, which are far more serious than superficial pin site problems. Superficial infection, dermatitis, and muscle atrophy are more common but less severe complications. Recognizing these red-flag signs is essential for urgent escalation of care.
questions.question: A patient with a halo vest develops a complication specific to pin penetration. What is the MOST likely presentation?

options: Reliable contraction of one residual muscle
Absence of any residual limb scarring
Full passive range at the elbow joint
questions.explanation: Myoelectric control depends on the ability to generate a detectable, repeatable EMG signal, which requires reliable voluntary contraction and relaxation of at least one residual muscle group. While two sites improve control options, one site is the functional minimum. Cognitive ability to learn the control pattern is also required, but the muscular requirement is the limiting physical factor.
questions.question: A myoelectric prosthesis user struggles to achieve consistent muscle signals. What is the MINIMUM physical requirement for successful myoelectric control?

questions.explanation: Hydraulic or pneumatic knee units provide swing or combined swing-and-stance phase control that adapts to changing cadence, an advantage over the single-cadence limitation of basic single-axis constant-friction knees, making them well suited to K3-level patients with variable walking speed needs. This functional benefit comes with trade-offs of higher cost, weight, and maintenance. Understanding this trade-off supports patient counseling about realistic expectations for their prescribed knee unit.
options: Complete elimination of any maintenance requirements
Guaranteed compatibility with all prosthetic feet regardless of design
Reduced weight compared to all other knee types
Ability to adapt swing and/or stance phase control to variable walking cadence
questions.question: A physiotherapist is assessing a patient with a new transfemoral prosthesis using a hydraulic knee unit. What is the primary clinical advantage of this knee type over a basic single-axis constant-friction knee for a K3 level patient?

questions.explanation: The TES belt is made of the same neoprene material used for transtibial suspension sleeves and wraps around the waist above the iliac crests. The Silesian belt instead attaches anteriorly and laterally and passes over the opposite iliac crest without full waist encirclement. Both are simple auxiliary suspension methods for lower activity users.
questions.question: Which suspension option for a transfemoral prosthesis uses a neoprene sleeve that surrounds the waist above the iliac crests?

questions.explanation: Comfort, which depends on achieving an appropriate distribution of forces between the residual limb and socket, is the most critical aspect of prosthetic prescription, since a poorly fitting or uncomfortable socket limits mobility and often leads to rejection of the device. Cosmesis and component brand are secondary considerations after comfort and functional component selection are established. This principle guides the overall prescription sequence, starting with socket design.
questions.question: Following an amputation, which factor is considered most critical to establishing overall comfort and acceptance of a lower limb prosthesis?
options: The total weight of the completed prosthesis alone
The color match of the prosthetic skin cover
Appropriate distribution of forces between the residual limb and socket
The specific brand of prosthetic components used
The cosmetic covering material selected for the limb

questions.explanation: A hip flexion contracture commonly produces uneven step length during successive double support, as the contracture limits terminal hip extension needed for a symmetric stride. Addressing this typically requires physical therapy focused on stretching and gait retraining rather than a simple prosthetic adjustment. Contractures should ideally be prevented early through positioning and range-of-motion exercises after amputation.
options: Excessive heel rise during initial swing
Jerky knee motion at loading response
Medial or lateral socket thrust at mid-stance
questions.question: A patient with an amputation has significant hip flexion contracture on the residual limb side. What gait deviation is this most likely to cause in successive double support?

options: Phantom sensation only occurs in upper limb amputees, never lower limb
Phantom sensation always requires opioid medication management
Phantom sensation is a nonpainful awareness of the amputated limb, whereas phantom pain is painful
Phantom sensation and phantom pain are identical clinical entities
Phantom pain is a normal, expected, nonpainful experience
questions.explanation: Phantom sensation is defined as the nonpainful awareness of the amputated limb, while phantom pain specifically refers to painful sensation perceived as arising from the amputated portion. This distinction is important for patient education, since phantom sensation is a common and generally nonpathological experience that does not necessarily require the same treatment approach as phantom pain. Clarifying this difference can reduce unnecessary patient anxiety about normal phantom sensations.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is educating a patient about phantom limb sensation shortly after amputation. What distinguishes phantom sensation from phantom pain?

questions.explanation: While weak hip abductors are a recognized cause of lateral trunk bending over the prosthesis, this can be addressed through gait training and strengthening as part of the rehabilitation program, and clinical judgment is used to weigh overall candidacy rather than applying an absolute exclusion criterion. This reflects the individualized, multifactorial nature of prosthetic candidacy decisions. Even if some compensatory pattern persists, functional prosthetic use may still provide meaningful benefit to the patient.
options: Prosthetic fitting is only appropriate once hip strength is completely normalized
A structured strengthening and gait training program may improve function even though some compensatory gait pattern may persist
Gait deviations from hip abductor weakness cannot be improved through any therapy
Hip abductor strength has no bearing on gait quality with a prosthesis
Hip abductor weakness always precludes any prosthetic fitting regardless of severity
questions.question: A physiotherapist is asked why a patient with a transfemoral amputation and significant hip abductor weakness might still be considered for prosthetic fitting despite anticipated gait deviations. What is the most appropriate clinical reasoning?

options: Automatic correction of any residual limb pain
Complete elimination of any prosthetic maintenance needs
Guaranteed reduction in overall prosthesis weight
Elastic energy storage during loading is returned at push-off to assist propulsion
Elimination of the need for any gait training
questions.question: A physiotherapist is educating a patient with a new prosthetic limb on the significance of dynamic response (energy-storing) feet. What functional benefit should be emphasized during running or jumping activities?
questions.explanation: Dynamic response feet store elastic energy during limb loading and mid-stance, returning it at push-off to assist propulsion, which is particularly beneficial during running and jumping activities for higher activity level users. However, objective evidence for reduced oxygen consumption is mixed and mainly evident at faster walking speeds. Setting realistic patient expectations about this benefit is an important part of patient education.

options: Malalignment only affects cosmetic appearance with no functional consequence
Malalignment exclusively affects contralateral upper limb function
Abnormal forces that can be transmitted to more proximal joints and contribute to pain
Malalignment cannot contribute to any pain symptoms
Malalignment has no relationship to extrinsic residual limb pain
questions.question: A physiotherapist is treating a patient whose prosthetic socket alignment appears to be contributing to abnormal, asymmetric wear patterns and reports of pain. What broader consequence of malaligned lower limb prostheses should the therapist be alert to?
questions.explanation: Malalignment of lower limb prostheses can create abnormal forces that contribute to extrinsic residual limb pain and may also affect more proximal joints, illustrating that prosthetic alignment issues can have effects beyond the immediate residual limb. This broader perspective supports a comprehensive assessment approach when a patient reports new or worsening pain with prosthesis use. Referral to the prosthetist for alignment reassessment may be warranted based on these findings.

questions.question: Which gait aid provides the widest base of support and is therefore appropriate for patients requiring maximal balance assistance, though it interferes with reciprocal gait?
questions.explanation: A standard walker provides a wider base of support than canes or crutches, offering greater stability for patients needing maximal balance assistance, ataxic patients, or those with a substantial fear of falling. However, its use requires bilateral grasp and arm strength and interferes with the development of a normal reciprocal gait pattern. Wheeled variants can help patients with incoordination who struggle to lift the device.

A key functional advantage of Lofstrand crutches is that the hand piece can be released without losing the crutch since the forearm cuff maintains its position, freeing the hands for tasks such as opening doors. Despite this advantage, good upper extremity strength and adequate trunk balance remain minimum requirements for safe use. Reinforcing correct cuff positioning ensures this functional benefit is realized safely.
questions.question: A physiotherapist notices a patient using Lofstrand crutches has difficulty maintaining the forearm cuff position correctly. What functional consequence is most relevant to reinforce during training?
options: The hand can be released from the grip without dropping the crutch, freeing the hand for tasks
The crutches provide no weight-bearing relief at all
The crutches require no adjustment for correct forearm cuff height
The forearm cuff eliminates the need for any upper extremity strength
The crutches are contraindicated for any patient with trunk imbalance
Radiographic evidence of adequate healing with stability
Completion of an arbitrary time period
A patient request without other findings
questions.question: A physiotherapist reviews radiographs of a patient in a TLSO for a thoracolumbar fracture. What clinical finding MOST strongly supports orthosis discontinuation?
questions.explanation: Discontinuation of a spinal orthosis should be based on objective evidence of adequate bony healing and confirmed clinical stability rather than arbitrary time frames, insurance limits, or patient preference alone. Minor skin irritation usually warrants modification rather than discontinuation. Radiographic and clinical confirmation of healing remains the clinical gold standard for this decision.

questions.question: A patient asks what factor most influences how effectively a spinal orthosis limits intersegmental motion. What should the physiotherapist explain?
options: The total cost of the device
Fit intimacy and three-point pressure application
questions.explanation: Effective control of intersegmental spinal motion depends primarily on how intimately the orthosis conforms to the trunk and how well the three-point pressure system is applied, since a loose-fitting brace cannot transmit corrective forces effectively regardless of design. Wearing time and body habitus can influence outcomes but are not the primary mechanical determinant. Proper fit is the foundation of orthotic effectiveness.

In bilateral upper limb loss, asymmetry of components is often more functional than mirrored devices, because a wrist flexion unit on the dominant side allows the hand to approach the body for tasks like feeding and hygiene. Identical bilateral devices limit positioning versatility. This individualized prescription improves independence in activities of daily living.
questions.question: A patient with bilateral transradial amputation reports difficulty performing two-handed tasks. What prosthetic feature should the physiotherapist recommend?
options: A wrist flexion unit on the dominant side

questions.question: Which prehospital cervical collar is generally used for short-term immobilization during trauma transport but is considered less reliable for long-term unstable spine management?
questions.explanation: Extrication collars such as the Stifneck are designed for short-term prehospital immobilization during transport and, per cadaveric study, do not provide significant mechanical immobilization for an unstable cervical spine. Devices such as the Miami J and Aspen collars are instead used for long-term management after the acute prehospital phase. This distinction guides appropriate transition of care after initial trauma stabilization.

questions.question: A patient develops contact dermatitis from prolonged cervical collar wear. What is the MOST appropriate intervention?
questions.explanation: Contact dermatitis from a cervical orthosis requires both symptomatic treatment, such as topical steroids, and identification and removal of the causative allergen, which may be the collar material or a cleaning product used on the skin or device. Stopping cervical stabilization entirely could compromise spinal safety if it is still clinically required. Addressing the skin reaction while maintaining necessary stabilization is the balanced approach.
options: Apply topical steroids and identify the allergen source
Add more padding beneath the collar
Continue the current collar without modification

questions.explanation: Hyperhidrosis, while not itself indicative of underlying disease, is a common finding related to heat and occlusion within the prosthetic socket environment. This differs from contact dermatitis, which reflects a hypersensitivity or irritant reaction to specific liner or socket materials. Management strategies differ depending on which specific dermatologic process is present.
questions.question: Which skin condition of the residual limb is not itself indicative of underlying disease but is commonly noted in association with prosthesis wear and heat buildup?

options: It eliminates any need for patient feedback
It is universally more accurate than instrumented gait analysis
It does not provide quantitative information and is limited by the speed and complexity of human locomotion
It always provides fully quantitative kinetic data
It requires no clinical experience to perform accurately
questions.explanation: Informal visual gait analysis does not provide quantitative information and has limitations due to the speed and complexity of human locomotion, especially when gait deviations and compensations coexist.
