questions.question: A physiotherapist is asked to help train a patient in donning a Syme prosthesis with a removable medial window design. What functional limitation should the patient be counseled about regarding this design?
options: Complete inability to bear weight through the residual limb
Complete elimination of any suspension needed
Reduced socket strength and less favorable cosmesis compared to other Syme designs
Mandatory use of a wheelchair at all times
Inability to wear any type of shoe
questions.explanation: The removable medial window socket design for Syme amputation allows easy donning over the bulbous residual limb but has the disadvantages of poor cosmesis and reduced socket strength due to the window cutout. Alternative designs such as the expandable wall or stovepipe liner may be considered if these drawbacks are problematic. Patient education about these trade-offs supports informed shared decision-making regarding prosthetic options.

questions.question: Which type of foot orthosis is designed to change the alignment of skeletal structures using rigid materials such as thermoplastics or carbon composites?
questions.explanation: Corrective orthoses use rigid materials to actively change the alignment of foot skeletal structures, whereas accommodative devices made from soft foams cushion an already deformed foot without correcting alignment. This distinction guides material selection based on treatment goals. Corrective devices demand more meticulous fitting to avoid pressure injury.

questions.question: A physiotherapist assessing a transfemoral prosthesis user notices circumduction of the prosthetic limb during swing phase. Which underlying cause should the therapist investigate first?
options: Poor socket rotation causing whips at heel strike
Inadequate knee flexion because the knee unit is too stiff, or the prosthesis is too long
Weak hip extensors during loading response
Excessive heel lever causing early knee flexion
Inadequate toe lever causing an early drop-off
questions.explanation: Circumduction of the prosthetic limb during swing is most commonly linked to inadequate knee flexion from excessive knee stiffness or a prosthesis that is too long, both of which impair toe clearance. Adjusting knee friction/damping or prosthesis length addresses the underlying mechanical cause. This differs from whips, which instead relate to excessive socket rotation rather than limb length or knee stiffness.

The balanced forearm orthosis (BFO) is a wheelchair-mounted device attaching to a forearm trough, assisting patients with spinal cord injury in feeding, grooming, and accessing household technology. A universal cuff instead is a simpler hand-worn device for holding utensils. Both serve the goal of attaching assistive devices, but the BFO provides greater proximal support.
questions.question: Which upper limb orthosis is essentially a wheelchair-mounted accessory that attaches to a forearm trough to assist ADLs in spinal cord injury?

options: Pin site care is solely the responsibility of the patient with no caregiver involvement
Pin sites require attention only if pain is completely absent
Regular wound care at the pin sites due to frequent complications
Pin sites need attention only during the first 24 hours after application
No specific pin site care is required once the halo is applied
questions.explanation: Pin site complications are a frequent occurrence with halo vest use and require regular vigilant wound care, making caregiver education about ongoing pin site monitoring an essential discharge teaching point. This is distinct from a one-time check, since complications such as loosening or infection can develop over the course of treatment. Physiotherapists working with these patients should reinforce this education alongside their functional mobility training.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is instructing caregivers on halo vest pin site care prior to discharge. What is emphasized as a frequent and important area requiring vigilant attention?

questions.explanation: Excessive heel lever produces abrupt heel contact with rapid knee flexion during loading response. Realigning the foot and softening heel stiffness reduces the abrupt loading moment at the knee. Increasing stiffness would worsen the abrupt heel strike rather than correct it.
questions.question: A patient with a transtibial amputation has excessive heel lever causing an abrupt heel strike with rapid knee flexion. Which prosthetic adjustment is most appropriate?
options: Lengthen the prosthetic shank by two centimeters
Switch to a rigid keel SACH foot design
Add a rotator unit to the pylon assembly
Increase the heel cushion stiffness only
Realign the prosthetic foot and reduce heel stiffness

questions.explanation: Routine follow-up for a new upper limb prosthesis user should occur initially 4 to 6 weeks after delivery, then every 2 to 6 months until a definitive prosthesis is prescribed, after which yearly visits generally suffice. This graduated schedule allows close monitoring during the early adaptation period when problems are more likely. Reducing visit frequency too early risks missing correctable fit or training issues.
options: Only annual visits starting immediately after delivery
Every 4 to 6 weeks initially, then every 2 to 6 months until definitive fitting
Only a single visit at delivery with no further follow-up needed
Daily visits for the first three months
Every 6 months from the very first visit
questions.question: Which upper limb prosthetic follow-up schedule is recommended shortly after delivery of a new prosthesis, before transitioning to less frequent visits?

options: Adding a rotator adaptor to the pylon
Discontinuing prosthesis use until surgery is performed
Switching to a stiffer prosthetic foot
Stretching exercises targeting hip flexor length combined with gait retraining
Immediate socket replacement by the prosthetist
questions.explanation: Hip flexion contracture leading to uneven step length is addressed primarily through physical therapy focused on stretching and gait retraining rather than a prosthetic component change. Contracture management is most effective when initiated early in the postoperative period through positioning and range-of-motion exercises. Persistent significant contractures may still require reassessment of prosthetic alignment as an adjunct measure.
questions.question: During transfemoral gait training, a therapist observes uneven step length attributed to a hip flexion contracture. What is the most appropriate physiotherapy-led intervention?
A physiotherapist is asked to help select an appropriate assistive device for a patient with significant fear of falling and severe sensory ataxia. Which device offers the greatest base of support?
questions.explanation: A standard walker provides a wider base of support than canes or crutches, making it appropriate for patients requiring maximal balance assistance, such as those with sensory ataxia or substantial fear of falling. This benefit must be balanced against its bulk and interference with reciprocal gait patterns. The therapist should still monitor for excessive emotional or physical dependence on the device over time.

Boutonniere deformity presents with PIP flexion and DIP hyperextension, and a ring orthosis is used to block further PIP flexion. Swan-neck deformity is the reverse pattern, with PIP hyperextension and DIP flexion, requiring a reversed ring design. Recognizing the deformity pattern determines proper orthotic orientation.
questions.question: Which finger deformity is characterized by flexion at the proximal interphalangeal joint and hyperextension at the distal interphalangeal joint, treatable with a ring orthosis blocking PIP flexion?

questions.explanation: Microprocessor-controlled knees use an onboard computer to continuously adjust knee resistance according to sensed gait parameters, offering energy savings and adaptability but at the highest cost and heaviest weight among knee options. Simpler mechanical knees such as single-axis or weight-activated designs lack this adaptive real-time control. This complexity is generally reserved for higher-functioning users who can benefit from adaptive control.
questions.question: Which prosthetic knee control mechanism uses an onboard computer to adjust resistance in real time based on gait parameters?

questions.explanation: It is generally best to don a TLSO while supine, which allows the orthosis to be properly aligned before the patient moves to sitting or standing. Donning it loosely or in an improper position diminishes its stabilizing effect. This instruction is a key part of patient and caregiver education for safe orthosis use.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is educating a patient fitted with a custom-molded plastic thoracolumbosacral body jacket about proper donning technique. What position is recommended for donning the orthosis?
options: Supine position to ensure proper alignment
Seated position with trunk flexed forward
Side-lying position with knees drawn to chest

questions.question: Which body-powered upper limb terminal device provides a lateral pinch grip and is activated by cable tension to open against spring or rubber-band closing force?
questions.explanation: The voluntary-opening hook, such as the Dorrance designs, is opened by cable tension while springs or rubber bands provide the closing prehensile force, typically 5 to 10 lb. Voluntary-closing devices instead allow the user to generate variable grip force but require sustained cable tension to maintain grasp. Hooks provide better visualization of grasped objects than cosmetic hands.

questions.question: For a hip disarticulation prosthesis, which prosthetic knee is most commonly selected to reduce overall weight and complexity?
options: Polycentric four-bar knee with hydraulic swing control
questions.explanation: The endoskeletal hip joint used for hip disarticulation prostheses typically pairs with a constant-friction knee that includes an extension assist, helping to reduce overall prosthesis weight given the added proximal hip joint component. Lightweight materials such as titanium or carbon graphite composite are also preferred at this level. Locking joints can still be added if additional stability is required.

options: Whether the ambient room temperature is appropriate
Whether the patient prefers a different cosmetic foam cover
Whether the socket fit and suspension are secure and properly aligned
Whether the patient is wearing an unrelated wristwatch
Whether the patient's shoe color matches the prosthesis
questions.explanation: Jerky knee motion at loading response is classically linked to a loose socket, poor alignment, or inadequate suspension, making socket fit and suspension security the first areas to check when this symptom is reported. Addressing this mechanical cause directly targets the source of instability rather than unrelated cosmetic factors. This systematic troubleshooting approach reflects sound clinical reasoning in prosthetic gait assessment.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is asked to help troubleshoot a patient's report of an uncomfortable, jerky sensation at the knee during initial contact while using a transtibial prosthesis with a supracondylar cuff strap. What should be checked first?

questions.explanation: In pediatric upper limb prosthetic care, the device often becomes an aid rather than a full replacement for lost function, and considerations such as the age for introducing myoelectric control must account for the child's developmental stage. This nuanced understanding helps set realistic expectations for families and supports appropriate multidisciplinary timing decisions. Physiotherapists contribute observational and functional developmental information relevant to these discussions.
options: Pediatric patients require no adaptation period for prosthetic use
Myoelectric fitting age is standardized identically across all children
The prosthesis always fully replaces normal hand function from the first fitting
Pediatric prosthetic fitting timing has no relevance to developmental milestones
The prosthesis functions more as an assistive aid than a full functional replacement, especially early on
questions.question: A physiotherapist is asked to contribute to a multidisciplinary discussion regarding pediatric prosthetic fitting timing for a young child with an upper limb deficiency. What general principle applies to the prosthesis in this population?
What effect does increased muscle tone from an upper motor neuron injury have on tissue pressures generated by an otherwise appropriately designed static orthosis?
questions.explanation: Increased tone from upper motor neuron injury generates much higher tissue pressures within a static orthosis than would occur in a flaccid limb, necessitating additional padding and a more careful wearing schedule to prevent skin breakdown. This differs from the typically low, well-tolerated pressures seen with static positioning splints on a flaccid limb. Recognizing this risk is essential when prescribing splints for spastic upper extremities.
options: It only affects dynamic orthoses, never static designs
It always decreases the pressure generated at bony prominences
It has no effect on tissue pressure generated by a static device
It generates much higher tissue pressures, requiring additional padding and a careful wearing schedule
It eliminates the need for any wearing schedule

questions.question: A physiotherapist is assisting a patient in a soft cervical collar following a whiplash injury. Based on available evidence, what should guide the treatment plan beyond simply providing the collar?
questions.explanation: Randomized studies have shown that patients who engaged in early mobilization and active exercise reported less pain and disability at both 6 weeks and 6 months compared with those managed with a soft collar alone, and collar-wearing patients took longer to return to work. This evidence supports incorporating physiotherapist-guided active exercise rather than relying on collar immobilization as sole treatment. Recognizing the psychological dependency and muscle atrophy risks of prolonged bracing supports this more active management approach.
options: Collar use should always be extended indefinitely for best results
The soft collar alone is proven to be the most effective long-term treatment
Complete immobilization for many months is the preferred approach
Early active mobilization and physical therapy exercise are associated with better outcomes than prolonged collar use alone
No exercise program is needed once a soft collar is provided
Determining that no intervention is possible
Rigid immobilization of all upper limb joints
Weighted orthoses providing stability via inertia
questions.question: A patient with Parkinson's disease and severe upper limb tremor is referred for orthotic management. What intervention is MOST appropriate?
questions.explanation: Weighted wrist or hand orthoses increase the inertia of the limb segment, which can dampen the amplitude of tremor and improve functional control during tasks such as eating or writing. Rigid immobilization would eliminate function entirely rather than improving control. This inertial damping approach is a recognized strategy for tremor management.

questions.question: Which UE amputation level typically shows the highest rate of continued long-term prosthetic acceptance among unilateral amputees?
questions.explanation: Approximately 90% of individuals with a transradial amputation continue to use a prosthesis occasionally, a notably higher rate than more proximal levels such as shoulder disarticulation or forequarter amputation, which have high rejection rates. Transhumeral amputees show intermediate acceptance around 40%. This pattern reflects the greater functional benefit prostheses provide at more distal levels.

The three-point control concept applies a strong corrective force at the joint level with counterforces applied both proximal and distal to that joint, forming the biomechanical basis of nearly all orthotic designs. Without an adequate counterforce, the orthosis cannot effectively control joint position or motion. This principle applies equally to upper and lower limb orthotic devices.
questions.question: Which biomechanical principle underlies the use of the three-point control concept in nearly all upper and lower limb orthotic designs?
options: Two equal forces applied at the same point cancel all joint motion
Orthotic control requires no counterforce if material is sufficiently rigid
Force is applied only proximal to the joint with no distal counterforce
A strong force applied at a joint is balanced by counterforces applied proximal and distal to it
A single large force applied only distal to the joint controls all motion

questions.question: Approximately what pressure range is generally tolerated by skin for only 2 to 4 hours continuously before risking tissue injury, according to orthotic tissue tolerance data?
questions.explanation: Higher pressures of 100 to 300 mm Hg are tolerated for only 2 to 4 hours continuously, whereas lower pressures of 20 to 50 mm Hg may be tolerated for up to 12 hours a day. This data, adapted from seating research, informs orthotic wearing schedules to avoid skin breakdown at bony prominences. Clinicians must balance stretching effectiveness against these tissue tolerance limits.

options: An oval distal contour matching the forearm
questions.question: A patient with a transradial amputation and intact forearm rotation needs a new socket. Which socket feature is essential to preserve pronation-supination?
questions.explanation: Preserving active pronation-supination requires the socket to closely match the natural oval, radial-ulnar shape of the forearm so rotational forces transfer directly to the prosthesis. A rigid anterior panel or excessive proximal trim restricts this motion. Matching anatomical contour is the key design principle for rotation-preserving sockets.

options: Only terminal stance push-off force generation
Only late loading response knee flexion control
Only initial double support weight acceptance
Only the transition into single-limb stance
Swing phase, by preventing plantarflexion and foot drag
questions.explanation: An AFO for footdrop primarily addresses the swing phase by preventing excessive plantarflexion, thereby improving toe clearance and preventing dragging or catching of the foot. While AFOs can also influence stance-phase knee mechanics depending on design, addressing swing-phase foot position is a primary goal in footdrop management. This focus guides both AFO selection and functional gait training goals.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is treating a patient with a new AFO for footdrop following a peripheral nerve injury. During gait analysis, what specific phase of gait is the AFO primarily intended to improve regarding limb clearance?

questions.explanation: The Williams orthosis is unique among rigid LSOs in that it encourages flexion while limiting extension and lateral motion, thereby reducing lumbar lordosis through oblique lateral uprights. The Knight and chairback braces instead limit flexion and extension symmetrically without encouraging a specific directional motion. This distinct mechanical goal differentiates the Williams design from other rigid lumbosacral orthoses.
questions.question: Which lumbosacral orthosis encourages spinal flexion while limiting extension and lateral motion, thereby reducing lumbar lordosis?

questions.explanation: Polycentric knees use multiple linked axes that shift the instantaneous center of rotation throughout the gait cycle, closely replicating the changing axis of the natural knee joint. This provides enhanced stance stability and toe clearance during swing compared to a fixed single-axis design. The benefit is biomechanical fidelity, not simplicity, weight, or cost.
questions.question: A patient asks why a polycentric prosthetic knee was chosen over a single-axis knee. What biomechanical advantage should be explained?
options: Changing center of rotation matching knee motion
It improves ground clearance during swing only
It passively absorbs shock at heel strike only
It enhances mediolateral stability during stance only
It reduces all vertical loading forces
It stores energy in stance for push-off release
questions.question: A patient with a dynamic response prosthetic foot asks how it improves walking efficiency. What should the physiotherapist explain?
questions.explanation: Dynamic response feet are designed with a flexible keel that deforms under load during stance, storing elastic energy that is released at terminal stance to assist forward propulsion. This mimics the push-off function of the natural ankle-foot complex. The other listed functions are secondary or inaccurate descriptions of this mechanism.

questions.question: A patient asks the purpose of a sacroiliac orthosis. What should the physiotherapist explain?
questions.explanation: A sacroiliac orthosis applies circumferential compression around the pelvis to stabilize the sacroiliac joints, reducing pain associated with instability or hypermobility at this joint. It does not address leg length, disc pathology, or scoliosis, which require different interventions. Compression-based stabilization is its specific mechanical function.

options: The collar improves peripheral vision while driving
The collar eliminates the need for mirror checks
The collar has no measurable effect on driving performance
The collar allows for faster vehicle acceleration and braking
The collar increases the driver's blind spot, affecting merging and lane changes
questions.question: A physiotherapist is providing patient education for someone who will drive while wearing a rigid cervical collar. What specific safety point should be emphasized based on research findings?
questions.explanation: Research has shown that wearing a cervical collar, such as the Philadelphia collar, increases the driver's blind spot and results in slower driving speeds, which can affect safe merging and lane changes. Patients should be counseled about this increased blind spot as part of return-to-driving education. This finding directly informs safe practice recommendations for collar-wearing patients who plan to resume driving.

questions.question: A patient with C6-level tetraplegia retains wrist extension strength but lacks finger flexor and intrinsic hand strength. Which orthosis best restores functional grasp?
questions.explanation: The tenodesis prehension or flexor hinge orthosis uses active wrist extension to drive three-jaw chuck pinch, making it ideal for C6 tetraplegia where wrist extensors remain functional but finger flexors do not. Static wrist orthoses are used for conditions like carpal tunnel syndrome rather than motor substitution. The design specifically converts wrist motion into functional grasp.
options: Static wrist-hand orthosis for carpal tunnel syndrome

questions.explanation: Multiaxis feet incorporate joints that allow motion in multiple planes, such as inversion, eversion, and rotation, enabling the foot to conform to irregular surfaces rather than forcing the residual limb to absorb the unevenness. This terrain accommodation reduces shear stress on the limb during outdoor ambulation. Energy storage and weight are not the defining features of multiaxis design.
questions.question: A prosthetist recommends a multiaxis ankle-foot assembly for a patient who frequently walks on grass and uneven ground. What is the rationale?
A physiotherapist is assessing a patient using a rocker sole shoe modification intended to offload pressure under a specific metatarsal head. What key fitting detail should be verified?
questions.explanation: If a rocker sole is expected to offload an area of plantar pressure, the apex of the rocker must be positioned proximal to that pressure area for the modification to be effective. Incorrect apex placement can fail to achieve the intended pressure relief or even worsen symptoms. This detail is essential when evaluating whether a prescribed rocker sole is functioning as intended.
options: The apex of the rocker must always be positioned at the very toe tip
The apex of the rocker must be positioned proximal to the area needing pressure relief
The rocker sole must always be combined with a heel elevation
The rocker sole requires no specific apex placement to be effective
The rocker sole functions identically regardless of apex position
Removing scatter rugs and installing stair rails given reduced stride length and slower gait
Avoiding any home environment assessment since risk is unaffected
Removing all stair rails to simplify the home layout
Adding thick decorative rugs throughout the home for cushioning
Encouraging faster walking speed to compensate for balance loss
questions.explanation: Because a halo vest reduces stride length, slows gait speed, and impairs balance, discharge planning should include removal of fall hazards such as scatter rugs and installation of stair rails, along with a formal home safety evaluation. This directly translates the known biomechanical effects of the halo vest into concrete injury-prevention recommendations. A home visit by the rehabilitation or home care team is recommended to identify and address specific hazards.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is planning discharge education for a patient with a new halo vest regarding fall prevention at home. Which specific home modification should be prioritized based on known gait changes?

questions.explanation: Exoskeletal prostheses have a rigid, load-bearing outer shell that withstands rough handling and harsh environments better than the modular components of an endoskeletal design, making them suitable for heavy manual labor. Endoskeletal designs are generally preferred for ease of alignment adjustment and lighter weight, the opposite of the priorities here. Durability under demanding conditions is the deciding factor for this patient.
questions.question: A heavy laborer asks why an exoskeletal prosthesis was recommended over an endoskeletal design. What is the PRIMARY reason?

A physiotherapist is treating a patient after rotator cuff repair who has been placed in a static shoulder-elbow-wrist-hand orthosis (airplane splint). What early complication must the therapist help prevent through timely mobilization once medically cleared?
questions.explanation: Static positioning of the shoulder in an airplane splint after conditions such as rotator cuff repair requires care to mobilize the glenohumeral joint as soon as medically appropriate to prevent adhesive capsulitis. This reflects the balance between protecting a surgical repair and preventing secondary joint stiffness. Physiotherapists play a central role in timing and progressing this mobilization safely.

options: Additional finger padding at the DIP joint
questions.question: A physiotherapist notices a patient's dynamic hand-finger orthosis, intended to stretch a PIP flexion contracture, is instead producing MCP hyperextension. What design feature is likely missing?
questions.explanation: Failure to provide an MCP extension block can allow the orthosis to create hyperextension across the MCP joint instead of achieving the intended PIP stretch, undermining the therapeutic goal. Adding this block redirects the corrective force appropriately toward the PIP joint. This illustrates how a missing structural feature can produce an unintended and counterproductive orthotic effect.

questions.question: A physiotherapist is training a patient with insensate feet in the use of new orthopedic shoes. What wearing schedule should be recommended initially?
options: Immediate full-day wear with no monitoring
Wearing the shoes only while sleeping
A gradually increasing schedule starting at about 2 hours per day with regular skin inspection
Wearing the shoes only once per week for short trials
No wearing schedule is necessary if the shoe fits well visually
questions.explanation: In patients with sensory loss in the feet, new shoes should be worn using a gradually increasing schedule starting at approximately two hours per day, followed by removal of shoes and socks for careful skin inspection. This cautious approach reduces the risk of unnoticed pressure injury in insensate skin. This principle mirrors the graded wearing schedule used for new prosthetic sockets in individuals with amputation.

questions.question: A physiotherapist is treating a patient with residual limb pain described as aching and diffuse, worsened by prosthesis wear, without evidence of neuroma or infection. What should the therapist assess first?
questions.explanation: Extrinsic residual limb pain results from a mismatch between the socket and the shape or volume of the residual limb, or from malalignment, making socket fit and alignment the first area to assess in the absence of intrinsic pathology such as neuroma or infection. Correcting fit or referring to the prosthetist for socket modification is the appropriate next step. This systematic approach avoids unnecessary medical workup when a mechanical cause is more likely.
options: Socket fit and alignment for a possible mismatch between limb and socket
Excessive knee flexion range in the prosthetic knee unit
Excessive dynamic response in the prosthetic foot
Hip flexion contracture or gait insecurity
questions.question: A physiotherapist is helping a patient troubleshoot a transtibial prosthesis that causes an uncomfortable socket sensation specifically during successive double support in gait. Besides socket fit, what other contributing factor should be considered?
questions.explanation: Uneven step length and discomfort during successive double support can result from hip flexion contracture or general gait insecurity, in addition to socket fit issues, requiring both physical therapy intervention and possible socket adjustment. Addressing only the socket without considering contracture or confidence-related factors may leave the underlying problem unresolved. A comprehensive assessment approach considers both mechanical and functional contributing factors.

options: Inability to actively flex or abduct
questions.question: A patient with a shoulder disarticulation prosthesis using a passive shoulder unit reports difficulty reaching overhead. What is the PRIMARY limitation responsible?
questions.explanation: Passive shoulder units must be manually pre-positioned by the other hand because they cannot actively flex or abduct under the user's own muscular effort. This makes dynamic overhead reaching impossible without external repositioning. Weight and cosmesis are secondary concerns compared to this fundamental lack of active joint motion.

questions.question: Which knee unit type provides only constant swing-phase control without stance-phase control, and is considered excellent for pediatric users?
questions.explanation: The single-axis constant-friction knee is simple, durable, and low-maintenance, but it only offers constant swing-phase control with no stance control, making it useful for pediatric patients who can voluntarily control knee stability. More complex knees add stance control at the cost of increased weight and maintenance. Selection depends on the user's control ability and activity level.

questions.question: A physiotherapist is working with a K2-level individual with a transtibial amputation whose activity is limited to low-level environmental barriers such as curbs and uneven surfaces. Which prosthetic foot category most appropriately matches this functional level?
questions.explanation: A flexible keel foot provides a smoother rollover than a rigid keel SACH foot and accommodates general mobility needs for low-to-moderate activity individuals, making it an appropriate match for a K2-level patient managing low-level environmental barriers. Highly specialized athletic feet would exceed this patient's functional demand and cost-effectiveness considerations. Matching component complexity to K-level supports both function and resource stewardship.
options: Full multiaxial dynamic response foot for elite athletics
Vertical shock pylon foot for high-impact sports

questions.explanation: Stable Jefferson fractures without significant ligamentous instability can often be managed initially with a rigid cervical collar and careful clinical and radiographic follow-up to ensure ongoing stability. A soft collar lacks sufficient rigidity for this fracture pattern, while surgery is reserved for unstable injuries. This conservative approach reflects standard management of stable upper cervical fractures.
questions.question: A patient sustains a Jefferson fracture, a C1 burst fracture. What initial management is MOST appropriate for a stable pattern?
options: No treatment is necessary at all
Immediate surgical fusion in all cases
Rigid cervical collar with close monitoring

questions.explanation: Torque absorbers are inserted within the pylon to allow transverse plane rotation between the foot and socket, dissipating rotational shear forces that would otherwise be transmitted directly to the residual limb during turning. Without this component, twisting motions create uncomfortable torque at the skin-socket interface. Addressing rotation specifically, rather than weight or heel height, resolves this complaint.
questions.question: A transfemoral prosthesis user complains of residual limb discomfort during turning movements. What component addition is MOST likely to help?
options: A torque absorber reducing rotational shear

questions.explanation: The PTB-supracondylar (PTBSC) socket extends its sidewalls above the femoral condyles for enhanced mediolateral stability and self-suspension. The PTBSCSP variant adds anterior extension over the patella for additional stiffness and sensory feedback. Both are typically reserved for short residual limbs needing extra control.
questions.question: Which transtibial socket variant provides high medial and lateral walls extending over the femoral condyles to enhance self-suspension?
Which suspension harness is most commonly used for light to normal duty activities in transradial and transhumeral body-powered prostheses?
questions.explanation: The figure-8 harness is simple, durable, and adjustable, making it the most commonly used suspension for light to normal duty body-powered prosthetic activities. The shoulder saddle and chest strap is reserved for heavier lifting or when axillary pressure is intolerable. Self-suspending sockets avoid harnessing altogether but are limited to certain amputation levels.

Patients with a custom body jacket are generally instructed to wear the orthosis at all times when on an incline greater than 30 degrees, though this instruction is often individualized and may be modified by the surgeon, such as to allow removal for showering. This specific activity-based instruction is a practical detail the physiotherapist should reinforce during patient education. Clarifying any surgeon-specific modifications avoids confusion about brace-wearing expectations.
options: Only when the patient is asleep
Never, since the brace is optional at all activity levels
Whenever the patient is on an incline greater than 30 degrees
questions.question: A physiotherapist is assessing a patient's understanding of orthotic wearing precautions for a custom TLSO following spinal fusion. When is the patient generally instructed the brace must be worn at all times, unless modified by the surgeon?

questions.explanation: A rigid dressing controls edema, protects the residual limb from trauma, and maintains consistent compression, which collectively promote faster wound healing and allow earlier progression through the rehabilitation program. Soft dressings allow wound visualization more easily but provide less effective edema and shape control. The clinical outcome benefit outweighs convenience factors like cost or ease of application.
questions.question: A patient with a transtibial amputation receives a rigid post-operative dressing instead of a soft dressing. What is the PRIMARY advantage?
options: Faster healing and better rehabilitation outcomes
Allows better visualization of the wound

questions.explanation: Choke syndrome results from excessive proximal socket constriction that restricts venous and lymphatic return while allowing distal tissue to bulge, so the correction is to fabricate a socket with a total contact fit that relieves the proximal constriction. Increasing tightness or adding sock plies would worsen the constriction. Elevation and topical agents do not address the underlying mechanical cause.
questions.question: A transtibial prosthesis user develops choke syndrome with distal limb swelling. What is the MOST effective management?
options: A new socket with reduced proximal constriction
Suction suspension with a one-way valve
PTB total contact hard socket alone
Waist belt with anterior fork strap
questions.question: A prosthetic user reports pistoning and delayed suspension security when running. Which transtibial suspension category best minimizes pistoning?
questions.explanation: Suction suspension creates a partial vacuum within the socket during swing, which most effectively minimizes pistoning compared to straps or sleeves. Sleeves and cuff straps are general-purpose but allow more vertical movement. Vacuum-assisted designs extend this same suction principle further.

Early prosthetic use should begin with brief wearing periods of 15 to 20 minutes, followed by removal to inspect the skin for irritation, with tolerance gradually increased over subsequent days to weeks. This graded schedule protects fragile, newly loaded skin from breakdown while permitting adaptation. Rushing to extended wear risks pressure injury and delays rehabilitation progress.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is educating a new prosthesis user on skin inspection routine. What is the most appropriate initial wearing schedule to recommend?
options: Avoid all prosthesis use until the definitive limb is fitted
Wear the prosthesis for a full 8-hour workday immediately
Wear the prosthesis only overnight during the first week
Wear the prosthesis for 15 to 20 minutes, then remove it to check the skin
Wear the prosthesis continuously for the first 24 hours

questions.explanation: An inadequate toe lever in the prosthetic foot can cause the limb to feel unstable and collapse early in late stance, described as drop-off, which disrupts the smooth transition into swing and increases stumbling risk. This differs from circumduction or trunk lean, which are compensations for clearance problems rather than stance instability. Identifying the toe lever issue directs the correct prosthetic adjustment.
questions.question: A patient frequently catches their toe during swing phase, causing stumbling. Which gait deviation does this suggest?
options: Early knee flexion or drop-off in stance

questions.question: A voluntary-opening terminal device requires cable adjustment. What tension setting is MOST appropriate for daily function?
questions.explanation: Voluntary-opening terminal devices rely on a controlled balance between sufficient closing force to grip objects and manageable opening effort through the cable. Moderate tension allows full opening without excessive fatigue while maintaining comfortable use throughout the day. Extremes of tension either limit function or cause user fatigue.
options: Moderate tension for opening and comfort
Maximum tension to allow full opening
Minimal slack with light opening force
Superior anatomical conformity for pressure control
questions.question: A patient asks why a custom-molded TLSO was chosen over a prefabricated design. What should be explained?
questions.explanation: Custom-molded TLSOs are fabricated directly from an impression or scan of the individual patient's torso, producing superior anatomical conformity that allows more precise and even distribution of corrective pressure compared to prefabricated designs. Prefabricated braces offer immediate availability but at the expense of this individualized fit. Pressure control and biomechanical effectiveness are the primary advantages of custom fabrication.

questions.question: A patient performing precision assembly work at a factory requests prosthetic hand modification. Which terminal device feature is MOST suitable?
options: Narrow fingers with good visual access
questions.explanation: Precision tasks require the worker to see exactly where small components are being placed, so a terminal device with narrow fingers and an unobstructed view of the workpiece is ideal. High grip force is more relevant to heavy labor than fine assembly. Visual access directly supports the dexterity needed for small-parts work.

questions.question: A physiotherapist is helping select an appropriate cane handle style for a patient with significant hand arthritis who reports discomfort with a standard C-handle. What alternative handle design should be considered?
options: A heavier wooden cane with the same C-handle
A functional or ortho-eze handle that centers over the cane shaft
A three-legged cane with the same C-handle
A cane with no handle grip at all
A longer cane shaft with no handle modification
questions.explanation: A functional or ortho-eze handle better conforms to the natural angle of the hand and is centered over the cane shaft, reducing the bending moment and strain on the wrist and fingers compared to a standard C-handle, making it more suitable for patients with hand pathology such as arthritis. This alternative does come at increased cost, which should be discussed with the patient. Selecting the appropriate handle design directly addresses the patient's specific comfort complaint.

options: Continued brace use can lead to trunk muscle weakness and atrophy, requiring a concurrent exercise program
Muscle strength always improves automatically during brace wear
Exercise programs are unnecessary once a brace is removed
Atrophy risk applies only to cervical, not thoracolumbar, orthoses
Trunk muscles are unaffected by any duration of orthotic use
questions.explanation: As with other spinal orthoses, continued use of a lumbosacral or thoracolumbar orthosis results in weakness and atrophy of trunk muscles, meaning an exercise program should be provided concomitantly with brace use and continued after weaning. This principle guides the physiotherapist's role in coordinating an appropriate strengthening program throughout the bracing period rather than only at brace discontinuation. Recognizing this risk supports proactive rather than reactive rehabilitation planning.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is treating a patient transitioning out of a custom TLSO body jacket after a compression fracture. What general principle applies regarding trunk muscle conditioning during and after brace use?

options: Rigid internal fixation through the orthosis
Complete elimination of all limb movement
A hydraulic effect from a snug cylindrical soft-tissue chamber
Traction applied continuously through pin sites
Direct compression of the fracture ends together
questions.explanation: A fracture orthosis relies on a closely fitting cylindrical component that compresses the soft tissue into an incompressible fluid-like chamber, converting vertical load into lateral and oblique stabilizing forces around the fracture. This concept is based on evidence that functional activity, rather than complete immobilization, stimulates healing. Rigid internal fixation is a separate surgical approach, not part of the orthosis mechanism.
questions.question: What is the primary biomechanical mechanism by which a fracture orthosis stabilizes a healing long bone fracture without rigid immobilization?

options: The cane works only by distracting the patient's attention from pain
A properly positioned cane decreases the muscular force needed to stabilize the joint, reducing joint reaction forces
The cane increases joint reaction forces but reduces perceived pain independently
The cane provides no measurable change in joint loading
The cane functions solely as a psychological placebo with no biomechanical effect
questions.explanation: A properly positioned cane can decrease the amount of muscle force necessary to stabilize a joint, which in turn leads to attenuation of joint reaction forces and decreased pain symptoms, particularly relevant in conditions like hip osteoarthritis. This biomechanical explanation supports the clinical practice of cane prescription for joint pain rather than viewing it purely as a psychological aid. Understanding this mechanism helps the physiotherapist explain the rationale for cane use to patients who may be reluctant to adopt an assistive device.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is reviewing a patient's cane use for balance support and notes the cane substantially reduces reported joint discomfort at the hip during stance. What is the proposed mechanism behind this symptomatic improvement?
Which prosthetic component allows a transfemoral prosthesis user to rotate the leg for tasks such as donning shoes or entering a vehicle?
questions.explanation: A rotator adaptor can be added to the pylon of a transfemoral prosthesis to allow the leg to be rotated for activities such as donning clothing or shoes or sitting comfortably in a vehicle. This differs from the vertical shock pylon, which addresses vertical impact absorption rather than rotation. Both components can be incorporated into an endoskeletal transfemoral prosthesis design.
options: Rotator adaptor in the pylon assembly
Transverse rotator at the ankle only

questions.question: Which KAFO design eliminates the thigh and calf bands and hip joint, relying on the ligament of Bijelow-type anatomical structures for stability in spinal cord injury patients?
questions.explanation: The Scott-Craig orthosis eliminates the lower thigh and calf bands and hip joint typical of an HKAFO, reducing weight and simplifying donning while relying on rigid connections and anatomical ligamentous structures for stability. It uses a bail-type knee lock and rigid ankle joints set in slight dorsiflexion. This design is specifically favored in spinal cord injury rehabilitation for its lighter weight.
options: Conventional metal KAFO with pelvic band
Louisiana State University reciprocating gait orthosis

questions.question: A physiotherapist is training a patient with a new transtibial prosthesis to negotiate uneven terrain after mastering level-surface ambulation. According to standard gait training progression, what should have been mastered immediately before this stage?
options: Advanced athletic cutting and rapid directional change maneuvers
Unsupervised community distance ambulation across varied outdoor terrain
Ambulation on level surfaces with equal step lengths and no lateral trunk bending
Complete simulation of complex workplace and vocational tasks
Fully independent driving skills using adaptive vehicle controls
questions.explanation: Following mastery of ambulation on flat, level surfaces with attention to transfers, knee stability, equal step lengths, and avoiding lateral trunk bending, techniques for managing uneven terrain, stairs, ramps, and curbs are introduced next in a structured progression. This stepwise approach ensures foundational gait quality before adding environmental complexity. Skipping steps in this progression risks reinforcing compensatory gait patterns on more challenging surfaces.

Donning a rigid TLSO while supine allows gravity to assist in achieving a neutral, well-aligned spinal position, improving the accuracy of the fit and the effectiveness of the corrective forces once standing. Standing donning makes consistent alignment more difficult to control. Patient and caregiver education on this supine technique supports correct daily application.
questions.question: A patient is being taught how to don a TLSO body jacket correctly. What positioning technique is recommended?
options: Supine positioning to optimize alignment and fit
Positioning does not affect device fit
Donning only by a trained orthotist

questions.explanation: Age has inconsistently predicted prosthetic success except in very advanced age, generally above 80 to 85 years, implying that other factors such as wound healing, contractures, and cognitive ability play a more consistent role in determining rehabilitation potential. This nuance is important because clinicians should not automatically exclude older patients from prosthetic candidacy based on age alone. Instead, a comprehensive functional assessment guides candidacy decisions.
questions.question: Which factor is identified as inconsistently predictive of prosthetic rehabilitation success, becoming significant mainly in very advanced age groups?

options: Fine motor tasks requiring intact sensory feedback
Bilateral simultaneous lifting of heavy loads
Basic control of the terminal device and elbow lock/unlock sequence
questions.explanation: Initial UE prosthetic training focuses on acquiring control of the terminal device and, for a transhumeral prosthesis, the elbow lock and unlock sequence, before progressing to more complex functional or vocational tasks. Establishing these foundational control skills is necessary before ADL tasks such as feeding can be reliably performed. This graded approach mirrors general motor learning principles applied to prosthetic rehabilitation.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is asked to assist in early ADL training for a patient with a new short transhumeral prosthesis who has difficulty positioning the terminal device for feeding tasks. What early skill should be emphasized before progressing to complex tasks?

questions.explanation: The solid ankle cushion heel (SACH) foot is durable, lightweight, and inexpensive, making it appropriate for K1-K2 level users limited to level-surface walking. Dynamic response and multiaxial feet are reserved for higher activity levels requiring energy return or terrain adaptation. Matching foot complexity to activity level avoids unnecessary cost and maintenance.
questions.question: Which prosthetic foot category is most appropriate for a low-activity individual (K1-K2) who ambulates mainly on level surfaces?

questions.explanation: Whips, defined as rotation of the prosthetic foot during initial swing, are caused by excessive socket rotation and are corrected by adjusting the socket fit rather than the knee or foot components. This differs from circumduction, which instead relates to inadequate knee flexion or prosthesis length. Precise terminology helps ensure the prosthetist addresses the correct mechanical issue.
options: Inadequate knee flexion requiring friction adjustment
Excessive heel lever requiring foot realignment
Hip flexion contracture requiring stretching alone
Weak hip extensors requiring strengthening alone
Excessive socket rotation requiring socket fit adjustment
questions.question: A physiotherapist is progressing a transfemoral amputee's gait training and notices whips (rotation of the prosthetic foot) at initial swing. What should be communicated to the prosthetic team?

questions.explanation: A single-axis foot allows controlled plantarflexion and dorsiflexion adjusted by durometer bumpers, which reduces knee-bending moments during loading and improves knee stability. This makes it useful for elderly transfemoral users or those with a short residual limb needing better knee stabilization. The trade-off is increased weight and maintenance compared to other foot designs.
options: Rigid keel with no ankle motion
Single-axis sagittal plane motion at the ankle
Low-profile foot design for Syme fitting
questions.question: Which prosthetic foot feature is primarily responsible for reducing knee-buckling forces during limb loading in individuals with a proximal amputation?

options: Soft dressing with elastic bandage wrap
Rigid dressing used for an immediate postoperative prosthesis
questions.explanation: A rigid dressing can be fashioned into an immediate or early postoperative prosthesis (IPOP) by attaching a pylon and foot, enabling limited weight bearing and edema control soon after surgery. Soft dressings and shrinkers manage edema but do not permit early weight bearing. Rigid dressing use requires experienced teams to monitor the residual limb closely.
questions.question: Which wound dressing option after lower limb amputation allows immediate to early weight bearing through an attached pylon and foot?

questions.explanation: Once the residual limb has stabilized, the average life expectancy for a lower limb prosthesis before replacement is generally 3 to 5 years. This timeline reflects gradual component wear and evolving patient needs rather than sudden failure alone. Yearly clinic visits help monitor when replacement becomes necessary.
options: Only after complete socket failure occurs
Only when the user reaches a new K-level
questions.question: At what approximate interval should a stable, well-fitting lower limb prosthesis typically be expected to require full replacement?

options: Physical therapy is contraindicated throughout collar use
Frequent diagnostic imaging is strongly recommended to detect possible instability
No further imaging is ever required once the collar is applied
The collar guarantees permanent bony stability without monitoring
The patient may discontinue collar use at any time without medical guidance
questions.explanation: For selected stable upper cervical fractures managed with rigid collars instead of a halo, frequent diagnostic imaging to detect possible instability is strongly recommended as part of the treatment protocol. This reflects the balance between the cost-effectiveness and reduced risk of collar use against the need for careful monitoring given the collar's less rigid immobilization compared to a halo. Physiotherapists should reinforce the importance of attending scheduled imaging and follow-up appointments.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is educating a patient recovering from a stable upper cervical spine fracture managed with a rigid collar rather than a halo device. What should the patient understand about ongoing monitoring?

questions.question:
Answer the following on the regulation of body pH:
1. Describe the regulation of body pH under these headings: sources of volatile and fixed acids, chemical buffering, the respiratory response and the renal response (bicarbonate handling and urinary buffers).
2. Explain why fixed acids accumulate in certain states (uncontrolled diabetes mellitus, starvation, alcoholism, protein metabolism).
3. Distinguish between carbonic (volatile) acid and non-carbonic (fixed) acids, and between the three lines of defence.
questions.answerText:
1. Regulation of pH:
• Acids are produced continuously and threaten the pH of extracellular and intracellular fluids; H2CO3 is in equilibrium with CO2, which leaves through the lungs, so arterial H2CO3 is set by respiratory activity.
• Chemical buffering in extracellular and intracellular fluids and bone is the first line of defence; it minimises pH change but removes no acid or base.
• Respiratory response is the second line: breathing removes CO2 as fast as it forms and large acid loads stimulate breathing, lowering H2CO3.
• Renal response: the burden of removing excess H+ falls on the kidneys, which excrete H+ combined with urinary buffers (for example phosphate), add new HCO3- to the ECF, reabsorb filtered bicarbonate through carbonic anhydrase-dependent steps and excrete the anions liberated from strong acids (phosphate, chloride, sulphate); the kidneys also excrete H+ in excess acid or HCO3- in excess base.
2. Basis of accumulation:
• Incomplete fatty acid oxidation in uncontrolled diabetes mellitus, starvation and alcoholism produces ketone body acids (acetoacetic and hydroxybutyric acids); incomplete carbohydrate metabolism produces lactate.
• Oxidation of proteins and amino acids produces strong acids such as H2SO4, HCl and H3PO4.
3. Distinctions:
• Carbonic acid is volatile and removed by the lungs; non-carbonic (fixed) acids are unaffected by breathing, are buffered and are excreted by the kidneys.
• First line: chemical buffers; second: respiratory; third: renal.

1. Sensory pathway:
• Receptors are biological transducers converting mechanical, thermal or other energy into electrical potentials and action potentials; structurally a receptor is a specialised dendritic ending, often encapsulated.
• General senses: exteroceptive, proprioceptive and interoceptive (for example bladder distension); special senses: sight, hearing, taste, smell, equilibrium.
• Classes by stimulus: mechanoreceptors (Merkel's discs, Meissner's, Pacinian and Ruffini corpuscles, hair follicle plexus), thermoreceptors (cold and warm), nociceptors (free endings), electromagnetic receptors (rods and cones) and chemoreceptors (taste, smell, oxygen, osmolality); teloceptors detect distant stimuli.
• Chain: first-order neuron from the receptor to the spinal cord (or medulla), second-order neuron to the thalamus, third-order neuron to the sensory cortex; all senses relay in the thalamus except olfaction.
2. Properties and modifiers:
• Fast-adapting afferents end in Meissner's corpuscles (FA1) and Pacinian corpuscles (FA2); slow-adapting afferents end in Merkel's discs (SA1) and Ruffini endings (SA2); type I units have small, well-defined receptive fields and type II wider fields.
• Cold spots are 4 to 10 times more numerous than warm spots (lips 15 to 25, fingers 3 to 5, trunk about 1 per cm2).
• Merkel's discs signal steady touch and texture, Meissner's corpuscles light touch and low-frequency vibration, Pacinian corpuscles pressure and vibration, Ruffini endings continuous deformation.
3. Damage:
• Inability to judge shape (astereognosis) and amorphosynthesis follow cortical and association area damage.
• Brown-Sequard syndrome: loss of position, vibration and light touch on the same side and of pain, heat and cold on the opposite side.
questions.question:
Answer the following on sensory receptors and the sensory pathway:
1. Describe the sensory system as a control pathway: the receptor as transducer, classes of receptors, the three-neuron chain to the cortex and the relay in the thalamus.
2. State the fibre and receptor properties (adaptation, receptive field, spot density) and the factors that alter receptor response.
3. Explain the physiological basis of the signs when the sensory pathway is damaged.

questions.answerText:
1. Fat digestion and absorption:
• Bile is required for fat digestion and absorption; the gallbladder stores and concentrates it, and it reaches the duodenum when digestion takes place.
• Pancreatic lipase with colipase converts triglyceride to monoglyceride and fatty acids (optimum pH 8.0); cholesterol esterase and phospholipase A2 also act.
• Fatty acids, monoglycerides, cholesterol and phospholipids with bile salts form micelles that carry lipids to the epithelium; in the smooth endoplasmic reticulum triglycerides and cholesterol esters are re-formed, and in the Golgi they are packaged with apoprotein B into chylomicrons or very low density lipoprotein (VLDL) particles.
• These leave the cell by exocytosis and enter lymph vessels (lacteals) or the venous system; lymph absorbs fatty acids and fats as chyle and transports lipids to the bloodstream.
• The absorptive surface is enlarged by folds, villi and microvilli.
2. Basis of vulnerability:
• Vitamin K is fat-soluble and is absorbed into the blood along with fats, so vitamin K deficiency occurs if fat absorption is impaired.
• Liver cells need vitamin K to make clotting factors; in liver disease the nonfunctional liver cells fail to produce procoagulants and also bile, which is required for fat and vitamin K absorption.
• Vitamin K deficiency is common in newborns and after systemic antibiotics; dietary lack is rarely a problem because bacteria in the large intestine produce vitamin K; the result is abnormal and often severe bleeding.
3. Distinctions:
• Micelles are bile salt aggregates in the lumen carrying fatty acids, monoglycerides, cholesterol and phospholipids to the epithelium; chylomicrons are lipoprotein particles assembled inside the cell (with apoprotein B) for export.
• Lymphatic route: lacteals carry lipids to the bloodstream as chyle; venous route: absorbed material enters the venous system directly.
questions.question:
Answer the following on the digestion and absorption of fats:
1. Describe fat digestion and absorption under these headings: role of bile and the gallbladder, pancreatic lipase and colipase, formation of micelles, uptake by the intestinal epithelium, formation of chylomicrons and VLDL, and routes into the circulation.
2. Explain why impaired fat absorption is more serious in some states (for example liver disease) and how it leads to a bleeding disorder.
3. Distinguish between micelles and chylomicrons, and between the lymphatic and venous routes of absorbed nutrients.

Answer the following on tubular reabsorption and secretion:
1. Describe tubular reabsorption and secretion under these headings: definition, mechanisms, handling in the proximal tubule, loop of Henle, distal tubule and collecting duct, and the tubular maximum and renal threshold.
2. Explain how tubular handling changes in dehydration and why a substance appears in the urine when its plasma concentration is high.
3. Distinguish between reabsorption and secretion, and between tubular maximum and renal threshold.
questions.answerText:
1. Tubular handling:
• Reabsorption transports water and some molecules from the filtrate back to the plasma; secretion is the reverse; the differential concentration gradient plays a major role.
• Mechanisms: passive diffusion, facilitated diffusion, active transport, symport (with Na+) and osmosis.
• Segments: the proximal tubule does uncontrolled reabsorption (about 67% of water osmotically with solutes, about 65% of sodium actively, phosphate about 85%, and a substance almost 100% reabsorbed by active transport with Na+); the loop of Henle sets the osmotic gradient (about 15% of water in the descending limb, about 25% of sodium in the thick ascending limb); the distal tubule reabsorbs about 8% of water and about 5% of sodium; the collecting duct reabsorbs a variable amount, with 5% of sodium under aldosterone; H+ is secreted along the tubule.
• About 99% of the filtrate is reabsorbed and urine flow is about 1 ml/min.
• Tubular maximum (Tm) and renal threshold are shown for glucose on a graph of plasma concentration at a GFR of 125 ml/min.
2. Changes:
• In dehydration a large proportion of the water in the filtrate is reabsorbed into the plasma to maintain homeostasis.
3. Distinctions:
• Reabsorption moves substances from tubular lumen to peritubular capillary plasma; secretion moves them from plasma into the tubular lumen.
• Tubular maximum is the maximum transport rate; renal threshold is the plasma concentration at which the substance begins to appear in the urine.

1. Brain waves:
• Origin: synchronised electrical pulses from masses of neurons communicating with each other; detected by scalp sensors with an EEG (electroencephalograph); speed is measured in Hertz.
• Gamma 40 to 100 Hz (highest): binding of senses, cognition, information processing, learning, perception, REM sleep.
• Beta 12 to 40 Hz (high, low amplitude): conscious focus, memory, problem solving; increased by caffeine and stimulants.
• Alpha 8 to 12 Hz (moderate): relaxation; bridges conscious and subconscious mind; alpha blocking occurs when stressed.
• Theta 4 to 8 Hz (slow): creativity, emotional connection, intuition, restorative sleep.
• Delta 0 to 4 Hz (slowest): deep restorative sleep, immune system, natural healing; commonest in infants and children, and less with age.
• All five appear during waking but one is dominant according to the state of consciousness.
2. Excess and deficiency:
• Gamma: too much gives anxiety, high arousal, stress; too little gives ADHD, depression, learning disabilities.
• Beta: too much gives anxiety, stress, inability to relax; too little gives ADHD, daydreaming, depression, poor cognition.
• Alpha: too much gives daydreaming and inability to focus; too little gives anxiety, high stress, insomnia, OCD.
• Theta: too much gives ADHD, depression, hyperactivity, impulsivity; too little gives anxiety, poor emotional awareness, stress.
• Delta: too much gives brain injuries, learning problems, inability to think, severe ADHD; too little gives inability to rejuvenate, poor sleep.
3. Wider effects:
• The ability to move flexibly through frequencies plays a large role in managing stress, focusing and sleeping well.
• Delta activity is involved in unconscious bodily functions such as regulating heart beat and digestion, so abnormal delta may affect body function and learning.
• No single band is better than the others; each serves a purpose.
questions.question:
Answer the following on brain waves and the EEG:
1. Describe brain waves under these headings: origin, detection by EEG, and the five bands (gamma, beta, alpha, theta, delta) with their frequency ranges and optimal functions.
2. State how excess and deficiency of each band relate to common disorders.
3. Explain why a disturbance of brain wave production may affect wider mental and bodily function.

questions.answerText:
1. Functions:
• Air passages: nasal cavity, pharynx, larynx, trachea, primary bronchi, secondary (lobar), tertiary (segmental) bronchi, bronchioles, terminal bronchioles (each bronchiole gives rise to 50 to 80), respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts and alveolar sacs; they filter, moisten, warm and conduct air; the conducting portion ends at the terminal bronchioles.
• Mucus from goblet cells and submucosal glands humidifies and filters air; ciliated epithelium (about 200 cilia per cell beating 10 to 20 times per second, upward in the lower tract and downward in the nose) moves trapped particles, forming the mucociliary escalator.
• Alveoli: about 300 million, area about 70 m2, each in a basket of capillaries; type I cells permit rapid diffusion and type II cells (5%) secrete surfactant that prevents collapse; the pulmonary circulation and alveoli together form the respiratory membrane.
• Muscles: diaphragm and external intercostals (inspiration); internal intercostals and abdominal muscles in forced expiration.
2. Disorders:
• Respiratory disorders are irregular or abnormal functioning, physiological or anatomical, resulting from genetics, allergies, lifestyle (smoking), air pollution and infections.
• Categories: airway disease, lung tissue disease and lung circulation disease; examples are asthma, COPD, emphysema, occupational disorders, sinusitis and lung cancer.
• Restrictive diseases (fibrosis, sarcoidosis) reduce volumes; obstructive diseases (emphysema, chronic bronchitis, asthma) increase residual volume; emphysema destroys alveolar walls.
• Drug groups: bronchodilators, antihistamines, antitussives, decongestants, expectorants, leukotriene modifiers, lung surfactants and mucolytics.
3. Distant effects:
• Impaired gas exchange reduces oxygen delivery to all tissues and reduces CO2 removal, changing blood pH.
• Pulmonary embolism dangerously impairs the ability to obtain oxygen; left heart failure backs blood into the lungs as pulmonary oedema.
• Smoking raises carbon monoxide occupancy of haemoglobin to as much as 10%.
questions.question:
Answer the following on the functions of the respiratory tract and lungs:
1. Describe the functions of the air passages, lungs and pulmonary circulation under these headings: pathway of air, mucus and cilia (mucociliary escalator), alveoli and surfactant, and the respiratory muscles.
2. State how the components relate to common respiratory disorders (airway, lung tissue and lung circulation disease) and the factors that cause them.
3. Explain why a respiratory disturbance may affect a distant organ or system.

questions.answerText:
1. Phototransduction:
• Each photoreceptor has an outer segment (stacked saccules with photochemical, modified cilium), inner segment (rich in mitochondria), nucleus and synaptic body.
• Rods contain rhodopsin (scotopsin plus 11-cis retinal), which decomposes when it absorbs light; cones contain colour pigments.
• Cascade: light forms metarhodopsin II, which activates transducin, which activates phosphodiesterase, which hydrolyses cGMP; cGMP separates from the Na+ channel, so the channels close and Na+ conductance into the outer segment falls; metarhodopsin II is inactivated by rhodopsin kinase.
• Receptor potential: more Na+ leaves than leaks in, so the inside becomes more negative (hyperpolarisation from about -40 mV in dark to -70/-80 mV in light), greater with more light energy.
• The pigment layer contains melanin, which prevents reflection of light, and stores vitamin A, a precursor of rhodopsin.
2. Basis of sensitivity changes:
• Nyctalopia (night blindness) is named in the rhodopsin-retinal visual cycle; the pigment layer stores vitamin A, a precursor of rhodopsin, and dark adaptation reforms rhodopsin from retinal, opsins and vitamin A.
• In dark adaptation retinal, opsins and vitamin A are converted back to rhodopsin (maximal in about 20 minutes; cones adapt first and rods later, more lastingly); in light adaptation much of the photochemical is reduced to retinal and opsins and retinal to vitamin A, lowering sensitivity.
• Sildenafil inhibits retinal phosphodiesterase and can cause blue-green colour blindness.
3. Rods versus cones:
• Rods: rhodopsin, vision at low light levels (scotopic), no colour vision, about 120 million; discs are separate from the plasma membrane.
• Cones: colour pigments (blue 445 nm, green 535 nm, red 570 nm), active at higher light levels (photopic), colour vision, about 6 million, concentrated in the fovea; membrane is continuous with the plasma membrane.
questions.question:
Answer the following on phototransduction in the retina:
1. Describe phototransduction under these headings: structure of rods and cones, rhodopsin and the visual cycle, the biochemical cascade, the receptor potential, and the differences between rods and cones.
2. Explain the physiological basis of night blindness and of retinal sensitivity changes in light and dark.
3. Distinguish between rods and cones.

Answer the following on the functions of the kidney:
1. Describe the functions of the kidney under these headings: excretion, regulation of fluid, ions and acid-base balance, hormones synthesised or degraded, and the roles of the parts of the nephron.
2. State how the regulatory components of the nephron and the kidney's hormonal roles relate to common pathologies of excess and deficiency.
3. Explain why kidney disturbance may affect a distant organ or system and cause a functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
1. Functions of the kidney:
• The renal system produces, transports and stores urine (kidneys, ureters, bladder, urethra and their muscles).
• Regulates osmolality of body fluids by excreting dilute or concentrated urine; regulates plasma Na+, K+, Ca2+, Mg2+, Cl-, bicarbonate, phosphate and sulphate; regulates extracellular fluid volume by controlling Na+ and water excretion; helps regulate arterial pressure by adjusting Na+ excretion and producing renin.
• Acid-base balance: excretes H+ when there is excess acid or HCO3- when there is excess base; synthesises ammonia.
• Eliminates urea, uric acid (purine metabolism) and creatinine (muscle metabolism), and excretes drugs and toxic compounds.
• Hormones: major production sites of erythropoietin and 1,25-dihydroxy vitamin D3; degrades insulin, glucagon and parathyroid hormone; synthesises prostaglandins, thromboxane A2 and kallikrein (which leads to kinins).
• Nephron: glomerulus filters protein-free plasma into Bowman's capsule; proximal tubule does uncontrolled reabsorption and secretion; loop of Henle sets the medullary osmotic gradient; distal tubule and collecting duct do variable, controlled reabsorption of Na+ and water and secretion of K+ and H+; the juxtaglomerular apparatus produces substances that control kidney function.
2. Pathologies:
• Plasma urea nitrogen and creatinine are measures of kidney function, and GFR is an index of the kidneys' functionality (normal 125 ml/min).
• Hypercalcaemia occurs, for example, in renal failure; alkaline phosphatase is raised in kidney disorders.
3. Distant effects:
• Erythropoietin is made mainly by the kidneys and stimulates red cell production, so kidney function links to blood.
• The kidneys convert vitamin D into its active form, allowing calcium absorption in the small intestine.
• Kidney control of Na+, water and renin affects arterial blood pressure and extracellular fluid volume; acid-base regulation depends on kidney excretion of H+ and addition of HCO3- to the ECF.

1. Volumes and capacities:
• Spirometry measures air volumes and capacities; a volume is one phase of the respiratory cycle and a capacity is the sum of two or more volumes.
• Tidal volume about 500 ml; inspiratory reserve volume about 3000 ml; expiratory reserve volume about 1100 ml; residual volume about 1200 ml.
• Inspiratory capacity = TV + IRV = 3500 ml; vital capacity = TV + IRV + ERV = 4600 ml; functional residual capacity = RV + ERV = 2300 ml; total lung capacity = RV + ERV + TV + IRV = 5800 ml.
• Pulmonary ventilation = respiratory rate x tidal volume = 12 x 500 = 6000 ml/min; alveolar ventilation = (tidal volume - dead space) x respiratory rate = (500 - 150) x 12 per minute.
• All volumes and capacities are about 20 to 25% less in women than in men and greater in athletic persons than in small asthenic persons.
2. Disease patterns:
• Restrictive disease makes it harder to get air in: decreased VC, TLC, RV and FRC; examples are fibrosis, sarcoidosis, muscular diseases and chest wall deformities.
• Obstructive disease makes it harder to get air out: decreased VC but increased TLC, RV and FRC; examples are emphysema, chronic bronchitis and asthma.
3. Distinctions:
• Anatomical dead space is the volume of all passageways from the nose to the terminal bronchiole; physiological dead space adds non-functioning and poorly perfused alveoli, and in normal lungs the two are equal.
• Pulmonary ventilation is the total air moved per minute; alveolar ventilation is the air reaching the gas exchange areas per minute, that is with the dead space subtracted.
questions.question:
Answer the following on lung volumes and capacities:
1. Describe lung volumes and capacities under these headings: spirometry, the four volumes, the four capacities, minute and alveolar ventilation, and dead space.
2. Explain how restrictive and obstructive lung diseases alter the volumes and capacities.
3. Distinguish between anatomical and physiological dead space, and between pulmonary ventilation and alveolar ventilation.

Answer the following on the cardiac cycle:
1. Describe the cardiac cycle under these headings: definition of systole and diastole, phases, pressure and volume changes, and heart sounds.
2. Explain why ventricular filling remains possible when atrial contraction is lost (for example in atrial fibrillation) and how valve disease alters the pumping of the heart.
3. Distinguish between the first and second heart sounds, and between isovolumetric contraction and isovolumetric relaxation.
questions.answerText:
1. Cardiac cycle:
• Definition: the repeating pattern of contraction (systole) and relaxation (diastole); both atria contract almost simultaneously and both ventricles about 0.1 to 0.2 second later; diastolic systemic arterial pressure is about 80 mmHg.
• Isovolumetric contraction: ventricular pressure rises, the AV valves snap shut, and the ventricles neither fill nor eject.
• Ejection: when ventricular pressure exceeds aortic (about 120 mmHg) and pulmonary artery (about 25 mmHg) pressure the semilunar valves open; afterwards the semilunar valves close and arterial pressures fall to about 80 and 8 mmHg while ventricular pressure falls to about 0 mmHg; the dicrotic notch is a brief rise in aortic pressure from backflow.
• Isovolumetric relaxation: all valves are closed while ventricular pressure falls below atrial pressure.
• Rapid filling: the AV valves open when ventricular pressure falls below atrial pressure.
• Atrial contraction: empties the final blood into the ventricles.
• Volumes: about 80 ml at end of systole, about 130 ml after passive filling, active atrial filling adds about 25% (to 150 ml), and about 70 ml is ejected.
• Heart sounds: closing of valves gives "lub-dub".
2. Basis of disturbance:
• Passive filling dominates, which explains why filling is still possible in atrial fibrillation.
• Valve disease: regurgitation is leakage because the valve does not close completely (blood flows back into the atria or ventricles); stenosis is narrowing or stiffening that suppresses flow, so the heart pumps with increased force; mitral valve prolapse is also listed.
3. Distinctions:
• First sound ("lub"): closure of the AV valves during isovolumetric contraction at the start of systole; second sound ("dub"): closure of the semilunar valves when ventricular pressure falls below arterial pressure at the start of diastole.
• Isovolumetric contraction: pressure rises, AV valves shut, semilunar valves not yet open; isovolumetric relaxation: pressure falls, both valve sets closed.

1. Functions:
• The thalamus is a sensory way-station for the rest of the brain and is important through its connections with other limbic structures.
• All general and special senses have an obligate relay in the thalamus; the only exception is olfaction.
• The ventrobasal complex has the ventral posterolateral nucleus (medial lemniscal fibres), ventral posteromedial nucleus (trigeminal fibres) and posterior thalamic nuclei (anterolateral system); third-order fibres go to the somatosensory cortex; intralaminar nuclei receive relays from the reticular nuclei.
• Role in somatic sensation: relays tactile information to the cortex, works with the brainstem in the discrimination of pain and temperature, and receives regulatory corticofugal fibres (mainly inhibitory) from the cortex.
2. Pathologies:
• Thalamic syndrome: blockage by thrombosis of the posterior cerebral artery supplying the posteroventral thalamus, and the nucleus degenerates.
• Effects: loss of pain sensation from the opposite side of the body, ataxia, a higher threshold for sensory perception after some weeks, extreme unpleasantness or pleasantness of many affective sensations, and enhanced sensitivity to pain.
• Secondary hyperalgesia arises from facilitation of sensory transmission due to a lesion in the spinal cord or thalamus.
3. Distant effects:
• Because sensory pathways cross, thalamic damage causes loss of pain on the opposite side of the body.
• The deficit also includes ataxia, which is an inability to control body movements precisely.
questions.question:
Answer the following on the functions of the thalamus:
1. Describe the functions of the thalamus under these headings: relay of sensation, nuclei and their inputs, projection to the cortex, role in pain and temperature, and corticofugal regulation.
2. State how its components relate to common pathologies (the thalamic syndrome and related excess and deficiency).
3. Explain why a thalamic disturbance may affect a distant part of the body and cause a functional deficit.

Answer the following on the white blood cells:
