• Memory: essential for the formation of new memories about past experiences and for retrieval; it underlies declarative (explicit) memory of facts and events, which depends on the medial temporal lobe and the hippocampal-entorhinal relationship; implicit memory is the learning of skills and conditioned and emotional responses; it plays a critical role in short-term memory, which is necessary to establish long-term patterns.
• Spatial function: understanding spatial relations, with the dentate gyrus and dorsal hippocampus generating new adult-born granule cells that support pattern separation, and the left hippocampus involved in recall of spatial memories.
• It helps control corticosteroid production.
2. Pathologies:
• Damage usually causes profound difficulty forming new memories (anterograde amnesia) and may affect access to earlier memories (retrograde amnesia), usually extending some years before the damage.
• Alzheimer's disease is a progressive degenerative disease, mostly in the elderly, with memory loss, irritability, confusion and ultimately hallucinations and death.
3. Distant effects:
• Lesions do not affect old established memories, which involve association areas in the frontal lobe and the parieto-temporo-occipital cortex; the hippocampus becomes less important in storage over time.
• The hippocampus sends output to the hypothalamus through the fornix.

questions.question:
Answer the following on the cerebrospinal fluid, meninges and blood-brain barrier:
1. Describe the functions of the meninges, cerebrospinal fluid (formation, circulation, functions) and blood-brain barrier (structure, functions).
2. State how the components relate to common pathologies of excess and deficiency and the causes of CNS disorders.
3. Explain why a disturbance of these protective systems may affect distant parts of the nervous system and cause a functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
1. Functions:
• Meninges: three layers from outside inward, the dura mater (thick, lines the skull), the arachnoid mater (thin, web-like; the subdural space lies between them) and the pia mater (follows the folds; the subarachnoid space lies between arachnoid and pia).
• CSF: clear colourless fluid produced by ependymal cells in the choroid plexuses and absorbed in the arachnoid granulations; volume about 150 ml, production about 550 ml/day, turnover about 3.7 times per day.
• Formation: plasma is passively filtered across the choroidal capillary endothelium, then water and ions are secreted across the choroidal epithelium (HCO3-, Cl- and K+ through apical channels, with aquaporins for water); CSF is nearly protein-free.
• Circulation: lateral ventricles, interventricular foramina, third ventricle, cerebral aqueduct, fourth ventricle, then the subarachnoid space through the median and lateral apertures and the central canal of the cord.
• Functions: buoyancy (brain of about 1500 g behaves as 25 to 50 g), protection as a shock absorber, prevention of ischaemia (reducing CSF lowers intracranial pressure and aids perfusion), homeostasis and removal of waste.
• Blood-brain barrier: a selective semipermeable border formed by tight junctions between brain capillary endothelial cells and choroid epithelial cells, with astrocyte end-feet and pericytes; it keeps out pathogens, limits large or hydrophilic molecules, allows hydrophobic molecules (O2, CO2, hormones) and small polar molecules, and actively transports glucose.
2. Pathologies:
• Clinical significance: hydrocephalus, lumbar puncture, anaesthesia and chemotherapy, kernicterus and drug administration.
• Causes of CNS disorders: trauma, infections (cryptococcal meningitis, malaria, leprosy, viruses), degeneration (Parkinson's disease), structural defects (anencephaly), tumours, autoimmune disorders (acute disseminated encephalomyelitis attacks myelin) and stroke.
• Cerebral oedema (swelling from the inflammatory response) may compress and kill brain tissue.
3. Distant effects:
• Metabolic waste diffuses into CSF and is removed into the blood as CSF is absorbed, so failure of drainage affects the whole brain.
• Stroke from interrupted blood supply kills tissue in the affected area, giving loss of function.

1. Synaptic transmission:
• A synapse is the junction where an axon terminal contacts another neuron or cell; the sending neuron is presynaptic and the receiving neuron postsynaptic; types are electrical, chemical and conjoint; by connectivity they are axodendritic, axosomatic or axoaxonic.
• Chemical synapse: cleft 20 to 50 nm wide; presynaptic button with synaptic vesicles (about 50 nm) and dense core vesicles (about 100 nm); active zones release transmitter and the postsynaptic density holds receptors.
• Requirements: synthesis and packing of neurotransmitter into vesicles, vesicle release in response to an action potential, an electrical or biochemical response in the postsynaptic neuron, removal of transmitter from the cleft, and all done very rapidly.
• Events: action potential enters the terminal, voltage-gated Ca2+ channels open, Ca2+ activates proteins so vesicles fuse and release transmitter by exocytosis, the transmitter binds the postsynaptic receptor, whose inner ionophore has an ion channel component (cation channels excite, anion channels inhibit) and a G-protein second messenger component (opens ion channels or activates enzymes that make second messengers).
• Fate: cleared by diffusion, enzymatic degradation, presynaptic reuptake then degradation or recycling, uptake by glia, or uptake by the postsynaptic neuron with desensitisation.
• Transmitters include acetylcholine, serotonin, GABA, dopamine, norepinephrine, endorphins and glutamate.
2. Clinical basis:
• Understanding synaptic transmission is necessary for the actions of psychoactive drugs, the causes of mental disorders and the neural basis of learning and memory; transmitters must be cleared to permit another round of transmission.
• Alzheimer's disease shows deterioration of memory, reasoning and language with low acetylcholine and loss of ACh neurons.
• Too much dopamine is involved in schizophrenia, cocaine and nicotine mimic dopamine, and loss of dopamine neurons in the substantia nigra causes Parkinson's disease.
3. Electrical versus chemical synapses:
• Electrical: direct transfer of ionic current through gap junctions, bidirectional, cells electronically coupled, very fast, common in non-neuronal cells and important in development.
• Chemical: transmitter released across a cleft, with receptors that convert the signal into a chemical or membrane potential change.
questions.question:
Answer the following on synaptic transmission:
1. Describe synaptic transmission under these headings: types of synapse, parts of a chemical synapse, requirements, sequence of events, the receptor components and the fate of neurotransmitters.
2. Explain the clinical basis of disturbances of synaptic transmission: why neurotransmitter imbalance is important in certain diseases and drugs.
3. Distinguish between electrical and chemical synapses.

Answer the following on the diffusion of oxygen and carbon dioxide (mechanism of gaseous exchange):
1. Describe gas exchange between the alveoli and the pulmonary capillaries under these headings: composition of inspired, alveolar and expired air, the respiratory membrane, Fick's law and the factors governing diffusing capacity, and normal diffusing capacities.
2. Explain why gas exchange is impaired in certain states (emphysema, oedema, fibrosis, removal of a lung) and how diffusing capacity increases in exercise.
3. Distinguish between alveolar air and inspired air, and between alveolar air and expired air.
questions.answerText:
1. Gas exchange:
• Air compositions: alveolar air is partially replaced by atmospheric air at each breath, oxygen constantly diffuses into the capillaries, carbon dioxide diffuses from the blood into alveolar air, and dry inspired air is humidified in the passages.
• Respiratory membrane: a fluid layer with surfactant, alveolar epithelium, epithelial basement membrane, thin interstitial space, capillary basement membrane and capillary endothelium; thickness averages about 0.6 micrometre and is as little as 0.2 micrometre in places.
• Fick's law: diffusing capacity is proportional to pressure gradient x surface area / thickness; solubility and molecular weight give the diffusion coefficient (proportional to S/square root of MW); diffusing capacity is the volume of gas that diffuses each minute for a 1 mmHg pressure difference.
• Values: for oxygen 21 ml/min/mmHg at rest, rising to about 65 (three times); for CO2 about 400 to 450 at rest, rising to about 1200 to 1300 in exercise.
• Alveoli: about 300 million alveoli of 0.3 to 0.5 mm diameter with total area about 70 square metres, each in a basket of pulmonary capillaries; type I cells allow rapid diffusion and type II cells secrete surfactant.
2. Impaired exchange and exercise:
• Removing a lung halves the surface area; in emphysema alveolar walls dissolve and area falls up to fivefold, and with a fall to one third or one quarter of normal exchange is impeded even at rest.
• Oedema and fibrosis increase membrane thickness; a thickness of two to three times normal interferes significantly with exchange.
• Exercise raises diffusing capacity by opening previously dormant capillaries or dilating open ones, increasing surface area, and by a better ventilation-perfusion ratio.
3. Distinctions:
• Alveolar versus inspired air: partial replacement per breath, continual O2 uptake, CO2 addition and humidification.
• Alveolar versus expired air: dead space air mixes with alveolar air, so expired air has higher oxygen tension and lower carbon dioxide tension than alveolar air.

questions.question:
Answer the following on the functions of the hypothalamus:
1. Describe the functions of the hypothalamus under these headings: connections and inputs, autonomic, endocrine and behavioural functions, internal sensors, and the roles of its regions (satiety and feeding areas, preoptic area, suprachiasmatic nucleus).
2. Explain why a disturbance of the hypothalamus may affect a distant organ or system.
questions.answerText:
1. Functions:
• The hypothalamus is the primary output node of the limbic system; it is connected with the frontal lobes, septal nuclei and brain stem reticular formation through the medial forebrain bundle and receives input from the hippocampus via the fornix and from the amygdala via the ventral amygdalofugal pathway and stria terminalis.
• It has centres for sexual, endocrine, behavioural and autonomic functions; autonomic functions are controlled through projections to the brain stem.
• Inputs: from most of the body, olfaction, the viscera and the retina; internal sensors for temperature, osmolarity, glucose and sodium; receptors for steroid hormones and for appetite signals such as leptin and orexin.
• Regions: the ventromedial nucleus is a satiety area and the lateral hypothalamic area a feeding centre; the preoptic area (greatest sexual dimorphism) with the septal nuclei projects gonadotropin releasing hormone to the median eminence; the suprachiasmatic nucleus receives direct retinal input and entrains circadian rhythms.
• The lateral hypothalamus releases orexin, which activates the arousal system; the posterior tuberomammillary hypothalamus is the source of histamine projections.
2. Distant effects:
• It controls temperature and osmolarity regulation, endocrine functions and appetite, and produces sexual responses that combine autonomic, endocrine and behavioural elements.
• Through the brain stem it influences autonomic organs, and through the median eminence it influences the gonads.
• The hypothalamus is one of the last areas of the brain to develop.

questions.question:
Answer the following on the conducting system of the heart and the electrocardiogram:
1. Describe the conducting system as a control pathway: initiator (pacemaker), conduction route through the SA node, AV node, bundle of His, bundle branches and Purkinje fibres, and how ECG leads record it.
2. State the normal ECG values (durations and amplitudes of waves, intervals and segments), the factors that alter them and the compensatory role of the Purkinje fibres.
3. Explain the physiological basis of the ECG changes when the pathway fails or is damaged.
questions.answerText:
1. Conducting system:
• The system consists of special conducting cells and fibres (not nervous tissue) that self-excite, conduct rapidly and coordinate the chambers; both atria contract together and first, then both ventricles.
• SA node: primary impulse initiator and physiological pacemaker; generates about 75 impulses per minute.
• AV node: secondary pacemaker and conduit; the atria are separated from the ventricles by a cartilaginous septum that cannot conduct, so the AV node is the only pathway; it delays the impulse about 0.1 second.
• Bundle of His: the initial segment penetrating the fibrous trigone into the interventricular septum; it allows only forward movement of action potentials and bifurcates into right and left bundle branches.
• Purkinje fibres: subendocardial branches extending to the apex and then up the ventricular walls; they have many more gap junctions than AV nodal cells, giving almost instantaneous transmission to the ventricle.
• ECG: electrodes on the skin record current spreading from the heart; there are bipolar leads (I, II, III), unipolar limb leads (aVR, aVL, aVF) and chest leads V1 to V6, twelve in all.
2. Normal values and modifiers:
• P wave (atrial depolarisation) 0.1 s, 0.1 to 0.12 mV; QRS (ventricular depolarisation) 0.08 to 0.10 s; T wave (ventricular repolarisation) 0.2 s, 0.3 mV; PR interval 0.12 to 0.2 s; ST segment 0.08 s; RR interval 0.8 s (one cardiac cycle, used for heart rate).
• Compensation: the rapid Purkinje conduction compensates for the delay at the AV node and lets the ventricles contract shortly after the atria.
• Ion levels and other factors that change the trace include potassium (hyperkalemia, hypokalemia), calcium and thyrotoxicosis.
3. Basis of ECG changes in failure:
• P wave: taller and wider in atrial enlargement; absent in hyperkalemia, atrial fibrillation or sinoatrial block.
• PR interval: prolonged in bradycardia and first degree heart block; shortened in tachycardia.
• QRS: prolonged in bundle branch block and hyperkalemia.
• ST segment: elevated in myocardial infarction, left bundle branch block, acute pericarditis; depressed in acute myocardial ischaemia, posterior infarction, ventricular hypertrophy, hypokalemia.
• T wave: tall and broad-based in acute ischaemia; flat or inverted in myocardial infarction, ventricular hypertrophy, pericarditis; U wave prominent in hypokalemia.

questions.question:
Answer the following on the functions of the autonomic nervous system:
1. Describe the functions of the autonomic nervous system under these headings: position in the nervous system, sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions, their opposing actions and the neurotransmitters.
2. State how the regulatory divisions relate to common disturbances of excess and deficiency.
3. Explain why a disturbance of autonomic function may affect a distant organ and cause a functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
1. Functions:
• The autonomic nervous system is the involuntary branch of the efferent peripheral system, consisting of motor nerves only, with sympathetic, parasympathetic (and enteric) divisions; somatic fibres supply skeletal muscle (voluntary) using acetylcholine.
• Sympathetic: the "fight-or-flight" system, responding to unusual stimuli and increasing activity (the "E" division: exercise, excitement, emergency, embarrassment); it controls internal organs in high-stress activity and increases heart rate.
• Parasympathetic: "housekeeping"; conserves energy and maintains daily functions (the "D" division: digestion, defecation, diuresis); it decreases heart rate and controls organs during normal activity.
• The two divisions have opposite effects on the same organs.
• Transmitters: norepinephrine from sympathetic endings and epinephrine from the adrenal medulla; acetylcholine from parasympathetic endings.
2. Disturbances:
• If the vagus nerve were cut the heart would lose its tone and heart rate would rise by about 25 beats per minute.
• High vagal activity produces the resting bradycardia of trained athletes.
3. Distant effects:
• Sympathetic stimulation causes vasoconstriction, which raises blood pressure and reduces flow in the constricted region.
• Sympathetic and parasympathetic action on the SA node changes heart rate and cardiac output.
• Autonomic centres in the hypothalamus and medulla link emotion and organ function.

1. Auditory pathway:
• Ear structure: the external ear (pinna, meatus, tympanic membrane) gathers sound; the middle ear (auditory tube, ossicles, oval and round windows, tensor tympani and stapedius) transmits it; the cochlea has three coiled tubes, scala vestibuli, scala media and scala tympani, with Reissner's membrane between the first two and the basilar membrane, carrying the organ of Corti, between the last two.
• Receptors: one row of inner hair cells and 3 to 4 rows of outer hair cells, on the basilar membrane and embedded in the tectorial membrane; when the basilar membrane vibrates the cilia bend, mechanically gated cation channels open and K+ and Ca2+ enter, depolarising the cell (resting potential about -60 mV), voltage-gated Ca2+ channels open, transmitter is released and the cochlear nerve endings fire; bending towards the scala tympani hyperpolarises.
• Pathway: first-order neurons synapse, second-order neurons cross, then the lateral lemniscus, another synapse and the auditory radiation; collateral fibres run to the reticular activating system and the vermis of the cerebellum.
2. Coding and protection:
• Loudness is coded by amplitude, frequency of firing and recruitment of new hair cells; pitch by frequency.
• The tensor tympani and stapedius protect against loud noise and mask low-frequency sounds in loud environments.
• Direction of sound is determined by the time lag between the ears and by the difference in intensity between the ears.
3. Deafness:
• Conduction deafness: impaired sound transmission in the external or middle ear, from a wax plug, foreign bodies, destruction of ossicles or a thickened eardrum.
• Nerve deafness: damage to the hair cells or neural pathways, from aminoglycoside antibiotics, loud noise, a tumour of cranial nerve VIII or vascular damage in the medulla.
questions.question:
Answer the following on hearing and the auditory pathway:
1. Describe the auditory system as a control pathway: conduction of sound through the external, middle and inner ear, the receptor (hair cells), the afferent pathway to the cortex and the collateral connections.
2. State how loudness and pitch are coded, the protective mechanism against loud sound and how direction is determined.
3. Explain the physiological basis of the signs of conduction deafness and nerve deafness.

questions.answerText:
1. Functions:
• Liver: metabolic regulation (stores absorbed nutrients and vitamins and releases them as needed), haematological regulation (plasma protein production and removal of old RBCs), bile production, detoxification of toxins and heparin formation.
• Bile: secreted by liver cells at a constant rate of about 40 ml per hour; required for fat digestion and absorption; between meals the sphincter of Oddi is closed and bile is stored and concentrated in the gallbladder, then delivered to the duodenum.
• Gallbladder: a pear-shaped sac under the liver (fundus, body, neck) with capacity of 30 to 50 ml; it concentrates bile by absorbing water, stores bile, selectively absorbs bile salts, keeps the bile acid, excretes cholesterol and secretes mucus; the neck continues as the cystic duct, which joins the common hepatic duct to form the bile duct.
• The biliary system consists of the liver, gallbladder and bile ducts.
2. Pathologies:
• Most clotting factors are plasma proteins synthesised by the liver; when the liver cannot make its usual procoagulants abnormal and often severe bleeding occurs.
• Causes range from an easily resolved vitamin K deficiency (common in newborns and after systemic antibiotics) to near-total loss of liver function as in hepatitis or cirrhosis.
• Vitamin K is fat-soluble and absorbed with fats; in liver disease the failing cells make neither procoagulants nor the bile needed for fat and vitamin K absorption.
• Bilirubin and enzymes such as aspartate transaminase and alkaline phosphatase are markers of liver damage; excess bilirubin from red cell breakdown is taken up by the liver and secreted in bile.
3. Distant effects:
• Liver failure shows as bleeding because clotting factors are synthesised in the liver.
• Impaired bile flow causes vitamin K deficiency, and bacteria in the large intestine, which normally produce vitamin K, cannot compensate if fat absorption is impaired.
• Liver cirrhosis is listed as a cause of blood disorders, and the liver's failure to make plasma proteins and remove old RBCs affects the blood.
questions.question:
Answer the following on the liver and biliary system:
1. Describe the functions of the liver, bile and gallbladder under these headings: metabolic and haematological functions, synthesis and secretion of bile, storage and concentration of bile, and delivery to the duodenum.
2. State how liver and biliary function relate to pathologies of deficiency, especially of clotting and fat absorption.
3. Explain why liver disturbance may affect distant organs and cause a functional deficit.

Answer the following on venous return and the control of blood pressure:
1. Describe the system that returns blood to the heart and regulates blood pressure: determinants of venous return, the structures and forces that aid it, and the vascular and neural effectors of blood pressure.
2. State the normal values (venous pressures, blood storage, cardiac output) and the factors that raise or lower venous return and blood pressure.
3. Explain the physiological basis of the signs and symptoms when the pathway fails.
questions.answerText:
1. Venous return and pressure control:
• Venous return is determined by total blood volume and venous pressure; veins are more compliant than arteries and act as capacitance vessels.
• Aids: sympathetic activity contracts venous smooth muscle and reduces compliance; the skeletal muscle pump squeezes veins; the thoracic-abdominal pressure difference promotes flow; one-way valves prevent backflow, and blood also relies on gravity and inertia.
• Blood pressure controls: hormones and autonomic signals alter heart rate and contraction strength; sympathetic vasoconstriction narrows arteries and raises pressure while vasodilation widens them; blood volume and viscosity also affect pressure.
• Flow relation: flow = pressure difference/resistance; precapillary sphincters and metarterioles regulate capillary flow.
2. Values and modifiers:
• Veins store about 70% of blood volume; pressure is about 10 mmHg at the venules and about 0 mmHg at the vena cava-right atrium junction; mean venous pressure is about 2 mmHg; cardiac output at rest is about 5 L/min (4 to 6).
• Raise return: sympathetic venoconstriction, muscle pump, higher blood volume, exercise; lower: blood loss.
• Raise pressure: greater contractile force and heart rate, vasoconstriction, higher blood volume, thicker viscous blood.
• Lower pressure: vasodilation after the fight-or-flight response or under hormones and chemicals.
3. Failure:
• Blood loss and extremely rapid heartbeat decrease stroke volume.
• Right-sided heart failure causes peripheral oedema and left-sided failure pulmonary oedema.

1. Gustatory pathway:
• Taste buds lie in papillae of the tongue (fungiform, foliate, circumvallate) and in the epiglottis, palate and pharynx; a bud (50 to 100 cells) contains basal, sustentacular and gustatory receptor cells around a taste pore; each is innervated by about 50 nerve fibres.
• Modalities: salty (Na+ through ENaC, blocked by amiloride, releasing glutamate), sour (H+ through ENaC and HCN channels), umami (glutamate on metabotropic mGluR4), bitter (T2R G-protein-coupled receptors and gustducin) and sweet (T1R3 receptors coupled to gustducin).
• First-order neurons: anterior two-thirds through the chorda tympani of the facial nerve, posterior one-third through the glossopharyngeal nerve, other parts through the vagus nerve; fibres pass to the nucleus of the solitary tract, then to the thalamus, then to the gustatory cortex at the foot of the postcentral gyrus and the insula; taste reflex fibres run to the salivatory nuclei.
2. Modifiers:
• Receptor potentials rise with tastant concentration; the response adapts to a lower level within seconds and the tastant is washed away by saliva; smell and food texture contribute to flavour.
• Aging and tobacco abuse diminish taste, and drugs (cisplatin, penicillamine, captopril, vitamin B3) and zinc deficiency can cause ageusia.
3. Abnormalities:
• Ageusia (absence), hypogeusia (diminished) and dysgeusia or parageusia (disturbed).
• Damage to the lingual or glossopharyngeal nerve causes ageusia and hypogeusia; neurological disorders (vestibular schwannoma, Bell palsy, familial dysautonomia, multiple sclerosis, some infections) also impair taste.
questions.question:
Answer the following on taste (gustation):
1. Describe the gustatory pathway as a control system: taste buds and receptor cells, transduction for each taste modality, first-order nerves, brainstem relay, thalamus and cortex.
2. State the normal features (numbers of buds and fibres, adaptation) and the factors that alter taste sensitivity.
3. Explain the physiological basis of the taste abnormalities.

Answer the following on the functions of the amygdala:
1. Describe the functions of the amygdala under these headings: location, connections, inputs and outputs, and coordination of behavioural, autonomic and endocrine responses.
2. State how amygdala activity relates to common pathologies of excess and deficiency (effects of lesions and stimulation).
3. Explain why a disturbance of the amygdala may affect distant organs and cause a functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
1. Functions:
• Location: in the anterior temporal lobe within the uncus.
• Connections: reciprocal connections with the thalamus, hypothalamus, septal nuclei, orbital frontal cortex, cingulate gyrus, hippocampus, parahippocampal gyrus and brain stem; the olfactory bulb is the only area that inputs to the amygdala without receiving reciprocal projections.
• Function: a critical centre for coordinating behavioural, autonomic and endocrine responses to environmental stimuli, especially those with emotional content; it coordinates responses to stress and integrates reactions involved in survival, particularly to stress and anxiety; it responds mostly to fear and anxiety.
• Olfaction: the smell pathway to the amygdala is involved in emotional responses to odours.
2. Pathologies:
• Lesions of the amygdala reduce responses to stress, particularly conditioned emotional responses.
• Stimulation produces behavioural arousal and can produce directed rage reactions.
3. Distant effects:
• Because it coordinates autonomic and endocrine responses, its disturbance alters stress responses in organs throughout the body.
• Its link to the hypothalamus (via the stria terminalis and ventral amygdalofugal pathway) carries its output to autonomic and endocrine centres.

questions.question:
Answer the following on the cardiac action potential and automaticity:
1. Describe the electrical activity of heart muscle under these headings: resting membrane potential, phases and ionic basis of the ventricular action potential, pacemaker potential and automaticity, refractory period, and excitation-contraction.
2. Explain why the long action potential and refractory period protect the heart, and why disturbed ion concentrations (for example hyperkalemia) disturb cardiac function.
3. Distinguish between autorhythmic (pacemaker) cells and contractile cells, and between the SA node and the AV node as pacemakers.
questions.answerText:
1. Cardiac electrical activity:
• Resting membrane potential is about -90 mV; there is rapid depolarisation to about +20 mV, partial repolarisation, a slow repolarisation (plateau) and then rapid repolarisation.
• Ionic basis: depolarisation opens sodium channels and the inward sodium current causes further depolarisation; calcium channels open more slowly and keep the membrane depolarised, maintaining the plateau; outward potassium flow is initially reduced and then increases, repolarising the membrane.
• Automaticity: action potentials arise spontaneously within the cells (myogenic); instead of a constant resting potential there is a steady depolarising (pacemaker) potential, and the rhythm is driven by the fastest pacemaker cells, normally the SA node; autorhythmic cells use calcium influx rather than sodium for the rising phase.
• Refractory period: cardiac cells are absolutely refractory for the whole action potential; a second action potential cannot be generated for up to 350 ms (absolute refractory period about 250 ms).
• Contraction: achieved through the release of calcium; cardiac muscle is striated, branched and rich in mitochondria, joined by intercalated discs that allow free passage of ions, so it behaves as a functional syncytium and contracts as a unit.
2. Protection and vulnerability:
• The prolonged action potential protects against pump failure caused by sustained contraction and sets the upper rate of contraction at 3 to 4 beats per second.
• Intra- and extracellular ion concentrations must be maintained for normal heart function; on the ECG hyperkalemia gives an absent P wave and a prolonged QRS, and hypokalemia gives a prominent U wave.
• Acidosis and increased extracellular K+ reduce contractility.
3. Distinctions:
• Autorhythmic cells initiate action potentials with unstable pacemaker potentials, whereas contractile cells have a stable resting potential of about -90 mV and produce the plateau action potential that drives contraction.
• The SA node is the primary pacemaker and physiological pacemaker; the AV node is the secondary pacemaker and normally acts as a conduit and delays the impulse about 0.1 second.

questions.question:
Answer the following on the transport of oxygen in the blood:
1. Describe oxygen transport under these headings: forms of transport, haemoglobin binding, amount released at the tissues (utilization coefficient), the oxygen-haemoglobin dissociation curve and the factors that shift it.
2. Explain why carbon monoxide poisoning is so dangerous and how tissues with higher metabolic needs obtain more oxygen.
3. Distinguish between oxyhaemoglobin and deoxyhaemoglobin, and between oxyhaemoglobin and carboxyhaemoglobin.
questions.answerText:
1. Oxygen transport:
• Forms: dissolved in plasma 0.3 ml/100 ml (1.5%) and combined with haemoglobin 19.4 ml/100 ml (98.5%); 100 ml of blood at full saturation carries 19.7 ml of oxygen.
• Haemoglobin: four globin chains each with one haem; each haem binds one O2 at its ferrous ion, so one Hb carries up to four O2, loosely and reversibly.
• Release: arterial blood (PO2 95 mmHg, 97% saturated) holds about 19.4 ml/100 ml and falls to 14.4 ml (PO2 40 mmHg, 75% saturated) in the tissues, so about 5 ml is delivered per 100 ml; this 22% is the utilization coefficient; the remainder is a venous reserve that can sustain life for 4 to 5 minutes; in strenuous exercise the coefficient rises to 75 to 80%.
• Dissociation curve: at low PO2 it rises slowly, then rapidly, then levels off near 100% saturation; binding of the first O2 changes Hb shape and raises affinity for the next; high PO2 in pulmonary capillaries loads O2 and low PO2 in tissue capillaries unloads it.
• Shifts to the right (promoting unloading): low ambient PO2 in active tissues, raised temperature, 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate (BPG, raised by fever or exercise) and raised PCO2 with lowered pH (Bohr effect).
2. Basis of vulnerability:
• Carbon monoxide binds the ferrous ion of haemoglobin to form carboxyhaemoglobin, competes with oxygen for the same site and binds 210 times as tightly, tying up haemoglobin for a long time.
• Less than 1.5% of Hb is occupied by CO in most nonsmokers, up to 3% in residents of polluted cities and up to 10% in heavy smokers; 0.1% CO in air binds 50% of Hb and 0.2% is quickly lethal.
• Active tissues consume O2 rapidly, keeping tissue PO2 low, warmer and more acidic, so the curve shifts right and utilization may reach 80% in exercising muscle.
3. Distinctions:
• Oxyhaemoglobin (HbO2) is Hb bound to O2; deoxyhaemoglobin (HHb) has no oxygen bound.
• Oxyhaemoglobin binds oxygen reversibly and loosely; carboxyhaemoglobin (HbCO) is formed by CO, which competes for the same site with 210 times the affinity.

questions.question:
Answer the following on refraction and accommodation in the eye:
1. Describe the optical system of the eye under these headings: structures and their refractive roles, the mechanism of accommodation for near and far vision, and the nerve supply.
2. Explain why refractive errors and loss of accommodation are commoner in certain states (ageing, eyeball length, corneal or lens shape).
3. Distinguish between myopia and hyperopia, and between accommodation for near and for distant objects.
questions.answerText:
1. Refraction and accommodation:
• Cornea: anterior modification of the sclera, refractive index 1.38, provides most of the refractive power; lens: transparent elastic capsule, refractive index 1.4, held by suspensory ligaments attached to the ciliary body; aqueous humour (1.33) nourishes the cornea and lens and vitreous humour (1.34) lies behind; the iris has circular fibres that constrict and radial fibres that dilate the pupil.
• Near vision: the ciliary muscle contracts, the suspensory ligaments relax, the lens becomes more spherical and refractive power rises (20 to 34 diopters); parasympathetic signals from the third cranial nerve stimulate it and sympathetic stimulation has little or no effect.
• Distant vision: the ciliary muscle relaxes, the ligaments tighten, the lens flattens and refractive power falls.
2. Basis of disturbance:
• Presbyopia: with age the lens is larger, thicker and less elastic with denatured proteins; dioptric strength falls from about 14 in a child to less than 2 by ages 45 to 50 and about 0 by 70; corrected with bifocal glasses.
• Hyperopia: short eyeball or weak lens system; myopia: long eyeball or too much refractive power; astigmatism: unequal lens curvature in two planes, corrected with a cylindrical lens; keratoconus: bulging cornea, corrected with a contact lens; cataract: lens opacity from protein denaturation, mainly in older people, treated by surgical replacement.
3. Distinctions:
• Myopia (nearsightedness): rays focus in front of the retina, corrected with a concave (diverging) lens; hyperopia (farsightedness): rays focus behind the retina, corrected with a convex (converging) lens.
• Near accommodation: contracted ciliary muscle, relaxed ligaments, spherical lens; distant: relaxed muscle, taut ligaments, flat lens; emmetropia is sharp focus with the ciliary muscle completely relaxed.

1. Functions and composition:
• Blood is a connective tissue with formed elements suspended in a plasma matrix but no fibre elements; it is the medium for metabolic activities, transport (oxygen, nutrients, carbon dioxide, nitrogenous wastes, hormones), protection (prevents fluid loss from damaged vessels, phagocytic WBCs, plasma antibodies) and homeostasis.
• Organisation: plasma is 55% of whole blood (a straw-coloured liquid, 91.5 to 92% water, 7 to 9% proteins, 1% solutes with Na+ the major solute) and formed elements 45% (mainly RBCs, plus leucocytes and platelets).
• Plasma constituents: organic nutrients (glucose, fats, amino acids, vitamins), inorganic ions (bicarbonate, phosphate, sulphate, chloride, calcium, potassium, sodium, magnesium), secretions such as enzymes (ALT, AST, SOD) and hormones, dissolved gases (O2, CO2), metabolic products (urea, bilirubin, creatinine) and plasma proteins (about 7%; fibrinogen, albumin, globulin and antibodies).
• Functions of plasma: transport of cells, food, waste and hormones; fibrinogen for clotting; homeostasis; globulin gives rise to antibodies for immunity.
• Formed elements: RBCs transport oxygen, help carry CO2, regulate acid-base balance and assist clot formation; neutrophils phagocytose and prevent spread of infection; eosinophils attack parasites and phagocytose antigen-antibody complexes; basophils secrete substances mediating hypersensitivity; lymphocytes mediate specific immunity (B cells humoral, T cells cellular); platelets initiate clotting and plug damaged vessels.
• Normal ranges: RBC men 4.6 to 6.2 x 10^12/L and women 4.2 to 5.4 x 10^12/L; Hb men 14 to 16 g/dl and women 12 to 16 g/dl; PCV men 42 to 52% and women 37 to 47%; platelets about 250 x 10^9/L.
2. Plasma constituents and pathology:
• Glucose: diabetes mellitus (Type 1 IDDM and Type 2 NIDDM).
• Calcium and phosphorus (bone formation): hypercalcaemia, for example in renal failure, or hypocalcaemia in malnutrition; sodium, potassium and chloride (cell osmosis, nerve impulses): dehydration and neuronal loss.
• Enzymes: alkaline phosphatase is elevated in liver, kidney and bone disorders; aspartate transaminase is elevated in hepatocellular damage, cardiac muscle damage, haemolysis and after exercise.
• Dissolved gases: CO2 is a measure of blood acidity and alkalinity, for example in severe vomiting and diarrhoea.
• Metabolic products: bilirubin measures liver function; urea nitrogen and creatinine measure kidney function; lipids, proteins and lipoproteins are markers in diabetes mellitus, cardiovascular disease and obesity.
• Blood disorders: reduced cell numbers (anaemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia), increased numbers (polycythemia), increased immune proteins (multiple myeloma), leukaemias, bleeding and clotting disorders, lymphomas, myeloproliferative and plasma cell disorders, spleen disorders.
3. Why a distant organ is affected:
• Symptoms of blood disorders could indicate a disorder of almost any part of the body and are vague and nonspecific.
• Blood disorders may result from diseases of other organs (for example infections, atrophy of the gastric mucosa and liver cirrhosis) or from drugs, accidents and malnutrition.
• Blood is the medium that supplies nutrients and oxygen and removes waste from every cell, so an altered plasma constituent or cell count (for example a falling calcium, sodium or oxygen-carrying capacity) alters the environment of cells in bone, nerve and other tissues.
• Blood is also the source of the plasma-based defence and clotting systems, so its disorders show as infection, bleeding or clotting problems wherever they occur.
questions.question:
Answer the following on blood and plasma:
1. Describe the functions of blood and of plasma under these headings: composition (plasma constituents and formed elements), functions of plasma, functions of the formed elements, and how plasma proteins and other constituents are used.
2. State how plasma constituents relate to common pathologies of excess and deficiency (glucose, calcium, sodium, enzymes, dissolved gases, metabolic products, plasma proteins) and how blood disorders present.
3. Explain why a disturbance of blood or plasma may show up in a distant organ or system and cause a functional deficit.

Answer the following on the transport of carbon dioxide in the blood:
1. Describe carbon dioxide transport under these headings: the three chemical forms, the reactions in the red cell, the chloride shift, and the reverse reactions in the lungs.
2. Explain why active tissues unload more oxygen (the link between CO2 loading, hydrogen ions and oxygen dissociation).
3. Distinguish between the chloride shift and the reverse chloride shift, and between carbaminohaemoglobin and bicarbonate transport.
questions.answerText:
1. CO2 transport:
• About 4 ml of CO2 is transported from tissues to lungs in each 100 ml of blood: 10% dissolved, 30% combined with haemoglobin and plasma proteins as carbamino-Hb (CO2 reacts with the amino group), and 60% as HCO3-.
• In the red cell dissolved CO2 reacts with water to form carbonic acid, catalysed by carbonic anhydrase (about 5000-fold faster); carbonic acid dissociates into H+ and HCO3-; most H+ combine with haemoglobin.
• Chloride shift: bicarbonate diffuses out of the red cell into plasma while chloride diffuses in, so venous red cells contain more chloride than arterial cells.
• In the lungs the reactions reverse: as haemoglobin loads oxygen its affinity for H+ declines, H+ dissociates and combines with HCO3- entering the red cell, chloride moves out (reverse chloride shift), free CO2 is regenerated and diffuses into the alveolus, together with CO2 released from carbaminohaemoglobin and dissolved CO2.
2. Link to oxygen unloading:
• Active tissues generate extra CO2, which raises H+ and lowers pH; this shifts the oxygen-haemoglobin curve to the right (Bohr effect) and promotes oxygen availability.
• CO2 loading releases hydrogen ions in the erythrocyte, and hydrogen ions promote O2 dissociation.
3. Distinctions:
• Chloride shift occurs in the tissues (HCO3- out, Cl- in); the reverse chloride shift occurs in the lungs (Cl- out, HCO3- in).
• Carbaminohaemoglobin carries about 30% of CO2 bound to the amino group of Hb; bicarbonate carries about 60%, formed through carbonic anhydrase.

questions.question: Which muscle depresses the hyoid bone after swallowing?
questions.explanation: The sternohyoid is an infrahyoid muscle that depresses the hyoid bone and larynx after swallowing. All infrahyoid muscles (sternohyoid, sternothyroid, thyrohyoid, omohyoid) serve this function. They are innervated by the ansa cervicalis (C1-C3) except thyrohyoid which receives C1 fibers via the hypoglossal nerve.

questions.question: Which structure lies in the rectovesical pouch in males?
questions.explanation: The rectovesical pouch is the peritoneal reflection between the bladder and rectum in males. It is the lowest part of the peritoneal cavity in males when upright and can contain loops of small intestine (ileum). Fluid collections or abscesses may accumulate here. In females, the analogous space is the rectouterine pouch (of Douglas), which is deeper.

questions.question: The trochanteric fossa, medial to the greater trochanter, receives the insertion of which muscle?
questions.explanation: The trochanteric fossa, located on the medial surface of the greater trochanter, receives the insertion of obturator externus. This differs from other short rotators (piriformis, obturator internus, gemelli) which insert into the upper border of the greater trochanter. Knowledge of this distinction is important in hip replacement approaches.

Resisted elbow extension primarily tests triceps brachii strength, particularly the medial head which is most active in this action. Anconeus provides minor assistance. Weakness suggests radial nerve injury or C7 nerve root pathology.
questions.question: What muscle action is tested by resisted elbow extension?

questions.explanation: The portal vein forms at approximately the L1/L2 vertebral level posterior to the neck of the pancreas through the confluence of the superior mesenteric vein (from the right) and splenic vein (from the left), anterior to the inferior vena cava. The inferior mesenteric vein typically joins the splenic vein before this confluence. The portal vein then ascends obliquely to the right in the free edge of the lesser omentum (hepatoduodenal ligament) to reach the porta hepatis, where it divides into right and left branches. It measures approximately 8 cm in length and receives the left and right gastric veins.
questions.question: The portal vein is formed at which vertebral level?

questions.explanation: Parietal (oxyntic) cells in the gastric glands of the stomach fundus and body secrete hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor. The acid creates an optimal pH for pepsin activation and kills ingested bacteria. Intrinsic factor is essential for vitamin B12 absorption in the terminal ileum. Parietal cell loss or dysfunction can cause achlorhydria and pernicious anemia.
questions.question: Which cells produce hydrochloric acid in the stomach?
Which type of inguinal hernia passes through the deep ring?
questions.explanation: Indirect inguinal hernias pass through the deep inguinal ring lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels, following the path of the spermatic cord. They are the most common type of inguinal hernia and can be congenital (due to persistent processus vaginalis) or acquired. Direct inguinal hernias protrude through the posterior wall of the inguinal canal medial to the inferior epigastric vessels.

Femoral hernias pass through the femoral ring (the medial compartment of the femoral sheath, normally occupied by a lymph node) and emerge below the inguinal ligament through the saphenous opening (fossa ovalis) in the deep fascia of the thigh. They are more common in women but overall less common than inguinal hernias. They have a high risk of strangulation due to the rigid boundaries of the femoral ring.
questions.question: Where does a femoral hernia emerge?

questions.explanation: The sternal angle (angle of Louis) is located at the junction between the manubrium and body of sternum, corresponding to the level of the second costal cartilage. This landmark lies at the vertebral level of T4/T5 and marks important anatomical boundaries. It is also the level of tracheal bifurcation and the beginning and end of the aortic arch.
questions.question: Which costal cartilage articulates with the sternal angle?
What type of hernia is most common?
questions.explanation: Hiatus hernias (both sliding and rolling types) are far more common than congenital diaphragmatic hernias. They occur in middle-aged and older adults due to weakening of the tissues around the esophageal hiatus. Sliding hernias are much more common than rolling (para-esophageal) hernias.

questions.question: Which ligament connects the epiglottis to the hyoid bone?
questions.explanation: The hyoepiglottic ligament connects the anterior surface of the epiglottis to the upper border of the hyoid bone. The thyroepiglottic ligament attaches the epiglottis to the thyroid cartilage. The epiglottis is also connected to the tongue by the median and lateral glossoepiglottic folds. These ligaments maintain epiglottic position during swallowing.

The lumbar plexus is formed by the anterior (ventral) rami of L1, L2, L3, and the upper part of L4 nerve roots within the substance of the psoas major muscle. The lower part of L4 joins with L5 to form the lumbosacral trunk, which contributes to the sacral plexus. The lumbar plexus gives rise to several important nerves including the iliohypogastric, ilioinguinal, genitofemoral, lateral femoral cutaneous, femoral, and obturator nerves, as well as branches to the psoas and quadratus lumborum muscles.
questions.question: Which spinal nerve roots contribute to the lumbar plexus?
Which structure forms the posterior wall of the lesser sac?
questions.explanation: The posterior wall of the lesser sac (omental bursa) is formed by peritoneum covering the pancreas, left kidney, left suprarenal gland, and the posterior two layers of the greater omentum. The lesser sac is bounded anteriorly by the stomach, lesser omentum, and greater omentum; superiorly by the caudate lobe of the liver and diaphragm; and inferiorly by the transverse mesocolon. It communicates with the greater sac through the epiploic foramen (foramen of Winslow).

questions.question: The foramen ovale transmits which additional structure besides V3?
questions.explanation: The foramen ovale transmits the mandibular nerve (V3), accessory meningeal artery, lesser petrosal nerve, and an emissary vein connecting the cavernous sinus with the pterygoid plexus. The accessory meningeal artery supplies the trigeminal ganglion and dura. Foramen ovale is located in the greater wing of the sphenoid bone.

questions.question: What are the cusps of the mitral valve?
questions.explanation: The mitral (bicuspid) valve has two cusps: anterior (aortic) and posterior (mural). The anterior cusp is larger and more mobile, positioned between the mitral orifice and aortic orifice, while the posterior cusp is shorter and attached to more of the annular circumference. Mitral valve prolapse and stenosis are common pathological conditions affecting this valve.

questions.question: Which artery can be used for coronary bypass?
questions.explanation: The internal thoracic (internal mammary) artery is commonly used for coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG). It is dissected from the chest wall while maintaining its origin from the subclavian artery, then anastomosed to a coronary artery (usually left anterior descending). It provides excellent long-term patency.

questions.question: Which structure passes posterior to the epiploic foramen?
questions.explanation: The inferior vena cava, covered by parietal peritoneum, forms the posterior boundary of the epiploic foramen (foramen of Winslow), along with the right crus of the diaphragm. This anatomical relationship is clinically significant because the IVC can be compressed in the Pringle maneuver when the hepatoduodenal ligament (anterior boundary containing the portal triad) is manually compressed or clamped to control hepatic bleeding. The proximity of the IVC also means that the foramen provides a potential route for hemorrhage into the lesser sac following IVC injury.

questions.question: What is the most common congenital renal anomaly?
questions.explanation: Duplicated (duplex) collecting system is the most common congenital renal anomaly, occurring in 0.5-1% of the population. It can be complete (two separate ureters) or incomplete (ureters join before entering bladder). The upper pole moiety ureter inserts more medially and inferiorly in the bladder (Weigert-Meyer rule) and is prone to obstruction, while the lower pole ureter is prone to reflux.

questions.question: The vocal ligament is the thickened upper edge of which membrane?
questions.explanation: The vocal ligament is the thickened free upper edge of the cricothyroid membrane (conus elasticus). It extends from the vocal process of the arytenoid to the posterior surface of the thyroid cartilage. The ligament is covered by mucosa to form the true vocal cord.

questions.question: Which vein drains the fundus of the stomach?
questions.explanation: The short gastric veins drain the fundus of the stomach and flow into the splenic vein. There are typically 4-5 short gastric veins that pass through the gastrosplenic ligament. In portal hypertension, these veins can become dilated and form part of the portosystemic collateral circulation, potentially leading to gastric varices and bleeding.

questions.question: The stylomastoid artery is a branch of which vessel?
questions.explanation: The stylomastoid artery arises from the posterior auricular artery and enters the stylomastoid foramen to supply the facial nerve in its bony canal, the mastoid air cells, and the stapedius muscle. It anastomoses with the petrosal branch of the middle meningeal artery. The artery follows the facial nerve through the temporal bone.

questions.question: Which nerve innervates the pyramidalis muscle?
questions.explanation: The pyramidalis muscle, a small triangular muscle anterior to the lower rectus abdominis (base on pubis, apex on linea alba), is innervated by the subcostal nerve (T12). This muscle is variably present (absent in about 20% of individuals) and functions to tense the linea alba. The subcostal nerve also contributes to innervation of the abdominal wall muscles and overlying skin. The pyramidalis lies within the rectus sheath and represents a derivative of the rectus abdominis. Its clinical significance is minimal.

The superior gluteal nerve (L4, L5, S1) exits the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen above the piriformis muscle (the only structure exiting above piriformis), passes between gluteus medius and minimus, and supplies these muscles plus tensor fasciae latae. All other structures exit below piriformis. The nerve does not actually pierce piriformis but rather exits superior to it. Piriformis serves as an important anatomical landmark in the gluteal region, dividing structures exiting the greater sciatic foramen into suprapiriform (superior gluteal vessels and nerve) and infrapiriform groups (all others including sciatic nerve).
questions.question: Which muscle is pierced by the superior gluteal nerve?

questions.explanation: The posterior wall of the stomach lies anterior to the body of the pancreas, separated by the lesser sac (omental bursa). The anterior surface of the pancreatic body is covered by the peritoneum of the posterior wall of the lesser sac. This relationship is clinically important as pancreatic disease can cause epigastric pain.
questions.question: Which structure lies anterior to the body of the pancreas?

questions.explanation: The appendix has abundant lymphoid follicles in both the lamina propria and submucosa, unlike other parts of the intestine where lymphoid tissue is confined to the lamina propria. These follicles often extend into the submucosa, sometimes obliterating the clear boundary between layers. The appendix functions as a component of gut-associated lymphoid tissue (GALT).
questions.question: Which layer of the appendix contains abundant lymphoid tissue?

questions.explanation: The azygos vein receives: right superior intercostal vein, lower eight right posterior intercostal veins, right bronchial vein, middle esophageal veins, and the hemiazygos and accessory hemiazygos veins from the left side. It drains much of the thoracic wall and mediastinal structures.
questions.question: Which veins drain into the azygos vein?

questions.explanation: Claw hand deformity results from ulnar nerve injury causing paralysis of intrinsic hand muscles. Hyperextension occurs at the metacarpophalangeal joints with flexion at the interphalangeal joints due to unopposed long flexor and extensor action. The deformity is more pronounced in the ring and little fingers.
questions.question: What nerve is affected in claw hand deformity?

questions.explanation: The suspensory ligament of the ovary (infundibulopelvic ligament), a lateral extension of the broad ligament, contains the ovarian vessels (artery and vein) and nerves passing from the lateral pelvic wall to the ovary. This ligament extends from the ovary to the lateral pelvic wall and must be carefully ligated during oophorectomy to control the ovarian vessels. The ovarian ligament (ligament of the ovary) connects the ovary to the uterus and contains no significant vessels. The broad ligament is a double layer of peritoneum extending from the lateral pelvic wall to the uterus, with the ovarian vessels running in its superior lateral extension.
questions.question: Which peritoneal ligament contains the ovarian vessels?
What does the lesser splanchnic nerve supply?
questions.explanation: The lesser splanchnic nerve arises from T10-11 ganglia, pierces the diaphragm, and synapses in the aorticorenal ganglion. It provides sympathetic innervation primarily to the kidneys and suprarenal glands. Some fibers may also reach midgut derivatives. The nerve carries both efferent sympathetic and visceral afferent fibers.

Gastric ulcers most commonly occur along the lesser curvature, particularly at the incisura angularis and junction of body and antrum. This distribution reflects the exposure to gastric acid and the vulnerability of this area to ischemia. Duodenal ulcers are more common overall than gastric ulcers, but gastric ulcers have higher malignancy potential.
questions.question: Which part of the stomach is most common site for gastric ulcers?

questions.explanation: Adductor magnus uniquely has two parts with different nerve supplies: the adductor part (obturator nerve, L2, L3, L4) and the hamstring part (tibial division of sciatic nerve). This dual origin and nerve supply reflects its dual embryological origin. Biceps femoris similarly has two heads with different nerve divisions of the sciatic nerve.
questions.question: Which thigh muscle has TWO different nerve supplies from two different divisions of two different named nerves?

questions.explanation: The cricoarytenoid joint permits rotation and sliding movements of the arytenoid cartilages, which directly control vocal cord abduction and adduction. Tension changes occur primarily through cricothyroid joint movement, not cricoarytenoid articulation. The L-shaped base of the arytenoid pivots at the cricoarytenoid joint to open or close the rima glottidis.
questions.question: The cricoarytenoid joint allows which specific movement of the vocal cords?
The greater splanchnic nerve carries preganglionic fibers from which spinal levels?
questions.explanation: The greater splanchnic nerve contains preganglionic sympathetic fibers from the T5-T9 levels of the spinal cord, which synapse in the celiac ganglion. This nerve pierces the diaphragm separately or with the sympathetic trunk and provides sympathetic innervation to the foregut derivatives (stomach, liver, gallbladder, pancreas, spleen, and small intestine to mid-duodenum) via the celiac plexus. The lesser splanchnic nerve (T10-T11) supplies the midgut, while the least splanchnic nerve (T12) and lumbar splanchnic nerves supply the hindgut and pelvic organs via the superior and inferior mesenteric plexuses.

questions.question: The femoral nerve emerges from which muscle's lateral border?
questions.explanation: The femoral nerve (L2, L3, L4), the largest branch of the lumbar plexus, emerges from the lateral border of the psoas major muscle near the inguinal ligament and descends in the groove between psoas and iliacus. It enters the thigh beneath the inguinal ligament, lateral to the femoral artery in the femoral triangle. Other branches emerging from psoas major's lateral border include the iliohypogastric, ilioinguinal, and lateral femoral cutaneous nerves. The obturator nerve, in contrast, emerges from the medial border of psoas, while the genitofemoral nerve pierces through its anterior surface.

questions.question: What produces opposition of the thumb?
questions.explanation: is the primary muscle producing opposition of the thumb, bringing the thumb across the palm to touch the little finger. This movement involves flexion, abduction, and medial rotation at the carpometacarpal joint. The muscle is supplied by the recurrent branch of the median nerve.

Pancoast tumor (superior sulcus tumor) is a lung cancer arising in the apex of the lung. Due to its location, it can invade the brachial plexus (causing arm pain and weakness), sympathetic chain (causing Horner's syndrome), and ribs (causing pain). Patients present with shoulder/arm pain rather than typical lung symptoms.
questions.question: What is Pancoast tumor?

questions.explanation: Both rectus femoris and sartorius cross both the hip and knee joints. Rectus femoris originates from the anterior inferior iliac spine and inserts via the patellar ligament to the tibial tuberosity. Sartorius originates from the anterior superior iliac spine and inserts into the superior medial surface of the tibia. The three vasti only cross the knee joint.
questions.question: Which two muscles in the anterior thigh compartment cross BOTH the hip and knee joints?

options: Anterior flexes, middle abducts, posterior extends
questions.question: How do the three deltoid portions contribute differently to shoulder function?
questions.explanation: The deltoid's three portions have distinct actions: anterior fibers flex and medially rotate, middle fibers abduct (15-90�), posterior fibers extend and laterally rotate. This multipennate architecture allows the same muscle to produce different movements depending on which fibers are active.

The descending colon is derived from the embryological hindgut, along with the distal third of the transverse colon, sigmoid colon, rectum, and upper anal canal. Hindgut structures are supplied by the inferior mesenteric artery and receive parasympathetic innervation from the pelvic splanchnic nerves. The midgut-hindgut junction occurs at approximately the left third of the transverse colon.
questions.question: Which embryological origin corresponds to the descending colon?

questions.explanation: The ductus deferens (vas deferens) hooks around the lateral side of the inferior epigastric artery at the deep inguinal ring, crossing from lateral to medial as it leaves the spermatic cord to descend into the pelvis. This relationship is surgically important during hernia repair and vasectomy. After crossing the external iliac vessels at the pelvic brim, the vas continues posteromedially across the obturator nerve and vessels and the ureter before reaching the posterior surface of the bladder where it dilates to form the ampulla and joins the seminal vesicle duct.
questions.question: The ductus deferens passes medial to which vessel?
Which hip joint ligament reinforces the posterior aspect of the fibrous membrane and attaches medially to the ischium just posteroinferior to the acetabulum?
questions.explanation: The ischiofemoral ligament reinforces the posterior aspect of the fibrous membrane. It attaches medially to the ischium posteroinferior to the acetabulum and laterally to the greater trochanter deep to the iliofemoral ligament. Like all three extracapsular hip ligaments, it becomes taut during extension, stabilizing the joint in the standing position.

The median (central) cricothyroid ligament connects the anterior aspects of the cricoid and thyroid cartilages. It is subcutaneous in the midline between the cricothyroid muscles. This ligament is crossed by the cricothyroid arterial anastomosis and is the site for emergency cricothyroidotomy.
questions.question: The median cricothyroid ligament connects which two cartilages?

questions.explanation: commonly results from repetitive overhead throwing activities. This is particularly seen in baseball pitchers, tennis players, and swimmers. Repetitive impingement of the rotator cuff tendons under the acromion causes inflammation, degeneration, and potential tears.
questions.question: Which condition involves repetitive overhead throwing?
The posterior third of the tongue receives general and special sensory from which nerve?
questions.explanation: The glossopharyngeal nerve (IX) provides both general sensation and taste (special sensation) to the posterior third of the tongue. The anterior two-thirds receives general sensation from the lingual nerve (V3) and taste from chorda tympani (VII). Motor supply to all tongue muscles is from the hypoglossal nerve except palatoglossus.

questions.question: The nasal bones articulate superiorly with which bone?
questions.explanation: The paired nasal bones articulate superiorly with the frontal bone at the frontonasal suture. Laterally, they attach to the frontal processes of the maxillae, and inferiorly to the upper lateral nasal cartilages. Fractures of the nasal bones are the most common facial fractures. The bones provide support for the nasal bridge.

options: Medial genicular and small saphenous veins
questions.explanation: The popliteal vein is formed at the distal border of popliteus by the union of the anterior and posterior tibial veins. It traverses the popliteal fossa in the same fibrous sheath as the popliteal artery and terminates at the adductor hiatus to become the femoral vein. The small saphenous vein also drains into the popliteal vein.
questions.question: The popliteal vein is formed at the distal border of popliteus by the union of which two deep leg veins?
Which condition involves synovial sheath inflammation in the carpal tunnel?
questions.explanation: Carpal tunnel syndrome commonly results from tenosynovitis (inflammatory reactions in synovial sheaths) of tendons traversing the tunnel. Excess fluid from inflammation compresses the median nerve within the confined space. This is one of the most common causes of carpal tunnel syndrome.

questions.question: The great saphenous vein passes posterior to which bony knee landmark, approximately a hand's breadth posterior to the medial border of the patella?
questions.explanation: The great saphenous vein passes posterior to the medial condyle of the femur (approximately a hand's breadth posterior to the medial border of the patella). This is a key landmark for identifying the vein during varicose vein surgery and for cannulation. At the ankle, it ascends anterior to the medial malleolus.

questions.question: The superior mesenteric artery syndrome involves compression of which structure?
questions.explanation: Superior mesenteric artery syndrome results from compression of the third (horizontal) part of the duodenum between the superior mesenteric artery anteriorly and the aorta (and spine) posteriorly. This typically occurs when the aortomesenteric angle decreases (normally 25-60 degrees) due to loss of the mesenteric fat pad, which can result from rapid weight loss, cachexia, scoliosis surgery, or growth spurts in adolescents. Symptoms include postprandial epigastric pain, nausea, vomiting, and early satiety. Left renal vein compression between the SMA and aorta is called nutcracker syndrome, a different condition.

The accessory pancreatic duct (duct of Santorini), when present, drains the upper part of the head of the pancreas and opens into the duodenum at the minor duodenal papilla. This papilla is located approximately 2 cm proximal to the major papilla. The accessory duct frequently communicates with the main pancreatic duct.
questions.question: Where does the accessory pancreatic duct open into the duodenum?
What causes swan neck deformity?
questions.explanation: Swan neck deformity involves PIP joint hyperextension with DIP joint flexion. This can result from volar plate insufficiency, FDS tendon injury, or chronic inflammatory arthritis. The deformity resembles a swan's neck in profile. It's the opposite of boutonniere deformity.
options: Central slip rupture with DIP extension deformity
Volar plate or FDS rupture with hyperextension
Hip joint itself (L3 innervates the hip)
questions.explanation: The L3 sclerotome includes the hip joint, which receives innervation partly from the femoral nerve (L2, L3, L4). Pain from L3 root pathology can be referred to the hip joint, and hip joint disease can refer pain along L3 dermatomal distribution to the anterior thigh and knee. This bidirectional referral is explained by Hilton's law and the concept of sclerotome overlap between spinal levels.
questions.question: In the lower limb, the term 'sclerotome' refers to the area of bone and deep structures supplied by a single spinal nerve root. Hip pain from L3 sclerotome involvement can mimic pain from which structure?
Which rotator cuff muscle does NOT fuse with the glenohumeral joint capsule?
questions.explanation: All four rotator cuff muscles (subscapularis, supraspinatus, infraspinatus, and teres minor) fuse with the lateral part of the joint capsule. Their tendons blend with the capsule to form the rotator cuff. The resting tone of these muscles helps stabilize the joint by pulling the humeral head into the glenoid cavity.

Phrenic nerve injury causes paralysis of the corresponding hemidiaphragm, which becomes elevated and moves paradoxically upward during inspiration. Causes include surgical trauma (especially cardiac surgery), tumors, neurological disease, and cervical spine injury. Bilateral phrenic nerve injury causes severe respiratory compromise. The phrenic nerve can be stimulated to pace the diaphragm in some patients.
questions.question: Which nerve injury causes diaphragmatic paralysis?
The internal spermatic fascia is derived from which structure?
questions.explanation: The internal spermatic fascia, the innermost of the three fascial coverings of the spermatic cord, is derived from the transversalis fascia as the cord structures pass through the deep inguinal ring. This fascia is continuous with the transversalis fascia at the margins of the deep ring. Moving outward, the next layer is the cremasteric muscle and fascia (from internal oblique and transversus abdominis), and the outermost layer is the external spermatic fascia (from external oblique aponeurosis at the superficial ring). These three layers enclose the contents of the spermatic cord and represent contributions from each layer of the anterior abdominal wall.

questions.question: How is chylothorax initially managed?
questions.explanation: Initial management of chylothorax is conservative: chest tube drainage, nutritional support with medium-chain triglyceride (MCT) diet or total parenteral nutrition (TPN) to reduce chyle production, and treatment of underlying cause. Many cases resolve with conservative management. Persistent cases (>2 weeks, >1L/day drainage) may require surgical intervention.

questions.question: The rectovesical pouch in males is located at which level from the anus?
questions.explanation: The rectovesical pouch (Douglas pouch in males), the peritoneal reflection between the rectum posteriorly and the urinary bladder anteriorly, lies approximately 7.5 cm from the anus. This represents the lowest extent of the peritoneal cavity in males when in the upright position, making it a common site for fluid accumulation (blood, pus, ascites) that can be drained transrectally. In females, the corresponding rectouterine pouch (of Douglas) lies lower at about 5.5 cm from the anus (7.5 cm from the vaginal orifice) due to the interposed uterus between rectum and bladder.

questions.question: Which vessel specifically supplies the bed of the submandibular gland?
questions.explanation: Branches of the facial and lingual arteries supply the submandibular gland, with the facial artery providing the primary vascular supply. The facial artery passes deep to the gland before crossing the mandible. Venous drainage follows corresponding veins to the internal jugular system.

questions.question: The ureter crosses which muscle as it descends?
questions.explanation: The ureter descends on the anterior surface of the psoas major muscle in the abdomen, passing over the tips of the lumbar vertebral transverse processes. It is crossed anteriorly by the testicular/ovarian vessels and runs posterior to the peritoneum throughout its abdominal course. At the pelvic brim, the ureter crosses the bifurcation of the common iliac artery (or external iliac artery) to enter the pelvis, where it runs along the lateral pelvic wall before turning medially to reach the bladder. In females, it passes beneath the uterine artery ("water under the bridge").

The medial meniscus is C-shaped and firmly attached to the tibial (medial) collateral ligament at its midpoint. This attachment makes it less mobile and more vulnerable to injury than the lateral meniscus. The tibial collateral ligament and medial meniscus are often torn together in contact sports as part of the classic 'unhappy triad.'
questions.question: The medial meniscus is C-shaped and firmly adheres to which extracapsular ligament, making it more vulnerable to sporting injury?
The lumbar plexus is formed within which muscle?
questions.explanation: The lumbar plexus is formed within the substance of the psoas major muscle from the anterior (ventral) rami of L1, L2, L3, and the upper part of L4 nerve roots. The plexus gives rise to branches that emerge from different borders of the muscle: lateral border (iliohypogastric, ilioinguinal, lateral femoral cutaneous, femoral nerves), anterior surface (genitofemoral nerve), and medial border (obturator nerve). The psoas major also receives direct motor innervation from L1-L4 nerve roots. The lumbar plexus supplies the anterior abdominal wall, external genitalia, and anterior and medial thigh.

The vomer forms the posteroinferior part of the bony nasal septum. The perpendicular plate of the ethmoid forms the posterosuperior portion. The septal cartilage forms the anterior part. The maxillary and palatine crests provide inferior support. Septal deviation commonly occurs at the junction of vomer and cartilage.
questions.question: Which structure forms the skeleton of the nasal septum posteroinferiorly?

questions.explanation: Wrist drop results from radial nerve injury, which has nerve root values C5, C6, C7, C8, and T1. However, C7 is the most critical root for wrist extension. Complete radial nerve palsy affects all extensor muscles and causes the characteristic wrist drop deformity.
questions.question: Which nerve root value is predominantly involved in wrist drop?
Where does the middle cardiac vein run?
questions.explanation: The middle cardiac vein runs in the posterior interventricular groove alongside the posterior interventricular artery and drains into the coronary sinus at its termination. It drains the posterior walls of both ventricles and the posterior interventricular septum, corresponding to the territory of the posterior interventricular artery. It is the second largest cardiac vein.

Trabeculae carneae are irregular muscular ridges that project from the inner surface of the ventricles. They prevent the walls from adhering to each other during contraction, increase ventricular surface area, and may contribute to ventricular contraction. Some are attached at both ends (ridges), some at one end (bridges like the moderator band), and some are free (papillary muscles).
questions.question: What is the function of trabeculae carneae?

questions.explanation: The aryepiglotticus muscle, running in the aryepiglottic fold, pulls the arytenoid cartilages forward toward the epiglottis, closing the laryngeal inlet during swallowing. It acts like a purse-string sphincter. The muscle is supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve. The thyroepiglotticus and thyroarytenoid muscles assist in this protective function.
questions.question: Which muscle pulls the arytenoid cartilages forward toward the epiglottis?
The processus vaginalis normally obliterates when?
questions.explanation: The processus vaginalis, an evagination of peritoneum that accompanies the descending testis through the inguinal canal, normally obliterates during the first year of life, leaving only the distal portion as the tunica vaginalis surrounding the testis. Failure of complete obliteration leads to various clinical conditions: patent processus vaginalis allows peritoneal fluid to flow into the scrotum (communicating hydrocele) or permits herniation of abdominal contents (congenital indirect inguinal hernia). Partial obliteration with persistence of intermediate portions creates encysted hydroceles of the cord. Complete patency occurs in about 20% of adults.

questions.question: The patella, embedded in the quadriceps and patellar tendon, serves as a pulley with what biomechanical benefit?
options: Increases the weight of the quadriceps
Increases mechanical advantage in knee extension
questions.explanation: The patella is a true sesamoid bone serving as a pulley that improves the angle of pull of the quadriceps tendon, resulting in greater mechanical advantage in knee extension. Patellectomy significantly reduces knee extension strength. The patella slides within the trochlear groove during knee movements and is protected by thick hyaline cartilage on its posterior surface.

Hesselbach's triangle (inguinal triangle) is bounded medially by the lateral border of the rectus abdominis muscle, laterally by the inferior epigastric artery, and inferiorly by the inguinal ligament. The floor of this triangle consists of transversalis fascia (reinforced medially by the conjoint tendon), representing a potential weak area in the posterior wall of the inguinal canal. Direct inguinal hernias protrude through this triangle medial to the inferior epigastric artery, in contrast to indirect hernias which emerge lateral to the artery through the deep inguinal ring.
questions.question: Which muscle forms the medial boundary of Hesselbach's triangle?

questions.explanation: McBurney's point marks the base of the appendix and is located at the junction of the lateral third and medial two-thirds of a line from the right anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus. This is the point of maximum tenderness in acute appendicitis and guides the surgical incision. The tip of the appendix, however, can vary considerably in position.
questions.question: Which structure marks the base of the appendix on the surface?

questions.explanation: The head of the pancreas lies in the concavity formed by the C-shaped duodenum and indents the medial aspect of the second (descending) part. The pancreatic head is intimately related to the duodenum, particularly the second part where the bile and pancreatic ducts enter. This close relationship means that pancreatic head disease often affects the duodenum and vice versa.
questions.question: Which structure indents the second part of the duodenum medially?
What is the most common complication of scaphoid fracture?
questions.explanation: are the most common complications of scaphoid fracture due to the unique blood supply. The proximal fragment often fails to heal due to inadequate blood supply. Early diagnosis and appropriate immobilization are essential to prevent these complications.

questions.question: Which structure lies in the cavernous sinus lateral wall?
questions.explanation: The lateral wall of the cavernous sinus contains (from superior to inferior): oculomotor nerve (III), trochlear nerve (IV), ophthalmic division (V1), and maxillary division (V2). The internal carotid artery and abducens nerve (VI) pass through the sinus cavity itself. Cavernous sinus thrombosis can affect all these structures causing ophthalmoplegia and sensory loss.

questions.question: What are the approximate dimensions of an adult kidney?
questions.explanation: Each adult kidney is approximately 10 cm long, 5 cm wide, and 2.5 cm thick, resembling a large bean in shape. The left kidney is typically slightly longer and narrower than the right. Kidney size is clinically important, as small kidneys may indicate chronic disease while enlarged kidneys suggest acute processes or masses.

The head of the pancreas lies within the C-shaped curve formed by the duodenum, specifically nestled in the concavity of the second, third, and fourth parts of the duodenum. The head is the broadest part of the pancreas. A portion of the head, the uncinate process, extends to the left behind the superior mesenteric vessels.
questions.question: Which part of the pancreas lies within the concavity of the duodenum?

questions.explanation: Biceps brachii is most effective as a supinator when the elbow is flexed at 90� (maximum mechanical advantage). As a flexor, it's most effective when the forearm is in mid-prone position. When fully supinated, the tendon is wrapped around the radius, reducing flexion efficiency.
questions.question: How does forearm position affect biceps function?
options: Supination optimal with flexed elbow, flexion optimal mid-pronation

questions.question: The superior orbital fissure transmits which cranial nerves?
questions.explanation: The superior orbital fissure transmits oculomotor (III), trochlear (IV), ophthalmic division of trigeminal (V1), and abducens (VI) nerves. It also transmits the superior ophthalmic vein. The fissure is bounded by the greater and lesser wings of the sphenoid. The optic nerve passes through the separate optic canal.
