questions.explanation: The esophageal hiatus (at T10 level, formed by muscle fibers from the right crus of the diaphragm that loop around the esophagus) transmits the esophagus and the anterior and posterior vagal trunks (formed from the vagus nerves). The vagal trunks provide parasympathetic innervation to the abdominal viscera up to the splenic flexure. The left gastric artery and vein may also pass through or near this opening. The aorta, thoracic duct, and azygos vein pass through the aortic hiatus at T12, while the IVC passes through the caval opening at T8.
questions.question: Which structure passes through the esophageal hiatus?

questions.explanation: Cockett's perforators are the clinically most important perforating veins in the lower leg, connecting the posterior arch vein (a tributary of the great saphenous vein) to the posterior tibial veins. Their incompetence leads to venous hypertension in the gaiter area of the leg (lower medial aspect), causing lipodermatosclerosis and venous ulcers. Perforator incompetence is addressed surgically or with thermal ablation.
questions.question: Varicose veins of the great saphenous system result from incompetence of the saphenofemoral junction and perforating veins. The longest perforating vein, connecting the posterior arch vein to the posterior tibial veins, is named what?
Which forearm muscle is supplied by the anterior interosseous nerve?
questions.explanation: is supplied by the anterior interosseous nerve, a branch of the median nerve. This nerve also supplies the lateral half of flexor digitorum profundus and pronator quadratus. Anterior interosseous syndrome results in inability to flex the thumb interphalangeal joint and index finger distal interphalangeal joint.

The ulnar nerve is compressed in cubital tunnel syndrome as it passes through the cubital tunnel posterior to the medial epicondyle. This is the most common site of ulnar nerve entrapment. Symptoms include numbness in the ulnar one and one-half fingers and hand muscle weakness.
questions.question: Which nerve is compressed in cubital tunnel syndrome?
Which structure separates the right and left atria internally?
questions.explanation: The interatrial septum is the thin wall separating the right and left atria. It contains the fossa ovalis, a thumbprint-sized oval depression representing the site of the foramen ovale in the fetus. The limbus fossae ovalis is the prominent margin of the fossa. In approximately 25% of people, the foramen ovale remains probe-patent without functional significance.

The celiac trunk emerges from the anterior aspect of the abdominal aorta immediately below the aortic hiatus of the diaphragm, anterior to the upper part of the first lumbar vertebra (L1). It quickly trifurcates into the left gastric, splenic, and common hepatic arteries, providing the principal arterial supply to foregut derivatives. The celiac ganglion and plexus surround the origin of this vessel, receiving preganglionic sympathetic fibers from the greater splanchnic nerve.
questions.question: The celiac trunk typically arises at which vertebral level?

questions.explanation: The knee joint is the largest and most complex joint in the body, primarily classified as a hinge-type synovial joint. It has two articulations: the tibiofemoral joint (femur with tibia, bearing most body weight) and the patellofemoral joint (femur with patella). Despite being hinge-like, the knee also allows rotation during the screw-home mechanism.
questions.question: Despite its complexity with two articulations, the knee joint is primarily classified as which type of synovial joint?

questions.explanation: The tracheobronchial lymph nodes (superior and inferior) lie at and around the tracheal bifurcation. They receive lymph from the lungs, bronchi, trachea, and heart. These nodes are important in lung cancer staging. Efferents form the bronchomediastinal trunks which drain to the venous system or lymphatic ducts.
questions.question: What drains to tracheobronchial lymph nodes?
Which condition causes pleural inflammation?
questions.explanation: Pleurisy (or pleuritis) is inflammation of the pleura lining the lungs. It usually occurs in conjunction with pneumonia and other lung infections. Characteristic symptoms include sharp chest pain that worsens with breathing or coughing. The inflamed pleural surfaces may produce a friction rub audible on auscultation.

questions.question: Which reflex tests C5 nerve root integrity?
questions.explanation: The biceps reflex tests C5 nerve root integrity (with C6 contribution). The reflex is elicited by tapping the biceps tendon in the cubital fossa while the elbow is partially flexed. Absence or diminution suggests C5 nerve root pathology or musculocutaneous nerve injury.

questions.question: The vas deferens crosses which vessel during its pelvic course?
questions.explanation: The vas deferens crosses superior to the external iliac vessels at the pelvic brim, then curves medially, crossing over (anterior to) the obturator nerve and vessels and the ureter before reaching the posterior surface of the bladder. At the inguinal region, the vas deferens "hooks" around the lateral side of the inferior epigastric artery, crossing it from lateral to medial as it exits the deep inguinal ring. This relationship is surgically important during hernia repair and vasectomy. The vas is easily palpable in the spermatic cord and feels like a firm cord or thick string.

questions.question: Which structure marks the junction between the smooth and rough parts of the right atrium?
questions.explanation: The crista terminalis is a prominent vertical muscular ridge on the internal right atrial wall that marks the junction between the smooth-walled posterior sinus venarum (derived from the sinus venosus) and the rough-walled anterior part with pectinate muscles (derived from the primitive atrium). Externally, this corresponds to the sulcus terminalis groove.

questions.question: What position does the heart occupy mediastinally?
questions.explanation: The heart and pericardium are the main contents of the middle mediastinum, which also contains the ascending aorta, pulmonary trunk, parts of the phrenic nerves, and the main bronchi. The middle mediastinum is the central compartment of the inferior mediastinum.

The falciform ligament is a sickle-shaped fold of peritoneum that attaches the liver to the anterior abdominal wall and diaphragm. It extends from the umbilicus to the liver, dividing the liver into anatomical right and left lobes on the diaphragmatic surface. The free inferior edge contains the ligamentum teres (round ligament).
questions.question: Which ligament connects the liver to the anterior abdominal wall?

questions.explanation: Nine flexor tendons accompany the median nerve through the carpal tunnel: four tendons each of flexor digitorum superficialis and profundus, plus the flexor pollicis longus tendon. These tendons are enclosed in synovial sheaths within the tunnel.
questions.question: What structure accompanies the median nerve through the carpal tunnel?
Which bone contains the foramen rotundum?
questions.explanation: The foramen rotundum is located in the greater wing of the sphenoid bone, transmitting the maxillary nerve (V2). It connects the middle cranial fossa with the pterygopalatine fossa. The foramen is round in shape, distinguishing it from the oval foramen ovale.

questions.question: How many vessels exit through the greater sciatic foramen?
questions.explanation: Six vessels exit through the greater sciatic foramen: superior gluteal artery and vein, inferior gluteal artery and vein, and internal pudendal artery and vein. Together with seven nerves and the piriformis muscle, they constitute the 14 structures passing through this critical anatomical gateway from the pelvis to the gluteal region.

The left internal thoracic artery is preferred for coronary bypass because of its proximity to the left anterior descending coronary artery. The right internal thoracic may also be used for right coronary or circumflex vessels. Using arterial grafts (vs. saphenous vein) provides superior long-term patency rates.
questions.question: Which side internal thoracic is preferred for bypass?

questions.explanation: The female urethra is approximately 4 cm (1.5 inches) long and extends from the internal urethral orifice of the bladder to the external urethral orifice in the vestibule. It is embedded in the anterior vaginal wall and passes through the urogenital diaphragm. The shorter length makes females more susceptible to urinary tract infections.
questions.question: What is the length of the female urethra?

questions.explanation: During pericardiocentesis (needle aspiration of pericardial fluid), the needle is typically inserted in the left 5th or 6th intercostal space near the sternum or at the infrasternal (subxiphoid) angle. The internal thoracic (mammary) artery, which runs about 1 cm lateral to the sternum, is at risk if the needle is inserted too laterally. The phrenic nerves run laterally between the pericardium and mediastinal pleura.
questions.question: Which structure is most at risk during pericardiocentesis?

questions.explanation: The gastrosplenic ligament contains the short gastric vessels (4-6 small arteries and veins) that pass from the splenic vessels near the hilum to supply the gastric fundus, and the left gastroepiploic (gastro-omental) vessels that run along the greater curvature. The splenic artery and vein themselves course through the splenorenal ligament (along with the pancreatic tail), not the gastrosplenic ligament. During splenectomy, the gastrosplenic ligament is divided, requiring careful ligation of these vessels. The gastrosplenic ligament represents part of the dorsal mesogastrium and connects the greater curvature to the splenic hilum.
questions.question: Which structure lies in the free edge of the gastrosplenic ligament?
What is a thymoma?
questions.explanation: A thymoma is a neoplasm (tumor) arising from the epithelial cells of the thymus gland. It is the most common primary tumor of the anterior mediastinum in adults. Thymomas are often associated with myasthenia gravis (about 30-50% of thymoma patients develop MG). Treatment typically involves surgical resection.

The costomediastinal recess is located behind the sternum where the costal pleura doubles back to become mediastinal pleura. It is more conspicuous on the left side in the region around the cardiac notch. This recess allows for cardiac expansion without lung compression.
questions.question: Where is the costomediastinal recess located?
The greater omentum is attached to which part of the transverse colon?
questions.explanation: The greater omentum (specifically its posterior two layers after folding back from the inferior descent) attaches to the anterior surface (and superior border) of the transverse colon and its mesocolon. The omentum hangs like an apron from the greater curvature of the stomach, descends anterior to the small intestine, then folds back on itself and fuses with the transverse colon and mesocolon before continuing to the posterior abdominal wall. This four-layered structure contains fat and can wall off inflamed organs (giving it the name "abdominal policeman"), provides insulation, and allows mobility of abdominal contents.

questions.question: The transversalis fascia forms which covering of the spermatic cord?
questions.explanation: The internal spermatic fascia, the innermost fascial covering of the spermatic cord, is derived from the transversalis fascia at the margins of the deep inguinal ring. Moving outward, the next layer is the cremasteric muscle and fascia (from internal oblique and transversus abdominis), and the outermost layer is the external spermatic fascia (from external oblique aponeurosis). These three concentric layers are acquired as the processus vaginalis descends through the layers of the anterior abdominal wall during testicular descent. The tunica vaginalis is the closed peritoneal sac surrounding the testis, derived from the processus vaginalis.

questions.question: Which vein receives the inferior mesenteric vein?
questions.explanation: The inferior mesenteric vein typically drains into the splenic vein posterior to the body of the pancreas, though anatomical variations exist (occasionally draining into superior mesenteric vein or the portal vein directly). The IMV ascends from the pelvis on the left side of the inferior mesenteric artery, receiving sigmoid and left colic tributaries. After joining the splenic vein, blood flows to the confluence with the superior mesenteric vein behind the neck of the pancreas, forming the portal vein. This pathway ensures blood from the hindgut reaches the liver for processing.

questions.question: The ACL is slack during knee flexion and taut during full extension. It prevents posterior displacement of the femur on the tibia and which other movement?
questions.explanation: The ACL prevents posterior displacement of the femur on the tibia (or anterior displacement of the tibia on the femur) and hyperextension of the knee joint. When the knee is flexed at a right angle, the tibia cannot be pulled anteriorly because it is held by the intact ACL. ACL rupture is detected by a positive anterior drawer test.

questions.question: Which structure lies in the hypoglossal triangle?
questions.explanation: The hypoglossal nerve (XII) lies in the hypoglossal triangle (muscular triangle), a subdivision of the anterior triangle bounded by the midline, superior belly of omohyoid, and sternocleidomastoid. The triangle also contains the infrahyoid muscles and thyroid gland. The nerve passes from the carotid triangle into the muscular triangle.

options: At the Achilles tendon insertion on the calcaneus
At the origin from the lateral femoral condyle
At the musculotendinous junction of the medial gastrocnemius head
questions.explanation: Gastrocnemius strain (tennis leg) typically occurs at the musculotendinous junction of the medial head of gastrocnemius, where the thick muscle belly transitions to the thin Achilles tendon. It occurs during sudden push-off activities and presents with acute posterior calf pain. The medial head is more commonly strained than the lateral because it is larger and generates greater force.
questions.question: Gastrocnemius strain ('tennis leg') typically occurs at which specific location within the muscle?

questions.explanation: Achalasia is a motility disorder characterized by failure of the lower esophageal sphincter to relax during swallowing and loss of normal esophageal peristalsis. This causes dysphagia to both solids and liquids, regurgitation, and progressive esophageal dilation. Treatment includes pneumatic dilation, Heller myotomy, or peroral endoscopic myotomy (POEM).
questions.question: What causes achalasia?

questions.explanation: Sartorius (the tailor's muscle) acts on two joints. At the hip: it flexes, abducts, and laterally rotates the thigh. At the knee: it flexes the leg and medially rotates when the knee is flexed. The combined action of both sartorii brings the lower limb into the cross-legged sitting position typical of traditional tailors.
options: Extends hip and flexes the knee only
Adducts the hip and extends the knee
Flexes, abducts, and laterally rotates hip; flexes and medially rotates knee
Flexes hip and laterally rotates the knee joint only
Abducts the hip and extends the knee only
questions.question: The sartorius muscle, the longest muscle in the body, performs which complete combination of actions?
Which muscle opens the auditory tube during swallowing?
questions.explanation: The tensor veli palatini muscle opens the auditory (Eustachian) tube during swallowing by pulling on the membranous lateral wall. The levator veli palatini also contributes. Salpingopharyngeus assists in opening the tube. This mechanism equalizes middle ear pressure with atmospheric pressure.

The cricoid cartilage is located at the C6 vertebral level. The lower border marks the transition from pharynx to esophagus and from larynx to trachea. This level also corresponds to where the carotid tubercle of C6 can be palpated and the carotid artery compressed. The middle cervical sympathetic ganglion lies at this level.
questions.question: The cricoid cartilage is located at which vertebral level?

questions.explanation: The inferior mediastinum has three subdivisions: anterior (in front of the heart), middle (contains the heart), and posterior (behind the heart). The superior mediastinum lies above the horizontal plane through T4. This classification helps in understanding the location of mediastinal structures and pathology.
questions.question: How many subdivisions does inferior mediastinum have?
Tibial nerve injury in the tarsal tunnel (tarsal tunnel syndrome) presents with pain and paraesthesia on the sole of the foot. Which action is specifically lost?
questions.explanation: Tarsal tunnel syndrome results from compression of the tibial nerve in the tarsal tunnel beneath the flexor retinaculum. It presents with pain, burning, and paraesthesia on the sole of the foot and intrinsic muscle weakness. Plantarflexion of the toes and intrinsic muscle function are impaired. Tinel's sign may be positive over the tarsal tunnel at the medial ankle.
options: Plantarflexion of toes and plantar sensation

questions.explanation: Cardiac tamponade occurs when fluid accumulates in the pericardial cavity rapidly or in large amounts, increasing intrapericardial pressure. This compresses the heart chambers, particularly the right atrium and ventricle, impairing venous return and cardiac filling. Clinical signs include Beck's triad: hypotension, elevated JVP, and muffled heart sounds. Emergency pericardiocentesis may be life-saving.
questions.question: What is cardiac tamponade?

questions.explanation: The lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm is the sensory continuation of the musculocutaneous nerve after it supplies the anterior arm muscles. It provides sensation to the lateral aspect of the forearm from elbow to wrist. This nerve emerges lateral to the biceps tendon in the cubital fossa.
questions.question: What provides sensory innervation to the lateral forearm?

questions.explanation: The hepatic artery proper, ascending in the free edge of the lesser omentum (hepatoduodenal ligament) as part of the portal triad, divides near the porta hepatis into right and left hepatic arteries that supply the corresponding lobes of the liver. The right hepatic artery gives off the cystic artery to the gallbladder. Significant anatomical variation exists in hepatic arterial anatomy (occurring in up to 45% of individuals), including replaced or accessory right hepatic arteries from the superior mesenteric artery and replaced or accessory left hepatic arteries from the left gastric artery.
questions.question: The hepatic artery proper typically divides into which branches?

questions.explanation: The esophagus has four anatomical constrictions where it is narrowed. The first is at its origin (C6 level, 15 cm from incisors) where the cricopharyngeus muscle forms the upper esophageal sphincter. These constrictions are clinically important as sites where foreign bodies lodge and where esophageal pathology commonly occurs.
questions.question: Which constriction is at the esophageal origin?

questions.explanation: Plantar interossei adduct (PAD - Plantar ADduct) and dorsal interossei abduct (DAB - Dorsal ABduct) in reference to the second digit (2nd ray), which is the anatomical axis of the foot. This is the same concept as the hand interossei, but referenced to different rays (middle finger for hand, second toe for foot). All interossei also flex the metatarsophalangeal joints.
questions.question: The fourth layer of foot muscles contains plantar interossei (3 muscles) and dorsal interossei (4 muscles). Plantar interossei adduct and dorsal interossei abduct in reference to which axis?

questions.explanation: Old platelets, like old erythrocytes, are recognized and destroyed by macrophages in the splenic cords. The spleen also serves as a reservoir for approximately one-third of the body's platelet pool. After splenectomy, platelet counts typically rise (thrombocytosis) due to loss of platelet sequestration and destruction. Splenic platelets can be rapidly mobilized in stress or hemorrhage.
questions.question: What happens to old platelets in the spleen?
Which structure forms the primary passive support of the mandible?
questions.explanation: The sphenomandibular ligament runs from the spine of the sphenoid to the lingula of the mandible and provides primary passive support. The stylomandibular ligament is merely a thickening of the parotid capsule and contributes minimally to joint support. Other ligaments provide secondary stabilization or perform different mechanical functions in the temporomandibular complex.

questions.question: At which vertebral level does the renal artery arise from the aorta?
questions.explanation: The renal arteries arise from the abdominal aorta at approximately the level of the L2 vertebral body, just inferior to the origin of the superior mesenteric artery. The right renal artery is longer than the left and passes posterior to the inferior vena cava to reach the right kidney. Each renal artery divides into five segmental arteries that are functionally end arteries.

The biceps reflex predominantly tests the C6 nerve root, though C5 also contributes. The reflex is elicited by tapping the biceps tendon in the cubital fossa. Absence or diminution of this reflex suggests C6 nerve root or musculocutaneous nerve pathology.
questions.question: Which nerve root is predominantly tested by the biceps reflex?
Why do foreign bodies enter the right bronchus?
questions.explanation: The wider and more vertical course of the right main bronchus allows foreign particles to enter into it more easily than the left. The left bronchus is longer, narrower, and more horizontally oriented. This anatomical difference is clinically significant in aspiration and foreign body lodgment.

questions.question: Which coronary artery typically gives rise to the SA nodal artery?
questions.explanation: The sinoatrial nodal artery arises from the right coronary artery in approximately 60% of people, and from the left circumflex artery in about 40%. It courses posteriorly around the superior vena cava-atrial junction to supply the SA node. Occlusion can cause sinus node dysfunction, though collateral circulation often provides some protection.

questions.question: The 'unhappy triad' of the knee involves simultaneous injury to which three structures following a valgus force with the foot planted?
questions.explanation: The 'unhappy triad' of the knee (O'Donoghue's triad) consists of simultaneous injury to the anterior cruciate ligament, medial meniscus, and tibial (medial) collateral ligament. This injury occurs classically in American football when a valgus force is applied to a planted, slightly flexed knee. The tight adherence of the medial meniscus to the tibial collateral ligament explains their combined injury.
options: PCL, lateral meniscus, and fibular collateral ligament
ACL, lateral meniscus, and fibular collateral ligament
PCL, lateral meniscus, and tibial collateral ligament
ACL, medial meniscus, and tibial collateral ligament
ACL, medial meniscus, and ACL and fibular collateral ligament

questions.question: Where do posterior mediastinal lymph nodes lie?
questions.explanation: Posterior mediastinal lymph nodes lie in the posterior mediastinum alongside the esophagus and descending thoracic aorta. They receive lymph from the esophagus, posterior diaphragm, pericardium, and posterior intercostal spaces. Efferents drain primarily to the thoracic duct.

questions.question: The three fascial compartments of the thigh are separated by septa passing from the fascia lata to which bony structure?
questions.explanation: Three fascial septa pass from the inner aspect of the fascia lata to the linea aspera of the femur, dividing the thigh into anterior, medial, and posterior compartments. Each compartment has distinct nerves, muscles, and vessels. Understanding compartment anatomy is critical in managing thigh compartment syndrome following trauma.

Lymphangiography involves injecting contrast into pedal lymphatics to visualize the lymphatic system and thoracic duct, potentially identifying the site of leakage. This procedure is technically challenging and rarely performed. Modern alternatives include lymphoscintigraphy or high-resolution MRI. Diagnosis is usually made by pleural fluid analysis showing characteristic chyle properties.
questions.question: What imaging localizes a chyle leak?

questions.explanation: The hemiazygos vein is formed by the union of the left ascending lumbar vein and left subcostal vein. It ascends on the left side of the vertebral column in the posterior mediastinum, crosses at T8-9, and drains into the azygos vein. It receives lower left posterior intercostal veins.
questions.question: What forms the hemiazygos vein?
The posterior cerebral artery is a terminal branch of which vessel?
questions.explanation: The posterior cerebral arteries are the terminal branches of the basilar artery, which bifurcates at the upper border of the pons. They supply the occipital lobes, inferior temporal lobes, and parts of the thalamus. The posterior communicating arteries connect them to the internal carotid system.

Each foot has 26 bones: 7 tarsals, 5 metatarsals, and 14 phalanges (the great toe has 2 phalanges; the other four toes each have 3 phalanges). Understanding foot bone anatomy is fundamental to podiatry, orthopaedics, and diagnosis of stress fractures, Lisfranc injuries, and other foot pathologies.
questions.question: Podiatry is the medical specialty dealing with the study and care of the feet. The foot has how many bones in total (tarsals + metatarsals + phalanges)?

questions.explanation: The superior vesical arteries (usually multiple branches) arise from the patent part of the umbilical artery and supply the superior surface and upper lateral surfaces of the bladder. The umbilical artery is obliterated distally (becoming the medial umbilical ligament) but remains patent proximally. The inferior vesical artery (in males) or vaginal artery (in females) supplies the bladder base.
questions.question: Which artery supplies the superior surface of the bladder?
Which artery typically does NOT arise from the abdominal aorta?
questions.explanation: The deep circumflex iliac artery arises from the external iliac artery (just above the inguinal ligament, near the origin of the inferior epigastric artery), not from the abdominal aorta. It runs laterally along the inguinal ligament and iliac crest, supplying the lower abdominal wall muscles. The abdominal aorta gives rise to paired visceral branches (inferior phrenic, suprarenal, renal, gonadal), unpaired visceral branches (celiac, SMA, IMA), paired parietal branches (four lumbar arteries), and the unpaired median sacral artery posteriorly, before bifurcating into right and left common iliac arteries at L4 level.

questions.question: Which procedure examines the bronchial tree?
questions.explanation: Bronchoscopy is the procedure that allows direct visualization and examination of the trachea and bronchial tree using a flexible or rigid bronchoscope. It can be used diagnostically (to visualize lesions, take biopsies, obtain specimens) or therapeutically (to remove foreign bodies, control bleeding, place stents).

Fourteen structures exit through the greater sciatic foramen: one muscle (piriformis), seven nerves (sciatic, posterior cutaneous nerve of the thigh, superior gluteal, inferior gluteal, nerve to obturator internus, nerve to quadratus femoris, and pudendal nerves), and six vessels (superior and inferior gluteal arteries and veins, and internal pudendal artery and vein).
questions.question: How many total structures exit through the greater sciatic foramen?

questions.explanation: The left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein at approximately a right angle, while the right testicular vein drains directly into the inferior vena cava at an acute angle. This anatomical asymmetry explains the higher incidence (90%) of left-sided varicoceles, as the longer venous column, perpendicular drainage, and potential compression of the left renal vein by the superior mesenteric artery (nutcracker phenomenon) create higher venous pressure. The pampiniform plexus of veins in the spermatic cord converges to form a single testicular vein at the deep inguinal ring.
questions.question: Which vessel drains the left testis?
Which structure separates the supracolic from the infracolic compartment?
questions.explanation: The transverse mesocolon, a broad fold of peritoneum connecting the transverse colon to the posterior abdominal wall, divides the peritoneal cavity into supracolic and infracolic compartments. The supracolic compartment contains the stomach, liver, spleen, and lesser sac, while the infracolic compartment is further divided into right and left infracolic spaces by the mesentery of the small intestine. These spaces communicate laterally via the paracolic gutters. The root of the transverse mesocolon crosses the descending (second) part of the duodenum and head of pancreas, serving as an important surgical landmark.

questions.question: The cremasteric artery is typically a branch of which vessel?
questions.explanation: The cremasteric artery arises from the inferior epigastric artery (a branch of the external iliac artery) near the deep inguinal ring and accompanies the spermatic cord through the inguinal canal. It supplies the cremaster muscle and anastomoses with the testicular artery and artery of the vas deferens, contributing to the arterial supply of the spermatic cord coverings. The genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve also enters the cord at the deep ring to innervate the cremaster muscle, which elevates the testis in response to cold or cremasteric reflex stimulation.

questions.question: How many cusps form the pulmonary valve?
questions.explanation: The pulmonary valve has three semilunar (half-moon shaped) cusps: anterior, right, and left. Behind each cusp is a pulmonary sinus. The valve opens during right ventricular systole to allow blood into the pulmonary trunk and closes during diastole to prevent backflow. Unlike AV valves, semilunar valves have no chordae tendineae or papillary muscles.

Compression of the common fibular nerve at the neck of the fibula paralyzes the anterior and lateral compartments of the leg, causing foot drop (inability to dorsiflex) and loss of eversion of the foot. Sensory loss occurs on the dorsum of the foot and lateral leg. The patient walks with a high-stepping gait to compensate for the foot drop.
options: Posterior leg compartment; loss of plantarflexion strength
Medial compartment of thigh; loss of adduction
Anterior compartment only; loss of dorsiflexion only
Posterior compartment of leg; calcaneal gait
Anterior and lateral compartments; foot drop and loss of eversion
questions.question: Compression of the common fibular nerve around the neck of the fibula results in paralysis of which compartments and what clinical presentation?
What forms the anterior boundary of posterior mediastinum?
questions.explanation: The posterior mediastinum is bounded anteriorly by the pericardium (which forms the heart in the middle mediastinum). Posteriorly, it is bounded by the thoracic vertebrae from T5 to T12. The posterior mediastinum contains the esophagus, descending aorta, azygos system, thoracic duct, and sympathetic trunks.

questions.question: What structures pass through the splenorenal ligament?
questions.explanation: The splenorenal (lienorenal) ligament extends from the hilum of the spleen to the anterior surface of the left kidney and contains the splenic vessels, tail of the pancreas, and associated lymph nodes. The tail of the pancreas extends into this ligament to reach the splenic hilum. This ligament represents a portion of the dorsal mesogastrium.

questions.question: What percentage of the rectum is covered by peritoneum anteriorly?
questions.explanation: Only the upper third of the rectum is covered by peritoneum on its anterior surface, the middle third has peritoneum on its front only, and the lower third is completely devoid of peritoneal covering. Posteriorly, the rectum is retroperitoneal throughout its length. This peritoneal relationship creates the rectovesical pouch in males and rectouterine pouch in females.

The carrying angle (approximately 170� in males, more in females) allows the forearm to clear the hip during walking and permits objects to be carried clear of the body. Excessive carrying angle (cubitus valgus) can predispose to ulnar nerve problems at the elbow.
questions.question: What is the clinical significance of the carrying angle?
options: Allows arm to clear hip, prevents body collision
Serves to limit range of elbow motion

questions.question: The ophthalmic artery is a branch of which vessel?
questions.explanation: The ophthalmic artery is the first major branch of the internal carotid artery after it exits the cavernous sinus. It enters the orbit through the optic canal with the optic nerve. Branches include the central retinal artery, which is an end artery supplying the retina.

The long head of biceps (originating from supraglenoid tubercle) contributes to glenohumeral stability and resists superior humeral head displacement. The short head (coracoid origin) provides more direct flexion power. Both heads function in elbow flexion and supination, but the long head has additional shoulder stabilization role.
options: Long head for stability, short head for power
questions.question: How do the two heads of biceps contribute differently to function?
Which space lies proximal to the carpal tunnel in the forearm?
questions.explanation: The space of Parona extends from the proximal margin of the carpal tunnel to the mid-forearm. Its roof is formed distally by flexor digitorum profundus tendons and proximally by the belly of flexor digitorum superficialis. The floor consists of pronator quadratus distally and interosseous membrane proximally.

The iliacus muscle is part of the posterior abdominal wall, not the anterior wall, originating from the iliac fossa and inserting with psoas major onto the lesser trochanter of the femur as the iliopsoas tendon. The anterior abdominal wall muscles include three flat muscles (external oblique, internal oblique, and transversus abdominis) and two vertical muscles (rectus abdominis and pyramidalis). The iliacus is innervated by the femoral nerve and functions primarily as a hip flexor, while the anterior abdominal wall muscles are involved in trunk movement and increasing intra-abdominal pressure.
questions.question: Which muscle is NOT part of the anterior abdominal wall?

questions.explanation: The spongy (penile) urethra begins where the membranous urethra exits the urogenital diaphragm and extends through the corpus spongiosum to the external urethral meatus at the tip of the glans penis. It is approximately 15 cm long and has two dilated portions: the intrabulbar fossa in the bulb and the navicular fossa in the glans.
questions.question: Where does the spongy urethra begin?

questions.explanation: The styloglossus muscle arises from the styloid process and inserts into the side of the tongue. It retracts and elevates the tongue during swallowing. Like all tongue muscles except palatoglossus, it is innervated by the hypoglossal nerve (XII). The muscle interdigitates with the hyoglossus.
questions.question: Which muscle originates from the styloid process and inserts on the tongue?

questions.explanation: The breast is separated from the deep fascia covering the underlying muscles by a layer of loose areolar tissue called the retromammary space. This space allows the breast some mobility over the pectoralis major muscle. The space is important surgically as it provides a plane for mastectomy.
questions.question: What separates the breast from deep fascia?

questions.explanation: Bronchial and pulmonary arteries anastomose at the precapillary level, creating connections between the systemic and pulmonary circulations. This anastomosis allows some mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood. The bronchial circulation comprises only about 1-2% of cardiac output.
questions.question: At which level do bronchial arteries anastomose?

questions.explanation: The fundus of the gallbladder projects beyond the inferior border of the liver at the tip of the right 9th costal cartilage, where it may contact the anterior abdominal wall. This location corresponds approximately to the point where the lateral edge of the right rectus abdominis crosses the right costal margin (at the transpyloric plane). The fundus is the only part of the gallbladder completely covered by peritoneum on all surfaces. When the gallbladder is distended or inflamed (acute cholecystitis), the fundus becomes palpable at this location, and deep palpation causes inspiratory arrest (Murphy's sign).
questions.question: The gallbladder fundus projects beyond which liver border?
Medial rotation at the hip joint is primarily performed by which three muscles?
options: Gluteus medius, minimus, and tensor fasciae latae
questions.explanation: Medial rotation at the hip joint is performed primarily by gluteus medius (anterior fibers), gluteus minimus (anterior fibers), and tensor fasciae latae. Lateral rotation is performed by obturator internus and externus, gemellus superior and inferior, quadratus femoris, piriformis, and posterior fibers of gluteus medius and maximus.

questions.question: The broad ligament contains which structure?
questions.explanation: The broad ligament is a double layer of peritoneum extending from the lateral pelvic wall to the uterus, containing multiple structures: the uterine tube in its superior free edge (mesosalpinx), the round ligament of uterus in its anteroinferior portion, the ovarian ligament posteriorly, and the ovarian vessels in its lateral extension (suspensory ligament of ovary/infundibulopelvic ligament). The broad ligament is divided into mesosalpinx (above ovary), mesovarium (posterior, supporting ovary), and mesometrium (below ovary, containing uterine vessels). It does not provide significant uterine support despite its name.

questions.question: The posterior tibial artery enters the sole of the foot through which structure, then divides into medial and lateral plantar arteries?
questions.explanation: The posterior tibial artery enters the sole of the foot through the tarsal tunnel (formed by the flexor retinaculum and medial ankle bones), accompanying the tibial nerve. It then divides into medial and lateral plantar arteries, supplying the plantar foot and contributing to the toes via the deep plantar arch. Its pulse is palpated inferoposterior to the medial malleolus.

questions.question: Which structure is NOT retroperitoneal?
questions.explanation: The transverse colon is intraperitoneal, suspended by the transverse mesocolon from the posterior abdominal wall. The ascending and descending colon are secondarily retroperitoneal (covered by peritoneum anteriorly only), as is most of the duodenum (except the first 2 cm) and the pancreas (except the tail which extends into the splenorenal ligament). Secondarily retroperitoneal structures were initially suspended by mesentery during development but became fused to the posterior body wall. Primarily retroperitoneal organs (kidneys, suprarenal glands, ureters, aorta, IVC) were never suspended by mesentery.

questions.question: Which flexure of the colon is located at a higher position?
questions.explanation: The splenic (left colic) flexure is positioned higher than the hepatic (right colic) flexure and also forms a more acute angle. The splenic flexure is attached to the diaphragm by the phrenicocolic ligament. This higher position of the left flexure is clinically significant in colonoscopy and surgical procedures.

Dupuytren's contracture results from progressive fibrosis of the palmar aponeurosis. Longitudinal bands thicken forming cords that cause progressive flexion contracture of fingers, typically ring and little fingers. The condition has genetic predisposition and is more common in males of Northern European descent.
questions.question: What causes Dupuytren's contracture?
What muscle action is lost in Saturday night palsy?
questions.explanation: Saturday night palsy results from radial nerve compression in the axilla, causing paralysis of wrist and finger extensors. This produces the characteristic "wrist drop" deformity. The condition is named for arm compression against a chair back during intoxicated sleep.

questions.question: Which structure lies immediately medial to the medial pterygoid muscle?
questions.explanation: The superior constrictor muscle of the pharynx lies medial to the medial pterygoid muscle, separated by a thin fascial layer. The medial pterygoid forms part of the lateral wall of the infratemporal fossa. This relationship is important when accessing the pharyngeal space surgically.

questions.question: Which nerve is at risk in supracondylar fractures of the humerus?
questions.explanation: The median nerve is at risk in supracondylar fractures of the humerus, along with the brachial artery. These injuries are common in children from falls on outstretched hands. Nerve damage can cause loss of thumb opposition and sensation in the lateral three and one-half fingers.

questions.question: What produces flexion at the wrist joint?
options: Flexor carpi ulnaris and radialis, flexor digitorum superficialis
questions.explanation: Flexion at the wrist is produced mainly by flexor carpi ulnaris and flexor carpi radialis muscles. The flexor digitorum superficialis provides assistance to this movement. All wrist movements are performed by forearm muscles crossing the wrist joint.

questions.question: Which nerve provides motor supply to diaphragm?
questions.explanation: The phrenic nerve (C3, 4, 5) provides the entire motor supply to the diaphragm. Each phrenic nerve supplies its corresponding half of the diaphragm up to the margin of the esophageal opening. Injury to the phrenic nerve results in paralysis of that hemidiaphragm with consequent elevation.

The olecranon fits into the olecranon fossa during extension while the coronoid fits into the coronoid fossa during flexion. This reciprocal architecture allows full range elbow motion (0-150�) while providing bony stability. The radial fossa accommodates the radial head during flexion.
questions.question: What is the functional significance of the olecranon-coronoid architecture?
Which artery supplies the majority of blood to the greater curvature of the stomach?
questions.explanation: The left gastroepiploic (gastro-omental) artery, a branch of the splenic artery, is the dominant vessel supplying the greater curvature of the stomach, anastomosing with the smaller right gastroepiploic artery from the gastroduodenal trunk. These vessels run along the greater curvature within the gastrocolic ligament, giving branches to both anterior and posterior surfaces of the stomach. The short gastric arteries contribute to the fundus but represent a minor component of the greater curvature blood supply.

questions.question: Which hamstring muscle has a short head originating from the linea aspera and NOT from the ischial tuberosity?
questions.explanation: Biceps femoris has two heads: the long head from the ischial tuberosity (in common with semitendinosus) and the short head from the linea aspera and lateral supracondylar line of the femur. The short head does not cross the hip joint and is supplied by the common fibular division (not tibial division) of the sciatic nerve.

questions.question: What connects the papillary muscles to the valve cusps?
questions.explanation: Chordae tendineae (heart strings) are thin, strong tendinous cords that connect the papillary muscles to the free edges and ventricular surfaces of the AV valve cusps. They prevent the valve cusps from prolapsing into the atrium during ventricular contraction. Rupture of chordae tendineae causes acute valvular regurgitation, often requiring surgical repair.

questions.question: The internal anal sphincter is formed from which layer?
questions.explanation: The internal anal sphincter is a thickening of the circular smooth muscle layer of the rectum, extending from the anorectal junction to approximately the level of the white line of Hilton, covering the upper three-quarters of the anal canal. It is under autonomic (involuntary) control, receiving sympathetic innervation (L1-L2 via hypogastric plexuses) that promotes contraction and parasympathetic innervation (S2-S4 via pelvic splanchnic nerves) that causes relaxation. This sphincter maintains resting anal tone and unconscious fecal continence, while the external anal sphincter (striated voluntary muscle supplied by inferior rectal nerve) provides voluntary control.

questions.question: Which structure forms the roof of the nasopharynx?
questions.explanation: The roof of the nasopharynx is formed by the body of the sphenoid bone and the basilar part of the occipital bone. The pharyngeal tonsil (adenoids) lies in the mucosa of this roof and posterior wall. The clivus (posterior cranial base) forms the anatomical background to this region.

questions.question: What is the primary function of the thoracic cage?
questions.explanation: The thoracic cage primarily functions to protect the lungs, heart, and great vessels from external trauma. Additionally, it provides attachment points for muscles of the thorax, upper limb, abdomen, and back. The cage also plays a vital role in the mechanics of respiration through its elastic properties.

questions.question: What is the anatomical position of the glenohumeral joint capsule's weakest area?
questions.explanation: The glenohumeral joint capsule is weakest inferiorly, making this the most common site for dislocation. The capsule is thin and lax to allow wide range of movement, particularly abduction. Superior movement of the humeral head is prevented by the coraco-acromial arch rather than capsular strength.

questions.question: The main pancreatic duct typically joins the bile duct at which location?
questions.explanation: The main pancreatic duct (duct of Wirsung) typically joins the common bile duct within the wall of the second (descending) part of the duodenum to form the hepatopancreatic ampulla (ampulla of Vater), which opens at the major duodenal papilla. The accessory pancreatic duct (duct of Santorini), when patent, opens separately at the minor duodenal papilla approximately 2 cm proximal to the major papilla. Anatomical variations exist, including separate openings of the pancreatic and bile ducts (pancreas divisum). The junction is surgically significant during ERCP and pancreaticoduodenectomy (Whipple procedure).

The bicipital aponeurosis reinforces the cubital fossa roof and protects the brachial artery and median nerve during venipuncture. It distributes biceps force to the ulna and forearm fascia. Historically recognized as the grace of God tendon for protecting vital structures during bloodletting.
questions.question: What is the functional significance of the bicipital aponeurosis?
options: Provides muscle attachment to bicipital fascia
Reinforces cubital fossa, protects neurovascular structures

questions.question: At which rib level is the axilla base formed?
questions.explanation: The base of the axilla is formed by skin, subcutaneous tissue, and axillary fascia spanning from the fourth rib. This base is concave and forms the floor of the axillary space. The axillary fascia is continuous with the pectoral fascia anteriorly and latissimus dorsi fascia posteriorly.

The occipital artery participates in the cruciate anastomosis at the suboccipital region along with branches of the vertebral artery and deep cervical artery. This anastomosis provides collateral circulation to the brain and spinal cord. The occipital artery also anastomoses with the posterior auricular and superficial temporal arteries on the scalp.
questions.question: Which artery anastomoses to form the cruciate anastomosis?

questions.explanation: The base of the heart is formed primarily by the left atrium and a small portion of the right atrium. It is the posterior surface facing the vertebral column and esophagus. The four pulmonary veins enter the left atrium at the base. The term "base" refers to the posterior aspect, opposite to the apex, not to the inferior surface.
questions.question: Which chamber primarily forms the base of the heart?

questions.explanation: The internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve provides sensory innervation above the vocal cords, including the epiglottis and vestibule. Below the cords, sensation is supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve. This division is clinically important for regional anesthesia during laryngoscopy.
questions.question: The superior laryngeal nerve's internal branch provides sensation to which region?

questions.explanation: The scala vestibuli and scala tympani communicate at the apex of the cochlea through the helicotrema. Both scalae contain perilymph. Sound vibrations travel up the scala vestibuli, through the helicotrema, and back down the scala tympani. The basilar membrane separates the scala tympani from the scala media (cochlear duct).
questions.question: The scala vestibuli communicates with the scala tympani through which structure?

questions.explanation: The epiploic foramen (foramen of Winslow) has the hepatoduodenal ligament (free right edge of lesser omentum) containing the portal triad as its anterior boundary. The superior boundary is formed by the caudate lobe of liver covered with peritoneum, the inferior boundary by the first part of the duodenum (superior or horizontal part), and the posterior boundary by the inferior vena cava covered with parietal peritoneum and the right crus of the diaphragm. This opening, typically admitting two fingers, provides the only communication between the greater and lesser peritoneal sacs.
questions.question: Which structure forms the anterior boundary of the epiploic foramen?

questions.explanation: The posterior wall of the axilla is formed by subscapularis on the anterior surface of the scapula superiorly, and teres major and latissimus dorsi inferiorly. The posterior axillary fold extends farther inferiorly than the anterior wall and can be grasped between fingers.
questions.question: Which muscles form the posterior wall of the axilla?
Which is the most medial, most superficial, and weakest muscle of the adductor group, uniquely crossing both hip and knee joints?
questions.explanation: Gracilis is the most medial, most superficial, and weakest member of the adductor group. It is the only member to cross both the hip and knee joints. Its tendon joins sartorius and semitendinosus at the pes anserinus on the medial tibia. It is used as a donor muscle in gracilis free flap reconstructive surgery due to its consistent anatomy.

questions.question: What causes esophageal varices?
questions.explanation: Esophageal varices develop due to portal hypertension (commonly from liver cirrhosis). Elevated portal venous pressure causes dilation of the portosystemic anastomoses at the lower esophagus. These dilated, tortuous veins (varices) can rupture, causing massive, life-threatening hematemesis. Treatment includes endoscopic banding and beta-blockers.

McBurney's (gridiron) incision for appendectomy divides (cuts) the external oblique aponeurosis in the direction of its fibers, then splits (separates) the internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles in the direction of their fibers. This muscle-splitting approach preserves the neurovascular supply and provides good healing with reduced hernia risk. The incision is centered on McBurney's point.
questions.question: Which muscle does McBurney's incision divide?

questions.explanation: To drain the apical (superior) segment of the lower lobe, the patient should lie prone with the head turned to one side. This position allows gravity to assist drainage of secretions from this segment. Different positions are used for postural drainage of different bronchopulmonary segments.
questions.question: What position drains apical lower lobe segment?

questions.explanation: The greater and lesser splanchnic nerves pierce the crura of the diaphragm through two lesser apertures in each crus. The hemiazygos vein also pierces the left crus. The sympathetic trunks pass behind the diaphragm deep to the medial arcuate ligament without piercing the diaphragm itself.
questions.question: Through which opening do splanchnic nerves pass?
Which ligament suspends the lens of the eye?
questions.explanation: The suspensory ligament (zonules of Zinn) connects the lens equator to the ciliary processes. These zonular fibers transmit tension from the ciliary muscle to the lens capsule, controlling lens shape for accommodation. When ciliary muscle contracts, zonular tension decreases, allowing the elastic lens to become more spherical for near vision.

questions.question: How many papillary muscles are in the right ventricle?
questions.explanation: The right ventricle typically has three papillary muscles (anterior, posterior, and septal) corresponding to the three cusps of the tricuspid valve. Each papillary muscle gives chordae tendineae to two adjacent cusps. The left ventricle has only two papillary muscles (anterior and posterior), which are larger and stronger, each providing chordae to two cusps of the mitral valve.

questions.question: The anterior arch of C1 articulates with which structure?
questions.explanation: The anterior arch of the atlas (C1) has a facet on its posterior surface that articulates with the dens (odontoid process) of the axis (C2). The transverse ligament of the atlas holds the dens against this facet. This atlantoaxial joint allows rotation of the head. Fracture or ligamentous injury can cause atlantoaxial instability.

questions.question: What is the most lateral bony point in the shoulder region?
questions.explanation: The greater tubercle of the humerus is the most lateral bony point in the shoulder region. It projects laterally below and in front of the acromial angle. This prominence can be palpated and felt to move during rotation of the humerus.

The left lung has several impressions on its mediastinal surface including: cardiac impression (the largest), aortic arch groove, descending aorta groove, subclavian artery groove, esophageal and tracheal grooves, and brachiocephalic vein groove. The aortic impressions are particularly prominent.
questions.question: What impression is on the left lung medially?

questions.explanation: Superficial and deep parotid lymph nodes lie within or on the parotid gland substance. They drain the scalp, auricle, external acoustic meatus, and parotid gland itself. Efferents pass to the superficial and deep cervical nodes. The presence of lymph nodes within the gland complicates parotid tumor surgery and influences surgical planning.
questions.question: Which lymph nodes are located in the parotid gland?

questions.explanation: There are three taeniae coli on the large intestine: the free taenia, mesocolic taenia, and omental taenia. These bands converge at the root of the appendix and disappear at the rectosigmoid junction. The taeniae are approximately 1 cm wide and their contraction creates the characteristic sacculated appearance of the colon.
questions.question: How many taeniae coli are present on the colon?

questions.explanation: The pterygomaxillary fissure is a vertical opening between the lateral pterygoid plate (posteriorly) and the maxilla (anteriorly), connecting the infratemporal and pterygopalatine fossae. The maxillary artery and mandibular nerve branches pass through this fissure. It forms the lateral boundary of the pterygopalatine fossa.
questions.question: The pterygomaxillary fissure connects which two regions?
options: Middle cranial fossa and pterygopalatine fossa

questions.explanation: The superficial palmar arch is formed primarily by the ulnar artery with contribution from the superficial palmar branch of the radial artery. The arch curves across the palm at the level of the distal border of the fully extended thumb. It gives rise to three common palmar digital arteries.
questions.question: Which artery forms the main contribution to the superficial palmar arch?

questions.explanation: The parietal peritoneum lining the anterior abdominal wall receives blood supply from the same vessels that supply the overlying abdominal wall: superior and inferior epigastric arteries, deep circumflex iliac artery, and lumbar arteries. The peritoneum overlying the diaphragm is supplied by the musculophrenic and phrenic arteries, while that in the pelvis is supplied by branches of the internal iliac artery. The visceral peritoneum covering the organs receives its blood supply from the arteries supplying those organs (celiac trunk, superior and inferior mesenteric arteries). Venous and lymphatic drainage follows arterial supply patterns.
questions.question: The parietal peritoneum of the anterior abdominal wall is supplied by which vessels?
What passes through the aortic hiatus?
questions.explanation: The aortic hiatus at T12 transmits the descending thoracic aorta (which continues as the abdominal aorta), the thoracic duct, and sometimes the azygos and hemiazygos veins. This is the lowest and most posterior of the three main openings. It lies between the crura rather than through them.

options: Five: calcaneus, talus, navicular, cuboid, one cuneiform
Seven: talus, calcaneus, cuboid, navicular, and three cuneiforms
Six: talus, calcaneus, navicular, cuboid, and two cuneiforms
Eight: talus, calcaneus, cuboid, navicular, and four cuneiforms
Seven: talus, calcaneus, navicular, cuboid, and three metatarsals
questions.question: The foot contains how many tarsal bones, and what are they?
questions.explanation: The foot contains seven tarsal bones: talus, calcaneus, cuboid, navicular, and three cuneiform bones (medial, intermediate, and lateral). The 26 bones of the foot include 7 tarsals, 5 metatarsals, and 14 phalanges. Understanding tarsal anatomy is fundamental to interpreting foot radiographs and managing tarsal fractures.

questions.question: The azygos vein passes through which diaphragmatic opening?
questions.explanation: The azygos vein passes through the aortic hiatus of the diaphragm (at T12 level) along with the aorta and thoracic duct, posterior to the diaphragmatic crura. The aortic hiatus is actually a midline gap between the crura rather than a true opening in the diaphragmatic muscle. The azygos vein drains the posterior thoracic and abdominal walls and provides important collateral circulation between the superior and inferior vena cavae. It arches over the right main bronchus to drain into the superior vena cava. The hemiazygos vein may also pass through the aortic hiatus.

questions.question: How many bronchopulmonary segments exist in right lung?
questions.explanation: The right lung contains ten bronchopulmonary segments: three in the upper lobe (apical, posterior, anterior), two in the middle lobe (lateral, medial), and five in the lower lobe (superior/apical, medial basal, anterior basal, lateral basal, posterior basal). Each segment is functionally independent.

DVT most commonly begins in the posterior tibial and fibular veins of the calf, often in valve sinuses where flow is stagnant. From here, thrombus can propagate proximally into the popliteal and femoral veins. The deep veins are the primary concern because thrombus there can embolize to the pulmonary circulation, causing potentially fatal pulmonary embolism. Superficial thrombophlebitis occurs in the saphenous veins.
questions.question: Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) most commonly develops in the deep veins of the leg. Which two veins are most commonly involved initially?
The tail of the pancreas extends into which ligament?
questions.explanation: The tail of the pancreas extends laterally and slightly superiorly, reaching to within 1 cm of the splenic hilum in approximately 75% of individuals, lying within the splenorenal ligament along with the splenic artery and vein. This relationship is surgically significant during splenectomy, as the pancreatic tail must be identified and preserved to prevent iatrogenic pancreatitis or pancreatic fistula. The body of the pancreas lies anterior to the splenic vein (which runs along its posterior surface) and behind the posterior wall of the lesser sac (omental bursa), separated from it by the gastrosplenic ligament.

The right renal artery passes posterior to both the right renal vein and the inferior vena cava as it courses from the aorta (at L1-L2 level, just below the superior mesenteric artery) to the right kidney hilum. The right renal artery is longer than the left due to the aorta's left-sided position. Both renal arteries also pass posterior to the corresponding psoas major muscle and ureter. The arteries typically divide into anterior and posterior divisions before entering the hilum, supplying corresponding segments of the kidney. The right artery may give off the inferior suprarenal artery.
questions.question: The right renal artery passes posterior to which structure?

questions.explanation: Each ureter is approximately 25 cm long, extending from the renal pelvis to the urinary bladder. The ureter descends on the psoas major muscle, crosses the pelvic brim at the bifurcation of the common iliac artery, and enters the bladder at the lateral angles of the trigone. It is a muscular tube that propels urine by peristaltic contractions.
questions.question: How long is the ureter in adults?
What is the significance of the median nerve's dual cord origin?
questions.explanation: The median nerve's formation from lateral and medial cords ensures it receives contributions from all nerve roots (C5-T1) except sometimes C5. This broad root distribution explains why isolated cord injuries may only partially affect median nerve function. The distinctive M-shaped formation in the axilla is clinically recognizable.
options: Has no clinical or anatomical significance
Supply from both lateral and medial cords

questions.question: The pes anserinus on the superior medial tibia is formed by the combined insertion of which three muscles?
questions.explanation: The pes anserinus (goose's foot) is formed by the common tendinous insertion of sartorius, gracilis, and semitendinosus on the superior medial surface of the tibia. These three muscles belong to three different thigh compartments yet all cross both the hip and knee joints and share this common insertion. Pes anserinus bursitis is a clinical condition here.

questions.question: Which ligament connects the lesser curvature of the stomach to the liver?
questions.explanation: The gastrohepatic ligament (pars flaccida) forms the membranous portion of the lesser omentum, extending from the lesser curvature of the stomach and first part of the duodenum to the liver (extending to the fissure for ligamentum venosum and porta hepatis). It contains the right and left gastric vessels along the lesser curvature, and in some individuals, an aberrant or replaced left hepatic artery arising from the left gastric artery. The lesser omentum is continuous with the hepatoduodenal ligament (pars condensa), which forms its thickened free right edge containing the portal triad.

The posterior fontanelle (lambda) is located at the junction of the sagittal and lambdoid sutures where the occipital and parietal bones meet. It is triangular and smaller than the anterior fontanelle. The posterior fontanelle typically closes by 2-3 months of age. Delayed closure may indicate hydrocephalus or skeletal dysplasia.
questions.question: The posterior fontanelle is located at which suture junction?
Which structures pass through the sternocostal triangle?
questions.explanation: The sternocostal triangles (foramina of Morgagni) are small gaps between the sternal and costal attachments of the diaphragm. The superior epigastric vessels (terminal branches of internal thoracic artery and vein) and lymphatic vessels pass through these triangles. They connect the thoracic and abdominal cavities and are potential sites for diaphragmatic hernias.

questions.question: Which muscle retracts the angle of the mouth laterally?
questions.explanation: The risorius muscle retracts the angle of the mouth laterally, producing a grin or grimace. It arises from the parotid fascia and inserts into the angle of the mouth. The muscle is innervated by the buccal branch of the facial nerve. It works with zygomaticus major in smiling. Some individuals lack this muscle.

questions.question: What structure passes superficial to the flexor retinaculum?
questions.explanation: The palmaris longus tendon (when present) passes superficial to the flexor retinaculum and inserts into it along with the palmar aponeurosis. The ulnar nerve and artery also pass superficial to the retinaculum through Guyon's canal. All flexor tendons and the median nerve pass deep to the retinaculum through the carpal tunnel.

questions.question: The incisive foramen transmits which nerve?
questions.explanation: The incisive foramen (canal) in the anterior hard palate transmits the nasopalatine nerves, which provide sensation to the anterior palate. The foramen also transmits terminal branches of the greater palatine vessels. The nasopalatine nerve is a branch of the maxillary nerve via the pterygopalatine ganglion.

questions.question: Which nerve may be injured during appendectomy?
questions.explanation: The genitofemoral nerve (L1, L2), emerging through the anterior surface of psoas major, may be at risk during appendectomy if the appendix has a retrocecal position or if dissection extends medially. The nerve's genital branch enters the inguinal canal at the deep ring, while the femoral branch passes beneath the inguinal ligament. Injury can cause sensory loss over the upper anterior thigh (femoral branch) and anterior scrotum/labium majus (genital branch), along with loss of the cremasteric reflex. The ilioinguinal nerve may also be at risk during gridiron or Lanz incisions for appendectomy.

Portal vein thrombosis causes portal hypertension by obstructing blood flow to the liver, leading to increased pressure in the portal system. This can cause splenomegaly, ascites, and development of portosystemic collaterals including esophageal varices, hemorrhoids, and caput medusae. Causes include hypercoagulable states, cirrhosis, pancreatitis, and abdominal sepsis. Chronic thrombosis may lead to cavernous transformation of the portal vein.
questions.question: Which condition results from portal vein thrombosis?

questions.explanation: Peyer's patches are aggregated lymphoid nodules characteristic of the ileum, especially prominent in the terminal ileum. These are permanent features of the gut-associated lymphoid tissue (GALT) that play a crucial role in intestinal immunity. Peyer's patches are absent in the jejunum and located on the antimesenteric border of the ileum.
questions.question: Which lymphoid structures are characteristic of the terminal ileum?

questions.explanation: Lymph vessels from the anterior part of intercostal spaces drain into anterior intercostal nodes that lie along the internal thoracic artery. From these nodes, lymph passes to the parasternal nodes. Posterior intercostal lymphatics drain into posterior intercostal nodes in the posterior mediastinum.
questions.question: Where do anterior intercostal lymphatics drain?

questions.explanation: The Circle of Willis is situated around the pituitary infundibulum and optic chiasma at the base of the brain. It provides collateral circulation when major arteries become occluded. The circle includes anterior cerebral, anterior communicating, internal carotid, posterior communicating, and posterior cerebral arteries.
options: Internal acoustic meatus and jugular foramen
Superior orbital fissure and optic canal
questions.question: The Circle of Willis is located around which anatomical structures?
What is the function of anconeus muscle?
questions.explanation: Anconeus is a small muscle that assists triceps brachii in elbow extension. It is located on the posterior aspect of the elbow, blending with the lateral head of triceps. The muscle is supplied by the radial nerve.

questions.question: What guides surgical segmental resection?
questions.explanation: Intersegmental veins running in the connective tissue septa between segments serve as guides for surgical separation during segmentectomy. The surgeon can identify these veins and use them to define segmental boundaries, allowing precise resection of diseased segments while preserving healthy lung tissue.

The femoral triangle is bounded superiorly by the inguinal ligament, laterally by the sartorius, and medially by the adductor longus. Its floor is formed by the iliopsoas laterally and the pectineus medially. Its roof is the fascia lata and cribriform fascia. It contains the femoral nerve, artery, vein, and deep inguinal lymph nodes arranged laterally to medially (NAVEL from lateral).
questions.question: The femoral triangle is bounded by which three structures?
options: Inguinal ligament, sartorius, and adductor longus
Inguinal ligament, adductor magnus, and iliopsoas
Iliac crest, sartorius, and adductor longus
Inguinal ligament, rectus femoris, and adductor magnus

questions.explanation: The superior constrictor muscle forms the floor (bed) of the tonsillar fossa, separated from the tonsil by the tonsillar capsule. The palatoglossus and palatopharyngeus form the anterior and posterior pillars respectively. Loose areolar tissue separates the capsule from the superior constrictor, facilitating surgical dissection.
questions.question: Which structure forms the floor of the tonsillar fossa?
Which muscle is paralyzed causing winged scapula?
questions.explanation: Paralysis of serratus anterior causes scapular winging due to weakness of the most powerful scapular protractor. The long thoracic nerve (C5, C6, C7) supplies this muscle. Winging becomes more apparent when pushing against resistance, as the medial border lifts away from the chest wall.

questions.question: Which movements must occur together for full shoulder abduction beyond 90 degrees?
questions.explanation: Full shoulder abduction beyond 90 degrees requires synchronized glenohumeral abduction and scapular upward rotation (scapulohumeral rhythm). For every 3 degrees of abduction, approximately 2 degrees occur at the glenohumeral joint and 1 degree from scapular rotation. This demonstrates upper limb integrated function.
options: Glenohumeral abduction and scapular upward rotation

questions.explanation: The thyroid gland is bound to the larynx and trachea by the pretracheal fascia. This attachment causes the thyroid to move with the larynx during swallowing. The isthmus overlies the second to fourth tracheal rings while the lobes extend from the thyroid cartilage downward.
questions.question: The thyroid gland is attached to which laryngeal structure?

questions.explanation: The right phrenic nerve passes through the superior and middle mediastinum descending on the right side of the superior vena cava (SVC) and heart. The left phrenic nerve similarly descends on the left side of the heart. Both nerves terminate in the diaphragm, providing motor and sensory innervation.
questions.question: Which nerve descends on the right side of SVC?
Which muscle is the ONLY abductor of the vocal cords?
questions.explanation: The posterior cricoarytenoid muscle is the sole abductor of the vocal cords, externally rotating the arytenoid cartilages. All other intrinsic laryngeal muscles are adductors or tensors of the vocal cords. Bilateral paralysis of this muscle causes life-threatening airway obstruction requiring immediate intervention.

The ligamentum venosum is the fibrous remnant of the fetal ductus venosus, which shunted oxygenated blood from the umbilical vein to the inferior vena cava during intrauterine life. It lies in a fissure on the visceral surface of the liver between the caudate and left lobes. After birth, when the ductus venosus closes, it becomes the ligamentum venosum.
questions.question: Which structure lies in the fissure for the ligamentum venosum?
What position drains apical pneumothorax?
questions.explanation: For draining a pneumothorax (air), which accumulates in the non-dependent (uppermost) part of the pleural cavity, the patient should be sitting upright. Air rises, so chest drain insertion for pneumothorax is typically in the 2nd intercostal space in the midclavicular line (anteriorly and superiorly) to access the apex where air collects.

The great auricular nerve (C2-C3) provides sensory innervation to the skin over the parotid gland and lower auricle. The auriculotemporal nerve carries postganglionic parasympathetic secretomotor fibers (not sensory to the gland). The facial nerve traverses the gland but doesn't innervate it. Parotid surgery risks great auricular nerve injury causing numbness.
questions.question: Which nerve supplies the parotid gland with sensory fibers?

questions.explanation: The right and left bundle branches divide into Purkinje fibers, which form a subendocardial network that rapidly conducts the impulse throughout the ventricular myocardium. Purkinje fibers are larger than regular cardiac myocytes with fewer myofibrils, specialized for rapid conduction rather than contraction. They ensure coordinated ventricular contraction from apex to base.
questions.question: Into which fibers do the bundle branches terminate?

questions.explanation: The splenic artery is the largest branch of the celiac trunk and has a characteristic tortuous course along the superior border of the pancreas. It runs from right to left within the splenorenal ligament before dividing into 5-7 branches at the splenic hilum. The artery gives off numerous pancreatic branches, short gastric arteries, and the left gastroepiploic artery.
questions.question: Which is the largest branch of the celiac trunk?

questions.explanation: The root (origin) of the mesentery is approximately 15 cm long, extending obliquely from the duodenojejunal flexure to the ileocaecal junction. Despite this short root attachment, the mesentery fans out to accommodate the 5-6 meters of small bowel. The root crosses the third part of the duodenum, aorta, IVC, right psoas muscle, and right gonadal vessels.
questions.question: What is the approximate length of the mesentery root attachment?
Which lymph nodes receive drainage from the chin?
questions.explanation: The submental lymph nodes lie between the anterior bellies of the digastric muscles and drain the chin, central lower lip, floor of mouth, and tip of tongue. Efferents pass to submandibular and jugulo-omohyoid nodes. These nodes are examined when staging oral cavity cancers.

questions.question: What epithelium lines the urinary bladder?
questions.explanation: The urinary bladder is lined by transitional epithelium (urothelium), a specialized stratified epithelium that can stretch and accommodate changes in bladder volume without tearing. When the bladder is empty, the epithelium appears thick with 5-6 cell layers; when distended, it thins to 2-3 layers. This epithelium is impermeable to salts and water.

The arytenoid cartilage comprises 40% of the vocal cord, while the remaining 60% is membranous (cricovocal ligament covered by mucosa). This anatomical proportion is important for understanding vocal cord pathology and surgical planning. The cartilaginous portion provides the posterior attachment point for the vocal ligament.
questions.question: What percentage of the vocal cord structure consists of the arytenoid cartilage?

questions.explanation: The ulnar nerve supplies all the interossei (palmar and dorsal) and the medial two lumbricals (to ring and little fingers). It also supplies the hypothenar muscles, adductor pollicis, and the medial head of flexor pollicis brevis. The lateral two lumbricals are supplied by the median nerve.
questions.question: Which intrinsic hand muscles are supplied by the ulnar nerve?
options: All interossei and medial two lumbricals

questions.question: The danger triangle of the face drains venously to which structure?
questions.explanation: The danger triangle connects via the angular and ophthalmic veins to the cavernous sinus without intervening valves. Facial infections in this region can lead to cavernous sinus thrombosis through retrograde venous spread. The triangle is bounded by the corners of the mouth and the bridge of the nose.

questions.question: The facial vein commonly anastomoses with which intracranial structure?
questions.explanation: The facial vein communicates with the cavernous sinus via the superior ophthalmic vein and deep facial vein to the pterygoid plexus. These connections lack valves, allowing bidirectional flow. Infections in the danger triangle of the face can spread to the cavernous sinus, causing cavernous sinus thrombosis.

The conjoint tendon (inguinal falx or conjoined tendon) is formed by the fusion of the aponeuroses of the internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles as they insert onto the pubic crest and pectineal line. This structure reinforces the posterior wall of the inguinal canal in its medial third, opposite the superficial inguinal ring. Weakness or absence of the conjoint tendon in Hesselbach's triangle (bounded by lateral border of rectus, inguinal ligament, and inferior epigastric artery) predisposes to direct inguinal hernias. The external oblique does not contribute to the conjoint tendon; instead, its aponeurosis forms the anterior wall of the canal and the superficial ring.
questions.question: Which muscle's fibers contribute to the conjoint tendon?
Which nerve roots form the upper trunk of the brachial plexus?
questions.explanation: The upper trunk is formed by union of C5 and C6 nerve roots. Injury to the upper trunk causes Erb's paralysis with characteristic policeman's tip hand deformity. The upper trunk gives rise to the suprascapular nerve and nerve to subclavius.

questions.question: Which artery supplies blood to the gallbladder?
questions.explanation: The cystic artery, most commonly arising from the right hepatic artery within Calot's triangle (75% of cases), provides the primary blood supply to the gallbladder. It typically divides into superficial (supplying the peritoneal surface) and deep (supplying the hepatic surface) branches. Anatomical variations are common, with the cystic artery occasionally arising from the left hepatic, common hepatic, gastroduodenal, or superior mesenteric arteries. Careful identification during cholecystectomy is essential to avoid injury to aberrant vessels or the right hepatic artery. The gallbladder may also receive small arterial branches from the liver bed.

Complete section of a phrenic nerve results in complete paralysis and eventual atrophy of the corresponding half of the diaphragm. The paralyzed hemidiaphragm shows paradoxical movement: moving upward during inspiration and downward during expiration. Unilateral paralysis is often asymptomatic; bilateral causes severe respiratory compromise.
questions.question: What happens with complete phrenic nerve section?
Which structure indents each renal papilla?
