questions.explanation: Each renal papilla (apex of a renal pyramid) is indented by a cup-shaped minor calyx that collects urine. There are typically 8-12 minor calyces in each kidney. Two or three minor calyces unite to form a major calyx, and 2-3 major calyces join to form the renal pelvis.

questions.question: The medial wall of the orbit is formed primarily by which bone?
questions.explanation: The medial orbital wall is formed primarily by the orbital plate (lamina papyracea) of the ethmoid bone. This thin bone separates the orbit from ethmoidal air cells. Fractures can cause orbital emphysema when air enters from the sinuses. The lacrimal bone contributes anteriorly.

The greater splanchnic nerve, after synapsing in the celiac ganglion, provides sympathetic innervation to foregut-derived organs including the stomach, liver, gallbladder, pancreas, spleen, small intestine, and proximal colon (to the splenic flexure). It also carries visceral afferent fibers for pain sensation from these organs.
questions.question: Which organs receive greater splanchnic innervation?

questions.explanation: Maisonneuve fracture involves a high (proximal) fibular fracture combined with disruption of the tibiofibular syndesmosis (inferior tibiofibular ligament complex) and interosseous membrane. This creates a unstable ankle mortise (syndesmotic diastasis) despite the intact lateral ankle. It is caused by an external rotation force. The high fibular fracture may be missed if only the ankle is radiographed.
questions.question: Proximal fibular fractures (Maisonneuve fracture) associated with ankle injuries disrupt which ligament, creating ankle instability?
What causes peau d'orange appearance?
questions.explanation: Infiltration of Cooper's ligaments by breast cancer leads to their shortening, producing tethering of the skin with a characteristic dimpled appearance resembling orange peel (peau d'orange). This is an important clinical sign of locally advanced breast cancer. The dimpling becomes more apparent when the patient raises her arms.

questions.question: Which duct drains the majority of the pancreatic tissue?
questions.explanation: The main pancreatic duct of Wirsung begins in the tail and runs through the entire length of the gland, receiving numerous tributaries along its course. It drains the majority of pancreatic tissue and usually joins the common bile duct to form the hepatopancreatic ampulla. This ampulla opens at the major duodenal papilla in the second part of the duodenum.

The tympanic plexus on the promontory of the middle ear is formed primarily by the tympanic branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve (Jacobson's nerve). Contributions also come from the caroticotympanic nerves (sympathetic). The plexus provides sensation to the middle ear mucosa. The lesser petrosal nerve arises from this plexus.
questions.question: The tympanic plexus is formed primarily by which nerve?

questions.explanation: The subcostalis muscle is an incomplete sheet on the inner surface of the lower ribs near their angles. Its fibers cross more than one intercostal space (unlike intercostal muscles which span single spaces). It is part of the innermost layer of thoracic wall muscles.
questions.question: What is the subcostal muscle?

questions.explanation: The portal tract (portal triad) is located at the corners of hepatic lobules and contains branches of the portal vein, hepatic artery, and bile duct, surrounded by connective tissue. Some also include lymphatic vessels. The portal triad delivers blood and removes bile from the hepatic lobule. The hepatic artery provides oxygen; the portal vein provides nutrients and metabolites from the GI tract.
questions.question: Which hepatic structure contains the portal triad?

questions.explanation: The gastrosplenic ligament contains the short gastric vessels (arteries and veins, 4-6 pairs) passing from the splenic vessels near the hilum to the gastric fundus, and the left gastroepiploic vessels running to the greater curvature. The splenic artery, splenic vein, and tail of the pancreas run in the splenorenal ligament, not the gastrosplenic ligament. These two ligaments together connect the spleen to the stomach and posterior abdominal wall. Division of the gastrosplenic ligament is necessary during splenectomy, requiring ligation of the short gastric and left gastroepiploic vessels to devascularize the spleen.
questions.question: Which structure passes through the gastrosplenic ligament?

questions.explanation: The lesser sciatic foramen transmits five structures: the pudendal nerve, nerve to obturator internus, internal pudendal artery and vein, and the tendon of obturator internus. The sciatic nerve exits through the greater sciatic foramen. The lesser sciatic foramen enables re-entry into the perineum from the gluteal region.
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT among the structures passing through the lesser sciatic foramen?

options: T12�L5 vertebrae, intervening discs, and all lumbar transverse processes
L1-L5 vertebral bodies only, no disc or process
T12-L4 vertebral bodies only without processes
L2-S1 vertebral levels and intervening discs
questions.question: The psoas major originates from which vertebral levels, including transverse processes?
questions.explanation: Psoas major originates from the sides of T12-L5 vertebrae and their intervening discs, as well as from the transverse processes of all lumbar vertebrae. It inserts into the lesser trochanter together with iliacus (forming iliopsoas). A psoas abscess from vertebral tuberculosis can track along this muscle to present as a groin swelling.

options: Extension of the thigh at the hip
Flexion of the leg at the knee
Extension of the trunk when thigh and knee are flexed
Medial rotation of the leg by biceps femoris
Lateral rotation of the leg by biceps femoris when knee is flexed
questions.explanation: Biceps femoris laterally rotates the leg when the knee is flexed, NOT medially rotates it. Semitendinosus and semimembranosus medially rotate the leg when the knee is flexed. This opposing rotation between the medial and lateral hamstrings provides the knee with important rotational control during walking and athletic movements.
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a correct action of the hamstring muscles?
How many arterial arcades typically supply the ileum?
questions.explanation: The ileum is supplied by 3 to 6 tiers of arterial arcades formed by branches of the superior mesenteric artery. These multiple arcades provide collateral circulation and ensure adequate blood supply to the bowel. In contrast, the jejunum typically has only 1 to 2 arterial arcades with longer vasa recta.

questions.question: Which structure serves as the anatomical landmark within the greater sciatic foramen, defining the relationship of all other structures to it?
questions.explanation: The piriformis muscle is the landmark structure in the greater sciatic foramen. All other structures are described relative to it: the superior gluteal nerve and vessels pass above it, while all seven other nerves and five vessels pass below it. This anatomical knowledge is essential for safe gluteal intramuscular injections.

questions.question: Which nerve is at risk in medial epicondyle fractures?
questions.explanation: The ulnar nerve passes behind the medial epicondyle in the ulnar groove, making it vulnerable to injury in medial epicondyle fractures. Damage causes numbness in the ulnar one and one-half fingers and weakness of intrinsic hand muscles. This can result in claw hand deformity.

options: The cuboid and calcaneus being wedge-shaped
The intermediate and lateral cuneiforms being wedge-shaped
The plantar surfaces of all tarsals being flat
questions.question: Which factor provides the bony contribution to the transverse arch, with the intermediate and lateral cuneiforms being specifically wedge-shaped?
questions.explanation: The intermediate and lateral cuneiforms are wedge-shaped, with their broader surfaces dorsally and narrower surfaces plantarly, providing the bony factor to the transverse arch. The ligaments (deep transverse metatarsal ligament and interosseous ligaments), the muscle fibularis longus, the transverse head of adductor hallucis, and slips of tibialis posterior all contribute to maintaining this arch.

The sentinel lymph node is the first lymph node to receive drainage from a tumor. It is identified during sentinel node biopsy using radioactive tracer or blue dye. If the sentinel node is negative for cancer, downstream nodes are unlikely to be involved, potentially avoiding extensive lymph node dissection.
questions.question: What is a sentinel lymph node?
Which enzyme in pancreatic juice digests proteins?
questions.explanation: Trypsinogen is the inactive precursor (zymogen) of trypsin, a protease that digests proteins. It is activated by enterokinase in the duodenum to form trypsin, which then activates other pancreatic proteases (chymotrypsinogen, proelastase, procarboxypeptidase) in a cascade. Pancreatic juice contains multiple proteases, each cleaving peptide bonds at specific amino acid sequences. Premature activation within the pancreas causes acute pancreatitis.

The lesser sciatic foramen is bounded by the lesser sciatic notch of the ischium, the sacrospinous ligament superiorly, and the sacrotuberous ligament inferiorly. The pudendal nerve and internal pudendal vessels exit the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen (below piriformis), hook around the ischial spine, and re-enter the pelvis through the lesser sciatic foramen to reach the pudendal canal in the lateral wall of the ischioanal fossa. The tendon of obturator internus also exits through this foramen. The sciatic nerve exits only through the greater sciatic foramen without re-entering the pelvis.
questions.question: Which structure passes through the lesser sciatic foramen?
What are white rami communicantes?
questions.explanation: White rami communicantes carry preganglionic sympathetic fibers from spinal nerves T1-L2 to the sympathetic trunk. They are white because the preganglionic fibers are myelinated. These fibers originate from intermediolateral cell columns in the thoracolumbar spinal cord. White rami exist only at T1-L2 levels.

The anal columns of Morgagni are 6-10 permanent longitudinal mucosal folds in the upper 15 mm of the anal canal, above the pectinate line, containing terminal radicles of the superior rectal veins (portal system). The lower ends of adjacent columns are connected by anal valves (semilunar mucosal folds), forming the pectinate (dentate) line. Superior to each valve is a small recess called an anal sinus, into which anal glands open. The columns have a plum-red color in living subjects due to the underlying internal rectal venous plexus, and internal hemorrhoids develop from these vascular columns.
questions.question: The anal columns (of Morgagni) are found in which part of the anal canal?

questions.explanation: Auerbach's (myenteric) plexus is located between the circular and longitudinal layers of the muscularis externa throughout the gastrointestinal tract. It controls gut motility, including peristalsis and segmentation. Damage to this plexus (as in Chagas disease or Hirschsprung disease) causes severe motility disorders. It contains both excitatory and inhibitory motor neurons.
questions.question: Where is Auerbach's plexus located in the gut wall?

options: Special sensory (taste) from anterior two-thirds tongue
questions.explanation: The chorda tympani carries special sensory (taste) fibers from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and parasympathetic secretomotor fibers to submandibular and sublingual glands. It branches from the facial nerve in the mastoid, crosses the middle ear, and joins the lingual nerve. Damage causes loss of taste on the ipsilateral anterior tongue.
questions.question: The chorda tympani nerve carries which type of fibers?

questions.explanation: The upper lateral quadrant is the safe zone for intramuscular injections in the gluteal region. This avoids the sciatic nerve, which courses midway between the ischial tuberosity and the greater trochanter. Injections in other quadrants risk sciatic nerve injury, causing foot drop and sensory loss.
questions.question: The safe quadrant for intramuscular injection in the gluteal region is which of the following?
Which arteries supply the bronchial tree?
questions.explanation: The bronchial arteries supply the bronchial tree from the main bronchi to the respiratory bronchioles. Two left bronchial arteries arise from the descending thoracic aorta, and one right bronchial artery arises from the third right posterior intercostal artery. These vessels provide oxygenated blood to airway structures.

The suspensory ligament of the ovary (infundibulopelvic ligament), a lateral extension of the broad ligament, suspends the ovary from the lateral pelvic wall and contains the ovarian artery (from aorta) and ovarian vein (to IVC on right, left renal vein on left), along with ovarian nerves and lymphatics. This ligament must be clamped and divided during oophorectomy. The ovarian ligament connects the ovary to the uterus medially, while the broad ligament provides only indirect support via the mesovarium. The round ligament extends from uterus to labium majus via the inguinal canal.
questions.question: The ovary is suspended by which ligament from the pelvic wall?

questions.explanation: The sphenopalatine foramen in the medial wall of the pterygopalatine fossa connects it with the nasal cavity. The foramen is located between the sphenoid bone and orbital process of the palatine bone. The sphenopalatine artery and nasopalatine nerve pass through it to supply the nasal cavity and septum.
questions.question: The pterygopalatine fossa communicates with the nasal cavity through which opening?

questions.explanation: The pancreatic acinus is the functional exocrine secretory unit, consisting of pyramid-shaped serous (enzyme-secreting) acinar cells arranged around a small lumen. The acinus is drained by an intercalated duct lined by centroacinar cells. Multiple acini drain into larger ducts, which eventually form the main pancreatic duct. The pancreas structurally resembles the parotid gland.
questions.question: What is the exocrine secretory unit of the pancreas called?

questions.explanation: On either side of the superior thoracic aperture, the opening is closed by the dense suprapleural membrane (also called Sibson's fascia). In the midline, structures pass between the neck and thorax. This membrane is a tent-shaped extension of endothoracic fascia that covers the apex of each lung.
questions.question: What closes the superior thoracic aperture laterally?

questions.explanation: The brachial artery is the main arterial supply to the arm and represents the continuation of the axillary artery. It begins at the inferior border of teres major and ends in the cubital fossa opposite the neck of the radius. Under cover of the bicipital aponeurosis, it divides into radial and ulnar arteries.
questions.question: Which artery provides the main arterial supply to the arm?
How many pulmonary veins emerge from each lung?
questions.explanation: Two pulmonary veins (superior and inferior) emerge from each lung, for a total of four pulmonary veins entering the left atrium. These veins carry oxygenated blood from the lungs to the heart. The openings of the pulmonary veins into the left atrium have no valves.

questions.question: The carotid body is a chemoreceptor sensitive to changes in which substance?
questions.explanation: The carotid body is a chemoreceptor sensitive to decreased arterial oxygen (hypoxemia), increased carbon dioxide (hypercapnia), and decreased pH (acidosis). It is located at the carotid bifurcation and is innervated by the glossopharyngeal nerve. The carotid sinus (baroreceptor) monitors blood pressure changes.

The pudendal nerve and internal pudendal vessels exit the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen (below piriformis), hook around the ischial spine (covered by sacrospinous ligament), and re-enter the pelvis through the lesser sciatic foramen to reach the pudendal canal (Alcock's canal) in the lateral wall of the ischioanal fossa. This unique course makes the pudendal nerve vulnerable to compression at the ischial spine (pudendal neuralgia). The nerve to obturator internus follows a similar course. No other major structures pass through both foramina; the sciatic nerve and other gluteal region structures exit only through the greater sciatic foramen.
questions.question: Which structure passes through both greater and lesser sciatic foramina?

questions.explanation: The transverse head of adductor hallucis originates from the plantar ligaments of the metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joints. Together with the oblique head (from bases of metatarsals 2-4), it inserts into the lateral side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the first digit. The transverse head contributes to maintaining the transverse arch by drawing the metatarsal heads together.
questions.question: The adductor hallucis has two heads. The transverse head originates from which structure and contributes to maintaining which arch?
options: Bases of metatarsals 2-4; medial longitudinal arch
Plantar ligaments of MTP joints; transverse arch

questions.explanation: Piriformis syndrome occurs when the sciatic nerve is compressed by a hypertrophied or spasmodic piriformis muscle. The sciatic nerve normally passes below piriformis; in approximately 10-15% of individuals, part or all of the nerve passes through the muscle, increasing vulnerability. It presents with buttock pain radiating down the posterior thigh (mimicking lumbar disc herniation) and is exacerbated by sitting.
questions.question: Piriformis syndrome causes buttock and posterior thigh pain by compressing which nerve as it passes through or near the piriformis muscle?
Which bone accounts for approximately one-quarter of a person's total height and averages 45 cm in length?
questions.explanation: The femur is the longest and strongest bone in the body, averaging 45 cm in length. It accounts for approximately one-quarter of a person's total height. The femur articulates with the acetabulum superiorly and the patella and tibia inferiorly.

questions.question: Which imaging best visualizes the mediastinum?
questions.explanation: CT (computed tomography) scan with contrast is the best imaging modality for visualizing mediastinal structures. It provides excellent detail of masses, lymphadenopathy, vascular structures, and anatomical relationships. MRI is also excellent, particularly for vascular and cardiac structures. Chest X-ray provides basic information but limited detail.

questions.question: Which structure forms the floor of the posterior triangle?
questions.explanation: The floor of the posterior triangle is formed by the prevertebral fascia covering splenius capitis, levator scapulae, and scalene muscles (anterior, middle, posterior). The subclavian artery and brachial plexus emerge between the scalene muscles. The accessory nerve crosses the triangle superficially on this floor. Cervical lymph nodes lie within the triangle.

The infraorbital foramen on the anterior surface of the maxilla transmits the infraorbital nerve (continuation of maxillary nerve V2) and vessels. The nerve emerges about 1 cm below the infraorbital margin. It provides sensation to the lower eyelid, lateral nose, and upper lip. The foramen is a landmark for regional anesthesia.
questions.question: The infraorbital foramen transmits which nerve?

questions.explanation: The pleural cavities are lined by mesothelium, a specialized layer of simple squamous epithelial cells. This smooth lining produces pleural fluid that lubricates the surfaces. The visceral pleura covers the lung surface while the parietal pleura lines the thoracic cavity walls.
questions.question: Which type of tissue lines the pleural cavities?

questions.explanation: Serratus anterior is the most powerful protractor of the scapula, pulling it forward around the chest wall. Paralysis of this muscle causes scapular winging, where the medial border of the scapula protrudes from the back. The muscle is supplied by the long thoracic nerve (C5, C6, C7).
questions.question: What is the primary action of serratus anterior?

questions.explanation: Barrett's esophagus is a premalignant condition where the normal stratified squamous epithelium of the lower esophagus is replaced by metaplastic columnar epithelium (intestinal metaplasia). This occurs due to chronic gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). It increases the risk of esophageal adenocarcinoma and requires surveillance.
questions.question: What is Barrett's esophagus?
Which vein receives the left renal vein?
questions.explanation: Both right and left renal veins drain into the inferior vena cava. The left renal vein is approximately three times longer than the right and crosses anterior to the aorta to reach the IVC. The left renal vein receives the left suprarenal vein, left gonadal (testicular or ovarian) vein, and communicates with the ascending lumbar vein.

questions.question: What is the functional significance of extensor expansion?
questions.explanation: The extensor expansion (extensor hood) distributes extensor digitorum force and coordinates intrinsic hand muscle action with extrinsic extensors. Intrinsic muscles insert into the expansion, enabling their unique MCP flexion with IP extension action. This complex structure allows coordinated finger movements essential for precision grip.
options: Distributes extensor force, coordinates intrinsic-extrinsic action

questions.explanation: The pericardiacophrenic vessels (branches of internal thoracic artery and vein) accompany the phrenic nerve on each side as it descends through the thorax to the diaphragm. These vessels supply the pericardium, pleura, and diaphragm. The phrenic nerve lies between the fibrous pericardium and mediastinal pleura.
questions.question: Which vessels run with the phrenic nerve?

questions.explanation: Proximal hamstring avulsion (ischial tuberosity avulsion) occurs during sudden forceful hip flexion with the knee extended, as in the full stride of sprinting. This violent stretch exceeds the tensile strength of the proximal hamstring attachment. Athletes present with acute posterior thigh pain and inability to sprint. MRI confirms the degree of retraction of the avulsed hamstring.
options: Sudden forceful hip flexion with knee extended (sprint stride)
Slow walking on flat ground at low speed
Passive knee extension while lying down
questions.question: Hamstring injuries are common in sprinting athletes. Which specific action most commonly causes a proximal hamstring avulsion?
What is the safest chest drain insertion site?
questions.explanation: The "safe triangle" for chest drain insertion is bounded by: anterior border of latissimus dorsi, lateral border of pectoralis major, a line superior to the horizontal level of the nipple (in males), and an apex below the axilla. This typically corresponds to the 5th intercostal space in the midaxillary line. This location minimizes risk to neurovascular structures and breast tissue.

questions.question: Which muscle forms the floor of the posterior abdominal wall?
questions.explanation: The posterior abdominal wall is formed by multiple muscles: psoas major (medially, originating from lumbar vertebrae), quadratus lumborum (laterally, between 12th rib and iliac crest), and iliacus (below iliac crest, in iliac fossa). Together these muscles, along with the diaphragm superiorly and the lumbar vertebrae and their processes, create the musculoskeletal framework of the posterior abdominal wall. The transversus abdominis wraps around from the anterolateral wall to attach to these structures. These muscles are covered anteriorly by psoas fascia, quadratus lumborum fascia, and iliac fascia respectively, with retroperitoneal organs and vessels lying anterior to these fascial layers.

The conjoint tendon (inguinal falx), formed by the fusion of the internal oblique and transversus abdominis aponeuroses, forms the medial part of the posterior wall and medial boundary of the inguinal canal. Weakness here predisposes to direct inguinal hernias. The lateral part of the posterior wall is formed by the transversalis fascia.
questions.question: Which structure forms the medial boundary of the inguinal canal?

questions.explanation: Retraction (adduction) of the scapula is produced by combined action of middle fibers of trapezius and the rhomboid muscles. During retraction, the lateral end of the clavicle moves backward along with the scapula. This movement is important for pulling actions.
questions.question: What is the primary muscle for scapular retraction?

questions.explanation: Patellofemoral syndrome is closely associated with weakness of the vastus medialis oblique (VMO), the distal oblique fibers of vastus medialis. VMO weakness allows the patella to track laterally in the trochlear groove, causing increased patellofemoral contact pressure and pain. VMO strengthening exercises (terminal knee extension, shallow squats) are the cornerstone of rehabilitation.
questions.question: Patellofemoral syndrome (anterior knee pain) is characterized by pain around the patella, aggravated by stairs and squatting. Which muscle weakness most contributes to this condition?
Which structure lies in the hepatoduodenal ligament's free edge?
questions.explanation: The hepatoduodenal ligament (pars condensa, the thickened free right edge of the lesser omentum) contains the portal triad: portal vein (posteriorly), common bile duct (anteriorly and to the right), and hepatic artery proper (anteriorly and to the left). The relationship is remembered as "DAV" from right to left anteriorly (Duct, Artery, Vein). This ligament forms the anterior boundary of the epiploic foramen and is the structure compressed during the Pringle maneuver to control bleeding during hepatic surgery. Lymph nodes and autonomic nerve plexuses also course through this ligament.

Olfactory nerve axons from the nasal epithelium pass through multiple foramina in the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone. These first-order sensory neurons synapse in the olfactory bulb above the cribriform plate. Head trauma can shear these delicate fibers causing anosmia.
questions.question: The olfactory nerves pass through which structure?

questions.explanation: The promontory on the medial wall of the tympanic cavity is formed by the basal turn of the cochlea. The facial nerve canal runs above it. The oval and round windows are also located on the medial wall. The tympanic plexus lies on the promontory providing sensation to the middle ear mucosa.
questions.question: Which structure forms the medial wall of the tympanic cavity?
Which muscle fibers form the conjoint tendon?
questions.explanation: The conjoint tendon (inguinal falx) is formed by the fusion of the aponeuroses of the internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles, inserting onto the pubic crest and pectineal line. This tendon reinforces the posterior wall of the inguinal canal in its medial third, opposite the superficial inguinal ring. Weakness or absence of the conjoint tendon in the area medial to the inferior epigastric artery predisposes to direct inguinal hernias, which protrude through Hesselbach's triangle bounded by the lateral border of rectus abdominis, inguinal ligament, and inferior epigastric vessels.

options: Bases of all five metatarsals only
Three cuneiforms and navicular bones only
Navicular and talus bones only proximally
Calcaneus and cuboid of the lateral column only
Three cuneiforms and cuboid proximally; five metatarsal bases distally
questions.question: The transverse arch is formed proximally by which bones?
questions.explanation: The transverse arch is formed proximally by the three cuneiforms and the cuboid, and distally by the bases of the five metatarsals. When both feet are approximated, the medial borders form a complete transverse arch, with each foot representing a half dome. The intermediate and lateral cuneiforms are wedge-shaped, contributing the bony factor to the transverse arch.

The anterior and lateral cutaneous branches of the 4th to 6th intercostal nerves supply the breast. These nerves convey sensory fibers to the skin, sympathetic fibers to blood vessels, and fibers to smooth muscle in the overlying skin and nipple. Pain from breast pathology follows these dermatomes.
questions.question: Which intercostal nerves supply the breast?

questions.explanation: The posterior portion of the hard palate is formed by the horizontal plates of the palatine bones. The anterior portion is formed by the palatine processes of the maxillae. The hard palate separates the oral and nasal cavities and provides a rigid surface for the tongue during mastication.
questions.question: Which bone forms the hard palate posteriorly?

questions.explanation: The renal vessels (particularly the renal veins attached to the IVC) are the main structures preventing excessive descent of the kidneys. The renal fascia provides minimal support. Loss of perirenal fat (in cachexia) can lead to nephroptosis (floating kidney), where the kidney descends excessively with positional changes, potentially causing ureteric kinking and obstruction.
questions.question: What prevents the kidney from descending more than normal?

questions.explanation: Coxa valga, with a neck-shaft angle increased above normal, is associated with congenital dislocation of the femoral head. It results in a relatively longer limb and altered gait mechanics. In contrast, coxa vara, with a reduced neck-shaft angle, follows fracture of the neck of femur.
questions.question: Coxa valga, with an increased neck-shaft angle of the femur, is characteristically associated with which clinical condition?
options: Fracture of the neck of femur
Congenital dislocation of the femoral head

questions.question: The superior mesenteric vein receives blood from all EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The superior mesenteric vein receives tributaries corresponding to branches of the superior mesenteric artery (jejunal, ileal, ileocolic, right colic, middle colic veins) plus the right gastroepiploic vein and inferior pancreaticoduodenal veins. The inferior mesenteric vein typically drains into the splenic vein (behind the pancreas) rather than the superior mesenteric vein, though variations exist. The SMV ascends to the right of the SMA, passes anterior to the third part of the duodenum and uncinate process of pancreas, and joins the splenic vein behind the neck of the pancreas to form the portal vein.

The mesentery of the small intestine, with its oblique root extending from the duodenojejunal flexure (L2, left of midline) to the right sacroiliac joint (S1, right of midline), divides the infracolic compartment into right and left infracolic spaces. These spaces communicate laterally with the right and left paracolic gutters respectively. The paracolic gutters are depressions lateral to the ascending and descending colon where peritoneal fluid can track between the pelvis and upper abdomen. The right paracolic gutter communicates with the hepatorenal recess, providing a pathway for infection spread.
questions.question: Which structure separates the right and left paracolic gutters?

questions.explanation: The right lung is divided into three lobes (superior, middle, and inferior) by two fissures: the oblique and horizontal fissures. The left lung has only two lobes (superior and inferior) separated by the oblique fissure. The presence of a middle lobe makes the right lung larger than the left.
questions.question: How many lobes does the right lung contain?
Which lymph node is found in the femoral canal?
questions.explanation: Cloquet's node (node of Rosenmuller) is the most superior of the deep inguinal lymph nodes, located in the femoral canal (femoral ring) and receives lymph from the superficial and deep inguinal nodes. It drains to the external iliac nodes. The femoral canal is the medial compartment of the femoral sheath (lateral to the lacunar ligament, medial to the femoral vein) and represents a potential weakness where femoral hernias occur. Virchow's node is in the left supraclavicular fossa, Sister Mary Joseph node at the umbilicus, and Calot's node in Calot's triangle.

The superior and inferior lingular segments of the left upper lobe are anatomically equivalent to the middle lobe of the right lung. The lingula is a tongue-like projection of the left upper lobe that occupies the space below the cardiac notch. Both are supplied similarly by their respective bronchi.
questions.question: What are the lingular segments?
Which nerve is compressed in pronator teres syndrome?
questions.explanation: The median nerve is compressed between the two heads of pronator teres in pronator teres syndrome. This entrapment neuropathy causes forearm pain and median nerve sensory symptoms. Unlike carpal tunnel syndrome, palm sensation is affected as compression occurs proximal to the palmar cutaneous branch.

questions.question: Which nerve is at risk in crutch palsy?
questions.explanation: Crutch palsy results from radial nerve compression in the axilla due to improperly fitted crutches pressing against the nerve. This causes wrist drop and loss of finger extension. The condition is preventable by ensuring crutches are properly adjusted to avoid axillary pressure.

The lateral cricoarytenoid muscle adducts (closes) the vocal cords by internally rotating the arytenoid cartilages. Other adductors include the interarytenoid and thyroarytenoid muscles. All adductors are supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve. Bilateral adductor paralysis causes airway obstruction.
questions.question: Which muscle adducts the vocal cords?
The right crus of the diaphragm arises from which vertebral bodies?
questions.explanation: The right crus of the diaphragm arises from the anterolateral surfaces of the bodies and intervertebral discs of L1, L2, and L3 vertebrae (sometimes extending to L4), while the left crus arises from only L1 and L2 (sometimes L3). Both crura contribute to forming the esophageal hiatus, with muscle fibers from the right crus (and sometimes left) looping around the esophagus to create a muscular sphincter mechanism. The crura also form boundaries of the aortic hiatus, with the median arcuate ligament connecting them anterior to the aorta at T12 level.

The superior mesenteric vessels (artery and vein) and the root of the mesentery cross anteriorly to the horizontal (third) part of the duodenum. This anatomical relationship is clinically significant as compression by these vessels can cause superior mesenteric artery syndrome. The third part of the duodenum crosses the vertebral column from right to left at the L3 level.
questions.question: Which vessel crosses anterior to the horizontal (third) part of the duodenum?

questions.explanation: Lund's node (Calot's node) is located within Calot's triangle, bounded by the cystic duct, common hepatic duct, and inferior surface of the liver. This lymph node frequently becomes enlarged in cases of cholecystitis or cholangitis and may be removed during cholecystectomy. Calot's triangle is an important surgical landmark for identifying the cystic artery, which typically lies within this triangle. Careful dissection of this area is crucial during laparoscopic cholecystectomy to avoid injury to the hepatic ducts or right hepatic artery.
questions.question: Which lymph node is characteristically found in Calot's triangle?
The superior gluteal nerve (L4, L5, S1) supplies which muscles?
options: Gluteus medius, minimus, and tensor fasciae latae
questions.explanation: The superior gluteal nerve (L4, L5, S1) supplies gluteus medius, gluteus minimus, and tensor fasciae latae. It exits the greater sciatic foramen above piriformis. Injury to this nerve (during posterior hip surgery or gluteal injections) causes Trendelenburg sign due to loss of hip abduction and medial rotation. It carries no cutaneous branches.

The vas deferens (ductus deferens) develops from the mesonephric duct (Wolffian duct) in males under the influence of testosterone. In females, the mesonephric duct regresses due to absence of testosterone, while the paramesonephric duct (M?llerian duct) develops into the fallopian tubes, uterus, and upper vagina. The epididymis also develops from the mesonephric duct, while the seminal vesicles arise as outgrowths from the distal mesonephric duct. The prostate and bulbourethral glands develop from the urogenital sinus. Understanding embryology helps explain congenital anomalies of the reproductive tract.
questions.question: The vas deferens is derived from which embryological structure?

questions.explanation: Glucagon is produced by alpha cells in the pancreatic islets (islets of Langerhans) and increases blood glucose by promoting hepatic glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis. It opposes insulin action. Glucagon secretion is stimulated by low blood glucose, amino acids, and sympathetic stimulation. Alpha cells constitute about 20% of islet cells and are located peripherally in the islets.
questions.question: Which hormone is produced by the pancreatic alpha cells?

questions.explanation: The ulnar nerve passes through Guyon's canal (ulnar tunnel) at the wrist alongside the ulnar artery. The canal is bounded by the pisiform and hook of hamate. Compression here causes ulnar tunnel syndrome affecting hand muscles but sparing forearm muscles.
questions.question: Which nerve passes through Guyon's canal?

questions.explanation: The popliteus muscle weakly flexes the knee and unlocks it from full extension by rotating the femur 5 degrees on a fixed tibia (or medially rotating the tibia on an unplanted limb). It originates from the lateral femoral condyle and lateral meniscus, inserting on the posterior tibia. It is innervated by the tibial nerve (L4, L5, S1).
questions.question: The popliteus muscle 'unlocks' the knee from full extension by rotating the femur by how many degrees on the fixed tibia?

questions.explanation: Flexor carpi ulnaris and extensor carpi ulnaris work synergistically to produce pure wrist adduction (ulnar deviation). By contracting simultaneously, they balance flexion and extension forces while producing adduction. This demonstrates how muscles from different compartments can cooperate for specific movements.
questions.question: Which muscles work synergistically to produce pure wrist adduction?
The femoral ring is bounded medially by which structure?
questions.explanation: The femoral ring (the medial compartment of the femoral sheath) is bounded medially by the lacunar ligament (Gimbernat's ligament), laterally by the femoral vein, anteriorly by the inguinal ligament, and posteriorly by the pectineal ligament (Cooper's ligament) and pectineus muscle covered by fascia. The femoral ring normally contains a lymph node (Cloquet's node) and loose connective tissue. It represents a potential site of weakness where femoral hernias can occur (more common in women), protruding through the ring into the femoral canal. The rigid boundaries make strangulation a risk in femoral hernias.

questions.question: At which vertebral level does the rectum commence?
questions.explanation: The rectum begins as a continuation of the sigmoid colon at the level of the third sacral vertebra (S3). It extends approximately 13 cm (5 inches) before terminating as the anal canal one inch below the tip of the coccyx. The rectum follows the curvature of the sacrum and coccyx, forming the sacral and perineal flexures.

questions.question: Which nerve provides parasympathetic innervation to the submandibular gland?
questions.explanation: Preganglionic parasympathetic fibers in the chorda tympani (from facial nerve) synapse in the submandibular ganglion suspended from the lingual nerve. Postganglionic fibers supply the submandibular and sublingual glands. Sympathetic fibers from the superior cervical ganglion also reach the gland via the facial artery plexus.

options: Right costal margin at 9th costal cartilage
questions.explanation: The fundus of the gallbladder typically reaches the anterior abdominal wall at the tip of the right 9th costal cartilage, where the lateral edge of the right rectus abdominis muscle crosses the right costal margin (approximately at the transpyloric plane). This surface marking corresponds to the point where the gallbladder may contact the anterior abdominal wall, making it palpable when distended or inflamed. Murphy's sign (inspiratory arrest with deep palpation at this point due to pain) indicates acute cholecystitis. The fundus is the only part of the gallbladder completely covered by peritoneum.
questions.question: The gallbladder fundus typically lies at which anatomical landmark?

questions.explanation: is the only rotator cuff muscle that performs medial (internal) rotation of the humerus. It lies on the anterior surface of the scapula, filling the subscapular fossa. The other rotator cuff muscles (supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor) are located posteriorly.
questions.question: Which rotator cuff muscle performs medial rotation of the humerus?
The inferior vena cava is formed at which vertebral level?
questions.explanation: The inferior vena cava is formed by the union of the right and left common iliac veins at the level of the fifth lumbar vertebra (L5), to the right of the midline and anterior to the right common iliac artery. From this point, it ascends on the right side of the aorta, anterior to the vertebral column, receiving tributaries in an asymmetric pattern. The IVC passes through the diaphragm (caval opening in central tendon) at T8 level to enter the thorax and immediately empties into the right atrium. The formation level (L5) is slightly lower than the aortic bifurcation (L4).

questions.question: The fibular (lateral) collateral ligament is separated from the lateral meniscus by the tendon of which muscle?
questions.explanation: The tendon of popliteus passes deep to the fibular collateral ligament, separating it from the lateral meniscus. This is why the lateral meniscus is more freely movable than the medial meniscus. The popliteus tendon also creates a gap in the posterior fibrous capsule allowing its passage. The biceps femoris tendon is split by the fibular collateral ligament at the fibular head.

questions.question: The calcaneal tendon reflex (ankle jerk) tests which nerve roots when elicited by tapping the Achilles tendon?
questions.explanation: The calcaneal tendon (Achilles) reflex tests the S1 and S2 nerve roots. The reflex arc involves the tibial nerve (both afferent and efferent), the S1-S2 spinal cord segments, and the gastrocnemius and soleus muscles. An absent ankle jerk is a hallmark of S1 root compression (commonly from L5/S1 disc herniation). The knee jerk tests L3 and L4.

questions.question: What type of hernia occurs through the oesophageal hiatus?
questions.explanation: A sliding hiatal hernia is the most common type of diaphragmatic hernia (95% of hiatal hernias), where the gastroesophageal junction and part of the stomach slide up through the oesophageal hiatus into the thorax. This is often associated with gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). In paraesophageal hernias, the gastroesophageal junction remains in place, but part of the stomach herniates alongside the esophagus.

The white pulp of the spleen consists of lymphoid tissue surrounding central arterioles (periarterial lymphoid sheaths - PALS) and lymphoid nodules. It is the site of immune surveillance and antibody production in response to blood-borne antigens. The white pulp contains predominantly T lymphocytes in the PALS and B lymphocytes in the lymphoid follicles.
questions.question: What is the primary immunological function of splenic white pulp?

questions.explanation: Adjacent bronchopulmonary segments are separated by connective tissue septa. Intersegmental veins run in these septa and serve as guides for surgically separating segments. The septa act as natural barriers preventing spread of infection between segments (though cancer and tuberculosis can break through).
questions.question: What separates adjacent bronchopulmonary segments?

questions.explanation: The deep facial vein connects the facial vein with the pterygoid venous plexus in the infratemporal fossa, draining deep facial structures. The pterygoid plexus drains via the maxillary vein to the retromandibular vein. This valveless connection provides a route for infection spread between face and cavernous sinus.
options: Deep facial vein to pterygoid plexus
questions.question: Which vein drains the deep face?
Which condition is associated with rupture of the biceps long head?
questions.explanation: Biceps long head tendon rupture typically occurs in elderly individuals with degenerative tendon changes. The muscle belly retracts distally creating the characteristic "Popeye" sign. Despite dramatic appearance, functional deficit is surprisingly minimal as the short head remains intact and compensates adequately.

is a small triangular muscle that assists the triceps brachii in elbow extension. It lies on the lateral aspect of the elbow, blending with the triceps. Both muscles are supplied by the radial nerve and work together to extend the elbow.
questions.question: Which muscle assists triceps in elbow extension?

questions.explanation: The bare area of the liver, the part of the posterior surface devoid of peritoneal covering and in direct contact with the diaphragm, receives blood supply from the right phrenic artery (and sometimes left phrenic artery). This triangular area is bounded by the reflections of the coronary and right triangular ligaments. The bare area lies between the two layers of the coronary ligament and is continuous with the inferior vena cava, which is embedded in a groove on the posterior surface. Small diaphragmatic veins from the bare area drain directly into the IVC.
questions.question: Which artery supplies the bare area of the liver?

questions.explanation: The supraspinatus muscle initiates the first 0-15 degrees of shoulder abduction. The middle fibers of the deltoid then take over from 15-90 degrees. Beyond 90 degrees, scapular rotation by trapezius and serratus anterior is essential for achieving full overhead abduction.
questions.question: Which muscles initiate the first 0-15 degrees of shoulder abduction?

questions.explanation: The superior laryngeal nerve (from the vagus) divides into internal and external branches. The internal branch pierces the thyrohyoid membrane to provide sensation above the vocal cords. The external branch descends to innervate the cricothyroid muscle. Damage to the external branch affects voice pitch control.
questions.question: The superior laryngeal nerve divides into which two branches?
The medial pterygoid muscle inserts on which structure?
questions.explanation: The medial pterygoid muscle inserts on the medial surface of the mandibular angle and ramus, forming a sling with the masseter on the lateral surface. It arises from the medial surface of the lateral pterygoid plate and pterygoid fossa. The muscle elevates and protrudes the mandible. It is innervated by the nerve to medial pterygoid (V3).

The esophagus, vagus nerves, and thoracic duct all pass through both the superior and posterior mediastinum. The esophagus descends from the neck through the superior mediastinum into the posterior mediastinum before piercing the diaphragm at T10. Understanding these relationships is important for interpreting imaging.
questions.question: Which structure lies in both superior and posterior mediastinum?

questions.explanation: The fundus is the dilated, dome-shaped portion of the stomach that lies superior to the level of the cardiac orifice and cardiac notch. It is usually filled with gas and is in contact with the left dome of the diaphragm. The fundus can be distinguished radiographically as the gas bubble seen in upright chest X-rays.
questions.question: Which part of the stomach lies superior to the cardiac notch?
The jugulo-omohyoid node drains which structure primarily?
questions.explanation: The jugulo-omohyoid lymph node (principal node of the tongue) is located where the omohyoid muscle crosses the internal jugular vein. It receives drainage from the tip and anterior tongue (along with submental nodes). The node is part of the inferior deep cervical chain. Enlargement suggests anterior oral cavity or tongue pathology.

The seminal vesicles are located posterior to the fundus (base) of the urinary bladder, lateral to the ampulla of the vas deferens, anterior to the rectum (separated by rectovesical fascia), and superior to the prostate gland. They are elongated, lobulated structures that produce approximately 70% of seminal fluid volume, which is alkaline and contains fructose (energy for sperm), prostaglandins, and clotting factors. The duct of each seminal vesicle joins the ampulla of the corresponding vas deferens to form the ejaculatory duct, which passes through the prostate to open into the prostatic urethra.
questions.question: The seminal vesicles are located posterior to which structure?

questions.explanation: The porta hepatis transmits the portal vein, proper hepatic artery (and its right and left branches), right and left hepatic ducts, nerves (sympathetic and parasympathetic), and lymphatic vessels. These structures, except the hepatic ducts, enter the liver while the ducts exit. The portal triad (portal vein, hepatic artery, bile duct) is enclosed by the hepatoduodenal ligament at the free edge of the lesser omentum.
questions.question: Which structure passes through the porta hepatis?

questions.explanation: The superior mesenteric artery is the principal vessel supplying midgut derivatives, extending from just distal to the major duodenal papilla to the junction of the proximal two-thirds and distal one-third of the transverse colon. It originates from the abdominal aorta at the L1 level, immediately below the celiac trunk. Its branches include the inferior pancreaticoduodenal, jejunal, ileal, ileocolic, right colic, and middle colic arteries, providing blood to the duodenum (distal to ampulla), jejunum, ileum, cecum, appendix, ascending colon, and right two-thirds of transverse colon.
questions.question: The superior mesenteric artery supplies which embryological division of the gut?
Which nerve is the largest branch of the brachial plexus?
questions.explanation: The radial nerve (C5-T1) is the largest branch of the brachial plexus and the most frequently injured. It arises from the posterior cord and supplies all extensor muscles of the upper limb. The nerve is particularly vulnerable in the spiral groove of the humerus.

questions.question: The suspensory muscle of the duodenum (ligament of Treitz) arises from which structure?
questions.explanation: The suspensory muscle of the duodenum (ligament of Treitz) is a fibromuscular band arising from the right crus of the diaphragm near the esophageal hiatus (some sources describe both crura contributing), passing posterior to the pancreas to insert onto the duodenojejunal flexure and sometimes the horizontal part of the duodenum. It supports the duodenojejunal junction at the posterior abdominal wall and marks the transition from fixed (retroperitoneal) duodenum to mobile (intraperitoneal) jejunum. This landmark is important surgically and radiologically, as widening of the angle suggests a mass in the pancreatic head.

questions.question: Which artery anastomoses with the superior rectal artery?
questions.explanation: The superior rectal artery (terminal continuation of the inferior mesenteric artery) anastomoses with the middle rectal artery (from anterior division of internal iliac) in the wall of the rectum, creating a portosystemic anastomosis between portal (superior rectal vein to inferior mesenteric vein to portal vein) and systemic (middle rectal vein to internal iliac vein to IVC) venous systems. The inferior rectal artery (from internal pudendal) also anastomoses with these vessels at the level of the anal canal. In portal hypertension, these anastomoses may become varicose, contributing to rectal varices (internal hemorrhoids above the pectinate line).

questions.question: Which organism are asplenic patients most susceptible to?
questions.explanation: Asplenic patients (post-splenectomy or functional asplenia) are particularly susceptible to infections with encapsulated bacteria: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae type b, and Neisseria meningitidis. The spleen is crucial for opsonization and clearance of these organisms. Asplenic patients require vaccination against these organisms and may need prophylactic antibiotics (penicillin or amoxicillin).

questions.question: Which vessel lies in the gastrosplenic ligament?
questions.explanation: The gastrosplenic ligament, connecting the greater curvature of the stomach (fundus region) to the hilum of the spleen, contains the short gastric vessels (4-6 small arteries and veins from the splenic artery and vein). The left gastroepiploic vessels also pass through this ligament after arising from the splenic vessels near the hilum. The splenic artery and vein themselves run in the splenorenal ligament (along with the tail of the pancreas), not the gastrosplenic ligament. During splenectomy, the gastrosplenic ligament must be divided, ligating the short gastric and left gastroepiploic vessels.

The brachial artery bifurcates in the cubital fossa opposite the neck of the radius. This division occurs under cover of the bicipital aponeurosis into the radial artery (superficial) and ulnar artery (deeper). The cubital fossa provides a triangular space for this important vascular division.
questions.question: At what location does the brachial artery typically bifurcate into radial and ulnar arteries?

questions.explanation: The cremasteric reflex (elevation of the testis when the inner thigh is stroked) is mediated by the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve (L1-L2). The sensory stimulus from the femoral branch travels to L1-L2, and the motor response via the genital branch causes contraction of the cremaster muscle. Absence of this reflex may indicate testicular torsion.
questions.question: What is the cremasteric reflex mediated by?
Which muscle abducts and flexes the shoulder?
questions.explanation: fibers produce both shoulder flexion and assist with abduction. The anterior fibers also contribute to medial rotation. The deltoid muscle as a whole is multipennate, with different fiber groups producing different movements.

The sphincter of Oddi (sphincter ampullae) surrounds the hepatopancreatic ampulla (ampulla of Vater), controlling the release of bile and pancreatic juice into the second part of the duodenum. The sphincter choledochus surrounds the terminal bile duct just before its junction with the pancreatic duct, while the sphincter pancreaticus surrounds the terminal pancreatic duct. The sphincter of Oddi coordinates the flow from both ducts, relaxing in response to cholecystokinin during digestion and contracting between meals to allow bile storage in the gallbladder.
questions.question: The hepatopancreatic ampulla is surrounded by which sphincter?
At which location is the external intercostal muscle deficient?
questions.explanation: The external intercostal muscle is deficient anteriorly at the costochondral junction and is replaced by the external (anterior) intercostal membrane. This fibrous membrane continues the plane of the muscle to the sternum. The internal intercostal muscle conversely is deficient posteriorly at the angle of the rib.

questions.question: What maintains negative intrapleural pressure?
questions.explanation: The elastic recoil of the lungs pulling inward, opposed by the chest wall's tendency to spring outward, creates and maintains the negative (sub-atmospheric) pressure in the pleural cavity. This negative pressure is essential for keeping the lungs expanded and prevents their collapse.

Seven tendons insert into the greater trochanter: gluteus medius, gluteus minimus, piriformis, obturator internus, obturator externus, gemellus superior, and gemellus inferior. The concentration of these insertions makes the greater trochanter a key landmark in hip anatomy. Avulsion fractures at this site carry significant functional implications.
questions.question: How many tendons insert into the greater trochanter of the femur?

questions.explanation: Cholecystokinin (CCK) is released by I cells in the duodenal and jejunal mucosa in response to fats and proteins. It stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion from acinar cells and contraction of the gallbladder. Secretin, released in response to acid in the duodenum, stimulates pancreatic bicarbonate secretion from duct cells. Both hormones work synergistically to produce adequate pancreatic juice.
questions.question: Which hormone stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion?
The pterygoid venous plexus communicates with which important venous structure?
questions.explanation: The pterygoid venous plexus communicates with the cavernous sinus via emissary veins and deep facial veins. This valveless connection allows spread of infection from the infratemporal fossa to the cranial cavity. The plexus receives maxillary, middle meningeal, and deep temporal veins.

questions.question: Which muscle attaches to the pectineal line?
questions.explanation: The conjoint tendon (formed by fusion of internal oblique and transversus abdominis aponeuroses) inserts onto the pubic crest and pectineal line (pecten pubis), reinforcing the posterior wall of the inguinal canal medially. The pectineal ligament (Cooper's ligament) also attaches to the pectineal line and is used in some hernia repairs (Cooper's ligament repair). The rectus abdominis originates from the pubic crest and symphysis, not the pectineal line. The lacunar ligament (medial extension of the inguinal ligament) also attaches to the pectineal line.

The median cubital vein connects the basilic and cephalic veins superficially in the cubital fossa. This vein is commonly used for venipuncture, blood sampling, and intravenous infusions due to its prominence and accessibility. It lies superficial to the bicipital aponeurosis, which historically protected deeper structures during bloodletting.
questions.question: Which vein is commonly used for venipuncture in the cubital fossa?
Which sinus receives the great cerebral vein?
questions.explanation: The straight sinus receives the great cerebral vein (of Galen) and the inferior sagittal sinus. It runs in the junction of the falx cerebri and tentorium cerebelli. The sinus drains into the confluence of sinuses (typically preferentially into the left transverse sinus). Deep cerebral structures drain via this pathway.

questions.question: Which muscle is responsible for intorsion of the eye?
questions.explanation: The superior oblique is the primary intortor of the eye, also producing depression and abduction. The muscle passes through the trochlea before inserting on the posterolateral superior eyeball. It is innervated by the trochlear nerve (IV). Superior oblique palsy causes vertical diplopia, worse on downward gaze and head tilt to the affected side.

The cribriform plate is the horizontal portion of the ethmoid bone forming the roof of the nasal cavity and floor of the anterior cranial fossa. It contains numerous foramina transmitting olfactory nerve fibers. The crista galli projects superiorly from the midline. Fractures cause CSF rhinorrhea and anosmia from shearing of olfactory nerve fibers.
questions.question: The cribriform plate is part of which bone?

questions.explanation: Only the parietal pleura has somatic sensory innervation from intercostal and phrenic nerves, making it sensitive to pain. The visceral pleura has no somatic sensory nerve supply and receives only autonomic vasomotor innervation. This explains why pleural pain is sharp and well-localized to the chest wall.
questions.question: Which pleura has somatic sensory innervation?

options: Fascia lata of the thigh only
Camper's fascia of the anterior abdominal wall
Transversalis fascia anteriorly and iliac fascia posteriorly
questions.explanation: The femoral sheath is a prolongation of the transversalis fascia anteriorly and the iliac fascia posteriorly, enclosing the femoral artery, femoral vein, and the femoral canal (containing lymphatics). The femoral nerve lies outside the femoral sheath. A femoral hernia passes through the femoral canal into the femoral sheath inferior to the inguinal ligament.
questions.question: The femoral sheath is a prolongation of which fascia, enclosing the femoral vessels and the femoral canal?
Which structure lies between the pretracheal and prevertebral fascia?
questions.explanation: The pharynx, esophagus, larynx, trachea, and thyroid gland lie between the pretracheal and prevertebral fascia. The pretracheal fascia encloses these visceral structures while the prevertebral fascia covers the vertebral column and associated muscles. The retropharyngeal space lies between these fascial layers posteriorly.

questions.question: Which carpal bones form the medial side of the carpal arch base?
questions.explanation: The medial side of the carpal arch base is formed by the pisiform bone and the hook of the hamate. The lateral side is formed by the tubercles of the scaphoid and trapezium bones. The flexor retinaculum bridges across this arch, converting it into the carpal tunnel.

questions.question: Which part of the male urethra is least distensible?
questions.explanation: The membranous urethra is the shortest (1-2 cm), narrowest, and least distensible part of the male urethra. It passes through the urogenital diaphragm (deep perineal pouch) surrounded by the external urethral sphincter (sphincter urethrae muscle). This segment is most vulnerable to traumatic injury, particularly in pelvic fractures, and is the most difficult to dilate or catheterize.

questions.question: What nerve provides sensation to the regimental badge area?
questions.explanation: The superior lateral brachial cutaneous nerve, the sensory continuation of the axillary nerve, provides sensation to the skin over the deltoid muscle ("regimental badge" area). Loss of sensation in this area indicates axillary nerve injury. Testing sensation here helps diagnose nerve damage in shoulder trauma.

questions.question: The iliotibial band syndrome (runner's knee) involves friction of the iliotibial tract over which bony landmark during running?
questions.explanation: Iliotibial band syndrome involves repetitive friction of the iliotibial tract over the lateral femoral epicondyle during the flexion-extension cycle of running. This creates pain and inflammation at the lateral aspect of the knee. It is particularly common in long-distance runners. Treatment includes stretching, foam rolling, and correcting biomechanical factors such as hip abductor weakness.

questions.question: The transpyloric plane intersects which vertebral level?
questions.explanation: The transpyloric plane is an important anatomical landmark that passes through the first lumbar vertebra (L1), situated midway between the suprasternal notch and pubic symphysis. This plane transects numerous vital structures including the pylorus, neck of pancreas, origins of superior mesenteric artery and portal vein, duodenojejunal junction, and the hila of both kidneys. It serves as a crucial reference point for clinical examination and surgical procedures in the upper abdomen.

questions.question: Which test demonstrates ulnar nerve palsy?
questions.explanation: demonstrates ulnar nerve palsy by revealing adductor pollicis weakness. When gripping paper between thumb and index finger, the patient compensates for weak thumb adduction by flexing the thumb interphalangeal joint (using median nerve-supplied flexor pollicis longus). This abnormal flexion indicates ulnar nerve dysfunction.

The caudate lobe, although anatomically part of the right lobe, is functionally part of the left lobe based on blood supply and biliary drainage. It receives blood from both right and left hepatic arteries and drains bile into both right and left hepatic ducts. Similarly, the quadrate lobe receives blood from the left hepatic artery and drains into the left hepatic duct.
questions.question: Which lobe of the liver is functionally part of the left lobe?
The inferior mesenteric artery typically arises at which vertebral level?
questions.explanation: The inferior mesenteric artery originates from the anterior aspect of the abdominal aorta at the level of the third lumbar vertebra (L3), approximately 3-4 cm above the aortic bifurcation. This vessel supplies hindgut derivatives, including the left one-third of the transverse colon, descending colon, sigmoid colon, rectum, and upper anal canal. Its main branches include the left colic artery, sigmoid arteries (2-4 branches), and the superior rectal artery, which represents its terminal continuation descending into the pelvis.

questions.question: The long plantar ligament, an important supporter of the lateral longitudinal arch, passes from the calcaneus to which structures?
options: Sustentaculum tali of calcaneus and talus
All five metatarsal bases and the navicular
Base of 1st metatarsal and medial cuneiform
Plantar surface of cuboid and bases of 3rd�5th metatarsals
questions.explanation: The long plantar ligament (longest ligament in the foot) passes from the plantar surface of the calcaneus to the ridges on the plantar surface of the cuboid and the bases of the 3rd-5th metatarsals. It is a primary support for the lateral longitudinal arch. In combination with the short plantar (plantar calcaneocuboid) ligament, it forms the floor of the fibularis longus tendon groove on the cuboid.

options: Loss of dorsalis pedis pulse only
Palpable popliteal fossa pulsation with possible arterial bruit
questions.question: A popliteal aneurysm is clinically detected by which finding, with an additional auscultatory sign?
questions.explanation: A popliteal artery aneurysm (dilation beyond 50% of normal diameter) can be detected by a palpable pulsation in the popliteal fossa. An arterial bruit may also be heard on auscultation. The popliteal pulse requires deep palpation as the artery lies deep. Slight knee flexion relaxes the fascia to facilitate palpation.

questions.question: What percentage of pancreatic tissue is endocrine?
questions.explanation: Only about 1-2% of the pancreatic tissue consists of endocrine islets of Langerhans, with the remaining 98-99% being exocrine acinar tissue that produces digestive enzymes. Despite representing such a small proportion, the islets are crucial for glucose homeostasis. There are approximately 1 million islets in the human pancreas, most concentrated in the tail.

questions.question: What maintains gastroesophageal junction competence?
questions.explanation: Multiple factors maintain gastroesophageal junction competence preventing reflux: intrinsic LES tone, extrinsic compression by right crus sling fibers, acute angle of gastric entry (angle of His), positive intraabdominal pressure on the abdominal esophageal segment, and mucosal rosette at the cardia. Disruption causes GERD.

The suprasternal space (of Burns) lies between the investing and pretracheal layers of deep cervical fascia above the manubrium. It contains the jugular venous arch, lymph nodes, and fat. The space extends laterally behind the sternocleidomastoid muscles. Infections can collect here forming a suprasternal abscess.
questions.question: Which space lies between the pretracheal and investing layers of deep cervical fascia?
The small saphenous vein arises on the lateral side of the foot and ascends posterior to which malleolus before entering the popliteal vein?
questions.explanation: The small saphenous vein arises from the union of the dorsal vein of the little toe with the dorsal venous arch and ascends posterior to the lateral malleolus. It then passes along the lateral border of the calcaneal tendon, ascends between the heads of gastrocnemius, and empties into the popliteal vein in the popliteal fossa.

The submandibular ganglion is suspended from the lingual nerve by two branches in the submandibular region. Preganglionic parasympathetic fibers arrive via the chorda tympani, synapse in the ganglion, and postganglionic fibers supply the submandibular and sublingual glands. Sympathetic and sensory fibers pass through without synapsing.
questions.question: The submandibular ganglion is suspended from which nerve?

questions.explanation: Efferent lymph vessels from the deep popliteal lymph nodes travel along the femoral vessels to reach the inguinal lymph nodes. Afferent vessels reach the popliteal nodes from the knee joint and lymphatics accompanying leg arteries. Superficial popliteal nodes receive lymph from the region accompanying the small saphenous vein.
questions.question: Efferent lymph vessels from the deep popliteal lymph nodes travel along which vessels to reach the inguinal lymph nodes?

questions.explanation: The middle cranial fossa accommodates the temporal lobes of the brain laterally and the pituitary gland centrally. The floor is formed by the greater wings and body of the sphenoid and the petrous and squamous parts of the temporal bones. The fossa is wider than the anterior fossa. Multiple foramina pierce its floor.
questions.question: Which cranial fossa contains the temporal lobes?

questions.explanation: The inferior phrenic arteries are usually the first branches of the abdominal aorta, arising immediately after it passes through the aortic hiatus at T12, though they may arise from the celiac trunk. They supply the inferior surface of the diaphragm and give off superior suprarenal arteries. Each artery has a medial and lateral branch.
questions.question: From which vessel do the inferior phrenic arteries usually arise?

options: Roof: inferior fibula; walls: tibia bilaterally; floor: calcaneus
Roof: inferior tibia; walls: medial (tibial) and lateral (fibular) malleoli; floor: trochlea tali
Roof: superior surface of talus; walls: tibia; floor: calcaneus
Roof: superior tibia; walls: talus on both sides; floor: navicular
Roof: fibula; walls: medial and lateral malleoli; floor: navicular
questions.explanation: The ankle joint (mortise) is formed by: the roof (inferior surface of the tibia), the lateral wall (lateral malleolus from the fibula), the medial wall (medial malleolus from the tibia), and the floor (superior surface of the talus, the trochlea tali). This mortise-and-tenon configuration provides inherent bony stability, especially during dorsiflexion.
questions.question: The ankle (talocrural) joint is formed by three bony components. Which correctly describes the roof, walls, and floor?
How many separate joints are formed collectively by the 19 bones of the hand?
questions.explanation: The 19 bones of the hand (metacarpals and phalanges) collectively form 14 separate joints. These include the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints connecting fingers to palm and interphalangeal (IP) joints between finger segments. All are synovial joints with articular cartilage covering the bone surfaces.

questions.question: At which intercostal space does nipple usually lie?
questions.explanation: In males and most young nulliparous women, the nipple lies opposite the 4th intercostal space, approximately 10 cm from the anterior midline. This position is variable in females and changes with age, pregnancy, and parity. The position is more constant in males.

questions.question: Which muscle tenses the vocal cords?
questions.explanation: The cricothyroid muscle is the only muscle that tenses (lengthens) the vocal cords by tilting the thyroid cartilage forward on the cricoid. It is supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve. All other intrinsic laryngeal muscles are supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

Delta cells (D cells) comprise about 5-10% of islet cells and produce somatostatin, which inhibits both insulin and glucagon secretion, acting as a paracrine regulator. They are located peripherally in the islets. Somatostatin also inhibits growth hormone release from the pituitary (hence the name) and has widespread inhibitory effects on the GI tract.
questions.question: Which cells in pancreatic islets produce somatostatin?
Which vessel supplies the cecum?
questions.explanation: The cecum receives its blood supply from the ileocolic artery (terminal branch of the superior mesenteric artery), which divides into superior and inferior branches. The inferior branch gives rise to anterior and posterior cecal arteries that supply the corresponding surfaces of the cecum. The ileocolic artery also gives off the appendicular artery (to appendix) and ileal branches. The superior branch of the ileocolic artery anastomoses with the right colic artery along the ascending colon. The cecum's venous drainage follows the arterial pattern, with ileocolic vein draining to the superior mesenteric vein.

Female breasts start developing at puberty under hormonal influence (estrogen and progesterone). They remain rudimentary in males throughout life. Most breast development in females occurs during the later months of pregnancy and lactation when the glandular tissue proliferates and becomes functional.
questions.question: At what age does female breast development begin?
At which vertebral level does the duodenojejunal flexure lie?
questions.explanation: The duodenojejunal flexure is located at the level of the second lumbar vertebra (L2), approximately 2.5 cm to the left of the midline. This junction is supported by the suspensory muscle of the duodenum (ligament of Treitz), a fibromuscular band. The flexure marks the transition from the retroperitoneal duodenum to the intraperitoneal jejunum.

questions.question: The subtalar joint (talocalcaneal joint) primarily allows which movements of the foot?
questions.explanation: The subtalar joint (talocalcaneal joint) primarily allows inversion and eversion of the foot, with associated adduction and abduction. These movements occur at the subtalar joint and midtarsal joints together. True dorsiflexion and plantarflexion occur at the ankle (talocrural) joint. The summit of the lateral longitudinal arch is at the subtalar articulation.
options: Dorsiflexion and plantarflexion at the ankle
Circumduction only, without inversion or eversion
Inversion and eversion (with associated adduction and abduction)
Pronation and supination of the ankle

questions.explanation: In forced expiration, the abdominal muscles (rectus abdominis, internal/external obliques, transversus abdominis) contract forcibly. This pushes the abdominal viscera upward against the relaxed diaphragm, forcing it higher into the thorax. Quadratus lumborum also contracts to pull down the 12th rib.
questions.question: Which muscles aid forced expiration?

questions.explanation: The lower border of the soft palate marks the boundary between the nasopharynx above and the oropharynx below. The soft palate can elevate to close off the nasopharynx during swallowing. The pharyngeal isthmus connects these two regions and can be voluntarily controlled.
questions.question: Which structure marks the junction between the nasopharynx and oropharynx?

questions.explanation: The hepatorenal recess (Morison's pouch), located between the right lobe of the liver and the right kidney, is the most dependent (lowest) part of the peritoneal cavity when supine in males. This makes it a common site for fluid accumulation (blood, pus, ascites) in the supine position, detectable by ultrasound. In females, the rectouterine pouch (of Douglas) is the most dependent part. The hepatorenal recess communicates with the right subphrenic space superiorly and the right paracolic gutter inferiorly, providing pathways for fluid spread.
questions.question: Which peritoneal recess is the most dependent in the supine male?
Which sinus drains into the superior meatus?
questions.explanation: The posterior ethmoidal air cells drain into the superior meatus. The middle meatus receives drainage from the frontal, maxillary, and anterior ethmoidal sinuses. The inferior meatus receives the nasolacrimal duct. The sphenoethmoidal recess receives drainage from the sphenoid sinus.

questions.question: Which nerve passes through the mandibular notch?
questions.explanation: The masseteric nerve (from anterior division of V3) passes through the mandibular notch with the masseteric artery to supply the masseter muscle. It also provides articular branches to the temporomandibular joint. The nerve crosses lateral to the temporomandibular joint and deep to the tendon of temporalis muscle.

questions.question: What is the function of the marginal zone in the spleen?
questions.explanation: The marginal zone, located between the white pulp and red pulp, contains specialized marginal zone B lymphocytes and macrophages that capture blood-borne antigens and particulate matter. It is the first site of contact between blood-borne antigens and the immune system. Marginal zone B cells can rapidly differentiate into antibody-producing cells without requiring T cell help.

The tegmen tympani (thin plate of petrous temporal bone) forms the roof of the tympanic cavity, separating it from the middle cranial fossa and temporal lobe. Fractures or erosion can cause CSF otorrhea or meningitis. The tegmen also roofs the mastoid antrum. It represents the superior wall of the middle ear cavity.
questions.question: Which structure forms the roof of the tympanic cavity?
Which carpal bone can undergo anterior dislocation following a fall on a dorsiflexed wrist?
questions.explanation: Anterior dislocation of the lunate can occur when falling on a dorsiflexed wrist. The displaced lunate compresses structures within the carpal tunnel, causing carpal tunnel syndrome symptoms. This manifests as paresthesia in median nerve distribution and weakness of thenar muscles.

questions.question: Which glands open into the female urethra?
questions.explanation: Skene's glands (paraurethral glands) are small glands that open via ducts on either side of the external urethral orifice in females. They are homologous to the male prostate and secrete mucus. They can become infected causing urethritis or form cysts. Bartholin's glands (greater vestibular glands) are homologous to Cowper's glands and open into the vestibule lateral to the vaginal orifice.

questions.question: Where do hilar lymphatics ultimately drain?
questions.explanation: Lymph vessels from the lung drain into hilar (bronchopulmonary) nodes, and efferent lymphatics ultimately drain into the brachiocephalic vein. The lymph passes through pulmonary nodes, bronchopulmonary nodes, and tracheobronchial nodes before reaching the venous system. This pathway is important in cancer metastasis.

questions.question: The ansa cervicalis provides motor innervation to which muscle group?
questions.explanation: The ansa cervicalis (C1-C3) provides motor innervation to the infrahyoid strap muscles: sternohyoid, sternothyroid, and omohyoid. The thyrohyoid receives C1 fibers that travel with the hypoglossal nerve. These muscles depress the hyoid bone and larynx after swallowing.

extends the interphalangeal joint of the thumb and assists with extension at the metacarpophalangeal and carpometacarpal joints. Its tendon forms the medial border of the anatomical snuffbox. The muscle is supplied by the posterior interosseous nerve.
