questions.question: What is the primary extensor of the thumb interphalangeal joint?

questions.explanation: The laryngeal ventricle (sinus of Morgagni) is a space between the true vocal fold below and the false vocal fold (vestibular fold) above. It extends laterally into the saccule, which contains mucous glands that lubricate the vocal cords. The lateral wall is formed by the thyroid cartilage.
questions.question: Which space lies between the vocal and vestibular folds?

questions.explanation: The body of the stomach extends from the cardiac orifice to the level of the incisura angularis, a constant notch on the lesser curvature. This angular notch serves as a reliable anatomical landmark separating the body from the pyloric portion. The incisura angularis becomes more prominent when the stomach is distended.
questions.question: What defines the lower limit of the body of the stomach?

questions.explanation: has no bony attachment distally; it inserts into the flexor retinaculum and palmar aponeurosis. This muscle is absent in approximately 15% of people without functional deficit. It can be used as a tendon graft source in reconstructive surgery.
questions.question: Which forearm muscle has no bony attachment distally?
Which sinus opens into the inferior meatus?
questions.explanation: The inferior meatus receives the opening of the nasolacrimal duct beneath the inferior turbinate. No paranasal sinuses drain into the inferior meatus. The maxillary, frontal, and anterior ethmoidal sinuses drain into the middle meatus. The posterior ethmoidal cells drain into the superior meatus. The sphenoid drains into the sphenoethmoidal recess.

questions.question: Which structure prevents superior displacement of the humeral head?
questions.explanation: The coraco-acromial arch (formed by coracoid process, acromion, and coracoacromial ligament) prevents superior displacement of the humeral head. The joint capsule is weak superiorly, making this bony-ligamentous arch essential for stability. Rotator cuff muscles provide dynamic stability but the arch provides the structural barrier.

The ureter has three normal physiological constrictions: (1) at the pelviureteric junction where the renal pelvis joins the ureter, (2) where it crosses the pelvic brim at the bifurcation of the common iliac artery, and (3) at the vesicoureteric junction where it pierces the bladder wall. These are the most common sites for ureteric stone impaction.
questions.question: At how many points is the ureter typically constricted?
What is the primary function of the glenoid labrum?
questions.explanation: The glenoid labrum is a fibrocartilaginous ridge surrounding the glenoid cavity that deepens the cavity, reducing dislocation risk. It increases the articular surface area and provides attachment for some glenohumeral ligaments. This structure contributes significantly to glenohumeral joint stability despite the joint's high mobility.

options: Tibialis anterior tendon, deep fibular nerve, dorsalis pedis artery
Tibialis posterior, FDL, posterior tibial vessels and tibial nerve, FHL
Fibularis longus, fibularis brevis, sural nerve, small saphenous vein
Extensor hallucis longus, extensor digitorum longus, anterior tibial artery
questions.explanation: The tarsal tunnel contains the following structures passing from anterior to posterior (using the mnemonic Tom, Dick And Very Nervous Harry): Tibialis posterior tendon, flexor Digitorum longus tendon, posterior tibial Artery and Veins, tibial Nerve, and flexor Hallucis longus tendon. Compression within this tunnel causes tarsal tunnel syndrome with plantar foot pain and paraesthesia.
questions.question: The tarsal tunnel is formed by the flexor retinaculum and bones of the medial ankle. Which structures pass through it from anterior to posterior?

questions.explanation: The brachioradialis reflex predominantly tests the C6 nerve root. The reflex is elicited by tapping the brachioradialis tendon at the distal forearm. Absence or diminution suggests C6 nerve root or radial nerve pathology proximal to the elbow.
questions.question: What nerve root is predominantly tested by the brachioradialis reflex?
Which lymphatic structure drains lymph from the right upper quadrant of the body?
questions.explanation: The right lymphatic duct drains lymph from the right half of the head, neck, thorax, and right upper limb. It is formed by the union of right jugular, subclavian, and bronchomediastinal trunks. The duct enters the right venous angle (junction of right internal jugular and subclavian veins).

questions.question: What prevents the AV valves from prolapsing into the atria?
questions.explanation: Chordae tendineae attach the free edges and ventricular surfaces of the AV valve cusps to the papillary muscles, preventing the cusps from prolapsing into the atria during ventricular systole when intraventricular pressure is high. Papillary muscles contract just before ventricular contraction, tensing the chordae. Rupture of chordae tendineae causes severe valve regurgitation requiring urgent surgical repair.

Above the pectinate line, lymphatic drainage is to internal iliac nodes (following the superior rectal vessels). Below the pectinate line, drainage is primarily to superficial inguinal nodes. This difference is clinically important in anal cancer spread: tumors above the line metastasize to pelvic nodes, while those below spread to inguinal nodes.
questions.question: What drains the area above the pectinate line in the anal canal?
The hepatic veins drain directly into which structure?
questions.explanation: The hepatic veins (right, middle, and left, plus small inferior veins) drain directly into the inferior vena cava just below the diaphragm, representing the final pathway for blood that has perfused the hepatic sinusoids. The hepatic veins have no valves and run intersegmentally (between liver segments), in contrast to portal vein and hepatic artery branches which run within segments. The caudate lobe has separate small veins draining directly into the IVC, allowing it to maintain function in Budd-Chiari syndrome (hepatic vein thrombosis). The close relationship between hepatic veins and IVC is critical in liver transplantation surgery.

Semitendinosus joins sartorius and gracilis at the pes anserinus on the superior medial surface of the tibia. As its name implies, semitendinosus has a long rounded distal tendon. All three pes anserinus muscles cross both the hip and knee joints from three different compartments, making this insertion a multi-compartment landmark.
questions.question: Semitendinosus inserts into the medial surface of the superior part of the tibia, joining which two muscles to form the pes anserinus?

questions.explanation: The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve supplies the cricothyroid muscle. This is the only intrinsic laryngeal muscle not supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve. The nerve descends with the superior thyroid artery. Damage affects vocal cord tension and causes voice fatigue and difficulty with pitch variation.
questions.question: Which nerve supplies the cricothyroid muscle?

questions.explanation: The puborectalis muscle, part of the levator ani complex, forms a U-shaped sling that loops around the anorectal junction, creating the anorectal angle of approximately 90 degrees by pulling the rectum anteriorly toward the pubic symphysis. This angle is a critical component of the fecal continence mechanism, as relaxation of puborectalis during defecation straightens the anorectal angle to facilitate evacuation. Damage to the puborectalis (such as during childbirth or surgery) or its nerve supply (pudendal nerve and direct branches from S3-S4) can lead to fecal incontinence. The muscle is in tonic contraction at rest.
questions.question: Which muscle's contraction causes the anorectal angle?
What type of synovial joint is the elbow classified as?
questions.explanation: The elbow joint is classified as a synovial hinge (ginglymus) joint, allowing uniaxial movement. Articulation occurs between the trochlea and capitulum of the humerus with the trochlear notch of the ulna and radial head respectively. This configuration permits flexion and extension movements.

The azygos vein lies posterior and to the right of the esophagus in the posterior mediastinum. The descending aorta lies posterior and to the left of the esophagus. The thoracic duct lies posterior to the esophagus. The vagus nerves form plexuses around the esophagus.
questions.question: Which vein lies posterior to the esophagus?

questions.explanation: The neck of the bladder is the most fixed part, anchored by the puboprostatic ligaments (in males) or pubovesical ligaments (in females) and the lateral ligaments of the bladder. The remainder of the bladder is relatively mobile, allowing it to expand superiorly into the abdomen when full. The neck surrounds the internal urethral orifice.
questions.question: Which part of the bladder is most fixed in position?
Tibialis posterior, inverting the foot and plantarflexing the ankle, primarily supports which arch of the foot?
questions.explanation: Tibialis posterior is the primary dynamic supporter of the medial longitudinal arch. It inserts into the tuberosity of the navicular, all three cuneiform bones, cuboid, sustentaculum tali, and bases of the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th metatarsals. Rupture of the tibialis posterior tendon leads to progressive adult flatfoot deformity (acquired pes planus).

Reticulocytes (immature red blood cells still containing RNA) normally comprise 0.5-1.5% of circulating red blood cells, representing the daily replacement of senescent erythrocytes. The reticulocyte count increases in hemolysis or bleeding (compensatory bone marrow response) and decreases in bone marrow failure or nutritional deficiencies. The spleen removes excessive RNA from reticulocytes (pitting function).
questions.question: What is the normal percentage of reticulocytes in peripheral blood?
The pharyngeal recess (of Rosenm�ller) is located in which region?
questions.explanation: The pharyngeal recess (fossa of Rosenm�ller) is a depression in the lateral wall of the nasopharynx behind the torus tubarius (Eustachian tube opening). Nasopharyngeal carcinomas commonly arise in this recess. The recess is bounded anteriorly by the tubal elevation and posteriorly by the adenoid pad. Deep cervical lymph nodes receive drainage from this region.

questions.question: Which rib level marks the base of breast vertically?
questions.explanation: The base of the breast extends vertically from the 2nd to 6th rib. Transversely, it extends from the sternal edge to the mid-axillary line. The axillary tail of Spence extends from the upper outer quadrant into the axilla. These landmarks are important for clinical breast examination.

questions.question: What is gynecomastia?
questions.explanation: Gynecomastia is enlargement of the male breast due to proliferation of glandular tissue. It can be physiological (neonatal, pubertal, elderly) or pathological (hormonal imbalance, drugs, liver disease, tumors). The condition is usually bilateral but may be asymmetric. True gynecomastia must be distinguished from fat accumulation.

options: Calcaneus, talus, navicular, and first metatarsal
Calcaneus, navicular, cuboid, and all metatarsals
Calcaneus, cuboid, and all five metatarsals
questions.question: The lateral longitudinal arch is formed by which bones and is described as more rigid and making more contact with the ground?
questions.explanation: The lateral longitudinal arch is formed by the calcaneus, cuboid, and the 4th and 5th metatarsals. Its summit is the subtalar articulation. It is smaller, more rigid, more stable than the medial arch, and makes more contact with the ground. It bears body weight before the medial arch comes into play and has limited mobility, built to transmit weight.

The incisive canal opens inferiorly into the oral cavity at the incisive fossa in the anterior hard palate. Superiorly, it communicates with the nasal cavity. The canal transmits the nasopalatine nerve and terminal branches of the greater palatine vessels. Embryologically, it marks the fusion of the primary and secondary palates.
questions.question: The incisive canal opens into which structure?
What are internal hemorrhoids dilations of?
questions.explanation: Internal hemorrhoids are dilations of the internal rectal venous plexus (superior rectal veins) above the pectinate line. They are covered by insensate rectal mucosa and are therefore painless. External hemorrhoids are dilations of the external rectal venous plexus (inferior rectal veins) below the pectinate line, covered by sensitive anoderm, making them painful. Portal hypertension can cause internal hemorrhoids.

questions.question: Which carpal bone is most commonly fractured due to falls on an outstretched hand?
questions.explanation: The scaphoid bone crosses two rows of carpal bones forming a hinge, making it vulnerable to heavy stress during falls on outstretched hands. The fracture commonly occurs through the middle of the bone or causes complete separation into two pieces. Risk of avascular necrosis exists due to single arterial blood supply entering at the distal end.

The cisterna chyli (receptaculum chyli) receives the intestinal trunk (draining abdominal viscera via pre-aortic nodes), right and left lumbar trunks (draining lower limbs, pelvis, and posterior abdominal wall), and sometimes the lower intercostal lymphatic trunks. It represents a dilated sac at the origin of the thoracic duct, located at L1-L2 level, anterior to the vertebral column, posterior and to the right of the aorta, posterior to the right crus of the diaphragm. The thoracic duct ascends from the cisterna through the aortic hiatus to traverse the posterior mediastinum and drain into the junction of left subclavian and internal jugular veins.
questions.question: The cisterna chyli receives lymph from which trunks?
The maxillary sinus ostium opens into which structure?
questions.explanation: The maxillary sinus ostium opens into the middle meatus through the hiatus semilunaris. This high opening impairs natural drainage when standing upright. The sinus is the largest paranasal sinus and is present in rudimentary form at birth.

Circumduction at the shoulder joint is a sequential combination of flexion, abduction, extension, and adduction movements. This creates a conical movement pattern of the limb. Multiple muscles act in coordinated sequence to produce this composite movement.
questions.question: What produces circumduction at the shoulder joint?

questions.explanation: The deep group of the posterior compartment contains four muscles: popliteus, flexor hallucis longus, flexor digitorum longus, and tibialis posterior. The superficial group contains three muscles: gastrocnemius, soleus, and plantaris. All muscles of the posterior compartment are supplied by the tibial nerve. It is the largest of the three leg compartments.
questions.question: The deep group of the posterior leg compartment contains how many muscles?

questions.explanation: The cervical pleura extends approximately one inch (2.5 to 4 cm) above the medial third of the clavicle. This superior extension of the parietal pleura is reinforced by the suprapleural membrane. Understanding this anatomy is important because the pleura can be injured during procedures in the lower neck.
questions.question: How high above the clavicle does cervical pleura extend?
The root of the transverse mesocolon crosses which part of the duodenum?
questions.explanation: The root of the transverse mesocolon attaches to the inferior border of the pancreas and crosses the second (descending) part of the duodenum as it extends from right to left across the posterior abdominal wall. This attachment divides the peritoneal cavity into supracolic (containing stomach, liver, spleen) and infracolic (containing small intestine and colon) compartments. The root also crosses anterior to the head of the pancreas and the superior mesenteric vessels. This anatomical relationship is important during surgical mobilization of the transverse colon and in understanding the spread of peritoneal infections.

The sigmoid colon receives its blood supply from 2-4 sigmoid arteries (sigmoidal arteries), branches of the inferior mesenteric artery. These arteries descend in the sigmoid mesocolon, anastomosing with each other and with branches from the left colic artery superiorly and the superior rectal artery inferiorly, contributing to the marginal artery along the mesenteric border. Sudeck's point, at the rectosigmoid junction (approximately 15 cm from anal verge), represents a watershed area where the last sigmoid artery anastomoses with the superior rectal artery and is vulnerable to ischemia.
questions.question: Which artery supplies the sigmoid colon?

questions.explanation: The jugulodigastric lymph nodes are located below the angle of the mandible where the posterior belly of digastric crosses the internal jugular vein. They are commonly enlarged in tonsillitis and are therefore called tonsillar nodes. These are part of the superior deep cervical lymph node chain.
questions.question: Which lymph nodes are commonly called the tonsillar nodes?
The nasolacrimal duct is formed by which two bones?
questions.explanation: The nasolacrimal canal is formed by the lacrimal bone and maxilla, housing the nasolacrimal duct. The duct drains tears from the lacrimal sac to the inferior meatus. The valve of Hasner at the inferior opening prevents retrograde airflow. Obstruction requires dacryocystorhinostomy surgery.

During inspiration, diaphragmatic contraction causes the muscle to descend (central tendon is relatively fixed by the pericardium and IVC), increasing thoracic volume and decreasing intrathoracic pressure (creating negative pressure that draws air in). Simultaneously, abdominal volume decreases and intra-abdominal pressure increases, displacing abdominal viscera downward and forward. The diaphragm is responsible for about 75% of the work of quiet breathing.
questions.question: What is the effect of diaphragmatic contraction during inspiration?
What muscle weakness occurs in carpal tunnel syndrome?
questions.explanation: Carpal tunnel syndrome causes weakness of thenar muscles (abductor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis, flexor pollicis brevis) due to median nerve compression. This results from compression of the recurrent branch of the median nerve. Thumb opposition and abduction are particularly affected.

The extensor digitorum brevis and extensor hallucis brevis, the only intrinsic muscles on the dorsum of the foot, are innervated by the deep fibular nerve (L5, or S1, or both). They aid the extensor digitorum longus in extending the four medial toes and the extensor hallucis longus in extending the great toe at the metatarsophalangeal joint.
questions.question: The muscles of the dorsum of the foot include the extensor digitorum brevis (EDB) and extensor hallucis brevis (EHB). They are innervated by which nerve?

options: Forearm flexion and supination weakened, lateral forearm numbness
questions.explanation: Musculocutaneous nerve injury greatly weakens forearm flexion (biceps and brachialis loss) and supination (biceps loss). Sensation is lost over the lateral forearm through the lateral cutaneous nerve. Some weak flexion remains through brachioradialis (radial nerve) and pronator teres (median nerve).
questions.question: How does the musculocutaneous nerve injury affect function?
Which nerve provides sensation to the upper eyelid?
questions.explanation: The supraorbital and supratrochlear nerves (branches of the frontal nerve from V1) provide sensation to the upper eyelid and forehead. The lacrimal nerve supplies the lateral upper lid. Infratrochlear nerve supplies the medial canthus and side of nose. These are all branches of the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve.

The superior intercostal artery (from costocervical trunk of subclavian artery) gives off the first and second posterior intercostal arteries. These are the only posterior intercostal arteries not arising from the thoracic aorta. This arrangement provides collateral circulation if the thoracic aorta is obstructed.
questions.question: What supplies the first two intercostal spaces?

questions.explanation: The testicular arteries arise directly from the anterior aspect of the abdominal aorta, just inferior to the renal arteries at approximately the L2 vertebral level, reflecting the embryological origin of the testes in the posterior abdominal wall. These long, slender arteries descend obliquely across the psoas major muscle, ureter, and external iliac vessels before entering the deep inguinal ring as part of the spermatic cord. The right testicular artery crosses anterior to the inferior vena cava, while the left crosses anterior to the left renal vein, then both pass through the inguinal canal to supply the testes.
questions.question: The testicular artery typically arises from which vessel?
What causes mallet finger deformity?
questions.explanation: Mallet finger deformity results from extensor tendon avulsion from the distal phalanx (terminal extensor tendon rupture). This causes inability to actively extend the distal interphalangeal joint, which droops in flexion. The injury commonly occurs from forced flexion of an extended fingertip.
options: Extensor tendon avulsion at distal phalanx

questions.explanation: The right border of the heart on a chest X-ray is formed by the right atrium. The left border is formed primarily by the left ventricle with a small contribution from the left atrial appendage superiorly. The superior border is formed by the great vessels (aorta and pulmonary artery).
questions.question: What forms the right heart border radiographically?

questions.explanation: The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve arises in the forearm proximal to the carpal tunnel, so palm sensation is preserved. Only sensation in the lateral three and one-half fingers (palmar aspect) is affected by carpal tunnel syndrome. This distinguishes it from more proximal median nerve injuries.
questions.question: What sensation is preserved in carpal tunnel syndrome?

options: Crossing one leg over the other (adduction)
questions.question: The obturator nerve exits the pelvis through the obturator foramen. Obturator nerve injury may cause difficulty with which activity due to adductor weakness?
questions.explanation: Obturator nerve injury (as can occur with obturator hernia, difficult childbirth, or pelvic fractures) causes weakness of the adductor muscles, making it difficult to cross one leg over the other (adduction). Sensory loss occurs on the medial side of the thigh. The obturator nerve does not supply the knee directly (though the posterior division gives a branch to the knee joint capsule).

The lumbar sympathetic chain enters the abdomen from the thorax by passing beneath the medial arcuate ligament (lumbocostal arch), which extends from the body of L1 vertebra to the tip of the L1 transverse process over the psoas major muscle. The chain then descends along the medial border of psoas major on the anterolateral aspects of the lumbar vertebral bodies, with the right chain posterior to the inferior vena cava and the left along the left margin of the aorta. It typically contains four lumbar ganglia that give off gray rami communicantes to all lumbar nerves and lumbar splanchnic nerves to autonomic plexuses.
questions.question: The lumbar sympathetic chain enters the abdomen through which opening?

options: Segmented bony arches supported by muscles and ligaments
Rigid flat bone platform without arching
Phalanges arranged in a single arch only
questions.explanation: The human foot achieves its two basic functions through a segmented skeleton arranged in arches (longitudinal and transverse), supported by muscles and ligaments. This arrangement enables efficient locomotion, sparing of foot structures, and shock absorption. The arches allow the foot to adapt to uneven surfaces and serve as resilient springs to absorb shocks as in jumping.
questions.question: The two basic functions of the human foot are supporting body weight and providing leverage for locomotion. These are achieved through which structural arrangement?

questions.explanation: Vagal (parasympathetic) stimulation decreases heart rate (negative chronotropy), decreases conduction velocity through the AV node, and slightly decreases contractility. The vagus nerve releases acetylcholine, which acts on muscarinic receptors (M2) in the SA node, AV node, and atrial muscle. The right vagus preferentially affects the SA node; the left vagus affects the AV node.
questions.question: Which effect does vagal stimulation have on the heart?

questions.explanation: The splenic red pulp filters blood and removes old, damaged, or abnormal erythrocytes through selective retention and phagocytosis by macrophages in the splenic cords. It also stores platelets (about one-third of the body's platelet pool) and serves as a reservoir for iron recycled from hemoglobin. The red pulp comprises about 75% of splenic tissue.
questions.question: What is the function of splenic red pulp?

questions.explanation: Bile salts are actively reabsorbed in the terminal ileum and returned to the liver via the portal circulation (enterohepatic recirculation). About 95% of bile salts are recycled this way, conserving the bile salt pool. Ileal disease or resection disrupts this circulation, leading to bile salt malabsorption, steatorrhea, and potential bile salt diarrhea.
questions.question: Which segment absorbs bile salts for enterohepatic recirculation?

questions.explanation: The external acoustic meatus measures approximately 2.9 cm in length from the concha to the tympanic membrane. The lateral one-third is cartilaginous containing cerumen glands, while the medial two-thirds is bony. Understanding this anatomy is essential for safe otoscopic examination and foreign body removal.
questions.question: The external acoustic meatus is what total length?
What arches over the left lung root?
questions.explanation: The aortic arch passes over and in front of the left lung root. The left lung root lies within the concavity of the aortic arch. This anatomical relationship is visible on chest X-rays and CT scans and is important for understanding mediastinal anatomy.

questions.question: Which muscle forms the posterior pillar of the fauces?
questions.explanation: The palatopharyngeus muscle forms the posterior pillar (palatopharyngeal arch) of the fauces. The palatoglossus forms the anterior pillar. The tonsillar fossa lies between these two pillars. Both muscles descend from the soft palate but have different innervation patterns.

questions.question: Fractures of the fibular neck are particularly associated with injury to which nerve, causing foot drop?
questions.explanation: Fractures of the fibular neck are particularly associated with injury to the common fibular nerve, which winds around this subcutaneous location. Injury causes foot drop (loss of dorsiflexion), loss of eversion (superficial fibular nerve), and sensory loss on the dorsum of the foot and anterolateral leg. The nerve is also vulnerable to pressure from tight plasters or prolonged crossing of the legs.

questions.question: What controls the external urethral sphincter?
questions.explanation: The external urethral sphincter is composed of skeletal muscle and is under voluntary somatic control via the pudendal nerve (S2-S4). This sphincter can be consciously contracted to prevent or interrupt micturition. In males, it surrounds the membranous urethra; in females, it surrounds the middle third of the urethra at the urogenital diaphragm.

questions.question: Which layer of the spermatic cord is derived from transversalis fascia?
questions.explanation: The internal spermatic fascia is derived from the transversalis fascia at the deep inguinal ring. The cremasteric muscle and fascia are derived from the internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles. The external spermatic fascia is derived from the external oblique aponeurosis at the superficial inguinal ring. These layers represent the layers of the abdominal wall through which the testis descended.

questions.question: The anterior fontanelle is located at the junction of which sutures?
questions.explanation: The anterior fontanelle (bregma) is located at the junction of the coronal, sagittal, and frontal (metopic) sutures where the frontal and parietal bones meet. It is diamond-shaped and typically closes by 18-24 months. The fontanelle allows skull molding during birth and accommodates brain growth. Bulging indicates increased intracranial pressure.

questions.question: Which nerve accompanies the deep brachial artery through the spiral groove?
questions.explanation: The radial nerve accompanies the profunda brachii (deep brachial) artery through the spiral groove of the humerus. The nerve winds around the posterior shaft of the humerus between the medial and lateral heads of triceps. This close relationship makes the nerve vulnerable to injury in humeral shaft fractures.

questions.question: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head following a femoral neck fracture is most likely due to disruption of which artery?
questions.explanation: The medial femoral circumflex artery wraps around the posterior side of the femur, supplying the femoral neck and head via retinacular vessels. In femoral neck fractures, this artery is easily damaged, leading to avascular necrosis of the femoral head. This is the most critical complication of intracapsular femoral neck fractures.

questions.question: Pes cavus is characterized by an exaggeration of the longitudinal arch with toes dorsiflexed at metatarsophalangeal joints and plantarflexed at interphalangeal joints. What is the alternative name for this toe deformity?
questions.explanation: Pes cavus (high arched foot) presents with exaggeration of the longitudinal arch. The toes are dorsiflexed at metatarsophalangeal joints and plantarflexed at interphalangeal joints, creating a deformity called claw foot. Pes cavus is associated with neurological conditions such as Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease and Friedrich's ataxia.

questions.question: Which structure forms the anterior wall of the axilla's superficial layer?
questions.explanation: The anterior wall of the axilla is formed by the pectoralis major muscle and the pectoral fascia associated with it. The pectoralis minor and clavipectoral fascia form a deeper layer. The anterior axillary fold, formed by pectoralis major bridging from thoracic wall to humerus, represents the inferiormost graspable part.

questions.question: Which vessels enter the liver at the porta hepatis?
questions.explanation: The porta hepatis (gateway of the liver) is a transverse fissure through which the portal vein, hepatic artery, and hepatic ducts pass. The portal vein and hepatic artery enter the liver while the hepatic ducts (right and left) exit. Lymphatic vessels and nerves also traverse the porta hepatis, which is bounded by the hepatoduodenal ligament.

questions.question: The femoral pulse is palpated at the mid-inguinal point, defined as the midpoint between which two bony landmarks?
questions.explanation: The femoral pulse is palpated at the mid-inguinal point, the midpoint between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis. At this point the femoral artery lies lateral to the femoral vein and medial to the femoral nerve. This is distinct from the midpoint of the inguinal ligament, which overlies the femoral canal.
options: Pubic tubercle and anterior superior iliac spine
Medial malleolus and anterior superior iliac spine
Inguinal ligament and the femoral condyle
Anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis
Pubic crest and posterior superior iliac spine

questions.explanation: In males, the spermatic cord passes through the deep inguinal ring (an opening in the transversalis fascia lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels). In females, the round ligament of the uterus passes through. The ilioinguinal nerve passes through the superficial inguinal ring but not the deep ring - it enters the canal by piercing the internal oblique muscle.
questions.question: What passes through the deep inguinal ring?

questions.explanation: The ligamentum teres hepatis (round ligament of the liver), representing the obliterated left umbilical vein, runs from the umbilicus to the liver within the free inferior border of the falciform ligament. Upon reaching the liver, it continues in a fissure on the visceral surface between the left and quadrate lobes before joining the left branch of the portal vein. The ligamentum teres may remain patent in portal hypertension, allowing portosystemic anastomosis through paraumbilical veins, potentially leading to caput medusae. At the umbilicus, it connects to the median umbilical ligament (obliterated urachus).
questions.question: The ligamentum teres hepatis is found in which structure?
Where does central diaphragmatic pain refer?
questions.explanation: Irritation of the central part of the diaphragm (supplied by phrenic nerve C3-5) causes referred pain to the shoulder-tip because the supraclavicular nerves (C3, 4) supply the skin over the shoulder. This occurs in conditions like pleurisy, pericarditis, or subphrenic abscess affecting the central diaphragm.

questions.question: The rectus abdominis muscle inserts onto which structures?
questions.explanation: The rectus abdominis originates from the pubic crest and pubic symphysis and inserts superiorly onto the xiphoid process and the costal cartilages of ribs 5-7. The muscle is intersected by three or four tendinous intersections that are firmly adherent to the anterior rectus sheath, creating the characteristic "six-pack" appearance in individuals with low body fat. These intersections represent remnants of the segmental myotomes from which the muscle develops and typically occur at the level of the xiphoid process, umbilicus, and midway between these landmarks.

The diaphragmatic pleura is the portion of parietal pleura that covers the superior surface of the diaphragm. It reflects onto the thoracic wall to become continuous with the costal pleura. The diaphragmatic pleura receives sensory innervation from the phrenic nerve centrally and intercostal nerves peripherally.
questions.question: Which pleura covers the diaphragm's superior surface?

questions.explanation: The maxillary division (V2) of the trigeminal nerve exits the middle cranial fossa through the foramen rotundum in the greater wing of the sphenoid. It enters the pterygopalatine fossa where it gives off branches before continuing as the infraorbital nerve. The foramen rotundum is round in shape, hence its name.
questions.question: The maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve exits the skull through which opening?

questions.explanation: The piriform fossa (recess) is bounded medially by the aryepiglottic fold and laterally by the thyroid cartilage and thyrohyoid membrane. The internal laryngeal nerve and superior laryngeal vessels lie in the mucosa of the piriform fossa. Foreign bodies commonly lodge in this recess. The fossa is part of the laryngopharynx.
questions.question: The piriform fossa is bounded medially by which structure?

questions.explanation: The renal fascia (Gerota's fascia), a condensation of connective tissue, encloses the kidney, perirenal fat, and suprarenal gland on each side, forming a distinct compartment. It consists of anterior and posterior layers that fuse laterally but remain open medially and inferiorly, allowing potential communication between the two sides medially and extension of infection or hemorrhage inferiorly. The fascia separates the perirenal space (containing kidney, suprarenal gland, and perirenal fat) from the posterior pararenal space posteriorly and anterior pararenal space anteriorly. This fascial envelope is important in limiting the spread of renal infections and tumors.
questions.question: The renal fascia (Gerota's fascia) encloses which structures?

questions.explanation: The areola is a dark pink-brownish circular area of skin (22-60 mm in diameter) that surrounds the nipple. Its color varies with parity and race, darkening during the second month of pregnancy. The areola contains Montgomery's glands (areola glands) which enlarge during pregnancy and lactation.
questions.question: What structure surrounds the nipple?

questions.explanation: The spleen is situated in the left hypochondriac region, lying obliquely along the long axis of the 9th, 10th, and 11th ribs in the left upper quadrant. It is protected by the rib cage and cannot normally be palpated unless enlarged. The spleen is related anteriorly to the stomach (via the gastrosplenic ligament), posteriorly to the left kidney (via the splenorenal ligament), superiorly to the diaphragm, and inferiorly to the left colic flexure (supported by the phrenicocolic ligament). The splenic notch on its superior border is a characteristic feature visible on imaging.
questions.question: The spleen is located in which abdominal region?

questions.explanation: The lingual artery arises from the external carotid at the level of the hyoid bone and is closely related to the hypoglossal nerve. The nerve crosses superficial to the artery as it loops forward. The artery divides into dorsal lingual, deep lingual, and sublingual branches. The hyoglossus muscle separates superficial from deep structures.
questions.question: Which artery accompanies the hypoglossal nerve?
The superior rectal artery crosses which vessel at S3 level?
questions.explanation: The superior rectal artery (terminal continuation of the inferior mesenteric artery) descends into the pelvis within the sigmoid mesocolon and crosses the left common iliac vessels (artery and vein) at approximately the S3 vertebral level before dividing into right and left branches that descend along the rectum. This anatomical relationship makes the superior rectal vessels vulnerable to injury during operations on the sigmoid colon or rectum. The artery eventually terminates by piercing the muscular wall of the rectum and anastomosing with the middle rectal (from internal iliac) and inferior rectal (from internal pudendal) arteries.

questions.question: Which structure passes through the internal acoustic meatus?
questions.explanation: The internal acoustic meatus transmits the facial nerve (VII), vestibulocochlear nerve (VIII), and labyrinthine artery. The facial nerve continues through the facial canal to exit at the stylomastoid foramen. Acoustic neuromas typically arise in this region from Schwann cells of the vestibular nerve.

questions.question: Where are intersegmental veins located?
questions.explanation: Intersegmental veins (tributaries of pulmonary veins) run in the connective tissue septa between adjacent bronchopulmonary segments. These veins act as anatomical guides during surgical segmentectomy, helping surgeons identify and separate individual segments without excessive bleeding.

The foramen lacerum is closed in life by fibrocartilage. Only small meningeal vessels and the greater petrosal nerve pass through its superior aspect. The internal carotid artery passes above it in the foramen's upper part but does not traverse it. In dried skulls, the foramen appears as a large opening.
questions.question: The foramen lacerum is closed in life by which structure?

questions.explanation: The greater curvature is supplied by the right and left gastroepiploic (gastroomental) arteries, which anastomose along the greater curvature. The left gastroepiploic arises from the splenic artery and supplies the upper greater curvature; the right gastroepiploic arises from the gastroduodenal artery and supplies the lower greater curvature. The short gastric arteries supply the fundus portion of the greater curvature.
questions.question: Which artery supplies the greater curvature of the stomach?

questions.explanation: Semitendinosus, semimembranosus, and the long head of biceps femoris are all innervated by the tibial division of the sciatic nerve (L5, S1, S2). The exception is the short head of biceps femoris, which is supplied by the common fibular division. The sciatic nerve is the largest nerve in the body.
questions.question: Semitendinosus, semimembranosus, and the long head of biceps femoris are all innervated by which division of the sciatic nerve?
Which structure separates the tympanic cavity into superior and inferior compartments?
questions.explanation: The tympanic cavity is a single air-filled space without compartmentalization, though the articular disc divides the temporomandibular joint into compartments. The cavity extends into mastoid air cells posteriorly via the aditus ad antrum. The Eustachian tube provides communication with the nasopharynx.

questions.question: At which vertebral level is the caval opening?
questions.explanation: The caval opening for the inferior vena cava is located at the level of T8 in the central tendon. It also transmits terminal branches of the right phrenic nerve and a few lymphatic vessels. This is the highest and most anterior of the three main diaphragmatic openings.

questions.question: The main blood supply to the medial compartment of the thigh comes from which two arteries?
questions.explanation: The medial fascial compartment of the thigh receives its blood supply from the profunda femoris (deep femoral) artery via its perforating branches and from the obturator artery. The nerve supply is from the obturator nerve (L2, L3, L4). The profunda femoris is the major blood supply to all three thigh compartments via its perforating branches.

questions.question: Where is the cardiac notch located?
questions.explanation: The cardiac notch is a deep indentation on the anterior border of the left lung created by the apex of the heart. This notch is located at the level of the fourth costal cartilage. Below the cardiac notch, the lung forms a tongue-like projection called the lingula.

A fracture of the neck of femur characteristically results in coxa vara, reducing the neck-shaft angle below the normal 125-135 degrees. Coxa valga with an increased neck-shaft angle follows congenital dislocation of the femoral head. These deformities have different biomechanical implications for gait and joint loading.
questions.question: A fracture of the neck of femur characteristically produces which angular deformity of the hip?

questions.explanation: Mammary glands are modifications of sweat glands and are therefore ectodermal in origin. They develop from the mammary ridge (milk line) which extends from axilla to groin in the embryo. In humans, most of this ridge disappears except in the pectoral region where breasts develop.
questions.question: What embryonic structure forms mammary glands?
What drains blood from the breast?
questions.explanation: Blood from the breast drains into both the axillary veins (via lateral thoracic and thoracoacromial tributaries) and the internal thoracic veins (via perforating veins). During pregnancy and lactation, these veins become prominent and engorged. Venous drainage pathways are important routes for cancer metastasis.

questions.question: The adductor tubercle is an important bony landmark on the medial aspect of the distal femur. Which tendon inserts here?
questions.explanation: The adductor tubercle on the medial aspect of the distal femur receives the insertion of the hamstring part of adductor magnus. This is the part of adductor magnus supplied by the tibial division of the sciatic nerve. The adductor tubercle is palpable on physical examination and serves as an important landmark in knee surgery (origin of the tibial collateral ligament is just above it).

questions.question: The pubofemoral ligament of the hip joint limits which two movements?
questions.explanation: The pubofemoral ligament supports the hip joint inferomedially and limits extension and abduction. It is triangular, attaching superiorly to the iliopubic eminence and obturator crest, inferiorly merging with the capsule and lower band of the iliofemoral ligament. Strain of this ligament produces groin pain worsened by extension and abduction.

Calot's triangle (cystohepatic triangle) is bounded by the cystic duct inferiorly, common hepatic duct medially, and inferior surface of the liver (or right lobe) superiorly. Within this triangle lies the cystic artery (typically arising from the right hepatic artery) and Lund's lymph node (Calot's node), which may be enlarged in cholecystitis or cholangitis. The triangle serves as a crucial surgical landmark during laparoscopic cholecystectomy for identifying and safely isolating the cystic duct and artery (the "critical view of safety") before ligation and division. Anatomical variations in this region are common and must be carefully identified.
questions.question: Which structure lies within Calot's triangle?

questions.explanation: The profunda femoris artery (deep femoral artery) arises from the posterolateral aspect of the femoral artery approximately 5 cm below the inguinal ligament. It is the largest branch of the femoral artery and the main blood supply to the thigh muscles via perforating branches, medial and lateral femoral circumflex arteries.
questions.question: The profunda femoris artery arises from the femoral artery at what distance below the inguinal ligament?
Which procedure divides the vagal trunks to reduce acid secretion?
questions.explanation: Vagotomy involves division of the vagal trunks or branches to reduce gastric acid secretion and was historically performed for peptic ulcer disease. Truncal vagotomy (dividing the main trunks) requires a drainage procedure (pyloroplasty) as it impairs gastric emptying. Highly selective vagotomy (dividing only the branches to the acid-secreting fundus/body) preserves antral innervation and pyloric function.

In a rolling (para-esophageal) hiatus hernia, the cardia remains in its normal position and the cardioesophageal junction is intact. The fundus of the stomach rolls up through the hiatus in front of the esophagus. Patients may have epigastric discomfort and dysphagia but no reflux.
questions.question: Which hernia maintains competent cardia?
What causes frozen shoulder?
questions.explanation: Frozen shoulder results from adhesive capsulitis, causing progressive restriction of glenohumeral joint motion. The joint capsule becomes thickened and contracted. The condition typically progresses through freezing, frozen, and thawing phases over 1-3 years.

options: Stable scapula essential for efficient glenohumeral motion
questions.question: What is the functional relationship between scapular stability and glenohumeral mobility?
questions.explanation: A stable scapular base is essential for efficient glenohumeral motion. Scapular stabilizers (serratus anterior, rhomboids, trapezius) provide a fixed base from which glenohumeral muscles can act. Scapular winging demonstrates how loss of stability compromises shoulder function despite intact glenohumeral muscles.

questions.question: The posterior tibial pulse is palpated at which surface anatomical location?
options: Anterior surface of the ankle between malleoli
Dorsum of foot lateral to extensor hallucis longus
Midway between lateral malleolus and calcaneus
questions.explanation: The posterior tibial pulse is palpated inferoposteriorly to the medial malleolus, where the artery curves to enter the tarsal tunnel and then the sole of the foot. The dorsalis pedis pulse is found on the dorsum of the foot, just lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon. The four main pulse points of the lower limb are femoral, popliteal, posterior tibial, and dorsalis pedis.

questions.question: Which structure is at risk during splenectomy?
questions.explanation: The tail of the pancreas extends into the splenorenal ligament to reach the splenic hilum and is at risk of injury during splenectomy. The splenic vessels in the splenorenal ligament must be carefully ligated. Pancreatic fistula is a recognized complication of splenectomy. The tail represents about 30% of pancreatic tissue but is rarely the site of surgical disease.

The posterior (Moore's) approach to the hip must carefully protect the sciatic nerve, which runs midway between the ischial tuberosity and the greater trochanter. The approach involves splitting gluteus maximus and detaching the short external rotators (piriformis, obturator internus, gemelli) from the greater trochanter. These rotators must be reattached to reduce the risk of posterior hip dislocation postoperatively.
questions.question: The posterior approach to the hip (Moore's approach) identifies which nerve as the critical structure to protect, found running midway between the ischial tuberosity and greater trochanter?
options: Posterior cutaneous nerve of the thigh

questions.explanation: The glossopharyngeal nerve (IX) provides both general sensation and taste (special sensation) to the posterior third of the tongue. The anterior two-thirds receives general sensation from the lingual nerve (V3) and taste from chorda tympani (VII). Motor innervation to all tongue muscles is from the hypoglossal nerve except palatoglossus (pharyngeal plexus).
questions.question: Which nerve provides general sensation to the posterior third of the tongue?

questions.explanation: Avascular necrosis is a well-recognized complication of talar neck fractures, classified by the Hawkins system. The talus receives its blood supply from branches of the posterior tibial, anterior tibial, and fibular arteries entering through its non-articular portions. Displaced talar neck fractures disrupt these vessels. Hawkins sign (subchondral osteopenia on radiograph at 6-8 weeks) is a favorable sign indicating intact blood supply.
questions.question: Osteonecrosis (avascular necrosis) of the talus is a known complication of which type of ankle/foot injury due to the talus having no direct muscle attachments and a tenuous blood supply?

questions.explanation: The gluteal tuberosity is located below the greater trochanter and serves as the insertion point for gluteus maximus. The trochanteric fossa, medial to the greater trochanter, receives the insertion of obturator externus. Knowing these distinctions is critical in hip replacement surgery.
questions.question: Which surface landmark on the femur, below the greater trochanter, represents the insertion of the gluteus maximus?
In a hip replacement (total hip arthroplasty), the posterior approach risks injury to which nerve that can cause foot drop?
questions.explanation: The posterior approach to the hip joint risks injury to the sciatic nerve, which passes posterior to the hip joint separated from it by the obturator internus, gemelli, and quadratus femoris. Sciatic nerve injury during hip surgery causes foot drop (common fibular division injury), posterior leg weakness, and extensive sensory loss. Careful positioning and nerve monitoring minimize this risk.

Wharton's duct (submandibular duct) is approximately 5 cm long and opens at the sublingual papilla beside the frenulum. The duct runs forward on the hyoglossus muscle between the lingual and hypoglossal nerves. Stone formation is more common in this duct than in Stensen's duct due to its upward course and mucoid secretions.
questions.question: What is the approximate length of Wharton's duct?

questions.explanation: The reflected attachment of semimembranosus forms the oblique popliteal ligament, which strengthens the fibrous capsule of the knee posteriorly. Semimembranosus inserts primarily into the posterior part of the medial condyle of the tibia. The arcuate popliteal ligament is a separate structure arising from the posterior fibular head.
questions.question: The reflected attachment of the semimembranosus tendon forms which structure posteriorly in the knee?

questions.explanation: The valleculae (spaces between the tongue base and epiglottis) receive sensory innervation from the internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (vagus). The glossopharyngeal nerve also contributes sensation to this region. Foreign bodies commonly lodge in the valleculae. These spaces are bounded by the median and lateral glossoepiglottic folds.
questions.question: The vallecular receives sensory innervation from which nerve?
What is the significance of the axillary sheath?
questions.explanation: The axillary sheath is a fascial extension of the prevertebral fascia that encloses the axillary artery and brachial plexus cords. This tubular sheath provides a pathway for these structures through the axilla. Local anesthetic can be injected into this sheath for brachial plexus blocks.
options: Encloses axillary artery and brachial plexus

questions.question: The popliteal artery terminates at the inferior border of popliteus by dividing into which two initial divisions?
questions.explanation: The popliteal artery terminates at the inferior border of the popliteus muscle by dividing into the anterior tibial artery and the tibioperoneal trunk. The tibioperoneal trunk then divides into the posterior tibial artery and fibular (peroneal) artery. The popliteal artery gives five genicular branches contributing to the genicular anastomosis.
options: Anterior tibial artery and tibioperoneal trunk
Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial arteries
Peroneal artery and posterior tibial artery directly

questions.explanation: The transverse colon is completely invested by peritoneum and suspended by the transverse mesocolon, making it freely mobile. This complete peritoneal covering classifies it as intraperitoneal. The ascending and descending colons are retroperitoneal, while the sigmoid colon and appendix also have mesenteries.
questions.question: Which part of the large intestine is completely intraperitoneal?

questions.explanation: The left gonadal (testicular or ovarian) vein drains into the left renal vein, while the right gonadal vein drains directly into the inferior vena cava. The left renal vein also receives the left suprarenal vein and communicates with the ascending lumbar vein. This arrangement makes the left testicular vein more prone to varicocele formation.
questions.question: Which vein drains into the left renal vein?

questions.explanation: The roof of the inguinal canal is formed by the arching lowest fibers of the internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles, along with contributions from the transversalis fascia. These arching fibers cross from lateral to medial, forming the superior boundary of the canal. The internal oblique muscle also contributes to the anterior wall laterally, where its fibers arise from the inguinal ligament. The conjoint tendon (formed by the fusion of internal oblique and transversus abdominis aponeuroses) reinforces the posterior wall medially but does not form the roof.
questions.question: Which structure forms the roof of the inguinal canal?

questions.explanation: The phrenic nerve (C3, C4, C5) provides sensory innervation to the central diaphragm, including both the pleural and peritoneal surfaces, in addition to its motor supply to the entire diaphragm. Irritation of the diaphragmatic peritoneum (such as in subphrenic abscess, perforated peptic ulcer, or ruptured spleen) can cause referred pain to the shoulder tip via the phrenic nerve, as both derive from the C3-C5 dermatomes. The peripheral parts of the diaphragm receive sensory innervation from the lower six intercostal nerves and subcostal nerve.
questions.question: Which nerve provides sensory innervation to the central part of the diaphragm?
Which vessel supplies the scalp in the occipital region?
questions.explanation: The occipital artery, a branch of the external carotid, supplies the posterior scalp. It ascends on the back of the neck, pierces the trapezius attachment, and runs in the dense connective tissue layer of the scalp. The artery accompanies the greater occipital nerve. Scalp lacerations in this region can cause significant bleeding.

The two sesamoid bones at the head of the first metatarsal are embedded within the tendons of flexor hallucis brevis (medial and lateral heads). They protect the tendons from compression during weight-bearing and increase the mechanical advantage of flexor hallucis brevis. Sesamoiditis (inflammation of sesamoid bones) causes plantar pain under the first metatarsal head and is common in dancers and runners.
questions.question: Sesamoid bones at the head of the first metatarsal are embedded in the tendons of which muscle?
Which cartilage caps the apex of the arytenoid?
questions.explanation: The corniculate cartilages (cartilages of Santorini) are small conical nodules of elastic cartilage that sit on the apex of each arytenoid cartilage. They are located in the posterior part of the aryepiglottic folds. The cuneiform cartilages lie more anteriorly in the aryepiglottic folds. Both are visible on laryngoscopy as small elevations.

The medial cutaneous nerve of the arm (C8, T1) from the medial cord provides sensation to the medial aspect of the arm. The intercostobrachial nerve (T2) also contributes to sensation in the axilla and medial arm. Both can be affected in axillary surgery or trauma.
questions.question: What nerve provides sensation to the medial arm?
The dorsalis pedis artery is the continuation of which artery as it crosses the ankle to enter the foot?
questions.explanation: The dorsalis pedis artery begins as the anterior tibial artery enters the foot at the ankle. It passes over the dorsal tarsal bones and then moves toward the sole, anastomosing with the lateral plantar artery to form the deep plantar arch. It supplies the tarsal bones and dorsal metatarsals, and contributes to the toes via the deep plantar arch.

questions.question: What is spontaneous pneumothorax most common in?
questions.explanation: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax is most common in young (20-40 years), tall, thin males. It typically results from rupture of apical pleural blebs (small air-filled sacs). Risk factors include smoking, Marfan syndrome, and family history. Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax occurs in patients with underlying lung disease (COPD, asthma, cystic fibrosis).

The lower trunk is formed by union of C8 and T1 nerve roots. Injury to the lower trunk causes Klumpke's paralysis with claw hand deformity. The lower trunk continues as the medial cord after giving off no branches in the neck.
questions.question: Which nerve roots form the lower trunk?
The stylomastoid foramen transmits which cranial nerve?
questions.explanation: The facial nerve exits the skull through the stylomastoid foramen after traversing the facial canal. It then enters the parotid gland and divides into five terminal branches. Damage at this location causes complete ipsilateral facial paralysis including loss of taste to anterior two-thirds of tongue.

A cervical rib (arising from C7) can compress the lowest trunk of the brachial plexus as it arches over the rib at the thoracic inlet. This causes T1 symptoms: pain and paresthesias along the ulnar border of the forearm and wasting of the small muscles of the hand.
questions.question: Where can cervical rib compress the brachial plexus?

questions.explanation: The red pulp comprises approximately 76-79% of normal splenic tissue and consists of blood-filled sinusoids and splenic cords (cords of Billroth). The red pulp is responsible for filtering blood, removing old or damaged erythrocytes, and recycling iron. It appears red due to the large number of red blood cells in the sinusoids.
questions.question: Which component comprises the majority of splenic tissue?
Which kidney is more commonly affected by renal cell carcinoma?
questions.explanation: Renal cell carcinoma affects both kidneys with approximately equal frequency, though some studies show a slight left-sided predominance. It typically presents in the 60-70 age group and is more common in males. The classic triad of flank pain, hematuria, and palpable mass is present in only 10-15% of cases. Most are now detected incidentally on imaging.

questions.question: What indicates diaphragmatic paralysis radiographically?
questions.explanation: Radiographically, diaphragmatic paralysis is recognized by elevation of the affected hemidiaphragm and paradoxical movement. On fluoroscopy, the paralyzed hemidiaphragm moves upward during inspiration (instead of descending) due to passive displacement by abdominal pressure. This is called the "sniff test."

questions.question: The facial artery crosses which border of the mandible?
questions.explanation: The facial artery crosses the inferior border of the mandible at the anterior edge of the masseter muscle, where its pulse can be palpated. After crossing, it ascends toward the medial canthus as the angular artery. The artery winds around the mandible from the neck to reach the face. Facial vein crosses more anteriorly.

questions.question: What is the approximate weight of an adult liver?
questions.explanation: The adult liver weighs approximately 1500 grams, constituting about 2.5% of total body weight in healthy adults. The liver is the largest internal organ and the largest gland in the human body. In newborns, the liver is proportionally larger, contributing to the characteristic protuberant abdomen of infants.

Lumbricals originate from flexor digitorum profundus tendons (unique among hand muscles). This means lumbrical contraction (causing MCP flexion and IP extension) also reduces profundus tension. This coupling enables the delicate coordination needed for precision movements like writing.
options: This attachment has no special anatomical significance
FDP origin couples DIP flexion with IP extension
questions.question: What is the functional significance of lumbrical muscle origin?
What sensation is lost in ulnar nerve palsy at the wrist?
questions.explanation: Ulnar nerve palsy at the wrist causes sensory loss over the medial one and one-half fingers (little finger and ulnar half of ring finger) on both palmar and dorsal aspects. The dorsal ulnar cutaneous branch arises proximal to the wrist, so its distribution may be spared depending on injury level.

questions.question: The hindfoot consists of which two bones?
questions.explanation: The hindfoot consists of the talus and the calcaneus. The calcaneus (heel bone) is the largest and strongest bone, absorbing shock and leveraging movement. The talus (ankle bone) articulates with the tibia and fibula superiorly and with the calcaneus inferiorly and navicular anteriorly, allowing ankle movement and weight transfer to the foot.

The quadratus lumborum receives innervation from the subcostal nerve (T12) and the upper lumbar nerves (L1-L3 or L4), reflecting its position as the most lateral muscle of the posterior abdominal wall. This muscle originates from the iliolumbar ligament and adjacent iliac crest, inserting onto the medial half of the inferior border of the 12th rib and the transverse processes of the upper lumbar vertebrae. It functions to fix the 12th rib during inspiration, extend the lumbar vertebral column bilaterally, and produce lateral flexion when acting unilaterally.
questions.question: The quadratus lumborum muscle is innervated by which nerves?

questions.explanation: The perforating branches of the profunda femoris artery consist of three or four arteries that perforate the adductor magnus muscle, contributing to the supply of the medial and posterior thigh muscles. The lateral femoral circumflex artery supplies the lateral thigh, while the medial femoral circumflex artery supplies the femoral head and neck.
questions.question: The perforating branches of the profunda femoris artery perforate which muscle to supply the posterior and medial thigh?

questions.explanation: Polymastia is the presence of extra (supernumerary) breast tissue, which can occur anywhere along the embryonic mammary ridge (milk line) from axilla to groin. This is distinct from polythelia (extra nipples only). Supernumerary breast tissue can undergo the same pathological changes as normal breasts.
questions.question: What defines polymastia?

questions.explanation: The quadratus plantae assists flexor digitorum longus in flexing the lateral four digits. This assistance is needed because the tendons of flexor digitorum longus approach the digits from a medially oblique direction; quadratus plantae corrects this pull to a more longitudinal direction. It originates from the medial and lateral plantar surfaces of the calcaneus and is innervated by the lateral plantar nerve.
questions.question: The second layer of foot muscles contains the quadratus plantae and lumbricals. The quadratus plantae assists which extrinsic muscle in flexing the lateral four digits?
What are Montgomery's glands?
questions.explanation: The areola glands of Montgomery are intermediate in structure between lactiferous and sweat glands. They are greatly enlarged in pregnancy and lactation as subcutaneous tubercles. Their oily secretion acts as a protective lubricant during lactation, preventing nipple cracking.

questions.question: The external anal sphincter is composed of which muscle type?
questions.explanation: The external anal sphincter is composed of striated (skeletal) voluntary muscle under somatic control via the inferior rectal nerve (branch of pudendal nerve, S2-S4) and perineal branch of S4. It surrounds the entire length of the anal canal external to the internal sphincter and is divided into subcutaneous, superficial, and deep parts. The external sphincter provides voluntary control of defecation and maintains continence, particularly during sudden increases in intra-abdominal pressure. In contrast, the internal anal sphincter (derived from thickened rectal circular smooth muscle) is under involuntary autonomic control and maintains baseline anal tone.

questions.question: The modified Harris Hip Score and Oxford Hip Score are patient-reported outcome measures used to assess which joint?
questions.explanation: The Harris Hip Score (modified) and Oxford Hip Score are validated patient-reported outcome measures used to assess pain, function, and quality of life following hip conditions and hip replacement surgery. The Oxford Hip Score uses 12 questions covering pain and function, with a range of 0-48 (48 being best). These are standard outcome measures used in arthroplasty registries globally, including the Nigerian context of the MDCN setting.

questions.question: Which muscle closes the vestibule of the larynx during swallowing?
questions.explanation: The aryepiglotticus muscle closes the laryngeal vestibule during swallowing by pulling the arytenoid cartilages toward the epiglottis. The thyroepiglotticus and thyroarytenoid muscles assist in this protective function. The aryepiglottic folds form the lateral margins of the laryngeal inlet.

The external anal sphincter, composed of skeletal muscle and innervated by the inferior rectal nerve (branch of pudendal nerve), is under voluntary control and can be consciously contracted to prevent or defer defecation. The internal anal sphincter (smooth muscle, autonomic control) maintains resting anal tone. The puborectalis muscle contributes to the anorectal angle and fecal continence.
questions.question: Which structure controls voluntary defecation?

questions.explanation: Renal and ureteric pain is typically felt in the loin (flank) and radiates to the groin and genitalia, following the T10-L1 dermatomes. Upper ureteric/renal pelvis obstruction causes loin pain, mid-ureteric obstruction causes iliac fossa pain, and lower ureteric obstruction causes suprapubic pain with urinary frequency. This radiation pattern is characteristic of renal colic from ureteric stones.
questions.question: Where is referred pain from renal pathology typically felt?

questions.explanation: L3 root compression presents with quadriceps weakness (knee extension), reduced patellar reflex (L3 component), and sensory changes on the anteromedial thigh and medial leg. The femoral nerve (L2, L3, L4) supplies the quadriceps, and the knee jerk is primarily L3 and L4. Pure L3 compression spares the dorsiflexors (L4, L5) and plantarflexors (S1, S2).
questions.question: A patient presents with weakness of knee extension and reduced patellar reflex but intact hip and ankle function. Which nerve root is most likely compressed?
The external spermatic fascia is derived from which layer?
questions.explanation: The external spermatic fascia is the outermost covering of the spermatic cord, derived from the external oblique aponeurosis as the cord passes through the superficial inguinal ring. The three concentric fascial coverings of the cord (from outside to inside) are: external spermatic fascia (from external oblique), cremasteric muscle and fascia (from internal oblique and transversus abdominis), and internal spermatic fascia (from transversalis fascia). Each layer is acquired as the processus vaginalis and accompanying structures descend through the layers of the anterior abdominal wall during testicular descent.

questions.question: The fibular (peroneal) artery is a branch of which vessel, making it an indirect branch of the popliteal artery?
questions.explanation: The fibular (peroneal) artery arises from the tibioperoneal trunk, which is one of the two terminal divisions of the popliteal artery (the other being the anterior tibial artery). The tibioperoneal trunk then divides into the posterior tibial artery and the fibular artery. The fibular artery descends alongside the fibula in the posterior compartment.

options: Iliopsoas tendon snapping over the femoral head
Hamstring tendon snapping over the ischial tuberosity
Iliotibial band snapping over the greater trochanter
Rectus femoris tendon snapping over the anterior inferior iliac spine
Gluteus medius tendon snapping over the lesser trochanter
questions.question: The snapping hip syndrome (coxa saltans) involves a palpable and audible snap during hip flexion and extension. External snapping involves which structure snapping over which prominence?
questions.explanation: External coxa saltans involves the iliotibial band (or tensor fasciae latae) snapping over the greater trochanter during hip flexion and extension. Internal coxa saltans involves the iliopsoas tendon snapping over the iliopectineal eminence or the femoral head. Intra-articular snapping is due to loose bodies or labral tears. External snapping is most common and associated with trochanteric bursitis.

questions.question: Where does the thoracic sympathetic trunk lie?
questions.explanation: The thoracic sympathetic trunk lies anterolateral to the vertebral bodies, just lateral to the anterior longitudinal ligament. It descends from the neck through the superior mediastinum and posterior mediastinum. Each trunk has 11-12 segmental ganglia, though the first thoracic ganglion often fuses with the inferior cervical ganglion.

questions.question: Which artery is the main blood supply to the face?
questions.explanation: The facial artery is the main arterial supply to the face, arising from the external carotid artery. It winds around the mandible anterior to the masseter and ascends toward the medial canthus. Branches include superior and inferior labial, lateral nasal, and angular arteries.

questions.question: The great auricular nerve is derived from which spinal segments?
questions.explanation: The great auricular nerve arises from the cervical plexus (C2-C3) and provides sensation to the skin over the parotid gland, lower ear, and angle of the mandible. It emerges at the posterior border of sternocleidomastoid and ascends on that muscle. The nerve is at risk during parotid surgery and facelift procedures.

questions.question: Which branches arise from the first part of the axillary artery?
questions.explanation: The first part of the axillary artery (from lateral border of first rib to upper border of pectoralis minor) gives off only one branch. This is the superior (highest) thoracic artery. The second part gives two branches while the third part gives three branches.

questions.question: Which structure separates the greater and lesser peritoneal sacs?
questions.explanation: The lesser omentum forms the anterior boundary of the lesser sac, separating it from the greater sac anteriorly along with the posterior wall of the stomach. This double-layered peritoneal fold extends from the lesser curvature of the stomach and first part of duodenum to the liver. The lesser omentum consists of the hepatogastric ligament (its membranous portion) and the hepatoduodenal ligament (its thickened free right edge containing the portal triad), with the latter forming the anterior boundary of the epiploic foramen.

questions.question: What is the functional relationship between wrist position and finger function?
options: Wrist position affects finger flexor/extensor length affecting grip
questions.explanation: Wrist position affects finger flexor and extensor muscle lengths through tenodesis effect. Wrist extension tightens finger flexors enhancing grip while passively flexing fingers. Wrist flexion tightens extensors causing passive finger extension. This relationship is exploited in tenodesis grip for spinal cord injury patients.

questions.question: Which hamstring muscle originates from the ischial tuberosity and inserts into the posterior part of the medial condyle of the tibia?
questions.explanation: Semimembranosus originates from the ischial tuberosity and inserts into the posterior part of the medial condyle of the tibia. Its reflected attachment forms the oblique popliteal ligament. Semimembranosus is named for its membranous (flat, broad) proximal tendon, in contrast to semitendinosus which has a long round distal tendon.

Pes planus (flat foot) is characterized by collapse of the medial longitudinal arch. The foot print of a flat foot shows increased contact with the ground medially. It can be flexible (reversible on tip-toeing) or rigid. Common causes include tibialis posterior tendon rupture, spring ligament laxity, and obesity. It can lead to secondary knee and hip pain.
options: Transverse arch first then longitudinal arches
questions.question: Pes planus (flat foot) is a deformity characterized by collapse of which arch?

questions.explanation: The saphenous nerve is the terminal cutaneous branch of the femoral nerve (L3, L4). It runs with the great saphenous vein along the medial leg, from the knee to the medial malleolus and then to the medial side of the foot. It provides cutaneous sensation to the medial leg, ankle, and foot. It is at risk during stripping of the great saphenous vein for varicose vein surgery or coronary bypass grafting.
options: Common fibular nerve; great saphenous vein
questions.question: The saphenous nerve is the terminal cutaneous branch of which nerve and runs with which vein throughout most of the leg?
Which muscles, posteriorly related to the hip joint, separate it from the sciatic nerve?
questions.explanation: Posteriorly, the obturator internus, the gemelli, and the quadratus femoris separate the hip joint from the sciatic nerve. Superiorly, piriformis and gluteus minimus are related. Anteriorly, iliopsoas, pectineus, and rectus femoris are anterior relations. Inferiorly, the tendon of obturator externus is found. These relations are vital during posterior hip surgery.
options: Obturator internus, gemelli, and quadratus femoris

questions.question: The dorsum of the foot receives cutaneous innervation from several nerves. Which nerve supplies the skin between the 1st and 2nd toes on the dorsum?
questions.explanation: The deep fibular nerve supplies the skin of the first web space (between the 1st and 2nd toes) on the dorsum of the foot. The superficial fibular nerve supplies most of the dorsum of the foot. The saphenous nerve supplies the medial side (first metatarsal area), while the sural nerve supplies the lateral side (digiti minimi area). This pattern is important in assessing nerve injuries.

The fovea capitis transmits blood from the obturator artery via the ligamentum teres (ligament of the head of femur). This vascular route is clinically important, as fractures of the femoral neck can disrupt primary blood supply and lead to avascular necrosis.
questions.question: The fovea capitis of the femoral head transmits blood from which artery to the femoral head?

questions.explanation: The subacromial bursa is the largest bursa in the body, positioned between the supraspinatus tendon and the coraco-acromial arch. It protects the supraspinatus tendon against friction with the acromion during arm abduction. Inflammation of this bursa is responsible for several shoulder pathologies including rotator cuff tendonitis.
questions.question: Which bursa is the largest in the body and lies between supraspinatus and the coraco-acromial arch?
How many borders does each lung possess?
questions.explanation: Each lung has three borders: anterior, posterior, and inferior. The anterior border is where the costal and mediastinal surfaces meet. The posterior border is thick and extends from C7 to T10. The inferior border separates the base from the costal and mediastinal surfaces.

options: Teres major, teres minor, long head of triceps, surgical neck of humerus
Subscapularis, teres major, latissimus dorsi, humerus
Teres minor, teres major, long head of triceps, lateral head of triceps
Deltoid, teres minor, long head of triceps, humerus
questions.explanation: The quadrangular space is bounded superiorly by teres minor, inferiorly by teres major, medially by the long head of triceps, and laterally by the surgical neck of humerus. Through this space pass the axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral vessels. Injury to these structures can occur with shoulder trauma.
questions.question: Which muscles form the boundaries of the quadrangular space in the axilla?
What replaces thymic tissue in adults?
questions.explanation: In adults, the involuting thymus is progressively replaced by adipose (fatty) tissue. This normal age-related change is called thymic involution. Despite fatty replacement, some functional thymic tissue usually persists even in elderly individuals. On CT scans, the adult thymus appears as fatty tissue in the anterior mediastinum.

On the left side, the pleural reflection passes inferomedially to the level of the fourth costal cartilage, where it deviates to the left margin of the sternum. This creates a shallow notch corresponding to the cardiac notch of the left lung. This differs from the right side where the pleura descends vertically in the median plane.
questions.question: At which costal cartilage does left pleural reflection deviate?

questions.explanation: The quadrate lobe, despite being part of the anatomical right lobe (located between the gallbladder fossa and falciform ligament), functionally belongs to the left lobe as it receives its blood supply from the left hepatic artery and drains bile via the left hepatic duct. The functional division of the liver (Couinaud's classification) is based on vascular supply and biliary drainage rather than external anatomical features. The main portal fissure (containing the middle hepatic vein) separates functional right and left lobes, running from the gallbladder fossa to the IVC, placing the quadrate and caudate lobes functionally on the left.
questions.question: The quadrate lobe of the liver receives blood from which branch?

questions.explanation: The flexor pollicis brevis is one of the thenar muscles supplied by the recurrent branch of the median nerve.
