The superior pancreaticoduodenal artery (from gastroduodenal) divides into anterior and posterior branches that descend on their respective surfaces of the pancreatic head, anastomosing with corresponding anterior and posterior branches of the inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery (from SMA). This rich anastomotic network provides collateral circulation between celiac and SMA systems.

questions.question: Which nerve innervates the cremaster muscle?
questions.explanation: The cremaster muscle receives motor innervation from the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve (L1, L2), which enters the inguinal canal through the deep inguinal ring and travels within the spermatic cord. The cremasteric reflex (elevation of the testis in response to stroking the inner thigh) tests this nerve and the L1-L2 cord segments. The ilioinguinal nerve provides sensory innervation to the skin of the scrotum and adjacent thigh but does not innervate the cremaster muscle. The cremasteric artery (from inferior epigastric) provides vascular supply to the cremaster muscle and travels alongside the nerve.

questions.question: Which vein forms the continuation of the sigmoid sinus?
questions.explanation: The internal jugular vein begins at the jugular foramen as the continuation of the sigmoid sinus. It descends in the carotid sheath lateral to the carotid arteries. At the base of the neck, it joins the subclavian vein to form the brachiocephalic vein. The vein receives the facial, lingual, pharyngeal, and thyroid veins.

The sural nerve is typically formed in the middle third of the leg (or sometimes in the lower popliteal fossa) when the medial sural cutaneous nerve (from the tibial nerve) unites with the sural communicating branch (from the common fibular nerve). It then descends to pass posterior to the lateral malleolus and supply the lateral side of the leg, ankle, and lateral heel. Its predictable course makes it valuable for nerve grafting.
questions.question: The medial sural cutaneous nerve and the sural communicating branch of the common fibular nerve unite to form the sural nerve. At what level does this union typically occur?
options: In the popliteal fossa immediately after bifurcation
In the middle third of the leg or lower popliteal region
At the superior angle of the popliteal fossa
At the ankle level near the malleolus only
Just posterior to the lateral malleolus at the ankle

questions.explanation: The ovarian artery (arising from the aorta at L2) descends obliquely across the psoas major muscle, crosses anterior to the ureter and the common iliac vessels (or external iliac vessels), then enters the suspensory ligament of the ovary to reach the ovary in the pelvis. This long course reflects the ovary's embryological origin high on the posterior abdominal wall. The artery anastomoses with the uterine artery in the broad ligament. In males, the testicular artery follows a similar course but continues through the inguinal canal. The ovarian artery's relationship to the ureter is surgically important.
questions.question: The ovarian artery crosses which structure anteriorly?
What muscle initiates finger extension at interphalangeal joints?
questions.explanation: extend the interphalangeal joints while simultaneously flexing the metacarpophalangeal joints. This coordinated action is essential for precision grip and fine motor control. Extensor digitorum extends the metacarpophalangeal joints but cannot independently extend interphalangeal joints without intrinsic muscle assistance.

questions.question: The femoral canal, the medial compartment of the femoral sheath, contains which structures and is the site of which type of hernia?
questions.explanation: The femoral canal, the most medial compartment of the femoral sheath, normally contains lymphatics and loose connective tissue. It is the site of femoral hernias, which are more common in women (due to their wider pelvis and femoral ring). Femoral hernias emerge below and lateral to the pubic tubercle (unlike inguinal hernias above and medial to it). They are at high risk of strangulation due to the rigid femoral ring.
options: Lymphatics and loose connective tissue; femoral hernia
Femoral artery and nerve; femoral hernia

questions.question: Which muscle is NOT supplied by the pharyngeal plexus?
questions.explanation: The stylopharyngeus muscle is supplied solely by the glossopharyngeal nerve (IX), not the pharyngeal plexus. All other pharyngeal muscles receive innervation from the pharyngeal plexus (vagus via cranial accessory). The stylopharyngeus elevates the pharynx and larynx during swallowing. It is the only structure supplied by the motor component of IX.

questions.question: Which muscle can be absent without functional deficit?
questions.explanation: is absent in approximately 15% of people without any functional deficit. When present, it inserts into the flexor retinaculum and palmar aponeurosis. The tendon is commonly harvested for use in tendon grafts and reconstructive procedures.

The sternoclavicular joint connects the medial end of the clavicle to the manubrium of the sternum. This synovial joint is the sole bony articulation linking the shoulder girdle to the axial skeleton. Posteriorly lie important structures including the common carotid artery and internal jugular vein.
questions.question: Which joint in the shoulder girdle provides the only bony link to the axial skeleton?

questions.explanation: The internal carotid artery enters the skull through the carotid canal in the petrous temporal bone. It ascends through the carotid canal, passes above the foramen lacerum, traverses the cavernous sinus, and emerges to give off the ophthalmic artery. The sympathetic carotid plexus surrounds the artery in the canal.
questions.question: The internal carotid artery enters the skull through which opening?
The middle colic artery divides into which branches?
questions.explanation: The middle colic artery (from the superior mesenteric artery) enters the transverse mesocolon and divides into right and left branches that supply the transverse colon. The right branch anastomoses with the right colic artery (from SMA), while the left branch anastomoses with the ascending branch of the left colic artery (from inferior mesenteric artery), forming the marginal artery of Drummond at the splenic flexure. This anastomotic connection between SMA and IMA territories provides important collateral circulation. Variation in the middle colic artery is common; occasionally it may be absent or arise as two separate vessels.

During expiration, the right dome of the diaphragm reaches as high as the fifth rib due to the upward bulge of the right lobe of the liver. The left dome ascends to the fifth intercostal space. With maximal inspiration, the domes flatten out considerably, descending several centimeters.
questions.question: At which rib does right dome reach during expiration?
Which structure separates the oral cavity from the oropharynx?
questions.explanation: The palatoglossal arch (anterior pillar of fauces) forms the boundary between the oral cavity and oropharynx. The arch contains the palatoglossus muscle and extends from the soft palate to the side of the tongue. The isthmus of fauces is the opening between the oral cavity and oropharynx, bounded by these arches.

questions.question: The inguinal ligament extends between which two points?
questions.explanation: The inguinal ligament represents the rolled-under, thickened inferior border of the external oblique aponeurosis, extending from the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) laterally to the pubic tubercle medially. It serves as a retinaculum bridging the subinguinal space through which pass the iliopsoas muscle, femoral vessels and nerve, and lymphatics entering/leaving the thigh. The inguinal ligament forms the inferior boundary (floor) of the inguinal canal and the base of Hesselbach's triangle. The lacunar ligament represents its medial extension, reflecting posteriorly to attach to the pectineal line.

The "critical zone" in the supraspinatus tendon has relatively poor vascularity, located approximately 1cm from its humeral insertion. This hypovascular area is more susceptible to degenerative changes and tears. The zone's poor blood supply impairs healing after injury.
questions.question: What is the significance of the critical zone in the supraspinatus tendon?

questions.explanation: The thoracic duct begins as the cisterna chyli anterior to L1 vertebra, formed by lumbar and intestinal trunks. It ascends through the aortic hiatus into the thorax. At the root of the neck, it arches forward to enter the left venous angle (junction of left internal jugular and subclavian veins).
questions.question: The thoracic duct begins at which vertebral level?

questions.explanation: The third layer of foot muscles contains three muscles: flexor hallucis brevis, adductor hallucis, and flexor digiti minimi brevis. Flexor hallucis brevis and adductor hallucis are supplied by branches of the medial and lateral plantar nerves respectively. The adductor hallucis assists in maintaining the transverse arch of the foot by drawing the metatarsals medially.
questions.question: The third layer of foot muscles contains three muscles. Which combination is correct?
options: Abductor hallucis, flexor digitorum brevis, abductor digiti minimi
Plantar interossei, dorsal interossei, flexor hallucis brevis
Flexor hallucis brevis, adductor hallucis, flexor digiti minimi brevis
Flexor hallucis brevis, abductor hallucis, flexor digiti minimi brevis

questions.explanation: The tibiofibular ligament (syndesmosis) and interosseous membrane maintain the integrity of the tibiofibular mortise, ensuring that the distal tibia and fibula remain properly spaced for stable articulation with the trochlea tali. Disruption of the syndesmosis (high ankle sprain or Maisonneuve fracture) significantly destabilizes the ankle joint and requires surgical fixation.
questions.question: The tibiofibular ligament and interosseous membrane form part of the ankle joint supports. These structures maintain which relationship between the tibia and fibula at the ankle?
options: They allow free rotation between tibia and fibula
They maintain tibiofibular mortise integrity for stable talus articulation
They create the lateral wall of the ankle
They only protect the interosseous vessels
They provide primary stability against valgus stress

questions.explanation: The splanchnic nerves are branches of the thoracic sympathetic trunk that carry preganglionic sympathetic fibers to the abdominal viscera. The greater splanchnic nerve arises from T5-9 ganglia, the lesser from T10-11, and the least (when present) from T12. They pierce the diaphragm to reach abdominal ganglia.
questions.question: What are the splanchnic nerves?
Tibialis anterior strain causes pain along the anterolateral shin during walking or running. Which specific action does the injured muscle perform that is impaired?
questions.explanation: Tibialis anterior dorsiflexes the ankle and inverts the foot. Strain of this muscle impairs these actions, causing pain during the heel-strike phase of gait (when the muscle eccentrically controls foot plantarflexion) and during active dorsiflexion. Shin splints (medial tibial stress syndrome) can involve the tibialis anterior among other muscles. Anterior compartment syndrome also affects it acutely.

questions.question: Which vessels cross anterior to the third part of the duodenum?
questions.explanation: The superior mesenteric artery and vein cross anteriorly over the third (horizontal) part of the duodenum. This anatomical relationship can cause superior mesenteric artery (SMA) syndrome, where the duodenum is compressed between the SMA and the aorta, leading to intestinal obstruction. The third part of the duodenum passes from right to left across the vertebral column at L3.

is the primary adductor of the thumb, bringing it toward the palm. It is supplied by the ulnar nerve, unlike the other thenar muscles. The muscle has two heads (oblique and transverse) that converge on the base of the proximal phalanx.
questions.question: Which muscle is the primary adductor of the thumb?

questions.explanation: The eparterial bronchus is the right upper lobar bronchus, so named because it arises above (epi-) the pulmonary artery. All other bronchi are hyparterial (below the pulmonary artery). This anatomical feature is unique to the right lung and has embryological significance.
questions.question: What is the eparterial bronchus?
Which artery supplies the upper third of the anal canal?
questions.explanation: The superior rectal artery (continuation of the inferior mesenteric artery) supplies the upper two-thirds of the anal canal above the pectinate line. The middle rectal arteries (from internal iliac) and inferior rectal arteries (from internal pudendal) supply the lower third. This mixed blood supply creates a watershed area prone to ischemia.

The interureteric ridge (interureteric fold) is a smooth muscular ridge connecting the two ureteric orifices and forms the posterior boundary (base) of the trigone. The trigone is a smooth triangular area on the internal bladder base with the two ureteric orifices forming the superolateral angles and the internal urethral orifice forming the inferior angle.
questions.question: Which structure forms the posterior boundary of the bladder trigone?

questions.explanation: The anterior ethmoidal foramen in the medial orbital wall transmits the anterior ethmoidal nerve (from nasociliary) and vessels (from ophthalmic artery). These structures supply the anterior ethmoidal air cells, frontal sinus, and upper nasal cavity. The foramen is located between the ethmoid and frontal bones at the frontoethmoidal suture.
questions.question: The anterior ethmoidal foramen transmits which structures?
What nerve provides motor innervation to all thenar muscles?
questions.explanation: Thenar muscles receive dual innervation: the recurrent branch of the median nerve supplies abductor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis, and superficial head of flexor pollicis brevis. The ulnar nerve supplies the deep head of flexor pollicis brevis and sometimes contributes to other thenar muscles.

questions.question: Which structure separates the frontal lobe from the orbit?
questions.explanation: The thin orbital plate (roof) of the frontal bone separates the frontal lobe of the brain from the orbital contents. Fractures can cause CSF leakage into the orbit. The anterior cranial fossa lies above this plate. The frontal sinus may pneumatize into this region of the frontal bone.

questions.question: Which vessels supply the esophagus in thorax?
questions.explanation: In the thorax, the esophagus is supplied by esophageal branches arising directly from the anterior aspect of the descending thoracic aorta. Additional supply comes from the inferior thyroid artery superiorly and left gastric artery inferiorly. Bronchial arteries also contribute small branches. Venous drainage follows a similar pattern.

The foramen ovale in the greater wing of the sphenoid transmits the mandibular division (V3) of the trigeminal nerve. It also transmits the accessory meningeal artery, lesser petrosal nerve, and an emissary vein. The nerve supplies muscles of mastication and provides sensation to the mandibular region.
questions.question: The foramen ovale transmits which nerve?

questions.explanation: The caudate lobe of the liver, despite being part of the anatomical right lobe, is functionally independent, receiving blood from both right and left hepatic arteries and draining bile into both right and left hepatic ducts. It also has separate venous drainage directly into the IVC via small hepatic veins, independent of the main right, middle, and left hepatic veins. This unique drainage explains why the caudate lobe may hypertrophy in cirrhosis (where it maintains direct IVC access) and why it can function in Budd-Chiari syndrome when the main hepatic veins are occluded. The caudate process extends from the caudate lobe toward the porta hepatis.
options: Both right and left hepatic ducts
questions.question: The caudate lobe of the liver drains bile into which duct?

questions.explanation: Displaced clavicle fractures risk injury to the subclavian vessels and brachial plexus trunks that pass immediately posterior to the bone. The subclavius muscle provides some protection, but severe displacement can damage these vital structures. Posteriorly, the common carotid artery and internal jugular vein are also at risk.
questions.question: Which structure is at risk in displaced clavicle fractures?

questions.explanation: The lymphatic drainage of the upper ureter is to the lateral aortic (para-aortic) lymph nodes, while the pelvic portion drains to the internal and external iliac nodes. This lymphatic drainage pattern follows the blood supply. The lateral aortic nodes are located around the origin of the renal arteries at the L1-L2 level.
questions.question: Which lymph nodes drain the upper ureter?

questions.explanation: The suprapleural membrane is attached at its apex to the transverse process of the seventh cervical vertebra (C7). Laterally, it attaches to the internal border of the first rib and its costal cartilage. Medially, it blends with the fascia covering structures passing through the superior thoracic aperture.
questions.question: To which structure is the suprapleural membrane attached apically?

questions.explanation: An emissary vein passes through the foramen ovale connecting the cavernous sinus with the pterygoid venous plexus. Other emissary veins include those passing through the foramen spinosum (middle meningeal vein), mastoid foramen (sigmoid sinus), and parietal foramina (superior sagittal sinus). These valveless connections allow bidirectional flow and infection spread.
questions.question: Which foramen transmits the emissary vein connecting the cavernous sinus?
The cruciate anastomosis, at the level of the lesser trochanter, provides collateral connection between the femoral arteries and which major vessel?
questions.explanation: The cruciate anastomosis is situated at the level of the lesser trochanter and is formed by the inferior gluteal artery, medial and lateral femoral circumflex arteries, and the first perforating branch of the profunda femoris. Together with the trochanteric anastomosis, it provides collateral connection between the femoral arteries and the internal iliac arteries.

The prostate gland is classically described as having five lobes: anterior (fibromuscular, no glandular tissue), posterior (palpable on digital rectal exam, common site of carcinoma), median (between ejaculatory ducts, may enlarge to cause bladder outlet obstruction), and right and left lateral lobes (largest, common site of benign prostatic hyperplasia). Modern zonal anatomy describes peripheral zone (70%, site of most cancers), central zone (25%, around ejaculatory ducts), transitional zone (5%, surrounds urethra, site of BPH), and anterior fibromuscular stroma. The median lobe may project into the bladder when enlarged, causing urinary symptoms.
questions.question: The prostate is divided into how many lobes?

questions.explanation: The saphenous nerve supplies the medial side of the leg, ankle, and medial side of the foot down to the first metatarsophalangeal joint. It is the terminal cutaneous branch of the femoral nerve, descending with the great saphenous vein. It exits the adductor canal with the saphenous branch of the descending genicular artery and provides sensation along the medial leg from knee to hallux.
options: Only the medial knee and distal thigh region
Medial leg down to the ankle only
Only the medial thigh, groin, and inner knee
The entire medial foot including the sole
Medial leg, ankle, and medial foot to the first MTP joint
questions.question: The saphenous nerve, the largest cutaneous branch of the femoral nerve, supplies the medial side of the leg and foot down to which level?

questions.explanation: Trochanteric bursitis is a common cause of hip pain that is more likely to involve women. It is most often caused by overuse or direct trauma to the joint. It presents as lateral hip pain that may radiate down the thigh and is aggravated by lying on the affected side or climbing stairs.
questions.question: Trochanteric bursitis at the tip of the greater trochanter is more likely to occur in which gender and due to what mechanism?

questions.explanation: The posterior intercostal veins lie deepest in the costal grooves and contain valves that direct blood flow posteriorly. The neurovascular bundle arrangement from superior to inferior is vein-artery-nerve (VAN). The veins are the largest and most superior structures in this arrangement.
questions.question: Which structure lies deepest in the costal groove?

questions.explanation: The spinal accessory nerve (XI) provides motor innervation to the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles. Additional proprioceptive fibers from C2-C3 may contribute. Unilateral contraction of sternocleidomastoid turns the face to the opposite side and tilts the head ipsilaterally. Bilateral contraction flexes the neck.
questions.question: The sternocleidomastoid muscle is innervated by which nerve?
What percentage of the pancreas is exocrine tissue?
questions.explanation: Approximately 99% of the pancreatic tissue is exocrine, consisting of acinar cells that secrete digestive enzymes. Only about 1% consists of endocrine tissue in the form of pancreatic islets (islets of Langerhans). The exocrine pancreas produces 1.5-2 liters of pancreatic juice daily containing enzymes for protein, carbohydrate, and fat digestion.

questions.question: Which papillae on the tongue do NOT contain taste buds?
questions.explanation: Filiform papillae are the most numerous papillae but do not contain taste buds; they provide the rough texture of the tongue. Fungiform, circumvallate, and foliate papillae all contain taste buds. The circumvallate papillae are arranged in a V-shape along the sulcus terminalis.

questions.question: How many secondary ossification centres does the hip bone have in total?
questions.explanation: The hip bone has five secondary ossification centres: two for the iliac crest, two for the Y-shaped cartilage of the acetabulum, and one for the ischial tuberosity. All five fuse by 20-25 years of age. The three primary centres (ilium, ischium, pubis) appear in the 2nd, 4th, and 5th months of intrauterine life, respectively.

The posterior auricular artery arises from the posterior aspect of the external carotid artery above the level of the digastric and stylohyoid muscles. It supplies the auricle, scalp behind the ear, and gives off the stylomastoid artery (which supplies the facial nerve and middle ear structures). The artery ascends between the parotid gland and mastoid process.
questions.question: The posterior auricular artery is a branch of which vessel?

questions.explanation: The thymus consists of two elongated lobes and is a large organ in the fetus, occupying the thoracic cavity behind the sternum. It secretes lymphopoietin and plays a crucial role in T-lymphocyte maturation. After puberty, the thymus undergoes involution and is gradually replaced by adipose tissue.
questions.question: How many lobes does the thymus consist of?

questions.explanation: The hepatic portal vein forms posterior to the neck of the pancreas at approximately the L1/L2 level through the confluence of the superior mesenteric vein (from the right) and splenic vein (from the left), anterior to the inferior vena cava. The inferior mesenteric vein typically joins the splenic vein before this confluence. From its formation, the portal vein ascends obliquely to the right within the hepatoduodenal ligament to reach the porta hepatis, where it divides into right and left branches. The portal vein measures approximately 8 cm in length and has no valves.
questions.question: The hepatic portal vein is formed posterior to which structure?

questions.explanation: Rectus femoris is the only quadriceps component that crosses the hip joint, originating from the anterior inferior iliac spine. Therefore, it can both extend the leg at the knee and flex the thigh at the hip. The three vasti originate from the femur itself and only cross the knee joint.
questions.question: Which muscle is the ONLY component of the quadriceps that crosses the hip joint and can therefore flex the thigh?

questions.explanation: The right lung in a healthy adult male weighs approximately 600 grams when filled with air, while the left lung weighs about 550 grams. The lungs are spongy, elastic organs that are pinkish in healthy individuals. In city dwellers, they may appear darker due to accumulation of carbon particles.
questions.question: What is the lung weight in a healthy adult male?

questions.explanation: The middle suprarenal artery (from the abdominal aorta) is unique in that it supplies the medulla directly without first passing through the cortex, carrying preganglionic sympathetic fibers directly to chromaffin cells (modified postganglionic neurons). The superior suprarenal artery (from inferior phrenic) and inferior suprarenal artery (from renal) supply primarily the cortex. This direct arterial supply to the medulla allows rapid hormone release (epinephrine and norepinephrine) in response to stress. The suprarenal glands have rich arterial supply from three sources but limited venous drainage (one vein each side).
questions.question: Which artery supplies the suprarenal medulla directly?

questions.explanation: The pudendal canal (Alcock's canal) is a fascial tunnel in the lateral wall of the ischiorectal fossa, formed by the splitting of the obturator fascia covering the obturator internus muscle. It contains the pudendal nerve and internal pudendal vessels as they pass from the lesser sciatic foramen toward the perineum. The pudendal nerve (S2-S4) provides motor innervation to perineal muscles and sensory innervation to the external genitalia and perineum. Pudendal nerve block can be performed by injecting anesthetic near the ischial spine where the nerve re-enters the pelvis.
questions.question: Which structure is located in the pudendal canal?
What are gray rami communicantes?
questions.explanation: Gray rami communicantes carry postganglionic sympathetic fibers from sympathetic ganglia back to all spinal nerves for distribution to blood vessels, sweat glands, and arrector pili muscles throughout the body. They are "gray" because postganglionic fibers are unmyelinated. Gray rami exist at all spinal levels unlike white rami.

The stapedius muscle reflex activates bilaterally at sound levels above 80 dB SPL to protect the cochlea. This acoustic reflex increases ossicular chain stiffness and attenuates low-frequency sounds. Testing this reflex provides valuable information about facial nerve and auditory pathway integrity.
questions.question: At what sound pressure level does the stapedius reflex typically activate?

questions.explanation: The pancreas extends obliquely across the posterior abdominal wall from the C-shaped curve of the duodenum (head) to the splenic hilum (tail) at approximately L1-L2 vertebral levels, though the tail may extend slightly higher. The head lies at L1-L2, the neck crosses L1, and the body and tail run along L1-L2 as they extend to the left. The pancreas is secondarily retroperitoneal (except the tail, which extends into the splenorenal ligament), lying anterior to the splenic vein, superior mesenteric vessels, aorta, IVC, left kidney, and left suprarenal gland.
questions.question: The pancreas lies at which vertebral levels?

questions.explanation: The differential diagnosis for anterior mediastinal masses is remembered by the "4 T's": Thymus (thymoma, thymic hyperplasia), Thyroid (retrosternal goiter, thyroid cancer), Teratoma (and other germ cell tumors), and Terrible lymphoma (Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphoma). Age and imaging characteristics help narrow the differential.
questions.question: What is the differential for anterior mediastinal mass?

questions.explanation: The obturator artery typically arises from the anterior division of the internal iliac artery, descending along the lateral pelvic wall to exit the pelvis through the obturator canal (superior to obturator membrane) with the obturator nerve. However, anatomical variation is common (25-30% of cases), with the obturator artery sometimes arising as an aberrant or accessory vessel from the inferior epigastric artery (a branch of external iliac), passing along the pelvic brim to reach the obturator foramen. This "aberrant obturator artery" is at risk during hernia repair as it may run along the margin of the femoral ring.
questions.question: The obturator artery is a branch of which vessel?

questions.explanation: The foramen of Morgagni is located anteriorly between the xiphoid and costal origins of the diaphragm. Hernias through this opening (Morgagni hernias) are less common than Bochdalek hernias but can allow omental fat or intestine to herniate into the anterior mediastinum. They are usually asymptomatic.
questions.question: Where is Morgagni's foramen located?
Where does the axillary tail extend?
questions.explanation: The axillary tail (of Spence) is a process that extends from the upper lateral part of the breast into the axilla. It passes through an opening in the deep fascia and may reach as far as the third rib. Cancer in the axillary tail presents as an axillary mass.

questions.question: What muscles produce lateral rotation of the humerus?
questions.explanation: Lateral (external) rotation of the humerus is produced by infraspinatus, teres minor, and posterior fibers of the deltoid. The infraspinatus and teres minor are two of the four rotator cuff muscles. This movement rotates the arm away from the midline, making the thumb point laterally.

questions.question: What causes Horner's syndrome in Klumpke's paralysis?
questions.explanation: Horner's syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhydrosis, enophthalmos) in Klumpke's paralysis results from injury to sympathetic fibers traveling with the T1 nerve root. These sympathetic fibers supply the head and neck. The association indicates severe lower trunk injury affecting both motor and sympathetic components.

The superior thyroid artery is typically the first branch of the external carotid artery, arising just below the carotid bifurcation. It descends to supply the thyroid gland and gives off the superior laryngeal artery. The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve accompanies this artery and innervates the cricothyroid muscle.
questions.question: The superior thyroid artery is typically the first branch of which vessel?

questions.explanation: Rotator cuff muscles provide dynamic stability through their resting tone, actively compressing the humeral head into the glenoid cavity. The muscles form a tendinous cuff blending with the joint capsule, providing circumferential reinforcement. This active stabilization is essential given the joint's inherent bony instability.
options: Through passive ligament and capsule action
Rotator cuff compresses humeral head into glenoid cavity
questions.question: How do the rotator cuff muscles stabilize the glenohumeral joint?
Which vein ascends in the anterior interventricular groove?
questions.explanation: The great cardiac vein ascends in the anterior interventricular groove alongside the anterior interventricular artery, then curves left in the coronary groove to become the coronary sinus. It drains the areas supplied by the left coronary artery (anterior left ventricle, anterior interventricular septum, and parts of right ventricle). It is the largest tributary of the coronary sinus.

The great saphenous vein has 10-12 valves that are more numerous in the leg than in the thigh. These valves are usually located just inferior to the perforating veins. Perforating veins also contain valves directing blood from superficial to deep venous systems. Incompetence of these valves leads to varicose veins most commonly in the leg.
questions.question: The great saphenous vein has 10-12 valves. These are more numerous in which segment of the vein?

questions.explanation: The lesser sac (omental bursa) communicates with the greater sac through the epiploic foramen (foramen of Winslow, foramen of Winslow), bounded anteriorly by the hepatoduodenal ligament, posteriorly by the IVC and right crus of diaphragm, superiorly by the caudate lobe of liver, and inferiorly by the first part of the duodenum. This communication allows peritoneal fluid to flow between the two sacs and permits spread of infection or hemorrhage. The foramen typically admits two fingers and can be used surgically to access the lesser sac. Foramina of Morgagni and Bochdalek are diaphragmatic defects, not communications between peritoneal sacs.
questions.question: The lesser sac communicates with the greater sac through which opening?
The patellar ligament, described as the distal part of the quadriceps tendon, ultimately attaches to which bony prominence?
questions.explanation: The patellar ligament passes from the apex and adjoining margins of the patella to the tibial tuberosity. It is a strong thick fibrous band representing the distal continuation of the quadriceps tendon. It blends with the medial and lateral patellar retinacula (aponeurotic expansions of vastus medialis and lateralis) providing additional stability.

questions.question: Which bone contains the cribriform plate?
questions.explanation: The cribriform plate is part of the ethmoid bone and forms the roof of the nasal cavity. It contains multiple foramina transmitting olfactory nerve fibers from the nasal epithelium to the olfactory bulb. The crista galli projects upward from the cribriform plate for attachment of the falx cerebri.

The portal vein forms posterior to the neck of the pancreas by the union of the superior mesenteric and splenic veins. It is approximately 8 cm long and ascends behind the first part of the duodenum to the porta hepatis, where it divides into right and left branches. It receives the left and right gastric veins, cystic vein, and paraumbilical veins during its course.
questions.question: Where does the portal vein form anatomically?

questions.explanation: At the superior angle of the popliteal fossa, the sciatic nerve divides into the common fibular nerve (laterally, following the medial border of biceps femoris) and the tibial nerve (medially). From lateral to medial: common fibular nerve, tibial nerve, popliteal vein, then popliteal artery (deepest). This arrangement changes inferiorly as the popliteal vein crosses to lie posterior to the artery.
questions.question: In the popliteal fossa, the popliteal artery lies deepest and the tibial nerve most superficially. In what order, from lateral to medial, are the structures arranged superiorly within the fossa?
options: Popliteal artery, popliteal vein, tibial nerve, common fibular nerve
Tibial nerve, common fibular nerve, popliteal vein, popliteal artery
Common fibular nerve, popliteal artery, popliteal vein, tibial nerve
Common fibular nerve, tibial nerve, popliteal vein, popliteal artery
Popliteal vein, popliteal artery, tibial nerve, common fibular nerve
Ligaments of the joint and adjacent bone
Muscles moving the joint and skin covering their insertion
Tendons crossing the joint and adjacent bursae
Articular cartilage and synovial membrane only
questions.question: Hilton's law states the nerve supplying a joint also supplies which other two structures?
questions.explanation: Hilton's law states: 'The nerve supplying the joint also supplies the muscles moving the joint and the skin covering the insertion of these muscles.' This explains why patients with hip joint disease may refer pain to the knee, as the posterior division of the obturator nerve supplies both joints. It is fundamental in understanding referred pain patterns.

questions.question: What is the functional relationship between finger flexor sublimis and profundus?
questions.explanation: Flexor digitorum superficialis flexes PIP joints independently of DIP joints. Flexor digitorum profundus flexes DIP joints and contributes to PIP and MCP flexion, providing power grip force. This two-layer arrangement enables independent or combined finger joint flexion for varied hand positions.
options: Both tendons have identical flexor function
FDS flexes PIP joints, FDP flexes DIP joints

questions.explanation: The vertebral arteries give off anterior spinal arteries before joining to form the basilar artery. The two anterior spinal arteries unite to form a single vessel descending in the anterior median fissure. The vertebral arteries also give off posterior spinal arteries. These vessels supply the cervical spinal cord before receiving reinforcement from segmental arteries.
questions.question: The vertebral artery gives off which spinal branch?

questions.explanation: The median nerve passes between the humeral and ulnar heads of pronator teres muscle. Compression at this site causes pronator teres syndrome, an entrapment neuropathy. This produces pain in the proximal forearm and sensory symptoms in the median nerve distribution.
questions.question: What nerve passes between the two heads of pronator teres?

questions.explanation: The tendons of the four quadriceps components unite to form the quadriceps tendon, which continues as the patellar ligament (also called patellar tendon) with the patella embedded within as a sesamoid bone. This inserts into the tibial tuberosity. The patellar retinacula are aponeurotic expansions that provide additional lateral stability.
questions.question: The quadriceps tendon continues as which structure, with the patella embedded within it, attaching to the tibial tuberosity?

questions.explanation: The thoracic duct drains into the left venous angle (junction of left internal jugular and subclavian veins). It collects lymph from the entire body except the right upper quadrant. The duct begins at the cisterna chyli (L1-L2), ascends through the thorax, and arches over the left subclavian artery to reach the venous angle.
questions.question: Which lymphatic duct drains into the left venous angle?
What provides collateral drainage in SVC obstruction?
questions.explanation: In SVC obstruction, the azygos venous system (along with intercostal veins and other collaterals) provides alternative drainage pathways for blood from the upper body to reach the right atrium. These collateral vessels dilate significantly. Prominent dilated veins may be visible on the chest wall and abdomen, directing flow from above downward.

questions.question: Which layer of the anterior abdominal wall contains Scarpa's fascia?
questions.explanation: Scarpa's fascia is the deep membranous layer of the superficial fascia of the anterior abdominal wall, found inferior to the umbilicus. Superficial to it lies Camper's fascia, the fatty superficial layer. Scarpa's fascia continues inferiorly as the superficial perineal fascia (Colles' fascia) in the perineum and the dartos muscle and fascia in the scrotum. This fascial layer is clinically important as it can limit the spread of extravasated urine or blood in the superficial perineal space, directing fluids superiorly toward the anterior abdominal wall.

The thoracic duct begins at the level of L1 as a continuation of the cisterna chyli, which is formed by the union of left and right lumbar trunks and the intestinal trunk. It ascends through the aortic opening of the diaphragm into the thoracic cavity. The duct eventually terminates by draining into the left venous angle after receiving additional lymphatic tributaries.
questions.question: Which structure represents the continuation of cisterna chyli?
Which ligaments anchor the bladder neck in males?
questions.explanation: The puboprostatic ligaments extend from the posterior aspect of the pubic bones to the prostate and bladder neck in males, anchoring these structures. In females, the equivalent structures are the pubovesical ligaments. The lateral ligaments of the bladder (containing superior vesical vessels) also contribute to bladder support and fixation.

questions.question: Which position tests for carpal tunnel syndrome?
questions.explanation: Phalen's test (passive wrist flexion for 60 seconds) provokes carpal tunnel syndrome symptoms by increasing pressure within the tunnel. Reproduction of paresthesia in the median nerve distribution within one minute is considered positive. The reverse Phalen's test uses wrist extension.

questions.question: What produces medial rotation of the humerus at the shoulder?
options: Subscapularis, pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi, teres major
questions.explanation: Medial (internal) rotation of the humerus is produced by subscapularis, pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi, teres major, and anterior fibers of deltoid. This movement rotates the arm toward the midline so the thumb points medially. These muscles are predominantly anterior or on the subscapular surface.

Pronator quadratus is supplied by the anterior interosseous nerve, a branch of the median nerve. This nerve also supplies flexor pollicis longus and the lateral half of flexor digitorum profundus. The pronator quadratus is the deepest muscle in the anterior forearm.
questions.question: Which nerve supplies pronator quadratus?

questions.explanation: Brachioradialis is unique as an anterior compartment muscle (flexor) supplied by the radial nerve, which typically supplies extensors. This reflects its developmental origin from extensor muscle mass despite its eventual anterior position. It flexes the forearm most effectively from mid-prone position.
options: Anterior compartment flexor with radial nerve supply
questions.question: How does the brachioradialis differ from other radial nerve-supplied muscles?

questions.explanation: The costodiaphragmatic recess is located inferiorly between the costal and diaphragmatic pleura and is by far the more clinically important of the two pleural recesses. It is shallow during inspiration and becomes deeper during expiration. This recess can accumulate fluid in pleural effusions and is the site for thoracentesis.
questions.question: Where is the costodiaphragmatic recess most clinically important?
Which structure is at risk in hook of hamate fracture?
questions.explanation: The ulnar nerve is at risk in hook of hamate fracture as it passes through Guyon's canal adjacent to this structure. The deep branch of the ulnar nerve curves around the hook of the hamate. Fracture can cause motor weakness of intrinsic hand muscles with or without sensory symptoms.

questions.question: Which ganglion contains cell bodies for taste from the anterior tongue?
questions.explanation: The geniculate ganglion of the facial nerve contains cell bodies of sensory neurons carrying taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue via chorda tympani. The ganglion is located at the genu (bend) of the facial canal in the temporal bone. Herpes zoster infection (Ramsay Hunt syndrome) causes facial paralysis and painful vesicles.

questions.question: The superior oblique muscle is innervated by which cranial nerve?
questions.explanation: The superior oblique muscle is innervated by the trochlear nerve (IV), the only extraocular muscle not supplied by the oculomotor nerve except lateral rectus (abducens). The superior oblique passes through the trochlea (pulley) on the medial orbital roof. It intorts, depresses, and abducts the eye.

The left phrenic nerve pierces the left dome of the diaphragm to supply the abdominal surface. The right phrenic nerve passes through the caval opening in the central tendon. Both phrenic nerves provide motor supply to the entire diaphragm and sensory supply to its central portion.
questions.question: Which nerve pierces the left dome of diaphragm?
What causes cubital tunnel syndrome?
questions.explanation: Cubital tunnel syndrome results from ulnar nerve compression as it passes through the cubital tunnel posterior to the medial epicondyle. This is the most common site of ulnar nerve entrapment. Symptoms include numbness in the ulnar one and one-half fingers and intrinsic hand muscle weakness.

The upper lateral quadrant of the buttock receives cutaneous innervation from L1 and T12. This is distinct from the upper medial quadrant (L1, 2, 3 and S1, 2, 3), lower medial quadrant (S1, 2, 3), and lower lateral quadrant (L2, 3). Clinical dermatomal mapping in this region can help identify the level of spinal pathology.
questions.question: Which cutaneous nerves supply the upper lateral quadrant of the buttock?

questions.explanation: Elevation of the scapula is caused by contraction of upper and middle fibers of trapezius and levator scapulae muscles. This movement is associated with elevation of the lateral end and depression of the medial end of the clavicle. Shoulder shrugging demonstrates this action.
questions.question: Which muscles elevate the scapula?
options: Upper and middle trapezius, levator scapulae

questions.explanation: Pericardiocentesis is typically performed by inserting a needle just to the left of the xiphoid process, angled upward and posteriorly toward the left shoulder at about 30-45 degrees. This avoids the internal thoracic vessels and enters the pericardial cavity inferior to the heart. The procedure is performed under ECG and/or ultrasound guidance.
questions.question: Where is the ideal location for pericardiocentesis?

questions.explanation: The descending genicular artery is a branch of the femoral artery, contributing superomedially to the genicular anastomosis. The five genicular branches of the popliteal artery are: lateral superior, medial superior, middle, lateral inferior, and medial inferior genicular arteries. The anterior tibial recurrent artery contributes inferolaterally.
questions.question: The descending genicular artery, contributing to the genicular anastomosis superomedially, is a branch of which artery?
How many posterior intercostal arteries does aorta give?
questions.explanation: The descending thoracic aorta gives off nine pairs of posterior intercostal arteries supplying the lower nine intercostal spaces (3rd-11th). The upper two spaces are supplied by the superior intercostal artery from the costocervical trunk. The subcostal arteries (below the 12th rib) are also given off by the thoracic aorta.

is the most commonly torn rotator cuff muscle due to its position under the acromion. Repetitive overhead activities and age-related degeneration increase tear risk. The painful arc (pain during mid-abduction) is characteristic of supraspinatus tendonitis or tears.
questions.question: Which rotator cuff muscle is most commonly torn?
What forms the anorectal angle?
questions.explanation: The puborectalis muscle (part of levator ani) forms a sling around the anorectal junction, creating an approximately 90-degree anorectal angle that contributes to fecal continence. During defecation, the puborectalis relaxes, straightening the anorectal angle to allow passage of feces. Paradoxical contraction of this muscle during defecation causes obstructed defecation syndrome.

questions.question: Which parasympathetic ganglion is associated with the pterygopalatine fossa?
questions.explanation: The pterygopalatine ganglion is located in the pterygopalatine fossa and is one of four parasympathetic ganglia of the head. It receives preganglionic fibers via the greater petrosal nerve and provides secretomotor innervation to lacrimal and nasal glands. The ganglion also transmits sympathetic and sensory fibers without synapsing.

The visceral pleura receives its arterial supply from branches of both the bronchial and pulmonary arterial systems. Venous drainage is to the pulmonary veins. Unlike the parietal pleura, the visceral pleura has no somatic sensory innervation and receives only autonomic vasomotor nerve supply.
questions.question: Which vessels supply blood to the visceral pleura?
Which structure marks the junction of the foregut and midgut blood supply?
questions.explanation: The major duodenal papilla (ampulla of Vater) in the second part of the duodenum marks the embryological and vascular transition between foregut (supplied by celiac trunk) and midgut (supplied by superior mesenteric artery). The superior pancreaticoduodenal artery (from gastroduodenal, ultimately from celiac trunk) supplies the duodenum and pancreatic head above this point, while the inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery (from SMA) supplies structures below it. This dual blood supply creates an anastomotic arcade providing collateral circulation between the two major arterial territories and reflects the embryological division of the primitive gut.

questions.question: Which muscle forms the medial wall of the orbit?
questions.explanation: The medial wall of the orbit is formed by bone (primarily the orbital plate of ethmoid), not muscle. The medial rectus muscle lies within the orbit adjacent to this bony wall. The thin lamina papyracea of the ethmoid separates the orbit from the ethmoidal air cells.

questions.question: How do extrinsic and intrinsic factors contribute to shoulder stability?
questions.explanation: Shoulder stability requires both extrinsic factors (rotator cuff muscles, long head of biceps, negative intra-articular pressure, scapular position) and intrinsic factors (glenoid labrum, glenohumeral ligaments, joint capsule). Loss of either extrinsic or intrinsic factors increases dislocation risk.
options: Both extrinsic and intrinsic stabilizers are essential

questions.question: What forms the superficial cardiac plexus?
questions.explanation: The cardiac plexus is formed by sympathetic fibers from the cervical and upper thoracic sympathetic ganglia and parasympathetic fibers from the vagus nerves. The superficial cardiac plexus lies beneath the aortic arch, while the deep plexus lies between the arch and tracheal bifurcation. These plexuses distribute fibers to the conducting system, coronary vessels, and myocardium.

questions.question: What sign indicates coarctation on chest X-ray?
questions.explanation: Rib notching on chest X-ray is a characteristic sign of aortic coarctation. The dilated, tortuous intercostal arteries (providing collateral circulation) erode the inferior margins of the posterior ribs (typically 3rd-8th ribs bilaterally). This creates scalloped indentations visible on radiographs. The first two ribs are usually spared.

The anterior bellies of the right and left digastric muscles form the lateral boundaries of the submental triangle. The hyoid bone forms the base (inferior boundary), and the mylohyoid muscle forms the floor. The triangle contains submental lymph nodes and is located in the midline below the chin.
questions.question: The anterior belly of the digastric forms part of which triangle?

The hip abductor moment is critical in preventing pelvic drop during single-leg stance. If the moment arm of the hip abductors (gluteus medius) is surgically reduced (e.g., by a high femoral offset prosthesis), what is the clinical consequence?
questions.explanation: Reducing the moment arm of the hip abductors (by medializing the hip center or using a low-offset prosthesis) means the abductor muscles must generate greater force to produce the same abductor moment needed to stabilize the pelvis. This increased muscle force also increases the hip joint reaction force, potentially accelerating bearing surface wear in hip replacements. Restoring femoral offset is therefore biomechanically important.
options: Improved hip abductor muscle strength reducing the limp overall
Improved Trendelenburg gait pattern after total hip arthroplasty
Reduced abductor moment arm requiring greater muscle force and increased joint reaction force
No clinical consequence for gait or joint loading
Reduced knee and ankle pain from altered load distribution only

questions.question: Which feature distinguishes the large intestine from the small intestine externally?
questions.explanation: The taeniae coli are three longitudinal muscle bands that are characteristic external features of the large intestine (colon) but absent from the rectum and anal canal. These bands are shorter than the colon itself, causing sacculations (haustra) to form. The small intestine has a complete, continuous longitudinal muscle layer without taeniae.

The pulmonary ligament is a loose fold of pleura that hangs down below the root of the lung. It is formed by the continuity of visceral and parietal pleura inferior to the hilum. It forms a sleeve allowing for expansion of the pulmonary veins during increased venous return.
questions.question: Where is the pulmonary ligament located?
Which procedure drains pleural fluid?
questions.explanation: Thoracentesis is the procedure to drain fluid from the pleural cavity by inserting a needle or catheter. It is performed just above the upper border of a rib to avoid the neurovascular bundle. The costodiaphragmatic recess is the usual site for this procedure.

Vastus lateralis is the largest component of the quadriceps femoris, lying on the lateral side of the thigh. It originates from the greater trochanter and lateral lip of the linea aspera. All four quadriceps components converge into the quadriceps tendon, which continues as the patellar ligament inserting into the tibial tuberosity.
questions.question: Which component of the quadriceps femoris is the largest and lies on the lateral side of the thigh?

questions.explanation: The ankle joint is more stable during dorsiflexion because the trochlea tali (superior articular surface of the talus) is wider anteriorly. During dorsiflexion, this wider part engages the mortise more tightly, increasing bony congruence and stability. In plantarflexion, the narrower posterior talus is in the mortise, creating relative instability and increased susceptibility to inversion sprains.
options: The wider anterior trochlea tali fits more snugly in the mortise during dorsiflexion
The deltoid ligament is placed under increased tension in dorsiflexion
The calcaneus supports the talus more during dorsiflexion
The Achilles tendon tightens and mechanically limits further dorsiflexion
The lateral ligaments are tighter in dorsiflexion only
questions.question: The ankle joint is more stable during dorsiflexion than plantarflexion. Why is this so?

questions.explanation: The spring ligament (plantar calcaneonavicular ligament) is the most critical ligament maintaining the medial longitudinal arch. It bridges the sustentaculum tali of the calcaneus to the navicular, directly supporting the head of the talus. Rupture of the spring ligament leads to progressive collapse of the medial longitudinal arch and adult acquired flatfoot deformity.
questions.question: Which ligament is the most important structure maintaining the medial longitudinal arch, bridging the sustentaculum tali to the navicular?

questions.explanation: Extrinsic thumb muscles (abductor pollicis longus, extensor pollicis longus and brevis, flexor pollicis longus) provide power and basic positioning. Thenar muscles provide fine motor control and opposition. This combination enables the thumb's unique versatility in human hand function.
questions.question: How do extrinsic thumb muscles complement thenar muscles?
options: Extrinsic muscles for precision grip only
Extrinsic for power grip, thenar for precision control

questions.question: Tibialis anterior dorsiflexes and inverts the foot. It inserts into which specific structures?
questions.explanation: Tibialis anterior inserts into the medial and inferior surfaces of the medial cuneiform and the base of the first metatarsal. It originates from the lateral condyle and superior half of the lateral surface of the tibia and interosseous membrane. It is the most powerful dorsiflexor and inverts the foot, active throughout the swing phase of gait.
options: Base and styloid process of the 5th metatarsal only
Medial and inferior surfaces of medial cuneiform and base of 1st metatarsal
Navicular tuberosity and the adjacent medial cuneiform bone
Bases of the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th metatarsal bones
Calcaneus via the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon posteriorly

questions.question: Which condition causes anterior dislocation of the lunate?
questions.explanation: Anterior dislocation of the lunate occurs from falling on a dorsiflexed wrist. The lunate is forced anteriorly and compresses the carpal tunnel contents including the median nerve. This causes carpal tunnel syndrome symptoms with paresthesia and thenar muscle weakness. The lunate also risks avascular necrosis.

The superior thoracic aperture is bounded posteriorly by the first thoracic vertebra (T1). Anteriorly, it is bounded by the superior border of the manubrium sterni. Laterally, the medial borders of the first ribs and their costal cartilages complete the boundaries of this important opening.
questions.question: Which structure bounds the superior thoracic aperture posteriorly?
How many lobes does the mammary gland contain?
questions.explanation: The mammary gland is formed of 15-20 lobes, each consisting of numerous lobules. The lobes and lobules are separated by interlobar and interlobular fibrous and fatty tissue called the ligaments of Cooper. Each lobe drains through its own lactiferous duct, which opens onto the nipple summit.

questions.question: Which cranial nerve supplies sensory innervation to the oropharynx?
questions.explanation: The glossopharyngeal nerve provides sensory innervation to the oropharynx, including the tonsillar region and posterior third of tongue. The vagus nerve also contributes sensation to the valleculae via the internal laryngeal branch. Referred otalgia from pharyngeal lesions occurs via glossopharyngeal pathways.

questions.question: Which muscle forms the right crus of the diaphragm?
questions.explanation: The right crus of the diaphragm arises from the bodies and intervertebral discs of the upper three lumbar vertebrae (L1-L3), while the left crus arises from only the upper two lumbar vertebrae (L1-L2). The crura are tendinous structures that ascend to insert into the central tendon. The right crus is longer and stronger, and some of its fibers form a muscular sling around the oesophageal hiatus.

The dorsal venous arch lies in the subcutaneous tissue over the heads of the metatarsal bones. It drains medially into the great saphenous vein (via the dorsal vein of the great toe) and laterally into the small saphenous vein (via the dorsal vein of the little toe). This arch is the origin point of both major superficial veins of the lower limb.
questions.question: The dorsal venous arch of the foot drains medially into the great saphenous vein and laterally into which vein?

questions.explanation: The left gastric artery is the smallest of the three branches of the celiac trunk (along with splenic and common hepatic arteries), arising at the T12/L1 level. It ascends to the cardioesophageal junction, giving off esophageal branches to the abdominal esophagus, then descends along the lesser curvature of the stomach in the lesser omentum, anastomosing with the right gastric artery. It supplies both surfaces of the stomach along the lesser curvature. An aberrant or replaced left hepatic artery may arise from the left gastric artery, running in the gastrohepatic ligament.
questions.question: The left gastric artery arises from which vessel?

questions.explanation: Sympathetic efferents from the thoracic sympathetic trunk cause bronchodilation and inhibit secretion from bronchial glands. This is clinically important in conditions like asthma where bronchodilators (sympathomimetics) are used therapeutically. Parasympathetic stimulation from the vagus causes bronchoconstriction.
questions.question: What causes bronchodilation in the lungs?
Which structure marks the transition from foregut to midgut?
questions.explanation: The major duodenal papilla represents the embryological junction between foregut and midgut derivatives, marking the transition from celiac to superior mesenteric arterial supply. The duodenum proximal to this point receives blood from the celiac trunk (via gastroduodenal and superior pancreaticoduodenal arteries), while the portion distal to it is supplied by the superior mesenteric artery (via inferior pancreaticoduodenal arteries). This vascular watershed reflects the embryological division of the primitive gut tube and has important implications for the blood supply and venous/lymphatic drainage patterns.

questions.question: Which muscle elevates the first rib?
questions.explanation: The scalene muscles fix and elevate the first rib during inspiration. With the first rib fixed, the external and internal intercostal muscles elevate the other ribs upward toward it. The scalene muscles are accessory muscles of respiration and are particularly active during forced inspiration.

The superior epigastric artery is the other terminal branch of the internal thoracic artery. It descends behind the rectus abdominis muscle supplying it and the anterior abdominal wall. It anastomoses with the inferior epigastric artery (from external iliac), providing collateral circulation between subclavian and external iliac arteries.
questions.question: Which artery supplies the anterior body wall superiorly?

questions.explanation: The inferior rectal nerve (branch of the pudendal nerve, S2-S4) provides somatic sensory innervation to the anal canal below the pectinate line, making this region sensitive to pain, touch, and temperature. The inferior rectal nerve also provides motor innervation to the external anal sphincter. Above the pectinate line, the anal canal receives autonomic innervation (from inferior hypogastric plexus), making it insensitive to pain but responsive to stretch. This difference explains why internal hemorrhoids (above pectinate line) are painless while external hemorrhoids (below the line) are painful.
questions.question: Which nerve provides sensory innervation below the pectinate line?

questions.explanation: The testes drain lymph directly to the para-aortic (lumbar) lymph nodes at the L1-L2 level, corresponding to their embryological origin high on the posterior abdominal wall and their arterial supply from the abdominal aorta. Lymphatics accompany the testicular vessels through the spermatic cord, inguinal canal, and over the pelvic brim to reach these nodes. In contrast, the scrotum drains to superficial inguinal nodes. This lymphatic drainage pattern is clinically crucial in testicular cancer staging and explains why metastases first appear in para-aortic nodes rather than inguinal nodes (unless the scrotal skin is also involved).
questions.question: Which lymph nodes receive drainage from the testis?

questions.explanation: The anterior tibial artery gives off the anterior tibial recurrent artery, which ascends to the front of the knee to contribute inferolaterally to the genicular anastomosis. This vessel pierces the anterior tibialis muscle and anastomoses with the inferior lateral genicular artery. Knowledge of this anastomosis is important for understanding collateral circulation when the popliteal artery is occluded.
questions.question: The anterior tibial artery runs through the anterior compartment and enters the foot as the dorsalis pedis artery. It gives off which branch that contributes to the genicular anastomosis?
Which vein drains directly into the inferior vena cava?
questions.explanation: The hepatic veins (right, middle, and left) drain directly into the inferior vena cava just below the diaphragm, representing the final pathway for blood that has passed through the hepatic sinusoids. Unlike other veins, hepatic veins have no valves. The portal vein and its tributaries (splenic, superior mesenteric, and inferior mesenteric veins) carry nutrient-rich but deoxygenated blood to the liver, where it mixes with oxygenated blood from the hepatic artery in the sinusoids before draining via hepatic veins. The hepatic veins and their relationship to IVC are crucial landmarks in liver surgery and transplantation.

Osgood-Schlatter disease is traction apophysitis at the tibial tuberosity, where the patellar ligament inserts during the growth phase. It affects adolescents (boys aged 12-15, girls aged 8-13) who are active in jumping and running sports. Repeated quadriceps contractions pull on the incompletely ossified tibial tuberosity. Treatment is activity modification and physiotherapy.
questions.question: Osgood-Schlatter disease involves traction apophysitis at which site in adolescents?

questions.explanation: Posterior interosseous syndrome results from compression of the posterior interosseous nerve as it passes through the supinator muscle. This causes weakness of finger and thumb extensors. Unlike complete radial nerve palsy, wrist extension is preserved as extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis are supplied proximal to the compression.
questions.question: What causes posterior interosseous syndrome?

questions.explanation: The levator anguli oris is innervated by the buccal branch of the facial nerve. It elevates the angle of the mouth during smiling. The muscle arises from the canine fossa of the maxilla and inserts into the angle of the mouth. It lies deep to levator labii superioris and zygomaticus minor muscles.
questions.question: The levator anguli oris muscle is innervated by which nerve branch?

options: Dual arterial supply proximally and distally
Direct branches from radial artery proximally
questions.explanation: Only one small artery enters the scaphoid bone at the end closest to the thumb (distal end). This unique blood supply pattern makes the scaphoid vulnerable to avascular necrosis following fracture. The proximal fragment may lose blood supply if fracture tears the artery.
questions.question: What is the primary blood supply to the scaphoid bone?

questions.explanation: The superficial lymphatics of the lower limb accompany the great saphenous vein and drain to the superficial inguinal lymph nodes. The deep lymphatics accompany the deep vessels and drain to the deep inguinal and then external iliac nodes. The popliteal nodes drain the posterior leg and lateral foot (accompanying the small saphenous vein). Lymphedema of the lower limb can follow radical inguinal lymph node dissection.
questions.question: The lymphatics of the lower limb follow the saphenous vein and drain to which lymph node group?

questions.explanation: The inferior boundary is where the medial pterygoid muscle attaches to the mandible near its angle. The fossa has no distinct floor but is limited inferiorly by this muscular attachment. Superiorly, it is bounded by the greater wing of the sphenoid.
questions.question: Which structure forms the inferior boundary of the infratemporal fossa?
Which structure prevents food from entering the nasopharynx during swallowing?
questions.explanation: The soft palate elevates and tenses during swallowing to close off the nasopharynx, preventing nasal regurgitation. Levator veli palatini elevates while tensor veli palatini tenses the palate. The uvula contacts the posterior pharyngeal wall (Passavant's ridge) to complete the seal.

options: Adductor hallucis, all interossei, lateral three lumbricals, and flexor digiti minimi brevis
All lumbricals and interossei of the foot only
Only the flexor digiti minimi brevis of the little toe
Abductor digiti minimi of the lateral plantar group alone
All intrinsic foot muscles except the abductor hallucis
questions.question: The lateral plantar nerve (S1, S2) is analogous to the ulnar nerve of the hand. It supplies which muscles as its deep branch?
questions.explanation: The deep branch of the lateral plantar nerve (analogous to the deep branch of ulnar nerve) supplies adductor hallucis, all plantar and dorsal interossei, the lateral three lumbricals, and flexor digiti minimi brevis. The superficial branch of the lateral plantar nerve supplies flexor digiti minimi brevis and provides cutaneous branches to the lateral one and a half toes.

The septal cusp of the tricuspid valve is attached to the interventricular septum, while the anterior and posterior cusps are attached to the anterior and posterior ventricular walls respectively. The septal cusp receives chordae tendineae from the septal and posterior papillary muscles. Ventricular septal defects near the membranous septum can affect this cusp's support.
questions.question: Which valve cusp is attached to the interventricular septum?
Where is coarctation typically located?
questions.explanation: Aortic coarctation is typically located just distal to the left subclavian artery origin, near the site of the ligamentum arteriosum (remnant of ductus arteriosus). This is called juxtaductal coarctation. Less commonly, it may be preductal or postductal. The stenosis reduces blood flow to the lower body.

questions.question: The pterygopalatine fossa communicates with the orbit through which opening?
questions.explanation: The inferior orbital fissure connects the pterygopalatine fossa with the orbit. The fissure is bounded by the greater wing of sphenoid, maxilla, and palatine bone. The maxillary nerve continues through this fissure as the infraorbital nerve. The infraorbital and zygomatic nerves and vessels pass through this communication.

questions.question: The urinary bladder receives parasympathetic innervation from which spinal segments?
questions.explanation: The urinary bladder receives parasympathetic innervation from the pelvic splanchnic nerves (nervi erigentes) arising from the S2, S3, and S4 spinal segments. These preganglionic fibers synapse in ganglia within the bladder wall and stimulate contraction of the detrusor muscle (for micturition) while relaxing the internal urethral sphincter. Sympathetic innervation (L1-L2 via lumbar splanchnic nerves and superior hypogastric plexus) has the opposite effect, promoting urine storage by relaxing the detrusor and contracting the internal sphincter. Somatic innervation of the external urethral sphincter comes from the pudendal nerve (S2-S4), allowing voluntary control.

questions.question: What nerve is at risk in Bennett's fracture?
questions.explanation: The superficial branch of the radial nerve courses over the base of the first metacarpal and is at risk in Bennett's fracture (intra-articular fracture-dislocation of the thumb metacarpal base). Injury can cause numbness over the dorsum of the thumb and radial side of the hand.

The flexor carpi radialis tendon lies in a groove between the attachments of the flexor retinaculum to bone, not within the carpal tunnel itself. The carpal tunnel contains the median nerve, four tendons each of flexor digitorum superficialis and profundus, and the flexor pollicis longus tendon. These structures are enclosed within synovial sheaths.
questions.question: Which structure does NOT pass through the carpal tunnel?
Which condition causes boutonniere deformity?
questions.explanation: Boutonniere deformity results from rupture of the central slip of the extensor mechanism over the proximal interphalangeal joint. This causes PIP joint flexion with DIP joint hyperextension. The lateral bands slip volarward, creating the characteristic deformity. Common after PIP joint injuries.

questions.question: Into which vessel do the hepatic veins drain?
questions.explanation: The hepatic veins (typically two or three major veins: right, middle, and left) drain directly into the inferior vena cava just below the diaphragm. These veins are intersegmental in distribution, draining adjacent hepatic segments. The attachment of these large veins to the IVC helps anchor the liver in position within the abdominal cavity.

The subscapular bursa communicates with the shoulder joint cavity through an oval gap between the superior and middle glenohumeral ligaments. This direct communication is clinically significant as it allows spread of infection or inflammatory processes between the bursa and joint. The subacromial bursa does not normally communicate with the joint.
questions.question: Which structure communicates with the shoulder joint cavity through the subscapular bursa?

questions.explanation: The femoral nerve (L2, L3, L4) lies lateral to the femoral artery as it exits beneath the inguinal ligament, outside the femoral sheath (which contains only the femoral artery, vein, and canal). The mnemonic NAVEL (Nerve, Artery, Vein, Empty/Lymphatics) describes the lateral to medial arrangement. The femoral nerve rapidly divides into branches in the femoral triangle.
questions.question: The femoral nerve (L2, L3, L4) exits the pelvis beneath the inguinal ligament. It lies in which position relative to the femoral artery?

questions.explanation: The foramen of Bochdalek (pleuroperitoneal canal) is located posterolaterally in the diaphragm. Failure of the pleuroperitoneal membrane to close this opening results in a congenital diaphragmatic hernia. These hernias are more common on the left side and can allow abdominal viscera to herniate into the thorax.
questions.question: Where is Bochdalek's foramen located?
Which ligament forms the free edge of the lesser omentum?
questions.explanation: The hepatoduodenal ligament forms the thickened free right edge of the lesser omentum, extending from the first part of the duodenum to the porta hepatis. It contains the portal triad (portal vein posteriorly, common bile duct anteriorly and to the right, hepatic artery proper anteriorly and to the left) and forms the anterior boundary of the epiploic foramen. The hepatoduodenal ligament can be compressed manually (Pringle maneuver) to control hepatic bleeding by temporarily occluding inflow to the liver. The gastrohepatic ligament forms the membranous portion of the lesser omentum.

questions.question: Which structure passes through esophageal hiatus?
questions.explanation: The esophageal hiatus at T10 transmits the esophagus, anterior and posterior vagal trunks, esophageal branches of left gastric vessels, and lymphatic vessels. The hiatus is formed by muscle fibers of the right crus of the diaphragm. Some right crus fibers form a sling around the esophagus.

questions.question: The patellar reflex (knee jerk) tests which nerve roots?
questions.explanation: The patellar reflex (knee jerk) tests the L3 and L4 nerve roots. The reflex arc involves the femoral nerve (both afferent and efferent), the L3-L4 spinal cord segments, and the quadriceps femoris muscle. An absent or diminished knee jerk suggests L3 or L4 root pathology, commonly from disc herniation at the L2/3 or L3/4 levels. The Achilles tendon reflex tests S1 and S2.

questions.question: Which condition is characterized by paresthesia in median nerve distribution?
questions.explanation: is characterized by paresthesia in the median nerve distribution (thumb, index, middle, and lateral half of ring finger). Symptoms are often worse at night and may be relieved by shaking the hand. The condition results from median nerve compression within the carpal tunnel.

The sigmoid colon drains to sigmoid nodes along the sigmoid arteries, then to inferior mesenteric nodes around the inferior mesenteric artery origin. These eventually drain to para-aortic (lateral aortic) nodes. In colorectal cancer, lymph node involvement follows this drainage pattern and is crucial for staging. The lymphatic spread of left-sided colon cancers differs from right-sided cancers. questions.question: Which lymph nodes drain the sigmoid colon?
The arcuate line represents the inferior limit of which structure?
questions.explanation: The arcuate line (linea semicircularis) marks the inferior border of the posterior rectus sheath, located approximately midway between the umbilicus and pubic symphysis. Above this line, the posterior sheath is formed by the posterior lamina of the internal oblique aponeurosis and the aponeurosis of transversus abdominis. Below the arcuate line, all aponeurotic layers pass anterior to the rectus abdominis, leaving only transversalis fascia and parietal peritoneum posteriorly. This creates an area of weakness exploited by direct inguinal hernias and inferior epigastric vessel injuries.

The calcaneal apophysis (posterior calcaneal epiphysis) is a classic example of an atavistic epiphysis. Traction epiphyses arise at tendinous insertions, while pressure epiphyses form articular surfaces. Traction apophysitis of the calcaneal apophysis in adolescents is known as Sever's disease.
questions.question: An atavistic epiphysis represents a vestigial bone once separate in ancestral species. Which of the following is a classic example in the lower limb?

questions.explanation: The olfactory bulbs lie on the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone in the anterior cranial fossa. Olfactory nerve fibers from the nasal epithelium pass through the cribriform foramina to synapse in the bulbs. The olfactory tracts extend posteriorly from the bulbs. Head trauma can shear these delicate fibers causing anosmia.
questions.question: Which space contains the olfactory bulbs?
What is the normal carrying angle of the fully extended forearm?
questions.explanation: The long axis of the fully extended ulna makes an angle of approximately 170 degrees with the long axis of the humerus. This carrying angle represents the way the forearm angles away from the body when carrying objects. The obliquity is more pronounced in females than males.

questions.question: Which neurovascular structure is the DEEPEST within the popliteal fossa, running closest to the articular capsule of the knee joint?
questions.explanation: The popliteal artery is the deepest structure in the popliteal fossa, running closest to the articular capsule of the knee joint. This proximity makes the popliteal artery particularly vulnerable in posterior knee dislocations and tibial plateau fractures. The arrangement from deep to superficial is: artery, vein, then tibial nerve.

questions.question: What is the functional significance of the scapular anastomoses?
options: Collateral circulation bypassing proximal subclavian obstruction
questions.explanation: Scapular anastomoses provide crucial collateral circulation connecting first part of subclavian artery with third part of axillary artery. This enables continued limb perfusion even with proximal arterial obstruction. The anastomoses involve suprascapular, dorsal scapular, and circumflex scapular arteries.

The tendon of biceps femoris at its insertion on the lateral side of the head of fibula is split into two parts by the fibular (lateral) collateral ligament of the knee joint. The common fibular nerve closely follows the medial border of the biceps femoris tendon and winds around the neck of the fibula. Injury to biceps femoris or the fibular head can therefore damage the common fibular nerve.
questions.question: The tendon of biceps femoris at its fibular head insertion is split into two parts by which ligament?

questions.explanation: The inferior epigastric artery arises from the external iliac artery just above the inguinal ligament, medial to the deep inguinal ring. It ascends obliquely along the medial margin of the deep ring, passing medial to it (an important landmark distinguishing direct from indirect inguinal hernias), and enters the rectus sheath by piercing the transversalis fascia at the arcuate line. Within the sheath, it ascends posterior to the rectus abdominis muscle and anastomoses with the superior epigastric artery, providing an important collateral pathway between subclavian (via internal thoracic) and external iliac arterial systems.
