questions.question: The inferior epigastric artery arises from which vessel?
Which lymph nodes are located along the external jugular vein?
questions.explanation: The superficial cervical lymph nodes lie along the external jugular vein in the superficial cervical fascia. They receive drainage from the scalp and superficial neck structures. Efferent vessels drain to the deep cervical nodes. These nodes are distinct from the deep cervical chain along the internal jugular vein.

questions.question: The posterior ethmoidal foramen transmits which structures?
questions.explanation: The posterior ethmoidal foramen in the medial orbital wall transmits the posterior ethmoidal nerve (from nasociliary) and vessels (from ophthalmic artery). These structures supply the posterior ethmoidal air cells and sphenoid sinus. The foramen is located between the ethmoid and sphenoid bones, posterior to the anterior ethmoidal foramen.

questions.question: Which artery forms an anastomosis across the median cricothyroid ligament?
questions.explanation: Small cricothyroid arterial branches from the superior thyroid arteries anastomose across the median cricothyroid ligament. This anastomosis crosses the ligament horizontally and must be considered during emergency cricothyroidotomy. The vessels typically run superiorly along the cricothyroid membrane.

The palatine tonsil drains to the superior deep cervical nodes, particularly the jugulodigastric node at the angle of the jaw. The soft palate and posterior tongue also drain to these nodes. The jugulodigastric node is also called the tonsillar node due to enlargement during tonsillitis.
questions.question: The superior deep cervical lymph nodes receive drainage from which structure?
The superior hypogastric plexus continues inferiorly as which structure?
questions.explanation: The superior hypogastric plexus (at the L5-S1 level, anterior to the sacral promontory) divides into right and left hypogastric nerves, which descend into the pelvis alongside the rectum to contribute to the right and left inferior hypogastric (pelvic) plexuses. The hypogastric nerves carry postganglionic sympathetic fibers. The inferior hypogastric plexuses also receive the pelvic splanchnic nerves (preganglionic parasympathetic, S2-S4) and branches from the sacral sympathetic ganglia. The combined plexuses supply pelvic viscera with both sympathetic and parasympathetic innervation.

questions.question: Which artery supplies the majority of the nasal septum?
questions.explanation: The sphenopalatine artery (from maxillary artery) provides the dominant blood supply to the nasal septum via posterior septal branches. The anterior ethmoidal artery and superior labial artery contribute anteriorly. Kiesselbach's plexus in the anteroinferior septum is the most common site of epistaxis.

questions.question: Which nerve provides motor innervation to the entire diaphragm?
questions.explanation: The phrenic nerves (C3-C5, with C4 being most important - "C3,4,5 keeps the diaphragm alive") provide all motor innervation to the diaphragm and most of its sensory innervation. Each phrenic nerve supplies the ipsilateral half of the diaphragm. Peripheral parts receive additional sensory innervation from intercostal and subcostal nerves, but these provide no motor supply.

Calot's triangle (cystohepatic triangle) has three boundaries: the cystic duct inferiorly, the common hepatic duct medially (not a vein, despite the question's misdirection), and the inferior surface of the liver superiorly. Within this triangle lie the cystic artery and Calot's lymph node. The correct answer addresses that the common hepatic duct (not a vein) forms the medial boundary. Understanding this triangle's anatomy is crucial for safe cholecystectomy, as the cystic artery must be identified within it before ligation. Anatomical variations in this region are common.
questions.question: Which vein forms the left border of the hepatocystic triangle (Calot's)?

options: Bone shape alone maintains the arches
Muscle tone alone determines arch height
Bone shape, muscle tone, and ligament strength
Tendon length, joint capsule, and synovial fluid
questions.explanation: The arches of the foot are maintained by three factors: the shape of the bones, the strength of the ligaments, and the tone of the muscles. All three work together to maintain normal arch height. In pes planus (flat foot), ligamentous laxity and muscle weakness combine with bony changes to flatten the medial longitudinal arch.
questions.question: The arches of the foot are described as being maintained by three factors. Which combination is correct?
Which vertebral level corresponds to the transpyloric plane?
questions.explanation: The transpyloric plane, passing midway between the suprasternal notch and pubic symphysis (or midway between xiphoid and umbilicus), corresponds to the level of the first lumbar vertebra (L1) and the lower border of vertebra T12. This important surgical landmark crosses numerous structures: pylorus of stomach (when supine), neck of pancreas, origin of the SMA and portal vein, duodenojejunal flexure, hila of both kidneys, fundus of gallbladder, root of transverse mesocolon, origin of IMA (at L3), and tips of ninth costal cartilages. The plane is used to define upper and lower abdominal regions in the nine-region scheme.

The fovea centralis is a depression in the center of the macula lutea, representing the area of most acute vision. It contains only cones (no rods) and has minimal overlying retinal layers to reduce light scatter. The fovea is located temporal to the optic disc. Macular degeneration causes central vision loss.
questions.question: The fovea centralis is located in which structure?

questions.explanation: The first part (superior part) of the duodenum, specifically its first 2 cm (duodenal cap or bulb), is the only portion that is intraperitoneal and mobile, being connected to the liver by the hepatoduodenal ligament. The remainder of the first part and all of the second, third, and fourth parts are secondarily retroperitoneal and fixed to the posterior abdominal wall. This mobility makes the duodenal bulb vulnerable to anterior displacement by posterior masses (e.g., pancreatic head tumors). The mobile first part is also the most common site of peptic ulceration.
questions.question: Which part of the duodenum is most mobile?

questions.explanation: The two ureteric orifices form the superolateral angles (corners) of the triangular trigone. The internal urethral orifice forms the inferior angle. The interureteric ridge connects the two ureteric orifices forming the base of the triangle. The trigone remains smooth even when the bladder is empty, unlike the rest of the bladder mucosa which is rugose when empty.
questions.question: Which structure forms the lateral boundary of the bladder trigone?
Which structure lies posterior to the head of the pancreas?
questions.explanation: The inferior vena cava lies posterior to the head of the pancreas (separated by the right renal vein and sometimes the third part of the duodenum), along with the right renal artery and vein, aorta, and origin of the superior mesenteric artery. The superior mesenteric vein ascends posterior to the neck of the pancreas (not the head), where it joins the splenic vein to form the portal vein. The common bile duct runs in a groove on (or through) the posterior surface of the pancreatic head before joining the main pancreatic duct.

The thoracic duct ascends through the posterior mediastinum and veers to the left at the level of the T5 vertebra. At the root of the neck, it arches forwards and descends to enter the left venous angle. This anatomical course is crucial for understanding lymphatic drainage patterns in the thorax.
questions.question: At which vertebral level does the thoracic duct turn laterally?

options: Single artery to each digit only
Dual proper digital arteries with extensive anastomoses
questions.question: How do digital arteries ensure blood supply to fingertips?
questions.explanation: Each finger receives two proper palmar digital arteries (one on each side from common digital arteries). These anastomose extensively, providing redundant blood supply. Additional dorsal digital arteries contribute. This rich vascular network protects fingertip perfusion critical for hand function.

De Quervain's tenosynovitis involves inflammation of the first dorsal compartment containing abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis tendons. Repetitive thumb and wrist motion causes the condition. Finkelstein's test (ulnar deviation of wrist with thumb flexed in palm) reproduces pain.
questions.question: What causes de Quervain's tenosynovitis?

questions.explanation: The pleural cavity normally contains a small amount of serous (pleural) fluid that acts as a lubricant between the visceral and parietal pleural surfaces. This fluid is continuously produced and absorbed, maintaining a thin film that facilitates smooth lung movement during respiration.
questions.question: What contains the pleural fluid normally?

questions.explanation: The iliopsoas is the primary flexor of the hip joint, formed by the fusion of iliacus and psoas major. Their combined tendon inserts into the lesser trochanter, which is its traction epiphysis. The iliopsoas is active in walking, running, and sitting up. Weakness of iliopsoas is assessed by resisted hip flexion in the seated position.
questions.question: Which muscle is the primary flexor of the hip joint, described as the great flexor, with its traction epiphysis being the lesser trochanter?

questions.explanation: Gluteus maximus has little action during ordinary gentle walking on level ground. It acts mainly in rising from sitting, straightening up, walking upstairs, and running. This is a critical clinical distinction in assessing gluteal function and designing rehabilitation after injury.
questions.question: Despite being the great extensor of the hip joint, gluteus maximus has little action during which of the following?

questions.explanation: The portal vein, positioned posteriorly within the hepatoduodenal ligament (posterior to the bile duct and hepatic artery), forms part of the anterior boundary of the epiploic foramen. The entire hepatoduodenal ligament (containing the portal triad) constitutes the anterior boundary. The portal vein is the most posterior structure within this ligament, closest to the foramen. Injury to the portal vein during surgical manipulation near the epiploic foramen can cause massive hemorrhage into the lesser sac. The foramen can be occluded by compressing the hepatoduodenal ligament between thumb and fingers (Pringle maneuver).
questions.question: Which vein forms the anterior boundary of the epiploic foramen?
Which condition causes thenar muscle wasting?
options: Median nerve palsy or carpal tunnel
questions.explanation: Thenar muscle wasting occurs with median nerve palsy or chronic carpal tunnel syndrome. The recurrent branch of the median nerve supplies the thenar muscles (abductor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis, flexor pollicis brevis). Chronic compression leads to visible flattening of the thenar eminence.

options: Pronator teres for fine control only
Pronator teres for power/speed, pronator quadratus for sustained/slow pronation
questions.explanation: Pronator teres is active during rapid or forceful pronation, while pronator quadratus is the primary muscle for slow, sustained pronation. The quadratus maintains pronated position during precision tasks. This demonstrates functional specialization among synergistic muscles.
questions.question: What is the functional relationship between pronator teres and pronator quadratus?

questions.explanation: The hypoglossal canal is located in the occipital bone above the anterolateral margin of the foramen magnum. It transmits the hypoglossal nerve (XII) from the posterior cranial fossa to the neck. The canal is about 1 cm long. Skull base fractures involving this canal can cause tongue paralysis.
questions.question: Which bone contains the hypoglossal canal?

questions.explanation: The vertebral arteries enter the cranial cavity through the foramen magnum after ascending through the transverse foramina of cervical vertebrae C1-C6. They unite at the pontomedullary junction to form the basilar artery. The vertebral arteries give off the posterior inferior cerebellar arteries before joining.
questions.question: The vertebral arteries enter the skull through which opening?

questions.explanation: The popliteus is considered an intra-articular muscle because part of its tendon runs within the joint capsule of the knee. It passes through a gap in the posterior fibrous capsule (the popliteal hiatus) between the fibular collateral ligament and the lateral meniscus. Popliteal tendinopathy causes posterolateral knee pain during downhill walking when the PCL and popliteus are most active.
questions.question: The popliteus muscle originates from the lateral surface of the lateral femoral condyle and also from the lateral meniscus. It is considered an intra-articular muscle because part of its tendon runs within which structure?
Which ligament connects the coracoid process to the acromion of the scapula?
questions.explanation: The coracoacromial ligament runs between the coracoid process and acromion of the scapula. Unlike other shoulder ligaments, it does not cross a joint or permit movement. It forms part of the coraco-acromial arch that prevents superior displacement of the humeral head.

questions.question: Which muscle fibers are directed downward and forward?
questions.explanation: The external intercostal muscle is the most superficial intercostal muscle with fibers directed downward and forward. It extends from the rib tubercle posteriorly to the costochondral junction anteriorly. The muscle is deficient anteriorly where it is replaced by the anterior intercostal membrane.

Rupture of the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon typically occurs in middle-aged men during sudden powerful plantarflexion or push-off movements (such as jumping or sprinting). The patient feels a sharp pain, as if struck from behind. Simmond's (Thompson's) test confirms rupture: squeezing the calf with the patient prone fails to produce plantarflexion of the foot.
options: Children; direct blow to the heel
Middle-aged men; sudden powerful plantarflexion or push-off
Young female athletes; chronic overuse with no acute event
Infants; congenital deficiency of the tendon
questions.question: Rupture of the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon typically occurs in which demographic and in what mechanism?

questions.explanation: The lateral cord lies lateral to the second part of the axillary artery (behind pectoralis minor). The medial cord lies medially and the posterior cord lies posteriorly to the second part. Below pectoralis minor, the cords give rise to their terminal branches.
questions.question: Which cord lies lateral to the second part of the axillary artery?

questions.explanation: The deep fascia of the gluteal region is continuous with the fascia lata of the thigh. The superficial fascia, thick in women and impregnated with large quantities of fat, accounts for the prominence of the buttock. This fascial continuity has clinical implications for spread of infections between gluteal and thigh compartments.
questions.question: The deep fascia of the gluteal region is continuous inferiorly with which named structure of the thigh?

options: Both lateral and medial pectoral nerves
questions.question: What nerve supplies pectoralis major?
questions.explanation: Pectoralis major receives dual innervation from both lateral pectoral nerve (C5, C6) and medial pectoral nerve (C8, T1). The lateral pectoral nerve is the primary supply. The medial pectoral nerve must pierce pectoralis minor to reach pectoralis major.

questions.question: Which surface of the femoral neck carries the intertrochanteric line, a broad rough area that is the attachment for the iliofemoral ligament?
questions.explanation: The anterior surface of the femoral neck carries the intertrochanteric line, which is broad and rough and serves as attachment for the iliofemoral ligament. The posterior aspect carries the prominent intertrochanteric crest. These landmarks delineate the intracapsular portion of the femoral neck.

options: They become lax to allow free extension
questions.question: During extension of the hip joint, the three extracapsular ligaments behave in which manner due to their spiral orientation?
questions.explanation: The fibers of all three extracapsular hip ligaments are oriented in a spiral fashion around the hip joint, causing them to become taut when the joint is extended. This stabilizes the joint in standing and reduces the amount of muscle energy required to maintain upright posture, demonstrating an important energy-conserving mechanism in bipedal locomotion.

The maxillary antrum and ethmoid sinuses are present in rudimentary form at birth. The frontal and sphenoid sinuses become evident around age seven. This developmental pattern explains why frontal sinusitis is rare in young children. All sinuses reach full development by late adolescence.
questions.question: Which paranasal sinus is present in rudimentary form at birth?

questions.explanation: Houston's third transverse rectal fold is the most constant and prominent, located at the level of S5 vertebra, approximately 5 cm above the anus. If this fold completely encircles the rectum, it is called Nelaton's sphincter. This fold divides the rectum into an upper chamber (containing the pre-allantoic part of the hindgut that can hold feces without triggering the defecation reflex) and a lower chamber (derived from the post-allantoic cloaca that is sensitive to distension). The fold helps support the weight of feces and prevents passage during instrumentation.
questions.question: Houston's third valve in the rectum is located at which vertebral level?

questions.explanation: The lateral compartment contains fibularis longus and fibularis brevis, both supplied by the superficial fibular nerve (L5, S1, S2). Their primary actions are eversion of the foot and weak plantarflexion of the ankle. Fibularis longus also supports the transverse arch by crossing the sole. Lateral compartment injury impairs the ability to evert the foot.
options: Inversion and adduction of the foot
questions.question: The two lateral compartment muscles, both supplied by the superficial fibular nerve, primarily perform which actions?

questions.explanation: The external anal sphincter, composed of voluntary striated muscle, receives motor innervation from the inferior rectal nerve (branch of the pudendal nerve, S2-S4) and perineal branch of S4. This allows voluntary control of defecation and anal continence. The pudendal nerve provides somatic innervation, making the external sphincter unlike the internal sphincter (smooth muscle under involuntary autonomic control). Damage to the pudendal nerve (during childbirth, surgery, or chronic straining) can lead to fecal incontinence. The pudendal nerve also provides sensory innervation to the anal canal below the pectinate line.
questions.question: Which nerve supplies the external anal sphincter?
Why are esophageal constrictions clinically important?
questions.explanation: The four esophageal constrictions are clinically important because they are: (1) sites where swallowed foreign bodies or large food boluses lodge, (2) sites where strictures tend to form, (3) sites where esophageal cancer commonly develops, and (4) areas of resistance during esophagoscopy. The narrowest point is at the cricopharyngeus.

questions.question: Which structure separates the maxillary sinus from the orbit?
questions.explanation: The thin orbital plate of the maxilla forms the roof of the maxillary sinus and the floor of the orbit. The infraorbital nerve and vessels run in a groove on this surface. Fractures can cause orbital contents to herniate into the sinus (blow-out fracture). Dental roots may project into the sinus floor.

The midfoot consists of five of the seven tarsal bones: navicular, cuboid, and three cuneiform bones. The midfoot meets the forefoot at the five tarsometatarsal (TMT) joints. The three cuneiforms articulate proximally with the navicular. The midfoot provides a stable platform and distributes forces between the hindfoot and forefoot during gait.
options: Talus, calcaneus, navicular, cuboid, and one cuneiform
All three cuneiforms and the first two metatarsals
Three cuneiforms, cuboid, and the talus
questions.question: The midfoot consists of five of the seven tarsal bones. Which bones constitute the midfoot?

questions.explanation: Anterior compartment syndrome initially affects the tibialis anterior and the deep fibular nerve running within the compartment. Early symptoms include foot dorsiflexion weakness and pain on passive toe flexion (stretching the anterior compartment muscles). Paraesthesia in the first web space (deep fibular nerve territory) is an early sign. Fasciotomy within 6 hours prevents permanent muscle necrosis and nerve damage.
options: Fibularis longus; loss of foot eversion first
Soleus; first presenting as loss of plantarflexion
Extensor hallucis longus; toe extension loss first
Tibialis anterior; initial loss of dorsiflexion with deep fibular nerve symptoms
Gastrocnemius; presenting first as loss of ankle plantarflexion power
questions.question: In compartment syndrome of the anterior leg compartment, which muscle is affected first, causing which specific neurological deficit?

questions.explanation: Nerve injury level critically affects presentation: proximal median nerve injury affects all forearm flexors and hand muscles; carpal tunnel syndrome spares forearm muscles. Similarly, ulnar nerve injury at elbow affects forearm flexors; wrist injury doesn't. Injury level determines which muscles and sensory territories are affected.
options: Proximal injuries affect more muscles than distal injuries
questions.question: How does nerve injury level affect clinical presentation?
From which aortic sinus does the right coronary artery arise?
questions.explanation: The right coronary artery arises from the right (anterior) aortic sinus of the ascending aorta. It runs in the right atrioventricular groove, giving off branches to the right atrium, SA node (in 60% of people), right ventricle, and posterior interventricular septum. In right-dominant circulation (70% of people), it gives rise to the posterior interventricular artery.

There are 15-20 lactiferous ducts that open by the same number of openings on the summit of the nipple. Each duct drains one lobe of the mammary gland. Deep to the areola, each duct has a dilated portion called the lactiferous sinus where milk can be stored.
questions.question: How many lactiferous duct openings are on nipple?

questions.explanation: The medial plantar nerve is analogous to the median nerve in the hand. It is the larger terminal branch and supplies the medial three and a half digits (great, 2nd, 3rd, and medial half of the 4th), the skin of the medial plantar surface, abductor hallucis, flexor digitorum brevis, flexor hallucis brevis, and the first lumbrical. The lateral plantar nerve is analogous to the ulnar nerve.
questions.question: The medial plantar nerve (L4, L5) is the larger terminal branch of the tibial nerve. It is analogous to which nerve in the hand?
The otic ganglion provides parasympathetic innervation to which gland?
questions.explanation: The otic ganglion provides postganglionic parasympathetic secretomotor fibers to the parotid gland via the auriculotemporal nerve. Preganglionic fibers arrive via the lesser petrosal nerve from the glossopharyngeal nerve. The ganglion lies in the infratemporal fossa medial to the mandibular nerve below the foramen ovale.

The OK sign tests anterior interosseous nerve function by assessing flexor pollicis longus and flexor digitorum profundus to the index finger. Inability to form the OK sign indicates anterior interosseous nerve palsy. The patient cannot flex the interphalangeal joint of the thumb and distal interphalangeal joint of the index finger.
questions.question: What muscle action is tested by the OK sign?

questions.explanation: The round ligament of the uterus passes through the deep inguinal ring (homologous to the spermatic cord in males), traverses the inguinal canal, exits through the superficial inguinal ring, and terminates in the subcutaneous tissue of the labium majus. It represents the distal gubernaculum (the proximal part becoming the ovarian ligament). The round ligament contains smooth muscle, vessels, and nerves, and helps maintain the anteverted position of the uterus. Rarely, indirect inguinal hernias can occur in females alongside the round ligament (canal of Nuck).
questions.question: The round ligament of the uterus passes through which opening?

questions.explanation: The common bile duct descends posterior to the first (superior) part of the duodenum (retroduodenal portion), then continues behind or embedded in the posterior surface of the head of the pancreas (infraduodenal portion). It finally passes through the wall of the second (descending) part of the duodenum (intraduodenal portion), joining the main pancreatic duct to form the hepatopancreatic ampulla, which opens at the major duodenal papilla. This posterior relationship means that duodenal ulcers in the first part can erode into the bile duct or gastroduodenal artery. The duct's pancreatic portion may be compressed by pancreatic head tumors.
questions.question: The common bile duct passes posterior to which part of the duodenum?
What causes tennis elbow?
questions.explanation: "Tennis elbow" is lateral epicondylitis involving inflammation of the common extensor origin at the lateral epicondyle. Repetitive wrist extension and gripping activities cause microtears and degeneration at the extensor carpi radialis brevis origin. Pain is reproduced by resisted wrist extension.

The lateral pterygoid muscle divides the maxillary artery into three parts: mandibular (first), pterygoid (second), and pterygopalatine (third). Each part gives off specific branches to supply deep facial structures. The third part enters the pterygopalatine fossa through the pterygomaxillary fissure.
questions.question: The maxillary artery is divided into how many parts by the lateral pterygoid muscle?
Which plane passes through the iliac tubercles?
questions.explanation: The transtubercular plane is a horizontal plane passing through the iliac tubercles (projections on the outer lips of the iliac crests about 5 cm posterior to the anterior superior iliac spines) at the level of the L5 vertebral body. Along with the subcostal plane (through the lowest points of the costal margin at L3), it defines the superior boundaries of the right and left inguinal (iliac) regions. This plane also approximates the level of the bifurcation of the abdominal aorta and the confluence of common iliac veins to form the inferior vena cava.

questions.question: Which part of diaphragm arises from xiphoid process?
questions.explanation: The sternal part of the diaphragm arises from two small slips from the deep surface of the xiphoid process. The costal part arises from the inner aspects of the lower six ribs and costal cartilages. The vertebral part arises from the crura and arcuate ligaments.

produces both flexion and supination of the forearm. It is most powerful as a supinator when the elbow is flexed at 90 degrees. The muscle has two heads proximally but a common tendon distally inserting on the radial tuberosity.
questions.question: Which muscle produces both flexion and supination of the forearm?

questions.explanation: The basilar artery is formed by the union of the two vertebral arteries at the pontomedullary junction. It ascends in the pontine groove and terminates by dividing into the two posterior cerebral arteries. Branches include pontine, anterior inferior cerebellar, superior cerebellar, and labyrinthine arteries.
questions.question: The basilar artery is formed by the union of which vessels?

questions.explanation: Peyer's patches are most numerous and largest in the terminal ileum, with 20-30 patches typically present in the last 60 cm of ileum. They are permanent aggregates of lymphoid follicles in the lamina propria and submucosa, located on the antimesenteric border. M cells in the epithelium overlying Peyer's patches sample antigens for immune surveillance. They can become inflamed in conditions like typhoid fever.
questions.question: Where are Peyer's patches most concentrated?
Which lymph nodes lie along the sternum?
questions.explanation: The parasternal (internal thoracic) lymph nodes lie along the internal thoracic vessels, approximately 1 cm from the lateral border of the sternum. They receive lymph from the anterior chest wall, medial breast, diaphragm, and upper abdominal wall. Efferents drain to the bronchomediastinal trunks and brachiocephalic veins.

The Eustachian (pharyngotympanic) tube opens into the lateral wall of the nasopharynx, connecting it with the middle ear cavity. The tubal elevation and tubal tonsil surround the opening. Tensor veli palatini and salpingopharyngeus muscles open the tube during swallowing to equalize middle ear pressure.
questions.question: Which opening connects the nasopharynx to the middle ear?
The superficial inguinal ring is an opening in which structure?
questions.explanation: The superficial inguinal ring is a triangular defect in the external oblique aponeurosis, located immediately superior and medial to the pubic tubercle. Its margins, called the medial and lateral crura, are connected superiorly by intercrural fibers and give attachment to the external spermatic fascia. The superficial ring represents the external opening of the inguinal canal and transmits the spermatic cord in males or round ligament in females, along with the ilioinguinal nerve. The ring is larger in males than females, contributing to the higher incidence of inguinal hernias in males.

After splenectomy, patients have increased susceptibility to infections, particularly from encapsulated bacteria (Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Neisseria meningitidis). This is due to loss of the spleen's role in antibody production and filtration of blood-borne pathogens. Other organs (liver, bone marrow) can partially compensate for splenic function, but immunization and antibiotic prophylaxis are necessary in asplenic patients.
questions.question: What happens to the spleen after splenectomy?

questions.explanation: During inspiration, ribs 7-10 move laterally in a "bucket handle" movement, increasing the lateral (transverse) dimensions of the thoracic cavity. The upper ribs (2-7) move in a "pump handle" fashion, increasing anteroposterior diameter by pushing the sternum forward. These movements are coordinated during breathing.
questions.question: Which ribs produce bucket-handle movement?
Which muscle tenses the tympanic membrane?
questions.explanation: The tensor tympani muscle tenses the tympanic membrane by pulling the malleus medially. It is innervated by the nerve to medial pterygoid (V3). The muscle arises from the Eustachian tube and bony canal above it. Contraction dampens excessive vibrations and reduces sensitivity to low-frequency sounds. It works synergistically with stapedius.

The ilioinguinal nerve (L1) passes through the superficial inguinal ring after traversing the inguinal canal, unlike the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve which travels within the spermatic cord through both deep and superficial rings. The ilioinguinal nerve runs between internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles, enters the inguinal canal, and emerges through the superficial ring to provide sensory innervation to the skin of the upper medial thigh, root of penis and anterior scrotum (males), or mons pubis and labium majus (females). Entrapment following hernia repair can cause chronic groin pain.
questions.question: Which structure passes through the superficial inguinal ring in males?

questions.explanation: Bochdalek hernias are the most common type of congenital diaphragmatic hernia, occurring through a posterolateral defect in the diaphragm due to failure of the pleuroperitoneal membrane to close. They are more common on the left side (85%) and allow abdominal viscera to herniate into the thorax, potentially causing respiratory distress in newborns. They represent a failure of normal diaphragm development.
questions.question: Which type of congenital diaphragmatic hernia is most common?
The anterior ethmoid artery is a branch of which parent vessel?
questions.explanation: The anterior ethmoidal artery is a branch of the ophthalmic artery from the internal carotid system. It supplies the anterior and middle ethmoidal air cells and frontal sinus. The artery enters the nasal cavity through the anterior ethmoidal foramen and supplies the anterior nasal septum.

The medial and lateral intermuscular septa attach from the deep brachial fascia to the humerus, dividing the arm into anterior (flexor) and posterior (extensor) compartments. Each compartment contains muscles with similar functions and common innervation. This organization is essential for understanding compartment syndromes.
questions.question: How do the medial and lateral intermuscular septa organize the arm?

questions.explanation: The narrowest point of the esophagus is at its origin at the level of the cricoid cartilage (C6) where the cricopharyngeus muscle forms the upper esophageal sphincter. This is the most common site for foreign body impaction and the site requiring most care during esophagoscopy to avoid perforation.
questions.question: What is the narrowest point of esophagus?
The cruciate anastomosis is at the level of the lesser trochanter. Which four arteries specifically constitute this anastomosis?
questions.explanation: The cruciate anastomosis at the level of the lesser trochanter is constituted by four arteries: inferior gluteal artery (IGA), medial femoral circumflex artery (MFCA), lateral femoral circumflex artery (LFCA), and the first perforating branch of the profunda femoris artery. Together with the trochanteric anastomosis, it provides collateral circulation between the internal iliac and femoral artery systems.
options: IGA, obturator artery, MFCA, and LFCA branches
SGA, IGA, MFCA, and LFCA arterial branches
IGA, MFCA, LFCA, and 1st perforating branch of profunda femoris
SGA, IGA, obturator, and 1st perforating branch
MFCA, LFCA, popliteal, and descending genicular

questions.explanation: The thymus reaches its maximum size at puberty, after which it undergoes involution (gradual shrinkage). In adults, much of the thymic tissue is replaced by adipose tissue, though some functional tissue persists. Despite involution, the adult thymus continues to produce T cells, though at a reduced rate.
questions.question: When does the thymus reach maximum size?
Which ligament arches over the psoas major muscle?
questions.explanation: The medial arcuate ligament is a tendinous arch in the diaphragm that arches over the psoas major muscle, extending from the body of L1 or L2 vertebra to the tip of the transverse process. The sympathetic trunk passes deep to (posterior to) this ligament as it enters the abdomen. The ligament forms part of the lumbar attachment of the diaphragm.

The diaphragm is highest in the supine position and after a large meal due to upward pressure from abdominal viscera. When lying on one side, the dependent (lower) diaphragm is considerably higher than the uppermost one. Position affects diaphragm function and is clinically relevant.
questions.question: Which position elevates the diaphragm highest?
The posterior superior iliac spine (PSIS) corresponds to the level of which sacral segment?
questions.explanation: The posterior superior iliac spine (PSIS) corresponds to the level of S2. This is a clinically important landmark for epidural and spinal anesthesia, as well as for assessing pelvic symmetry in musculoskeletal examination. The highest point of the iliac crest corresponds to the level of L4, used for lumbar puncture guidance.

questions.question: The testicular artery arises at which vertebral level?
questions.explanation: The testicular arteries (and ovarian arteries in females) arise from the anterior aspect of the abdominal aorta at the L2 vertebral level, just inferior to the renal arteries. This high origin reflects the embryological development of the gonads on the posterior abdominal wall before testicular descent or ovarian migration. The long testicular arteries descend obliquely across the psoas major, ureter, and external iliac vessels, enter the deep inguinal ring, and travel through the inguinal canal as part of the spermatic cord to reach the testes in the scrotum.

Pulmonary embolism occurs when the pulmonary artery is obstructed by air, blood clot, fat, tumor cells, or other foreign particles. This can result in respiratory distress, chest pain, and potentially fatal cardiovascular collapse. Risk factors include prolonged immobilization, surgery, and hypercoagulable states.
questions.question: What condition involves pulmonary artery obstruction?

questions.explanation: The sympathetic trunk does not innervate voluntary (skeletal) muscles, which are innervated by somatic motor neurons. The sympathetic system innervates cardiac muscle, smooth muscle in blood vessels and organs, sweat glands, and various viscera. Sympathetic fibers reach the body wall via gray rami communicantes.
questions.question: Which structure does the sympathetic trunk NOT innervate?

questions.explanation: The middle ribs (4-9) are most commonly fractured because they are longest and least protected. The upper two ribs are protected by the clavicle, and the lower two floating ribs are mobile and therefore swing free, avoiding fracture. Rib fractures are uncommon in children due to chest wall elasticity.
questions.question: Which rib is most commonly fractured?
What principle explains joint innervation from muscles crossing it?
questions.explanation: states that nerves supplying muscles that move a joint also supply the joint itself. This explains why the wrist joint receives innervation from median, radial, and ulnar nerves. The principle helps predict joint innervation patterns throughout the body.

Four pulmonary veins (two from each lung) drain oxygenated blood from the lungs and open into the left atrium. These veins have no valves at their orifices. The superior and inferior pulmonary veins from each side carry blood from the respective lobes of the lungs.
questions.question: How many pulmonary veins open into left atrium?
The popliteal artery begins where the femoral artery passes through which structure in the lower thigh?
questions.explanation: The popliteal artery begins when the femoral artery passes through the adductor hiatus, a tendinous gap in the lower part of adductor magnus. It then descends through the popliteal fossa and terminates at the inferior border of popliteus. The femoral artery travels through the adductor canal in the anterior thigh before reaching the hiatus.

questions.question: Which muscle elevates the soft palate?
questions.explanation: The levator veli palatini elevates the soft palate during swallowing to close the nasopharynx. The muscle arises from the petrous temporal bone and Eustachian tube cartilage. It is supplied by the pharyngeal plexus (vagus via cranial accessory). Bilateral paralysis causes nasal regurgitation and hypernasal speech.

The adult urinary bladder has a capacity of approximately 400-600 ml, with the desire to void typically occurring at about 150-250 ml and strong urgency at 400-500 ml. The bladder is highly distensible due to its muscular wall (detrusor muscle) and transitional epithelium lining. Capacity can be reduced in pathological conditions or increased with chronic retention.
questions.question: What is the typical capacity of an adult urinary bladder?
Which chamber has the thickest myocardial wall?
questions.explanation: The left ventricular wall is 8-12 mm thick, approximately three times thicker than the right ventricle (3-5 mm), reflecting the higher pressure it must generate to pump blood through the systemic circulation. The left ventricle forms the apex and most of the left border and diaphragmatic surface of the heart. It contains two papillary muscles (anterior and posterior).

questions.question: The palatine tonsil receives its blood supply primarily from which artery?
questions.explanation: The tonsillar branch of the facial artery provides the main blood supply, entering at the lower pole. Additional supply comes from ascending palatine (facial), ascending pharyngeal, dorsal lingual, and lesser palatine arteries. The paratonsillar vein descends from the soft palate across the capsule and is regularly divided during tonsillectomy.

questions.question: What are splenic cords composed of?
questions.explanation: Splenic cords (cords of Billroth) in the red pulp consist of a meshwork of reticular fibers and reticular cells, with macrophages, lymphocytes, plasma cells, and various blood cells in the interstices. Blood from open-ended capillaries percolates through these cords before re-entering the circulation via sinusoids. Macrophages in the cords phagocytose old red cells and foreign particles.

questions.question: The right suprarenal vein drains directly into which vessel?
questions.explanation: The right suprarenal vein is short and drains directly into the inferior vena cava on its posterior aspect, while the left suprarenal vein drains into the left renal vein (along with the left testicular/ovarian and left inferior phrenic veins). This asymmetric venous drainage mirrors the pattern of testicular/ovarian veins. The suprarenal glands receive blood from three arteries (superior, middle, and inferior suprarenal arteries from inferior phrenic, aorta, and renal artery respectively) but drain via only one or two veins, creating a rich arterial supply with limited venous drainage.

questions.question: A fracture of the neck of femur causing coxa vara also disrupts the blood supply to the femoral head. Which named clinical complication most specifically results from this vascular disruption?
questions.explanation: Fracture of the neck of femur disrupts the retinacular blood vessels (mainly the medial femoral circumflex artery), leading to avascular necrosis (osteonecrosis) of the femoral head. This is the most specific complication, occurring in approximately 15-35% of displaced intracapsular femoral neck fractures. It results in segmental collapse of the femoral head and severe hip arthritis if untreated.
options: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head

questions.explanation: The fabella is an accessory sesamoid bone occasionally found in the tendon of the lateral head of gastrocnemius, at the posterolateral aspect of the knee. It is present in approximately 10-30% of individuals. It can cause posterolateral knee pain (fabella syndrome) when it compresses the common fibular nerve or irritates the popliteus tendon. It is typically visible on lateral knee radiographs.
questions.question: The fabella is a sesamoid bone occasionally found in which muscle's tendon near the knee?
Which nerve loops around the ligamentum arteriosum?
questions.explanation: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve (branch of left vagus) loops around the aortic arch and ligamentum arteriosum before ascending in the groove between trachea and esophagus to reach the larynx. The right recurrent laryngeal nerve loops around the right subclavian artery. This asymmetry reflects embryological development.

questions.question: What is Horner's syndrome triad?
questions.explanation: Horner's syndrome results from interruption of sympathetic innervation to the eye and face, characterized by: (1) ptosis (drooping eyelid from paralysis of M?ller's muscle), (2) miosis (constricted pupil from unopposed parasympathetic action), and (3) anhidrosis (absent sweating on ipsilateral face). Pancoast tumors invading the sympathetic chain commonly cause this.

questions.question: Which impression is largest on the left lung?
questions.explanation: The cardiac impression on the left lung is larger than that on the right lung because the heart is positioned more to the left side. The left ventricle forms most of the heart's left border and creates a large concave impression on the left lung's mediastinal surface.

questions.question: The hepatic flexure is related posteriorly to which structure?
questions.explanation: The hepatic (right colic) flexure is related posteriorly to the lower part of the right kidney and anteriorly to the liver and gallbladder. This relationship means that right renal pathology may manifest as right upper quadrant pain mimicking hepatobiliary disease. The hepatic flexure is more mobile than the splenic flexure, attached to the posterior abdominal wall by the hepatocolic ligament (part of the greater omentum). The flexure receives blood supply from the right colic artery (from SMA) and right branch of the middle colic artery, with anastomoses forming the marginal artery.

The anterior vagal trunk is formed mainly from the left vagus nerve as it descends on the anterior surface of the oesophagus. This trunk enters the abdomen on the anterior surface of the oesophagus and supplies the anterior gastric surface. It also gives off a large hepatic branch and a pyloric branch.
questions.question: Which nerve forms the anterior vagal trunk supplying the stomach?

questions.explanation: During inspiration, expansion of the thoracic cavity (through rib elevation and diaphragm descent) increases intrathoracic volume and creates negative pressure within the chest. This negative pressure draws air into the lungs. The pleural cavity pressure becomes more negative, preventing lung collapse.
questions.question: What creates negative intrathoracic pressure?

questions.explanation: The palatoglossal arch (anterior pillar of fauces) forms the posterior boundary of the oral cavity proper, separating it from the oropharynx. The arch extends from the soft palate to the side of the tongue and contains the palatoglossus muscle. The isthmus of fauces is the opening between the two palatoglossal arches connecting the oral cavity with the oropharynx.
questions.question: Which structure forms the posterior boundary of the oral cavity proper?

questions.explanation: The superficial inguinal lymph nodes drain lymph from the lower limb, perineum, gluteal region, and lower anterior abdominal wall (below the umbilicus). Their efferents drain to the deep inguinal lymph nodes, which then drain to the external iliac nodes, common iliac nodes, and ultimately the para-aortic nodes. This drainage pattern explains why infections of the foot can present with inguinal lymphadenopathy.
options: Lower limb only; draining to external iliac nodes
Lower limb, perineum, gluteal region, lower anterior abdominal wall; deep inguinal nodes
Only the genitalia; draining to internal obturator nodes
Only the lower limb below the knee; popliteal nodes
Only the gluteal region; internal iliac nodes
questions.question: The superficial inguinal lymph nodes drain which areas of the body, and their efferents drain to which deep node group?
The anterior cranial fossa contains which lobe of the brain?
questions.explanation: The anterior cranial fossa accommodates the frontal lobes of the brain. The floor is formed by the orbital plates of the frontal bone, cribriform plate of ethmoid, and lesser wings of sphenoid. The crista galli provides attachment for the falx cerebri. Fractures can cause CSF rhinorrhea through the cribriform plate.

questions.question: Through which opening does the sympathetic trunk enter the abdomen?
questions.explanation: The sympathetic trunks enter the abdomen from the thorax by passing deep to (posterior to) the medial arcuate ligaments. They descend on the anterolateral aspects of the lumbar vertebral bodies, giving off lumbar splanchnic nerves. The greater and lesser splanchnic nerves pierce the crura to enter the abdomen.

A small area of the posterior surface of the stomach near the cardia (where the two layers of lesser omentum separate to enclose the stomach) is "bare" and in direct contact with the left crus of the diaphragm, lacking peritoneal covering. This represents the only part of the stomach not completely invested by peritoneum. The rest of the stomach is completely covered by visceral peritoneum: anteriorly and posteriorly by peritoneum continuous with the greater and lesser omenta, and along its curvatures where the gastrosplenic, gastrohepatic, and gastrocolic ligaments attach. The bare area can be a site where gastric perforation communicates directly with the retroperitoneum.
questions.question: Which part of the stomach is LEAST covered by peritoneum?

questions.explanation: The palatine processes of the right and left maxillae form the anterior three-quarters of the hard palate. The horizontal plates of the palatine bones form the posterior quarter. The hard palate separates the oral and nasal cavities. The incisive foramen transmits the nasopalatine nerve anteriorly.
questions.question: Which bone forms the hard palate anteriorly?

questions.explanation: The superior sagittal sinus lies in the attached superior border of the falx cerebri. It begins at the foramen cecum and runs posteriorly to the confluence of sinuses. The sinus receives superior cerebral veins and communicates with scalp veins via emissary veins. Arachnoid granulations project into it for CSF absorption.
questions.question: Which sinus lies within the falx cerebri?
Which liver segment receives blood from the left hepatic artery?
questions.explanation: The quadrate lobe, although anatomically part of the right lobe, is functionally part of the left lobe as it receives blood from the left hepatic artery and drains bile into the left hepatic duct. Similarly, the caudate lobe receives blood from both right and left hepatic arteries. This functional division is based on blood supply and biliary drainage rather than external anatomical features.

The transverse cervical nerve (C2-C3) emerges from the posterior border of sternocleidomastoid and provides sensation to the anterior and lateral neck. It is a branch of the cervical plexus. The nerve crosses the sternocleidomastoid horizontally. Cervical plexus block affects this nerve causing anterior neck anesthesia.
questions.question: The transverse cervical nerve provides sensation to which area?

questions.explanation: The inguinal canal does not have distinct medial or lateral walls; instead, it has anterior and posterior walls, a roof, and a floor. The internal oblique muscle contributes to the anterior wall in the lateral third of the canal (where its fibers arise from the inguinal ligament) and forms part of the roof with the transversus abdominis muscle through their arching fibers. The external oblique aponeurosis forms the entire length of the anterior wall, the transversalis fascia (reinforced medially by conjoint tendon) forms the posterior wall, and the inguinal ligament forms the floor.
questions.question: Which muscle forms the lateral wall of the inguinal canal?
Which muscle separates the subphrenic from the subhepatic space?
questions.explanation: The falciform ligament divides the subphrenic space into right and left components, separating the right subphrenic space from the left. The right subphrenic space communicates posteriorly with the hepatorenal recess (Morison's pouch), the most dependent part of the peritoneal cavity in the supine position, making it a common site for fluid accumulation. The left subphrenic space is bounded by the falciform ligament on the right, the diaphragm superiorly and anteriorly, the stomach and spleen posteriorly, and the anterior layer of the left triangular ligament laterally.

questions.question: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head can also occur after dislocation of the hip joint without fracture. How long after dislocation should the hip be reduced to minimize avascular necrosis risk?
questions.explanation: Emergency reduction of a dislocated hip should ideally be performed within 6 hours to minimize the risk of avascular necrosis of the femoral head. Prolonged dislocation stretches and compresses the retinacular vessels supplying the femoral head. The risk of avascular necrosis increases significantly after 6 hours. Posterior hip dislocations, the most common type, also risk sciatic nerve injury.

questions.question: Which artery is most at risk during frontal sinus surgery?
questions.explanation: The anterior ethmoidal artery crosses the roof of the ethmoid sinuses and is at risk during frontal and ethmoidal sinus surgery. It is a branch of the ophthalmic artery and supplies the anterior ethmoidal cells, frontal sinus, and anterior nasal cavity. Damage can cause orbital hematoma or CSF leak.

questions.question: The anterior compartment of the leg contains four muscles. Which of the following does NOT belong to this compartment?
questions.explanation: The anterior compartment of the leg contains four muscles: tibialis anterior, extensor digitorum longus, extensor hallucis longus, and fibularis tertius. Fibularis longus belongs to the lateral compartment, along with fibularis brevis. All anterior compartment muscles are innervated by the deep fibular nerve (L4, L5). Paralysis of these muscles causes foot drop.

The right bronchomediastinal trunk drains lymph from the right side of the thorax. It joins with right jugular and right subclavian trunks to form the right lymphatic duct. Alternatively, these three trunks may drain independently into the right venous angle. The left bronchomediastinal trunk usually drains into the thoracic duct.
questions.question: Which lymphatic trunk drains the right side of the thorax?
Which vessel crosses anterior to the ureter in the female pelvis?
questions.explanation: In the female pelvis, the uterine artery crosses superior (above) to the ureter near the lateral fornix of the vagina - remembered by the phrase "water under the bridge." This relationship is clinically crucial during hysterectomy to avoid inadvertent ureteric injury during ligation of the uterine artery. The ureter runs along the lateral wall of the pelvis to reach the bladder.

is not part of the rotator cuff; it acts as a medial rotator and adductor of the humerus. The four rotator cuff muscles are supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, and subscapularis. These muscles fuse with the joint capsule and stabilize the glenohumeral joint.
questions.question: Which muscle is NOT part of the rotator cuff?
Extensor hallucis longus, innervated by the deep fibular nerve, originates from which structure?
questions.explanation: Extensor hallucis longus originates from the middle part of the anterior surface of the fibula and the adjacent interosseous membrane. It inserts into the dorsal aspect of the base of the distal phalanx of the great toe and is innervated by the deep fibular nerve (L4, L5). It extends the great toe, dorsiflexes the ankle, and can assist with foot inversion.
options: Superior half of lateral surface of tibia
Middle anterior fibula and interosseous membrane
Inferior third of anterior fibula only

questions.question: What is overwhelming post-splenectomy infection (OPSI)?
questions.explanation: Overwhelming post-splenectomy infection (OPSI) is a rare but life-threatening condition characterized by fulminant sepsis that can progress to death within hours. It occurs in 0.1-0.4% of splenectomized patients per year, with mortality rates of 50-70%. It is most commonly caused by encapsulated bacteria, particularly Streptococcus pneumoniae. Prevention includes vaccination and antibiotic prophylaxis.

questions.question: Which artery supplies the appendix?
questions.explanation: The appendicular artery, a branch of the ileocolic artery (which itself arises from the superior mesenteric artery), supplies the vermiform appendix. It runs in the free margin of the mesoappendix to reach the tip of the appendix. This end-artery arrangement (with minimal collateral supply) means that thrombosis or inflammation affecting the appendicular artery can lead to appendiceal ischemia and necrosis. The artery's location in the mesoappendix requires careful ligation during appendectomy. Variations in the arterial supply are uncommon, but occasionally the appendicular artery may arise directly from a posterior cecal artery.

questions.question: Which muscle produces both shoulder adduction and medial rotation?
questions.explanation: produces shoulder adduction, extension, and medial rotation. It is a powerful muscle forming part of the posterior axillary fold. The muscle is commonly used in reconstructive surgery and is supplied by the thoracodorsal nerve.

questions.question: Which muscle attaches to the white line of Hilton?
questions.explanation: The corrugator cutis ani muscle, formed by fusion of fibers from the longitudinal muscle layer of the rectum and the levator ani, inserts into the skin of the anal canal at the white line (intersphincteric line, or white line of Hilton). This line represents the lower border of the internal anal sphincter and the intermuscular groove between the internal and external anal sphincters. Some longitudinal muscle fibers also blend with the puborectalis anteriorly and extend to form the rectourethralis muscle (muscle of Roux) in males, extending toward the urethra.

questions.question: Which vessel forms the left heart border?
questions.explanation: The left border of the heart on a chest X-ray is formed almost entirely by the left ventricle, with a small contribution from the left atrial appendage superiorly. This border extends from the 2nd left costal cartilage to the apex beat in the 5th intercostal space.

The vertebral artery ascends through the transverse foramina (foramina transversaria) of cervical vertebrae C1-C6. It enters the foramen of C6 and ascends to C1, then passes posteriorly around the lateral mass of atlas before entering the foramen magnum. The vertebral vein accompanies the artery through these foramina.
questions.question: Which artery passes through the transverse foramina of cervical vertebrae?

questions.explanation: The pterygomaxillary fissure forms the lateral boundary, connecting the pterygopalatine fossa with the infratemporal fossa. The anterior wall is formed by the posterior surface of the maxilla. The medial wall consists of the perpendicular plate of the palatine bone.
questions.question: Which structure forms the lateral boundary of the pterygopalatine fossa?

questions.explanation: A hip pointer is a contusion of the iliac crest and anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS), resulting from a direct blow in contact sports such as American football. It is extremely painful due to the multiple muscle attachments in this area. Tensor fasciae latae and sartorius originate from the ASIS and iliac crest respectively. Treatment is ice, NSAIDs, and activity modification.
questions.question: The 'hip pointer' is a contusion of which anatomical structure, common in contact sports?
options: Anterior superior iliac spine and iliac crest

questions.question: What is the ligamentum arteriosum?
questions.explanation: The ligamentum arteriosum is the fibrous remnant of the fetal ductus arteriosus, which connected the pulmonary artery to the aorta in fetal circulation, bypassing the non-functional fetal lungs. It closes functionally at birth and becomes a fibrous cord extending from the left pulmonary artery to the aortic arch.

The lateral femoral circumflex artery (LFCA) has three branches: ascending (to the hip joint and gluteal region), transverse (encircling the femur laterally), and descending (contributing superolaterally to the genicular anastomosis around the knee). The descending branch travels between vastus intermedius and vastus lateralis muscles and provides one of the anastomotic connections at the knee.
questions.question: The lateral femoral circumflex artery has three named branches. Which of these descends distally to contribute to the genicular anastomosis?
The ischiopubic rami fuse with each other at which approximate age?
questions.explanation: The ischiopubic rami fuse with each other at approximately 7-8 years of age. The secondary ossification centres of the hip bone (for the iliac crest, Y-shaped cartilage of the acetabulum, and ischial tuberosity) all fuse completely by 20-25 years of age.

questions.question: Which cord of the brachial plexus gives rise to the ulnar nerve?
questions.explanation: The ulnar nerve arises from the medial cord of the brachial plexus (C7, C8, T1). The medial cord also gives rise to the medial pectoral nerve, medial cutaneous nerve of arm and forearm, and the medial root of the median nerve. Injury to the medial cord affects all these structures.

The lateral pterygoid assists in opening the jaw against resistance (along with gravity, mylohyoid, geniohyoid, and anterior belly of digastric). The suprahyoid muscles provide the main force when opening against resistance. Lateral pterygoid protrudes and depresses the mandible. All other muscles of mastication (masseter, temporalis, medial pterygoid) close the jaw.
questions.question: Which muscle opens the jaw against resistance?

questions.explanation: The first thoracic nerve is atypical because it has no anterior cutaneous branch. Instead, it has a large branch that joins the brachial plexus, corresponding to its lateral cutaneous branch. The second thoracic nerve is also atypical, giving rise to the intercostobrachial nerve.
questions.question: Which thoracic nerve lacks an anterior cutaneous branch?

options: Flattens the medial longitudinal arch of the foot
Has no significant effect on any foot arch
Progressively flattens the transverse arch of the midfoot
Raises the medial longitudinal arch, converting foot to a rigid push-off lever
Only affects the lateral longitudinal arch of the foot
questions.explanation: The windlass mechanism (described by Hicks, 1954) involves tensioning of the plantar aponeurosis as the toes dorsiflexed during push-off. This raises the medial longitudinal arch, shortens the foot, and converts it into a rigid lever for efficient propulsion. This mechanism is impaired in flatfoot (pes planus) and hallux rigidus, reducing push-off efficiency.
questions.question: The 'windlass mechanism' of the foot refers to tensioning of the plantar aponeurosis during toe dorsiflexion. What effect does this have on the foot arches?
The pampiniform plexus drains into which vein?
questions.explanation: The pampiniform plexus, a network of 8-12 veins in the spermatic cord surrounding the testicular artery, drains into a single testicular vein at the deep inguinal ring. The right testicular vein drains directly into the inferior vena cava at an acute angle, while the left testicular vein typically drains into the left renal vein at a right angle. This venous plexus serves as a countercurrent heat exchanger, cooling arterial blood before it reaches the testes. The higher incidence of left-sided varicoceles reflects the longer course and perpendicular drainage of the left testicular vein.

The great saphenous vein is formed by the union of the dorsal vein of the great toe and the dorsal venous arch of the foot. It ascends anterior to the medial malleolus, passes posterior to the medial condyle of the femur, and empties into the femoral vein after traversing the saphenous opening. It has 10-12 valves.
questions.question: The great saphenous vein, the longest vein in the body, is formed at the foot by the union of which structures?
options: Medial marginal vein and dorsal venous arch
Dorsal vein of great toe and dorsal venous arch
Dorsal vein of great toe and posterior tibial vein
Small saphenous vein and dorsal venous arch
Anterior tibial vein and dorsal venous arch

questions.question: The buccinator muscle is pierced by which structure?
questions.explanation: The buccinator muscle is pierced by the parotid (Stensen's) duct before the duct opens into the oral vestibule opposite the upper second molar. The muscle forms the muscular component of the cheek and is innervated by the buccal branch of the facial nerve. It compresses the cheek against the teeth during chewing.

questions.question: Which factor most limits shoulder joint stability?
questions.explanation: The shoulder's extreme mobility comes at the expense of stability. The shallow glenoid cavity (1:4 disproportion with humeral head) and lax joint capsule are necessary for wide range of motion but compromise stability. Dynamic stability from rotator cuff muscles partially compensates.

The platysma is a muscle of facial expression innervated by the cervical branch of the facial nerve. It lies in the superficial cervical fascia and extends from the chest to the mandible. The muscle tenses the skin of the neck and can depress the mandible and lower lip. Facial nerve paralysis causes platysmal weakness.
questions.question: The platysma muscle is innervated by which nerve?

questions.explanation: The supinator muscle is the primary supinator of the forearm, wrapping around the proximal radius. The biceps brachii is a powerful accessory supinator, especially when the elbow is flexed. The deep branch of the radial nerve passes between the two heads of the supinator muscle.
questions.question: Which muscle is the primary supinator of the forearm?
Which structure forms the floor of the cubital fossa?
questions.explanation: The floor of the cubital fossa is formed by two muscles: the brachialis muscle superiorly and the supinator muscle inferiorly. The roof is formed by skin, superficial and deep fascia, reinforced by the bicipital aponeurosis. The fossa contains important neurovascular structures from medial to lateral.

Superior vena cava (SVC) syndrome results from obstruction or compression of the SVC, impairing venous return from the head, neck, and upper extremities. Most cases are caused by malignancy (lung cancer, lymphoma, metastases) compressing the SVC in the mediastinum. Clinical features include facial swelling, neck vein distension, and upper body edema.
questions.question: What causes superior vena cava syndrome?
The hyoglossus muscle separates which two important arteries?
questions.explanation: The hyoglossus muscle is a key surgical landmark separating the lingual artery into three parts: above, on, and below the muscle. The hypoglossal nerve and lingual vein lie superficially on the muscle. Deep lingual and sublingual arteries arise from the lingual artery in relation to this muscle.

questions.question: What connects breast skin to deep fascia?
questions.explanation: The ligaments of Cooper are fibrous strands that connect the skin with the deep fascia of pectoralis major, passing through the breast tissue. They provide structural support to the breast. Infiltration of these ligaments by breast cancer causes their shortening, producing the characteristic peau d'orange appearance.

The rectovesical pouch (between bladder and rectum in males) is the lowest part of the peritoneal cavity when standing or sitting and is a common site for fluid collection, abscesses, or metastatic deposits. In females, the rectouterine pouch (of Douglas) is even deeper and is the most dependent peritoneal space, which can be accessed via the posterior vaginal fornix.
questions.question: Which pouch in males is the most dependent peritoneal space?

questions.explanation: The mesoappendix is a triangular fold of peritoneum extending from the terminal ileum and its mesentery to the entire length of the appendix (base to tip), connecting it to the posterior abdominal wall. The appendicular artery (from ileocolic artery) runs in the free edge of the mesoappendix to supply the appendix. During appendectomy, the mesoappendix must be divided and the appendicular artery ligated. The mesoappendix contains fat, lymph nodes, and vessels. Occasionally, the mesoappendix may be short, leaving the distal appendix without mesenteric coverage.
questions.question: The mesoappendix is attached to which part of the appendix?

options: Only the fascial sheath around the femoral vessels
questions.explanation: Thigh compartment syndrome most commonly affects the anterior compartment, usually following femoral shaft fractures with significant hematoma formation, crush injuries, or arterial injuries. The anterior compartment contains the quadriceps muscles and femoral neurovascular bundle. Rising compartment pressure impairs perfusion, causing ischemia. Fasciotomy must include all three thigh compartments to ensure complete decompression.
questions.question: Compartment syndrome of the thigh is less common than leg compartment syndrome. Which compartment of the thigh is most commonly affected following a femoral fracture?

questions.explanation: Needle decompression for tension pneumothorax is performed in the 2nd intercostal space in the midclavicular line on the affected side. A large-bore needle or cannula is inserted just above the 3rd rib (to avoid neurovascular bundle of 2nd intercostal space). This provides immediate temporary relief until a chest tube can be inserted.
questions.question: Where is needle decompression performed?
What connects the two crura anteriorly?
questions.explanation: The median arcuate ligament is a fibrous arch that unites the right and left crura anteriorly across the aortic hiatus at the T12 level. It forms the superior boundary of the aortic hiatus through which the aorta, thoracic duct, and sometimes azygos vein pass. Occasionally, this ligament can compress the celiac trunk causing median arcuate ligament syndrome.

questions.question: The internal jugular vein begins at which anatomical location?
questions.explanation: The internal jugular vein begins at the jugular foramen as a continuation of the sigmoid sinus. It descends in the carotid sheath lateral to the internal and common carotid arteries. The vein joins with the subclavian vein to form the brachiocephalic vein.

questions.question: Which recess is deeper during expiration?
questions.explanation: The costodiaphragmatic recess is shallow during inspiration when the lung expands into it, and becomes deeper during expiration when the lung retracts. This recess is clinically important as it is the site where pleural fluid accumulates in effusions and is the target for thoracentesis.

questions.question: What nerve innervates the wrist joint?
options: Anterior and posterior interosseous nerves only
questions.explanation: The wrist joint is innervated by branches from three nerves following Hilton's law: median nerve (anterior interosseous branch), radial nerve (posterior interosseous branch), and ulnar nerve (deep and dorsal branches). This follows the principle that nerves supplying muscles moving a joint also supply the joint.

Hamman's sign (also called Hamman's crunch) is a crunching or clicking sound synchronous with the heartbeat, heard on auscultation over the precordium in pneumomediastinum. It's caused by the heart beating against air-filled tissue. The sign is named after Dr. Louis Hamman who described it in 1939.
questions.question: What clinical sign suggests pneumomediastinum?
Adductor brevis lies deep to which two muscles of the medial compartment?
questions.explanation: Adductor brevis lies deep to pectineus and adductor longus. It originates from the body and inferior ramus of the pubis and inserts into the pectineal line and proximal part of the linea aspera. It is innervated by the anterior division of the obturator nerve (L2, L3, L4) and adducts the thigh and to some extent flexes it.

questions.question: At what age does the appendix typically reach its adult position?
questions.explanation: The appendix reaches its definitive adult position by puberty. In infants and young children, the appendix has a relatively higher position, which explains why appendicitis in children may present with higher abdominal pain. The growth of the cecum pulls the appendix to a lower position. The base of the appendix remains constant at the confluence of the three taeniae coli.

questions.question: Which structure forms the anterior boundary of the posterior triangle of the neck?
questions.explanation: The posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle forms the anterior boundary of the posterior triangle. The anterior border of trapezius forms the posterior boundary, and the middle third of the clavicle forms the base. The apex is where the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius meet at the superior nuchal line.

The detrusor muscle is the smooth muscle layer forming the bladder wall and consists of three poorly defined layers: inner longitudinal, middle circular, and outer longitudinal. During bladder filling, the detrusor relaxes; during micturition, it contracts to expel urine. The detrusor is innervated by parasympathetic fibers (pelvic splanchnic nerves S2-4) for contraction.
questions.question: What muscle forms the bladder wall?

questions.explanation: The left gastric vein typically drains directly into the portal vein near its origin behind the neck of the pancreas, though it may occasionally drain into the splenic vein. The left gastric vein receives esophageal tributaries from the abdominal esophagus, creating an important portosystemic anastomosis with esophageal veins draining to the azygos system. In portal hypertension, these anastomotic channels dilate to form esophageal varices, which can rupture causing life-threatening hemorrhage. The coronary vein is an alternative name for the left gastric vein, following the course of the left gastric artery along the lesser curvature.
questions.question: The left gastric vein drains into which vessel?

questions.explanation: Trigger finger involves stenosis of the flexor tendon sheath, particularly at the A1 pulley. A nodule develops on the flexor tendon that catches on the pulley during finger flexion/extension, causing triggering or locking. Release of the A1 pulley is curative.
questions.question: Which structure is involved in trigger finger?

questions.explanation: In Erb's paralysis, the affected arm hangs by the side in an adducted and medially rotated position. The forearm assumes an extended and pronated posture, creating the "policeman's tip" or "porter's tip" hand deformity. This results from paralysis of muscles supplied by C5-C6 nerve roots.
questions.question: What is the characteristic position of the forearm in Erb's paralysis?
Which nerve injury causes inability to form OK sign?
questions.explanation: injury causes inability to properly form the OK sign. This tests flexor pollicis longus (thumb IP flexion) and flexor digitorum profundus to index finger (DIP flexion). Patients cannot touch the thumb tip to index fingertip in a rounded configuration.

questions.question: The perforating branches of the profunda femoris artery perforate which muscle to reach the posterior compartment of the thigh?
questions.explanation: The perforating branches (three or four) of the profunda femoris artery perforate the adductor magnus to supply the muscles of the medial and posterior thigh. This anatomical relationship is important during surgical approaches to the posterior thigh, where inadvertent cutting of perforating vessels can cause significant hemorrhage. They are the main blood supply to the hamstring muscles.

questions.question: Which part of the kidney contains the renal pyramids?
questions.explanation: The renal medulla is the inner part of the kidney containing 10-12 renal pyramids (medullary pyramids). Each pyramid has its base directed toward the cortex and its apex (renal papilla) projecting medially into a minor calyx. The pyramids contain the loops of Henle and collecting ducts, giving them a striated appearance due to parallel tubules.

questions.question: The sphenoid sinus drains into which location?
questions.explanation: The sphenoid sinuses drain into the sphenoethmoidal recess above the superior concha. These sinuses lie within the body of the sphenoid bone and vary greatly in size. Close relationship to the optic nerve and carotid artery makes sphenoid surgery particularly challenging.

questions.question: Where does the internal thoracic artery arise?
questions.explanation: The internal thoracic (internal mammary) artery arises from the first part of the subclavian artery. It descends vertically behind the upper six costal cartilages, approximately 1 cm from the lateral border of the sternum. It gives off anterior intercostal arteries, perforating branches, and terminates as superior epigastric and musculophrenic arteries.

questions.question: Which enzyme activates trypsinogen in the duodenum?
questions.explanation: Enterokinase (enteropeptidase) is a brush border enzyme produced by duodenal enterocytes that converts inactive trypsinogen to active trypsin by cleaving a small peptide. Trypsin then activates other pancreatic proteases through a cascade mechanism. This activation mechanism ensures that proteases are inactive within the pancreas and are only activated in the duodenal lumen, protecting the pancreas from autodigestion.

questions.question: The central artery of the retina is a branch of which vessel?
questions.explanation: The central artery of the retina is a branch of the ophthalmic artery. It is an end artery running in the center of the optic nerve to supply the inner layers of the retina. Occlusion causes sudden painless loss of vision. The artery enters the optic nerve about 12 mm behind the eyeball.

The jejunum constitutes approximately 40% of the total length of the small intestine beyond the duodenum. This represents about 2.5 meters of the 5-6 meter total small bowel length. The jejunum is characterized by being thicker-walled, more vascular, and having more prominent plicae circulares than the ileum.
questions.question: What percentage of the small intestine length does the jejunum constitute?

questions.explanation: The musculocutaneous nerve has nerve root values C5, C6, and C7. It arises from the lateral cord of the brachial plexus. The nerve supplies three muscles (biceps, brachialis, coracobrachialis) before continuing as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm.
questions.question: What nerve root value is the musculocutaneous nerve?
Which structure forms the falciform ligament's free edge?
questions.explanation: The ligamentum teres (round ligament of the liver) is the obliterated umbilical vein that runs in the free inferior edge of the falciform ligament from the umbilicus to the liver. It joins the left branch of the portal vein at the inferior end of the fissure for the ligamentum teres. In portal hypertension, paraumbilical veins accompanying the ligamentum teres may recanalize, forming caput medusae.

The falciform ligament (and lesser omentum) develops from the ventral mesentery, while the greater omentum, splenorenal ligament, gastrosplenic ligament, and transverse mesocolon all derive from the dorsal mesentery. The ventral mesentery, present only in the region of the foregut, gives rise to the falciform ligament (connecting liver to anterior abdominal wall), the lesser omentum (connecting liver to lesser curvature and proximal duodenum), and the coronary and triangular ligaments (connecting liver to diaphragm). The liver and gallbladder develop within the ventral mesentery, explaining their peritoneal relationships.
questions.question: Which structure is derived from the ventral mesentery?
