Which ligament connects the ovary to the uterus?
questions.explanation: The ovarian ligament (ligament of the ovary) connects the ovary to the uterus, extending from the uterine pole of the ovary to the lateral angle of the uterus just below the uterine tube attachment. It represents the proximal remnant of the gubernaculum (the distal remnant becoming the round ligament of the uterus). The ligament lies within the broad ligament (between its layers) and contains no significant vessels. The suspensory ligament of the ovary (infundibulopelvic ligament) connects the ovary to the lateral pelvic wall and contains the ovarian vessels; it is not directly attached to the uterus.

questions.question: The kidney hilum is located at which vertebral level?
questions.explanation: The renal hilum is positioned at the level of the transpyloric plane, which corresponds to the first lumbar vertebra (L1), though the kidneys themselves extend from approximately T12 to L3. At the hilum, structures are arranged from anterior to posterior as vein, artery, and pelvis (VAP), though the renal vein is most anterior and superior. The left kidney typically sits slightly higher than the right due to the presence of the liver on the right side.

The lateral border of the pronator teres muscle forms the medial (ulnar) boundary of the cubital fossa. The lateral boundary is formed by the medial border of brachioradialis muscle. The floor consists of brachialis and supinator muscles while the roof is formed by fascia and bicipital aponeurosis.
questions.question: Which muscle forms the medial boundary of the cubital fossa?
The knee joint stability depends primarily on muscles. Which muscle group is described as the MOST important in stabilizing the knee joint?
questions.explanation: The quadriceps femoris is the most important muscle group for stabilizing the knee joint. The inferior fibers of vastus medialis and lateralis are particularly important stabilizers. Quadriceps weakness leads to instability especially on stairs and inclines. Rehabilitation after any knee injury or surgery focuses heavily on quadriceps strengthening exercises.

The splenic red pulp is the primary site for destruction of old, damaged, or abnormal erythrocytes (red blood cells). After their normal lifespan of approximately 120 days, erythrocytes become less flexible and are selectively engulfed by macrophages in the splenic cords. The iron from hemoglobin is recycled, while other components are degraded.
questions.question: Which cells are predominantly destroyed in the splenic red pulp?
The hypoglossal canal transmits which cranial nerve?
questions.explanation: The hypoglossal canal in the occipital bone transmits the hypoglossal nerve (XII). The nerve provides motor innervation to all intrinsic and most extrinsic muscles of the tongue except palatoglossus. Unilateral paralysis causes the tongue to deviate toward the paralyzed side when protruded.

The vaginal artery typically arises from the anterior division of the internal iliac artery (though it may arise from the uterine artery) and descends to supply the vagina. It gives off numerous branches to the anterior and posterior vaginal walls, anastomosing with branches from the uterine artery superiorly and internal pudendal artery inferiorly. This rich anastomotic network provides extensive collateral circulation to the vagina. The vagina also receives blood supply from the middle rectal and internal pudendal arteries. The upper vagina drains via uterine veins, while the lower vagina drains via internal pudendal veins.
questions.question: The vaginal artery typically arises from which vessel?

questions.explanation: The Thomas test assesses tightness of the hip flexors (primarily iliopsoas). The patient lies supine and holds one knee to the chest (flattening the lumbar lordosis). If the opposite hip cannot remain flat on the table (flexes up), this indicates hip flexor contracture. This is commonly found in patients with lumbar disc disease, hip osteoarthritis, and those who sit for prolonged periods.
questions.question: The Thomas test assesses tightness of which muscle group, with the patient supine and one hip fully flexed against the chest?
Which nerve carries pain sensation from the parietal peritoneum covering the diaphragm?
questions.explanation: The phrenic nerves carry pain sensation from the parietal peritoneum and parietal pleura covering the central part of the diaphragm. Irritation here causes referred pain to the C3-C5 dermatomes (neck and shoulder, especially shoulder tip). Peripheral parts of the diaphragm receive sensory supply from the lower intercostal and subcostal nerves, with referred pain to the trunk wall.

questions.question: Which structure contains the portal triad?
questions.explanation: The hepatoduodenal ligament, forming the thickened free right edge of the lesser omentum, contains the portal triad: the portal vein (posteriorly), hepatic artery proper (anteriorly and to the left), and common bile duct (anteriorly and to the right). This ligament extends from the porta hepatis to the superior border of the first part of the duodenum. The portal triad arrangement is crucial for the Pringle maneuver, where the hepatoduodenal ligament is compressed to control bleeding during hepatic surgery.

Klumpke's paralysis involves the C8-T1 nerve roots of the lower trunk of the brachial plexus. This typically results from undue abduction of the arm, such as clutching a tree branch during a fall. The resulting claw hand deformity occurs due to paralysis of intrinsic hand muscles and ulnar flexors.
questions.question: Which nerve root values are primarily involved in Klumpke's paralysis?
The pterygopalatine fossa communicates with the middle cranial fossa through which opening?
questions.explanation: The foramen rotundum provides direct communication between the pterygopalatine fossa and the middle cranial fossa, transmitting the maxillary nerve. The pterygoid canal connects with the foramen lacerum region, not the middle cranial fossa proper. This anatomical relationship is crucial for understanding trigeminal nerve pathways and regional anesthesia.

The aortic hiatus is located at the T12 vertebral level, posterior to the diaphragm (technically behind rather than through it). It is formed by the median arcuate ligament connecting the right and left crura. It transmits the aorta, thoracic duct, and sometimes the azygos vein. As it's posterior to the diaphragm, aortic flow is not impeded during diaphragmatic contraction.
questions.question: At which level is the aortic hiatus located?

questions.explanation: The external spermatic fascia, the outermost covering of the spermatic cord, is derived from the external oblique muscle's aponeurosis as the cord passes through the superficial inguinal ring. Moving inward, the next layer is the cremasteric muscle and fascia (from internal oblique and transversus abdominis), and the innermost fascial layer is the internal spermatic fascia (from transversalis fascia at the deep inguinal ring). The dartos muscle is in the scrotal wall, not directly covering the cord. These concentric layers are acquired sequentially as structures descend through abdominal wall layers.
questions.question: The spermatic cord receives its external covering from which muscle?

questions.explanation: The pulmonary plexuses (anterior and posterior to the roots of the lungs) contain both parasympathetic fibers from the vagus nerve and sympathetic fibers from the sympathetic trunk. These plexuses provide the autonomic innervation to the lungs and bronchial tree. The visceral pleura receives only vasomotor supply from these nerves.
questions.question: Which plexus provides autonomic supply to lungs?
The ankle joint allows primarily which movements?
questions.explanation: The ankle joint (talocrural joint) primarily allows dorsiflexion and plantarflexion, with a small degree of rotation. Inversion and eversion occur primarily at the subtalar joint (talocalcaneal articulation) and midtarsal joints. The talocrural joint has a range of approximately 20 degrees dorsiflexion and 50 degrees plantarflexion in a healthy adult.

questions.question: Where does the posterior vagal trunk primarily distribute after entering the abdomen?
questions.explanation: The posterior vagal trunk, formed mainly from the right vagus nerve, sends a large branch to the celiac and superior mesenteric plexuses. This distribution extends vagal innervation to the intestines as far as the splenic flexure and to the pancreas. The remaining branches supply the posterior surface of the stomach.

lumbrical canals are present in the hand as potential spaces surrounding the tendon of each lumbrical muscle. These canals lie between the index, middle, ring, and little fingers. Proximally they are continuous with one of the palmar spaces and can serve as routes for infection spread.
questions.question: How many lumbrical canals are present in the hand?

questions.explanation: Lacteal vessels (lymphatic capillaries) in intestinal villi coalesce to form larger lymphatic vessels that drain to lymph nodes along the mesenteric border of the intestine (juxta-intestinal nodes), then to nodes along the vascular arcades in the mesentery (intermediate nodes), followed by nodes at the root of the mesentery along the superior mesenteric artery (superior mesenteric nodes), and finally to pre-aortic nodes (celiac, superior mesenteric, inferior mesenteric groups) before reaching the cisterna chyli and thoracic duct. This stepwise progression through multiple nodal stations allows for filtering and immune surveillance of intestinal lymph.
questions.question: The lacteal vessels in intestinal villi drain into which nodes first?
Which immune cells are found in splenic white pulp?
questions.explanation: The splenic white pulp consists primarily of T and B lymphocytes organized around central arterioles (periarterial lymphoid sheaths - PALS containing T cells) and in lymphoid follicles (containing B cells). The white pulp is responsible for immune surveillance of blood-borne antigens and antibody production. It represents about 15-25% of splenic tissue and increases in infections.

The diaphragm develops from four embryological structures: (1) septum transversum (forming central tendon), (2) dorsal esophageal mesentery, (3) peripheral rim from body wall, and (4) pleuroperitoneal membranes (closing the pleuroperitoneal canals). Incomplete fusion of these components leads to congenital diaphragmatic hernias.
questions.question: How many structures contribute to diaphragm development?

questions.explanation: The peripheral part of the diaphragm (including the crura) receives sensory fibers from the lower six or seven intercostal and subcostal nerves. The central part receives sensory fibers from the phrenic nerves (C3-5). This dual innervation explains the referral patterns of pain from diaphragmatic irritation.
questions.question: Which nerves supply peripheral diaphragm sensory fibers?
Where is the thoracic duct located initially?
questions.explanation: The thoracic duct begins at L1 and ascends in the posterior mediastinum, initially posterior to the esophagus. At T5, it moves to the left side of the esophagus and continues upward into the superior mediastinum where it arches forward to drain into the left venous angle.

questions.question: Five bones uniquely possess epiphyseal plates at BOTH ends. Which set correctly identifies all five?
questions.explanation: Most long bones have only one epiphyseal plate at one end; however, five bones are unique in having epiphyseal plates at both ends: femur, tibia, fibula, humerus, and radius. This feature is important in understanding growth patterns and fracture management in these bones.

questions.question: Which bone forms the prominence of the cheek?
questions.explanation: The zygomatic bones form the prominence of the cheeks and lie on the inferolateral sides of the orbits. They articulate with the frontal, sphenoid, temporal, and maxillary bones. The bone has a broad connection with the maxilla medially and forms part of the zygomatic arch laterally. Fractures cause flattening of the malar eminence.

questions.question: The arcuate line of the rectus sheath is typically found at which level?
options: Level of anterior superior iliac spine
questions.explanation: The arcuate line (linea semicircularis) marks the inferior border of the posterior rectus sheath, located approximately midway between the umbilicus and pubic symphysis, roughly at the level of the anterior superior iliac spine. Below this line, all three aponeurotic layers (external oblique, internal oblique, and transversus abdominis) pass anteriorly to the rectus abdominis muscle, leaving only transversalis fascia posteriorly. This anatomical feature creates a potential weakness that may be involved in direct inguinal hernias.

In flail chest (from multiple rib fractures creating a free-floating segment), the affected segment moves paradoxically: sucking inward during inspiration (when intrathoracic pressure decreases) and bulging outward during expiration (when pressure increases). This ineffective breathing causes hypoventilation, hypoxia, and impaired secretion clearance. Treatment includes positive pressure ventilation.
questions.question: What causes paradoxical breathing in flail chest?
Which nerve supplies the first dorsal interosseous muscle?
questions.explanation: The ulnar nerve supplies all interosseous muscles including the first dorsal interosseous. This muscle is easily visible and palpable on the dorsum of the hand between the thumb and index finger. Testing its strength (finger abduction) helps assess ulnar nerve function.

produces both extension and adduction (ulnar deviation) at the wrist joint. It works with flexor carpi ulnaris to produce pure adduction by balancing extension and flexion forces. The muscle is located in the posterior forearm compartment.
questions.question: Which muscle extends and adducts the wrist?

questions.explanation: is supplied by the median nerve, not the musculocutaneous nerve. The musculocutaneous nerve supplies only three muscles: biceps brachii, brachialis, and coracobrachialis (BBC). After supplying these muscles, it continues as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm.
questions.question: Which muscle is NOT supplied by the musculocutaneous nerve?
The posterior compartment of the thigh is supplied primarily by perforating branches of which artery?
questions.explanation: The posterior compartment of the thigh is supplied by perforating branches of the profunda femoris artery, consisting of three or four arteries perforating adductor magnus. The profunda femoris is the main blood supply to all three thigh compartments. The inferior gluteal artery provides additional supply to the proximal hamstrings via descending branches.

The maxillary vein is formed from the pterygoid venous plexus in the infratemporal fossa. It joins the superficial temporal vein to form the retromandibular vein within the parotid gland. The pterygoid plexus communicates with cavernous sinus and facial veins without valves.
questions.question: Which vein drains the pterygoid venous plexus?
The subclavian artery becomes the axillary artery at which landmark?
questions.explanation: The subclavian artery becomes the axillary artery at the lateral border of the first rib. The artery is divided into three parts by the anterior scalene muscle. The vertebral, internal thoracic, and thyrocervical trunk typically arise from the subclavian. The costocervical trunk arises from the second part posteriorly.

questions.question: What prevents premature activation of pancreatic enzymes?
questions.explanation: The pancreas produces protease inhibitors (particularly pancreatic secretory trypsin inhibitor, PSTI) that prevent premature activation of trypsinogen within the pancreas. Enzymes are also stored as inactive zymogens in secretory granules. Premature intrapancreatic activation of trypsinogen (which then activates other proteases) causes acute pancreatitis with autodigestion of pancreatic tissue.

Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) requires intrinsic factor, secreted by gastric parietal cells, for absorption in the terminal ileum. Intrinsic factor binds to B12, protecting it from degradation and facilitating its receptor-mediated uptake by ileal enterocytes. Lack of intrinsic factor (from parietal cell destruction in pernicious anemia or gastrectomy) causes B12 deficiency and megaloblastic anemia.
questions.question: Which vitamin requires intrinsic factor for absorption?

questions.explanation: The anterior ethmoidal artery (from ophthalmic artery) descends through the anterior ethmoidal foramen to supply the anterior superior nasal septum and lateral nasal wall. It anastomoses with branches of the sphenopalatine artery posteriorly. The artery also supplies the anterior ethmoidal cells and contributes to the blood supply of the frontal sinus.
questions.question: Which artery supplies the anterior nasal septum superiorly?
Which lymph nodes drain the ovary?
questions.explanation: The ovaries drain lymph directly to the para-aortic (lumbar) lymph nodes at the L1-L2 level, following the ovarian vessels along which the lymphatics ascend. This drainage pattern reflects the ovary's embryological origin high on the posterior abdominal wall near the kidneys. In contrast, the uterine fundus drains to para-aortic nodes via lymphatics following the ovarian vessels, while the uterine body drains to external iliac nodes, and the cervix drains to external iliac, internal iliac, and sacral nodes. The upper vagina drains to internal iliac nodes, while the lower vagina drains to superficial inguinal nodes.

Avulsion of the medial epicondyle commonly results from valgus stress to the elbow, seen in throwing athletes (tennis elbow). The common flexor origin and ulnar collateral ligament attachment create a strong pull. Repetitive throwing or acute valgus force can avulse this growth center in children or the epicondyle in adults.
questions.question: Which injury commonly causes avulsion of the medial epicondyle?
Which nerve is at risk during surgical neck fractures of the humerus?
questions.explanation: The axillary nerve runs in close proximity to the surgical neck of the humerus, making it vulnerable to injury in fractures of this region. Damage results in paralysis of the deltoid muscle and loss of sensation over the regimental badge area. These fractures are especially common in elderly people with osteoporosis.

questions.question: Which structure is palpable in the anatomical snuffbox?
questions.explanation: The scaphoid bone forms the floor of the anatomical snuffbox and is palpable in this space. Tenderness in the snuffbox following wrist injury suggests possible scaphoid fracture. The radial artery pulse can also be felt crossing the snuffbox floor.

The pterygoid hamulus is a hook-like process at the inferior end of the medial pterygoid plate of the sphenoid bone. The tensor veli palatini tendon hooks around it before inserting into the soft palate. The hamulus can be palpated intraorally posterior to the maxillary tuberosity. Fractures cause palatal dysfunction.
questions.question: The pterygoid hamulus is part of which bone?

questions.explanation: Goblet cells that secrete mucus are abundant in the large intestinal mucosa and increase in number toward the rectum. The mucus lubricates the passage of increasingly solid feces and protects the mucosa. Large intestinal crypts (of Lieberk?hn) lack villi and contain mainly goblet cells and absorptive colonocytes. Paneth cells are found only in the small intestine.
questions.question: Which cells are characteristic of the large intestinal mucosa?
Which vessel typically runs in the splenorenal ligament?
questions.explanation: The splenorenal ligament connects the hilum of the spleen to the anterior surface of the left kidney and contains the splenic artery and vein, along with the tail of the pancreas (extending to within 1 cm of the splenic hilum in about 75% of individuals). The splenic vessels run a tortuous course along the superior border of the pancreatic body and tail before entering this ligament. The ligament represents the left portion of the dorsal mesogastrium. During splenectomy, the tail of the pancreas within this ligament must be identified and preserved to prevent pancreatic injury and subsequent pancreatitis or pseudocyst formation.

questions.question: Where does the azygos vein originate?
questions.explanation: The azygos vein is formed by the union of the right ascending lumbar vein and right subcostal vein at the level of L1-L2. It enters the thorax through the aortic hiatus of the diaphragm at T12. It represents the embryonic right posterior cardinal vein.

questions.question: Which bone contains the foramen spinosum?
questions.explanation: The foramen spinosum is located in the greater wing of the sphenoid bone, posterolateral to the foramen ovale. It transmits the middle meningeal artery and meningeal branch of the mandibular nerve. The foramen is located at the spine of the sphenoid. Accessory meningeal arteries may also pass through this foramen.

The sphenoid sinus lies within the body of the sphenoid with the clivus and pons posterior to it. The pituitary fossa is superior, and the cavernous sinuses with internal carotid arteries are lateral. The optic chiasm lies superiorly. Trans-sphenoidal pituitary surgery accesses the fossa through the sphenoid sinus.
questions.question: The sphenoid sinus relates posteriorly to which structure?
Which structure marks the beginning of the anal canal?
questions.explanation: The anal canal begins at the anorectal junction (where the rectum pierces the pelvic diaphragm formed by the levator ani muscle), located approximately one inch (2.5 cm) below and anterior to the tip of the coccyx. At this level, the puborectalis sling creates the anorectal angle. The anal canal extends approximately 3.8-4 cm to the anus (anal verge). The pectinate line divides the anal canal into upper (endodermal) and lower (ectodermal) parts. The white line of Hilton marks the lower border of the internal sphincter.

The taeniae coli represent three longitudinal bands where the outer longitudinal smooth muscle layer of the colon is thickened and concentrated, running from cecum to rectosigmoid junction. The three bands are: taenia libera (free, anteriorly on ascending and descending colon), taenia mesocolica (at mesenteric attachment), and taenia omentalis (at omental attachment). Between the taeniae, the longitudinal muscle is thin, allowing the circular muscle to create sacculations (haustra). The taeniae converge at the base of the appendix, providing a surgical landmark. At the rectosigmoid junction (about 15 cm from anus), the taeniae spread to form a complete longitudinal muscle layer in the rectum.
questions.question: The taeniae coli are thickenings of which muscle layer?
Where is the AV node situated?
questions.explanation: The AV node is located in the lower part of the interatrial septum, within the triangle of Koch (bounded by the tricuspid annulus, coronary sinus orifice, and tendon of Todaro). It receives the impulse from the SA node and, after a physiological delay allowing atrial contraction, transmits it to the ventricles via the bundle of His. Its blood supply is typically from the right coronary artery.

questions.question: What structure is torn in gamekeeper's thumb?
questions.explanation: "Gamekeeper's thumb" (skier's thumb when acute) involves a tear of the ulnar collateral ligament of the thumb metacarpophalangeal joint. This causes thumb instability affecting pinch grip strength. The injury historically occurred in gamekeepers from repetitive stress while killing rabbits.
options: Ulnar collateral ligament of thumb MCP

questions.question: Abductor hallucis, the most medially placed first layer foot muscle, is innervated by which nerve and performs which action?
questions.explanation: Abductor hallucis is innervated by the medial plantar nerve (S2, S3) and performs abduction and flexion of the first digit (hallux). It originates from the medial tubercle of the calcaneal tuberosity, the flexor retinaculum, and plantar aponeurosis. It inserts into the medial side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the first digit.
options: Lateral plantar nerve; adducts and flexes 1st digit
Deep fibular nerve; extends and abducts 1st digit
Medial plantar nerve; abducts and flexes 1st digit
Medial plantar nerve; flexes and inverts foot

questions.question: The celiac ganglion receives preganglionic fibers via which nerve?
questions.explanation: The celiac ganglion, the largest of the prevertebral (preaortic) ganglia, receives preganglionic sympathetic fibers primarily via the greater splanchnic nerve (T5-T9), with contributions from the lesser splanchnic nerve (T10-T11). These preganglionic fibers synapse in the ganglion, and postganglionic fibers distribute along arterial branches from the celiac trunk to supply foregut derivatives. The vagus nerve also contributes parasympathetic fibers to the celiac plexus, but these pass through without synapsing. The celiac plexus surrounds the origin of the celiac trunk and is the largest autonomic plexus in the body.

Circular venous plexuses are found at the base of the nipple. Veins corresponding to the arteries drain the breast, ultimately into the axillary and internal thoracic veins. The superficial veins often become prominent and dilated during pregnancy and lactation.
questions.question: Where are circular venous plexuses located?

questions.explanation: The body of the pancreas is one of the major structures forming the posterior relations or stomach bed. The stomach bed is separated from the stomach by the lesser sac (omental bursa). Other structures in the stomach bed include the left kidney, left suprarenal gland, splenic artery, transverse mesocolon, and diaphragm.
questions.question: Which structure lies in the stomach bed posteriorly?

questions.explanation: Saturday night palsy affects the radial nerve due to compression against the humerus, typically from sleeping with the arm over a chair back. This causes wrist drop and loss of finger extension. Sensory loss over the dorsum of the hand may also occur.
questions.question: What nerve is affected in Saturday night palsy?

questions.explanation: produces both wrist flexion and wrist abduction (radial deviation). It is a prominent muscle in the anterior forearm, easily palpable lateral to palmaris longus. The muscle is supplied by the median nerve.
questions.question: Which muscle produces wrist flexion and abduction?

questions.explanation: The suprapatellar bursa extends approximately 3-5 cm above the superior pole of the patella, beneath the quadriceps tendon, and communicates freely with the knee joint cavity. In knee effusions, fluid accumulates in this bursa as well as the joint space, creating the characteristic fluctuant fullness above the patella. Aspiration is performed by needle insertion into the suprapatellar pouch.
options: 3�5 cm above the superior patellar pole beneath the quadriceps tendon
1 cm above the superior pole of the patella
To the level of the anterior superior iliac spine
Only to the level of the patella
10 cm above the patella into the anterior thigh
questions.question: The knee joint has a synovial membrane that is extensive. The suprapatellar bursa communicates with the knee joint cavity and is clinically important because it extends how far above the patella?
Which nerve is compressed in radial tunnel syndrome?
questions.explanation: Radial tunnel syndrome involves compression of the posterior interosseous nerve (deep branch of radial nerve) in the proximal forearm. Compression typically occurs at the arcade of Frohse (fibrous arch at the proximal edge of supinator). Unlike radial nerve palsy, wrist extension is preserved as the extensor carpi radialis muscles are supplied proximal to the compression.

The middle cardiac vein ascends in the posterior interventricular groove alongside the posterior interventricular artery and drains into the coronary sinus near its termination in the right atrium. It drains blood from the posterior walls of both ventricles and the posterior interventricular septum. It is the second largest cardiac vein after the great cardiac vein.
questions.question: Which vein accompanies the posterior interventricular artery?
Which enzyme in pancreatic juice digests nucleic acids?
questions.explanation: Pancreatic juice contains DNAase and RNAase (nucleases) that digest deoxyribonucleic acid and ribonucleic acid respectively into nucleotides. These nucleotides are further broken down by intestinal enzymes into nucleosides and bases for absorption. The pancreas secretes all major classes of digestive enzymes: proteases, lipases, amylase, and nucleases, making it essential for complete digestion.

questions.question: Which condition compresses structures at thoracic inlet?
questions.explanation: Thoracic outlet syndrome results from compression of nerves (brachial plexus) or vessels (subclavian artery/vein) at the superior aperture of the thorax. Causes include cervical rib, abnormal first rib, scalene muscle abnormalities, or trauma. Symptoms include arm pain, paresthesias, and vascular changes.

options: Superficial at medial epicondyle and Guyon canal
Runs in a deep and well-protected anatomical position
questions.question: How does the ulnar nerve's path make it vulnerable to injury?
questions.explanation: The ulnar nerve is vulnerable at two main sites: posterior to the medial epicondyle where it's subcutaneous and easily traumatized (cubital tunnel), and at the wrist in Guyon's canal. At both locations, the nerve lies in confined spaces with minimal soft tissue protection.

questions.question: The femoral artery passes through the adductor hiatus in adductor magnus to continue as which artery?
questions.explanation: The femoral artery passes through the adductor hiatus, a tendinous gap in the lower part of adductor magnus, to become the popliteal artery in the popliteal fossa. The femoral vein similarly traverses the adductor hiatus to become the popliteal vein. The adductor canal lies superior to the adductor hiatus.

questions.question: What is a Zenker's diverticulum?
questions.explanation: Zenker's diverticulum is a pharyngeal pouch (false diverticulum) that herniates through Killian's dehiscence (area of weakness between the thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus muscles). It occurs in the hypopharynx just above the upper esophageal sphincter. Patients present with dysphagia, regurgitation, halitosis, and risk of aspiration.

The anterior ethmoidal artery (from ophthalmic artery) supplies the anterior superior nasal septum. The sphenopalatine artery supplies the posterior septum while the superior labial artery supplies anteroinferiorly. These vessels anastomose in Little's area (Kiesselbach's plexus), the most common site of anterior epistaxis.
questions.question: Which artery supplies the nasal septum anteriorly?
What deformity results from paralysis of intrinsic hand muscles?
questions.explanation: deformity results from paralysis of intrinsic hand muscles, particularly in ulnar nerve injury. There is hyperextension at the metacarpophalangeal joints and flexion at the interphalangeal joints. This occurs due to unopposed action of long flexors and extensors without intrinsic muscle balance.

In the bare area of the liver, there is no peritoneum between the liver and the diaphragm - they are in direct contact. This area is bounded by the superior and inferior layers of the coronary ligament. The direct contact allows potential spread of infection between the liver and thorax, and provides a route for extraperitoneal collateral circulation.
questions.question: Which structure separates the liver bare area from the diaphragm?

questions.explanation: The midtarsal joint (Chopart's joint) consists of two articulations working in concert: the talonavicular joint medially and the calcaneocuboid joint laterally. Movements at this joint complement subtalar movements to produce overall foot inversion and eversion. Chopart's amputation is performed through this joint for distal foot pathology, preserving the hindfoot for a functional stump.
questions.question: The midtarsal (transverse tarsal) joint is formed by which two articulations working together?

questions.explanation: The "dinner fork deformity" in Colles' fracture results from posterior displacement of the distal radial fragment. When viewed laterally, the wrist resembles an upside-down dinner fork with the handle representing the forearm and the fork head representing the displaced hand segment.
questions.question: What produces the dinner fork deformity?
The transverse sinus lies in the attached border of which dural fold?
questions.explanation: The transverse sinuses lie in the attached posterior border of the tentorium cerebelli, extending from the internal occipital protuberance to the petrous temporal bone. They receive blood from the superior sagittal sinus (or confluence) and drain into the sigmoid sinuses. The tentorium separates the cerebellum from the occipital lobes.

questions.question: What structure indents the apex of each renal pyramid?
questions.explanation: Each renal papilla (apex of a renal pyramid) is indented by a cup-shaped minor calyx that collects urine draining from the collecting ducts. There are typically 8-12 minor calyces per kidney. Two to three minor calyces unite to form a major calyx, and 2-3 major calyces join to form the renal pelvis.

questions.question: Which cells in the gastric mucosa produce pepsinogen?
questions.explanation: Chief (peptic or zymogenic) cells in the gastric glands of the fundus and body secrete pepsinogen, the inactive precursor of pepsin. Pepsinogen is activated to pepsin by gastric acid (HCl) and autocatalytically by pepsin itself. Pepsin begins protein digestion in the stomach, working optimally at pH 1.5-2. Chief cells are basophilic due to abundant rough endoplasmic reticulum for protein synthesis.

questions.question: The posterior division of the obturator nerve supplying both the hip and knee joints explains which clinical observation?
questions.explanation: The posterior division of the obturator nerve supplies both the hip and knee joints, explaining the well-known clinical phenomenon of referred pain to the knee in hip joint disease. Children with Perthes disease or slipped femoral epiphysis classically present with knee pain. This is a critical clinical pearl applying Hilton's law practically.
options: Quadriceps weakness in obturator nerve injury
Referred pain to the knee in hip joint disease
Loss of adduction in knee joint pathology
Hip pain referred to the lumbar spine
Groin pain referred to the ankle

questions.question: The basilar artery terminates at which vertebral level?
questions.explanation: The basilar artery terminates at the upper border of the pons by dividing into the two posterior cerebral arteries. It is formed by union of the vertebral arteries at the pontomedullary junction. The artery gives off pontine, anterior inferior cerebellar, superior cerebellar, and labyrinthine branches during its course.

The sella turcica (Turkish saddle) is a depression in the body of the sphenoid bone housing the pituitary gland. It is bounded anteriorly by the tuberculum sellae and posteriorly by the dorsum sellae. The cavernous sinuses lie laterally. Trans-sphenoidal pituitary surgery accesses this region through the sphenoid sinus.
questions.question: Which bone contains the sella turcica?

questions.explanation: When a bone has an epiphysis at both ends, the nutrient canal is directed away from the more actively growing end. Hughes captured this in the mnemonic 'to the elbow I go, from the knee I flee,' indicating the direction of nutrient arteries in the humerus and lower limb bones respectively.
questions.question: In bones with epiphyses at both ends, the nutrient canal is directed away from which structure?

questions.explanation: The ureter descends on the anterior surface of the psoas major muscle (over the tips of the transverse processes of the lumbar vertebrae), passing from lateral to medial as it descends toward the pelvic brim. It is crossed anteriorly by the testicular/ovarian vessels and lies posterior to the peritoneum throughout its abdominal course. The ureter crosses the bifurcation of the common iliac artery (or the external iliac artery) at the pelvic brim, providing a consistent landmark. The relationship to psoas major is maintained until the ureter reaches the pelvic inlet, where it enters the pelvis.
questions.question: The ureter descends on the anterior surface of which muscle?

questions.explanation: Sliding hiatal hernia (type I) accounts for about 95% of hiatal hernias. The gastroesophageal junction and a portion of the stomach slide up through the esophageal hiatus into the thorax. It is associated with gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). Paraesophageal hernias (types II-IV) account for 5% and involve herniation of stomach alongside a normally positioned gastroesophageal junction.
questions.question: What is the most common type of hiatal hernia?

questions.explanation: The anterior interosseous nerve supplies deep flexor muscles (flexor pollicis longus, radial half of flexor digitorum profundus, pronator quadratus) while the posterior interosseous nerve supplies all posterior forearm extensors. This complementary distribution ensures complete innervation of forearm muscles from the radial and median nerves.
options: Anterior for deep flexors, posterior for extensors
Anterior for extensors, posterior for flexors
questions.question: How do the anterior and posterior interosseous nerves complement each other?
Which nerve may be injured during inguinal hernia repair?
questions.explanation: The ilioinguinal nerve (L1), running through the inguinal canal between the internal oblique and external oblique, and emerging through the superficial inguinal ring, is at risk during inguinal hernia repair. Injury can cause chronic postoperative groin pain and sensory loss over the medial thigh and anterior scrotum/labium majus. The nerve should be identified and preserved during herniorrhaphy. The genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve (running within the spermatic cord) is also vulnerable. The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve runs lateral to the inguinal canal and may be injured during lateral approaches.

questions.question: Which of the following muscles is NOT among the six small lateral rotators of the hip joint?
questions.explanation: The six small lateral rotators of the hip joint are: quadratus femoris, obturator internus, gemellus superior, gemellus inferior, obturator externus, and piriformis. Gluteus medius is primarily an abductor and medial rotator of the hip, not a lateral rotator. Gluteus medius is sometimes referred to as the 'rotator cuff of the hip' for its stabilizing role.

questions.question: How many posterior intercostal arteries arise from thoracic aorta?
questions.explanation: Nine pairs of posterior intercostal arteries arise from the thoracic aorta, supplying the lower nine intercostal spaces. The upper two spaces receive their posterior intercostal arteries from the superior intercostal artery. Each posterior intercostal artery gives branches to muscles, skin, parietal pleura, and the breast.

In adults, the Eustachian tube lies at 45� to the horizontal plane, whereas in infants it is only 10�. This more vertical orientation in children predisposes them to middle ear infections. The tube is approximately 31-38 mm long with the posterior third being osseous.
questions.question: The Eustachian tube in adults lies at what angle to the horizontal plane?

questions.explanation: The cricothyroid joint between the inferior horn of the thyroid cartilage and cricoid cartilage allows anteroposterior tilting (rotation). This movement elongates or shortens the vocal cords, changing their tension. Cricothyroid muscle contraction tilts the thyroid cartilage forward, tensing the cords. The joint is a synovial joint with a capsule and ligaments.
questions.question: The cricothyroid joint allows which movement?

questions.explanation: Subscapularis is supplied by the upper subscapular nerve (C5, C6) and lower subscapular nerve (C5, C6). Both nerves arise from the posterior cord. The lower subscapular nerve also supplies teres major muscle.
questions.question: What nerve supplies subscapularis muscle?
Which structure forms the most concave impression on the splenic visceral surface?
questions.explanation: The gastric impression is the largest and most concave of the impressions on the splenic visceral surface, reflecting contact with the fundus and greater curvature of the stomach. It lies between the superior and intermediate borders. Other impressions include renal (from left kidney), colic (from splenic flexure), and pancreatic (from pancreatic tail).

options: Second part of duodenum to sigmoid colon
Duodenojejunal flexure to right sacroiliac joint
questions.question: The root of the mesentery extends from which two points?
questions.explanation: The root of the mesentery of the small intestine extends obliquely from the duodenojejunal flexure (at approximately L2, left of midline) to the right sacroiliac joint (at approximately S1, right of midline), a distance of about 15 cm. Along this short root, approximately 6-7 meters of small intestine (jejunum and ileum) is attached. The root crosses the third (horizontal) part of the duodenum, abdominal aorta, IVC, right ureter, right psoas major muscle, and right testicular/ovarian vessels. This oblique orientation allows the small intestine maximum mobility while maintaining vascular supply and creating the characteristic radiating pattern of jejunal and ileal vessels.

The lamina papyracea (orbital plate) of the ethmoid bone forms the thin medial wall of the orbit. It separates the orbit from the ethmoidal air cells. The name papyracea (paper-like) reflects its extreme thinness. Ethmoidal infections can erode through this wall causing orbital cellulitis or abscess.
questions.question: The lamina papyracea forms the medial wall of which structure?

questions.explanation: The hip joint is a multiaxial ball and socket type of synovial joint, the largest and second largest weight-bearing joint in the human body. It allows movements in all three planes: flexion/extension in the sagittal plane, abduction/adduction in the frontal plane, and medial/lateral rotation in the transverse plane.
questions.question: The hip joint is specifically classified as which type of synovial joint?

questions.explanation: The true vocal cords are covered by stratified squamous non-keratinized epithelium, which is firmly adherent to the underlying vocal ligament without submucosa. This accounts for the pearly white avascular appearance on laryngoscopy. The rest of the larynx is lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium.
questions.question: What epithelium lines the true vocal cords?
The inferior alveolar artery is a branch of which vessel?
questions.explanation: The inferior alveolar artery arises from the first (mandibular) part of the maxillary artery. It descends with the inferior alveolar nerve to enter the mandibular foramen, supplying the mandibular teeth and bone. The mylohyoid branch supplies the mylohyoid muscle. The mental artery emerges through the mental foramen.

The left colic artery (first branch of the inferior mesenteric artery) divides into ascending and descending branches near the descending colon. The ascending branch runs superiorly to supply the left (distal) third of the transverse colon and splenic flexure, anastomosing with the left branch of the middle colic artery (from SMA) to complete the marginal artery. The descending branch runs inferiorly along the descending colon, anastomosing with branches of the sigmoid arteries. This anastomotic pattern creates collateral circulation between superior and inferior mesenteric arterial territories, though the splenic flexure (Griffiths' point) remains a watershed area vulnerable to ischemia.
questions.question: The left colic artery typically divides into which branches?

questions.explanation: The posterior wall of the lesser sac (omental bursa) is formed by peritoneum covering the pancreas, left kidney, left suprarenal gland, superior pole of the left kidney, and the posterior two layers of the greater omentum fused to the transverse mesocolon. The lesser sac is bounded anteriorly by the stomach, lesser omentum, and greater omentum (anterior two layers); superiorly by the caudate lobe of liver and diaphragm; inferiorly by the transverse colon and mesocolon; and communicates with the greater sac through the epiploic foramen. Collections in the lesser sac appear on imaging as fluid between stomach and pancreas.
questions.question: Which structure forms the posterior boundary of the lesser sac?

options: A single extensor tendon controls finger extension
Extrinsic extensors and intrinsics interact via extensor expansion
questions.question: How does the extensor mechanism coordinate finger extension?
questions.explanation: The extensor mechanism involves complex interaction between extensor digitorum (extrinsic) and intrinsic muscles through the extensor expansion. Intrinsic muscles (lumbricals, interossei) insert into lateral bands of the expansion, enabling MCP flexion with IP extension. This coordination is essential for normal finger function.

The superior mesenteric artery and vein pass between the two peritoneal layers of the mesentery along with lymph nodes, lymphatic vessels, nerves, and fat. These vessels provide the primary blood supply and drainage for the jejunum and ileum. The superior mesenteric artery gives off 15-18 branches that form the arterial arcades.
questions.question: Which structures pass between the two layers of the mesentery?

questions.explanation: The moderator band (septomarginal trabecula) is a muscular bridge extending from the interventricular septum to the base of the anterior papillary muscle. It carries the right bundle branch of the conducting system, ensuring coordinated activation of the papillary muscles. It prevents overdistention of the ventricle and was historically important for determining ventricular orientation.
questions.question: Which structure carries the right bundle branch in the right ventricle?

questions.explanation: The bare area of the liver is located on the diaphragmatic surface where the liver is in direct contact with the diaphragm without intervening peritoneum. This area is bounded by the superior and inferior layers of the coronary ligament. The bare area is clinically significant as infections can spread directly between the liver and thorax.
questions.question: Which area of the liver is devoid of peritoneal covering?

options: Lateral tibial plateau of the knee
Tibial tuberosity on the anterior tibia
Posterior aspect of the medial knee
Lateral joint line of the knee
Medial tibia, 5�7 cm below the knee joint line
questions.explanation: Pes anserinus bursitis presents with pain, swelling, and tenderness at the medial aspect of the tibia, approximately 5-7 cm below the knee joint line, at the common insertion of sartorius, gracilis, and semitendinosus. It is common in obese patients with knee osteoarthritis and is associated with valgus knee deformity. Treatment includes local steroid injection and physiotherapy.
questions.question: The pes anserinus is located on the medial surface of the tibia. Pes anserinus bursitis presents with pain at which specific location?
The superior thyroid artery gives off which laryngeal branch?
questions.explanation: The superior thyroid artery gives off the superior laryngeal artery, which accompanies the internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve through the thyrohyoid membrane. The artery supplies the laryngeal structures above the vocal cords. The cricothyroid branch runs with the external laryngeal nerve to supply the cricothyroid muscle and anastomoses across the midline.

extends the metacarpophalangeal joint of the thumb. Its tendon forms the lateral border of the anatomical snuffbox along with abductor pollicis longus. The muscle is supplied by the posterior interosseous nerve.
questions.question: What produces thumb extension at the metacarpophalangeal joint?
Which nerve is compressed causing handlebar palsy?
questions.explanation: "Handlebar palsy" results from ulnar nerve compression at the wrist (Guyon's canal) due to prolonged pressure from bicycle handlebars. This causes weakness of intrinsic hand muscles and numbness in ulnar nerve distribution. The condition is common in long-distance cyclists.

at the wrist joint (ulnar deviation) is produced by the combined action of extensor carpi ulnaris and flexor carpi ulnaris. These muscles work synergistically despite being in different compartments. The wrist joint permits movement along two axes as an ellipsoid synovial joint.
questions.question: Which movement at the wrist joint is produced by extensor carpi ulnaris and flexor carpi ulnaris?
What nerve supplies the first and second lumbricals?
questions.explanation: The lateral two lumbricals (to index and middle fingers) are supplied by the median nerve. The medial two lumbricals (to ring and little fingers) are supplied by the ulnar nerve. This dual innervation pattern is unique among hand muscles.

questions.question: What structure occupies the free edge of the falciform ligament?
questions.explanation: The ligamentum teres (round ligament of the liver) occupies the free inferior edge of the falciform ligament. It is the obliterated remnant of the umbilical vein, which carried oxygenated blood from the placenta to the fetus. The ligamentum teres extends from the umbilicus to the left branch of the portal vein at the porta hepatis.

questions.question: Which cruciate ligament becomes taut during knee flexion and is the stronger of the two cruciate ligaments?
questions.explanation: The posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) arises from the posterior intercondylar area of the tibia and attaches to the medial condyle of the femur. It becomes taut during flexion of the knee and is the stronger of the two cruciate ligaments. In a weight-bearing flexed knee (walking downhill), the PCL is the main stabilizing factor preventing anterior displacement of the femur.

questions.question: Which structure forms the roof of the carpal tunnel?
questions.explanation: The flexor retinaculum is a thick connective tissue structure forming the roof of the carpal tunnel. It bridges between the hook of hamate and pisiform medially to the scaphoid and trapezium laterally. This converts the carpal arch into a tunnel through which flexor tendons and median nerve pass.

The internal thoracic vein accompanies the artery of the same name, draining blood from the anterior chest wall, upper abdomen, and breast. It ascends to drain into the brachiocephalic vein on each side. The vein receives tributaries corresponding to the arterial branches.
questions.question: Which vein accompanies the internal thoracic artery?
The cystic artery typically arises from which vessel?
questions.explanation: The cystic artery most commonly (in about 75% of cases) arises from the right hepatic artery within Calot's triangle (bounded by the cystic duct, common hepatic duct, and inferior surface of the liver). However, significant anatomical variations exist, with the cystic artery occasionally arising from the left hepatic, gastroduodenal, or even superior mesenteric artery. The artery typically passes posterior to the common hepatic duct before reaching the gallbladder, where it divides into superficial (supplying the peritoneal surface) and deep (supplying the hepatic surface) branches. Careful identification during cholecystectomy prevents inadvertent injury to aberrant vessels.

questions.question: The proper hepatic artery lies in which position within the portal triad?
questions.explanation: Within the hepatoduodenal ligament (free edge of lesser omentum), the structures of the portal triad are arranged from anterior to posterior and right to left as: bile duct (anteriorly and to the right), hepatic artery proper (anteriorly and to the left), and portal vein (posteriorly). This arrangement is sometimes remembered as "DAV" reading from right to left anteriorly (Duct, Artery, Vein). The hepatic artery typically lies anterior to the portal vein and to the left of the bile duct, though anatomical variations are common. Lymph nodes and autonomic nerve plexuses also travel through the hepatoduodenal ligament.

The superior epigastric artery is a terminal branch of the internal thoracic artery (which arises from the subclavian artery), not the abdominal aorta. It descends through the thorax, enters the rectus sheath by passing between the sternal and costal attachments of the diaphragm, and anastomoses with the inferior epigastric artery (from external iliac artery), providing an important collateral pathway between subclavian and external iliac systems. The abdominal aorta gives rise to paired visceral branches (suprarenal, renal, gonadal), unpaired visceral branches (celiac, SMA, IMA), paired parietal branches (inferior phrenic, four lumbar), and the unpaired median sacral artery.
questions.question: Which artery does NOT arise from the abdominal aorta?

questions.explanation: Lymphatic drainage from the stomach first passes to regional lymph node groups along the lesser curvature (left and right gastric nodes), greater curvature (left and right gastroepiploic nodes), and around the cardia (paracardial nodes). From these first-tier nodes, lymph flows to second-tier nodes along the celiac trunk and its branches (celiac, hepatic, and splenic nodes), then to pre-aortic nodes, and finally to the cisterna chyli and thoracic duct. This extensive lymphatic drainage explains the potential for widespread metastases in gastric cancer and the need for extended lymphadenectomy in curative surgery.
questions.question: Which lymph nodes receive direct drainage from the stomach?

questions.explanation: The oesophageal hiatus in the diaphragm is located at the level of the tenth thoracic vertebra (T10). The oesophagus passes through the muscular part of the right crus of the diaphragm at this level. This hiatus also transmits the anterior and posterior vagal trunks and oesophageal branches of the left gastric vessels.
questions.question: Which vertebral level corresponds to the oesophageal opening in the diaphragm?
The parotid duct crosses which muscle superficially?
questions.explanation: The parotid (Stensen's) duct crosses the masseter muscle superficially before turning medially to pierce the buccinator. The duct runs parallel to and one finger's breadth below the zygomatic arch. Accessory parotid tissue (socia parotidis) may be present on the masseter along the duct. Facial nerve branches lie deep to the duct.

The gastrocolic ligament, part of the greater omentum, connects the greater curvature of the stomach to the transverse colon. It contains the right and left gastroepiploic vessels along the greater curvature and represents the anterior two layers of the greater omentum before they descend and fold back. Division of the gastrocolic ligament provides surgical access to the lesser sac (omental bursa) and is a key step in gastric surgery, transverse colectomy, and pancreatic surgery. The avascular plane (relatively avascular window) between the gastroepiploic vessels and transverse colon can be developed to enter the lesser sac with minimal bleeding.
questions.question: The gastrocolic ligament connects the stomach to which structure?

options: Ischium; loose connective tissue and fat
questions.explanation: The acetabular fossa is the non-articular part of the acetabulum, formed mainly by the ischium. It contains loose connective tissue and a pad of fat. The articular surface is the horseshoe-shaped lunate surface covered by hyaline cartilage. The fossa is deficient inferiorly at the acetabular notch, bridged by the transverse acetabular ligament.
questions.question: The non-articular portion of the acetabulum (acetabular fossa) is formed mainly by which bone and contains what?
What is the function of palmar interossei?
questions.explanation: Palmar interossei (PAD - Palmar ADduct) produce finger adduction, moving fingers toward the middle finger axis. There are three palmar interossei muscles compared to four dorsal interossei. All interossei also flex the metacarpophalangeal joints and extend the interphalangeal joints.

The masseter, temporalis, and medial pterygoid muscles elevate the mandible during mastication. The masseter originates from the zygomatic arch and inserts on the lateral surface of the mandibular angle and ramus. It is innervated by the masseteric nerve from V3. Bilateral contraction closes the mouth and clenches the teeth.
questions.question: Which muscle elevates the mandible during mastication?
Which nerve supplies rhomboid muscles?
questions.explanation: The dorsal scapular nerve (C5) supplies the rhomboid major and minor muscles, and often the levator scapulae. The nerve pierces and may supply scalenus medius before descending along the vertebral border of the scapula. Injury affects scapular retraction.

The duodenum is primarily retroperitoneal except for the first 2 cm of the superior (first) part, which is intraperitoneal and mobile, connecting to the liver via the hepatoduodenal ligament. The descending (second), horizontal (third), and ascending (fourth) parts are all secondarily retroperitoneal, having been covered by peritoneum during development but subsequently becoming fixed to the posterior abdominal wall. The duodenojejunal flexure marks the transition from retroperitoneal duodenum to intraperitoneal jejunum and is supported by the suspensory muscle of the duodenum (ligament of Treitz).
questions.question: Which part of the duodenum is retroperitoneal?

questions.explanation: The superior hypogastric plexus lies anterior to the lower part of the abdominal aorta and its bifurcation, extending from approximately L4 to the upper part of the sacrum, anterior to the L5 vertebra and sacral promontory. It represents the continuation of the aortic (intermesenteric) plexus and receives lumbar splanchnic nerves carrying preganglionic sympathetic fibers. The plexus divides inferiorly into right and left hypogastric nerves, which descend into the pelvis to join the inferior hypogastric (pelvic) plexuses. The superior hypogastric plexus can be blocked or surgically divided to treat intractable pelvic pain.
questions.question: The superior hypogastric plexus is located at which vertebral level?

questions.explanation: The oval window (fenestra vestibuli) in the medial wall of the middle ear is closed by the footplate of the stapes, held in place by the annular ligament. The stapes transmits vibrations from the ossicular chain to the perilymph of the inner ear. Otosclerosis causes abnormal bone growth fixing the stapes, resulting in conductive hearing loss.
questions.question: The oval window is closed by which structure?
The vermiform appendix typically arises from which part of the cecum?
questions.explanation: The vermiform appendix arises from the posteromedial wall of the cecum, approximately 2-3 cm below the ileocecal junction. The three taeniae coli of the cecum converge at the base of the appendix, serving as a reliable landmark for locating it during surgery. While the base of the appendix has a relatively constant position, its tip can be found in various locations: retrocecal (65%), pelvic (31%), subcecal (2.3%), preileal (1%), or postileal (0.4%). The appendicular artery, a branch of the ileocolic artery, runs through the mesoappendix to supply the appendix.

questions.question: Into which vein does the splenic vein primarily drain?
questions.explanation: The splenic vein joins with the superior mesenteric vein posterior to the neck of the pancreas to form the hepatic portal vein. The splenic vein runs from left to right along the posterior surface of the pancreas. It receives the short gastric veins, left gastroepiploic vein, pancreatic veins, and inferior mesenteric vein.

questions.question: Gastrocnemius can only plantarflex the ankle effectively under which condition?
options: When the knee is fully extended
questions.explanation: Gastrocnemius is unique in that it plantarflexes the ankle only effectively when the knee is extended, because it crosses the knee joint. When the knee is flexed, gastrocnemius becomes relatively ineffective, and soleus becomes the primary plantarflexor. Gastrocnemius also flexes the leg at the knee and is innervated by the tibial nerve (S1, S2).

questions.question: Which muscle closes the eyelid?
questions.explanation: The orbicularis oculi muscle closes the eyelids. It has orbital, palpebral, and lacrimal parts. The muscle is innervated by the facial nerve (VII). The palpebral portion produces gentle closure (blinking), while the orbital portion produces tight closure (squinting). Facial nerve palsy causes inability to close the eyelid (lagophthalmos).

questions.question: The psoas major muscle receives innervation from which nerve roots?
questions.explanation: The psoas major muscle is innervated by the ventral rami of lumbar nerves L1 through L4, which emerge from the lumbar plexus formed within the substance of the muscle itself. This segmental innervation pattern corresponds to the muscle's extensive vertebral origins from the bodies, transverse processes, and intervertebral discs of T12 through L5. The muscle serves as the chief flexor of the thigh at the hip joint and also assists in lateral flexion of the lumbar vertebral column when acting unilaterally.

questions.question: Which artery supplies the vermiform appendix?
questions.explanation: The appendicular artery, a branch of the ileocolic artery (from the superior mesenteric artery), provides the blood supply to the vermiform appendix. It runs through the free edge of the mesoappendix, making it vulnerable during surgical mobilization of the appendix. This is typically an end artery with minimal collateral supply, so thrombosis can lead to appendiceal ischemia and necrosis. The artery may give off a recurrent branch that ascends toward the ileocecal junction. Variations include occasional origin from a posterior cecal artery or rarely from the superior mesenteric artery directly.

The scapular anastomoses provide collateral circulation connecting the first part of the subclavian artery with the third part of the axillary artery. This involves suprascapular artery, dorsal scapular artery, and circumflex scapular artery. The anastomoses allow blood flow to the limb even with proximal vessel obstruction.
questions.question: What connects the first part of the subclavian artery with the third part of the axillary artery?
The greater trochanter is classified as which type of epiphysis, and which muscle exerts traction upon it, drawing it upward, medially, and backward?
questions.explanation: The greater trochanter is a traction epiphysis; gluteus medius pulls it upward, medially, and backward. Traction epiphyses arise at tendon insertions rather than at articular ends, unlike pressure epiphyses. The quadrate tubercle marks where the epiphyseal line crosses the intertrochanteric crest.

The levator palpebrae superioris is innervated by the oculomotor nerve (III). M�ller's muscle (superior tarsal muscle), a smooth muscle also elevating the lid, is innervated by sympathetics. Oculomotor palsy causes ptosis (drooping eyelid) along with eye movement deficits. Horner's syndrome causes mild ptosis from sympathetic loss.
questions.question: The levator palpebrae superioris is innervated by which nerve?
The recurrent laryngeal nerve ascends in which anatomical groove?
questions.explanation: The recurrent laryngeal nerve ascends in the tracheoesophageal groove between the trachea and esophagus. This location makes it vulnerable during thyroid surgery. The left recurrent nerve loops under the aortic arch while the right loops under the subclavian artery.

The psoas major muscle lies posteromedially to each kidney, forming part of its posterior relation. A psoas abscess can cause confusion with renal pathology due to this proximity. The quadratus lumborum lies directly posterior to the mid-portion of the kidney, while the transversus abdominis and its aponeurosis lie posterolaterally.
questions.question: Which muscle lies immediately medial to the kidney?
Which lymph node group drains the skin of the umbilicus?
questions.explanation: Lymphatic drainage from skin of the anterior abdominal wall follows the watershed principle: above the umbilicus drains to axillary nodes, below the umbilicus drains to superficial inguinal nodes, and the umbilicus itself drains primarily to superficial inguinal nodes though some drainage may occur to both axillary and inguinal nodes. The deep abdominal wall lymphatics drain along the deep vessels (superior epigastric, inferior epigastric, lumbar) to internal thoracic, external iliac, and para-aortic nodes. Metastatic tumor deposits at the umbilicus (Sister Mary Joseph node) typically indicate advanced intra-abdominal malignancy spreading via lymphatics or direct extension.

The fossa ovalis is the remnant of the foramen ovale, which allowed blood to bypass the fetal lungs by shunting from the right to left atrium in utero. Functional closure occurs at birth with the first breath, though anatomical fusion may take months to years. A patent foramen ovale persists in about 25% of adults without usually causing problems.
questions.question: What is the fossa ovalis a remnant of?
Which structure is most posterior in superior mediastinum?
questions.explanation: The esophagus is the most posterior structure in the superior mediastinum. From superficial to deep, the contents include: thymus gland, great veins (brachiocephalic veins and SVC), great arteries (aortic arch and branches), nerves (vagus and phrenic), trachea, esophagus, and thoracic duct.

options: Over the superior border of the interosseous membrane
Anterior to the interosseous membrane superficially
Through the fibular notch of the tibia
Through an opening in the interosseous membrane
questions.explanation: The anterior tibial artery passes through an opening (hiatus) in the interosseous membrane between the tibia and fibula to reach the anterior compartment. It runs down the entire length of the leg into the foot, where it becomes the dorsalis pedis artery at the ankle. It also gives the anterior tibial recurrent artery contributing to the genicular anastomosis.
questions.question: The anterior tibial artery passes through which structure to reach the anterior compartment of the leg?
What is the action of the long head of triceps at the shoulder?
questions.explanation: The long head of triceps crosses both the shoulder and elbow joints, performing extension at the shoulder. At the elbow, all three heads of triceps work together to produce extension. The long head originates from the infraglenoid tubercle of the scapula.

questions.question: The plantar aponeurosis is the most important passive structure maintaining the medial longitudinal arch. It stretches from the calcaneal tuberosity to which structures?
options: Bases of all five proximal phalanges
Bases of all five metatarsal bones
Heads of all metatarsals and bases of proximal phalanges
Only the first metatarsophalangeal joint exclusively
All tarsal bones as a group
questions.explanation: The plantar aponeurosis (plantar fascia) stretches from the calcaneal tuberosity (medial tubercle) to the heads of all metatarsals and the bases of the proximal phalanges. During toe extension (dorsiflexion) in push-off phase of gait, this aponeurosis is tensioned, raising the arch in a windlass mechanism. Plantar fasciitis involves inflammation at the calcaneal attachment.

The gastrosplenic ligament, a peritoneal fold connecting the greater curvature of the stomach (fundus region) to the hilum of the spleen, contains the short gastric arteries and veins (vasa brevia). These 4-6 small vessels branch from the splenic artery and vein near the splenic hilum to supply the gastric fundus. The left gastroepiploic vessels run in the greater omentum along the greater curvature, while the splenic vessels themselves course through the splenorenal ligament connecting the spleen to the left kidney, along with the tail of the pancreas.
questions.question: The gastrosplenic ligament contains which vessels?
The spleen develops in relation to which mesentery?
questions.explanation: The spleen develops within the dorsal mesogastrium (greater omentum) during embryonic development, explaining its position in the left upper quadrant and its peritoneal attachments. The gastrosplenic ligament (part of the dorsal mesogastrium) connects it to the greater curvature of the stomach, while the splenorenal ligament attaches it to the left kidney. Although the spleen is not a gastrointestinal organ, it receives its blood supply from the celiac trunk (via splenic artery) due to this developmental relationship. The tail of the pancreas also develops in the dorsal mesogastrium, extending into the splenorenal ligament.

During inspiration, the diaphragm contracts, causing its domes and central tendon to descend and flatten. This increases the vertical dimension of the thoracic cavity. As the diaphragm descends, abdominal viscera are pushed downward and the intrathoracic volume increases, reducing intrathoracic pressure.
questions.question: What happens to diaphragm during inspiration?

questions.explanation: The left lower lobe typically contains four (sometimes five) bronchopulmonary segments: superior (apical), anterior basal, lateral basal, and posterior basal. The medial basal segment is often absent or fused with the anterior basal segment on the left side, unlike the right lower lobe which consistently has five segments.
questions.question: How many segments are in left lower lobe?

questions.explanation: Two-thirds of the breast's base lies on the pectoralis major muscle. The inferolateral one-third lies on the serratus anterior and external oblique muscles. The deep fascia of these muscles forms the posterior boundary of the retromammary space behind the breast.
questions.question: Which muscle lies deep to the breast medially?
Which portion of the axillary artery lies behind pectoralis minor?
questions.explanation: The second part of the axillary artery lies directly behind (posterior to) the pectoralis minor muscle. This anatomical relationship is used to divide the artery into three parts. The second part gives off two branches: the thoracoacromial and lateral thoracic arteries.

questions.question: The kidney is located at which vertebral levels?
questions.explanation: The kidneys extend from approximately T12 to L3 vertebral levels, with the hilum positioned at the L1 level (transpyloric plane). The right kidney typically sits slightly lower than the left (by about half a vertebra) due to the presence of the liver superiorly. The upper poles are closer to the midline and are related to the diaphragm and ribs (left kidney: ribs 11-12; right kidney: rib 12), while the lower poles are further from the midline. The kidneys lie obliquely, with the upper poles more posterior and closer together than the lower poles.

options: Provide redundant blood supply with extensive anastomoses
questions.explanation: The superficial and deep palmar arches provide redundant blood supply to the hand through extensive anastomoses. This collateral circulation protects hand perfusion even with single artery occlusion. The arches interconnect via perforating branches and palmar metacarpal communications.
questions.question: What is the functional relationship between the two palmar arches?

questions.explanation: The retromandibular vein (formed by union of maxillary and superficial temporal veins) passes through the parotid gland substance. It divides into anterior and posterior divisions within the gland. The anterior division joins the facial vein; the posterior joins the posterior auricular vein to form the external jugular. The facial nerve and external carotid artery also traverse the gland.
questions.question: Which vein passes through the parotid gland?
What lies in the anterior mediastinum primarily?
questions.explanation: The anterior mediastinum (between the sternum and pericardium) contains primarily the thymus gland (or its remnant in adults), fatty tissue, and lymph nodes. In children, the thymus is prominent; in adults, it is largely replaced by fat. This space can be involved in thymomas or lymphomas.

questions.question: Which structure prevents reflux at the gastroesophageal junction?
questions.explanation: Although no anatomical sphincter exists, a physiological lower esophageal sphincter (LES) mechanism prevents reflux at the gastroesophageal junction. This involves: (1) increased smooth muscle tone in the distal esophagus, (2) acute angle of entry (angle of His), (3) compression by the right crus of the diaphragm, (4) positive intra-abdominal pressure on the abdominal esophagus. LES dysfunction causes gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD).

questions.question: The median umbilical fold contains which structure?
questions.explanation: The median umbilical fold (single, midline structure) is raised by the median umbilical ligament, which represents the obliterated urachus (embryonic connection between bladder apex and umbilicus). The paired medial umbilical folds contain the medial umbilical ligaments (obliterated umbilical arteries), while the paired lateral umbilical folds contain the inferior epigastric vessels (patent). The obliterated umbilical vein forms the ligamentum teres hepatis and runs in the free edge of the falciform ligament, not in an umbilical fold. These folds create fossae on the internal surface of the anterior abdominal wall that are clinically significant as potential sites of herniation.

questions.question: Which hormone stimulates gastric acid secretion?
questions.explanation: Gastrin is produced by G cells in the pyloric antrum and stimulates parietal cells to secrete hydrochloric acid and stimulates chief cells to secrete pepsinogen. Its release is stimulated by stomach distention, peptides, and vagal stimulation. Gastrin secretion is inhibited by low pH (negative feedback) and by somatostatin from D cells.

The superior boundary of the epiploic foramen (foramen of Winslow) is formed by the caudate lobe (caudate process) of the liver covered with peritoneum. The inferior boundary is the first part of the duodenum, the anterior boundary is the hepatoduodenal ligament containing the portal triad, and the posterior boundary is the inferior vena cava covered with parietal peritoneum along with the right crus of the diaphragm. The foramen provides communication between the greater and lesser peritoneal sacs and typically admits two fingers, serving as a surgical landmark and potential route for accessing the lesser sac.
questions.question: Which structure forms the superior boundary of the epiploic foramen?
Which muscle depresses the lower lip?
questions.explanation: The depressor labii inferioris depresses and everts the lower lip. It arises from the mandible and inserts into the skin of the lower lip. The muscle is innervated by the marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve. Depressor anguli oris acts primarily on the angle of the mouth, though it assists in lowering the lip.

The epiploic foramen (foramen of Winslow) has the bile duct within the hepatoduodenal ligament as its anterior boundary, not medial. The superior boundary is the caudate lobe of the liver, the inferior boundary is the first part of the duodenum, the anterior boundary is the hepatoduodenal ligament containing the portal triad (portal vein, hepatic artery, and bile duct), and the posterior boundary is the inferior vena cava covered by parietal peritoneum. This opening typically admits two fingers and provides communication between the greater and lesser sacs.
questions.question: Which vessel marks the medial boundary of the epiploic foramen?
Which part of the humerus is most commonly associated with radial nerve injury?
questions.explanation: The radial nerve winds around the spiral groove of the humerus accompanied by profunda brachii vessels. Midshaft humeral fractures frequently damage the radial nerve at this location. This results in wrist drop due to paralysis of extensor muscles and sensory loss over the dorsal hand.

(Cozen's test) or middle finger extension (Maudsley's test) provocates lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow) pain. This stresses the common extensor origin, particularly extensor carpi radialis brevis. Pain at the lateral epicondyle indicates inflammation of the extensor origin.
questions.question: Which test provocates lateral epicondylitis pain?
Which nerve is at risk during submandibular gland surgery?
questions.explanation: All three nerves are at risk during submandibular gland surgery. The marginal mandibular nerve crosses the lower border of the mandible superficially. The hypoglossal nerve lies deep to the gland on hyoglossus. The lingual nerve lies above the gland in contact with the submandibular duct. Careful surgical technique preserves these structures.

questions.question: The retropharyngeal space lies between which two fascial layers?
questions.explanation: The retropharyngeal space lies between the buccopharyngeal fascia (covering the pharynx) and the prevertebral fascia. This potential space extends from the skull base to the mediastinum. Infections here can spread to the posterior mediastinum causing mediastinitis.

The "dinner fork deformity" in Colles' fracture is caused by posterior displacement of the distal radial fragment. When viewed from the side, the wrist resembles the shape of an upside-down dinner fork. The ulnar styloid process is commonly avulsed in conjunction with the radial fracture.
questions.question: What causes the dinner fork deformity to be visible?
From how many lumbar vertebrae does right crus arise?
questions.explanation: The right crus arises from the front of the bodies of the upper three lumbar vertebrae (L1-L3) and their intervertebral discs. The left crus is smaller and arises only from L1 and L2. Some muscle fibers from the right crus form a sling around the esophageal opening.

The internal iliac artery, formed by the bifurcation of the common iliac artery at the L5/S1 level (pelvic brim), descends into the pelvis and typically divides into anterior and posterior divisions at the level of the first sacral vertebra (S1), near the greater sciatic foramen. The posterior division gives off the iliolumbar, lateral sacral, and superior gluteal arteries (all parietal branches), while the anterior division supplies both parietal structures (obturator, internal pudendal, inferior gluteal) and viscera (umbilical, inferior vesical, middle rectal, uterine/vaginal in females, prostatic in males).
questions.question: The internal iliac artery typically divides into anterior and posterior divisions at which vertebral level?
What causes handlebar palsy in cyclists?
questions.explanation: "Handlebar palsy" results from ulnar nerve compression at the wrist (Guyon's canal) due to prolonged pressure from bicycle handlebars.
