This causes weakness of intrinsic hand muscles and sensory changes in ulnar nerve distribution. Long-distance cyclists are particularly susceptible.

The radial nerve primarily supplies extensor muscles but also innervates brachioradialis (elbow flexor) and extensor carpi radialis longus (proximal to lateral epicondyle). This reflects developmental muscle group origins. Brachioradialis, despite being anatomically anterior (flexor compartment), is functionally and embryologically an extensor group muscle.
options: Does not supply any flexor muscles
Supplies brachioradialis flexor despite being an extensor nerve
questions.question: How does the radial nerve supply both flexors and extensors?

questions.explanation: Lateral compartment (fibular compartment) syndrome is confirmed by testing the superficial fibular nerve: eversion strength of the foot (fibularis longus and brevis) and sensation on the dorsum of the foot (superficial fibular nerve cutaneous distribution). In the anterior compartment, the deep fibular nerve is tested (first web space sensation and dorsiflexion). These clinical tests guide emergency fasciotomy decision-making.
options: Deep fibular nerve; first web space sensation and dorsiflexion
Superficial fibular nerve; dorsal foot sensation and eversion strength
questions.question: The peroneal (fibular) compartment syndrome is a less common variant of leg compartment syndrome. Which specific nerve function is tested to confirm lateral compartment integrity?
Which layer directly surrounds the kidney outside the fibrous capsule?
questions.explanation: Perirenal (perinephric) fat is a layer of adipose tissue that lies outside the fibrous capsule and inside the renal fascia (Gerota's fascia). It cushions and protects the kidney. The renal fascia encloses both the kidney and suprarenal gland, while pararenal fat lies external to the renal fascia and forms part of the retroperitoneal fat.

The left kidney extends higher than the right, with its upper pole reaching the 11th rib, while the right kidney's upper pole typically reaches the 12th rib. Both kidneys lie on the diaphragm superiorly, which separates them from the pleura and lungs. The left kidney's higher position reflects the asymmetry caused by the liver on the right.
questions.question: Which rib typically crosses the upper pole of the left kidney?

questions.explanation: The dorsalis pedis pulse is palpated on the dorsum of the foot, just lateral to the tendon of the extensor hallucis longus. The dorsalis pedis artery (continuation of the anterior tibial artery) runs between the extensor hallucis longus tendon medially and the extensor digitorum longus tendon laterally. Absence of this pulse, along with the posterior tibial pulse, indicates peripheral arterial disease.
questions.question: The dorsalis pedis pulse is palpated on the dorsum of the foot. It is found just lateral to the tendon of which muscle?
Which nerve supplies the fibrous pericardium and parietal serous pericardium?
questions.explanation: The phrenic nerves (C3-C5) provide somatic sensory innervation to the fibrous pericardium and parietal layer of serous pericardium. Pain from pericardial irritation is therefore sharp and well-localized, often referred to the shoulder (C4 dermatome). The visceral pericardium receives autonomic innervation and is insensitive to pain.

questions.question: Which compartment contains the brachial artery in the arm?
questions.explanation: The brachial artery lies in the anterior compartment of the arm, medial to the biceps brachii. It is accompanied by the median nerve and basilic vein. The artery is separated from the posterior compartment by the medial intermuscular septum.

questions.question: The trochanteric anastomosis, providing the main blood supply to the head of femur, is formed by which four arteries?
questions.explanation: The trochanteric anastomosis is formed by four arteries: superior gluteal (SGA), inferior gluteal (IGA), medial femoral circumflex (MFCA), and lateral femoral circumflex (LFCA) arteries. Disruption of this anastomosis in femoral neck fractures leads to avascular necrosis of the femoral head.

questions.question: What procedure accesses the heart anteriorly?
questions.explanation: Median sternotomy (vertical splitting of the sternum) is the standard approach for cardiac surgery, providing excellent access to the heart, great vessels, and anterior mediastinum. The sternum is later rewired together. This approach causes less pain and respiratory compromise than lateral thoracotomy.

questions.question: Which muscle protracts the eyeball?
questions.explanation: The inferior oblique muscle is the only extraocular muscle that protracts (brings forward) the eyeball along with extorsion, elevation, and abduction. It arises from the maxilla at the anteromedial orbital floor and inserts on the posterolateral inferior eyeball. The muscle is innervated by the oculomotor nerve (III). It has no relationship with the common tendinous ring.

questions.question: The kidney is related posteriorly to which muscle?
questions.explanation: The posterior surface of each kidney lies on the diaphragm superiorly, then from medial to lateral on the psoas major, quadratus lumborum, and transversus abdominis muscles, separated from them by the perinephric fat, renal fascia, and pararenal fat. The subcostal, iliohypogastric, and ilioinguinal nerves descend obliquely posterior to the kidney on these muscles. The left kidney is related to ribs 11 and 12 posteriorly (protected by the rib cage), while the right kidney is related only to rib 12. These posterior relations are important when considering retrograde surgical approaches to the kidney or complications of renal trauma.

questions.question: The posterior superior alveolar nerve supplies which teeth?
questions.explanation: The posterior superior alveolar nerve (branch of maxillary nerve) supplies the upper molar teeth except the mesiobuccal root of the first molar (supplied by middle superior alveolar). The nerve descends on the maxillary tuberosity and enters the posterior superior alveolar foramina. It also supplies the maxillary sinus mucosa and buccal gingiva.

Each renal artery typically divides into five segmental arteries: apical, anterosuperior, anteroinferior, inferior, and posterior. These are functional end arteries with no significant anastomoses, meaning occlusion of one causes infarction of that segment. This segmental anatomy allows partial nephrectomy without affecting remaining segments. Four segmental arteries arise from the anterior division; one (posterior) from the posterior division.
questions.question: How many segmental arteries typically supply each kidney?
Which component of the quadriceps femoris lies deepest, between the vastus medialis and lateralis?
questions.explanation: Vastus intermedius lies deep to the rectus femoris, between the vastus medialis and lateralis. It originates from the anterior and lateral surfaces of the shaft of the femur and inserts via the common quadriceps tendon and patellar ligament to the tibial tuberosity. It is innervated by the femoral nerve (L2, L3, L4) and extends the leg at the knee.

questions.question: What connects superior and inferior epigastric arteries?
questions.explanation: The superior and inferior epigastric arteries anastomose within the rectus sheath behind the rectus abdominis muscle. This provides an important collateral pathway between the subclavian artery (via internal thoracic and superior epigastric) and the external iliac artery (via inferior epigastric), bypassing the abdominal aorta.

in nerve injuries causes vasomotor changes including arteriolar dilation (making skin warmer) and loss of sweating (making skin drier). Long-standing cases develop trophic changes with dry, scaly skin and cracked nails. These changes are seen in Klumpke's paralysis and other severe nerve injuries.
questions.question: What causes vasomotor changes in nerve injuries?

questions.explanation: The bicipital aponeurosis reinforces the roof of the cubital fossa, protecting the brachial artery and median nerve during venipuncture. Historically, this structure was called the "grace of God" tendon because it protected vital deeper structures during bloodletting. The median cubital vein lies superficial to this protective layer.
questions.question: Which structure protects the brachial artery and median nerve during venipuncture?

questions.explanation: The pectinate line represents the mucocutaneous junction where endoderm-derived hindgut epithelium meets ectoderm-derived proctodeal epithelium at the level of the anal valves. Above this line, the anal canal has columnar epithelium, venous drainage to portal circulation, lymphatic drainage to internal iliac nodes, and autonomic innervation. Below the line, it has stratified squamous epithelium, systemic venous drainage, lymphatic drainage to superficial inguinal nodes, and somatic (pudendal) innervation.
questions.question: The pectinate line in the anal canal marks the junction between which embryological structures?
What movements occur at the shoulder girdle during arm abduction?
questions.explanation: During shoulder joint abduction, the shoulder girdle undergoes upward rotation of the scapula. This scapular movement is essential for achieving full arm abduction beyond 90 degrees. The trapezius and serratus anterior muscles produce this upward rotation of the scapula.

The elbow joint capsule is weak anteriorly and posteriorly, allowing extensive flexion-extension movement. The medial and lateral collateral ligaments provide essential stability. This capsular laxity in the movement plane while maintaining stability perpendicular to it exemplifies structure-function relationships.
options: Allows full flexion-extension with ligament support
questions.question: How does the elbow joint capsule weakness affect function?

questions.explanation: The "prayer" position (pressing palms together with fingers extended) tests median nerve function, particularly flexor digitorum superficialis. Inability to maintain all fingers in full extension with palms pressed together suggests median nerve pathology. This is a reverse of Phalen's test for carpal tunnel syndrome.
questions.question: Which nerve is tested by the prayer position?

questions.explanation: The SA node is located in the upper part of the crista terminalis in the right atrium, near the junction of the superior vena cava and right atrium. It consists of specialized pacemaker cells that spontaneously depolarize, initiating the cardiac impulse at a rate of 60-100 bpm. It is the primary pacemaker, overriding other potential pacemaker sites due to its faster rate.
questions.question: Where is the SA node located anatomically?
Which olecranon bursa lies in subcutaneous connective tissue?
questions.explanation: The subcutaneous olecranon bursa is located in the subcutaneous connective tissue directly over the olecranon process. This bursa can become inflamed from repeated trauma, causing olecranon bursitis known as "student's elbow" or "miner's elbow." The other two bursae are the intratendinous and subtendinous types.

questions.question: Which structure extends between adjacent renal pyramids?
questions.explanation: Renal columns (columns of Bertin) are extensions of cortical tissue that project between adjacent pyramids from the cortex to the renal sinus. They contain interlobar arteries and veins. The cortical tissue in the columns and over the bases of pyramids contains the renal corpuscles and convoluted tubules. Enlarged renal columns can mimic renal masses on imaging.

"Ape hand" deformity results from thenar muscle paralysis due to median nerve injury. The thenar eminence flattens and the thumb falls back in the plane of the palm. Opposition and abduction of the thumb are lost, creating a hand resembling that of an ape.
questions.question: Which muscle is paralyzed in ape hand deformity?

questions.explanation: The ulnar nerve's course around the medial epicondyle means elbow flexion stretches the nerve. Prolonged flexion (sleeping with bent elbow) can cause compression symptoms. This positional sensitivity explains why cubital tunnel syndrome symptoms may worsen at night and why sleeping with extended elbows helps.
options: Elbow flexion stretches nerve around medial epicondyle
questions.question: How does the ulnar nerve's course make hand position affect its function?
Which structure separates the caudate lobe from the quadrate lobe?
questions.explanation: The porta hepatis (transverse fissure) separates the caudate lobe (posterosuperiorly) from the quadrate lobe (anteroinferiorly) on the visceral surface of the liver. The porta hepatis contains the portal vein, hepatic artery, hepatic ducts, lymphatics, and nerves entering or leaving the liver. The caudate lobe is bounded by the porta hepatis anteriorly, the IVC groove posteriorly, and the fissure for the ligamentum venosum on the left. The quadrate lobe is bounded by the porta hepatis posteriorly, the gallbladder fossa on the right, and the fissure for the ligamentum teres on the left.

The parietal peritoneum receives sensory innervation from the same nerves that supply the overlying body wall region: phrenic nerve (C3-C5) for the central diaphragmatic peritoneum, lower six intercostal and subcostal nerves (T7-T12) for the peripheral diaphragmatic and abdominal wall peritoneum, and lumbar nerves for the pelvic peritoneum. This explains why peritoneal irritation produces well-localized, sharp, somatic pain referred to specific dermatomes. In contrast, the visceral peritoneum is insensitive to touch, temperature, and laceration, being innervated only by autonomic nerves that mediate poorly localized visceral pain in response to stretch, ischemia, or chemical irritation.
questions.question: Which nerve provides sensory innervation to the parietal peritoneum?
Which muscles are responsible for scapular protraction?
questions.explanation: Scapular protraction (abduction) is produced by serratus anterior and pectoralis minor muscles. During protraction, the lateral end of the clavicle moves forward along with the scapula. This movement is used in punching, pushing, and reaching forward actions.

options: Deep hand structures and palmar metacarpal arteries
questions.explanation: The deep palmar arch (formed primarily by radial artery) supplies blood to deep hand structures and gives off palmar metacarpal arteries. These metacarpal arteries provide important contributions to digital blood supply. The arch lies approximately 1cm proximal to the superficial arch.
questions.question: What is the primary function of the deep palmar arch?

questions.explanation: The scapulothoracic "joint" is not a true anatomical joint but a functional articulation between the scapula and thoracic wall. It allows scapular movements (elevation, depression, protraction, retraction, rotation) essential for positioning the glenoid cavity. Muscle action rather than ligaments controls this "joint."
questions.question: What is the significance of the scapulothoracic joint?
options: Functional articulation allowing scapular mobility on thorax

questions.explanation: The pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2-S4) provide parasympathetic innervation to hindgut derivatives (distal third of transverse colon, descending colon, sigmoid colon, rectum, and upper anal canal). The vagus nerve provides parasympathetic supply to foregut and midgut derivatives (up to the proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon). Sympathetic supply is via lumbar splanchnic nerves and the inferior mesenteric plexus.
questions.question: Which parasympathetic nerve supplies the hindgut derivatives?
What provides sensation to the palmar aspect of the thumb?
questions.explanation: The median nerve provides sensation to the palmar aspect of the thumb, index, middle, and lateral half of the ring finger. This sensory distribution is preserved in anterior interosseous syndrome (pure motor branch) but affected in carpal tunnel syndrome and more proximal median nerve injuries.

Splenic sinusoids are lined by discontinuous endothelium composed of elongated endothelial cells (stave cells) oriented parallel to blood flow with gaps (slits) of 2-3 ?m between them. This discontinuous arrangement allows flexible cells to pass through but retains rigid or damaged cells. The basement membrane is also discontinuous. This structure is unique to the spleen and facilitates its filtering function.
questions.question: Which cells line the splenic sinusoids?

questions.explanation: The "painful arc" sign is characteristic of rotator cuff pathology, particularly supraspinatus tendonitis or tears. Pain occurs specifically during the middle range of abduction (60-120 degrees) when the greater tubercle and supraspinatus tendon pass under the acromion. Pain is absent at the start and end of abduction.
questions.question: Which condition is characterized by the painful arc sign?

options: Quadriceps (rectus femoris) muscle tear or contusion
Adductor muscle strain of the thigh
Piriformis syndrome from external hip rotation
questions.explanation: Myositis ossificans traumatica can complicate contusions or tears of the quadriceps muscle in the anterior thigh, particularly direct blows (common in contact sports). Heterotopic bone forms within the healing hematoma over 4-8 weeks. Premature massage or passive stretching accelerates its formation. It can cause restriction of knee flexion. Most cases resolve with time and physiotherapy.
questions.question: Myositis ossificans is pathological bone formation within muscle that may complicate which injury about the anterior thigh?

questions.explanation: The mylohyoid muscle forms the muscular floor of the oral cavity, separating it from the neck. It arises from the mylohyoid line of the mandible and inserts into the median raphe and hyoid bone. The muscle is innervated by the mylohyoid nerve from the mandibular division. It elevates the floor of the mouth during swallowing.
questions.question: Which muscle forms the floor of the oral cavity?

options: L1 and T12 vertebral levels only
questions.question: The cutaneous innervation of the upper medial quadrant of the buttock is derived from which spinal segments?
questions.explanation: The upper medial quadrant of the buttock receives cutaneous innervation from L1, 2, 3 and S1, 2, 3. The upper lateral quadrant receives L1 and T12. The lower medial quadrant receives S1, 2, 3, and the lower lateral quadrant receives L2, L3. This dermatomal pattern helps localize spinal pathology.

Pneumothorax is the presence of air in the potential space between the pleural layers, causing lung collapse. This can occur spontaneously, traumatically, or iatrogenically. Hemothorax involves blood, empyema involves pus, and pleural effusion involves abnormal fluid accumulation in the pleural cavity.
questions.question: What condition results from air in pleural cavity?
Which trunk branches from the aortic arch first?
questions.explanation: The brachiocephalic trunk is the first and largest branch of the aortic arch. It ascends to the right and divides behind the right sternoclavicular joint into the right common carotid and right subclavian arteries. The left common carotid and left subclavian arteries arise directly from the arch.

questions.question: What causes Jersey finger?
questions.explanation: Jersey finger results from avulsion of flexor digitorum profundus from the distal phalanx. This commonly occurs in the ring finger when a player's finger catches in another player's jersey during tackle attempts. Inability to flex the distal interphalangeal joint is diagnostic.

Posterior mediastinal masses are most commonly neurogenic tumors arising from sympathetic ganglia (ganglioneuroma, neuroblastoma), peripheral nerves (schwannoma, neurofibroma), or paraganglia (paraganglioma). Esophageal lesions, thoracic duct cysts, and extramedullary hematopoiesis can also occur posteriorly. In children, neuroblastoma is common.
questions.question: What typically causes posterior mediastinal masses?

questions.explanation: The lateral ligaments of the ankle are: the anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL), the posterior talofibular ligament (PTFL), and the calcaneofibular ligament (CFL). The ATFL is the weakest and most commonly injured in ankle sprains. The CFL is the intermediate in strength, and the PTFL is the strongest. Together they stabilize the lateral side of the ankle joint.
options: Anterior tibiotalar, posterior tibiotalar, and calcaneofibular
Anterior talofibular, tibiocalcaneal, and posterior talofibular
Anterior talofibular, posterior talofibular, and calcaneofibular
questions.question: The lateral ligaments of the ankle include which three named ligaments?

questions.explanation: The phrenic nerve (C3, C4, C5) provides sensory innervation to the central diaphragm (both pleural and peritoneal surfaces). Irritation of the diaphragmatic peritoneum (from subphrenic abscess, ruptured spleen, perforated peptic ulcer, ectopic pregnancy, liver inflammation, or cholecystitis) can cause referred pain to the shoulder tip (C3-C5 dermatomes) via the phrenic nerve. This is called Kehr's sign when associated with splenic rupture. The peripheral diaphragm receives sensory innervation from the lower intercostal and subcostal nerves, referring pain to the chest wall and upper abdomen.
questions.question: Which nerve may cause referred pain to the shoulder?
The inferior mesenteric vein typically drains into which vessel?
questions.explanation: The inferior mesenteric vein typically drains into the splenic vein posterior to the body of the pancreas, though variations exist (occasionally draining into the superior mesenteric vein or the confluence of splenic and superior mesenteric veins). The IMV ascends from the pelvis, receiving sigmoid and left colic tributaries, and runs to the left of the inferior mesenteric artery. It passes anterior to the left psoas, left ureter, and left gonadal vessels before reaching the splenic vein. From there, blood flows via the splenic vein to join the superior mesenteric vein, forming the portal vein behind the pancreatic neck.

The great cerebral vein (of Galen) is formed by union of internal cerebral veins and basal veins, draining into the straight sinus. The straight sinus then joins the superior sagittal sinus at the confluence of sinuses. Deep cerebral structures drain via this venous pathway.
questions.question: The great cerebral vein of Galen drains into which sinus?
Which nerve branch arises from the lateral cord?
questions.explanation: The lateral pectoral nerve (C5, C6) arises from the lateral cord and primarily supplies pectoralis major muscle. The lateral cord also gives rise to the musculocutaneous nerve and the lateral root of the median nerve. It lies lateral to the second part of the axillary artery.

The subcostal plane is a horizontal transverse plane passing through the inferior margins of the 10th costal cartilages (lowest point of the costal margin) on each side, corresponding to the upper border of the third lumbar vertebra (L3). Together with the transtubercular plane (L5 level) and the two vertical midclavicular planes, it defines the nine regions of the abdomen. The subcostal plane marks important anatomical landmarks including the origin of the inferior mesenteric artery, the level of the pylorus in some individuals, and the approximate position of the inferior border of the liver.
questions.question: The subcostal plane passes through which vertebral level?

questions.explanation: The most common cause of phrenic nerve paralysis is surgical trauma, particularly during cardiac surgery, thoracic surgery, or neck dissection. The nerve runs along the lateral aspect of the pericardium between the mediastinal pleura and pericardium, making it vulnerable. Other causes include tumors, cervical spine disease, neurological disorders, and idiopathic paralysis.
questions.question: What is the most common cause of phrenic nerve paralysis?
Which axillary node group lies on pectoralis minor?
questions.explanation: The pectoral (anterior) group of axillary lymph nodes lies on the pectoralis minor muscle along the lateral thoracic vessels. This group receives most of the lymphatic drainage from the breast. From here, lymph passes to the central and then apical nodes before reaching the subclavian lymph trunk.

The testes drain lymph directly to the para-aortic (lumbar) lymph nodes at the L1-L2 level, bypassing the inguinal and iliac nodes. This drainage pattern follows the testicular vessels and reflects the embryological origin of the testes high on the posterior abdominal wall. In testicular cancer, metastases first appear in para-aortic nodes, not inguinal nodes (unless scrotal skin is involved). The scrotum drains to superficial inguinal nodes. This explains why orchiectomy for testicular cancer requires high ligation of the spermatic cord at the deep inguinal ring to include regional lymphatics.
questions.question: The testicular lymphatics drain to which nodes?

questions.explanation: Pectineus is primarily supplied by the femoral nerve (L2, L3), but may also receive innervation from the obturator nerve. It originates from the superior ramus of the pubis and inserts into the pectineal line of the femur just inferior to the lesser trochanter. It acts to adduct and flex the thigh and assists with medial rotation.
questions.question: The pectineus muscle receives primary innervation from the femoral nerve and a variable additional supply from which nerve?

questions.explanation: The pulmonary artery is the most superior structure in the root of both lungs. The main bronchus lies posterior to the vessels. The superior and inferior pulmonary veins are the most inferior structures in the root. This anatomical arrangement is constant and important during surgery.
questions.question: Which vessel is superior in the lung root?

options: Femoral rollback during knee flexion, improving flexion range
Anterior knee stability against tibial translation only
Patellar tracking and extensor alignment correction
questions.explanation: The primary biomechanical argument for retaining the PCL in total knee replacement is that it provides femoral rollback during knee flexion: as the knee flexes, the PCL pulls the femoral condyles posteriorly, increasing flexion range and reducing quadriceps force needed for stair climbing. PCL-substituting (posterior-stabilized) designs use a cam and post mechanism to replicate this rollback when the PCL is sacrificed.
questions.question: In a total knee replacement (TKR), the posterior cruciate ligament is either retained or resected. The primary biomechanical argument for retaining the PCL is that it provides which function?

questions.explanation: The ureter is crossed anteriorly by the testicular vessels (in males) or ovarian vessels (in females) near the pelvic brim, as these vessels descend from their aortic origins at L2 level toward the deep inguinal ring (males) or ovary (females). The ureter then crosses the bifurcation of the common iliac artery (or proximal external iliac artery) before entering the pelvis. In females, the ureter is subsequently crossed by the uterine artery approximately 1.5 cm lateral to the cervix ("water under the bridge"), an important surgical relationship during hysterectomy. The superior vesical artery travels with the ureter in the pelvis but does not cross it.
questions.question: The ureter is crossed anteriorly at the pelvic brim by which vessel?

questions.explanation: The base of the vermiform appendix has a constant anatomical location at the posteromedial wall of the cecum where the three taeniae coli converge, approximately 2-3 cm below the ileocecal junction. This convergence provides a reliable surgical landmark for locating the appendix during appendectomy, even when the appendix tip occupies a variable position (retrocecal, pelvic, subcecal, pre-ileal, or post-ileal). McBurney's point (one-third the distance from ASIS to umbilicus) represents the surface marking of the appendix base and is the site of maximal tenderness in appendicitis, but is not the actual anatomical landmark for finding the appendix during surgery.
questions.question: The appendix base is located at which anatomical landmark?

questions.explanation: The long thoracic nerve (C5, C6, C7) supplies serratus anterior, giving branches to each muscle digitation. The nerve descends on the superficial surface of the muscle and is vulnerable to injury during axillary surgery. Damage causes scapular winging.
questions.question: What nerve supplies serratus anterior?

questions.explanation: The superficial branch of the radial nerve passes over the scaphoid bone in the anatomical snuffbox. Scaphoid fracture or associated swelling can compress this nerve branch. This causes numbness over the dorsal thumb and radial side of the hand without motor deficit.
questions.question: Which nerve is at risk in scaphoid fracture?

questions.explanation: The mylohyoid muscle arises from the mylohyoid line on the internal surface of the mandible. The muscle forms the floor of the mouth, separating oral cavity from neck. Below the mylohyoid line, the submandibular gland rests in the submandibular fossa. The mylohyoid nerve (V3) innervates the muscle.
questions.question: The mylohyoid line of the mandible provides attachment for which muscle?
The superficial inguinal ring transmits which structure in females?
questions.explanation: In females, the round ligament of the uterus passes through the inguinal canal and exits via the superficial inguinal ring to terminate in the subcutaneous tissue and labium majus. The ilioinguinal nerve also passes through the superficial ring in both sexes (after traversing the canal). The round ligament is homologous to the gubernaculum testis in males (proximal gubernaculum becomes the ovarian ligament in females). Indirect inguinal hernias are much less common in females but can occur alongside the round ligament in the canal of Nuck (persistent processus vaginalis in females).

questions.question: Morton's neuroma is a painful condition of the foot involving perineural fibrosis of a digital plantar nerve. In which intermetatarsal space does it most commonly occur?
questions.explanation: Morton's neuroma most commonly occurs in the third intermetatarsal space (between the 3rd and 4th metatarsal heads), where the medial and lateral plantar nerves communicate, creating a larger nerve prone to compression. It presents with burning pain and paraesthesia in the 3rd and 4th toes, aggravated by tight footwear and weight-bearing. Mulder's click is a clinical sign on examination.

Hoarseness after cardiac surgery often results from injury to the left recurrent laryngeal nerve during manipulation of the aortic arch or ligamentum arteriosum. The nerve's close relationship to the aorta makes it vulnerable during surgery. Injury causes paralysis of the ipsilateral vocal cord, resulting in hoarseness and weak voice.
questions.question: What causes hoarseness after cardiac surgery?

questions.explanation: The suprascapular artery accompanies the suprascapular nerve through the suprascapular notch into the supraspinous fossa. Unlike the nerve which passes under the superior transverse scapular ligament, the artery passes over it. Both structures then pass through the spinoglenoid notch to reach the infraspinous fossa.
questions.question: What artery typically accompanies the suprascapular nerve through the supraspinous fossa?

questions.explanation: The coronary sinus, the main venous drainage vessel of the heart, opens into the right atrium between the inferior vena cava orifice and the tricuspid valve. It lies in the posterior part of the coronary (atrioventricular) groove and receives the great, middle, and small cardiac veins, along with other tributaries. A small Thebesian valve may partially cover its orifice.
questions.question: Into which chamber does the coronary sinus drain?

options: They're antagonists: pronator teres pronates, biceps supinates
questions.explanation: Pronator teres and biceps brachii are antagonistic for forearm rotation: pronator teres produces pronation while biceps produces supination. However, both can contribute to elbow flexion when pronation/supination resistance is present. This demonstrates how muscles can be synergistic for one motion while antagonistic for another.
questions.question: What is the functional relationship between pronator teres and biceps?
Which artery supplies the body of the pancreas?
questions.explanation: The body and tail of the pancreas receive arterial supply from the splenic artery through numerous small pancreatic branches (dorsal pancreatic, greater pancreatic, caudal pancreatic arteries) as the splenic artery courses along the superior border of the pancreas. The head of the pancreas is supplied by the superior and inferior pancreaticoduodenal arteries forming anterior and posterior arcades. The pancreas has a rich blood supply with extensive anastomoses, though the pancreatic neck region may be relatively less vascular. The intimate relationship between the splenic artery and pancreas means that pancreatic pathology can affect the artery.

The posterior interosseous nerve (deep branch of radial nerve) passes between the two heads of the supinator muscle. Compression at this site causes posterior interosseous syndrome with weakness of finger and thumb extensors but preserved wrist extension. The superficial branch of the radial nerve does not pass through supinator.
questions.question: What nerve passes through the supinator muscle?
What is the functional relationship between wrist flexors and extensors in grip?
questions.explanation: During grip, wrist extensors isometrically contract to stabilize the wrist in slight extension. This prevents wrist flexion as finger flexors contract, optimizing finger flexor length-tension relationship for maximum grip force. This synergistic stabilization demonstrates functional muscle interaction.
options: Wrist extensors stabilize wrist enabling grip strength

questions.question: From which vessel do inferior phrenic arteries arise?
questions.explanation: The inferior phrenic arteries are the first branches of the abdominal aorta and supply the inferior surface of the diaphragm. The right inferior phrenic artery gives off the suprarenal artery. These arteries are important in collateral circulation and can be a source of bleeding in trauma.

options: It originates from the rim of the acetabulum
It is supplied exclusively by the obturator nerve
Does not cross the hip joint; supplied by the common fibular nerve
It inserts into the medial tibial condyle distally
It is classified as a medial compartment muscle
questions.explanation: The short head of biceps femoris does not cross the hip joint (originating from the linea aspera, not the ischial tuberosity) and therefore cannot extend the hip. It is supplied by the common fibular division of the sciatic nerve, unlike all other hamstrings which are supplied by the tibial division. It only flexes the knee and laterally rotates the leg when the knee is flexed.
questions.question: The short head of biceps femoris differs from the other hamstrings in which critical way?

options: Sural nerve and posterior cutaneous nerve of thigh
Tibial nerve and common fibular nerve
questions.question: The sciatic nerve is the largest nerve in the body. At the level of the popliteal fossa, it divides into which two terminal branches?
questions.explanation: The sciatic nerve divides at the superior angle of the popliteal fossa (or sometimes higher in the thigh or even within the pelvis) into the tibial nerve (medial and larger) and the common fibular nerve (lateral and smaller). The tibial nerve innervates the posterior compartment of the leg and intrinsic muscles of the sole, while the common fibular nerve innervates the anterior and lateral leg compartments.

questions.question: Which structure separates the thenar and midpalmar spaces of the hand?
questions.explanation: The medial palmar septum joins the border of the palmar aponeurosis to the palmar border of the third metacarpal bone. This septum separates the thenar space (thumb side) from the midpalmar space (ulnar side). Each space contains specific flexor tendons and lumbrical muscles.

questions.question: From which artery does the proper hepatic artery arise?
questions.explanation: The proper hepatic artery arises from the common hepatic artery, which is a branch of the celiac trunk. The common hepatic artery divides into the proper hepatic artery and the gastroduodenal artery. The proper hepatic artery then divides into right and left hepatic arteries that supply the corresponding lobes of the liver.

questions.question: Which ligament extends from the lesser curvature to the liver?
questions.explanation: The lesser omentum extends from the lesser curvature of the stomach to the liver and consists of the hepatogastric and hepatoduodenal ligaments. The hepatogastric portion specifically connects the lesser curvature to the liver. This double layer of peritoneum carries the left and right gastric vessels along the lesser curvature.

The hepatic portal vein forms behind the neck of the pancreas at approximately the L1/L2 vertebral level through the confluence of the superior mesenteric and splenic veins, anterior to the inferior vena cava. The inferior mesenteric vein typically joins the splenic vein before this confluence, though variations exist. From its formation, the portal vein ascends obliquely to the right within the hepatoduodenal ligament (free edge of lesser omentum) to reach the porta hepatis, where it divides into right and left branches. It measures approximately 8 cm in length and lacks valves.
questions.question: The hepatic portal vein is formed at which vertebral level?

questions.explanation: All the abdominal wall muscles work together to increase intra-abdominal pressure: the diaphragm contracts and descends, while the rectus abdominis, external oblique, internal oblique, and transversus abdominis contract simultaneously to compress the abdominal contents. This coordinated action is essential for defecation, micturition, parturition (childbirth), coughing, sneezing, and vomiting. The transversus abdominis is particularly important for this function. Weakness of abdominal wall muscles (from aging, pregnancy, or surgery) can impair these functions and predispose to hernias.
questions.question: Which muscle assists in raising intra-abdominal pressure?

questions.explanation: The thoracic duct terminates by draining into the left venous angle (junction of left internal jugular and left subclavian veins). Before termination, it receives the left jugular, subclavian, and bronchomediastinal lymph trunks. The duct has no valve at its termination.
questions.question: Where does the thoracic duct terminate?

questions.explanation: The pterygopalatine ganglion hangs from the maxillary nerve (V2) by two pterygopalatine (sensory) branches in the pterygopalatine fossa. Parasympathetic fibers arrive via the nerve of the pterygoid canal (greater petrosal + deep petrosal). Postganglionic fibers supply the lacrimal gland and nasal/palatine mucosa. Sympathetic fibers pass through without synapsing.
questions.question: The pterygopalatine ganglion is suspended from which nerve?
What structure passes through the foramen cecum in adults?
questions.explanation: In only 1% of adults, a nasal emissary vein passes through the foramen cecum connecting nasal veins with the superior sagittal sinus. In most adults, the foramen is obliterated. In the fetus, this foramen transmitted the anterior extension of the developing superior sagittal sinus.

questions.question: The sustentaculum tali is a medial shelf of the calcaneus that supports the head of the talus and carries the groove for which tendon?
questions.explanation: The sustentaculum tali is a medial shelf of the calcaneus that supports the head of the talus and carries the groove for the flexor hallucis longus tendon on its inferior surface. It also receives the insertion of the tibialis posterior tendon and serves as the attachment for the spring ligament (plantar calcaneonavicular ligament) and the deltoid ligament medially.

The internal urethral sphincter is composed of smooth muscle (a thickening of the detrusor muscle at the bladder neck) and is under involuntary autonomic control. It is controlled by sympathetic innervation (hypogastric nerves), which causes contraction to maintain continence and prevent retrograde ejaculation in males. It relaxes during micturition under parasympathetic control.
questions.question: What is the internal urethral sphincter composed of?
Which epithelium lines the anal canal above the pectinate line?
questions.explanation: Above the pectinate (dentate) line, the anal canal is lined by simple columnar epithelium (rectal-type mucosa) forming the columns of Morgagni. Below the pectinate line, it transitions to stratified squamous non-keratinized epithelium (in the intermediate zone) and then stratified squamous keratinized epithelium (in the cutaneous zone). The pectinate line marks the junction of endoderm and ectoderm.

questions.question: Fibularis longus crosses the sole diagonally after turning medially in a groove on which bone, ultimately inserting into the base of the 1st metatarsal and medial cuneiform?
questions.explanation: After descending in the lateral compartment and passing behind the lateral malleolus, fibularis longus turns medially in a groove on the plantar surface of the cuboid, crossing the sole diagonally to insert into the base of the 1st metatarsal and medial cuneiform. This unique oblique course allows it to support the transverse arch of the foot.

questions.question: Which rib does the costal pleural reflection cross midaxillarily?
questions.explanation: The costal line of pleural reflection passes obliquely, crossing the tenth rib in the midaxillary line (MAL). It crosses the eighth rib in the midclavicular line and becomes continuous posteriorly with the vertebral lines at the neck of the twelfth rib. This surface marking is crucial for safe thoracentesis.

questions.question: Which structure forms the medial boundary of the carotid triangle?
questions.explanation: The carotid triangle is bounded by the sternocleidomastoid (posterolaterally), superior belly of omohyoid (inferiorly), and posterior belly of digastric (superiorly). The triangle contains the carotid bifurcation, internal jugular vein, vagus nerve, and several other structures. It is a subdivision of the anterior triangle of the neck.

Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune neuromuscular disease characterized by antibodies against acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction. This causes muscle weakness and fatigue that worsens with activity and improves with rest. Common symptoms include ptosis, diplopia, dysphagia, and weakness. Treatment includes anticholinesterases, immunosuppression, and sometimes thymectomy.
questions.question: What is myasthenia gravis?
Which nerve is at risk during clavicle fracture?
questions.explanation: The subclavian vessels and brachial plexus trunks pass behind the medial third of the clavicle, separated only by the subclavius muscle. Fracture of the clavicle, especially displaced fractures, can injure these neurovascular structures. The subclavius muscle provides some protection.
options: Subclavian vessels and brachial plexus trunks

questions.question: Which structure receives blood from both celiac and superior mesenteric arteries?
questions.explanation: The transverse colon has a dual blood supply: the right two-thirds from the middle colic branch of the superior mesenteric artery (midgut supply) and the left third from the left colic branch of the inferior mesenteric artery (hindgut supply). The junction between these territories forms the marginal artery (of Drummond) and represents the watershed area most vulnerable to ischemia.

questions.question: At which vertebral level does the inferior vena cava pierce the diaphragm?
questions.explanation: The inferior vena cava passes through the caval opening (foramen venae cavae) in the central tendon of the diaphragm at the T8 vertebral level, the highest of the three major diaphragmatic openings. This opening also transmits branches of the right phrenic nerve. The esophageal hiatus (T10 level) transmits the esophagus and vagal trunks, while the aortic hiatus (T12 level) transmits the aorta, thoracic duct, and azygos vein. The IVC opening dilates during inspiration as the diaphragm contracts and descends, facilitating venous return to the heart.

questions.question: What shape is the central tendon?
questions.explanation: The central tendon of the diaphragm is shaped like three leaves (trifoliate). It has no bony attachments but is partially fused with the inferior surface of the fibrous pericardium. All the muscular fibers of the diaphragm insert into this central tendon.

questions.question: Which segment is most dependent when supine?
questions.explanation: The superior (apical) segment of the lower lobe is the most dependent position in the supine position. This explains why abscess formation is more common in this segment and in the posterior segment of the upper lobe, as secretions pool in dependent areas during recumbency.

questions.question: Which nerve roots form the phrenic nerve?
questions.explanation: The phrenic nerve is formed from cervical nerve roots C3, C4, and C5 ("C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive"). It provides the entire motor supply to the diaphragm. The long course from neck to diaphragm reflects the embryological migration of the diaphragm from the cervical region.

Beck's triad comprises three clinical signs of cardiac tamponade: (1) hypotension (due to reduced cardiac output), (2) elevated jugular venous pressure/JVP (due to impaired venous return), and (3) muffled/distant heart sounds (due to fluid surrounding the heart). Pulsus paradoxus (excessive decrease in systolic BP during inspiration) is another important sign.
questions.question: What are Beck's triad signs?
How do the thenar and hypothenar muscles differ functionally?
questions.explanation: Thenar muscles provide thumb mobility essential for opposition and precision grip. Hypothenar muscles provide little finger mobility and contribute to power grip by cupping the hand. The specialized thumb movements made possible by thenar muscles are uniquely human characteristics.
options: Thenar for thumb mobility/opposition, hypothenar for little finger mobility
Thenar for power, hypothenar for precision
Thenar for extension, hypothenar for flexion

questions.question: What is the primary action of brachioradialis?
questions.explanation: Brachioradialis is primarily a flexor of the forearm, most effective when the forearm is in mid-pronation position. It also assists with both pronation from supinated position and supination from pronated position, returning the forearm to neutral. The muscle is supplied by the radial nerve despite being an anterior compartment muscle.

questions.question: Which artery supplies the thyroid gland inferiorly?
questions.explanation: The inferior thyroid artery arises from the thyrocervical trunk (a branch of the subclavian artery) and ascends to supply the lower poles of the thyroid gland. The recurrent laryngeal nerve has an intimate relationship with this artery, passing either anterior or posterior to it. The superior thyroid artery supplies the upper poles.

questions.question: How many segments are in right lower lobe?
questions.explanation: The right lower lobe contains five bronchopulmonary segments: superior (apical), medial basal, anterior basal, lateral basal, and posterior basal. The superior segment is also called the apical segment of the lower lobe and is the most dependent segment when lying supine.

The round ligament of the liver (ligamentum teres hepatis) represents the obliterated left umbilical vein, which carried oxygenated blood from the placenta to the fetus. It runs from the umbilicus to the liver within the free inferior margin of the falciform ligament, then continues in a fissure on the visceral surface between the left and quadrate lobes before joining the left branch of the portal vein. In portal hypertension, paraumbilical veins accompanying the ligamentum teres may recanalize, creating a portosystemic anastomosis that can produce caput medusae (dilated superficial veins radiating from the umbilicus). The obliterated ductus venosus forms the ligamentum venosum.
questions.question: Which structure does the round ligament of the liver represent?

questions.explanation: The medial arcuate ligament is a thickening of the fascia covering the anterior surface of psoas major muscle. It extends from the side of the body of L2 vertebra to the tip of the transverse process of L1. The lateral arcuate ligament overlies quadratus lumborum muscle.
questions.question: What does the medial arcuate ligament overlie?

questions.explanation: results from compression of the median nerve within the carpal tunnel. This causes sensory disturbances in the lateral three and one-half fingers (palmer aspect) and weakness of thenar muscles. The condition commonly occurs from inflammatory reactions in flexor tendon synovial sheaths or space-occupying lesions.
questions.question: What condition results from median nerve compression in the carpal tunnel?

questions.explanation: Lateral cord injury paralyzes muscles supplied by the musculocutaneous nerve (biceps, coracobrachialis, brachialis) and muscles supplied by the median nerve except those in the hand. This results from damage to both the musculocutaneous nerve and lateral root of median nerve. Wrist and finger flexion is lost along with forearm flexion.
questions.question: Which muscles are paralyzed in injury to the lateral cord of the brachial plexus?
options: Biceps, coracobrachialis, and forearm median muscles

questions.question: What is the weakest part of the clavicle?
questions.explanation: The junction of the middle and outer third of the clavicle is the weakest point. Most clavicular fractures occur at this location from indirect forces transmitted through the limb during falls. The medial fragment is typically displaced superiorly by sternocleidomastoid while the lateral fragment is displaced inferiorly by arm weight.

questions.question: Which structures form the boundaries of the cervicoaxillary canal (apex of axilla)?
options: First rib, clavicle, and superior scapular border
questions.explanation: The apex of the axilla forms the cervicoaxillary canal, providing passage between the neck and axilla. It is bounded by the first rib medially, the clavicle anteriorly, and the superior border of the scapula posteriorly. Arteries, veins, lymphatics, and nerves traverse this opening to reach or leave the upper limb.

questions.question: What is the only electrical connection between atria and ventricles?
questions.explanation: The bundle of His (AV bundle) is the only normal electrical connection between the atria and ventricles, as the fibrous skeleton of the heart electrically insulates these chambers. It arises from the AV node, penetrates the fibrous skeleton, and divides into right and left bundle branches in the interventricular septum. Accessory pathways (e.g., WPW syndrome) can create additional abnormal connections.

The lateral femoral circumflex artery (LFCA) and its descending branch provide the vascular pedicle for the anterolateral thigh (ALT) free flap, one of the most commonly used free flaps in reconstructive surgery. The ALT flap is based on septocutaneous or musculocutaneous perforators from the descending branch of the LFCA, running in the intermuscular septum between vastus lateralis and rectus femoris.
questions.question: The lateral femoral circumflex artery (LFCA) is important as a source vessel for which reconstructive flap frequently used in plastic surgery?
The hilum of the spleen faces which direction?
questions.explanation: The hilum of the spleen faces anteromedially toward the stomach, receiving the splenic artery (which divides into 5-6 branches before entering) and giving exit to the splenic vein. The gastrosplenic ligament connects the hilum to the greater curvature of the stomach and contains the short gastric and left gastroepiploic vessels. The splenorenal ligament connects the hilum to the left kidney and contains the splenic vessels and tail of the pancreas. The splenic hilum typically shows a distinct notch (splenic notch) on its superior border, a characteristic feature visible on cross-sectional imaging.

The lateral wall of the ischiorectal (ischioanal) fossa is formed by the obturator internus muscle covered by obturator fascia, which contains the pudendal canal (Alcock's canal) housing the pudendal nerve and internal pudendal vessels. The medial wall is formed by the levator ani and external anal sphincter. The fossa is bounded posteriorly by the gluteus maximus and sacrotuberous ligament, anteriorly by the posterior border of the urogenital diaphragm, and inferiorly by skin. The fossa contains fat and is a potential space for abscess formation.
questions.question: Which muscle forms the lateral wall of the ischiorectal fossa?
Which ligament connects the spleen to the greater curvature?
questions.explanation: The gastrosplenic (gastrolienal) ligament extends from the hilum of the spleen to the greater curvature of the stomach. It is part of the greater omentum and contains the short gastric vessels and left gastroepiploic vessels. This ligament provides vascular connections between the spleen and stomach.

The pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2-S4) carry preganglionic parasympathetic fibers that synapse in terminal ganglia within or very near the walls of the pelvic organs they supply (bladder, rectum, reproductive organs). This is characteristic of parasympathetic innervation, where the preganglionic fibers are long and synapse close to or within the target organ, while postganglionic fibers are very short. The fibers travel via the inferior hypogastric plexus to reach their destinations but do not synapse there. The pelvic splanchnics also provide parasympathetic innervation to the distal hindgut from the splenic flexure to the upper anal canal.
questions.question: The pelvic splanchnic nerves synapse in which location?
The appendicular lymph nodes drain into which nodal group?
questions.explanation: Lymphatic drainage from the appendix passes through lymph nodes in the mesoappendix to the ileocolic lymph nodes along the ileocolic artery, which subsequently drain to superior mesenteric lymph nodes along the superior mesenteric artery. From there, lymph flows to the pre-aortic nodes and eventually to the cisterna chyli and thoracic duct. This drainage pattern follows the arterial supply (appendicular artery from ileocolic artery from SMA). Enlarged ileocolic nodes may be palpable in appendicitis and can contribute to diagnostic imaging findings in acute abdominal conditions.

questions.question: What are Rotter's nodes?
questions.explanation: Rotter's nodes (interpectoral nodes) lie between the pectoralis major and minor muscles. They are part of the axillary lymphatic drainage pathway. During modified radical mastectomy, these nodes may be removed along with the pectoral fascia. Their involvement affects staging and prognosis.

questions.question: Which segment of colon has the largest diameter?
questions.explanation: The cecum is the widest part of the large intestine (approximately 7.5 cm in diameter), and the diameter gradually decreases toward the sigmoid colon. This variation in diameter is clinically significant in colonic obstruction: according to Laplace's law, the cecum is most likely to perforate in cases of distal large bowel obstruction due to its larger diameter and thinner wall.

questions.question: The rectouterine pouch (of Douglas) lies between which structures?
questions.explanation: The rectouterine pouch (pouch of Douglas, cul-de-sac) is the peritoneal reflection between the uterus anteriorly and the rectum posteriorly, representing the most inferior extent of the peritoneal cavity in females (approximately 5.5 cm from the anus and 7.5 cm from the vaginal orifice). It is bounded laterally by the uterosacral ligaments and can be accessed through the posterior vaginal fornix for drainage of pelvic abscesses (culdocentesis) or laparoscopic procedures. Fluid, blood, or pus in the peritoneal cavity gravitates to this pouch in supine or standing positions, making it clinically significant.

questions.question: What comprises the central tendon of the diaphragm?
questions.explanation: The central tendon is a strong aponeurosis of dense fibrous tissue forming the central portion of the diaphragm. It is trifoliate (three-leafed) in shape, resembling a clover leaf. The heart rests on its superior surface within the pericardium. The caval opening pierces the central tendon at the junction of the right leaflet with the middle leaflet.

questions.question: The marginal artery of Drummond connects which two arterial systems?
questions.explanation: The marginal artery of Drummond (marginal artery of the colon) is a continuous arterial arcade running along the mesenteric border of the colon, connecting the superior mesenteric and inferior mesenteric arterial territories. It is formed by anastomoses between the ileocolic, right colic, middle colic, left colic, and sigmoid arteries. This vessel provides crucial collateral circulation to the colon and is particularly important at the splenic flexure, where the superior and inferior mesenteric arterial distributions meet. The weakest point in this anastomotic chain occurs at Griffiths' point (splenic flexure) and Sudeck's point (rectosigmoid junction).

questions.question: Into which vein does the right inferior phrenic vein drain?
questions.explanation: The right inferior phrenic vein usually drains directly into the inferior vena cava. The left inferior phrenic vein is usually double, with one branch draining into the IVC and the other frequently joining the left suprarenal vein, which then drains into the left renal vein. These veins drain blood from the inferior surface of the diaphragm.

The tricuspid valve has three cusps: anterior (largest), posterior (smallest), and septal. These cusps are attached to a fibrous ring (annulus) and prevented from prolapsing into the atrium by chordae tendineae connecting to papillary muscles. The valve prevents backflow from the right ventricle to the right atrium during ventricular systole.
questions.question: How many cusps compose the tricuspid valve?

questions.explanation: The middle colic artery (from the superior mesenteric artery) and middle colic veins (to superior mesenteric vein) pass through the transverse mesocolon to supply the transverse colon. The root of the transverse mesocolon attaches to the inferior border of the pancreas and crosses the descending duodenum, serving as an important surgical landmark dividing the peritoneal cavity into supracolic and infracolic compartments. The superior mesenteric vessels lie posterior to the transverse mesocolon, while the inferior mesenteric vessels lie posterior to the peritoneum, not within the mesocolon itself.
questions.question: Which structure passes through the transverse mesocolon?

questions.explanation: The female external urethral orifice opens into the vestibule, the space between the labia minora, approximately 2.5 cm posterior to the clitoris and immediately anterior to the vaginal opening. The orifice is surrounded by the external urethral sphincter and may be difficult to visualize in some women. Paraurethral (Skene's) glands open on either side of the orifice.
questions.question: Where does the female urethra open externally?

questions.explanation: The transverse acetabular ligament bridges across the acetabular notch, converting it into a foramen for vessels and nerves, and serves as the base of attachment for the ligament of the head of femur (ligamentum teres). The acetabular labrum is a fibrocartilaginous rim attached to the margin of the acetabulum that deepens it.
questions.question: The transverse acetabular ligament converts the acetabular notch into a foramen. It also serves as the base of attachment for which intracapsular ligament?
Which left upper lobe segments are fused?
questions.explanation: In the left upper lobe, the apical and posterior segments typically fuse to form a single apicoposterior segment. The left upper lobe therefore typically contains: apicoposterior, anterior, superior lingular, and inferior lingular segments. This fusion accounts for the lower total segment count.

questions.question: How do intrinsic and extrinsic hand muscles work together?
options: Extrinsic for power grip, intrinsic for precision
questions.explanation: Extrinsic hand muscles (arising in forearm) provide power for grip and basic finger movements. Intrinsic hand muscles (arising in hand) provide precision movements, finger positioning, and the unique lumbrical action (MCP flexion with IP extension). This combination enables both powerful and precise hand function.

questions.question: What produces scapular depression?
questions.explanation: Depression of the scapula is produced by lower fibers of trapezius and pectoralis minor muscles. This movement lowers the shoulder and is opposite to elevation. It occurs when lowering the arm from an elevated position or during downward reaching.

questions.question: The genitofemoral nerve pierces which muscle?
questions.explanation: The genitofemoral nerve (L1, L2) emerges through the anterior surface of the psoas major muscle at approximately the L3/L4 level, unlike other branches of the lumbar plexus which emerge from its lateral border. After piercing psoas, it descends on the muscle's anterior surface, dividing into genital and femoral branches. The genital branch enters the deep inguinal ring to supply the cremaster muscle and scrotal/labial skin, while the femoral branch passes beneath the inguinal ligament lateral to the femoral artery to supply skin over the femoral triangle.

questions.question: Why is the left recurrent laryngeal nerve longer?
questions.explanation: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve is longer than the right because of the embryological descent of the heart and great vessels. As the heart descends from the neck into the thorax, it carries the aortic arch (and the nerve looping under it) downward. The right subclavian artery descends less, so the right nerve is shorter.

questions.question: How many fascicles does the left bundle branch divide into?
questions.explanation: The left bundle branch divides into two main fascicles: anterior and posterior (some describe a third, septal fascicle). The anterior fascicle supplies the anterior and lateral left ventricular wall; the posterior fascicle supplies the posterior and inferior wall. Left bundle branch block or fascicular blocks (hemiblocks) cause characteristic ECG patterns and may indicate underlying cardiac disease.

questions.question: Which lymph nodes are the final common drainage for the stomach?
questions.explanation: All lymph from the stomach eventually drains to the celiac lymph nodes located around the celiac trunk on the posterior abdominal wall. The lymphatic drainage follows the arterial supply: left and right gastric nodes drain to celiac nodes, as do the gastroepiploic and short gastric nodes (via pancreaticosplenic nodes). This lymphatic pathway is important in gastric cancer staging and spread.

questions.question: Tibialis posterior and fibularis longus are described as important stabilizers at the ankle. Which action does tibialis posterior perform at the ankle?
questions.explanation: Tibialis posterior plantarflexes the ankle and inverts the foot. It is innervated by the tibial nerve (L4, L5) and inserts into the tuberosity of the navicular and multiple other tarsal and metatarsal bones. It is also the primary dynamic maintainer of the medial longitudinal arch. Its rupture leads to progressive flat foot and valgus deformity at the ankle.
options: Eversion and abduction of the foot

questions.question: What nerve root is predominantly tested by the triceps reflex?
questions.explanation: The triceps reflex predominantly tests the C7 nerve root. The reflex is elicited by tapping the triceps tendon just above the olecranon. Absence or diminution suggests C7 nerve root or radial nerve pathology.

The appendix drains to ileocolic lymph nodes located along the ileocolic artery, which then drain to superior mesenteric nodes. Appendiceal lymphoid tissue is abundant, earning it the nickname "intestinal tonsil." In appendicitis, lymph nodes may become enlarged and palpable. Metastatic disease from appendiceal tumors follows this lymphatic drainage pattern.
questions.question: Which lymph nodes drain the appendix?
Which muscle elevates the hyoid bone and pharynx during swallowing?
questions.explanation: The stylopharyngeus muscle elevates the pharynx and hyoid bone during swallowing, supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve. The infrahyoid muscles (sternohyoid, sternothyroid, thyrohyoid, omohyoid) depress the hyoid. Longitudinal pharyngeal muscles collectively raise the pharynx to engulf the food bolus.

The thyroid cartilage is shield-shaped with two laminae meeting in the midline to form the laryngeal prominence (Adam's apple). This prominence is more acute and prominent in males. The thyroid cartilage protects the vocal cords and provides anterior attachment for the vocal ligaments.
questions.question: Which cartilage forms the Adam's apple (laryngeal prominence)?

questions.explanation: The aortic hiatus, located at the T12 vertebral level between the two crura of the diaphragm (posterior to the median arcuate ligament), transmits the aorta, thoracic duct, and azygos vein (and sometimes hemiazygos vein). The esophagus and vagal trunks pass through the esophageal hiatus at T10, while the inferior vena cava traverses the caval opening in the central tendon at T8. The aortic hiatus is actually a midline gap between the crura rather than a true opening in the diaphragm, which means structures passing through it are not constricted during diaphragmatic contraction.
questions.question: The aortic hiatus transmits which structures besides the aorta?

options: Medial sural cutaneous nerve and sural communicating branch of common fibular nerve; lateral side of leg and ankle
Medial sural cutaneous nerve (from tibial nerve) and lateral sural cutaneous nerve (from common fibular nerve); lateral side of leg, ankle, and foot
Saphenous nerve and medial sural cutaneous nerve; medial leg and foot
Both sural nerves from tibial nerve; posterior leg entirely
Posterior cutaneous nerve of thigh and medial sural cutaneous nerve; posterior thigh and leg
questions.explanation: The sural nerve is formed by the union of the medial sural cutaneous nerve (from the tibial nerve in the popliteal fossa) and the sural communicating branch of the common fibular nerve. It supplies the skin of the lateral side of the leg, ankle, and lateral heel. The sural nerve is commonly harvested as a nerve graft in peripheral nerve reconstruction surgery.
questions.question: The sural nerve is formed by the union of which two nerves and supplies which area of the lower limb?
The lingual tonsil is located on which surface of the tongue?
questions.explanation: The lingual tonsil is lymphoid tissue on the posterior third (dorsal surface) of the tongue behind the sulcus terminalis. It forms part of Waldeyer's ring with the palatine and pharyngeal tonsils. The lingual tonsil is covered by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium with crypts. Hypertrophy can cause airway obstruction or dysphagia.

questions.question: Which nerve passes through the quadrangular space?
questions.explanation: The axillary nerve passes through the quadrangular space accompanied by the posterior circumflex humeral vessels. The space is bounded by teres minor superiorly, teres major inferiorly, long head of triceps medially, and surgical neck of humerus laterally. Injury can occur with shoulder trauma or humeral neck fractures.

Metatarsal stress fractures (March fractures) most commonly affect the second metatarsal in soldiers, runners, and military recruits after unaccustomed prolonged walking or running. The second metatarsal is the most stable midfoot ray (most protected by its surrounded cuneiforms) but is subjected to repetitive bending forces. They typically present with pain in the forefoot that worsens with activity and is relieved by rest.
questions.question: Stress fractures of the metatarsals (March fractures) most commonly affect which metatarsal in soldiers and long-distance runners?
Which vessels supply the superior diaphragmatic surface?
questions.explanation: The superior surface of the diaphragm is supplied by pericardiacophrenic and musculophrenic arteries (branches of the internal thoracic artery) and the superior phrenic arteries (from the thoracic aorta). The pericardiacophrenic artery accompanies the phrenic nerve. The musculophrenic artery is a terminal branch of the internal thoracic artery.

questions.question: What percentage of body weight does the adult heart represent?
questions.explanation: The adult heart weighs approximately 250-350 grams, representing about 0.5% of total body weight (roughly 1/200th of body weight). The heart size is often compared to a closed fist. The male heart is typically slightly larger and heavier than the female heart, correlating with body size differences.

questions.question: Which nerve supplies latissimus dorsi?
questions.explanation: The thoracodorsal nerve (C7, C8) from the posterior cord supplies latissimus dorsi muscle. The nerve descends along the posterior axillary wall with the thoracodorsal artery. Preservation of this nerve is important during axillary surgery to maintain shoulder function.

questions.question: Which cartilage lies in the aryepiglottic fold?
questions.explanation: The cuneiform cartilages (cartilages of Wrisberg) are small rod-shaped elastic cartilages lying in the aryepiglottic folds anterior to the corniculate cartilages. They produce small elevations on the mucosal surface visible during laryngoscopy. The cartilages strengthen the aryepiglottic folds. Some individuals may lack these cartilages.

The Achilles (calcaneal) tendon inserts into the posterior surface of the calcaneus via the calcaneal tuberosity. The gastrocnemius, soleus, and plantaris muscles all contribute to the calcaneal tendon. The calcaneal tendon is the strongest tendon in the body but is frequently ruptured in sudden powerful plantarflexion, such as in a jump landing. Bursae lie posterior and anterior to the tendon.
questions.question: The calcaneus is the largest and strongest bone of the foot and its primary function is to absorb shock and leverage movement. Where is the Achilles tendon inserted on the calcaneus?
The dorsalis pedis artery is the continuation of the anterior tibial artery on the dorsum of the foot. It anastomoses with the lateral plantar artery to form which arch?
questions.explanation: The dorsalis pedis artery passes over the dorsal tarsal bones and then moves inferiorly toward the sole, anastomosing with the lateral plantar artery to form the deep plantar arch. Via this arch, it contributes to the supply of the toes. The dorsal venous arch lies in the subcutaneous tissue over the heads of the metatarsal bones.

There is little anastomosis between the arteries (branches of pulmonary artery) supplying adjacent bronchopulmonary segments. This anatomical feature allows individual segments to be surgically resected without significantly affecting neighboring segments. Each segment functions as an independent unit.
questions.question: What is unique about segmental blood supply?
How does wrist position affect grip strength?
questions.explanation: Maximum grip strength occurs with the wrist in 20-30� extension. This position optimally lengthens finger flexors for maximum tension development while stabilizing the wrist. Full flexion or extension reduces grip strength due to passive insufficiency or active insufficiency of finger flexors.
options: Wrist position does not affect grip strength
Strongest grip in full wrist flexion
Grip strongest with wrist in slight extension
Strongest grip in full wrist extension
Strongest grip in neutral wrist position

questions.explanation: The axillary nerve is at risk in anterior shoulder dislocation due to its course around the surgical neck of the humerus. The nerve can be stretched or damaged when the humeral head displaces anteriorly. This results in deltoid paralysis and sensory loss over the regimental badge area.
questions.question: What nerve is at risk in anterior shoulder dislocation?
Where does the right bundle branch travel?
questions.explanation: The right bundle branch descends in the interventricular septum and crosses to the right ventricular free wall via the moderator band (septomarginal trabecula) to reach the anterior papillary muscle. From there, it divides into Purkinje fibers that spread throughout the right ventricle. This pathway ensures coordinated right ventricular contraction and explains why the moderator band is functionally important.

questions.question: What is clinical significance of esophageal venous drainage?
questions.explanation: The esophageal veins form an important portosystemic anastomosis where portal venous blood (from lower esophagus draining to left gastric vein) connects with systemic venous blood (middle and upper esophagus draining to azygos system and brachiocephalic veins). In portal hypertension, these veins dilate to form esophageal varices which can rupture.

questions.question: How many leaves does the central tendon of the diaphragm have?
questions.explanation: The central tendon is trifoliate (three-leafed), resembling a clover leaf with right, left, and middle (anterior) leaflets. The right leaflet is the largest. The caval opening pierces the central tendon at the junction of the right and middle leaflets. The heart in its pericardium rests on the superior surface of the central tendon.

questions.question: What is the stellate ganglion?
questions.explanation: The stellate ganglion is formed by fusion of the inferior cervical ganglion with the first thoracic ganglion. It lies anterior to the neck of the first rib. Stellate ganglion block (local anesthetic injection) can provide sympathetic blockade for upper limb pain or vascular conditions. Damage causes Horner's syndrome.

Inversion sprains of the ankle most commonly damage the anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL) first, as it is the weakest of the three lateral ankle ligaments. The ATFL runs from the anterior aspect of the lateral malleolus to the lateral surface of the talus and is taut in plantarflexion, the position in which inversion sprains typically occur. With more severe inversion, the CFL is next to be torn.
questions.question: Inversion sprains of the ankle most commonly damage which ligament first?

questions.explanation: The left suprarenal vein drains into the left renal vein (along with the left testicular/ovarian and left inferior phrenic veins), while the right suprarenal vein drains directly into the inferior vena cava. This asymmetric venous drainage mirrors that of the testicular/ovarian veins. The suprarenal glands have a rich arterial supply from three sources (superior, middle, and inferior suprarenal arteries from the inferior phrenic artery, abdominal aorta, and renal artery respectively) but typically have only a single venous drainage pathway, creating a high arterial-to-venous ratio favoring hormone secretion.
questions.question: Which vein drains the left suprarenal gland?

questions.explanation: Afferent (sensory) nerve fibers from the kidneys travel with sympathetic nerves and enter the spinal cord at T10-T12 and L1 segments. This explains the referred pain pattern of renal colic, which radiates from the loin to the groin along the distribution of these dermatomes. Ureteric pain follows a similar pattern as the ureter shares this innervation.
questions.question: Which spinal segments provide afferent innervation from the kidney?

questions.explanation: The superior mesenteric vessels (artery and vein) form a groove on the posterior aspect of the pancreatic neck as they pass behind it. The neck is the constricted portion connecting the head to the body. Anteriorly, the neck is related to the pylorus of the stomach.
questions.question: Which vessels form a groove on the posterior aspect of the pancreatic neck?
Which muscle crosses the sole diagonally in a groove on the cuboid, and in so doing provides the most important muscular support for the transverse arch?
questions.explanation: Fibularis longus crosses the sole of the foot diagonally in a groove on the plantar surface of the cuboid, inserting into the base of the first metatarsal and medial cuneiform. This diagonal course provides critical support to the transverse arch by pulling the first metatarsal medially and maintaining the dome of the transverse arch. It is the most important muscular support for this arch.

questions.question: What is the functional significance of the mobile 4th and 5th metacarpals?
options: Allow cupping of hand for power grip
questions.explanation: The mobile 4th and 5th metacarpals (articulating with hamate) allow palmar cupping for power grip. This adaptation enables the hand to conform to cylindrical objects. The 2nd and 3rd metacarpals are relatively fixed, providing a stable platform for precision grip.

The common carotid artery typically bifurcates at the level of C4, corresponding to the upper border of the thyroid cartilage. The carotid sinus (baroreceptor) and carotid body (chemoreceptor) are located at this bifurcation. Carotid endarterectomy is performed at this crucial anatomical location.
questions.question: At which vertebral level does the common carotid artery typically bifurcate?

options: Hip 90�, knee 90�, posterior force applied to the proximal tibia
Hip at 45 degrees flexion, knee in extension
Hip flexed, knee extended, valgus stress applied
Patient prone on table with knee extended passively
Patient standing while performing a single-leg squat
questions.question: The posterior cruciate ligament prevents anterior displacement of the femur on the tibia. Clinically, PCL injury causes a positive posterior drawer test. In what clinical position is this test performed?
questions.explanation: The posterior drawer test for PCL integrity is performed with the patient supine, the hip at 90 degrees and the knee at 90 degrees. A posterior force is applied to the proximal tibia. Excessive posterior translation indicates PCL rupture. The starting position is important: if the tibia is already posteriorly sagged (posterior sag sign), an apparent positive anterior drawer sign may mimic ACL injury.

The buccopharyngeal fascia is a thin layer covering the buccinator muscle and pharyngeal constrictor muscles externally. It is continuous anteriorly over the buccinator and posteriorly over the constrictors. The retropharyngeal space lies between this fascia and the prevertebral fascia. The fascia blends with the pterygomandibular raphe.
questions.question: The buccopharyngeal fascia covers which structure?
Which muscle flexes the elbow when the forearm is pronated?
