questions.explanation: The medial umbilical fold is created by the peritoneum covering the medial umbilical ligament, which represents the obliterated umbilical artery. There are paired medial umbilical folds (one on each side), in contrast to the single median umbilical fold in the midline formed by the urachus remnant (median umbilical ligament). Between the median and medial folds lies the supravesical fossa, while the medial inguinal fossa (site of direct inguinal hernias) lies between the medial and lateral umbilical folds, the latter being raised by the inferior epigastric vessels.

questions.question: Where in the spleen are blood-borne bacteria primarily filtered?
questions.explanation: Blood-borne bacteria and particulate matter are primarily filtered and phagocytosed by macrophages in the red pulp cords and sinusoids. Blood flowing through the spleen is exposed to numerous macrophages that can recognize and remove opsonized bacteria and foreign particles. This filtering function is lost after splenectomy, increasing infection susceptibility.

questions.question: Which part of the colon lacks taeniae coli?
questions.explanation: The rectum lacks taeniae coli, haustra, and appendices epiploicae, unlike the cecum and colon. At the rectosigmoid junction (approximately 15 cm from the anus, at S3 level), the three taeniae spread out to form a complete outer longitudinal muscle layer encircling the rectum. The rectum can be distinguished from sigmoid colon by this absence of taeniae, its fixed retroperitoneal position, and presence of transverse folds (Houston's valves). The taeniae coli converge at the base of the appendix on the cecum, providing a surgical landmark.

Froment's sign indicates ulnar nerve palsy, demonstrating weakness of adductor pollicis. When attempting to grip paper between thumb and index finger, the patient compensates by flexing the thumb interphalangeal joint (using flexor pollicis longus supplied by median nerve). This flexion indicates inability to adduct the thumb normally.
questions.question: Which nerve is involved in Froment's sign?

questions.explanation: The anterior two-thirds (oral part) of the tongue develops from the first pharyngeal arch (two lateral lingual swellings and median tuberculum impar). The posterior third (pharyngeal part) develops from the third arch (copula). The second arch contribution is overgrown. This embryologic division explains the different nerve supplies.
questions.question: The anterior two-thirds of the tongue develops from which pharyngeal arch?

options: Dorsal cutaneous branch of ulnar nerve
questions.explanation: The superficial branch of the radial nerve supplies sensation to the dorsal aspect of the lateral three and one-half digits and the dorsal hand. The dorsal cutaneous branch of the ulnar nerve supplies the medial side. The posterior interosseous nerve has no cutaneous distribution.
questions.question: Which nerve supplies sensation to the dorsum of the hand?

questions.explanation: The right kidney's anterior surface is related superiorly to the right lobe of the liver (hepatorenal recess), the second part of the duodenum medially, and the right colic flexure and ascending colon inferiorly. Small intestine loops may also contact its anterior surface. The liver creates the largest impression on the right kidney's anterior surface.
questions.question: Which organ lies anterior to the right kidney?
The cochlear aqueduct connects the scala tympani with which space?
questions.explanation: The cochlear aqueduct (perilymphatic duct) connects the scala tympani with the subarachnoid space, allowing communication between perilymph and cerebrospinal fluid. The aqueduct opens at the base of the petrous temporal bone. The vestibular aqueduct separately connects the endolymphatic system with the posterior cranial fossa. Patency varies among individuals.

The pelvic splanchnic nerves (nervi erigentes) arising from S2-S4 spinal segments provide parasympathetic innervation to the bladder. These nerves stimulate detrusor muscle contraction and inhibit the internal urethral sphincter, promoting micturition. Sympathetic innervation from T11-L2 via the hypogastric plexus promotes urine storage by relaxing the detrusor and contracting the internal sphincter.
questions.question: Which nerves provide parasympathetic innervation to the bladder?
The menisci deepen the articular surface and act as which functional structures in the knee joint?
options: Shock absorbers and joint space deepeners
Attachment points for cruciate ligaments only
Blood vessel channels for synovial membrane
Lubricating pads reducing synovial fluid production
questions.explanation: The menisci are crescentic plates of fibrocartilage that deepen the tibial articular surface and act as shock absorbers. They are thicker at external margins and taper toward the center. Meniscal tears are among the most common knee injuries in athletes. The lateral meniscus is more freely movable than the medial meniscus.

options: Median for power, ulnar for precision muscles
Median for thenar precision, ulnar for hypothenar power and intrinsics
questions.explanation: The median nerve supplies thenar muscles enabling precise thumb opposition for precision grip. The ulnar nerve supplies hypothenar muscles, all interossei, and medial lumbricals, providing intrinsic muscle coordination and power grip contribution. Together they enable both precision and power hand functions.
questions.question: What is the functional relationship between median and ulnar nerves in the hand?

questions.explanation: The iliofemoral ligament (ligament of Bigelow) is one of the strongest ligaments in the body, triangular and Y-shaped. Its apex attaches to the anterior inferior iliac spine and its base to the intertrochanteric line. It reinforces the joint anteriorly, prevents overextension while standing, and reduces the muscle energy needed to maintain upright posture.
questions.question: Which Y-shaped hip ligament, described as one of the strongest in the body, has its apex attached to the anterior inferior iliac spine?

questions.explanation: The lumbosacral triangle (Marcille's triangle) has the medial border of psoas major forming its lateral boundary, with the body of L5 vertebra medially and the ala of sacrum as its base. The floor consists of the transverse process of L5 and the iliolumbar ligament. This triangle is clinically significant as the ureter crosses the common iliac vessels at its lateral angle, making it an important landmark during pelvic surgery.
questions.question: Which muscle forms the lateral boundary of the lumbar triangle of Marcille?
What fluid occupies the pericardial cavity?
questions.explanation: The pericardial cavity contains 15-50 ml of serous pericardial fluid, an ultrafiltrate of plasma produced by the serous pericardium. This thin film of fluid acts as a lubricant, allowing the heart to beat with minimal friction between the visceral and parietal layers of serous pericardium. Excess fluid accumulation causes pericardial effusion and potential cardiac tamponade.

questions.question: Which interossei muscles produce finger abduction?
questions.explanation: (four muscles) produce finger abduction, moving fingers away from the middle finger axis. Palmar interossei (three muscles) produce finger adduction toward the middle finger. All interossei are supplied by the ulnar nerve and contribute to metacarpophalangeal joint flexion.

The middle colic artery (from the superior mesenteric artery) passes superiorly into the transverse mesocolon to supply the transverse colon, dividing into right and left branches. The middle colic veins (draining to the superior mesenteric vein) also pass through the mesocolon. The root of the transverse mesocolon is attached to the inferior border of the pancreas and anterior surface of the second part of the duodenum, crossing from right to left. The superior mesenteric vessels themselves lie posterior to the transverse mesocolon, not within it.
questions.question: Which vessel passes through the transverse mesocolon?

questions.explanation: The obturator nerve (L2, L3, L4), formed within the psoas major from the lumbar plexus, emerges from the medial border of the muscle at the pelvic brim. It descends along the lateral wall of the pelvis, passing above the obturator vessels to reach the obturator foramen, through which it exits the pelvis to enter the medial compartment of the thigh. This medial emergence distinguishes it from other lumbar plexus branches (iliohypogastric, ilioinguinal, lateral femoral cutaneous, and femoral nerves) which emerge from the lateral border, except for the genitofemoral nerve which pierces the anterior surface of psoas.
questions.question: The obturator nerve emerges from which border of psoas major?

questions.explanation: The inferior alveolar nerve (a branch of V3) enters the mandibular foramen on the medial surface of the mandibular ramus. It travels in the mandibular canal supplying the lower teeth and emerges at the mental foramen as the mental nerve. The mylohyoid nerve branches before entering the foramen to supply mylohyoid and anterior digastric.
questions.question: The inferior alveolar nerve enters the mandible through which opening?

questions.explanation: The submandibular triangle is bounded superiorly by the body of the mandible, anteroinferiorly by the anterior belly of digastric, and posteroinferiorly by the posterior belly of digastric. The floor is formed by mylohyoid and hyoglossus muscles. The triangle contains the submandibular gland, facial artery and vein, and submandibular lymph nodes.
questions.question: Which muscle forms the lateral boundary of the submandibular triangle?

questions.explanation: The primary ossification centre for the ilium appears at the 2nd month of intrauterine life. The ischium's primary centre appears during the 4th month, and the pubis during the 5th month. At birth, the hip bone is ossified except for the iliac crest, the Y-shaped cartilage, and a strip along the inferior margin.
questions.question: A primary ossification centre for the ilium appears at which gestational period?
Which artery typically supplies the SA node?
questions.explanation: The sinoatrial (SA) nodal artery arises from the right coronary artery in approximately 60% of people and from the left circumflex artery in 40%. The SA node is located in the superior part of the crista terminalis near the junction of the superior vena cava and right atrium. It is the primary pacemaker of the heart, initiating approximately 60-100 beats per minute.

In males, the seminal vesicles and ampullae of the vas deferens lie posterior to the bladder base, and the rectum lies posterior to these structures, separated by the rectovesical fascia (Denonvilliers' fascia). The rectovesical pouch of peritoneum separates the upper part of the bladder from the rectum. In females, the vagina lies directly posterior to the bladder.
questions.question: What lies posterior to the male urinary bladder?

questions.explanation: The nutrient artery, also called the medullary artery, is the main blood supply to the diaphysis of a long bone. It enters through the nutrient canal and nutrient foramen, branching within the medullary cavity. The epiphysis, metaphysis, and periosteum all have their own distinct arterial supplies from separate named vessels.
questions.question: The nutrient artery (medullary artery) is best described as the main artery of which part of a long bone?
Which space infection can spread to lumbrical canals?
questions.explanation: The thenar space can readily spread infection into the connective tissue canals surrounding the lumbricals. Proximally, the thenar space communicates with the space of Parona. Distally, it is continuous with lumbrical canals, which then connect to web spaces, providing routes for infection spread.

questions.question: Which muscle forms the anatomical snuffbox floor?
questions.explanation: The scaphoid and trapezium bones form the floor of the anatomical snuffbox. The boundaries are formed by tendons of abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis laterally, and extensor pollicis longus medially. The radial artery crosses the floor.

The right gastric artery usually arises from the hepatic artery proper near the porta hepatis, though it may occasionally branch from the gastroduodenal or left hepatic artery. It descends to the pylorus, then ascends along the lesser curvature of the stomach within the lesser omentum, anastomosing with the left gastric artery (the smallest but most consistent branch of the celiac trunk). This anastomotic network along the lesser curvature provides collateral circulation and must be carefully ligated during gastric resections to avoid ischemia or bleeding.
questions.question: The right gastric artery typically arises from which vessel?

questions.explanation: Incisions of the breast should be made in a radial direction (from the nipple outward) to avoid cutting through the lactiferous ducts, which are arranged radially from the nipple. Circumferential incisions would transect multiple ducts. Radial incisions also follow Langer's lines for better cosmetic results.
questions.question: How should breast incisions be oriented?

questions.explanation: The anterior belly of the digastric is innervated by the mylohyoid nerve, a branch of the inferior alveolar nerve (V3). The posterior belly is supplied by the facial nerve. This dual innervation reflects the embryologic origin from first and second pharyngeal arches respectively.
questions.question: The anterior belly of the digastric muscle is innervated by which nerve?
Which part of the pancreas is most commonly affected by tumors?
questions.explanation: Pancreatic head tumors are most common (60-70% of pancreatic cancers), followed by body (15-20%) and tail (10-15%). Head tumors often present earlier due to biliary obstruction causing jaundice. Body and tail tumors may grow larger before detection as they don't obstruct the bile duct. The head's proximity to the duodenum and bile duct makes surgical resection (Whipple procedure) more complex.

questions.question: At what vertebral level does the pharynx transition to the esophagus?
questions.explanation: The pharynx extends from the base of the skull to the lower border of the cricoid cartilage at C6, where it becomes continuous with the esophagus. This landmark corresponds to the level where the cricopharyngeus muscle acts as a sphincter. The transition zone is clinically significant for foreign body impaction and surgical access considerations.

The sacrotuberous and sacrospinous ligaments stabilize the sacrum, prevent its rotation under body weight, and form both sciatic foramina together with bones. They do not transmit the obturator nerve, which exits through the obturator foramen to supply the medial compartment of the thigh via its anterior and posterior divisions.
options: Stabilize the sacrum at the sacroiliac joint
Prevent rotation of sacrum by vertebral column weight
Form the greater sciatic foramen with bones
Transmit the obturator nerve to the medial thigh
Form the lesser sciatic foramen with bones
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a function of the sacrotuberous and sacrospinous ligaments?
Which renal artery typically passes posterior to the inferior vena cava?
questions.explanation: The right renal artery is longer than the left and passes posterior to the inferior vena cava to reach the right kidney. The left renal artery has a shorter, more direct course from the aorta to the left kidney. Both arteries arise at approximately L1-L2 level, just inferior to the superior mesenteric artery origin.

options: Directly into the lesser trochanter of the proximal femur
Into the ischial tuberosity rather than into the trochanter
Into the rim of the acetabulum directly without turning
Turns 90� around the ischium then inserts into the greater trochanter's upper border
Into the trochanteric fossa on the medial femur
questions.question: The obturator internus exits the pelvis through the lesser sciatic foramen. Where does its tendon turn to insert?
questions.explanation: The obturator internus tendon exits through the lesser sciatic foramen, turns nearly 90 degrees around the smooth lesser sciatic notch (using the ischium as a pulley), and then inserts into the upper border of the greater trochanter of the femur. The gemelli muscles (superior and inferior) arise from the edges of the lesser sciatic notch and merge with the obturator internus tendon, acting as its 'cheeks.'

questions.question: Which structure passes through the foramen transversarium?
questions.explanation: The vertebral artery and accompanying veins pass through the foramina transversaria (transverse foramina) of cervical vertebrae C1-C6. The artery typically enters at C6 and ascends to C1. The stellate ganglion lies anterior to C7 transverse process, which usually lacks a foramen transversarium. Spinal nerves exit via intervertebral foramina posteriorly.

questions.question: The popliteal artery is the deepest structure in the popliteal fossa and is most vulnerable in which clinical scenario?
options: Knee joint effusion without ligament injury
Posterior knee dislocation and tibial plateau fractures
questions.explanation: The popliteal artery is most vulnerable in posterior knee dislocations and tibial plateau fractures because it runs closest to the posterior joint capsule. Posterior dislocation puts direct traction on the artery and can cause intimal tear or complete transection. Assessment of distal pulses (dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial) is mandatory after knee dislocation before any reduction attempt.

The median nerve is the only nerve passing through the carpal tunnel. It enters the hand between the tendons of flexor digitorum superficialis and lies anterior to the flexor digitorum profundus tendons. Compression of this nerve within the tunnel causes carpal tunnel syndrome.
questions.question: Which nerve passes through the carpal tunnel?
Which part of the duodenum crosses anterior to the abdominal aorta?
questions.explanation: The third (horizontal or inferior) part of the duodenum crosses anterior to the abdominal aorta, the inferior vena cava, the right psoas major muscle, the right ureter, and the right testicular/ovarian vessels at approximately the L3 vertebral level. This portion of the duodenum runs transversely from right to left and is crossed anteriorly by the superior mesenteric artery and vein, with the root of the mesentery of the small intestine crossing it obliquely. Superior mesenteric artery syndrome can occur when the third part of the duodenum is compressed between the SMA anteriorly and the aorta posteriorly.

questions.question: What percentage of lymph drains to axillary nodes?
questions.explanation: Approximately 75% of lymph from the breast drains into the axillary nodes, primarily the pectoral (anterior) group. About 20% drains to the internal mammary (parasternal) chain. The lower quadrants may drain to inferior phrenic (abdominal) nodes. This drainage pattern is crucial in cancer staging.

options: Hyperextension of the knee with foot planted
Hyperflexion of the knee in a flexed position
Direct blow to the medial knee causing varus stress
Lateral knee blow with foot planted, causing valgus force and external rotation
Twisting injury with foot in the air (open-chain)
questions.question: The 'unhappy triad' of the knee is also called O'Donoghue's triad. What is the mechanism of injury most commonly responsible?
questions.explanation: O'Donoghue's unhappy triad results from a direct blow to the lateral side of the knee with the foot planted on the ground. This creates a valgus force with external rotation of the tibia, simultaneously stressing the ACL (rotatory force), medial meniscus (compression), and tibial collateral ligament (valgus distraction). This injury pattern is classic in American football 'clipping' injuries.

questions.question: The lingual artery typically arises from which parent vessel?
questions.explanation: The lingual artery is a branch of the external carotid artery arising at the level of the hyoid bone. It supplies the tongue through dorsal lingual, deep lingual, and sublingual branches. The artery passes deep to the hyoglossus muscle, which serves as a key surgical landmark.

Superior gluteal nerve (L4, L5, S1) palsy causes weakness of gluteus medius, gluteus minimus, and tensor fasciae latae. This results in a Trendelenburg gait (pelvis drops to the opposite side during swing phase). Bilateral superior gluteal nerve palsy causes a characteristic waddling gait. This nerve is at risk during posterior surgical approaches to the hip.
questions.question: Superior gluteal nerve palsy results in which specific gait abnormality?
options: Waddling gait due to hip flexor weakness
Scissor gait due to adductor spasticity
High-stepping gait due to foot drop
Antalgic gait due to hip pain
Trendelenburg gait due to gluteus medius and minimus weakness

questions.explanation: The medial longitudinal arch is formed by the calcaneus, talus, navicular, three cuneiform bones, and the 1st-3rd metatarsals. Its summit is the superior articular facet of the talus, making the talus the keystone of this arch. It is larger, higher, more mobile, and more resilient than the lateral longitudinal arch, dynamically changing most during movement.
options: Calcaneus, talus, navicular, three cuneiforms, and 1st-3rd metatarsals
Talus, navicular, cuboid, and three metatarsals
Calcaneus, cuboid, navicular, and two cuneiforms
Calcaneus, talus, and first metatarsal only
questions.question: The medial longitudinal arch has the greatest height and is formed by which bones?

questions.explanation: The ACL arises from the anterior intercondylar area of the tibia (just posterior to the medial meniscus attachment) and attaches to the lateral condyle of the femur. It is the weaker of the two cruciate ligaments with relatively poor blood supply. It becomes taut in full extension and prevents posterior displacement of the femur on the tibia.
questions.question: The anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) arises from the anterior intercondylar area of the tibia and attaches to which femoral condyle?
options: Anterior surface of medial femoral condyle

questions.explanation: When the thigh and knee are flexed, the hamstrings extend the trunk. This action is important in activities such as rising from a forward-flexed position and in postural control. The hamstrings also flex the leg at the knee and extend the thigh at the hip. Semitendinosus and semimembranosus medially rotate the leg, while biceps femoris laterally rotates it when the knee is flexed.
questions.question: When the thigh and knee are already flexed, the hamstring muscles perform which action on the trunk?

questions.explanation: The anal canal above the pectinate line is derived from endoderm (hindgut), while the portion below originates from ectoderm (proctodeum). This embryological distinction explains the different characteristics of the two regions: superior to the pectinate line, the mucosa is columnar, venous drainage is to the portal system via superior rectal veins, lymphatic drainage is to internal iliac nodes, and innervation is autonomic (insensitive to pain). Below the line, the epithelium is stratified squamous, venous drainage is systemic (middle and inferior rectal veins), lymph drains to superficial inguinal nodes, and sensory innervation is via the inferior rectal nerve (painful).
questions.question: Which portion of the anal canal is derived from endoderm?

questions.explanation: The middle colic artery arises from the right side of the superior mesenteric artery as it emerges from beneath the pancreas, ascending into the transverse mesocolon. It divides into right and left branches that supply the transverse colon; the right branch anastomoses with the right colic artery (from SMA), while the left branch anastomoses with the left colic artery (from IMA) forming the marginal artery of Drummond. This anastomotic connection between superior and inferior mesenteric arterial territories creates an important collateral pathway in cases of vascular compromise.
questions.question: The middle colic artery is a branch of which vessel?

questions.explanation: allows independent extension of the index finger, supplementing extensor digitorum action. This is particularly useful for pointing while making a fist. The muscle is located in the posterior forearm and supplied by the posterior interosseous nerve.
questions.question: What produces index finger independent extension?

questions.explanation: The body of the stomach is the most anterior part, lying against the anterior abdominal wall in the epigastric region when the stomach is empty. The fundus extends superiorly and posteriorly beneath the left dome of the diaphragm, while the pyloric antrum angles to the right and posteriorly. The stomach's position varies with body position, respiratory phase, and degree of filling. When distended, the stomach extends inferiorly and the greater curvature becomes more anterior. The anterior surface is related to the diaphragm, anterior abdominal wall, left lobe of liver, and anterior abdominal wall.
questions.question: Which part of the stomach is most anterior?

questions.explanation: Scapular winging results from serratus anterior paralysis due to long thoracic nerve injury. The medial border of the scapula protrudes from the back, particularly evident during pushing movements. The serratus anterior is the most powerful protractor of the scapula and its loss dramatically affects scapular stability.
questions.question: What causes scapular winging?

questions.explanation: The lateral arcuate ligament is a tendinous arch that extends from the tip of the transverse process of L1 to the 12th rib, arching over the quadratus lumborum muscle. It provides attachment for some of the muscular fibers of the diaphragm. The subcostal nerve (T12) and vessels pass deep to this ligament.
questions.question: Over which muscle does the lateral arcuate ligament arch?

questions.explanation: Abscess formation is more common in the posterior segment of the upper lobe and the apical (superior) segment of the lower lobe because these are the most dependent positions when lying supine. Aspiration of infected material tends to gravitate to these segments, especially during sleep.
questions.question: Where is abscess formation most common?
How do upper left intercostal veins drain?
questions.explanation: The upper three left posterior intercostal veins typically join to form the left superior intercostal vein, which crosses the aortic arch and drains into the left brachiocephalic vein. This provides a direct connection to the superior vena cava system without crossing to the right side.

questions.question: Erector spinae and gluteus maximus work together during which functional activity?
questions.explanation: Gluteus maximus and erector spinae work together in rising from a forward-flexed position, simultaneously extending the hip and the trunk respectively. Gluteus maximus is the great extensor of the hip, particularly powerful in these loaded extension tasks. Weakness of either muscle group causes difficulty in rising from bending and is assessed in clinical examination of low back and hip pathology.
options: Hip abduction while in single-leg stance
Dorsiflexing the ankle during the swing phase of walking
Rising from a forward-flexed position (simultaneous hip and trunk extension)
Rotating the trunk in a sitting position

questions.question: The geniculate ganglion is associated with which cranial nerve?
questions.explanation: The geniculate ganglion is the sensory ganglion of the facial nerve located at the genu (bend) of the facial canal. It contains cell bodies of neurons carrying taste from the anterior tongue via chorda tympani. Herpes zoster infection here causes Ramsay Hunt syndrome with facial palsy and vesicles.

A pleural friction rub is caused by inflamed visceral and parietal pleural surfaces rubbing against each other during respiration. The sound is typically described as creaking or grating and occurs in both inspiration and expiration. It is heard when pleural fluid is absent or minimal.
questions.question: What causes pleural friction rub?

questions.explanation: The right vagus nerve descends to the right side of the trachea, forms the posterior esophageal plexus, and continues into the abdomen as the posterior gastric nerve. The left vagus descends between the left common carotid and left subclavian arteries, forms the anterior esophageal plexus, and continues as the anterior gastric nerve.
questions.question: Where does the right vagus form plexus?
Which vessel supplies blood to the middle ear?
questions.explanation: The middle ear receives blood from multiple tympanic arteries: superior tympanic (middle meningeal), inferior tympanic (ascending pharyngeal), anterior tympanic (maxillary), and posterior tympanic (stylomastoid branch of posterior auricular). This rich vascular supply reflects the metabolic needs of the middle ear mucosa and ossicles.

questions.question: The sciatic nerve (L4, 5; S1, 2, 3) curves downward at which position between the ischial tuberosity and the greater trochanter?
questions.explanation: The sciatic nerve curves downward midway between the ischial tuberosity and the greater trochanter. It has a side of danger (medial side, closer to the ischial tuberosity) and a side of safety (lateral side). The quadratus femoris forms a protective muscular layer over the nerve as it passes posterior to the hip joint.

The deep palmar arch is formed by the radial artery and deep palmar branch of the ulnar artery. It lies approximately one centimeter proximal to the superficial palmar arch at the level of the proximal border of the extended thumb. It gives off palmar metacarpal arteries and perforating branches.
options: One centimeter distal to wrist joint
One centimeter proximal to superficial arch
questions.question: At what level does the deep palmar arch lie in the hand?
What imaging study visualizes the bronchial tree?
questions.explanation: A bronchogram is a radiographic study where contrast medium is introduced into the bronchial tree to visualize its anatomy. This procedure has largely been replaced by CT bronchography and virtual bronchoscopy. Knowledge of bronchopulmonary segments helps in correctly interpreting bronchograms and planning interventions.

The anterior interosseous nerve being purely motor (no cutaneous branches) means injury produces pure motor deficit (weak thumb IP flexion, index finger DIP flexion, pronation) without sensory symptoms. This can lead to delayed diagnosis as patients lack the paresthesia typical of other nerve compression syndromes.
options: Injury causes motor deficit without sensory loss
questions.question: What is the significance of the anterior interosseous nerve being purely motor?
Which part of the male urethra is surrounded by the external sphincter?
questions.explanation: The external urethral sphincter (sphincter urethrae, voluntary striated muscle) surrounds the membranous urethra as it passes through the deep perineal space (urogenital diaphragm). This sphincter provides voluntary control of micturition and is innervated by the pudendal nerve (S2-S4). The prostatic urethra is surrounded by the internal urethral sphincter (smooth muscle under autonomic control) at the bladder neck. The membranous urethra is the shortest (1-2 cm) and least distensible part, making it vulnerable to injury during instrumentation and the most common site of urethral rupture in pelvic fractures.

The apex of the heart is formed by the inferolateral part of the left ventricle and is the most inferior and lateral cardiac point. It lies deep to the left 5th intercostal space in the midclavicular line in adults (4th space in children). The apex beat (point of maximal impulse) can normally be palpated at this location during systole.
questions.question: What is the most inferior part of the heart?
What is the smallest independently resectable lung unit?
questions.explanation: The bronchopulmonary segment is the smallest part of the lung that can be surgically removed without affecting adjacent regions. Each segment has its own tertiary bronchus, arterial supply, and venous drainage. Segmentectomy preserves more lung tissue than lobectomy while treating localized disease.

questions.question: The middle meningeal artery typically arises from which artery?
questions.explanation: The middle meningeal artery arises from the first (mandibular) part of the maxillary artery. It enters the skull through the foramen spinosum and supplies the dura mater and calvarium. The artery runs in grooves on the inner skull surface. Rupture causes epidural hematoma with the classic lucid interval.

The detrusor muscle is composed of smooth muscle arranged in three poorly defined layers (inner longitudinal, middle circular, outer longitudinal). It is under involuntary control via autonomic innervation. Parasympathetic stimulation (via pelvic splanchnic nerves) causes detrusor contraction for micturition; sympathetic stimulation (via hypogastric nerves) causes relaxation for urine storage.
questions.question: What type of muscle forms the detrusor muscle?

questions.explanation: Smooth muscle cells disposed in a predominantly circular direction and radiating from the nipple base cause nipple erection. Their contraction, induced by cold, tactile, or emotional stimuli, causes erection of the nipple and wrinkling of the surrounding areola. This is an involuntary response.
questions.question: Which muscle causes nipple erection?

questions.explanation: The lesser petrosal nerve carries preganglionic parasympathetic fibers from the inferior salivatory nucleus via the glossopharyngeal nerve and tympanic plexus. Fibers synapse in the otic ganglion. Postganglionic fibers reach the parotid gland via the auriculotemporal nerve. This pathway controls parotid secretion. Damage causes reduced salivary flow.
questions.question: The lesser petrosal nerve carries fibers from which nucleus?

options: A fascial tunnel from the posterior compartment
questions.explanation: The Achilles tendon does not have a true synovial tendon sheath like finger flexor tendons. Instead, it is surrounded by a paratenon (peritenon), a loose connective tissue sheath that allows tendon gliding and contains blood vessels. Two bursae are adjacent: the retrocalcaneal bursa (between tendon and calcaneus) and the superficial calcaneal bursa (between tendon and skin). Inflammation of the paratenon causes peritendinitis (Achilles peritendinitis).
questions.question: The Achilles tendon is the thickest and strongest tendon in the body. It does NOT have a true tendon sheath but instead has which covering?
Where does the right upper lobar bronchus branch?
questions.explanation: The right upper lobar bronchus (also called eparterial bronchus) is given off outside the hilum of the lung, above the pulmonary artery. This is in contrast to the left lung where the main bronchus divides within the hilum into two lobar (secondary) bronchi. This anatomical arrangement is clinically significant.

questions.question: Which muscle forms the medial wall of the inguinal canal?
questions.explanation: The inguinal canal does not have distinct medial and lateral walls; instead, it has anterior and posterior walls, a roof, and a floor. The canal runs obliquely (downward, forward, and medially) from the deep inguinal ring to the superficial inguinal ring, approximately 4 cm in length. The anterior wall is formed by external oblique aponeurosis (entire length) and internal oblique laterally; posterior wall by transversalis fascia (entire length) and conjoint tendon medially; roof by arching fibers of internal oblique and transversus; floor by inguinal ligament. Understanding this anatomy is crucial for hernia repair.

questions.question: At which vertebral level does the inferior mesenteric artery arise?
questions.explanation: The inferior mesenteric artery arises from the anterior surface of the abdominal aorta at approximately the level of the third lumbar vertebra (L3), about 3-4 cm above the aortic bifurcation. It supplies the hindgut derivatives: distal third of transverse colon, descending colon, sigmoid colon, and upper rectum. Its first branch is the left colic artery.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Down syndrome (trisomy 21): a congenital chromosomal disorder causing intellectual impairment and physical abnormalities including short stature and a broad facial profile; recognisable at birth.

(b)
• Features: hypotonia, growth failure, poor Moro reflex, flat face and nasal bridge, up-slanting eyes with epicanthic folds, Brushfield spots, short neck with loose skin, low-set small ears, macroglossia with small flat-roofed mouth, micrognathia, single palmar crease, small hands and feet, clinodactyly, hypoplastic fifth finger, hyperextensible joints, strabismus.
• Associated: cognitive delay and learning disability, congenital heart disease (about 1 in 3), neurological defects, leukaemia and cancer, thyroid, eye and ear disorders, Alzheimer's disease. Predisposing: boys and girls equally affected; about 1 in 865 live births in Nigeria.

(c)
• An error in cell division gives an extra chromosome 21 (47 instead of 46 chromosomes); the additional genetic material causes the physical and developmental condition. Non-disjunction (trisomy 21) accounts for about 95% and is not hereditary; mosaic Down syndrome occurs in 1-2%.
• Gait: ligamentous laxity, hypotonia and leg weakness cause hip abduction and external rotation, knee hyperextension, and foot pronation/eversion; children walk with feet wide apart, knees stiff and feet turned out. Locking knees, widening the base and rotating feet outward increase stability but cause uneven weight distribution, painful walking, poor endurance and higher energy expenditure.

(d)
• Delayed neuropsychomotor development, global hypotonia and ligament laxity lead to abnormal postural control and instability. PT role: improve muscle strength, developmental milestones, balance and coordination, physical fitness and gait; provide assistive devices.
• Aims: help the person live a long productive life, facilitate optimal movement patterns and minimise abnormal compensatory movement patterns.
questions.question:
A newborn has a rounded, flat face with a flat nasal bridge, up-slanting almond-shaped eyes with skin folds at the inner corners and tiny white spots on the iris, a short neck with loose neck skin, small round low-set ears, a tongue that tends to stick out, a single palmar crease, small hands and feet, generalised hypotonia and a poor Moro reflex.
(a) Give the diagnosis.
(b) Describe the clinical features, associated problems and predisposing factors.
(c) Explain the pathophysiology.
(d) Outline the physiotherapy management.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Cerebral palsy, spastic type (hypertonia, tight muscles). The stage is childhood; the lesion is non-progressive but the picture changes with growth.

(b)
• History (birth, immunisation, drug history), general observation (respiratory distress, temperature, colour), head and neck deformity, trunk and abdominal muscle assessment, tone, PROM and AROM. Classification by GMFCS level I-V (age-based, motor function), topographical distribution and severity.
• Expected findings from the case: hypertonia, weak tight trunk, limited painful PROM in both extremities, limited left AROM.

(c)
Short- and long-term goals are not separately stated. General aims: enable the child to achieve potential physical independence and fitness in the community, minimise physical impairments, improve quality of life of the child and family.

(d)
• Approaches: Bobath/NDT (reflex-inhibiting patterns, key points of control head/neck, shoulder and pelvic girdles), neuromuscular electrical stimulation, exercise therapy, hydrotherapy, body-weight-supported treadmill, conductive education, CIMT, Vojta, sensory integration, suit therapy; muscle education with braces for spasticity; PNF techniques (hold-relax, contract-relax).
• Medical/adjunct: botulinum toxin for painful spastic muscles, orthopaedic surgery, selective dorsal rhizotomy, adaptive equipment (wheelchairs, walkers), occupational and speech therapy.

(e)
Athetoids are not given muscle education; botulinum toxin dosing rests on expert opinion.

(f)
• Education: caregivers and family play a major role in the rehabilitation programme, which must be individualised.
• Diagnostic note: the mother had earlier stopped exercise therapy because of no visible improvement; early assessment and treatment give better results.
questions.question:
An 11-year-old boy is carried into the clinic on his mother's back because he cannot walk, crawl, stand, sit or talk. He was born by caesarean section and did not cry until pinched. At 5 years he began rolling, grasping and trying to rise. He startles when things drop. Examination shows weak, tight trunk and abdominal muscles, hypertonia, limited and painful passive range in both extremities, and left upper-limb active range limited but pain free while the right is normal.
(a) State the diagnosis, the type and the stage.
(b) State the assessment tools/tests and the expected findings.
(c) State the short-term and long-term goals.
(d) Name the treatment approach and techniques.
(e) State the precautions/contraindications.
(f) State the patient/caregiver education.

A patient has sudden episodes of severe facial pain radiating over the jaw and cheek region on one side. The pain is attributed to compression of the nerve by a blood vessel.
(a) Give the diagnosis.
(b) State the clinical features and predisposing factors.
(c) Explain the anatomy and pathophysiology.
(d) Outline the physiotherapy management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Trigeminal neuralgia (tic douloureux) of the trigeminal nerve (CN V).

(b)
Severe facial pain that commonly radiates to the mandibular and maxillary regions; other trigeminal impairment: facial numbness, weakness of chewing, loss of facial/mouth sensation, abnormal reflexes. Causes: blood vessel compression, tumour, multiple sclerosis, facial trauma. In MS it is one of the brainstem demyelination features (trigeminal neuralgia).

(c)
CN V originates from the brainstem, has sensory and motor functions and three branches: ophthalmic V1 (eye, forehead, nose), maxillary V2 (mid-face, cheeks, upper lip), mandibular V3 (lower face, jaw, lips, tongue); it also supplies the muscles of mastication. Pain arises from nerve compression or damage. Related conditions: trigeminal neuropathy (diabetes, vitamin deficiency, infection, trauma) and neuritis (infection, autoimmune, trauma).

(d)
• Assessment: sensory (pain, temperature, light and deep touch, all three divisions with eyes closed), motor (jaw opening, closing, lateral movement, temporalis and masseter contraction), jaw jerk and masseter reflexes.
• Goals: manage pain and improve sensory function; enhance motor function for mastication. Treatment: TENS, interferential therapy, sensory re-education (graded textures and temperatures), jaw strengthening exercises.

(a)
• Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (Lou Gehrig's disease), the commonest and fatal motor neuron disease of adults; limb onset (70-80%) with lower-limb onset shown by tripping, foot drop, slapping gait, loss of bulk/strength. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by EMG, NCV, biopsy and imaging, and needs LMN signs, UMN signs and progression within or between regions.
• El Escorial criteria (1994, revised 1998): clinically definite (UMN and LMN signs in 3 of 4 regions, or bulbar plus two spinal), probable, probable laboratory-supported, possible.

(b)
• Aetiology mostly unknown; 5-10% familial (autosomal dominant; about 20% of these have SOD1 mutations); proposed mechanisms: oxidative stress, neurotoxicity, excitotoxicity, impaired axonal transport, protein aggregation, apoptosis, lifestyle.
• Pathophysiology: progressive loss of UMNs (cortex, corticospinal tracts), brainstem nuclei (V, VII, IX, X, XII) and anterior horn cells; surviving axons sprout and reinnervate until about 50% of motor units are lost, then impairments appear; spread is contiguous within regions.

(c)
History: painless, gradual weakness, cramps, twitching, speech/swallowing/breathing problems. LMN signs: fasciculations, weakness, atrophy, hypotonia, hyporeflexia. UMN signs: spasticity, hyperreflexia, pathological reflexes. Also bulbar, respiratory and cognitive/behavioural status; sensation, eye movements, bladder/bowel and skin are usually preserved. ADL: Schwab and England scale (100% independent to 10% totally dependent).

(d)
Problems: muscle weakness (cervical extensors with head drop, upper and lower limbs), gait impairment and reduced mobility (difficulty with sit-to-stand), cramps, spasticity, shoulder pain, dysarthria, dysphagia and aspiration risk, respiratory weakness, fatigue, contractures, cognitive/behavioural change.

(e)
• Goals: maximise function and independence through restorative and compensatory interventions, promote health in early stages, prevent complications, provide adaptive equipment, and give education, psychological support and community resources.
• Interventions: soft collar (mild-moderate) or semirigid/rigid collar (moderate-severe) for neck weakness; adaptive equipment, sling and wrist/hand splints for UL weakness; ROM, stretching and joint mobilisation for shoulder pain; breathing exercises, positioning and rest-activity balance for respiratory weakness.
• Ankle-foot orthosis, ROM and mobilisation for leg weakness; firm cushion (2-3 in) or raised chair for sit-to-stand; massage and stretching for cramps; slow prolonged stretch, passive ROM, positioning and splinting for spasticity; chin tuck, head/trunk positioning, communication devices and food-consistency changes for dysarthria/dysphagia.
• Progression: early/early-middle stage restorative and preventive; later compensatory (cane, AFO, wheelchair for fatigue, unsteadiness or falls). Prognosis is better with younger onset, limb onset and good psychological well-being.
questions.question:
A man in his late 50s reports insidious, painless, slowly progressive weakness beginning in his legs with tripping, stumbling and a slapping gait (foot drop), loss of muscle bulk, muscle twitching, and stiffness with brisk reflexes in some limbs. Sensation is unchanged and no other cause is evident.
(a) State the probable diagnosis and how it is confirmed.
(b) Describe the aetiology and pathophysiology.
(c) Describe your physiotherapy assessment (history and objective findings) and the ADL scale you would use.
(d) List the problems.
(e) State the goals and interventions of physiotherapy management and how they change as the disease progresses.

(a) Describe the physiotherapy management of cranial nerve damage (olfactory, optic, oculomotor, trigeminal, facial, accessory), stating goals and interventions for each.
(b) State the assessment and outcome measures used.
(c) Explain how complications and secondary impairments of these nerve lesions are prevented or managed.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Overall aim: restore function, reduce symptoms and improve quality of life, individualised to specific deficits with exercise, education and functional training.
• CN I (anosmia, hyposmia, hyperosmia, dysosmia after trauma, infection or surgery): olfactory training and sensory re-education. CN II (glaucoma, ischaemic optic neuropathy, optic neuritis, NMOSD): visual rehabilitation and compensatory strategies. CN III (ptosis, dilated pupil, 'down and out' eye, diplopia): eye exercises, strengthening/coordination exercises, facial massage, patching and prism glasses.
• CN V (trigeminal neuralgia, neuropathy, neuritis): goals pain relief, sensory function and mastication; TENS, interferential therapy, sensory re-education with textures and temperatures, jaw strengthening (opening/closing, lateral movements).
• CN VII (Bell's palsy, Ramsay Hunt, trauma, otitis): goals restore function and symmetry and reduce synkinesis; facial exercises, mirror and biofeedback re-education, electrical stimulation used cautiously, massage.
• CN XI (palsy after neck surgery, tumour, GBS): goals restore sternocleidomastoid and trapezius function, neck/shoulder mobility; shrugs and neck flexion/extension strengthening, NMES, ROM (neck rotation, shoulder abduction), functional training.

(b)
• Assessment: CN I - aromatic substances (coffee, vanilla, cinnamon), one nostril at a time, avoid alcohol/ammonia; CN II - visual acuity, colour, fields, pupillary and accommodation reflexes, funduscopy; CN III - H-pattern eye following, total palsy limits all gaze except abduction and intorsion.
• CN V - sensation over forehead, cheek, jaw (pin), mastication, jaw and masseter reflexes; CN VII - symmetry, eyebrow raise, eye closure, cheek puff, teeth, taste, corneal reflex; CN XI - shoulder shrug, sternocleidomastoid and head rotation against resistance.

(c)
• Accessory palsy causes head-turning difficulty, shoulder drooping and impaired abduction beyond 90 degrees; iatrogenic damage occurs in neck surgery.
• Oculomotor palsy: abnormal head posture and misalignment managed with patching and prism glasses; trochlear palsy can cause neck pain from head tilt.
• Diplopia complicates depth perception and daily tasks (reading, driving, stairs); abducens palsy in children can cause amblyopia if untreated.
• CN VIII disorders: vestibular rehabilitation (gaze stabilisation, habituation), balance aids, home modifications to prevent falls; CN IX/X/XII: swallowing exercises, dietary modification and speech therapy.
• Trigeminal weakness affects mastication and facial pain, treated by TENS/IFT and jaw exercises.

(a)
NTDs are birth defects of the brain, spine or spinal cord from a defect in neurulation (neural plate, folds, tube) in the first month of pregnancy, open (exposed neural tissue) or closed; spina bifida is incomplete closure of the fetal spinal column. The commonest NTDs are spina bifida and anencephaly.

(b)
Exact cause unknown; multifactorial (genetic, nutritional, environmental); insufficient maternal folic acid intake is a key factor.

(c)
• Occulta: mildest and commonest (10-20% of people), skin-covered, may show a dimple, dark hair patch or fatty deposit, rarely causes symptoms. Closed NTDs: malformed fat, bone or meninges, few symptoms or incomplete paralysis with urinary/bowel dysfunction.
• Meningocele: fluid and meninges protrude through a vertebral opening, no neural elements. Myelomeningocele: most severe, neural elements exposed, usually no skin cover. Other NTDs: anencephaly (stillborn/die soon after birth), encephalocele, hydranencephaly, iniencephaly, Chiari malformation (cerebellum bulges into spinal canal).

(d)
• Flaccid or spastic paralysis, sensory loss at pelvis/lower limbs, urinary and bowel incontinence, scoliosis, hip dysplasia/dislocation, club foot, hip/knee contractures, hydrocephalus, trunk hypotonia, delayed automatic postural reactions; osteoporosis if mobility is severely restricted.
• Cognitive effects on memory, learning, concentration and language processing; 6 in 10 have normal intelligence, about half of whom have some learning disability; difficulty with complex motor tasks such as tying laces.

(e)
Symptoms vary with the type and level of involvement from mild to severe: in myelomeningocele exposed neural elements cause partial or complete paralysis below the opening (may be unable to walk), whereas a meningocele has no neural elements and may cause few or no symptoms.

(f)
Research indicates that insufficient dietary folic acid (a B vitamin) is a key factor in causing spina bifida and other NTDs; prenatal vitamins contain folic acid, and adequate intake before and after conception reduces NTD risk.

(g)
Meningocele: sac of fluid without spinal cord in it, little or no nerve damage, minor disability. Myelomeningocele: sac holds part of the spinal cord and nerves, which are damaged, causing moderate to severe disability and leg motor impairment.

(h)
• Maximise independence in standing, transferring and walking; provide mobility aids (walkers, cane) and equipment; maintain or improve muscle strength and length; balance and coordination exercises to prevent falls.
• Anticipate and prevent contractures; positioning and postural advice; wheelchair skills; orthotic devices; achieve milestones (sitting, crawling, standing); improve ADL independence, posture and confidence.
questions.question:
(a) Define neural tube defects and spina bifida and state their embryological basis.
(b) State the causes and risk factors.
(c) Describe the types of spina bifida and the other neural tube defects.
(d) Describe the clinical features.
(e) Explain why the severity of disability varies with the type and level of spina bifida.
(f) Explain the importance of folic acid in the mother's diet.
(g) Distinguish between meningocele and myelomeningocele.
(h) Outline the physiotherapy management.

During assessment of a patient with an intracranial lesion the physiotherapist finds an acute loss of consciousness, a dilated pupil on one side with an absent light reflex on that side, an eye that will not turn upwards, and weakness of the opposite side of the body.
(a) Identify the cranial nerve involved and the probable pathological process.
(b) State how the nerve and the other nerves supplying eye movement are examined and which functions are affected.
(c) State the differential conditions.
(d) Give the clinical reasoning for the physiotherapy plan.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Oculomotor nerve (CN III): unilateral dilated pupil with absent light reflex and/or an eye that will not turn upwards. Probable process: uncal herniation with raised intracranial pressure (or an internal carotid aneurysm). Uncal herniation occurs when a brain lesion overwhelms the ability of the three cranial components to compensate for pressure increases; cardinal signs are acute loss of consciousness, ipsilateral pupillary dilation and contralateral hemiparesis.

(b)
• Examination: pupil size and light reflex; eye movements are tested by drawing an 'H' with a finger or pen for the patient to follow with the head still, reporting blurred or double vision. CN IV and VI are examined with the same eye movements. Total CN III palsy limits gaze in all fields except abduction and intorsion; incomplete palsy gives partial limitation.
• Functions affected: CN III supplies the superior, medial and inferior recti and inferior oblique (elevation, adduction, depression, external rotation), the levator palpebrae (lid elevation), the sphincter pupillae (constriction) and the ciliary muscle (accommodation). Palsy gives ptosis, dilated pupil, a 'down and out' eye and diplopia. CN IV (superior oblique) gives depression, intorsion, abduction; CN VI (lateral rectus) gives abduction.

(c)
Differentials: internal carotid aneurysm versus uncal herniation; other causes of CN III damage are trauma, posterior communicating artery aneurysm, microvascular ischaemia (diabetes) and compressive tumours; raised ICP from swelling, abnormal fluid dynamics or haematoma (extradural, subdural, intracerebral), subarachnoid haemorrhage.

(d)
• Reasoning: raised ICP can cause herniation in severe cases, so in the acute stage positioning and management are used to control intracranial pressure.
• Minimise activities that raise intrathoracic pressure; avoid neck flexion or positions that compromise cerebral venous drainage, while remaining mindful of cerebral perfusion.
• Promote respiratory function, prevent complications, assess sensorimotor deficit and cranial nerve involvement; treat as often as the patient tolerates, in short sessions with rest periods.
• For the eye deficit itself: eye exercises, strengthening and coordination exercises, facial massage, patching and prism glasses.

questions.question:
A patient with long-standing diabetes mellitus presents with aching pain, numbness and loss of joint position sense in the feet and asymmetrical wasting and weakness of the iliopsoas, quadriceps and hip adductors.
(a) Identify the condition and its risk factors.
(b) State the complications and secondary impairments.
(c) Outline the prevention and physiotherapy management options.
(d) Justify one physiotherapy option.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Diabetic neuropathy - distal symmetrical sensory neuropathy plus proximal motor neuropathy, in a polyneuropathy pattern (sensory loss progresses distal to proximal). Risk factor: diabetes mellitus; recovery depends on glycaemic control. Diabetes is also listed among causes of sensory disturbance, trochlear/oculomotor nerve palsy (microvascular ischaemia) and neuropathy generally.

(b)
Pain, numbness, loss of joint position sense (unsteadiness), wasting and weakness of proximal muscles, deformity, oedema and sensory loss risks; cranial nerve palsies from microvascular ischaemia; sensory loss can lead to injury. Alcoholic neuropathy is a comparable pattern (myalgia, dysaesthesia, autonomic dysfunction, ataxia).

(c)
• Prevention: control blood glucose (and blood pressure in microvascular palsies). Physiotherapy per neuropathy aims: relieve pain (massage, TENS, cautious thermotherapy); control oedema (bandaging, elevation); strengthen weak muscles with electrical stimulation and exercise; maintain ROM by passive movement and stretching; prevent deformity by splinting; restore function.
• Balance and coordination exercises follow from the loss of joint position sense; graded therapeutic exercises for weakness.

(d)
Justification for graded strengthening: proximal motor weakness and wasting of iliopsoas, quadriceps and adductors impair function, and graded therapeutic exercise and electrical stimulation are listed for weak muscle in neuropathies. Recovery is tied to glycaemic control, so exercise complements medical control.

(a)
• Five groups cause acute noncompressive myelopathy: demyelination, infection, inflammation, vascular, neoplastic/paraneoplastic. MS: usually partial myelopathy (Brown-Sequard, 'sensory useless hand'), Lhermitte's sign, previous episodes with recovery; MRI cord lesions under 2 segments, peripheral (lateral/posterior columns); brain white-matter lesions; CSF oligoclonal bands and raised IgG index.
• NMO: relapsing demyelination of optic nerves and cord, commoner in Asians and Africans, about 90% female, severe deficits, associated autoimmune disease (SLE, Sjogren's, thyroid), NMO-IgG highly specific (over 90%) and sensitive (over 70%); MRI long cord lesions over 3 segments with swelling and gadolinium enhancement.
• ADEM: monophasic, brain and sometimes cord, fever, encephalopathy and/or myelopathy after a viral illness, commoner in children; MRI large confluent white-matter lesions of the same age; CSF pleocytosis; about 25% later meet MS criteria.
• Acute idiopathic transverse myelitis: commonest cause of acute myelitis, peaks at 10-19 and 30-39 years, preceding fever/viral illness, acute or subacute onset with back pain at lesion level, rapid flaccid paralysis, sensory level, impaired sphincter control.

(b)
• Infections (viral, bacterial, fungal, parasitic: systemically ill, fever, meningismus, CSF pleocytosis and raised protein); vascular (cord infarction, AV fistula, bleeding into malformations); paraneoplastic (e.g. CRMP5 with small cell lung carcinoma); nutritional - subacute combined degeneration from vitamin B12 deficiency (also copper deficiency, nitrous oxide); tabes dorsalis.
• Compressive causes: tumours, epidural abscess or haematoma, herniated disc, vertebral pathology, with warning signs of neck/back pain, bladder disturbance and sensory symptoms.

(c)
• Lhermitte's sign (electric-shock sensation on neck flexion) reflects posterior column irritation and is typical of MS; short peripheral lesions favour MS whereas cord lesions over 3 segments with swelling favour NMO.
• Transverse myelitis may be the first sign of MS, NMO or another non-compressive myelopathy; affectation is as for other spinal cord injuries.

(d)
• MS: relapsing, small short cord lesions, oligoclonal bands, previous episodes. NMO: optic nerve plus long cord lesions, NMO-IgG, severe. ADEM: monophasic, encephalopathy, large confluent brain lesions of the same age, more in children.
• CIS contrast: NMOSD shows longitudinally extensive lesions with AQP4 antibodies; ADEM has encephalopathy which CIS lacks.
• MS demyelination: oligodendrocyte destruction, plaque formation and scarring with a chronic course; classification benign, relapsing-remitting, secondary progressive, primary progressive.
• Physiotherapy for these cord conditions follows the SCI plan and MS management (stretching, submaximal exercise, walking aids, avoid overheating).
questions.question:
(a) Describe multiple sclerosis, neuromyelitis optica, acute disseminated encephalomyelitis and acute idiopathic transverse myelitis under the headings of definition, epidemiology, clinical features and investigation findings.
(b) State the other causes of noncompressive myelopathy.
(c) Explain the clinical significance of Lhermitte's sign and of the length of the cord lesion on MRI.
(d) Distinguish between MS, NMO and ADEM.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• CN IX, X and XII are the bulbar nerves (medulla oblongata) concerned with swallowing, taste, speech and head/shoulder movement. CN IX exits by the jugular foramen and has 5 fibre types: taste from posterior third of tongue, stylopharyngeus motor, sensation from ear skin/tympanic membrane, parasympathetic to the parotid, visceral sensation from pharynx.
• CN X ('wandering') exits the jugular foramen with IX and XI, passes the carotid sheath, neck, thorax and abdomen; sensory to external acoustic meatus, larynx, laryngopharynx, viscera and epiglottis taste; motor to pharynx, soft palate, larynx; parasympathetic to trachea, bronchi, GI tract and heart rhythm. CN XII arises from the medulla, exits via the hypoglossal canal, and supplies all tongue muscles except palatoglossus (purely motor).

(b)
• CN IX: causes meningioma, metastases (bronchial, breast), styloid infection; signs neuropathic pain of posterior tongue, pharynx and ear, loss of taste, decreased saliva, dysphagia, hearing loss; glossopharyngeal neuralgia. CN X: dysphagia, dysphonia, hoarseness, dyspnoea, cough/choking, bradycardia/tachycardia, blood pressure change, arrhythmia, GI symptoms, drooling, slurred speech, loss of gag reflex.
• CN XII palsy: uncommon; head and neck malignancy or penetrating trauma; tongue deviates towards the damaged side on protrusion, wasting and fasciculations on the affected side; impaired articulation of lingual sounds, oral phase swallowing, tongue mobility.

(c)
• Assessment IX/X: cough (X), open mouth and say 'ah' with tongue depressor - soft palate should rise centrally; gag reflex only if bulbar impairment is suspected (uncomfortable). X also: swallowing and voice evaluation, heart rate variability, BP on standing, EMG/NCS, endoscopy, tilt-table, Valsalva, cold pressor, respiratory sinus arrhythmia tests.
• XII assessment: inspect tongue at rest (atrophy, fasciculation, asymmetry), protrusion, strength against cheek or depressor, articulation ('tip-top', 'light-tight', 'la-la-la').
• Management IX: speech and language therapy, dietary modification, swallowing exercises, feeding tubes, pain medication (carbamazepine, gabapentin, amitriptyline), nerve decompression surgery. XII: corticosteroids, antivirals if herpes simplex, tumour surgery, botulinum toxin for spasticity, swallowing exercises (supraglottic, Masako), speech therapy, NMES, postural training, adaptive equipment.

(d)
CN IX and X both pass through the jugular foramen, so a lesion there can involve both.

(e)
CN XII is purely somatic motor to the tongue muscles, so a lower motor neuron lesion weakens the muscles on that side; the unopposed side pushes the tongue towards the weak side, with wasting and fasciculations.

(f)
• Unilateral weakness suggests a lower motor neuron lesion; bilateral weakness suggests an upper motor neuron lesion.
• Vagus visceral effects are why cardiovascular, GI and respiratory symptoms accompany vagal damage.
• Together CN IX, X and XII control swallowing, taste, speech and head and shoulder movement; CN X also carries parasympathetic supply to the heart, GI tract and airways.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the glossopharyngeal, vagus and hypoglossal nerves: origin, course, fibre types and functions.
(b) Describe the causes, clinical features and impairments of damage to each nerve.
(c) State the assessment and management.
(d) Explain why CN X is likely to be affected when CN IX is damaged.
(e) Explain why tongue deviation and wasting occur in hypoglossal palsy.
(f) Distinguish between unilateral and bilateral hypoglossal weakness.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII) / cochlear and vestibular apparatus - sensorineural hearing loss (sound localises to the normal ear; AC greater than BC). Nerve arises from pons/medulla nuclei, exits at the cerebellopontine angle and passes the internal acoustic meatus to the inner ear.

(b)
Cochlear part: hearing; vestibular part: balance and spatial orientation (utricle, saccule, semicircular canals). Impairment: hearing loss, tinnitus, vertigo, nystagmus, poor coordination, falls, nausea/vomiting.

(c)
• Acoustic neuroma (vestibular schwannoma: progressive unilateral hearing loss, tinnitus, balance issues), Meniere's disease, vestibular neuritis, labyrinthitis, BPPV (Dix-Hallpike), conductive loss (Weber localises to the affected ear; BC better than AC). NF2 also causes bilateral 8th nerve tumours.
• Investigations: audiometry, ENG/VNG, MRI/CT, caloric test, posturography.

(d)
Balance disorders: vestibular rehabilitation therapy (balance exercises to reduce dizziness, gaze stabilisation, habituation exercises), Romberg for monitoring balance, walking aids and home modifications to prevent falls. Medical: hearing aids, cochlear implants, corticosteroids, antivertigo drugs, surgery (labyrinthectomy, vestibular nerve section), tinnitus sound therapy and CBT.
questions.question:
A patient has progressive unilateral hearing loss, ringing in the ear, difficulty understanding speech in noise, dizziness with nystagmus, and loss of balance. On tuning fork testing the sound is heard louder in the normal ear (Weber), and air conduction is better than bone conduction (Rinne).
(a) Identify the lesion site and the system affected.
(b) State the affected functions.
(c) State the differential conditions.
(d) Give the clinical reasoning for the physiotherapy plan.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Traumatic spinal cord injury with spinal shock; completeness (AIS A-E) and neurological level to be determined.

(b)
• SCI: about 80% traumatic (falls, road accidents, violence), commonest at 20-39 years and in males (4:1). Spinal shock is a transient physiological disruption of cord function immediately after injury: complete loss of reflexes, slow heart rate, low BP, flaccid paralysis, sensory loss, paralytic ileus, atonic bladder with retention; lasts minutes to months with gradual return of reflexes.
• Acute care: proper handling and transfer; airway, breathing (monitor rate, pattern, colour, distress, especially cervical injury), circulation (atropine for heart rate); spinal stabilisation (halo-traction, Gardner-Wells or cone callipers for C-spine; postural reduction for T-spine and below); immobilisation appliances.

(c)
• Continuous assessment. Subjective: when, where, what, how, and after that. Objective: vital signs, skin, limb placement, tubes and external connections; completeness (AIS A = no voluntary anal contraction, bulbocavernosus reflex present; B-E = sacral sparing); neurological level; all sensory modalities including pain.
• Also spasticity (Ashworth, Tardieu), function (Katz index, FIM, SCIM) and associated injuries (brain injury, fractures, peripheral nerve injury).

(d)
Problems: paralysis and sensory loss by level (e.g. C4 poor cough, diaphragmatic breathing, hypoventilation), respiratory compromise, autonomic disturbance, bladder and bowel dysfunction, spasticity, pain; risks of osteoporosis, heterotopic ossification, urosepsis, VTE/PE, pressure ulcers, orthostatic hypotension, autonomic dysreflexia (above T6); psychosocial and existential concerns.

(e)
• The plan is not a blanket one; it follows the analysis of findings and a physical diagnosis. Aims: maintain/improve respiratory function and treat/prevent complications; maintain and strengthen innervated muscles and facilitate functional patterns; treat pain; train function and facilitate reintegration; address psychosocial concerns; evaluate with outcome measures.
• Progression follows level: e.g. C6 needs help with dressing and bed-chair-car transfers, C7-C8 dress, eat, drive and transfer independently, T5-T9 manual wheelchair and independent personal care, L2-S5 walking with aids; assistive devices and community reintegration are part of the plan.
questions.question:
A young man is brought in after a road traffic accident with immediate flaccid paralysis, loss of sensation and absent reflexes below the injury, a slow heart rate and low blood pressure.
(a) State the diagnosis.
(b) Describe the aetiology and pathophysiological state.
(c) Describe your physiotherapy assessment (subjective and objective).
(d) Draw up the problem list.
(e) State the plan of physiotherapy management, goals and how it progresses.

A man in his 50s reports lightning-like pains in the legs, unsteadiness with a slapping gait, numbness, loss of reflexes and sensory incontinence, and X-ray shows a Charcot joint. He was infected with syphilis about 15-20 years ago and was not treated.
(a) State the probable diagnosis.
(b) Describe the pathophysiology and aetiology.
(c) Describe your physiotherapy assessment (subjective and objective findings).
(d) Draw up the problem list.
(e) State the physiotherapy management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Tabes dorsalis (syphilitic myelopathy), a tertiary-syphilis complication of untreated infection, with a latent period of about 15-20 years.

(b)
Syphilis that is untreated can involve the nervous system: meningovascular syphilis in 2-3%, general paresis in 2-5%, tabes dorsalis in 1-5%. Tabes is a sensory disorder involving the dorsal spinal roots, with demyelination of the posterior column of the white matter.

(c)
Symptoms: weakness, lightning (lancinating) pain, autonomic dysfunction, sensory incontinence, impotence, faecal incontinence. Signs: sensory ataxia (tabetic/slapping gait), hypoaesthesia, depressed or lost reflexes, pain and temperature loss with trophic changes such as Charcot joints and perforating foot ulcers. Investigation: syphilis serological testing.

(d)
Problems: sensory ataxia and impaired balance/posture, muscle weakness, pain, sensory loss, incontinence, joint damage (Charcot) and foot ulcers, autonomic dysfunction.

(e)
• Medical treatment is antibiotics. Physiotherapy: improve balance and posture (which may be due to the primary damage), strengthen weak muscles, balance and coordination exercises.
• Sensory-ataxia principle for reference: patients rely more on visual or auditory information about leg or foot position (high-stepping gait).

questions.question:
After a lymph node biopsy in the posterior triangle of the neck, a patient has difficulty shrugging one shoulder, a drooping shoulder, difficulty turning the head to the opposite side, muscle wasting in the neck and upper back, and cannot abduct the arm beyond 90 degrees.
(a) State the diagnosis and cause.
(b) State the assessment tools/tests and expected findings.
(c) State the treatment goals.
(d) Name the treatment approach and techniques.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Accessory nerve (CN XI) palsy, here iatrogenic (surgery in the posterior triangle of the neck: lymph node biopsy, parotidectomy, carotid endarterectomy). Other causes: trauma, tumours, infection, idiopathic, compression, GBS. Nerve has cranial root (medulla) and spinal root (C1-C5/6) supplying sternocleidomastoid and trapezius.

(b)
Shoulder shrug test against resistance (weakness/asymmetry); sternocleidomastoid test (neck flexion against resistance while turning to opposite side); head rotation against resistance. Expected: weak or paralysed muscles, difficulty turning the head to the opposite side, unable to shrug, atrophy, fasciculations, possible swallowing difficulty.

(c)
Goals: restore function of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius; improve shoulder and neck mobility.

(d)
Strengthening (shoulder shrugs, neck flexion and extension), neuromuscular electrical stimulation to activate muscles and prevent atrophy, ROM exercises (neck rotations, shoulder abduction) to prevent stiffness, functional training to reduce compensatory movement.

(a)
• Developed by Karel (physician, worked with children with CP) and Berta Bobath (physiotherapist); traditional care used massage, heat and passive movement; Berta's observations led to techniques based on movement and relaxation; she stressed inhibition, and treatment is individualised, not a fixed set of exercises.
• Key concepts: problem-solving approach; emphasis on motor control; systems integration; plasticity (neuroplasticity, cortical and muscle plasticity); motor learning; holistic (sensory, perceptual, adaptive behaviour), multidisciplinary, patient-centred, function over movement.

(b)
• Assessment uses the ICF: history taking, functional activity, body functions and structures, clinical reasoning, outcome measures, evaluation and documentation.
• Treatment aims: inhibit abnormal released patterns of coordination, facilitate higher integrated automatic postural reactions, encourage voluntary activity, and channel tonic reflex activity into normal function using spasticity-inhibiting patterns.
• Principles: avoid movements that raise tone or cause abnormal responses on the paretic side; develop normal posture and movement patterns (functional postural patterns rather than developmental sequences); include the hemiplegic side to restore symmetry and use; change quality of movement and function.
• Techniques: reflex-inhibiting patterns, sensorimotor experience, facilitation techniques, key points of control (head/neck, shoulder and pelvic girdles); sensory re-education with verbal, visual and tactile cues paired with active movement; strengthening with body weight, gravity, resistance bands.
• Indications: neurological deficits such as hemiplegia and paediatric neurological impairments.

(c)
• Rationale/effects: improved postural control and alignment, weight transfer for balance and transfers, tone management, better quality of movement, relearning of functional activities through task-oriented training of the affected side. Case: an 81-year-old woman with right paralysis and aphasia achieved all goals in a year and lived independently.
• Benefits: individualised ICF-based therapy, active patient engagement, goal-oriented task focus, usable in children.

(d)
• Bobath aims to inhibit abnormal released patterns and integrate the affected side into normal postural reactions and functional tasks, whereas Brunnstrom deliberately uses primitive reflexes and limb synergies in stages.
• Choice therefore rests on the described aims: quality of movement, symmetry and inhibition of tone (Bobath) versus staged use of synergies and reflexes with recovery sequence (Brunnstrom).
• Limitations of Bobath: lack of standardisation, focus on impairments more than function, selection and individual variability, complexity and time intensity; further research needed on specific benefits and long-term results.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the origin and key concepts of the Bobath approach.
(b) State its assessment framework, treatment principles and techniques, and its indications.
(c) State its rationale and expected effects in neurological rehabilitation.
(d) Explain the basis for choosing the Bobath approach over an alternative approach in a patient with hemiplegia.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Purpose: identify which components of the nervous system are affected, locate the problem and screen at-risk patients. A complete assessment has five steps: cranial nerves, reflexes, motor system, sensory system, coordination and gait, together with intellect (memory, orientation, calculation), new learning, judgment and perception.
• History: presenting complaint (site, onset, duration, sudden or gradual, trauma), associated symptoms (headache, numbness, pins and needles, weakness, unsteadiness, stiffness, clumsiness, nausea, visual disturbance, altered consciousness), past and family history, systemic enquiry; tools: reflex hammer, Snellen chart, pen light, cotton swabs, paper clips.
• Reflexes graded 0 (absent), 1+ hypoactive, 2+ normal, 3+ hyperactive without clonus, 4+ hyperactive with clonus: Achilles S1-S2, patellar L3-L4, biceps C5-C6, triceps C6-C7, brachioradialis C5-C6.
• Motor: muscle appearance (wasted/normal), tone (flaccid, clonic, normal), involuntary movements, strength 0-5 (0 none, 1 visible contraction, 2 not against gravity, 3 against gravity, 4 against some resistance, 5 normal); e.g. deltoid C5, biceps C5-C6, triceps C6-C7, finger abduction T1, hip adduction L2-L4, abduction L4-S1, plantar flexion S1-S2, great-toe extension L5.
• Sensory: pin prick, light touch, position sense, stereognosis (identify coin or pen), graphesthesia (number written on palm), extinction. Coordination: rapid alternating movements, finger-to-nose, Romberg (feet together, eyes closed 5-10 s), gait (walk and turn, heel-to-toe, toes, heels, hop, knee bend, rise from sitting).
• Cranial nerves: CN V sensation over forehead, cheek and jaw with a sharp implement plus temporalis/masseter power; CN III pupil size and light reflex; CN VIII Weber and Rinne; CN XII tongue protrusion against cheek resistance.

(b)
Precautions: be ready to catch the patient during the Romberg test; a light-touch, closed-eye set-up avoids visual cues in sensory tests.

(c)
• Positive Romberg (unstable) indicates a vestibular or proprioceptive problem; astereognosis without dorsal column lesion suggests a parietal sensory cortex lesion; a unilaterally dilated pupil with absent light reflex suggests aneurysm or uncal herniation; apraxia (movement failure despite intact strength and comprehension) signals cortical damage.
• Ataxia types: sensory (high-stepping, relies on vision), vestibular (wide-based staggering, lost equilibrium reactions), cerebellar (dysmetria, dyssynergia, dysdiadochokinesia, intention tremor); sensory disturbance causes include diabetes, thiamine deficiency and neurotoxins.

(d)
• In the pronator drift test the patient extends both arms forward, closes the eyes and counts to 10; with upper-extremity weakness the affected arm pronates and falls.
• This is one of the most sensitive tests for upper-extremity weakness, which is the basis for using it; resisted testing (deltoid, biceps, triceps, finger abduction) grades the strength.
• Rinne test (comparison): compares air with bone conduction, and normal is air conduction greater than bone conduction.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the components of a complete neurological assessment and the procedures for motor, sensory, reflex, coordination and gait testing.
(b) State the precautions to observe.
(c) State what the findings indicate (rationale and expected clinical meaning).
(d) Explain the basis for using the pronator drift test to detect upper-extremity weakness.

questions.answerText:
(a)
