• A neurophysiological approach developed by Margaret Rood in 1940, based on the reflex/hierarchical model of the CNS: activating or deactivating sensory receptors (interaction of somatic, autonomic and psychic factors) to regulate motor behaviour in people with motor-control problems; motor patterns develop from primitive reflexes through proper sensory stimuli.
• Principles: normalisation of tone by appropriate sensory stimuli; ontogenic developmental sequence (assess current level, aim for the next); purposeful movement; repetition for motor learning.
• Concepts: mobility (phasic) muscles are fast glycolytic, superficial, one-joint, tire rapidly and give skilled movement; stability (tonic) muscles are slow oxidative, deep, co-contract for joint stability and tire slowly.
• Ontogenic sequences: motor (supine withdrawal, roll over, pivot prone, neck co-contraction, prone on elbow, quadruped, standing, walking) and vital functions (inspiration, expiration, sucking, swallowing liquids, phonation, chewing and swallowing solids, speech).

(b)
• Sensory receptors stimulated by summation act on anterior horn cell excitability: proprioceptive, exteroceptive, vestibular and special sense receptors. Autonomic manipulation: sympathetic activation for hypotonic, somnolent patients; parasympathetic activation for hypertonic, hyperkinetic, hyperexcitable patients.
• Techniques: facilitatory (tapping/percussion, vibration, quick stretch, resistance) and inhibitory (prolonged stretch, sustained pressure, rhythmic rocking).
• Indications: motor-control problems, for example stroke (improved mobility, balance, strength, ROM and gait) and paediatric spastic cerebral palsy; combined with exercise, gait training, functional mobility and occupational therapy.
• Precautions: population, age group, contraindications, risks and safety measures appear only as headings.

(c)
• Appropriate sensory input evokes or inhibits the desired muscle response, normalises tone and rebuilds motor engrams from reflex to skilled movement. Case: a 6-year-old with spastic CP had, after six months, lower tone, smoother coordinated movement and more independent sitting, standing and assisted walking.
• Case insights: early intervention, consistent sensory-motor technique application and family involvement are important.

(d)
• Facilitatory techniques (with sympathetic activation) are chosen to raise activity in hypotonic, somnolent patients; inhibitory techniques (with parasympathetic activation) to reduce excessive tone in hypertonic, hyperkinetic patients such as the spastic child.
• Today only some Rood techniques are common in practice, though current evidence supports valid components.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the origin, principles and basic concepts of Rood's approach.
(b) State its techniques and indications.
(c) State its rationale and expected effects.
(d) Explain the basis for choosing facilitatory rather than inhibitory techniques (or the reverse) in a given patient.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Hydrocephalus (build-up of CSF in the ventricles; here acquired/obstructive after haemorrhage blocks CSF exit from the ventricles). Risk factors: prematurity before 34 weeks or under 1.8 kg (high risk of intraventricular haemorrhage), recent head trauma, meningitis, tumours, subarachnoid haemorrhage, genetic aqueductal stenosis, neural tube defects such as spina bifida.

(b)
Pressure from excess CSF damages brain tissue and causes a spectrum of impairment in brain function: seizures, vomiting, sleepiness, poor feeding, deficits in muscle tone and strength, poor responsiveness to touch, poor growth, later poor balance and coordination, developmental delay, learning and cognitive problems, incontinence.

(c)
• Prevention: prenatal care to reduce premature birth, adequate folic acid before and after conception (NTDs), prompt treatment of infections such as meningitis, helmets and careful handling to prevent head injury, safe home to prevent falls.
• Medical: shunt system (shunt, catheter, one-way valve) diverting CSF to the abdomen (or heart chamber/lung area). Physiotherapy: promote milestones (sitting, standing, crawling), independent mobility, balance and coordination exercises, stretching/strengthening, confidence, stamina.
• Teaching is task-oriented and intermittent rather than rote; problem-solving by the child; family-centred, transdisciplinary care in natural environments.

(d)
Task-oriented, family-centred milestone training is justified because the common goal is increased functional activity and motor learning depends on child problem-solving. Prognosis is difficult to predict (cause, associated disorders, timeliness, treatment success).
questions.question:
A premature infant born before 34 weeks and weighing under 1.8 kg develops intraventricular haemorrhage. The head is enlarging rapidly, the fontanel is bulging, the eyes are fixed downward, and the infant is irritable and feeds poorly.
(a) Identify the condition and the risk factors.
(b) State the complications and secondary impairments.
(c) Outline the preventive measures and management options, including physiotherapy.
(d) Justify one physiotherapy option.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Erb's palsy, a form of obstetric brachial plexus palsy (OBPP), from injury to the upper roots (C5, C6).

(b)
Features: affects muscles of the ipsilateral shoulder and elbow; waiter's/porter's tip position; contractures are liable to occur in these positions without treatment. Predisposing: baby weight (single most significant), breech delivery, birth canal disproportion.

(c)
• Brachial plexus: ventral rami C5-C8 and most of T1; C5+C6 form the upper trunk, C7 the middle, C8+T1 the lower; trunks divide into anterior and posterior divisions forming lateral, medial and posterior cords, which give the musculocutaneous, median, ulnar, radial and axillary nerves. Injury of the roots at birth interrupts these pathways (peripheral nerve lesion, LMN).
• Brachial plexus lesions are the most severe upper-limb nerve injuries; Klumpke's paralysis (C8, T1) is the less common lower-root form causing claw hand.

(d)
• Prognosis: about 90% recover fully in 3-6 months; surgery only for severe cases or fixed deformity.
• Physiotherapy after confirming the diagnosis: passive ROM stretching to prevent deformity, tactile stimulation, positioning, taping (e.g. kinesiotape), electrical stimulation, facilitation of normal movement patterns while inhibiting substitutions.
• Splint if severe: shoulder abducted to shoulder level and externally rotated, elbow semi-flexed, forearm supinated, wrist usually extended.
• Older children: play activities for ROM and strength; promote independence in washing, eating, dressing; maximise hand function; encourage positive self-image with parents' involvement.
questions.question:
A newborn delivered by breech, with a high birth weight, lies with the arm at the side of the trunk, internally rotated at the shoulder, unable to bend the elbow or supinate the forearm, and with the fingers clenched (waiter's tip position).
(a) Give the diagnosis.
(b) State the clinical features and predisposing factors.
(c) Explain the pathophysiology and the anatomy involved.
(d) Outline the physiotherapy management.

A patient has progressive weakness of the arms and legs, chronic severe pain and stiffness, loss of pain and temperature sensation in a cape-like distribution, but preserved proprioception and vibration sense. The arms show lower motor neuron paralysis, the legs bilateral spastic paralysis with a positive Babinski response, and there is loss of bladder function. Horner's syndrome may be present.
(a) Identify the lesion site and the system affected.
(b) State the affected functions and explain the sensory pattern.
(c) State the differential conditions.
(d) Give the clinical reasoning for the physiotherapy plan.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Syringomyelia: cystic expansion (syrinx) in the spinal canal from obstruction of CSF flow; common in the brain stem and cervical regions (central cervical cord). Communicating type: Chiari malformation; non-communicating: post-traumatic, post-infection (meningitis), tumour, haemorrhage.

(b)
The cyst damages the anterior white commissure where pain and temperature fibres (lateral spinothalamic tract) cross, giving cape-like loss, while the posterior columns are spared so proprioception and vibration are preserved. Arm LMN paralysis reflects destruction of anterior horn cells; bilateral spastic leg paralysis with Babinski reflects long-tract involvement; bladder function is lost.

(c)
Differentials among cord syndromes: central cord syndrome (arm weakness greater than leg, loss of pain and temperature, burning in the arms, partial bowel/bladder dysfunction; also caused by trauma and intrinsic cord tumours); anterior cord (all functions lost except posterior column functions); Brown-Sequard (ipsilateral motor loss, contralateral pain/temperature loss); posterior cord (profound ataxia).

(d)
• Medical management: surgery to remove the syrinx or aspiration of CSF; physiotherapy assessment and management follow the SCI plan.
• Assessment: continuous, with vital signs, skin, limb placement; completeness and neurological level; all sensory modalities; spasticity (Ashworth, Tardieu); function (Katz index, FIM, SCIM); associated injuries.
• Treatment: maintain/improve respiratory function and prevent complications; maintain and strengthen innervated muscles and facilitate functional patterns of activity; treat pain; train function and reintegration; address psychosocial concerns; evaluate with outcome measures.
• Reasoning: mixed LMN (arms) and UMN (legs) signs, sensory dissociation, pain and bladder loss determine an individualised, non-blanket plan.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the early detection and diagnosis of cerebral palsy in infancy and the barriers to early diagnosis.
(b) Describe the physiotherapy and related management from infancy through childhood, stating the goals and interventions and the classification/outcome tools.
(c) Explain how complications and secondary impairments are prevented or managed.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Diagnosis often occurs at 12-24 months in high-income countries and up to 5 years in low-resource settings, after the optimal window for interventions that use developing-brain plasticity. A 2017 guideline says CP can often be diagnosed under 6 months, even at 3 months corrected age, by combining tools with clinical reasoning.
• Best tools under 5 months in high-risk infants: General Movements Assessment (sensitivity 98%, specificity 91% at fidgety age), MRI at term-equivalent age, and Hammersmith Infant Neurological Examination; cranial ultrasound lowers age at diagnosis. Hand Assessment of Infants is used for unilateral CP.
• Barriers: no definitive biomarker, fear of false positives, difficult conversations, wish to exclude every treatable differential, lack of cure and of evidence for early intervention, and lack of definite signs on traditional examination. Half of children with CP have no newborn risk factor such as prematurity.
• Diagnosis and classification are separate in infants; early diagnosis allows access to CP-specific early interventions (e.g. baby constraint-induced movement therapy) and early psychological support for parents.

(b)
• Management starts with very early assessment and treatment and must be individualised, age-appropriate and multidisciplinary (developmental, physical, medical, surgical, pharmacological, technical) with the family playing a major role; aim: physical independence and fitness in the community and better quality of life.
• Physiotherapy: Bobath/NDT, neuromuscular electrical stimulation, exercise therapy, hydrotherapy, body-weight-supported treadmill, patterning, conductive education, CIMT, Vojta, sensory integration, suit therapy; balance training; adaptive equipment. Botulinum toxin (reinjection every 4-6 months), orthopaedic surgery and selective dorsal rhizotomy, occupational therapy and speech therapy.
• Classification and outcome tools: GMFCS levels I-V by age band (0-2, 2-4, 4-6, 6-12, 12-18) based on head control, transitions, walking and running; combined with tools for extent and location and documentation of upper-limb function and speech; Hypertonicity Assessment Tool for older children.

(c)
• Secondary problems listed: feeding/swallowing difficulty, seizures, scoliosis, hip dislocation, contracture, constipation/incontinence, GORD, sleep problems, learning disability, eye problems.
• Prevention/management: physiotherapy to prevent muscle weakening and contracture, adaptive equipment, braces and orthotics (facilitated by reducing tone), botulinum toxin, orthopaedic surgery for scoliosis and hip dislocation, speech and language therapy for communication and swallowing.
• Total-body involvement carries a higher risk of complications; the damage is non-progressive but the picture changes with growth.
• Neuroplasticity - growth of new cells, repair of damaged cells and reorganisation - is the biological basis for early intervention.

(a)
• Developed by Australian physiotherapists Janet Carr and Roberta Shepherd (University of Sydney), applying neuroscience findings on motor control and relearning. It is a task-oriented technique to regain or improve motor control after neurological damage, grounded in brain reorganisation even in adulthood.
• Rationale: neuroplasticity, task specificity, meaningful context, active participation. Procedure rests on three factors: elimination of unnecessary muscle activity, feedback and practice; the therapist needs analysis, decision making, action taking and re-evaluation skills.
• Seven sections: upper limb function, orofacial function, sitting up from supine, sitting, standing up and sitting down, standing, walking.
• Steps: analyse the task (missing components, timing errors, lack of muscle activity, excessive activity, compensations); practise missing components (30-60 min or more, or twice daily; brief instructions; verbal and visual feedback; manual guidance; monitor alignment); practise the activity (increase complexity and variety, decrease feedback and guidance); transfer learning (opportunity and consistency of practice, relatives and staff, reinforcement, stimulating environment).

(b)
• Applications: reaching and grasping, walking and stairs, balance and transfers, communication, self-care. Guiding principles: task-oriented therapy, motor plus cognitive and perceptual function, movement on the injured side, cues, discourage compensation, avoid muscle shortening (spasticity), lively functional setting.
• Challenges for patients: cognitive demands, time-intensive, frustration with slow progress. For therapists: time constraints, advanced skills, physical demands, limited evidence base.

(c)
• Benefits: functional gains in ADL, enhanced neuroplasticity through repetition, increased motor control and independence, confidence and motivation, transfer to real life.
• Therapist benefits: structured goal-oriented framework, possibly shorter therapy, patient-centred goals, creativity and problem solving.

(d)
• It is chosen when task-specific, functional relearning is wanted for reaching, walking, transfers and self-care, with the patient actively participating.
• It often complements other therapies for holistic rehabilitation and is tailored to each patient with gradual progression and positive reinforcement.
• Factors affecting motor learning (verbal instruction, session variability, active participation and motivation, chance to make mistakes, postural control, memory, feedback) support this choice.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the motor relearning programme (Carr and Shepherd): its origin, rationale, procedure and the sections it covers.
(b) State its indications and challenges.
(c) State its rationale and expected effects.
(d) Explain the basis for choosing the motor relearning programme in a patient with a neurological deficit.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Clinically isolated syndrome (CIS), optic neuritis type: a first episode of CNS inflammation and demyelination lasting at least 24 h, not due to fever/infection; a possible precursor of MS, especially with brain lesions on MRI. Stage: usually a monophasic first event that may progress to relapsing-remitting MS.
• Other types: brainstem syndrome and spinal cord syndrome (transverse myelitis). Mechanism: autoimmune attack on CNS myelin (T and B cells cross the blood-brain barrier) causing inflammation, demyelination and axonal injury.

(b)
• Tools: detailed history (onset, duration, pattern, previous episodes, triggers, family history); neurological examination of vision, movement, coordination, sensation, reflexes; gait/balance (TUG, Berg Balance Scale); Oxford muscle grading; fatigue severity; visual and sensory impairments.
• Expected: vision loss or blurring, pain on eye movement, colour desaturation, diplopia, vertigo; investigations show white-matter lesions on MRI (periventricular, juxtacortical, infratentorial), oligoclonal bands in CSF, slowed optic-nerve conduction on VEP.

(c)
Goals: improve mobility and reduce spasticity; enhance coordination and balance; reduce fatigue and improve endurance; educate on energy conservation and safe movement; preserve function and prevent deconditioning.

(d)
• Exercise-based approach: strengthening of affected limbs; static and dynamic balance training (one-leg stand, stepping tasks, coordination drills, BOSU ball, wobble board, tandem walk); gait re-education with cane/walker as needed; stretching for tightness.
• Aerobic exercise (walking, stationary cycling, aquatic, treadmill) starting at low intensity (Borg 3-4) and progressing gradually; fatigue management with the 4 P's (Prioritize, Plan, Pace, Position) and breathing exercises.

(e)
• Medical: IV methylprednisolone then oral prednisolone; disease-modifying therapy if high MS risk (interferon beta, glatiramer acetate, dimethyl fumarate, teriflunomide; monoclonal antibodies if risk very high).
• Symptom management: fatigue; neuropathic pain (gabapentin, pregabalin, duloxetine); psychological and social support; surgery only for other underlying conditions.

(f)
Education: energy conservation and safe movement, pacing with the 4 P's, early detection and follow-up (MRI) because not all CIS becomes MS, and awareness of possible relapse, residual deficits or cognitive change; physiotherapy and education empower the patient and improve quality of life.
questions.question:
A young adult presents with a first episode of neurological symptoms lasting at least 24 hours and not caused by fever or infection: loss of vision in one eye, pain on eye movement and poor colour vision. MRI shows white-matter lesions.
(a) State the diagnosis, its type and the stage of the disease process.
(b) List the physiotherapy assessment tools and tests you would use and the findings expected.
(c) State the treatment goals.
(d) Name the treatment approach and the specific interventions.
(e) State the other (medical) management.
(f) Outline the education you would give the patient.

A woman who had paralytic poliomyelitis in childhood now reports, some 30-40 years later, new muscle weakness, fatigue, pain, muscle atrophy, cold intolerance and breathing difficulty. She has residual disability but no viral shedding.
(a) State the probable diagnosis.
(b) Describe the underlying condition, its pathophysiology and aetiology.
(c) Describe your physiotherapy assessment (subjective and objective findings).
(d) Draw up the problem list.
(e) State the physiotherapy management and how it is progressed.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Post-polio syndrome: occurs in 25-40% of cases of paralytic polio after a latent period of 30-40 years, with permanent residual disability, no shedding of polio virus, and commoner in females.

(b)
• Poliomyelitis is a contagious viral infection of the anterior horn cells of the grey matter and motor nuclei of cranial nerves (a lower motor neuron disease). Anterior horn cells are somatotopically organised (medial cells serve proximal muscles, lateral cells distal muscles) and each supplies hundreds to thousands of muscle fibres.
• Infection is non-paralytic in most cases; paralytic polio is about 1% of infections, in spinal, bulbar and bulbospinal forms. Paralytic polio gives asymmetrical flaccid paralysis with diminished deep tendon reflexes, legs more than arms, proximal more than distal; respiratory, facial, pharyngeal, laryngeal and tongue muscles may be paralysed.

(c)
Subjective: onset of weakness, fatigue, pain, cold intolerance, swallowing/speech and breathing difficulty, history of acute polio. Objective: muscle strength and atrophy, tone and reflexes (LMN pattern), bulbar function and respiratory function.

(d)
Muscle weakness, fatigue, pain, muscle atrophy, cold intolerance, bulbar dysfunction, respiratory problems, muscle tightness and contracture.

(e)
• Relieve pain with TENS, hot packs and hydrotherapy; strengthen weak muscle with graded therapeutic exercise; manage fatigue with endurance training; treat tightness and contracture with stretching.
• Progression follows grading of exercise.

(a)
Parkinson's disease (idiopathic parkinsonism, the 'shaking palsy'/paralysis agitans): progressive degenerative disorder of the basal ganglia.

(b)
• Cardinal features: bradykinesia (slowness with loss of amplitude/speed), rest tremor (4-5 Hz pill-rolling), rigidity (cogwheel, flexor and extensor), postural and gait impairment (stooped posture, falls). Also freezing, festinating gait, hypomimia, drooling, fixed postures, fatigue, swallowing/communication difficulty, autonomic and cognitive change.
• Symptoms start on one side; tremor at onset predicts slower progression; early non-motor signs: loss of smell, constipation, REM sleep behaviour disorder, mood disorder, orthostatic hypotension. Subtypes: tremor-dominant, akinetic-rigid, postural instability/gait difficulty.
• Predisposing: age (about 1% over 55, 2.6% by 85; mean onset 58-62; young onset under 40 in up to 10%); genetic and environmental influences; secondary parkinsonism from infection, toxins (manganese, carbon monoxide, cyanide, ethanol), drugs (chlorpromazine, haloperidol, thioridazine, reserpine), tumours, hypothyroidism, atypical (multiple system atrophy).

(c)
• Loss of dopamine-producing neurons in the substantia nigra (pars compacta) with dopamine deficiency in the corpus striatum (caudate, putamen); 60-80% of cells are lost before symptoms appear.
• Dopamine falls while acetylcholine is relatively increased, so excessive excitatory output activates skeletomotor and fusimotor systems via corticospinal, reticulospinal and rubrospinal pathways, causing rigidity and bradykinesia; tremor may relate to low serotonin; norepinephrine loss may explain fatigue and blood-pressure change.

(d)
• No cure; medical (anticholinergics, levodopa/carbidopa, dopamine agonists, amantadine) and surgical (stereotaxic lesions to reduce tremor and rigidity) care. PT goals: full functional ROM, prevent contractures and faulty posture, prevent disuse atrophy, posture/balance awareness and safety, functional gait, keep vital capacity/chest expansion/speech, endurance.
• Means: ROM exercise; strengthen weak elongated extensors and stretch tight flexors; rhythmic, reciprocal, rotational functional mobility from dependent to upright positions; relaxation techniques; balance training starting with slow weight shifts; diaphragmatic and basal breathing exercises.
• Gait training: lengthen stride, broaden base, increase trunk rotation and arm swing, heel-toe pattern, weight transference, regular walking; daily aerobic walking; teach gestes antagonistes; assistive devices; educate patient and family on medication, regular exercise and avoiding inactivity.
questions.question:
A middle-aged or elderly person has a rhythmic pill-rolling tremor of one hand at rest that disappears with active movement and during sleep, slowness and difficulty initiating movement, stiffness with a cogwheel feel, a stooped posture, reduced facial expression, and small accelerating steps with sudden episodes of being unable to move. Symptoms began on one side of the body.
(a) Give the diagnosis.
(b) Describe the clinical features and the predisposing factors.
(c) Explain the pathophysiology.
(d) Outline the physiotherapy management.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Prematurity (before 32 weeks): greater chance of CP; babies born very early survive more often now but have medical problems that put them at risk. Low birth weight (under 1,500 g; also under 2,500 g) increases the chance.
• Jaundice: bilirubin builds up in the blood; untreated severe jaundice causes kernicterus, which can cause CP (may follow ABO/Rh incompatibility that breaks red cells down too fast). Maternal thyroid problems (also intellectual disability or seizures) give a slightly higher risk.
• Another risk not present in this history: birth complications (placental detachment, uterine rupture, cord problems) that disrupt oxygen supply.

(b)
Feeding, drooling and swallowing difficulties; constipation/urinary incontinence; seizures; sleep problems; GORD; scoliosis; easily dislocating hips; learning disability (about half); speech, hearing and eye problems. Musculoskeletal problems: muscle weakening, deterioration and contracture. Complications are more likely when the whole body is involved.

(c)
• Preventing secondary problems: very early assessment, diagnosis and treatment; physiotherapy to prevent weakening, deterioration and contracture; adaptive equipment (wheelchairs, walkers); braces.
• Other options: botulinum toxin for spastic/dystonic muscles (reversible, re-injection every 4-6 months; aids bracing); orthopaedic surgery (range, scoliosis, hip dislocation); selective dorsal rhizotomy (severe leg tightness); occupational and speech therapy.
• Physiotherapy options: Bobath/NDT, neuromuscular electrical stimulation, exercise therapy, hydrotherapy, body-weight-supported treadmill, patterning, conductive education, constraint-induced therapy, Vojta, sensory integration, suit therapy. Historical approaches: Phelps, Fay, Collis, Brunnstrom, Kabat (PNF).

(d)
• Bobath/NDT justified: reflex-inhibiting patterns inhibit abnormal tone; the child gets the sensation of more normal tone and movement and is prepared for movement and mature postural reactions using key points of control (head/neck, shoulder and pelvic girdles).
• Programme must be individualised, age- and function-appropriate, multidisciplinary, aimed at physical independence and fitness in the community, with the family playing a major role; neuroplasticity (growth of new cells, repair, reorganisation) supports early intervention.
questions.question:
A child was born before the 32nd week of pregnancy with a birth weight below 1,500 g. The neonate developed severe jaundice, and the mother has a thyroid problem. By the age of 2-3 years the child shows stiff muscles, poor muscle control and delayed motor development.
(a) Identify the risk factors in this history that predispose to cerebral palsy and state how each acts.
(b) State the complications and secondary impairments the child may develop.
(c) Outline the preventive measures and the physiotherapy and other management options available.
(d) Justify one physiotherapy option you would select.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• X: upper motor neuron lesion (first-order neurons; descending pyramidal/corticospinal and extrapyramidal pathways: reticulospinal, vestibulospinal, tectospinal, rubrospinal) that control the lower motor neurons. Bilateral involvement gives pseudobulbar palsy.
• Y: lower motor neuron lesion (final common pathway: anterior horn cells, peripheral nerve, neuromuscular junction, muscle). Involvement of VII, IX, X, XII gives bulbar palsy.

(b)
Both lose voluntary movement (paresis or paralysis): UMNs convey impulses for voluntary motor activity and control the LMNs, which carry the final motor output to muscle.

(c)
• UMN: stroke (contralateral corticospinal tract hemiplegia), cord lesions, MS, TBI, tumours. LMN: anterior horn cell disease (poliomyelitis), peripheral nerve lesions and neuropathies, neuromuscular junction disease (myasthenia gravis), myopathies. ALS shows LMN signs superimposed on UMN signs.
• Contrast: UMN = slight wasting, spasticity/hypertonia, hyperreflexia with clonus, diminished superficial reflexes, no fasciculation. LMN = marked atrophy, flaccidity/hypotonia, diminished or absent reflexes, unaltered superficial reflexes, fasciculation.

(d)
UMN pattern: plan addresses spasticity and abnormal reflexes and facilitates voluntary movement (PNF, Brunnstrom, Bobath, Rood, motor relearning). LMN pattern: plan addresses flaccid weakness and atrophy with strengthening and electrical muscle stimulation, ROM to prevent deformity and splinting.
questions.question:
Patient X has loss of voluntary movement with only slight muscle wasting, increased tone with ankle clonus, brisk reflexes, diminished superficial reflexes and a Babinski sign. Patient Y has loss of voluntary movement with marked muscle atrophy, flaccidity, fasciculations, diminished or absent reflexes and intact superficial reflexes.
(a) Identify the type and site of lesion in each patient.
(b) State the functions affected.
(c) State the differential conditions for each.
(d) Give the clinical reasoning for the physiotherapy plan.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Guillain-Barré syndrome is an acute demyelinating polyneuropathy: acquired and immune-mediated, preceded by respiratory or GIT infection; immunisation, surgery or lead exposure may precipitate it.
• Epidemiology: incidence 1-2 per 100,000, higher in men, no geographical clustering, any age but commonest between 30 and 50 years.
• Drug management (usually within the nadir): steroids, immunoglobulin therapy, plasmapheresis.

(b)
• Polyneuropathies are disorders of peripheral nerves with sensory and motor involvement, symmetrical, with sensory loss progressing distal to proximal. Diabetic: distal symmetrical sensory neuropathy (aching pain, numbness, loss of joint position sense) and proximal motor neuropathy (asymmetrical wasting/weakness of iliopsoas, quadriceps, hip adductors); recovery depends on glycaemic control.
• Alcoholic: secondary to long-term alcohol abuse; weakness progresses from the feet proximally, myalgia, dysaesthesia, autonomic dysfunction, ataxia. Other causes: HIV/AIDS, leprosy, renal disease, neoplasm and malignancies.

(c)
Physiotherapy: maintain respiratory function with pulmonary exercises; strengthen weak muscles with graded therapeutic exercises; prevent deformities with ROM and stretching; relieve pain with thermotherapy used cautiously; electrical stimulation.

(d)
GBS: acute, demyelinating, post-infectious/immune, respiratory risk, treated with immunotherapy and plasmapheresis. Diabetic neuropathy: occurs in patients with diabetes, distal sensory (and proximal motor) picture, outcome tied to glycaemic control.

(e)
• Mononeuritis: one nerve involved (e.g. carpal tunnel syndrome). Mononeuritis multiplex: multiple peripheral nerves involved over time. Polyneuritis/polyneuropathy: symmetrical involvement in a glove-and-stocking pattern.
• Neuritis can be due to viral infection, mechanical injury, vascular causes, toxins/allergy and metabolic disease.
• GBS is also mentioned as a cause of accessory nerve neuropathy, and OMAS is often initially misdiagnosed as GBS, which has a distinct pattern of nerve damage.
• Neuropathies are also a cause of the sensory disturbance that physiotherapists test for, along with diabetes mellitus, thiamine deficiency and neurotoxins.
questions.question:
(a) Define Guillain-Barré syndrome and describe its aetiology, epidemiology and medical management.
(b) Describe polyneuropathy, including diabetic and alcoholic neuropathy and other causes.
(c) State the physiotherapy management of Guillain-Barré syndrome.
(d) Distinguish between Guillain-Barré syndrome and diabetic neuropathy.
(e) Distinguish between mononeuritis, mononeuritis multiplex and polyneuropathy.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Parkinson's disease, Hoehn-Yahr stage III. Scale: I minimal or absent, unilateral; II minimal bilateral or midline, balance not impaired; III impaired righting reflexes, unsteadiness on turning or rising, some restriction but independent; IV all symptoms severe, standing/walking only with assistance; V confined to bed or wheelchair.

(b)
• Assess rigidity to passive movement and limits on active movement; goniometry for active/passive ROM; stopwatch movement time to quantify bradykinesia; posture (forward-flexed posture shifting centre of gravity); endurance (hills, stairs); gait (freezing, festinating gait, difficulty initiating); strength; flexibility; breathing/pulmonary function; balance and home safety.
• Laboratory tests, EEG and CT help exclude other causes.

(c)
Goals: promote full functional ROM; prevent contractures and faulty posture; prevent disuse atrophy and weakness; enhance awareness of posture, balance reactions and safety; promote functional gait; maintain vital capacity, chest expansion and speech; maintain or improve endurance.

(d)
• Restorative exercise programme: ROM; strengthen weak elongated extensors while stretching shortened flexors; mobility exercise from functional movement patterns, rhythmic and reciprocal, with postural and rotational activities, progressing from dependent to upright unsupported positions.
• Balance: begin with low-velocity weight shifts in sitting and standing. Gait: lengthen stride, broaden base, increase trunk rotation and arm swing, heel-to-toe, weight transference, regular walking. Breathing: diaphragmatic and basal chest wall exercises. Conditioning: daily walking.

(e)
Postural instability is a major cause of falls, so safety awareness and home changes are emphasised; drug adverse effects (dizziness, dyskinesias, confusion, hallucinations) should be noted.

(f)
Educate patient and family about PD and the goals of medical and rehabilitation care, about medications (purpose, side effects, dose), the importance of regular exercise and avoidance of prolonged inactivity.
questions.question:
A patient with Parkinson's disease has impaired righting reflexes and unsteadiness when turning or rising from a chair. Some activities are restricted but the patient lives independently and continues some employment.
(a) State the disease stage and describe the staging scale.
(b) List the assessment tools and tests and the findings expected.
(c) State the treatment goals.
(d) Name the treatment approach and techniques.
(e) State the precautions.
(f) Outline patient and family education.

(a) Describe neurodynamics and the mechanical behaviour of the nervous system, including areas where nerves are vulnerable.
(b) State the neurodynamic tests, the procedure of assessment, and the principles and indications of neural mobilisation.
(c) State the rationale and expected effects of neural mobilisation.
(d) Explain the basis for choosing indirect treatment (posture and ergonomic advice) over direct mobilisation of the nervous system.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Neurodynamics is the science of the interaction between mechanics and physiology of the nervous system; it involves placing mechanical stress on the nervous system to evaluate length and mobility of its components.
• The CNS is a dynamic organ with plastic and elastic properties, mechanically and physiologically continuous. Tissues adjacent to the nervous system that can move independently are the mechanical interface; pathology there can abnormally move nerves and raise tension in the nerve.
• The nervous system adapts to load by elongation, sliding, change in cross-sectional area, angulation and compression; sensitisers can further provoke responses.
• Vulnerable sites: tunnels (carpal and tarsal), branches (medial and lateral plantar nerves), hard interfaces (radial nerve in the spinal groove) and superficial nerves; damaged nerves show altered conduction, loss of elasticity and mechanosensitivity.

(b)
• Assessment: the therapist passively moves limb and trunk to gauge mobility and sensitivity of the nervous system and to identify disorders suitable for mobilisation (inflammatory or biomechanical); structures moved include neuraxis, meninges and nerve roots.
• Tests: straight leg raise, slump test, upper limb neurodynamic tests, passive neck flexion test (Lhermitte's).
• Neural mobilisation treats adverse neurodynamics; approaches: direct mobilisation with sliders and tensioners, treatment of the mechanical interface and related tissues, and indirect treatment by postural advice and ergonomic design.

(c)
• Rationale: restore the dynamic balance between movement of neural tissues, reduce intrinsic pressure on neural tissue and promote optimum physiological function.
• Neuroadaptation (the processes by which the initial effects of a drug or exercise are enhanced or attenuated) is a related concept.

(d)
• Indirect treatment addresses the mechanical interface and causes of adverse loading by changing posture and workstation design.
• Choice depends on the findings of the neurodynamic examination (inflammatory versus biomechanical compromise).

questions.question:
(a) Describe the mechanisms and classification of traumatic brain injury.
(b) Describe the physiotherapy management in the acute stage and in the rehabilitation phase, stating goals and interventions.
(c) State the assessment/outcome measures available.
(d) Explain how complications and secondary impairments are prevented or managed.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• TBI arises from external forces (direct contact with the skull or a penetrating object, acceleration/deceleration, blast). Primary injury occurs at impact: contact injury (contusion, laceration, intracerebral haematoma), acceleration/deceleration (diffuse axonal injury, tissue tearing, haemorrhage), blast (oedema, contusion, DAI, haematoma).
• Secondary injury develops over hours to days from hypoxaemia, hypotension, ischaemia, oedema and raised ICP, leading to herniation in severe cases; results in extradural (middle meningeal bleed), subdural or intracerebral haematoma and subarachnoid haemorrhage. Severity (mild, moderate, severe) is classified by Glasgow Coma Scale, duration of loss of consciousness and post-traumatic amnesia.

(b)
• Acute stage: control ICP through positioning and management; minimise activities that raise intrathoracic pressure; avoid neck flexion or positions that impede cerebral venous drainage while maintaining perfusion; promote respiratory function; prevent complications; assess sensorimotor deficit and cranial nerves; treat as often as tolerated in short sessions with rests.
• Impairments to address: cognitive (attention, memory, executive function, information processing), physical (motor function, balance, endurance, fatigue, deconditioning), behavioural and psychosocial.
• Rehabilitation interventions: task-oriented approach (extensive task-specific practice induces neuroplastic change), gait and balance training (tandem walking), constraint-induced therapy, electrical stimulation, resistance training, splints, dual-task training, PNF, patient/family/caregiver education.
• Technology: robot-assisted gait training (more repetitions, better neuroplasticity), virtual reality for motor and cognitive training (motivation, repetition, real-time feedback), computer-based cognitive rehabilitation, telerehabilitation, non-invasive neuromodulation devices.
• Assistive devices chosen by a team (PT, counsellors, physicians, engineers) according to function, tasks and environment: aids for daily living (grab bars, ramps, adapted utensils, nonslip surfaces), mobility technology (wheelchairs, scooters, stairlifts), seating and positioning, augmentative communication.

(c)
Severity measures: Glasgow Coma Scale, duration of coma and post-traumatic amnesia.

(d)
• Complications: post-concussion syndrome, chronic traumatic encephalopathy, PTSD and adjustment disorders, plus fatigue and deconditioning. Secondary-injury prevention is through ICP control, respiratory promotion and careful positioning.
• Fatigue and deconditioning are addressed by resistance training and graded functional practice.
• DAI: widespread tearing of white-matter fibres causing immediate unconsciousness and, in severe form, cognitive, memory and motor deficits; may not be visible initially on CT/MRI.
• Family and caregiver education and a team approach support the recovery process, which relies on neuroplasticity from repetition.

(a)
Group of non-progressive but often changing motor impairment syndromes from lesions/anomalies of the developing brain (before, during or after birth); chronic, non-fatal, non-curable; affects movement and posture (motor cortex).

(b)
Low birth weight (under 2,500 g, especially under 1,500 g); premature birth (before 37 weeks, especially before 32); birth complications (placental detachment, uterine rupture, cord problems reduce oxygen); jaundice/kernicterus (bilirubin; ABO/Rh incompatibility); maternal thyroid problems, intellectual disability or seizures.

(c)
• Motor type: spastic/pyramidal (commonest, about 80%); non-spastic/extrapyramidal = dyskinetic (athetoid, dystonic) and ataxic (rarest); mixed. Topography: monoplegia, diplegia, hemiplegia, paraplegia, triplegia, double hemiplegia, tetraplegia, quadriplegia, pentaplegia.
• Severity: mild (moves without assistance), moderate (needs braces, medication, adaptive technology), severe (wheelchair); GMFCS levels I-V, a universal system based on what the child can do, combined with other systems.

(d)
Exaggerated reflexes, stiff muscles, poor coordination/balance; floppy or stiff baby, delayed development (cannot sit or roll by 6 months), feeding/swallowing difficulty, prefers one side; not walking by 12-18 months. Associated: seizures, learning disability (about half), mental retardation in 25-50%, speech/hearing/vision problems, drooling, GORD, constipation/incontinence, sleep problems, scoliosis, hip dislocation.

(e)
The damage is non-progressive, but the picture changes as the undamaged nervous system develops and the child grows; symptoms become more or less evident with age and are usually noticeable only in the first 2-3 years.

(f)
Spastic quadriplegia involves the trunk and the muscles controlling mouth, tongue and windpipe, making eating and talking difficult; babies may have sucking and swallowing problems and a weak or shrill cry.

(g)
• Spastic: increased tone (hypertonia), tight muscles that cannot relax, stiff joints, exaggerated reflexes. Dyskinetic: tone fluctuates between loose and tight with slow writhing (athetosis/chorea) or jerky involuntary movements of face, neck, limbs, trunk.
• Dyskinetic also: drooling, speech difficulty, facial expression problems; dystonic form holds body and neck stiff. Non-spastic CP shows decreased or fluctuating tone (hypotonia).
• Ataxic form (for contrast): uncoordinated jerky movements, poor balance, intention tremor, feet wide apart.

(h)
• Spastic diplegia: stiffness mainly in the legs (arms mildly affected), scissoring gait, toe walking, poor coordination and balance.
• Spastic hemiplegia: one side (arm and leg) involved, with movement difficulty mainly in the arm on the affected side.

(a)
Traumatic brain injury with diffuse axonal injury (DAI) and secondary brain injury; severity is classed as mild, moderate or severe using the Glasgow Coma Scale, period of loss of consciousness and post-traumatic amnesia.

(b)
• External force (skull contact, penetrating object, acceleration/deceleration, blast). DAI = widespread tearing of white-matter fibres causing immediate unconsciousness; common in high-speed vehicle accidents; sites: parasagittal white matter, corpus callosum, pontine-mesencephalic junction; microscopic so may not be visible on CT/MRI initially.
• Secondary injury over hours to days: hypoxaemia, hypotension, ischaemia, oedema, raised ICP (swelling, abnormal fluid dynamics or haematoma) with possible herniation; extradural haematoma from middle meningeal vessels, subdural haematoma from bridging veins, intracerebral haematoma, subarachnoid haemorrhage.

(c)
Assess sensorimotor deficit and cranial nerve involvement, respiratory function; cognitive (attention, memory, executive function, processing), physical (motor function, balance, endurance, fatigue, deconditioning), behavioural and psychosocial status.

(d)
Raised ICP and respiratory risk, cognitive deficits, motor and balance deficits, fatigue and deconditioning, behavioural/psychosocial problems; complications post-concussion syndrome, CTE, PTSD and adjustment disorders.

(e)
• Acute: position and manage to control ICP; minimise activities that raise intrathoracic pressure; avoid neck flexion or positions impeding venous drainage but keep cerebral perfusion; promote respiratory function; prevent complications; treat as often as tolerated in short sessions with rests.
• Rehabilitation: task-oriented approach with extensive practice, gait and balance training (tandem walking), constraint-induced therapy, electrical stimulation, resistance training, splints, dual-task training, robot-assisted gait training, virtual reality and computer-based cognitive rehabilitation, telerehabilitation, neuromodulation devices.
• Assistive technology chosen by a team (PT, counsellors, physicians, engineers): aids for daily living, mobility technology, seating and positioning, augmentative communication; educate patient, family and caregivers.
questions.question:
A young man is brought in after a high-speed motor vehicle accident with immediate loss of consciousness. CT and MRI initially look normal. Hours later he deteriorates with raised intracranial pressure.
(a) State the probable diagnosis.
(b) Explain the pathophysiology and aetiology.
(c) Describe your physiotherapy assessment (subjective and objective).
(d) Draw up the problem list.
(e) State the physiotherapy management, goals and progression.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• PNF: promoting or hastening the response of the neuromuscular mechanism by stimulating proprioceptors; a motor-learning approach that improves motor function and facilitates maximal contraction using proprioceptive, cutaneous and auditory input.
• History: Herman Kabat (late 1930s-40s) used it on CP and other neurological conditions; stimulating distal segments stimulates proximal proprioceptors; based on Sherrington's irradiation, reciprocal innervation and inhibition; Kabat (1951): all people have untapped potential.
• Neurophysiology: stretch reflex (muscle spindles sense length and rate of change), Golgi tendon organs (tension), autogenic inhibition (stretched muscle relaxes, protective), reciprocal inhibition (antagonist relaxes when agonist contracts); facilitation raises and inhibition lowers motor-neuron excitability (reduces spasticity).

(b)
• Principles: manual contact (lumbrical grip), verbal cues (push, hold, pull, relax), vision, resistance throughout movement, traction/approximation, stretch, timing (distal before proximal), irradiation and reinforcement, diagonal patterns, body position/mechanics; patient must learn the pattern.
• Patterns: mass movement diagonals that are spiral and cross the midline (UL D1 and D2 flexion/extension; LL D1 and D2; scapular patterns), used bilaterally as symmetrical, reciprocal or asymmetrical combinations.
• Techniques: agonistic (rhythmic initiation, combination of isotonics, repeated stretch); antagonistic (dynamic reversals, stabilizing reversals, rhythmic stabilization); relaxation (hold-relax, contract-relax, slow reversal-hold-relax).
• Indications: rhythmic initiation for difficulty initiating, ataxia or rigidity; combination of isotonics for poor eccentric control; stabilizing reversals for weakness/instability; dynamic reversals for reduced AROM, fatigue, hypertonia; rhythmic stabilization for limited ROM, pain, joint instability, poor balance.
• Precautions: positive, pain-free approach; relaxation techniques done in comfort below pain; condition level may require modification.

(c)
Rationale/expected effects: increase strength, flexibility, ROM, coordination and functional mobility; facilitate weak muscles and reduce spasticity; improve motor control, gait and balance in stroke and TBI; used in neurological and orthopaedic rehabilitation.

(d)
• Hold-relax: strong isometric contraction in the agonist pattern at the point of limited ROM, then relax (2-3 s) and passive movement into the new range with a 10-15 s stretch; repeated until no more gain.
• Chosen because it is effective when ROM is reduced by muscle tightness or when pain is part of the limitation, and it is performed below the pain level.
• Contract-relax (alternative): strong small-range isotonic contraction of the restricting muscles with emphasis on the rotators, held 7-9 s, then relax and move into new range; used when tightness or guarding limits motion needed for function.
questions.question:
(a) Define proprioceptive neuromuscular facilitation (PNF), outline its history and its neurophysiological basis.
(b) State the principles, patterns, techniques, indications and precautions of PNF.
(c) State the rationale and expected effects of PNF in neurological rehabilitation.
(d) Explain the basis for choosing hold-relax rather than contract-relax in a patient with limited range of motion.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• A broad term for rare, lifelong, progressive neurological disorders (brain, spine, peripheral nerves) that can cause tumours in brain, cord, organs, skin and bone; skin lesions are most common in children; manifest in early childhood and adolescence. Main types: tuberous sclerosis, neurofibromatosis and Sturge-Weber disease.
• Causes: all congenital and genetically inclined; TS and NF are autosomal dominant (many TS cases are new mutations; NF1 chromosome 17, NF2 chromosome 22, 30-50% new mutations); Sturge-Weber is sporadic (cause unknown).

(b)
• Tuberous sclerosis: benign tumours (tubers) in brain and retina and many organs; intellectual disability, developmental delay, seizures, learning disability, autism, skin lesions, kidney and cardiopulmonary complications. NF1: café-au-lait spots, neurofibromas, Lisch nodules, hearing loss, headaches, seizures, scoliosis.
• NF2 (bilateral acoustic neurofibromatosis): eighth nerve tumours with hearing loss, balance problems, meningioma, noticed at 18-22 years. Schwannomatosis: multiple painful schwannomas, vestibular nerve spared. Sturge-Weber: port-wine stain in trigeminal (ophthalmic/maxillary) distribution, meningeal angioma, ipsilateral eye glaucoma; Roach types I-III.
• Diagnosis: history and examination, blood/genetic tests, X-ray, MRI, CT, EEG, eye examination, biopsy.

(c)
Incurable, so symptoms are managed by an interdisciplinary team. Medical: laser for port-wine stain, medication for glaucoma and seizures, surgery (hemispherectomy or focal resection, trabeculotomy, tube shunt), genetic counselling. Physiotherapy: start early; strengthening/resistive exercise; spasticity management and orthoses; CIMT; prevent deformity; maximise independence.

(d)
Residual embryonic blood vessels steal blood from the rest of the cortex ('vascular steal'), causing hypoxic injury and increasing calcification around the angioma, which raises the risk of seizures and neurological deficit; tissue hypertrophy also leads to calcification.

(e)
• NF1: more common, von Recklinghausen's disease, chromosome 17, café-au-lait spots, neurofibromas and Lisch nodules, about 1 in 3,000-4,000 births.
• NF2: rarer (about 1 in 25,000), chromosome 22, bilateral 8th nerve tumours (hearing loss, balance and walking problems), meningioma; café-au-lait spots and skin nodules less common.
• When NF and TS occur together they are called phakomatoses.
• Sturge-Weber effects: seizures (usually within 24 months), hemiparesis, developmental delay, headaches, glaucoma, blindness if untreated, buphthalmos.
• Neurocutaneous conditions are lifelong; positive reinforcement builds self-esteem and independence, and the full extent of disease may only be revealed as the child grows.
questions.question:
(a) Define neurocutaneous syndrome and list its types and causes.
(b) Describe tuberous sclerosis, neurofibromatosis (types 1 and 2, schwannomatosis) and Sturge-Weber disease under the headings of clinical features, pathophysiology and diagnosis.
(c) State the medical and physiotherapy management.
(d) Explain why the neurological symptoms of Sturge-Weber disease are progressive.
(e) Distinguish between neurofibromatosis type 1 and type 2.

(a) Describe the epidemiology and aetiology of spinal cord injury.
(b) Classify spinal cord injury by completeness, level and syndrome.
(c) Describe spinal shock and the clinical features of injury by level.
(d) Explain why autonomic dysreflexia occurs in injuries above T6.
(e) Explain the sensory findings in Brown-Sequard syndrome.
(f) Distinguish between anterior cord and central cord syndromes.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Incidence is higher between 20 and 39 years, male:female about 4:1; about 80% traumatic (falls, road accidents, violence); about 20% non-traumatic (tumour, degenerative and vascular conditions, infection, toxins, birth defects).

(b)
Complete = AIS A (no voluntary anal contraction/sacral sparing, bulbocavernosus reflex present); incomplete = AIS B-E (any S4-S5 sparing), determined between 24 h and 1 month. Neurological level = lowest segment with normal sensory and motor function on both sides. Syndromes: anterior, posterior, central cord, Brown-Sequard, conus medullaris/cauda equina.

(c)
• Spinal shock: transient physiological loss of reflexes immediately after injury with slow heart rate, low BP, flaccid paralysis, sensory loss, paralytic ileus and atonic bladder; lasts minutes to months and gives way to hyper-excitability (strong early spasticity suggests an incomplete lesion).
• By level: C1-C3 fully dependent and ventilated; C4 breathes unaided but with poor cough and hypoventilation; C5 shoulder/elbow flexion; C6 wrist extension; C7-C8 hand movements, can dress, eat, drive, transfer; T1-T4 paraplegia; T5-T9 manual wheelchair; T10-L1 partial lower-body paralysis; L2-S5 some knee, hip, foot movement, walking with aids.
• Complications: osteoporosis, heterotopic ossification, bladder/bowel dysfunction with urosepsis, VTE, pulmonary embolism, pressure ulcers, orthostatic hypotension, bradycardia, autonomic dysreflexia.

(d)
Above T6, descending excitatory and inhibitory input to sympathetic neurons is lost, so noxious stimuli below the lesion trigger unopposed autonomic stimulation with vasoconstriction below T6, vasodilation above, raised heart rate and a massive, life-threatening rise in BP.

(e)
The lateral spinothalamic tract crosses almost immediately, so pain and temperature loss is contralateral to the lesion; posterior columns stay on the same side, so proprioception/stereognosis loss is ipsilateral; motor loss is ipsilateral, with bowel and bladder usually normal.

(f)
• Anterior cord: commonest; flexion injury with compression by bone fragments or a disc; variable motor function, loss of pain and temperature but preserved vibration and proprioception; poor prognosis.
• Central cord: cervical, older patients with degenerative change (spondylosis) or hyperextension; upper limbs weaker than lower; flaccid arms (LMN) with spastic legs; loss of pain and temperature; burning in the arms; partial bowel/bladder dysfunction.
• Brown-Sequard: hemicord (stab injury, tumour, inflammation); ipsilateral motor loss, contralateral pain/temperature loss, normal bladder/bowel, usually walks with bracing. Posterior cord: hyperextension, profound ataxia, Lhermitte's sign on neck flexion.
• Conus medullaris: avulsion of lumbar/sacral roots, UMN or LMN, with or without sacral reflexes. Cauda equina: peripheral nerve damage with flaccid paralysis, saddle anaesthesia and intractable pain relieved only by rest.
• Assessment uses AIS for completeness, Ashworth/Tardieu for spasticity, and Katz index, FIM or SCIM for function.

questions.question:
An 81-year-old woman who lives alone presents with paralysis of the right side of her body (only some finger movement retained) and difficulty speaking, although she understands what is said to her. She can sit unsupported on a plinth but cannot actively move or right herself, uses a wheelchair, and needs help with transfers and dressing. She can feed herself and has no significant cognitive deficit.
(a) State the most probable diagnosis and explain how the side of the lesion accounts for her presentation.
(b) Describe the pathophysiology and aetiology of the condition, including its main types.
(c) Outline your physiotherapy assessment (subjective and objective), naming the systems examined and the tools you would use.
(d) Draw up a problem list of primary and secondary impairments.
(e) State the goals and guiding principles of physiotherapy management.
(f) Describe your interventions in the early, middle and late recovery stages and how you would progress treatment.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Stroke (CVA) with hemiplegia: a left-hemisphere lesion gives right hemiparesis with aphasia and motor-planning deficits (a right CVA gives spatial neglect, poor insight/judgment, impulsiveness). Hemiplegia = total paralysis of one side of the body from brain damage.

(b)
Stroke = sudden, specific neurological deficit of vascular origin. Ischaemic: atherothrombotic occlusion of large/small arteries, cardiac emboli, cerebral hypoperfusion. Haemorrhagic: arterial wall/aneurysmal rupture (intracerebral or subarachnoid). Other causes of hemiplegia: tumour, trauma, MS/demyelinating disease, infection, congenital (CP).

(c)
• Assess mental function and speech; motor system (tone, power, ROM, reflexes); sensory system (superficial, deep, cortical); cranial nerves, pain, cardio-respiratory system, balance, gait, ADL.
• Tools: Fugl-Meyer, ARAT, Wolf Motor Function, Motor Assessment Scale, STREAM, Rivermead Mobility Index; Modified Barthel, FIM; Berg, TUG, Functional Reach; VAS/McGill/NRS (pain); MMSE, Zung depression scale; Stroke-Specific QoL, SF-12/36.

(d)
• Primary: weakness (UE more than LE), loss of selective motor control (stereotyped synergies), abnormal tone (flaccidity to spasticity), asymmetrical weight-bearing and increased sway, sensory disturbance, abnormal reflexes, impaired rolling/transfers/ADL, language impairment.
• Secondary: contractures and deformities, DVT (calf pain, swelling, discolouration), shoulder pain/shoulder-hand syndrome, hand and foot oedema, anxiety/depression, urinary and bowel problems.

(e)
Goals: help the patient relearn skills, regain maximum independence and best quality of life (for her: walk, independent ADL, return home). Principles: problem-solving approach; active motor relearning; functional performance (muscles facilitated in movement patterns, not in isolation); repetition.

(f)
• Early stage (2-6 weeks; start once medically stable, 24-36 h; at least 45 min daily as tolerated): positioning, ROM, electrical and sensory stimulation, active-assisted exercise, rhythmic initiation, bed activities, respiratory exercises.
• Middle (spastic) stage: tone reduction (prolonged stretch, ice, slow stroking); weight-bearing, trunk, hand and pelvic control; supported standing in parallel bars with orthosis; bed mobility and transfers. Late stage: PNF for timing/coordination, stepping, gait and balance training, stair climbing.
• For her: improve postural control and alignment, facilitate weight transfer for balance, movement and transfers, explore arm recovery alongside posture. Other options: FES, EMG biofeedback, NDT/task-oriented approach, splint, walking aids, CIMT, mirror therapy, robot-assisted therapy, VR, motor imagery.
• Prognosis/progression: most UL gain in first 3 months; no voluntary return after a week or after 6 months is unfavourable; poor signs = prolonged flaccidity, severe proximal spasticity, no hand movement for 4-6 weeks. Success depends on early rehabilitation, extent of injury, attitude, team skill, family cooperation.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the physiotherapy management of multiple sclerosis in the relapse phase and the remission/stable phase, stating the goals and interventions.
(b) Explain how complications and secondary impairments of multiple sclerosis are prevented or managed, including the precautions to observe.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Medical background: corticosteroids (methylprednisolone) for relapses; disease-modifying therapies (interferon beta, glatiramer acetate, fingolimod, natalizumab). Physiotherapy works alongside them to improve functional independence, prevent secondary complications and maintain quality of life.
• Overall goals: minimise progression, maintain optimum functional independence, prevent or reduce secondary complications, maintain respiratory function, conserve energy and manage fatigue, educate patient and family.
• Relapse phase: gentle positioning and pressure relief, passive or assisted active ROM, bed mobility training, gentle respiratory exercises, prevention of joint stiffness and maintenance of circulation.
• Remission/stable phase: spasticity management (stretching, positioning, tone-reducing techniques), strengthening, balance and coordination training, gait training with assistive devices, fatigue strategies, low-to-moderate aerobic exercise, ADL retraining.
• Strengthening: begin early before impairments develop, low-to-moderate intensity, frequent repetitions, short bouts with 1-5 min rest; resistance (isokinetic, progressive resistive, hydrotherapy) and PNF; aerobic work after a low-level graded exercise test.
• Stretching: static stretches (supine, sitting, wall) held 30-60 s; weight-bearing and postural control exercises; Frenkel coordination exercises; static and dynamic balance training; splinting and adaptive equipment.
• Symptom-specific: spasticity (stretching, splinting, positioning); fatigue (energy conservation, education); bladder (pelvic floor strengthening, bladder training education); pain/sensory problems (desensitisation, positioning).

(b)
• Contractures and stiffness: positioning, ROM, stretching, splinting; pulmonary complications: respiratory exercises; deconditioning and weakness: strengthening and aerobic training; falls: specialised balance and proprioception training.
• Incontinence: bladder training; spasticity and ataxia: stretching and Frenkel exercises; posture and stability: core strengthening; mobility: canes, walkers or wheelchairs assessed and taught.
• Precautions: avoid overworking and balance rest with exercise; exercise in a cool environment because raised core temperature worsens symptoms (Uhthoff's phenomenon); use electrotherapy with caution.
• Prognosis is highly variable; early DMT improves long-term outcome, progressive forms (especially PPMS) do worse; intensity of physiotherapy depends on the degree of disability.

questions.question:
An infant is born with an open sac on the back through which the spinal cord and nerves protrude, with no skin covering. The mother's diet had insufficient folic acid.
(a) State the diagnosis and the risk factors.
(b) State the complications and secondary impairments that may develop.
(c) Outline the preventive measures and the physiotherapy management options.
(d) Justify one physiotherapy option.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Myelomeningocele, the most severe form of spina bifida (neural elements exposed through the vertebral opening). Neural tube fails to close in the first month; cause is multifactorial (genetic, nutritional, environmental) and insufficient maternal folic acid is a key factor.

(b)
• Flaccid or spastic paralysis below the opening, loss of sensation at pelvis and lower limbs, urinary and bowel incontinence, hydrocephalus, trunk hypotonia, delayed automatic postural reactions.
• Musculoskeletal: scoliosis, hip dysplasia/dislocation, club foot, hip/knee contracture, osteoporosis with severe mobility restriction. Cognitive: effects on memory, learning, concentration and language; learning disability in about half of those with normal intelligence.

(c)
• Prevention: adequate folic acid (prenatal vitamins contain it) before and after conception. Secondary problems: anticipate and prevent contractures, positioning and postural advice, maintain strength and length, balance and coordination exercises to prevent falls.
• Options: maximise independence in standing, transferring and walking; mobility aids (walkers, cane) and equipment; orthotic devices; wheelchair skills; achieve milestones (sitting, crawling, standing); improve ADL independence, posture, strength, balance and confidence.

(d)
Justification from the stated aims: paralysis, weakness and deformity limit function, so priority is independence in standing, transferring and walking supported by aids and orthoses, while positioning and stretching prevent contractures.

questions.question:
(a) Describe opsoclonus myoclonus ataxia syndrome (definition, pathophysiology, clinical features, investigations and medical management).
(b) Describe the physiotherapy management, stating goals, interventions and challenges/strategies.
(c) Explain how long-term deficits and relapses are managed, and state the prognosis.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• OMAS (Kinsbourne syndrome, 'dancing eye syndrome') is a rare neuroinflammatory disorder of opsoclonus, myoclonus, ataxia and behavioural/sleep disturbance; about 1 in 10,000,000 yearly; mainly 6-36 months but can occur in adults.
• Pathophysiology: autoimmune, often paraneoplastic (neuroblastoma) or post-infectious; antibodies attack cerebellar neurons, disrupting motor control; cerebellar involvement causes ataxia and myoclonus and oculomotor pathways cause opsoclonus. Diagnosis needs 3 of 4 core features (opsoclonus, myoclonus, ataxia, behavioural/sleep disturbance); often misdiagnosed as acute cerebellar ataxia or GBS.
• Other features: dysarthria/mutism, tremor, developmental regression, vomiting. Investigations: MRI/CT, tumour screening (CT/MRI chest and abdomen, MIBG, PET), CSF (often normal), EEG (usually normal).
• Medical: high-dose corticosteroids, IV immunoglobulin, rituximab for moderate/severe or relapse; surgical resection of neuroblastoma; acetazolamide or levetiracetam for myoclonus.

(b)
• Goals: improve balance and coordination, enhance gross and fine motor skills, support milestones, reduce fall risk, improve functional independence.
• Interventions: balance training (one-leg standing, wobble board, tandem walking); coordination (ball tossing, obstacle courses, rhythmic activities); gentle resistance for limb, trunk and head muscles; gait training with walkers; sensory integration for proprioception and vestibular function.
• Challenges: relapsing course needs ongoing assessment; behavioural issues affect compliance; long-term neurological sequelae. Strategies: play-based therapy (games, music), adjust intensity to severity and fatigue, involve caregivers for consistency and monitoring.

(c)
• Long-term care: ongoing rehabilitation for residual ataxia or motor delay, support for school reintegration and ADL, regular reassessment.
• Prognosis: most children improve with early aggressive immunotherapy; residual cognitive, behavioural or motor deficits are common; better outcomes with early diagnosis and high-intensity therapy.
• Interdisciplinary collaboration improves outcomes; interventions are tailored to ataxia and myoclonus and adapted to the relapsing nature.

(a)
• Myasthenia gravis: autoimmune, chronic, idiopathic disease of the neuromuscular junction; antibodies against acetylcholine receptors (or MuSK) destroy receptors and impair ACh binding, causing fluctuating weakness that escalates with activity (fatigability). Thymoma in about 15%; peak onset women 20-30s, men 40-60s.
• Stage/type: begins as ocular MG (ptosis, diplopia; if restricted to eye muscles for 3 years it usually stays ocular) and in about 85% becomes generalised; other types: congenital, transient neonatal, juvenile. Myasthenic crisis = acute exacerbation with respiratory failure needing intubation and ventilation.

(b)
Diagnosis: physical examination, antibody tests, repetitive nerve stimulation, edrophonium (Tensilon) test, chest CT/MRI. Findings: ptosis, diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia, chewing difficulty, limited facial expression, nasal voice with nasal regurgitation, weak neck, proximal and possibly asymmetric limb weakness, respiratory muscle weakness.

(c)
Goals: plan activity around peak energy, maintain pulmonary function and avoid fatigue and stress.

(d)
Approach: plan exercises around the peak of energy; graded low-to-medium-intensity exercise; maximal resistance with low repetition; pulmonary exercises. Medical: acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (pyridostigmine) first line, steroids/mycophenolate, plasmapheresis, immunoglobulin, thymectomy.

(e)
Precautions: avoid strenuous exercise and stress; avoid extreme heat or cold. Watch for myasthenic crisis (severe respiratory weakness, a medical emergency) triggered by infection, surgery/physiological stress, fatigue, laxatives, heat (sauna, hot tubs, sunbathing) and drugs such as quinolones, beta-blockers, magnesium.

(f)
Education content is not separately listed; the management advice to convey is pacing activity to peak energy, avoiding heat, stress, fatigue and triggering drugs, and recognising respiratory distress and swallowing problems (coughing or choking while drinking, aspiration risk).
questions.question:
A woman in her 20s-30s presents with drooping eyelids, double vision, slurred and nasal-sounding speech, difficulty swallowing with fluid coming back through the nose, and muscle weakness that worsens with repeated activity and improves with rest. A thymoma is found.
(a) State the diagnosis and the stage/type of the disease.
(b) State the assessment tools and tests and the findings expected.
(c) State the treatment goals.
(d) Name the treatment approach and technique.
(e) State the precautions and contraindications.
(f) Outline patient education.

(a) Describe the physiotherapy management of stroke in the early, middle and late recovery stages, stating the goals and interventions of each stage.
(b) State the outcome measures available for monitoring stroke rehabilitation.
(c) Explain how complications and secondary impairments after stroke are prevented or managed.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Early (acute) stage: lasts 2-6 weeks (varying flaccid stage); start when medically stable (24-36 h); at least 45 min daily as tolerated. Goals: minimise tone abnormalities, maintain ROM, mobilise in early functional activities.
• Early means: positioning, ROM exercises, electrical stimulation, sensory stimulation (stroking, stretch, superficial/deep pressure), motor relearning (active-assisted exercise, rhythmic initiation, bed activities), respiratory exercises and postural drainage; acute care also prevents abnormal patterns and hemineglect and strengthens weak muscles.
• Middle (spastic) stage goals: minimise spasticity, promote functional use of the hemiplegic side, improve postural control and independent balance, independence in bed mobility/transfers, ambulation.
• Middle means: tone reduction (prolonged stretch, ice, slow stroking); weight-bearing and trunk control, hand function, pelvic control; supported standing between parallel bars, orthosis.
• Late stage: many movements regained, tone near normal; remaining deficits are timing and coordination. Means: PNF, stepping activities, gait and balance training, stair climbing; post-acute rehabilitation adds strengthening, functional training and community reintegration.
• Other protocols: FES, EMG biofeedback, motor relearning, NDT/PNF, task-oriented approach, cardiorespiratory training, splints/orthoses, walking aids; recent advances: CIMT, mirror therapy, robot-assisted therapy, virtual reality, mental practice/motor imagery.

(b)
• General tools: Fugl-Meyer, ARAT, Wolf, Motor Assessment Scale, STREAM, Rivermead Mobility Index, Chedoke-McMaster; Modified Barthel, FIM; Berg, Postural Assessment Scale, TUG, Functional Reach.
• Also pain scales (VAS, McGill, NRS), quality of life (SS-QOL, SF-12/36), mental state (MMSE, Zung). Prognostic markers: UL gain mainly in first 3 months; no return after 6 months is unfavourable.

(c)
• Contractures/deformities: positioning, ROM, stretching, splint/orthosis. DVT (calf pain, tenderness, swelling, discolouration), shoulder pain/shoulder-hand syndrome and hand/foot oedema are listed.
• Psychological problems (anxiety, depression) and urinary/bowel problems are listed as complications; acute/sub-acute complications include aspiration, bronchopneumonia, UTI, decubitus ulcers, joint stiffness, PE and seizures. Respiratory exercises and postural drainage are the stated respiratory measures.
• Rehabilitation is delivered by a team (PT, OT, speech therapy) in stroke units; success depends on early rehabilitation, extent of brain injury, patient attitude, team skill and family/caregiver cooperation.
• Treatment principles that limit secondary problems: active participation, repetition, function-focused practice, and a problem-solving approach in which the therapist defines the cause of the movement disorder and selects strategies.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the physiotherapy management of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis across the stages of the disease, stating the goals and interventions.
(b) State the assessment and outcome measures.
(c) Explain how complications and secondary impairments are prevented or managed.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• ALS has no cure; rehabilitation maximises function, independence and quality of life, and the PT role varies with team setting and reason for referral.
• Role: promote independence through restorative and compensatory interventions; promote health in early and early-middle stages through restorative and preventive interventions; provide adaptive equipment and alternative methods as the disease progresses; prevent complications throughout; give education, psychological support and community resources.
• Cervical weakness: soft foam collar for mild-moderate, semirigid or rigid collar for moderate-severe weakness. Dysarthria/dysphagia (with nutritionist): head/trunk control and sitting position, chin tuck, communication devices, food-consistency changes, family education.
• Upper limb weakness: adaptive equipment, sling for painful subluxed shoulder, wrist/hand splints. Shoulder pain: modalities, ROM, passive stretching, joint mobilisation, education on joint support.
• Respiratory weakness: balance activity and rest, breathing exercises, positioning. Leg weakness: orthoses (ankle-foot brace prevents toe drag), ROM, mobilisation; sit-to-stand: firm 2-3 in cushion, raised chair or lifting cushions (needs trunk control).
• Cramps and spasticity: massage and stretching, slow prolonged stretch, passive ROM, positioning, splinting. Devices: cane for one weaker leg or mild balance deficit; wheelchair for excessive fatigue, unsteadiness or falls.

(b)
Assessment: history; LMN and UMN signs; bulbar and respiratory status; Schwab and England ADL scale (100% independent to 10% totally dependent); El Escorial categories for diagnosis.

(c)
• Painful joint contractures from immobility (rare), shoulder subluxation/adhesive capsulitis, aspiration or choking, secretion retention and ineffective cough, fatigue, pain and falls are the listed problems.
• Prevention/management: ROM, splinting and positioning for contracture and shoulder problems; swallowing strategies and diet modification for aspiration; breathing exercises and positioning for respiratory weakness; orthoses and aids for falls.
• Skin integrity is usually maintained because sensation and bladder/bowel control are preserved; sensation, eye movements and bladder/bowel function are typically spared.
• Prognosis: younger onset and limb onset do better; psychological well-being is linked to longer survival (mortality 6.8 times higher with distress), so psychological support is part of care.
• Median survival is about 3 years, and management aims to maintain independence and function for as long as possible.

(a)
• Reflexes are automatic subconscious responses; the reflex arc has receptor, sensory neuron, interneuron, motor neuron and effector. Stretch reflex: stretch activates muscle spindles (Ia and II afferents; gamma efferents to intrafusal fibres), alpha motor neurons contract the muscle and inhibit the antagonist; monosynaptic, e.g. patellar tap contracts quadriceps and relaxes hamstrings.
• Golgi tendon reflex: contraction activates Golgi tendon organs, which inhibit the contracting muscle and activate the antagonist (protects against tearing). Withdrawal (flexor) reflex: pain excites flexors and inhibits extensors; crossed-extensor: ipsilateral flexion with contralateral extension to stabilise posture.
• Testing: biceps (finger on tendon, forearm flexes), triceps (short tendon near elbow, forearm extends), Achilles/ankle jerk (plantar flexion), abdominal (stroke skin toward midline, umbilicus moves), cremasteric (stroke inner thigh, testis elevates). Root levels: Achilles S1-S2, patellar L3-L4, biceps C5-C6, triceps C6-C7, brachioradialis C5-C6.

(b)
Grades: 0 absent; 1+ hypoactive; 2+ normal; 3+ hyperactive without clonus; 4+ hyperactive with clonus.

(c)
• Stretch reflexes maintain healthy muscle tone; Golgi organs inform the brain of muscle state. The brain sets muscle length and the stretch reflex maintains it, so it is important for muscle tone and upright posture.
• Clinical meaning: UMN lesions give hyperreflexia with clonus, diminished superficial reflexes, Babinski sign; LMN lesions give diminished or absent reflexes with intact superficial reflexes.
• Abnormal retention of primitive reflexes and postural reactions are components of motor development assessed in children.

(d)
• The stretch reflex has a single synapse and directly links muscle length to alpha-motor-neuron output, maintaining tone and posture, whereas the withdrawal reflex is polysynaptic and pain-driven.
• The deep tendon reflex is polysynaptic in this description, with inhibitory interneurons relaxing the ipsilateral flexor.
• Stretch reflex is the physiological basis for PNF principles (initial stretch and re-stretch) and for autogenic and reciprocal inhibition.
• Reflex theory: reflexes as the basis of movement (Sherrington).
questions.question:
(a) Describe the reflex arc and the stretch, Golgi tendon, withdrawal and crossed-extensor reflexes, with the procedure for testing the deep tendon and superficial reflexes.
(b) State the grading of reflexes.
(c) State the rationale and clinical meaning of reflex testing.
(d) Explain the basis for using the monosynaptic stretch reflex rather than the withdrawal reflex to assess muscle tone and posture.

A child has a flat red-purple birthmark on the face around the eye and forehead present since birth, seizures beginning in the first two years, weakness of one side of the body, developmental delay, and an enlarged, high-pressure eye on the same side as the birthmark.
(a) Give the diagnosis.
(b) State the clinical features and predisposing factors.
(c) Explain the pathophysiology.
(d) Outline the physiotherapy management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Sturge-Weber disease (encephalotrigeminal angiomatosis): a sporadic neurocutaneous disorder of the meninges (pia and arachnoid), facial skin and ipsilateral eye.

(b)
• Face: port-wine stain in the ophthalmic and maxillary trigeminal divisions, light pink at birth becoming dark red/purple, with hypertrophy and facial asymmetry.
