CNS: seizures (most in first 24 months, higher developmental-delay risk), hemiparesis, developmental delay, learning disorders/ADHD, headaches (often before 10 years). Eye: glaucoma (first year or age 5-9), blindness if untreated, buphthalmos.
• Predisposing: cause unknown and sporadic; relatives may have milder haemangiomas; early onset is seen with bilateral involvement. Roach Scale: type I face, meninges and eye; type II face only; type III meninges only.

(c)
Embryonic blood vessels fail to regress, leaving residual vessels that form angiomas on the face, meninges and eye. Hypertrophy and calcification cause seizures and focal deficits; the 'vascular steal' phenomenon deprives the cortex of blood, causing hypoxic injury and progressive neurological deficit.

(d)
• Medical: laser for port-wine stain, glaucoma and seizure medication, surgery (hemispherectomy or focal resection, trabeculotomy, tube shunt). Physiotherapy: start early; address hemiparesis and weakness with strengthening/resistive exercise; spasticity management and orthosis; CIMT to promote use of involved limbs and prevent neglect; interdisciplinary team; genetic counselling is advised for related disorders.
• Management aims to prevent or limit deformity and achieve independence at home and in the community, with positive reinforcement to build self-esteem.

(a)
• Modifiable: hypertension (the most significant), previous TIA (markedly raises recurrence risk), diabetes mellitus, cigarette smoking, physical inactivity, obesity; also atrial fibrillation/cardiac disease, hyperlipidaemia, sickle cell disease, carotid disease, alcohol and drug abuse, oral contraceptives, meningitis. Non-modifiable: age, sex, race (commoner in blacks, partly through higher hypertension, diabetes, obesity), heredity/family history, prior stroke, TIA or heart attack.
• Stroke is ischaemic (atherothrombotic, cardio-embolic, hypoperfusion) or haemorrhagic (intracerebral, subarachnoid); a TIA is transient focal ischaemia (under 24 h) without infarction. Time is brain: about 2 million neurons are lost per minute.

(b)
• Acute (under 7 days): cerebral oedema, raised ICP, hydrocephalus, haemorrhagic transformation, seizures, herniation; hypoxia, hypertension, hyperglycaemia, aspiration, cardiac arrhythmias, inappropriate ADH secretion.
• Sub-acute (over 7 days): seizures, depression, DVT and pulmonary embolism, bronchopneumonia, UTI, septicaemia, decubitus ulcers, joint stiffness, weight loss. Secondary impairments: contractures, shoulder pain/shoulder-hand syndrome, hand and foot oedema, urinary/bowel problems, anxiety.

(c)
• Prevention: control multiple risk factors by lifestyle change and drug therapy: lower blood pressure and cholesterol, diet low in salt and saturated fat and rich in fruit, vegetables and fish oils, regular exercise, no smoking. Care levels: primary prevention, acute treatment, secondary prevention, rehabilitation.
• Acute medical care: IV tPA (alteplase/tenecteplase) within the first three hours is the gold standard for ischaemic stroke; thrombolysis, endovascular revascularisation, antithrombotics, stroke units.
• Physiotherapy: acute stage (respiratory function, prevent abnormal patterns and hemineglect, strengthen weak muscles, positioning, ROM); post-acute (strengthening, balance, functional rehabilitation, gait retraining, community reintegration); options include FES, NDT/PNF, task-oriented approach, biofeedback, splints.

(d)
Task-oriented motor relearning is justified because treatment is problem-solving, active, aimed at functional performance and needs repetition; regular exercise is also a listed prevention strategy. Poor prognostic factors to monitor: older age, haemorrhagic stroke, incontinence, poor wrist extension, comorbidity, depression, poor social support.
questions.question:
A patient with high blood pressure (above 160/95), diabetes mellitus, cigarette smoking, physical inactivity and obesity, who has had a previous transient ischaemic attack, now presents with a stroke.
(a) Identify the modifiable and non-modifiable risk factors relevant to stroke.
(b) State the complications and secondary impairments that may follow.
(c) Outline the preventive measures and the physiotherapy management options.
(d) Justify one physiotherapy option.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Motor control = interaction of the CNS, the body and the environment to produce purposeful coordinated movement. Reflex theory (Sherrington): reflexes are the basis of movement, each response becomes the stimulus for the next. Hierarchical theory (Jackson): top-down control, CNS maturation drives change, reflexes dominate after CNS damage.
• Systems theory: movement arises from interaction of many systems plus gravity and inertia, and the initial condition affects movement. Motor programming: central motor patterns and central pattern generators (spinal programs) plus higher-level programs. Dynamic action theory: parts interact and organise without instructions from a higher centre. Parallel distributed processing: serial and parallel processing in neural networks.

(b)
• Reflex: use sensory input, stimulate good reflexes, inhibit primitive ones (Bobath concept partly based on it); limits: reflex cannot be the basic unit, cannot explain varied responses to one stimulus or voluntary movement.
• Hierarchical: identify and prevent primitive reflexes, reduce hyperactive stretch, facilitate normal patterns; limits: does not explain reflex dominance in normal adults (withdrawal) and developmental variation.
• Systems: identifiable functional tasks, practice under varied conditions, modify the environment; limits: very broad, limited focus on organism-environment interaction. Motor programming: abnormal movement may reflect faulty pattern generators/programs, retrain movements important to function; limits: CNS is not the sole determinant and ignores musculoskeletal/environmental variables.
• Dynamic action: predicts how a system acts and searches for physical explanations; limit: minimises the role of the CNS. Parallel distributed processing: brain as network of interacting cells.

(c)
• Purpose of neurorehabilitation: cement existing abilities, retrieve lost abilities, foster new skills (ability is relatively permanent; skill can be acquired). Postural control and balance programmes are more effective when they include multidimensional tasks rather than a single area.
• Factors affecting motor learning: verbal instructions, characteristics and variability of training sessions, active participation and motivation, the option of making mistakes, postural control, memory and feedback.

(d)
• Systems theory supports identifiable functional tasks, varied practice and environmental modification; reflex/hierarchical views rest on stimulating good reflexes and inhibiting primitive ones.
• Motor learning is a change in capacity for skilled action from practice or experience that must be relatively permanent; it cannot be measured directly.
• Motor-control stages: random reflex-based movement, static postural control, controlled mobility, skill; motor-learning phases: cognitive, associative, autonomous.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the theories of motor control (reflex, hierarchical, systems, motor programming, dynamic action, parallel distributed processing).
(b) State the clinical implications and limitations of each.
(c) State the rationale for applying motor control theory in neurorehabilitation.
(d) Explain the basis for preferring the systems or task-oriented view over the reflex or hierarchical view in stroke rehabilitation.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Autoimmune, chronic, idiopathic disease of the neuromuscular junction with decreased acetylcholine receptors from antibody-mediated attack; first described by Thomas Willis in 1672; 'snowflake disease'. Prevalence 77-150 per 100,000, bimodal (women 20-30s, men 40-60s; overall W:M 3:2).
• Aetiology: anti-AChR antibodies, anti-MuSK antibodies (needed for formation and maintenance of the NMJ), thymoma in about 15%, rare hereditary forms. Types: congenital, transient neonatal, juvenile, generalised, ocular.
• Pathophysiology: normally ACh from the nerve binds nicotinic receptors on muscle, opening ion gates and causing contraction; in MG antibodies bind and destroy AChRs at the motor end plate and impair ACh binding on remaining receptors.

(b)
• Features: ptosis and diplopia (commonest initial), dysarthria, dysphagia, chewing difficulty, limited facial expression ('snarling'), intercostal/diaphragm/pharyngeal weakness, nasal voice and regurgitation, proximal (possibly asymmetric) limb weakness, neck weakness.
• Diagnosis: physical examination, antibody tests, repetitive nerve stimulation, edrophonium (Tensilon) test, chest CT/MRI. Management: acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (pyridostigmine) first line, steroids and steroid-sparing mycophenolate, plasmapheresis, immunoglobulin, thymectomy.
• Physiotherapy: plan exercise around peak energy; low-to-medium intensity, graded; maximal resistance with low repetition; pulmonary exercises; avoid strenuous exercise, stress, and extreme heat or cold.

(c)
• Antibody-mediated loss of AChRs impairs transmission, so voluntary weakness escalates with continued activity (fatigability) and improves with rest.
• Myasthenic crisis: acute exacerbation with respiratory failure needing intubation and ventilation (medical emergency); triggers: infection, surgery or physiological stress, fatigue, laxatives, heat, and drugs (quinolones, beta-blockers, magnesium).

(d)
• Ocular MG: weakness confined to extraocular muscles (if restricted for 3 years it will likely remain ocular). Generalised MG: in about 85% of patients weakness spreads to limb and bulbar muscles.
• Complications include respiratory failure and aspiration from dysphagia.
questions.question:
(a) Define myasthenia gravis and describe its epidemiology, aetiology, classification and pathophysiology.
(b) Describe the clinical features, diagnosis and management.
(c) Explain why weakness worsens with repeated activity and how a myasthenic crisis arises.
(d) Distinguish between ocular and generalised myasthenia gravis.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Neurorehabilitation helps people with nervous-system injury or disease improve physical and cognitive function, minimise symptoms and regain independence. Core aspects: individualised, multidisciplinary (PT, OT, speech-language, psychology), restoration plus compensation, focus on function, attention to psychological and social needs.
• Conditions that benefit: stroke, TBI, SCI, MS, Parkinson's disease, muscular dystrophy, neuropathies. Phase model: based on severity of injury and symptoms, measured with the Barthel Index, and the phase determines treatment.
• Phase A acute treatment (intensive care). Phase B early rehabilitation (consciousness severely impaired, intensive care still needed; measures aim to improve consciousness). Phase C further rehabilitation (partial mobilisation). Phase D medical rehabilitation (after early mobilisation).
• Phase E secondary rehabilitation (professional, social and domestic reintegration). Phase F activating rehabilitation (activating care for patients in a vegetative state).

(b)
• The outcome measure named is the Barthel Index.
• CBR is a community-development strategy for rehabilitation, equal opportunities, poverty reduction and social inclusion; matrix components: health, education, livelihood, social, empowerment. Components: community assessment and goal setting, functional training (mobility, ADL), assistive devices and home modification, patient/caregiver education, psychosocial support and reintegration.
• Principles of community neurorehabilitation: holistic patient-centred care, multidisciplinary teamwork, inclusion of patients and families, accessibility and affordability, continuity of care, early intervention, brain plasticity, task-oriented approach.
• PT role in CBR: early intervention and prevention of complications, individualised exercise programmes, training caregivers in safe handling, transfers and home exercises, promoting participation, facilitating assistive devices, advocacy.

(c)
• Complications such as contractures and pressure ulcers are prevented by early intervention and caregiver training in the community.
• Challenges: limited staff, equipment and funding; stigma, beliefs, low literacy, poverty; transport and accessibility; poor hospital-community coordination.
• Strategies: engage community leaders and volunteers, use tele-rehabilitation and mobile health, train community health workers, develop low-cost locally made assistive devices.
• Case: a 55-year-old rural man with left hemiparesis after stroke: teach family transfer techniques, gait training with a walking stick, home adaptations for safety, and social participation through local support groups.
questions.question:
(a) Define neurological rehabilitation and describe the phase model (goals of each phase).
(b) State the outcome measures for the phases and the interventions and principles of community-based rehabilitation.
(c) Explain how complications are prevented and how challenges to community-based rehabilitation are managed.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Neurofibromatosis type 1 (von Recklinghausen's disease): café-au-lait spots, neurofibromas, Lisch nodules. Congenital, autosomal dominant, gene on chromosome 17, about 1 in 3,000-4,000 births; a parent with NF has a 50/50 chance of an affected child; 30-50% of cases are new mutations; males and females equally affected.

(b)
• Brain tumours (high rate), malignant change in under 1% of neurofibromas; hearing loss, headaches, seizures, scoliosis, facial pain or numbness, intellectual disability in up to 1%, learning problems, hyperactivity; muscle weakness, sensation problems, spasticity or flaccidity.
• For comparison, NF2 (chromosome 22, about 1 in 25,000) causes eighth cranial nerve tumours with hearing loss, balance and walking difficulty and meningioma; schwannomatosis causes multiple painful schwannomas with the vestibular nerve spared.

(c)
• Prevention: genetic counselling (recurrence risks and available testing). Treatment is symptomatic because the condition is lifelong and incurable; interdisciplinary team (paediatrician, neurologist, neurosurgeon, orthopaedic surgeon, ophthalmologist, nurse, rehabilitation team); biopsy/imaging/genetic tests for diagnosis.
• Physiotherapy: intervention focused on hemiparesis and muscle weakness, started early before speech and ambulation are established; muscle strengthening/resistive exercise; spasticity management and orthosis; constraint-induced movement therapy; prevent deformities; maximise capability at home and community; positive reinforcement.

(d)
CIMT justified: it promotes use of the involved limbs and prevents neglect. Strengthening and orthoses are justified by weakness and spasticity.
questions.question:
A child of a parent known to have neurofibromatosis has light brown skin patches, skin tumours along nerves, and small nodules on the iris that appeared around adolescence. The child has hearing loss, headaches, scoliosis and learning problems.
(a) Identify the condition and its risk factors.
(b) State the complications and secondary impairments.
(c) Outline the prevention and physiotherapy management options.
(d) Justify one physiotherapy option.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Signe Brunnstrom (1950s) facilitated return of normal movement using reflexes, synergies and sensory stimulation. Principle 1: normal movement needs muscles working synergistically, which is lost after CNS damage and improves in recovery. Principle 2: recovery follows a sequence.
• Sequence: no voluntary movement; spasticity and basic reflexes appear; voluntary control of reflexes (spasticity may rise); basic patterns develop and spasticity falls; individual movements and near-normal coordination; normal function.
• Six stages: 1 flaccidity (prevent contracture, keep ROM); 2 mass movement (facilitate with reflexes and synergies); 3 associated reactions; 4 early voluntary movement (strengthen, coordinate); 5 late voluntary movement (skills, function); 6 skilled movement (maximise function and independence).

(b)
• Therapist assesses remaining movement potential, picks facilitation by level and severity, progresses from assisted or reflex-driven to voluntary movement, trains key muscles of arm, hand and leg, uses touch and pressure cues, then advances to complex tasks and daily activities.
• Indications: stroke (most applicable), spinal cord injury, brain injury, Parkinson's disease, multiple sclerosis. In CP it provokes primitive/synergistic patterns and uses tonic neck, lumbar and labyrinthine reflexes, then righting reflexes and balance.
• Limitations: time-intensive, needs patient understanding and cooperation, may not address specific functional goals, resource-intensive, unsuitable for all, lacks standardisation; needs skilled therapists.

(c)
Rationale/effects: stretch tight muscles, recover voluntary movement, improve the sequence of functional activities, posture, ROM, strength, coordination, motor control, functional mobility and independence; reduce spasticity and pain.

(d)
• It suits a patient whose recovery is progressing through the described stages with reflexes and synergies that can be built on, because treatment is chosen by stage of recovery and remaining movement potential.
• Alternatives: PNF (stretching and facilitation to improve ROM and motor performance) and Bobath (inhibition of abnormal patterns).
• Its first principle (synergistic muscle action) and second principle (staged recovery) justify progressing treatment stage by stage.
• The approach offers a systematic method aligned with motor-recovery principles after stroke or other neurological conditions.
• Effectiveness depends on skilled, experienced therapists for proper assessment, progression and individual adaptation.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the principles and stages of the Brunnstrom approach.
(b) State the technique, indications and limitations.
(c) State its rationale and expected effects.
(d) Explain the basis for choosing the Brunnstrom approach over an alternative approach in a patient recovering from stroke.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Build-up of CSF in the ventricles that enlarges them and presses on the brain, damaging tissue; commoner in infants. CSF is formed by the choroid plexus, circulates through ventricles, cisterns and subarachnoid space and is absorbed into blood by the arachnoid villi; third and fourth ventricles connect via the aqueduct of Sylvius, and CSF exits through the foramina of Luschka and Magendie.

(b)
Congenital (present at birth: fetal events or genetic) or acquired (at/after birth from injury or disease, any age); communicating or non-communicating (obstructive).

(c)
Genetic abnormalities (aqueductal stenosis), developmental disorders (NTDs such as spina bifida, encephalocele), intraventricular haemorrhage of prematurity, meningitis, tumours, head injury, subarachnoid haemorrhage. Risks: recent head trauma; premature infants born before 34 weeks or under 1.8 kg.

(d)
• Infants: large or rapidly enlarging head, bulging fontanel, vomiting, sleepiness, irritability, poor feeding, seizures, downward-fixed eyes (sunsetting), poor tone and strength, poor responsiveness, poor growth.
• Older children/adults: headache then vomiting, nausea, papilloedema, blurred/double vision, sunsetting, poor balance and coordination, gait disturbance, urinary incontinence, lost developmental progress, lethargy, personality or cognitive change, memory loss.

(e)
Clinical neurological evaluation and cranial imaging (ultrasound, CT, MRI) or pressure monitoring. Treated mostly by a shunt (catheter and one-way valve) diverting CSF from a ventricle to the abdominal cavity, or to a heart chamber or lung area, for absorption.

(f)
PT aims: milestones (sitting, standing, crawling), independent mobility, balance and coordination, stretching/strengthening, confidence, stamina; task-oriented, problem-solving practice with family-centred care in natural environments. Prognosis is hard to predict (cause, associated disorders, timely diagnosis, treatment success). Prevention: prenatal care, folic acid, prompt treatment of infection, helmets, safe home.

(g)
The infant skull can expand because the sutures have not closed, so the head enlarges; in older children and adults the skull cannot expand, so pressure symptoms such as headache and papilloedema appear.

(h)
Narrowing of the aqueduct of Sylvius between the third and fourth ventricles blocks CSF flow along the narrow passage, so CSF accumulates and the ventricles enlarge (non-communicating type).

(i)
• Communicating: flow is blocked after CSF leaves the ventricles, and the ventricles remain open to one another.
• Non-communicating (obstructive): flow is blocked along one or more narrow passages connecting the ventricles.
• Hydrocephalus can occur at any age but is commoner in infants; CSF is continually produced, circulated and absorbed, and the blood-CSF barrier lies at the choroid plexus epithelium.
questions.question:
(a) Define hydrocephalus and describe normal CSF production and circulation.
(b) Classify hydrocephalus.
(c) State the causes and risk factors.
(d) Describe the clinical features in infants and in older children/adults.
(e) State how it is diagnosed and medically managed.
(f) Outline the physiotherapy management, prognosis and prevention.
(g) Explain why infants and older children/adults present differently.
(h) Explain why aqueductal stenosis causes hydrocephalus.
(i) Distinguish between communicating and non-communicating hydrocephalus.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Subacute combined degeneration of the cord (myeloneuropathy) due to vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency, with dorsal column, corticospinal tract and peripheral nerve involvement. Anaemia is usual but may be absent.

(b)
Dorsal columns: postural sense (proprioception), vibration, sensory ataxia. Corticospinal tract: weakness and spasticity. Peripheral nerves: paraesthesiae of feet or hands. Wider B12 effects: dementia and optic nerve impairment.

(c)
• Copper deficiency and nitrous oxide (laughing gas) toxicity ('anaesthetic paresthetica' after surgical or dental procedures) give a similar picture. Other myelopathies: tabes dorsalis (dorsal column, syphilis serology), MS, NMO, transverse myelitis, vascular cord infarction, paraneoplastic myelopathy, compressive lesions, polyneuropathy.
• Treatment of the cause: parenteral hydroxocobalamin.

(d)
• Sensory ataxia and weakness require assessment of sensation (including position sense), reflexes, strength, coordination and gait; Romberg is positive in proprioceptive loss.
• By analogy with tabes dorsalis, the plan is to improve balance and posture and strengthen weak muscles with balance and coordination exercises.
• Reasoning is limited to the site of lesion (posterior columns, lateral corticospinal tracts, peripheral nerves) explaining the mixed sensory-motor signs.
questions.question:
A patient has symmetrical tingling of the feet, increasing difficulty walking from a mix of weakness and loss of position sense, dementia and impaired vision. Examination indicates involvement of the dorsal columns, the corticospinal tracts and the peripheral nerves. Anaemia is present.
(a) Identify the lesion site/level or system affected.
(b) State the affected functions.
(c) State the differential conditions.
(d) Give the clinical reasoning for the physiotherapy plan.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Neuroplasticity is the ability of the brain/CNS to change activity by reorganising structure, function or connections in response to stimuli, learning, injury or development, lifelong but less rapid in adults; changes may be beneficial, neutral or negative (plasticity does not equal a positive outcome). Types: structural (modifying neural connections) and functional (modifying functional characteristics of neurons).
• Mechanisms: angiogenesis, synaptic plasticity (long-term potentiation and depression, receptor up/down-regulation), neurogenesis and axonal sprouting (hippocampus, olfactory bulb, cerebellum in adults), synaptogenesis and pruning, neuronal migration, collateral sprouting, functional reorganisation.
• Principles: use it or lose it; use it and improve it; specificity; repetition; intensity; time; salience; age (younger brains); transference; interference. Drivers: skill acquisition and motor-learning principles.

(b)
• Motor control = ability to maintain and change posture and movement from neurologic and mechanical processes (motor, cognitive, perceptual); stages: random movements (mobility), static postural control (stability), controlled mobility, skill. Sensation cues reflexive movement, gives feedback and reinforces posture.
• Motor learning = acquiring or adapting motor skills through practice and experience; phases: cognitive (novice, high error, needs guidance), associative (errors detected and corrected, less reliance on instruction), autonomous (automatic, little attention). Constraints: biomechanical (ROM, strength), weak cognition/memory, growth and maturation, adolescence.

(c)
• After stroke, brain or spinal cord injury the treatment approach is based on the brain's ability to change, reorganise and recover; harnessed through practice and repetition; positive effects include new skills, improved motor control, sensory recovery, memory and slowing pathology; negative effects include altered motor control and amplified pain.
• Neuroplastic techniques in PT: motor learning, biofeedback, task analysis and task-specific training, Bobath, CIMT, PNF; other listed therapies: FES, treadmill with body-weight support, virtual reality.
• Clinically it occurs after stroke, TBI, MS and Parkinson's disease; environment and motivation play a key role.

(d)
• The principles of specificity and repetition state that the nature of training dictates the nature of brain change and that sufficient repetition is needed to induce plasticity; intensity and salience also matter.
• Task-specific interventions with extensive practice induce beneficial neuroplastic change and restore function in TBI; robot-assisted gait training allows more repetitions.
• Interference: bad habits can interfere with learning of good ones, supporting correct, specific practice.
questions.question:
(a) Define neuroplasticity and describe its types, mechanisms and principles.
(b) Describe motor control and motor learning, including the stages of each and the constraints.
(c) State the rationale and expected effects of harnessing neuroplasticity in neurological physiotherapy.
(d) Explain the basis for choosing task-specific, repetitive training over non-specific exercise.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Radial nerve lesion (Saturday night palsy) - a peripheral nerve (lower motor neuron) lesion. The nerve may be compressed in the axilla (incorrect crutch use, arm over chair) or damaged in mid-shaft humerus fractures, supracondylar fractures and fracture/dislocation of the elbow.

(b)
Inability to extend the wrist and fingers; loss of wrist extension weakens the finger flexors' grip; anaesthesia on the dorsum of the hand, which causes minimal disability.

(c)
• Axillary nerve lesion: inability to abduct the arm, deltoid wasting, minimal sensory loss (shoulder dislocation, surgical-neck fracture). Median nerve: thenar paralysis with 'monkey hand' and lateral palm anaesthesia. Ulnar nerve: weak ulnar deviation, loss of 3rd/4th finger movements, ulnar-side anaesthesia. Brachial plexus (C5-T1) injury and cervical root lesions are other possibilities.
• Nerve injury type: neurapraxia (conduction block, full spontaneous recovery), axonotmesis (Wallerian degeneration, slower recovery) or neurotmesis (surgical repair).

(d)
• LMN lesion gives weakness or paralysis, atrophy, diminished reflexes and sensory loss, so the plan follows the aims of nerve-injury care: relieve pain (massage, TENS, cautious thermotherapy), control oedema (bandaging, elevation, positioning), strengthen with electrical muscle stimulation and exercise.
• Maintain or increase ROM with passive movement and stretching; prevent deformity by splinting; restore function through functional exercise. Recovery, if the axon is disrupted, proceeds proximal to distal, beginning within about 3 weeks.
questions.question:
After falling asleep with his arm hanging over the back of a chair, a man cannot extend his wrist or fingers, his grip is weak, and he has an area of numbness on the back of the hand. Deltoid function and thumb/finger movements of the palm side are otherwise intact.
(a) Identify the nerve lesion and the level/site.
(b) State the affected functions.
(c) State the differential conditions.
(d) Give the clinical reasoning for the physiotherapy plan.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Acute: proper handling and transfer; airway (patent), breathing (monitor rate, pattern, colour, distress, especially C-spine), circulation (atropine to restore heart rate); spinal stabilisation from pre-hospital stage - halo-traction, Gardner-Wells tongs or cone callipers for the cervical spine, postural reduction for thoracic spine and below; immobilisation appliances.
• Rehabilitation plan is not a blanket one and depends on findings with a physical diagnosis: maintain/improve respiratory function and treat/prevent complications; maintain and strengthen innervated muscles and facilitate functional activity patterns; treat pain; train function and facilitate reintegration; address psychosocial and existential concerns.
• Function by level guides goals: C5 head, neck, shoulder and elbow flexion; C6 wrist extension, help with dressing and transfers; C7-C8 dress, eat, drive, transfer; T5-T9 manual wheelchair and independent personal care; L2-S5 walking with aids. Assistive devices and community reintegration (working with family and employers) complete the plan.

(b)
• Assessment is continuous: subjective (when, where, what, how, after that) and objective (vital signs, skin, limb placement, tubes); AIS A-E for completeness (sacral sparing, bulbocavernosus reflex); neurological level with zone of partial preservation; sensory modalities; spasticity by Ashworth and Tardieu; function by Katz index, FIM and SCIM; associated injuries.
• Evaluate progress with outcome measures; the AIS and the Frenkel scale are set as an assignment to compare for concurrent validity, merits and demerits.

(c)
• Osteoporosis, heterotopic ossification, bladder and bowel dysfunction with urosepsis, venous thromboembolism, pulmonary embolism, pressure ulcers, orthostatic hypotension and bradycardia, autonomic dysreflexia are the listed problems.
• Autonomic dysreflexia (injury above T6): noxious stimulation below the lesion causes vasoconstriction below T6, vasodilation above, raised heart rate and massive hypertension; it is life-threatening.
• Spinal shock: flaccid paralysis, low BP and slow heart rate, atonic bladder, paralytic ileus; reflexes return gradually, and strong spasticity soon after injury indicates an incomplete lesion.
• Respiratory deterioration implies an ascending lesion from oedema or hypoxia and is monitored; C4 patients have a poor cough and hypoventilation.
• Related conditions managed on the same plan: syringomyelia (surgery to remove the syrinx, CSF aspiration; assessment and management as for SCI).
• Incomplete injury syndromes influence prognosis: anterior cord poor; Brown-Sequard usually walks, sometimes with bracing.
• Psychosocial and existential concerns and pain are treated throughout the course.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the management of spinal cord injury in the acute (trauma) stage and in the rehabilitation stage, stating the goals and interventions.
(b) State the assessment and outcome measures.
(c) Explain how the special problems and complications of spinal cord injury are prevented or managed.

questions.answerText:
(a)
A peripheral nerve lesion interrupts the pathway between CNS and periphery. It is a lower motor neuron lesion: flaccidity and atonia, loss of power, diminished or lost reflexes, trophic skin changes, muscle atrophy, arrested bone growth in children, loss of sensation and pain. Causes: sharp objects, gunshot or stab wounds, machinery, fracture/dislocation, birth injury (Erb's palsy), road accidents, entrapment.

(b)
By axon behaviour: neurapraxia (Sunderland I): local conduction block, architecture intact, mild reversible, spontaneous complete recovery. Axonotmesis (II and III): axon damaged, connective tissue intact, Wallerian degeneration, loss of motor, sensory and autonomic function, fibrillation, slower proximal-to-distal recovery. Neurotmesis (IV and V): trunk interrupted, stumps separated, all modalities lost, surgical repair may help.

(c)
Wallerian (anterograde) degeneration occurs distal to the injury: axon fragmentation and myelin disintegration begin within hours, axonal continuity is lost by 48-96 h, macrophages clear debris, and the process is complete by 5-8 weeks leaving Schwann cells in the endoneurial sheath; regeneration starts within 3 weeks and continues for months.

(d)
• Signs: pain, muscle weakness or paralysis, loss of sensory modalities (including proprioception and stereognosis), oedema, deformity. Aims: relieve pain (massage, TENS, cautious thermotherapy); control oedema (bandaging, elevation, positioning); strengthen (electrical muscle stimulation, exercise).
• Further aims: maintain or increase ROM (passive movement, stretching); prevent deformity by splinting; restore function through functional exercise.
• Common sites: brachial plexus (C5-T1), axillary nerve (shoulder dislocation, surgical-neck fracture), radial nerve (humeral fracture, crutch pressure, Saturday night palsy), median nerve (wrist, carpal tunnel), ulnar nerve (medial epicondyle fracture); sciatic and common peroneal injuries.

(e)
Neurapraxia preserves the axon, so recovery is spontaneous and complete; in axonotmesis the connective tissue is intact so chances are high but recovery is slow; in neurotmesis the trunk is disrupted with retrograde degeneration and loss of neuronal cell bodies, which limits recovery.

(f)
Unlike the CNS, the PNS is not protected by the vertebral column and skull, leaving it exposed to toxins and mechanical injury; nerves are also vulnerable in tunnels, at branches, at hard interfaces and near the surface.

(g)
Neurapraxia: axon preserved, no Wallerian degeneration, full spontaneous recovery. Neurotmesis: trunk divided, Wallerian and retrograde degeneration, cell-body loss, surgery indicated because spontaneous recovery may not occur.

(h)
• Mononeuritis: one nerve (e.g. carpal tunnel syndrome). Mononeuritis multiplex: several nerves affected over time. Polyneuritis/polyneuropathy: symmetrical involvement in a glove-and-stocking pattern.
• Causes of neuritis: viral infection, mechanical injury, vascular, toxins/allergy, metabolic.
• Peripheral nerve lesions alone rarely threaten life but interfere considerably with functional attainment; upper-limb nerve injuries outnumber lower-limb ones.
questions.question:
(a) Define peripheral nerve lesions and state their causes and clinical features.
(b) Classify nerve injuries.
(c) Describe Wallerian degeneration and regeneration.
(d) State the signs and symptoms and the aims of physiotherapy management.
(e) Explain why recovery differs among the three types of nerve injury.
(f) Explain why peripheral nerves are vulnerable to injury.
(g) Distinguish between neurapraxia and neurotmesis.
(h) Distinguish between mononeuritis, mononeuritis multiplex and polyneuritis.

(a) Describe the psychosocial and ethical considerations in neurorehabilitation and the phases of adjustment of patients and families.
(b) State the roles and interventions of the rehabilitation team.
(c) Explain how psychosocial and ethical problems are prevented or managed.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Neurorehabilitation addresses physical, psychological, social and ethical dimensions, which strongly influence outcomes and quality of life. Emotional impact: depression, anxiety, frustration and anger, loss of identity and self-esteem; cognitive issues: memory loss, attention deficits, executive dysfunction.
• Adjustment: patients and families pass through stages of grief - denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance; cultural beliefs and values affect coping. In stroke survivors (Kerr, 1963): crisis/shock, therapy (hopeful of full recovery), realisation (deficit may be permanent; depression in 50%, with suicidal tendency, dependence, hostility), adjustment (acceptance varies with culture).
• Ethical principles: autonomy and informed consent (clear communication adapted to cognition and language; involve family when capacity is lacking but respect dignity); confidentiality; beneficence and non-maleficence (balance aggressive rehabilitation with tolerance and quality of life); justice and equity (fair access regardless of socioeconomic status, gender, ethnicity, disability severity).
• End-of-life: decisions on life-sustaining treatment, palliative care, advance directives and DNR orders discussed sensitively. Other dilemmas: autonomy versus safety, bias in treatment, over-reliance on new technology, transition to the community.

(b)
• Team: physiotherapists, occupational and speech therapists, psychologists, social workers, spiritual care providers; ongoing communication with patients and families for complex decisions.
• Physiotherapist tasks in the community setting: train caregivers, promote participation, advocate for rights, facilitate assistive devices; phases of rehabilitation (A-F) determine treatment.

(c)
• Early psychological assessment and intervention improves outcomes; counselling, education and realistic goal-setting are provided by professionals.
• Social support: family and caregiver involvement, support groups and peer counselling, community reintegration to reduce isolation and improve participation.
• Stroke-specific: recognition of depression at the realisation stage; cooperation of family and caregivers and the survivor's attitude support success.
• Community factors (stigma, beliefs, low literacy, poverty) are handled by engaging community leaders, training community health workers and using tele-rehabilitation.
• Confidentiality: protect privacy and share information only with authorised persons.

questions.question:
A patient wakes with sudden weakness of one side of the face, a drooping eyelid and mouth, inability to smile symmetrically, loss of taste on the front of the tongue on that side, and increased sensitivity to sound in that ear, with tearing and drooling.
(a) State the diagnosis and its cause.
(b) State the assessment tools and tests and expected findings.
(c) State the treatment goals.
(d) Name the treatment approach and techniques.
(e) State the precautions/contraindications.
(f) State the differential conditions.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Bell's palsy: the most common cause of acute facial nerve (CN VII) paralysis, with sudden unilateral facial weakness; believed to be due to viral infection causing inflammation and swelling of the nerve.

(b)
• Facial symmetry test; motor tests (raise eyebrows, close eyes, puff cheeks, show teeth); sensory/taste test; corneal reflex. Expected findings: asymmetry with drooping eyelid and mouth, inability to smile symmetrically, loss of taste in the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, hyperacusis, tearing or drooling.
• Anatomy: CN VII arises from the pons, passes through the internal acoustic meatus, supplies facial expression muscles (temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular, cervical branches), taste from anterior two-thirds of tongue, and salivary and lacrimal glands.

(c)
Goals: restore muscle function and symmetry; reduce synkinesis (involuntary muscle movements).

(d)
Facial exercises (smiling, frowning, raising eyebrows, closing eyes tightly); neuromuscular re-education (mirror exercises, biofeedback); electrical stimulation; massage to reduce stiffness and improve circulation.

(e)
Use electrical stimulation cautiously to avoid disrupting nerve regeneration.

(f)
Differentials/other causes of facial paralysis: Ramsay Hunt syndrome (varicella-zoster reactivation with painful rash around ear, face or mouth, hearing loss, vertigo), traumatic facial nerve injury (temporal bone fracture, surgery; neurapraxia to neurotmesis), chronic otitis media (ear pain, discharge, hearing loss).

(a)
Multiple sclerosis (MS): chronic demyelinating disease of the CNS with the classical triad of nystagmus, scanning speech (cerebellar dysarthria) and intention tremor.

(b)
• Sensory symptoms first (paraesthesia/dysaesthesia); optic neuritis (blurring, diplopia); nystagmus (cerebellar); leg weakness (corticospinal); ataxia, clumsiness, lurching gait; dysarthria, dysphagia; fatigue; cognitive change; autonomic dysfunction and incontinence; Lhermitte's sign, trigeminal neuralgia, spasticity and brisk reflexes. Courses: relapsing-remitting (commonest), secondary progressive, primary progressive, progressive-relapsing.
• Predisposing: onset 20-40 years (peak 25-35); women affected about twice as often; genetic susceptibility; viral infection (Epstein-Barr); vitamin D deficiency; smoking; temperate latitudes; other autoimmune disease.

(c)
• An environmental trigger (virus) causes a delayed autoimmune attack in a genetically susceptible person: T and B cells infiltrate the CNS, causing inflammation and patches of demyelination in the white matter of brain and spinal cord.
• Oligodendrocytes are destroyed so axons cannot be remyelinated and are left exposed; inflammation causes axon damage and plaque formation; plaques are replaced by glial scar. Sites: optic nerve, corticospinal tract, posterior column, cerebellar peduncle; axonal damage and neurodegeneration produce permanent deficits.
• Diagnosis: clinical evidence of multiple lesions separated in time; MRI (best; white-matter lesions); CSF oligoclonal bands/raised gammaglobulin; evoked potentials on nerve conduction studies.

(d)
• Medical: corticosteroids for acute exacerbation, anti-spasticity drugs (baclofen, botulinum toxin), analgesics, anticholinergics for bladder, immunomodulators. PT goals: minimise progression, maintain functional independence, prevent complications, maintain respiratory function, conserve energy and manage fatigue, educate patient and family.
• Means: stretching, moderate submaximal active exercise, low-to-moderate strengthening with short bouts and rests, aerobic and PNF work, Frenkel coordination, static/dynamic balance, weight-bearing, ambulation with walking aids, splinting and adaptive equipment; positioning and ROM during relapse.
• Precautions: avoid overworking; exercise in a cool environment (heat and exercise worsen symptoms, Uhthoff's phenomenon); electrotherapy with caution.
questions.question:
A young adult presents with nystagmus, slow scanning speech with long pauses and an intention tremor. There is also fatigue, muscle weakness in the legs, and urinary incontinence.
(a) Give the diagnosis.
(b) Describe the clinical features and the predisposing factors.
(c) Explain the pathophysiology.
(d) Outline the physiotherapy management.
