questions.explanation: Honey should be avoided in infants under 12 months because it can contain Clostridium botulinum spores, which can cause infant botulism, a serious and potentially fatal illness, due to the infant's immature gut flora being unable to control spore germination. Well-cooked, appropriately textured foods such as mashed vegetables, fortified cereal, and pureed fruit are safe and recommended. This specific caution about honey is an important safety message for caregivers.
questions.question: A mother asks which foods should be avoided in infants under 12 months due to safety concerns. The nurse should specifically caution against:

options: mild allergic reaction to dressing material
questions.explanation: Sudden chest pain, dyspnoea, and tachycardia following prolonged surgery, particularly orthopaedic procedures with periods of immobility, should raise strong suspicion of pulmonary embolism from venous thromboembolism, requiring urgent assessment and escalation. This presentation is inconsistent with simple anxiety, surgical site pain, or normal recovery, all of which lack this specific combination of cardiorespiratory symptoms.
questions.question: A patient in recovery develops sudden severe chest pain, dyspnoea, and tachycardia several hours after a long orthopaedic procedure. The nurse should have a high index of suspicion for

options: Lying on the right side with the affected lung down
Lying on the left side with the good lung down
Flat on the back regardless of the affected side
Prone with the head turned to the right side
Sitting upright with legs elevated above heart level
questions.question: A patient with unilateral lung disease affecting the right lung is being positioned to optimize oxygenation. The nurse should position the patient:
questions.explanation: Positioning the unaffected lung in the dependent position takes advantage of gravity to increase blood flow to the better-functioning lung, improving ventilation-perfusion matching. This principle, 'good lung down,' is applied in unilateral lung disease to optimize oxygenation. It differs from bilateral disease management, where positioning strategies vary.

questions.question: A woman with placenta praevia has her placental location classified using ultrasound. Which finding defines a major degree of praevia?
options: The placenta lies in the upper uterine segment only
The placenta is more than five centimetres from the os
The placenta lies near but not touching the os
The placenta is implanted at the uterine fundus
The placenta completely covers the internal cervical os
questions.explanation: A major placenta praevia is defined as one where the placenta completely or partially covers the internal cervical os, precluding safe vaginal delivery. Minor degrees, where the placental edge lies in the lower segment without covering the os, may still permit vaginal birth depending on precise distance. This classification guides mode of delivery planning.

options: whole pieces of hard raw food
questions.question: A nurse advises a mother on the appropriate food texture progression for her 7-month-old infant. The most appropriate texture at this age is:
questions.explanation: By around seven months, infants are typically ready to progress from smooth purees to mashed or slightly lumpy soft foods, which helps develop oral motor skills needed for chewing and later speech development. Progressing texture too slowly can delay acceptance of more varied foods later. Whole hard pieces remain a choking hazard and should be avoided until the infant is developmentally ready for finger foods.

options: Two lateral swellings and tuberculum impar
questions.explanation: The anterior 2/3 (oral part) of the tongue develops from two lateral lingual swellings and the tuberculum impar, all from the 1st pharyngeal arch. The posterior 1/3 (pharyngeal part) develops from the copula (hypobranchial eminence) of the 3rd pharyngeal arch. These parts are separated by the linguo-gingival swelling.
questions.question: The anterior 2/3 of the tongue develops from which pharyngeal arch structures?

questions.explanation: IMCI utilises every sick child visit as an opportunity to update the child's vaccination status. If a child is not fully immunised for age and there are no contraindications to vaccination, all overdue vaccines should be given during the same visit, even if the child is mildly ill. Missing this opportunity to vaccinate can result in preventable illness. Only children with high fever, severe illness, or specific contraindications should have vaccination deferred to the next visit.
options: Refer the child to the immunisation clinic only if healthy
Defer immunisation until the current illness is fully resolved
Give all overdue vaccines if no contraindication is present
Advise the mother to bring the child next week for vaccines
Document the missed vaccines without giving any today
questions.question: IMCI child assessment always includes asking about immunisation status. If a child is not fully immunised for age, the nurse should:

questions.explanation: Massage therapy provides analgesic benefit primarily by promoting local blood circulation and reducing muscle tension, both of which can decrease pain associated with muscle tightness and spasm. It also may stimulate the release of endogenous pain-modulating substances and provide psychological relaxation benefit. It works as an adjunct to, rather than a replacement for, other indicated treatments.
options: Eliminating the need for any physical therapy
Permanently altering the client's pain threshold
Promoting local circulation and reducing muscle tension
questions.question: A nurse implementing massage therapy for a client with chronic muscle tension explains that it primarily provides analgesic benefit through which mechanism?

questions.explanation: The pulmonary valve has three semilunar (half-moon shaped) cusps: anterior, right, and left. Behind each cusp is a pulmonary sinus. The valve opens during right ventricular systole to allow blood into the pulmonary trunk and closes during diastole to prevent backflow. Unlike AV valves, semilunar valves have no chordae tendineae or papillary muscles.
questions.question: How many cusps form the pulmonary valve?
The Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome, a recognised complication of PID, is characterised by:
options: Ovarian cyst formation with torsion risk
Perihepatic inflammation causing right upper quadrant pain
Bilateral tubal blockage without any pain symptoms
questions.explanation: Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome results from spread of infection, typically gonococcal or chlamydial, from the pelvis to the liver capsule, producing perihepatic adhesions and right upper quadrant pain that can mimic cholecystitis. It is a recognised extragenital complication of ascending pelvic inflammatory disease. Awareness of this presentation prevents misdiagnosis and ensures appropriate antibiotic management targeting the underlying pelvic infection.

questions.question: During puerperal sepsis management, thromboprophylaxis is administered using:
options: Aspirin 75mg daily to reduce platelet aggregation
Enoxaparin as a low molecular weight heparin agent
Warfarin to maintain INR in therapeutic anticoagulant range
Clopidogrel 75mg daily for antiplatelet prophylaxis only
questions.explanation: Thromboprophylaxis during puerperal sepsis management is achieved with enoxaparin, a low molecular weight heparin. If the woman is breastfeeding, she may need a pump to assist with breastfeeding during this period. Note that NSAIDs should be used with caution when infection is confirmed to be due to Group A Streptococcus, as they may delay diagnosis and alter host defence mechanisms.

Postoperative infection rates reflect the results of care delivered to patients and therefore represent an outcome measure in the Donabedian model, distinguishing it from structure, which concerns resources and conditions, and process, which concerns the specific activities and procedures carried out during care.
questions.question: A hospital measures the rate of postoperative wound infections following surgical nursing procedures to assess care quality. This measure is BEST classified as which component of the Donabedian model?
A midwife caring for a woman recognises that ongoing severe pain in the second stage, out of proportion to contractions and unrelieved by usual measures, together with a rigid abdomen, may indicate:
options: Placental abruption or uterine rupture requiring urgent assessment
Expected finding as the second stage progresses
Reassuring finding needing no further action
questions.explanation: Severe, disproportionate pain with a rigid, tender abdomen suggests a serious complication such as placental abruption or uterine rupture, both of which are obstetric emergencies requiring urgent assessment and intervention. These findings should never be assumed to be simply intensifying normal labour pain. Prompt recognition allows for timely life-saving management for both mother and fetus.

options: Critically ill but with potential for recovery with maximal intervention
Patients with acute reversible illness requiring temporary organ support
Stable patients who are too well to need intensive care interventions
Monitored patients needing only hemodynamic stabilization measures
Terminally ill with irreversible conditions facing imminent death
questions.explanation: Priority 4 Category B includes patients with terminal and irreversible illness facing imminent death – they are 'too sick to benefit' from ICU care. This contrasts with Category A, who are 'too well to benefit.' Examples include severe irreversible brain damage and metastatic cancer unresponsive to therapy.
questions.question: Priority 4 Category B patients in the ICU are those who are:

questions.explanation: Continuous electronic fetal monitoring (CTG/cardiotocography) is mandatory throughout oxytocin augmentation. Oxytocin can cause uterine hyperstimulation (tachysystole - more than 5 contractions in 10 minutes), causing fetal hypoxia. Continuous CTG allows early identification of fetal compromise, enabling timely oxytocin dose reduction or discontinuation. Intermittent auscultation is insufficient during oxytocin infusion.
questions.question: During oxytocin augmentation, which form of fetal monitoring is mandatory?
options: Every 15 minutes for contractions and FHR assessment
Every 5 minutes auscultation while adjusting the infusion
Every 30 minutes with assessment of contraction strength
Every 60 minutes when the target contraction rate is reached

questions.question: Which cranial nerves emerge from the medulla?
questions.explanation: The glossopharyngeal (IX), vagus (X), accessory (XI), and hypoglossal (XII) cranial nerves emerge from the medulla oblongata. The hypoglossal nerve emerges between the pyramid and olive, while IX, X, and XI emerge posterior to the olive.

Reminiscing activities individualized to a patient's past hobbies and interests help seniors with dementia feel contented and peaceful, reduce stress, enhance positive feelings, and minimize challenging behaviors such as wandering. These activities do not cure the underlying disease, nor do they replace pharmacological treatment, and they do not restore complex skills such as independent driving. They also do not eliminate the ongoing need for caregiver support, which remains essential throughout the disease course.
options: To reduce stress, enhance positive feelings, and minimize challenging behaviors such as wandering
To eliminate the need for caregiver support
To cure the underlying disease process
To fully restore the client's ability to drive independently again someday soon eventually
To completely replace the ongoing need for cholinesterase inhibitors entirely
questions.question: A nurse incorporates reminiscing activities, such as looking through old photographs and listening to favorite music, into the care of a client with dementia. What is the primary intended benefit of these activities?

questions.explanation: Twin pregnancies carry a higher risk of postpartum haemorrhage because uterine overdistension can impair effective contraction after birth, increasing the likelihood of atony. Malpresentation and cord prolapse risks are also increased, not decreased, due to the presence of two fetuses and often unstable lies. Delivery mode must be carefully planned and is not guaranteed to be vaginal for both twins.
questions.question: A midwife caring for a woman with twin pregnancy in labour anticipates a HIGHER risk of which complication compared with singleton labour?
options: Postpartum haemorrhage due to uterine overdistension
Guaranteed vaginal delivery of both twins

questions.question: A nurse caring for a patient recovering from a TIA explains that, unlike acute complications such as falls, there are generally what kind of long-term complications associated specifically with TIA itself?
questions.explanation: While patients can experience acute complications during a TIA such as falls leading to fractures or hematomas, there are no documented long-term complications of transient ischemic attacks themselves. Permanent paralysis, guaranteed dementia, ventilator dependence, and certain seizure development are not accurate descriptions of TIA outcomes.
options: Permanent paralysis in nearly all patients
No long-term complications, though falls can occur

questions.explanation: While nurses play an important supportive and clarifying role in the consent process, the physician performing the procedure holds primary responsibility for disclosing its specific risks and obtaining informed consent, so the nurse should clarify her role, reinforce the patient's questions, and ensure the physician provides the detailed procedural risk disclosure.
options: explain all surgical risks fully herself as requested
refuse to discuss the procedure at all with the patient
guess at the likely risks to satisfy the patient
tell the patient to research the risks independently online
clarify her role and involve the physician for procedural risks
questions.question: A patient requests that her nurse, rather than a physician, explain the details of an upcoming surgical procedure's risks. The nurse's MOST appropriate action is to
A patient with a family history of retinoblastoma is found to carry a germline mutation in the RB1 gene. The RB1 gene product normally functions as a tumour suppressor by:
options: Regulating progression through the cell cycle checkpoint
questions.explanation: The retinoblastoma protein is a critical regulator of the cell cycle, normally restraining progression from the G1 to S phase by binding and inhibiting transcription factors required for DNA synthesis. Loss of functional retinoblastoma protein removes this checkpoint control, allowing unregulated cell cycle progression and contributing to tumorigenesis. This central role in cell cycle regulation explains why RB1 mutations are implicated in a wide range of human cancers beyond retinoblastoma itself.

questions.question: A patient's healing wound shows fibroblast recruitment and proliferation driven by growth factors released from degranulating platelets. Platelet-derived growth factor in wound healing is sourced from which cells?
questions.explanation: Platelet-derived growth factor is released by activated platelets at the time of injury and is subsequently also produced by macrophages and endothelial cells, contributing to sustained fibroblast and smooth muscle cell recruitment throughout the proliferative phase. This multi-source production ensures a continued supply of the growth factor as healing progresses beyond the initial haemostatic response. Its actions include chemotaxis and mitogenic stimulation of connective tissue cells essential for granulation tissue formation.

Methotrexate, the most commonly used disease-modifying antirheumatic drug in rheumatoid arthritis, requires regular liver function and full blood count monitoring due to its potential for hepatotoxicity and bone marrow suppression. Blood glucose, thyroid function, urinalysis for glucose and blood pressure monitoring are not the primary safety concerns with this specific medication. This monitoring priority guides safe long-term therapy.
options: Regular liver function and full blood count monitoring
questions.question: A client with rheumatoid arthritis is prescribed methotrexate. Which nursing monitoring priority is MOST important during this therapy?

options: Malaria rapid diagnostic test, as fever with rash is common in malaria-endemic settings
Blood culture to identify the causative organism before initiating treatment
Haemoglobin level to differentiate viral from bacterial causes of the fever and rash
Koplik's spots on the buccal mucosa to confirm or exclude a measles diagnosis
Urine culture to exclude urinary source of fever before attributing it to the rash
questions.question: A child aged 3 years presents with high fever, cough, runny nose, red watery eyes, followed by a rash starting on the face and spreading to the body. The FIRST diagnostic step is to assess for:
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of high fever, cough, runny nose, red watery eyes (the '3 Cs' plus fever), followed by a rash starting on the face and spreading to the body, strongly suggests measles. The first diagnostic step is to assess for Koplik's spots on the buccal mucosa, which are pathognomonic of measles and appear 1 to 2 days before the rash. Early clinical diagnosis enables prompt isolation to prevent community spread and initiation of supportive care including vitamin A supplementation.

options: The number of previous surgeries performed at the facility
The surgeon's personal preference for teaching content
The insurance coverage available for the procedure
The hospital's standard preoperative teaching checklist alone
The patient's current level of understanding and specific concerns
questions.question: When assessing a patient's need for preoperative information, the nurse should FIRST evaluate:
questions.explanation: Assessment should begin by identifying what the patient already understands and what specific concerns they hold, allowing teaching to be tailored rather than generic. A standard checklist alone may miss individual gaps or misconceptions. Individualised assessment ensures teaching time is used efficiently and addresses the patient's actual needs.

questions.question: The nursing management of a woman with APH includes educating mothers during antenatal visits. Which sign should mothers specifically be taught to report immediately?
questions.explanation: Mothers should be educated during antenatal visits to immediately report any episode of vaginal bleeding, as this could represent APH from placenta praevia, abruption, or other causes requiring urgent evaluation. Delays in reporting bleeding episodes can lead to significant maternal and fetal morbidity and mortality. Health professionals should provide clear verbal and written information about warning signs and when to seek emergency care.

Monitoring CD4+ T lymphocyte count and HIV viral load assesses the overall HIV disease status and immune function, which directly predicts the risk of ocular opportunistic infections. Low CD4 counts (below 200 cells/mm³) indicate severe immune compromise and heightened risk for conditions such as CMV retinitis, toxoplasma retinochoroiditis, and other sight-threatening infections. This systemic monitoring is essential for guiding the timing and intensity of prophylactic and therapeutic ocular interventions.
questions.question: The nursing intervention of 'monitoring CD4 count and HIV viral load' for a patient with ocular HIV manifestations is PRIMARILY to:
options: Monitor for antiretroviral drug toxicity causing ocular side effects
Assess the overall HIV disease status to predict risk of ocular complications
Establish whether the patient qualifies for intraocular steroid injection
Determine the dose of topical anti-inflammatory medications required
Determine the need for prophylactic antibiotic eye drops

questions.question: Which of the following CORRECTLY describes the complication of Sturge-Weber syndrome associated with a port wine stain?
options: Port wine stain with Sturge-Weber causes bilateral renal agenesis
Port wine stain associated with aortic coarctation and Turner syndrome
Port wine stain causing progressive skin thickening and necrosis
Port wine stain associated with VSD and pulmonary hypertension
Port wine stain mimicking distribution of ophthalmic branch of trigeminal nerve associated with glaucoma and epilepsy
questions.explanation: When a port wine stain mimics the distribution of the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve, further malformations in the eyes (glaucoma), meninges, or brain (epilepsy) may be suspected. This is known as Sturge-Weber syndrome. Parents and the child may need substantial psychological support.

questions.question: A nurse uses the Nursing Interventions Classification system to select interventions for a patient with the nursing diagnosis 'Ineffective Peripheral Tissue Perfusion' related to diabetes. What is the primary purpose of using a standardised classification system like NIC in this context?
options: To replace the need for individualised patient assessment
To determine the patient's medical diagnosis definitively
To calculate the patient's medication dosages automatically
To eliminate the need for documentation of care provided
To provide a standardised, evidence-based language for planning and communicating nursing care
questions.explanation: Standardised classification systems such as the Nursing Interventions Classification provide a consistent, evidence-based terminology that supports clear communication among healthcare providers and consistency in care planning and evaluation across different settings. This structured language complements, rather than replaces, individualised clinical judgement and assessment for each specific patient. Using such systems supports quality and continuity of nursing care.

Atherosclerosis roughens vessel endothelium, allowing platelet adherence and activation. Inflammation and endothelial damage similarly promote thrombus formation by exposing subendothelial collagen and tissue factor, initiating coagulation cascades in intact vessels.
questions.question: What promotes inappropriate thrombus formation?

options: Prevent sexual transmission of hepatitis B and its complications
Reduce the viral load of hepatitis B in already infected individuals
Provide cross-protection against hepatitis C viral infection
Treat existing hepatitis B infection before starting contraception
Screen high-risk populations for hepatitis B surface antigen
questions.explanation: Hepatitis B vaccination in family planning settings is offered to prevent new hepatitis B infection, which is sexually transmitted and can cause chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma. Vaccination before sexual exposure provides lasting protection. Family planning settings are an important point of contact for vaccination of at-risk individuals who may not otherwise access vaccination services. Hepatitis B vaccination has no therapeutic effect on existing infection.
questions.question: In the prevention strategies for HIV and STIs, hepatitis B vaccination is recommended in family planning settings primarily to:

options: Permanent loss of all allergic sensitivity
Immediate resolution with no further risk
Spontaneous cure of the underlying allergy
questions.question: A nurse caring for a patient recovering from anaphylaxis several hours ago should monitor for which possible complication before discharge?
questions.explanation: A biphasic anaphylactic reaction can occur hours after apparent resolution of initial symptoms, even without further allergen exposure, making a period of observation essential before safe discharge. Patients should be educated to seek immediate care if symptoms recur. This risk underscores the importance of extended monitoring after severe allergic reactions.

options: Be refrigerated and used within 48 hours of thawing
Be left at room temperature to slowly reach feeding temperature
Never be refrozen and discarded if any remains after feeding
Be warmed in a microwave for quick and safe preparation
Be kept at room temperature for up to 4 hours after thawing
questions.question: A breastfeeding mother asks about storing expressed breast milk. The nurse should advise that thawed breast milk should:
questions.explanation: Thawed breast milk should never be refrozen. It should be thawed in a cup or bowl of warm water (not left to cool at room temperature). After feeding, any milk remaining in the feeding container should be discarded and not saved for a later feeding. Breast milk that is refrigerated should not be left to cool at room temperature but thawed in warm water to maintain nutritional and immunological properties.

questions.question: Sympathetic stimulation of the bladder:
questions.explanation: Sympathetic fibers via hypogastric nerves (T10-L2) cause detrusor relaxation through β3-adrenergic receptors and internal sphincter contraction through a1-adrenergic receptors, promoting urine storage. This system is dominant during bladder filling. a1-blockers (tamsulosin) relax the internal sphincter and prostatic smooth muscle, improving urinary flow in benign prostatic hyperplasia. β3-agonists (mirabegron) enhance bladder relaxation for overactive bladder.

questions.question: A client is diagnosed with osteoarthritis that has no prior event or disease associated with its onset. This is classified as:
questions.explanation: Primary, or idiopathic, osteoarthritis has no prior event or disease related to its development, distinguishing it from secondary osteoarthritis which results from previous joint injury or inflammatory disease. Rheumatoid, septic, and gouty arthritis are inflammatory or infectious joint conditions with different etiologies entirely. This classification helps guide assessment of contributing history during evaluation.

A microtome is the specialized instrument used to cut tissue blocks into thin sections (typically 3–10 μm) that allow light transmission for microscopy. The cryostat is a variant used for frozen sections. A centrifuge separates components and an autoclave sterilizes, neither producing histological sections.
questions.question: A student views a specimen and finds it cannot be examined directly because of its thickness. Which instrument is most appropriate to produce thin translucent sections?
The Recovery Nurse's postoperative responsibility for wound and surgical site care includes:
options: Inspecting for infection, bleeding, and reporting concerns to the team
Administering systemic antibiotics for confirmed SSI management
Removing sutures or staples once the wound appears healed
Performing wound debridement and re-dressing as indicated
Irrigating the surgical wound with antiseptic solution routinely
questions.explanation: The recovery nurse inspects the surgical site for signs of infection, bleeding, or other complications, provides appropriate care, and reports any concerns to the surgical team. Active wound interventions such as debridement or suture removal are beyond the recovery nurse's scope; their role is assessment, monitoring, and communication.

questions.question: A patient receiving a large-volume field block for hernia repair should be monitored closely because the cumulative local anaesthetic dose increases the risk of
options: delayed wound healing at the site
immediate cardiac arrest without warning signs
questions.explanation: Large-volume local anaesthetic infiltration increases the total dose administered and therefore the risk of systemic absorption reaching toxic plasma concentrations, producing central nervous system and cardiovascular toxicity. This is why maximum weight-based doses must be calculated and adhered to during extensive field blocks. Toxicity typically presents with warning signs before progressing to cardiac arrest, rather than occurring without warning.

Veins of the breast drain into both the axillary and internal thoracic veins. The pattern follows the arterial supply. During pregnancy and lactation, these veins become engorged and may be visible through the skin. Venous drainage is important in the spread of breast cancer.
questions.question: Which veins drain the breast?
What happens during incompatible blood transfusion?
questions.explanation: Incompatible transfusions cause recipient antibodies to bind donor red cell antigens, causing agglutination (clumping). Agglutinated cells block small vessels and undergo hemolysis (rupture), releasing hemoglobin into plasma, potentially causing kidney failure and death.

options: No significant change in medication sensitivity
Reduced drug effect requiring higher initial doses
Excessive sedation and increased fall risk
Improved alertness compared to younger adults
Faster drug clearance requiring more frequent dosing
questions.explanation: Older adults often have increased sensitivity to sedative medications due to pharmacodynamic changes in the central nervous system, leading to excessive sedation and a heightened risk of falls, even at standard adult doses. This is the opposite of reduced effect requiring higher doses. This heightened sensitivity underlies the geriatric prescribing principle of starting at lower doses.
questions.question: A nurse caring for an older client prescribed a new sedative medication should recognise the priority safety concern related to age-related pharmacodynamic changes as increased risk of:
A nurse assessing an older client's nutritional status uses the Mini Nutritional Assessment tool and identifies a risk for malnutrition. The most appropriate next step is to:
questions.explanation: A positive malnutrition risk screening should prompt a more comprehensive nutritional evaluation and development of an appropriate intervention plan, which may include dietary modification, supplementation, or further investigation of underlying causes. Jumping directly to invasive interventions like parenteral nutrition without further assessment, or dismissing the screening result, would not be appropriate. Timely follow-up on screening results supports proactive nutritional care.
options: Immediately begin total parenteral nutrition without further assessment
Restrict the client's diet further to simplify meal planning
Wait several months before any further nutritional evaluation
Initiate a comprehensive nutritional evaluation and intervention plan
Disregard the finding since screening tools are unreliable

questions.question: The average age of menarche is:
questions.explanation: The average age of menarche (first menstrual period) is 11 years, though there is individual variation. Menarche typically occurs 2-3 years after the onset of breast development and represents a later stage of pubertal development. It indicates maturation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis sufficient to support menstrual cycling.

options: It guarantees the client will never experience side effects
It eliminates the need for further pain assessment
It maintains consistent drug levels and prevents pain escalation
It reduces the total medication cost significantly
It is used only if the client requests it
questions.question: A nurse plans to administer prescribed analgesics on a scheduled, around-the-clock basis for a client with predictable postoperative pain, rather than only as needed. What is the PRIMARY rationale for this scheduling approach?
questions.explanation: Scheduled, around-the-clock analgesic administration for predictable, ongoing pain maintains more consistent blood drug levels, preventing the pain from escalating to a more severe, harder-to-control level between doses, compared with waiting until pain becomes significant before administering an as-needed dose. This proactive approach is a recognised best practice for managing predictable acute pain, such as in the early postoperative period. Ongoing assessment remains necessary to evaluate effectiveness and adjust the regimen as needed.

questions.question: A patient reports noticing patches of skin that have lost pigmentation on the hands and around the mouth. The nurse recognises this as vitiligo and considers it may coexist with which category of disease?
questions.explanation: Vitiligo results from autoimmune destruction of melanocytes and frequently coexists with other autoimmune endocrine disorders such as Addison's disease and Hashimoto's thyroiditis, reflecting a shared predisposition to autoimmune conditions. Recognising this association can prompt screening for other autoimmune endocrine disease in a patient presenting with vitiligo. This differs from infectious or purely nutritional causes of skin changes.
options: Viral infections of the skin exclusively
Autoimmune endocrine disorders such as Addison's disease or Hashimoto's thyroiditis
Nutritional deficiency of vitamin A exclusively

questions.explanation: Pre-eclampsia is defined as new-onset hypertension developing after twenty weeks gestation in a previously normotensive woman, accompanied by proteinuria or evidence of other maternal organ dysfunction such as renal or liver impairment. This distinguishes it from chronic hypertension, which predates pregnancy or the twenty-week threshold. Accurate definition guides correct diagnosis and subsequent management planning.
questions.question: A woman diagnosed with pre-eclampsia asks how this condition is defined in relation to her blood pressure and gestational age. What is the standard definition?
options: Hypertension present before conception in any woman
Elevated blood pressure only during the first trimester
New hypertension after twenty weeks with proteinuria or organ dysfunction
Hypertension diagnosed exclusively in the postpartum period
Any blood pressure reading above the non-pregnant baseline

questions.explanation: Low health literacy requires the nurse to use plain, simple language, combined with visual aids, demonstrations, and return demonstrations to ensure understanding. Providing dense written materials in technical language would exacerbate the comprehension barrier rather than address it.
questions.question: When a nurse identifies that a patient has low health literacy, the MOST appropriate adaptation to preoperative teaching is to:
options: Shorten the teaching session to avoid overwhelming the patient
Provide more detailed written handouts in technical language
Ask the patient's family to take over the educational process
Use simple language, visuals, and demonstration techniques
Refer the patient to a specialist health educator for teaching

questions.explanation: The subcostal plane is a horizontal transverse plane passing through the inferior margins of the 10th costal cartilages (lowest point of the costal margin) on each side, corresponding to the upper border of the third lumbar vertebra (L3). Together with the transtubercular plane (L5 level) and the two vertical midclavicular planes, it defines the nine regions of the abdomen. The subcostal plane marks important anatomical landmarks including the origin of the inferior mesenteric artery, the level of the pylorus in some individuals, and the approximate position of the inferior border of the liver.
questions.question: The subcostal plane passes through which vertebral level?
A newborn with a suspected fractured clavicle following a difficult vaginal delivery is most likely to present with which clinical finding?
options: Bilateral absence of the Moro reflex entirely
Hyperextension of both lower limbs bilaterally
Complete facial asymmetry when crying vigorously
Persistent bulging of the anterior fontanelle
Asymmetric or absent Moro reflex on the affected side
questions.explanation: A fractured clavicle typically causes pain on movement of the affected arm, leading to an asymmetric or absent Moro reflex on that side, along with possible crepitus or a palpable bony irregularity over the clavicle itself. Bilateral Moro absence, facial asymmetry, and fontanelle bulging suggest entirely different underlying pathologies. Clavicular fractures generally heal well with simple supportive measures such as gentle handling and pinning the sleeve to clothing.

questions.question: Which patient scenario most appropriately justifies escalating from Step 2 to Step 3 of the WHO analgesic ladder?
options: Patient with mild headache requesting stronger analgesia
Patient requesting opioids for social or recreational purposes
Patient with uncontrolled cancer pain despite maximum weak opioid doses
Patient with mild arthritis pain not responding to paracetamol alone
Patient with acute ankle sprain requiring immediate post-injury pain relief
questions.explanation: The WHO analgesic ladder mandates escalation from Step 2 (weak opioids) to Step 3 (strong opioids) when pain is not adequately controlled despite reaching the maximum recommended dose of a Step 2 agent. This scenario - a cancer patient with uncontrolled pain at maximum weak opioid doses - is the prototype indication for strong opioid initiation. The ladder is designed to match analgesic potency to pain severity systematically, avoiding both undertreatment and inappropriate use of potent analgesics for mild pain.

A red, inflamed appearance on the ectocervix may represent cervical erosion (ectropion), infection, or, rarely, a precancerous lesion. The appropriate step is to collect a Pap smear to rule out cervical dysplasia and a cervical swab to exclude infection, particularly STIs such as chlamydia or gonorrhoea. This ensures a systematic and evidence-based approach before initiating any treatment.
options: Immediately initiate antibiotic therapy for PID
Perform a Pap smear and cervical swab for investigation
Proceed with IUD insertion without further workup
Reassure the patient that this is always benign
Refer immediately to a gynaecological oncologist

A patient's surgical wound is examined one week after injury and shows an established bed of new vessels and fibroblasts filling the defect. By five to seven days after wounding, granulation tissue:
questions.explanation: By five to seven days, granulation tissue has typically become well established, filling the wound space with proliferating fibroblasts and new capillaries, though it continues to mature and remodel over subsequent weeks. At this stage tensile strength remains far below normal, and the tissue has not yet been replaced by mature collagenous scar. This timeline is clinically useful for anticipating the expected appearance of a healing wound at follow-up assessment.
options: Has not yet begun to form
Is completely replaced by mature scar
Has fully regained normal tensile strength
Fills the wound space and continues to mature
impaired gas exchange related to anaemia
deficient fluid volume related to blood loss
risk for infection related to open wound
altered nutrition related to poor intake
questions.question: A postpartum woman with heavy ongoing blood loss develops tachycardia, pallor, and reduced consciousness. The most appropriate nursing diagnosis reflecting this presentation is:
questions.explanation: Tachycardia, pallor, and altered consciousness after significant blood loss reflect hypovolaemia, making 'deficient fluid volume related to excessive blood loss' the most fitting nursing diagnosis. This guides prioritised interventions such as intravenous fluid resuscitation and blood transfusion. Ongoing vital sign monitoring evaluates response to treatment.

options: The goal is fully met and can be discontinued
The goal has failed completely and should be abandoned
The goal is partially met, requiring continued or revised interventions
No evaluation can be made without further laboratory testing
The goal was never appropriate and should be deleted
questions.question: A nurse is evaluating whether a care plan goal for a patient with diabetes has been met. The patient's most recent HbA1c has improved but remains above the target range. How should the nurse document this evaluation?
questions.explanation: When a patient shows some improvement toward a goal but has not yet reached the specific target, this represents partial goal achievement, prompting the nurse to continue or adjust interventions rather than concluding the goal was either fully met or a complete failure. This nuanced evaluation reflects the ongoing, dynamic nature of the nursing process. Recognising partial progress allows for more tailored ongoing care planning.

questions.question: Semitendinosus, semimembranosus, and the long head of biceps femoris are all innervated by which division of the sciatic nerve?
questions.explanation: Semitendinosus, semimembranosus, and the long head of biceps femoris are all innervated by the tibial division of the sciatic nerve (L5, S1, S2). The exception is the short head of biceps femoris, which is supplied by the common fibular division. The sciatic nerve is the largest nerve in the body.

questions.question: A patient with a persistent foreign body embedded in soft tissue develops a firm nodule on biopsy showing aggregates of epithelioid macrophages. This pattern of chronic inflammation is termed:
questions.explanation: Granulomatous inflammation is a distinctive pattern of chronic inflammation characterised by aggregates of activated macrophages, called epithelioid cells, often surrounding an indigestible foreign material or a poorly degradable pathogen. It represents an attempt by the immune system to wall off an agent it cannot easily eliminate. Foreign body granulomas, tuberculous granulomas, and sarcoidosis are all examples of this pattern with differing underlying causes.

questions.question: A patient taking levothyroxine for hypothyroidism asks the nurse the best way to take this medication for optimal absorption. What should the nurse advise?
options: Take it with a large meal to improve absorption
Take it on an empty stomach each morning, before eating
Take it at bedtime with dairy products
Take it together with calcium or iron supplements
Take it only when symptoms of hypothyroidism appear
questions.explanation: Levothyroxine absorption is significantly reduced by food, particularly dairy, and by certain supplements such as calcium or iron, so it is recommended to take it on an empty stomach in the morning, separated by 30 to 60 minutes from food or other medications, to ensure consistent absorption. Taking it inconsistently or with interfering substances can lead to fluctuating hormone levels and difficulty achieving stable control. This teaching point is essential for effective long-term management of hypothyroidism.

options: Permanent guardianship established immediately at the very first sign of any cognitive impairment
All decisions must be made by the healthcare provider without client input
Complete and immediate withdrawal of all treatment until full capacity is formally re-established again
Regular assessment of decision-making capacity and maximizing supported decision-making within the client's fluctuating capacity
Reliance exclusively on family members for all decisions without assessing the client
questions.question: The principle of autonomy in elder care requires that healthcare providers ensure which of the following when caring for older adults with fluctuating cognitive capacity?
questions.explanation: Respecting autonomy in clients with fluctuating cognitive capacity requires regular assessment of their current decision-making capacity and maximizing supported decision-making within whatever capacity the client retains at any given time, involving proxy decision-makers only when the client genuinely cannot decide. Having providers make all decisions without client input, establishing permanent guardianship at first cognitive impairment, withdrawing all treatment, and relying exclusively on family without assessing the client each violate the principle of autonomy by failing to engage the client's own decision-making to its fullest extent.

questions.question: The nursing care plan for a patient with hyperthyroidism includes the goal of maintaining core temperature below 37.5°C. Which nursing intervention directly addresses this goal?
options: Providing a cool environment and lightweight bed coverings
Administering corticosteroids to reduce thyroid inflammation
Encouraging high-calorie fluid intake to meet metabolic needs
Restricting physical activity to conserve metabolic heat
Monitoring TSH levels to evaluate treatment effectiveness
questions.explanation: Hyperthyroidism causes hyperthermia (elevated body temperature) due to the increased metabolic rate driven by excess thyroid hormone. The nursing intervention of providing a cool environmental temperature and lightweight bed coverings (such as a single sheet rather than blankets) directly reduces the thermal burden on the patient and promotes heat dissipation. This comfort-focused nursing intervention addresses the symptom of heat intolerance and elevated temperature, which is the physiological basis of the nursing goal stated.

questions.question: Which antihypertensive drug is absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy due to its teratogenic effects on the fetal kidney?
options: ACE inhibitors (e.g., enalapril/lisinopril) — cause fetal renal agenesis
Labetalol — associated with fetal growth restriction
Methyldopa — causes haemolytic anaemia in neonates
questions.explanation: ACE inhibitors (enalapril, lisinopril, ramipril, captopril) and ARBs (losartan, valsartan) are absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy (all trimesters, though most dangerous in second and third trimesters). They cause fetal renal tubular dysgenesis, oligohydramnios (from lack of fetal urine production), pulmonary hypoplasia, limb contractures, skull hypoplasia, and intrauterine fetal death. Women on ACE inhibitors must be switched to a safe alternative (methyldopa, labetalol, or nifedipine) before or immediately upon confirming pregnancy.

Esophageal adenocarcinoma has surpassed squamous cell carcinoma as the predominant type in Western countries, with incidence rising dramatically. It typically arises in the distal esophagus from Barrett's esophagus (intestinal metaplasia from chronic GERD). Risk factors include GERD, Barrett's esophagus, obesity, smoking, and white race/male sex. Squamous cell carcinoma predominates globally and in the proximal/mid esophagus, associated with smoking, alcohol, achalasia, caustic injury, and tylosis. Both present late with dysphagia and weight loss. Treatment involves esophagectomy with neoadjuvant chemoradiation; prognosis is poor (15-20% 5-year survival).
questions.question: The most common type of esophageal cancer in Western countries is:

questions.explanation: Immobilizing or bracing a painful body part reduces pain by restricting movement at the injured or inflamed site, thereby decreasing mechanical stimulation of nociceptors in the affected tissues. Movement of an injured area stretches and compresses damaged structures, activating mechanoreceptors and exacerbating pain. By limiting this movement, immobilization reduces nociceptive input, prevents further tissue damage during the healing phase, and provides a stable environment for repair. It is particularly effective for acute fracture pain, joint inflammation, and musculoskeletal injuries.
questions.question: Immobilization or bracing of a painful body part as a nursing intervention achieves pain relief through which mechanism?
options: Blocking afferent pain signals through transcutaneous electrical current
Replacing pharmacological analgesia in post-fracture pain management
Increasing circulation to the painful area, reducing inflammatory mediators
Restricting movement of the painful part to reduce mechanical nociceptive stimulation
Stimulating endogenous opioid release through sustained mechanical pressure
Hyperglycaemia and excessive weight gain in the first week
High Apgar scores with respiratory depression only
Polycythaemia, hypoglycaemia, and difficulty maintaining temperature
Exomphalos and diaphragmatic hernia requiring immediate surgery
Excessive jaundice due to high haemoglobin levels only
questions.explanation: SGA babies at birth may experience: decreased oxygen levels, low Apgar scores, meconium aspiration, hypoglycaemia, difficulty maintaining normal temperature, and polycythaemia. These complications arise from impaired intrauterine nutrition and adaptation. Management requires careful monitoring, thermoregulation, and blood sugar checks.
questions.question: Which of the following complications is MOST likely to affect an SGA baby at birth?

options: Neurons as supporting cells and oligodendrocytes as conducting cells
Neurons that conduct impulses and mitotically capable neuroglia that provide support
Astrocytes that conduct and Schwann cells that only support in CNS
Microglia that conduct and astrocytes that provide energy
Both neuroglia and neurons conduct impulses equally
questions.explanation: The nervous system has two fundamental cell categories: neurons are the electrically excitable conducting cells that transmit electrochemical impulses, and neuroglia or glial cells are the non-conducting support cells far more numerous than neurons that retain the ability to undergo mitosis. The term neuroglia means nerve glue reflecting the originally conceptualized function of physically supporting neurons.
questions.question: The two main cell types in nervous tissue and their primary distinction are which of the following?

questions.explanation: Leukocytosis, an elevation of the circulating white blood cell count, commonly rises to fifteen to twenty thousand cells per microlitre during the acute-phase response to infection, driven by accelerated release of leukocytes from the bone marrow reserve. Bacterial infections classically produce neutrophilia, whereas some viral infections may instead cause a relative lymphocytosis. Marked leukocytosis supports a clinical suspicion of ongoing acute inflammation such as appendicitis.
questions.question: A patient with acute appendicitis has a full blood count showing a white cell count of 18,000 cells per microlitre. This finding, typical of the acute-phase response, is termed:
Where does deoxygenated blood from the heart drain?
questions.explanation: Most cardiac venous blood drains through the coronary sinus into the right atrium. Some blood drains through small cardiac veins directly into right chambers. This deoxygenated blood mixes with systemic venous return before pulmonary circulation.

questions.question: A client with type 2 diabetes admits to stopping their metformin two weeks ago due to nausea and is now confused with severe hyperglycaemia. Which factor MOST likely precipitated this presentation?
questions.explanation: Stopping diabetes medications accounts for a significant proportion of Hyperosmolar Hyperglycaemic State presentations because uncontrolled hyperglycaemia develops rapidly without treatment. Excessive fluids, increased activity, vaccination and improved dietary control would not precipitate this hyperglycaemic emergency. Medication history is therefore essential when assessing a client presenting this way.

questions.question: A nurse caring for a patient with polycythaemia secondary to chronic hypoxic lung disease should prioritise monitoring for:
options: Signs of bleeding from low platelet count
Signs of anaemia such as pallor
Signs of thrombosis such as calf swelling
questions.explanation: Chronic hypoxia drives excessive erythropoietin release, raising red cell mass and blood viscosity, which predisposes to venous and arterial thrombosis. Nurses should assess for calf tenderness, swelling, and chest pain suggestive of clot formation. Adequate hydration and mobility help reduce this risk.

Fertility returns rapidly after stopping combined oral contraceptives because the hormones do not accumulate or cause lasting suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis. Many women can conceive within the very first cycle off the pill. This rapid return distinguishes COCs from injectable progestins, where return of fertility can be delayed by several months.
questions.question: A client asks how quickly fertility returns after discontinuing combined oral contraceptive pills. The correct response is that fertility:
options: Returns only after a mandatory six-month wait
Is permanently reduced after five years of use
Requires ovulation induction drugs to restore
Remains suppressed for approximately two years
Returns promptly, often within the same cycle

questions.question: Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) is listed as a control measure for STIs. PEP is most effective when initiated:
questions.explanation: Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) is most effective when initiated within 72 hours of potential exposure, and earlier initiation provides greater protection. PEP involves a course of antiretroviral medications taken for 28 days to prevent HIV infection after potential exposure. The 72-hour window is a critical clinical guideline, and PEP should ideally be started as soon as possible after exposure. It is listed as a key STI control strategy alongside contact tracing and treatment.
options: Within 24 hours of potential exposure only
Within one week of potential exposure
At any time within one month of exposure
Only after laboratory confirmation of exposure

questions.explanation: Severe hypoxemia with respiratory distress requires immediate intervention with supplemental oxygen to prevent further tissue hypoxia and organ damage. Diagnostic workup and detailed history-taking should follow stabilization of the patient's airway and breathing. This reflects the airway-breathing-circulation priority framework used in emergency assessment.
questions.question: A patient in the emergency department has an oxygen saturation of 85% on room air with signs of severe respiratory distress. The nurse's priority action is to:
options: Obtain a detailed medication history first
Schedule a chest X-ray before any treatment
Wait for arterial blood gas results before acting
Encourage the patient to breathe more slowly

questions.question: A diabetic patient reports sudden vision changes and blurry vision between scheduled review visits. What should the patient do immediately?
questions.explanation: Diabetic patients should contact their eye doctor right away if their vision suddenly changes or becomes blurry, spotty, or hazy between appointments. Sudden visual change may indicate acute vitreous haemorrhage, retinal detachment, or rapid proliferative retinopathy requiring urgent intervention. Prompt reporting and specialist assessment can prevent irreversible vision loss.
options: Wait for the next scheduled annual review
Apply lubricating eye drops and monitor
Genetic testing of embryos before ovarian stimulation begins
Fertilisation of oocytes in the laboratory before any ovarian stimulation
Ovarian stimulation to produce multiple mature follicles for oocyte retrieval
Retrieving the male partner's sperm for cryopreservation before stimulation
Transfer of embryos into the uterus before follicle development
questions.explanation: In vitro fertilisation begins with controlled ovarian hyperstimulation using gonadotrophin injections to stimulate the ovaries to produce multiple mature follicles. This is followed by oocyte retrieval (egg collection) using ultrasound-guided needle aspiration, fertilisation of retrieved oocytes with prepared sperm in the laboratory, embryo culture for 3 to 5 days, and finally embryo transfer into the uterine cavity. Genetic testing (PGT) may be performed on embryos before transfer if indicated.
questions.question: In counselling a couple about in vitro fertilisation (IVF), the nurse should explain that the first step in the IVF process involves:

questions.explanation: The nurse anesthetist (CRNA) conducts a comprehensive preoperative assessment evaluating medical history, anesthesia risks and contraindications, allergies, and formulates an appropriate anesthesia plan. This assessment is the foundation for safe anesthesia administration and intraoperative patient management.
options: Wound care education and postoperative activity restrictions
Patient's understanding of the surgical procedure and consent
Preoperative laboratory values and imaging for surgical clearance
Nutritional status and bowel preparation compliance
Medical history, anesthesia risks, allergies, and anesthesia planning
questions.question: The nurse anesthetist's preoperative assessment specifically evaluates:
A nurse explains growth monitoring to a group of mothers attending a child welfare clinic. She defines growth monitoring as the regular assessment and recording of a child's:
questions.explanation: Growth monitoring involves the regular measurement and recording of anthropometric indicators such as weight, height or length, and head circumference over time, plotted against standard reference charts to track a child's growth trajectory. This ongoing process allows early identification of growth faltering or malnutrition. It differs from a single one-off measurement, as trends over time are more informative than isolated readings.

questions.question: A nurse caring for a client in a new plaster of Paris cast checks the exposed fingers for colour and warmth every hour. Which complication is this monitoring intended to detect EARLY?
questions.explanation: The nursing care of a patient in a plaster of Paris cast should include checking for early signs of compartment syndrome, such as changes in colour, warmth, sensation and movement, since a tight cast can constrict swelling tissue and compromise circulation. Malunion, non-union, osteomyelitis and chronic regional pain syndrome are later complications that would not present with these acute hourly changes. Early detection through frequent monitoring prevents permanent tissue damage.

questions.question: A nurse counsels a client that after a high-risk sexual exposure, starting specific antiretroviral medication within a limited time window can prevent HIV acquisition. What is this intervention called, and when is it most effective?
questions.explanation: Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) involves antiretroviral medication started as soon as possible after a high-risk exposure, ideally within 72 hours, to reduce the likelihood of HIV transmission. Delay in initiation reduces its effectiveness significantly. This differs from pre-exposure prophylaxis, which is taken before potential exposure.
options: Post-exposure prophylaxis, most effective when started soon after exposure
Pre-exposure prophylaxis, most effective when started before exposure
Contact tracing, most effective when started after diagnosis
Vaccination, most effective when started in childhood
Syndromic management, most effective when started after symptoms appear

questions.explanation: Residual volume (RV) is the volume of air that remains in the lungs even after the most forceful expiration, averaging about 1200 mL. This air cannot be expelled voluntarily and serves critical functions including preventing alveolar collapse between breaths and allowing continuous gas exchange. The presence of residual volume ensures that the lungs never completely empty, maintaining some oxygen availability and preventing the airways from collapsing completely.
questions.question: Residual volume averages approximately:

options: Extreme hunger requiring immediate nasogastric tube feeding
Severe systemic illness preventing the child from swallowing
Dehydration so severe that the child cannot open their mouth
Oral thrush preventing swallowing of fluids or breast milk
Extreme fatigue from fever preventing effort of suckling
questions.question: The IMCI symptom of 'unable to drink or breastfeed' is a general danger sign because it indicates:
questions.explanation: Inability to drink or breastfeed in IMCI is a general danger sign because it reflects severe systemic illness that impairs the child's level of consciousness, swallowing reflex, or energy to the point where they cannot feed. This sign indicates a very sick child who requires urgent hospital care. It should be distinguished from a child who is not hungry after a recent meal - inability means the child cannot drink even when fluid is actively offered, indicating a critical level of illness.

Fat embolism syndrome is a serious complication that most commonly follows fractures of long bones, presenting with respiratory distress, confusion and a characteristic petechial rash within one to two days of injury. Compartment syndrome presents with localised limb findings rather than systemic respiratory and neurological symptoms. Deep vein thrombosis, tuberculosis and osteomyelitis present with different characteristic features not matching this acute triad.
questions.question: A client with a long bone fracture develops sudden respiratory distress, confusion, and a petechial rash 24 to 48 hours after injury. Which complication does the nurse suspect?
During physical assessment of a client with a painful, inflamed joint, the nurse notes increased skin temperature on palpation over the area. What does this finding most likely indicate?
questions.explanation: Increased skin temperature over a painful joint on palpation typically indicates local inflammation, often accompanied by redness and swelling, which is contributing to the client's pain experience. This physical finding supports and corroborates the client's subjective pain report. Correlating physical assessment findings with self-reported pain provides a more complete clinical picture.
options: A completely unrelated skin infection only
Local inflammation contributing to the client's pain
Reduced blood flow to the joint
A normal finding requiring no further assessment

questions.question: Which bone forms the prominence of the cheek?
questions.explanation: The zygomatic bones form the prominence of the cheeks and lie on the inferolateral sides of the orbits. They articulate with the frontal, sphenoid, temporal, and maxillary bones. The bone has a broad connection with the maxilla medially and forms part of the zygomatic arch laterally. Fractures cause flattening of the malar eminence.

options: facilitate access while coordinating timely physician discussion
refuse to ever release results directly to patients
release the results with no further explanation offered
tell the patient the results do not exist yet
withhold results indefinitely until the patient forgets
questions.explanation: Patients generally have a right to access their own test results, and the nurse's appropriate role is to facilitate this access while coordinating timely discussion with the physician to ensure the patient receives adequate context and support in understanding potentially significant findings, rather than outright refusing or indefinitely delaying access.
questions.question: A patient requests a copy of test results before her physician has reviewed and discussed them with her. The nurse's MOST appropriate response is to
A client newly diagnosed with bone cancer expresses fear about possible amputation and changes in body image. Which nursing referral is MOST appropriate to support emotional adjustment?
questions.explanation: Referral to a psychologist or spiritual advisor provides emotional support for clients and families dealing with fears, concerns, and feelings related to cancer diagnosis and possible amputation. Dietary counselors, surgical technicians, pharmacy staff, and radiology technologists address different aspects of care unrelated to psychosocial adjustment. Addressing body image concerns is part of holistic nursing management for bone tumor clients.

Mullerian agenesis, also known as Mayer-Rokitansky-Kuster-Hauser syndrome, presents with primary amenorrhoea due to congenital absence of the uterus and upper vagina, while normal secondary sexual characteristics develop because ovarian function and hormone production remain intact. A blind-ending vagina on examination is a classic finding. Karyotyping and imaging help confirm the diagnosis and guide further management.
questions.question: A woman presents with primary amenorrhoea at seventeen years of age, and examination reveals a blind-ending vagina with normal secondary sexual characteristics. Which condition is most consistent with this presentation?
options: Polycystic ovary syndrome, with anovulatory cycles
Premature ovarian insufficiency, with early menopause
Mullerian agenesis, with absent uterus and upper vagina
Turner syndrome, with associated short stature

questions.explanation: Catecholamines (epinephrine, norepinephrine) are released during stress, hypoglycemia, and sympathetic activation. They increase heart rate, blood pressure, glucose mobilization, and metabolic rate. Catecholamines are critical counter-regulatory hormones protecting against hypoglycemia and mediating stress responses.
questions.question: Catecholamines are released during:

questions.explanation: In triage systems adapted alongside IMCI, colour coding typically follows: Red = Emergency (immediate life-saving intervention needed - equivalent to IMCI general danger signs), Yellow = Priority (needs prompt assessment and treatment - equivalent to IMCI severe classifications without immediate danger signs), Green = Routine care (stable, can wait - equivalent to non-severe IMCI classifications). This colour coding streamlines care in busy health facilities and ensures the sickest children receive care first.
questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes how the IMCI triage colour classification system works in most adapted national protocols?
options: Red = routine care, Yellow = priority, Green = emergency care
Red = emergency, Yellow = priority, Green = routine care
Green = emergency, Red = routine, Yellow = priority care
Red = urgent referral, Yellow = home care, Green = hospital
Green = mild, Yellow = severe, Red = very severe classification

questions.explanation: Viral myocarditis causes direct inflammatory damage to cardiac myocytes, which can impair contractility and disrupt the conduction system. This places the patient at risk for both acute heart failure and life-threatening arrhythmias. Close cardiac monitoring is essential during the acute phase of illness.
questions.question: A nurse caring for a patient with suspected myocarditis following a recent viral illness should monitor closely for:
options: Signs of anaemia related to bleeding
Signs of chronic kidney disease only
Signs of heart failure and arrhythmia
Signs of peptic ulcer disease only

questions.explanation: A diet with excessive phosphorus relative to calcium, often from high consumption of processed foods and carbonated beverages, can negatively affect calcium balance and bone health, making the ratio between these minerals clinically relevant in osteoporosis management. Eliminating phosphorus entirely is neither necessary nor appropriate, as it is an essential nutrient. Balanced intake of both minerals supports optimal bone health in older adults.
options: Calcium intake should always be lower than phosphorus intake overall
Phosphorus intake has no relationship to calcium balance
Excess phosphorus intake relative to calcium can impair calcium balance
Phosphorus should be entirely eliminated from the diet completely
The ratio between these minerals has no clinical relevance
questions.question: A nurse caring for an older client with osteoporosis provides dietary counselling regarding calcium intake. Which teaching point about the calcium-to-phosphorus ratio is most accurate?

questions.explanation: A low cognitive screening score indicates the need for further comprehensive evaluation to determine the underlying cause, which could include dementia, delirium, depression, or other reversible conditions, rather than an immediate definitive diagnosis. Screening tools identify the need for further assessment, not a final diagnosis on their own. Communicating findings promptly to the team supports timely, accurate diagnosis and care planning.
options: Communicate findings to the team for further comprehensive evaluation
Assume normal ageing and take no further action at all
Inform the family the client will require permanent institutionalisation
Disregard the score since screening tools are never useful
Immediately diagnose the client with dementia based on this score
questions.question: A nurse using a standardised cognitive screening tool notes an older client scores significantly below the expected range for education level. The nurse's most appropriate next step is to:
GABA (gamma-aminobutyric acid) primarily functions as which neurotransmitter type?
questions.explanation: GABA is the brain's principal inhibitory neurotransmitter, used by approximately 30% of central synapses. GABA-A receptors are chloride channels producing fast inhibition, while GABA-B receptors are metabotropic G-protein-coupled receptors causing slower, prolonged inhibition. GABAergic interneurons regulate circuit excitability; insufficient GABA function contributes to epilepsy and anxiety disorders.

questions.question: A nurse caring for a mechanically ventilated patient with ARDS notes the physician has ordered prone positioning. This intervention primarily aims to:
questions.explanation: Prone positioning in ARDS improves oxygenation by promoting more uniform lung aeration and better ventilation-perfusion matching, particularly in the previously dependent lung regions. It is a recognised adjunct therapy for severe hypoxaemia, not a replacement for ventilator support or a preventive measure against infection. Careful monitoring is required during and after repositioning due to risks such as line dislodgement.
options: Reduce the need for any sedation medication
Replace the need for ongoing haemodynamic monitoring
Eliminate the requirement for positive pressure ventilation
Prevent all future episodes of pneumonia entirely
Andropause always begins before age 40 in all men
Andropause causes complete loss of fertility in all men
Andropause involves an abrupt single-day hormonal cessation
Andropause lacks a clear endpoint like menstruation
Andropause is unrelated to testosterone levels
questions.question: A 53-year-old man reports a gradual, several-year decline in energy, libido, and muscle mass, without any abrupt cessation of a defined reproductive cycle. Why does andropause differ importantly from menopause in this respect?
questions.explanation: Unlike menopause, which has a clear clinical endpoint marked by 12 months of amenorrhoea, andropause involves a gradual, variable testosterone decline without a universally defined endpoint, and many men retain some fertility. This makes diagnosis of andropause less clear-cut than menopause. Recognising this difference is important for accurate counselling of male clients.

Transitional epithelium of the bladder is classified as a stable, or quiescent, tissue because its cells normally exhibit a low level of replication but retain the capacity to undergo rapid proliferation in response to injury or increased demand. This differs from labile tissues, such as the epidermis or gut epithelium, which divide continuously throughout life, and from permanent tissues, such as cardiac myocytes and neurons, which have essentially no regenerative capacity in adulthood. This intermediate regenerative capacity allows the bladder epithelium to repair itself effectively following injury while normally remaining relatively quiescent.
questions.question: A patient's bladder wall biopsy shows transitional epithelium capable of stretching and returning to its original shape. In terms of regenerative capacity, this epithelium is classified as which type of tissue?
A patient's healing wound at three weeks shows a pale, flattened scar rather than the earlier raised, red appearance. This maturation and blanching is accomplished PRIMARILY by:
questions.explanation: Scar maturation and blanching during the remodelling phase occur as the dense capillary network of granulation tissue regresses through programmed cell death of endothelial cells, reducing the vascularity and causing the scar to fade from red to pale. Simultaneously, collagen is reorganised into thicker, more organised bundles that increase tensile strength. This regression of vasculature is a normal and expected part of the transition from granulation tissue to mature scar.
options: Increased neutrophil infiltration into the scar
Reduced vascularity as capillaries regress during remodelling
New collagen deposition without any vessel change
Continued active angiogenesis at the same rate

questions.explanation: Phalen's test (passive wrist flexion for 60 seconds) provokes carpal tunnel syndrome symptoms by increasing pressure within the tunnel. Reproduction of paresthesia in the median nerve distribution within one minute is considered positive. The reverse Phalen's test uses wrist extension.
questions.question: Which position tests for carpal tunnel syndrome?

questions.explanation: Cytokine release syndrome (CRS) is the most important acute toxicity of CAR-T cell therapy, resulting from massive immune activation and cytokine release (particularly IL-6) following CAR-T cell engagement with tumour cells. It manifests as high fever, hypotension, tachycardia, and in severe cases, multiorgan dysfunction. Management includes tocilizumab (IL-6 receptor antagonist) and corticosteroids for severe cases, with ICU-level supportive care. Nurses must monitor vital signs frequently and respond swiftly to early CRS signs in the first 1–14 days post-infusion.
options: Severe constipation from bowel motility inhibition
Liver failure from direct hepatic cell toxicity
Cytokine release syndrome (CRS) with hyperpyrexia and hypotension
Deep vein thrombosis from CAR-T cell aggregation
questions.question: The nurse caring for a patient receiving CAR-T cell therapy for lymphoma must be specifically prepared for which life-threatening toxicity?

options: the inner square remains lighter than the outer circle
the vial has been stored at the correct temperature
the expiry date has not yet passed
inner square colour matches or exceeds the outer circle
the vaccine appears clear without particulate matter
questions.explanation: A vaccine vial monitor indicates cumulative heat exposure, and the vaccine should not be used once the inner square has changed colour to match or become darker than the surrounding circle, signalling that the vaccine has likely lost potency due to heat exposure. Checking the vial monitor is a simple, practical field method for assessing vaccine viability even when continuous temperature logging is unavailable. This check should be performed before every vaccine administration, in addition to verifying the expiry date.
questions.question: A nurse checks a vaccine vial monitor before administering a dose to a child. The vaccine should NOT be used when the vaccine vial monitor indicates:

options: Its large bulk and dual blood supply
Its ability to plantarflex the ankle
Its broad origin from the ischial tuberosity
Its dual nerve supply from femoral and obturator nerves
Its consistent neurovascular pedicle and manageable dimensions
questions.question: The gracilis muscle is frequently used as a free flap in reconstructive surgery. It is most suitable because of which anatomical feature?
questions.explanation: The gracilis muscle is frequently used in reconstructive surgery because of its consistent neurovascular pedicle (medial femoral circumflex artery perforators and the obturator nerve), manageable length and bulk, and relatively small donor site morbidity. It is used for facial reanimation, limb reconstruction, and dynamic graciloplasty for sphincter reconstruction in fecal incontinence.

questions.question: A client with Cushing Syndrome has a bone density scan revealing significant loss of bone mass. Which mechanism BEST explains this complication?
options: Cortisol suppresses osteoblast activity and calcium absorption
Cortisol stimulates excess vitamin D synthesis
questions.explanation: Chronic glucocorticoid excess suppresses osteoblast function and reduces intestinal calcium absorption, leading to progressive bone loss and osteoporosis in Cushing Syndrome. This catabolic bone effect is a well-recognised long-term complication of hypercortisolism. Parathyroid breakdown, phosphate retention, vitamin D stimulation and thyroid conversion are not the primary mechanisms responsible.

questions.question: A neonate with ophthalmia neonatorum develops an ineffective breathing pattern. The nurse administers oxygen PRIMARILY to:
options: Prevent corneal drying from increased respiratory rate
Eliminate the Chlamydia organisms from the respiratory tract
Correct dyspnea and improve oxygenation in the neonate
Stimulate surfactant production in the premature neonate
Reduce the intraocular pressure elevated by crying and distress
questions.explanation: Oxygen is administered to a neonate with an ineffective breathing pattern to correct dyspnea and improve oxygenation. In neonates with ophthalmia neonatorum complicated by respiratory involvement (especially from Chlamydia, which can cause pneumonia), inadequate gas exchange leads to hypoxemia that must be addressed urgently. Respiratory assessment, positioning, suctioning of secretions, and oxygen administration are key nursing interventions to maintain adequate respiratory function.

Achondroplasia is an autosomal dominant condition caused by a defect in the ossification of the epiphyseal plate. It presents with a disproportionately large head, very short limbs, and pronounced lumbar lordosis. Cognitive development is typically not impaired. No specific treatment is required for the condition itself, though supportive care and psychological support for parents are important components of management.
questions.question: Achondroplasia is caused by which genetic mechanism and presents with which combination of features?
options: Multifactorial inheritance associated with maternal vitamin D deficiency
Autosomal dominant condition with large head, short limbs, and lordosis
Autosomal recessive mutation causing severe cognitive impairment
X-linked recessive inheritance affecting male infants exclusively
Chromosomal trisomy causing intellectual disability and cardiac defects
Cracked nipple leading to haematoma formation
Mastitis progressing toward breast abscess formation
Breast engorgement from inadequate emptying of milk
Normal colostrum ejection causing transient inflammation
Retained placental fragment causing reflux mastitis
questions.question: A puerperal woman presents with a hard, red, and painful area confined to one lobe of the breast, accompanied by a fever and rigors. This is most consistent with:
questions.explanation: Mastitis is an infection of the breast tissue confined to one lobe, presenting with a hard, red, painful, and tender affected area accompanied by systemic signs of infection including pyrexia and rigors. It typically follows cracked nipples or breast engorgement. If mastitis is not promptly treated with antibiotics, it may progress to abscess formation requiring surgical drainage in addition to systemic antibiotic therapy.

options: Encourage the patient to cough forcefully
Administer back blows only in a seated position
Perform abdominal thrusts to dislodge the object
Provide reassurance and continue monitoring closely
Offer sips of water to clear the throat
