Acute mitral regurgitation from loss of leaflet support
questions.explanation: Sudden loss of chordal support allows the mitral leaflet to flail, producing acute, often severe mitral regurgitation with a new loud murmur and rapid symptom onset. This contrasts with the gradual symptom progression typically seen in chronic valve disease. Recognising this acute presentation is important because it often requires urgent medical and potentially surgical management.
questions.question: A physiotherapist assessing a patient after a suspected chordae tendinae rupture notices sudden worsening breathlessness and a new loud murmur. What is the most likely explanation for this acute presentation?
Which pathway correctly traces the flow of oxygenated blood after it leaves the lungs?
options: Pulmonary artery to right atrium to right ventricle to aorta
Venae cavae to right atrium to left ventricle to aorta
Pulmonary veins to left atrium to left ventricle to aorta
Pulmonary veins to right atrium to left ventricle to pulmonary artery
Aorta to left atrium to left ventricle to pulmonary veins
questions.explanation: Oxygenated blood returns from the lungs via the pulmonary veins into the left atrium, then passes through the mitral valve into the left ventricle. From there it is ejected through the aortic valve into the aorta for systemic distribution. This completes the pulmonary to systemic transition within the circulatory pathway.

options: Resting heart rate and total blood volume
Systolic blood pressure and diastolic blood pressure
Maximal cardiac output and maximal oxygen extraction by the tissues
Respiratory rate and tidal volume alone
Body mass index and resting metabolic rate
questions.question: Maximal oxygen consumption, or VO2 max, is best described as the product of which two physiological variables?
questions.explanation: VO2 max reflects the combined capacity of the cardiovascular system to deliver oxygen, measured as maximal cardiac output, and the ability of tissues to extract that oxygen. Training improves both components, raising overall aerobic capacity. This measure is often used to gauge cardiorespiratory fitness and guide exercise prescription intensity.

questions.question: A patient recently diagnosed with heart failure asks the physiotherapist why fluid restriction has been recommended by their physician. What is the most accurate explanation to relay?
questions.explanation: In heart failure, restricting fluid intake helps reduce circulating volume and limit the congestive symptoms such as breathlessness and oedema associated with fluid overload. This works alongside, rather than replacing, diuretic medication in overall management. Explaining this rationale supports patient understanding and adherence to broader lifestyle recommendations.
options: Fluid restriction directly strengthens the heart muscle itself
Fluid restriction eliminates the need for any diuretic medication
Fluid restriction has no relationship to symptom control
Fluid restriction is only relevant to patients with kidney disease
Reducing fluid intake helps limit fluid overload and associated congestive symptoms

questions.question: Which statement best explains why hypoxaemia often develops before hypercapnia in early restrictive lung disease?
options: Oxygen has a much smaller molecule than carbon dioxide
Carbon dioxide diffuses far more readily across a thickened membrane than oxygen
Carbon dioxide production decreases before oxygen use falls
Hyperventilation always lowers oxygen delivery first
The respiratory centre is insensitive to falling oxygen levels
questions.explanation: Because carbon dioxide is far more soluble and diffuses more easily than oxygen, early membrane thickening impairs oxygen transfer before carbon dioxide elimination is affected. Patients therefore often hyperventilate to compensate, which can further lower PaCO2. Hypercapnia typically only appears once disease is advanced and ventilation can no longer compensate.

options: Directly increasing heart muscle contractile force
Controlling the tone of the blood vessels to reduce cardiac workload
Increasing fluid retention within the circulation
Blocking electrical conduction through the atrioventricular node
Increasing resistance to blood ejection from the ventricle
questions.question: Vasodilators such as nitrates and calcium channel blockers are used in heart failure management primarily to achieve which effect?
questions.explanation: Vasodilators reduce the resistance the heart must pump against, easing the workload on a failing ventricle. This differs from diuretics, which target fluid volume, and digitalis, which targets contractile force. Together these drug classes address different aspects of the pathophysiology in heart failure.

options: Avoiding all forms of supervised walking indefinitely
Avoiding any communication with the healthcare team
Avoiding heavy lifting and straining activities such as the Valsalva manoeuvre
Avoiding routine follow-up appointments after surgery
Avoiding education about their surgical procedure
questions.question: A patient is scheduled to begin outpatient cardiac exercise following recent coronary bypass surgery. Which precaution specifically relates to avoiding excessive intrathoracic pressure during early exercise?
questions.explanation: Heavy lifting and straining sharply raise intrathoracic pressure and cardiac workload, both of which are specifically avoided in the early period after cardiac surgery to protect the healing sternotomy and reduce cardiovascular strain. Supervised walking and structured education, by contrast, are core safe components of early rehabilitation. This distinction helps guide appropriate exercise selection during early recovery.

options: Complete immobilisation of the chest wall to prevent any movement
Deep breathing exercises combined with adequate pain relief and positioning
Withholding all analgesia to encourage voluntary deep breathing
Vigorous unsupported percussion regardless of pain level
Avoiding any breathing exercises until the wound has fully healed
questions.question: A patient recovering from thoracic surgery has shallow breathing due to incisional pain, resulting in reduced basal lung expansion. Which physiotherapy technique is most appropriate to directly address this specific problem?
questions.explanation: Encouraging deep breathing exercises, supported by adequate pain control and appropriate positioning, helps overcome the shallow breathing pattern caused by incisional pain after thoracic surgery. Withholding analgesia would likely worsen compliance with breathing exercises rather than help. This approach directly targets the mechanical limitation caused by pain rather than ignoring or overcorrecting for it.

Chest percussion is contraindicated in the presence of rib fractures because it risks further injury and pain. Shaking is also contraindicated in similar structural risk situations, so a gentler technique or alternative method should be selected instead. Reviewing case notes before any hands-on technique is an essential safety step in ICU physiotherapy.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is about to perform chest percussion on a ventilated ICU patient and notices the case notes document recent rib fractures. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Proceed with percussion at a reduced force over the fracture site
Avoid chest percussion and select an alternative airway clearance technique
Proceed with percussion only on the unaffected side without further precaution
Delay all treatment for one week without reassessment
Proceed with vibrations at maximal intensity instead

questions.explanation: Circuit training rotates patients through several low to moderate intensity stations such as cycling, arm ergometry and stepping. This variety distributes workload across different muscle groups while allowing close monitoring during initial stages. Continuous conditioning activities like walking or swimming are typically introduced later as tolerance improves.
questions.question: Which training method involves several exercise stations performed in rotation and is recommended during the initial stages of cardiac exercise programmes?

questions.explanation: Certain groups may face additional barriers to accessing or completing rehabilitation, including social, financial or physical challenges. Recognising these groups allows the multidisciplinary team to adapt programmes to improve equity of access and outcomes. Special consideration does not mean exclusion, but rather tailored support.
questions.question: Which factor is emphasised as needing special consideration when planning cardiac rehabilitation for certain patient groups?
options: Only young athletic males with no comorbidities
Only patients who have never smoked
Only patients with private health insurance
Only patients living in urban areas
Women, the elderly, people with low income and people with physical disability

questions.question: Special consideration should be given to informal carers during cardiac rehabilitation for which reason?
questions.explanation: Family members or informal carers often provide practical and emotional support that reinforces the goals set during rehabilitation. Involving them helps ensure continuity of care once the patient returns home. This support does not substitute for professional medical or therapeutic input, but complements it.
options: They are legally required to attend every hospital appointment
They must independently prescribe the patient's medications
They replace the need for professional medical follow-up
They are responsible for performing the patient's surgery

questions.explanation: Excess positive fluid balance can lead to fluid accumulating within the pulmonary interstitium and alveoli, producing what is commonly described as wet lungs or pulmonary oedema. This can worsen gas exchange and increase secretion viscosity difficulties. Recognising this risk helps guide appropriate chest physiotherapy and positioning decisions.
questions.question: A large positive fluid balance recorded on an intensive care chart may specifically predispose the patient to which pulmonary complication?
options: Pulmonary embolism from a peripheral clot
Pulmonary oedema, described as wet lungs
Improved lung compliance from reduced surface tension
Widening of the major central airways
Complete absence of any airway abnormality
questions.explanation: Because airway resistance rises sharply as luminal radius decreases, bronchoconstriction is a common and significant cause of both increased resistance and audible wheeze during ventilation. Identifying this mechanism helps guide appropriate medical and physiotherapy management, which may include bronchodilator therapy alongside secretion clearance techniques. Reassessment after intervention helps confirm improvement.
questions.question: A ventilated patient develops rising airway resistance and audible wheeze on auscultation. Which underlying mechanism most directly explains this finding?

Permanently restricting the patient to bed rest for safety
Avoiding all patient and family education indefinitely
Allaying anxiety and depression while offsetting the harmful effects of bed rest

questions.question: Which of the following is listed as a specific goal of the initial phase of cardiac rehabilitation?
questions.explanation: Early goals focus on psychological reassurance and counteracting the physical deconditioning that prolonged bed rest can cause. These goals support a gradual, safe return toward activities of daily living. Later phases build on this foundation with more structured exercise and lifestyle education.

questions.question: Which physical property allows the lung to return to its resting volume after inspiration?
options: Active contraction of expiratory muscles at rest
Rigidity of the bony thoracic cage
questions.explanation: Lung tissue contains elastic fibres that stretch during inspiration and recoil passively during quiet expiration. This recoil, not muscular effort, drives normal tidal expiration. Loss of elastic recoil, as in emphysema, causes air trapping.

questions.question: A reduction in airway lumen diameter during an asthma attack is mainly caused by which combination of factors?
options: Cartilage collapse, alveolar fibrosis and hyperinflation
Smooth muscle contraction, mucosal oedema and secretions
Diaphragmatic weakness, pleural thickening and effusion
Loss of surfactant, atelectasis and consolidation
Rib cage stiffness, kyphosis and reduced compliance

questions.explanation: In atrial fibrillation, multiple chaotic electrical wavelets circulate through the atria instead of a single coordinated impulse. Complete absence of electrical activity in both atria and ventricles
Regular, coordinated atrial contraction at a normal rate
Isolated ventricular ectopic beats with a normal atrial rhythm

Continuous prone positioning maintained for twenty-four hours
Upright sitting maintained continuously without repositioning

questions.question: A patient in the ICU is unconscious and paralysed, requiring prolonged nursing care. Which positioning approach is specifically recommended for this patient?

Intrapleural pressure rising above alveolar pressure
Alveolar pressure falling below atmospheric pressure

questions.question: During normal quiet inspiration, which pressure gradient chiefly drives air movement into the alveoli?

questions.explanation: Vibrations are contraindicated in the presence of metastasis affecting the ribs or spine because the mechanical force could risk pathological fracture or increased pain. questions.question: A physiotherapist is treating a patient with known spinal metastases in the ICU and is selecting a manual technique for secretion clearance. Which technique is specifically contraindicated by this finding?

questions.explanation: Although individual small airways have a narrow lumen, their total cross-sectional area is large, which lowers combined resistance. questions.question: Airway resistance is highest and airflow most turbulent in which region of the tracheobronchial tree?

questions.explanation: Airway resistance is inversely related to the fourth power of the airway radius, so even small reductions in lumen size sharply increase resistance. Bronchoconstriction is therefore a major contributor to increased work of breathing. This relationship explains why bronchodilators are so effective in reducing breathlessness.

options: Less complete oxygen extraction with greater lactate production
No measurable change in oxygen extraction efficiency
More complete oxygen extraction with less increase in lactate production

This reduces reliance on anaerobic metabolism, resulting in less lactate accumulation compared with an untrained individual. This adaptation is part of the explanation for why regular exercise benefits patients with heart disease.
questions.question: Better distribution of blood to trained muscle fibres following exercise training produces which net physiological effect for a given workload?
Which set of symptoms represents the classic hallmark presentation of restrictive lung disease?
questions.explanation: Restrictive lung disease classically produces slowly progressive breathlessness on exertion, along with a persistent dry, non-productive cough. Exercise tolerance declines as lung volumes and diffusion capacity fall. These features differ from the productive cough of infection or the wheeze of obstructive airway disease.

Wheeze, chest tightness and nocturnal cough
Progressive dyspnoea, dry cough and reduced exercise tolerance

questions.question: Which pulmonary condition listed among interstitial causes of restrictive dysfunction is granulomatous in nature?
questions.explanation: Sarcoidosis produces non-caseating granulomas within the lung interstitium, which can progress to fibrosis if untreated. This granulomatous inflammation distinguishes it from the scarring pattern of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. Both ultimately reduce lung compliance and volumes.

questions.question: A ventilated patient's chart shows a persistently elevated inflation pressure. What is the most appropriate initial physiotherapy consideration?
questions.explanation: A rising inflation pressure during mechanical ventilation may reflect retained secretions, bronchospasm or reduced lung compliance, all of which are relevant to physiotherapy assessment and treatment planning. Identifying the underlying cause helps guide whether chest physiotherapy, repositioning or medical review is the priority. Removing a patient from ventilation is a medical decision, not a physiotherapy action.
options: Increase mobilisation intensity immediately without further assessment
Discontinue all monitoring of the ventilator settings
Assess for retained secretions or reduced lung compliance contributing to the raised pressure
Assume the finding is unrelated to any respiratory pathology

questions.question: Chronic stress is thought to contribute to cardiovascular risk primarily through which mechanism?
questions.explanation: Prolonged stress can elevate blood pressure over an extended period and trigger the release of platelets that promote clot formation. This combination increases the likelihood of thrombotic cardiovascular events over time. Stress management techniques are therefore often incorporated into comprehensive cardiac risk reduction programmes.
options: Sustained elevation of blood pressure and release of clot-forming platelets
Direct destruction of red blood cells
Permanent paralysis of the autonomic nervous system
Immediate calcification of the coronary arteries
Complete suppression of the immune system
Worsened restriction of lung volumes on the affected side
No change in chest expansion under any circumstances
Improved chest expansion and lung volumes on the affected side
Immediate development of new interstitial fibrosis
Immediate onset of unrelated cardiac arrhythmia
questions.question: A patient with a large pleural effusion undergoes therapeutic drainage. Following the procedure, which change would the physiotherapist most expect on reassessment?
questions.explanation: Removing fluid that was compressing the adjacent lung typically allows improved expansion and lung volumes on the previously affected side. This reflects the pleural cause of restriction being directly addressed by the drainage procedure. Physiotherapy assessment before and after such procedures helps document objective improvement in respiratory function.

questions.question: A patient with atrial fibrillation presents to physiotherapy for cardiac rehabilitation. On pulse assessment, the physiotherapist notes an irregularly irregular rhythm. What is the most appropriate immediate consideration before beginning exercise?
options: Proceeding with maximal intensity exercise regardless of rhythm control
Ignoring the pulse finding since it is expected in all cardiac patients
Confirming the patient's rhythm is adequately controlled and reviewing anticoagulation status
Assuming the patient requires immediate resuscitation without further assessment
Cancelling all future rehabilitation sessions permanently
questions.explanation: Before exercising a patient with atrial fibrillation, it is important to confirm that their heart rate is adequately controlled and to be aware of their anticoagulation status given the associated stroke risk. This assessment ensures exercise intensity is appropriately calibrated and safe. Ongoing monitoring during sessions remains important given the potential for rhythm-related symptoms.

options: Optimising functional exercise tolerance within symptom limits
Aggressive postural drainage to clear thick secretions
High-intensity resistance training of respiratory muscles
Prolonged bed rest to conserve oxygen consumption
Vigorous chest percussion regardless of symptoms
questions.question: Which management priority is most important for a physiotherapist treating a patient with restrictive lung disease due to advanced pulmonary fibrosis?
questions.explanation: Because fibrotic lung disease is progressive and secretions are not usually the primary problem, therapy focuses on maintaining functional capacity and managing breathlessness during activity. Pacing and controlled breathing techniques help the patient remain as active as tolerated. Aggressive secretion clearance techniques are generally unnecessary and may worsen dyspnoea.

options: Understanding the course of rehabilitation and supporting resumption of life at home
Learning to independently adjust the patient's cardiac medication doses
Learning to perform diagnostic cardiac imaging themselves
Taking over all decisions from the healthcare team entirely
Avoiding any involvement in the patient's recovery process
questions.explanation: Family education focuses on helping relatives understand the rehabilitation process and supporting practical planning for the patient's return home. This does not extend to clinical decision-making or technical medical tasks, which remain the responsibility of the healthcare team. Well-informed family support can meaningfully reinforce the patient's own rehabilitation efforts.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is educating a cardiac rehabilitation patient's family about their role during the recovery process. Which statement best reflects the recommended focus of this family education?

options: Only the patient's admission date to the hospital
Respiratory parameters including minute volume, inflation pressure and secretions
Only the visiting hours schedule for family members
Only the brand of ventilator being used
Only the colour of the patient's hospital gown
questions.explanation: Intensive care charts document respiratory information such as minute volume, inflation pressure if ventilated, breathing pattern, cough presence and secretion characteristics. Reviewing these parameters before treatment helps the physiotherapist judge the patient's current respiratory status and treatment needs. This system-specific review is part of the broader systematic ICU assessment approach.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is asked to review a mechanically ventilated patient's readiness for chest physiotherapy. According to standard ICU practice, which finding on the intensive care chart should be reviewed first?
Which congenital heart defect is characterised by the aorta arising from the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery from the left ventricle?
questions.explanation: In transposition of the great vessels, the two main arteries are switched, so oxygenated and deoxygenated blood circulate in separate parallel loops. This produces severe cyanosis unless a mixing lesion exists between the circuits. Surgical correction soon after birth is usually required for survival.

questions.question: A patient with Guillain-Barre syndrome develops progressive weakness and reduced vital capacity on serial spirometry. Which physiotherapy consideration is most urgent in this scenario?
options: Immediate aggressive postural drainage regardless of muscle strength
Close monitoring of respiratory muscle strength and ventilatory capacity for deterioration
Discharge planning without any further respiratory monitoring
High-intensity resistance training of the limbs as the priority
Ignoring respiratory status since the disease is neuromuscular
questions.explanation: Because Guillain-Barre syndrome can progressively weaken the respiratory muscles, close monitoring of vital capacity and respiratory function is critical to detect deterioration that may require urgent ventilatory support. This neuromuscular cause of restrictive dysfunction differs from parenchymal lung disease, but still carries significant respiratory risk. Physiotherapy input should be closely coordinated with medical staff monitoring disease progression.

questions.question: A diagnostic tool that directly measures intracardiac pressures via an inserted catheter is best described as which of the following?
questions.explanation: Cardiac catheterisation involves threading a catheter into the heart chambers or coronary vessels to measure pressures directly and visualise coronary anatomy with contrast. This invasive technique provides detailed haemodynamic data unavailable from non-invasive imaging alone. It is often used to confirm and treat coronary artery disease in the same procedure.

options: Acute renal failure with fluid overload
Severe hypertension unrelated to fluid status
questions.question: A central venous pressure reading lower than the normal range in an intensive care patient most likely indicates which condition?
questions.explanation: A central venous pressure below the normal range of zero to six suggests reduced circulating volume, consistent with dehydration. Conversely, a reading above six suggests overhydration, which risks progressing to pulmonary oedema and respiratory failure if uncorrected. This measurement helps guide fluid management decisions in critically ill patients.

options: Only the cardiac surgeon working alone
Physician, nurse, occupational therapist, nutritionist, psychologist and social worker
A single rehabilitation aide with no other input
Only family members without professional involvement
questions.question: Who typically coordinates the multidisciplinary cardiac rehabilitation team alongside the physiotherapist?
questions.explanation: Cardiac rehabilitation is delivered by a multidisciplinary team that addresses medical, nutritional, psychological and social needs together. Each professional contributes a distinct area of expertise toward the shared goal of comprehensive recovery. This team-based structure distinguishes cardiac rehabilitation from a purely medical or purely exercise-based intervention.

options: Small muscle group exercise always produces lower heart rate responses
Large muscle group exercise has no established physiological rationale
Isolated small muscle group training is always safer in coronary disease
Muscle group selection has no relevance to cardiac workload
Large muscle group exercise reduces the disproportionate haemodynamic strain seen with smaller muscle group work
questions.question: A physiotherapist is asked to justify prioritising aerobic exercise using large muscle groups for a patient with coronary artery disease rather than isolated small muscle group training. What is the most accurate justification?
questions.explanation: Exercise using small, upper body muscle groups tends to increase hemodynamic demand and cardiac strain disproportionately relative to the workload achieved, compared with large muscle group activities such as walking. Selecting large muscle group exercise helps minimise unnecessary cardiac strain in patients with underlying coronary disease. This principle directly informs exercise mode selection during cardiac rehabilitation prescription.

As mitral regurgitation worsens, backflow into the left atrium raises left atrial pressure, which is transmitted back into the pulmonary circulation, causing congestion and breathlessness. This mechanism explains why exertional dyspnoea often correlates with the severity of regurgitation. Monitoring symptom progression helps guide timing of further medical or surgical intervention.
options: Rising left atrial pressure leading to pulmonary congestion
Falling right atrial pressure improving venous return
Reduced pulmonary vascular resistance improving gas exchange
Increased right ventricular contractility compensating fully
Decreased left ventricular preload reducing symptoms
questions.question: A physiotherapist is treating a patient with confirmed mitral regurgitation who reports increasing breathlessness on exertion. Which underlying haemodynamic change most directly explains this worsening symptom?

options: Greater increase in heart rate for the same submaximal workload
Lower increase in heart rate and cardiac output for a given submaximal workload
Reduced stroke volume for any given workload
Increased resting heart rate at all times
Decreased efficiency of oxygen extraction by muscles
questions.explanation: Trained individuals achieve a given submaximal workload with a smaller rise in heart rate and cardiac output than untrained individuals, reducing cardiac strain. This occurs partly because trained muscles extract oxygen more efficiently, lessening the demand placed on the heart. This adaptation is one reason exercise training benefits patients with underlying coronary disease.
questions.question: Which cardiovascular adaptation to regular exercise training benefits patients with underlying heart disease?

questions.explanation: Turbulent blood flow across a stenotic or incompetent valve typically produces an audible murmur, the timing and location of which help identify the specific valve involved. Associated features may include exertional breathlessness or fatigue depending on severity. Detecting a new or changed murmur is often the first clue to underlying valvular pathology.
options: A completely silent precordium with no audible sounds
An abnormal heart murmur on auscultation
A perfectly regular pulse with no other findings
Total absence of any exercise limitation
Normal heart sounds with no additional findings
questions.question: Which clinical feature would most likely be expected in a patient with significant valvular heart disease?

questions.explanation: Preventative interventions specifically focus on reducing impairment and promoting general health, including respiratory physiotherapy to enhance chest health, distinct from restorative interventions aimed at regaining lost movement or compensatory strategies using unaffected limbs. This distinction is useful for appropriately categorising and communicating treatment goals within a multidisciplinary rehabilitation plan. Airway clearance techniques fall specifically within this preventative category.
options: Preventative interventions promoting general respiratory health
Restorative interventions targeting motor recovery of the limbs only
Compensatory interventions targeting use of the unaffected side only
Interventions focused solely on vocational retraining
Interventions focused solely on cognitive rehabilitation
questions.question: A patient recovering from traumatic brain injury with associated chest involvement requires airway clearance support. Which category of physiotherapeutic intervention specifically targets enhancing chest health in this context?

questions.explanation: Rheumatic heart disease develops after childhood streptococcal infection triggers an autoimmune response damaging the heart valves. Because it develops after birth due to an external infectious trigger, it is classified as acquired rather than congenital. It most commonly affects the mitral and aortic valves.
questions.question: In the general classification of cardiovascular disease, rheumatic heart disease is typically categorised under which heading?

questions.explanation: Infective endocarditis can directly damage or perforate valve leaflets, leading to new or worsening regurgitation as a direct consequence of the infectious process. This differs from age-related degenerative or congenital causes, which have a different underlying mechanism and timeline. Recognising the infectious cause is important for guiding both medical treatment and monitoring for further valvular deterioration.
options: Complete regeneration of normal valve tissue during infection
Direct damage to the valve leaflets from the infective process
Congenital absence of the mitral valve discovered incidentally
Age-related calcification unrelated to the recent infection
Pregnancy-related volume changes unrelated to infection
questions.question: A patient recovering from infective endocarditis develops new mitral regurgitation. Which underlying valvular change most likely explains this new finding?

questions.explanation: Scar tissue formed after infarction does not conduct electrical impulses normally, creating a substrate for abnormal rhythms. It also does not contract, which can impair overall mechanical pumping function to some degree. This combination of electrical and mechanical consequences is why long-term cardiac monitoring remains important after infarction.
options: Complete regeneration of fully functional new heart muscle
Permanent immunity to any further cardiac events
Total normalisation of mechanical pumping function
Elimination of any future need for cardiac monitoring
questions.question: Following myocardial infarction, scarring of the healed myocardium can predispose the heart to which long-term complication?

questions.explanation: Digitalis glycosides increase the force of myocardial contraction, helping to improve cardiac output in heart failure. Diuretics instead reduce fluid retention, while vasodilators and sympatholytics primarily act on vascular tone. Each drug class targets a different component of the overall heart failure management strategy.
questions.question: Pharmacological management of heart failure aimed at increasing the force of myocardial contraction typically involves which class of drug?
The classic symptom of peripheral artery disease that occurs during walking and resolves with rest is termed which of the following?
questions.explanation: Intermittent claudication describes cramping muscle pain, typically in the calf, brought on by walking and relieved by rest due to inadequate arterial blood supply during exertion. It reflects the mismatch between oxygen demand and restricted arterial delivery. This symptom is a key clinical clue distinguishing peripheral artery disease from other causes of leg pain.

In true shunt physiology, blood bypasses ventilated alveoli entirely, so increasing inspired oxygen concentration has limited effect on overall arterial oxygenation. This differs from hypoventilation or mild diffusion problems, which typically respond well to supplemental oxygen. Recognising a shunt-dominant pattern is important because it may indicate a need for more advanced respiratory support, such as recruitment strategies or ventilation.
options: Simple hypoventilation fully responsive to supplemental oxygen
Mild diffusion impairment fully correctable with oxygen alone
Pure dead space ventilation unrelated to oxygenation problems
Normal ventilation-perfusion matching throughout the lung
A significant intrapulmonary shunt from unventilated but perfused lung tissue
questions.question: A patient with severe hypoxaemia is started on supplemental oxygen but shows minimal improvement in oxygen saturation. Which underlying mechanism is most likely responsible for this poor response?

questions.explanation: Atrial fibrillation predisposes to thrombus formation within a poorly contracting atrium, and embolisation of this thrombus can cause a stroke presenting with sudden focal neurological deficit. This risk is significantly higher without adequate anticoagulation. Recognising this potential presentation requires immediate emergency medical assessment rather than continuation of the rehabilitation session.
options: A simple vasovagal response to mild exertion
An expected and harmless side effect of exercise
A normal variant requiring no further evaluation
Thromboembolic stroke arising from atrial thrombus
A minor musculoskeletal strain unrelated to cardiac rhythm
questions.question: A patient with known atrial fibrillation who is not on anticoagulation develops sudden weakness on one side of the body during a rehabilitation session. What is the most likely explanation for this presentation?

questions.explanation: A ventricular septal defect is a hole in the muscular or membranous wall separating the ventricles. Blood typically shunts from the higher-pressure left ventricle to the right, increasing pulmonary blood flow. Large defects can lead to pulmonary hypertension and right ventricular strain over time.
questions.question: An abnormal opening between the left and right ventricles allowing blood to shunt between chambers describes which congenital defect?
Diuretics are used in heart failure management primarily to achieve which therapeutic effect?
questions.explanation: Diuretics promote renal excretion of sodium and water, reducing circulating fluid volume and relieving congestion in heart failure. This differs from the contractility-boosting action of digitalis or the vasodilatory action of nitrates. Reducing fluid overload helps ease symptoms such as breathlessness and peripheral oedema.
options: Increasing the force of myocardial contraction
Before any circuit training has been attempted
Only during the very first rehabilitation session
Exclusively during the acute inpatient phase immediately after the event
During the later stages, once initial tolerance has been established
Only after the patient has stopped attending rehabilitation
questions.question: Continuous conditioning activities such as swimming and cycling are typically introduced at which point in a cardiac rehabilitation programme?
questions.explanation: Circuit-type training is generally used first because it allows close monitoring and variety across multiple short work stations. Once tolerance and confidence improve, continuous activities of longer duration, such as swimming or cycling, are gradually introduced. This progression reflects the graded increase in workload central to safe cardiac exercise prescription.

questions.question: Provision of locally relevant written information about cardiac rehabilitation and support groups primarily serves which purpose?
questions.explanation: Written materials reinforce verbal education, giving patients a reliable reference they can revisit after discussions with the healthcare team. Connecting patients with local support groups helps sustain motivation and provides peer encouragement. This resource complements rather than replaces direct clinical contact and supervised rehabilitation activities.
options: Replacing the need for any verbal explanation from the healthcare team
Serving only as a legal record with no educational value
Substituting entirely for supervised exercise sessions
Reinforcing patient understanding and connecting them with ongoing community support
Eliminating the need for follow-up medical appointments

questions.explanation: By stage five, activity has progressed from partial self-care and short chair sitting toward longer supervised walks with active pulse monitoring. This graded increase reflects improving cardiovascular tolerance as recovery advances. Stage seven activities involve even greater distances and stair climbing in preparation for discharge.
questions.question: During which inpatient stage does a patient typically begin walking approximately three hundred metres twice daily while practising pulse counting?

options: Acute bronchospasm of the airway smooth muscle
Bacterial infection of the lung parenchyma
Mechanical obstruction of the central airway
Accumulation of air within the pleural cavity
Progressive interstitial fibrosis of the lung
questions.question: Connective tissue disease causes restrictive lung dysfunction chiefly through which process?
questions.explanation: Conditions such as systemic sclerosis and rheumatoid disease can trigger chronic inflammation that leads to interstitial fibrosis. This scarring stiffens the lung and reduces its compliance and volume, producing a restrictive pattern. Because it is progressive, early physiotherapy and monitoring of exercise tolerance are important.

options: Sexual activity must be avoided permanently after any cardiac event
Avoid sexual activity within an hour of eating or consuming a heavy meal
There is no need to consider timing relative to meals at all
Sexual activity should only occur immediately after heavy exercise
Sexual activity is always contraindicated during outpatient rehabilitation
questions.question: A patient recovering from myocardial infarction wants to know when they may resume sexual activity. Based on standard cardiac rehabilitation guidance regarding energy conservation, which advice is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Breathing control, body positioning and energy conservation strategies are used to help minimize symptoms during activities such as sexual activity after a cardiac event. Patients are specifically advised to avoid sexual activity within an hour of eating, or following a heavy meal, to reduce cardiac workload at that time. This guidance forms part of broader patient education about resuming daily activities safely.

Atherosclerotic plaque build-up in the coronary arteries progressively narrows blood flow to the myocardium, producing ischaemic heart disease. This acquired condition contrasts with the structural defects present from birth in congenital disease. Its risk factors include hypertension, hyperlipidaemia and smoking.
questions.question: Which acquired condition is most commonly caused by long-standing atherosclerosis of the coronary arteries?

questions.explanation: Stage one activities include partial self-care, self-feeding, dangling legs at the bedside and gentle range of motion exercises performed in bed. This represents the earliest and most conservative level of inpatient mobilisation. Progression to later stages depends on the patient's tolerance and ongoing haemodynamic stability.
questions.question: A patient is three days post myocardial infarction, certified haemodynamically stable, and is currently performing partial self-care, self-feeding and dangling legs at the bedside. Which inpatient cardiac rehabilitation stage does this correspond to?

questions.explanation: Echocardiography uses ultrasound to create real-time images of cardiac structures, allowing assessment of chamber dimensions, wall motion and valve competence. Electrocardiography instead records electrical activity, while chest radiography gives only a general silhouette of heart size. Echocardiography is therefore a first-line structural diagnostic tool.
questions.question: Which diagnostic tool provides direct visualisation of cardiac chamber size, wall motion and valve function using sound waves?

questions.explanation: Fluctuating intracranial pressure can occur in poorly sedated patients in response to physiotherapy procedures or environmental stimuli, making consistent, safe intracranial pressure levels necessary before intervention. This reflects the direct clinical guidance that physiotherapy procedures require stable intracranial pressure in neurologically vulnerable patients. Close liaison with medical staff is important when readings are unstable.
questions.question: A physiotherapist reviewing an ICU patient's neurological status notes fluctuating intracranial pressure readings. What is the most appropriate consideration before performing physiotherapy procedures?
options: Proceed with treatment regardless of intracranial pressure readings
Ignore neurological findings since they are unrelated to physiotherapy
Increase environmental stimulation to test the patient's response
Ensure intracranial pressure is at a consistent, safe level before proceeding with intervention
Discontinue all future neurological monitoring immediately

questions.explanation: Stenosis of the pulmonary artery obstructs blood leaving the right ventricle, forcing it to work harder to maintain pulmonary flow. Over time this can cause right ventricular hypertrophy as a compensatory response. Severe stenosis may require surgical or catheter-based correction.
questions.question: Narrowing of the pulmonary artery in a congenital heart lesion primarily produces which haemodynamic consequence?
options: Increased resistance to left ventricular outflow
Reversal of flow through the aorta
Increased resistance to right ventricular outflow

questions.question: Which piece of equipment commonly found in the intensive care unit is used to assist breathing through an endotracheal tube or tracheostomy?
questions.explanation: A mechanical ventilator delivers controlled breaths to patients unable to maintain adequate spontaneous ventilation, typically via an endotracheal tube or tracheostomy. Haemofiltration equipment instead manages acute renal failure, while suction pumps clear secretions. Recognising each device's function helps the physiotherapist interpret a patient's overall clinical picture.

questions.question: A physiotherapist is asked to assist in early recognition of a deteriorating ICU patient before airway obstruction complicates any resuscitation attempt. Which action reflects correct initial resuscitation preparation?
questions.explanation: Before starting resuscitation efforts, it is important to check that the airway is clear, removing any obstruction such as vomited material or broken teeth. An obstructed airway can render subsequent rescue breaths or compressions ineffective. This basic airway check is a foundational first step in any resuscitation sequence.
options: Begin chest compressions before assessing the airway at all
Delay any airway check until after ten minutes of observation
Check and clear the airway of any obstruction such as vomited material before proceeding
Assume the airway is automatically clear in every patient
Proceed directly to advanced ventilator settings without airway assessment

questions.explanation: A yellow skin colour on ICU observation is described as indicating renal or liver failure, distinct from the blue discolouration of cyanosis associated with hypoxaemia or hypercapnia. Recognising these colour-based clinical signs helps the physiotherapist appreciate the broader systemic status of a critically ill patient. This observation complements, but does not replace, formal laboratory investigation.
questions.question: A physiotherapist notices a patient's skin has a yellow discolouration during an ICU assessment. According to standard ICU observation principles, what does this most likely indicate?
options: Normal skin colour requiring no further action
Dehydration alone with no organ involvement
Immediate open heart surgery in every case
Risk factor modification and pharmacological management
Permanent cessation of all physical activity
Isolated psychological counselling without medical therapy
questions.explanation: Most acquired cardiovascular diseases are initially managed with lifestyle change and medication targeting the underlying risk factors, such as hypertension or hyperlipidaemia. Surgery or invasive procedures are typically reserved for cases refractory to conservative management or with critical anatomy. Physiotherapy plays a supportive role within this broader management plan.
questions.question: Which broad treatment category is generally prioritised first in the overall management of most acquired cardiovascular diseases?
A patient with chronic bronchiectasis produces large volumes of purulent sputum daily. Which physiotherapy technique is most directly indicated to assist clearance of these secretions?
questions.explanation: Bronchiectasis is characterised by chronic excess sputum production, making postural drainage combined with manual techniques an appropriate mainstay of physiotherapy management, provided no specific contraindications such as haemoptysis are present. This differs from restrictive conditions like fibrosis, where secretion clearance is not usually the primary problem. Regular review ensures the chosen technique remains appropriate as the patient's condition evolves.
options: Strict avoidance of any airway clearance technique indefinitely
Breathing control exercises alone with no manual component
Complete bed rest without any positional changes
Oxygen therapy alone without any secretion clearance technique
Postural drainage combined with manual techniques such as percussion or vibration as appropriate

questions.question: During an ICU ward round, a physiotherapist observes a chest drain producing a large volume of fresh blood. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
questions.explanation: A sudden increase in fresh blood from a chest drain may indicate an urgent complication requiring prompt medical assessment rather than continuation of routine physiotherapy. Communicating significant chart or clinical findings promptly to the wider team is a core professional responsibility. Physiotherapy treatment should generally be paused until the situation has been reviewed.
options: Proceed with vigorous chest percussion as planned
Alert medical or nursing staff promptly for further assessment
Remove the chest drain independently to inspect the site
Ignore the finding since drainage volume is not clinically relevant
Increase the intensity of mobilisation immediately

questions.question: A patient with confirmed cardiomyopathy asks whether their condition is the same as coronary artery disease. What is the most accurate clarification?
options: Both terms describe exactly the same underlying condition
Cardiomyopathy always results from coronary artery blockage
Coronary artery disease mainly affects the cardiac valves
Cardiomyopathy affects heart muscle, not the coronary vessels
Cardiomyopathy only affects the electrical conduction system
questions.explanation: Cardiomyopathy refers to disease intrinsic to the heart muscle itself, affecting its structure or contractile function, whereas coronary artery disease specifically involves narrowing of the coronary vessels supplying the myocardium with blood. Although ischaemic damage from coronary disease can eventually contribute to a form of cardiomyopathy, the two terms describe distinct primary processes. Clarifying this distinction helps patients understand their specific diagnosis and its implications.

options: Reducing the frequency of necessary medical observations
Eliminating the need for family communication entirely
Avoiding any explanation of procedures to the patient
Maintaining dignity and a supportive, orientating environment for the patient
Replacing the need for pain relief medication
questions.question: Recognising the intensive care patient as a person, rather than focusing solely on their equipment and monitors, primarily supports which aspect of care?
questions.explanation: Even within the technological environment of intensive care, patients benefit from having their dignity respected and being oriented to time, place and the details of their care. This non-clinical consideration works alongside, not instead of, medical monitoring and treatment. A supportive atmosphere can positively influence psychological wellbeing during a highly stressful admission.

options: A normal expected finding requiring no further evaluation
Complete resolution of all coronary artery disease
An unrelated skin irritation from the ergometer seat
A simple side effect of correct exercise technique
Exercise-induced angina from insufficient coronary blood flow relative to demand
questions.explanation: Exercise increases myocardial oxygen demand, and if coronary blood flow cannot meet this increased demand due to underlying atherosclerosis, angina can occur during exertion and typically resolves with rest. This is an important safety signal requiring the exercise session to stop and be reassessed. It may also indicate the need for review of the exercise prescription intensity or further cardiology assessment.
questions.question: A patient recovering from an acute myocardial infarction reports new pain that occurs specifically during ergometer cycling and resolves promptly with rest. What is the most likely explanation for this presentation?

options: Alveolar consolidation reducing effective lung volume without significantly narrowing the airways
Chronic destruction of alveolar walls typical of emphysema
Loss of airway cartilage causing dynamic airway collapse
Excess mucus plugging causing diffuse small airway obstruction
questions.question: A patient recovering from severe pneumonia has reduced lung volumes and shows a restrictive pattern on spirometry with a normal expiratory ratio. Which explanation best accounts for this pattern?
questions.explanation: Pneumonia fills alveolar spaces with inflammatory exudate, reducing effective lung volume while leaving airway calibre relatively unaffected, producing a restrictive rather than obstructive pattern. This explains why the ratio of forced expiratory volume to forced vital capacity remains normal despite reduced overall volumes. Physiotherapy in this context focuses on secretion clearance and lung re-expansion as consolidation resolves.

questions.question: During an outpatient cardiac rehabilitation class, a patient reports new chest discomfort while cycling on the ergometer. What is the most appropriate immediate physiotherapist action?
options: Stop the exercise immediately and assess the patient's symptoms and vital signs
Encourage the patient to push through discomfort to complete the set workload
Increase the exercise intensity to test symptom reproducibility
Ignore the complaint since chest discomfort is expected during exercise
Delay any assessment until the end of the full session
questions.explanation: New chest discomfort during exercise may indicate myocardial ischaemia and requires immediate cessation of activity along with prompt clinical assessment. Continuing or increasing exercise intensity in this situation could precipitate a serious cardiac event. Vigilant monitoring for such symptoms is a core safety responsibility during supervised cardiac exercise sessions.

Meticulous hand washing involving both scrubbing and rinsing between patient contacts is specifically emphasised as a key infection control measure in the ICU. Additional measures include appropriate gowning, gloving and mask use, particularly after contact with bodily fluids. These combined practices help protect vulnerable, critically ill patients from cross-infection.
options: Meticulous hand washing with scrubbing and rinsing between patients
Wearing the same gloves for all patients throughout the shift
Avoiding hand hygiene when running short on time
Relying solely on room ventilation to prevent infection spread
Sharing equipment between patients without cleaning
questions.question: A physiotherapist working in the ICU wants to reduce the risk of cross-infection between critically ill patients. Which specific practice is most directly emphasised for this purpose?

questions.explanation: Pregnancy increases circulating blood volume and cardiac output, which can worsen the haemodynamic burden on an already incompetent valve such as one affected by mitral regurgitation. This is why pregnancy is listed as a specific risk factor for symptomatic decompensation of pre-existing valve disease. Close monitoring throughout pregnancy is recommended for women with known valvular disease.
options: A perfectly healthy heart with no additional risk
Complete absence of any valve tissue
A valve that has already been surgically removed
Normal valve function with no prior disease
questions.question: Which valvular condition is most likely to be exacerbated haemodynamically by the increased blood volume seen in pregnancy?
A patient recovering from myocardial infarction is scheduled for a graded exercise tolerance test before starting outpatient exercise. What is the primary clinical purpose of this test?
questions.explanation: A supervised exercise tolerance test with ECG monitoring identifies the workload at which a patient develops angina or ischaemic changes, known as the angina threshold. This information is then used to safely calibrate the intensity of the exercise prescription. It also helps detect any exercise-induced arrhythmias requiring further medical attention.
options: Determining the patient's blood type before any further treatment
Identifying the angina threshold under supervised ECG monitoring to guide exercise prescription
Replacing the need for any medication review
Assessing visual acuity before hospital discharge

questions.question: Auscultation of the chest during intensive care physiotherapy assessment is performed primarily to determine which finding?
questions.explanation: Auscultation with a stethoscope allows direct assessment of air entry and any abnormal added sounds such as crackles or wheezes. It is recommended both before and after treatment to evaluate the immediate effect of chest physiotherapy. This clinical skill complements, rather than replaces, information available on the monitoring charts.
options: Whether breath sounds are normal, reduced, absent or accompanied by added sounds
The exact numerical oxygen saturation reading
The precise blood pressure value at that moment
The patient's total fluid balance for the day
The current central venous pressure reading

questions.question: Which intensive care equipment is specifically used to manage acute renal failure in a critically ill patient?
questions.explanation: Haemofiltration equipment removes waste products and excess fluid from the blood when the kidneys can no longer perform this function adequately. This differs from a ventilator, which supports breathing, or a nasogastric tube, which is used for feeding or decompression. Recognising the purpose of each device helps the physiotherapist understand the overall clinical priorities for that patient.

questions.question: Which beneficial cardiovascular change is expected in the heart itself following sustained aerobic training?
questions.explanation: Aerobic conditioning strengthens the myocardium, increasing its size modestly and improving stroke volume with each beat. This allows the same cardiac output to be achieved at a lower heart rate. Faster heart rate recovery after exercise is another marker of improved cardiovascular fitness from training.
options: A decrease in stroke volume at rest
A reduction in the size of the heart muscle
An increase in resting heart rate
An increase in stroke volume and size of the heart muscle
A decreased rate of heart rate recovery after exercise

questions.explanation: Non-modifiable risk factors, including heredity, male sex, increasing age and race, cannot be altered through medication or lifestyle change. Modifiable factors such as smoking, cholesterol and blood pressure can be actively addressed to lower cardiovascular risk. Recognising which category a risk factor belongs to helps target realistic prevention strategies.
questions.question: Which of the following is classified as a non-modifiable risk factor for cardiovascular disease?

options: Only the small joints of the fingers
Only the joints of the cervical spine
Only the joints of the foot and ankle
The hip, shoulder girdle and glenohumeral joints
questions.explanation: The hip, shoulder girdle and glenohumeral joints are particularly susceptible to progressive limitation of movement in immobile or unconscious patients and require particular attention during passive movement sessions. Maintaining full joint range, muscle extensibility and venous return are the stated aims of these passive movements. Neglecting these key joints increases the risk of long-term contracture.
questions.question: While performing passive range of motion exercises on an unconscious ICU patient, which joints should receive particular attention due to their susceptibility to progressive limitation?
Inpatient cardiac rehabilitation activities can typically begin how soon after a cardiac event, once the patient is certified stable?
questions.explanation: Early mobilisation, once clinical stability is confirmed by both physiotherapist and physician judgement, typically starts within three to five days following the cardiac event. This timing balances the harms of prolonged bed rest against the risks of premature exertion. Progression through further inpatient stages then follows a graded approach.
options: Three to five days after the event
Immediately within the first hour after the event
Only after six full months of complete bed rest
Not until after formal hospital discharge
Only once the patient has returned fully to work

questions.explanation: Severe spinal curvature alters the shape and volume of the thoracic cavity, mechanically limiting lung expansion. This is a musculoskeletal cause because the deformity lies in the bony chest wall rather than the lung itself. Physiotherapy for these patients often emphasises postural correction and breathing exercises.
questions.question: A musculoskeletal cause of restrictive lung dysfunction would most likely involve which structural abnormality?
options: Severe kyphoscoliosis distorting the thoracic cage

questions.question: Which of the following best distinguishes acquired heart disease from congenital heart disease?
questions.explanation: Acquired heart disease arises later in life from causes such as coronary artery disease, infection, or valve degeneration, rather than being present from birth. Congenital disease instead results from abnormal cardiac development in utero. This distinction is important for guiding both diagnostic timing and management strategy.
options: It develops after birth from factors such as infection, ischaemia or degeneration
It is always present and diagnosed at birth
It always results from a chromosomal abnormality
It never affects the cardiac valves
It cannot be treated with surgery

questions.explanation: The home exercise programme principle recommends maintaining the same exercise level achieved at discharge for the first two weeks before considering any increase. This cautious approach ensures the transition from supervised inpatient activity to independent home exercise is safe. Gradual progression and diligent follow-up appointments are also emphasised in this phase.
options: Maximal intensity exercise immediately from day one at home
Avoiding any exercise entirely for two months at home
Exercise only under continuous hospital supervision at home
Doubling exercise intensity immediately upon leaving hospital
The same level reached at hospital discharge, for two weeks
questions.question: A patient beginning the home exercise programme phase of cardiac rehabilitation asks about the appropriate starting exercise level. What is the recommended initial approach?

questions.explanation: Exercise duration typically starts at around ten to fifteen minutes and gradually increases toward thirty to sixty minutes per session as tolerance improves. Frequency is generally set at three to four sessions per week. This gradual, monitored progression minimises risk while steadily building cardiorespiratory fitness.
options: An immediate jump to maximal duration and frequency in the first session
Gradual increase in duration and frequency as fitness level improves
A fixed duration and frequency that never changes throughout the programme
Random variation in duration with no relationship to fitness level
Complete avoidance of any increase regardless of tolerance
questions.question: Which principle should guide progression of exercise duration and frequency for a patient in outpatient cardiac rehabilitation?

options: Complete elimination of the need for any airway clearance techniques
Immediate normalisation of upper airway humidification function
Total resolution of any risk of chest infection
Enhanced natural cough effectiveness compared with normal breathing
Increased tracheal secretion production due to mucosal irritation
questions.question: A physiotherapist is planning treatment for a patient recently placed on mechanical ventilation via an endotracheal tube. Which physiological consequence of the tube itself should be anticipated?
questions.explanation: The presence of an endotracheal or tracheostomy tube irritates the tracheal mucosa, increasing mucus secretion, while also bypassing the nose's normal humidifying function and impairing effective coughing. These combined effects increase the risk of secretion retention and chest infection. This is why breathing exercises, suctioning and humidification become particularly important in ventilated patients.

Sustained high blood pressure forces the left ventricle to work against elevated resistance over time, leading initially to compensatory hypertrophy and eventually to pump dysfunction and heart failure if uncontrolled. This progression underlies why early and effective blood pressure control is emphasised as a key preventive strategy. Physiotherapy-supported lifestyle measures contribute to this control alongside pharmacological treatment.
questions.question: A patient with longstanding untreated hypertension develops symptoms and signs consistent with heart failure. Which pathophysiological link best explains this progression?
options: Chronic pressure overload leading to ventricular hypertrophy and eventual pump failure
Hypertension has no established relationship with heart failure development
Sudden viral infection is the only possible explanation for this progression
Hypertension always resolves spontaneously without any cardiac consequence
Reduced blood pressure over time always prevents heart failure entirely

questions.explanation: An atrioventricular canal defect results from incomplete fusion of the endocardial cushions during development, affecting the septa and valves simultaneously. This produces a combined defect involving both atrial and ventricular communication with valve abnormalities. It is commonly associated with chromosomal conditions such as Down syndrome.
questions.question: An atrioventricular canal defect primarily involves abnormal development of which cardiac structures?
options: The aorta and pulmonary artery only
The coronary arteries and cardiac conduction system
The atrial septum, ventricular septum and atrioventricular valves
The great veins entering the right atrium

questions.question: During a ward round, a physiotherapist notes a cardiac patient walking seventy-five metres at an average pace with supervision to the bathroom, while also being taught pulse counting. Which inpatient stage is this patient in?
questions.explanation: Stage four introduces short supervised ambulation of about seventy-five metres alongside teaching the patient to monitor their own pulse. This is a step up from stage three, which involves shorter, slower walking distances. Learning pulse counting at this stage supports self-monitoring as activity progresses further.

questions.question: Which activity should generally be avoided in the early period after myocardial infarction due to increased cardiac strain?
questions.explanation: Heavy lifting and straining sharply raise intrathoracic pressure and cardiac workload, both of which can be hazardous soon after infarction. Supervised low-intensity activity, breathing exercises and education are, by contrast, core safe components of early rehabilitation. Avoiding the Valsalva manoeuvre specifically helps prevent sudden haemodynamic swings during recovery.
options: Gentle postural correction and stretching exercises
Heavy lifting and straining, such as the Valsalva manoeuvre
Structured patient and family education sessions

questions.explanation: Patients are generally encouraged to participate in a range of leisure activities such as walking, jogging, cycling, swimming, golf, gardening and dancing, chosen according to individual preference and functional capacity. This promotes long-term adherence to an active lifestyle beyond the formal rehabilitation programme. High-contact competitive sports would generally require more individualised risk assessment before recommendation.
options: Only high-contact competitive sports regardless of cardiac status
Activities such as walking, swimming, cycling and gardening, according to patient preference
Complete avoidance of all leisure activity indefinitely
Only activities performed in a hospital setting under continuous ECG monitoring
Exclusively sedentary hobbies with no physical component
questions.question: A cardiac rehabilitation patient asks which leisure activities are generally encouraged as part of ongoing recovery. Which of the following best reflects appropriate guidance?

options: Eliminating the need for any rest throughout the session
Allowing higher work intensity at each station through built-in rest periods
Producing maximal fatigue as quickly as possible
Avoiding any increase in heart rate during exercise
Preventing all forms of aerobic adaptation
questions.explanation: By alternating work periods with rest intervals, interval training allows patients to reach a higher peak intensity than they could sustain continuously. This approach is particularly useful for deconditioned cardiac patients who need graded intensity increases. It can be introduced at any stage of the rehabilitation programme.
questions.question: Interval training in cardiac rehabilitation is specifically designed to achieve which physiological benefit?

options: Thickened ventricular walls with a small chamber cavity
Rigid ventricular walls with normal chamber size
Absent ventricular septum with free communication
Calcified valve leaflets with normal chamber size
Enlarged ventricular chambers with reduced contractile force
questions.question: Dilated cardiomyopathy typically produces which characteristic change in cardiac structure and function?
questions.explanation: In dilated cardiomyopathy, the ventricular chambers stretch and enlarge while the muscle itself weakens, reducing the force of contraction. This leads to a fall in ejection fraction and eventually symptoms of heart failure. It contrasts with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, where the walls thicken rather than the chamber dilating.

questions.question: Which class of medication is used to relieve acute angina symptoms by reducing venous return and cardiac workload?
questions.explanation: Sublingual nitroglycerin acts quickly to dilate veins, reducing venous return and myocardial workload, which relieves anginal pain. Beta-blockers are used for longer-term reduction of cardiac workload, while potassium channel activators may also relieve symptoms. None of the unrelated drug classes listed have a direct role in acute anginal symptom relief.

A restrictive pattern with a positive family history raises suspicion for a hereditary or connective tissue related interstitial process, such as certain familial forms of pulmonary fibrosis. This differs from acquired causes like infection or effusion, which would not typically show a familial pattern. Further specific investigation would be needed to confirm the exact underlying interstitial diagnosis.
options: An acute infectious pneumonia unrelated to family history
An interstitial or connective tissue related fibrotic process
A simple musculoskeletal chest wall deformity
An isolated pleural effusion of unknown cause
A straightforward case of reversible bronchospasm
questions.question: A patient presents with progressive dyspnoea, and pulmonary function testing shows reduced total lung capacity with a normal expiratory flow ratio. Family history reveals a similar condition in a parent. Which broad category of restrictive lung disease should be considered first?
A physiotherapist is asked to perform manual hyperinflation on a ventilated ICU patient. What is the primary clinical goal of this technique?
options: Permanently replacing the need for mechanical ventilation
Reducing the patient's heart rate directly
Improving aeration of the alveoli and assisting removal of retained secretions
Eliminating the need for any further suctioning
Increasing the patient's blood pressure directly
questions.explanation: Manual hyperinflation delivers larger than normal breaths to improve aeration of underventilated alveoli and help mobilise retained secretions toward the central airways for removal. It is generally combined with other chest physiotherapy techniques rather than used in isolation. It does not replace the ventilator or directly target haemodynamic parameters such as heart rate or blood pressure.

questions.question: Which of the following diagnostic tools is most useful for assessing the electrical rhythm and conduction pattern of the heart?
questions.explanation: An electrocardiogram records the heart's electrical activity, making it the primary tool for identifying arrhythmias and conduction abnormalities. Echocardiography instead assesses structure and function rather than electrical timing. Radiography provides only an anatomical silhouette without functional or electrical detail.

questions.question: Central cyanosis becomes clinically visible once deoxygenated haemoglobin in arterial blood reaches approximately what concentration?
questions.explanation: Cyanosis appears once absolute deoxyhaemoglobin concentration exceeds roughly five grams per decilitre. This is why severely anaemic patients may appear pale rather than cyanosed despite significant hypoxaemia. Conversely, polycythaemic patients may appear cyanosed at higher oxygen saturations.

questions.question: A patient with known kyphoscoliosis presents with a restrictive pattern on pulmonary function testing. Which physiotherapy approach is most directly relevant to this specific underlying cause?
questions.explanation: Because the restriction in kyphoscoliosis arises from a mechanical chest wall deformity rather than lung tissue or airway disease, physiotherapy emphasises postural correction and breathing exercises adapted to the altered chest wall mechanics. Bronchodilator technique and secretion clearance are less relevant here since the underlying cause is skeletal rather than airway-based. An individualised approach considers the specific structural limitation present.
options: Postural correction exercises and breathing techniques addressing chest wall mechanics
Bronchodilator inhaler technique training as the primary focus
Postural drainage targeting excess bronchial secretions
High-intensity strength training of the diaphragm alone
Airway stenting to relieve central airway obstruction
When there is no pulse and no breathing, or pulse only with no breathing
Only when the patient specifically requests resuscitation verbally
Only after seventy-two hours of continuous observation
Only if the patient is fully conscious at the time
Only when blood pressure is within the normal range
questions.question: An ICU patient is due for cardiopulmonary resuscitation training review. Which statement correctly reflects when cardiac resuscitation is indicated according to standard guidance?
questions.explanation: Cardiac resuscitation is indicated when there is loss of consciousness with no pulse and no breathing, or in situations where a pulse is still felt but breathing has stopped, in which case rescue breathing alone may be needed. Recognising these specific scenarios ensures the correct urgent response is applied. Immediate action in these situations is time-critical for patient survival.

Pneumonia fills alveolar spaces with inflammatory exudate, reducing effective lung volume and compliance, giving a restrictive pattern. The other listed conditions are classically obstructive, affecting airway calibre and expiratory flow rather than lung volume. This distinction guides differing physiotherapy approaches for airway clearance versus volume restoration.
questions.question: Which infectious condition is listed as a cause of restrictive rather than obstructive lung dysfunction?

questions.explanation: Because exercise may provoke angina, having accessible, non-expired antianginal medication readily available during physiotherapy is an important safety measure. This precaution allows prompt treatment if symptoms occur during a session. Ongoing monitoring and clear communication with the patient about warning symptoms further supports safe exercise participation.
questions.question: Before beginning exercise in a patient with a history of angina, which safety precaution is specifically recommended?
options: Withholding all medication until after the session is finished
Ensuring the patient's prescribed antianginal medication is not expired and is accessible during physiotherapy
Ensuring the patient has eaten a large heavy meal beforehand
Scheduling exercise immediately after a full night without sleep
Avoiding any communication with the patient about their symptoms

questions.question: In a patient with impaired ventilation-perfusion matching, which combination best describes classic shunt physiology?
options: Perfused alveoli that are poorly or not ventilated
Ventilated alveoli that are poorly or not perfused
Equal ventilation and perfusion throughout the lung
Alveoli that are neither ventilated nor perfused
Increased ventilation with decreased perfusion uniformly
questions.explanation: A shunt occurs when blood passes through the lungs without contacting adequately ventilated alveoli, as in consolidation or atelectasis. This blood returns to the systemic circulation still relatively deoxygenated. Unlike dead space, true shunt hypoxaemia responds poorly to supplemental oxygen alone.

questions.question: A patient with restrictive lung disease due to a pleural cause is most likely to have which underlying condition?
questions.explanation: A large pleural effusion compresses the adjacent lung, preventing full expansion and reducing lung volumes. This is classified as a pleural cause because the pathology lies in the pleural space rather than the lung tissue. Draining the effusion typically improves the restrictive pattern.

questions.question: A patient with peripheral artery disease reports calf pain that consistently occurs after walking a fixed distance and resolves with rest. Which physiotherapy approach is most appropriate as part of their management?
questions.explanation: Supervised, structured walking exercise programmes are a recommended conservative management strategy for intermittent claudication in peripheral artery disease, helping to improve walking distance over time through physiological adaptation. Complete inactivity would likely worsen rather than improve symptoms and function. Exercise progression should be graded and monitored to ensure safety and adherence.
options: Complete avoidance of all walking activity indefinitely
Immediate surgical bypass without any conservative trial
High-intensity sprinting to rapidly build tolerance
Bed rest until all symptoms have completely resolved
Structured, supervised walking exercise programme to improve walking distance

questions.question: Pulmonary perfusion is normally greatest in which region of the upright lung?
questions.explanation: Gravity increases hydrostatic pressure in the pulmonary vessels toward the dependent lung base. This raises blood flow to the base compared with the apex in an upright person. Ventilation is also greater at the base, helping to match ventilation and perfusion.

Awareness of the type and position of lines, catheters and monitoring leads is essential to plan safe mobilisation without dislodging vital equipment. This awareness allows the physiotherapist to modify positioning and movement technique accordingly. Removing lines is not within the physiotherapist's role and mobilisation should proceed thoughtfully rather than being avoided or rushed.
options: Identifying and safely managing all lines, catheters and monitoring equipment during movement
Removing all lines and catheters before any mobilisation attempt
Ignoring the lines completely since they rarely affect mobility planning
Mobilising the patient as quickly as possible without any planning
Delaying mobilisation indefinitely regardless of clinical stability
questions.question: A physiotherapist is asked to mobilise a patient in the ICU who has multiple intravenous lines, a central venous line and a urinary catheter in place. What is the most important initial consideration before starting mobilisation?
