questions.answerText:
A(i) Pulmonary function tests: spirometry (FEV1, FVC), lung volumes (TLC, RV), diffusion capacity (DLCO).
A(ii) Dyspnoea scales: Modified Medical Research Council (mMRC) dyspnoea scale, and the Borg dyspnoea scale.
A(iii) Exercise capacity: the 6-minute walk test (6MWT) and the shuttle walk test.
A(iv) Quality of life: St. George's Respiratory Questionnaire (SGRQ) and the Chronic Respiratory Questionnaire (CRQ).
A(v) Muscle strength and endurance: handgrip strength and quadriceps strength.
B. Disease-specific outcome measures are chosen according to the condition: COPD uses PFTs, dyspnoea scales, 6MWT and SGRQ; asthma adds the Asthma Control Test (ACT); cystic fibrosis adds the Cystic Fibrosis Questionnaire (CFQ); and lung cancer adds quality-of-life questionnaires such as the EORTC QLQ-C30.
B. A precaution in interpretation is that a normal chest X-ray shows clear lungs and a healthy heart with no nodules, tumors or masses.
B. An abnormal finding such as an enlarged heart, fluid build-up, broken ribs, cysts or masses should prompt reassessment of the treatment plan.
C. Basis: these outcome measures assess the effectiveness of physiotherapy interventions and monitor changes in respiratory function.
C. They allow physiotherapists to adjust treatment plans accordingly, since respiratory diseases range from mild and self-limiting conditions to life-threatening diseases that make gas exchange difficult.
C. Effect on function: X-ray imaging reveals abnormalities of the chest and lungs that help clinicians assess disease progression and show how well the heart and lungs are working, which underlies the functional deficits these outcome measures are designed to capture.
C. Physiotherapy management directed by these measures includes breathing exercises, airway clearance techniques, mobilization and exercise, and education and behavioural change, aimed at restoring respiratory function.
questions.question:
A. Describe the assessment of the respiratory system for physiotherapy purposes under: (i) pulmonary function tests (ii) dyspnoea scales (iii) exercise capacity tests (iv) quality of life measures (v) muscle strength and endurance measures.
B. State precautions relevant to respiratory assessment and management.
C. Explain the basis of these outcome measures and their effect on function.

A. Describe fluoroscopy under: (i) principle (ii) indications (iii) how contrast is used (iv) advantages.
B. State when fluoroscopy is the preferred imaging choice.
C. Compare fluoroscopy with plain (fixed-plate) radiography.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Principle: fluoroscopy is a special X-ray technique that produces real-time images on a television monitor.
A(ii) Indications: it is used to help guide catheters into place in the heart during cardiac catheterization.
A(ii) Further indications: it is also used to guide an endoscope during endoscopic surgery.
A(iii) Use of contrast: with fluoroscopy, contrast material is injected into a blood vessel.
A(iii) Use of contrast (continued): the physician can then watch the real-time movement of the contrast material to determine if there are blockages in circulation.
A(iv) Advantages: it allows the physician to watch real-time movement, which is not possible with a static fixed-plate X-ray image.
B. Fluoroscopy is preferred when real-time visualization is required, such as to determine if there are blockages in circulation, or to guide catheters or an endoscope into place during a procedure.
C. Fixed-plate (plain) X-rays produce a single static image based on the density and composition of the structures the beam passes through, and are useful for diagnosing fractures, joint dislocation and pulmonary pathology.
C. Fluoroscopy, by contrast, produces continuous real-time images on a monitor rather than a single static image.
C. Fluoroscopy specifically uses injected contrast material to visualize moving structures such as blood flow, which a plain radiograph cannot show.
C. Radiography more broadly refers to multiple modalities: mammography and DEXA are examples of low-energy projectional radiography.
C. Fluoroscopy and angiography are special applications used for real-time imaging, while CT uses computed reconstruction to generate a cross-sectional image.

questions.question:
A. Describe the physiotherapy assessment/outcome measures used for a patient with a fracture under: (i) range of motion (ii) length (iii) pain (iv) function/balance.
B. State the factors and precautions that determine whether the first line of treatment is surgical or non-surgical.
C. Explain the basis of these outcome measures and their effect on function.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Range of motion: goniometer.
A(ii) Length: tape measure.
A(iii) Pain: visual analogue scale (VAS).
A(iv) Function/balance: DASH (Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder and Hand), and the Berg balance scale.
B. The type of fracture: some fractures are stable and can heal on their own with immobilization, while others are unstable and require surgery to fix the broken bone.
B. The severity of the fracture: more severe fractures may require more aggressive treatment, such as surgery or traction, before physiotherapy can begin.
B. The patient's overall health and fitness: patients who are otherwise healthy and fit may be able to start physiotherapy earlier than those with other medical conditions or who are less active.
B. Appropriate immobilization is imperative to injury healing, and nonsurgical reduction is indicated only when the fracture severity allows for direct reduction, with surgical reduction required in more severe cases.
C. Basis: X-rays provide essential information about the location, severity and healing progress of a fracture, which helps physiotherapists monitor the healing process and make adjustments to the treatment plan as needed.
C. They also help identify potential complications such as nonunion or malunion, and educate the patient about their injury and the importance of following the treatment plan.
C. Effect on function: in the early stage, pain management, movement exercises and strengthening exercises help to prevent stiffness, maintain joint mobility and support the fracture as it heals, with balance and gait training helping patients regain coordination and walk safely again.
C. In the later stage, functional activities help patients return to their normal activities such as work, sports and hobbies, alongside scar management and psychological support.

A(i) Subjective assessment: history.
A(i) Mechanism of injury: traumatic incident, or repeated overstretching.
A(i) Mechanism of injury (continued): shallow or abnormally formed joint surfaces (congenital), or rheumatoid arthritis or other disease of the ligaments and tissue around the joint.
A(i) Age and occupation of the patient.
A(i) Pain and the characteristics of the symptoms.
A(ii) Objective assessment: observation of symmetry - the shape and position of the joint - and observation of swelling.
A(ii) Associated clinical signs: the joint is visibly deformed, with swelling and discoloration.
A(ii) Further signs: limited ability to move the joint, with intense pain.
A(ii) Additional signs: bruising, instability of the joint, and loss of ability to move the joint.
B. Clinical basis: a dislocation occurs when the bones in a joint become separated or knocked out of their usual positions, which accounts for the visible deformity.
B. Disruption of the joint and surrounding tissue accounts for the pain, swelling and instability; dislocations can be very painful and cause the affected joint area to be unsteady or immobile.
C. Any joint in the body can become dislocated; if the joint is only partially dislocated it is called a subluxation, whereas in a dislocation the bones are completely separated or knocked out of their usual positions in the joint.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the subjective assessment of a patient with a suspected joint dislocation.
A(ii) Describe the objective assessment of a patient with a suspected joint dislocation.
B. Explain the clinical basis for the findings obtained on this assessment.
C. Distinguish between a dislocation and a subluxation.

questions.answerText:
(i) Risk factors: family history, gender, age, alcohol consumption, being overweight, taking certain medications, and other conditions such as type 2 diabetes, high cholesterol and fats in the blood, chronic kidney disease, and osteoarthritis.
(i) The clinical picture itself is a red flag: sudden and excruciating painful episodes affecting the joint at the base of the big toe, with redness, swelling and extreme tenderness.
(ii) Complications if missed: the chronic phase of gout can lead to the development of tophi (visible deposits of urate crystals under the skin), with erosive and cyst-like changes and gouty destruction at multiple joints seen on imaging over time.
(iii) Laboratory investigations: a uric acid blood test showing a high level of uric acid, and joint fluid analysis - a synovial fluid sample examined under a microscope for urate crystals, which is the definitive diagnostic test.
(iii) Imaging investigations: X-ray, ultrasound, CT scan, and MRI.
(iv) Decision: physiotherapy management is appropriate as a supportive role - pain relief with cryotherapy, therapeutic ultrasound and TENS during acute flare-ups, gentle ROM exercises once the flare subsides, joint protection with rest and temporary immobilization, and patient education on lifestyle modification.
(iv) Justification: the medical management of gout (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, corticosteroids, prophylaxis, and correction of hyperuricemia) and surgical management (resection of joints, arthroplasty, arthrodesis of painful joints) address the underlying disease process, so physiotherapy works alongside rather than in place of medical management, restoring functional ability and reducing gout-related disability.
questions.question:
A 55-year-old man presents with a sudden, excruciatingly painful, red, swollen and extremely tender first metatarsophalangeal joint.
(i) State the risk factors and red flags relevant to this presentation.
(ii) State the complications if the condition is missed.
(iii) State the special tests and investigations used to confirm the diagnosis.
(iv) Discuss whether physiotherapy referral or physiotherapy management is the more appropriate decision at this stage, and justify the choice.

A. Describe the laboratory diagnosis of gout under: (i) the uric acid blood test (ii) joint fluid analysis - procedure (iii) joint fluid analysis - interpretation.
B. Explain the clinical basis for these tests.
C. Distinguish the uric acid blood test from joint fluid analysis.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Uric acid blood test: gout occurs when uric acid builds up in the bloodstream and forms crystals in the joints.
A(i) Uric acid blood test (continued): a blood test that shows a high level of uric acid could help confirm a diagnosis of gout.
A(ii) Joint fluid analysis procedure: this is done by taking a sample of synovial fluid through a needle inserted into the joint.
A(iii) Joint fluid analysis interpretation: the fluid is then examined under a microscope for urate crystals.
A(iii) Interpretation (continued): a gout flare is marked by the presence of monosodium urate (MSU) crystals in synovial fluid obtained from affected joints or bursas, visualized by direct examination of a fluid sample using compensated polarized light microscopy.
B. Clinical basis: identifying urate crystals in fluid from an affected joint is the definitive diagnostic test for the diagnosis of gout.
B. Gouty arthritis is characterised by tissue deposition of monosodium urate crystals as a result of hyperuricaemia, which can lead to an acute attack of gout or the formation of tophi.
B. In practice, joint fluid analysis is applied to only a minority of patients diagnosed as having gout.
C. The uric acid blood test is a simple blood sample that measures the level of uric acid in the bloodstream.
C. Joint fluid analysis instead requires sampling synovial fluid directly from the affected joint via a needle, and is the definitive diagnostic test for gout.
C. The presence of a high uric acid level on the blood test only helps to confirm a diagnosis rather than being definitive on its own.
C. Imaging tests are also used alongside these laboratory tests, including X-ray, ultrasound, CT scan and MRI.

(i) Provisional diagnosis: femoral neck stress fracture.
(ii) Supporting findings: an overuse injury characterized by a hairline crack in the femoral neck, caused by repetitive stress, bone insufficiency and biomechanical factors.
(iii) Imaging of choice: MRI, which is highly sensitive and preferred for early diagnosis.
(iv) Expected findings: a coronal MR STIR image shows a femoral neck stress fracture with greater than 50% neck involvement.
(v) Physiotherapy management: MRI provides detailed images of soft tissues, bones and joints, helping physiotherapists accurately diagnose the condition; by identifying the extent and specific location of the injury, MRI helps develop targeted treatment plans including specific exercises, manual therapy techniques and other interventions tailored to the patient's needs; early detection through MRI can prevent further damage and complications, which is particularly important for athletes, and MRI can be used to monitor the healing process and assess the effectiveness of the treatment plan, allowing adjustments where necessary.
questions.question:
A young athlete presents with an overuse injury characterized by a hairline crack in the femoral neck, caused by repetitive stress, bone insufficiency and biomechanical factors.
(i) State the provisional diagnosis.
(ii) State the supporting history and physical examination findings.
(iii) State the imaging modality of choice, with justification.
(iv) State the expected imaging findings.
(v) Outline the physiotherapy management.

An MRI of the spine shows a paraspinal abscess, vertebral body collapse and cord compression.
(i) Identify the imaging modality and the structures/lesion shown.
(ii) State the structures affected or compressed.
(iii) State the differential diagnoses.
(iv) Give the clinical reasoning that links the imaging to the physical findings.
questions.answerText:
(i) Imaging modality: MRI. The image shows a Potts spine (spinal tuberculosis) with paraspinal abscess, vertebral body collapse and cord compression; Potts spine is commonly known as spinal tuberculosis, an extrapulmonary form of TB caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and Pott's paraplegia occurs when the spine is involved.
(ii) Structures affected/compressed: the vertebral body (collapsed), the paraspinal soft tissue (abscess formation), and the spinal cord (compression); in a related MRI case, tuberculosis of the spine also showed destruction of the T11-T12 disc interspace with an abscess, while vertebral body alignment remained normal.
(iii) Differential diagnoses: other conditions seen on spinal MRI that can mimic this picture include discitis/osteomyelitis (an acute or inflammatory process of bone secondary to infection with pyogenic organisms, bacteria, fungi or mycobacteria), an epidural abscess, metastatic bone disease, and a spinal tumor such as a glioma, astrocytoma, ependymoma or meningioma.
(iv) Clinical reasoning: the spinal cord may be compressed by bone, hematoma, abscesses, tumors, or a ruptured or herniated disk, and symptoms can include back pain, abnormal sensations, muscle weakness, or impaired bladder and bowel control; diagnosis is based on the symptoms together with the result of a physical examination and/or magnetic resonance imaging, so the cord compression and abscess seen on MRI explain the neurological findings, and MRI is able to detect subtle changes in the vertebral column that may be an early sign of infection or tumor, being more sensitive than CT for evaluating abscesses and soft tissue masses near the spinal cord.

A(i) Assessment of pacemaker placement: X-ray helps confirm the correct position of the pacemaker generator and leads within the body, ensuring optimal function and preventing complications.
A(ii) Detection of lead complications: X-ray can reveal problems with the pacemaker leads, such as fractures, migration or perforations, which may necessitate intervention.
A(iii) Evaluation of implant integrity: X-ray can identify any damage or malfunction of the pacemaker device itself.
A(iv) Post-operative monitoring: regular X-rays after pacemaker implantation help monitor any changes in device position or lead integrity.
B. Patients with a pacemaker should avoid high-voltage power lines and radio transmitters.
B. Patients with a pacemaker should also avoid magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) machines, magnetic therapy massagers, and gas-powered appliances.
B. Fractures of the leads are often triggered by physical exertion using the upper limbs, such as weightlifting, or by trauma in this location, so patients with implanted devices are commonly advised to avoid such activities.
C. Densities on an X-ray reflect tissue composition: air appears black, fat appears slightly darker, and water/soft tissue appears mid-grey.
C. Bone appears white, and metal appears even whiter than bone, which is why medical devices like pacemakers and implants are easily visible on X-ray.
C. X-rays can reveal complications such as pacemaker electrode perforation of the heart and fracture of a lead.
C. X-rays can also reveal pneumothorax, and Twiddler's syndrome, where the patient unknowingly manipulates the device in the chest pocket, causing lead displacement and device malfunction.
C. Effect on function: X-rays provide a visual confirmation of the position of pacemaker leads within the heart and blood vessels, which is helpful for physiotherapists in understanding potential limitations or risk associated with specific exercises or activities, especially those involving movements that could put stress on the leads.
questions.question:
A. Describe the role of chest X-ray in monitoring a patient with a cardiac pacemaker under: (i) assessment of pacemaker placement (ii) detection of lead complications (iii) evaluation of implant integrity (iv) post-operative monitoring.
B. State the precautions/contraindications relevant to a patient with a pacemaker.
C. Explain the basis of pacemaker-related radiographic findings and their effect on function.

questions.answerText:
(i) Conditions requiring a cardiac pacemaker: bradycardia (a slow heart rate typically below 60 beats per minute), heart block, sick sinus syndrome, atrial fibrillation, heart failure, and cardiogenic shock, all of which pacemakers help by regulating heart rate and rhythm.
(ii) Complications if missed: thrombophlebitis, infection, myocardial perforation, lead dislodgement, pneumothorax, haemothorax, lead fracture, thrombosis, and Twiddler's syndrome, where the patient unknowingly manipulates the pacemaker device in the chest pocket, causing lead displacement and malfunction of the device.
(iii) Special tests/investigations: chest X-ray, typically involving at least two views - a postero-anterior (PA) view giving a two-dimensional view of the lead, and a lateral (LAT) view giving a third dimension to help evaluate the lead tip location.
(iv) Decision: physiotherapy referral back to the cardiology/medical team is the more appropriate immediate decision given the suspected device complication.
(iv) Justification: X-rays help identify problems with the pacemaker leads, such as fractures, migration or perforations, which may necessitate intervention, and evaluate implant integrity for damage or malfunction; once the device issue is medically addressed, X-rays continue to provide physiotherapists with a visual confirmation of the position of pacemaker leads, helpful for understanding potential limitations or risk associated with specific exercises or activities, especially those involving movements that could put stress on the leads.
questions.question:
A patient with a cardiac pacemaker presents with chest pain and shortness of breath, and is found to have unknowingly manipulated the device in the chest pocket.
(i) State the risk factors/conditions that led to pacemaker implantation.
(ii) State the complications if a pacemaker-related problem is missed.
(iii) State the special tests/investigations used to confirm the diagnosis.
(iv) Discuss whether physiotherapy referral or physiotherapy management is the more appropriate decision at this stage, and justify the choice.

A degenerative spine radiograph/MRI in an older patient shows features of spondylosis affecting the neck.
(i) State the diagnosis.
(ii) State the predisposing factors and pathophysiology.
(iii) State the physical and imaging assessment findings.
(iv) Outline the physiotherapy management.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: cervical spondylosis.
(ii) Predisposing factors/pathophysiology: spondylosis is a degenerative disease that affects the spine, causing pain and other issues; it is a common result of aging, but not everyone experiences symptoms; spinal osteoarthritis (OA) is a degenerative process defined radiologically by joint space narrowing, osteophytosis, subchondral sclerosis and cyst formation, and spondylosis commonly occurs in the neck (cervical spondylosis) or lower back (lumbar spondylosis).
(iii) Physical and imaging assessment: some people experience no symptoms, while others feel stiffness and/or pain in the neck, shoulders, or between the shoulder blades; the condition can lead to a variety of problems, including herniated disks and bone spurs; MRI of a normal cervical and lumbar spine is compared against the degenerative changes seen in spondylosis.
(iv) Physiotherapy management: patient education; exercise therapy (strengthening and flexibility exercises); manual therapy; electrotherapy; and recommendation of orthotics and assistive devices, aimed at improving joint mobility, reducing pain, and enhancing overall quality of life, since the underlying degeneration cannot be reversed but symptoms can be managed.

questions.question:
A patient sustains a wrist injury and imaging demonstrates a lunate dislocation.
(i) Outline the history.
(ii) Outline the physical examination sequence relevant to this presentation.
(iii) State the interpretation of the findings.
(iv) State the indicated imaging.
(v) State the joint structures and nerve supply at risk.
(vi) State the precautions relevant to management.
questions.answerText:
(i) History: wrist joint dislocation is one of the classifications of upper limb dislocation, occurring at the wrist joint between the distal end of the radius and the articular disc above and the scaphoid, lunate and triquetral bones below.
(ii) Physical examination sequence: inspection for joint deformity; observation for swelling and discoloration; assessment of range of motion, which is limited; assessment for intense pain and instability; the wrist is a synovial ellipsoid joint, with anterior and posterior ligaments strengthening the capsule, a medial ligament attached to the ulnar styloid process and triquetral bone, and a lateral ligament attached to the radial styloid process and scaphoid bone.
(iii) Interpretation: the findings are consistent with wrist dislocation (lunate).
(iv) Indicated imaging: X-ray of the wrist joint, compared against a normal wrist joint X-ray.
(v) Structures/nerve at risk: the anterior and posterior ligaments, the medial ligament (ulnar styloid to triquetral bone) and the lateral ligament (radial styloid to scaphoid bone); nerve supply of the wrist joint is from the anterior interosseous nerve and the deep branch of the radial nerve.
(vi) Precautions: dislocations can be very painful and cause the affected joint to be unsteady or immobile, so management includes reduction technique (closed reduction or traction), immobilization with a splint, cryotherapy for pain, and progressive range-of-motion and strengthening exercises (isometric, then resistance) as healing allows.

questions.question:
A 34-year-old presents with fever, chills, a cough productive of phlegm, chest pain on breathing and coughing, fatigue and shortness of breath.
(i) State the provisional diagnosis.
(ii) State the supporting history and physical examination findings.
(iii) State the imaging modality of choice, with justification.
(iv) State the expected imaging findings.
(v) Outline the physiotherapy management.
questions.answerText:
(i) Provisional diagnosis: pneumonia.
(ii) Supporting findings: fever, chills, cough with phlegm or pus, chest pain during breathing or coughing, fatigue, and shortness of breath.
(iii) Imaging of choice: chest X-ray, since it is a quick, noninvasive test of the lungs, heart, blood vessels, airways, ribs and diaphragm, chest radiographs are the most common film taken in medicine, and pneumonia is very commonly diagnosed by chest radiograph.
(iv) Expected imaging findings: whitish spots (infiltrates) that identify an infection, for example right upper-lobe pneumonia bounded inferiorly by the horizontal fissure, with blunting at the right costophrenic angle due to an accompanying pleural effusion; the trachea remains centralized in pneumonia.
(v) Physiotherapy management - breathing exercises: diaphragmatic breathing, inspiratory muscle training, yoga breathing exercises.
Airway clearance techniques: chest physiotherapy, postural drainage, percussion, vibration.
Mobilization and exercise: aerobic exercise, strength training, flexibility exercises.
Education and behavioural changes: smoking cessation, breathing techniques, energy conservation strategies.

questions.question:
A. Describe the physical examination for benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) under: (i) what is checked (ii) the digital rectal exam.
B. Explain the clinical basis for these physical examination findings.
C. Distinguish the physical examination from the medical/laboratory tests used in BPH diagnosis.
questions.answerText:
A(i) What is checked: discharge from the urethra, and enlarged or tender lymph nodes in the groin.
A(i) What is checked (continued): a swollen or tender scrotum, and taps on specific areas of the patient's body.
A(ii) The digital rectal exam is also performed as part of the physical examination.
B. Clinical basis: a physical exam may help diagnose benign prostatic hyperplasia.
B. During the exam a health care provider most often examines a patient's body for signs related to the enlarged prostate gland and associated urinary tract changes.
B. Benign prostatic hyperplasia is a condition in which the prostate gland - which secretes fluid that nourishes and protects sperm and sits in front of the rectum, just below the bladder - becomes enlarged and not cancerous.
B. This is why physical findings cluster around the groin, scrotum and rectal region.
C. Physical exam findings are distinct from medical tests, which a urologist uses to help diagnose lower urinary tract problems related to BPH and recommend treatment.
C. Medical tests include urinalysis, and a prostate-specific antigen (PSA) blood test.
C. Medical tests also include urodynamic tests, and cystoscopy.
C. Medical tests further include transrectal ultrasound, and biopsy.
C. The physical exam is a hands-on bedside assessment of the body, while the medical tests are laboratory, imaging or instrumented investigations that provide additional diagnostic information beyond what the physical exam can reveal.

(i) Imaging modality: chest X-ray. The abnormality shown is a pneumothorax, the presence of air or gas in the pleural cavity between the lungs and the chest wall, causing collapse of the lung; radiograph findings show lucency (dark) around the edge of the lung.
(ii) Structures affected: air enters the pleural cavity and is trapped during expiration; buildup of air increases intrathoracic pressure, and if the buildup is large enough it can collapse the lung, shift the mediastinum away from the tension pneumothorax, and compromise venous filling of the heart.
(iii) Differential diagnoses: pleural effusion, an excessive accumulation of fluid in the pleural cavity showing as a white area at the base of the lung on radiograph; pulmonary fibrosis and atelectasis; and pneumonia, which shows whitish infiltrates identifying infection.
(iv) Clinical reasoning: for pleural effusion, the trachea should not be centralized and should be seen away from the affected lung; for pulmonary fibrosis and atelectasis, the trachea should also not be centralized but should be seen towards the affected lung; for pneumonia, the trachea should be centralized; this rule applies provided only one lung field is affected, so checking the position of the trachea on the chest X-ray, together with the clinical presentation of sudden chest pain, shortness of breath, rapid heart rate and fatigue, links the imaging appearance to the underlying diagnosis.
questions.question:
A chest X-ray shows lucency (dark) around the edge of the lung with absence of lung markings in the affected area.
(i) Identify the imaging modality and the abnormality shown.
(ii) State the structures affected.
(iii) State the differential diagnoses.
(iv) Give the clinical reasoning that links the imaging to the physical findings.

A. Describe the technique of application of therapeutic ultrasound under: (i) setting up and testing the equipment (ii) preparation of the patient (iii) method of application.
B. Explain the clinical basis of the Fountain test.
C. Distinguish between continuous and pulsed ultrasound.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Setting up and testing: connect the machine to the main power supply through the cable, fit the transducer jack tightly to the output socket, and keep all controls at zero before turning on the apparatus.
A(i) Setting up (continued): set the timer for two minutes and perform the Fountain test.
A(ii) Preparation of the patient: place the patient in a comfortable position, sitting or lying, based on the area to be treated; expose the part to be treated and ensure it is well supported.
A(ii) Preparation (continued): drape the rest of the body appropriately for modesty; partially stretch out tightened soft tissue or shortened tendon, ligament or muscle; carry out treatment in a screened-off, well-lit and aerated area.
A(iii) Method of application: the commonest method is direct contact of the transducer on the skin surface over the target tissue.
A(iii) Method (continued): indirect methods used for irregular areas with bony prominences and thin tissue cover include the water bath method and the water bag method; specialized application includes phonophoresis and combined ultrasound with iontophoresis.
B. The Fountain test involves putting a few drops of water on the transducer head with its face up, then gradually increasing the intensity by turning the knob clockwise until bubbles of the water drops are observed.
B. The Fountain test indicates that the machine has a satisfactory output of ultrasound energy, and the duration must be limited to a few seconds before reducing the intensity back to zero.
C. Continuous ultrasound is the continuous delivery of ultrasound throughout the treatment period.
C. Pulsed ultrasound is the delivery of ultrasound during only a portion of the treatment period.
C. Pulsed ultrasound is produced when the high-frequency alternating current is delivered to the transducer for only a limited proportion of the treatment time, as determined by the selected duty cycle.
C. Pulsing the ultrasound minimises its thermal effects.

questions.question:
A patient sustains an elbow injury following a fall onto an outstretched hand.
(i) Outline the history.
(ii) Outline the physical examination sequence relevant to this presentation.
(iii) State the interpretation of the findings.
(iv) State the indicated imaging.
(v) State the joint structures and nerve supply at risk.
(vi) State the precautions relevant to management.
questions.answerText:
(i) History: elbow dislocation in adults is, after shoulder, the second most commonly dislocated joint, and in children under 10 years elbow dislocation is the most common type of joint dislocation.
(ii) Physical examination sequence: inspection for joint deformity; observation for swelling and discoloration; assessment of range of motion, which is limited; assessment for intense pain and instability; the elbow joint is a compound synovial hinge joint between the trochlea and capitulum of the humerus and the trochlear notch of the ulna and head of the radius, with lateral and medial (anterior, posterior and transverse band) ligaments.
(iii) Interpretation: the findings are consistent with elbow joint dislocation.
(iv) Indicated imaging: X-ray of the elbow joint, compared against a normal elbow joint X-ray.
(v) Structures/nerve at risk: the lateral ligament (attached to the lateral epicondyle and the annular ligament) and the medial ligament (anterior, posterior and transverse bands); nerve supply of the elbow joint is from branches of the median, ulnar, musculocutaneous and radial nerves.
(vi) Precautions: dislocations can be very painful and cause the affected joint to be unsteady or immobile, so management includes reduction technique (closed reduction or traction), immobilization with a splint, and cryotherapy for pain, followed by range-of-motion exercises and, later, isometric and resistance strengthening exercises.

questions.question:
A patient presents with lateral elbow pain that is the most common overuse injury of the elbow, involving the extensor muscles of the forearm.
(i) State the diagnosis.
(ii) State the predisposing factors and pathophysiology.
(iii) State the physical and imaging assessment findings.
(iv) Outline the physiotherapy management.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: lateral epicondylitis, also known as "tennis elbow".
(ii) Predisposing factors/pathophysiology: it is a tendinopathy injury involving the extensor muscles of the forearm; most commonly the extensor carpi radialis brevis (ECRB) is involved, but others may include extensor digitorum, extensor carpi radialis longus and extensor carpi ulnaris; it is the most common overuse injury in the elbow.
(iii) Physical and imaging assessment: on MRI, a coronal T2-weighted image with fat saturation shows the common extensor tendon appearing thickened with increased T2 signal.
(iv) Physiotherapy management: MRI provides detailed images of soft tissues, bones and joints that help physiotherapists accurately diagnose the condition; by identifying the extent and specific location of the injury, MRI helps physiotherapists develop targeted treatment plans, which can include specific exercises, manual therapy techniques and other interventions tailored to the patient's needs; MRI can also be used to monitor the healing process and assess the effectiveness of the treatment plan, allowing adjustments to be made if necessary.

(i) History: forced abduction, external rotation and extension of the arm, which is the usual mechanism for the most common type of shoulder dislocation.
(ii) Physical examination sequence: inspection for a visibly deformed joint; observation for swelling and discoloration; assessment of range of motion, which is limited; assessment for intense pain and instability of the joint; the shoulder joint is a synovial ball-and-socket articulation between the rounded head of the humerus and the shallow, pear-shaped glenoid cavity of the scapula, strengthened by the glenohumeral, transverse humeral and coracohumeral ligaments.
(iii) Interpretation: the findings are consistent with a shoulder (glenohumeral) dislocation, described according to the direction the humerus exits the joint; anterior dislocation accounts for greater than 95% of cases, and can be further divided into subcoracoid, subglenoid or subclavicular positions of the humeral head.
(iv) Indicated imaging: X-ray of the shoulder joint, AP view.
(v) Structures/nerve at risk: the glenohumeral ligaments, the transverse humeral ligament, and the coracohumeral ligament; nerve supply of the shoulder joint is from the axillary and suprascapular nerves.
(vi) Precautions: dislocations can be very painful and cause the affected joint to be unsteady or immobile, so management includes reduction technique (closed reduction or traction), immobilization with a splint to hold the joint in place and prevent further injury, and cryotherapy to enhance relaxation and reduce pain, followed by range of motion and strengthening exercises as tolerated.

A. Describe the radiographic appearance of rheumatoid arthritis under: (i) hallmark findings (ii) staging (iii) hand and foot features (iv) other joints affected.
B. Relate these radiographic findings to the underlying pathology.
C. Explain how these findings guide physiotherapy assessment and management.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Hallmark findings: periarticular osteopenia and joint space narrowing, often accompanied by marginal erosions.
A(ii) Staging: stage 1 shows no destructive changes on X-ray; stage 2 shows periarticular osteoporosis and subchondral bone destruction but no joint deformity.
A(ii) Staging (continued): stage 3 shows cartilage and bone destruction in addition to joint deformity and periarticular osteoporosis; stage 4 shows bony or fibrous ankylosis along with stage 3 features.
A(iii) Hand features: erosive subluxation, most marked at the metacarpophalangeal joints, with ulnar deviation; degenerative change at the ulnar-carpal articulation; osteopaenia particularly of the metacarpophalangeal regions; fused carpal bones and bone erosion at the ulnar-carpal articulation.
A(iii) Foot features: symmetrical changes at the phalanges, marginal erosion at the metatarsophalangeal joints, bony ankylosis between metatarsophalangeal joints, and fused ankle joints.
A(iv) Other joints: rheumatoid arthritis can also be seen in the shoulder, elbow and knee joints, including reduction in joint space of the knee.
B. These findings result from chronic inflammation and destruction of the synovium, leading to damage to the adjacent cartilage and bone.
B. Rheumatoid arthritis is a chronic autoimmune disease in which the immune system attacks the synovium (lining) of joints, leading to inflammation, pain and eventually joint damage.
B. It typically starts in small peripheral joints and progresses to proximal joints if untreated.
C. X-ray imaging helps clinicians assess disease progression and joint damage, guiding decisions such as joint protection advice, functional splinting and assistive devices for affected joints.
C. The findings inform physiotherapy goals: improving disease-management knowledge, pain control using TENS, improving activities of daily living, and improving joint stiffness/range of motion.
C. Further goals: preventing or controlling further joint damage, and improving strength, fatigue levels, quality of life, aerobic condition, and stability and coordination.

A(i) Common views: Posterior-Anterior (PA), the most common and preferred view, with the beam travelling from back to front.
A(i) Further views: Anterior-Posterior (AP), less preferred as the heart and mediastinum appear less clear, used when the patient cannot stand; and the Lateral view, which complements the frontal view to help localize lesions.
A(ii) Normal features: a normal chest X-ray shows clear lungs, a healthy heart and a clearly outlined chest cavity, with no visible nodules, tumors or masses.
A(iii) Systematic approach - the regions to check can be summarised by the letters ABCDEF: Airways (including hilar adenopathy), Breast shadows, Bones (rib fractures, lytic lesions).
A(iii) ABCDEF continued: Cardiac silhouette (cardiac enlargement), Costophrenic angles (pleural effusions), Diaphragm (free air), Edges (fibrosis, pneumothorax, pleural thickening), Extrathoracic tissues, Fields (alveolar flooding) and Failure (alveolar air space disease with vascularity).
B. Pneumonia shows whitish infiltrates identifying infection, with the trachea remaining centralized.
B. Pneumothorax shows lucency (dark) around the edge of the lung, from air leaking into the space between lung and chest wall.
B. Pleural effusion shows a white area at the base of the lung, from excess fluid in the pleural space; the trachea is away from the affected lung, unlike in fibrosis or atelectasis where it is drawn towards the affected side.
B. COPD, asthma, cystic fibrosis and emphysema each show hyperinflated lungs and a flattened diaphragm, while lung cancer shows a large white-grey mass and interstitial lung disease shows ground-glass opacification with volume loss and linear opacities.
C. An abnormal chest X-ray highlights atypical characteristics such as an enlarged heart, fluid build-up, broken ribs, cysts or masses that clinicians use to assess disease progression.
C. X-ray imaging plays a crucial role in the diagnosis and management of respiratory diseases, revealing abnormalities of the chest and lungs that help clinicians assess disease progression and show how well the heart and lungs are working.
C. These findings thereby guide physiotherapy interventions such as breathing exercises, airway clearance techniques, mobilization and exercise, and patient education.
questions.question:

questions.answerText:
A(i) Principle: a narrow beam of X-rays is aimed at the patient and quickly rotated around the body, producing signals processed by computer into cross-sectional "slices".
A(i) Principle (continued): these slices can be digitally stacked into a three-dimensional image, allowing easier identification and location of structures, tumors or abnormalities.
A(ii) Indications: possibly life-threatening conditions such as haemorrhage, blood clots or cancer; imaging the head for injuries, tumors, clots leading to stroke, or haemorrhage.
A(ii) Further indications: imaging the lungs for tumors, pulmonary embolism, excess fluid, emphysema or pneumonia; and complex bone fractures, severely eroded joints or bone tumors.
A(iii) Advantages: it is noninvasive, safe and well-tolerated, and provides a highly detailed look at many different parts of the body.
A(iii) Advantages (continued): it has revolutionised medicine by showing diseases that could previously only be found at surgery or autopsy.
A(iv) Disadvantages/risks: it uses X-rays, and all X-rays produce ionizing radiation with the potential to cause biological effects in living tissue.
A(iv) Further risk: the biggest potential risk is a serious allergic reaction to the contrast (dye) sometimes used, and intravenous dye can damage the kidneys, particularly if kidney disease is already present.
A(v) In pregnancy: a CT scan poses no known risk to the baby if the area imaged is not the abdomen or pelvis, but if abdominal or pelvic imaging is needed, doctors prefer exams that do not use radiation, such as MRI or ultrasound, unless there is an emergency or time constraint.
B. CT is preferred when imaging complex bone fractures, severely eroded joints, or bone tumors, since it usually produces more detail than a conventional X-ray, and it is useful for evaluating the brain, neck, spine, chest, abdomen, pelvis and sinuses.
C. CT and MRI are similar to each other in that both produce cross-sectional images that appear to open the body up, but they provide a different view of the body than an X-ray; MRI uses a magnetic field and radiowaves to produce images, while CT uses X-rays.
C. Both CT and MRI are better than plain X-ray for evaluating soft tissues such as the brain, liver and abdominal organs and for visualizing subtle abnormalities not apparent on regular X-ray.

questions.answerText:
(i) Provisional diagnosis: knee osteoarthritis.
(ii) Supporting findings: joint pain especially with movement, morning stiffness that improves with activity, reduced range of motion, joint tenderness, crepitus (grating sensation), bony enlargement and potential joint deformity, common in the elderly.
(iii) Imaging of choice: MRI, which helps to detect injury to the soft tissue, loss of joint space and the presence of osteophytes.
(iv) Expected findings: marginal osteophytes on a coronal T1-weighted image in a patient without articular cartilage loss; well-defined subchondral bone marrow lesions with subchondral cysts and marrow oedema at the patellofemoral compartment on sagittal T1-weighted and STIR images in more severe cases, with severe (full-thickness) articular cartilage loss and osteophyte formation; femoral cartilage loss and femoral bone marrow lesions with incident subchondral bone attrition at the tibia are also seen.
(v) Physiotherapy management: patient education; exercise therapy - strengthening and flexibility exercises; manual therapy; electrotherapy; and recommendation of orthotics and assistive devices, since physiotherapy is an important aspect of osteoarthritis management, helping patients improve their joint mobility, reduce pain, and enhance their overall quality of life.

A. Describe the safety screening/precautions for a patient about to undergo spinal MRI under: (i) implants (ii) contrast agents (iii) pregnancy (iv) noise (v) claustrophobia.
B. State the red flags/limitations relevant to this screening.
C. Explain the basis of these precautions and their effect on the patient.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Implants: people with implants, particularly those containing iron - pacemakers, vagus nerve stimulators, implantable cardioverter-defibrillators, loop recorders, insulin pumps, cochlear implants, deep brain stimulators, and capsules from capsule endoscopy - should not enter an MRI machine.
A(ii) Contrast agents: patients with severe renal failure who require dialysis may risk a rare but serious illness called nephrogenic systemic fibrosis (NSF) that may be linked to certain gadolinium-containing agents.
A(iii) Pregnancy: while no effects have been demonstrated on the fetus, it is recommended that MRI scans be avoided as a precaution, especially in the first trimester when the fetus's organs are being formed, and a contrast agent, if used, could enter the fetal bloodstream.
A(iv) Noise: loud noise, commonly referred to as clicking and beeping, with sound intensity up to 120 decibels in certain MRI scanners, may require special ear protection.
A(v) Claustrophobia: people with even mild claustrophobia may find it difficult to tolerate long scan times inside the machine.
B. Although MRI does not emit the ionizing radiation found in X-ray and CT imaging, it does employ a strong magnetic field that extends beyond the machine and exerts very powerful forces on objects made of iron, some steels, and other magnetizable objects, strong enough to fling a wheelchair across the room, so patients should notify their physicians of any form of medical implant prior to an MRI scan.
B. Limitations relevant to safety screening also include the requirement for patient stillness and an inability to assess tissue functionality.
B. Further limitations include challenges in interpretation for certain conditions.
C. Basis: current guidelines recommend that dialysis patients should only receive gadolinium agents when essential.
C. Dialysis should be performed as soon as possible after the scan to remove the agent from the body promptly.
C. Familiarization with the machine and process, as well as visualization techniques, sedation and anaesthesia, provide patients with mechanisms to overcome the discomfort of claustrophobia and long scan times.
C. Effect on patient: a person who is very large may not fit into certain types of MRI machines due to weight limits on the scanners, and MRI is generally not recommended for seriously injured patients because traction devices and life-support equipment may distort the MR images and must therefore be kept away from the area being imaged.

questions.question:
A patient involved in a road traffic accident presents with a deformed, painful hip and inability to bear weight.
(i) Outline the history.
(ii) Outline the physical examination sequence relevant to this presentation.
(iii) State the interpretation of the findings.
(iv) State the indicated imaging, with the views used.
(v) State the structure at risk and the associated complication.
(vi) State the precautions relevant to management.
questions.answerText:
(i) History: hip dislocation is the displacement of the femur head from the acetabulum; it typically takes a major force to dislocate the hip, and car accidents and falls from significant heights are common causes, so other injuries like broken bones often occur with the dislocation; a hip dislocation is a serious medical emergency requiring immediate treatment.
(ii) Physical examination sequence: inspection for a visibly deformed joint; observation for swelling and discoloration; assessment of range of motion, which is limited; assessment for intense pain and inability to bear weight; the hip is a weight-bearing ball-and-socket joint, with the acetabulum shaped like a cup and the femur head shaped like a ball, stabilised mainly by the capsule and surrounding muscles and ligaments.
(iii) Interpretation: the findings are consistent with a hip dislocation, which can be congenital (developmental dysplasia of the hip) or acquired through trauma, most commonly posterior.
(iv) Indicated imaging: X-ray of the hip joint, in postero-anterior and lateral views, compared against a normal hip joint.
(v) Structure at risk/complication: time to reduction is crucial, as the longer the dislocation persists, the greater the risk of avascular necrosis in the affected part.
(vi) Precautions: closed relocation of the hip is done by a traction force performed in the opposite direction of the dislocation, with the hip in 90-degree flexion, preferably under general or regional anaesthesia and muscle relaxation to prevent greater damage to cartilage and soft tissue; after relocation, hip stability should be tested carefully, and a period of bed rest might be recommended depending on stability and the extent of soft tissue injury; complete rehabilitation following hip dislocation can take 3-6 months, with gait re-education using assistive devices to limit weight-bearing initially.

(i) Diagnosis: rheumatoid arthritis.
(ii) Predisposing factors: consumption of food rich in polyunsaturated oils, smoking or exposure to pollution, age, obesity, female gender, family history (interaction between genotype and environment), low vitamin D intake, and a history of viral infection such as Epstein Barr virus.
(ii) Pathophysiology: a chronic autoimmune disease in which the immune system attacks the synovium (lining) of joints, leading to inflammation, pain and eventually joint damage; it typically starts in small peripheral joints, is usually symmetric, and progresses to involve proximal joints if left untreated.
(iii) Physical assessment: polyarthritis of the small joints of the hands - proximal interphalangeal, metacarpophalangeal joints and wrist; morning stiffness usually lasting greater than an hour; deformities in advanced stages such as ulnar deviation, boutonniere deformity and swan-neck deformity; systemic features such as fatigue, low-grade fever, weight loss and rheumatoid nodules.
(iii) Imaging assessment: X-ray shows periarticular osteopenia and joint space narrowing, often with marginal erosions, resulting from chronic inflammation and destruction of the synovium; MRI and ultrasound of the joints detect erosions earlier than X-ray and are more sensitive than clinical examination for synovitis and joint effusion.
(iv) Physiotherapy management: exercise therapy (range-of-motion exercises, aerobic exercise, stabilisation/coordination exercises, starting moderate and progressing to high-intensity as tolerated); joint protection advice with functional splinting and assistive devices; massage therapy to improve function, reduce pain and improve flexibility; pain control using TENS; and patient education, aiming to improve activities of daily living, joint stiffness, strength, fatigue levels, quality of life, aerobic condition, and stability and coordination.

questions.answerText:
(i) Imaging modality: MRI (coronal, fat-suppressed). The lesion shown is calcific tendinitis, a painful shoulder disorder characterized by either single or multiple deposits in the rotator cuff tendon or subacromial bursa.
(ii) Structures affected: the rotator cuff (supraspinatus) tendon, shown with a focus of chronic calcification and an associated full-thickness supraspinatus tendon tear; the accuracy of MRI in identifying calcific deposits is around 95%, but it is more useful in cases of chronic calcific tendinitis.
(iii) Differential diagnoses: other injuries to the shoulder joint listed alongside calcific tendinitis include frozen shoulder, shoulder dislocation, and rotator cuff tear.
(iv) Clinical reasoning: frozen shoulder is defined by restriction of passive movements in all planes, from painful, gradual loss of active and passive shoulder motion resulting from fibrosis and contracture of the joint capsule, which is a different mechanism from the focal calcific deposit and tendon tear seen here; MRI provides detailed images of soft tissues, bones and joints, helping physiotherapists accurately diagnose conditions such as ligament tears, meniscus injuries and cartilage damage, and by identifying the extent and specific location of the injury, MRI helps physiotherapists develop targeted treatment plans tailored to the patient's needs.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Choice of apparatus/setting up: if a non-luminous lamp is chosen, switch it on 5 minutes before treatment to allow warm-up time; a luminous lamp does not require warm-up time.
A(i) Setting up (continued): the apparatus should be in working order and the voltage of the emitter noted, usually 250 to 1000 watts.
A(ii) Patient position/explanation: position the patient suitably and well supported, with the area to be treated exposed; explain the nature and effect of the treatment to the patient.
A(iii) Examination and testing: examine the skin to be treated and test thermal sensation.
A(iv) Application: set the lamp at 50-75 cm for a large lamp (750-1000 watts) or 40-45 cm for a small lamp.
A(iv) Application (continued): intensity is controlled by distance - doubling the lamp-to-skin distance reduces intensity to one quarter, and tripling it reduces intensity to one ninth; for acute conditions duration should be 10 to 15 minutes, and for chronic conditions 30 minutes.
A(v) End of treatment: cover the area exposed with a dry towel, remove the lamp to a safe location, inspect the area for erythema produced, and ask the patient how he or she is feeling.
B. Clinical basis: heat will render the patient's perception of a rise in temperature, and this failure to detect excessive heat may result in a burn.
B. Patients on strong analgesics have a raised pain threshold and cannot determine whether the intensity of heat is too much, so testing thermal sensation before treatment is a precaution against burn injury.
C. Luminous generators consist of a tungsten filament in a large glass envelope containing inert gas at low pressure, heated to about 3000 degrees.
C. Luminous generators emit a continuous spectrum in the infrared and visible region, extending from short IR to visible light to UVR (UVR is absorbed in the glass), and are sometimes called radiant heat.
C. Non-luminous generators consist of a coil of wire wrapped around a cylindrical ceramic insulator, or wires embedded in insulation ceramic that is then heated; short/luminous IRR (700-1500 nm) penetrates to the dermis and superficial subcutaneous tissues, while long/non-luminous IRR (1500-12000 nm) penetrates only to about 2 mm, up to the superficial dermis.

An 80-year-old woman falls at home and presents with hip pain and inability to weight-bear.
(i) State the risk factors and red flags relevant to this presentation.
(ii) State the complications if the fracture is missed.
(iii) State the special tests and investigations used to confirm the diagnosis.
(iv) Discuss whether physiotherapy referral or physiotherapy management is the more appropriate decision at this stage, and justify the choice.
questions.answerText:
(i) Risk factors: femoral neck fractures are associated with low-energy falls in the elderly, essentially all fractures in elderly women being associated with low bone density; other general fracture risk factors include increasing age, gender, low body weight, family history of bone disease, smoking and excessive alcohol consumption, inadequate calcium and vitamin D intake, previous fractures, and certain medications such as corticosteroids.
(i) Red flag: pain is usually intense and localized to the fracture site, with limited range of motion and inability to bear weight.
(ii) Complications if missed: distal femur and femoral shaft fractures can result in limb shortening and deformities if not treated appropriately; general complications of missed fractures include nonunion or malunion.
(iii) Special tests/investigations: history and physical examination, followed by X-ray, which is a diagnostic tool used to image any bone in the body, with bones appearing white, soft tissue in shades of grey, and air appearing black.
(iv) Decision: physiotherapy referral for orthopaedic/medical management is the more appropriate immediate decision.
(iv) Justification: physiotherapy is often an important part of fracture management, but it is not always the first line of treatment, since orthopaedic physicians are usually the first to see patients as a fracture is an emergency condition; the first line of treatment depends on the type of fracture, its severity, and the patient's overall health and fitness, with appropriate immobilization being imperative to healing before physiotherapy - such as early-stage pain management, gentle range-of-motion exercises, strengthening exercises, and balance and gait training - can begin.

questions.question:
A 65-year-old man presents with urinary frequency, urgency, a weak urine stream and nocturia.
(i) State the risk factors and red flags relevant to this presentation.
(ii) State the complications if the condition is missed.
(iii) State the special tests and investigations used to confirm the diagnosis.
(iv) Discuss whether physiotherapy referral or physiotherapy management is the more appropriate decision at this stage, and justify the choice.
questions.answerText:
(i) Risk factors: age 40 years and older, family history of benign prostatic hyperplasia, medical conditions such as obesity, heart and circulatory disease and type 2 diabetes, lack of physical exercise, and erectile dysfunction.
(i) Red flags requiring immediate medical care: urinary frequency of eight or more times a day, urinary urgency, trouble starting a urine stream, a weak or interrupted stream, dribbling at the end of urination, nocturia, urinary retention, urinary incontinence, pain after ejaculation or during urination, and urine of unusual colour or smell.
(ii) Complications if missed: acute urinary retention, chronic urinary retention, blood in the urine, urinary tract infections, bladder damage, kidney damage, and bladder stones.
(iii) Special tests/investigations - physical exam: checking for discharge from the urethra, enlarged or tender lymph nodes in the groin, a swollen or tender scrotum, taps on specific areas of the body, and a digital rectal exam.
(iii) Medical tests: urinalysis, a prostate-specific antigen (PSA) blood test, urodynamic tests, cystoscopy, transrectal ultrasound, and biopsy.
(iv) Decision: physiotherapy management in a supportive role is appropriate - pelvic floor (Kegel) exercises, which can relieve symptoms by strengthening the muscles around the bladder and penis, helping with waking to urinate at night, weak stream, leakage and urgency.
(iv) Justification: physiotherapy plays a supportive role in managing BPH and may not directly treat the condition, so treatment options such as lifestyle changes, medications, minimally invasive procedures and surgery remain part of medical management, while physiotherapy exercises and lifestyle modification, including physical activity and posture awareness, contribute to overall well-being alongside that medical care.

A(i) Joint space changes: joint space narrowing.
A(ii) Bone changes: subchondral sclerosis, osteophytosis (osteophyte formation), joint erosions, bone marrow lesions, and subchondral cyst formation (geodes).
A(iii) Soft tissue changes: synovitis.
B. Degenerative arthritis, also commonly called osteoarthritis, is a joint disease characterized by the breakdown of cartilage within joints, leading to pain, stiffness and reduced range of motion, most often affecting the knees, hips, hands and spine; it is considered a "wear and tear" condition primarily associated with aging and overuse of joints.
B. Osteoarthritis can be primary (idiopathic, with a strong genetic component, primarily affecting middle-aged women) or secondary, arising from abnormal mechanical forces such as occupational stress or obesity, previous joint injury, prior surgery, crystal deposition, or inflammatory arthritis.
C. MRI can detect bone marrow changes and cartilage loss, both of which are early osteoarthritis changes not visible on radiographs.
C. Articular cartilage is best assessed using fluid-sensitive sequences with fat suppression, and contrast administration enhances the visualization of synovitis.
C. The clinical presentation of joint pain especially with movement, morning stiffness that improves with activity, and reduced range of motion, together with these imaging findings, guides physiotherapy management.
C. Further clinical presentation includes tenderness, crepitus, bony enlargement and potential deformity.
C. Physiotherapy management includes patient education, exercise therapy (strengthening and flexibility exercises), manual therapy, electrotherapy, and recommendation of orthotics and assistive devices.
C. Physiotherapy helps patients improve joint mobility, reduce pain, and enhance overall quality of life.
C. Since osteoarthritis cannot be reversed, imaging and clinical findings are used to guide treatments that reduce pain and help the patient move better, alongside medical and, where needed, surgical management such as arthroplasty for patients who have failed non-operative interventions due to severe degeneration.
questions.question:

B. Relate these findings to the underlying pathology.
C. Explain how these findings guide physiotherapy assessment and management.

A. Describe the MRI appearance of the spine under: (i) normal features (ii) spondylosis (iii) disc herniation (iv) spinal stenosis (v) tuberculosis of the spine (Potts spine).
B. Relate these imaging findings to the underlying pathologies.
C. Explain how these findings guide physiotherapy assessment and management.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Normal features: on T1-weighted images, cerebrospinal fluid appears dark, muscles grey, spinal cord grey, and an intact hydrated disc grey; on T2-weighted images, cerebrospinal fluid appears bright, the spinal cord light grey, and an intact hydrated disc bright.
A(ii) Spondylosis: a degenerative process defined radiologically by joint space narrowing, osteophytosis, subchondral sclerosis and cyst formation, commonly seen in the cervical or lumbar spine.
A(iii) Disc herniation: a localized displacement of disc material beyond the limits of the intervertebral disc space, arising from rupture of the annulus fibrosus and leakage of the nucleus pulposus beyond the margins of the annulus, seen on T2-SPIR sagittal images as herniated lumbar discs, for example at L5-S1.
A(iv) Spinal stenosis: the narrowing of the spinal canal and nerve root canal along with enlargement of the facet joints, most commonly caused by osteoarthritis and the natural aging process, but can also develop from injury or previous surgery.
A(v) Tuberculosis of the spine (Potts spine): MRI shows a long T1 signal, long T2 signal, and a high short-T inversion recovery signal in the sagittal plane; a related case showed the abscess and subsequent destruction of the disc interspace with vertebral body alignment remaining normal, and paraspinal abscess with vertebral body collapse and cord compression.
B. Vertebral fracture is seen on T1-weighted MRI as low signal at the fracture level, with T2-weighting showing bone marrow oedema, and osteoporotic-type fractures show preservation of some marrow fat with a fluid-filled cavity acutely, and fat filling the marrow cavity when chronic.
B. Symptoms of spinal stenosis include pain, numbness, weakness and cramping, and in severe cases a loss of bladder or bowel control and sexual dysfunction.
B. Symptoms of spondylosis include stiffness and/or pain in the neck, shoulders, or between the shoulder blades, which can lead to herniated disks and bone spurs.
C. The spinal cord may be compressed by bone, hematoma, abscesses, tumors, or a ruptured or herniated disk.
C. Diagnosis is based on symptoms together with the result of a physical examination and/or MRI.
C. MRI is able to detect subtle changes in the vertebral column that may be an early sign of infection or tumor, and is more sensitive than CT for evaluating tumors, abscesses and other soft tissue masses near the spinal cord.
C. This guides physiotherapy toward targeted assessment and monitoring of the specific structures involved.

A(i) PA (Posterior-Anterior) view: the most common and preferred chest X-ray; the X-ray beam travels from the back (posterior) to the front (anterior).
A(i) PA view (continued): the patient stands with the chest against the film, arms raised or to the sides, shoulders rolled forward, and holds their breath for a clearer image of the heart and lungs.
A(ii) AP (Anterior-Posterior) view: less preferred, as the heart and mediastinum appear less clear; the beam travels from the front (anterior) to the back (posterior).
A(ii) AP view (continued): it is taken with the patient standing, sitting, or lying down if they cannot stand.
A(iii) Lateral view: a side-view X-ray, often complementing the frontal view, which helps localize lesions for 3D analysis.
A(iii) Lateral view (continued): the patient stands with one shoulder against the plate, hands raised overhead, and holds their breath for clarity.
B. The PA view is the normal and best view for a chest X-ray, especially for assessing the cardiothoracic ratio, and is preferred whenever the patient is able to stand.
B. The AP view is used when the patient cannot stand, but the heart will be slightly magnified in this view.
C. In PA views the heart is further from the film, while in AP views the heart is closer to the film, so the heart appears slightly bigger in the AP view.
C. The further an object or person is from the film, the smaller it appears, and the closer it is, the bigger it appears.
C. If the X-ray is taken in an AP view, then the cardiothoracic ratio cannot be reliably concluded upon.
C. Mediastinal width (using a PA view) is normally less than 8 cm, and this measurement is distorted by the AP projection.
questions.question:
A. Describe chest X-ray views under: (i) PA view (ii) AP view (iii) lateral view.
B. State when the PA view is preferred over the AP view.
C. Compare the PA and AP views in terms of cardiothoracic ratio assessment.

A. Describe the imaging appearance of gout arthritis under: (i) X-ray views/joints affected (ii) X-ray abnormal findings (iii) MRI findings.
B. Relate these imaging findings to the underlying pathology.
C. Explain how these findings guide physiotherapy assessment and management.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Joints affected on X-ray: the hand, elbow, shoulder, knee, foot (first metatarsophalangeal joint), and even the cervical spine can show gouty involvement.
A(ii) Abnormal X-ray findings: erosive and cyst-like changes about multiple joints of the hand and ulnar styloid with soft tissue nodules; punched-out peri-articular erosion of the digits.
A(ii) Further X-ray findings: a large tophus seen as a soft tissue mass; severe erosive lesion of the glenoid cavity in gouty shoulder arthritis.
A(ii) Further X-ray findings (continued): multiple tophi deposits in the collateral ligaments and iliotibial tract bursa at the knee; erosion of bone at the tibial tuberosity; and gouty arthropathy of the first metatarsophalangeal joint.
A(iii) MRI findings: tophi seen in the metatarsal joint, and gouty erosion at the ankle joint.
B. X-rays in gout show the presence of tophi (urate crystal deposits) and joint damage due to repeated flare-ups.
B. This reflects tissue deposition of monosodium urate crystals as a result of hyperuricaemia, which can lead to acute gouty attacks or the formation of tophi.
B. Tophi appear to continually recruit monocytes that differentiate into macrophages, and tophi also continually remodel, usually presenting with intermittent painful attacks followed by long periods of remission.
C. Understanding the radiographic features of gout aids in distinguishing it from other types of arthritis and in monitoring long-term joint health.
C. Physiotherapy management is guided toward pain relief (cryotherapy, therapeutic ultrasound, TENS) during acute flare-ups, and improved joint mobility through gentle ROM exercises once the flare subsides.
C. Joint protection through rest and temporary immobilization, avoiding prolonged immobilization, and restoration of functional abilities.
C. Patient education on lifestyle modification, posture and exercises to prevent flare-ups.

A(i) Pain assessment: Visual Analogue Scale (VAS), measuring pain intensity on a 0-10 scale.
A(ii) Range of motion assessment: goniometry, an inclinometer for more precise measurement, and the sit-and-reach test for hip and knee replacements to assess lower limb flexibility.
A(iii) Strength assessment: Manual Muscle Testing (MMT) grading muscle strength on a 0-5 scale; handgrip strength test for upper limb replacements; and isokinetic dynamometry.
A(iv) Functional mobility and gait assessment: for lower limb replacements - Timed Up and Go Test (TUG), Six-Minute Walk Test (6MWT), gait analysis, and the stair climbing test; for upper limb replacements - the DASH score and the Shoulder Pain and Disability Index (SPADI).
A(v) Balance and proprioception assessment: Berg Balance Scale (BBS), Single-Leg Stance Test, and Functional Reach Test.
B. Hip precautions for total hip replacement include avoiding flexion greater than 90 degrees.
B. Other precautions include preventing complications such as deep vein thrombosis (DVT), contractures and joint stiffness.
B. Weight-bearing progression should be observed as advised following lower limb replacement.
C. Basis: using standardized outcome measures ensures objective tracking of patient progress, and these tools help guide rehabilitation goals and adjustments in therapy.
C. A combination of pain, ROM, strength, function and quality-of-life measures provides a comprehensive assessment.
C. Effect on function: goals of physiotherapy management include pain management, restoring joint mobility, and improving muscle strength.
C. Further goals include enhancing functional mobility (gait training, stair climbing, transfers), preventing complications, and improving balance and proprioception, especially after lower limb replacements.

questions.answerText:
(i) Imaging modality: CT scan. The lesion is an epidural hematoma (EDH), a type of head injury that occurs when there is bleeding between the skull and the dura mater, the outermost layer of the brain's protective covering; CT features include a bi-convex shape, most frequently beneath the squamous part of the temporal bone, and the lesion is hyperdense, somewhat heterogeneous, and sharply demarcated.
(ii) Structures affected: the space between the skull and the dura mater, with the tip of the associated bleed shown to compress the underlying brain tissue; the cause is usually an artery that is torn by a skull fracture.
(iii) Differential diagnoses: subdural hematoma (bleeding between the dura mater and the brain tissue itself, which on CT is acutely crescentic and hyperdense, becomes nearly isodense in the subacute stage, and hypodense with an enhancing membrane in the chronic stage); intracerebral hemorrhage (bleeding within the brain tissue itself); and diffuse axonal injury (widespread axonal damage with midline shift and loss of white matter on CT).
(iv) Clinical reasoning: an epidural hematoma is a life-threatening condition that requires emergency surgery, with symptoms including severe headache and loss of consciousness; a subdural hematoma is the most common type of traumatic intracranial mass lesion; the distinct CT density pattern of each lesion, together with the clinical presentation, allows the type and age of the bleed to be identified and links the imaging findings to the patient's neurological signs.

questions.answerText:
(i) Provisional diagnosis: rheumatoid arthritis.
(ii) Supporting findings: polyarthritis of small joints of the hands - proximal interphalangeal, metacarpophalangeal joints and wrist - usually symmetric; morning stiffness that may last up to several hours, usually greater than an hour; possible "trigger finger" from flexor tenosynovitis; systemic symptoms of fatigue, malaise, low-grade fever and weight loss, and rheumatoid nodules.
(iii) Imaging of choice: X-ray of both hands and feet is usually obtained for the presence of erosions, the pathognomonic feature of rheumatoid arthritis, although plain radiograph does not show the early changes of the disease; MRI and ultrasound detect erosions earlier than X-ray and are more sensitive than clinical examination for synovitis and joint effusion.
(iv) Expected findings: the hallmark radiographic finding is periarticular osteopenia and joint space narrowing, often accompanied by marginal erosions, resulting from chronic inflammation and destruction of the synovium leading to damage of the adjacent cartilage and bone; staging ranges from no destructive change, through periarticular osteoporosis and subchondral bone destruction without deformity, to cartilage and bone destruction with joint deformity, and finally bony or fibrous ankylosis.
(v) Physiotherapy management: exercise therapy (ROM exercises, aerobic exercise, stabilisation/coordination exercises) starting moderate and progressing to high intensity as tolerated; joint protection advice with functional splinting and assistive devices; massage therapy; patient education; and pain control using TENS, aiming to improve activities of daily living, joint stiffness/range of motion, strength, fatigue, quality of life, aerobic condition, and stability and coordination.

A. Describe plain radiography under: (i) principle (ii) indications/common applications (iii) contraindications (iv) advantages (v) risks/safety.
B. State when plain radiography is the preferred first imaging choice.
C. Compare plain radiography with CT.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Principle: radiography is performed by transmitting ionizing electromagnetic radiation through bony structures and soft tissue, producing an image based on the absorption of X-ray photons.
A(i) Principle (continued): plain radiographs use a heterogeneous beam of X-rays projected toward a detector, creating an image based on the density and composition of the intervening objects.
A(ii) Indications: diagnosis of fractures or joint dislocation; demonstration of proper alignment and stabilization of bony fragments following fracture treatment; guidance for orthopedic surgery; assessment for trauma; evaluation of osteomyelitis.
A(ii) Further indications: diagnosis of pneumonia, atelectasis, pleural effusion, asthma, COPD and other pulmonary pathology; evaluation of cardiomegaly, arthritis, scoliosis, bone cancer and growth plates; and location of foreign objects in soft tissue.
A(iii) Contraindications: pregnant or potentially pregnant women should avoid X-rays because of an increased risk that a developing fetus will develop leukemia during childhood if exposed to X-ray radiation.
A(iv) Advantages: it is the most commonly used diagnostic imaging study, and is a painless, non-invasive way to help diagnose problems such as broken bones, tumors, dental decay and the presence of foreign bodies.
A(v) Risks/safety: low-dose exposure to X-rays creates minimal cell damage and minimal risk when performed in an accredited facility.
A(v) Risks/safety (continued): there is also a slight risk of an allergic reaction to the contrast material or dye used in certain X-rays.
B. It is the most commonly used diagnostic imaging study, useful in detecting abnormalities within the body such as broken bones, tumors, dental decay and foreign bodies.
C. CT scan works on the same principle as fixed plate X-rays, only with a CT scan an X-ray tube rotates around the individual, taking hundreds of images compiled by computer to produce a two-dimensional cross-section of the body.
C. A conventional X-ray, by contrast, provides a two-dimensional image and requires the patient to be moved manually to image the same region from a different angle.
C. Other common imaging techniques such as MRI and ultrasound do not use X-rays at all, unlike both plain radiography and CT.

A(i) Principle: MRI uses strong magnetic fields and radio waves to produce detailed internal images; the magnetic field aligns the hydrogen nuclei of the body, and the radio wave disturbs this alignment.
A(i) Principle (continued): the body detects the release of energy as the nuclei return to their original position; imaging can be obtained in the axial, sagittal and coronal planes.
A(ii) Common sequences: the most frequently used MRI sequences for the spine are T1-weighted, T2-weighted, and STIR (short tau inversion recovery); STIR is especially helpful for diagnosing acute pathologies like inflammation and detecting vertebral oedema.
A(iii) Indications: acute and chronic back pain, disc herniations, spinal stenosis, tumors and infections, and post-surgical follow-up.
A(iv) Advantages: non-invasive and radiation-free; allows better visualization of the spinal cord, ligaments, discs, vessels and other soft tissues than CT or radiographs.
A(iv) Advantages (continued): the gadolinium contrast material is less likely to cause an allergic reaction than the iodine-based contrast used for X-rays and CT; it is the preferred method for assessing complications of surgery, including bleeding, scarring, infection and recurrence of a herniated disk.
A(v) Limitations: cost and availability; limited ability to assess bone detail compared with CT; the need for the patient to remain perfectly still.
A(v) Limitations (continued): implants and other metallic objects can make clear images difficult to obtain, and it is generally not recommended for seriously injured patients because traction devices and life-support equipment may distort the images.
B. MRI is the modality of choice for identifying injuries to soft-tissue structures - the posterior ligamentous complex, spinal cord, intervertebral discs and adjacent muscles.
B. It is the gold standard for the spinal canal, thecal sac, cord, disc and nerve roots.
C. MRI is very good for detecting fractures, but not as sensitive or precise as CT.
C. CT is instead the imaging modality of choice when there is a high or moderate index of suspicion of spine injury in a trauma setting, and has been shown to be more accurate at identifying thoracolumbar injuries than plain X-ray.
