questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: congenital hip dislocation, also known as developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH).
(ii) Predisposing factors/pathophysiology: it occurs with an incidence that varies between 1.5 and 20 per 1000 births and is 8 times more common in girls than boys, explained by the greater mobility of the hip in women; more than 80% of clinically unstable hips noted at birth resolve spontaneously; hip dislocation is the displacement of the femur head from the acetabulum, and all newborn babies have their hips assessed for DDH within a few days of birth and at six weeks so that treatment can commence early if necessary.
(iii) Physical and imaging assessment: the ball-and-socket joint of the hip anatomy consists of the acetabulum, shaped like a cup, and the femur head, shaped like a ball; radiographs are compared to a normal hip joint to identify the displacement.
(iv) Physiotherapy management: aims of physiotherapy management for dislocation include improving physical function, reducing the risk of occurrence of the condition and secondary impairment, improving muscle strength, power and endurance, achieving active range of motion, and improving the ability to perform activities of daily living; management includes reduction technique, immobilization with a splint, range-of-motion exercises, and strengthening exercises such as isometric and resistance exercises, progressed as tolerated.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Diagnosis: Osteoarthritis of the shoulder, also known as periarthritis shoulder.

(b)
Mechanism: hypersecretion of synovial fluid with an inflamed, thickened, hypertrophied synovial membrane; softened, roughened, worn articular cartilage; sclerosis, eburnation and cyst formation of subchondral bone; osteophytes at the articular surfaces; and bony ankylosis.

(c)
Clinical features/assessment: age over 60 years, insidious onset, morning stiffness, dull aching pain aggravated by joint use and relieved by rest, swelling or deformity, muscular wasting, crepitus, and painful restricted movement, without systemic manifestations; X-ray shows asymmetric joint space narrowing and osteophytes at the joint margins, with MRI revealing early changes missed on X-ray.

(d)
Management: conservative treatment is the treatment of choice, comprising physiotherapy (SWD or IR therapy, exercises); surgery is rarely indicated.

(e)
Physiotherapy treatment: muscle-strengthening exercises (active and passive), traction, heat therapy (SWD/IRR), massage (stroking, compression), ambulation aids where applicable, acupuncture/acupressure and yoga therapy, aimed at relieving pain, strengthening muscles, mobilizing joints, improving coordination and minimizing deformity.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Diagnosis: Osteochondritis of the patella (lesion usually found anywhere on the patella, especially its femoral surface).

(b)
Surgical procedure: Excision of the osteochondritic lesion with removal of loose bodies.

(c)
Post-operative physiotherapy: Post-operative immobilization for 2-3 weeks, with after-care physiotherapy - assisted passive exercises by the physiotherapist progressed to free active exercises by the patient.

(a)
Diagnosis: Acromegaly (hyperpituitarism occurring after closure of the epiphyses).

(b)
Predisposing factors/pathophysiology: a benign adenoma (or carcinoma) of the anterior pituitary lobe, or a transient (fugitive) cause, produces overactivity of the hyperactive eosinophilic portion of the anterior pituitary with excessive growth hormone; onset may be before closure of the epiphyses of the long bones (gigantism) or after closure (acromegaly).

(c)
Management: hormonal therapy (progesterone, growth hormone/somatostatin); radiotherapy is the treatment of choice for a sensitive tumour without visual field loss; surgery (cryohypophysectomy) is rarely required, as patients are a poor risk on account of heart and chest problems and a difficult surgical approach, and is indicated when radiotherapy is hazardous or visual fields are markedly reduced.

(d)
Physiotherapy management: physiotherapy does not play a prominent part, but the physiotherapist advises moderate regular exercise, and may be involved in planning and teaching a programme of activities for the individual patient.

(a)
Indication: amputation for peripheral vascular disease, where medical and surgical procedures have failed to furnish adequate nutrition to the limb, performed to save life and preserve remaining function, on grounds of unrelieved ischemic pain, infection, or gangrene.

(b)
Procedure named: amputation through the leg (below-knee amputation) at the ideal level of 15 cm below the medial tibial condyle, bone length varying between 12 and 18 cm based on patient height.

(c)
Preoperative phase: physical, social and psychological assessment; strengthening exercises for shoulder extensors and adductors, elbow extensors, hand grip, hip extensors, adductors and abductors; mobilizing exercises for hip and knee; bed exercises; transfer practice; wheelchair mobility training. Postoperative preprosthetic phase: control of wound-site or phantom limb pain and anxiety with adequate analgesics and sedatives. Prosthetic phase: referral to an artificial limb fitting centre after stump healing (usually 2 to 3 weeks postoperatively).

(d)
Precautions: longer stumps are poorly adapted to a prosthesis and prone to breakdown from poor circulation; a short stump cannot be fitted comfortably and may require excision of fibula and additional muscle bulk; the stump's bony base must be broad and smooth, with the scar kept away from the pressure area.

(e)
Functional outcome: the stump and prosthesis together should restore two functions, walking and static weight bearing, provided the skin coverage can withstand weight-bearing pressure.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Axillary (circumflex) nerve injury.

(b)
Mechanism: direct trauma (blow, gunshot, stab), fall from height, road/street accident, or fracture-dislocation of the humerus; the deltoid and teres minor become paralysed and wasted.

(c)
Deformity: arm hanging by the side of the chest; deltoid thin, soft, flabby in old lesions; power: deltoid paralysed, unable to raise a flexed elbow against resistance; loss of sensation and reflexes along the outer side of the arm; skin cold, glazed and smooth. Assessment: test deltoid by asking the patient to raise the flexed elbow from the side against resistance; electrical stimulation via needles along the posterior border of deltoid; X-ray shoulder.

(d)
Conservative treatment: immobilization of the arm in a relaxation (right-angled) position using splints to relax deltoid and spinati, forearm flexed and supinated to relax biceps, brachialis and supinator; physiotherapy.

(e)
Surgical treatment for compression from fracture-dislocation: exploration and suturing of the nerve, postoperative immobilization with a POP cast, stitches removed through a window in the cast, exercises in an abduction brace, and occupational therapy; results of suturing are usually unsatisfactory.

(a)
Definition: varicose veins are a disorder of veins whereby the vein is dilated, lengthened, and tortuous, usually occurring in the leg veins, though spermatic, oesophageal, and haemorrhoidal veins may also be affected.

(b)
• Aetiology: congenital (arteriovenous fistula), traumatic, inflammatory, postural (erect posture), pregnancy (venous obstruction), and metabolic causes.
• Pathogenesis: impaired venous pump from congenital paucity of non-return valves (especially the saphenofemoral and saphenopopliteal valves), muscle weakness/wasting, and stretched deep fascia, resulting in dilated superficial veins and leakage of blood under high pressure into the superficial system.

(c)
Clinical features: aching or burning discomfort, fatigue or pain in the legs on prolonged standing, cramps, itching, eczematoid dermatitis; usually bilateral, with dilated, tortuous, elongated visible veins, pigmented thinned skin, and postphlebitic swelling.

(d)
Investigations: CBC, ESR, blood sugar, Color Doppler (venous), ultrasound, MRI; Trendelenburg's test determines competency of valves in the superficial and communicating venous systems.

(e)
Complications: ulceration from direct trauma, haemorrhage from an ulcerating varix, thrombophlebitis of superficial veins, and eczema.

(f)
• Differentiation: chronic venous insufficiency is characterized by progressive edema of the leg, especially the lower leg, and secondary changes in the skin and subcutaneous tissues, usually occurring from changes secondary to deep thrombophlebitis (damaged valves).
• Varicose veins are instead primarily a disorder of superficial vein dilation from valvular incompetence, which may itself be a precursor or contributing cause to later chronic venous insufficiency.

(g)
• Management: conservative treatment includes elastic stockings, leg-elevation exercises, and injection (sclerosing) therapy for cosmetic reasons or after failed stripping.
• Surgical treatment for failed conservative measures: high ligation of the long saphenous vein at the saphenofemoral junction, stripping of the saphenous vein, ligation of secondary veins, and ligation of the short saphenous vein at the saphenopopliteal junction.
• Physiotherapy management for varicose veins: exercises with legs raised while remaining ambulant to maintain venous circulation.
• Physiotherapy for chronic venous insufficiency follows the same principle of leg elevation and exercise to support venous return and reduce progressive edema.

The femoral condyles - periarticular fractures of the distal femur.

A patient over 60 years old with dull aching knee pain aggravated by weight-bearing and relieved by rest, morning stiffness, crepitus and painful restricted movement is diagnosed with osteoarthritis of the knee and undergoes joint replacement surgery.
(a) What is the diagnosis and what surgery/procedure has been named?

questions.answerText:
(a)
Diagnosis: Osteoarthritis (degenerative joint disease) of the knee; surgical procedures for osteoarthritis include excision of osteophytes, excision of loose bodies, arthroscopic débridement, synovectomy, reconstruction (débridement of the joint), arthroplasty (joint replacement), and arthrodesis.

(b)
Postoperative physiotherapy: immobilization of the joint with Buck's traction for one week, followed by exercises as soon as possible until restoration of quadriceps power.

(c)
Precautions: the joint is kept immobilized in Buck's traction for the first week before exercises are commenced.

(d)
Expected outcome: restoration of quadriceps power with exercises given as soon as possible after the period of immobilization.

(a)
Diagnosis: congenital torticollis (wryneck).

(b)
Predisposing factors: history of obstructed labour. Pathophysiology: a fibromatosis tumor within the sternocleidomastoid muscle; muscle fibres are replaced by diffuse infiltration of fibroblasts arranged in an organoid pattern, forming a thickened acellular mass of disorganized fascial tissue.

(c)
Management: transient torticollis (about 20% of cases) requires no treatment. Surgical treatment, indicated for persistent cases, includes sternocleidomastoid release at the clavicle or mastoid, tumor excision, or tenotomy; postoperative POP casts or braces are usually not effective.

(d)
Physiotherapy management: manipulation (stretching) of the neck three times daily for a couple of months, followed by free active exercises.

A two-week-old infant, born after obstructed labour, presents with the head tilted towards the affected side and the chin pointing to the opposite side, with a swollen sternocleidomastoid muscle.
(a) What is the diagnosis?
(b) What are the predisposing factors and pathophysiology?
(c) What is the medical/surgical management?
(d) What is the physiotherapy management?

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Mechanism, direct trauma: violence.
• Mechanism, indirect trauma: sudden quadriceps contraction, repetitive strain activity (RSA), sports injury (weight lifting, jumps, martial arts), or degenerative rupture in the elderly after trivial injury (e.g. stumbling).

(b)
• Types, by site: rupture may occur at the tendon-muscle junction (e.g. quadriceps extensor just above the patella) or through the muscle belly itself (e.g. rectus femoris at mid-thigh level); may follow normal or unusual physical activity/stress.
• Types, commonly ruptured structures: rectus femoris, biceps brachii (muscles); quadriceps femoris tendon, supraspinatus tendon, patellar tendon, biceps brachii tendon, tendocalcaneus, extensor pollicis longus, extensor digitorum communis (tendons).

(c)
• Deformity/clinical signs: pain; a gap visible and palpable on contracting the affected muscle; local tenderness; movements painful and restricted.
• Investigation: X-ray, AP and lateral views, to rule out bony injury.

(d)
Complications: torn muscle fibres/tendon with extravasation of blood and haematoma formation.

(e)
• Management principles, conservative: rest; pressure dressings; analgesics/NSAIDs; antibiotics.
• Management principles, surgical: performed as soon as possible especially in a young person/laborer; muscle repaired with interrupted silk mattress sutures; tendon apposed without tension, lacerated parts excised, large ruptured tendons repaired using fascia lata strips across the repair line; after care by POP cast or splint.

(f)
• Physiotherapy management, stage 1 (during immobilization): support provided with a splint.
• Physiotherapy management, stage 2 (as pain subsides): active exercises encouraged for joint movement and muscle strengthening.
questions.question:
Describe rupture of muscles and tendons under the following headings:
(a) Mechanism of injury
(b) Types
(c) Deformity
(d) Complications
(e) Management principles
(f) Physiotherapy management at each stage

questions.answerText:
(a)
Definition: supracondylar fracture is a fracture of the distal humerus, going through the thinnest portion of the bone, proximal to the trochlea and capitulum, often through the apices of the coronoid and olecranon fossae or through the metaphysis.

(b)
Epidemiology: the most common elbow injury in children (60%), becoming less common with increasing age; usually under 8 years, peak age 5-7 years; boys are affected more than girls.

(c)
Mechanism: extension type is the commonest type (95-97%).

(d)
Clinical features: mild swelling to gross deformity, arm held to the side, reduced movement at the elbow, S-shaped configuration.

(e)
• Treatment: fractures with neurovascular affectation are treated as a surgical emergency; undisplaced fractures are managed with a splint; displaced fractures require open reduction and internal fixation.
• Precaution: to minimise compartment syndrome risk, the elbow should be immobilised at about 30 degrees of flexion in the emergency room and 60-70 degrees after surgery.

(f)
• Clinical basis: nerve injuries occur in about 7% (radial greater than median greater than ulnar) and vascular injuries in about 1%, with open fractures in less than 1%.
• Continued: complications include vascular insufficiency of the brachial artery, compartment syndrome, cubitus varus ("gunstock") deformity and Volkmann's ischaemic contracture, reflecting the proximity of the neurovascular bundle to the thin distal humerus in the growing skeleton.

(g)
• Distinguishing feature 1: the extension type is the commonest pattern of supracondylar fracture, accounting for 95-97% of cases.
• Distinguishing feature 2: the flexion type is the less common pattern.
• Distinguishing feature 4: both types share the risk of nerve injury, vascular injury to the brachial artery, and the S-shaped deformity described for supracondylar fracture generally.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Central cord syndrome.

(b)
Occurs with hyperextension injuries of the neck in older patients due to haemorrhage into the grey matter, leading to flaccid paralysis of the upper limb.

(c)
Anterior cord syndrome (severe compression fractures/axial loading, complete muscle paralysis with joint position sense, vibration and deep pressure sensation intact, poor prognosis for motor recovery); posterior cord syndrome (depressed fractures of the posterior arch, minimal motor/proprioception/deep pressure loss, persistent ataxia is a common complication); Brown-Sequard syndrome (paresis with spasticity on the side of the lesion and blunting of pain/thermal sensibility on the opposite side); cauda equina syndrome (perianal anaesthesia, sphincter and bladder dysfunction).

(d)
The cervical spine is susceptible to injury because it is highly mobile, has relatively small vertebral bodies, and supports the head, which is heavy and acts as a lever; stability is provided by two functional vertical columns (anterior column supporting compressive load, posterior column resisting tensile stress), and the injury remains stable as long as one column is intact.

(e)
Before evaluating the cervical region, test the alar and transverse ligaments for laxity, and do not proceed with range-of-motion exercises if laxity is found; use cervical collars for a short period to prevent healing in a faulty position; use massage and muscle-setting techniques to maintain circulation and promote relaxation; do not stretch if muscle guarding is found.
questions.question:

Describe rupture of the extensor tendon (Mallet Finger) under the following headings:
(a) Mechanism of injury
(b) Types
(c) Deformity
(d) Complications
(e) Management principles
(f) Physiotherapy management at each stage
questions.answerText:
(a)
Mechanism of injury: forced flexion of the finger from the extension position, causing the extensor tendon to tear its attachment to the phalanx (an avulsion injury).

(b)
Types: avulsion of the extensor tendon at its bony attachment.

(c)
• Deformity: persistent flexion of the terminal phalanx.
• Further clinical signs: pain; swelling; local tenderness; loss of extension of the terminal phalanx.
• Investigation: X-ray of the hand, AP and lateral views.

(d)
Complications: failure of conservative treatment necessitating surgery.

(e)
• Management principle, conservative: a splint applied in hyperextension at the DIP joint for 5 weeks.
• Management principle, surgical (indicated on failure of conservative treatment): arthrodesis in extreme cases of failure.

(f)
• Physiotherapy management, stage 1: heat pad therapy or IRR; accessory movement exercises to mobilize the finger joints; massage by finger kneading to mobilize the tendon and reduce swelling.
• Physiotherapy management, stage 2: passive stretching applied by the physiotherapist to restore flexion; the physiotherapist teaches the patient how to hold the middle phalanx initially in extension and practice flexion, progressing by increasing flexion of the PIP joint.
• Physiotherapy management, stage 3: an extensor splint is worn until full control is achieved.

questions.question:
An infant presents with a convex sole, the talus and calcaneus positioned in equinus, and the forefoot dorsiflexed at the midtarsal joints, with deep creases on the dorsolateral aspect of the foot.
(a) What structure or joint is involved?
(b) What deformity or functional impairment results?
(c) What are the differential diagnoses?
(d) What is the clinical reasoning for the physiotherapy plan?
questions.answerText:
(a)
Structure/joint involved: the talus (distorted plantarward and medially) and calcaneus (in equinus), with the navicular displaced onto the dorsal aspect of the talar head, and contracted capsules, ligaments, and tendons on the dorsum of the foot.

(b)
Deformity: this is congenital rocker bottom flat foot (vertical talus), showing flattening of the medial longitudinal arch with a convex sole, and restricted, painful movement of the tarsal joints.

(c)
Differential diagnoses: the flexible type of congenital flat foot caused by postural factors, distinguished by the sole not being convex.

(d)
Clinical reasoning: conservative measures (moulding into inversion, wedging casts, braces, or modified shoes with raised inner borders) tend to fail with recurrence, so surgical release of contracted soft structures and stabilization of the tarsals is usually preferred; postoperatively the physiotherapist's role centres on advice regarding suitable footwear, with or without arch support, since painless flat feet in children generally require no active treatment while painful cases need footwear guidance.

(a)
• Delayed union - pathology: a fracture that has not healed in the expected time for the type of fracture, patient and method of repair.
• Continued, causes/presentation: caused by inadequate blood supply, severe soft tissue damage, periosteal stripping, excessive traction, insufficient splintage or infection; features are persistent pain at the fracture site, instability, non-weight bearing, disuse muscle atrophy, with X-rays showing a visible fracture line and very little callus.
• Non-union - pathology: the fracture has not healed and is not likely to do so without intervention; healing has stopped and the gap is filled with fibrous tissue (pseudoarthrosis).
• Continued, causes/presentation: caused by instability at the fracture site, inadequate stabilisation, inadequate blood supply, poor surgical technique, infection, excessive gap or bone loss, or excessive/improper implants; presents with painless movement at the fracture site, and X-rays show rounded, smooth, sclerotic ends (atrophic or hypertrophic).
• Malunion - pathology/causes: fragments join in an unsatisfactory position (angulation, rotation or shortening), caused by failure to reduce a fracture adequately, failure to hold reduction, or gradual collapse of comminuted/osteoporotic bone; features are deformity and shortening with limitation of movement.

(b)
• Perkins' time table, upper limb: callus is visible at 2-3 weeks, union at 4-6 weeks, consolidation at 6-8 weeks.
• Perkins' time table, lower limb: callus is visible at 2-3 weeks, union at 8-12 weeks, consolidation at 12-16 weeks - delayed and non-union are defined against this expected timetable.

(c)
• Distant functional deficit: joint stiffness commonly follows fracture immobilisation, affecting the knee, elbow, shoulder and small hand joints, caused by oedema and fibrosis of the capsule/ligaments/muscle, or adhesion of soft tissue to itself or underlying bone.
• Continued: malunion causing angulation greater than 15 degrees in a long bone, marked rotational deformity, or shortening greater than 3cm in a lower limb can alter loading and function at joints away from the fracture site.

(d)
• Physiotherapy management: prevention by exercise and correct joint positioning if splinted; once stiffness has occurred, prolonged physiotherapy, with intra-articular adhesions treated by gentle manipulation under anaesthesia followed by continuous passive motion, and adherent/contracted tissue released by operation.
• Surgical management, delayed union: conservative treatment eliminates the possible cause with continued immobilisation and exercise; operative treatment (internal fixation and bone grafting) is indicated when union is delayed more than 6 months with no signs of callus.
• Surgical management, non-union/malunion: vascular non-union is treated with rigid immobilisation and open reduction/compression with cancellous bone graft; avascular non-union requires opening the medullary canal, debriding sclerotic bone, rigid fixation and cancellous bone graft; malunion is treated by osteotomy and internal fixation, or a raised boot for shortening.

(b) State how these relate to the causes and clinical presentation of each (Perkins' time table).
(c) Explain how these complications may lead to a distant functional deficit such as joint stiffness.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Diagnosis: Osgood-Schlatter disease (epiphysitis of the tibial tuberosity).

(b)
Predisposing factors/pathophysiology: Etiology is unknown, genetic, traumatic (sports trauma), or infective; the tibial epiphysis undergoes partial separation; commoner in boys, aged 10-15 years; X-ray shows partial separation of the tongue-shaped portion of the epiphysis from the shaft.

(c)
Medical/surgical management: Conservative - bedrest, avoiding strenuous exercises, diathermy (SWD, infrared), strapping, analgesics/NSAIDs/antibiotics, and a cylinder walking cast for 8-10 weeks. Surgical (rarely indicated, for failure of conservative measures) - excision of the bony prominence (Thomson) or insertion of bone pegs (Bosworth), with a cylinder walking cast (groin to toes) for 2 weeks post-operatively.

(d)
Physiotherapy management: Assisted passive exercises by the physiotherapist progressed to free active exercises by the patient.
questions.question:
A 13-year-old boy presents with pain and limping following sports activity, with an unduly prominent tibial tubercle, local tenderness, and pain on walking and running.
(a) What is the diagnosis?
(b) What are the predisposing factors and pathophysiology of this condition?
(c) Outline the medical/surgical management.
(d) Outline the physiotherapy management.

Following a stab injury to the knee, a patient develops a contaminated wound with hematoma formation, extravasation of blood and subsequent diffuse cellulitis around the joint.
(a) What are the risk factors that predispose a joint wound to this course?
(b) What are the early and late complications?
(c) What are the conservative versus surgical management options, and which would you justify as the treatment of choice?
(d) What is the role of physiotherapy?
questions.answerText:
(a)
Risk factors: direct trauma (blow, stab, gunshot), road/traffic accidents, sports injuries, and fall from a height.

(b)
Complications: torn tissues, contused adjoining structures, extravasation of blood, hematoma, infected wound, diffuse cellulitis, abscess formation, reactivated infection, and later scarring and contracture of soft tissues.

(c)
• Conservative treatment is the treatment of choice: toilet of the wound, antiseptic dressing, antibiotics, analgesics and NSAIDs, and immobilization of the affected joint, followed by aftercare immobilization with Buck's traction.
• Surgical treatment is indicated only for synovitis or a remnant foreign body, and consists of aspiration of the joint (diagnostic and therapeutic), exploration of the wound/soft tissue, and débridement of the wound with exploration of the joint.

(d)
Physiotherapy role: active and passive exercises started once acute symptoms have subsided, with restoration of function induced slowly to avoid reactivating synovitis or infection; special exercises to restore quadriceps power at the earliest; walking allowed with the aid of a long leg brace, which is not discarded until a satisfactory range of motion, especially extension, is restored.

questions.question:
A patient presents after a fall downstairs with pain in the ankle, local tenderness, a clicking sensation on moving the joint, weakness, and painful restricted movements.
(a) What is the diagnosis?
(b) Describe the mechanism of injury and the pathology involved.
(c) State the clinical features and physiotherapy assessment findings in this condition.
(d) What are the definitive treatment options?
questions.answerText:
(a)
Diagnosis: Internal derangement of the ankle joint (chronic sprain of ankle).

(b)
Mechanism/pathology: Direct trauma (violence, road/street accident, sports injury, or fall downstairs) injures the deltoid ligament, ruptures the lateral ligament, or causes dislocation/subluxation (traumatic predisposing factors), or produces an angulated tibia or fibula (deformity); this tears the capsule/synovia and ruptures the deltoid and lateral ligaments.

(c)
Clinical features/assessment findings: Pain; local tenderness; clicking of the joint on moving the ankle; weakness; movements painful and restricted.

(d)
Definitive treatment options: Repair for ruptured ligaments; reduction (closed or open) for dislocation/subluxation; osteotomy for an angulated tibia or fibula; followed by assisted passive exercises by the physiotherapist progressed to free active exercises by the patient.

questions.question:
A child presents with pain, swelling, local tenderness, a limp, and restricted knee movement, with muscular weakness.
(a) What structure or joint is involved?
(b) What is the resulting deformity or functional impairment?
(c) What are the differential diagnoses?
(d) What is the clinical reasoning for the physiotherapy plan?
questions.answerText:
(a)
Structure/joint involved: the semimembranosus bursa, which forms one large sac separating the tendon and medial head of gastrocnemius, and often communicates with a bursa separating gastrocnemius from the back of the knee joint.

(b)
Functional impairment: pain, swelling, local tenderness, limp, movements of the knee painful and restricted, and muscular weakness; common in children.

(c)
Differential diagnoses: lipomas; xanthomas; fibrosarcoma.

(d)
Clinical reasoning: conservative measures (rest, immobilization, diathermy, analgesics/NSAIDs, intra-articular corticosteroid injection, antibiotics) are tried first; surgical treatment (aspiration and injection, incision and drainage, excision of the cyst) is reserved since it is not required in most cases, with postoperative immobilization of the knee by a posterior splint for 2 weeks; physiotherapy - heat therapy (SWD/IRR or heating pad therapy) and, as pain subsides, active exercises for joint movement and muscle strengthening - follows either pathway.

questions.question:
(a) Define and classify gangrene.
(b) What are the causes/aetiology?
(c) What are the clinical features?
(d) What investigations are used?
(e) What are the complications?
(f) Distinguish dry gangrene from moist gangrene.
(g) Outline the management, including the physiotherapy management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Definition: gangrene is death with putrefaction of macroscopic portions of tissue, usually affecting the distal part of a limb, the appendix, small intestine, gallbladder, pancreas, or testis.
• Classification: clinical types are dry and moist gangrene.

(b)
Aetiology: traumatic (crush injuries, pressure sores), infective (boils, carbuncles, gas gangrene, scrotal gangrene), physical agents (burns, scalds, frostbite, trench feet, acids, alkalies, electricity, X-ray radiation), and secondary causes summarized by the mnemonic RESTED (Raynaud, ergot, senile, thrombosis, embolism, diabetes).

(c)
Clinical features: skin colour changes from haemoglobin breakdown and iron sulphide formation; pain as rest pain or intermittent claudication in senile gangrene; swelling in gas gangrene; fever in infective gangrene; muscles appear brick red, green, or black.

(d)
Investigations: CBC, ESR; WR for syphilis; urine for diabetes; Color Doppler; X-ray.

(e)
Complications: spread by local extension, infection, or skipping; may necessitate amputation as a life-saving measure.

(f)
• Differentiation: dry gangrene shows the part becoming dry, wrinkled, discoloured, and greasy, typical of traumatic gangrene and frostbite, with the line of demarcation appearing quickly.
• Moist gangrene shows the part becoming swollen and discoloured, with the epidermis raised in blebs and crepitus on palpation from gas formation, typical of acute appendicitis, strangulated intestine and hernia; in atherosclerosis and embolism the line of demarcation is very slow.

(g)
• Preventive treatment: refraining from smoking, alcohol, and cold exposure, and protecting pressure areas.
• Conservative treatment: analgesics, NSAIDs, vasodilators (Papaverine, methyldopa, reserpine), and local care to keep the part dry and well-aerated.
• Surgical treatment: amputation, classified as conservative, semi-conservative, or radical (definitive), depending on the adequacy of demarcation and blood supply.
• Physiotherapy management: explaining treatment and teaching strengthening exercises; breathing and foot exercises as soon as possible to prevent DVT; recording skin temperature and colour for postoperative complications; avoiding strenuous exercise after arterial grafting, with walking allowed after 2 to 3 days.

questions.question:
Describe rupture of the ulnar collateral ligament (Gamekeeper's Thumb) under the following headings:
(a) Mechanism of injury
(b) Types
(c) Deformity
(d) Management principles
(e) Physiotherapy management at each stage
questions.answerText:
(a)
Mechanism of injury: direct violence - forced abduction of the thumb.

(b)
Types of injury described: incomplete tear or undisplaced avulsion fracture, versus complete tear or rotated fracture of the ulnar collateral ligament.

(c)
• Deformity: persistent flexion of the terminal phalanx.
• Further clinical signs: pain; local tenderness.
• Movements: of the thumb painful and restricted, especially grasping.
• Investigation: X-ray of the thumb, AP and lateral views.

(d)
• Management principle, indication and method for incomplete tear/undisplaced avulsion fracture: plaster fixation using a scaphoid-type cast for 6 weeks.
• Management principle, indication and method for complete tear/rotated fracture: surgical repair of the torn ligament and open reduction of the fracture, with after-care plaster fixation (scaphoid-type cast) for 6 weeks.

(e)
• Physiotherapy management, heat therapy: SWD/IRR or heating pad therapy.
• Physiotherapy management, exercise: as pain subsides, active exercises for joint movement and muscle strengthening.

questions.question:
An adult aged between 30 and 50 years presents with low backache and pain radiating down the thigh and leg.
(a) What are the risk factors for this condition?
(b) What are its complications?
(c) What are the conservative and surgical management options, and which would you justify choosing?
(d) What is the role of physiotherapy?
questions.answerText:
(a)
Risk factors: postural factors; deformity, e.g. kyphosis, scoliosis; spondylitis; vertebral osteophytes; violent actions such as sneezing, coughing, or lurching.

(b)
Complications: nerve root or spinal cord compression can cause neurologic deficit, including bowel or bladder compromise in severe cases

(c)
Conservative (symptomatic): bedrest; physiotherapy (heat therapy, massage, supervised back and leg exercises once acute backache and sciatica subside); traction for muscle spasm; a lumbar belt/back brace; analgesics, NSAIDs. Surgical: indicated in about 10% of cases when nerve root or spinal cord compression causes neurologic deficit, advised only where bowel or bladder function is compromised; conservative treatment must be attempted first, and recovery after surgery may take 3-12 months. Conservative management is justified as first-line since surgery is reserved for the minority with neurologic compromise.

(d)
Physiotherapy role: heat/ice packs to alleviate leg pain, especially in the initial phase; low back exercises performed 2-3 times daily.

(a)
• Definition: an aneurysm is a sac filled with blood that is in direct communication with the interior of an artery.
• Classification: true (fusiform, saccular, dissecting), false, and arteriovenous fistula (congenital or acquired).

(b)
Aetiology: traumatic, inflammatory, and infective (bacterial or syphilitic) causes.

(c)
Clinical features: intrinsic signs are a pulsatile, reducible swelling along the course of an artery, a palpable thrill, and an auscultated bruit; extrinsic signs are pressure effects on adjoining veins, nerves, bones, joints, trachea or oesophagus, and backache.

(d)
Investigations: CBC shows anaemia; ESR raised; blood sugar; Color Doppler; arteriography is confirmatory.

(e)
Complications/terminations: consolidation (spontaneous cure), rupture, or infection.

(f)
• Differentiation: a congenital arteriovenous fistula produces a structural effect, with veins becoming dilated, tortuous and thick-walled (arterialized).
• An acquired arteriovenous fistula instead produces a physiological effect, with arterial blood shunting into veins, resulting in high pulse pressure, left ventricular enlargement, and cardiac failure.

(g)
• Management is surgical: choice of treatment depends on arteriographic findings.
• Surgical techniques include ligation and excision, exclusion with grafting, excision with grafting, or reconstructive aneurysmorrhaphy.
• Physiotherapy management includes explaining treatment and teaching strengthening exercises, breathing and foot exercises to prevent DVT, and recording skin temperature and colour for postoperative complications.
• After femoral-popliteal grafting, strenuous exercise is avoided, walking is allowed after 2 to 3 days, and walking pattern is corrected daily as distance is increased.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Structure involved: the ulnar nerve, stretched in its groove behind the medial epicondyle of the humerus due to an increased carrying angle (cubitus valgus) following the earlier fracture.

(b)
Deformity: claw hand with clawing of the little and ring fingers, from paralysis of flexor carpi ulnaris, the medial half of flexor digitorum profundus, and the short muscles of the hand; the card test is unable to be performed (unable to grip a card between thumb and palm).

(c)
Differential diagnoses: this delayed presentation is consistent with tardy (delayed) ulnar nerve palsy from cubitus valgus, as distinct from an acute ulnar nerve division from direct trauma at the elbow or wrist (cuts, fractures of the medial epicondyle, dislocation of the elbow, Monteggia fracture-dislocation, or Colles fracture).

(d)
Clinical reasoning: since the deformity follows a chronic carrying-angle change rather than acute laceration, the definitive surgical option is anterior transposition of the ulnar nerve, with postoperative POP cast immobilization; physiotherapy planning should focus on exercises and occupational therapy following the cast period, and advice on movement and reassurance about recovery, since tardy palsy results from chronic stretching rather than nerve division.
questions.question:
A patient sustains a supracondylar fracture of the humerus in childhood. Years later, the hand shows clawing of the little and ring fingers, wasting of the hypothenar eminence and intermetacarpal spaces, and inability to grip a card between the thumb and palm.
(a) What structure or joint is involved?
(b) What deformity or functional impairment results?
(c) What are the differential diagnoses?

(a) Define injury to the infrapatellar pad of fat.
(b) State the etiology/mechanism.
(c) State the clinical features.
(d) State the investigation used.
(e) Explain how this condition affects function.
(f) Outline the surgical and rehabilitation management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Definition: injury to the infrapatellar pad of fat is one of the recognised internal derangements of the knee joint.

(b)
Etiology/mechanism: When hypertrophied, the fat pad may be nipped between the femur and tibia during extension of the knee.

(c)
Clinical features: History of pain and locking of the knee without being followed by sudden unlocking, unlike medial meniscus injury; local tenderness over the sides of the ligamentum patellae.

(d)
Investigation: X-ray of the knee (AP and lateral views) for any bony lesion.

(e)
• Effect on function: The knee locks due to nipping of the hypertrophied fat pad during extension, but this locking is not followed by the sudden unlocking seen in medial meniscus injury, so extension in particular is functionally affected.
• Effect on function (continued): Local tenderness over the sides of the ligamentum patellae further limits comfortable knee extension.

(f)
• Surgical management: Excision of the hypertrophied fat.
• Rehabilitation: Assisted passive exercises by the physiotherapist.
• Rehabilitation (continued): Progressed to free active exercises by the patient.

questions.question:
A 32-year-old man is involved in a road traffic accident and sustains a knee dislocation. On examination there is gross knee deformity, swelling and instability of the knee.
(a) State the most likely diagnosis.
(b) Name the surgery/procedure indicated.
(c) State the nerve/vessel/structure at risk.
(d) Outline the post-operative rehabilitation and physiotherapy considerations.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Knee dislocation, a medical emergency, given its rarity and the coexistent vascular injury that is a major complication and can lead to limb loss.

(b)
Vascular repair surgery for the coexistent vascular injury, together with surgery for the associated ligamentous injury.

(c)
Vascular assessment is essential; complications include vascular damage to the popliteal artery and popliteal vein, and nerve damage to the peroneal nerve.

(d)
A long rehabilitation programme is required, with return to full activity taking about 9-12 months. Postsurgical rehabilitation varies depending on the ligaments injured and repaired; passive and active movements are performed as tolerated (most patients lose some range of motion and do not recover it fully). Exercises in extension are performed in the first postoperative week; range-of-motion exercises stressing full extension and flexion are used from the 7th-10th week; strength training using closed kinetic chain exercises (e.g. squats) begins from the 11th-24th week; advanced strength and proprioceptive training is used from the 25th-36th week; the patient can return to sport/heavy work at the 37th week.

(a)
Acute suppurative (infective) arthritis is an acute inflammation of a joint due to infection, usually monoarticular, or acute in one/more joints with subacute/mild involvement in others if polyarticular. Chronic suppurative arthritis is a polyarticular infection with slight joint effusion, considerable synovial/periarticular edema, and adhesion/stiffness formation, following untreated or unsuccessfully managed acute infection.

(b)
• Aetiology, acute: direct - compound fractures involving the joint, penetrating wounds, operations, intra-articular aspiration or injection; local extension from a neighbouring focus (e.g. osteomyelitis of the femoral neck into the hip joint); indirect - hematogenous spread from skin, respiratory or genitourinary infection.
• Aetiology, chronic: bacterial, viral, fungal or parasitic infection; transmission primary (direct intrusion of microorganisms into the joint) or secondary (hematogenous, mostly via arteries).
• Organisms for both: Staphylococcus, Streptococcus, Pneumococcus, Gonococcus, Meningococcus, Haemophilus influenzae, gram-negative bacilli, Mycobacterium; smallpox, measles, mumps viruses; Actinomyces, blastomyces, coccidioides fungi; Echinococcus granulosus.

(c)
• Clinical features, acute: common in children; knee and hip commonly affected; sudden onset; severe pain; fever with chills and prostration; swelling; hot, red skin; local tenderness; movements painful and restricted.
• Clinical features, chronic: common in adults; knee and hip commonly affected; slow onset; mild to moderate continuous pain; fever may or may not be present; skin red, grey or pale; increasing deformity; sinus formation; movements painful and restricted.

(d)
• Investigations, both: CBC; leukocytosis on TLC/DLC; raised ESR; blood culture; synovial fluid analysis showing leukocytosis; smear and culture study of the causative organism.
• Investigations, specific: acute - X-ray normal in early cases, later demineralization, bony erosion, joint space narrowing, followed by osteomyelitis and periostitis; chronic - X-ray shows demineralization, bony erosion, progressive joint space narrowing, infarction or cavitation.

(e)
Complications: chronic suppurative arthritis may lead to soft tissue abscess (e.g. pelvic abscess), persistent infection, pathological fracture, pathological dislocation of the hip, and fibrous or bony ankylosis from destruction of articular cartilage.

(f)
• Distinguishing acute vs chronic: acute has a sudden onset with severe symptoms, commonly in children, whereas chronic has a slow, persisting, less severe course in adults with sinus formation and increasing deformity as hallmark features.
• Management, both: conservative - bedrest, immobilization by traction or splint, elevation of the part, warm fomentation, antibiotics, analgesics, fluids orally or IV; surgical - aspiration of the joint, incision and drainage; chronic disease may also need débridement, saucerization, arthrodesis, or amputation.
• Physiotherapy management, both: heat therapy (SWD/IRR); non-weight bearing free active exercises through full range; gait re-education with crutches progressed to sticks once pain subsides; hydrotherapy (buoyancy-resisted exercises) additionally used in the chronic form; early mobilization to prevent muscle atrophy and stiff joints.
questions.question:
(a) Define and classify suppurative arthritis.
(b) What is the causes/aetiology?
(c) What are the clinical features?
(d) What investigations are used?
(e) What are the complications?
(f) Distinguish between acute and chronic suppurative arthritis.

A 28-year-old man sustains a high-energy fall and presents with hip pain, non-weight bearing status, thigh deformity, leg length discrepancy and tenderness in the proximal thigh region.
(a) State the risk factors for this condition.
(b) Outline the possible complications.
(c) Discuss the conservative and surgical management options and justify one option for this patient.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Due to high-energy trauma in younger age groups (20-40 years) or low-energy trauma in older age groups (over 60 years); the subtrochanteric area (lesser trochanter to 5cm distal) accounts for 10-30% of fractures around the hip; strong muscular forces at the fracture site deform the fracture fragments and make reduction difficult.

(b)
Significantly higher rates of malunion, non-union and comminution compared with other proximal femoral fractures.

(c)
Conservative options for the trochanteric region include Buck's traction, hip spica cast, or Bohler-Braun splint. Surgical fixation is justified in this young, high-energy patient because strong muscular deforming forces make closed reduction difficult to maintain, and (as with other femoral fractures known to require surgery) surgical repair heals more rapidly with a better outcome and allows earlier mobilisation.

(a)
• Definition: infective (septic) arthritis is the invasion of a joint by an infectious agent resulting in joint inflammation, with redness, heat and pain in a single joint and decreased ability to move it, usually of rapid onset.
• Classification: acute suppurative arthritis is usually monoarticular, or if polyarticular, acute in one or more joints while subacute or mild in others; organisms include bacteria (Staphylococcus, Streptococcus, Pneumococcus, Gonococcus, Meningococcus, Haemophilus influenzae, gram-negative bacilli, Mycobacterium tuberculosis or bovis), viruses (smallpox, measles, mumps), fungi (Actinomyces, blastomyces, coccidioides) and parasites (Echinococcus granulosus).

(b)
• Causes: direct (compound fractures involving the joint, penetrating wounds, operations, diagnostic procedures such as intra-articular aspiration/injection) or local (extension from a neighbouring focus, e.g. osteomyelitis of the femoral neck).
• Transmission: primary (direct intrusion of microorganisms into the joint) or secondary (haematogenous, through the bloodstream, mostly via the arteries).

(c)
• Clinical features: common in children, commonly affecting the knee and hip, with sudden onset, severe pain, fever with chills and prostration, swelling, and local tenderness.
• Further features: hot red skin over the joint, and movements that are painful and restricted.

(d)
• Investigations: CBC with TLC and DLC showing leukocytosis, raised ESR, and blood culture.
• Further investigations: synovial fluid analysis showing leukocytosis with smear and culture study of the causative organism, and X-ray, normal early but later showing demineralization, bony erosion and joint space narrowing, followed by osteomyelitis and periostitis.

(e)
• Complications: chronic arthritis from delayed diagnosis or inadequate early treatment, soft tissue (pelvic) abscess formation, and persistent infection.
• Further complications: pathological fracture at the site of extensive bone necrosis, pathological dislocation of the hip, and ankylosis (fibrous or bony) from partial or complete destruction of the articular cartilage.

(f)
• Suppurative arthritis from a wound of the joint is more difficult to manage than the haematogenous type, with a less favourable prognosis.
• Infection from a wound may spread through fascial planes to cause diffuse cellulitis or abscess, with reactivation of infection or scar contracture more likely after surgery or manipulation, unlike haematogenous spread.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Definition: the scaphoid fracture is the commonest carpal fracture.

(b)
Classification/management basis: managed conservatively if displacement is less than 1mm; managed by internal fixation if displacement is greater than 1mm or the fracture is open.

(c)
Aetiology: results from a fall on an outstretched hand.

(d)
• Clinical features: pain in the anatomical snuffbox; often not visible on initial radiographs.
• Continued: if clinical suspicion exists despite a negative initial X-ray, the wrist is placed in a cast and reimaged at 10 days.

(e)
Treatment: conservative - immobilisation in a cast for 9-12 weeks if displacement is less than 1mm; internal fixation if displaced more than 1mm or open.

(f)
• Clinical basis: there is a risk of avascular necrosis of the scaphoid because the fracture can injure the radial artery, which supplies the bone.
• Continued: interruption of this blood supply is why scaphoid fractures are treated cautiously even when initial imaging is negative, with reimaging at 10 days to avoid missing a fracture that could progress to avascular necrosis if untreated.

(g)
• Distinguishing feature 1: scaphoid fracture typically follows a fall on an outstretched hand and presents with pain localised to the anatomical snuffbox, often without gross deformity.
• Distinguishing feature 2: Colles' fracture is also caused by a fall on an outstretched hand but involves the distal radius with dorsal displacement, producing an obvious dinner-fork wrist deformity.
• Distinguishing feature 3: Colles' fracture presents with severe pain worsened by grip and hand movement, swelling and tenderness of the wrist and hand, unlike the more localised snuffbox tenderness of scaphoid fracture.
• Distinguishing feature 4: scaphoid fracture carries a specific risk of avascular necrosis due to its precarious blood supply, a complication not characteristically described for Colles' fracture in the same way.

Both are mycotic (fungal) infections of bones and joints, usually secondary to a primary pulmonary infection; coccidioidomycosis and histoplasmosis are the two forms described, with histoplasmosis being rare and skeletal lesions single or multiple.

(b)
• Coccidioidomycosis is due to mycotic infection with coccidioidomycosis; histoplasmosis is due to mycotic infection with histoplasmosis.
• Pathogenesis (both): villonodular synovitis, granulomatous lesions in the cancellous bone of the vertebrae or near the ends of long bones, local bone atrophy, focal cystic destruction, abscess formation, sinus formation; the initial phase of pulmonary infection in both is characterized by arthralgia and periarticular swelling especially of the knees and ankles.

(c)
Clinical features (both): pain; swelling; local tenderness; reddish skin; septic-type arthritis; abscess; sinus formation.

(d)
Investigations (both): CBC, ESR; complement fixation test; microscopic appearance of spherules containing endospores; culture of synovial fluid for detection of coccidioides immitis; X-rays of bone showing rarefaction simulating tuberculosis.

(e)
Complications: abscess formation and sinus formation are described for both, with chronic bone infection possible.

(f)
• Distinguishing the two conditions: coccidioidomycosis and histoplasmosis have essentially the same clinical, investigative and pathogenetic features; the principal difference is that histoplasmosis is rare, with skeletal lesions that may be single or multiple, and its granulomatous lesions are not characteristic.
• Conservative management, coccidioidomycosis: immobilization of joints by splint or plaster cast; avoidance of weight bearing; antibiotics - Amphotericin B.
• Conservative management, histoplasmosis: immobilization of joints by splint or plaster cast; avoidance of weight bearing; analgesics/NSAIDs; antibiotics - Amphotericin B.
• Surgical management (both): curettage or saucerization for chronic bone infection; amputation for progressive stubborn bone infection; synovectomy for more advanced joint infection; débridement of the local/focal lesion for more advanced joint infection.
• After care (both): physiotherapy and exercises.
• Physiotherapy management (both): immobilization by splints, braces, etc. to provide comfort or protect weak osteoporotic bone from fracture; assisted passive exercises progressed to free active exercises for free joint movement and to strengthen weak muscles.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the pathology and stages of post-traumatic osteoarthritis.
(b) State how this relates to intra-articular fracture.
(c) Explain how the condition may spread its effect to cause functional deficit and joint deformity.
(d) Outline the physiotherapy and surgical management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Pathology, early stage: post-traumatic osteoarthritis follows a joint fracture with severely damaged articular cartilage, developing within a period of months.
• Pathology, late stage: years after the joint injury, cartilage heals but an irregular joint surface may cause localised stress, leading to secondary osteoarthritis.

(b)
• Relation to intra-articular fracture: fractures that extend into a joint usually damage the cartilage at the ends of the bones in the joint; normally this smooth, protective cartilage enables joints to move smoothly, but damaged cartilage tends to scar, causing osteoarthritis that makes joints stiff and limits range of motion.
• Continued: the knee, elbow and shoulder are particularly likely to become stiff after such injury, especially in older people; some fractures can make a joint unstable, further increasing the risk of repeated injury and osteoarthritis.
• Continued: surgery is often needed to repair the damaged cartilage after an intra-articular fracture, since afterwards the cartilage is less likely to scar, and if scarring occurs it tends to be less severe.

(c)
• Spread to functional deficit/deformity: clinical features of established osteoarthritis are pain, stiffness, swelling, deformity and restricted movement.
• Continued: because the irregular joint surface causes localised stress across the whole joint, not merely the original fracture line, the functional deficit extends to overall joint motion and load-bearing capacity, not just the site of the original break.
• Continued: appropriate treatment of the original fracture, often including a cast or splint, can help prevent this permanent joint deformity and instability from developing.

(d)
• Physiotherapy management: physical therapy is usually needed to prevent stiffness and help the joint move as normally as possible after an intra-articular fracture.
• Continued: for established post-traumatic osteoarthritis - pain relief with analgesics and anti-inflammatory agents, and joint mobility measures through physiotherapy.
• Continued: load reduction through weight reduction is also part of management.
• Surgical management: realignment osteotomy is used in the younger patient, while arthroplasty is used in patients over 60 years.

questions.question:
An adolescent presents with a rounded back, stiffness in the upper back, and tight hamstrings, developing gradually with poor posture during growth.
(a) What structure or joint is involved?
(b) What deformity or functional impairment results?
(c) What are the differential diagnoses?
(d) What is the clinical reasoning for the physiotherapy plan?
questions.answerText:
(a)
Structure involved: the thoracic spine, showing increased posterior convexity (abnormal rounding of the upper back).

(b)
Deformity: kyphosis, with a rounded back, stiffness in the upper back, and tight hamstrings; in severe cases complications include an irreversible hunch, persistent back pain, weakness or numbness in the limbs, breathing difficulties, and loss of bladder control.

(c)
Differential diagnoses: postural kyphosis (commonest amongst adolescents, from abnormal development of the spine and surrounding muscles related to poor posture); Scheuermann's kyphosis (also develops in adolescence but can become more severe than postural kyphosis); and congenital kyphosis (present from birth from abnormal spinal development in the womb, which can rapidly worsen with age).

(d)
Clinical reasoning: since postural and Scheuermann's kyphosis receive non-surgical treatment, physiotherapy aims to strengthen the back and abdominal muscles (knee rolls, pelvic tilting, knees to chest) to relieve pressure on the spine and improve posture, with a spinal brace added for Scheuermann's kyphosis; because physiotherapy cannot alter a structural curve once there is a change in bone structure, congenital kyphosis (which can rapidly worsen) is instead managed by arthrodesis, so the physiotherapy plan differs according to which of the three types is identified.

(a)
Mechanism: fracture-dislocation of the cervical spine or shoulder joint, road/street accident, fall from height, direct violence, or rarely operative trauma while excising the elbow; forced hyperabduction of the arm, as when a falling person tries to hold an object (e.g. failing to obtain a foothold on a moving train or bus), avulses the nerve roots from the spinal cord.

(b)
Type: lower lesion of the brachial plexus due to involvement of the eighth cervical and first thoracic nerve roots, sometimes also the seventh cervical.

(c)
Deformity: clawhand with the first phalanx extended and the second and third phalanges flexed, with the forearm flexed at the elbow.

(d)
Complications: muscular wasting of the hand muscles (hypothenar) in late cases; loss of muscle power, tone, sensations and reflexes along the inner side of the forearm, hand, and little finger; Horner's syndrome from paralyzed cervical sympathetic fibres, comprising partial ptosis, enophthalmos, myosis, and anhydrosis.

(e)
Healing: recovery likely within a few weeks in many cases; neurotmesis lesions have a poorer prognosis.

(f)
• Management: conservative treatment as soon as possible with immobilization of the arm in a relaxation position (right-angled, forearm flexed and supinated) with physiotherapy.
• Surgical treatment is indicated for neurotmesis lesions: exploration of the brachial plexus, often with little recovery due to difficulty approximating retracted torn nerve ends, and suturing, better performed by suturing two nerve roots to one trunk.

(g)
• Physiotherapy at the acute stage: advice on carrying out as much movement of the limb as possible and reassurance about recovery of normal function.
• Physiotherapy during immobilization: the relaxation position is maintained by splints while movement is encouraged as tolerated.
• Physiotherapy following surgical exploration: continues alongside the conservative approach of movement encouragement and reassurance.
• Segmental innervation of C8, T1 governs the intrinsic muscles of the hand, flexors of the fingers, and flexor carpi ulnaris, explaining the clawhand and flexion loss at the wrist and fingers.
• Overall recovery is likely to occur within a few weeks in many cases, but ongoing advice and reassurance remain central to physiotherapy care.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Definition: a fracture is a complete or incomplete break in a bone resulting from the application of excessive force; it could result from high-force impact, stress, pathology, or trivial injury, and certain medical conditions that weaken bone produce a pathological fracture.

(b)
Causes/risk factors: individuals with high activity levels are at greater risk; up to age 50 more men suffer fractures than women due to occupational hazards, but after age 50 women are more prone to fractures than men; specific disease risk factors include Paget's disease, rickets, osteogenesis imperfecta, osteoporosis, bone cancer and tumours.

(c)
• Classification, position/completeness: non-displaced - ends retain normal position; displaced - ends out of normal alignment; complete - broken all the way through; incomplete - not broken all the way through.
• Continued: broadly, all fractures are classified as closed (simple) or open (compound); a fracture line further classifies fractures as linear, oblique, transverse, longitudinal or spiral; fragments may also be described as comminuted, angulated, displaced, impacted, avulsed or segmental.

(d)
Symptoms: pain, which increases with attempted movement.

(e)
Diagnosis: begins with the individual's own observation of symptoms.

(f)
• Clinical basis, position of bone ends: non-displaced fracture ends retain their normal position while displaced fracture ends show disruption of normal alignment with deformity of the segments separate from one another, guiding whether reduction is required before immobilisation.
• Clinical basis, completeness: a complete fracture is broken all the way through the bone while an incomplete fracture (such as a greenstick fracture from bending or crushing forces, seen in children's bones) is not broken all the way through, reflecting the greater flexibility of immature bone.
• Continued: an open (compound) fracture involves a break in the skin, exposing bone and causing additional soft tissue injury and possible infection, whereas a closed (simple) fracture is not obvious as the skin remains intact - this classification determines infection risk and urgency of treatment.

(g)
• Distinguishing feature 1: a fracture is a break in the continuity of bone.
• Distinguishing feature 2: a dislocation is movement of a bone or joint away from its normal position, representing an anatomical disruption of a joint (luxation - total separation between two articulating bones; subluxation - incomplete dislocation/separation), often including tearing of ligaments, distinct from a break within the bone itself.
• Distinguishing feature 3: an injury may be classified as a fracture-dislocation when a fracture involves the bony structures of a joint with associated dislocation of that same joint, showing the two entities can coexist.

A patient sustains a high-energy impact injury and radiographs show an intra-articular fracture of the distal tibia disrupting the weight-bearing articular surface.
(a) Identify the structure/lesion involved.
(b) State the structures affected.
(c) List the differential fracture patterns (classification).
(d) Discuss the clinico-anatomical and functional reasoning for the presentation.
(e) State the physiotherapy management priorities.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Distal tibia (pilon) fracture.

(b)
Intra-articular fracture of the distal end of the tibia, disrupting the distal tibial weight-bearing articular surface; caused by high-energy impact, with the fracture pattern dictated by the position of the foot and talus at the time of impact.

(c)
Ruedi and Allgower classification: Type I - minimal displacement; Type II - significant displacement of the joint surface; Type III - impaction and comminution of the articular surface; also by injury position - plantar flexion injury (posterior lip fragment), neutral ankle (anterior and posterior fragments), dorsiflexion injury (anterior lip fragment).

(d)
25-50% of patients have additional injuries, reflecting the high-energy nature of the mechanism; clinical features (inability to bear weight, marked pain and swelling, evidence of soft tissue injury and deformity) relate directly to the degree of articular disruption.

(e)
Treatment goals are to obtain an anatomical articular reduction, restore axial alignment, maintain joint stability, achieve fracture union, and regain functional and pain-free weight bearing and motion while avoiding infection and wound complications; nondisplaced fractures with good skin condition are managed with calcaneal traction followed by cast immobilisation (long leg cast for 6 weeks) or ankle bracing/splinting.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Definition: Baseball pitcher's shoulder is often occupational and is caused by repeated severe strains of the joint.

(b)
Etiology: Occupational (repeated strains); sports injury.

(c)
Pathogenesis: Injury to a single or multiple structures; degenerated arthritic changes; irritated capsule and synovium causing irritation of the radial nerve; exostosis formed on the glenoid; frayed or degenerated rotator cuff tendons caused by repeated snubbing of the cuff over the humeral head and greater tuberosity.

(d)
• Clinical features: Pain referred to the deltoid region; local tenderness.
• Clinical features (continued): Movements of the shoulder painful and restricted.

(e)
Investigations: CBC, ESR; X-ray of the shoulder (AP and lateral views).

(f)
• Effect on function: Movements of the shoulder are painful and restricted, consistent with the occupational, repeated-strain nature of the condition.
• Effect on function (continued): The irritated capsule and synovium may irritate the radial nerve, and frayed/degenerated rotator cuff tendons further impair shoulder movement.

(g)
• Conservative management: Warm fomentation; analgesics/NSAIDs.
• Conservative management (continued): Local infiltration with injection lignocaine 1% 2 ml with hydrocortisone.
• Surgical management: Exploration.
• Rehabilitation: Assisted passive exercises by the physiotherapist progressed to free active exercises by the patient.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Pathology/stages: initial assessment includes airway/breathing/circulation assessment, careful physical and neurovascular examination, antibiotics and tetanus prophylaxis, local irrigation of 1-2 litres, sterile compressive dressings and splinting of the realigned fracture.
• Primary surgery: objectives of initial surgical management are preservation of life and limb, wound debridement, definitive injury assessment, and fracture stabilisation; thorough operative debridement is the standard of care for all open fractures.
• Wound closure: the open wound is initially left open to prevent anaerobic conditions and facilitate drainage/repeat debridement, though renewed evidence supports primary closure once adequately debrided; skin cover and soft tissue reconstruction should be done early, as infection risk increases if the wound is open for more than 7 days.

(b)
• Grade-infection/non-union relation: infection rates rise with Gustilo grade - 0-2% for Type I, 2-7% for Type II, 10-25% for Type IIIA, 10-50% for Type IIIB, and 25-50% for Type IIIC, with an amputation rate of 50% for Type IIIC.
• Continued: fracture healing time also lengthens with grade, from 21-28 weeks for Type I up to 30-35 weeks for Type III; delayed/non-union in severe injuries with bone loss is anticipated, with bone grafting usually delayed 6 weeks until soft tissues have soundly healed.
• Continued: host factors also predict infection - patients with any immunocompromising risk factor (from a list of 14 such factors, including advanced age, current nicotine use, diabetes mellitus and systemic immunodeficiency) have an increased risk of infection.

(c)
• Spread to osteomyelitis: most acute infections are caused by pathogens acquired in the hospital rather than at the time of injury - only about 18% of infections are caused by the same organism initially isolated on perioperative culture, indicating a largely nosocomial source.
• Continued: when wounds are left open for more than 2 weeks they become prone to nosocomial contaminants such as Pseudomonas and other Gram-negative bacteria, and currently most open fracture infections are caused by Gram-negative rods and Gram-positive staphylococci.
• Continued: if infection becomes established in bone, it constitutes osteomyelitis; pitfalls and complications of inadequately managed open fracture include infection leading to delayed union, non-union, malunion and loss of function.
• Continued: antibiotic timing matters - starting antibiotics within 3 hours is associated with a 4.7% infection rate versus 7.4% if delayed beyond 3 hours, reinforcing the importance of early, adequate antimicrobial cover in preventing spread to bone infection.

(d)
• Rehabilitation implications: types of fracture stabilisation influence rehabilitation - a splint is a good option if operative fixation is not required, internal fixation is used once the wound is clean with soft tissue coverage available, and external fixation is used for dirty wounds or extensive soft tissue injury.
• Continued: weight bearing and mobilisation progression are guided by wound healing status, soft tissue coverage, and radiographic evidence of healing, alongside the general principles of maintaining range of motion, isometric exercise during immobilisation, and progressive mobilisation, strengthening and gait retraining once healing allows.

An 82-year-old woman sustains a simple fall at home. Radiographs confirm an intertrochanteric fracture of the femur. She complains of hip and groin pain, is unable to lift the affected lower limb, and there is swelling and tenderness over the greater trochanter with no obvious deformity.
(a) State the risk factors for this condition.
(b) Outline the possible complications.
(c) Discuss the conservative and surgical management options and justify one option for this patient.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Advancing age and increased number of comorbidities; increased dependency in activities of daily living; a history of other osteoporosis-related fractures; female gender; a history of falls and gait abnormalities; poor vision; decreased muscle power; low blood pressure; decreased reflexes; vascular disease; coexisting musculoskeletal pathology.

(b)
Infection; non-union, malunion and delayed union; massive blood loss/haemorrhagic shock; thromboembolism, including pulmonary embolism, to which hip fracture greatly increases the risk; joint stiffness; and, because immobilisation is a particular problem in older people, blood clots, pressure sores, loss of muscle tissue and deterioration in physical conditioning.

(c)
Conservative management includes Buck's traction, a hip spica cast, or a Bohler-Braun splint. Doctors are increasingly using surgery to repair or replace the broken hip because it shortens the time patients must remain immobilised, enables the patient to walk (with a walker) often on the first day after surgery, and allows physical therapy to begin promptly; surgery is justified for this patient because, if not treated surgically, hip fractures require months of immobilisation in bed, and immobilisation in older people is more likely to cause blood clots, pressure sores, loss of muscle tissue and deterioration in physical conditioning than early surgical mobilisation.

questions.question:
(a) Describe rickets and osteomalacia under the headings of definition, aetiology, clinical features and investigations.
(b) Explain how the disease affects function.
(c) Outline the conservative, surgical and rehabilitation management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Definition: a disturbance of the mineral-matrix ratio due to reduced mineralization; rickets is the childhood deficiency disease due to lack of vitamin D, and osteomalacia is its adult form, common in females, with tetany occurring in advanced cases.
• Aetiology: inadequate intestinal absorption of calcium and phosphorus, from lack of calcium alone or lack of/resistance to vitamin D; risk factors include lack of sunshine, a diet poor in natural fats and oils, immobilization/lack of exercise, and neoplastic disease.
• Clinical features: a flabby child with a pot belly and sweating of the head; diminished stature, bending of the leg bones, spinal deformities, rickety rosary of the ribs, and aching bones.
• Further clinical features: muscular weakness and paralysis.
• Investigations: low serum calcium and phosphate, elevated alkaline phosphatase, and low urinary calcium and phosphate.
• Further investigations: a positive bone densitometer test, and X-ray showing cupping and blurring of the epiphyseal line, demineralization and bowing.

(b)
• Effect on function: deformed, bowed long bones and spinal deformity (kyphosis followed by scoliosis) impair posture, gait and growth.
• Function is further affected by muscular weakness and paralysis.

(c)
• Conservative management: a high-calcium diet, milk, cod liver oil and meat extracts, calcium gluconate/lactate 5-20 g/day, vitamin D (2-5 K units/day for rickets, 25-100 K units/day for osteomalacia and renal rickets), and sunlight exposure.
• Further conservative management: deformities corrected by splinting, and osteoclasis by manipulation; pancreatic insufficiency is treated with pancreatic enzyme and a high calcium intake.
• Surgical management: osteotomy, in older children and adults.
• Rehabilitation/physiotherapy management: regular exercise, especially weight-bearing, under the supervision and teaching of the physiotherapist.

(a)
Diagnosis: Hyperparathyroidism, due to diffuse hyperplasia of all the parathyroids or a localized tumour (adenoma, or rarely carcinoma).

(b)
Surgery: Parathyroidectomy, the only curative treatment, indicated for an adenoma of the parathyroid or hyperplasia of the parathyroids; a transverse incision is made following a crease of the neck, the flap is dissected up to the level of the pomum adami, the thyroid gland is exposed through a vertical median incision into the fasciomuscular planes from the hyoid bone to the suprasternal space of Burns, the parathyroid tumour is sought by sight and touch, and the tumour is excised (or, alternatively, three-quarters of a hyperplastic parathyroid is excised).

(c)
Postoperative phase: calcium plus vitamin D (calciferol) is given as 4 g of calcium lactate and 1K units of calciferol with 1 L of milk orally once daily for 3 days, continued for 6 months; physiotherapy consists of exercises and SWD/IRR.

(d)
Preoperative precaution: 4 g of calcium lactate and 1K units of calciferol with 1 L of milk orally once daily for 3 days before surgery; IV fluids are given to minimize formation of calcium phosphate renal stones, and hemodialysis may be life-saving if needed.
questions.question:
A patient with body aches, joint pains and backache, pathological fractures of the spine, ribs or long bones, renal calculi with polyuria and polydipsia, constipation, and nausea and vomiting is found to have a raised serum calcium with a reciprocally low serum phosphate.
(a) What is the diagnosis?
(b) What surgery/procedure is indicated, and what does it involve?
(c) Describe the post-operative physiotherapy and medical care by phase.
(d) What precautions apply preoperatively and postoperatively?

questions.answerText:
(a)
Indication: amputation through the thigh, indicated where end-bearing amputation at the distal femur is achievable and preferred over a higher amputation level.

(b)
Procedure named: amputation through the thigh (above-knee amputation), end-bearing type, providing a long leverage and a direct end-bearing surface that eliminates pressure from the prosthesis on the perineum.

(c)
Preoperative phase: physical, social and psychological assessment; strengthening of shoulder extensors and adductors, elbow extensors, hand grip, hip extensors, adductors and abductors; mobilizing exercises for hip and knee; transfer and wheelchair training. Postoperative preprosthetic phase: control of wound-site or phantom limb pain and anxiety with analgesics and sedatives. Prosthetic phase: referral to an artificial limb fitting centre after stump healing (usually 2 to 3 weeks postoperatively).

(d)
Precautions/drawback: a bulky knee mechanism, whose prosthetic hinges may fail to control rapid swing of the shin during gait due to friction.

(e)
Functional outcome: the stump and prosthesis together should restore walking and static weight bearing, with the bony base of the weight-bearing surface broad and smooth and the scar kept away from the pressure area.
questions.question:
A patient requires a thigh-level amputation. The surgeon selects an end-bearing amputation at the level of the distal end of the femur, covering the stump's end with suitable weight-bearing tissue.
(a) What is the diagnosis/indication for amputation?
(b) What surgery/procedure is named?
