(a) Define Perthes disease and state its pathogenesis.
(b) State the causes/etiology.
(c) State the clinical features.
(d) State the investigation used.
(e) Distinguish Perthes disease from osteochondritis dissecans of the hip.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Definition: Perthes disease (coxa plana, pseudocoxalgia) is a disability characterized by limping, muscular wasting, and restricted movements of the hip joint, present mostly in boys between the ages of 5 and 15 years.
• Pathogenesis: The femoral head becomes flattened, fragmented, and condensed.

(b)
Causes/etiology: Unknown; genetic; traumatic.

(c)
Clinical features: Commoner in boys; age 5-15 years; pain and limp are early symptoms; deformity with the limb adducted and externally rotated; muscular wasting; abduction and internal rotation restricted, while flexion and extension are free and painless.

(d)
Investigation: X-ray of the pelvis (AP view) shows marked incongruity, flattening of the femoral head, and the femur displaced upwards, confirmed by Shenton's line.

(e)
• Distinguishing feature - age group: Perthes disease occurs mostly in boys aged 5-15 years, whereas osteochondritis dissecans of the hip has no specific age group stated, its etiology instead being traumatic (intra-articular fracture) or degenerative (osteoarthritis).
• Distinguishing feature - pathology: In Perthes disease the femoral head itself becomes flattened, fragmented, and condensed, whereas in osteochondritis dissecans of the hip there is avascular necrosis of the subchondral bone with the overlying cartilage usually remaining intact, so a loose body is usually not formed.
• Distinguishing feature - natural history: without treatment, osteochondritis dissecans of the hip leads to collapse of the area and development of osteoarthritis.
• Distinguishing feature - investigation: Perthes disease shows marked incongruity, flattening of the femoral head, and upward femoral displacement confirmed by Shenton's line, whereas osteochondritis dissecans of the hip shows a loose body or bodies on X-ray of the pelvis.
• Distinguishing feature - conservative management: Perthes disease is managed conservatively with bedrest, traction, diathermy, and analgesics/NSAIDs, whereas osteochondritis dissecans of the hip is managed conservatively with restricted weight bearing, immobilization by traction, and walking with crutches without weight-bearing.
• Distinguishing feature - surgical management: Perthes disease, if conservative measures fail, is managed by drilling of the proximal femoral epiphysis, correction of disturbed soft tissues, trochanteric osteotomy, or arthrodesis, whereas osteochondritis dissecans of the hip is managed by drilling (small lesion), drilling with cancellous bone packing (large lesion), or excision with removal of loose bodies (detached area).

questions.question:
(a) Describe the mechanism, types, clinical features and complications of Monteggia and Galeazzi fractures.
(b) State the safe site/precautions for reduction and immobilisation of these injuries.
(c) Explain the anatomical/biomechanical basis of the deformity seen in these fracture-dislocations.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Mechanism, Monteggia: fall on the hand with forceful pronation of the forearm if the body is twisting at the moment of impact; sometimes the causal force is hyperextension.
• Mechanism, Galeazzi: fall on an outstretched hand, usually with a rotation force; the radius fractures in its lower third and the inferior radio-ulnar joint subluxates or dislocates.
• Types, Monteggia: a fracture of the shaft of the ulna associated with dislocation of the proximal radio-ulnar joint and the radiocapitellar joint (in children the ulnar injury may be an incomplete/greenstick fracture).
• Types, Galeazzi: a fractured radius with dislocation of the distal radioulnar joint, and is more common than the Monteggia fracture.
• Clinical features, Monteggia: obvious ulnar deformity, the dislocated radial head masked by swelling, pain and tenderness on the lateral side of the elbow; the wrist and hand should be examined for signs of radial nerve injury.
• Clinical features, Galeazzi: prominence or tenderness over the lower end of the ulna, pain and laxity of the radio-ulnar joint on wrist rotation, ulnar nerve paresis.
• Complications, Galeazzi: malunion due to loss of longitudinal support for the distal fragment, cross union, compartment syndrome.

(b)
• Safe site/precautions, Monteggia: the ulna is reduced and fixed with a plate and screws; stability must be tested through a full range of motion, and flexion, extension and rotation can commence postoperatively once the elbow is stable; with unstable elbows, immobilisation in plaster with the elbow flexed is used for 6 weeks.
• Safe site/precautions, Galeazzi: conservative treatment in children; open reduction and internal fixation in adults.

(c)
• Biomechanical basis, Monteggia: the radial head usually dislocates forwards while the upper third of the ulna fractures and bows forwards, so the deformity reflects the anterior displacement of the radial head relative to the fractured, bowed ulna.
• Biomechanical basis, Galeazzi: the radius fractures in its lower third and this shortening/angulation removes the longitudinal support for the distal radioulnar joint, allowing the joint to subluxate or dislocate, which is why malunion here specifically arises from loss of longitudinal support for the distal fragment.
• Continued: in both injuries, the single-bone fracture (ulna in Monteggia, radius in Galeazzi) destabilises the parallel forearm bone's joint (proximal radioulnar/radiocapitellar in Monteggia; distal radioulnar in Galeazzi), producing the characteristic combined fracture-dislocation pattern.

(a)
• Definition: the trophic affection of joints, developing frequently in weight-bearing joints.
• Aetiology: tabes dorsalis, syringomyelia, diabetic neuropathy, or alcohol neuropathy.
• Clinical features: trophic changes develop in weight-bearing joints, resulting in destruction of the joint.
• Further clinical feature: genitourinary manifestations of dysuria and pyouria have been noted.
• Investigations: X-ray shows marked destruction of the joint, sclerosis, and fragmentation.

(b)
• Effect on function: the affected weight-bearing joint (hip, knee, ankle or spine) becomes progressively destroyed, impairing weight-bearing and mobility.
• Function is further affected by the accompanying genitourinary symptoms of the underlying neuropathic disease.

(c)
• Conservative management: symptomatic — rest, analgesics and NSAIDs, and antibiotics.
• Surgical management (general): arthrodesis is the surgical procedure of choice.
• Surgical management (regional): osteotomy or reconstruction for a destroyed femoral head/neck at the hip; arthrodesis for the knee, with postoperative immobilization in a POP spica for 2-3 months and a knee brace for a year; arthrodesis, or talectomy plus tibiocalcaneal arthrodesis for a markedly destroyed avascular talus, at the ankle; and arthrodesis for the spine.
• Rehabilitation/physiotherapy management: muscle-strengthening exercises (active and passive), traction, heat therapy (SWD/IRR), and wax bath therapy.
• Further rehabilitation: hydrotherapy, massage (stroking, compression), ambulation aids, and acupuncture/acupressure and yoga therapy.
questions.question:
(a) Describe Charcot's joint under the headings of definition, aetiology, clinical features and investigations.
(b) Explain how it affects function.
(c) Outline the conservative, surgical and rehabilitation (physiotherapy) management.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Structure/joint involved: Epiphysitis affecting the epiphysis of one single or multiple vertebrae in the thoracic region, commoner in boys aged 10-15 years, of unknown, genetic, or traumatic (sports trauma) etiology.

(b)
Deformity: Kyphosis (round) of the thoracic spine, compensated by lordosis of the lumbar spine below it, and round shoulders; local tenderness; pain on walking/running.

(c)
Clinical reasoning for the physiotherapy plan: As surgical treatment is rarely indicated, management is conservative - bedrest, analgesics/NSAIDs, diathermy (SWD, infrared, wax bath), a brace, and active exercise - with physiotherapy progressing assisted passive exercises by the physiotherapist to free active exercises by the patient.
questions.question:
An adolescent presents with pain and a round (kyphotic) deformity of the thoracic spine compensated by lordosis of the lumbar spine and round shoulders, with local tenderness and pain on walking; X-ray shows irregular anterosuperior and anteroinferior angles of the vertebral bodies at the site of the normal epiphysis.
(a) What structure/joint is involved?
(b) What is the deformity present?
(c) What is the clinical reasoning for the physiotherapy plan?

(a) Define hallux valgus.
(b) State the aetiology.
(c) Describe the pathogenesis/deformity.
(d) Describe the clinical diagnosis and investigations.
(e) Explain how hallux valgus affects function.
(f) Outline the conservative, surgical, and rehabilitation management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Definition: a deformity of the foot characterized by valgus of the phalanges of the great toe with an angulated metatarsophalangeal joint, a medially prominent first metatarsal head (the 'bunion'), and varus of the first metatarsal.

(b)
Aetiology: congenital, traumatic, or inflammatory.

(c)
Pathogenesis/deformity: abducted big toe, often with an associated hammer toe of the second toe.

(d)
Diagnosis: agonizing pain; swelling (bunion) over the first metatarsophalangeal joint; local tenderness; difficulty wearing shoes; difficulty running and brisk walking. Investigation: X-ray shows osteophytic outgrowths and malalignment of the bones.

(e)
Effect on function: pain and deformity impair shoe wearing, running, and brisk walking.

(f)
• Conservative treatment: generally unsatisfactory, involving low-heeled, wide-fronted shoes with straight inner borders.
• Surgical treatment is the treatment of choice, indicated for marked discomfort and gross deformity: the Keller operation excises the base of the proximal phalanx, augmented by osteotomy of the base of the first metatarsal; the McBride operation, for middle-aged and younger patients with moderate deformity, frees the adductor hallucis tendon and reattaches it to the first metatarsal.
• The Lapidus operation corrects varus of the first metatarsal and narrows the wide angle at the bases of the first and second metatarsals; the Duncan McKeever operation performs arthrodesis of the first metatarsophalangeal joint.
• Postoperative care: after the Keller operation, fixation is removed after 2 weeks and partial walking increased gradually in a modified shoe with arch support for 6 months; after the McBride operation, partial weight bearing on the heel is allowed after 2 weeks; after the Lapidus operation, a corset stay holds the toe in position for 4 weeks then wide shoes for 6 weeks; after the Duncan McKeever operation, weight bearing in a hallux valgus splint shoe is permitted after 1 week.
• Rehabilitation in conservative cases: the physiotherapist helps with intrinsic muscle strengthening (especially adductor hallucis) and gives advice on suitable footwear and correct gait.
• In surgical cases, postoperative physiotherapy includes strengthening intrinsic muscles and walking re-education.
• Footwear advice throughout emphasizes well-fitting, comfortable shoes with a straight inner side and a snugly fitting upper edge.

(a)
Patella fracture.

(b)
The patella - a hard triangular bone in an exposed position in front of the knee joint, separated from the skin by a subcutaneous bursa, influenced by the line of pull of the quadriceps and its attachment to the tibial tubercle via the patellar tendon; caused by compressive forces (direct blow on the knee, fall on the knee cap, car collision) or a sudden tensile force on knee hyperflexion.

(c)
Undisplaced fracture; displaced fracture (transverse, lower pole, comminuted, osteochondral, vertical); open fracture.

(d)
The subcutaneous location renders the patella vulnerable to fracture; because the patella improves the efficiency of knee extension during the last 30 degrees of extension and acts as a bony shield for the femoral condyle cartilage, disruption produces inability to extend the knee/perform a straight leg raise, intra-articular effusion and haemarthrosis.

(e)
Early weight bearing as tolerated with crutches or a walker, performed with the knee fully extended; splinting of the knee with a knee immobiliser or hinged brace locked in extension while weight bearing; active, active-assisted and gravity-assisted flexion initiated while sitting, with heel slides in supine; isometric quadriceps strengthening as soon as comfort allows, and active extension against gravity in the early postoperative period; resistive exercises in extension are delayed until the extensor mechanism has healed (6-12 weeks), and passive range of motion for flexion is delayed until the fracture and soft tissue repair are healed.
questions.question:
A cyclist falls directly onto the knee cap. Examination shows a palpable defect at the knee, with inability to extend the knee or perform a straight leg raise.
(a) Identify the structure/lesion involved.
(b) State the structures affected.
(c) List the differential fracture patterns (classification).
(d) Discuss the clinico-anatomical and functional reasoning for the presentation.
(e) State the physiotherapy management priorities.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Burst fracture of the thoracolumbar spine.

(b)
Failure of the anterior and middle columns of the spine due to axial loading; the entire vertebra is evenly crushed, often with retropulsion of bone fragments into the spinal canal; the concentration of axial forces occurs at the thoracolumbar junction, and 60-70% of thoracolumbar fractures occur in the T11-L2 region, which is biomechanically weak for stress.

(c)
In all suspected spinal injuries, assume the spinal cord is injured until proven otherwise; move the patient as little as possible until an X-ray rules out a fracture; postural reduction is required for thoracolumbar injuries.

(d)
Below L2, compression fractures are treated conservatively while fracture-dislocations require open reduction and internal fixation with Harrington instruments; in difficult cases or with gross displacement, internal fixation with Harrington rods is used.
questions.question:
A construction worker falls from a height and lands in a seated position. He complains of severe back pain at the thoracolumbar junction.
(a) State the most likely diagnosis.
(b) Explain the pathological/biomechanical basis (mechanism of injury).
(c) Outline the acute management and immobilisation.
(d) Outline the definitive conservative or surgical treatment.

A mountain climber presents with a reducible swelling over the belly of the arm muscle that decreases or disappears on muscle contraction, with pain on exertion, fatigue and disability.
(a) What structure or joint is involved?
(b) What is the resulting deformity or functional impairment?
(c) What are the differential diagnoses?
(d) What is the clinical reasoning for the physiotherapy plan?
questions.answerText:
(a)
Structure involved: the biceps brachii tendon, dislocating from the intertubercular groove.

(b)
Functional impairment: swelling over the belly of the muscle, commonly over the intertubercular groove, reducible and decreasing in size or disappearing on muscle contraction; pain on exertion; fatigue; disability.

(c)
Differential diagnoses: torn muscle (a gap appears between the two torn segments on muscle contraction); varicose veins; angiomas.

(d)
Clinical reasoning: management is required only when symptoms are severe and disabling, so conservative treatment (avoiding strenuous activity/exertion, analgesics/NSAIDs, elastic support) is reasoned as first-line; when surgery (fixation of the tendon in the intertubercular groove) is performed, physiotherapy follows postoperative immobilization by an arm pouch or sling for 2 weeks, with heat therapy (SWD/IRR or heating pad therapy) and, as pain subsides, active exercises for joint movement and muscle strengthening.

questions.question:
An infant presents with a hypoplastic, misshapen scapula lying more superiorly than normal, restricted abduction movement, and the head tilted towards the affected side.
(a) What is the diagnosis?
(b) What are the predisposing factors and pathophysiology?
(c) What is the medical/surgical management?
(d) What is the physiotherapy management?
questions.answerText:
(a)
Diagnosis: congenital elevation of the scapula (Sprengel's deformity).

(b)
Predisposing factors: aetiology unknown. Pathophysiology: hypoplastic and misshapen scapula lying superiorly in relation to the thoracic cage; in the severe form the scapula is very small and highly elevated with the inferior angle internally rotated.

(c)
Management: mild deformity and disability require no treatment. Severe deformity and disability require surgical treatment: release of muscles or excision of the scapula (for cosmetic factor); physiotherapy is continued regularly for a couple of months.

(d)
Physiotherapy management: providing passive stretching and positioning the baby to correct the deformity; teaching the mother how to perform passive stretching, hold the baby, and position the baby in the cot; the physiotherapist continues observation until satisfied the process is carried out properly, and monitors the baby at regular intervals until no further treatment is required.

questions.question:
A young athlete sustains a high-energy injury to the ankle during a sporting activity, presenting with foot oedema, ankle deformity and joint tenderness.
(a) State the risk factors for this condition.
(b) Outline the possible complications.
(c) Discuss the conservative and surgical management options and justify one option for this patient.
questions.answerText:
(a)
High-energy injury; occurs with associated fractures; the ankle is normally a very stable joint because of the stability of the tibiotalar joint, so dislocation reflects the severity of the causative force.

(b)
Chronically painful and unstable ankle; avascular necrosis of the talus; nerve injury and damage; foot necrosis and gangrene.

(c)
Management may be conservative or surgical; surgical stabilisation is justified for this high-energy sporting injury because the described rehabilitation protocol is a post-operative programme - ankle isometrics in a boot splint with no range-of-motion exercises until after 4 weeks, gait training with crutches, followed by partial and then full weight bearing, joint mobilisations, strengthening/balance work, and sport-specific training from week 12 onward.

(a)
Displaced femoral neck fracture (Garden type III or IV).

(b)
Femoral neck fracture usually occurs with minor falls or twisting injuries in the elderly; it results from low-energy trauma acting on bone weakened by osteoporosis, poor physical conditioning, malnutrition, impaired vision, neurologic disease and poor balance. Displacement of the fracture fragments disrupts the vascular supply attached to the femoral neck, raising the risk of avascular necrosis from 7% to 37%.

(c)
Analgesia; protection, rest, ice, compression and elevation; the limb is kept non-weight bearing; realignment (reduction) of the displaced fragments; immobilisation of the joints above and below the fracture (e.g. traction) pending definitive treatment.

(d)
Hip and thighbone fractures are known to heal more rapidly and have a better outcome when surgically repaired; internal fixation (open reduction and internal fixation) restores the bone's shape and alignment; joint replacement (arthroplasty) may be needed when the fracture severely damages the upper end of the femur; surgery allows earlier walking and return to daily activity than prolonged bed rest.
questions.question:
A 68-year-old woman presents after a fall at home. She is unable to bear weight on the right leg, which lies shortened and externally rotated at the hip, and she complains of groin pain.
(a) State the most likely diagnosis.
(b) Explain the pathological/biomechanical basis (mechanism of injury) of this condition.
(c) Outline the acute management and immobilisation of this patient.
(d) Outline the definitive conservative or surgical treatment of this condition.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Galeazzi fracture - fractured radius with dislocation of the distal radioulnar joint; more common than the Monteggia fracture.

(b)
Caused by a fall on an outstretched hand, usually with a rotation force; the radius fractures in its lower third and the inferior radio-ulnar joint subluxates or dislocates.

(c)
Conservative treatment in children; open reduction and internal fixation in adults.
questions.question:
A patient falls on an outstretched hand with a rotational force and presents with prominence and tenderness over the lower end of the ulna, and pain with laxity of the radio-ulnar joint on wrist rotation.
(a) State the most likely diagnosis.
(b) Explain the pathological/biomechanical basis (mechanism of injury).
(c) Outline the definitive conservative or surgical treatment.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Pathology: osteogenesis imperfecta is a genetic collagen mutation that manifests with fragile bones.
• Severity spectrum, severe forms: babies are born with multiple fractures.
• Severity spectrum, mild forms: the condition may not be detected until later in childhood, after the child begins walking, presenting as a fracture resulting from an insignificant injury.
• Diagnosis: Type I collagen and DNA tests help differentiate osteogenesis imperfecta from abuse.

(b)
• Relation to recurrent fracture: because the underlying collagen defect makes bone fragile, the child sustains fractures from insignificant injury, and medical management is symptomatic rather than curative.
• Relation to bone bowing: surgery (most frequently internal fixation of long bones) aims to minimise the incidence of fracture and avoid bone bowing, which compounds bone stress; this is especially beneficial in children with marked bowing and frequent fracture.

(c)
• Spread to skeletal deformity/impaired ambulation: repeated fracture and progressive bowing of long bones compound bone stress, creating a cycle in which deformed bone is more prone to further fracture and mechanical stress during weight bearing and ambulation.
• Continued: bisphosphonate drugs are taken for weeks to months to be effective, improving bone density, reducing bone pain, and improving ambulation potential - indicating that untreated disease affects the child's ability to bear weight and ambulate normally.
• Continued: internal fixation of long bones is specifically used to prevent this bowing-fracture cycle from progressively worsening skeletal alignment and function.

(d)
• Physiotherapy management: provides the caregiver/older child with information on safety and prevention of recurrent fractures, including avoiding rough-house play and contact sports.
• Continued: plans and instructs the child in an aggressive yet safe exercise and standing programme to help the child develop strength and endurance.
• Continued: aims to maintain or increase range of motion, and to promote bone mineralisation through weight bearing; provides consultation for braces and adaptive equipment selection.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the pathology of osteogenesis imperfecta and its severity spectrum.
(b) State how this relates to recurrent fracture and bone bowing.
(c) Explain how the condition may spread its effect to cause skeletal deformity and impaired ambulation.
(d) Outline the physiotherapy management.

(a) State the mechanism of injury to the medial meniscus of the knee.
(b) State the types of this injury.
(c) State the deformity/clinical findings produced.
(d) State the investigation used.
(e) State the management principles for this injury.
(f) Explain the physiotherapy management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Mechanism (context): Traumatic injury to the medial meniscus is the commonest cause of internal derangement of the knee joint.
• Mechanism (detail): The flexed knee is subjected to rotational and abduction strain from a road/street accident or sports injury (especially footballers); the knee momentarily opens up on the medial side, and the meniscus is sucked inside and nipped between the condyles of femur and tibia, resulting in a tear.

(b)
• Types: Tear, rupture, or vertical splitting of the medial meniscus.
• Types (continued): Repeated strains lead to a "bucket handle" tear, and the torn meniscus becomes displaced.

(c)
• Clinical findings: Usually a footballer; history of locking of the knee followed by sudden unlocking and effusion.
• Clinical findings (continued): Local tenderness; McMurray's test positive.

(d)
Investigation: X-ray of the knee (AP and lateral views) to rule out any bony lesion.

(e)
• Management principles (conservative): Rest, analgesics, elastic crepe bandage or knee cap, SWD/IRR, and local massage.
• Management principles (surgical): Meniscectomy.

(f)
• Physiotherapy management: Assisted passive exercises by the physiotherapist.
• Physiotherapy management (continued): Progressed to free active exercises by the patient.

questions.question:
Describe displacement of the peroneal tendons under the following headings:
(a) Mechanism/aetiology
(b) Types/pathogenesis
(c) Deformity
(d) Management principles
(e) Physiotherapy management at each stage
questions.answerText:
(a)
Mechanism/aetiology: congenital (a congenitally shallow groove of the lateral malleolus, or total absence of the groove); direct trauma (violence/blow); sports injury (common amongst mountain climbers, skiers, marchers, athletes); repetitive strain activity.

(b)
Types/pathogenesis: mechanical impairment with loss of fulcrum pull - on contraction, the tendons/muscle fibers dislocate from their normal position on the posterior aspect of the lateral malleolus to lie over the lateral aspect of the distal third of the fibula.

(c)
• Deformity/clinical signs: swelling of the ankle, over its lateral aspect, large or small; pain on exertion; fatigue; disability.
• Differential diagnosis: torn muscle (a gap appears between torn segments on contraction); varicose veins; angiomas.

(d)
• Management principle, conservative (when symptoms are severe and disabling): avoidance of strenuous physical activity/exertion; analgesics/NSAIDs; elastic support.
• Management principle, surgical (treatment of choice): reconstruction, with postoperative immobilization by a POP cast above the ankle with the ankle at 90 degrees for 1 month; walking allowed after 1 month.

(e)
• Physiotherapy management, stage 1 (during immobilization): heat therapy (SWD/IRR or heating pad therapy).
• Physiotherapy management, stage 2 (as pain subsides): active exercises for joint movement.
• Physiotherapy management, stage 3: active exercises for muscle strengthening.

(a)
• Mechanism: commonly known as an acceleration-deceleration cervical injury; results from sharp hyperextension and flexion of the neck that damages muscles, ligaments, discs and nerve tissue.
• Continued: commonly results from rear-end automobile accidents.
• Types: padded headrests, air bags and seat belts with shoulder harnesses now common in cars have reduced the incidence of this type of traumatic injury.
• Clinical features: symptoms are often delayed 12-24 hours if the injury is mild; produces moderate to severe anterior and posterior neck pain; within several days the anterior pain diminishes but the posterior pain persists or intensifies; may also cause dizziness, gait disturbance, vomiting, headache, nuchal rigidity, neck muscle asymmetry, and rigidity or numbness in the arms.
• Complications: full cervical spine X-rays are required to rule out cervical fracture; if X-rays are negative, examination focuses on motor ability and sensation below the cervical spine to detect nerve root compression.

(b)
• Precautions: in all suspected spinal injuries assume the spinal cord is injured until proven otherwise, and any patient with suspected whiplash requires careful transportation; until an X-ray rules out a cervical fracture, move the patient as little as possible.
• Continued: before evaluating the cervical region, test the alar and transverse ligaments for possible laxity; do not proceed with range-of-motion exercises if laxity is found.
• Continued: use cervical collars for a short period of time only, to ensure the affected area does not heal in a faulty position.
• Continued: use massage and muscle-setting techniques to maintain circulation and promote relaxation; if muscle guarding is found, do not perform stretching.

(c)
• Biomechanical basis: the injury results from sharp hyperextension and flexion of the neck, i.e. the head continues moving relative to the sudden deceleration/acceleration of the torso.
• Continued: this rapid, forced hyperextension-then-flexion sequence damages the muscles, ligaments, discs and nerve tissue of the cervical spine without necessarily producing a visible fracture, which is why the prognosis for whiplash is generally excellent, with symptoms usually subsiding with treatment.
• Continued: the delay in symptom onset (12-24 hours in mild injury) reflects the soft-tissue nature of the damage, as inflammatory swelling develops after the initial biomechanical insult.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the mechanism, types, clinical features and complications of whiplash injury.
(b) State the precautions regarding the use of cervical collars and range-of-motion exercise.
(c) Explain the biomechanical basis of the hyperextension-flexion injury pattern.

A young woman presents with symmetrical bilateral pallor and cyanosis of the fingers followed by bright redness on exposure to cold.
(a) What is the diagnosis?
(b) What are the predisposing factors and pathophysiology?
(c) What is the medical and surgical management?
(d) What is the physiotherapy management?
questions.answerText:
(a)
Raynaud's disease.

(b)
A vasomotor disorder characterized by intermittent spasm of the digital arterioles; common among women; affects the upper limbs more than the lower; peripheral pulses remain normal; attributable to abnormal sensitivity in the direct response of the arterioles to cold. Aetiology: cold exposure. Pathogenesis, during attack: cold exposure causes abrupt spasm of arterioles, metabolite accumulation in the capillary circulation, dilated capillaries filled with slowly flowing deoxygenated blood, a swollen dusky part, obliterative changes in peripheral vessels, necrosis, and dry gangrene; post-attack: relaxed arterioles, dilated capillaries filled with oxygenated blood, and reddish hands.

(c)
Conservative: protection from cold (wearing gloves), keeping the body warm, avoiding pulp and nailbed infections, avoiding smoking, vasodilator drugs (reserpine, methyldopa, papaverine). Surgical: sympathectomy (preganglionic section of the thoracic sympathetic chain), indicated for severe attacks.

(d)
Physiotherapy management: active exercises to increase circulation flow; contrast baths - the physiotherapist instructs the patient to immerse hands or feet in a hot bath for 3 minutes then a cool bath for 1 minute, to accelerate peripheral blood flow; connective tissue massage, beginning with the sacral and lumbar area followed by the limbs, may provide symptomatic improvement.

(a)
Diagnosis: Kohler's disease (also known as Freiberg's disease).

(b)
Predisposing factors: aetiology unknown. Pathophysiology: degenerative changes occurring in the head of the second or third metatarsal.

(c)
Management: conservative treatment with analgesics (paracetamol, NSAIDs) and avoiding narrow-toed shoes. Surgical treatment is the treatment of choice: excision of the metatarsal head, or remodeling the head and excising the proximal half of the proximal phalanx; weight bearing is permitted after 1 week postoperatively.

(d)
Physiotherapy management: corrective/protective orthosis (hallux valgus splint).

questions.answerText:
(a)
Mechanism at the elbow: supracondylar fractures of the humerus in children, fractures of the medial epicondyle, dislocations of the elbow, Monteggia fracture-dislocation, direct trauma, road/street accident, operative excision of the elbow, or cubitus valgus deformity (tardy palsy). At the wrist: cuts, fractures of the lower radius (Colles fracture).

(b)
Types: acute ulnar nerve division at the elbow or wrist, and tardy (delayed) ulnar nerve palsy from increased carrying angle (cubitus valgus) stretching the nerve in its groove behind the medial epicondyle.

(c)
Deformity: claw hand, i.e. clawing of the little and ring fingers.

(d)
Complications: muscular wasting of the hypothenar eminence and intermetacarpal spaces; paralysis of flexor carpi ulnaris and the medial half of flexor digitorum profundus, plus the short muscles of the hand; sensory loss of muscle pain, joint sense, pressure sense, and cutaneous sensation (little finger); skin cold, glazed, smooth.

(e)
Healing: results of suturing are usually unsatisfactory for acute division; tardy palsy managed by anterior transposition addresses the ongoing mechanical stretch.

(f)
• Management principles: conservative treatment with immobilization in a universal arm pouch, analgesics/NSAIDs, and physiotherapy exercises. Surgical treatment for compression from fracture-dislocation or wounds involves exploration and suturing of the nerve ends. Tardy ulnar palsy is managed by anterior transposition of the ulnar nerve in front of the medial epicondyle.
• Testing: interossei tested by spreading/closing fingers, straightening the 2nd and 3rd phalanges, and the card test; adductor pollicis and first palmar interosseous tested by grasping a book (terminal phalanx of thumb flexes immediately in ulnar palsy) and gripping a card between thumb and palm.
• Investigation also includes electrical stimulation in situ and Tinel's sign, elicited after a couple of months by tapping over the nerve course from below upward until tingling is felt, the level shifting distally as regeneration progresses.

(g)
• Physiotherapy after acute nerve suturing: postoperative POP cast for about 4 to 6 weeks, stitches removed after 2 days through a window in the cast, followed by exercises and occupational therapy.
• Physiotherapy after anterior transposition for tardy ulnar palsy: postoperative POP cast for about 4 to 6 weeks, stitches removed after 2 days, followed by exercises and occupational therapy.
• Physiotherapy management overall may not require extensive treatment as recovery is likely within a few weeks in many cases, with advice on movement and reassurance about recovery being important.
• Factors affecting outcome include the nerve injured, infection, time to secondary suture, muscle tone maintenance, operative technique, and postoperative cooperation and vicarious movements.

A young adult presents with a localized bulging swelling near the end of a long bone, with pain, local tenderness, painful restricted movement of the adjoining joint, and muscular weakness and wasting; a pathological fracture has occurred through the lesion.
(a) What is the diagnosis?
(b) Describe the mechanism of the underlying pathology.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Diagnosis: Aneurysmal bone cyst, a localized bulging mass covered by a thin, often incomplete shell of bone, occurring most often in the large long bones and occasionally the flat bones and vertebrae, located nearer one end than the middle of the shaft.

(b)
Mechanism: aetiology is uncertain, possibly vascular disorders (hemorrhage, venous dilatations) or trauma (parosteal myositis ossificans); a thin bone shell forms the outer surface while the interior is loculated by connective tissue septa forming lakes of dark blood that oozes profusely without pulsation, with variable ossification and localized giant cell reaction within the septa, and pathological fracture.

(c)
Clinical features/assessment: pain, swelling, local tenderness, painful restricted movement of the adjoining joint, muscular weakness and wasting, and pathological fracture; X-rays show a localized bulging mass with a thin bone shell, striking heavy trabeculations or loculation and slight irregular cortical erosion; needle aspiration biopsy is done to rule out malignancy.

(d)
Conservative management: analgesics and NSAIDs, and warm fomentation, SWD or IR therapy.

(e)
Definitive treatment: surgery, indicated on failure of conservative treatment, comprising curettage of lesions in long bones or excision of expanded vertebral lesions with adjoining involved tissue, followed by physiotherapy exercises as aftercare.

(a)
Definition: Chondromalacia of the patella is degeneration of its articular cartilage; it usually results in osteoarthritis of the knee joint, the patellofemoral joint usually being the first joint in the body to undergo degenerative changes.

(b)
Causes/etiology: Direct trauma (violence), recurrent subluxation or dislocation of the patella, fractured patella, or internal derangement of the knee; predisposing factors are obesity and a disturbed quadriceps mechanism (knee lockings).

(c)
Clinical features: Deep-seated subpatellar pain; swelling; local tenderness; crepitus; locking of the knee; movements of the knee and patella painful and restricted.

(d)
Investigation: X-rays of the knee (AP and lateral views), which may show fracture, dislocation, or degenerative changes.

(e)
Complications: Degeneration of the articular cartilage frequently results in osteoarthritis of the knee joint, with the joint becoming arthritic and ankylosed.

(f)
• Distinguishing feature - pathology: Chondromalacia of the patella is a degeneration of the articular cartilage of the patella, whereas osteochondritis of the patella is an avascular necrosis of the bone with degeneration and loose body formation.
• Distinguishing feature - etiology: Chondromalacia of the patella arises from direct trauma, recurrent subluxation/dislocation, fractured patella, or internal derangement of the knee, with obesity and disturbed quadriceps mechanism as predisposing factors; osteochondritis of the patella arises traumatically from fracture or fracture-dislocation, or degeneratively from osteoarthritis.
• Distinguishing feature - site: Osteochondritis of the patella is usually found anywhere on the patella, especially its femoral surface, whereas chondromalacia of the patella affects the articular cartilage of the patellofemoral joint generally.
• Distinguishing feature - investigation findings: Chondromalacia of the patella may show fracture, dislocation, or degenerative changes on X-ray, whereas osteochondritis of the patella shows a loose body or bodies on X-ray of the knee joint.
• Distinguishing feature - surgical management: Chondromalacia of the patella is managed surgically (for internal derangement of the knee or arthritic lesions) by exploration of the knee joint, shaving of the involved cartilage, arthroplasty, or patellectomy/patelloplasty; osteochondritis of the patella is managed surgically by excision of the osteochondritic lesion and removal of loose bodies, for a detached osteochondritic area.
• Distinguishing feature - after care: Chondromalacia of the patella after care includes an elastic crepe bandage for 1 week and quadriceps/hamstring exercises with early weight bearing using crutches, whereas osteochondritis of the patella after care is post-operative immobilization for 2-3 weeks followed by physiotherapy.
• Distinguishing feature - predisposing factors: chondromalacia of the patella is associated with obesity and a disturbed quadriceps mechanism, whereas osteochondritis of the patella has a traumatic or degenerative aetiology.

Regarding infective (septic) arthritis:
(a) What is the mechanism of spread of infection to the joint?
(b) What types of transmission and organisms are involved?
(c) What deformity/joint destruction results?
(d) What are the complications?
(e) How does management/healing proceed?
(f) What are the management principles?
(g) Explain the physiotherapy management at each stage.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Mechanism: direct spread (compound fractures involving the joint, penetrating wounds, operations, or diagnostic procedures such as intra-articular aspiration/injection).
• Further mechanism: local extension from a neighbouring focus (e.g. osteomyelitis of the femoral neck), or indirect haematogenous spread (bacteraemia/septicaemia from an infective focus in the skin, upper respiratory tract or genitourinary tract).

(b)
• Types of transmission: primary (direct intrusion of microorganisms into the joint) or secondary (haematogenous, through the bloodstream, mostly via the arteries).
• Types of organisms: bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites, as listed under aetiology; pathogenesis varies with the patient's age, and in infants and children a metaphyseal abscess forms and enters the joint, causing partial or complete destruction of the articular cartilage.

(c)
Deformity/joint destruction: ankylosis (fibrous or bony), from partial or complete destruction of the articular cartilage.

(d)
• Complications: chronic arthritis (from delayed diagnosis or inadequate early treatment), soft tissue abscess formation, and persistent infection.
• Further complications: pathological fracture at the site of extensive bone necrosis, and pathological dislocation of the hip.

(e)
Healing/course: early mobilization is mandatory to prevent muscle atrophy and joint stiffness once the inflammation is resolving.

(f)
• Management principles (conservative): bedrest, immobilization by traction or splint, elevation of the part, warm fomentation, antibiotics, and analgesics/fluids orally or intravenously.
• Management principles (surgical): aspiration of the joint, and incision and drainage.

(g)
• Physiotherapy management: joint rest by splints or traction, isometric exercises of the muscles surrounding the affected joint during the resolving phase of inflammation, and non-weight-bearing free active exercises through full range.
• Further physiotherapy: gait re-education, mandatory initially with crutches for partial weight-bearing, progressing to walking sticks once pain has diminished, and early mobilization.

(a)
Diagnosis: median nerve injury at the wrist.

(b)
Mechanism: trauma at the wrist including cuts, blow, gunshot injury, Colles fracture of the lower end of the radius, dislocation of the semilunar bone, or carpal tunnel syndrome; pronator teres, flexor carpi radialis, palmaris longus, flexor digitorum sublimis, flexor pollicis longus, the lateral half of flexor digitorum profundus, and pronator quadratus, plus the thenar muscles, are paralysed by stretching or severing of the nerve.

(c)
Features: 'ape thumb' deformity; thenar eminence wasting; flexor carpi radialis paralysis causing ulnar deviation of the hand on resisted flexion; flexor pollicis longus paralysis with inability to flex the terminal phalanx of the thumb; sensory loss at the thumb, index and middle finger tips; trophic changes in the terminal phalanx of the index finger. Assessment: pen test (unable to touch a pen held above the thumb with the hand flat, palm up), opponens test (unable to touch each fingertip with the thumb tip), electrical stimulation, and Tinel's sign.

(d)
Conservative treatment: immobilization in a universal arm pouch, analgesics/NSAIDs, and physiotherapy exercises.

(e)
Surgical treatment: exploration and suturing for compression from fracture-dislocation or wounds; carpal tunnel decompression for unrelieved carpal tunnel symptoms; excision of the lunate (with or without prosthetic replacement) for avascular necrosis with median nerve compression; postoperative POP cast for about 4 to 6 weeks, stitches removed after 2 days, followed by exercises and occupational therapy.

A patient presents with pain, local tenderness, and painful, restricted movements of the hip, with difficulty in walking. An X-ray of the pelvis shows a loose body within the joint, with the weight-bearing area of the femoral head involved.
(a) What are the risk factors for this condition?
(b) What are the late complications of this condition?
(c) Discuss the management options, conservative versus surgical, and justify one approach.
(d) What is the physiotherapy role?
questions.answerText:
(a)
Risk factors: Traumatic - intra-articular fracture; degenerative - osteoarthritis.

(b)
Complications: Late - without treatment, the area collapses and osteoarthritis develops.

(c)
Management options: Conservative - weight bearing restricted (may help revascularization of the avascular bone and preservation of the overlying cartilage), immobilization by traction, and walking with crutches without weight-bearing on the affected leg. Surgical - drilling (small lesion) to restore revascularization, drilling with cancellous bone packing (large lesion) to maintain the contour of the articular surface, or excision of the osteochondritic lesion with removal of loose bodies (detached area), followed by immobilization for 2-3 weeks and physiotherapy. Surgical treatment is justified once the osteochondritic area is detached, since conservative measures alone cannot remove an already-separated fragment.

(d)
Physiotherapy role: Assisted passive exercises by the physiotherapist progressed to free active exercises by the patient.

(a)
Definition/classification: vein thrombosis is classified as superficial (thrombophlebitis) and deep vein thrombosis (phlebothrombosis); DVT shows minimal inflammatory element with a soft, loose thrombus.

(b)
• Aetiology: traumatic, surgical (postoperative immobility), sedentary physical inactivity, childbirth, debilitating illness (typhoid fever), cardiovascular disease (hypertension, MI, CHF), stroke, and metabolic causes. Predisposing factors: age, infection, obesity, prolonged immobilization, anaemia, dehydration, shock, IV drug use, and venous obstruction.
• Pathogenesis follows Virchow's triad: vessel wall trauma, venous stasis, and hypercoagulation.

(c)
Clinical features: early stages symptomless; dull ache, tight feeling or frank pain increased on exertion; swollen calf; distended peripheral veins; local tenderness; fever; rising pulse rate; positive Homans sign; a tender, hard, cord-like vein; pale or cyanotic, cool skin.

(d)
Investigations: CBC, ESR, blood sugar, ultrasound, Color Doppler (venous), chest X-ray, MRI.

(e)
Complications: pulmonary embolism obstructing pulmonary circulation with lung infarction, and chronic venous insufficiency.

(f)
• Differentiation: DVT has minimal inflammatory element with a soft, loose thrombus more prone to detaching and embolizing.
• Superficial thrombophlebitis instead forms a hard thrombus firmly adherent to the venous wall, presenting as an indurated, red, tender, cord-like vein (often the long saphenous vein), usually without constitutional reaction, and anticoagulants are usually not indicated for it.

(g)
• Preventive management for DVT: better than cure; during surgery legs are well-padded, stockinged, and elevated by about 20 degrees; postoperatively legs are massaged and exercised.
• Medical management: adequate hydration, analgesics/NSAIDs, anticoagulants (oral aspirin/warfarin or parenteral heparin/LMWH) continued for 10 days, and thrombolytics (urokinase or streptokinase) where indicated.
• Surgical treatment: indicated when thrombus becomes detached (rare), via ligation of the femoral vein (when anticoagulants are contraindicated) or thrombectomy/embolectomy (when conservative measures fail).
• Physiotherapy management: exercises with legs raised while remaining ambulant to maintain venous circulation.

(a)
High-speed trauma is the paramount cause - high-speed driving, falls or jumps from significant height, gunshot wounds to the lower leg; the tibia is subcutaneous, so the incidence of open fracture is high.

(b)
Graded by the Gustilo and Anderson classification (Type I: wound less than 1cm, minimal contamination and soft tissue injury; Type II: wound 1-10cm, moderate contamination/comminution; Type III: periosteal stripping and soft tissue coverage required, may need vessel repair); infection rates rise with grade (0-2% Type I up to 25-50% Type III); internal bleeding can lead to compartment syndrome due to the compartmental anatomy of the lower leg; reduced blood supply in the distal third predisposes to delayed union and non-union.

(c)
Gustilo Type I injuries can be treated the same way as a comparable closed fracture; operative fixation is required when fractures are unstable, with options including plating, external fixation, intramedullary nailing and, in severe cases, amputation. Surgical debridement and fixation is justified for this open fracture because thorough operative debridement is the standard of care for all open fractures, restores length, alignment and rotation, provides an ideal environment for soft-tissue healing, reduces wound infection and dead space, and reduces the inflammatory response.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Definition/classification: bone tuberculosis is one of the forms of extrapulmonary tuberculosis, an inflammation of bones and joints due to Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection; it is a slow, unrelenting manifestation of systemic disease, mostly secondary to a primary focus in the respiratory or gastrointestinal tract, affecting above all the spine, long bones and joints.
• Aetiology and transmission: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (acid-fast); hematogenous spread from a primary focus.
• Pathogenesis: tuberculous osteitis originates in the cancellous bone by lodging of blood-borne bacilli, mostly at the ends of long bones (intra-articular), resulting in tuberculous arthritis (except Pott's disease of the spine), with subperiosteal abscess and discharging sinus formation.
• Clinical features: insidious onset and course; affects ends of long bones and short bones of hand and feet; dull aching pain; swelling of the bone; weakness; shiny pale skin; thickened periosteum due to edema, with possible subperiosteal abscess; pathognomonic sinuses.
• Investigations: CBC, ESR; sputum tests for active tuberculosis (smear microscopy for acid- and alcohol-fast bacilli, nucleic acid amplification test, culture); Mantoux test; Heaf test; synovial fluid/tissue exudate analysis for acid-fast bacilli; biopsy of the lesion or regional lymph node; X-ray showing bone destruction (caries) as rarefaction of bone with a cavity containing small sequestrae, with recalcification at the healing stage.
• Complications: cold abscess; sinus formation; paraplegia (in spinal tuberculosis).

(b)
Effect on function: the disease causes dull aching pain, bone swelling, weakness, and discharging sinuses, with paraplegia occurring in spinal involvement, so joint and bone function is progressively compromised.

(c)
• Conservative management: hygienic atmosphere and fresh air; bedrest; immobilization by splint or plaster; a balanced, nutritious diet; appropriate treatment of associated pulmonary, genitourinary or gastrointestinal lesions.
• Chemotherapy: systemic antitubercular agents in combination, including isoniazid (most effective, given with other agents), streptomycin (less effective, reserved for resistant organisms, may cause 8th cranial nerve injury), PAS, ethambutol (relatively safer, affects visual acuity, avoided in infants and young children), rifampicin, and pyrazinamide (toxic hepatitis).
• Surgical management: aspiration of the joint for early-stage synovitis; arthrotomy (biopsy, synovectomy, débridement, bone grafting) for subacute hypertrophic lesions; curettage or bone grafting for extra-articular bone lesions; excision of bones and joints for extensive sinuses and secondary infection; arthrodesis or amputation for extensive destruction of bone and cartilage; postoperative immobilization by a double hip spica with the hip in 40 degree abduction.
• Rehabilitation/physiotherapy management: assisted exercises provided by the physiotherapist.
• Additional note on the spinal form (tuberculous spondylitis/Pott's disease): perispinal or discharging cold abscesses of the spine may be palpable externally depending on size, involved vertebrae and adjoining structures, or produce pressure symptoms on the spinal cord or pharynx.

(a)
Definition: a deformity of the foot characterized by a transverse ridge or bar of bone at the anterior plantar edge of the calcaneal tuberosity, its sharp free edge mostly pointing towards the toes, developing at the attachment of the plantar fascia and extending into the fascia itself.

(b)
Aetiology: unknown.

(c)
Pathogenesis/types: plantar fasciitis developing into a spur; types are large but painless, large and painful, or rudimentary.

(d)
Diagnosis: pain, swelling, deformity, and disability with painful walking. Investigation: X-ray foot (AP and lateral views) shows a transverse ridge or bar of bone at the anterior plantar edge of the calcaneal tuberosity.

(e)
Effect on function: painful walking and disability, particularly with weight bearing on the affected heel.

(f)
• Conservative treatment: painless spurs require no treatment; painful spurs are managed with hot wet packs, infrared therapy, short-wave therapy, analgesics, NSAIDs, oral corticosteroids, and a sponge in the shoe heel.
• Surgical treatment: excision of the spur, indicated when pain is disabling and persistent despite conservative measures.
• Postoperative care: weight bearing is permitted after 2 weeks.
• Rehabilitation: walking supported with a sponge in the heel of the shoe.
• Alternatively, walking is supported with metatarsalgia gel support.
• These supportive measures are used both before surgery (as conservative care) and after surgery (as part of rehabilitation) to reduce pressure on the healing heel.
• Physiotherapy management for calcaneal spur follows the same supportive footwear approach used for related forefoot conditions such as plantar callosities and metatarsalgia.

Diagnosis: Acute suppurative (septic) arthritis, commonly affecting the knee or hip in a child.

(b)
Mechanism/pathology: infection reaches the joint directly (compound fracture, penetrating wound, operation, intra-articular aspiration or injection), by local extension from a neighbouring focus such as osteomyelitis of the femoral neck, or indirectly through the bloodstream from an infected focus in the skin, upper respiratory tract or genitourinary tract; in infants and children a metaphyseal abscess forms and enters the joint, destroying the articular cartilage partially or completely.

(c)
Clinical features/assessment findings: sudden onset, severe pain, fever with chills and prostration, swelling, hot red skin, local tenderness, and painful, restricted movement; confirmed by leukocytosis on CBC/TLC/DLC, raised ESR, positive blood culture, leukocytosis on synovial fluid analysis with organism on smear and culture, and X-ray that is normal early but later shows demineralization, bony erosion and narrowing of the joint space, followed by osteomyelitis and periostitis.

(d)
Immediate/conservative management: bedrest, immobilization of the joint by traction or splint, elevation of the part, warm fomentation, antibiotics, and analgesics and fluids given orally or intravenously.

(e)
Definitive treatment: aspiration of the joint, or incision and drainage.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Definition: Osgood-Schlatter disease (epiphysitis of the tibial tuberosity) is a disability characterized by pain, limping, an unduly prominent tibial tubercle, and restricted sports activities, mostly in boys between the ages of 10 and 15 years.
• Pathogenesis: The tibial epiphysis undergoes partial separation.

(b)
Causes/etiology: Unknown; genetic; traumatic (sports trauma); infective.

(c)
• Clinical features - demographics: Commoner in boys; age 10-15 years.
• Clinical features - presentation: Pain; deformity of a prominent tibial tubercle; local tenderness; walking/running painful.

(d)
Investigation: X-ray shows partial separation of the tongue-shaped portion of the epiphysis from the shaft.

(e)
• Distinguishing feature - site: Osgood-Schlatter disease affects the tibial tuberosity, producing a prominent tibial tubercle, whereas Sever's disease (apophysitis of the os calcis) affects the heel, producing a prominent heel.
• Distinguishing feature - pathogenesis: In Osgood-Schlatter disease the tibial epiphysis is partially separated, whereas in Sever's disease the epiphysis becomes fragmented and irregular.
• Distinguishing feature - investigation: Osgood-Schlatter disease shows partial separation of the tongue-shaped epiphysis on X-ray, whereas Sever's disease shows fragmentation and irregularity of the epiphysis.
• Distinguishing feature - age range: Both conditions are commoner in boys aged 10-15 years, so the site of the deformity (tibial tubercle versus heel) is the distinguishing clinical feature rather than age.

(a)
Diagnosis: congenital coxa vara.

(b)
Predisposing factors: overweight; aetiology otherwise unknown, though it may be caused by injury such as fracture. Pathophysiology: a progressive decrease in the angle between the femoral neck and shaft, from an abnormal epiphyseal plate with irregularly arranged cells in defective cartilage, atypical ossification, osteoporotic adjacent metaphyseal bone with atrophic trabeculae, excess irregularly arranged connective tissue, and delayed ossification.

(c)
Management: conservative treatment is of little or no value, as the deformity increases as the child becomes older and heavier until the greater trochanter lies superior to the femoral head, potentially developing pseudarthrosis of the femoral neck. Surgical treatment is osteotomy of the femur to correct the angle between the neck and shaft.

(d)
Physiotherapy management: may not be required in non-surgical cases except strengthening of muscles, especially the hip abductors, and re-education of gait. Post-surgery, the physiotherapist mobilizes the hip, strengthens muscles around the hip joint, and re-educates walking.
