(a)
Definition: Scheuermann's disease is epiphysitis affecting the epiphysis, usually of one single or multiple vertebrae in the thoracic region, mostly in adolescents, characterized by deformity, pain, and disability.

(b)
Causes/etiology: Unknown; genetic; traumatic (sports trauma).

(c)
Clinical features: Commoner in boys; age 10-15 years; pain; deformity of kyphosis (round) of the thoracic spine compensated by lordosis of the lumbar spine below it, with round shoulders; local tenderness; walking/running painful.

(d)
Investigation: X-ray shows irregular anterosuperior and anteroinferior angles of the vertebral bodies at the site of the normal epiphysis.

(e)
• Distinguishing feature - age group: Scheuermann's disease occurs mostly in adolescents (boys aged 10-15 years), whereas Calve's disease occurs mostly in infants or very small children.
• Distinguishing feature - vertebral involvement: Scheuermann's disease usually affects one single or multiple vertebrae in the thoracic region, whereas Calve's disease usually affects one single vertebra.
• Distinguishing feature - etiology: Calve's disease has birth trauma as its traumatic cause, whereas Scheuermann's disease has sports trauma.
• Distinguishing feature - deformity: Scheuermann's disease produces kyphosis of the thoracic spine with compensatory lumbar lordosis and round shoulders, whereas Calve's disease produces a prominent spine deformity.
• Distinguishing feature - differential diagnosis: tuberculosis is a differential diagnosis of Calve's disease.
• Distinguishing feature - management: Scheuermann's disease is managed conservatively with bedrest, analgesics/NSAIDs, diathermy, a brace, and active exercise, whereas Calve's disease is managed conservatively with bedrest, diathermy, analgesics, and strapping with adhesive plaster; surgery is rarely indicated in both.
questions.question:
(a) Define Scheuermann's disease and state its pathogenesis.
(b) State the causes/etiology.
(c) State the clinical features.
(d) State the investigation used.
(e) Distinguish Scheuermann's disease from Calve's disease.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Diagnosis: injury of the nerve of Bell (long thoracic/external respiratory nerve).

(b)
Mechanism: direct trauma (blow, gunshot, stab), carrying a heavy weight on the shoulder, road/street accident, or operative complications on the breast or chest wall; serratus anterior becomes paralysed and wasted from stretching or severing of the nerve.

(c)
Features: winging of the scapula with the vertebral border and inferior angle unduly prominent; serratus anterior thin, soft, flabby in old lesions; power lost, unable to raise the arm above the shoulder or push forward; loss of sensation and reflexes along the outer side of the arm; skin cold, glazed, smooth. Assessment: ask the patient to raise the arm or push forward, noting the winging; electrical stimulation with needles either side of the nerve; X-ray chest.

(d)
Conservative treatment: immobilization of the arm in a relaxation position (right-angled, splints to relax deltoid and spinati; forearm flexed and supinated) with physiotherapy.

(e)
Surgical treatment for compression factors: exploration and suturing of the nerve, with results usually unsatisfactory; scapula may be steadied by transferring a slip of pectoralis major to the inferior angle of the scapula; postoperative POP cast immobilization, stitches removed through a window in the cast, exercises in an abduction brace, and occupational therapy.
questions.question:
A patient who has been carrying a heavy weight on the shoulder presents with winging of the scapula, the vertebral border and inferior angle unduly prominent, and is unable to raise the arm above the shoulder or push forward.
(a) What is the diagnosis?
(b) What is the mechanism of injury and pathology?
(c) What are the clinical features and physiotherapy assessment findings?
(d) What is the immediate and conservative management?
(e) What are the definitive treatment options?

questions.answerText:
(a)
Diagnosis: Injury to the medial meniscus (tear, rupture, or vertical splitting), the commonest cause of internal derangement of the knee, and especially common in footballers.

(b)
Mechanism/pathology: The flexed knee is subjected to rotational and abduction strain; the knee momentarily opens up on the medial side, the meniscus is sucked inside and gets nipped between the condyles of femur and tibia, resulting in a tear; repeated strains lead to a "bucket handle" tear.

(c)
Clinical features/assessment findings: History of locking of the knee followed by sudden unlocking and effusion; local tenderness; McMurray's test positive; movements painful and restricted.

(d)
Immediate/conservative management: Rest; analgesics; elastic crepe bandage or knee cap; SWD/IRR; local massage.

(e)
Definitive treatment options: Meniscectomy, followed by assisted passive exercises by the physiotherapist progressed to free active exercises by the patient.
questions.question:
A footballer sustains a twisting injury to a partly flexed knee during a sudden change of direction. He develops a history of the knee locking, followed by sudden unlocking and swelling of the joint, with tenderness along the joint line and a positive McMurray's test.
(a) What is the diagnosis?
(b) Describe the mechanism of injury and the pathology involved.
(c) State the clinical features and physiotherapy assessment findings in this condition.
(d) Outline the immediate and conservative management.
(e) What are the definitive treatment options?

An infant presents with pain, a prominent spine deformity, local tenderness, and pain on walking; X-ray shows a flattened and irregular sclerosed articular surface of a single vertebra.
(a) What structure/joint is involved?
(b) What is the deformity present?
(c) What are the differential diagnoses?
(d) What is the clinical reasoning for the physiotherapy plan?
questions.answerText:
(a)
Structure/joint involved: Epiphysitis affecting the epiphysis of usually one single vertebra, mostly in infants or very small children; etiology is unknown, genetic, or traumatic (birth trauma), with pathogenesis being a flattened and irregular sclerosed articular surface of the vertebra.

(b)
Deformity: A prominent spine deformity, with local tenderness and painful walking/running.

(c)
Differential diagnoses: Tuberculosis.

(d)
Clinical reasoning for the physiotherapy plan: As surgical treatment is rarely indicated, hardly any deformity or disability occurring in later life, conservative management is favoured - bedrest, diathermy (SWD, infrared), analgesics, and strapping with adhesive plaster - with physiotherapy as after-care using SWD/IR and exercises progressing from assisted passive exercises by the physiotherapist to free active exercises by the patient.

questions.question:
A 70-year-old woman falls onto her outstretched hand. She presents with a swollen, deformed wrist described as having a "dinner fork" appearance.
(a) State the most likely diagnosis.
(b) Explain the pathological/biomechanical basis (mechanism of injury).
(c) Outline the acute management and immobilisation.
(d) Outline the definitive conservative or surgical treatment.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Colles' fracture - fracture of the distal radius with dorsal displacement of the hand.

(b)
Usually results from a fall on an outstretched hand (FOOSH); the classic "dinner fork" deformity reflects the dorsal displacement of the distal fragment.

(c)
Splinting/casting; instability criteria that increase the likelihood of requiring operative management include dorsal tilt greater than 20 degrees, a comminuted fracture, avulsion of the ulnar styloid process, intra-articular displacement greater than 1mm, and loss of radial height greater than 2mm.

(d)
Undisplaced fractures are treated in a cast; fractures with angulation/displacement are treated by closed reduction; fractures with significant angulation/displacement require open reduction and internal fixation.

questions.question:
(a) State the mechanism of injury in internal derangement of the radioulnar joints.
(b) State the types/predisposing factors of this condition.
(c) State the clinical findings produced, including the relevant investigations.
(d) State the pathogenesis of this condition.
(e) State the management principles for this condition.
(f) Explain the physiotherapy management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Mechanism: Direct trauma - violence, road/street accident, sports injury, or fall downstairs.

(b)
• Types (traumatic predisposing factors): Injured articular disc; injured ulnar collateral ligament; ruptured distal radioulnar ligaments; dislocation/subluxation.
• Types (deformed predisposing factors): Angulated radius or ulna; enlarged ulnar head.

(c)
• Clinical findings: Pain; local tenderness; clicking joint on rotation of the forearm; prominent ulnar head; weakness of grip and of the wrist.
• Investigations: X-ray of the wrist (AP and lateral views) to rule out any bony lesion; MRI of the wrist.

(d)
Pathogenesis: a torn articular disc, torn ulnar collateral ligament, and ruptured distal radioulnar ligaments.

(e)
• Management principles - torn articular disc: Excision of the disc.
• Management principles - ruptured ligaments: Repair.
• Management principles - dislocation/subluxation and angulation: Reduction (closed or open) for dislocation/subluxation; osteotomy for angulated radius or ulna.

(f)
• Physiotherapy management: Assisted passive exercises by the physiotherapist.
• Physiotherapy management (continued): Progressed to free active exercises by the patient.

questions.question:
An elderly patient sustains a rupture of the quadriceps tendon just above the patella through a zone of degeneration.
(a) What is the diagnosis?
(b) What surgery/procedure is named for definitive treatment?
(c) What is the post-operative physiotherapy by phase?
(d) What precautions and contraindications apply?
questions.answerText:
(a)
Ruptured quadriceps femoris tendon.

(b)
Surgery: repair of the tendon. Postoperative: a long leg cast applied with the knee flexed and foot in equinus position, with wire sutures protruding through the cast; after care - removal of cast and wires after 4 weeks, then a walking cast for a further 4 weeks.

(c)
During fixation: non-weight bearing walking progressed to weight-bearing walking; teaching functional activities with crutches; exercises to maintain mobility of the toes, knee and hip joints and muscle power. Post fixation: non-weight bearing exercises started immediately; massage to mobilize the tendon and reduce swelling; passive stretching to restore flexion; weight-bearing exercises started once pain subsides; a knee brace worn until full control achieved; rehabilitation depending on age and occupation, including hopping, skipping, jumping, running.

(d)
Precautions: immobilization in the long leg cast with the knee flexed and foot equinus is maintained until removal of the cast and wires at 4 weeks; weight bearing is withheld until the walking-cast stage and until pain subsides.

(a)
Definition: loose bodies of the knee are one of the recognised internal derangements of the knee joint, presenting as loose bodies within the joint.

(b)
Etiology/mechanism: Direct violence.

(c)
Clinical features: History of locking of the knee at different angles each time.

(d)
Investigation: X-ray of the knee (AP and lateral views).

(e)
• Effect on function: The knee locks at different angles each time, indicating a loose body moving freely within the joint and mechanically blocking movement.
• Effect on function (continued): This locking impairs a normal, consistent range of movement of the knee.

(f)
• Surgical management: Surgical removal of the loose body/bodies.
• Rehabilitation: Assisted passive exercises by the physiotherapist.
• Rehabilitation (continued): Progressed to free active exercises by the patient.
questions.question:
(a) Define loose bodies of the knee.
(b) State the etiology/mechanism.
(c) State the clinical features.
(d) State the investigation used.
(e) Explain how this condition affects function.
(f) Outline the surgical and rehabilitation management.

A patient with an old rupture of the anterior cruciate ligament and the tibial collateral ligament of the knee, causing persisting instability, is scheduled for surgical reconstruction using the Hey Groves (modified) procedure.
(a) What is the diagnosis?
(b) Name the surgical procedure.
(c) Describe the post-operative physiotherapy by phase.
(d) What precautions/contraindications apply?
questions.answerText:
(a)
Diagnosis: Old rupture of the anterior cruciate and tibial collateral ligaments of the knee, causing anterior instability with recurrent episodes of internal derangement of the knee.

(b)
Surgical procedure: Reconstruction of the old ruptured anterior cruciate and tibial collateral ligaments (Hey Groves - modified).

(c)
Post-operative physiotherapy by phase: A long leg cast is applied with the knee flexed to 15 degrees; exercises begin from 1 week; the cast is removed after 4 weeks; walking in a brace then continues for 3 months; assisted passive exercises by the physiotherapist are progressed to free active exercises by the patient.

(d)
Precautions/contraindications: Reconstruction is of little practical value where the articular surfaces are damaged; the muscles controlling the joint (quadriceps, hamstring, gastrosoleus) must be strong enough, otherwise the joint will be unstable/flail; the age and general health of the patient must be considered, as an elderly, debilitated patient may be better managed in a brace or with a cane/crutches; surgery cannot fully restore the structure and function of the original ligaments.

(a)
Diagnosis: Charcot's joint (a trophic affection of a weight-bearing joint), here due to diabetic neuropathy; arthrodesis is the surgical procedure of choice for the knee.

(b)
Postoperative physiotherapy: immobilization in a POP spica for 2-3 months, with aftercare of walking with knee support (brace).

(c)
Precautions: postoperative immobilization in a POP spica for 2-3 months.

(d)
Expected outcome: walking with knee support (brace) for a year as aftercare.
questions.question:
A patient with diabetic neuropathy presents with marked destruction of the knee joint, with sclerosis and fragmentation seen on X-ray, and undergoes surgical fusion of the joint.
(a) What is the diagnosis and what surgery/procedure is named as the procedure of choice?
(b) Describe the post-operative physiotherapy by phase.
(c) What precautions/immobilization apply postoperatively?
(d) What is the expected functional outcome?

(a) Describe the pathology and stages of acute compartment syndrome.
(b) State how this relates to supracondylar and tibial fractures.
(c) Explain how compartment syndrome may spread its effect to cause a permanent contracture deformity.
(d) Outline the emergency and physiotherapy management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Pathology: compartment syndrome occurs when pressure is too high within the fascia, described as an ischaemia-oedema cycle, causing massive compromise of circulation to the area.
• Causes: overly tight bandages, splints or casts, fracture, dislocation, crush injury, vascular injury, soft-tissue injury, bleeding disorder, or fluid leakage/oedema.
• Clinical presentation: the first sign is searing or burning pain out of proportion to the injury; other features are sensory deficit, progressive muscle weakness, tense swollen area, elevated compartment pressures, and loss of pulses (a late sign); neurologic symptoms include paraesthesias and paralysis of involved muscles.

(b)
• Relation to supracondylar fracture: associated forearm fractures and elbow flexion greater than 90 degrees increase compartment pressures, which is why supracondylar fracture requires the elbow to be immobilised at about 30 degrees in the emergency room and 60-70 degrees after surgery.
• Relation to tibial fracture: internal bleeding in the leg can lead to compartment syndrome due to the compartmental anatomy of the tibial section of the lower limb, and compartment syndrome is also more likely with certain lower leg fractures and a Lisfranc fracture of the foot.

(c)
• Spread to permanent contracture: within 4-6 hours after onset, neuromuscular damage is irreversible, and the limb can become useless within 24-48 hours.
• Continued: possible results of acute compartment syndrome include infection, motor weakness, and Volkmann's contracture - a deformity of the hand, fingers and wrist caused by a lack of blood flow to the muscles of the forearm.
• Continued: if enough tissue dies from the raised pressure, part of the limb may have to be amputated - so the localised rise in fascial pressure spreads its ischaemic effect distally to the hand and fingers, producing a fixed contracture deformity far from the original injury; without prompt treatment the syndrome can be fatal.

(d)
• Emergency management: monitor compartment pressures.
• Continued: fasciotomy may be performed to relieve pressure, and the wound is packed and dressed after fasciotomy.
• Continued: if a cast causes persistent or worsening pain, feels excessively tight, or causes new numbness or weakness, it must be removed immediately, as these symptoms may indicate compartment syndrome; a splint does not increase this risk in the way a snug cast does.
• Physiotherapy management: once medically stabilised, physiotherapy follows the general principles for fracture rehabilitation - maintenance of range of motion of unaffected joints, isometric exercise where movement is not allowed, and, post-immobilisation, mobilising stiff joints and strengthening weak muscles to re-educate movement.

(a)
• Definition: Internal derangement of the joint mainly applies to various affections (intra-articular or extra-articular, or both), mostly caused by trauma, that interfere with the joint's functioning.
• Classification (knee): Injury to collateral ligaments (commonly medial); injury to meniscus or cartilage (commonly medial); cysts of the lateral meniscus; injury to cruciate ligaments; injury to the infrapatellar pad of fat; fracture of the tibial spine; loose bodies.

(b)
• Causes/mechanism: Disturbed joint mechanics, mostly following trauma.
• Frequency: Internal derangements of the knee joint are much more common than those of other joints.

(c)
• Clinical features: Pain, local tenderness, and painful and restricted movements of the joint; stability of the knee is provided by its muscles and tendons, ligaments, capsule, menisci, and the contours of the bones.
• Movements of the knee: Flexion and extension.

(d)
Investigation: X-ray of the knee (AP and lateral views), to rule out any bony lesion.

(e)
Complication: In injury to the medial collateral ligament, by further continued strain the cruciate ligament, especially the anterior one, may rupture.

(f)
Distinguishing feature:
• ACL injury: abnormal forward movement of the tibia over the femur, and the knee can be hyperextended.
• PCL injury: the tibia is forced backwards, producing abnormal backward movement of the tibia over the femur.
• Management of a PCL injury is the same as that for an ACL injury.
questions.question:
(a) Define internal derangement of the knee joint (IDK) and classify the different types of internal derangement it comprises.
(b) State the causes/mechanism responsible for internal derangement of the knee.
(c) State the clinical features found in internal derangement of the knee.
(d) State the investigation used in internal derangement of the knee.
(e) State a complication that may follow continued strain in an injury to the medial collateral ligament of the knee.
(f) Distinguish between an anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury and a posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) injury of the knee.

A middle-aged patient presents with shoulder pain following a trivial injury; the tendon rupture may be complete or incomplete.
(a) What is the diagnosis?
(b) What is the mechanism of injury and pathogenesis?
(c) What are the clinical features and physiotherapy assessment findings?
(d) What is the immediate and conservative management?
(e) What are the definitive treatment options?
questions.answerText:
(a)
Ruptured supraspinatus tendon.

(b)
Mechanism of injury: direct trauma, repetitive strain activity (RSA), sports injury. Pathogenesis: extravasation of blood within the muscle sheath, at the site of injury or at a distance from it, with an inflamed subacromial bursa.

(c)
Clinical features/assessment findings: pain; a gap visible and palpable at the site of rupture; local tenderness; movements painful and restricted.

(d)
Conservative treatment (symptomatic): rest; analgesics, NSAIDs; antibiotics; physiotherapy (IR, SWD, massage, exercises); immobilization by an arm pouch; intra-articular injection of steroid (hydrocortisone/triamcinolone) plus lignocaine plain 1%.

(e)
Definitive treatment: surgical repair of complete/incomplete tears, with physiotherapy as after care - heat therapy (SWD/IRR or heating pad therapy) and, as pain subsides, active exercises for joint movement and muscle strengthening.

questions.question:
(a) Define spondylolisthesis.
(b) State the aetiology.
(c) Describe the pathogenesis.
(d) Describe the clinical diagnosis and investigations.
(e) Explain how spondylolisthesis affects function.
(f) Outline the conservative, surgical, and rehabilitation management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Definition: spondylolisthesis is an anomaly characterized by slipping forward of a lower lumbar vertebra, usually the fifth, through the plane of the intervertebral disc below it, carrying with it the whole of the upper part of the spine.

(b)
Aetiology: unknown, hereditary, incidence about 5%, equal in men and women.

(c)
Pathogenesis: the essential lesion is separation of the body of the vertebra from the posterior articulation, lamina, and spinous process, due to defective pedicles that normally hold these two parts of the vertebra together.

(d)
Diagnosis: occurs in younger age groups; aching pain around the loin radiating into the legs; weakness of the lower limbs; the trunk appears short with a transverse furrow encircling the trunk between the ribs and iliac crests, prominent upper edge of the sacrum with a depression above it. Investigations: X-ray AP and lateral views confirms the diagnosis, showing a congenital defect in pedicle development.

(e)
Effect on function: pain and weakness of the lower limbs, together with the shortened trunk deformity, can incapacitate a person for work.

(f)
• Conservative treatment: rest, local heat (shortwave diathermy, infrared heat), lumbosacral belt or corset, and analgesics.
• Surgical treatment: usually not required, but indicated in a younger patient with an acute condition, or with persistent low backache and radiating pain into the buttocks and thighs incapacitating the person for work.
• Postoperative care: rest on a firm bed for 8 weeks, followed by brace fitting and the patient allowed up.
• Rehabilitation: physiotherapist's advice on posture, back care, and lifting technique is mandatory.
• Active exercises, once acute pain has subsided, are mandatory to strengthen the back extensor muscles; weight loss is usually appropriate.
• Mobilizations may be appropriate to restore movement to levels of the lumbar spine above the level of the lesion.
• Heat therapy (SWD/IRR or heat pad) and a lumbosacral belt or corset are also part of physiotherapy management.

questions.question:
(a) Describe plantar fibromatosis (plantar fasciitis) under the following headings: definition and classification, aetiology, pathogenesis, clinical features, investigations, differential diagnosis.
(b) Explain how it affects function.
(c) Outline the conservative, surgical and rehabilitation management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Definition/classification: plantar fasciitis is the inflammation of the plantar fascia, similar in histology and pathogenesis to palmar fasciitis, with variation peculiar to the anatomy of the foot.
• Aetiology: traumatic; inflammatory; infective; metabolic.
• Pathogenesis: most often affects the medial part of the plantar fascia; proliferated fibroblasts blend with the fascia beneath the tarsal bones, producing nodular thickening of the plantar fascia.
• Clinical features: pain; swelling; local tenderness.
• Investigations: CBC, ESR, blood sugar; X-ray of the foot, AP and lateral views.
• Differential diagnosis: fibrosarcoma (difficult to differentiate histologically); synovial sarcoma.

(b)
Effect on function: pain, swelling and local tenderness of the plantar fascia impair weight bearing and walking.

(c)
• Surgical management (treatment of choice, to avoid recurrence): block resection of the plantar fascia; after care - bedrest with the leg elevated for several days, followed by full weight bearing.
• Rehabilitation/physiotherapy management: heat therapy (SWD/IRR or heating pad therapy).
• Physiotherapy exercises: as pain subsides, the physiotherapist encourages active exercises for joint movement and muscle strengthening.

(a)
Diagnosis: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury.

(b)
Surgical procedure: ORIF (screw fixation), since the anterior tibial spine is fractured; where the ACL itself is avulsed, re-attachment or ACL replacement using the tendon of semitendinosus is the treatment of choice; associated tears of the medial collateral ligament and medial meniscus are repaired.

(c)
Post-operative physiotherapy: After care includes physiotherapy, with assisted passive exercises by the physiotherapist progressed to free active exercises by the patient.

(d)
Precautions/contraindications: Isolated tears of the ACL are uncommon and are usually associated with tears of the medial collateral ligament and/or medial meniscus, which must also be addressed at surgery; where the anterior tibial spine is intact, a plaster cylinder for 6 weeks with after-care physiotherapy is used instead of surgery.
questions.question:
A patient sustains direct violence to the knee and presents with abnormal forward movement of the tibia over the femur, with the knee able to be hyperextended; X-ray shows the anterior tibial spine to be fractured, and surgery is planned.
(a) What is the diagnosis?
(b) Name the surgical procedure.
(c) Describe the post-operative physiotherapy.
(d) What precautions/contraindications apply?

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Definition/classification: acute sciatica occurs suddenly and usually heals within several days to weeks; the severity relates directly to the amount of tissue injury, and the source of pain may lie in the spinal joints, discs, nerves, or muscles and ligaments; it is described as most resistant to treatment because its aetiology may remain obscure even after careful physical and radiological examination.
• Aetiology: traumatic (RSA, sports injury, lifting heavy weight); inflammatory (tuberculosis, spondylitis); infection of the genitourinary, gastrointestinal or nervous system; endocrinal (diabetes); neoplastic (vertebral or pelvic tumors); degenerative (PIVD, spondylosis, spondylolisthesis).
• Clinical features: pain down the thigh and leg; positive straight leg raise (SLR) test; positive forward bending test.
• Investigations: hemogram, TLC and DLC, ESR; X-ray of the lumbosacral spine; myelography; CT scan.

(b)
Effect on function: pain radiating down the thigh and leg, provoked by the SLR and forward bending tests, restricts spinal and lower-limb movement and causes significant suffering and economic loss.

(c)
• Conservative management, general measures: bedrest; heat therapy (infrared, short-wave diathermy); traction; lumbar belt; analgesics; NSAIDs.
• Specific treatment: treatment of the underlying cause.
• Surgical management: indicated only in limited cases, namely PIVD and spinal tumors.
• Rehabilitation/physiotherapy management: heat/ice - heat and/or ice packs are readily available and help alleviate leg pain, especially in the initial phase.
• Physiotherapy exercises: low back exercises performed 2-3 times daily.
• Prognosis note: sciatica is described as most resistant to treatment and often difficult to treat satisfactorily because its aetiology may remain obscure.
questions.question:
(a) Describe acute sciatica under the following headings: definition and classification, aetiology, clinical features, investigations.
(b) Explain how it affects function.
(c) Outline the conservative, surgical and rehabilitation management.

A patient sustains a rupture of the patellar tendon at the lower border of the patella following direct trauma.
(a) What is the diagnosis?
(b) What surgery/procedure is named for definitive treatment?
(c) What is the post-operative physiotherapy by phase?
(d) What precautions and contraindications apply?
questions.answerText:
(a)
Ruptured patellar tendon.

(b)
Surgery: repair of the tendon. Postoperative: a long leg cast is applied with the knee flexed and foot in an equinus position, with wire sutures protruding through the cast; the cast and wires are removed after 4 weeks, then a walking cast applied for a further 4 weeks.

(c)
During fixation: non-weight bearing walking progressed to weight-bearing walking; the physiotherapist teaches functional activities with crutches; exercises to maintain mobility of the toes, knee and hip joints and muscle power. Post fixation: non-weight bearing exercises started immediately; massage to mobilize the tendon and reduce swelling; passive stretching by the physiotherapist to restore flexion; weight-bearing exercises started once pain subsides; a knee brace worn until full control is achieved; rehabilitation depending on age and occupation, including hopping, skipping, jumping, running.

(d)
Precautions: the leg remains immobilized in the cast with the knee flexed and foot equinus until removal of the cast and wires at 4 weeks; weight bearing is withheld during fixation and progressed only through the walking-cast stage once pain subsides.

questions.question:
A patient sustains a fracture of the middle of the shaft of the humerus and subsequently presents with wrist drop, unable to extend the wrist, thumb and metacarpophalangeal joints against resistance with the forearm in mid-prone position.
(a) What structure or joint is involved?
(b) What deformity or functional impairment results?
(c) What are the differential diagnoses?
(d) What is the clinical reasoning for the physiotherapy plan?
questions.answerText:
(a)
Structure involved: the radial (musculospiral) nerve, paralysing triceps and the supinators and extensors of the wrist, fingers, and thumb.

(b)
Deformity: wrist drop, with loss of joint sense usually unaffected but loss of cutaneous sensation over the dorsum of the forearm and back of the hand; the deficit is confirmed by testing with the forearm in mid-prone position, unable to extend the wrist, thumb and MP joints against resistance.

(c)
Differential diagnoses: the mechanism (fracture of the mid-shaft of the humerus) points specifically to radial nerve injury, distinguishing it from median nerve injury (ape thumb) or ulnar nerve injury (claw hand), which occur from different fracture/dislocation sites at the elbow or wrist.

(d)
Clinical reasoning: management follows the standard nerve injury approach, with conservative immobilization in a universal arm pouch and physiotherapy exercises, or surgical exploration and suturing for compression from fracture-dislocation, followed by a POP cast, physiotherapy of assisted passive movements progressing to free active exercises, and occupational therapy, since results of suturing are usually unsatisfactory.

questions.question:
(a) Define and classify osteomyelitis of bone.
(b) What is the causes/aetiology?
(c) What are the clinical features?
(d) What investigations are used?
(e) What are the complications?
(f) Distinguish between acute and chronic osteomyelitis.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Osteomyelitis is an infection of the bone; classified as acute osteomyelitis (acute inflammation of bone due to infection) and chronic osteomyelitis (its reparative stage after missed diagnosis or inadequate treatment of acute infection, or an indolent slowly progressive process).

(b)
• Aetiology, direct: compound fractures, penetrating wounds, operations, diagnostic procedures such as intramedullary aspiration or injection.
• Aetiology, indirect: hematogenous spread from infective foci in the skin, upper respiratory tract, or genitourinary tract; organisms include bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites (Staphylococcus, Streptococcus, Pneumococcus, Gonococcus, Meningococcus, Haemophilus influenzae, gram-negative bacilli, Mycobacterium; smallpox, measles, mumps viruses; Actinomyces, blastomyces, coccidioides fungi; Echinococcus granulosus).

(c)
• Clinical features, acute: common in children; affects bone ends (metaphysis) of tibia, femur, humerus; sudden onset, severe pain, fever with chills and prostration, hot red swollen skin, local tenderness.
• Clinical features, chronic: history of trauma; mild insidious symptoms; unremitting pain; recurrent fever; redness of overlying skin; periodic or constant discharging sinuses; movements free initially, later painful and restricted.

(d)
• Investigations, acute: CBC, hematocrit; leukocytosis on TLC/DLC; raised ESR; blood culture; aspiration with smear and culture sensitivity; urinalysis; X-ray normal early, later rarefaction of the metaphysis and subperiosteal bone formation.
• Investigations, chronic: hemogram shows anemia; leukocytosis; raised ESR; blood culture; X-ray may show a sequestrum, increased bone density, involucrum and new bone formation, resorption of sclerosed bone; CT scan to localize occult infection.

(e)
• Complications, acute: chronic osteomyelitis; suppurative arthritis; soft tissue abscess formation; pathological fracture; deformity (e.g. manus valgus); Brodie's abscess.
• Complications, chronic: septic arthritis; amyloidosis; pathological fracture; deformity or shortening.

(f)
• Distinguishing acute vs chronic: acute has sudden onset, severe pain, marked fever with chills, surgery avoided in the first 2-3 days, and is treated by incision and drainage plus decompression of the medullary canal by burr holes.
• Chronic has an insidious, unremitting course with periodic discharging sinuses, and additionally requires sequestrectomy, curettage, saucerization, or amputation to forestall amyloidosis.
• Physiotherapy management for both: heat therapy (SWD/IRR or heating pad therapy); as pain subsides the physiotherapist encourages active exercises for joint movement and muscle strengthening.

(a)
Diagnosis: Injury to the medial (tibial) collateral ligament of the knee.

(b)
Mechanism/pathology: A forcible abduction strain on the extended leg (road/street accident, sports injury, fall downstairs, or direct violence) causes a tear of the anterior portion of the deep layer, or an avulsion/rupture; the injury is usually associated with injury to the medial meniscus because of the attachment of its deeper fibres to the meniscus, and further continued strain may rupture the anterior cruciate ligament.

(c)
Clinical features/assessment findings: Pain on the medial side of the knee; local tenderness; movements of the knee painful and restricted, especially abduction.

(d)
Immediate/conservative management: Analgesics; elastic crepe bandage or knee cap; SWD/IRD; local massage; rest.

(e)
Definitive treatment options: Surgical repair of the collateral ligament, repair of the medial meniscus (torn peripheral attachment), and repair of the ACL; post-operatively a long leg cast is applied with the knee flexed to 10-15 degrees with active quadriceps and hamstring exercises, the cast and stitches removed after 2 weeks, a walking cylindrical cast applied from groin to above the ankle with walking using crutches, and the walking cast removed after 6 weeks.
questions.question:
A patient sustains a forcible abduction strain to the extended leg following a road accident, and presents with pain on the medial side of the knee, local tenderness, and painful, restricted movement, especially abduction.
(a) What is the diagnosis?
(b) Describe the mechanism of injury and the pathology involved.
(c) State the clinical features and physiotherapy assessment findings in this condition.
(d) Outline the immediate and conservative management.
(e) What are the definitive treatment options?

questions.answerText:
(a)
Risk factors/aetiology: direct trauma causing arterial or (rarely) venous obstruction; immobilization by tight splints or casts; spasmodic local arterial spasm with reflex spasm of the collateral vascular supply due to arterial trauma; most often follows a supracondylar fracture of the humerus, and occasionally fractures of both bones of the forearm (radius and ulna).

(b)
Complications: impending signs - severe pain in the forearm flexor muscles post fracture; confirmed (established) signs - claw hand deformity (flexed phalanges with flexed wrist, unable to extend the fingers), impaired sensations, pallor or cyanosis of the fingers, impaired radial pulse; irreparable ischemic nerve damage can cause contracture, deformity, or paralysis.

(c)
First aid (ASAP): reduction of the fracture; removal of pressure from the front of the elbow by bivalving or removing the cast/splint and cutting dressings to the skin; partial extension of the joint; sympathetic nerve block (injection of papaverine) to relieve vascular spasm. Surgical (indicated for impending or established VIC): fasciotomy plus arteriectomy; sympathectomy; postoperative immobilization of the arm in a cast in the extended position. Surgery is justified once impending or established VIC is present, since first-aid measures alone address prevention rather than reversing established ischemic damage.

(d)
Physiotherapy role: children usually mobilize quickly once fixation (POP) is removed and thereby do not require any treatment; however, sometimes the physiotherapist has to teach the child free active exercises (in the presence of parents) as encouragement.

Describe tibial shaft fracture under
(a) Epidemiology
(b) Aetiology
(c) Complications
(d) Treatment (conservative and surgical)
(e) Physiotherapy
(f) Explain the clinical basis for why tibial shaft fractures are prone to becoming open fractures and to delayed/non-union.
(g) Distinguish tibial shaft fracture from tibial plateau fracture.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Epidemiology: isolated tibial fracture occurs in 23% of tibial shaft fractures, while both tibia and fibula are fractured together in 77%; fractures can be closed or open; 2 tibial shaft fractures occur per 1000 orthopaedic injuries, mostly in young and middle-aged people, with teenage males reported to have the highest incidence.

(b)
Aetiology: high-speed trauma is paramount - high-speed driving, falls or jumps from significant height, gunshot wounds to the lower leg.

(c)
Complications: reduced blood supply in the distal one-third due to segmental fractures; the tibia is known for delayed union and non-union in this area; internal bleeding can lead to compartment syndrome due to the compartmental anatomy of the lower limb.

(d)
• Treatment, conservative: closed fractures with minimal displacement/stable reduction are treated non-operatively with a long leg cast (application delayed 3-5 days to allow swelling to diminish), extending from mid-thigh to the metatarsal heads with the ankle at 90 degrees and knee extended, for 6-8 weeks with frequent radiographs.
• Treatment, surgical: operative fixation is required when fractures are unstable; options include plating, external fixation, intramedullary nailing and, in some cases, amputation.

(e)
Physiotherapy: a tibial fracture splint allows more movement of the knee and ankle, protects the tibial fracture and decreases stiffness after the fracture has healed.

(f)
• Clinical basis, open fracture risk: the tibia is subcutaneous, hence the incidence of open fracture is high.
• Clinical basis, delayed/non-union: only 5% of tibial shaft fractures need operative treatment, as most respond well to conservative treatment, but the reduced blood supply in the distal one-third predisposes this area specifically to delayed union and non-union.

(g)
• Distinguishing feature 1: tibial shaft fracture involves the mid-diaphysis of the tibia, most commonly from high-speed trauma, and is managed largely conservatively with a long leg cast.
• Distinguishing feature 2: tibial plateau fracture involves the proximal tibia and its articular surface, caused by a force directed medially, laterally, or both with axial loading (commonly vehicle-pedestrian collision, fall from height, industrial accident or sports injury).
• Distinguishing feature 3: tibial plateau fracture presents with severe knee pain, swelling, valgus deformity and joint instability, graded by the Schatzker classification, unlike tibial shaft fracture, which presents with diffuse leg pain/deformity.
• Distinguishing feature 4: tibial plateau fracture is managed with protected weight bearing and early range-of-knee motion in a hinged fracture brace, whereas tibial shaft fracture is more often managed in a long leg cast with the knee extended.

(a)
• Mechanism: occurs when pressure is too high within the fascia; causes include overly tight bandages, splints or casts, fracture, dislocation, crush injury, vascular injury, soft-tissue injury, bleeding disorder, and fluid leakage or oedema.
• Sites at risk: more likely with certain fractures of the lower leg, certain arm fractures, or a Lisfranc fracture of the foot; also associated with supracondylar fracture of the humerus and midfoot crush injuries.
• Clinical features: pain disproportionate to the injury, sensory deficit, progressive muscle weakness, tense swollen area, elevated compartment pressures, loss of pulses (a late sign).
• Continued: the first sign is searing/burning pain out of proportion to the injury.
• Complications: infection, motor weakness, Volkmann's contracture (a deformity of the hand, fingers and wrist from lack of blood flow to the forearm muscles); if enough tissue dies, part of the limb may have to be amputated.

(b)
• Precautions: within 4-6 hours after onset, neuromuscular damage is irreversible, and the limb can become useless within 24-48 hours, so compartment pressures must be monitored.
• Continued: a splint, which does not completely encircle the limb, allows room for expansion and does not increase the risk of compartment syndrome, unlike a snugly fitted cast.
• Continued: if a cast causes persistent or worsening pain, feels excessively tight, or causes new numbness or weakness, it must be removed immediately, as these symptoms may indicate compartment syndrome.
• Continued: fasciotomy may be performed to relieve pressure, and the wound is packed and dressed after fasciotomy.

(c)
• Biomechanical basis: compartment syndrome develops when injured muscles swell after a limb is broken; because swelling occurs within a closed fascial compartment, it raises pressure on and compresses nearby blood vessels, reducing or blocking blood flow to the limb.
• Continued: this is described as an ischaemia-oedema cycle - reduced blood flow causes further tissue oedema, which further raises compartmental pressure, worsening ischaemia, and with reduced perfusion tissue in the limb may be damaged or die.
• Continued: the elbow is specifically immobilised at about 30 degrees of flexion in the emergency room and 60-70 degrees after surgery for supracondylar fracture to minimise the compartment-pressure-raising effect of greater flexion.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Mechanism: A forcible abduction strain on the extended leg, due to a road/street accident, sports injury, fall downstairs, or direct violence.

(b)
Types: A tear of the anterior portion of the deep layer, or an avulsion or rupture of the ligament.

(c)
• Clinical findings: Pain on the medial side of the knee, local tenderness, and movements of the knee painful and restricted, especially abduction.
• Anatomy: The ligament is a long, flat band, wider in the middle, running from the medial epicondyle of the femur (below the adductor tubercle) to the medial tibial condyle and upper tibial shaft, fused with the fibrous capsule.
• Investigation: X-ray of the knee (AP and lateral views), to rule out any bony lesion.

(d)
Complication: By further continued strain, the cruciate ligament, especially the anterior one, may rupture.

(e)
Associated injury: the injury is usually associated with injury to the medial meniscus, because of the attachment of its deeper fibres to the meniscus.

(f)
• Management principles (conservative): Analgesics, elastic crepe bandage or knee cap, SWD/IRD, local massage, and rest.
• Management principles (surgical): Repair of the collateral ligament, repair of the medial meniscus (torn peripheral attachment), and repair of the ACL.

(g)
• Physiotherapy - post-operative phase: A long leg cast is applied with the knee flexed to 10-15 degrees with active quadriceps and hamstring exercises; the cast and stitches are removed after 2 weeks.
• Physiotherapy - walking phase: A walking cylindrical cast is applied from the groin to above the ankle, walking with crutches, and the walking cast is removed after 6 weeks.
• Physiotherapy - exercise progression: Assisted passive exercises by the physiotherapist are progressed to free active exercises by the patient.

Describe fracture of the clavicle under
(a) Definition/anatomy
(b) Classification
(c) Aetiology
(d) Clinical features
(e) Treatment
(f) Explain the clinical basis for why the middle third of the clavicle is the most common fracture site.
(g) Distinguish clavicle fracture from scapular fracture.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Definition/anatomy: the clavicle is an S-shaped long curved tubular bone lying horizontally across the root of the neck, articulating with the sternum medially (sternoclavicular joint) and the acromion of the scapula laterally (acromioclavicular joint).

(b)
Classification (Allman): Type 1 - middle third (80%); Type 2 - outer/lateral third (15%); Type 3 - inner/medial third (5%).

(c)
Aetiology: direct traumatic impact or fall on the shoulder (87%); direct impact to the clavicle (7%); fall on an outstretched hand (6%); in children, non-traumatic causes include tumour, rickets, osteogenesis imperfecta and physical abuse.

(d)
Clinical features: pain and tenderness at the site of injury, local bruising, obvious deformity and swelling; the patient supports the injured limb with the other hand with the head tilted toward the injured side.

(e)
• Treatment: fractures unite with or without treatment, usually in 3-6 weeks; conservative management (sling or figure-of-eight for 2-4 weeks with shoulder ROM exercises) is used for most non-displaced fractures.
• Continued: surgical fixation is rarely indicated except for lateral one-third fracture, neurovascular injury or nonunion.
• Physiotherapy: sling for 2-4 weeks followed by active motion, with hand, wrist and elbow exercises during immobilisation; strengthening at 6-8 weeks; full activity including sports at 3 months.

(f)
Clinical basis: the middle third is the most common fracture site because it is the thinnest part of the bone, the junction of the two main curves of the shaft, and the site of entrance of the nutrient artery; the outer fragment typically displaces below the inner fragment.

(g)
• Distinguishing feature 1: clavicle fracture commonly follows direct impact or a fall on the shoulder and presents with local deformity and swelling over the clavicle, with the patient tilting the head toward the injured side.
• Distinguishing feature 2: scapular fracture is uncommon due to the bone's protected location and surrounding muscle (supraspinatus, infraspinatus, subscapularis), and results from high-energy trauma with 60-98% of cases having associated injuries.
• Distinguishing feature 3: scapular fracture presents with bruising over the scapula/chest, shoulder pain on movement with the arm held immobile, and tenderness at the fracture site, and is managed with a sling for comfort with repeated checks for shoulder dislocation.
• Distinguishing feature 4: reduction is usually necessary for displaced clavicle fractures affecting the lateral third, whereas reduction is usually unnecessary for scapular fractures, which are managed with rest in a sling.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the mechanism, types (Winquist-Hansen classification), clinical features and complications of femoral shaft fracture.
(b) State the safe site/precautions for skeletal traction as a method of holding reduction.
(c) Explain the biomechanical basis of the hip external rotation and abduction deformity seen with this fracture.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Mechanism: a common injury due to major violent trauma, averaging 1 per 10,000 people, more common in people between 25 and 65 years; high-energy causes include RTA, gunshot wounds, collision, fall from height, crush, sport; low-energy causes include stress fractures, osteoporosis, cancer.
• Types (Winquist-Hansen): Grade 1 - no comminution; Grade 2 - bone fragment with short transverse or oblique fracture; Grade 3 - bone fragment greater than 50% of cortex intact; Grade 4 - larger bone fragment leaving less than 50% of the cortex in contact; Grade 5 - segmental comminution.
• Clinical features: diffuse pain or ache, hip usually externally rotated and abducted, limb length discrepancy, weakness of the thigh muscles, inability to bear weight.
• Complications, loss of alignment/infection/union problems: loss of joint alignment, infection, non-union, malunion, delayed union.
• Continued, systemic and joint complications: massive blood loss/haemorrhagic shock, avascular necrosis, nerve injury, heterotopic ossification, joint stiffness/deformities, thromboembolism, fat embolism.

(b)
• Precautions: management options include skeletal traction (8-12 weeks), external fixation, intramedullary nailing (union rates greater than 95%), or plate fixation.
• Continued: the femur is surrounded by massive musculature, which provides excellent blood supply but also generates strong deforming forces during traction, so alignment must be checked and maintained throughout the traction period.
• Continued: fractures known to require surgery, such as femoral shaft fractures, heal more rapidly with a better outcome, and surgery shortens the time patients must remain immobilised; prognosis depends on the severity of injury, adequacy of the reduced bone fragments, and adequacy of fixation.

(c)
• Biomechanical basis: the femur is a long tubular bone, anteriorly bowed forward, with an oblique course from the neck to the distal end.
• Continued: the massive musculature surrounding the femur (including the hip flexors, abductors and external rotators attaching around the proximal fragment) pulls the proximal fragment into external rotation and abduction once the shaft is fractured and the normal bony lever is lost, producing the diffuse pain, externally rotated and abducted hip position, and limb length discrepancy described clinically.
• Continued: because these deforming forces make reduction difficult to maintain, sustained skeletal traction or rigid internal fixation is required to counteract them during healing.
• Continued: rigid internal fixation with an intramedullary nail achieves union rates greater than 95% by neutralising this muscular pull throughout healing.

questions.question:
A patient over 60 years old with a sedentary lifestyle and a history of squatting, climbing stairs and prolonged standing presents with dull aching hip pain worsened by weight-bearing and relieved by rest, morning stiffness and restricted painful movement, and X-ray shows asymmetric narrowing of the joint space with osteophytes at the joint margins.
(a) What is the diagnosis (also known by what synonym for the hip)?
(b) What are the predisposing factors and pathophysiology?
(c) What is the medical/surgical management?
(d) What is the physiotherapy/occupational therapy management?
questions.answerText:
(a)
Diagnosis: Osteoarthritis of the hip, also known as coxa magna.

(b)
Predisposing factors/pathophysiology: advancing age over 60 years, a sedentary life, being overweight, wrong posture and misuse of the joint, and strenuous exercise including regular use of stairs; pathologically there is hypersecretion of synovial fluid with an inflamed, thickened, hypertrophied synovial membrane, softened, roughened and worn articular cartilage, sclerosis, eburnation and cyst formation in the subchondral bone, osteophytes at the articular surfaces, and bony ankylosis.

(c)
Management: analgesics and NSAIDs (with caution for NSAID toxicity in the elderly), intra-articular steroid injection (hydrocortisone acetate 25 mg/mL plus 1% plain lignocaine 1 mL); the conservative treatment of choice for the hip is generally preferred, with arthrodesis rarely indicated.

(d)
Occupational therapy/physiotherapy management: joint protection and conservation by avoiding joint stress such as squatting, ascending/descending stairs and prolonged standing; general physiotherapy modalities include muscle-strengthening exercises (active and passive), traction, heat therapy (SWD/IRR), wax bath therapy, hydrotherapy, massage (stroking, compression), ambulation aids (walking stick, walker, crutches, braces/belts), acupuncture/acupressure and yoga therapy.

(a)
Ankylosing spondylitis.

(b)
A crippling, chronic inflammatory disease of unknown aetiology, affecting mostly young men (20-40 years), involving mainly the spine and sacroiliac joints, peripheral joints and extra-articular structures

(c)
No specific treatment is known. Conservative (general measures): bedrest; warm fomentation; deep breathing exercises; drugs - analgesics, NSAIDs, corticosteroids. Surgical (indicated in severe flexion deformity of the spine): osteotomy (wedge) of the spine.

(d)
Physiotherapy management: regular physiotherapy is essential; exercises - active (patient puts joints through range of motion), passive (someone puts the joints through range of motion), isometric (muscle contracted but not shortened), isotonic (muscle contracted and shortened); heat therapy (infrared, short-wave diathermy); radiotherapy for symptomatic relief (with high incidence of leukemia as a side effect).
questions.question:
A young man aged between 20 and 40 years presents with low backache radiating down the thighs and legs, morning stiffness, and restricted chest expansion.
(a) What is the diagnosis?
(b) What are the predisposing factors and pathophysiology?
(c) What is the medical and surgical management?
(d) What is the physiotherapy management?

questions.answerText:
(a)
Risk factors: direct trauma (fractures/fracture-dislocations), supracondylar fracture of the humerus, fall from height, sports injury, exposure to cold or heat, and cardiovascular conditions (arteriosclerosis, embolism, thrombosis); smoking and extreme cold/heat exposure are precipitating factors.

(b)
Complications: severe persisting post-reduction pain, loss of distal pulses (radial, popliteal, dorsalis pedis), anaesthesia, and paralytic muscle; progression leads to muscle replaced by fibrous tissue causing ischemic contracture and/or paralysis (clawhand deformity).

(c)
Conservative management: cautious chiropody and avoidance of heating/freezing the ischemic part; analgesics, NSAIDs, vasodilators, paravertebral block, and anticoagulants (heparin, dicoumarol/warfarin). For impending Volkmann's contracture, fasciotomy and arteriectomy are the justified surgical procedures, since early diagnosis and management may relieve the agony before established contracture sets in; established contracture instead requires tendon lengthening, muscle origin transfer, bone shortening, or carpectomy.

(d)
Physiotherapy: postoperative immobilization of the arm with a forearm brace followed by physiotherapy exercises as after-care.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Diagnosis: Polyostotic fibrous dysplasia (osteitis fibrosa cystica); the combination of brown spots with ragged margins and true precocious puberty is known as Albright's syndrome, which may be associated with hyperthyroidism and acromegaly.

(b)
Predisposing factors/pathophysiology: the aetiology is unknown; there is generalized bone resorption causing diffuse cystic changes widely scattered throughout the skeleton, mostly affecting the long bones and skull, with bone cysts and pathological fractures; in the congenital type, bone and cartilage fail to form and are replaced by fibrous tissue; it is a congenital dysplasia, not a metabolic disorder, though it is often mistaken for osteitis fibrosa generalisata due to hyperparathyroidism as both show bone cysts and fractures.

(c)
Management: there is no specific treatment; conservative treatment is warm fomentation, SWD or IR therapy, analgesics and NSAIDs, and calcitonin, which may be tried in acute disease though results are inconclusive; surgery is indicated for correction of deformities such as fractures or an expanding orbital cyst.

(d)
Physiotherapy management: regular exercise, especially weight-bearing, under the supervision and teaching of the physiotherapist, and heat therapy (SWD/IRR).

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Definition: a familial condition due to maldevelopment of bones of cartilage origin, characterised by markedly diminished stature with the limbs, in particular, stunted.
• Aetiology: unknown.
• Clinical features: diminished stature, shortened legs, arms resembling flippers with fingertips reaching only to the greater trochanters, and fingers diverging like the spokes of a wheel.
• Further clinical features: a skull with a cartilaginous base smaller than the vertex, a prominent forehead, a depressed nose, weakened muscles, a gait of short steps, and normal mental development.
• Investigations: CBC, ESR, and X-rays of the skull, spine, pelvis and limbs.

(b)
• Effect on function: shortened legs and weakened muscles produce a gait of short steps.
• The stunted limbs (flipper-like arms, diverging fingers) affect manual and locomotor function generally.
• Mental development remains normal, and patients are usually employed in circuses.

(c)
• Surgical management: leg lengthening, indicated for the shortened legs.
• Rehabilitation/physiotherapy management: regular exercise, especially weight-bearing, under the supervision and teaching of the physiotherapist.
• Further rehabilitation: SWD/IRR (heat therapy).

A woman past the fifth decade of life presents with shoulder pain, worst at night and aggravated by movement, with restricted shoulder motion.
(a) What is the diagnosis?
(b) What are the predisposing factors and pathophysiology?
(c) What is the medical and surgical management?
(d) What is the physiotherapy management?
questions.answerText:
(a)
Periarthritis shoulder (syn. scapulohumeral periarthritis, frozen shoulder).

(b)
It is an inflammatory disorder of multiple aetiology involving primarily the soft tissue. Predisposing factors: traumatic (fracture or dislocation); inflammatory (rheumatoid arthritis); degenerative (osteoarthritis); common in women past the 5th decade.

(c)
Management aims: pain relief, restoration of movement, and treatment of the underlying cause. Conservative: rest; avoiding aggravating strenuous exercises; improving posture; analgesics/NSAIDs; intra-articular injection of hydrocortisone plus lignocaine. Surgical (on failure of conservative measures): exploration, with physiotherapy as after care.

(d)
Physiotherapy management: exercises (isometric and other exercises to maintain muscle power and flexibility of the shoulder muscles); heat therapy (SWD/IRR).

questions.question:
Describe Colles' fracture under
(a) Definition
(b) Classification/instability criteria
(c) Aetiology
(d) Clinical features
(e) Treatment
(f) Explain the clinical basis for why this fracture typically occurs in elderly women via a fall on the outstretched hand.
(g) Distinguish Colles' fracture from Smith's fracture.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Definition: Colles' fracture is a fracture of the distal radius with dorsal displacement of the hand, producing a "dinner fork" deformity, named after Abraham Colles.

(b)
Classification/instability criteria: dorsal tilt greater than 20 degrees, comminuted fracture, avulsion of the ulnar styloid process, intra-articular displacement greater than 1mm, loss of radial height greater than 2mm - these increase the likelihood of requiring operative management.

(c)
Aetiology: usually results from a fall on an outstretched hand (FOOSH).

(d)
Clinical features: severe pain that worsens with grip and hand movements; swelling and tenderness of the wrist and hand; obvious wrist deformity.

(e)
• Treatment: undisplaced - cast; with angulation/displacement - closed reduction; with significant angulation/displacement - open reduction and internal fixation.
• Physiotherapy: the immediate post-surgical phase (day 1-10) focuses on early range of motion of fingers, elbow and shoulder and minimising oedema, with the involved limb non-weight bearing and no lifting, pushing, pulling or forceful gripping.

(f)
• Clinical basis: an outstretched hand acting to break a fall transmits force through the wrist onto the distal radius; elderly women are commonly affected because reduced bone density associated with osteoporosis predisposes the distal radius to fracture from this fall pattern.
• Continued: the resultant dorsal displacement of the distal fragment produces the characteristic dinner-fork deformity described for this fracture.

(g)
• Distinguishing feature 1: Colles' fracture is a fracture of the distal radius with dorsal displacement of the hand.
• Distinguishing feature 2: Smith's fracture is a fracture of the distal radius with volar (palmar) displacement, caused by a fall onto a flexed wrist rather than an outstretched hand, and is named after Robert William Smith.
• Distinguishing feature 3: management of Smith's fracture follows similar principles - undisplaced fractures are treated with a cast, while significant angulation/displacement requires open reduction and internal fixation.
• Distinguishing feature 4: Robert William Smith was involved in an academic argument with Colles regarding the position of the so-called Colles' fracture, reflecting the opposite displacement direction of the two injuries.

(a)
Acute osteomyelitis (acute pyogenic infection of bone/acute osteitis).

(b)
Aetiology: direct - compound fractures, penetrating wounds, operations, diagnostic procedures such as intramedullary aspiration or injection; indirect - hematogenous spread from infective foci in the skin, upper respiratory tract, or genitourinary tract. Organisms: bacteria (Staphylococcus, Streptococcus, Pneumococcus, Gonococcus, Meningococcus, Haemophilus influenzae, gram-negative bacilli, Mycobacterium); viruses (smallpox, measles, mumps); fungi (Actinomyces, blastomyces, coccidioides); parasites (Echinococcus granulosus).

(c)
Clinical features/assessment findings: common in children; commonly affects the tibia, femur, humerus at the bone ends (metaphysis); sudden onset; severe pain; fever with chills and prostration; swelling; hot, red skin; local tenderness over the bone; joint swelling absent initially, may present later; movements free initially, later painful and restricted.

(d)
Conservative treatment: bedrest; immobilization by splint or traction; elevation of the part; warm fomentation; antibiotics (bactericidal agents preferred); analgesics; fluids orally or IV; blood transfusion if necessary. Treatment should start as soon as possible after diagnosis; surgical measures avoided during the first 2-3 days of acute infection, especially in infants and young children.

(e)
Definitive treatment: incision and drainage of the abscess under general anaesthesia; decompression of the medullary canal by burr holes; postoperative immobilization by POP cast or splint with the ankle in neutral position and knee in 20 degree flexion; physiotherapy thereafter - heat therapy (SWD/IRR or heating pad therapy) and, as pain subsides, active exercises for joint movement and muscle strengthening.
questions.question:
A child presents with sudden severe bone pain, fever with chills, and a hot, red, swollen area over a long bone.
(a) What is the diagnosis?
(b) What is the mechanism of injury/pathogenesis?
(c) What are the clinical features and physiotherapy assessment findings?
(d) What is the immediate and conservative management?
(e) What are the definitive treatment options?

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Pathology: myositis ossificans is heterotopic ossification in the muscles after an injury.
• Stages/causes: thought to be due to muscle damage; can occur without a local injury, e.g. in an unconscious or paraplegic patient.
• Sites: usually occurs in dislocation of the elbow, or after a blow to the brachialis, deltoid or quadriceps muscle.

(b)
• Relation to elbow dislocation: myositis ossificans usually occurs in dislocation of the elbow or after a blow to the brachialis, so it is a recognised complication in the region of the elbow.
• Relation to supracondylar fracture: supracondylar fracture of the humerus (the most common elbow injury in children) similarly carries risks of complications in this region, such as vascular insufficiency of the brachial artery, compartment syndrome, cubitus varus deformity, and Volkmann's ischaemic contracture, reflecting the vulnerability of the soft tissues around the elbow following trauma in this region.

(c)
• Spread to joint stiffness/ankylosis: clinical features of myositis ossificans are pain, soft tissue tenderness, local swelling, joint stiffness and limitation of movement.
• Continued: X-rays are normal early, later showing fluffy calcification in the soft tissue.
• Continued: in extreme cases, bone bridges the joint, producing complete loss of movement, described as extra-articular ankylosis - heterotopic bone formation in the muscle spreads its effect to fix the adjacent joint itself, beyond the original muscle injury.
• Continued: this parallels joint stiffness generally, caused by oedema and fibrosis of the capsule, ligaments and muscle around a joint, or adhesion of soft tissue to itself or underlying bone, following immobilisation after fracture or dislocation.

(d)
• Physiotherapy, early stage: the joint should be rested in the early stage.
• Continued: gentle active movements are then introduced.
• Continued: when the condition has stabilised, excision of the bony mass may be performed, and anti-inflammatory drugs may reduce joint stiffness.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Definition: cervical spondylosis (syn. degenerative arthritis) is a degenerative condition characterized by degeneration of the intervertebral discs.
• It features bony ridges running across the anterior surface of the neural canal, and osteophytes from the neurocentral joints of Luschka projecting backwards into the intervertebral foramen; common in persons above 35 years of age.
• Aetiology: direct trauma (violence); repetitive strain activity (RSA); fall from a height; degenerative changes (osteoarthritis).
• Clinical features: pain referred to the occipital or post-auricular areas and between the shoulder blades; fever and night sweats; weight loss.
• Further clinical features: swelling over the nape of the neck; numbness of the arms and fingers; movements of the neck and shoulder painful and restricted.
• Investigations: X-rays of the cervical spine (AP and lateral views) show straightening of the spine with loss of normal anterior convexity, reduced disc space, and osteophyte formation as a late finding.
• Further investigation: MRI, to demonstrate nerve root or spinal cord compression.

(b)
Effect on function: the condition may be symptomless, or may cause neurological symptoms with painful, restricted neck and shoulder movement.

(c)
• Conservative management: ice packs or warm fomentation, SWD or IR therapy; a cervical collar for a short (2-week) period to avoid muscle atrophy; a cervical brace; cervical traction (continuous or periodic); analgesics plus NSAIDs; exercises.
• Surgical management: excision of involved nerves; arthrodesis; division of dentate ligaments; relief of intraforaminal compression by osteophytes on multiple nerve roots; fasciectomy; after care includes wearing a collar for 1 month.
• Rehabilitation/physiotherapy management: exercises of the neck started as soon as possible after surgery.
• Ongoing physiotherapy: isometric and other exercises to maintain muscle power and flexibility of the neck muscles.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the mechanism, types (instability criteria), clinical features and complications of Colles' fracture.
(b) State the precautions for closed reduction and casting of this fracture.
(c) Explain the biomechanical basis of the "dinner fork" deformity.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Mechanism: fracture of the distal radius with dorsal displacement of the hand, usually resulting from a fall on an outstretched hand; named after Abraham Colles.
• Types/instability criteria: dorsal tilt greater than 20 degrees, comminuted fracture, avulsion of the ulnar styloid process, intra-articular displacement greater than 1mm, and loss of radial height greater than 2mm increase the likelihood of requiring operative management.
• Clinical features: severe pain that worsens with grip and hand movements, swelling and tenderness of the wrist and hand, obvious wrist deformity (the "dinner fork" appearance).

(b)
• Precautions: undisplaced fractures are managed in a cast.
• Continued: fractures with angulation/displacement are managed with closed reduction.
• Continued: fractures with significant angulation/displacement are managed with open reduction and internal fixation.
• Continued: postoperatively, in the immediate phase (day 1-10), the wrist is kept non-weight bearing with no lifting, pushing, pulling or forceful gripping, using a custom volar wrist orthotic or wrist cock-up splint, with the arm elevated above heart level when resting to manage oedema.

(c)
• Biomechanical basis: a fall onto an outstretched hand transmits force along the forearm to the distal radius.
• Continued: this force drives the distal radial fragment into dorsal displacement/angulation relative to the shaft.
• Continued: the dorsally displaced, angulated distal fragment, together with the hand it carries, produces the characteristic "dinner fork" silhouette when the wrist is viewed from the side.
• Continued: instability criteria such as dorsal tilt greater than 20 degrees and loss of radial height greater than 2mm reflect the degree of this dorsal angulation and collapse, which is why more severe deformity by these criteria predicts the need for surgical rather than closed management.

(a)
Anatomy: the proximal humerus comprises four main osseous segments - the humeral head, lesser tuberosity, greater tuberosity and the humeral shaft; the shoulder has the greatest joint range of motion due to a shallow glenoid fossa that is only 25% of the humeral head, with stability provided mainly by soft tissue.

(b)
Epidemiology: proximal humeral fractures account for 4-6% of all fractures and 45% of all humeral fractures; 75% occur in patients older than 60 years, more common in older women; in young individuals, high-energy trauma causes the fracture, mostly as part of polytrauma.

(c)
Aetiology: three main loading modes - compressive loading of the glenoid onto the humeral head, bending forces at the surgical neck, and tension forces of the rotator cuff at the greater and lesser tuberosities; the most common cause is a fall onto an outstretched upper extremity from standing height in older, osteoporotic women.

(d)
• Clinical features: painful and restricted shoulder; obvious deformity indicative of glenohumeral dislocation; swelling and ecchymosis are common.
• Continued: nerve damage is uncommon, but there is a risk of vascular injury.

(e)
Treatment: minimally displaced fractures - analgesia and sling for 3-4 weeks; displaced fractures - open reduction and internal fixation; complications include shoulder stiffness, dislocation and unstable shoulder.

(f)
• Clinical basis: 75% of humerus fractures occur in patients older than 60, more common in older women, and the most common mechanism is a fall onto an outstretched upper extremity from standing height in older, osteoporotic women - the reduced bone density of osteoporosis renders the proximal humerus vulnerable to fracture from this relatively low-energy fall.
• Continued: in contrast, young individuals require high-energy trauma, usually as part of polytrauma, to sustain the same injury, reflecting their stronger bone stock.

(g)
• Distinguishing feature 1: anatomical neck fractures are uncommon.
• Distinguishing feature 2: anatomical neck fractures have a poor prognosis because of interference with the vascular supply to the humeral head.
• Distinguishing feature 3: the surgical neck of the humerus, distal to the tuberosities, is a common site for fractures.
• Distinguishing feature 4: surgical neck fractures result from the three loading modes described and are the fracture pattern typically produced by a fall onto an outstretched arm
