A patient requires amputation through the forearm at the junction of the middle and distal thirds, to provide an adequately long stump for powerful activation of the artificial limb.
(a) What is the diagnosis/indication for amputation?
(b) What surgery/procedure is named?
(c) What is the post-operative physiotherapy by phase?
(d) What are the precautions and contraindications?
(e) What is the expected functional outcome?
questions.answerText:
(a)
Indication: amputation through the forearm, upper limb amputation being mainly due to trauma.

(b)
Procedure named: amputation through the forearm at the junction of the middle and distal thirds.

(c)
Physiotherapy management: occupational therapist plays a vital role in functional rehabilitation; assisted exercises followed by a free active exercise regimen

(d)
Precautions: short forearm stumps are less effective in activating the prosthesis and are more difficult to fit, so the site is deliberately chosen at the junction of the middle and distal thirds rather than more proximally; the end of the stump is smoothened with a terminal scar.

(e)
Functional outcome: pronation and supination are preserved at this amputation level, allowing a functionally adequate stump for powering the artificial limb.

questions.question:
An elderly patient with an old rupture of the collateral and cruciate ligaments of the knee is assessed for possible ligament reconstruction; movements of the knee are painless but restricted, with muscle weakness and variable swelling and tenderness.
(a) What are the risk factors for this condition?
(b) What are the late complications of this condition?
(c) Discuss the management options, conservative versus surgical, and justify one approach.
(d) What is the physiotherapy role?
questions.answerText:
(a)
Risk factors: Traumatic etiology, with damaged articular surfaces, torn ligaments, torn menisci, arthritic changes, and a degenerative joint; the reactions of acute trauma are absent, making the joint chronically unstable though diagnosis is more precise.

(b)
Complications: Late - with damaged articular surfaces, reconstruction of the ligaments is of little practical value; if the muscles controlling the joint (quadriceps, hamstring, gastrosoleus) are not strong enough, the joint becomes unstable/flail; surgery cannot fully restore the structure and function of the original ligaments.

(c)
Management options: Surgical reconstruction is the only management option described. Preoperative criteria considered include the age and general health of the patient (an elderly, debilitated patient may be better managed in a brace or with a cane/crutches rather than surgery), the condition of the articular surfaces, the strength of the controlling muscles, and which particular ligaments are ruptured (a collateral ligament with valgus/varus instability and recurrent IDK is reconstructed; a cruciate ligament with anterior/posterior instability alone does not justify reconstruction, though the ACL may be reconstructed for persisting instability). Given the typically poor muscle strength of an elderly, debilitated patient, conservative management with a brace, cane or crutches is justified over surgical reconstruction.

(d)
Physiotherapy role: Assisted passive exercises by the physiotherapist progressed to free active exercises by the patient.

questions.question:
A diabetic patient presents with claw toes, callosities, diffuse pain, impaired sensation, and absent reaction of hyperemia in the foot, with muscles appearing brick red to black.
(a) What are the risk factors for this condition?
(b) What are the early and late complications?
(c) What are the conservative and surgical management options, and which would you justify?
(d) What is the physiotherapy role?
questions.answerText:
(a)
Risk factors: three combined factors, namely peripheral neuritis causing trophic changes, atheroma of arteries causing ischemia, and hyperglycemia lowering tissue resistance to infection.

(b)
Complications: dry or moist gangrene, diffuse pain, impaired sensation with vasomotor disturbance, absent reaction of hyperemia, brick red/green/black muscle discoloration, loss of reflexes, and claw toes with callosities; progression may require amputation as a life-saving measure.

(c)
Management: conservative treatment includes control of diabetes by diet, exercise, and insulin or antidiabetic drugs, analgesics/NSAIDs, vasodilators, and local care keeping the part dry and well-aerated. Surgical treatment, justified when conservative measures fail to salvage the limb, is amputation as a life-saving measure, using conservative, semi-conservative, or radical (definitive) regional amputation of the leg depending on demarcation and blood supply.

(d)
Physiotherapy role: explaining treatment and teaching strengthening exercises; breathing and foot exercises (active toe and ankle movements) as soon as possible to prevent DVT; recording skin temperature and colour for postoperative complications; avoiding strenuous exercise after arterial grafting, with walking allowed after 2 to 3 days and walking pattern corrected daily.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old man falls from a height and lands on his heel. He presents with pain in the affected heel.
(a) State the most likely diagnosis.
(b) Discuss the predisposing factors and pathophysiology of this condition.
(c) Outline the management, including the physiotherapy role.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Calcaneal fracture.

(b)
Occurs in patients aged 30-50 years, with peak incidence at 45 years; males are affected 5 times more than females; commonly caused by motor vehicle accidents or falls from a height. There is a high rate of associated injuries with falls from height, including lumbar compression fractures and forearm fractures; ankle, femur and elbow fractures are also common. Fractures are classified as extra-articular or intra-articular.

(c)
For intra-articular joint fracture, open reduction and internal fixation is usually necessary. For extra-articular fracture, a Robert Jones dressing, bulky compression dressing, rest, ice and elevation, with orthopaedic follow-up care. Physiotherapy role: soft tissue massage, joint mobilisation, electrotherapy (e.g. ultrasound, TENS), taping or bracing, which are vital to hasten healing; a short leg cast/splint/protective boot/CAM walker is used for 4-6 weeks, with non-weight bearing followed by progressive partial then full weight bearing over another 4-6 weeks.

(a)
Ruptured biceps tendon (long head).

(b)
Mechanism of injury: direct violence; RSA; fall from a height; neoplastic. Rupture is usually spontaneous, due to a degenerative (wear and tear) ageing process, and usually affects middle and old aged persons.

(c)
Clinical features/assessment findings: pain; swelling - a bulge in the lower end of the upper arm becomes prominent on flexing the elbow against resistance; local tenderness; movements of the shoulder and elbow restricted.

(d)
Conservative treatment (indication: incomplete tear): immobilization with an arm sling/pouch; analgesics and NSAIDs; SWD or IRR heat therapy.

(e)
Definitive treatment (indication: complete tear or an old tear): surgery - repair of the torn muscle; after care - rest in an arm sling/pouch with the elbow flexed for 3 weeks; physiotherapy thereafter - heat therapy (SWD/IRR or heating pad therapy) and, as pain subsides, active exercises for joint movement and muscle strengthening.
questions.question:
A middle-aged/elderly patient sustains a spontaneous rupture of the long head of biceps after a trivial injury, on a background of degenerative wear and tear.
(a) What is the diagnosis?
(b) What is the mechanism of injury and pathogenesis?
(c) What are the clinical features and physiotherapy assessment findings?
(d) What is the immediate and conservative management?
(e) What are the definitive treatment options?

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Mechanism: developmental defects, localized and temporary cessation of ossification, and abnormal periosteal growth.
• Pathogenesis: grossly the lesional tissue is friable, vividly rusty coloured, with discrete bright yellow foci; histologically these are cellular fibromas containing giant cells and clusters of macrophages containing lipid or iron, and are developmental defects or hamartomas.

(b)
• Type — metaphyseal defect: usually in the first decade, small, innocuous and asymptomatic, occurring most often in the distal femoral metaphysis, with X-rays showing small bowl-shaped defects located eccentrically, sclerosed and scalloped bony margins and absent peripheral cortex.
• Type — nonosteogenic fibroma: usually in the second decade, in the long bones of the lower limb (tibia and fibula), rarely multiple, with X-rays showing sclerotic and scalloped bony margins and trabeculated or loculated lesions.

(c)
• Complications: pain, swelling, and local tenderness.
• Further complications: painful restricted movement of the adjoining joint, muscular weakness/wasting, and pathological fracture.

(d)
Evolution/healing: metaphyseal defects exist for about 2-3 years and then disappear gradually, with the occupied area ossifying and resuming a normal trabecular pattern.

(e)
• Management principles (conservative): analgesics and NSAIDs, and warm fomentation, SWD or IR therapy.
• Management principles (surgical, indicated on failure of conservative treatment): curettage of lesions in long bones, or excision of expanded vertebral lesions with adjoining involved tissue.

(f)
• Physiotherapy management: regular exercise, especially weight-bearing, under the supervision and teaching of the physiotherapist.
• Further physiotherapy: SWD/IRR.
questions.question:
Regarding metaphyseal fibrous defect and non-osteogenic fibroma:
(a) What is the mechanism/developmental basis?

questions.answerText:
(a)
Structure involved: compression of the neurovascular structures supplying the upper limb.

(b)
Functional impairment: pain radiating to the nape of the neck, axilla, shoulder girdle, arm, forearm and hand; paresthesia of the volar aspect of the 4th and 5th digits, aggravated at night or by strenuous exercise; muscular weakness and atrophy; vascular changes - pallor of the fingers on elevation of the arm, cold sensitivity, digital gangrene; deep reflexes unaffected.

(c)
Differential diagnoses: osteoarthritis of the cervical spine; periarthritis of the shoulder; cervicobrachial pain syndromes.

(d)
Clinical reasoning: conservative treatment (rest, avoidance of aggravating strenuous exercises, improving posture, analgesics/NSAIDs) is tried first, since surgery is more likely to relieve the neurological rather than the vascular component and is reserved for failure of conservative measures (surgical decompression of nerves); physiotherapy management focuses on isometric and other exercises to maintain muscle power and flexibility of the neck muscles.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Indication: amputation through the ankle where sound tissues remain round the heel, fulfilling the criteria for the bone level at the distal end of the tibia, 0.5 cm above the ankle joint.

(b)
Procedure named: Syme amputation, the classical example of an end-bearing stump.

(c)
After care: sutures removed after 2 weeks; walking cast applied until shrinkage is complete; prosthesis then applied. Physiotherapy: occupational therapy plays a vital role in functional rehabilitation, with assisted exercises followed by a free active exercise regimen.

(d)
Precautions: from a permanent efficiency standpoint it is not an ideal amputation, since the skin pad forms a firm, non-mobile weight-bearing surface with a lifespan of 5 to 10 years, after which re-amputation with a 15 cm tibial stump becomes mandatory.

Functional outcome: the patient can put weight on the leg even without a prosthesis, since the end of the stump is formed by heel skin already accustomed to weight bearing, giving good early functional use pending eventual re-amputation.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Ruptured tendocalcaneus (Achilles tendon).

(b)
Mechanism of injury: direct trauma; RSA; sports injury. Pathogenesis: extravasation of blood within the muscle sheath, at the site of injury or at a distance from it.

(c)
Clinical features/assessment findings: pain; a gap visible and palpable at the site of rupture; local tenderness; movements painful and restricted. (Differential diagnosis: rupture of the plantaris tendon, in younger patients.)

(d)
Conservative treatment: rest; pressure dressings; analgesics, NSAIDs; antibiotics.

(e)
Definitive treatment (of choice): surgery - suturing of the tendon; postoperatively a long leg cast is applied with the knee flexed and foot in an equinus position, with wire sutures protruding through the cast; after care - removal of the cast and wires after 4 weeks, then a walking cast for a further 4 weeks.

(a) Define and classify gigantism and acromegaly.
(b) What are the causes?
(c) What are the clinical features?
(d) What investigations are used?
(e) What are the complications?
(f) Distinguish gigantism from acromegaly.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Definition: hyperpituitarism due to overactivity (excessive growth hormone) of the anterior pituitary lobe, formed by a benign adenoma, occurring before closure of the epiphyses of the long bones (gigantism) or after their closure (acromegaly).
• Classification/pathogenesis: caused by a hyperactive eosinophilic portion of the anterior pituitary lobe, with onset before or after closure of the epiphyses of the long bones.

(b)
• Causes: tumours of the anterior pituitary lobe (benign adenoma, carcinoma).
• Further causes: transient (fugitive) acromegaly.

(c)
• Clinical features: excessive growth of the hands (increased glove size), feet (increased shoe size), jaw (protruded lower jaw), malar bones, separation of teeth, chest (increased AP diameter) and internal organs, with kyphosis, big hands reaching down to the knees, and a protruded lower jaw (Gorilla type).
• Further features: amenorrhea, headache, sweating, weakness, aches and pains in the limbs and backache, hypotension, and loss of visual fields.

(d)
• Investigations: CBC, ESR, elevated serum inorganic phosphorus, elevated BMR, low FSH level, glycosuria, hyperglycaemia and hypercalciuria.
• Further investigations: normal T4 and PBI, eye examination possibly showing bitemporal hemianopsia, and skull X-ray possibly showing a large sella with destroyed clinoids, large frontal sinuses, thickened skull and long bones, and dorsal kyphosis.

(e)
• Complications: pressure on adjoining structures, and carpal tunnel syndrome.
• Further complications: cord compression due to large discs, rupture of the tumour into the brain or sinuses, and heart failure.

(f)
• Gigantism occurs when hyperpituitarism begins before closure of the epiphyses of the long bones, so excess growth hormone acts on bones still capable of longitudinal growth.
• Acromegaly occurs when hyperpituitarism begins after closure of the epiphyses, producing the characteristic thickening and deformity of bone and soft tissue rather than increased height.

questions.question:
(a) State the mechanism of injury in internal derangement of the temporomandibular joint.
(b) State the types of this condition.
(c) State the clinical findings produced, including the relevant investigations.
(d) State the management principles for this condition.
(e) Explain the physiotherapy management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Mechanism: Direct trauma - violence, road/street accident, sports injury, fall downstairs, or degeneration of the disc or degenerative arthritis.

(b)
• Types: Degenerated articular disc, either torn or wrinkled.
• continued: Degenerative arthritic changes of the joint.

(c)
• Clinical findings: Pain; local tenderness; snapping or popping of the joint; movements painful and restricted.
• Investigations: X-rays of the TM joint (AP and lateral views) to rule out any bony lesion; MRI of the TM joint.

(d)
• Management principles (conservative): Rest; analgesics/NSAIDs; warm fomentation; immobilization with a mandibular splint.
• Management principles (surgical, usually contraindicated unless pain is severe and not relieved by conservative measures): Excision of the disc for a torn articular disc; repair for ruptured ligaments.
• Management principles (surgical, continued): Reduction (closed or open) for dislocation/subluxation; resection of the mandibular condyle for degenerative arthritis or recurrent subluxation.

(e)
• Physiotherapy management: Assisted passive exercises by the physiotherapist.
• Physiotherapy management (continued): Progressed to free active exercises by the patient.

(a)
Mechanism/aetiology: traumatic (violence), repetitive strain activity, sports injury, or an inflammatory cause.

(b)
Types/pathogenesis: thickening of the flexor tendon or a constriction in the tendon sheath as it enters the fibro-osseous tunnel at the level of the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint; in infants several fingers of both hands are often affected, whereas in adults usually a single finger or thumb is affected.

(c)
• Deformity: difficulty in flexing or extending the affected finger, with snapping or triggering of the distal joint - little force suddenly releases the finger with a click.
• Further clinical signs: a nodule is palpated opposite the MP joint of the affected finger.
• Investigation: X-ray of the hand, AP and lateral views.

(d)
• Management principle, conservative: active exercises; analgesics and NSAIDs.
• Management principle, surgical (indicated on failure of conservative treatment): slitting the fibro-osseous tunnel at the level of the constriction, followed by physiotherapy as after care.

(e)

• Physiotherapy management, stage 2: wax bath therapy.
• Additional physiotherapy technique described: massage by finger kneading to mobilize the tendon and reduce swelling, with passive stretching to restore flexion and progressive increase of PIP joint flexion.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Whiplash (acceleration-deceleration cervical injury).

(b)
Commonly results from rear-end automobile accidents; results from sharp hyperextension and flexion of the neck that damages muscles, ligaments, discs and nerve tissue. Symptoms are often delayed 12-24 hours if the injury is mild; anterior pain diminishes within several days while posterior pain persists or intensifies; may also cause dizziness, gait disturbance, vomiting, headache, nuchal rigidity, neck muscle asymmetry and rigidity/numbness in the arms.

(c)
Full cervical spine X-rays are required to rule out cervical fracture; if X-rays are negative, physical examination focuses on motor ability and sensation below the cervical spine to detect nerve root compression; the prognosis is excellent, with symptoms usually subsiding with treatment. Physiotherapy role: test the alar and transverse ligaments for laxity before evaluating the cervical region and avoid range-of-motion exercises if laxity is found; use cervical collars for a short period to avoid healing in a faulty position; use massage and muscle-setting techniques to maintain circulation and promote relaxation; avoid stretching if muscle guarding is present.
questions.question:
A driver involved in a rear-end automobile collision presents with moderate to severe anterior and posterior neck pain that developed within several hours, later associated with dizziness and headache.
(a) State the most likely diagnosis.
(b) Discuss the predisposing factors and pathophysiology of this condition.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Mechanism: Direct violence (for both ACL and PCL injury); in PCL injury specifically, the tibia is forced backwards.

(b)
Types: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury and posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) injury; isolated tears are uncommon, and ACL injury is usually associated with tears of the medial collateral ligament and/or medial meniscus.

(c)
• Clinical findings (ACL): Abnormal forward movement of the tibia over the femur; the knee can be hyperextended.
• Clinical findings (PCL): Abnormal backward movement of the tibia over the femur.
• Investigation: X-ray of the knee (AP and lateral views), for any bony lesion.

(d)
Complications: Associated tears of the medial collateral ligament and/or medial meniscus, in the case of ACL injury.

(e)
• Management principles (conservative, ACL): A plaster cylinder for 6 weeks, if the anterior tibial spine is intact, with after-care physiotherapy.
• Management principles (surgical, ACL): ORIF (screw fixation) if the anterior tibial spine is fractured; re-attachment or ACL replacement (using the tendon of semitendinosus), the treatment of choice if the ACL is avulsed; repair of associated tears of the medial collateral ligament and medial meniscus.
• Management principles (PCL): Management of a PCL injury is the same as for an ACL injury.

(f)
• Physiotherapy management: Assisted passive exercises by the physiotherapist.
• Physiotherapy management (continued): Progressed to free active exercises by the patient.

(a) Define coccygodynia.
(b) State its etiology.
(c) State its pathogenesis.
(d) State the clinical features.
(e) State the investigation used.
(f) Explain how this condition affects function.
(g) Outline the conservative, surgical, and rehabilitation management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Definition: Coccygodynia (coccydynea) is a painful coccyx; it may be of functional origin, or may be organic, resulting either from rigidity of the sacrococcygeal joint or from traumatic arthritis of this joint without rigidity.

(b)
• Etiology (traumatic): Violence, fall from a height, sports injury.
• Etiology (other): Functional; organic; spasmodic.

(c)
Pathogenesis: Arthritic changes.

(d)
Clinical features: a painful coccyx, with painful sitting due to pressure on the bone.

(e)
Investigation: X-rays of the pelvis (AP view).

(f)
• Effect on function (functional type): Pain often decreases without treatment or is increased by any treatment, especially in highly nervous persons.
• Effect on function (organic type): Painful sitting occurs due to pressure on the bone from a rigid sacrococcygeal joint.

(g)
• Conservative management: Rest, warm fomentation/SWD/IR, analgesics/NSAIDs, and local infiltration with injection lignocaine 1% (1-5 ml) plain, mixed with 1 ml of triamcinolone, hydrocortisone acetate, or methylprednisolone.
• Surgical indications: Organic coccygodynea with a rigid sacrococcygeal joint and painful sitting, and traumatic arthritis developed in a movable sacrococcygeal joint; the surgery is coccygectomy.
• Surgical contraindications: Functional coccygodynea, traumatic arthritis with low backache, and acute injuries of the sacrococcygeal joint.
• Rehabilitation/after care: Toilet of the wound with full care to prevent infection; physiotherapy - assisted passive exercises by the physiotherapist progressed to free active exercises by the patient.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the mechanism, types, clinical features and complications of cervical spine injury based on the two-column theory of stability.
(b) State the safe site/precautions for skull traction (halo) in cervical spine injury.
(c) Explain the biomechanical basis of two-column stability and its failure.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Mechanism: injuries of the vertebral column cluster at junctional areas of stress concentration - the craniocervical junction, the cervicothoracic junction, and the thoracolumbar junction, where a rigid segment meets a more flexible segment.
• Types: based on direction of injury force - Type A compression, Type B distraction, Type C rotational; categorised further into compression fracture, burst fracture, flexion-distraction injury, and fracture-dislocation.
• Continued: mechanisms include axial loading, flexion force, hyperextension force, flexion-rotation force, hyperextension-rotation, and lateral flexion.
• Clinical features: general indicators of cervical spine instability include involvement of more than one vertebral column, increased or reduced disc space height, increased interspinous distance, facet joint widening, and vertebral compression greater than 25%.
• Complications: cervical spine injuries are less common but more life-threatening than thoracic and lumbar injuries, mostly from whiplash and head injuries; ligament injuries of the spine often heal poorly, causing chronic pain and instability.

(b)
• Precautions: minor compression fractures of the transverse process and spinous process are treated by immobilisation in a collar until the pain has gone.
• Continued: dislocations/subluxations are promptly reduced and rigidly immobilised by skull traction with a 'halo' screwed into the diploe of the skull, and stability is assessed after 3 months.
• Continued: a comprehensive history is necessary, with assessment of respiratory function, evaluation of vertebral injury and neurological impairment level, and review of associated injuries, before instituting or removing traction; routine AP/lateral radiographs are essential and oblique views help avoid superimposing parts.

(c)
• Biomechanical basis: cervical spine stability is provided by two functional vertical columns - the anterior column (vertebral bodies, disc spaces, longitudinal ligaments, annulus fibrosus), which supports compressive load, and the posterior column (pedicles, facets, laminae, spinous processes, posterior ligament complex), which resists tensile stress.
• Continued: as long as one column is intact, the injury is stable; failure of both columns produces instability.
• Continued: the cervical spine is especially susceptible to such failure because it is highly mobile, has relatively small vertebral bodies, and supports the head, which is heavy and acts as a lever.
• Continued: this is also why bilateral facet dislocation (subluxation greater than half the AP diameter of the vertebral body below it) is extremely unstable with a high incidence of spinal cord injury, since it represents failure of both columns.

(a)
Definition: Raynaud's disease is a spasmodic condition, usually in women, affecting the upper limb more than the lower, in which the digital arteries respond excessively to vasospastic stimuli. Buerger's disease (thromboangiitis obliterans) is an episodic and segmental inflammatory and thrombotic disorder of the arteries and veins, mostly in the limbs, especially the lower, usually terminating in gangrene.

(b)
Aetiology: Raynaud's disease is of unknown cause, related to direct trauma from extreme cold exposure, emotional distress, and abnormal sympathetic nervous system activity. Buerger's disease is of unknown cause, associated with a collagen disorder, tobacco/cigarette smoking, and abnormal sympathetic nervous system activity.

(c)
• Clinical features of Raynaud's disease: family history of a vasospastic phenomenon; women aged 15 to 40; pain precipitated by cold and relieved by warmth; intermittent attacks of pallor or cyanosis in the fingers (rarely toes); cold, pale, numb skin with trophic changes; muscle wasting.
• Clinical features of Buerger's disease: mainly signs of arterial insufficiency; men aged 20 to 40; mostly legs affected; persisting, aching or gnawing rest pain and intermittent claudication; cold, pale, numb skin with trophic changes; muscle wasting; diminished sensation; absent or impaired pulses.

(d)
Investigations for both: CBC, ESR, WR (for syphilis), urine for diabetes, Color Doppler, X-ray.

(e)
Complications: gangrene, particularly in Buerger's disease, which usually terminates in gangrene.

(f)
• Differentiation: Raynaud's disease shows symmetrical, bilateral colour changes, mostly in young women, with arterial pulsations not affected.
• Buerger's disease differs by comparatively younger men (20 to 40), predominant lower limb involvement, and impaired or absent pulses; further differentials for Buerger's disease include arteriosclerosis obliterans (older age, hyperlipidemia, vessel calcification, no phlebitis), scleroderma (skin involvement precedes vascular changes), and frostbite (history of cold exposure).

(g)
• Management for Raynaud's disease: conservative treatment includes preventive avoidance of cold exposure, warmth, analgesics/NSAIDs, and vasodilators; surgical sympathectomy is indicated for frequent severe attacks.
• Management for Buerger's disease: conservative treatment includes preventive avoidance of smoking and trauma to the feet, warm stockings, analgesics/NSAIDs, vasodilators, and exercises; surgical sympathectomy aims to eliminate vasospasm, aid collateral circulation, relieve rest pain and claudication, and may precede amputation, which is indicated for gangrene.
• Physiotherapy for Raynaud's disease: active exercises to increase circulatory flow; contrast baths (hot bath 3 minutes, cool bath 1 minute); massage, treating the sacral and lumbar area before the limbs.
• Physiotherapy for Buerger's disease: Buerger's exercises, a pattern of positions encouraging collateral circulation development, repeated 4 to 5 times daily, with improvement determined by decreasing time required for skin colour to change.

(b)
Types/pathogenesis: it is a space-occupying lesion due to median nerve compression in the wrist at the level of the carpal tunnel; any condition that reduces the space of the carpal canal may initiate the symptoms.

(c)

(d)

(e)

Describe femoral neck fracture under the following headings:
(a) Definition
(b) Classification
(c) Aetiology
(d) Clinical features
(e) Treatment
(f) Explain the clinical basis for why femoral neck fracture prevalence increases with age.
(g) Distinguish between Garden type I/II and Garden type III/IV femoral neck fractures.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Definition: femoral neck fracture is a break in the continuity of bone at the neck of the femur, usually from a fall or twisting injury.

(b)
• Classification - Garden: based on displacement (I incomplete; II complete undisplaced; III complete with partial displacement; IV complete with total displacement).
• Classification - Pauwels: based on the angle between the fracture line and the horizontal (I less than 30 degrees, stable; II 30-70 degrees, less stable; III greater than 70 degrees, unstable).

(c)
• Aetiology: minor falls/twisting injuries in the elderly; high-energy trauma in the young; can complicate sickle cell disease; stress in athletes and osteoporotic elderly individuals.
• Predisposing factors: poor physical conditioning, malnutrition, impaired vision, neurologic disease, poor balance, muscle atrophy, anatomic variation.

(d)
• Clinical features, Garden I/II: hip internal rotation, hip pain, may be unable to bear weight.
• Clinical features, Garden III/IV: inability to bear weight, groin pain, hip external rotation, leg length discrepancy.

(e)
Treatment: hip/thighbone fractures heal more rapidly with a better outcome when surgically repaired (internal fixation or joint replacement/arthroplasty).

(f)
Clinical basis: prevalence rises sharply with age - only 2% of fractures occur below age 50 versus 80% above age 50, and prevalence is higher in institutionalised geriatric and cognitively impaired patients, reflecting the cumulative effect of osteoporosis, falls risk and reduced bone quality with ageing.

(g)
• Distinguishing feature 1: Garden I/II are non-displaced (incomplete or complete without displacement) fractures.
• Distinguishing feature 2: Garden III/IV are displaced (partial or total displacement) fractures, clinically differentiated by inability to bear weight, external rotation and leg length discrepancy.
• Distinguishing feature 3: displacement in Garden III/IV raises the risk of avascular necrosis from 7% to 37%, unlike the non-displaced Garden I/II pattern.

(a)
• Mechanism/definition: an open fracture is a break in the skin and underlying soft tissue leading directly into or communicating with the fracture and its haematoma.
• Types (Gustilo and Anderson): Type I - wound less than 1cm, minimal contamination and soft tissue injury, simple fracture pattern; Type II - wound 1-10cm, moderate contamination and comminution; Type III - periosteal stripping and soft tissue coverage required, may require vessel repair in severe cases (subdivided IIIA, IIIB, IIIC).
• Clinical/grading correlation: infection rates rise from 0-2% (Type I) through 2-7% (Type II) to 10-50% (Type III).
• Continued: fracture healing extends from 21-28 weeks (Type I) to 30-35 weeks (Type III), with a 50% amputation rate associated with Type IIIC.
• Complications: infection leading to delayed union, non-union, malunion and loss of function; Type IIIC (major vascular injury requiring repair) carries increased risk of amputation and infection.

(b)
• Precautions, timing: thorough operative debridement is the standard of care for all open fractures, even though evidence shows no significant difference in infection whether surgery occurs before or after 6 hours from injury; adequacy of debridement and time to soft-tissue coverage matter more than strict time to theatre.
• Continued: if presenting late at night, the patient can be kept until morning or at least within 24 hours, unless there is neurovascular compromise, gross soft-tissue contamination, or compartment syndrome.
• Precautions, irrigation: copious irrigation is recommended - 3 litres (one bag) for Type I, 6 litres (two bags) for Type II, and 9 litres (three bags) for Type III wounds.
• Continued: the open wound should initially be left open to prevent anaerobic conditions and facilitate drainage/repeat debridement, though renewed evidence supports primary closure once adequately debrided, with contraindications including inadequate debridement, gross contamination, farm-related or freshwater injuries, delay beyond 12 hours, or compromised tissue viability.

(c)
• Anatomical basis: isolated tibial fracture occurs in 23% of tibial shaft fractures, and both tibia and fibula fracture together in 77% of cases.
• Continued: the tibia is subcutaneous, hence the incidence of open fracture is high.
• Continued: reduced blood supply in the distal one-third of the tibia due to segmental fractures also makes this region known for delayed union and non-union, compounding the risk once a wound is open, which is why the tibia is used as the model bone for the Gustilo and Anderson classification.

(a)
• Mechanism: a rise of serum calcium with a reciprocal fall of serum phosphate, causing withdrawal of calcium from bones, increased urinary excretion of calcium and decreased urinary excretion of phosphate.
• Further mechanism: rarefaction of bones (osteoporosis), formation of bone cysts (osteitis fibrosa cystica), pathological fractures, and renal calculi from calciuria.

(b)
Types/causes: diffuse hyperplasia of all the parathyroids, or a localized tumour (adenoma, or rarely carcinoma) in one of them.

(c)
• Complications/manifestations: skeletal — body aches, joint pains, backache, and pathological fractures of the spine, ribs or long bones.
• Further complications: urinary tract (renal calculi, polyuria, polydipsia, uraemia), gastrointestinal (constipation, peptic ulcer), and hypercalcaemia manifestations (nausea, vomiting, anorexia, restlessness, prostration, tachycardia and hypertension).

(d)
• Preoperative preparation: 4 g of calcium lactate and 1K units of calciferol with 1 L of milk orally once daily for 3 days before surgery.
• Postoperative healing: the same calcium lactate and calciferol regimen with milk, continued for 6 months.

(e)
• Management principles (conservative): IV fluids to minimize calcium phosphate renal stone formation, diuretics (furosemide), hemodialysis (may be life-saving), and calcitonin to lower serum calcium.
• Management principles (surgical, the only curative treatment): parathyroidectomy, indicated for an adenoma or hyperplasia of the parathyroids, via a transverse neck incision, exposure of the thyroid gland, and excision of the tumour or three-quarters of a hyperplastic parathyroid.

(f)
• Physiotherapy management: exercises.
• Further physiotherapy: SWD/IRR.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Definition: a chronic, progressive arthropathy characterised by degeneration (architectural deterioration) of articular cartilage and by hypertrophy (bone formation) at the articular margins, without systemic manifestations; it is the commonest type of arthritis worldwide, commonly affecting the hands, feet, spine and large weight-bearing joints such as the hips and knees.
• Classification: primary (idiopathic, syn. polyarticular degenerative) and secondary (syn. monarticular degenerative) osteoarthritis.

(b)
• Causes of primary osteoarthritis: unknown aetiology, usually active in several joints at the same time, rarely occurring under 40 years, and commonly affecting the DIP joints.
• Causes of secondary osteoarthritis: pre-existing joint disorders — congenital anomaly; trauma to the articular cartilage (intra-articular fracture/dislocation, or extra-articular bony block/torn muscle or tendon); inflammatory disease (rheumatoid arthritis); infection (septic arthritis, tuberculosis); an endocrinal cause (diabetes mellitus); a metabolic cause (hyperparathyroidism); or a neuropathic cause (tabes dorsalis); risk factors include advancing age over 60, sedentary life, being overweight, wrong posture/misuse of the joint, and strenuous exercise including regular stair use.

(c)
• Clinical features: age over 60, insidious onset, morning stiffness, and dull aching pain aggravated by joint use/weight-bearing and relieved by rest, without systemic manifestations.
• Further features: swelling or deformity, muscular wasting, crepitus, and painful restricted movement.

(d)
• Investigations: X-ray showing asymmetric narrowing of the joint space and osteophytes at the joint margins.
• Further investigations: MRI, which may reveal early changes missed on X-ray, and CT scan, indicated in cervical or lumbar spondylosis associated with neurological manifestations.

(e)
• Complications: the progressive joint changes described — synovitis, cartilage wear, subchondral sclerosis/cysts, osteophytes and bony ankylosis.
• Further complication: osteoarthritis itself is noted as a complication of other conditions, such as Paget's disease, from altered mechanics and muscular weakness.

(f)
• Primary osteoarthritis is of unknown cause, tends to be polyarticular and active in several joints at once, rarely occurs before 40 years, and commonly affects the DIP joints.
• Secondary osteoarthritis is monarticular, developing in a joint with a pre-existing congenital, traumatic, inflammatory, infective, endocrinal, metabolic or neuropathic disorder.

(a)
Mechanism/aetiology: direct trauma; vascular embolism; occurs in army/police personnel or athletes due to long marches or races.

(b)
Types/pathogenesis: strenuous exercise results in edema and micro-haemorrhages in the muscles of the anterior compartment of the leg; muscle ischemia develops due to pressure from the edema, leading to muscle necrosis, fibrosis, contractures, paresis and deformities.

(c)
• Deformity: develops in late cases due to fibrous contractures.
• Further clinical signs: common in younger persons, more in males than females; acute pain after strenuous march or exercise; swelling; localized erythema of the skin; loss of function of the anterior tibial, extensor digitorum longus and extensor hallucis longus muscles; paresis between the 1st and 2nd toes (peroneal nerve); diminished or absent dorsalis pedis pulse.

(d)
Complications: contractures, paresis, and deformities in late/established cases.

(e)
• Management principle (surgical, treatment of choice): fasciotomy of the crural fascia; arteriectomy; sympathectomy.
• Postoperative care: immobilization of the leg in a cast in the extended position.

(f)
• Physiotherapy management, stage 1: rest using splints.
• Physiotherapy management, stage 2: heat therapy (SWD/IRR or heat pad therapy).
• Physiotherapy management, stage 3: postoperative exercises under the supervision of the physiotherapist.

Structure/imaging: osteoarthritis of the wrist and of the joints of the hand; X-ray shows asymmetric narrowing of the joint space and osteophytes at the joint margins, with MRI able to reveal early changes missed on X-ray.

(b)
Functional impairment: morning stiffness, dull aching pain aggravated by joint use and relieved by rest, swelling or deformity, muscular wasting, crepitus, and painful restricted movement, without systemic manifestations.

(c)
Differential consideration: primary (idiopathic, polyarticular degenerative) osteoarthritis is of unknown cause, is often active in several joints at once, rarely occurs under 40 years, and commonly affects the DIP joints; secondary (monarticular degenerative) osteoarthritis affects a joint due to a pre-existing disorder such as a congenital anomaly, trauma to the articular cartilage, inflammatory disease (rheumatoid arthritis), infection (septic arthritis, tuberculosis), an endocrinal cause (diabetes mellitus), a metabolic cause (hyperparathyroidism), or a neuropathic cause (tabes dorsalis).

(a)
Mechanism: traction force during obstructed labour (forced delivery of the fetus), road/street accident, fall of a heavy weight on the shoulder, or direct violence (blow, gunshot).

(b)
Type: upper lesion of the brachial plexus due to involvement of the fifth and sixth (and sometimes sixth) cervical nerve roots, from an increased angle between the neck and shoulder.

(c)
Deformity: arm hangs by the side, adducted and internally rotated; elbow fully extended; forearm fully pronated; wrist and fingers flexed.

(d)
Complications: muscular wasting (thin, soft, flabby in lesions of long duration); loss of muscle power, tone, sensations and reflexes; skin cold, glazed and smooth, with vasomotor changes (pallor, cyanosis, redness, shiny scaly skin, brittle nails) in irritating lesions.

(e)
Healing: recovery is likely to occur within a few weeks in many cases, though neurotmesis lesions carry a poorer prognosis.

(f)
• Management principles: conservative treatment as soon as possible with immobilization of the arm in a relaxation position (right-angled at shoulder, forearm flexed and supinated) to relax deltoid, spinati, biceps, brachialis, and supinator, together with physiotherapy.
• Surgical treatment is indicated for neurotmesis lesions: exploration of the brachial plexus (often yielding little recovery due to difficulty approximating retracted torn nerve ends) and suturing, which is a difficult procedure, so it is often better to suture two nerve roots to one trunk.

(g)
• Physiotherapy at the acute stage: advice on carrying out as much movement of the limb as possible and reassurance about recovery of normal function, since recovery is likely within a few weeks in many cases.
• Physiotherapy during immobilization: the arm is held in the relaxation position by splints while gentle movement is encouraged as tolerated.
• Physiotherapy following surgical exploration: continues alongside the conservative approach of encouraging movement and providing reassurance.
• Segmental innervation affected includes deltoid, spinati, rhomboids, teres minor, biceps, brachialis, brachioradialis, and supinator, explaining the loss of abduction at the shoulder.
• Overall, physiotherapy management may not require extensive treatment as recovery is likely within a few weeks, but ongoing patient advice and reassurance remain central to care.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is an inflammatory syndrome that primarily involves the vascular and connective tissues of multiple organs, resulting in multiple local and systemic manifestations. Scleroderma (progressive systemic sclerosis) refers to a range of long-term, progressive disorders in which the skin and connective tissues tighten and harden, occurring in localized and systemic forms.

(b)
• SLE is associated with viral infection (myxoviruses - measles and parainfluenza type I, and Epstein-Barr virus, demonstrated in capillary endothelial cells) and heredity, with an altered immune mechanism causing necrotizing vasculitis.
• Scleroderma is of unknown aetiology, with insidious connective tissue proliferation in the dermis and multiple internal organs, with early and progressive small arterial involvement disproportionate to the fibrosis.

(c)
• Clinical features, SLE: systemic - fever, sweating, weight loss, weakness, malaise, fatigue; skin - erythematous butterfly rash on the face or sun-exposed areas; eyes - corneal opacity, exudative retinopathy; also lung, cardiovascular, hematopoietic, gastrointestinal, hepatic, renal, musculoskeletal (myalgia, arthralgia, myositis, polyarthritis, synovial nodules and cysts), CNS, and lymphatic involvement.
• Clinical features, scleroderma: common in middle-aged women; localized and systemic forms; stiffness and sweating of the hands and feet with ulceration of fingers and toes; positive Raynaud's phenomenon; skin hard, thick, parched, glossy, pigmented, calcified around joints; joint arthritis; GI tract (dysphagia, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea); chest, cardiovascular, CNS and renal involvement.

(d)
• Investigations, SLE: CBC (normochromic/normocytic or hemolytic anemia); positive Coombs test; mild leukopenia with lymphopenia; raised ESR; elevated serum globulin IgG; antinuclear antibodies present; low serum complement; positive RA factor; LE cells in blood and tissues (diagnostic); abnormal LFT; false positive STS; urine showing proteinuria, hematuria, casts; skin and kidney biopsy detecting antibody fluorescence.
• Investigations, scleroderma: raised ESR; elevated serum globulin; LE phenomenon or increased antinuclear antibodies; urine proteinuria and casts; X-ray showing subcutaneous calcification, osteoporosis, bone destruction; plain abdominal X-ray showing loss of peristalsis.

(e)
• Complications/prognosis, SLE: mild disease improves with corticosteroid therapy; fulminant disease may cause death within a few weeks despite treatment.
• Complications/prognosis, scleroderma: prognosis better in young women; survival rate around seven years, with death occurring due to renal or cardiac failure or infection.

(f)
• Distinguishing the two conditions: SLE is primarily a vasculitic, multisystem inflammatory disease with a characteristic butterfly facial rash and LE cells in the blood, whereas scleroderma is characterized by hardening/tightening of the skin and connective tissue with Raynaud's phenomenon and calcinosis, without the LE-cell serology of SLE.
• Management, SLE: symptomatic and supportive; high-caloric, high-vitamin diet with iron supplements; avoidance of sunlight/ultraviolet and cold exposure; drugs - corticosteroids, antimalarials (chloroquine, caution for toxic retinopathy), antibiotics, analgesics, immunosuppressive agents.
• Management, scleroderma, and physiotherapy for both: scleroderma is managed symptomatically, avoiding cold exposure, with vasodilators and corticosteroids; physiotherapy for scleroderma comprises passive movements to stretch and mobilize skin and fascia, skin rolling, kneading and possible active exercise, while for SLE the affected joints during active exacerbation are treated as for rheumatoid arthritis, with a daily active exercise programme devised between exacerbations.

(b)
Complications: tophi - nodular masses of urate crystals deposited in soft tissues

(c)
General measures: rest with the limb raised; control of body weight; control of alcohol intake; a purine-restricted diet (e.g. red meat, pulses, cheese); plenty of oral fluids; control of hypertension and hyperlipidemia. Drugs: NSAIDs (indomethacin, naproxen, diclofenac), colchicine (IV colchicine given rarely), allopurinol, probenecid; corticosteroids used only when NSAIDs and colchicine are non-effective; intra-articular injection indicated in monoarticular gout. Only this medical/drug-based management is described rather than a distinct surgical option, so medical management as above is the justified approach.

(d)
Physiotherapy role: physiotherapy and occupational therapy intervention can ameliorate or prevent problems with activities of daily living or employment.
questions.question:
A patient develops sudden agonizing pain, swelling, redness and warmth of the first metatarsophalangeal joint, beginning at night.
(a) What are the risk factors for this condition?
(b) What are its complications?
(c) What are the conservative and surgical management options, and which would you justify choosing?
(d) What is the role of physiotherapy?

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Mechanism: aetiology is uncertain, possibly vascular disorders (hemorrhage, venous dilatations) or trauma (parosteal myositis ossificans).
• Pathogenesis: a thin shell of bone forms the outer surface while the interior is loculated by connective tissue septa forming lakes of dark blood that oozes profusely without pulsation.

(b)
• Gross type: lesions vary markedly in gross structure — some are entirely vascular, others contain connective tissue that is markedly ossified.
• Histological type: no characteristic tissue; principal features are connective tissue septa with adjoining large unlined spaces, varying ossification, and localized giant cell reaction within the septa.

(c)
• Complications: pathological fracture.
• The lesion is diagnosed via X-rays showing a localized bulging mass with heavy trabeculations or loculation and slight irregular cortical erosion.

(d)
Aftercare: after surgery, aftercare is physiotherapy exercises.

(e)
• Management principles (conservative): analgesics and NSAIDs, and warm fomentation, SWD or IR therapy.
• Management principles (surgical, indicated on failure of conservative treatment): curettage of lesions in long bones, or excision of expanded vertebral lesions with adjoining involved tissue.

(f)
• Physiotherapy management: regular exercise, especially weight-bearing, under the supervision and teaching of the physiotherapist.
• Further physiotherapy: heat therapy (SWD/IRR or heat pad therapy); needle aspiration biopsy is used to rule out malignancy.
questions.question:
Regarding aneurysmal bone cyst:
(a) What is the mechanism of the underlying pathology?
(b) What gross and histological types are seen?
(c) What are the complications?
(d) How does management/aftercare proceed?
(e) What are the management principles?
(f) Explain the physiotherapy management.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Mechanism: Direct trauma - violence, road/street accident, sports injury, or fall downstairs.

(b)
• Types (traumatic predisposing factors): Injured deltoid ligament; ruptured lateral ligament; dislocation/subluxation.
• Types (deformed predisposing factor): Angulated tibia or fibula.

(c)
• Clinical findings: Pain; local tenderness; clicking of the joint on moving the ankle; weakness; movements painful and restricted.
• Investigations: X-ray of the ankle (AP and lateral views) to rule out any bony lesion; MRI of the ankle.

(d)
Pathogenesis: a torn capsule/synovia, with ruptured deltoid and lateral ligaments.

(e)
• Management principles - ruptured ligaments: Repair.
• Management principles - dislocation/subluxation: Reduction (closed or open).
• Management principles - angulated tibia or fibula: Osteotomy.

(f)
• Physiotherapy management: Assisted passive exercises by the physiotherapist.
• Physiotherapy management (continued): Progressed to free active exercises by the patient.
questions.question:
(a) State the mechanism of injury in internal derangement of the ankle joint (chronic sprain of ankle).
(b) State the types/predisposing factors of this condition.
(c) State the clinical findings produced, including the relevant investigations.
