Describe pelvic ring fracture under
(a) Anatomy
(b) Classification
(c) Mechanism
(d) Clinical features
(e) Treatment
(f) Explain the clinical basis for why the posterior ligament complex determines pelvic stability.
(g) Distinguish Tile type B from Tile type C pelvic fractures.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Anatomy: the pelvis comprises the sacrum and two innominate bones (ilium, ischium, pubis), joined anteriorly at the symphysis pubis and posteriorly at the paired sacroiliac joints.

(b)
Classification: the two most common systems are Tile and Young; Tile is comprehensive and predicts the need for operative intervention but not morbidity or mortality; Young is based on mechanism of injury, predicts associated injury and estimates mortality but excludes more minor injuries.

(c)
Mechanism: low-energy injuries result in fractures of individual bones (avulsion, low-energy fall, or straddle-type injury); high-energy injuries (RTA, pedestrian-struck, motorcycle accident, fall from height, crush) result in pelvic ring disruption.

(d)
Clinical features: pelvic instability may result in leg-length discrepancy with shortening or a markedly rotated lower extremity; lumbosacral plexus and nerve root injuries may be present.

(e)
• Treatment: fractures amenable to non-operative treatment include lateral impaction injuries with less than 1.5cm displacement, pubic rami fractures with no posterior displacement, and symphyseal gapping less than 2.5cm, managed with protected weight bearing and serial radiographs.
• Continued: if posterior ring displacement exceeds 1cm, weight bearing should be stopped and operative treatment considered.

(f)
• Clinical basis: anterior support structures (symphysis pubis, pubic rami) provide about 40% of pelvic strength, while posterior support structures (sacroiliac complex, sacroiliac ligaments, iliolumbar ligaments) provide about 60%.
• Continued: the posterior sacroiliac ligaments provide most of the stability, with the sacrotuberous ligament maintaining vertical stability and the sacrospinous ligament maintaining rotational control when the posterior sacroiliac ligaments are intact - this is why the degree of posterior structure disruption defines the pelvic stability grade.

(g)
• Distinguishing feature 1: Tile Type B is a partially stable pelvis with incomplete posterior structure disruption, comprising open-book injury (B1), lateral compression injury (B2), and contralateral/bucket-handle injury (B3).
• Distinguishing feature 2: Tile Type C is an unstable pelvis with complete disruption of posterior structures, comprising unilateral injury (C1), bilateral injury with one side Type B and one side Type C (C2), and bilateral Type C injury (C3).
• Distinguishing feature 3: Type B fractures are rotationally unstable but vertically stable, whereas Type C fractures are both rotationally and vertically unstable.
• Distinguishing feature 4: radiographic instability signs (sacroiliac displacement of 5mm in any plane, posterior fracture gap, avulsion of the L5 transverse process/sacral border/ischial spine) guide whether operative fixation is required, particularly in Type C injuries.

(a)
Diagnosis: Charcot's joint of the hip; osteotomy is indicated where the femoral head and neck are destroyed, with reconstruction or arthrodesis as further surgical options.

(b)
Postoperative physiotherapy: the general modalities used for Charcot's joint are muscle-strengthening exercises, traction, heat therapy (SWD/IRR), wax bath therapy, hydrotherapy, massage, ambulation aids, and acupuncture/acupressure and yoga therapy.

(c)
Precautions: osteotomy is indicated specifically where the femoral head and neck are destroyed.
questions.question:
A patient with a destroyed and avascular femoral head and neck due to a neuropathic joint undergoes surgical reconstruction of the hip.
(a) What is the diagnosis and what surgery/procedure is named for a destroyed femoral head and neck?
(b) Describe the post-operative physiotherapy by phase.
(c) What precautions apply to the choice of surgery at the hip?

A young female patient presents with a bony hard swelling in the lower part of the neck, tingling and numbness along the medial side of the forearm and hand, and wasting of the thenar/hypothenar eminence.
(a) What is the diagnosis?
(b) What is the mechanism of injury and pathology?
(c) What are the clinical features and physiotherapy assessment findings?
(d) What is the immediate and conservative management?
(e) What are the definitive treatment options?
questions.answerText:
(a)
Diagnosis: cervical rib syndrome.

(b)
Mechanism: direct trauma (stretching or pressing injury); the lower trunk (C8, D1), formed at the anterior border of scalenus medius immediately above the first rib, is stretched or pressed by an elevated cervical rib pushing between the nerve and the first rib. It is rare (about 1%), more frequent on the right side, and more common in females than males, occurring in younger (puberty) or older (from disease or weakness) patients.

(c)
Features: symptomless, or a bony hard lump in the lower neck; sensory tingling, numbness and pain along the medial forearm and hand; motor wasting of the thenar or hypothenar eminence with weakness; vasomotor sweating of the hand or gangrene. Assessment: X-ray neck (AP and lateral, rib mostly non-visible), CT scan.

(d)
Conservative treatment: postural relief from arm elevation using an arm support; short-wave diathermy or infrared therapy; analgesics and NSAIDs.

(e)
Surgical treatment: timely extraperiosteal excision of the cervical rib and its periosteum; physiotherapy management may not be required as recovery is likely within a few weeks, though advice on movement and reassurance may be needed.

questions.question:
Regarding Paget's disease of bone:
(a) What is the mechanism/pathogenesis?
(b) What types are recognized?
(c) What deformity results?
(d) What are the complications?
(e) How does the disease course/management proceed?
(f) What are the management principles?
(g) Explain the physiotherapy management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Mechanism/pathogenesis: bones become thickened, softened, deformed and fractured, and vertebrae collapse.

(b)
• Types: the disease may affect a single bone or multiple bones, often only a portion of a single bone.
• It affects the spine (usually lumbar region), skull, sternum, ribs, humerus, hipbone, femur and tibia in descending order, sparing small bones, and in a long bone begins at one end and advances to the other.

(c)
• Deformity: bowing of the leg.
• Further deformity: an enlarged skull and thickened facial bones.

(d)
• Complications: pathological fractures of weight-bearing bones such as the femur and tibia.
• Further complications: osteoarthritis, from altered mechanics and muscular weakness.

(e)
Course/management: there is no specific treatment to control the progress of the disease.

(f)
• Management principles (conservative, for relief of pain): analgesics/NSAIDs, and radiotherapy for severe bony pain.
• Management principles (surgical): osteotomy, for relief of pain due to faulty mechanics.

(g)
• Physiotherapy management: required for relief of pain and tenderness of the muscles, and to assist the patient in becoming mobile as soon as possible.
• Further physiotherapy: also required for the fractures or osteoarthritis that may develop as complications; investigations used include diagnostic X-ray showing Paget bone formed/destroyed, a thickened skull and wedged vertebrae.

(a)
Risk factors: Direct trauma/violence, recurrent subluxation or dislocation of the patella, fractured patella, and internal derangement of the knee; obesity and a disturbed quadriceps mechanism (knee lockings) are predisposing factors.

(b)
Complications: Late - degeneration of the articular cartilage frequently results in osteoarthritis of the knee joint, with the patellofemoral joint usually the first joint to undergo degenerative changes, and the joint may become ankylosed.

(c)
Management options: Conservative (symptomatic) - analgesics/NSAIDs, and closed reduction of any fracture or fracture-dislocation. Surgical - indicated for internal derangement of the knee or arthritic lesions, comprising exploration of the knee joint, shaving of the involved cartilage, arthroplasty, or patellectomy/patelloplasty, followed by an elastic crepe bandage for 1 week, quadriceps/hamstring exercises, and weight bearing with crutches as soon as possible. Surgery is justified once arthritic lesions or internal derangement are present, since symptomatic conservative treatment alone will not address the underlying joint damage.

(d)
Physiotherapy role: Assisted passive exercises by the physiotherapist progressed to free active exercises by the patient.
questions.question:
A patient presents with deep-seated pain beneath the patella, swelling, local tenderness, crepitus, locking of the knee, and painful, restricted movements of the knee and patella.
(a) What are the risk factors for this condition?
(b) What are the late complications of this condition?
(c) Discuss the management options, conservative versus surgical, and justify one approach.
(d) What is the physiotherapy role?

questions.answerText:
(a)
Diagnosis: Osteoarthritis of the elbow.

(b)
Predisposing factors/pathophysiology: advancing age over 60 years, sedentary life, being overweight, wrong posture and misuse of the joint, and strenuous exercise including regular use of stairs; pathology involves synovitis with a thickened hypertrophied synovial membrane, softened worn articular cartilage, subchondral sclerosis, eburnation and cysts, marginal osteophytes and bony ankylosis.

(c)
Management: the conservative treatment of choice is physiotherapy (SWD or IR therapy, exercises); surgery is rarely indicated, except where loose bodies interfere with joint functioning.

(d)
Physiotherapy management: muscle-strengthening exercises (active and passive), traction, heat therapy (SWD/IRR), massage (stroking, compression), acupuncture/acupressure and yoga therapy, aimed at relieving pain, strengthening muscles, mobilizing joints, improving coordination and minimizing deformity.
questions.question:
A patient over 60 years old presents with dull aching elbow pain aggravated by use and relieved by rest, morning stiffness, crepitus, and painful restricted movement, with X-ray showing asymmetric joint space narrowing and marginal osteophytes.
(a) What is the diagnosis?
(b) What are the predisposing factors and pathophysiology?
(c) What is the medical/surgical management?
(d) What is the physiotherapy management?

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Stage 1, Haematoma: due to tearing of blood vessels, within seconds of injury a haematoma forms at the fracture site, and small portions of bone immediately adjacent to the fracture die and are gradually absorbed.
• Stage 2, Periosteal and endosteal proliferation: cells proliferate from the deep surface of the periosteum, forming osteoblast precursors around each fragment, while endosteal cells gradually bridge the bone ends as the haematoma is reabsorbed.
• Stage 3, Callus formation: the proliferating cells mature as osteoblasts or, in some instances, as chondroblasts, which form cartilage found in varying amounts at the fracture site.
• Stage 4, Consolidation: osteoblastic activity changes the primary callus to bone with a lamellar structure, and union is complete by the end of this stage.
• Stage 5, Remodelling: the bone adapts by strengthening along the lines of stress imposed upon it, and surplus bone is gradually removed; healing is confirmed by absence of pain on weight bearing/movement, no tenderness at the fracture site, blurring of the fracture line on X-ray, and full functional ability.

(b)
• Relation to delayed union: delayed union is a fracture that has not healed in the expected time, caused by inadequate blood supply, severe soft tissue damage, periosteal stripping, excessive traction, insufficient splintage or infection, showing a visible fracture line with little callus on X-ray.
• Relation to non-union: non-union is a fracture unlikely to heal without intervention - healing has stopped and the gap is filled by fibrous tissue (pseudoarthrosis), with X-rays showing rounded, smooth, sclerotic fracture ends (atrophic - avascular; or hypertrophic - excessive bone unable to bridge the gap).

(c)
• Effect on distant structures: factors affecting healing include type of bone, revascularisation of devitalised tissue, the mechanical environment of the fracture, type of fixation, age, medications and smoking.
• Continued: joint stiffness commonly follows fracture immobilisation, affecting the knee, elbow, shoulder or small hand joints, caused by oedema and fibrosis of the capsule/ligaments/muscle or adhesion of soft tissue to itself or underlying bone.
• Continued: myositis ossificans (heterotopic ossification in muscle) can occur at a distance from the fracture itself, such as after elbow dislocation or a blow to the brachialis, deltoid or quadriceps, producing pain, swelling, joint stiffness and, in extreme cases, complete loss of movement.

(d)
• Physiotherapy during immobilisation: maintenance of full range of motion of all joints not splinted; exercise all muscles, isometrically where no movement is allowed; encourage functional activities and independence.
• Physiotherapy post-immobilisation: mobilise stiff joints; strengthen weak muscles; restore equilibrium; re-educate movement (free exercise, hydrotherapy, PNF hold-relax, suspension therapy, passive mobilisation) and retrain independence.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the pathology and stages of fracture healing.
(b) State how these stages relate to complications such as delayed union and non-union.
(c) Explain why complications of fracture healing may affect a distant structure and cause functional deficit.
(d) Outline the physiotherapy management during and after immobilisation.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Tibial plateau fracture.

(b)
The lateral and/or medial tibial condyle and the articulating surface (made up of hyaline cartilage) at the proximal end of the tibia; caused by a force directed medially, laterally, or both, with axial compressive loading (commonly vehicle-pedestrian collision, fall from a height, industrial accident, or sports injury); 80% are RTAs and 20% sports-related.

(c)
Schatzker classification: I - simple split of the lateral condyle; II - depressed split of the lateral condyle; III - fracture with depression of the central articulating surface; IV - fracture of the medial condyle; V - fractures of both condyles with the articulating surface still connected to the tibial shaft; VI - combined condylar and subcondylar fractures with disconnection of the shaft from the articulating surface.

(d)
Force directed medially with axial loading is the most common mechanism; the valgus deformity and joint instability reflect the direction of the deforming force and the degree of articular depression/condylar involvement.

(e)
Protected weight bearing with early range-of-knee-motion in a hinged fracture brace; isometric quadriceps exercises progressing to passive, active-assisted and active range-of-knee-motion exercises; partial weight bearing for 8-12 weeks progressing to full weight bearing.
questions.question:
A pedestrian involved in a road traffic accident presents with severe pain and swelling at the knee, valgus deformity, local tenderness and medial or lateral instability. Radiographs are obtained.
(a) Identify the structure/lesion involved.
(b) State the structures affected.
(c) List the differential fracture patterns (classification).
(d) Discuss the clinico-anatomical and functional reasoning for the presentation.
(e) State the physiotherapy management priorities.

(a) Describe the mechanism of injury of the three types of peripheral nerve injury.
(b) Describe the types (neurapraxia, axonotmesis, neurotmesis).
(c) Describe the resulting deformity/functional loss.
(d) Describe the complications of each type.
(e) Describe the healing/recovery pattern of each type.
(f) State the management principles.
(g) Explain the physiotherapy management at each stage.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Mechanism: these injuries follow trauma such as fractures, dislocations, cuts, stabs or gunshot wounds affecting a peripheral nerve.

(b)
Types: neurapraxia is a concussion injury with momentary loss of conduction without organic damage; axonotmesis involves rupture of axons with an intact neural sheath; neurotmesis involves partial or complete division of both the neural sheath and nerve fibres.

(c)
Deformity/functional loss: depends on the specific nerve injured; for example, ulnar injury produces claw hand, median injury produces ape thumb, radial injury produces wrist drop.

(d)
Complications: axonotmesis shows incomplete recovery; neurotmesis shows deceptive recovery of both sensory and motor function

(e)
Healing: neurapraxia recovery is almost complete as no structural regeneration is needed; axonotmesis and neurotmesis require regeneration along the nerve course, assessed by Tinel's sign shifting distally over time.

(f)
• Management principles: conservative treatment with immobilization in a relaxation position and physiotherapy; surgical treatment (exploration and suturing) is indicated for neurotmesis lesions, with results usually unsatisfactory, better to suture two nerve roots to one trunk where applicable.
• Factors affecting suture results: nerve injured, infection causing delayed recovery, time factor (early secondary suture yields better results than delayed suture), and muscle tone maintenance.
• Operative factors: poor haemostasis, failure to prevent torsion and tension, and irritating suture material.
• Postoperative factors: infection, non-cooperating patient, and vicarious movements where adjoining muscles fail to share the paralysed function.

(g)
• Physiotherapy at the acute/postoperative stage: patient may need advice on carrying out as much movement of the limb as possible and reassurance about recovery of normal function.
• Physiotherapy following surgery: assisted passive movements progressing to free active exercises, along with occupational therapy.
• Ongoing physiotherapy: assessment made by the physiotherapist along with the team (doctors, nurses, occupational therapist, speech therapist, psychologist) to plan appropriate treatment.

questions.question:
A patient presents after direct trauma to the forearm from a road accident, with pain, local tenderness, a clicking sensation on rotation of the forearm, a prominent ulnar head, and weakness of grip and wrist.
(a) What is the diagnosis?
(b) Describe the mechanism of injury and the pathology involved.
(c) State the clinical features and physiotherapy assessment findings in this condition.
(d) What are the definitive treatment options?
questions.answerText:
(a)
Diagnosis: Internal derangement of the radioulnar joints.

(b)
Mechanism/pathology: Direct trauma (violence, road/street accident, sports injury, or fall downstairs) injures the articular disc or the ulnar collateral ligament, ruptures the distal radioulnar ligaments, or causes dislocation/subluxation (traumatic predisposing factors), or produces an angulated radius or ulna, or an enlarged ulnar head (deformity); this tears the articular disc and ulnar collateral ligament, and ruptures the distal radioulnar ligaments.

(c)
Clinical features/assessment findings: Pain; local tenderness; clicking joint on rotation of the forearm; prominent ulnar head; weakness of grip and of the wrist.

(d)
Definitive treatment options: Excision of the disc for a torn articular disc; repair for ruptured ligaments; reduction (closed or open) for dislocation/subluxation; osteotomy for an angulated radius or ulna; followed by assisted passive exercises by the physiotherapist progressed to free active exercises by the patient.

(a)
Diagnosis: Sever's disease (apophysitis of os calcis).

(b)
Predisposing factors/pathophysiology: Etiology unknown, genetic, traumatic (sports trauma), infective, or endocrinal; the epiphysis becomes fragmented and irregular; commoner in boys, aged 10-15 years; X-ray shows fragmentation and irregularity of the epiphysis.

(c)
Medical/surgical management: Conservative - bedrest, avoiding strenuous exercises, diathermy (SWD, infrared, wax bath), analgesics/NSAIDs, and a shoe cut away at the back to relieve pressure with a raised heel to relax the calf muscles. Surgical (rarely indicated, for failure of conservative measures) - excision.

(d)
Physiotherapy management: Assisted passive exercises by the physiotherapist progressed to free active exercises by the patient.
questions.question:
A 12-year-old boy presents with pain, limping, an unduly prominent heel, and pain on walking and running following sports activity.
(a) What is the diagnosis?
(b) What are the predisposing factors and pathophysiology of this condition?
(c) Outline the medical/surgical management.
(d) Outline the physiotherapy management.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Structure/imaging: the vertebral body has sustained a compression (crush) fracture; X-ray shows demineralization of the spine, pelvis and limbs, and bone densitometry (BMD, recorded as a T score against a healthy young adult and a Z score against a person of the same age and sex) may show early bone mineral loss, with quantitative CT or MRI as further tests.

(b)
Functional impairment: pain, particularly low backache, ranging from asymptomatic to severe, with deformity and an increased risk of further fracture (e.g. fracture neck of femur, Colles' fracture) as the bone loss exceeds 30%.

(c)
Associated/secondary causes: prolonged immobilization (traumatic), rheumatoid arthritis/tuberculosis/syphilis (inflammatory), lack of androgens (senile osteoporosis) or lack of estrogens (postmenopausal osteoporosis), hypopituitarism/hypogonadism, hyperthyroidism (thyrotoxicosis), hyperparathyroidism, excess ACTH or corticosteroids (Cushing's syndrome), diabetes mellitus, pregnancy, calcium deficiency, and multiple myeloma; risk factors include age over 60 years, female sex, alcohol abuse, smoking, poor diet, a sedentary lifestyle, lack of physical activity, and prolonged use of heparin or corticosteroids.

(d)
Physiotherapy plan/reasoning: regular exercise, especially weight-bearing exercise, carried out under the supervision and teaching of the physiotherapist, alongside a high-protein diet adequate in calcium, stopping smoking, reducing alcohol intake, calcium and vitamin D, and analgesics/NSAIDs.
questions.question:
An elderly postmenopausal woman on prolonged corticosteroid therapy presents with backache and is found on X-ray to have a compression (crush) fracture of a vertebral body, with demineralization of the spine, pelvis and limbs.
(a) What structure/joint is involved and what does the imaging show?
(b) What deformity, gait or functional impairment would you expect?
(c) What are the differential/associated causes for this bone fragility?
(d) What is your clinical reasoning for the physiotherapy plan?

A patient presents with a history of trauma, unremitting bone pain, recurrent fever, and a periodically discharging sinus of long standing.
(a) What are the risk factors for this condition?
(b) What are its complications?
(c) What are the conservative and surgical management options, and which would you justify choosing?
(d) What is the role of physiotherapy?
questions.answerText:
(a)
Risk factors: anxiety, overwork, or other debilitating conditions; it represents the reparative stage of acute osteomyelitis following missed diagnosis or inadequate treatment.

(b)
Complications: septic arthritis; amyloidosis; pathological fracture; deformity or shortening.

(c)
Conservative (general measures): bedrest; immobilization by splint or traction; elevation of the part; warm fomentation; antibiotics; analgesics; fluids orally or IV. Surgical: incision and drainage of abscess; sequestrectomy and curettage; saucerization; amputation to forestall amyloid disease. Surgery is justified once a sequestrum or persistent discharging sinus is present, since conservative measures alone cannot remove dead, infected bone; postoperatively a POP cast is applied with a window cut over the wound for dressings.

(d)
Physiotherapy role: heat therapy (SWD/IRR or heating pad therapy); as pain subsides the physiotherapist encourages the patient to perform active exercises for joint movement and muscle strengthening.

(a)
75% of humerus fractures occur in patients older than age 60, more common in older women; the most common cause is a fall onto an outstretched upper extremity from standing height in older, osteoporotic women; in young individuals, high-energy trauma causes the fracture, mostly as part of polytrauma; the fracture results from compressive loading of the glenoid onto the humeral head, bending forces at the surgical neck, and tension forces of the rotator cuff at the tuberosities.

(b)
Shoulder stiffness, dislocation, unstable shoulder; nerve damage is uncommon, but there is a risk of vascular injury; anatomical neck fractures have a poor prognosis because of interference with the vascular supply to the humeral head.

(c)
Minimally displaced fractures are managed with analgesia and a sling for 3-4 weeks; displaced fractures are managed with open reduction and internal fixation. Conservative sling treatment is justified in this minimally displaced pattern because the surgical neck, distal to the tuberosities, is the common fracture site with generally good outcomes when minimally displaced, avoiding the risks of surgery while allowing early active shoulder motion.
questions.question:
An elderly woman falls onto her outstretched arm and presents with a painful, restricted shoulder, swelling and ecchymosis.
(a) State the risk factors for this condition.
(b) Outline the possible complications.
(c) Discuss the conservative and surgical management options and justify one option for this patient.

A child develops sudden onset of a hot, red, painful, swollen single joint (knee or hip), with fever and chills.
(a) What is the diagnosis?
(b) What surgery/procedure is named for definitive treatment?
(c) What is the post-operative physiotherapy by phase?
(d) What precautions and contraindications apply?
questions.answerText:
(a)
Acute suppurative arthritis.

(b)
Surgical procedures: aspiration of the joint; incision and drainage; amputation.

(c)
Physiotherapy by phase: rest to the joint by traction or splintage; heat therapy (SWD/IRR or heat pad therapy); non-weight bearing free active exercises to move the affected joints through the full range; gait re-education, mandatory with crutches progressed to sticks once pain has subsided; early mobilization mandatory to prevent muscle atrophy and stiff joints.

(d)
Precautions: the joint is rested and immobilized by traction or splint, with weight bearing withheld and only free active (non-weight bearing) exercise permitted until pain subsides, after which crutches are progressed to sticks.

questions.question:
A child in the first decade of life has a small, asymptomatic, eccentric defect in the distal femoral metaphysis noted incidentally on X-ray, while an older child or young adult has a similar-appearing lesion in the tibia or fibula with pain, swelling and local tenderness.
(a) What are the risk factors/developmental basis for these lesions?
(b) What are the early and late complications?
(c) What are the conservative versus surgical management options, and which would you justify?
(d) What is the role of physiotherapy?
questions.answerText:
(a)
Developmental basis: developmental defects, localized and temporary cessation of ossification, and abnormal periosteal growth; metaphyseal defects are usually small, innocuous and asymptomatic, occurring in children in the first decade, and exist for about 2-3 years before the occupied area ossifies and resumes a normal trabecular pattern, occurring most often in the distal femoral metaphysis; when such a defect fails to follow its usual evolutionary course it forms a nonosteogenic fibroma, usually seen in the second decade in the long bones of the lower limb (tibia and fibula), and unlike metaphyseal defects, nonosteogenic fibromas are rarely multiple.

(b)
Complications: pain, swelling, local tenderness, painful restricted movement of the adjoining joint, muscular weakness and wasting, and pathological fracture.

(c)
Conservative treatment is analgesics and NSAIDs, and warm fomentation, SWD or IR therapy. Surgical treatment is indicated on failure of conservative treatment, and consists of curettage of lesions in long bones or excision of expanded vertebral lesions with adjoining involved tissue.

(d)
Physiotherapy role: regular exercise, especially weight-bearing, under the supervision and teaching of the physiotherapist, and SWD/IRR.

(a)
Mechanism: Direct trauma - violence, road/street accident, sports injury, or fall downstairs.

(b)
• Types (traumatic predisposing factors): Injured interosseous ligament; ruptured tibiofibular ligaments; dislocation or subluxation.
• Types (deformed predisposing factor): Angulated tibia or fibula.

(c)
• Clinical findings: Pain; local tenderness; weakness; movements painful and restricted.
• Investigations: X-ray of the ankle (AP and lateral views) to rule out any bony lesion; MRI of the ankle.

(d)
Pathogenesis: a torn interosseous ligament with ruptured tibiofibular ligaments.

(e)
• Management principles - ruptured ligaments: Repair.
• Management principles - dislocation/subluxation: Reduction (closed or open).
• Management principles - angulated tibia or fibula: Osteotomy.

(f)
• Physiotherapy management: Assisted passive exercises by the physiotherapist.
• Physiotherapy management (continued): Progressed to free active exercises by the patient.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Definition: Osteochondritis dissecans is an area of subchondral bone that undergoes avascular necrosis, with degenerative changes usually occurring in the overlying cartilage; unless interrupted by surgical or conservative measures, the necrotic bone and overlying cartilage separate gradually from the adjacent bone and cartilage, forming a loose body.
• Classification/types: Synovial chondromatosis; traumatic loose bodies (by fracture); detached osteophytes (due to degenerative changes).

(b)
• Causes/etiology: Traumatic (intra-articular fracture); degenerative (osteoarthritis).
• Pathogenesis: Avascular necrosis of the subchondral bone, with the overlying cartilage degenerated and loose body formation.

(c)
Clinical features: Affects the knee, elbow, shoulder, ankle, or hip; swelling; local tenderness; movements painful and restricted; disability with difficulty in walking.

(d)
Investigation: X-ray of the affected joint shows loose body(s).

(e)
Complications: loose body formation; for the hip specifically, without treatment the area collapses and osteoarthritis develops.

(f)
• Distinguishing feature - cartilage/loose body: In osteochondritis dissecans of the hip, the cartilage overlying the avascular fragment of bone usually remains intact and a loose body ultimately is not formed, unlike the general/knee pattern where a loose body does form.
• Distinguishing feature - site: Osteochondritis dissecans of the hip affects the weight-bearing area of the femoral head, whereas of the knee it is usually found on the medial femoral condyle near the attachment of the posterior cruciate ligament, though it may occur on the lateral femoral condyle or the inferomedial surface of the patella.
• Distinguishing feature - natural history: without treatment, osteochondritis dissecans of the hip leads to collapse of the area and development of osteoarthritis.
• Distinguishing feature - investigation: Osteochondritis dissecans of the hip is investigated with an X-ray of the pelvis (AP view), whereas of the knee it is investigated with an X-ray of the knee joint.
• Distinguishing feature - surgical management: Osteochondritis dissecans of the hip is managed surgically by drilling (small lesion) or drilling with cancellous bone packing (large lesion), or excision with removal of loose bodies (detached area); osteochondritis dissecans of the knee is managed surgically by excision of the lesion with removal of loose bodies when the area is detached.

(a)
Structure/joint involved: The synovium (synovial membrane) of the knee joint, responding to trauma with hypersecretion of synovial fluid, synovial effusion, and a distended knee; there may be hemarthrosis from injured bone, cruciate ligaments, menisci, synovium or capsule, with blood clots in intra-articular fractures; the synovial fluid becomes acidic, becomes fibrosed, and adhesions form with chronic synovitis showing hypertrophy and proliferation of synovial folds.

Functional impairment: Movements of the knee are painful and restricted, with weakness, lethargy and anorexia, and fever that may or may not be present.

(c)
Differential diagnoses: Acute suppurative arthritis; hemophilic joints; internal derangement of the knee (IDK).

Clinical reasoning for the physiotherapy plan: Management follows the precise diagnosis reached from detailed history, physical examination and investigations (including X-rays); once aspiration of the knee has been carried out to relieve pain, prevent stretching of the synovium/capsule/ligaments, and analyze the synovial fluid, an elastic crepe bandage is applied and aspiration is repeated every 3rd or 4th day; the physiotherapist then progresses assisted passive exercises to free active exercises by the patient.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Mechanism: fractures of the pelvis and upper end of femur, dislocations of the hip, direct trauma (blow, gunshot, stab), road/street accident, or operative complications from excision of malignant tumors of the femur or hindquarter amputations.

(b)
Types: the sciatic nerve itself, and its two terminal divisions, the lateral popliteal (common peroneal) nerve and the medial popliteal (tibial) nerve.

(c)
Deformity: sciatic nerve injury produces 'foot drop' with complete paralysis below the knee; lateral popliteal nerve injury (from fracture or excision of the upper fibula, knee fracture-dislocation, or lateral collateral ligament injury) also produces foot drop from loss of dorsiflexion; medial popliteal (tibial) nerve injury produces talipes calcaneovalgus from paralysis of the calf muscles and sole.

(d)
Complications: paralysis of all hamstrings with sciatic injury; muscular wasting; loss of muscle pain sensation, joint sense (ankle, foot, toe joints), and pressure sense beyond the metatarsal heads; loss of cutaneous sensation below the knee; skin cold, glazed, smooth, with trivial trophic changes.

(e)
Healing: results of suturing are usually more satisfactory when the tibial nerve component is affected than when the peroneal component is involved.

(f)
• Management: conservative treatment with immobilization of the leg and physiotherapy exercises. Surgical treatment for compression from fracture-dislocation or wounds involves exploration of the nerve from its emergence at the sciatic notch to its point of division, and suturing.
• Testing: dorsiflexion of the ankle tested with the foot on its lateral border, the leg hanging from the end of the bed, against resistance, unable to dorsiflex the foot.
• Investigation includes electromyography (since electrical stimulation in situ is difficult due to the nerve's deep position), a skin resistance test as confirmatory, and Tinel's sign after a couple of months, the level shifting distally with regeneration.

(g)
• Physiotherapy after nerve suturing: postoperative immobilization with splints for about 4 to 6 weeks, stitches removed after 2 days through a window in the cast.
• Physiotherapy assessment: the physiotherapist, along with the team (doctors, nurses, occupational therapist, speech therapist, psychologist), assesses the case and plans treatment.
• Physiotherapy treatment: assisted passive movements progressing to free active exercises, along with occupational therapy.
• Investigations also include X-ray of the pelvis, knee, and ankle to assess the injury and guide the management plan.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the pathology and stages of avascular necrosis following fracture.
(b) State how this relates to the femoral neck and scaphoid fractures specifically.
(c) Explain how avascular necrosis may spread its effect to cause secondary osteoarthritis of a joint.
(d) Outline the physiotherapy and surgical management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Pathology: avascular necrosis is circumscribed bone necrosis caused by interruption of arterial blood flow or slowing of venous outflow leading to inadequate perfusion.
• Common sites: femoral head, femoral condyles, humeral head, capitulum of the humerus, scaphoid (proximal part), talus (body), lunate.
• Associated conditions/features: Perthes' disease, epiphyseal infection, sickle cell disease, Caisson disease, Gaucher's disease, alcohol abuse and high-dosage corticosteroid use; clinical features are joint pain, stiffness, swelling and restricted movement, with X-rays showing increased bone density, subarticular fracturing and bone deformity.

(b)
• Relation to femoral neck fracture: with displacement of the femoral neck, the risk of avascular necrosis jumps from 7% to 37%, because displacement disrupts the vascular supply attached to the femoral neck; trauma-caused femoral neck fractures are also usually associated with multiple injuries and high rates of avascular necrosis.
• Relation to scaphoid fracture: there is a risk of avascular necrosis of the scaphoid due to injury of the radial artery which supplies it, and displaced navicular body fractures similarly have a high incidence of avascular necrosis and require open reduction and internal fixation.
• Continued: this is also true of the talus, which has a fragile blood supply because of its large articular surface and lack of tendon/muscle attachments, so displaced talar neck fracture predisposes to avascular necrosis, as does ankle dislocation.

(c)
• Spread to secondary osteoarthritis: post-traumatic osteoarthritis occurs when a joint fracture severely damages the articular cartilage, and within months damaged cartilage begins to scar.
• Continued: years after joint injury, secondary osteoarthritis develops as cartilage heals with an irregular joint surface that causes localised stress.
• Continued: avascular necrosis similarly produces subarticular fracturing and bone deformity that alter joint surface congruity and predispose to secondary degenerative change, producing pain, stiffness, swelling, deformity and restricted movement.

(d)
• Physiotherapy management: avoid weight bearing on the necrotic bone.
• Continued: for established secondary osteoarthritis - pain relief with analgesics and anti-inflammatory agents, physiotherapy for joint mobility, and load reduction through weight reduction.
• Surgical management: revascularisation using vascularised bone grafts, excision of the avascular segment and replacement by prostheses for avascular necrosis; realignment osteotomy (young patient) or arthroplasty (patients over 60 years) for established secondary osteoarthritis.

(a)
Diagnosis: Rickets (the childhood deficiency disease due to lack of vitamin D).

(b)
Mechanism: inadequate absorption of calcium and phosphorus from the intestine, due to lack of calcium alone or lack of/resistance to vitamin D; epiphyseal cartilages become enlarged, the zone of provisional calcification is absent or irregular, newly formed bone trabeculae are osteoid tissue lacking calcium salts, and medullary spaces fill with vascular fibrocellular tissue instead of normal bone marrow, resulting in deformed bones.

(c)
Clinical features/assessment: diminished stature from retarded bony growth (especially femur and tibia), bending of the leg bones, spinal deformities (kyphosis followed by scoliosis from faulty posture), rickety rosary from beading of the costochondral junctions, aching bones, and muscular weakness/paralysis; confirmed by low serum calcium and phosphate, elevated alkaline phosphatase, low urinary calcium and phosphate, a positive bone densitometer test, and X-ray showing cupping and blurring of the epiphyseal line, demineralization and bowing.

(d)
Conservative management: a high-calcium diet, milk, cod liver oil and meat extracts; calcium gluconate or lactate 5-20 g/day; vitamin D (2-5 K units/day for rickets); sunlight exposure; deformities corrected by splinting; osteoclasis by manipulation.

(e)
Definitive treatment: osteotomy, in older children and adults.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Definition: a localized bulging mass covered with a thin and often incomplete shell of bone.
• Classification: lesions usually occurring in older children and young adults, most often in the large long bones, and occasionally the flat bones and vertebrae; in a tubular bone the lesion is located nearer to one end than to the middle of the shaft; it may be considered a clinical and radiological entity rather than a pathological one.

(b)
• Causes: uncertain aetiology.
• Further causes: possibly vascular disorders (hemorrhage, venous dilatations) or trauma (parosteal myositis ossificans).

(c)
• Clinical features: pain, swelling, and local tenderness.
• Further features: painful and restricted movement of the adjoining joint, muscular weakness and wasting, and pathological fracture.

(d)
• Investigations: X-rays showing a localized bulging mass covered with a thin shell of bone, striking heavy trabeculations or loculation, and slight irregular cortical erosion.
• Further investigations: needle aspiration biopsy, to rule out malignancy.

(e)
• Complications: pathological fracture.
• Further complications: pathological fracture.

(f)
Differential diagnoses: giant cell tumour and chondromyxoid fibroma.

(a)
Diagnosis: Kohler's disease (osteochondritis of the os scaphoid tarsal/navicular).

(b)
Predisposing factors/pathophysiology: Etiology unknown, genetic, or traumatic (sports trauma); the navicular epiphysis becomes fragmented and irregular, with a flattened head of the talus; commoner in boys, aged 5-10 years; X-ray shows fragmentation and irregularity of the epiphysis, with a disc-like scaphoid.

(c)
Medical/surgical management: Conservative - bedrest, avoiding strenuous exercises, diathermy (SWD, infrared, wax bath), analgesics/NSAIDs, strapping support, and a shoe cut away at the back with a raised heel to relax the calf muscles. Surgical (rarely indicated, for failure of conservative measures) - arthrodesis of the midtarsal joints (talonavicular and calcaneocuboid).

(d)
Physiotherapy management: Assisted passive exercises by the physiotherapist progressed to free active exercises by the patient.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Definition: a rare fibrocystic disease of bone manifesting as softening, bending and often fracture, usually mistaken for osteitis fibrosa generalisata due to hyperparathyroidism, as both show bone cysts and fractures; it is not a metabolic disorder but a congenital dysplasia in which bone and cartilage fail to form and remain as fibrous tissue; with brown spots of ragged margins and true precocious puberty it is called Albright's syndrome, and may be associated with hyperthyroidism and acromegaly.
• Aetiology: unknown.
• Clinical features: usually presenting in the second decade of life with painless swelling of the skull, ribs, pelvis, upper femur, tibia, metatarsals, metacarpals and phalanges.
• Further clinical features: pathological fractures, deformities, brown pigmentation of the skin, and, in females, true precocious puberty with early secondary sex characters and fast skeletal growth.
• Investigations: normal serum calcium and phosphorus, elevated alkaline phosphatase, and elevated urinary hydroxyproline.
• Further investigations: X-rays showing rarefaction and expansion of the affected bones or hyperostosis especially of the base of the skull, with fractures and deformities, and confirmatory bone biopsy.

(b)
• Effect on function: pathological fractures and deformity of the limb (e.g. shepherd's crook deformity of the femur) impair limb function.
• Function may be further affected by blindness due to orbital involvement, and by thyrotoxicosis.

(c)
• Conservative management: no specific treatment; warm fomentation, SWD or IR therapy, and analgesics and NSAIDs.
• Further conservative management: calcitonin may be tried in acute disease, though results are inconclusive.
• Surgical management: indicated for correction of deformities (fractures, expanding orbital cyst).
• Rehabilitation/physiotherapy management: regular exercise, especially weight-bearing, under the supervision and teaching of the physiotherapist, and heat therapy (SWD/IRR).

(a)
Palmar fibromatosis (syn. palmar fasciitis; Dupuytren's contracture).

(b)
Predisposing factors: unknown; hereditary/familial; traumatic (occupational hazard); inflammatory; metabolic; common in middle age, more in men than women. Pathophysiology: a primary disorder of the collagen substance of the fibrous tissue; the lesion starts as a fibroblastic nodule in the subcutaneous palmar fascia, passing through proliferative, involutional and residual stages, mostly starting near the base of the ring or little finger and drawing that finger into the palm.

(c)
Management, early case: night splintage and active exercises with gentle stretching of the fingers by the patient; radiotherapy has a limited role in the early phase. Surgical: fasciotomy - subcutaneous (elderly, arthritic, or poor health), partial (small affected area, immature nodule, early contracture from a fascial cord), or complete (younger patient with disabling contracture); postoperative immobilization by a splint for 1 week.

(d)
Physiotherapy management: heat therapy (SWD/IRR or heating pad therapy); as pain subsides the physiotherapist encourages active exercises for joint movement and muscle strengthening.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Definition: an abnormal development, usually of the acetabulum, proximal femur, and soft structures of the hip joint, often familial or hereditary, usually occurring during the first two years after birth (rarely before birth), more common among girls.
• Classification: three types by severity: femoral head in a normal position within an abnormal acetabulum; subluxation with the femoral head partially beneath the acetabular roof; and the head fully dislocated from the acetabulum.

(b)
Aetiology: unknown.

(c)
Clinical features: at birth, clinical signs may be absent, requiring periodic examination; suggestive findings include asymmetry of skin creases on the inner thighs, leg shortening, restricted abduction, positive Ortolani sign, and telescoping of the flexed and adducted thigh.

(d)
Investigations: X-ray pelvis at birth and during infancy (ill-defined); observation of the acetabular index, Hilgenreiner's line, Perkins' line, Shenton's arcuate line, and Ponseti's Y coordinate; arthrography for diagnosis of mild dysplasia, subluxation/dislocation status, and reducibility.

(e)
Complications: untreated dislocation progresses to established deformity with gait abnormality and hip instability persisting into later childhood.

(f)
• Differentiation of early signs (infancy): no single sign is diagnostic; suggestive findings are skin-crease asymmetry, leg shortening, restricted abduction, positive Ortolani sign (clicking on entry and exit of the femoral head into the acetabulum), and telescoping.
• Differentiation of late signs (childhood): waddling (bilateral) or lurching (unilateral) gait, shortening above the greater trochanter (Nelaton's line), a prominent greater trochanter, lordosis, a widened perineum (bilateral), absent femoral pulsation, restricted abduction, and a positive Trendelenburg sign.

(g)
• Management in infancy: conservative treatment with abduction of the thighs using a pillow or folded diaper, later an abduction splint; children 1 to 2 years old receive skeletal traction for 2 weeks prior to closed reduction under anaesthesia, followed by a POP dual hip spica ('frog leg' plaster) with hips flexed 90 degrees, fully abducted and externally rotated, for 8 weeks, with X-ray checks at 8-week intervals.
• In late childhood, satisfactory closed skeletal reduction needs no further treatment; unsatisfactory closed reduction requires open reduction (skeletal traction followed by open reduction) to achieve anatomic and functional restoration, with postoperative POP double hip spica; arthrodesis is reserved for late unreduced cases over 12 years.
• Physiotherapy management: early conservative treatment may not require extensive physiotherapy after fixation removal, though hydrotherapy is beneficial for encouraging leg mobility.
• Following open reduction, the child may require a more active mobilizing programme with strengthening exercises and walking re-education.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Snapping (syn. clicking) joints are defined as the ability to produce sounds (loud clicks) from otherwise apparently normal joints; two main sources of these sounds/clicks are intra-articular menisci of joints, and the sliding of tendons over bony anatomical prominences near the joints, which may be habitual.
• Snapping hip is an audible, palpable or visible snap usually produced by a tense fascial band catching while sliding over the superior margin of the greater trochanter when the hip is flexed, adducted or internally rotated. Snapping knee is due to a congenital discoid cartilage that slips to produce a snap or click.

(b)
• Aetiology, snapping hip: voluntary (painless); involuntary (painful and habitual); traumatic (subluxation of the hip); inflammatory (osteochondritis); bursitis (trochanteric); loose bodies. Pathogenesis: the thickened posterior border of the ilio-tibial band, or the thickened anterior border of gluteus maximus near its insertion, slides forwards and backwards over the prominence of the greater trochanter (an obsessive neurosis in the involuntary form).
• Aetiology, snapping knee: congenital - a discoid cartilage (a solid disc, thicker in the centre than at the periphery) that slips to produce a snap/click, with no neurotic element; pathogenesis - the solid discoid cartilage, thicker centrally than peripherally, is slippery and produces the snap.

(c)
• Clinical features, snapping hip: usually painless, occasionally painful and habitual; snap/click voluntarily produced.
• Clinical features, snapping knee: common amongst adolescents; snap/click loudly audible even at a distance; the knee is hyperactive though dislocating.

(d)
Investigations: snapping hip is diagnosed clinically; snapping knee is investigated with X-rays of the knee, AP and lateral views.

(e)
• Distinguishing the two conditions: snapping hip arises from a fascial band or tendon sliding over the greater trochanter and is often habitual/neurotic in nature, whereas snapping knee arises from a congenital discoid meniscal cartilage in adolescents with no neurotic element, producing a loud, distance-audible click.
• Management, snapping hip: rarely requires surgery as it is usually painless and patients often prefer no treatment once the (mostly neurotic) cause is explained; surgery (excision of the fascia at the level of the greater trochanter) is indicated only for very severe snapping/clicking, with active exercises as after care once the wound heals.
• Management, snapping knee: surgical excision of the discoid disc is the treatment of choice for very severe snapping/clicking, followed by exercises.
• Physiotherapy management (both): heat therapy (SWD/IRR or heating pad therapy) and, as pain subsides, active exercises for joint movement and muscle strengthening.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Mechanism: fractures of the middle of the shaft of the humerus, fractures and dislocations of the upper end of the humerus, supracondylar fracture of the humerus, fracture-dislocations of the lower end of the humerus, direct trauma (blow, gunshot, stab), road/street accident, or operative complications from excision of malignant tumors of the humerus or prolonged tourniquet application.

(b)
Types: injury anywhere along the course of the nerve, which is primarily motor, supplying triceps, anconeus, brachioradialis, the lateral fourth of brachialis anticus, and extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis in the arm, and the supinators and wrist/finger/thumb extensors in the forearm.

(c)
Deformity: wrist drop.

(d)
Complications: muscular wasting; paralysis of triceps and the wrist and finger extensors; loss of muscle pain sensation in the paralysed muscles, with joint sense usually unaffected; loss of cutaneous sensation over the dorsum of the forearm and back of the hand; trophic changes usually trivial.

(e)
Healing: results of suturing are usually unsatisfactory.

(f)
• Management: conservative treatment with immobilization in a universal arm pouch and physiotherapy exercises. Surgical treatment for compression from fracture-dislocation or wounds involves exploration of the nerve and suturing.
• Testing: with the forearm in mid-prone position, the patient is asked to extend against resistance, unable to extend the wrist, thumb and MP joints; also tested by asking the patient to flex against resistance to observe triceps standing out.
• Investigation includes electrical stimulation in situ and Tinel's sign after a couple of months, the level of tingling shifting distally with regeneration.

(g)
• Physiotherapy after nerve suturing: postoperative POP cast for about 4 to 6 weeks, stitches removed after 2 days through a window in the cast.
• Physiotherapy assessment: the physiotherapist, along with the team (doctors, nurses, occupational therapist, speech therapist, psychologist), assesses the case and plans treatment accordingly.
• Physiotherapy treatment: assisted passive movements progressing to free active exercises, along with occupational therapy.
• Overall, physiotherapy management may not require extensive treatment in milder cases as recovery is likely within a few weeks, but advice on movement and reassurance remain important throughout.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Definition: Kohler's disease (osteochondritis of the os scaphoid tarsal) is a disability characterized by pain, disability, and restricted sports activities, mostly in boys between the ages of 5 and 10 years, due to osteochondritis of the navicular epiphysis.
• Pathogenesis: Fragmented, irregular navicular epiphysis, with a flattened head of the talus.

(b)
Causes/etiology: Unknown; genetic; traumatic (sports trauma).

(c)
Clinical features: Commoner in boys; age 5-10 years; pain; deformity of a prominent foot at the dorsum near the ankle; local tenderness; walking/running painful.

(d)
Investigation: X-ray shows fragmentation and irregularity of the epiphysis, with a disc-like scaphoid.

(e)
• Distinguishing feature - bone affected: Kohler's disease affects the navicular epiphysis of the foot, whereas Freiberg's disease affects the head of the second or third metatarsal.
• Distinguishing feature - age: Kohler's disease occurs mostly in boys aged 5-10 years, whereas Freiberg's disease is described as occurring mostly in young adults, although its diagnosis section states an age of 10-15 years.
• Distinguishing feature - deformity: Kohler's disease produces a prominent foot deformity at the dorsum near the ankle, whereas Freiberg's disease produces a prominent foot deformity at the dorsum near the metatarsal head.
• Distinguishing feature - investigation: Kohler's disease shows fragmentation and irregularity of the epiphysis with a disc-like scaphoid on X-ray, whereas Freiberg's disease shows a flattened articular surface and irregular sclerosed head of the metatarsal.
• Distinguishing feature - conservative management: Kohler's disease is managed with strapping support in addition to the general conservative measures, whereas Freiberg's disease is managed with a shoe fitted with a metatarsal bar.
• Distinguishing feature - surgical management: Kohler's disease, if surgery is needed, is treated by arthrodesis of the midtarsal joints (talonavicular and calcaneocuboid), whereas Freiberg's disease, if surgery is needed, is treated by excision of the metatarsal head.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Definition: a group of foot deformities whereby the sole of the foot is no longer plantigrade, varying from the entire foot in equinus and varus with the forefoot adducted and a cavus deformity, to a much less severe form with mild equinus and varus, mostly accompanied by internal torsion of the tibia.
• Classification: congenital and acquired types.

(b)
Aetiology: unknown, or muscular imbalance between the calf muscles, tibialis anterior, and tibialis posterior versus the peronei.

(c)
Clinical features: contracture of the medial plantar ligaments, deltoid ligament, posterior tibial tendon, abductor hallucis, tendocalcaneus, joint capsules, and the anterior tibial tendon, with the talus deviated medially and plantarward, its head prominent subcutaneously on the dorsum of the foot, the navicular displaced medially and rotated, the cuboid displaced medially, and the calcaneus displaced medially in varus.

(d)
Investigations: X-ray of the feet, spine, and pelvis.

(e)
Complications: without early treatment the deformity becomes progressively more difficult to correct with increasing age; failure of conservative treatment necessitates surgery, which becomes more extensive with older age.

(f)
• Differentiation: the congenital type is usually bilateral, with normal-appearing skin, subcutaneous tissue and muscles, a transverse crease across the medial sole, and callosities and bursae in a walking child.
• The acquired type is usually unilateral, with cold, cyanotic skin showing trophic changes and no transverse crease, wasted flaccid muscles (infantile paralysis) or spastic muscles (upper motor neuron lesion), and thin bones of the affected leg.

(g)
• Management: conservative treatment should begin within the first two weeks after birth, manipulating into over-correction, confirmed by post-reduction X-ray, and immobilized with plaster of Paris at regular intervals, Denis Browne splints, or a rigid-shank, low-lateral-wedge shoe.
• Surgical treatment is indicated on failure of conservative treatment: children under 10 years have soft-tissue procedures only, as bones are insufficiently ossified for arthrodesis; children 5 to 10 years may have tendon lengthening and osteotomy (Dwyer); children over 10 years have advanced ossification permitting arthrodesis. Postoperative long leg cast for 2 weeks, with a further POP cast of 8 to 12 weeks if deformity persists.
• Physiotherapy management: passive stretching carried out as soon as possible after birth while the foot is relatively mobile, fixing the lower tibia and flexing the knee to protect the epiphyses, correcting the plantar flexion deformity by pressure on the heel, with adhesive strapping to hold the corrected position, replaced weekly.
• If the child has already started walking, a walking plaster cast is applied; after fixation removal, physiotherapy aims to maintain the corrected position with passive movements and active dorsiflexion and eversion exercises, and an ambulatory child requires a surgical shoe or ankle-foot splint walker.

(a)
• Mechanism: direct trauma such as a blow, stab or gunshot wound, road/traffic accidents, sports injuries, or a fall from a height.
• Pathogenesis: torn tissues, contusion of adjoining structures, and extravasation of blood leading to hematoma and an infected wound.

(b)
• Types of organisms: gram-positive cocci (Staphylococcus aureus, Staphylococcus albus), gram-positive sporing bacilli (Clostridia welchii, Clostridia tetani), and gram-negative bacilli (Escherichia coli, Klebsiella, Proteus, Pseudomonas pyocyanea, bacteroids).
• Transmission: self-infection or cross-infection from other persons.

(c)
• Complications: hematoma (localized hemorrhage), infected wound, diffuse cellulitis, and abscess formation.
• Further complications: reactivated infection and scarring with contracture of soft tissues; the knee joint, with its extensive synovium, is more immune to infection than the bones, tendons or periarticular structures.

(d)
Healing/recovery: exercises (active and passive) are started once acute symptoms have subsided, with restoration of function induced slowly, since inducing it too quickly may cause residual synovitis or reactivate infection.

(e)
• Management principles (conservative, treatment of choice): toilet of the wound, antiseptic dressing, antibiotics, analgesics and NSAIDs, and immobilization of the affected joint, with aftercare immobilization using Buck's traction.
• Management principles (surgical, indicated for synovitis or a remnant foreign body): aspiration of the joint (diagnostic and therapeutic), exploration of the wound/soft tissue, and débridement of the wound with exploration of the joint.

(f)
• Physiotherapy management: special exercises are required to restore quadriceps power at the earliest possible stage.
• Walking is allowed with the aid of a long leg brace, not discarded until a satisfactory range of motion, especially extension, is restored; investigations used include CBC, ESR, blood culture, culture of aspirated fluid/pus, and AP and lateral X-rays.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Definition: spina bifida is failure of fusion of the vertebral arches, usually with associated maldevelopment of the spinal cord and membranes.
• Types: spina bifida occulta (commonest, no protrusion of cord or membranes), meningocele, meningomyelocele, syringomyelocele (rarest, dilated central canal of spinal cord), and myelocele.

(b)
Aetiology: unknown.

(c)
Pathogenesis: spina bifida occulta involves a fibrous band connecting skin to the spinal theca, so growth pulls the theca and nerve roots; meningocele contains CSF only; meningomyelocele has the spinal cord or cauda equina adherent to the sac; syringomyelocele shows a dilated central canal of the spinal cord; myelocele shows CSF discharging from the central canal.

(d)
Diagnosis: swelling over the lumbosacral region, talipes, skin depression, patch of hair, trophic ulcers, discharging CSF sinus, muscular weakness or paralysis of the legs in advanced cases, and incontinence of urine and faeces. Investigations: transillumination test distinguishes meningocele from meningomyelocele; X-ray lumbosacral spine reveals bony deficiency.

(e)
Effect on function: sensory impairment (anaesthesia) predisposes to pressure sores, and muscular weakness or paralysis of the legs impairs mobility, with incontinence also affecting function.

(f)
• Surgical management is the treatment of choice, provided as soon as possible by a neurosurgeon (spina bifida repair) and orthopedic surgeon (lower limb deformity correction); mandatory preoperative neurological examination to detect areas of anaesthesia.
• Rehabilitation: the physiotherapist makes an assessment soon after diagnosis and discusses findings with the team to form an overall plan.
• Assessment techniques for posture and movement follow normal developmental patterns for the child's age; areas of anaesthesia are noted specifically to prevent pressure sores.
• Treatment provides forced stimulation to encourage active movement, teaching parents to assist and encourage the child.
• As activity develops, the physiotherapist follows the normal sequence of movement: sitting, rolling, crawling, and finally standing; passive movements are carried out to prevent contractures.
• The physiotherapist tries to prevent deformities through correct posture and teaches parents to watch for signs of pressure over pressure areas.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Definition: an affection of the palmar fascia characterized by localized thickening of the palmar aponeurosis involving the overlying skin of the palm, with a tendency to contract, drawing the affected fingers into fixed flexion, mostly starting near the base of the ring or little finger.

(b)
Aetiology: unknown, hereditary/familial, or traumatic (occupational hazard).

(c)
Pathogenesis: a primary disorder of the collagen substance of the fibrous tissue; the lesion starts as a fibroblastic nodule in the subcutaneous palmar fascia, passing through proliferative, involutional, and residual stages.

(d)
Diagnosis: occurs in middle age, more common in men than women; flexed proximal and middle phalanx with the terminal phalanx unaffected; in advanced cases permanent joint changes render straightening futile; skin of the palm becomes adherent and puckered. Investigation: X-ray hand, AP and lateral views.

(e)
Effect on function: progressive flexion contracture of the ring or little finger draws it into the palm, impairing hand opening and grip function, with advanced cases becoming permanently fixed.

(f)
• Conservative treatment: in early cases, night splintage and active exercises with gentle finger stretching by the patient; radiotherapy has a limited role in the early phase.
• Surgical treatment: fasciotomy, performed subcutaneously in elderly, arthritic, or poor-health patients, or partially for a small affected area with an immature nodule or early contracture from a fascial cord, or completely in younger patients with a disabling contracture.
• Postoperative care: immobilization by a splint for 1 week, followed by active exercises.
• Rehabilitation: physiotherapy exercises, assisted initially by the physiotherapist and progressing to active exercises under supervision.
• Manipulative therapy is also used as part of rehabilitation.
• Massage therapy forms part of the physiotherapy programme.
• Wax bath therapy is included in physiotherapy management to aid soft tissue mobility and comfort.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Anatomy: the talus is divided into the body, head, neck, posterior and lateral processes; it articulates with the tibia, fibula, calcaneus and navicular; 60% is covered by articular cartilage and nearly 70% of the entire surface area is articular surface, accounting for 90% of ankle range of motion.

(b)
Epidemiology: talus fractures account for 0.1 to 0.85% of all fractures and 5-7% of foot fractures; talar neck fractures constitute 30-50% of talus fractures.

(c)
Aetiology: frequently occurs in a young, active, mobile population following high-velocity trauma; talar neck fractures are caused by foot hyper-dorsiflexion, direct axial load, or a fall from height.

(d)
Clinical features: intense pain, inability to move the ankle, gross pedal oedema, distortion of the normal contours of the ankle and foot.

(e)
• Treatment, conservative: below-knee cast for 6-12 weeks - ankle in slight plantarflexion for 4 weeks, followed by a short leg walking cast for 2-8 weeks; once secure union is achieved, active range of motion and progressive weight bearing as tolerated is started.
• Treatment, surgical: open reduction internal fixation or external fixation followed by a below-knee cast for 6-12 weeks postoperatively; displaced fractures usually require surgical fixation.

(f)
• Clinical basis: the talar neck is thin and has approximately 15-20 degrees of medial deviation, making it the area most vulnerable to fracture.
• Continued: the talus has no tendon or muscle attachments, and because of its large articular surface and lack of musculotendinous attachments it has a fragile blood supply, so displacement at the neck readily disrupts this supply, predisposing to avascular necrosis.

(g)
• Distinguishing feature 1: talar neck fractures constitute 30-50% of talus fractures and are specifically caused by hyper-dorsiflexion, direct axial load, or fall from height.
• Distinguishing feature 2: talar neck fractures carry a recognised avascular necrosis risk due to disruption of the fragile blood supply at this thin, vulnerable segment.
• Distinguishing feature 4: both patterns fall under the general talus fracture presentation of intense pain, inability to move the ankle and gross pedal oedema, with displaced fractures of either pattern usually requiring surgical fixation.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Mechanism at the elbow: supracondylar fractures of the humerus in children, dislocations of the elbow joint, direct trauma, road/street accident, or operative excision of the elbow. At the wrist: cuts, Colles fracture of the lower radius, dislocation of the semilunar bone, or carpal tunnel syndrome.

(b)
Types: injury at elbow level and injury at wrist level, including compressive carpal tunnel syndrome.

(c)
Deformity: 'ape thumb', with the thumb lying in the same plane as the other metacarpals.

(d)
Complications: muscular wasting of the thenar eminence; flexor carpi radialis paralysis causing the hand to deviate ulnarward when flexed against resistance; flexor pollicis longus paralysis causing inability to flex the terminal phalanx of the thumb; sensory loss of muscle pain, joint sense, pressure sense, and cutaneous sensation at the thumb, index and middle finger tips; trophic changes in the terminal phalanx of the index finger.

(e)
Healing: results of suturing are usually unsatisfactory.

(f)
• Management: conservative treatment with immobilization in a universal arm pouch, analgesics/NSAIDs, and physiotherapy exercises. Surgical treatment for compression from fracture-dislocation or wounds involves exploration and suturing; carpal tunnel decompression is indicated for unrelieved symptoms of carpal tunnel syndrome; excision of the lunate (with or without prosthetic replacement) is indicated for avascular necrosis with median nerve compression.
• Testing: interossei (spread/close fingers, straighten 2nd/3rd phalanges, card test); abductor pollicis brevis via the pen test (touching a pen held in front of the flat, upturned palm); opponens pollicis by touching each fingertip with the thumb tip; flexor pollicis longus by bending the terminal phalanx of the thumb.
• Investigation includes electrical stimulation in situ and Tinel's sign, elicited after a couple of months, the level of tingling shifting distally as regeneration progresses.

(g)
• Physiotherapy after nerve suturing: postoperative POP cast for about 4 to 6 weeks, stitches removed after 2 days through a window in the cast, followed by exercises and occupational therapy.
• Physiotherapy after carpal tunnel decompression: exercises follow once symptoms have been relieved by decompression.
• Physiotherapy management overall may not require extensive treatment as recovery is likely within a few weeks in many cases, with advice on movement and reassurance being central.
• Factors affecting outcome include the nerve injured, infection, time to secondary suture, muscle tone maintenance, operative technique, and postoperative cooperation.

(a) Define and classify rickets and osteomalacia.
(b) What are the causes?
(c) What are the clinical features?
(d) What investigations are used?

(f) Distinguish rickets from osteomalacia.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Definition: a disturbance of the mineral-matrix ratio due to reduced mineralization; rickets is a deficiency disease due to lack of vitamin D (a component of natural fats and oils), and osteomalacia is the adult form of rickets.
• Classification: osteomalacia is common in females, and tetany may occur in advanced cases of either; both are prevalent in African, ASEAN and North Chinese populations.

(b)
• Causes: inadequate absorption of calcium and phosphorus from the intestine, due to lack of calcium alone or lack of/resistance to vitamin D.
• Further causes (osteomalacia in adults): disorders of fat absorption (diarrhoea, gastrectomy, pancreatitis, sprue), renal calcium or phosphorus losses (vitamin D resistant rickets), Fanconi's syndrome, or a mesenchymal tumour; risk factors include lack of sunshine, a diet poor in natural fats and oils, immobilization/lack of exercise, and neoplastic disease.

(c)
• Clinical features: a flabby child with a pot belly and sweating of the head; diminished stature from retarded bony growth (especially femur and tibia), bending of the leg bones and spinal deformities.
• Further features: increased width of shaft from increased epiphyses, rickety rosary from beading of the costochondral junctions, deformed (bowed) legs with an increased anterior curve of the femur and coxa vara, kyphosis followed by scoliosis, aching bones especially long bones and ribs, and muscular weakness/paralysis.

(d)
• Investigations: CBC, ESR, blood urea, low serum calcium and phosphate, and elevated alkaline phosphatase.
• Further investigations: low urinary calcium and phosphate, a positive bone densitometer test, and X-ray showing cupping and blurring of the epiphyseal line, demineralization and bowing.

(e)
• Complications: bony deformities of the legs and spine (bowing, kyphosis, scoliosis).
• Further complications: muscular weakness and paralysis.

(f)
• Rickets is the deficiency disease of childhood, affecting the growing epiphyseal cartilage of long bones (femur and tibia) and producing bowing, rickety rosary of the ribs and stunted stature.
• Osteomalacia is the adult form, common in females, and in adults is more often associated with disorders of fat absorption, renal calcium/phosphorus loss, Fanconi's syndrome or a mesenchymal tumour rather than the childhood growth-plate presentation.

(a)
Supracondylar fracture of the humerus, extension type - the commonest type (95-97%) and the most common elbow injury in children, usually under 8 years, peak age 5-7 years, more common in boys.

(b)
Open reduction and internal fixation for displaced fractures; fractures with neurovascular affectation are treated as a surgical emergency.

(c)
The fracture runs through the thinnest portion of the distal humerus, proximal to the trochlea and capitulum, often through the apices of the coronoid and olecranon fossae; nerve injuries occur in about 7% (radial greater than median greater than ulnar); vascular injury (brachial artery) occurs in about 1%; complications include vascular insufficiency of the brachial artery, compartment syndrome, cubitus varus ("gunstock") deformity, and Volkmann's ischaemic contracture.

(d)
To minimise the risk of compartment syndrome, the elbow should be immobilised at about 30 degrees of flexion in the emergency room and 60-70 degrees of flexion after surgery; undisplaced fractures are managed with a splint.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Rheumatoid arthritis (syn. atrophic arthritis) is a chronic inflammatory disease characterized by symmetric polyarthritis often leading to serious morbidity. Reiter's syndrome is a clinical tetrad of unknown aetiology consisting of polyarthritis, urethritis, conjunctivitis/uveitis and mucocutaneous manifestations.

(b)
• Rheumatoid arthritis is of unknown cause, possibly due to auto-immunity or infection.
• Reiter's syndrome is of unknown aetiology, predisposed by venereal contact (unprotected intercourse) or diarrhoea, occurring commonly in young men, often within 4 weeks of intercourse with an infected partner.
• Epidemiology: rheumatoid arthritis has an incidence of 1 to 3% in the general population, female:male ratio 3:1, age 20-40 years; Reiter's syndrome occurs commonly in young men.

(c)
• Clinical features, rheumatoid arthritis: morning stiffness; symmetric joint swelling; arthritis of hand joints (PIP, MCP, wrist), toes, ankles, knees; subcutaneous nodules over bony extensor aspects; warmth, local tenderness, fever, malaise, weight loss, sweating, paresthesia, scleritis, iritis.
• Clinical features, Reiter's syndrome: asymmetrical arthritis usually of large weight-bearing joints (knee, ankle), sacroiliitis, ankylosing spondylitis; insidious onset with articular stiffness, painful and restricted movements relieved by rest, valgus or varus knee deformity, joint effusion; conjunctivitis, uveitis; stomatitis, keratoderma, balanitis, urethritis; carditis, aortic regurgitation; fever, malaise, weight loss.

(d)
• Investigations, rheumatoid arthritis: CBC, ESR; rheumatoid factor (latex particle agglutination); quantitative immunoglobulins (IgA, IgM, IgG); X-ray of wrists and hands showing early osteoporosis and cartilage erosion at the joint periphery.
• Investigations, Reiter's syndrome: CBC (anemia); elevated ESR; positive Wassermann reaction; auto-antibody screen; positive rheumatoid factor; X-ray of the knees, ankle, spine and chest.

(e)
Complications: for Reiter's syndrome, most signs disappear within days to weeks, but the arthritis may continue for months to years.

(f)
• Distinguishing the two conditions: rheumatoid arthritis is a symmetric polyarthritis of unknown cause affecting mainly women aged 20-40, diagnosed by at least 4 of 7 criteria (morning stiffness, symmetric joint swelling, hand/toe/ankle/knee arthritis, subcutaneous nodules, positive rheumatoid factor, radiologic changes), whereas Reiter's syndrome is an asymmetric arthritis of large joints in young men with a venereal or diarrhoeal trigger, combined with urethritis, conjunctivitis/uveitis and mucocutaneous lesions.
• Management, rheumatoid arthritis: rest (complete bedrest in severe systemic/articular involvement, brief rest in mild cases); heat and cold for muscle relaxation and analgesia; drugs - NSAIDs with or without analgesics, corticosteroids, disease-modifying agents (chloroquine, sulfasalazine, methotrexate, cyclosporin), gold, newer anti-TNF therapy.
• Management, Reiter's syndrome, and physiotherapy for both: Reiter's syndrome is treated conservatively and symptomatically with analgesics and NSAIDs, and antibiotics; physiotherapy for rheumatoid arthritis includes indoor physiotherapy (bedrest, splintage, exercises, advice) and outdoor physiotherapy (muscle power work, joint range exercises, hydrotherapy), while for Reiter's syndrome it includes heat or ice packs for pain relief and regular exercises 2-3 times daily.
