questions.question:
(a) Describe syphilis of bones and joints under the following headings: definition and classification, aetiology and transmission, clinical features, investigations.
(b) Explain how it affects function.
(c) Outline the conservative, surgical and rehabilitation management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Definition/classification: syphilis of bones and joints is an inflammation of the bones and joints caused by the spirochaetal infection Treponema pallidum, which may occur during any stage of congenital or acquired systemic disease; tertiary joint lesions are now rarely seen since the disease is usually detected early and treated effectively.
• Aetiology and transmission: Treponema pallidum (syn. Spirochaeta pallida); hematogenous spread from a primary focus.
• Clinical features, congenital syphilis: Clutton's joints - bilateral, painless hydrops of the knee in a child.
• Clinical features, acquired syphilis: secondary stage - arthralgia and hydrarthrosis (fleeting bone pains due to periostitis); tertiary stage - diffuse periosteal gumma, usually forming in the tibia, clavicle and manubrium; the pathognomonic lesion is painless, symmetrical hydrops with free and painless mobility.
• Investigations: X-ray (syphilitic osteitis not diagnostic, bone production more pronounced than bone destruction); CBC showing leukocytosis; positive Wassermann serological reaction.

(b)
• Effect on function: joint lesions are usually painless with free mobility, but residual disability can occur from destruction of the joint in advanced cases.
• Complications: residual disability of joints due to destruction

(c)
• Conservative/medical management: immobilization to provide comfort or protect weak osteoporotic bone from fracture; preventive measures (avoiding sex with an unknown person, condom use, good hygiene); antibiotic - procaine penicillin 2.4 million units IM into each buttock once daily.
• Systemic management: lesions of bones and joints respond markedly and promptly to adequate chemotherapy of the systemic disease using benzyl penicillin (penicillin G).
• Surgical management (indication: residual disability of joints due to destruction): synovectomy for thickened synovial membrane; arthrodesis for destroyed articular surfaces of the joint.
• Rehabilitation/physiotherapy management: immobilization by splints, braces, etc. to provide comfort or protect weak osteoporotic bone from fracture.
• Physiotherapy exercises: assisted passive exercises provided by the physiotherapist, progressed to free active exercises for free joint movement and to strengthen weak muscles.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the pathology/levels of amputation and the stages of psychological adjustment.
(b) State how this relates to phantom limb pain and residual limb pain.
(c) Explain how amputation may spread its effect to cause functional and psychosocial impact.
(d) Outline the physiotherapy management across its phases.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Definition: amputation is the surgical removal of a body part in part or in full, different from disarticulation, which means removal of a part through a joint; causes include severe infection with extensive tissue damage, gangrene, trauma, congenital deformity, necrosis, peripheral arterial disease, malignant tumour, and conditions affecting blood flow such as diabetes.
• Levels, lower limb: hindquarter amputation, hip disarticulation, above-knee amputation, knee disarticulation, below-knee amputation (the most commonly performed), Syme's amputation, Chopart's amputation, Lisfranc's amputation.
• Stages of psychological adjustment: shock and denial, grief and mourning, acceptance, and reconstruction.

(b)
• Relation to phantom limb pain: phantom limb pain is the feeling of pain in a missing body part after amputation, localised in the region of the removed body part, experienced by over half of people with amputation.
• Continued: most people have it in the first 6 months after amputation with intensity/frequency decreasing thereafter, though some still have phantom pain up to 2 years post-amputation; triggers include fatigue, stress, anxiety, depression, infection, blood flow issues, and pressure/swelling on the stump.
• Relation to residual limb pain: residual limb pain affects the remaining part of the limb (the stump), with causes including post-operative pain, peripheral nerve neuroma at the end of cut peripheral nerves, and prosthetic pain from an ill-fitting prosthesis.

(c)
• Spread to functional/psychosocial impact: amputation has a huge psychological impact, similar to the loss of a loved one.
• Continued: it brings difficulty coping with loss of function/sensation and changes in body image perception.
• Continued: specific implications include depression and anxiety, body image issues, trauma, and adjustment challenges in daily life; complications of amputation (oedema and swelling, wound infection, muscle weakness, muscle tightness and contractures, joint instability, autonomic dysfunction, somatosensory impairment) further compound the functional impact.

(d)
• Physiotherapy, pre-operative/acute phases: pre-operative phase focuses on patient education, preparation, and strengthening exercises if possible; the acute post-operative phase (0-2 weeks) focuses on pain management, wound care, positioning and mobility, and preventing complications.
• Continued: the sub-acute phase (2-6 weeks) involves strengthening/ROM exercises, mobility training and scar management; the pre-prosthetic phase (from 6 weeks) focuses on strengthening/conditioning and shaping the residual limb.
• Continued: the prosthetic training phase involves learning to use the prosthesis, gaining mobility/independence and functional training; overall goals throughout are promoting healing, preventing complications, and maximising function and independence.

questions.question:
Regarding Charcot's (neuropathic) joint:
(a) What is the mechanism/cause?
(b) What regional types of surgery are used?
(c) What deformity/joint change results?
(d) What are the complications?
(e) How does postoperative healing proceed?
(f) What are the management principles?
(g) Explain the physiotherapy management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Mechanism/cause: trophic changes in weight-bearing joints.
• Causes: tabes dorsalis, syringomyelia, diabetic neuropathy, or alcohol neuropathy.

(b)
• Regional surgery — hip: osteotomy (for a destroyed femoral head and neck), reconstruction, or arthrodesis.
• Regional surgery — knee, ankle and spine: arthrodesis is the surgical procedure of choice for the knee and ankle (with talectomy plus tibiocalcaneal arthrodesis for a markedly destroyed, avascular talus), and arthrodesis is also used for the spine.

(c)
Deformity/joint change: X-ray shows marked destruction of the joint, sclerosis, and fragmentation.

(d)
Complications: joint destruction, with genitourinary manifestations of dysuria and pyouria noted.

(e)
• Postoperative healing (knee): immobilization in a POP spica for 2-3 months.
• Aftercare (knee): walking with knee support (brace) for a year.

(f)
• Management principles (conservative, symptomatic): rest, analgesics and NSAIDs, and antibiotics.
• Management principles (surgical): arthrodesis, as above by joint.

(g)
• Physiotherapy management: muscle-strengthening exercises (active and passive), traction, and heat therapy (SWD/IRR).
• Further physiotherapy: wax bath therapy, hydrotherapy, massage (stroking, compression), ambulation aids, and acupuncture/acupressure and yoga therapy.

questions.question:
(a) Describe osteoporosis under the headings of definition, aetiology, clinical features and investigations.
(b) Explain how it affects function.
(c) Outline the conservative and rehabilitation management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Definition: a progressive systemic disease characterized by reduced bone mass and deteriorating bone tissue (matrix), resulting in increased bone fragility, so a fracture may occur with minor injury once bone loss exceeds 30%.
• Aetiology: primary (unknown) or secondary — traumatic (prolonged immobilization), inflammatory (rheumatoid arthritis, tuberculous, syphilitic), endocrinal (lack of androgens/senile, lack of estrogens/postmenopausal, hypopituitarism/hypogonadism, hyperthyroidism, hyperparathyroidism), excess ACTH/corticosteroids (Cushing's syndrome), diabetes mellitus, pregnancy, calcium deficiency, or multiple myeloma; risk factors include age over 60, female sex, alcohol abuse, smoking, poor diet, sedentary lifestyle, lack of exercise, and prolonged heparin/corticosteroid use.
• Clinical features: ranges from asymptomatic to severe backache (low backache), with fracture as the most common finding.
• Investigations: serum calcium, phosphate and alkaline phosphatase are normal; X-ray shows demineralization of the spine, pelvis and limbs.
• Further investigations: bone densitometry (BMD), recorded as a T score (against a healthy young adult) or a Z score (against a person of the same sex and age), used for early diagnosis, along with quantitative CT and MRI.

(b)
• Effect on function: fractures most commonly occur at the neck of femur and the vertebral body (compression/crush fracture), impairing mobility and independence.
• Fracture may also occur at the wrist (Colles' fracture).
• Function is further affected by deformity resulting from vertebral compression.

(c)
• Conservative management (diet and lifestyle): a high-protein diet adequate in calcium (milk and milk products), stopping smoking, and reducing alcohol intake.
• Conservative management (medical): calcium and vitamin D, and analgesics/NSAIDs.
• Rehabilitation/physiotherapy management: regular exercise, especially weight-bearing exercise, under the supervision and teaching of the physiotherapist.

(a)
Congenital scoliosis is a congenital disorder characterized by a lateral curved spine caused by anomalies of one or more vertebrae. Idiopathic scoliosis is a deformity of the spine with lateral curves, deviation of vertebrae from the midline, and abnormal vertebral rotation, which the patient cannot correct or maintain corrected.

(b)
Congenital scoliosis aetiology: anomalies such as hemivertebrae, failure of segmentation of posterior elements, and muscular or ligamentous contractures. Idiopathic scoliosis is primary in about 80% of cases (cause unknown); secondary (20%) causes include congenital spinal anomalies, trauma, poliomyelitis, empyema, neurofibromatosis, muscular dystrophy, Friedreich's ataxia, and cerebral palsy.

(c)
Pathogenesis: in congenital scoliosis, a primary curve is a single sharp lateral curve, with secondary curves developing with growth. In idiopathic scoliosis, primary curves develop structural changes (wedging, angulation, rotation) simultaneously and do not correct spontaneously, while secondary curves develop these changes more slowly and retain longer the ability to correct spontaneously.

(d)
Diagnosis: cervical curves show a short, thick neck with restricted movement; dorsal curves show deformity; lumbar curves show accompanying kyphosis; shortening may occur; high dorsal curves show elevated shoulder, prominent scapula, and projected ribs (razorback). Investigations: X-ray spine, MRI, CT scan; curves measured by Cobb's method or Ferguson's method.

(e)
Effect on function: deformity causes visible trunk asymmetry, restricted movement, and in severe cases can affect posture and comfort; the physiotherapist cannot alter a structural curve once there is a change in bone structure.

(f)
• Conservative treatment: maintenance of posture, leg lengthening by a shoe lift, and Milwaukee brace to control and correct rapidly increasing scoliosis; turnbuckle and localizer casts are also used.
• Surgical treatment: excision of the hemivertebra for congenital scoliosis; for idiopathic scoliosis, arthrodesis of the spine aims to correct and maintain correction, indicated in a growing child with an increasing curve, an adolescent with severe trunk asymmetry, or an older patient with uncontrollable pain.
• Rehabilitation: in non-surgical cases the physiotherapist teaches the child to hold a correct position and perform active exercises to strengthen trunk muscles, monitoring progress and posture deterioration.
• In surgical cases, the physiotherapist teaches the child to adjust to the new posture and strengthen muscles to hold the position and perform normal function.
• Hydrotherapy is a helpful modality once the child mobilizes freely.
• Physiotherapy may provide symptomatic relief for pain and discomfort from stretching of soft tissue structures.
• In certain cases it may be possible to prevent further deterioration by positioning and strengthening muscles, even though the structural curve itself cannot be reversed.
questions.question:

(b) State the aetiology of each.
(c) Describe the pathogenesis (primary vs secondary curves).
(d) Describe the clinical diagnosis and investigations.
(e) Explain how scoliosis affects function.
(f) Outline the conservative, surgical, and rehabilitation management.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Risk factors: severe polytrauma with multiple fractures, injury to bone marrow or adipose tissue, fractures of osteoporotic bone, atheromatous plaque, blood clots from thrombosed veins or cardiac sources, and vegetations from cardiac valves.

(b)
Complications: cerebral effects (drowsiness, restlessness, delirium, narrow pupils, fever, coma) and pulmonary effects (dyspnea, cyanosis, chest pain, striate retinal haemorrhages, petechial haemorrhages, frothy mouth); regional effects include hemiplegia (brain), blindness (eyes), pulmonary embolism (lungs), gangrene of intestinal loop (mesentery), loin pain and hematuria (kidneys), splenomegaly (spleen), and limb pain, pallor, and gangrene.

(c)
Management: emergency measures include admission to A&E, input/output monitoring, IV fluids (5% dextrose), vasodilators (Papaverine), heparin, antibiotics, and analgesics. Surgical treatment is closed reduction or ORIF of fractures, aiming for the best fixation with least manipulation and surgery; this surgical fixation is justified since stabilizing the fracture source reduces ongoing embolization.

(d)
Physiotherapy role: encouraging foot exercises with the leg elevated and remaining ambulant to maintain venous circulation; in severe cases the patient may be confined to bed for a short period, with treatment modified according to the patient's condition.
questions.question:
A patient with multiple long-bone fractures following severe polytrauma develops drowsiness, restlessness, dyspnea, cyanosis, and petechial haemorrhages over the anterior chest and conjunctival sac.
(a) What are the risk factors for this condition?
(b) What are the early and late complications?
(c) What are the conservative and surgical management options, and which would you justify?
(d) What is the physiotherapy role?

questions.answerText:
(a)
Mallet fracture.

(b)
Occurs at the insertion of the terminal finger extensor mechanism into the dorsal portion of the distal phalanx; caused by an axial load to the tip of an extended finger, leading to forced flexion at the DIP joint; includes a bone fragment attached to the terminal extensor mechanism. Referral for surgical management is indicated for fractures involving greater than 30% of the intra-articular surface and those associated with volar subluxation of the distal phalanx.

(c)
Splinting of the DIP joint in extension for eight weeks; extension is always maintained during treatment because any flexion can affect healing and may extend the treatment period. Physiotherapy role: passive stretching to correct residual soft tissue tightness (care taken not to dislocate the joint), heat treatment, soft tissue massage, and active and assisted active finger exercises.
questions.question:
A basketball player sustains an axial load to the tip of an extended finger and is unable to actively extend the distal interphalangeal joint.
(a) State the most likely diagnosis.
(b) Discuss the predisposing factors and pathophysiology of this condition.
(c) Outline the management, including the physiotherapy role.

A patient sustains a direct blow to the elbow and presents with a palpable gap over the olecranon and inability to extend the elbow against resistance.
(a) State the most likely diagnosis.
(b) Name the surgery/procedure indicated.
(c) State the nerve/vessel/structure at risk.
(d) Outline the post-operative rehabilitation and physiotherapy considerations.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Olecranon fracture, transverse type, due to forced contraction of the triceps muscle; common in osteoporotic patients.

(b)
Displaced transverse fracture is treated with open reduction and internal fixation.

(c)
Injury to the ulnar nerve is a recognised complication.

(d)
Following operation, early mobilisation should be encouraged; undisplaced transverse fractures are immobilised in a cast at about 60 degrees of elbow flexion for 2-3 weeks before exercises begin.

(a)
• Mechanism: a relatively rare injury due to the stability of the knee joint; caused by high-energy trauma/high-speed injuries - motor vehicle accidents, auto-pedestrian, industrial injuries, falls from height, sport injuries.
• Types, descriptive (direction of tibial displacement): anterior - hyperextension injury; posterior - axial load on a flexed knee (e.g. dashboard injury); medial, lateral, or rotatory - corresponding forces.
• Types, Schenck classification (ligamentous involvement): KD I - either ACL or PCL; KD II - ACL and PCL only; KD III - ACL, PCL and MCL or LCL; KD IV - ACL, PCL, MCL and LCL; KD V - multiligamentous injury with periarticular fracture; C denotes arterial injury and N denotes nerve injury.
• Clinical features: gross knee deformity, knee swelling and immobility, associated fractures, knee pain and instability.
• Complications: vascular damage to the popliteal artery and popliteal vein, nerve damage to the peroneal nerve, knee stiffness and osteoarthritis, chronically unstable and painful knee, limb damage/amputation.

(b)
• Precautions: knee dislocation is a medical emergency requiring vascular assessment before definitive management, given that coexistent vascular injury is a major complication that can lead to limb loss.
• Continued: management includes surgery and vascular repair where indicated, followed by a long rehabilitation programme, with return to full activity taking about 9-12 months.
• Continued: nonoperative treatment involves 6-8 weeks of non-weight bearing with passive and active range-of-motion training and muscle strengthening, with a brace limiting ROM from 90 degrees of flexion to 45 degrees of extension at the early rehabilitation stage.

(c)
• Biomechanical basis: knee dislocation is rare precisely because of the inherent stability of the knee joint, so its occurrence signals a high-energy mechanism.
• Continued: the popliteal artery lies in close anatomical proximity behind the knee joint, so the high-energy displacement of the tibia relative to the femur that disrupts the cruciate and collateral ligaments also places tensile and shearing stress on the popliteal vessels.
• Continued: this is why coexistent vascular injury to the popliteal artery/vein is a major complication that can lead to limb loss, and why the peroneal nerve, which also courses close to the joint, is at similar risk.
• Continued: the Schenck classification's C and N suffixes reflect this correlation between ligamentous disruption and neurovascular injury risk.

(b) State the precautions regarding vascular assessment before reduction.
(c) Explain the biomechanical basis for the risk of popliteal artery injury in this condition.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Trochanteric bursitis is inflammation of the trochanteric bursa, a large synovial sac separating the aponeurotic part of gluteus maximus from the lower part of the outer aspect of the greater trochanter of the femur. Ischiogluteal bursitis (Weaver's Bottom) is inflammation of the ischiogluteal bursa, which separates the gluteus maximus muscle from the ischial tuberosity.

(b)
• Aetiology (both): traumatic or frictional; inflammatory (pyogenic, tuberculous); rheumatic (RA, gout, rheumatic fever); the inflammation of the bursa is rarely primary, rather resulting from tendinitis of the glutei tendons of the hip due to recurrent friction, and ischiogluteal bursitis is usually caused by constant irritation/friction, occurring most often in persons with a sedentary occupation (e.g. weavers).
• Pathogenesis (both): inflamed synovium, effusion, fibrosis, and ankylosis.

(c)
Clinical features (both): pain; swelling; local tenderness; limp; movements of the hip painful and restricted.

(d)
Investigations (both): CBC, ESR, blood sugar, blood uric acid; X-ray of the hip, which in trochanteric bursitis may show synovitis and calcific deposits, and in ischiogluteal bursitis may show synovial effusion and calcific deposits.

(e)
• Distinguishing the two conditions: trochanteric bursitis affects the bursa over the greater trochanter and is linked to glutei tendinitis, whereas ischiogluteal bursitis affects the bursa over the ischial tuberosity and is specifically associated with sedentary/friction occupations such as weaving.
• Conservative management (both): rest; immobilization (traction, for trochanteric bursitis); diathermy; analgesics/NSAIDs; injection of intra-articular corticosteroid with local anaesthetic (hydrocortisone acetate or triamcinolone acetonide with lignocaine); antibiotics.
• Surgical management (both): aspiration and injection of an appropriate drug; incision and drainage; excision of the entire bursa.
• After care (both): physiotherapy.
• Physiotherapy management (both): heat therapy (SWD/IRR or heating pad therapy).
• Physiotherapy exercises (both): as pain subsides, active exercises for joint movement and muscle strengthening.
questions.question:
(a) Define and classify trochanteric bursitis and ischiogluteal bursitis (Weaver's Bottom).
(b) What is the causes/aetiology and pathogenesis of each?
(c) What are the clinical features?
(d) What investigations are used?
(e) Distinguish between trochanteric bursitis and ischiogluteal bursitis.

A patient with tabes dorsalis develops marked destruction and avascularity of the talus, confirmed on X-ray by joint destruction, sclerosis and fragmentation.
(a) What are the risk factors/causes for this joint destruction?
(b) What are the early and late complications?
(c) What are the conservative versus surgical management options for the ankle, and which would you justify?
(d) What is the role of physiotherapy?
questions.answerText:
(a)
Causes: tabes dorsalis, syringomyelia, diabetic neuropathy, and alcohol neuropathy, producing trophic changes in weight-bearing joints.

(b)
Complications: joint destruction, and genitourinary manifestations of dysuria and pyouria have been noted with this condition.

(c)
Conservative treatment is symptomatic: rest, analgesics and NSAIDs, and antibiotics. Surgical treatment for the ankle is arthrodesis, the procedure of choice, with talectomy plus tibiocalcaneal arthrodesis indicated where the talus is markedly destroyed and avascular.

(d)
Physiotherapy role: muscle-strengthening exercises (active and passive), traction, heat therapy (SWD/IRR), wax bath therapy, hydrotherapy, massage (stroking, compression), ambulation aids (walking stick, walker, crutches, braces/belts), and acupuncture/acupressure and yoga therapy.

(a)
• Pathology: algodystrophy (complex regional pain syndrome), previously known as Sudeck's atrophy, is a post-traumatic reflex sympathetic dystrophy.
• Sites: usually seen in the foot or hand.
• Trigger: occurs after a relatively trivial injury.

(b)
• Relation to trivial hand/foot injury: because algodystrophy is described as occurring after relatively trivial injury of the foot or hand, it can follow minor trauma that might otherwise be expected to resolve without significant sequelae.
• Continued: this contrasts with the major-trauma complications described elsewhere (such as compartment syndrome or myositis ossificans), showing that the severity of the initiating injury does not predict the severity of this particular complication.

(c)
• Early clinical features: continuous, burning pain; in the early stage, local swelling, redness and warmth are present.
• Later clinical features: atrophy of the skin and muscles develops later, and movements are grossly restricted.
• Spread of effect: X-rays show patchy rarefaction of the bones (patchy osteoporosis), demonstrating that the process spreads beyond the original site of trivial injury to affect the skin, muscle and underlying bone of the limb segment.
• Continued: this progression from localised early swelling/redness/warmth to widespread skin and muscle atrophy with gross movement restriction and patchy bone rarefaction shows how a trivial local injury can produce a disabling regional condition.

(d)
• Drug management: anti-inflammatory drugs; sympathetic block or sympatholytic drugs (guanethidine).
• Physiotherapy management: elevation and active exercises.
• Continued: these are applied together with the drug measures above to address both the pain/sympathetic component and the resulting stiffness/atrophy as the condition evolves from its early swelling/redness/warmth stage into its later atrophic, movement-restricted stage.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the pathology and stages of algodystrophy (complex regional pain syndrome).
(b) State how this relates to relatively trivial injury of the hand or foot.
(c) Explain how the condition may spread its effect to cause skin and muscle atrophy with joint restriction.
(d) Outline the drug and physiotherapy management.

A patient falls on an outstretched hand and presents with tenderness on pressure over the radial head and pain on pronation and supination.
(a) State the most likely diagnosis.
(b) Name the surgery/procedure indicated.
(c) Outline the post-operative rehabilitation and physiotherapy considerations.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Radial head fracture, caused by impaction of the radial head against the capitulum, causing the radial head to split or crack.

(b)
Displaced fractures are treated with open reduction and internal fixation.

(c)
Undisplaced fractures are held in a collar and cuff for 3 weeks, with active flexion, extension and rotation encouraged; the prognosis for this injury is very good.

questions.question:
(a) Define and classify Paget's disease.
(b) What are the causes?
(c) What are the clinical features?
(d) What investigations are used?
(e) What are the complications?
(f) Distinguish Paget's disease from polyostotic fibrous dysplasia.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Definition: a nonsystemic localized skeletal affection of bones (osteitis deformans), which may affect a single or multiple bones, often involving only a portion of a single bone.
• Classification: it affects the spine (usually the lumbar region), skull, sternum, ribs, humerus, hipbone, femur and tibia in descending order of frequency, and spares the small bones.

(b)
Causes: unknown.

(c)
• Clinical features: pain, backache, and local tenderness.
• Further features: deformity with bowing of the leg, an enlarged skull, and thickened facial bones.

(d)
• Investigations: X-ray is diagnostic, showing Paget bone formed or destroyed, a thickened skull, and wedged vertebrae.
• Further investigations: in long bones, Paget's disease begins at one end and advances to the other end.

(e)
• Complications: pathological fractures of weight-bearing bones such as the femur and tibia.
• Further complications: osteoarthritis, from altered mechanics and muscular weakness.

(f)
• Paget's disease is a nonsystemic localized skeletal affection of unknown cause, with bones thickened, softened, deformed and fractured, and vertebrae collapsed.
• Polyostotic fibrous dysplasia is a congenital dysplasia (not a metabolic disorder) with generalized bone resorption and diffuse cystic changes where bone and cartilage fail to form and are replaced by fibrous tissue, and is often mistaken for osteitis fibrosa generalisata due to hyperparathyroidism, from which it is distinguished by not being a metabolic disorder.

questions.question:
A 7-year-old boy presents with a limp and hip pain of gradual onset. On examination there is muscular wasting, the limb is held adducted and externally rotated, and abduction and internal rotation of the hip are restricted while flexion and extension remain free and painless.
(a) What is the diagnosis?
(b) What are the predisposing factors and pathophysiology of this condition?
(c) Outline the medical/surgical management.
(d) Outline the physiotherapy management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Diagnosis: Perthes disease (coxa plana, pseudocoxalgia).

(b)
Predisposing factors/pathophysiology: Etiology is unknown, genetic, or traumatic; the femoral head becomes flattened, fragmented, and condensed; commoner in boys than girls, aged 5-15 years; X-ray of the pelvis (AP view) shows marked incongruity, flattening of the femoral head, and the femur displaced upwards, confirmed by Shenton's line.

(c)
Medical/surgical management: Conservative - bedrest, traction, diathermy (SWD, infrared), analgesics/NSAIDs. Surgical (for failure of conservative measures) - drilling of the proximal femoral epiphysis, correction of disturbed soft tissues, trochanteric osteotomy, or arthrodesis with the hip fixed in flexion and adduction.

(d)
Physiotherapy management: Assisted passive exercises by the physiotherapist progressed to free active exercises by the patient.

questions.question:
(a) Describe osteoarthritis under the headings of definition, aetiology, clinical features and investigations.
(b) Explain how it affects function.
(c) Outline the conservative, surgical and rehabilitation management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Definition: a chronic, progressive arthropathy characterised by degeneration of articular cartilage and hypertrophy of bone at the articular margins, without systemic manifestations; it is the commonest form of arthritis worldwide, commonly affecting the hands, feet, spine and large weight-bearing joints such as the hips and knees.
• Aetiology: primary (idiopathic, of unknown cause) or secondary, due to a pre-existing congenital, traumatic, inflammatory (rheumatoid arthritis), infective (septic arthritis, tuberculosis), endocrinal (diabetes mellitus), metabolic (hyperparathyroidism) or neuropathic (tabes dorsalis) disorder; risk factors include advancing age over 60, sedentary life, being overweight, wrong posture/misuse of the joint, and strenuous exercise including regular stair use.
• Clinical features: insidious onset after age 60, morning stiffness, and dull aching pain aggravated by joint use/weight-bearing and relieved by rest, without systemic manifestations.
• Further clinical features: swelling or deformity, muscular wasting, crepitus, and painful restricted movement.
• Investigations: X-ray shows asymmetric narrowing of the joint space and osteophytes at joint margins; MRI may reveal early changes missed on X-ray; CT scan is indicated in cervical or lumbar spondylosis with neurological manifestation.

(b)
• Effect on function: pain and restricted, crepitant movement of the affected joints (hands, feet, spine, hips, knees) impair weight-bearing and mobility.
• Function is further affected by muscular wasting.
• Function is further affected by any resulting swelling or deformity.

(c)
• Conservative/preventive management: joint protection and conservation by avoiding joint stress (squatting, ascending/descending stairs, prolonged standing, long walks), muscle-strengthening exercises, traction, heat therapy, massage, ambulation aid devices, acupuncture/acupressure, and yoga therapy.
• Medical management: analgesics and NSAIDs (with caution for toxicity in the elderly), and intra-articular steroid injection.
• Surgical management: excision of osteophytes, excision of loose bodies, arthroscopic débridement, synovectomy, reconstruction, arthroplasty (joint replacement), or arthrodesis.
• Rehabilitation/physiotherapy management: aimed at relieving pain, strengthening muscles, mobilizing joints, improving coordination and minimizing deformity, through exercises, traction, heat therapy, wax bath therapy (for hands and feet), hydrotherapy, massage, orthoses and acupuncture/yoga therapy.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the mechanism, types, clinical features and complications of thoracolumbar spinal injuries.
(b) State the precautions/safe approach for skull traction in unstable spinal injuries.
(c) Explain the biomechanical basis of column failure and kyphotic deformity in these injuries.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Mechanism: fractures of the spine are commonly caused by indirect violence to the head, shoulders or buttocks; main injuring forces include flexion, extension, compression and rotation, often combined; 60-70% of thoracolumbar fractures occur in the T11-L2 region, which is biomechanically weak for stress.
• Types, compression and burst fracture: compression fracture is failure of the anterior column; burst fracture is failure of the anterior and middle columns due to axial loading, the entire vertebra evenly crushed with possible retropulsion into the spinal canal, most common at the thoracolumbar junction.
• Types, flexion-distraction and fracture-dislocation: flexion-distraction/seat-belt injury is failure of the posterior and middle columns under tension, from sudden upper-body forward flexion while the lower body is stationary; fracture-dislocation is failure of all three columns, the most unstable pattern, highly associated with neurological deficits.
• Clinical features: over 65% of thoracic fracture cases are asymptomatic; when symptomatic - chronic thoracic/lumbar pain, slower gait, decreased range of motion, impaired pulmonary function, increased kyphosis (especially in osteoporotic patients), and neurological deficits from spinal canal narrowing that can present as late as 1.5 years post-injury.
• Complications: with greater forces, the spinal cord and nerve roots may be crushed or compressed, and the same forces may tear the meninges and impair blood supply to the cord; unmanaged symptoms lead to decreased physical function, decreased performance of activities of daily living, increased risk of disability, and vertebral deformities associated with increased risk of future fractures.

(b)
• Precautions: in all suspected spinal injuries, assume the spinal cord is injured until proven otherwise, and move the patient as little as possible until an X-ray rules out a fracture.
• Continued: dislocations/subluxations of the cervical spine are promptly reduced and rigidly immobilised by skull traction (with a 'halo' screwed into the diploe of the skull), and stability is assessed after 3 months.
• Continued: for thoracolumbar injuries, postural reduction is required; in difficult cases or with gross displacement, internal fixation with Harrington rods is used; below L2, compression fractures are treated conservatively while fracture-dislocation requires open reduction and internal fixation.

(c)
• Biomechanical basis: spinal stability is provided by three columns (Denis three-column theory); trauma focused into the middle column is sufficient to cause instability, categorised as first-degree (mechanical), second-degree (neurological), or third-degree (combined).
• Continued: compression fracture is failure of the anterior column alone; burst fracture is failure of both anterior and middle columns, making it more severe and carrying a higher risk of neurologic injury; fracture-dislocation is failure of all three columns, making it the most unstable.
• Continued: this progression from anterior-only to all-three-column failure explains the progression from stable compression injury to unstable fracture-dislocation.
• Continued: the resulting kyphotic deformity reflects the degree of anterior column height loss relative to the posterior elements.

(a)
• Mechanism: extension type is the commonest type (95-97%), most common in children under 8 years (peak 5-7 years), affecting boys more than girls, and becoming less common with increasing age.
• Types: the fracture goes through the thinnest portion of the distal humerus, proximal to the trochlea and capitulum, often running through the apices of the coronoid and olecranon fossae or through the metaphysis.
• Clinical features: mild swelling to gross deformity, arm held to the side, reduced movement at the elbow, S-shaped configuration.
• Complications, nerve/vascular: nerve injuries occur in about 7% (radial greater than median greater than ulnar), vascular injuries in about 1%, and open fractures in less than 1%.
• Continued: further complications include vascular insufficiency of the brachial artery, compartment syndrome, cubitus varus deformity, and Volkmann's ischaemic contracture.

(b)
• Precautions: fractures with neurovascular affectation are treated as a surgical emergency.
• Continued: to minimise the risk of compartment syndrome, the elbow should be immobilised at about 30 degrees of flexion in the emergency room and 60-70 degrees of flexion after surgery.
• Continued: undisplaced fractures are managed with a splint; displaced fractures require open reduction and internal fixation.
• Continued: associated forearm fractures and elbow flexion greater than 90 degrees increase compartment pressures, which is why the flexion angle during splinting/positioning must be carefully limited.

(c)
• Biomechanical basis: the fracture line runs through the thinnest, weakest portion of the distal humerus just above the trochlea and capitulum, a site closely related to the brachial artery and median/radial/ulnar nerves as they cross the elbow.
• Continued: vascular insufficiency of the brachial artery and compartment syndrome can occur when the fracture fragments and associated swelling compress these neurovascular structures, particularly when the elbow is flexed beyond the safe range.
• Continued: cubitus varus deformity results from malunion of the fracture with the distal fragment tilted into varus relative to the humeral shaft, which is why the elbow flexion angle used in emergency splinting (about 30 degrees) and postoperative positioning (60-70 degrees) is specifically limited, to reduce compartment pressure and protect the brachial artery from the increased tension greater flexion would create.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the mechanism, types, clinical features and complications of supracondylar fracture of the humerus with particular reference to neurovascular injury.
(b) State the precautions for elbow positioning during splinting to minimise complications.
(c) Explain the biomechanical basis of the cubitus varus ("gunstock") deformity.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Risk factors: the aetiology is unknown; the disease is a nonsystemic localized skeletal affection that may affect a single or multiple bones, often only a portion of a single bone, most often the spine (usually the lumbar region), skull, sternum, ribs, humerus, hipbone, femur and tibia in descending order of frequency, sparing the small bones.

(b)
Complications: pathological fractures of weight-bearing bones such as the femur and tibia, and osteoarthritis from altered mechanics and muscular weakness.

(c)
There is no specific treatment to control progress of the disease. Conservative treatment is for relief of pain: analgesics/NSAIDs, and radiotherapy for relief of severe bony pain. Surgical treatment (osteotomy) is justified only for relief of pain due to faulty mechanics.

(d)
Physiotherapy role: required for relief of pain and tenderness of the muscles and to assist the patient in becoming mobile as soon as possible, and also for the fractures or osteoarthritis that may develop as complications of the disease.
questions.question:
An older patient presents with backache, local tenderness, bowing of the leg and an enlarged skull with thickened facial bones; X-ray shows thickened, softened, deformed and fractured bone with wedged vertebrae.
(a) What are the risk factors for this condition?
(b) What are the early and late complications?
(c) What are the conservative versus surgical management options, and which would you justify?
(d) What is the role of physiotherapy?

questions.answerText:
(a)
Talar neck fracture.

(b)
Talar neck fractures frequently occur in a young, active, mobile population following a history of high-velocity trauma, and are caused by foot hyper-dorsiflexion, direct axial load, or a fall from height. The talar neck is thin, with approximately 15-20 degrees of medial deviation, making it the area most vulnerable to fracture. The talus has no tendon or muscle attachments, and because of its large articular surface and lack of musculotendinous attachments it has a fragile blood supply, so displacement readily disrupts this supply and predisposes to avascular necrosis.

(c)
Conservative management is a below-knee cast for 6-12 weeks, with the ankle in slight plantarflexion for 4 weeks followed by a short leg walking cast for 2-8 weeks; once secure union is achieved, active range of motion and progressive weight bearing as tolerated is started. Displaced fractures usually require surgical fixation (open reduction and internal fixation, or external fixation), followed by a below-knee cast for 6-12 weeks postoperatively. The physiotherapy role is to progress active range of motion and weight bearing as tolerated once union is secure.
questions.question:
A young, active man presents following a fall from a height with intense pain in the ankle, inability to move the ankle, gross pedal oedema, and distortion of the normal contours of the ankle and foot.
(a) State the most likely diagnosis.
(b) Discuss the predisposing factors and pathophysiology of this condition.
(c) Outline the management, including the physiotherapy role.

A motorcyclist involved in a high-energy road traffic accident presents with pelvic pain, and an AP pelvic radiograph is obtained showing disruption of the pelvic ring.
(a) Identify the structure/lesion involved.
(b) State the structures affected.
(c) List the differential fracture patterns (classification).
(d) Discuss the clinico-anatomical and functional reasoning for the presentation.
(e) State the physiotherapy management priorities.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Pelvic ring disruption (fracture of the sacrum and/or innominate bones - ilium, ischium, pubis).

(b)
Anterior support structures (symphysis pubis, pubic rami - about 40% of pelvic strength) and/or posterior support structures (sacroiliac complex, sacroiliac ligaments, iliolumbar ligaments - about 60% of pelvic strength); radiographic signs of instability include sacroiliac displacement of 5mm in any plane, a posterior fracture gap, or avulsion of the L5 transverse process, lateral border of the sacrum, or ischial spine.

(c)
Tile classification: Type A - stable, posterior structures intact; Type B - partially stable, incomplete posterior disruption; Type C - unstable, complete posterior disruption. Young classification: lateral compression, AP compression, or vertical shear injury.

(d)
High-energy injuries (RTA, pedestrian-struck, motorcycle accident, fall from height, crush) cause pelvic ring disruption, whereas low-energy injuries cause fractures of individual bones; pelvic instability may result in leg-length discrepancy with shortening or a markedly rotated lower extremity, and lumbosacral plexus/nerve root injury may be present.

(e)
Fractures amenable to non-operative treatment (lateral impaction injuries with less than 1.5cm displacement, pubic rami fractures with no posterior displacement, symphyseal gapping less than 2.5cm) are managed with protected weight bearing using a walker or crutches and serial radiographs; during the acute phase, keep muscles proximal to the injury strong with active exercises; during the post-healing clinical-union phase, use active and active-assistive exercise and avoid passive stretching/resistive exercise, allowing only partial weight bearing; during the post-healing complete-union phase, use resistive exercise and stretching with full weight bearing.

questions.question:
(a) Define baseball pitcher's elbow.
(b) State its etiology.
(c) State its pathogenesis.

(f) Explain how this condition affects function.
(g) Outline the conservative and surgical management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Definition: baseball pitcher's elbow is often occupational and is caused by repeated severe strains of the joint.

(b)
Etiology: Occupational (repeated strains); sports injury.

(c)
Pathogenesis: Traumatic arthritis; thickened synovial membrane; fibrillated cartilage; spurred junction of bone and cartilage; loose bodies in the joint.

(d)
• Clinical features: Pain over the front of the medial humeral condyle; swelling; local tenderness.
• Clinical features (continued): Movements of the elbow painful and restricted.

(e)
Investigations: CBC, ESR; X-ray of the elbow (AP and lateral views).

(f)
• Effect on function: Movements of the elbow are painful and restricted due to traumatic arthritis, a thickened synovial membrane, fibrillated cartilage, and loose bodies within the joint.
• Effect on function (continued): A spurred junction of bone and cartilage further contributes to the mechanical disturbance of joint movement.

(g)
• Conservative management: Warm fomentation; analgesics/NSAIDs.
• Conservative management (continued): Local infiltration with injection lignocaine 1% 2 ml with hydrocortisone.
• Surgical management: Excision of osteophytes (from the origin of the common flexor group of muscles, the olecranon, and the olecranon fossa); dividing the deep fascia covering the pronator teres.
• Rehabilitation: Assisted passive exercises by the physiotherapist progressed to free active exercises by the patient.

(a)
• Definition/classification: acute low back pain is low back pain present for up to six weeks, experienced as aching, burning, stabbing, sharp or dull; it is most often caused by a sudden injury to the muscles and ligaments supporting the back, with pain from muscle spasm or a strain/tear in the muscles and ligaments.
• Aetiology: traumatic (RSA, sports injury, falls, lifting heavy weight); inflammatory (osteomyelitis, discitis, sacroiliitis, ankylosing spondylitis, spondyloarthropathies, prostatitis, endometritis, appendicitis, cholecystitis); endocrinal and metabolic (diabetes, thyroid disorders, osteoporosis); degenerative (spondylosis, spondylolisthesis, prolapsed disc); postural (habitual, spinal deformity such as kyphosis, scoliosis); neoplastic (carcinoma colon).
• Clinical features: lumbar or dorsal pain during the night; buttock pain if affecting one side; heel pain; pain that may worsen on rest (inflammation) or on activity (mechanical), and may be aggravated by coughing or sneezing; pain may or may not radiate to the thigh or legs depending on nerve root compression; muscle spasm; deformity (kyphosis or scoliosis); local tenderness; movements painful and restricted; neurological deficit.
• Investigations: hemogram, ESR, TLC and DLC, RA factor; X-ray of the lumbosacral spine (AP and lateral views); MRI; myelogram; CT scan.

(b)
Effect on function: pain and muscle spasm restrict spinal movement and may radiate to the thigh and legs when nerve roots are compressed, impairing mobility and posture.

(c)
• Conservative management, general measures: bedrest; physiotherapy; heat therapy (infrared, short-wave diathermy); traction; lumbar belt.
• Further conservative management: analgesics, NSAIDs; antibiotics to control infection if present.
• Specific treatment: epidural block; treatment of the underlying cause.
• Rehabilitation/physiotherapy management: heat therapy (SWD/IRR); traction; lumbar belt.
• Physiotherapy exercises: back exercises performed regularly, 2-3 times daily.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Fracture of the clavicle, middle third (Allman Type 1, 80% of clavicle fractures).

(b)
Direct traumatic impact or a fall on the shoulder accounts for 87% of cases. The middle third is the commonest site because it is the thinnest part of the bone, the junction of the two main curves of the shaft, and the site of entrance of the nutrient artery. Non-traumatic causes in children include tumour, rickets, osteogenesis imperfecta and physical abuse.

(c)
Clavicle fractures unite with or without treatment, usually in 3-6 weeks. Non-operative treatment (sling or figure-of-eight bandage for 2-4 weeks) with range-of-motion exercises to the shoulder is used for most non-displaced fractures. Surgical fixation with an internal fixation plate is rarely indicated, except for lateral one-third fractures, neurovascular injury or nonunion. Physiotherapy role: sling for 2-4 weeks followed by active motion, with hand, wrist and elbow exercises during immobilisation; strengthening exercise at 6-8 weeks once pain-free motion and radiographic union are evident; full activity including sports at 3 months.

Loss of joint alignment; infection; non-union, malunion, delayed union; massive blood loss resulting in haemorrhagic shock; avascular necrosis; nerve injury; heterotopic ossification; joint stiffness and deformities; thromboembolism, fat embolism.

questions.question:
(a) A patient presents with polydipsia, polyuria and unexplained weight loss, and a random plasma glucose is 220 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L or more).
(b) Identify the diagnosis suggested by this result and presentation.
(c) State the diagnostic principle/criteria applied.
(d) List other laboratory criteria that could alternatively be used to confirm this diagnosis.
(e) State the sample handling requirement for the glucose specimen used in this assessment.
questions.answerText:
(b)
• This presentation and result meet the criterion for diabetes mellitus (DM): random glucose greater than or equal to 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) accompanied by classic symptoms (polydipsia, polyuria and unexplained weight loss).
(c)/(d)
• Alternative diagnostic criteria for DM are: two fasting glucose measurements equal to or greater than 126 mg/dL (>=7.0 mmol/L); HbA1c equal to or greater than 6.5% (confirmed by repeat testing); random glucose >=200 mg/dL accompanied by an unequivocal complication of DM such as DKA; or a 2-hour post-load glucose >=11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL) during an OGTT.
• Normal fasting glucose is <5.6 mmol/L (100 mg/dL), impaired fasting glucose is 5.6-6.9 mmol/L (100-125 mg/dL); normal HbA1c is <5.6%, and pre-diabetic HbA1c is 5.7-6.4%.
(e)
• Samples for glucose assay must be drawn into sodium fluoride or fluoride oxalate tubes (grey top), because fluoride inhibits the glycolytic enzyme enolase by binding magnesium, preventing glucose from being metabolised by cells in the sample tube before analysis.
• Given the random glucose of 220 mg/dL with the classic symptoms described, this patient meets the stated diagnostic criterion for diabetes mellitus without needing to await a fasting or OGTT result.

(b)
• This is the NBT-PABA (bentiromide/BTP) test, based on hydrolysis by chymotrypsin of a synthetic tripeptide, administered orally with a test meal to stimulate pancreatic secretion.
(c)
• BTP is hydrolysed by chymotrypsin in the duodenum to release PABA, which is absorbed, metabolised in the liver, and excreted by the kidney; in pancreatic insufficiency there is low chymotrypsin, leading to less peptide hydrolysis and therefore less PABA excreted in urine or found in serum.
(d)
• A control substance (such as C-PABA or PAS) is given, typically on a second day, because low recovery of the control substance would suggest decreased intestinal absorption or decreased renal excretion rather than pancreatic insufficiency; here the control substance is recovered normally, so a non-pancreatic cause of low PABA recovery is excluded.
(e)
• PEI = (test substance in urine x 100)/(control substance in urine); since the control substance recovery is normal and test substance recovery is 25% (well below the normal 48-72%, about 60% average), the PEI is low.
• This low PEI, with normal control substance recovery, is consistent with pancreatic insufficiency, since PABA excretion is significantly decreased in pancreatic insufficiency while defective intestinal absorption, altered transit time, or impaired renal excretion have been excluded by the normal control result.
• It should be noted that the NBT-PABA test is less sensitive than fecal elastase-1, so this finding may be considered alongside or confirmed by fecal elastase-1 measurement.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• The metabolic derangements are: metabolic acidosis, respiratory acidosis, metabolic alkalosis, respiratory alkalosis, and mixed picture (largely compensational).
(b)
• In metabolic acidosis, the primary abnormality is reduction of (HCO3-), changes in pCO2 being secondary; when HCO3- is reduced in pH = pK + log(HCO3-/PCO2), the pH will fall.
• In respiratory acidosis, there is an increase in pCO2 due to CO2 retention; if pCO2 is increased in the equation pH = (HCO3-)/PCO2, pH will fall.
• In metabolic alkalosis, there is primarily an increase in the concentration of bicarbonate in the ECF, reducing hydrogen ion concentration, with reduced bicarbonate reabsorption leading to bicarbonate excretion in urine.
• In respiratory alkalosis, there is a fall in pCO2 which reduces the ratio of pCO2 to bicarbonate concentration in the pH equation.
• A mixed disorder occurs when a patient has more than one primary disturbance, such as an acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease together with diabetic ketoacidosis, in which case PaCO2 and HCO3- may move in opposite directions.
(c)
• If it is a respiratory problem, the metabolic system tries to compensate, and vice versa; a compensatory response generally improves the pH but never completely restores it.
• Compensation for metabolic acidosis occurs through stimulation of the respiratory centre, causing hyperventilation to 'wash out' CO2 and avoid a change in pH.
• Compensation for respiratory acidosis occurs by acceleration of the carbonic anhydrase mechanism in erythrocytes and renal tubular cells, resulting in high HCO3- and normal or no change in pH.
• Compensation for metabolic alkalosis occurs largely by induction of respiratory acidosis through CO2 retention.
• Compensation for respiratory alkalosis occurs by a compensatory fall in the drive of the carbonic anhydrase system to reclaim bicarbonate in the kidneys and erythrocytes, leading to a fall in HCO3- to minimise the change in pH.
• Because compensation is never complete, terms such as partial and full compensation are used, and failing to recognise this may lead to misclassification of whether the primary disorder is respiratory or metabolic.
questions.question:
