questions.answerText:
(a)
• Renal function tests can be divided into tests for glomerular function (serum urea, serum creatinine, clearance tests) and tests for tubular function (urine concentration test, dilution test, para-amino-hippuric acid clearance test, acidification test).
• Urine examination is important for assessing both glomerular and tubular function.
• Normal reference ranges include serum urea 15-45 mg/dL, serum creatinine 0.6-1.2 mg/dL, serum uric acid, total protein 6.4-8.1 g/dL, serum albumin 3.2-4.6 g/dL, and serum electrolytes (Na, K, Cl, phosphate, calcium).
(b)
• Urinalysis is applied by examining appearance (blood, colour, turbidity), specific gravity and osmolality, pH, glucose, protein and urinary sediments.
• Glucose in urine reflects either increased blood glucose or a low renal threshold/tubular disorder; proteinuria (normal <200 mg/24h) may arise from overflow, glomerular leak, decreased tubular reabsorption of protein, or renal-origin protein.
• Urine sediment microscopy looks for cells, casts (Tamm-Horsfall protein) and fat droplets: red cell casts indicate glomerular disease (haematuria), white cell casts with polymorphs and bacteriuria indicate pyelonephritis, and lower UTI shows polymorphs without casts.
(c)
• A fresh sample is stated to be equal to a valid sample; urinalysis therefore assumes the sample tested reflects the patient's current urine composition and cellular content.
• If the sample is not fresh, cells and casts seen on microscopy may degrade, and colour or turbidity changes could reflect standing artefact rather than true pathology (e.g. infection, nephrotic syndrome or chyle causing turbidity).
• Specific gravity sticks measure ionic species only (not glucose), so this must be considered alongside the true clinical context when interpreting concentration.
• Because acute glomerulonephritis classically shows haematuria, cells and casts, while chronic glomerulonephritis shows less sediment, a degraded or non-fresh sample could blur this distinction and lead to misclassification of disease chronicity.
• Colouration of urine can arise from many causes (methylene blue, pseudomonas, riboflavin for blue-green; haemoglobin, myoglobin, phenolphthalein, porphyrins, rifampicin for pink-orange-red; haemoglobin, myoglobin, red cells, homogentisic acid, L-DOPA, melanin, methyldopa for red-brown-black), so an old or contaminated sample risks a false colour-based conclusion.
• Overall, since biochemical testing rarely establishes the cause of renal disease on its own (mainly used for screening for damage and monitoring progression), an invalid (non-fresh, poorly collected) sample removes even this limited but important diagnostic value.
questions.question:
(a) List the types of tests used to assess renal function, dividing them into tests of glomerular function and tests of tubular function.
(b) State how urinalysis is applied as part of the assessment of both glomerular and tubular function.
(c) Explain why a falsely collected or non-fresh urine sample would invalidate the interpretation of urinalysis findings.

(a) List the risk factors for cardiovascular disease (CVD) described as non-modifiable and modifiable, together with lipid-related and other independent risk factors.
(b) State how LDL-C, HDL-C, total cholesterol and total triglyceride laboratory values are applied to predict risk of coronary heart disease (CHD).
(c) Explain why oxidised LDL and Lipoprotein(a) are each considered to promote atherosclerosis.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Non-modifiable risk factors for CVD include age, sex, family history of CVD, and ethnic background; modifiable risk factors include smoking, raised blood pressure and raised cholesterol.
• Other risk factors listed include high ApoB, high triglycerides, hyperhomocysteinaemia, hypertension, family history, diabetes, physical inactivity, abnormally low HDL, and smoking.
• Genetic hyperlipidaemias listed include familial hypercholesterolaemia, familial combined hyperlipidaemia, familial dyslipidaemia and familial dysbetalipoproteinaemia.
(b)
• Laboratory values predicting risk of CHD are: LDL-C >130 mg/dL, HDL-C <35 mg/dL, total cholesterol (TC) >200 mg/dL, and total triglycerides (TG) >150 mg/dL.
• LDL-C is calculated using the Friedewald formula: LDL-C = TC - HDL-C - (TG/5) (in mg/dL units); an inverse relationship exists between HDL and coronary artery disease, so the LDL/HDL-C ratio is often used as a predictor.
(c)
• Oxidised LDL is taken up more rapidly by macrophages than new LDL, via scavenger receptors on macrophages that invade artery walls, generating foam cells that invade smooth muscle cells of vessel walls.
• This uptake leads to production of fatty streaks, precursors of fibrous plaque, and elicits cholesterol deposition in artery walls, allowing atherosclerosis/coronary artery disease to develop.
• Agents that prevent oxidation (anti-oxidants) are protective, while agents that potentiate oxidation, such as cigarette smoke, are associated with increased risk, underlining the central role of LDL oxidation in this mechanism.
• Lipoprotein(a) is a small LDL-like particle attached to apolipoprotein(a), a large glycoprotein, and is easily modified by oxidation.
• Lp(a) resembles plasminogen, which allows it to function as a tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) inhibitor, thereby preventing clot dissolution and leading to coronary artery occlusion.
• Because Lp(a) combines an LDL-like (cholesterol-carrying, oxidisable) particle with this anti-fibrinolytic action, it is considered an independent cardiovascular risk factor distinct from LDL cholesterol alone.
• Together, oxidised LDL (via foam cell formation and plaque deposition) and Lp(a) (via oxidation and impaired clot dissolution) represent two separate but reinforcing mechanisms by which lipoprotein abnormalities promote atherosclerosis.

questions.question:
(a) Describe cystatin-C as a marker of renal function under the headings of its molecular characteristics, production and route of elimination.
(b) State the setting in which cystatin-C is proposed as an alternative to plasma creatinine.
(c) Explain why cystatin-C correlates better with a reference clearance method than plasma creatinine does.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Cystatin-C is a cysteine proteinase inhibitor with a molecular weight of about 13000 and a small size with high pI, meaning it is freely filtered at the glomerulus.
• It has a constant production rate by all nucleated cells and no known extra-renal excretion routes.
(b)
• Cystatin-C is proposed as an alternative marker of GFR in the same clinical setting as plasma creatinine and creatinine clearance, that is, for estimating renal function without the complexity of inulin clearance.
(c)
• The correlation of 1/[cystatin C] with Cr-EDTA clearance is r=0.81, which is better than the correlation of 1/[Plasma Creatinine] with the same reference method, at r=0.51.
• Cystatin-C is not influenced by muscle mass, diet or the subject's sex, unlike plasma creatinine.
• Because plasma creatinine concentration is derived from muscle mass, which is related to body mass, age and sex, it has high between-subject variability that is unrelated to renal function itself.
• Cystatin-C's constant production rate by all nucleated cells removes this muscle-mass-related source of variability.
• Since cystatin-C has no known extra-renal excretion route, changes in its plasma concentration should more purely reflect changes in glomerular filtration rather than changes in production or non-renal elimination.
• Creatinine, by contrast, undergoes some tubular secretion (inhibited by cimetidine), which causes creatinine clearance to overestimate true GFR, particularly in renal failure.
• The small size and high pI of cystatin-C ensure it is freely filtered at the glomerulus in the same way that an ideal clearance marker should be.
• These combined properties (constant production, no extra-renal excretion, free filtration, and no dependence on muscle mass, diet or sex) explain the stronger correlation of cystatin-C with the Cr-EDTA reference clearance.
• This is why cystatin-C's correlation coefficient (r=0.81) is superior to that of plasma creatinine (r=0.51) with the same gold-standard clearance measurement.

(a)
• Indirect tests of pancreatic function include fecal lipid, the fat absorption test, and serum carotene (beta-carotene or vitamin A absorption test).
• These are grouped as indirect laboratory tests, alongside the N-benzoyl-L-tyrosyl-p-aminobenzoic acid (PABA/NBT-PABA) test.
(b)
• This group of tests is based on the fact that proper pancreatic function is essential for normal intestinal absorption of certain substances.
• This is because the pancreas is the major source of amylase, lipase and proteolytic enzymes needed to digest starch, fat and protein respectively.
• A decrease in pancreatic function therefore causes decreased absorption of starch, fat and protein, with a parallel increase in excretion of these food materials in the stool.
(c)
• In pancreatic deficiency, a microscopic examination of stool shows undigested cell nuclei and meat fibres, called creatorrhea.
• It also shows increased fat, called steatorrhea.
• It also shows increased starch, called amylorrhea.
• These three findings (creatorrhea, steatorrhea, amylorrhea) directly reflect the loss of proteolytic, lipase and amylase activity respectively, since undigested protein, fat and starch pass through to the stool instead of being absorbed.
• Because indirect tests such as fecal lipid and the fat absorption test measure this same downstream consequence (malabsorbed fat reaching the stool), they detect pancreatic exocrine insufficiency indirectly rather than by measuring pancreatic secretion itself.
• Serum carotene (vitamin A) absorption is similarly reduced when fat malabsorption impairs the uptake of this fat-soluble vitamin, providing another indirect marker of pancreatic exocrine insufficiency.
• As with other indirect tests, these measures reflect pancreatic function or intestinal absorption generally and do not diagnose a specific disorder, due to overlap between normal individuals and those with pancreatic disease.
questions.question:
(a) List the indirect (non-direct) tests of pancreatic function based on intestinal absorption, including fecal lipid, the fat absorption test and serum carotene.
(b) State the principle underlying why a decrease in pancreatic function affects these indirect tests.
(c) Explain why microscopic examination of stool in pancreatic deficiency shows creatorrhea, steatorrhea and amylorrhea.

(a) Describe the mechanisms by which the gastrointestinal tract and the kidney participate in bicarbonate handling.
(b) State the clinical setting in which disturbances of this mechanism become apparent.
(c) Explain the basis of the metabolic alkalosis that occurs in pyloric stenosis and the hyperchloraemic acidosis that occurs after ureteric transplantation into the ileum.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• The parietal cells of the stomach secrete H+ into the gastric lumen together with Cl-; as HCl enters the lumen, HCO3 diffuses into the ECF, accounting for the post-prandial 'alkaline tide'.
• In the healthy subject, this is rapidly corrected by HCO3- secretion, mainly by the pancreas, as food passes down the intestinal tract.
• As fluid passes down the intestinal tract, HCO3 enters and Cl- leaves the lumen by a reversal of the gastric mucosal mechanism, so gastric loss of Cl- and gain of HCO3 are finally corrected.
• Urinary buffers (phosphate and ammonia) are brought into play when bicarbonate concentration becomes reduced in acidotic states; ammonia is produced during deamination of glutamine in renal tubular cells by glutaminase, and the ammonium ion formed is passed out in urine, promoting loss of excess H+.
(b)
• Disturbances become apparent clinically in conditions such as pyloric stenosis, severe diarrhoea, and after ureteric transplantation into the ileum, ileal loops or the colon.
(c)
• In pyloric stenosis, gastric HCl secretion continues but is not matched by the normal duodenal reabsorption/correction because the pylorus is obstructed, so the alkaline tide effect is not corrected, producing metabolic alkalosis.
• Loss of H+ from the GI tract by vomiting, as in pyloric stenosis or nasogastric tube drainage, is listed as a cause of metabolic alkalosis.
• After ureteric transplantation into the ileum, ileal loops or the colon, there is preferential reabsorption of urinary Cl- by the intestinal Cl-/HCO3 exchange mechanism.
• This explains the hyperchloraemic acidosis (normal anion-gap acidosis) associated with this operation, since Cl- is reabsorbed while HCO3- is lost into the lumen.
• Loss of HCO3- from the GIT, as in severe diarrhoea or pancreatic fistula, is also a cause of metabolic acidosis.
• Loss of HCO3- in urine, as in uretero-enterostomy or proximal renal tubular acidosis, similarly produces metabolic acidosis.
• These mechanisms show that the same GIT/renal bicarbonate-handling pathway, when disrupted in different directions, can produce either an alkalosis (pyloric stenosis) or an acidosis (ureteric transplantation into bowel).

(b)
• This is a mixed acid-base disorder, occurring when the patient has more than one primary disturbance.
(c)
• It should be recorded/reported by describing that the arterial blood gas measurement shows inadequate compensation, or PaCO2 and HCO3- moving in opposite directions, rather than the single-disorder pattern expected from either problem alone.
• This indicates that two separate primary processes are occurring together: a respiratory disturbance from the COPD exacerbation (expected to raise PaCO2, respiratory acidosis) and a metabolic disturbance from diabetic ketoacidosis (expected to lower HCO3-, metabolic acidosis).
(d)
• Because compensation for a single primary disorder generally improves, but never fully restores, the pH, a compensating response would usually make PaCO2 and HCO3- move in the same overall direction as far as pH correction is concerned; instead here two primary disorders exist simultaneously.
(e)
• Recognising a mixed disorder means the clinician should identify and separately manage each underlying cause (the respiratory condition and the diabetic ketoacidosis) rather than assuming a single disturbance with compensation.
• Both processes are treated as full, primary contributors to the acid-base disturbance, so correction of the metabolic ketoacidosis (as in metabolic acidosis generally) and support of ventilation for the respiratory component (as in respiratory acidosis) are both needed.
• This example is given specifically to illustrate a mixed disorder as distinct from an uncomplicated primary disturbance with compensation.
• The overall action is therefore to recognise, from the finding of PaCO2 and HCO3- both being abnormal in a way inconsistent with simple compensation, that more than one primary acid-base process is present and each should be addressed on its own merits.
questions.question:
(a) A patient with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease develops an acute exacerbation together with diabetic ketoacidosis, and the arterial blood gas shows PaCO2 and HCO3- moving in opposite directions.
(b) Identify the type of acid-base disturbance illustrated by this combination.
(c) State how this is recorded/reported in an arterial blood gas interpretation.
(d) State what this pattern indicates about the patient's acid-base status.
(e) State the action that follows from recognising this pattern.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Non-invasive tests include amino acid consumption test, fecal chymotrypsin, fecal elastase-1, NBT-PABA, pancreolauryl, and C-mixed chain triglyceride (C-MCT) absorption.
• Fecal chymotrypsin is based on reduction in secretion of pancreatic enzymes with direct measurement of the enzyme in feces; residual enzyme activity is stable for several days at 20 degrees C.
• Pancreatic elastase-1 is a pancreatic-specific protease present in pancreatic juice, not degraded during passage through the gut, present in feces at five- to six-fold higher concentration than in pancreatic juice, and determined by ELISA using two monoclonal antibodies specific to the human enzyme; pancreatic enzyme supplements do not interfere with the test.
(b)
• Low fecal elastase (<200 microgram/g) after 4 weeks of age is indicative of pancreatic insufficiency and provides supporting evidence for a diagnosis of cystic fibrosis.
• In children with cystic fibrosis, the test discriminates between those with and without pancreatic insufficiency, and both fecal chymotrypsin and elastase have shown 100% sensitivity for detecting pancreatic insufficiency in cystic fibrosis, with elastase showing more sensitivity.
• In adults, fecal elastase-1 measurement has high sensitivity for detecting severe and moderate chronic pancreatitis and a high sensitivity/high negative predictive value for discriminating pancreatic from non-pancreatic diarrhoea, though it is not specific for pancreatitis, as it detects moderate to severe impairment of pancreatic exocrine secretion from any cause.
(c)
• Fecal chymotrypsin output in stool correlates poorly with chymotrypsin secretion in duodenal contents when both are measured after secretin-CCK stimulation.
• In patients without pancreatic disease, the incidence of falsely low fecal chymotrypsin results is 10-15%, which may be due to voluminous stools (>300 g/day, giving less enzyme per gram of feces), inadequate food intake, partial gastrectomy, or mucosal disease (coeliac disease) causing inadequate stimulation of pancreatic secretion, or obstruction to the bile duct.
• Voluminous stools dilute the enzyme concentration per gram, even if the total amount excreted is not reduced, giving an apparently low result.
• Inadequate food intake reduces the physiological stimulus for pancreatic secretion, so a low chymotrypsin level may reflect reduced stimulation rather than true pancreatic insufficiency.
• Coeliac (mucosal) disease impairs release of hormones from the duodenal mucosa that would normally stimulate the pancreas, again lowering measured chymotrypsin without primary pancreatic disease.
• In pancreatic insufficiency itself, a falsely normal fecal chymotrypsin result is seen in about 50% of cases, showing that both false-low and false-normal results are recognised limitations of this particular test.
questions.question:
(a) List the non-invasive tests of exocrine pancreatic function described, including fecal chymotrypsin, fecal elastase-1, NBT-PABA, pancreolauryl and the C-mixed chain triglyceride test.
(b) State how fecal elastase-1 is applied in the diagnosis of pancreatic insufficiency in cystic fibrosis.
(c) Explain why factors such as voluminous stools, inadequate food intake, partial gastrectomy and coeliac disease can cause a falsely low fecal chymotrypsin result.

(a) List the metabolic actions of insulin described for glucose uptake, glycolysis, glycogen synthesis, triglyceride synthesis, gluconeogenesis, protein synthesis, and ketogenesis/lipolysis.
(b) State the clinical setting in which measurement of fasting glucose, 2-hour post-OGTT glucose and HbA1c is applied.
(c) Explain why oral glucose stimulates more insulin secretion than intravenous glucose.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Insulin promotes glucose uptake in muscle and adipose tissue by causing GLUT4 channels to move to the cell membrane; once inside cells, glucose is phosphorylated and converted to glycogen or used for energy.
• Insulin promotes glycolysis by stimulating formation of fructose 2,6-bisphosphate, a potent activator of phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1) and an inhibitor of fructose 1,6-bisphosphatase, preventing glucose from being converted back via gluconeogenesis.
• Insulin increases glycogen synthesis in the liver by activating glycogen synthase while deactivating glycogen phosphorylase, and increases triglyceride synthesis by activating acetyl-CoA carboxylase (which forms malonyl-CoA, the rate-limiting step of fatty acid synthesis).
• Insulin inhibits gluconeogenesis partly by inhibiting fat and protein breakdown, promotes protein synthesis, and blocks ketogenesis and lipolysis by inhibiting fatty acid release from adipocytes and blocking fatty acid entry into liver mitochondria via raised malonyl-CoA.
(b)
• Normal fasting glucose is <5.6 mmol/L (100 mg/dL); impaired fasting glucose is 5.6-6.9 mmol/L (100-125 mg/dL); diabetes mellitus is diagnosed at fasting glucose >=7.0 mmol/L (126 mg/dL).
• Normal 2-hour post-OGTT (or post glucose load) glucose is <7.8 mmol/L (140 mg/dL); impaired glucose tolerance is 7.8-11.0 mmol/L; diabetes is diagnosed at 2-hour post-load glucose >=11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL).
• Normal HbA1c is <5.6%; pre-diabetic HbA1c is 5.7-6.4%; diabetes mellitus HbA1c is 6.5% or more; two fasting glucose measurements >=126 mg/dL, or HbA1c >=6.5% confirmed by repeat testing, or a random glucose >=200 mg/dL with classic symptoms or an unequivocal complication such as DKA, also diagnose diabetes.
(c)
• The gradual evacuation of gastric contents allows good time for absorption and utilisation of glucose given orally.
• GLP-1 (glucagon-like insulinotropic peptide), a gastrointestinal hormone released from the duodenum in response to dietary carbohydrate ingestion, stimulates insulin secretion by beta cells of the pancreas.
• Because oral glucose triggers this additional GLP-1-mediated (incretin) pathway of insulin release, in addition to the direct effect of the rising blood glucose itself, oral glucose stimulates more insulin secretion than the same amount of glucose given intravenously.
• Intravenous glucose bypasses the gut entirely, so it raises blood glucose without triggering GLP-1 release from the duodenum.
• This is also relevant to sample handling: samples for glucose assay are drawn into sodium fluoride or fluoride oxalate tubes, since fluoride inhibits the glycolytic enzyme enolase by binding magnesium, preventing glucose from being metabolised by cells in the tube before analysis.

questions.question:
(a) A patient's investigation shows unmeasured cations (calcium 5, magnesium 2, potassium 4 mmol/L) totalling 11 mmol/L, and unmeasured anions (protein 15, phosphate 2, sulphate 1, organic acid 5 mmol/L) totalling 23 mmol/L.
(b) State the appropriate test/calculation for assessing this patient's acid-base/electrolyte status from these values.
(c) Describe the principle behind this calculation.
(d) State the materials/data required to perform it.
(e) List sources of error or conditions that could alter the result, and the precautions needed.
questions.answerText:
(b)
• The appropriate calculation is the anion gap, used clinically to detect the potential of metabolic disorders affecting electrolyte balance.
(c)
• The anion gap is the difference between the usually unmeasured cations and the usually unmeasured anions; it is commonly calculated in practice as (Na+ + K+) - (Cl- + HCO3-).
• Using the given values, the anion gap = 23 - 11 = 12 mmol/L, which is within the normally quoted range of 15-20 mmol/L in the general description (though the worked example itself gives 12 mmol/L).
(d)
• The materials/data required are the plasma or serum concentrations of sodium, potassium, chloride and bicarbonate (or, as tabulated here, the individual unmeasured cations calcium, magnesium and potassium, and unmeasured anions protein, phosphate, sulphate and organic acid).
(e)
• The anion gap increases when unmeasured anions such as phosphates and sulphates increase in the blood and HCO3 falls in acidosis, as in diabetic ketoacidosis, lactic acidosis, uraemia, salicylate poisoning, methanol poisoning or alcoholic ketoacidosis ("DR MAPLES").
• The anion gap decreases in hypocalcaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hypoalbuminaemia, hypercalcaemia, paraproteins, underestimation of Na+, and hypertriglyceridaemia.
• Because so many non-acid-base conditions (protein level, paraproteins, calcium/magnesium changes) can shift the gap, its diagnostic accuracy is stated to be in doubt, so results should be interpreted alongside the clinical picture rather than in isolation.
• As a precaution, the same set of electrolytes (Na+, K+, Cl-, HCO3-) should be used consistently each time the gap is calculated, and any unusual protein or paraprotein state should be considered before interpreting an abnormal result.

(a)
• There are three phases of the digestive process: the cephalic or neurogenic phase, the gastric phase, and the intestinal phase.
• The intestinal phase begins when the weakly acidic digestive products of proteins and lipids enter the duodenum; local and neural stimulations lead to release of several gastrointestinal hormones, including cholecystokinin (CCK) and secretin.
• Cholecystokinin is released in the duodenum in response to the presence of fat, protein and HCl; secretin is released by gastric acid in the duodenum.
(b)
• CCK and secretin act together to potentiate gastrin action and augment pancreatic and biliary secretion, and this combined stimulation is used in the secretin-CCK test of pancreatic function.
(c)
• CCK principally stimulates gallbladder contraction, secretion of enzymes, bicarbonate, insulin and glucagon from the pancreas, and stimulates intestinal motility and stomach contraction.
• Secretin augments the effect of CCK on gallbladder contraction and pancreatic secretions, stimulates pepsinogen secretion by the stomach, inhibits gastrin and gastric acid secretion, and, in contrast to CCK, reduces gastric and duodenal motility.
• Contraction of the stomach mixes and chemically breaks down food into a mucus-containing mixture called chyme, which is then moved through the pylorus into the duodenum.
• Additional gastrin is released as the upper duodenal mucosa contacts partially digested proteins and lipids, as well as gastric HCl, and gastrin's action is further potentiated by CCK.
• Because secretin inhibits gastrin and gastric acid secretion while CCK potentiates gastrin action, the two hormones act as counterbalancing regulators of gastric acid output once food reaches the duodenum.
• Similarly, because CCK stimulates gastric contraction while secretin reduces gastric and duodenal motility, the two hormones have opposing effects on motility that together regulate the rate of gastric emptying and chyme delivery.
• This complementary relationship (CCK stimulating enzyme/bicarbonate output and gallbladder contraction, secretin augmenting bicarbonate/gallbladder response but opposing motility and acid secretion) underlies the ecbolic (enzyme) function tested by giving secretin followed by CCK.
• It also explains why the secretin-CCK test, rather than secretin alone, is needed to assess pancreatic enzyme secretion, since secretin alone evaluates only the hydrokinetic (volume/bicarbonate) function.
questions.question:
(a) List the phases of the digestive process and the gastrointestinal hormones released during the intestinal phase.
(b) State the setting in which cholecystokinin (CCK) and secretin act together in the assessment of digestive function.
(c) Explain the differing and complementary effects of CCK and secretin on gallbladder contraction, pancreatic secretion and gastric/duodenal motility.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Anion gap is the difference between the usually unmeasured cations and the usually unmeasured anions; it is commonly calculated as (Na+ + K+) - (Cl- + HCO3-).
• Unmeasured cations (calcium 5, magnesium 2, potassium 4 mmol/L) total about 11 mmol/L; unmeasured anions (protein 15, phosphate 2, sulphate 1, organic acid 5 mmol/L) total about 23 mmol/L, giving an anion gap of about 12 mmol/L.
• The osmolal gap is a measure of low molecular weight substances or compounds in plasma other than sodium, potassium, urea and glucose that contribute to plasma osmolality.
• The osmolal gap indicates the presence of substances such as ethanol, methanol, ethylene glycol, drugs, lactate, mannitol or hydroxybutyrate.
(b)
• The anion gap is used clinically to detect the potential of metabolic disorders affecting electrolyte balance, especially to help classify a metabolic acidosis.
• The osmolal gap is used when poisoning with substances such as methanol or ethylene glycol, or another unmeasured osmotically active substance, is suspected.
(c)
• Increases in the anion gap occur when unmeasured anions such as phosphates and sulphates increase in blood and HCO3 falls in acidosis (as in "DR MAPLES" causes: diabetic ketoacidosis, renal failure/uraemia, methanol poisoning, alcoholic ketoacidosis, paraldehyde, lactic acidosis, ethylene glycol, salicylate poisoning).
• Decreases in the anion gap occur in hypoalbuminaemia, hypercalcaemia, paraproteins, underestimation of Na+, and hypertriglyceridaemia.
• Because so many different physiological and analytical conditions (protein concentration, paraproteins, unmeasured cations like calcium and magnesium) can shift the calculated gap in either direction, its diagnostic accuracy is in doubt.
• The gap can therefore be altered by non-acid-base conditions, such as changes in albumin, that have nothing to do with the presence or absence of an acidosis.
• This means an apparently normal or abnormal anion gap does not always reliably confirm or exclude the presence of a high-anion-gap acidotic process.
• For this reason, the anion gap and osmolal gap are best interpreted together with the clinical picture and other tests rather than in isolation.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the anion gap and the osmolal gap under the headings of definition, components and normal values.
(b) State the clinical setting in which each gap is used.
(c) Explain the reasoning behind the caution that the diagnostic accuracy of the anion gap is in doubt.

questions.answerText:
(b)
• The patient has alkalaemia (pH 7.5, above the normal 7.35-7.45 range).
• The PaCO2 is low (4 kPa/30 mmHg) while HCO3- (24 mmol/L) is essentially at the upper end of normal, so the respiratory component (PaCO2) is the cause.
(c)
• The principle applied is that pH is determined by the ratio of HCO3-/PCO2, so a low PaCO2 (loss of this acidic gas) can account for an alkaline pH even when HCO3- is not raised.
(d)
• First ask whether there is an acid-base abnormality at all, and whether the pH is outside the normal range (here it is, at 7.5, confirming alkalaemia).
• Next ask whether it is the respiratory (PaCO2) or the metabolic (HCO3-) component that is abnormal; here PaCO2 is low while HCO3- is normal.
• Then ask whether this abnormal component tells the same story as the pH, i.e. whether a low PaCO2 is consistent with alkalaemia; a low PaCO2 (loss of acidic gas) is indeed consistent with an alkaline pH.
• Finally consider whether there is any compensation; if it is a respiratory problem, the metabolic system tries to compensate and vice versa, though a compensatory response never completely restores the pH.
(e)
• The expected finding is therefore respiratory alkalosis as the primary disorder in this patient, since the PaCO2 is low and accounts for the alkalaemia while the HCO3- remains normal.
• This is directly consistent with the example of a patient with alkalaemia (pH 7.5), PaCO2 4 kPa (30 mmHg) and HCO3- 24 mmol/L, where the respiratory component is identified as the cause.
questions.question:

(b) Identify the acid-base abnormality present and which component (respiratory or metabolic) is the primary cause.
(c) State the underlying biochemical principle used to reach this interpretation.
(d) Describe the correct step-by-step approach used to interpret this arterial blood gas result.
(e) State the expected finding and its interpretation for this patient.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Urine specific gravity is measured as part of routine analysis, or on timed specimens after fluid restriction for more exact information, using either a urinometer or a refractometer; reference range for a 24-hour specimen is 1.015-1.025, rising to above 1.025 after fluid restriction.
• In the dilution test, after overnight water deprivation the patient takes 1200 mL of water in half an hour, and urine specific gravity is measured in samples collected over the next 4 hours; at least one sample should show specific gravity of 1.003 or below.
• In the urine concentration test, in chronic kidney disease the kidney loses the ability to concentrate urine, and a low fixed specific gravity is indicative of chronic kidney disease.
(b)
• Specific gravity using a urinometer works on the principle that the hydrometer sinks to a level characteristic of the specific gravity of the specimen, read from calibrations on the stem.
• Specific gravity using a refractometer works on the principle that the refractive index and specific gravity of urine are both related functions of the quantity and type of dissolved substance present, so refractive index can be correlated with specific gravity.
• Urine osmolality measurement is preferred as part of a concentration test because it measures the true osmotic concentration of the urine; in normal individuals it falls to about 50 mOsm/kg after excessive fluid intake and can rise to 1200 mOsm/kg with severe fluid restriction, with 300-900 mOsm/kg seen on average fluid intake.
(c)
• Increased amounts of abnormal substances such as glucose and protein may partially invalidate the specific gravity-osmolality correlation, because heavy molecules such as protein, glucose or iodine-containing compounds affect specific gravity substantially more than they affect osmolality.
• Specific gravity is a measure of the density of urine relative to water, and while density usually bears a constant relationship to osmolality, there may occasionally be a remarkable divergence between the two.
• Because water excretion is determined, in part, by the osmolality of body fluid compartments, osmolality is a more direct physiological measure of the kidney's concentrating ability than density.
• A random urine specimen osmolality of 850 mOsm/kg H2O after 12-hour fluid restriction is considered normal, whereas in the absence of fluid restriction an osmolality of 600 mOsm/kg or higher is assumed normal.
• In chronic progressive renal failure the concentrating ability of tubules is diminished, and in diabetes insipidus urine osmolality is extremely low, both of which are more reliably shown by osmolality than by specific gravity when heavy solutes are present.
• For this reason, measurement of urine osmolality, especially as part of the concentration test, is preferred over specific gravity measurement in accessing the concentrating ability of the kidney.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the urine concentration test and the dilution test under the headings of principle, procedure and expected findings.
(b) State how urine specific gravity and urine osmolality are each applied in assessing the kidney's concentrating ability.
(c) Explain why urine osmolality measurement is considered more valid than specific gravity in assessing the kidney's concentrating ability.

(a) Describe the three cell types of the body of the stomach and their secretions, alongside the cells of the cardiac and pyloric zones.
(b) State how knowledge of these zones and cell types is applied in understanding the functions of the stomach.
(c) Explain the physiological basis for why vagotomy results in a decrease in the volume and acidity of gastric secretion.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• The cardiac zone (including the fundus) contains mucus-secreting surface epithelial cells, which also secrete group II pepsinogens, and several types of endocrine-secreting cells.
• The body of the stomach contains four cell types: surface epithelial cells (secrete mucus), parietal/oxyntic cells (the main, possibly only, source of hydrochloric acid, also secreting intrinsic factor), chief/zymogen/peptic cells (secrete group I and II pepsinogen), and neck chief cells/mucus cells (secrete mucus and pepsinogen).
• Enterochromaffin cells, among the endocrine-secreting cells, secrete serotonin.
• The pyloric zone, subdivided into the antrum, pyloric canal and sphincter, secretes mucus, pepsinogen and gastrin, but NO HCl.
(b)
• Functions of the stomach include accepting, mixing, storing and discharging food into the duodenum, enzyme secretion, and intrinsic factor and hydrochloric acid secretion.
• This zonal and cellular arrangement is applied clinically to understand the site of production of acid (parietal cells) versus the site of gastrin production (pyloric antrum), and to interpret conditions such as achlorhydria.
(c)
• The cephalic (neurogenic) phase of digestion is initiated by intake of food, its sight, smell and taste, stimulating the cerebral cortex and subsequently the vagal nuclei, mediated chemically by acetylcholine from postganglionic parasympathetic nerve endings acting on gastric parietal cells.
• The vagus stimulates gastric chief and parietal (oxyntic) cells to secrete pepsinogen and HCl.
• In the gastric phase, HCl is released partly by direct stimulation of the parietal cells by the vagus nerve, and partly by local distension of the antrum stimulating antral cells (via vagal nerve) to secrete gastrin, which in turn causes HCl release from parietal cells.
• Since both the cephalic and gastric phases of HCl secretion depend heavily on vagal stimulation of the parietal cells (directly, and indirectly through gastrin release), removing this vagal input by vagotomy removes a major drive for both pepsinogen and HCl secretion.
• Vagotomy therefore results in a decrease in the volume and acidity of gastric secretion because it interrupts the neural pathway that normally stimulates parietal and chief cells.
• This is consistent with the description that vagotomy and subtotal gastrectomy (Billroth II) can give invalid results with tests such as the Lundh meal, since the normal hormonal/neural stimulation of the pancreas and stomach is altered by these procedures.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the stimuli used for gastric secretion testing, including test meals, caffeine/alcohol, histalog, gastrin/pentagastrin and insulin.
(b) State the clinical setting requiring physician administration and blood pressure monitoring during gastric stimulation testing.
(c) Explain the reasoning behind giving antihistamine before histalog injection and monitoring systolic blood pressure.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Test meals, such as toast with water or tea (Ewald meal), are a stimulus with the advantage of no undesirable side reactions but the disadvantage of weak stimulant ability.
• Caffeine (caffeine sodium benzoate, 500 mg in 200 mL water) or alcohol (3.5 mL ethanol in 50 mL water) may also be admitted into the stomach through a gastric tube, with similar advantages and disadvantages to test meals.
• Histalog (3-beta-aminoethyl pyrazole dihydrochloride) is a potent stimulus for gastric HCl secretion, commonly dosed at 1.5 mg/kg body weight, with maximum stimulation achieved at 1.7-2.0 mg/kg; peak HCl secretion occurs 90-120 minutes after injection.
• Gastrin is the natural and most powerful stimulus for gastric HCl secretion, administered as a single subcutaneous dose of 2 microgram/kg or 1 microgram/kg intramuscularly, or by continuous intravenous infusion (67 microgram/hour) or single IV injection (50 microgram); stimulation with gastrin is 20% greater than maximum stimulation with histamine.
• Pentagastrin, a synthetic compound with similar physiological action to gastrin, is a potent stimulus requiring a higher dose (6 microgram/kg subcutaneously) for maximal stimulation.
• Insulin-induced hypoglycaemia stimulates the vagal medullary nuclei and causes increased gastrin and HCl secretion; 20 units of insulin is administered to decrease blood glucose to less than 45 mg/dL.
(b)
• Histalog administration must be given by the physician, and the systolic blood pressure must not be less than 110 mmHg during the test.
(c)
• Disadvantages of histalog include acute erosive gastritis, gastric bleeding and anaphylactic shock, which are serious adverse reactions requiring careful supervision.
• Because anaphylactic shock is a risk, some clinicians advocate administering antihistamine 30 minutes before the histalog injection, to reduce the severity of any hypersensitivity reaction.
• Monitoring that systolic blood pressure remains at or above 110 mmHg is a safeguard against unrecognised hypotension or an evolving anaphylactic/shock reaction during the test.
• Because histalog carries these risks of serious adverse reactions (erosive gastritis, gastric bleeding, anaphylactic shock), it must be administered by the physician rather than by laboratory staff alone.
• These same safety considerations explain why physician administration and blood pressure monitoring are specifically emphasised for histalog, compared with the lower-risk test meal, caffeine or alcohol stimuli.

(a)
• The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation expresses the relationship between pH and a buffer pair; in aqueous solution the pH is determined by the concentration ratio of the acid to its conjugate base: pH = pKa + log(HCO3-/H2CO3).
• Because H2CO3 cannot be measured directly, CO2 is substituted for H2CO3, giving pH = pK + log(HCO3-/CO2).
• The pK for the HCO3-/H2CO3 buffer pair is 6.1, and pCO2 is 0.23 in kilopascals (0.03 in mmHg), giving pH = 6.1 + log(HCO3-/(PCO2 x 0.23)).
• Normal blood pH is 7.35-7.45; a patient has acidosis or acidaemia when blood pH is below 7.35 and alkalosis or alkalaemia when it is above 7.45.
(b)
• The equation and anion gap are applied together in the interpretation of arterial blood gas results in acidaemia, particularly when there is metabolic acidosis (low pH and low HCO3-).
(c)
• If there is metabolic acidosis, that is, low pH and low HCO3-, it may be useful to take the additional step of calculating the anion gap.
• The anion gap is the difference between the unmeasured cations (Na+ and K+) and the unmeasured anions (chloride and bicarbonate), normally between 15-20 mmol/L.
• The anion gap increases when unmeasured anions such as phosphates and sulphates increase in the blood and HCO3 falls in acidosis, so it helps identify the cause of a metabolic acidosis.
• Causes of increased anion gap acidosis include ketoacidosis (uncontrolled diabetes mellitus, starvation), lactic acidosis, shock and salicylate over-dosage.
• Causes of normal anion gap acidosis include loss of HCO3- from the GIT (severe diarrhoea, pancreatic fistula) and loss of HCO3- in urine (uretero-enterostomy, proximal renal tubular acidosis, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors).
• The converse pattern (decreased anion gap) occurs in metabolic alkalosis, so calculating the gap outside of acidosis would not add the same diagnostic value.
• Thus the anion gap step is reserved for acidaemia with a metabolic (low HCO3-) component, where it helps distinguish among possible causes of the acidosis.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation, stating its components and the normal values used within it.
(b) State the clinical setting in which the equation and the anion gap are applied together.
(c) Explain the reasoning behind calculating the anion gap only when metabolic acidosis (low pH and low HCO3-) is present.

(a) A patient known to have insulinoma presents with hunger, sweating, nausea, dizziness, nervousness and mental confusion, and the blood glucose result is below the normal lower reference limit.
(b) Identify the condition indicated by these symptoms and result.
(c) State the principle behind why these symptoms occur.
(d) List the laboratory investigations appropriate for this patient.
(e) State the classification/category into which this patient's cause of the condition falls.
questions.answerText:
(b)
• This is hypoglycaemia, involving decreased plasma glucose levels below the normal lower reference limit.
(c)
• The observable symptoms and warning signs of hypoglycaemia are all related to the central nervous system; symptoms include increased hunger, sweating, nausea and vomiting, dizziness, nervousness and shaking, blurring of speech and sight, and mental confusion, matching this patient's presentation.
(d)
• Laboratory investigations listed for assessing glucose disorders include fasting blood sugar, random blood sugar, 2-hour post-prandial glucose, and insulin estimation.
(e)
• Current classification separates patients into those who appear healthy and those who are sick; among healthy-appearing patients are those with a compensated coexistent disease, and causes listed explicitly include insulinoma, islet hyperplasia/nesidioblastosis, factitial hypoglycaemia from insulin or sulfonylurea, severe exercise, and ketotic hypoglycaemia.
• Since this patient has known insulinoma, the hypoglycaemia falls into the "healthy-appearing patient with a compensated coexistent disease" category rather than the "sick person" category (in which hypoglycaemia may be due to illness or drug-illness interaction, or be iatrogenic in hospitalised patients).
• Insulin estimation would be a particularly relevant investigation in this patient, alongside fasting blood glucose, given the known diagnosis of insulinoma as the underlying cause of the hypoglycaemic episode.

(b)
• This is the standing plasma test for chylomicrons: plasma is placed in a refrigerator (4°C) overnight, and chylomicrons accumulate as a floating "cream" layer.
(c)
• The principle is that the larger and less dense chylomicrons form a creamy layer on the surface on standing, while smaller and denser VLDL and IDL particles do not rise and instead cause diffuse turbidity if present in excess; LDL and HDL particles are too small to scatter light and do not contribute to turbidity.
(d)
• Because fasting plasma from normal individuals contains only VLDL, LDL and HDL particles, chylomicrons in fasting plasma are abnormal.
• Finding a creamy layer in this fasting sample therefore indicates the presence of chylomicrons, which should not normally be present after fasting, suggesting significantly disturbed triglyceride/chylomicron metabolism.
(e)
• The appropriate follow-up is to measure total cholesterol, triglycerides, HDL and LDL directly (since lipoprotein electrophoresis is no longer a common laboratory test) and to note that a very high triglyceride level (e.g. >400 mg/dL) would be consistent with the presence of chylomicrons or remnants.
• Given the presence of chylomicrons, any subsequent LDL-cholesterol calculation by the Friedewald formula would be unreliable, since that formula assumes chylomicrons are not significant contributors to total cholesterol in a fasting sample.
questions.question:
(a) A fasting plasma sample is placed in the refrigerator at 4 degrees C overnight, and the following morning a floating creamy layer is observed on top of a sample that otherwise appears clear underneath.
(b) Identify the test being performed and the finding observed.
(c) State the principle behind this test.
(d) State the significance of finding this creamy layer in a fasting sample.
(e) State the follow-up laboratory approach that would now be appropriate.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Antidiuretic hormone is produced from the supra-optic nucleus of the hypothalamus and stored in the posterior pituitary.
• Its release is triggered by increased plasma tonicity or osmolality, and by reduced pressure from blood loss or heart failure accompanied by hyponatraemia (absent tonic inhibitory control in baroreceptors of the left atrium and great vessels).
• ADH release is suppressed by expanded plasma volume or reduced osmolality.
• Its site of action is the distal renal tubules, where it increases the reabsorption of water from aquaporin channels, leading to production of a small volume but concentrated urine.
• ADH release stimulates insertion of aquaporins (water channels) into the luminal membranes of cells in the renal collecting ducts, otherwise impermeable to water, allowing passive movement of water down the concentration gradient generated by the countercurrent system.
(b)
• Disturbances of ADH action are assessed clinically in conditions such as diabetes insipidus, SIADH, dehydration and water excess/overload.
(c)
• Increase in plasma osmolality induces the sensation of thirst and stimulates ADH release, so plasma osmolality reflects the stimulus for ADH secretion.
• Urine osmolality reflects the kidney's response to that stimulus; comparing the two shows whether the kidney is responding appropriately.
• In chronic progressive renal failure the concentrating ability of the tubules is diminished, while in polyuria due to diabetes insipidus urine osmolality is extremely low, so urine osmolality alone cannot distinguish renal failure from diabetes insipidus without knowing the plasma/ hydration state.
• Water deficiency raises plasma osmolality and produces highly concentrated urine with hypernatraemia and haemoconcentration; water excess is associated with hyponatraemia and dilute urine.
• Since ADH release is suppressed by expanded plasma volume, a properly interpreted water balance assessment needs to relate the urine concentrating response to the prevailing plasma osmolality and volume status.
• This paired interpretation therefore distinguishes appropriate renal concentration of urine from an abnormality of either ADH secretion or renal tubular responsiveness.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the mechanism of antidiuretic hormone (ADH) action, including its site of production, storage, triggers for release and site and mechanism of action.
(b) State the clinical setting in which ADH-related disturbances of water balance are assessed.
(c) Explain the reasoning behind measuring urine and plasma osmolality together when assessing water balance disorders rather than urine osmolality alone.

questions.answerText:
(b)
• Continuous ECG monitoring alongside repeat plasma potassium measurement is appropriate, since this is true hyperkalaemia (pseudo-hyperkalaemia from haemolysis has been excluded) with cardiac findings including tall T wave and widened QRS complex.
(c)
• Calcium Chloride (or Gluconate), 10 mL of 10% solution, is given IV with ECG monitoring; this antagonises the effect of hyperkalaemia on heart muscle, though it does not alter the net potassium concentration.
• Glucose 50g with 20 units of soluble insulin by IV injection is then used to lower plasma K+ within about 30 minutes by increasing K+ entry into cells; in an emergency 10 units of soluble insulin may be added to 1L of 10% glucose.
• Alternatively, 40 mL of 8.5% NaHCO3 (40 mmol of bicarbonate) may be injected over 5 minutes if metabolic acidosis is present; this solution is hyperosmolal.
(d)
• Materials required: 10% calcium chloride or calcium gluconate solution, 50g glucose with 20 units soluble insulin (or 10 units insulin in 1L of 10% glucose), and 8.5% NaHCO3 as an alternative when acidosis is present, together with continuous ECG monitoring equipment.
(e)
• Calcium should never be added to bicarbonate solutions because calcium carbonate is poorly soluble in water, so these two agents must be given as separate infusions.
• If too much calcium is given, hypercalcaemia may itself cause cardiac arrest, so calcium administration must be carefully monitored by ECG and not repeated indiscriminately.
questions.question:
(a) A hospitalised patient develops a plasma potassium of 6.8 mmol/L with tall T waves and a widened QRS complex on ECG, and haemolysis of the sample has been excluded.
(b) State the test/monitoring appropriate for this specimen finding.
(c) Describe the principle behind the immediate treatment appropriate to this specimen finding.
(d) List the materials/agents required for emergency treatment.
(e) State the precaution that must be observed regarding two of the treatment agents used together.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Normal serum electrophoresis distinguishes five main groups: albumin, alpha1-globulin, alpha2-globulin, beta-globulin and gamma-globulin (immunoglobulins).
• Albumin fraction example: albumin itself, the main plasma protein, reduces tissue water accumulation and transports many substances.
• Alpha1-globulin example: alpha1-antitrypsin, which inactivates trypsin and other proteolytic enzymes and reduces damage from inflammation; alpha2-globulin examples include haptoglobin (haemoglobin-binding protein) and caeruloplasmin (a copper-containing enzyme involved in iron metabolism).
• Beta-globulin examples include transferrin (iron transport) and LDL (cholesterol delivery to tissue); gamma-globulin examples include IgG (major immunoglobulin, long-term immunity), IgM (initial-response immunoglobulin), C-reactive protein (inflammatory response mediator) and fibrinogen (a coagulation factor found only in plasma, not serum).
(b)
• Reduction in all protein fractions may occur in severe malnutrition, sometimes due to malabsorption, while an increase may occur in haemoconcentration.
• In chronic inflammatory response there is a rise in gamma-globulins due to increased immunoglobulin synthesis.
• Cirrhosis of the liver shows a characteristic pattern of reduced albumin and alpha1, with markedly raised gamma-globulins.
• Nephrotic syndrome shows a typical pattern of reduced albumin, alpha1 and gamma-globulins, with an increase in alpha2-globulin concentration.
(c)
• Serum is used rather than plasma for electrophoresis because fibrinogen interferes with the final interpretation of the electrophoretic pattern.
• Fibrinogen, a coagulation factor found only in plasma (not serum), would otherwise appear as an additional band that could be mistaken for a beta- or gamma-globulin abnormality.
• Since serum is obtained after clotting has removed fibrinogen, the resulting pattern more cleanly reflects only the five recognised fractions (albumin, alpha1, alpha2, beta, gamma).
• Using serum therefore avoids the confounding effect of fibrinogen on the shape and interpretation of the electrophoretic strip, which is important when trying to recognise specific disease patterns such as those of cirrhosis or nephrotic syndrome.
questions.question:
(a) List the electrophoretic fractions of serum protein and give one protein example with its function from each fraction.
(b) State how serum protein electrophoresis is applied in distinguishing patterns of disease such as nephrotic syndrome and cirrhosis of the liver.
(c) Explain why serum, rather than plasma, is used for protein electrophoresis.

questions.answerText:
(b)
• The BAO/PAO ratio is calculated and can be expressed as a percentage (BAO/PAO x 100 = %BAO/PAO) or as a fraction.
(c)
• In gastric analysis, basal condition is one in which the patient is at complete rest with no visual, auditory or olfactory stimuli, such as during sleep, which is why a 12-hour nocturnal collection is used for basal acid output.
(d)
• Using the given values, BAO/PAO = 8/30 = 0.27, or 27% (%BAO/PAO).
(e)
• According to the reference ranges given, a BAO/PAO fraction of 0.20-0.40 (20-40%) is consistent with gastric or duodenal ulcer.
• A ratio below 0.20 (<20%) would be normal, or seen in gastric ulcer and gastric carcinoma; a ratio of 0.40-0.60 (40-60%) suggests possible duodenal ulcer or Zollinger-Ellison syndrome; a ratio above 0.60 (>60%) is seen in Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.
• Since this patient's ratio of 0.27 (27%) falls in the 20-40% range, the result is consistent with gastric or duodenal ulcer rather than normal findings or Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.
• Correlating this with the separate BAO and PAO reference ranges (BAO 5-15 mmol/h suggesting possible duodenal ulcer; PAO 5-20 mmol/h normal/gastric ulcer) supports the same interpretation, and the action that follows is to proceed with further diagnostic evaluation for peptic ulcer disease rather than Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.

• Red cell casts with haematuria and proteinuria suggest glomerular disease, specifically a pattern of acute glomerulonephritis (haematuria, cells, casts).
(c)
• The principle is that red cell casts, being formed within the renal tubules from Tamm-Horsfall protein trapping red cells, indicate that bleeding is originating from the glomerulus/nephron itself, rather than lower in the urinary tract.
• This contrasts with a lower urinary tract infection, which shows polymorphs without casts, and with pyelonephritis, which shows white cell casts with polymorphs and bacteriuria.
(d)
• A fresh sample is required, since a fresh sample is equal to a valid sample for microscopic examination of freshly passed urine sediment; a non-fresh sample risks degradation of casts and cells before they can be identified.

• The interpretation to record is that this pattern (haematuria with cells and casts) is consistent with acute glomerulonephritis, a glomerular rather than lower urinary tract disorder, whereas chronic glomerulonephritis would be expected to show less sediment.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• The secretin test is based on the principle that maximum secretion of pancreatic juice and bicarbonate output are related to the functional mass of pancreatic tissue; it gives a direct measure of the secretion rate and the concentration of bicarbonate and other pancreatic juice.
• Secretin is administered as 1 Crick-Harper-Raper (CHR) unit/kg body weight intramuscularly, or 2 CHR units/kg/hour by continuous intravenous infusion in 0.15 mol/L sodium chloride; secretin preparations from different manufacturers differ greatly in potency.
• Stimulation by secretin alone allows evaluation only of the hydrokinetic function of the pancreas (volume secretion, bicarbonate secretion); pancreatic enzyme secretion is inconsistent with secretin alone.
• The secretin-CCK test, stimulation with secretin followed by CCK, allows assessment of enzyme secretion, referred to as the ecbolic function, and is the most satisfactory test for measuring pancreatic secretory capacity.
(b)
• The secretin-CCK test is used to separate patients with normal from those with impaired pancreatic function, and is more sensitive than results obtained with the Lundh meal.
• The Lundh meal provides inadequate or no stimulation in the presence of mucosal diseases such as coeliac disease, due to impaired release of hormones from the duodenal mucosa, and gives invalid results after vagotomy and subtotal gastrectomy (Billroth II).
(c)
• At least 50% of the acinar cells must have been destroyed before signs of pancreatic insufficiency begin to surface, and almost 90% of the acinar cells would have been damaged before clinical signs of pancreatic insufficiency become evident.
• This is attributed to the large functional reserve of the pancreas.
• Because of this reserve, even a test as sensitive as secretin-CCK stimulation can only detect insufficiency once a substantial proportion of pancreatic tissue has already been destroyed.
• There is a great overlap between results observed in normal individuals and those with pancreatic disorders, further limiting early detection.
• Both direct tests (secretin, secretin-CCK) and indirect/non-invasive tests measure pancreatic function or intestinal absorption but do not diagnose a specific disorder.
• For these combined reasons, no pancreatic function test can detect the early stages of pancreatic disease.
questions.question:

questions.answerText:
(a)
• NBT-PABA (also known as BTP or bentiromide) is based on hydrolysis by chymotrypsin of a synthetic tripeptide; it is administered orally with a test meal to stimulate pancreatic secretion.
• BTP is hydrolysed by chymotrypsin in the duodenum to release PABA, which is absorbed in the intestinal tract and metabolised in the liver to hippurate, PABA glucuronide and PABA acetylate, then excreted by the kidney.
• In pancreatic insufficiency, there is low chymotrypsin, leading to less peptide hydrolysis and therefore less chromogen excreted in urine or found in serum; PEI = (test substance in urine x 100)/(control substance in urine).
• Normally about 60% (48-72%) of the orally administered dose is recovered in urine, and in pancreatic insufficiency PABA excretion is significantly decreased.
(b)
• A control substance (given orally on a second day, such as C-PABA or p-aminosalicylic acid/PAS given with the NBT-PABA) is co-administered/used because low recovery of the control substance in urine is suggestive of decreased intestinal absorption or decreased renal excretion, rather than pancreatic insufficiency.
(c)
• Defective intestinal absorption, caused by intestinal disease, can reduce the amount of PABA absorbed regardless of how much chymotrypsin has released it, lowering urinary/serum PABA independent of pancreatic function.
• Variations in transit time, caused by impairment in hepatic conjugation as seen in liver disease, can alter how much PABA is converted and excreted in the test period, confounding interpretation.
• Impaired renal excretion can reduce urinary recovery of PABA even if it has been normally released and absorbed, again mimicking a falsely low result suggestive of pancreatic insufficiency.
• Because these three non-pancreatic factors can each lower the apparent NBT-PABA result, a control substance step is required to distinguish a true pancreatic cause from an intestinal, hepatic or renal cause.
• The disadvantage of PABA is that it is not as sensitive as fecal elastase-1, a further reason for confirming abnormal results with another method.
• This is similar to the pancreolauryl (fluorescein dilaurate, FDL) test, which is also repeated on a second day using free fluorescein to correct for individual variability in intestinal absorption, hepatic conjugation and urinary excretion.
• Both tests therefore build in a control/correction step precisely because absorption, conjugation and excretion factors unrelated to the pancreas can distort the apparent measure of pancreatic enzyme activity.
questions.question:

(b)
• The test is the dye excretion test using indocyanine green (ICG), used to evaluate a patient with suspected liver disorder but without jaundice, and also to investigate hepatic blood flow.
(c)
• The principle is that these lipophilic dyes are cleared in the liver and excreted into bile as the intact parent compound and/or its conjugates, with uptake by hepatocytes believed to be a carrier-mediated active transport process.
• Elimination of the dye depends on the hepatic blood flow, patency of the biliary tree, and hepatic parenchymal function.
(d)/(e)
• In apparently healthy individuals, ICG clearance ranges from 6.5-14 mL/min/kg.
• If the patient's result falls within this normal range, it suggests that hepatic blood flow, biliary patency and parenchymal function are not significantly impaired.
• ICG is preferred over the historically used bromosulfophthalein (BSP), because BSP caused fatal hypersensitivity reactions in some patients and other reactions such as nausea, syncope, headache, chills and thrombophlebitis, whereas ICG has a lower incidence of side effects.
• A normal ICG clearance in a patient with suspected but unconfirmed liver disease (without jaundice) is therefore reassuring evidence against significant impairment of hepatic blood flow or excretory function, though the test does not differentiate between intra- and extra-hepatic cholestasis.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Lipids can be broadly subdivided into five groups: sterol derivatives (cholesterol, cholesteryl esters, steroid hormones, bile acids, vitamin D), fatty acids (short, medium, long chain, prostaglandins), glycerol esters (triglycerides, diglycerides, monoglycerides, phosphoglycerides), sphingosine derivatives (sphingomyelin, glycosphingolipids), and terpenes/isoprene polymers (vitamins A, E and K).
• The four main lipids present in plasma are fatty acids, triglycerides, phospholipids and cholesterol.
(b)
• Cholesterol (a sterol derivative) is measured as total cholesterol, LDL-cholesterol and HDL-cholesterol; triglycerides (glycerol esters) are measured directly; these are the routinely reported components of a lipid profile.
• Lipoproteins (chylomicrons, VLDL, IDL, LDL, HDL) are the macromolecular complexes that transport these lipid classes in plasma, since lipids are relatively insoluble in aqueous solution.
(c)
• Blood for lipid measurement should be collected after at least 12 hours of fasting, and strenuous exercise should be avoided 2-3 hours before blood drawing.
• Change of position from 30 minutes supine to 30 minutes standing results in an increase in total cholesterol concentration, due to haemodilution when supine and haemoconcentration when upright.
• If the patient is not properly fasted, chylomicrons (which are usually low or absent in fasting plasma) may be present, and the Friedewald formula assumes the patient is fasting.
• Non-fasting specimens can contain chylomicrons, and a triglyceride level >400 mg/dL indicates their presence (or the presence of remnants), invalidating the Friedewald calculation of LDL cholesterol.
• Prolonged venous occlusion by tourniquet use is associated with higher cholesterol values, another handling error that would distort the result.
• Haemolysis during blood drawing or handling results in higher cholesterol levels, again an error unrelated to the patient's true lipid status.
• For serum, blood should be allowed to clot for at least half an hour before centrifugation; failing to do so could yield an inaccurate separation and erroneous result.
• Because the Friedewald equation specifically requires a fasting sample with triglycerides not exceeding 4.5 mmol/L, failure to fast for 12 hours undermines the validity of the calculated LDL-cholesterol result specifically, in addition to affecting total cholesterol and triglyceride measurements generally.

(a)
• Proximal tubular function tests include phosphate reabsorption, aminoaciduria, glycosuria and fractional HCO3- excretion.
• Distal tubular function tests include acidification (ammonium chloride load) and concentration (water deprivation with DDAVP).
• Other tubular tests described include the urine concentration test (specific gravity), the dilution test, and the para-amino-hippuric acid (PAH) clearance test.
• In the urine concentration test, in chronic kidney disease the kidney loses the ability to concentrate urine, and a low fixed specific gravity is indicative of chronic kidney disease.
(b)
• Tests of tubular function are applied when glomerular filtration markers (urea, creatinine, clearance) are normal but a tubular defect, such as renal tubular acidosis, is suspected, since RTA is not a glomerular lesion.
(c)
• In the acidification test, the ability to acidify urine is tested after administering 0.1 g/kg ammonium chloride in gelatin-coated form.
• Ammonium chloride is metabolised to produce an acid load (via release of H+ and Cl-), which the normal kidney should be able to excrete by acidifying the urine.
• In renal tubular acidosis, the distal tubular cells have abnormal permeability to H+ (Type 1) or a carbonic anhydrase defect (Type 2), so they cannot lower urine pH normally even when given this acid load.
• Testing the ability to acidify urine after this load therefore distinguishes patients with a distal or proximal acidifying defect from those with normal tubular H+ handling.
• This is analogous to the dilution test, where an oral water load (1200ml in half an hour after overnight water deprivation) is used to test whether the tubules can appropriately produce a dilute urine, at least one sample expected to show specific gravity of 1.003 or below.
• Both the acidification and dilution/concentration tests work on the same principle: giving a physiological challenge (acid load or water load/deprivation) and observing whether the tubules respond appropriately.
• This is why RTA testing specifically requires an acidification (ammonium chloride) challenge rather than relying on baseline urea, creatinine or GFR, which remain normal in this tubular disorder.

(b)
• This is the determination of free hydrochloric acid in gastric residue.
(c)
• The principle is that a known amount of gastric residue is titrated with NaOH, 0.10 mol/L, to a pH of 3.5 using a pH meter, or until Toepfer's reagent added to the gastric juice takes on a salmon colour; titration to this endpoint detects essentially all free HCl because it is the only strongly ionised acid in gastric content.
(d)
• Calculation: Free HCl (mmol/L) = (mL of NaOH x 0.1 x 1000)/(mL of gastric juice titrated); since 5 mL of sample was titrated, this simplifies to Free HCl (mmol/L) = mL of NaOH x 20.
(e)
• Free HCl = 3.2 x 20 = 64 mmol/L.
• This falls within the reference range given for free acid after stimulation with pentagastrin (10-130 mmol/L), which is consistent with the sample having been collected after gastric stimulation rather than in the unstimulated (0-40 mmol/L) state.
• Before titrating, the pH of the specimen should first be checked; if it had been above 3.5, no free acid would be present and the specimen should not have been titrated, instead requiring a gastric stimulus to be given first.
• Because titration beyond pH 3.5 would overestimate the HCl concentration, while titrating only to pH 3.5 could under-estimate free H+ that has already reacted with gastric constituents, the reported value of 64 mmol/L should be understood as the operationally defined free acid rather than an absolute measure of every hydrogen ion secreted.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Glucosuria is classified into hyperglycaemic glucosuria and normoglycaemic or renal glucosuria.
• Normoglycaemic (renal) glucosuria is seen in congenital renal glucosuria (a congenital defect in renal tubular reabsorption of glucose), acquired renal disease (e.g. nephritis), pregnancy (increased GFR), and injection of phlorhizin (inhibition of the SGLUT transporter in renal tubules).
• Hyperglycaemic glucosuria occurs when blood glucose exceeds the renal threshold (180 mg/dL), as seen in diabetes mellitus, stress (epinephrine glucosuria), and alimentary glucosuria (due to increased rate of glucose absorption following gastrectomy or gastrojejunostomy).
(b)
• The renal threshold is the maximum rate of reabsorption of glucose by the renal tubules, normally about 180 mg/dL; all glucose in blood is filtered through the kidneys and is normally completely returned to the blood by tubular reabsorption.
• If blood glucose exceeds this threshold, or if the threshold is abnormally low, glucosuria results.
(c)
• In normoglycaemic (renal) glucosuria, the renal threshold itself is abnormally low, for example due to a congenital defect in tubular reabsorption, acquired renal disease, pregnancy (increased GFR), or inhibition of the tubular glucose transporter (SGLUT) by phlorhizin.
• Because the defect lies in the kidney's capacity to reabsorb glucose rather than in the blood glucose concentration, glucose can appear in urine even though the blood glucose level itself remains within the normal range.
• In pregnancy, an increased GFR delivers a greater filtered load of glucose to the tubules, which may exceed their reabsorptive capacity even at a normal blood glucose level.
• In hyperglycaemic glucosuria, by contrast, the tubular reabsorptive mechanism itself is intact, but the filtered glucose load exceeds it because blood glucose is above 180 mg/dL, as in diabetes mellitus or stress-induced hyperglycaemia.
• Alimentary glucosuria occurs due to an increased rate of glucose absorption following gastrectomy or gastrojejunostomy, producing a transient rise in blood glucose above the threshold rather than a primary tubular defect.
• This distinction (tubular defect versus exceeded filtered load) is why glucosuria must always be interpreted together with a simultaneous blood glucose measurement.
• Without pairing urine glucose with blood glucose, a clinician could not tell whether glucosuria reflects true hyperglycaemia or an isolated renal (tubular) abnormality.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the classification of glucosuria into hyperglycaemic glucosuria and normoglycaemic (renal) glucosuria.
(b) State how the renal threshold for glucose is applied in distinguishing these two types.
(c) Explain why glucosuria can occur even when blood glucose is normal.

(a) List the hormones involved in the regulation of blood glucose, distinguishing insulin from the counter-regulatory hormones.
(b) State the setting in which cortisol, thyroxine and somatostatin each raise or otherwise affect plasma glucose levels.
(c) Explain why a hormonal imbalance, rather than glucose itself, is described as the underlying cause of hyperglycaemia.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Several factors regulate blood glucose level: regulation by different tissues and organs (liver and extra-hepatic tissue such as kidney, gastrointestinal tract, skeletal muscle and adipose tissue), and hormones, namely insulin and counter-regulatory hormones (glucagon, glucocorticoids, growth hormone and adrenaline).
• Insulin is described as a very important hormone in glucose metabolism, promoting glucose uptake, glycolysis, glycogen synthesis and triglyceride synthesis while inhibiting gluconeogenesis, ketogenesis and lipolysis.
• Control of blood glucose is under two major hormones, insulin and glucagon, both produced by the pancreas, with other hormones and neuroendocrine substances also exerting some control.
(b)
• Decreased levels of cortisol stimulate the anterior pituitary to release ACTH, which stimulates the adrenal cortex to release cortisol, increasing plasma glucose by converting liver glycogen to glucose and promoting gluconeogenesis.
• The thyroid gland is stimulated by thyroid-stimulating hormone to release thyroxine, which increases plasma glucose levels by increasing glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis and intestinal absorption of glucose.
• Somatostatin, produced by the D-cells of the islets of Langerhans, increases plasma glucose levels by inhibiting insulin, glucagon, growth hormone and other endocrine hormones.
(c)
• Hyperglycaemia is an increase in plasma glucose levels which occurs as a result of hormonal imbalance.
• Causes of hyperglycaemia listed include deficiency of insulin (absolute or relative, as in diabetes mellitus) and increases of anti-insulin hormones such as adrenaline, glucocorticoids, thyroxine and pituitary growth hormone.
• Because glucose itself is simply the substrate being regulated, and its level rises or falls according to the balance between insulin and these counter-regulatory hormones, an abnormal glucose level reflects an underlying disturbance in that hormonal balance rather than a primary fault in glucose itself.
• This is illustrated by conditions such as Cushing's syndrome/adrenal tumours (excess glucocorticoids), hyperthyroidism (excess thyroxine) and acromegaly (excess growth hormone), all of which raise plasma glucose through hormone excess rather than a primary pancreatic defect.
• Stress-related hyperglycaemia (infection, trauma, cerebrovascular accident) and pancreatic causes (glucagonoma, pancreatitis) or drugs (steroids, thiazides) similarly act by altering the hormonal balance controlling glucose rather than by any direct action on glucose.
• This is why hyperglycaemia is defined specifically as resulting from hormonal imbalance, rather than simply as an excess of dietary or absorbed glucose.

(a)
• Base units are the standard units of measurement for the seven international system of quantities, a basic set from which all other SI units can be derived.
• Derived units are derived mathematically from two or more base units.
• Supplementary units conform to the SI but have not been classified as either base or derived; at present only the radian (for plane angles) and the steradian (for solid angles) are classified this way.
• The Systeme Internationale d'Unites (SI) was accepted internationally in 1960, succeeding earlier absolute systems based on the centimeter-gram-second (CGS) and meter-kilogram-second (MKS) systems.
(b)
• A reference value is a value obtained by observation or measurement of a particular type of quantity on a reference individual; diagnosis in medical practice is essentially made by comparison with known outcomes, so reference values are needed for all tests, from both healthy individuals and patients with relevant diseases.
(c)
• Reporting of laboratory results is often expressed in terms of substance concentration (e.g. moles) or the mass of a substance (e.g. mg/dL, g/dL, g/L, mEq/L, IU) rather than in SI units, and these familiar/traditional units can cause confusion during interpretation.
• It has been recommended that analytes be reported using moles of solute per volume of solution (substance concentration) and that the litre be used as the reference volume.
• Any meaningful quantitative laboratory result consists of two components: the actual numeric value and a label identifying the units, where the number describes the numeric value and the unit defines the physical quantity or dimension (mass, length, time or volume).
• Because mass-based units (mg/dL, g/dL) do not directly indicate the number of molecules or ions present, comparing results across different substances or laboratories using different traditional units risks misinterpretation.
• Molar (mole per litre) reporting standardises the expression of concentration in terms of the actual number of particles, which is more directly relevant to the biochemical/physiological reactions being assessed.
• Reference limits describe the observed variation of values in a selected subset of reference individuals, while clinical decision limits provide optimum separation among clinical categories for differential diagnosis; both are more comparably applied when a consistent (molar) unit system is used.
• This is also why the requirements of comparison specify that all quantities compared should be of the same type and that laboratory results should be produced using adequately standardised methods, which is easier to achieve when a single internationally agreed unit system (SI, with molar concentration) is used.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the SI system of units under the headings of base, derived and supplementary units.
(b) State the setting in which the concept of a reference value is applied in interpreting a laboratory result.
(c) Explain the reasoning behind recommending that analytes be reported as moles of solute per litre rather than as mass concentration.

questions.answerText:
(b)
• The Friedewald formula is used to calculate LDL cholesterol: LDL-C = TC - HDL-C - (TG/5), applicable in mg/dL units (or LDLchol = tChol - HDLchol - [triglycerides]/2.2 in the equivalent mmol/L-based version).
• This equation assumes the patient is fasting, since VLDL is taken as 55% TG and 12% cholesterol, and that plasma triglyceride does not exceed 4.5 mmol/L (approximately 400 mg/dL); it also assumes chylomicrons, IDL and Lp(a) are not significant contributors to total cholesterol.
(c)/(d)
• LDL-C = 220 - 40 - (150/5) = 220 - 40 - 30 = 150 mg/dL.
• Comparing to the laboratory values that predict risk of CHD (LDL-C >130 mg/dL, HDL-C <35 mg/dL, TC >200 mg/dL, TG >150 mg/dL), this patient's LDL-C (150 mg/dL) and TC (220 mg/dL) both exceed the risk thresholds, while HDL-C (40 mg/dL) and TG (150 mg/dL) are at or just within the borderline levels, indicating an increased risk profile for CHD.
(e)
• If a future triglyceride result exceeds 400 mg/dL, this indicates the presence of chylomicrons (or remnants), invalidating the assumptions of the Friedewald formula, since non-fasting specimens or high triglyceride states can contain chylomicrons.
• In that situation, the Friedewald-calculated LDL-C should not be relied upon, and a direct LDL cholesterol measurement method should instead be used.
