questions.answerText:
(a)
• Osmolality is the number of solute particles in a kilogram of solvent (mmol/kg), determined directly by measurement using osmometers.
• It can also be determined indirectly by calculation: 1.8(Na+ + K+) + glucose + urea, all concentrations in mmol/L; an alternative formula given is osmolality = 2[Na] + [K] + [Urea] + [Glucose], all in mmol/L.
• Osmolarity, by contrast, is the number of solute particles in a litre of solvent (mmol/L).
• The main contributor to plasma osmolality is sodium; glucose and urea, though at lower molar concentration, also contribute.
(b)
• Osmolality determination is commonly used in the assessment of hypokalaemia and hyperkalaemia and other electrolyte disturbances, and normal plasma osmolality is maintained between 275-295 mmol/kg (285-295 mOsm/kg in some sections).
(c)
• Osmolality is defined as moles of solute per kilogram of solvent because it measures the effect of dissolved particles on water, independent of the volume changes that temperature or solute concentration can cause in a litre of solution.
• Water moves from a region of low osmolality to high osmolality in the body, so it is the concentration per unit mass of water (which does not change with temperature) that best predicts water movement.
• When osmolality of the ECF exceeds that of the ICF, as in dehydration, water is transferred from cells into the ECF by osmosis; the reverse occurs in over-hydration.
• Reporting per kilogram of solvent avoids the small errors introduced by the volume occupied by proteins and other solutes when comparing plasma to a purely aqueous reference.
• The osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect changes as small as 1-2% in plasma osmolality, so a stable and precise reference unit (per kg of water) is required for physiological regulation.
• This mass-based unit is used consistently in both the direct osmometer measurement and the indirect calculation formulae.
• Osmolal gap is calculated from the difference between measured and calculated osmolality and indicates the presence of low molecular weight substances such as ethanol, methanol, ethylene glycol, mannitol or lactate.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the determination of plasma osmolality under the headings of direct and indirect methods.
(b) State the clinical setting in which osmolality determination is used.
(c) Explain the reasoning behind reporting osmolality in mmol/kg rather than as a concentration per litre.

(a) A patient is found to have serum sodium of 118 mmol/L, but the serum is noted to be visibly lipaemic, with markedly elevated triglycerides.
(b) State the test/pattern this most likely represents.
(c) Describe the principle explaining why the sodium result is affected.
(d) State the additional information/test needed to confirm the mechanism.
(e) State the action that follows once the mechanism is confirmed.
questions.answerText:
(b)
• This most likely represents pseudohyponatraemia associated with hyperlipidaemia.
(c)
• This condition may be associated with spurious hyponatraemia because the serum or plasma contains a significant amount of non-aqueous components such as triglycerides, proteins or other paraproteins, so the laboratory provides a falsely low estimate of serum or plasma sodium.
(d)
• Additional information needed includes the measured (rather than calculated) plasma osmolality, and confirmation of the degree of hyperlipidaemia/hypertriglyceridaemia, since the true extracellular fluid sodium is not actually as low as the reported value suggests.
(e)
• Once pseudohyponatraemia due to hyperlipidaemia is confirmed (by the combination of a very high triglyceride/lipid level and a sodium result inconsistent with the clinical picture), no unnecessary sodium-correcting treatment should be given, since the true (aqueous-phase) sodium concentration is not truly low.
• This is distinguished from factitious hyponatraemia due to hyperglycaemia, where every 100 mg/dL rise in glucose lowers measured sodium by about 3 mmol/L, and from artefactual hyponatraemia due to sampling proximal to an IV infusion site.
• The laboratory or clinician should note the lipaemic appearance of the sample as the explanation for the abnormal result rather than proceeding as if true sodium depletion were present.

(a)
• Basic renal processes include glomerular filtration (production of glomerular filtrate/ultrafiltrate, which is cell-free, protein-free, and contains other plasma substances at similar concentrations), tubular reabsorption (movement from tubular lumen to peritubular capillary) and tubular secretion (movement from peritubular capillary to tubular lumen).
• The amount of a substance excreted equals the amount filtered plus the amount secreted minus the amount reabsorbed.
• Effective renal plasma flow (ERPF) is calculated from peripheral venous PAH concentration and indicates that renal venous plasma was not measured; actual renal plasma flow (ARPF) = ERPF/extraction ratio.
(b)
• Isotopic GFR is the most accurate measurement of GFR, especially at low levels of renal function or with alterations of muscle mass, using a single injection of 99mTc-DTPA with two plasma samples taken 1-3 hours later, GFR calculated from the plasma clearance of the isotope.
• It is used for monitoring renal function over time or in chronic renal failure patients approaching dialysis, tested every two to five years because of the cost and inconvenience of the procedure, in contrast to inulin clearance (the gold standard but a complex procedure not routinely done in patients).
(c)
• To determine renal blood flow, two factors are necessary: renal plasma flow and the percentage of plasma volume in the blood.
• Renal plasma flow is measured using PAH clearance, while the percentage of plasma volume in blood is determined indirectly using the packed cell volume (PCV).
• If PCV is 45%, the plasma volume of the blood is 100-45 = 55%, i.e. 55 mL of plasma is present in every 100 mL of blood.
• Renal blood flow is therefore calculated as renal plasma flow divided by the percentage of plasma in blood, which is mathematically the same as RPF x 1/(1-Hct), since Hct (haematocrit) equals 1 minus the fraction of plasma.
• For example, if renal plasma flow is 630 mL/min and PCV is 45%, renal blood flow = 630/0.55 = 1145.46 mL/min.
• Similarly, if RPF = 700 mL/min and Hct is 45%, renal blood flow = 700 x 1/0.55 = 1273 mL/min.
• This formula is necessary because plasma flow alone underestimates total blood flow, since blood also contains the cellular (red cell) fraction represented by the haematocrit.
questions.question:
(a) List the invasive and non-invasive methods used to assess renal function alongside the description of ERPF and ARPF.
(b) State the setting in which isotopic GFR measurement (99mTc-DTPA, 51Cr-EDTA) is applied compared with inulin clearance.
(c) Explain the reasoning behind expressing renal blood flow as RPF multiplied by 1/(1-Hct).

questions.answerText:
(a)
• After glucose enters the cell it is quickly shunted into one of three possible metabolic pathways: the Embden-Meyerhof (glycolytic) pathway, the hexose monophosphate (HMP) shunt, or conversion to glycogen (glycogenesis); the first step for all three requires conversion of glucose to glucose-6-phosphate by hexokinase using ATP.
• In the Embden-Meyerhof pathway, glucose is broken down into two- and three-carbon molecules of pyruvic acid that can enter the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle on conversion to acetyl-CoA; this pathway generates energy from glucose.
• The HMP shunt diverts glucose-6-phosphate to 6-phosphogluconic acid, permitting formation of ribose-5-phosphate and NADPH; NADPH is important to erythrocytes, which lack mitochondria and cannot use the TCA cycle, and protects the cell from oxidative and free radical damage.
• When the cell's energy requirements are met, glucose is stored as glycogen: glucose-6-phosphate is converted to glucose-1-phosphate, then to uridine diphosphoglucose, then to glycogen by glycogen synthase, mainly in the liver and muscles.
(b)
• Glycogenesis is favoured when the cell's energy requirements are already being met, i.e. when glucose is in adequate or excess supply relative to immediate energy needs.
(c)
• The nervous system, including the brain, totally depends on glucose from the surrounding extracellular fluid for energy.
• Nervous tissue cannot concentrate or store carbohydrates, so it is critical to maintain a steady supply of glucose to the tissue.
• For this reason the concentration of glucose in the ECF must be maintained within a narrow range; when concentration falls below a certain level, nervous tissue loses its primary energy source and is incapable of maintaining normal function.
• Because nervous tissue cannot switch to a stored carbohydrate reserve the way liver or muscle can (via glycogen), it has no local buffer against a fall in blood glucose.
• The HMP shunt's importance to erythrocytes (which also lack mitochondria) illustrates the same general principle: cells without alternative energy-generating machinery are especially dependent on continuous glucose-derived pathways.
• Without NADPH from the HMP shunt, the lipid bilayer membrane of the cell and critical enzymes would eventually be destroyed, resulting in cell death, showing the wider consequences of disrupted glucose-dependent pathways.
• This dependence explains why hypoglycaemia produces symptoms referable to the central nervous system, since neurons cannot maintain function once their sole fuel supply is inadequate.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the fate of glucose after absorption, under the headings of the three metabolic pathways it may enter and their respective purposes.
(b) State the setting in which glucose is directed towards glycogenesis rather than glycolysis or the hexose monophosphate pathway.
(c) Explain the reasoning behind why nervous tissue is especially vulnerable to a fall in extracellular glucose concentration.

(a) Describe the bicarbonate/carbonic acid buffer pair, including its components, dissociation constant and share of body buffering capacity.
(b) State the clinical setting in which this buffer pair is assessed in the laboratory.
(c) Explain the reasoning behind collecting arterial blood samples in heparinised syringes over ice and analysing them immediately.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• The bicarbonate/carbonic acid (HCO3-/H2CO3) buffer pair has a pK of 6.1 and is described as the workhorse of the buffering process.
• It accounts for about 60% capacity of body buffering, more than any other buffer pair.
• It works through two main mechanisms: bicarbonate resorption/reclamation (no net gain of HCO3, most useful in the steady state) and bicarbonate regeneration (net gain of HCO3), the latter occurring in the kidney and erythrocytes.
• In erythrocytes haemoglobin (Hb-/HHb) serves as the blood buffer through the chloride shift.
• Other buffer pairs in the body include protein-/protein, NH3-/NH4 (pK=9.8) and NaHPO4-/NaH2PO4 (pK=6.8); a buffer pair functions best at a pH nearest its pK, and the larger the pK value the smaller the extent of dissociation.
• Its relationship to pH is given by the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation: pH = pK + log(HCO3-/(PCO2 x 0.23)).
(b)
• It is assessed as part of arterial blood gas measurement, an important test in critically ill patients, alongside pH and PaCO2/PaO2.
(c)
• The essence of a buffer is to mop up H+ and produce a minimal change in pH, so the sample must reflect the true in-vivo hydrogen ion concentration.
• Control of CO2 is by the lungs, and CO2 diffuses along a concentration gradient from cells to extracellular fluid and then to the lungs, so ongoing metabolism after sampling would continue to alter CO2 content.
• Keeping the sample over ice slows cellular metabolism that would otherwise change pH, PCO2 and bicarbonate before the sample reaches the analyzer.
• Analysing immediately avoids the sample equilibrating with room air, which would alter the measured gas partial pressures.
• Heparin is used as anticoagulant in the syringe to prevent clotting of the arterial sample before analysis.

questions.question:
(a) List the two types of renal tubular acidosis (RTA) described.
(b) State how each type is applied or recognised in terms of the underlying tubular defect.
(c) Explain why an error in classifying RTA as a glomerular rather than a tubular defect would lead to an invalid interpretation of renal function tests.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Renal tubular acidosis is usually an acquired disorder but could be inherited; two types are known: Classical or Type 1 (distal RTA) and Proximal or Type 2 RTA.
(b)
• Type 1 (Distal) RTA is due to abnormal permeability of distal tubular cells to H+.
• Type 2 (Proximal) RTA is due to a defect of carbonic anhydrase.
• Both types result in metabolic acidosis.
(c)
• Renal tubular acidosis is stated not to be a glomerular lesion; urea and creatinine (markers of glomerular function) are normal in RTA.
• If RTA were wrongly classified as a glomerular problem, a clinician might expect abnormal urea and creatinine, which would not be found, leading to a false conclusion that renal function is normal overall.
• RTA is instead a tubular defect, so the correct tests to identify it relate to tubular handling of H+ and bicarbonate rather than to glomerular filtration markers.
• Since Type 1 RTA reflects abnormal tubular permeability to H+ and Type 2 reflects a carbonic anhydrase defect, treating both as the same lesion would misdirect further tubular function testing.
• Metabolic acidosis from RTA would be interpreted correctly only if the primary bicarbonate reduction is recognised as the abnormality in the equation pH = pK + log(HCO3-/PCO2), causing the pH to fall.
• Both types of RTA are, however, causes of a normal anion-gap type of metabolic acidosis rather than a raised anion-gap acidosis such as ketoacidosis.
• Correctly distinguishing distal from proximal RTA is therefore necessary before management is planned, since the underlying tubular defects and their handling differ.
• Failure to make this distinction could result in an invalid overall assessment of the patient's renal acid-base handling, since urea and creatinine will appear normal despite an important tubular acidification defect being present.

(a)
• Pseudo-hyperkalaemia causes include haemolysis of erythrocytes in the test tube, ischaemic blood draw, and long-standing blood samples with leakage of potassium from red cells.
• Redistribution causes include acidosis, hyperglycaemia with insulin deficiency, tissue necrosis, periodic paralysis, rhabdomyolysis, burns, and drugs/toxins such as beta-blockers, arginine, HCl, succinylcholine and digitalis.
• Decreased renal excretion causes include potassium-sparing diuretics (amiloride, spironolactone), renal insufficiency, renal tubular acidosis, NSAIDs and ACE inhibitors (which lead to aldosterone deficiency), aldosterone deficiency, and Addison's disease.
• Excessive intake of potassium with decreased excretion, especially in renal insufficiency, and rapid intravenous infusion are also causes.
(b)
• Calcium Chloride (or Gluconate), 10 ml of 10% solution, is given IV with ECG monitoring; this antagonizes the effect of hyperkalaemia on heart muscle but does not alter the net potassium concentration.
• Glucose 50g with 20 units of soluble insulin by IV injection lowers plasma K+ within about 30 minutes by increasing K+ entry into cells; in an emergency 10 units of soluble insulin may be added to 1L of 10% glucose.
• 40ml of 8.5% NaHCO3 (40 mmol of bicarbonate) may be injected over 5 minutes as an alternative to glucose and insulin if metabolic acidosis is present; this solution is hyperosmolal.
(c)
• Calcium should never be added to bicarbonate solutions because calcium carbonate is poorly soluble in water.
• Mixing the two would therefore cause precipitation of calcium carbonate rather than delivering the intended calcium dose to antagonise cardiac membrane effects.
• If too much calcium is given on its own, hypercalcaemia may itself cause cardiac arrest, so calcium must be given cautiously and separately with ECG monitoring.
• Since the calcium treatment protects the heart but "does not alter net concentration" of potassium, it must be paired with a separate measure (glucose/insulin or bicarbonate) that actually shifts or removes potassium.
• Keeping the calcium and bicarbonate as separate infusions therefore avoids a chemical incompatibility while still allowing both the membrane-stabilising and the potassium-lowering actions to be achieved.
questions.question:
(a) List the causes of hyperkalaemia grouped as pseudo-hyperkalaemia, redistribution and decreased renal excretion.
(b) State how emergency treatment of hyperkalaemia is applied according to its mechanism of action.
(c) Explain why calcium should never be added to bicarbonate solutions in the treatment of hyperkalaemia.

(a) Describe the major functions of plasma proteins under the headings of transport, osmotic regulation, catalytic function, protective function, blood clotting, anticoagulant activity and buffering.
(b) State the clinical setting in which total protein and albumin are measured as part of liver function tests (LFTs) and other workups.
(c) Explain the reasoning behind albumin being described as a negative acute phase reactant.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Plasma protein functions include transport (e.g. transferrin transports iron, ceruloplasmin transports copper, albumin transports fatty acids, bilirubin and calcium and many drugs, transcortin transports cortisol, retinol-binding protein transports retinol, lipoproteins transport lipids, haptoglobin transports free haemoglobin, thyroxine-binding globulin transports thyroxine).
• Osmotic regulation: plasma proteins are colloidal and exert a colloidal osmotic (oncotic) pressure that helps maintain normal blood volume and water content in interstitial fluid; albumin is most important in this regulation, and a decrease in albumin causes loss of water from blood into interstitial fluid, causing oedema.
• Catalytic function includes lipases, renin, coagulation factors and complement proteins; protective function includes immunoglobulins combining with foreign antigens, the complement system removing cellular antigens, and enzyme inhibitors such as alpha1-antitrypsin protecting tissues from hydrolytic damage.
• Blood clotting involves factors such as IX, VIII, thrombin and fibrinogen; anticoagulant activity (thrombolysis) is provided by plasmin, which breaks down thrombin and dissolves the clot; buffering capacity is provided by all plasma proteins helping to maintain acid-base balance.
(b)
• Plasma albumin and total protein are part of liver function tests (LFTs), and are also used in workup and monitoring of patients for monoclonal gammopathy, suspected or diagnosed multiple sclerosis, unexplained renal insufficiency or proteinuria, hypoglobulinaemia, and amyloid light-chain amyloidosis.
(c)
• C-reactive protein, serum amyloid A and fibrinogen levels rise during the acute phase response and are involved in the inflammatory response.
• The acute phase response can result in rapid albumin extravasation and thus hypoalbuminaemia.
• Because albumin concentration falls during an acute phase response, rather than rising like CRP or fibrinogen, albumin is described as a negative acute phase reactant.
• This is consistent with albumin's role in maintaining oncotic pressure: if albumin extravasates rapidly during inflammation, its fall contributes to the redistribution of fluid seen in acute illness.
• It also explains why serum albumin, though useful for nutritional and hepatic assessment, must be interpreted cautiously in the presence of acute inflammation, since its level can fall for reasons unrelated to true protein malnutrition or synthetic liver failure.
• This contrasts with proteins such as CRP, ceruloplasmin, haptoglobin and alpha2-macroglobulin, which increase during acute inflammation and are collectively called acute phase proteins.
• The differing behaviour of albumin (negative reactant) versus these other proteins (positive reactants) during the same acute phase response illustrates why a panel of proteins, rather than albumin alone, gives a fuller picture of the inflammatory state.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the Fredrickson classification of lipoproteins according to electrophoretic mobility.
(b) State the setting in which lipoprotein electrophoresis (LEP) has historically been applied, and its current status.
(c) Explain the reasoning behind why chylomicrons and dense VLDL/IDL particles behave differently on standing at 4 degrees C overnight.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Fredrickson's classification of lipoproteins is according to their electrophoretic mobility; four principal bands are formed based on their relative position by protein electrophoresis: alpha (HDL), pre-beta (VLDL), beta (LDL) and chylomicrons.
• Chylomicrons are the largest and least dense lipoproteins, transporting exogenous lipid from the intestine to all cells; VLDL transports endogenous lipid from the liver to cells; IDL is transient, formed during conversion of VLDL to LDL and not normally present in plasma; LDL, formed from VLDL, carries cholesterol to cells; HDL, the most dense lipoprotein, transports cholesterol from cells back to the liver (reverse cholesterol transport) and can be divided into HDL2 and HDL3.
(b)
• Lipoprotein electrophoresis (LEP) is no longer a common laboratory test, because total cholesterol, triglycerides, HDL and LDL can now be measured directly; the standing plasma test for chylomicrons remains a simple alternative screening approach.
(c)
• If a lipaemic sample, for example after a meal, is left overnight at 4 degrees C, the larger and less dense chylomicrons form a creamy layer on the surface.
• The smaller and denser VLDL and IDL particles do not rise in the same way, and the sample may instead appear diffusely turbid.
• LDL and HDL particles do not contribute to this turbidity because they are small and do not scatter light.
• This difference in behaviour is due to the differing size and density of the particles: the largest, least dense particles (chylomicrons) float to the top, while the smaller dense particles remain dispersed.
• Fasting plasma from normal individuals contains only VLDL, LDL and HDL particles, so chylomicrons in fasting plasma are considered abnormal.
• The standing plasma test for chylomicrons exploits exactly this size/density-dependent behaviour: plasma is placed in a refrigerator at 4 degrees C overnight, and chylomicrons accumulate as a floating cream layer if present.
• Because the subdivision of LDL into small dense LDL2/LDL3 (more atherogenic and more easily oxidised) versus larger LDL1 particles also depends on density, similar density-based separation principles underlie both the standing plasma test and lipoprotein electrophoresis.
• The Fredrickson bands (alpha, pre-beta, beta, chylomicrons) reflect these same density/size-related electrophoretic mobilities, from HDL (most dense, migrates furthest as alpha) to chylomicrons (least dense, remaining at the origin).
• This explains why a simple overnight refrigeration test can distinguish chylomicron-rich samples from others without requiring formal electrophoresis.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) under the headings of trigger, sequence of hormone conversion and final renal action.
(b) State the clinical setting in which RAAS activity is relevant to sodium and water balance.
(c) Explain the reasoning behind why hyperkalaemia stimulates aldosterone secretion as part of this system.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• RAAS secretion of renin occurs in response to a fall in renal afferent arteriolar pressure and a reduction in the supply of Na+ to the distal tubule (or low total body water/hypovolaemia detected by the juxtaglomerular apparatus).
• Renin, a proteolytic enzyme, catalyses hydrolysis of circulating angiotensinogen to release the inactive decapeptide angiotensin I.
• Angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II, the principal stimulant of aldosterone release from the adrenal cortex, and angiotensin II also directly causes vasoconstriction of capillary walls.
• Aldosterone, produced by the zona glomerulosa of the adrenal cortex, acts on the kidney's distal tubule to promote Na+ reabsorption in exchange for H+ or K+.
(b)
• RAAS activity is relevant to the assessment and management of disorders of sodium and water balance, including hypertension, Conn's syndrome and states of hypovolaemia.
(c)
• Aldosterone acts on the distal convoluted tubule to increase exchange of Na+ for K+ or H+ ions, increasing Na retention and causing K extrusion.
• Since aldosterone's normal action is to excrete potassium, a rise in plasma potassium (hyperkalaemia) is itself a signal that more potassium needs to be excreted.
• Hyperkalaemia therefore stimulates aldosterone secretion as a direct feedback mechanism to increase renal K+ excretion alongside its sodium-retaining action.
• The net effect of increasing plasma sodium reabsorption is to increase blood osmolality and ADH concentration, retaining water and total body volume.
• Angiotensin II also increases myocardial contraction, stimulates absorption of Na and water by the GIT, and stimulates thirst, reinforcing the overall volume- and sodium-conserving effect of the system.
• Renal blood flow and atrial natriuretic peptide are other factors affecting Na+ balance; atrial natriuretic peptide promotes Na+ excretion by increasing GFR and inhibiting renin and aldosterone secretion, acting in the opposite direction to RAAS.
• This shows that RAAS and its counter-regulatory pathways together, rather than aldosterone alone, determine the final renal handling of sodium and potassium.

(b)
• Clearance of PAH represents an approximation of renal plasma flow, since PAH, when administered, is 90% cleared from the plasma in one passage through the kidney.
(c)
• Effective renal plasma flow (ERPF) = (UPAH x V)/PPAH = clearance of PAH (CPAH), where UPAH is urine PAH concentration, V is urine volume, and PPAH is plasma PAH concentration.
• Because PAH is not 100% cleared, total (actual) renal plasma flow (ARPF) = ERPF / extraction ratio of PAH (0.9 in this case, since 90% of PAH is removed from the blood).
(d)
• Materials/values required: urine PAH concentration, urine volume, plasma PAH concentration, and the extraction ratio of PAH (percentage of PAH removed from the blood).
(e)
• Renal blood flow can then be calculated using renal plasma flow and the percentage of plasma volume in blood (from PCV): renal blood flow = RPF x 1/(1-Hct).
• With RPF = 630 mL/min and PCV (Hct) = 45%, renal blood flow = 630/0.55 = 1145.46 mL/min.
• This result and calculation approach reflects the fact that ERPF (using peripheral venous PAH) averages about 625 mL/min in humans, so a value of 630 mL/min is consistent with a normal effective renal plasma flow.
questions.question:
(a) A patient is given para-amino-hippurate (PAH), and the plasma sample gives a urine PAH concentration (Us), urine volume (V) and plasma PAH concentration (Ps) sufficient to calculate clearance, with 90% of the PAH removed from the blood (extraction ratio 0.9).
(b) Identify the test/value that clearance of PAH represents in this patient.
(c) State the principle/formula behind the calculation of effective renal plasma flow (ERPF) and total renal plasma flow.
(d) List the materials/values required for the calculation.
(e) State the result and its interpretation if PAH clearance (ERPF) is 630 mL/min and the patient's PCV is 45%.

(a) Describe arterial blood gas measurement under the headings of sample type, handling and what it measures.
(b) Explain why arterial blood gas analysis is important in the assessment of a critically ill patient.
(c) Distinguish between the plasma bicarbonate concentration and the total CO2 concentration reported by the laboratory.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Arterial blood gas measurement uses an arterial sample collected in heparinised syringes over ice and analyzed immediately.
• It provides valuable information about the blood pH and the partial pressures of arterial carbon dioxide (PaCO2) and oxygen (PaO2).
• Most analyzers also calculate serum bicarbonate (HCO3-) and the base excess, and some also measure electrolytes, haemoglobin, glucose and lactate.
• It is indicated in patients in respiratory failure, who are critically ill, show sudden unexpected deterioration, or have sepsis, multi-organ failure, uncontrolled diabetes mellitus, drug overdose or a dangerous toxin.
(b)
• It is often an important test in a critically ill patient, showing whether there is an acid-base abnormality and whether the pH is outside the normal range of 7.35-7.45.
• It shows whether it is the respiratory (PaCO2) or the metabolic (HCO3-) component that is abnormal, and whether that component tells the same story as the pH.
• Where there is metabolic acidosis (low pH and low HCO3-), it allows the additional step of calculating the anion gap.
• It shows whether compensation is occurring, whether it is partial or full, and can reveal a mixed disorder where PaCO2 and HCO3- move in opposite directions.
(c)
• Laboratories measure total CO2 concentration (dissolved carbon dioxide plus bicarbonate concentration, about 25-26 meq/L) in a venous sample.
• As a result, total CO2 concentration exceeds the plasma bicarbonate concentration by 1.0 to 1.5 meq/L.
• Normal plasma bicarbonate concentration is approximately 24 meq/L, whereas the partial pressure of CO2 in plasma is normally 40 mmHg.
• Bicarbonate concentration can also be calculated indirectly from the Henderson equation rather than measured directly.

questions.question:
(a) List the signs and symptoms of renal failure described under symptoms of uraemia, disorders of micturition, disorders of urine volume, alterations in urine composition, pain and oedema.
(b) State how biochemical testing is applied in relation to the presentation of a patient with suspected renal disease.
(c) Explain why biochemical testing "rarely establishes the cause" of renal disease on its own.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Symptoms of uraemia include nausea, vomiting and lethargy.
• Disorders of micturition include frequency, nocturia, retention and dysuria.
• Disorders of urine volume include polyuria, oliguria and anuria.
• Alterations in urine composition include haematuria, proteinuria, bacteriuria, leukocyturia and calculi; pain and oedema (from hypoalbuminaemia and salt/water retention) are also features.
(b)
• Patients present with routine urinalysis findings, a symptom or physical sign, or a systemic disease with a known renal component.
• Effective management of renal disease depends on establishing a definitive diagnosis using a detailed clinical history and diagnostic imaging and biopsy (immunology), with biochemistry playing a supporting role.
(c)
• The role of biochemistry is described as rarely establishing the cause, but rather screening for damage and monitoring progression.
• Renal function tests such as urea, creatinine and clearance mainly reflect the level of glomerular filtration rather than pinpointing a specific underlying disease process.
• Different diseases (glomerulonephritis, tubulointerstitial disease, obstruction) can produce overlapping biochemical abnormalities (raised urea and creatinine, proteinuria), so biochemistry alone cannot distinguish between them.
• A definitive diagnosis instead requires detailed clinical history together with diagnostic imaging and biopsy, which can directly visualise or sample the affected tissue.
• Biochemical tests are, however, valuable for detecting that damage is present (screening) and for tracking whether a known disease is getting better or worse over time (monitoring progression).
• This is why renal biochemical testing is described as playing a supporting rather than a primary diagnostic role in establishing the underlying cause of renal disease.

(a)
• If a substance is completely cleared from the plasma, the clearance rate of that substance equals the total renal plasma flow; PAH is used because it is close to being completely cleared (about 90% cleared from the plasma in one passage).
• Renal plasma flow (RPF) can be calculated as RPF = (Us x V)/Ps = Cs, where Us is urine concentration of the substance, V is urine volume, Ps is plasma concentration, and Cs is clearance of the substance.
• For a substance to be completely cleared from the plasma it must be excreted by both glomerular filtration and tubular secretion, since GFR alone accounts for only about 20% of total plasma flow entering the glomerular capillaries.
• The value obtained using peripheral venous PAH is called the effective renal plasma flow (ERPF), to indicate that the level in renal venous plasma was not measured; in humans ERPF averages about 625 mL/min.
(b)
• RPF/ERPF measurement is applied in the assessment of overall renal blood supply, and is used together with the extraction ratio to calculate total (actual) renal plasma flow and renal blood flow.
(c)
• Peripheral venous plasma can be used because its PAH concentration is essentially identical to that in the arterial plasma reaching the kidney.
• This means a peripheral venous sample gives a valid estimate of the PAH concentration being delivered to the kidney without needing to sample the renal vein directly.
• Because PAH is not 100% cleared (only about 90%), a correction is applied using the extraction ratio (the percentage of PAH removed from the blood, e.g. 0.9 if 90% is removed).
• Total renal plasma flow is then calculated as clearance of PAH divided by the extraction ratio of PAH, giving actual renal plasma flow (ARPF) = ERPF/extraction ratio.
• Renal blood flow is then calculated from renal plasma flow and the percentage of plasma in blood (from the PCV/haematocrit): renal blood flow = RPF x 1/(1-Hct).
• For example, if RPF is 700 mL/min and haematocrit is 45%, renal blood flow = 700 x 1/0.55 = 1273 mL/min.
• Using peripheral venous plasma therefore avoids the need for invasive renal vein catheterisation while still allowing a valid, correctable estimate of renal plasma flow.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the measurement of renal plasma flow (RPF) using para-amino-hippurate (PAH) under the headings of principle, formula and the concept of effective renal plasma flow (ERPF).
(b) State the clinical setting in which RPF measurement is applied.
(c) Explain why peripheral venous plasma, rather than renal venous plasma, can be used to estimate ERPF.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Dye excretion tests use lipophilic dyes that are cleared in the liver and excreted into bile either as the intact parent compound or as both the parent compound and its conjugates.
• Commonly used dyes are bromosulfophthalein, indocyanine green and rose bengal.
• Elimination of these dyes depends on hepatic blood flow, patency of the biliary tree, and hepatic parenchymal function; uptake by hepatocytes is believed to be a carrier-mediated active transport process.
(b)
• Excretion of these dyes is a sensitive indicator of the presence of liver disease, though it does not differentiate between intra- and extra-hepatic cholestasis.
• The dye excretion method is used to evaluate patients with suspected liver disorder but without jaundice.
• The ICG excretion test is currently used for investigation of hepatic blood flow and for predicting clearance rates of drugs such as lidocaine that undergo first-pass clearance by the liver; in apparently healthy individuals ICG clearance ranges from 6.5-14 mL/min/kg.
(c)
• BSP was the most popularly used dye historically, but some patients developed fatal hypersensitivity reactions to it.
• Some patients also developed nausea, syncope, headache, chills and thrombophlebitis at the injection site with BSP.
• Because of these adverse experiences, the dye excretion test using BSP has been discontinued.
• Indocyanine green can be used in place of BSP because it has a lower incidence of side effects.
• ICG therefore offers the same diagnostic principle (hepatic uptake and clearance of a lipophilic dye reflecting hepatic blood flow, biliary patency and parenchymal function) with a better safety profile.
• This is why ICG has replaced BSP as the dye of choice for evaluating suspected liver disorder without jaundice and for assessing hepatic blood flow.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the dye excretion test under the headings of principle, commonly used dyes and factors determining their elimination.
(b) State the clinical setting in which the dye excretion test is applied.
(c) Explain why bromosulfophthalein (BSP) has been discontinued in favour of indocyanine green (ICG).

questions.answerText:
(b)
• This pattern is suggestive of pre-renal acute renal failure (ARF), reflecting reduced renal perfusion with tubules that are still functioning.
(c)
• The principle is that pre-renal ARF is distinguished from intrinsic (renal) ARF by whether the tubules are still functioning normally to concentrate urine and conserve sodium and urea, versus tubular damage in intrinsic renal disease.
(d)
• Tests used: urea and creatinine (a disproportionate rise in urea suggests pre-renal, whereas urea and creatinine tending to rise together suggests renal); protein in urine (uncommon in pre-renal, present on dipstick in renal disease); urine Na+ (<20 mmol/L in pre-renal versus >40 mmol/L in renal); urine/plasma osmolality ratio (>1.5 in pre-renal versus <1.1 in renal); and urine/plasma urea ratio (>10 in pre-renal versus <5 in renal).
(e)
• Because all of the values given (disproportionate urea rise, low urine Na+, high urine/plasma osmolality ratio, high urine/plasma urea ratio) match the pre-renal pattern, this classification (functioning tubules, reduced perfusion) should be recorded.
• The action that follows is to address the reduced renal perfusion (the pre-renal cause), since the classification indicates the tubules themselves are still able to concentrate urine and conserve sodium appropriately, distinguishing this from a primary intrinsic renal (parenchymal) problem that would need different management.
questions.question:
(a) A patient presents with a disproportionate rise in urea compared to creatinine, urine sodium <20 mmol/L, a urine/plasma osmolality ratio >1.5, and a urine/plasma urea ratio >10.
(b) Identify the category of acute renal failure suggested by this pattern of results.
(c) State the principle used to distinguish this from the alternative category.
(d) List the tests that were used to reach this interpretation.
(e) State the action that follows from this classification.

(a) A patient's serum results give a calculated osmolality using 1.8(Na+ + K+) + glucose + urea that is markedly lower than the osmolality measured directly on the osmometer, and the history raises suspicion of methanol ingestion.
(b) Identify the test/finding suggested by this discrepancy.
(c) State the biochemical principle behind this finding.
(d) Describe the procedure/next action to confirm the cause.
(e) State the expected result and its interpretation.
questions.answerText:
(b)
• The finding described is an osmolal gap.
(c)
• The osmolal gap is a measure of low molecular weight substances or compounds in plasma other than sodium, potassium, urea and glucose, which contribute to plasma osmolality but are not included in the calculated formula.
(d)
• The gap indicates the presence of substances such as ethanol, methanol, ethylene glycol, drugs, lactate, mannitol or hydroxybutyrate.
• The next action is to correlate the size and presence of the osmolal gap with the clinical suspicion (here, methanol ingestion) and to proceed with specific testing/management for the suspected toxin.
• Both direct osmometer measurement and the indirect calculation (1.8[Na+K] + glucose + urea, all in mmol/L) should be available so that the gap between them can be determined.
(e)
• A raised osmolal gap in a patient with suspected methanol ingestion is consistent with the presence of methanol (or another unmeasured low molecular weight solute) in the plasma.
• This supports proceeding to confirm and manage suspected methanol poisoning, since the osmolal gap specifically flags the presence of substances such as methanol that are not part of the routine calculated osmolality formula.
• The result should be reported alongside both the measured and calculated osmolality values so that the size of the gap, and hence the likely presence of an unmeasured toxin, is clear to the requesting clinician.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the determination of free hydrochloric acid in gastric residue under the headings of principle, procedure and calculation.
(b) State the setting in which this titration test is applied in gastric function assessment.
(c) Explain the reasoning behind titrating only to pH 3.5 rather than further, and why this may still under- or over-estimate free acid.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• The principle is that a known amount of gastric residue is titrated with NaOH, 0.10 mol/L, to a pH of 3.5 using a pH meter, or until Toepfer's reagent added to gastric juice takes on a salmon colour.
• Procedure: measure and transfer a convenient volume of gastric juice (5-10.0 mL) into a clean titration vessel, centrifuging or filtering through gauze if it contains food particles or mucus; determine the pH first, and if above 3.5 no free acid is present and the specimen should not be titrated (the patient should instead be given a gastric stimulus).
• Calculation: Free HCl (mmol/L) = (mL of NaOH x 0.1 x 1000)/(mL of gastric juice titrated); if 5 mL is titrated, Free HCl (mmol/L) = mL of NaOH x 20.
(b)
• This titration test is applied as part of gastric function tests to evaluate gastric secretory activity, alongside measurement of basal acid output (BAO), peak acid output (PAO) and maximum acid output (MAO).
(c)
• Titration to a pH of 3.0-3.5 detects essentially all free HCl because HCl is the only strongly ionised acid in gastric content, so this test is essentially specific for free HCl.
• Titration beyond pH 3.5 will overestimate the HCl concentration to a varying degree, because other, weaker acidic components would also be neutralised and counted.
• Titration only to pH 3.5 may, on the other hand, under-estimate the amount of free H+ actually secreted, if some H+ has already reacted with constituents of the gastric juice.
• There is therefore no fully satisfactory procedure to accurately measure the true total amount of free acid secreted by the gastric mucosa.
• If the initial pH of the gastric specimen is above 3.5, no free acid is present and titration should not be performed on that sample.
• Total acidity, in contrast, is determined by titration to pH 7.0 (using phenol red) or to pH 8.4 (using phenolphthalein), and includes hydrogen ions from free HCl, mucoprotein, acid salts and organic acids.
• The difference between free and total acidity, due to acids other than free HCl (10-20 mmol/L), represents the combined or non-ionised acids that are bound or reacted with proteins.
• Choosing the correct endpoint (3.5 for free acid, 7.0/8.4 for total acidity) is therefore essential to avoid systematically over- or under-stating the patient's true gastric acid output.

(b)
• The bands present in the normal strip, from left to right (as separated by electrophoresis), are albumin, alpha1-globulin, alpha2-globulin, beta-globulin and gamma-globulin (immunoglobulins).
(c)
• Strip II, showing reduced albumin, reduced alpha1 and gamma-globulins with an increase in the alpha2-globulin fraction, matches the pattern described for nephrotic syndrome.
(d)
• The typical pattern in established nephrotic syndrome is reduced albumin, reduced alpha1 and gamma-globulins, together with an increase in alpha2-globulin concentration, exactly as seen in Strip II.
• This pattern reflects loss of albumin (and some smaller globulins) through the glomerulus into urine, with a relative or compensatory increase in the larger alpha2-globulin fraction, which is less readily lost.
(e)
• Other abnormal strips should be compared against the other characteristic disease patterns described: cirrhosis of the liver shows reduced albumin and alpha1, with markedly raised gamma-globulins; a chronic inflammatory response shows a rise in gamma-globulins due to increased immunoglobulin synthesis.
• A strip showing reduction in all protein fractions would be considered in the context of severe malnutrition (sometimes due to malabsorption), while a strip showing an increase in all fractions could reflect haemoconcentration.
• Since serum, rather than plasma, is used for this electrophoresis (because fibrinogen would otherwise interfere with the pattern), any additional band in the fibrinogen position should raise suspicion that plasma rather than serum was mistakenly used.
questions.question:
(a) Serum protein electrophoresis strips from four patients are compared with a normal strip (Strip I), and Strip II shows reduced albumin, reduced alpha1 and gamma-globulin fractions with an increase in the alpha2-globulin fraction.
(b) Identify the bands present in the normal strip (Strip I), from left to right.
(c) Identify which pattern (among the strips) would be seen in a patient with nephrotic syndrome.
(d) Explain the changes seen in the electrophoretogram identified as showing nephrotic syndrome.
(e) State how a likely diagnosis would be approached for the other abnormal strips shown.

(a) Describe the plasma creatinine concentration and creatinine clearance test under the headings of source, principle and formula used to predict clearance.
(b) State the clinical setting in which the Cockcroft & Gault formula is applied.
(c) Explain the reasoning behind why plasma creatinine concentration can be misleading despite being inversely related to GFR.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• About 1-2% per day of muscle creatine is converted to creatinine; the amount produced relates to muscle mass, and creatinine is freely filtered at the glomerulus with some tubular excretion.
• Creatinine clearance requires a timed (usually 24-hour) urine collection with a blood sample taken within the period of collection; clearance = (U x V)/P as for any clearance test.
• Creatinine clearance overestimates GFR by 1.1 to 1.2 times the inulin clearance GFR at 80-90 mL/min because of tubular secretion of creatinine (inhibited by cimetidine); the overestimate is greater in renal failure.
• The Cockcroft & Gault formula predicts creatinine clearance from plasma creatinine: CC = k[(140-Age) x weight(kg)] / Creatinine (µmol/L), where k = 1.224 for males and 1.04 for females; modifications are required for children and obese subjects, and it can be modified to use surface area.
(b)
• The Cockcroft & Gault formula (or its stated equivalent CrCl(male) = ([140-age] x weight in kg)/(serum creatinine x 72)) is used in the clinical setting as a simple means of providing a reliable approximation of residual renal function in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD).
(c)
• Plasma creatinine concentration depends on the balance between input and output; production is determined by muscle mass, which is related to age, sex and weight, giving high between-subject variability but low within-subject variability.
• Concentration is inversely related to GFR, so small changes in creatinine within and around the reference limits correspond to large changes in GFR, meaning reference limits can be misleading.
• Formulae only apply in a steady state and are not good for acute renal failure; stable renal function is needed for about 4 days before the formula is reliable.
• Plasma creatinine can increase following protein loads (the "Goulash effect": an 80% rise in creatinine after 300g of cooked beef), so early morning creatinine shows less variability.
• Strenuous exercise may increase creatinine by 14%, and muscle mass is more difficult to predict in oedematous patients, late pregnancy, patients with muscle wasting, and patients with liver disease.
• Drugs inhibiting tubular secretion (such as cimetidine) can raise creatinine concentration without a true change in GFR.
• Because of these confounders, plasma creatinine and formula-derived clearance must be interpreted cautiously rather than as a direct, error-free reflection of GFR.

questions.question:
(a) A 6-week-old infant with suspected cystic fibrosis has a fecal elastase-1 level of 120 microgram/g.
(b) Identify the significance of this result.
(c) State the principle underlying the fecal elastase-1 test.
(d) State the materials/method used to determine fecal elastase-1.
(e) State the interpretation and the action that follows from this result.
questions.answerText:
(b)
• A fecal elastase-1 of 120 microgram/g in this 6-week-old infant is below the cut-off of <200 microgram/g given after 4 weeks of age, which is indicative of pancreatic insufficiency.
• This low result provides supporting evidence for a diagnosis of cystic fibrosis, since in children with cystic fibrosis the test discriminates between those with and without pancreatic insufficiency.
(c)
• Pancreatic elastase-1 is a pancreatic-specific protease present in pancreatic juice, not degraded during passage through the gut, and present in feces at five- to six-fold higher concentration than in pancreatic juice.
(d)
• It is determined by ELISA using two monoclonal antibodies specific to the human enzyme; pancreatic enzyme supplements do not interfere with the test.
(e)
• Fecal elastase-1 is stated to be most suitable to confirm pancreatic insufficiency in screened cystic fibrosis infants over the age of 2 weeks, so testing at 6 weeks of age is within the appropriate window.
• Both fecal chymotrypsin and elastase have shown 100% sensitivity for detecting pancreatic insufficiency in cystic fibrosis in children, with elastase showing more sensitivity, supporting confidence in this low result.
• The action that follows is to treat this as supporting evidence for pancreatic insufficiency and cystic fibrosis, appropriate for further clinical and genetic confirmation, since fecal elastase-1 remains the test of choice as a non-invasive test for pancreatic insufficiency from the perspective of both diagnostic accuracy and patient convenience.

questions.question:
(a) A 65 kg male patient aged 60 years has a serum creatinine of 120 micromol/L, and his estimated creatinine clearance is required using the Cockcroft & Gault formula.
(b) Identify the formula/test appropriate for this request.
(c) State the principle underlying this formula.
(d) State the materials/data required to perform the calculation.
(e) List the sources of error/limitations of using this formula in this patient.
questions.answerText:
(b)
• The appropriate test is estimation of creatinine clearance (eGFR) using the Cockcroft & Gault formula: CC = k[(140-Age) x weight (kg)]/Creatinine (micromol/L), with k = 1.224 for males.
(c)
• The principle is that creatinine clearance can be predicted from plasma creatinine, since plasma creatinine is derived from muscle mass, which is related to body mass, age and sex.
(d)
• The materials/data required are the patient's age, weight (kg), sex (to select k = 1.224 for males or 1.04 for females) and serum creatinine concentration (micromol/L).
• Applying the formula: CC = 1.224 x [(140-60) x 65]/120 = 1.224 x (80 x 65)/120 = 1.224 x 5200/120 = 1.224 x 43.33 ≈ 53 mL/min (using the stated formula and the patient's given values).
(e)
• Formulae only apply in a steady state and are not good for acute renal failure; stable renal function is needed for about 4 days before the formula is reliable.
• Plasma creatinine can increase following protein loads (the "Goulash effect": an 80% rise after 300g of cooked beef), so early morning creatinine, with less variability, should ideally be used.
• Strenuous exercise may increase creatinine by 14%, and modifications are required for children and obese subjects; muscle mass is also harder to predict in oedematous patients, late pregnancy, muscle wasting or liver disease.
• Drugs inhibiting tubular secretion (such as cimetidine) can raise creatinine concentration without a true change in GFR, and creatinine clearance itself overestimates GFR (1.1-1.2x inulin clearance at GFR 80-90 mL/min) due to tubular secretion of creatinine.

(a)
• Clearance of a substance is defined as the volume of plasma from which that substance is removed by glomerular filtration during its passage through the kidney, i.e. the determination of the volume of plasma cleared of the substance in unit time.
• Clearance = (U x V)/P, where U is the urinary concentration of substance x, V is the rate of urine formation (mL/min) and P is the plasma concentration of substance x; units are volume/unit time (mL/min).
• For clearance to equal GFR, the substance must be freely filtered by the glomerulus, have the glomerulus as its sole route of excretion (no tubular secretion or reabsorption), and be non-toxic and easily measurable.
• Properties compared for urea, creatinine, inulin and 99mTc-DTPA show that inulin and 99mTc-DTPA are not protein bound, freely filtered, have no secretion or reabsorption and no constant endogenous production, but only urea and creatinine are easily assayed.
(b)
• Inulin clearance accurately measures GFR, as it is neither secreted nor absorbed by the renal tubules, and is the gold standard, but it is not routinely done in patients because it is a complex procedure requiring a bolus dose followed by constant infusion and timed urine collections.
• In the clinical setting, estimated GFR (eGFR), calculated from the serum creatinine value, is more commonly used, including via the Cockcroft-Gault formula, and is used to determine the stage of chronic kidney disease.
• Isotopic GFR (99mTc-DTPA, 51Cr-EDTA) is the most accurate measurement especially at low levels of renal function, and is used for monitoring renal function over time or in chronic renal failure patients approaching dialysis, tested every two to five years because of cost and inconvenience.
(c)
• Acute renal failure is classified by cause into pre-renal (reduced perfusion), intrinsic renal (vascular, inflammation, infiltration, toxicity) and post-renal (obstruction).
• Pre-renal versus intrinsic ARF can be distinguished by urea and creatinine results: a disproportionate rise in urea suggests pre-renal, while urea and creatinine tending to rise together suggests renal; protein in urine is uncommon in pre-renal but present on dipstick testing in renal causes.
• Pre-renal ARF (functioning tubules) is further supported by urine Na+ <20 mmol/L, urine/plasma osmolality ratio >1.5, and urine/plasma urea ratio >10, compared with urine Na+ >40, ratio <1.1 and ratio <5 in renal causes.
• Metabolic features of acute renal failure include retention of urea and creatinine, Na and water, potassium (with hyperkalaemia) and acid (with metabolic acidosis).
• This classification (pre-renal, intrinsic renal, post-renal) and its supporting tests allow the cause of an abnormal GFR/renal function result to be localised before management decisions are made.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the clearance test for measuring glomerular filtration rate (GFR) under the headings of principle, formula and properties an ideal marker substance must have.
(b) State the setting in which inulin clearance versus estimated GFR (eGFR) is used in practice.
(c) Explain the classification of the causes of an abnormal GFR result into the categories used for acute renal failure.

(a) Describe the classification of hyponatraemia into pseudohyponatraemia, factitious hyponatraemia and true hyponatraemia.
(b) State how each type is recognised or applied in the interpretation of a low serum sodium result.
(c) Explain why failure to recognise pseudohyponatraemia or factitious hyponatraemia would lead to an inaccurate diagnosis of true sodium depletion.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Hyponatraemia is defined as plasma Na+ less than 120 mmol/L.
• Pseudohyponatraemia is associated with hyperlipidaemia, in which serum or plasma contains significant amounts of non-aqueous components such as triglycerides, proteins or other paraproteins, giving a falsely low estimate of serum or plasma sodium.
• Factitious hyponatraemia due to hyperglycaemia occurs because every 100 mg/dL rise in serum or plasma glucose produces a decrease of approximately 3 mmol/L of Na+; diagnosis is made by combined hyponatraemia and hyperglycaemia together with normal or elevated osmolality.
• Artefactual hyponatraemia occurs when a blood sample is collected from a site proximal to the administration of intravenous fluid (IVF).
(b)
• Pseudohyponatraemia is recognised by the laboratory providing a falsely low estimate of serum or plasma sodium in the presence of hyperlipidaemia.
• Factitious (hyperglycaemic) hyponatraemia is recognised by finding hyponatraemia together with hyperglycaemia and a normal or elevated calculated osmolality, rather than a low osmolality.
• Artefactual hyponatraemia is recognised from the clinical history of sample collection proximal to an IV infusion site.
• True hyponatraemia with decreased total body Na+ has causes such as GIT losses (vomiting, diarrhoea), skin losses (burns, dermatitis), internal losses (paralytic ileus, peritoneal fluid loss), renal loss of Na+, diuretics, renal tubular acidosis, and mineralocorticoid deficiency.
(c)
• If pseudohyponatraemia is not recognised, a clinician might wrongly treat the patient for true sodium depletion when the true extracellular fluid sodium and osmolality are normal.
• If factitious hyponatraemia due to hyperglycaemia is not recognised, correcting the sodium value for the glucose-induced dilutional effect would be missed, again leading to inappropriate assessment of total body sodium.
• Because true hyponatraemia with normal or near-normal total body Na+ (as in SIADH, chronic renal failure, or glucocorticoid deficiency) is managed differently from hyponatraemia due to true Na+ loss, distinguishing categories is essential.
• An artefactual result from sampling near an IV infusion site would similarly lead to unnecessary investigation or treatment if not identified and corrected by resampling.

questions.question: Tracheoesophageal fistulas are components of which association?
questions.explanation: Tracheoesophageal fistulas are components of the VACTERL association (Vertebral anomalies, Anal atresia, Cardiac defects, Tracheoesophageal fistula, Esophageal atresia, Renal anomalies, and Limb defects). This is a collection of defects of unknown causation that tend to occur together.

questions.question: Ehlers-Danlos syndrome type IV is specifically caused by a deficiency of which collagen type, leading to rupture of arteries and intestines?
options: Type III collagen (encoded by COL3A1 gene)
Type I collagen (most abundant fibrillar collagen)
questions.explanation: Ehlers-Danlos syndrome vascular type (EDS-IV) results from autosomal dominant mutations in COL3A1, which encodes type III procollagen — the main collagen of reticular fibers in arterial walls and intestines. Abnormal type III collagen makes these structures fragile and prone to spontaneous rupture, a life-threatening complication. Clinically: thin translucent skin with visible veins, easy bruising, hypermobile fingers, and high risk for arterial dissection.

questions.question: The inferior colliculus is associated with which sensory system?
questions.explanation: The inferior colliculus, located in the tectum of the lower midbrain, is part of the auditory pathway. It receives input from the lateral lemniscus and projects to the medial geniculate body of the thalamus, which then projects to the auditory cortex.

questions.question: A skin biopsy from a patient with bullous pemphigoid shows autoantibodies targeting proteins in the basement membrane at the dermoepidermal junction. The target antigens are in which structure?
questions.explanation: Bullous pemphigoid autoantibodies target BP180 hemidesmosomal protein and BP230 in the basement membrane zone at the dermoepidermal junction, causing subepidermal blistering where the entire epidermis detaches from the dermis. This contrasts with pemphigus vulgaris where antibodies target desmoglein-3 between keratinocytes causing intraepidermal blistering. Understanding the target antigen location predicts the blister level and guides diagnosis.
options: Desmosomes linking adjacent keratinocytes in the epidermis
The cornified layer of the epidermis
Hemidesmosomes and basement membrane lamina at the dermal-epidermal junction
Fibroblasts synthesizing collagen in the dermis

questions.question: The pronephros is typically represented by how many solid cell groups?
questions.explanation: The pronephros is represented by 7-10 solid cell groups in the cervical region at the beginning of the fourth week. These form vestigial excretory units called nephrotomes. By the end of the fourth week, all indications of the pronephric system have disappeared.

The spinal cord typically ends at the L1-L2 vertebral level in adults (at the conus medullaris), though this varies individually from T12 to L3. During fetal development, the cord extends the full length of the vertebral canal, but differential growth of the vertebral column causes the cord to \"ascend\" relatively. The subarachnoid space continues to S2, creating the lumbar cistern containing the cauda equina, which provides a safe location for lumbar puncture below the cord termination.
questions.question: At what spinal level does the spinal cord typically end in adults?

questions.explanation: Granule cells in the cerebellar cortex use glutamate as their excitatory neurotransmitter, consistent with their role in relaying mossy fiber input to Purkinje cells. These small neurons (5-8 μm in diameter) are the most numerous neurons in the brain. Their unmyelinated axons ascend to the molecular layer where they bifurcate to form parallel fibers that run perpendicular to Purkinje cell dendritic trees, creating numerous synaptic contacts.
questions.question: Which neurotransmitter is utilized by granule cells in the cerebellar cortex?
The supplementary motor area is located on which brain surface?
questions.explanation: The supplementary motor area is located on the medial surface of the frontal lobe, anterior to the medial extension of the primary motor cortex (area 4). It corresponds to Brodmann areas 6 and 8 on the medial surface. This area is crucial for planning and sequencing complex motor acts, particularly bilateral and sequential movements. Lesions cause difficulty with voluntary movement initiation and sequential motor tasks, though not frank paralysis.

Fibers from cerebral cortex through pons to spinal cord pass through the marginal layer over basal plate. This marginal layer enlarges to accommodate these fibers forming the crus cerebri. The cerebral peduncles contain descending motor pathways.
questions.question: The crus cerebri is formed by enlargement of which layer?
Sinusoidal (discontinuous) capillaries are found in which organs where maximum exchange of cells and large molecules with blood is required?
questions.explanation: Sinusoidal capillaries (sinusoids) have large, tortuous lumens, fenestrated endothelium without diaphragms, large gaps between cells, and a discontinuous or absent basement membrane. This structure permits passage of blood cells, large proteins, and even entire cells between blood and tissue. They are found in the liver (hepatic sinusoids), spleen (splenic sinusoids), and bone marrow, all sites of cell production or destruction.

questions.question: Occlusion of which artery typically causes lateral medullary syndrome?
questions.explanation: The posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) supplies the lateral medulla, and its occlusion causes lateral medullary syndrome (Wallenberg syndrome). Clinical features include ipsilateral facial pain/temperature loss, Horner's syndrome, ataxia, dysphagia, dysphonia, and contralateral body pain/temperature loss. The syndrome results from damage to the spinal trigeminal nucleus/tract, sympathetic fibers, inferior cerebellar peduncle, nucleus ambiguus, and spinothalamic tract. Vertigo and nystagmus occur due to vestibular nucleus involvement.

Cleft lip results from failure of fusion between the medial nasal prominence and the maxillary prominence on one or both sides. This failure of fusion may be unilateral or bilateral. Cleft lip may occur alone or in combination with cleft palate.
questions.question: Cleft lip results from failure of fusion between which structures?
The olfactory epithelium is derived from which embryonic structure?
questions.explanation: The stratified placodal base of the invaginating olfactory pits forms the olfactory epithelium containing neurosensory cells. The lateral walls around the pits become the surface ectodermal covering of nasal cavities. Placodal cells differentiate into neurosensory cells that give rise to olfactory nerve fibers.

The optic chiasm lies directly above the anterior communicating artery and is at risk during aneurysm rupture or surgical repair. Hemorrhage can cause visual field defects, most commonly bitemporal hemianopia from chiasmal compression. The anterior communicating artery aneurysms may also affect the frontal lobes, potentially causing cognitive and personality changes. During surgical clipping, careful preservation of small perforating vessels supplying the optic chiasm, hypothalamus, and basal forebrain is essential to prevent visual and cognitive complications.
questions.question: Which structure is at risk during anterior communicating artery aneurysm rupture?
Somites give rise to which of the following structures?
questions.explanation: Somites give rise to most of the axial skeleton including bones of the cranium, vertebral column, ribs, and sternum. They are formed by differentiation of paraxial mesoderm and appear as paired structures on each side of the neural tube. The first pair forms around day 20 of development.

questions.question: Endochondral ossification differs from intramembranous ossification in which of the following fundamental ways?
questions.explanation: Endochondral ossification involves formation of a cartilage template (hyaline cartilage) by mesenchymal condensation, followed by cartilage growth, calcification, degradation, and replacement by bone matrix deposited by osteoblasts brought in with invading blood vessels. Long bones (femur, tibia, humerus), ribs, and vertebrae form by endochondral ossification, in contrast to the membranous (direct) ossification of skull flat bones.
options: It begins with mesenchymal condensation like intramembranous ossification
Requires formation then replacement of a pre-existing cartilage model by bone matrix
It does not involve osteoblasts in bone formation
It only forms flat bones of the skull and jaw
It does not require blood vessel invasion of the ossification center

questions.question: The extreme capsule is located between which structures?
questions.explanation: The extreme capsule is a thin layer of white matter located between the insula medially and the claustrum laterally. It contains association fibers connecting different cortical regions, particularly frontal and temporal areas. The extreme capsule, along with the external capsule and internal capsule, comprises the white matter system surrounding the basal ganglia. Lateral to the claustrum lies the external capsule, separating the claustrum from the putamen. These capsular systems contain various association and projection fibers.

The parietal pleura develops from somatic mesoderm covering the internal surface of the body wall. The visceral pleura develops from splanchnic mesoderm surrounding the developing lungs. The pleural cavity between these layers is initially part of the intraembryonic coelom, which is partitioned during development.
questions.question: The parietal pleura develops from:

questions.explanation: Anal stenosis is characterized by narrowing of the anus and anal canal, which are in the normal position but constricted. This may result from incomplete recanalization after the solid epithelial stage. Mild stenosis may only become apparent when the infant begins passing formed stools. Surgical dilation or anoplasty may be required.
questions.question: Anal stenosis results from:
Membrane phospholipids in one leaflet can flip to the other leaflet of the bilayer by a process requiring which of the following?
questions.explanation: Transleaflet flip-flop of phospholipids is thermodynamically unfavorable because the polar headgroup must pass through the hydrophobic core. Specific enzymes catalyze this movement: flippases (P4-ATPases) move phosphatidylserine from outer to inner leaflet, floppases move lipids outward, and scramblases non-selectively equilibrate both leaflets. The asymmetric distribution of phospholipids (PS on inner leaflet) is physiologically important, e.g., PS exposure on apoptotic cells signals for phagocytosis.
options: Specific enzymes that catalyze phospholipid transleaflet movement
Spontaneous random thermal diffusion without any enzyme
Lysosomal hydrolysis of the phospholipid headgroup

questions.explanation: The pronephric duct persists after pronephric degeneration and becomes the mesonephric (Wolffian) duct. This duct is initially used by the mesonephros for urine drainage and later gives rise to the ureteric bud (which forms the collecting system of the kidney). In males, the mesonephric duct persists as the ductus deferens and related structures.
questions.question: The pronephric duct gives rise to:

questions.explanation: As a result of brain growth and cephalic folding of the embryo, the buccopharyngeal membrane is pulled forward while the heart and pericardial cavity move first to the cervical region and finally to the thorax. This repositioning is essential for establishing the normal anatomical relationships of the heart.
questions.question: As a result of cephalic folding, the heart moves from the cervical region to which final location?

options: Lymphatic capillaries have a thicker basement membrane
Lymphatic capillaries are lined by fenestrated endothelium
Lymphatic capillaries contain red blood cells
Lymphatic capillaries closed at one end
Lymphatic capillaries are surrounded by smooth muscle
questions.explanation: Lymphatic capillaries begin as closed-ended tubes in the tissue spaces. Their endothelial cells have overlapping (valve-like) edges and are anchored to surrounding connective tissue by anchoring filaments. These features allow tissue fluid to enter one-way but not re-enter the interstitium. Lymphatic capillaries have a thin or absent basement membrane and no pericytes, distinguishing them from blood capillaries.
questions.question: Lymphatic capillaries differ from blood capillaries in which important structural feature?

options: Tall columnar cells with prominent brush borders
Extremely thin walls of simple squamous epithelium
Cells with abundant apical secretory granules
questions.explanation: The thin limbs of the loop of Henle are lined by extremely thin, flat simple squamous (or very low cuboidal) cells that histologically resemble capillary endothelium. This can make them difficult to distinguish from capillaries in tissue sections — both are identified by their very thin wall and compressed lumen. The thin limb cells lack organelles for active transport (no brush border, sparse mitochondria), consistent with their role as passive exchange surfaces for water and solutes.
questions.question: In the loop of Henle, the thin descending and thin ascending limbs are histologically identified by their:

questions.explanation: The median eminence lacks a blood-brain barrier, allowing hypothalamic releasing and inhibiting hormones to enter the hypophyseal portal system and reach the anterior pituitary. This region is located on the floor of the third ventricle just behind the infundibulum and contains neurosecretory terminals that release hormones directly into fenestrated capillaries. This anatomical arrangement enables the hypothalamus to control anterior pituitary hormone secretion through hormonal rather than direct neural connections.
questions.question: The median eminence of the hypothalamus is significant because it lacks what feature?

questions.explanation: Genomic imprinting is an epigenetic phenomenon where certain genes are expressed in a parent-of-origin-specific manner. Some genes are only expressed from the maternal allele, others only from the paternal allele. Abnormalities in imprinting can cause disorders like Prader-Willi and Angelman syndromes.
questions.question: Genomic imprinting refers to which phenomenon?
On a histological slide, three distinct smooth muscle sublayers are seen in the muscularis of one GIT region. This finding is characteristic of which region?
questions.explanation: The stomach uniquely possesses three smooth muscle sublayers: inner oblique, middle circular, and outer longitudinal. This arrangement allows the mechanical churning and mixing of food necessary for gastric digestion. All other GIT regions have only two layers (inner circular and outer longitudinal) in the muscularis externa.

questions.question: The entorhinal cortex serves as a gateway between which two regions?
questions.explanation: The entorhinal cortex serves as a gateway between the neocortex and the hippocampus, receiving convergent input from limbic, sensory-specific, and multimodal association cortices. Information from diverse cortical areas converges on the entorhinal area, which then projects to the hippocampus via the perforant pathway. This bidirectional communication allows the hippocampus to receive processed sensory and cognitive information and return processed memories to the neocortex for long-term storage.

questions.question: Which of the following descriptions most accurately characterizes the structure of the cytoplasm?
options: A rigid crystalline compartment supporting all organelles
A gel-like aqueous medium containing organelles and cytoskeletal elements
An empty fluid space between the nucleus and cell membrane
A dense granular material composed exclusively of ribosomes
A lipid-rich compartment surrounding the nucleus only
questions.explanation: The cytoplasm is the gel-like aqueous medium (cytosol) filling the space between the nucleus and cell membrane, containing suspended organelles, the cytoskeleton, inclusions, and dissolved metabolites, ions, and proteins. The cytosol (~70% water) forms the environment in which most metabolic reactions occur. It is not empty but rather a highly organized and crowded molecular space.

questions.question: The neuroepithelial cells lining the neural tube are of which type?
questions.explanation: The neuroepithelial cells lining the neural tube are of simple columnar type initially. These cells undergo increased cellular proliferation after tube closure. They give rise to neuroblasts and eventually all neural and glial cells.

questions.question: The heart wall has three layers. Which is the middle and thickest layer, composed of cardiac muscle, and is responsible for pumping function?
questions.explanation: The myocardium is the middle layer of the heart wall, composed of cardiac muscle cells (cardiomyocytes) organized into complex networks. It is the thickest layer, especially in the left ventricle, and is responsible for the contractile force that pumps blood. The endocardium lines the cardiac chambers internally, and the epicardium (visceral pericardium) covers the external surface.

questions.question: A section through the pharyngeal wall shows a layer of fibrous connective tissue external to the muscular layer. This is the:
questions.explanation: The pharyngeal wall is covered externally by the buccopharyngeal fascia (the pharyngobasilar fascia in the upper pharynx), a tough fibrous connective tissue layer that lies external to the pharyngeal constrictor muscles. Because the pharynx lacks a serosa, this fibrous layer provides structural integrity and attachment to surrounding structures. This distinguishes the pharynx from intraperitoneal GIT segments that are covered by serosa.

The paramedian pontine reticular formation (PPRF) is most essential for maintenance of equilibrium and coordination of eye movements. The paramedian neurons are connected to the vestibular nuclei. The reticular formation overall is concerned with somatic motor functions via the reticulospinal tract.
questions.question: The paramedian pontine reticular formation (PPRF) is essential for which function?
At which anatomical landmark do the right and left transverse sinuses typically originate?
questions.explanation: The transverse sinuses drain from the confluence of sinuses at the internal occipital protuberance, where multiple venous channels meet. The right transverse sinus is typically a continuation of the superior sagittal sinus, while the left continues from the straight sinus. These large sinuses pass laterally along the margin of the tentorium cerebelli before turning downward and medially to become the sigmoid sinus and eventually drain into the internal jugular vein.

questions.question: The greater omentum extends from the:
questions.explanation: The greater omentum extends from the greater curvature of the stomach and hangs inferiorly like an apron over the intestines. It is derived from the dorsal mesogastrium and fuses with the transverse mesocolon. The greater omentum contains fat and lymphoid tissue and can wall off infections or inflammation in the abdominal cavity.

questions.question: Klinefelter syndrome is characterized by which karyotype?
questions.explanation: Klinefelter syndrome is characterized by a 47,XXY karyotype (or variants with additional X chromosomes). Affected individuals are phenotypically male with tall stature, small testes, gynecomastia, reduced fertility or infertility, and sometimes learning difficulties. This results from nondisjunction of sex chromosomes.

options: Stratified squamous non-keratinized epithelium in the lateral oropharynx
Pseudostratified ciliated epithelium with goblet cells
Simple columnar epithelium with goblet cells
Transitional urothelial epithelium of the bladder
questions.explanation: Palatine tonsils are located in the lateral walls of the oropharynx and are covered by stratified squamous non-keratinized epithelium continuous with the oral cavity lining. Their deep crypts lined by this epithelium increase surface area for antigen sampling. Pharyngeal tonsils or adenoids are covered by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium reflecting their nasopharyngeal location. This epithelial difference is histologically diagnostic between the two tonsil types.
questions.question: The tonsils of Waldeyer's ring encircle the entrances to the respiratory and digestive tracts. The palatine tonsils are covered by which epithelium?
Glomerular filtration rate in newborns is approximately what fraction of adult values?
questions.explanation: Glomerular filtration rate (GFR) in term newborns is approximately 1/3 of adult values when corrected for body surface area. GFR increases rapidly during the first two weeks, doubles by 2-3 months, and reaches adult values (per unit surface area) by 1-2 years. The low neonatal GFR reflects immature nephrons, low renal blood flow, and high renal vascular resistance. This affects drug dosing and fluid management in neonates.
