questions.explanation: The corpus callosum develops from the lamina terminalis, which thickens to form commissural pathways connecting the cerebral hemispheres. Development proceeds from anterior to posterior, with the genu and body forming before the splenium. The anterior commissure and hippocampal commissure also develop from the lamina terminalis. Developmental abnormalities can cause partial or complete agenesis of the corpus callosum, sometimes compensated by enlargement of the anterior commissure. The lamina terminalis represents the rostral-most end of the neural tube.

questions.question: The inferior olivary complex is a characteristic feature of which medullary level?
questions.explanation: The inferior olivary complex (principal, medial accessory, and dorsal accessory olivary nuclei) is a characteristic feature of the mid-medulla level. The olive appears as a prominent landmark on the ventral surface of the medulla. It projects to the cerebellum via climbing fibers.

questions.question: The classic signs of inflammation described by Celsus include all of the following EXCEPT which of the following?
questions.explanation: The cardinal signs of inflammation described by Celsus (1st century CE) are: redness (rubor), heat (calor), swelling (tumor), and pain (dolor), to which Galen later added disturbed function (functio laesa). Pallor (pallidus — whiteness) is notably absent; in fact inflammation typically causes redness, the opposite of pallor. The five cardinal signs remain the clinical hallmark of acute inflammation.

questions.question: The PAS (Periodic Acid-Schiff) reaction stains reticular fibers positively for which of the following reasons?
options: High lipid content in their core protein
questions.explanation: PAS positivity of reticular fibers reflects their high content of carbohydrate side chains (sugar chains) associated with type III collagen and associated glycoproteins. The periodic acid oxidizes adjacent hydroxyl groups in sugars, generating aldehydes that react with Schiff reagent to produce magenta color. This carbohydrate-linked reactivity also underlies argyrophilia in silver staining.
Wallerian degeneration occurs to the distal part of a cut axon. Nutrients for axonal integrity come from the cell body. The distal segment degenerates without this support.
questions.question: Wallerian degeneration occurs in which part of a cut axon?
Principal neurons are divided into which types?
questions.explanation: Principal neurons divide into projection/tract neurons (forming tracts) and root neurons (forming spinal nerve roots). Interneurons like Renshaw cells provide local circuits. This organization allows complex spinal functions.

questions.question: The definitive urinary bladder develops from which embryonic structure?
questions.explanation: The definitive urinary bladder develops from the urogenital sinus (part of the cloaca). The allantois contributes to formation of the urachus (median umbilical ligament). The trigone of the bladder is derived from incorporated portions of the mesonephric ducts.

questions.question: Megacystis (enlarged bladder) may result from:
questions.explanation: Megacystis (enlarged bladder) commonly results from posterior urethral valves in males, which cause bladder outlet obstruction. The increased pressure leads to bladder wall hypertrophy and trabeculation. Prolonged obstruction can cause bilateral hydronephrosis and renal damage. Diagnosis is often made prenatally by ultrasound. Endoscopic valve ablation is the treatment.

questions.question: The dentate nucleus projects primarily to which structure?
questions.explanation: The dentate nucleus projects primarily to the contralateral red nucleus and ventrolateral thalamus via the superior cerebellar peduncle, which decussates in the midbrain. From the thalamus, fibers reach the motor and premotor cortices, completing the cerebrocerebellar loop. The dentate receives input from lateral cerebellar hemispheres (neocerebellum) and is involved in planning and timing of movements. Dentate nucleus lesions cause intention tremor, dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia, and impaired motor learning.

questions.question: Primary villi are formed by which structure growing into the syncytiotrophoblast?
questions.explanation: On day 13, cytotrophoblast grows outward into the syncytiotrophoblast in a finger-like manner, forming primary villi. These villi are the first stage in placental villous development. They will later become secondary villi (with mesenchymal core) and tertiary villi (with blood vessels).

Parietal cells produce both HCl and intrinsic factor. Intrinsic factor is essential for the absorption of vitamin B12 (cobalamin) in the terminal ileum. Destruction of parietal cells leads to intrinsic factor deficiency, preventing B12 absorption and causing megaloblastic anemia — termed pernicious anemia. This is one of the most important clinical correlates of gastric histology.
questions.question: A patient with pernicious anemia is found to have autoantibodies destroying parietal cells. Which essential substance becomes deficient as a direct consequence?
Lateral reticulospinal tract originates from which structure?
questions.explanation: Lateral reticulospinal tract originates from medullary reticular system. Fibers run in lateral white column facilitating anterior horn cells. It helps control posture and movement.

The terminal sac period extends from 26 weeks to birth, during which terminal sacs (primitive alveoli) form and capillaries establish close contact with the epithelium. The epithelium thins from cuboidal to squamous, creating the blood-air barrier. Surfactant production by type II pneumocytes begins during this period.
questions.question: The terminal sac period of lung development extends from:

questions.explanation: The central nervous system (brain and spinal cord) is concerned with integration, analysis and response to information. The peripheral nervous system receives sensory information and delivers responses. Together they form the complete nervous system.
questions.question: The central nervous system is concerned with which functions?

questions.explanation: Layer V (internal pyramidal layer) contains medium to large pyramidal cells, including the giant pyramidal cells of Betz that are characteristic of the primary motor cortex. These large neurons send their axons down the corticospinal tract to control voluntary movement. The internal band of Baillarger, a horizontal layer of nerve fibers, is also found in this layer, contributing to intracortical connectivity.
questions.question: In the six-layered neocortex, which layer contains the giant pyramidal cells of Betz?

questions.explanation: Neuronal cell bodies lack centrioles, consistent with the neurons' permanent post-mitotic state (amitotic nature). Centrioles are essential for organizing the mitotic spindle during cell division; since neurons do not divide, centrioles are dispensable and absent. All other listed organelles are present and functional in neuronal cell bodies.
questions.question: The cell body (soma) of a neuron contains most organelles typical of other cells but specifically lacks which of the following?
Hemiballismus typically results from lesions of which structure?
questions.explanation: Hemiballismus (violent, involuntary flinging movements of the contralateral limbs) typically results from lesions of the subthalamic nucleus (STN), most commonly from small strokes. STN lesions reduce excitation of GPi, decreasing GPi inhibition of the thalamus (similar to excessive direct pathway activity). This causes excessive, uncontrolled movements. Treatment may include dopamine blockers or GABAergic drugs to increase inhibition. Deep brain stimulation of STN for Parkinson's disease must be carefully controlled to avoid inducing hemiballismus.

The CNS is an ectodermal derivative that begins differentiation in the 3rd intrauterine week. The slipper-shaped neural plate thickens rostral to the primitive node at this time. This marks the beginning of neurulation and the formation of the nervous system.
questions.question: The neural plate begins to differentiate in humans during which intrauterine week?
Which of the following correctly describes the components of whole blood and their approximate proportions?
options: Equal parts plasma, leukocytes, and erythrocytes
questions.explanation: Blood consists of approximately 55% plasma which is 90% water with proteins including albumin immunoglobulins and clotting factors plus electrolytes and solutes, and 45% formed elements by volume known as the hematocrit. The formed elements comprise erythrocytes accounting for approximately 99% of cells, leukocytes of five types, and platelets which are cell fragments. This ratio is maintained by continuous hematopoiesis in bone marrow.

questions.question: Rexez's laminae number how many zones?
questions.explanation: Rexed found that spinal cord cell clusters are arranged into 10 zones or laminae (I-X). This replaced the older nuclear terminology. Each lamina has specific functions and connections.

questions.question: When a cell is described as 'excitable' or 'irritable' in the context of membrane physiology, this specifically means which of the following?
questions.explanation: Excitable cells (neurons, muscle cells, some gland cells) are capable of responding to stimuli by rapidly reversing their membrane potential (action potential/depolarization). All cells maintain an electrical potential across their membrane, but only excitable cells can rapidly and significantly change this potential to propagate a signal. This property is the basis of nerve impulse transmission and muscle contraction.
options: It can rapidly change its membrane electrical potential in response to stimuli
It is easily damaged by mechanical force
It secretes large quantities of hormones in response to signals
It undergoes rapid division when stimulated
It migrates toward the source of a chemical signal

questions.question: The tail of the caudate nucleus is connected to which structure?
questions.explanation: The tail of the caudate nucleus curves inferiorly following the lateral ventricle and terminates by merging with the amygdala in the temporal lobe. This anatomical relationship reflects the C-shaped development of the caudate following the lateral ventricle. The caudate has a large head bulging into the anterior horn, a body along the lateral ventricle body, and a tail extending into the temporal lobe. Striatopallidal fibers (cell bridges) connect the caudate and putamen through the internal capsule, confirming their unity as the striatum.

questions.question: Transitional epithelium (urothelium) of the bladder has umbrella cells on its luminal surface. These cells are characterized by which unique structural feature adapting them to stretch?
questions.explanation: Umbrella cells (superficial cells) of the urothelium have rigid, thickened apical plaques (asymmetric unit membranes composed of uroplakins — specific barrier proteins) and cytoplasmic fusiform vesicles. When the bladder is empty, excess membrane is stored as invaginated vesicles. During bladder filling, the vesicles fuse with the plasma membrane, adding membrane to accommodate distension. Uroplakins also create the highly effective barrier preventing urine from diffusing back into the tissue.
options: Large surface area with asymmetric unit membranes (plaques)
Tight junctions only, without special membrane features

questions.question: Caudal regression syndrome affects which body systems?
questions.explanation: Caudal regression syndrome (sacral agenesis) affects the lower limbs and caudal structures including lumbosacral spine, lower limbs, urogenital system, and hindgut. Severity ranges from minor sacral hypoplasia to complete absence of sacral and lumbar vertebrae with fused lower limbs (sirenomelia). The syndrome is associated with maternal diabetes and has high mortality.

questions.question: Erythropoietin (EPO) is produced primarily by which kidney cell type in response to hypoxia?
options: Principal cells of the collecting duct
questions.explanation: Erythropoietin is produced predominantly by peritubular interstitial cells (EPO-producing cells, which resemble fibroblasts) in the renal cortex and outer medulla in response to hypoxia via HIF-2α activation. A smaller amount is produced in the liver. Renal failure causes EPO deficiency and normochromic, normocytic anemia. Recombinant EPO is used therapeutically in renal anemia.

questions.question: Crossed renal ectopia is characterized by:
questions.explanation: Crossed renal ectopia is characterized by both kidneys located on the same side of the body, with one kidney having crossed to the opposite side. The kidneys are usually fused. The ureters enter the bladder in their normal positions. This rare anomaly results from abnormal migration during development.

questions.question: Canaliculi in bone serve which of the following critical physiological functions?
options: Allow osteoclasts to migrate between different bone surfaces
Store calcium phosphate reserves for blood calcium regulation
Serve as channels for osteoblast migration during bone remodeling
Provide direct routes for nerve fibers to reach osteocytes
Allow osteocytes to exchange nutrients with blood vessels via gap junctions
questions.explanation: Canaliculi are minute tunnels radiating from each osteocyte lacuna, containing cytoplasmic processes of osteocytes that form gap junctions with adjacent osteocytes. Since metabolites cannot diffuse through calcified matrix, this canalicular network creates a 'bucket brigade' relay system for nutrients, oxygen, hormones, and waste products between blood vessels in Haversian canals and the most distant osteocytes. Osteocytes also sense mechanical strain through canalicular fluid flow.

questions.question: Betz cells are characteristic of which cortical layer?
questions.explanation: Giant pyramidal cells of Betz are characteristic of layer V (internal pyramidal layer) specifically in the primary motor cortex. These are among the largest neurons in the central nervous system, with cell bodies up to 100 μm in diameter. Betz cells send their axons down the corticospinal tract, directly influencing spinal motor neurons. Although Betz cells are a hallmark of the primary motor cortex, they represent only about 3% of corticospinal neurons, with most coming from smaller layer V pyramidal cells.
Interneurons (association or connecting neurons) connect one neuron with another. They are most abundant in the CNS. In reflexes, they connect sensory to motor neurons.
questions.question: Interneurons connect which structures?
The crus cerebri is formed from which embryonic structure?
questions.explanation: The marginal layer of each basal plate in the mesencephalon enlarges and forms the crus cerebri (cerebral peduncles). These crura serve as pathways for nerve fibers descending from the cerebral cortex to lower centers in the pons and spinal cord (corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts).

The lens placode becomes visible at Carnegie stage 13 (approximately 28 days). At this stage, other features include the 4th pair of pharyngeal arches, appearance of upper and lower limb buds, an attenuated tail, and closure of the caudal neuropore. The lens placode is the primordium of the lens of the eye.
questions.question: The lens placode first becomes visible at which Carnegie stage?

questions.explanation: Mature alveoli with well-developed epithelial-endothelial (capillary) contacts develop during the alveolar period, which extends from 8 months of gestation through childhood. The majority of alveoli (5/6ths) form postnatally during the first 10 years. This continued development explains why lung growth continues after birth.
questions.question: Mature alveoli have well-developed epithelial-endothelial contacts during:
How many levels are in the motor system hierarchy?
questions.explanation: Six levels are implicated in movement: motor units, spinal cord, brainstem nuclei, basal ganglia, cerebellum, and motor/association cortex. Commands cascade down through levels. It is a parallel hierarchical system.

options: Replacement of alveoli by fibrous tissue
Collapse of alveoli with no fluid
Widening of alveolar septa with pale
questions.explanation: Pulmonary edema is characterized histologically by widening of the alveolar septa (interstitial edema from fluid accumulation) and flooding of the alveolar spaces with a pale, homogeneous eosinophilic proteinaceous fluid (alveolar edema). In cardiogenic pulmonary edema, hemosiderin-laden macrophages ('heart failure cells') may be present from previous episodes. Severe acute pulmonary edema manifests as intra-alveolar hyaline membranes (as in ARDS).
questions.question: The interstitium of the lung between alveolar septa and bronchioles is normally very thin. Accumulation of edema fluid in this space (pulmonary edema) manifests histologically as:
Carnegie stage 11 corresponds to approximately how many days of development?
questions.explanation: Carnegie stage 11 corresponds to approximately 24 days of development. At this stage, the embryo shows the mandibular (1st) and hyoid (2nd) pharyngeal arches, is slightly curved with head and tail folds, and has a prominent heart. The rostral neuropore is closing at this stage.

options: Aldosterone receptors in the collecting duct
questions.question: The renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) is activated when juxtaglomerular cells secrete renin. Renin acts on which substrate to begin the cascade?
questions.explanation: Renin is a protease enzyme secreted by juxtaglomerular cells that cleaves angiotensinogen — a glycoprotein produced by the liver — to form angiotensin I (a decapeptide). ACE (in pulmonary endothelium) then converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II. Angiotensin II causes vasoconstriction and stimulates aldosterone secretion from the adrenal cortex, increasing sodium reabsorption and blood pressure. ACE inhibitors block this step therapeutically.

Tooth development requires reciprocal inductive interactions between mesenchyme (neural crest-derived) and epithelium (ectodermal). The epithelium induces the mesenchyme to form dental papilla and dental follicle, while the mesenchyme induces the epithelium to form enamel organ. Both tissues are required.
questions.question: Tooth development requires inductive stimuli from which tissue?

questions.explanation: Primary ossification centers appear in the skeleton (skull and long bones) during 9-12 weeks. During this period, there is also rapid growth in body length, decrease in relative head growth compared to earlier stages, and beginning of erythropoiesis by the liver and spleen.
questions.question: During which weeks do primary ossification centers appear in the skeleton?

questions.explanation: The bladder in newborns is located partly in the abdomen, projecting above the pelvic brim. As the pelvis enlarges with growth, the bladder descends to become entirely a pelvic organ by adulthood. This explains why the bladder is more easily palpable abdominally in infants. The peritoneal reflection is also higher in infants.
questions.question: The bladder in newborns is located:
Ventral motor roots form approximately in which week?
questions.explanation: The axons of the basal plate neurons coalesce and exit through the marginal layer to form the ventral motor root about the 4th week. These roots carry motor impulses to skeletal muscles. They combine with dorsal sensory roots to form spinal nerves.

Haustra (singular: haustrum) are created because the three teniae coli are shorter than the total length of the colon. Their tonic contraction gathers the colon wall into pouches between them. Haustra disappear in conditions like ulcerative colitis (lead-pipe colon on imaging) due to loss of normal colonic architecture. They facilitate segmental mixing and slow colonic transit.
questions.question: Haustra are saccular pouches visible on the outer surface of the colon. They are produced by which mechanism?
options: Distension of the colon wall by fecal material
Submucosal lymphoid tissue causing outward protrusion
Hypertrophy of the circular muscle layer

questions.explanation: The septum pellucidum is a thin, translucent membrane separating the anterior horns and bodies of the lateral ventricles in the midline. It consists of two parallel laminae with a potential cavity between them (cavum septum pellucidum, present in fetuses and sometimes persisting in adults). The septum extends from the inferior surface of the corpus callosum to the superior surface of the fornix. It contains septal nuclei that are part of the limbic system and involved in emotional processing.
questions.question: The septum pellucidum separates which structures?

questions.explanation: Volkmann's canals (perforating canals) run perpendicular or oblique to the long axis of bone, connecting adjacent Haversian canals to each other and to the periosteum and marrow cavity. They are the primary route by which blood vessels from the marrow cavity reach the Haversian canals of individual osteons. Unlike Haversian canals, Volkmann's canals are NOT surrounded by concentric lamellae.
options: Volkmann's canals contain larger blood vessels and no nerves
Volkmann's canals run parallel to the long axis of the bone
Volkmann's canals run perpendicular to the long axis of bone
Volkmann's canals are absent in mature bone and present only during development
Volkmann's canals are only found in spongy bone trabeculae
questions.question: Volkmann's canals in compact bone differ from Haversian canals primarily in which of the following ways?
The bile canaliculi between hepatocytes are sealed by which intercellular junctions to prevent bile from leaking into the space of Disse?
questions.explanation: Bile canaliculi are sealed from the perisinusoidal space by tight junctions (zonulae occludentes) between adjacent hepatocytes. This prevents bile — which contains potentially toxic bile salts — from leaking into the space of Disse and entering the bloodstream. Disruption of these tight junctions in cholestasis leads to regurgitation of bile into the hepatic sinusoids, causing jaundice.

questions.question: Ectopic gastric mucosa in Meckel's diverticulum can cause:
questions.explanation: Ectopic gastric mucosa in Meckel's diverticulum can produce acid, leading to peptic ulceration of adjacent ileal mucosa and bleeding. Pancreatic acini may also be present. These heterotopic tissues make Meckel's diverticulum clinically significant despite being a common anatomical variant. The classic presentation is painless rectal bleeding.

A urachal fistula results from complete patency of the urachus, causing urine to leak from the umbilicus. Normally, the urachus obliterates to form the median umbilical ligament. Partial persistence can result in a urachal cyst or sinus. These abnormalities require surgical correction to prevent infection.
questions.question: A urachal fistula results in:
Patent urachus is characterized by:
questions.explanation: Patent urachus is characterized by persistent communication between the bladder and umbilicus, resulting in urine drainage from the umbilicus. This represents complete failure of urachus obliteration. The condition is evident at birth and requires surgical repair to prevent infection and establish normal urinary drainage.

options: Changing the curvature of the cornea through ciliary muscle contraction
Rotating the eyeball to shift the angle of refraction
Adjusting aqueous humor volume in the anterior chamber
Ciliary muscle contraction reduces zonular tension, allowing the lens to round up
Pupil constriction reducing spherical aberration for near objects
questions.question: The lens of the eye achieves accommodation for near vision by which mechanism?
questions.explanation: Accommodation for near vision involves ciliary muscle contraction which relaxes the circular zonular fibers attached to the lens, allowing the elastic lens to recoil into a more spherical shape with greater refractive power to focus near objects on the retina. For far vision, ciliary muscle relaxes causing zonular fibers to tighten and flatten the lens. The lens loses elasticity with age causing presbyopia with reduced near vision accommodation.

The intraparietal sulcus divides the lateral parietal cortex into superior and inferior parietal lobules. The superior parietal lobule (above the sulcus) is involved in spatial processing, visuomotor coordination, and mathematical cognition. The inferior parietal lobule (below the sulcus) includes the supramarginal and angular gyri, involved in language, reading, and multimodal sensory integration. The intraparietal sulcus itself contains areas involved in visually-guided reaching, attention, and numerical processing.
questions.question: The intraparietal sulcus divides the parietal lobe into which lobules?

questions.explanation: The spinal dura mater extends beyond the conus medullaris and covers the filum terminale, blending with the dura at the level of the second sacral vertebra (S2). Beyond this point, the filum terminale continues as the coccygeal ligament attached to the coccyx. The subdural cavity separates the dura from the arachnoid mater and is filled with a thin film of fluid.
questions.question: At what vertebral level does the spinal dura mater covering the filum terminale blend with other structures?

questions.explanation: The overlying marginal layer of the alar plate enlarges with neuroblast waves forming the tectum. This creates the longitudinal elevations that become colliculi. The tectum is dorsal to the cerebral aqueduct.
questions.question: The tectum is formed from which mesencephalic region?

questions.explanation: Cranial nerves contain branchial and special efferent/afferent components unlike spinal nerves. They are irregularly spaced. Some contain only motor or sensory components.
questions.question: Cranial nerves differ from spinal nerves in which way?

questions.explanation: The fusiform gyrus, particularly the fusiform face area (FFA) on the inferior temporal surface, is specialized for face recognition and processing. This region shows preferential activation to faces compared to other visual stimuli. Damage to this area, particularly bilaterally, causes prosopagnosia (face blindness), where patients cannot recognize familiar faces despite normal visual acuity and object recognition. The FFA is part of the ventral visual stream specialized for object identification.
questions.question: Which cortical region is specialized for face recognition?
Lumbar puncture is safest below which vertebral level?
questions.explanation: Lumbar puncture is safest below L2 where only cauda equina nerve roots are present (cord ends at L1 in adults). Epidural anesthesia also utilizes this safe zone. The subarachnoid space extends to S2.

options: Synthesizing albumin for plasma oncotic pressure
Storing vitamin A in lipid droplets which is the function of hepatic stellate cells
Phagocytosing aged erythrocytes and bacteria from portal blood; antigen presentation
questions.question: Kupffer cells in the liver sinusoids are the most numerous tissue macrophages in the body. They perform which primary functions?
questions.explanation: Kupffer cells are liver-resident macrophages lining the hepatic sinusoids representing approximately 80 to 90% of all fixed tissue macrophages in the body. They phagocytose aged RBCs contributing to heme and bilirubin metabolism, bacteria from portal blood as first defense against gut-derived pathogens, endotoxin or LPS, immune complexes, and cellular debris. They are part of the MPS and contribute to liver inflammation in alcoholic hepatitis and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease.

Cells of the nervous system are derived from three different origins. Neuroepithelium gives rise to neurons, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, and ependymal cells. Neural crest cells give rise to Schwann cells. Mesoderm gives rise to microglia, the immune cells of the central nervous system.
questions.question: Microglia cells in the nervous system are derived from which source?

questions.explanation: The primary visual cortex (Brodmann area 17) is located along the calcarine sulcus on the medial surface of the occipital lobe, extending to the occipital pole. This striate cortex receives direct input from the lateral geniculate nucleus via the optic radiations. The visual association areas (Brodmann areas 18 and 19) surround the primary visual cortex and are involved in higher-order visual processing and interpretation.
questions.question: The primary visual cortex is located along which sulcus on the medial surface of the occipital lobe?

questions.explanation: The Circle of Willis is an anastomotic channel between the internal carotid and vertebrobasilar arterial systems located around the infundibulum of the pituitary and optic chiasma at the brain base. This collateral circulation can provide alternative blood flow pathways when major arteries become occluded. The circle is formed by the anterior communicating artery, anterior cerebral arteries, internal carotid arteries, posterior communicating arteries, and posterior cerebral arteries.
questions.question: The Circle of Willis provides collateral circulation between which two major arterial systems?

options: Between the endothelium and the GBM
Between the GBM and podocyte foot processes
questions.explanation: Bowman's space (urinary space) is the crescent-shaped cavity between the visceral epithelium (podocytes) covering the glomerular capillaries and the parietal epithelium (simple squamous cells) lining the outer wall of Bowman's capsule. Ultrafiltrate crosses the filtration barrier into this space, then flows into the proximal convoluted tubule. In glomerulonephritis with crescents, proliferating parietal epithelial cells and infiltrating macrophages fill Bowman's space, compressing the glomerular tuft.
questions.question: The renal corpuscle consists of the glomerular tuft and Bowman's capsule. The urinary space (Bowman's space) is located between which two structures?

questions.explanation: When an active osteoblast secreting matrix becomes entrapped in the matrix it has produced, it transforms into an osteocyte. Osteocytes reside in lacunae and maintain the surrounding matrix through limited secretion and resorption. They extend cytoplasmic processes through canaliculi, connecting to neighboring osteocytes and to vascular channels, functioning as the primary mechanosensory cells of bone that regulate remodeling in response to mechanical loading.
questions.question: An osteoblast that becomes completely surrounded by the bone matrix it has secreted is henceforth called which of the following?

questions.explanation: Tetralogy of Fallot consists of four cardiovascular alterations: pulmonary stenosis (narrow ventricle outflow region), large ventricular septal defect, overriding aorta that arises directly above the septal defect, and right ventricular hypertrophy. Atrial septal defect is not part of this tetralogy.
questions.question: Tetralogy of Fallot includes all of the following features EXCEPT:
Neurofilaments provide which function?
questions.explanation: Neurofilaments (neurofibrils) provide structural rigidity to neurons. They are part of the cytoskeleton. Microtubules facilitate axonal transport of materials.

General sensation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is provided by the lingual branch of the mandibular nerve (CN V3). Special taste sensation to this region is from the chorda tympani (CN VII). The posterior one-third receives both general and taste sensation from the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX).
questions.question: General sensation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is provided by which nerve?

questions.explanation: The DCT is lined by simple cuboidal cells with NO brush border (or only minimal microvilli), making the lumen appear relatively clear and larger compared to the PCT. PCT cells, in contrast, have a prominent brush border that significantly reduces the apparent lumen diameter. Both have abundant mitochondria and basolateral infoldings, but the absence of a brush border is the key histological criterion distinguishing DCT from PCT.
questions.question: The distal convoluted tubule (DCT) differs from the proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) in which histological characteristic?
options: DCT has a brush border while PCT does not
DCT cells have more mitochondria than PCT cells
DCT is lined by cuboidal cells with no brush border, while PCT
DCT cells are taller and more eosinophilic than PCT cells
DCT has a larger lumen than PCT

questions.explanation: The cell bodies of first-order sensory neurons are located in the posterior root ganglia. Their peripheral processes reach receptors. Their central processes enter the spinal cord via posterior nerve roots.
questions.question: Where are the cell bodies of first-order sensory neurons located?
The basilar artery is formed by union of which vessels?
questions.explanation: The basilar artery is formed by the union of the two vertebral arteries at the pontomedullary junction. It ascends along the ventral surface of the pons in the pontine groove (basilar sulcus) and terminates by dividing into the two posterior cerebral arteries at the upper border of the pons. The basilar artery gives off pontine arteries, anterior inferior cerebellar artery, labyrinthine artery, and superior cerebellar arteries, supplying the pons, cerebellum, and inner ear.

The anterior choroidal artery supplies optic tract, lateral geniculate body, optic radiation, uncus, amygdala, hippocampus, internal capsule, lentiform nucleus and thalamus. Its occlusion causes multiple deficits. It arises from the internal carotid.
options: Optic tract, internal capsule, lentiform nucleus, thalamus
questions.question: The anterior choroidal artery supplies which structures?

questions.explanation: Enterocytes have numerous, densely packed apical microvilli that form the brush border (striated border). Each microvillus is supported by a core of actin filaments and is coated by a glycocalyx rich in digestive enzymes (disaccharidases, peptidases). This brush border enormously amplifies absorptive surface area. Deficiency or damage to the brush border enzymes causes malabsorption syndromes.
questions.question: Enterocytes (absorptive cells) of the small intestine are characterized by which ultrastructural feature on their apical surface?

questions.explanation: Damage to the prefrontal cortex (Brodmann areas 9, 10, 11) typically results in personality changes and impaired judgment, planning, and social behavior. Patients may become disinhibited, emotionally labile, or apathetic, with poor impulse control and decision-making. The famous case of Phineas Gage, who suffered prefrontal damage from an iron rod, demonstrated dramatic personality changes despite preserved motor and sensory function, highlighting the prefrontal cortex's role in executive function and social behavior.
questions.question: Damage to the prefrontal cortex typically results in changes to what aspect of behavior?

questions.explanation: The pineal gland secretes melatonin which regulates circadian rhythms. It develops from the diencephalon roof plate. Light inhibits melatonin secretion. It influences sleep-wake cycles.
questions.question: The pineal gland secretes which hormone?

questions.explanation: Polar bodies are small cells with minimal cytoplasm that result from asymmetric division during oogenesis. They contain genetic material but lack the cytoplasm and organelles needed for development. Polar bodies are nonfunctional cells that degenerate and serve to discard excess chromosomes.
questions.question: Polar bodies are characterized by which feature?
The substantia nigra is located in which brain region?
questions.explanation: The substantia nigra is located in the midbrain, separating the tegmentum from the crus cerebri (basis pedunculi). It contains dopaminergic neurons that project to the striatum. Degeneration of these neurons causes Parkinson's disease.

questions.question: The superior olivary nucleus is part of which pathway?
questions.explanation: The superior olivary nucleus, found at the upper pons level, is part of the auditory pathway. It receives input from the cochlear nuclei bilaterally and projects to the lateral lemniscus and inferior colliculus. It is involved in sound localization.

questions.question: The blastocystic cavity is also known as which structure?
questions.explanation: Shortly after the morula enters the uterus on day 4, fluid from the uterine cavity passes through the zona pellucida to form a single fluid-filled space called the blastocystic cavity, primitive chorionic cavity, or blastocoele. This transforms the morula into a blastocyst.

Modified ependymal cells covering the choroid plexus are primarily responsible for CSF production through active secretion and ultrafiltration of blood plasma. These specialized epithelial cells are connected by tight junctions that form the blood-CSF barrier, selectively regulating the passage of substances from blood vessels into the CSF. The choroid plexus consists of highly vascularized pia mater covered by a single layer of these specialized ependymal cells.
questions.question: Which cells are primarily responsible for CSF production in the choroid plexus?
The internal capsule is formed by axons dividing which structure?
questions.explanation: Axons from cortical neurons coalesce and pass through the corpus striatum dividing it into caudate and lentiform nuclei. The dividing axonal bundle forms the internal capsule. This creates the characteristic appearance of basal ganglia.

During zygotene, the second stage of prophase I, pairing (synapsis) of homologous chromosomes occurs. During leptotene (first stage), chromosomes become visible. During pachytene (third stage), crossing over occurs. During diplotene (fourth stage), homologous chromosomes begin to separate.
questions.question: The zygotene stage of prophase I is characterized by which event?

questions.explanation: Initially, the foregut is separated from the stomodeum by the buccopharyngeal membrane. This membrane breaks down so that the foregut opens to the exterior. At this stage, the head is represented by a bulge caused by the developing brain, and the pericardium occupies the region of the future thorax.
questions.question: The stomodeum is initially separated from the foregut by which membrane?

questions.explanation: The cingulate gyrus is located above the corpus callosum on the medial surface of the cerebral hemisphere, separated from superior structures by the cingulate sulcus. This gyrus forms part of the limbic system and extends from the region of the genu to behind the splenium of the corpus callosum. The paracentral lobule caps the medial end of the central sulcus, while the precuneus lies in the superior parietal region.
questions.question: On the medial cerebral surface, which gyrus lies immediately above the corpus callosum?

questions.explanation: Lumbar puncture is typically performed at the L3-L4 or L4-L5 interspace, below the termination of the spinal cord at L1-L2 in adults. This allows access to the lumbar cistern, which contains CSF and the cauda equina (nerve roots), without risking direct injury to the spinal cord. The subarachnoid space extends to S2, providing a safe window for CSF sampling and measurement of opening pressure.
questions.question: At which vertebral level is lumbar puncture typically performed to access CSF safely?
Rapid eye movements begin during which week?
questions.explanation: Rapid eye movements begin during the 21st week of development. This coincides with substantial weight gain and maturation of the central nervous system. The fetus can also respond to noise (blink-startle responses) at 22-23 weeks.

Patau syndrome results from trisomy 13 (47,XX,+13 or 47,XY,+13). Features include holoprosencephaly, cleft lip and palate, polydactyly, cardiac defects, and severe intellectual disability. Like trisomy 18, most affected infants die within the first year of life.
questions.question: Patau syndrome results from trisomy of which chromosome?

questions.explanation: Heparin within mast cell granules is a sulfated glycosaminoglycan that acts locally as an anticoagulant by activating antithrombin III, which inhibits clotting factors. The local anticoagulant effect may facilitate cell migration through connective tissue during inflammatory responses. Clinically, heparin extracted from mast cell-rich tissues (lung, intestinal mucosa) is used as a therapeutic anticoagulant.
questions.question: Mast cell granules contain heparin, which acts locally in connective tissue as which of the following?
options: A vasoconstrictor reducing blood flow to inflamed areas
An antibacterial peptide directly killing bacteria
An anticoagulant preventing blood clot formation in the tissue
A growth factor stimulating fibroblast proliferation

questions.question: Nephrons are formed until:
questions.explanation: Nephrons continue to form until birth, with over 1 million nephrons eventually present in each kidney. After birth, no new nephrons are formed, though existing ones continue to mature. Kidney maturation continues postnatally, but nephrogenesis (formation of new nephrons) is complete before birth.

questions.question: The gallbladder concentrates bile by actively absorbing which substance from bile?
questions.explanation: The gallbladder epithelium actively absorbs sodium (via NaCl cotransporters) and water follows osmotically, concentrating the bile 5- to 10-fold. This is the primary function of the tall columnar epithelial cells, which have apical microvilli, lateral interdigitations, and basal infoldings to maximize active transport. Disruption of this process contributes to gallstone formation.

questions.question: The acini of the parotid gland are entirely serous while those of the sublingual gland are predominantly mucous. This distinction is based on which histological features?
options: Serous cells are cuboidal with central nuclei while mucous cells have irregular nuclei
Serous acini are larger than mucous acini
Serous cells have basophilic granular cytoplasm; mucous cells have pale vacuolated cytoplasm
Serous glands lack any connective tissue stroma
Mucous cells stain with eosin while serous cells stain with hematoxylin only
questions.explanation: Serous acinar cells have round central nuclei and basophilic granular cytoplasm due to abundant rough ER and apical zymogen granules containing digestive enzymes like amylase. Mucous acinar cells have flattened or crescent-shaped basal nuclei pushed against the base by large apical mucin-filled vacuoles giving pale clear cytoplasm in routine sections. Mixed glands like submandibular have both, often with serous demilunes capping mucous acini.

Amniocentesis is typically performed after 14 weeks when there is about 200 ml of amniotic fluid, and 20-30 ml can be safely withdrawn. The procedure is performed under ultrasound guidance. The risk of inducing an abortion is approximately 0.5%.
questions.question: Amniocentesis for genetic testing is typically performed after which week?
The nasal placodes are formed by inductive influence of which structure?
questions.explanation: On both sides of the frontonasal prominence, the ectoderm shows localized thickening called nasal or olfactory placodes. These are formed by the inductive influence of the ventral part of the forebrain. The placodes develop into nasal pits, which are primordia of the anterior nares and nasal cavities.

questions.question: Mesonephric ridges, which indicate sites of future kidneys, appear during which week?
questions.explanation: Mesonephric ridges appear during the 5th week of development and indicate the sites of the developing kidneys. During this week, the brain grows rapidly, the face contacts the heart prominence, the hyoid (2nd) arch overgrows the 3rd and 4th arches forming the cervical sinus, and upper limbs show elbows and hand plates.

questions.question: Which layer of the gastrointestinal tract wall contains the Meissner plexus of autonomic nerves?
questions.explanation: The submucosal (Meissner) plexus is located within the submucosa of the GIT wall. It regulates glandular secretion and local blood flow. This is distinct from the myenteric plexus found between the muscle layers of the muscularis externa.

The rich vascularity of the gastric lamina propria serves multiple critical functions: it delivers CO2, water, and substrates needed for acid production; it transports oxygen to support the high metabolic activity of parietal and chief cells; it carries regulatory hormones and neural signals to epithelial cells; and it rapidly clears absorbed substances and waste products. Any disruption of this blood supply (as in mucosal ischemia) quickly compromises the gastric mucosal barrier.
options: Direct absorption of digested nutrients in the stomach
Supply of substrates for HCl synthesis
questions.question: A researcher studying the stomach notices that the lamina propria is highly vascularized to support gastric pits and glands. This rich vascularity is essential for which function?

questions.explanation: The largest gray matter aggregate is the thalamus, with other aggregates lateral to it known as basal ganglia. The forebrain consists largely of white matter with buried gray matter. The thalamus serves as a sensory relay station.
questions.question: The largest gray matter aggregate in the forebrain is which structure?

options: The inactive form produced in the skin and liver is 25-hydroxyvitamin D. Which enzyme in the kidney converts this to the active form?
questions.explanation: The proximal tubular cells of the kidney (specifically the proximal convoluted and straight tubules) express 1-alpha-hydroxylase (CYP27B1), which converts 25-hydroxyvitamin D (calcidiol, produced in the liver) to 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3 (calcitriol) — the biologically active form. Calcitriol increases intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption and promotes renal calcium reabsorption. Chronic kidney disease impairs 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity, causing vitamin D deficiency and renal osteodystrophy.
questions.question: The kidney activates vitamin D. The inactive form produced in the skin and liver is 25-hydroxyvitamin D. Which enzyme in the kidney converts this to the active form?
Cortical neuron settling occurs in which pattern?
questions.explanation: Settling of neurons in their definitive cortical position occurs in an inside-out fashion. Earlier-born neurons occupy deeper layers while later-born neurons migrate past them. This establishes the six-layered cortical structure.

questions.question: The membranous labyrinth contains which fluid?
questions.explanation: The membranous labyrinth (derived from otic vesicle) contains endolymph. The bony labyrinth spaces contain perilymph. Endolymph has high potassium and low sodium concentration.

questions.question: The maxillary process of the first arch forms all EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The dorsal part of the maxillary process forms the premaxilla, maxilla, zygomatic bone, and part of the temporal bone. The mandible is formed from mesenchyme surrounding Meckel's cartilage in the mandibular process (dorsal part) of the first arch, not from the maxillary process.

questions.question: The centroacinar cells of the pancreas are unique cells found within the lumen of pancreatic acini. Their primary function is:
questions.explanation: Centroacinar cells are the initial cells of the ductal system that extend into the lumen of the acinus. They secrete water and bicarbonate (stimulated by secretin) into the duct lumen, forming the aqueous component of pancreatic juice. This alkaline fluid neutralizes gastric acid in the duodenum. Cystic fibrosis impairs centroacinar cell function, causing thickened pancreatic secretions and ductal obstruction.

questions.question: What percentage of the cerebral cortex is neocortex?
questions.explanation: Approximately 90% of the human cerebral cortex is neocortex (isocortex), characterized by the typical six-layered architecture. The remaining 10% consists of allocortex (archicortex and paleocortex) with three layers, found in phylogenetically older structures like the hippocampus and olfactory cortex. The expansion of neocortex, particularly association areas, is a hallmark of human brain evolution and correlates with advanced cognitive abilities including language, abstract reasoning, and complex social behavior.

questions.question: Which cells in the cerebellar cortex are the sole output neurons?
questions.explanation: Purkinje cells are the sole output neurons of the cerebellar cortex, sending their axons to the deep cerebellar nuclei and vestibular nuclei. These large neurons have extensively branched dendritic trees arranged in a single plane perpendicular to the cerebellar folia. Purkinje cells use GABA as their neurotransmitter and exert inhibitory control over the deep cerebellar nuclei, modulating cerebellar output to other brain regions.

The hippocampal commissure (psalterium or commissure of the fornix) is a thin sheet of transverse fibers connecting the two crura of the fornix inferior to the splenium of the corpus callosum. While called the hippocampal commissure, it actually connects the fornices and may exchange some fibers between hippocampi. It is a small commissure compared to the corpus callosum and anterior commissure. The hippocampal commissure is part of the complex white matter architecture of the limbic system beneath the splenium.
questions.question: The hippocampal commissure (psalterium) connects which structures?

questions.explanation: The pyramidal decussation occurs at the lower medulla where 75-90% of corticospinal fibers cross. This creates contralateral motor control. The crossing is visible externally. Uncrossed fibers form anterior corticospinal tract.
questions.question: The pyramidal decussation occurs at which level?

questions.explanation: The pyloric sphincter regulates the rate of gastric emptying into the duodenum, ensuring that chyme is released in small, manageable quantities for digestion and absorption. It prevents duodenal contents from refluxing back into the stomach. Pyloric stenosis (hypertrophy of this sphincter) in infants causes projectile vomiting and is corrected surgically. The sphincter responds to both neural (vagal) and hormonal (gastrin, secretin, CCK) signals.
questions.question: The pyloric sphincter is a thickening of the circular smooth muscle layer at the gastroduodenal junction. Its primary function is to:
options: Prevent acid from entering the stomach
Regulate the emptying of gastric contents
Generate peristaltic waves in the stomach
Produce mucus to neutralize gastric acid

questions.question: The tunica adventitia of blood vessels is primarily composed of which tissue?
questions.explanation: The tunica adventitia is the outermost layer of blood vessels, composed predominantly of dense irregular connective tissue containing type I collagen fibers, fibroblasts, and elastic fibers. It anchors the vessel to surrounding tissues and prevents overdistension. The adventitia also contains vasa vasorum (supplying the vessel wall), nervi vasorum (autonomic nerves), and lymphatic vessels.

questions.question: The palatine tonsil develops from which pharyngeal pouch?
questions.explanation: The ventral part of the second pharyngeal pouch forms the palatine tonsil. The dorsal part of the second pouch joins the dorsal part of the first pouch to contribute to formation of the external auditory meatus. The palatine tonsil is a lymphoid organ of the oropharynx.

questions.question: Central cord syndrome typically affects which tracts predominantly?
options: Central fibers affecting upper limbs more
questions.explanation: Central cord syndrome affects central fibers (upper limb representation in corticospinal tract) more than peripheral. Upper limbs are affected more than lower. It often follows hyperextension injury. There is sacral sparing.

questions.question: Which dural venous sinus is formed by the union of the great cerebral vein and inferior sagittal sinus?
questions.explanation: The straight sinus is formed by the union of the great cerebral vein (of Galen) with the inferior sagittal sinus. It runs posteriorly along the junction of the falx cerebri and tentorium cerebelli, continuing mainly with the left transverse sinus. This sinus is a major drainage pathway for deep cerebral structures and plays a crucial role in venous return from the brain.

After PNS injury, Schwann cells and their basal lamina form continuous tubes called bands of Büngner within the neurilemma that guide regenerating axon sprouts from the proximal cut end toward the target organ at approximately 1–3 mm per day. The neurilemma's guidance role and growth factor secretion explain why peripheral nerves can regenerate while CNS axons generally cannot, since CNS oligodendrocytes lack this guiding tube and produce inhibitory molecules.
questions.question: The neurilemma formed by Schwann cells plays a critical role in peripheral nerve regeneration primarily by providing which of the following?
options: The signal for Wallerian degeneration of the proximal stump
Cellular tubes guiding regenerating axon sprouts toward their target organs
New myelin directly without any axon present
The blood-nerve barrier preventing macrophage entry
Inhibitory proteoglycans that prevent aberrant regeneration

questions.question: PICA supplies which structures?
questions.explanation: Posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) approaches cerebellum to supply its inferior surface. As it curves around brainstem, it supplies choroid plexus of 4th ventricle and lateral medulla. PICA occlusion causes lateral medullary syndrome.
options: Inferior cerebellar surface and lateral medulla

questions.explanation: The true vocal cords (vocal folds) are covered by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium, which can withstand the mechanical trauma of rapid vibration during phonation. The false vocal cords and most of the larynx above the vocal folds are covered by respiratory epithelium (pseudostratified ciliated columnar). This sharp epithelial transition at the vocal folds is the basis for the distinction between supraglottic, glottic, and subglottic laryngeal carcinomas.
questions.question: The larynx contains true and false vocal cords. The TRUE vocal cords (vocal folds) are covered by which epithelium, reflecting their vibratory function?

questions.explanation: The trigone of the bladder is derived from the caudal ends of the mesonephric ducts, which become incorporated into the bladder wall. Although the trigone has mesodermal origin, the rest of the bladder epithelium is endodermal from the urogenital sinus. The trigone is the triangular area between the ureteric and urethral openings.
questions.question: The trigone of the bladder is derived from:

questions.explanation: The accessory pancreatic duct (of Santorini), when present, opens at the minor duodenal papilla, located approximately 2 cm proximal to the major papilla. It represents the proximal part of the dorsal pancreatic bud duct. The main pancreatic duct (of Wirsung) opens at the major duodenal papilla along with the common bile duct.
questions.question: The accessory pancreatic duct (of Santorini) opens at:
Ureteral ectopia in females may result in:
questions.explanation: Ureteral ectopia in females, where the ureter opens into the urethra or vagina (distal to the urinary sphincter), results in continuous urinary incontinence despite normal voiding. The ectopic ureter bypasses the sphincter mechanism. In males, ectopic ureters usually open into structures proximal to the external sphincter and don't cause incontinence. Surgical reimplantation is required.

The reticular formation is a loosely arranged network of neurons distributed throughout the brainstem (midbrain, pons, and medulla) wherever there are no specific neural tracts or nuclei. It forms the core of the brainstem and serves as a relay between various brain regions.
questions.question: The reticular formation is located in which region?
Pulmonary fibrosis results from excessive collagen deposition in the lung interstitium. The primary cell type responsible for collagen synthesis in pulmonary fibrosis is the:
questions.explanation: In pulmonary fibrosis, myofibroblasts are the primary collagen-producing cells responsible for progressive lung scarring. They arise from local fibroblasts (activated by TGF-β from macrophages), from epithelial-mesenchymal transition of alveolar epithelial cells, and from circulating fibrocytes. Activated myofibroblasts express alpha-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA) and continuously deposit collagen type I, progressively replacing alveolar architecture and impairing gas exchange.

options: Right heart failure causing hepatic congestion
questions.explanation: Centrilobular (Zone 3) necrosis corresponds to hepatocyte death around the central veins — precisely where Zone 3 hepatocytes are located. These cells are most vulnerable to ischemia because they are furthest from the portal blood supply. Right heart failure causes venous congestion (nutmeg liver) with centrilobular necrosis. Acetaminophen toxicity also causes centrilobular necrosis via CYP2E1-mediated toxicity (concentrated in Zone 3).
questions.question: A liver biopsy shows centrilobular necrosis (necrosis around the central veins). This pattern of injury is most consistent with which condition?
The loop of Henle is part of:
questions.explanation: The loop of Henle is part of the excretory unit (nephron), which is derived from the metanephric blastema. Each nephron consists of Bowman's capsule, proximal convoluted tubule, loop of Henle, and distal convoluted tubule. The distal tubule connects to a collecting tubule (derived from the ureteric bud).

questions.question: The myelencephalon forms which adult structure?
questions.explanation: The myelencephalon is the caudal portion of rhombencephalon that forms the medulla oblongata. The dorso-lateral wall is opened up. Basal and alar plates are separated by sulcus limitans.

options: Increase urea reabsorption in collecting ducts
questions.question: Interstitial cells of the renal medulla produce prostaglandins. These prostaglandins act on the kidney to produce which effect?
questions.explanation: Renal medullary interstitial cells produce prostaglandins (primarily PGE2 and PGI2) that have local vasodilatory effects on renal vasculature, counteracting excessive renal vasoconstriction. They also inhibit tubular sodium reabsorption, promoting natriuresis. NSAIDs, by inhibiting prostaglandin synthesis, can cause renal vasoconstriction and sodium retention — particularly dangerous in states of reduced renal perfusion.

options: Filtration of blood plasma through slit diaphragms
Structural support of capillary loops, phagocytosis
questions.question: The mesangium is the supporting tissue of the glomerulus between and within the glomerular capillary loops. Mesangial cells perform which functions?
questions.explanation: Mesangial cells are specialized pericyte-like cells within the mesangium (matrix between glomerular capillary loops). Their functions include: structural support and anchoring of glomerular capillaries; phagocytosis and removal of immune complexes, macromolecules, and cellular debris; contraction/relaxation to regulate capillary surface area available for filtration; and secretion of cytokines. In IgA nephropathy, mesangial IgA immune complex deposition causes mesangial cell proliferation and matrix expansion.

questions.question: In the spinal cord, sacral fibers of the spinothalamic tract are positioned where?
questions.explanation: Sacral fibers are lateral while cervical fibers are medial in the spinothalamic tract. Crude touch fibers are more medial than pain and temperature fibers. This somatotopic organization is maintained throughout the tract.

D cells (delta cells) are enteroendocrine cells producing somatostatin, which acts as a potent paracrine inhibitor. Somatostatin inhibits gastrin secretion from G cells (reducing the stimulus for HCl production) and directly inhibits parietal cells and enterochromaffin-like (ECL) cells. This provides a local negative feedback loop regulating gastric acid secretion. H. pylori infection suppresses D cell function, contributing to hypergastrinemia.
questions.question: Somatostatin-producing D cells in the gastric antrum act as paracrine inhibitors of acid secretion. When stimulated, they primarily inhibit which cell type?
Which of the following features best distinguishes the 10× eyepiece lens from a 10× objective lens in terms of function within a compound microscope?
questions.explanation: The objective lens creates an enlarged real, inverted intermediate image of the specimen based on its proximity to the object. The eyepiece then acts as a magnifying glass to further enlarge this intermediate image for the observer's eye. Only the objective lens determines resolving power; the eyepiece simply increases perceived magnification without improving resolution.
options: The eyepiece magnifies the actual specimen while the objective produces a virtual image
The objective creates an enlarged real image; the eyepiece further magnifies it
Both lenses function identically with only placement differing
The eyepiece lens improves resolving power; the objective only magnifies
The objective is adjusted by the coarse focus; the eyepiece by the fine focus

questions.explanation: Lysosomes fuse with phagosomes containing engulfed microorganisms to form phagolysosomes, where lysosomal hydrolases (active at pH ~4.5) digest the bacterial components. This is the primary intracellular killing mechanism of macrophages. The acidic pH of lysosomes both activates the hydrolases and denatures many bacterial proteins, contributing to efficient destruction.
questions.question: Phagocytosis of bacteria by a macrophage involves fusion of the phagosome with lysosomes to form a phagolysosome. This process specifically demonstrates which organelle's function?

In the GIT, chemical digestion is aided by secretions from glands within the wall itself and from accessory digestive organs. Which three accessory organs contribute exocrine secretions to the GIT lumen?
questions.explanation: The three principal accessory digestive organs contributing exocrine secretions to the GIT lumen are: salivary glands (amylase, mucus, lipase), liver via bile (bile salts for fat emulsification, bilirubin for excretion), and pancreas (digestive enzymes: lipase, amylase, proteases; bicarbonate from ductal cells). The gallbladder stores and concentrates bile but is not an exocrine gland per se. The spleen has no digestive secretory function.

questions.question: The sarcomere, the basic contractile unit of skeletal and cardiac muscle, is precisely defined as the region between which of the following?
options: Two M lines in the center of the A band
Two H zones within adjacent A bands
The I band boundaries of adjacent A bands
questions.explanation: The sarcomere is the functional contractile unit of striated muscle, defined as the segment between two consecutive Z lines. Each sarcomere contains one A band flanked by two half-I bands. During contraction, Z lines move closer together as actin slides over myosin according to the sliding filament mechanism, shortening the sarcomere. The A band width remains constant during contraction while the I band and H zone narrow.

The internal cerebral veins drain deep structures including the thalamus, basal ganglia, and deep white matter of the cerebral hemispheres. These paired veins run posteriorly in the roof of the third ventricle and unite beneath the splenium of the corpus callosum to form the great vein of Galen. The great vein then drains into the straight sinus. Thrombosis of deep cerebral veins is less common than superficial thrombosis but can cause hemorrhagic infarction of deep structures.
questions.question: Which venous structure drains the deep white matter of the cerebral hemispheres?

questions.explanation: Fingerprints and footprints result from the microscopic ridge structures formed by the papillary layer of the dermis. These ridges create unique patterns that remain constant throughout life unless disrupted. The patterns are genetically determined and established during intrauterine development.
questions.question: Fingerprints and footprints result from the arrangement of:
The movement of a molecule across a membrane requiring carrier proteins, driven by a concentration gradient, without ATP expenditure, is BEST classified as which of the following?
questions.explanation: Facilitated diffusion uses integral membrane carrier proteins or channels to move substances down their concentration gradient, requiring no ATP. Simple diffusion moves lipid-soluble molecules directly through the bilayer without carriers. Osmosis is specifically water movement, and active transport requires ATP to move substances against gradients. Facilitated diffusion is intermediate: it needs proteins (like simple diffusion does not) but not energy (unlike active transport).

Neural crest cells give rise to many structures including dorsal root ganglia, autonomic ganglia, Schwann cells, melanocytes, adrenal medulla, and leptomeninges. Motor neurons of the spinal cord are derived from the basal plate of the neural tube, not from neural crest cells.
questions.question: Which structure do neural crest cells NOT contribute to forming?
Congenital megacolon (Hirschsprung disease) most commonly affects:
questions.explanation: Congenital megacolon (Hirschsprung disease) most commonly affects the sigmoid colon and rectum (approximately 80% of cases). About 3% of cases involve the entire colon. The aganglionic segment lacks peristalsis, causing proximal bowel distention. The condition results from failure of neural crest cell migration.

questions.question: The abducens nucleus innervates which extraocular muscle?
questions.explanation: The abducens nucleus (CN VI) innervates the lateral rectus muscle, which abducts the eye (moves it laterally away from the nose). The nucleus is located in the lower pons beneath the facial colliculus on the floor of the fourth ventricle. The abducens nerve has the longest intracranial course of any cranial nerve, making it vulnerable to damage from increased intracranial pressure. Lesions cause medial deviation of the eye (esotropia) and inability to abduct, resulting in horizontal diplopia.

questions.question: Marfan syndrome results from mutations in which gene, affecting which structural protein of the elastic fiber system?
questions.explanation: Marfan syndrome results from autosomal dominant mutations in the FBN1 gene encoding fibrillin-1, a glycoprotein that forms the microfibrillar scaffold essential for elastin deposition and elastic fiber integrity. Without functional fibrillin-1, elastic fibers lack mechanical resistance, causing aortic aneurysm/dissection, lens dislocation, and skeletal abnormalities (tall stature, arachnodactyly). Aortic rupture is the major life-threatening complication.
options: COL3A1 gene encoding type III collagen
COL1A1 gene encoding type I collagen
FBN1 mutation affecting fibrillin-1, the elastin scaffolding protein

questions.explanation: Cartilage is a specialized connective tissue where chondrocytes are embedded within lacunae in a firm, gel-like matrix. Its most distinctive feature is avascularity — cartilage contains no blood vessels, nerves, or lymphatics; it receives nutrition by diffusion through the matrix from surrounding perichondrium or synovial fluid. This avascularity explains the slow healing of cartilage injuries compared to vascularized tissues.
questions.question: Cartilage is classified as which of the following tissue types and is characterized by which unique feature that distinguishes it from most other connective tissues?
options: Muscle tissue with highly specialized contractile cells
Avascular tissue with sparse cells in a firm matrix
Epithelial tissue lining the joint cavities
Specialized adipose tissue for joint cushioning

questions.explanation: The genu (anterior bend) of the corpus callosum primarily connects the frontal poles and prefrontal cortex bilaterally. The forceps minor, formed by fibers radiating anteriorly from the genu, connects the orbital and medial frontal cortices. The genu is important for bilateral coordination of executive functions, emotional processing, and social cognition. Damage to the genu may contribute to executive dysfunction, emotional dysregulation, and impaired interhemispheric transfer of prefrontal information. The genu is the first portion of the corpus callosum to show thinning in normal aging.
questions.question: The genu of the corpus callosum primarily connects which regions?

options: Yellow, white, and blue cartilage based on their color under light microscopy
Fibrocartilage, hyaline, and elastic cartilage — identical in all characteristics
Hyaline (most common), fibrocartilage (richest in cells), and elastic (most rigid type)
Dense, loose, and reticular cartilage based on matrix composition
Hyaline (fine collagen), elastic (elastic fibers), and fibrocartilage (type I collagen bundles)
questions.explanation: The three cartilage types are: hyaline cartilage (most abundant; homogeneous glassy matrix with fine type II collagen fibrils; found in trachea, costal cartilages, articular surfaces); elastic cartilage (contains elastic fibers providing flexibility; found in ear pinna, epiglottis); and fibrocartilage (contains thick bundles of type I collagen for tensile strength; found in intervertebral discs, pubic symphysis, menisci). Each type serves distinct biomechanical functions.
questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes the three types of cartilage and their distinguishing characteristics?

questions.explanation: Total magnification is calculated by multiplying the ocular lens magnification by the objective lens magnification (10 × 40 = 400×). Addition of the two values is a common misconception that gives an incorrect result. This principle applies consistently across all compound microscope configurations.
questions.question: The total magnification achieved when a 10× ocular lens is combined with a 40× objective lens is which of the following?
Hydroxyapatite crystals in bone matrix have the chemical formula Ca10(PO4)6(OH)2 and constitute what proportion of bone's dry weight?
questions.explanation: Inorganic matter (mainly hydroxyapatite) represents approximately 50% of the dry weight of bone matrix. Calcium and phosphorus are the most abundant mineral elements, with significant amounts of bicarbonate, citrate, magnesium, potassium, and sodium also present. The remaining ~50% of dry weight is organic matrix (mainly type I collagen). This mineral-organic balance creates the unique combination of hardness and resilience in bone.

questions.question: In females, the mesonephric duct remnant may persist as:
questions.explanation: In females, the mesonephric duct may persist as Gartner's duct, a vestigial structure in the lateral vaginal wall. The epoophoron and paroophoron in the broad ligament also represent mesonephric remnants. These structures are usually clinically insignificant but may occasionally form cysts. In males, the mesonephric duct becomes the ductus deferens and related structures.

questions.question: The premotor cortex (area 6) is primarily involved in which function?
questions.explanation: The premotor cortex (Brodmann area 6), located anterior to the primary motor cortex, is involved in planning and organizing movements based on sensory cues, particularly visual guidance of movement. It programs complex movement sequences before execution by the primary motor cortex. Lesions cause apraxia, difficulty performing learned motor tasks despite normal strength and coordination, particularly affecting reaching and grasping movements guided by visual input.
options: Planning movements based on sensory cues

questions.explanation: Ependymal cells are cylindrical cells lining cavities in brain and spinal cord containing CSF. They play a role in CSF production, transport and circulation. They form a filter regulating CSF-CNS exchange.
questions.question: Ependymal cells line which structures?
The bronchopulmonary segments are the smallest independently functional lung units with their own bronchus, artery, and vein. Which surgical implication arises from this segmental anatomy?
questions.explanation: Because each bronchopulmonary segment has its own segmental bronchus and artery (note: veins run in intersegmental septa between segments), individual segments can be surgically resected (segmentectomy) while preserving adjacent healthy lung tissue. This is advantageous in patients with limited pulmonary reserve who cannot tolerate lobectomy. Understanding segmental anatomy is also critical for interpreting chest CT, bronchoscopy findings, and postural drainage positions.
options: Only entire lobes can be surgically removed
Individual bronchopulmonary segments can be surgically resected
Each segment has its own pleural covering preventing pneumothorax
Segments are too small to be identified radiologically
Segments share venous drainage making individual resection impossible

questions.explanation: Adult cardiomyocytes are terminally differentiated cells with extremely limited regenerative capacity. In response to increased mechanical load (pressure overload from aortic stenosis or hypertension), the heart adapts by increasing the size of individual cardiomyocytes (hypertrophy), adding more sarcomeres in parallel (concentric hypertrophy) or in series (eccentric hypertrophy). The total cell number does not increase (no hyperplasia). This compensatory hypertrophy eventually becomes maladaptive, leading to heart failure.
questions.question: Cardiac hypertrophy in response to pressure overload (e.g., aortic stenosis) involves enlargement of individual cardiomyocytes. This is called:
The first two ossicles (malleus and incus) derive from which arch?
questions.explanation: The first two ossicles (malleus and incus) derive from cartilage of 1st pharyngeal arch. The stapes is from the 2nd arch. The tympanic cavity gradually envelopes these ossicles.

questions.question: The duodenum receives bile and pancreatic secretions through the ampulla of Vater. The sphincter controlling this ampulla is the:
questions.explanation: The sphincter of Oddi is a complex of smooth muscle surrounding the distal common bile duct, main pancreatic duct, and ampulla of Vater as they traverse the duodenal wall. It regulates the flow of bile and pancreatic juice into the duodenum and prevents reflux of duodenal contents into the biliary and pancreatic ducts. CCK causes relaxation of the sphincter of Oddi, while somatostatin causes contraction. Sphincter of Oddi dysfunction can mimic biliary colic.

Spongy (cancellous/trabecular) bone consists of a three-dimensional lattice of bone trabeculae (thin struts and plates) with interconnected marrow-filled spaces, providing a lightweight yet strong architecture for weight-bearing and hematopoiesis. Compact bone forms the dense cortex with cylindrical osteons. Both types contain osteocytes in lacunae, but spongy bone's trabeculae are too thin to require Haversian canal systems.
questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes spongy (cancellous) bone compared to compact (cortical) bone?
options: Spongy bone is denser and forms the cortex of long bones
Spongy bone contains Haversian systems like compact bone
Spongy bone has no cells and is composed entirely of mineral
Spongy bone is found only in flat bones and absent in long bones
Spongy bone has a lattice-like trabecular structure with marrow-filled spaces
Polyploidy of a single myoblast nucleus through repeated karyokinesis without cytokinesis
Invasion of fibroblasts into the muscle fiber
Fusion of multiple myoblasts into a single multinucleated fiber
Amitotic replication unique to skeletal muscle cells
Satellite cell proliferation within adult muscle fibers
questions.question: Skeletal muscle fibers are multinucleated. This multinuclearity arises during development from which of the following processes?
questions.explanation: Skeletal muscle fibers develop embryologically by fusion of numerous mononucleated myoblasts, mesodermal precursors, into a single elongated syncytium with hundreds of peripherally placed nuclei. This multinucleated state reflects the syncytial origin. Satellite cells, positioned between the sarcolemma and basal lamina, serve as the adult muscle stem cell pool for regeneration after injury but do not fuse to form the original fiber during embryogenesis.

questions.question: Primordial germ cells first appear in which location?
questions.explanation: Both male and female germ cells have a common origin from primordial germ cells in the posterior wall of the yolk sac. These cells start migrating by the 4th week and reach the gonad by the 5th week, where they differentiate into either spermatogonia or oogonia.

questions.question: The respiratory diverticulum appears during which week?
questions.explanation: The respiratory diverticulum (lung bud) appears during the 4th week as an outgrowth from the ventral wall of the foregut. This location is controlled by transcription factor TBX4, upregulated by retinoic acid from adjacent mesoderm. The bud induces formation and promotes growth and differentiation of the lungs.

After birth, when lung circulation begins and pressure in the left atrium increases, the valve of the foramen ovale is pressed against the septum secundum. This obliterates the foramen ovale and separates the right and left atria. Functional closure occurs immediately, but anatomical closure may take several months.
questions.question: After birth, the valve of the foramen ovale is pressed against which structure?

questions.explanation: When a foreign body is too large for a single macrophage to engulf, multiple macrophages can fuse to form multinucleated foreign body giant cells. These cells accumulate at invasion sites and sites of chronic inflammation, attempting to isolate and destroy the foreign material. This fusion response is a hallmark histological feature of granulomatous inflammation.
questions.question: When macrophages encounter a foreign body too large to phagocytose (e.g., a splinter), they may fuse together to form which of the following structures?
Bipolar neurons with a dendrite at one end and an axon at the other are found predominantly in which locations?
questions.explanation: Bipolar neurons are spindle-shaped with a single dendrite at one pole and a single axon at the opposite pole. They are specialized sensory neurons found in the retina as bipolar cells, in the cochlear spiral ganglion as first-order auditory neurons, in the vestibular ganglion, and in the olfactory epithelium. Their simple two-process form reflects their specialized role as first-order sensory transducer cells.
options: Motor neurons of the spinal cord ventral horn
Retinal, cochlear, and olfactory epithelium sensory neurons

questions.explanation: By the 4th month, the epidermis has its definitive arrangement of five layers: stratum basale, stratum spinosum, stratum granulosum, stratum lucidum, and stratum corneum.
