These layers represent progressive stages of keratinocyte differentiation. The entire process from basal layer to desquamation takes approximately 15-30 days.
questions.question: The five definitive layers of the epidermis are established by which fetal month?
The circumferences of the head and abdomen become equal at approximately which week?
questions.explanation: The circumferences of the head and abdomen become approximately equal at 36 weeks. The crown-rump length is about 360 mm and weight about 3400 grams at this time. The fetus is growing more slowly before birth compared to earlier weeks.

The Edinger-Westphal nucleus provides parasympathetic (GVE) innervation to the sphincter pupillae muscle (causing pupillary constriction) and ciliary muscle (controlling lens accommodation) via the oculomotor nerve. These preganglionic fibers synapse in the ciliary ganglion, with postganglionic fibers reaching the eyeball. Damage to the Edinger-Westphal nucleus or oculomotor nerve causes a dilated pupil that doesn't constrict to light (due to unopposed sympathetic activity) and impaired accommodation.
questions.question: The Edinger-Westphal nucleus provides parasympathetic innervation to which structures?
The nucleus ambiguus contains which functional component?
questions.explanation: The nucleus ambiguus contains special visceral efferent (SVE) neurons that innervate branchial arch-derived muscles of the larynx, pharynx, and soft palate via cranial nerves IX, X, and XI. The SVE component is more lateral than GSE but medial to visceral afferent components in the brainstem's mediolateral nuclear organization. These muscles, though striated and voluntary, are classified as \"special visceral\" because they develop from branchial arch mesoderm rather than somitic mesoderm.

The anterior limb of the internal capsule is positioned between the head of the caudate nucleus medially and the lentiform nucleus laterally. It contains frontopontine fibers traveling from the frontal cortex to pontine nuclei, which then relay to the cerebellum. These fibers pass through the thalamus and occupy the medial part of the cerebral peduncle base, playing a role in corticopontocerebellar pathways.
questions.question: The anterior limb of the internal capsule lies between which two structures?
Varicose veins are dilated, tortuous superficial veins caused by incompetent venous valves. Histologically, varicose veins show which changes compared to normal veins?
questions.explanation: Varicose veins show irregular remodeling of the vein wall: areas of smooth muscle hypertrophy alternating with atrophy and fibrosis in the media, intimal thickening, adventitial fibrosis, and calcification. Valve leaflets are thickened and fibrotic (incompetent). The irregular contraction of the remodeled smooth muscle makes varicose veins tortuous. These changes result from chronic venous hypertension due to gravitational stress and valve failure.
options: Thinning of all vessel wall layers with normal valve architecture
Replacement of venous wall by arterial tissue
Cartilaginous metaplasia of the vein wall

questions.question: The globus pallidus is divided into how many segments?
questions.explanation: The globus pallidus is divided into external (GPe) and internal (GPi) segments by the medial medullary lamina (internal medullary lamina of the pallidum). These segments have different connections and functions: GPe projects mainly to the subthalamic nucleus and striatum (indirect pathway), while GPi projects to the thalamus (VA/VL nuclei) representing a major basal ganglia output. The globus pallidus has a pale appearance (hence \"pale globe\") due to the large number of myelinated fibers passing through it. It is the pallidum portion of the lentiform nucleus.

questions.question: Horizontal cells of Cajal are primarily found in which age group?
questions.explanation: Horizontal cells of Cajal are fusiform neurons found predominantly in neonates in layer I (molecular layer) of the cortex. These cells are transient developmental neurons involved in organizing cortical circuitry during early brain development. They largely disappear or become incorporated into mature cortical circuits after the neonatal period. Their presence in the acellular molecular layer of the developing cortex suggests a role in guiding migrating neurons and establishing early cortical connections.

questions.question: The cerebellum functions to perform which task?
questions.explanation: The cerebellum compares information from cortex, brainstem and somatosensory system, then corrects deviations from intended movement. It does not initiate movement. It coordinates and modulates ongoing movements.

questions.question: The phallic part of the urogenital sinus gives rise to:
questions.explanation: The phallic part of the urogenital sinus gives rise to the penile (spongy) urethra in males and the vestibule in females. This portion grows toward and into the genital tubercle. In males, the terminal glandular urethra is formed by an ectodermal cord that grows inward from the glans and later canalizes.

questions.question: The laryngeal cartilages are derived from which pharyngeal arches?
questions.explanation: The laryngeal cartilages (thyroid, cricoid, arytenoid, corniculate, cuneiform) are derived from the 4th and 6th pharyngeal arches. The muscles of the larynx are also derived from these arches. This explains their innervation by branches of the vagus nerve (superior and recurrent laryngeal nerves).

questions.question: The folds of the stomach mucosa and submucosa visible to the naked eye when the stomach is empty are called:
questions.explanation: The rugae are longitudinal folds of the gastric mucosa and submucosa visible when the stomach is empty. They allow the stomach to expand greatly when filled with food. These folds flatten as the stomach distends. Plicae circulares are found in the small intestine and cannot be flattened, distinguishing them from gastric rugae.

Bowman's capsule develops from metanephric vesicles, which form from the metanephric blastema. These vesicles elongate to form S-shaped tubules. One end of the tubule invaginates to form Bowman's capsule around a developing glomerulus. The other end connects to a collecting tubule, establishing continuity of the nephron.
questions.question: Bowman's capsule develops from:

options: Subepithelial immune deposits on electron microscopy
questions.question: Interstitial nephritis is inflammation of the renal interstitium. The characteristic histological finding of acute interstitial nephritis (typically drug-induced) is:
questions.explanation: Acute interstitial nephritis (AIN) is characterized histologically by edema and dense inflammatory infiltrate in the renal interstitium — predominantly lymphocytes, plasma cells, monocytes, and characteristically eosinophils (suggesting drug-induced type). Tubular injury (tubulitis — inflammatory cells invading the tubular epithelium) is a key feature. Glomeruli are typically normal or show minor changes. NSAIDs, beta-lactam antibiotics, and PPIs are common causes. AIN is an important reversible cause of acute kidney injury.

questions.question: The ventral pallidum projects primarily to which thalamic nucleus?
questions.explanation: The ventral pallidum (output structure of ventral striatum) projects primarily to the mediodorsal (MD) nucleus of the thalamus, which then projects to prefrontal cortex. This forms the limbic basal ganglia loop involved in motivation, emotion, and executive function rather than motor control. The ventral pallidum also projects to other limbic structures including hypothalamus and brainstem. This pathway parallels the motor loop (dorsal striatum → GPi → VA/VL → motor cortex) but serves limbic rather than motor functions.

questions.question: The substantia nigra pars reticulata is functionally similar to which structure?
questions.explanation: The substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr) is functionally similar to the globus pallidus internal segment (GPi), both serving as major output structures of the basal ganglia. Both use GABA as their neurotransmitter and project to the thalamus (VA/VL, and additionally SNr to superior colliculus for saccadic eye movements). SNr and GPi tonically inhibit thalamic neurons, with movement occurring when this inhibition is reduced. Embryologically, SNr and GPi derive from the same structure, while SNc (dopaminergic portion) has different origins.

questions.question: The muscular interventricular septum develops in the floor of the ventricle and grows toward which structure?
questions.explanation: The muscular interventricular septum develops in the floor of the ventricle and grows toward the AV cushions but stops short, leaving the interventricular foramen. The membranous IV septum later forms by fusion of three components: right bulbar ridge, left bulbar ridge, and AV cushions, closing this foramen.

There are three natural constrictions of the ureter where ureteric stones commonly lodge: (1) ureteropelvic junction (UPJ); (2) as the ureter crosses the common iliac vessels at the pelvic brim; (3) ureterovesical junction (UVJ) — the narrowest point. The UVJ is the most common site for stone impaction because the ureter passes obliquely through the bladder wall (antireflux mechanism), creating the narrowest luminal diameter. Stones >5mm at the UVJ are unlikely to pass spontaneously.
questions.question: The ureter descends retroperitoneally and crosses anterior to the common iliac artery. At which anatomical location does the ureter have the narrowest caliber, making it a common site for ureteral stone impaction?
options: At the ureterovesical junction (UVJ) as it enters the bladder
At the pelvic brim crossing anterior to iliac vessels

questions.explanation: Aneuploidy refers to an abnormal number of individual chromosomes (not complete sets). This includes monosomy (loss of one chromosome) and trisomy (gain of one chromosome). Aneuploidy usually results from nondisjunction during meiosis and is the most common type of chromosomal abnormality.
questions.question: Aneuploidy refers to which chromosomal condition?

questions.explanation: By the end of the 8th week (final week of the embryonic period), the head takes up approximately half of the embryo. At this stage, all regions of limbs are apparent, limbs can move, the neck is established, intestines are still in the umbilical cord, and sexual differences exist but external sex cannot yet be determined.
questions.question: By the end of the 8th week, which measurement equals approximately half the embryo?
Which glial cell type acts as the macrophage of the CNS performing phagocytic functions?
questions.explanation: Microglia are the resident immune and phagocytic cells of the CNS derived from bone marrow monocyte precursors not neuroectoderm. They continuously survey the CNS parenchyma and respond to injury or infection by proliferating, migrating to the site, phagocytosing debris and pathogens, and presenting antigens. They are the CNS equivalent of the peripheral tissue macrophage within the Mononuclear Phagocyte System.

questions.question: The submucosal Meissner's plexus and myenteric Auerbach's plexus together constitute which nervous system component?
options: Intrinsic GI nervous system with independent control of motility and secretion
The sympathetic chain ganglia innervating the intestine
The somatic motor system controlling intestinal smooth muscle
The central nervous system extension into the gut wall
The lymphatic plexus draining intestinal villi
questions.explanation: The enteric nervous system is a complex intrinsic neural network within the GI wall containing approximately 500 million neurons organized into Meissner's submucosal plexus which regulates secretion and blood flow and Auerbach's myenteric plexus between circular and longitudinal muscle layers which controls motility. The ENS can function autonomously without input from the CNS and is often called the second brain. It is derived from neural crest cells and contains as many neurons as the spinal cord.

options: Presence of thick type I collagen bundles alternating with rows of chondrocytes
Abundance of elastic fibers providing flexibility and shape memory
Absence of any perichondrium and lack of any collagen fibers
Presence of hydroxyapatite mineralization identical to bone
Having the thinnest matrix with the highest water content of all cartilage types
questions.explanation: Fibrocartilage contains alternating layers of hyaline cartilage matrix and thick bundles of type I collagen fibers, with chondrocytes arranged in rows between the collagen bundles. This combination provides both compressive resistance from the proteoglycan matrix and high tensile strength from thick type I collagen, making it ideal for intervertebral discs, menisci, and pubic symphysis that must withstand both compression and tension.
questions.question: Fibrocartilage, found in intervertebral discs and pubic symphysis, is distinguished from hyaline and elastic cartilage by which of the following?

questions.explanation: The submucosa consists of dense irregular connective tissue that houses larger caliber blood vessels, lymphatics, and lymphoid tissue. This is in contrast to the lamina propria, which contains loose connective tissue with smaller vessels. The submucosa also contains the Meissner plexus of autonomic nerves.
questions.question: In a cross-section of the GIT wall, the layer identified as having the densest connective tissue with large blood and lymph vessels is the:
The secondary oocyte completes meiosis II at which time?
questions.explanation: The secondary oocyte is arrested in metaphase II and is ovulated in this state. It only completes meiosis II if fertilization occurs. The penetration of the sperm triggers completion of meiosis II, with extrusion of the second polar body. Without fertilization, the oocyte degenerates.

questions.question: Laminae I-IV are concerned with which sensations?
questions.explanation: Laminae I-IV are concerned with exteroceptive sensations (pain, temperature, touch). Laminae V-VI process proprioceptive information. This dorsoventral organization reflects functional specificity.

Weibel-Palade bodies are rod-shaped, membrane-bound storage granules in endothelial cells containing von Willebrand factor (vWF) and P-selectin. Upon stimulation by histamine, thrombin, or complement, they degranulate within seconds. Released vWF multimers bind to exposed subendothelial collagen and recruit platelets (platelet adhesion). P-selectin is inserted into the endothelial membrane, mediating rolling of neutrophils and monocytes — the first step of inflammatory cell emigration.
questions.question: The Weibel-Palade body is an organelle unique to vascular endothelial cells. Its contents include von Willebrand factor and P-selectin. When rapidly released (degranulation) in response to histamine or thrombin, these contents cause:

questions.explanation: The incisive foramen forms the midline landmark between the primary palate (derived from the intermaxillary segment) and the secondary palate (derived from the palatine shelves of the maxillary prominences). Anteriorly, the palatine shelves fuse with the primary palate at this location.
questions.question: The incisive foramen marks the junction between which two structures?
The circle of Willis provides which benefit?
questions.explanation: The circle of Willis provides collateral circulation if one vessel is occluded. It connects anterior and posterior circulations. Anatomical variations are common. Complete circles occur in only about 50% of people.

questions.question: Which nucleus controls the muscles of the tongue?
questions.explanation: The hypoglossal nucleus (CN XII) in the medulla controls the intrinsic and extrinsic muscles of the tongue (except palatoglossus, which is innervated by the vagus nerve via the nucleus ambiguus). This GSE nucleus lies beneath the hypoglossal trigone on the floor of the fourth ventricle near the midline. Unilateral lesions cause tongue deviation toward the affected side due to unopposed action of the contralateral genioglossus muscle, while bilateral lesions cause severe dysarthria and dysphagia.

questions.question: The gastric mucosa undergoes rapid renewal. Surface mucous cells of the stomach are replaced approximately every:
questions.explanation: Surface mucous cells of the stomach are among the most rapidly renewed cells in the body, with a turnover rate of approximately 3–7 days. This rapid replacement is driven by the pluripotent stem cells in the isthmus of gastric glands, which continuously produce new cells that migrate upward to the surface. This rapid renewal is essential for maintaining mucosal integrity against the highly acidic and proteolytic gastric environment.

From the renal papilla outward — through the minor calyces, major calyces, renal pelvis, ureter, and bladder — the entire collecting system is lined by transitional epithelium (urothelium). This barrier epithelium is impermeable to urea and urine, preventing urine reabsorption. Transitional epithelium can stretch considerably (2–6 layers when relaxed versus 2–3 when distended).
questions.question: The renal papilla is the apex of a medullary pyramid where urine drains into the minor calyx. It contains the openings of papillary ducts (ducts of Bellini). The epithelium lining the minor calyx that receives this urine is:
DiGeorge sequence results from abnormal development of which pharyngeal pouches?
questions.explanation: DiGeorge sequence results from abnormal development of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches, leading to thymic hypoplasia or aplasia and parathyroid abnormalities. This syndrome is often associated with cardiac defects and is related to deletion of chromosome 22q11.2.

The caudate nucleus and putamen are joined by interconnecting fibers through anterior internal capsule forming corpus striatum. These fibers create striations visible on sections. The corpus striatum receives most basal ganglia input.
questions.question: The corpus striatum consists of which structures?

questions.explanation: Wernicke's area is located in superior temporal gyrus of dominant hemisphere. It controls language comprehension. Lesions cause receptive aphasia. Patients speak fluently but with poor comprehension.
questions.question: Wernicke's area is located in which lobe?

options: Thymic lobule with cortex and medulla
Lymph node germinal center with B cells
Peyer's patches: ileal submucosal aggregates of lymphoid follicles
questions.question: A section through the ileum shows dome-shaped protrusions overlying lymphoid aggregates with follicle-associated epithelium containing M cells. This structure corresponds to which of the following?
questions.explanation: Peyer's patches are identified histologically as submucosal lymphoid aggregates underlying the intestinal epithelium in the ileum. Their characteristic features include multiple secondary follicles with germinal centers, a dome-shaped villus-free follicle-associated epithelium overlying each aggregate, M cells interspersed in the FAE, and an interfollicular zone containing T lymphocytes. These features distinguish Peyer's patches from solitary intestinal lymphoid nodules and other GALT structures.

The anterior commissure connects corresponding regions of the temporal lobes and olfactory structures of the two cerebral hemispheres. It has a smaller anterior portion connecting the olfactory bulbs and tracts, and a larger posterior portion connecting the temporal lobes including the amygdalae. The anterior commissure crosses in the lamina terminalis at the anterior wall of the third ventricle, anterior to the columns of the fornix. It is phylogenetically older than the corpus callosum and remains important for interhemispheric transfer of olfactory and temporal lobe information.
questions.question: The anterior commissure connects which structures?

A tissue section shows a gland composed of spherical follicles filled with homogeneous pink material lined by a single layer of cuboidal cells. This histological picture is most consistent with which of the following organs?
questions.explanation: The thyroid gland has a pathognomonic histological appearance of spherical follicles filled with eosinophilic homogeneous colloid which is iodinated thyroglobulin, lined by a single layer of follicular cells. The height of the follicular epithelium reflects activity: flat squamous cells in inactive thyroid and tall columnar cells in hyperstimulated thyroid. No other endocrine gland has this follicular colloid-filled architecture, making thyroid histology immediately recognizable.
options: Colloid-filled follicles lined by follicular epithelium
Parathyroid gland with chief cell cords
Pituitary gland with acidophils and basophils

questions.explanation: The celiac trunk supplies the abdominal foregut derivatives, including the abdominal esophagus, stomach, proximal duodenum (to the ampulla of Vater), liver, gallbladder, and pancreas. The superior mesenteric artery supplies the midgut, and the inferior mesenteric artery supplies the hindgut.
questions.question: The celiac trunk supplies which embryonic gut division?

questions.explanation: In the trachea and main bronchi, cartilage forms C-shaped rings. As bronchi branch, cartilage becomes irregular plates. At the level of bronchioles (< 1mm diameter), cartilage is completely absent, and the wall depends on elastic fibers and smooth muscle for support. Loss of cartilage at the bronchiolar level contributes to dynamic airway collapse during forced expiration in emphysema.
options: Irregular plates → C-rings → absent at bronchioles
C-rings → complete rings → absent at alveoli
C-rings remain constant in all bronchi
Cartilage is absent from bronchi but present in bronchioles
C-rings → irregular plates → absent at bronchioles
questions.question: As the bronchial tree branches, cartilage in the airway walls undergoes a specific structural change. Which sequence accurately describes this transformation?

questions.explanation: CNS white matter appears white due to the high lipid content of myelin sheaths wrapping the axons running through it. The lipid-rich myelin is white-appearing in fresh tissue and provides electrical insulation for saltatory conduction. Gray matter contains neuronal cell bodies, dendrites, unmyelinated axons, and most synapses, and appears gray due to the absence of myelin and the presence of many nuclei and neuropil.
questions.question: The white matter of the CNS appears white because it consists predominantly of which of the following?
options: Cell bodies of neurons containing pale cytoplasm
Myelinated axons with high lipid content appearing white
Blood vessels with whitish tunica adventitia
Collagen fibers providing structural support to the CNS

questions.explanation: Widened vestibular aqueduct is characteristic of Pendred syndrome, not Treacher Collins syndrome. Treacher Collins syndrome results from abnormal development of first and second pharyngeal arch derivatives. It includes malformed auricles, external auditory canal atresia, middle and inner ear anomalies, micrognathia, and facial bone hypoplasia.
questions.question: Treacher Collins syndrome is characterized by all of the following EXCEPT:

questions.explanation: The triad is the functional calcium-release unit of skeletal muscle excitation-contraction coupling, consisting of one transverse tubule, which is an invagination of the sarcolemma that rapidly propagates the action potential, flanked by two terminal cisternae of the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Voltage sensors called dihydropyridine receptors in the T-tubule mechanically open ryanodine receptors in the SR, releasing calcium into the cytoplasm to trigger contraction.
options: The M line of the sarcomere
The sarcolemma and its overlying myelin sheath
The Z line and attached titin proteins
One T-tubule flanked by two SR terminal cisternae
questions.question: In skeletal muscle, which structure represents the functional unit for calcium release that triggers contraction?

questions.explanation: The perineal body is formed from the tip of the urorectal septum at the point where it meets and divides the cloacal membrane. The perineal body is an important fibromuscular structure in the perineum where several muscles converge. It provides support for pelvic organs and is clinically important during childbirth and pelvic surgery.
questions.question: The perineal body is formed from:
Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) levels are increased in which conditions?
questions.explanation: Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) is produced by the fetal liver, yolk sac, and intestine. AFP levels are increased in maternal serum and amniotic fluid in cases of neural tube defects (NTDs) and ventral wall defects (VWDs). AFP is decreased in Down syndrome and trisomy 18.

Onuf's nucleus is located in lamina IX of S1-4 segments supplying anal and urethral sphincters. It is sexually dimorphic and resists degeneration in motor neuron disease. It provides somatic control of sphincters.
questions.question: Onuf's nucleus is located in which lamina and segments?

questions.explanation: The trigone of the bladder has mesodermal origin, derived from the caudal ends of the mesonephric ducts. The remainder of the bladder epithelium is endodermal, derived from the urogenital sinus. This dual origin explains the different epithelial characteristics: the trigone has unique smooth muscle and different innervation patterns.
questions.question: The trigone of the bladder has which embryological origin?

questions.explanation: There are seven functional components: somatic efferent, special visceral efferent, general visceral efferent, general visceral afferent, special visceral afferent, general somatic afferent, special somatic afferent. Each has specific nuclei.
questions.question: How many functional components can cranial nerve fibers belong to?
The cornea is formed from how many sources?
questions.explanation: The cornea forms from three sources: epithelial layer from surface epithelium, substantia propria from mesoderm (continuous with sclera), and epithelial layer over anterior chamber. This creates the transparent refractive structure.

questions.question: A urachal cyst results from:
questions.explanation: A urachal cyst results from partial persistence of the urachus, with the central portion remaining patent while the ends close. This creates a fluid-filled cyst between the bladder and umbilicus. Urachal cysts may become infected and require surgical excision. Complete patency results in a urachal fistula, while persistence at the bladder end causes a urachal sinus.

questions.question: An antibody produced by a plasma cell is specific for which of the following characteristics of the antigen that stimulated its production?
options: The molecular weight of the antigen only
The carbohydrate component of the antigen exclusively
The overall three-dimensional shape of the entire antigen molecule
The specific epitope (antigenic determinant) on the antigen
The foreign origin of the antigen regardless of its structure
questions.explanation: Each antibody recognizes a specific epitope (the precise molecular shape of a small region of the antigen) rather than the entire antigen or its molecular weight. Antibodies raised against one epitope will react with any molecule displaying that same or similar epitope (cross-reactivity). This exquisite epitope-specificity is the molecular basis of immunological specificity and is exploited in diagnostic tests and therapeutic antibodies.

questions.question: The insula is covered by opercula from which lobes?
questions.explanation: The insula (island of Reil) is buried in the depth of the lateral sulcus and covered by opercula (lips) from the frontal, parietal, and temporal lobes. These overlying cortical regions must be retracted to visualize the insular cortex. The insula is divided into anterior and posterior portions by the central insular sulcus and is involved in interoception, emotion, autonomic control, taste processing, and possibly pain perception. Insular strokes can cause subtle deficits including ageusia, autonomic dysfunction, and sometimes pure motor or sensory deficits.
Corticonuclear fibers pass through the corona radiata to the genu of internal capsule. They synapse with cranial nerve nuclei in brainstem. Those traveling beyond midbrain run on medial side of crus.
questions.question: Corticonuclear fibers pass through which part of internal capsule?

questions.explanation: Neuroblasts have a large deeply stained nucleus and pale cytoplasm, distinguishing them from other cell types. They arise from neuroepithelial cells after closure of the neural tube. These cells differentiate into neurons of various types.
questions.question: Neuroblasts are characterized by which features?
options: Large deeply stained nucleus, pale cytoplasm

questions.question: Which cranial nerves have nuclei in the mesencephalon basal plate?
questions.explanation: The somatic efferent nuclei in the basal plate are CN3 and CN4, which supply extraocular muscles. CN3 also contains the Edinger-Westphal nucleus. These motor nuclei are medially placed in the tegmentum.

questions.question: A protein that spans the entire phospholipid bilayer, with domains both inside and outside the cell, is classified as which of the following?
questions.explanation: Integral (transmembrane) proteins span the entire thickness of the lipid bilayer and have exposed domains on both the cytoplasmic and extracellular faces. They include receptors, ion channels, transporters, and structural proteins (like integrins). Unlike peripheral proteins, they cannot be extracted without disrupting the membrane with detergents.

The cerebral aqueduct (aqueduct of Sylvius) connects the third ventricle to the fourth ventricle, allowing CSF to flow between these cavities. This narrow channel runs through the midbrain dorsal to the cerebral peduncles and ventral to the tectum. Obstruction of the cerebral aqueduct, whether congenital or acquired, causes obstructive hydrocephalus with dilation of the lateral and third ventricles while the fourth ventricle remains normal or small.
questions.question: Through which structure does CSF flow from the third to the fourth ventricle?

questions.explanation: Renal ectopia refers to an abnormally positioned kidney, most commonly pelvic kidney (failure to ascend) or crossed renal ectopia (kidney on wrong side). Simple ectopic kidneys are usually unilateral and asymptomatic. The ectopic kidney may receive blood supply from nearby vessels and is prone to trauma, infection, and obstruction due to its abnormal position.
questions.question: Renal ectopia refers to:

questions.explanation: The inner epithelial lining of the mucosa acts as the primary barrier separating the potentially harmful luminal environment from underlying tissues. This epithelium is also the interface for absorption and secretion. The lamina propria, submucosa, and other layers provide structural support but are not the primary barrier.
questions.question: Which component of the GIT wall forms an important physical barrier between luminal contents and the body's deeper tissues?
The dentate nucleus projects primarily to which structure via the superior cerebellar peduncle?
questions.explanation: The dentate nucleus, the largest deep cerebellar nucleus, projects primarily to the contralateral red nucleus and thalamus (specifically the ventrolateral nucleus) via the superior cerebellar peduncle. These projections then relay to the motor cortex, completing a cerebrocerebellar loop important for planning and coordination of voluntary movements. The dentate nucleus receives input from the lateral cerebellar hemispheres and is involved in timing and precision of movements.

ADH (vasopressin), released from the posterior pituitary in response to increased plasma osmolality or decreased blood volume, acts on V2 receptors on principal cells of the collecting duct. This triggers insertion of aquaporin-2 water channels into the apical membrane, making the collecting duct permeable to water. Water then moves osmotically into the hypertonic medullary interstitium, concentrating the urine. Absence of ADH causes diabetes insipidus.
questions.question: The collecting duct plays a central role in final urine concentration. Which hormone directly acts on principal cells of the collecting duct to insert aquaporin-2 channels?

questions.explanation: As a follicle grows beyond the primary stage, stromal cells surrounding the granulosa cell layer differentiate into theca cells. The theca organizes into two layers: theca interna (secretes androgens under LH stimulation, which granulosa cells aromatize to estrogens) and theca externa (fibrous structural support). This two-cell, two-gonadotropin model of sex steroid synthesis is fundamental to understanding ovarian function and PCOS pathophysiology.
questions.question: In the development of ovarian follicles, thecal cells differentiate from which surrounding ovarian structure?
At birth, the spinal cord ends at which vertebral level?
questions.explanation: At birth, the spinal cord ends at the lower border of L3, while in adulthood it ends at L2/L3 boundary. At 3 months of intrauterine life, it extends the entire length of the vertebral column. This differential growth creates the cauda equina.

questions.question: Lysosomes are organelles that contain hydrolytic enzymes and primarily function to perform which of the following?
questions.explanation: Lysosomes are membrane-bound vesicles containing over 50 acid hydrolases active at pH ~4.5, enabling intracellular digestion of phagocytosed material (heterophagy), worn-out organelles (autophagy), and cellular debris. Their role in fusing with phagosomes (forming phagolysosomes) is central to macrophage-mediated immunity. Lysosomal storage diseases result from deficiency of specific hydrolases.
options: Digest ingested material, worn-out organelles, and debris

questions.explanation: Crossing over (exchange of chromosome segments between homologous chromosomes) occurs during prophase I of meiosis, specifically during the pachytene stage. This occurs at points called chiasmata and results in new combinations of genes, increasing genetic diversity.
questions.question: Crossing over between homologous chromosomes occurs during which meiotic stage?

questions.explanation: The fourth ventricle communicates with the subarachnoid space through three openings: the midline foramen of Magendie and the two lateral foramina of Luschka. The foramen of Magendie opens into the cerebellomedullary cistern (cisterna magna), while the foramina of Luschka open into the pontine cistern at the cerebellopontine angles. These openings are critical for CSF circulation; their obstruction causes internal hydrocephalus with dilated ventricles.
questions.question: Which foramen allows CSF to exit the fourth ventricle into the subarachnoid space?
The lesser omentum contains which structures in its free edge?
questions.explanation: The lesser omentum contains the portal triad (hepatic artery, portal vein, and bile duct) in its free right edge, known as the hepatoduodenal ligament. This free edge forms the anterior boundary of the epiploic foramen (of Winslow). The hepatogastric ligament is the portion extending between liver and lesser curvature of stomach.

Dysmetria is impaired distance or range judgment in voluntary movements, manifesting as overshooting (hypermetria) or undershooting (hypometria) when reaching for targets. It reflects the cerebellum's role in calibrating movement amplitude and direction. Dysmetria is tested by finger-nose-finger and heel-shin tests where patients overshoot or undershoot the target. This deficit results from impaired internal models of movement dynamics and inability to use sensory feedback effectively to correct ongoing movements, seen with cerebellar hemisphere lesions.
questions.question: Dysmetria is best defined as:

questions.explanation: Ask-Upmark kidney refers to segmental renal hypoplasia with focal cortical scarring and atrophy, typically affecting the upper pole. It may be congenital or acquired (from vesicoureteral reflux). The condition is associated with hypertension. Histologically, it shows decreased nephrons in affected segments with irregular scarring. It differs from true renal hypoplasia, which involves the entire kidney.
questions.question: Ask-Upmark kidney refers to:
Extrahepatic biliary atresia typically presents with:
questions.explanation: Extrahepatic biliary atresia typically presents with jaundice developing soon after birth due to obstruction of bile flow. This is the most common serious anomaly of the biliary system. If uncorrected surgically, it leads to progressive liver damage and death. Early diagnosis and surgical intervention (Kasai procedure) are critical.

questions.question: The chorion frondosum forms which part of the placenta?
questions.explanation: The chorion frondosum (villous chorion) forms the fetal portion of the placenta. This is the part of the chorion where villi are well-developed and persist, in contrast to the chorion laeve (smooth chorion) where villi degenerate. The chorion frondosum is located at the embryonic pole.

questions.question: The posterior spinocerebellar tract enters cerebellum via which peduncle?
questions.explanation: Posterior spinocerebellar tract fibers synapse with thoracic nucleus cells and run to cerebellum via inferior cerebellar peduncle. They travel through the medulla. This pathway conveys proprioceptive information.

Intermediate filaments (8–12 nm) provide the primary mechanical support for cells, reinforcing their shape against deformation and anchoring the nucleus and other organelles. Different cell types express different intermediate filament proteins (vimentin in mesenchymal cells, cytokeratins in epithelial cells, desmin in muscle, neurofilaments in neurons). Their stability makes them useful as cell-type identification markers in pathology.
options: Generate contractile forces in non-muscle cells
Form mitotic spindle during cell division
Reinforce the cell mechanically and maintain organelle position
Transport vesicles from ER to Golgi
questions.question: Intermediate filaments, the cytoskeletal elements between actin and microtubules in diameter, primarily serve which of the following roles?

options: It eliminates the need for tissue fixation
It achieves greater magnification than electron microscopy
It stains all nuclei uniformly without antibodies
It visualizes tissue sections in real time without preparation
Fluorescent-labeled antibodies localize specific antigens with high specificity
questions.explanation: Immunofluorescence uses antibodies conjugated to fluorescent dyes to bind specific tissue antigens, allowing precise localization of target molecules with high sensitivity. When excited by specific wavelengths of light, the fluorescent labels emit distinguishable colors pinpointing the molecule's location. This technique is invaluable in diagnostic pathology and research for identifying specific cell types and disease markers.
questions.question: Which of the following fluorescence microscopy properties makes it particularly useful for localizing specific proteins or antibodies in tissues?
Langerhans cells first appear in fetal skin at:
questions.explanation: Langerhans cells, which are antigen-presenting cells of the immune system, appear in fetal skin at 6 weeks of gestation. They demonstrate functional activity at around 12-14 weeks of gestation. These cells are part of the skin-associated lymphoid tissue (SALT) and play crucial roles in adaptive immunity.

The hyaloid vessels, which invade the optic cup through the choroid fissure, primarily supply the developing lens during intrauterine life. These vessels form a delicate network between the lens and retina. After birth, the hyaloid vessels normally regress, and their persistence can form cords or cysts.
questions.question: Hyaloid vessels primarily function to supply which developing structure during intrauterine life?

questions.explanation: The lamina propria is composed of loose connective tissue — not dense fibrous collagen. It contains blood vessels, lymphatics, lymphocytes, plasma cells, smooth muscle cells, and small glands. Dense connective tissue is a feature of the submucosa, not the lamina propria.
questions.question: The lamina propria of the GIT mucosa characteristically contains all of the following EXCEPT:

questions.explanation: Skeletal muscle has classic triads with one T-tubule flanked by two SR terminal cisternae. Cardiac muscle has dyads with one T-tubule and one SR cistern. Additionally, skeletal muscle excitation-contraction coupling is entirely SR-dependent through mechanical linkage via dihydropyridine-ryanodine receptor interaction, while cardiac muscle requires calcium-induced calcium release from SR triggered by calcium entry through L-type channels. This difference explains why cardiac muscle is affected by extracellular calcium concentration while skeletal is not.
questions.question: The triad of excitation-contraction coupling in skeletal muscle differs from the dyad in cardiac muscle in which of the following ways?
options: Skeletal muscle uses dyads while cardiac muscle uses triads
Both cardiac and skeletal muscle use identical triads
Cardiac muscle has no T-tubules unlike skeletal muscle
Skeletal muscle does not require calcium release from SR for contraction
Skeletal: two SR cisternae per T-tubule (triads); cardiac: one SR cisterna (dyads)

questions.question: On a histological section, the pharyngeal wall shows skeletal muscle throughout with no smooth muscle. This distinguishes the pharynx from the esophagus because the esophagus contains:
options: Smooth muscle throughout its entire length
Cardiac muscle in the lower third
Skeletal muscle only in the upper third, mixed
Exclusively smooth muscle in its upper third
questions.explanation: The pharynx contains skeletal muscle throughout, reflecting its role in the voluntary phase of swallowing. The esophagus differs markedly: the upper third has skeletal muscle (voluntary deglutition), the middle third has mixed skeletal and smooth muscle (transition), and the lower third has smooth muscle only (involuntary peristalsis). This progressive change from skeletal to smooth muscle is a classic and regularly examined feature of esophageal histology.

questions.question: Nephrocalcinosis is calcification of the renal parenchyma. It is associated with which metabolic condition causing elevated urinary calcium and supersaturation of calcium salts?
questions.explanation: Nephrocalcinosis (renal parenchymal calcification) is most commonly caused by hypercalciuria from primary hyperparathyroidism (elevated PTH increases renal calcium loss) and distal renal tubular acidosis (RTA type 1 — inability to acidify urine causes calcium phosphate supersaturation). Other causes include medullary sponge kidney, hyperoxaluria, and sarcoidosis (elevated calcitriol). Dystrophic calcification can also occur in areas of papillary necrosis or chronic pyelonephritis.

questions.question: Hirschsprung disease results from failure of:
questions.explanation: Hirschsprung disease results from failure of neural crest cells to migrate into the wall of the colon, causing absence of parasympathetic ganglia in affected segments. This leads to loss of peristalsis, fecal retention, and abdominal distention (megacolon). The sigmoid colon and rectum are most commonly affected.

The paraventricular nucleus (lining the third ventricle) and supraoptic nucleus (above the optic chiasma) of the anterior hypothalamic group produce oxytocin and antidiuretic hormone (ADH/vasopressin). These peptide hormones are synthesized in the neuronal cell bodies, transported down axons through the pituitary stalk, and released from nerve terminals in the posterior pituitary (neurohypophysis). These nuclei have rich blood supply and are connected to the neurohypophysis via the hypothalamohypophyseal tract.
questions.question: Which hypothalamic nuclei are specifically involved in producing oxytocin and ADH?
The malleus and incus ossicles are derived from which pharyngeal arch cartilage?
questions.explanation: The first two auditory ossicles, malleus and incus, are derived from the cartilage of the first pharyngeal arch (Meckel's cartilage). The third ossicle, the stapes, is derived from the second pharyngeal arch (Reichert's cartilage). These ossicles become embedded in mesenchyme as the tympanic cavity develops.

questions.question: The leptomeninges consist of which layers?
questions.explanation: Mesenchyme surrounding neural tube forms primordial meninges. The outer layer thickens into dura mater. The inner layer forms arachnoid and pia mater (leptomeninges).

The definitive kidney formed from the metanephros becomes functional near the 12th week, when urine begins to be passed into the amniotic cavity. During fetal life, the placenta performs excretory functions. Urine mixed with amniotic fluid is swallowed by the fetus and recycled through the kidneys.
questions.question: The definitive kidney becomes functional near which week?

options: The wall of the heart ventricular myocardium
The iris and ciliary body of the eye
questions.explanation: The ventricular myocardium of the heart is composed of cardiac muscle not smooth muscle. Cardiac muscle is a striated involuntary muscle type restricted to the heart and great vessel roots. Smooth muscle forms the walls of hollow viscera including GI tract, bladder, and uterus, the tunica media of blood vessel walls, airways, and the iris and ciliary body of the eye.
questions.question: The prominent locations of smooth muscle in the body include all of the following EXCEPT which of the following?
The heart and blood vessels are derived from which germ layer?
questions.explanation: The heart and all blood vessels are mesodermal in origin. The mesoderm constitutes the cardiogenic field or area, which is closely related to the pericardial cavity and heart tube. This cardiogenic mesoderm differentiates to form the endocardium, myocardium, and epicardium.

questions.question: The urethra in females is shorter than in males. The female urethra is lined by which epithelium in its middle portion?
questions.explanation: The female urethra (approximately 4cm long) transitions from transitional epithelium near the bladder to non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium near the external urethral orifice, with patches of pseudostratified or stratified columnar epithelium in between. This epithelial variability makes the female urethra susceptible to ascending infections, contributing to the higher incidence of UTIs in women compared to men.

questions.question: How many types of glial cells exist?
questions.explanation: There are 4 types of glial cells: astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, microglia, and ependymal cells. Each has different morphology, function and origin. They do not participate directly in synaptic interactions.

questions.question: The spinal cord measures approximately what length in adults?
questions.explanation: The spinal cord measures about 42-45 cm in adults and 1.5 cm in diameter. It is enclosed within the vertebral canal covered by meninges. It extends from foramen magnum to conus medullaris.

The internal capsule carries both ascending (thalamocortical) and descending (corticospinal, corticobulbar) fibers. It is a crucial white matter structure. Lesions cause significant deficits. It separates basal ganglia.
questions.question: The internal capsule carries which fibers?
The most common cause of bilateral hydronephrosis in male fetuses is:
questions.explanation: The most common cause of bilateral hydronephrosis in male fetuses is posterior urethral valves (PUV), which cause bladder outlet obstruction. PUV are membranous folds in the posterior urethra that obstruct urinary flow. Prenatal ultrasound shows bilateral hydroureteronephrosis, distended bladder, and oligohydramnios. Postnatal endoscopic valve ablation is required. Severe cases cause renal dysplasia and chronic kidney disease.

questions.question: The parathyroid glands contain chief cells and oxyphil cells. The function of oxyphil cells is which of the following?
options: They produce PTH as the sole parathyroid hormone source
They produce calcitonin supplementing thyroid C cells
They produce aldosterone in hypoparathyroid states
They are the sole producers of vitamin D binding protein
Post-pubertal cells with abundant mitochondria; may be exhausted chief cells
questions.explanation: Oxyphil cells appear after puberty in increasing numbers and have abundant mitochondria giving them their eosinophilic granular cytoplasm. Their function remains incompletely understood. They are thought to represent a transitional or exhausted form of chief cells that may retain some limited PTH secretory capacity. In parathyroid adenoma and hyperplasia, oxyphil cells may proliferate. They do not have the prominent Golgi or secretory granules of active chief cells.

questions.question: In the tunica adventitia of large arteries, which structural proteins provide tensile strength and prevent overdistension?
questions.explanation: The tunica adventitia is rich in type I collagen fibers (providing tensile strength and preventing overdistension at high pressures) and type III collagen (providing flexibility). Elastin fibers in the adventitia provide elasticity, while type I collagen acts as a 'safety net' limiting vessel diameter when maximally distended. Vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome involves type III collagen deficiency, causing fragile vessel walls prone to spontaneous arterial rupture.

Chorionic villus sampling (CVS) has a risk of fetal loss of approximately 1%. Trophoblast cells are obtained by needle through the mother's abdominal and uterine wall under ultrasound guidance. There is also a risk of limb defects if the procedure is performed too early (before 10 weeks).
questions.question: Chorionic villus sampling (CVS) has what risk of fetal loss?

questions.explanation: The choroid fissure is a ventral invagination of optic stalk into which hyaloid vessels grow. Nerve fibers from neural retina converge to the optic stalk. The fissure normally closes completely.
questions.question: The choroid fissure allows entry of which structure?

questions.explanation: The caudate nucleus is comma-shaped with demonstrable bulbous head, body and tail attached to amygdaloid body. Its convexity projects into the ventricle. Internal capsule fibers run in its concavity.
questions.question: The caudate nucleus has which shape?
Golgi Type I neurons are characterized by which feature?
questions.explanation: Golgi Type I neurons are large multipolar cells like Purkinje and pyramidal cells. They have long axons projecting to distant targets. Golgi Type II are small multipolar cells.

The foramen cecum marks the site of origin of the thyroid gland at the junction of the anterior two-thirds and posterior one-third of the tongue. It represents the point where the thyroglossal duct originally descended from the floor of the pharynx. This is a normal anatomical landmark in adults.
questions.question: The foramen cecum marks the origin of which structure?

questions.explanation: Muscles of the first pharyngeal arch include the muscles of mastication (temporalis, medial and lateral pterygoids), anterior belly of digastric, mylohyoid, tensor tympani, and tensor palatini muscles. These muscles are innervated by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V).
questions.question: Muscles of mastication are derived from which pharyngeal arch?

questions.explanation: The atrioventricular cushions initially divide the AV canal into right and left AV canals. Lateral AV cushions then appear and further narrow the canals, which are later closed by the formation of valves. The endocardial cushions are crucial for proper heart septation.
questions.question: The atrioventricular (AV) cushions initially divide the AV canal into how many canals?
Parallel fibers in the cerebellar cortex are formed by axons of which cells?
questions.explanation: Parallel fibers are the unmyelinated axons of granule cells that ascend to the molecular layer and bifurcate, running parallel to the cerebellar folia (perpendicular to Purkinje cell dendritic trees). Each parallel fiber synapses with hundreds of Purkinje cells along its length, while each Purkinje cell receives input from approximately 200,000 parallel fibers. This arrangement allows widespread distribution of mossy fiber input and enables the cerebellum to integrate diverse information for motor coordination.

questions.question: Damage to the posterior two-thirds of the internal capsule's posterior limb primarily affects which system?
questions.explanation: The anterior two-thirds of the posterior limb contains corticospinal fibers traveling from cortical motor areas to anterior horn cells of the spinal cord. These fibers form the pyramidal tract, most of which decussate in the lower medulla to form the lateral corticospinal tract. Hemorrhage or thrombosis of the lenticulostriate arteries in this region results in contralateral skeletal muscle paralysis and affects Broca's speech area when the left side is involved.

The posterior cerebral artery connects to internal carotid by posterior communicating artery completing the circle of Willis. This allows anastomotic blood flow during occlusion. It is an important collateral circulation.
questions.question: The circle of Willis is completed by which arteries?

questions.explanation: Fetal lobulation represents a normal developmental stage where the surface of the kidney shows distinct lobes corresponding to individual pyramids. This lobulation is prominent in fetal and neonatal kidneys but typically disappears during infancy as growth smooths the surface. Persistent lobulation into childhood is usually a benign variation. True scarring (from reflux or infection) creates irregular, retracted areas, not smooth lobules.
questions.question: Fetal lobulation of the kidneys represents:

questions.explanation: Contraction of muscles depends on pattern and rate of firing of spinal motor neurons. These are bombarded by an array of pathways. Motor neurons are the final common pathway.
questions.question: Muscle contraction depends on the firing pattern of which cells?

options: Fixed tissues take up stain more selectively
Cells rapidly deteriorate through drying out and autolysis after removal
Fixation prevents tissue shrinkage during microtomy
Unfixed tissues react with embedding media
Blood supply continues to alter tissue composition after removal
questions.explanation: After removal from the body, tissues lose their blood supply, causing cellular enzymes (lysosomes) to begin digesting cellular components (autolysis) and the tissue to dry out. Immediate fixation halts these processes by cross-linking proteins and denaturating enzymes. Delay in fixation results in artefacts that compromise histological and diagnostic interpretation.
questions.question: Which of the following correctly explains why tissue fixation must be performed immediately after tissue removal from the body?
The structural resilience of bone — its ability to resist fracture — is attributed primarily to which of its components?
questions.explanation: Bone's unique mechanical properties result from its composite structure: the mineral phase (hydroxyapatite ~50% dry weight) provides compressive hardness and rigidity, while the organic matrix (type I collagen ~35% dry weight) provides tensile strength and resilience. Demineralized bone is flexible and tough like rubber; deproteinized bone is brittle and shatters easily. The combination creates the optimal structural material found nowhere else in nature.
options: The vascular channels in Haversian systems
The osteocyte network in lacunae and canaliculi
The non-collagenous proteins like osteocalcin and osteopontin only
The inorganic mineral component hydroxyapatite alone
Organic type I collagen provides resilience; mineral phase provides hardness

questions.explanation: A pelvic kidney results from failure of normal ascent from the pelvis to the abdomen. The kidney remains in the pelvis, often receiving blood supply from nearby vessels (iliac or aortic branches). Pelvic kidneys are usually functional and asymptomatic but may be prone to infection, obstruction, or trauma. They should not be mistaken for pathology.
questions.question: A pelvic kidney results from:

questions.explanation: Somatic efferent CN12 forms a motor column continuous cranio-caudally and supplies tongue muscles. It is the most medial motor column. Lesions cause tongue deviation.
questions.question: CN XII supplies which structure?

questions.explanation: Tendons are the functional link between muscle and bone that transmit contractile force to the skeleton, producing movement. They form by convergence of the three muscle connective tissue layers at the muscle's ends, consisting predominantly of parallel type I collagen bundles of dense regular connective tissue with sparse tenocytes aligned between the fiber bundles. Tendons are among the strongest biological tissues per unit cross-sectional area.
questions.question: Which connective tissue element specifically transmits the force of skeletal muscle contraction to the skeleton?
options: Convergence of epimysium, perimysium, and endomysium
Endomysium surrounding individual muscle fibers directly

questions.question: The acrosome of the sperm is derived from which organelle?
questions.explanation: The acrosome forms from the Golgi apparatus during spermiogenesis. It contains enzymes (including hyaluronidase and acrosin) that are essential for penetrating the corona radiata and zona pellucida during fertilization. Acrosome formation is one of the key events in spermiogenesis.

questions.question: Neuroglia are approximately how many times more numerous than neurons?
questions.explanation: Neuroglia are about 10 times more numerous than neurons. They are supporting cells with functional interdependence with neurons. They maintain neuronal health and signaling ability.

questions.question: The sulcus limitans in mesencephalon separates which regions?
questions.explanation: The sulcus limitans forms the boundary between the basal (motor) and alar (sensory) portions in mesencephalon. The basal plate contains motor cell groups. The alar plate mediates sensory functions.

The trigeminal sensory nuclei (main sensory, spinal, and mesencephalic nuclei) represent the general somatic afferent (GSA) column, receiving pain, temperature, touch, and proprioception from the face and head via cranial nerve V. The GSA column is lateral to visceral afferent components in the brainstem organization. The spinal trigeminal nucleus extends from the pons through the medulla to the upper cervical spinal cord, while the main sensory nucleus processes discriminative touch and the mesencephalic nucleus handles proprioception.
questions.question: Which nucleus represents the general somatic afferent column in the brainstem?
Pancreatic acinar cells synthesize and store digestive enzymes as inactive zymogens to prevent autodigestion. Trypsinogen is the key precursor enzyme activated in the duodenal lumen by which enzyme?
questions.explanation: Trypsinogen, secreted by pancreatic acinar cells, is activated in the duodenal lumen by enterokinase (enteropeptidase) — a specific protease anchored to the duodenal brush border epithelium. Active trypsin then activates all other pancreatic zymogens (chymotrypsinogen, proelastase, procarboxypeptidase) in a cascade. In acute pancreatitis, premature intrapancreatic activation of trypsinogen (by cathepsin B or other triggers) initiates this destructive cascade within the pancreas itself.

Meckel's diverticulum can result from persistence of the vitelline duct (yolk stalk). This is the most common congenital malformation of the gastrointestinal tract, occurring in about 2% of the population. It is typically located about 2 feet from the ileocecal valve on the ileum.
questions.question: Meckel's diverticulum represents persistence of which embryonic structure?

questions.explanation: Type II pneumocytes (alveolar epithelial cells) begin producing surfactant around 24 weeks (late 6th to early 7th month). Surfactant reduces surface tension in alveoli, preventing collapse during expiration. Insufficient surfactant production is a major cause of respiratory distress syndrome in premature infants.
questions.question: Type II pneumocytes begin producing surfactant around:
Nissl bodies together with Golgi apparatus serve which function?
questions.explanation: Nissl bodies (RER) together with Golgi bodies are the neuron's biosynthetic machinery. They manufacture neurotransmitters which neurons secrete in large quantities. Products are transported to axon terminus.

The intraembryonic coelom appears as a horseshoe-shaped cavity in the cardiogenic area and lateral mesoderm during the 4th week of development. The bend of this cavity indicates the future pericardial cavity, while the limbs indicate future pleural and peritoneal cavities. This structure initially opens laterally into the extraembryonic coelom.
questions.question: The intraembryonic coelom first appears as a horseshoe-shaped cavity in which week of development?
Duplication of the ureter results from:
questions.explanation: Duplication of the ureter results from development of two ureteric buds from the mesonephric duct instead of one. Complete duplication produces two separate ureters, while incomplete duplication (bifid ureter) produces a Y-shaped ureter. The duplicated ureter may have ectopic opening into the urethra or vagina.

questions.question: Meningomyelocele involves herniation of which structures?
questions.explanation: Meningomyelocele (spina bifida cystica) involves herniation of meninges and spinal cord through vertebral defect. It causes neurological deficits. It requires surgical repair. It is associated with hydrocephalus.

questions.question: The sclera of the eye primarily serves which function?
options: Generating aqueous humor through active transport
Tough fibrous outer coat maintaining eyeball shape
Controlling pupil size through involuntary muscle contraction
Regulating intraocular pressure through trabecular drainage
questions.explanation: The sclera is the tough opaque white fibrous outer coat continuous with the cornea anteriorly formed by densely packed randomly interwoven collagen bundles. It maintains the globe's shape against intraocular pressure, protects intraocular contents, and provides attachment sites for the six extraocular muscles. Its irregular collagen arrangement compared to the cornea's regular lattice makes it opaque rather than transparent.

questions.question: The internal carotid artery supplies approximately which portion of cerebral blood flow?
questions.explanation: The internal carotid artery and its branches supply the anterior two-thirds of the brain, constituting the anterior circulation. This includes most of the cerebral hemispheres, basal ganglia, and internal capsule. The vertebrobasilar system and posterior cerebral arteries form the posterior circulation, supplying the brainstem, cerebellum, occipital lobes, and inferior temporal regions.

questions.question: Renal agenesis on ultrasound may show which associated finding?
questions.explanation: Bilateral renal agenesis shows oligohydramnios (decreased amniotic fluid) on ultrasound because the fetus cannot produce urine. Unilateral renal agenesis typically shows normal amniotic fluid because the contralateral kidney produces adequate urine. Other ultrasound findings in bilateral renal agenesis include non-visualization of kidneys and bladder. Oligohydramnios impairs ultrasound visualization and causes Potter sequence.

Greatest length (GL) is used to measure embryos during the 3rd and early 4th weeks when the embryo is relatively straight. After this period, crown-rump length (CRL) or sitting height is used as the neck-rump measurement. Crown-heel length (CHL) or standing height may also be used for measurements.
questions.question: The greatest length (GL) measurement is used to measure embryos during which weeks?
Umbilical herniation with intestines occurs during which week?
questions.explanation: Umbilical herniation with intestine occurs during the 7th week of development. This is a normal developmental event. During this week, notches also appear between the digital rays of the hand. The intestines herniate into the umbilical cord due to rapid growth and limited abdominal space.

questions.question: The paraxial mesoderm gives rise to which head structure?
questions.explanation: The paraxial mesoderm gives rise to all voluntary muscles of the craniofacial region, the floor of the brain case, a small portion of the occipital region, dermis and connective tissues in the dorsal head region, and meninges caudal to the prosencephalon.

options: Na+/K+-ATPase pumping H+ into the lumen
Passive diffusion of H+ through tight junctions
Na+/H+ exchanger on the apical membrane
questions.explanation: Parietal cells secrete HCl via H+/K+-ATPase (the proton pump) on the intracellular canalicular membranes. This enzyme pumps H+ into the canalicular lumen in exchange for K+, driven by ATP hydrolysis. CO2 + H2O (via carbonic anhydrase) generates H+ and HCO3-. Cl- enters the lumen via Cl- channels. Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs like omeprazole) irreversibly block H+/K+-ATPase, the most effective pharmacological reduction of gastric acid.
questions.question: The stomach secretes approximately 2–3 liters of gastric juice daily. The acidic gastric juice is produced by parietal cells via which molecular mechanism?
The spleen performs which of the following multiple functions?
questions.explanation: The spleen has three main functions: blood filtration where red pulp macrophages in splenic cords and sinuses remove aged damaged or parasitized RBCs and blood-borne pathogens; immune function where white pulp contains T cell periarterial lymphoid sheaths and B cell lymphoid follicles that mount immune responses to blood-borne antigens; and blood reservoir storing approximately 200 mL blood released during sympathetic activation.
options: Produces thymic hormones for T cell maturation
Filters lymph from peripheral tissues only
Is the primary site of red blood cell production in adults
Functions only as an iron storage organ
Filters blood, removes old RBCs, and provides immune surveillance

questions.explanation: At 3rd month IUL, spinal cord length equals vertebral column length. Differential growth causes disparity. In newborns it ends at L2/3, in adults at L1.
questions.question: At the 3rd month of intrauterine life, where does the spinal cord end?

questions.explanation: The cauda equina consists of lumbosacral nerve roots that descend almost parallel to the filum terminale. This results from the differential growth of the vertebral column and spinal cord. The obliquity of spinal nerves increases caudally.
questions.question: The cauda equina is formed by which structures?

questions.explanation: Smooth ER (SER) is the primary site of lipid synthesis, steroid hormone biosynthesis, and detoxification. Steroid-secreting cells (adrenocortical cells, Leydig cells, luteal cells) are therefore rich in SER. Unlike rough ER, SER lacks ribosomes and appears smooth in electron micrographs. The agranular appearance reflects its functional specialization for lipid metabolism rather than protein synthesis.
questions.question: A cell produces large quantities of steroid hormones. Which organelle is most likely most abundant in this cell's cytoplasm?
Most neurons in the CNS are which type?
questions.explanation: Most neurons in the CNS are multipolar with many dendrites and one axon. This includes Purkinje cells, pyramidal cells and motor neurons. Bipolar neurons are found in special sensory organs.

questions.question: Polycystic kidney disease (PKD) causes progressive replacement of renal parenchyma by cysts. The autosomal dominant form (ADPKD) involves mutations in which genes?
questions.explanation: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) is caused by mutations in PKD1 (encoding polycystin-1, chromosome 16 — 85% of cases) or PKD2 (encoding polycystin-2, chromosome 4 — 15% of cases). Polycystins are membrane proteins involved in mechanosensation, cell-cell and cell-matrix interactions, and fluid flow sensing. Their dysfunction causes collecting duct cells to proliferate and form cysts. ADPKD is the most common hereditary kidney disease, causing end-stage renal disease in 50% of patients by age 60.

questions.question: The planum temporale is typically larger in which hemisphere?
questions.explanation: The planum temporale, located on the superior temporal surface posterior to Heschl's gyrus, is typically larger in the left hemisphere (approximately 65% of individuals). This asymmetry is present from early development and correlates with language dominance, as the planum temporale is part of Wernicke's area involved in language comprehension. This represents one of the clearest anatomical asymmetries between hemispheres and may relate to left hemisphere specialization for language in most individuals.

options: Hyaluronic acid and heparan sulfate predominantly
Type II collagen and aggrecan proteoglycan
questions.question: Ground substance of bone matrix contains which important non-collagenous proteins that participate in mineralization regulation?
questions.explanation: Bone matrix non-collagenous proteins include osteocalcin which binds calcium and regulates mineral crystal growth, osteopontin which mediates osteoclast attachment and cell signaling, and bone sialoprotein which nucleates hydroxyapatite crystallization. These proteins are synthesized by osteoblasts and regulate mineralization. Osteocalcin is also used as a serum marker of bone formation activity in metabolic bone disease assessment.

questions.question: The GI tract develops primarily from which germ layer?
questions.explanation: The GI tract develops primarily from the endodermal germ layer, which forms the epithelial lining of the digestive tube. The endoderm covers the ventral surface of the embryo and forms the roof of the yolk sac. The connective tissue, smooth muscle, and blood vessels are mesodermal derivatives.

The left sixth aortic arch is connected to the aorta through the ductus arteriosus during fetal life. This allows blood from the right ventricle to bypass the non-functioning fetal lungs and enter the systemic circulation. The ductus arteriosus normally closes after birth.
questions.question: The ductus arteriosus connects the left sixth aortic arch to which vessel during fetal life?
The internal carotid system consists of which arteries?
questions.explanation: The internal carotid system consists of anterior and middle cerebral arteries, anterior choroidal and posterior communicating arteries. The internal carotid bifurcates alongside the optic chiasma. It supplies most of the cerebral hemispheres.

options: Two layers from the start of the esophagus
No muscularis mucosae in the esophagus
A single longitudinal layer in the upper
questions.question: The esophageal muscularis mucosae is noteworthy because it consists of:
questions.explanation: The muscularis mucosae of the esophagus begins as a single longitudinal layer in the upper esophagus and develops into two layers (inner circular + outer longitudinal) in the lower esophagus. This is an important histological feature distinguishing the esophagus from the stomach, where the muscularis mucosae has two layers throughout. This developmental variation in the esophageal muscularis mucosae is a reliable landmark for esophageal identification.

questions.question: Esophageal atresia is often associated with:
questions.explanation: Esophageal atresia is most commonly associated with tracheoesophageal fistula (TEF). The most frequent combination is proximal esophageal atresia with distal TEF. These defects result from abnormal development of the tracheoesophageal septum that separates the respiratory diverticulum from the foregut. Polyhydramnios often accompanies these defects.

options: Fundus/body secrete mucus; cardia/pylorus secrete acid
All regions secrete equal amounts of mucus and acid
Cardia/pylorus secrete mucus; fundus/body secrete acid
Pylorus is the sole site of pepsinogen production
Cardia is the only region with parietal cells
questions.explanation: The cardia and pylorus contain glands that predominantly produce mucus to protect the mucosa at junctional zones. The fundus and body contain the main gastric glands with parietal cells (HCl and intrinsic factor) and chief cells (pepsinogen). This regional specialization ensures protection at the gastroesophageal and gastroduodenal junctions.
questions.question: Histologically, the fundus and body of the stomach are identical, while the cardia and pylorus are similar. The primary secretory difference between these regions is:

questions.explanation: Occlusion of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) causes lateral medullary syndrome (Wallenberg syndrome), affecting structures in the lateral medulla. This results in ipsilateral facial pain and temperature loss, Horner's syndrome, ataxia, and contralateral body pain and temperature loss. The syndrome also includes dysphagia, dysphonia, and vertigo due to involvement of the nucleus ambiguus, vestibular nuclei, and spinothalamic tract.
questions.question: Which vessel's occlusion typically causes lateral medullary syndrome?

options: Oropharynx has pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium; nasopharynx has stratified squamous
Both have identical pseudostratified columnar epithelium
Oropharynx has non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium
Oropharynx has transitional epithelium; nasopharynx has simple columnar
Both have non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium
questions.explanation: The nasopharynx is a respiratory passageway lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar (respiratory) epithelium with goblet cells, continuous with the nasal cavity epithelium. The oropharynx and laryngopharynx are food-conducting passages that transition to non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium to withstand mechanical abrasion during swallowing. This epithelial transition at the pharyngeal isthmus is clinically relevant in nasopharyngeal carcinoma.
questions.question: Which structural feature distinguishes the oropharynx histologically from the nasopharynx?

questions.explanation: The vestibular apparatus detects two types of motion through distinct receptor organs: the maculae of the utricle and saccule contain hair cells with overlying otolithic membranes carrying calcium carbonate crystals called otoliths that respond to linear acceleration and gravity; and the cristae ampullares in the three semicircular ducts oriented in the three planes of space detect angular acceleration and rotation. Together these five receptor organs provide complete three-dimensional vestibular sensing.
options: Sound vibrations converted to nerve impulses
Macular otolith organs (linear) and semicircular cristae (angular acceleration)
Only static head position without any dynamic movement detection
questions.question: The vestibular apparatus of the inner ear detects which types of motion through its specialized sensory receptor structures?

questions.explanation: The cloacal membrane is composed of endoderm (lining the cloaca) and ectoderm (surface covering) without intervening mesoderm. This bilaminar membrane closes the caudal end of the hindgut. When the urorectal septum divides the cloaca, it also divides the cloacal membrane into the urogenital membrane ventrally and anal membrane dorsally. Both membranes normally rupture during the 7th-9th weeks.
questions.question: The cloacal membrane is composed of:
Hepatocytes are the main functional cells of the liver. Which description best characterizes their light microscopic appearance?
options: Small dark nuclei with scanty cytoplasm
Elongated fusiform cells with dark basophilic cytoplasm
Cuboidal cells with apical microvilli and basal nuclei
Large polygonal eosinophilic cells with round nuclei
questions.explanation: Hepatocytes are large polygonal cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm reflecting their high metabolic activity (rich in mitochondria, ER, and glycogen). They have round, vesicular nuclei with prominent nucleoli, and about 25% are binucleate — a feature of polyploidy indicating high metabolic demand. These features readily distinguish hepatocytes from other liver cell types.

questions.question: In the context of intracellular protein degradation, the ubiquitin-proteasome system primarily degrades which of the following categories of proteins?
questions.explanation: The ubiquitin-proteasome system is the cell's primary mechanism for selective degradation of cytoplasmic proteins, particularly those that are misfolded, damaged by oxidative stress, or short-lived regulatory proteins (cyclins, transcription factors). Proteins are tagged with ubiquitin chains that direct them to the 26S proteasome for ATP-dependent proteolysis. This system is distinct from lysosomal degradation of extracellular and membrane proteins.
options: Extracellular matrix proteins secreted by fibroblasts
Misfolded, damaged, or short-lived regulatory cytoplasmic proteins
Membrane lipids in the phospholipid bilayer

questions.question: Which muscle of the tongue is NOT supplied by the hypoglossal nerve?
questions.explanation: The palatoglossus muscle is supplied by the pharyngeal branch of the vagus nerve (CN X), not the hypoglossal nerve. All other tongue muscles (intrinsic muscles, genioglossus, hyoglossus, styloglossus) are supplied by the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII).

Endochondral ossification of long bones begins around week 12 of gestation when periosteal cells in the midregion of the cartilage model switch from producing chondroblasts to producing osteoblasts. A periosteal bone collar forms first by intramembranous ossification, followed by vascular invasion and formation of the primary ossification center by endochondral ossification. Secondary ossification centers in epiphyses typically develop postnatally.
options: At birth when oxygen tension increases
questions.question: During endochondral ossification, the primary ossification center forms in the midregion (diaphysis) of the cartilage model at approximately which gestational age in the human fetus?

questions.explanation: The blood-air barrier consists of: (1) the thin cytoplasm of Type I pneumocytes, (2) a fused basement membrane shared between the pneumocyte and endothelial cells (the thinnest part of the barrier), and (3) the thin cytoplasm of the capillary endothelium. The total thickness is approximately 0.2–0.5 μm. This minimal diffusion distance allows rapid O2/CO2 exchange by passive diffusion.
options: Type I pneumocyte → capillary endothelium → basement membrane
Type I pneumocyte → fused basement membrane → capillary endothelium
Type II pneumocyte → basement membrane → capillary endothelium
questions.question: The blood-air barrier across which gas exchange occurs in the lung consists of which three layers in correct sequence from alveolar air to capillary blood?
