Capillaries are classified into three types based on their endothelium. Which type is found in the kidney glomeruli, pancreatic islets, and intestinal villi, and is characterized by cytoplasmic pores called fenestrations?
questions.explanation: Fenestrated capillaries have numerous transcytoplasmic pores (fenestrae, ~80nm diameter) covered by thin diaphragms. They are found in organs with high filtration/secretion/absorption requirements: kidney glomeruli, intestinal villi, endocrine glands, and choroid plexus. The fenestrae increase permeability to water and small molecules compared to continuous capillaries. In the glomerulus, fenestrae lack diaphragms to maximize filtration.

questions.question: The inferior cerebellar peduncle contains primarily which type of fibers?
questions.explanation: The inferior cerebellar peduncle (restiform body) contains primarily afferent fibers to the cerebellum, including the dorsal spinocerebellar tract, olivocerebellar fibers, vestibular afferents, and reticular formation inputs. A small efferent component includes cerebellovestibular and cerebelloreticular projections from the fastigial nucleus and flocculonodular lobe. The inferior peduncle connects the medulla to the cerebellum and is the main route for proprioceptive and vestibular information entering the cerebellum.

questions.question: The cloacal membrane disappears during which week?
questions.explanation: The cloacal membrane disappears during the 7th week, after the urorectal septum has divided it into anal and urogenital membranes. This breakdown exposes a ventral urogenital opening and a dorsal anal opening. The tip of the urorectal septum forms the perineal body.

questions.question: The ostium secundum forms in the septum primum by which process?
questions.explanation: Before closure of the ostium primum is complete, programmed cell death produces perforations in the upper portion of the septum primum. Coalescence of these perforations forms the ostium secundum. This allows continued right-to-left shunting of blood in the fetal circulation.

questions.question: Which artery is most commonly involved in berry aneurysm formation?
questions.explanation: The anterior communicating artery is the most common site for berry (saccular) aneurysm formation, accounting for approximately 30-35% of intracranial aneurysms. Other common sites include the posterior communicating artery junction with internal carotid and middle cerebral artery bifurcation. These aneurysms form at arterial bifurcations where hemodynamic stress is greatest and the vessel wall lacks normal medial layer support. Rupture causes subarachnoid hemorrhage with sudden severe headache (\"thunderclap headache\"), meningismus, and potential complications.

questions.question: The outer longitudinal smooth muscle layer of the GIT is continuous throughout EXCEPT at which region where it forms three longitudinal bands?
questions.explanation: In the colon (large intestine), the outer longitudinal smooth muscle of the muscularis externa is not a complete circumferential sheet but is condensed into three distinct longitudinal bands — the teniae coli (taenia libera, taenia mesocolica, and taenia omentalis). This unique arrangement is a defining histological and anatomical feature of the colon. The teniae converge at the base of the appendix, which has a complete longitudinal layer.

questions.question: Extraocular muscles develop from which embryonic structures?
questions.explanation: Extraocular muscles form from the first three somitomeres (pre-otic head mesoderm). Each somitomere contributes specific muscles. They are innervated by cranial nerves III, IV, and VI.

Cholangiocytes are reliably identified by immunostaining for cytokeratin 7 (CK7) — a type II intermediate filament characteristic of biliary epithelial cells and some hepatic progenitor cells. CK7 positivity differentiates bile duct cells from hepatocytes (which are negative for CK7 but express albumin). CK7 immunostaining is used in liver biopsies to identify ductular reactions, bile duct proliferation, and metastatic carcinomas of biliary origin.
questions.question: The interlobular bile ducts in the portal tracts are lined by cuboidal to low columnar epithelial cells called cholangiocytes. Which immunohistochemical marker is most useful for identifying these cells?

options: Vitamin D deficiency causing impaired mineralization of osteoid
Increased osteoblast activity without corresponding osteoclast activity
Excess osteoclast-mediated bone resorption with fibrous tissue replacement
Deficiency of type I collagen synthesis by osteoblasts
Failure of endochondral ossification at the growth plate
questions.explanation: Osteitis fibrosa cystica results from primary or secondary hyperparathyroidism, where excess PTH chronically stimulates osteoclasts to resorb bone matrix. The removed bone is replaced by fibrous tissue and hemorrhagic cysts called brown tumors. Histologically, increased osteoclast activity with tunneling resorption, fibrous stroma, and cyst formation are the characteristic findings.
questions.question: Osteitis fibrosa cystica is the bone disease associated primarily with which of the following?

questions.explanation: Lateral vestibulospinal tract originates from lateral vestibular nucleus of medulla. It controls trunk and limb girdle musculature. It facilitates extensor muscles for postural maintenance.
questions.question: Lateral vestibulospinal tract originates from which nucleus?

questions.explanation: The three concentric tunics of the eye are: the outer fibrous tunic consisting of the sclera which is white and protective and the cornea which is transparent and refractive; the middle vascular tunic or uvea consisting of the choroid for nutrition, the ciliary body for accommodation and aqueous humor production, and the iris for pupil control; and the inner nervous tunic which is the retina containing photoreceptors and neurons for vision.
questions.question: The eye is composed of three concentric layers. From outside to inside these are correctly named as which of the following?
options: Uveal tract → Fibrous tunic → Nervous tunic
Fibrous (sclera/cornea), vascular uvea, and nervous tunic (retina)

questions.question: The canalicular period is characterized by formation of:
questions.explanation: The canalicular period (16-26 weeks) is characterized by division of terminal bronchioles into respiratory bronchioles, which then divide into alveolar ducts. Primitive alveoli begin forming, and capillaries establish close contact with developing air spaces. Fetuses born at the end of this period may survive with intensive care.

The motor nucleus of the trigeminal nerve (CN V) innervates the muscles of mastication (masseter, temporalis, medial and lateral pterygoids) plus the mylohyoid, anterior belly of digastric, tensor veli palatini, and tensor tympani. These muscles are derived from the first branchial arch, making this an SVE component. The motor nucleus is located in the lateral upper pons. Lesions cause weakness of jaw closure with deviation toward the affected side due to unopposed pterygoid action.
questions.question: The motor nucleus of the trigeminal nerve innervates which group of muscles?

questions.explanation: The amygdala is particularly involved in determining the storage location of memories and their emotional significance, especially those related to fear and emotional experiences. It receives extensive sensory input from all modalities and projects widely to cortical and subcortical structures. The amygdala works closely with the hippocampus, with the hippocampus handling explicit memory formation and the amygdala processing the emotional context and significance of experiences.
questions.question: Which structure of the limbic system is primarily involved in memory storage location?
The double bubble sign on imaging indicates:
questions.explanation: The "double bubble" sign indicates distension of both the stomach and the duodenum proximal to an obstruction, typically duodenal atresia. One bubble represents the air-filled stomach, and the second represents the dilated duodenal segment. The pyloric canal appears as an air-free space between the two bubbles.

The corpus albicans (white body) is the hyalinized scar that remains after the corpus luteum degenerates. It appears as an irregular, eosinophilic mass of collagenous connective tissue on histological sections. It gradually diminishes in size over months. Older ovaries contain multiple corpora albicantia, reflecting the number of previous ovulations and luteal cycles throughout reproductive life.
options: A fluid-filled structure with granulosa cells lining its wall
A cluster of primordial follicles with flattened cells
A dark, hemorrhagic structure following ovulation
A mass of white, hyalinized fibrous tissue
A collection of interstitial cells secreting androgens
questions.question: Which of the following best describes the histological appearance of the corpus albicans?
The fourth ventricle is bounded laterally by which structures?
questions.explanation: The fourth ventricle is bounded laterally by the cerebellar peduncles (superior, middle, and inferior), which form its walls as they course between the brainstem and cerebellum. The superior cerebellar peduncles form the upper lateral boundaries, while the inferior peduncles (with the gracile and cuneate tubercles) form the lower lateral boundaries. The floor is the rhomboid fossa formed by the posterior pons and medulla, while the roof is formed by the superior medullary velum and inferior medullary velum with cerebellum.

In the interval between any two adjoining pharyngeal arches, the endoderm extends outward forming the pharyngeal pouch, while the ectoderm dips inward to form the pharyngeal cleft. These pouches and clefts are separated only by thin membranes at specific locations.
questions.question: The endoderm extends outward between pharyngeal arches to form which structure?

questions.explanation: Microglia are of mesenchymal origin and invade the CNS in the later half of gestation. They are cigar-shaped with fine processes and serve as phagocytic cells. Unlike other glial cells, they are not neuroectodermal in origin.
questions.question: Microglia are derived from which embryonic origin?

options: They have the thickest walls of any vessel
Their endothelium expresses the highest levels
They have the highest blood pressure
They are always located adjacent to lymph nodes
questions.question: Postcapillary venules are the primary site of leukocyte emigration during inflammation. This preferential emigration is because:
questions.explanation: Postcapillary venules are the primary sites of leukocyte-endothelial interaction during inflammation. Their endothelium rapidly upregulates adhesion molecules (P-selectin from Weibel-Palade bodies within minutes, E-selectin and ICAM-1/VCAM-1 via NF-κB over hours) in response to inflammatory mediators like histamine, TNF-α, and IL-1. The relatively low flow velocity in these vessels facilitates the rolling, adhesion, and transmigration cascade of neutrophils and monocytes.

options: Action potentials jumping node to node, dramatically increasing conduction speed
They are sites of synaptic transmission between neurons
They represent areas where myelin synthesis is slowest
They contain the highest density of potassium channels for repolarization
They allow Schwann cells to phagocytose damaged axon segments
questions.question: The nodes of Ranvier enable saltatory conduction of action potentials. This increases conduction velocity by which mechanism?
questions.explanation: Nodes of Ranvier are unmyelinated gaps approximately 1 micrometer wide where voltage-gated sodium channels are concentrated. Action potentials are regenerated only at nodes jumping from node to node in saltatory conduction which is approximately 50 times faster than continuous conduction and requires less energy since fewer membrane areas need repolarization. Multiple sclerosis disrupts myelin converting saltatory to continuous slower conduction causing the characteristic delayed nerve conduction.

The Edinger-Westphal nucleus is the parasympathetic component of the oculomotor nuclear complex in the upper midbrain. It provides parasympathetic innervation to the sphincter pupillae (pupil constriction) and ciliary muscle (accommodation). It is essential for the pupillary light reflex.
questions.question: The Edinger-Westphal nucleus is associated with which cranial nerve?

questions.explanation: Pierre Robin sequence is also known as first arch sequence. It consists of abnormalities affecting the head and face, including micrognathia (small lower jaw), glossoptosis (posteriorly placed tongue), and airway obstruction. These features result from underdevelopment of first arch structures.
questions.question: Pierre Robin sequence is also known as which type of developmental anomaly?
Which gyrus is located between the two arms of the Y-shaped calcarine and parieto-occipital sulci junction?
questions.explanation: The cuneus gyrus is positioned between the two arms of the Y-shaped configuration formed by the calcarine and parieto-occipital sulci on the medial surface. The precuneus lies above the upper arm and limb of this Y-shaped structure, while the lingual gyrus is located below it at the inferomedial border. This region contains the primary visual cortex along the calcarine sulcus.

questions.question: A sickle-shaped projection of meningeal dura dividing cerebral hemispheres houses which venous sinus in its upper margin?
questions.explanation: The falx cerebri is the sickle-shaped projection extending from the crista galli to the internal occipital protuberance, dividing the two cerebral hemispheres. Its upper convex margin is attached to the cranial vault and contains the superior sagittal sinus. The free crescentic lower margin houses the inferior sagittal sinus, while the straight sinus is located at its posterior junction with the tentorium cerebelli.

options: They are not enclosed by a membrane
They degrade proteins by proteolysis exclusively
They arise from the Golgi apparatus during biogenesis
They do not contain any enzymes
They use oxidative reactions rather than hydrolysis
questions.question: Peroxisomes differ from lysosomes primarily in which of the following aspects?
questions.explanation: Peroxisomes perform oxidative reactions using molecular oxygen to generate hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) as an intermediate, which is then detoxified by catalase within the same organelle. They oxidize very long chain fatty acids (beta-oxidation), metabolize glyoxylate, and detoxify alcohol. Lysosomes use acid hydrolases at low pH, whereas peroxisomes oxidize substrates at neutral pH — a fundamental mechanistic difference.

The JGA has three components: (1) juxtaglomerular (granular) cells — modified smooth muscle of the afferent arteriole that secrete renin; (2) macula densa — specialized DCT cells that sense NaCl concentration and signal to JG cells; (3) extraglomerular mesangial cells (lacis cells) — mediators between macula densa and JG cells. Together they regulate renin release and hence blood pressure via the RAAS.
options: Podocytes, mesangial cells, and parietal cells
Collecting duct cells, juxtaglomerular cells, and podocytes
Macula densa, vasa recta, and PCT cells
Distal tubule cells, podocytes, and parietal epithelium
questions.question: The juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA) is a specialized structure that regulates blood pressure and filtration. Which three components make up the JGA?

questions.explanation: Type II pneumocytes (pneumonocytes) are cuboidal cells with characteristic lamellar bodies — the organelles that synthesize and store pulmonary surfactant. Surfactant (dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine + proteins) reduces alveolar surface tension, preventing alveolar collapse. Deficiency in premature infants causes neonatal respiratory distress syndrome. Type II cells also serve as progenitors for Type I pneumocytes after lung injury.
questions.question: Type II pneumocytes represent only 5% of alveolar surface but have a critical metabolic function. This function is:

questions.explanation: The metanephric blastema (metanephric mesenchyme) is induced by the ureteric bud. Reciprocal induction between these two tissues is essential for kidney development. The ureteric bud induces the blastema to form nephrons (excretory units), while the blastema induces the ureteric bud to branch and form the collecting system.
questions.question: The metanephric blastema is induced by:
Microfilaments of actin within the cytoskeleton primarily enable cells to perform which of the following functions?
questions.explanation: Actin microfilaments (7 nm diameter) are the thinnest cytoskeletal filaments and generate the forces necessary for cell shape changes, movement, and cell division through dynamic polymerization and depolymerization. They are concentrated beneath the plasma membrane forming the cell cortex. They work with myosin motors in muscle contraction and in non-muscle cell motility.
options: Give the cell rigid structural support
Act as tracks for organelle movement

questions.question: The adrenal medulla is derived from which embryonic source?
questions.explanation: The adrenal medulla is derived from neural crest cells, specifically from sympathetic ganglion precursors. These cells migrate to the developing adrenal gland and differentiate into chromaffin cells that secrete epinephrine and norepinephrine. The adrenal cortex is derived from mesoderm.

Pyloric stenosis is characterized by hypertrophy of the pyloric sphincter musculature, causing extreme narrowing of the pyloric lumen. This results in projectile, non-bilious vomiting approximately one hour after feeding. It is one of the most common stomach abnormalities in infants and shows male predominance.
questions.question: Pyloric stenosis is characterized by:

options: Schwann cells in peripheral nerve myelin
Oligodendrocytes as CNS myelin-producing cells targeted by autoimmune attack
Microglia phagocytosing myelin debris as a secondary response
Neurons in the gray matter predominantly
questions.question: A patient with multiple sclerosis has plaques of demyelination in the CNS white matter. The cell type most directly damaged in this condition is which of the following?
questions.explanation: Multiple sclerosis is an autoimmune demyelinating disease where T cells and antibodies target CNS myelin and oligodendrocytes. Loss of myelin disrupts saltatory conduction causing the variable neurological symptoms of optic neuritis weakness sensory loss and ataxia. CNS regeneration is limited because oligodendrocytes lack the neurilemma guidance provided by Schwann cells and inhibitory molecules prevent axon regrowth through plaques.
Motor neurons carry messages to effector organs (muscles and glands). They are efferent, carrying messages away from the CNS. They originate in the CNS and extend to the periphery.
questions.question: Motor neurons carry messages to which structures?

options: Finger-like mucosal projections into the lumen
Lymphoid follicles scattered in the lamina propria
Goblet cell clusters in the epithelium
questions.question: The crypts of Lieberkühn in the small intestine are structurally defined as:
questions.explanation: Intestinal glands — the crypts of Lieberkühn — are simple tubular glands that extend through the full thickness of the mucosal lamina propria. They open at the base of the villi and contain stem cells, goblet cells, Paneth cells, and enteroendocrine cells. They are the proliferative compartment of the intestinal epithelium, constantly renewing the villous epithelium.

questions.question: The developing kidney is an example of which type of induction?
questions.explanation: Renal tubules of the kidney develop through reciprocal induction between ureteric bud (from mesonephric duct) and metanephric mesenchyme. The ureteric bud induces the mesenchyme to form nephrons, while the mesenchyme induces branching of the ureteric bud to form collecting system.

questions.question: Melanocytes in the skin are derived from which source?
questions.explanation: Melanocytes are pigment-producing cells derived from neural crest. They migrate from the neural crest to the developing skin, hair follicles, and eyes. Absence of melanocytes or their pigment production results in albinism. Neural crest cells also give rise to other pigmented cells.

Duplicated collecting system (duplicated ureter and renal pelvis) is the most common congenital anomaly of the urinary system, occurring in about 1% of the population. It results from premature division of the ureteric bud or development of two separate buds. Most cases are asymptomatic, though they may predispose to urinary tract infections.
questions.question: The most common congenital anomaly of the urinary system is:
The inferior parathyroid gland develops from which pharyngeal pouch?
questions.explanation: The inferior parathyroid gland develops from the dorsal part of the third pharyngeal pouch in the 5th week. It develops along with the thymus and descends with it into the thorax. There are four parathyroid glands total, with the superior pair developing from the fourth pouch.

questions.question: The falciform ligament is derived from:
questions.explanation: The falciform ligament is derived from the ventral mesogastrium and connects the liver to the anterior abdominal wall. It contains the ligamentum teres (obliterated umbilical vein) in its free edge. The falciform ligament divides the liver into right and left anatomical lobes and extends from the diaphragm to the umbilicus.
The dorsal septum is formed by enlargement of the alar plate. The ventral fissure forms from basal plate enlargement. These landmarks divide the white matter into funiculi.
questions.question: The dorsal septum is formed by enlargement of which plate?

questions.explanation: On day 9, the blastocyst is deeply embedded in the endometrium and the defect is plugged with a fibrin clot. Spaces called lacunae appear within the syncytiotrophoblast. These lacunae will later fill with maternal blood to establish uteroplacental circulation.
questions.question: Lacunae appear in the syncytiotrophoblast on which day?

questions.explanation: Volvulus (twisting) of the midgut can result from malrotation, which creates a narrow mesenteric base predisposing to twisting around the superior mesenteric artery. This can cause intestinal obstruction and ischemia. Midgut volvulus is a surgical emergency requiring prompt intervention to prevent bowel necrosis. It typically presents with bilious vomiting in infants.
questions.question: Volvulus of the midgut can result from:

questions.explanation: First-order neurons lie in vestibular or Scarpa's ganglion in internal auditory meatus. Peripheral processes receive information from semicircular canal and otolith hair cells. Central processes form vestibular nerve.
questions.question: First-order vestibular neurons are located in which ganglion?

questions.explanation: Pancreas development depends on interactions between endoderm (which forms the pancreatic epithelium and islets) and associated mesoderm. The mesoderm provides permissive inductive signals that allow the endodermal cells to follow their predetermined pancreatic differentiation pathway.
questions.question: Pancreatic development requires which type of tissue interaction?

questions.explanation: Beta cells are the most numerous cells in the islets (60–70%), predominantly located in the central core. They secrete insulin in response to elevated blood glucose, amino acids, and GIP. Insulin promotes glucose uptake by muscle and adipose tissue and inhibits hepatic glucose production. Autoimmune destruction of beta cells causes Type 1 diabetes; insulin resistance and beta cell exhaustion characterize Type 2 diabetes. Beta cells can be identified by specific immunostaining for insulin.
questions.question: Which cell type in the islets of Langerhans is most numerous, centrally located, and secretes the hormone critical for glucose uptake?
The urogenital ridge gives rise to:
questions.explanation: The urogenital ridge, a longitudinal elevation of intermediate mesoderm on either side of the dorsal aorta, gives rise to both the urinary system (nephrogenic cord portion) and the reproductive system (gonadal ridge portion). This explains why renal and genital anomalies often occur together. The close developmental relationship also explains why some structures (mesonephric duct) serve both systems.

questions.question: At 12 weeks, the cerebellum consists of which parts?
questions.explanation: At 12 weeks, a central vermis and 2 lateral dilated cerebellar hemispheres are identified. A transverse fissure separates upper and lower parts. The cerebellum continues developing postnatally.

Transitional epithelium or urothelium is the specialized epithelium lining the renal pelvis, ureters, bladder, and proximal urethra. When the bladder is empty it appears stratified cuboidal to columnar with large rounded umbrella cells at the surface; when distended it stretches to appear much thinner and more squamous. The umbrella cells are joined by tight junctions forming an impermeable barrier and have specialized cytoplasmic plaques containing uroplakin proteins resistant to urine.
questions.question: In the classification of epithelium, the urinary bladder epithelium that can change from columnar to squamous depending on distension is specifically called which of the following?
Sensory decussation in the medulla involves fibers from which nuclei?
questions.explanation: The sensory decussation in the upper closed medulla involves internal arcuate fibers from the gracile and cuneate nuclei crossing the midline to form the medial lemniscus. These nuclei receive and process fine touch, vibration, and proprioceptive information from the dorsal columns of the spinal cord. After decussation, the medial lemniscus ascends through the brainstem to reach the ventral posterolateral nucleus of the thalamus.

options: Blood supply, innervation, and lymphatic drainage
questions.question: The pectinate line is clinically significant because it marks differences in:
questions.explanation: The pectinate line marks differences in blood supply (superior rectal artery above, inferior rectal artery below), innervation (visceral above, somatic below), lymphatic drainage (internal iliac nodes above, superficial inguinal nodes below), and epithelium (columnar above, stratified squamous below). These differences reflect the dual embryological origin of the anal canal.

questions.question: The angular gyrus is involved primarily in which function?
questions.explanation: The angular gyrus (Brodmann area 39) in the inferior parietal lobule is crucial for reading, integrating visual word recognition with language comprehension. It caps the posterior end of the superior temporal sulcus and serves as a multimodal association area connecting visual, auditory, and somatosensory information. Dominant hemisphere lesions cause alexia (inability to read) and agraphia (inability to write), as well as Gerstmann syndrome (acalculia, finger agnosia, left-right disorientation, agraphia). The angular gyrus is unique to humans and great apes, correlating with language capabilities.

options: Decreased osteoclast activity causing excessive bone density
Increased osteoblast apoptosis reducing bone formation
Inflammatory destruction of bone collagen matrix
Unmineralized osteoid accumulation from impaired bone mineralization
Complete absence of osteoid synthesis by osteoblasts
questions.question: Vitamin D deficiency in children causes rickets while in adults it causes osteomalacia. The underlying histological defect common to both is which of the following?
questions.explanation: Vitamin D deficiency impairs intestinal calcium absorption and bone mineralization. Without adequate calcium and phosphate, osteoblasts continue to produce osteoid but it cannot be mineralized, accumulating as wide seams of unmineralized matrix. In children, the epiphyseal plate also fails to mineralize properly causing characteristic bowing of weight-bearing bones and epiphyseal widening in rickets. In adults the same osteoid accumulation causes bone pain and stress fractures of osteomalacia. The tetracycline labeling distance is reduced in osteomalacia.

questions.question: Type I pneumocytes cover approximately 95% of the alveolar surface. Their primary structural characteristic is:
questions.explanation: Type I pneumocytes (type I alveolar cells) are extremely thin, squamous epithelial cells covering about 95% of the alveolar surface. Their thinness (0.2 μm) minimizes the diffusion distance for O2 and CO2 across the blood-air barrier. They cannot divide and are renewed from Type II pneumocytes. Damage to Type I cells (as in ARDS) severely impairs gas exchange.
options: Cuboidal shape with numerous lamellar bodies
Extremely thin, flattened cells allowing rapid gas

questions.question: The renal hilum transmits which structures between the kidney and its surroundings?
questions.explanation: The renal hilum is a vertical fissure on the medial border of the kidney through which pass (from anterior to posterior): the renal vein, renal artery, and ureter. Lymphatics and the renal nerve plexus (sympathetic fibers from the renal plexus) also pass through the hilum. The hilum leads to the renal sinus — a fatty space containing the major and minor calyces, renal pelvis, and major vessels.
options: Renal artery, renal vein, and ureter
Renal vein, ureter, and sympathetic nerves only

questions.explanation: Fibers from the cervical region travel with fasciculus cuneatus to form the cuneocerebellar tract. They exit through the inferior cerebellar peduncle. This pathway conveys upper limb proprioceptive information.
questions.question: The cuneocerebellar tract carries information from which region?

questions.explanation: Arachnoid villi are evaginations of the arachnoid mater that protrude into the dura mater and are visible from the third year of life. Their number increases proportionately with age from the seventh year onward, eventually pitting the inner surface of the cranium. These structures communicate with the venous sinuses and are crucial for cerebrospinal fluid absorption into the venous system.
questions.question: The arachnoid villi begin to appear and increase with age. From which year of life do they become consistently visible?
The endothelium lining blood vessels is metabolically active and produces multiple vasoactive substances. Which endothelial product causes vasodilation and inhibits platelet aggregation?
questions.explanation: Endothelial cells produce nitric oxide (NO, via eNOS stimulated by shear stress) and prostacyclin (PGI2), both of which cause vasodilation and inhibit platelet aggregation, maintaining vascular homeostasis. In contrast, damaged endothelium produces less NO/PGI2 and releases endothelin-1 (vasoconstrictor), PAI-1 (pro-thrombotic), and von Willebrand factor (platelet adhesion). This balance between vasodilatory and vasoconstrictive endothelial products underlies the pathogenesis of atherosclerosis and hypertension.

Respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) in premature infants primarily results from insufficient surfactant production by immature type II pneumocytes. Without adequate surfactant, alveoli collapse during expiration, requiring greater effort for breathing. Treatment includes surfactant replacement therapy and respiratory support.
questions.question: Respiratory distress syndrome in premature infants primarily results from:
What is the approximate total volume of cerebrospinal fluid in an adult?
questions.explanation: The total cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) volume in an adult is approximately 150 mL, with about 30 mL in the ventricles and 120 mL in the subarachnoid space. CSF is produced at a rate of approximately 0.4 mL/min (about 600 mL/day), resulting in a complete turnover 3-4 times daily. This continuous production and reabsorption maintains constant intracranial pressure and provides metabolic support to the brain.

options: Anaerobic glycolysis for ATP production in erythrocytes
The pentose phosphate pathway producing NADPH to regenerate glutathione
The synthesis of 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate for oxygen affinity regulation
questions.explanation: Erythrocytes depend entirely on the pentose phosphate pathway for NADPH production since they lack mitochondria. NADPH is essential for regenerating reduced glutathione via glutathione reductase, which protects erythrocyte membranes and hemoglobin from oxidative damage. G6PD deficiency impairs this protection making RBCs vulnerable to oxidative stress from drugs such as primaquine, fava beans, or infection-induced reactive oxygen species, causing hemolysis. G6PD deficiency is the most common enzymatic RBC disorder worldwide.
questions.question: Deficiency of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase in erythrocytes leads to hemolytic anemia triggered by oxidative stress from drugs or infections. This is because G6PD is essential for which metabolic pathway in erythrocytes?
Astrocytes serve as which intermediary?
questions.explanation: Astrocytes are large stellate cells serving as metabolic intermediaries for neurons. Their processes attach to capillaries and neurons. They form the inner layer of blood-brain barrier.

questions.question: The vermis of the cerebellum projects to which deep nucleus?
questions.explanation: The vermis (midline cerebellum) projects to the fastigial nucleus, the most medial deep cerebellar nucleus. The fastigial nucleus then projects to the vestibular nuclei, reticular formation, and contralateral motor cortex, influencing proximal limb muscles, trunk, and posture. This medial cerebellar system (vermis-fastigial-vestibulospinal/reticulospinal) controls balance, posture, and axial movements. Vermal lesions cause truncal ataxia with difficulty sitting and standing, wide-based gait, and titubation (rhythmic head tremor).
The trigger zone is at the junction of axon and cell body (axon hillock). Here summation of signals can produce action potential. This area has the lowest threshold for generating action potentials.
questions.question: The axon hillock is also known as which region?

questions.explanation: The facial motor nucleus innervates all muscles of facial expression, including orbicularis oculi, orbicularis oris, buccinator, frontalis, and platysma, plus the stapedius, stylohyoid, and posterior belly of digastric. These muscles derive from the second branchial arch (SVE component). The nucleus is located in the lower pons, with its axons looping around the abducens nucleus before exiting the brainstem. Upper motor neuron lesions spare forehead muscles due to bilateral innervation, while lower motor neuron lesions cause complete hemifacial paralysis.
questions.question: The facial motor nucleus innervates which group of muscles?
Peyer's patches are aggregated lymphoid nodules found predominantly in which segment of the small intestine?
questions.explanation: Peyer's patches are large aggregates of lymphoid follicles located predominantly in the distal ileum, where they can extend from the lamina propria into the submucosa. They are part of the gut-associated lymphoid tissue (GALT) and play a crucial role in immune surveillance of intestinal contents. Isolated lymphoid nodules are distributed throughout the small intestine but aggregated patches characterize the ileum.

questions.question: What histological feature characterizes the inner surface of the arachnoid mater?
questions.explanation: The inner surface of the arachnoid mater is lined with low cuboidal mesothelium that flattens at intervals. The outer surface contains white fibrous and elastic fibers arranged in layers. Nervous plexuses from cranial nerves V, VII, and XI supply the arachnoid, providing sensory innervation to this delicate meningeal layer.

questions.question: Paneth cells are found at the base of intestinal crypts and are best characterized by which morphological and functional feature?
questions.explanation: Paneth cells are distinctive for their large, apical, eosinophilic secretory granules that contain antimicrobial substances including alpha-defensins (cryptdins), lysozyme, and secretory phospholipase A2. These secretions play a critical role in innate immunity by regulating microbial colonization of the intestinal crypts. They are among the longest-lived cells in the intestinal epithelium.
options: Abundant mucin granules for mucus secretion

questions.explanation: On day 13, new cells from the hypoblast migrate to the inner part of Heuser's membrane. Spaces develop within these cells to form the definitive (secondary) yolk sac, which is smaller than the primitive yolk sac. The primitive yolk sac is pushed aside and eventually degenerates.
questions.question: The definitive (secondary) yolk sac forms on which day?

options: Inward toward the lumen and outward toward the serosa
Both upward to surface and downward to secretory gland
Only upward toward the gastric pit
Only downward toward the base of the gland
questions.explanation: Pluripotent stem cells in the isthmus of gastric glands undergo asymmetric division. Daughter cells can migrate upward to replace surface mucous cells lining the pits and stomach lumen, or migrate downward to replace specialized secretory cells (parietal, chief, mucous neck cells) in the gland base. This bidirectional migration ensures continuous mucosal renewal.
questions.question: Stem cells in gastric glands are pluripotent and located in the isthmus. These cells are capable of moving in which two directions?
The appendix is initially located at which part of the cecum?
questions.explanation: The appendix initially arises from the distal (apical) end of the cecum during the 6th week. Due to unequal growth of the cecal wall, with the right side growing more rapidly, the appendix comes to lie on the medial side of the cecum. This explains the variable positions of the appendix in adults (retrocecal, pelvic, etc.).

options: Glandular columnar epithelium with goblet cells
questions.question: Lingual tonsils located at the base of the tongue are covered by which epithelium?
questions.explanation: Lingual tonsils located in the lamina propria at the root of the tongue are covered by stratified squamous epithelium reflecting their location within the oral cavity where mechanical abrasion from food necessitates a protective stratified squamous surface. This is the same epithelial type as palatine tonsils. In contrast pharyngeal tonsils have respiratory pseudostratified ciliated epithelium reflecting their nasopharyngeal location.

questions.question: Which statement about the muscularis mucosae is MOST accurate?
options: It is composed of skeletal muscle in the upper GIT
It is the thickest layer of the GIT wall
It contains the myenteric plexus between its two sublayers
It generates peristaltic waves throughout the GIT
questions.explanation: The muscularis mucosae is a thin layer of smooth muscle that separates the mucosa from the submucosa. Its contractions produce local movements of the mucosa, improving contact with luminal contents. It should not be confused with the muscularis externa, which drives peristalsis. The myenteric plexus lies between the layers of the muscularis externa, not mucosae.

options: Position of all joints at any time
questions.question: Posture is defined as which composite?
questions.explanation: Posture is a composite of the position of all body joints at any given time. Movement is caused by muscle contraction and relaxation. Muscles are broadly divided into flexors and extensors.

The neural tube formed during neurulation has two openings: the cranial (anterior) neuropore and the caudal (posterior) neuropore. The cranial neuropore closes on day 25, while the caudal neuropore closes on day 27. Failure of these neuropores to close results in neural tube defects.
questions.question: On which day does the cranial neuropore typically close?

questions.explanation: The choroid is a highly vascularized layer between the sclera and retinal pigment epithelium that provides the sole blood supply to the outer one-third of the retina including photoreceptors and RPE. The inner two-thirds of the retina receive blood from the central retinal artery. Choroidal blood flow is the highest per gram of tissue in the body reflecting the extremely high metabolic demand of photoreceptors. Age-related macular degeneration involves abnormal choroidal neovascularization.
questions.question: The choroid layer of the uveal tract primarily serves which function for the retina?
options: Regulating light entry through pupil diameter changes
Producing vitreous humor for the posterior chamber
Focusing light on the retina through refractive power
Providing oxygen and nutrients to the outer retinal layers including photoreceptors
Converting light energy to neural impulses in the photoreceptor layer

questions.explanation: Polycystic kidney disease is characterized by multiple cysts throughout the kidney parenchyma that can lead to renal failure. There are autosomal dominant (adult) and autosomal recessive (infantile) forms. The cysts result from abnormal development of collecting tubules and nephrons. Childhood or adulthood onset depends on the genetic form.
questions.question: Polycystic kidney disease is characterized by:
The mesonephros begins functioning during which week?
questions.explanation: The mesonephros begins functioning during the 5th week, with urine draining along the mesonephric duct into the cloaca. The mesonephric kidney continues functioning as an interim kidney until the 10th week. By this time, the permanent metanephric kidneys have developed sufficiently.

questions.question: The thyroid gland reaches its final position in the neck during which week?
questions.explanation: The thyroid gland reaches its final position in the 7th week in the neck, anterior to the trachea. The two lobes become connected by an isthmus attached to the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th tracheal rings. The thyroglossal duct becomes solid and normally disappears as the gland descends.

options: Reticular fiber networks in lymph nodes
questions.explanation: In bone osteons, collagen fibers within adjacent lamellae are oriented at right angles to one another, creating anisotropy detectable with polarized light. Lamellae with fibers parallel to the polarizer appear dark (extinct) while those with perpendicular fibers appear bright, producing the characteristic alternating pattern. This structural arrangement gives bone its mechanical strength and resistance to multidirectional stress.
questions.question: A tissue section examined under polarized light shows alternating bright and dark layers corresponding to perpendicular collagen fiber orientation. This is most characteristic of which structure?

options: Structural support and semipermeable barrier for molecular traffic
Synthesizing proteins for secretion outside the cell
Detoxifying foreign substances entering the cell
questions.question: The function of the cell membrane is best described as which of the following?
questions.explanation: The cell membrane provides structural integrity to the cell and, through its selectively permeable nature, controls which molecules enter and exit. Transport can be passive (down concentration gradient) or active (requiring energy, against gradient). The membrane also mediates cell signaling through surface receptors and cell-to-cell recognition through the glycocalyx.

questions.question: The Mononuclear Phagocyte System (MPS) includes all of the following EXCEPT which of the following?
questions.explanation: The MPS includes all tissue macrophages regardless of location: Kupffer cells (liver), alveolar macrophages (lung), osteoclasts (bone), microglia (CNS), Langerhans cells (skin), and dendritic cells (lymph nodes). Mast cells, however, are NOT part of the MPS — they originate from a separate progenitor cell distinct from monocytes and are not phagocytic macrophages. This distinction is frequently tested.

questions.question: Mastication is the mechanical breakdown of food in the oral cavity. The oral mucosa over the hard palate and gingiva is lined by which type of epithelium adapted for mechanical trauma?
questions.explanation: The masticatory mucosa covering the hard palate and gingiva (gums) is lined by keratinized stratified squamous epithelium to withstand the significant mechanical forces during chewing. The lining mucosa of the cheeks, lips, and floor of mouth is non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium, allowing flexibility. The specialized mucosa of the tongue dorsum contains papillae and taste buds.

questions.question: Which midbrain structure receives direct input from the retina for visual reflexes?
questions.explanation: The superior colliculus in the tectum receives direct input from the retina and is involved in visual reflexes, particularly controlling rapid eye movements and orienting responses to visual stimuli. The superior colliculus also receives input from visual cortex and projects through tectospinal and tectobulbar tracts. The inferior colliculus receives auditory input from the cochlea and is involved in auditory reflexes and sound localization.

questions.question: Odontoblasts (which produce dentin) are derived from which source?
questions.explanation: Odontoblasts, which produce dentin of teeth, are derived from neural crest cells (specifically from the dental papilla). Ameloblasts, which produce enamel, are derived from oral ectoderm (enamel organ). Tooth development requires reciprocal induction between neural crest-derived mesenchyme and ectodermal epithelium.

questions.question: The ureter is lined by which type of epithelium that can accommodate changes in volume and distension?
questions.explanation: The entire urinary collecting system from the renal pelvis to the bladder is lined by transitional epithelium (urothelium). In the relaxed state, it appears 5–6 cells thick with characteristic dome-shaped (umbrella) cells at the surface. When distended, it becomes 2–3 cells thick as cells flatten out. This remarkable ability to accommodate volume changes without losing barrier function is unique to urothelium.

options: It is produced continuously and drains like aqueous humor
It is a free-flowing liquid with no gel structure
It contains photoreceptors embedded within its matrix
It is replaced by fresh fluid every few hours
Stable gelatinous gel not replaced throughout life, stabilizing the eyeball
questions.question: The vitreous humor fills the space between the lens and retina. It differs from aqueous humor in which of the following ways?
questions.explanation: Vitreous humor is a stable transparent gel of 98% water with 2% type II collagen and hyaluronic acid filling the vitreous chamber. Unlike aqueous humor which continuously circulates, vitreous is not replaced and the same gel present in infancy persists throughout adult life. It maintains the spherical shape of the eyeball supports the lens anteriorly and keeps the retina pressed against the choroid. Liquefaction with aging contributes to floaters and increased risk of retinal detachment.

Frozen sections prepared by cryostat allow histological examination within minutes during surgery, enabling the pathologist to determine whether tumor margins are clear or if a suspicious lesion is malignant before the surgeon closes. Paraffin processing takes 12–24 hours and cannot be used when immediate results are needed. The trade-off is slightly inferior morphological quality compared to paraffin sections.
questions.question: A frozen section technique using a cryostat rather than paraffin embedding is most advantageous in which of the following clinical situations?
The transverse mesocolon fuses with:
questions.explanation: The transverse mesocolon fuses with the greater omentum but maintains its mobility. This creates a four-layered structure posterior to the stomach. The fusion occurs as the greater omentum grows inferiorly from the greater curvature. Despite fusion, the transverse colon retains significant mobility unlike the ascending and descending colons.

Accessory (supernumerary) renal arteries represent persistence of embryonic vessels that normally regress as the kidney ascends. They are common (occurring in 25-30% of individuals) and are usually clinically insignificant. However, an accessory artery crossing the ureteropelvic junction can cause obstruction. These vessels are end arteries and must be preserved during surgery to prevent renal infarction.
questions.question: Accessory renal arteries represent:

questions.explanation: Fingernails reach the fingertips by the 32nd week of gestation, while toenails reach toe tips by the 36th week. Development of fingernails precedes toenails by approximately 4 weeks. Nails begin developing at the tips of digits around the 10th week as thickened areas called nail fields.
questions.question: Fingernails reach the fingertips by approximately:

questions.explanation: T follicular helper cells in germinal centers provide critical help to B cells through: CD40L-CD40 interaction which is the contact-dependent signal preventing B cell apoptosis and driving proliferation; IL-21 which drives somatic hypermutation and promotes plasma cell differentiation; and IL-4 which promotes class switching to IgG1 and IgE. Without Tfh help, B cells in germinal centers undergo apoptosis rather than completing affinity maturation. This Tfh-B cell interaction is disrupted in common variable immunodeficiency.
questions.question: The germinal center reaction in secondary follicles requires T follicular helper cells providing which signals to activate B cells?
options: CD8 cytotoxic signals killing infected B cells
Mast cell degranulation and histamine release signals
Neutrophil oxidative burst and degranulation signals
CD40L–CD40 and IL-21/IL-4 driving B-cell proliferation and class switching

questions.question: The adrenal glands develop from:
questions.explanation: The adrenal glands have dual embryological origin: the cortex develops from intermediate mesoderm (coelomic epithelium) and the medulla from neural crest cells (sympathetic ganglion cells). During kidney ascent, the adrenals remain in their original position at the superior poles. Initially, the adrenal glands are much larger relative to the kidneys than in adults, and the fetal cortex (which produces fetal zone steroids) involutes after birth.

The epidermis is derived entirely from surface ectoderm, which provides the epithelial component of skin. The dermis, in contrast, develops from mesoderm. This dual origin explains the distinct tissue types and functions of these two skin layers.
questions.question: The epidermis is derived from which embryonic germ layer?

options: Unmineralized organic bone matrix secreted by osteoblasts before mineralization
Fully mineralized compact bone in the cortex
The inorganic mineral phase of bone after calcification
The cartilage template before endochondral ossification begins
The vascular connective tissue in Haversian canals
questions.explanation: Osteoid is the unmineralized organic matrix of bone, composed primarily of type I collagen (95%) and non-collagenous proteins (osteocalcin, osteopontin, bone sialoprotein). It is secreted by osteoblasts and constitutes a thin seam of matrix that awaits mineralization. Accumulation of osteoid without subsequent mineralization characterizes osteomalacia (adult) and rickets (children), typically due to vitamin D deficiency.
questions.question: Osteoid is the term for which of the following bone tissue components?
Demyelination results in which consequence?
questions.explanation: Loss of myelin sheath (demyelination) has serious effects on neuron function. Myelin maintains axonal integrity and speeds conduction. Multiple sclerosis is a demyelinating disease.

questions.question: The calcarine sulcus contains which functional area?
questions.explanation: The calcarine sulcus on the medial occipital surface contains the primary visual cortex (area 17, striate cortex) along its banks. The upper and lower lips of the sulcus represent the inferior and superior visual fields respectively, with macular (central) vision represented posteriorly near the occipital pole. The stria of Gennari, a prominent myelinated fiber layer, gives the name \"striate cortex\" and is visible grossly. Posterior cerebral artery strokes affecting this region cause contralateral homonymous hemianopia with characteristic macular sparing.

questions.question: Fibrous astrocytes are mainly seen in which location?
questions.explanation: Fibrous astrocytes are seen mainly in white matter and serve a repair function after neuronal damage. Protoplasmic astrocytes are in gray matter. Astrocytes can partially envelop cell bodies.

The respiratory center is primarily located in the pons, with additional respiratory control centers in the medulla. The pontine respiratory group (pneumotaxic center) modulates the respiratory rhythm generated by medullary centers. The pons also contains the apneustic center, which influences the duration of inspiration. These centers work together to maintain normal respiratory patterns and respond to chemoreceptor input.
questions.question: The respiratory center is primarily located in which part of the brainstem?
Surfactant secretion by type II pneumocytes begins during which weeks?
questions.explanation: Secretion of surfactant (a surface-active lipid) begins during 21-25 weeks. Surfactant maintains the patency of developing alveoli of the lungs and prevents collapse. Adequate surfactant production is essential for survival of premature infants; deficiency causes respiratory distress syndrome.

questions.question: The inferior colliculus receives input from which tract?
questions.explanation: Fibers from superior olivary nucleus via lateral lemniscus ascend to inferior colliculus in midbrain. From here they ascend via inferior quadrigeminal brachium to medial geniculate body. The inferior colliculus is an auditory relay nucleus.

Interphase is the preparatory phase preceding mitosis during which the cell grows (G1 and G2 phases) and replicates its DNA (S phase). Nutrients are accumulated and the cell size increases substantially. Interphase occupies the majority of the cell cycle duration in most dividing cells.
questions.question: In eukaryotic cells, the phase during which the cell grows, accumulates nutrients, and duplicates its DNA before mitosis is specifically called which of the following?

questions.explanation: The primitive streak continues to produce mesoderm until the early 4th week, after which it regresses and becomes an insignificant structure in the sacrococcygeal region. It normally degenerates and disappears by the end of the 4th week. Persistence of the primitive streak results in a sacrococcygeal teratoma.
questions.question: By the end of which week does the primitive streak normally degenerate and disappear?

questions.explanation: The blood-brain barrier is formed primarily by astrocyte foot processes inducing tight junctions in endothelial cells. It protects brain from toxins. It restricts drug delivery. Some areas lack this barrier.
questions.question: The blood-brain barrier is formed primarily by which cells?

questions.explanation: The general visceral efferent (GVE) column includes the Edinger-Westphal nucleus (midbrain), superior and inferior salivatory nuclei (pons and medulla), and dorsal vagal nucleus (medulla). These parasympathetic nuclei control smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, and glandular secretions. The GVE column lies lateral to somatic efferent nuclei but medial to afferent components in the brainstem's functional organization, providing autonomic control via cranial nerves III, VII, IX, and X.
questions.question: Which cranial nerve nuclei represent the general visceral efferent column?
Which nuclei lie lateral to the red nucleus in the subthalamus?
questions.explanation: The subthalamic nuclei lie lateral to the red nucleus and substantia nigra in the subthalamus, which is located between the midbrain and thalamus. These lens-shaped nuclei receive afferent input from the globus pallidus and form part of the efferent pathway for the corpus striatum. The subthalamic nuclei are involved in motor control; their damage or dysfunction (as in hemiballismus) causes violent, involuntary flinging movements of the contralateral limbs.

questions.question: The metanephric blastema is derived from:
questions.explanation: The metanephric blastema (metanephric mesenchyme) is derived from intermediate mesoderm in the sacral region. This mesenchyme condenses around the ureteric bud and, through reciprocal induction, differentiates to form the nephrons (excretory units) of the permanent kidney. Without proper interaction between ureteric bud and metanephric mesenchyme, the kidney fails to develop.

questions.question: Which commissure connects the olfactory areas of both cerebral hemispheres?
questions.explanation: The anterior commissure connects the olfactory areas and temporal lobes of both cerebral hemispheres, crossing anterior to the columns of the fornix at the anterior wall of the third ventricle. It consists of two parts: a smaller anterior portion connecting the olfactory bulbs and tracts, and a larger posterior portion connecting the temporal lobes. The anterior commissure is phylogenetically older than the corpus callosum and remains important for interhemispheric olfactory and temporal lobe communication.

The metanephric kidney initially develops in the sacral region (pelvic area) opposite S1-S2 vertebrae at approximately 5 weeks. It subsequently "ascends" to reach its final lumbar position (T12-L3) by 9 weeks through differential growth of the caudal embryo. During ascent, the kidney undergoes medial rotation and acquires new arterial supply from progressively higher aortic levels.
questions.question: The metanephric kidney initially develops in which region?
The urinary bladder wall contains the detrusor muscle, which is composed of which type of muscle and how is it arranged?
questions.explanation: The detrusor muscle of the bladder is composed of three interwoven layers of smooth muscle: inner longitudinal, middle circular, and outer longitudinal. Unlike the GIT where layers are distinct, the bladder muscle layers are less clearly defined and fibers run in multiple directions, giving the bladder its unique distensibility. The internal urethral sphincter at the bladder neck is a thickening of the circular smooth muscle.
options: Smooth muscle in three interwoven layers
Cardiac muscle in a single layer
Two layers of smooth muscle (circular only)
Mixed skeletal and smooth muscle in two layers

questions.question: The glossopharyngeal nerve stylopharyngeus muscle receives which fibers?
questions.explanation: The glossopharyngeal nerve (IX) SVE fibers supply stylopharyngeus muscle (3rd arch derivative). It also has GVE (parotid), GVA (posterior tongue/pharynx), SVA (posterior tongue taste) and GSA components.

questions.question: Glucagon is secreted by which islet cell type in response to hypoglycemia, and what is its primary target organ?
questions.explanation: Alpha cells (approximately 25% of islet cells, predominantly located at the periphery) secrete glucagon in response to hypoglycemia, amino acids, and sympathetic stimulation. Glucagon's primary target is the liver (hepatocytes), where it stimulates glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, raising blood glucose. The paracrine inhibition of alpha cells by beta cell insulin and delta cell somatostatin within the islet is an important local regulatory mechanism.

questions.question: How many layers compose the amnion histologically?
questions.explanation: The amnion is histologically composed of five layers: cellular layer, basement membrane, compact layer, fibroblast layer, and outer spongy layer. The amnion is a transparent grayish membrane that lines the chorion and covers the fetal surface of the placenta and umbilical cord.

Nondisjunction (failure of separation of homologous chromosomes in anaphase I or sister chromatids in anaphase II) can result in abnormal gametes. Normal gametes have 23 chromosomes (22 + X or 22 + Y). Nondisjunction produces gametes with 24 chromosomes (23 + X or 23 + Y) or 22 chromosomes (21 + X or 21 + Y).
questions.question: Nondisjunction during oogenesis can result in gametes with which chromosome number?
Lumbar puncture is performed safely because of which developmental feature?
questions.explanation: The apparent ascent of the spinal cord creates a safe zone below L2/L3 for lumbar puncture. Only nerve roots of the cauda equina are present at this level. This reduces the risk of direct spinal cord injury.

questions.question: Which cells are derived from the external granular layer?
questions.explanation: The external granular layer gives rise to granule, Purkinje, and Golgi II neurons by the 6th month. Basket and stellate cells derive from the marginal layer. These neurons form the cerebellar cortex circuitry.

questions.question: The hypoglossal nerve supplies which muscles?
questions.explanation: The hypoglossal nerve (XII) has only GSE fibers supplying intrinsic and most extrinsic tongue muscles (except palatoglossus which is CN X). It exits between pyramid and olive. Lesions cause tongue deviation.

questions.question: At what gestational age is the fetus considered viable with intensive care?
questions.explanation: Fetuses born at 22-25 weeks (extremely low birth weight, ELBW, usually less than 1000 grams) may survive with expert intensive postnatal care, though survival rates and long-term outcomes vary. Viability has improved with advances in neonatal care, including surfactant therapy and ventilatory support.

The peritoneal cavity loses its connection with the extraembryonic coelom during the 10th week of development. Initially, the greater part of each limb of the intraembryonic coelom opens laterally into the extraembryonic coelom. Horizontal folding brings the limbs together ventrally and eventually closes this connection.
questions.question: The peritoneal cavity loses its connection with the extraembryonic coelom during which week?

questions.explanation: Histamine is the primary early vasoactive mediator of increased vascular permeability in acute inflammation. Released rapidly from mast cell and basophil granules upon activation, histamine causes postcapillary venule endothelial cell contraction, widening intercellular gaps and allowing fluid, proteins, and leukocytes to escape into the tissue. This increase in permeability produces the edema (tumor) and contributes to redness and heat.
questions.question: Increased vascular permeability during inflammation is primarily caused by the action of which vasoactive substance?
options: Histamine from mast cells and basophils

questions.explanation: The interventricular foramen (foramen of Monro) connects each lateral ventricle to the third ventricle, allowing CSF to flow between these spaces. This foramen is located just behind the anterior column of the fornix and is also the point where the choroid plexus of the lateral ventricle becomes continuous with that of the third ventricle. Obstruction of one foramen causes unilateral ventricular dilation, while bilateral obstruction affects both lateral ventricles.
questions.question: The lateral ventricles communicate with the third ventricle through which opening?

questions.explanation: Mesenchyme around cochlear duct becomes cartilage which undergoes vacuolization giving 2 perilymph-filled spaces. These are scala vestibuli and scala tympani separated from cochlear duct. The duct contains endolymph.
questions.question: Perilymph-filled spaces include which structures?
The tracheal epithelium contains Basal cells, goblet cells, and ciliated cells. Which additional specialized cell type is found in the tracheal epithelium that monitors airway chemicals?
questions.explanation: Brush cells (tuft cells) are solitary chemosensory cells found in the respiratory epithelium, including the trachea and bronchi. They have a characteristic tuft of blunt microvilli on their apical surface and express taste receptor proteins (T2R bitter taste receptors). When activated by bitter compounds (bacterial metabolites, irritants), they trigger rapid cholinergic reflexes causing bronchoconstriction and mucus secretion as a defense mechanism.

questions.question: In the mediolateral arrangement of brainstem nuclei, which component is most medial?
questions.explanation: General somatic efferent (GSE) nuclei are the most medial in the brainstem's mediolateral arrangement, reflecting the original organization of the neural tube where motor nuclei were ventral/medial and sensory nuclei were dorsal/lateral. The complete medial-to-lateral sequence is: GSE (oculomotor, trochlear, abducens, hypoglossal), SVE (motor V, facial, ambiguus), GVE (Edinger-Westphal, salivatory, dorsal vagal), GVA/SVA (solitary), GSA (trigeminal sensory), and SSA (cochlear, vestibular).

options: Formation of a cartilage template that is subsequently replaced by bone
Endochondral replacement of previously formed cartilage
Mesenchyme cells differentiating directly into osteoblasts without a cartilage intermediate
Migration of osteoblasts from the marrow cavity to the periosteum
Dedifferentiation of mature osteocytes into osteoprogenitor cells
questions.question: Intramembranous ossification, which forms flat bones of the skull, begins with which of the following initial events?
questions.explanation: Intramembranous ossification begins with the condensation (aggregation) of mesenchyme cells in a highly vascularized region, followed by their direct differentiation into osteoblasts without any cartilage intermediate. These osteoblasts secrete osteoid (collagen + ground substance) that subsequently mineralizes, forming primary ossification centers. The skull bones, mandible, clavicle, and some facial bones form by this direct membrane bone formation pathway.

questions.question: Cells from the primitive streak that displace the hypoblast form which layer?
questions.explanation: Some epiblast cells from the primitive streak displace the hypoblast to form the intraembryonic endoderm. Other cells from the deep surface of the primitive streak form mesenchyme or mesoblast, which develops into intraembryonic mesoderm. The remaining epiblast cells form the intraembryonic ectoderm.

questions.question: The optic radiation passes through which part of internal capsule?
questions.explanation: Nerve fibers from lateral geniculate body travel to visual cortex (area 17) through optic radiation in retrolentiform part of internal capsule. The radiation sweeps around the lateral ventricle. Lesions cause characteristic visual field defects.

questions.question: The anterolateral system is concerned with which sensations?
questions.explanation: The anterolateral pathway (lateral spinothalamic tract) is concerned with crude touch, pain, temperature, itch and sexual sensations. Cell bodies are in posterior root ganglia. Fibers synapse with substantia gelatinosa cells.

The resting (reserve) zone consists of typical hyaline cartilage with small, quiescent chondrocytes showing no morphological changes — it acts as a reservoir of cells for the proliferative zone. Moving toward the diaphysis: proliferative zone (rapid division in columns), hypertrophic zone (large cells accumulating glycogen), calcified cartilage zone (matrix calcification, chondrocyte death), and ossification zone (endochondral bone deposition by invading osteoblasts).
options: The resting zone is where chondrocytes rapidly divide in columns
The proliferative zone shows hypertrophied chondrocytes accumulating glycogen
The hypertrophic zone is where cartilage matrix becomes calcified
Resting zone: quiescent hyaline chondrocytes with no morphological changes
The ossification zone consists only of dying chondrocytes with no bone formation
questions.question: The epiphyseal (growth) plate allows long bones to grow in length. This process involves five histological zones; which zone is correctly described?

questions.explanation: General visceral efferent nuclei supply involuntary muscles of gut, heart and respiratory system. These are parasympathetic preganglionic neurons. They regulate autonomic functions.
questions.question: General visceral efferent nuclei in myelencephalon supply which structures?
options: Involuntary muscles of gut, heart, respiratory system

questions.question: Neurotransmitters are transported to axon terminus by which structures?
questions.explanation: Neurotransmitter molecules are transported to axon terminus by microfilaments and microtubules. This is called axoplasmic flow or axonal transport. The transport can be anterograde or retrograde.

Medullary sponge kidney is characterized by cystic dilation of collecting ducts in the renal pyramids, giving a sponge-like appearance. It is usually bilateral and often asymptomatic but may cause nephrolithiasis (kidney stones), hematuria, or urinary tract infections. The condition is typically diagnosed in young adults. The cortex and glomeruli are normal. It represents a developmental abnormality of collecting duct formation.
questions.question: Medullary sponge kidney is characterized by:
Injury to the reticular formation can result in which condition?
questions.explanation: The reticular activating system is critical for existence of the conscious state. Injury to the reticular formation can result in irreversible coma. The reticular formation effects consciousness, attention, and sleep through its connections with the thalamus, hypothalamus, and cerebral cortex.

Parathormone (PTH) from parathyroid glands raises blood calcium by stimulating osteoclast-mediated bone resorption (releasing stored calcium), increasing renal calcium reabsorption, and promoting intestinal calcium absorption via vitamin D activation. Calcitonin (from thyroid C cells) opposes PTH by suppressing bone resorption (inhibiting osteoclasts) and increasing osteoid calcification. This PTH-calcitonin axis is the primary calcium homeostasis mechanism.
options: PTH raises blood calcium by stimulating bone resorption; calcitonin suppresses resorption
Calcitonin raises blood calcium; parathyroid hormone lowers it
Both hormones raise blood calcium through osteoclast activation
Parathyroid hormone only acts on kidneys with no effect on bone
Calcitonin stimulates osteoclast activity while parathyroid hormone activates osteoblasts
questions.question: Blood calcium levels are regulated by two hormones with opposing effects on bone resorption. Which of the following correctly describes this hormonal regulation?

questions.explanation: The cerebellar cortex is organized into parasagittal zones and microzones with specific input-output relationships, despite its uniform histological appearance. Purkinje cells are arranged in parasagittal bands that project to specific regions of deep nuclei, and these zones receive climbing fiber input from specific olivary subdivisions. Within zones, smaller microzones (\~1mm wide) may represent functional units. This modular organization allows different cerebellar regions to control specific body parts and motor functions independently.
questions.question: The cerebellar cortex follows which organizational principle?

questions.explanation: The ileocecal valve (Bauhin's valve) is a mucosal fold reinforced by thickened circular muscle that controls the flow of ileal content into the cecum and prevents reflux of the heavily colonized large intestinal content into the relatively sterile small intestine. This barrier function is critical for preventing small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO). Surgical removal or incompetence of the ileocecal valve predisposes to SIBO.
options: Prevention of reflux of colonic bacterial
Production of mucus for fecal lubrication
questions.question: The ileocecal valve is a mucosal fold at the junction of the ileum and cecum. Its primary histological function is:

questions.explanation: The forceps minor is formed by the laterally extending fibers of the genu of the corpus callosum and connects the frontal cortex of both hemispheres. In contrast, the forceps major is formed by fibers of the splenium and connects the occipital cortex bilaterally. The corpus callosum is the largest commissural fiber bundle, providing asymmetrical connections between corresponding cortical areas of the two hemispheres.
questions.question: Which commissural fiber connects the frontal cortex of both cerebral hemispheres?
The anterior spinal artery supplies which region of the medulla?
questions.explanation: The anterior spinal artery supplies the medial medulla, including the pyramids, medial lemniscus, and hypoglossal nucleus. Occlusion causes medial medullary syndrome with contralateral hemiplegia (pyramid damage), contralateral loss of fine touch and proprioception (medial lemniscus), and ipsilateral tongue paralysis with deviation toward the lesion side (hypoglossal nucleus). This contrasts with lateral medullary syndrome caused by PICA occlusion, demonstrating the distinct vascular territories of the medulla.

TORCH is an acronym for congenital infections: Toxoplasmosis, Other (syphilis, VZV, HIV, parvovirus B19), Rubella, Cytomegalovirus, and Herpes simplex. Influenza is not typically included in TORCH infections. These infections can cause serious fetal abnormalities when contracted during pregnancy.
questions.question: TORCH infections include all of the following EXCEPT:
Unilateral renal agenesis is often associated with:
questions.explanation: Unilateral renal agenesis is often associated with ipsilateral genital anomalies (absent vas deferens in males, uterine anomalies in females) because both systems develop from adjacent mesoderm and share inductive interactions. The condition results from failure of ureteric bud formation or degeneration of the metanephric blastema. Most cases are compatible with normal life if the contralateral kidney is normal.

options: Destroying aged erythrocytes and recycling iron from hemoglobin
Synthesizing transferrin for iron transport in blood
Storing iron only in bone marrow without degrading erythrocytes
Producing erythropoietin to stimulate red blood cell production
Converting bilirubin to iron in the gallbladder
questions.question: In the body, macrophages participate in iron metabolism by performing which of the following specific functions?
questions.explanation: Macrophages of the spleen (red pulp), liver (Kupffer cells), and bone marrow phagocytose aged or damaged erythrocytes, break down hemoglobin, and recycle iron (releasing it for new hemoglobin synthesis) and heme (converted to bilirubin). This erythrophagocytosis and iron recycling is a critical metabolic function. Macrophages also participate in extrahepatic bile production through this heme degradation pathway.

At the end of the 4th week, five mesenchymal prominences can be recognized surrounding the stomodeum: one frontonasal prominence, two mandibular prominences, and two maxillary prominences. These prominences are derived from neural crest cells and play crucial roles in facial development.
questions.question: At the end of the 4th week, how many mesenchymal prominences surround the stomodeum?
The epithalamus includes all of the following structures EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The epithalamus consists of the pineal gland, habenular nuclei, posterior commissure, and stria medullaris, but not the mammillary bodies (which are part of the posterior hypothalamus). The epithalamus is the smallest and phylogenetically oldest part of the diencephalon, located in the posterior and superior region. It is concerned with autonomic (respiratory and cardiovascular), endocrine (thyroid function), and reproductive functions, integrating olfactory and limbic information.

Kupffer cells (hepatic macrophages) are derived from mesenchyme of the septum transversum, along with fibrous tissue and hematopoietic tissue. The hepatic epithelial cells (hepatocytes and bile duct epithelium) are derived from endoderm of the hepatic diverticulum. This dual origin creates the complex cellular composition of the liver.
questions.question: Kupffer cells in the liver are derived from:

options: Neurons cannot produce new proteins after development
Neurons cannot receive synaptic signals from more than one cell
Neurons cannot transmit action potentials to adjacent cells
Neurons cannot develop myelin sheaths in the CNS
Destroyed neurons cannot be replaced since they lack the ability to divide
questions.explanation: The permanent post-mitotic state of neurons means that destroyed neurons are not replaced by new neurons through division. This is why CNS injuries from stroke or trauma and neurodegenerative diseases cause permanent functional deficits proportional to the neurons lost. Limited adult neurogenesis in specific brain regions represents a minor exception. This amitotic nature also explains why brain tumors arise from glial cells as gliomas rather than from neurons.
questions.question: Neurons are described as amitotic. The most significant clinical consequence of this property is which of the following?
The marginal layer is formed by which components?
questions.explanation: The axons of the mantle layer neurons coalesce in the outermost layer forming the marginal layer. This layer eventually becomes the white matter of the CNS. The myelination of these axons gives it the white appearance.

Gastroschisis differs from omphalocele by having no covering membranes; the viscera are bathed directly in amniotic fluid. The defect occurs to the right of the umbilicus through a ruptured abdominal wall defect. It is less commonly associated with other anomalies compared to omphalocele.
questions.question: Gastroschisis differs from omphalocele by having:

questions.explanation: The rectum differs from the rest of the large intestine in that the teniae coli spread out into a complete longitudinal muscle layer (no longer forming three bands), and haustra are absent — giving the rectum a smooth, non-sacculated outline. This smooth muscle coat contributes to the rectal reservoir function. The rectum is lined by simple columnar epithelium with goblet cells, transitioning to stratified squamous in the anal canal.
options: Is lined by stratified squamous epithelium
Has no teniae coli, as the longitudinal muscle is
Contains Brunner's glands in its submucosa
Has three distinct layers of muscularis externa
questions.question: The rectum differs from the sigmoid colon histologically in that the rectum:
The lens develops from which tissue?
questions.explanation: Surface epithelium of frontonasal prominence is induced by optic vesicles to form lens placodes. Placodes invaginate to form lens vesicles which develop lens fibers. The lens is entirely ectodermal.

The thymic cortex is densely packed with thymocytes undergoing positive selection and cortical epithelial cells forming a blood-thymus barrier. The medulla is less cellular and contains more mature T cells undergoing negative selection for self-tolerance, macrophages, dendritic cells, and Hassall's corpuscles which are whorls of keratinized epithelial cells unique to the thymus involved in regulatory T cell induction.
options: Cortex: densely packed immature thymocytes; medulla: mature T cells, less cellular
Cortex contains mostly B lymphocytes while medulla contains mostly T lymphocytes
