questions.explanation: A microtome is the specialized instrument used to cut tissue blocks into thin sections (typically 3–10 μm) that allow light transmission for microscopy. The cryostat is a variant used for frozen sections. A centrifuge separates components and an autoclave sterilizes, neither producing histological sections.
questions.question: A student views a specimen and finds it cannot be examined directly because of its thickness. Which instrument is most appropriate to produce thin translucent sections?
The auricle is formed from how many mesenchymal proliferations?
questions.explanation: The auricle develops from six mesenchymal proliferations (auricular hillocks), 3 on each side of meatus at dorsal ends of 1st and 2nd pharyngeal arches. These hillocks later fuse to form the definitive auricle.

questions.question: The pancreatic acinar cells produce digestive enzymes. Which morphological feature distinguishes them from islet cells?
options: Acinar cells are pale-staining with irregular nuclei
Acinar cells are large cells with central nuclei and clear cytoplasm
Acinar cells are pyramidal with basophilic cytoplasm and apical zymogen granules
Acinar cells are arranged in cords surrounded by fenestrated capillaries
questions.explanation: Pancreatic acinar cells are pyramidal or triangular cells with intensely basophilic basal cytoplasm (due to abundant rough ER for enzyme synthesis) and acidophilic apical zymogen granules (containing inactive digestive enzymes). They are arranged in rounded secretory units (acini). Islet cells (of Langerhans), in contrast, are paler-staining, spherical cells arranged in cords with rich capillary networks.

questions.question: The lentiform nucleus consists of which structures?
questions.explanation: The lentiform nucleus consists of outer putamen and inner globus pallidus. It is biconvex in shape. The putamen is lateral and larger than the medial globus pallidus.

questions.question: Which structures develop from the metencephalon?
questions.explanation: The metencephalon is the point of formation of both the pons and cerebellum. Pontine nuclei migrate into the developing pons. The rhombic lips differentiate into cerebellar plates.

questions.question: The tunica muscularis of the esophagus in its middle third contains both skeletal and smooth muscle. These two muscle types can be distinguished histologically because skeletal muscle has:
options: A single central nucleus and faint cross-striations
A single peripheral nucleus without cross-striations
questions.explanation: Skeletal muscle fibers can be identified histologically by their multiple peripheral nuclei (pushed to the periphery by myofibrils), prominent cross-striations (due to regular sarcomere arrangement), and large diameter. Smooth muscle cells have a single central nucleus, no cross-striations, and are spindle-shaped. Cardiac muscle has central nuclei, cross-striations, and intercalated discs. These features allow confident identification of muscle type in the esophageal wall.

questions.question: Plasma cells are responsible for antibody production and are derived from which precursor cell type?
options: B lymphocytes following antigen activation and maturation
questions.explanation: Plasma cells are terminally differentiated B lymphocytes that have undergone antigen activation, B cell receptor signaling, and somatic hypermutation, resulting in high-affinity antibody-secreting cells. They are the primary humoral immune effector cells, producing thousands of antibody molecules per second. Their unique morphology (eccentric clock-face nucleus, basophilic cytoplasm) reflects extreme adaptation for protein secretion.

questions.question: The cornea as part of the eye's optical apparatus provides approximately what proportion of the eye's total refractive power?
options: Two-thirds of total refractive power; primary refraction site
All refractive power without the lens
Only 10 percent of total refractive power
Equal contribution to the lens of 50 percent each
questions.explanation: The cornea provides approximately two-thirds of the total refractive power of the eye at about 43 diopters of the approximately 58 total, making it the primary refractive surface. The lens provides the remaining one-third and fine-tunes focus through accommodation. The cornea's refractive power is fixed while the lens changes shape. Corneal transparency depends on its regular collagen fiber arrangement, avascularity, and the endothelial fluid pump.

questions.question: The series of events in a cell leading to its division and duplication is collectively called which of the following?
questions.explanation: The cell cycle is the complete series of events from cell growth through DNA duplication to division into daughter cells. It encompasses both interphase (growth and DNA replication) and the mitotic (M) phase. The term mitogenesis describes factors stimulating cell division, not the cycle itself.

questions.question: The medial geniculate body projects to auditory cortex via which pathway?
questions.explanation: From medial geniculate body in thalamus, fibers project to auditory cortex in temporal lobe via acoustic radiation. The radiation passes through sublenticular portion of internal capsule. The auditory cortex is in Heschl's gyrus.

questions.question: All mammalian cells contain a cytoplasm and a nucleus EXCEPT which of the following?
questions.explanation: Mature mammalian erythrocytes are unique in lacking a nucleus (anucleate) as well as most other organelles including mitochondria. This anucleate state is achieved during terminal differentiation and maximizes space for hemoglobin, optimizing oxygen-carrying capacity. All other cell types listed retain both nucleus and cytoplasm throughout their functional lifespan.

questions.question: How many spermatozoa result from one spermatogonium that enters meiosis?
questions.explanation: One spermatogonium (type B) differentiates into one primary spermatocyte. Meiosis I produces two secondary spermatocytes. Meiosis II produces four spermatids. Spermiogenesis converts each spermatid into a spermatozoon, yielding four spermatozoa from each primary spermatocyte.

The right main bronchus gives rise to three secondary bronchi, corresponding to the three lobes of the right lung. The left main bronchus forms two secondary bronchi for the two lobes of the left lung. These appear as lateral outpocketings during the early 5th week.
questions.question: The right main bronchus gives rise to how many secondary bronchi?
The vertebral arteries fuse to form which artery?
questions.explanation: Vertebral arteries run alongside medulla and fuse at pontomedullary junction to form basilar artery. Before fusion they give off three branches. The basilar artery supplies the brainstem and cerebellum.

questions.question: The infundibulum together with Rathke's pouch forms which gland?
questions.explanation: The infundibulum alongside Rathke's pouch from the oral cavity forms the pituitary gland. It sits in the sella turcica. The cephalic flexure makes this connection topographically possible.

questions.question: Which structure does NOT develop from the dorsal pancreatic bud?
questions.explanation: The uncinate process does NOT develop from the dorsal pancreatic bud; it develops from the ventral bud along with part of the head. The dorsal bud forms the body, tail, and remainder of the head of the pancreas. The accessory pancreatic duct (when present) is formed from the proximal part of the dorsal bud duct.

questions.question: The liver produces the majority of serum proteins. Which protein, synthesized exclusively by hepatocytes, is the most abundant in plasma and maintains oncotic pressure?
questions.explanation: Albumin is synthesized exclusively by hepatocytes (approximately 12g/day) and is the most abundant plasma protein (35–50 g/L). It maintains plasma oncotic pressure (preventing edema), transports fatty acids, bilirubin, hormones, and drugs, and acts as a buffer. In chronic liver failure, reduced albumin synthesis causes hypoalbuminemia, leading to peripheral edema and ascites. Serum albumin level is a sensitive marker of synthetic function in chronic liver disease.

questions.question: Primary oocytes are arrested in which stage of meiosis until puberty?
questions.explanation: Primary oocytes begin meiosis I during fetal life but are arrested in prophase I (specifically diplotene stage) until puberty. At puberty, with each ovarian cycle, one or more primary oocytes complete meiosis I to form secondary oocytes, which are then arrested in metaphase II.

The massa intermedia (interthalamic adhesion) is present in approximately 60-80% of individuals, connecting the two thalami across the third ventricle. Its size varies considerably when present, and it may be absent in 20-40% of normal individuals without apparent functional consequence. This gray matter bridge does not transmit nerve fibers between the thalami and is not considered a true commissure. Its presence or absence has no known clinical significance, though it can serve as a radiographic landmark.
questions.question: The massa intermedia is present in approximately what percentage of individuals?

questions.explanation: Hypospadias results from incomplete fusion of the urethral folds on the ventral surface of the penis, leaving the urethral opening on the underside rather than at the tip. Severity varies from glandular (near tip) to penoscrotal. It is one of the most common congenital anomalies in males. Associated chordee (ventral curvature) often requires surgical correction.
questions.question: Hypospadias results from:

questions.explanation: Truncal ataxia with relatively preserved limb coordination suggests lesions of the vermis and flocculonodular lobe (medial cerebellum). These regions control axial muscles, posture, and balance through connections with vestibular and reticular systems. Patients have difficulty sitting and standing without support (truncal ataxia), wide-based gait, and difficulty with tandem walking, but finger-nose and heel-shin tests may be relatively normal. This pattern is seen in alcoholic cerebellar degeneration affecting anterior-superior vermis and in medulloblastomas (especially in children).
questions.question: Truncal ataxia with relatively preserved limb coordination suggests lesions in which cerebellar region?
Damage to which hypothalamic nuclei would primarily affect appetite regulation?
questions.explanation: The ventromedial nuclei (oval-shaped, anterior to the mammillary bodies) and dorsomedial nuclei (above the ventromedial) of the middle hypothalamic group play crucial roles in appetite regulation and satiety. The ventromedial nucleus serves as a \"satiety center\" while lateral hypothalamic areas function as a \"feeding center.\" Lesions of the ventromedial nuclei lead to hyperphagia and obesity, while lateral area lesions cause loss of appetite and weight loss.

Satellite cells are the adult stem cells of skeletal muscle, residing between the sarcolemma and the overlying basal lamina. They are normally quiescent but are activated by muscle injury, proliferate, and either fuse with damaged fibers or form new fibers, providing the limited but genuine regenerative capacity of skeletal muscle. Progressive depletion of satellite cells contributes to the sarcopenia seen with aging.
options: Between sarcomeres inside muscle fibers where they synthesize myosin
Within the endomysium where they produce collagen for muscle connective tissue
At the neuromuscular junction where they remyelinate motor nerves
In the perimysium where they differentiate into fibroblasts after injury
Between the sarcolemma and overlying basal lamina, serving as adult muscle stem cells
questions.question: Satellite cells in skeletal muscle are located in which specific position and serve which primary function?

questions.explanation: The flocculonodular lobe constitutes the archicerebellum and is phylogenetically the oldest part of the cerebellum, closely related to vestibular function. It consists of the nodulus (vermis) and paired flocculi (hemispheres), separated from the rest of the cerebellum by the posterolateral fissure. This lobe receives input from vestibular nuclei and is essential for maintaining balance and equilibrium; damage results in truncal ataxia and nystagmus.
questions.question: Which cerebellar lobule is phylogenetically the oldest and related to vestibular function?

questions.explanation: The white line (anocutaneous line) is located approximately 2 cm superior to the anus and marks where the anal epithelium changes from columnar to stratified squamous keratinized epithelium. This is distinct from the pectinate (dentate) line, which is more superior and marks the embryological junction between endoderm and ectoderm. Both lines have clinical significance.
questions.question: The white line (anocutaneous line) is located approximately how many centimeters above the anus?

options: All three layers are identical and have no specific order
questions.explanation: Each aortic valve cusp has three layers: (1) Ventricularis (ventricular surface) — rich in elastic fibers, allows elastic recoil; (2) Spongiosa (middle) — loose connective tissue with glycosaminoglycans, acts as shock absorber; (3) Fibrosa (aortic surface) — dense collagen, provides structural strength. These layers are arranged from the ventricular inflow surface outward. This trilaminar architecture is designed to withstand repetitive mechanical stress over 3 billion cardiac cycles in a lifetime.
questions.question: The aortic valve consists of three semilunar cusps. The histological layers of each cusp from the ventricular (inflow) to the aortic (outflow) surface are:

questions.explanation: Rugae are most prominent in the fundus and body of the stomach and are formed by redundant folding of both the mucosa and submucosa when the stomach is empty. As the stomach fills and distends, rugae flatten. They differ from plicae circulares of the small intestine (permanent, cannot flatten) and are created by the greater distensibility of the gastric wall. Rugae orientation is longitudinal, guiding fluid along the lesser curvature toward the pylorus.
questions.question: In which portion of the gastric wall are rugae most prominent, and what determines their formation?
options: They are uniform throughout all gastric regions and are formed by muscularis externa folding
Most prominent in the pyloric region; formed by mucosal gland hyperplasia
They are found only at the greater curvature of the stomach
Formed only by muscularis mucosae contraction with no submucosal component

questions.explanation: The white pulp of the spleen consists of the periarteriolar lymphoid sheath containing predominantly T lymphocytes encircling the central arteriole, and adjacent lymphoid follicles containing B lymphocytes that form germinal centers during immune responses. Together they constitute the immunologically active white pulp compartment strategically positioned for contact with blood-borne antigens. The marginal zone between white and red pulp contains marginal zone B cells and macrophages bridging innate and adaptive immunity.
options: Red pulp with venous sinuses and splenic cords
Trabecular framework and capsule of the spleen
White pulp T-cell PALS and B-cell follicles as immunologically active zones
Marginal zone alone without organized lymphocyte aggregates
Perivascular sheath containing only vascular smooth muscle cells
questions.question: A spleen histology section shows a periarteriolar lymphoid sheath surrounding a central artery and an adjacent lymphoid follicle with a germinal center. These structures collectively constitute which of the following?

questions.explanation: In the metencephalon, the dorsolateral parts of the alar plates bend medially and form the rhombic lips, which give rise to the cerebellum. The remaining portion of the metencephalon forms the pons. This bending is due to the pontine flexure.
questions.question: The rhombic lips of the metencephalon give rise to which structure?
Brown-Séquard syndrome results from which lesion?
questions.explanation: Brown-Séquard syndrome results from hemisection of spinal cord. It causes ipsilateral motor loss and proprioception loss, contralateral pain/temperature loss. It demonstrates crossed pathways. Pure forms are rare.

options: Resting → proliferative → hypertrophic → calcified cartilage → ossification
Ossification zone then calcified zone then hypertrophic zone then proliferative zone then resting zone
Only three zones exist: proliferative hypertrophic and ossification
Calcified zone is immediately adjacent to the resting zone
The proliferative zone is closest to the diaphysis
questions.explanation: The epiphyseal plate from epiphyseal to diaphyseal side has five zones: resting zone with quiescent hyaline cartilage chondrocytes; proliferative zone with rapidly dividing chondrocytes in longitudinal columns; hypertrophic zone with enlarged chondrocytes accumulating glycogen; calcified cartilage zone where matrix calcifies as chondrocytes die; and ossification zone where endochondral bone tissue appears as blood vessels and osteoblasts invade. This progression drives longitudinal bone growth.
questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes the five zones of the epiphyseal growth plate from the epiphyseal to the diaphyseal side?

options: A central nutrient foramen surrounded by randomly arranged trabecular bone
Concentric lamellae surrounding a central Haversian canal with blood vessels and nerves
A solid block of mineralized matrix with no canal system
Interconnecting trabeculae with red marrow in all spaces
A single osteocyte surrounded by ground substance only
questions.question: Compact (cortical) bone is organized into cylindrical structures called osteons (Haversian systems), each of which consists of which of the following?
questions.explanation: Each osteon (Haversian system) is the basic structural unit of compact bone, consisting of 5–20 concentric lamellae of mineralized matrix (with alternating collagen fiber orientations) surrounding a central Haversian canal containing small arterioles, venules, nerves, and loose connective tissue. Osteocytes reside in lacunae between lamellae and communicate via canaliculi that penetrate all lamellae to reach the central canal.

The thyroglossal duct initially connects the developing tongue and thyroid gland. The foramen cecum becomes thickened below the surface to form this duct. The tip of the duct becomes bilobed, and cells proliferating at this bifid end form the two lobes of the thyroid gland.
questions.question: The thyroglossal duct connects which two structures during development?

questions.explanation: Pores of Kohn are natural fenestrations (1–15 μm) in the walls between adjacent alveoli in adult lungs. They allow collateral ventilation — movement of air between alveoli via pathways that bypass conventional airways. This is protective in obstructive lung disease as alveoli distal to an obstructed airway can still receive air via the pores. However, they also allow bacterial spread between alveoli during pneumonia, contributing to consolidation patterns.
options: They allow collateral ventilation between alveoli when
They are pathological openings only seen in emphysema
They are sites of gas exchange
They allow fluid to drain into lymphatics
They are channels for surfactant distribution
questions.question: Pores of Kohn are small openings in alveolar septa connecting adjacent alveoli. Their functional significance is:

questions.explanation: The subarachnoid cavity communicates with the fourth ventricle through the central foramen of Magendie and the two lateral foramina of Luschka. This communication allows cerebrospinal fluid to flow from the ventricular system into the subarachnoid space surrounding the brain and spinal cord. The subarachnoid cavity terminates at the level of S2 and contains cerebrospinal fluid throughout its extent.
questions.question: Through which foramina does the subarachnoid cavity communicate with the ventricular system?
Bipolar neurons in dorsal root ganglia send processes to which locations?
questions.explanation: The medial process of bipolar dorsal root ganglion neurons enters the marginal layer of the alar plate. It ends in the dorsal horn or ascends to higher centers. The peripheral process extends to sensory receptors in the body.

questions.question: The dermis of the skin is derived from which embryonic source?
questions.explanation: The dermis of the face is derived from neural crest cells, while dermis in the dorsal region of the head comes from paraxial mesoderm, and dermis of the body wall comes from lateral plate mesoderm. The epidermis is derived from surface ectoderm throughout the body.

Perforating branches of the posterior cerebral artery supply the cerebral peduncle, substantia nigra, red nucleus, and other midbrain structures, as well as the thalamus (via thalamogeniculate and thalamoperforating arteries). These small vessels are crucial for blood supply to deep structures. Occlusion of thalamic perforating branches causes thalamic syndrome (Dejerine-Roussy syndrome) with contralateral sensory loss, pain (thalamic pain), and possible hemiataxia. Midbrain perforating vessel occlusion can cause various brainstem syndromes.
questions.question: Perforating branches of the posterior cerebral artery supply which structures?
Islets of Langerhans constitute which functional component of the pancreas?
options: Exocrine pancreas secreting digestive enzymes into the duodenum
Connective tissue stroma of the pancreas
questions.explanation: Islets of Langerhans are clusters of endocrine cells scattered throughout the pancreatic parenchyma. They contain alpha cells (glucagon), beta cells (insulin — most numerous, centrally located), delta cells (somatostatin), and PP cells (pancreatic polypeptide). These hormones are secreted directly into the rich capillary networks within islets. The islets constitute only about 2% of pancreatic mass but have profound metabolic importance.

Connective tissue mast cells (found in skin, peritoneal cavity) contain heparin as their predominant proteoglycan in granules, while mucosal mast cells (in intestinal mucosa and lung) contain chondroitin sulfate instead of heparin. Mucosal mast cells are also smaller than connective tissue mast cells. This biochemical distinction has implications for anticoagulant activity at different body sites.
options: Their surface receptors for IgE differ fundamentally
Connective tissue mast cells lack histamine while mucosal mast cells contain it
Connective tissue mast cells contain heparin; mucosal mast cells contain chondroitin sulfate
Connective tissue mast cells are found in the intestinal mucosa
questions.question: Two types of mast cells exist in connective tissue; the key difference between connective tissue mast cells and mucosal mast cells is which of the following?

questions.explanation: Voluntary movements require the entire motor system from cortex to muscles. Simple rhythms need only spinal circuits. Complex movements need multiple levels of hierarchy.
questions.question: Voluntary movements require which system?
The nasal placodes appear on approximately which day of development?
questions.explanation: Nasal placodes appear around day 30 as thickenings on the right and left of the anteroinferior portion of the frontal prominence. They are located above the stomodeum and below the forebrain. These placodes appear after optic and otic placodes and after the neural tube has completely closed.

questions.question: Hair cells of the organ of Corti develop from which embryonic ridge?
questions.explanation: The outer ridge of epithelial cells in the cochlear duct forms rows of hair cells, which are the sensory cells of the auditory system. These hair cells are covered by the tectorial membrane. The inner ridge forms other supporting structures of the organ of Corti.

Woven bone is the primary bone type formed rapidly during fetal development and fracture healing, with randomly arranged collagen fibers and more osteocytes per unit volume, providing structural support quickly but with inferior mechanical strength. It is subsequently replaced by lamellar bone through remodeling, which has precisely organized parallel collagen lamellae in alternating orientations conferring superior mechanical properties. Pathological persistence of woven bone occurs in Paget's disease and osteosarcoma.
options: Woven bone is more mineralized than lamellar bone
Lamellar bone forms faster than woven bone
Woven bone contains more osteocytes per unit volume
Regularly organized collagen lamellae providing superior mechanical strength
They are mechanically identical with only age-related differences
questions.question: The transition from woven bone to lamellar bone during development and fracture healing is important because of which difference between the two bone types?

questions.explanation: The alveolar septa contain: Type I pneumocytes (lining most of the surface), Type II pneumocytes (surfactant production), capillary endothelial cells, a shared basal lamina, elastic fibers (allowing alveolar recoil during expiration), collagen fibers (structural support), and occasional alveolar macrophages. Smooth muscle cells are NOT present in alveolar septa — they are found in bronchioles and pulmonary vessels. Loss of elastic fibers causes alveolar collapse (emphysema).
questions.question: The alveolar septa (interalveolar walls) are the thin tissue partitions between adjacent alveoli. Their structural components include all of the following EXCEPT:

questions.explanation: A thyroglossal cyst results from persistence of a portion of the thyroglossal duct. The duct normally becomes solid and disappears, but if portions persist, they can form cysts anywhere along the path of thyroid descent from the foramen cecum to the final position in the neck.
questions.question: A thyroglossal cyst results from persistence of which embryonic structure?

options: All contents of the cell including the nucleus
Only the membrane-bound organelles within the cell
The soluble aqueous phase of the cytoplasm, excluding organelles
The gel-like material found only within the nucleus
The extracellular fluid immediately surrounding the cell
questions.explanation: The cytosol is the soluble, aqueous phase of the cytoplasm in which organelles are suspended; it excludes membrane-bound organelles, cytoskeletal elements, and inclusions. The cytoplasm encompasses everything between the plasma membrane and nuclear envelope, including both the cytosol and all organelles. The distinction matters when discussing metabolic reactions that occur 'in the cytosol' (glycolysis) versus 'in the cytoplasm' more broadly.
questions.question: The 'cytosol' is distinguished from the 'cytoplasm' in that the cytosol specifically refers to which of the following?
The postcentral sulcus runs parallel to which structure?
questions.explanation: The postcentral sulcus runs parallel and posterior to the central sulcus, separating the postcentral gyrus (primary somatosensory cortex) from the superior and inferior parietal lobules posteriorly. This sulcus marks the posterior boundary of the primary somatosensory cortex (areas 3, 1, 2). The region between the postcentral and central sulci contains the postcentral gyrus, which has a somatotopic organization (sensory homunculus) similar to the motor homunculus of the precentral gyrus.

questions.question: Compaction of blastomeres occurs at which cell stage?
questions.explanation: At the 2- and 4-cell stages, blastomeres are loosely bound. With the third division producing 8 cells, compaction occurs, producing tightly bound cells. This compaction maximizes cell-to-cell contact and is essential for subsequent differentiation into inner cell mass and trophoblast.

The stria vascularis is a specialized epithelium on the lateral wall of the cochlear duct containing marginal cells, intermediate cells, and basal cells with extensive ion transport machinery including Na-K-ATPases and KCNJ10 potassium channels. It maintains the endolymph composition of high potassium and low sodium and generates the endocochlear potential of approximately +80 mV. This large potential difference drives potassium through mechanosensitive channels in hair cell stereocilia amplifying the transduction current.
options: Spiral ganglion neurons secreting potassium into the scala media
Basilar membrane vibration generating piezoelectric potentials
Stria vascularis maintaining high-K+ endolymph and the positive endocochlear potential
Outer hair cells through their electromotile activity
The round window membrane oscillating against the tectorial membrane
questions.question: The endocochlear potential of approximately +80 mV in the scala media endolymph is generated by which structure and serves which function?
Melanocytes originate from which embryonic source?
questions.explanation: Melanocytes are neural crest derivatives that migrate into the embryonic epidermis during the first three months of development. They migrate to the dermo-epidermal junction where they differentiate from melanoblasts. One melanocyte typically associates with 30-40 keratinocytes, forming an epidermal-melanin unit.

questions.question: A person with 69 chromosomes has which condition?
questions.explanation: Triploidy (69 chromosomes, three complete sets) is a lethal condition usually resulting from fertilization of an egg by two sperm (dispermy) or failure of meiotic division. Most triploid conceptuses are spontaneously aborted. Tetraploidy (92 chromosomes) is even rarer and also lethal.

questions.question: Alveoli at birth are approximately what fraction of the adult number?
questions.explanation: At birth, alveoli number approximately 1/6th of the adult number. The remaining 5/6ths develop postnatally, primarily during the first 10 years of life. This continued alveolar development explains why lung function continues to improve during childhood. Factors affecting early lung development can have lifelong consequences.

questions.question: The choroid plexus extends into which parts of the lateral ventricle?
questions.explanation: The choroid plexus of the lateral ventricle extends through the body, trigone (atrium), and inferior horn, but is absent from the anterior and posterior horns. It enters through the choroid fissure, the cleft between the fornix and thalamus where pia mater invaginates into the ventricle. The choroid plexus is continuous with that of the third ventricle through the interventricular foramen. In the inferior horn, the choroid plexus lies in the choroid fissure between the fimbria and the stria terminalis.

Malrotation of the midgut can lead to volvulus, which is rotation of an intestinal loop around a branch of the superior mesenteric artery. This can cause intestinal obstruction or even gangrene. Volvulus requires emergency surgical intervention to prevent bowel ischemia and necrosis.
questions.question: Malrotation of the midgut can lead to:

questions.explanation: Elastic fibers require special staining techniques because they are not well visualized by H&E. Weigert's resorcin-fuchsin and orcein stains specifically stain elastic fibers dark blue-black or brown, allowing their visualization in vessels, lung, and ligamentum flavum. Silver stains, by contrast, stain reticular (type III collagen) fibers. This differential staining is important for diagnosing conditions affecting elastic tissue (e.g., emphysema, aortic aneurysm).
options: Type IV collagen of basement membranes
questions.question: Which connective tissue fiber type is best demonstrated by the Weigert's or orcein staining techniques?

questions.explanation: The cells of nervous system are divided into neurons (excitable cells transmitting signals) and neuroglia (supporting cells). Neurons together with neuroglia make up nervous tissue. Each cell type has specialized functions.
questions.question: The two main categories of nervous system cells are which?

questions.explanation: Langerhans cells are specialized antigen-presenting macrophages resident in the skin epidermis, named after Paul Langerhans who also described the pancreatic islets. They capture antigens entering through the skin and migrate to draining lymph nodes to present antigens to T lymphocytes, initiating adaptive immune responses. They are part of the MPS and contain characteristic tennis racket-shaped cytoplasmic Birbeck granules.
questions.question: Which connective tissue cell type acts as an antigen-presenting cell (APC) in the skin epidermis and is specifically named after the scientist who described it?

questions.explanation: Most of the esophagus is located in the neck and thorax, where it lacks peritoneal covering and is therefore surrounded by adventitia — loose connective tissue that blends with surrounding structures. Only the short intraabdominal segment of the esophagus is covered by serosa (peritoneum). This has surgical significance as it affects how esophageal leaks are managed.
options: The portion at the gastroesophageal junction
questions.question: The adventitia, rather than serosa, covers the esophagus in which portion?

questions.explanation: Cortical neurons migrate in an inside-out pattern with earlier-born neurons in deeper layers. Later neurons migrate past them to superficial layers. This establishes six-layered cortex. Radial glia guide migration.
questions.question: Cortical neurons migrate in which pattern?

questions.explanation: Layer II (external granular layer) primarily contains small granule cells and stellate interneurons that process and distribute information within local cortical circuits. These neurons have short axons and extensive dendritic arbors, facilitating lateral connections within the cortex. Interneurons use GABA as their neurotransmitter and provide inhibitory modulation of pyramidal cell activity, shaping cortical responses to inputs and maintaining proper excitatory-inhibitory balance essential for normal cortical function.
questions.question: The external granular layer of the cortex primarily contains which neurons?
The straight gyrus (gyrus rectus) is located where?
questions.explanation: The straight gyrus (gyrus rectus) is located on the inferior medial frontal surface, medial to the olfactory sulcus and lateral to the interhemispheric fissure. It is a straight, narrow gyrus running anteroposteriorly along the medial inferior frontal lobe. The olfactory bulb and tract lie lateral to it in the olfactory sulcus. The gyrus rectus is part of the orbitofrontal cortex and involved in decision-making and impulse control; damage can contribute to frontal lobe syndrome.

questions.question: Adipocytes (fat cells) in connective tissue are specialized for which of the following primary functions?
questions.explanation: Adipocytes are highly specialized connective tissue cells derived from mesenchyme that store neutral fat (triglycerides) as a single large droplet (unilocular white adipose tissue) or multiple small droplets (multilocular brown adipose tissue). Their metabolic functions include energy storage/release, thermal insulation, organ cushioning, and (importantly recognized now) endocrine signaling through adipokines like leptin and adiponectin.
options: Synthesis and secretion of immunoglobulins by plasma cells
Phagocytosis of debris from tissue injury
Secretion of histamine during allergic reactions
Cytoplasmic storage of neutral lipids for energy and insulation

questions.explanation: Hematopoiesis (blood cell formation) first occurs in the yolk sac wall and allantois during the third week. It later shifts to the liver (6 weeks), then to the spleen (12 weeks), and finally to the bone marrow (which becomes the primary site by 28 weeks and throughout life).
questions.question: Hematopoiesis first occurs in which embryonic location?

questions.explanation: Embryonic CSF begins to form in the 5th week of IUL. Fluid-filled spaces appear in leptomeninges and coalesce to form subarachnoid space. This separates arachnoid from pia mater.
questions.question: Embryonic CSF begins to form in which week of IUL?

questions.explanation: The gastric mucus layer (primarily secreted by surface mucous cells) acts as a physicochemical barrier protecting the gastric epithelium from the highly acidic (pH ~2) and pepsin-containing gastric juice. Disruption of this mucus barrier is central to the pathogenesis of peptic ulcers. The mucus also contains bicarbonate which further neutralizes acid at the mucosal surface.
options: Protecting the mucosa from self-digestion by HCl and pepsin
Anchoring the epithelial cells to the lamina propria
questions.question: The gastric mucosa's surface is covered by a thick mucus layer. What is the primary role of this mucus layer?
Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) is an autoimmune disease targeting intrahepatic bile ducts. The characteristic histological finding in early PBC is:
questions.explanation: The pathognomonic early histological lesion of primary biliary cholangitis is the 'florid duct lesion' — granulomatous inflammation with a dense lymphocytic and plasma cell infiltrate surrounding and destroying the interlobular bile ducts. This is mediated by autoreactive T cells targeting mitochondrial antigens (anti-mitochondrial antibodies/AMA are serological markers). Progressive bile duct destruction leads to cholestasis, fibrosis, and eventually cirrhosis.
options: Granulomatous destruction of interlobular bile ducts
Periportal fibrosis with plasma cell infiltrate

questions.question: Ankyloglossia results from:
questions.explanation: Ankyloglossia (tongue-tie) is characterized by an unusually short, thick lingual frenulum that may decrease tongue mobility. It is a congenital oral anomaly that can affect speech and feeding. Severe cases may require surgical intervention (frenulotomy) to improve tongue movement.

questions.question: Damage to the paracentral lobule would primarily affect:
questions.explanation: The paracentral lobule on the medial surface of the hemisphere contains the motor and sensory representations for the lower limb and perineum, straddling the medial continuation of the central sulcus. Lesions cause contralateral leg weakness and sensory loss, potentially with bladder dysfunction if the representation for the perineum is affected. Anterior cerebral artery strokes affecting this region produce characteristic lower limb deficits with relative sparing of arm and face, distinguishing them from middle cerebral artery strokes.

The frontal eye field is located in Brodmann area 8 in the middle frontal gyrus, controlling voluntary eye movements and visual attention. It also contributes to areas 6 and 9 in some classifications. Stimulation of this area causes conjugate eye deviation toward the opposite side, while lesions cause inability to voluntarily direct gaze contralaterally. The frontal eye fields work with the superior colliculus and PPRF to coordinate saccadic eye movements and visual scanning.
questions.question: The frontal eye field is located in which area?

questions.explanation: Fixation is the process that preserves structural integrity by halting autolysis and enzymatic degradation immediately after tissue removal. Without fixation, cells deteriorate rapidly through processes like drying out and autolysis. Common fixatives include formalin (formaldehyde-based) which cross-links proteins to stabilize cell architecture.
questions.question: The process by which cell structure is preserved after tissue removal, preventing rapid deterioration, is specifically called which of the following?
The gustatory cortex is located in which region?
questions.explanation: The gustatory (taste) cortex is located in the inferior part of the postcentral gyrus and adjacent opercular region (Brodmann area 43), near the somatosensory representation of the tongue. This area receives taste information from the ventral posteromedial nucleus of the thalamus, which in turn receives input from the nucleus solitarius via the gustatory pathway. The gustatory cortex processes taste quality, intensity, and affective components of taste perception.

options: Study of living organisms using electron beams
Study of tissues derived from 'histos' and 'logia'
Study of cells using biochemical markers only
Anatomical study limited to the gross level
Study of body fluids and their components
questions.question: Which of the following correctly defines histology in terms of its Greek etymological roots?
questions.explanation: Histology derives from the Greek 'histos' meaning web or tissue, and 'logia' meaning the study of a science. It specifically focuses on the microscopic anatomy of cells and tissues. Understanding this etymology distinguishes histology from gross anatomy, cytology, and biochemistry.

questions.question: The tensor tympani muscle is innervated by which division of the trigeminal nerve?
questions.explanation: The tensor tympani muscle is derived from the first pharyngeal arch and is innervated by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V3). It attaches to the malleus and dampens sound. The tensor veli palatini (also first arch) is also innervated by CN V3.
Internal ear development starts around day 22 with otic placode thickening beside the myelencephalon. This invaginates to form otic vesicles. The placode is surface ectoderm.
questions.question: The otic placode first appears on which day of intrauterine life?

questions.explanation: The pars opercularis (opercular part) of the inferior frontal gyrus, along with the pars triangularis, comprises Broca's motor speech area (Brodmann areas 44 and 45) in the dominant hemisphere. The pars opercularis is the posterior portion, bounded posteriorly by the precentral sulcus and anteriorly by the ascending ramus of the lateral sulcus. Damage causes expressive (Broca's) aphasia with non-fluent, effortful speech, agrammatism, and relatively preserved comprehension. In the non-dominant hemisphere, this region may be involved in prosody (emotional tone of speech).
questions.question: The pars opercularis of the inferior frontal gyrus corresponds to which area?
The GIT wall is described as a hollow tube with four layers. Which layer represents the structural foundation providing tensile strength to resist luminal pressure?
questions.explanation: The submucosa, composed of dense irregular connective tissue rich in collagen type I and elastic fibers, provides the primary tensile strength to the GIT wall. This is why surgeons place sutures through the submucosa during intestinal anastomoses — it is the holding layer. In conditions like diverticular disease, weakness of the submucosa and muscularis allows mucosal herniation through the wall.

The placenta is a fetomaternal organ composed of two portions: the fetal portion (from the chorionic sac, specifically the chorion frondosum) and the maternal portion (from the endometrium, specifically the decidua basalis). These two portions are intimately connected but do not mix blood directly.
questions.question: The placenta is composed of which two portions?
The digestive tract functions as a hollow tube. Which region demonstrates the most dramatic variation in the diameter of its lumen under normal physiological conditions?
questions.explanation: The stomach is the most dilated portion of the digestive tract and has the greatest capacity for luminal expansion. When empty, its mucosa forms longitudinal folds called rugae. As the stomach fills, these rugae flatten, allowing enormous increase in lumen diameter. No other segment of the GIT matches this degree of distensibility.

Hassall's corpuscles are spherical structures in the thymic medulla composed of concentrically arranged keratinized medullary epithelial cells forming onion-skin-like whorls. They appear in increasing numbers with age and thymic involution. Recent evidence shows they produce thymic stromal lymphopoietin that activates medullary dendritic cells to induce regulatory T cells contributing to self-tolerance. They are pathognomonic for thymic tissue identification in histological sections.
questions.question: The Hassall's corpuscles found exclusively in the thymic medulla are composed of which of the following?
options: Clusters of mature T lymphocytes expressing CD8
Keratinized epithelial whorls involved in regulatory T cell induction
Macrophages that have phagocytosed dying thymocytes
Type IV collagen deposits forming the blood-thymus barrier

questions.question: The interposed nucleus consists of which two nuclei?
questions.explanation: The interposed nucleus consists of the emboliform (wedge-shaped) and globose (rounded) nuclei, which are functionally similar and considered together as the interposed nucleus in humans (though separate in lower mammals). The paravermal zone projects to these nuclei, which then project via the superior cerebellar peduncle to the contralateral red nucleus and thalamus. The interposed nucleus influences distal limb muscles and is involved in correcting ongoing movements. Lesions cause limb ataxia and intention tremor.

A caudal neuroepithelial thickening on the dorsal surface evaginates around the 7th week to form the pineal body. It sits on the mesencephalon. The pineal gland secretes melatonin and regulates circadian rhythms.
questions.question: The pineal body develops from which structure?

questions.explanation: The intermaxillary segment has three components: the upper jaw component (carries four incisor teeth), the labial component (forms the philtrum of the upper lip), and the palatal component (forms the triangular primary palate). The segment forms by fusion of the two medial nasal prominences.
questions.question: The philtrum of the upper lip is formed from which component of the intermaxillary segment?
During cell cycle arrest, a cell accumulates in which phase if it fails to complete DNA replication?
questions.explanation: DNA replication occurs during the S (synthesis) phase of interphase; if replication is incomplete or damaged, checkpoint mechanisms arrest the cell in S phase or at the S/G2 boundary. Checkpoints prevent progression to mitosis until DNA integrity is confirmed. Arrest in S phase occurs when replication forks stall or when DNA damage is detected during replication.

Vernix caseosa is a white, greasy substance composed of sebum (from sebaceous glands) and desquamated peridermal cells. It covers fetal skin and protects against constant exposure to amniotic fluid with its high urine content. Vernix also facilitates birth by providing lubrication.
questions.question: Vernix caseosa is composed of:

questions.explanation: Just beyond the choroid plexus bearing region, neuroblast proliferation forms the slightly thickened hippocampus. This portion gets buried within the enlarging cortex. It bulges into the cavity of the lateral ventricle.
questions.question: The hippocampus is formed from which region?

questions.explanation: The roof plate ependymal layer in addition to surrounding vascular mesenchyme forms the choroid plexus. This occurs in regions where neuroblast proliferation fails. The choroid plexus produces cerebrospinal fluid.
questions.question: The choroid plexus of lateral ventricles is formed by which structures?
The substantia propria of the cornea develops from which embryonic layer?
questions.explanation: The outer layer of mesenchymal tissue overlying the anterior aspect of the eye forms the substantia propria of the cornea. Vacuolization of this mesenchymal tissue creates the anterior chamber. The inner mesenchymal layer forms the iridopupillary membrane, which later disappears to establish communication between anterior and posterior chambers.

questions.question: Upper motor neuron signs include which features?
questions.explanation: Upper motor neuron signs include spastic paralysis, hyperreflexia, Babinski sign and clonus. Lower motor neuron signs include flaccid paralysis and hyporeflexia. This distinction aids localization. UMN lesions are above anterior horn.

The most serious consequence of oligohydramnios is pulmonary hypoplasia (underdeveloped lungs), which is often lethal. Normal amniotic fluid is essential for lung development through fetal breathing movements and adequate thoracic space. Severe oligohydramnios, especially in the second trimester, prevents normal lung development. Affected neonates cannot maintain adequate gas exchange after birth.
questions.question: The most serious consequence of oligohydramnios is:
Aqueous humor fills the anterior and posterior chambers of the eye and is produced by which structure?
questions.explanation: Aqueous humor is produced by the ciliary body's non-pigmented epithelium through active secretion from blood plasma. It flows from the posterior chamber through the pupil into the anterior chamber and drains at the iridocorneal angle through the trabecular meshwork into Schlemm's canal. Impaired drainage in glaucoma increases intraocular pressure damaging the optic nerve. Aqueous humor provides nutrients to the avascular lens and cornea.
options: The corneal endothelium through active secretion
The ciliary body epithelium by active secretion from capillaries
The vitreous humor flowing into the anterior chamber
The iris stroma through filtration of plasma

questions.question: The lung pleura is composed of two layers — visceral and parietal. Both are lined by which cell type?
questions.explanation: Both the visceral (lung) and parietal (chest wall, diaphragm, mediastinum) pleura are lined by a continuous layer of mesothelial cells — simple squamous epithelial cells of mesodermal origin. Mesothelial cells produce lubricating serous fluid that allows friction-free lung movement during breathing. In pleural mesothelioma (associated with asbestos exposure), these cells undergo malignant transformation. Mesothelial cells are identified immunohistochemically by calretinin, WT1, and CK5/6.
Ganglion cells of CN VIII migrate along cochlear coils to form spiral ganglion. Peripheral processes extend to organ of Corti hair cells. Central processes form the cochlear nerve.
questions.question: The spiral ganglion is formed by which cells?

questions.explanation: The loop of Henle becomes functionally mature at approximately 1 year of age. At birth, infant kidneys cannot concentrate urine as effectively as adult kidneys because the loops of Henle are short and the medullary concentration gradient is not fully developed. This explains why infants produce dilute urine and are vulnerable to dehydration. Concentrating ability gradually improves during the first year.
questions.question: The loop of Henle becomes functionally mature:
A histology slide shows an outermost layer composed of mesothelium overlying loose connective tissue. This layer is correctly identified as the:
questions.explanation: Wait — the correct answer here requires careful distinction: The serosa is an outermost layer covered by mesothelium (peritoneum) for intraperitoneal organs. The adventitia is a connective tissue layer WITHOUT mesothelium for retroperitoneal organs. When mesothelium is present, the correct term is serosa. Answer: C (Serosa) — mesothelium is the hallmark of serosa/peritoneal covering.

questions.question: The enteric nervous system (ENS) is called the 'second brain'. What is the total approximate number of neurons in the ENS?
questions.explanation: The ENS contains approximately 100 million (10^8) neurons — more than the spinal cord — organized into the myenteric and submucosal plexuses. This vast neuronal network enables autonomous regulation of GIT motility, secretion, and blood flow, earning the ENS its designation as the 'second brain.' The ENS communicates bidirectionally with the CNS via the vagus nerve and sympathetic pathways.

questions.question: The epithelium lining the respiratory tract from nasal cavity to small bronchi is characterized as which type and what is the functional significance of its goblet cells?
questions.explanation: Respiratory epithelium from nasal cavity through trachea and bronchi to small bronchioles is pseudostratified ciliated columnar with goblet cells. Goblet cells secrete viscous mucus that forms a protective blanket trapping inhaled particles, pathogens, and allergens. Approximately 200 cilia per cell beat at 10 to 15 Hz in coordinated waves propelling the mucus blanket with its trapped particles toward the pharynx for clearance. This mucociliary escalator is the primary mechanical defense of the respiratory tract, impaired in smoking and primary ciliary dyskinesia.
options: Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells; mucociliary escalator
Simple squamous epithelium optimized for gas exchange
Stratified squamous keratinized epithelium for mechanical protection
Transitional epithelium capable of changing shape
Simple cuboidal epithelium with secretory function only

questions.explanation: Taste buds are formed by inductive interaction between epithelial cells of the tongue and invading gustatory nerve cells from the chorda tympani branch of the facial nerve (CN VII). This interaction is essential for taste bud development in the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.
questions.question: Taste buds form by inductive interaction between epithelial cells and which nerve?
Failure of recanalization of the anal membrane results in:
questions.explanation: Failure of recanalization of the anal membrane, which normally occurs during the 9th week, results in imperforate anus. The anal membrane forms at the junction of the proctodeum (ectoderm) and hindgut (endoderm). Temporary occlusion by epithelial proliferation is normal, but failure of subsequent recanalization causes this anomaly.

questions.question: Which cranial nerves emerge from the medulla?
questions.explanation: The glossopharyngeal (IX), vagus (X), accessory (XI), and hypoglossal (XII) cranial nerves emerge from the medulla oblongata. The hypoglossal nerve emerges between the pyramid and olive, while IX, X, and XI emerge posterior to the olive.

The facial nerve (VII) SVE fibers supply 2nd pharyngeal arch derivatives (muscles of facial expression, stapedius, stylohyoid, posterior digastric). It also has GVE, SVA and GSA components. It exits at pontomedullary junction.
questions.question: The facial nerve supplies which pharyngeal arch derivatives?
Neural crest cells migrate to which position relative to the neural tube?
questions.explanation: As the neural tube detaches from surface ectoderm, neural crest cells migrate dorsolaterally on each side of the neural tube to form the neural crest. The neural crest then separates into right and left parts lying on the dorsolateral aspect of the neural tube, giving rise to dorsal root ganglia.

Amniotic fluid is derived from active secretion by amniotic epithelium, transudation from fetal circulation, fetal urine (important source in later pregnancy), and transudation from maternal circulation. The fetal liver does not directly contribute to amniotic fluid production.
questions.question: Amniotic fluid is derived from all sources EXCEPT:
The anterior lobe of the cerebellum receives proprioceptive input primarily from which pathway?
questions.explanation: The anterior lobe (paleocerebellum) receives proprioceptive input primarily from the spinocerebellar tracts (dorsal and ventral), carrying information about muscle length, tension, and joint position from the body. This input allows the anterior lobe to regulate muscle tone and coordinate posture and locomotion. The spinocerebellar pathways provide unconscious proprioception, unlike the dorsal column system which carries conscious proprioception. Anterior lobe lesions cause gait ataxia and limb incoordination, particularly affecting proximal muscles.

questions.question: Proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) cells have numerous apical microvilli (brush border) and extensive basolateral infoldings. These adaptations are designed for:
questions.explanation: The PCT reabsorbs approximately 65% of the glomerular filtrate — including virtually all glucose and amino acids, most sodium, water, potassium, and bicarbonate. The brush border greatly increases the apical surface area, while basolateral infoldings and abundant mitochondria support the energy-intensive Na+/K+-ATPase-driven active transport. PCT cells are the most metabolically active cells in the kidney.

The small intestine is the primary site of nutrient absorption. Its mucosa is extensively modified with plicae circulares, villi, and microvilli to maximize surface area. Digested macromolecules — amino acids, monosaccharides, fatty acids — cross the epithelium here into blood and lymphatic vessels for systemic distribution.
questions.question: The main macromolecules broken down during GIT digestion include proteins, complex carbohydrates, nucleic acids, and fats. The products of digestion are absorbed primarily through the lining of which structure?
Motor output is guided by which input?
questions.explanation: Motor output is guided by sensory input which fine-tunes motion activities. Eyes, balance organs, and receptors in skin, muscles and joints monitor response. Many adjustments are controlled by lower levels.

questions.question: Embryonic induction is involved in development of all EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Embryonic induction is involved in development of many organs including eyes (lens, optic cup), ears, limbs, kidney, teeth, hair, salivary glands, and pancreas. Blood cell development (hematopoiesis) occurs through intrinsic differentiation programs rather than classical tissue-to-tissue induction.

The stomach body (and fundus) is characterized by simple columnar epithelium with gastric pits and glands (invaginations into the lamina propria), absence of villi, and a uniquely three-layered muscularis externa (oblique, circular, longitudinal). The colon also lacks villi but has only two distinct muscularis layers arranged as teniae coli. The three-layered muscularis is the key distinguishing feature pointing to the stomach.
questions.question: A section of GIT stained with H&E shows mucosa with simple columnar epithelium invaginating into the lamina propria, NO villi, and a thick muscularis externa with three distinct layers. Which region is MOST likely depicted?
Convolutions of cerebral cortex occur in which gestational period?
questions.explanation: In the latter quarter of gestation, expansion of cerebral cortex exceeds cranial vault capacity resulting in convolutions. The degree of convolutions relates directly to behavioral and neuronal complexity. This folding increases surface area.

questions.question: The lateral motor pathways primarily control which muscles?
questions.explanation: Lateral motor pathways (corticospinal and rubrospinal) primarily control limb muscles for skilled movements. Medial pathways control trunk and proximal muscles. This is the proximal-distal rule of motor organization.

questions.question: The liver parenchyma is predominantly composed of hepatocytes, but which additional cell type lines the hepatic sinusoids and has fenestrated cytoplasm?
questions.explanation: Hepatic sinusoidal endothelial cells (LSECs) are specialized endothelial cells with numerous transcytoplasmic pores (fenestrae) arranged in groups called sieve plates. This fenestrated structure allows free passage of plasma and macromolecules (but not blood cells) between the sinusoidal blood and the space of Disse, facilitating hepatocyte exchange. Loss of fenestration in hepatic disease impairs liver function.

questions.question: At which Carnegie stage does the caudal neuropore close?
questions.explanation: The caudal neuropore closes at Carnegie stage 13, which corresponds to approximately 28 days of development. At this stage, the 4th pair of pharyngeal arches appear, upper and lower limb buds are visible, lens placodes are present, and the tail is attenuated. This closure is critical for normal neural tube development.

Barrett's esophagus is defined histologically by the presence of specialized intestinal metaplasia — simple columnar epithelium with goblet cells — replacing the normal non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium of the esophagus. The goblet cells (staining blue/purple with alcian blue stain) are the pathognomonic feature. Barrett's esophagus is a premalignant condition increasing the risk of esophageal adenocarcinoma approximately 30- to 125-fold.
questions.question: A biopsy from the gastroesophageal junction shows simple columnar epithelium with occasional goblet cells — features NOT expected in normal esophageal tissue. This histological finding is diagnostic of:

questions.explanation: The cecal swelling (diverticulum) in the caudal limb of the midgut loop marks the primordium of both the cecum and appendix. This swelling appears during the 6th week. The appendix initially arises from the distal end of the cecum but shifts to the medial side with unequal cecal wall growth.
questions.question: The cecal swelling marks the future:

questions.explanation: Oligohydramnios (amniotic fluid volume <500 ml) is most commonly associated with renal agenesis or other urinary tract abnormalities that prevent fetal urine production. This can result in Potter sequence: pulmonary hypoplasia, limb deformities, and characteristic facial features. Polyhydramnios is associated with esophageal atresia and anencephaly.
questions.question: Oligohydramnios (too little amniotic fluid) is most commonly associated with which condition?

questions.explanation: Hematoxylin is a basic (positively charged at acidic pH after mordanting) dye that is attracted to the negatively charged phosphate groups of nucleic acids — DNA in nuclei and RNA in nucleoli, ribosomes, and rough ER. This explains why cell nuclei stain blue-purple (basophilic) while collagen-rich cytoplasm and extracellular matrix stain pink (eosinophilic) with eosin in H&E. The degree of basophilia reflects RNA/ribosome content.
questions.question: Hematoxylin stains nuclei blue-purple in H&E sections. This basophilic staining occurs because nuclei predominantly contain which of the following?
options: Lipids in cell membranes with negative surface charges
Myofilaments of actin and myosin in the sarcomere
Collagen fibers with hydroxylysine and hydroxyproline residues
Phosphate groups on nucleic acids attract the cationic hematoxylin dye

questions.question: The medullary rays of the kidney are radial striations visible in the cortex extending from the medullary pyramids. They contain which structures?
questions.explanation: Medullary rays (Ferrein's pyramids) are radial extensions of medullary tissue into the cortex. They contain the straight (pars recta) portions of proximal and distal tubules and the cortical portions of collecting ducts — all running parallel to each other in a radial direction. In contrast, the cortical labyrinth (cortex between medullary rays) contains the renal corpuscles, proximal convoluted tubules, and distal convoluted tubules.
options: Renal corpuscles and proximal convoluted tubules
Loop of Henle thin limbs only

questions.explanation: Third-order neurons from superior olivary nucleus form lateral lemniscus ascending the brainstem to inferior colliculus. Some fibers synapse with nucleus of lateral lemniscus. The lateral lemniscus is a major ascending auditory pathway.
questions.question: The lateral lemniscus is formed by neurons from which nucleus?

questions.explanation: Localized dilatations (ampullae) develop at one end of each semicircular duct where cristae ampullae differentiate. These are specialized receptor areas for equilibrium. They are also present in utricle and saccule.
questions.question: Cristae ampullae are specialized receptors for which function?

questions.explanation: The middle third of the esophagus is characterized by its mixed muscularis containing both skeletal and smooth muscle, lining of non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium, and the absence of serosa (covered by adventitia). These three features together uniquely identify the middle esophagus in histological sections. The stomach has simple columnar epithelium and the trachea has pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium.
questions.question: A histological section shows a tube with stratified squamous epithelium, a thick muscularis with mixed skeletal and smooth muscle, and no serosa. This most likely represents which structure?

questions.explanation: The wall of the fused neural tube is composed of neuroepithelial cells arranged in a pseudostratified epithelium. These neuroepithelial cells give rise to neurons, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, and ependymal cells. Microglia are derived from mesoderm, and Schwann cells from neural crest.
questions.question: The wall of the neural tube is initially composed of which type of cells?

options: Principal cells reabsorb H+; intercalated cells reabsorb Na+
Both cell types perform identical functions
Principal cells secrete aldosterone; intercalated cells secrete ADH
Principal cells are responsible for potassium reabsorption only
questions.question: Principal cells and intercalated cells are the two main cell types of the collecting duct. Which statement correctly distinguishes their functions?
questions.explanation: Principal cells (most numerous in collecting duct) have aldosterone-regulated ENaC channels for Na+ reabsorption and ROMK channels for K+ secretion; ADH-regulated aquaporin-2 insertion mediates water reabsorption. Intercalated cells manage acid-base balance: Type A intercalated cells secrete H+ (via H+/K+-ATPase and H+-ATPase) and reabsorb HCO3- for acid excretion. Type B intercalated cells secrete HCO3- and reabsorb H+ for base excretion. This functional specialization is critical for renal acid-base regulation.

The reticulospinal tract carries descending projections from reticular formation neurons to spinal cord motor neurons, modulating muscle tone, posture, and voluntary movements. The medial (pontine) reticulospinal tract facilitates extensor tone, while the lateral (medullary) reticulospinal tract facilitates flexor tone. These tracts are important for maintaining posture, modulating reflex activity, and controlling proximal limb muscles during locomotion and reaching movements.
questions.question: The reticular formation influences spinal cord activity through which tract?

questions.explanation: The sphenoparietal sinus runs along the posterior edge of the lesser wing of the sphenoid bone and drains into the anterior portion of the cavernous sinus. This small sinus receives veins from the dura and bone in the frontal and parietal regions. It represents one of several venous channels feeding into the cavernous sinus, which serves as a major venous collecting system at the skull base receiving blood from orbital, facial, and cerebral sources.
questions.question: The sphenoparietal sinus drains into which structure?

questions.explanation: The allantois first appears around day 16 as a small diverticulum projecting from the caudal end of the yolk sac into the connecting stalk. In humans, the allantois is vestigial and contributes to bladder development and formation of the urachus. In other species, it plays important roles in waste storage and gas exchange.
questions.question: The allantois first appears around which day of development?
The liver is described as a modified exocrine gland. This classification reflects which feature of hepatocytes?
options: They secrete hormones into the bloodstream
They store glycogen like endocrine cells
They secrete bile into the bile canaliculi,
questions.explanation: Hepatocytes function as exocrine secretory cells by producing bile — approximately 600–1000 mL daily — which they secrete into bile canaliculi. Bile drains through the intrahepatic and extrahepatic biliary tree into the duodenum where it aids fat digestion. This secretory product (bile) traveling through a duct system to a body surface (duodenum) is the defining characteristic of an exocrine gland. Hepatocytes also have endocrine functions (producing plasma proteins, clotting factors) making the liver a uniquely multifunctional organ.

questions.question: The thyroid gland first appears in which week as an epithelial proliferation?
questions.explanation: The thyroid gland is the first endocrine gland to develop, appearing in the 4th week from endoderm as an epithelial proliferation in the floor of the pharynx. After pharyngeal arch formation, it develops at the site of the foramen cecum, located behind the tuberculum impar (median tongue swelling).

The facial colliculus is formed by the facial nerve (CN VII) wrapping around the abducens nucleus (CN VI) before exiting the brainstem. This occurs at the level of the lower pons. The facial nucleus is located in the ventrolateral pontine tegmentum.
questions.question: The facial colliculus in the floor of the fourth ventricle is formed by which nerve?
The prostate gland develops from:
questions.explanation: The prostate gland develops from endodermal epithelial outgrowths (buds) of the pelvic part of the urogenital sinus, which penetrate surrounding mesenchyme. Development is stimulated by dihydrotestosterone from the fetal testes. The mesenchyme forms the fibromuscular stroma, while the endoderm forms the glandular epithelium. Prostatic development continues through puberty.

questions.question: Which Carnegie stage corresponds to the appearance of webbed digits of the hand?
questions.explanation: Carnegie stage 22 corresponds to the 8th week when webbed digits of the hand are present. This is the final week of the embryonic period. At this stage, notches are also present between digits of the foot, the tail is still present, and the scalp vascular plexus is visible.

questions.question: Gastrulation converts the bilaminar disc into a trilaminar disc during which week of development?
questions.explanation: Gastrulation is the process whereby the bilaminar germ disc is converted into a trilaminar germ disc during the 3rd week of development. This process begins with formation of the primitive streak and results in the differentiation of the three germ layers: ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm.

options: Systemic elastic tissue disease with aortic dissection as a major complication
Cartilage throughout the body affected causing severe degenerative arthritis
Compact cortical bone affected causing repeated pathological fractures
Lymphoid tissue affected causing severe progressive immunodeficiency
Skeletal muscle affected causing dilated or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
questions.question: A patient with Marfan syndrome has mutations in the FBN1 gene. Which tissue type is most critically affected and what is the life-threatening complication?
questions.explanation: Marfan syndrome from FBN1 fibrillin-1 mutations primarily affects tissues rich in elastic fibers since fibrillin-1 scaffolds elastin deposition. The aorta with its high elastic fiber content and constant high-pressure pulsatile stress is most critically affected, with progressive dilatation leading to aneurysm formation and potentially fatal acute aortic dissection or rupture. Additional manifestations include lens dislocation from zonular fiber weakness, and skeletal features from abnormal bone and connective tissue.
A nerve is a bundle of many nerve fibers (axons and dendrites of neurons). A neuron is a single nerve cell. This distinction is important for anatomical understanding.
questions.question: A nerve is defined as which structure?
Centrioles are organelles present in most cells but conspicuously absent in neurons. Their absence in neurons is most consistent with which of the following characteristic of neurons?
options: Neurons do not require energy from mitochondria
Neurons are amitotic and cannot divide
questions.explanation: Centrioles organize the mitotic spindle during cell division, a function unnecessary in neurons since they are amitotic (permanently post-mitotic after final differentiation). The absence of centrioles is directly consistent with the inability of neurons to undergo mitosis and therefore regenerate after destruction. This is why CNS neuron loss (e.g., in stroke, trauma) is permanent.

questions.question: How many pharyngeal arches are formed during development?
questions.explanation: Six pharyngeal arches are formed during development, though the fifth arch is rudimentary and typically regresses. These arches appear as bars of mesoderm that grow dorso-ventrally in the side wall of the foregut. Each arch contains skeletal elements, muscles, nerves, and an arterial arch.

questions.question: Spina bifida results from failure of closure of which structure?
questions.explanation: Spina bifida results from failure of closure of the posterior (caudal) neuropore along with failure of the vertebral arches to fuse. Failure of the anterior (cranial) neuropore to close results in anencephaly. These conditions are collectively known as neural tube defects (NTDs).

options: Glycocalyx → phospholipid bilayer → cytoskeleton → receptor proteins
Nucleus → cytoplasm → membrane proteins → extracellular matrix
Interior protein network → phospholipid bilayer → glycocalyx
Microtubules → smooth ER → plasma membrane → collagen
questions.explanation: From the intracellular side outward: the interior protein network (cytoskeletal attachments) interfaces with the cytoplasmic face of the phospholipid bilayer (containing integral and peripheral proteins), and the extracellular face is decorated with the glycocalyx (carbohydrate chains constituting cell surface markers). This inside-to-outside sequence reflects the structural and functional organization of the plasma membrane.
questions.question: The four molecular components of the cell membrane listed from the inside of the cell outward would include which of the following sequences?
The cochlea's hair cells located in the organ of Corti are activated by which mechanism?
questions.explanation: Sound-induced vibration travels through perilymph causing the basilar membrane to vibrate, deflecting the stereocilia of hair cells that are anchored to or near the tectorial membrane. Deflection opens mechanically-gated potassium and calcium channels in the stereocilia tips. The resulting depolarization triggers neurotransmitter release at the hair cell basolateral surface, activating afferent cochlear nerve fibers that transmit auditory information to the brainstem.
options: Direct electrical stimulation from the cochlear nerve
Pressure changes in the perilymph of the scala tympani
Endolymph temperature changes in the scala media
Basilar membrane vibration deflects stereocilia, opening ion channels
Blood flow pulsations through the stria vascularis

questions.question: What is the primary fissure that separates the anterior from the posterior lobe of the cerebellum?
questions.explanation: The primary fissure is the deepest fissure on the cerebellar surface, separating the anterior lobe (paleocerebellum) from the larger posterior lobe (neocerebellum). The anterior lobe receives proprioceptive input from the spinal cord and controls muscle tone. The posterior lobe receives input from the contralateral cerebral cortex via pontocerebellar pathways and is concerned with coordination of voluntary motor function.

questions.question: Section of the corpus callosum results in which syndrome?
questions.explanation: Section of the corpus callosum (callosotomy) results in split-brain syndrome, where the hemispheres function independently and cannot share information. Classic findings include inability to verbally identify objects placed in the left hand (information goes to right hemisphere which lacks language), inability to execute verbal commands with the left hand, and various visual field anomalies. Callosotomy has been performed to control intractable epilepsy, preventing seizure propagation between hemispheres. Agenesis of the corpus callosum can occur developmentally with variable symptoms.

questions.question: The vitelline duct connects the midgut loop to:
questions.explanation: The vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct connects the midgut loop to the yolk sac and persists until the end of the 10th week. Normally, this duct completely obliterates. Incomplete obliteration can result in Meckel's diverticulum, vitelline cyst, vitelline fistula, or fibrous cord connecting ileum to umbilicus.

questions.question: Collagen type IV found in basement membranes has which of the following structural characteristics that distinguish it from fibrillar collagens?
questions.explanation: Type IV collagen forms a non-fibrillar sheet-like or meshwork structure rather than fibrillar bundles. Type IV collagen molecules assemble into polygonal networks through end-to-end and lateral associations, forming the structural scaffolding of all basement membranes. Basement membranes also contain laminin, perlecan, nidogen, and other non-collagenous components. Goodpasture syndrome involves autoantibodies against type IV collagen in glomerular and alveolar basement membranes.
options: Forms thick parallel bundles like type I collagen
Organizes into reticular fibers staining with silver salts
Forms non-fibrillar sheet-like networks rather than fibrillar bundles
Is produced exclusively by chondrocytes in cartilage
Contains no triple helical domains unlike other collagens

questions.question: Which cells form the blood-brain barrier?
questions.explanation: Astrocytes are star-shaped glial cells mainly protoplasmic in the mantle layer and fibrous in the marginal layer. They form the blood-brain barrier through their perivascular end-feet. They also provide metabolic support to neurons.

Granule cells constitute over 90% of cerebellar cortex neurons and are among the smallest and most numerous neurons in the entire brain (estimated 50-100 billion). Despite their small size (5-8 μm), their overwhelming numbers and extensive parallel fiber connections make them crucial for cerebellar computation. Each granule cell receives input from only a few mossy fibers but contacts hundreds of Purkinje cells via its bifurcating parallel fiber axon, enabling massive divergence and information distribution.
questions.question: What percentage of cerebellar cortex neurons are granule cells?
The cerebellum contains approximately what percentage of the brain's total neurons?
questions.explanation: The cerebellum, despite representing only about 10% of brain volume, contains approximately 50% or more of the brain's total neurons, primarily due to the enormous number of tiny granule cells. This massive neural substrate supports the cerebellum's computational functions in motor coordination, timing, and learning. The highly regular, repetitive architecture allows uniform processing across the cerebellar cortex, with local circuits repeated millions of times. This computational capacity underlies the cerebellum's roles in motor control, cognitive functions, and motor learning.

Ballooning is more pronounced in the dorsal part of the telencephalon forming the cerebral cortex. The ventral part consists largely of the corpus striatum. This differential growth creates the characteristic cerebral hemisphere shape.
questions.question: Which portion of the telencephalon undergoes ballooning?

questions.explanation: In the pyloric region, gastric pits are notably deep — occupying approximately half the mucosal thickness — while the associated glands are shorter and more coiled.
