In the fundus and body, the glands are longer and pits shallower by proportion. This morphological difference is a key histological criterion for distinguishing pyloric from fundic/body mucosa.
questions.question: Gastric pits are invaginations of the surface epithelium into the lamina propria. The ratio of gastric pit depth to total gland length is GREATEST in which gastric region?

questions.explanation: All decidua (decidua basalis, decidua capsularis, and decidua parietalis) are shed at birth along with the placenta and fetal membranes. The decidua is the modified endometrium of pregnancy. After delivery, the endometrium regenerates from the basal layer.
questions.question: All decidual layers are shed at which time?
The Edinger-Westphal nucleus supplies which muscle?
questions.explanation: The general visceral efferent nucleus of Edinger-Westphal supplies the sphincter pupillary muscle. It is laterally placed relative to the somatic motor nuclei. This parasympathetic nucleus controls pupillary constriction.

The thyroid gland is unique among endocrine glands in storing its hormones extracellularly within thyroid follicles, spherical structures lined by follicular cells and filled with colloid which is iodinated thyroglobulin. When stimulated by TSH, follicular cells endocytose the colloid, cleave thyroid hormones from thyroglobulin, and secrete T3 and T4 into the bloodstream. This extracellular storage allows a 2 to 3 month hormone reserve.
questions.question: The thyroid gland stores thyroid hormones extracellularly in which unique structure?
options: Thyroid follicles filled with colloid containing iodinated thyroglobulin
Dense-core secretory granules within follicular cells
Thymic Hassall's corpuscles in the medulla
Intracellular lipid droplets in follicular cells

questions.question: Congenital cataracts resulting from rubella infection typically occur when maternal infection happens between:
questions.explanation: Rubella infection between 4-7 weeks of gestation is particularly teratogenic to lens development, causing congenital cataracts. This critical period corresponds to active lens fiber formation and differentiation. Genetic factors can also cause congenital cataracts independent of infection.

During primary embryonic induction, the mesoderm (particularly the notochord and prechordal mesoderm) serves as the primary inducer of neural tissue. These structures secrete factors like noggin, chordin, and follistatin that induce the overlying ectoderm to form neural tissue.
questions.question: Which structure serves as the primary inducer during primary embryonic induction?
The flocculonodular lobe is separated by which structure?
questions.explanation: A transverse fissure separates the cerebellar plate into upper and lower parts. It separates the vermis from the nodule and hemisphere from the flocculus. This creates the flocculonodular lobe.

options: Ascending and anterior rami of lateral sulcus
questions.question: The pars triangularis is bounded by which structures?
questions.explanation: The pars triangularis (triangular part) of the inferior frontal gyrus is bounded by the ascending and anterior horizontal rami of the lateral sulcus, forming a triangular region. Along with the pars opercularis, it forms Broca's area in the dominant hemisphere. This region is involved in phonological and syntactic processing in language production. The triangular configuration created by the diverging rami of the lateral sulcus makes this gyrus readily identifiable on lateral brain views.

questions.question: The volume of amniotic fluid at mid-pregnancy is approximately:
questions.explanation: The volume of amniotic fluid is about 400 ml at mid-pregnancy. It reaches about 1000 ml at 36-38 weeks, then decreases later to be scanty in post-term pregnancy. The fluid is continuously turned over, with approximately 500 ml replaced every hour.

The lamina terminalis forms the anterior wall of the third ventricle, extending from the anterior commissure above to the optic chiasm below. This thin membrane represents the rostral end of the neural tube and is the site where the cerebral hemispheres initially evaginated during development. The anterior commissure traverses the lamina terminalis, connecting the temporal lobes and olfactory structures. The lamina terminalis, along with the optic chiasm and hypothalamus, forms the anterior border of the diencephalon.
questions.question: Which structure marks the anterior boundary of the third ventricle?

questions.explanation: The internal elastic lamina is most prominent in muscular (distributing) arteries such as the femoral, radial, and coronary arteries. It appears as a wavy, bright eosinophilic band on H&E staining and stains black with Verhoeff elastic stain. Muscular arteries also have an external elastic lamina separating the media from the adventitia. These landmarks help distinguish muscular arteries from elastic arteries in histological sections.
questions.question: The internal elastic lamina is a prominent layer separating the tunica intima from the tunica media. It is best developed in which type of artery?

questions.explanation: About 90% of anterolateral tract fibers synapse with reticular formation rather than going directly to thalamus. They connect to thalamus via interneurons forming the spinoreticulothalamic pathway. This mediates arousal and affective pain components. ## CRANIAL NERVES
questions.question: The spinoreticulothalamic pathway comprises what percentage of anterolateral fibers?
Insulin production by the pancreas begins around:
questions.explanation: Insulin production begins around the 10th week of pancreatic development, while glucagon production begins around the 15th week. The endocrine cells develop from pancreatic epithelium and aggregate to form islets of Langerhans. These islets are surrounded by exocrine pancreatic tissue.

Sebaceous glands develop from buds of the epidermal root sheaths of hair follicles. The glandular buds grow into surrounding connective tissue and branch to form alveoli and ducts. Central cells of the alveoli break down to form the oily secretion called sebum.
questions.question: Sebaceous glands develop from:

questions.explanation: In the third week of development, mesenchymal cells from the primitive node form the notochordal process. This process extends cranially between the ectoderm and endoderm to reach the prechordal plate. The primitive pit extends into the notochordal process to form the notochordal canal.
questions.question: The notochordal process extends cranially to which structure?

questions.explanation: Wallerian degeneration occurs distal to injury because the axon segment is cut off from cell body nutrients. The proximal segment may regenerate in PNS. CNS regeneration is limited. Schwann cells aid PNS regeneration.
questions.question: Wallerian degeneration occurs in which direction from injury?
Collagen type I is found predominantly in which of the following tissues?
questions.explanation: Type I collagen is the most abundant protein in the human body, forming thick fibrillar bundles in dermis, bone, tendons, ligaments, fascia, and the corneal stroma. It provides high tensile strength. Type II collagen is specific to cartilage and vitreous, type III (reticular) predominates in loose connective tissues and vessels, and type IV forms non-fibrillar sheets in basement membranes.

questions.question: Invasion of trophoblast cells into the endometrium is mediated by which molecules?
questions.explanation: The second stage of implantation involves invasion of trophoblast cells into the endometrium. This invasion is mediated by adhesion molecules including integrins, laminin, and fibronectin. These molecules allow the trophoblast to penetrate the endometrial stroma.

questions.question: Type I alveolar epithelial cells function primarily in:
questions.explanation: Type I alveolar epithelial cells are extremely thin, squamous cells that cover most of the alveolar surface and function primarily in gas exchange. They form the epithelial component of the blood-air barrier. Type II cells produce surfactant, while type I cells facilitate diffusion. Type I cells cannot divide and are replaced by differentiation of type II cells.

The external band of Baillarger is a layer of horizontal nerve fibers found in layer IV (internal granular layer) of the cortex, representing thalamocortical and corticocortical connections. In the primary visual cortex, this band is especially prominent and visible to the naked eye as the stria of Gennari, giving the name \"striate cortex\" to area 17. These horizontal fibers facilitate intracortical communication and integration of information across cortical columns.
questions.question: Which band of horizontal fibers characterizes layer IV of the cortex?

questions.explanation: The embryonic period (weeks 3-8) is the most critical period for teratogenic effects because this is when organogenesis occurs. Exposure to teratogens during this period can cause major structural abnormalities. The fetal period is primarily growth and maturation, so teratogens typically cause functional deficits rather than major structural defects.
questions.question: The most critical period for teratogenic effects is during which developmental period?

questions.explanation: In membranous nephropathy, subepithelial immune complex deposits cause the GBM to appear diffusely thickened on light microscopy. With silver methenamine staining, the GBM shows characteristic 'spike and dome' or 'spike' formation — projections of GBM material growing up between and around the subepithelial deposits. Immunofluorescence shows granular IgG and C3 deposits in a peripheral (capillary wall) pattern. This is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults.
questions.question: In membranous nephropathy, immune complexes deposit on the subepithelial aspect of the GBM (between the GBM and podocyte foot processes). On light microscopy, the GBM shows:
options: No visible changes on light microscopy

questions.question: The homunculus in the motor cortex represents which body part largest?
questions.explanation: The motor homunculus represents hand and face disproportionately large reflecting their fine motor control. Trunk and leg have smaller representation. This is Penfield's motor map. It demonstrates cortical organization based on function.

questions.question: Frontopontinecorticospinal fibers pass through which part of internal capsule?
questions.explanation: Corticopontine fibers arise from cortex passing through internal capsule: frontopontine through anterior limb. Others pass through retrolentiform part. They synapse with pontine nuclei in the crus

Each intestinal villus contains a central lymphatic channel called a lacteal. Lacteals absorb dietary long-chain fatty acids and fat-soluble vitamins packaged as chylomicrons. The absorbed lipids travel through the lymphatic system to the thoracic duct before entering the bloodstream — bypassing the portal circulation. This is why certain fat-soluble drugs avoid hepatic first-pass metabolism.
questions.question: The central lymphatic vessel within each intestinal villus is called:
Chief (zymogen) cells of the gastric glands are characterized by which secretory product?
questions.explanation: Wait — Chief cells secrete pepsinogen (converted to pepsin by HCl) and gastric lipase. Gastrin is secreted by G-cells (enteroendocrine cells). The correct answer is C: Chief (zymogen) cells are basophilic cells in the base of gastric glands that produce pepsinogen and gastric lipase. Answer: C.

Vernix caseosa is formed from fatty secretions from fetal sebaceous glands and dead epithelial cells. It covers the fetal skin during 17-20 weeks and protects the skin from abrasions, chapping, and hardening that could result from exposure to amniotic fluid. It is a white, cheese-like substance.
options: Fatty secretions and dead epithelial cells
questions.question: Vernix caseosa is formed from which substances?

questions.explanation: Osteomalacia involves vitamin D deficiency leading to failure of osteoid mineralization, with accumulation of unmineralized osteoid seams and soft, painful bones. Osteitis fibrosa cystica (von Recklinghausen disease of bone) results from hyperparathyroidism causing excessive osteoclast activity, which removes both mineral and organic matrix and replaces it with fibrous tissue and cysts. Tetracycline labeling diagnostically distinguishes these opposite metabolic bone disorders.
questions.question: Osteomalacia (adult) and osteitis fibrosa cystica represent opposite extremes of bone pathology because of which of the following?
options: Osteomalacia involves osteoclast hyperactivity; osteitis fibrosa involves mineralization failure
They both result from identical biochemical defects in collagen synthesis
Osteomalacia involves excessive mineralization; osteitis fibrosa involves matrix dissolution
Osteomalacia involves impaired mineralization; osteitis fibrosa involves excess osteoclast activity
They are the same disease at different ages

questions.question: The trapezoid body is formed by axons crossing from which nuclei?
questions.explanation: Axons of second-order neurons from cochlear nucleus form trapezoid body as they cross midline to contralateral superior olivary nucleus. Other crossing fibers form dorsal and intermediate acoustic striae. This allows bilateral hearing.

questions.question: The fundic glands of the stomach body contain a characteristic cell type not found in the pyloric or cardiac regions. This cell type is:
questions.explanation: Parietal (oxyntic) cells are the defining cell type of the fundic and body glands of the stomach. They are large, pyramidal, eosinophilic cells that produce HCl and intrinsic factor. The cardiac and pyloric glands are predominantly mucous glands lacking parietal cells (or with very few in transitional zones). The unique presence of parietal cells in fundic glands is therefore the key histological criterion for identifying this region.

questions.question: Which component of the cell membrane stabilizes the phospholipid bilayer, increases its rigidity, and regulates fluidity?
questions.explanation: Cholesterol molecules intercalated between phospholipid tails regulate membrane fluidity: at high temperatures, cholesterol restricts phospholipid movement reducing fluidity; at low temperatures it prevents tight packing, maintaining fluidity. This temperature-buffering role is essential for membrane function across physiological temperature ranges. Cholesterol constitutes approximately 30–40% of mammalian plasma membrane lipids.

options: Random arrangement of collagen fibers with abundant ground substance
Predominantly elastic fibers with few collagen fibers
Large amounts of adipose cells with sparse collagen
Parallel bundles of collagen fibers with sparse fibroblasts aligned along fibers
Predominantly reticular fibers forming a supporting meshwork
questions.explanation: Dense regular connective tissue is characterized by closely packed, parallel bundles of type I collagen fibers, with few but elongated fibroblasts (tenocytes) aligned between the fiber bundles. This parallel arrangement provides maximal tensile strength in a single direction — ideal for tendons and ligaments that must withstand strong unidirectional forces. The sparse ground substance and cells reflect prioritization of mechanical performance over cellular activity.
questions.question: Dense regular connective tissue, as found in tendons and ligaments, is characterized by which of the following structural features?
Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (NRDS) occurs in premature infants due to surfactant deficiency. Antenatal corticosteroids are given to accelerate fetal lung maturity by stimulating:
questions.explanation: Corticosteroids (betamethasone, dexamethasone) given antenatally accelerate fetal lung maturity by binding glucocorticoid receptors in Type II pneumocytes, stimulating maturation and increasing synthesis of dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (DPPC) — the main surfactant phospholipid. This reduces surface tension in alveoli, decreasing the risk of NRDS. Lecithin:sphingomyelin (L:S) ratio >2 in amniotic fluid indicates adequate surfactant maturity.

questions.question: Which structure divides the thalamus from the hypothalamus?
questions.explanation: The alar plate cells are divided into dorsal thalamus and ventral hypothalamus by the hypothalamic sulcus. Thalamic cells proliferate rapidly causing inward bulging. The hypothalamus regulates homeostatic functions.

questions.question: Unipolar neurons are exemplified by which cells?
questions.explanation: Unipolar neurons are exemplified by dorsal root ganglion cells. They have one process that divides into peripheral and central branches. They are actually pseudounipolar developmentally.

The caudate nucleus and putamen together constitute the striatum (corpus striatum in older terminology), which is the main input structure of the basal ganglia. These two nuclei have similar cellular composition and connections, appearing as a single C-shaped structure during development before being separated by the developing internal capsule. The striatum receives massive input from the cerebral cortex (corticostriatal projections) and from the substantia nigra (dopaminergic nigrostriatal pathway). The striatum is divided into ventral striatum (limbic system) and dorsal striatum (motor system).
questions.question: The caudate nucleus and putamen together constitute which structure?
A fracture that heals correctly undergoes a sequence that includes which stage where fibrocartilage temporarily bridges the fracture gap?
options: Inflammatory phase with neutrophil predominance only
Hard callus phase with lamellar bone formation only
Remodeling phase where osteoclasts remove excess bone
Primary bone healing without any cartilage formation
Fibrocartilage callus later replaced by woven bone via endochondral ossification
questions.explanation: Fracture healing proceeds through: (1) hematoma and inflammatory phase, (2) soft callus phase where periosteal cells produce fibrocartilage bridging the gap via endochondral ossification, (3) hard callus phase where cartilage is replaced by woven bone, and (4) remodeling phase where woven bone is replaced by lamellar bone. Cells involved include osteocytes, osteoblasts, osteoclasts, and fibroblasts.

The dorsal column system in posterior funiculus is concerned with discriminative touch and kinesthesia. Peripheral receptors include mechanoreceptors, muscle spindles, and joint receptors. Fibers travel as gracile and cuneate fasciculi.
questions.question: The dorsal column system is concerned with which sensations?

questions.explanation: The lesser omentum extends between the liver and stomach (lesser curvature), connecting the lesser curvature of the stomach to the inferior surface of the liver. It develops from the ventral mesogastrium. The lesser omentum contains the hepatic artery, portal vein, and bile duct in its free edge.
questions.question: The lesser omentum extends between:

questions.explanation: The tympanic membrane is formed by contributions from all three germ layers. The external epithelial lining comes from ectoderm of the first pharyngeal cleft, the middle fibrous layer from mesoderm, and the internal lining from endoderm of the first pharyngeal pouch (tubotympanic recess).
questions.question: The tympanic membrane receives contributions from which embryonic layers?
Cranial nerve VI nucleus is located in which plate?
questions.explanation: The basal plate neuroblasts differentiate into neurons arranged into motor nuclei including CN6 for extraocular muscles. This is the somatic efferent component. CN6 specifically innervates the lateral rectus muscle.

questions.question: The basal ganglia consist of how many main nuclei?
questions.explanation: The basal ganglia consist of caudate nucleus, lentiform nucleus, amygdaloid body and claustrum. The lentiform nucleus further divides into putamen and globus pallidus. These nuclei modulate motor function.

questions.question: The mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve is the motor nerve of which arch?
questions.explanation: The motor nerve of the first pharyngeal arch is the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V). The sensory nerves are the ophthalmic, maxillary, and mandibular divisions of CN V. Each pharyngeal arch has its own specific nerve supply.

Acute inflammation is characterized by vascular changes and neutrophil (PMN) infiltration as the dominant cellular response, typically resolving within days. Chronic inflammation (lasting weeks to months) features a mononuclear cell infiltrate (lymphocytes, macrophages, plasma cells), tissue destruction, and attempts at healing/fibrosis. The temporal and cellular differences reflect distinct immunological mechanisms and different tissue repair outcomes.
options: Only chronic inflammation involves vascular changes
Acute inflammation always leads to tissue fibrosis
Chronic inflammation lacks any cellular component
Acute: neutrophil-dominated; chronic: lymphocytes, macrophages, fibrosis
questions.question: Acute inflammation differs from chronic inflammation histologically primarily in which of the following?
The collecting system of the kidney (collecting tubules and ducts) is derived from which embryological structure, distinct from the nephrons?
questions.explanation: Kidney development involves two distinct embryological components: (1) the ureteric bud (metanephric diverticulum), which branches from the mesonephric (Wolffian) duct and gives rise to the collecting system — collecting tubules, papillary ducts, calyces, renal pelvis, and ureter; (2) the metanephric mesenchyme (blastema), which is induced by the ureteric bud to undergo mesenchymal-to-epithelial transition, forming the nephrons (glomeruli, proximal tubules, loop of Henle, distal tubules). Failure of ureteric bud induction causes renal agenesis.

The eponychium (cuticle) is formed from the stratum corneum of the epithelium of the proximal nail fold. Initially, this band covers the developing nail completely, but later degenerates and persists only at the nail base. The eponychium protects the nail matrix from infection.
questions.question: The eponychium (cuticle) is formed from:

questions.explanation: The middle cerebral artery supplies the primary motor cortex in the precentral gyrus, the primary somatosensory cortex in the postcentral gyrus, and large portions of the frontal, parietal, and temporal lobes. It also supplies the internal capsule through its lenticulostriate branches. Occlusion of this artery results in severe contralateral motor and sensory deficits, often with aphasia if the dominant hemisphere is affected.
questions.question: The middle cerebral artery supplies which functional area critical for motor control?

questions.explanation: The amygdaloid body is a group of gray matter at the tip of the tail of caudate nucleus. It lies on the roof of the inferior horn of lateral ventricle. It connects with frontal, temporal and olfactory lobes.
questions.question: The amygdaloid body is located at which position?

questions.explanation: The renal papillae (apices of renal pyramids) are formed by convergence of collecting ducts from each pyramid. The papillae project into minor calyces, and collecting duct openings (papillary ducts of Bellini) at the papillae drain urine into the calyces. Each kidney has 8-12 papillae corresponding to pyramids. Papillary necrosis can occur in certain disease states.
questions.question: The renal papillae are formed by:
The urachus later becomes which adult structure?
questions.explanation: The allantois plays a significant role in development of the urinary bladder through the urachus, which later becomes the median umbilical ligament. The urachus connects the apex of the bladder to the umbilicus. Persistence of the urachal lumen can result in urachal cysts or fistulas.

questions.question: Vestibular fibers project to extraocular muscle nuclei via which pathway?
questions.explanation: Vestibular fibers project to extraocular muscle nuclei (CN3, 4, 6) via ascending component of medial longitudinal fasciculus. This helps control conjugate eye movements. This is the basis of the vestibulo-ocular reflex.

Barrett's esophagus is a metaplastic condition where the normal non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium of the esophagus is replaced by intestinal-type simple columnar epithelium with goblet cells (specialized intestinal metaplasia). This occurs due to chronic gastroesophageal acid reflux and carries a risk of progression to esophageal adenocarcinoma.
questions.question: A 45-year-old develops Barrett's esophagus. Histologically, this condition is characterized by replacement of normal esophageal epithelium with:
options: Intestinal-type columnar epithelium with goblet cells

questions.explanation: Over 50% of corticospinal fibers synapse with anterior horn cells of cervical segments. Lumbosacral segments receive about 25%. This reflects the greater innervation density of upper limb muscles.
questions.question: What percentage of corticospinal fibers synapse with cervical anterior horn cells?

questions.explanation: Juxtaglomerular cells are modified smooth muscle cells in the wall of the afferent arteriole at the vascular pole of the glomerulus. They contain renin stored in secretory granules and release it in response to: decreased stretch from low blood pressure sensed by baroreceptors in the afferent arteriole; decreased sodium delivery sensed by macula densa cells; and sympathetic beta-1 adrenergic stimulation. Renin cleaves angiotensinogen to angiotensin I initiating the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone axis.
questions.question: The juxtaglomerular apparatus of the kidney consists of juxtaglomerular cells macula densa cells and extraglomerular mesangial cells. The juxtaglomerular cells perform which function?
options: Filtering blood directly in place of the glomerulus
Producing erythropoietin to stimulate red blood cell production
Secreting aldosterone in direct response to angiotensin II stimulation
Secretes renin in response to low perfusion, low sodium, and sympathetic activation
Phagocytosing damaged and apoptotic glomerular mesangial cells

questions.question: The nipple typically rises from the mammary pit:
questions.explanation: After birth, nipples rise from mammary pits through proliferation of surrounding connective tissue of the areola. In newborn infants, nipples are poorly formed and depressed. Late in fetal life, the epidermis at the site of mammary gland origin becomes depressed, forming a shallow mammary pit.

questions.question: The mesonephric tubules in males contribute to formation of:
questions.explanation: In males, some caudal mesonephric tubules persist to form the efferent ductules connecting the testis to the epididymis. The mesonephric duct itself becomes the ductus deferens, epididymis, and ejaculatory duct. In females, mesonephric structures largely degenerate, with only vestigial remnants (epoophoron, paroophoron) persisting.

questions.question: The blood-CSF barrier is formed by which cellular junction?
questions.explanation: The blood-CSF barrier is formed by tight junctions (zonulae occludentes) between choroid plexus epithelial cells, restricting paracellular diffusion of substances from blood into CSF. Unlike the blood-brain barrier (formed by endothelial tight junctions), the blood-CSF barrier is at the epithelial level, with the underlying capillaries being fenestrated. This barrier actively transports nutrients into CSF, removes waste products, and prevents entry of many drugs and toxins, while allowing water and small lipophilic molecules to pass relatively freely.

Arterioles are small muscular vessels (diameter < 0.3 mm) whose tunica media contains 1–3 layers of smooth muscle cells. Contraction or relaxation of this smooth muscle changes the arteriolar diameter, directly controlling peripheral vascular resistance and blood flow distribution. This is the primary mechanism regulating blood pressure at the tissue level and is the target of antihypertensive drugs like calcium channel blockers.
questions.question: Arterioles are the principal site of peripheral vascular resistance. This resistance is regulated by contraction of smooth muscle in which layer?

questions.explanation: Proteins such as fibroblast growth factor (FGF) and activin, belonging to peptide growth factors, play key roles in programming mesodermal cells to induce overlying ectoderm to differentiate into neural structures. These factors are part of the complex signaling that establishes the nervous system.
questions.question: Which growth factor plays a key role in programming mesodermal cells to induce neural structures?

questions.explanation: The nucleolus is the dense region within the nucleus where ribosomal RNA genes are actively transcribed (by RNA polymerase I) and ribosome subunits are assembled before export to the cytoplasm. Cells with high protein synthesis rates (e.g., plasma cells, secretory cells) have prominent, enlarged nucleoli. Nucleoli appear eosinophilic/amphiphilic in H&E sections due to their RNA content.
questions.question: The nucleolus visible within the cell nucleus is specifically the site of which of the following biosynthetic activities?
options: Ribosomal RNA synthesis and ribosome assembly

questions.question: Temporary occlusion of the laryngeal lumen results from:
questions.explanation: Temporary occlusion of the laryngeal lumen results from rapid proliferation of the laryngeal epithelium. This is followed by vacuolization and recanalization, creating the laryngeal ventricles bounded by vocal cord folds. Failure of proper recanalization can result in laryngeal atresia or webs, which are rare but serious anomalies.

The right and left endothelial heart tubes fuse to form a single tube that shows a series of four dilations: bulbus cordis, ventricle (primitive ventricle), atrium (primitive atrium), and sinus venosus. These dilations represent the primordial chambers of the developing heart.
questions.question: The endocardial heart tubes fuse to form a single tube showing how many dilations?

questions.explanation: The tympanic membrane consists of three layers: ectodermal lining at bottom of auditory meatus, endodermal lining of tympanic cavity, and intermediate connective tissue layer. It separates external from middle ear.
questions.question: The tympanic membrane is composed of how many layers?
Which meningeal structure creates a tent-like covering over the cerebellum with its apex directed anteriorly?
questions.explanation: The tentorium cerebelli has an elevated mid-anterior portion that slopes downward toward the periphery, creating a tent-like structure. It is attached posteriorly to the transverse ridge of the occipital bone and laterally to the superior angle of the petrous temporal bone. This structure separates the cerebellum from the occipital lobes of the cerebrum and contains a large U-shaped opening for the brainstem.

The maxillary and sphenoidal sinuses develop before birth as diverticula from the nasal cavity. The frontal and ethmoid sinuses develop after birth. Enlargement of all sinuses is associated with overall facial skeleton growth, providing space for jaw development and teeth eruption.
questions.question: Which paranasal sinuses develop before birth?
The ureteric bud arises from which structure?
questions.explanation: The ureteric bud (metanephric diverticulum) sprouts from the distal end of the mesonephric duct at about 5 weeks. This outgrowth induces the surrounding intermediate mesoderm to form metanephric blastema. Reciprocal induction between the ureteric bud and metanephric blastema is essential for proper kidney development.

Bronchopulmonary segments are established by the formation of tertiary (segmental) bronchi. There are ten on the right and eight on the left. Each segment represents a functional unit of lung tissue supplied by a segmental bronchus and its branches.
questions.question: Bronchopulmonary segments are established by formation of:
Which brain vesicle gives rise to the cerebral hemispheres?
questions.explanation: The telencephalon is the portion of the prosencephalon that gives rise to the cerebral hemispheres and cortex. The ballooning of the lateral portions forms this structure by the 5th week. It undergoes massive growth compared to the midline diencephalic portion.

The fourth aortic arch on the left side gives rise to the arch of the aorta. The first and second arches form the carotid arteries, the third forms parts of the internal carotid, the fifth disappears, and the sixth forms the pulmonary arteries. The right fourth arch contributes to the right subclavian artery.
questions.question: Which aortic arch gives rise to the left arch of the aorta?

questions.explanation: Implantation begins on day 7 and ends on day 13. The blastocyst is enclosed within the zona pellucida and lies free in the uterus cavity before implantation. The zona pellucida must disappear before implantation can occur.
questions.question: Implantation of the blastocyst begins on which day?
Ectopic lung lobes may arise from:
questions.explanation: Ectopic lung lobes may arise from the trachea or esophagus rather than from the normal bronchial tree. These accessory lung buds develop independently. Ectopic lobes are usually non-functional and may become infected. They result from abnormal budding of the respiratory diverticulum or foregut.

questions.question: The anterior chamber is formed by which process?
questions.explanation: Space formed in mesenchyme splits it into iridopupillary membrane and substantia propria of cornea. The iridopupillary membrane later disappears allowing anterior and posterior chambers to communicate. This creates the aqueous pathway.

questions.question: The corona radiata is continuous with which structure inferiorly?
questions.explanation: The corona radiata is the fan-shaped array of projection fibers that radiates from the internal capsule to reach all parts of the cerebral cortex. These fibers converge as they descend to form the internal capsule, which then continues as the cerebral peduncle in the midbrain. The corona radiata contains both ascending fibers (thalamocortical) and descending fibers (corticospinal, corticobulbar, corticopontine). Strokes affecting the corona radiata can produce deficits similar to internal capsule strokes but may be more variable depending on the specific fiber involvement.

The pretectal nucleus is located at the junction between the midbrain and diencephalon and plays a crucial role in the pupillary light reflex. It receives input from the retina via the optic nerve and projects bilaterally to the Edinger-Westphal nuclei, which then send parasympathetic fibers via the oculomotor nerve to constrict the pupils. This explains the consensual light reflex where light in one eye causes both pupils to constrict.
questions.question: The pretectal nucleus is specifically involved in which reflex pathway?

questions.explanation: The first urine is produced around 12 weeks when the metanephric kidney becomes functional and glomerular filtration begins. Urine is excreted into the amniotic cavity and becomes a major component of amniotic fluid in the second half of pregnancy. Fetal urine is hypotonic compared to fetal plasma. The placenta handles waste excretion; the kidneys primarily regulate fluid balance.
questions.question: The first urine is produced around:

questions.explanation: The external ear (auricle) develops from six auricular hillocks (3 on each side) at dorsal ends of 1st and 2nd pharyngeal arches. These surround the 1st pharyngeal cleft. The hillocks later fuse.
questions.question: The external ear develops from which pharyngeal structures?
The implantation defect in the endometrium is filled with which structure?
questions.explanation: The third stage of implantation involves reparation of the implantation defect in the endometrium. The defect in the epithelium is filled with a closing plug (operculum) consisting of a blood clot and cellular debris. This seals the implantation site.

options: They disappear entirely in the ileum
They gradually assume a finger-like shape
questions.question: The duodenal villi are typically described as leaf-shaped. How does their shape change as you progress to the ileum?
questions.explanation: Intestinal villi transition from broad, leaf-shaped forms in the duodenum to more slender, finger-like projections in the ileum. This progressive shape change reflects adaptation for absorption. The villi are tallest and most densely packed in the jejunum, which is the primary site of nutrient absorption, and become shorter in the ileum.

The hepatic diverticulum appears as a ventral bud from the caudal part of the foregut during the 4th week. This diverticulum grows into the septum transversum and divides into a larger cranial part (liver primordium) and smaller caudal part (gallbladder and cystic duct).
questions.question: The hepatic diverticulum appears during which week?

options: All cardiomyocytes simultaneously receive stimuli from motor nerves
Cardiac muscle has uniform calcium sensitivity throughout all cells
Identical sarcomere length in all cardiomyocytes at rest
Gap junctions at intercalated discs propagate action potentials to all connected cells
Shared sarcoplasmic reticulum across all adjacent cardiomyocytes
questions.explanation: Gap junctions within the intercalated discs allow direct ion flow particularly sodium and potassium between adjacent cardiomyocytes, enabling action potentials to spread rapidly throughout the entire myocardium. This electrical coupling makes the heart function as a coordinated syncytium where when one cell is excited all connected cells are excited in sequence. This explains the all-or-nothing nature of cardiac contractions.
questions.question: Which of the following best describes the property of cardiac muscle that makes it function as a coordinated unit?
The membranous urethra in males is derived from:
questions.explanation: The membranous urethra in males is derived from the pelvic part of the urogenital sinus, along with the prostatic urethra. This is the shortest and least distensible portion of the male urethra, passing through the urogenital diaphragm. It contains the external urethral sphincter (voluntary muscle from surrounding mesenchyme).

Neural systems serve three general functions: sensory systems, motor systems, and association systems. Sensory systems gather information. Motor systems produce responses. Association systems integrate and process. ## NEURULATION AND ANOMALIES
questions.question: Neural systems serve how many general functions?

questions.explanation: During the 4th week, the septum transversum lies opposite the 3rd to 5th cervical somites. Myoblasts from these somites migrate to the developing diaphragm, bringing their nerve fibers with them. This establishes the phrenic nerve supply which persists despite the descent of the diaphragm.
questions.question: The phrenic nerve supply to the diaphragm originates from which cervical somites?
The zona glomerulosa, fasciculata, and reticularis are the three zones of the adrenal cortex. Which zone primarily produces mineralocorticoids (aldosterone)?
questions.explanation: The zona glomerulosa is the outermost zone of the adrenal cortex and is the exclusive site of aldosterone synthesis (it uniquely expresses aldosterone synthase/CYP11B2). Aldosterone regulates sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion in the renal collecting duct. The zona fasciculata (middle, largest zone) produces cortisol (glucocorticoids), and the zona reticularis (innermost) produces weak androgens (DHEA). The adrenal medulla secretes catecholamines (epinephrine, norepinephrine).

HPV infects the reserve cells (basal stem cells) at the squamocolumnar junction of the cervical transformation zone. These cells express alpha-6 integrin (HPV receptor) and have active proliferative capacity. After HPV integration, high-risk HPV oncoproteins E6 (degrading p53) and E7 (inactivating pRb) dysregulate cell cycle control, leading to CIN (cervical intraepithelial neoplasia) and ultimately invasive squamous cell carcinoma. HPV vaccination targets high-risk types (16, 18) to prevent this malignant transformation.
questions.question: The cervical transformation zone (TZ) is the most common site of HPV-related neoplasia. Human papillomavirus infects which specific cell type at the TZ that serves as the origin of cervical cancer?

questions.explanation: Progressive systemic sclerosis (scleroderma) involves pathological overproduction of collagen by activated fibroblasts, resulting in fibrosis of multiple organs including skin, GI tract, lungs, kidneys, and muscles. The histological hallmark is replacement of normal tissue architecture by dense collagen bundles. The hardening (sclero-) and organ dysfunction reflect the replacement of functional tissue with excessive collagen.
questions.question: Progressive systemic sclerosis (scleroderma) is characterized histologically by which of the following?
options: Deficiency of collagen leading to tissue atrophy
Selective loss of elastic fibers in skin
Excessive collagen accumulation in skin, digestive tract, and muscles
Mast cell infiltration causing widespread anaphylaxis
Replacement of connective tissue by adipose tissue

questions.explanation: Addison's disease destroys all cortical zones causing: cortisol deficiency from zona fasciculata destruction producing weakness fatigue hypoglycemia and impaired stress response; aldosterone deficiency from zona glomerulosa destruction causing salt wasting hyponatremia hyperkalemia hypotension and salt craving; and adrenal androgen deficiency from zona reticularis destruction. Loss of negative feedback causes excess ACTH and MSH from the anterior pituitary producing the characteristic bronzed hyperpigmentation especially in sun-exposed areas and pressure points.
questions.question: A patient with Addison's disease has primary adrenal insufficiency destroying the entire adrenal cortex. Which combination of hormonal deficiencies and clinical features would result?
options: Excess aldosterone and cortisol causing hypertension
Cortisol deficiency, aldosterone deficiency, and ACTH-driven hyperpigmentation
Deficiency of epinephrine causing bradycardia only
Isolated aldosterone deficiency without cortisol effects

questions.question: Myelin sheaths in the axon serve which function?
questions.explanation: Myelin sheaths make excellent insulators which help impulse conduction through saltatory conduction. They are formed by oligodendrocytes in CNS and Schwann cells in PNS. Nodes of Ranvier are gaps between myelin segments.

questions.question: The amniotic cavity appears as spaces within which layer on day 8?
questions.explanation: On day 8, spaces occur within the epiblast layer to form the amniotic cavity. This cavity will expand greatly and eventually surrounds the entire embryo. The cells lining the amniotic cavity are derived from epiblast and are called amnioblasts.

questions.question: Celiac disease (gluten-sensitive enteropathy) causes villous atrophy in the small intestine. The histological hallmark of established celiac disease is:
options: Total villous atrophy with crypt hyperplasia
Replacement of columnar epithelium by stratified squamous epithelium
questions.explanation: Celiac disease (Marsh classification) is characterized histologically by: total or subtotal villous atrophy (flattening of intestinal villi), crypt hyperplasia (compensatory elongation of crypts), and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes (IELs > 25 per 100 enterocytes). These changes are most severe in the proximal small intestine (duodenum and proximal jejunum) and improve on a gluten-free diet. The changes reflect immune-mediated destruction of enterocytes triggered by gliadin peptides.

questions.question: The basal plate of the neural tube forms which functional component?
questions.explanation: The basal plate forms most of the ventral portion of the nervous system including the motor portion of the spinal cord and brainstem. The alar plate forms the dorsal portions, devoted mainly to sensory processing. This patterning is established by signals including Sonic hedgehog (SHH) and bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs).

questions.question: Surface mucous cells lining the gastric pit produce alkaline mucus. This mucus is chemically distinguished from the mucus of the mucous neck cells in that it is:
questions.explanation: Surface mucous cells produce thick, alkaline, insoluble mucus (containing MUC5AC mucin) that forms the protective gel-like layer adherent to the gastric epithelium. This alkaline mucus traps bicarbonate ions, creating a pH gradient from ~7 at the mucosa surface to ~2 in the gastric lumen. Mucous neck cells secrete soluble, less alkaline (slightly acidic) mucus (MUC6) that lubricates the gland lumen and acts as a precursor to surface mucous cells.

Adrenal medullary chromaffin cells are modified postganglionic sympathetic neurons that upon preganglionic sympathetic stimulation via acetylcholine release catecholamines predominantly epinephrine at 80% and norepinephrine at 20% directly into the bloodstream. This hormonal output mediates the systemic fight-or-flight response including increased heart rate, blood pressure, blood glucose through glycogenolysis, and bronchodilation.
questions.question: Chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla secrete which hormones in response to sympathetic nerve stimulation?

questions.explanation: The definitive metanephric kidney begins functioning at approximately 12 weeks gestation when glomerular filtration commences. Before this, the mesonephros serves as the interim kidney. Although the metanephric kidney is functional by 12 weeks, it doesn't perform true excretory function during fetal life - the placenta handles waste removal. The fetal kidneys primarily regulate amniotic fluid volume.
questions.question: The definitive kidney begins functioning at approximately:

questions.explanation: The supramarginal gyrus in the inferior parietal lobule caps (arches over) the posterior upturned end of the lateral (Sylvian) sulcus. It corresponds to Brodmann area 40 and is involved in phonological processing, reading, and perception of space. In the dominant hemisphere, lesions can cause conduction aphasia (impaired repetition with relatively preserved comprehension and fluent speech) and components of Gerstmann syndrome. The supramarginal gyrus is part of the parietal association cortex integrating somatosensory and language functions.
questions.question: The supramarginal gyrus caps which sulcus?

questions.explanation: Collagen fibers derive their tensile strength from the triple-helical structure of collagen protein and the cross-linking between fibrils. Elastic fibers are composed of elastin (a cross-linked rubber-like protein providing extensibility) surrounded by fibrillin-containing microfibrils (providing structural scaffolding). The distinct molecular architectures of collagen versus elastin-fibrillin directly determine the different mechanical properties.
options: Their staining affinity with H&E staining
Their cellular origin (fibroblasts vs. mast cells)
Their presence in specific organs only
The diameter of their constituent fibrils
questions.question: Collagen fibers possess greater tensile strength than elastic fibers, while elastic fibers possess superior elasticity. These structural differences primarily reflect differences in which of the following?
Which nucleus in the medulla is responsible for motor control of the larynx and pharynx?
questions.explanation: The nucleus ambiguus lies laterally in the medulla and contains motor cell bodies that innervate skeletal muscles of the larynx, soft palate, pharynx, and upper esophagus via cranial nerves IX, X, and XI. This nucleus is crucial for swallowing, phonation, and maintaining airway patency. Lesions affecting the nucleus ambiguus result in dysphagia, dysphonia, and potential aspiration due to impaired swallowing coordination.

The spinal trigeminal nucleus extends continuously from the pons through the medulla to approximately C2-C3 of the spinal cord, where it merges with the substantia gelatinosa. This long rostrocaudal extent allows somatotopic organization, with different regions processing pain and temperature from different facial areas (onion-skin distribution). The rostral portions process perioral sensation while caudal portions process more peripheral facial regions, explaining the pattern of sensory loss in lesions at different levels.
questions.question: Which cranial nerve nucleus is continuous from the pons through the medulla to the spinal cord?

questions.explanation: Uniparental disomy occurs when both homologs of a chromosome pair are inherited from one parent with no contribution from the other parent. This can result in abnormalities if the genes are subject to genomic imprinting, where expression depends on parent of origin.
questions.question: Uniparental disomy refers to which situation?

questions.explanation: The amygdala consists of groups of neurons connected to the tip of the tail of the caudate nucleus, lying on the roof of the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle anterior to the hippocampus. This almond-shaped complex modulates the association between different sensory modalities and exerts emotional control over sensory input. The amygdala is involved in fear conditioning, emotional memory, and social behavior; bilateral damage causes Klüver-Bucy syndrome with emotional blunting and hypersexuality.
questions.question: The amygdala is located at the tip of which structure?

questions.explanation: If splitting occurs at the bilaminar disc stage (after formation of the amniotic cavity), monozygotic twins will share a common placenta, common chorionic cavity, and common amniotic cavity. This is the rarest and most dangerous type, with risk of cord entanglement and twin-to-twin transfusion.
questions.question: Monozygotic twins sharing both amniotic and chorionic cavities result from splitting at which stage?

questions.explanation: Initially 2 longitudinal elevations form, then a transverse furrow separates them creating 4 colliculi. These are inferior and superior colliculi on both sides of median sulcus. They serve as relay centers for auditory and visual impulses.
questions.question: How many colliculi are formed in the mesencephalon?

questions.explanation: The secondary palate is formed in the 6th week from the palatine shelves derived from the maxillary prominences. Anteriorly, the palatine shelves fuse with the primary palate. The incisive foramen marks the midline landmark between the primary and secondary palate.
questions.question: The secondary palate develops from which structures?

questions.explanation: A ventral thickening of the neuroepithelium results in formation of the mamillary body. It is functionally related to the hypothalamus. The mamillary bodies are involved in memory and emotional responses.
questions.question: The mamillary body is formed from which region?
Which structure induces formation of the neural plate?
questions.explanation: Neural plate formation is induced by the underlying notochord and adjacent mesoderm. The notochord secretes neural inducing factors that cause the overlying ectoderm to thicken and form the neural plate. This induction is the first step in formation of the central nervous system.

questions.question: The A band of a sarcomere corresponds to which ultrastructural components?
options: Full thick myosin filament length including regions overlapping actin at both ends
The region containing only thin actin filaments with no myosin
The H zone where thin filaments overlap maximally
The region between Z lines exclusive of all thick filaments
questions.explanation: The A band corresponds to the full length of thick myosin filaments including the regions where thin actin filaments overlap with myosin at both ends. The central H zone within the A band contains only thick myosin filaments with no actin overlap at rest. During contraction, actin slides inward narrowing the H zone and I band while the A band width remains constant — a key observation confirming the sliding filament model.

questions.question: The first stage of labor involves which process?
questions.explanation: The first stage of labor involves thinning, shortening, and dilation of the cervix from 0 to 10 cm. This is the longest stage of labor. The second stage involves delivery of the fetus, and the third stage involves delivery of the placenta and fetal membranes.

questions.question: Cardiac muscle cells differ from skeletal muscle cells in several ways. Which feature is UNIQUE to cardiac muscle?
questions.explanation: Intercalated discs are specialized junctional complexes unique to cardiac muscle. They contain fascia adherens (anchoring myofibrils), desmosomes (mechanical coupling), and gap junctions (electrical coupling via connexins). Gap junctions allow rapid propagation of action potentials, making the heart function as an electrical syncytium. Skeletal muscle lacks intercalated discs; its cells are multinucleate with peripheral nuclei, unlike the central single nucleus of cardiomyocytes.
options: Presence of actin and myosin filaments
Striated pattern due to sarcomere arrangement
Dependence on oxygen for sustained function

questions.explanation: Shortly after the ostium secundum forms, a second crescent-shaped fold (septum secundum) appears to the right of the septum primum. The septum secundum never forms a complete partition. The opening left by the septum secundum is called the foramen ovale.
questions.question: The septum secundum forms as a crescent-shaped fold in which direction from the septum primum?

questions.explanation: Meningomyelocele is a cystic form of spina bifida where both meninges and spinal cord tissue protrude through the vertebral defect. Other forms include spina bifida occulta (hidden, minimal defect) and meningocele (only meninges protrude). These result from failure of posterior neuropore closure.
questions.question: Meningomyelocele is a type of which congenital anomaly?
The precentral sulcus runs parallel to which major sulcus?
questions.explanation: The precentral sulcus runs parallel and anterior to the central sulcus, separating the precentral gyrus (primary motor cortex) from the more anterior frontal cortex. Between the precentral sulcus and superior and inferior frontal sulci lie the superior, middle, and inferior frontal gyri. The precentral sulcus is variable in configuration but generally follows the orientation of the central sulcus. This sulcus helps identify the precentral gyrus containing the primary motor cortex (Brodmann area 4).

The striatum receives dopaminergic input primarily from the substantia nigra pars compacta via the nigrostriatal pathway. This dopamine modulates striatal activity and is essential for normal movement control. Degeneration of these dopaminergic neurons causes Parkinson's disease with bradykinesia, rigidity, and tremor. The ventral striatum (nucleus accumbens) also receives dopamine from the ventral tegmental area via the mesolimbic pathway, involved in reward and motivation. Dopamine in the striatum has complex effects, exciting the direct pathway and inhibiting the indirect pathway.
questions.question: The striatum receives dopaminergic input from which structure?

questions.explanation: The perisinusoidal space of Disse separates the surface of hepatocytes from the endothelium of hepatic sinusoids. Hepatocyte microvilli project into this space, maximizing exchange of substances between blood and hepatocytes. Stellate cells (Ito cells) also reside in the space of Disse and store vitamin A. In hepatic fibrosis, stellate cells activate and deposit collagen, obliterating the space of Disse.
questions.question: The space of Disse is the perisinusoidal space that lies between:
options: The central vein and portal tract

questions.question: The hippocampus forms which boundary of the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle?
questions.explanation: The hippocampus forms the medial part of the floor of the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle, while the collateral eminence forms the lateral part. The tail of the caudate nucleus forms the roof of the inferior horn, ending anteriorly in convexities formed by the amygdaloid body and pes hippocampi. The alveus, a layer of white matter fibers on the ventricular surface of the hippocampus, continues as the fimbria of the fornix.

Mucous neck cells are irregular in shape with a round nucleus and apical secretory granules, unlike the tall columnar surface mucous cells. Their mucus secretion is acidic (less alkaline) compared to the alkaline mucus of surface cells. MNCs are located in the necks of gastric glands and function as progenitor cells for other gland cell types.
options: MNCs are taller and more columnar than surface mucous cells
MNCs secrete more alkaline mucus than surface mucous cells
MNCs line the gastric pits, whereas surface cells line the glands
MNCs produce pepsinogen, unlike surface mucous cells
MNCs are irregular with round nucleus and acidic mucus
questions.question: Mucous neck cells (MNCs) differ from surface mucous cells in which important characteristic?

questions.explanation: The trigeminal nerve (V) has SVE (motor nucleus in pons) and GSA (sensory nuclei extending from midbrain to upper cervical cord). It is the largest cranial nerve. It provides sensation to most of the head.
questions.question: The trigeminal nerve has nuclei in which brainstem levels?

questions.explanation: Reciprocal induction involves interactions between different tissues in which cells in one tissue express a set of inductive signals to which cells in the other tissue respond. The responding cells then express signals that affect the inducing tissue. Many organs develop through reciprocal induction.
questions.question: Reciprocal induction involves which type of interaction?
Hepatocytes in Zone 1 (periportal) of the hepatic acinus are specialized for which metabolic function?
options: Bile pigment processing and bilirubin conjugation only
Lipid synthesis and detoxification of drugs
Urea cycle and albumin synthesis equally in all zones
questions.explanation: Zone 1 (periportal) hepatocytes receive well-oxygenated blood rich in nutrients and are therefore specialized for oxygen-dependent processes: oxidative phosphorylation, fatty acid oxidation, gluconeogenesis, and amino acid metabolism (including urea synthesis). Zone 3 (centrilobular) hepatocytes, receiving less oxygen, are specialized for glycolysis, lipogenesis, and drug biotransformation (high CYP450). This metabolic zonation explains why different liver diseases affect different zones.

questions.question: A rectovesical fistula connects the rectum to:
questions.explanation: A rectovesical fistula is an abnormal communication between the rectum and urinary bladder. This results from incomplete separation of the cloaca by the urorectal septum. Boys with high anorectal malformations may have rectovesical or rectourethral fistulas. These require surgical correction to separate the systems.

During postpartum uterine involution, macrophages are massively recruited to phagocytose and degrade the dramatically increased extracellular matrix and cellular components that supported pregnancy. Macrophages release collagenase and other matrix metalloproteinases that break down excess collagen. This process exemplifies the physiological remodeling role of macrophages beyond pathological scenarios.
questions.question: Following parturition, the involution of the uterus (reduction back to normal size) is accomplished primarily through which of the following cellular mechanisms?
options: Hormonal inhibition of collagen synthesis by fibroblasts
Macrophage-mediated phagocytosis and degradation of excess tissue components
Neutrophil-driven enzymatic degradation of smooth muscle
Adipocyte differentiation replacing uterine muscle tissue

questions.question: Neural induction occurs by preventing ectoderm from forming which tissue?
questions.explanation: Neural induction occurs by preventing ectoderm from forming epidermis through neutralization of BMPs. Neural inducers (noggin, chordin, follistatin) bind BMPs. This allows default neural fate.

options: Lipid droplets dissolved during histological processing create a spongy appearance
They have a meshwork of interconnected cell processes
They contain large amounts of glycogen creating empty-appearing spaces
They are post-apoptotic cells with fragmented nuclei
questions.question: The zona fasciculata of the adrenal cortex produces cortisol. The cells in this zone appear vacuolated or spongy in histological sections because of which characteristic?
questions.explanation: The cells of zona fasciculata are called spongiocytes because their abundant cytoplasmic lipid droplets containing stored cholesterol esters which are the substrate for steroid hormone synthesis are dissolved by organic solvents during standard histological dehydration and clearing, leaving a characteristic spongy or vacuolated cytoplasm. In electron microscopy they are rich in smooth ER for steroidogenesis and mitochondria with tubular cristae.

The indirect pathway inhibits movement by increasing GPi/SNr output, thereby increasing inhibition of the thalamus. The pathway proceeds: cortex → striatum (D2 receptors) → GPe → STN → GPi/SNr → thalamus → cortex. Striatal activation inhibits GPe, which disinhibits STN (glutamatergic), which then excites GPi, increasing thalamic inhibition. Dopamine inhibits the indirect pathway (via D2 receptors), reducing movement inhibition. Loss of dopamine in Parkinson's disease increases indirect pathway activity, contributing to bradykinesia and rigidity.
questions.question: The indirect pathway of the basal ganglia inhibits movement by:

questions.explanation: Ciliated columnar cells are the most numerous cells in the respiratory epithelium of the conducting airways. Each cell bears approximately 300 cilia on its apical surface. Coordinated ciliary beating propels the mucus blanket (produced by goblet cells) with trapped particles toward the pharynx — the mucociliary escalator. Dysfunction of cilia (as in primary ciliary dyskinesia) leads to chronic respiratory infections.
questions.question: Respiratory epithelium (pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium) lines most of the conducting airways. Which cell type in this epithelium is most numerous?
Edwards syndrome is caused by trisomy of which chromosome?
questions.explanation: Edwards syndrome is caused by trisomy 18 (47,XX,+18 or 47,XY,+18). It is characterized by severe developmental abnormalities including clenched fists with overlapping fingers, rocker-bottom feet, cardiac defects, and profound intellectual disability. Most affected infants die within the first year.

Adipose tissue is classified as a specialized connective tissue because adipocytes are mesenchymally derived (like all connective tissue cells) and are embedded in a connective tissue framework of reticular fibers. The specialization lies in the extreme adaptation of adipocytes for lipid storage and metabolic signaling. Like other connective tissues, it has an ECM (though sparse) and derives from the same mesodermal origin.
options: It contains large quantities of type I collagen fibers
It forms protective sheaths around peripheral nerves
It produces antibodies in response to infection
Adipocytes derived from mesenchyme and classified within connective tissue
It replaces bone marrow in adults
questions.question: In the classification of connective tissue, adipose tissue is considered a specialized connective tissue because of which of the following?

questions.explanation: M cells are specialized epithelial cells overlying Peyer's patches that lack a conventional brush border and instead have an irregular apical surface. They transcytose antigens, bacteria, and macromolecules from the intestinal lumen to the underlying lymphoid tissue for immune processing. This makes them critical portals for mucosal immunity but also pathogen entry points.
questions.question: M cells (microfold cells) in the small intestinal epithelium overlie Peyer's patches. Their primary function is:
Second-order auditory neurons are located in which nuclei?
questions.explanation: Cochlear nerve terminates in dorsal and ventral cochlear nuclei in pons containing second-order neurons. Their axons form trapezoid body and acoustic striae. Most fibers cross to contralateral superior olivary nucleus.

questions.question: Spina bifida occulta involves which structure?
questions.explanation: Spina bifida occulta involves failure of vertebral arch fusion without neural tissue exposure. It is often asymptomatic. A tuft of hair may mark the site. It is the mildest form.

Neurulation accomplishes three major things: creation of neural tube (CNS), creation of neural crest (diverse cell types), and creation of overlying epidermis. This establishes the basic body plan. It is a critical developmental period.
questions.question: Neurulation accomplishes how many major things?

questions.explanation: "Apple peel" atresia involves a large segment of the midgut loop derivatives (jejunum and ileum). A short segment of intestine distal to the atresia is coiled around the remnant of the superior mesenteric artery, resembling an apple peel. This results from vascular accidents rather than failure of recanalization.
questions.question: "Apple peel" atresia involves:

questions.explanation: Striatal medium spiny neurons use GABA (gamma-aminobutyric acid) as their primary neurotransmitter, providing inhibitory output to GPe (indirect pathway) or GPi/SNr (direct pathway). These neurons comprise approximately 95% of striatal neurons and are the principal projection neurons. Different populations express either D1 receptors (direct pathway, also release substance P and dynorphin) or D2 receptors (indirect pathway, also release enkephalin). Medium spiny neurons integrate cortical (glutamatergic) and dopaminergic inputs to modulate basal ganglia output.
questions.question: Which neurotransmitter is used by striatal medium spiny neurons?

options: Within the lumen of the rete testis
questions.explanation: Leydig cells (interstitial cells) are located in the connective tissue stroma between the seminiferous tubules of the testis. They are large, polygonal cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm (rich in smooth ER and mitochondria for steroidogenesis) and often contain Reinke crystals (elongated protein inclusions). LH from the pituitary stimulates Leydig cells to synthesize and secrete testosterone, which is essential for spermatogenesis, secondary sexual development, and male reproductive function.
questions.question: Interstitial cells of Leydig in the testis produce testosterone. They are found in which location within the testis?
The nucleus accumbens is part of which striatal division?
questions.explanation: The nucleus accumbens is the main component of the ventral striatum, located at the junction of the caudate and putamen inferiorly. Unlike the dorsal striatum (involved in motor control), the ventral striatum is part of the limbic system involved in reward, motivation, addiction, and emotion. It receives dopaminergic input from the ventral tegmental area (mesolimbic pathway) and projects to the ventral pallidum. The nucleus accumbens is critically involved in addiction, with drugs of abuse causing dopamine release in this region.

Goblet cells are unicellular mucous glands scattered throughout the intestinal epithelium. They produce and secrete mucins that form the protective mucus layer overlying the epithelium. Their numbers increase from duodenum to rectum. Deficiency of mucus production, as seen in inflammatory bowel disease, exposes the epithelium to luminal damage.
questions.question: Which cell type in the intestinal epithelium produces mucus to lubricate and protect the intestinal lining?
Which cortical area is responsible for understanding written language?
questions.explanation: The angular gyrus (Brodmann area 39) in the inferior parietal lobe is crucial for reading and understanding written language, integrating visual word recognition with language comprehension. It connects visual cortex (recognizing letter shapes) with Wernicke's area (language comprehension). Lesions of the angular gyrus in the dominant hemisphere cause alexia (inability to read) and agraphia (inability to write), as well as elements of Gerstmann syndrome including acalculia and left-right disorientation.

The first mitotic division occurs 24-30 hours after fertilization, producing a 2-cell stage embryo. The second division produces a 4-cell stage, the third division produces an 8-cell stage, and subsequent divisions produce 16-32 cells forming the morula by day 3.
questions.question: The first mitotic division of the zygote occurs approximately how many hours after fertilization?
The double bubble sign on ultrasound is characteristic of which condition?
questions.explanation: The "double bubble sign" on prenatal ultrasound or postnatal X-ray is characteristic of duodenal atresia. The two bubbles represent the distended stomach and proximal duodenum, with absence of gas distally due to the obstruction. This condition is associated with Down syndrome in about 30% of cases.

The hallmark of nephrotic syndrome at the ultrastructural level is effacement (fusion/retraction) of podocyte foot processes, which eliminates the slit diaphragms that are the final size-selective filter. Without slit diaphragms, proteins — primarily albumin — leak freely into the filtrate, causing proteinuria. In minimal change disease, foot process effacement is the only ultrastructural abnormality (no deposits, normal light microscopy). This effacement is reversible with corticosteroid treatment in minimal change disease.
questions.question: The nephrotic syndrome is characterized by massive proteinuria (>3.5g/day), hypoalbuminemia, edema, and hyperlipidemia. The podocyte lesion that results in loss of selective filtration is:

options: Phagocytosis of pathogens in capillary walls
Production of basement membrane proteins only
Structural support, regulation of capillary diameter,
questions.explanation: Pericytes are contractile cells embedded within the basement membrane of capillaries and postcapillary venules. They provide structural support, regulate capillary diameter (microvascular tone), and have stem cell-like properties, being able to differentiate into smooth muscle cells and other mesenchymal cells. Pericyte loss is associated with diabetic retinopathy and capillary dysfunction.
questions.question: Pericytes are cells that wrap around the outside of capillaries and small venules. Their primary functions include:

questions.explanation: The three levels of surface amplification in the small intestine, from the smallest to the largest scale, are: microvilli (submicroscopic, forming the brush border), villi (finger-like mucosal projections visible with light microscopy), and plicae circulares (macroscopic permanent mucosal-submucosal folds). Together they increase the luminal surface area approximately 600-fold compared to a simple tube.
questions.question: The surface amplification structures of the small intestinal mucosa, listed in increasing order of microscopic scale, are:
The tunica intima of blood vessels consists of which three components in the correct sequence from the lumen outward?
questions.explanation: The tunica intima is the innermost layer of blood vessels and consists of: (1) endothelium — a single layer of squamous cells lining the lumen, (2) a basement membrane, and (3) a subendothelial layer of loose connective tissue. In larger arteries, the intima is separated from the tunica media by the internal elastic lamina (IEL). The endothelium is metabolically active, producing NO, prostacyclin, and von Willebrand factor.
options: Basement membrane → smooth muscle → elastic lamina
Endothelium → external elastic lamina → smooth muscle

questions.question: Cerebellar lesions cause which type of deficit?
questions.explanation: Cerebellar lesions cause ataxia (incoordination), dysmetria (overshooting), intention tremor, and dysdiadochokinesia. There is no paralysis or sensory loss. Deficits are ipsilateral to lesion. The cerebellum coordinates movement.

questions.question: Congenital hydrocele results from:
questions.explanation: Congenital hydrocele results from patent processus vaginalis allowing peritoneal fluid to accumulate around the testis. Unlike an indirect inguinal hernia (where bowel can enter), a hydrocele contains only fluid. Communicating hydroceles vary in size with position/activity. Most resolve spontaneously by age 1-2 years as the processus vaginalis obliterates. Persistence beyond this age may require surgical repair.

Striation results from the precise sarcomeric organization of thick and thin filaments within myofibrils: A bands appear dark under polarized light because overlapping thick and thin filaments are anisotropic while I bands appear light because thin filament-only regions are isotropic. The sarcomere repeating unit from Z line to Z line creates the characteristic banding pattern identical in skeletal and cardiac muscle but absent in smooth muscle which lacks sarcomeres.
options: Regular arrangement of mitochondria between individual adjacent myofibrils
Periodic arrangement of lysosomes distributed throughout the sarcoplasm
Dense aggregates of glycogen granules accumulated between adjacent Z lines
Dark A bands (myosin + actin) alternating with light I bands (actin only)
Arrangement of T-tubules and SR creating alternating membrane densities
questions.question: The structural basis of striation in skeletal and cardiac muscle involves which of the following?
The small intestine renews its epithelium approximately every 3–5 days. This rapid renewal protects against environmental damage but also makes the intestinal epithelium particularly vulnerable to:
questions.explanation: The high proliferative rate of intestinal stem cells makes the intestinal epithelium one of the most sensitive targets of cytotoxic chemotherapy and radiation therapy, which preferentially damage rapidly dividing cells. This accounts for the GI toxicity (mucositis, diarrhea, nausea, vomiting) seen with these treatments. Intestinal stem cells in the crypts are the primary target, and their loss leads to villous atrophy and malabsorption.

questions.question: The right and left main bronchi appear during which week?
questions.explanation: The right and left main bronchi appear during the early 5th week as lateral outpocketings of the lung bud. The right bronchus subsequently divides to form three secondary bronchi, while the left forms two. This asymmetric branching establishes the foundation for the three-lobed right lung and two-lobed left lung.

questions.question: The frontonasal prominence gives rise to which facial structures?
questions.explanation: The frontonasal prominence forms the forehead, dorsum (bridge) and apex (tip) of the nose. It also contributes to formation of the medial nasal prominences and the nasal septum. The lateral aspects of the nose develop from the lateral nasal prominences.

questions.question: Lymph nodes filter lymph and contain B cell follicles and T cell zones. The germinal center of a lymphoid follicle represents:
questions.explanation: Germinal centers are specialized microenvironments within secondary lymphoid follicles where antigen-activated B cells undergo rapid clonal expansion (centroblasts → centrocytes), somatic hypermutation of immunoglobulin genes (affinity maturation), and class-switch recombination. The resulting high-affinity antibody-secreting plasma cells and long-lived memory B cells are the products of the germinal center reaction. Abnormal germinal centers are the origin of most B-cell lymphomas.
options: The primary B cell zone in a non-stimulated lymph node
The T cell-rich area around the follicle
A site of active B cell proliferation, somatic hypermutation,
The site of T cell receptor gene rearrangement

questions.explanation: After 90-degree clockwise rotation (viewed from above), the stomach's original dorsal border becomes the left surface and forms the greater curvature. The original ventral border becomes the right surface and forms the lesser curvature. The original left surface becomes anterior, and the original right surface becomes posterior. This rotation explains the vagal nerve distribution.
questions.question: The stomach's original dorsal border becomes which surface after rotation?

questions.explanation: The intrinsic muscles of the larynx are derived from the sixth pharyngeal arch. The fourth arch gives rise to the cricothyroid, levator palatini, and constrictor muscles of the pharynx. Both fourth and sixth arches contribute to formation of laryngeal cartilages.
questions.question: Intrinsic muscles of the larynx are derived from which pharyngeal arch?

questions.explanation: Recanalization of the esophageal lumen normally occurs by the end of the embryonic period (8th week). During the 4th-7th weeks, epithelial proliferation partly or completely obliterates the lumen temporarily. Failure of proper recanalization leads to esophageal stenosis or atresia. This process of obliteration and recanalization occurs throughout the GI tract.
questions.question: Recanalization of the esophageal lumen normally occurs by:

questions.explanation: On day 9, some hypoblast cells migrate and form a thin membrane termed the exocoelomic membrane of Heuser. Heuser's membrane together with hypoblast cells lines the blastocystic cavity, forming the primitive (primary) yolk sac.
questions.question: Heuser's membrane is formed by migration of cells from which layer?

options: Membrane-bound compartments interacting with each other and surroundings
Tissues — collections of cells with similar function
questions.question: Life, with the exception of viruses, is characterized by which of the following structural units as the basic organizational level?
questions.explanation: All life (except viruses) is composed of cells, which are defined as aqueous, membrane-bound compartments that interact with each other and their environment. This is the foundational principle of cell theory, established by Schleiden, Schwann, and Virchow. Viruses are excluded because they lack cellular structure, metabolic machinery, and cannot reproduce independently.

Hepatic stellate cells (Ito cells) normally store vitamin A as retinyl esters in lipid droplets within the space of Disse. Upon activation by cytokines released during liver injury, they transform into myofibroblasts, proliferate, and deposit collagen type I and III in the space of Disse. This is the central mechanism of hepatic fibrosis and cirrhosis, which is a major cause of liver failure worldwide.
questions.question: Hepatic stellate cells (Ito cells) are pericytes of the liver sinusoids. When activated in response to liver injury, their primary pathological role is:
options: Synthesis of albumin to compensate for liver failure
