questions.explanation: Colloids are formed within the thyroid gland by the 11th week of development. The thyroid gland becomes functional by the 12th week of development. This timing is important for normal fetal development as thyroid hormones are essential for brain development.
questions.question: Colloid formation in the thyroid gland occurs by which week?

questions.explanation: In the resting state, tropomyosin physically blocks myosin-binding sites on actin. When calcium is released from the SR, it binds troponin C as part of the troponin-tropomyosin complex on thin filaments, causing a conformational change that moves tropomyosin away from the myosin binding sites on actin. This exposes the binding sites allowing myosin cross-bridges to attach and the power stroke to occur.
options: Tropomyosin to displace it from actin binding sites
Titin to reduce the sarcomere resting length
Troponin C moves tropomyosin to expose actin's myosin-binding sites
Actin directly to activate its ATPase activity
questions.question: During skeletal muscle contraction, calcium ions bind to which protein to initiate the actin-myosin interaction?
Lanugo helps to hold which substance on the fetal skin?
questions.explanation: Lanugo is fine, downy hair that appears during 17-20 weeks and helps hold the vernix caseosa on the skin. Lanugo is usually shed before birth or shortly after. Premature infants often have more lanugo than full-term infants.

questions.question: In which zone of the epiphyseal growth plate do chondrocytes actively divide and arrange themselves in longitudinal columns parallel to the long axis of the bone?
questions.explanation: The proliferative zone is characterized by rapid mitotic division of chondrocytes that organize into longitudinal columns stacked like coins and oriented parallel to the bone's long axis. This zone is responsible for actual bone lengthening through interstitial growth. The columns of cells reflect the directional pressure of growth and guide subsequent events of hypertrophy calcification and replacement by bone in the zones closer to the diaphysis.

questions.question: Which GIT wall layer contains the largest concentration of lymphoid tissue including Peyer's patches?
questions.explanation: Lymphoid tissue in the GIT is distributed throughout the mucosa (lamina propria contains diffuse lymphoid tissue and isolated nodules) and the submucosa (where larger aggregates like Peyer's patches can extend). The gut-associated lymphoid tissue (GALT) constitutes the largest immunological organ in the body. This strategic positioning allows surveillance of luminal antigens at the interface between the external environment and internal tissues.

questions.question: A histological section shows a segment of gut with no villi, extremely numerous goblet cells, and three distinct longitudinal muscle bands. This is most consistent with:
questions.explanation: The combination of absent villi, abundant goblet cells, and teniae coli (three bands of longitudinal muscle) is pathognomonic for the colon. The colon lacks villi entirely, unlike all three segments of the small intestine. Goblet cells are more numerous in the colon than anywhere else in the GIT. The teniae coli are the most distinctive gross and microscopic feature of the colon.

questions.question: Crossed fused renal ectopia most commonly involves:
questions.explanation: In crossed fused renal ectopia, both kidneys are most commonly on the left side (though right-sided can occur). One kidney crosses the midline during development and fuses with the other. The ureters still insert normally in the bladder on their respective sides. The fused kidneys typically function normally. Various fusion patterns exist (inferior, sigmoid, lump, disc). The condition is usually discovered incidentally.

questions.question: Lenticulostriate arteries are branches of which artery?
questions.explanation: Lenticulostriate arteries are numerous small branches from middle cerebral artery supplying deep diencephalic and telencephalic structures. They supply internal capsule and basal ganglia. They are prone to hemorrhage (stroke arteries).

questions.question: The pons is formed by enlargement of which layer?
questions.explanation: Passage of fibers from cerebral cortex to spinal cord through the marginal layer over basal plate enlarges it. This enlargement forms the pons. Pontine nuclei from the alar region also migrate into this structure.

The canal of the neural tube differentiates into the ventricles of the brain and the central canal of the spinal cord. The neural tube itself gives rise to the brain and spinal cord tissue. This establishes the basic fluid-filled cavities of the CNS.
questions.question: The neural canal differentiates into which structures?

questions.explanation: Reichert's cartilage is the cartilage of the second pharyngeal arch. Its dorsal part forms the stapes, styloid process of temporal bone, and stylohyoid ligament. The ventral part forms the lesser horn of the hyoid bone and the upper part of the body of the hyoid bone.
questions.question: Reichert's cartilage is associated with which pharyngeal arch?

options: Esophagus has C-shaped hyaline cartilage; trachea does not
Esophagus has respiratory epithelium; trachea has stratified squamous epithelium
Esophagus has hyaline cartilage rings; trachea has smooth muscle
questions.question: Which feature correctly distinguishes the esophagus from the trachea in histological cross-sections?
questions.explanation: The esophagus is lined by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium appropriate for food passage, while the trachea is lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium (respiratory epithelium) with goblet cells for air conditioning. Additionally, the trachea contains C-shaped hyaline cartilage rings in its wall, which are absent from the esophagus. These features together make esophageal versus tracheal identification straightforward histologically.

The mesentery of the small intestine acquires its final attachment line running obliquely from the duodenojejunal junction (left of L2 vertebra) to the ileocecal junction (right sacroiliac joint). This fan-shaped mesentery allows mobility of the jejunum and ileum. The attachment line changes during fixation as the ascending and descending colons become retroperitoneal.
questions.question: The mesentery of the small intestine acquires its final attachment line between:
The dorsal column nuclei (gracile and cuneate) are found at which level?
questions.explanation: The dorsal column nuclei (nucleus gracilis and nucleus cuneatus) are characteristic features of the lower medulla (caudal to the pyramidal decussation level). These nuclei receive and relay sensory information from the dorsal columns (fasciculus gracilis and fasciculus cuneatus).

questions.question: Which component forms the largest portion of the fetal diaphragm but represents a smaller portion in infants?
questions.explanation: The pleuroperitoneal membranes form a large portion of the fetal diaphragm but represent a relatively smaller portion in infants due to differential growth. The body wall contributes the peripheral muscular part, while the septum transversum forms the central tendon. The dorsal mesentery of the esophagus forms the crura.

Folding of the embryo occurs in both the median (longitudinal) and horizontal (transverse) planes. Median plane folding includes the head fold and tail fold, which result from differential growth of the embryonic structures. This folding converts the flat embryonic disc into a cylindrical embryo.
questions.question: Longitudinal folding of the embryo occurs in which plane?

questions.explanation: Lymphoid tissue including isolated nodules may extend from the lamina propria into the submucosa, but Peyer's patches are particularly notable in the distal ileum and can extend into the submucosa. The lamina propria is the primary site of diffuse lymphoid tissue. Option D is most accurate: both mucosa and submucosa can contain lymphoid tissue.
questions.question: In which layer of the GIT would you find lymphoid tissue such as isolated nodules or Peyer's patches?
The myelencephalon develops into which adult brain structure?
questions.explanation: The myelencephalon is a brain vesicle that gives rise to the medulla oblongata. It differs from the spinal cord in that its lateral walls are everted. Alar and basal plates separated by the sulcus limitans can be clearly distinguished in the myelencephalon.

questions.question: Polycystic kidney disease (autosomal recessive form) typically presents:
questions.explanation: The autosomal recessive form of polycystic kidney disease typically presents in infancy or early childhood with enlarged kidneys and progressive renal failure. This contrasts with the autosomal dominant form (adult polycystic kidney disease), which usually presents in the third or fourth decade. Both forms involve multiple renal cysts but differ in age of onset and inheritance pattern.

questions.question: The dermal papillae contain all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Melanocyte cell bodies are located in the basal layer of the epidermis, not in dermal papillae. Dermal papillae project upward into the epidermis and contain capillaries, sensory nerve endings, and connective tissue. These papillae are especially prominent in thick skin areas like palms and soles.

The two anterior cerebral arteries are interconnected by the anterior communicating artery before entering longitudinal fissure. This connection is part of the circle of Willis. It allows collateral blood flow.
questions.question: The two anterior cerebral arteries are interconnected by which artery?
Which structure forms the lateral boundary of the fourth ventricle in the pons?
questions.explanation: The superior cerebellar peduncle forms the lateral boundary of the fourth ventricle in the pontine region, connecting the cerebellum to the midbrain. These peduncles contain primarily efferent fibers from the deep cerebellar nuclei, particularly the dentate nucleus, projecting to the contralateral red nucleus and thalamus. The superior cerebellar peduncles form the roof of the cranial part of the fourth ventricle along with the superior medullary velum.

The endocardium is lined on its luminal surface by endothelium — a single layer of simple squamous cells continuous with the endothelium of blood vessels. Beneath the endothelium are a subendothelial layer of connective tissue and a deeper layer of smooth muscle and connective tissue. In the atria, the endocardium also contains ANP-secreting granules in the myocardium below it.
questions.question: The endocardium of the heart is lined by which cell type on its luminal surface?

questions.explanation: Purkinje cells use GABA (gamma-aminobutyric acid) as their inhibitory neurotransmitter, exerting powerful inhibitory control over deep cerebellar nuclei and vestibular nuclei. All Purkinje cell output is inhibitory, making the cerebellum fundamentally an inhibitory structure. Deep cerebellar nuclei neurons are tonically active and receive continuous inhibitory input from Purkinje cells; modulation of this inhibition controls cerebellar output. Loss of Purkinje cells (as in degenerative disorders) removes inhibition, causing hypermetria and other cerebellar signs.
questions.question: Which neurotransmitter do Purkinje cells use?

questions.explanation: The vestibular nerve synapses in the vestibular nuclei in the pons. There are four vestibular nuclei: superior, inferior, medial and lateral. These project to multiple targets for balance and eye movement control.
questions.question: The vestibular nerve synapses in which brainstem nuclei?

questions.explanation: Scanning speech (scanning dysarthria) is characteristic of cerebellar lesions, particularly vermal lesions. Speech becomes slow, slurred, and broken into separate syllables with irregular rhythm and abnormal stress patterns, sounding staccato or explosive. This reflects impaired coordination of respiratory, laryngeal, and articulatory muscles involved in speech production. Patients separate syllables abnormally and may have irregular volume. Unlike Broca's aphasia (motor planning deficit) or dysarthria from motor cortex lesions, scanning speech specifically reflects cerebellar timing and coordination deficits.
questions.question: Scanning speech is characteristic of lesions in which structure?
The neurenteric canal forms a temporary communication between which two cavities?
questions.explanation: The proximal part of the notochordal canal forms the neurenteric canal, which provides temporary communication between the amniotic cavity and the yolk sac. The neural plate, groove, and tube are bathed in amniotic fluid that reaches them through the neurenteric canal. This canal is a transient structure.

questions.question: The appendix is a blind-ended tubular appendage of the cecum. Its histological hallmark that distinguishes it from the rest of the large intestine is:
questions.explanation: The appendix is characterized histologically by the presence of numerous lymphoid follicles that may extend from the mucosa into the submucosa. This prominent lymphoid tissue has led to the appendix being called a gut tonsil or abdominal tonsil. It is thought to function in immune surveillance. In chronic inflammation, this lymphoid tissue may atrophy in elderly individuals.

questions.question: Cells of Martinotti are primarily found in which cortical layer?
questions.explanation: Cells of Martinotti are multipolar neurons found predominantly in the deeper layers, particularly layer VI (multiform layer), though they can be found throughout the cortex. These interneurons have ascending axons that reach the molecular layer (layer I), where they synapse on apical dendrites of pyramidal cells. Martinotti cells provide feedback inhibition, modulating cortical excitability and contributing to vertical information processing across cortical layers.

The superior parathyroid gland develops from the fourth pharyngeal pouch in the 5th week, along with contributions to thyroid gland formation. It remains in the neck region along with the thyroid gland. The inferior parathyroid from the third pouch descends with the thymus.
questions.question: The superior parathyroid gland develops from which pharyngeal pouch?

questions.explanation: Vestibular nuclei project to spinal cord through lateral and medial vestibulospinal tracts for equilibrium maintenance. Lateral tract facilitates extensors. Medial tract controls neck muscles.
questions.question: Vestibular nuclei project to spinal cord via which tracts?
The first major induction phenomenon occurs during which developmental stage?
questions.explanation: The first major induction phenomenon occurs during the final stages of gastrulation of most animal embryos. This primary embryonic induction involves the mesoderm inducing the overlying ectoderm to develop into the neural tube. This establishes the basic body plan.

questions.question: Mast cell granules stained metachromatically with toluidine blue produce which of the following colors?
questions.explanation: Metachromasia refers to the property of certain dyes, including toluidine blue, to color tissue components differently from their own intrinsic color. Mast cell granules contain heparin (a sulfated glycosaminoglycan) which shifts the color from the dye's native blue to purple or violet. This color shift is diagnostic for identifying mast cells in tissue sections.

questions.question: Medial reticulospinal tract has which effect on anterior horn cells?
questions.explanation: Medial reticulospinal tract from pontine reticular system runs in anterior white column inhibiting anterior horn cells. Lateral tract facilitates them. Together they modulate motor neuron activity.

questions.question: Which structure receives projections from the lateral geniculate body?
questions.explanation: The lateral geniculate body (nucleus), part of the posterior thalamic group, receives fibers from the optic tract and projects via the optic radiations to the primary visual cortex (area 17) along the calcarine sulcus. This six-layered nucleus maintains retinotopic organization and is the principal relay station for visual information from the retina to the cortex. Each layer receives input from either the ipsilateral or contralateral eye, forming the basis for binocular vision.

questions.question: The thymus develops from which pharyngeal pouch?
questions.explanation: The thymus develops from the endoderm of the ventral part of the third pharyngeal pouch in the 5th week. It is large at birth, reaches full size at puberty, and shrinks in old age. It has both cranial (neck) and caudal (thorax) parts and is invaded by vascular mesoderm containing lymphoblasts.

questions.question: The dura mater serves multiple functions in the cranial cavity. Which layer acts as the periosteum of the skull?
questions.explanation: The endosteal layer of the dura mater is the tough, fibrous outer layer that adheres closely to the inner surface of the cranial bones, serving as their periosteum. This adherence is most prominent around the skull base and sutures, providing structural support. The meningeal layer is the inner layer that folds to create projections dividing the cranial cavity into compartments.

questions.question: The anterior spinocerebellar tract exits to cerebellum via which peduncle?
questions.explanation: Anterior spinocerebellar fibers decussate and lie on the cord's margin, exiting via superior cerebellar peduncle. They synapse with posterior horn cells in lower lumbar and sacral segments. They do not synapse with thoracic nuclei.

The lateral geniculate body is part of the thalamus receiving visual input. It projects to primary visual cortex via optic radiations. It has six layers with specific organization. It is a relay station for vision.
questions.question: The lateral geniculate body is part of which structure?

questions.explanation: Vitamin B12 bound to intrinsic factor (IF, produced by gastric parietal cells) is specifically absorbed in the terminal ileum via cubilin receptors on enterocyte surfaces. This is a critical location because surgical resection or Crohn's disease affecting the terminal ileum will cause B12 malabsorption and megaloblastic anemia. The terminal ileum also specifically absorbs bile salts (enterohepatic circulation) — their malabsorption leads to bile salt-induced diarrhea.
questions.question: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) is absorbed in which specific region of the intestine after binding to intrinsic factor?

questions.explanation: Treacher Collins syndrome (mandibulofacial dysostosis) results from abnormal neural crest cell development. It is characterized by deformities of the ears, eyes, cheekbones, and chin. The severity varies from mild to severe, and complications may include breathing problems, vision issues, cleft palate, and hearing loss.
questions.question: Treacher Collins syndrome results from abnormal development of which cells?
The chorion is histologically composed of how many layers?
questions.explanation: The chorion is histologically composed of four layers: cellular layer, dense reticulum, pseudo-basement membrane, and outer trophoblast. The chorion is the outer membrane of the fetal membranes, is in contact with the uterine wall, and is attached to the margins of the placenta.

The cochlear and vestibular nuclei represent the special somatic afferent (SSA) component, receiving auditory and vestibular information from the inner ear via cranial nerve VIII. The SSA column is the most lateral in the brainstem's mediolateral organization. These nuclei are located at the pontomedullary junction, with the vestibular nuclei positioned more medially and the cochlear nuclei more laterally. The SSA modality represents specialized mechanoreceptors from the otic placode rather than general surface ectoderm.
questions.question: The cochlear and vestibular nuclei represent which functional component?

questions.explanation: Ankyloglossia is commonly known as tongue tie. It results from an abnormally short lingual frenulum that restricts tongue movement. This can interfere with breastfeeding in infants and speech development in children. Treatment may involve surgical release of the frenulum.
questions.question: Ankyloglossia is also known as which condition?
The cingulum is best described as:
questions.explanation: The cingulum is a major association fiber bundle running within the cingulate gyrus, connecting frontal, parietal, and temporal lobes along the medial hemispheric surface. It carries fibers from the entorhinal cortex to the hippocampus and connects components of the limbic system. The cingulum curves around the splenium of the corpus callosum to reach the parahippocampal gyrus and hippocampus. Damage can cause memory impairment and emotional dysregulation, reflecting its role in the limbic system.

The three layers from innermost outward are: (1) fibrous (true) capsule — tightly adherent to renal parenchyma; (2) adipose (perinephric fat) capsule — layer of perinephric fat providing cushioning; (3) renal (Gerota's) fascia — outer fibrous layer anchoring the kidney to surrounding structures. This fat layer acts as a protective shock absorber. In thin patients, loss of perinephric fat contributes to renal ptosis (nephroptosis).
questions.question: The kidney is enclosed by three layers of supporting tissue. Which layer, immediately adjacent to the renal capsule externally, consists of perinephric fat?
Eosinophils are most characteristically elevated in which clinical conditions?
questions.explanation: Eosinophils are classically elevated in IgE-mediated allergic diseases including asthma atopic dermatitis and food allergy, and in parasitic helminth infections. Their bilobed nucleus and prominent orange-red granules containing major basic protein and eosinophil peroxidase allow cytotoxic killing of parasites too large to phagocytose. Eosinophil recruitment is directed by IL-5 from T helper 2 cells and eotaxin from tissue cells.

questions.question: The third ventricle is derived from the cavity of which vesicle?
questions.explanation: The canal of the neural tube differentiates to form various ventricles including the third ventricle from diencephalon. Lateral ventricles derive from telencephalon. The fourth ventricle originates from the rhombencephalon.

Neural crest cells migrate into the developing heart and contribute to formation of the conotruncal (aorticopulmonary) septum, which divides the truncus arteriosus into the aorta and pulmonary trunk. Abnormalities in neural crest migration can result in conotruncal defects like persistent truncus arteriosus or transposition of great vessels.
questions.question: The conotruncal septum of the heart is formed by cells from which source?

questions.explanation: The facial nerve (CN VII) contains both special visceral efferent (SVE) fibers to facial expression muscles from the facial motor nucleus, and general visceral efferent (GVE) parasympathetic fibers to lacrimal and salivary glands from the superior salivatory nucleus. The facial nerve also carries special visceral afferent (taste) from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue via the nervus intermedius. This complex functional composition makes the facial nerve one of the most complicated cranial nerves.
questions.question: Which cranial nerve contains both SVE and GVE components?
The regeneration potential differs among the three muscle types. Which of the following correctly ranks their regenerative capacity?
questions.explanation: Smooth muscle has the highest regenerative potential and can fully regenerate from surviving smooth muscle cells. Skeletal muscle has limited but real regeneration through satellite cell activation. Cardiac muscle has minimal regeneration; after myocardial infarction, lost cardiomyocytes are replaced by fibrous scar tissue rather than functional myocardium, causing permanent loss of contractile function proportional to the infarct size.
options: All three types have identical regenerative potential
Smooth > Skeletal > Cardiac in regenerative capacity
Myelin sheath formation by Schwann cells
Calcium influx triggering exocytosis of vesicles
Axon hillock integrating graded potentials into action potentials
Retrograde axonal transport of trophic factors
questions.question: The axon hillock of a neuron is specifically important because it is the site of which of the following?
questions.explanation: The axon hillock is the specialized region at the junction of the cell body and axon containing the highest density of voltage-gated sodium channels and the lowest threshold for action potential generation. It functions as the integration point that sums excitatory and inhibitory postsynaptic potentials and fires an action potential only when depolarization reaches threshold, making it the decision-making point of the neuron.

The I band consists only of thin actin filaments without any overlapping thick myosin filaments. Each I band is bisected by a Z disc to which the thin filaments are anchored. During contraction, actin filaments slide deeper into the A band, narrowing the I band and H zone but not the A band. The degree of I band narrowing reflects the degree of muscle shortening.
options: Only thick myosin filaments with no actin
Both thick and thin filaments in maximum overlap
The M line with myomesin cross-linking thick filaments
Only titin spanning from M line to Z disc
Thin actin filaments only, bisected by the Z disc; no myosin overlap
questions.question: The I band of a sarcomere which appears light under polarized microscopy contains which of the following?

questions.explanation: Mesenchyme is the embryonic loose connective tissue consisting of sparse, undifferentiated stellate (star-shaped) cells that can give rise to all adult connective tissue types (fibroblasts, chondrocytes, osteoblasts, adipocytes, smooth muscle cells). The cells are embedded in a watery matrix with minimal collagen. It is found in the mesodermal layer of early embryos and persists in Wharton's jelly of the umbilical cord.
questions.question: Mesenchyme, the embryonic connective tissue from which all adult connective tissues are derived, is best characterized by which of the following?
options: Dense collagen bundles with polarized epithelial cells
Abundant mature elastic fibers and fibroblasts throughout
Sparse stellate cells in watery matrix with few collagen fibers
Completed differentiated adipocytes in an embryonic setting
Organized lymphoid follicles with germinal centers

questions.explanation: The superior longitudinal fasciculus is a major association fiber system connecting the frontal, parietal, occipital, and temporal lobes within the same hemisphere. It arches over the insula deep to the lateral surface and includes several components: SLF I (superior parietal-frontal connections), SLF II (inferior parietal-frontal), and SLF III (supramarginal gyrus-frontal). The arcuate fasciculus, connecting Wernicke's and Broca's areas, is sometimes considered part of SLF. Damage can cause conduction aphasia and visuospatial deficits.
questions.question: The superior longitudinal fasciculus connects which regions?
The ventral posterolateral nucleus of the thalamus receives input from which ascending tract?
questions.explanation: The ventral posterolateral (VPL) nucleus receives input from the medial lemniscus (carrying fine touch, vibration, and proprioception), spinothalamic tract (pain and temperature), and trigeminal lemniscus. This nucleus is part of the lateral group of thalamic nuclei and projects to the primary somatosensory cortex in the postcentral gyrus. The VPL nucleus maintains somatotopic organization, preserving the spatial arrangement of body representation from periphery to cortex.

questions.question: At what vertebral level does the internal jugular vein begin?
questions.explanation: The internal jugular vein begins at the jugular foramen as a continuation of the sigmoid sinus, representing the primary venous drainage pathway from the brain. It descends in the neck within the carotid sheath alongside the internal carotid artery and vagus nerve. The jugular foramen is located at the skull base between the petrous temporal bone and occipital bone. The internal jugular vein receives additional tributaries in the neck before joining the subclavian vein to form the brachiocephalic vein.

options: The superior colliculus directly without any relay
Lateral geniculate nucleus projecting to the occipital visual cortex
The medial geniculate nucleus of the thalamus
The inferior colliculus which processes visual information
questions.question: The primary visual cortex located in the occipital lobe receives input from the retina through which relay station?
questions.explanation: The main visual pathway from retina to cortex: retinal ganglion cell axons form the optic nerve, partially decussate at the optic chiasm where nasal fibers cross, form the optic tract, and synapse in the lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus. Geniculocalcarine fibers project through the optic radiation to the primary visual cortex in area 17 of the occipital lobe. The superior colliculus receives a separate projection involved in eye movement control. The medial geniculate nucleus handles auditory information.
Sensory neurons are afferent, carrying messages toward the brain or spinal cord. They transmit information from receptors to the CNS. Their cell bodies are in sensory ganglia.
questions.question: Sensory neurons are described as which type?

questions.explanation: Parietal cell acid secretion is stimulated by three pathways: (1) acetylcholine — released by vagal (parasympathetic) nerve terminals acting on M3 muscarinic receptors; (2) gastrin — from G cells acting on CCK-B receptors; (3) histamine — from ECL cells acting on H2 receptors. All three pathways converge on the H+/K+-ATPase. This explains why H2 blockers and PPIs are effective in treating peptic ulcers regardless of the primary trigger.
questions.question: Gastric acid secretion is stimulated by three pathways. Which neurotransmitter/hormone is released by nerve terminals in the stomach to directly stimulate parietal cells?
The optic nerve carries which functional component?
questions.explanation: The optic nerve (II) has only special somatic afferent component for vision. It conveys visual information from the retina. It is actually a CNS tract, not a true peripheral nerve.

questions.question: Neurulation is completed by the end of which week with closure of the neural tube?
questions.explanation: Neurulation is the process involved in formation of the neural plate, neural groove, neural folds, and fusion of the folds to form the neural tube. The process is completed by the end of the 4th week with closure of the neural tube. The neural tube is the primordium of the central nervous system.

Intention tremor increases as the limb approaches its target during goal-directed voluntary movement, particularly near the end of movement. It is absent or minimal at rest and with supported posture, distinguishing it from Parkinsonian resting tremor (which decreases with voluntary movement). Intention tremor reflects impaired cerebellar correction of ongoing movements---as the limb approaches the target, increasing precision is required, and cerebellar inability to make fine adjustments becomes apparent. Lesions of the dentate nucleus and superior cerebellar peduncle typically cause pronounced intention tremor.
questions.question: Intention tremor differs from resting tremor in that it:

questions.explanation: Cogwheel rigidity is a feature of Parkinson's disease (basal ganglia dysfunction), not cerebellar ataxia. Cerebellar ataxia includes intention tremor (tremor increasing during goal-directed movement), dysmetria (overshooting or undershooting targets), dysdiadochokinesia (inability to perform rapid alternating movements), past-pointing (missing targets), decomposition of movement (breaking complex movements into components), scanning dysarthria, and hypotonia. These deficits reflect impaired motor coordination, timing, and motor learning rather than the rigidity seen in basal ganglia disorders.
questions.question: Cerebellar ataxia is characterized by all EXCEPT:

questions.explanation: Each primary oocyte produces only one ovum. During meiosis I, the primary oocyte produces one secondary oocyte and one first polar body. During meiosis II, the secondary oocyte produces one mature ovum and one second polar body. The polar bodies are nonfunctional and degenerate.
questions.question: In females, how many ova result from each primary oocyte?
The splenium of the corpus callosum primarily connects which cortical regions?
questions.explanation: The splenium (posterior portion) of the corpus callosum primarily connects the occipital and posterior parietal lobes bilaterally, transferring visual and spatial information between hemispheres. The forceps major, formed by fibers radiating from the splenium, connects the occipital cortices. Lesions of the splenium can cause alexia without agraphia (inability to read in the left visual field despite intact writing) by disconnecting the right visual cortex from the left language areas. The splenium also contains fibers from the posterior temporal lobes.

The pia and arachnoid mater (collectively called leptomeninges) are derived from neural crest cells. The dura mater is derived from mesoderm. Schwann cells, which myelinate peripheral nerves, are also derived from neural crest, while oligodendrocytes (CNS myelin) come from neural tube.
questions.question: The pia and arachnoid mater (leptomeninges) are derived from which source?
Which cranial nerve emerges from the dorsal surface of the brainstem?
questions.explanation: The trochlear nerve (CN IV) is unique as the only cranial nerve emerging from the dorsal surface of the brainstem, specifically from below the inferior colliculus. It courses ventrally around the brainstem between the superior cerebellar and posterior cerebral arteries. All other cranial nerves (except CN IV) emerge from the ventral surface of the brainstem, making the trochlear nerve's dorsal emergence a distinguishing anatomical feature.

Vesicoureteral reflux is graded I-V based on the extent of reflux and degree of system dilation: Grade I (ureter only), Grade II (ureter and pelvis, no dilation), Grade III (mild dilation), Grade IV (moderate dilation with blunted calyces), Grade V (severe dilation with tortuous ureter). Higher grades have greater risk of renal scarring and may require surgical correction. Lower grades often resolve spontaneously.
questions.question: Vesicoureteral reflux is graded from I-V based on:
options: Extent of reflux and system dilation

questions.question: The organ of Corti develops from which structure?
questions.explanation: Epithelial cells of cochlear duct form inner and outer ridges. The outer ridge forms rows of hair cells (sensory cells) covered by tectorial membrane. Together these form the organ of Corti.

questions.question: Collecting tubules are derived from:
questions.explanation: Collecting tubules are derived from the ureteric bud through repeated branching (approximately 15 generations). The ureteric bud gives rise to the entire collecting system: ureter, renal pelvis, major and minor calyces, and collecting tubules. The metanephric blastema forms the nephrons (glomeruli and tubules from Bowman's capsule to distal convoluted tubule).

options: Producing digestive enzymes for nutrient absorption
M cell antigen sampling initiating mucosal secretory IgA responses
Secreting mucus to protect the intestinal epithelium
Absorbing vitamin B12 through intrinsic factor
questions.question: The GALT including Peyer's patches in the ileum serves which primary immunological function?
questions.explanation: Peyer's patches are aggregated lymphoid follicles in the ileum covered by follicle-associated epithelium containing M cells that sample luminal antigens by transcytosis and deliver them to underlying dendritic cells. This triggers mucosal immune responses culminating in secretory IgA production which is secreted back into the gut lumen to neutralize pathogens. Salmonella and Vibrio cholerae exploit M cells for invasion into the submucosa.

questions.question: Broca's area is located in which lobe?
questions.explanation: Broca's area is located in the inferior frontal gyrus of the dominant (usually left) frontal lobe. It controls speech production. Lesions cause expressive aphasia. Patients understand but cannot speak fluently.

Intussusception is characterized by invagination of one segment of intestine into itself, causing obstruction. It most commonly occurs at the ileocecal junction. Unlike volvulus, which is twisting around the mesenteric axis, intussusception involves telescoping of bowel. It can occur as a complication of malrotation.
questions.question: Intussusception is characterized by:

options: Are muscular arteries throughout with no elastic component
Have thinner walls relative to their lumen size
Carry oxygenated blood at high pressure
Have no smooth muscle in the media
Carry both arterial and venous blood simultaneously
questions.question: The pulmonary vasculature carries deoxygenated blood from the right heart to the lungs and oxygenated blood back to the left heart. Pulmonary arteries differ from systemic arteries in that they:
questions.explanation: Pulmonary arteries operate at much lower pressures than systemic arteries (pulmonary systolic pressure ~25 mmHg vs. 120 mmHg systemically). Correspondingly, pulmonary arteries have thinner walls relative to their lumen diameter and contain more elastic tissue compared to systemic arteries of similar size. In pulmonary arterial hypertension, the media of pulmonary arteries undergoes smooth muscle hypertrophy and intimal fibrosis, increasing wall thickness and pulmonary vascular resistance.

The liver develops from the hepatic diverticulum of the foregut, not from the primitive pharynx. The primitive pharynx gives rise to the thyroid gland, parathyroid glands, thymus gland, tympanic cavity, and contributes to trachea and lung development. These structures develop from pharyngeal pouches and floor of the pharynx.
questions.question: The primitive pharynx gives rise to all EXCEPT:
Pain modulation by the reticular formation primarily involves which neurotransmitter system?
questions.explanation: Pain modulation by the reticular formation primarily involves serotonergic neurons from the raphe nuclei, which project to the spinal cord dorsal horn and inhibit pain transmission. This descending pain control system also involves noradrenergic neurons from the locus coeruleus and endogenous opioid mechanisms in the periaqueductal gray. These systems can be activated by stress, attention, and certain medications, explaining phenomena like stress-induced analgesia and placebo effects.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes the structural and functional difference between myelin in the PNS versus CNS?
options: PNS myelin is thicker but has fewer lamellae than CNS myelin
CNS myelin contains more cholesterol than PNS myelin
PNS myelin has identical protein composition to CNS myelin
Both CNS and PNS myelin are produced by identical Schwann cells
PNS Schwann cell myelin enables regeneration; CNS oligodendrocyte myelin does not
questions.explanation: PNS myelin is produced by Schwann cells where one Schwann cell myelinates one internode of one axon, and the Schwann cell cytoplasm and basal lamina form the neurilemma tube that guides axon regeneration. CNS myelin is produced by oligodendrocytes where one oligodendrocyte myelinates segments of multiple axons through cytoplasmic processes, without forming a cellular tube, and CNS environment contains inhibitory factors preventing regeneration. PNS myelin contains P0 protein as the major structural protein while CNS myelin contains MBP and PLP.

Simple renal cysts in children (unlike adults, where they're common and benign) usually indicate underlying disease such as tuberous sclerosis, von Hippel-Lindau disease, or other syndromes. Isolated simple cysts are rare in children. Any cystic renal lesion in a child warrants investigation for syndromic or genetic conditions. Simple cortical cysts become increasingly common with age in adults.
questions.question: Simple renal cysts in children usually indicate:
The stomach rotates approximately how many degrees around its longitudinal axis?
questions.explanation: The stomach rotates approximately 90 degrees clockwise around its longitudinal axis (when viewed from above). This rotation causes the original left side to become the ventral (anterior) surface and the original right side to become the dorsal (posterior) surface. This explains the innervation pattern by vagus nerves.

The mesencephalon (midbrain vesicle) gives rise to the midbrain in the adult brain. The three primary brain vesicles are prosencephalon (forebrain), mesencephalon (midbrain), and rhombencephalon (hindbrain). These later subdivide into five secondary brain vesicles.
questions.question: The mesencephalon gives rise to which adult brain structure?
The embedding medium used in standard paraffin histology processing primarily provides tissues with which of the following properties?
questions.explanation: Paraffin wax infiltrates dehydrated tissue and, upon solidifying, provides the mechanical support necessary for cutting thin, consistent sections (3–10 μm) on a microtome. The wax must be removed (deparaffinization) before staining since it interferes with water-based stains. Embedding is a critical intermediate step between fixation and staining.
options: Firmness to support sectioning on the microtome

questions.question: The intermediate horn is limited to which spinal segments?
questions.explanation: The intermediate horn is limited to the region of T1 to T12 and L2-L3 spinal segments. Neuroblast aggregation between basal and alar plates forms this structure. It contains neurons of the sympathetic portion of the autonomic nervous system.

On days 11 and 12, syncytiotrophoblast lacunae establish connections with maternal stromal capillaries to form sinusoids. This marks the beginning of uteroplacental circulation, allowing maternal blood to flow through the lacunae and provide nutrients and oxygen to the developing embryo.
questions.question: Sinusoids are established in the syncytiotrophoblast on which days?

questions.explanation: The neural tube forms three brain flexures: the cephalic (midbrain) flexure which is ventral, the cervical flexure at the junction of hindbrain and spinal cord which is ventral, and the pontine flexure which is dorsal. There is no lumbar flexure in brain development.
questions.question: Brain flexures include all of the following EXCEPT:
Esophageal glands proper are located in which layer of the esophageal wall?
questions.explanation: Esophageal glands proper are small mucous glands located in the submucosa throughout the esophagus. They produce mucus that lubricates the passage of food boluses. In contrast, esophageal cardiac glands are found in the mucosa near the gastroesophageal junction. This submucosal location is a useful histological landmark for identifying esophageal tissue.

In the late secretory phase, falling progesterone (and estrogen) levels trigger intense vasospasm of the spiral arteries of the stratum functionalis. This ischemia causes breakdown of the functionalis. The subsequent reperfusion causes lysis of the ischemic tissue, which sloughs as menstrual flow. Prostaglandins (particularly PGF2α) mediate this spiral artery vasospasm. Excessive prostaglandin production causes dysmenorrhea; NSAIDs treat dysmenorrhea by inhibiting prostaglandin synthesis.
questions.question: In the late secretory phase of the endometrial cycle (days 25–28), just before menstruation, the endometrium shows which specific vascular change?

questions.explanation: Fetal movements (quickening) are typically felt by the mother during 17-20 weeks. Coordinated limb movements actually begin earlier (13-16 weeks), but they are too weak to be felt. Quickening is an important milestone in prenatal development and pregnancy monitoring.
questions.question: Fetal movements are first felt by the mother during which weeks?

questions.explanation: Folic acid supplementation (400-800 mcg daily) before conception and during early pregnancy significantly reduces the risk of neural tube defects (NTDs) such as spina bifida and anencephaly. Folic acid is essential for DNA synthesis and cell division during the critical period of neural tube closure.
questions.question: Folic acid supplementation during pregnancy is primarily recommended to prevent which abnormality?

questions.explanation: Inductive forces from pigmented outer optic cup layer cause surrounding lateral plate mesoderm to form choroid (vascularized, pigmented) and sclera (tough outer layer). Sclera is continuous with dura around optic nerve.
questions.question: The choroid and sclera are formed from which tissue?
Amniotic fluid volume in the third trimester is primarily regulated by:
questions.explanation: Amniotic fluid volume in the third trimester is primarily regulated by fetal swallowing (removes ~500-1000 ml/day) and fetal urination (produces ~800-1200 ml/day). This dynamic balance maintains normal fluid volume. Disruption of either process leads to polyhydramnios (impaired swallowing from GI obstruction or neurological problems) or oligohydramnios (impaired urination from renal/urinary anomalies).

questions.question: Maternal blood enters the intervillous spaces through which vessels?
questions.explanation: Maternal blood enters the intervillous spaces through spiral arteries, which become less convoluted and increase in diameter during pregnancy. This increases maternal blood flow to the placenta for gaseous exchange. Deoxygenated maternal blood flows back through endometrial veins.

questions.question: Omphalocele is covered by which membrane layers?
questions.explanation: Omphalocele is covered by both peritoneal and amniotic membranes, creating a translucent sac. The umbilical cord inserts into the apex of the sac. This covering differentiates omphalocele from gastroschisis, where bowel is exposed directly to amniotic fluid without membrane coverage. The membrane may rupture during or after delivery.

In anaphylactic shock, mast cell degranulation releases preformed histamine which rapidly causes bronchospasm and increased vascular permeability causing hypotension and urticaria. Newly synthesized leukotrienes LTC4 and LTD4 (slow-reacting substances of anaphylaxis) sustain bronchoconstriction more potently than histamine. Platelet activating factor contributes to hypotension. Treatment with epinephrine reverses bronchospasm through beta-2 receptor stimulation and hypotension through alpha-1 vasoconstriction.
options: IgE directly causing smooth muscle contraction
Complement C5a causing mast cell activation
questions.question: A patient presents with anaphylactic shock after a bee sting. The life-threatening bronchospasm and hypotension are primarily mediated by which substances released from mast cells?
The gracile fasciculus carries information from which body region?
questions.explanation: The gracile fasciculus (medial) carries discriminative touch and proprioception from lower limb and trunk. The cuneate fasciculus (lateral) carries similar information from upper limb. They ascend in posterior columns.

questions.question: The Circle of Willis provides anastomosis between which major arterial systems?
questions.explanation: The Circle of Willis provides important anastomotic connections between the internal carotid (anterior circulation) and vertebrobasilar (posterior circulation) systems. It consists of the anterior communicating artery connecting the anterior cerebral arteries, the posterior communicating arteries connecting the internal carotid to the posterior cerebral arteries, and the posterior cerebral arteries themselves. This arrangement allows collateral blood flow when one major vessel is occluded, though anatomical variations and incomplete circles are common.

questions.question: The renal cortex contains granular-appearing regions because of which structures concentrated there?
questions.explanation: The granular appearance of the renal cortex results from the presence of numerous renal corpuscles (glomeruli enclosed in Bowman's capsule) and convoluted tubules (proximal and distal). These structures give the cortex its characteristic granular texture on gross and histological examination. The medullary pyramids, in contrast, contain straight tubules (loops of Henle, collecting ducts) giving them a striated appearance.

The superior salivatory nucleus provides parasympathetic innervation to the lacrimal gland, submandibular gland, and sublingual gland via the facial nerve and its branches. Preganglionic fibers travel in the nervus intermedius, synapsing in the pterygopalatine ganglion (for lacrimal gland) or submandibular ganglion (for submandibular and sublingual glands). This parasympathetic stimulation increases secretion from these glands, important for eye lubrication and saliva production.
questions.question: The superior salivatory nucleus provides parasympathetic innervation to which glands?

options: A primary oocyte arrested in meiosis I surrounded by a single layer of flattened follicular
A primary oocyte surrounded by several layers of granulosa cells with a zona pellucida
A secondary oocyte with a fully formed antrum
A secondary oocyte surrounded by cumulus oophorus
A mature egg with zona pellucida and corona radiata only
questions.question: The female ovary contains follicles at various stages of development. Primordial follicles consist of:
questions.explanation: Primordial follicles consist of a primary oocyte arrested in prophase I of meiosis, surrounded by a single layer of flattened (squamous) follicular cells. These are the smallest and most numerous follicles in the ovary and represent the ovarian reserve. Activation of primordial follicles triggers their transition to primary follicles, where follicular cells become cuboidal and begin proliferating.

questions.question: Potter sequence is characterized by all EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Potter sequence is characterized by oligohydramnios (not polyhydramnios), which leads to pulmonary hypoplasia, limb deformities, and characteristic facial features (low-set ears, epicanthal folds, flattened nose). The sequence results from bilateral renal agenesis or severe bilateral renal dysplasia. The condition is lethal due to pulmonary hypoplasia preventing adequate breathing after birth.

questions.question: A histology student examines a lymph node section and identifies a region with large dividing B cells surrounded by a mantle zone of small B cells. This structure is specifically called which of the following?
options: Primary follicle without germinal center or immune activation
Thymic cortex undergoing T-cell positive selection
Secondary follicle with germinal center indicating active immune response
questions.explanation: A secondary follicle with a germinal center forms in lymph nodes when antigen-activated B cells undergo clonal expansion within the center, forming the germinal center with large proliferating centroblasts and smaller centrocytes. This is surrounded by a mantle zone of small naive B cells forming a dark rim. Secondary follicles indicate active humoral immune responses with ongoing somatic hypermutation and affinity maturation. Primary follicles are smaller and uniformly cellular without germinal centers.

questions.question: Lanugo hair is characterized by being:
questions.explanation: Lanugo is fine, soft, lightly pigmented downy hair that appears around the 12th week and is the first hair to develop. It is replaced by coarser hairs during the perinatal period. Lanugo persists over most of the body but is eventually replaced by vellus or terminal hairs.

questions.question: Multiple sclerosis is characterized by which pathology?
questions.explanation: Multiple sclerosis is characterized by demyelination in CNS (oligodendrocyte damage). It causes varied neurological symptoms. It is an autoimmune disease. Plaques form in white matter.

questions.question: The peripheral nervous system is divided into which divisions?
questions.explanation: The peripheral nervous system is divided into somatic NS (voluntary) and autonomic NS (involuntary). Somatic controls skeletal muscles and receives sensory information. Autonomic controls involuntary functions like heart rate.

At birth, closure of the lumen of the umbilical arteries results in formation of the median umbilical ligaments. Closure of the umbilical vein forms the ligamentum teres in the liver, and closure of the ductus venosus forms the ligamentum venosum. These changes redirect blood flow after birth.
questions.question: At birth, closure of the umbilical arteries results in formation of which structure?

questions.explanation: The prosencephalon (forebrain) divides into telencephalon and diencephalon. The telencephalon gives rise to the cerebral hemispheres (cortex, white matter, and basal nuclei), while the diencephalon forms the thalamus and hypothalamus. This subdivision occurs during formation of secondary brain vesicles.
questions.question: The telencephalon develops from which primary brain vesicle?
Which structure marks the posterior limit of the thalamus?
questions.explanation: The posterior commissure marks the posterior limit of the thalamus, located at the junction between the diencephalon and midbrain dorsal to the cerebral aqueduct. The anterior limit of the thalamus is the interventricular foramen (foramen of Monro). The thalamus extends from the third ventricle medially to the posterior limb of the internal capsule laterally, with its posterior expansion called the pulvinar overlying the geniculate bodies.

The filum terminale is a condensation of pia mater extending from the conus medullaris. It anchors the spinal cord to the coccyx. This structure is important anatomically for lumbar puncture procedures.
questions.question: The filum terminale is formed from which tissue?

questions.explanation: The 4th week witnesses differentiation of the cranial neural tube into 3 primary brain vesicles. These are the prosencephalon, mesencephalon, and rhombencephalon arranged cranio-caudally. By the 5th week, these increase to five secondary vesicles.
questions.question: How many primary brain vesicles form during the 4th week?
The musculature of the tongue develops from which embryonic structure?
questions.explanation: Tongue musculature develops from occipital myotomes (somites). These myoblasts migrate into the developing tongue, bringing their nerve supply (hypoglossal nerve, CN XII) with them. This is why the hypoglossal nerve innervates all intrinsic and most extrinsic tongue muscles.

questions.question: The fourth ventricle is derived from which embryonic structure?
questions.explanation: The canal of the neural tube in the rhombencephalon forms the fourth ventricle. Both metencephalon and myelencephalon contribute to it. It has a characteristic diamond shape due to the pontine flexure.

questions.question: Bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs) during neurulation are neutralized by which molecules?
questions.explanation: Three main neural inducers present in the notochord and primitive node are noggin, chordin, and follistatin. These molecules are secreted and bind to bone morphogenetic proteins (especially BMP-4), thus neutralizing them. This neutralization is essential for neural induction to occur.

questions.question: The fetal period begins at which week after fertilization?
questions.explanation: The fetal period begins at 9 weeks after fertilization and ends at birth. It is characterized by rapid body growth and differentiation of tissues and organs that were established during the embryonic period. The major events are maturation and growth rather than organogenesis.

The sulcus limitans is a longitudinal groove that separates the alar plate (dorsal, sensory) from the basal plate (ventral, motor) in the developing neural tube. This boundary is clearly visible in the spinal cord and brainstem regions and represents a fundamental functional division of the nervous system.
questions.question: The sulcus limitans separates which two plates in the developing neural tube?
Spermiogenesis involves all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Spermiogenesis is the structural modification of spermatids (which have already completed meiosis) into spermatozoa. It involves cytoplasm shedding, nucleus condensation, formation of neck, middle piece and tail, and acrosome formation. Meiotic division occurs earlier during conversion of spermatocytes to spermatids.

questions.question: The septum transversum contributes to formation of:
questions.explanation: The septum transversum, a thick plate of mesoderm, contributes to formation of both the central tendon of the diaphragm and the fibrous/connective tissue stroma of the liver. The hepatic diverticulum grows into the septum transversum during the 4th week. This mesodermal tissue provides the structural framework for the developing liver.

The buccopharyngeal membrane, an ectodermal-endodermal membrane at the cranial end of the foregut, ruptures during the 4th week. This establishes an open connection between the oral cavity and the primitive gut. Before rupture, the membrane temporarily bounds the foregut anteriorly.
questions.question: The buccopharyngeal membrane ruptures during which week?

questions.explanation: The notochord degenerates and disappears as the bodies of the vertebrae form during development. However, it persists as the nucleus pulposus of each intervertebral disc. The notochord initially defines the primordial axis of the embryo and indicates the future site of vertebral bodies.
questions.question: The notochord ultimately persists as which adult structure?

options: A single lipid membrane with no pores that completely isolates nuclear contents
A double membrane perforated by nuclear pores regulating nucleocytoplasmic exchange
A rigid structure composed entirely of intermediate filaments
A membrane identical in composition to the plasma membrane
A structure that only allows RNA to exit while blocking all proteins from entering
questions.question: Which of the following describes the structure and function of the nuclear envelope?
questions.explanation: The nuclear envelope consists of inner and outer lipid membranes separated by the perinuclear space (continuous with ER lumen). Nuclear pore complexes (~120 nm diameter) perforate both membranes and mediate selective bidirectional traffic: mRNAs and ribosome subunits exit to cytoplasm while transcription factors, histones, and polymerases enter. The outer nuclear membrane is continuous with rough ER.

questions.question: Capillary hemangiomas are benign vascular tumors. On histological examination, they consist of:
questions.explanation: Capillary hemangiomas are composed of closely packed, small caliber vascular channels lined by a single layer of benign endothelial cells. The channels are thin-walled (like capillaries) and are filled with red blood cells. The stroma contains minimal supporting connective tissue. Strawberry hemangiomas in infants are the most common type, involuting spontaneously. Cavernous hemangiomas have larger, dilated blood-filled spaces with thin walls.
options: Closely packed, small, thin-walled blood-filled channels

questions.question: Which cellular deterioration process occurring after tissue removal involves self-digestion by the cell's own enzymes?
questions.explanation: Autolysis is self-digestion resulting from release of lysosomal enzymes within dying cells, which hydrolyze cellular components. It is a key reason why tissues must be fixed immediately after removal. Necrosis is a broader term for cell death, while apoptosis is programmed cell death distinct from autolysis.

questions.question: The enteroendocrine cell type in the small intestine that releases cholecystokinin (CCK) in response to fat and protein is the:
questions.explanation: I cells are enteroendocrine cells of the duodenum and jejunum that release cholecystokinin (CCK) in response to dietary fat and protein. CCK stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion, gallbladder contraction, and relaxation of the sphincter of Oddi. S cells release secretin in response to acid; K cells release GIP (glucose-dependent insulinotropic peptide); G cells release gastrin; L cells release GLP-1 and GLP-2. This is a frequently tested aspect of GIT endocrinology.

Migration results in 6-layered cortical arrangement from molecular to multiform layers. Each layer consists of neurons of specified composition and function. This laminar organization is characteristic of neocortex.
questions.question: How many cortical layers are formed through neuronal migration?
Neural tube formation involves how many major stages?
questions.explanation: Neurulation involves four major stages: transformation of general ectoderm into a thickened neural plate, shaping the plate so it becomes narrower and longer, lateral folding of the neural plate, and fusion of the two most lateral apical surfaces of the neural folds.

questions.question: The three cell types found in bone tissue and their respective primary functions are best described by which of the following?
options: Osteoblasts (synthesize osteoid), osteocytes (maintain matrix), and osteoclasts (resorb bone)
Fibroblasts, macrophages, and adipocytes performing structural roles
Osteoblasts and osteocytes performing identical functions with no resorption cells
questions.explanation: Bone has three distinct cell types with complementary roles: osteoblasts are active matrix-synthesizing cells that produce osteoid (unmineralized matrix); osteocytes are mature osteoblasts entrapped in lacunae that maintain the matrix and act as mechanosensors; and osteoclasts are large multinucleated cells (monocyte-derived) that resorb bone through acid and lysosomal enzyme secretion. The balance between osteoblast and osteoclast activity determines bone mass.

questions.question: Primary optic vesicles develop from which structure?
questions.explanation: Primary optic vesicles develop as outpocketings of primitive forebrain in 4th week. They touch surface ectoderm inducing lens placode formation. The vesicles then invaginate forming optic cups.

The efferent arterioles of juxtamedullary nephrons descend into the medulla as the vasa recta (straight vessels) rather than forming cortical peritubular capillaries. The descending and ascending vasa recta form a hairpin loop parallel to the loop of Henle. This countercurrent exchange in the vasa recta allows solutes to cycle (salt and urea recirculate) without being washed out of the medullary interstitium, maintaining the osmotic gradient essential for urine concentration.
questions.question: The efferent arteriole of juxtamedullary nephrons is different from cortical nephrons in that it gives rise to:

questions.explanation: Turner syndrome results from monosomy X (45,X karyotype), where there is only one X chromosome and no second sex chromosome. Affected individuals are phenotypically female with characteristic features including short stature, ovarian dysgenesis, webbed neck, and cardiovascular abnormalities.
questions.question: Turner syndrome results from which sex chromosome constitution?

questions.explanation: The kidneys "ascend" from the pelvis to the abdomen primarily between weeks 6-9, reaching their final position by the 9th week. This apparent ascent occurs through disproportionate growth of the embryo, particularly in the lumbar and sacral regions. During ascent, the kidneys rotate 90 degrees medially and acquire new blood supply from progressively higher aortic branches.
questions.question: The kidneys ascend from the pelvis primarily between which weeks?
Second-order neurons of the anterolateral tract are located in which laminae?
questions.explanation: Second-order neurons with cell bodies in lamina I and V connect via interneurons in the anterolateral system. Their fibers decussate ventral to the central canal. They form the anterolateral tract.

questions.question: The ascending and descending colons become retroperitoneal through:
questions.explanation: The ascending and descending colons become secondarily retroperitoneal when their mesenteries press against and fuse with the posterior abdominal wall. This fusion obliterates the potential space behind these structures. The transverse and sigmoid colons retain their mesenteries and remain intraperitoneal. This anatomical arrangement has important surgical implications.

questions.question: The placental barrier becomes progressively thinner due to which process?
questions.explanation: Maturation of villi occurs throughout fetal development. The chorionic villi become thinner, providing a minimal barrier to diffusion, while the number of fetal capillaries within them increases. The cytotrophoblast and its core become thinned out so fetal capillaries are separated from maternal blood only by thin layers.

questions.question: The choroid plexus of the fourth ventricle is formed from which structures?
questions.explanation: The ependymal lining of roof plate alongside vascular mesenchyme forms the choroid plexus. This produces cerebrospinal fluid in the fourth ventricle. The choroid plexus hangs into the ventricular cavity.

First-order neurons of auditory pathway are in spiral ganglion close to cochlea. They are bipolar neurons with peripheral processes reaching organ of Corti hair cells. Central processes form cochlear nerve terminating in cochlear nuclei.
questions.question: First-order auditory neurons are located in which structure?

questions.explanation: Asthma causes reversible airway changes including goblet cell hyperplasia (mucus hypersecretion), subepithelial collagen deposition (thickened reticular basement membrane), smooth muscle hypertrophy/hyperplasia (increased bronchoconstriction potential), and eosinophilic/mast cell/T-lymphocyte infiltration. Destruction of alveolar walls (emphysematous change) is NOT part of asthma — it is a feature of emphysema (a separate COPD entity). This distinction is critical for understanding asthma pathophysiology.
questions.question: Asthma is characterized by reversible bronchoconstriction, airway hyperresponsiveness, and inflammation. The histological changes in the asthmatic airway include all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Goblet cell hyperplasia and mucus hypersecretion

questions.explanation: Primordial germ cells appear in the endodermal lining of the yolk sac wall. These cells later migrate to the developing gonads to form oogonia and spermatogonia. The yolk sac also functions in early blood development and contributes endoderm to various organs.
questions.question: Primordial germ cells appear in the endodermal lining of which structure?

questions.explanation: Structures at 0.5 nm are well below the resolving limit of light microscopy (0.2 μm = 200 nm), requiring an electron microscope. The transmission electron microscope achieves resolution of ~0.1 nm, making it suitable for visualizing macromolecules and subcellular structures. Phase contrast and fluorescence microscopes are variants of light microscopy with the same inherent resolution limit.
questions.question: A histologist wishes to visualize structures that are 0.5 nm in size. Which microscope should be used?

questions.explanation: The myenteric (Auerbach) plexus is located between the circular and longitudinal layers of the muscularis externa. It controls the peristaltic movements of the gut wall essential for propulsion of luminal contents. The Meissner plexus, in contrast, primarily regulates secretion and mucosal blood flow.
questions.question: Which autonomic nerve plexus is solely responsible for coordinating local peristaltic contractions of the muscularis externa?
The renal medulla is organized into pyramids separated by renal columns. Renal columns (columns of Bertin) are composed of:
options: Medullary tissue extending toward the cortex
Inward extensions of cortical tissue between
questions.explanation: Renal columns (columns of Bertin) are inward projections of cortical tissue that separate adjacent medullary pyramids. They contain interlobar arteries and veins, as well as cortical nephrons extending into the columns. Prominent renal columns can be mistaken for renal masses on imaging — an important radiological consideration. They represent the normal infolding of cortex between the lobes of the kidney.

The ascending reticular activating system (ARAS) connects reticular formation neurons to the thalamus, hypothalamus, and cortex, mediating consciousness, attention, and the sleep-wake cycle. The ARAS integrates sensory input from multiple modalities and maintains cortical arousal. Damage to the ARAS in the brainstem can cause coma or persistent vegetative state, while functional changes contribute to sleep disorders and alterations in consciousness.
questions.question: The reticular formation's role in consciousness is primarily mediated through which system?

questions.explanation: If splitting of monozygotic twins occurs at the 2-cell stage, they will have separate placentas, separate amniotic cavities, and separate chorionic cavities. If splitting occurs at the early blastocyst stage, they have a common placenta and common chorionic cavity but separate amniotic cavities.
questions.question: Monozygotic twins with separate placentas result from splitting at which stage?
Wharton's jelly is composed of which tissue type?
questions.explanation: Wharton's jelly is a mucous connective tissue (gelatinous connective tissue) that surrounds and protects the umbilical blood vessels within the umbilical cord. It prevents compression and kinking of the vessels. The cord is typically 30-90 cm in length and 1-2 cm in diameter.

questions.question: The liver in the 5th-10th weeks comprises what percentage of total body weight?
questions.explanation: During weeks 5-10, the rapidly growing liver comprises about 10% of total body weight, filling a large part of the abdominal cavity. This disproportionate size contributes to physiological herniation of the midgut. As other organs grow, the liver's relative size decreases. The large fetal liver reflects its hematopoietic function.
The alar plate has similar arrangement to basal plate but with sensory nuclei. Somatic afferent nuclei (CN8, CN5) for ear and head surface. Special visceral afferent (CN9) for tongue taste.
questions.question: The alar plate of myelencephalon contains which nuclei?

questions.explanation: Dense irregular connective tissue has collagen fiber bundles oriented randomly in multiple planes, conferring tensile strength resistant to forces from all directions rather than a single direction. This is optimal for skin dermis, organ capsules, joint capsules, and the tunica albuginea, which must withstand multidirectional mechanical stresses. The irregular arrangement distinguishes it functionally and structurally from the unidirectional dense regular type.
questions.question: Dense irregular connective tissue, found in the dermis of skin and organ capsules, differs from dense regular connective tissue in which of the following ways?
options: Collagen bundles arranged randomly to resist tearing from all directions
It contains only elastic fibers arranged haphazardly
It is composed entirely of reticular fibers
It has a much lower collagen content than loose connective tissue
Its fiber bundles run parallel like those of tendons

questions.question: The omental bursa (lesser sac) forms as a result of:
questions.explanation: The omental bursa (lesser sac) forms as a result of 90-degree rotation of the stomach around its longitudinal axis. This rotation pulls the dorsal mesogastrium to the left, creating a space behind the stomach. The omental bursa communicates with the greater peritoneal cavity through the epiploic foramen.

The cerebellum develops from the rhombic lips, which are dorsolateral parts of the alar plates of the metencephalon. The pontine flexure causes these lips to compress cephalocaudally, forming the cerebellar plate. This plate initially shows a midline vermis and two lateral hemispheres, then develops fissures that divide it into lobes. The flocculonodular lobe is the first to differentiate phylogenetically and ontogenetically.
questions.question: During development, which embryonic structure gives rise to the cerebellum?
The spinal cord consists of how many segments?
questions.explanation: The spinal cord has 31 segments: 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, 1 coccygeal. Each segment gives rise to a pair of spinal nerves. Segments are defined by nerve root emergence.

Piebaldism is an autosomal dominant trait characterized by localized lack of melanin in patches of skin and/or hair, often presenting with a white forelock. Unlike generalized albinism (autosomal recessive), piebaldism shows a predictable inheritance pattern. The condition results from mutations affecting melanocyte development or migration.
questions.question: Piebaldism is inherited as:
The preparation of tissue sections for electron microscopy differs from light microscopy preparation in requiring which of the following?
questions.explanation: Electron microscopy requires ultra-thin sections (50–100 nm) because electrons cannot penetrate thicker tissue. Specimens are fixed with glutaraldehyde and osmium tetroxide, embedded in epoxy resin (not paraffin), cut on an ultramicrotome, and contrast-stained with heavy metals (uranium, lead) that scatter electrons differentially. These differences from light microscopy preparation are fundamental.
options: Ultra-thin sections stained with heavy metal salts
Routine H&E staining and glass slides

questions.explanation: Rathke's pouch is an ectodermal outpocketing from the roof of the primitive oral cavity. It meets the downward extension of the diencephalon (infundibulum). Together they form the anterior and posterior lobes of the pituitary respectively.
questions.question: Rathke's pouch originates from which structure?

questions.explanation: Fibronectin in loose connective tissue ECM and laminin in basement membranes are adhesive multidomain glycoproteins that mediate cell attachment to the extracellular matrix. They have binding sites for both matrix components like collagen and heparan sulfate proteoglycans and for cell surface integrin receptors, acting as molecular bridges linking cells to their surrounding matrix. This adhesion is critical for cell migration, differentiation, and signaling. Fibronectin has RGD sequences recognized by multiple integrin heterodimers.
options: Providing tensile strength like type I collagen
Adhesive glycoproteins mediating cell-ECM attachment via integrin receptors
Catalyzing collagen cross-linking like lysyl oxidase
Inhibiting protease degradation of the ECM
questions.question: Fibronectin and laminin are glycoproteins of the extracellular matrix that primarily serve which function?
Myelin is produced in the peripheral nervous system by which specific cell type?
questions.explanation: In the peripheral nervous system, Schwann cells produce myelin by spirally wrapping their cytoplasm around a single axon segment compacting the membrane into the myelin sheath. In the CNS, oligodendrocytes produce myelin and can myelinate segments of multiple axons simultaneously unlike Schwann cells which myelinate only one axon segment each. This difference has important implications for regeneration after nerve injury.

Cri-du-chat (cat cry) syndrome results from deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5 (5p-). Affected infants have a characteristic high-pitched cry resembling a cat's cry, microcephaly, intellectual disability, and distinctive facial features. The severity depends on the size of the deletion.
questions.question: Cri-du-chat syndrome results from deletion of which chromosome?

questions.explanation: Nissl substance or rough ER is present throughout the cell body and extends into the main dendritic trunks but is notably absent from the axon hillock and throughout the entire axon. This distribution reflects the specialized function of the axon as an electrical conductor rather than a protein synthesis compartment. Proteins synthesized in the cell body are transported to axon terminals via axonal transport mechanisms.
options: Axon hillock and entire axonal arborization
questions.question: Nissl substance is absent from which two regions of the neuron?
The medial geniculate body primarily relays which sensory modality?
questions.explanation: The medial geniculate body receives auditory information from the inferior colliculus via the lateral lemniscus and projects to the primary auditory cortex (areas 41, 42) in the superior temporal gyrus. This thalamic nucleus is part of the posterior nuclear group and maintains tonotopic organization, preserving frequency representation from the cochlea to the auditory cortex. Bilateral representation ensures that unilateral thalamic lesions rarely cause complete deafness.

The decidua capsularis overlies the developing fetus and separates the fetus from the uterine lumen, forming a capsule around the fetus. As the embryo grows, the decidua capsularis expands to meet the decidua parietalis, eventually fusing together and obliterating the uterine cavity.
questions.question: The decidua capsularis initially covers which structure?

questions.explanation: Brodmann area 4 corresponds to the primary motor cortex in the precentral gyrus, characterized by the presence of giant pyramidal (Betz) cells in layer V. This area controls voluntary movements of contralateral body parts with somatotopic organization (motor homunculus). Electrical stimulation of area 4 produces discrete movements of specific body parts, while lesions cause contralateral weakness or paralysis, particularly affecting distal limb and facial muscles.
questions.question: Brodmann area 4 corresponds to which functional cortical area?

questions.explanation: At the end of the fourth week, a sickle-shaped crest (septum primum) grows from the roof of the common atrium into the lumen. The two limbs of this septum extend toward the endocardial cushions in the atrioventricular canal. The opening between the septum primum and endocardial cushions is called the ostium primum.
questions.question: The septum primum grows from the roof of the common atrium toward which structure?
The body of the corpus callosum connects which cortical areas?
questions.explanation: The body (trunk) of the corpus callosum connects the premotor, supplementary motor areas, and primary motor cortices bilaterally, as well as parietal association areas. These connections coordinate bilateral motor activities and transfer somatosensory information between hemispheres. The body represents the largest and longest portion of the corpus callosum, containing approximately 200-250 million fibers in humans. It is topographically organized with more anterior regions connecting frontal areas and more posterior regions connecting parietal areas.

The external capsule is a thin layer of white matter separating the claustrum laterally from the putamen (lateral portion of lentiform nucleus) medially.
