It contains association fibers and some projection fibers connecting cortical regions. The external capsule lies between the more lateral extreme capsule and the more medial internal capsule. These white matter layers interdigitate with gray matter structures (insula, claustrum, lentiform nucleus) forming the complex architecture of the basal forebrain region.
questions.question: The external capsule separates which structures?

questions.explanation: The cortical labyrinth is the region of the renal cortex between the medullary rays. It contains: renal corpuscles (glomeruli with Bowman's capsule), proximal convoluted tubules (PCT), and distal convoluted tubules (DCT). Medullary rays, in contrast, contain the straight segments of tubules (pars recta of PCT and DCT) and the cortical collecting ducts running in parallel toward the medulla. This architectural division is essential for interpreting renal biopsy findings.
questions.question: The renal cortex can be divided into the cortical labyrinth and medullary rays. The cortical labyrinth specifically contains:
options: Loops of Henle and collecting ducts

questions.explanation: Zone 1 (periportal zone) of the hepatic acinus is located adjacent to the portal tract (the short axis of the acinus) and therefore receives blood first as it enters the sinusoids. This zone has the highest oxygen tension and nutrient concentration, making it most metabolically active for oxidative metabolism and gluconeogenesis. Zone 1 is also most susceptible to toxic injury from substances absorbed via the portal circulation.
questions.question: Which zone of the hepatic acinus receives the most oxygenated blood and the highest concentration of nutrients?

questions.explanation: The fundus and body of the stomach are histologically identical, both containing branched tubular gastric glands with parietal cells, chief cells, mucous neck cells, and enteroendocrine cells. The cardia and pylorus are histologically similar to each other, containing predominantly mucus-secreting glands. This regional identity is consistently tested in histology examinations.
questions.question: The stomach is divided into four regions. Which pair of regions is histologically IDENTICAL?

questions.explanation: Meckel's diverticulum is typically located approximately two feet (60 cm) from the ileocecal valve on the antimesenteric border of the ileum. It follows the "rule of 2s": 2% prevalence, 2 feet from ileocecal valve, 2 inches long, and may contain 2 types of ectopic tissue (gastric mucosa and pancreatic acini).
questions.question: The most common site for Meckel's diverticulum is:
The inferior mesenteric artery supplies derivatives of which embryonic gut?
questions.explanation: The inferior mesenteric artery (IMA) supplies derivatives of the hindgut, including the left 1/3 to 1/2 of the transverse colon, descending colon, sigmoid colon, rectum, and superior part of the anal canal. The foregut is supplied by the celiac artery, and the midgut by the superior mesenteric artery.

questions.question: Vestibular fibers reach the cerebellum via which peduncle?
questions.explanation: Some vestibular fibers project to cerebellum via inferior cerebellar peduncle to the flocculonodular lobe. This is important for balance and coordination. The cerebellum integrates vestibular information.

The globus pallidus internal segment (GPi) projects primarily to the ventral anterior (VA) and ventral lateral (VL) nuclei of the thalamus, which then project to motor and premotor cortex. This represents the main output pathway of the basal ganglia motor loop. GPi neurons are GABAergic and tonically active, continuously inhibiting thalamic neurons; movement occurs when this inhibition is reduced by the direct pathway or increased by the indirect pathway. Pallidotomy (surgical GPi lesioning) was performed for Parkinson's disease before deep brain stimulation became available.
questions.question: Which structure is the primary output target of GPi?
The basal vein of Rosenthal primarily drains which structures?
questions.explanation: The basal vein of Rosenthal drains deep structures including the insula, basal ganglia, and medial temporal lobe. It courses around the cerebral peduncle and joins the great vein of Galen along with the internal cerebral veins. This vein receives tributaries from the anterior perforated substance, insular region, and inferior horn of the lateral ventricle. Occlusion can cause hemorrhagic infarction of the temporal lobe and basal ganglia, often with severe neurological deficits.
options: Deep structures and medial temporal lobe

questions.explanation: The portal lobule is defined by bile flow rather than blood flow. It is organized as a triangle with the portal tract at its center, and central veins at the three corners. Bile produced by hepatocytes flows from the periphery (near central veins) toward the central portal tract, the opposite direction of blood flow. This model emphasizes the exocrine secretory function of hepatocytes.
questions.question: In the portal lobule model of liver organization, what structure is at the center of the lobule?
The organ of Corti converts sound waves into which signals?
questions.explanation: The organ of Corti converts sound waves into nerve impulses by depolarization of hair cell membranes. These impulses are picked and propagated by the cochlear nerve. The cochlea is tonotopically organized.

Monosomy X (Turner syndrome, 45,X) is the only viable human monosomy. All autosomal monosomies are lethal and result in early miscarriage. Even monosomy X has a high rate of spontaneous abortion; about 99% of 45,X conceptuses are lost during pregnancy.
questions.question: The only viable human monosomy is which condition?

questions.explanation: Dorsal root ganglia contain large pseudounipolar sensory neurons whose single T-shaped process divides into a peripheral branch to sensory receptors and a central branch entering the spinal cord. Each neuron is surrounded by satellite cells which are glial cells that regulate the local ionic environment around the neuron cell body. The entire ganglion is enclosed in dense connective tissue continuous with the epineurium of the nerve.
questions.question: A section through the dorsal root ganglion would show which cell types?
options: Multipolar motor neurons with ventral horn characteristics
Large pseudounipolar neurons with satellite glia in a connective tissue capsule
Bipolar neurons identical to retinal bipolar cells
Interneurons connecting ascending sensory and descending motor pathways
Oligodendrocytes that exclusively produce myelin in the CNS

questions.question: The mesenchyme for head and neck formation is derived from all EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The mesenchyme for formation of the head and neck region is derived from paraxial mesoderm, lateral plate mesoderm, neural crest cells, and ectodermal placodes. Endoderm contributes to epithelial linings of pharyngeal pouches but not to mesenchymal structures. Each of these sources contributes specific tissues.

questions.question: Which of the following statements correctly describes the histological difference between arteries and veins of similar caliber?
questions.explanation: Arteries have a thicker tunica media relative to lumen diameter containing more smooth muscle and elastic fibers to withstand high arterial blood pressure. The internal elastic lamina is prominent in arteries. Veins have a thinner media, larger lumen relative to wall thickness, prominent tunica adventitia, and many have valves to prevent backflow. The ratio of lumen diameter to wall thickness is much higher in veins reflecting lower venous pressure.
options: Thicker tunica media and smaller lumen-to-wall ratio compared to veins
Veins have a thicker media and smaller lumen than arteries
Arteries and veins are histologically identical
Veins have more elastic laminae than arteries
Arteries lack a tunica adventitia while veins have a prominent one

questions.question: The pronephros completely disappears by the end of:
questions.explanation: The pronephros completely disappears by the end of the 4th week, leaving no functional structures. It represents the first of three kidney systems to develop and appears in the cervical region. The pronephric duct, however, persists and is used by the mesonephros, eventually becoming the mesonephric (Wolffian) duct.

questions.question: Which reticular area is most essential for maintaining equilibrium?
questions.explanation: The paramedian pontine reticular formation (PPRF) is most essential for maintaining equilibrium and controlling horizontal eye movements. It integrates vestibular, visual, and proprioceptive information to coordinate eye and head movements during balance maintenance. The PPRF also contains premotor neurons for horizontal gaze and works closely with the vestibular nuclei. Lesions cause gaze palsies and difficulty maintaining stable gaze during head movements.

options: Rickets due to vitamin D deficiency
Osteoporosis from reduced bone mineral density
Osteosarcoma arising from osteoblast precursor cells
Arrested longitudinal growth causing short stature before full height
Osteomalacia from impaired bone matrix mineralization
questions.explanation: The epiphyseal growth plate is responsible for longitudinal bone growth through endochondral ossification. Premature closure, whether from trauma, infection, or corticosteroids, arrests longitudinal growth of that bone. If bilateral, this leads to short stature proportional to the extent and timing of premature closure. Conversely, delayed closure as in growth hormone excess before puberty leads to gigantism.
questions.question: Which condition would most directly result from premature closure of the epiphyseal growth plate?

questions.explanation: The inferior salivatory nucleus provides parasympathetic innervation exclusively to the parotid gland via the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX). Preganglionic fibers travel in the tympanic nerve (Jacobson's nerve), then as the lesser petrosal nerve, synapsing in the otic ganglion. Postganglionic fibers join the auriculotemporal nerve to reach the parotid gland. Parasympathetic stimulation increases parotid secretion, producing watery saliva rich in enzymes.
questions.question: The inferior salivatory nucleus provides parasympathetic innervation to which gland?
In nephrotic syndrome caused by minimal change disease, which specific structural change is visible ONLY on electron microscopy?
questions.explanation: Minimal change disease (lipoid nephrosis) shows no abnormalities on light microscopy (hence 'minimal change') and no immune deposits on immunofluorescence. The ONLY abnormality is diffuse effacement (fusion) of podocyte foot processes on electron microscopy. This loss of the slit diaphragm causes massive proteinuria. Minimal change disease is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children and responds dramatically to corticosteroids, with foot process effacement reversing on treatment.

questions.question: Which nucleus in the limbic system directly regulates endocrine and autonomic functions?
questions.explanation: While the amygdala regulates aspects of emotional behavior and influences autonomic and endocrine function through connections with the hypothalamus, it is actually the hypothalamus (part of the diencephalon involved in limbic function) that directly regulates endocrine and autonomic functions. The amygdala sends efferents to hypothalamic nuclei that control heart rate, respiration, blood pressure, feeding, and sexual behavior, serving as a link between emotional processing and physiological responses.

The LES is a physiological (not anatomical) sphincter formed by a zone of increased circular smooth muscle tone in the distal 3–4 cm of the esophagus. Histologically, this segment shows greater smooth muscle density and specialized myogenic/neurogenic tone. Both intrinsic myogenic properties and extrinsic factors (angle of His, diaphragmatic compression) contribute. Failure of LES relaxation causes achalasia; inadequate tone causes GERD.
questions.question: The lower esophageal sphincter (LES) is a physiological sphincter. Histologically, the increased smooth muscle tone of the LES is maintained by:
options: A distinct anatomical ring of skeletal muscle
A cartilaginous ring supporting the sphincter
A fold of mucosa acting as a one-way valve
Increased density of smooth muscle cells
External compression by the right crus of the diaphragm only

questions.explanation: The urorectal septum divides the cloaca into the ventral urogenital sinus and the dorsal rectum/cranial anal canal. This septum grows from mesoderm at the junction between the connecting stalk and yolk sac. By the 7th week, it fuses with the cloacal membrane, dividing it into anal and urogenital membranes.
questions.question: The urorectal septum divides the cloaca into:

questions.explanation: The corticomedullary junction represents the meeting point between the adrenal cortex derived from mesodermal coelomic epithelium and the adrenal medulla derived from neural crest cells that migrated and became encapsulated by the cortex. Histologically the boundary shows the transition from cortical zona reticularis cells to larger medullary chromaffin cells with their prominent eosinophilic granules. This dual developmental origin explains why cortical and medullary function is regulated by entirely different signaling systems.
options: The site of aldosterone synthesis switching to cortisol production
A watershed zone with the lowest blood supply
The location of the adrenal capsule blood vessels
A region containing only adipocytes with no endocrine cells
Boundary between mesodermal cortex and neural crest-derived chromaffin medulla
questions.question: The corticomedullary junction of the adrenal gland is significant histologically because it represents which of the following?

questions.explanation: Sphincter and dilator pupillae muscles are unique smooth muscles formed from neuroectoderm of optic cup. Ciliary muscles form from lateral plate mesoderm. This dual origin reflects the complex iris development.
questions.question: Sphincter and dilator pupillae muscles develop from which tissue?

questions.explanation: Mitochondria contain their own circular DNA (mtDNA), 70S ribosomes, and double membrane — features consistent with endosymbiotic origin from an ancient alpha-proteobacterium engulfed by a proto-eukaryotic cell. Mitochondrial ribosomes are sensitive to the same antibiotics that inhibit bacterial ribosomes. mtDNA is inherited maternally in most species and is used for phylogenetic and forensic analysis.
questions.question: Which cellular organelle is correctly described as having its own DNA and ribosomes, and is thought to have originated from endosymbiosis with an ancient bacterium?

options: They remain constant throughout the conducting airways
They are replaced by type II pneumocytes
questions.question: Goblet cells in the respiratory epithelium produce mucus. As airways become smaller (bronchioles), what happens to goblet cell numbers?
questions.explanation: Goblet cells are abundant in the trachea and large bronchi but decrease progressively as airways branch and narrow. In bronchioles, goblet cells are largely replaced by club cells (Clara cells) as the predominant secretory cell type. Terminal bronchioles have no goblet cells and no mucous glands. This is why inhaled particles reaching bronchioles are cleared by club cell secretions and alveolar macrophages rather than the mucociliary escalator.

questions.question: The epithelial lining of the oral cavity and esophagus differs from the rest of the GIT in that it is specifically:
questions.explanation: The oral cavity, esophagus, and anal canal are lined by stratified squamous epithelium due to the mechanical stress encountered at these sites. The rest of the GIT is lined by simple columnar epithelium specialized for secretion and absorption. This distinction is critical for histological identification of these regions.

The lower intercostal nerves supply sensory fibers to the peripheral region of the diaphragm, which is derived from the body wall. This peripheral portion brings its own nerve supply with it during development. The phrenic nerve supplies sensory fibers to all other parts of the diaphragm and motor supply to all diaphragmatic muscles.
questions.question: Which nerve supplies sensory fibers to the peripheral region of the diaphragm?

questions.explanation: During the pseudoglandular period (5-16 weeks), branching continues to form terminal bronchioles, but respiratory bronchioles and alveoli are not yet present. The lung resembles a gland histologically during this period. Respiration is not possible if a fetus is born during this stage.
questions.question: During the pseudoglandular period (5-16 weeks), which structures are absent?
How many sets of motor nuclei are in the myelencephalon basal plate?
questions.explanation: Three sets of motor nuclei are identified in the basal plate: somatic efferent, special visceral efferent, and general visceral efferent. These form continuous motor columns. They innervate different target structures.

questions.question: The neural plate begins to invaginate to form the neural groove on approximately which day?
questions.explanation: About day 18, the neural plate begins to invaginate to form the neural groove. The neural plate itself forms around day 15 as a slipper-shaped thickening of the surface ectoderm. This invagination is induced by interkinetic migration of neuroectodermal cells and formation of somites.

questions.question: The stylopharyngeus muscle is derived from which pharyngeal arch?
questions.explanation: The stylopharyngeus muscle is the only muscle derived from the third pharyngeal arch. The skeletal elements of this arch include the greater horn of the hyoid bone and the inferior part of the body of the hyoid bone. The nerve of the third arch is the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX).

The lesser omentum is derived from the ventral mesogastrium, not the dorsal mesogastrium. The dorsal mesogastrium gives rise to the greater omentum, gastrosplenic ligament, and lienorenal ligament. The ventral mesogastrium also forms the visceral peritoneum of the liver and falciform ligament.
questions.question: The dorsal mesogastrium gives rise to all EXCEPT:
Unilateral renal agenesis affects which kidney more commonly?
questions.explanation: Unilateral renal agenesis more commonly affects the left kidney and occurs in approximately 1 in 1000 neonates. Males are more frequently affected than females. The condition usually causes no symptoms because the contralateral kidney undergoes compensatory hypertrophy and performs the function of both kidneys.

options: Sensorineural hearing loss from hair cell damage
Central hearing loss from brainstem damage
Mixed hearing loss with retrocochlear component
Fixed stapes preventing vibration transmission: conductive hearing loss
questions.explanation: Otosclerosis involves abnormal bony remodeling that fixes the stapes footplate in the oval window preventing its normal piston-like movement. Since the stapes footplate normally transmits vibrations from the ossicular chain into the cochlear perilymph, its fixation blocks sound transmission to the inner ear causing conductive hearing loss. The inner ear hair cells are unaffected so sensorineural function is intact. Stapedectomy with prosthesis replacement restores hearing in most cases.
questions.question: The middle ear ossicle pathology in otosclerosis where abnormal bone formation fixates the stapes footplate causes which hearing deficit?

questions.explanation: The pontine flexure is dorsal (opens dorsally) unlike cephalic and cervical flexures which are ventral. It is responsible for the diamond shape of the 4th ventricle. It provides the template for cerebellar development.
questions.question: The pontine flexure is characterized as which type?

options: To allow free passage of all water-soluble molecules
To provide binding sites for all hormones
To form a selectively permeable barrier controlling molecular entry and exit
To anchor cells permanently to the extracellular matrix
To generate electrical potential differences across the membrane
questions.question: The cell membrane consists of a phospholipid bilayer in which the hydrophilic heads face outward and hydrophobic tails face inward. This arrangement primarily serves which of the following functions?
questions.explanation: The phospholipid bilayer arrangement with polar (hydrophilic) heads facing the aqueous environments (cytoplasm and extracellular fluid) and nonpolar (hydrophobic) tails forming the interior creates a selectively permeable barrier. This barrier controls which molecules can enter or exit the cell based on size, charge, and lipid solubility. Specialized transport proteins embedded in the bilayer mediate the passage of ions and polar molecules.

questions.question: Glial cells are produced after the production of which cells?
questions.explanation: Glial cells are produced by the neuroepithelial cells following the production of neurons. They differentiate into astrocytes in the mantle layer and oligodendrocytes in the marginal layer. This temporal sequence ensures proper nervous system organization.

questions.question: Which organ system does NOT primarily develop through epithelial-mesenchymal interactions?
questions.explanation: Most inductive processes during embryonic development involve epithelial-mesenchymal interactions, including development of kidneys, gastrointestinal derivatives, respiratory system, and skin appendages. Skeletal muscles develop primarily from somitic mesoderm through intrinsic differentiation programs rather than epithelial-mesenchymal induction.

The pars orbitalis (orbital part) is the most anterior portion of the inferior frontal gyrus, located anterior to the anterior horizontal ramus of the lateral sulcus and above the orbital surface of the frontal lobe. While the pars opercularis and triangularis comprise Broca's area, the pars orbitalis is more involved in cognitive and emotional processing as part of the orbitofrontal cortex. This region participates in decision-making, impulse control, and processing reward-related information.
questions.question: The pars orbitalis is the most anterior part of which gyrus?
The accessory nerve has which two roots?
questions.explanation: The accessory nerve (XI) has cranial (from medulla) and spinal (from C1-C5) roots both with SVE fibers. Spinal root supplies trapezius and sternocleidomastoid. Cranial root joins vagus.

questions.question: The glycocalyx, which surrounds the cell membrane, is composed primarily of which of the following?
questions.explanation: The glycocalyx is a fuzzy extracellular coat composed of carbohydrate chains covalently attached to membrane proteins (glycoproteins) and lipids (glycolipids). It plays roles in cell recognition, adhesion, and protection from mechanical damage. Its presence is detectable in electron micrographs as an electron-dense coating on the outer surface of the plasma membrane.

questions.question: Which objective lens is designated as the 'oil immersion' lens in a compound microscope and at what magnification?
questions.explanation: The 100× objective lens is the oil immersion lens, requiring immersion oil between the lens and coverslip to prevent light refraction. It provides the highest magnification and best resolving power of the objective lenses in the standard set (4×, 10×, 40×, 100×). Without oil, light bends at the air-glass interface, drastically reducing resolution and brightness.
options: 4× lens used for scanning wide fields
100× lens used with immersion oil for highest magnification
40× lens used for most detailed cellular work
60× lens standard in all compound microscopes

questions.explanation: Arrector pili muscles differentiate from mesenchyme surrounding the hair follicle and attach to the dermal root sheath and papillary dermis. Their contraction causes depression of skin at their attachment and elevation around hair shafts (goosebumps). These muscles are poorly developed in axillary hairs and absent in eyebrow and eyelash hairs.
questions.question: The arrector pili muscles are derived from:

options: Safe house for beneficial gut bacteria
Primary site of bile acid recycling
questions.explanation: One proposed functional role of the appendix is as a 'safe house' or reservoir for beneficial commensal bacteria. The lymphoid-rich, biofilm-protected lumen of the appendix may harbor bacteria that can reseed the colon following diarrheal illnesses that clear the normal gut microbiome. While controversial, this hypothesis explains the appendix's unusual anatomy. The appendix is also thought to play a role in immune education in early childhood.
questions.question: The appendix is a vestigial structure often considered functionless, yet it contains abundant lymphoid tissue. Current understanding suggests the appendix may function as a:
Double ureter with complete duplication results from:
questions.explanation: Complete double ureter results from development of two separate ureteric buds from the mesonephric duct, each inducing separate collecting systems. The ureters may remain separate to the bladder or join before entering. According to the Weigert-Meyer rule, the ureter from the upper pole inserts more medially and inferiorly in the bladder and may be ectopic or obstructed.

questions.question: The periderm (epitrichium) is typically replaced completely by which gestational week?
questions.explanation: The periderm, which is the outermost layer of early fetal skin, is completely replaced by the 21st week of gestation. Peridermal cells continually undergo keratinization and desquamation, being replaced by cells from the basal layer. Exfoliated peridermal cells contribute to the formation of vernix caseosa.

questions.question: Plicae circulares are permanent circular folds of the small intestine. They differ fundamentally from gastric rugae in that:
questions.explanation: Plicae circulares (valves of Kerckring) are permanent folds that cannot be flattened even when the intestine is fully distended, unlike gastric rugae which flatten as the stomach fills. Structurally, plicae contain a core of submucosa covered by mucosa. They are best developed in the jejunum and serve to increase surface area for absorption.
options: Plicae contain mucosa only while rugae contain all four layers
Plicae are found only in the ileum while rugae are throughout the stomach
Plicae cannot be flattened while rugae flatten when distended
Plicae are temporary folds while rugae are permanent
Plicae are formed by muscularis externa while rugae are formed by mucosa
Conduct signals toward the cell body from neurons or receptors
Carry impulses away from the cell body to effectors
Produce action potentials at the axon hillock
Synthesize neurotransmitters for synaptic vesicle release
questions.question: Dendrites are classified as afferent processes because they perform which function?
questions.explanation: Dendrites are the receptive input surfaces of neurons classified as afferent because they transmit incoming electrochemical signals toward the cell body. They have elaborate branching that increases receptor surface area. The postsynaptic receptors on dendritic spines receive neurotransmitters from presynaptic axon terminals generating graded potentials that summate at the axon hillock to generate or inhibit action potentials.

questions.question: At what gestational week does the lens vesicle separate from the surface ectoderm?
questions.explanation: By the 5th week of development, the lens vesicle has completely separated from the surface ectoderm and lies free within the rim of the optic cup. This separation allows the lens vesicle to develop independently while maintaining its position. The lens vesicle then undergoes further differentiation to form the definitive lens structure.

The cranial neuropore closes on the 25th intrauterine day in conjunction with the cervical closure site. The caudal neuropore closes 2 days later on day 27. Failure of neuropore closure results in neural tube defects.
questions.question: On which intrauterine day does the cranial neuropore close?

options: Secondary response is slower and weaker than primary response
Primary and secondary responses are identical in magnitude and timing
Secondary response produces only IgM while primary produces IgG
Secondary response requires a different antigen than primary response
Faster, more robust response with higher-affinity switched antibodies due to memory cells
questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes the sequence of events in secondary immune response compared to primary immune response?
questions.explanation: The secondary immune response is faster with antibody production beginning within 1 to 3 days versus 5 to 10 days; achieves higher antibody titers by 10 to 100 fold; produces predominantly class-switched high-affinity antibodies IgG IgA or IgE rather than the IgM of the primary response; and is sustained for longer. This enhanced secondary response results from clonal expansion of memory B and T cells generated during the germinal center reaction of the primary response. This is the immunological basis for vaccination and immunological memory.

The combination of eccentric nucleus with clock-face chromatin arrangement and strongly basophilic cytoplasm (due to abundant rough ER for antibody synthesis) is pathognomonic for plasma cells. These cells are terminally differentiated B lymphocytes specialized for immunoglobulin production. The well-developed Golgi body adjacent to the nucleus creates the paranuclear pale zone called the 'Hof.'
questions.question: A histology student observes a tissue section where cells show large basophilic cytoplasm with eccentric nuclei having a clock-face chromatin pattern. These cells are most likely which of the following?

questions.explanation: The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) is the nerve of the third pharyngeal arch. It provides both motor and sensory innervation to structures derived from this arch, including the stylopharyngeus muscle and portions of the tongue (posterior one-third).
questions.question: The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) supplies which pharyngeal arch?
Kidneys attain their adult position by which week?
questions.explanation: The kidneys attain their adult position in the abdomen by the 9th week of development. This "ascent" occurs through disproportionate growth of the lumbar and sacral regions. During ascent, the kidneys rotate medially approximately 90 degrees, bringing their hila to face anteromedially. Blood supply changes from iliac to aortic branches.

questions.question: Which sinus is located at the attachment of the falx cerebelli?
questions.explanation: The occipital sinus is located at the posterior attachment of the falx cerebelli in the midline, extending from the internal occipital protuberance to the posterior margin of foramen magnum. It is the smallest of the major dural sinuses and drains into the confluence of sinuses above or the marginal sinus around the foramen magnum. The occipital sinus lies between the two layers of the falx cerebelli and receives small veins from the cerebellar hemispheres.

options: Two ureteric buds on same side
questions.question: Supernumerary kidney results from:
questions.explanation: Supernumerary kidney results from development of two separate ureteric buds on the same side, each inducing separate metanephric tissue. This is extremely rare and differs from duplicated collecting system (bifid ureter), where a single ureteric bud branches early. Each supernumerary kidney has its own blood supply, ureter, and collecting system.

Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) typically presents in the third or fourth decade of life with hypertension, hematuria, flank pain, or renal insufficiency. It is caused by mutations in PKD1 or PKD2 genes. This contrasts with autosomal recessive PKD, which presents in infancy. ADPKD is one of the most common hereditary diseases.
questions.question: Congenital polycystic kidney disease (autosomal dominant) typically presents in:
Weibel-Palade bodies are found exclusively in endothelial cells. These organelles are used as a definitive immunohistochemical marker of endothelial cell origin using antibodies against:
questions.explanation: Von Willebrand factor (vWF, also known as Factor VIII-related antigen) stored in Weibel-Palade bodies is the most specific immunohistochemical marker of endothelial cell origin. It is routinely used in surgical pathology to confirm vascular tumors (hemangiomas, angiosarcomas) and to identify endothelial cells in tissue sections. CD31 (PECAM-1) is another highly sensitive endothelial marker. CD68 marks macrophages; smooth muscle actin marks smooth muscle cells.

The superior cerebellar artery forms just before basilar bifurcation, supplies upper pons, superior cerebellar surface and caudal midbrain. It runs below the tentorium cerebelli. Occlusion causes cerebellar and sensory deficits.
questions.question: The superior cerebellar artery supplies which structures?
options: Superior cerebellum, upper pons, caudal midbrain

questions.question: Fusion of neural groove edges begins in which region?
questions.explanation: Fusion of the neural groove edges begins in the cervical region and proceeds in cephalocaudal directions. A more cranial site of closure occurs in the forebrain region. This dual closure mechanism ensures complete neural tube formation by day 27.

questions.question: The nasal conchae (turbinates) increase nasal airway resistance and serve which functions as air passes over them?
questions.explanation: The nasal conchae create turbulent airflow that brings inspired air into close contact with the moist, warm, mucosa-covered surfaces. This allows the nasal cavity to filter (via mucus and cilia), humidify (to near 100% relative humidity), and warm inspired air to near body temperature before it reaches the lungs. The rich submucosal vasculature (cavernous plexus) of the inferior turbinate regulates blood flow for temperature control — alternating congestion (nasal cycle).

questions.question: Which ventricle contains the largest volume of CSF?
questions.explanation: The lateral ventricles contain the largest volume of CSF among the ventricles, comprising most of the approximately 30 mL found in the ventricular system. The lateral ventricles are the largest cavities due to their extensive C-shaped configuration following the cerebral hemisphere contours. The third and fourth ventricles are smaller, slit-like cavities, while the cerebral aqueduct is a narrow channel. The subarachnoid space contains approximately 120 mL, much more than the ventricular system.
Failure of anterior neuropore closure (day 25) causes anencephaly. This results in absence of brain and cranial vault. It is incompatible with life. Posterior neuropore failure causes spina bifida.
questions.question: Closure of the cranial neuropore occurs on day 25. Failure causes which anomaly?

options: Total paralysis and sensory loss below lesion
questions.explanation: Complete cord transection causes total paralysis and sensory loss below lesion level. Initially there is spinal shock. Later upper motor neuron signs develop. Autonomic dysfunction occurs.
questions.question: Complete spinal cord transection causes which clinical picture?
Which type of cortical neuron is characterized by extensive dendritic trees in a single plane?
questions.explanation: Pyramidal cells, the principal neurons of the cerebral cortex, are characterized by pyramid-shaped cell bodies and extensive dendritic trees that spread in a cone shape, primarily in planes perpendicular to the cortical surface. Their apical dendrites extend toward the cortical surface, while basal dendrites spread laterally. Pyramidal cells have long axons projecting to other cortical areas, subcortical structures, or spinal cord, making them the main output neurons of the cortex.
Lumbar puncture accesses the subarachnoid space containing CSF. It is performed below L2 where only nerve roots are present. It samples CSF for diagnosis. It can measure CSF pressure.
questions.question: Lumbar puncture accesses which space?
The basal ganglia modulate which aspects of movement?
questions.explanation: The basal ganglia offer supraspinal control over skeletal muscle movement, modulating rate, range and coordination. They do not initiate movement but refine it. Lesions cause movement disorders.

questions.question: The secondary oocyte is released at ovulation and arrested at which stage of meiosis?
questions.explanation: At ovulation, the secondary oocyte is arrested at metaphase II of meiosis. The first meiotic division is completed just before ovulation, expelling the first polar body. Meiosis II is only completed if fertilization occurs, when the sperm's penetration provides the activating signal. The second polar body is then expelled. If not fertilized, the secondary oocyte degenerates without completing meiosis. This arrest mechanism prevents parthenogenetic activation.

questions.question: The cell membrane acts as a semipermeable barrier; which of the following molecules can most freely cross it by simple diffusion WITHOUT requiring a transport protein?
questions.explanation: Small, nonpolar molecules like O2 and CO2 cross the phospholipid bilayer by simple diffusion because they are lipid-soluble and have no charge. Large molecules (DNA, proteins), charged ions (Na+, K+), and polar molecules (glucose, ATP) cannot cross the hydrophobic core of the bilayer without protein-mediated transport. This selective permeability is central to cellular homeostasis.

General sensory innervation to the anterior 2/3 of the tongue is provided by the lingual nerve, a branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V3). Special taste sensation from this area is provided by the chorda tympani branch of the facial nerve (CN VII).
questions.question: General sensation from the anterior 2/3 of the tongue is provided by:
The pia mater forms specialized structures within the ventricles. What are these vascular structures called?
questions.explanation: The pia mater invaginates into the ventricles forming the tela choroidea and choroid plexus, which are responsible for cerebrospinal fluid production. These highly vascular structures consist of blood vessels held together by fine areolar tissue covered by ependymal cells. The cranial pia closely invests the brain surface, dipping into sulci and cerebellar laminae, while maintaining its delicate vascular nature.

questions.question: The neck is formed by elongation of the region between which two structures?
questions.explanation: The neck is formed by elongation of the region between the stomodeum and pericardium. This elongation is caused by descent of the developing heart and appearance of the pharyngeal (branchial) arches in the 4th and 5th weeks of development. The developing brain is separated from the future thorax by the stomodeum.

options: Bile ductules → Canals of Hering → common bile duct → duodenum
Interlobular ducts → Canals of Hering → bile ductules → common hepatic duct
Bile canaliculi → sinusoids → central vein → hepatic vein
Canals of Hering → bile ductules → interlobular bile ducts → intrahepatic ducts →
Bile canaliculi → space of Disse → portal vein → duodenum
questions.question: Bile canaliculi are spaces between adjacent hepatocyte plasma membranes. Bile flows from canaliculi in which sequential pathway toward the duodenum?
questions.explanation: Bile flows from bile canaliculi (between hepatocytes) to Canals of Hering (transitional channels at the periphery of lobules), then to bile ductules, interlobular bile ducts, intrahepatic ducts, right and left hepatic ducts, common hepatic duct, and finally joins the cystic duct to form the common bile duct which empties into the duodenum at the ampulla of Vater.

Facilitated diffusion moves substances down their concentration gradient through specific membrane protein channels or carriers, requiring no energy expenditure (ATP). GLUT transporters move glucose down its gradient from high extracellular to lower intracellular concentrations. By contrast, primary active transport (e.g., Na+/K+ ATPase) uses ATP to move substances against concentration gradients.
questions.question: In the context of membrane transport, the movement of glucose into a cell via a glucose transporter (GLUT) without requiring direct ATP expenditure but utilizing a concentration gradient is classified as which of the following?
Which layer of the esophageal wall contains a rich venous plexus clinically significant in portal hypertension?
questions.explanation: The submucosal venous plexus of the lower esophagus forms portosystemic anastomoses between the portal venous system and systemic venous circulation. In portal hypertension, blood is diverted through these vessels causing esophageal varices — dilated submucosal veins. Rupture of esophageal varices can cause life-threatening hemorrhage.

questions.question: The classic hepatic lobule is described as hexagonal. Which structure is located at the CENTER of this lobule?
questions.explanation: The classic hepatic lobule is centered on the central vein (terminal hepatic venule). Portal tracts — containing branches of the hepatic artery, portal vein, and bile duct — are located at the periphery (corners of the hexagon). Blood flows from the portal tracts centripetally through sinusoids toward the central vein, while bile flows in the opposite direction toward the bile ducts in the portal tracts.

questions.question: The white pulp of the spleen consists primarily of which of the following?
options: Red blood cells and erythroid precursors
Periarterial T cell sheaths and B cell-containing follicles
questions.explanation: Splenic white pulp consists of lymphoid tissue arranged around central arteries: the periarteriolar lymphoid sheath is a cuff of T lymphocytes directly surrounding the central arteriole, and lymphoid follicles which are B cell-rich zones that enlarge to form germinal centers during immune responses are adjacent to the PALS. This arrangement positions immune cells optimally for contact with blood-borne antigens carried in the central arteriole.

Cerebrospinal fluid is produced at approximately 0.4 mL/min, totaling about 600 mL per day. With a total CSF volume of about 150 mL, this results in complete CSF turnover 3-4 times daily. This constant production and absorption maintains stable intracranial pressure and ensures continuous waste removal and nutrient delivery. Production rate is relatively constant and independent of intracranial pressure, while absorption rate varies with pressure, providing a homeostatic mechanism.
questions.question: What is the approximate production rate of cerebrospinal fluid?

questions.explanation: Oligodendrocytes produce myelin sheath enveloping axons in the CNS. Schwann cells do this in the PNS. One oligodendrocyte can myelinate multiple axon segments.
questions.question: Oligodendrocytes produce myelin in which location?
The Golgi apparatus is primarily responsible for which of the following cellular functions?
options: Sorting, modifying, and packaging proteins for secretion
Generating cellular energy through oxidative phosphorylation
Detoxification of drugs and metabolic byproducts
questions.explanation: The Golgi apparatus receives proteins from the rough ER, modifies them (glycosylation, phosphorylation, proteolytic cleavage), sorts them, and packages them into vesicles directed to the cell surface (secretion), lysosomes, or other organelles. It functions as the cell's postal sorting and processing center. The 'cis' face receives from the ER while the 'trans' face dispatches vesicles.

The lenticulostriate arteries (lateral striate arteries) are small perforating branches of the middle cerebral artery that supply the basal ganglia and internal capsule. These vessels are particularly vulnerable to hypertensive damage and are common sites of intracerebral hemorrhage (\"hemorrhagic stroke\"). Occlusion or rupture of these arteries causes contralateral hemiplegia due to internal capsule involvement, often with severe permanent deficits. They are sometimes called \"arteries of stroke\" due to their clinical significance.
questions.question: The lenticulostriate arteries are branches of which vessel?

options: T cell positive selection on MHC molecules
Plasmacytoid dendritic cell production of type I interferons
B cell clonal expansion, hypermutation, affinity maturation, and class switching
Mast cell IgE production following allergen exposure
questions.explanation: Germinal centers form in secondary lymphoid follicles when antigen-activated B cells with T cell help undergo rapid clonal expansion. Within germinal centers, activation-induced cytidine deaminase causes somatic hypermutation of immunoglobulin variable regions; selection retains high-affinity mutants in affinity maturation; class switch recombination changes immunoglobulin isotype from IgM to IgG, IgA, or IgE; selected cells differentiate into long-lived plasma cells or memory B cells.
questions.question: The germinal center within a lymph node secondary follicle is the site of which critical immunological process?

questions.explanation: Bone serves as the body's major reservoir of calcium accounting for 99% of body calcium, which is released into or deposited from blood under hormonal control by PTH, calcitonin, and vitamin D. Adult bone undergoes continuous remodeling at approximately 10% of the skeleton per year through coordinated osteoclast resorption followed by osteoblast formation. This metabolic activity is reflected in the rich vascular supply essential for delivering hormones and nutrients to bone cells.
options: Bone does not participate in calcium homeostasis
Bone matrix is completely stable and undergoes no remodeling after skeletal maturity
Osteocytes are permanently quiescent after being trapped in lacunae
Bone is a calcium and phosphate reservoir continuously remodeled for blood mineral homeostasis
Bone marrow is metabolically inactive in adult life
questions.question: Bone tissue is described as highly vascularized and metabolically active. Which of the following best reflects this metabolic activity?
Anterior spinal artery syndrome spares which sensation?
questions.explanation: Anterior spinal artery syndrome affects ventral 2/3 of cord sparing posterior columns. Proprioception and vibration are preserved. Motor function, pain and temperature are lost. It results from anterior spinal artery occlusion.

questions.question: During wound healing, which type of collagen is initially deposited by fibroblasts in the proliferative phase and what subsequently replaces it?
options: Type IV collagen is deposited first then replaced by type I
Type I collagen is deposited first without any subsequent change
Type III collagen deposited first, then replaced by type I during remodeling
Type II collagen is deposited only then replaced by type III
Elastic fibers are deposited first before any collagen
questions.explanation: The proliferative phase beginning approximately days 3 to 5 post-injury involves fibroblasts invading the wound and initially depositing type III collagen forming provisional granulation tissue. Over weeks to months during the remodeling phase type III collagen is progressively replaced by stronger type I collagen and cross-linking increases gradually restoring tensile strength reaching maximum approximately 80% of original. This temporal collagen transition is fundamental to wound healing biology.

questions.question: During return to the abdomen, which intestinal segment returns first?
questions.explanation: During return of herniated intestines (10th week), the small intestine loops (cranial limb) return first and are situated to the right of the dorsal mesentery. The large intestine follows, with the cecum being the last to return. This sequence is important for proper intestinal positioning.

questions.question: Familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) involves APC gene mutations leading to hundreds of colonic polyps. These polyps arise from the abnormal proliferation of which cells?
questions.explanation: Colorectal polyps in FAP arise from the uncontrolled proliferation of crypt stem cells (colonocytes) in the base of colonic crypts. Normally, the APC protein controls Wnt signaling to regulate stem cell proliferation. Bi-allelic APC loss leads to unrestrained crypt cell division and upward migration, forming adenomatous polyps. Without prophylactic colectomy, virtually all FAP patients develop colorectal cancer by age 40.
options: Goblet cells in the lamina propria
Smooth muscle cells of the muscularis
Stem cells in the base of colonic crypts

questions.question: Renal columns (of Bertin) are composed of:
questions.explanation: Renal columns (of Bertin) are composed of cortical tissue that extends between the pyramids down to the renal sinus. They contain cortical nephrons and interlobular vessels. Prominent columns are normal variants but can be mistaken for masses on imaging. The columns represent the cortical tissue separating adjacent renal pyramids.

questions.question: Which germ layer gives rise to the epithelial lining of the respiratory tract?
questions.explanation: The endoderm gives rise to the epithelial lining of the respiratory tract (pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi, and lungs). The connective tissue, cartilage, and smooth muscle of the respiratory system are derived from splanchnic mesoderm. The yolk sac endoderm contributes to this epithelium.

The vesical (upper) part of the urogenital sinus gives rise to most of the urinary bladder and is continuous with the allantois (which becomes the urachus). The pelvic part forms the prostatic and membranous urethra in males or the entire urethra in females. The phallic part grows toward the genital tubercle.
questions.question: The vesical part of the urogenital sinus gives rise to:

questions.explanation: Accessory (ectopic) pancreatic tissue is most commonly found in the stomach wall, duodenum, or jejunum. It represents aberrant pancreatic tissue that develops outside the normal pancreas, usually in the GI tract wall. Most accessory pancreatic tissue is asymptomatic and discovered incidentally, though it may rarely cause obstruction or bleeding.
questions.question: Accessory pancreatic tissue is most commonly found in:

options: Large pale erythrocytes with hypersegmented neutrophils
Target cells with a central dense area surrounded by a pale ring
Small pale (microcytic hypochromic) red cells with increased central pallor
questions.explanation: Iron deficiency anemia results in microcytic hypochromic erythrocytes because insufficient iron limits hemoglobin synthesis causing smaller RBCs with less hemoglobin per cell. The peripheral smear shows: microcytosis with MCV less than 80 fL; hypochromia with increased central pallor occupying more than one-third of the cell diameter; and anisocytosis and poikilocytosis with variable size and shape. Large hyperchromic macrocytic cells with hypersegmented neutrophils indicate B12 or folate deficiency megaloblastic anemia instead.
questions.question: The peripheral blood smear of a patient with iron deficiency anemia would show erythrocytes with which morphological abnormalities?

questions.explanation: Nephron formation (nephrogenesis) is complete at birth, with over 1 million nephrons in each kidney. No new nephrons form after birth, though existing ones continue to mature and grow. This finite nephron number explains why kidney disease in childhood can have lifelong consequences. Low birth weight and prematurity are associated with reduced nephron number.
questions.question: Which statement about nephron formation is correct?

questions.explanation: Each renal pyramid has its base facing the cortex and its apex (papilla) projecting into a minor calyx. The papilla contains the openings of the papillary ducts (of Bellini), which drain urine collected from multiple collecting ducts. The minor calyces then drain into major calyces, then the renal pelvis, and finally the ureter. There are typically 8–18 renal pyramids per kidney.
questions.question: The renal medulla contains renal (medullary) pyramids. The apex (papilla) of each pyramid is directed toward:

questions.explanation: Continuous addition of neuroblasts reduces the neural canal into a minute central canal. This occurs as the mantle layer thickens. The central canal is lined by ependymal cells.
questions.question: The central canal is reduced from which structure?
The gallbladder develops from which part of the hepatic diverticulum?
questions.explanation: The gallbladder develops from the smaller caudal part of the hepatic diverticulum. The larger cranial part forms the liver parenchyma. The stalk of the diverticulum connecting these parts becomes the cystic duct. The bile duct forms from the stalk connecting to the duodenum. These structures undergo temporary occlusion and recanalization.

The luteal phase (from ovulation to the onset of menstruation) is consistently approximately 14 days in all women with normal cycles, regardless of total cycle length. This is because it corresponds to the fixed lifespan of the corpus luteum (14 ± 2 days) in the absence of pregnancy. Cycle length variation arises from differences in the follicular phase (proliferative phase duration). This constancy is the basis of counting back 14 days from the next expected period to estimate ovulation date.
questions.question: The female reproductive cycle is approximately 28 days. The interval between ovulation and menstruation (luteal phase) is consistently which duration?
The laryngeal muscles are derived from which pharyngeal arches?
questions.explanation: The laryngeal muscles are derived from the 4th and 6th pharyngeal arches. The cricothyroid muscle (4th arch) is innervated by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve. The intrinsic laryngeal muscles (6th arch) are innervated by the recurrent laryngeal nerve. Both nerves are branches of the vagus.

questions.question: Which vein connects the superficial and deep venous systems?
questions.explanation: The basal vein of Rosenthal serves as an important connection between superficial and deep venous systems, receiving tributaries from superficial structures like the insula and temporal lobe while draining into the deep system via the great vein of Galen. The superficial middle cerebral vein also provides connections, draining superficial lateral structures into either the cavernous sinus or deep system. These connections allow alternative drainage pathways if one system becomes thrombosed.

questions.question: Which cells in the respiratory epithelium serve as stem cells capable of regenerating other epithelial cell types after injury?
questions.explanation: Basal cells are the stem cells of the pseudostratified respiratory epithelium. They are small, triangular cells attached to the basement membrane but not reaching the luminal surface. After injury, basal cells proliferate and differentiate into ciliated cells, goblet cells, and other cell types to restore the epithelium. This regenerative capacity is critical for airway repair after viral infections and toxic exposures.

options: Stimulating thyroid hormone production by follicular cells
Raising blood calcium by stimulating osteoclasts
Regulating sodium reabsorption in the kidney
Mediating the stress response through cortisol release
Suppresses bone resorption and increases calcification, lowering blood calcium
questions.explanation: Parafollicular C cells scattered between thyroid follicles produce calcitonin which lowers blood calcium by inhibiting osteoclast activity reducing bone resorption and promoting calcium deposition in bone. It opposes parathyroid hormone action. While important pharmacologically for treating Paget's disease and hypercalcemia, calcitonin's physiological role in human calcium homeostasis is less critical than that of PTH.
questions.question: Parafollicular C cells of the thyroid gland produce calcitonin which has which physiological action?

options: Ventral (saccule, cochlear duct) and dorsal (utricle, semicircular canals)
questions.question: The otic vesicle divides into which parts?
questions.explanation: The otic vesicle divides into ventral part (saccule and cochlear duct) and dorsal part (utricle, semicircular canals, endolymphatic duct). All form the membranous labyrinth. This occurs in the 4th-5th week.

questions.question: Macrophages originate from which precursor cells in the bone marrow and subsequently differentiate in connective tissues?
questions.explanation: Macrophages originate from monocyte precursor cells produced in the bone marrow, which circulate in the blood and then migrate into connective tissues where they differentiate into tissue macrophages. This monocyte-macrophage lineage is part of the Mononuclear Phagocyte System (MPS). The process of differentiation involves changes in size, surface markers, and the acquisition of pronounced phagocytic capacity.

questions.question: Obstruction of the cerebral aqueduct causes which type of hydrocephalus?
questions.explanation: Obstruction of the cerebral aqueduct causes non-communicating (obstructive) hydrocephalus, where CSF cannot flow from the lateral and third ventricles to the fourth ventricle and subarachnoid space. This results in progressive dilation of the lateral and third ventricles with elevated intraventricular pressure, while the fourth ventricle remains normal or small. Congenital aqueductal stenosis is a common cause of infantile hydrocephalus, while tumors compressing the aqueduct can cause acquired obstruction in adults.

At the beginning of the 3rd week, epiblast cells proliferate and migrate to the median plane of the germ disc, forming the primitive streak. As the primitive streak elongates, its cranial part forms the primitive node. The primitive groove appears in the streak and is continuous with the primitive pit.
questions.question: The primitive streak first appears at which location on the embryonic disc?

questions.explanation: The pontine flexure, which is a dorsal flexure, is responsible for the diamond shape of the fourth ventricle. This flexure also serves as a template for development of the cerebellum. The other brain flexures (cephalic and cervical) are ventral flexures.
questions.question: The pontine flexure is responsible for the shape of which structure?

questions.explanation: Resolving power refers to the minimum distance between two points that can be distinguished as separate. The compound light microscope achieves approximately 0.2 micrometers, compared to normal human eye resolution of ~100 micrometers. This limit is governed by the wavelength of visible light and the numerical aperture of the objective lens.
questions.question: The maximum resolving power of a standard compound light microscope is closest to which of the following values?

questions.explanation: Intrahepatic bile ducts are lined by cholangiocytes — simple cuboidal epithelium in smaller ducts transitioning to simple columnar epithelium in larger ducts. These cells regulate bile composition through secretion and reabsorption. Cholangiocytes are targets of autoimmune destruction in primary biliary cholangitis and primary sclerosing cholangitis, causing progressive biliary cirrhosis.
questions.question: Cholangiocytes are the epithelial cells lining the bile ducts. What type of epithelium lines the large intrahepatic bile ducts?

questions.explanation: The pontine respiratory centers (pneumotaxic and apneustic centers) in the pons modulate the basic respiratory rhythm generated by medullary respiratory centers. The pneumotaxic center (parabrachial nuclei) limits inspiration, promoting rhythmic breathing, while the apneustic center prolongs inspiration. These centers integrate input from chemoreceptors, mechanoreceptors, and higher centers to adjust breathing rate and depth. Lesions can cause abnormal respiratory patterns like apneustic breathing (prolonged inspiratory gasps).
questions.question: Which nucleus is responsible for generating rhythmic breathing patterns?

questions.explanation: The posterior intermediate sulcus is present only in T6 and above, dividing posterior column into gracile and cuneate fasciculi. Below T6, only gracilis is present. This reflects upper limb proprioceptive input.
questions.question: The posterior intermediate sulcus is present in which segments?
The stria terminalis runs parallel to which structure?
questions.explanation: The amygdala's efferent bundle (stria terminalis) runs parallel to the concavity of caudate nucleus. It carries output from the amygdala to hypothalamus and other structures. It is visible in the floor of lateral ventricle.

questions.question: Which structure forms from the pars iridica retinae of the optic cup?
questions.explanation: The anterior 1/5th of the inner layer of the optic cup, called pars iridica retinae, forms the inner layer of the iris. The pars ciliaris retinae forms the ciliary body epithelium. These anterior derivatives of the optic cup do not develop photoreceptors like the posterior portions.

options: Both flow in the same direction from portal tracts to central vein
Blood flows from central vein to portal tracts; bile flows centripetally
Blood and bile flow randomly through the lobule
Blood flows centrifugally from central vein; bile flows toward the central vein
Blood flows from portal tracts toward central vein
questions.explanation: Blood flows centripetally — from the portal tracts at the periphery through the sinusoids toward the central vein (terminal hepatic venule) at the center of the classic lobule. Bile, however, flows centrifugally — from bile canaliculi between hepatocytes toward the bile ductules in the portal tracts. This counter-current arrangement is essential for understanding hepatic pathology patterns in various liver diseases.
questions.question: In the liver, the hepatic artery and portal vein supply blood that flows through hepatic sinusoids. The direction of blood flow relative to bile flow is:

questions.explanation: The aorticopulmonary septum divides the truncus arteriosus into the aorta and pulmonary trunk. It forms by fusion of pairs of opposing ridges (truncal and bulbar ridges) that grow in a spiral fashion, not straight. This spiral arrangement is crucial for proper alignment of the great vessels.
questions.question: The aorticopulmonary (AP) septum forms by fusion of ridges that grow in what pattern?

questions.explanation: The nigrostriatal pathway connects substantia nigra to the striatum using dopamine as neurotransmitter. Degeneration of this pathway causes Parkinson's disease. This is one of the major afferent pathways to basal ganglia.
questions.question: The nigrostriatal pathway connects which structures?

questions.explanation: The superior 2/3 of the anal canal (endodermal portion) is supplied by the superior rectal artery, a branch of the inferior mesenteric artery. The inferior 1/3 (ectodermal portion) is supplied by the inferior rectal artery from the internal pudendal artery. This reflects the dual embryological origin of the anal canal.
questions.question: The superior 2/3 of the anal canal is supplied by:

questions.explanation: The placenta produces hormones including progesterone, estrogens (especially estriol), human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), and human placental lactogen (somatomammotropin). It does not produce follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), which is secreted by the anterior pituitary gland.
questions.question: The placenta produces all of the following hormones EXCEPT:

questions.explanation: The remaining part of the septum primum (after the upper part gradually disappears) becomes the valve of the foramen ovale. This creates a valvular aperture that allows blood to flow from right to left but not from left to right during fetal life.
questions.question: The valve of the foramen ovale is formed by which structure?
Which of the following correctly distinguishes primary from secondary lymphoid organs?
options: Primary organs filter lymph while secondary organs filter blood
Primary organs for lymphocyte development; secondary organs for immune responses
Primary organs are larger than secondary organs
Secondary organs develop before primary organs in embryogenesis
They are functionally identical with only anatomical location differing
questions.explanation: Primary lymphoid organs are the sites where lymphocytes develop and acquire antigen recognition capability: bone marrow for B cells and thymus for T cells. Secondary lymphoid organs including lymph nodes, spleen, tonsils, Peyer's patches, and MALT are where mature naive lymphocytes encounter antigens and mount adaptive immune responses. This distinction reflects the two-stage model of lymphocyte differentiation: antigen-independent in primary organs and antigen-dependent in secondary organs.

This is a Type I immediate hypersensitivity reaction. Prior peanut exposure sensitized the patient with plasma cells producing peanut-specific IgE that coated tissue mast cells via high-affinity FcεRI receptors. Re-exposure causes IgE crosslinking on mast cells triggering rapid degranulation within minutes. Released histamine causes urticaria, vasodilation, and bronchoconstriction while leukotrienes sustain bronchospasm. Systemic mast cell activation causes the full anaphylaxis syndrome.
options: Peanut allergens crosslink mast cell IgE, triggering degranulation and mediator release
T cell-mediated cytotoxicity against peanut-sensitized cells
Complement activation by IgM antibodies against peanut proteins
Neutrophil-mediated release of reactive oxygen species
B cell direct recognition of peanut antigen causing plasma cell activation
questions.question: A 30-year-old patient develops urticaria and bronchoconstriction within minutes of eating peanuts. This reaction is mediated by which mechanism?
The vestibulocochlear nerve divisions are both which component?
questions.explanation: Both cochlear and vestibular divisions of CN VIII are special somatic afferent for hearing and balance. They carry information from inner ear receptors. The nerve enters at the cerebellopontine angle.
Special visceral afferent fibers of CN9 supply taste buds of the tongue. CN9 also has general visceral afferent for pharyngeal sensation. It is a mixed cranial nerve.
questions.question: CN9 special visceral afferent supplies which structure?
Somatic afferent nuclei CN8 and CN5 receive information from which structures?
questions.explanation: Somatic afferent nuclei CN8 and CN5 receive information from the ear and head surface. CN8 carries hearing and balance information. CN5 carries general sensation from the face.

Attachment of the blastocyst to the endometrial epithelium is mediated by L-selectin on the trophoblast and its receptor on the endometrial epithelium. This is the first stage of implantation and occurs after the zona pellucida has disappeared.
questions.question: Attachment of the blastocyst to endometrial epithelium is mediated by which molecule on the trophoblast?

questions.explanation: The superior cerebellar peduncle decussates in the lower midbrain at the level of the inferior colliculus. After decussation, fibers continue to the contralateral red nucleus and thalamus (ventrolateral nucleus). This decussation explains why cerebellar lesions cause ipsilateral deficits---the cerebellum influences the contralateral motor cortex, which then sends crossed corticospinal fibers back to the ipsilateral side. The decussating fibers are visible in cross-sections of the lower midbrain.
questions.question: The superior cerebellar peduncle decussates at which level?
The ampulla of Vater marks the boundary between:
questions.explanation: The ampulla of Vater (where the common bile duct opens into the duodenum) marks the boundary between foregut and midgut. This anatomical landmark corresponds to the junction between celiac artery and superior mesenteric artery blood supply. The foregut extends from the oral cavity to this point.

options: Collecting tubules converging on minor calyx
questions.question: Renal pyramids are formed by:
questions.explanation: Renal pyramids are formed by collecting tubules of the 5th and successive generations that elongate considerably and converge on each minor calyx. The tubules run parallel to each other, creating the striated appearance of the pyramids. Each pyramid with its overlying cortex represents a renal lobe. The apex of each pyramid (papilla) projects into a minor calyx.

questions.question: In the visual pathway, fibers from the nasal retina project to which side?
questions.explanation: Visual stimuli are represented on retina in reverse. At optic chiasma, medial (nasal retina) fibers cross to the contralateral side. This allows each hemisphere to process the opposite visual field.

options: Medial nasal and two maxillary prominences
questions.explanation: The upper lip is formed in the 6th week by fusion of the medial nasal prominence and the two maxillary prominences. The lower lip and jaw are formed by fusion of the two mandibular prominences in the midline. The cheeks and maxilla are formed by fusion of the maxillary prominences.
questions.question: The upper lip is formed by fusion of which structures?

questions.explanation: Superior colliculi serve as synaptic relay centers for visual impulses and control eye movements. Inferior colliculi relay auditory impulses. Both are part of the tectum of the midbrain.
questions.question: Superior colliculi serve as relay centers for which modality?
Mossy fibers in the cerebellum originate from which sources?
questions.explanation: Mossy fibers originate from pontine nuclei (relaying cortical information), spinal cord (spinocerebellar tracts), vestibular nuclei, and reticular formation. These are the primary afferent fibers to the cerebellum, synapsing on granule cells in the granular layer. Granule cells then send parallel fibers to synapse on Purkinje cell dendrites. Mossy fibers provide detailed information about motor commands, sensory feedback, and vestibular signals, allowing the cerebellum to compare intended with actual movements.

Brown fat (brown adipose tissue) forms during 17-20 weeks and is an important site of heat production in the newborn. It is located primarily in the neck, between the scapulae, around the kidneys, and around the adrenal glands. Brown fat helps maintain body temperature after birth.
questions.question: Brown fat, which is important for heat production, forms during which period?

questions.explanation: Superficial cerebral veins drain the cortex and superficial white matter, primarily emptying into the superior sagittal sinus and other dural sinuses. These veins run in the subarachnoid space and penetrate the arachnoid and dura to reach the sinuses. Unlike systemic veins, cerebral veins lack valves, making them susceptible to retrograde thrombosis. Superior cerebral veins drain into the superior sagittal sinus, while inferior veins drain into transverse and sigmoid sinuses or deep venous system.
questions.question: Superficial cerebral veins primarily drain into which structure?

questions.explanation: Connective tissue derives its name from its fundamental function of connecting or binding cells and tissues together throughout the body. It maintains the form of organs and serves as a structural framework for other tissue types. Unlike epithelium, muscle, and nerve (which consist mainly of cells), connective tissue's dominant component is the extracellular matrix.
options: It forms the outer covering of all organs
It generates electrical impulses through gap junctions
It absorbs and secretes fluids in body cavities
It provides contractile force for body movement
It connects and binds cells and tissues together
questions.question: Connective tissue derives its name from which of the following primary functional characteristics?
At the level of the superior colliculus, which nucleus is located close to the midline?
questions.explanation: The oculomotor nucleus is located close to the midline ventral to the cerebral aqueduct at the level of the superior colliculus. The Edinger-Westphal nucleus (parasympathetic component) lies cranial to the main oculomotor nucleus. The oculomotor nerve fibers pass through the red nucleus, which lies lateral and ventral to the nucleus, before emerging from the medial aspect of the cerebral peduncle.

The urorectal septum is derived from mesoderm at the junction between the connecting stalk and yolk sac. This septum grows toward the cloacal membrane, separating the hindgut from the allantois. It divides the cloaca into urogenital sinus ventrally and anorectal canal dorsally.
questions.question: The urorectal septum is derived from mesoderm at the junction between:
The vagus nerve wanders as far as which structure?
questions.explanation: The vagus nerve (X) wanders as far as the transverse colon providing parasympathetic innervation. It has SVE (pharynx, larynx), GVE (thoracic/abdominal viscera), GVA, GSA and SVA components. It is the main parasympathetic nerve.

questions.question: A student observes glands within the lamina propria on a GIT slide. These glands most likely represent:
questions.explanation: The lamina propria frequently contains small glands which open into the lumen, forming part of the secretory apparatus of the GIT. These are region-specific — gastric glands in the stomach, intestinal crypts in the intestines. Brunner's glands are specific to the duodenal submucosa, not the lamina propria.

options: Neurons as supporting cells and oligodendrocytes as conducting cells
Neurons that conduct impulses and mitotically capable neuroglia that provide support
Astrocytes that conduct and Schwann cells that only support in CNS
Microglia that conduct and astrocytes that provide energy
Both neuroglia and neurons conduct impulses equally
questions.question: The two main cell types in nervous tissue and their primary distinction are which of the following?
questions.explanation: The nervous system has two fundamental cell categories: neurons are the electrically excitable conducting cells that transmit electrochemical impulses, and neuroglia or glial cells are the non-conducting support cells far more numerous than neurons that retain the ability to undergo mitosis. The term neuroglia means nerve glue reflecting the originally conceptualized function of physically supporting neurons.

questions.question: The lateral ventricles develop from which embryonic structure?
questions.explanation: The lateral ventricles develop from the cavity of the telencephalon. The third ventricle develops from the diencephalon cavity, the cerebral aqueduct from the mesencephalon cavity, and the fourth ventricle from the rhombencephalon cavity (metencephalon and myelencephalon).

Paneth cells at the base of small intestinal crypts are the primary niche cells for intestinal Lgr5+ stem cells. Paneth cells provide essential stem cell maintenance signals including Wnt3a (activating the Wnt/β-catenin pathway), Delta-like ligands (Notch signaling), and EGF family members. This direct physical and signaling contact between Paneth cells and stem cells is essential for intestinal regeneration. In colonic crypts, Paneth-like cells or stromal cells fulfill this niche function.
questions.question: The intestinal stem cell niche is located at the base of intestinal crypts, where Lgr5+ stem cells reside. These stem cells are maintained by signals from which adjacent supporting cell type?

questions.explanation: The action potential is a transient reversal of the electrochemical gradient across the axolemma, caused by sequential opening of voltage-gated sodium channels (depolarization) followed by potassium channels (repolarization). It propagates along neuronal processes and axons, transmitting signals to other neurons, muscles, and glands. The all-or-nothing nature of action potentials ensures signal fidelity over long axonal distances.
options: Permanent irreversible change in the neuron's membrane composition
Passive diffusion of glucose across the neuronal membrane
Release of neurotransmitters directly into the bloodstream
Synthesis of new proteins at the axon terminal
Reversal of ionic gradient propagated along the neuronal plasma membrane
questions.question: An action potential in a neuron is specifically characterized by which of the following?

questions.explanation: Nissl substance (or Nissl bodies) are the basophilic granular patches in neuronal cytoplasm that represent stacked rough ER cisternae with densely attached ribosomes. They reflect the neuron's high demand for new protein synthesis to maintain its extensive axonal and dendritic processes. Chromatolysis (dissolution of Nissl substance) following axonal injury is a histological sign of neuronal stress.
questions.question: The Nissl substance visible in neuronal cell bodies under light microscopy corresponds to which ultrastructural organelle?
The vestibular nuclei receive input from which structure?
questions.explanation: The vestibular nuclei receive input from the semicircular canals (detecting angular acceleration) and otolith organs (utricle and saccule, detecting linear acceleration and head position) via the vestibular division of CN VIII. These nuclei are located at the pontomedullary junction in the floor of the fourth ventricle, lateral to the medial sulcus. The vestibular nuclei project to the spinal cord (vestibulospinal tract), cerebellum, extraocular motor nuclei, and thalamus, coordinating balance, posture, and eye movements.

options: Anywhere along the entire colon equally
At the points where vasa recta (blood vessels)
Only in the sigmoid colon, not other regions
questions.question: Colonic diverticula are herniations of mucosa and submucosa through the muscularis externa. They form preferentially at which anatomical site?
questions.explanation: Colonic diverticula (false diverticula) form at natural weak points in the muscularis where the vasa recta (arterial branches supplying the mucosa) penetrate the circular muscle layer. The increased intraluminal pressure from a low-fiber diet forces the mucosa and submucosa to herniate through these weak points. Diverticulosis is most common in the sigmoid colon where intraluminal pressures are highest due to the narrow lumen.

questions.question: The yolk sac is connected to the midgut by which structure?
questions.explanation: The yolk sac is connected to the midgut by a narrow yolk stalk (also called the vitelline duct). The yolk sac is a pear-shaped remnant of about 5 mm in diameter by 20 weeks, after which it is very small and usually not visible. It can persist as Meckel's diverticulum.

options: Fixed cells permanently anchored to alveolar walls
Cells producing surfactant in the alveolus
Cells secreting IgA into the alveolus
Free cells in the alveolar lumen phagocytosing particles
questions.question: Alveolar macrophages (dust cells) are derived from blood monocytes and patrol the alveolar surface. They are most accurately described as:
questions.explanation: Alveolar macrophages are free, mobile cells within the alveolar spaces and alveolar walls that phagocytose inhaled particles, microorganisms, surfactant, and cellular debris.
