They contain ingested carbon particles (making them 'dust cells') and hemosiderin in heart failure (making them 'heart failure cells'). After phagocytosis, they migrate to the mucociliary escalator or lymphatics for clearance.

questions.question: The claustrum is located between which two structures?
questions.explanation: The claustrum is a thin sheet of gray matter located between the insula medially (separated by the extreme capsule) and the putamen laterally (separated by the external capsule). This structure has extensive reciprocal connections with nearly all cortical areas, suggesting a role in integrating multimodal sensory information or coordinating cortical activity. Despite its extensive connectivity, the function of the claustrum remains debated, with theories ranging from attention and salience detection to binding of sensory features or consciousness. It follows the contour of the insula.

Lateral (horizontal) folding rolls the sides of the embryonic disc and turns part of the yolk sac into the embryo as midgut. The rest is left outside as the yolk stalk and is incorporated into the umbilical cord. This folding brings the ventral body wall together and establishes the tubular gut.
questions.question: Horizontal folding of the embryo results in incorporation of which structure into the midgut?
The metencephalon is the cranial portion of which vesicle?
questions.explanation: The metencephalon is the cranial portion of the rhombencephalon formed by differential growth. It has well-defined basal and alar plates. The pontine flexure separates it from the myelencephalon.

questions.question: A cell that is actively secreting proteins would be expected to have especially abundant amounts of which of the following?
options: Peroxisomes and centrioles of the cytoskeleton
Rough ER, Golgi apparatus, and secretory vesicles
questions.explanation: Protein secretion requires synthesis at rough ER ribosomes, modification and packaging in the Golgi apparatus, and transport of secretory vesicles to the cell surface for exocytosis. Cells specialized for protein secretion (pancreatic acinar cells, antibody-secreting plasma cells) are therefore characterized by abundant rough ER (basophilic cytoplasm) and prominent Golgi complex. This constellation of organelles defines the secretory pathway.

Intervillous spaces are filled with maternal blood from spiral arteries. Maternal blood bathes the chorionic villi, allowing exchange of nutrients, gases, and wastes between maternal and fetal circulations without direct contact. Blood flows from spiral arteries and drains into endometrial veins.
questions.question: Intervillous spaces contain which substance?

questions.explanation: The transverse temporal gyri (Heschl's gyri) located on the superior surface of the superior temporal gyrus within the lateral sulcus contain the primary auditory cortex (Brodmann areas 41 and 42). Usually 1-3 transverse gyri run obliquely across the superior temporal surface, perpendicular to the long axis of the temporal lobe. These gyri receive auditory input from the medial geniculate nucleus via the auditory radiations and process sound frequency, intensity, and temporal patterns. Bilateral lesions cause cortical deafness.
questions.question: The transverse temporal gyri (of Heschl) contain which functional area?
The caudal limb of the midgut loop gives rise to:
questions.explanation: The caudal limb of the midgut loop gives rise to the lower portion of the ileum, cecum, appendix, ascending colon, and proximal 2/3 of the transverse colon. The cranial limb forms the distal duodenum, jejunum, and upper ileum. The hindgut forms the distal 1/3 of transverse colon through the upper anal canal.

options: Multiple peripheral nuclei, identical to typical skeletal muscle fibers
Uniform smooth histological appearance without visible cross-striations
Intercalated discs with gap junctions for coupling and desmosomes for cohesion
Satellite cells providing regeneration after myocardial infarction
Voluntary motor control through upper alpha motor neurons
questions.explanation: Intercalated discs are the unique structural feature of cardiac muscle at the junctions between cardiomyocytes. They contain gap junctions that electrically couple adjacent cells allowing rapid action potential propagation throughout the myocardium creating a functional syncytium; desmosomes providing mechanical cohesion during vigorous contraction; and fascia adherens for myofibril anchoring. This organization enables the coordinated, rhythmic heart contractions.
questions.question: Cardiac muscle is unique among the three muscle types in possessing which structural feature?

options: Preventing T cells from leaving the thymus prematurely
Blocking antibody production within the thymus
Filtering out aged erythrocytes before they enter lymphoid tissue
Educating T cells on self-MHC to generate a self-tolerant repertoire
questions.explanation: The blood-thymus barrier consists of capillary endothelium with tight junctions, pericytes, perivascular connective tissue, and enveloping cortical epithelial cells. It prevents blood-borne antigens from reaching developing thymocytes in the cortex, ensuring that T cells are educated exclusively on self-MHC and self-peptide complexes presented by thymic epithelial cells. This controlled environment is essential for generating a self-tolerant T cell repertoire avoiding autoimmunity.
questions.question: The blood-thymus barrier in the thymic cortex prevents circulating antigens from reaching developing thymocytes. This serves which critical immunological function?

questions.explanation: The visceral pleura is derived from splanchnic mesoderm covering the outside of the developing lungs. The parietal pleura develops from somatic mesoderm lining the body wall. The pleural cavity forms between these two layers as the lungs expand into the body cavity.
questions.question: The visceral pleura is derived from:

questions.explanation: The subthalamus is involved in control of micturition, generation of rhythmic movements, and motor regulation through connections with the basal ganglia. Deep brain stimulation of the subthalamic nucleus has proven effective in treating late-stage Parkinson's disease, reducing tremor, rigidity, and bradykinesia. The subthalamus is present only in mammals and represents a transitional zone between the thalamus/hypothalamus and the midbrain.
questions.question: The subthalamus is primarily involved in control of which function?

questions.explanation: The brush border of enterocytes is embedded with numerous disaccharidases (sucrase, maltase, lactase) and peptidases responsible for terminal digestion of carbohydrates and proteins. Lactase deficiency causes lactose intolerance — the most common brush border enzyme deficiency. These enzymes are part of the glycocalyx covering the microvilli and are directly linked to absorption.
questions.question: Enterocytes in the small intestinal villi contain which enzyme system on their brush border that is critical for final carbohydrate digestion?
The duodenum becomes secondarily retroperitoneal because:
questions.explanation: The duodenum becomes secondarily retroperitoneal as it rotates to the right and loses its dorsal mesentery through fusion with the posterior abdominal wall. The pancreas, developing in the duodenal mesentery, also becomes retroperitoneal. Only the first inch of duodenum retains its mesentery as the hepatoduodenal ligament.
options: Its mesentery fuses with posterior wall

questions.question: The intermediate mesoderm in the sacral region gives rise to:
questions.explanation: The intermediate mesoderm in the sacral region gives rise to the metanephric blastema (metanephric mesenchyme), which forms the nephrons of the permanent kidney. More cranially, intermediate mesoderm gives rise to the pronephros (cervical) and mesonephros (thoracolumbar). The gonads develop from intermediate mesoderm but in a different region (urogenital ridge).

Red bone marrow fills the spaces of cancellous bone and is the site of hematopoiesis — the continuous production of all formed elements of blood: erythrocytes, leukocytes, and megakaryocytes which produce platelets. Yellow marrow (fat-filled) predominates in adult long bone shafts but can revert to active red marrow during increased demand such as severe anemia or hemorrhage.
options: Mineral storage exclusively without any cellular function
Hematopoiesis — production of erythrocytes, leukocytes, and platelets
Synthesis of cortical bone matrix as the primary source
Production of cartilage matrix for endochondral ossification
Secretion of parathyroid hormone to regulate blood calcium
questions.question: The bone marrow housed in cancellous bone serves which of the following essential functions?
The primary palate is formed from which component of the intermaxillary segment?
questions.explanation: The palatal component of the intermaxillary segment forms the triangular primary palate. Cranially, the intermaxillary segment is continuous with the rostral part of the nasal septum formed by the frontonasal prominence. The primary palate forms only a small part of the adult hard palate.

questions.question: How many pairs of cranial nerves exist?
questions.explanation: There are 12 pairs of cranial nerves numbered I-XII from their cranio-caudal arrangement. Three are purely sensory, five purely motor, four mixed. They differ from spinal nerves in several features.

options: Thick, viscous, and cellular (late luteal phase mucus)
Thick and plug-like due to progesterone action
Thin, watery, acellular, and forms a ferning pattern on drying
questions.question: The cervical mucus changes in consistency throughout the menstrual cycle. At the time of ovulation, cervical mucus is maximally permeable to sperm because it becomes:
questions.explanation: At ovulation, high estrogen levels cause cervical mucus secreted by endocervical glands to become thin, watery, acellular, and highly elastic (spinnbarkeit — can be drawn into long strings). When dried on a glass slide, ovulatory mucus forms a characteristic ferning (arborization) pattern due to NaCl crystallization. This change facilitates sperm penetration. After ovulation, progesterone converts cervical mucus to thick, viscous, cellular mucus forming a 'plug' impenetrable to sperm.

Horseshoe kidney, present in 0.2% of the population, usually results from fusion of the inferior poles of the kidneys. The fused kidney typically lies in the hypogastric region because normal ascent is prevented by the root of the inferior mesenteric artery. Most cases are asymptomatic as the collecting system develops normally.
questions.question: A horseshoe kidney results from fusion of the kidneys at which pole?
Smooth muscle of the GI tract wall achieves peristalsis through which organization of its muscle layers?
questions.explanation: The GI tract wall contains an inner circular smooth muscle layer encircling the tube and an outer longitudinal smooth muscle layer running along its length. Coordinated contraction where the inner circular layer contracts while the outer longitudinal layer relaxes produces peristaltic waves that propel luminal contents aborally. The myenteric plexus of Auerbach between these layers coordinates their activity.
options: Inner circular and outer longitudinal smooth muscle in coordinated waves
Inner longitudinal and outer circular smooth muscle layers
Inner striated and outer smooth muscle layers
Inner oblique and outer transverse layers only
A single layer with spiral orientation throughout

questions.question: Venous drainage from deep cerebral structures ultimately empties into which sinus?
questions.explanation: Deep cerebral veins drain structures like the diencephalon and basal ganglia, converging to form the internal cerebral veins and basal veins of Rosenthal. These join to form the great vein of Galen, which empties into the straight sinus. The straight sinus then drains into the confluence of sinuses at the internal occipital protuberance, eventually reaching the transverse and sigmoid sinuses before emptying into the internal jugular vein.

The foregut extends from the oral cavity to the ampulla of Vater (opening of the bile duct into the duodenum). This division is based on arterial supply, with the celiac trunk supplying foregut derivatives. The midgut extends from the ampulla of Vater to the proximal 2/3 of the transverse colon.
questions.question: The foregut extends from the oral cavity to:
The cavernous sinus drains primarily into which structure?
questions.explanation: The cavernous sinus drains primarily into the superior and inferior petrosal sinuses, with the inferior petrosal sinus providing the main outflow to the internal jugular vein. The superior petrosal sinus drains into the transverse sinus. The cavernous sinus also has connections to facial veins through the superior and inferior ophthalmic veins, providing a route for facial infections to spread intracranially. Cavernous sinus thrombosis can result from facial infections, causing ophthalmoplegia, orbital edema, and potential bilateral involvement.

questions.question: A branchial fistula results from persistence of which structure?
questions.explanation: A branchial fistula results from persistence of a pharyngeal cleft (external) communicating with a pharyngeal pouch (internal), creating an abnormal passage from the pharynx to the external skin surface. Most commonly, this involves the second pharyngeal cleft and second pouch.

questions.question: The aqueduct of Sylvius connects which ventricles?
questions.explanation: The canal of the neural tube in the mesencephalon forms the aqueduct of Sylvius connecting third and fourth ventricles. This narrow channel allows CSF flow between ventricles. Blockage causes hydrocephalus.

options: They are the most numerous cells lining gastric pits
They release hormones into the bloodstream
They produce HCl and intrinsic factor
They are exclusively found in the pyloric glands
They stain intensely with PAS reagent for mucus
questions.explanation: Enteroendocrine cells (also called APUD cells or diffuse neuroendocrine cells) are scattered throughout the GIT epithelium and release hormones and peptides — such as gastrin, somatostatin, and secretin — into the lamina propria vasculature. They are characterized by basal granules visible on electron microscopy. They constitute the largest endocrine system in the body.
questions.question: Enteroendocrine cells in the stomach are best characterized by which feature?
Oligohydramnios is commonly associated with:
questions.explanation: Oligohydramnios (decreased amniotic fluid) is commonly associated with bilateral renal agenesis or severe renal dysfunction because the fetus cannot produce urine. Oligohydramnios causes Potter sequence: pulmonary hypoplasia, limb deformities, and characteristic facial features. The condition is incompatible with life due to pulmonary hypoplasia and renal failure.

questions.question: Which Brodmann areas constitute the primary somatosensory cortex?
questions.explanation: Brodmann areas 3, 1, and 2 in the postcentral gyrus constitute the primary somatosensory cortex, processing touch, proprioception, and vibration from the contralateral body. Area 3 receives the main thalamic input, while areas 1 and 2 process this information further. These areas maintain somatotopic organization (sensory homunculus) with disproportionate representation of hands and face. Lesions cause contralateral sensory loss, particularly affecting fine discriminative touch and position sense.

questions.question: The flocculonodular lobe connects primarily with which system?
questions.explanation: The flocculonodular lobe (archicerebellum) connects primarily with the vestibular nuclei, receiving input from and projecting to these structures. This phylogenetically oldest part of the cerebellum is crucial for maintaining balance and equilibrium, controlling eye movements (vestibulo-ocular reflex), and coordinating head movements. Lesions cause truncal ataxia (difficulty standing and walking with wide-based gait), nystagmus, and vertigo but typically spare limb coordination. The nodulus also receives direct input from vestibular receptors.

questions.question: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia most commonly occurs through which defect?
questions.explanation: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia commonly occurs through a posterolateral defect in the diaphragm, most frequently on the left side. This defect results from incomplete fusion of the pleuroperitoneal membranes with other diaphragmatic components. The herniation causes the left lung to show hypoplasia due to compression by abdominal viscera.

options: Large, pale cells with abundant glycogen,
questions.question: Purkinje fibers are part of the cardiac conduction system. Histologically, they are distinguished from ordinary cardiomyocytes by being:
questions.explanation: Purkinje fibers are modified cardiomyocytes of the subendocardial conduction system. Histologically, they are characteristically large, pale cells with central vacuoles (due to abundant glycogen), peripherally displaced myofibrils, and more prominent nuclei than working cardiomyocytes. They stain lightly with H&E due to glycogen. Purkinje fibers conduct action potentials rapidly to the ventricular myocardium, coordinating ventricular contraction. They are embedded in the subendocardial connective tissue.

The reticular formation nuclei are divided into three main columns based on neuron size and location: the paramedian (raphe) nuclear group in the midline, the central/medial column with large magnocellular neurons, and the lateral column with small parvocellular neurons. These columns have different connections and functions, with medial nuclei having long ascending and descending projections, while lateral nuclei modulate cranial nerve function and receive sensory input.
questions.question: The reticular formation is divided into how many main nuclear columns?

questions.explanation: The anterior 2/3 (oral part) of the tongue develops from two lateral lingual swellings and the tuberculum impar, all from the 1st pharyngeal arch. The posterior 1/3 (pharyngeal part) develops from the copula (hypobranchial eminence) of the 3rd pharyngeal arch. These parts are separated by the linguo-gingival swelling.
questions.question: The anterior 2/3 of the tongue develops from which pharyngeal arch structures?
options: Two lateral swellings and tuberculum impar

questions.question: Cervical enlargement corresponds to innervation of which structure?
questions.explanation: Cervical (C5-T1) and lumbar (L1-S2) enlargements correspond to increased gray matter for upper and lower limb innervation respectively. More neurons are needed for fine motor control. The cord diameter increases at these levels.

questions.question: The most common cell type in the brain is which?
questions.explanation: Astrocytes are the most common cells in the brain, outnumbering neurons 10:1. They provide metabolic support, form blood-brain barrier, and regulate extracellular environment. They are essential for neuronal function.

At the optic chiasm, nasal (medial) retinal fibers cross to the opposite side. Temporal fibers remain ipsilateral. This allows each hemisphere to process the contralateral visual field. Chiasm lesions cause bitemporal hemianopia.
questions.question: The optic chiasm is characterized by decussation of which fibers?

options: Membrane proteins are fixed in place within a rigid lipid framework
Lipids exist in a solid gel phase stabilized by cholesterol exclusively
Membrane proteins float freely within a fluid phospholipid bilayer like a mosaic
The membrane is composed only of proteins with lipids as minor components
All membrane components move in a synchronized coordinated pattern
questions.explanation: The fluid mosaic model describes the plasma membrane as a fluid phospholipid bilayer (the 'fluid' component) in which membrane proteins are embedded and can diffuse laterally (the 'mosaic' pattern). Cholesterol modulates the fluidity. The model replaced earlier static membrane models and explains the dynamic lateral movement of membrane components observed in experiments like FRAP (fluorescence recovery after photobleaching).
questions.question: The 'fluid mosaic model' of cell membrane structure, proposed by Singer and Nicolson, best describes which of the following?
The thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle is impermeable to water but actively transports NaCl. Which transporter on the apical membrane of thick ascending limb cells accomplishes this?
questions.explanation: The Na+/K+/2Cl- cotransporter (NKCC2) on the apical membrane of thick ascending limb (TAL) cells transports 1 Na+, 1 K+, and 2 Cl- into the cell using the electrochemical gradient created by basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase. This is the primary mechanism for NaCl reabsorption in the TAL, generating the medullary osmotic gradient. Loop diuretics (furosemide, bumetanide) inhibit NKCC2, reducing NaCl reabsorption and preventing medullary gradient formation, producing a potent diuretic effect.

questions.question: A normal human somatic cell contains how many chromosomes?
questions.explanation: Normal human somatic cells contain 46 chromosomes: 22 pairs of autosomes and 1 pair of sex chromosomes (XX in females, XY in males). Gametes (sperm and ova) contain 23 chromosomes (haploid number). The diploid number is restored at fertilization.

The upper third of the esophagus contains skeletal muscle (for voluntary swallowing), the middle third contains mixed skeletal and smooth muscle, and the lower third contains smooth muscle only. This gradation reflects the transition from voluntary to involuntary control of swallowing. This is a classic and frequently tested histological feature of the esophagus.
questions.question: The upper third of the esophagus contains which type of muscle in its muscularis externa?
High endothelial venules (HEVs) are specialized post-capillary venules found in lymphoid organs. Their distinctive tall, cuboidal endothelial cells facilitate which process?
options: Naïve lymphocyte homing from blood into
questions.explanation: High endothelial venules in lymph nodes (and other peripheral lymphoid organs) have tall, cuboidal endothelial cells that express specialized adhesion molecules (peripheral node addressins/MAdCAM-1, PNAd) and chemokines (CCL21/CCL19). Naïve lymphocytes expressing L-selectin and CCR7 adhere to and migrate through these HEVs into the lymph node parenchyma for immune surveillance — lymphocyte homing. HEVs are the primary route of lymphocyte recruitment to lymph nodes under steady-state conditions.

Hepatic sinusoids are derived from the vitelline veins, which form a plexus around the developing hepatic cords. The hepatic cords (derived from endoderm) anastomose around these endothelium-lined spaces to create the characteristic sinusoidal architecture. The sinusoids eventually receive blood from both hepatic artery and portal vein.
questions.question: Hepatic sinusoids are derived from:
Erythropoiesis shifts from the liver to which organ by the end of the 28th week?
questions.explanation: By the 28th week, the spleen has been an important site of hematopoiesis, but hematopoiesis shifts to the bone marrow by the end of this week. Earlier, erythropoiesis occurs primarily in the liver (starting around 6 weeks) and later in the spleen (starting around 12 weeks).

DNA is not a component of the plasma membrane; it resides in the nucleus (and mitochondria/chloroplasts in eukaryotes). The plasma membrane consists of the phospholipid bilayer, integral and peripheral proteins, cholesterol for fluidity regulation, and the glycocalyx (carbohydrate chains of glycoproteins and glycolipids). Confusing membrane components with nuclear components is a common conceptual error.
questions.question: The components of the cell membrane include all of the following EXCEPT which of the following?
Undescended testis (cryptorchidism) most commonly involves:
questions.explanation: Cryptorchidism most commonly involves retention in the inguinal canal (70% of cases). Abdominal retention accounts for about 20%, and other locations 10%. The condition may be bilateral or unilateral (right side more common). Orchiopexy (surgical placement into scrotum) is recommended by 12-18 months to preserve fertility and reduce malignancy risk.

questions.question: The transverse furrow in the alar plate creates which structures?
questions.explanation: A transverse furrow separates the two initial longitudinal elevations in the alar plate marginal layer. This creates 4 colliculi: inferior and superior on both sides. They form the quadrigeminal plate.

questions.question: The optic vesicles develop as outpocketings from which embryonic structure?
questions.explanation: The optic vesicles arise as paired outpocketings from the primitive forebrain during the 4th week of development. These vesicles subsequently invaginate to form the double-walled optic cup. The optic vesicles maintain their attachment to the brain through the optic stalk, which later transforms into the optic nerve.

The pharyngeal constrictor muscles (superior, middle, inferior) are derived from the fourth pharyngeal arch and are innervated by the vagus nerve (CN X) via the pharyngeal plexus. These muscles are essential for swallowing. The stylopharyngeus (from third arch) is innervated by CN IX.
questions.question: The pharyngeal constrictors are innervated by which cranial nerve?

questions.explanation: In portal hypertension (e.g., from liver cirrhosis), increased pressure in the portal venous system is transmitted to the submucosal venous plexus of the lower esophagus via portosystemic anastomoses. This causes dilation of these submucosal veins into esophageal varices. Variceal rupture during vomiting or Valsalva can cause massive, life-threatening upper GI hemorrhage. Endoscopic band ligation or sclerotherapy is used to obliterate these vessels.
questions.question: The esophageal wall contains a rich submucosal venous plexus. In which pathological condition does this plexus become clinically life-threatening?

questions.explanation: The ureter has two smooth muscle layers in its upper two-thirds (inner longitudinal and outer circular) and three layers in its lower third near the bladder (inner longitudinal, middle circular, outer longitudinal). Peristaltic waves generated by pacemaker cells in the renal pelvis propel urine downward toward the bladder. The oblique entry of the ureter into the bladder wall creates a valve mechanism preventing vesicoureteral reflux during bladder filling and micturition.
questions.question: The renal pelvis collects urine from the major calyces and connects to the ureter. What type of smooth muscle arrangement in the ureter drives urine downward by peristalsis?
options: Two layers — inner circular, outer longitudinal throughout
Skeletal muscle in the upper third
No peristalsis — urine flows by gravity alone

questions.explanation: Potter facies is characterized by low-set ears, prominent epicanthal folds, flattened nose, and receding chin, but NOT hypertelorism (widely-spaced eyes). Instead, there is often hypotelorism (closely-spaced eyes). These facial features result from oligohydramnios and compression. The term "Potter sequence" encompasses the full spectrum of oligohydramnios effects including pulmonary hypoplasia and limb deformities.
questions.question: Potter facies is characterized by all EXCEPT:
Most tissues require slicing into thin sections before microscopic examination primarily because of which of the following reasons?
options: To prevent contamination of the specimen
To allow staining solutions to penetrate faster
They are too thick for transmitted light to pass through
To reduce the size of the specimen on the slide
To improve resolution of the electron microscope
questions.explanation: Light microscopy requires transmitted light to pass through specimens, but intact tissues or organs are too thick to allow adequate light transmission. Thin sections, typically 3–10 micrometers, are mounted on glass slides to achieve the translucency required for microscopic examination. This is the fundamental reason for the sectioning step in histological preparation.

The cisterna magna (cerebellomedullary cistern) is the largest subarachnoid cistern, located between the cerebellum, medulla, and occipital bone. It receives CSF from the fourth ventricle via the foramen of Magendie and serves as a major reservoir in the subarachnoid space. The lumbar cistern is also significant, extending from L2 (where the spinal cord ends) to S2 (where the dural sac terminates), containing the cauda equina and serving as the site for lumbar puncture.
questions.question: Which cistern is the largest subarachnoid CSF reservoir?

questions.explanation: Approximately 15% of the cardiac output reaches the brain to sustain its constant metabolic activity and high energy demands. The brain is highly dependent on continuous blood supply, with loss of consciousness occurring within about 5 seconds of interrupted blood flow. Irreversible brain damage occurs if the brain is deprived of blood for more than 4-5 minutes due to its limited capacity for anaerobic metabolism.
questions.question: What percentage of cardiac output normally reaches the brain under physiological conditions?
Congenital lung cysts are formed by:
questions.explanation: Congenital lung cysts are formed by dilation of terminal or larger bronchi. These cysts may be single or multiple and can cause respiratory compromise if large. They result from abnormal branching morphogenesis or obstruction during development. Large cysts may require surgical resection.

questions.question: The basic functional components of a neuron are which of the following?
questions.explanation: Every neuron has three basic structural components: the cell body or soma containing the nucleus and organelles; dendrites which are usually multiple short branching processes that receive incoming signals and are afferent; and a single axon which is typically long conducting signals away from the cell body to targets and is efferent. Additional features include the axon hillock for impulse initiation and synaptic terminals.
options: Cell body, nucleus, and mitochondria only
Soma, Schwann cell, and myelin sheath
Cell body, dendrites (afferent), and a single axon (efferent)
Axon, two dendrites, and a terminal bouton
Node of Ranvier, axon hillock, and synaptic cleft

questions.explanation: Ring chromosomes form when deletions occur at both ends of a chromosome, and the broken ends fuse together to form a ring structure. This results in loss of genetic material from both chromosome arms. The clinical effects depend on which genes are lost.
questions.question: Ring chromosomes result from which process?
The anterolateral system decussates at which level?
questions.explanation: Anterolateral system fibers ascend 1-2 segments after entry before decussating ventral to central canal. This creates a small ipsilateral zone. Decussation is more oblique cervically, transverse lumbosacral.

options: Neutrophils and eosinophils of innate immunity
Megakaryocytes and platelets of the myeloid lineage
Macrophages and dendritic cells of the Mononuclear Phagocyte System
questions.question: Monocytes in the bloodstream are precursors that differentiate into which cell types upon emigrating into tissues?
questions.explanation: Monocytes circulate in blood for 1 to 3 days before emigrating into tissues where they differentiate into tissue-resident macrophages including Kupffer cells, alveolar macrophages, microglia, and osteoclasts, or into dendritic cells depending on tissue-specific signals. This monocyte-macrophage-dendritic cell lineage comprises the MPS. Monocytes are identified by their kidney-shaped nucleus and represent 2 to 8 percent of blood leukocytes.

questions.question: The RET gene mutation is associated with:
questions.explanation: RET gene mutations are associated with Hirschsprung disease. RET is a tyrosine kinase receptor involved in neural crest cell migration. Mutations impair the migration of neural crest cells into the distal colon, resulting in absence of ganglia. Genetic testing can help diagnose and counsel families about recurrence risks.

questions.question: Polyhydramnios may be associated with which fetal condition?
questions.explanation: Polyhydramnios (excessive amniotic fluid, usually >2000 ml) may be associated with esophageal atresia or other conditions that prevent the fetus from swallowing amniotic fluid. It can also occur with anencephaly, where there is excessive CSF production. Oligohydramnios (too little fluid) is associated with renal agenesis.

questions.question: The main sensory nucleus of the trigeminal nerve primarily processes which sensation?
questions.explanation: The main sensory nucleus of the trigeminal nerve, located in the upper pons, processes discriminative (fine) touch and tactile localization from the face, similar to the dorsal column-medial lemniscus system for the body. It receives input from mechanoreceptors via the trigeminal nerve and projects to the contralateral thalamus (VPM nucleus) via the trigeminal lemniscus. The spinal trigeminal nucleus processes pain and temperature, while the mesencephalic nucleus handles proprioception from jaw muscles and teeth.

questions.question: Which of the following disciplines is NOT listed as essential for better knowledge of tissue biology in the context of histological study?
questions.explanation: The core disciplines essential for tissue biology include biochemistry, molecular biology, physiology, immunology, and pathology — but pharmacokinetics is not among them. Pharmacokinetics deals with drug absorption, distribution, and metabolism, which is outside the foundational scope of tissue biology. This distinction is important for understanding the integrative basis of histological science.

options: Diapedesis through capillary and postcapillary venule walls
Rupture of capillary walls during inflammation
questions.question: Leukocytes migrate from blood vessels into connective tissue predominantly through which of the following mechanisms?
questions.explanation: Leukocytes (white blood cells) squeeze through the endothelial cell junctions of capillaries and postcapillary venules into connective tissue by a process called diapedesis (also called extravasation or transmigration). This process increases dramatically during inflammation in response to chemotactic signals. Selectins facilitate initial rolling, integrins mediate firm adhesion, and PECAM-1 facilitates transmigration.

Vascular smooth muscle cells in the tunica media are connected by gap junctions (containing connexins), which allow direct electrical and chemical coupling between adjacent cells for coordinated vasoconstriction and vasodilation. They also have dense bodies (equivalent to Z-lines in striated muscle) on the inner surface of the plasma membrane and in the cytoplasm, which anchor actin and intermediate filaments of the contractile apparatus. This arrangement allows the smooth muscle to generate sustained tension.
questions.question: The tunica media of muscular arteries is composed predominantly of circular smooth muscle cells. These cells are connected to each other and to the extracellular matrix by which junction allowing coordinate contraction?
The midgut loop rotates a total of how many degrees?
questions.explanation: The midgut loop undergoes a total rotation of 270 degrees counterclockwise around the axis of the superior mesenteric artery. An initial 90-degree rotation occurs while in the umbilical cord, followed by an additional 180-degree rotation during return to the abdomen. This rotation is essential for proper intestinal positioning.

ADH and oxytocin are produced by hypothalamic neurons in supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei respectively and released from the posterior pituitary or neurohypophysis not the anterior pituitary. The anterior pituitary or adenohypophysis secretes GH, Prolactin, ACTH, TSH, LH, FSH, and MSH. This distinction is essential for understanding pituitary disorders where anterior and posterior functions are independently affected.
questions.question: The anterior pituitary secretes multiple tropic hormones. Which of the following is correctly identified as a posterior pituitary hormone not an anterior pituitary hormone?
The mucosa of the stomach is protected from self-digestion by a gastric mucosal barrier. Which component is NOT part of this barrier?
questions.explanation: The gastric mucosal barrier consists of: mucus layer (traps bicarbonate), bicarbonate secretion (creates alkaline microenvironment at mucosa surface), tight junctions (prevent acid backflow), rapid cell renewal (replaces damaged cells), and rich blood supply. Pepsinogen granules in chief cells are precursors to the digestive enzyme pepsin — they are part of the digestive mechanism, not the protective barrier. NSAIDs disrupt the barrier by inhibiting prostaglandin synthesis.
options: Mucus layer secreted by surface mucous cells
Bicarbonate secreted beneath the mucous layer
Tight junctions between surface epithelial cells

questions.explanation: Myelination of the white matter begins in the 2nd trimester and continues postnatally. Oligodendrocytes are responsible for myelination in the CNS. They appear as small cells with round deeply stained nuclei.
questions.question: Oligodendrocytes begin myelination in which trimester?

options: Third and body of lateral ventricles
questions.question: Posterior choroidal arteries form choroid plexus of which ventricles?
questions.explanation: Posterior choroidal arteries form choroid plexus of 3rd and body of lateral ventricles. They arise from posterior cerebral artery. The choroid plexus produces cerebrospinal fluid.

The prostatic and membranous parts of the male urethra develop from the pelvic part of the urogenital sinus. The penile (spongy) urethra develops from the phallic part of the UGS. The terminal glandular urethra develops from an ectodermal ingrowth. This explains the different epithelial types along the urethra.
questions.question: The prostatic urethra in males develops from:

questions.explanation: H&E staining is the standard general-purpose histological stain because hematoxylin colors nuclei blue-purple (basophilic structures) while eosin stains cytoplasm, collagen, and other acidophilic structures pink. This combination provides the clearest overview of tissue architecture and cell types. It remains the cornerstone of diagnostic pathology worldwide.
options: It visualizes only collagen fibers selectively
It stains nuclei blue-purple and cytoplasm/collagen pink
It specifically marks reticular fibers black
It detects polysaccharides by turning them red
It requires no prior fixation of the tissue
questions.question: Which of the following characteristics makes hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining the most commonly used technique in routine histology?
A vitelline fistula is characterized by:
questions.explanation: A vitelline fistula represents complete persistence of the vitelline duct, creating a communication between the ileum and umbilicus. Meconium (intestinal contents) oozes out of the umbilicus. This requires surgical repair to close the fistula and restore intestinal continuity. It differs from a urachal fistula, which would drain urine.

The mammillary nuclei (medial and lateral) belong to the posterior hypothalamic group and are visible as paired prominences on the inferior surface of the hypothalamus. These nuclei receive input from the hippocampus via the fornix and project to the anterior thalamic nuclei via the mammillothalamic tract, forming a key link in the Papez circuit. The mammillary nuclei are involved in memory processing and learning; their damage (as in Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome) causes severe memory impairment.
questions.question: The mammillary nuclei are part of which hypothalamic group?
What characterizes the venous drainage system of the brain compared to systemic veins?
questions.explanation: Cerebral veins and dural sinuses lack valves, unlike systemic veins, making them susceptible to retrograde flow and thrombosis propagation. This valve-less system allows blood to flow in either direction depending on pressure gradients. The sinuses are lined only by endothelium without smooth muscle, making them rigid channels that don't collapse. This anatomy means infections can spread readily through the venous system, and elevated intracranial pressure directly impedes venous drainage, potentially worsening cerebral edema.

questions.question: The claustrum is shaped like which structure?
questions.explanation: The claustrum is a saucer-shaped thin lamina of gray matter lateral to putamen. It is separated from the putamen by external capsule. Its function remains somewhat unclear.

The cardiac and vasomotor centers are located in the medulla oblongata. The reticular formation helps automatically regulate beating of the heart, breathing and respiratory functions, and digestion in the gastrointestinal tract via these centers. These are vital autonomic functions.
questions.question: The cardiac and vasomotor centers are located in which part of the brainstem?

options: Hyaline cartilage, elastic cartilage, and vitreous body
questions.explanation: Type II collagen is the principal collagen of cartilage (both hyaline and elastic types) and the vitreous body of the eye. Its fibrils are finer than type I collagen and are embedded in the proteoglycan-rich cartilage matrix. Chondrocytes are the cell type that synthesizes type II collagen. Autoimmune destruction of type II collagen characterizes relapsing polychondritis and contributes to joint cartilage loss in rheumatoid arthritis.
questions.question: Type II collagen is specifically found in which of the following tissue locations?

questions.explanation: The mesonephros functions as an interim kidney for approximately 4 weeks (from weeks 6-10 of development). It appears late in the 4th week and degenerates toward the end of the first trimester. In males, some caudal tubules persist to form parts of the reproductive system, but in females, the mesonephros disappears almost completely.
questions.question: The mesonephros functions for approximately how many weeks?

questions.explanation: The ANS is the visceral motor division controlling involuntary functions including heart rate, digestion, glandular secretion, smooth muscle tone, and pupil size. It uses a two-neuron chain where a preganglionic neuron in the CNS synapses in an autonomic ganglion on a postganglionic neuron that innervates the target organ, unlike the somatic motor system using a single motor neuron. The ANS subdivides into sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions.
options: The ANS uses myelinated fibers exclusively
The ANS controls voluntary skeletal muscle contractions
The ANS is located only in the brain without peripheral components
The ANS uses only a single neuron between CNS and target
Two-neuron chains controlling involuntary visceral functions below conscious awareness
questions.question: The autonomic nervous system is distinguished from the somatic nervous system primarily by which of the following?

questions.explanation: All lymphatic drainage ultimately returns to the bloodstream via the thoracic duct (draining left body below the diaphragm, left head/neck/arm) emptying into the left subclavian-jugular angle, and the right lymphatic duct (draining right head/neck/arm, right thorax) emptying into the right subclavian-jugular angle. This return of lymph to the venous circulation maintains plasma volume, returns plasma proteins, and allows immune cells to recirculate.
questions.question: The lymphatic system begins with lymphatic capillaries in tissues. These ultimately drain into lymphatic ducts that empty into the venous circulation at which anatomical sites?

questions.explanation: The sliding filament model explains contraction through cross-bridge cycling: calcium binds troponin exposing myosin-binding sites on actin; myosin heads attach to actin; the power stroke pivots the head pulling actin toward the M line; ATP binding causes myosin head release; and ATP hydrolysis re-cocks the head. Repeated cycling slides actin over myosin, shortening the sarcomere without changing the length of individual filaments.
questions.question: In the sliding filament model of muscle contraction, shortening of the sarcomere is produced by which molecular events?
options: Shortening of individual myosin and actin filaments
Enzymatic degradation of titin elastic proteins
Disassembly of Z line proteins releasing actin filaments
Cross-bridge cycling: myosin heads bind actin, pivot, release, and re-cock
Calcium directly shortening thick filaments through conformational change

questions.question: The vagina is lined by stratified squamous epithelium that is not keratinized. The glycogen content of vaginal epithelial cells is metabolized by Lactobacillus species to lactic acid, maintaining the vaginal pH at:
questions.explanation: Lactobacillus species (dominant members of the normal vaginal microbiome) metabolize glycogen stored in vaginal epithelial cells to lactic acid. This maintains vaginal pH at approximately 3.8–4.5 — an acidic environment that inhibits colonization by pathogenic bacteria and fungi. Estrogen promotes glycogen deposition in vaginal epithelium; postmenopausal women have reduced estrogen, less glycogen, and higher vaginal pH, predisposing to atrophic vaginitis and bacterial vaginosis.

options: Permanent irreversible change in the neuron membrane composition
Passive diffusion of glucose across the neuronal membrane
Release of neurotransmitters directly into the bloodstream
Synthesis of new proteins at the axon terminal
Voltage-gated sodium channels open, causing sodium influx and rapid depolarization
questions.explanation: The action potential begins when membrane depolarization reaches threshold activating voltage-gated sodium channels, causing rapid sodium influx down its electrochemical gradient from high extracellular to low intracellular concentration. This rapid sodium entry reverses the membrane potential from approximately -70 mV to +30 mV. Subsequent potassium efflux through delayed rectifier channels repolarizes the membrane. The all-or-nothing nature ensures signal fidelity over long axonal distances.
questions.question: An action potential in a neuron is characterized as a reversal of the ionic gradient propagated along the neuronal plasma membrane. What triggers the initial depolarization?

questions.explanation: The kidneys "ascend" from the pelvis to the abdomen primarily due to disproportionate growth in the caudal region of the embryo. As the lumbar and sacral regions grow, the kidneys appear to move cranially. They attain their adult position by the 9th week and simultaneously rotate medially approximately 90 degrees.
questions.question: The kidneys ascend from the pelvis to the abdomen primarily due to:

questions.explanation: The fornix is the main output pathway of the hippocampus, formed by continuation of the fimbria as a flat band of white matter. The columns of the fornix pass anteriorly to reach the septal nuclei and mammillary bodies, while posterior projections reach the thalamus. The fornix is a crucial component of the Papez circuit, connecting the hippocampus with other limbic structures involved in memory processing and emotional regulation.
questions.question: Which structure forms the main output pathway of the hippocampus?
The lens develops in response to induction from which structure?
questions.explanation: The lens develops from surface ectoderm in response to induction from the optic vesicle (an outgrowth of the diencephalon). The optic vesicle induces the overlying ectoderm to form the lens placode, which then invaginates to form the lens vesicle.

The pupillary light reflex develops during 30-34 weeks as the nervous system matures. At this stage, the upper and lower limbs have a chubby appearance, the skin is pink and smooth, and infants born at 32 weeks usually survive with proper medical care.
questions.question: The pupillary light reflex develops during which weeks?
Basophils in blood circulation are functionally similar to mast cells in tissues. They share which structural and functional characteristics?
options: Both have IgE receptors and histamine-filled basophilic granules mediating allergy
Both are derived from identical progenitor cells in bone marrow
Both undergo fusion to form multinucleated giant cells
Both are phagocytic cells that can kill intracellular bacteria
Both produce type I collagen for wound repair
questions.explanation: Basophils in blood and mast cells in tissues share: high-affinity IgE receptors FcεRI; large basophilic granules containing histamine heparin and proteases; and the ability to mediate IgE-dependent immediate hypersensitivity reactions upon antigen-IgE crosslinking. Despite these functional similarities they are separate lineages from different progenitors. Basophils originate from common myeloid progenitors while mast cells arise from a distinct progenitor that matures in tissues under local signals.

options: Neural crest cells for all muscle types
questions.question: Muscle cells are described as being of mesodermal origin. This means all three muscle types derive from which embryonic germ layer?
questions.explanation: All three muscle types are of mesodermal origin, differentiating from mesodermal precursor cells during embryogenesis. Skeletal muscle derives from paraxial mesoderm in somites; cardiac muscle from splanchnic lateral plate mesoderm; and smooth muscle from lateral plate mesoderm and splanchnic mesoderm. Neural crest cells contribute to smooth muscle of head and neck blood vessels but the primary origin of muscle is mesodermal.

The juxtaglomerular apparatus develops from specialized cells in the distal convoluted tubule (macula densa) and the afferent arteriole (juxtaglomerular cells). This structure regulates renal blood flow and glomerular filtration rate through the renin-angiotensin system. It forms during late fetal development and continues maturing postnatally. The JGA is important for blood pressure regulation and fluid homeostasis.
questions.question: The juxtaglomerular apparatus develops from:

questions.explanation: Motor neurons with meter-long axons cannot rely on diffusion to supply synaptic terminals with neurotransmitters, organelles, and trophic factors synthesized in the cell body. Fast anterograde axonal transport (via kinesin on microtubule tracks at ~400 mm/day) and retrograde transport (via dynein at ~200 mm/day) are essential for neuronal survival and function. Disruption of axonal transport underlies several neurodegenerative diseases.
options: The need for axonal transport to deliver organelles from cell body to distant terminals
The necessity for multiple nuclei to support such a long cell
The requirement for lysosomes at each node of Ranvier
The generation of a large number of synaptic vesicles in the cell body only
The need for peroxisomes to oxidize myelin along the axon length
questions.question: A neuron with an axon 1 meter long (e.g., motor neuron to the foot) demonstrates which cellular challenge most dramatically?

questions.explanation: Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) is the most compatible with survival to term and beyond among autosomal trisomies. Trisomies 13 and 18 are compatible with survival to term but usually result in death within the first year. Most other autosomal trisomies are lethal in utero.
questions.question: Which autosomal trisomy is most compatible with survival to term?
The hippocampus is important for which function?
questions.explanation: The hippocampus is important for memory formation, especially declarative memory. It is part of the limbic system. Bilateral damage causes anterograde amnesia. It is affected early in Alzheimer disease.

questions.question: The reticular formation consists of approximately how many nuclei?
questions.explanation: The reticular formation consists of more than 100,000 brainstem nuclei. These nuclei are divided into three subgroups: paramedian nuclear group, central/medial column group (magnocellular), and lateral group (parvocellular column). They acquire different names in different parts of the brainstem.

options: Functional obstruction with failure of relaxation
questions.question: Hirschsprung's disease results from absence of the myenteric and submucosal plexuses in a segment of colon. This leads to which functional consequence?
questions.explanation: In Hirschsprung's disease, absence of ganglion cells (aganglionosis) in the myenteric and submucosal plexuses of the affected bowel segment means it cannot relax — it remains in a state of tonic contraction, creating a functional obstruction. The proximal bowel dilates massively (megacolon) due to retained feces and gas. Diagnosis requires rectal biopsy showing absence of ganglion cells. Treatment is surgical resection of the aganglionic segment.

The external auditory meatus develops from the dorsal portion of the first pharyngeal cleft, forming the meatal plug. Initially, the epithelium proliferates and fills the meatus temporarily. Later recanalization occurs to establish the patent external auditory canal.
questions.question: The external auditory meatus develops from which pharyngeal structure?
Ureteropelvic junction obstruction most commonly results from:
questions.explanation: Ureteropelvic (UPJ) obstruction in children most commonly results from intrinsic narrowing or a crossing vessel (accessory lower pole renal artery) compressing the ureter. UPJ obstruction is the most common cause of hydronephrosis detected on prenatal ultrasound. Treatment (pyeloplasty) is indicated for symptoms, progressive hydronephrosis, or declining renal function.

The cerebellum coordinates movement by continuously comparing intended movements (from motor cortex via pontocerebellar pathway) with actual movements (from proprioceptive feedback via spinocerebellar pathways). This comparison allows error detection and correction, enabling smooth, accurate movements. The climbing fiber system from the inferior olive provides error signals when movement doesn't match intention, driving motor learning and adaptation. This feed-forward control allows anticipatory adjustments and explains why cerebellar damage causes intention tremor as movements progress.
questions.question: The cerebellum coordinates movement by comparing:

questions.explanation: M cells (microfold cells) overlie the dome epithelium of Peyer's patches in the ileum. They lack a brush border, have an irregular apical surface with short microfolds, and contain a basolateral pocket housing lymphocytes and macrophages. M cells transcytose luminal antigens, bacteria, and viruses to the underlying lymphoid tissue for immune processing. Pathogens such as Salmonella, Yersinia, and poliovirus exploit M cells as entry points into the body.
questions.question: In the ileum, specialized cells overlie Peyer's patches and sample luminal antigens. These are the:

options: Both by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium
Endocervix by transitional epithelium; ectocervix by simple columnar
Endocervix by simple columnar mucus-secreting epithelium
Endocervix by pseudostratified ciliated columnar; ectocervix by keratinized squamous
questions.explanation: The endocervix (canal) is lined by simple columnar mucus-secreting epithelium with endocervical glands (Nabothian follicles when obstructed). The ectocervix (visible portion) is lined by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium continuous with the vagina. The squamocolumnar junction (SCJ/transformation zone) is where these two epithelia meet, and is the critical zone where most cervical intraepithelial neoplasias (CIN) and invasive cervical cancers originate, particularly after HPV infection.
questions.question: The endocervix is lined by which epithelium, while the ectocervix is lined by what type?
The brainstem consists of which three parts?
questions.explanation: The brainstem consists of three parts: the midbrain (mesencephalon), pons (part of metencephalon), and medulla oblongata (myelencephalon). The brainstem is the lowest part of the brain, acting as a pathway between the upper brain and spinal cord, and containing centers for vital functions.

questions.question: The semicircular canals develop from which portion of the otic vesicle?
questions.explanation: Three disc-like flattened outpocketings develop from the utricular portion of the otic vesicle to form the semicircular canals. The central portions of these outpocketings oppose and fuse, then disappear, leaving the peripheral unfused parts. These peripheral portions become the semicircular ducts housed within the semicircular canals.

questions.question: The extraembryonic mesoderm adjacent to the cytotrophoblast is termed which type?
questions.explanation: Extraembryonic mesoderm adjacent to the cytotrophoblast (and amnion) is called somatopleuric extraembryonic mesoderm. Extraembryonic mesoderm adjacent to the primitive yolk sac is called splanchnopleuric extraembryonic mesoderm. These terms are analogous to the intraembryonic mesoderm layers.

questions.question: The process of erythropoiesis involves a series of precursor stages. Which of the following correctly sequences erythroid development from earliest to most mature in bone marrow?
questions.explanation: Erythropoiesis progresses: proerythroblast (large cell with prominent nucleolus basophilic cytoplasm) to basophilic erythroblast (active ribosome synthesis) to polychromatic erythroblast (hemoglobin accumulation mixed colors) to orthochromatic erythroblast (pyknotic nucleus pink cytoplasm) where the nucleus is extruded to form a reticulocyte (still contains ribosomes staining with supravital dyes) which matures into an erythrocyte. This 5 to 7 day process is driven by erythropoietin from the kidney.
options: Proerythroblast → basophilic → polychromatic → orthochromatic erythroblast → reticulocyte → erythrocyte
Myeloblast then promyelocyte then myelocyte then metamyelocyte then erythrocyte
Lymphoblast then prolymphocyte then lymphocyte then erythrocyte
Stem cell directly producing mature erythrocytes without intermediate stages

questions.question: Which thalamic nuclei group projects to the cingulate gyrus?
questions.explanation: The anterior nuclei group of the thalamus receives afferents from the mammillary bodies via the mammillothalamic tract and projects to the cingulate gyrus, forming part of the Papez circuit involved in emotion and memory. These nuclei are separated from other thalamic groups by the anterior limbs of the internal medullary lamina. The anterior nuclei are part of the limbic system and play a role in regulating emotional tone and recent memory.

questions.question: The inferior olivary nucleus is characterized by what shape when viewed in cross-section?
questions.explanation: The inferior olivary nucleus appears as a crenated C-shaped strip of gray matter with its open end (hilus) facing the opposite cerebellar peduncle. This distinctive folded appearance is easily recognizable in cross-sections of the open medulla. The inferior olivary nucleus receives input from multiple sources and projects climbing fibers to the contralateral cerebellar cortex via the inferior cerebellar peduncle, playing a crucial role in motor learning.

Hair development first becomes recognizable in the eyebrows, upper lip, and chin regions, beginning around the 9th-12th week. Hair does not become easily visible until approximately the 20th week. This craniocaudal progression reflects the general pattern of embryonic development.
questions.question: Hair follicle development begins in which body regions first?

questions.explanation: The thalamus comprises approximately 80% of the diencephalon and forms most of the lateral wall of the third ventricle. It is the largest collection of gray matter within the cerebral hemisphere and serves as a major relay and integration center for sensory and motor information. The remaining diencephalon consists of the hypothalamus (forming the lower lateral wall and floor), epithalamus (including the pineal gland and habenula), and subthalamus.
questions.question: The thalamus comprises what percentage of the diencephalon?

options: Lateral lingual swellings and tuberculum impar
questions.explanation: The anterior two-thirds of the tongue is formed by fusion of the two lateral lingual swellings and the tuberculum impar (first median swelling). The posterior one-third is formed by the cranial part of the hypobranchial eminence (second median swelling called the cupola).
questions.question: The anterior two-thirds of the tongue is formed by fusion of which structures?

questions.explanation: Appendices epiploicae are small peritoneal pouches filled with adipose tissue attached to the outer surface of the colon along the teniae coli. They are a distinctive anatomical feature of the large intestine absent in the small intestine and rectum. Torsion or infarction of appendices epiploicae can mimic acute appendicitis or diverticulitis clinically.
questions.question: Appendices epiploicae are small fat-filled peritoneal pouches on the surface of the colon. Their histological composition is:
Which of the following correctly classifies connective tissue into its two main fiber systems?
options: Collagen, reticular, and elastic fiber systems
Only collagen fibers and only elastic fibers
Reticular and smooth muscle fiber systems
Type I and Type II collagen systems only
questions.explanation: The two fiber systems in connective tissue are the collagen system (comprising collagen fibers and reticular fibers, both made of collagen protein) and the elastic system (comprising elastic, elaunin, and oxytalan fibers containing elastin and fibrillin). Collagen provides tensile strength while elastic fibers allow extensibility and recoil. The classification into these two systems reflects both compositional and functional differences.

questions.question: Describe the key difference between Type I and Type II pneumocytes in the lung alveolar lining.
options: Type I pneumocytes produce surfactant while Type II provide structural coverage
Type II pneumocytes line 95 percent of the alveolar surface while Type I produce mucus
Type I cells are cuboidal with abundant lamellar bodies while Type II cells are squamous
Type I pneumocytes cover 95% of alveolar surface for gas exchange; Type II produce surfactant
questions.explanation: Type I pneumocytes are extremely thin squamous cells covering approximately 95% of the alveolar surface area providing the minimum diffusion distance for gas exchange. Type II pneumocytes are cuboidal cells occupying only 5% of the surface but constituting approximately 60% of alveolar epithelial cells by number. Type II cells produce pulmonary surfactant stored in lamellar bodies and released by exocytosis to reduce alveolar surface tension and prevent collapse. Type II cells also serve as progenitors replacing Type I cells after injury.
The nucleus is large, pale staining with a prominent nucleolus (RNA store). It is surrounded by a double-layered membrane. The nucleolus produces ribosomal RNA.
questions.question: The nucleus of a neuron contains which structure prominently?
The minor calyces are formed from:
questions.explanation: The minor calyces are formed from enlarged third and fourth generation branches of the ureteric bud, which absorb the collecting tubules of these generations. The second generation forms major calyces, and the first division forms the renal pelvis. Subsequent generations (5th onward) form collecting tubules and ducts. Understanding this branching pattern helps explain calyceal anatomy and anomalies.

Renal arteries are considered end arteries because they have no significant anastomoses with other vessels - each segmental artery supplies a specific renal segment without collateral circulation. Occlusion of a renal artery or its branches causes infarction of the supplied tissue. This is clinically important during surgery, trauma, or embolism. Accessory renal arteries are also end arteries and must be preserved.
questions.question: Renal arteries are considered end arteries because:
The processus vaginalis normally:
questions.explanation: The processus vaginalis, an evagination of peritoneum that precedes testicular descent through the inguinal canal, normally obliterates after testicular descent (except for portion covering testis = tunica vaginalis). Patent processus vaginalis allows communication between peritoneal cavity and scrotum, predisposing to indirect inguinal hernia or hydrocele. Obliteration usually occurs shortly before or after birth.

questions.question: The azygos lobe is an accessory lobe of the right lung created by an anomalous azygos vein cutting through the lung tissue. Histologically, the tissue within the azygos lobe is:
questions.explanation: The azygos lobe is an anatomical variant (found in approximately 1% of people) where the azygos vein migrates through the lung during development, carrying a double layer of pleura (visceral and parietal) with it to form an accessory fissure. The tissue within the azygos lobe is otherwise completely normal pulmonary parenchyma. It is clinically significant because it can be mistaken for a pathological lesion on chest radiography and may complicate surgical procedures.

questions.question: Which neurotransmitters are involved in basal ganglia pathways?
questions.explanation: Several neurotransmitters are involved in different basal ganglia pathways including acetylcholine, dopamine, glutamate, and serotonin. This chemical complexity allows fine motor control. Neurotransmitter imbalances cause movement disorders.

questions.question: Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis is characterized by accumulation of surfactant lipids and proteins in alveoli. The deficiency that causes most cases is:
options: Deficiency of surfactant proteins A and D
Excess production of type I collagen
Loss of ciliary function in bronchioles
questions.explanation: Most cases of pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (PAP) are autoimmune, caused by antibodies against granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF). GM-CSF is required for terminal differentiation and surfactant-catabolizing function of alveolar macrophages. Without functional GM-CSF signaling, macrophages cannot clear surfactant, which accumulates in alveoli. Histologically, alveoli are filled with PAS-positive, acellular, granular material. Treatment is whole-lung lavage.

options: Dense mucin granules in the cytoplasm
High content of rough ER for protein
questions.question: Zymogenic (chief) cells contain abundant basophilic rough endoplasmic reticulum and produce pepsinogen. The basophilia of these cells reflects which feature?
questions.explanation: Chief (zymogenic) cells are basophilic because they contain an extensive rough endoplasmic reticulum (rER) for the high-volume synthesis and processing of the zymogen pepsinogen. The rER contains RNA, which stains basophilically with hematoxylin. Apical acidophilic zymogen granules are also present. This combination of basal basophilia with apical granules is the hallmark of zymogenic/serous cells throughout the body.

questions.question: Which of the following describes the histological appearance of the spleen when the organ is freshly sectioned, without tissue processing?
options: Entirely white throughout with no distinction between areas
Entirely red pulp throughout without white pulp areas
Yellow-gray coloration throughout due to extensive adipose tissue infiltration
Uniformly brown from bile pigment and hemosiderin accumulation
Dark red pulp from blood cells and white-gray nodules of white pulp
questions.explanation: A fresh cut section of the spleen shows easily distinguishable red pulp which appears dark red due to its massive blood content in sinuses and cords, and white pulp which appears as white or gray nodular areas along the branches of the splenic artery. The white pulp lymphoid nodules were originally described as Malpighian bodies or corpuscles in the unfixed spleen where this macroscopic distinction is most visible. Processing changes these appearances.

The decidua basalis forms the maternal portion of the placenta. The fetal portion is formed by the chorion frondosum. The decidua basalis is the part of the endometrium located beneath the implanted embryo, where maternal blood vessels are modified to supply the placenta.
questions.question: The decidua basalis forms which part of the placenta?

questions.explanation: The genu of the internal capsule contains corticonuclear (corticobulbar) fibers traveling from the cerebral cortex to motor nuclei of cranial nerves in the brainstem. These fibers control voluntary movements of facial muscles, tongue, pharynx, and larynx. Lesions of the genu can result in dysarthria, dysphagia, and facial weakness, particularly affecting muscles of the lower face contralaterally due to the predominantly crossed nature of these projections.
questions.question: Fibers in the genu of the internal capsule primarily belong to which system?

questions.explanation: Rods number approximately 120 million and contain rhodopsin, are extremely sensitive to low light, provide monochromatic peripheral vision, and are distributed throughout the retina except the fovea. Cones number approximately 6 to 7 million and come in three types for trichromatic color vision concentrated at the fovea centralis for maximum visual acuity. Cone-dominated foveal vision requires bright light.
options: Rods provide color vision and cones detect low light and movement
Both rods and cones function identically in all light conditions
Rods detect dim light and provide achromatic vision; cones detect color and high-acuity vision
Rods are concentrated at the fovea centralis and cones are in the peripheral retina
Only cones are present in humans as rods are vestigial structures
questions.question: The retina's rods and cones differ in which of the following ways?
The adrenal gland's zona glomerulosa produces aldosterone regulated by the renin-angiotensin system. Which stimulus directly acts on zona glomerulosa cells to stimulate aldosterone production?
options: ACTH from the anterior pituitary exclusively
Low serum sodium without any other stimulus
Cortisol feedback through negative feedback mechanism
Angiotensin II and elevated potassium stimulating zona glomerulosa cells
questions.explanation: Zona glomerulosa aldosterone synthesis is regulated by two primary stimuli: angiotensin II generated by the renin-angiotensin system in response to decreased renal perfusion, decreased sodium, or sympathetic activation; and elevated serum potassium which directly depolarizes zona glomerulosa cells opening calcium channels. While ACTH provides permissive support for aldosterone production in stress, the principal regulators are angiotensin II and potassium. Aldosterone increases renal sodium reabsorption and potassium excretion.

questions.question: The first breath after birth is initiated primarily by:
questions.explanation: The first breath after birth is initiated primarily by increased carbon dioxide levels and decreased pH in the blood, which stimulate respiratory centers in the brainstem. Other factors include temperature change, tactile stimulation, and decreased oxygen. Surfactant facilitates breathing but does not initiate it.

The Papez circuit is a closed neural loop starting and ending in the hippocampus: hippocampus → fornix → mammillary bodies → mammillothalamic tract → anterior thalamic nuclei → internal capsule → cingulate gyrus → cingulum → parahippocampal gyrus/entorhinal cortex → hippocampus. This circuit was originally proposed as the anatomical substrate for emotion but is now recognized as crucial for memory formation and retrieval. Damage to any component can cause memory impairment.
questions.question: The Papez circuit begins and ends in which structure?

options: One or two centrally placed nuclei
Multiple peripherally placed nuclei like skeletal muscle
A single very large lobulated nucleus
Multiple nuclei arranged only at the intercalated disc
questions.explanation: Cardiomyocytes are mononucleated and occasionally binucleated cells with centrally placed nuclei, in contrast to skeletal muscle fibers with multiple peripheral nuclei reflecting their syncytial origin from myoblast fusion. The central nuclear position in cardiac muscle reflects that cardiomyocytes are individual cells joined at intercalated discs rather than true syncytia. This distinction is diagnostically useful in differentiating cardiac from skeletal muscle in tissue sections.
questions.question: Cardiac muscle cells have which of the following nuclear arrangement that distinguishes them from skeletal muscle fibers?

questions.explanation: Microtubules (25 nm diameter, hollow cylinders of tubulin dimers) provide structural rigidity to maintain cell shape and serve as tracks for motor proteins (kinesins and dyneins) carrying organelles and vesicles throughout the cell. They also form the mitotic spindle during cell division. Their dynamic instability allows rapid reorganization in response to cellular needs.
questions.question: Microtubules within the cytoskeleton serve which of the following primary functions?
options: Provide the contractile force for muscle contraction
Generate cell surface projections like microvilli
Provide rigidity and tracks for organelle movement

questions.question: Neuroblasts in the mantle layer of the spinal cord give rise to which structure?
questions.explanation: Neuroepithelial cells of the spinal cord first produce neuroblasts which form the mantle layer, which becomes the gray matter of the spinal cord. The marginal layer contains nerve fibers and becomes the white matter when myelinated. Ependymal cells line the central canal.

questions.question: The alar plate houses neurons for which function?
questions.explanation: The dorsal alar plate houses neurons that subserve sensory modalities throughout the CNS. The ventral basal plate houses neurons for motor modalities. This dorsoventral organization is maintained throughout the spinal cord and brainstem.

questions.question: The sinoatrial (SA) node is located in the wall of the right atrium. The artery supplying the SA node arises from which coronary artery in most individuals?
questions.explanation: The sinoatrial nodal artery supplies the SA node and arises from the right coronary artery (RCA) in approximately 55–60% of individuals and from the left circumflex artery in the remaining 40–45%. This is clinically important because RCA territory myocardial infarctions (inferior MI) can cause sinus node dysfunction (bradycardia, sick sinus syndrome). Understanding coronary artery anatomy and conduction system blood supply is essential for interpreting ECG changes in MI.

Meckel's cartilage is the cartilage of the first pharyngeal arch, specifically in the mandibular process (dorsal part). The mesenchyme surrounding Meckel's cartilage forms the mandible. Meckel's cartilage itself forms the anterior ligament of malleus and the sphenomandibular ligament.
questions.question: Meckel's cartilage is found in which pharyngeal arch?
Dendrites are characterized by high density of which proteins?
questions.explanation: Dendrites have high density of ribosomes and cytoskeletal proteins (neurofilaments). They increase surface area and have dendritic spines. The number of inputs depends on dendritic arbor complexity.

Superior sagittal sinus thrombosis typically presents with bilateral leg weakness (and possibly paraplegia) because the parasagittal cortex containing leg motor and sensory areas drains into this sinus. Venous infarction of these areas causes bilateral lower extremity deficits. Additional features include headache, seizures, papilledema from elevated intracranial pressure, and potential hemorrhagic infarction. The presentation may be subacute, distinguishing it from arterial stroke, and requires imaging showing the absence of flow in the sinus.
questions.question: Thrombosis of the superior sagittal sinus typically presents with what finding?
The endometrium in the proliferative phase is stimulated by estrogen from developing follicles. Which histological changes characterize this phase?
questions.explanation: During the proliferative phase (days 5–14), rising estrogen levels stimulate endometrial growth: glands multiply and become slightly tortuous, stromal cells proliferate actively (mitoses visible), and the endometrium thickens from ~0.5mm (just after menstruation) to ~5mm. In the early proliferative phase, glands are narrow and straight; they become more tortuous later. This phase is dominated by mitotic activity in preparation for the secretory (luteal) phase.
options: Proliferation of glands (becoming slightly tortuous), mitoses in glands
Straight glands with narrow lumens and compact stroma; thin endometrium
Coiled (spiral) glands with secretory vacuoles, subnuclear glycogen

questions.question: The principal route of venous drainage is through which system?
options: Cerebral veins to dural sinuses to internal jugular
questions.explanation: The principal venous drainage route is through cerebral veins into dural venous sinuses and ultimately internal jugular vein. Emissary veins connect extracranial veins with dural sinuses. A basilar plexus also exists.

questions.question: Schwann cells myelinate axons in which location?
questions.explanation: Myelination is a function of Schwann cells in axons outside the spinal cord. The portion within the SC is myelinated by oligodendrocytes. This division of labor distinguishes peripheral from central myelination.

questions.question: The ventral pancreatic bud gives rise to:
questions.explanation: The ventral pancreatic bud gives rise to the uncinate process and part of the head of the pancreas. The dorsal bud forms most of the pancreas including the body, tail, and remainder of the head. The two buds fuse as the duodenum rotates, bringing the ventral bud dorsally.
options: Uncinate process and part of head

questions.explanation: The umbilical cord typically contains two arteries and one vein surrounded by Wharton's jelly. The umbilical arteries carry deoxygenated blood from the fetus to the placenta, while the umbilical vein carries oxygenated blood from the placenta to the fetus. Single umbilical artery is associated with congenital anomalies.
questions.question: The umbilical cord typically contains how many blood vessels?

questions.explanation: Reticular fibers, composed mainly of type III collagen, are not visible in routine H&E preparations but are stained black by silver impregnation due to their argyrophilic nature. This property reflects their high carbohydrate content associated with the sugar chains on these fibers. PAS also stains them positively due to the same sugar chain content.
questions.question: Reticular fibers are best visualized in histological sections by impregnation with which of the following staining methods?

options: Absence of associated ribosomes on its cytoplasmic surface
Role in lipid synthesis and detoxification
Ribosomes-studded membrane for secretory and membrane protein synthesis
Located only in the cell periphery near the plasma membrane
Serves as the primary site of ATP production
