It is invariably lethal due to pulmonary insufficiency. Amniotic fluid is essential for normal fetal lung development.

Juxtamedullary nephrons (approximately 15% of nephrons) have long loops of Henle that penetrate deep into the medulla. Their long ascending limbs actively transport more NaCl, creating a deeper and steeper medullary osmotic gradient. This allows the formation of highly concentrated urine when ADH is present. The vasa recta, which run alongside these loops, maintain this gradient via countercurrent exchange.
questions.question: The kidney has cortical and juxtamedullary nephrons. Juxtamedullary nephrons have longer loops of Henle that extend deeper into the medulla. Their primary functional advantage is:

questions.explanation: The bulbus cordis gives rise to the smooth part of the right ventricle, while the primitive ventricle forms the trabeculated parts of both ventricles. The proximal part of the bulbus is called the conus cordis, and the distal part is the truncus arteriosus, which is continuous with the aortic sac.
questions.question: The bulbus cordis eventually forms which adult heart structure?

The cell division process by which a single-celled fertilized egg ultimately develops into a mature organism and by which certain tissues (skin, blood) are continuously renewed is best described as which of the following?
questions.explanation: The cell-division cycle is both the mechanism for embryonic development from a single fertilized egg and the continuous renewal of cells in self-renewing tissues like skin and blood. Disruption of this cycle underlies both developmental defects and malignancies. Terminal differentiation, by contrast, is the process by which cells stop dividing and specialize.

The blastocyst consists of an outer cell layer (trophoblast) and a group of centrally located cells called the inner cell mass or embryoblast. The embryoblast gives rise to the embryo proper, while the trophoblast gives rise to the chorion and ultimately the fetal part of the placenta.
questions.question: The inner cell mass of the blastocyst is also termed which structure?

questions.explanation: Exstrophy of the bladder is a ventral body wall defect in which bladder mucosa is exposed externally. This rare anomaly (2/100,000 live births) results from failure of mesoderm migration to the ventral midline. The exposed bladder mucosa is continuous with abdominal skin, and the condition requires surgical correction.
questions.question: Exstrophy of the bladder is characterized by:

questions.explanation: The pectinate line marks the junction between endodermal and ectodermal portions of the anal canal. Above this line, the anal canal is endodermal (from hindgut), while below it is ectodermal (from proctodeum). This junction has clinical significance regarding blood supply, innervation, lymphatic drainage, and epithelial type.
questions.question: The pectinate line in the anal canal marks the junction between:
The collateral eminence in the lateral ventricle is caused by indentation from which structure?
questions.explanation: The collateral eminence is a bulge on the floor of the posterior and inferior horns of the lateral ventricle caused by the indentation of the collateral sulcus from the inferior surface of the temporal lobe. This eminence runs longitudinally along the floor lateral to the hippocampus in the inferior horn. The collateral sulcus on the brain's inferior surface creates this inward bulge into the ventricular cavity.
Corticospinal fibers run in the anterior 2/3rd of posterior limb of internal capsule. They occupy the middle 2/3rd of midbrain crus. Cranial fibers are more medial than caudal fibers.
questions.question: Corticospinal fibers occupy which part of the internal capsule?
The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies which pharyngeal arch?
questions.explanation: The recurrent laryngeal nerve, a branch of the vagus nerve (CN X), supplies the sixth pharyngeal arch. The superior laryngeal nerve supplies the fourth arch. These nerves innervate the muscles and provide sensation to structures derived from their respective arches.

Binary fission is the asexual reproductive process of prokaryotes where a cell copies its single circular chromosome and splits into two identical daughter cells. Unlike eukaryotic mitosis, it does not involve a nuclear membrane, spindle apparatus, or condensed chromosomes. It is the primary method of reproduction in bacteria.
questions.question: Cell division in prokaryotes, which lack a nucleus, occurs by a process termed which of the following?

options: Mitochondria with chromatolysis indicating increased ATP demand
Golgi apparatus with chromatolysis indicating secretory cell activation
Lipofuscin granules with chromatolysis indicating cellular aging
Rough ER with ribosomes; chromatolysis indicates neuronal injury after axonal damage
Melanin granules with chromatolysis indicating decreased dopamine production
questions.question: The Nissl substance visible in neuronal cell bodies corresponds to which ultrastructural organelle and what does its dissolution (chromatolysis) indicate?
questions.explanation: Nissl bodies are stacks of rough ER visible with basic dyes in neuronal cell bodies reflecting the neuron's high capacity for protein synthesis. Chromatolysis is the dissolution of Nissl substance occurring as the histological hallmark of the axonal reaction after peripheral axon injury, characterized by cell body swelling, nuclear eccentricity, and dispersal of Nissl substance as the neuron redirects synthetic activity toward axon regeneration proteins.

questions.question: Hematopoiesis in the liver begins during which week?
questions.explanation: Hematopoiesis begins in the liver during the 6th week, giving the organ a dark red color. The liver serves as the major hematopoietic organ during fetal life. By the 9th week, the rapidly growing liver comprises about 10% of total body weight.

Failure of the urorectal septum to completely divide the cloaca results in persistent cloaca, where urogenital and anorectal systems remain connected. This is more common in females and results in a single perineal opening. Associated anomalies may include hydrocolpos and urinary tract obstruction. Surgical reconstruction is required.
questions.question: Failure of the urorectal septum to reach the cloacal membrane results in:
Bilateral renal agenesis results in:
questions.explanation: Bilateral renal agenesis results in oligohydramnios (decreased amniotic fluid) because little or no urine is excreted into the amniotic cavity. This condition is incompatible with postnatal life and occurs in approximately 1 in 3000 births. The condition has a multifactorial etiology and may be associated with other urogenital anomalies.

questions.question: The periosteum surrounding bone differs from the perichondrium surrounding cartilage primarily in which fundamental way?
options: Both have identical inner layers containing the same stem cells
Periosteum contains only fibroblasts without any progenitor function
Periosteum inner layer with osteoprogenitor cells capable of producing osteoblasts
The perichondrium is more vascularized than the periosteum
They are structurally identical with the same cellular composition
questions.explanation: Both periosteum (over bone) and perichondrium (over cartilage) have an outer fibrous and an inner cellular layer, but their inner layers contain different progenitor cells. The periosteal inner layer contains osteoprogenitor cells giving rise to osteoblasts, while the perichondrial inner layer contains chondroprogenitor cells giving rise to chondroblasts. This distinction is critical for understanding bone and cartilage repair mechanisms.

questions.question: High anorectal malformations are characterized by:
questions.explanation: High anorectal malformations are characterized by the rectum ending above the levator ani muscle, often with a fistula to the urinary tract (males) or vagina (females). Low malformations involve the rectum ending below the levator ani. This classification is important for surgical planning, as high malformations require more extensive reconstruction.

questions.question: The cochlear nuclei process information from which frequency ranges somatotopically?
questions.explanation: The cochlear nuclei maintain tonotopic organization, preserving the frequency representation from the cochlea, with different regions processing different sound frequencies systematically. High frequencies are represented dorsally and low frequencies ventrally in the dorsal cochlear nucleus. This tonotopic map is maintained through the auditory pathway to the cortex. The ventral cochlear nucleus processes temporal patterns important for speech, while the dorsal nucleus processes frequency and spectral information.

questions.question: The muscularis mucosae of the small intestine consists of which arrangement of smooth muscle?
options: Three layers — oblique, circular, and longitudinal
Inner circular and outer longitudinal thin layers
questions.explanation: The muscularis mucosae of the small intestine consists of two thin layers of smooth muscle: an inner circular and an outer longitudinal layer. Isolated smooth muscle cells from the muscularis mucosae extend into the lamina propria and up into the villi, where their contraction pumps lymph through the lacteals, facilitating fat absorption. This is distinct from the much thicker muscularis externa.

After menopause, estrogen withdrawal causes progressive endometrial atrophy. The postmenopausal endometrium becomes very thin (< 4mm on ultrasound), composed of a small amount of fibrous stroma with widely spaced, small, straight, inactive glands lined by low cuboidal cells with no mitoses. This atrophic endometrium is the expected finding. Unexpected endometrial thickening (> 4mm on TVUS) in a postmenopausal woman warrants investigation to exclude endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma.
questions.question: In a postmenopausal woman, the endometrium typically becomes thin and atrophic due to estrogen deficiency. Histologically, the postmenopausal endometrium shows:
options: Thin mucosa with small, straight, inactive glands

questions.question: A histology student is instructed to make drawings of tissue sections observed under the light microscope. This practice is specifically aimed at achieving which primary objective?
questions.explanation: Making drawings of observed tissue sections trains students to carefully observe and accurately record the spatial arrangement of cells and tissue components. This active observation develops the ability to identify tissue types and pathological changes from microscopic examination. It is a core component of histology practical training.
options: Memorizing staining patterns by color alone
Learning to operate the microscope mechanically
Accurate recognition of cellular and tissue architecture

questions.explanation: The trochlear nerve (IV) is unique as it exits dorsally from the brainstem. It has only GSE fibers supplying superior oblique muscle. It decussates before exiting.
questions.question: The trochlear nerve is unique because it exits where?

courses.title: Biochemistry II

questions.question:
A. Describe the classification of membrane transport proteins under the following headings: channel proteins, carrier proteins, and the types of carrier-mediated transport (uniport, symport, antiport).
B. Relate defects in specific membrane transport proteins to the named clinical disorders that result.
C. Explain why a defect confined to a single transport protein, such as CFTR, produces a functional deficit in several distant organs.
questions.answerText:
A. Channel proteins form transmembrane pores across the bilayer through which selected ions diffuse down their electrochemical gradient; they are generally built from four, five or six protein subunits assembled to form a pore, and channels are gated (ligand-gated, voltage-gated, or mechanically-gated), with transport through channels not requiring additional energy input. Carrier proteins bind specific molecules or ions, diffuse through the membrane and release the substance on the other side, with binding causing the carrier to change shape; carriers are much slower than channels. Carrier-mediated transport is classified as uniport (one solute transported), and co-transport, which is either symport (two solutes transported in the same direction) or antiport (two solutes transported in opposite directions).
B. Cystinuria results from a failure of the renal proximal tubules to reabsorb cysteine filtered by the glomerulus, due to defects in either of the two protein subunits of the cysteine transporter. Sitosterolemia results from mutations in either ABCG5 or ABCG8, causing unrestricted absorption of plant sterols and cholesterol. Hartnup disorder results from deficiency in SLC6A19 (system B(0) neutral amino acid transporter 1), impairing transport of neutral amino acids across epithelial cells of the renal proximal tubules and intestinal mucosa. Liddle's syndrome is caused by dysregulation of the epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) due to a mutation at the 16p13-p12 locus. Cystic fibrosis is characterised by abnormal transport of chloride and sodium across an epithelium, caused by mutations in the gene for the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) protein.
C. Cystic fibrosis affects most critically the lungs, and also the pancreas, liver and the intestine, because it is characterised by abnormal transport of chloride and sodium across an epithelium, leading to thick, viscous secretions; since CFTR-dependent chloride and sodium transport is a shared property of the epithelial linings of these different organs, a single gene mutation that disrupts this one transport protein produces the same abnormal secretion defect wherever that epithelium is found, so the functional deficit appears simultaneously in several distant organs rather than being confined to one site.

A(i) Haemoglobin is a protein composed of globin (a polypeptide, synthesised by the rough endoplasmic reticulum) and the pigment heme; each haemoglobin molecule (a globular protein) consists of 4 heme groups and 4 linear (globin) proteins, each binding to a heme.
Haemoglobin is a chromoprotein of molecular weight 64,458 Dalton; each molecule carries four molecules of oxygen and each gram of haemoglobin can carry 1.34 ml of oxygen; about 6.25 grams of haemoglobin is synthesised each day to replace haemoglobin lost through normal RBC destruction.
A(ii) A heme group consists of an iron (Fe) ion held in a heterocyclic ring known as a porphyrin; the porphyrin ring consists of four pyrrole molecules cyclically linked together by methine (methenyl) bridges, with the iron ion bound at the centre.
Iron in haemoglobin is in the ferrous (6-coordination) form: 4 bonds bind protoporphyrin, 1 binds to histidine of the globin, and 1 is free to bind O2 or CO2.
A(iii) Heme synthesis starts with glycine and succinyl-CoA reacting, with vitamin B6 as cofactor, to produce aminolevulinic acid via the ALA synthase reaction, the regulatory (rate-limiting) step; further steps occur partly in the cytoplasm before the molecule returns to the mitochondria where protoporphyrin is formed.
Protoporphyrin binds to ferrous iron while globin is synthesised in the rough endoplasmic reticulum; protoporphyrin, ferrous iron and globin then combine to form haemoglobin.
B(i) In the ferric form, haemoglobin has one bond missing and is malfunctional; heme and globin are not isolated but are bound together via iron.
When O2 binds to iron the process is called oxygenation (not oxidation), and oxygen is transported through the circulation in molecular form (O2); the oxidation state of the iron does not change during normal oxygen binding.
Oxidation of Fe2+ to Fe3+ occurs only occasionally; the oxidised form, methaemoglobin, is then no longer able to bind O2, so the proportion of methaemoglobin is normally kept low, which is the basis for the requirement that iron remain ferrous.
C(i) Haemoglobin is a tetramer, made up of four subunits, a quaternary structure of protein, that reversibly combines with oxygen and transports it.
Myoglobin, in contrast, is a monomer with a structure similar to haemoglobin, present in muscles, representing a tertiary structure of protein, and functions in the storage of oxygen rather than its transport.
Different types of haemoglobin arise from different types of globin, not heme: adults have mainly HbA with a small amount of HbA2, while the fetus has HbF.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the composition of the haemoglobin molecule.
A(ii) Describe the structure of heme and the iron coordination within it.
A(iii) Describe the synthesis of haemoglobin.
B(i) Explain the biochemical basis for why iron in haemoglobin must remain in the ferrous state.
C(i) Distinguish between haemoglobin and myoglobin.

questions.answerText:
(i) A red blood cell enzyme disorder should be assumed in cases of persistent normocytic haemolytic anaemia with these exclusions; the diagnosis is pyruvate kinase (PK) deficiency, the most common enzyme deficiency of glycolysis and nucleotide metabolism, causing hereditary nonspherocytic haemolytic anaemia (HNSHA).
(ii) The glycolytic pathway is affected, specifically the pyruvate kinase step.
(iii) Continuously impaired ATP generation causes a lack of sufficient energy; ATP is required for maintenance of glycolysis, the electrolyte red cell/plasma gradient, glutathione synthesis, membrane phospholipid asymmetry, and purine/pyrimidine metabolism, resulting in chronic haemolytic anaemia.
(iv) PK enzymatic activity is usually decreased, ATP levels are usually decreased, and 2,3-DPG levels are increased due to the metabolic block at the PK step.
(v) The precise mechanism of red cell destruction is unknown; ATP depletion initiates a series of events leading to premature destruction of young PK-deficient red cells in the spleen, with premature destruction and apoptosis of red cell progenitors also possibly contributing to the pathogenesis.
questions.question:
An infant presents with chronic haemolytic anaemia; haemoglobin abnormalities and antiglobulin reactions have been excluded, spherocytes are absent, and osmotic fragility is normal.
(i) What is the diagnosis?
(ii) Which pathway and enzyme is defective?
(iii) What is the metabolic basis of the haemolysis?
(iv) What biochemical findings would be expected in the red cell?
(v) What is the proposed mechanism of red cell destruction?

questions.answerText:
A(i) Gastrin is released from G cells in the antral region of the stomach (also pancreatic endocrine cells, pituitary and extra-antral G cells); targets are parietal cells (HCl), chief cells (pepsinogen) and enterochromaffin-like (ECL) cells (histamine).
A(ii) Synthesised in the antrum as preprogastrin then progastrin (21-aa signal peptide, 37-aa N-terminal extension, gastrin-34, 9-aa C-terminal extension); stored in secretory granules; prohormone convertases remove the extensions, giving glycine-extended gastrin and amidated gastrin (G-34, G-17). Fasting gastrin is mainly G-34, post-meal mainly G-17 (cleared faster).
A(iii) Stimulated by antral distension, vagal stimulation (bombesin/GRP), partially digested protein and small peptides (aromatic amino acids strongest) and hypercalcaemia (calcium-sensing receptors). Inhibited by acid in the stomach (negative feedback, direct on G cells and via somatostatin from D cells) and by secretin, GIP, VIP, glucagon and calcitonin.
A(iv) Stimulates parietal cell HCl secretion, maturation and fundal growth; chief cell pepsinogen; increases antral motility and relaxes the pyloric sphincter (faster gastric emptying); acid aids protein digestion and absorption of iron, calcium, vitamin B12 and thyroxin.
- Mechanism: directly on parietal cells and indirectly via CCK2/gastrin receptors on ECL cells (histamine, the major stimulus); G protein - phospholipase C - PIP2 to IP3 (Ca2+ release from ER) and DAG (protein kinase C) - HCl secretion; gastrin does not change cAMP.
B(i) Zollinger-Ellison syndrome: excess gastrin, often from a gastrinoma (mostly benign) of the duodenum or pancreas; the pentagastrin test investigates hypergastrinaemia.
- Autoimmune gastritis: attack on parietal cells causes hypochlorhydria, a rise in gastric pH and elevated gastrin; loss of all parietal cells gives achlorhydria and loss of negative feedback (gastrin is also elevated in pernicious anaemia).
- Mucolipidosis type IV: constitutive achlorhydria with plasma gastrin mean 1507 pg/mL (range 400-4100; normal 0-200), useful for diagnosis; chronic gastritis from H. pylori infection may also raise gastrin.
C(i) Gastrin also induces pancreatic secretion and gallbladder emptying, relaxes the ileocecal valve, contributes to the gastrocolic reflex and may affect lower oesophageal sphincter tone; it is also present in parts of the nervous system.
- Gastrin amide acting through the CCK2 receptor has important roles in epithelial proliferation in the GI tract; gut hormones are involved in the pathogenesis of mucosal atrophy, neoplasm and cancers.
- Progastrin-derived peptides drive proliferation in the colon, differentiation of gastric epithelium and proliferation in the stomach.
- Acid secretion pathways are neural, paracrine and hormonal.

questions.question:
A saturated fatty acyl CoA undergoes one round of mitochondrial β-oxidation.
(i) Name the pathway and the organelle in which it occurs.
(ii) Name in order the enzymes and intermediates of the round.
(iii) State the fate of the reduced cofactors and of the acetyl CoA.
(iv) Name the step whose electron handling differs in the peroxisome and describe the difference.
(v) Describe the variant arrangement of two peroxisomal enzymes.
questions.answerText:
(i) β-oxidation of saturated fatty acids, occurring in the mitochondrion.
(ii) Acyl CoA dehydrogenase (FAD) converts fatty acyl CoA to trans-Δ2-enoyl CoA.
(ii) Enoyl CoA hydratase adds water stereospecifically to give 3-L-hydroxyacyl CoA.
(ii) 3-L-hydroxyacyl CoA dehydrogenase (NAD+) gives β-ketoacyl CoA.
(ii) β-ketoacyl CoA thiolase (acyl CoA acetyltransferase) gives acetyl CoA and a fatty acyl CoA 2 carbon atoms shorter.
(iii) FADH2 is reoxidised by the mitochondrial electron transport chain; reduction of O2 to water beginning at the coenzyme Q stage gives 2 ATPs per electron pair.
(iii) Acetyl CoA is oxidised via the citric acid cycle, generating additional FADH2 and NADH that are reoxidised through phosphorylation to form ATP.
(iv) The first dehydrogenation: in the peroxisome it uses FAD but the electrons are transferred directly to oxygen, not through the electron transport chain.
(iv) Peroxisomal oxidation is therefore less efficient by 2 ATPs per C2 cycle, and the H2O2 formed is split to H2O and O2 by catalase.
(v) Peroxisomal enoyl-CoA hydratase and 3-L-hydroxyacyl CoA dehydrogenase activities occur in a single polypeptide; the reactions are identical to those of the mitochondrial system.

(i) Acyl CoA dehydrogenase is bypassed in each of the problems.
(ii) Each bypass leads to one fewer FADH2 and 1.5 fewer ATPs than in the β-oxidation of the saturated counterpart.
(iii) Problem 1: a β,γ (cis Δ3) double bond after the third round; enoyl CoA isomerase converts it to trans-Δ2.
(iii) Problem 2: a Δ4 double bond (even numbered carbon) met in the 5th round; NADPH-dependent 2,4-dienoyl CoA reductase gives trans-3-enoyl CoA, which 3,2-enoyl CoA isomerase converts to trans-2-enoyl CoA.
(iv) Acyl CoA dehydrogenase is bypassed twice during β-oxidation of linoleyl CoA.
(iv) Therefore 2 fewer FADH2 and 3 fewer ATPs are generated compared with β-oxidation of stearoyl CoA (18:0).
(iv) Each bypass removes one FADH2 and 1.5 ATPs, so two bypasses remove 2 FADH2 and 3 ATPs.
questions.question:
The energy yield from β-oxidation of linoleyl CoA is compared with that of stearoyl CoA (18:0), its saturated counterpart.
(i) Identify the enzyme step that is bypassed in the unsaturated substrate.
(ii) State the effect of each bypass on FADH2 and ATP.
(iii) Distinguish the two situations in which a bypass occurs and the enzymes that resolve each.
(iv) State the overall deficit compared with stearoyl CoA and explain the reasoning.

questions.answerText:
(i) The diagnosis is Liddle's syndrome.
(ii) This syndrome is caused by dysregulation of an epithelial sodium channel (ENaC), found at the surface of certain cells called epithelial cells, found in the kidneys, lungs, and sweat glands.
(iii) The dysregulation of ENaC is due to a genetic mutation at the 16p13-p12 locus.

questions.question:
A young patient presents with hypertension and is found to have low serum potassium. Genetic testing reveals a mutation at the 16p13-p12 locus.
(i) What is the diagnosis?
(ii) What transport protein/channel is affected, and where in the body is it normally found?
(iii) What is the mechanism by which this mutation causes the clinical picture?

A patient presents with cyanosis that does not improve with oxygen therapy; the blood sample appears chocolate-brown in colour.
(i) What is the diagnosis, and what is the underlying chemical change in haemoglobin?
(ii) What is the biochemical mechanism by which this change occurs?
(iii) How is this normally corrected in the body, and why can patients tolerate it up to a point?
(iv) What is the genetic classification of the enzyme deficiency that can cause this condition?
questions.answerText:
(i) The diagnosis is methaemoglobinaemia; methaemoglobin is a derivative of haemoglobin in which the ferrous (Fe2+) ions are oxidised to the ferric (Fe3+) state, and the ferric heme of methaemoglobin is unable to bind oxygen.
(ii) During oxygenation, one electron is partially transferred from iron to the bound oxygen, forming a ferric-superoxide (Fe3+-O2-) anion complex; during deoxygenation, some of the oxygen leaves as a superoxide (O2-) radical, leaving the iron in the ferric state, forming methaemoglobin.
(iii) Several potential mechanisms exist to reduce methaemoglobin back to haemoglobin, but only the NADH-dependent reaction catalysed by cytochrome b5 reductase (previously called NADH diaphorase or methaemoglobin reductase) is physiologically important; patients can tolerate methaemoglobin levels as high as 40% because of physiological adaptations, including polycythaemia, changes in the concentration of 2,3-DPG and pH, and altered synthesis of globin chains, although they can decompensate when exposed to oxidising agents.
(iv) There are two types of cytochrome b5 reductase deficiency: Type I, in which only red blood cells are affected, and Type II, which affects all cell types; most patients with cytochrome b5 reductase deficiency do not have symptoms.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the five classes of human immunoglobulins.
A(ii) Describe the light-chain types.
A(iii) Describe the general functions of immunoglobulins.
B(i) Explain the biochemical basis for why IgG is the principal immunoglobulin protecting the newborn.
C(i) Distinguish between IgG and IgM.
questions.answerText:
A(i) The five immunoglobulin classes are based on differences in heavy-chain constant-region amino acid sequences: IgG (gamma heavy chains), IgM (mu heavy chains), IgA (alpha heavy chains), IgD (delta heavy chains), IgE (epsilon heavy chains).
IgG properties: major serum immunoglobulin; the only antibody that crosses the placenta; fixes complement; binds to Fc receptors on phagocytes, mediating opsonization.
IgA properties: 2nd highest serum immunoglobulin; the major secretory immunoglobulin, found in saliva, tears, and respiratory, intestinal and genital tract secretions; does not fix complement unless aggregated; binds to Fc receptors on some cells.
IgM properties: 3rd highest serum immunoglobulin; the first immunoglobulin made by the fetus and by B cells, produced early in the primary response; described as the most efficient immunoglobulin; fixes complement; binds Fc receptors; also a B cell surface immunoglobulin.
IgD properties: 4th highest serum immunoglobulin; a B cell surface immunoglobulin; does not bind complement. IgE properties: least common serum immunoglobulin; a monomer with an extra domain (CH4); mediates allergic reactions and fights parasitic infections (anthelmintic action); does not fix complement.
A(ii) Immunoglobulins are also classified by light-chain type, based on differences in the amino acid sequence of the light-chain constant region, into kappa (κ) and lambda (λ) light chains.
A(iii) The general functions of immunoglobulins are antigen binding, which can result in protection of the host and depends on the antibody's valency, and effector functions, including fixation of complement and binding to various cells such as phagocytes for opsonization.
B(i) IgG is the only antibody that crosses the placenta, and most of the protection for a foetus or newborn comes from maternal IgG crossing the placenta during pregnancy, because the human foetus and newborn have limited immune responses of their own.
Only intact IgG or its Fc fragment can cross the placenta (Fab or F(ab')2 cannot), which is the structural basis for IgG, and not IgM or the other classes, being the principal protector of the newborn.
C(i) IgM is the first immunoglobulin made by the fetus and by B cells, produced early in the primary immune response and described as the most efficient immunoglobulin, whereas IgG is the major serum immunoglobulin overall.
Both IgG and IgM fix complement and bind Fc receptors, but only IgG crosses the placenta; IgM is additionally a B cell surface immunoglobulin, a property also shared by IgD.
Thus IgM is distinguished by being the earliest and most efficient response immunoglobulin with a B cell surface role, while IgG is distinguished by being the major, longer-term serum immunoglobulin uniquely capable of placental transfer for newborn protection.

(i) Goitre (enlargement of the thyroid gland) due to iodine deficiency in the diet.
(ii) Dietary iodine deficiency; dietary iodine is very scarce in many parts of the world.
(iii) The thyroid, located in the neck, releases thyroxin (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3); these are tyrosine derivatives that require the addition of iodine for bioactivity, so an intricate mechanism has evolved for accumulating and retaining iodine.
- Thyroid hormones regulate the rate of metabolism and are essential for normal physical and mental development; T3 and T4 act through intracellular receptors (entering cells by facilitated diffusion), and T3 is also formed from precursor in the periphery.
- Oversecretion of thyroxin causes nervousness and weight loss; undersecretion causes cretinism (mental retardation, small size) in children.

A(i) GI hormones are chemical messengers regulating secretion, absorption, digestion and gut motility; they are a large family of peptides secreted by endocrine cells widely distributed in the GI mucosa and pancreas; with more than 50 gut hormone genes the gut is the largest endocrine organ. They act as endocrine, autocrine, paracrine and neurocrine agents.
A(ii) Gastrin family: gastrin and CCK. Secretin family: secretin, glucagon, GIP, VIP and glicentin. Neurocrine peptides (neurotensin, bombesin-like peptides, substance P, somatostatin) have no structural similarity to other GI peptides and very short plasma half-lives.
A(iii) Gastrin: 17 amino acids (little gastrin 17, big gastrin 34); antral gastric mucosa and duodenum; released by amino acids and partially digested protein and by vagal stimulation on distension; stimulates HCl and pepsinogen; inhibited by HCl and other GI hormones.
- Secretin: 27 amino acids; duodenal mucosa; released by acidification from gastric HCl; stimulates pancreatic HCO3- to neutralise HCl, reduces gastric and duodenal motility and inhibits gastrin release and gastric acid secretion.
- CCK: full activity in the C-terminal 8-amino-acid peptide; duodenum and jejunum; released by products of lipid and protein digestion; stimulates gallbladder emptying and pancreatic enzyme and HCO3- secretion (enhancing secretin), inhibits gastric emptying; has a role in satiety.
- GIP (glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide): 42 amino acids; small intestine; released by glucose in the GIT; stimulates insulin release and inhibits gastric acid secretion, motility and emptying.
B(i) Stomach: gastrin, ghrelin (stimulates appetite and gastric emptying), somatostatin; duodenum and jejunum: CCK, secretin, GIP; ileum: GLP-1 (increases insulin secretion) and neurotensin; colon: peptide YY (inhibits food intake); enteric nerves: VIP, neuropeptide Y, galanin, substance P.
- Gut hormones also modulate mucosal growth and are involved in the pathogenesis of gut mucosal atrophy, neoplasm and cancers; growth factors throughout the gut drive proliferation and differentiation and trefoil peptides give mucosal protection and repair.
C(i) Distant actions: CCK and secretin stimulate pancreatic secretion; CCK stimulates gallbladder contraction; GIP, GLP-1 and secretin stimulate insulin release; enteroglucagon inhibits insulin secretion; pancreatic polypeptide inhibits pancreatic and biliary secretion; VIP releases hormones from pancreas, gut and hypothalamus.
- Six receptor classes: muscarinic cholinergic, gastrin-CCK, bombesin and related peptides, physalaemin-substance P, secretin and VIP, and cholera toxin.
- Two intracellular routes that do not cross over: Ca2+ mobilisation with phosphatidylinositol turnover to diacylglycerol and inositol phosphates (gastrin, CCK), and adenylate cyclase with cAMP (secretin); they converge at some point, for example in amylase secretion.
- Some peptides have unclear actions (calcitonin gene-related peptide, growth hormone-releasing factor, substance P); chromogranin A is a secretory protein.

A(i) Made in beta cells as preproinsulin (signal sequence, proinsulin): translation and translocation, folding, oxidation and signal-peptide cleavage; ER export, Golgi transport and vesicle packaging; protease cleavage liberates C-peptide; carboxypeptidase E produces mature insulin (A and B chains).
A(ii) Glucose enters through GLUT2, is metabolised, raising ATP:ADP; K-ATP channel closure depolarises the membrane, voltage-dependent Ca2+ channels open, intracellular Ca2+ rises and stored insulin granules are released by exocytosis; Ca2+ also activates insulin gene expression via CREB.
- Other modulators: neural signals, the amino acids leucine and arginine and GIP (gut hormone released after food) stimulate release; epinephrine decreases it.
A(iii) Insulin binds the alpha subunits of its heterotetrameric receptor; the beta-subunit tyrosine kinase phosphorylates the receptor (ATP to ADP), then IRS-1, PI3-kinase and Akt, giving GLUT4 translocation (glucose uptake) and mTOR (P70 S6K, 4E-BP1) for protein synthesis; MAP kinases (ERK1,2) alter gene expression.
- Actions: promotes glucose uptake in muscle and adipose tissue, glycolysis, glycogen synthesis, protein synthesis (active amino acid transport) and uptake of K+ and phosphate; stops gluconeogenesis, glycogenolysis, lipolysis, ketogenesis and proteolysis; in adipocytes promotes fat storage; centrally lowers feeding and raises energy expenditure.
A(iv) Insulin is internalised with its receptor in an endocytic vesicle; acidification dissociates insulin, which is degraded in endosomes (cytosolic or peroxisomal degradation also proposed); the receptor is recycled to the cell surface.
B(i) C-peptide assay; glucose tests (fasting, random and post-prandial blood sugar); insulin autoantibody (IAA) assay; oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT).
C(i) Absolute (type 1) or relative (type 2: insulin resistance with dysfunctional beta cells) deficiency gives hyperglycaemia and glycosuria; glucose in urine carries water, causing dehydration.
- Loss of insulin's 'stop' actions: increased breakdown of fat and tissue protein causes weight loss; increased gluconeogenesis from amino acids gives negative nitrogen balance; lipemia (raised lipid, fatty acid, cholesterol).
- Increased ketone body production by the liver with incomplete tissue utilisation causes ketosis and ketonuria; circulating keto acids lower blood pH (acidosis).
- Long-term: increased tendency to develop cataract in the eye and arteriosclerotic lesions of blood vessels.
- Hyperinsulinism (islet-cell tumours of beta cells) and oversecretion of insulin produce low blood sugar, showing the opposite deficit.

questions.question:
A. Describe nutritional assessment under the following headings: definition, the ABCDE approach to data collection, and examples of validated screening/assessment tools.
B. State how malnutrition risk relates to hospital outcomes and complications.
C. Explain why, in critically ill patients, metabolic derangement due to illness, injury or infection can produce a distant, systemic effect on nutritional status that cannot be corrected by nutrition support alone.
questions.answerText:
A. Nutritional assessment is "the evaluation of nutrition needs of individuals based upon appropriate biochemical, anthropometric, physical, and dietary data to determine nutrient needs and recommended appropriate nutrition intake including enteral and parenteral nutrition" (American Dietetic Association). A full nutrition assessment follows a systematic approach to data collection, summarised as A-B-C-D-E: Anthropometry, Biochemical data, Clinical signs and symptoms/medical condition, Dietary intake, and Exercise (energy balance/expenditure), considering current level, history and changes, and including both subjective data (e.g. signs/symptoms, appetite) and objective data (e.g. lab results). Examples of validated assessment tools include the Malnutrition Screening Tool (MST), the Short Nutritional Assessment Questionnaire (SNAQ), the Mini Nutritional Assessment (MNA, for identifying malnutrition in the elderly, considering dietary intake, weight change/BMI/muscle circumferences, functional impairment and psychological issues), and the Subjective Global Assessment (SGA, based on medical history and physical examination, classifying patients as A: well nourished, B: moderately malnourished or suspected of malnutrition, or C: severely malnourished).
B. Malnutrition is associated with increased length of stay in hospital, increased complications, increased hospital costs and increased mortality rates, as well as wasting, reduced energy and effects on wellness, especially in the young.
C. Critically unwell patients may be well nourished but at high nutritional risk; illness, injury and infection cause metabolic derangements that may have a significant effect on nutritional status and may lead to malnutrition, and such derangements cannot be corrected by nutrition support alone. Patients at high nutritional risk therefore require early nutritional intervention and close monitoring, because the metabolic disturbance driving their nutritional decline originates from the systemic illness process itself rather than from inadequate intake alone, so it produces its effect on nutritional status body-wide rather than being resolved simply by providing nutrients.

A(i) β-oxidation occurs in the peroxisome as well as the mitochondrion; in animals it shortens very long chain fatty acids (>22 carbon atoms) to facilitate their degradation by the mitochondrial system.
A(i) In plants, fatty acid oxidation occurs exclusively in the peroxisomes and glyoxysomes (specialised peroxisomes).
A(ii) There is no carnitine requirement; very long chain fatty acids diffuse in, are activated by peroxisomal very long chain acyl CoA synthetase to CoA esters and are oxidised directly.
A(iii) Reaction 1: an FAD-dependent dehydrogenation with electrons transferred directly to oxygen; the H2O2 formed dissociates to H2O and O2 through catalase.
A(iii) Reaction 2: enoyl-CoA hydratase and 3-L-hydroxyacyl CoA dehydrogenase activities occur in a single polypeptide, with reactions identical to the mitochondrial system.
A(iii) Reaction 3: peroxisomal thiolase, which has a different chain length specificity from its mitochondrial counterpart.
B(i) Peroxisomal thiolase is almost inactive with acyl CoAs of length C8 or less, so fatty acids are incompletely oxidised by peroxisomes.
B(i) Because electrons pass directly to oxygen without the electron transport chain and oxidative phosphorylation, peroxisomal oxidation is less efficient by 2 ATPs for each C2 cycle.
C(i) Acyl CoAs shortened by peroxisomal β-oxidation are converted to their carnitine esters.
C(i) Most of these substrates diffuse passively out of the peroxisome to the mitochondrion, where they are oxidised further.
C(i) The shorter chain acyl products are linked to carnitine for transport to the mitochondrion.
C(i) The peroxisome contains both a carnitine acyl transferase and a transferase specific for long chain acyl groups, although entry does not depend on carnitine esters.

A(i) Vitamins are classified based on solubility into nine water-soluble vitamins (the B vitamin complex and vitamin C) and four fat-soluble vitamins (vitamins A, D, E and K); all absorption takes place in the small intestine, but fat-soluble and water-soluble vitamins differ in absorption and bioavailability, and solubility also influences digestion, transportation, storage and excretion.
A(ii) Bioavailability of vitamins varies with the amount present in a specific food, the method of preparation (raw, fermented, cooked), the efficiency of digestion and absorption, individual nutritional status, and whether the vitamin is in natural or synthetic form; fat-soluble vitamins are generally less bioavailable than water-soluble vitamins, and vitamins from plant foods are generally less bioavailable than those from animal foods.
B. Fat-soluble vitamins are attached to proteins in foods, released in the stomach, absorbed in the duodenum, and packaged in chylomicrons for transport in the lymph and bloodstream; the liver is the main storage site for vitamin A, and to a lesser extent for vitamins K and E, while vitamin D is mainly stored in fat and muscle tissue, so these vitamins can build up in the body to the point of toxicity. Water-soluble vitamins, by contrast, are absorbed with water directly into the bloodstream (mostly in the duodenum and jejunum), are not stored in the body, and excess intake is excreted through the urine.
C. Water-soluble vitamins are absorbed with water directly into the bloodstream, mostly in the duodenum and jejunum, are not stored, and any excess is excreted in the urine. Fat-soluble vitamins are attached to proteins in food and released in the stomach, absorbed in the duodenum, packaged into chylomicrons for transport in lymph and blood, and stored mainly in the liver (vitamin A, and to a lesser extent K and E) or in fat and muscle tissue (vitamin D); a lack of dietary fat can lead to deficiency of fat-soluble vitamins, and unlike water-soluble vitamins, they can accumulate to toxic levels.

(i) The child has kwashiorkor, the oedematous form of protein-calorie malnutrition (PCM); marasmus (non-oedematous PCM) is the other type, and both represent the critical end of a spectrum of varying degrees of protein-calorie deficiency.
(ii) The oedema results mainly from a decreased albumin concentration due to a severe negative protein balance, with the liver rapidly losing protein and muscle protein loss being progressive; the fatty liver is due to an inability to mobilise fat; blood glucose is usually normal but there is an increased tendency to hypoglycaemia on fasting, and glucose tolerance tests give a diabetic type of curve with low insulin secretion.
(iii) Total plasma proteins are reduced mainly from decreased albumin, beta-globulins are decreased while gamma-globulin is normal or increased (so its percentage contribution is high); specific transport proteins such as transferrin, ceruloplasmin, retinol-binding protein, alpha- and beta-lipoproteins, thyroxin, aldosterone-binding proteins and cortisol-binding proteins are decreased; the plasma free amino acid pattern is abnormal; steatorrhoea occurs even on a diet practically devoid of fat; serum vitamin A and E levels are consistently lower than normal; serum potassium and magnesium are decreased due to diarrhoea and vomiting; mild acidosis occurs from decreased renal acidification; total serum calcium is low because of the affected protein-bound fraction; and serum enzymes such as amylase, pseudocholinesterase and alkaline phosphatase have reduced activity.

(ii) Goitre results from a deficiency of iodine in soils in areas far from the sea; over 90% of the body's iodine is stored in the thyroid, present in only minute amounts (15-20 mg) in the body, so dietary/environmental iodine deficiency is the predisposing factor. Fetal iodine deficiency (severe maternal deficiency) is the specific predisposing factor for cretinism.
(iii) Iodine is required to produce thyroid hormones, which control cell metabolism and neuromuscular tissue growth and development, especially fetal-perinatal brain development; iodine deficiency disorders (IDD) therefore span fetal iodine deficiency (resulting in abortion, stillbirth, congenital defects, mental retardation, paraplegia, deaf-mutism, dwarfism, psychomotor defects, cretinism and infant mortality), neonatal iodine deficiency (neonatal goitre, hypothyroidism, infant mortality), IDD in children and adolescents (impaired mental and physical development, goitre, hypothyroidism), and IDD in adults (goitre, hypothyroidism, impaired mental function, and iodine-induced hyperthyroidism).
(iv) Interventions for the prevention of IDD include universal iodisation of salt, as well as iodisation of water (e.g. in China, Malaysia) and iodisation of oil in countries where there is no salt iodisation.

questions.answerText:
(i) The diagnosis is glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency, the most common metabolic disorder of the red blood cell, affecting more than 400 million people worldwide, with X-chromosome-linked hereditary transmission — women may be heterozygous or homozygous, and men are hemizygous.
(ii) The hexose monophosphate (HMP) shunt pathway metabolises 5% to 10% of the glucose used by the red blood cell and is critical for protecting red cells against oxidant injury; G6PD deficiency causes inadequate levels of reduced glutathione (GSH), so the cell is unable to withstand oxidative stress, and is commonly characterised by acute haemolytic episodes triggered by oxidative stressors such as fava beans, infections and certain medications (favism).
(iii) Management is supportive during the acute haemolytic crisis, with avoidance of the oxidant triggers such as fava beans, infections and the implicated medications.
(iv) G6PD deficiency is frequent in Africans and protects them from malaria, because Plasmodium falciparum is dependent on the HMP shunt and reduced glutathione for its optimum growth in the red blood cell, and one theory is that cells infected with the parasite are cleared more rapidly by the spleen.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Uptake of bilirubin by the liver is mediated by a carrier protein (receptor); on the smooth endoplasmic reticulum, bilirubin is conjugated with glucuronic acid, the major conjugate, catalysed by UDP glucuronyl transferase.
Conjugated bilirubin is water-soluble and is secreted by hepatocytes into the biliary canaliculi; it is converted to stercobilinogen (urobilinogen), which is colourless, by bacteria in the gut.
Stercobilinogen is oxidised to stercobilin, which is coloured, and excreted in the faeces; some stercobilin may be re-absorbed by the gut and re-excreted by either the liver or kidney.
B(i) Prehepatic (haemolytic) jaundice results from excess production of bilirubin, beyond the liver's ability to conjugate it, following haemolysis; excess red cell lysis is commonly due to autoimmune disease, haemolytic disease of the newborn (Rh- or ABO-incompatibility) or structurally abnormal red cells such as sickle cell disease, giving high plasma unconjugated bilirubin.
Intrahepatic jaundice reflects impaired uptake, conjugation, or secretion of bilirubin due to generalised liver (hepatocyte) dysfunction, so hyperbilirubinaemia is usually accompanied by other abnormalities in biochemical markers of liver function.
Posthepatic jaundice is caused by obstruction of the biliary tree; plasma bilirubin is conjugated and other biliary metabolites such as bile acids accumulate, giving pale-coloured stools and dark urine; in incomplete obstruction, urobilin is absent from the urine.
C(i) Neonatal jaundice is common, particularly in premature infants, is transient (resolves in the first 10 days), and is due to immaturity of the enzymes involved in bilirubin conjugation.
High levels of unconjugated bilirubin are toxic to the newborn because, due to its hydrophobicity, it can cross the blood-brain barrier.
This causes a type of mental retardation known as kernicterus, a distant/systemic functional deficit arising from a defect in the hepatic conjugation step of the pathway.
If bilirubin levels are judged too high, phototherapy with UV light is used to convert bilirubin to a water-soluble, non-toxic form; exchange blood transfusion is used to remove excess bilirubin.
Phenobarbital is often administered to the mother prior to induced labour of a premature infant, as it crosses the placenta and induces synthesis of UDP glucuronyl transferase.
Jaundice within the first 24 hours of life, or which takes longer than 10 days to resolve, is usually pathological and needs further investigation.

Fatty acids, monoglycerides, lysophosphatidylcholine and free cholesterol enter from mixed micelles and are re-esterified in the smooth ER: long-chain fatty acids (>14 C) with monoglycerides to triglyceride and with lysophosphatidylcholine to lecithin; cholesterol is esterified by ACAT.

A(iii) In blood the nascent chylomicron receives apo C (including C-II) and apo E from HDL, a circulating reservoir; apo C-II makes it able to activate lipoprotein lipase (LPL), and it becomes a mature chylomicron.
A(iv) LPL hydrolyses core triglyceride to fatty acids and monoglycerides, taken up locally; surface phospholipid, free cholesterol and apo Cs are transferred to HDL; the chylomicron returns apo C-II to HDL but keeps apo E, becoming a 30-50 nm remnant.

B(i) LPL sits on the vascular endothelium of tissues with a high requirement for triglyceride: skeletal and cardiac muscle (energy), adipose tissue (storage) and the lactating mammary gland (milk).
C(i) As the core shrinks, triglyceride content falls and the particle becomes relatively richer in cholesterol and protein; the overcrowded surface materials pass to HDL, leaving a cholesteryl-ester-enriched, triglyceride-depleted remnant.

- Blood from large veins reaches the lungs and peripheral capillaries (adipose tissue, muscle) before the liver, which may protect the liver from lipid overload after a meal.
- Composition: 1-2% protein, 85-88% triglyceride, ~8% phospholipid, ~3% cholesteryl ester, ~1% cholesterol; largest (up to 1000 nm) and least dense (<0.95) lipoprotein.
- Apolipoproteins: apo A-I, II, IV, B-48, C-I, II, III, E and H; when many are absorbed the lymph draining the small intestine appears milky.

questions.question:
During β-oxidation of an unsaturated fatty acyl CoA, a double bond at an even-numbered carbon atom is met in the fifth round.
(i) State the factor that causes the difficulty and the intermediate formed.
(ii) State the complication for the next enzyme step.
(iii) Describe the enzymes that resolve it, with their cofactor requirement, and justify why the second enzyme is needed.
(iv) State the effect on FADH2 and ATP.
questions.answerText:
(i) The presence of a double bond at an even numbered carbon atom (Δ4) results in the formation of 2,4-dienoyl CoA.
(ii) 2,4-dienoyl CoA is a poor substrate for enoyl CoA hydratase, so the Δ4 double bond inhibits the action of hydratase.
(iii) NADPH-dependent 2,4-dienoyl CoA reductase reduces the Δ4 double bond and yields trans-3-enoyl CoA.
(iii) To proceed along the β-oxidation pathway, trans-3-enoyl CoA must first be isomerised to trans-2-enoyl CoA by 3,2-enoyl CoA isomerase.
(iii) Justification: enoyl CoA hydratase catalyses stereospecific addition of water to a trans α,β double bond, which the trans-2 form provides.
(iv) Acyl CoA dehydrogenase is bypassed, leading to one fewer FADH2 and 1.5 fewer ATPs than in the saturated counterpart.

(i) He has a high LDL and low HDL; LDL carriers are often referred to as "bad cholesterol" while HDL carriers are typically referred to as "good cholesterol."
(ii) Synthesis of the LDL receptor is suppressed by high intracellular cholesterol; the decreased synthesis of LDL receptor prevents excessive cholesterol uptake by cells, but has the deleterious consequence that excess dietary cholesterol remains in the blood as LDL. HDL, on the other hand, is manufactured by the liver to remove excess materials left over by LDL carriers, a process called reverse cholesterol transport, moving through the bloodstream to scrape cholesterol deposits off blood vessel walls and transferring them to VLDL and LDL carriers for return to the liver, where excess fats or cholesterol are converted into bile and excreted through the large intestines.
(iii) Bacterial and viral infections, and some inflammatory disease states, decrease HDL and increase VLDL production by the liver.
(iv) High blood levels of HDL correlate with a low incidence of atherosclerosis; the changes associated with inflammation (decreased HDL and increased VLDL) can lead to increased risk of atherosclerosis if prolonged, because cells that no longer need cholesterol leave LDL carriers to travel the bloodstream still loaded with cholesterol, and this cholesterol material can be dropped onto blood vessel walls and arteries, leading to blood vessel and artery blockages.
questions.question:

questions.answerText:
A(i) Mitochondria contain 3 acyl CoA dehydrogenases, with specificities for short-, medium- and long-chain fatty acyl CoAs.
A(ii) The reaction is thought to involve the removal of a proton at Cα.
A(ii) It also involves the transfer of a hydride ion equivalent from Cβ to FAD.
A(iii) The product is an enoyl CoA (trans-Δ2), with FAD reduced to FADH2.
B(i) FADH2 is reoxidised by the mitochondrial electron transport chain through a series of electron transfer reactions.
B(i) The series includes ETF and ETF:ubiquinone oxidoreductase, coenzyme Q, and oxygen reduced to water.
B(i) Reduction of oxygen to water beginning at the coenzyme Q stage results in synthesis of 2 ATPs per electron pair transferred.
C(i) The peroxisomal reaction also involves an FAD cofactor.
C(i) The abstracted electrons are transferred directly to oxygen rather than passing through the electron transport chain.
C(i) There is thus no concomitant oxidative phosphorylation, making peroxisomal oxidation less efficient by 2 ATPs for each C2 cycle.
C(i) The H2O2 produced dissociates to H2O and O2 through peroxisomal catalase.
C(i) The enzymes of the two organelles differ, although the same chemical changes result.

(i) Diabetes mellitus: hyperglycaemia and glycosuria with other early features (weight loss, ketosis and ketonuria, acidosis, dehydration, negative nitrogen balance, lipemia, tendency to cataract and arteriosclerotic lesions).
(ii) C-peptide assay; glucose tests (fasting blood sugar FBS, random blood sugar RBS, post-prandial glucose PPS); insulin autoantibody (IAA) assay; oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT).
(iii) Preproinsulin (signal sequence) - proinsulin; the C-peptide is liberated when proteases cleave proinsulin in the secretory vesicle; carboxypeptidase E then produces mature insulin (A chain and B chain).
(iv) The beta cells of the pancreatic islets: their glucose-stimulated release depends on GLUT2, ATP:ADP, K-ATP channel closure, depolarisation and Ca2+ entry; beta-cell dysfunction occurs in type 2 diabetes and islet-cell tumours of beta cells cause hyperinsulinism.
(v) Juvenile type (type 1): in children, due to an absolute deficiency of insulin.
- Maturity-onset type: usually associated with obesity; MODY results from mutations in pancreatic glucokinase or specific nuclear transcription factors.
- Secondary diabetes: hyperfunction of an insulin antagonist gives relative insufficiency of insulin (acromegaly - excess growth hormone; Cushing's disease - excess glucocorticoids; hyperthyroidism).
- Type 2 diabetes: a combination of insulin resistance and dysfunctional beta cells.

questions.answerText:
A(i) The lac operon is an inducible operon, usually off by default; it contains genes coding for enzymes used in the hydrolysis and metabolism of lactose, and by itself the lac repressor is active and switches the lac operon off.
A(ii) A molecule called an inducer inactivates the repressor to turn the lac operon on; when lactose is absent, the repressor is active and no RNA is made; when lactose is present, allolactose (the inducer) inactivates the repressor, and RNA polymerase transcribes the operon into an mRNA encoding beta-galactosidase, permease and transacetylase.
This is negative gene regulation, because the operon is switched off by the active form of the repressor, the product of a regulatory gene.
A(iii) Some operons are also subject to positive control through a stimulatory protein, catabolite activator protein (CAP), an activator of transcription; when glucose (E. coli's preferred food source) is scarce, CAP is activated by binding cyclic AMP (cAMP).
Activated CAP attaches to the promoter of the lac operon and increases the affinity of RNA polymerase, accelerating transcription; when glucose levels increase, CAP detaches from the lac operon and transcription returns to a normal rate.
A(iv) When lactose is present and glucose is scarce (cAMP level high), abundant lac mRNA is synthesised, because active CAP-cAMP binds the CAP site and RNA polymerase binds efficiently.
When lactose is present but glucose is also present (cAMP level low), CAP is inactive, RNA polymerase is less likely to bind, and only a little lac mRNA is synthesised; CAP also helps regulate other operons encoding enzymes used in catabolic pathways.
B(i) The regulatory step is the combined status of the repressor-operator interaction (inactivated by the inducer allolactose) together with the CAP-cAMP-promoter interaction, both of which govern whether RNA polymerase can transcribe the structural genes efficiently.
C(i) If the repressor cannot be inactivated by the inducer (regulation disrupted at the negative-control step), the operon would remain off (no RNA made) even when lactose is available for metabolism.
Conversely, if CAP cannot bind cAMP or attach to the promoter (regulation disrupted at the positive-control step), RNA polymerase would be less likely to bind even when lactose has inactivated the repressor, so only little lac mRNA would be synthesised despite lactose being present.
This shows that inducible enzymes, which usually function in catabolic pathways, have their synthesis induced by a chemical signal, and that the lac operon integrates negative control (repressor/inducer) and positive control (CAP/cAMP) to match enzyme production to substrate and energy-source availability.
Disruption of either regulatory mechanism therefore uncouples lactose-metabolising enzyme production from the cell's actual need, either preventing induction when lactose is present or preventing efficient transcription when glucose is also present.

A. Describe the activation of a fatty acid before oxidation under the following headings:
A(i) enzymes, their chain-length specificity and locations;
A(ii) the two-stage reaction with substrates and products;
A(iii) the fate of the pyrophosphate produced.
B(i) Explain why the reaction is driven to completion in the cell.
B(ii) State the ATP cost of forming fatty acyl-CoA.
C(i) Distinguish between the site of fatty acid activation and the site of fatty acid oxidation, and between the acyl adenylate intermediate and the acyl CoA product.
questions.answerText:
A(i) A family of at least 3 acyl CoA synthetases (thiokinases) catalyses the activation.
A(i) They differ according to their chain length specificities.
A(i) They are associated with either the ER or the outer mitochondrial membrane.
A(ii) Fatty acid is primed in an ATP-dependent acylation: fatty acid + ATP gives acyl adenylate mixed anhydride + PPi.
A(ii) The acyl adenylate reacts with H-SCoA to give acyl CoA + AMP.
A(iii) PPi is hydrolysed (with H2O) to 2 Pi by the ubiquitous inorganic pyrophosphatase.
A(iii) This hydrolysis is highly exergonic.
B(i) The highly exergonic hydrolysis of pyrophosphate completes the reaction in the cell.
B(ii) 2 ATP equivalents are required for fatty acyl-CoA formation (subtracted in the net yield of palmitate oxidation).
C(i) Activation occurs in the cytosol whereas oxidation occurs in the mitochondrion.
C(i) The acyl adenylate is a mixed anhydride intermediate (R-CO-O-P-adenosine); the acyl CoA is the CoA thioester product (R-CO-SCoA) formed with release of AMP.
C(i) A long chain fatty acyl CoA cannot enter the inner mitochondrial membrane directly; its acyl portion is first transferred to carnitine.

(i) Folic acid deficiency often occurs in alcoholics, women who are pregnant, people who have problems with absorption (with inflammatory bowel disorders such as ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease), and people taking certain prescribed medicines (like methotrexate and cholestyramine); it may also happen due to a lack of dietary consumption.
(ii) Symptoms of folic acid (vitamin B9) deficiency include mood disorders, depression, growth retardation, macrocytic anaemia, glossitis, and gastro-intestinal disorders; more extreme cases can include weakness, fatigue, mood instability, breathing problems, anorexia, diarrhoea, weight loss, headaches and palpitations. Folate deficiency has also been linked with coronary artery disease and peripheral vascular disease. The daily requirement for folic acid increases substantially during pregnancy, and pregnant women who are folate deficient have an elevated risk of giving birth to infants with low birth weight, prematurity, and/or neural tube defects.
(iii) The Centre for Disease Control and the United States Public Health Service have estimated that an intake of 400 micrograms of folic acid each day could possibly result in the prevention of almost 70% of birth defects. Justification: because folic acid deficiency in pregnancy is directly linked to neural tube defects and this specific intake level is stated to prevent most such defects, periconceptional folic acid supplementation at this dose is an appropriate management option. Sources of folate include dark-green and leafy vegetables (including cabbage), citrus fruits, beans, legumes, liver and fortified grain products.

Testing shows hypoglycaemia and lactic acidosis after milk formula or fruit, and enzyme testing shows a deficiency of fructose 1-phosphate aldolase. Her 3-year-old brother has a marked aversion to fruit.
(i) State the diagnosis.

questions.answerText:

questions.question:
A strict vegan presents with tiredness, weakness and pallor. Investigations reveal megaloblastic anaemia. She also reports numbness and tingling in her hands and feet and difficulty walking.
(i) What is the diagnosis?
(ii) What predisposing factors account for her deficiency?
(iii) What is the pathophysiological basis of her haematological and neurological findings?
(iv) What is the management of this condition?
questions.answerText:
(i) The diagnosis is vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency.
(ii) Vitamin B12 only comes from animal sources, where it is found tied to proteins; therefore, strict vegetarians or vegans who don't consume any animal-based foods are the people most likely to have a deficiency. Cobalamin is absorbed in the intestines and needs a secretion from the stomach called gastric intrinsic factor for effective absorption; those deficient in gastric intrinsic factor absorb much less vitamin B12 and may therefore suffer from a deficiency.
(iii) Vitamin B12 is required for the body to absorb, store and activate folate to its coenzyme forms, and works with folate to facilitate cell replication and produce red blood cells; a deficiency causes megaloblastic anaemia (in particular pernicious anaemia), which is identical to folic acid deficiency, with signs including pallor of skin, headache, fatigue, syncope, shortness of breath and palpitations. Cobalamin also plays a vital role in maintaining the health of the central nervous system and in protecting against nerve damage; nerves are encased in a fatty sheath composed of myelin, and those with vitamin B12 deficiency display irregular damage to myelin sheaths, which can result in paralysis, nerve and neurological damage. Neurological problems can include numbness or tingling in the hands and feet, progressive neuropathy, weakness in the legs and problems walking, and these neurological problems may occur without any haematological problems.
(iv) These symptoms (the general and haematological symptoms) can be totally reversed through vitamin B12 treatment; however, depending on severity, neurologic disorders resulting from a cobalamin deficiency may or may not be reversible through treatment.

questions.question:
The same acyl CoA is oxidised in a mitochondrion and in a peroxisome.
(i) Identify the two pathways and the substrates the peroxisomal system handles in animals.
(ii) Name the step that differs and the cofactor involved in both.
(iii) State the ATP difference per cycle and the by-product involved.
(iv) Identify the enzyme with low activity toward short acyl CoAs and the threshold.
(v) State how acyl groups reach each organelle.
questions.answerText:
(i) Mitochondrial β-oxidation and peroxisomal β-oxidation; the peroxisomal system shortens very long chain fatty acids (>22 carbon atoms) in animals for degradation by the mitochondrial system.
(i) The same chemical changes occur, although the enzymes in the two organelles are different.
(ii) The first dehydrogenation; both use an FAD cofactor.
(ii) In mitochondria the FADH2 is reoxidised through the electron transport chain; in peroxisomes the electrons go directly to oxygen.
(iii) Peroxisomal oxidation is less efficient by 2 ATPs for each C2 cycle; the H2O2 formed dissociates to H2O and O2 through catalase.
(iv) Peroxisomal thiolase is almost inactive with acyl CoAs of length C8 or less, so fatty acids are incompletely oxidised by peroxisomes.
(v) Mitochondrion: acyl groups are carried as carnitine esters (carnitine palmitoyl transferases I and II and a specific carrier protein).
(v) Peroxisome: no carnitine requirement; very long chain fatty acids diffuse in and are activated by peroxisomal very long chain acyl CoA synthetase.
(v) Shortened products are converted to carnitine esters by peroxisomal carnitine acyl transferase for export to the mitochondrion.

A(i) Activation occurs in the cytosol, by acyl CoA synthetases associated with the ER or the outer mitochondrial membrane.
A(ii) A long chain acyl CoA cannot enter the inner mitochondrial membrane directly; the acyl portion is transferred to carnitine by carnitine palmitoyl transferases I and II with a specific carrier protein.
A(iii) β-oxidation occurs in the mitochondrion and, for very long chain fatty acids in animals, also in the peroxisome.
A(iv) In plants, fatty acid oxidation occurs exclusively in the peroxisomes and glyoxysomes.
B(i) The acyl CoA synthetases (at least 3) differ according to chain length specificities; a very long chain acyl CoA synthetase is found in the peroxisome.
B(i) Mitochondria contain 3 acyl CoA dehydrogenases with specificities for short-, medium- and long-chain fatty acyl CoAs.
B(i) The peroxisomal system shortens very long chain fatty acids (>22 carbon atoms) so that the mitochondrial system can degrade them.
B(i) Peroxisomal thiolase is almost inactive with acyl CoAs of length C8 or less, so peroxisomal oxidation is incomplete.
C(i) The 3-step process carrying acyl groups from cytosolic fatty acyl-CoA into the matrix is rate-limiting for fatty acid oxidation.
C(i) Carnitine acyl transferase I is inhibited by malonyl-CoA.
C(i) Since oxidation occurs in the mitochondrion, restricting entry limits the acyl groups available for mitochondrial oxidation.
C(i) Peroxisomal β-oxidation does not depend on carnitine esters for entry, but its shortened products are converted to carnitine esters to reach the mitochondrion.

A(i) Very long chain fatty acids diffuse into the peroxisome; there is no carnitine requirement for transport of the fatty acyl-CoA into it.
A(i) They are activated by peroxisomal very long chain acyl CoA synthetase to CoA esters and oxidised directly.
A(ii) The peroxisome contains both a carnitine acyl transferase and a transferase specific for long chain acyl groups.
A(ii) Acyl CoAs shortened by peroxisomal β-oxidation are thereby converted to their carnitine esters.
A(iii) The shorter chain acyl products are linked to carnitine for transport to the mitochondrion.
A(iii) Most of these substrates diffuse passively out of the peroxisome.
A(iv) The destination is the mitochondrion, where they are oxidised further.
B(i) Peroxisomal thiolase has a different chain length specificity from its mitochondrial counterpart.
B(i) It is almost inactive with acyl CoAs of length C8 or less, so fatty acids are incompletely oxidised.
C(i) In the first dehydrogenation the electrons are transferred directly to oxygen rather than through the electron transport chain and oxidative phosphorylation.
C(i) Peroxisomal oxidation is therefore less efficient by 2 ATPs for each C2 cycle.
C(i) The H2O2 formed dissociates to H2O and O2 through peroxisomal catalase.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe cholesterol biosynthesis under the following headings: the four stages of synthesis, and the enzymes of the first stage (acetate to mevalonate).
A(ii) State the rate-determining step of cholesterol synthesis and how the pathway is regulated.
C. Distinguish between the cytosolic and mitochondrial fates of the enzymes thiolase and HMG-CoA synthase.
questions.answerText:
A(i) All 27 carbons of cholesterol are derived from acetyl-CoA. There are four stages of cholesterol synthesis: (1) Acetate → Mevalonate, by three cytosolic enzymes: thiolase, hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA synthase (forming beta-hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA, HMG-CoA), and HMG-CoA reductase; (2) Mevalonate → Isopentenyl pyrophosphate (IPP), and IPP ⇌ Dimethylallyl pyrophosphate (DMP) by isopentenyl pyrophosphate isomerase; (3) IPP + DMP → Squalene; (4) Squalene → Cholesterol, via squalene → 2,3-oxidosqualene (catalysed by squalene epoxidase, requiring NADPH), 2,3-oxidosqualene → lanosterol, and lanosterol → cholesterol by 19 steps.
A(ii) The synthesis of mevalonate is irreversible and is the rate-determining step in cholesterol synthesis; HMG-CoA reductase can be inhibited by cholesterol.
C. The cytosolic forms of thiolase and HMG-CoA synthase are involved in cholesterol synthesis, converting acetate to mevalonate as the first stage of the four-stage cholesterol synthesis pathway, whereas the corresponding mitochondrial enzymes are instead involved in ketone body (acetoacetate) synthesis, showing that the same reaction sequence in a different cellular compartment serves a different metabolic fate.

questions.question:
After the third round of β-oxidation of an unsaturated fatty acyl CoA, the resulting enoyl-CoA carries a cis double bond between the β and γ carbons.
(i) Identify the problem and the products of the first three rounds.
(ii) State the factor that makes the compound unsuitable for the next enzyme.
(iii) Describe the enzymatic correction and the product.
(iv) State the effect on energy yield compared with the saturated counterpart.
questions.answerText:
(i) This is the β,γ double bond problem, occurring after the third round; the three rounds give 3 NADH, 3 FADH2 and 3 acetyl CoA.
(ii) The resulting cis β,γ double bond containing enoyl CoA is not a substrate for enoyl CoA hydratase.
(iii) Enoyl CoA isomerase converts the cis Δ3 double bond to the more stable ester conjugated trans-Δ2 form.
(iii) Such compounds are normal substrates of enoyl-CoA hydratase, so β-oxidation can then continue.
(iv) Acyl CoA dehydrogenase is bypassed, giving one fewer FADH2 and 1.5 fewer ATPs than the saturated counterpart.

questions.question:
A young boy presents with progressive muscle weakness; serum creatine kinase (CK) is found to be markedly elevated, more than 50 times the baseline level.
(i) Which enzyme is the key biochemical marker here, and where is it normally distributed?
(ii) Which organ is affected, and to what degree in this specific condition?
(iii) What other conditions can also raise this marker, and how would the degree of elevation help differentiate them?
(iv) How would you reason biochemically from the pattern described to support the diagnosis?
questions.answerText:
(i) Creatine kinase (CK) is the key marker; it is primarily involved in ATP regeneration and storage, and its activity is highest in striated muscle, heart muscle and brain, with negligible presence in liver and erythrocytes; CK is a dimeric enzyme of B (brain) and M (muscle) subunits forming isoenzymes CK-1 (BB), CK-2 (MB), CK-3 (MM) and CK-mt (mitochondrial), with CK-3 responsible for almost all CK enzyme activity.
(ii) Skeletal muscle is affected; in Duchenne muscular dystrophy, CK is elevated to more than 50 times the baseline level.
(iii) CK activity is also elevated in damage involving muscle or brain generally, including after myocardial infarction, in cerebral ischaemia, acute cerebrovascular disease, head injury and neurological interventions, in Reye's syndrome (CK more than 70-fold over control), and up to 5 times normal in about 60% of hypothyroid subjects; CK serum activity is also a function of muscle mass, being lower in females than males and higher in muscular individuals.
(iv) The very large magnitude of CK elevation (>50x baseline) in a young boy, far greater than the moderate rises seen in thyroid disease or the more focal rises seen in CNS conditions, together with the tissue distribution of the CK-3 (MM) isoenzyme in skeletal muscle, supports a primary skeletal muscle (dystrophic) origin for the elevated enzyme.

A(i) Located at the top of each kidney ('suprarenal'); each is really two endocrine glands, the outer adrenal cortex and the inner adrenal medulla, secreting unrelated chemicals that all help with extreme situations.
A(ii) Cortex: lipid-based steroid hormones (corticosteroids) made from cholesterol: mineralocorticoids (aldosterone), glucocorticoids (cortisol, the most abundant) and androgens (testosterone precursors such as DHEA). Medulla: epinephrine and norepinephrine.
- Glucocorticoids raise blood glucose by gluconeogenesis (fats and proteins to glucose), are anti-inflammatory (useful in rheumatoid arthritis and asthma), depress cell-mediated immunity and help prevent transplant rejection.
- Aldosterone promotes renal sodium reabsorption (maintaining blood pressure), reduces sodium loss in sweat and increases taste sensitivity to sodium; adrenaline raises blood sugar, heartbeat and breathing rate.
A(iii) Stress: hypothalamic CRH - anterior pituitary ACTH - glucocorticoid secretion (the sympathetic nervous system can also stimulate); feedback loops link stimuli, hypothalamus, anterior pituitary, adrenal cortex and tissues; ACTH triggers all three classes of steroid.
- Aldosterone is stimulated by a fall in blood sodium, a rise in blood potassium, angiotensin II and ACTH; aldosterone is made in the zona glomerulosa, glucocorticoids in the zona fasciculata and zona reticularis.
B(i) Primary hyperaldosteronism: one or both adrenals make too much aldosterone: unilateral adenoma (2/3), bilateral hyperplasia (1/3), carcinoma, unilateral hyperplasia or familial types I and II (each <1%); it is 'secondary' if the cause lies outside the adrenals.
- Cushing's syndrome: hypersecretion of adrenal hormones, especially glucocorticoids. Addison's disease: hyposecretion of the cortex, usually cortisol and aldosterone, with low blood glucose and sodium, severe dehydration, fatigue, loss of appetite and abdominal pain.
- Androgen excess: adrenal testosterone excess causes premature puberty in young boys; in females (adrenal cortex is a major androgen source) it gives a masculine pattern of body hair and even cessation of menstruation.
C(i) Cushing's is usually caused by an ACTH-secreting pituitary tumour (a distant gland driving the cortex), rarely by an adrenal cortex tumour, and can result from glucocorticoid therapy for a disorder such as rheumatoid arthritis or to prevent organ rejection.
- Target-tissue effects then follow: kidney (sodium), sweat glands, taste cells, liver (glucose), immune cells; DHEA is converted in peripheral tissues to testosterone and estrogen.
- Undersecretion of adrenaline results in inability to deal with stress.

(i) The diagnosis is an erythropoietic porphyria — either congenital erythropoietic porphyria or erythropoietic protoporphyria.
(ii) Congenital erythropoietic porphyria results from deficiency of uroporphyrinogen III synthase; erythropoietic protoporphyria results from deficiency of ferrochelatase.
(iii) Porphyrias are genetic diseases in which activity of one of the enzymes of heme synthesis is decreased; this leads to accumulation of porphyrinogens in the skin and tissues, with spontaneous oxidation of porphyrinogens to porphyrins causing photosensitivity.
(iv) Symptoms include skin rashes and blisters early in childhood, and cholestatic liver cirrhosis with progressive liver failure.
(v) These conditions are classified as erythropoietic porphyrias (as opposed to hepatic porphyrias), caused by hereditary or acquired defects in heme synthesis; treatment for porphyrias includes medical support for vomiting and pain, hemin (which decreases ALA synthase synthesis), and avoidance of sunlight and precipitating drugs or factors.
