questions.answerText:
A(i) Twenty-carbon derivatives of arachidonic acid (20:4), made in almost every tissue in small amounts from essential fatty acids (linoleic acid); prostaglandins are derivatives of prostanoic acid with a 5-carbon ring formed by C8-C12 and two side chains.
A(ii) Arachidonate from phospholipid (phospholipase A2) is cyclised by cyclooxygenase (prostaglandin endoperoxide synthase) to PGG2 then PGH2; cell-specific synthases convert PGH2 to prostaglandins and thromboxanes; the 5-lipoxygenase route forms leukotrienes (LTA4, LTC4, LTD4, LTE4) and competes with COX for substrate.
- Naming: the E type has a keto group at C9 and the F type a hydroxyl; subscripts 1, 2, 3 give the number of double bonds; thromboxanes have an oxygen-interrupted (oxane) ring; leukotrienes have three conjugated double bonds.
A(iii) They act locally as paracrine hormones, are not stored, have very short half-lives and are degraded at the site of production; PGE raises cAMP and PGF raises cGMP.
- PGE, PGA and PGI2 are vasodilators lowering blood pressure; PGE1 and PGE2 cause inflammation; PGE2 and PGF2-alpha induce labour and terminate pregnancy; pyrogens raise hypothalamic PGE2 (fever) and PGE2 with histamine and bradykinin causes pain.
- PGE inhibits gastric secretion, stimulates pancreatic secretion and intestinal motility; PGE is a bronchodilator whereas PGF constricts bronchial muscle; PGE increases GFR, urine output and Na+ and K+ excretion, decreases lipolysis and increases glycogen formation; PGI2 inhibits, and TXA2 and PGE2 promote, platelet aggregation.
B(i) Corticosteroids inhibit phospholipase A2 (preventing arachidonic acid formation); aspirin irreversibly acetylates serine in COX; indomethacin reversibly inhibits COX; ibuprofen and meclofenamate also inhibit COX.
C(i) Blocking COX lowers prostaglandins and thromboxanes, relieving pain, fever and inflammation; low-dose aspirin irreversibly inhibits COX-1 and reduces heart attack and stroke; side effects include GI irritation, ulcers and bleeding, and aspirin-triggered asthma when COX blockade diverts substrate to leukotrienes.
- COX-1: constitutive, present in most tissues, homeostatic role (protects gastric mucosa), not influenced by steroids or increased by cytokines or bacteria.
- COX-2: inducible after inflammation or trauma, found in immunocompetent cells, pathophysiological role (pain, inflammation, fever), induced by interleukin-1 and inhibited by steroids; COX-2-selective drugs exploit its side pocket (Val523 versus Ile523).
- Tylenol is thought to act through COX-3, an alternatively spliced form of COX-1.
- Thromboxanes are made by platelets and promote clot formation and reduced blood flow at the clot.

A(i) Control point 1: the 3-step process by which fatty acyl groups are carried from cytosolic fatty acyl-CoA into the mitochondrial matrix is rate-limiting.
A(ii) Control point 2: carnitine acyl transferase I is inhibited by malonyl-CoA.
A(iii) Control point 3: β-hydroxyacyl CoA dehydrogenase is inhibited when the [NADH]/[NAD+] ratio is high.
A(iv) Control point 4: high concentrations of acetyl-CoA inhibit thiolase.
B(i) Malonyl-CoA is the first intermediate in the cytosolic biosynthesis of long chain fatty acids from acetyl CoA.
B(i) It acts when the liver is amply supplied with glucose and actively making triacylglycerols from excess glucose.

questions.question:
A child on a diet lacking orange, yellow and dark green vegetables presents with difficulty seeing in dim light, dry and scaly skin, and increased susceptibility to infections. His mother is pregnant and in her third trimester.
(i) Identify the nutrient deficiency responsible for the child's findings.
(ii) What organ/structure is chiefly affected, and what other body tissues are affected by this deficiency?
(iii) What is the differential concern for the mother given her stage of pregnancy?
(iv) Give the clinico-biochemical reasoning linking this nutrient to the child's eye and skin findings.
questions.answerText:
(i) The nutrient deficiency responsible is vitamin A deficiency. Vitamin A is the name for a group of fat-soluble compounds with four isoprenoid units joined in a head-to-tail fashion; there are two main forms, provitamin A carotenoids (beta-carotene and other carotenoids) and preformed vitamin A (retinol), with retinol being the most easily used, active form, and all other forms converted to retinol before use.
(ii) Vitamin A (retinol) promotes healthy eye function and aids the eyes in adjusting to light changes when going from bright to dark environments; a deficiency can cause night blindness as well as other eye and vision problems. It also promotes the growth and health of body cells and tissues, particularly in the mouth, digestive tract and lungs, and helps regulate the immune system and guard against bacterial infection; deficiency can therefore also cause altered skin appearance (dry and/or scaly skin), increased susceptibility to infectious diseases, and decreased function of lung and intestinal tissues in severe cases.
(iii) Vitamin A is especially crucial for pregnant women, as it aids in postpartum tissue repair; a deficiency can cause problems during pregnancy, particularly in the third trimester when demand for the vitamin is particularly high, and can result in night blindness in the mother, plus problems related to the placenta and possibly low birth weight of the baby.
(iv) Vitamin A promotes healthy eye function and aids adjustment to changes in light, so its deficiency causes night blindness; it also promotes growth and health of body cells and tissues (mouth, digestive tract, lungs) and acts as an antioxidant neutralising free radicals, so its deficiency also produces dry, scaly skin and increased susceptibility to infection, consistent with the child's presentation. Dietary sources include orange and yellow fruits such as mango, orange and red vegetables such as carrot, red pepper, pumpkin, sweet potatoes and tomatoes, and green or dark green leafy vegetables, along with braised liver and fortified foods and cereals.

(i) Complications of treatment: NSAIDs can cause gastrointestinal irritation, ulcers and bleeding; glucocorticoid therapy (for rheumatoid arthritis or to prevent organ rejection) can produce Cushing's syndrome (hypersecretion of adrenal hormones, especially glucocorticoids) and depresses the cell-mediated immune response.
(ii) Options: glucocorticoids/corticosteroids (potent anti-inflammatory effect, useful in rheumatoid arthritis; they inhibit phospholipase A2 and so prevent formation of arachidonic acid); aspirin (irreversible COX inhibitor); indomethacin (reversible COX inhibitor); ibuprofen and other NSAIDs.
- Justification for a corticosteroid: all eicosanoids (prostaglandins, thromboxanes, leukotrienes) derive from arachidonic acid, so blocking its formation at phospholipase A2 lowers all of them, whereas NSAIDs act one step later on COX; corticosteroids also inhibit COX-2.
- Aspirin is non-selective (COX-1 and COX-2) with many side effects; COX-1 is not influenced by steroid administration, whereas inducible COX-2 (which maintains inflammation) is inhibited by steroids.

(i) Alpha thalassaemia results from mutation of one or more of the 4 alpha globin genes on chromosome 16; the severity of disease depends on the number of genes affected, and results in an excess of beta globins.
(ii) Silent carriers (heterozygotes, 3 functional alpha globin genes) have no symptoms, but thalassaemia could potentially appear in their offspring; alpha thalassaemia trait (2 functional globin genes) results in smaller, lighter-coloured blood cells with no serious symptoms except slight anaemia; alpha thalassaemia major (no functional globin genes) results in death before birth (embryonic lethality).
(iii) Specific treatment protocols are not well defined by genotype, but based on the outcomes described, alpha thalassaemia major is the most clinically urgent form, since it causes embryonic lethality, whereas the silent carrier and trait forms cause no serious symptoms and mainly carry reproductive/genetic-counselling significance for offspring.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Located in the inner mitochondrial membrane; protons can pass from the intermembrane space to the matrix only through ATP synthase. It consists of F1 and F0: F1 has five types of polypeptide chains (alpha3, beta3, gamma, delta, epsilon); F0 contains the proton channel (10-14 c subunits, plus a and b2 subunits).
A(ii) Chemiosmotic hypothesis: ATP synthesis and electron transport are coupled by the proton gradient across the mitochondrial membrane; the gradient acts through a binding-change mechanism in which the 3 beta subunits promote ADP and Pi binding, ATP synthesis and ATP release.
- Each c subunit has 2 alpha helices, one carrying an aspartic acid residue; the a subunit has two proton half-channels (cytosolic and matrix).
- A proton entering the half-channel neutralises the charge on aspartate, so the c ring can rotate and the proton passes into the matrix; the c ring is linked to the gamma and epsilon subunits, so they rotate, and this rotation promotes ATP synthesis.
A(iii) Each 360-degree rotation of the gamma subunit synthesises 3 ATP; 10 protons generate 3 ATP, about 3 protons per ATP (plus 1 proton used to move ATP out).
- P/O ratio (ATP per 2 electrons to oxygen): NADH, 10 protons pumped / 4 per ATP = 2.5; FADH2, 6 / 4 = 1.5.
B(i) Oligomycin binds directly to the F0 subunit and blocks proton flow through the channel; DCCD forms covalent bonds to a glutamate residue of the c subunit of F0, blocking the proton channel, so rotation and ATP synthesis cease.
- Uncouplers (2,4-dinitrophenol, dicumarol, FCCP) act differently: they carry protons across the inner membrane, collapsing the gradient; the energy is lost as heat and oxygen is consumed even without ADP.
- Respiration rate is controlled by the supply of ADP: oxygen is consumed only when ADP is added and stops when it is all converted to ATP.
C(i) F1: the catalytic head; the beta subunits bind ADP and Pi, synthesise and release ATP (binding-change mechanism).
- F0: the membrane-embedded proton channel; proton flow through F0 (c ring, a and b2 subunits) drives rotation of the gamma subunit.
- Blocking F0 (oligomycin, DCCD) stops proton flow and ATP synthesis.

questions.question:

questions.answerText:
(i) The process is an ATP-dependent acylation that forms fatty acyl-CoA.
(i) It is catalysed by a family of at least 3 acyl CoA synthetases (thiokinases) that differ according to their chain length specificities.
(i) The enzymes are associated with either the ER or the outer mitochondrial membrane.
(ii) Fatty acid + ATP gives acyl adenylate mixed anhydride + PPi (acyl CoA synthetase).
(ii) Acyl adenylate reacts with H-SCoA to give acyl CoA + AMP.
(iii) Pyrophosphate is hydrolysed to 2 Pi (with H2O) by the ubiquitous inorganic pyrophosphatase.
(iii) This hydrolysis is highly exergonic and completes the reaction in the cell.
(iv) 2 ATP equivalents are required for fatty acyl-CoA formation.
(iv) Activation occurs in the cytosol but oxidation occurs in the mitochondrion.
(iv) A long chain fatty acyl CoA cannot enter the inner mitochondrial membrane directly; its acyl portion is first transferred to carnitine.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the chain composition of immunoglobulins.
A(ii) Describe the variable and constant regions of immunoglobulins.
A(iii) Describe the hinge region.
A(iv) Describe the domain structure of immunoglobulins.
B(i) Explain the clinical basis for why only IgG (of all the antibody classes) protects the newborn before and after birth.
C(i) Distinguish between the Fab fragment and the Fc fragment.
questions.answerText:
A(i) All immunoglobulins are built from a four polypeptide-chain basic unit: two identical light chains (23kD) and two identical heavy chains (50-70kD).
Heavy and light chains, and the two heavy chains, are held together by inter-chain disulphide bonds and non-covalent interactions; intra-chain disulphide bonds also occur within each chain.
A(ii) Both heavy and light chains divide into variable (V) and constant (C) regions based on amino acid sequence variability.
Light chain: VL and CL, each about 110 amino acids; Heavy chain: VH (110 amino acids) and CH (330-440 amino acids).
A(iii) The hinge region is where the arms of the antibody form a Y shape and is called the hinge because of flexibility in the molecule at this point.
A(iv) The molecule folds into globular domains, each containing an intra-chain disulphide bond: light chain domains VL and CL; heavy chain domains VH, CH1-CH3 (or CH4).
Carbohydrates are attached to the CH2 domain in most immunoglobulins.
B(i) Only IgG can cross the placenta because only the gamma-chain has constant domains that bind placental cells.
Most protection for a foetus or newborn comes from maternal IgG crossing the placenta, since the foetus/newborn has limited immune responses.
Intact IgG or Fc fragments of IgG can cross the placenta, but Fab or F(ab')2 fragments cannot.
C(i) Papain digestion breaks the hinge region before the H-H inter-chain disulphide bonds, forming two Fab fragments (light chain plus VH and CH1) that contain the antigen-binding sites.
Papain digestion also produces the Fc fragment (CH2 and CH3 domains), easily crystallized, which mediates the effector functions of the antibody.

A(i) Outer membrane: reasonably permeable, containing porins (VDAC). Inner membrane: relatively impermeable, and impermeable to charged molecules, NAD+ and NADH; it carries the respiratory chain and ATP synthase.
A(ii) Inner membrane: the respiratory complexes (three proton pumps and one link to the citric acid cycle) and ATP synthase. Matrix: citric acid cycle, pyruvate oxidation and most NADH production (the NADH site of Complex I faces the matrix).
- Intermembrane space: where protons accumulate (proton motive force) and where cytochrome c operates; carriers (ATP-ADP translocase, phosphate, dicarboxylate, tricarboxylate, pyruvate carriers) and shuttles link matrix and cytosol.
A(iii) Believed origin is endosymbiosis; evidence: mitochondrial DNA, machinery for transcription and translation, and a genome similar to that of bacteria.
B(i) Complex I: rotenone (insecticide, fish poison), amytal (barbiturate) and Demerol (painkiller) block oxidation of the Fe-S clusters. Complex II: 2-thenoyltrifluoroacetone and carboxin. Complex III: antimycin A1 (blocks Cyt bH to Q at the QN site).
- Complex IV: cyanide and azide (bind Fe3+ of Cyt a3) and carbon monoxide (Fe2+); cells have few Cyt a3 molecules, so small amounts of cyanide or azide are lethal, whereas CO acts largely on haemoglobin and needs a large quantity.
- ATP synthase: oligomycin (F0) and DCCD (c subunit). ATP-ADP translocase: atractyloside (plant glycoside) blocks ATP-ADP exchange and stops oxidative phosphorylation.
- Uncouplers (2,4-dinitrophenol, dicumarol, FCCP): hydrophobic weak acids that carry protons across the inner membrane, collapsing the gradient; energy is lost as heat.
C(i) Blocking electron flow leaves carriers before the block fully reduced and those after it oxidised; ATP formation, coupled through the proton gradient, falls. Efficiency is normally ~54% (about 30-32 ATP per glucose depending on the shuttle).
- Useful uncoupling: brown adipose tissue (hibernating and newborn animals, including humans) is rich in mitochondria; thermogenin (UCP-1) opens a passive proton channel, collapsing the pH gradient to generate heat, and fatty acids activate UCP-1.
- Partial reduction of O2 gives superoxide and peroxide; cells protect themselves with superoxide dismutase and catalase.
- The proton motive force also drives transport of charged molecules across the inner membrane.

A(i) The ATP-ADP translocase (an antiporter) lets ATP exit and ADP enter the mitochondrion, the two movements being coupled; it has a single nucleotide binding site that binds ADP and ATP with equal affinity.
- Because of the negative matrix charge, ATP4- is exported about 30 times faster than ADP3- is imported; the net exchange of one negative charge out of the matrix decreases the proton motive force.
A(ii) Phosphate carrier: electroneutral symport of Pi with H+ (secondary active transport); with the translocase it exchanges ADP + Pi for ATP at the cost of one proton. Dicarboxylate carrier: antiport of malate, succinate and fumarate with phosphate; tricarboxylate carrier: antiport of citrate + H+ for malate; pyruvate carrier: symport of pyruvate and a proton into the matrix.
A(iii) Glycerol 3-phosphate shuttle (muscle): cytosolic G3P dehydrogenase reduces dihydroxyacetone phosphate to glycerol 3-phosphate using NADH; G3P crosses the outer membrane through a porin and is reoxidised by FAD-dependent G3P dehydrogenase on the inner membrane, giving FADH2 that passes electrons to coenzyme Q (QH2 to Complex III).
- Malate-aspartate shuttle (heart and liver): cytosolic oxaloacetate is reduced to malate by malate dehydrogenase using NADH; malate enters via the dicarboxylate or tricarboxylate carrier and is reoxidised to oxaloacetate and NADH in the matrix, which feeds Complex I; oxaloacetate is transaminated to aspartate and alpha-ketoglutarate, aspartate leaves and transaminates alpha-ketoglutarate in the cytosol to reform oxaloacetate.
B(i) The inner membrane is impermeable to NAD+ and NADH, yet cytosolic NADH must be reoxidised to keep glycolysis going: anaerobically by lactate dehydrogenase; aerobically its electrons must be shuttled into the matrix.
- Atractyloside (a plant glycoside) binds the translocase when its nucleotide binding site faces the intermembrane space, completely blocking ATP-ADP translocation and stopping oxidative phosphorylation.
- The proton gradient's potential energy also drives active transport of charged molecules, to which the inner membrane is otherwise impermeable.
C(i) Glycerol 3-phosphate shuttle: electrons transferred to FAD (FADH2 to Q), 1.5 ATP per NADH, essentially irreversible, found in muscle.
- Malate-aspartate shuttle: electrons delivered to matrix NAD+ (NADH to Complex I), 2.5 ATP per NADH, completely reversible, found in heart and liver.
- Net ATP from glucose oxidation: 30 with the glycerophosphate shuttle versus 32 with the malate-aspartate shuttle (about two more ATP).
- Energy efficiency of 32 ATP per glucose is 1600/2937 kJ/mol, about 54%.

A(i) Bile acids (bile salts) are polar derivatives of cholesterol made in the liver, secreted with bile via the gallbladder and bile duct into the duodenum; at physiological pH they are anions with detergent properties.
A(ii) Above the pK and above 2-5 mM (the critical micellar concentration) they reversibly aggregate into micelles, 40-600 Angstrom in size depending on bile acid concentration and the bile acid:lipid ratio; hydrophobic parts face away from water and hydrophilic groups stay exposed; four bile acid molecules can form a simple micelle.
A(iii) Mixed micelles are disk-shaped: phospholipids and fatty acids form a bilayer with bile acids at the hydrophilic edges; cholesterol is solubilised within mixed phospholipid-bile acid micelles.
- The fluid layer next to the cell surface is poorly mixed, so flux is by diffusion; micelles raise the effective concentration by up to 1000-fold compared with single fatty acids and are the major vehicle carrying lipid from lumen to cell surface.
- Pancreatic lipase (activated by colipase, which needs tryptic removal of an NH2-terminal decapeptide) gives fatty acids and 2-monoacylglycerols; phospholipase A2 (activated by trypsin) gives lysophospholipids, powerful detergents; a less specific esterase acts on cholesterol and vitamin A esters.
B(i) Efficient absorption needs enough bile acids to solubilise hydrolysed lipids; without them triacylglycerol absorption does not stop completely but is drastically reduced, relying on the slight water solubility of free fatty acids and monoacylglycerols.
- Unabsorbed lipids reach the lower intestine, where a small part is metabolised by bacteria and the bulk is excreted in stool (steatorrhoea).
- For cholesterol and vitamins A and K, which are even less water-soluble, bile acid secretion is absolutely necessary; the esterase and phospholipase A2 also require bile acids for activity.
C(i) Micelles are equilibrium structures of well-defined size, much smaller than emulsion droplets, and their bile acids are in equilibrium with free bile acids.
- Emulsion arises when acid-stable gastric lipase releases surfactive fatty acids, monoacylglycerols and phospholipids, increasing lipid-water interfacial area and dispersing the lipid phase into smaller droplets; pancreatic lipase then acts at the emulsion interface.
- After micellar delivery, uptake is by diffusion through the plasma membrane; fatty acids and monoacylglycerols are almost completely absorbed, cholesterol less efficiently.
- Five phases: hydrolysis, solubilisation, uptake with resynthesis of triacylglycerol, chylomicron packaging, and exocytosis into lymph.

(i) The pituitary gland: a round organ about the size of a pea (about 1 cm in diameter) behind the bridge of the nose at the base of the brain; it secretes 9 different hormones.
(ii) Its hormones affect growth, blood pressure, regulation of pregnancy, breast milk production, sex organ function in both sexes, thyroid gland function, metabolism, water regulation by the kidneys and temperature regulation.
- The anterior lobe (adenohypophysis) releases ACTH, which triggers production of adrenal cortical steroids, and glycoprotein hormones (TSH, LH, FSH).
(iii) Oversecretion of growth hormone: gigantism in childhood and acromegaly in adults (bones of the face, hands and feet enlarge); undersecretion: dwarfism in childhood.
- An ACTH-secreting pituitary tumour is the usual cause of Cushing's syndrome (excess glucocorticoids).
(iv) Growth hormone regulates cell growth by binding to growth hormone receptors on target cells; hormones act only on tissues (target cells) that carry their specific receptors, and endocrine output is regulated by positive and negative feedback.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Glucose is metabolised in the red blood cell by two major pathways: the glycolytic ("energy-producing") pathway and the hexose monophosphate shunt ("protective pathway"); the HMP shunt metabolises 5% to 10% of the glucose used by the RBC.
A(ii) Glycolysis converts glucose through glucose-6-phosphate, fructose-6-phosphate, fructose-1,6-diphosphate and downstream intermediates to pyruvate/lactate, generating ATP and 2,3-diphosphoglycerate (2,3-DPG), which modulates haemoglobin oxygen affinity.
Glycolysis is the only pathway that supplies ATP to the RBC; it also provides NADH for reduction of methaemoglobin by NADH-cytochrome b5 reductase, and 2,3-DPG binds haemoglobin, decreasing its oxygen affinity and helping deliver oxygen to tissues.
A(iii) In the oxidative stage of the HMP shunt, glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase converts glucose-6-phosphate to 6-phosphogluconolactone, producing NADPH ("reducing power"); NADPH is required by glutathione reductase, which reduces oxidised glutathione (GSSG) to reduced glutathione (GSH), needed for elimination of peroxide and protection of protein -SH groups.
A(iv) ATP generated by glycolysis is utilised for phosphorylation of sugars and proteins, ATPase-driven ion pumps, maintenance of membrane asymmetry, and maintenance of red cell shape and deformability via the ATP-dependent cytoskeleton.
A red blood cell enzyme disorder should be suspected in persistent normocytic haemolytic anaemia where haemoglobin abnormalities and antiglobulin reactions are excluded, spherocytes are absent, and osmotic fragility is normal.
B(i) Enzyme deficiencies fall into two groups: deficiencies of glycolysis and nucleotide metabolism, of which pyruvate kinase (PK) deficiency is the most common cause.
The second group is deficiencies of the HMP shunt and glutathione metabolism, of which glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency is the most common, being the most common metabolic disorder of the RBC, affecting more than 400 million people worldwide.
Other enzymopathies include pyrimidine 5' nucleotidase deficiency (the third most common cause of enzymatic haemolysis, an autosomal recessive disorder), cytochrome b5 reductase deficiency, and familial 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate deficiency.
C(i) In glycolytic enzyme deficiencies such as PK deficiency, continuously impaired ATP generation causes a lack of sufficient energy for glycolysis, electrolyte gradients, glutathione synthesis, membrane phospholipid asymmetry and purine/pyrimidine metabolism, leading to chronic haemolytic anaemia.
ATP depletion initiates a series of events leading to premature destruction of young PK-deficient red cells, mainly in the spleen, with red blood cell enzymopathies generally causing hereditary nonspherocytic haemolytic anaemia (HNSHA), mostly through extravascular haemolysis.
In G6PD deficiency, inadequate NADPH generation from the HMP shunt leaves inadequate levels of reduced glutathione, so the cell cannot withstand oxidative stress, presenting as acute haemolytic episodes triggered by oxidant drugs, foods (favism), or infection.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Mitochondrial: fatty acyl CoAs, handled by 3 acyl CoA dehydrogenases (short-, medium- and long-chain); peroxisomal: very long chain fatty acids (>22 carbon atoms) in animals.
A(ii) Mitochondrion: acyl groups enter as carnitine esters (carnitine palmitoyl transferases I and II and a carrier protein); peroxisome: no carnitine requirement, very long chain fatty acids diffuse in and are activated by a very long chain acyl CoA synthetase.
A(iii) Both first oxidations use FAD; mitochondrial FADH2 is reoxidised by the electron transport chain, whereas peroxisomal electrons pass directly to oxygen.
A(iv) Peroxisomal enoyl-CoA hydratase and 3-L-hydroxyacyl CoA dehydrogenase occur in a single polypeptide; their reactions are identical to those of the mitochondrial system.
B(i) Without the electron transport chain and oxidative phosphorylation for the first step, peroxisomal oxidation is less efficient by 2 ATPs per C2 cycle.
B(i) The H2O2 formed dissociates to H2O and O2 through peroxisomal catalase.
B(i) Peroxisomal thiolase is almost inactive with acyl CoAs of length C8 or less, so fatty acids are incompletely oxidised.
C(i) The thiolases of the two organelles differ in chain length specificity.
C(i) In animals, peroxisomal β-oxidation shortens very long chain fatty acids so that the mitochondrial system can degrade them.
C(i) Peroxisomal end products are linked to carnitine and diffuse to the mitochondrion for further oxidation.
C(i) Mitochondrial acetyl CoA is oxidised via the citric acid cycle to generate FADH2 and NADH for ATP formation.
C(i) In plants, fatty acid oxidation occurs exclusively in peroxisomes and glyoxysomes.

questions.question:
Linoleyl CoA, an unsaturated fatty acyl CoA, is degraded by β-oxidation.
(i) State the products of the first three rounds.
(ii) Identify the enzymatic difficulty that arises after the third round and the enzyme that resolves it.
(iii) Name the form of the intermediate that enoyl-CoA hydratase can accept.
(iv) Identify the step that is bypassed in this situation.
(v) Describe the second difficulty that arises in the fifth round and how it is handled.
questions.answerText:
(i) Three rounds of β-oxidation use 3 NAD+, 3 FAD and 3 CoA-SH and give 3 NADH, 3 FADH2 and 3 acetyl CoA.
(ii) After the third round the cis β,γ (Δ3) double bond containing enoyl CoA is not a substrate for enoyl CoA hydratase.
(ii) Enoyl CoA isomerase converts the cis Δ3 double bond to the more stable ester conjugated trans-Δ2 form.
(iii) The trans-Δ2 form; such compounds are normal substrates of enoyl-CoA hydratase, so β-oxidation can then continue.
(iv) Acyl CoA dehydrogenase is bypassed.
(v) In the 5th round a double bond at an even numbered carbon atom (Δ4) results in 2,4-dienoyl CoA, a poor substrate for enoyl CoA hydratase.
(v) NADPH-dependent 2,4-dienoyl CoA reductase reduces the Δ4 double bond and yields trans-3-enoyl CoA.
(v) 3,2-enoyl CoA isomerase then isomerises trans-3-enoyl CoA to trans-2-enoyl CoA, and β-oxidation continues.

questions.question:
A sailor on a long voyage with a diet lacking fresh fruit and vegetables develops fatigue, muscle weakness, joint and muscle aches, bleeding gums and leg rashes. Later he develops loose teeth and delayed wound healing.
(i) Identify the nutrient deficiency responsible for these findings.
(ii) What pathway/process is affected by this deficiency that explains the bleeding gums, loose teeth and delayed wound healing?
(iii) Why can humans not synthesise this nutrient, unlike many other animals?
(iv) Give the clinico-biochemical reasoning for the full-blown clinical picture (scurvy) that develops if the deficiency is prolonged.
questions.answerText:
(i) The nutrient deficiency responsible is vitamin C (ascorbic acid) deficiency.
(ii) Among the functions of vitamin C is the hydroxylation of proline and lysine for collagen synthesis; vitamin C also helps to repair and regenerate tissues. The bleeding gums, loose tooth, gingivitis and delayed wound healing seen in scurvy relate to this role in collagen synthesis.
(iii) Many animals can synthesise ascorbic acid from glucose via the uronic acid pathway; however, humans cannot synthesise vitamin C, due to deficiency of the enzyme L-gulonolactone oxidase, and therefore vitamin C needs to be taken in the diet.
(iv) Deficiency symptoms include fatigue, muscle weakness, joint and muscle aches, bleeding gums and leg rashes; prolonged deficiency can cause scurvy, a rare but potentially severe illness characterised by general weakness, anaemia, swollen joints, loose tooth, gingivitis (gum disease), susceptibility to infections, skin haemorrhages, delayed wound healing, bone fragility and osteoporosis. Sources of vitamin C include green leafy vegetables, citrus fruits, mango, paw-paw and watermelon, the absence of which (as on a long sea voyage) explains the sailor's presentation.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe fatty acid biosynthesis under the following headings: site of occurrence, source of acetyl-CoA and its transfer from mitochondria, and formation of malonyl-CoA.
A(ii) State the overall stoichiometry of palmitate synthesis from acetyl-CoA and malonyl-CoA.
C. Distinguish between the enzyme/cofactor used to transfer reducing equivalents for fatty acid synthesis and the regulatory enzyme that commits acetyl-CoA to fatty acid synthesis.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Fatty acid synthesis occurs mainly in the liver and adipocytes in mammals; when glucose is plentiful, large amounts of acetyl-CoA are produced by glycolysis and can be used for fatty acid synthesis, while glucose oxidation in the pentose phosphate pathway provides NADPH for fatty acid synthesis. Acetyl-CoA from catabolism of carbohydrates and amino acids is exported from mitochondria via the citrate transport system, with cytosolic NADH also converted to NADPH; two molecules of ATP are expended for each round of this cyclic pathway, and one molecule of NADPH is produced for each acetyl-CoA transferred from the mitochondria, producing 8 NADPH for one palmitate produced. Malonyl-CoA is formed by acetyl-CoA carboxylase, a biotin-containing enzyme in which a carboxybiotin intermediate is formed and hydrolysis of ATP catalyses the reaction; this is the regulatory site for fatty acid biosynthesis.
A(ii) The overall stoichiometry of palmitate synthesis is: Acetyl-CoA + 7 Malonyl-CoA + 14 NADPH + 14 H+ → Palmitate + 7 CO2 + 14 NADP+ + 8 HS-CoA + 6 H2O.
C. NADPH (generated via the citrate transport system and the pentose phosphate pathway) supplies the reducing equivalents for fatty acid synthesis, whereas acetyl-CoA carboxylase, a biotin-containing enzyme that forms a carboxybiotin intermediate using ATP hydrolysis, is the regulatory enzyme that converts acetyl-CoA to malonyl-CoA and is the regulatory site for fatty acid biosynthesis.

A(i) Hydrophobic core of cholesteryl esters, triglycerides, fatty acids and fat-soluble vitamins; surrounding hydrophilic layer of apolipoproteins, phospholipids and cholesterol; particles range from 10 to 1000 nm.
A(ii) Classified by density: the higher the protein-to-lipid ratio, the higher the density, the smaller the size and the lower the molecular weight; classes are chylomicron, VLDL, IDL, LDL and HDL.
- Chylomicron: intestine, transports dietary fats and cholesterol; VLDL: liver, exports triacylglycerol/endogenous fats; IDL: from VLDL; LDL: final stage of VLDL catabolism; HDL: transports cholesterol from tissues to liver and takes part in VLDL and chylomicron metabolism.
A(iii) Chylomicron: largest (1000 nm), least dense (<0.95); 1-2% protein, 85-88% triglyceride, ~8% phospholipid, ~3% cholesteryl ester, ~1% cholesterol; apo A-I, II, IV, B-48, C-I, II, III, E. VLDL: 25-90 nm; 5-12% protein, 50-55% triglyceride; apo B-100, C-I, II, III, E.
- IDL: 40 nm, density ~1.0; 10-12% protein, 24-30% triglyceride, 32-35% cholesteryl ester; same apolipoproteins as VLDL; taken up by liver or becomes LDL. LDL: 26 nm, density ~1.04; 20-22% protein, 37-48% cholesteryl ester; apo B-100. HDL: 6-12.5 nm, density ~1.12; ~55% protein; apo A-I, II, IV, C, D, E.
B(i) The 'good and bad' labels refer to the transport vehicles, not to different cholesterol molecules. LDL is the main carrier of cholesterol and cholesteryl esters (over half of plasma lipoprotein) and can drop cholesterol onto vessel walls, causing blockages; high LDL correlates with coronary atherosclerosis.
- HDL scrapes cholesterol from vessel walls and peripheral tissues and returns it to the liver (reverse cholesterol transport); low HDL (<35 mg/dL) may raise coronary risk whereas high HDL (>55 mg/dL) appears protective.
B(ii) LDL is taken up when apo B-100 binds the hepatic LDL receptor (clathrin-coated vesicle, then lysosome); free cholesterol delivered to the ER inhibits further uptake and synthesis, and high intracellular cholesterol suppresses LDL-receptor synthesis.
- Diets high in saturated fat and cholesterol raise hepatocyte cholesterol, LDL receptors fall and plasma LDL rises; LDL-receptor gene defects (familial hypercholesterolaemia) elevate LDL and cause premature coronary atherosclerosis.
C(i) Function: LDL carries cholesterol from liver to tissues; HDL carries cholesterol from tissues to liver (source of apo C and E; LCAT activated by apo A-I esterifies cholesterol; transfers cholesteryl esters to VLDL and LDL).
- Composition: LDL is larger (26 nm), less dense (~1.04), 20-22% protein, mostly cholesteryl ester, apo B-100 only; HDL is smallest (6-12.5 nm), densest (~1.12), ~55% protein, many apolipoproteins (apo A-I, II, IV, C, D, E).
- Fate: LDL is taken up by receptor-mediated endocytosis; HDL is made as a protein-rich particle in liver and intestine and returns to the liver, which excretes excess cholesterol as bile acids; normal fasting HDL is 1.0-2.0 g/L.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the normal shape, size and count of red blood cells.
A(ii) Describe the variations in RBC shape.
B(i) State how these shape variations relate to specific anaemias/conditions.
C(i) Explain how RBC destruction leads to a distant, systemic effect.
questions.answerText:
A(i) RBCs (erythrocytes) are non-nucleated formed elements of the blood; they are normally disc-shaped and bi-concave, with the central portion thinner and the periphery thicker; diameter is about 7.2 microns (6.9-7.5), thickness 2.2 microns at the periphery and 1 micron at the centre.
Their red colour is due to haemoglobin; normal counts are about 5 million/cu mm in males and 4.5 million/cu mm in females; average life span of RBCs is about 120 days, and they are destroyed in the reticuloendothelial system, mostly in the capillaries of the spleen, termed the "graveyard of RBCs".
A(ii) Variations in RBC shape include: crenation (shrinkage, as in a hypertonic solution), spherocytosis (globular form, as in a hypotonic solution), elliptocytosis (elliptical shape, in certain anaemias), sickle cell (crescent shape, as in sickle cell anaemia), and poikilocytosis (unequal, deformed shapes such as flask or hammer forms due to a deformed cell membrane).
B(i) Elliptocytosis occurs in certain anaemias, and sickle-shaped cells are characteristic specifically of sickle cell anaemia, while spherocytosis and crenation relate to abnormal osmotic environments rather than intrinsic haemoglobin disease.
A red blood cell enzyme disorder should be suspected in persistent normocytic haemolytic anaemia where spherocytes are absent and osmotic fragility is normal, distinguishing enzymopathy-related haemolysis from membrane or haemoglobin disorders.
Erythropoiesis (origin, maturation and development of erythrocytes) occurs at different sites in fetal life: the mesoblastic stage (yolk sac, first trimester), hepatic stage (liver, spleen, lymphoid organs, second trimester), and myeloid stage (bone marrow and liver, third trimester).
C(i) Hemolysis is the destruction of formed elements of the blood, or breakdown of red blood cells to liberate haemoglobin; fragility is the susceptibility of RBCs to haemolysis.
Normally plasma and RBCs are in equilibrium, but when this equilibrium is disturbed the cells are affected; conditions in which haemolysis occurs include hemolytic jaundice, antigen-antibody reactions, and poisoning by chemicals or toxins.
When cells become older, the cell membrane becomes fragile, and destruction occurs mostly in the capillaries of the spleen as part of normal ageing of the RBC at the end of its 120-day life span.
Excess RBC lysis in prehepatic (haemolytic) jaundice results in bilirubin production beyond the liver's ability to conjugate it, giving high plasma concentrations of unconjugated bilirubin.
This links a local event in the red cell (destruction in the spleen) to a distant, systemic functional deficit: the liver's conjugating capacity is overwhelmed, and unconjugated bilirubin accumulates in the plasma.
Thus an intrinsic RBC defect that alters normal biconcave shape and shortens red cell survival (e.g. sickle cell disease) can manifest systemically as chronic haemolysis and jaundice, illustrating how a cellular/membrane change produces a distant, organ-level (hepatic/biliary) consequence.

A(i) Apoptosis can be triggered by various stimuli from outside or inside the cell; the extrinsic pathway (death receptor pathway) is triggered by death activators binding to cell-surface receptors, such as TNF-alpha and Fas ligand (FasL), while the intrinsic (mitochondrial) pathway is generated by signals arising within the cell.
In the extrinsic pathway, TNF-alpha binds to the TNF receptor and FasL binds to the cell-surface receptor Fas (CD95), leading to receptor-mediated caspase activation at the Death Inducing Signalling Complex (DISC).
In the intrinsic pathway, the mitochondria contribute to and accelerate apoptosis by releasing apoptogenic proteins such as cytochrome C and endonuclease G; ATP synthesis is abrogated, redox molecules such as NADH, NADPH and glutathione are oxidised, and reactive oxygen species (ROS) are increasingly generated.
A(ii) Caspases specifically cleave their substrates after aspartate residues, and are synthesised in the cell as inactive zymogens called procaspases.
Proapoptotic caspases are divided into initiator caspases (procaspases-2, -8, -9 and -10) and executioner caspases (procaspases-3, -6 and -7); executioner caspases have only short prodomains, whereas initiator caspases have long prodomains containing death effector domains (DED).
Via their prodomains, initiator caspases are recruited to and activated at death-inducing signalling complexes; caspase 8 is the initiator caspase of the extrinsic pathway, and caspase 9 is the initiator caspase of the intrinsic pathway.
A(iii) The Bcl-2 family of proteins regulates apoptosis and comprises two types: pro-apoptotic members (e.g. Bax, Bad, Bid) and anti-apoptotic members (e.g. Bcl-2 and Bcl-xl); the sensitivity of cells to apoptotic stimuli depends on the balance between the pro- and anti-apoptotic proteins.
B(i) Apoptosis is described as a programmed cell death that removes cells whose existence would harm the proper functioning of the organism; too much of this premature apoptosis often leads to the onset of the ageing process.
This relates apoptosis, through its balance of pro- and anti-apoptotic Bcl-2 family proteins, to the pathology of accelerated cellular ageing when the balance is disturbed towards excess pro-apoptotic activity.
C(i) Because apoptosis at the level of a single cell is executed by caspase cascades triggered either by surface death receptors or by mitochondrial release of apoptogenic proteins and reactive oxygen species, disturbance of this balance across many cells accumulates into tissue-level change.
Ageing itself is a progressive decline in multiple organ systems (reproductive, metabolic, physical and cognitive), and premature/excess apoptosis is stated to contribute to the onset of this whole-body ageing process.
Thus a cellular-level defect in the balance of pro- and anti-apoptotic Bcl-2 proteins, acting through the caspase cascade of the extrinsic and intrinsic pathways, is linked to a distant, systemic functional deficit — accelerated, multi-organ ageing.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the two main triggering pathways of apoptosis.
A(ii) Describe the role of caspases.
A(iii) Describe the role of the Bcl-2 family of proteins.
B(i) State how these mechanisms relate to a specific pathology when their balance is disturbed.
C(i) Explain how excess/premature apoptosis at the cellular level produces a distant, whole-body functional deficit.

questions.answerText:
(i) Beta thalassaemia results from mutations on chromosome 11, with hundreds of possible mutations in the beta globin gene, making beta thalassaemia more diverse than the alpha form; the trait is seen most commonly in people of Mediterranean (including North African, Italian and Greek), Middle Eastern, Indian, African, Chinese, and Southeast Asian ancestry.
(ii) Beta thalassaemia major is characterised by complete absence of beta globin, an enlarged spleen, lightly coloured blood cells, and severe anaemia beginning months after birth, with paleness, delays in growth and development, and bone marrow expansion; untreated beta thalassaemia major can lead to child death due to heart failure.
(iii) Management options are regular blood transfusion (which helps prevent severe anaemia and allows more normal growth and development), medications targeting red blood cell production such as erythropoietin, and chronic transfusion in conjunction with chelation therapy (desferoxamine) to reduce iron overload; regular blood transfusion combined with chelation therapy is the most justified option, since beta thalassaemia major requires chronic transfusions together with chelation therapy specifically to reduce the iron burden that chronic transfusion itself produces.
questions.question:
An infant presents at several months of age with severe anaemia, growth delay, and an enlarged spleen. A blood film shows small, pale (lightly coloured) red cells.
(i) What are the risk factors for this condition?
(ii) What are its complications?
(iii) What are the management options, and which would you justify as most important?

A child with asthma, whose attacks are usually triggered by allergens or exercise, develops bronchoconstriction after taking aspirin.
(i) State the most likely diagnosis.
(ii) Explain the biochemical basis of the attack, including what aspirin does to the enzymes of arachidonic acid metabolism and which mediator produces the airway effect.
(iii) State the immediate management.
(iv) State the definitive treatment options.
questions.answerText:
(i) Aspirin-triggered asthma: asthma with bronchoconstriction whose triggers include allergens, exercise and aspirin.
(ii) The acetyl group of aspirin binds serine in cyclooxygenase (COX) and blocks both COX-1 and COX-2, so arachidonic acid can no longer enter the active site to form prostaglandins.
- Blocking COX leaves the 5-lipoxygenase (5-LIPOX) pathway open, so the arachidonic acid substrate becomes leukotrienes (LTs): a surge in LT production.
- Leukotriene D4 (derived from LTA4) contracts the muscle lining the airways; overproduction of leukotrienes causes the asthmatic attack. Leukotrienes are potent proinflammatory agents with three conjugated double bonds.
- Prostaglandin E is a bronchodilator whereas PGF constricts bronchial muscle; PGE and PGF oppose each other in the lungs.
(iii) Immediate management: discontinue aspirin and other NSAIDs; use direct bronchodilators (e.g. albuterol).
(iv) Definitive treatment: 5-LIPOX inhibitors and LT-receptor inhibitors; corticosteroids; anti-IgE antibodies.
- Leukotriene synthesis is a target of anti-asthmatic drugs such as prednisone.

A(i) Exocrine function: pancreatic juice is released into the small intestine through a duct. Endocrine function: the islets of Langerhans, ductless, release hormones directly into the bloodstream.
A(ii) Islets secrete insulin (from beta cells) and glucagon, plus somatostatin (inhibits insulin and glycogen production) and pancreatic polypeptide (influences pancreatic exocrine function and nutrient metabolism).
- Insulin promotes movement of glucose from blood into cells; glucagon promotes glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis and ketogenesis, is triggered by low blood glucose, protein ingestion and exercise, and increases hepatic glucose production.
A(iii) Insulin stimulates glucose uptake by cells and glucagon promotes conversion of glycogen to glucose; endocrine control uses positive and negative feedback.
- Oversecretion of insulin results in low blood sugar; undersecretion results in high blood sugar and can lead to diabetes; insulin release is stimulated by blood glucose (also leucine, arginine, GIP and neural signals) and decreased by epinephrine.
B(i) Type 1 (juvenile): absolute insulin deficiency; maturity-onset type: usually with obesity, and MODY from mutations in pancreatic glucokinase or nuclear transcription factors; type 2: insulin resistance with dysfunctional beta cells.
- Secondary diabetes: hyperfunction of insulin antagonists (acromegaly, Cushing's disease, hyperthyroidism) gives relative insulin insufficiency; hyperinsulinism may result from islet-cell tumours involving beta cells.
- Diagnosis: C-peptide assay, fasting, random and post-prandial glucose, insulin autoantibody (IAA) assay and oral glucose tolerance test.
C(i) Diabetes causes hyperglycaemia and glycosuria with dehydration from water lost with urinary glucose; breakdown of fat and tissue protein gives weight loss; increased gluconeogenesis gives negative nitrogen balance; lipemia develops.
- Ketosis with ketonuria and acidosis (lowered blood pH from keto acids) follow; distant tissues show an increased tendency to cataract of the eye and arteriosclerotic lesions of blood vessels.
- Insulin also acts on the brain: raised central insulin signalling lowers feeding behaviour and raises energy expenditure, whereas reduced signalling raises feeding and lowers expenditure.
- Insulin also acts on liver, muscle and adipocyte (glycogen and fat synthesis, glucose uptake, reduced lipolysis), so its loss disturbs all three tissues.

A(i) Enoyl CoA hydratase and 3-L-hydroxyacyl CoA dehydrogenase (β-hydroxyacyl CoA dehydrogenase).
A(ii) Following dehydrogenation of the fatty acyl CoA to an enoyl CoA, hydratase catalyses stereospecific addition of water to its substrate's trans α,β double bond.
A(ii) The product, 3-L-hydroxyacyl CoA, is the substrate of the dehydrogenase, which oxidises this secondary alcohol to a ketone.
A(iii) NAD+ is the oxidising agent of the dehydrogenase; NADH + H+ and β-ketoacyl CoA are formed.
B(i) A cis β,γ double bond containing enoyl CoA is not a substrate for enoyl CoA hydratase; enoyl CoA isomerase converts cis Δ3 to trans-Δ2.
B(i) 2,4-dienoyl CoA is a poor substrate for enoyl CoA hydratase; NADPH-dependent 2,4-dienoyl CoA reductase and 3,2-enoyl CoA isomerase are needed.
B(i) Compounds with a trans-2 double bond are normal substrates of enoyl-CoA hydratase, so β-oxidation can then continue.
C(i) Hydratase adds water to the double bond to give an alcohol; the dehydrogenase oxidises that alcohol to a ketone.
C(i) The first oxidation uses FAD (giving FADH2); the third step uses NAD+ (giving NADH).
C(i) Each round produces 1 NADH and 1 FADH2.
C(i) The thiolase reaction then cleaves β-ketoacyl CoA into acetyl CoA and a new acyl CoA 2 carbon atoms shorter.
C(i) Acyl CoA dehydrogenase is bypassed in the unsaturated problems, giving one fewer FADH2 per bypass.

A(i) All start from cholesterol. ACTH activates a cytoplasmic esterase that frees cholesterol from cholesteryl esters; the ACTH-dependent StAR protein carries free cholesterol into the mitochondrion, where cytochrome P450 side-chain cleavage enzyme (P450scc) forms pregnenolone.
A(ii) Aldosterone: pregnenolone to progesterone (3beta-OHSD and 5,4-isomerase, smooth ER), 21-hydroxylase to 11-deoxycorticosterone, 11beta-hydroxylase (mitochondrial) to corticosterone, 18-hydroxylase to 18-OH corticosterone, 18-hydroxydehydrogenase to aldosterone.
- Cortisol: 17alpha-hydroxylase, 21-hydroxylase and 11beta-hydroxylase act on pregnenolone; the final step converts 11-deoxycortisol to cortisol, the most potent natural glucocorticoid in humans.
- Testosterone: 17,20-lyase forms DHEA from 17-OH pregnenolone; DHEA gives androstenedione via 3beta-OHSD and 5,4-isomerase (or from 17-OH progesterone via P450C17); 17beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase makes testosterone.
A(iii) Steroid-secreting cells have abundant smooth ER and lipid droplets; steroids diffuse across the plasma membrane (no exocytosis) and travel in blood bound to serum globulin because they are so hydrophobic.
- The hormone enters cells and binds its receptor (surface and/or nucleus); the hormone-receptor complex pairs to form a dimer, migrates to the nucleus and binds specific hormone response elements in DNA, switching genes on or off.
A(iv) Testosterone is metabolised by two pathways: oxidation at C17 in many tissues, including liver, gives less active 17-ketosteroids; a less efficient pathway in target tissues (testis, prostate) reduces the A-ring double bond to form dihydrotestosterone (DHT), a potent metabolite.
- Plasma DHT in the adult male is about one-tenth of total testosterone; the testes secrete 50-100 micrograms of DHT daily.
B(i) Mineralocorticoids in the zona glomerulosa; glucocorticoids in the zona fasciculata and zona reticularis; adrenal androgens are weak (the testes are the main source of testosterone in males, but the adrenal cortex is a major androgen source in females).
C(i) Cortisol deficiency (Addison's disease) lowers blood glucose; aldosterone deficiency lowers sodium and causes severe dehydration; glucocorticoid excess is Cushing's syndrome; excess adrenal androgen causes premature puberty in boys and masculinisation in females.
- Production of all three classes is triggered by ACTH from the anterior pituitary; the final product depends on the cell type and its enzymes (progesterone is a hormone and a precursor of glucocorticoids, mineralocorticoids, testosterone and estrogens).
- Testosterone is an obligatory intermediate in the synthesis of estradiol and DHT.

A(i) Ageing can be defined as the progressive loss of function of an organism, leading to increasing mortality; it is a multifactorial process influenced and modified by various genetic, biochemical and other systems working together. The key signalling networks regulating ageing are: hormonal signalling (insulin and insulin-like signalling); nutrient sensing and signalling (dietary restriction, i.e. restriction of food intake without malnutrition); mitochondria and ROS signalling (controlling cellular energy levels, reactive oxygen species production/detoxification and apoptosis); and genome surveillance signalling pathways (DNA repair and telomere maintenance).
A(ii) The first example of a specific pathway controlling longevity came from studies of Caenorhabditis elegans (worms); mutations that reduce the activity of the insulin receptor DAF-2 or the phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K)/AGE-1 extend lifespan in adult worms by more than 100%. The DAF-2 gene encodes the insulin-like growth factor 1 receptor in C. elegans. The insulin receptor mediates its effects via the PI3K-AKT(PKB)/SGK signalling pathway, which culminates in the negative regulation of the Forkhead transcription factor FOXO/DAF-16; insulin signalling regulates ageing in a conserved manner from worms to mammals, with FOXO (in mammals)/Daf-16 (in C. elegans) as the key downstream regulator integrating signals from these pathways, playing a crucial role in ageing and longevity.
B. Mutations that reduce the activity of the insulin receptor DAF-2 or PI3K/AGE-1 extend lifespan in adult worms by more than 100%, because reduced signalling through this pathway leads to negative regulation being lifted from the Forkhead transcription factor FOXO/DAF-16, which is the key downstream regulator integrating signals from these pathways and plays a crucial role in ageing and longevity.
C. Hormonal signalling in ageing operates through insulin and insulin-like signalling, exemplified by the DAF-2/PI3K/FOXO pathway. Nutrient sensing and signalling, in contrast, operates through dietary restriction, which is restriction of food intake without malnutrition; these are listed as two separate networks among the four key signalling networks regulating ageing, alongside mitochondria/ROS signalling and genome surveillance signalling.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe ageing and the key signalling networks that regulate it, naming the four networks.
A(ii) Describe the hormonal (insulin/insulin-like) signalling network in detail, including the organism in which it was first characterised and the downstream transcription factor involved.
B. Explain the biochemical basis for how mutations in this pathway extend lifespan.
C. Distinguish between hormonal signalling and nutrient-sensing signalling as networks regulating ageing.

questions.answerText:
(i) Acyl CoA synthetases (thiokinases): a family of at least 3 that differ according to their chain length specificities.
(i) Mitochondrial acyl CoA dehydrogenases: 3, with specificities for short-, medium- and long-chain fatty acyl CoAs.
(i) Peroxisomal thiolase: a different chain length specificity from its mitochondrial counterpart; almost inactive with acyl CoAs of length C8 or less.
(ii) Synthetases: associated with either the ER or the outer mitochondrial membrane (a very long chain acyl CoA synthetase is in the peroxisome).
(ii) Dehydrogenases: mitochondria; thiolase: peroxisomes.
(iii) Synthetase: ATP-dependent acylation giving acyl CoA + AMP (pyrophosphate released).
(iii) Dehydrogenase: removal of a proton at Cα and transfer of a hydride ion equivalent from Cβ to FAD.
(iii) Thiolase: forms acetyl CoA and a new acyl CoA 2 carbon atoms shorter.
(iv) Because peroxisomal thiolase is almost inactive with acyl CoAs of C8 or less, fatty acids are incompletely oxidised by peroxisomes.
questions.question:
Three enzyme families in fatty acid oxidation are described by their chain length preference: one activates fatty acids, one removes the first pair of hydrogens in the mitochondrion, and one cleaves in the peroxisome.
(i) Identify each family and its chain length behaviour.
(ii) State the location of each.
(iii) Differentiate the reactions they catalyse.
(iv) Explain why the peroxisomal one leads to incomplete oxidation.

A(i) Describe the general characteristics of ageing.
A(ii) Describe the free radical theory and mitochondrial DNA theory of ageing.
A(iii) Describe the telomere theory of ageing.
B(i) State how these mechanisms relate to specific accelerated-ageing diseases.
C(i) Explain how a defect in these mechanisms produces a distant, multi-organ (systemic) functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Ageing is a progressive decline in multiple organ systems affecting reproductive, metabolic, physical and cognitive function and survival; summarised characteristics include increased mortality with increasing age, changes in the chemical composition of the body, a broad spectrum of progressive deteriorative changes, reduced ability to adapt to environmental changes, and increasing vulnerability to disease.
A(ii) The free radical theory, the most developed and accepted theory, proposes that elevated levels of oxygen-derived free radicals cause damage to biochemical molecules via oxidation of proteins and lipids and mutation of DNA; free radicals are products of cell metabolism in the mitochondria, lysosome and peroxisome, and antioxidants reduce this harm by scavenging free radicals, delaying ageing.
The mitochondrial DNA theory proposes that progressive accumulation of somatic mutations in mitochondrial DNA over an individual's lifetime leads to a decline in the bio-energetic function of mitochondria and contributes to ageing; increased free radical generation is due to 1-2% of oxygen leaking from the electron transport chain, and mitochondrial DNA has no protective histone.
A(iii) The telomere (Hayflick) theory states that after each cell division, telomere is lost, resulting in a decline in life span because of incomplete DNA replication; oxidative stress increases the rate of telomere shortening; telomerase, which replaces lost telomeres, is active in germ cells, stem cells and cancer cells, preventing them from experiencing the Hayflick limit.
Other theories of ageing include the evolution theory, glycation theory, wear-and-tear theory, neuroendocrine-immuno theory, and error catastrophe theory; the glycation theory suggests glucose acts as a mediator of ageing through the non-enzymic reaction between glucose and tissue protein.
B(i) Accelerated ageing diseases include Werner syndrome, Bloom's syndrome, Down's syndrome, Xeroderma pigmentosum, Cockayne syndrome, and Ataxia telangiectasia.
These diseases are grouped together because they represent genetic conditions in which the mechanisms underlying normal ageing are disrupted, so that the characteristic features of ageing appear prematurely.
Longevity (length or period of a person's life expectancy) is influenced by gender, diet and nutrition, genetics and lifestyle; genes account for 25% of what determines longevity.
C(i) Because mitochondrial free-radical damage and telomere shortening occur at the level of individual cells, but ageing is described as affecting reproductive, metabolic, physical and cognitive function together, a defect in these basic cellular mechanisms manifests as decline across multiple, distant organ systems rather than in one organ alone.
Calorie restriction (CR), a dietary regimen restricting calories while maintaining adequate nutrition, has been shown to increase lifespan in yeast, fish, rodents and monkeys, and produces metabolic alterations including reduced temperature, decreased plasma insulin, decreased T4/T3, and reduced lipid peroxidation.
Modulators of ageing include hormesis (mild stress upregulating gene expression and repair pathways), gene therapy (inducing telomerase expression), and nutraceuticals (reducing reactive oxygen species and lipid oxidation).
Thus a single underlying cellular defect, such as impaired DNA repair or persistent oxidative damage, is presented as the basis for the multi-organ, systemic functional decline that characterises both normal ageing and the accelerated-ageing diseases listed.

A(i) The starting substrate is a long chain fatty acyl CoA formed in the cytosol, which cannot enter the inner mitochondrial membrane directly.
A(i) Its acyl portion is first transferred to carnitine (4-trimethylamino-3-hydroxybutyrate), a compound occurring in both plants and animal tissues.
A(ii) Carnitine palmitoyl transferases I and II transfer a variety of acyl groups.
A(ii) They are found on the external and internal surfaces of the inner mitochondrial membrane.
A(iii) A specific carrier protein mediates the translocation.
A(iii) It transports acyl carnitine into the mitochondria while transporting free carnitine in the opposite direction.
A(iv) On the inside, acyl CoA is regenerated (with release of carnitine) by carnitine palmitoyl transferase II.
A(iv) Oxidation of the acyl group then occurs in the mitochondrion.
B(i) The 3-step process is rate-limiting for fatty acid oxidation and an important point of regulation.
B(ii) Carnitine acyl transferase I is inhibited by malonyl-CoA.
C(i) Malonyl-CoA is the first intermediate in the cytosolic biosynthesis of long chain fatty acids from acetyl CoA.
C(ii) The inhibition occurs when the liver is amply supplied with glucose as fuel and is actively making triacylglycerols from excess glucose.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the origin (initiation) of the coagulation cascade via its two pathways.
A(ii) Describe the course of the cascade through to fibrin formation.
A(iii) Describe the regulation of coagulation by the body's anticlotting mechanisms.
A(iv) Describe the fate of the clot after formation.
B(i) State the regulatory stage of the cascade that governs entry into the final common pathway.
C(i) Explain the biochemical basis of a bleeding disorder that results when a clotting factor is deficient.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Prothrombinase (prothrombin activator) is formed in two ways: the extrinsic pathway (tissue factor pathway), triggered by tissue trauma and tissue thromboplastin, and the intrinsic pathway (contact activation pathway), triggered by endothelial damage and collagen exposure; factors I, V, VII, X are involved in the extrinsic pathway, and factors I, II, V, VIII, IX, X, XI, XII in the intrinsic pathway.
A(ii) There are three major stages: Stage 1, formation of the prothrombinase complex; Stage 2, conversion of prothrombin to thrombin; Stage 3, conversion of fibrinogen to fibrin (Stages 2 and 3 together form the final common pathway).
In the presence of prothrombinase and calcium, prothrombin is converted to thrombin, which increases its own rate of formation by positive feedback and activates factors V and VIII; factor VIIIa is the co-factor of factor IXa, and together they form the "tenase" complex, which activates factor X.
Thrombin converts fibrinogen (a plasma protein produced by the liver) to fibrin, and also activates factor XIII (fibrin stabilising factor), which in the presence of calcium stabilises the fibrin polymer through covalent bonding of fibrin monomers.
A(iii) Under physiological conditions intravascular clotting does not normally occur, because of continuous circulation of blood, a smooth endothelial lining, the presence of natural anticoagulant heparin produced by the liver, and because all clotting factors are normally kept inactive.
Heparin, produced by mast cells (abundant in liver and lungs) and secreted also by basophils, prevents clotting by combining with and activating antithrombin III, which then inactivates factors IX, X, XI and XII.
A(iv) After clot formation, the clot starts contracting (clot retraction), mediated by the contractile proteins actin, myosin and thrombosthenin; after about 30-45 minutes a straw-coloured fluid called serum oozes out of the clot.
Fibrinolysis, the lysis of a blood clot inside the vessel, requires plasmin (fibrinolysin), formed from the inactive glycoprotein plasminogen, synthesised in the liver; fibrinolysis helps remove the clot from the lumen of the vessel.
B(i) The formation of the prothrombinase complex, particularly the tenase-complex-driven activation of factor X, is the key regulatory point governing entry into the final common pathway.
C(i) Factor VIII is the antihaemophilic factor, involved in the intrinsic pathway alongside factors IX (Christmas factor), X (Stuart factor), XI, and XII.
Because factors V, VIII, IX, X, XI and XII participate in forming the prothrombinase/tenase complexes that generate thrombin, deficiency of any one of these factors interrupts the cascade before thrombin and fibrin can be generated adequately.
This explains why a deficiency of a clotting factor manifests as a bleeding tendency: without sufficient thrombin generation, fibrinogen is not adequately converted to the fibrin polymer needed to form a stable, retractile clot.

questions.question:
A patient presents with fatigue, loss of appetite and abdominal pain, and is found to have severe dehydration, low blood glucose and low blood sodium.
(i) State the diagnosis.
(ii) Explain the pathophysiology, naming the hormones involved, their normal actions and their control.
questions.answerText:
(i) Addison's disease: hyposecretion (undersecretion) of the adrenal cortex, usually involving cortisol and aldosterone.
(ii) Cortisol (glucocorticoid) raises blood glucose by stimulating gluconeogenesis in the liver, especially the conversion of fats and proteins to glucose; its deficiency explains the low blood glucose.
- Aldosterone (mineralocorticoid) acts on the kidney to promote sodium reabsorption into the blood, maintaining blood volume and blood pressure, and reduces sodium loss in sweat; its deficiency explains the low sodium and severe dehydration.
- Both are corticosteroids made from cholesterol in the adrenal cortex; production is triggered by ACTH from the anterior pituitary (CRH from the hypothalamus drives ACTH) and controlled by feedback loops.
- Aldosterone is also stimulated by a drop in blood sodium, a rise in blood potassium and angiotensin II.

questions.question:
A 40-year-old woman is noted to have an excessive accumulation of body fat. She is found to have high triglycerides and total cholesterol, and reports snoring with breathing pauses at night.
(i) What are the risk factors that predispose to the development of this condition?
(ii) What complications and health problems is she at increased risk of as a result of this condition?
(iii) What management approach would you consider, and justify one option based on the recognised classification of the condition?
questions.answerText:
(i) Obesity has various causes, including single-gene mutations, damage to the ventromedial hypothalamus, genetic factor, diet, lifestyle, drugs, and endocrine disorders.
(ii) Obesity increases the risk of diseases and health problems such as coronary heart disease, Type 2 diabetes, cancers (breast, endometrial and colon), hypertension, dyslipidaemia (for example, high triglycerides or high total cholesterol), stroke, liver and gallbladder disease, sleep apnoea and respiratory problems, osteoarthritis (degeneration of cartilage and its underlying bone within a joint) and gynaecological problems (abnormal menses, infertility); these conditions can cause or contribute to premature death and substantial disability.
(iii) There are various classifications or types of obesity, including that based on the results of the Yorkshire Health Study Cohort; researchers suggest that the medical community could recognise the different sub-categories of obesity and treat them separately in order to battle the disease more effectively. Justification: since this patient's obesity may reflect a specific recognised sub-category rather than a single uniform disease, management directed at her particular sub-category (as opposed to a one-size-fits-all approach), rather than a one-size-fits-all approach, is the more appropriate option.

(i) The diagnosis is rickets (the childhood form of vitamin D deficiency; the adult form is osteomalacia).
(ii) Rickets can result from various reasons, including lack of ultraviolet radiation, dietary deficiency, renal tubular defects, familial hypophosphataemia, inborn errors of vitamin D metabolism, intestinal malabsorption of fat, chronic renal failure and cadmium poisoning; the concern here is occurrence as a result of the absence of vitamin D in the diet, or lack of exposure to ultraviolet radiation. Those at highest risk of vitamin D deficiency include older people, people with darker complexions, people who live in areas with limited sunlight, people who don't go outdoors, people with a problem absorbing dietary fat, and obese or overweight people.
(iii) There is decreased absorption of dietary calcium and phosphorus, so hydroxyapatite formation is decreased and plasma calcium tends to decline; in response, the parathyroid glands release parathyroid hormone, which accelerates bone resorption and phosphate excretion to maintain plasma ionised calcium. In bone, calcification of cartilage and new osteoid is inhibited and bones become soft; flat bones and the shafts of long bones become distorted, and the cartilaginous growth sites at the ends of bones overgrow, resulting in knobby deformities. In infants and children, serum calcium may be normal or low, phosphorus is low, and alkaline phosphatase is quite elevated.
(iv) Prevention and treatment of dietary rickets includes enrichment of milk with 400 I.U. of vitamin D per quart, and eating fatty fish (e.g. salmon, sardines and mackerel), fish oils (including cod liver oil and other fish liver oils) and eggs; getting adequate exposure to sunlight is also one of the most important sources of vitamin D.
questions.question:

(i) What is the diagnosis?
(ii) What predisposing factors account for this condition?
(iii) What is the pathophysiological basis of the bone changes and biochemical findings?
(iv) What management/prevention would you institute?

questions.answerText:

Acetylcholine is synthesised from choline and acetylcoenzyme-A by choline acetyltransferase in the cytoplasm, then transported into and stored in vesicles, and removed by hydrolysis by acetylcholinesterase. Serotonin is synthesised from the amino acid tryptophan; within the brain it is localised mainly in nerve pathways emerging from the raphe nuclei, a group of nuclei at the centre of the reticular formation in the midbrain, pons and medulla, and these serotonergic pathways spread extensively throughout the brainstem, cerebral cortex and spinal cord. In general, neurotransmitters are stored in vesicles at the end of axons and released into the synaptic cleft when a nerve impulse reaches the axon terminal, then diffuse across the synapse and bind to receptors on the receiving cell, and are removed rapidly by enzymes that break them down.
B. The most common antidepressants are called selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs); they are considered relatively safe and cause fewer side effects than other kinds of medications used to treat depression.
C. Acetylcholine is transmitted within cholinergic pathways concentrated mainly in specific regions of the brainstem, thought to be involved in cognitive functions, especially memory; severe damage to these pathways is the probable cause of Alzheimer's disease, with something on the order of a 90% loss of acetylcholine in the brains of people suffering from Alzheimer's, a major cause of senility. An imbalance of serotonin in the brain is thought to contribute to depression, anxiety, poor mood, sexual dysfunction and stress; low serotonin levels lead to an increased appetite for carbohydrates and trouble sleeping, which are also associated with depression and other emotional disorders, and have also been tied to migraines, irritable bowel syndrome and fibromyalgia.
questions.question:

B. State the mechanism by which the most common class of antidepressant drugs acts on the serotonin system.

A patient develops hypocalcaemia after thyroid surgery in which excessive parathyroid tissue was inadvertently removed.
(i) State the diagnosis.
(ii) Name the procedure implicated and give the anatomical landmarks of the glands concerned (number, position, blood supply).
(iii) Name the structure at risk in the procedure and the cells that produce the hormone.
(iv) Explain the biochemical consequences of losing the hormone.
(v) State the variants of this disorder that must be distinguished.
questions.answerText:
(i) PTH-deficient hypoparathyroidism: reduced or absent synthesis of parathyroid hormone (PTH), often due to inadvertent removal of excessive parathyroid tissue; hypocalcaemia results and 1,25-(OH)2-D also falls (bihormonal).
(ii) Procedure: thyroid (or parathyroid) surgery. Landmarks: four small parathyroid glands lying on the dorsal (posterior) side of the thyroid gland; their blood supply is from the thyroid arteries.
(iii) Structure at risk: the parathyroid tissue; PTH is released by chief cells, which contain receptors for Ca2+.
(iv) PTH normally raises plasma Ca2+ by mobilising Ca2+ from bone, enhancing renal (distal tubule) reabsorption and indirectly increasing intestinal absorption by stimulating 1,25-(OH)2-D synthesis; it lowers plasma phosphate by inhibiting renal phosphate reabsorption.
- Without PTH these actions are lost, so plasma Ca2+ falls (hypocalcaemia is invariably associated with hypoparathyroidism).
(v) PTH-ineffective hypoparathyroidism: synthesis of biologically inactive PTH.
- Pseudohypoparathyroidism (PTH-resistant): defect in the PTH receptor-adenylate cyclase complex, with mutation in the Gs-alpha subunit; patients are also resistant to TSH, glucagon and gonadotropins.

(i) The process is β-oxidation; the function of fatty acid oxidation is to generate metabolic energy.
(i) Activation occurs in the cytosol but oxidation occurs in the mitochondrion; each round produces 1 NADH, 1 FADH2 and 1 acetyl CoA.
(ii) Palmitoyl-CoA (C16) undergoes 7 rounds of β-oxidation.
(ii) These yield 7 FADH2, 7 NADH and 8 acetyl CoA.
(iii) The 8 acetyl CoA are oxidised in the citric acid cycle, yielding 8 GTP, 24 NADH and 8 FADH2.
(iii) The FADH2 and NADH are reoxidised through phosphorylation to form ATP.
(iv) The total is 31 NADH and 15 FADH2.
(iv) Oxidative phosphorylation of the 31 NADH yields 93 ATPs.
(iv) Oxidative phosphorylation of the 15 FADH2 yields 30 ATPs.
(iv) 2 ATP equivalents required for fatty acyl-CoA formation are subtracted.
(iv) The net yield is 129 ATP per palmitate molecule.
(iv) Complete oxidation of a fatty acid is a highly exergonic process that yields numerous ATPs.
