A. Describe the origin, forms, and distribution/functions of vitamin D in the body.
B. State the intervention used for the prevention and treatment of dietary rickets.
C. Explain the biochemical basis of the bone deformity that follows vitamin D deficiency.
questions.answerText:
A. Vitamin D is primarily obtained through exposure to sunlight, although it is difficult to obtain sufficient quantities through diet alone; there are three primary forms of vitamin D in the body: (1) cholecalciferol (vitamin D3), formed when pre-vitamin D in the skin is exposed to ultraviolet rays; (2) calcidiol (calcifediol), the stored form found in fat, muscle, blood and the liver, which regulates how much active vitamin D the body can make; and (3) calcitriol, the active steroid-hormone form produced by hydroxylation of calcidiol in the kidneys (and other tissues). Vitamin D functions include helping the body absorb and utilise calcium and phosphorus to keep bones and teeth strong, bolstering the immune system, regulating cell differentiation and limiting excessive cell multiplication, acting as an anti-inflammatory agent, and helping control blood sugar levels.
B. Prevention and treatment of dietary rickets includes enrichment of milk with 400 I.U. of vitamin D per quart, and eating fatty fish (e.g. salmon, sardines and mackerel), fish oils (including cod liver oil and other fish liver oils) and eggs.
C. In vitamin D deficiency there is decreased absorption of dietary calcium and phosphorus, so hydroxyapatite formation is decreased and plasma calcium tends to decline; in response, the parathyroid glands release parathyroid hormone, which accelerates bone resorption and phosphate excretion to maintain plasma ionised calcium. In bone, calcification of cartilage and new osteoid is inhibited and bones become soft; flat bones and the shafts of long bones become distorted in both children and adults, and in children the cartilaginous growth sites at the ends of bones overgrow, resulting in knobby deformities.

questions.question:
In an animal cell, a fatty acid with more than 22 carbon atoms must be degraded.
(i) Identify the organelle in which its oxidation begins and state the role of that pathway.
(ii) Explain how the fatty acid enters and is activated.
(iii) Describe the first reaction and how its electrons and by-product are handled.
(iv) State what happens to the shortened products for final oxidation.
questions.answerText:
(i) The peroxisome; peroxisomal β-oxidation shortens very long chain fatty acids (>22 carbon atoms) to facilitate their degradation by the mitochondrial β-oxidation system.
(i) It produces the same chemical changes as the mitochondrial pathway, although the enzymes in the two organelles differ.
(ii) There is no carnitine requirement for transport of fatty acyl-CoA into the peroxisome.
(ii) Very long chain fatty acids diffuse into the compartment and are activated by a peroxisomal very long chain acyl CoA synthetase to form their CoA esters.
(ii) They are then oxidised directly.
(iii) The first reaction involves an FAD cofactor, but the abstracted electrons are transferred directly to oxygen rather than through the electron transport chain with oxidative phosphorylation.
(iii) The H2O2 produced dissociates to H2O and O2 through peroxisomal catalase.
(iv) The shorter chain acyl products are linked to carnitine for transport to the mitochondrion for further oxidation; most diffuse passively out of the peroxisome.

A(i) Fatty acyl CoA is dehydrogenated by acyl CoA dehydrogenase, with FAD as acceptor, giving FADH2 and an enoyl CoA (trans-Δ2).
A(i) Mitochondria contain 3 acyl CoA dehydrogenases with specificities for short-, medium- and long-chain fatty acyl CoAs.
A(ii) Enoyl CoA hydratase catalyses stereospecific addition of water to the trans α,β double bond to form 3-L-hydroxyacyl CoA.
A(iii) 3-L-hydroxyacyl CoA dehydrogenase oxidises this secondary alcohol to a ketone using NAD+ as its oxidising agent, giving β-ketoacyl CoA + NADH + H+.
A(iv) The thiolase reaction (β-ketoacyl CoA thiolase / acyl CoA acetyltransferase) forms acetyl CoA and a new acyl CoA 2 carbon atoms shorter.
A(iv) Each round of β-oxidation produces 1 NADH, 1 FADH2 and 1 acetyl CoA.
B(i) FADH2 is reoxidised by the mitochondrial electron transport chain through a series of electron transfer reactions (ETF and ETF:ubiquinone oxidoreductase to coenzyme Q).
B(i) Reduction of oxygen to water beginning at the coenzyme Q stage results in the synthesis of 2 ATPs per electron pair transferred.
B(ii) When the [NADH]/[NAD+] ratio is high, β-hydroxyacyl CoA dehydrogenase is inhibited.
B(ii) High concentrations of acetyl-CoA inhibit thiolase.
C(i) Oxidation of acetyl CoA via the citric acid cycle generates additional FADH2 and NADH.
C(i) These are reoxidised through phosphorylation to form ATP.

questions.question:
A patient presents with severe upper abdominal pain radiating to the back, of a few hours' duration; blood is sent for pancreatic enzyme estimation.
(i) Which biochemical markers would be used, and what is their normal tissue distribution?
(ii) What time course of change would be expected in the marker specific to this condition?
(iii) What other source could give a similar rise, and how would you differentiate it?
(iv) How would you reason biochemically to support a pancreatic rather than an alternative origin?
questions.answerText:
(i) Amylase and lipase are used; amylase hydrolyses complex carbohydrates containing alpha-D-glucose units and is highly concentrated in the pancreas and saliva, being also present in striated muscle, adipose tissue, lung, ovaries, fallopian tubes, semen and testes; lipase hydrolyses glycerol esters of long-chain fatty acids, attacking ester bonds at carbons 1 and 3 to produce two moles of fatty acid and one mole of 2-acylglycerol, and is used specifically as a measure of pancreatic disease such as obstruction of the pancreatic duct.
(ii) In acute pancreatitis, serum amylase activity increases within 2 to 12 hours of the onset of disease, reaches maximal levels between 12-72 hours, and normalises by the 3rd-4th day.
(iii) Salivary gland disease, due to infection (mumps), surgical trauma, other trauma or tumours, can also lead to high amylase activity in the serum, so a raised amylase alone does not confirm a pancreatic source.
(iv) Because lipase is specifically used as a measure of pancreatic disease and amylase requires calcium ions and is activated by chloride and bromide with a pH optimum of 7.0, a concurrently raised lipase together with the characteristic early-onset time course of amylase (rising within 2-12 hours) supports a pancreatic rather than a salivary gland origin for the enzyme elevation.

questions.question:
A patient with familial hypercholesterolaemia has a defect in the gene encoding the LDL receptor and an elevated plasma LDL.
(i) Identify the risk factors that determine or worsen the plasma LDL and the atherosclerotic risk.
(ii) State the complications.
(iii) State the management options and justify one.
questions.answerText:
(i) Defects in the LDL receptor gene (familial hypercholesterolaemia) elevate plasma LDL.
- Diets high in saturated fat and cholesterol raise hepatocyte cholesterol, so hepatic LDL receptors fall and plasma LDL rises (high intracellular cholesterol suppresses LDL-receptor synthesis).
- Low HDL (<35 mg/dL) may be associated with increased risk of coronary atherosclerosis whereas high HDL (>55 mg/dL) appears protective; bacterial and viral infections and some inflammatory states decrease HDL and increase hepatic VLDL production, raising atherosclerosis risk if prolonged.
(ii) Elevated plasma LDL and premature coronary atherosclerosis; LDL drops cholesterol onto blood vessel walls and arteries, which can lead to vessel and artery blockages.
(iii) Lipid-lowering medication is indicated, aimed at reducing plasma LDL and cardiovascular risk.
- Related mechanisms: LDL receptors are located mainly in the liver, where receptor number is regulated by hepatocyte cholesterol content; HDL mediates reverse cholesterol transport, accepting excess cholesterol from extrahepatic tissues and delivering it to the liver for breakdown and excretion (as bile acids).

questions.question:
A very long chain fatty acid is being oxidised in a peroxisome.
(i) State the factors that limit the extent of its oxidation.
(ii) State the consequences for energy yield and for the by-product formed.
(iii) Describe the route by which the shortened acyl products are disposed of and justify why it is needed.
questions.answerText:
(i) Peroxisomal thiolase has a different chain length specificity from its mitochondrial counterpart.
(i) It is almost inactive with acyl CoAs of length C8 or less, so fatty acids are incompletely oxidised by peroxisomes.
(ii) In the first dehydrogenation the abstracted electrons are transferred directly to oxygen rather than through the electron transport chain.
(ii) There is no concomitant oxidative phosphorylation, so peroxisomal oxidation is less efficient by 2 ATPs for each C2 cycle.
(ii) The H2O2 produced dissociates to H2O and O2 through peroxisomal catalase.
(iii) The peroxisome contains a carnitine acyl transferase (and a transferase specific for long chain acyl groups); acyl CoAs shortened by peroxisomal β-oxidation are converted to carnitine esters.
(iii) Most of these substrates diffuse passively out of the peroxisome to the mitochondrion, where they are oxidised further.
(iii) Justification: in animals peroxisomal β-oxidation shortens very long chain fatty acids (>22 carbon atoms) to facilitate their degradation by the mitochondrial β-oxidation system.

A(i) The nucleosome is the basic unit of DNA packaging, formed from DNA wound around a protein core of two copies each of four histone types (H2A, H2B, H3, H4); a fifth histone, H1, serves as a linker histone.
A(ii) The 30 nm chromatin fibre consists of a DNA-protein complex coiled with six nucleosomes per turn; the 30 nm fibre forms looped domains (a 300 nm diameter structure) attached to a non-histone scaffold protein.
Looped domains form a 700 nm structure attached to the inside of the nuclear membrane, and 700 nm units form the chromosome (1,400 nm diameter); chromosome structure comprises the chromatid, centromere, short arm (p) and long arm (q).
A(iii) Chromosomes are classified by centromere position: acrocentric (short arm so short it is hard to observe, e.g. chromosomes 13, 14, 15, 21, 22), metacentric (arms roughly equal, which may form by balanced translocation), sub-metacentric (unequal arm lengths), telocentric (centromere at the terminal, not found in humans), sub-telocentric, and holocentric (entire chromosome length acts as centromere, e.g. C. elegans).
B(i) Most balanced reciprocal translocation carriers are healthy and asymptomatic, with an incidence of about 1 in 500 to 1 in 625 human newborns.
About 6% of carriers have symptoms such as autism, intellectual disability, or congenital anomalies, caused by a gene disrupted or dysregulated at the breakpoint of the translocation.
Carriers of balanced translocations have an increased risk of producing gametes with unbalanced chromosomal translocations, leading to miscarriages or abnormal offspring, which is the basis of the reproductive risk despite the carrier's own good health.
C(i) A reciprocal translocation is usually an exchange of material between non-homologous chromosomes; it is generally harmless and may be found through prenatal diagnosis.
A Robertsonian translocation involves two acrocentric chromosomes fusing near the centromere region with loss of the short arms, forming a single metacentric chromosome.
The resulting karyotype in a Robertsonian translocation carrier leaves only 45 chromosomes, since two chromosomes have fused; this has no direct effect on phenotype because the only genes on the short arms of acrocentrics are common to all of them and present in variable copy number.
The most common Robertsonian translocation in humans involves chromosomes 13 and 14, seen in about 0.97 per 1000 newborns; carriers of Robertsonian translocations are not associated with phenotypic abnormality themselves.
Both types of translocation carrier share the same underlying risk of producing unbalanced gametes leading to miscarriage or abnormal offspring, for example a Robertsonian translocation of chromosome 21 raising the risk of a child with Down syndrome.

A(ii) Describe higher-order chromatin packaging (the 30 nm fibre and looped domains).
A(iii) Describe the structural types of chromosomes based on centromere position.
B(i) Explain the clinical basis for why balanced translocation carriers are usually asymptomatic yet still at reproductive risk.
C(i) Distinguish between reciprocal translocation and Robertsonian translocation.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Three rounds of β-oxidation give 3 NADH, 3 FADH2 and 3 acetyl CoA.
A(ii) Problem 1: a β,γ (cis Δ3) double bond after the third round; enoyl CoA isomerase converts it to the trans-Δ2 form.
A(iii) Problem 2: a Δ4 double bond in the 5th round gives 2,4-dienoyl CoA; NADPH-dependent 2,4-dienoyl CoA reductase gives trans-3-enoyl CoA, which 3,2-enoyl CoA isomerase converts to trans-2-enoyl CoA.
A(iv) After correction, β-oxidation continues.
B(i) Problem 1: the cis β,γ double bond containing enoyl CoA is not a substrate for enoyl CoA hydratase.
B(i) Problem 2: 2,4-dienoyl CoA is a poor substrate for enoyl CoA hydratase.
B(i) In both cases a trans-2 form, a normal substrate of enoyl-CoA hydratase, is generated so that β-oxidation can continue.
C(i) Acyl CoA dehydrogenase is bypassed in each problem.
C(i) Each bypass leads to one fewer FADH2 and 1.5 fewer ATPs than the saturated counterpart.
C(i) FADH2 is reoxidised by the electron transport chain, with reduction of oxygen to water from the coenzyme Q stage giving 2 ATPs per electron pair.
C(i) Acyl CoA dehydrogenase is bypassed twice for linoleyl CoA, giving 2 fewer FADH2 and 3 fewer ATPs than stearoyl CoA (18:0).
C(i) Each round of the saturated pathway produces 1 NADH, 1 FADH2 and 1 acetyl CoA.

A(i) Phosphatidic acid, diacylglycerol and triacylglycerol are all synthesised from fatty acyl-CoA and glycerol-3-phosphate or dihydroxyacetone phosphate; the acyltransferases are not completely specific for any particular acyl-CoA with respect to chain length or degree of unsaturation, though in human adipose tissue triacylglycerols, the 1-acyl group is mostly saturated (especially C-16 palmitoyl) and the 2-acyl group is mostly unsaturated (especially C-18, cis-oleyl). Both ATP and CTP are required to activate ethanolamine and choline; the activated metabolites then react with 1,2-diacylglycerol to generate phosphatidylethanolamine and phosphatidylcholine. Phosphatidylserine can be obtained from phosphatidylethanolamine and serine by an exchange reaction.
A(ii) Both phosphatidylinositol and phosphatidylglycerol are derived from phosphatidic acid; CTP is required to activate phosphatidic acid to form CDP-diacylglycerol.
C. Phosphatidylethanolamine and phosphatidylcholine are synthesised by first using ATP and CTP to activate ethanolamine or choline, which then react with 1,2-diacylglycerol; phosphatidylinositol and phosphatidylglycerol, in contrast, are synthesised from phosphatidic acid via CTP-dependent activation of phosphatidic acid to CDP-diacylglycerol.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the biosynthesis of glycerophospholipids under the following headings: precursors of phosphatidic acid/diacylglycerol/triacylglycerol, and the synthesis of phosphatidylethanolamine, phosphatidylcholine and phosphatidylserine.
A(ii) Describe the synthesis of phosphatidylinositol and phosphatidylglycerol.

A(i) β-ketoacyl CoA thiolase (acyl CoA acetyltransferase).
A(ii) The thiolase reaction is the final stage of β-oxidation.
A(ii) It forms acetyl CoA and a new acyl CoA which is 2 carbon atoms shorter than the one that began the cycle.
A(iii) Each round of β-oxidation produces 1 NADH, 1 FADH2 and 1 acetyl CoA.
B(i) Oxidation of acetyl CoA via the citric acid cycle generates additional FADH2 and NADH.

B(i) For palmitoyl-CoA: 7 rounds give 7 FADH2, 7 NADH and 8 acetyl CoA; the 8 acetyl CoA in the citric acid cycle give 8 GTP, 24 NADH and 8 FADH2.
B(i) Complete oxidation of a fatty acid is highly exergonic and yields numerous ATPs.
C(i) Peroxisomal thiolase has a different chain length specificity from its mitochondrial counterpart.
C(i) It is almost inactive with acyl CoAs of length C8 or less, so fatty acids are incompletely oxidised by peroxisomes.
C(i) High concentrations of acetyl-CoA, a product of the reaction, inhibit thiolase.

questions.question:
A patient is found to have excessive aldosterone production from one or both adrenal glands.
(i) Identify the gland, its position, its subdivisions and the layer responsible.
(ii) State the structures affected by the hormone and what normally stimulates it.
(iii) List the differential pathologies, including causes of adrenal hormone excess.
(iv) Give the clinical-biochemical reasoning that distinguishes them.
questions.answerText:
(i) The adrenal (suprarenal) glands lie at the top of each kidney; each is two endocrine glands, the outer cortex and the inner medulla. Aldosterone is a mineralocorticoid made from cholesterol in the zona glomerulosa of the cortex.
(ii) Kidney (promotes sodium reabsorption into the blood, helping maintain blood pressure), sweat glands (reduces sodium loss) and taste cells (increases sensitivity to sodium sources).
- Aldosterone is stimulated by a drop in blood sodium, a rise in blood potassium, angiotensin II and ACTH.
(iii) Primary hyperaldosteronism (adrenal cause): unilateral adenoma (2/3), bilateral hyperplasia (1/3), unilateral carcinoma (<1%), unilateral hyperplasia (<1%), familial types I and II (<1%); secondary hyperaldosteronism when the cause lies outside the adrenal glands.
- Other adrenal hormone excess: Cushing's syndrome (glucocorticoid excess, usually from an ACTH-secreting pituitary tumour, rarely an adrenal cortex tumour, or from glucocorticoid therapy); androgen excess (premature puberty in boys; masculine hair pattern and cessation of menstruation in females).
(iv) 'Primary' means the problem lies in the adrenal glands themselves; unilateral disease (one gland) is separated from bilateral disease (both glands).
- Cushing's syndrome involves glucocorticoids (cortisol, which promotes gluconeogenesis, breaks down fat and protein and is anti-inflammatory) whereas aldosterone acts on sodium handling; adrenal steroid production is triggered by pituitary ACTH.

A. Biosynthesis of triacylglycerols (TGs) occurs in the intestinal mucosa cells, adipose tissue and liver; TGs are used primarily for energy storage and also provide insulation for survival in cold climates in some animals. In the liver and adipose tissue, TGs are synthesised by diacylglycerol acyltransferase, an enzyme found on the cytoplasmic face of the endoplasmic reticulum; in the intestinal mucosa, TG synthesis is initiated when TGs in the small intestine are degraded into 2-monoacylglycerols and free fatty acids, which are absorbed and converted by monoacylglycerol acyltransferase into diacylglycerol, which then forms TGs. Degradation begins with bile salts, amphipathic compounds synthesised from cholesterol in the liver, stored in the gall bladder and released into the small intestine after a fatty meal, converting dietary fats into mixed micelles of bile salts, monoacylglycerols and fatty acids; TGs are also hydrolysed by gastric and/or pancreatic lipases, which adsorb to the water-lipid interface and convert TGs into fatty acids, monoacylglycerols, glycerol and diacylglycerols, which diffuse into intestinal epithelial cells and are reconverted to TG and packaged with dietary cholesterol and specific proteins into chylomicrons.
B. When hormones such as epinephrine and glucagon are secreted in response to low blood glucose levels, they activate the enzyme adenylyl cyclase in the adipocyte plasma membrane, which produces the intracellular second messenger cAMP; a cAMP-dependent protein kinase phosphorylates and thereby activates hormone-sensitive triacylglycerol lipase, which catalyses hydrolysis of the ester linkages of triacylglycerols.
C. The fatty acids released pass from the adipocyte into the blood, where they bind to the blood protein serum albumin; serum albumin, which makes up about half of the total serum protein, noncovalently binds as many as 10 fatty acids per protein monomer, and bound to this soluble protein the otherwise insoluble fatty acids are carried to tissues such as skeletal muscle, heart and renal cortex, where they dissociate from albumin and are transported into cells to serve as fuel.
questions.question:
A. Describe the biosynthesis and degradation of triacylglycerols, including the sites of synthesis, the enzymes involved, and the role of bile salts and lipases in digestion.
B. State the hormonal mechanism by which stored triacylglycerol is mobilised when blood glucose is low.
C. Explain the biochemical basis of how the released fatty acids are transported to and used by tissues such as skeletal muscle, heart and renal cortex.

A patient is found to have markedly raised blood gastrin (hypergastrinaemia) due to a gastrin-producing tumour that is mostly benign.
(i) State the diagnosis.
(ii) Name the test used to investigate the hypergastrinaemia.
(iii) Give the sites of the tumour and the normal sites of gastrin production.
(iv) State the structures affected by the excess hormone and how it acts on them.
(v) Describe the molecular forms (variants) of gastrin and their behaviour.
questions.answerText:
(i) Zollinger-Ellison syndrome: gastrin produced at excessive levels, often as a result of a gastrinoma (mostly benign).
(ii) The pentagastrin test is performed to investigate hypergastrinaemia (high blood gastrin).
(iii) Tumour sites: duodenum or pancreas. Normal gastrin: G cells in the antral region of the stomach (also pancreatic endocrine cells, pituitary and extra-antral G cells).
(iv) Parietal cells (HCl secretion, parietal cell maturation and fundal growth); chief cells (pepsinogen); ECL cells via CCK2/gastrin receptors, releasing histamine which acts in a paracrine way on parietal cells (the major stimulus for acid secretion).
- Signalling: G protein - phospholipase C - PIP2 hydrolysed to IP3 (releases Ca2+ from the endoplasmic reticulum) and DAG (activates protein kinase C) - phosphorylation - HCl secretion; gastrin does not change cAMP.
- Also increases antral motility and gastric emptying (relaxes the pyloric sphincter), induces pancreatic secretion and gallbladder emptying, relaxes the ileocecal valve and contributes to the gastrocolic reflex; also regulates epithelial proliferation.
(v) Preprogastrin - progastrin (21-aa signal peptide, 37-aa N-terminal extension, gastrin-34, 9-aa C-terminal extension) - glycine-extended gastrins - amidated gastrins G-34 (big) and G-17 (little).
- Fasting gastrin is mostly G-34 (cleared more slowly); the main form released after a meal is G-17; all forms are equally potent at the receptor.

(i) The diagnosis is neonatal jaundice, common particularly in premature infants and usually transient, resolving in the first 10 days of life.
(ii) It is predisposed by prematurity and by immaturity of the enzymes involved in bilirubin conjugation, particularly UDP glucuronyl transferase.
(iii) High levels of unconjugated bilirubin are toxic to the newborn because, owing to its hydrophobicity, it can cross the blood-brain barrier and cause a type of mental retardation known as kernicterus.
(iv) If bilirubin levels are judged too high, phototherapy with UV light is used to convert bilirubin to a water-soluble, non-toxic form; exchange blood transfusion is used to remove excess bilirubin; phenobarbital may be given to the mother before an induced labour of a premature infant, as it crosses the placenta and induces synthesis of UDP glucuronyl transferase; jaundice within the first 24 hours of life, or lasting longer than 10 days, is usually pathological and needs further investigation.

questions.answerText:
A. The sphingolipids, like the phospholipids, are composed of a polar head group and two nonpolar tails; the core of sphingolipids is the long-chain amino alcohol, sphingosine. The sphingolipids include the sphingomyelins and glycosphingolipids (the cerebrosides, sulfatides, globosides and gangliosides); sphingomyelins are the only sphingolipid class that are also phospholipids. The initiation of synthesis of the sphingoid bases takes place via the condensation of palmitoyl-CoA and serine, occurring on the cytoplasmic face of the endoplasmic reticulum and catalysed by the pyridoxal phosphate-dependent enzyme, serine palmitoyl transferase (SPT); SPT is the rate-limiting enzyme of the sphingolipid biosynthesis pathway and is a heterodimeric enzyme composed of two main catalytic subunits, SPTLC1 and SPTLC2 or SPTLC3.
B. Sphingolipids are components of all membranes but are particularly abundant in the myelin sheath; the myelin sheath is a multilayered structure that protects and insulates cells of the central nervous system, and in human myelin, sphingolipids constitute about 25% of the total lipid.
C. Degradation of sphingolipids occurs in the lysosomes by a family of hydrolytic enzymes; these degradative pathways are of great medical interest because of their relationship to a group of congenital diseases called sphingolipidoses (also known as lipid storage diseases). Each disease condition is characterised by deficiency of the degradative enzyme, with concomitant accumulation within the lysosome of the substrate for the deficient enzyme; most of these diseases are autosomal recessive. General symptoms of sphingolipidoses include mental retardation, premature death, psychomotor degeneration, gastrointestinal problems, fatigue, anaemia, and enlarged spleen and liver.
questions.question:
A. Describe the biosynthesis of sphingolipids under the following headings: the core structural component, initiation of synthesis, and the rate-limiting enzyme.
B. State the significance of the myelin sheath as a site of sphingolipid concentration.
C. Explain the biochemical basis of the group of diseases called sphingolipidoses that result when sphingolipid degradation is defective.

A(i) Describe how enzymes are used in clinical diagnosis, including the three groups of plasma enzymes.
A(ii) Describe the cellular/organ localisation of the major diagnostic enzymes.
B(i) State how the organ distribution of these enzymes relates to the diseases in which each is characteristically raised.
C(i) Explain how a rise in one such enzyme allows disease in a distant organ to be inferred from a blood sample.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Clinical enzymology applies enzyme analysis to the diagnosis and management of disease; enzymes are predominantly localised intracellularly and secreted into serum in only very low active amounts, so a rise in a specific serum enzyme indicates tissue or cellular damage and release of intracellular enzyme into body fluids.
Plasma enzymes are classified into three groups: plasma-specific enzymes (e.g. pro-coagulants such as thrombin, factor XII, factor X), secreted enzymes inconsequential to plasma function (e.g. lipase, lactate dehydrogenase, alkaline phosphatase), and cellular/organ-specific enzymes involved in tissue metabolism (e.g. aminotransferases, alkaline phosphatase, dehydrogenases).
A(ii) In eukaryotic cells, enzymes are localised in specific organelles: respiratory/TCA enzymes in mitochondria, transaminases and drug-metabolising enzymes in the liver, glycolytic enzymes in the cytosol, and nutrient-transport enzymes in the cell membrane.
Relevant diagnostic enzymes include AST, ALT, creatine kinase (CK), alkaline phosphatase (ALP), gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT), lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), acid phosphatase (ACP) with prostate specific antigen, plasma cholinesterase, lipase and amylase.
B(i) AST and ALT are present in liver, heart and muscle; tissue injury elevates both in circulation, and they help diagnose liver carcinoma, viral hepatitis, and heart or pancreatic disease; ALT is more liver-specific, so its rise indicates hepatocyte damage.
CK is highest in striated muscle, heart muscle and brain, and forms isoenzymes CK-1 (BB, brain), CK-2 (MB, heart/muscle), CK-3 (MM, skeletal muscle/heart); it is elevated in muscular dystrophy, myocardial infarction, cerebral ischaemia, head injury and Reye's syndrome, and moderately in hypothyroidism.
LDH is composed of H and M subunits forming five isoenzymes with tissue-specific distribution (LDH1,2 cardiac muscle; LDH4,5 liver; LDH3 lung/platelets); it is elevated in myocardial infarction, viral hepatitis, malignant disease and muscular dystrophy.
ALP is a family of membrane-bound zinc metalloenzyme isoenzymes found in intestinal epithelium, kidney tubules, osteoblasts, bile canaliculi/sinusoidal membrane of liver, and placenta; it is elevated in rickets, osteomalacia, Paget's disease, metastatic carcinoma and biliary obstruction/liver disease.
Amylase and lipase are concentrated in the pancreas (and salivary glands for amylase); amylase rises in acute pancreatitis and in salivary gland disease such as mumps, surgical trauma or tumours.
C(i) Because each enzyme has a characteristic tissue distribution, a disproportionate elevation of one enzyme relative to others (e.g. CK-MB with AST/LDH1,2 rather than ALT) points to damage in a distant organ such as the heart rather than the liver or skeletal muscle.
Enzyme levels in blood are also controlled by cell proliferation, intracellular distribution, the rate of extrication of enzyme from cells, and inactivation, degradation and plasma elimination kinetics, which are affected by the individual's health status.
Serum enzyme assessment is therefore of diagnostic and prognostic significance, allowing the biochemical detection of damage to organs distant from the sampled blood, reflecting an underlying systemic functional deficit in that organ.

questions.question:
A long-chain fatty acyl-CoA cannot cross the inner mitochondrial membrane directly, yet its acyl group reaches the matrix. Two enzyme activities on opposite surfaces of the membrane and a specific protein are involved.
(i) Identify the carrier compound and the enzymes involved.
(ii) State the location and reaction of each enzyme and the role of the protein.
(iii) Distinguish the two enzymes and state the movement of free carnitine.
(iv) Explain the reasoning by which this 3-step process is regarded as controlling oxidation.
questions.answerText:
(i) The carrier compound is carnitine (4-trimethylamino-3-hydroxybutyrate), which occurs in both plants and animal tissues; the acyl portion of the acyl CoA is transferred to it.
(i) The enzymes are carnitine palmitoyl transferases I and II, which can transfer a variety of acyl groups.
(ii) They are found on the external and internal surfaces of the inner mitochondrial membrane.
(ii) Carnitine palmitoyl transferase I converts acyl CoA + carnitine to acyl carnitine + CoA.
(ii) A specific carrier protein mediates translocation, transporting acyl carnitine into the mitochondria.
(iii) Carnitine palmitoyl transferase I acts on the external surface and II on the internal surface, where acyl CoA and carnitine are regenerated.
(iii) The carrier protein transports free carnitine in the opposite direction to acyl carnitine.
(iv) The 3-step process is rate-limiting for fatty acid oxidation and an important point of regulation.
(iv) Carnitine acyl transferase I is inhibited by malonyl-CoA.

(i) The diagnosis is sickle-cell anaemia (sickle-cell disorder/disease), a common genetic condition due to a haemoglobin disorder resulting from inheritance of mutant haemoglobin genes from both parents (homozygous inheritance, e.g. Hb SS); heterozygous inheritance of two different abnormal haemoglobin genes, such as Hb SC, is also recognised.
(ii) Normal haemoglobin is a 4-chain tetramer of 2 alpha and 2 beta chains; in HbS, valine is substituted for glutamic acid in both beta chains (HbSS), due to a single point mutation at the sixth position of the beta globin chain, which has thymine instead of adenine.
(iii) Classical treatment of sickle cell disease comprises pain treatment, antibiotherapy, transfusion, and rehydration.
(iv) Emerging therapeutic agents include anti-adhesion therapy, HbF augmentation, anti-oxidative therapy, bone marrow transplantation, and gene therapy.

A. There are two main types of nutrients: macronutrients and micronutrients. Macronutrients include carbohydrates, proteins, and fats, and provide the body with energy. Micronutrients include vitamins and minerals, and help regulate various bodily processes. Water is also considered an essential nutrient.
B. A deficiency in macronutrients, particularly protein and energy together, leads to protein-calorie malnutrition (kwashiorkor and marasmus). Deficiency of specific micronutrients leads to specific nutritional disorders: for example, iodine deficiency leads to iodine deficiency disorders (goitre, cretinism), vitamin A deficiency leads to night blindness, vitamin D deficiency leads to rickets and osteomalacia, vitamin B1 deficiency leads to beriberi, vitamin B3 deficiency leads to pellagra, vitamin B12 deficiency leads to megaloblastic/pernicious anaemia and neurological disease, vitamin B9 (folate) deficiency leads to macrocytic anaemia and neural tube defects, and vitamin C deficiency leads to scurvy.
C. Iodine is required to produce thyroid hormones, which control cell metabolism and neuromuscular tissue growth and development, especially fetal-perinatal brain development; because the mother's dietary/environmental iodine deficiency limits the thyroid hormone available to the developing fetus, the deficiency (which originates outside the fetus, in maternal diet/soil iodine content) produces its functional deficit at a distant site, the fetal brain, resulting in fetal iodine deficiency manifestations such as mental retardation, dwarfism, psychomotor defects and cretinism.
questions.question:

A. Describe the classification of lipoproteins under the following headings: origin/source, density, and main lipid components/apolipoproteins.
B. State how the different lipoprotein classes relate to the development of atherosclerosis.
C. Explain why a change in the regulation of the LDL receptor produces a distant, systemic effect (elevated circulating cholesterol and its consequences on the blood vessel wall).
questions.answerText:
A. Lipoproteins are classified based on their density: the chylomicron (largest, lowest density, highest in triacylglycerols, derived from intestinal absorption of dietary lipids); VLDL (very low density lipoprotein, derived from the liver for export of triacylglycerol, second highest in triacylglycerol content); IDL (intermediate density lipoprotein, derived from triacylglycerol depletion of VLDL); LDL (low density lipoprotein, representing a final stage in the catabolism of VLDL, highest in cholesteryl esters as a percentage of weight, containing apolipoprotein B-100); and HDL (high density lipoprotein, highest in density due to a high protein/lipid ratio, involved in cholesterol transport and also in VLDL and chylomicron metabolism).
B. LDL carriers are often referred to as "bad cholesterol": cells that no longer need cholesterol leave LDL particles to travel the bloodstream still loaded with cholesterol, which can be dropped onto blood vessel walls and arteries, leading to blood vessel and artery blockages. HDL carriers are typically referred to as "good cholesterol" and remove excess material left over by LDL through reverse cholesterol transport, scraping cholesterol deposits off blood vessel walls and transferring them to VLDL and LDL for delivery to the liver; high blood levels of HDL correlate with low incidence of atherosclerosis, while bacterial and viral infections and some inflammatory disease states decrease HDL and increase VLDL production by the liver, which, if prolonged, can increase the risk of atherosclerosis.
C. Synthesis of the LDL receptor is suppressed by high intracellular cholesterol; this decreased synthesis of LDL receptor prevents excessive cholesterol uptake by cells, but has the deleterious consequence that excess dietary cholesterol remains in the blood as LDL. Because the cholesterol that does enter cells locally down-regulates the receptor that clears LDL from the whole circulation, a change confined to intracellular cholesterol handling in individual cells produces a distant, systemic rise in circulating LDL, with cholesterol material able to deposit on blood vessel walls and arteries throughout the body, leading to blood vessel and artery blockages.

A. Iron: the total amount of Fe in the human body is 4 to 5 g, about 75% of which is found in haemoglobin, the pigment for the red colour of erythrocytes; it is required for synthesis of the iron-porphyrin proteins haemoglobin, myoglobin, cytochromes and cytochrome oxidase, and is absorbed only in its Fe2+ form, with iron in meat best absorbed and that in cereals poorly absorbed. Zinc: present in many NAD/NADP-linked dehydrogenases and also in DNA/RNA polymerases, hence its importance in replication and transmission of genetic information; over 80 enzymes are known to require Zn as part of their prosthetic groups, including alcohol dehydrogenase, carbonic anhydrase, DNA/RNA polymerases and carboxypeptidase. Copper: required for proper utilisation of Fe in the body, present in the active group of lysyl oxidase (an enzyme that makes the cross-linkages between polypeptide chains in collagen and elastin), and essential for the synthesis of cytochrome oxidase (which contains both Fe and Cu); it is also necessary for proper development of connective tissue and blood vessels, with about 2.5-5.0 mg/day required, and is abundant in organ meats, seafood, vegetables and nuts, but absent in dairy products. Iodine: over 90% of iodine is stored in the thyroid, present in only minute amounts (15-20 mg) in the body, and is required to produce thyroid hormones, which control cell metabolism and neuromuscular tissue growth and development, especially fetal-perinatal brain.
B. Fe deficiency is one of the most common nutritional disorders, common in children, in adolescent girls and in women in their reproductive years. Iodine deficiency (goitre) results from a deficiency of iodine in soils in areas far from the sea; severe iodine deficiency of mothers leads to cretinism in their children.
C. Copper is required for proper utilisation of iron in the body, and it is essential for the synthesis of cytochrome oxidase, an enzyme that contains both iron and copper, linking copper directly to iron-dependent function. Copper is also present in the active group of lysyl oxidase, the enzyme that makes the cross-linkages between polypeptide chains in collagen and elastin, and is necessary for proper development of connective tissue and blood vessels, explaining its role in connective tissue integrity.

A malnourished man with a history of alcohol abuse presents with dermatitis and skin lesions on the face and hands, mouth ulceration, diarrhoea, and disorientation with depression.
(i) What risk factors are responsible for this man's condition?
(ii) What complications/manifestations has he developed as a result of this condition?
(iii) What dietary management would you recommend, and justify this option based on how the deficient nutrient is normally obtained?
questions.answerText:
(i) Pellagra usually occurs due to alcohol abuse, malnutrition (especially in the light of a very low protein diet), and in those who have multiple nutrient deficiencies.
(ii) The primary symptoms of pellagra include skin problems (dermatitis, skin lesions on the face, arms and hands, inflamed skin); mouth problems (canker sores, mouth irritation, ulceration or swelling of the tongue); digestive problems (diarrhoea, nausea, vomiting, poor appetite); mental impairment (disorientation, dementia, depression, irritability, emotional instability); and, since niacin is vital for energy production, general fatigue, muscular weakness and loss of appetite.
(iii) Niacin is naturally found in many foods, including meat (especially liver), fish, nuts, legumes, herbs, dairy (e.g. milk and cheese), fruits, vegetables, enriched whole grain products (e.g. cereals) and brewer's yeast. Justification: because small amounts of niacin are manufactured in the body from the amino acid tryptophan but this is inefficient and cannot meet daily demands, dietary correction with niacin-rich foods is preferable to relying on endogenous synthesis alone, which is inefficient.

(i) The patient has beriberi, specifically wet beriberi (which affects the heart and circulatory system, and in extreme cases can cause heart failure), with features also of Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome (cerebral beriberi).
(ii) Vitamin B1 (thiamin) functions along with other B vitamins to allow the body to metabolise carbohydrates, fat and protein into energy, and is particularly vital for turning carbohydrates into energy in the brain; it also helps maintain normal heart function and supports normal function of the nervous system. Wernicke encephalopathy and Korsakoff syndrome are two forms of brain damage caused by thiamine deficiency: Wernicke encephalopathy damages the thalamus and hypothalamus, causing confusion, memory loss, loss of muscle coordination and visual problems such as rapid eye movement and double vision; Korsakoff syndrome is the result of permanent damage to the region of the brain where memories form, causing loss of memory, the inability to form new memories, and hallucinations. Symptoms of wet beriberi include shortness of breath during physical activity, waking up short of breath, rapid heart rate and swollen lower legs.
(iii) A vitamin B1 deficiency can happen due to factors such as over-dieting, abusing alcohol, liver disorders and kidney dialysis; thiamin deficiency is particularly widespread among alcoholics, since chronic alcohol abuse lowers the quantity of vitamin B1 absorbed by the body, as alcohol blocks thiamin absorption and damages the lining of the small intestine, disrupting normal nutrient absorption.
(iv) To prevent beriberi, a healthy, balanced diet including foods rich in thiamine should be taken, such as vegetables, beans and legumes, meat, fish, whole grains, nuts, dairy, yeast, and products made with fortified grains (e.g. breads, rice, pasta, cereals).

(i) Aspartate transaminase (AST), creatine kinase (CK), and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) are used; AST is present in liver, heart and muscle; CK is highest in striated muscle, heart muscle and brain, existing as isoenzymes CK-1 (BB, brain), CK-2 (MB, heart and muscle) and CK-3 (MM, skeletal muscle and heart); LDH exists as five isoenzymes, with LDH1 and LDH2 specific to cardiac muscle.
(ii) AST rises 6-8 hours after the onset of chest pain, reaches its highest serum level at 18-24 hours, and returns to pre-infarction levels by the 4th-5th day; in myocardial infarction, serum LDH activity is typically more than 3 times normal, and may exceed 10 times normal.
(iii) AST and ALT are also raised in liver carcinoma, viral hepatitis and pancreatic disease, and AST/ALT are also raised (2-8 times normal) in skeletal muscle diseases such as progressive muscular dystrophy, dermatomyositis and crush injury; however, in myocardial infarction, ALT activity is within the normal range or only slightly increased, distinguishing cardiac from hepatic injury.
(iv) The combination of a raised CK-2 (MB) isoenzyme with an AST time course (rising at 6-8 hours, peaking at 18-24 hours, normalising by day 4-5) and near-normal ALT supports a diagnosis of myocardial infarction rather than liver or skeletal muscle disease, since this tissue-specific isoenzyme pattern and the relatively normal ALT are not features of hepatic or muscular dystrophic damage.

A(i) Electrons come from NADH and FADH2. NADH enters at NADH-Q oxidoreductase (Complex I); FADH2 from succinate enters at succinate-Q reductase (Complex II); both feed coenzyme Q (ubiquinone).
A(ii) Complex I: NADH to FMN (prosthetic group) to iron-sulfur clusters to coenzyme Q (oxidised Q, semiquinone, reduced QH2); NADH + Q + 5H+(matrix) gives NAD+ + QH2 + 4H+(cytosolic side).
- Complex II: FADH2 to Fe-S clusters to Q, with no protons pumped. Complex III (Q-cytochrome c oxidoreductase; 3 hemes and an Fe-S cluster): Q to cytochrome b to Fe-S to cytochrome c1 to cytochrome c, coupled to proton transport by the Q cycle; cytochromes carry only electrons (heme iron Fe2+/Fe3+).
A(iii) Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase; cytochromes a and a3; CuA/CuA, heme a, heme a3-CuB) reduces oxygen to water; oxygen accepts the electrons because of its high electronegativity.
- Partial reduction of O2 gives superoxide and peroxide, handled by superoxide dismutase (2O2- + 2H+ to O2 + H2O2) and catalase (2H2O2 to O2 + 2H2O).
A(iv) Each electron transfer is an exothermic redox reaction whose energy moves H+ into the intermembrane space; Complex I pumps 4 protons and cytochrome c oxidase pumps 4 additional protons (8 removed from the matrix in total).
- Per 2 electrons, NADH gives 10 protons pumped (P/O 2.5) and FADH2 gives 6 (P/O 1.5); the rate depends on the distance between donor and acceptor, the free-energy change and the supply of ADP.
B(i) Complex I: rotenone, amytal, Demerol. Complex II: 2-thenoyltrifluoroacetone, carboxin. Complex III: antimycin A1 (Cyt bH to Q at the QN site).
- Complex IV: cyanide, azide and carbon monoxide bind the iron of cytochrome a3 (cyanide and azide when ferric, CO when ferrous); their acute toxicity reflects the few Cyt a3 molecules present.
C(i) With O2 and an electron donor such as NADH present, carriers before the block become fully reduced and carriers after it are completely oxidised.
- Electron flow and proton pumping stop, so proton-gradient-coupled ATP synthesis ceases; the toxicity of cyanide is solely from arrest of electron transport.
- In intact mitochondria oxygen is consumed only when ADP is added, and consumption stops when the ADP is converted to ATP.

(i) The diagnosis is cystinuria, a disorder associated with excess cysteine in the urine; cystine is the oxidised disulfide homodimer of two cysteines.
(ii) Cystinuria is an autosomal recessive disorder that results from a failure of the renal proximal tubules to reabsorb cysteine that was filtered by the glomerulus; the disorder results from defects in either of the two protein subunits of the cysteine transporter.
(iii) In addition to excess cysteine in the urine, the disorder is also associated with increased urinary excretion of the dibasic amino acids arginine, lysine and ornithine; however, clinical consequences are only associated with the increased urinary cysteine, and this is due to the poor solubility of this homodimeric compound (cystine).
(iv) The cysteine transporter affected in cystinuria is distinct from the renal cysteine transporter (i.e. it is a separate transport system from other renal amino acid transporters).

A(i) Describe the classification of enzyme structure into simple and complex (holo-) enzymes.
A(ii) Describe cofactors, including prosthetic groups and coenzymes.
A(iii) Describe the role of vitamins as coenzyme precursors.
B(i) Explain the biochemical basis for why certain vitamins must be supplied in the diet as coenzyme precursors.
C(i) Distinguish between a prosthetic group and a coenzyme.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Enzymes are structurally classified as simple enzymes (protein only) or complex/holoenzymes (a protein part, the apoenzyme, plus a non-protein part, the cofactor); the enzyme without its non-protein moiety is the apoenzyme and is inactive, while the holoenzyme is the active enzyme with its non-protein component.
A(ii) Some enzymes require non-protein molecules called cofactors for activity; cofactors can be inorganic (e.g. metal ions such as Mg, Cu, Zn, Fe-S clusters) or organic compounds (e.g. flavin or heme).
Cofactors can also be classed as prosthetic groups, tightly bound/permanently associated with an enzyme by covalent interactions (e.g. the heme prosthetic group of haemoglobin, pyridoxal phosphate, FMN, FAD, metalloenzymes), or as coenzymes, which are loosely bound to the apoenzyme.
Coenzymes are small organic molecules that transfer a chemical group from one enzyme to another; examples of groups carried include the hydride ion carried by NAD or NADP, the acetyl group carried by coenzyme A, and methyl groups carried by folates.
A(iii) Many vitamins are coenzyme precursors; many organisms are unable to synthesise certain portions of essential cofactors, so these substances must be present in the diet, and many coenzymes were originally discovered as growth factors for microorganisms.
The vitamins in the human diet that are coenzyme precursors are all water-soluble vitamins.
B(i) Because the vitamins that serve as coenzyme precursors are water-soluble, and organisms cannot synthesise certain portions of these essential cofactors themselves, they are not stored to any great extent in the body.
This is the basis for the requirement that such vitamins be regularly present in the diet, since without dietary supply the corresponding apoenzymes cannot be converted to active holoenzymes.
C(i) A prosthetic group is tightly bound, usually covalently, to the apoenzyme, so that it becomes a permanent part of the enzyme, as in the heme group of haemoglobin or pyridoxal phosphate, FMN and FAD bound to their respective enzymes.
A coenzyme, by contrast, is a large organic molecule that is only loosely (non-covalently) bound to the apoenzyme, participating directly in catalysis but not remaining permanently attached to any one enzyme molecule.
Both are cofactors needed for the holoenzyme to be catalytically active, but a prosthetic group is a fixed structural component of a single enzyme, whereas a coenzyme behaves more like a co-substrate that shuttles a chemical group between different enzymes.
The heme groups of enzymes such as catalase and peroxidase, and metalloenzymes generally, are examples of prosthetic-group cofactors, while NAD/NADP and coenzyme A are examples of coenzyme-type cofactors that act as chemical-group carriers.

(i) These are acute hepatic porphyrias caused by hereditary or acquired defects in enzymes of heme synthesis: variegate porphyria results from deficiency of protoporphyrinogen oxidase, and hereditary coproporphyria results from deficiency of coproporphyrinogen oxidase.
(ii) These deficiencies cause an accumulation of porphyrins resulting in cutaneous manifestations; photosensitivity is a common symptom, attributable to elevated levels of light-absorbing pathway intermediates and their degradation products, with skin damage on light exposure resulting from the formation of superoxide radicals; porphyrins are also excreted in excessive amounts in urine and stool, which may become port-wine coloured at very high levels.
(iii) Treatment options for porphyrias include medical support for vomiting and pain, hemin (which decreases ALA synthase synthesis), and avoidance of sunlight and precipitating drugs or factors; for the cutaneous presentation described, avoidance of sunlight and protection of the skin from light is the most directly justified option, since protection of the skin from light is specifically indicated for cases with cutaneous manifestations.
questions.question:
An adult presents with blistering skin lesions on sun-exposed areas together with occasional episodes of abdominal pain.
(i) What are the enzyme defects (risk factors) that can cause this presentation?
(ii) What are the complications/manifestations of this group of conditions?
(iii) What management options are available, and which is most directly justified by the presentation described?

questions.answerText:
(i) Diabetes mellitus (insulin deficiency; the juvenile type 1 form is due to an absolute deficiency of insulin) with ketosis, ketonuria and acidosis.
- Other features of early diabetes: negative nitrogen balance (increased gluconeogenesis from amino acids), lipemia (raised lipid, fatty acid and cholesterol), and increased tendency to cataract and arteriosclerotic lesions; glucose in urine carries water, causing dehydration.
(ii) With insufficient insulin, extrahepatic tissues cannot take up glucose efficiently to use as fuel or convert to fat, and the 'stop' signals on lipolysis, ketogenesis, proteolysis and gluconeogenesis are lost.
- Malonyl CoA (starting material for fatty acid synthesis) is not formed, so it does not inhibit carnitine acyl transferase I; fatty acids enter mitochondria and are degraded to acetyl CoA.
- Acetyl CoA cannot pass through the citric acid cycle because cycle intermediates are drawn off for gluconeogenesis; the accumulating acetyl CoA accelerates ketone body formation (acetoacetate, D-beta-hydroxybutyrate, acetone) beyond the capacity of extrahepatic tissues to oxidise them.
- The raised acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate lower blood pH (acidosis); extreme acidosis can lead to coma and death.
questions.question:
A patient with untreated diabetes presents with hyperglycaemia, glycosuria, weight loss and dehydration; ketones are found in the blood and urine and the blood pH is lowered.
(i) State the diagnosis.
(ii) Explain the biochemical basis of the ketosis and acidosis.

A patient is found to have hypercalcaemia that is often asymptomatic and hard to diagnose, and the loss of calcium homeostasis is due to hormone excess.
(i) Identify the gland that regulates calcium and give its number, position, cells and blood supply.
(ii) State the structures affected by the hormone and the effects on calcium and phosphate.
(iii) List the differential pathologies.
(iv) Give the clinical-biochemical reasoning that separates the causes and describe how the body defends against hypercalcaemia.
questions.answerText:
(i) The parathyroid glands: four small glands on the dorsal side of the thyroid gland, supplied by the thyroid arteries; PTH is released by chief cells, which contain Ca2+ receptors.
(ii) PTH acts directly on bone (Ca2+ resorption) and on the kidney (Ca2+ reabsorption in the distal tubule; inhibits phosphate reabsorption so phosphate is excreted) and indirectly on the intestine by stimulating 1,25-(OH)2-D synthesis; the net effect is raised plasma Ca2+ and lowered plasma phosphate.
(iii) Primary hyperparathyroidism: excess PTH from adenomatous or hyperplastic parathyroid tissue; hypercalcaemia results from combined PTH-induced bone resorption, intestinal calcium absorption and renal tubular reabsorption, plus excessive 1,25-(OH)2-D production.
- Hypercalcaemia of malignancy (excessive bone resorption) by three mechanisms: 1,25-(OH)2-D synthesis by lymphomas; local osteolytic hypercalcaemia (20% of cases); humoral hypercalcaemia through over-expression of PTH-related protein (PTHrP).
(iv) PTHrP has three forms, each about twice the size of native PTH, with marked structural homology; it binds the same receptor and reproduces the full spectrum of PTH activities.
- PTH secretion is inversely related to plasma Ca2+ (maximal below 3.5 mg/dL, maximally inhibited above 5.5 mg/dL); 1,25-(OH)2-D inhibits PTH gene expression; phosphate exerts no direct control.
- Defences against hypercalcaemia: decreased PTH secretion, decreased renal Ca2+ reabsorption, decreased 1,25-(OH)2-D, decreased intestinal Ca2+ absorption and decreased bone resorption.

(i) The diagnosis is acute intermittent porphyria, one of the acute hepatic porphyrias.
(ii) It results from a deficiency of Uroporphyrinogen I synthase (Porphobilinogen Deaminase), an enzyme of the heme biosynthesis pathway.
(iii) This deficiency results in accumulation of the precursors of porphyrins in the liver, namely delta-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) and porphobilinogen (PBG); the accumulation causes occasional episodes of severe neurological symptoms, including acute bouts of abdominal pain and mental confusion, and can cause permanent nerve damage and even death if not treated promptly.
(iv) Porphyrins build up in the body and are excreted in the urine and stool in excessive amounts, and at very high levels cause the urine to have a port-wine colour.
(v) Porphyrias are genetic diseases in which activity of one of the enzymes of heme synthesis is decreased, grouped into erythropoietic and hepatic (acute or chronic) porphyrias, caused by hereditary or acquired defects in heme synthesis; when an acute attack is confirmed, urgent treatment is with an injection of human hemin, and management includes prevention of attacks by avoiding causal factors and protection of the skin from light where cutaneous manifestations occur.
questions.question:
A young adult presents with recurrent episodes of severe abdominal pain accompanied by mental confusion; the urine is noted to darken on standing.
(i) What is the diagnosis?
(ii) Which enzyme in the heme biosynthetic pathway is deficient?
(iii) What is the metabolic basis of the presentation?
(iv) What biochemical/laboratory findings would be expected?
(v) What is the genetic classification of this condition, and how is an acute attack managed?

A person exposed to a small quantity of cyanide develops acute, potentially lethal toxicity.
(i) State the diagnosis.
(ii) Explain the biochemical basis, including the site of action and why a small quantity is lethal.
questions.answerText:
(i) Acute cyanide poisoning: inhibition of electron transport at Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase).
(ii) Cyanide (like azide and carbon monoxide) binds tightly to the iron coordinated in cytochrome a3; cyanide and azide bind when the iron is ferric (Fe3+), carbon monoxide when it is ferrous (Fe2+). This blocks electron transfer to oxygen (the reduction of O2 to water).
- With the block in the presence of O2 and an electron donor, the carriers before the block become fully reduced and those after it completely oxidised.
- ATP formation (oxidative phosphorylation) is coupled to electron transfer through the proton gradient, so it stops; the toxicity of cyanide is solely from its ability to arrest electron transport.
- A small quantity is lethal because animals have relatively few molecules of cytochrome a3; carbon monoxide needs a large quantity to kill because it is toxic through its affinity for the heme iron of haemoglobin, of which animals carry many molecules.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the origin/default state of the trp operon.
A(ii) Describe the course of trp operon regulation (repressor-operator interaction).
A(iii) Describe the role of the corepressor.
A(iv) Describe the fate of transcription in the presence versus absence of tryptophan.
B(i) State the key regulatory control point of the trp operon.
C(i) Explain the biochemical consequence when this regulatory mechanism is disrupted.
questions.answerText:
A(i) By default the trp operon is on, and the genes for tryptophan synthesis (trpE, trpD, trpC, trpB, trpA) are transcribed; E. coli can synthesise the amino acid tryptophan under the control of the trp operon.
An operon is the entire stretch of DNA that includes the operator, the promoter, and the structural genes they control; the regulatory switch is a segment of DNA called the operator, usually positioned within the promoter.
A(ii) The operon can be switched off by a protein repressor, the product of a regulatory gene, which prevents transcription by binding to the operator and blocking RNA polymerase.
The repressor can be in an active or inactive form depending on the presence of other molecules; a corepressor is a molecule that cooperates with the repressor protein to switch the operon off.
A(iii) When tryptophan is present, it binds to the trp repressor protein as its corepressor, activating the repressor; the repressor is active only in the presence of its corepressor, tryptophan.
A(iv) When tryptophan is absent, the repressor is inactive and the operon is on, so RNA polymerase transcribes the genes into mRNA, which is translated into the polypeptide subunits of the tryptophan-synthesising enzymes.
When tryptophan is present, the active repressor binds the operator and no RNA is made from the structural genes, so the trp operon is repressed (turned off) when tryptophan levels are high.
B(i) The key regulatory control point is the binding of the corepressor tryptophan to the repressor protein, which determines whether the repressor can bind the operator and block RNA polymerase.
This makes the trp operon a repressible operon: it is usually on, and it is switched off by the corepressor-activated repressor.
C(i) If the repressor cannot be activated by its corepressor (regulatory binding disrupted), the operon would remain on and the tryptophan-synthesising enzymes would continue to be transcribed regardless of tryptophan availability.
Because repressible enzymes such as those of the trp operon usually function in anabolic pathways and are normally repressed by high levels of the end product, failure of this feedback repression removes the negative control that normally governs expression of the trp operon.
This illustrates negative gene regulation: the trp operon is switched off by the active form of the repressor, and any disruption of repressor-corepressor binding removes this switch, leaving the biosynthetic genes constitutively transcribed regardless of tryptophan levels.

questions.question:
An infant of Ashkenazi Jewish descent presents with progressive nervous system degeneration, mental retardation and blindness. The parents are informed the condition is usually fatal by age three to four.
(i) What is the diagnosis?
(ii) What enzyme is deficient, and what substance accumulates as a result?
(iii) Where does the accumulation particularly occur, and what is the mode of inheritance?
(iv) Why is the disease more common among Ashkenazi Jews even though it is rare in the general population?
(v) What management/preventive strategy is available for this condition?
questions.answerText:
(i) The diagnosis is Tay-Sachs disease, the best known of the sphingolipidoses (lipid storage diseases), originally described in 1881.
(ii) Tay-Sachs disease is a deficiency of the lysosomal enzyme beta-N-acetyl hexosaminidase A; the deficiency causes accumulation of the ganglioside called GM2.
(iii) The GM2 ganglioside accumulates particularly in the brain; the disease is devastating, causing nervous system degeneration, mental retardation, blindness and death, usually by the age of three or four. Most sphingolipidoses, including this one, are autosomal recessive.
(iv) Though the disease is rare in the general population, the defective gene is relatively common among Ashkenazic Jews.
(v) In its management, attention has been focused on prenatal detection; in fact, this was one of the first genetic diseases to be diagnosed in conjunction with amniocentesis. Genetic counselling can also predict and avert many inheritable diseases.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the origin (starting substrates) of heme biosynthesis.
A(ii) Describe the course of the pathway.
A(iii) Describe the regulation of the pathway.
A(iv) Describe the fate/end product of the pathway.
B(i) State the rate-limiting/regulatory step of the pathway.
C(i) Explain the biochemical basis of a disorder that results when this pathway is disrupted.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Heme synthesis begins with condensation of glycine and succinyl-CoA, with decarboxylation, to form delta-aminolevulinic acid (ALA); the reaction is catalysed by ALA synthase using pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6) as cofactor.
A(ii) One ALA condenses with another ALA to form porphobilinogen (PBG), catalysed by ALA dehydratase; four molecules of PBG condense, via hydroxymethylbilane and uroporphyrinogen III, to form the porphyrin ring.
Uroporphyrinogen III is converted to coproporphyrinogen III, transported back into the mitochondria, converted to protoporphyrin IX, and iron (Fe2+) is added by ferrochelatase to form heme.
The first and last three reactions occur in the mitochondria, the intervening steps in the cytoplasm; major sites of heme synthesis are the liver and bone marrow (erythroblasts), and mature red blood cells cannot synthesise heme as they lack mitochondria.
A(iii) Regulation occurs mainly at ALA synthase, by repression: heme acts as a corepressor, inhibiting transcription of the ALA synthase gene (feedback/end-product inhibition).
ALA synthase is also allosterically inhibited by hematin, which forms when excess free heme (without globin to bind) has its Fe2+ oxidised to Fe3+; hematin also inhibits translocation of ALA synthase into the mitochondria.
Heme synthesis is also inhibited by heavy metals (lead), which inhibit the steps catalysed by ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase; lack of vitamin B6, or drugs such as INH that reduce pyridoxal phosphate availability, can also affect heme synthesis.
A(iv) The pathway culminates in heme, the prosthetic group of haemoglobin, myoglobin, cytochromes, catalase, peroxidase and tryptophan pyrrolase.
B(i) The committed and rate-limiting step of the pathway is the ALA synthase-catalysed reaction.
C(i) Porphyrias are genetic diseases in which activity of one of the enzymes of heme synthesis is decreased, so that cells do not convert porphyrins to heme normally.
This causes accumulation of ALA and PBG and/or porphyrinogens, with a corresponding decrease in heme; spontaneous oxidation of porphyrinogens to porphyrins in skin and tissues causes photosensitivity, while accumulation of ALA and PBG produces neuropsychiatric signs and symptoms.
Symptoms vary depending on which enzyme is affected, the severity of the deficiency, and whether heme synthesis is affected primarily in the liver or in developing erythrocytes (hepatic vs erythropoietic porphyria).

A. There are three major buffering systems and a minor one. The protein buffer system: if pH climbs, the carboxyl group of an amino acid acts as a weak acid, and if pH drops, the amino group acts as a weak base. The haemoglobin buffer system: hydrogen ions are buffered by haemoglobin, preventing pH changes as PCO2 rises or falls. The carbonic acid-bicarbonate buffer system: CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3 ⇌ H+ + HCO3−; the pH is balanced by the presence of both a weak acid (H2CO3) and its conjugate base (HCO3−), so that any excess acid or base introduced is neutralised. The minor phosphate buffer system consists of dihydrogen phosphate ions (as the hydrogen ion donor/acid) and hydrogen phosphate ions (as the hydrogen ion acceptor/base).
B. The phosphate buffer operates in the internal fluid of all cells (buffers pH in the intracellular fluid, ICF). The carbonic acid-bicarbonate buffer system buffers changes caused by organic and fixed acids in the body, and it only functions when the respiratory system and control centres are working normally; the lungs help regulate pH through this buffer system by changing respiratory rate (respiratory compensation), while the kidneys help regulate pH through renal compensation by releasing H+ into urine and reabsorbing HCO3− into the blood plasma.
C. The carbonic acid-bicarbonate buffer system cannot protect the extracellular fluid from pH changes due to increased or depressed CO2 levels, and is limited by the availability of bicarbonate ions (bicarbonate reserve); failure of this buffer system to function normally results in acid-base imbalance (irregular pH) in the blood, which, because the bicarbonate ion is transported in the blood plasma to the lungs and dehydrated back into CO2 for exhalation, means that a defect in this single buffering mechanism has consequences for overall blood pH rather than being confined to one local site.
questions.question:
A. Describe the buffer systems of the body under the following headings: the protein buffer system, the haemoglobin buffer system, the carbonic acid-bicarbonate buffer system, and the phosphate buffer system.
B. State the fluid compartment or organ in which each of these buffer systems chiefly operates.
C. Explain why failure of the bicarbonate buffer system produces a distant, whole-body effect (acid-base imbalance in the blood) rather than a localised one.

A newborn is found on karyotyping to have only 45 chromosomes, with the long arm of chromosome 21 fused onto the long arm of chromosome 14.
(i) What is the diagnosis?
(ii) What predisposing chromosomal mechanism underlies this presentation?
(iii) What is the pathophysiological basis of the karyotype described, and why are carriers usually unaffected?
questions.answerText:
(i) The diagnosis is Down syndrome, which in a minority of cases (5% or less) is caused by a Robertsonian translocation of the chromosome 21 long arm onto the long arm of chromosome 14.
(ii) Carriers of Robertsonian translocations involving chromosome 21 have a higher chance of having a child with Down syndrome; a Robertsonian translocation involves two acrocentric chromosomes fusing near the centromere region with loss of the short arms, forming a metacentric chromosome.
(iii) The resulting karyotype leaves only 45 chromosomes in the carrier, since two chromosomes have fused; this has no direct effect on phenotype in the carrier because the only genes on the short arms of acrocentric chromosomes are common to all of them and present in variable copy number, so carriers of Robertsonian translocations are not themselves associated with phenotypic abnormalities, though there is a risk of unbalanced gametes leading to miscarriage or abnormal offspring such as a child with Down syndrome.

questions.question:
A. Describe the cell-surface hormone receptors under the following headings:
A(i) domains and structural variants;
A(ii) second messenger systems and the hormones that use each.
B. B(i) Explain the biochemical basis of pseudohypoparathyroidism, including the resistance to several hormones.
C. C(i) Distinguish between hormones acting through intracellular receptors (Group I) and through cell-surface receptors (Group II).
questions.answerText:
A(i) Cell-surface receptors are integral membrane proteins with three domains: extracellular (ligand-binding), transmembrane (hydrophobic stretches anchoring the receptor in the bilayer) and cytoplasmic (the effector region, interacting with other molecules to generate second messengers).
- Variants: simple single-pass receptors (many growth factor receptors); multi-subunit receptors such as the insulin receptor (alpha2beta2 heterotetramer linked by disulfide bonds; extracellular alpha subunit binds insulin, beta subunit has a tyrosine kinase domain, as do IGF-I and EGF receptors); seven-pass receptors (beta-adrenergic).
- Receptors may interact with other membrane proteins and cluster after hormone binding.
A(ii) The hormone is the first messenger; binding generates second messengers (signal transduction). cAMP: epinephrine, norepinephrine, glucagon, LH, FSH, TSH, calcitonin, PTH, ADH, ACTH, CRH, somatostatin.
- Ca2+/phosphoinositides: gastrin, cholecystokinin, angiotensin II, vasopressin, GnRH, oxytocin, TRH, substance P; cGMP: atrial natriuretic factor, nitric oxide; kinase or phosphatase cascades: insulin, growth hormone, prolactin, IGFs, EGF, erythropoietin.
B(i) Pseudohypoparathyroidism is PTH-resistant hypoparathyroidism due to a defect in the PTH receptor-adenylate cyclase complex (a mutation in the Gs-alpha subunit); PTH acts through the cAMP second messenger.
- Patients are also resistant to TSH, glucagon and gonadotropins, which likewise signal through cAMP.
C(i) Group I (steroids, iodothyronines, calcitriol, retinoids): lipophilic, carried by transport proteins, long half-life (hours to days), intracellular receptor, and the receptor-hormone complex is the mediator.
- Group II (peptides, proteins, catecholamines): hydrophilic, no transport proteins, short half-life (minutes), plasma-membrane receptor; mediators are cAMP, cGMP, Ca2+, phosphoinositides and kinase cascades.
- Group I mechanism: steroids diffuse across the membrane (thyroid hormone by facilitated diffusion) and bind receptors that act as ligand-dependent transcription factors.
- These receptors have an amino-terminus, a DNA-binding domain and a carboxy-terminal ligand-binding domain, plus a nuclear localisation sequence and a dimerisation domain.
- The hormone-receptor dimer binds hormone response elements in DNA and modulates gene expression, whereas Group II signals act at the membrane through second messengers.

courses.title: Immunology

questions.question: Which proteolytic enzyme generates two Fab fragments and one Fc fragment?
questions.explanation: Papain digestion cleaves immunoglobulin molecules at the hinge region, producing two identical antigen-binding fragments (Fab) and one crystallizable fragment (Fc). The Fab fragments retain antigen-binding capability while the Fc fragment mediates effector functions. This enzymatic cleavage provided crucial insights into immunoglobulin structure and function.

questions.question: How do tumor antigen-specific CTLs eliminate tumor cells?
questions.explanation: Tumor antigen-specific cytotoxic T lymphocytes directly lyse tumor cells through cell-mediated cytotoxicity mechanisms. CTLs recognize tumor antigens presented on MHC class I molecules and release cytotoxic granules. This direct killing mechanism is a primary defense against malignant cells.

Specificity arises from complementary three-dimensional structures between epitopes and paratopes, allowing precise molecular recognition. The unique arrangement of amino acids in CDRs creates binding sites complementary to specific epitopes. This lock-and-key fit underlies the exquisite specificity that enables antibodies to distinguish closely related antigens.
questions.question: What determines the specificity of antigen-antibody interactions?

questions.explanation: Counter immunoelectrophoresis detects antibodies against specific antigens, including applications like detecting hepatitis B antibodies or antibodies in systemic lupus erythematosus. The technique's speed advantage over passive diffusion makes it useful for certain diagnostic applications. However, it has largely been replaced by more sensitive modern methods.
questions.question: What can counter immunoelectrophoresis detect?
Which immunoglobulin exists only in membrane-bound form?
questions.explanation: IgD exists predominantly in membrane-bound form on naive B cells, with negligible serum concentrations. Its primary role is as a B cell antigen receptor rather than a secreted antibody. The membrane form differs from potential secreted forms through alternative RNA splicing that determines the C-terminal sequence.

IgG is the predominant antibody in secondary immune responses, appearing after the initial IgM response to provide long-term immunity. It constitutes approximately 75% of total circulating immunoglobulins. IgG's longer half-life of about three weeks ensures sustained antibody-mediated protection.
questions.question: What is the predominant immunoglobulin in secondary immune responses?

questions.explanation: Although immune responses against cancer develop during malignancy, they are often insufficient to prevent tumor cell growth. Tumors employ multiple escape mechanisms that undermine immune effectiveness. Cancer immunotherapy aims to augment these inadequate natural responses to therapeutic levels.
options: They are insufficient to prevent growth
questions.question: Why are natural anti-tumor immune responses often insufficient?

questions.explanation: IL-4 and IL-13 are critical cytokines that drive B cell class switching to IgE production in Type I hypersensitivity. These cytokines are primarily secreted by TH2 cells during allergen sensitization. The CD40:CD40L interaction is also essential for activating AICD enzyme in B cells for isotype switching.
questions.question: Which cytokines are essential for B cell isotype switching to IgE production?

questions.explanation: Secondary lymphoid organs are sites where immune cells encounter antigens and initiate adaptive immune responses against pathogens. These organs provide optimal microenvironments for lymphocyte-antigen interactions and cellular activation. Their architecture facilitates efficient immune surveillance and response generation.
questions.question: Secondary lymphoid organs primarily function as sites where what occurs?

questions.explanation: Tumor suppressor genes function primarily to restrain cell growth and maintain controlled cellular proliferation. When these genes lose function through mutation or deletion, regulation of cell growth is lost. This results in unrestricted cell proliferation, contributing significantly to cancer development.
questions.question: What is the primary function of tumor suppressor genes?

questions.explanation: IFN-α, IFN-β, and IFN-γ are all used in cancer cytokine therapy, either individually or in combination. Each interferon type provides distinct but overlapping immunostimulatory effects against tumors. Their use represents an important component of cancer immunotherapy approaches.
questions.question: Which interferons are used in cancer cytokine therapy?
How are cancer cell differences recognized by immunity?
questions.explanation: Mutational events, translocations, and genetic abnormalities within cancer cells are distinguished as 'alter-self' rather than completely foreign. These subtle differences between tumor and normal cells can trigger immune responses. However, the alter-self nature makes recognition more challenging than foreign pathogen recognition.

questions.question: What technique uses radial immunodiffusion for complement estimation?
questions.explanation: Single radial immunodiffusion (Mancini technique) is used for laboratory estimation of complement factors through precipitation rings. This quantitative immunological method measures protein concentration. Ring diameter correlates with antigen concentration.

questions.question: What characterizes tumor growth compared to normal tissue?
questions.explanation: Tumor growth exceeds that of normal tissue and is uncoordinated with body needs. The growth persists excessively even after cessation of the initial stimulus. This autonomous, unregulated proliferation distinguishes malignant from reactive processes.

questions.question: The bone marrow serves as the maturation site for which cell types?
questions.explanation: Bone marrow is specifically identified as the maturation site for B cells, monocytes, dendritic cells, and granulocytes. These cells complete their development in the marrow before entering circulation. T cells, by contrast, migrate to the thymus for maturation.

questions.question: How many constant domains do IgM and IgE heavy chains contain?
questions.explanation: IgM and IgE heavy chains possess four constant domains (CH1, CH2, CH3, CH4) but lack a hinge region. This contrasts with IgG, IgA, and IgD, which have three constant domains and a hinge region. The additional constant domain in IgM and IgE contributes to their larger molecular size and distinct structural properties.

Membrane-bound and soluble regulatory proteins exist to protect host cells from unintended complement-mediated lysis and tissue damage. Without regulation, complement would attack self-tissues. Pathogens lack these protective regulators.
questions.question: Why do regulatory proteins exist in complement?
What prevents neutrophils from engulfing basement membrane in Goodpasture's syndrome?
questions.explanation: Unlike microbes, the glomerular basement membrane is a fixed tissue structure that cannot be engulfed by neutrophils.
