questions.explanation: Atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis typically occurs at the vessel ostia in older patients with vascular risk factors such as smoking and hypertension, and is the most common cause of renal artery stenosis overall. Fibromuscular dysplasia instead typically affects younger women with mid or distal vessel involvement. Recognising the cause guides appropriate risk factor management.

questions.question: A patient with chronic pancreatitis undergoes cross-sectional imaging showing ductal dilation, parenchymal calcification, and gland atrophy together. This combination of findings is considered highly specific for which diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The triad of ductal dilation, parenchymal calcification, and glandular atrophy on imaging is highly specific for chronic pancreatitis, reflecting longstanding fibrosis and recurrent injury to the gland. Acute oedematous pancreatitis, in contrast, typically shows glandular swelling without calcification or atrophy, reflecting a single acute inflammatory episode rather than chronic structural damage. Recognising this imaging triad supports a confident diagnosis of chronic rather than acute disease.

PCOS causes hyperandrogenism through excess ovarian androgen production (testosterone, androstenedione, DHEAS), which stimulates sebaceous gland hyperplasia and sebum overproduction. This, combined with follicular hyperkeratosis and P. acnes (C. acnes) colonisation, drives acne in women with PCOS. Anti-androgen therapies (cyproterone acetate, spironolactone) and combined oral contraceptives are effective in this context.
options: Elevated oestrogen levels directly stimulating sebaceous glands
Elevated cortisol from chronic stress activating sebocytes
Hyperandrogenism from excess ovarian androgen production stimulating sebaceous glands
Elevated prolactin directly stimulating P. acnes
Reduced FSH levels causing follicular maturation arrest
questions.question: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) contributes to acne in women through which primary hormonal mechanism?

questions.explanation: SARS-CoV-2 possesses a lipid envelope that is readily disrupted by soap, which dissolves the lipid membrane and inactivates the virus, explaining why handwashing with soap is highly effective against enveloped viruses like coronaviruses. Non-enveloped viruses are generally more resistant to this mechanism. This structural vulnerability underpinned key public health hygiene messaging during the pandemic.
options: Exclusive transmission through airborne particles only
Its lipid envelope, which soap readily disrupts
Complete absence of any outer membrane
A rigid cell wall similar to bacteria
A thick protective protein coat resistant to soap
questions.question: During the COVID-19 pandemic, hand hygiene with soap was emphasised as highly effective disinfection. This effectiveness relates to which structural feature of SARS-CoV-2?
Liver cirrhosis links both hepatitis B and C to hepatocellular carcinoma risk. Which additional carcinogenic mechanism is recognised as unique to hepatitis B but absent in hepatitis C?
questions.explanation: Hepatitis B virus DNA can integrate directly into the host hepatocyte genome, potentially causing oncogenic mutations even in the absence of cirrhosis, a mechanism not shared by hepatitis C virus, which is an RNA virus lacking this integration capability. This explains why HCC can occasionally arise in HBV-infected patients without cirrhosis. Hepatitis C-related HCC, by contrast, almost always occurs in the setting of established cirrhosis.
options: Direct viral DNA integration into host DNA

questions.explanation: Adenocarcinoma is the most common lung cancer subtype (~40% of cases), typically peripheral in origin, arising from Clara cells or type II alveolar cells. It may not cause symptoms until extrathoracic metastases have developed due to its peripheral location. Histologically it shows glandular formation. It is increasingly common in non-smokers, particularly women, and shows EGFR mutations.
questions.question: Adenocarcinoma of the lung is MOST accurately described as:
options: Peripheral tumour, 40% of lung cancers, glandular histology
Central tumour arising from bronchial mucosa near the hilum
Associated with cavitation in a proximal bronchus
Predominantly affecting central bronchi with sputum cytology positivity
Characterised by keratin pearls on histology

questions.explanation: Peptide and protein hormones are generally hydrophilic and cannot cross the cell membrane, so they bind cell surface receptors and activate intracellular second messenger cascades to exert their effects. This contrasts with steroid hormones, which are lipophilic and act on intracellular or nuclear receptors after crossing the cell membrane directly. Understanding this distinction explains differences in hormone onset and duration of action.
questions.question: A patient's peptide hormone binds to a cell surface receptor, triggering an intracellular signalling cascade rather than entering the nucleus directly. This is characteristic of which hormone class mechanism?
options: Thyroid hormone acting via direct DNA binding
Peptide and protein hormones acting via second messenger systems
Vitamin D acting via cell surface ion channels exclusively
Steroid hormones acting via intracellular nuclear receptors
Catecholamines acting via intracellular gene transcription only

questions.explanation: Comprehensive Type 2 DM management includes: continuous diabetes education, lifestyle modification (dietary changes, physical exercise, weight loss), pharmacotherapy starting with metformin and escalating as needed, blood pressure and lipid management, and regular screening for complications. While some patients may never require insulin, others will need it as beta cell function declines. Cardiovascular risk factor management is equally important as glycaemic control.
questions.question: Which statement about Type 2 DM management is CORRECT?
options: All Type 2 DM patients require insulin from diagnosis
Lifestyle modification is ineffective in Type 2 DM
Type 2 DM never requires insulin therapy
BP and lipid management is not relevant in Type 2 DM
Management includes diabetes education, lifestyle changes, and stepwise pharmacotherapy
Increased peripheral resistance raising diastolic pressure
Diastolic backflow with raised stroke volume
Reduced stroke volume lowering systolic pressure
questions.explanation: In aortic regurgitation, blood regurgitates from the aorta into the left ventricle during diastole, dropping diastolic pressure, while a compensatory increase in stroke volume raises systolic pressure. This combination produces the wide pulse pressure and collapsing (water-hammer) pulse. It is a classic peripheral sign of significant regurgitant flow.
questions.question: A patient with aortic regurgitation has a wide pulse pressure and a bounding, collapsing peripheral pulse. This haemodynamic pattern occurs because:

questions.explanation: A hepatic bruit on auscultation over the liver is a highly characteristic finding of hepatocellular carcinoma due to the hypervascular nature of the tumour. While not universally present, when heard, it is almost pathognomonic and should prompt urgent investigation for HCC.
questions.question: In HCC, which finding on physical examination is almost pathognomonic and distinguishes it from simple hepatomegaly?
Lupus pernio in sarcoidosis is a SPECIFIC cutaneous manifestation. Where does it characteristically occur and what does it represent histologically?
questions.explanation: Lupus pernio is a specific dermatological manifestation of sarcoidosis appearing as raised, indurated, violet-purple plaques on the cheeks, nose, ears, and lips. It represents granulomatous infiltration of the dermis and is associated with chronic sarcoidosis, indicating systemic involvement including pulmonary fibrosis and bone involvement. It differs from erythema nodosum which is a reactive phenomenon.
options: Cheeks and nose; purple granulomatous lesions

questions.question: Which organism is the MOST common cause of community-acquired bacterial meningitis in adults worldwide?
questions.explanation: STREPTOCOCCUS PNEUMONIAE (pneumococcus) is the most common cause of adult community-acquired bacterial meningitis, accounting for ~50% of cases. It has the highest mortality and morbidity including hearing loss and cognitive impairment. Neisseria meningitidis is second in young adults. H. influenzae has been dramatically reduced by Hib vaccination.

Ingestion of Entamoeba histolytica cysts leads to amoebic liver abscess, not pyogenic abscess. Pyogenic liver abscesses arise from bacterial spread via the portal vein (appendicitis, diverticulitis), biliary system (cholangitis, cholecystitis), arterial route, or direct extension from adjacent structures.
questions.question: Sources of pyogenic liver abscess include all of the following EXCEPT:
In the management of acute pancreatitis, early aggressive IV fluid resuscitation (within the first 24-48 hours) aims PRIMARILY to:
questions.explanation: Early aggressive IV fluid resuscitation in acute pancreatitis (typically Ringer's lactate solution preferred over normal saline) aims to restore intravascular volume, maintain haemodynamic stability, and ensure adequate renal and splanchnic perfusion to prevent acute kidney injury and pancreatic necrosis. Significant fluid sequestration into the retroperitoneum and gut (third-spacing) occurs in severe pancreatitis, necessitating large volume replacement.
options: Prevent renal failure by maintaining renal perfusion and replacing third-space losses
Reduce serum amylase to diagnostic levels
Dissolve pancreatic calculi with alkaline fluids

questions.explanation: Aflatoxin B1, produced by Aspergillus flavus contaminating stored grains and nuts, is a potent hepatocarcinogen that synergises with chronic hepatitis B infection to significantly increase hepatocellular carcinoma risk in endemic regions. Other mycotoxins listed have different, less directly hepatocarcinogenic profiles. Public health measures to reduce food contamination help lower this cancer risk.
questions.question: A patient in a region with high dietary exposure to a mycotoxin produced by Aspergillus flavus has increased risk of hepatocellular carcinoma. This mycotoxin is:

questions.explanation: Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) is the most common chromosomal abnormality associated with congenital heart disease, with 50% of Down syndrome patients having a CHD. Common lesions include AV canal defects (AVSD), VSD, ASD, and others. About 8% of all CHD cases are primarily due to chromosomal factors. Trisomy 18 has CHD in 80% and Trisomy 13 in 40%, but both are less prevalent than Down syndrome.
questions.question: The most common chromosomal abnormality associated with CHD is:

options: Polymicrobial with E. coli, Klebsiella, and Streptococcus
questions.question: Pyogenic liver abscesses are most commonly caused by which microbiological pattern?
questions.explanation: Most pyogenic liver abscesses are polymicrobial, reflecting their origin from abdominal sources (e.g., appendicitis, cholangitis). The most frequently isolated organisms are Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Proteus, Pseudomonas, and Streptococcus species in various combinations.

Ziehl-Neelsen staining identifies acid-fast bacilli, characteristic of Mycobacterium tuberculosis, which resist decolourisation due to their waxy mycolic acid cell wall, making this the classic rapid screening test for suspected pulmonary tuberculosis in a patient with this clinical and radiological picture. Gram staining is instead used to differentiate typical bacterial pathogens, not mycobacteria. Culture and nucleic acid amplification tests are used to confirm and further characterise the organism after initial smear positivity.
options: Viral inclusion bodies suggestive of influenza
questions.question: A patient presents with a two-week history of cough, night sweats, and weight loss. Chest X-ray shows upper lobe cavitation. Sputum is sent for Ziehl-Neelsen staining. What is this test MOST specifically designed to detect?

questions.explanation: Polycystic ovary syndrome causes acne through excess ovarian (and sometimes adrenal) androgen production, which stimulates sebaceous gland activity and follicular hyperkeratinisation in a manner similar to other androgen-driven acne. Recognising this hormonal driver is important because it may prompt investigation for PCOS in women with acne accompanied by menstrual irregularity or hirsutism. Cortisol and thyroid hormone changes are not the primary mechanism in this classic association.
questions.question: A woman with acne, irregular menstrual cycles, and evidence of hyperandrogenism on investigation is diagnosed with a common endocrine condition contributing to her skin disease. Which hormonal mechanism links this condition to acne?
options: Excess ovarian androgen production stimulating sebaceous glands

questions.question: Mineralocorticoid excess (primary hyperaldosteronism) characteristically causes:
questions.explanation: Primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn's syndrome) causes hypertension without oedema, with hypokalaemia. Aldosterone excess stimulates renal sodium retention (raising BP) and potassium excretion (causing hypokalaemia). Despite sodium retention, oedema does not develop because of an 'escape phenomenon' where increased renal pressure eventually limits sodium retention. This distinguishes it from secondary hyperaldosteronism (e.g., heart failure) where oedema is prominent.

questions.question: An ECG in an elderly patient shows complete dissociation between P waves and QRS complexes with a slow, regular ventricular escape rhythm. This finding indicates:
questions.explanation: Complete AV block features total dissociation between atrial and ventricular activity, with the ventricles driven by an independent, usually slow, escape rhythm. This often requires pacemaker insertion, especially if symptomatic. Lesser degrees of block show partial or intermittent conduction rather than complete dissociation.

questions.question: A 22-year-old tall, thin male presents with sudden pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness. Chest X-ray shows a visible lung edge with absent lung markings peripheral to it. What is the MOST likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A tall, thin young male with sudden pleuritic pain and a visible lung edge with absent peripheral markings on chest X-ray is the classic presentation of primary spontaneous pneumothorax, typically due to rupture of a subpleural bleb in an otherwise healthy lung. Tension pneumothorax specifically requires additional signs of mediastinal shift and haemodynamic compromise, not simply described here. Recognising typical demographic and radiological features helps distinguish this from other acute chest presentations.

questions.question: A 9-year-old presents two weeks after a sore throat with migratory polyarthritis, a new pansystolic murmur, and involuntary jerky movements. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: The combination of migratory polyarthritis, new-onset carditis (murmur), and chorea following a preceding streptococcal pharyngitis is classic for acute rheumatic fever, meeting Jones criteria. It results from an autoimmune cross-reaction to group A streptococcal antigens. Early recognition allows secondary prophylaxis to prevent recurrent carditis.

questions.question: A patient develops symptomatic bradycardia with hypotension after a myocardial infarction. The first-line pharmacological treatment is:
questions.explanation: Atropine is the first-line drug for symptomatic bradycardia with haemodynamic instability, acting by blocking vagal tone to increase heart rate. If ineffective, transcutaneous pacing or inotropic support may be required. Adenosine and verapamil are used for tachyarrhythmias, not bradycardia.

options: Inferior vena cava filter placement alone
questions.explanation: Massive pulmonary embolism causing haemodynamic collapse or cardiac arrest is an indication for emergency thrombolytic therapy, aiming to rapidly dissolve the obstructing clot and restore pulmonary blood flow, given the otherwise very high mortality risk of this presentation if treated with anticoagulation alone, which does not actively dissolve existing clot burden. Inferior vena cava filters prevent further embolisation but do not address the existing life-threatening clot. Recognising massive PE with haemodynamic instability as a thrombolysis indication, distinct from stable submassive or low-risk PE, is critical for appropriately urgent management.
questions.question: A patient with a massive pulmonary embolism presents with cardiac arrest due to obstructive shock. Which treatment is MOST appropriate as an emergency intervention in this haemodynamically catastrophic presentation?

questions.explanation: Carbimazole (and its active metabolite methimazole, and propylthiouracil—PTU) belongs to the thionamide class of antithyroid drugs. They inhibit thyroid peroxidase (TPO), the enzyme responsible for oxidising iodide and coupling iodinated tyrosines to form T4 and T3. PTU additionally inhibits peripheral conversion of T4 to T3. These drugs do not destroy thyroid tissue or block release of preformed hormone; hence, clinical effect is delayed until stored hormone is depleted (usually 4–6 weeks).
options: Inhibiting thyroid peroxidase, preventing thyroid hormone synthesis
Blocking TSH receptors on thyroid cells
Blocking thyroid hormone release from follicles
Blocking peripheral conversion of T4 to T3 only
questions.question: A patient is prescribed carbimazole for Graves' thyrotoxicosis. The mechanism of action of carbimazole is:
A patient with suspected cholecystitis has Murphy's sign positive on palpation. A succussion splash is also elicited. What does the succussion splash SPECIFICALLY indicate?
questions.explanation: A positive succussion splash (fluid sloshing sound when the patient is shaken) indicates retained gastric content ? a specific sign of gastric outlet obstruction. Murphy's sign is positive in cholecystitis. Ascites is detected by shifting dullness and fluid thrill, not succussion splash, which requires an air-fluid interface in the stomach.

options: Glycopeptide antibiotics alone as sole therapy
Beta-lactam antibiotics alone as sole therapy
questions.explanation: Legionella species are intracellular organisms that lack a typical bacterial cell wall targeted by beta-lactam antibiotics, so effective treatment requires antibiotics with good intracellular penetration such as macrolides (for example, azithromycin) or fluoroquinolones (for example, levofloxacin), which are the recommended first-line agents. Beta-lactams alone would be ineffective against this organism despite their utility against typical pneumococcal pneumonia. Recognising the atypical, intracellular nature of Legionella is essential for selecting appropriate empirical or targeted antibiotic therapy when this pathogen is suspected or confirmed.
questions.question: A patient with severe community-acquired pneumonia due to Legionella is being treated. Which antibiotic class is MOST appropriate given the intracellular nature of this organism?

questions.explanation: Both licensed meningococcal vaccines protect against serogroups A, C, Y, and W-135 but crucially provide no immunity against serogroup B, which causes approximately one-third of meningococcal meningitis cases. The difficulty in developing serogroup B vaccine relates to molecular mimicry between group B capsular polysaccharide and human neural tissue.
questions.question: Current licensed meningococcal vaccines provide immunity against serogroups A, C, Y, and W-135 but NOT against which serogroup responsible for approximately one-third of meningococcal cases?

questions.explanation: Aspergillus flavus, a common mould contaminating stored groundnuts and grains in tropical regions, produces aflatoxin B1, a potent hepatocarcinogen. Repeated dietary exposure to aflatoxin B1 causes p53 mutations and is a major cause of hepatocellular carcinoma in sub-Saharan Africa.
questions.question: Aflatoxin B1 produced by which fungal species is a major risk factor for hepatocellular carcinoma?
Endomyocardial fibrosis (EMF) is classified as which type of cardiomyopathy?
questions.explanation: Endomyocardial fibrosis (EMF) is the most common form of restrictive cardiomyopathy in sub-Saharan Africa and tropical regions. It is characterised by fibrosis of the endocardium and subendocardial myocardium, particularly affecting the apices of both ventricles, obliterating the ventricular cavity. It restricts filling without dilating the ventricle. Its aetiology is unclear but may be related to hypereosinophilia.

questions.question: The FIRST-LINE treatment for Stage 1 hypertension without compelling indications is:
options: Lifestyle modification with consideration of pharmacotherapy
Immediate ACE inhibitor at maximum dose
Diuretic therapy only, never lifestyle modification
questions.explanation: For Stage 1 hypertension, lifestyle modification (DASH diet, sodium restriction, weight loss, physical activity, limiting alcohol) is the cornerstone of initial management and may suffice for some patients. Pharmacotherapy is added if BP remains uncontrolled after 3–6 months of lifestyle measures or if cardiovascular risk is high. ACE inhibitors, ARBs, calcium channel blockers, and thiazide diuretics are all evidence-based first-line options.

Tiotropium is a long-acting muscarinic antagonist (LAMA) that blocks M3 receptors in airway smooth muscle, reducing bronchoconstriction and mucus secretion. Unlike ipratropium (short-acting), tiotropium is given once daily. In COPD management, LAMAs are first-line bronchodilators for maintenance therapy. They reduce exacerbation frequency and improve quality of life.
questions.question: Tiotropium (Spiriva) is classified as which type of bronchodilator used in COPD management?

questions.explanation: Huntington's disease, which causes chorea, is classified as a hyperkinetic movement disorder—characterised by excessive, involuntary movements. Parkinsonian syndromes (Parkinson's, PSP, MSA, CBD) are hypokinetic disorders characterised by poverty of movement and bradykinesia.
questions.question: Which of the following neurological conditions is classified as a hyperkinetic movement disorder?

questions.explanation: A doughy abdominal texture on palpation is a classic though non-specific finding associated with tuberculous peritonitis, resulting from thickened peritoneum and low-grade chronic inflammatory exudate. It differs from the acute rigidity of peritonitis from perforation. Recognising this sign in an appropriate clinical context should prompt investigation for tuberculosis.
questions.question: A patient's abdomen on palpation feels unusually firm with a 'doughy' quality without clear rebound tenderness. This finding should raise suspicion for:

In hepatocellular carcinoma, the combination of HBV and HCV accounts for approximately 80% of cases. Which additional carcinogen from food contamination plays an important aetiological role in sub-Saharan Africa?
questions.explanation: Viral hepatitis (HBV and HCV combined) accounts for approximately 80% of HCC worldwide. Aflatoxin B1, produced by Aspergillus flavus contaminating mouldy groundnuts and grains, is the most potent hepatocarcinogen relevant in sub-Saharan Africa. Aflatoxin causes a specific p53 mutation (249 arginine substitution) characteristic of HCC in aflatoxin-exposed populations.
options: 80% of cases; Aflatoxin from mouldy food
40% of cases; Ochratoxin from spoiled beans
APACHE II score only for ICU patients
questions.explanation: RANSON'S CRITERIA (or Glasgow/modified Glasgow score) stratify acute pancreatitis severity. =3 Ranson's criteria indicate SEVERE pancreatitis with high risk of local (necrosis, pseudocyst, abscess) and systemic complications. The BISAP score is simpler (BUN, impaired mental status, SIRS, age >60, pleural effusion). CURB-65 is for pneumonia; MELD for chronic liver disease.
questions.question: A patient presents with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back with elevated serum amylase (3× normal). Which scoring system is used to stratify severity and predict complications in acute pancreatitis?

options: Excess circulating thyroid hormone affecting tissues
Autoimmune destruction of the thyroid gland
questions.question: Thyrotoxicosis is defined as the clinical syndrome resulting from:
questions.explanation: Thyrotoxicosis is the clinical syndrome resulting from exposure of body tissues to excess circulating thyroid hormone levels. It can be caused by various conditions: Graves' disease (most common—TSH receptor antibodies), toxic multinodular goitre, thyroid adenoma, thyroiditis (subacute, painless), or exogenous thyroid hormone excess. Hyperthyroidism refers specifically to excess thyroid hormone production, whereas thyrotoxicosis includes all sources of excess T3/T4.

questions.question: Among proposed triggers for sarcoidosis, which microorganisms have been most implicated in its pathogenesis?
questions.explanation: Among proposed environmental triggers for sarcoidosis, spirochetes (e.g., Propionibacterium acnes) and mycobacterial antigens (including M. tuberculosis-related peptides) have been most consistently implicated by molecular and immunological evidence. However, no single causative organism has been confirmed, and sarcoidosis remains of unknown aetiology.

options: Lumbar puncture first, then CT brain and MRI
IV antibiotics, then CT brain, then LP if safe
Wait 24 hours to see full clinical evolution and response
questions.question: A young woman presents with acute onset of left-sided weakness, headache, and fever. Which investigation sequence is MOST appropriate when both meningitis and stroke are in the differential?
questions.explanation: When both meningitis and stroke are differential diagnoses, the principle is: START IV ANTIBIOTICS IMMEDIATELY (never delay for investigations), then CT brain (to exclude mass lesion and assess for stroke), then LP if CT shows no contraindication. Antibiotics started before LP marginally affect culture sensitivity but this small loss is far outweighed by the catastrophic consequences of delayed treatment in bacterial meningitis.

Vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol) is synthesised in the Malpighian layer (comprising the stratum spinosum and stratum basalis) when 7-dehydrocholesterol is converted by UV-B radiation. This pro-vitamin is then hydroxylated in the liver and kidney to form active 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3. Melanin competitively absorbs UV, explaining reduced vitamin D synthesis in dark-skinned individuals.
questions.question: The skin's vitamin D production occurs in which specific epidermal layer under UV radiation?
Thymectomy in myasthenia gravis is most clearly beneficial in which group of patients?
options: Patients under 60 years with generalised MG and thymic hyperplasia or thymoma
All MG patients regardless of thymus status
Purely ocular MG patients under 40 years
Patients in myasthenic crisis requiring ventilation
questions.explanation: Thymectomy is most clearly beneficial in patients with generalised MG who are under 60 years of age with thymic hyperplasia (germinal centre formation) or thymoma. The thymus contains myoid cells bearing AChR, which drive the autoimmune response. Thymectomy can induce remission or significantly reduce immunosuppression requirements.

questions.question: Cryptogenic organising pneumonia (COP) is BEST described as:
questions.explanation: COP (formerly BOOP) is an interstitial lung disease characterised by organising fibrous plugs in alveolar ducts and alveoli. It presents with sub-acute flu-like illness, cough, and bilateral patchy consolidation on CT. Bronchoalveolar lavage shows mixed cellularity. Crucially, COP responds dramatically to corticosteroids (60mg prednisolone) with near-complete radiological resolution. Relapse is common on steroid withdrawal.
options: A bacterial pneumonia caused by atypical organisms
Irreversible fibrosis of the lung parenchyma
Obstructive lung disease from bronchial mucus plugging
Interstitial lung disease with alveolar fibrous plugs

questions.explanation: An apnoea-hypopnoea index above 30 events per hour is classified as severe obstructive sleep apnoea, reflecting frequent airway obstruction episodes during sleep associated with significant oxygen desaturation and increased cardiovascular risk. Mild and moderate categories correspond to lower index ranges, typically 5-15 and 15-30 respectively. This severity classification guides decisions regarding continuous positive airway pressure therapy initiation.
questions.question: A patient with obstructive sleep apnoea undergoes overnight polysomnography showing an apnoea-hypopnoea index of 35 events per hour. Which severity category does this MOST correctly represent?
A patient with fever and a target-shaped (erythema migrans) skin lesion after a tick bite in a Lyme disease-endemic area develops facial nerve palsy weeks later. Which organism causes this disease?
questions.explanation: Lyme disease is caused by the spirochaete Borrelia burgdorferi, transmitted by Ixodes tick bites, with erythema migrans being the characteristic early skin manifestation. If untreated, the infection can disseminate to cause neurological complications such as facial nerve palsy, as well as cardiac and joint involvement. Doxycycline is the treatment of choice for most stages of the disease.

options: eGFR falling below 15 ml/min without symptoms
Uraemic symptoms: pericarditis, encephalopathy, refractory fluid overload, or hyperkalaemia
Patient preference for transplant over dialysis
Rising creatinine on two consecutive measurements
questions.question: In CKD stage 5, which criterion defines the need to START renal replacement therapy URGENTLY?
questions.explanation: Urgent RRT indications include uraemic complications: pericarditis (fibrinous inflammation), encephalopathy (confusion/seizures), refractory fluid overload, and life-threatening hyperkalaemia. While planning RRT at eGFR <15 (CKD G5) is appropriate, eGFR alone rarely dictates urgent initiation. Elective initiation based on symptoms and biochemistry allows optimal preparation for the patient's chosen modality.

questions.question: Which clinical feature distinguishes Cushing's DISEASE from Cushing's SYNDROME due to adrenal adenoma?
options: Presence of striae and easy bruising
Central fat distribution in both equally
questions.explanation: Cushing's disease specifically refers to pituitary-dependent Cushing's syndrome caused by a pituitary ACTH-secreting adenoma (corticotroph adenoma). Here, ACTH is elevated, driving bilateral adrenal cortical hyperplasia. In contrast, adrenal adenoma causing Cushing's syndrome autonomously produces cortisol, suppressing ACTH (low ACTH). The clinical features of hypercortisolaemia are similar, but ACTH measurement distinguishes the source (ACTH-dependent vs. ACTH-independent).

questions.question: A patient presents with the 'five D's' of brainstem disease: dysphagia, dysarthria, diplopia, dysaesthesia, and dizziness. Which additional finding would MOST specifically confirm brainstem rather than cortical pathology?
options: Contralateral hemiplegia with upper motor neuron signs only
Homonymous visual field defect with normal motor examination
Ipsilateral cranial nerve palsy with contralateral limb weakness
questions.explanation: Ipsilateral cranial nerve palsy combined with contralateral limb (long tract) signs ? the 'crossed syndrome' ? is the hallmark of brainstem localization. This occurs because cranial nerve nuclei are ipsilateral while motor tracts cross in the pyramids. This pattern cannot be explained by a single supratentorial (cortical) lesion.

questions.question: The Jones Criteria for diagnosis of rheumatic fever include all of the following MAJOR criteria EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Fever is a MINOR criterion (not a major criterion) in the Jones Criteria for diagnosing rheumatic fever. The MAJOR criteria are: Carditis, Polyarthritis, Chorea (Sydenham's), Erythema marginatum, and Subcutaneous nodules. MINOR criteria include fever (38.2–38.9°C), arthralgia (only if polyarthritis is not present as major), elevated ESR/CRP, and prolonged PR interval. Diagnosis requires 2 major or 1 major + 2 minor criteria plus evidence of preceding streptococcal infection.

questions.question: A patient on dialysis develops uraemic pericarditis. The FIRST clinical sign to detect is:
questions.explanation: Pericardial friction rub is the earliest clinical sign of uraemic pericarditis, heard best with the patient leaning forward. It is scratchy and multi-phasic. As the effusion enlarges, the rub may disappear and tamponade signs develop (Beck's triad: hypotension, elevated JVP, muffled heart sounds). Urgent dialysis or pericardiocentesis may be required. Haemorrhagic pericardial effusion is common in uraemia.
options: Muffled heart sounds from large effusion

questions.question: In the pathophysiology of DKA, insulin deficiency leads to increased lipolysis, producing which substrates for hepatic ketogenesis?
questions.explanation: In DKA, absolute insulin deficiency disinhibits hormone-sensitive lipase in adipose tissue, causing massive lipolysis and release of free fatty acids (FFAs) into the circulation. The liver converts these FFAs via beta-oxidation to acetyl-CoA, which is then channelled into ketone body synthesis (acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate). This hepatic overproduction of ketones, combined with reduced peripheral utilisation, results in the ketonaemia and metabolic acidosis of DKA.

questions.question: A patient with spinal cord compression above a certain level develops a spastic bladder with urgency, while lesions below this level cause a flaccid, retentive bladder. This distinction is primarily determined by involvement relative to which level?
options: The peripheral pudendal nerve only, unrelated to cord level
questions.explanation: Spinal cord lesions above the sacral micturition centre typically produce a spastic, hyperreflexic bladder with urgency, while lesions at or below this level, including the conus medullaris or cauda equina, produce a flaccid, areflexic bladder with retention. This distinction guides both diagnostic localisation and appropriate bladder management strategy. Careful assessment of the level of injury informs expected sphincteric dysfunction pattern.

questions.question: Sphincteric dysfunction in spinal cord disease — lesions above which spinal level cause spastic bladder (urgency) versus flaccid bladder (retention) below?
questions.explanation: Lesions above the conus medullaris (S2–S4) cause spastic bladder (detrusor hyperreflexia)—urgency, frequency, and incontinence—due to loss of supraspinal inhibition. Conus or cauda equina lesions (S2–S4) cause flaccid bladder (overflow incontinence, retention) due to lower motor neuron damage to the sacral micturition reflex arc.

questions.question: A patient has adequate circulating insulin levels but persistent hyperglycaemia due to defective receptor signalling in target tissues. This mechanism of endocrine disease is best described as:
questions.explanation: When hormone levels are adequate but tissues fail to respond appropriately, this reflects target tissue resistance, exemplified by insulin resistance in type 2 diabetes. This differs mechanistically from deficiency states where hormone production itself is inadequate. Distinguishing resistance from deficiency guides different therapeutic strategies.
options: Excess hormone-binding protein reducing free hormone
Ectopic hormone production by a tumour
Short bones of hands and feet; lacy/trabecular pattern
questions.question: In sarcoidosis, bone involvement (2% of cases) most commonly affects which part of the skeleton?
questions.explanation: When sarcoidosis involves bone, it most characteristically affects the SHORT BONES of the hands and feet (phalanges), producing lacy trabecular pattern or 'donut' (ring) lesions representing granulomatous infiltration with surrounding sclerosis ? called osseous sarcoidosis or sarcoid dactylitis. Patients may have associated skin involvement (lupus pernio) and systemic disease.

questions.question: Tobacco smoking is responsible for approximately what percentage of lung cancer cases?
questions.explanation: Active tobacco smoking is responsible for approximately 90% of all lung cancer cases (78% in men, 90% in women). Tobacco smoke contains more than 300 harmful substances with at least 40 known potent carcinogens. The remaining cases are attributed to passive smoking (25% of non-smokers' lung cancers), occupational exposures, radon, and other environmental factors.

options: Tinea capitis caused by Microsporum species
questions.question: A Woods lamp examination would be MOST useful in confirming which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation: The Woods lamp emits UV light and causes certain Microsporum species (e.g., M. audouinii, M. canis) causing tinea capitis to fluoresce a characteristic green-yellow colour. It is also useful for identifying erythrasma, vitiligo, and porphyria. Trichophyton species do not fluoresce, limiting its utility for all tinea capitis cases.

questions.question: The rate of fingernail growth is approximately:
questions.explanation: Fingernails grow at approximately 0.1 mm/day, equating to about 3 mm/month. Toenails grow approximately three times more slowly (1 mm/month), necessitating longer antifungal treatment courses for toenail onychomycosis. Growth rate is affected by age, season, dominant hand, nutritional status, and systemic disease, making it a useful indirect marker of general health.

Vitamin B12 deficiency damages the posterior columns and lateral corticospinal tracts, producing combined loss of proprioception and vibration with spastic weakness, while sparing the pain and temperature carried in the spinothalamic tract. This dissociation distinguishes it from anterior spinal artery syndrome, which spares posterior columns. Early recognition and B12 replacement can prevent irreversible cord damage.
questions.question: A patient with pernicious anaemia develops bilateral loss of vibration and proprioception with spastic weakness but preserved pain and temperature sensation. Which condition is MOST likely?
options: Subacute combined degeneration of the cord

questions.explanation: In primary adrenal insufficiency, loss of negative feedback leads to markedly elevated ACTH, a precursor of melanocyte-stimulating hormone, which stimulates melanocytes and causes hyperpigmentation, particularly in sun-exposed areas, scars, and mucous membranes. This distinguishes primary from secondary adrenal insufficiency, where ACTH is low and pigmentation does not occur. It is a useful clinical clue at the bedside.
questions.question: A patient with Addison's disease is noted to have darkening of skin creases and buccal mucosa. This hyperpigmentation results from:
options: Elevated ACTH cross-reacting with melanocyte-stimulating receptors
Direct effect of low cortisol on melanocytes

questions.explanation: Dapsone can precipitate severe haemolytic anaemia in patients with G6PD deficiency due to oxidative stress on red blood cells lacking adequate protective enzyme activity, presenting with pallor, jaundice, and dark urine. Screening for G6PD deficiency before starting dapsone, where feasible, helps anticipate and mitigate this risk. Aplastic anaemia and immune thrombocytopenia are recognised but distinct haematological reactions, less specifically linked to the G6PD mechanism.
questions.question: A patient with G6PD deficiency is started on dapsone as part of multidrug therapy for leprosy and subsequently develops severe dark urine and pallor. Which haematological complication has most likely occurred?

questions.explanation: WHO classifies lepromatous (LL), borderline lepromatous (BL), and borderline (BB) leprosy as multibacillary (MB), reflecting high bacterial load. Tuberculoid (TT) and borderline tuberculoid (BT) are paucibacillary (PB). The distinction is crucial for determining MDT duration: MB requires 12 months, PB only 6 months.
questions.question: In the WHO classification of leprosy, which types are classified as multibacillary (MB)?

questions.explanation: For patients with severe, treatment-resistant obesity, bariatric surgery is considered the only intervention capable of producing substantial, sustained long-term weight loss, along with durable improvement in obesity-related comorbidities such as diabetes and hypertension. Non-surgical measures such as diet, exercise, and pharmacotherapy typically produce more modest and less durable weight loss in this severity category. This is why surgical referral is considered once conservative measures have failed in appropriately selected patients.
questions.question: A patient with morbid obesity and a BMI of 45 kg per square metre has failed multiple supervised dietary and pharmacological weight loss attempts. Which intervention is considered the only therapeutic modality offering sustained long-term weight loss in this group?
Mononeuritis multiplex in sarcoidosis involves which pattern of neural damage that distinguishes it from symmetric peripheral neuropathy?
options: Painful, asymmetric damage to multiple separate nerves
Proximal muscle weakness without sensory loss
questions.explanation: Mononeuritis multiplex (peripheral nervous system sarcoidosis, 5% of cases) causes painful, ASYMMETRICAL, ASYNCHRONOUS sensory AND motor neuropathy involving at least 2 separate peripheral nerve territories simultaneously. This multi-focal pattern distinguishes it from symmetric peripheral neuropathy. Causes include sarcoidosis, vasculitis, diabetes, leprosy, and HIV.

HBV DNA integrates into the host hepatocyte genome, potentially disrupting tumour suppressor genes and activating oncogenes directly—a carcinogenic mechanism independent of cirrhosis. HCV, being an RNA virus, does not integrate into host DNA; it causes HCC primarily through cirrhosis-mediated chronic inflammation.
questions.question: Liver cirrhosis is the most important risk factor linking Hepatitis B and C to HCC. Which additional risk factor is unique to HBV (absent for HCV)?
options: Integration of viral DNA into host hepatocyte genome
Perinatal transmission with prolonged viral carriage

questions.explanation: Irritant contact dermatitis is a non-immunological toxic reaction that will occur in anyone (regardless of prior exposure) if the concentration or duration of the irritant exceeds the threshold for that individual's skin. There is no requirement for prior sensitisation or immunological memory. Patch testing is negative as it does not depend on T-cell sensitisation.
options: Spreads beyond the contact area in sensitised individuals
Occurs in ALL individuals above a threshold concentration of the irritant
questions.question: Irritant contact dermatitis is distinct from allergic contact dermatitis in that it:
HIV destroys CD4+ T cells progressively. The asymptomatic period between initial infection and AIDS development averages approximately how long?
questions.explanation: The average asymptomatic period between initial HIV infection and development of AIDS (defining opportunistic infections or CD4 < 200) is approximately 8-10 years in untreated individuals. During this period, viral replication continues and CD4 cells decline progressively. Antiretroviral therapy dramatically extends this asymptomatic period.

questions.question: Addison's disease is caused by PRIMARY adrenal insufficiency, which MOST commonly results from:
questions.explanation: In developed countries, the most common cause of primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease) is autoimmune destruction of the adrenal cortex (up to 80% of cases), often associated with other autoimmune conditions. In developing countries, tuberculosis is a major cause. Other causes include fungal infections, bilateral adrenalectomy, and infiltrative diseases. The adrenal destruction affects both glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid production, causing the full clinical syndrome.

questions.question: In a patient with bilateral facial palsy, anterior uveitis, parotid swelling, and fever, which investigations are MOST appropriate to confirm sarcoidosis?
questions.explanation: Heerfordt's syndrome requires confirmation by HISTOLOGICAL EVIDENCE of non-caseating granulomas. BRONCHOSCOPY with BAL (showing increased CD4:CD8 ratio > 3.5) and transbronchial biopsy has the highest diagnostic yield (50-90% of pulmonary sarcoidosis). Serum ACE is supportive but non-specific. CT chest guides biopsy site selection.
options: Liver biopsy and renal biopsy simultaneously
Serum ACE, chest CT, and biopsy for non-caseating granulomas
Skin biopsy of uninvolved skin only

questions.question: A patient on chemotherapy is warned that fingernails will show a temporary growth arrest visible weeks later as a transverse groove. Which nail sign should the clinician look for at follow-up?
questions.explanation: Beau's lines are transverse depressions in the nail plate caused by temporary cessation of matrix activity during a systemic insult such as chemotherapy. Because the nail grows distally at a fairly constant rate, the groove appears weeks after the illness, at a distance from the cuticle proportional to elapsed time. This differs from Mees' lines, which are white transverse bands linked to arsenic poisoning.

options: Hepatitis B surface antigen alone without further markers
Hepatitis B core antibody IgG (anti-HBc IgG)
questions.explanation: HBeAg positivity indicates active viral replication and correlates with high infectivity in chronic hepatitis B infection, guiding decisions regarding antiviral therapy and transmission risk counselling. Anti-HBs instead indicates immunity, either from vaccination or resolved infection. Monitoring HBeAg status helps track disease activity and treatment response over time.
questions.question: A patient with chronic hepatitis B is found to have a serological marker indicating active viral replication and high infectivity. This marker is:

options: All patients regardless of oxygen need
Only patients not requiring any oxygen
Patients requiring oxygen or ventilatory support
Only patients within 24 hours of symptom onset
questions.explanation: Dexamethasone has been shown to reduce mortality specifically in COVID-19 patients requiring supplemental oxygen or mechanical ventilation, reflecting benefit from dampening the hyperinflammatory response driving severe disease at this stage. In contrast, corticosteroids showed no benefit and a trend toward harm in patients with mild disease not requiring oxygen, likely by impairing early viral clearance. This stage-dependent effect illustrates the importance of matching immunomodulatory treatment to disease severity.
questions.question: A patient with COVID-19 pneumonia requiring supplemental oxygen is being considered for corticosteroid therapy. According to major clinical trial evidence, which patients benefit MOST from dexamethasone?

questions.explanation: Latent tuberculosis infection describes a state where Mycobacterium tuberculosis is present in the body in a dormant form, controlled by the immune system, without clinical symptoms, radiographic abnormality or infectiousness to others. A positive tuberculin skin test or interferon-gamma release assay reflects prior exposure and immune sensitisation rather than active disease. Isoniazid preventive therapy reduces the risk of progression to active disease, particularly in high-risk groups such as those with HIV.
questions.question: A patient with a positive tuberculin skin test but no symptoms, normal chest x-ray and no evidence of active disease is diagnosed with which condition?

options: Autosomal dominant with mutation in LMX1B gene
questions.explanation: Nail-patella syndrome is inherited as an autosomal dominant condition caused by mutations in the LMX1B gene encoding a transcription factor. Features include absence/hypoplasia of the patella, congenital nail dystrophy (triangular lunulae are characteristic), skeletal abnormalities, and renal involvement (glomerulonephritis with haematuria and albuminuria, with 20% developing CRF).
questions.question: The Nail-patella syndrome (hereditary osteo-onychodysplasia) is inherited as which pattern?

questions.explanation: Melanonychia (brown-black nail pigmentation) can be induced by several drugs including antimalarials (chloroquine, hydroxychloroquine), chemotherapeutic agents, minocycline, zidovudine, and arsenic. Drug-induced melanonychia typically affects multiple nails and resolves after stopping the medication. Solitary longitudinal melanonychia should raise concern for a nail matrix tumour or melanoma, warranting biopsy.
questions.question: A patient on long-term chloroquine for malaria prophylaxis develops brown-black streaks in multiple nails. This represents:
In telogen effluvium, hair shedding occurs approximately how long after the precipitating event?
questions.explanation: Telogen effluvium characteristically presents with diffuse hair shedding approximately 3-5 months after a precipitating event (e.g., severe illness, surgery, postpartum, severe psychological stress). This delay reflects the time taken for the prematurely converted anagen hairs to complete the telogen phase and shed. Identifying events 3-5 months prior is key to diagnosing the trigger.

Intraperitoneal methotrexate instillation is used as palliative treatment for malignant ascites in advanced gastric carcinoma. It creates a cytotoxic environment in the peritoneal cavity that reduces peritoneal tumour burden and fluid production, providing symptomatic relief from tense ascites.
questions.question: Methotrexate instillation is used in gastric carcinoma specifically to manage which complication?

questions.explanation: Todd's paralysis (post-ictal paresis) is transient focal weakness occurring after a motor seizure, lasting minutes to hours. It reflects neuronal exhaustion in the motor cortex following seizure discharge. Jacksonian march describes the spread of motor seizure activity. Todd's paralysis must be distinguished from stroke in emergency settings.
questions.question: Following a simple partial motor seizure, a patient develops transient weakness of the same limb for several hours. What is the CORRECT term for this phenomenon?

options: Produces comedones as its primary lesion
Predominantly affects teenagers and young adults
Is caused by Propionibacterium acnes (C. acnes) colonisation
Is effectively treated with topical retinoids as first line
Flushing and telangiectasia without comedones, in middle age
questions.explanation: Rosacea is distinct from acne vulgaris in several key ways: it is characterised by flushing, persistent erythema, telangiectasia, and papulopustules WITHOUT comedones (which are present in acne vulgaris). It predominantly affects middle-aged fair-skinned adults (unlike acne vulgaris which peaks in adolescence). Triggers include heat, alcohol, spicy foods, and sun. Treatment includes topical metronidazole, azelaic acid, and systemic tetracyclines.
questions.question: Acne rosacea differs from acne vulgaris in that rosacea:

options: Renal fluid retention from hypoxia-induced EPO production
Repeated sympathetic activation and hypoxia-induced endothelial dysfunction
Increased aldosterone from renin release during apnoeic episodes
Right heart failure increasing venous pressure
Nocturnal cortisol surges from repeated arousal
questions.question: Obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) contributes to secondary hypertension through which MAIN mechanism?
questions.explanation: In OSA, repeated apnoeic episodes cause acute hypoxia and hypercapnia, triggering sympathetic nervous system activation (surges of catecholamines) and oxidative stress. Over time, this leads to persistent sympathetic activation, endothelial dysfunction, impaired baroreceptor reflex, and secondary hypertension. OSA is a common reversible cause of resistant hypertension. CPAP therapy reduces blood pressure in OSA-related hypertension.

questions.question: A patient with a longstanding anxiety disorder presents with light-headedness and perioral tingling during an acute panic episode. Arterial blood gas shows pH 7.50, PaCO2 26 mmHg, and HCO3 22 mmol/L. What is the MOST likely underlying acid-base disturbance?
questions.explanation: Hyperventilation during panic attacks causes excessive CO2 elimination, producing acute respiratory alkalosis with elevated pH and low PaCO2, with bicarbonate remaining relatively normal since renal compensation for acute respiratory disturbances takes hours to days to develop. This explains the classic symptoms of perioral and peripheral tingling caused by reduced ionised calcium related to the alkalosis. Recognising hyperventilation as the underlying trigger allows targeted reassurance and controlled breathing techniques as first-line management.

options: Thinning of the entire epidermis to a single cell layer
Thickening of the stratum spinosum due to increased keratinocyte proliferation
Accumulation of neutrophils in the stratum corneum
questions.question: Acanthosis, a histological finding in chronic eczema and psoriasis, refers specifically to:
questions.explanation: Acanthosis is thickening of the stratum spinosum due to increased keratinocyte proliferation, seen in chronic eczema, psoriasis, and acanthosis nigricans. In psoriasis it is accompanied by elongated rete ridges and parakeratosis. In eczema it is part of the transition from acute spongiotic to chronic lichenified disease. It corresponds clinically to the palpable thickness of lichenified skin.

Brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) and NT-proBNP are secreted by ventricular myocytes in response to increased wall stress and stretch, making them sensitive markers of heart failure. Markedly elevated BNP in a dyspnoeic patient strongly suggests cardiac failure. Normal BNP effectively rules out heart failure. Mildly elevated BNP can be seen in other conditions including PE and renal failure.
questions.question: A 60-year-old presents with dyspnoea. His BNP is markedly elevated. This finding is MOST suggestive of:

questions.explanation: HCC in black Africans presents at a younger mean age (<30 years) compared to Asian and Western populations (>50 years), reflecting early HBV vertical transmission (perinatal exposure) and high-level aflatoxin exposure from contaminated food. This contrasts sharply with the Western pattern of HCC on alcoholic cirrhosis.
questions.question: Hepatocellular carcinoma in black Africans differs from the global pattern in that it presents at a:
options: Lower rate despite high HBV prevalence

questions.explanation: HIV lacks its own ribosomes and relies entirely on host cell ribosomes to translate viral mRNA into precursor polyproteins (Gag, Pol, Env). This dependence on host ribosomes is why antibiotics (which target bacterial ribosomes) are ineffective against HIV and why antiviral drugs target viral-specific enzymes.
questions.question: During HIV biosynthesis inside host cells, which machinery translates viral mRNA into precursor polyproteins?
The CORRECT method for collecting nail specimens for mycology in suspected onychomycosis is:
questions.explanation: For nail mycological specimens, clippings and scrapings must be collected from the most proximal advancing edge of the onycholysis where viable fungi are most concentrated. Distal nail clippings may yield only dead organisms or debris, producing false-negative results. Sufficient material is needed for KOH microscopy (rapid result) and culture on Sabouraud's medium (species identification in 2-4 weeks).
options: A surface swab of the nail plate is sufficient
Clippings from the most distal free edge of the nail
Clippings and scrapings from the most proximal advancing edge of onycholysis
A punch biopsy of the nail bed as the only reliable method

questions.explanation: Metronidazole is the antibiotic of choice for amoebic liver abscess, targeting the trophozoites of Entamoeba histolytica. Aspiration is added for large or complicated abscesses to reduce volume, relieve pressure, and speed resolution. A luminal amoebicide (diloxanide) is added to eliminate intestinal cysts.
questions.question: The drug of choice for amoebic liver abscess is:
The treatment of eczema with calcineurin inhibitors (e.g., tacrolimus) is particularly useful because they:
questions.explanation: Calcineurin inhibitors suppress T-cell-mediated inflammation through inhibition of calcineurin-dependent transcription, without the glucocorticoid receptor pathway. Critically, they do not cause skin atrophy, making them suitable for long-term use on the face and flexures where corticosteroids are risky. They are considered steroid-sparing agents in atopic dermatitis management.
options: Provide bactericidal effect on Staphylococcus aureus
Suppress inflammation without causing skin atrophy
Are the most potent anti-inflammatory agents available topically
Replace the skin barrier deficiency in atopic dermatitis
Reduce pruritus by blocking histamine H1 receptors peripherally

questions.question: Urological causes of haematuria that are TYPICALLY painless include all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Painless haematuria is the classic presentation of urological malignancies (RCC, TCC of bladder/ureter), TB of urinary tract, and glomerulonephritis. Ureteric calculus (renal colic) is characteristically PAINFUL—the sudden severe colicky loin-to-groin pain distinguishes it from other causes. Any painless haematuria in an adult should be investigated urgently to exclude malignancy, particularly in those over 50 or with risk factors (smoking, chemical exposure).

Rose spots are characteristic of typhoid fever and appear as few to 30 blanching, salmon-pink, macular or maculopapular lesions (2-4mm) on the trunk (abdomen and lower chest). They appear in the first week, last 3-4 days, and are due to S. typhi emboli in dermal capillaries. They are seen in only about 30% of patients and may be difficult to detect in dark-skinned individuals, requiring careful examination.
options: Purpuric non-blanching lesions on the lower limbs
Blanching salmon-pink macular or maculopapular lesions on the trunk
Vesicular lesions on the palms and soles
Petechiae distributed on the upper chest
Fixed erythematous plaques on the face
questions.question: Rose spots in typhoid fever are BEST described as:
Which chromosomal loci are implicated in colorectal carcinogenesis through allelic losses?
questions.explanation: Colorectal carcinoma involves allelic losses on chromosomes 5q (APC gene), 18q (DCC/SMAD4), and 17p (p53), along with K-ras mutations. This multistep genetic model (Vogelstein sequence) represents the adenoma-carcinoma pathway, progressing from normal epithelium through polyp to carcinoma.

Consistent improvement away from work, particularly during holidays, is a classic feature of occupational contact dermatitis. The history should explore potential sensitisers or irritants at the workplace and hobbies. Patch testing is the key investigation to identify the causative allergen in allergic contact dermatitis.
questions.question: A 35-year-old man presents with skin lesions that worsen at work but improve consistently during holidays. This pattern is MOST suggestive of:
A 65-year-old presents with new-onset temporal headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, and visual disturbance. The most urgent concern is:
questions.explanation: Giant cell (temporal) arteritis in patients typically over 50 presents with headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, and can rapidly cause irreversible visual loss if untreated. High-dose corticosteroids should be started urgently even before biopsy confirmation when suspicion is high. Delay significantly increases the risk of permanent blindness.
options: Giant cell arteritis risking permanent blindness

questions.question: Which investigation is the gold standard for diagnosing a bleeding peptic ulcer AND provides therapeutic options simultaneously?
questions.explanation: Upper GI endoscopy is both diagnostic and therapeutic for bleeding ulcers, allowing direct visualization of the bleeding point and simultaneous haemostasis via diathermy, haemoclip application, or injection of vasoconstrictors. It provides definitive diagnosis and can prevent surgery in many cases.

questions.question: Which investigation is MOST useful for quantifying the severity and reversibility of obstructive uropathy?
questions.explanation: Renal ultrasound is the first-line investigation for obstructive uropathy, showing hydronephrosis (dilated calyces/pelvis), hydroureter (if present), and importantly renal cortical thickness (which reflects functional parenchyma). Thick cortex suggests reversible obstruction; thin cortex indicates established parenchymal loss. USS is non-invasive, radiation-free, and readily available.
options: Bladder catheterisation to measure residual urine

questions.question: The MOST important side effect of aminoglycoside antibiotics used in TB treatment is:
options: Optic neuritis causing colour vision loss
questions.explanation: Aminoglycosides (streptomycin, kanamycin, amikacin) used in MDR-TB treatment cause nephrotoxicity (proximal tubular damage, AKI) and ototoxicity (irreversible cochlear damage causing hearing loss, and vestibular damage causing balance disturbance). Baseline and monthly audiometry and renal function monitoring are mandatory. Ethambutol causes optic neuritis; INH causes peripheral neuropathy; Rifampicin causes hepatotoxicity.

Asteatotic eczema predominantly affects elderly patients whose skin becomes excessively dry due to age-related reductions in sebum production and natural moisturising factors. The characteristic 'crazy paving' or 'lichen field' pattern of fine cracked fissures is distinctive. Treatment centres on liberal use of emollients and avoiding soap and excessive bathing. Mild topical corticosteroids address active inflammation.
options: Young atopic adults during winter months
Elderly patients with dry skin from reduced sebum production
Infants in the first 3 months of life
questions.question: Asteatotic eczema (eczema craquelé) is MOST commonly encountered in which patient group?

questions.explanation: The posterior cerebral artery supplies the occipital visual cortex, so its occlusion produces contralateral homonymous hemianopia. Macular sparing occurs because the occipital pole receives dual blood supply from the middle cerebral artery collaterals. This pattern distinguishes cortical from optic tract lesions.
questions.question: A patient presents with sudden contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing after a stroke. Which artery is occluded?
A child with atopic dermatitis develops sudden painful clustered vesicles with punched-out erosions over existing eczematous skin, accompanied by fever. Which complication should be suspected?
questions.explanation: Eczema herpeticum is a disseminated herpes simplex infection superimposed on eczematous skin, presenting with monomorphic punched-out vesicles and systemic upset, and is a dermatological emergency requiring prompt antiviral therapy. Impetiginised eczema instead produces honey-coloured crusting from bacterial superinfection rather than punched-out vesicles. Recognising this distinction avoids delay in starting aciclovir.

options: Initial right-to-left shunt from birth with worsening pulmonary hypertension
Fixed pulmonary stenosis with no shunt
Spontaneous closure of VSD with complete resolution
Bidirectional shunt at atrial level only
questions.question: Eisenmenger syndrome refers to:
questions.explanation: Eisenmenger syndrome occurs when a chronic left-to-right shunt (from VSD, ASD, or PDA) causes sufficient pulmonary vascular disease and pulmonary arterial hypertension that pulmonary vascular resistance exceeds systemic vascular resistance, reversing the shunt direction to right-to-left. This causes cyanosis, clubbing, and erythrocytosis. Once established, Eisenmenger syndrome is irreversible, making early surgical closure of the defect essential to prevent this complication.

questions.question: The characteristic Wickham's striae of lichen planus histologically correspond to which epidermal change?
questions.explanation: Wickham's striae in lichen planus histologically correspond to focal areas of hypergranulosis (increased thickness of the stratum granulosum) beneath the epidermal surface. Clinically, they appear as fine white reticulate lines or network on the LP papule surface. The band-like lymphocytic infiltrate at the dermoepidermal junction and basal cell damage (liquefaction degeneration) are the other key histological features of LP.
options: Munro microabscesses in the stratum corneum

questions.explanation: Capsule endoscopy is particularly useful for visualising the mid small bowel, a region beyond the reach of standard upper endoscopy and colonoscopy, making it valuable for investigating obscure gastrointestinal bleeding or small bowel pathology. Other segments listed are already accessible by conventional endoscopic techniques. This unique capability defines its main clinical indication.
questions.question: A patient undergoes capsule endoscopy for suspected small bowel bleeding. This investigation is specifically valuable because it visualises which segment that is otherwise difficult to access?
options: The oesophagus, already well seen on upper endoscopy
The rectum, already well seen on colonoscopy
The mid small bowel beyond the reach of standard endoscopy
The sigmoid colon, already well seen on colonoscopy
The stomach, already well seen on upper endoscopy

questions.question: Which diuretic is an aldosterone antagonist used in heart failure to reduce mortality?
questions.explanation: Spironolactone (and eplerenone) is an aldosterone antagonist (mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist) that has been shown in the RALES and EPHESUS trials to reduce mortality in heart failure with reduced EF. It blocks aldosterone's sodium-retaining and potassium-excreting effects, reducing cardiac remodelling. The main adverse effects are hyperkalaemia and gynaecomastia.

questions.question: A patient with linitis plastica type gastric cancer requiring surgery is best managed with which extent of gastric resection?
questions.explanation: Diffuse infiltrative gastric cancers such as linitis plastica typically require total gastrectomy because the disease often extends beyond visible margins throughout the stomach wall, making partial resection inadequate for clearance. This differs from localised early gastric cancers, where lesser resections may suffice. Recognising the histological subtype guides appropriate surgical extent.

options: Reynold's pentad; septic shock from cholangitis
Mirizzi syndrome; gallstone impaction at Hartmann's pouch
Courvoisier's law; malignant obstruction of the CBD
questions.explanation: COURVOISIER'S LAW states that in obstructive jaundice, a palpable non-tender gallbladder is unlikely to be caused by gallstones (chronic stone disease causes fibrosis and shrinkage). It implies MALIGNANT OBSTRUCTION ? most commonly carcinoma of the head of the pancreas. This sign combined with painless progressive jaundice demands urgent CT abdomen and CA19-9.
questions.question: A 70-year-old presents with painless obstructive jaundice and a non-tender distended gallbladder. This combination is known as which eponymous sign and what does it implicate?

questions.explanation: Isotretinoin is a powerful teratogen capable of causing severe congenital malformations if taken during pregnancy, so strict pregnancy prevention programmes with reliable contraception and monthly pregnancy testing are mandatory for women of childbearing potential. It does not cause permanent infertility, and its teratogenicity is independent of any interaction with hormonal contraceptive efficacy. This is one of the most safety-critical prescribing points in dermatology.
questions.question: A young woman on isotretinoin for severe nodulocystic acne must use effective contraception throughout treatment. What is the primary reason for this requirement?
options: Isotretinoin interacts with hormonal contraceptives to cause pregnancy
Isotretinoin causes chromosomal abnormalities in sperm
Isotretinoin increases the risk of ectopic pregnancy

questions.explanation: Tetralogy of Fallot produces reduced pulmonary blood flow from right ventricular outflow obstruction, giving pulmonary oligaemia on chest X-ray, along with a boot-shaped cardiac silhouette from right ventricular hypertrophy. This distinguishes it from lesions with increased pulmonary blood flow, which typically show pulmonary plethora. Recognition guides urgent paediatric cardiology referral.
questions.question: A cyanotic infant has a chest X-ray showing decreased pulmonary vascular markings (oligaemia) alongside a boot-shaped heart. This combination is most suggestive of:

questions.explanation: The zona glomerulosa is the outermost layer of the adrenal cortex and the sole site of aldosterone (mineralocorticoid) production. Its secretion is controlled primarily by the renin-angiotensin system and serum potassium levels. Aldosterone acts on distal kidney tubules to promote sodium reabsorption and potassium excretion, playing a critical role in long-term blood pressure regulation. Complete failure of aldosterone secretion leads to lethal dehydration and hyperkalaemia.
questions.question: The adrenal cortex is divided into three zones. Which zone produces aldosterone?

options: The pancreas, through direct beta-cell destruction
The heart, through left ventricular hypertrophy and failure
questions.question: A hypertensive patient's chronic uncontrolled disease most commonly damages which target organ, contributing significantly to morbidity and mortality?
questions.explanation: Chronic uncontrolled hypertension most commonly leads to cardiac target organ damage, including left ventricular hypertrophy, heart failure, and coronary artery disease, alongside renal and cerebrovascular complications. This makes the heart a principal organ of concern in long-term hypertension management. Regular cardiovascular risk assessment is therefore essential in hypertensive patients.

questions.question: A patient with suspected bleeding peptic ulcer requires an investigation that can both confirm the diagnosis and provide immediate treatment. The most appropriate choice is:
questions.explanation: Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy is the gold standard for bleeding peptic ulcers, allowing direct visualisation of the bleeding source and simultaneous therapeutic intervention such as clipping or injection. Barium studies and plain X-rays offer no therapeutic capability and are less sensitive for active bleeding. This dual diagnostic-therapeutic role makes endoscopy the investigation of choice.

options: Iron induces viral hepatitis B reactivation
Iron directly activates oncogenic KRAS mutations
Iron chelates p53 tumour suppressor protein
Iron-induced free radical generation causing hepatocyte DNA damage and cirrhosis
Iron promotes aflatoxin uptake by hepatocytes
questions.question: Haemochromatosis as a risk factor for hepatocellular carcinoma operates through which mechanism?
questions.explanation: In haemochromatosis, excess hepatic iron generates reactive oxygen species (hydroxyl radicals via Fenton reaction) that cause oxidative DNA damage, lipid peroxidation, and hepatocyte death, ultimately producing cirrhosis. HCC risk in haemochromatosis is 200 times higher than the general population, primarily through cirrhosis-mediated carcinogenesis.

COPD patients with chronic hypercapnia lose their sensitivity to CO2 as a respiratory stimulant and rely on hypoxic drive (low PaO2) to maintain ventilation. Excessive supplemental oxygen corrects hypoxia, removing the hypoxic drive, leading to further CO2 retention, respiratory acidosis, and CO2 narcosis (confusion, drowsiness, coma). This is prevented by using controlled low-concentration oxygen (24-28%) via Venturi mask in acute COPD exacerbations.
options: New onset bacterial pneumonia causing Type I failure
Carbon monoxide poisoning from improper equipment
CO2 narcosis from oxygen suppressing hypoxic drive
Pulmonary embolism causing acute respiratory failure
questions.question: A patient with known COPD develops new onset confusion and drowsiness following increased home oxygen therapy. ABG shows pH 7.22, PaCO2 78 mmHg, PaO2 68 mmHg. What is the MOST likely explanation?

questions.explanation: Strict blood pressure control targeting <130/80 mmHg using RAAS inhibitors (ACE inhibitors or ARBs) is the single most effective strategy to slow CKD progression. RAAS inhibition reduces intraglomerular pressure, proteinuria, and inflammatory/fibrotic signalling. These benefits are independent of BP reduction. Both in diabetic and non-diabetic CKD, BP control is paramount.
questions.question: The single MOST important modifiable risk factor for slowing CKD progression is:

questions.explanation: Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea is sudden breathlessness that awakens the patient from sleep, caused by reabsorption of dependent oedema and nocturnal fluid redistribution increasing venous return. It typically improves after sitting up or standing for some minutes. This distinguishes it from simple positional orthopnoea.
questions.question: A patient in heart failure develops sudden severe breathlessness two hours after falling asleep, improved by sitting upright. This is characteristic of:

questions.explanation: Hepatitis D virus (HDV) is a defective RNA virus that cannot replicate independently; it requires HBV surface antigen for its assembly and release. HDV can occur as co-infection (simultaneous HBV+HDV) or superinfection (HDV in a chronic HBV carrier), the latter carrying worse prognosis.
questions.question: Which hepatitis virus requires the helper function of HBV for its replication?

options: Seizure-free AND off all anticonvulsants for 6 months
questions.question: A patient with focal epilepsy has been seizure-free for 2 years on carbamazepine and wishes to drive. The standard seizure-free period before driving licence reinstatement is typically:
questions.explanation: Most regulatory bodies (including Nigeria's Federal Road Safety Corps framework) require a minimum of 1 YEAR SEIZURE-FREE before a patient with epilepsy may drive a private motor vehicle. Commercial vehicle licensing requires longer seizure-free periods. Physicians have a duty to counsel epileptic patients about driving restrictions.

options: Increased renal clearance of clotting factors
questions.explanation: Nephrotic syndrome causes urinary loss of antithrombin III, a key natural anticoagulant, along with other regulatory proteins, contributing to a hypercoagulable state that increases risk of venous thromboembolism, including notably renal vein thrombosis. Hepatic fibrinogen synthesis is actually increased, not reduced, as a compensatory response to hypoalbuminaemia, further contributing to the prothrombotic state. Recognising this thrombotic risk is important for considering prophylactic anticoagulation in severe nephrotic syndrome.
questions.question: A patient with nephrotic syndrome and severe hypoalbuminaemia is found to have an increased risk of venous thromboembolism. Which mechanism MOST directly explains this hypercoagulable state?

questions.explanation: Roseola infantum, caused by human herpesvirus 6, classically presents with several days of high fever in an otherwise well-appearing infant, with the rash appearing only as the fever resolves, a sequence known as 'rash after fever'. This temporal pattern distinguishes it from measles and rubella, where rash and fever typically overlap. Febrile seizures can occur during the high fever phase due to the rapid temperature rise.
questions.question: An infant develops several days of high fever followed by a sudden drop in temperature coinciding with the appearance of a diffuse rose-pink rash on the trunk. Which diagnosis is MOST likely?

A patient with long-standing uncontrolled hypertension and benign nephrosclerosis is counselled on management priorities. Which specific intervention is MOST important to slow further progression of this renal pathology?
questions.explanation: Strict blood pressure control is the most important intervention to slow progression of hypertensive nephrosclerosis, directly addressing the underlying vascular injury mechanism driving this form of chronic kidney disease, typically using renin-angiotensin system blockers as preferred agents given their additional renoprotective haemodynamic effects. While statins and aspirin have cardiovascular benefits, they do not directly address the primary renal vascular pathology in the same way as blood pressure control. Recognising blood pressure management as the central therapeutic priority reflects the well-established causal relationship between hypertension severity and renal disease progression.
options: Aspirin therapy as the primary measure
High-dose diuretic therapy alone regardless of pressure
Statin therapy as the primary measure
Dietary protein restriction as the primary measure

questions.question: Discoid (nummular) eczema is characterised by which DISTINCTIVE morphology?
questions.explanation: Discoid (nummular) eczema presents as well-defined, coin-shaped eczematous plaques, typically on the limbs and trunk. This circular configuration is diagnostically distinctive and can mimic tinea corporis; KOH microscopy of scale differentiates between the two. It tends to be chronic and recurrent and may be aggravated by xerosis, stress, and alcohol. Potent topical corticosteroids are the first-line treatment.
options: Diffuse erythema and lichenification of the entire lower leg
Well-demarcated coin-shaped (discoid) plaques on the limbs and trunk
Deep-seated vesicles confined to the palms and soles

questions.question: A patient's liver function tests show alkaline phosphatase markedly elevated out of proportion to aminotransferase levels. This pattern is most consistent with which hepatic condition?
questions.explanation: A disproportionate rise in alkaline phosphatase relative to aminotransferases suggests a cholestatic or obstructive pattern of liver injury, such as biliary obstruction or infiltrative disease, rather than primarily hepatocellular injury as seen in acute viral hepatitis. This biochemical pattern helps direct further imaging toward biliary tree evaluation. Distinguishing hepatocellular from cholestatic patterns is a key step in liver disease work-up.

Approximately 14% of COVID-19 patients develop severe disease requiring hospitalisation and supplemental oxygen, while approximately 5% require ICU admission for critical illness including ARDS and multi-organ failure. The majority (~80%) experience only mild or uncomplicated illness.
questions.question: Approximately what percentage of COVID-19 patients develop severe disease requiring hospitalisation and oxygen support?

questions.explanation: Approximately 60% of gastric cancers occur in the antral and pyloric region of the stomach. The body and greater curvature account for 20–30%, while the cardia accounts for only 5–20%. Location influences surgical approach (partial vs. total gastrectomy).
questions.question: Gastric cancer most commonly presents in the:
Which is the MOST common target organ affected by longstanding uncontrolled hypertension?
