Anagen effluvium results from hair shaft fracture caused by antimitotic chemotherapy agents (antimetabolites, alkylating agents, mitotic inhibitors) that arrest hair matrix cell division during the active growth phase. Unlike telogen effluvium, the hair does not complete its cycle but fractures, causing abrupt and rapid hair loss. It is generally reversible after cessation of the causative drug.
options: Hormonal changes causing premature telogen conversion
Hair shaft fracture due to chemotherapy agents inhibiting hair matrix mitosis
Autoimmune follicle destruction targeting anagen follicles
questions.question: Anagen effluvium most commonly results from which mechanism?

options: It increases filling time, causing more efficient pumping
It reduces ventricular filling time, decreasing stroke volume
questions.question: Tachyarrhythmia can precipitate heart failure MAINLY because:
questions.explanation: Sustained tachyarrhythmia precipitates heart failure by reducing diastolic filling time, which decreases left ventricular preload and stroke volume. Additionally, the rapid rate increases myocardial oxygen demand while impairing coronary perfusion (which occurs in diastole). Prolonged tachycardia can cause tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy. Restoring sinus rhythm or controlling rate often dramatically improves cardiac function.

questions.question: A patient with severe necrotising pancreatitis is scored using a validated prognostic system, and a score of 3 or more at 48 hours is calculated. What does this specific threshold predict?
questions.explanation: A Ranson score of 3 or more at 48 hours is associated with a significantly increased risk of mortality and severe complications in acute pancreatitis, prompting closer monitoring, often in a higher level of care setting. It does not itself mandate emergency surgery, since most acute pancreatitis, even severe cases, is initially managed supportively rather than operatively. This scoring system helps stratify prognosis rather than dictate a specific intervention.
options: Increased mortality and severe disease course
No need for further imaging or monitoring
Absolute contraindication to any fluid resuscitation
Muscle wasting and fasciculations with low tone
The presence of spasticity and hyperreflexia
questions.question: On examination, a patient has muscle wasting, fasciculations, and reduced reflexes in the affected limb. This clinical pattern differentiates a lower motor neuron lesion from an upper motor neuron lesion primarily because of:
questions.explanation: Lower motor neuron lesions classically produce flaccid weakness with reduced tone, diminished or absent reflexes, muscle wasting, and fasciculations, reflecting loss of direct innervation to the muscle. This contrasts sharply with the spasticity and hyperreflexia of upper motor neuron lesions. Recognising these distinguishing features guides accurate neurological localisation.

Group B Streptococcus (GBS) is the leading cause of neonatal meningitis in the first 3 months of life globally, acquired during passage through the birth canal (early-onset) or from the environment (late-onset). Gram-negative organisms (E. coli, Klebsiella) are the second most common group. Neisseria meningitidis and S. pneumoniae predominate in older children and adults.
questions.question: In a neonate with suspected meningitis in the first 3 months of life, which organism is the MOST common cause in sub-Saharan Africa?

questions.explanation: Because early gastric cancer confined to the mucosa or submucosa carries a low risk of lymph node involvement, selected cases can be curatively managed with less invasive endoscopic resection rather than radical gastrectomy with extensive lymphadenectomy. This significantly reduces treatment-related morbidity. Careful staging is required to confirm eligibility for this less invasive approach.
options: Radical total gastrectomy with extended lymphadenectomy is always mandatory
Chemotherapy alone is the only effective option
The disease is always already metastatic at diagnosis
Endoscopic resection alone may be curative in selected cases
questions.question: A patient with early gastric cancer confined to the mucosa or submucosa is found to have a very low likelihood of lymph node metastasis. This clinical significance means that:
The MAIN advantage of AZATHIOPRINE over corticosteroids as a long-term steroid-sparing agent in MG is:
questions.explanation: AZATHIOPRINE is used as a STEROID-SPARING agent to allow reduction of corticosteroid dose, avoiding long-term steroid side effects. Its ONSET IS SLOW (6-12 months to full effect). TPMT enzyme activity must be checked BEFORE starting ? TPMT-deficient patients develop life-threatening myelosuppression. Regular full blood count monitoring is essential during treatment. SUBTOPIC 5: GASTROINTESTINAL DISEASES  (Questions 126?165)
options: No need for monitoring blood counts
Avoidance of steroid side effects with a steroid-sparing effect ? though onset of benefit is slow
Safe in all patients including those with TPMT deficiency

questions.question: Which statement is TRUE regarding the pulmonary valve?
questions.explanation: The pulmonary valve is one of the two semilunar valves (the other being the aortic valve). It separates the right ventricle from the pulmonary artery and opens during ventricular systole to allow blood ejection into the pulmonary circulation. Like all semilunar valves, it has three cusps and prevents backflow during diastole.
options: It separates right atrium from right ventricle
It connects left ventricle to aorta

questions.explanation: Erythema nodosum leprosum (Type 2 reaction) occurs exclusively in patients near the lepromatous end of the spectrum, reflecting an immune complex-mediated response to bacillary antigens, and presents with tender nodules, fever, and systemic symptoms. Type 1 reversal reactions instead occur more centrally in the borderline spectrum and are driven by a shift in cell-mediated immunity rather than immune complexes. Distinguishing the two reactions guides appropriate treatment choice.
questions.question: A patient with borderline lepromatous leprosy develops tender erythematous nodules, fever, and joint pains several months into multidrug therapy. Which reaction is this, and at which end of the leprosy spectrum does it exclusively occur?
options: Type 1 reversal reaction, at the tuberculoid end
Lucio's phenomenon, at the indeterminate stage
Type 1 reversal reaction, at the lepromatous end
Erythema nodosum leprosum, at the lepromatous end
Erythema nodosum leprosum, at the tuberculoid end

questions.question: The '10 kg weight loss benefit' in obesity management includes all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: A 10 kg weight loss in obese patients produces well-quantified benefits: >20% fall in total mortality, >30% fall in diabetes-related deaths, >40% fall in obesity-related cancer deaths, and a 50% fall in fasting glucose. While blood pressure falls by approximately 10mmHg systolic per 10kg, this is a reduction — not a complete cure of hypertension, which depends on the duration, severity, and presence of end-organ damage.
options: More than 30% fall in diabetes-related deaths
More than 40% fall in obesity-related cancer deaths
Complete cure of essential hypertension in all patients
More than 20% fall in total mortality
High-dose oral sodium chloride tablets alone
Loop diuretic without any fluid restriction
Hypertonic saline for all cases regardless of severity
questions.explanation: Fluid restriction is the standard first-line management for SIADH-related hyponatraemia in mild to moderate, asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic cases, reducing water intake relative to ongoing antidiuretic hormone-driven water retention. Aggressive normal saline can paradoxically worsen hyponatraemia in SIADH because the retained free water exceeds the sodium delivered, an important and often tested distinction from other causes of hyponatraemia. Hypertonic saline is reserved for severe, symptomatic cases such as seizures, not routine mild presentations.
questions.question: A patient with syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion is found to have hyponatraemia, inappropriately concentrated urine, and clinical euvolaemia. Which first-line management approach is MOST appropriate for mild to moderate cases?

questions.explanation: Sarcoidosis characteristically produces non-caseating granulomas on histology, distinguishing it from tuberculosis, which typically shows caseating (necrotising) granulomas with central cheese-like necrosis. This histological distinction is an important diagnostic clue, particularly in regions where tuberculosis is common and clinical presentations may overlap. Additional microbiological and clinical correlation supports the final diagnosis.
questions.question: A patient with sarcoidosis is found to have granulomatous inflammation on biopsy, characterised by non-caseating granulomas. This histological feature helps distinguish sarcoidosis from which important differential diagnosis that typically shows caseating granulomas?

questions.explanation: Kayser-Fleischer rings are copper deposits in the Descemet membrane of the cornea, pathognomonic for Wilson's disease, a disorder of impaired copper excretion due to ATP7B gene mutations. Copper accumulation in the basal ganglia produces movement disorders and dysarthria, while hepatic deposition causes liver disease. Reduced serum caeruloplasmin supports the diagnosis.
questions.question: A young patient with liver disease, dysarthria and a copper-coloured ring around the cornea is diagnosed with a metabolic disorder. Which sign is being described?

questions.explanation: Cyclophosphamide is metabolised to acrolein which is excreted in urine and causes haemorrhagic cystitis (dysuria, haematuria) and increases risk of urothelial (bladder) carcinoma. Prevention requires adequate hydration, mesna (a uroprotective agent), and emptying bladder frequently. Cumulative dose monitoring helps limit bladder cancer risk. Other toxicities include myelosuppression, gonadotoxicity, and infections.
options: Peripheral neuropathy from direct neurotoxic effect
questions.question: Cyclophosphamide used in glomerulonephritis treatment requires monitoring for which specific complication?

options: Flexural distribution with sparing of extensor surfaces
Symmetrical involvement of elbows and knees
Face, neck V, hands; sparing shaded areas
questions.question: When examining the distribution of skin lesions, which pattern would MOST suggest a photosensitive dermatosis?
questions.explanation: Photosensitive dermatoses characteristically affect sun-exposed areas including the face, V of the neck, dorsum of hands, and forearms, while typically sparing shaded areas such as under the chin, behind the ears, and upper eyelids. Polymorphic light eruption and drug-induced photosensitivity follow this pattern. The history of outdoor exposure and seasonality corroborates the diagnosis.

options: Barium delays surgical intervention by 24 hours
questions.explanation: Barium peritonitis is a lethal complication that occurs when barium sulfate leaks through a perforation into the peritoneal cavity. The dense, inert material causes a severe chemical peritonitis with very high mortality, making water-soluble contrast the preferred alternative.
questions.question: In a patient with suspected perforated peptic ulcer, barium studies are contraindicated primarily because:
A patient with Prader-Willi syndrome develops severe childhood-onset obesity driven by hyperphagia. What is the underlying genetic mechanism of this syndrome?
options: Autosomal recessive mutation affecting the leptin receptor only
X-linked recessive mutation affecting appetite regulation
Loss of paternal genes on chromosome 15
Mitochondrial DNA deletion affecting energy metabolism
questions.explanation: Prader-Willi syndrome results from loss of function of paternally expressed genes in the 15q11-q13 region, commonly due to paternal deletion or maternal uniparental disomy, leading to hypothalamic dysfunction, hyperphagia, and severe obesity from early childhood. This differs mechanistically from isolated leptin receptor mutations, which cause a distinct, rarer monogenic obesity syndrome. Recognising the genetic basis helps distinguish syndromic from simple polygenic obesity.

questions.question: An occupational health physician wants to confirm that a factory worker's hand dermatitis is caused by a specific chemical used at the workbench, rather than being irritant in nature. Which investigation should be arranged?
questions.explanation: Patch testing applies suspected allergens under occlusion to the back for 48 hours, with delayed readings, to identify type IV delayed hypersensitivity responsible for allergic contact dermatitis. Skin prick and RAST testing instead detect immediate IgE-mediated (type I) reactions and are not useful for contact allergy. This distinction determines which investigation confirms an occupational allergen.

questions.question: Which investigation is recommended for confirming H. pylori infection in a patient with dyspepsia prior to endoscopy?
options: Urea breath test or stool antigen
questions.explanation: The urea breath test (UBT) and stool antigen test are the RECOMMENDED non-invasive tests for confirming active H. pylori infection in uncomplicated dyspepsia (test-and-treat strategy). Both detect active infection rather than past exposure (unlike serology). Endoscopy with biopsy (CLO test, histology, culture) is used when endoscopy is indicated for other reasons.

The STOOP mnemonic for AKI causes includes: Sepsis and hypoperfusion (most common), Toxicity from drugs and contrast agents, Obstetric causes (APH, PPH, eclampsia), Obstruction of urinary tract (post-renal), and Parenchymal kidney disease (glomerulonephritis, malignancy). This framework helps systematic evaluation of AKI aetiology in clinical practice.
questions.question: The 'STOOP' mnemonic for causes of AKI stands for:
options: Sepsis, Toxicity, Obstruction, Obstetric, Parenchymal kidney disease
Shock, Toxins, Oestrogenic states, Oligaemia, Pyelonephritis

questions.explanation: Giant cell (temporal) arteritis is a large vessel vasculitis that almost exclusively affects individuals over 50 years of age. It involves the aorta and its main branches, particularly the carotid and temporal arteries. Clinical features include headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, and visual disturbance (visual loss due to ischaemic optic neuropathy is a feared complication). It is associated with polymyalgia rheumatica and responds dramatically to high-dose corticosteroids.
questions.question: Giant cell (temporal) arteritis predominantly affects patients over which age?
Acute epiglottitis in children is potentially life-threatening primarily because it causes:
questions.explanation: Acute epiglottitis causes rapid, severe swelling of the epiglottis and surrounding supraglottic tissues, which can occlude the upper airway completely, leading to asphyxiation. The child typically presents in a 'tripod' position (leaning forward) with drooling, stridor, and high fever. Airway management is the immediate priority before any examination.

options: Oral bile acid dissolution therapy alone
questions.question: A patient with symptomatic gallstones causing recurrent cholecystitis is being considered for definitive treatment. The preferred management is:
questions.explanation: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy is the preferred definitive treatment for symptomatic gallstone disease causing recurrent cholecystitis, offering low morbidity and preventing recurrent attacks and complications. Conservative measures such as dietary modification or dissolution therapy are less effective and not definitive. Surgery addresses the underlying cause rather than just symptoms.

questions.question: The prodromal phase of acute viral hepatitis is characterised by all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Jaundice characterises the icteric phase that follows the prodromal phase, not the prodromal phase itself. The prodromal phase features constitutional symptoms: anorexia, nausea, vomiting, fatigue, dark urine, and clay-coloured stools—before visible jaundice appears.

questions.question: Which organism is most directly implicated in both MALT lymphoma and adenocarcinoma of the stomach?
questions.explanation: Helicobacter pylori is a WHO Class I carcinogen strongly associated with both gastric adenocarcinoma and MALT lymphoma. Anti-H. pylori therapy can be curative for early MALT lymphoma and eradicating H. pylori reduces gastric cancer risk.

options: Fever and neck stiffness with normal conscious level and no focal signs
Headache and photophobia in a febrile patient
Suspected viral meningitis with normal CT brain
Severe headache with papilloedema, reduced GCS, and focal neurological signs
questions.explanation: LP is CONTRAINDICATED without prior CT brain when there are features of RAISED INTRACRANIAL PRESSURE: papilloedema, reduced GCS (< 13), focal neurological signs, or immunocompromise. LP in this context risks TONSILLAR HERNIATION and death. ANTIBIOTICS must be started immediately while awaiting imaging ? never delay antibiotics for the CT or LP.
questions.question: In which clinical scenario is lumbar puncture ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED without prior neuroimaging?

options: Free subdiaphragmatic gas on an erect film
questions.explanation: Free air under the diaphragm on an erect chest or abdominal X-ray indicates pneumoperitoneum, strongly supporting perforation of a hollow viscus such as a duodenal ulcer. This is a key radiological sign guiding urgent surgical referral. Its absence does not entirely exclude perforation but its presence is highly suggestive.
questions.question: A plain abdominal X-ray is obtained in a patient with suspected perforated duodenal ulcer. Which finding would support this diagnosis?
Acitretin, a systemic retinoid used in psoriasis, is classified as a teratogen. This means female patients must avoid pregnancy during treatment and for how long AFTER stopping?
questions.explanation: Acitretin is highly teratogenic, and female patients must avoid pregnancy during treatment and for 2 years after stopping due to the drug's long half-life in tissue stores. This is in contrast to isotretinoin, which requires only 1 month of post-treatment contraception. Acitretin may be converted to etretinate in the presence of alcohol, which has an even longer elimination half-life.

Interstitial lung disease (fibrosing alveolitis/IPF) causes a restrictive ventilatory defect: reduced TLC, FVC, and functional residual capacity with a preserved or supranormal FEV1/FVC ratio (because fibrosis makes lungs stiffer but doesn't narrow airways). DLCO is reduced from impaired alveolar-capillary gas exchange. This pattern contrasts with obstructive defects (COPD, asthma) where TLC is increased and FEV1/FVC reduced.
options: Obstructive: reduced FEV1/FVC with normal TLC
Restrictive: reduced TLC, FVC, preserved or elevated FEV1/FVC
Normal spirometry with reduced DLCO only
Hyperinflation with increased TLC and RV
questions.question: Which pulmonary function pattern is EXPECTED in early interstitial lung disease (fibrosing alveolitis)?

questions.explanation: A palpable epigastric mass appearing 4-6 weeks after an episode of acute pancreatitis is most likely a pancreatic pseudocyst — a collection of pancreatic fluid enclosed by fibrous tissue (not a true epithelial cyst) that develops when disrupted pancreatic ducts leak digestive fluid. Diagnosis is confirmed by ultrasound or CT. Management depends on size and symptoms; many resolve spontaneously, while larger or symptomatic pseudocysts require drainage.
options: Splenic artery aneurysm from perivascular inflammation
Pancreatic adenocarcinoma arising from chronic inflammation
Pancreatic pseudocyst from walled-off necrotic fluid
Duodenal haematoma from pancreatic enzyme erosion
questions.question: A patient presents with severe acute pancreatitis and develops a palpable epigastric mass 4-6 weeks after the initial attack. The MOST likely diagnosis is:

options: Allergic contact dermatitis is limited to the contact area and does not spread
Irritant contact dermatitis involves T-cell sensitisation and may spread beyond the contact area
Allergic contact dermatitis occurs in sensitised individuals and is an immunological reaction that may spread
Irritant contact dermatitis requires prior sensitisation before it can occur
Both types require prior sensitisation for the initial reaction
questions.explanation: Allergic contact dermatitis (ACD) is a T-cell-mediated (Type IV) delayed hypersensitivity reaction that occurs only in previously sensitised individuals and characteristically spreads beyond the contact area due to its immunological nature. Irritant contact dermatitis (ICD) is a direct toxic reaction requiring no prior sensitisation and is confined to the area of exposure. Minute amounts of allergen can trigger ACD in sensitised individuals.
questions.question: Which of the following BEST distinguishes allergic contact dermatitis from irritant contact dermatitis?

options: Resting PaO2 persistently below 7.3 kPa on room air
Resting PaO2 above 10 kPa on room air
Oxygen saturation of exactly 95% on room air
FEV1 alone without any oxygen level assessment
questions.explanation: Long-term oxygen therapy is indicated in COPD patients with a resting PaO2 persistently below 7.3 kPa (or below 8 kPa with evidence of cor pulmonale or polycythaemia) measured on room air on at least two occasions when clinically stable, since this level of therapy has been shown to improve survival in this specific patient group by reducing pulmonary hypertension progression. Higher oxygen levels or isolated exertional symptoms alone do not meet this evidence-based threshold for long-term therapy. Correct patient selection is essential since long-term oxygen therapy provides survival benefit specifically in this hypoxaemic population, not in all COPD patients.
questions.question: A patient with cor pulmonale secondary to COPD is assessed for long-term oxygen therapy eligibility. Which specific criterion is MOST commonly used to determine appropriateness of this therapy?

options: Freezing of gait and postural instability
Anosmia, REM behaviour disorder, constipation, depression
questions.question: Non-motor features of Parkinson's disease that may PRECEDE motor symptoms by years are BEST summarised as:
questions.explanation: Non-motor PRODROMAL features of Parkinson's disease that may precede motor symptoms by 5-20 years include: anosmia (Braak stage 1-2), REM sleep behaviour disorder (high predictive value), constipation (enteric nervous system involvement), and depression. These represent Lewy body pathology beginning in olfactory bulb and dorsal vagal nucleus before reaching the substantia nigra.

options: Posterior structures poorly seen on PA view
questions.explanation: The lateral chest X-ray view complements the PA view by better demonstrating posterior structures and specific chamber enlargements, such as left atrial enlargement, that may be obscured on a single frontal projection. The cardiothoracic ratio is calculated from the PA view, not the lateral. This makes the lateral view a useful adjunct in selected cardiac assessments.
questions.question: A patient's chest X-ray lateral view is requested specifically because it is most helpful for assessing:
Grey Turner's sign and Cullen's sign in acute pancreatitis represent:
questions.explanation: Grey Turner's sign is ecchymosis (bruising) in one or both flanks, and Cullen's sign is ecchymosis in the periumbilical region. Both signs result from retroperitoneal haemorrhage tracking through fascial planes and indicate severe haemorrhagic pancreatitis. Their presence signifies a serious prognosis and the need for intensive monitoring.
options: Flank and periumbilical ecchymosis from retroperitoneal haemorrhage respectively
Palpable epigastric mass from pancreatic pseudocyst

questions.question: A patient on anti-tuberculous therapy develops peripheral neuropathy with tingling and numbness in the feet. Which drug is responsible and which supplement prevents this?
questions.explanation: Isoniazid causes peripheral neuropathy by increasing renal excretion of pyridoxine and interfering with its metabolism, which is required for neurotransmitter synthesis in peripheral nerves. Co-administration of pyridoxine (vitamin B6) prevents this complication and is routinely given, especially in malnourished patients, pregnant women and those with diabetes or HIV. Neuropathy is dose-related and more common with higher isoniazid doses.

questions.question: A 70-year-old with diabetes develops sudden painless monocular visual loss described as 'a curtain descending.' Fundoscopy shows a pale, oedematous retina with a 'cherry-red spot.' This MOST represents:
questions.explanation: Sudden painless monocular visual loss with a cherry-red spot at the fovea surrounded by pale (infarcted) retina is the classic presentation of CENTRAL RETINAL ARTERY OCCLUSION ? a retinal stroke. The fovea appears red because it is supplied by the choroidal circulation while the surrounding retina becomes white from ischaemia. Risk factors mirror those for stroke: DM, hypertension, atrial fibrillation.

questions.question: A patient on antiretroviral therapy develops paradoxical worsening of a pre-existing opportunistic infection shortly after starting treatment, due to recovering immune function. What is this phenomenon called?
questions.explanation: Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome occurs when a rapidly recovering immune system mounts an exaggerated inflammatory response against a pre-existing, often subclinical, infection after antiretroviral therapy is started. It typically occurs within weeks to months of treatment initiation and can mimic worsening infection or treatment failure. Management usually involves continuing antiretroviral therapy while treating the underlying infection and using corticosteroids if severe.

questions.question: A child with a 'slapped cheek' facial rash followed by a lacy, reticular rash on the limbs is diagnosed with an infection that can cause aplastic crisis in patients with haemolytic disorders. Which virus is responsible?
questions.explanation: Parvovirus B19 causes erythema infectiosum (fifth disease), characterised by a bright red 'slapped cheek' facial rash followed by a lacy, reticular rash on the trunk and limbs. Because the virus directly infects erythroid progenitor cells, it can precipitate transient aplastic crisis in patients with underlying chronic haemolytic conditions such as sickle cell disease. Infection during pregnancy also carries a risk of fetal hydrops due to severe fetal anaemia.

questions.question: A patient develops acute bacterial meningitis. Which CSF glucose pattern is MOST consistent with pyogenic bacterial meningitis?
questions.explanation: A CSF/plasma glucose ratio BELOW 0.5 (50%) indicates hypoglycorrhachia ? characteristic of bacterial meningitis. A ratio of 0.24 is far below 0.5, indicating severe hypoglycorrhachia. Normal ratio is =0.6. In viral meningitis, glucose is usually normal (ratio 0.6-0.8). In TB and fungal meningitis, glucose is moderately reduced.

questions.question: In the normal conduction pathway, after leaving the SA node, impulses reach the AV node PRIMARILY through:
questions.explanation: After impulse generation at the SA node, electrical activation spreads through both atria via interatrial conduction pathways and internodal tracts to reach the AV node. The AV node then introduces a physiological delay before transmitting the impulse to the bundle of His, bundle branches, and Purkinje fibres to the ventricles. This delay allows atrial contraction to complete before ventricular contraction begins.
options: Direct muscle-to-muscle conduction via working myocytes
Intermodal tracts in the right atrium

questions.explanation: The tricuspid valve is the right-sided atrioventricular valve, separating the right atrium from the right ventricle. It has three leaflets (hence 'tri') and ensures unidirectional blood flow from right atrium into right ventricle. The mitral (bicuspid) valve serves the analogous role on the left side.
questions.question: Which valve separates the right atrium from the right ventricle?

questions.explanation: Keratinocytes undergo a maturation journey from the stratum basalis to the stratum corneum in approximately 28 days. This process involves progressive loss of organelles and nuclei as cells differentiate. Understanding this timeline is clinically important in evaluating treatment responses in conditions like psoriasis.
questions.question: What is the approximate transit time for a basal keratinocyte to reach the stratum corneum?

questions.explanation: Chronic analgesic use, particularly combinations including NSAIDs, reduces renal prostaglandin synthesis, which normally helps maintain adequate blood flow to the relatively hypoxic renal medulla and papillae; this reduction in medullary perfusion over prolonged use can lead to ischaemic papillary necrosis, a recognised complication of analgesic nephropathy. This mechanism, while related to prostaglandin inhibition similarly to other NSAID renal effects, specifically targets the vulnerable medullary microcirculation over chronic use rather than causing acute haemodynamic changes alone. Recognising analgesic nephropathy as a distinct, chronic cause of papillary necrosis is important for identifying and addressing this potentially preventable cause of progressive renal impairment.
questions.question: A patient with long-standing analgesic overuse, including combined aspirin and paracetamol preparations, develops chronic kidney disease with papillary necrosis on imaging. Which mechanism MOST directly explains this analgesic-related renal papillary injury?
options: Increased medullary blood flow causing injury
Direct bacterial infection of the papillae
Direct crystal deposition within papillae only
Direct immune complex deposition in papillae
Reduced medullary blood flow from prostaglandin inhibition

questions.question: Projectile vomiting in a 6-week-old infant is pathognomonic of which condition?
questions.explanation: Projectile vomiting in an infant is pathognomonic of infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (IHPS). The hypertrophied pyloric muscle causes gastric outlet obstruction, leading to forceful, non-bilious vomiting. This is a surgical emergency requiring pyloromyotomy.

options: Excessive, dysregulated immune activation and cytokine release
Simple dehydration causing inflammatory markers to rise
Complete absence of any immune response
Isolated allergic reaction to the virus
questions.explanation: Severe COVID-19 can trigger a dysregulated, excessive immune response with massive release of pro-inflammatory cytokines, termed a cytokine storm, contributing to widespread tissue damage and multi-organ dysfunction. This differs from a normal, well-regulated immune response to infection. Recognising this mechanism has guided the use of immunomodulatory therapies such as corticosteroids in severe disease.
questions.question: A critically ill COVID-19 patient develops a hyperinflammatory state with markedly elevated inflammatory markers. This cytokine storm results primarily from which mechanism?

options: Repetitive nerve stimulation showing decremental response, PLUS single-fibre EMG showing increased jitter
questions.explanation: Electrophysiological confirmation of MG: (1) REPETITIVE NERVE STIMULATION showing =10% DECREMENTAL response (75-80% sensitive for generalised MG); and (2) SINGLE-FIBRE EMG (most sensitive test ? 95%) showing increased JITTER. Anti-MuSK antibodies are important but electrophysiology confirms diagnosis even when antibodies are negative.
questions.question: What is the MOST appropriate investigation to confirm MG in a patient with fatigable ptosis and negative anti-AChR antibodies?

questions.explanation: Colicky pain from hollow viscus obstruction becoming CONSTANT indicates strangulation ? ischaemia of the obstructed bowel wall from vascular compromise. This is a surgical emergency. Pure obstruction causes intermittent colicky pain; strangulation adds constant pain, fever, peritonism, and systemic sepsis indicating bowel necrosis.
questions.question: A patient develops colicky abdominal pain becoming constant, associated with fever and peritonism. Which transition in pain character indicates progression from simple obstruction to strangulation?
options: Pain changing from epigastric to umbilical
Colicky pain becoming constant, indicating strangulation
Pain radiating to the back suggesting pancreatic involvement
Pain relieved by vomiting suggesting psychogenic cause
Pain worsened by eating indicating peptic ulcer

questions.question: A patient with Parkinson's disease demonstrates increased resistance to passive limb movement with a ratchet-like, jerky quality. This finding is termed:
options: Flaccidity of lower motor neuron origin
questions.explanation: Cog-wheeling rigidity, a ratchet-like resistance felt during passive movement often combined with an underlying tremor, is characteristic of parkinsonism, reflecting increased basal ganglia-mediated muscle tone. This differs from the velocity-dependent resistance of pyramidal spasticity. Recognising this specific quality of rigidity supports clinical diagnosis of Parkinson's disease or related parkinsonian syndromes.

options: Neural tube defects and neurodevelopmental delay
questions.question: Valproate is used for multiple seizure types. Which TERATOGENIC risk is MOST important to counsel women of childbearing age about before prescribing?
questions.explanation: Sodium valproate is a MAJOR TERATOGEN. Neural tube defects (spina bifida ? 1-3%) and NEURODEVELOPMENTAL effects (10-40% of children have cognitive impairment, autism, or developmental delay) are the most significant risks. Valproate should be AVOIDED in women of childbearing potential unless no alternatives exist, with mandatory contraception and risk disclosure.

Lithium is one of the most well-established drugs known to precipitate or exacerbate psoriasis. Other significant culprits include beta-blockers, antimalarial agents, systemic steroids (rebound effect on withdrawal), and interferon. Patients with psoriasis should be counselled about these triggers, and alternative medications considered where clinically feasible.
questions.question: Which drug is MOST commonly associated with precipitating or exacerbating psoriasis?

A patient's examination shows impaired ability to name common objects despite intact vision and comprehension, along with right-left confusion. This combination would most strongly suggest a lesion in which hemisphere?
questions.explanation: Language-related deficits such as anomia, along with features of Gerstmann syndrome including right-left confusion, typically localise to the dominant, usually left, cerebral hemisphere, reflecting its specialisation for language and certain calculation and spatial functions. Non-dominant hemisphere lesions more typically produce neglect and visuospatial deficits instead. Recognising hemisphere-specific deficit patterns aids accurate localisation.

questions.question: A patient with chronic hypercapnic respiratory failure secondary to severe kyphoscoliosis is being evaluated for long-term ventilatory support. Which underlying mechanism MOST directly explains his hypoventilation in this condition?
options: Primary alveolar destruction impairing gas exchange
Primary neuromuscular junction failure impairing effort
Restricted chest wall movement impairing ventilation
Primary pulmonary vascular disease impairing perfusion
questions.explanation: Severe kyphoscoliosis mechanically restricts normal chest wall expansion, reducing effective tidal volume and increasing the work of breathing, eventually leading to chronic alveolar hypoventilation and hypercapnic respiratory failure, distinct from the alveolar or airway pathology seen in intrinsic lung diseases such as COPD or pulmonary fibrosis. This restrictive chest wall mechanism explains why long-term nocturnal non-invasive ventilation is often an effective supportive treatment, by mechanically assisting the impaired ventilatory pump rather than treating lung parenchymal disease. Recognising this distinct pathophysiological category guides appropriate respiratory support strategy selection.

options: Trauma-induced epidermal hyperproliferation at the basal layer
Vascular thrombosis at the trauma site
questions.explanation: The Köbner phenomenon occurs in both psoriasis and lichen planus because cutaneous trauma triggers a shared cascade of basal keratinocyte hyperproliferation and inflammatory cell recruitment in genetically predisposed skin. This explains why new, disease-specific lesions appear at sites of injury in either condition. Wickham's striae and Munro microabscesses are instead specific histological features unique to lichen planus and psoriasis respectively, not the shared trauma-response mechanism.
questions.question: A patient with psoriasis notices new plaques developing precisely along a recent surgical scar. Which shared pathological mechanism links this finding to a similar phenomenon seen in lichen planus?

questions.explanation: Uraemic pericarditis is an absolute indication for urgent initiation of renal replacement therapy, as it reflects severe uraemic toxicity that can progress to pericardial effusion and tamponade if untreated, and typically resolves with adequate dialysis rather than anti-inflammatory medications alone, which do not address the underlying uraemic cause. NSAIDs should also be used cautiously given the risk of further renal impairment and bleeding in uraemic patients. Recognising uraemic pericarditis as a dialysis-urgent complication, rather than a condition to manage symptomatically, is an essential clinical teaching point.
questions.question: A patient with chronic kidney disease stage 5 not yet on dialysis develops uraemic pericarditis with a pericardial friction rub and chest pain. What is the MOST appropriate definitive management for this complication?
options: High-dose oral corticosteroids as definitive treatment
Oral colchicine alone as definitive treatment

questions.explanation: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is a leading cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes, characterised by asymmetric septal hypertrophy causing outflow obstruction and arrhythmia risk. Intense exertion can precipitate fatal ventricular arrhythmias in undiagnosed cases. Pre-participation echocardiographic screening can detect this abnormality.
questions.question: A young athlete collapses during a marathon. Post-mortem echocardiography would most likely reveal asymmetric septal hypertrophy in which underlying condition?
Zanamivir exerts its antiviral effect against influenza by which mechanism?
options: Preventing viral uncoating inside host cells
questions.explanation: Zanamivir inhibits the neuraminidase surface enzyme of influenza A and B viruses, preventing new viral particles from being released from infected host cells and limiting spread. It is delivered by dry powder inhalation and reduces symptom duration and complications in high-risk patients. Oseltamivir has the same mechanism but is orally administered.

Chronic eczema is characterised histologically by acanthosis, thickening of the epidermis with elongated rete ridges, reflecting a prolonged reparative and hyperproliferative response to ongoing inflammation. Acute eczema, by contrast, is dominated by spongiosis and intraepidermal vesicle formation from intercellular oedema. Recognising which histological pattern predominates helps correlate clinical stage with underlying pathology.
questions.question: A patient with eczema is being taught the difference between acute and chronic disease stages. Which histological feature predominates in CHRONIC rather than acute eczema?

questions.explanation: As potassium rises, ECG changes progress from peaked T waves ? prolonged PR interval ? widened QRS ? sine wave pattern ? ventricular fibrillation. The broad complex sine wave pattern represents severe, potentially fatal hyperkalemia requiring immediate treatment (IV calcium gluconate, insulin/glucose, sodium bicarbonate) and urgent RRT. Peaked T waves alone are an earlier, less immediately dangerous sign.
questions.question: Hyperkalemia in AKI is a renal replacement therapy (RRT) indication. Which ECG change is MOST URGENTLY alarming for hyperkalemia?
options: Broad complex rhythm, sine wave pattern

questions.question: During high-quality CPR in adults, chest compressions should be performed at a rate of:
questions.explanation: Current resuscitation guidelines recommend performing chest compressions at a rate of 100–120 compressions per minute during CPR in adults. This rate optimises coronary and cerebral perfusion pressure. The compression depth should be at least 5 cm (2 inches) with full chest recoil allowed between compressions. The ratio of compressions to ventilations is 30:2 for healthcare providers.

questions.question: A patient at high risk of tumour lysis syndrome before chemotherapy is given prophylactic rasburicase. Which mechanism MOST directly explains how this agent reduces the risk of associated acute kidney injury?
questions.explanation: Rasburicase is a recombinant urate oxidase enzyme that converts uric acid into the more soluble compound allantoin, which is more readily excreted by the kidneys, reducing the risk of uric acid crystal precipitation and consequent acute kidney injury during tumour lysis syndrome. This differs from allopurinol, which instead reduces new uric acid production by inhibiting xanthine oxidase but does not break down existing uric acid. Understanding this distinct enzymatic mechanism explains why rasburicase is often preferred for rapid uric acid reduction in high-risk tumour lysis situations.
options: Enzymatic breakdown of uric acid into soluble allantoin
Increased renal blood flow independent of uric acid
Direct chelation of released phosphate ions
Direct binding and removal of potassium ions

questions.explanation: SCLC exhibits aggressive behaviour with rapid growth and early spread to distant sites, exquisite sensitivity to chemotherapy and radiation, and frequent association with paraneoplastic syndromes (SIADH, Cushing's, Lambert-Eaton). Unlike NSCLC, surgery is rarely appropriate because SCLC is usually disseminated at diagnosis. Untreated median survival is only 3 months.
options: Exquisite sensitivity to surgery as primary treatment
Tendency to exfoliate cells into sputum
questions.question: Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) is MOST distinct from non-small cell lung cancer because of which characteristic?

questions.explanation: The enzyme 5-alpha reductase converts weaker androgens (particularly testosterone) to dihydrotestosterone (DHT) within sebaceous glands. DHT is significantly more potent than testosterone in stimulating sebaceous gland activity and sebum production. This explains why anti-androgenic agents like finasteride (5-alpha reductase inhibitors) can be effective in androgen-driven acne.
questions.question: In the pathogenesis of acne, the enzyme 5-alpha reductase within the skin converts weaker androgens to which potent androgen?

questions.explanation: Murphy's sign—inspiratory arrest during deep right subcostal palpation due to pain—is the hallmark of acute cholecystitis, indicating inflammation of the gallbladder. A positive sign occurs when the inflamed gallbladder descends against the examiner's fingers during inspiration.
questions.question: A positive Murphy's sign on abdominal palpation is most specific for which condition?
The Starling curve in heart failure is SHIFTED in which direction compared to normal?
options: Upward and to the right only
questions.explanation: In heart failure, the Frank-Starling curve is flattened and shifted downward and to the right, meaning for any given filling pressure (preload), the cardiac output is reduced compared to a normal heart. The diseased heart can still show some preload-dependent increase in output but reaches a plateau at lower levels. This is the basis for understanding why diuresis helps—reducing excessive preload.

options: To calculate total body fat percentage directly
To replace the need for BMI measurement entirely
questions.question: A clinician measures a patient's waist and hip circumference as part of an obesity assessment. What is the primary purpose of calculating the waist-hip ratio in this context?
questions.explanation: The waist-hip ratio is used as a surrogate marker of central, visceral fat distribution, which correlates more strongly with cardiometabolic risk than total body fat or BMI alone. It does not measure total body fat percentage directly and is used alongside, rather than as a replacement for, BMI in comprehensive obesity assessment. A higher ratio indicates greater central adiposity and increased cardiovascular risk.

questions.question: A 16-year-old has seizures provoked only by flickering light or TV screens. Under ILAE 2009 classification, the aetiology is BEST categorised as:
questions.explanation: Photosensitive epilepsy (seizures triggered by flickering light) is classified as GENETIC epilepsy with a REFLEX trigger in the 2010 ILAE paradigm. The photoparoxysmal EEG response is a genetically determined trait. Valproate is first-line; carbamazepine is contraindicated. Patients should avoid flickering lights, computer games, and video patterns.

In central diabetes insipidus, the kidneys retain their ability to respond to ADH, so administering desmopressin (a synthetic ADH analogue) results in appropriate urine concentration, confirming a deficiency of endogenous ADH secretion rather than renal resistance. Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus would show no such response due to renal insensitivity to ADH. This distinction guides appropriate treatment selection.
questions.question: A patient with excessive thirst and dilute urine is found to have an intact response to desmopressin, with urine concentrating appropriately after administration. This confirms the diagnosis of:
A patient's hormonal regulation of thirst and water balance is primarily governed by which axis?
questions.explanation: Thirst and water balance are primarily regulated through the hypothalamic-posterior pituitary axis via antidiuretic hormone, which controls renal water reabsorption in response to plasma osmolality changes. While the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system also contributes to volume regulation, ADH is the principal hormone specifically governing water balance. Disorders of this axis include diabetes insipidus and SIADH.

questions.question: A patient with severe hyponatraemia of 108 mmol/L presenting with seizures is treated with hypertonic saline. Which complication is MOST important to avoid by not correcting the sodium too rapidly?
questions.explanation: Rapid correction of chronic severe hyponatraemia risks osmotic demyelination syndrome, a serious and often irreversible neurological injury caused by rapid osmotic shifts damaging myelin in the pons and other brain regions, so sodium correction is carefully limited to a maximum recommended rate, typically no more than 8-10 mmol/L in 24 hours in chronic cases. Acute, symptomatic hyponatraemia with seizures does warrant initial rapid partial correction with hypertonic saline, but subsequent correction must still be carefully controlled. Recognising this risk underpins the cautious, staged approach to correcting significant hyponatraemia.

questions.question: Which risk factor for gastric carcinoma is associated with the HIGHEST attributable risk, making it the most important modifiable cause?
questions.explanation: H. pylori infection is the most important risk factor for gastric adenocarcinoma, classified as a Group I carcinogen by WHO. It causes chronic atrophic gastritis progressing through intestinal metaplasia to dysplasia and carcinoma (Correa cascade). Eradication reduces but does not eliminate risk. H. pylori has the highest population-attributable risk of all risk factors.

questions.question: A patient is counselled on exercise recommendations for sustained weight reduction. According to standard sports medicine guidance, what is the minimum recommended weekly exercise duration for meaningful weight reduction in obese patients?
questions.explanation: Standard exercise guidance for meaningful weight reduction in obese patients recommends approximately 150 to 250 minutes of moderate-intensity activity per week, an amount shown to produce measurable weight loss and improved cardiometabolic risk when combined with dietary change. Lower durations are generally more appropriate for general health maintenance rather than active weight reduction. This guidance underpins structured lifestyle intervention programmes for obesity.

questions.question: The 'peek sign' in myasthenia gravis refers to which clinical observation indicating incomplete orbicularis oculi closure?
questions.explanation: The 'peek sign' is observed when asking the patient to close their eyes tightly: in MG, eyelid closure is incomplete due to orbicularis oculi weakness, and the SCLERA IS VISIBLE between the lids (the eyes 'peek'). This sign of eyelid closure weakness is distinct from ptosis (levator weakness). It is a useful bedside test for orbicularis weakness in suspected MG.
options: Downward deviation of the eye on upgaze
Sclera visible between partially closed eyelids

questions.question: A patient with acute kidney injury is found to have a fractional excretion of sodium below 1%. Which category of AKI does this finding MOST strongly suggest?
questions.explanation: A fractional excretion of sodium below 1% suggests intact tubular sodium reabsorption in response to reduced renal perfusion, characteristic of prerenal AKI where the kidney tubules remain functionally intact but underperfused. In contrast, acute tubular necrosis typically shows a fractional excretion of sodium above 2% due to impaired tubular reabsorptive capacity. This distinction helps guide whether fluid resuscitation (prerenal) or supportive management of intrinsic damage (ATN) is the appropriate initial approach.

questions.question: A patient with chronic hepatitis C is being evaluated for treatment. Which class of drugs has revolutionised cure rates by achieving sustained virological response in most patients?
questions.explanation: Direct-acting antivirals, which target specific steps of the hepatitis C viral lifecycle such as the NS3/4A protease, NS5A and NS5B polymerase, have transformed hepatitis C treatment, achieving sustained virological response (functional cure) in over 95% of patients with short, well-tolerated oral regimens. This represents a dramatic improvement over older interferon-based regimens, which had lower efficacy and significant side effects. Hepatitis C, unlike hepatitis B, can now be cured rather than only suppressed.

ACTIVE HBV REPLICATION is determined by HBeAg positivity, HIGH HBV DNA levels (>2000 IU/mL for treatment threshold), and ELEVATED ALT (indicating ongoing hepatocellular damage). The INACTIVE CARRIER state has HBeAg-negative, anti-HBe positive, low/undetectable HBV DNA, and NORMAL ALT. This distinction is critical for deciding who needs antiviral treatment (entecavir, tenofovir).
options: HBeAg status and HBV DNA level
questions.question: In Hepatitis B, the key difference between chronic hepatitis B with HIGH viral replication versus inactive carrier state is BEST determined by:

options: A lower motor neuron facial palsy
An upper motor neuron facial palsy
questions.question: A patient has facial weakness affecting only the lower half of one side of the face, sparing the forehead, which can still wrinkle normally. This pattern indicates:
questions.explanation: In upper motor neuron facial palsy, the forehead is spared due to bilateral cortical innervation of the upper facial muscles, so only the lower face is weak, contralateral to the cortical lesion. In contrast, a lower motor neuron facial palsy (such as Bell's palsy) affects the entire ipsilateral face including the forehead. This distinction is a classic and clinically important localising sign.

Septic arthritis is a medical emergency because bacterial enzymes and the host inflammatory response can destroy articular cartilage within days, leading to permanent joint damage if treatment is delayed. Joint aspiration for synovial fluid analysis and culture should be performed urgently before starting empirical antibiotics whenever possible. Staphylococcus aureus is the most common causative organism in adults.
options: Risk of irreversible cartilage destruction from septic arthritis
Risk of avascular necrosis only in the hip
questions.question: A patient presents with a hot, swollen, acutely painful single joint with restricted range of movement and fever. Joint aspiration is planned. What is the MOST urgent reason for rapid diagnosis and treatment?

questions.explanation: Chronic subdural haematoma typically occurs in the elderly because cerebral atrophy stretches the bridging veins, making them more susceptible to rupture even after minor trauma. The gradual accumulation of blood over weeks explains the delayed and often subtle presentation with headache and cognitive change. This must be distinguished from acute subdural haematoma, which presents rapidly after major trauma.
questions.question: A patient with a subdural haematoma from a fall three weeks ago now presents with progressive headache and confusion, worse than expected for a minor injury of that age. Which population is MOST at risk of this delayed presentation?

questions.explanation: A persistently worsening pH despite appropriately optimised non-invasive ventilation settings indicates failure of this modality to adequately support the patient's ventilation, and should prompt consideration of invasive mechanical ventilation to prevent further deterioration and potential respiratory arrest. Improving parameters, including pH, PaCO2, oxygenation, and clinical distress, instead indicate successful response to non-invasive support. Regular reassessment with blood gases within the first hours of initiating non-invasive ventilation is essential to identify early treatment failure requiring escalation.
questions.question: A patient with type 2 respiratory failure is monitored using serial arterial blood gases during non-invasive ventilation. Which specific parameter trend would MOST strongly indicate a need to consider invasive mechanical ventilation instead?
options: Stable pH with improving oxygen saturation
Mild persistent hypoxaemia with normal pH
Persistently worsening pH despite optimised NIV settings
Gradually improving PaCO2 over several hours
Improving respiratory rate and reduced distress
Sickle cell disease causing sickling crises
questions.explanation: The direct Coombs test detects IgG antibodies or complement fixed to the surface of red blood cells. It is positive in autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (warm AIHA), drug-induced haemolysis (methyldopa, penicillin), and haemolytic disease of the newborn. In HUS/TTP and G6PD deficiency, the Coombs test is negative (non-immune haemolysis). This distinguishes immune from non-immune causes of haemolytic anaemia.
questions.question: Direct Coombs test (direct antiglobulin test) is positive in haemolytic anaemia associated with:

options: Direct viral invasion of coagulation factor-producing hepatocytes
Suppression of anticoagulant protein C and protein S exclusively
Viral integration into platelet DNA causing thrombocytosis
Cytokine-mediated endothelial damage, activation of coagulation cascade, consumption of clotting factors, and hypercoagulable state ? evidenced by markedly elevated D-dimer
questions.explanation: COVID-19 causes a HYPERCOAGULABLE STATE through: (1) CYTOKINE STORM causing widespread ENDOTHELIAL DAMAGE activating coagulation; (2) INFLAMMATORY MEDIATORS stimulate tissue factor expression; (3) PLATELET ACTIVATION by virus; (4) CONSUMPTION of coagulation factors (DIC pattern). The result is dramatically elevated D-dimer and marked thromboembolic risk. Therapeutic anticoagulation is used in hospitalised patients.
questions.question: What is the SPECIFIC mechanism by which SARS-CoV-2 disrupts the coagulation system, contributing to the high rate of thromboembolic complications?

questions.explanation: Aldosterone is synthesised in the outermost zona glomerulosa of the adrenal cortex, which lacks the enzyme required for cortisol synthesis but possesses aldosterone synthase. Cortisol is instead produced in the zona fasciculata, and androgens in the zona reticularis. This zonal specialisation underlies the distinct regulation of each hormone class.
questions.question: A biochemistry review of the adrenal cortex confirms that aldosterone is produced by which specific zone?

questions.explanation: The left atrium receives oxygenated blood from the four pulmonary veins after blood has been oxygenated in the lungs. From the left atrium, blood flows through the mitral valve into the left ventricle, and then is ejected into the aorta for systemic circulation. The right atrium receives deoxygenated blood from the systemic circulation via the superior and inferior venae cavae.
questions.question: Which cardiac chamber receives oxygenated blood directly from the pulmonary veins?
The '4 Ps' of lichen planus describe the characteristic lesion. Which set correctly represents ALL four Ps?
questions.explanation: The classic '4 Ps' of lichen planus are Pruritic, Polyglonal (irregular polygon shape), Purple (or gray in dark-skinned individuals), and Papule. Wickham's striae (fine white reticulate network) are an additional characteristic feature seen with the application of mineral oil or under a dermatoscope. These features help distinguish LP from other papulosquamous conditions.

BB leprosy is the most immunologically unstable part of the spectrum. Without treatment, patients tend to downgrade towards the lepromatous end (LL), reflecting declining CMI. With treatment or spontaneously, they may upgrade toward the tuberculoid end as a reversal (Type 1) reaction. The annular lesions with a punched-out centre are characteristic of BB disease.
questions.question: In the Ridley & Jopling classification, borderline (BB) leprosy is described as 'the most unstable part of the spectrum.' This means BB patients tend to:
options: Remain stable throughout their disease course
Downgrade towards lepromatous leprosy if untreated or upgrade as a reversal reaction
Always progress to pure neural leprosy
Develop ENL more commonly than Type 1 reactions

questions.explanation: Uraemic fetor (ammonia-like breath odour from urea breakdown by oral bacteria) and uraemic frost (white crystalline deposits on skin from urea precipitation as sweat evaporates) are features of advanced (severe) renal failure. Other features of severe uraemia include asterixis (flapping tremor), pericarditis, encephalopathy, and Kussmaul breathing from metabolic acidosis.
questions.question: Uraemic fetor and frost are features of which stage of renal disease?

A patient with suspected acute interstitial nephritis has the causative antibiotic stopped. Which additional treatment is MOST commonly considered if renal function does not improve within a few days of drug withdrawal?
questions.explanation: If renal function does not improve promptly after stopping the causative drug in acute interstitial nephritis, a short course of corticosteroids is often considered to reduce ongoing interstitial inflammation and improve renal recovery, based on observational evidence, though robust randomised trial data remains limited. More aggressive immunosuppression such as cyclophosphamide is not routinely used for this generally reversible, drug-induced condition. Recognising drug withdrawal as the primary intervention, with steroids as an adjunct for incomplete recovery, guides appropriate stepwise management.

Cortisol (glucocorticoid) is produced predominantly in the zona fasciculata, the middle and largest zone of the adrenal cortex. Its secretion is regulated by ACTH from the anterior pituitary, which is in turn regulated by CRH from the hypothalamus. Cortisol has broad metabolic effects including gluconeogenesis, anti-inflammatory action, and immunosuppression. Its secretion follows a circadian rhythm with peak levels in early morning.
questions.question: Cortisol is produced MAINLY in which zone of the adrenal cortex?

A teenager presents with well-defined pink patches with fine scale limited to the soles and weight-bearing areas of the feet, worse in trainers, sparing the web spaces, with negative skin scrapings for fungal elements. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Juvenile plantar dermatosis characteristically affects the weight-bearing forefoot and sole with glazed erythema, sparing the web spaces, and is linked to occlusive footwear and sweating rather than fungal infection, distinguishing it from tinea pedis, which usually involves the web spaces and shows positive scrapings. This clinical and mycological distinction avoids unnecessary antifungal treatment. Contact dermatitis to dyes would more likely correspond to the shoe's contact pattern rather than weight-bearing zones specifically.

questions.question: The clinical triad of anorexia, asthenia, and anaemia (3As) is most associated with which GI malignancy?
questions.explanation: The 3As—anorexia, asthenia (weakness), and anaemia—constitute a classic non-specific presentation of gastric carcinoma. This triad often causes diagnostic delay as symptoms mimic benign gastritis. High index of clinical suspicion is required, especially in patients over 40 with new dyspeptic symptoms.

questions.question: A 60-year-old smoker with COPD has a room-air ABG showing PaO2 55 mmHg and PaCO2 50 mmHg with compensated pH. Which oxygen delivery approach is MOST appropriate to avoid worsening his hypercapnia?
options: High-flow oxygen to achieve saturation above 98%
No supplemental oxygen regardless of saturation
Controlled low-flow oxygen with target saturation 88-92%
Oxygen only during sleep at high flow
questions.explanation: In chronic CO2 retainers, controlled low-flow oxygen aimed at a target saturation of 88-92% avoids suppressing the hypoxic respiratory drive and worsening hypercapnic respiratory failure, while still correcting dangerous hypoxaemia. High-flow oxygen aiming for near-normal saturation can precipitate acute respiratory acidosis in this group. Titrated oxygen therapy with regular ABG monitoring is standard practice in acute COPD exacerbations.

Struvite stones, composed of magnesium ammonium phosphate, form in alkaline urine generated by urease-producing bacteria such as Proteus mirabilis, which hydrolyse urea to ammonia, and characteristically grow rapidly to fill the renal pelvis and calyces as staghorn calculi. Effective treatment requires both stone removal and eradication of the underlying infection to prevent recurrence. Recognising this infection-stone relationship guides both urological and antimicrobial management strategies.
questions.question: A patient with a large staghorn calculus is found to have recurrent urinary tract infections with urease-producing organisms such as Proteus. Which stone composition is MOST characteristically associated with this presentation?

questions.explanation: Petechiae are punctate haemorrhagic spots approximately 1-2mm in diameter representing small foci of bleeding. Ecchymoses (bruises) are macular areas of haemorrhage greater than 2mm. Purpura refers to elevated blood-filled lesions. These distinctions are important in assessing coagulation disorders and vasculitis.
questions.question: Petechiae are defined as punctate haemorrhagic spots of approximately what diameter?

questions.explanation: AIDS is defined by either a CD4+ T cell count below 200 cells/µL OR the presence of an AIDS-defining illness. Below 200 cells/µL, prophylaxis for PCP and other opportunistic infections is mandatory. Below 50 cells/µL, MAC prophylaxis is added. The CD4:CD8 ratio also falls progressively in HIV disease.
questions.question: A 22-year-old with HIV presents with CD4 count 180 cells/µL. Which CD4 count level is used for the defining threshold for AIDS diagnosis?

questions.explanation: Ethambutol carries a specific risk of optic neuritis, causing reduced visual acuity and impaired red-green colour discrimination, so baseline and periodic visual assessment is recommended during treatment, with prompt discontinuation if visual changes occur. Isoniazid is instead associated with peripheral neuropathy, mitigated by co-administered pyridoxine. Rifampicin is notable for hepatotoxicity and orange discolouration of body fluids, a different monitoring concern.
questions.question: A patient newly diagnosed with pulmonary tuberculosis is started on standard four-drug therapy. Which drug in this regimen MOST specifically requires baseline and ongoing visual acuity and colour vision monitoring?

questions.explanation: Alport's syndrome is a hereditary nephritis caused by mutations in type IV collagen (COL4A3, A4, A5 genes). The classic triad includes progressive renal failure, sensorineural hearing loss (nerve deafness), and ocular abnormalities (anterior lenticonus). It is X-linked in most cases (COL4A5), affecting males more severely. Electron microscopy shows characteristic thinning and thickening/splitting of the GBM.
questions.question: Alport's syndrome is an inherited glomerular disease characteristically associated with which combination?
options: Renal failure, nerve deafness, ocular abnormalities
Minimal change disease with nephrotic syndrome
Positive hair pull test over the entire scalp
questions.question: A young woman on tight braided hairstyles for years develops thinning specifically at the frontal and temporal hairline with retained fine hairs closer to the margin. Examination confirms no scalp scarring elsewhere. What pathognomonic sign supports the diagnosis of traction alopecia?
questions.explanation: The fringe sign, retention of a thin rim of hair along an otherwise receded frontal or temporal margin, is described as pathognomonic for traction alopecia resulting from chronic mechanical tension on hair follicles. Exclamation mark hairs and yellow dots are instead classic trichoscopic features of alopecia areata. Recognising the fringe sign helps direct a change in hairstyling practice before permanent scarring develops.

In androgenetic alopecia, dihydrotestosterone acts on genetically susceptible follicles to progressively shorten the anagen phase and shrink follicle size over successive cycles, a process termed miniaturisation that converts terminal hairs into vellus-like hairs. This differs from scarring processes, which permanently destroy the follicle rather than shrink it. Because the follicle is preserved, miniaturisation is potentially responsive to treatments like minoxidil and finasteride.
questions.question: A man with male pattern hair loss is told the underlying process involves progressive shortening of the anagen phase and shrinkage of hair follicle size over successive cycles. What is this process called?

questions.explanation: Cyclosporine is a calcineurin inhibitor that selectively suppresses T-lymphocyte activation by blocking the calcineurin-dependent transcription of interleukin-2 and other inflammatory cytokines. It is highly effective for severe psoriasis but is limited by nephrotoxicity and hypertension with long-term use, necessitating regular monitoring of renal function and blood pressure.
questions.question: Which systemic agent for psoriasis works by selectively inhibiting calcineurin, thereby blocking T-lymphocyte activation?

questions.explanation: The zona reticularis is the innermost layer of the adrenal cortex and produces androgens, mainly dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) and DHEA sulfate (DHEA-S). These weak androgens are converted peripherally to testosterone and oestrogen. In females, adrenal androgens contribute to libido and secondary sexual characteristics. Excess androgen production (e.g., in congenital adrenal hyperplasia or adrenal tumours) causes virilisation in women.
questions.question: Which zone of the adrenal cortex produces DHEA and DHEA-sulfate (androgens)?
A patient has diabetes mellitus with thyrotoxicosis and Addison's disease. This combination of multiple gland failures suggests:
options: Secondary endocrine failure from a single pituitary adenoma
questions.explanation: The simultaneous failure of multiple endocrine glands due to autoimmune destruction is called Autoimmune Polyglandular Syndrome (APS). APS Type II (Schmidt syndrome) typically includes Addison's disease with either thyroid autoimmunity (Graves' or Hashimoto's) and/or Type 1 diabetes mellitus. This is distinct from MEN syndrome, where multiple endocrine tumours (hyperfunction) occur. APS Type I (APECED) is rarer and includes hypoparathyroidism and adrenal failure.

Borderline (BB) leprosy is the MOST IMMUNOLOGICALLY UNSTABLE position on the leprosy spectrum. Without treatment, BB patients typically DOWNGRADE toward lepromatous leprosy. With reversal reactions, they may move toward tuberculoid. BB skin lesions are annular with broad irregular borders and characteristic punched-out centres. The instability makes BB particularly important to identify and treat promptly.
options: Most stable part of the spectrum near tuberculoid pole
Most unstable spectrum position; downgrades toward LL
Exclusively neural leprosy without skin lesions
questions.question: Borderline (BB) leprosy has a characteristic annular ring-shaped lesion with a 'punched-out' centre. Which immunological position does BB represent on the leprosy spectrum?

questions.explanation: Pterygium unguis (forward growth of the proximal nail fold onto the nail plate) is the most characteristic nail change of lichen planus. It results from destruction of the nail matrix by the inflammatory process, causing the nail fold to adhere to the nail plate. Other nail LP features include longitudinal ridging, thinning, and anonychia in severe cases.
questions.question: Pterygium formation of the nail is MOST characteristic of which condition?

questions.explanation: In LEMS, reflexes are ABSENT or reduced at rest but TRANSIENTLY RETURN (post-tetanic potentiation) after brief sustained muscle contraction as calcium accumulates presynaptically. This characteristic ? absent reflexes that transiently normalise post-exercise ? is unique to LEMS and distinguishes it from MG (where reflexes are preserved). Electrophysiology confirms this finding.
options: Reflexes absent in LEMS but transiently return after contraction
Both conditions show absent reflexes that do not return with activity
Reflexes are brisk in MG and absent in LEMS regardless of activity
Both conditions have normal reflexes throughout
MG shows brisk reflexes and LEMS shows diminished reflexes unaffected by exercise
questions.question: Which statement about reflexes in LEMS versus MG is MOST accurate?

questions.explanation: Normal arterial oxygen saturation (SaO2) is 95-100%. A value of 85-90% would indicate significant hypoxaemia requiring urgent assessment. The other values listed—PaO2 80-100 mmHg, PaCO2 35-45 mmHg, pH 7.35-7.45, and HCO3 20-30 mmol/L—are all within the normal physiological range.
questions.question: Normal arterial blood gas values include all of the following EXCEPT:

questions.explanation: Pink frothy sputum, bilateral basal crackles, orthopnoea, and marked hypoxia describe acute pulmonary oedema. Immediate management includes: sitting the patient upright, high-flow oxygen (face mask), IV furosemide (40-80mg) for fluid removal, and nitrates (GTN spray/infusion) to reduce preload. Morphine reduces anxiety and preload. If refractory, NIV (CPAP) or intubation may be required.
questions.question: A patient with progressive breathlessness has exertional dyspnoea, bilateral basal crackles, and pink frothy sputum. SpO2 is 82%. The MOST appropriate immediate treatment is:

questions.explanation: PTRA with stenting is both the definitive diagnostic and therapeutic procedure for haemodynamically significant renal artery stenosis. Under fluoroscopic guidance, a catheter crosses the stenotic lesion, balloon dilation opens the artery, and a stent maintains patency. It can cure renovascular hypertension in fibromuscular dysplasia and may improve BP control in atherosclerotic stenosis. CT angiography and duplex USS diagnose but don't treat the lesion.
questions.question: In a patient with suspected renal artery stenosis causing renovascular hypertension, which investigation provides both diagnosis AND potential treatment?

questions.explanation: Prevention of calcium oxalate/phosphate stones: (1) High fluid intake to dilute urine (>2.5L/day), reducing stone crystallisation. (2) Thiazide diuretics reduce urinary calcium excretion by increasing tubular reabsorption. (3) Adequate dietary calcium (not restriction)—calcium binds dietary oxalate in the gut, reducing oxalate absorption and urinary excretion. Citrate supplementation inhibits crystal formation. Avoiding excess oxalate foods (spinach, nuts) is also helpful.
options: High oxalate diet and calcium restriction
Alkalinising urine with citrate for all stone types equally
High fluid intake, thiazides, and dietary calcium with meals
Vitamin D supplementation to improve calcium absorption
Protein-rich diet to reduce urinary calcium excretion
questions.question: Urinary calcium oxalate or calcium phosphate stones can be PREVENTED by which dietary and pharmacological measures?

questions.explanation: In pyogenic liver abscess, alkaline phosphatase is characteristically elevated disproportionately compared to aminotransferases, reflecting biliary canalicular inflammation rather than hepatocellular necrosis. This pattern helps distinguish abscess from viral or alcoholic hepatitis on initial LFT interpretation.
questions.question: Alkaline phosphatase is disproportionately elevated compared to aminotransferases in which hepatic condition?
Which finding on inspection of a patient before formal examination most reliably suggests a focal CNS lesion?
questions.explanation: Neglect of one side of the body (hemispatial neglect) is a focal cortical sign indicating non-dominant parietal lobe pathology, detectable on mere inspection. It localizes the lesion before formal examination begins. Other options reflect systemic rather than focal CNS pathology.

questions.question: A patient undergoing chemotherapy notices near-total scalp hair loss within two to three weeks of starting treatment, far more rapidly than typical postpartum shedding. What mechanism explains this rapid pattern?
questions.explanation: Anagen effluvium results from a toxic insult, such as chemotherapy, abruptly halting mitotic activity in actively growing anagen follicles, causing rapid, extensive hair loss within days to a few weeks, in contrast to the delayed shedding of telogen effluvium which follows a lag of around two to three months. This rapid timeline is the key distinguishing clinical feature. Hair regrowth typically follows once the offending agent is stopped.
options: Abrupt arrest of actively growing (anagen) follicles
Premature conversion of follicles to telogen phase
Chronic traction on the hair shaft

questions.question: A patient with Parkinson's disease is noted to have progressively smaller handwriting as they continue writing a sentence. This finding is termed:
questions.explanation: Micrographia, characterised by progressively smaller handwriting, is a recognised feature of Parkinson's disease, reflecting bradykinesia affecting fine motor control during sustained repetitive movement. This contrasts with macrographia, which can occur in some cerebellar conditions. Recognising this subtle sign can support early clinical suspicion of parkinsonism.

Chronic kidney disease reduces renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity, impairing conversion of vitamin D to its active form, which reduces intestinal calcium absorption and contributes to hypocalcaemia, clinically demonstrated by a positive Chvostek's sign reflecting neuromuscular hyperexcitability. This hypocalcaemia, alongside phosphate retention, drives the secondary hyperparathyroidism characteristic of CKD-mineral bone disease. Recognising this vitamin D-mediated mechanism explains the rationale for active vitamin D analogue supplementation in managing CKD-related hypocalcaemia.
options: Excess vitamin D increasing calcium absorption
Reduced active vitamin D reducing intestinal calcium absorption
questions.question: A patient with chronic kidney disease develops hypocalcaemia and tetany. Chvostek's sign is positive on examination. Which underlying mechanism MOST directly explains this finding?
The MOST common cardiac rhythm identified in adult out-of-hospital cardiac arrest is:
questions.explanation: Ventricular fibrillation (VF) is the most common rhythm in adult out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, occurring in approximately 65–85% of monitored arrests. It is a chaotic, disorganised ventricular rhythm without effective cardiac output. Early defibrillation is the critical intervention for VF, with survival decreasing by approximately 10% for each minute without defibrillation. CPR buys time until defibrillation is available.

questions.question: In HBV infection, which serological marker indicates active viral replication and high infectivity?
questions.explanation: HBeAg positivity alongside elevated serum HBV DNA levels indicates active viral replication and high infectivity. HBeAg is a secreted protein reflecting nucleocapsid gene expression; its persistence beyond 3 months suggests transition to chronic HBV infection with ongoing replication.

questions.question: A 60-year-old with chronic alcoholism develops progressive jaundice, ascites, spider naevi, gynaecomastia, palmar erythema, and asterixis. AFP is 1,800 ng/mL. The MOST likely diagnosis explaining ALL findings is:
questions.explanation: Decompensated cirrhosis explains the spider naevi, gynaecomastia, palmar erythema, asterixis, and ascites. Superimposed HCC explains the elevated AFP (1,800 ng/mL). This combination requires urgent evaluation for HCC. Regular surveillance of cirrhotic patients with ultrasound and AFP every 6 months enables earlier detection and better outcomes.
options: Wilson's disease with acute liver failure
Viral hepatitis A with fulminant failure

questions.question: A patient with liver cirrhosis is noted to have nails showing a proximal white portion occupying roughly half the nail, sharply demarcated from a distal reddish-brown portion. What is this specific nail pattern called?
questions.explanation: Half-and-half nails, or Lindsay's nails, describe a sharply demarcated proximal white and distal brown or pink nail pattern, most classically associated with chronic kidney disease, though also reported with other systemic illnesses including liver disease. This differs from Terry's nails, where only a very narrow distal pink band remains against an almost entirely white nail. Precise pattern recognition helps differentiate among several superficially similar systemic nail signs.

options: Hard keratin plate forming the visible nail body
The visible pale crescent at the proximal nail base
Epithelium beneath the free edge of the nail plate
