questions.question: Which echocardiographic finding is MOST consistent with dilated cardiomyopathy?
questions.explanation: In dilated cardiomyopathy, echocardiography classically shows a dilated left ventricle (and often other chambers), globally reduced wall motion (hypokinesis), and low ejection fraction (less than 50%). Functional mitral regurgitation occurs due to dilation of the mitral annulus. Spontaneous contrast may be seen. BNP is markedly elevated. The overall appearance contrasts with the thickened walls seen in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

questions.question: A comatose patient has a Glasgow Coma Scale eye-opening score of 2. What does this represent?
questions.explanation: The eye-opening component of the Glasgow Coma Scale is scored from one to four, with a score of two indicating eye opening only in response to a painful stimulus. A score of four represents spontaneous opening, three represents opening to voice, and one represents no opening at all. This component reflects arousal rather than awareness.

questions.question: Adiponectin, a hormone secreted by adipose tissue, is UNIQUE in that its levels are INVERSELY related to body fat mass. Its protective roles include:
options: Directly stimulating cortisol release from the adrenal cortex
Stimulating food intake and promoting energy storage
Improving insulin sensitivity, reducing atherosclerosis risk, and having anti-inflammatory effects
questions.explanation: Adiponectin is inversely proportional to body fat mass — obese individuals have paradoxically low adiponectin despite excess adipose tissue. Its protective roles include improving insulin sensitivity (anti-diabetic), reducing endothelial inflammation and atherosclerosis risk (cardioprotective), and anti-inflammatory effects on macrophages. The fall in adiponectin with increasing obesity contributes mechanistically to metabolic syndrome.

questions.question: Surgery for chronic duodenal ulcer disease is typically only indicated for which complication?
questions.explanation: Surgeons are typically called in for complications of chronic duodenal ulcer: uncontrolled haemorrhage, perforation (causing peritonitis), or pyloric stenosis (causing gastric outlet obstruction). Medical management with PPIs and H. pylori eradication is the mainstay for uncomplicated duodenal ulcer disease.
options: Recurrent ulceration despite two antibiotic courses
Pain unresponsive to single PPI course
Duodenal ulcer greater than 1 cm in diameter

questions.question: The MOST common cardiac valve affected in rheumatic heart disease is:
questions.explanation: The mitral valve is the most commonly affected valve in rheumatic heart disease, involved in over 90% of cases, due to the high pressure in the left heart during systole. The aortic valve is the second most commonly affected, often involved alongside the mitral valve. Tricuspid and pulmonary valve involvement is uncommon. Mitral stenosis is the classic valvular lesion of chronic rheumatic heart disease.

Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease) causes aldosterone deficiency, leading to sodium loss and potassium retention. The resulting hyponatraemia (low sodium) and hyperkalaemia (high potassium) are characteristic electrolyte abnormalities. Cortisol deficiency also contributes to hyponatraemia through inappropriate ADH secretion. Hypoglycaemia may also occur due to impaired gluconeogenesis. In an acute Addisonian crisis, severe hypotension, hyponatraemia, and hyperkalaemia may be life-threatening.
questions.question: In Addison's disease (primary adrenal insufficiency), which electrolyte pattern is EXPECTED?

options: Below the kidneys on the pelvic brim
Behind the pancreas in the mesentery
questions.question: The adrenal glands are located:
questions.explanation: The adrenal glands (also known as suprarenal glands) are paired endocrine glands located on top of each kidney in the retroperitoneal space. The right adrenal gland is triangular (pyramidal) and the left is crescent-shaped. Each gland has two functionally distinct regions: the outer cortex (producing steroid hormones) and the inner medulla (producing catecholamines). Their intimate relationship with the kidneys and renal vessels is important in surgical anatomy.

The coronary arteries run along the epicardium (the outer layer of the heart wall, also called visceral pericardium). They then penetrate into the myocardium to supply blood. The endocardium lines the inner chambers. In severe coronary artery disease, these epicardial vessels develop plaques that obstruct blood flow.
questions.question: Which layer of the heart wall contains the coronary arteries on its surface?

options: A rhythm disorder of the heart
Heart's inability to meet metabolic demands
Structural abnormality of heart valves only
Failure of the heart to maintain rate above 60 bpm
Loss of consciousness due to cardiac cause
questions.explanation: Heart failure is defined as the inability of the heart to pump sufficient blood to meet the metabolic demands of the body tissues, or when it can only do so at the cost of an elevated filling pressure. It is a syndrome, not a disease, resulting from various structural or functional cardiac disorders. Both systolic and diastolic dysfunction can lead to this clinical syndrome.
questions.question: Heart failure is BEST defined as:

options: Normal venous anatomy in obese patients
Simple superficial varicose veins of the abdominal wall
Recanalisation of the paraumbilical veins due to portal hypertension
questions.explanation: Caput medusae results from portal hypertension forcing blood through recanalised paraumbilical veins that connect the portal system to the systemic venous circulation via the umbilicus, producing visibly distended veins radiating from that point. It is a classic sign of significant portal hypertension, often accompanying cirrhosis. Its presence indicates advanced portosystemic collateral formation.
questions.question: A patient with cirrhosis and portal hypertension has distended veins radiating outward from the umbilicus. This finding is termed caput medusae and reflects:
Cystic fibrosis causes obstructive lung disease through which PRIMARY mechanism?
options: Chronic neutrophilic airway inflammation from bacterial colonisation
Smooth muscle hyperreactivity from IgE-mediated allergy
Alveolar destruction from neutrophil elastase deficiency
Interstitial fibrosis from recurrent viral pneumonia
questions.explanation: Cystic fibrosis is caused by CFTR gene mutations causing thick, viscid mucus production that impairs mucociliary clearance. Chronic bacterial colonisation (Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staphylococcus aureus) causes persistent neutrophilic airway inflammation, bronchiectasis, progressive airway obstruction, and respiratory failure. Pancreatic insufficiency and infertility are other manifestations. Median survival has improved to >40 years with modern treatment.

options: A gland regulated solely by portal blood flow from the anterior pituitary
A gland that only responds to peripheral hormone feedback
An extension of hypothalamic neurons storing and releasing hormones
A structure with no connection to the hypothalamus
An independent endocrine gland synthesising its own hormones
questions.question: A patient's posterior pituitary is functionally best described as:
questions.explanation: The posterior pituitary is functionally an extension of hypothalamic neurons, which synthesise ADH and oxytocin in the hypothalamus and transport them via axons for storage and release from the posterior pituitary. This differs from the anterior pituitary, which independently synthesises its hormones under hypothalamic releasing factor control. Understanding this anatomy explains the distinct regulation of posterior pituitary hormones.

options: Calcium channel blockade at presynaptic terminal
questions.explanation: Myasthenia gravis is caused by antibodies against acetylcholine receptors (AChR) at the neuromuscular junction, causing fatigable weakness worsening with activity. The anti-AChR antibodies block receptor sites, accelerate receptor degradation, and cause complement-mediated damage. LEMS involves presynaptic calcium channels, not postsynaptic receptors.
questions.question: A 28-year-old woman presents with ptosis and diplopia worsening in the evening. She notes difficulty chewing by the end of meals. The MOST likely underlying mechanism is:

questions.explanation: Hand psoriasis is classified as psoriasis, not hand eczema, even though it may clinically overlap. Recognised types of hand dermatitis include irritant contact, allergic contact, atopic, pompholyx, hyperkeratotic fissured, and nummular hand eczema. Distinguishing hand psoriasis from hand eczema is clinically important as the treatments and long-term management differ significantly.
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a recognised type of hand eczema?

questions.explanation: The ulnar nerve at the elbow is one of the most commonly affected peripheral nerves in Type 1 (reversal) reactions in leprosy, and sudden nerve tenderness with new motor or sensory deficit represents a medical emergency requiring urgent corticosteroid treatment to prevent permanent nerve damage. Other superficial nerves such as the common peroneal and posterior tibial can also be affected, but the ulnar nerve is classically emphasised. Prompt recognition and treatment can prevent irreversible claw hand deformity.
questions.question: A patient with borderline leprosy develops a Type 1 reversal reaction causing sudden ulnar nerve tenderness and new hand weakness. Which nerve is classically most affected by this type of reaction?

A 23-year-old presents with first seizure during sleep (focal motor of right hand progressing to generalised tonic-clonic). MRI shows small cortical dysplasia in the left pre-central gyrus. Under the 2010 ILAE classification, the aetiology is BEST classified as:
questions.explanation: The 2010 ILAE paradigm: Genetic (formerly idiopathic), Structural/Metabolic (formerly symptomatic), and Unknown (formerly cryptogenic). Cortical dysplasia is a structural brain abnormality causing symptomatic focal epilepsy, classified as STRUCTURAL. This contrasts with GENETIC causes (channelopathies) and UNKNOWN causes where no cause is found.

questions.question: A patient with central obesity, purple abdominal striae, proximal muscle weakness, and easy bruising is suspected of having excess exposure to which hormone?
questions.explanation: Cushing's syndrome results from prolonged excess cortisol exposure, producing central obesity, purple striae, proximal myopathy, and easy bruising due to catabolic effects on skin and muscle. These features distinguish it from mineralocorticoid or catecholamine excess. Identifying the cause, whether pituitary, adrenal, or exogenous, guides specific treatment.

questions.question: A patient with chronic hepatitis develops superimposed acute liver decompensation and is found to be co-infected with a virus that requires HBV surface antigen for its own assembly. This co-infecting virus is:
questions.explanation: Hepatitis D virus is a defective virus that requires the presence of hepatitis B surface antigen to form its viral envelope and replicate, meaning it can only infect individuals who are also infected with HBV. Co-infection or superinfection with HDV often worsens the clinical course of chronic hepatitis B. Recognising this dependency explains why HDV testing is reserved for HBV-positive patients.

questions.question: SARS (2002-2003) had a case fatality rate of 10% and was ultimately contained. What primarily enabled containment of SARS but NOT SARS-CoV-2?
options: SARS had an effective vaccine developed quickly
SARS had lower viral load than SARS-CoV-2
SARS patients were infectious only after symptom onset
SARS had a shorter incubation period
questions.explanation: SARS was containable because patients became infectious only AFTER symptom onset, allowing effective isolation of symptomatic cases. SARS-CoV-2 is infectious up to 2 days BEFORE symptom onset (pre-symptomatic transmission ~23% of spread), making symptom-based isolation insufficient. Combined with asymptomatic transmission and longer infectious period, SARS-CoV-2 was far more difficult to contain.

options: The right main bronchus is wider and more vertical
The left lung has greater overall lung volume
The right lung has reduced blood supply generally
The right lung has fewer lobes than the left
The left main bronchus is shorter than the right
questions.explanation: The right main bronchus is wider, shorter, and more vertically oriented compared with the left main bronchus, making aspirated material more likely to preferentially enter the right lung, particularly the right lower lobe when a patient aspirates in an upright or semi-recumbent position. This anatomical predisposition explains why aspiration pneumonia classically localises to the right lower lobe, an important radiological clue supporting this specific aetiology. Recognising this pattern helps direct further clinical assessment toward risk factors for aspiration, such as swallowing dysfunction or reduced consciousness.
questions.question: A patient with aspiration pneumonia following a witnessed choking episode is noted to have infiltrates predominantly in the right lower lobe on chest X-ray. Which anatomical feature MOST directly explains this characteristic distribution?

options: Prolonged application of topical corticosteroids to the face
Contact allergy to lipstick or lip balm ingredients
Excessive cumulative sun exposure around the mouth
questions.explanation: Perioral dermatitis is a papulopustular eruption around the mouth and sometimes eyes, most commonly caused by prolonged topical corticosteroid use on the face. The condition paradoxically flares on initial steroid withdrawal before eventually clearing. Fluorinated toothpastes have also been implicated. Management involves stopping topical steroids and using tetracycline antibiotics or topical metronidazole for several months.
questions.question: Perioral dermatitis is MOST commonly triggered by:

options: Loss of efferent arteriolar constriction maintaining filtration
Increased renal blood flow overwhelming filtration
Direct toxic tubular injury from the drug
questions.question: A patient with renal artery stenosis due to fibromuscular dysplasia is started on an ACE inhibitor and subsequently develops acute kidney injury with a marked rise in creatinine. Which mechanism MOST directly explains this deterioration?
questions.explanation: In bilateral (or solitary kidney) renal artery stenosis, glomerular filtration is critically dependent on angiotensin II-mediated efferent arteriolar constriction to maintain filtration pressure despite reduced renal blood flow; ACE inhibitors abolish this compensatory mechanism, causing a sharp fall in glomerular filtration rate and acute kidney injury. This is why renal artery stenosis is a recognised contraindication to ACE inhibitor or ARB use, particularly in bilateral disease. Recognising this specific haemodynamic mechanism explains the paradoxical harm of an otherwise renoprotective drug class in this setting.

questions.question: The coronavirus structural protein responsible for mediating receptor binding and viral entry into host cells is:
questions.explanation: The Spike (S) glycoprotein, which gives coronaviruses their crown-like appearance, mediates receptor binding (to ACE2) and membrane fusion for viral entry. The M protein assists viral assembly, N protein regulates viral RNA synthesis, E protein plays a role in assembly/budding, and HE protein enhances mucosal uptake (only in beta coronaviruses OC43 and HKU1).

questions.question: A young lean patient presents with diabetes but tests negative for pancreatic autoantibodies and has a strong three-generation family history with onset before age 25. This pattern most suggests:
questions.explanation: Maturity-onset diabetes of the young is a monogenic form of diabetes characterised by autosomal dominant inheritance, early onset, and absence of autoimmune markers, distinguishing it from typical type 1 or type 2 diabetes. Recognising this pattern is important as management may differ from standard type 2 protocols. Genetic testing can confirm the diagnosis.

questions.question: Pursed lip breathing in emphysema patients is PRIMARILY a compensatory mechanism to achieve which goal?
questions.explanation: Pursed lip breathing creates back-pressure in the airways during expiration, preventing dynamic collapse of already weakened airways in emphysema. This extends expiration, reduces gas trapping, and improves gas exchange. It also allows patients to breathe more slowly and deeply, improving ventilatory efficiency.

questions.question: Steroid use in bacterial meningitis should be given at what timing relative to antibiotics?
options: With or before the first dose of antibiotics in non-HIV patients
6 hours before antibiotics to reduce inflammation
Only after culture results confirm sensitivity
questions.explanation: Dexamethasone should be given with or before the first dose of antibiotics in HIV-negative patients with bacterial meningitis. Early steroid use reduces the inflammatory response to bacterial lysis products, decreasing complications such as hearing loss and neurological sequelae, particularly in pneumococcal meningitis.

An elevated anion gap metabolic acidosis, as seen in diabetic ketoacidosis, reflects accumulation of unmeasured acid anions, in this case ketoacids, that are not accounted for in the standard sodium minus chloride and bicarbonate calculation, distinguishing it from normal anion gap acidosis caused by bicarbonate loss such as diarrhoea or renal tubular acidosis. The compensatory low PaCO2 reflects appropriate respiratory compensation (Kussmaul breathing) attempting to correct the acidaemia. Correctly calculating and interpreting the anion gap helps narrow the differential diagnosis of metabolic acidosis significantly.
options: Renal tubular acidosis with normal anion gap
Loss of bicarbonate through the gastrointestinal tract
Dilutional acidosis from excess intravenous fluid
questions.question: A patient with diabetic ketoacidosis has ABG showing pH 7.15, PaCO2 20 mmHg, and HCO3 10 mmol/L. Calculating the anion gap using sodium, chloride, and bicarbonate reveals a value of 24 mmol/L. What does this elevated anion gap MOST specifically indicate?

questions.explanation: Irritant contact dermatitis is characteristically limited to the area of exposure and is sharply marginated, reflecting its toxic mechanism rather than an immunological spreading response. Repeated exposure to irritants like latex, cleaning agents, and water in healthcare workers is a classic occupational scenario. The sharp demarcation distinguishes it from allergic contact dermatitis, which may spread beyond the contact area.
questions.question: A 25-year-old nurse develops a sharply marginated, weeping rash confined strictly to the areas of glove contact on her hands. Which type of eczema does this BEST describe?

questions.explanation: Sputum Gram stain provides rapid initial guidance (identifying Gram-positive diplococci for Streptococcus pneumoniae, Gram-negative rods for Klebsiella etc.), while culture and sensitivity identifies the causative organism and determines appropriate antibiotic. Blood cultures are essential for bacteraemic pneumonia. Procalcitonin helps distinguish bacterial from viral causes but doesn't identify the organism.
options: Full blood count and CRP only
questions.question: In community-acquired pneumonia, the most important investigation for guiding targeted antibiotic therapy is:

A child presents with periorbital oedema, frothy urine, and hypoalbuminaemia with heavy proteinuria on urinalysis. Renal biopsy shows effacement of podocyte foot processes on electron microscopy with no changes on light microscopy. What is the MOST likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Minimal change disease, the commonest cause of nephrotic syndrome in children, characteristically shows normal appearance on light microscopy with diffuse podocyte foot process effacement visible only on electron microscopy, and typically responds well to corticosteroid therapy. Membranous nephropathy and focal segmental glomerulosclerosis instead show distinct light microscopic changes such as basement membrane thickening or segmental scarring. Recognising this classic electron microscopy finding with otherwise normal light microscopy is diagnostic for minimal change disease.

WHO Class IV (ISN/RPS Class IV) lupus nephritis is diffuse proliferative GN involving >50% of glomeruli. It is the most severe and common class, with 'full house' immunofluorescence (IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, C1q deposits). It presents with haematuria, heavy proteinuria, hypertension, and rapidly declining GFR. Subendothelial deposits ('wire loops') are characteristic. Treatment: high-dose corticosteroids + cyclophosphamide or mycophenolate.
questions.question: Lupus nephritis (WHO Class IV) involves which histological finding on renal biopsy?
options: Minimal change with no immunoglobulin deposits
Segmental mesangial proliferation in <25% of glomeruli
Diffuse proliferative GN with 'full house' immunofluorescence
Focal necrosis with crescent formation exclusively

questions.question: A dermatologist explains that within the pilosebaceous unit, a specific enzyme converts a weaker circulating androgen into a much more potent form that drives sebaceous gland activity in acne. Which enzyme is this?
questions.explanation: 5-alpha reductase within the pilosebaceous unit converts testosterone into dihydrotestosterone, a far more potent androgen that stimulates sebaceous gland growth and sebum production, driving acne pathogenesis locally even when systemic androgen levels are normal. Aromatase instead converts androgens to oestrogens and is not central to acne pathogenesis. This local enzymatic amplification explains why some patients with normal serum androgens still develop significant acne.

In ADPKD, approximately 50% of patients develop end-stage renal disease by age 60 years. PKD1 mutations (chromosome 16) cause more severe disease with earlier renal failure compared to PKD2 mutations (chromosome 4). Hypertension, which occurs early, accelerates progression. Management focuses on BP control (tolvaptan may slow cyst growth), treating complications, and preparation for RRT.
questions.question: The 50% renal failure threshold in ADPKD occurs at approximately what age?

questions.explanation: Pregnant women, especially in their third trimester, have dramatically increased risk (mortality 15–25%) of fulminant hepatic failure from Hepatitis E virus infection. The mechanism may involve immune modulation of pregnancy and altered viral clearance, making HEV particularly dangerous in this group.
questions.question: Hepatitis E virus infection carries the highest risk of fulminant hepatitis in which specific patient population?

questions.explanation: ACE inhibitors reduce angiotensin II production, leading to arterial vasodilation (reducing afterload), venous dilation (reducing preload), reduced aldosterone secretion (reducing sodium retention), and prevention and reversal of adverse cardiac remodelling. These mechanisms collectively improve symptoms, reduce hospitalizations, and reduce mortality in HFrEF. They are a cornerstone of heart failure with reduced EF therapy.
questions.question: ACE inhibitors improve outcomes in heart failure PRIMARILY by:
Sudden inappropriate reduction of diuretic therapy in a heart failure patient is MOST likely to precipitate:
questions.explanation: Sudden withdrawal or inappropriate reduction of diuretics allows sodium and water retention to re-occur, rapidly increasing preload and triggering acute decompensation with fluid overload, pulmonary oedema, and peripheral oedema. This is one of the most common precipitants of heart failure decompensation. Patient education about medication adherence is critical in heart failure management.

Plasmodium falciparum characteristically shows delicate ring forms with double chromatin dots and frequent multiple infection of a single red cell, features that distinguish it from other species. It is the species responsible for the most severe and life-threatening malaria, including cerebral malaria. Rapid identification is essential because falciparum infection can progress rapidly to multi-organ failure.
questions.question: A child from a malaria-endemic area presents with fever, drowsiness, and a blood film showing ring forms with double chromatin dots and multiply infected red cells. Which Plasmodium species is MOST likely?

questions.explanation: HIV infection is notably NOT a risk factor for leprosy, unlike tuberculosis where HIV dramatically increases susceptibility. Leprosy susceptibility depends primarily on cell-mediated immune status specific to M. leprae antigens, and HIV's depletion of CD4+ T cells does not appear to meaningfully increase leprosy risk.
questions.question: Leprosy is endemic in Africa, Asia, and Latin America. Which factor is notably NOT a risk factor for leprosy transmission?
Analgesic nephropathy from chronic NSAID or phenacetin abuse causes which CHARACTERISTIC renal lesion?
options: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis with heavy proteinuria
Renal papillary necrosis with tubulo-interstitial nephritis
Crescentic GN with rapidly progressive renal failure
questions.explanation: Analgesic nephropathy from chronic NSAID/phenacetin abuse causes renal papillary necrosis (ischaemic necrosis of medullary papillae from prostaglandin inhibition reducing medullary blood flow) combined with chronic tubulo-interstitial nephritis. The necrotic papillae may calcify (ring shadows on X-ray) or slough into the collecting system. Clinical features include polyuria, nocturia, UTIs, haematuria, and gradually progressing CKD.

questions.question: Indeterminate leprosy has which clinical characteristic regarding its natural progression without treatment?
questions.explanation: Indeterminate leprosy shows 1-3 hypopigmented macules with slight sensory loss ? the EARLIEST stage of leprosy. Without treatment, 70% of cases HEAL SPONTANEOUSLY (due to effective cell-mediated immunity), while 30% progress to any form on the determinate spectrum. Early treatment prevents progression and nerve damage.
options: Predominantly affects internal organs not skin
Inadequate renal perfusion lowering GFR, no intrinsic damage
Obstruction of the urinary collecting system
questions.explanation: Pre-renal AKI occurs when renal perfusion is inadequate (hypovolaemia, low cardiac output, vasodilation), leading to decreased GFR without structural renal injury initially. If perfusion is restored promptly, kidney function recovers. Prolonged hypoperfusion can progress to intrinsic AKI (acute tubular necrosis). Pre-renal AKI is the most common cause of AKI worldwide.
questions.question: Pre-renal AKI results from which primary mechanism?

options: Hypertension with bilateral renal artery stenosis
Recurrent macroscopic haematuria following upper respiratory infections
Acute flank pain with fever from renal abscess
questions.question: IgA nephropathy (Berger's disease) is MOST characterised by which clinical feature?
questions.explanation: IgA nephropathy (Berger's disease) is the most common glomerulonephritis worldwide. It characteristically presents with recurrent episodes of macroscopic haematuria (visible blood in urine) often occurring 24-48 hours after upper respiratory tract infections (synpharyngitic haematuria). Diffuse mesangial IgA deposits are pathognomonic. Recurrent macroscopic haematuria is actually a favourable prognostic feature.

questions.question: Early defibrillation in VF is critical because survival decreases approximately how much for each minute without defibrillation?
questions.explanation: The probability of successful defibrillation and survival decreases by approximately 10% for every minute that VF persists without intervention. This is why the chain of survival concept emphasizes early recognition, early CPR, and early defibrillation. After 10 minutes of untreated VF, survival is very unlikely. Automated external defibrillators (AEDs) placed in public areas aim to shorten the time to defibrillation.

questions.question: Retroperitoneal fibrosis causing ureteric obstruction is MOST commonly associated with which drug?
questions.explanation: Methysergide (an ergot alkaloid used for migraine prophylaxis) is the classic drug-induced cause of retroperitoneal fibrosis, causing progressive bilateral ureteric obstruction. Other causes include aortic aneurysm, malignancy (lymphoma), radiation, and idiopathic Ormond's disease. Corticosteroids and tamoxifen are used in treatment. Withdrawal of methysergide alone may result in partial regression of fibrosis.

options: Is more potent as a neurotransmitter than epinephrine
10 times more potent in metabolic effects
questions.question: Epinephrine from the adrenal medulla differs functionally from norepinephrine as a neurotransmitter in that epinephrine:
questions.explanation: Epinephrine is 10 times more potent than norepinephrine in producing direct metabolic effects (glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis, lipolysis, bronchodilation). Norepinephrine, conversely, is more potent as a neurotransmitter at adrenergic synapses and has more pronounced alpha-adrenergic (vasoconstrictive) effects. Epinephrine acts on both alpha and beta receptors. This difference has practical implications: in anaphylaxis, epinephrine is the drug of choice; norepinephrine is preferred as a vasopressor in septic shock.

options: Early gallstone migration into the common bile duct
Superficial cellulitis of the abdominal wall
Retroperitoneal haemorrhage tracking to subcutaneous tissue
questions.question: A patient with severe acute pancreatitis develops bluish discolouration around the umbilicus and in the flanks several days into the illness. What do these findings, Cullen's and Grey Turner's signs, indicate?
questions.explanation: Cullen's sign (periumbilical bruising) and Grey Turner's sign (flank bruising) result from retroperitoneal haemorrhage tracking through tissue planes to reach the subcutaneous layer in severe necrotising pancreatitis, and their presence indicates severe disease with a worse prognosis. They are not related to simple bruising from examination or superficial skin infection. Recognising these signs should prompt escalation of monitoring and supportive care.

Close contacts of meningococcal meningitis require CHEMOPROPHYLAXIS to eradicate nasopharyngeal carriage and prevent secondary cases. Rifampicin (2 days) is the standard agent; single-dose ciprofloxacin is preferred for adults as it is more convenient. Ceftriaxone single IM dose is used in pregnant women.
questions.question: Which prophylactic antibiotic should be given to CLOSE CONTACTS of a confirmed meningococcal meningitis case to eradicate nasopharyngeal carriage?

A patient with type 1 renal tubular acidosis (distal) is found to have hypokalaemia, nephrocalcinosis, and an inability to acidify urine below pH 5.5 despite systemic acidosis. Which underlying tubular defect MOST directly explains this presentation?
questions.explanation: Type 1 (distal) renal tubular acidosis results from impaired hydrogen ion secretion by the distal tubule's intercalated cells, preventing adequate urinary acidification despite systemic acidosis, and is associated with hypokalaemia and nephrocalcinosis due to calcium phosphate precipitation in an inappropriately alkaline urine environment. This differs from type 2 (proximal) RTA, which results from impaired bicarbonate reabsorption in the proximal tubule instead. Recognising the specific tubular segment and defect involved helps distinguish the different renal tubular acidosis subtypes and their distinct complications.
options: Excess aldosterone action on collecting duct
Impaired distal tubular hydrogen ion secretion

questions.question: Vaccination remains the most effective prevention for bacterial meningitis. Meningococcal vaccine elicits protective bactericidal antibody levels in what percentage of recipients by day 28?
questions.explanation: Both licensed meningococcal vaccines elicit protective bactericidal antibody levels to all four covered serogroups (A, C, Y, W-135) in more than 97% of recipients by day 28. Mild local reactions and minor systemic symptoms (headache, fatigue, low-grade fever) may occur but the vaccines are highly immunogenic and safe.

questions.question: A CONTINUOUS (machinery) murmur best heard at the left infraclavicular area in a young patient suggests:
questions.explanation: Patent ductus arteriosus produces a continuous 'machinery' murmur heard best in the left infraclavicular region and first/second left intercostal space. The continuous nature (throughout systole and diastole) reflects persistent communication between the aorta and pulmonary artery, with left-to-right blood flow throughout the cardiac cycle. Premature infants are particularly susceptible to PDA. Indomethacin or surgical ligation are treatments.

questions.question: In which condition would synchronized cardioversion (not defibrillation) be the appropriate electrical treatment?
questions.explanation: Synchronised cardioversion is appropriate for organised rhythms (AF, atrial flutter, SVT, VT with pulse) where the shock is timed to the QRS complex to avoid the vulnerable T-wave period. Unsynchronised defibrillation (shock delivered randomly) is used only in VF and pulseless VT, where there is no organised rhythm to synchronise to. Delivering an unsynchronised shock to organised rhythm can precipitate VF. SUBTOPIC 4: VALVULAR HEART DISEASE, RHEUMATIC FEVER AND CARDIOMYOPATHIES

questions.question: The primary blood supply to the nail unit is from:
questions.explanation: The nail unit receives blood from paired proper digital arteries that form an anastomotic arcade within the nail bed. The rich vascular supply explains the characteristic pink colour of healthy nails and the potential for brisk bleeding from nail matrix injuries. Vascular compromise, as in peripheral arterial disease, leads to nail thinning, slow growth, and onycholysis.
options: Paired digital arteries forming an arcade
Periosteal capillaries of the distal phalanx

questions.explanation: Distal brown or 'half-and-half' nail discolouration (Lindsay's nails) is a general sign of chronic kidney disease, likely due to melanin deposition and anaemia. Along with pallor, pruritus, and hyperpigmentation, it is a dermatological manifestation of CKD. These signs reflect chronic uraemia and metabolic derangements accumulating over months to years of renal dysfunction.
questions.question: The Virchow's RENAL concept (not thrombosis) states that distal brown nail discolouration in kidney disease is a general sign of:

options: Irritant contact dermatitis from glove use
questions.explanation: A negative patch test to potential allergens (latex, rubber chemicals) in a healthcare worker with hand eczema confined to glove contact areas suggests irritant contact dermatitis from occlusion, sweat accumulation, and friction. This is the most common form of occupational hand dermatitis. Management involves barrier protection, moisturisers, and minimising wet work.
questions.question: A healthcare worker develops hand eczema after prolonged glove use, but patch testing to latex and rubber chemicals is negative. The MOST likely diagnosis is:

options: Elevated CRP, D-dimer, ferritin, IL-6, with lymphopenia
Isolated thrombocytopenia with normal inflammatory markers
Neutropenia with monocytosis and normal CRP
Elevated white cell count with predominantly eosinophils
questions.explanation: The COVID-19 cytokine storm is characterised by markedly elevated CRP, D-dimer (indicating coagulopathy and DIC risk), ferritin, LDH, IL-6, and TNF-alpha ? all proportionate to disease severity. Elevated D-dimer specifically predicts thromboembolic complications requiring anticoagulation. This immunological profile guides ICU management decisions.
questions.question: The 'cytokine storm' in severe COVID-19 is characterised by which specific laboratory pattern indicating a dysregulated immune response?

questions.explanation: SIADH causes hyponatraemia through inappropriate ADH (vasopressin) secretion causing excess water retention (dilutional hyponatraemia) without oedema or volume depletion. Causes include SCLC (most common paraneoplastic), CNS disorders, pulmonary diseases, and drugs. Diagnosis: hyponatraemia, low serum osmolality, inappropriately concentrated urine (>100 mOsm/kg), and euvolaemia. Treatment: fluid restriction ± vaptans.
questions.question: Which electrolyte abnormality is MOST commonly found in the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH)?

options: Any two of raised LDL, low triglycerides, hypotension, or hypoglycaemia
Any two of raised triglycerides, low HDL, hypertension, or hyperglycaemia
All five classic cardiovascular risk factors simultaneously
Elevated BMI alone without any biochemical criteria
A single abnormal lipid parameter only
questions.explanation: Metabolic syndrome is diagnosed when central obesity is accompanied by at least two of the following: raised triglycerides, low HDL cholesterol, raised blood pressure, or raised fasting glucose, reflecting a cluster of interrelated cardiometabolic risk factors. A single abnormal parameter alone, or BMI in isolation, is insufficient to make the diagnosis. Recognising the full criteria supports appropriate risk stratification and targeted lifestyle or pharmacological intervention.
questions.question: A patient is assessed for metabolic syndrome. Alongside central obesity, which combination of additional criteria would confirm this diagnosis?

questions.explanation: Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause of acute haematogenous osteomyelitis across all age groups, seeding the highly vascular metaphysis of long bones in children. Salmonella species are classically associated with osteomyelitis in patients with sickle cell disease, an important exception to remember. Prompt blood cultures and imaging, along with targeted antibiotics, are essential to prevent chronic bone infection and growth disturbance.
questions.question: A child presents with fever, refusal to bear weight on one leg, and localised bone tenderness. Blood cultures are pending. Which organism is the MOST common cause of acute haematogenous osteomyelitis in previously healthy children?

questions.explanation: Guttate psoriasis classically follows streptococcal pharyngitis and presents with numerous small, drop-shaped scaly papules scattered over the trunk and proximal limbs, differing from the larger, more chronic, well-demarcated plaques of chronic plaque psoriasis. It often resolves spontaneously but can herald chronic plaque disease later in life. The recent streptococcal infection is the key historical clue distinguishing it from other variants.
questions.question: A child recovers from a streptococcal throat infection and two weeks later develops numerous small, drop-like scaly papules scattered over the trunk. Which psoriasis variant is most consistent with this presentation?

questions.explanation: Lymphopenia occurs in approximately 80% of COVID-19 patients and is proportionate to disease severity ? deeper lymphopenia indicates more severe disease and poorer prognosis. Combined with elevated D-dimer and CRP, lymphopenia serves as an important severity marker. CD4+ lymphocytes are particularly affected. In HIV, CD4 lymphopenia is the defining feature.
questions.question: In COVID-19, lymphopenia occurs in what proportion of patients and is associated with:
Acne Cosmetica refers to acne caused by:
options: Comedogenic cosmetic products applied to the skin
Chlorinated hydrocarbon exposure in industrial settings
questions.explanation: Acne cosmetica is caused by exposure to comedogenic cosmetics, presenting as closed comedones and papulopustules predominantly on the chin and cheeks. The condition may take months to clear after stopping the offending product. Patients should be advised to use non-comedogenic cosmetic and skincare products.

options: Direct renal tubular lipid reabsorption defect
Direct urinary loss of lipoprotein lipase enzyme
Increased hepatic lipoprotein synthesis in response to hypoalbuminaemia
questions.explanation: In nephrotic syndrome, hypoalbuminaemia stimulates increased hepatic protein synthesis generally, including lipoproteins, contributing to hyperlipidaemia, while reduced lipoprotein lipase activity further impairs clearance of circulating lipids, together producing the characteristic dyslipidaemia associated with heavy proteinuria. This hepatic synthetic response is a compensatory mechanism related to low oncotic pressure rather than a primary lipid metabolism disorder. Recognising this mechanism explains why effectively treating the underlying nephrotic syndrome, rather than lipid-lowering therapy alone, is central to resolving the associated hyperlipidaemia.
questions.question: A patient with nephrotic syndrome is noted to have hyperlipidaemia alongside heavy proteinuria and hypoalbuminaemia. Which mechanism MOST directly explains this lipid abnormality?
In MG, the HLA haplotype associated with the disease is:
questions.explanation: Myasthenia gravis is associated with the HLA haplotype HLA-B8, DRw3, and possibly DQw2, indicating a genetic predisposition to autoimmune anti-AChR antibody production. This HLA association overlaps with other autoimmune diseases (type 1 diabetes, Graves' disease, SLE), explaining MG's frequent co-occurrence with other autoimmune conditions.

Catecholamines (epinephrine/adrenaline and norepinephrine/noradrenaline) are amino acid derivative hormones derived from the amino acid tyrosine. Like peptide hormones, they are water-soluble and act via cell surface receptors (alpha and beta adrenergic receptors). They have very short half-lives in circulation. This is in contrast to thyroid hormones (T3, T4), which are also amino acid derivatives but lipophilic and act on nuclear receptors.
questions.question: Catecholamine hormones (epinephrine, norepinephrine) are classified as which type of hormone?

questions.explanation: MRC Grade 3 = active movement against gravity through full range of motion, but not against any added resistance. Grade 0 = no contraction; Grade 1 = flicker; Grade 2 = movement only with gravity eliminated; Grade 4 = movement against resistance (reduced); Grade 5 = normal full power.
questions.question: The MRC scale for muscle power grades weakness from 0 to 5. Grade 3 specifically means:
options: Movement against gravity but not against resistance
Full movement against gravity and moderate resistance
Full power throughout range of motion

questions.explanation: Fluoroscopy provides real-time moving images allowing assessment of dynamic cardiac motion and detection of valve calcification. It is used during cardiac catheterization procedures and for assessing prosthetic valve function. Unlike static chest X-rays, fluoroscopy can detect abnormal calcification in the cardiac valves and pericardium.
questions.question: Fluoroscopy of the chest is used in cardiac investigation MAINLY to assess:

A patient presents with a single well-circumscribed, smooth, non-scarring bald patch on the scalp that developed over a few weeks, with normal surrounding skin and no inflammation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Alopecia areata most commonly presents as one or more well-defined, smooth, non-scarring round or oval patches of hair loss, often developing relatively quickly, without surface inflammation or scaling. Discoid lupus and central centrifugal cicatricial alopecia instead produce scarring with loss of visible follicular openings. The rapid onset and smooth non-scarring surface are the key discriminators here.

Plasmodium malariae is uniquely associated with quartan malarial nephropathy (QMN)—a progressive immune complex GN causing nephrotic syndrome in children and young adults in endemic areas. P. falciparum more commonly causes AKI through haemolysis, pigment nephropathy, and sepsis-related mechanisms. QMN has a poor prognosis with gradual progression to ESRD in 3-8 years and poor response to immunosuppressants.
questions.question: In the context of AKI in a malaria patient, which Plasmodium species is MOST associated with glomerular involvement causing nephrotic syndrome?
Succussion splash on abdominal examination several hours after the last meal strongly suggests:
questions.explanation: A positive succussion splash—heard by shaking the patient's abdomen—indicates retained fluid and gas in the stomach, a hallmark of gastric outlet obstruction. It should not be present hours after eating if gastric emptying is normal.

Influenza A undergoes both antigenic drift (minor changes) and antigenic shift (major changes creating new subtypes). Antigenic shift results in new haemagglutinin or neuraminidase combinations for which populations have no immunity, enabling pandemic spread. Influenza B is antigenically more stable and causes less severe epidemics.
options: Greater virulence of its envelope proteins
Its ability to cause secondary bacterial pneumonia
Frequent antigenic shift producing new subtypes
questions.question: Influenza virus type A is more likely to cause pandemics than type B primarily because of:

questions.explanation: Forced vital capacity is the preferred bedside measurement for monitoring respiratory muscle strength in neuromuscular conditions such as Guillain-Barre syndrome, since a declining trend, particularly below approximately 15-20mL/kg, predicts impending respiratory failure often before oxygen saturation or blood gases become abnormal, given the compensatory reserve of the respiratory system until muscle weakness becomes severe. Oxygen saturation and blood gases can remain deceptively normal until very late in progressive neuromuscular respiratory failure. Regular serial FVC monitoring allows proactive, rather than reactive, decisions about elective intubation before a respiratory crisis develops.
questions.question: A patient with Guillain-Barre syndrome develops progressive respiratory muscle weakness. Which bedside measurement is MOST useful for monitoring impending respiratory failure and guiding the timing of ventilatory support?
options: Oxygen saturation by pulse oximetry alone
Arterial blood gas oxygen level alone

questions.question: Growth hormone excess producing gigantism differs from acromegaly in that gigantism occurs:
questions.explanation: Gigantism results from excessive growth hormone secretion (usually from a pituitary adenoma) in children BEFORE epiphyseal fusion (growth plate closure). This causes linear growth excess and abnormally tall stature. Acromegaly occurs when GH excess develops AFTER epiphyseal closure in adults, causing bony and soft tissue enlargement without linear height gain (enlarged hands, feet, jaw, and viscera). Both are caused by pituitary GH-secreting adenomas.
options: From peripheral tissue resistance to GH

questions.explanation: Topical retinoids (tretinoin, adapalene, isotretinoin) are the treatment of choice for comedonal acne because they normalise follicular keratinisation, preventing comedo formation, and have an anti-inflammatory effect. They must be applied at bedtime as they are inactivated by light. Topical antibiotics target inflammatory lesions and are less effective for comedones alone.
questions.question: A 16-year-old with predominantly comedonal acne is started on treatment. Which topical agent is MOST appropriate as the primary treatment for comedonal acne?

questions.explanation: When plasma glucose exceeds the renal threshold, glucose spills into the urine, drawing water osmotically and causing polyuria; the resulting fluid loss stimulates thirst and compensatory polydipsia. This is a direct consequence of hyperglycaemia rather than a primary behavioural or hormonal disturbance. Correcting glycaemic control resolves these symptoms.
questions.question: A diabetic patient's polyuria and polydipsia are directly explained by which pathophysiological mechanism?
options: Direct toxic effect of glucose on the bladder wall
Osmotic diuresis from glucose exceeding renal tubular reabsorption capacity

questions.question: A 6-month-old infant is noted to have completely normal, silky terminal scalp hair, but the mother recalls the baby was born with fine unpigmented body hair that disappeared within weeks. What was that shed neonatal hair called?
questions.explanation: Lanugo is the fine, soft, unpigmented hair that covers the fetus and is typically shed just before or shortly after birth. It is replaced by vellus hair over most body sites and, later at puberty, by terminal hair in androgen-sensitive areas. Vellus hair is a separate, permanent short hair type rather than the shed fetal coat.

Seborrhoeic dermatitis affects sebum-rich areas: the scalp (causing dandruff), nasolabial folds, presternal area, retroauricular areas, and body folds. The interdigital spaces of the feet are not a typical seborrhoeic area; interdigital maceration there is more characteristic of tinea pedis or bacterial intertrigo. Mild scalp seborrhoeic dermatitis manifests simply as dandruff.
questions.question: Seborrhoeic dermatitis characteristically affects regions where sebaceous glands are most active. Which of the following is NOT a typical site of involvement?

questions.explanation: Diverticular disease affects predominantly the SIGMOID COLON in Western populations (95% of cases), reflecting the high intraluminal pressure in this narrow segment. Left iliac fossa pain, altered bowel habit, and flatulence are typical symptoms. Diverticulitis presents with left iliac fossa pain, fever, and leucocytosis. Diverticula can cause significant rectal bleeding.
questions.question: Colonic diverticular disease presenting as flatulence and altered bowel habit is MOST commonly located in which colonic segment?

questions.explanation: The relatively lower incidence of colorectal carcinoma in Africans compared to Westerners is largely attributed to dietary differences—specifically, higher dietary fibre and lower animal fat and protein intake. Dietary fibre reduces bowel transit time and dilutes carcinogens.
questions.question: Colorectal carcinoma in Africa is relatively uncommon compared to Western countries. This difference is primarily attributed to:
options: Genetic differences in p53 mutation rates
Higher dietary fibre and lower animal fat consumption

questions.question: Fungal lung disease caused by Pneumocystis jirovecii (formerly carinii) primarily affects which patient population?
questions.explanation: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) primarily affects immunocompromised patients, especially those with HIV/AIDS when CD4 count falls below 200 cells/µL. It presents with progressive dyspnoea, dry cough, fever, and bilateral interstitial infiltrates on CXR. Treatment is with high-dose co-trimoxazole. Prophylaxis with co-trimoxazole is given when CD4 <200.
options: Patients with COPD on systemic steroids

questions.explanation: A cardiac arrhythmia is defined as any abnormality of the cardiac rhythm, encompassing abnormalities of impulse formation, conduction, or both. This includes abnormal rates (bradycardia or tachycardia), irregular rhythms, or abnormal propagation of impulses. Arrhythmias range from benign to life-threatening and can cause palpitations, syncope, heart failure, or sudden death.
questions.question: A cardiac arrhythmia is BEST defined as:
options: Electrical abnormality of the cardiac rhythm
Failure of ventricles to fill adequately
Group IIB has exclusively ocular symptoms
Group IIB has bulbar involvement raising aspiration and airway risk
Group IIB responds better to anticholinesterases than IIA
Group IIB has no respiratory muscle involvement
Group IIB is exclusively seen in thymoma patients
questions.explanation: Group IIB (moderate generalised MG with BULBAR involvement) adds dysphagia, dysphonia, and dysarthria to generalised limb weakness. Bulbar involvement significantly raises the risk of aspiration pneumonia and airway compromise. The presence of bulbar involvement warrants more aggressive treatment and close monitoring of respiratory function.
questions.question: In the OSSERMAN classification, Group IIB (moderate generalised MG with bulbar symptoms) differs from Group IIA in which CLINICALLY CRITICAL way?
Papilloedema can be distinguished from papillitis (optic neuritis) by which MOST reliable clinical feature?
options: Papilloedema causes loss of visual acuity in all cases; papillitis preserves vision
Papilloedema only occurs bilaterally; papillitis is always unilateral
Papilloedema preserves visual acuity initially; papillitis reduces visual acuity
Papilloedema causes a relative afferent pupillary defect; papillitis does not
Papilloedema has haemorrhages at disc margin; papillitis does not
questions.explanation: PAPILLOEDEMA (raised ICP) causes disc swelling with NORMAL visual acuity initially ? no inflammation of optic nerve fibres ? with no pain and often bilateral swelling. PAPILLITIS (optic neuritis ? MS) causes disc swelling WITH REDUCED visual acuity, PAIN on eye movement, often unilateral, and a RAPD. Visual acuity is the most important distinguishing clinical feature.

The optic chiasm carries the decussating nasal retinal fibres from both eyes, which represent the temporal visual fields. Compression here, typically from a pituitary macroadenoma, therefore causes loss of the outer (temporal) visual field in both eyes, known as bitemporal hemianopia. This visual field pattern is a classic clue to a sellar or suprasellar mass.
questions.question: A patient with a pituitary tumour develops bitemporal hemianopia. Which structure is being compressed?
Kussmaul breathing pattern in renal failure results from:
questions.explanation: Kussmaul breathing (deep, regular, sighing respirations) is the respiratory compensation for severe metabolic acidosis, which commonly occurs in advanced renal failure. The respiratory centre responds to low pH by increasing depth and rate of breathing to blow off CO2, reducing carbonic acid and partially compensating the acidosis. It is named after Adolf Kussmaul who described it in diabetic coma. B. CKD Stage G4 C. CKD Stage G3b D. Nephrotic syndrome E. Pre-renal azotaemia Answer: C Explanation: KDIGO CKD staging: G1 =90, G2 60-89, G3a 45-59, G3b 30-44, G4 15-29, G5 <15 ml/min/1.73m². An eGFR of 28 falls in G3b, indicating moderately to severely decreased kidney function. CKD requires abnormalities persisting for >3 months. Staging guides management intensity and referral to nephrology. At G3b, preparation for renal replacement therapy should begin.
options: Chest wall rigidity from uraemic pleuritis

questions.question: A patient's endocrine physiology course notes that hormones exert widespread, sustained control over metabolism, growth, and reproduction, distinguishing endocrine signalling from neurotransmission mainly because hormones act via:
questions.explanation: Endocrine hormones are secreted into the bloodstream and can act on distant target tissues throughout the body, in contrast to neurotransmitters, which act rapidly across a synaptic cleft on an adjacent cell. This allows hormones to coordinate slower, more sustained physiological processes such as growth and metabolism. This fundamental difference underlies the distinct time courses of hormonal versus neural regulation.
options: The bloodstream to reach distant target tissues
Local paracrine diffusion only, never reaching distant sites
Direct synaptic contact with target cells only
Physical contact between adjacent cells only

questions.explanation: If seizures persist despite adequate benzodiazepine dosing, second-line intravenous agents such as phenytoin, valproate or levetiracetam are indicated to terminate status epilepticus before proceeding to general anaesthesia if seizures continue. Repeating benzodiazepines beyond the recommended doses increases the risk of respiratory depression without added benefit. Airway protection and continuous monitoring are essential throughout.
questions.question: A patient in status epilepticus has been seizing continuously for 25 minutes despite two doses of intravenous benzodiazepine. What is the MOST appropriate NEXT step?
options: A third dose of intravenous benzodiazepine
Intravenous phenytoin or an equivalent second-line agent

questions.explanation: Central centrifugal cicatricial alopecia typically affects women of African descent and is associated with chronic use of heat styling and chemical hair relaxers, producing progressive scarring hair loss beginning at the vertex and spreading outward. It is a scarring alopecia with permanent follicular destruction if unrecognised. Reducing traumatic hair practices is an important part of management alongside anti-inflammatory treatment.
questions.question: A middle-aged woman of West African descent who has used heated combs and chemical relaxers for years presents with progressive, centrally distributed scarring hair loss on the vertex spreading centrifugally. What is the most likely diagnosis?

questions.explanation: In pulmonary sarcoidosis, BAL characteristically shows elevated LYMPHOCYTES (lymphocytic alveolitis) with markedly increased CD4:CD8 T-cell ratio > 3.5:1 (normal ~1.5:1). A ratio > 3.5 has ~95% specificity for sarcoidosis. In contrast, hypersensitivity pneumonitis shows predominantly CD8 lymphocytes (low CD4:CD8 ratio). This immunological pattern reflects the Th1-driven immune response in sarcoidosis.
questions.question: In the BAL (bronchoalveolar lavage) finding MOST characteristic of sarcoidosis is:
options: Predominantly neutrophil differential with low CD4:CD8 ratio
Elevated T lymphocytes with markedly INCREASED CD4:CD8 ratio

questions.explanation: ST-elevation in the inferior leads II, III, and aVF localises infarction to the inferior wall of the left ventricle, typically supplied by the right coronary artery. Recognising this territory is important because inferior infarcts carry a risk of right ventricular involvement and bradyarrhythmias. Reciprocal ST depression is often seen in the lateral leads.
questions.question: A 45-year-old male presents with acute chest pain and an ECG showing ST-elevation in leads II, III, and aVF. This pattern indicates infarction of which cardiac territory?

A patient undergoes Roux-en-Y gastric bypass for morbid obesity. Postoperatively, their type 2 diabetes resolves rapidly, often before significant weight loss has occurred. Which comorbidity is best documented to improve substantially with this specific procedure?
questions.explanation: Roux-en-Y gastric bypass produces well-documented rapid and often weight-loss-independent improvement or resolution of type 2 diabetes, thought to relate to altered gut hormone signalling in addition to caloric restriction. While osteoarthritis symptoms can improve with weight loss over time, the effect is generally more gradual and mechanically mediated rather than an early metabolic resolution. This distinction is frequently highlighted when explaining the specific metabolic benefits of bypass surgery.

questions.question: A patient with poorly controlled diabetes develops facial pain, black necrotic nasal turbinate tissue and orbital swelling. Biopsy shows broad, non-septate hyphae branching at right angles. Which infection is MOST likely?
questions.explanation: Mucormycosis is an aggressive angioinvasive fungal infection strongly associated with poorly controlled diabetes and ketoacidosis, characterised histologically by broad, ribbon-like, non-septate hyphae branching at right angles, distinguishing it from the septate, acute-angle branching hyphae of Aspergillus. Rhino-orbital-cerebral involvement can progress rapidly with tissue necrosis, requiring urgent surgical debridement alongside amphotericin B. Delay in treatment carries very high mortality.

Indian ink (nigrosin) stain is specifically used to visualise the large polysaccharide capsule of Cryptococcus neoformans in CSF, appearing as clear halos against the dark background. Cryptococcal meningitis is a common AIDS-defining illness and life-threatening fungal infection in immunocompromised patients.
questions.question: The Indian ink stain in CSF analysis is specifically used to detect which organism causing meningitis?

options: Both cortisol and ACTH are markedly elevated
Cortisol elevated but ACTH only mildly raised
questions.explanation: In ectopic ACTH syndrome (e.g., from small cell lung carcinoma), the tumour autonomously produces ACTH (or ACTH-like molecules) independent of CRH or cortisol feedback. This results in both markedly elevated ACTH AND markedly elevated cortisol. High ACTH drives adrenocortical hyperplasia and excess cortisol production. Neither is suppressed by exogenous glucocorticoids (fails high-dose DST). This contrasts with adrenal adenoma Cushing's (high cortisol, suppressed ACTH).
questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes the relationship between cortisol and ACTH in Cushing's syndrome due to ectopic ACTH?
A patient with early mechanical bowel obstruction has high-pitched, frequent bowel sounds on auscultation. This finding reflects which phase of obstruction?
options: Early phase with increased peristaltic activity against the obstruction
Late phase with bowel ischaemia and silence
questions.explanation: In early mechanical obstruction, the bowel proximal to the blockage exhibits hyperactive, high-pitched peristalsis as it attempts to overcome the obstruction. As obstruction progresses and bowel becomes ischaemic or exhausted, sounds diminish and eventually become silent, suggesting a more advanced or complicated stage. Recognising this progression aids clinical assessment of obstruction severity.

questions.question: A pregnant woman develops glucose intolerance first recognised during her third trimester, resolving after delivery. This pattern is best classified as:
questions.explanation: Gestational diabetes mellitus refers to glucose intolerance with onset or first recognition during pregnancy, typically resolving after delivery, though it increases future risk of type 2 diabetes. It differs from pre-existing diabetes, which is diagnosed before pregnancy. Screening and management reduce maternal and fetal complications.

The characteristic reddish-brown, pasty aspirate described as 'anchovy paste' or 'chocolate sauce' is pathognomonic of amoebic liver abscess caused by Entamoeba histolytica. This material represents liquefied hepatic tissue and cellular debris from trophozoite invasion via the portal circulation.
questions.question: A hepatic abscess aspirate yielding reddish-brown material resembling 'anchovy paste' is diagnostic of:
options: Pyogenic liver abscess from E. coli
Amoebic liver abscess from Entamoeba histolytica

questions.explanation: In highly endemic areas (most of Africa), HAV infection is nearly universal in childhood. The MAJORITY of individuals are immune by age 10 years due to exposure to faecally contaminated food and water in early childhood. This exposure typically causes asymptomatic or mild infection in young children but potentially more severe disease in adults who escape early exposure.
questions.question: Hepatitis A is highly endemic in Africa. By what age have the MAJORITY of individuals in the community acquired immunity through natural infection?

options: Structural diversity even within the same coronavirus genus
Total absence of any envelope proteins in this virus family
Complete structural identity across all coronaviruses
Absence of any glycoproteins in coronaviruses generally
Exclusive presence in alpha coronaviruses only
questions.explanation: Coronaviruses within the same genus can show significant structural variation, such as the presence or absence of the haemagglutinin-esterase glycoprotein among different beta coronaviruses, reflecting evolutionary divergence even among closely related viruses. This variation influences aspects of viral biology and potential immune targets. Recognising such diversity is important when comparing pathogenicity and treatment approaches across coronavirus species.
questions.question: A microbiologist notes that the haemagglutinin-esterase glycoprotein is present in only certain coronaviruses. Among the major pathogenic human coronaviruses, this protein is notably absent in SARS-CoV-2 but present in some other beta coronaviruses, illustrating:

questions.explanation: Asbestos exposure alone increases lung cancer risk approximately 5-fold. Tobacco smoking alone increases risk approximately 15-fold. However, the combination of current smoking AND asbestos exposure has a synergistic (multiplicative) effect, increasing lung cancer risk to 80-90 times that of unexposed non-smokers. This demonstrates the critical synergism between occupational carcinogens and tobacco.
questions.question: Asbestos exposure multiplies the risk of lung cancer in smokers to how many times that of unexposed non-smokers?

questions.explanation: First-degree AV block is defined by a prolonged PR interval (greater than 200 milliseconds) with every atrial impulse still conducted to the ventricles, distinguishing it from higher degrees of block where some or all impulses fail to conduct. It is often asymptomatic and may not require specific treatment. Monitoring is appropriate to detect progression to higher-grade block.
questions.question: A patient's ECG shows a PR interval of 280 milliseconds with every P wave followed by a QRS complex. This finding is most consistent with:

questions.explanation: AIDS is defined by either a CD4+ T-cell count below 200 cells/µL or the development of an AIDS-defining illness (e.g., PCP, CMV retinitis, Kaposi's sarcoma, cerebral toxoplasmosis), regardless of CD4 count. Below 200/µL, the immune system is severely compromised and susceptible to opportunistic infections.
options: CD4 count below 200 cells/µL OR AIDS-defining illness
questions.question: AIDS is defined as late-stage HIV disease. Which immunological threshold defines progression to AIDS?
The MOST common cause of Cushing's syndrome in children is:
questions.explanation: Iatrogenic (exogenous) glucocorticoid therapy is the most common cause of Cushing's syndrome in both children and adults overall. In endogenous Cushing's syndrome, pituitary adenoma (Cushing's disease) is the most common cause in adults, while adrenal tumours are relatively more common in children. Ectopic ACTH secretion (e.g., from small cell lung cancer) is another important cause, typically with a rapid and severe presentation.

options: Reduced renin secretion from the kidney
Increased angiotensin II accumulation causing inflammation and vasoconstriction
questions.explanation: ACE2 normally converts angiotensin II to angiotensin 1-7 (anti-inflammatory). SARS-CoV-2 binding depletes ACE2, causing angiotensin II accumulation—promoting vasoconstriction, inflammation, and oxidative stress. This ACE2 depletion partly explains COVID-19's cardiovascular and pulmonary complications.
questions.question: SARS-CoV-2 binding to ACE2 depletes surface ACE2 activity. The physiological consequence of this depletion is:
A patient with dysphagia undergoes chromoendoscopy to highlight suspicious oesophageal mucosal areas. Definitive confirmation of oesophageal carcinoma still requires which additional step?
questions.explanation: While chromoendoscopy enhances visualisation of subtle mucosal abnormalities, definitive diagnosis of oesophageal carcinoma still requires histological confirmation via targeted biopsy of the suspicious area. Imaging techniques alone, however advanced, cannot provide tissue diagnosis. This biopsy confirmation is essential before planning definitive oncological treatment.
options: Histological biopsy of the abnormal area
Improved urine output and falling creatinine
questions.question: A patient with acute kidney injury secondary to hypovolaemia is given intravenous fluid resuscitation. Which parameter would MOST reliably confirm an adequate response to this treatment?
questions.explanation: Adequate response to fluid resuscitation in prerenal AKI is best confirmed by improved urine output and a subsequent trend toward normalising creatinine, reflecting restored renal perfusion and tubular function. Increased potassium or urea would instead suggest worsening, not improving, renal function. Monitoring these functional parameters, rather than unrelated laboratory values, guides ongoing fluid management decisions.

questions.question: A patient with widespread erythema, scaling, and skin failure affecting more than 90% of the body surface is admitted with hypothermia and high-output cardiac failure. Which psoriasis variant does this represent?
questions.explanation: Erythrodermic psoriasis involves diffuse erythema and scaling over nearly the entire skin surface, impairing thermoregulation and causing high fluid and protein losses that can precipitate cardiac failure, making it a dermatological emergency. Generalised pustular psoriasis instead features widespread sterile pustules with systemic toxicity rather than diffuse erythroderma as the defining feature. Recognising erythroderma as an emergency prompts urgent multidisciplinary admission.

Drug-induced hypersensitivity pneumonitis is classified under the hypersensitivity pneumonitis/pneumoconiosis category in the differential diagnosis of granulomatous lung disease. Other categories include infectious conditions (TB, fungal), vasculitides (GPA, EGPA), and foreign body granulomatosis—each requiring distinct treatment approaches.
questions.question: In sarcoidosis, the differential diagnosis of granulomatous lung disease includes hypersensitivity pneumonitis. Which aetiological category does drug-induced hypersensitivity pneumonitis fall under?

questions.explanation: Onychogryphosis (ram's horn deformity of the nail) is caused by trauma, peripheral vascular disease, chronic neglect, and old age. Psoriasis causes nail pitting, oil spots, onycholysis, and subungual hyperkeratosis but is not a direct cause of the specific ram's horn deformity of onychogryphosis. Liver cirrhosis causes Terry's nails, not onychogryphosis.
questions.question: Onychogryphosis (nail hypertrophy producing 'ram's horn' nails) is caused by all of the following EXCEPT:

questions.explanation: Discoid (nummular) eczema is classified as an endogenous eczema, meaning it arises from internal constitutional processes rather than identifiable external triggers. Other endogenous eczemas include atopic dermatitis, seborrhoeic dermatitis, pompholyx, and asteatotic eczema. Irritant and allergic contact dermatitis, photoallergic CD, and infective dermatitis are exogenous.
questions.question: Which of the following is an ENDOGENOUS form of eczema?

questions.explanation: Oliguria is defined as decreased urine output less than 400 ml/day (approximately 0.5 ml/kg/hr). Anuria is defined as absence of urine production (<100 ml/day). Polyuria is defined as urine output >3 litres/day. These definitions are clinically important for staging renal failure and guiding fluid management decisions. Oliguria in acute kidney injury is an important prognostic marker.
questions.question: Oliguria is defined as urine output below which threshold?
Altered tissue response to hormones is a mechanism of endocrine disease BEST exemplified by:
questions.explanation: Type 2 diabetes mellitus is the classic example of altered tissue response (resistance) as a mechanism of endocrine disease. Target tissues (liver, muscle, adipose) are resistant to insulin action despite normal or elevated insulin levels. Other examples include androgen insensitivity syndrome (resistance to androgens at receptor level) and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (renal resistance to ADH). In contrast, hypothyroidism represents underproduction, not resistance.

options: Direct DNA binding by the hormone
Immediate gene transcription by the hormone-receptor complex
Physical entry of the hormone into the nucleus
Cascade of intracellular signalling affecting cell function
questions.explanation: When a peptide hormone binds to its cell surface receptor, it triggers a cascade of intracellular signalling events—typically activation of second messenger systems (cAMP, IP3/DAG, tyrosine kinase pathways). This amplifies the signal and ultimately affects cellular function rapidly. This contrasts with steroid hormones, which enter the cell and directly interact with nuclear receptors to regulate gene transcription.
questions.question: The hormone receptor binding triggers which intracellular event for cell surface (peptide hormone) receptors?

options: Oxalate crystal deposition from dietary excess
Hypercalcaemia and hypercalciuria from excess calcitriol
questions.explanation: In sarcoidosis, granuloma-derived macrophages produce excess 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol), causing hypercalcaemia and hypercalciuria. The excess urinary calcium precipitates as calcium phosphate or calcium oxalate in renal tubules and parenchyma—nephrocalcinosis—and in the collecting system as nephrolithiasis (kidney stones).
questions.question: In sarcoidosis of the kidney, nephrocalcinosis occurs as a direct consequence of which metabolic derangement?

options: Chronic eczema and suspected allergic contact dermatitis
questions.explanation: Patch testing is the gold-standard investigation for identifying contact allergens in allergic contact dermatitis and is particularly useful in chronic eczema where an allergic aetiology is suspected. It involves application of standardised allergen panels for 48 hours under occlusion. It is not appropriate for urticaria or psoriasis where IgE or T-cell mechanisms differ.
questions.question: Patch testing is SPECIFICALLY indicated as an investigation in which clinical scenario?

questions.explanation: Trigeminal neuralgia causes brief, severe, lancinating unilateral facial pain in the distribution of the trigeminal nerve, often triggered by innocuous stimuli such as chewing, talking or touching the face. The neurological examination is typically normal, and vascular compression of the trigeminal nerve root is the most common underlying cause. Carbamazepine is the first-line pharmacological treatment.
questions.question: A patient describes brief, severe, electric shock-like unilateral facial pain triggered by chewing or touching the face, lasting seconds, with normal neurological examination. Which condition is MOST likely?

options: An autoimmune condition from T-cell attack on basal keratinocytes
A congenital eczematous disorder present from birth
A viral-induced papulosquamous eruption of the skin
A side effect of prolonged systemic corticosteroid use
Chronic eczema from repetitive scratching, perpetuating itch-scratch cycle
questions.explanation: Lichen simplex chronicus results from chronic repetitive scratching or rubbing of a localised area, creating a self-perpetuating itch-scratch-lichenification cycle. The skin becomes thickened with accentuated markings (lichenification). Common sites include the nape, ankles, and anogenital area. Management requires breaking the cycle with potent topical corticosteroids and addressing underlying psychological factors contributing to habitual scratching.
questions.question: Lichen simplex chronicus (neurodermatitis) is BEST described as:

options: Direct granulomatous infiltration of renal tubules
Uric acid deposition from tissue turnover
questions.explanation: Sarcoidosis kidneys are affected (5% of cases) predominantly through hypercalcaemia and hypercalciuria driven by macrophage-produced 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D. Calcium deposits in tubules and collecting ducts cause nephrocalcinosis, while calcium stones form in the collecting system. Interstitial nephritis from granulomatous infiltration also occurs but hypercalciuria is the primary mechanism for stones.
questions.question: A patient with sarcoidosis develops nephrocalcinosis and kidney stones. Which underlying mechanism is DIRECTLY responsible?
Which statement about hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) screening is MOST consistent with evidence-based practice for high-risk patients with cirrhosis?
options: Regular ultrasound surveillance combined with AFP monitoring for early detection
CT scan every 5 years is sufficient
Annual liver biopsy to detect dysplasia
No screening is beneficial as treatment outcomes are equally poor
questions.explanation: Regular ultrasonography (every 6 months) combined with serum AFP monitoring is recommended for HCC surveillance in high-risk patients (cirrhosis, chronic HBV/HCV). Early detection increases surgical candidacy ? early presentation with small tumours allows partial hepatectomy with 40-50% improvement in survival. AFP >400 ng/mL in a cirrhotic patient is virtually diagnostic of HCC.

questions.question: Bilateral renal artery stenosis as a cause of pre-renal AKI is PARTICULARLY dangerous when which class of drug is administered?
questions.explanation: In bilateral renal artery stenosis (or stenosis in a single kidney), GFR is maintained by angiotensin II-mediated efferent arteriolar constriction. ACE inhibitors/ARBs block angiotensin II, dilating the efferent arteriole and abruptly dropping GFR, precipitating AKI. This is a critical drug interaction to remember. Blood pressure and renal function must be monitored closely if these agents are used.

options: Requiring second messenger cascades for all effects
Diffusing across the cell membrane to bind intracellular receptors
Being unable to cross the cell membrane
Binding exclusively to cell surface receptors
questions.question: A researcher studying steroid hormone action confirms that these hormones typically act by:
questions.explanation: Steroid hormones are lipophilic and can diffuse directly across the cell membrane to bind intracellular or nuclear receptors, subsequently influencing gene transcription. This mechanism differs from peptide hormones, which rely on cell surface receptors and second messenger systems due to their hydrophilic nature. This property also explains the relatively slower onset but prolonged action of steroid hormones.

A cardiothoracic ratio exceeding 0.5 on a PA chest film indicates cardiomegaly, reflecting chamber dilation or hypertrophy. This ratio compares maximal transverse cardiac diameter to maximal thoracic diameter. Chronic hypertension causes left ventricular hypertrophy and eventual dilation, raising this ratio.
questions.question: A 50-year-old with long-standing hypertension develops a chest X-ray showing an enlarged cardiac silhouette. Which measurement threshold confirms cardiomegaly?

options: Identify fungal elements under UV light
Distinguish purpura from erythema by blanching
questions.explanation: Diascopy distinguishes between purpura (extravasated red blood cells that do not blanch on pressure) and erythema (dilated blood vessels that blanch on pressure). A glass slide or transparent spatula is pressed firmly against the lesion; blanching indicates vascular dilation, while non-blanching indicates extravascular haemorrhage.
questions.question: Diascopy in dermatological examination involves pressing a glass slide onto a lesion. Its PRIMARY purpose is to:
