questions.explanation: Adiponectin is unusual among adipokines in that its circulating levels fall as body fat mass increases, and it exerts insulin-sensitising, anti-inflammatory, and anti-atherogenic effects, so reduced adiponectin in obesity contributes to insulin resistance and increased cardiovascular risk. Leptin, resistin, and pro-inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-alpha and IL-6 typically rise with increasing adiposity, following the opposite pattern. This inverse relationship makes adiponectin a marker of interest in obesity-related metabolic research.

options: IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation (Type I hypersensitivity)
Immune complex deposition in vessels (Type III)
questions.explanation: Type 1 (reversal) reactions are Type IV delayed hypersensitivity reactions in which cell-mediated immunity suddenly increases in borderline leprosy patients. This causes acute inflammation in skin lesions and peripheral nerves, potentially causing rapid irreversible nerve damage. Prompt high-dose corticosteroids are essential to prevent permanent disability.
questions.question: Type 1 lepra reaction (reversal reaction) in borderline leprosy is immunologically mediated by which mechanism?

questions.explanation: SMALL CELL LUNG CARCINOMA (SCLC) accounts for approximately 60% of LEMS cases (paraneoplastic LEMS). SCLC cells express voltage-gated calcium channels (VGCCs) which trigger an immune response producing anti-VGCC antibodies that cross-react with presynaptic VGCCs at the neuromuscular junction. All patients with newly diagnosed LEMS should be screened for SCLC with CT chest.
questions.question: Which malignancy is MOST strongly associated with LEMS (Lambert-Eaton Myasthenic Syndrome) as a paraneoplastic syndrome?
Emphysema is pathologically defined as:
questions.explanation: Emphysema is defined pathologically as abnormal, permanent enlargement of air spaces distal to the terminal bronchioles, accompanied by destruction of their walls without obvious fibrosis. This alveolar destruction reduces gas exchange surface area and elastic recoil, causing air trapping, hyperinflation, and progressive dyspnoea. It is primarily caused by tobacco smoke and alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.
options: Mucus hypersecretion with airway wall thickening
Inflammatory cell infiltration of alveolar walls with granuloma formation
Permanent air-space enlargement distal to bronchioles with wall destruction
Fibrosis of alveolar walls from chronic hypoxia
Smooth muscle hypertrophy from chronic airway inflammation
Only half as strong as SARS-CoV
questions.question: The coronavirus spike protein binds ACE2 receptors on type 2 alveolar cells with what relative affinity compared to SARS-CoV (2002)?
questions.explanation: SARS-CoV-2 binds ACE2 receptors 10-20 times more strongly than the original SARS-CoV (2002-2003). This greater receptor affinity contributes to SARS-CoV-2's superior transmissibility, though SARS-CoV had higher case fatality. The higher binding affinity also explains why SARS-CoV-2 was not contained through symptom-based surveillance alone.

questions.question: A dermatologist biopsies perilesional skin from a patient with suspected autoimmune blistering disease and sends the tissue in a special transport medium rather than formalin. Which test is being requested?
questions.explanation: Direct immunofluorescence requires fresh or specially preserved perilesional tissue to detect in-vivo bound immunoglobulins and complement along the epidermal or basement membrane zone, confirming autoimmune bullous or connective tissue disease. Formalin fixation destroys the antigenicity needed for this test. Tzanck smears and patch tests use entirely different specimen types and cannot substitute.

courses.title: Opthalmology

questions.explanation: Phacodonesis (shimmering/trembling of the lens during eye movements) indicates partial zonular disruption (zonulysis) following blunt trauma. Complete zonular rupture leads to full lens dislocation (luxation) into the vitreous or anterior chamber. Iridodonesis (trembling iris) often accompanies phacodonesis and confirms zonular insufficiency.
questions.question: Phacodonesis (trembling lens) following blunt ocular trauma indicates:
options: Partial or complete disruption of the lens zonular fibres
Choroidal rupture at the posterior pole
Cataract formation occurring secondary to blunt trauma

questions.explanation: Behcet's disease characteristically causes bilateral occlusive retinal vasculitis with perivascular sheathing and recurrent hypopyon uveitis. The hallmark is a severe non-granulomatous panuveitis in a patient with the systemic triad of oral ulcers, genital ulcers, and skin lesions (erythema nodosum/pathergy). It is a major cause of blindness in the Middle East and Far East.
options: Multifocal choroidal granulomas with disc swelling
Occlusive retinal vasculitis with perivascular sheathing and recurrent vitritis
Exudative retinal detachment with sunset glow fundus
Unilateral retinal perivasculitis with hard exudates at the macula
Cotton-wool spots and flame-shaped hemorrhages from hypertensive retinopathy
questions.question: Behcet's disease uveitis is distinguished by which characteristic fundus finding?
A diabetic patient is found to have fine new vessels growing on the optic disc surface on fundoscopy. What stage of retinopathy does this represent?
questions.explanation: The presence of neovascularisation, whether on the disc or elsewhere in the retina, defines proliferative diabetic retinopathy, the most advanced and sight-threatening stage. These fragile new vessels are prone to bleeding into the vitreous and can cause tractional retinal detachment. Urgent panretinal photocoagulation is indicated at this stage.

questions.question: A premature infant on prolonged supplemental oxygen develops abnormal peripheral retinal vascularisation with a demarcation ridge on screening examination. Which condition is this?
questions.explanation: Retinopathy of prematurity results from disrupted normal retinal vascular development in premature infants, often exacerbated by supplemental oxygen exposure, leading to abnormal peripheral vessel growth and a characteristic demarcation ridge between vascularised and avascular retina. Severe cases can progress to tractional retinal detachment if untreated. Screening of at-risk premature infants allows timely laser treatment to halt progression.

options: No lens required; fixed focus only
questions.explanation: Myopic eyes are too long (anteroposteriorly), causing light to focus in front of the retina. Correction requires concave (diverging, minus-powered) lenses. During ophthalmoscopy, a minus number on the dial (red numbers) compensates for the patient's myopia and the examiner's refractive error to bring the fundus into clear focus. Green (plus) numbers are used for hyperopic patients.
questions.question: Myopic patients require which lens type for correction, and on the ophthalmoscope dial, which number setting brings their fundus into focus?

options: Apoptosis triggered by axonal flow obstruction, excitotoxicity, and ischaemia
Toxic retinal ganglion cell death from aqueous protein accumulation
Direct mechanical rupture of ganglion cell axons
Viral invasion of retinal ganglion cells
Immune complex deposition causing complement lysis
questions.explanation: Retinal ganglion cell death in glaucoma involves apoptosis triggered by multiple mechanisms including: axoplasmic flow obstruction at the lamina cribrosa, glutamate excitotoxicity, ischaemia from vascular dysregulation, and neurotrophic factor deprivation. These mechanisms are all exacerbated by elevated IOP but may persist even after IOP normalisation.
questions.question: The most significant mechanism of glaucomatous retinal ganglion cell death involves:

questions.explanation: Orbital cellulitis involves infection posterior to the orbital septum, producing proptosis, pain on eye movement, and restricted ocular motility, none of which occur in preseptal cellulitis confined anterior to the septum. Preseptal cellulitis presents with lid swelling and erythema without orbital signs. This distinction guides the urgency of imaging and treatment since orbital cellulitis carries higher risk of intracranial spread.
questions.question: A child presents with eyelid swelling, proptosis, restricted eye movement, and fever. Preseptal cellulitis has been excluded. Which feature supports this distinction?

questions.explanation: Recording the presenting complaint in the patient's exact words prevents premature diagnostic labeling. Using the patient's own description avoids the use of diagnostic terms (e.g., 'cataract', 'glaucoma') that may bias clinical assessment. This practice establishes an accurate baseline from which objective findings are later correlated.
options: Request fundoscopy immediately under standard examination conditions
Perform a visual field test in most clinical presentations
Record the complaint in the patient's exact words
questions.question: A 45-year-old man presents with gradual painless visual loss. During history taking, the MOST important initial step to establish the nature of the complaint is to:

options: Thyroid eye disease with superior limbal keratitis
Meibomian gland dysfunction with inferior staining
Congenital syphilis, tuberculosis, or Cogan's syndrome
questions.explanation: Interstitial keratitis (stromal vascularization and inflammation without primary epithelial involvement) in a young adult is classically associated with congenital syphilis (Hutchinson's triad: interstitial keratitis, notched incisors, and deafness), tuberculosis, and Cogan's syndrome (interstitial keratitis + vestibuloauditory dysfunction). Syphilis serology (FTA-ABS, TPHA) and chest X-ray should be performed.
questions.question: Interstitial keratitis in a young adult without obvious precipitating cause should prompt investigation for:
The MOST common cause of sudden painless unilateral visual loss in a patient aged over 60 years with cardiovascular risk factors is:
options: Non-arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy or central retinal artery occlusion
Central retinal vein occlusion with disc swelling
questions.explanation: In patients over 60 with cardiovascular risk factors, sudden painless unilateral visual loss is most commonly caused by non-arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy (NAION) or central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO). Both present with sudden, painless monocular visual loss. Giant cell arteritis must be urgently excluded with ESR/CRP in all such patients over 50 to prevent bilateral blindness.

The ciliary muscle, which contracts to allow lens rounding for near focus, is supplied by parasympathetic fibres travelling with the third nerve. Its paralysis removes accommodative ability even though distance vision through an undilated portion of the pupil may be preserved. This is why near vision complaints often accompany third nerve palsy.
questions.question: A patient with third nerve palsy is unable to accommodate for near vision despite normal visual acuity for distance. This loss of accommodation results from paralysis of the

options: Dry eye (keratoconjunctivitis sicca) from secondary Sjögren's syndrome
questions.question: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) MOST commonly causes which ocular manifestation?
questions.explanation: Keratoconjunctivitis sicca (dry eye) is the most common ocular manifestation of SLE, associated with secondary Sjögren's syndrome. Other SLE eye manifestations include retinal vasculitis (lupus retinopathy with cotton-wool spots), scleritis, episcleritis, and optic neuritis. Hydroxychloroquine for SLE can cause bull's-eye maculopathy requiring annual screening.

questions.question: A patient presents following blunt trauma with a fixed, dilated pupil that does not react to light or accommodation. What is the likely cause?
questions.explanation: Blunt trauma can mechanically damage the iris sphincter muscle, resulting in a traumatic mydriasis that is poorly reactive to light. This differs from a relative afferent pupillary defect caused by optic nerve damage, which still shows some reactivity. Careful examination helps distinguish structural iris damage from neurological causes.

questions.question: Which type of glaucoma shows IOP within normal range but progressive optic disc cupping and field loss?
questions.explanation: Normal-tension (low-tension) glaucoma features progressive optic cupping and visual field loss despite IOP consistently within 10–21 mmHg. Vascular insufficiency and increased optic nerve susceptibility to normal pressures are proposed mechanisms. It is more prevalent in Japanese populations and women.

questions.question: A patient develops sudden painless visual loss with curtain-like shadow from below. Fundoscopy shows a convex grey-brown elevation of the retina. The diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment (RRD) presents with sudden painless visual loss, preceded by flashes (photopsia) and floaters (vitreous detachment). The classic 'curtain' or 'shadow' rising from the periphery follows as the detachment progresses. Fundoscopy shows an elevated, corrugated grey retina with one or more retinal breaks. Urgent surgical repair (vitrectomy, scleral buckle) is required.

options: Observe and manage conservatively in the majority of documented cases as commonly encountered in practice
Apply topical antibiotics only based on typical clinical findings during routine ophthalmic assessment
Reposition uveal prolapse and suture laceration with 10-0 nylon for cornea
questions.question: For a Grade 1 corneo-scleral laceration presenting within 24 hours, the CORRECT surgical management is:
questions.explanation: For a Grade 1 corneo-scleral laceration presenting within 24 hours, the uveal prolapse should be repositioned and the laceration repaired with 10-0 nylon sutures for the cornea. If the presentation exceeds 24 hours, the uvea should be excised (abscised) before wound closure to prevent infection. Timely repair is critical to prevent infection, hypotony, and sympathetic ophthalmia.

Approximately 90% of cases of congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction resolve spontaneously within the first year of life through natural canalization of the duct. Initial conservative management includes topical antibiotics and massage of the lacrimal sac. Probing and syringing are reserved for cases persisting beyond 12–18 months.
questions.question: Congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction (CNLDO) typically resolves spontaneously in what percentage of cases within the first year of life?

questions.explanation: Retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) results from disruption of normal retinal vascular development in premature infants. Premature infants have incompletely vascularised retinas; supplemental oxygen causes vasoconstriction and vaso-obliteration. When oxygen is reduced, hypoxic retina releases VEGF, driving abnormal neovascularisation. Screening and laser photocoagulation of avascular retina prevent blinding complications.
options: Genetic mutation affecting rod photoreceptor development pathways
Oxygen-induced retinal vascular changes in premature infants with immature retinal vasculature
questions.question: Retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) is caused primarily by:
Epidemic keratoconjunctivitis (EKC), a highly contagious eye disease, is caused by:
questions.explanation: Epidemic keratoconjunctivitis (EKC) is caused by adenovirus serotypes 8 and 19. It presents with acute follicular conjunctivitis, preauricular lymphadenopathy, and subepithelial corneal infiltrates causing photophobia and reduced vision. It spreads rapidly via contaminated hands and instruments. It is self-limiting with no specific antiviral treatment.

The Under-5 Mortality Rate (U5MR) is used as a surrogate indicator for the magnitude of childhood blindness because both reflect levels of poverty, malnutrition, vaccination coverage, and access to health services. Countries with higher U5MR tend to have higher rates of preventable causes of childhood blindness (vitamin A deficiency, measles, corneal scarring). This relationship underscores the shared socioeconomic determinants of child health.
questions.question: The U5MR (Under-5 Mortality Rate) is considered a useful surrogate indicator for:
options: Prevalence of adult-onset glaucoma based on typical clinical findings
The magnitude of childhood blindness in a country
Prevalence of refractive error in children in the majority of documented cases

questions.explanation: Optic nerve gliomas are uncommon benign tumors predominantly affecting children in the first decade. Up to 50% are associated with neurofibromatosis type 1. In patients with stable vision, observation with periodic examinations is appropriate since many remain static. Treatment (surgery, radiotherapy, or chemotherapy) is indicated only for progressive visual loss or growing tumor.
options: Immediate surgical excision to prevent spread
questions.question: In optic nerve glioma associated with neurofibromatosis type 1, the management of a child with stable vision is:

questions.explanation: Punctal occlusion blocks the tear drainage channels, allowing natural tears to remain on the ocular surface for a longer period, improving lubrication in patients with dry eye disease. This can reduce reliance on frequent artificial tear instillation and protect the cornea from exposure-related damage. Temporary plugs can be used as a trial before considering permanent occlusion.
options: Increase drainage of tears from the eye
Retain natural tears on the ocular surface for longer
Directly treat any underlying infection present
Reduce the natural production of tears
questions.question: A patient with severe dry eye and ongoing risk of corneal breakdown is considered for punctal occlusion. What is the therapeutic aim of this procedure?
Neovascular glaucoma (rubeosis iridis) is MOST commonly caused by:
options: Proliferative diabetic retinopathy or central retinal vein occlusion
Congenital glaucoma with markedly elevated intraocular pressure
questions.explanation: Neovascular glaucoma results from posterior segment ischaemia — most commonly proliferative diabetic retinopathy or central retinal vein occlusion. VEGF released by ischaemic retina stimulates iris neovascularisation (rubeosis iridis). Fibrovascular membrane covers the angle, causing progressive closure and intractable elevated IOP.

questions.question: A patient on chronic pilocarpine therapy for glaucoma complains of dim vision, particularly at night. What is the underlying reason?
options: Persistent pupillary constriction reducing retinal illumination
questions.explanation: Pilocarpine causes sustained miosis, which reduces the amount of light reaching the retina, particularly problematic in low-light conditions. This miotic pupil also worsens vision in patients with early lens opacities by increasing depth of focus effects. These visual side effects often limit long-term tolerability of the drug.

questions.question: A patient develops endophthalmitis several days after a penetrating eye injury. The MOST appropriate initial management is
options: immediate enucleation without trial of therapy
questions.explanation: Intravitreal antibiotic injection delivers high local drug concentrations directly to the site of infection, which is essential in post-traumatic endophthalmitis given the eye's limited penetration of systemic or topical drugs. Topical therapy alone is inadequate for intraocular infection. Enucleation is reserved for eyes that fail to respond or have no visual potential.

Trachoma, caused by repeated Chlamydia trachomatis infection, leads to chronic follicular conjunctivitis and subsequent conjunctival scarring. This scarring distorts the eyelid margin, causing eyelashes to turn inward and abrade the cornea, a condition called trichiasis. Untreated, this progresses to corneal opacification and blindness.
questions.question: A child in an endemic community presents with follicular conjunctivitis and later develops inturned eyelashes scarring the cornea. What is the underlying infection?
A patient recovering from radical neck dissection develops ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis on the operated side. This pattern is most consistent with injury to the
questions.explanation: Neck surgery can damage the sympathetic chain as it travels from the cervical ganglia toward the eye, corresponding to the second-order (preganglionic) segment. This explains the postoperative onset of the classic Horner's triad. Anhidrosis limited to the face confirms a lesion at or below the superior cervical ganglion.

Goldberg Stage V represents the most advanced stage of proliferative sickle cell retinopathy, characterised by vitreous hemorrhage and retinal detachment resulting from the fibrovascular proliferation of earlier stages. Earlier stages describe peripheral arteriolar occlusion and early neovascular changes without these severe complications. Recognising Stage V guides urgent surgical planning given the threat to vision.
questions.question: A patient with sickle cell disease and known proliferative retinopathy develops vitreous hemorrhage and tractional retinal detachment on examination. According to the Goldberg staging system, this represents

questions.explanation: In hereditary retinoblastoma, a germline mutation in one RB1 allele is already present in every cell, so only a single additional somatic mutation in the second allele is needed to trigger tumour formation. This explains why hereditary cases tend to be bilateral and present earlier than sporadic disease, which requires two independent somatic hits within the same cell. Understanding this model guides genetic counselling for affected families.
options: one inherited mutation plus one additional somatic mutation
two separate inherited mutations from each parent
a mutation acquired only after birth in every case
no additional mutation beyond the inherited one
questions.question: A child with bilateral retinoblastoma and a strong family history is found to carry a germline RB1 mutation. According to the two-hit hypothesis, tumour formation in this hereditary form requires
A farmer presents with a corneal ulcer following injury with a plant material, showing a feathery infiltrate with satellite lesions. What is the likely cause?
questions.explanation: Vegetable matter injuries are a classic risk factor for fungal keratitis, which characteristically produces a feathery, greyish infiltrate with satellite lesions distant from the main ulcer. Fungal ulcers often have a more indolent course than bacterial infections. Diagnosis requires scraping with fungal stains or culture, and antifungal therapy is prolonged.

options: Third-order neuron along the carotid artery
questions.question: A patient with a Pancoast's tumor develops classic features of Horner's syndrome. The lesion most likely affects the:
questions.explanation: A Pancoast's tumor arises at the apex of the lung and compresses the preganglionic (second-order) sympathetic fibers as they exit the upper thoracic spine. This classically produces Horner's syndrome as a paraneoplastic manifestation. The location—lung apex—specifically implicates the second-order neuron in the sympathetic chain.

options: Maintain adequate distance focus without effort
Generate sufficient zonular tension for clear far vision
Produce enough aqueous to compensate for near focus
Increase dioptric power to focus near objects on the retina
questions.explanation: In presbyopia, the ciliary muscle (and increasingly rigid lens) cannot generate the required increase in dioptric power to focus near objects on the retina. The convex addition lens supplements this lost accommodative amplitude, bringing near objects into focus. The reading addition needed equals the accommodation deficit.
questions.question: Presbyopia correction specifically requires a convergent lens because the weakened ciliary muscle can no longer:

questions.explanation: PACG is approximately 4 times more common in women than in men. Women generally have shorter axial lengths, smaller eyes, shallower anterior chambers, and more anteriorly positioned lenses — anatomical factors predisposing to angle closure. Women also develop PACG at older ages, typically in the sixth decade.
questions.question: The sex ratio for PACG shows approximately:
options: Equal distribution between men and women
More common in men over 70 years

questions.explanation: The reading addition required equals the accommodative deficit at near working distance. A +2.50 D addition means the patient's accommodation is deficient by 2.50 D for near tasks. Normal near accommodation for adults without presbyopia is approximately 4–6 D; presbyopia reduces this progressively beyond age 40.
questions.question: A patient needs a +2.50 D reading addition with normal distant VA. The accommodation amplitude is approximately:
options: Deficient by 2.50 D compared to required near accommodation
Completely absent; patient has no residual accommodation
Variable; presbyopia does not affect amplitude predictably
Sickle cell trait in a cousin
questions.explanation: A first-degree family history of glaucoma is one of the strongest risk factors for primary open-angle glaucoma, as the condition has a significant genetic component. The FSH section specifically asks about glaucoma in the family for this reason. Diabetes and hypertension are general risk factors for other ocular diseases but less specific to glaucoma.
questions.question: In a patient with suspected glaucoma, which family history item carries the MOST diagnostic significance?

questions.explanation: The Jones I (primary dye) test assesses the functional (physiological) drainage of tears through the lacrimal system under normal blinking conditions. Fluorescein dye is instilled in the conjunctival sac; recovery from the nose indicates functional patency. If negative, Jones II (secondary dye) test checks for anatomical structural patency.
questions.question: The Jones primary dye test (Jones I) assesses which component of the lacrimal drainage function?
options: Structural patency of the nasolacrimal duct under pressure
Goblet cell density of the conjunctival surface
Aqueous tear secretion rate by the lacrimal gland
Functional lacrimal drainage and pump mechanism
Resistance of the valve of Rosenmuller to reflux
As iris depigmentation spots in chronic PACG
In the vitreous following secondary glaucoma
At the optic disc margin as green-yellow haemorrhages
As corneal dystrophic deposits in PACG
As anterior subcapsular lens opacities after acute PACG
questions.question: Glaukomflecken are characteristically found:
questions.explanation: Glaukomflecken are small, irregular anterior subcapsular lens opacities from ischaemia of the anterior lens during an acute angle-closure attack. They are pathognomonic evidence of a previous acute PACG episode and may remain visible on slit-lamp for years after the attack, confirming a history of prior acute PACG.

questions.question: A patient with seasonal allergic conjunctivitis is prescribed sodium cromoglicate drops for prevention rather than acute relief. Its mechanism of action is to
questions.explanation: Sodium cromoglicate stabilises mast cell membranes, preventing the release of histamine and other inflammatory mediators upon allergen exposure. Because it acts prophylactically rather than reversing already-released mediators, it is less useful for treating an acute flare. This distinguishes it from antihistamines, which block receptors after mediator release.
options: stabilise mast cell membranes and prevent degranulation

questions.explanation: The pin-hole allows only one ray of light from each point to pass through the principal axis to the retina, eliminating peripheral aberrations from refractive errors. This creates a focused image on the retina regardless of the refractive state. It helps confirm that reduced VA is due to refractive error rather than structural ocular pathology.
questions.question: The pin-hole creates a clear image regardless of refractive state because it:
options: Increases the depth of field beyond the far point
Allows only paraxial rays through the principal axis to the retina
Enlarges the retinal image by reducing magnification
Stimulates pupillary dilation to enhance retinal illumination
Bypasses the corneal refractive pathway entirely

questions.question: A patient presents after blunt trauma with diplopia on upward gaze, sunken appearance of the eye, and numbness of the cheek. What structure is entrapped?
options: Superior oblique muscle in the roof
Inferior rectus muscle in an orbital floor fracture
Medial rectus muscle in medial wall
Lateral rectus muscle in the wall
questions.explanation: This presentation is classic for a blow-out fracture of the orbital floor, where the inferior rectus or surrounding tissue becomes entrapped, restricting upward gaze. Infraorbital nerve involvement, running through the floor, causes cheek numbness. Enophthalmos results from orbital volume expansion into the maxillary sinus.

options: Absence of any lens in the eye
A pre-existing narrow anterior chamber angle
questions.explanation: Pharmacological pupillary dilation can precipitate acute angle closure in eyes with a pre-existing anatomically narrow angle, as the dilated iris bunches into the angle recess and obstructs aqueous outflow. Screening programmes should be aware of this risk and provide clear safety advice to patients after dilation. Eyes known to have narrow angles may require prophylactic iridotomy before routine dilation.
questions.question: A patient develops sudden loss of vision, severe pain, and a fixed, dilated pupil following pupillary dilation drops used for a diabetic eye screening appointment. What underlying anatomical risk factor predisposed to this event?

questions.explanation: Pilocarpine produces sustained pupillary constriction and ciliary muscle spasm, causing dim vision, browache, and accommodative difficulty, especially troublesome in younger patients. These side effects reduce compliance compared with once-daily prostaglandin analogues. Newer agents also require less frequent dosing.
questions.question: Why is pilocarpine less favoured today compared with prostaglandin analogues for chronic glaucoma therapy?
options: It raises intraocular pressure over time
It causes miosis and accommodative spasm

questions.explanation: A hypopyon represents accumulated inflammatory cells settling under gravity in the anterior chamber and signals a severe, often infective or markedly inflammatory process such as endophthalmitis, infectious keratitis, or severe uveitis. It is not seen in mild superficial conditions like conjunctivitis or dry eye. Its presence mandates urgent ophthalmic assessment.
questions.question: A patient with anterior chamber inflammation is found to have a visible horizontal layer of white cells settling in the lower anterior chamber. This finding, called a hypopyon, is MOST indicative of
options: severe anterior uveitis or infectious keratitis

questions.question: Anisometropia, if severe and uncorrected in childhood, most commonly leads to:
options: Convergent strabismus in the better eye
Amblyopia in the more ametropic eye
Nuclear cataract in the dominant eye
questions.explanation: Anisometropia (unequal refraction between the two eyes) forces the visual cortex to suppress the blurry image from the more ametropic eye. If left untreated during the critical period of visual development (birth to ~8 years), this leads to amblyopia — reduced vision from disuse in that eye despite no structural defect.

questions.question: Which trachoma sign in the WHO grading system represents the most advanced stage leading to blindness?
questions.explanation: Corneal opacity (CO) in the WHO trachoma grading system represents the most advanced stage of trachoma and directly causes blindness by obstructing the visual axis. It results from years of repeated Chlamydia trachomatis infections causing scarring (TS), trichiasis (TT), and mechanical abrasion of the cornea. CO-stage blindness is irreversible, making earlier intervention critical.

questions.question: A pedunculated conjunctival papilloma in a young patient is almost always caused by which organism?
questions.explanation: Pedunculated conjunctival papillomas in young patients are almost always caused by human papillomavirus (HPV). They are multiple, tend to recur after incomplete excision, and eventually regress spontaneously. Non-viral papillomas occur in older patients, are solitary, originate at the limbus, and have lower recurrence rates. Treatment is complete excision with cryotherapy or beta radiation. SUBTOPIC 5: DISEASES OF THE CORNEA

questions.question: Purulent discharge with lid swelling and conjunctival chemosis in a neonate is MOST suggestive of:
questions.explanation: Gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum presents within 2-5 days of birth with profuse purulent discharge, severe lid swelling, and conjunctival chemosis. Without treatment, Neisseria gonorrhoeae can penetrate the intact corneal epithelium causing corneal ulceration and perforation. Chemical conjunctivitis from silver nitrate is mild and self-limiting; viral conjunctivitis produces watery rather than purulent discharge.

questions.question: The International Clinical DR Disease Severity Scale classifies diabetic retinopathy without visible retinal abnormality as:
options: Mild NPDR as commonly encountered in practice
Moderate NPDR during routine ophthalmic assessment
questions.explanation: On the International Clinical DR Disease Severity Scale, eyes with no visible abnormalities on dilated fundoscopy are classified as 'No Apparent Retinopathy.' This category still requires regular surveillance (annual examination) as the patient may develop retinopathy with duration of diabetes and poor metabolic control. Subsequent categories progress through mild, moderate, and severe NPDR to PDR.

questions.question: A patient with a hyphema (blood in the anterior chamber) following blunt trauma should INITIALLY be managed with:
options: Immediate surgical evacuation of blood in the majority of documented cases
Conservative treatment: bed rest in Fowler's position to allow absorption
Topical antifungals and antibiotics based on typical clinical findings
questions.explanation: Initial conservative management of traumatic hyphema includes bed rest in Fowler's position (head elevated 30-45 degrees) to allow the blood to settle inferiorly and facilitate absorption without blocking the visual axis or drainage angle. Intraocular pressure must be monitored closely as elevated IOP is a major complication. Surgical intervention (paracentesis) is reserved for total hyphemas or uncontrolled IOP elevation.

questions.question: A patient presents with a dendritic corneal ulcer and reduced corneal sensation. Which treatment is contraindicated?
questions.explanation: Dendritic ulceration with reduced corneal sensation is characteristic of herpes simplex keratitis. Topical corticosteroids used alone without antiviral cover can worsen epithelial disease by promoting viral replication. Antiviral therapy, sometimes combined with cautious steroid use for stromal disease, is the appropriate approach.

questions.question: A child spills household detergent into the eye at home. This type of chemical injury is MOST commonly classified as
questions.explanation: Many household cleaning agents and detergents are alkaline, and alkali burns penetrate ocular tissue more deeply than acid burns because they cause liquefactive rather than coagulative necrosis. Recognising the likely alkaline nature of domestic chemical injuries prompts urgent and prolonged irrigation. This distinction affects both severity and management priorities.

options: Direct laser destruction of the ciliary body
Complete removal of the trabecular meshwork
Insertion of a permanent artificial cornea
Creation of a new drainage channel
Direct injection of medication into the vitreous
questions.question: A patient undergoes trabeculectomy for uncontrolled glaucoma. What is the basic surgical principle behind this procedure?
questions.explanation: Trabeculectomy creates a partial-thickness scleral flap allowing aqueous humour to bypass the diseased trabecular meshwork and drain into a subconjunctival space, forming a bleb. This lowers intraocular pressure by providing an alternative outflow pathway. Careful flap tension is required to balance adequate drainage against the risk of hypotony.

An external hordeolum arises from staphylococcal infection of the glands of Zeis or Moll, which are associated with the eyelash follicles at the lid margin. This produces a superficial, tender, pointing abscess unlike the deeper internal hordeolum from meibomian gland infection. Warm compresses and topical antibiotics usually suffice for resolution.
questions.question: A patient develops an acutely painful, tender swelling at the lash line with pointing toward the skin surface. Which structure is primarily infected?

questions.explanation: Vitamin A supplementation during measles does not treat the virus itself but replenishes stores rapidly depleted by the infection, reducing the risk of corneal xerosis, ulceration, and resultant blindness. It has no direct antiviral or antibacterial action and does not prevent transmission to others. This targeted preventive measure specifically protects ocular surface integrity during a high-risk illness.
options: prevent the spread of measles to contacts
shorten the duration of fever alone
prevent bacterial superinfection of the skin
reduce the risk of corneal xerosis and blindness during the illness
questions.question: A public health programme gives vitamin A supplementation to all children diagnosed with measles specifically to

options: Accumulation of gliosis in the nerve head
Abnormal vascular proliferation occurring within the optic cup
Swelling of axons within the optic nerve
Loss of neuroretinal rim tissue due to retinal ganglion cell death
questions.explanation: Optic disc cupping in glaucoma represents loss of neuroretinal rim tissue — the axons of retinal ganglion cells — as ganglion cells die progressively. As axons are lost, the optic cup enlarges relative to the disc (increased C/D ratio). In adults this damage is irreversible. In infants with congenital glaucoma, cupping may partially reverse with IOP normalisation.
questions.question: Glaucomatous optic disc cupping reflects which pathological process?

options: Focus longer on familiar compared to novel stimuli
Blink more frequently to high-contrast stimuli
Turn toward a patterned stimulus rather than a uniform gray target
Follow a slowly moving light target across the visual midline
Reach for objects in the illuminated temporal hemifield
questions.question: Preferential looking tests assess visual acuity in infants by exploiting the tendency of a child to:
questions.explanation: Preferential looking tests exploit the infant's innate tendency to look toward a patterned grating stimulus (alternating black and white stripes) over a plain gray target of equal average luminance. The finest grating the infant can see correlates with visual acuity. Infants with better vision can detect finer gratings.

questions.question: A patient presents with copious purulent discharge and rapidly progressive conjunctival injection within 24 hours of onset. Which feature classifies this presentation as hyperacute?
questions.explanation: Hyperacute conjunctivitis is defined by an extremely rapid onset, typically within 24 hours, with copious purulent discharge, most classically caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae. This rapid tempo distinguishes it from the more gradual onset of bacterial or viral conjunctivitis. Because of the risk of corneal invasion, it requires urgent systemic antibiotic treatment alongside topical therapy.

questions.question: Histological examination of a retinoblastoma specimen reveals rosette structures with photoreceptor differentiation. These structures, called Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes, are significant because they
questions.explanation: Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes reflect an attempt at photoreceptor differentiation within the malignant tumour and are a characteristic, diagnostically supportive histological feature of retinoblastoma. Their presence does not indicate benignity or resolution of disease. Recognising this feature helps confirm the diagnosis on pathological review after enucleation or biopsy.
options: confirm the tumour is entirely benign
rule out the need for further treatment
support the diagnosis by demonstrating retinal cell differentiation
indicate the tumour has completely resolved
Reduce aqueous humor production and lower IOP
Dilate the pupil, prevent posterior synechiae, and reduce ciliary spasm pain
Enhance corneal penetration of topical steroids
Stimulate lacrimal gland secretion for lubrication
Constrict the trabecular meshwork to improve aqueous drainage
questions.explanation: Cycloplegics are essential in anterior uveitis management for three purposes: (1) pupil dilation to prevent posterior synechiae between the iris and lens, (2) paralysis of the ciliary muscle to relieve photophobia and deep ciliary spasm pain, and (3) stabilizing the blood-aqueous barrier. Atropine 1% is used for severe uveitis; shorter-acting agents for mild disease.
questions.question: Anterior uveitis management uses cycloplegic drops (e.g., atropine, cyclopentolate) primarily to:

questions.explanation: High-velocity metallic injuries carry a significant risk of an intraocular foreign body, which is best localised using CT imaging or plain X-ray. MRI is contraindicated when a metallic foreign body is suspected due to the risk of movement causing further tissue damage. Prompt imaging guides surgical planning for removal.
questions.question: A patient presents after a high-speed metallic hammering injury with a small corneal wound and reduced vision. What investigation is most appropriate to localise a possible retained fragment?

questions.explanation: Wide-field fundus fluorescein angiography (FFA) is the most useful investigation for detecting peripheral retinal non-perfusion, arteriovenous anastomoses, and neovascularization in sickle cell retinopathy. Standard fundoscopy may miss peripheral lesions. FFA provides dynamic assessment of retinal circulation and guides laser treatment planning for sea-fan neovascularization. OCT is more useful for macular assessment.
questions.question: In the evaluation of sickle cell retinopathy, which investigation is MOST useful for detecting peripheral retinal non-perfusion?

questions.explanation: Goldmann applanation tonometry assumes a standard corneal thickness and rigidity when estimating intraocular pressure. A thinner-than-average cornea can cause the true pressure to be underestimated, while a thicker cornea can cause overestimation. Corneal pachymetry helps clinicians interpret pressure readings more accurately.
questions.question: Why is central corneal thickness measurement important before interpreting a Goldmann applanation tonometry reading?
options: Thin corneas can cause pressure underestimation
It replaces the need for gonioscopy
It determines the type of glaucoma present

questions.explanation: Ultraviolet radiation is the most important etiological factor for pterygium, which is more common in tropical regions with high UV exposure. Other contributing factors include dryness, wind, and dust (ocular surface irritants). Pathologically, elastotic degeneration of collagen and fibrovascular tissue growth occur. Simple excision has a 40–60% recurrence rate without adjunctive therapy.
questions.question: A pterygium is a degenerative lesion of the bulbar conjunctiva that has invaded the superficial cornea. The MOST important etiological factor is:
options: Meibomian lipid deposition on the corneal surface

questions.question: Treatment of pterygium recurrence can be prevented with all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Pterygium recurrence is reduced by adjuvant therapy after excision: beta radiation, mitomycin-C, 5-fluorouracil, conjunctival autograft, or amniotic membrane graft. Oral tetracycline is used in meibomian gland dysfunction management and has no established role in pterygium recurrence prevention. Simple excision alone has a 40–60% recurrence rate.

Retained iron-containing foreign bodies slowly release iron ions that deposit in ocular tissues, causing siderosis bulbi and progressive toxic damage to the retina and other structures. This process worsens over time rather than resolving spontaneously. Early removal is therefore recommended to prevent this complication.
options: resolution of any associated hyphema without harm
siderosis bulbi with progressive retinal toxicity
questions.question: A patient with a retained metallic intraocular foreign body declines surgical removal. Over subsequent months this untreated foreign body will MOST likely lead to
A patient develops optic disc pallor and reduced acuity following prior optic neuritis. Which of the following would be an atypical finding for simple optic atrophy alone?
questions.explanation: Optic atrophy from a unilateral or asymmetric prior optic nerve insult typically produces a relative afferent pupillary defect because of reduced conduction along the damaged nerve compared with the healthy fellow eye. Its absence would be atypical and should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis or evaluation for bilateral symmetric involvement. Pallor, reduced acuity, colour vision loss, and contrast sensitivity deficits are all expected accompaniments of optic atrophy.

Hutchinson's sign refers to vesicles on the tip or side of the nose, indicating involvement of the nasociliary branch of the trigeminal nerve, which also supplies the eye. Its presence strongly predicts subsequent ocular complications in herpes zoster ophthalmicus. Ophthalmology assessment is warranted whenever this sign is present.
questions.question: A patient recovering from chickenpox develops a vesicular rash along the forehead and tip of the nose with red eye. What sign predicts corneal involvement?
options: Vesicles on the nasal tip (Hutchinson's sign)

questions.explanation: Acanthamoeba keratoconjunctivitis is strongly associated with soft contact lens wear, particularly when lenses are cleaned or stored with tap water, homemade saline, or contaminated solutions. Acanthamoeba exists in soil, air, and water, and can colonize biofilm on contact lenses. It shows no response to conventional antimicrobial therapy; treatment uses chlorhexidine and PHMB drops.
questions.question: Acanthamoeba keratoconjunctivitis is most strongly associated with:
options: Newborns from infected mothers during delivery
Soft contact lens wearers using tap water or homemade saline
Elderly patients with reduced tear secretion
Swimming pool workers exposed to Candida-contaminated water

questions.explanation: Sickle cell retinopathy is driven by vaso-occlusion of peripheral retinal vessels by rigid, sickled red blood cells. This causes retinal ischemia, hypoxia, and infarction, which stimulates VEGF production and subsequent neovascularization (sea-fan lesions). The adhesion of sickled cells to activated endothelium and von Willebrand factor exacerbates vascular stasis. This mechanism parallels proliferative diabetic retinopathy pathogenesis.
questions.question: Sickle cell retinopathy is pathogenetically driven by which primary mechanism?
options: Elevated intraocular pressure compressing retinal vessels in the majority of documented cases
Autoimmune vasculitis of retinal arteries based on typical clinical findings
Vaso-occlusion of peripheral retinal vessels causing ischemia and neovascularization

questions.explanation: Topical steroids are contraindicated or dangerous in herpetic keratitis (they worsen dendritic ulcers) and fungal keratitis (promote fungal growth). They can also mask serious pathology by suppressing symptoms. Their use without diagnosis and specialist supervision can lead to corneal perforation and blindness. This is why guidelines strongly advise against prescribing steroids for undifferentiated red eye.
questions.question: In managing red eye, the MOST important reason to avoid prescribing topical steroids without ophthalmological consultation is:
options: Steroids increase corneal pigmentation during routine ophthalmic assessment
Steroids are ineffective for all eye conditions as commonly encountered in practice
Steroids can worsen herpetic and fungal infections, and mask serious pathology

questions.question: A patient develops endophthalmitis following penetrating eye injury. The MOST appropriate management is:
questions.explanation: Post-traumatic endophthalmitis (infection inside the eye) requires urgent intravitreal antibiotic injection (e.g., vancomycin and ceftazidime) to achieve therapeutic drug concentrations within the vitreous cavity. Vitrectomy may be added for severe cases to debulk the infective load and clear media. Topical or systemic antibiotics alone do not achieve adequate intraocular concentrations.
options: Intravitreal antibiotics with or without vitrectomy
Observation and re-assess in one week

questions.question: A patient with a family history of a lens dislocation syndrome is found to have an ectopic lens along with tall stature and long fingers. Which systemic condition should be considered?
questions.explanation: Marfan syndrome is an autosomal dominant connective tissue disorder associated with superotemporal lens subluxation, tall stature, arachnodactyly, and cardiovascular abnormalities such as aortic root dilation. This pattern of lens displacement direction helps distinguish it from homocystinuria, which more typically causes inferonasal lens subluxation. Recognising the systemic features is important because of the risk of life-threatening aortic complications.

Third nerve palsy paralyses the levator, superior, inferior, and medial recti along with the parasympathetic pupillary fibres, producing complete ptosis, a down-and-out eye, and a dilated fixed pupil. This combination is distinct from Horner's syndrome, where the pupil is small rather than dilated. Recognising the full pattern confirms third nerve rather than sympathetic involvement.
questions.question: A patient has a dilated, poorly reactive pupil together with complete ptosis and the eye deviated down and out. This combination localises the lesion to the

questions.explanation: Grade IV hypertensive retinopathy (malignant hypertension) is associated with diastolic blood pressure =130 mmHg and includes all features of Grade III plus papilledema (optic disc swelling) and macular star formation (hard exudates arranged in a star pattern around the fovea). Grade III corresponds to diastolic BP =110 mmHg with cotton wool spots and hemorrhages. Grade IV indicates severe end-organ damage.
questions.question: In hypertensive retinopathy, which grade is associated with a diastolic blood pressure =130 mmHg and papilledema?

questions.explanation: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (e.g., dorzolamide topically, acetazolamide systemically) reduce aqueous humor production by blocking the enzyme carbonic anhydrase in the ciliary epithelium, which is essential for bicarbonate formation needed in aqueous secretion. They are used as adjunctive or primary therapy in glaucoma. Systemic CAIs can cause metabolic acidosis and hypokalemia.
questions.question: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors reduce intraocular pressure through which mechanism?
options: Increasing uveoscleral outflow based on typical clinical findings
Lysing fibrin in the anterior chamber in the majority of documented cases
Inhibiting carbonic anhydrase in the ciliary body to reduce aqueous production

questions.question: A reading addition convex lens for presbyopia works by substituting for:
options: The dioptric loss from corneal flattening with age
The lost accommodative amplitude of the aging lens
The increased aqueous humor viscosity with age
The reduced pupil size causing decreased retinal illumination
The decreased rod sensitivity in the aging macular region
questions.explanation: With age, the crystalline lens hardens and the ciliary muscle weakens, reducing accommodative amplitude. An infant can accommodate 14 dioptres; by age 45 this falls to about 4 dioptres. The reading addition lens provides the supplemental converging power equivalent to the accommodative deficit, enabling near focus.

The Goldmann applanation tonometer is the gold standard for IOP measurement, using the Imbert-Fick principle — measuring force required to flatten a 3.06 mm corneal diameter. All other tonometers are calibrated against Goldmann readings. Corneal thickness deviations introduce measurement error.
questions.question: The gold standard instrument for measuring intraocular pressure is the:

questions.explanation: The British N system uses the type-setter's point system to specify letter size, where each point equals 1/72 inch. Near visual acuity charts using the N system are tested at 25–33 cm. For example, N5 letters measure 5/72 inches in height. This system is used for testing near VA in children over 6 and literate adults.
questions.question: Which chart is specifically designed for testing near visual acuity in children over 6 years using a type-setter point system?
A patient presents with an eye injury from a small metallic fragment and later develops a rusty brown discoloration of ocular tissues. What complication is this?
options: Chalcosis from a retained copper body
Siderosis from a retained iron foreign body
questions.explanation: Siderosis bulbi results from the slow toxic deposition of iron from a retained ferrous intraocular foreign body into ocular tissues, causing progressive pigmentary changes and retinal toxicity. This can lead to secondary glaucoma, cataract, and retinal degeneration if the foreign body is not removed. Electroretinography can help monitor toxic retinal effects.

questions.question: A patient has absent sensation on corneal touch but normal facial movement. Which nerve territory is most likely affected?
questions.explanation: Corneal sensation is carried by the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve, while the efferent blink response depends on the facial nerve. Normal facial movement with absent corneal sensation localises the lesion to the sensory afferent limb rather than the motor efferent limb. This distinguishes trigeminal from facial nerve pathology in the corneal reflex.

questions.question: Laser peripheral iridotomy (LPI) is the definitive treatment for which form of glaucoma?
questions.explanation: Laser peripheral iridotomy (LPI) creates a hole in the peripheral iris to bypass relative pupil block, equalizing pressure between the posterior and anterior chambers. This relieves iris bombé and opens the angle in primary angle-closure glaucoma (PACG). LPI is also prophylactically performed in the fellow eye of patients who have had an acute angle-closure episode, as the fellow eye is at high risk.
options: Primary open-angle glaucoma with normal angle
Primary angle-closure glaucoma from relative pupil block

questions.question: Retinal detachment can be classified as rhegmatogenous, tractional, or exudative. Which type occurs WITHOUT a retinal break?
questions.explanation: Exudative (serous) retinal detachment occurs without a retinal break. Fluid accumulates under the neurosensory retina from abnormal choroidal vascular leakage (choroidal melanoma, VKH, choroidal hemangioma, severe hypertension). The detachment is smooth, shifts with position, and resolves when the underlying cause is treated. Both rhegmatogenous and combined tractional-rhegmatogenous detachments require retinal breaks.
options: Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment from round atrophic holes
Rhegmatogenous from posterior vitreous detachment causing horseshoe tear
Exudative (serous) retinal detachment from choroidal tumor or VKH
Tractional RD with a coexisting retinal break (combined mechanism)
Rhegmatogenous from operculated hole in lattice degeneration

questions.explanation: Dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR) creates a new passage between the lacrimal sac and the nasal cavity, bypassing the obstructed nasolacrimal duct. It is the definitive treatment for nasolacrimal duct obstruction causing chronic dacryocystitis or epiphora. Canalicular obstruction requires conjunctivodacryocystorhinostomy (CDCR) as a different procedure.
questions.question: Dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR) is the definitive surgical procedure for which lacrimal drainage problem?
options: Lacrimal sac and nasolacrimal duct obstruction
Evaporative dry eye from meibomian gland disease

questions.question: Subconjunctival hemorrhage without pain or visual loss most commonly occurs due to:
questions.explanation: Subconjunctival hemorrhage most commonly results from spontaneous rupture of a small conjunctival blood vessel following Valsalva maneuvers (sneezing, coughing, straining), or occurs without identifiable cause. It is typically painless, does not affect vision, and resolves spontaneously within 1-2 weeks. Recurrent episodes in hypertensive patients warrant blood pressure assessment.

questions.question: A visual field of less than 5 degrees around fixation places a patient in which WHO visual handicap category?
questions.explanation: A central visual field (CVF) of less than 5 degrees around fixation corresponds to Category 4 visual handicap, regardless of the measured Snellen VA. Category 3 is assigned when CVF is less than 10 degrees but greater than 5 degrees around fixation. This highlights that visual field is as important as acuity in defining disability.

questions.question: During ophthalmic examination, the arterial-to-venous (A:V) ratio in the normal fundus is approximately:
questions.explanation: The normal arterial-to-venous ratio on fundoscopy is approximately 2:3, meaning arteries appear narrower than veins. Arteries appear bright red while veins appear purplish. A reduction in this ratio below 1:2 suggests significant arteriolar narrowing, as seen in hypertensive retinopathy.

questions.question: In ophthalmic history taking, past spectacle use is recorded under:
questions.explanation: Past ocular history (POH) specifically captures information about previous eye conditions, trauma, surgeries, and the use of spectacles or regular eye medications. The frequency of prescription changes and the date of the latest prescription provide valuable insight into the trajectory of refractive error or other ocular conditions. This differentiates POH from general past medical history.

questions.question: The major difference in the pathogenesis of hypertensive retinopathy Grade I–II versus Grade III–IV is:
options: Grade III–IV involves purely arteriosclerotic (chronic) changes based on typical clinical findings
Grades I–II are acute changes; Grades III–IV are chronic in the majority of documented cases
Grade III–IV involves only choroidal changes
Grades I–II are chronic arteriosclerotic; Grades III–IV include acute vascular damage
There is no pathological difference between grades
questions.explanation: Grades I and II hypertensive retinopathy represent chronic arteriosclerotic changes (arteriolar narrowing, AV nipping, copper/silver wiring) without active tissue damage. Grades III and IV represent acute vascular damage from severely elevated BP, including hemorrhages, cotton wool spots, hard exudates, and papilledema. This distinction explains why Grade III–IV correlates with markedly elevated diastolic pressures (=110 and =130 mmHg respectively).

questions.question: A child presents with bilateral leucocoria at an unusually young age and a strong family history of retinoblastoma in a parent. This clinical pattern strongly suggests
questions.explanation: Bilateral involvement, early age of onset, and a positive family history together strongly point toward a germline RB1 mutation underlying hereditary retinoblastoma, as opposed to sporadic disease which is typically unilateral and later in onset. Recognising this pattern prompts genetic counselling and testing for the child and at-risk relatives. It also guides the choice of imaging and long-term surveillance strategy.

questions.question: A patient with a recognised ocular emergency involving sudden painless visual loss, described using the mnemonic RSVP, most likely has which condition?
questions.explanation: The RSVP mnemonic (Red flag, Sudden, Vision loss, Painless) is used to highlight conditions such as retinal detachment, retinal vascular occlusion, and ischaemic optic neuropathy that present with sudden painless visual loss and require urgent ophthalmic assessment. Rapid recognition and referral are essential, as many of these conditions are time-critical for visual outcome. Delay can result in permanent, irreversible vision loss.

When maximal tolerated medical therapy fails to halt glaucomatous progression, surgical intervention becomes appropriate. Trabeculectomy creates an alternative aqueous outflow pathway, achieving lower pressures than drops alone. Continued observation without escalation risks further irreversible optic nerve damage.
options: Add a fifth topical agent immediately
Consider filtration surgery such as trabeculectomy
questions.question: A patient with chronic open-angle glaucoma on maximal medical therapy still has progressive field loss. What is the next logical step?

options: Topical and systemic pressure-lowering agents followed by iridotomy
Immediate enucleation of the affected eye
questions.explanation: Acute angle closure following pharmacological pupillary dilation requires prompt pressure-lowering treatment using topical and systemic agents to break the attack, followed by definitive treatment with laser peripheral iridotomy once the cornea has cleared sufficiently. Delay increases the risk of permanent optic nerve and angle damage. The fellow eye should also be assessed and treated prophylactically.
questions.question: A patient with sudden severe eye pain and haloes around lights following pupillary dilation for an eye examination is found to have an acute pressure rise. What emergency treatment sequence is appropriate?
In hyperviscosity syndrome (e.g., Waldenström macroglobulinaemia), the retinal findings include:
options: Anterior uveitis with posterior synechiae formation
Dilated tortuous retinal veins with haemorrhages and disc swelling
questions.explanation: Hyperviscosity syndrome (elevated serum IgM in Waldenström's) causes dilated, tortuous retinal veins ('sausage-link' tortuosity), dot-blot haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, and disc oedema — resembling bilateral central retinal vein occlusion. Plasmapheresis reduces viscosity and may resolve the retinal changes. The eye findings often precede systemic diagnosis.

questions.question: A patient with acute severe orbital pressure rise from retrobulbar haemorrhage requires emergency intervention. What surgical procedure provides rapid decompression?
questions.explanation: Lateral canthotomy with inferior cantholysis rapidly releases the lateral canthal tendon, allowing the globe to move forward and relieving compartment pressure within the orbit. This bedside emergency procedure can be performed without delay when vision is threatened by rising orbital pressure. It buys time for definitive management of the underlying cause of bleeding.

questions.question: A patient with dry, gritty eyes has a tear film that evaporates rapidly despite normal aqueous production. Which gland's secretion is deficient?
questions.explanation: Meibomian glands secrete the outer lipid layer of the tear film, which retards evaporation of the underlying aqueous layer. Dysfunction of this layer produces evaporative dry eye despite adequate aqueous tear production. This differs from aqueous-deficient dry eye caused by lacrimal gland failure.

The TVT study, a landmark RCT comparing Baerveldt tube shunt to trabeculectomy with MMC in eyes with prior surgery, showed similar IOP outcomes and medication use at 5 years. However, trabeculectomy had a higher rate of early complications (hypotony, flat anterior chamber) while tube shunts had later mechanical complications. Both are valid surgical options depending on clinical context.
options: Similar between tube shunt and trabeculectomy but with different complication profiles
Significantly better outcomes with tube shunt than trabeculectomy surgery
Tube shunts were only effective in aphakic eyes
Significantly better with trabeculectomy than tube shunt
questions.question: The Tube Versus Trabeculectomy (TVT) study showed that after 5 years, IOP control was:
The corticosteroid used most commonly for injection in posterior uveitis is:
questions.explanation: Triamcinolone acetonide is the most commonly used injectable corticosteroid for posterior uveitis, typically administered as a posterior sub-Tenon's or intravitreal injection. Its depot formulation provides sustained anti-inflammatory effect over weeks. Prednisolone tablets are used systemically for severe cases, while topical drops are insufficient for posterior segment inflammation.

questions.question: Hyperosmotic agents (e.g., IV mannitol) lower IOP in acute PACG by:
questions.explanation: Hyperosmotic agents (mannitol IV, glycerol oral) create an osmotic gradient between vitreous and blood plasma, drawing fluid from the posterior segment and reducing vitreous volume. This lowers IOP acutely. They are particularly useful in acute PACG when IOP needs urgent reduction to allow corneal clearing before definitive laser treatment.
options: Creating an osmotic gradient that draws fluid from the vitreous cavity
Reducing aqueous humour production via beta receptor blockade

questions.question: Glaucomatous visual field defects follow a characteristic pattern because they affect the nerve fiber layer. The FIRST detectable field defect in glaucoma is typically:
options: Inferior altitudinal defect from sudden ischemia
Homonymous quadrantanopia from optic radiation involvement
Paracentral or arcuate scotoma (Bjerrum scotoma) corresponding to RNFL loss
questions.explanation: Glaucomatous visual field defects follow the arcuate nerve fiber layer pattern. The earliest detectable defects are paracentral scotomas or arcuate scotomas (Bjerrum scotomas) in the Bjerrum area (10–20 degrees from fixation). These progress to nasal step defects and eventually to ring scotoma and tunnel vision. Central vision is preserved until late. Automated perimetry (Humphrey) detects these early defects.

Biodata serves to identify the patient, provide research statistics, and highlight demographic risk factors—but it does NOT establish a diagnosis. Clinical diagnosis requires correlation of history, examination, and investigations. Attempting to diagnose solely from biodata without examination is an unsafe clinical practice.
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a purpose of biodata collection in ophthalmic history taking?

options: Nerve fiber layer axonal debris (cystoid bodies) based on typical clinical findings
Lipoprotein and lipid-filled macrophages at the junction of normal and oedematous retina
Inflammatory cells infiltrating the inner retina
Fibrin deposits on the inner limiting membrane
Retinal pigment epithelial cells migrating into the retina in the majority of documented cases
questions.question: The pathological characteristic that distinguishes diabetic 'hard exudates' from 'cotton wool spots' is that hard exudates are composed of:
questions.explanation: Hard exudates are composed of lipoprotein and lipid-filled macrophages (foam cells) that accumulate at the boundary of normal and chronically oedematous retina, primarily in the outer plexiform layer. They appear as bright yellow-white deposits with distinct edges on fundoscopy. Cotton wool spots, by contrast, are composed of neuronal debris (axonal swellings/cystoid bodies) from ischemic infarcts of the nerve fiber layer.

questions.question: Meningeal inflammation is a recognized cause of third nerve palsy. Which of the following infective organisms would MOST likely be responsible?
questions.explanation: Infectious (bacterial or viral) meningitis causes meningeal inflammation that can irritate or compress cranial nerves, including CN III. Sarcoidosis, meningeal carcinomatosis, and lymphoma are also listed causes of meningeal CN III palsy. Staphylococcal infections and Chlamydia are not primary causes of meningeal CN III palsy.

questions.question: A patient develops sudden painless loss of a superior visual field arc following a disc haemorrhage noted at a previous glaucoma review. What does this haemorrhage typically indicate?
options: Normal ageing change of the disc
questions.explanation: A disc haemorrhage at the neuroretinal rim, also called a Drance haemorrhage, is a recognised sign of active and progressive glaucomatous optic nerve damage. It often precedes detectable visual field loss in the corresponding location. Its presence should prompt reassessment of treatment adequacy.

A bandage contact lens acts as a physical scaffold and protective covering for the denuded ocular surface, protecting the migrating epithelial cells from mechanical trauma from eyelid movement. It also reduces pain from exposed corneal nerves and provides a smooth surface for epithelial cell migration. This is particularly useful after the initial healing phase has begun.
options: Absorbs the chemical agent under standard examination conditions under standard examination conditions
Dilates the pupil for better healing in most clinical presentations in most clinical presentations
Protects the ocular surface epithelium as it migrates to cover the denuded area
questions.question: After chemical burn repair, a bandage contact lens is beneficial because it:

options: A white reflex in the pupil indicating lens opacity in the majority of documented cases
A raised, silvery-white, foamy triangular patch on the temporal bulbar conjunctiva
A dendritic ulcer on the corneal epithelium based on typical clinical findings
Follicular hypertrophy on the tarsal conjunctiva
questions.question: The Bitot's spot in xerophthalmia is BEST described as:
questions.explanation: A Bitot's spot (WHO classification X1B) is a raised, silvery-white, foamy, triangular patch of keratinized epithelium situated on the bulbar conjunctiva in the inter-palpebral area, most commonly temporal. It is an extension of the xerotic process in Vitamin A deficiency and represents metaplasia of the conjunctival epithelium. Bitot's spots in children younger than 5 are highly specific for VAD.

questions.question: Secondary glaucomas differ from primary glaucomas primarily in that they:
questions.explanation: Secondary glaucomas are associated with identifiable underlying conditions causing reduced outflow or increased IOP (e.g., uveitis, lens-induced, steroid-induced, neovascular glaucoma). Primary glaucomas have no identifiable systemic or ocular cause. Secondary glaucomas are often asymmetric or unilateral.
options: Have identifiable ocular or systemic causes
Orbital CT to exclude retrobulbar hematoma always
Topical steroid drops to accelerate absorption
questions.explanation: Subconjunctival hemorrhage — whether spontaneous or from mild trauma — typically resolves spontaneously within 2–3 weeks as blood is reabsorbed. No specific treatment is required. However, if associated with trauma causing proptosis or visual change, orbital CT should be performed to exclude retrobulbar hematoma. Recurrent spontaneous hemorrhages warrant investigation for coagulopathy.
questions.question: Subconjunctival hemorrhage appearing after minor trauma with no other findings MOST commonly requires:

options: Topical antibiotic eye drops alone in most clinical presentations
Oral antibiotics as outpatient treatment under standard examination conditions
Hospital admission with intravenous antibiotics and urgent imaging
questions.question: A patient with orbital cellulitis requires which IMMEDIATE management step?
questions.explanation: Orbital cellulitis is a vision- and life-threatening emergency requiring immediate hospital admission, high-dose intravenous antibiotics (typically a combination covering gram-positive, gram-negative, and anaerobic organisms), and urgent CT imaging of the orbit and sinuses to identify a subperiosteal or orbital abscess that may require surgical drainage. Delayed treatment risks optic nerve compression, septic cavernous sinus thrombosis, and intracranial spread.

Vitrectomy (surgical removal of the vitreous) is indicated in advanced diabetic eye disease for: severe persistent vitreous hemorrhage that fails to clear spontaneously (preventing laser treatment and causing visual loss), tractional retinal detachment involving or threatening the macula, and premacular hemorrhage. Mild-to-moderate proliferative retinopathy is treated with panretinal photocoagulation before vitrectomy is considered.
options: All cases of proliferative retinopathy regardless of severity as commonly encountered in practice
Clinically significant macular edema as first-line during routine ophthalmic assessment
Severe persistent vitreous hemorrhage or tractional retinal detachment threatening the macula
questions.question: Vitrectomy in advanced diabetic eye disease is specifically indicated for which complication?

questions.explanation: Although rare, intravitreal injections carry a small risk of introducing infection directly into the eye, causing endophthalmitis, which presents with pain, reduced vision, and hypopyon. This requires the same urgent diagnostic and treatment approach as postoperative endophthalmitis, including vitreous sampling and intravitreal antibiotics. Strict aseptic technique during injection reduces this risk.
options: Mild allergic reaction to the drug
questions.question: A patient develops sudden reduced vision and pain after intravitreal injection therapy for retinal disease, with hypopyon on examination. What complication must be urgently excluded?

options: Elevated IOP from ciliary muscle overexertion
Optic atrophy from chronic vascular nerve compression
questions.explanation: Hypermetropic children who accommodate excessively to overcome their refractive error activate the accommodation-convergence reflex. This can cause convergent strabismus (esotropia) because accommodation and convergence are neurologically linked. Correcting the hypermetropia with glasses typically resolves the accommodative esotropia.
questions.question: A hypermetropic child who accommodates forcefully to overcome the refractive error may develop which ocular complication?

questions.explanation: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is the most common eyelid malignancy, predominantly in Caucasians and elderly patients. It most commonly appears on the lower lid margin as a nodular, pearly lesion with rolled edges and central ulceration. It is locally invasive but rarely metastasizes. Squamous cell carcinoma is less common but more aggressive with metastatic potential.
questions.question: The most common eyelid tumor in Caucasians, typically arising on the lower lid margin with local invasion, is:

questions.explanation: In emmetropia, parallel light rays from infinity are focused exactly on the retina without any accommodative effort — the second principal focus falls precisely on the retinal surface. Myopia focuses light in front of the retina; hypermetropia focuses it behind. This perfect state requires no corrective lenses for distance.
options: At the nodal point of the crystalline lens
Exactly on the retina without accommodation
questions.question: In emmetropia, where does the second principal focus of parallel light rays from infinity fall?
Which bacterial organisms are uniquely capable of invading an INTACT corneal epithelium?
questions.explanation: Most bacteria require a breach in the corneal epithelium to cause keratitis. However, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Corynebacterium diphtheriae, Haemophilus aegyptius, and Listeria monocytogenes are uniquely virulent organisms capable of penetrating an intact corneal epithelium. This is why gonococcal infection can cause rapid corneal perforation even in apparently healthy eyes.
options: Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Corynebacterium diphtheriae, Haemophilus species, and Listeria
Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pneumoniae species

questions.explanation: Chrysiasis is the deposition of gold crystals in the corneal stroma from chronic gold salt administration for rheumatoid arthritis. It appears as fine golden-brown or purplish deposits in the deep stroma. Other drugs causing corneal deposits include chloroquine (whorl keratopathy), amiodarone (vortex/whorl pattern), and chlorpromazine. Tamoxifen causes crystalline maculopathy, not keratopathy.
questions.question: Chrysiasis is a corneal deposition disorder caused by chronic administration of which medication?

options: Direct bacterial infection of the iris
Release of VEGF from ischaemic retina
Chronic mechanical irritation of the iris
questions.question: A diabetic patient with advanced retinal ischaemia develops new vessels on the iris surface. What is the primary driver of this abnormal vessel growth?
questions.explanation: Chronic retinal ischaemia in advanced diabetic retinopathy stimulates the release of vascular endothelial growth factor, which diffuses forward and promotes abnormal new vessel growth on the iris surface, termed rubeosis iridis. This can progress to neovascular glaucoma if the angle becomes involved. Panretinal photocoagulation reduces this ischaemic drive.

Acute postoperative endophthalmitis presents within days of cataract surgery with pain, marked inflammation, hypopyon, and rapid visual decline, representing a sight-threatening emergency requiring urgent intravitreal antibiotic therapy. This must be distinguished from toxic anterior segment syndrome, which is typically less painful and occurs even earlier. Rapid diagnosis and treatment are critical to preserving vision in true infectious endophthalmitis.
questions.question: A patient develops sudden painful red eye with severe visual loss two days after uneventful cataract surgery, and the anterior chamber shows dense inflammatory cells and hypopyon. Which complication must be urgently excluded?
A patient presents with sudden painless visual loss and a red, swollen optic disc after a large-volume blood loss during childbirth. What is this condition called?
questions.explanation: Purtscher-like retinopathy can occur following severe systemic events such as major haemorrhage, producing multiple cotton-wool spots, retinal haemorrhages, and disc swelling due to microvascular occlusion. The exact mechanism involves complement-mediated leukoembolisation. Visual recovery is variable and depends on the extent of retinal ischaemia.

questions.question: Optic atrophy presents with disc pallor and reduced visual function. Which of the following does NOT cause optic atrophy?
questions.explanation: Refractive error alone does not cause optic atrophy. Optic atrophy results from: glaucoma, optic neuritis, compression (pituitary adenoma, orbital tumors), vascular (AION, CRAO), toxic/nutritional (methanol, tobacco-alcohol amblyopia, vitamin B12 deficiency), inflammatory, and hereditary causes (Leber's hereditary optic neuropathy). Refractive error may reduce visual acuity but does not damage the optic nerve.
options: Compression of the optic nerve by a pituitary adenoma
