questions.question: A young child presents with a white pupillary reflex noted on flash photography. Immediate referral is arranged due to concern for a life-threatening intraocular tumour. Which diagnosis must be excluded urgently?
questions.explanation: Leukocoria in a child is a red flag sign that must prompt urgent exclusion of retinoblastoma, the most common primary intraocular malignancy of childhood, because delayed diagnosis carries risk to life as well as vision. Other causes of leukocoria such as cataract, Coats disease, or persistent fetal vasculature are more common but must not be assumed without adequate examination. Fundus examination under anaesthesia and imaging help differentiate these causes.

questions.question: The MOST common site of scleral rupture following blunt trauma is:
questions.explanation: Scleral rupture from blunt trauma most commonly occurs at the limbus (just behind the corneal margin) or at the insertions of the extraocular muscles, where the sclera is thinnest and most vulnerable. These are also the sites of maximum stress concentration during antero-posterior compression. Subconjunctival haemorrhage may mask the rupture.
options: Just behind the corneal limbus or at extraocular muscle insertions parallel to the limbus
At the posterior pole near the optic nerve head
At the equator of the globe

questions.question: Herpes simplex keratitis MOST characteristically produces which pattern of corneal ulceration?
options: Dendritic (branching tree-like) ulcer staining with fluorescein
Hypopyon ulcer with a flat clean base
Deep posterior stromal vascularisation and scarring
questions.explanation: HSV keratitis characteristically produces a dendritic (branching, tree-like) epithelial ulcer with terminal bulbs, staining with fluorescein and rose Bengal. This pattern reflects viral spread along corneal epithelial cells. Recurrence causes disciform stromal keratitis (immune-mediated) and metaherpetic (trophic) geographic ulcers.

options: Pigment granules obstructing the trabecular meshwork
Lens protein leakage into the angle
questions.explanation: In pigment dispersion syndrome, posterior iris bowing causes mechanical rubbing against zonular fibres, releasing pigment granules into the aqueous. These granules deposit in and obstruct the trabecular meshwork, raising outflow resistance. This can progress to pigmentary glaucoma, particularly in young myopic males.
questions.question: A middle-aged woman presents with unilateral pigment dispersion, iris transillumination defects, and raised IOP. Which mechanism underlies her elevated pressure?

questions.explanation: In hereditary (germline) retinoblastoma, the first mutation (RB1 gene deletion on chromosome 13q14) is inherited through the germinal cells and is present in every cell of the body. The second somatic mutation then occurs in retinal cells to produce the tumor. This explains why hereditary RB is often bilateral, multifocal, and presents earlier than the sporadic form.
questions.question: Retinoblastoma follows the 'two-hit' Knudson hypothesis. In the hereditary (germline) form, how are the two mutations distributed?
options: Both mutations occur in somatic cells only as commonly encountered in practice
Both mutations occur simultaneously in retinal cells during routine ophthalmic assessment
No mutations are required in hereditary form
First mutation is inherited via germinal cells; second occurs in somatic cells

questions.question: A patient with sickle cell disease develops peripheral retinal neovascularisation described as having a fan-like configuration, differing from the pattern seen in diabetic retinopathy. What is this proliferative lesion called?
questions.explanation: Sickle cell retinopathy produces a characteristic peripheral 'sea fan' pattern of neovascularisation arising at the junction of vascular and avascular peripheral retina, distinct from the disc or diffuse neovascularisation typically seen in diabetic retinopathy. This occurs due to peripheral retinal ischaemia from sickled erythrocytes occluding small vessels. These fragile vessels are prone to bleeding into the vitreous cavity.

The outer retina, including photoreceptors, is avascular and relies on the choriocapillaris (derived from the short posterior ciliary arteries via the choroid) for oxygen and nutrients via diffusion. The central retinal artery supplies only the inner retinal layers. This dual blood supply is why separate occlusive diseases affect different retinal layers. SUBTOPIC 2: VISUAL ACUITY, REFRACTIVE ERRORS AND VISUAL HANDICAP
questions.question: Which component of the retina provides the ONLY blood supply to the photoreceptors and outer retinal layers?
options: Posterior ciliary arteries via the choroid

questions.explanation: Viral (adenoviral) conjunctivitis is self-limiting and requires only symptomatic treatment: cold compresses for comfort, topical vasoconstrictors, and lubricants. Antiviral preparations have no proven benefit for adenoviral infection. Topical steroids are generally avoided as they can prolong viral shedding. Prophylactic topical antibiotics may be considered to prevent secondary bacterial infection.
questions.question: The MOST appropriate treatment for viral conjunctivitis is:
options: Systemic acyclovir 400 mg five times daily for 14 days
Symptomatic treatment with cold compresses and vasoconstrictors
Topical prednisolone 1% drops four times daily immediately

questions.explanation: Angle recession (tearing of the anterior ciliary body face between circular and longitudinal muscles) is visible on gonioscopy as widening of the ciliary body band. Damage to trabecular meshwork cells increases outflow resistance, causing chronic open-angle glaucoma years after injury. Annual IOP monitoring is recommended in all eyes with angle recession.
questions.question: Angle recession following blunt ocular trauma predisposes to which type of glaucoma?
options: Acute angle-closure glaucoma from pupillary block
Chronic open-angle glaucoma from trabecular damage

questions.question: The afferent pupillary defect (RAPD/Marcus Gunn pupil) is detected using the swinging flashlight test. Its presence indicates:
questions.explanation: RAPD (relative afferent pupillary defect) indicates a defect in the afferent pupillary pathway (retina or optic nerve) on the affected side. When light swings to the affected eye, the pupil dilates rather than constricts (paradoxical dilation) due to reduced afferent input. It is a critical clinical sign of significant ipsilateral optic nerve or extensive retinal disease, e.g., optic neuritis, CRAO, advanced glaucoma.
options: Bilateral symmetric optic nerve damage equally
Ocular motor (efferent) paresis resulting from CN III palsy
Unilateral or asymmetric optic nerve or retinal disease on the side of the RAPD
Bilateral occipital cortex lesion from stroke
Degenerated red blood cell ghosts block the trabecular meshwork after vitreous haemorrhage
Pigment released from iris trauma occludes aqueous outflow drainage
Iris neovascularisation closes the angle after ischaemia
Inflammatory cells from chronic uveitis obstruct the anterior chamber angle
Lens protein leaks from a hypermature cataract
questions.question: Ghost-cell (haemolytic) glaucoma occurs when:
questions.explanation: Ghost-cell glaucoma occurs when old, degenerated erythrocytes (ghost cells) from a vitreous haemorrhage enter the anterior chamber via a disrupted anterior hyaloid and mechanically obstruct the trabecular meshwork. Their rigidity prevents deformation through trabecular spaces, causing elevated IOP. It is a recognised complication of vitreous haemorrhage.

options: Allergic conjunctivitis as commonly encountered in practice
Viral keratitis during routine ophthalmic assessment
questions.explanation: Hypopyon represents a collection of white blood cells (pus) settling by gravity in the inferior anterior chamber. It indicates severe intraocular infection (endophthalmitis) or intense inflammation (severe uveitis or corneal ulcer with anterior chamber spillover). It is a sight-threatening emergency requiring urgent ophthalmological assessment and treatment. It should never be dismissed as a minor finding.
questions.question: A hypopyon—a horizontal fluid level of white cells in the anterior chamber—is MOST indicative of:

options: Increasing antibiotic concentration and dosing frequency alone
Review of scraping results and empirical antifungal therapy if fungus suspected
Switching to topical vancomycin for MRSA coverage only
questions.explanation: A corneal ulcer with hypopyon not responding to antibiotics should prompt review of scraping results (Gram stain, KOH preparation) and reconsideration of the diagnosis. If KOH shows fungal hyphae or clinical features suggest fungal keratitis (feathery margins, satellite lesions, history of trauma), empirical antifungal therapy should be started. Misdiagnosing fungal as bacterial keratitis leads to catastrophic delay. SUBTOPIC 6: UVEAL DISEASES — UVEITIS AND UVEAL TUMOURS
questions.question: A corneal ulcer with a hypopyon that does NOT respond to broad-spectrum topical antibiotics after 48 hours should prompt:

options: Type III (immune complex) hypersensitivity to staphylococcal exotoxins
Direct invasion by Staphylococcus aureus from the lid margin
Type I IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation to pollen allergens
Direct extension of gonococcal conjunctival infection across the limbus
Autoimmune attack on corneal type IV collagen in the periphery
questions.explanation: Marginal ulcers (catarrhal ulcers) are peripheral corneal infiltrates with a clear lucid interval from the limbus, caused by a Type III immune complex hypersensitivity reaction to Staphylococcus aureus exotoxins from lid margin blepharitis. The bacteria themselves are not in the cornea. Treatment is topical antibiotic-steroid combination plus lid hygiene for the underlying blepharitis.
questions.question: Marginal corneal ulcer (catarrhal ulcer) at the peripheral cornea is caused by which mechanism?

questions.explanation: Microaneurysms are a hallmark early feature of diabetic retinopathy and are not a typical feature of pure hypertensive vascular change, which instead shows arteriolar narrowing, wiring, and nicking. This distinction helps when a patient has both conditions and the clinician needs to attribute specific fundus findings to the correct underlying disease. Recognising overlapping but distinguishable signs supports more accurate patient counselling.
questions.question: Comparing hypertensive and diabetic retinopathy on fundus examination, a feature that helps distinguish diabetic disease is the
A patient with Horner's syndrome has ptosis of the upper lid and elevation of the lower lid. The sympathetically innervated muscle responsible for BOTH findings is:
questions.explanation: Horner's syndrome (sympathetic pathway disruption) causes ptosis from denervation of Müller's superior tarsal muscle (upper lid) and upward displacement of the lower lid from paralysis of the inferior tarsal muscle. Together they reduce the palpebral fissure. The associated miosis is from paralysis of the iris dilator muscle.
options: Müller's superior tarsal muscle and inferior tarsal muscle
Superior rectus with its associated fascial extension
A technical error during surgical repair
Simple corneal scarring that will resolve
Severe posterior segment or optic nerve damage
Normal expected outcome of any repair
questions.explanation: Persistent no light perception vision despite successful anatomical repair of an open globe usually reflects severe underlying damage to the retina, choroid, or optic nerve that cannot be corrected surgically. This carries a poor visual prognosis regardless of further intervention. Preoperative and intraoperative findings help predict this outcome.
questions.question: A patient with an open globe injury undergoes primary surgical repair but has no light perception at final assessment. What does this most likely reflect?
Slit lamp examination in a patient with anterior uveitis reveals clumps of inflammatory cells adherent to the posterior corneal surface. What are these deposits called?
questions.explanation: Keratic precipitates are aggregates of inflammatory cells, including lymphocytes and macrophages, that settle on the corneal endothelium in anterior uveitis. Their size and distribution, such as large greasy mutton-fat deposits, can suggest a granulomatous process. This finding is a hallmark sign distinguishing active anterior chamber inflammation from other causes of red eye.

questions.question: A patient with narrow angles but no previous acute attack undergoes a preventive laser procedure. What is the aim of this treatment?
options: Permanently dilate the pupil for comfort
Create an opening bypassing pupillary block
Reduce corneal thickness for better vision
questions.explanation: Laser peripheral iridotomy creates a small opening in the peripheral iris, allowing aqueous humour to bypass the pupil and flow directly from the posterior to anterior chamber. This relieves pupillary block, deepening the anterior chamber angle and reducing the risk of future acute angle closure. It is offered prophylactically to patients with anatomically narrow but asymptomatic angles.

Chemical conjunctivitis from silver nitrate prophylaxis is a mild, self-limiting irritant reaction that resolves spontaneously without antimicrobial therapy, unlike infective causes which can progress to serious complications if untreated. Recognising this distinction prevents unnecessary antibiotic use for a benign, transient reaction. The timing, usually within the first day, also helps differentiate it from later-onset infective causes.
questions.question: A neonate develops chemical conjunctival irritation shortly after silver nitrate eye prophylaxis, which resolves within a day or two without treatment. This differs from infective ophthalmia neonatorum in that it is

questions.explanation: The visual field is classically described as an 'island of vision in a sea of darkness,' referring to the area of vision perceived simultaneously without eye movement. Visual field testing detects defects from glaucoma, retinal disease, and neurological lesions. Automated perimetry quantifies these defects.
questions.question: 'An island of vision in a sea of darkness' best describes which visual function?
Opticrom (sodium cromoglicate) is an anti-allergic agent that works by:
questions.explanation: Sodium cromoglicate (Opticrom) stabilizes mast cell membranes, preventing degranulation and the release of histamine and other inflammatory mediators in allergic conjunctivitis. It is a prophylactic agent most effective when used before allergen exposure. H1-receptor antihistamines (e.g., ketotifen, olopatadine) work differently by blocking the receptor rather than preventing mediator release.
options: Mast cell stabilization, preventing mediator release
Blocking histamine H1 receptors as commonly encountered in practice
Inhibiting prostaglandin synthesis during routine ophthalmic assessment

questions.question: A patient with HIV presents with a white, frothy, irregular retinal lesion along a vascular arcade with no haemorrhage. The MOST likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Pneumocystis jirovecii (formerly carinii) choroiditis presents as multiple, bilateral, yellow-white, round to oval choroidal lesions without vitritis or retinal involvement, typically in HIV patients with CD4 <100 cells/µL receiving inhaled (not systemic) pentamidine prophylaxis. It lacks the haemorrhage of CMV retinitis and the white exudate of toxoplasma. Systemic treatment with TMP-SMX is required.

Cataract surgery in diabetic patients can precipitate or worsen diabetic macular oedema (DMO) due to post-surgical inflammation, disrupted blood-ocular barrier, and VEGF up-regulation. Pre-operative fundus fluorescein angiography (FFA) and OCT assess macular status; significant DMO should ideally be treated with anti-VEGF or laser before surgery to optimize visual outcomes post-operatively.
options: Diabetes causes lens protein glycation preventing safe phacoemulsification
Diabetic corneas have increased risk of herpetic keratitis post-surgery
Surgery can unmask or worsen pre-existing diabetic macular oedema post-operatively
Hypoglycemia from perioperative fasting causes optic nerve ischemia
Diabetic patients cannot be adequately dilated for cataract surgery
questions.question: Cataract surgery in a diabetic patient should be performed with caution because:

questions.explanation: Focal laser photocoagulation targets individual microaneurysms and areas of focal leakage within the macular zone. Grid laser applies a grid of mild burns to areas of diffuse macular edema and non-perfusion. Both are distinct from PRP (used for PDR), which applies 1,500–2,000 large burns to the peripheral retina. Focal/grid laser is used for DMO, while PRP targets proliferative disease.
options: Panretinal scatter (PRP) to all quadrants as commonly encountered in practice in the majority of documented cases
Single-spot treatment to the optic disc during routine ophthalmic assessment based on typical clinical findings
Focal and/or grid pattern targeted to areas of leakage and edema at the macula
questions.question: Laser photocoagulation in diabetic macular edema uses which laser delivery pattern?
A shallow anterior chamber depth is a predisposing anatomical factor for which glaucoma type?
questions.explanation: A shallow anterior chamber predisposes to primary angle-closure glaucoma. Hyperopic (far-sighted) eyes have shorter axial lengths, thicker lenses, and shallower chambers, predisposing to relative pupillary block and angle closure. Anterior chamber depth assessment is crucial in screening high-risk individuals.

options: Ischemic optic neuropathy from giant cell arteritis
Multiple sclerosis as the most common association
Toxic optic neuropathy from methanol poisoning
questions.question: Optic neuritis in a young woman with unilateral painful loss of vision and an afferent pupillary defect raises concern for:
questions.explanation: Optic neuritis — painful unilateral visual loss with an afferent pupillary defect (RAPD), central scotoma, and reduced colour vision — in a young woman is most commonly associated with multiple sclerosis. The Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial (ONTT) showed 50% of patients develop MS within 15 years. MRI shows periventricular white matter lesions. IV methylprednisolone speeds visual recovery but does not improve final VA.

questions.question: A patient placed at 6 meters can only read the line that a normal person reads at 24 meters. What is their recorded visual acuity?
questions.explanation: Visual acuity is expressed as a fraction: numerator is the patient's testing distance (6 m) and denominator is the distance at which a normal eye can read that line (24 m). Therefore, VA = 6/24. Normal VA is 6/6. If a patient cannot read from 6 m, the test distance is reduced to 3 m, 1 m, or counting fingers (CF).

The Eclipse Sign is elicited by shining a pen torch from the temporal side of the cornea; a shadow cast on the nasal iris indicates a shallow anterior chamber. It is a simple bedside test to estimate anterior chamber depth before more formal assessment. A deep anterior chamber allows light to illuminate the full iris without shadow, while a shallow chamber casts a characteristic nasal shadow.
options: Shining a light directly into the pupil from the front
Using a slit lamp to measure the chamber depth
Applying pressure on the globe through the eyelid
Instilling fluorescein and using cobalt blue light
Shining a light from the temporal side of the cornea
questions.question: The Eclipse Sign used in anterior chamber assessment is elicited by:
A patient with peripheral sea-fan neovascularisation from sickle cell disease is at greatest risk of which vision-threatening complication?
questions.explanation: Sea-fan neovascularisation in sickle cell retinopathy consists of fragile abnormal vessels prone to spontaneous bleeding into the vitreous cavity. This can cause sudden visual loss from vitreous haemorrhage and, if traction develops, tractional retinal detachment. Regular monitoring allows timely laser treatment of high-risk lesions.
options: Vitreous haemorrhage from fragile new vessels

questions.question: A contact lens wearer presents with a painful corneal ulcer that has failed to respond to standard antibacterial therapy. What organism should be specifically considered?
questions.explanation: Acanthamoeba keratitis should be suspected in contact lens wearers with disproportionate pain and a corneal ulcer unresponsive to conventional antibacterial agents. Risk factors include exposure to contaminated water or poor lens hygiene. Diagnosis often requires corneal scraping with specific staining or culture techniques.

questions.question: An infant's acuity, tested using a rolling ball apparatus of decreasing size, is noted to be better than later testing confirms. Which is a recognised limitation of this method?
questions.explanation: The rolling ball test relies on observing whether the infant's eyes follow a moving ball of graded size, but subtle head or body cues from the examiner can lead the child to track the ball regardless of true resolving power. This produces a tendency to overestimate visual acuity compared with more controlled methods. Awareness of this limitation is important when interpreting results in preverbal children.

options: Inhibit Tenon's capsule fibroblast proliferation and prevent bleb scarring that causes surgical failure
Speed up aqueous drainage through the surgical fistula site
questions.explanation: Antimetabolites prevent fibroblastic scarring of the filtration bleb, which is the main cause of trabeculectomy failure. Mitomycin-C is more potent than 5-FU and is preferred in high-risk patients — young patients, Africans, aphakic/pseudophakic, or those with prior failed surgery. Proper application technique avoids complications such as hypotony and bleb leaks.
questions.question: Antimetabolites (mitomycin-C and 5-fluorouracil) are used in trabeculectomy to:

options: Starting intravitreal anti-VEGF immediately in most clinical presentations
Performing panretinal photocoagulation urgently under standard examination conditions
Optimizing blood sugar control to target HbA1c 6–7%
questions.explanation: Optimizing glycemic control to maintain HbA1c in the 6–7% range is the single most important systemic intervention to reduce the risk of developing and progressing diabetic retinopathy. This has been demonstrated in landmark trials (DCCT for Type 1, UKPDS for Type 2). Ocular treatments are important but secondary to systemic metabolic control in preventing retinopathy progression.
questions.question: A patient with diabetic retinopathy has HbA1c of 9.5%. The primary systemic intervention to reduce retinopathy progression is:
A 50-year-old with normal distance vision complains of blurred near vision that improves when reading material is held further away. Which condition is most likely?
questions.explanation: Presbyopia results from age-related loss of lens elasticity and reduced ciliary muscle efficiency, impairing the accommodative reserve needed for near work. Holding material further away reduces the accommodative demand and temporarily improves clarity. This typically develops in the fifth decade of life independent of pre-existing refractive error.

options: Trachomatous scarring stage (TS) occurring after scarring has developed
Trichiasis (TT) stage — treating established corneal abrasion
Active infectious trachoma stage (TF and TI) — reducing community prevalence of infection
Corneal opacity (CO) stage — reversing established blindness
questions.explanation: The Antibiotic component of SAFE targets active infectious trachoma (TF = trachomatous follicular inflammation; TI = trachomatous intense inflammation) by treating C. trachomatis infection with mass drug administration of azithromycin to reduce community infection prevalence below the elimination threshold (less than 5% TF in children aged 1–9 years). Azithromycin (1 g single dose in adults) is the antibiotic of choice.
questions.question: The SAFE strategy for trachoma control works because Surgery prevents blindness from trichiasis while Antibiotics target which stage of the disease?

questions.explanation: Orbital involvement (orbital inflammatory pseudotumour/orbital granuloma) is the most common ocular manifestation of granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA/Wegener's), occurring in 15–20% of patients. It causes proptosis, diplopia, and pain. Other ocular manifestations include scleritis (most common anterior segment finding), peripheral ulcerative keratitis, retinal vasculitis, and nasolacrimal duct obstruction.
questions.question: The MOST common ocular complication in patients with granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener's granulomatosis) is:

questions.explanation: The corneal endothelium maintains a relative state of dehydration via its bicarbonate pump, which is critical for transparency. Loss of endothelial cells leads to corneal oedema and opacity. Normal endothelial cell count is above 2400 cells/mm².
questions.question: Which layer of the cornea is responsible for maintaining corneal transparency through active dehydration?

questions.explanation: Each Snellen letter is designed so that the whole letter subtends 5 minutes of arc, while the bars and spaces (features/strokes) each subtend 1 minute of arc at the designated distance. This 1-minute-of-arc feature size equals the resolving power of one foveal cone. This standardizes the minimum angle of resolution (MAR) to 1 minute.
options: Strokes and gaps of letters subtend 5 min of arc at the design distance
Each letter subtends exactly 1 minute of arc at all distances
The letter occupies a visual angle equal to 5 degrees at design distance
Letter size is equivalent to the inverse of line distance in meters
The whole letter subtends 5 min of arc while each feature subtends 1 min of arc
questions.question: Which statement about the Snellen chart design principle is CORRECT?

questions.explanation: Persistent epithelial defects that fail to heal with standard lubrication may benefit from a bandage contact lens to protect the healing surface or punctal occlusion to increase tear film retention. Addressing any underlying cause, such as exposure or neurotrophic factors, is also important. More invasive options are reserved for cases refractory to these measures.
options: Stopping all treatment and observing only
Bandage contact lens or punctal plugs
questions.question: A patient develops a persistent, non-healing corneal epithelial defect despite standard lubrication after ocular surface surgery. What is an appropriate next step in management?
Acute primary angle-closure glaucoma presents characteristically with:
options: Mild discomfort only on exposure to bright light
Gradual, painless, progressive visual loss occurring over several months
Severe periocular pain, ciliary flush, corneal oedema, nausea, and vomiting
Morning headaches with no specific ocular signs
Bilateral simultaneous onset of severe headache
questions.explanation: Acute PACG is an ophthalmic emergency presenting with sudden severe periocular pain, ciliary congestion, corneal oedema (causing haloes), mid-dilated fixed pupil, shallow anterior chamber, and markedly elevated IOP (often 40–80 mmHg). Nausea and vomiting are frequent. The pain can mimic acute abdomen, leading to misdiagnosis.

questions.question: A child with a suspected intraocular metallic foreign body requires imaging, but MRI should be AVOIDED because it can
questions.explanation: A ferromagnetic intraocular foreign body can be violently displaced by the strong magnetic field of an MRI scanner, causing further intraocular damage. Plain X-ray or CT are safer alternatives for localising metallic fragments. This risk makes careful screening for magnetic metal essential before ordering MRI in trauma cases.
options: expose the child to ionising radiation
fail to detect any foreign body at all
require general anaesthesia in every case
cause displacement of the metallic fragment by the magnetic field

questions.explanation: Copper wiring reflects mild to moderate thickening of the arteriolar wall that alters the normal light reflex without completely obscuring the underlying blood column. This precedes the more advanced silver wiring seen with severe, longstanding hypertensive vascular change. Recognising this early sign supports staging the severity of hypertensive retinopathy.
questions.question: On fundoscopy of a hypertensive patient, retinal arterioles show a bright, copper-coloured light reflex. This appearance corresponds to
Fungal keratitis treatment requires a minimum duration of how many weeks of antifungal therapy?
questions.explanation: Fungal keratitis requires prolonged topical antifungal treatment for a minimum of 6 weeks due to the slow growth rate of fungi and difficulty of drug penetration into the stroma. Econazole 1%, natamycin, and imidazole (e.g., voriconazole) are used topically; systemic itraconazole or ketoconazole is added for severe cases. De-epithelialization may enhance drug penetration into the stroma. OPHTHALMOLOGY MCQ BANK MDCN Standard — 250 Objective Questions PART 2: Questions 151 – 250 SUBTOPIC 5: DISEASES OF THE CORNEA (CONTINUED)

options: Acute Vitamin A deficiency keratomalacia secondary infection
Direct viral invasion of the retina in the majority of documented cases
Measles encephalitis causing cortical blindness based on typical clinical findings
questions.question: In measles-related blindness in children, the pathway most commonly involves:
questions.explanation: Measles precipitates blindness through a cascade: the infection causes acute Vitamin A deficiency (via increased metabolic demand and decreased absorption), leading to xerophthalmia, keratomalacia, and corneal ulceration. Secondary bacterial infections exploit the immune suppression caused by measles. This pathway explains why Vitamin A supplementation during measles (3 doses over 2 weeks) is a WHO recommendation.

questions.question: Lid laceration involving the medial canthus should be assessed for:
options: Intraocular foreign body lodged at the angle
Corneal abrasion under the upper lid
Involvement of the lacrimal canaliculi requiring specialist repair
questions.explanation: Lid lacerations at the medial canthus must be assessed for involvement of the upper and lower lacrimal canaliculi (lacrimal drainage channels). Canalicular lacerations require specialist repair with silicone intubation (bicanalicular or monocanalicular stent) to maintain lacrimal drainage patency. Unrepaired canalicular lacerations cause epiphora (persistent tearing) permanently.

options: Application of a firm eye pad
questions.question: A patient presents with sudden proptosis, tense eyelids, and severely reduced vision shortly after facial trauma with retrobulbar bleeding. What is the most urgent management step?
questions.explanation: Orbital compartment syndrome from retrobulbar haemorrhage causes a rapid rise in orbital pressure, compressing the optic nerve and central retinal artery. Emergency lateral canthotomy and cantholysis decompresses the orbit immediately, and should not be delayed for imaging when vision is threatened. Rapid intervention can prevent permanent visual loss.

questions.question: A 2-year-old is brought in because a parent noticed a white reflection in one pupil on a flash photograph. This sign, called leucocoria, is MOST commonly caused in this age group by
questions.explanation: Leucocoria, or an abnormal white pupillary reflex, is the most common presenting sign of retinoblastoma, the leading intraocular malignancy of childhood. Conjunctivitis, refractive error, and subconjunctival hemorrhage do not produce this pupillary appearance. Recognising leucocoria on routine examination or photographs prompts urgent ophthalmic referral.

questions.question: Urgent lateral canthotomy and inferior cantholysis is performed in which emergency condition?
questions.explanation: Lateral canthotomy (cutting the lateral canthal tendon) and inferior cantholysis (cutting the inferior crus of the lateral canthal tendon) immediately decompresses the orbit by allowing the globe to displace anteriorly. It is the emergency bedside procedure for orbital compartment syndrome from retrobulbar haemorrhage, relieving pressure on the optic nerve and restoring ocular perfusion. Time to decompression is critical.
options: Orbital compartment syndrome from retrobulbar haemorrhage
Endophthalmitis occurring after recent cataract surgery
bacterial infection of the eyelid margin only
obstruction and infection of the nasolacrimal duct
questions.explanation: Dacryocystitis arises when nasolacrimal duct obstruction leads to stagnation of tears and secondary bacterial infection within the lacrimal sac. This differs from eyelid margin or corneal infections, which involve different anatomical structures. Recognising the obstructive cause guides management toward relieving the blockage in addition to antibiotics.
questions.question: A patient with tearing, swelling over the inner corner of the eye, and discharge on pressing the lacrimal sac area is diagnosed with dacryocystitis, which is PRIMARILY caused by

options: White elevated dome-shaped lesion with surrounding retinal detachment
Orange-pigmented lesion with drusen on the RPE surface
Flame-shaped haemorrhages over a flat hyperpigmented area
Dome-shaped or collar-stud shaped grey-brown mass with orange pigment and associated RD
Multiple white chorioretinal scars with pigment clumping
questions.question: Choroidal melanoma detected on fundoscopy typically appears as:
questions.explanation: Choroidal melanoma typically appears as a dome-shaped or collar-stud (mushroom) shaped grey-brown or pigmented mass. Orange pigment on the surface (lipofuscin deposits in RPE) is an important clinical sign. Associated exudative retinal detachment and shunt vessels are common. Diagnosis is confirmed by B-scan ultrasound (showing intrinsic vascularity) and fine needle aspiration biopsy.

Prolonged use of topical corticosteroids (e.g., prednisolone, dexamethasone) is associated with posterior subcapsular cataract formation and steroid-induced elevated intraocular pressure (ocular hypertension), potentially leading to steroid-induced glaucoma. These side effects necessitate careful monitoring during corticosteroid use. The '10P' mnemonic captures: cataract (posterior subcapsular) and Pressure elevation.
questions.question: Posterior subcapsular cataract and elevated intraocular pressure are well-recognized side effects of prolonged use of which class of ophthalmic medication?

questions.explanation: Orange lipofuscin pigment (lipofuscin deposits in degenerating RPE overlying the tumor) on the surface is the most clinically specific fundoscopic feature distinguishing choroidal melanoma from benign nevus. Other suspicious features include: subretinal fluid, height more than 2 mm, acoustic hollow on B-scan, margin touching the disc, and absence of drusen. Regular monitoring with B-scan ultrasound is required.
questions.question: The most specific clinical feature used to differentiate choroidal melanoma from a benign choroidal nevus on fundoscopy is:
options: Uniform flat dark pigmentation at the posterior pole
Presence of orange lipofuscin pigment on the tumor surface
Absence of drusen over the lesion surface
Adjacent choroidal vessels visible through the lesion
Location at the inferior fundus rather than posterior pole

questions.question: An infant with a periocular capillary haemangioma causing occlusion of the visual axis and risk of amblyopia requires prompt treatment. Which systemic agent is currently preferred?
questions.explanation: Oral propranolol has become the preferred first-line systemic treatment for problematic capillary haemangiomas because it induces rapid regression with a favourable safety profile compared with corticosteroids. Historically, systemic or intralesional steroids were used but carried greater side effect burden. Early treatment is essential to prevent deprivation amblyopia from visual axis occlusion.

Dacryocystitis is an infection of the lacrimal sac, most commonly resulting from obstruction of the nasolacrimal duct, which allows stasis and bacterial overgrowth. It presents as tender swelling at the medial canthus, redness, and epiphora, with potential discharge on pressure over the sac. Treatment involves antibiotics and, if recurrent, surgical correction of the obstruction (dacryocystorhinostomy).
questions.question: Dacryocystitis presenting as red eye is PRIMARILY caused by:
options: Infection of the lacrimal sac due to nasolacrimal duct obstruction
Inflammatory disease of the globe as commonly encountered in practice
Allergic reaction to eye drops during routine ophthalmic assessment

questions.explanation: High-risk PDR characteristics (NVD > 1/3 disc area, any NVD with vitreous haemorrhage, or NVE >1/2 disc area with vitreous haemorrhage) indicate urgent need for panretinal photocoagulation. The DRS (Diabetic Retinopathy Study) defined these criteria, showing 50% risk reduction in severe visual loss with prompt PRP. Delay risks catastrophic vitreous haemorrhage or traction detachment.
questions.question: The EYE finding in a diabetic patient that most directly indicates the need for URGENT laser treatment is:
options: High-risk characteristics of PDR: NVD >1/3 disc area or NVE with vitreous haemorrhage
Any degree of non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy present
Hard exudates in the nasal periphery

questions.explanation: Germline RB1 mutation carriers have an elevated lifetime risk of second primary cancers, including osteosarcoma and soft tissue sarcomas, well beyond the treated eye itself. This risk persists into adulthood, justifying lifelong surveillance rather than monitoring confined to the eye. Recognising this systemic risk shapes long-term follow-up planning for survivors.
questions.question: Long-term surveillance is recommended for survivors of hereditary retinoblastoma PRIMARILY because they carry an increased lifetime risk of
options: second primary malignancies outside the eye
recurrence limited only to the treated eye

questions.explanation: 5% povidone-iodine instilled into the conjunctival sac immediately before intraocular surgery is the most evidence-based antiseptic for reducing bacterial load and preventing post-operative endophthalmitis. It is cheap, effective against bacteria, fungi, and some viruses, and has an excellent safety profile in the eye. It is used in combination with intracameral cefuroxime.
questions.question: The SAFEST antiseptic for pre-operative conjunctival preparation before intraocular surgery is:

questions.explanation: WHO-recommended Vitamin A therapy for xerophthalmia (including keratomalacia) consists of age-appropriate doses given on Day 1, Day 2, and Day 14. The rapid two doses in the first 48 hours replenish hepatic and tissue stores quickly, while the Day 14 dose ensures sustained restoration. Oral administration is preferred; IM water-miscible preparations are used if oral administration is impossible due to vomiting or severe diarrhea.
questions.question: The recommended Vitamin A therapy dose for children with xerophthalmia who have keratomalacia (X3) is given on which days?

questions.explanation: TED predominantly affects females (F:M = 8:1). TSH-receptor stimulating IgG antibodies cross-react with TSH-receptors expressed on orbital fibroblasts, stimulating glycosaminoglycan production, water retention, and adipogenesis. This causes increased orbital volume within a fixed bony space, producing exophthalmos. Smoking significantly worsens prognosis.
options: Males predominantly; catecholamine excess causes exophthalmos
Equal sex distribution; parathyroid hormone stimulates orbital fibroblasts
Males predominantly; T4 directly stimulates retrobulbar fat hypertrophy
Females predominantly; autoimmune T-cell attack directly on extraocular muscle fibers
Females predominantly; TSH-R stimulating IgG causes glycosaminoglycan deposition in orbital fibroblasts
questions.question: Thyroid Eye Disease (TED) predominantly affects which gender and follows which pathophysiology?

questions.explanation: Posterior synechiae are adhesions between the posterior iris and the anterior lens capsule (or anterior vitreous face in aphakic patients). They form from fibrinous exudate during active uveitis. They can cause irregular pupil shape, impair aqueous flow (pupil block), and lead to iris bombé and secondary angle-closure glaucoma. Cycloplegics prevent and break early posterior synechiae.
questions.question: Posterior synechiae in uveitis refers to adhesions between the iris and which structure?
options: Anterior lens capsule or vitreous face

questions.question: The MOST potent class of topical IOP-lowering agents currently available is:
questions.explanation: Prostaglandin analogues (latanoprost, travoprost, bimatoprost, tafluprost) are the most potent topical IOP-lowering agents, reducing IOP by 25–35% from baseline. They are administered once daily (usually at night), have minimal systemic effects, and are recommended as first-line monotherapy in most international POAG guidelines.

questions.question: Which of the following is a correct supportive measure in managing infectious conjunctivitis to prevent spread?
options: Sharing towels with family members to build immunity
Using handkerchief repeatedly to wipe discharge from the eye
Frequent handwashing and avoiding sharing of towels or cosmetics
questions.explanation: Infectious conjunctivitis (bacterial and viral) is highly contagious and transmitted via direct contact. Preventing spread requires frequent handwashing, avoiding sharing towels, cosmetics, and eye drops, and abstaining from contact lens wear during infection. Using tissues rather than handkerchiefs and disposing of them immediately also reduces transmission risk.

AKC affects older patients (typically adults 20–50 years) with associated atopic dermatitis, has perennial (year-round) symptoms unlike VKC (seasonal), and involves both upper and lower lids. AKC is associated with higher risk of corneal complications, cataract, and secondary herpetic eye disease. VKC predominantly affects young males seasonally in warm climates.
questions.question: Atopic keratoconjunctivitis (AKC) is distinguished from VKC in that AKC typically affects:
options: Male children in warm climates with superior tarsal cobblestones
Older adults with associated atopic dermatitis and perennial symptoms
Young male adults with limbal Trantas dots and superior pannus
Infants with mucopurulent discharge from birth
Middle-aged women with systemic Sjogren's syndrome and KCS

questions.explanation: The lens epithelium relies on the Na-K-ATPase pump to keep the lens relatively dehydrated and transparent. Failure of this pump allows water imbibition and protein aggregation, causing opacification. This mechanism parallels the corneal endothelial pump but occurs in a different tissue.
questions.question: A patient with a mature cataract is scheduled for surgery. Which pump mechanism, if failing, would explain progressive lens opacification?
A patient with retinal detachment surgery develops recurrent detachment due to fibrocellular membrane formation on both retinal surfaces causing traction. Which complication is this?
questions.explanation: Proliferative vitreoretinopathy is the most common cause of failure after retinal detachment surgery, resulting from glial and retinal pigment epithelial cell proliferation forming contractile membranes on the retinal surface. These membranes generate traction that can reopen previous breaks or create new ones, leading to recurrent detachment. Its management often requires more complex vitreoretinal surgical techniques than the original repair.

questions.question: Fluorescein is classified as a diagnostic agent in ophthalmology. Its primary clinical use is to:
options: Highlight damage to corneal epithelial tissue
Dilate the pupil for examination as commonly encountered in practice
Reduce aqueous humor production during routine ophthalmic assessment
questions.explanation: Fluorescein is a water-soluble dye that stains areas of disrupted or absent corneal epithelium bright green under cobalt blue illumination. It is used to identify corneal abrasions, ulcers, dendrites, and to assess tear film breakup time. It serves no therapeutic purpose and does not affect intraocular pressure or pupillary size.

questions.question: A patient has recurrent unilateral chronic blepharoconjunctivitis unresponsive to standard treatment, and biopsy of a thickened lid lesion is recommended because a masquerading malignancy is suspected. Which tumour classically mimics benign lid disease?
questions.explanation: Sebaceous gland carcinoma can mimic chronic blepharitis or chalazion clinically, often leading to delayed diagnosis because of its indolent and masquerading presentation. Any atypical or recurrent chalazion-like lesion, especially in an older patient, warrants biopsy to exclude this aggressive tumour. Early recognition is important because of its potential for local invasion and metastasis.

questions.question: A patient presents with sudden flashes of light, floaters, and a curtain-like shadow progressing across the visual field. What symptom pattern is this most consistent with?
questions.explanation: The combination of photopsia, floaters, and a progressive curtain-like visual field defect is highly suggestive of retinal detachment, typically resulting from a retinal tear allowing fluid to accumulate beneath the retina. Urgent ophthalmic assessment and treatment are required to prevent further detachment and macular involvement. Prompt surgical repair offers the best chance of visual recovery.

Malignant hypertensive retinopathy occurs with severely elevated blood pressure and produces cotton wool spots, flame haemorrhages, hard exudates, and optic disc swelling reflecting acute end-organ damage to the retinal and choroidal circulation. Urgent blood pressure control is required to prevent further visual and systemic complications. This differs from arterial occlusion, which produces a pale, oedematous retina rather than diffuse haemorrhagic changes.
questions.question: A hypertensive patient develops sudden painless visual loss, and fundoscopy reveals cotton wool spots, flame haemorrhages, and disc swelling with a fundus appearance sometimes compared to a 'stormy sunset'. Which diagnosis is most likely?
In sickle cell disease, which genotype is associated with the WORST systemic disease but is NOT the most common cause of severe proliferative retinopathy?
questions.explanation: SS disease (homozygous sickle cell anemia) causes the most severe systemic disease with frequent painful crises and organ damage. Paradoxically, SC disease (compound heterozygous) is more commonly associated with severe proliferative sickle cell retinopathy, likely because SC red cells have higher viscosity. SS patients have more frequent crises that may promote auto-infarction of sea-fan neovascularization before it becomes established.

options: Areas of retinal nerve fibre infarction
Lipid and protein leakage from damaged vessels
questions.question: A diabetic patient's fundus examination reveals yellow, well-defined lipid deposits near the macula. What do these represent?
questions.explanation: Hard exudates in diabetic retinopathy result from chronic leakage of lipids and proteins through damaged retinal capillaries with breakdown of the blood-retinal barrier. Their presence near the fovea indicates a risk to central vision if macular oedema develops. Laser treatment can help reduce leakage in significant cases.

A brief summary distills scattered historical details into a coherent clinical picture that guides the examination plan. It is not a substitute for examination but a bridge toward it. This step sharpens the differential before objective findings are added.
options: list every drug the patient has used
consolidate key findings into a coherent working impression
replace the need for physical examination
questions.question: At the end of history taking, the clinician dictates a short clinical summary. Its PRIMARY purpose is to

options: Sporozoite stage transmitted by the vector
Cyst (double-walled cyst resistant to most antimicrobials)
questions.question: Acanthamoeba has a life cycle consisting of a trophozoite and which resistant form that complicates treatment?
questions.explanation: Acanthamoeba has a two-stage life cycle: an active feeding trophozoite and a hardy, dormant, double-walled cyst. The cyst is highly resistant to most disinfectants, biocides, and antimicrobial agents. This resistance of the cyst form makes Acanthamoeba keratitis difficult to treat and is why treatment requires prolonged courses (minimum 6–12 months) of polyhexamethylene biguanide (PHMB) and propamidine.

Orbital veins are valveless and drain into the cavernous sinus, allowing infection to spread intracranially. This creates the risk of cavernous sinus thrombosis, a life-threatening complication of orbital cellulitis. Prompt recognition and imaging are essential when systemic signs of sepsis appear.
questions.question: A patient with orbital cellulitis develops fever and reduced consciousness. The treating team is concerned about intracranial spread via which venous route?

questions.explanation: A Grade 1 laceration without uveal prolapse presenting early is best managed with primary surgical closure of the wound to restore globe integrity and reduce infection risk. Enucleation is reserved for non-salvageable eyes, not straightforward early lacerations. Delaying closure increases the risk of infection and further tissue loss.
questions.question: A patient presents within 24 hours with a Grade 1 corneo-scleral laceration without uveal prolapse. The CORRECT initial surgical approach is

options: Drainage of drops into the nasopharynx
Direct corneal toxicity from the drug
questions.explanation: Topical eye drops drain through the nasolacrimal duct into the nasopharynx, where dorzolamide can be tasted. This is a harmless but common complaint with carbonic anhydrase inhibitor drops. Punctal occlusion after instillation can reduce this effect.
questions.question: A patient using dorzolamide develops a bitter metallic taste after each dose. What explains this common complaint?
In the non-proliferative stage of sickle cell retinopathy, 'venous tortuosity' results from:
questions.explanation: Venous tortuosity in non-proliferative sickle cell retinopathy occurs because peripheral arteriovenous shunts divert blood from arterioles directly to venules, increasing venous return and volume in the posterior segment veins, causing them to become dilated and tortuous. This is one of the earliest ocular signs of sickling and reflects the peripheral vascular shunting at areas of arteriolar occlusion.
options: Vitreous traction on retinal veins in the majority of documented cases
Systemic hypertension compressing retinal veins based on typical clinical findings
Peripheral arteriovenous shunts increasing venous flow and causing tortuous dilation

questions.explanation: High myopia is recognised as an independent risk factor for primary open-angle glaucoma, partly due to structural changes in the lamina cribrosa and connective tissue. This can make glaucomatous damage harder to detect due to atypical disc appearance. Regular monitoring is therefore essential in myopic patients.
options: It protects completely against optic nerve damage
It only predisposes to congenital glaucoma
It is an independent risk factor for open-angle disease
It has no established relationship with glaucoma
questions.question: A young myopic patient is found to have an unusually deep anterior chamber and open angles on gonioscopy. How does high myopia relate to glaucoma risk?

questions.explanation: Chronic retinal ischaemia in proliferative diabetic retinopathy stimulates release of vascular endothelial growth factor, promoting new vessel growth on the iris and angle. These fibrovascular membranes obstruct aqueous outflow, causing a severe secondary glaucoma. Panretinal photocoagulation and anti-VEGF therapy are central to management.
questions.question: A diabetic patient with poorly controlled proliferative retinopathy develops a red, painful eye with high intraocular pressure and new iris vessels. What is the diagnosis?

questions.explanation: In the Seidel test, concentrated fluorescein is applied over the suspected wound site. Aqueous leaking through the wound dilutes the concentrated dye, creating a stream of bright green fluorescein flowing over the orange background — the Seidel sign. This confirms aqueous leakage from a wound, bleb, or perforation. A positive result requires urgent wound repair.
options: Fluorescein dilution creating a black stream over orange-stained cornea
Fluorescein concentration creating bright green fluorescence pooling
Fluorescein rivulet flowing over the orange background of the stained eye
Rose bengal staining of devitalized epithelial cells at wound edges
Lissamine green staining of the exposed stroma at the leak site
questions.question: The Seidel test detects aqueous leakage from a corneal wound or bleb. A positive Seidel test shows:
A patient several years after trabeculectomy develops sudden eye pain, redness, and discharge localised to the drainage bleb. Why is this considered a particularly serious complication?
questions.explanation: Blebitis represents infection localised to a thin-walled drainage bleb, which if untreated can rapidly progress to bleb-related endophthalmitis due to the direct communication between the ocular surface and the intraocular space. This requires urgent aggressive antibiotic treatment and close monitoring for signs of intraocular spread. Long-term risk persists for as long as the bleb remains present.
options: It is always a harmless, self-limiting condition
It never requires any antibiotic treatment
Infection can rapidly spread into the eye causing endophthalmitis
It only affects the external eyelid skin
It cannot progress beyond the conjunctiva

questions.question: Atropine 1% is classified as a mydriatic/cycloplegic. Its primary mechanism of action in the eye is:
options: Sympathomimetic stimulation of the dilator pupillae in most clinical presentations
Anticholinergic blockade of iris sphincter and ciliary muscle
Beta-1 adrenergic blockade under standard examination conditions
questions.explanation: Atropine is a competitive anticholinergic agent that blocks muscarinic receptors, paralyzing both the iris sphincter (causing mydriasis) and the ciliary muscle (causing cycloplegia/loss of accommodation). It is the most potent and long-acting cycloplegic available. Its long duration (up to 2 weeks) distinguishes it from shorter-acting agents like tropicamide.

questions.question: What percentage of POAG patients in West Africa typically present with blindness in at least one eye at initial diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Studies from West Africa including Nigeria consistently show 30–50% of POAG patients present with blindness in at least one eye at initial diagnosis. This reflects late presentation due to the asymptomatic nature of POAG, limited eye care access, and absence of systematic screening programmes targeting high-risk populations.

The posterior ciliary arteries supply the choroid and also contribute to the optic nerve head circulation via the circle of Zinn-Haller. Occlusion can therefore compromise both structures, unlike the central retinal artery, which supplies only the inner retina. This anatomical overlap is relevant in ischaemic optic neuropathy.
questions.question: A patient develops progressive retinal ischaemia after occlusion of a vessel that also supplies the optic nerve head. Damage to which structure explains combined retinal and optic nerve involvement?
Vitamin A deficiency causes ocular disease through which PRIMARY mechanism?
questions.explanation: Vitamin A (retinol) is required for rhodopsin synthesis (rod photoreceptor pigment) and for maintaining normal epithelial differentiation. Deficiency causes night blindness (earliest symptom), Bitot's spots (keratinised conjunctival plaques), xerophthalmia (corneal dryness), and ultimately keratomalacia (corneal melting) — a devastating, sight-threatening condition common in malnourished children.
options: Lens opacity resulting from absence of antioxidant vitamin A activity
Impaired production of rhodopsin and squamous metaplasia of conjunctival and corneal epithelium

questions.question: In granulomatous uveitis, which finding on the iris is characteristic of sarcoidosis?
questions.explanation: Granulomatous anterior uveitis from sarcoidosis characteristically shows Koeppe nodules (at the pupil margin) and Busacca nodules (in the iris stroma). Mutton-fat KPs are also characteristic. Sarcoidosis uveitis may also cause pars planitis, periphlebitis, and optic nerve granulomas. Chest X-ray and serum ACE levels are initial investigations.
options: Hypopyon with fibrin in anterior chamber

questions.question: A mediastinal mass causing Horner's syndrome would disrupt which order of sympathetic neuron?
options: First-order (hypothalamic-spinal) as commonly encountered in practice
questions.explanation: The second-order preganglionic sympathetic fibers leave the C8-T2 spinal cord and pass over the lung apex and through the mediastinum before synapsing at the superior cervical ganglion. A mediastinal mass compressing these fibers produces a preganglionic Horner's syndrome. Proper localization guides the search for the underlying pathology.

questions.question: Persistent corneal epithelial defect (PCED) after ocular surface surgery is managed by:
options: Amniotic membrane transplantation, bandage contact lens, or tarsorrhaphy
Vitrectomy to reduce traction on the cornea
questions.explanation: Persistent corneal epithelial defect (PCED) management focuses on promoting re-epithelialisation and protecting the exposed stroma. Amniotic membrane transplantation (AMT) provides growth factors and anti-inflammatory proteins to support healing. Bandage contact lenses reduce lid friction, and tarsorrhaphy (partial lid closure) protects the ocular surface. Treating underlying cause (e.g., dry eye, neurotrophic keratitis) is essential.

questions.question: A glaucoma patient using latanoprost notices gradual darkening and increased length of his eyelashes. What is the mechanism?
options: Melanocyte destruction in the iris stroma
Prolongation of hair growth anagen phase
questions.explanation: Prostaglandin analogues prolong the anagen (growth) phase of eyelash hair follicles, leading to longer, thicker, and more numerous lashes. They also increase melanogenesis, darkening periocular skin and iris colour. These are recognised cosmetic side effects rather than harmful reactions.

Hollenhorst plaques are cholesterol emboli that most commonly originate from atherosclerotic plaques in the carotid arteries, travelling to lodge at retinal arteriolar bifurcations. Their presence indicates significant systemic atherosclerotic disease and warrants further cardiovascular and carotid assessment. They are associated with an increased risk of stroke.
questions.question: A patient over 60 with vascular risk factors presents with sudden painless loss of vision in one eye and bright refractile particles seen at a retinal vessel branch point. What is the likely source of these particles?
options: Atherosclerotic plaque from the carotid artery

questions.question: Rhodopsin in the outer segment of rods is composed of:
questions.explanation: Rhodopsin is composed of the protein opsin bound to the chromophore 11-cis-retinal (a derivative of vitamin A). When light strikes rhodopsin, 11-cis-retinal isomerizes to all-trans-retinal, triggering a cascade that generates a neural impulse. Vitamin A deficiency impairs rhodopsin regeneration, causing night blindness.

Post-traumatic bacterial endophthalmitis, especially from virulent organisms like Bacillus cereus, can manifest within 12–24 hours of the open globe injury. B. cereus produces exotoxins causing a fulminant course with severe pain, rapid visual decline, and ring abscess. Early recognition and prompt intravitreal antibiotics are critical to salvaging the eye.
questions.question: Bacterial endophthalmitis after open globe repair presents within how many hours of injury?

questions.explanation: Anterior uveitis, or iridocyclitis, involves inflammation of the iris and ciliary body and is strongly associated with HLA-B27-related spondyloarthropathies such as ankylosing spondylitis. It presents acutely with pain, circumlimbal redness, and photophobia. This anterior involvement contrasts with posterior uveitis, which primarily affects the choroid and retina.
questions.question: A patient with ankylosing spondylitis develops sudden unilateral eye pain, redness concentrated around the limbus, and photophobia. Which layer of the uveal tract is primarily inflamed?
In a 58-year-old Nigerian man with IOP 32 mmHg, C/D ratio 0.8, dense arcuate scotoma on perimetry, and open angles, the MOST appropriate initial management is:
questions.explanation: This clinical scenario — elevated IOP, large C/D ratio, dense arcuate scotoma, and open angles — represents established moderate-to-advanced POAG requiring treatment. First-line medical therapy with the most potent class (prostaglandin analogue) is appropriate. Additional medications are added sequentially if target IOP is not achieved before considering surgery.

Fixed-dose combination drops (e.g., timolol + dorzolamide; timolol + bimatoprost) reduce the total number of daily drop instillations, simplifying regimens and significantly improving patient compliance. Non-compliance is a major challenge in asymptomatic chronic diseases like POAG. Simplifying the regimen is as important as drug potency.
questions.question: Fixed-dose combination glaucoma eyedrops are used primarily to:
options: Reduce the number of daily instillations and improve patient compliance
Avoid all systemic side effects from each individual agent used
Maximise IOP lowering beyond individual agents

questions.explanation: Leukocoria (absent red reflex replaced by white reflex) in a child is a medical emergency — retinoblastoma must be excluded immediately. Retinoblastoma is the most common primary intraocular malignancy of childhood and is life-threatening if it extends outside the eye. Other causes include Toxocara, PHPV, cataract, and Coats' disease, but retinoblastoma must always be excluded first.
questions.question: Leukocoria (white pupillary reflex) in a child should raise IMMEDIATE concern for which life-threatening intraocular tumor?
A patient presents with a red eye, severe pain, nausea, vomiting, hazy cornea, mid-dilated non-reactive pupil, and markedly elevated IOP. The MOST likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Acute angle-closure glaucoma presents with circumciliary injection, hazy cornea (corneal edema), a mid-dilated non-reactive pupil, and acutely elevated IOP, often accompanied by severe eye pain, headache, nausea, and vomiting. The mid-dilated pupil is pathognomonic—distinguishing it from uveitis where the pupil is typically miotic and irregular. Urgent IOP reduction is required to prevent permanent vision loss.

Tropicamide is a short-acting mydriatic that typically achieves adequate pupil dilation within 15 to 20 minutes of instillation. Waiting the correct interval avoids an incomplete or hazy fundus view. Premature examination risks missing peripheral retinal pathology.
questions.question: While dilating a patient's pupils for fundoscopy, the examiner selects tropicamide and expects adequate mydriasis after approximately

options: IOP alone (above 21 mmHg) in most clinical presentations
Visual field loss alone under standard examination conditions
Visual field optic nerve appearance other structural/functional tests
questions.explanation: Modern glaucoma diagnosis is no longer based on IOP alone, as many patients with elevated IOP never develop glaucoma (ocular hypertensives), and some with normal IOP develop glaucoma (normal-tension glaucoma). Current practice requires correlation of visual field loss, optic nerve head appearance (cupping), structural tests (OCT of retinal nerve fiber layer), and other factors for accurate diagnosis and management decisions.
questions.question: In glaucoma management, modern practice advocates diagnosing based on which combination of factors?

options: Maxillary branch of the trigeminal nerve (CN V2)
Ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve (CN V1)
questions.explanation: HZO follows reactivation of varicella-zoster virus (VZV) in the trigeminal ganglion, specifically involving the ophthalmic division (CN V1). Involvement of the nasociliary branch (Hutchinson's sign — vesicles on the tip of the nose) predicts ocular involvement. Features include painful dermatomal vesicular eruption, uveitis, scleritis, and various types of keratitis.
questions.question: Herpes zoster ophthalmicus (HZO) is caused by varicella-zoster virus and preferentially affects which nerve distribution?

options: The ionizing radiation increases the risk of second radiation-induced malignancies in RB1 mutation carriers
CT cannot visualize the intraocular tumor adequately
MRI is cheaper and faster than CT in all centers in most clinical presentations
CT causes the tumor to grow faster
Gadolinium contrast used in CT is nephrotoxic in children under standard examination conditions
questions.explanation: Children with germline RB1 mutations carry a constitutional mutation in every cell of the body, making them exquisitely susceptible to radiation-induced second malignancies (especially in the radiation field). CT uses ionizing X-radiation and is therefore avoided in favor of MRI (no ionizing radiation) for orbital/brain imaging in hereditary retinoblastoma. MRI also provides better soft tissue contrast for assessing optic nerve involvement and intracranial extension.
questions.question: For retinoblastoma patients with germline RB1 mutations, CT scanning of the orbits is avoided because:

options: overall vitamin A deficiency and childhood blindness risk in a population
prevalence of refractive error in adults
questions.explanation: Under-5 mortality is closely linked to the same nutritional and infectious burdens, such as vitamin A deficiency and measles, that drive childhood blindness in a population. High child mortality settings typically also have higher rates of preventable childhood blinding conditions. This makes it a practical, readily available proxy indicator for planning eye health interventions.
questions.question: A community eye health programme measures under-5 mortality rate as a surrogate marker mainly because it correlates with
Which layer of the tear film is secreted by meibomian glands and prevents tear evaporation?
options: IgA layer from conjunctival plasma cells
questions.explanation: The outer lipid layer of the tear film is secreted by the meibomian glands embedded in the tarsal plates. It reduces tear evaporation and maintains surface tension. Dysfunction of meibomian glands leads to evaporative dry eye, which is one of the most common causes of dry eye syndrome.

POAG is defined by an open anterior chamber angle with normal-appearing angle structures on gonioscopy, despite raised IOP. The increased outflow resistance in POAG lies at the cellular level within the trabecular meshwork — invisible on gonioscopy. This fundamentally distinguishes POAG from angle-closure glaucoma.
questions.question: POAG is characterised by which angle configuration on gonioscopy?
options: Closed angle with peripheral anterior synechiae
Open angle with normal trabecular appearance
Occludable angle with plateau iris configuration
Open angle with neovascularisation of the angle

questions.explanation: Plain X-rays of the orbit in AP and lateral views are the primary imaging tool for identifying radiopaque IOFBs (typically metallic fragments). The combination of both views allows 3D localization of the FB. A limbal ring may be used as a reference marker for more accurate localization. Organic IOFBs (wood, vegetable matter) are radiolucent and require CT or MRI.
questions.question: A plain X-ray of the orbit in two views (AP and lateral) is MOST useful for:
A hypertensive patient with sudden painless visual loss and fundus showing dilated, tortuous retinal veins with flame-shaped hemorrhages in all four quadrants has:
options: Proliferative diabetic retinopathy with preretinal hemorrhage
questions.explanation: Central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO) presents with sudden painless visual loss and the classic fundus appearance of 'stormy sunset' — dilated, tortuous retinal veins, flame-shaped hemorrhages in all four quadrants, disc swelling, and cotton-wool spots. BRVO affects only one quadrant/segment. Risk factors include hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and hyperviscosity. Anti-VEGF treats macular oedema.

questions.question: An acute PACG attack that goes untreated may lead to:
questions.explanation: Untreated acute PACG causes permanent, severe optic nerve damage from sustained extreme ischaemia at very high IOP. Progressive optic atrophy, irreversible visual field loss, and total blindness can result within hours to days. This underscores the critical nature of acute PACG as a true ophthalmic emergency requiring immediate treatment.
options: Retinal detachment as the primary complication
Permanent optic atrophy and irreversible blindness

questions.question: A patient undergoing cataract surgery has an intraocular lens power calculated using axial length and corneal curvature measurements. Which additional factor is essential for accurate lens power calculation?
questions.explanation: Intraocular lens power calculation formulas incorporate axial length, corneal curvature, and estimated postoperative anterior chamber depth to predict the correct lens power for target refraction. Errors in any of these measurements, particularly axial length, can lead to significant postoperative refractive surprise. Modern biometry techniques have improved the accuracy of these calculations compared with older methods.

questions.question: Retinal emboli (Hollenhorst plaques) appearing as bright yellow refractile bodies at retinal arteriolar bifurcations originate MOST commonly from:
questions.explanation: Hollenhorst plaques are bright yellow, refractile cholesterol crystals (Hollenhorst bodies) lodging at retinal arteriolar bifurcations. They originate from carotid artery atherosclerotic plaques. While often asymptomatic (or causing transient visual loss/amaurosis fugax), they indicate significant carotid artery disease and risk of stroke. Urgent carotid Doppler, antiplatelet therapy, and vascular surgery referral are indicated.

Beta-blockers such as timolol reduce cyclic AMP-mediated fluid secretion by the ciliary epithelium, thereby decreasing aqueous humour formation and lowering intraocular pressure. This mechanism differs from prostaglandin analogues, which primarily increase uveoscleral outflow. Choosing the correct class matters when combination therapy is being planned.
questions.question: A glaucoma patient is started on a topical agent that lowers intraocular pressure by reducing aqueous humour production at the ciliary epithelium. This class of drug is

questions.explanation: Normal IOP is 10–21 mmHg based on population studies. The mean is approximately 16 mmHg, and values beyond 21 mmHg (mean + 2 SDs) are considered elevated. This statistical definition does not equate to glaucoma diagnosis without associated optic nerve changes.
questions.question: The normal intraocular pressure range in the general population is:

questions.explanation: Ivermectin is the cornerstone of onchocerciasis control programs, including the WHO's Onchocerciasis Control Programme (OCP) and the African Programme for Onchocerciasis Control (APOC). Annual or biannual mass drug administration of ivermectin reduces microfilarial load, preventing the ocular inflammation and scarring that lead to blindness. It does not kill adult worms but suppresses microfilarial production for several months.
questions.question: Ivermectin is the primary pharmacological agent used in the control of which blinding condition?
A child with poor nutrition develops dry, foamy conjunctival patches and difficulty seeing at night. What deficiency should be suspected?
questions.explanation: Vitamin A deficiency impairs conjunctival epithelial differentiation, producing dry, keratinised patches known as Bitot's spots, alongside night blindness from impaired rod photoreceptor function. Severe deficiency can progress to corneal melting and perforation. Supplementation and dietary correction are essential to prevent blindness.

Disciform keratitis is an immune-mediated (not directly virally mediated) stromal reaction causing disc-shaped stromal edema, typically without significant infiltration or vascularization. It is highly responsive to topical steroids with antiviral prophylaxis. Keratic precipitates may be present under the disciform lesion. In contrast, necrotizing stromal keratitis involves direct viral destruction with cellular infiltration.
options: Direct viral invasion and necrosis of stromal keratocytes
Fungal hyphae penetrating the stroma via biofilm formation
Bacterial toxin-mediated lytic destruction of collagen lamellae
Immune complex deposition causing endotheliitis with disc-shaped stromal edema
Acanthamoeba cysts migrating through corneal stroma
questions.question: Disciform keratitis is the MOST common form of stromal disease in HSK. The pathophysiology involves:
Neurotrophic keratopathy occurs due to reduced or absent corneal sensation. Which of the following conditions does NOT cause neurotrophic keratopathy?
questions.explanation: Neurotrophic keratopathy results from loss of CN V1 corneal sensation, causing impaired healing, reduced blink reflex, and persistent epithelial defects. Causes include trigeminal nerve section, herpes simplex/zoster (which reduces corneal sensation), diabetes, and leprosy. Hypothyroidism alone does not directly cause neurotrophic keratopathy.

An external hordeolum (stye) is an acute staphylococcal infection of the Zeis glands (sebaceous glands of eyelashes) or the lash follicles in the anterior eyelid. An internal hordeolum involves the meibomian glands in the tarsus. Both present with pain and localized erythema, but external hordeolum points anteriorly toward the skin.
questions.question: An external hordeolum (stye) involves acute staphylococcal infection of which structure?
options: Glands of Zeis or lash follicles

questions.explanation: Proliferative diabetic retinopathy is defined by new blood vessel formation (neovascularisation) on the optic disc (NVD) or elsewhere on the retina (NVE) in response to VEGF from ischaemic retina. These fragile vessels can rupture (vitreous haemorrhage) or cause tractional retinal detachment, with severe, often irreversible visual loss.
questions.question: The hallmark finding that defines proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR) is:
options: Neovascularisation on the disc (NVD) or elsewhere (NVE)
Haemorrhages present in all four retinal quadrants

questions.question: Intra-arterial chemotherapy for retinoblastoma is administered via which vessel?
questions.explanation: Intra-arterial chemotherapy for retinoblastoma involves selective catheterization of the ophthalmic artery (typically via the internal carotid artery and interventional radiology techniques) to deliver high-dose chemotherapy directly to the eye. This approach achieves high intraocular drug concentrations while minimizing systemic side effects. It has significantly expanded globe-salvage rates for advanced intraocular retinoblastoma.
options: Central retinal artery directly in the majority of documented cases
External carotid artery based on typical clinical findings
Ophthalmic artery via selective catheterization through the internal carotid
Reduces retinal oxygen demand and VEGF drive
questions.question: A diabetic patient with proliferative retinopathy undergoes panretinal photocoagulation. What is the primary therapeutic mechanism of this treatment?
questions.explanation: Panretinal photocoagulation ablates areas of ischaemic peripheral retina, reducing the overall oxygen demand and thereby decreasing the production of vascular endothelial growth factor that drives neovascularisation. This indirect mechanism causes regression of new vessels rather than directly treating the vessels themselves. It is the standard treatment for proliferative diabetic retinopathy to prevent vitreous haemorrhage and tractional retinal detachment.

questions.question: The 'SAFE' strategy for trachoma control stands for:
questions.explanation: The WHO SAFE strategy for trachoma control stands for: Surgery (lid surgery for trichiasis/entropion), Antibiotics (mass drug administration with azithromycin for active trachoma), Facial cleanliness (face washing to reduce transmission), and Environmental improvements (access to water, sanitation, fly control). This comprehensive strategy targets all stages of the disease cycle and is the basis of the global trachoma elimination programme. SUBTOPIC 5: OCULAR TRAUMA
options: Selective treatment, Azithromycin, Face washing, Education
Surgical repair, Antiviral therapy, Fluorescein, Examination
Screening, Antibiotics, Filtering water, Environmental changes
Surgery, Antibiotics, Facial cleanliness, Environmental improvements

questions.explanation: Sympathetic ophthalmia is a rare bilateral granulomatous uveitis thought to result from an autoimmune response against previously sequestered uveal antigens exposed after penetrating trauma or surgery. It can affect the uninjured fellow eye weeks to years later. Enucleation of a severely damaged, blind eye within the appropriate window can reduce this risk.
options: Simple mechanical irritation of the fellow eye
Autoimmune reaction against exposed uveal antigens
questions.question: A patient with a penetrating eye injury develops inflammation in the fellow, uninjured eye months later. What is the mechanism of this condition?

questions.explanation: Arteriosclerotic changes in hypertensive retinopathy (copper wiring, silver wiring, arteriovenous nicking from vessel wall thickening) represent structural changes to the arteriolar wall that are irreversible and do NOT regress after blood pressure is controlled. By contrast, acute hypertensive changes (hemorrhages, cotton wool spots, hard exudates, and papilledema) typically improve over months once BP is effectively lowered. This distinction has important prognostic implications.
questions.question: The prognosis of hypertensive retinopathy: which change does NOT regress after blood pressure control?

options: Vascular dysregulation affecting optic nerve perfusion
questions.explanation: In normal-tension glaucoma, vascular factors such as nocturnal hypotension and impaired autoregulation of optic nerve head blood flow are thought to contribute to damage independent of pressure. This explains why some patients progress despite pressures within a statistically normal range. Management still centres on further lowering intraocular pressure.
