questions.question: A patient develops progressive visual field loss despite intraocular pressures consistently within the statistically normal range on multiple visits. What additional factor is commonly implicated?

options: The buccal mucosa as clustered white lesions
The bulbar conjunctiva as white spots in most clinical presentations
The hard palate as yellowish papules under standard examination conditions
The corneal epithelium as punctate staining
questions.question: Koplik's spots are a clinical feature of the prodromal phase of measles. They appear on:
questions.explanation: Koplik's spots are pathognomonic of measles and appear as small, clustered white or bluish-white lesions on an erythematous base on the buccal mucosa (inner cheeks) during the prodromal phase, 1–2 days before the rash appears. Their presence confirms measles diagnosis before the rash and allows early implementation of preventive measures including Vitamin A supplementation.

questions.question: Trachoma is caused by which specific serotypes of Chlamydia trachomatis?
options: Serotypes D-K (genital infections) in the majority of documented cases
Serotypes L1-L3 (lymphogranuloma venereum) based on typical clinical findings
questions.explanation: Trachoma is caused by Chlamydia trachomatis serotypes A, B, and C, which exclusively infect the conjunctiva and cause the characteristic chronic follicular conjunctivitis leading to blindness. Serotypes D-K cause genital infections, while L1-L3 cause lymphogranuloma venereum. This serotype specificity is critical for understanding the epidemiology and prevention of trachoma.

questions.question: Diabetic macular edema (DMO) is the MOST common cause of visual impairment in diabetic patients, particularly those with:
questions.explanation: Diabetic maculopathy (particularly macular edema) is the most common cause of visual impairment in diabetics, with a particular predilection for Type 2 diabetes patients who are typically older. Diffuse macular edema results from extensive capillary permeability changes. It can occur at any stage of retinopathy but is especially significant in the context of non-proliferative disease.

options: Meibomian gland dysfunction with secondary infection
GPC from poorly fitting contact lens
questions.explanation: Parinaud's oculoglandular syndrome is a granulomatous conjunctivitis with prominent preauricular or submandibular lymphadenopathy, caused by cat-scratch disease (Bartonella henselae), tularemia, sporotrichosis, or tuberculosis. It does not respond to topical antibiotics and requires systemic treatment. It is typically unilateral and associated with cat exposure or other animal contact.
questions.question: A patient presents with chronic unilateral follicular conjunctivitis with preauricular adenopathy and no response to topical antibiotics. Which diagnosis should be considered?

questions.explanation: Chloramphenicol is a broad-spectrum topical antibiotic effective against most common bacterial conjunctivitis pathogens (Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae). Acyclovir targets viral (herpetic) infections, natamycin is antifungal, and prednisolone is contraindicated as a monotherapy for bacterial infections. Chloramphenicol remains a first-line choice globally.
questions.question: A patient requires treatment for acute bacterial conjunctivitis. The MOST appropriate first-line antimicrobial would be:

questions.explanation: Corneal xerosis begins at the lower nasal quadrant of the cornea as punctate keratopathy, followed by progressive haziness, dryness, and loss of lustre. This location corresponds to the area most exposed to the palpebral fissure and most dependent on adequate tear film. Without treatment, it progresses to keratomalacia with corneal ulceration and permanent scarring.
questions.question: Corneal xerosis (WHO grade X2) in xerophthalmia begins in which quadrant of the cornea?

questions.explanation: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a gram-negative organism that causes particularly aggressive keratitis with rapid diffuse corneal necrosis and perforation. Treatment uses aminoglycosides (tobramycin/gentamicin) combined with fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin), which provide excellent gram-negative coverage. GNB keratitis requires urgent hospitalization and frequent topical dosing. Pseudomonal keratitis is the most common contact lens-associated bacterial keratitis.
questions.question: A patient with contact lens-associated bacterial keratitis caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa should be treated with which antibiotic class as first choice?
Which statement distinguishes glaucomatous optic neuropathy from non-arteritic ischaemic optic neuropathy?
questions.explanation: In glaucoma, cup enlargement (cupping) exceeds pallor — the cup is enlarged, but adjacent rim tissue retains its normal pink colour. In ischaemic optic neuropathy, pallor exceeds cupping — there is diffuse or sectoral disc pallor without significant cup enlargement. This 'cupping versus pallor' distinction is a key clinical differentiating feature.
options: Pallor always exceeds cupping in cases of glaucoma
Glaucoma always presents with sudden onset
Flame haemorrhages only occur in glaucoma
Cup enlargement exceeds pallor in glaucomatous optic neuropathy
Both conditions always cause an identical disc appearance

questions.question: Children with mental retardation require visual acuity assessment using behavioral methods regardless of age because:
options: Their crystalline lenses are uniformly hypermetropic
Their pupils do not respond normally to light stimuli presented
Standard charts underestimate their visual capacity
VEP is unreliable in this population
Matching optotype tests require cognitive ability to follow instructions
questions.explanation: Matching optotype tests require the child to identify or match symbols, letters, or pictures — tasks that demand cognitive cooperation and literacy ability. Children with mental retardation cannot reliably perform these matching tasks regardless of their chronological age. Behavioral tests (CSM fixation, preferential looking) assess vision without requiring cognitive matching.

options: Supplying glucose to the avascular cornea
Removing metabolic waste from the cornea
questions.question: Aqueous humour performs all of the following functions EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Aqueous humour maintains IOP, supplies nutrients (glucose, oxygen) to the avascular cornea and lens, and removes metabolic waste (lactate, CO2). Visual pigments such as rhodopsin are synthesised by photoreceptors in the retina through an entirely separate biochemical pathway unrelated to aqueous humour.

questions.question: A patient with recurrent attacks of acute angle-closure glaucoma in one eye requires a definitive procedure to prevent further attacks in both eyes. The MOST appropriate intervention is
questions.explanation: Laser peripheral iridotomy creates a permanent opening in the peripheral iris that equalises pressure between the anterior and posterior chambers, eliminating the pupillary block mechanism responsible for angle closure. Medical therapy alone only manages acute episodes without preventing recurrence. Because the fellow eye shares the same anatomical predisposition, prophylactic iridotomy is typically offered there as well.
options: repeated courses of oral acetazolamide alone
long-term pilocarpine drops without any procedure

questions.question: A patient with narrow angles on gonioscopy but normal IOP and no symptoms is classified as having which condition?
questions.explanation: A primary angle-closure suspect has an anatomically narrow angle on gonioscopy but no evidence of raised pressure, peripheral anterior synechiae, or optic nerve damage. Such patients are at risk of future angle closure and require monitoring or prophylactic iridotomy. This differs from established disease where damage has already occurred.

Rhabdomyosarcoma is the most common primary malignant orbital tumour in childhood and characteristically presents with rapidly progressive proptosis over days to weeks. Histology reveals small round blue cells, and prompt biopsy and staging are essential for treatment planning. Early recognition improves prognosis given the tumour's aggressive growth pattern.
questions.question: A child develops sudden rapid proptosis with a palpable orbital mass and systemic malaise. Biopsy confirms a small round blue cell tumour. Which diagnosis is most likely?
A clinician performs a swinging flashlight test and observes paradoxical dilation of the affected pupil when light swings from the healthy to the affected eye. What does this finding indicate?
questions.explanation: A relative afferent pupillary defect occurs when the affected optic nerve transmits a weaker light signal than the healthy eye, causing the pupil to paradoxically dilate when light is swung from the good eye to the affected eye. This finding localises the lesion to the afferent visual pathway, typically the optic nerve or extensive retinal disease. It is a key clinical sign used to assess unilateral or asymmetric optic nerve pathology.

questions.question: A patient with anterior uveitis has small nodules noted on the pupillary margin of the iris on examination. Sarcoidosis is suspected as the underlying cause. What are these nodules called?
questions.explanation: Koeppe nodules are small inflammatory nodules found at the pupillary margin of the iris and are characteristic of granulomatous anterior uveitis, commonly seen in sarcoidosis. Busacca nodules, in contrast, occur on the iris stroma away from the pupillary border. Their presence supports a granulomatous rather than non-granulomatous uveitis pattern, guiding further systemic investigation.

According to the 2008 Nigerian National Blindness Survey, glaucoma (predominantly POAG) is the second most common cause of blindness after cataract, with prevalence of 1.8% and glaucoma blindness prevalence of 0.7%. West African populations develop POAG at younger ages and experience more rapid progression compared to Caucasians.
options: POAG is uncommon in West Africa
POAG in West Africa has a better visual prognosis than in Caucasians
POAG in West Africa presents primarily in patients over 60 years
High myopia is the predominant risk factor in West African POAG
POAG is the second most common cause of blindness after cataract in Nigeria
questions.question: Which statement about POAG in Nigeria and West Africa is CORRECT?

questions.explanation: Disciform keratitis in herpes simplex disease results from an immune-mediated reaction against viral antigens at the level of the corneal endothelium, producing localised stromal oedema without significant active epithelial ulceration. This is the most common form of stromal involvement in herpetic keratitis. Management focuses on controlling the immune response with steroids under antiviral cover rather than treating active viral replication alone.
questions.question: A patient with a history of herpetic stromal keratitis develops disciform corneal oedema without significant epithelial breakdown. Which underlying process best explains this pattern?

questions.explanation: In Horner's syndrome, only the superior tarsal muscle (Muller's muscle)—a sympathetically innervated accessory lid elevator—is denervated, contributing approximately 1–2 mm of the total lid elevation. The main elevator, levator palpebrae superioris (innervated by CN III), remains intact. Therefore, the ptosis is partial (2 mm) rather than complete (as seen in CN III palsy where the levator is also paralyzed, causing 4–5 mm ptosis or complete ptosis).
options: Only Muller's muscle is denervated, which contributes 1–2 mm of lid elevation
The levator palpebrae is partially innervated by the sympathetic nervous system in the majority of documented cases
The third nerve is also partially affected in all Horner's cases based on typical clinical findings
Ptosis in Horner's worsens in bright light
The orbicularis oculi compensates for the ptosis
questions.question: Ptosis associated with Horner's syndrome is described as 'partial' rather than complete because:

questions.explanation: Aniseikonia is the condition where retinal images in the two eyes are unequal in size and shape due to differences in correcting lens magnification (from anisometropia). In uniocular aphakia, differences can be as high as 30%, which is intolerable and causes diplopia. Iseikonic lenses correct the disparity in image size.
questions.question: A patient with severe myopia corrected by spectacle lenses notices different image sizes in each eye causing diplopia. This condition is:

options: Irrigate the eye immediately with copious saline
Apply a rigid eye shield without pressure, nil by mouth, and arrange urgent surgery
Apply topical antibiotics and discharge with routine outpatient follow-up
Perform forced duction test to assess muscle entrapment
Instil mydriatic drops to examine the posterior segment
questions.question: The correct immediate management of a suspected open globe injury in the emergency setting is:
questions.explanation: An open globe injury is a surgical emergency. Immediate management: apply a rigid (Fox) shield over the eye WITHOUT pressure, avoid manipulation that could extrude intraocular contents, make the patient nil by mouth for anaesthesia, give systemic antibiotics and antiemetics, and arrange urgent surgical exploration and repair.

Systemic corticosteroids, like topical forms, can raise intraocular pressure through reduced trabecular outflow in susceptible individuals, termed steroid responders. Regular pressure monitoring throughout the course of steroid therapy allows early detection of this complication. Prompt recognition prevents progression to steroid-induced glaucomatous damage.
options: Regular intraocular pressure checks during steroid therapy
questions.question: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis on long-term oral prednisolone develops raised intraocular pressure. What monitoring should have been in place?
A clinician instils an orange dye onto the ocular surface before examining a suspected corneal abrasion under blue light. This diagnostic agent is
questions.explanation: Fluorescein stains areas of epithelial defect green under cobalt blue light, making it the standard agent for detecting corneal abrasions, ulcers, and Seidel-positive leaks. It is also used with applanation tonometry. Its diagnostic rather than therapeutic role distinguishes it from anaesthetics or antiseptics.

options: The procedure requires direct gonioscopic visualisation of the trabecular meshwork
Corneal clarity determines the child's visual prognosis
Hazy cornea means trabeculotomy is always preferred
questions.explanation: Goniotomy requires sufficient corneal clarity to allow the surgeon to directly visualise the anterior chamber angle structures through a goniolens during the procedure. In cases where corneal haze from elevated IOP prevents adequate angle visualisation, trabeculotomy ab externo — which does not require corneal clarity — is performed instead.
questions.question: In goniotomy for congenital glaucoma, the requirement for adequate corneal clarity is critical because:

questions.explanation: Acquired dacryocystitis most commonly results from obstruction at the level of the nasolacrimal duct, causing stasis and secondary infection within the lacrimal sac. This produces a tender swelling below the medial canthal tendon, distinguishing it from canalicular obstruction which occurs above this landmark. Pressure over the sac can express purulent material through the punctum.
questions.question: An adult develops chronic epiphora, and a swelling appears just below the medial canthal tendon that discharges pus with pressure. Where along the lacrimal drainage system is obstruction most likely?

questions.explanation: Herpetic disciform keratitis is immune-mediated, not directly viral. Management involves topical steroids to suppress the immune reaction combined with antiviral cover (oral aciclovir or topical aciclovir) to prevent viral reactivation. Steroids alone without antiviral cover risk reactivating epithelial HSV disease. Long-term oral aciclovir prophylaxis reduces recurrence rates.
options: Oral aciclovir with careful topical steroid use to control immune-mediated inflammation
Vitrectomy performed to remove persistent viral reservoirs
questions.question: The SAFEST treatment for herpetic stromal (disciform) keratitis is:

questions.explanation: Toxoplasma gondii is the most common cause of posterior uveitis globally in immunocompetent patients. It causes a focal necrotizing retinochoroiditis with vitreous haze (headlight-in-fog appearance). Most cases represent reactivation of congenital infection; primary acquisition occurs from undercooked meat or cat feces. Treatment is with pyrimethamine, sulfadiazine, and folinic acid.
options: Toxocara canis causing ocular larva migrans
questions.question: Ocular toxoplasmosis is the MOST common cause of posterior uveitis in immunocompetent individuals. The causative organism is:

options: IOP measurement based on typical clinical findings
Optical coherence tomography in the majority of documented cases
Conjunctival swab for microscopy, culture and sensitivity
questions.explanation: Conjunctival swab for microscopy, Gram staining, culture, and sensitivity (MCS) is the most useful investigation for differentiating bacterial from viral conjunctivitis and guiding antibiotic therapy. Gram staining can immediately reveal gram-negative diplococci (gonococcus) or gram-positive cocci. This is particularly important in neonates and severe cases. FBC and ESR may add supportive evidence for systemic infection.
questions.question: Which investigation is MOST useful in differentiating bacterial from viral conjunctivitis?

options: delayed onset of any surface damage
no tissue damage at the surface
coagulative necrosis that limits further tissue penetration
questions.explanation: Acids denature and precipitate surface proteins, forming a coagulum that acts as a barrier limiting further penetration into deeper tissues. Alkalis instead saponify lipid membranes, causing liquefactive necrosis that allows continued deep penetration and more severe damage. This mechanistic difference explains the generally better outcome after acid exposure.
questions.question: When comparing chemical burns, acid injuries generally have a BETTER prognosis than alkali injuries mainly because acids cause

questions.explanation: Phenylephrine is a sympathomimetic that stimulates alpha-1 adrenergic receptors on the dilator pupillae, causing mydriasis without cycloplegia (accommodation is preserved). Atropine causes both mydriasis AND cycloplegia through anticholinergic blockade. This distinction is clinically important when dilation is needed without affecting accommodation (e.g., to examine the fundus without blurring near vision).
questions.question: Phenylephrine at concentrations of 2.5%, 5%, or 10% is used as a mydriatic. Its mechanism differs from atropine in that it acts via:

questions.explanation: Gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum presents early, within the first few days of life, with hyperacute purulent discharge capable of penetrating an intact cornea and causing perforation. Chlamydial conjunctivitis typically presents later, around one to two weeks, with a milder mucopurulent discharge. Prompt systemic and topical antibiotic therapy is required to prevent corneal complications.
questions.question: A neonate develops profuse purulent discharge and marked lid swelling within 3 days of birth. Corneal perforation is a feared complication. Which organism is most likely responsible?

options: Accept the term and proceed to fundoscopy as commonly encountered in practice
Document 'vitreous floaters' in the notes during routine ophthalmic assessment
Discourage diagnostic terminology and ask for lay description
questions.explanation: Patients should be discouraged from using diagnostic terms like 'floaters', 'glaucoma', or 'cataract' as these may not accurately reflect their actual experience. Encouraging a lay description elicits a more precise symptom account. This approach reduces diagnostic anchoring and ensures that important differential diagnoses are not prematurely excluded.
questions.question: During ophthalmic history taking, a patient spontaneously uses the term 'floaters' to describe their symptom. The CORRECT clinical approach is to:

questions.explanation: Ethnic nationality is a key biodata element because certain ocular conditions have higher prevalence in specific ethnic groups (e.g., primary open-angle glaucoma is more common in Africans and Afro-Caribbeans). It also provides statistics for epidemiological research and helps identify population-specific risk factors. No other listed item serves this diagnostic function equally.
questions.question: Which component of ophthalmic biodata is MOST useful in identifying genetic risk factors for ocular disease?

questions.explanation: Cyclodiode laser cycloablation uses thermal energy to partially destroy the ciliary body epithelium responsible for aqueous production, thereby lowering intraocular pressure in eyes with severe, refractory glaucoma. It is typically reserved for eyes that have failed other surgical options due to its potential for significant complications. Careful patient selection is important given the risk of hypotony.
questions.question: A patient with severe refractory glaucoma who has failed multiple surgeries undergoes a procedure to reduce aqueous production by targeting the ciliary body. What is this treatment called?

questions.explanation: Watery discharge with preauricular adenopathy following a viral upper respiratory illness is characteristic of adenoviral conjunctivitis. Bacterial conjunctivitis more typically produces purulent rather than watery discharge. Recognising the viral pattern avoids unnecessary antibiotic prescription and guides hygiene advice to limit spread.
questions.question: A patient presents with red eye, watery discharge, tender preauricular lymph nodes, and a recent upper respiratory infection. This clinical picture MOST suggests

questions.explanation: Goldberg's staging of proliferative sickle cell retinopathy progresses from Stage I (peripheral arteriolar occlusion) through Stage V (fibrovascular proliferation with tractional retinal detachment). Stage III is the characteristic 'sea-fan' neovascularization. Stage V represents the most advanced and visually devastating stage, requiring vitrectomy and surgical retinal detachment repair.
questions.question: In the Goldberg staging system for proliferative sickle cell retinopathy, Stage V represents:
options: Peripheral arteriolar occlusion in most clinical presentations
Peripheral arteriovenous anastomoses under standard examination conditions

questions.explanation: Debridement of necrotic tissue is performed to remove a source of ongoing inflammation and to promote re-epithelization of the denuded corneal and conjunctival surface. Necrotic tissue harbors inflammatory mediators and bacteria that perpetuate tissue damage. After debridement, intensive topical antibiotics and a bandage contact lens protect the healing epithelium.
options: Necrotic tissue perpetuates inflammation and impairs epithelial healing
It eliminates the need for antibiotic treatment as commonly encountered in practice
It reverses ischemia of the anterior segment during routine ophthalmic assessment
questions.question: In chemical burns, debridement of necrotic tissue from the ocular surface is recommended because:

questions.explanation: Sympathetic ophthalmia is a rare but devastating bilateral granulomatous uveitis that develops in the fellow (sympathizing) eye weeks to decades after penetrating trauma or intraocular surgery to the exciting eye. It is thought to be an autoimmune reaction to uveal antigens exposed by injury. Enucleation of the exciting eye within 2 weeks may prevent it; after 2 weeks it may not.
questions.question: Sympathetic ophthalmia is a bilateral granulomatous panuveitis that develops after:
options: Acute angle closure glaucoma in the fellow eye
Severe chemical alkali burns affecting the cornea
Penetrating or perforating injury to one eye (exciting eye)
Intraocular surgery in an eye with pre-existing uveitis
Blunt trauma causing hyphaema without perforation

questions.explanation: The correct initial step in suspected bacterial keratitis is corneal scraping for microscopy (Gram stain, KOH), culture, and sensitivity testing before commencing antibiotics. This guides targeted antibiotic therapy. However, in severe/rapidly progressive cases, broad-spectrum empirical treatment is started concurrently while awaiting results. Corneal scraping also helps differentiate bacterial from fungal and viral etiologies.
questions.question: The initial step in management of suspected bacterial keratitis before starting antibiotics should be:
options: Starting broad-spectrum antibiotics empirically without any investigation
Performing penetrating keratoplasty to remove infected tissue
Prescribing oral doxycycline 100 mg daily for 6 weeks
Corneal scraping for microscopy, culture, and sensitivity testing

questions.explanation: Contact lens solutions are specifically formulated to maintain lens comfort, facilitate lens wearing, and ensure safety by cleaning and disinfecting lenses. These include wetting solutions, daily cleaners, multipurpose solutions, and enzymatic cleaners. Using corticosteroids or atropine for contact lens discomfort is inappropriate and potentially harmful.
questions.question: A contact lens wearer reports discomfort and reduced lens tolerance. The MOST appropriate class of solution to recommend is:
options: Fluorescein diagnostic drops in the majority of documented cases
Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors based on typical clinical findings

questions.explanation: Gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum presents within 24–48 hours of birth with hyperacute, profuse purulent discharge, severe eyelid oedema, and chemosis. Corneal ulceration and perforation can occur rapidly. Transmission is via passage through an infected birth canal. Crede's prophylaxis with 1% silver nitrate or antibiotic drops prevents it.
questions.question: Neonatal conjunctivitis (ophthalmia neonatorum) appearing within 24–48 hours of birth is MOST likely caused by:

questions.explanation: Silver wiring is an advanced chronic hypertensive retinopathy change where progressive fibroelastic intimal thickening completely obliterates the blood column, leaving only a bright silver or white vessel wall reflex. It represents severe, long-standing arteriolar sclerosis. Copper wiring is an earlier stage of the same pathological process.
questions.question: 'Silver wiring' of retinal arterioles in hypertensive retinopathy indicates:
options: Fresh red blood in the arteriolar lumen
Arteriovenous crossing changes (nipping) at multiple sites
Severe arteriolar sclerosis obliterating the blood column, leaving a white reflective vessel wall

questions.question: The MOST important initial step in evaluating any red eye is:
questions.explanation: A thorough history and careful eye examination provide the essential framework for correctly diagnosing the cause of red eye. The type of discharge, pain, visual change, history of trauma, contact lens use, and systemic illness all guide differentiation between benign and sight-threatening causes. Empiric treatment without diagnosis risks harm (e.g., steroids in herpetic disease).
options: Taking a thorough history and performing an eye examination to establish aetiology
Ordering CT scan of the orbits in most clinical presentations in the majority of documented cases
Measuring IOP in all cases under standard examination conditions based on typical clinical findings

questions.question: A patient with a history of acute angle closure in one eye is offered a prophylactic laser procedure on the fellow eye to prevent a future attack. Which procedure is indicated?
questions.explanation: Laser peripheral iridotomy creates an opening in the peripheral iris that relieves pupillary block, the primary mechanism underlying angle closure, and is used both to treat an acute attack and prophylactically in the anatomically narrow fellow eye. This differs from laser trabeculoplasty, which targets the trabecular meshwork in open-angle glaucoma. Prophylactic iridotomy significantly reduces the risk of a future angle closure attack in the untreated eye.

Posterior capsule opacification is the most common late complication following extracapsular cataract extraction, resulting from proliferation and fibrous metaplasia of residual lens epithelial cells on the posterior capsule. It causes gradual, painless blurring of vision that can be effectively treated with a simple laser capsulotomy. This complication is distinct from more acute postoperative issues such as endophthalmitis.
questions.question: A patient several months after extracapsular cataract extraction develops gradual blurring of vision due to fibrosis of the remaining lens capsule. Which complication is this?

questions.explanation: Viral conjunctivitis characteristically produces watery discharge, a follicular conjunctival response, and preauricular lymphadenopathy, often following a viral upper respiratory illness. Bacterial conjunctivitis instead tends to produce purulent discharge with a papillary reaction and lacks prominent adenopathy. This clinical pattern helps guide the decision to avoid unnecessary antibiotic treatment.
questions.question: A patient has watery discharge, follicular conjunctival reaction, and tender preauricular lymphadenopathy following a recent upper respiratory infection. Which aetiology best fits this combination?
The pathognomonic sign of posterior vitreous detachment (PVD) seen clinically is a:
questions.explanation: The Weiss ring is the pathognomonic sign of posterior vitreous detachment — a circular condensed ring of vitreous gel that was previously attached around the optic disc margin. It is seen floating in the vitreous. Shafer's sign (pigment cells in the vitreous — tobacco dust) indicates a retinal tear has occurred, requiring urgent retinal examination to exclude retinal detachment. SUBTOPIC 7: CATARACT, RETINAL AND OPTIC NERVE DISEASES
options: Cobweb-like vitreous condensation floating in the mid-vitreous cavity
Snowball opacities at the vitreous base
Weiss ring — circular condensation of former vitreoretinal adhesion at the disc
Tobacco-dust (Shafer's sign) of pigment in the vitreous
A boat-shaped hyphaema in the inferior anterior chamber

questions.question: Alpha-2 agonists are CONTRAINDICATED in neonates and infants because they cause:
questions.explanation: Alpha-2 agonists such as brimonidine are absolutely contraindicated in neonates and infants below 2 years of age. Systemic absorption through the nasolacrimal mucosa causes apnoea (cessation of breathing), hypotension, bradycardia, hypothermia, and CNS depression potentially leading to coma. This is a critical prescribing safety issue in paediatric ophthalmology.
options: Allergic blepharoconjunctivitis with lid swelling and erythema
Apnoea, bradycardia, and CNS depression from systemic absorption
Direct corneal toxicity from the medication
Drug-induced pupillary dilatation precipitating angle closure
Optic neuritis triggered by the drug
questions.question: A patient develops sudden severe eye pain, blurred vision, and haloes around lights after starting an anticholinergic medication for irritable bowel syndrome. What is the likely cause?
questions.explanation: Anticholinergic drugs cause pupillary dilatation, which can precipitate pupillary block in an anatomically predisposed narrow angle. This leads to acute rise in intraocular pressure, producing pain, blurred vision, and coloured haloes. Systemic drugs with anticholinergic effects should be used cautiously in such patients.

Bacterial conjunctivitis classically produces thick purulent discharge, while viral conjunctivitis produces a watery discharge, and this distinction remains the most practical clinical clue at the bedside. Other features such as swelling or age overlap considerably between the two. This simple observation guides whether antibiotic therapy is warranted.
questions.question: A clinician distinguishes bacterial from viral conjunctivitis primarily by noting the

options: Viral or chlamydial infection — follicles suggest bacterial
Follicles are always benign while papillae always indicate malignancy
A specific pattern for contact-lens related conjunctivitis only
Trachoma exclusively, while follicles suggest VKC
A nonspecific hyperplastic response to chronic irritation or allergy
questions.explanation: Papillae (central vascular core, polygonal shape) are a nonspecific hyperplastic response seen in bacterial conjunctivitis, VKC, GPC, and allergic conditions. Follicles (peripheral vascular channels, dome-shaped lymphoid aggregates) suggest viral, chlamydial, or toxic/drug reactions. Giant papillae (>1 mm) are characteristic of VKC and giant papillary conjunctivitis from contact lens use.
questions.question: Papillae in the conjunctiva have a central vascular core. This distinguishes them from follicles and is most significant because papillae suggest:

questions.explanation: A bull's-eye maculopathy pattern can result not only from drug toxicity such as hydroxychloroquine but also from inherited retinal dystrophies including cone-rod dystrophy. Electrophysiological testing helps distinguish between toxic and hereditary causes. Accurate diagnosis guides both drug management and genetic counselling where relevant.
questions.question: A patient with reduced vision and central retinal loss is found to have a ring-shaped area of pigment disturbance surrounding a relatively preserved fovea. Besides drug toxicity, what other cause should be considered?
A patient with a chalazion is advised on initial management before considering surgical incision. Which measure is recommended first?
questions.explanation: Warm compresses with gentle massage promote drainage of the obstructed meibomian gland and can resolve a chalazion without invasive intervention. This conservative approach is tried first because many chalazia resolve spontaneously with improved gland drainage. Surgical curettage or steroid injection is reserved for lesions that persist despite conservative measures.

questions.question: A patient with sickle cell disease has a fundus examination revealing pink-orange, elevated superficial haemorrhages near the retinal periphery. What is the term for this finding?
questions.explanation: Salmon patch haemorrhages in sickle cell retinopathy occur at the level of the mid-peripheral retina, appearing as pink-orange, elevated lesions from intraretinal bleeding following vaso-occlusion. Over time these can evolve and resolve, sometimes leaving a schisis cavity or iridescent spots. They are a marker of peripheral sickle vasculopathy.

questions.question: A patient develops chronic red eye and nodular scleral inflammation associated with kidney involvement and nasal crusting. Which systemic vasculitis should be suspected?
questions.explanation: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is an ANCA-associated vasculitis that frequently produces scleritis alongside renal and upper respiratory tract involvement including nasal crusting. Ocular involvement can be severe, including necrotising scleritis threatening globe integrity. Early immunosuppressive treatment is important to prevent both ocular and systemic complications.

Ophthalmia neonatorum is defined as conjunctival inflammation occurring within the first 28 days of life, reflecting the period during which infection acquired during delivery typically becomes apparent. This time-based definition helps distinguish it from later childhood conjunctivitis with different causes. Recognising this window prompts consideration of maternally transmitted pathogens in an affected neonate.
questions.question: A neonate develops conjunctivitis on day 3 of life following a vaginal delivery. Ophthalmia neonatorum is defined as conjunctivitis occurring within which period after birth?
Chemical burns to the eye that pose the GREATEST risk to vision are caused by:
questions.explanation: Alkali burns are the most dangerous ocular chemical injuries because alkalis penetrate rapidly through corneal stroma and anterior segment tissues via saponification of cell membranes, continuing to damage tissues for hours. Acids cause coagulative necrosis forming a protective barrier that limits penetration. Immediate prolonged irrigation is critical for both.
options: Dilute acids (pH 5–6) forming a coagulative barrier

questions.question: A diabetic patient's HbA1c is checked every few months as part of retinopathy risk assessment because this test BEST reflects
questions.explanation: HbA1c reflects glycation of haemoglobin proportional to average blood glucose exposure over roughly the preceding two to three months, making it a more stable marker of long-term control than a single glucose reading. It has no direct relationship with visual acuity or intraocular pressure. This makes it the preferred marker for correlating systemic control with retinopathy risk.
options: average blood glucose control over the preceding weeks to months
blood glucose at the exact moment of testing

questions.explanation: Smoking is an established modifiable risk factor for cataract and age-related macular degeneration, while heavy alcohol use has also been implicated in lens changes. Quantifying exposure gives a dose-related risk estimate. This information therefore directly informs counselling on modifiable risk.
questions.question: A clinician documents alcohol and cigarette consumption in quantified units during an ophthalmic history mainly because these habits are linked to
A child recovering from measles develops corneal ulceration and subsequent blindness. This complication is MOST directly related to
questions.explanation: Measles infection depletes vitamin A stores and increases metabolic demand, unmasking or worsening subclinical deficiency and precipitating corneal xerosis, ulceration, and blindness in malnourished children. This is why vitamin A supplementation during measles illness is a key preventive strategy. Recognising this link explains why measles remains a major indirect cause of childhood corneal blindness in vulnerable populations.
options: a primary bacterial keratitis unrelated to measles
underlying vitamin A deficiency worsened by the measles infection

questions.question: A patient in acute angle-closure crisis is given a topical agent that constricts the pupil and contracts the ciliary muscle to open the drainage angle. This drug is
questions.explanation: Pilocarpine is a direct-acting cholinergic agonist that causes miosis and ciliary muscle contraction, pulling the peripheral iris away from the trabecular meshwork. This mechanical opening of the angle helps relieve pupillary block in acute angle closure. It is therefore used as first-line emergency therapy alongside pressure-lowering agents.

questions.question: Staphylococcal blepharitis causes chronic ocular irritation primarily through:
options: Goblet cell hyperplasia from eyelid inflammation
Hypersensitivity to staphylococcal exotoxins and enzymes causing marginal keratitis
Viral reactivation in the lid margin
Direct corneal invasion and colonisation by staphylococci
questions.explanation: Chronic staphylococcal blepharitis causes ocular surface disease through multiple mechanisms: direct toxin (exotoxin) damage to corneal epithelium, Type IV hypersensitivity to staphylococcal antigens causing peripheral corneal infiltrates (marginal keratitis), and disruption of the tear film by abnormal lid margin secretions. Treatment includes eyelid hygiene, warm compresses, and topical antibiotics.

The Keith-Wagener-Barker classification designates Grade IV hypertensive retinopathy by the addition of optic disc swelling to the haemorrhages, exudates, and vascular changes seen in Grade III. This indicates malignant or accelerated hypertension requiring urgent blood pressure control. It carries significant risk of systemic complications including stroke and renal damage.
questions.question: A patient with long-standing poorly controlled hypertension is found to have retinal haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, and swelling of the optic disc. What grade of hypertensive retinopathy does this represent?
Anti-VEGF therapy for diabetic retinopathy works by targeting which pathological process?
questions.explanation: Anti-VEGF agents (e.g., bevacizumab, ranibizumab, aflibercept) block vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), which is elevated in the diabetic vitreous and drives both abnormal vascular permeability (causing macular edema) and neovascularization (causing proliferative disease). Blocking VEGF reduces leakage, regresses new vessels, and improves vision in both DMO and PDR. They are increasingly used as primary treatment or adjuncts to laser.
options: Pericyte proliferation causing capillary obstruction in the majority of documented cases
Excess VEGF-driven vascular permeability and neovascularization
Vitreous liquefaction from oxidative stress based on typical clinical findings

questions.question: Proliferative vitreoretinopathy (PVR) is the MOST common cause of failed retinal detachment surgery. The mechanism involves:
questions.explanation: PVR results from proliferation and contraction of RPE cells, glial cells, and macrophages that form membranes on the retinal surfaces. These membranes contract, creating fixed retinal folds that prevent the retina from reattaching. PVR is the leading cause of failed retinal detachment repair. Vitrectomy with membrane peeling and long-acting gas or silicone oil tamponade is required.
options: Contraction of epiretinal and subretinal membranes from RPE and glial cell proliferation
Incomplete laser or cryotherapy seal around retinal breaks
Silicone oil migration through the detachment into the subretinal space
Intraoperative choroidal haemorrhage causing irreversible detachment

questions.question: A 50-year-old teacher complains of difficulty reading fine print without blurring. Her distance vision remains 6/6. The MOST likely diagnosis is:
options: Early nuclear cataract causing myopic shift
Presbyopia from loss of accommodation with age
questions.explanation: Presbyopia is progressive loss of accommodation with age, beginning around 40–45 years. Infants accommodate approximately 14 dioptres, dropping to about 4 dioptres by age 45. It manifests as difficulty reading near objects while distance vision is preserved. Correction requires a convex addition lens.

Rhodopsin, composed of the protein opsin bound to the chromophore 11-cis retinal, is bleached by light and must be regenerated for continued rod function. Delayed regeneration slows dark adaptation, a feature seen in vitamin A deficiency. Iodopsin is the cone pigment and is not primarily responsible for this scotopic process.
questions.question: A patient's rod photoreceptors fail to regenerate visual pigment adequately after light exposure, causing delayed dark adaptation. Which molecule is deficient in regeneration?

options: Acute arterial embolism to the retina
Sluggish blood flow from elevated plasma viscosity
questions.explanation: Hyperviscosity syndrome, as seen in Waldenström macroglobulinaemia, causes sluggish retinal blood flow due to markedly increased plasma viscosity from abnormal protein production. This produces dilated, segmented retinal veins with haemorrhages and can progress to venous occlusion. Treatment of the underlying haematological condition, sometimes with plasmapheresis, improves the retinal findings.
questions.question: A patient with a plasma cell disorder causing markedly increased blood viscosity develops retinal venous dilation with sausage-like segmentation and haemorrhages. What is the underlying mechanism?
Bleb-related infection (blebitis) following trabeculectomy is serious because:
options: It can progress to devastating endophthalmitis via direct infection through the bleb
It only occurs in the first postoperative week
Scleral flap scarring inevitably follows infection
It is always caused by antifungal-resistant organisms specifically
questions.explanation: Blebitis (bleb-related infection) can rapidly progress to bleb-related endophthalmitis because the thin-walled bleb provides a direct conduit from the ocular surface into the anterior chamber. Avascular, overhanging, or late-bleb modifications increase risk. Urgent intravitreal antibiotics and hospitalisation are required once endophthalmitis is suspected.

A normal cup-to-disc ratio is 0.3 or less, indicating a small pale central cup within the larger pink optic disc. A ratio exceeding 0.6 is suspicious for glaucomatous optic nerve damage. Serial monitoring of the C:D ratio is essential in glaucoma screening and management.
questions.question: When performing fundoscopy, the optic cup-to-disc (C:D) ratio in a normal adult eye should be approximately:
The mnemonic FAST (Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to call) helps identify strokes. Similarly, 'RSVP' is used to describe which ocular emergency?
questions.explanation: The RSVP mnemonic for acute PACG stands for: Raised IOP, Severe pain (periocular), Vision blur (haloes, corneal oedema), and Photophobia. These are the cardinal features distinguishing acute PACG from other red eye conditions. Rapid recognition and urgent IOP lowering prevent permanent optic nerve damage and blindness.
options: Retinal Vein Occlusion — Red fundus, Shadows, Vision loss, Painless
Retinal Detachment — features: Red, Shadows, Vision loss, Pain
Acute PACG — Raised IOP, Severe pain, Vision blur, Photophobia
Central Retinal Artery Occlusion — painless sudden profound vision loss
Chemical burns — Redness, Stinging, Vision blur, Pain on irrigation

questions.question: Valsalva manoeuvre raises IOP primarily by:
questions.explanation: The Valsalva manoeuvre raises intrathoracic pressure, impedes venous return, and elevates episcleral venous pressure. Since aqueous drains into episcleral veins, elevated venous pressure reduces outflow and raises IOP. Straining, coughing, and lifting transiently raise IOP via this mechanism.

Treatment measures sought prior to formal consultation —including traditional eye medications—form part of the history of the presenting complaint (HPC). This information is critical for understanding disease progression, potential complications from prior treatment, and for anticipating drug interactions. It also completes the timeline of the illness narrative.
questions.question: A patient mentions taking traditional eye medications before presenting to the clinic. This information is BEST classified under which section of the ophthalmic history?

questions.explanation: Central retinal vein occlusion classically produces widespread flame and dot-blot haemorrhages in all four quadrants, dilated tortuous veins, and disc swelling, often described using the descriptive term 'blood and thunder' fundus. This appearance reflects venous stasis and secondary capillary damage throughout the retina. Ischaemic forms carry a higher risk of subsequent neovascular complications.
questions.question: A patient presents with widespread retinal haemorrhages in all quadrants, dilated tortuous veins, and disc swelling, described as a stormy sunset appearance. What is this classic presentation of?
Which type of intraocular lens (IOL) is implanted in the ciliary sulcus rather than the capsular bag?
questions.explanation: When the posterior capsule is ruptured during cataract surgery (intraoperative complication), a standard in-the-bag IOL cannot be used. Instead, a three-piece PCIOL can be placed in the ciliary sulcus (the groove between the iris and the anterior face of the capsule). If the capsule support is entirely absent, an ACIOL or scleral/iris-fixated IOL is used.
options: Sulcus-fixated PC IOL when posterior capsule is ruptured
Multifocal IOL used for presbyopia correction

questions.question: A 60-year-old man on timolol drops for glaucoma develops wheezing and dyspnoea on exertion. What best explains this?
questions.explanation: Topical timolol is a non-selective beta-blocker that can be systemically absorbed via the nasolacrimal duct. This absorption can precipitate bronchospasm in susceptible asthmatic patients. Cardioselective agents or alternative drug classes are preferred in such patients.

The first-order (central) sympathetic neurons originate in the hypothalamus and descend to synapse at the C8-T2 level of the spinal cord. From there, second-order (preganglionic) neurons leave and travel to the superior cervical ganglion. Third-order (postganglionic) fibers then travel along the internal carotid artery to the eye.
questions.question: The first-order sympathetic neuron supplying the eye originates from the:
options: Superior cervical ganglion in most clinical presentations
Ciliary ganglion under standard examination conditions
Hypothalamus and travels to C8-T2 spinal cord

questions.explanation: Both eyes of an individual typically share similar anterior segment anatomy, including a narrow angle configuration. The fellow eye therefore carries a high future risk of an acute attack. Prophylactic iridotomy is recommended to prevent this occurrence.
questions.question: Why is laser peripheral iridotomy performed on the fellow eye of a patient who has had an acute angle-closure attack?
options: The fellow eye shares the same anatomical predisposition
It improves the vision of the affected eye
It reduces systemic blood pressure risk
Giant cell arteritis causing vessel occlusion
Multiple sclerosis with optic nerve demyelination
Hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, and small optic disc cup (disc at risk)
Raised intracranial pressure causing disc swelling
Methanol toxicity causing bilateral optic nerve neuropathy
questions.explanation: NAION results from ischemic infarction of the optic nerve head supplied by the short posterior ciliary arteries. It presents with painless visual loss, altitudinal field defect, and disc swelling with peripapillary hemorrhages. Risk factors include hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, obstructive sleep apnea, and a structurally small optic disc cup ('disc at risk'). There is no proven effective treatment.
questions.question: The MOST important systemic risk factor for non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION) is:

options: Hypertensive retinopathy from severe malignant hypertension
Ocular ischaemic syndrome from carotid stenosis
Giant cell arteritis causing branch occlusion
questions.explanation: Eales' disease is an idiopathic obliterative perivasculitis predominantly affecting young adult males, causing peripheral retinal vasculitis, branch occlusions, peripheral non-perfusion, and neovascularization with recurrent vitreous haemorrhage. It is associated with tuberculin hypersensitivity and is more common in the Indian subcontinent and Middle East. Treatment is PRP for neovascularization.
questions.question: Retinal vasculitis causing bilateral branch occlusions and neovascularization in a young adult male should raise suspicion for:
A farmer sustains a corneal injury with vegetable matter and later develops a grey-white ulcer with feathery margins and hypopyon. Which organism is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: Fungal keratitis classically follows trauma involving vegetable or plant matter and produces a grey-white ulcer with indistinct, feathery margins, often accompanied by satellite lesions and hypopyon. This history of organic trauma is a key clue distinguishing fungal from bacterial keratitis. Prolonged antifungal therapy is required because fungal organisms penetrate deeply into corneal stroma.

Angioid streaks are crack-like bands in Bruch's membrane radiating from the optic disc. They are most strongly associated with pseudoxanthoma elasticum (PXE), also seen in sickle cell disease, Paget's disease, and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (mnemonic: PEPSA). Marfan syndrome is NOT associated with angioid streaks but with lens subluxation.
questions.question: Angioid streaks on fundoscopy are MOST strongly associated with which systemic condition?

options: Myasthenia gravis and third nerve palsy
Simple mechanical ptosis from lid edema
questions.explanation: Rapidly progressive ptosis with diplopia and marked diurnal variability (worse by evening) suggests myasthenia gravis, while ptosis with dilated pupil, ophthalmoplegia, and pain suggests third nerve palsy (possibly from posterior communicating artery aneurysm). Both require urgent neurological workup — myasthenia with Tensilon test and third nerve palsy with CT/MRI angiography.
questions.question: Ptosis that develops over days to weeks in an adult with diplopia and variable diurnal symptoms should be urgently investigated for:

questions.explanation: Visual acuity of BOTH eyes must be recorded at the first examination for medicolegal purposes in all eye injury cases. This provides a baseline that documents the extent of visual damage at presentation, which may be critical in legal proceedings, compensation claims, and assessment of prognosis. Failing to document this information can have serious medicolegal consequences.
questions.question: When taking a history in an eye injury case, which fact is MOST important for medicolegal documentation?
options: The brand of safety glasses worn
The duration of work on the day of injury in most clinical presentations
Visual acuity of both eyes at the time of first examination
The weather conditions at the time of injury under standard examination conditions

questions.question: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is classified as dry (non-exudative) or wet (exudative). The MOST aggressive vision-threatening form is:
options: Early dry AMD with soft drusen only
Drusenoid pigment epithelial detachment without CNV
questions.explanation: Wet (exudative) AMD with choroidal neovascularization (CNV) is the most aggressive form, causing rapid severe central visual loss from sub-retinal fluid, haemorrhage, and scarring. Although only 10–15% of AMD is wet, it accounts for 90% of severe visual loss from AMD. Treatment is intravitreal anti-VEGF injections (ranibizumab, bevacizumab, aflibercept), which have revolutionized the prognosis.

questions.question: Sympathetic ophthalmia is a rare but feared complication of which type of eye injury?
questions.explanation: Sympathetic ophthalmia is a rare bilateral granulomatous uveitis that occurs in the uninjured (sympathizing) eye following penetrating trauma to the fellow eye, particularly when uveal tissue is disrupted or prolapsed. It can occur weeks to decades after injury. Timely and meticulous primary repair of penetrating wounds significantly reduces this risk.
options: Thermal burn limited to the conjunctiva as commonly encountered in practice
Penetrating injury with uveal tissue disruption and delayed repair
Corneal abrasion with no uveal involvement during routine ophthalmic assessment
HIV/AIDS with CD4 count below 50 cells/µL
questions.question: CMV retinitis predominantly occurs in patients with:
questions.explanation: CMV retinitis is an opportunistic infection in severely immunocompromised patients, classically HIV/AIDS with CD4 <50 cells/µL. It is the most common cause of retinitis in AIDS patients. The fundus shows 'crumbled cheese and ketchup' — white retinal necrosis with haemorrhages along vascular arcades. Ganciclovir/valganciclovir is standard treatment.

In developed countries where gonococcal infection is relatively uncommon, Chlamydia trachomatis (serovars D–K) is now the most common cause of ophthalmia neonatorum. It requires systemic treatment with oral erythromycin or azithromycin to eradicate both ocular and nasopharyngeal infection, reducing the risk of pneumonitis. Both parents require testing and treatment.
questions.question: The commonest cause of neonatal conjunctivitis (ophthalmia neonatorum) in developed countries today is:
A contact lens wearer presents with ring-shaped corneal infiltrate, severe pain disproportionate to the clinical signs, and poor response to antibiotics. Which organism is MOST likely responsible?
questions.explanation: Acanthamoeba keratitis classically presents with a ring-shaped (annular) stromal infiltrate, severe pain disproportionate to signs (due to perineural inflammation), and a history of contact lens use with tap water. It is frequently misdiagnosed as HSV or bacterial keratitis initially, leading to treatment delays. Confocal microscopy aids diagnosis by visualizing cysts.

Chloramphenicol has broad Gram-positive and Gram-negative coverage and is widely used as first-line topical therapy for uncomplicated bacterial conjunctivitis. Antifungal and antiviral agents target different pathogen classes and would not treat bacterial infection. Corticosteroids alone would worsen an untreated bacterial infection.
questions.question: A patient with acute purulent bacterial conjunctivitis is prescribed a broad-spectrum topical agent as first-line therapy. The MOST appropriate choice is

questions.explanation: The seven bones of the orbit are the frontal, sphenoid, zygomatic, ethmoid, lacrimal, maxillary, and palatine bones. The temporal bone does not contribute to the orbit. Knowing the orbital anatomy is important for understanding the spread of infection, tumors, and orbital fracture patterns.
questions.question: The 7 bones forming the bony orbit include all of the following EXCEPT:

questions.explanation: Microaneurysms are the earliest and most characteristic sign of background (non-proliferative) diabetic retinopathy, representing outpouchings of weakened retinal capillary walls. They appear as small red dots on fundoscopy. The progression is: microaneurysms → dot/blot haemorrhages → hard exudates → cotton-wool spots (IRMA) → new vessel formation (proliferative DR).
questions.question: Diabetic retinopathy progresses from background to proliferative. The FIRST sign of background diabetic retinopathy is:
A child with developmental delay is unable to cooperate with verbal or matching acuity tests. Which category of test is most appropriate regardless of cognitive level?
questions.explanation: Behavioural methods such as preferential looking, fixation and following, and optokinetic responses do not require verbal cooperation or symbolic matching, making them suitable across all cognitive levels. Standard letter-based or matching charts assume a level of comprehension that children with developmental delay may not have. These objective behavioural tests provide a functional estimate of vision in such patients.

questions.question: Laser peripheral iridotomy (LPI) is the FIRST-LINE treatment for:
questions.explanation: LPI is the first-line treatment for pupil-block angle-closure glaucoma, both as emergency treatment after acute attacks and prophylactically in narrow angles. A small opening in the peripheral iris bypasses pupillary block, equalises pressure between posterior and anterior chambers, opens the angle, and prevents future attacks. Prophylactic LPI is also performed on the fellow eye.

options: Disc haemorrhages with statistically normal pressures
Rapid onset of severe eye pain
questions.explanation: Normal-tension glaucoma is characterised by optic disc cupping and visual field loss occurring despite intraocular pressures remaining within the statistically normal range. Disc haemorrhages are more frequently observed in this subtype. Vascular dysregulation is thought to contribute to nerve damage.
questions.question: Which clinical feature would make a clinician suspect normal-tension rather than high-tension glaucoma?
A patient with thyroid eye disease develops a red eye with injection concentrated over the horizontal rectus muscle insertions. This pattern reflects
options: inflammation localised to the horizontal extraocular muscles
questions.explanation: In thyroid eye disease, inflammatory infiltration preferentially affects the horizontal recti, producing characteristic injection overlying their insertions rather than diffuse conjunctival redness. This localised pattern is a useful clinical clue distinguishing it from infective or allergic causes of red eye. It reflects the underlying autoimmune myopathic process.

questions.question: According to the WHO classification (1993) of childhood blindness, the time of onset refers to:
questions.explanation: The WHO 1993 classification of childhood blindness is based on the anatomical site of the primary condition AND the time of onset of the underlying condition, which may differ from when visual loss actually became apparent. For example, a congenital cataract may cause visual loss detected at months, but onset is prenatal. This distinction is important for identifying preventable windows of intervention.
options: Age at diagnosis by an ophthalmologist
Time the parents first noticed the child's visual problem
Time of onset of visual impairment
Sudden onset unilateral pain and photophobia
questions.question: A patient with recurrent red eyes and joint stiffness is found to have HLA-B27 positive acute anterior uveitis. Which clinical feature is typical?
questions.explanation: HLA-B27 associated anterior uveitis typically presents acutely with unilateral eye pain, redness, and photophobia, often recurring in the same or the other eye over time. It is associated with systemic conditions such as ankylosing spondylitis and reactive arthritis. Prompt topical steroid and cycloplegic treatment reduces complications.

Phenylephrine acts on alpha-adrenergic receptors of the iris dilator muscle to produce mydriasis without significantly affecting the ciliary muscle, so accommodation is largely preserved. This differs from antimuscarinic agents like atropine, which cause both mydriasis and cycloplegia. It is often combined with tropicamide for a more complete dilation.
questions.question: A patient requires pupil dilation for fundoscopy without loss of accommodation, so the clinician selects an adrenergic agonist that produces mydriasis with minimal cycloplegia. This agent is
A patient with infective endocarditis is found to have retinal haemorrhages with pale centres on fundoscopy. What is the composition of the pale centre in these lesions?
options: Aggregated platelets, fibrin, or infective emboli
questions.explanation: Roth spots are retinal haemorrhages with a pale, white centre composed of fibrin-platelet aggregates or, in infective endocarditis, septic emboli, surrounded by blood. Although classically associated with endocarditis, they can also occur in leukaemia and severe anaemia. Their presence should prompt evaluation for the underlying systemic cause.

The ESCRS endophthalmitis study demonstrated that intracameral cefuroxime (1 mg/0.1 mL) at end of cataract surgery reduces post-operative endophthalmitis risk approximately 5-fold. This is the gold standard prophylaxis. Povidone-iodine conjunctival preparation before surgery is also essential and independently evidence-based.
options: Intracameral cefuroxime injection at end of surgery
Subconjunctival penicillin at end of surgery
questions.question: The MOST effective prophylaxis proven to reduce bacterial endophthalmitis after cataract surgery is:

questions.explanation: Sympathetic ophthalmia is an autoimmune bilateral granulomatous panuveitis mediated by T-lymphocytes sensitized to uveal antigens (melanin-associated antigens) exposed by the penetrating injury. These autoreactive T-cells can cross-react with the same antigens in the uninjured eye, producing bilateral uveitis. The latency period of weeks to years reflects the time needed for T-cell sensitization and tissue trafficking.
options: Aqueous humor drainage from the injured eye to the uninjured eye
Direct bacterial spread via the optic nerve to the contralateral eye
Autoimmune T-cell response to uveal antigens exposed by the penetrating injury
Elevated IOP in the injured eye causing vascular compromise in the opposite eye
Optic chiasm crossing of inflammatory signals
questions.question: Sympathetic ophthalmia involves the uninjured 'sympathizing' eye because of:

questions.explanation: Systemic beta-blocker side effects (bradycardia, bronchospasm, dyspnoea) from topical timolol require immediate drug discontinuation. Switching to a prostaglandin analogue provides effective IOP lowering without cardiovascular or respiratory side effects. Recognising systemic toxicity from topical ophthalmic agents is an essential clinical competency.
options: Reduce timolol to once daily dosing
Add an alpha agonist to timolol
Continue timolol and treat cardiac effects separately
Add an oral beta-blocker to counteract systemic effects
questions.question: In a patient with POAG on timolol eyedrops who develops bradycardia and bronchospasm, the MOST appropriate management is:
A patient with malignant hypertension develops disc swelling, flame hemorrhages, cotton wool spots, and macular star formation together. This grouped presentation is classified as
questions.explanation: The combination of disc oedema together with hemorrhages, cotton wool spots, and a macular star defines the most severe stage of hypertensive retinopathy, Grade IV, and signals malignant hypertension requiring urgent blood pressure reduction. Milder grades lack the disc swelling that distinguishes this stage. Recognising this constellation is an ocular emergency prompting immediate systemic evaluation.

options: represent fixed structural sclerosis that does not reverse with blood pressure control
only occur in patients without treatment
are entirely reversible within days of treatment
always resolve completely within one year
questions.question: A patient with longstanding, well-controlled hypertension still shows persistent arteriovenous nicking and arteriolar wiring on fundus examination. This is because these particular changes
questions.explanation: Chronic sclerotic changes such as arteriolar wiring and arteriovenous nicking reflect structural wall thickening that persists even after blood pressure is well controlled, unlike hemorrhages, cotton wool spots, or edema which can resolve with treatment. This helps clinicians distinguish old structural damage from ongoing active vascular injury. Recognising this distinction avoids over-interpreting persistent chronic signs as evidence of poor current control.

Normal intraocular pressure ranges from 10–21 mmHg, maintained by the balance between aqueous humor production by the ciliary body and drainage via the trabecular meshwork. A consistently elevated IOP above 21 mmHg is a major risk factor for glaucoma, though normal tension glaucoma also occurs.
questions.question: A normal intraocular pressure is maintained between which values (in mmHg)?

questions.explanation: Topical beta-blockers (e.g., timolol, betaxolol) reduce intraocular pressure by blocking beta-2 adrenergic receptors on the ciliary epithelium, thereby decreasing the production of aqueous humor. They are a mainstay of glaucoma treatment globally. Prostaglandin analogues work via increasing uveoscleral outflow, a different mechanism entirely.
options: Reducing aqueous humor production by the ciliary body
Increasing uveoscleral outflow based on typical clinical findings
Reducing vitreous humor volume in the majority of documented cases
questions.question: Beta-adrenergic receptor blockers used in glaucoma management reduce intraocular pressure by:

questions.explanation: VKH syndrome is an autoimmune panuveitis targeting melanocytes in the uvea, skin, inner ear, and meninges. Ocular features include bilateral exudative retinal detachment and disc swelling. Systemic features include sensorineural deafness, alopecia, poliosis (whitening of hair/lashes/brows), vitiligo, and meningismus. Oral corticosteroids are the mainstay of treatment.
questions.question: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada (VKH) syndrome is a bilateral panuveitis with systemic features that include:
options: Arthritis, anterior uveitis, urethritis, and skin lesions
Erythema nodosum, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, and uveitis
Choroidal hemangioma, port-wine stain, and glaucoma
Interstitial nephritis, uveitis, and tubulointerstitial inflammation

questions.explanation: Povidone-iodine has broad microbicidal activity and is applied to the periocular skin and conjunctival sac before intraocular surgery specifically to lower the risk of postoperative endophthalmitis. It functions as an antiseptic rather than a therapeutic antibiotic. This preoperative step is considered standard of care in ophthalmic surgery.
questions.question: Before intraocular surgery, the surgical field is cleaned with an antiseptic solution known to reduce postoperative endophthalmitis rates. This agent is

options: duration of diabetes and degree of glycemic control
questions.question: A patient with a 15-year history of poorly controlled diabetes develops progressive retinal changes. The strongest driver of this progression is
questions.explanation: Both the length of time a patient has had diabetes and how well blood glucose has been controlled are the most consistent determinants of diabetic retinopathy severity and progression. Unrelated patient characteristics such as blood group or eye colour have no bearing on retinal risk. This is why glycemic control is central to retinopathy prevention strategies.

questions.question: Herpes simplex blepharoconjunctivitis — the PRIMARY management principle is:
options: Topical/oral antiviral agents; steroids only for stromal complications
Emergency topical steroids to reduce inflammation
Immediate irrigation with normal saline and bandage contact lens
Systemic corticosteroids plus cycloplegics from the outset
Patching the eye for 48 hours and bed rest
questions.explanation: Herpes simplex blepharoconjunctivitis requires topical or oral antiviral therapy (acyclovir, trifluridine, or famciclovir). Topical steroids must be avoided in active epithelial HSV disease as they can enhance viral replication and worsen epithelial keratitis. Steroids are only used for immune-mediated stromal (disciform) keratitis, with concurrent antiviral cover. Cycloplegics are added if uveitis is present.

options: Choroidal rupture at the posterior pole
Commotio retinae (Berlin's oedema) at the macula
Retinal dialysis at the ora serrata
questions.explanation: Retinal dialysis is a circumferential tear at the ora serrata (the vitreoretinal junction anteriorly), often caused by blunt ocular trauma. It produces a peripheral retinal detachment that slowly extends posteriorly. The detachment may produce a ring-like peripheral visual field defect. Retinal dialysis is an important cause of traumatic retinal detachment, especially in young patients.
questions.question: The 'ring scotoma' following blunt ocular trauma is associated with:
Which management approach is INCORRECT for managing an acute dacryocystitis?
options: Oral or IV antibiotics targeting common pathogens
Immediate DCR surgery during acute infection phase
Incision and drainage if abscess forms
Definitive DCR after resolution of acute inflammation
questions.explanation: DCR surgery should NOT be performed during active acute dacryocystitis because of the risk of spreading infection. The correct approach is first to treat the acute infection with antibiotics and warm compresses, and if an abscess forms, to perform incision and drainage. Definitive DCR is planned after the acute inflammation has completely resolved.

Meibomian gland dysfunction alters the lipid composition of secretions, producing foam in the tear meniscus and unstable, rapidly evaporating tear film. This evaporative dry eye pattern differs from aqueous-deficient states, which show normal lipid layer function. Lid margin inflammation and telangiectasia often accompany the condition.
questions.question: A 45-year-old woman has lid margin redness, foamy tear meniscus, and rapid tear film breakup time. Which condition best explains these findings?

questions.explanation: Target intraocular pressure is individualised based on the severity of existing glaucomatous damage, with lower targets generally set for eyes with more advanced disease to reduce the risk of further progression. Eyes with only mild or early changes may tolerate a somewhat higher target pressure. This personalised approach balances treatment burden against the risk of further visual loss.
options: The eye with less advanced damage only
Both eyes should have identical targets always
Neither eye requires a defined target
The eye with the better vision only
The eye with more advanced glaucomatous damage
questions.question: A patient with advanced glaucomatous damage in one eye and early changes in the fellow eye is being counselled on treatment targets. In which eye should the target intraocular pressure generally be set lowest?

questions.explanation: Mydriatics dilate the pupil (mydriasis), allowing a wider view of the internal eye structures during fundoscopy and slit-lamp examination. Cycloplegic mydriatics (e.g., atropine, cyclopentolate) additionally paralyze the ciliary muscle, preventing accommodation—useful for objective refraction in children. Pilocarpine, by contrast, constricts the pupil and is used in glaucoma.
options: Dilate the pupil and possibly paralyze accommodation for better examination
Constrict the pupil for glare reduction as commonly encountered in practice
Kill bacteria on the eye surface during routine ophthalmic assessment
questions.question: A patient is prescribed mydriatics for ophthalmic examination. They ask about the purpose of the medication. The CORRECT explanation is that mydriatics:

questions.explanation: Sequencing multiple complaints helps determine whether they share a single underlying process or represent independent pathology. This timeline shapes the differential diagnosis before examination begins. It also directs which systems require closer review.
options: let the patient rank complaint severity
establish a clear timeline linking both complaints
treat both complaints as unrelated events
postpone history until fundoscopy is done
examine only the complaint mentioned first
questions.question: A patient reports two separate visual complaints that began weeks apart. The MOST useful history-taking step is to
Peters anomaly is characterised by which combination of findings?
questions.explanation: Peters anomaly is a developmental anterior segment disorder featuring central corneal leucoma (opacity) with posterior corneal defect and iridocorneal adhesions. The lens may be clear or cataractous. It is bilateral in 80% of cases, and 50% are associated with glaucoma. Management is complex, requiring corneal transplantation and glaucoma surgery.
options: Entire corneal vascularisation from the limbus
Central corneal opacity with posterior iridocorneal adhesions
Posterior synechiae with posterior lens opacity
Peripheral corneal vascularisation with limbal involvement
2 disc diameters temporal and 1.5 degrees below the horizon of the disc
Directly at the optic disc during routine ophthalmic assessment
Superior to the disc by 1 disc diameter as commonly encountered in practice
questions.explanation: The macula is approximately 2 disc diameters temporal to the optic disc and about 1.5 degrees below the horizon. It appears darker than the surrounding retina due to its high pigment content and lack of nerve fiber layer. The fovea centralis, responsible for highest visual acuity, lies at the center of the macula.
questions.question: The macula in fundoscopy is located approximately:

questions.explanation: Neovascularization of the disc, abbreviated NVD, describes new pathological vessels growing directly from the optic nerve head in response to retinal ischemia. This is distinct from IRMA, which describes intraretinal shunt vessels rather than true new vessel growth. NVD is a hallmark feature defining proliferative diabetic retinopathy.
questions.question: A diabetic patient's fundus examination reveals new abnormal vessels arising directly from the optic disc. This finding is abbreviated in retinal grading as
Ciliary muscle paralysis in third nerve palsy results in:
questions.explanation: The ciliary muscle, responsible for accommodation (near focusing), is innervated by the parasympathetic division of CN III via the ciliary ganglion. Paralysis of this muscle results in cycloplegia—inability to accommodate. This manifests as blurred near vision and is an additional feature distinguishing CN III palsy from other causes of diplopia.

questions.question: A patient with a mature cataract develops sudden severe eye pain, red eye, and markedly elevated intraocular pressure. Which mechanism explains this acute presentation?
questions.explanation: A markedly swollen, intumescent mature cataract can push the iris-lens diaphragm forward, precipitating acute angle closure known as phacomorphic glaucoma. This produces sudden pain, redness, and high intraocular pressure similar to primary angle closure but caused mechanically by lens swelling. Urgent cataract extraction relieves the pupillary block and lowers pressure definitively.

options: accept the term and proceed to biometry
document cataract as the presenting complaint
ask him to describe the symptom in his own words
questions.question: A 55-year-old describes his problem as 'cataract' before any examination is done. The BEST next action is to
questions.explanation: Diagnostic labels volunteered by patients may not reflect the true clinical picture. Asking for a lay description prevents premature anchoring on one diagnosis. This preserves an unbiased differential until objective findings are obtained.

questions.question: Among sickle cell genotypes, patients with haemoglobin SC disease characteristically have MILDER systemic disease but tend to have
questions.explanation: Paradoxically, patients with haemoglobin SC disease, despite generally milder systemic manifestations than haemoglobin SS disease, tend to develop more severe proliferative retinopathy, possibly related to relatively higher blood viscosity in less severely anaemic patients. This dissociation between systemic and ocular severity is a distinctive feature of sickle cell eye disease. Recognising this prevents underestimating retinopathy risk in genotypes with milder systemic disease.
options: more severe proliferative retinopathy than haemoglobin SS disease
only non-proliferative changes and never proliferative disease
retinopathy limited exclusively to the macula
identical retinopathy severity to haemoglobin SS disease

questions.explanation: Adult chlamydial conjunctivitis (serovars D–K) is an STI transmitted by autoinoculation from genital secretions. Unlike trachoma (serovars A–C in endemic areas), adult chlamydial conjunctivitis does not cause tarsal scarring or blindness. It presents as chronic follicular conjunctivitis and responds to systemic azithromycin or doxycycline.
options: Adult chlamydial conjunctivitis always scars the superior tarsus permanently
Trachoma is caused by Chlamydia serovars L1, L2, L3 instead of A-C
Adult chlamydial conjunctivitis is a sexually transmitted disease without tarsal scarring
Adult chlamydial conjunctivitis exclusively affects the inferior fornix
Trachoma causes follicular conjunctivitis in the inferior tarsal plate exclusively
questions.question: Adult chlamydial keratoconjunctivitis differs from trachoma in which important clinical feature?
