A 30-year-old man presents with acute unilateral red eye, watery discharge, and ipsilateral preauricular lymphadenopathy. No fever noted. The MOST likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Viral conjunctivitis classically presents with acute onset, unilateral (or bilateral) watery discharge, follicular conjunctivitis, and preauricular lymphadenopathy. Adenovirus is the most common cause of epidemic keratoconjunctivitis. Bacterial conjunctivitis lacks lymphadenopathy and has purulent discharge. Gonococcal keratoconjunctivitis has profuse purulent discharge and is a more dramatic presentation.

questions.question: Rifamycin as an ophthalmic antimicrobial is primarily effective against which pathogen category?
options: Herpes viruses in most clinical presentations
Chlamydia only under standard examination conditions
questions.explanation: Rifamycin (rifampicin) is an antibacterial agent with particular effectiveness against mycobacteria and a broad spectrum covering many gram-positive and some gram-negative organisms. In ophthalmic use, rifamycin eye drops have been used for bacterial conjunctivitis, including infections by organisms resistant to other agents. It is not antifungal or antiviral.

options: Reduce the duration of the consultation as commonly encountered in practice
Avoid the need for clinical examination during routine ophthalmic assessment
Put disease into perspective and guide clinical examination
Generate a final diagnosis before examination
questions.question: A brief clinical summary at the end of history taking in ophthalmology serves PRIMARILY to:
questions.explanation: A brief summary following history taking puts the disease into perspective and guides the focus of the subsequent clinical examination. It helps the clinician identify areas requiring more concentrated assessment. The summary does not replace examination but frames it meaningfully within the clinical context.

The STYCAR rolling balls test uses ten white polystyrene spheres of graded sizes (3.5 mm to 6 cm) rolled across a contrasting floor at 3 meters. The child's pursuit eye movements toward the ball indicate it has been seen; each size corresponds to a VA level. It is a behavioral test suitable for children under 2 years.
questions.question: In the STYCAR rolling balls test, how is the child's visual acuity inferred?
options: By matching letters on a key card held at 3 meters
By measuring VEP amplitude to alternating patterns
By noting pursuit eye movements toward rolling spheres of graded size
By assessing preferential looking toward grating patterns
By recording OKN responses to optokinetic drums

questions.explanation: Unexpectedly low (soft) IOP — hypotony — on tonometry is an important but sometimes overlooked sign of an open globe, indicating fluid loss from the eye. The intact conjunctiva may mask a scleral rupture. A careful search for scleral rupture is mandatory in all blunt trauma cases, especially under the extraocular muscle insertions where the sclera is thinnest.
questions.question: Which of the following is a sign of an open globe that may be MISSED on initial examination?

options: Seal the perforation and restore chamber depth
questions.explanation: Cyanoacrylate tissue adhesive is applied to seal a small corneal perforation, preventing further aqueous leakage and allowing the anterior chamber to reform. This temporising measure stabilises the eye while definitive treatment, such as a corneal graft, is planned. It does not treat the underlying infection, which must be managed with appropriate antimicrobial therapy.
questions.question: A perforating corneal ulcer with a small leak is treated with a tissue adhesive applied over the defect. What is the primary aim of this intervention?

options: Hexokinase pathway producing excess fructose based on typical clinical findings
Advanced glycation end-product (AGE) receptor binding in the majority of documented cases
Polyol pathway: glucose converted to sorbitol by aldose reductase
questions.explanation: The polyol (sorbitol) pathway is activated in hyperglycemia: aldose reductase converts excess intracellular glucose to sorbitol, which accumulates because it crosses cell membranes poorly. Sorbitol accumulation causes osmotic stress, reduced NADPH availability, and oxidative stress in retinal pericytes and endothelial cells. This mechanism, along with AGE formation and PKC activation, contributes to the retinal vascular damage of diabetic retinopathy.
questions.question: In the pathogenesis of diabetic retinopathy, intracellular sorbitol accumulation occurs via which pathway?

options: Dot/blot hemorrhages, hard and soft exudates, diffuse arteriolar narrowing, AV crossing defects
Only arteriovenous nipping and copper wiring in most clinical presentations in most clinical presentations
Isolated macular star without other changes under standard examination conditions under standard examination conditions
questions.explanation: Grade III (early malignant) hypertensive retinopathy includes dot and blot hemorrhages, both hard exudates (lipid deposits) and soft exudates (cotton wool spots), diffuse arteriolar narrowing, and arteriovenous crossing defects. Grade IV adds macular star formation and papilledema. Grades I and II are chronic changes without hemorrhages or exudates, representing arteriosclerosis only.
questions.question: In early malignant hypertensive retinopathy (Grade III), which combination of findings is CHARACTERISTIC?
Only 30–40% of all causes of childhood blindness are considered avoidable. The MAJORITY of avoidable causes are in which category?
questions.explanation: Among the 30–40% of avoidable childhood blindness causes, both treatable conditions (cataract, ROP, refractive errors, low vision) and preventable conditions (corneal scarring from Vitamin A deficiency, measles keratitis) contribute significantly. The relative proportion varies by region: preventable causes dominate in very low-income settings, while treatable causes (including ROP) are more prominent in middle-income countries.
options: Preventable causes (corneal scarring from VAD, measles)

questions.question: External beam radiotherapy (EBRT) is now rarely used in retinoblastoma because:
options: It is less effective than laser therapy for all tumor stages as commonly encountered in practice
It increases the risk of second non-ocular tumors, particularly in germline RB patients
It causes immediate blindness in all treated eyes during routine ophthalmic assessment
It is more expensive than intravenous chemotherapy
It is prohibited by international guidelines
questions.explanation: External beam radiotherapy dramatically increases the risk of second primary malignancies (e.g., osteosarcomas, soft tissue sarcomas) in children with germline retinoblastoma, as the entire body carries the RB1 mutation predisposing to radiation-induced cancers. Modern treatment protocols avoid EBRT and use intravenous chemotherapy, intra-arterial chemotherapy, and local treatments instead. EBRT is reserved for very specific situations.

The lacrimal gland is an exocrine gland located in the superior lateral quadrant of the orbit within the lacrimal fossa, in the frontal bone. It produces the aqueous component of the tear film. Lacrimal gland tumors typically cause an S-shaped deformity of the upper lid and axial or non-axial proptosis.
questions.question: The lacrimal gland is located in the:
options: Superior medial quadrant adjacent to the trochlea
Superior lateral quadrant within the lacrimal fossa
Inferior lateral quadrant of the orbit
Central orbital apex near the optic canal

questions.explanation: Diabetes mellitus is an established risk factor for POAG. Additional risk factors include increasing age, family history of glaucoma, African ancestry, high myopia, and thin central corneal thickness. The association with diabetes may reflect shared pathological mechanisms including vascular dysregulation affecting the optic nerve.
questions.question: Which systemic disease is an established risk factor for the development of primary open-angle glaucoma?

questions.explanation: The lowest target IOP is required in normal tension glaucoma (NTG) patients with progressive damage, because their optic nerves are damaged at 'normal' IOP levels, indicating exceptional optic nerve vulnerability. Target IOP in NTG is typically set at 30% below baseline (often <12–14 mmHg) to halt progression. This aggressive target reflects the optic nerve's sensitivity to even normal IOP levels in NTG.
questions.question: The 'target' IOP concept in glaucoma management means that the target is LOWEST in which patient group?
options: Patients with early glaucoma and high IOP
Patients with early POAG and wide rim tissue

questions.explanation: A drop in visual acuity signals that deeper ocular structures may be involved rather than a superficial, self-limiting process. Simple conjunctivitis or allergic irritation rarely affects central vision. This single red flag should prompt urgent slit-lamp assessment regardless of other findings.
questions.question: Among features of a red eye, which single finding MOST strongly suggests a sight-threatening cause requiring urgent referral?
A patient develops ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis following a radical neck dissection. The most likely affected structure is the:
questions.explanation: Radical neck dissection can damage the superior cervical ganglion or its postganglionic fibers, producing ipsilateral Horner's syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis). This is a well-documented surgical complication. The involvement of anhidrosis helps localize the lesion to the preganglionic or ganglionic level rather than the postganglionic carotid plexus.
options: Optic nerve as commonly encountered in practice
Ciliary ganglion during routine ophthalmic assessment

questions.question: A newborn develops purulent discharge, marked lid swelling, and conjunctival chemosis within the first days of life. This presentation is MOST suggestive of
questions.explanation: Purulent discharge with significant lid swelling and chemosis in a neonate is the hallmark presentation of ophthalmia neonatorum, most commonly from gonococcal or chlamydial infection acquired during delivery. This urgency reflects the risk of rapid corneal involvement. Prompt microbiological testing and systemic therapy are required.

Chemical ON caused by 1% silver nitrate (Crede's method of neonatal prophylaxis) is non-infective, transient, and self-limiting, typically resolving within 24–48 hours without treatment. It presents with mild conjunctival redness and watery discharge. By contrast, infective ON (gonococcal, chlamydial, bacterial) requires antimicrobial therapy. 2% povidone iodine is now preferred over silver nitrate for neonatal prophylaxis.
questions.question: Chemical (silver nitrate-induced) ophthalmia neonatorum differs from infective ON in that it is:
options: Purulent and associated with systemic disease
The most severe form requiring IV antibiotics
Associated with corneal ulceration in most cases
Bilateral and requires topical antiviral treatment
resolved retinopathy with no further risk
mild background disease needing no follow-up
severe non-proliferative disease requiring close follow-up
questions.question: According to the 4-2-1 rule used to define severe non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy, meeting even one of the specified criteria in all four quadrants, two quadrants, or one quadrant respectively indicates
questions.explanation: The 4-2-1 rule combines the extent of intraretinal hemorrhages, venous beading, and IRMA across the four retinal quadrants to identify eyes at high risk of progressing to proliferative disease. Meeting any one criterion classifies the eye as severe non-proliferative retinopathy, prompting closer monitoring or earlier intervention. This grading helps target treatment before frank neovascularization develops.

questions.question: A community health worker screens an illiterate farmer for visual acuity using a chart with a single optotype in different orientations. Which test is being used?
questions.explanation: The tumbling E chart uses a single letter E presented in different rotations, requiring the patient to indicate the direction of the open limbs rather than name letters. This makes it suitable for non-literate patients who cannot read standard alphabetic optotypes. It provides a reliable estimate of visual acuity without literacy requirements.

questions.question: A neonate develops copious purulent discharge and severe eyelid swelling on day two of life. What is the most urgent concern?
questions.explanation: Gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum presents very early with hyperacute, copious purulent discharge and marked lid oedema. Neisseria gonorrhoeae can rapidly invade an intact corneal epithelium, risking perforation within hours if untreated. Urgent systemic and topical antibiotic treatment is required to prevent blindness.

questions.question: A patient has both an entry and an exit wound in the globe following a projectile injury. This pattern of injury is classified as
questions.explanation: When a projectile creates two full-thickness wounds, one of entry and one of exit, the injury is termed perforating rather than simply penetrating, which involves only a single full-thickness wound. This distinction matters because perforating injuries carry a higher risk of posterior segment damage and retinal detachment. Recognising the pattern shapes the urgency and extent of surgical exploration.

questions.question: A patient with gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum requires antimicrobial therapy that reaches adequate tissue levels to prevent corneal perforation. The recommended route is
questions.explanation: Gonococcal infection can rapidly invade an intact corneal epithelium and cause perforation, so topical therapy alone is inadequate. Systemic antibiotics, typically a cephalosporin, achieve the tissue concentrations needed to eradicate the organism and prevent this complication. Topical treatment is used only as an adjunct, not as sole therapy.

Proliferative diabetic retinopathy is the most common overall cause of vitreous haemorrhage in adults, resulting from bleeding of fragile new vessels growing in response to retinal ischaemia. Other causes such as retinal tears, vein occlusion, and trauma also contribute but are individually less frequent than diabetic causes in most populations. Ultrasound is used to assess the retina when haemorrhage obscures direct visualisation.
questions.question: A patient develops sudden vitreous haemorrhage with no view of the fundus. In an adult population, which underlying condition is the most common overall cause?

options: Abrupt nasal angulation of vessels as they enter a deep undermined glaucomatous cup
Arteriovenous crossing changes on the retina
Abnormal choroidal neovascularisation occurring at the optic disc
Pallor extending beyond the cup margin
Pulsation of the central retinal artery
questions.question: Bayonetting of vessels at the optic disc in advanced glaucoma refers to:
questions.explanation: Bayonetting describes the abrupt angulation of blood vessels as they pass over the sharply undercut edge of a deep glaucomatous cup — vessels appear to bend at right angles as they dive deep, then seem to 'disappear and reappear.' This finding indicates advanced glaucomatous cupping with an overhanging cup edge.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the anatomical relationship between the medial orbital wall and adjacent sinuses?
options: Separated from ethmoid sinus by the lamina papyracea
Separated from the frontal sinus by a thick bony plate
Directly adjacent to the sphenoid sinus only
Bounded laterally by the maxillary sinus
Separated from nasal cavity by the palatine bone
questions.explanation: The medial wall of the orbit is separated from the ethmoid sinus by the lamina papyracea, a paper-thin bone that easily allows transmission of pathogens from sinusitis, leading to orbital cellulitis. This is why sinusitis is the most common cause of orbital cellulitis.

Primary open-angle glaucoma results from progressive optic nerve damage related to elevated intraocular pressure acting on the lamina cribrosa, compressing and disrupting retinal ganglion cell axons over time. Unlike angle closure, the drainage angle remains anatomically open, and pressure elevation occurs due to increased trabecular outflow resistance rather than mechanical obstruction. This gradual axonal loss produces the characteristic cupping and visual field defects.
questions.question: A 68-year-old with progressive tunnel vision and optic disc cupping is found to have an intraocular pressure of 28 mmHg. Which mechanism underlies the optic nerve damage in this open-angle presentation?

questions.explanation: Hyphema is defined as blood in the anterior chamber, typically from rupture of iris root or angle vessels following blunt trauma. It appears as a fluid level of blood in the anterior chamber. Mild hyphema may be visible only on slit-lamp; Grade IV (8-ball) hyphema fills the entire anterior chamber with dark blood.
questions.question: Hyphema is defined as:
options: Vitreous haemorrhage within the vitreous cavity
Blood in the anterior chamber of the eye

questions.explanation: In acute severe angle-closure crises, intravenous hyperosmotic agents such as mannitol rapidly draw fluid osmotically from the vitreous, producing a fast reduction in intraocular pressure. This provides urgent relief while definitive treatment, such as iridotomy, is arranged. Oral agents act more slowly and are used adjunctively.
questions.question: A patient presents with acutely painful red eye, corneal oedema, and IOP of 55 mmHg. Which initial medical measure acts fastest to lower pressure?

questions.explanation: Chronic open-angle glaucoma typically causes gradual, painless peripheral visual field loss that patients do not notice until damage is advanced, unlike acute angle closure which is painful and obvious. Without routine screening programmes, many cases are only detected once central vision is already threatened. This silent progression is a major driver of preventable blindness from glaucoma in under-resourced health systems.
questions.question: Most glaucoma cases in low-resource settings remain undiagnosed until late-stage visual loss mainly because the disease
options: always presents with severe pain early

questions.explanation: Corneal scraping for Gram stain, microscopy, and culture should be obtained before starting empirical antimicrobial therapy whenever possible, since this guides targeted treatment and identifies resistant or unusual organisms. Delaying treatment for results is avoided by starting broad-spectrum therapy immediately after sampling. Patching is avoided in suspected infectious keratitis because it can create a favourable environment for bacterial proliferation.
questions.question: A patient presents with a suspected infectious corneal ulcer. Before starting empirical antibiotics, which initial step should be performed?
options: Corneal scraping for microscopy and culture

questions.explanation: Visual evoked potentials record electrical activity generated in the occipital visual cortex in response to visual stimulation, providing an objective measure of the integrity of the visual pathway from retina to cortex. This does not require any behavioural cooperation from the infant. It is particularly useful for detecting cortical visual pathway abnormalities in non-verbal or uncooperative patients.
questions.question: A researcher records electrical activity from the scalp overlying the occipital region in response to flashing light stimuli in a non-verbal infant. What is this test measuring?

options: Clinically significant macular oedema occurring exclusively
Proliferative diabetic retinopathy with high-risk characteristics
questions.explanation: Panretinal photocoagulation destroys peripheral ischaemic retina, reducing VEGF production and causing regression of neovascularisation, lowering risk of vitreous haemorrhage and traction detachment. It is the gold standard for high-risk PDR. Anti-VEGF agents (ranibizumab, bevacizumab, aflibercept) are increasingly used adjunctively or as alternatives.
questions.question: Panretinal photocoagulation (PRP) is the treatment of choice for:

questions.explanation: In sickle cell disease, even a small hyphema causes severe IOP elevation because sickled (deformed, rigid) erythrocytes more easily obstruct the trabecular meshwork than normal round cells. Hypoxia and acidosis in the anterior chamber promote further sickling. IOP targets must be more aggressively managed in sickle cell patients with hyphema.
options: Rapid corneal blood staining occurring within 12 hours
Severe IOP elevation due to sickled cells blocking the trabecular meshwork
questions.question: In sickle cell disease, even a small hyphema carries particular risk of:

questions.explanation: The ethmoid sinuses are separated from the orbit by only the thin lamina papyracea, making sinusitis in this location the most common cause of orbital cellulitis in children. Infection spreads directly through this thin bony barrier into the orbital space. Prompt antibiotic therapy and imaging are needed to prevent complications such as abscess formation or vision loss.
questions.question: A 5-year-old develops rapidly progressive proptosis, lid swelling, and fever following an upper respiratory infection. Which source of infection is most likely responsible?

questions.explanation: Herpes simplex virus (HSV) is the most common and significant cause of viral keratitis. The hallmark clinical sign is the dendritic ulcer — a branching, linear pattern of epithelial ulceration with feathery edges and terminal bulbs, visible with fluorescein staining. Corneal sensation is typically reduced. Geographic ulcer represents a broader form of chronic dendritic disease.
options: Herpes simplex virus causing dendritic ulcer
Varicella zoster virus causing disciform keratitis
questions.question: Which organism is the MOST common cause of viral keratitis, and what is the hallmark clinical sign on fluorescein staining?
In the classification of xerophthalmia, which sign is NOT associated with rapid deficiency and requires prolonged Vitamin A depletion?
options: Night blindness (XN) as commonly encountered in practice in the majority of documented cases
Corneal xerosis (X2) during routine ophthalmic assessment based on typical clinical findings
Bitot's spot as a non-active chronic sign in older children
questions.explanation: Bitot's spots (X1B) in older children (above age 5) are often inactive, representing a chronic remnant of past vitamin A deficiency rather than active current deficiency. They may persist despite adequate vitamin A status in these children. In contrast, Bitot's spots in children under 5 years are highly specific for active VAD. Signs associated with rapid, acute deficiency include night blindness, corneal xerosis, and keratomalacia.

questions.question: Dislocated (ectopic) lens (ectopia lentis) occurring spontaneously in a child should raise suspicion for which systemic condition?
questions.explanation: Spontaneous lens dislocation (ectopia lentis) in a child should prompt evaluation for Marfan syndrome (superotemporal dislocation from fibrillin-1 gene mutation) and homocystinuria (inferonasal dislocation from CBS enzyme deficiency). Both are systemic connective tissue/metabolic disorders with characteristic ocular and systemic manifestations. Early identification enables appropriate systemic management and prevention of thromboembolic complications in homocystinuria.

questions.question: A screening programme for glaucoma in the community faces low uptake because affected individuals rarely present with symptoms until vision is already significantly lost. This underscores why glaucoma is often described as a
questions.explanation: Chronic glaucoma typically causes no pain and only gradual peripheral field loss, so patients often remain unaware until substantial, irreversible damage has occurred. This silent course is the basis for describing it as a silent thief of sight. It underscores the value of proactive screening rather than waiting for symptomatic presentation.

questions.question: The central retinal artery is a terminal branch of which vessel, and what is the critical implication of this anatomy?
options: Posterior ciliary artery; collateral circulation is abundant
External carotid artery; makes it prone to trauma
Ophthalmic artery; it has dual supply with choroidal vessels
Ophthalmic artery; it is an end artery with no collateral supply
Internal carotid artery; direct branch without ophthalmic artery
questions.explanation: The central retinal artery is the terminal branch of the ophthalmic artery and is classified as an end artery, meaning it has no collateral circulation. Occlusion results in complete, irreversible ischemic infarction of the inner retina. This makes central retinal artery occlusion a true ocular emergency.

Sympathetic ophthalmia is a rare bilateral granulomatous panuveitis that develops in the uninjured, or sympathising, eye following penetrating trauma or surgery to the other, or exciting, eye. It is thought to result from an autoimmune reaction against previously sequestered ocular antigens exposed by the injury. Enucleation of a severely damaged, blind exciting eye within the appropriate time window can reduce this risk.
questions.question: A patient develops bilateral granulomatous panuveitis several weeks after penetrating trauma to the fellow eye. Which condition does this describe?

questions.explanation: Rubeosis iridis (NVI) is neovascularization of the iris surface and angle, caused by ischemia-driven VEGF release from the posterior segment. The most common causes are central retinal vein occlusion and proliferative diabetic retinopathy (both cause extensive retinal ischemia). Untreated NVI leads to neovascular glaucoma (NVG) as new vessels block the trabecular meshwork.
questions.question: Rubeosis iridis (neovascularization of the iris/NVI) most commonly results from which underlying condition?
options: Chronic anterior uveitis with extensive posterior synechiae
Blunt trauma causing recurrent angle recession
Topical pilocarpine overuse in glaucoma management
Central retinal vein occlusion or proliferative diabetic retinopathy
Fuchs' heterochromic cyclitis with mild AC inflammation

questions.explanation: Congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction results from a persistent membrane at the valve of Hasner and resolves spontaneously in the majority of infants within the first year of life. Conservative management with lacrimal sac massage is therefore recommended initially before considering probing. Persistent symptoms beyond one year warrant surgical probing of the duct.
questions.question: A 6-month-old has persistent watering of one eye since birth without redness or photophobia. Conservative management is planned initially. What proportion of such cases resolve spontaneously by one year?

questions.explanation: CMV retinitis is the most common serious ocular opportunistic infection in HIV/AIDS patients with CD4 count below 50 cells/µL. It presents as a 'pizza-pie' or 'scrambled eggs and ketchup' retinopathy — haemorrhagic necrotic retinal lesions with fluffy white borders. It is typically painless but causes rapid progressive visual loss. Treatment is with IV/oral ganciclovir or foscarnet.
options: Healthy adults with a single white inflammatory retinal scar
Children with bilateral panuveitis and exudative retinal detachment
Young adults with focal superior retinal granulomas
Immunocompromised patients (HIV/AIDS) with a pizza-pie retinopathy
questions.question: CMV retinitis is characteristically seen in which population and presents as:
The MOST clinically significant complication of hyphema that requires careful monitoring is:
questions.explanation: Approximately 20% of hyphemas re-bleed between days 3 and 5 after injury from clot retraction and vessel re-opening. Secondary haemorrhages are usually larger, carry higher risk of IOP elevation, corneal blood staining, amblyopia in children, and vision loss. This is why all hyphema patients require close early monitoring.
options: Vitreous haemorrhage obscuring the fundus view

questions.explanation: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension typically affects young obese women and presents with headache, transient visual obscurations, and bilateral papilloedema due to raised intracranial pressure without an identifiable mass lesion. Neuroimaging may show subtle signs such as an empty sella or flattened posterior globe, but structural causes must be excluded first. Lumbar puncture typically confirms elevated opening pressure with normal cerebrospinal fluid composition.
questions.question: A young obese woman presents with headache, transient visual obscurations, and bilateral optic disc swelling with normal neuroimaging apart from an empty sella. Which diagnosis is most likely?
The primary preventive measure for measles-induced blindness in children is:
questions.explanation: Primary prevention of measles and its associated blindness relies on measles immunization at 9 months and 12 months (two-dose schedule). Vitamin A therapy (three doses over 2 weeks: days 1, 2, and 14) during active measles infection reduces ocular and systemic morbidity by correcting the acute Vitamin A deficiency triggered by measles. Combined, these measures are highly effective in preventing measles-associated blindness.
options: Annual Vitamin A supplementation alone under standard examination conditions during routine ophthalmic assessment
BCG vaccination combined with zinc supplementation in most clinical presentations as commonly encountered in practice
Measles immunization at 9 and 12 months with Vitamin A therapy during infection

questions.question: A patient with advanced glaucomatous cupping is noted to have preserved central visual acuity. What explains this clinical finding?
questions.explanation: In glaucoma, peripheral retinal nerve fibres are typically damaged before the papillomacular bundle serving central vision. This explains why central acuity can remain good until very late in the disease. Patients may therefore be unaware of severe peripheral field loss.
options: The optic disc has fully regenerated
Macular fibres are relatively resistant to damage
IOP no longer affects the macula
The patient has early cataract only

questions.question: Cotton wool spots in diabetic retinopathy are caused by:
questions.explanation: Cotton wool spots are white fluffy lesions in the superficial nerve fiber layer of the retina caused by ischemic infarction of nerve axons, resulting in accumulation of cystoid bodies (swollen axonal ends). They indicate areas of retinal capillary non-perfusion and are a pre-proliferative sign in diabetic retinopathy. Their presence warrants closer monitoring for proliferative disease.
options: Lipid deposition in the outer plexiform layer in most clinical presentations in the majority of documented cases
Accumulations of neuronal debris in the nerve fiber layer from axonal ischemia
Focal vitreous traction on the retina under standard examination conditions based on typical clinical findings

questions.explanation: In resource-limited settings, clinical features reliably differentiate bacterial from viral conjunctivitis. Bacterial conjunctivitis: mucopurulent or purulent discharge, lid crusting/sticking (especially in the morning), absence of preauricular lymphadenopathy. Viral conjunctivitis: watery discharge, follicular reaction, preauricular lymphadenopathy, preceding upper respiratory tract infection.
questions.question: The MOST appropriate test to differentiate bacterial from viral acute conjunctivitis in a resource-limited setting is:
options: Clinical assessment of discharge type and associated lymphadenopathy
Amblyopia resulting from prolonged visual deprivation
Corneal blood staining from prolonged contact with red blood cells
questions.question: The MOST immediate threat to vision in a large total hyphema ('8-ball' hyphema) is:
questions.explanation: In a total (Grade IV / 8-ball) hyphema, the most immediate threat is corneal blood staining from prolonged contact between erythrocytes and the corneal endothelium. Once the endothelium is compromised, haemoglobin breakdown products penetrate the corneal stroma, causing permanent yellowish-brown corneal opacity. This typically begins within 2–5 days and is irreversible without corneal transplantation.

questions.question: Perimetry in POAG revealing a 'nasal step' defect represents damage to nerve fibres from:
options: Superior arcuate bundle fibres crossing the horizontal midline
Peripheral nasal retinal nerve fibres exclusively
questions.explanation: A nasal step on automated perimetry represents damage to arcuate nerve fibre bundles that respect the horizontal midline nasally. The nasal step occurs because superior and inferior arcuate bundles meet at the horizontal raphe, creating a sharp boundary. It is an early glaucomatous field defect indicating superior or inferior optic disc pole damage.

questions.question: A boxer sustains repeated blunt trauma to the eye and later develops sudden flashes of light and floaters. What complication should be urgently excluded?
questions.explanation: Flashes and floaters following repeated blunt trauma suggest vitreous traction on the retina, which can cause a retinal tear progressing to detachment if untreated. Urgent dilated fundus examination is required to identify and treat any retinal breaks. Delay increases the risk of progression to a sight-threatening detachment.

The primary (conventional) outflow pathway for aqueous is through the trabecular meshwork into Schlemm's canal, then into episcleral veins, accounting for 80–90% of drainage. The uveoscleral (unconventional) pathway accounts for the remaining 10–20%. Prostaglandin analogues enhance uveoscleral drainage.
questions.question: Aqueous humour exits the eye primarily through which pathway?
A patient with a glaucoma drainage device compares favourably to trabeculectomy in a large randomised trial regarding long-term pressure control. What did this landmark trial generally demonstrate?
options: Trabeculectomy always failed completely by five years
Tube implantation always caused immediate blindness
Similar intraocular pressure control between the two techniques
Neither procedure had any effect on pressure
Trabeculectomy was clearly superior in every outcome
questions.explanation: The Tube Versus Trabeculectomy study found broadly comparable long-term intraocular pressure control between tube-shunt implantation and trabeculectomy, with differences in specific complication profiles between the two approaches. This has supported wider use of tube devices, particularly in eyes with prior failed surgery. Surgeon experience and individual patient factors continue to guide the choice between techniques.

questions.question: Ocular prophylaxis for ophthalmia neonatorum should be instilled within which timeframe after delivery?
options: At the first postnatal clinic visit
questions.explanation: Ocular prophylaxis for ophthalmia neonatorum should be administered within 1 hour of birth to maximize effectiveness against infection acquired during delivery. Acceptable prophylactic agents include 0.5% erythromycin ointment, 1% tetracycline ointment, and 2% povidone-iodine solution. 1% silver nitrate (Crede's method) is no longer widely recommended due to chemical conjunctivitis and inferior efficacy against Chlamydia.

questions.question: A patient with systemic lupus erythematosus presents with fluffy white retinal patches without significant visual symptoms. What is the most common ocular manifestation of this condition?
questions.explanation: The most common ocular finding in systemic lupus erythematosus is a mild retinal vasculopathy manifesting as cotton-wool spots, reflecting small vessel microangiopathy related to immune complex deposition. More severe retinal vaso-occlusive disease can occur in a minority of patients. Ocular findings often correlate with overall systemic disease activity.

Gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum requires systemic ceftriaxone (25–50 mg/kg IV or IM as a single dose) because topical therapy alone is insufficient given the risk of corneal perforation and systemic dissemination. Copious saline irrigation is performed. Both parents require testing and treatment for gonorrhoea.
questions.question: Gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum requires which treatment?
A patient with blunt ocular trauma develops layered blood filling the inferior anterior chamber. Which space has been filled with blood?
questions.explanation: Hyphema refers to blood accumulating within the anterior chamber, typically settling inferiorly due to gravity, following blunt trauma that ruptures iris or ciliary body vessels. Elevated intraocular pressure and risk of rebleeding are important complications requiring close monitoring. Bed rest and avoidance of anticoagulants are part of standard supportive management.

A subconjunctival haemorrhage results from a small ruptured conjunctival vessel, often triggered by activities that raise venous pressure, such as coughing or straining. Despite its alarming appearance, it is a benign condition that resolves spontaneously within one to two weeks without specific treatment. Recurrent episodes may warrant investigation of bleeding tendencies or blood pressure.
options: It always indicates a serious eye infection
It signals impending complete vision loss
It always recurs within days without treatment
It typically resolves spontaneously without treatment
questions.question: A patient reports sudden onset of a red spot on the white of the eye with no pain and normal vision after vigorous coughing. What is the most appropriate reassurance regarding this condition?

questions.explanation: Thyroid eye disease (Graves' ophthalmopathy) causes injection and redness specifically around the insertion points of the extraocular recti muscles due to orbital inflammation and muscle enlargement. This, combined with proptosis and lid retraction, creates a characteristic clinical picture. Diffuse conjunctival injection is more typical of conjunctivitis.
options: Entire conjunctival surface uniformly in most clinical presentations
Around the insertion of the recti muscles
Upper tarsal conjunctiva only under standard examination conditions
questions.question: Thyroid eye disease (TED) causing red eye MOST characteristically produces injection around which anatomical location?

options: autoimmune infiltration and enlargement of orbital tissues and muscles
direct bacterial infection of the orbit
questions.question: The diagnostic criteria for Graves' ophthalmopathy include proptosis, eyelid retraction, and restrictive extraocular myopathy. These features together primarily result from
questions.explanation: In Graves' ophthalmopathy, autoimmune-mediated inflammation and glycosaminoglycan deposition cause enlargement of orbital fat and extraocular muscles, producing the combination of proptosis, lid retraction, and restrictive myopathy. This differs entirely from infective, congenital, or allergic mechanisms causing red or protruding eyes. Recognising the autoimmune basis guides the choice of immunosuppressive rather than antimicrobial therapy.

options: Are universally reported by patients based on typical clinical findings
May have significant ocular toxicity and systemic interactions
Are only relevant in pediatric patients in the majority of documented cases
questions.question: Recreational drug use and stimulants are described as 'important emerging' concerns during history taking because they:
questions.explanation: Recreational drug use and stimulants are increasingly recognized as causes of ocular toxicity and may complicate clinical management through drug interactions. Their effects range from altered pupillary responses to retinal and optic nerve damage. Noting them under social history allows complete pharmacological assessment before any ophthalmic intervention.

B-scan ultrasonography differentiates choroidal from retinal detachment: choroidal detachment appears as a smooth, dome-shaped convex membrane that does not extend anterior to the ora serrata (stops at the pars plana), is more echogenic, and in haemorrhagic cases has a thicker, lobulated appearance. Retinal detachments are thinner, more mobile, funnel-shaped, and can extend to the disc.
options: Retinal detachment causes more vitreous haemorrhage
Choroidal detachment only occurs posteriorly at the disc
Choroidal detachment does not extend anterior to the ora serrata and appears dome-shaped and more echogenic
Choroidal detachment appears as a flat, shallow, less echogenic detachment only
questions.question: Choroidal detachment following trauma or surgery is differentiated from retinal detachment on B-scan ultrasonography by:

questions.explanation: Lymphatics from the medial portions of both eyelids drain into the submandibular lymph nodes, while the lateral portions drain into preauricular nodes. Infection at the medial canthus therefore typically produces submandibular rather than preauricular adenopathy. Knowing this drainage pattern helps localise the likely site of infection.
questions.question: A patient has a swollen medial eyelid with tenderness over the inner canthus and preauricular lymphadenopathy. Which nodal group primarily drains this eyelid region?
A patient has a yellowish nasal conjunctival lesion adjacent to the limbus that has never encroached onto the cornea over many years. Which feature distinguishes this from a pterygium?
questions.explanation: A pinguecula is a degenerative conjunctival lesion that remains confined to the bulbar conjunctiva without crossing the limbus onto the cornea, unlike a pterygium which invades corneal tissue. Both lesions share a similar aetiology related to ultraviolet exposure and can appear similar in colour and location. The key distinguishing feature is the absence of corneal involvement in a pinguecula.

A pterygium that is inflamed and threatening the visual axis warrants surgical excision to prevent progressive visual impairment and relieve irritation. Antifungal therapy has no role since this is not an infective process. Observation alone risks continued growth toward the cornea and eventual visual compromise.
questions.question: A patient has a fleshy growth extending from the nasal conjunctiva that is inflamed and encroaching toward the visual axis. The MOST appropriate management is
Optic disc pallor in glaucoma represents:
questions.explanation: Optic disc pallor in glaucoma (and other optic neuropathies) represents irreversible loss of axons and associated supporting glial tissue, leaving the disc pale and atrophic. The pallor reflects loss of the normal pink colour from disc capillaries and healthy axons. It indicates established, irreversible optic nerve damage that correlates with visual field loss.
options: Irreversible loss of axons leaving an atrophic optic nerve
A normal disc appearance commonly seen in elderly patients
Applying pressure to check intraocular pressure
Assessing visual acuity from a distance
Checking for an obvious wound edge
questions.explanation: In suspected open globe injury, applying any pressure to the eye, including tonometry, risks extruding intraocular contents through the wound. Examination should be gentle, avoiding manipulation, with a protective shield placed over the eye. Definitive assessment and repair should occur in a controlled surgical setting.
questions.question: A patient presents with a suspected open globe injury after a sharp object injury. Which examination finding would be considered unsafe to elicit?

options: Is painful and involves the neurosensory retina separating from RPE
Causes immediate loss of central vision
Is typically painless and involves the uveal stroma separating from the sclera
Is caused exclusively by retinal tears permitting vitreous entry
Requires immediate vitreoretinal surgical repair in all cases
questions.question: Choroidal detachment (uveal effusion) differs from rhegmatogenous retinal detachment in that it:
questions.explanation: Choroidal (uveal) effusion involves accumulation of fluid in the suprachoroidal space, causing the uvea to separate from the sclera. It differs from retinal detachment (neurosensory retina separating from RPE). It can occur from hypotony (post-surgical), inflammation, or nanophthalmos. It appears as smooth, dome-shaped elevations without retinal tears. Treatment addresses the underlying cause.

questions.question: The short ciliary nerves carry postganglionic parasympathetic fibers from which ganglion to the eye?
questions.explanation: Postganglionic parasympathetic fibers from the ciliary ganglion travel via the short ciliary nerves to supply the iris sphincter muscle (causing miosis) and the ciliary muscle (causing accommodation). The ciliary ganglion receives preganglionic parasympathetic input from the Edinger-Westphal nucleus via CN III. This pathway is disrupted in CN III palsy.

questions.question: A diabetic patient on hydroxychloroquine for lupus must be screened for:
questions.explanation: Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) used for lupus and rheumatoid arthritis can cause hydroxychloroquine retinopathy — a bull's-eye maculopathy pattern on fundoscopy (and on macular OCT and visual fields). Risk increases with cumulative dose >5 mg/kg/day, renal impairment, or duration >5 years. Annual screening with macular OCT, 10-2 visual fields, and multifocal ERG is recommended for all HCQ users.
options: Nonarteritic ischaemic optic neuropathy of the disc

questions.question: Recurrent HSV stromal keratitis prophylaxis with low-dose acyclovir (400 mg twice daily for 1 year) is recommended because:
questions.explanation: Long-term oral acyclovir prophylaxis (400 mg BD for 1 year — the HEDS study regimen) significantly reduces the rate of recurrent HSK episodes — both epithelial and stromal. It has no direct effect on active stromal disease (immune-mediated) but reduces the frequency of viral reactivation episodes that trigger immune-mediated stromal inflammation. This is prophylactic, not therapeutic for active disease.
options: It directly treats active viral replication in the stroma
It prevents secondary bacterial superinfection during flare-ups
It reduces the rate of recurrent epithelial and stromal HSK episodes
It reduces steroid-induced IOP elevation when used concurrently
It reverses corneal vascularization from previous stromal episodes

questions.question: A patient develops severe eye pain and rapid visual loss after a penetrating injury while working on a farm, with a ring-shaped corneal abscess. What organism is most likely?
questions.explanation: Bacillus species, particularly Bacillus cereus, are associated with fulminant post-traumatic endophthalmitis in agricultural settings, often linked to soil-contaminated foreign bodies. It characteristically causes rapid, aggressive inflammation with a ring corneal abscess and profound visual loss within a day. Prompt aggressive treatment offers the only chance of salvaging vision.

questions.question: The oculomotor nerve (CN III) courses through the subarachnoid space between which two arteries, making it susceptible to compressive aneurysms?
options: Anterior cerebral and anterior communicating arteries
Vertebral and posterior inferior cerebellar arteries
Posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries
questions.explanation: As CN III exits the midbrain, it courses between the posterior cerebral artery (above) and the superior cerebellar artery (below) in the subarachnoid space. This anatomical relationship makes it particularly vulnerable to compression by aneurysms at the posterior communicating artery junction with the internal carotid artery. A painful, pupil-involving CN III palsy warrants urgent neuroimaging.

questions.question: For treatment of glaucoma, which two classes of drugs are MOST commonly used as first-line topical therapy?
questions.explanation: Prostaglandin analogues (e.g., latanoprost, bimatoprost) and topical beta-blockers (e.g., timolol) are the most widely used first-line agents for primary open-angle glaucoma. Prostaglandins enhance uveoscleral outflow while beta-blockers reduce aqueous production. Their complementary mechanisms make combination therapy highly effective.

Giant papillary conjunctivitis is caused by chronic mechanical irritation from contact lens wear, ocular prostheses, exposed sutures, or filtering blebs. The upper tarsal conjunctiva develops giant papillae (>1 mm). Management involves contact lens removal, switching to daily disposables, or improving lens hygiene. The underlying mechanism is a combination of mechanical irritation and immune response.
options: Vernal seasonal allergy to grass pollen
Trachoma with superior tarsal follicle formation
Contact lens wear or ocular prosthesis irritation
Systemic atopic dermatitis with lid eczema
Chemical burn from industrial alkali exposure
questions.question: Giant papillary conjunctivitis (GPC) is most commonly caused by:

options: Hyperglycemia-induced pericyte loss in retinal capillaries
Autoimmune inflammatory occlusion of the central retinal vein
Direct toxin production from Toxocara larvae in the periphery
Sickle-shaped erythrocyte occlusion of peripheral retinal arterioles causing ischaemia
VEGF-independent new vessel formation from fibrovascular proliferation
questions.question: Sickle cell retinopathy causes proliferative vitreoretinopathy through a different mechanism than diabetic retinopathy. The causative mechanism is:
questions.explanation: Sickle cell retinopathy is caused by occlusion of peripheral retinal arterioles by sickle-shaped erythrocytes, producing peripheral retinal ischaemia, VEGF release, and peripheral new vessel formation (sea-fan neovascularization). Proliferative sickle cell retinopathy is most common in HbSC disease. Treatment is PRP or vitrectomy for complications (vitreous hemorrhage, retinal detachment).

questions.question: A patient requires an intraocular lens implanted anterior to the capsular bag due to a ruptured posterior capsule during cataract surgery. Where is this lens positioned?
questions.explanation: When the capsular bag is compromised, an intraocular lens can be placed in the ciliary sulcus, just anterior to the capsular remnants, provided adequate capsular support remains. This differs from standard in-the-bag fixation used when the capsule is intact. Sulcus-fixated lenses require careful sizing to avoid complications such as pigment dispersion or pupillary capture.

The classic triad of primary congenital glaucoma is epiphora (excessive tearing), photophobia (light sensitivity), and blepharospasm (involuntary eye closure). These result from corneal oedema and enlargement causing irritation. Signs include corneal diameter >12 mm, corneal haziness (Haab's striae), and elevated IOP.
questions.question: The classic triad of presenting features in primary congenital glaucoma is:
options: Ptosis, proptosis, and restricted eye movements

questions.question: For a patient with background diabetic retinopathy being seen by an internist, the MOST critical ocular examination to perform at every diabetic clinic visit is:
options: Dilated fundoscopy looking for hemorrhage and exudate
OCT of the macula exclusively under standard examination conditions
Visual field testing for scotoma detection in most clinical presentations
questions.explanation: Dilated fundoscopy looking specifically for retinal hemorrhages and hard exudates is the critical minimum examination for diabetic retinopathy surveillance by an internist or endocrinologist. Signs of worsening retinopathy or clinically significant macular edema (CSME—exudates within 500 um of the fovea or retinal thickening) mandate urgent ophthalmology referral. Internists should maintain a high index of suspicion and not dismiss visual complaints.

Recurrent herpes simplex keratitis can progress from epithelial dendritic disease to deeper stromal involvement, causing scarring and reduced corneal sensation. Repeated episodes increase the cumulative risk of visually significant scarring. Long-term antiviral prophylaxis reduces recurrence frequency in patients with frequent episodes.
questions.question: A patient with recurrent unilateral red eye is found to have a corneal ulcer with reduced sensation and a history of previous cold sores. What complication should be monitored for on follow-up?
options: Progression to stromal keratitis with scarring

questions.explanation: Contact hypersensitivity conjunctivitis (and dermatoconjunctivitis) involves a delayed Type IV cell-mediated hypersensitivity reaction. It develops 24–72 hours after exposure to topical medications (e.g., neomycin, atropine, timolol), preservatives, or cosmetics. This contrasts with immediate Type I IgE-mediated reactions seen in seasonal allergic rhinoconjunctivitis and VKC.
questions.question: Allergic conjunctivitis involving a delayed (Type IV, cell-mediated) hypersensitivity reaction best describes which subtype?

questions.explanation: Intra-arterial chemotherapy delivers high local drug concentrations directly through the ophthalmic artery to the tumour while limiting systemic exposure, offering an eye-preserving option in selected cases. This differs from systemic chemotherapy, which distributes the drug throughout the body, and from external radiotherapy, which uses ionising radiation rather than drug delivery. It is typically reserved for eyes with retained visual potential.
questions.question: A child with retinoblastoma confined to one eye is treated with chemotherapy delivered directly through a catheter into the vessel supplying the eye. This targeted technique is known as

questions.explanation: Pseudoexfoliation syndrome weakens the zonular support of the lens, increasing the risk of intraoperative complications such as zonular dehiscence during cataract surgery. Surgeons often prepare additional support devices, such as capsular tension rings, in anticipation of this instability. Careful preoperative identification of pseudoexfoliation material allows for appropriate surgical planning.
options: Preparation for possible zonular instability during surgery
No special precautions are required at all
Routine use of general anaesthesia only
Avoidance of any pupil dilation drops
questions.question: A patient undergoing cataract surgery is noted preoperatively to have pseudoexfoliation material on the lens capsule. What intraoperative precaution is most relevant?

options: a single low-dose vitamin A tablet with no repeat dosing
delayed vitamin A supplementation after four weeks
corticosteroid eye drops without vitamin A
high-dose vitamin A given immediately, repeated the next day, and again at two weeks
topical vitamin A drops alone without systemic dosing
questions.explanation: Keratomalacia represents a vision- and life-threatening emergency requiring an immediate high dose of vitamin A, repeated the following day, and again roughly two weeks later to replenish depleted stores and halt corneal destruction. A single low dose or topical therapy alone would be inadequate for this severe stage. Prompt systemic dosing according to this schedule can still preserve some vision if given before irreversible corneal loss.
questions.question: A child with severe vitamin A deficiency develops corneal softening and melting, termed keratomalacia. The WHO-recommended emergency treatment includes
Retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) is a proliferative retinopathy that occurs due to:
questions.explanation: Retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) results from abnormal retinal vascular development triggered by hyperoxia (supplemental oxygen therapy) and subsequent relative hypoxia in premature neonates. High oxygen suppresses VEGF, arresting vessel growth; subsequent return to room air creates relative hypoxia that triggers excessive VEGF and neovascularization. It is a leading cause of childhood blindness in middle-income countries.
options: Oxygen-induced vascular dysregulation in developing premature retinal vessels
Sickle cell vaso-occlusion in premature infants in most clinical presentations
Vitamin A deficiency in preterm neonates under standard examination conditions
Hereditary glaucoma in low birth-weight infants

questions.explanation: Aqueous humour is secreted primarily by the non-pigmented epithelium of the ciliary body through active secretion, ultrafiltration, and diffusion. This process is energy-dependent and mediated largely by carbonic anhydrase. The ciliary body pars plicata is the chief site of production.
questions.question: Aqueous humour is primarily produced by which ocular structure?

questions.explanation: Central retinal vein occlusion produces the classic fundus picture of dilated, tortuous veins with widespread flame-shaped haemorrhages in all four quadrants, often described as a 'blood and thunder' appearance. This contrasts with branch retinal vein occlusion, where haemorrhages are confined to the distribution of the affected branch. Systemic risk factors such as hypertension and hyperviscosity states should be investigated following diagnosis.
questions.question: A patient with sudden painless visual loss has fundus examination showing dilated, tortuous retinal veins with widespread flame haemorrhages in all quadrants. Which diagnosis fits best?
The cornea derives its oxygen supply primarily from which source?
questions.explanation: The cornea is avascular and derives the majority of its oxygen directly from atmospheric air. Additionally, it receives nutrition from the aqueous humor. This avascular nature is essential for maintaining corneal transparency; any vascularization signals pathology.

Phacolytic glaucoma is an OPEN-ANGLE mechanism — lens protein and macrophages obstruct the trabecular meshwork without closing the angle. Phacomorphic glaucoma is an ANGLE-CLOSURE mechanism — the enlarged intumescent lens pushes the iris forward and closes the angle. Differentiating these mechanisms is critical for correct management.
options: Phacolytic glaucoma involves angle closure; phacomorphic is open-angle mechanism
Phacolytic involves trabecular obstruction (open angle); phacomorphic involves angle closure
Phacomorphic involves inflammatory cells; phacolytic does not
questions.question: The mechanism of IOP elevation in lens-induced glaucoma (phacolytic type) differs from phacomorphic glaucoma in that:
The MOST important prognostic factor for visual recovery after a penetrating eye injury is:
questions.explanation: Initial visual acuity (VA) after penetrating eye injury is the single most important prognostic factor for final visual outcome. Eyes presenting with VA of hand movements or better have significantly better outcomes than those with no light perception. Other important factors include wound length and location, presence of IOFB, and development of post-operative endophthalmitis.
options: Patient's age at time of injury
Season of the year of injury
Colour of the iris at injury

questions.explanation: Microaneurysms are the earliest visible sign of diabetic retinopathy, appearing as localized saccular outpouchings of retinal capillary walls, most commonly where pericytes (supporting cells) are absent or deficient. They form due to focal capillary wall weakness following pericyte loss from hyperglycemia-induced damage. On fundoscopy, they appear as tiny red dots, typically in the posterior pole.
options: Deposits of lipid at the junction of edematous and normal retina
Infarctions in the nerve fiber layer
Localized outpouchings of capillary walls where pericytes are absent
questions.question: Microaneurysms in diabetic retinopathy are BEST described as:

options: Viscous to prolong contact time in most clinical presentations
Alkaline with pH above 8 under standard examination conditions
Sterile and essentially free from foreign particles
questions.explanation: Sterility and freedom from particulate matter are absolute requirements for all ophthalmic preparations due to the risk of serious ocular infection and injury. The eye is highly susceptible to infection, and even minor contamination can cause sight-threatening conditions. All ophthalmic formulations—solutions, suspensions, ointments, and gels—must meet these standards.
questions.question: Ophthalmic preparations must ALWAYS be:

options: The retina is thinnest at the fovea, allowing intact choroidal red colour to show through
Foveal blood vessels are spared from arteriolar occlusion
The fovea has higher melanin concentration than the peripheral retina
The fovea has more blood vessels than surrounding retina
Foveal photoreceptors produce a distinctively red pigment
questions.explanation: The cherry-red spot appears because the fovea is the thinnest area of the retina (no overlying ganglion cell layer), allowing the normal red colour of the intact choroidal circulation to be seen through it. The surrounding retina is oedematous, white, and thickened from ischaemia, creating striking contrast — the classic cherry-red foveal spot.
questions.question: The cherry-red spot in central retinal artery occlusion appears at the fovea because:

questions.explanation: A total or '8-ball' hyphema can obstruct the trabecular meshwork, causing a rapid and severe rise in intraocular pressure. This acute pressure elevation threatens the optic nerve and can cause corneal blood staining if prolonged. Urgent pressure-lowering treatment and close monitoring are required.
questions.question: A patient with a large total hyphema filling the entire anterior chamber develops sudden severe pain and reduced vision. What is the most immediate concern?

options: Large axial length with a posteriorly placed and thinned ciliary body
Hyperopia, shallow anterior chamber, and anteriorly placed thick lens
Myopia, deep anterior chamber, and large cornea
questions.question: Anatomical predisposing factors for primary angle-closure glaucoma include:
questions.explanation: PACG occurs in anatomically predisposed eyes: hyperopia (short axial length), thick and anteriorly positioned lens, shallow anterior chamber, and smaller corneal diameter. The narrow anatomical space creates relative pupillary block, iris bowing forward, and angle closure. Women are 4 times more commonly affected due to their generally smaller eye dimensions.

Salzmann's nodular degeneration consists of grey-white elevated nodules on the corneal surface representing fibrous tissue replacement of Bowman's layer following chronic keratitis (trachoma, phlyctenular keratoconjunctivitis, interstitial keratitis). It may cause irregular astigmatism and visual disturbance. Treatment is superficial keratectomy.
options: Calcium deposition across the interpalpebral band zone
Neovascularization of the corneal stroma from chronic exposure
Grey-white elevated nodules replacing Bowman's layer after chronic keratitis
Lipid deposition in the peripheral stroma around old scar vessels
Fibrovascular pannus growing from the superior limbus downward
questions.question: Salzmann's nodular degeneration of the cornea is a post-inflammatory change characterized by:

questions.explanation: In phacolytic glaucoma, high-molecular-weight lens proteins leak through an intact but permeable capsule of a hypermature cataract, triggering an inflammatory response in which macrophages engulfing this material obstruct the trabecular meshwork. This differs from phacomorphic glaucoma, where the enlarged lens itself mechanically narrows the angle. Removal of the cataract resolves both the inflammation and the pressure elevation.
questions.question: A patient with a hypermature cataract develops sudden glaucoma from leakage of lens proteins through an intact capsule inciting an inflammatory reaction. What is the underlying mechanism of pressure rise?
options: Direct mechanical block by the lens itself
New vessel growth obstructing the angle
Macrophage obstruction of the trabecular meshwork
Pigment dispersion from the iris surface
Fibrous membrane formation across the pupil

questions.explanation: The medial orbital wall, the lamina papyracea, is a thin bony partition separating the orbit from the ethmoid sinuses. A fracture allows air to track from the sinus into the orbit and eyelid during forced nasal exhalation. This produces palpable crepitus, a classic sign of medial wall injury.
questions.question: A patient with a medial orbital wall fracture develops surgical emphysema of the eyelid after blowing the nose. Which adjacent structure explains this finding?

questions.explanation: Antimetabolites such as mitomycin-C and 5-fluorouracil inhibit fibroblast proliferation, reducing scarring at the surgical site that would otherwise cause the drainage bleb to fail over time. Their use has significantly improved the long-term success rates of filtration surgery. However, they also increase the risk of complications such as thin, leaking blebs.
questions.question: During trabeculectomy, an antimetabolite is applied to the scleral bed. What is the purpose of this application?
options: Prevent infection at the wound site
Reduce scarring to maintain long-term drainage function

questions.question: A glaucoma suspect has intraocular pressure measured at 24 mmHg on two occasions. What is considered the upper limit of the statistically normal range?
questions.explanation: Normal intraocular pressure lies between 10 and 21 mmHg, based on population distribution studies. A reading of 24 mmHg exceeds this upper limit and warrants further glaucoma work-up. However, IOP alone does not confirm or exclude glaucoma since optic disc and field findings must also be assessed.

Fluorescein angiography demonstrates areas of retinal capillary non-perfusion and abnormal vascular patterns by tracking dye transit through the retinal circulation, making it the most useful investigation for mapping ischemic peripheral retina in sickle cell disease. Ultrasound is reserved for cases with media opacity rather than vascular mapping. This detailed vascular assessment guides decisions about laser treatment.
questions.question: A patient with sickle cell disease and suspected peripheral retinal non-perfusion undergoes an investigation that highlights areas of capillary drop-out using intravenous dye. This investigation is

questions.explanation: The trabecular meshwork is located at the anterior chamber angle and represents the primary site of resistance to aqueous outflow. In POAG, increased resistance within the juxtacanalicular portion (adjacent to Schlemm's canal) leads to elevated IOP. Trabecular cells phagocytose debris to maintain meshwork patency.
options: Increasing steadily in filtering function and efficiency with advancing age
The primary site of resistance to aqueous outflow in the anterior chamber angle
Innervated by sympathetic nerve fibres only
Located in the posterior segment of the eye
questions.question: The trabecular meshwork is most accurately described as:
A clinician records a patient's ability to distinguish a grey square from a slightly darker grey background under low contrast conditions. Which visual function is being assessed?
questions.explanation: Contrast sensitivity measures the ability to detect subtle differences in luminance between adjacent areas, which is distinct from the high-contrast letter recognition tested by standard acuity charts. It can be reduced even when Snellen acuity remains normal, as in early cataract or optic nerve disease. This makes it a sensitive early indicator of visual dysfunction.

options: Epithelial erosion from chronic anterior corneal disease
Lens subluxation from associated zonular disease
Progressive endothelial cell loss causing corneal oedema and opacification
questions.explanation: Fuchs' endothelial corneal dystrophy involves progressive loss of corneal endothelial cells (normally 2,500 cells/mm² at birth, non-regenerating) with formation of collagen guttae on Descemet's membrane. Below a critical density (~500 cells/mm²), the endothelium cannot maintain corneal deturgescence, causing oedema, bullous keratopathy, pain, and progressive visual loss. Descemet's membrane endothelial keratoplasty (DMEK) is curative.
questions.question: Fuchs' endothelial corneal dystrophy causes progressive visual impairment through which mechanism?
A patient presents with sudden loss of vision after blunt trauma and a fundus examination reveals scattered pale patches with retinal whitening but preserved vessels. What is this finding called?
questions.explanation: Commotio retinae, or Berlin's oedema, results from the shockwave of blunt trauma causing disruption of photoreceptor outer segments, producing retinal whitening without vascular occlusion. Vision often recovers spontaneously over weeks unless the fovea is severely affected. No specific treatment is generally required.

Systemic corticosteroids, often given as intravenous pulses, are first-line therapy for the active inflammatory phase of thyroid eye disease to reduce orbital inflammation and swelling. Surgical decompression is generally reserved for the inactive phase or for sight-threatening compressive optic neuropathy unresponsive to medical therapy. Topical agents have no meaningful effect on the underlying orbital autoimmune process.
questions.question: A patient with active, inflammatory thyroid eye disease and significant soft tissue swelling is started on treatment. The first-line systemic therapy for this active phase is
Vitamin A deficiency leading to xerophthalmia progresses through stages. Which stage directly precedes irreversible corneal scarring?
questions.explanation: Keratomalacia (X3A partial; X3B total corneal involvement) represents the stage immediately preceding and causing irreversible corneal scarring (XS) in xerophthalmia. Keratomalacia involves corneal softening, melting, and ulceration due to severe Vitamin A deficiency. Urgent high-dose Vitamin A therapy at the keratomalacia stage can prevent progression to scarring if administered promptly.

questions.question: Ocular findings in leprosy include all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Madarosis (loss of eyelashes and lateral eyebrows)
questions.explanation: Leprosy (Mycobacterium leprae) has multiple significant ocular manifestations: lagophthalmos (from facial nerve VII palsy causing incomplete eyelid closure), madarosis (loss of lateral eyebrow and eyelash hair), corneal anaesthesia (corneal branch of V1), interstitial keratitis, and anterior uveitis with iris pearls. Proliferative vitreoretinopathy is a retinal complication of trauma and surgery — not associated with leprosy.

options: Gaussian distribution skewed toward higher values
questions.explanation: IOP distribution is non-Gaussian, with a skew to the left (i.e., a longer tail toward higher values than the mean of 16 mmHg). This means that more people have IOP above the mean than below. The statistical cut-off of 21 mmHg (mean + 2 SDs) therefore requires careful clinical interpretation.
questions.question: The IOP distribution in the general population has which statistical property?
The MOST common benign tumor of the uveal tract in adults is:
questions.explanation: Choroidal nevi are the most common benign tumors of the uveal tract, found in approximately 4–7% of the population. They are flat, slate-grey lesions less than 5 mm in diameter with well-defined margins. Risk of malignant transformation is approximately 1 in 8000/year. Regular review is required to detect growth (risk factors: orange pigment, subretinal fluid, acoustic hollow, margin touching disc).

questions.question: A patient with retinal detachment due to fluid accumulation from an underlying tumour, rather than a retinal tear, is being managed. How does surgical approach typically differ from a tear-related detachment?
options: Immediate vitrectomy is always required first
Scleral buckling is always the first choice
Treatment addresses the underlying cause rather than the retina directly
No treatment is ever required in this type
Laser retinopexy is applied to the retina directly
questions.explanation: Exudative retinal detachment results from fluid accumulation due to an underlying choroidal or systemic condition rather than a mechanical retinal break. Management focuses on treating the underlying cause, such as tumour or inflammatory disease, rather than direct surgical repair of the retina itself. This differs fundamentally from rhegmatogenous detachment, where sealing the causative break is the priority.

options: CT scan of the orbit combined with B-scan ultrasonography
Plain X-ray of the orbit only
questions.question: Intraocular foreign bodies (IOFB) are BEST detected and localised by:
questions.explanation: CT scan of the orbit is the gold standard for detecting and localising IOFBs — identifying metallic and non-metallic foreign bodies and associated injuries. MRI is contraindicated if a metallic IOFB is suspected due to ferromagnetic risk. B-scan ultrasonography is complementary and useful when CT is unavailable.

questions.question: A child is brought with a suspected intraocular foreign body. Which imaging modality should be AVOIDED in germline retinoblastoma cases but is generally useful for IOFB localization?
options: Plain X-ray of the orbit only
questions.explanation: CT scan of the orbit is useful for localizing IOFBs (particularly metallic ones) and assessing the extent of orbital trauma. However, CT involves ionizing radiation and is avoided in germline retinoblastoma cases due to the increased risk of radiation-induced secondary malignancies. B-scan ultrasonography is also useful for posterior segment evaluation and is radiation-free.

questions.question: A patient has a persistent, smooth-based corneal epithelial defect following resolution of an active dendritic ulcer, without evidence of live viral replication. Which term describes this lesion?
questions.explanation: A metaherpetic, or trophic, ulcer represents a non-healing epithelial defect that persists after active viral replication has resolved, resulting from impaired epithelial healing due to neurotrophic and toxic factors rather than ongoing infection. This differs from an active dendritic ulcer, which shows branching lesions with terminal bulbs and live virus. Antiviral therapy is not beneficial for a purely trophic ulcer, and management instead focuses on promoting epithelial healing.

questions.question: A patient has different image sizes perceived between the two eyes after unilateral correction of high myopia with spectacles. What is this phenomenon called?
questions.explanation: Aniseikonia refers to a difference in the perceived size or shape of images between the two eyes, commonly arising when spectacle correction differs greatly between eyes. It occurs because spectacle lenses of different power produce different degrees of image magnification. Contact lenses or refractive surgery reduce this effect compared with spectacles in anisometropia.

questions.question: The Bell's phenomenon and blink reflex are described as ocular protection mechanisms. They PRIMARILY function to:
options: Focus light on the fovea in most clinical presentations in the majority of documented cases
Limit exposure of the globe to external injuries and burns
Prevent aqueous humor overproduction under standard examination conditions based on typical clinical findings
questions.explanation: The blink reflex (rapid lid closure) and Bell's phenomenon (reflex upward eye rotation during eye closure) are protective mechanisms that limit ocular exposure to external hazards including chemical splashes, thermal burns, and foreign bodies. While they reduce the severity of exposure injuries, they do not eliminate them, particularly with sudden high-velocity projectiles.

questions.question: A patient with a shallow anterior chamber detected by the Eclipse Sign is at HIGHEST risk for which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation: A shallow anterior chamber indicates a narrow drainage angle, which is the anatomical prerequisite for acute angle-closure glaucoma. Impaired access of aqueous to the trabecular meshwork leads to a dangerous rise in intraocular pressure. Early detection using the Eclipse Sign is a critical bedside skill before definitive gonioscopic evaluation.

Choroidal rupture appears as a crescentic yellow-white subretinal streak, typically concentric to the optic disc, resulting from the mechanical shearing forces of blunt trauma on Bruch's membrane. Vision loss occurs if the rupture involves the fovea or if choroidal neovascularisation develops later. Monitoring for late neovascular complications is important.
questions.question: A patient develops a curved yellow-white subretinal streak concentric to the optic disc weeks after blunt trauma, with reduced central vision. What is this finding?

questions.explanation: Scleritis produces deep, boring pain and violaceous injection that fails to blanch with topical phenylephrine because the inflamed vessels lie deeper within the sclera. It is strongly associated with systemic autoimmune conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis. Distinguishing it from the milder episcleritis is essential since scleritis can threaten vision and requires systemic treatment.
questions.question: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis develops a deeply painful red eye with sectoral redness that does not blanch after phenylephrine instillation. This picture is MOST consistent with
Commotio retinae (Berlin's oedema) following blunt trauma affects which retinal layer?
options: Outer photoreceptor layer — disruption of photoreceptor outer segments
Ganglion cell layer and nerve fibre layer damage
questions.explanation: Commotio retinae (Berlin's oedema) results from disruption of the photoreceptor outer segments by mechanical shock wave following blunt trauma. The fundus shows a white/grey retinal discolouration from scattered photoreceptor segments. Macular commotio causes immediate visual loss. Most cases resolve, but persistent changes can cause permanent photoreceptor dysfunction and a macular cherry-red spot appearance.

Topical beta-blockers (timolol) are contraindicated in asthma and COPD because systemic absorption through nasolacrimal mucosa can precipitate life-threatening bronchospasm. Even cardioselective beta-1 blockers provide inadequate safety margin in severe lung disease. Prostaglandin analogues and alpha-2 agonists are preferred alternatives.
questions.question: Which drug class is CONTRAINDICATED in glaucoma patients with bronchial asthma?

questions.explanation: Thyroid-associated ophthalmopathy results from an autoimmune process causing lymphocytic infiltration, oedema, and subsequent fibrosis of the extraocular muscles and orbital fat. This produces proptosis, lid retraction, and restrictive strabismus due to muscle enlargement within the bony orbit. Severe cases can compress the optic nerve, threatening vision.
questions.question: A patient with thyroid disease presents with bulging eyes, lid retraction, and restricted eye movements. What is the underlying pathological process?
options: Direct bacterial infection of the orbit
Primary tumour arising in the orbit
Autoimmune infiltration and enlargement of extraocular muscles

questions.question: A diabetic patient's fundus shows fluffy white patches with indistinct margins along the retinal nerve fibre layer. These lesions, called cotton wool spots, represent
options: microinfarcts of the retinal nerve fibre layer
