questions.explanation: Cotton wool spots are localised infarcts of the retinal nerve fibre layer caused by occlusion of precapillary arterioles, appearing as fluffy white patches with indistinct edges. They differ from hard exudates, which reflect lipid leakage rather than ischemia. Their presence indicates areas of retinal ischemia and disease progression.

KWB Grade IV hypertensive retinopathy adds papilloedema (optic disc oedema/swelling) to the Grade III features (haemorrhages, hard exudates, and cotton-wool spots). Grade IV represents malignant hypertension and is associated with hypertensive encephalopathy and a very poor short-term prognosis without urgent antihypertensive treatment.
questions.question: Keith-Wagener-Barker Grade IV hypertensive retinopathy is distinguished by the ADDITIONAL finding of:

options: Focus only on the more serious complaint based on typical clinical findings
Address both complaints together without order
Defer detailed history until after examination
Establish a timeline and order of progression for both complaints
Ask the patient to choose which to discuss first in the majority of documented cases
questions.explanation: When multiple presenting complaints exist, establishing a timeline and order of progression is essential to determine if they are related or independent processes. This structured approach helps determine causality, disease progression, and the most likely unifying diagnosis. It also guides the physical examination by prioritizing areas of concern.
questions.question: A patient presents with two simultaneous eye complaints. According to proper history-taking technique, the clinician should:

questions.explanation: A significant difference in refractive error between the two eyes prevents simultaneous clear focusing, and the brain suppresses the more blurred image over time. This chronic suppression during visual development produces anisometropic amblyopia even though the fundus and ocular structures appear normal. Early correction and occlusion therapy are needed to reverse the suppression if detected in time.
questions.question: A child with hypermetropia measuring +4.00 dioptres in one eye and +1.00 dioptre in the other, uncorrected since birth, later shows poor vision in the more hypermetropic eye despite a normal fundus. What is the primary underlying mechanism?

questions.explanation: Because the eye is a highly sensitive and easily infected surface, all ophthalmic preparations must be sterile, isotonic, and buffered to a tolerable pH to avoid irritation or infection. Colour and flavour are irrelevant to safety. This standard applies regardless of drug class or manufacturer.
options: sterile and formulated for ocular tolerability
questions.question: An eye clinic checks that every dispensed ophthalmic bottle is free of particulate matter, at an appropriate pH, and free from microbial contamination. These requirements exist because ophthalmic preparations must ALWAYS be

questions.explanation: Age is the strongest and most consistent risk factor for age-related cataract, with prevalence increasing dramatically after the fifth decade. Additional definite risk factors include diabetes, smoking, corticosteroid use, and prolonged sunlight exposure. Aspirin and antioxidants have been studied as potential protective factors rather than risk factors.
questions.question: The strongest and most consistent risk factor for the development of senile (age-related) cataract is:
Vernal keratoconjunctivitis (VKC) is MOST characteristic in which patient group?
questions.explanation: VKC predominantly affects young boys (prepubertal) in hot, dry climates (tropical Africa, Middle East) with an atopic background. It is seasonal (spring/summer) and presents with intense itching, giant papillae (cobblestones) on the upper tarsal conjunctiva, limbal follicles (Horner-Trantas dots), and shield corneal ulcers. Mast cell stabilisers and topical steroids are used.
options: Neonates exposed to infection during vaginal delivery
Young boys in hot, dry climates with an atopic background

questions.question: Phacolytic glaucoma is caused by:
questions.explanation: Phacolytic glaucoma is an open-angle glaucoma from a hypermature (Morgagnian) cataract. Liquefied lens protein leaks through a permeable capsule, activates macrophages, and these protein-laden macrophages obstruct the trabecular meshwork. The AC shows flare and cells without posterior synechiae. Cataract extraction is curative.
options: Trabecular obstruction by protein-laden macrophages from a hypermature cataract
Pigment dispersion from the posterior lens surface directly
Pupillary block by a dislocated lens
Angle closure from an intumescent lens

questions.explanation: WHO classification of blindness includes not only reduced central acuity but also severe visual field constriction, since a very narrow field severely limits functional vision even with preserved central acuity. A field of less than 10 degrees radius, or 5 degrees in some definitions, around fixation meets the criterion for blindness. This reflects the functional importance of peripheral vision for mobility and safety.
questions.question: A patient with severe peripheral field constriction to less than 5 degrees around fixation, despite retaining good central acuity, is classified under which WHO category?
Post-traumatic endophthalmitis, especially in agricultural settings, is MOST commonly caused by:
options: Bacillus cereus and Gram-positive organisms from soil or plant matter
questions.explanation: Post-traumatic endophthalmitis after open globe injuries in agricultural settings is commonly caused by Bacillus cereus and other Gram-positive soil organisms. Bacillus cereus causes particularly fulminant, rapidly devastating endophthalmitis. Prophylactic broad-spectrum antibiotics are given immediately after all open globe injuries.

Initial management of hyphema focuses on reducing rebleeding risk through rest with the head elevated to allow blood to settle inferiorly, along with a protective shield rather than a pressure patch. Aspirin and other agents that impair clotting are avoided because they increase rebleeding risk. Surgical washout is reserved for cases with uncontrolled pressure or corneal bloodstaining rather than used routinely at presentation.
questions.question: A patient with traumatic hyphema following blunt injury is admitted for observation. The MOST appropriate INITIAL management includes
options: immediate anterior chamber washout in every case
bed rest with head elevation and an eye shield
topical steroid drops without any monitoring
vigorous eye patching with firm pressure

questions.question: A patient with a suspected open globe injury is found to have a positive fluorescein streaming test. What does this finding confirm?
questions.explanation: The Seidel test uses fluorescein dye to detect aqueous humour leaking through a corneal or scleral wound, seen as a stream of dilution in the dye under blue light. A positive result confirms an open globe injury requiring urgent surgical repair. This simple bedside test is valuable in emergency assessment of trauma.
options: Presence of a corneal abrasion only
Active leakage of aqueous through a corneal wound

questions.question: A patient with a history of penetrating trauma years earlier develops chronically raised IOP in the same eye. Gonioscopy shows a torn, receded angle. What is this called?
questions.explanation: Blunt or penetrating trauma can tear the ciliary body face, widening and deepening the angle recess, a finding termed angle recession. Over subsequent years, this can lead to progressive trabecular meshwork dysfunction and secondary open-angle glaucoma. Lifelong monitoring of such eyes is essential even when initial pressures are normal.

questions.question: A patient requires a +2.50 dioptre reading addition to focus clearly at 33 centimetres despite having no distance refractive error. What does this addition substitute for?
questions.explanation: With age, the crystalline lens loses elasticity and the ciliary muscle becomes less efficient, reducing the eye's natural accommodative amplitude. A convex reading addition compensates for this lost accommodative power to allow clear near focus. This is the basis of presbyopic correction in reading glasses.

options: Ruptured globe with associated vitreous haemorrhage
Orbital floor fracture with inferior rectus entrapment
questions.explanation: The clinical triad of diplopia on upward gaze (restricted elevation), enophthalmos, and infraorbital nerve numbness (cheek/upper lip/teeth) following blunt trauma is classic for an orbital floor fracture with herniation or entrapment of the inferior rectus muscle into the maxillary sinus. CT scan confirms the fracture. Surgical repair is indicated for significant entrapment or cosmetic enophthalmos.
questions.question: A cyclist sustains blunt periorbital trauma and develops diplopia only on upward gaze with enophthalmos and numbness over the cheek. The MOST likely diagnosis is:

questions.explanation: Contrast sensitivity is the ability to perceive slight changes in luminance between regions that are not separated by definite borders. When impaired, it causes mild fogginess of vision even with preserved Snellen acuity. It is frequently affected in refractive errors, glaucoma, cataract, and optic nerve disease.
questions.question: Which visual function examines the ability to detect slight changes in luminance between regions without defined borders?
Band keratopathy complicating chronic uveitis is associated with which specific metabolic abnormality?
options: Elevated serum uric acid from gout
Elevated serum triglycerides causing corneal lipid deposition
Iron overload causing Kayser-Fleischer ring formation
Elevated serum calcium from sarcoidosis or hyperparathyroidism
questions.explanation: Band keratopathy is a complication of chronic uveitis (particularly juvenile idiopathic arthritis) and hypercalcemia (sarcoidosis, hyperparathyroidism, vitamin D excess). The calcium deposits form in Bowman's membrane. In the context of uveitis, local alkalinity from evaporation contributes. Treatment is chelation with EDTA after de-epithelialization.

The corneal stroma comprises approximately 90% of corneal thickness and is composed of regularly arranged collagen lamellae, keratocytes, and ground substance. The regular parallel arrangement of collagen fibers and relative dehydration are responsible for corneal transparency. Stromal swelling from endothelial pump failure causes opacification. Bowman's membrane is acellular and permanent when destroyed.
questions.question: The layer responsible for 90% of corneal thickness and strength, containing keratocytes and collagen, is the:

A hypertensive patient's fundus reveals disc swelling together with radiating yellow-white lipid deposits fanning out from the fovea. This macular star formation is a feature of which grade of hypertensive retinopathy?
questions.explanation: Grade IV hypertensive retinopathy is defined by the presence of optic disc swelling in addition to the vascular changes of earlier grades, and the associated macular star reflects lipid exudation along the radiating fibres of Henle's layer around the fovea. This grade indicates malignant hypertension requiring urgent blood pressure control. Recognising disc swelling as the defining feature distinguishes Grade IV from milder grades.

options: Cylindrical lens for one meridian only
questions.question: A myopic patient's second principal focus lies in front of the retina. The corrective lens of choice is:
questions.explanation: Myopia requires a concave (diverging) lens to diverge incoming parallel light rays so they converge further back, exactly on the retina. A convex lens would worsen myopia. Myopia occurs when the eyeball is too long or the dioptric power is too high. Patients can see near objects but not far clearly.

questions.question: The Catford drum overestimates visual acuity in infants. The TWO reasons for this overestimation are:
options: Short test distance and small target size
Moving target and short working distance
Large target size and reduced ambient illumination
Stationary target and long working distance
questions.explanation: The Catford drum overestimates visual acuity because: (1) the target is moving (oscillating), which requires less resolution than stationary targets, and (2) it is conducted at a short working distance (60 cm), which reduces the required spatial resolution. Despite this limitation, it provides useful behavioral information in infants.

questions.question: In the Eagling classification of ocular injuries, which grade involves a corneo-scleral laceration with lens damage?
questions.explanation: Eagling's classification grades ocular injuries as follows: Grade 1 involves a corneo-scleral laceration with uveal prolapse in the anterior segment; Grade 2 involves corneo-scleral laceration with lens damage; Grade 3 involves corneo-scleral laceration, lens damage, and vitreous loss; Grade 4 involves severe injury with extensive tissue damage. Correct grading is essential for guiding surgical repair decisions.

Roth spots are pale-centred retinal haemorrhages (white or pale centres within red haemorrhages) seen in bacterial endocarditis and other conditions. The white centre represents aggregates of fibrin, platelets, or inflammatory cells within the haemorrhage. Roth spots are not pathognomonic of endocarditis but indicate septic microemboli in the retinal vasculature.
options: New vessels on the disc margin
Yellow hard exudates in a circinate pattern
White fluffy lesions without any haemorrhage
Grey-green flame-shaped haemorrhages along vascular arcades
questions.question: The Roth spots seen on fundoscopy in bacterial endocarditis are characterised as:

options: Excellent function — best outcome with levator resection
Good function — standard levator resection is sufficient
Poor function — frontalis sling procedure required
Normal function; only aponeurotic repair is needed
questions.explanation: LPSA of 4 mm or less indicates poor levator function. When levator function is poor, a frontalis sling operation is required to connect the lid to the frontalis muscle. LPSA of 10 mm or more is excellent, allowing levator resection. LPSA 5–7 mm is fair (levator resection with caution), and 8 mm or more is good. Classifying levator function guides surgical planning.
questions.question: In ptosis classification, a Levator Palpebrae Superioris Action (LPSA) of less than 4 mm indicates:

questions.explanation: Rhabdomyosarcoma is the most common primary orbital malignancy of childhood, typically presenting between 8–10 years of age with sudden onset, rapid unilateral proptosis. It may also present with ptosis, strabismus, or a superonasal mass. Urgent biopsy is required; treatment is combined radiotherapy and chemotherapy with high cure rates.
questions.question: The MOST common primary orbital malignancy in childhood with sudden onset rapid proptosis is:
A patient with chronic granulomatous inflammation of the eye and skin lumps from an endemic region is diagnosed with ocular sarcoidosis. Which uveitis pattern is classic?
questions.explanation: Ocular sarcoidosis classically produces bilateral granulomatous anterior uveitis, characterised by large, greasy mutton-fat keratic precipitates on the corneal endothelium. Posterior segment involvement with vasculitis can also occur. Systemic evaluation for pulmonary and other organ involvement is important once ocular sarcoidosis is diagnosed.

An orbital floor (blowout) fracture from blunt trauma (e.g., tennis ball) typically causes: (1) diplopia from entrapment of the inferior rectus or inferior oblique, (2) reduced sensation in the upper teeth/gums due to infraorbital nerve injury, and (3) enophthalmos from increased orbital volume or fat herniation. Surgical repair is usually required.
options: Proptosis, restricted abduction, and corneal edema
Diplopia, reduced sensation upper teeth, and enophthalmos
questions.question: A blowout fracture of the orbit most commonly involves the floor. Which classic symptom triad results from entrapment of inferior rectus muscle?

questions.explanation: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada (VKH) syndrome is an autoimmune T-cell–mediated attack against melanocyte-containing tissues. The prodromal phase features meningism, headache, and tinnitus. The ocular phase causes bilateral granulomatous panuveitis with exudative retinal detachments. The convalescent phase produces depigmentation: vitiligo (skin), poliosis (white hair patches), and alopecia. High-dose systemic corticosteroids are mainstay treatment.
questions.question: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada (VKH) disease is characterised by bilateral panuveitis associated with:
options: Keratoconus and ectopia lentis with lens subluxation
Dermatological and neurological manifestations: alopecia, poliosis, vitiligo, tinnitus, meningism
RNFL dropout visible on OCT only
Partial lens subluxation creating a visible notch at the equator
Focal neuroretinal rim tissue loss creating a sharp notch in the disc margin
Indentation of the corneal surface by tonometry
Scoring of corneal epithelium using fluorescein
questions.question: 'Rim notching' in glaucomatous optic disc assessment refers to:
questions.explanation: Rim notching is a focal area of neuroretinal rim tissue loss creating a visible notch in the optic disc margin, most commonly at the inferior (6 o'clock) or superior (12 o'clock) pole. Notching corresponds to focal nerve fibre bundle loss and is associated with corresponding arcuate scotomas on perimetry.

options: Hemoglobin in the retinal vasculature radiating color to surrounding tissue in most clinical presentations in most clinical presentations
Reflection of light off the RPE and choroidal melanin and vasculature through the transparent retina
Luteal pigment in the macula coloring the entire retina
Oxidized rhodopsin producing a red fluorescence
Nerve fiber layer scattering of white light into red wavelengths under standard examination conditions under standard examination conditions
questions.explanation: The normal orange-red color of the fundus on ophthalmoscopy is produced by light reflecting off the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and the highly vascular choroid (containing abundant oxyhemoglobin) that shines through the transparent retina and RPE. Breaks in the RPE (e.g., in retinal detachment) appear pale/grey because the light scatters differently. The macula appears darker due to higher melanin and luteal pigment content.
questions.question: The normal retina appears 'red/orange' on fundoscopy because of:
Subhyaloid (preretinal) haemorrhage in the context of sudden raised intracranial pressure (e.g., subarachnoid haemorrhage) is called:
questions.explanation: Terson's syndrome is the occurrence of intraocular haemorrhage (subhyaloid/vitreous) associated with subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH) or other causes of sudden raised intracranial pressure. The mechanism involves sudden ICP rise transmitted to optic nerve sheath, rupturing peripapillary retinal vessels. It occurs in up to 13% of SAH cases and portends a worse prognosis.

options: Mantoux test and sputum culture for AFB
Serum angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) and chest X-ray
Serum lysozyme levels and gallium-67 scan alone
questions.explanation: Serum ACE (elevated in 60–90% of active sarcoidosis) combined with chest X-ray (bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy in stage I/II sarcoidosis) are the most useful initial investigations to confirm sarcoidosis in bilateral granulomatous uveitis. Gallium-67 scan shows lacrimal/salivary gland uptake. Tissue biopsy (lymph node, conjunctival granuloma, or Kveim test) provides definitive diagnosis.
questions.question: Which clinical investigation is MOST useful to confirm the diagnosis of sarcoidosis in a patient with bilateral granulomatous uveitis?

questions.explanation: Behcet's disease is characterised by recurrent oral and genital ulceration together with a severe, often bilateral, occlusive retinal vasculitis and hypopyon uveitis. The retinal vasculitis can cause branch vessel occlusion and secondary neovascularisation if untreated. Early aggressive immunosuppression is important to prevent irreversible visual loss in this condition.
questions.question: A patient with recurrent oral and genital ulcers develops a hypopyon uveitis with retinal vasculitis affecting both eyes. Which systemic condition is most likely?

questions.explanation: Prolonged corticosteroid use (systemic, topical ophthalmic, or inhaled) is the most important systemic cause of PSC in young patients. The mechanism involves direct steroid-induced metabolic disruption of lens epithelial cells at the posterior lens equator. PSC from steroids is dose- and duration-dependent. Patients on long-term steroids should undergo regular slit-lamp examination.
questions.question: The MOST important systemic association of posterior subcapsular cataract (PSC) in young patients is:
options: Hypertension causing anterior chamber angle compression
Prolonged systemic or topical corticosteroid use
Vitamin A deficiency causing lens dehydration
Hyperparathyroidism causing calcium deposition in the lens

questions.explanation: Toxoplasma gondii is the most common cause of posterior uveitis in immunocompetent individuals and characteristically produces a focal necrotising retinochoroiditis adjacent to a pre-existing pigmented scar from prior infection. The overlying vitritis produces a hazy appearance sometimes described as a headlight in fog. Recurrence often arises from reactivation at the edge of an old scar.
questions.question: An immunocompetent patient presents with a focal, white, fluffy retinochoroidal lesion adjacent to an old pigmented scar, causing vitritis. Which organism is the most likely cause?

questions.explanation: Chrysiasis refers to deposition of gold particles within the corneal stroma and other tissues following prolonged systemic gold therapy, producing a golden-brown discolouration. It is typically asymptomatic and does not impair vision, being an incidental finding on slit lamp examination. Discontinuation of gold therapy does not necessarily reverse the deposits, but they rarely cause functional problems.
questions.question: A patient on long-term gold salt therapy for rheumatoid arthritis develops golden-brown corneal deposits noted incidentally on slit lamp examination. What is this finding called?

questions.explanation: Grade I hyphema (blood filling less than one-third of the anterior chamber) is the most common presentation of traumatic hyphema. Grades II–IV represent increasing blood levels up to total (8-ball) hyphema. Secondary hemorrhage (rebleed) on days 3–5 is the most feared complication, often more severe than the primary bleed and can cause corneal staining and acute IOP rise.
questions.question: Hyphema (blood in the anterior chamber) following blunt trauma initially MOST commonly fills what proportion of the anterior chamber?
options: Less than one-third of the anterior chamber height
Exactly half the anterior chamber height
Three-quarters of the anterior chamber height
A micro-hyphema visible only with red cells in suspension

questions.question: A patient with sickle cell retinopathy shows a well-demarcated area of retinal pigment epithelial atrophy near the macula without any history of trauma. This non-proliferative feature is described as a
questions.explanation: The macular depression sign in sickle cell retinopathy reflects focal thinning from chronic microvascular occlusion affecting the perifoveal region, producing a subtle depression visible on careful examination. This differs from a macular star, which relates to hypertensive lipid exudation, and from a cherry-red spot associated with central retinal artery occlusion. Recognising it as a non-proliferative feature helps in staging disease severity.

questions.question: 'Pseudopapilloedema' differs from true papilloedema in that:
questions.explanation: Pseudopapilloedema (from optic disc drusen, small hypermetropic discs, or tilted discs) mimics true papilloedema but is NOT caused by elevated ICP. The disc appears elevated with irregular margins but without haemorrhages or exudates. Autofluorescence or B-scan ultrasound confirms buried drusen. Neuroimaging is required to exclude raised ICP in any case of apparent bilateral disc swelling.
options: It always causes visual field defects
It results from optic disc drusen or hypermetropia and has no associated ICP elevation
It is caused by chronically elevated intracranial pressure

questions.explanation: Physiological large cups are normal variants — the C/D ratio may be large (even up to 0.7–0.8), but the neuroretinal rim tissue is healthy and pink, IOP is normal, and there are no visual field defects. Distinguishing physiological from glaucomatous cupping requires assessment of rim tissue quality, IOP, corneal thickness, and perimetry.
questions.question: A physiological large optic cup differs from a glaucomatous cup in that:
options: It has healthy rim tissue, normal IOP, and no visual field defects
It always occurs in association with myopia
It typically has a larger C/D ratio than true glaucoma
It causes elevated IOP from birth
It is always bilateral and symmetrical

questions.question: Which local anaesthetic is used for topical anaesthesia in ophthalmic procedures?
questions.explanation: Tetracaine (amethocaine) hydrochloride eye drops are the standard topical ophthalmic local anaesthetic used for minor procedures such as foreign body removal, tonometry, and minor conjunctival surgery. Injectable xylocaine (lignocaine) with or without adrenaline is used for retrobulbar and peribulbar blocks for intraocular surgery. Bupivacaine is also used for blocks but not topically.

questions.question: Trachoma characteristically affects which part of the conjunctiva, and what is the sequence leading to blindness?
questions.explanation: Trachoma characteristically affects the superior tarsal conjunctiva (upper eyelid), producing follicles followed by scarring (Herbert's pits at the superior limbus). The resulting tarsal scarring causes entropion and trichiasis, leading to corneal abrasion and ultimately blindness. The WHO SAFE strategy (Surgery, Antibiotics, Facial cleanliness, Environmental improvement) aims to interrupt this cycle.
options: Inferior tarsal — follicles, inferior scarring, then ectropion
Superior tarsal — follicles, scarring, entropion, trichiasis, corneal ulceration
Bulbar conjunctiva — pannus, then corneal vascularization only
Marginal conjunctiva — keratinization, then corneal exposure

questions.explanation: In children, the elastic periosteum and bone spring back after fracture (trapdoor or 'white-eyed blow-out' fracture), trapping inferior rectus muscle between the bony edges without obvious radiological bone displacement. This causes acute oculocardiac reflex (nausea, vomiting, bradycardia) and diplopia with restricted elevation. Urgent surgical exploration is required within 24–48 hours.
options: Elastic paediatric bone springs back, trapping inferior rectus without radiological evidence of fracture
Infection is more common in paediatric orbital fractures
Children are significantly more prone to developing angle recession glaucoma
Orbital haemorrhage is always more extensive and severe in children
questions.question: A 'trapdoor' fracture of the orbital floor is particularly dangerous in children because:

questions.explanation: Arcus senilis is a common peripheral corneal opacity resulting from lipid deposition in the stroma, appearing as a grey-white ring separated from the limbus by a clear zone of normal cornea. It is a physiological finding of ageing and generally does not affect vision or require treatment. Its presence in a young patient, however, should prompt evaluation for hyperlipidaemia.
questions.question: An elderly patient has a grey-white ring of lipid deposition at the peripheral cornea with a clear zone separating it from the limbus. Which age-related change is this?

questions.explanation: Axenfeld-Rieger (A-R) syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder of anterior segment dysgenesis. Approximately 50% of cases develop glaucoma. The syndrome also features dental anomalies (hypodontia), facial abnormalities, and periumbilical skin changes. It is the most common mesodermal dysgenesis syndrome associated with congenital glaucoma.
questions.question: Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome is associated with glaucoma development in approximately what proportion of affected individuals?
Salmon patch hemorrhages and black sunbursts in sickle cell retinopathy represent:
options: Proliferative stages requiring immediate laser treatment as commonly encountered in practice
Non-proliferative lesions that may auto-infarct without treatment
End-stage disease with retinal detachment during routine ophthalmic assessment
questions.explanation: Salmon patches are equatorial intraretinal hemorrhages, while black sunbursts are patches of RPE hyperplasia—both are non-proliferative manifestations of sickle cell retinopathy. Many of these lesions auto-infarct and involute spontaneously without treatment in 20-60% of cases. Treatment is NOT routinely required for non-proliferative lesions, which distinguishes the management approach from proliferative diabetic retinopathy.

questions.question: Corneal bloodstaining following hyphema occurs when:
questions.explanation: Corneal bloodstaining (hemosiderosis corneae) occurs when hemoglobin from lysed red blood cells in a hyphema penetrates the corneal stroma, particularly when there is elevated IOP and concurrent corneal endothelial dysfunction. The hemoglobin is converted to hemosiderin, causing a yellow-brown discoloration that may take months to years to clear. Aggressive IOP management is essential to prevent this complication.
options: The cornea is vascularized by pannus formation in most clinical presentations in most clinical presentations
Topical steroids cause corneal iron deposition
Blood breakdown products penetrate the corneal stroma due to elevated IOP and corneal endothelial damage
Aqueous humor osmolarity changes cause stromal edema under standard examination conditions under standard examination conditions
a permanent cure requiring no follow-up ever
the lowest cost of all possible ophthalmic interventions
a high-impact, cost-effective restoration of sight
questions.question: A public health programme prioritises cataract surgical services above other interventions when resources are limited mainly because cataract surgery offers
questions.explanation: Cataract surgery reliably restores vision in a single procedure at relatively low cost per outcome achieved, making it one of the most cost-effective health interventions available. It does not prevent unrelated conditions like glaucoma or trachoma. This favourable cost-to-benefit ratio drives its prioritisation in blindness-prevention programmes with constrained resources.

options: Direct invasion of the optic nerve by Chlamydia trachomatis organisms
Secondary glaucoma from trabecular meshwork involvement
Autoimmune attack on retinal pigment epithelium
Tarsal scarring leading to entropion, trichiasis, and corneal abrasion/ulceration
questions.explanation: Trachoma causes blindness through a cascade: chronic chlamydial inflammation → superior tarsal conjunctival scarring → entropion (lid turns inward) → trichiasis (lashes abrade cornea) → corneal ulceration → corneal opacity and blindness. The WHO SAFE strategy (Surgery, Antibiotics, Facial cleanliness, Environmental improvement) aims to interrupt this cycle.
questions.question: Subepithelial conjunctival fibrous tissue replacement as seen in trachoma causes blindness through which mechanism?

questions.explanation: A cup-to-disc (C:D) ratio of 0.6 or above is suspicious for glaucomatous optic nerve damage, particularly if accompanied by notching of the neuroretinal rim, flame hemorrhages at the disc margin, or asymmetry between the two eyes. A C:D ratio of >0.3 is already above normal but 0.6 and above, combined with visual field changes, strongly indicates glaucomatous cupping. Asymmetry of >0.2 between eyes is also a warning sign.
options: 0.5 symmetrically as commonly encountered in practice
questions.question: The normal optic disc on fundoscopy has a pink rim (neuroretinal rim) with a pale central cup. The cup-to-disc ratio at which glaucomatous damage becomes MOST suspicious is:
A patient with sickle cell disease develops fan-shaped new vessel growth at the border between perfused and non-perfused peripheral retina. According to Goldberg staging, this corresponds to
questions.explanation: Sea-fan neovascularization arising at the junction of perfused and non-perfused peripheral retina defines Goldberg Stage III sickle cell retinopathy. Earlier stages describe vaso-occlusion and vascular remodelling without true new vessel growth, while later stages involve haemorrhagic or tractional complications of these fragile new vessels. Identifying Stage III is important because it is the point at which laser treatment is typically considered.
options: no defined stage in this classification

questions.question: A patient has a unilateral dendritic corneal ulcer with reduced corneal sensation and a history of recurrent cold sores. Which organism is the most common cause of this presentation?
questions.explanation: Herpes simplex virus is the most common cause of infectious dendritic keratitis, producing a branching ulcer with terminal bulbs best seen with fluorescein staining. Reduced corneal sensation is a hallmark feature that helps differentiate it from other causes of red eye. Recurrent orolabial herpes history supports reactivation of latent virus in the trigeminal ganglion.

options: New vessels growing from the retina into the vitreous
Laser burn scars from previous photocoagulation
Cotton wool spots resolving into pigmented scars
Arteriolar-venular shunts bypassing ischemic capillary beds within the retina
questions.question: Intraretinal microvascular abnormalities (IRMAs) in diabetic retinopathy are best described as:
questions.explanation: IRMAs are arteriolar-venular shunts that bypass areas of capillary non-perfusion, running from arterioles directly to venules within the retinal tissue without leaving the retinal plane. They are flat (intraretinal) and thus differ from true neovascularization, which grows above the retinal surface toward the vitreous. IRMAs indicate severe non-proliferative DR and signal impending progression to the proliferative stage.

The conjunctiva is anatomically divided into: (1) palpebral/tarsal conjunctiva covering the lid surface, (2) bulbar conjunctiva covering the eyeball up to the limbus, (3) forniceal conjunctiva in the recess (cul-de-sac) between the lid and globe, and (4) marginal conjunctiva at the lid margin where keratinization begins. Foreign bodies commonly lodge in the superior fornix.
questions.question: The conjunctiva is divided into which anatomical regions?
options: Nasal, temporal, superior, and inferior regions
Palpebral, bulbar, forniceal, and marginal regions
Tarsal, limbal, and corneal regions only
Anterior, posterior, superficial, and deep regions
Epithelial, stromal, and basement membrane regions

questions.question: In end-stage POAG, which visual field area is typically preserved LAST?
questions.explanation: In end-stage POAG, the central visual field (macular vision) and a small temporal crescent (from the nasal retina) are the last areas preserved, creating characteristic 'tunnel vision.' Loss of central vision represents functionally devastating, irreversible late-stage glaucoma and constitutes legal blindness in most jurisdictions.
options: Central field with a small temporal crescent

questions.question: The treatment of Acanthamoeba keratitis differs from bacterial and fungal keratitis in that it requires:
questions.explanation: Acanthamoeba keratitis requires specific treatment with chlorhexidine and polyhexamethylene biguanide (PHMB) drops, which target both the trophozoite and cyst forms. It shows no response to conventional antibacterial, antifungal, or antiviral therapy. The combination of these anti-acanthamoebic agents is used for prolonged treatment periods. Penetrating keratoplasty may be needed in refractory cases.
options: Oral doxycycline plus topical steroid combination
IV amphotericin B for 6 weeks minimum
Standard topical ciprofloxacin and tobramycin fortified drops

questions.question: A patient accommodates for near vision. Which of the following correctly describes the ciliary muscle state and lens shape during this process?
questions.explanation: During accommodation for near vision, the ciliary muscle contracts, which releases tension on the zonular fibers. The elastic lens then returns to a more rounded shape with increased dioptric power, enabling near focus. In the resting state, zonules are taut keeping the lens flat for distance vision.
options: Ciliary muscle contracts; zonules relax; lens rounds
Ciliary muscle relaxes; zonules tighten; lens flattens
Ciliary muscle relaxes; zonules loosen; lens rounds
Ciliary muscle contracts; zonules tighten; lens flattens
Ciliary muscle relaxes; zonules contract; lens thickens
Diffuse flame haemorrhages in all four quadrants, dilated tortuous veins, and disc swelling
Peripheral preretinal haemorrhages with sea fan neovascularisation present
Bilateral optic disc pallor without retinal haemorrhages
Pale white oedematous retina with cherry-red spot at fovea
questions.question: Central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO) fundus appearance is BEST described as:
questions.explanation: CRVO produces diffuse flame-shaped retinal haemorrhages in all four quadrants, tortuous dilated veins, cotton-wool spots, and disc swelling — classically described as a 'blood and thunder' or 'stormy sunset' fundus. Vision loss results from macular oedema. It is differentiated from CRAO by haemorrhages rather than pallor, and relatively preserved vision.

questions.question: Bitot's spots seen in vitamin A deficiency are characterised as:
options: Yellow deposits at the optic disc margin
Whitish lipid deposits in the central corneal stroma
Cotton-wool spots on the retinal surface
Foamy, triangular, whitish plaques on the bulbar conjunctiva in the interpalpebral zone
questions.explanation: Bitot's spots are foamy, triangular, greyish-white plaques on the bulbar conjunctiva in the interpalpebral zone (3 o'clock and 9 o'clock positions). They represent keratinised, desquamated conjunctival epithelium colonised by Corynebacterium xerosis. They are pathognomonic of vitamin A deficiency and indicate significant depletion requiring urgent supplementation.

The lamina cribrosa is a sieve-like meshwork of connective tissue located at the posterior scleral foramen (the opening in the sclera where the optic nerve exits the eye). In glaucoma, elevated IOP causes mechanical compression and distortion of the lamina cribrosa, obstructing axoplasmic flow in retinal ganglion cell axons and contributing to their death. SUBTOPIC 2: PRIMARY OPEN-ANGLE GLAUCOMA (POAG)
options: Located centrally within the trabecular meshwork tissue itself
At the pars plana of the ciliary body
At the posterior scleral foramen where the optic nerve exits the eye
questions.question: The lamina cribrosa, where glaucomatous damage is concentrated, is located:

questions.explanation: The orbicularis oculi is the muscle of lid protraction (closure), which narrows the palpebral fissure during blinking and assists in the lacrimal pump mechanism for tear drainage. It is innervated by CN VII. Facial nerve palsy causes lagophthalmos, exposing the cornea to desiccation.
questions.question: Which muscle narrows the palpebral fissure and assists in the lacrimal pump mechanism?

options: Rust-brown discoloration of the iris with retinal toxicity and degeneration
Optic disc cupping without IOP elevation in most clinical presentations
Cherry-red spot at the macula under standard examination conditions
questions.explanation: Haemosiderosis bulbi results from the slow release of ferrous ions from an iron-containing IOFB. The iron deposits throughout ocular tissues causing rust-brown discoloration of the iris, corneal endothelial damage, and toxic degeneration of retinal photoreceptors and neurons. The condition leads to progressive visual loss and blindness if the IOFB is not removed. ERG changes (reduced amplitude) are early indicators of retinal iron toxicity.
questions.question: Haemosiderosis bulbi from an untreated iron IOFB leads to which characteristic fundoscopic finding over time?
Corneal ectasia post-LASIK surgery most closely resembles which naturally occurring corneal condition?
questions.explanation: Post-LASIK ectasia is iatrogenic progressive corneal thinning and protrusion resembling keratoconus, caused by excessive stromal ablation or inadequate residual stromal bed (less than 250 microns). Risk factors include pre-existing forme fruste keratoconus, thin corneas, and high myopia. Preoperative corneal topography is essential to screen for keratoconus before LASIK.

questions.question: A patient has ptosis, a dilated pupil, and the eye deviates outward and downward, but abduction is preserved. Which nerve is affected?
questions.explanation: The oculomotor nerve supplies levator palpebrae, the pupillary sphincter, and all extraocular muscles except lateral rectus and superior oblique. Its palsy causes ptosis, mydriasis, and an eye pulled down and out by the unopposed muscles. Abduction is spared because lateral rectus is innervated by the abducens nerve.

questions.question: A patient on long-term topical corticosteroid for chronic uveitis develops gradually rising intraocular pressure and posterior lens opacity. These are recognised complications of
questions.explanation: Corticosteroids can raise intraocular pressure by reducing aqueous outflow and are well known to cause posterior subcapsular cataract with chronic use. Regular monitoring of pressure and lens clarity is required during steroid therapy for uveitis. This risk must be weighed against the benefit of controlling inflammation.

options: Exposure keratopathy from incomplete lid closure
questions.explanation: Leprosy can damage the facial and trigeminal nerves, causing lagophthalmos (incomplete eyelid closure) and reduced corneal sensation. This combination predisposes to exposure keratopathy, corneal ulceration, and secondary infection due to poor tear film distribution and blink reflex. Lubrication and eyelid surgery may be required to protect the cornea.
questions.question: A patient with lepromatous leprosy presents with reduced corneal sensation and lagophthalmos. What ocular complication is this patient at high risk of developing?

questions.explanation: Marcus Gunn jaw-winking syndrome is a congenital neurogenic ptosis caused by aberrant innervation between the pterygoid branch of CN V3 and the levator palpebrae superioris. Jaw movement causes the ptotic lid to retract or wink. It accounts for 5% of congenital ptosis. The synkinetic lid movement distinguishes it from other forms.
questions.question: Marcus Gunn jaw-winking syndrome is a form of ptosis classified as:
options: Pseudoptosis from ipsilateral hypotropia of the globe

questions.explanation: Vitrectomy is reserved for advanced complications such as persistent vitreous hemorrhage that fails to clear or tractional retinal detachment threatening the macula, both of which require mechanical removal of blood and fibrous tissue. Early or mild disease is managed medically or with laser rather than surgery. Recognising this threshold avoids premature or unnecessary surgical intervention.
questions.question: A diabetic patient undergoes vitrectomy for advanced eye disease. The MOST common indication for this procedure is
options: non-clearing vitreous hemorrhage or tractional retinal detachment

questions.question: A patient recovering from severe cerebral malaria is found to have retinal whitening and characteristic vessel discoloration on fundoscopy. What is the significance of these findings?
options: They are unrelated to the underlying illness
They correlate with disease severity and prognosis
They indicate an unrelated retinal dystrophy
questions.explanation: Malarial retinopathy, including retinal whitening, vessel colour changes, and haemorrhages, is a recognised finding in cerebral malaria and correlates with disease severity and helps distinguish cerebral malaria from other causes of coma in endemic areas. It also carries prognostic value for outcome. Fundoscopy can therefore aid diagnosis in unclear clinical presentations.

Phlyctenulosis is a delayed hypersensitivity reaction of the conjunctiva and cornea to microbial antigens, classically associated with tuberculosis or staphylococcal exposure. It presents as small nodular lesions with surrounding inflammation and marked photophobia. Treatment addresses the underlying trigger alongside topical anti-inflammatory therapy.
questions.question: A patient presents with painful nodular conjunctival lesions and pain with photophobia after tuberculosis exposure. What type of hypersensitivity reaction is this?

questions.explanation: Repeated inflammatory episodes in trachoma cause conjunctival scarring that distorts the lid margin, producing trichiasis in which lashes abrade the cornea and eventually cause opacification and blindness. Earlier WHO grades describe active inflammation without this mechanical corneal damage. Recognising the progression justifies early lid surgery to prevent this outcome.
options: mild conjunctival scarring without lash involvement
questions.question: A patient with far-advanced trachomatous scarring develops in-turned eyelashes rubbing against the cornea, ultimately causing corneal opacification. This end-stage complication reflects the WHO grade of
A young South Asian male presents with recurrent vitreous haemorrhage from peripheral retinal vasculitis and non-perfusion without an identifiable systemic cause. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Eales disease is an idiopathic peripheral retinal vasculitis predominantly affecting young males, causing peripheral capillary non-perfusion, neovascularisation, and recurrent vitreous haemorrhage. Its exact cause remains unclear, though associations with tuberculosis hypersensitivity have been proposed. Management includes laser photocoagulation of ischaemic areas and control of vitreous bleeding.

questions.question: Sickle cell disease produces its characteristic vaso-occlusive complications because:
questions.explanation: In sickle cell disease, the amino acid substitution of valine for glutamic acid at position 6 of the beta-globin chain causes hemoglobin S to polymerize and form rigid polymers under conditions of hypoxia, acidosis, and dehydration. This deforms red blood cells into the characteristic sickle shape that obstructs small vessels, causing vaso-occlusion, ischemia, and tissue infarction—the foundation of sickle cell pathophysiology.
options: Hemoglobin S is structurally identical to hemoglobin A as commonly encountered in practice
Iron overload from hemolysis destroys vessel walls
White blood cells in SCD are abnormally large during routine ophthalmic assessment
Hemoglobin S polymerizes under conditions of hypoxia and acidosis, deforming red blood cells

questions.question: The injectable form of local anaesthetic used for retrobulbar block in ophthalmic surgery is:
questions.explanation: Xylocaine (lignocaine) with or without adrenaline is the injectable local anaesthetic used for retrobulbar and peribulbar blocks in intraocular surgery. The addition of adrenaline prolongs the duration of anaesthesia by causing local vasoconstriction. Tetracaine is topical only, and pilocarpine/atropine/timolol are therapeutic ophthalmic agents, not anaesthetics.

questions.question: Peripheral laser scatter photocoagulation for sea-fan neovascularization in sickle cell retinopathy works by:
questions.explanation: Like panretinal photocoagulation in diabetic PDR, peripheral scatter laser in sickle cell retinopathy destroys ischemic peripheral retinal tissue—the source of VEGF production—thereby reducing the angiogenic stimulus for sea-fan neovascularization. This promotes regression of existing sea fans and reduces the risk of vitreous hemorrhage and retinal detachment. The laser is applied to non-perfused peripheral retina identified on FFA.
options: Directly coagulating the sea-fan neovascular fronds
Creating a barrier to prevent further vascular occlusion as commonly encountered in practice
Destroying ischemic peripheral retina to reduce VEGF, inducing regression of new vessels
Coagulating the vitreous base to prevent hemorrhage
Improving blood flow through the peripheral retinal arteries during routine ophthalmic assessment

questions.question: Acute retinal necrosis (ARN) is a severe necrotizing retinitis caused by herpesviruses. The typical sequence of events is:
questions.explanation: ARN (caused by VZV, HSV-1, or HSV-2) follows a characteristic sequence: peripheral full-thickness retinal whitening (necrotizing retinitis) progressing circumferentially, associated occlusive retinal arteritis, moderate to severe vitritis, and ultimately rhegmatogenous retinal detachment (through necrotic peripheral retinal holes) in 75% of untreated cases. IV acyclovir is urgent.
options: CMV retinitis → vitreous haemorrhage → disc swelling
Peripheral retinal whitening → vitritis → arteritis → retinal detachment
Macular oedema → exudative retinal detachment → optic atrophy
Central scotoma → progressive peripheral scotoma → hand movements only
Anterior uveitis → posterior synechiae → secondary glaucoma → blindness
It increases lacrimal gland stimulation reflexively
It reduces goblet cell turnover in the conjunctiva
It eliminates the evaporative component of dry eye
It stimulates accessory lacrimal gland secretion via CN V reflex
It prevents tear drainage, thereby increasing tear film retention time
questions.question: Dry eye management using punctal occlusion works because:
questions.explanation: Punctal occlusion (plugs or surgical cautery) blocks the drainage puncta, preventing tears from draining away. This increases tear retention time on the ocular surface, improving symptoms of aqueous-deficient dry eye. It is used in severe cases after topical lubricants and environmental modifications have been tried. Silicone plugs are reversible; cautery is permanent.

AAION is caused by giant cell arteritis (GCA/temporal arteritis), an inflammatory granulomatous vasculitis affecting medium and large vessels. It presents with sudden visual loss, disc oedema, elevated ESR/CRP, and systemic GCA symptoms. It is a medical emergency — immediate high-dose systemic corticosteroids prevent loss of the second eye.
questions.question: Arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy (AAION) is a complication of:

questions.explanation: Uveal (choroidal) metastases are the most common intraocular malignancy overall in adults. They originate primarily from breast carcinoma (most common in women) and lung carcinoma (most common in men), accounting for approximately 70% of uveal metastases. They appear as flat, creamy-white subretinal lesions, often multiple, associated with exudative retinal detachment.
options: Renal cell carcinoma and bladder cancer
Melanoma of the skin and ovarian carcinoma
questions.question: Orbital metastases to the uveal tract most commonly originate from which primary tumors in adults?

questions.explanation: Thyroid eye disease results from autoimmune lymphocytic infiltration and glycosaminoglycan deposition within the extraocular muscles and orbital fat, and predominantly affects women. This produces lid retraction, proptosis, and restrictive myopathy, most often involving the inferior and medial rectus muscles. It commonly occurs in association with Graves' hyperthyroidism but can also occur in euthyroid patients.
questions.question: A middle-aged woman presents with eyelid retraction, proptosis, and restrictive strabismus. Autoimmune infiltration of extraocular muscles is suspected. Which condition is most likely?

questions.explanation: Post-operative endophthalmitis requires intravitreal antibiotic injection (vancomycin for Gram-positive + ceftazidime or amikacin for Gram-negative coverage) as primary treatment, as systemic antibiotics achieve inadequate intraocular concentrations. The EVS study showed vitrectomy benefits eyes with vision of light perception only. Prompt treatment is essential.
questions.question: Post-operative endophthalmitis with hypopyon after intraocular surgery should be treated with:
options: Topical antibiotic drops used alone as monotherapy
Urgent intravitreal antibiotic injection (vancomycin + ceftazidime) with or without vitrectomy

questions.question: Horner's syndrome is characterized by a classic triad that includes ptosis, miosis, and:
questions.explanation: Horner's syndrome consists of ptosis (drooping upper lid), miosis (constricted pupil), anhidrosis (reduced sweating on the ipsilateral face), and hypochromia iridis (lighter iris colour). These result from interruption of the sympathetic pathway at any of the three neuron levels. Anhidrosis occurs because facial sweating is also under sympathetic control via the superior cervical ganglion.
options: Pupillary dilation as commonly encountered in practice

questions.explanation: Acute postoperative endophthalmitis is an ophthalmic emergency requiring rapid diagnosis through vitreous and aqueous sampling combined with immediate empirical intravitreal antibiotic therapy. Delay significantly worsens visual prognosis due to rapid intraocular tissue destruction by proliferating organisms. Vitrectomy may be required in severe cases.
questions.question: A patient recovering from cataract surgery develops sudden severe pain, marked visual loss, and hypopyon three days postoperatively. What is the priority investigation and action?
options: Observation with review in one week
Vitreous tap with immediate intravitreal antibiotics

questions.question: A patient with diabetic macular edema is treated with anti-VEGF injections. This therapy works by
options: blocking vascular endothelial growth factor to reduce leakage and neovascularization
sterilising the vitreous cavity of infection
questions.explanation: Anti-VEGF agents bind and neutralise vascular endothelial growth factor, a key driver of increased vascular permeability and abnormal vessel growth in diabetic eye disease. This reduces macular fluid accumulation and can regress early neovascularization. It has no direct effect on systemic glucose control or mechanical vitreous removal.

Chemical burns from household alkali agents (detergents, disinfectants, bleach, lye) are the most common type of domestic chemical eye injury. Alkali injuries are more severe than acid burns because alkalis cause liquefactive necrosis that allows continued deep tissue penetration. Immediate irrigation is the single most important first-aid step and should begin at the site of injury.
questions.question: Which type of eye injury is MOST associated with domestic accidents involving detergents and disinfectants?
Which of the following anti-infective agents is correctly matched with its primary indication?
questions.explanation: Acyclovir (Zovirax) is an antiviral agent specifically used for herpetic eye infections, including herpes simplex keratitis. Natamycin and voriconazole are antifungal agents. Chloramphenicol and gentamicin are antibacterials. Povidone-iodine has broad-spectrum antiseptic properties but is not a primary glaucoma treatment.

questions.question: An adult presents with unilateral chronic follicular conjunctivitis, mucopurulent discharge, and preauricular adenopathy lasting several weeks without resolution on standard antibacterial drops. Which organism should be suspected?
questions.explanation: Adult inclusion conjunctivitis caused by Chlamydia trachomatis serotypes D to K presents as a chronic follicular conjunctivitis that fails to respond to conventional antibacterial treatment, often accompanied by preauricular adenopathy. Unlike trachoma, this form is usually sexually transmitted and does not typically progress to severe scarring. Diagnosis requires specific testing since routine bacterial cultures will not identify the organism.

The red reflex test uses an ophthalmoscope or retinoscope held at arm's length to assess the uniformity and symmetry of the fundal red reflex through the pupil. An absent or white reflex (leucocoria) in one or both eyes is the most common presenting sign of retinoblastoma and warrants urgent evaluation. It also detects cataract, significant refractive error, and other media opacities in infants.
options: Refractive error under standard examination conditions
Retinoblastoma and other causes of leucocoria
Amblyopia from patching in most clinical presentations
questions.question: The red reflex test is most important for detecting which childhood ocular condition?

questions.explanation: Enucleation of the injured (exciting) eye within 2 weeks of a penetrating injury is the most effective way to prevent sympathetic ophthalmia. After 2 weeks, sensitisation may already have occurred and enucleation no longer reliably prevents the disease. High-dose systemic immunosuppression (steroids, steroid-sparing agents) is used to treat established sympathetic ophthalmia.
questions.question: Sympathetic ophthalmia is BEST prevented by:
options: Enucleation of the traumatised (exciting) eye within 2 weeks of injury
Prophylactic systemic steroids after every penetrating injury
Topical cyclosporine in the fellow eye
Bilateral enucleation after any eye trauma
Prophylactic laser photocoagulation of the fellow retina

questions.question: A 7-year-old is tested for near vision using a chart with graded print sizes designed specifically for school-age children rather than adults. Which type of chart is this?
questions.explanation: Standard adult reading charts such as the Jaeger chart use text passages that may not suit a school-age child's reading level or attention span. Paediatric near charts use age-appropriate print sizes and content to obtain a reliable near acuity measurement. This ensures the result reflects visual ability rather than reading comprehension limitations.

questions.question: A patient with thyroid eye disease develops progressive visual loss with an afferent pupillary defect due to optic nerve compression at the orbital apex. The MOST appropriate intervention is
questions.explanation: Compressive optic neuropathy from crowded orbital apex tissue in thyroid eye disease is an indication for urgent orbital decompression surgery to relieve pressure on the optic nerve and preserve vision. Lubricants and antihistamines address surface symptoms but do not relieve nerve compression. Recognising this sight-threatening complication distinguishes it from milder, cosmetic-only presentations.

questions.question: The MOST common cause of optic disc swelling in a 25-year-old obese woman with headache and pulsatile tinnitus but no focal neurological deficits is:
options: Cavernous sinus thrombosis from orbital cellulitis
questions.explanation: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH/pseudotumour cerebri) classically presents in young obese women with bilateral papilloedema, headache, pulsatile tinnitus, and transient visual obscurations, but without focal neurological signs. CSF opening pressure is elevated with normal composition. Risk factors include obesity, tetracycline, vitamin A excess, and OCP use. Treatment: weight loss, acetazolamide, and serial lumbar punctures.

questions.question: Fuchs' endothelial dystrophy causes progressive corneal decompensation due to:
options: Stromal fibrosis from recurrent herpetic disease
Accelerated endothelial cell loss producing guttata then corneal edema
Anterior segment ischemia from carotid artery disease
Calcium deposition in Bowman's layer blocking aqueous flow
Immune-mediated destruction of keratocytes in the stroma
questions.explanation: Fuchs' endothelial dystrophy is characterized by progressive endothelial cell loss with formation of guttata (excrescences on Descemet's membrane). As endothelial density falls below the critical threshold (~500 cells/mm²), the pump fails, causing stromal and then epithelial edema (bullous keratopathy). Treatment is endothelial keratoplasty (DSAEK or DMEK).

Normal cup-to-disc ratio is approximately 0.3–0.4, representing the physiological cupping. A CDR above 0.5, asymmetry between eyes (difference greater than 0.2), or progressive enlargement are suspicious for glaucoma. However, CDR alone is insufficient for diagnosis — structural optic nerve assessment (OCT RNFL) and functional testing (visual fields) are required.
questions.question: A normal optic disc has a cup-to-disc ratio (CDR) of approximately:

questions.explanation: In Africa and developing countries, phlyctenular keratoconjunctivitis is most commonly a Type IV (delayed) hypersensitivity reaction to Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigens. In developed countries, Staphylococcal antigens are the predominant trigger. The phlycten is a pink-white nodule at the limbus that can migrate centrally producing a leash of vessels. Treatment requires topical steroids.
questions.question: Phlyctenular keratoconjunctivitis is a hypersensitivity reaction MOST commonly to antigens of which organism in Africa?

questions.explanation: Avoidable blindness encompasses conditions that could have been prevented through public health measures or successfully treated with available interventions, such as cataract, trachoma, and vitamin A deficiency. This concept excludes conditions with no current effective intervention. Framing blindness this way focuses health system priorities on interventions with measurable impact.
questions.question: A blindness prevention programme defines certain cases as 'avoidable blindness.' This term specifically refers to blindness that is
options: either preventable or treatable with existing interventions

questions.explanation: Hypochromia iridis occurs in congenital or longstanding Horner's syndrome where sympathetic denervation prevents normal melanin development in the iris. The affected iris appears lighter (less pigmented) than the contralateral normal iris. This feature is most pronounced in congenital Horner's syndrome and may be subtle in acquired cases.
options: Increased iris pigmentation on the affected side in most clinical presentations
Lighter iris colour on the affected side due to sympathetic denervation
Loss of iris tissue due to trauma under standard examination conditions
questions.question: Hypochromia iridis in Horner's syndrome refers to:
A patient with a foreign-body sensation and a history of a metallic fragment striking the eye is BEST evaluated at the slit lamp using
questions.explanation: Fluorescein staining highlights the corneal epithelial disruption caused by a retained or previously embedded foreign body under blue light examination. Visual field and colour vision testing do not localise anterior segment injury. This targeted examination guides safe removal and assessment for penetration.

options: causes immediate loss of the eye
cannot be delivered to the orbit at all
increases the risk of secondary malignancies in radiation-exposed tissue
has no long-term risks in this population
is less effective than chemotherapy in every case
questions.question: External beam radiotherapy is now used less frequently in children with hereditary retinoblastoma mainly because it
questions.explanation: Children with germline RB1 mutations are already predisposed to secondary cancers, and external beam radiotherapy further increases this risk within the irradiated field, particularly for sarcomas. This has shifted practice toward alternatives such as chemotherapy and focal treatments that avoid this added risk. The decision to avoid radiotherapy reflects long-term cancer risk rather than a lack of short-term efficacy.

options: Superior cervical ganglion in the majority of documented cases
Pterygopalatine ganglion based on typical clinical findings
questions.question: The parasympathetic supply to the pupil for the light reflex originates from the:
questions.explanation: The Edinger-Westphal nucleus is the parasympathetic preganglionic nucleus within the rostral midbrain that mediates pupillary constriction and accommodation. Fibers from this nucleus travel with the oculomotor nerve (CN III) to synapse in the ciliary ganglion. Postganglionic fibers then reach the iris sphincter and ciliary muscle via the short ciliary nerves.

options: They are instilled into the conjunctival sac
They are applied to the lid margin only
They are the same as contact lens solutions
They include intracorneal, intravitreal, and retrobulbar injections
They are only used for topical anaesthesia
questions.question: Which statement about parenteral ophthalmic products is CORRECT?
questions.explanation: Parenteral ophthalmic products are preparations intended for injection directly into ocular tissues or surrounding structures, including intracorneal, intravitreal, and retrobulbar routes. Intravitreal injections (e.g., anti-VEGF agents, steroids) are increasingly used in the management of posterior segment diseases. They differ fundamentally from topical preparations instilled into the conjunctival sac.

Hydroxychloroquine retinal toxicity classically produces a bull's-eye maculopathy, with a ring of depigmentation surrounding a relatively preserved central fovea, visible on careful retinal imaging. Early detection through regular screening, including visual fields and imaging, allows discontinuation before irreversible central vision loss occurs. Risk increases with cumulative dose and duration of therapy.
questions.question: A patient on long-term hydroxychloroquine therapy for autoimmune disease is screened annually for a specific retinal toxicity. What pattern is characteristic of this toxicity?
A child develops unilateral leukocoria and a white raised retinal granuloma with eosinophilia and a history of exposure to puppies. Which parasite is responsible?
questions.explanation: Toxocara canis infection occurs when children ingest embryonated eggs from soil contaminated by infected dogs, leading to larval migration and formation of a granulomatous retinal mass. Peripheral eosinophilia and positive serology support the diagnosis in a child presenting with unilateral leukocoria or strabismus. This differs from toxoplasmosis, which is acquired through undercooked meat or cat faeces exposure.

Onchocerciasis is caused by Onchocerca volvulus, transmitted by Simulium (blackfly) near fast-flowing rivers in sub-Saharan Africa. Microfilariae dying in the corneal stroma trigger an immune reaction causing punctate keratitis progressing to sclerosing (blinding) keratitis. Posterior segment lesions (chorioretinopathy, optic atrophy) also occur. Treatment is annual ivermectin.
questions.question: Onchocerciasis (river blindness) causes blindness in tropical Africa through which ocular mechanism?
options: Direct larval invasion of the optic nerve sheath
Sclerosing keratitis from immune reaction to microfilariae in the cornea
Optic disc drusen from chronic microfilarial disc obstruction

questions.question: A patient with atopic disease develops recurrent seasonal itchy eyes with giant papillae under the upper eyelid. What condition is this?
questions.explanation: Vernal keratoconjunctivitis is a chronic allergic condition most common in young males with an atopic background, typically worsening in warm seasons. Giant papillae on the upper tarsal conjunctiva and intense itching are characteristic features. Severe cases can cause corneal shield ulcers threatening vision.

Eyelid retraction, giving a staring appearance with visible sclera above the limbus, is the most common clinical sign of thyroid eye disease and results from sympathetic overactivity and Müller's muscle involvement. This is the opposite finding to ptosis, which involves lid drooping. Recognising retraction as the hallmark sign helps distinguish thyroid eye disease from other causes of proptosis.
questions.question: On examination, a patient with thyroid eye disease shows the upper eyelid positioned above the normal margin, exposing more sclera than usual. This MOST common clinical sign is
A patient with recurrent herpes simplex stromal keratitis is started on daily low-dose oral acyclovir for a year. What is the primary goal of this regimen?
questions.explanation: Long-term low-dose oral acyclovir prophylaxis reduces the frequency of herpes simplex keratitis recurrences by suppressing viral reactivation, though it does not eliminate latent virus from the trigeminal ganglion. This strategy is particularly useful in patients with frequent stromal keratitis episodes that risk progressive corneal scarring. It does not reverse scarring already present from prior episodes.

questions.question: Which photoreceptor cells are responsible for color vision and are concentrated at the fovea centralis?
questions.explanation: Cones are responsible for color vision and best visual acuity and are concentrated in the fovea centralis. They require more light (photopic vision) and contain three types of photopigments: blue, green, and red. Rods are responsible for scotopic (dim light) vision.

options: has no risk of side effects in neonates
eliminates the need for maternal treatment
prevents chlamydial pneumonia developing from nasopharyngeal colonisation
works faster than topical therapy on the eye alone
avoids the need for any follow-up visits
questions.question: A neonate with chlamydial ophthalmia neonatorum is treated with systemic erythromycin rather than topical therapy alone mainly because systemic treatment additionally
questions.explanation: Chlamydia trachomatis often colonises the neonatal nasopharynx in addition to the conjunctiva, and topical treatment alone would not eradicate this reservoir, risking later chlamydial pneumonia. Systemic erythromycin treats both the ocular infection and this respiratory risk simultaneously. This dual benefit is the main reason systemic rather than topical-only therapy is recommended.

questions.question: A patient presents after blunt trauma with sudden onset of a ring-shaped visual field defect sparing central vision. What structure has typically been damaged?
questions.explanation: A ring scotoma following blunt trauma reflects damage to the peripheral retina, often related to peripheral retinal oedema or choroidal rupture, while the macula and central vision remain relatively preserved. This pattern differs from more central or diffuse visual loss seen with optic nerve injury. Careful peripheral fundus examination helps confirm the diagnosis.

options: Sphere power plus the full cylinder power
Cylinder power minus half the sphere power
The average of the two principal meridian powers
Sphere power divided by cylinder power
Sphere power plus half the cylinder power
questions.explanation: Spherical equivalent = sphere power + (cylinder power / 2). For example, -3.00 / -1.00 x 180 has a spherical equivalent of -3.50 D. It represents the average refractive power of both principal meridians and is used clinically to describe overall myopia/hypermetropia in astigmatic patients. It is the power of the best single sphere approximating the astigmatic correction.
questions.question: Spherical equivalent refraction is calculated from a full spectacle prescription as:
A diabetic patient with newly diagnosed mild background retinopathy is scheduled for follow-up. The MOST appropriate interval for repeat retinal screening in this scenario is
options: every five years regardless of severity
questions.explanation: Diabetic patients with mild background retinopathy are typically reassessed annually to detect early progression before it threatens vision, since retinopathy can advance silently. Waiting for symptoms risks missing sight-threatening changes at a treatable stage. More frequent review is reserved for more advanced disease.

questions.question: A patient using prolonged intravenous antibiotics and total parenteral nutrition develops blurred vision with fluffy white retinal and vitreous lesions in a string-of-pearls pattern. What organism is responsible?
questions.explanation: Candida endophthalmitis typically occurs in patients with risk factors such as prolonged intravenous access, parenteral nutrition, or immunosuppression, allowing haematogenous spread to the eye. It produces characteristic fluffy white chorioretinal lesions with vitritis, sometimes in a string-of-pearls pattern. Systemic and intravitreal antifungal therapy is required.

options: Myopia causes retinal detachment, which then secondarily raises the intraocular pressure
Myopic trabecular meshwork is less functional
Myopic discs have naturally larger cups, making glaucomatous cupping harder to detect
The cornea is thicker, giving falsely high IOP readings
questions.question: High myopia is associated with POAG susceptibility PARTLY because:
questions.explanation: Myopic optic discs naturally have larger physiological cups, making it more difficult to detect superimposed glaucomatous cupping. Myopic patients also tend to have thinner CCTs (underestimating IOP on applanation) and peripapillary tissues that may be more susceptible to pressure-related damage. High myopia is an independent risk factor for POAG.

Combined surgery addresses both visually significant cataract and uncontrolled glaucoma in a single operation, reducing the cumulative risks and recovery time of two separate procedures. It can also improve both vision and pressure control simultaneously. The decision depends on disease severity and surgeon expertise.
questions.question: Why might a patient with early cataract and coexisting glaucoma be considered for combined cataract-glaucoma surgery rather than separate procedures?
options: It reduces overall risk and improves patient convenience
It is the only way to remove cataract
It guarantees normalisation of pressure permanently
It avoids the need for postoperative drops entirely
It eliminates any risk of complications

questions.explanation: Benzalkonium chloride, a common preservative in multi-dose glaucoma bottles, can disrupt the tear film and cause chronic ocular surface toxicity with prolonged use. This manifests as redness, stinging, and dry eye symptoms, sometimes limiting compliance. Preservative-free formulations are considered for patients with significant surface disease.
questions.question: A glaucoma patient using multiple topical drops develops ocular surface redness and irritation attributed to a common preservative. Which preservative is typically implicated?

questions.explanation: A perforating injury involves a through-and-through laceration of the globe with both an entry wound (from where the missile entered) and an exit wound (from where it exited). A penetrating injury involves only an entry wound without exit. The distinction is clinically important as perforating injuries generally carry a worse prognosis and may require more complex surgical management.
questions.question: A patient sustains a through-and-through globe injury with both an entry and exit wound. This type of injury is BEST classified as:

questions.explanation: Dry eye syndrome results from deficient tear production or excessive evaporation, causing ocular surface irritation and redness. First-line treatment is topical lubricants (artificial tears) such as hydroxymethylcellulose, sodium hyaluronate, or carboxymethylcellulose to supplement the deficient tear film. Topical steroids may be used in specific inflammatory subtypes but are not first-line for all dry eye.
questions.question: In a patient with Dry Eye Syndrome (keratoconjunctivitis sicca) causing red eye, the MOST appropriate treatment is:

questions.explanation: Retinitis pigmentosa (RP) is characterized by progressive rod photoreceptor degeneration causing: night blindness (nyctalopia), tunnel vision (peripheral field loss), and the classic fundus triad of bone spicule pigmentation, attenuated retinal vessels, and waxy optic disc pallor. ERG shows markedly reduced rod responses. RP can be autosomal dominant, recessive, or X-linked.
questions.question: Which retinal dystrophy is characterized by progressive peripheral visual field loss, night blindness, and bone spicule pigmentation on fundoscopy?

questions.explanation: Laser peripheral iridotomy creates a small hole in the peripheral iris, allowing aqueous to flow directly from the posterior to the anterior chamber, bypassing the pupillary block that causes angle closure. It is the definitive treatment to prevent recurrent acute attacks of angle-closure glaucoma. Prophylactic iridotomy in the fellow eye is also recommended due to high risk of contralateral attack.
questions.question: A patient with acute angle-closure glaucoma (AACG) needs surgical intervention to prevent recurrence. The MOST appropriate procedure is:
Exfoliative glaucoma is characterised by deposition of which material in the trabecular meshwork?
questions.explanation: Pseudoexfoliation (exfoliative) glaucoma features accumulation of fibrillar pseudoexfoliative material on the anterior lens capsule, zonules, ciliary epithelium, and trabecular meshwork, physically obstructing aqueous outflow. It is one of the most common identifiable causes of secondary open-angle glaucoma worldwide.
options: Fibrillar pseudoexfoliative material from the lens capsule
Calcium crystal deposits from corneal decompensation
Melanin pigment released from the posterior iris surface

questions.question: A premature infant is assessed using a rotating drum with black and white stripes, and eye movements are observed. What visual response is being elicited?
questions.explanation: A rotating striped drum elicits optokinetic nystagmus, a reflexive eye movement consisting of slow pursuit of the moving stripe followed by a fast corrective saccade. Presence of this reflex indicates functioning visual pathways from retina to brainstem. This method can overestimate acuity in infants because subcortical pathways alone can drive the reflex.

questions.question: Gonioscopy in glaucoma classification is primarily used to distinguish:
questions.explanation: Gonioscopy is the clinical examination of the anterior chamber angle and is the definitive method for distinguishing open-angle from closed-angle glaucoma. The technique uses a goniolens and slit-lamp to visualise the trabecular meshwork, Schwalbe's line, scleral spur, and ciliary body band.

CN III innervates the SR, MR, IR, and IO muscles. Abduction is the action of the lateral rectus, which is innervated by CN VI, not CN III. Damage to CN III causes ptosis, pupil dilation, loss of accommodation, and medial gaze palsy.
questions.question: A patient with damage to CN III would LEAST likely present with which of the following?

questions.explanation: Ophthalmia neonatorum is defined as conjunctivitis (inflammation of the conjunctiva) occurring within the first 28 days of life—the neonatal period as defined by UNICEF. It is almost always bilateral and the most common infective cause is Chlamydia trachomatis (serotypes D-K). Gonococcal ON presents earlier (2-5 days) and is more severe.
questions.question: Ophthalmia neonatorum (ON) is defined as conjunctivitis occurring within the first:
