questions.explanation: Black sunburst lesions in sickle cell retinopathy arise from intraretinal haemorrhages that undergo resorption with subsequent migration of pigment into the surrounding retina. They represent a sequela of previous vaso-occlusive retinal damage. Their presence indicates chronic peripheral retinal vascular compromise from sickling.
questions.question: A patient with sickle cell disease has fundoscopy showing scattered dark, spiculated lesions in the peripheral retina. What is the underlying cause of these lesions?
options: Direct viral infection of the retina
Intraretinal haemorrhage with subsequent pigment migration

questions.explanation: Aqueous-deficient dry eye (keratoconjunctivitis sicca/KCS) results from lacrimal gland dysfunction, as occurs in Sjögren's syndrome. Sjogren's is a systemic autoimmune disease causing xerostomia and KCS, with or without a connective tissue disorder. Diagnosis is confirmed by Schirmer's test (under 5 mm wetting), salivary/lacrimal gland biopsy, and serological antibodies.
questions.question: Dry eye disease characterized by absent or abnormal tear protein production as in Sjogren's syndrome is classified as:
options: Evaporative dry eye from meibomian gland obstruction
Mucin-deficient dry eye from goblet cell loss
Lipid-deficient dry eye from lacrimal gland atrophy
Mixed mechanism from corneal epithelial dysfunction

questions.explanation: Aniseikonia is a condition where the size and shape of retinal images in the two eyes are unequal. It differs from anisometropia (unequal refractive states). The eyes can tolerate up to 5% difference; greater differences cause intolerable diplopia, particularly in uniocular aphakia (up to 30%).
options: Different refractive states between the two eyes
Color vision disparity between the two eyes
Unequal pupil sizes causing differential light entry
Unequal size and shape of retinal images between the two eyes
questions.question: Aniseikonia specifically refers to:

questions.explanation: Germline RB1 mutations causing hereditary retinoblastoma follow an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern with high but incomplete penetrance. Affected individuals are also at increased lifetime risk of secondary malignancies outside the eye. Genetic counselling is essential for families with a confirmed germline mutation given the implications for future offspring.
questions.question: A child is diagnosed with bilateral retinoblastoma and found to carry a germline RB1 mutation. What is the inheritance pattern of this mutation?

questions.explanation: Refractive error is cited as the fourth most important cause of blindness using strict criteria (VA <3/60) and is the second most important cause of low vision (VA <6/18). It is also noted as an important cause of blindness after age-related macular degeneration (46%) and glaucoma (17%). Correcting refractive errors with spectacles is among the most cost-effective interventions in blindness prevention.
questions.question: The VISION 2020 target disease that is the fourth most important cause of blindness (using the definition of VA <3/60) globally is:

options: Purulent discharge and periorbital edema in most clinical presentations in most clinical presentations
Hypopyon and corneal neovascularization under standard examination conditions under standard examination conditions
Cobblestone papillae on the upper tarsal conjunctiva and intense itching
questions.explanation: Vernal keratoconjunctivitis (VKC) is a chronic bilateral allergic condition with characteristic cobblestone (giant papillary) hypertrophy of the upper tarsal conjunctiva, severe itching, and ropy mucoid discharge. It predominantly affects young males in tropical climates. The cobblestone appearance is pathognomonic and distinguishes VKC from simple allergic conjunctivitis.
questions.question: Vernal keratoconjunctivitis (VKC) is BEST characterized by which clinical feature?

questions.explanation: While cup-to-disc ratio varies between individuals, a marked asymmetry of 0.2 or more between the two eyes of the same patient is considered suspicious for glaucomatous optic nerve damage rather than a normal anatomical variant. This finding warrants further assessment including intraocular pressure measurement and visual field testing. Symmetrical cupping is more reassuring but does not fully exclude bilateral glaucoma.
questions.question: A patient undergoing dilated fundus examination is found to have a cup-to-disc ratio of 0.9 in one eye and 0.3 in the fellow eye. What does this marked asymmetry suggest?
A patient with acute Horner's syndrome is noted to have only mild drooping of the upper lid rather than complete ptosis. This partial ptosis occurs because sympathetic loss affects only the
questions.explanation: The levator palpebrae superioris, which provides the main lifting force of the upper lid, is supplied by the oculomotor nerve and remains intact in Horner's syndrome. Only the sympathetically innervated Müller's muscle is lost, producing a mild rather than complete ptosis. This distinguishes Horner's ptosis from third nerve palsy ptosis.

Vitamin A is an essential component of rhodopsin, the visual pigment in rod photoreceptors responsible for vision in low light, so deficiency impairs rod function and produces night blindness before other signs appear. Cone-mediated colour vision is relatively preserved early in deficiency. Recognising night blindness as an early symptom allows intervention before progression to corneal xerosis.
options: regeneration of rhodopsin in retinal rod photoreceptors
questions.question: A child with vitamin A deficiency reports difficulty seeing in dim light while daytime vision remains normal. This night blindness occurs because vitamin A deficiency impairs
A patient notices a painless, well-demarcated area of bright red blood under the conjunctiva after a bout of coughing. This finding most commonly results from
options: a ruptured conjunctival vessel from raised venous pressure
questions.explanation: Sudden increases in venous pressure, such as from coughing, straining, or vomiting, can rupture a small conjunctival vessel, producing a painless subconjunctival hemorrhage that resolves without treatment. It causes no visual loss and does not require intervention beyond reassurance. Recognising its benign nature avoids unnecessary investigation.

questions.question: Solid dosage forms placed in the conjunctival sac designed for prolonged drug release are known as:
questions.explanation: Ocular inserts are solid dosage forms placed in the conjunctival sac that release active ingredients over a prolonged period, improving compliance and maintaining therapeutic drug levels. An example is the pilocarpine Ocusert system. They overcome the poor bioavailability of conventional eye drops and reduce the frequency of administration.

Gonococcal infection is typically transmitted to the neonate through direct contact with infected cervical and vaginal secretions during passage through the birth canal, rather than through transplacental, droplet, or feeding-related routes. This explains why maternal screening and treatment during pregnancy, along with prompt neonatal prophylaxis, are key preventive strategies. Recognising the mode of transmission clarifies why caesarean delivery may be considered in some high-risk maternal infections.
questions.question: Gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum is MOST commonly acquired by the neonate through
options: passage through an infected birth canal during vaginal delivery
postnatal droplet transmission from hospital staff

questions.explanation: The most common source of orbital cellulitis, especially in children, is spread from adjacent paranasal sinusitis (most commonly ethmoid sinusitis). The close anatomical relationship of the ethmoid sinuses to the medial orbital wall via the thin lamina papyracea facilitates direct bacterial spread. Immediate IV antibiotics are required.
questions.question: The most common cause of orbital cellulitis in children is:

questions.explanation: Cavernous haemangioma is the most common benign orbital tumour in adults and typically presents as slow, painless, axial proptosis without inflammatory features. It is well encapsulated, allowing complete surgical excision when symptomatic. This contrasts with malignant orbital tumours, which tend to grow rapidly and may show infiltrative margins.
questions.question: An adult presents with slowly progressive painless proptosis over years without inflammatory signs. Imaging reveals a well-circumscribed orbital mass. Which tumour is most likely?

questions.explanation: Soft contact lens-related chronic corneal hypoxia is the most common cause of superficial corneal neovascularization in developed countries. Hypoxia triggers VEGF release, stimulating vessel ingrowth from the limbus. Other causes include trachoma (superior pannus), chemical burns, and interstitial keratitis. Treatment involves improving oxygenation with high Dk lenses or anti-VEGF therapy.
questions.question: Corneal vascularization is pathological because the normal cornea is avascular. The MOST common cause of superficial corneal vascularization is:
options: Chemical alkali burn to the limbal stem cells

questions.explanation: Coagulase-negative staphylococci, particularly Staphylococcus epidermidis from the patient's own conjunctival and lid flora, are the most common organisms isolated in postoperative endophthalmitis following cataract surgery. This underlies the rationale for perioperative antiseptic preparation with povidone-iodine to reduce ocular surface bacterial load. Prompt intravitreal antibiotic therapy targeting likely organisms is critical while awaiting culture results.
questions.question: A patient develops endophthalmitis several days after cataract surgery. Which organism is most frequently implicated in this postoperative complication?

An elderly patient develops sudden painless visual loss with drusen-like deposits and new abnormal blood vessels growing beneath the retina causing haemorrhage. Which form of macular degeneration is this?
questions.explanation: Wet, or exudative, age-related macular degeneration is characterised by choroidal neovascularisation growing beneath the retina, leading to leakage, haemorrhage, and rapid visual decline compared with the slower progression of dry age-related macular degeneration. Anti-VEGF intravitreal therapy targets this abnormal vessel growth to slow or reverse visual loss. Prompt treatment is important because delayed intervention allows irreversible photoreceptor damage.

options: Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment from choroidal rupture
Vitreous hemorrhage from ruptured new vessels
questions.question: A patient with proliferative diabetic retinopathy develops sudden painless visual loss. The MOST likely cause is:
questions.explanation: Sudden, painless visual loss in proliferative diabetic retinopathy is most commonly caused by vitreous hemorrhage from the rupture of fragile new vessels (neovascularization at the disc—NVD, or elsewhere—NVE). These vessels lack proper tight junctions and bleed easily with minimal provocation (e.g., Valsalva, fluctuating BP). The hemorrhage obscures the vitreous cavity, causing sudden loss of vision. Management includes observation for spontaneous absorption or vitrectomy.

options: Lateral orbital wall (greater wing of sphenoid)
questions.question: A blow-out fracture of the orbit most commonly involves which orbital wall?
questions.explanation: Orbital blow-out fractures from blunt trauma (fist, ball) most commonly involve the orbital floor (inferior wall above the maxillary sinus), which is the thinnest wall. Fracture may entrap the inferior rectus, causing diplopia on upward gaze, enophthalmos, and infraorbital nerve numbness. Medial wall fractures (ethmoid sinus) are the second most common.

NVD stands for 'new vessels at the disc' (neovascularization at the optic disc), a hallmark of proliferative diabetic retinopathy. NVE refers to 'new vessels elsewhere' (away from the disc). NVD carries a particularly poor prognosis as it is associated with a high risk of vitreous hemorrhage and traction retinal detachment. Panretinal photocoagulation is the standard treatment.
questions.question: In proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR), neovascularization at the optic disc is abbreviated as:

A patient with posterior uveitis and suspected granulomatous inflammation is being investigated to exclude a treatable infectious cause before starting systemic immunosuppression. Which investigation is prioritised?
questions.explanation: Tuberculosis is an important and treatable infectious cause of granulomatous posterior uveitis, and its exclusion is prioritised because immunosuppressive therapy could worsen undiagnosed active tuberculosis. Investigations may include chest imaging, tuberculin skin testing, or interferon-gamma release assays. Missing this diagnosis before starting steroids or immunosuppressants can have serious systemic consequences.

Corticosteroids, even by inhaled or systemic routes, can reduce outflow facility through the trabecular meshwork by altering extracellular matrix turnover. This leads to a dose- and duration-dependent rise in intraocular pressure in susceptible individuals. Regular IOP monitoring is recommended during prolonged steroid therapy.
questions.question: A patient recently started on inhaled corticosteroids for asthma is later found to have elevated intraocular pressure. What is the likely explanation?

questions.explanation: As glaucomatous cupping expands, particularly the temporal neuroretinal rim, central retinal vessels are forced to shift toward the nasal aspect of the disc — termed nasalisation of disc vessels. This finding accompanies significant cup expansion and temporal rim loss and is a sign of advanced glaucomatous cupping.
options: Vessels are pushed nasally as temporal rim tissue thins and cup expands temporally
New abnormal vessels grow from the nasal side of the optic disc
questions.question: 'Nasalisation' of retinal vessels at the optic disc in POAG occurs because:

A contact lens wearer with a ring-shaped corneal infiltrate and pain disproportionate to clinical signs is treated empirically before culture results return. Which organism is most strongly suspected?
questions.explanation: Acanthamoeba keratitis is classically associated with contact lens wear, particularly with exposure to contaminated water, and produces severe pain out of proportion to clinical findings along with a characteristic ring infiltrate. This organism requires prolonged combination therapy with biguanide and diamidine agents rather than standard antibacterial treatment. Delayed diagnosis is common because early presentation can mimic herpetic keratitis.

Intraretinal microvascular abnormalities, or IRMAs, are dilated pre-existing capillaries that shunt blood around areas of non-perfused retina and are distinguished histologically from true new vessels since they remain within the retina rather than growing beyond the internal limiting membrane. Their presence is a marker of significant retinal ischemia. Recognising IRMA helps grade retinopathy severity even without frank neovascularization.
questions.question: A diabetic patient's fundus shows dilated, tortuous intraretinal vessels that act as shunts around areas of capillary non-perfusion, without true new vessel growth. These are termed

options: Bleeding into loose periorbital connective tissue
questions.explanation: The loose, distensible connective tissue of the eyelids allows blood from local vessel injury to spread easily, producing the characteristic bruised appearance known as a 'black eye'. This is usually a benign finding but should prompt examination to exclude underlying orbital or globe injury. Resolution typically occurs over one to two weeks.
questions.question: A patient sustains blunt trauma and develops bruising and swelling around both eyelids without direct eye injury. What is the underlying cause of this appearance?
Which is the SINGLE most common cause of blindness worldwide and MOST treatable?
questions.explanation: Cataract is the leading cause of blindness worldwide and is eminently treatable with a relatively simple and cost-effective surgical procedure (cataract extraction with intraocular lens implant). Full sight can be restored even after prolonged blindness. It accounts for a large proportion of the ophthalmic surgical workload globally, especially in Africa and Asia.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes the recommended blood pressure target for patients with hypertensive retinopathy?
questions.explanation: The recommended target for treating malignant hypertension causing hypertensive retinopathy is to reduce systemic blood pressure below 140/90 mmHg using appropriate antihypertensive agents. This target is based on cardiovascular outcome data. Rapid over-correction should be avoided in acute presentations as it can cause ischemic complications; controlled reduction over hours to days is preferred in hypertensive emergencies.
options: Any BP reduction regardless of target

questions.question: The MOST common infective cause of ophthalmia neonatorum globally is:
questions.explanation: Chlamydia trachomatis (serotypes D-K—the genital strain) is the most common infective cause of ophthalmia neonatorum globally. It is acquired during passage through an infected birth canal and typically presents 5-14 days after birth with mucopurulent discharge. Gonococcal ON (Neisseria gonorrhoeae) is less common but more severe and presents earlier (2-5 days). Chemical ON from silver nitrate is non-infective.

questions.question: A patient with pseudoexfoliation syndrome undergoing cataract surgery is at increased risk of which intraoperative complication?
questions.explanation: Pseudoexfoliative material deposits on zonular fibres, weakening their structural integrity over time. This predisposes to zonular dehiscence and lens subluxation during cataract surgery. Surgeons must plan for potential capsular support devices in these cases.

Children have more pliable bone that can spring back after fracture, trapping and strangulating the extraocular muscle in a trapdoor fashion with little external sign of injury. Severe pain, nausea, and an oculocardiac reflex response indicate significant muscle entrapment requiring urgent surgical release. Delay risks permanent muscle ischaemia and fibrosis.
options: Children never develop diplopia after trauma
Bone healing is always faster requiring no repair
Trapdoor fractures in children can cause muscle strangulation
Adults always require surgery regardless of severity
Children cannot develop enophthalmos at all
questions.question: A child sustains a similar orbital floor injury but shows severe pain, nausea, and vomiting with minimal external bruising. Why is urgent surgery indicated here more than in adults?
A patient undergoing refraction is asked to view through a small aperture, and vision improves markedly. What optical principle explains this improvement?
questions.explanation: A pinhole allows only a narrow central bundle of rays to enter the eye, reducing the blur circle produced by uncorrected refractive error. This improves image clarity regardless of the specific refractive error present. Failure to improve with a pinhole suggests a non-refractive cause of reduced vision.

questions.question: A young adult presents with unilateral corneal stromal haze, vascularisation, and photophobia without any preceding trauma or infection history. Which systemic condition should be investigated?
questions.explanation: Interstitial keratitis presenting without an obvious precipitating cause in a young adult classically raises suspicion for congenital or acquired syphilis, which produces immune-mediated stromal inflammation and vascularisation. Serological testing for syphilis is an important part of the work-up in such cases. Other causes such as tuberculosis or herpes can also produce interstitial keratitis but syphilis remains a classic association.

questions.question: In uveitic glaucoma, IOP may be elevated due to multiple mechanisms EXCEPT:
options: Trabecular meshwork obstruction by inflammatory cells and proteins
Increased aqueous production by the inflamed ciliary body
Peripheral anterior synechiae closing the angle
Posterior synechiae causing pupil block and iris bombé
questions.explanation: Uveitic glaucoma results from: (1) trabecular meshwork obstruction by inflammatory cells/proteins, (2) PAS angle closure, (3) pupil block from posterior synechiae, and (4) steroid-induced glaucoma. The inflamed ciliary body typically REDUCES aqueous production (not increases it), which is why IOP is often low or normal in acute anterior uveitis. Chronic inflammation and steroid use eventually raise IOP.

questions.question: The mode of inheritance of retinoblastoma when associated with a germline RB1 mutation is:
questions.explanation: Germline retinoblastoma mutations follow an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern with approximately 90% penetrance. Individuals with germline RB1 mutation have a 45% risk of transmitting it to offspring and are predisposed to bilateral/multifocal retinoblastoma and second primary cancers (osteosarcoma). Somatic (non-germline) mutations account for 60% of cases and are unilateral, non-heritable.

options: Leakage and bleeding from abnormal choroidal vessels
questions.question: An elderly patient presents with sudden distortion of central vision and a greyish-green subretinal lesion with associated haemorrhage. What is the mechanism of rapid visual loss in this condition?
questions.explanation: In neovascular (wet) age-related macular degeneration, abnormal choroidal vessels grow beneath the retina and leak fluid or blood, causing rapid distortion and loss of central vision. This differs from the slower progressive atrophy seen in the dry form of the disease. Anti-VEGF injections are the mainstay of treatment to reduce vessel leakage and preserve vision.

questions.question: At which time of day is IOP typically HIGHEST according to its diurnal rhythm?
questions.explanation: IOP follows a circadian rhythm and is typically highest in the early morning hours (6–8 AM) and lowest at night. The normal diurnal variation is 2–6 mmHg over 24 hours. This variation is clinically important when monitoring glaucoma patients, warranting phased tonometry.

questions.question: A patient cannot look down and inward with the affected eye and tilts the head away from the lesioned side to compensate. Which muscle is weak?
questions.explanation: The superior oblique muscle intorts and depresses the eye, most effectively when the eye is adducted. Its palsy causes vertical diplopia worst on looking down and in, and patients tilt the head to the opposite shoulder to minimise the deviation. This head tilt is a classic compensatory sign of fourth nerve palsy.

questions.question: Choroidal melanoma is the MOST common primary intraocular malignancy in adults. The MOST important prognostic factor is:
questions.explanation: The most important prognostic factor in choroidal melanoma is tumor size — specifically the largest basal diameter and height (classified as small, medium, or large by COMS criteria). Larger tumors have higher rates of metastasis (primarily to the liver). Other adverse prognostic factors include ciliary body involvement, epithelioid cell type, and monosomy 3 on cytogenetics.
options: Tumor size (largest basal diameter and height)

questions.explanation: Traditional eye remedies are a recognised cause of chemical injury and secondary infection in many communities. Establishing what was used and for how long guides toxicity assessment and treatment. This detail is captured under drug history, not family history.
options: refer for enucleation as a precaution
ignore it since it is not conventional therapy
specifically ask about type and duration of the substance used
questions.question: During history taking a farmer reports using native leaf extract in his eye before presenting with redness. This detail should prompt the clinician to
Night blindness (nyctalopia) in xerophthalmia occurs because Vitamin A deficiency impairs:
options: Cone photoreceptor function in the fovea
Aqueous humor production in dim light
questions.explanation: Night blindness is the earliest symptom of Vitamin A deficiency because retinol is an essential component of rhodopsin (visual purple), the photopigment in rod photoreceptors. Rods function in dim/scotopic conditions; their dysfunction causes difficulty adapting to darkness. Rhodopsin regeneration requires a constant supply of 11-cis-retinal derived from Vitamin A, making it acutely sensitive to deficiency states.

questions.question: A patient presents with sudden onset optic disc swelling that appears asymmetric and shows only mild pallor rather than true hyperaemic swelling. What alternative diagnosis should be considered before assuming raised intracranial pressure?
questions.explanation: Pseudopapilloedema, often due to optic disc drusen or a congenitally crowded disc, can mimic true papilloedema on routine examination but lacks the associated vascular congestion, haemorrhages, and cotton-wool spots of true disc swelling. Careful fundus examination and imaging, such as ultrasound or optical coherence tomography, help differentiate the two. This distinction avoids unnecessary neuroimaging or lumbar puncture.
options: Acute optic neuritis in both eyes
Two separate somatic mutations in each eye independently
Viral transmission causing bilateral simultaneous transformation
Autoimmune bilateral destruction of retinal photoreceptors
Bilateral ischaemic infarction of the developing retina
Germline RB1 mutation allowing second hit in multiple retinal cells
questions.question: Retinoblastoma bilateral in a child is MOST likely due to:
questions.explanation: Bilateral retinoblastoma is virtually always due to a germline (inherited or new germline) RB1 mutation following Knudson's two-hit hypothesis. The first hit is the inherited germline mutation (present in every cell), and the second somatic mutation occurs independently in multiple retinal cells in both eyes, leading to multiple bilateral tumors. Bilateral disease requires systemic chemotherapy.

options: Acute retinal necrosis from varicella-zoster virus
Branch retinal artery occlusion with localized whitening
questions.question: The 'headlight in fog' appearance on fundoscopy — a focal area of retinal whitening with overlying vitreous haze — is the characteristic presentation of which condition?
questions.explanation: Ocular toxoplasmosis presents as a focal necrotizing retinochoroiditis — a white area of active retinitis adjacent to an old pigmented chorioretinal scar ('satellite lesion'), with overlying vitreous inflammatory haze creating the 'headlight in fog' appearance. It is the most common cause of posterior uveitis in immunocompetent individuals. Treatment: pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine + folinic acid for 4–6 weeks.

options: A dark circular area of choroidal melanoma
A hypofluorescent area on FFA at the fovea in the majority of documented cases
An oval depression of the central macular reflex due to retinal atrophy and thinning
Subretinal fluid at the macula from choroidal neovascularization based on typical clinical findings
questions.explanation: The macular depression sign in sickle cell disease is an oval depression of the bright central macular reflex resulting from atrophy and thinning of the sensory retina at the macula, caused by macular arteriolar occlusion and ischemia. It is an asymptomatic non-proliferative lesion visible on biomicroscopy. OCT confirms the retinal thinning and may show macular thinning patterns characteristic of sickle cell maculopathy.
questions.question: In sickle cell disease, the non-proliferative feature described as a 'macular depression sign' refers to:

questions.explanation: Acquired dacryocystitis typically results from obstruction of the nasolacrimal duct, most commonly at its distal end near the valve of Hasner where it opens into the inferior nasal meatus. Obstruction causes tear stasis, secondary infection, and lacrimal sac distension. Treatment of acute dacryocystitis is antibiotics; definitive treatment is DCR.
questions.question: Acquired dacryocystitis most commonly occurs due to obstruction at which site in the lacrimal drainage system?

questions.explanation: Intraocular foreign body removal should ideally be performed within 24 hours of injury to minimize the risk of endophthalmitis, toxic damage from the IOFB material, and further mechanical injury to intraocular structures. Delay significantly increases the risk of siderosis (iron), chalcosis (copper), and infection. Emergency surgical removal is the standard of care.
questions.question: IOFB removal should ideally be performed within what timeframe of the injury?
A diabetic patient develops sudden mild optic disc swelling with minimal visual symptoms and good visual acuity, differing from typical ischaemic optic neuropathy. What is this condition called?
questions.explanation: Diabetic papillopathy is a distinct, usually self-limiting condition causing mild optic disc swelling in diabetic patients, often with disproportionately preserved visual function compared with typical ischaemic optic neuropathy. Its exact mechanism is unclear but may relate to microvascular changes. Most cases resolve spontaneously over several months without specific treatment.

In Graves' ophthalmopathy, the inferior rectus muscle is most commonly and most severely affected by glycosaminoglycan infiltration and fibrosis, causing restriction of upgaze (the inferior rectus tethers the globe preventing upward movement). This results in vertical diplopia on upgaze. The medial rectus is the second most commonly involved muscle. The characteristic muscle involvement pattern differs from neurogenic causes of diplopia.
questions.question: The diagnostic criteria for Graves' ophthalmopathy include proptosis, eyelid retraction, and restrictive myopathy. Which extraocular muscle is MOST commonly involved first?

questions.explanation: Documented growth of a choroidal lesion over serial examinations is the most reliable indicator of malignant transformation, distinguishing choroidal melanoma from a stable benign naevus. Other features such as subretinal fluid, orange lipofuscin pigment, and thickness also raise suspicion, but growth remains the most specific single feature. Serial photography and ultrasound are used to monitor lesions for interval change.
options: Size under 3 mm at first detection
questions.question: A patient with a pigmented choroidal lesion is being evaluated for malignant transformation. Which feature is most predictive of malignancy compared with a benign naevus?

options: Peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS) have formed, permanently closing the angle
The pupil was too small at the time of the LPI procedure
The lens is positioned too posteriorly
questions.explanation: Even after a technically successful laser peripheral iridotomy (eliminating pupillary block), the angle may remain closed if peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS) — fibrous adhesions between the peripheral iris and trabecular meshwork — have formed during a prolonged attack. PAS represent permanent angle closure. Early LPI (before PAS formation) is more likely to result in full angle opening. SUBTOPIC 4: OPHTHALMIC MICROBIOLOGY AND PATHOLOGY
questions.question: After laser peripheral iridotomy in angle-closure glaucoma, the angle may NOT fully open if:

questions.explanation: Aldose reductase converts excess intracellular glucose to sorbitol via the polyol pathway, and sorbitol accumulation contributes to osmotic and oxidative cellular damage implicated in diabetic retinopathy. This pathway is distinct from the enzymes involved in aqueous humour formation or neurotransmitter metabolism. Understanding this mechanism underlies research into aldose reductase inhibitors as a potential therapy.
questions.question: In the pathogenesis of diabetic retinopathy, excess glucose is converted to sorbitol within retinal cells through activation of the enzyme

options: Facial nerve palsy causing incomplete lid closure (lagophthalmos)
Recurrent HSV reactivation reducing corneal sensitivity
Sjögren's syndrome reducing aqueous tear production
Contact lens overwear causing chronic epithelial hypoxia
Band keratopathy with calcium deposition blocking the visual axis
questions.explanation: Exposure keratopathy results from inadequate coverage of the cornea by the eyelids, leading to desiccation of the inferior cornea. Facial nerve (CN VII) palsy is the most common cause due to orbicularis paralysis causing lagophthalmos (inability to fully close the eye). Other causes include proptosis, scarring of eyelids, and unconscious patients. Treatment is aggressive lubrication and tarsorrhaphy.
questions.question: Exposure keratopathy most commonly results from which underlying condition?
The MOST common type of glaucoma globally is:
questions.explanation: Primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) accounts for approximately 55% of all glaucoma cases worldwide, making it the most prevalent type. It is bilateral, chronic, and slowly progressive. POAG is particularly prevalent in West Africa and is a leading cause of irreversible blindness in Nigeria.

questions.question: In the management of clinically significant macular edema (CSME) in diabetic retinopathy, the MOST evidence-based treatment currently includes:
questions.explanation: Intravitreal anti-VEGF agents (e.g., bevacizumab, ranibizumab) have become the standard of care for CSME/center-involving DMO, demonstrating superior visual outcomes compared to focal laser alone in randomized controlled trials. They may be used in combination with focal grid laser photocoagulation. VEGF levels are elevated in the diabetic vitreous and are the primary driver of vascular permeability in DMO.
options: Vitrectomy as first-line for all cases as commonly encountered in practice
Intravitreal anti-VEGF injections with or without focal laser
Systemic corticosteroids as monotherapy during routine ophthalmic assessment

questions.question: A malnourished child has a foamy, triangular, keratinised patch on the temporal bulbar conjunctiva. This finding, called a Bitot's spot, is a manifestation of
questions.explanation: Bitot's spots are foamy, keratinised conjunctival lesions resulting from squamous metaplasia of the conjunctival epithelium due to vitamin A deficiency. Other vitamin or mineral deficiencies listed do not produce this specific ocular finding. Recognising this sign supports early vitamin A supplementation before progression to corneal involvement.

options: Forced and directive to save time
With the clinician completing sentences for the patient
Skipping HPC when PMH is informative
questions.explanation: History taking should flow seamlessly and naturally from one section to the next, without appearing forced or coerced. The patient should not feel pressured to respond at a specific pace. A comfortable, conversational approach improves the completeness and accuracy of information gathered, which is essential for correct diagnosis.
questions.question: The history-taking process in ophthalmology should ideally flow in what manner?

questions.explanation: Fungal keratitis characteristically shows a dry, raised, grey-white stromal infiltrate with feathery borders, satellite lesions (smaller infiltrates around main lesion), and a hypopyon. The lesion expands slowly despite antibiotics. Vegetative trauma history and the satellite lesion pattern strongly indicate fungal aetiology. Microscopy confirms hyphae.
questions.question: A corneal ulcer showing 'satellite lesions' surrounding the main infiltrate and a hypopyon is MOST suggestive of:
Vitamin A deficiency is a leading cause of childhood corneal blindness in low-income settings mainly through its effect on
options: abnormal lens protein synthesis causing cataract
direct toxic effect on the optic nerve
corneal epithelial integrity, leading to xerosis and ulceration
questions.explanation: Vitamin A deficiency impairs maintenance of the corneal and conjunctival epithelium, leading to progressive dryness, ulceration, and in severe cases keratomalacia, which can rapidly destroy the cornea and cause blindness. This differs mechanistically from cataract, glaucoma, or retinal pigment disorders. Recognising this pathway underlies the emphasis on vitamin A supplementation programmes for childhood blindness prevention.

An untreated internal hordeolum may progress to a chalazion — a chronic granulomatous inflammation of the meibomian gland resulting in a painless nodule. Chalazia are caused by retained meibomian secretions that escape into adjacent tissue. Recurrent chalazia must be biopsied to exclude sebaceous gland carcinoma.
questions.question: An internal hordeolum may spontaneously progress to a painless, slowly enlarging nodule called:

questions.explanation: The Eagling classification grades penetrating eye injuries by depth and involvement of intraocular structures, with uveal prolapse through a corneo-scleral wound representing a more advanced and serious grade. Recognising uveal involvement changes surgical urgency and prognosis. Superficial or adnexal injuries are graded separately and carry a better outlook.
questions.question: A patient sustains a penetrating injury with a corneo-scleral laceration and uveal tissue prolapsing through the wound. According to the Eagling classification, this represents a
options: more severe grade with uveal prolapse
Bilateral red eyes with purulent mucopurulent discharge present
Gradual onset of blurred vision with white fluffy vitreal 'snowball' opacities
Sudden onset of large vitreous haemorrhage
Acute onset of severe pain and hypopyon
questions.explanation: Candidal endophthalmitis presents insidiously with gradual blurred vision and characteristic white, fluffy, 'snowball' or 'string-of-pearls' vitreal opacities. It may also show white retinal/choroidal lesions. It occurs in immunocompromised patients or those on prolonged IV therapy/TPN with IV access. Systemic voriconazole and intravitreal amphotericin B are used.
questions.question: Fungal endophthalmitis (candidal) after prolonged IV therapy or immunosuppression presents with:
In ocular onchocerciasis, the initial corneal lesion (punctate keratitis) results from:
questions.explanation: The corneal lesions in onchocerciasis result from the host's immune response against dead and dying microfilariae in the corneal stroma, not from living organism toxicity. Living microfilariae are tolerated in corneal stroma; dead organisms trigger a violent inflammatory reaction. This is why ivermectin (which kills microfilariae rapidly) can transiently worsen ocular inflammation.
options: Living microfilariae secreting toxic enzymes dissolving stroma
Onchocerca adult worm migration through the corneal stroma
Bloodstream-derived antibodies depositing as immune complexes
Immune-mediated inflammation in response to dead and dying microfilariae
Trachomatous scarring preceding the keratitis in all cases

questions.question: Sympathetic ophthalmia following penetrating eye injury is best described as:
questions.explanation: Sympathetic ophthalmia is a rare bilateral granulomatous uveitis occurring weeks to years after penetrating injury or surgery to one eye (the 'exciting eye'). The uninjured fellow eye (the 'sympathising eye') develops T-cell–mediated autoimmune uveitis. Enucleation of the injured eye within 2 weeks of injury prevents sympathetic ophthalmia.
options: Corneal scarring following severe bilateral chemical burns
A bilateral granulomatous uveitis affecting the uninjured eye weeks to months after trauma
Bacterial endophthalmitis in the fellow eye
Inflammation of the injured eye only

questions.question: Prostaglandin analogues (e.g., latanoprost) lower IOP primarily by:
options: Increasing uveoscleral outflow via ciliary muscle remodelling
Decreasing aqueous production from the ciliary body
questions.explanation: Prostaglandin analogues such as latanoprost, travoprost, and bimatoprost lower IOP primarily by enhancing the uveoscleral (unconventional) outflow pathway through remodelling of the extracellular matrix of the ciliary muscle. They are the most potent single topical agents with once-daily dosing and minimal systemic effects.

Basal cell carcinoma is the most common eyelid malignancy in fair-skinned populations and typically arises on the lower lid as a pearly, telangiectatic nodule with locally invasive but rarely metastatic behaviour. It favours sun-exposed areas and grows slowly compared with more aggressive eyelid tumours. Complete surgical excision with clear margins is the treatment of choice.
questions.question: A fair-skinned elderly patient has a pearly nodule with rolled telangiectatic edges on the lower eyelid margin that has grown slowly over years without metastasis. Which tumour is most likely?
A patient is given atropine 1% before a cycloplegic refraction in a child. Its prolonged mydriatic and cycloplegic effect is explained by its action as a
questions.explanation: Atropine competitively blocks muscarinic receptors on the iris sphincter and ciliary muscle, preventing parasympathetic-mediated constriction and accommodation. Because it dissociates slowly from the receptor, its effects last considerably longer than agents like tropicamide. This makes it useful for cycloplegic refraction in children where accurate accommodation control is needed.

options: Haemorrhage occurring within the optic nerve sheath itself
Choroidal haemorrhage at the disc margin
Deep disc haemorrhage located within the lamina cribrosa region
Prelaminar (nerve fibre layer) haemorrhage from capillaries in the superficial disc
Central retinal artery rupture at the disc
questions.explanation: Flame-shaped or splinter haemorrhages at the optic disc margin in glaucoma originate from small capillaries in the prelaminar nerve fibre layer of the optic nerve head. The nerve fibre arrangement causes the blood to spread in a flame/splinter shape along nerve fibre bundles. These haemorrhages indicate active nerve fibre damage and are associated with accelerated glaucomatous progression. SUBTOPIC 3: ANGLE-CLOSURE AND CONGENITAL GLAUCOMA
questions.question: A 'flame-shaped' (splinter) haemorrhage confined to the disc margin in glaucoma indicates which layer of the optic nerve head is bleeding?

questions.explanation: Kayser-Fleischer rings are golden-brown or greenish deposits of copper in the peripheral corneal stroma (Descemet's membrane), best seen on slit-lamp. They are pathognomonic of Wilson's disease with neurological involvement. Present in virtually 100% of patients with neurological Wilson's disease. D-penicillamine treatment causes their regression.
questions.question: The characteristic corneal finding pathognomonic of Wilson's disease (hepatolenticular degeneration) is:
options: Interstitial keratitis with stromal vascular scarring
Kayser-Fleischer ring — golden-brown copper deposits in peripheral Descemet's membrane
Each infected individual infects 15–19 susceptible people on average
15–19 days are needed for full recovery in most clinical presentations
Only 15–19 strains of measles virus exist under standard examination conditions
questions.explanation: A reproductive rate (R0) of 15–19 means that in a fully susceptible population, each infected individual will on average infect 15–19 other people. This makes measles one of the most contagious human infections known. This high transmissibility means very high vaccination coverage (>95%) is needed for herd immunity to prevent community outbreaks.
questions.question: Measles is described as 'highly infectious' with a reproductive rate of 15–19. This means:

options: High imminent risk of severe proliferative retinopathy in most clinical presentations
Anemia-driven retinopathy risk requiring blood transfusion under standard examination conditions
Well-controlled systemic parameters associated with reduced retinopathy risk
questions.explanation: This profile reflects excellent systemic control: HbA1c 6.5% (target 6–7%), BP 128/78 mmHg (target <130/80 mmHg), total cholesterol 180 mg/dL (<200 mg/dL target), and normal hemoglobin. These optimally controlled systemic parameters are associated with reduced risk of developing and progressing diabetic retinopathy. Maintaining these targets alongside regular ophthalmic screening significantly reduces blindness from diabetic eye disease.
questions.question: A diabetic patient on follow-up has HbA1c 6.5%, BP 128/78 mmHg, cholesterol 180 mg/dL, and Hb 13 g/dL. This profile suggests:
A patient presents with irregular, branching reddish-brown lines radiating from the optic disc, and a history of a bone and blood disorder. What systemic condition is classically associated?
questions.explanation: Angioid streaks represent breaks in a thickened, calcified Bruch's membrane and are classically associated with pseudoxanthoma elasticum, alongside other conditions such as Paget's disease and sickle cell disease. They can predispose to choroidal neovascularisation, causing sudden visual loss if the macula is involved. Regular monitoring for this complication is important.

questions.question: A glaucoma patient develops elevated intraocular pressure despite normal aqueous production. Angle examination is open. Where is the outflow obstruction most likely located?
questions.explanation: In open-angle glaucoma the anterior chamber angle appears normal but resistance to aqueous outflow increases within the trabecular meshwork itself. This impairs drainage into Schlemm's canal and raises intraocular pressure gradually. Because the angle stays open, gonioscopy shows no mechanical blockage.

Keratoconus is classified as a non-inflammatory ectatic corneal disorder characterised by progressive thinning and conical protrusion of the cornea, leading to irregular astigmatism. It typically begins in adolescence and can progress until the third or fourth decade of life. This classification distinguishes it from inflammatory or infectious causes of corneal pathology.
questions.question: A young patient presents with progressive corneal thinning, irregular astigmatism, and a cone-shaped corneal protrusion confirmed on topography. Which classification best describes this disorder?

questions.explanation: Organic IOFBs (e.g., wood, vegetable matter, cilia) are particularly dangerous because they are radiolucent (not visible on plain X-ray), are not inert, and cause intense intraocular inflammation and infection risk. CT or MRI may be needed for localization. Immediate removal is critical as organic matter rapidly degrades, releasing inflammatory mediators and providing a nidus for infection.
questions.question: Organic IOFBs (wood, cilia) are particularly hazardous because they:
options: Are radiopaque and easily detected on X-ray based on typical clinical findings
Are completely inert and cause no tissue reaction in the majority of documented cases
Are not detectable on plain X-ray and cause intense organic inflammation
Are removed without vitrectomy in all cases

questions.question: A patient using long-term topical steroids after corneal transplant develops progressive optic disc cupping. What is the most appropriate next step?
questions.explanation: Steroid-induced glaucoma should be suspected when disc cupping develops during prolonged topical steroid use after ocular surgery. Gradual tapering of the steroid, balanced against graft rejection risk, along with pressure-lowering therapy, is required. Close monitoring prevents both graft failure and glaucomatous damage.
options: Increase steroid dose to reduce inflammation
Stop all treatment abruptly without review
Taper the steroid and monitor intraocular pressure
Ignore the finding as expected postoperatively

questions.question: Uveal effusion syndrome presents with choroidal and ciliary body detachment in eyes that are NOT inflamed and NOT hypotonus. The MOST likely underlying cause is:
questions.explanation: Uveal effusion syndrome is a rare condition characterized by bilateral spontaneous ciliochoroidal detachment in structurally abnormal eyes (typically nanophthalmic with abnormally thick sclera). The thickened sclera compresses the vortex veins, impairing choroidal venous drainage and promoting uveal effusion. Treatment is sclerectomy (vortex vein decompression) in symptomatic cases.
options: Severe hypertension causing exudative choroidal detachment
Systemic lupus erythematosus causing immune complex deposition
Post-operative complication from trabeculectomy bleb overfiltration
Nanophthalmos with abnormal scleral thickness impeding vortex vein drainage

questions.explanation: Chlamydial ophthalmia neonatorum (Chlamydia trachomatis) has an incubation period of 5–14 days after birth. It presents with mucopurulent discharge and eyelid swelling. Unlike gonococcal disease, systemic treatment (oral erythromycin or azithromycin) is required to eradicate the organism and prevent pneumonitis.
questions.question: Chlamydial ophthalmia neonatorum typically presents at what age after birth?

questions.explanation: Anterior uveitis is the most common form of uveitis and is most frequently associated with HLA-B27 positive seronegative spondyloarthropathies: ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis (Reiter's syndrome), psoriatic arthritis, and inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's, ulcerative colitis). HLA-B27 should be tested in all patients with recurrent anterior uveitis.
questions.question: Anterior uveitis (iridocyclitis) is MOST commonly associated with which systemic condition?

questions.explanation: The combination of proptosis, restricted ocular movement, marked lid swelling, and systemic fever indicates infection extending into the orbit itself, characteristic of orbital cellulitis. This is an ophthalmic and systemic emergency because of the risk of intracranial spread. Immediate imaging and intravenous antibiotics are required.
questions.question: A patient presenting with severe eyelid swelling, proptosis, restricted eye movement, and fever is MOST likely to have

questions.explanation: Medical CN III palsies (e.g., from diabetes, hypertension causing ischemia) typically spare the pupil because ischemia affects the inner core fibers while outer parasympathetic fibers remain intact. Surgical (compressive) palsies, such as from aneurysms, compress the outer pupillary fibers first, causing pupil involvement. This distinction guides urgency of investigation for aneurysm.
options: Medical palsy is more painful based on typical clinical findings
Medical palsy spares the pupil; surgical palsy involves the pupil
Surgical palsy involves only the inferior rectus in the majority of documented cases
questions.question: Which of the following features differentiates a 'medical' from a 'surgical' third nerve palsy?

questions.explanation: Nasal retinal fibres, which carry information from the temporal visual field, decussate at the optic chiasm and are vulnerable to midline compression by a pituitary mass. Temporal retinal fibres do not cross and are relatively spared. The result is bitemporal hemianopia.
questions.question: A child with a pituitary tumour develops loss of temporal visual fields in both eyes while central and nasal fields remain intact. Which fibres are compressed?

questions.explanation: Canalicular obstruction from Actinomyces (which forms casts/concretions in canaliculi) or other causes such as viral infection, 5-FU toxicity, or Stevens-Johnson syndrome, requires conjunctivodacryocystorhinostomy (CDCR) with insertion of a Jones tube for permanent drainage. Standard DCR is insufficient as it does not bypass canalicular obstruction.
questions.question: Canalicular obstruction from Actinomyces infection is treated definitively by:

questions.explanation: The internal limiting membrane forms the innermost boundary of the retina, adjacent to the vitreous cavity, and is composed of Muller cell footplates. Surgeons peel it during macular hole or epiretinal membrane surgery to relieve tangential traction. It lies anterior to the nerve fibre and ganglion cell layers.
questions.question: A patient undergoing vitrectomy has the innermost retinal layer stripped during membrane peeling. Which layer is this?

questions.explanation: Rubeosis iridis refers to abnormal new vessel growth on the iris surface, typically arising as a response to widespread retinal ischaemia releasing angiogenic factors such as VEGF. Untreated, these vessels can grow into the anterior chamber angle, leading to neovascular glaucoma. Common causes include proliferative diabetic retinopathy and central retinal vein occlusion.
questions.question: A patient develops new iris vessels growing across the pupillary margin and angle following extensive retinal ischaemia. Which term describes this neovascularisation?

questions.explanation: Corynebacterium diphtheriae causes diphtheritic (membranous) conjunctivitis characterised by formation of a true membrane (pseudomembrane) that bleeds when removed, adherent to the conjunctival surface. Systemic diphtheria is rare with vaccination but remains a concern in unimmunised populations. Urgent antitoxin and systemic penicillin are required in addition to local treatment.
questions.question: Which organism causes 'red eye' with a classic pseudomembrane on the conjunctival surface?

questions.explanation: Glaucomatous visual field defects follow an arcuate pattern that respects the horizontal midline because retinal nerve fibres are anatomically arranged in arcuate bundles converging on the optic disc above and below the horizontal raphe. Damage to these bundles at the optic nerve head produces field defects that reflect this underlying fibre architecture. This pattern differs from field defects caused by chiasmal or retrochiasmal lesions, which do not respect the horizontal midline in the same way.
questions.question: A patient with glaucoma has visual field testing showing an arcuate defect respecting the horizontal midline. Which anatomical feature explains this characteristic pattern?

options: Calcium hydroxyapatite crystals from aqueous humor
Fibrin clots from disrupted blood-aqueous barrier
Inflammatory cells and fibrin depositing on endothelium
Viral inclusion bodies from CMV endotheliitis
questions.question: Keratic precipitates (KPs) deposited on the corneal endothelium in uveitis are composed of:
questions.explanation: Keratic precipitates (KPs) are aggregates of inflammatory cells (lymphocytes, macrophages, plasma cells) and fibrin that deposit on the corneal endothelium due to inflammation. Mutton-fat KPs (large, greasy) suggest granulomatous uveitis (sarcoidosis, tuberculosis, leprosy, Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada). Fine stellate KPs suggest non-granulomatous or Fuchs' heterochromic cyclitis.

questions.question: Corneal collagen cross-linking (CXL) is the preferred treatment to halt progression in which corneal condition?
options: Keratoconus in a young patient with documented progression
Bacterial keratitis with progressive stromal thinning
questions.explanation: Corneal collagen cross-linking (CXL) using riboflavin drops and ultraviolet-A light strengthens corneal collagen bonds, halting progression in keratoconus. It is indicated in young patients with documented progression (increasing cone steepness on topography). CXL does not reverse existing ectasia but prevents further thinning and protrusion.

Pseudomonas aeruginosa is the most common and virulent cause of bacterial corneal ulcer in contact lens wearers, causing rapidly progressive stromal necrosis. The ulcer characteristically shows a grey-green necrotic infiltrate with undermined edges. Urgent fluoroquinolone treatment is required to prevent corneal perforation and permanent vision loss.
questions.question: The MOST common cause of bacterial corneal ulcer in contact lens wearers is:

questions.explanation: A flat, vascularised bleb with rising intraocular pressure suggests that scarring has occurred at the scleral flap or subconjunctival space, reducing aqueous outflow through the surgical drainage pathway, termed bleb failure. This may require additional medical therapy, bleb revision, or further surgical intervention. Regular postoperative monitoring helps detect this complication early.
options: Bleb failure from scarring at the drainage site
Early acute infection of the bleb
questions.question: Several months after trabeculectomy, a patient's bleb appears flat, vascularised, and the intraocular pressure has gradually risen again. What does this suggest?

questions.explanation: Gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum requires systemic treatment due to the risk of corneal perforation and systemic dissemination. IV/IM ceftriaxone 25-50 mg/kg (max 125 mg) stat is the treatment of choice, alongside hourly saline irrigation until discharge resolves. Topical therapy alone is insufficient for gonococcal ON due to the penetrative capacity of Neisseria gonorrhoeae.
questions.question: A patient with gonorrheal ophthalmia neonatorum is started on therapy. The antimicrobial route of choice is:
options: Topical chloramphenicol alone based on typical clinical findings
IV or IM ceftriaxone 25-50 mg/kg stat
Oral erythromycin for 2 weeks in the majority of documented cases
secondary rebleeding and rise in intraocular pressure
questions.question: A patient with traumatic hyphema requires close monitoring mainly because of the risk of
questions.explanation: Rebleeding into the anterior chamber after the initial hyphema carries a higher risk of significant intraocular pressure elevation and corneal bloodstaining than the original bleed. This complication typically occurs within the first few days after injury. Close monitoring of pressure and clot size during this period is therefore essential.

questions.question: The two most important risk factors for hypertensive retinopathy that are modifiable are:
questions.explanation: Among modifiable risk factors, systolic and diastolic blood pressure elevation are the most directly related to hypertensive retinopathy development and grade. Smoking contributes through vasoconstriction and endothelial dysfunction. Controlling blood pressure below 140/90 mmHg is the primary treatment, and smoking cessation reduces cardiovascular and retinal vascular risk. Age and race are non-modifiable risk factors.

options: Diffuse retinal whitening with cherry-red spot at the macula
Disc swelling with peripapillary hemorrhages in all four quadrants
A sector of superficial flame-shaped haemorrhages
Yellow sub-RPE deposits at the posterior pole
questions.question: Central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO) causes a characteristic fundus appearance of:
questions.explanation: CRAO causes infarction of the inner retina, producing diffuse retinal whitening/oedema from ischaemic cell swelling. The fovea, which is supplied by the choroidal circulation (not central retinal artery), remains red against the white ischaemic background, producing the pathognomonic cherry-red spot at the macula. Vision loss is sudden, profound, and painless. It is a true ocular emergency.

Sebaceous gland carcinoma is a rare but highly malignant eyelid tumor that frequently masquerades as a recurrent or atypical chalazion, causing significant diagnostic delay. Any chalazion that recurs after adequate treatment, is atypical, or occurs in an elderly patient should be biopsied to exclude sebaceous gland carcinoma. It has a high metastatic rate.
questions.question: Sebaceous gland carcinoma of the eyelid can masquerade as which benign condition, leading to delayed diagnosis?

questions.explanation: During acute PACG, the pupil is typically mid-dilated (4–5 mm) and fixed (non-reactive to light) because ischaemia from the extremely high IOP paralyses the iris sphincter muscle. This mid-dilated, fixed pupil is pathognomonic of acute PACG and helps distinguish it from other causes of acute painful red eye.
questions.question: The pupil in acute primary angle-closure glaucoma is characteristically:
options: Unequal but reactive in both eyes
Source of aqueous tear production for lubrication
First-line immunological defense secreting sIgA at the ocular surface
Regulator of intraocular pressure through anterior chamber drainage
questions.question: The conjunctiva's MALT (mucosal associated lymphoid tissue) functions primarily as a:
questions.explanation: Conjunctival MALT is located in the subepithelial layer and functions as a regional immunological defense, secreting secretory IgA (sIgA) at the ocular surface to neutralize pathogens. It also participates in immune surveillance. Disruption of MALT (by topical medications, surgery, or radiation) can impair local conjunctival immunity and increase susceptibility to infection.

options: Bacterial corneal ulcer with stromal infiltration
questions.explanation: Trachoma characteristically produces a superior corneal pannus — fibrovascular ingrowth from the superior limbus into the upper corneal stroma. This is caused by repeated episodes of active trachomatous inflammation (TF and TI stages) stimulating corneal vascularisation. Pannus formation, combined with trichiasis-induced scarring, contributes to progressive corneal opacity and blindness.
questions.question: Corneal pannus formation is a vascular ingrowth from the limbus MOST classically associated with:

options: a compressive lesion such as a posterior communicating artery aneurysm
questions.explanation: Pupil involvement in a third nerve palsy suggests external compression of the peripherally located parasympathetic fibres, classically from an expanding posterior communicating artery aneurysm. Pupil-sparing palsies are more typical of ischemic microvascular disease. This distinction determines whether urgent vascular imaging is required.
questions.question: A patient with a new third nerve palsy has a fully dilated, non-reactive pupil in addition to ptosis and ophthalmoplegia. This finding should raise urgent suspicion for

questions.explanation: Enucleation (surgical removal of the globe) is indicated in retinoblastoma when the tumor is advanced and fills most of the vitreous with no remaining visual potential, and when globe-conserving treatments are not feasible. In bilateral disease, the more severely affected eye may be enucleated while the fellow eye is treated conservatively. Advances in chemotherapy and focal treatments have greatly reduced the need for enucleation.
options: Advanced unilateral tumors filling the vitreous with no visual potential
Small unilateral tumors amenable to focal therapy under standard examination conditions
As initial treatment in all cases regardless of stage in most clinical presentations
questions.question: Enucleation of the eye in retinoblastoma is indicated in which clinical scenario?

questions.explanation: Alkali burns continue to penetrate and damage tissue as long as the causative agent remains in contact with the eye, so immediate and copious irrigation is the single most important first step. Delaying irrigation to apply medication allows ongoing tissue destruction. All other interventions follow only after adequate irrigation and pH normalisation.
options: copious irrigation of the ocular surface
questions.question: A patient presents immediately after an alkali splash to the eye. The FIRST and MOST critical management step is

questions.explanation: Iron-containing IOFBs release ferrous ions over time, causing haemosiderosis—toxic iron deposition that damages the corneal endothelium, causes stromal staining, and leads to death of retinal neuronal cells (siderosis bulbi). Copper IOFBs cause chalcosis. The toxicity profile of the IOFB material determines the urgency and approach to removal.
questions.question: A metallic intraocular foreign body (IOFB) that remains untreated will MOST likely cause:
options: Haemosiderosis with toxic damage to corneal endothelium and retinal neurons
Spontaneous resolution over time as commonly encountered in practice in most clinical presentations
Gradual reduction in IOP during routine ophthalmic assessment under standard examination conditions

questions.question: A child is found to have one eye significantly more myopic than the other, left uncorrected for several years. Which visual consequence is most likely?
questions.explanation: Unequal refractive error between the eyes, or anisometropia, deprives the more ametropic eye of a clear retinal image during the critical period of visual development. The brain suppresses the blurred image, leading to amblyopia if uncorrected. Early detection and correction are essential to prevent permanent visual loss.

questions.question: In a patient with established diabetic retinopathy, which follow-up interval is recommended for background (mild NPDR) retinopathy?
questions.explanation: For mild-to-moderate non-proliferative (background) diabetic retinopathy without clinically significant macular edema, annual or 6-monthly ophthalmic review is recommended depending on systemic control and other risk factors. More frequent review (3-monthly) is required for severe NPDR, PDR, or CSME. Waiting only until symptoms develop is unsafe as significant retinopathy can exist without symptoms until vision is irreversibly lost.

options: New vessel formation at the optic disc in most clinical presentations in most clinical presentations
Ischemia of the nerve fiber layer under standard examination conditions under standard examination conditions
Hard exudate deposition along venous walls
Microaneurysm formation at venous branch points
Thickening of the arteriolar wall compressing the underlying vein at crossing points
questions.explanation: Gunn's sign (AV nicking/nipping) occurs because hypertension causes arteriosclerotic thickening and increased rigidity of the arteriolar wall. At arteriovenous crossing points, where artery and vein share a common adventitial sheath, the thickened arteriolar wall compresses the underlying vein, causing apparent constriction, deflection, or banking of blood in the vein distal to the crossing. This is a classic sign of chronic hypertensive retinopathy.
questions.question: Gunn's sign (arteriovenous nipping) in hypertensive retinopathy results from:

options: Raised IOP exceeding 21 mmHg in both eyes
Retinal detachment occurring secondary to vitreous traction forces
Progressive degeneration of the lens causing gradual visual loss
A progressive optic neuropathy with cupping and visual field loss
Inflammation of the uveal tract with IOP rise
questions.question: Which statement BEST defines glaucoma as a disease?
questions.explanation: Glaucoma is fundamentally a progressive optic neuropathy characterised by optic nerve head cupping and visual field loss. Raised IOP is a major risk factor but not the defining criterion, as evidenced by normal-tension glaucoma. Optic nerve damage and field changes are the disease hallmarks.

questions.question: In the management of acute iridocyclitis (anterior uveitis), which drug combination is MOST appropriate?
questions.explanation: Acute anterior uveitis is managed with a cycloplegic mydriatic (to prevent synechiae formation by dilating and resting the pupil) and topical corticosteroids (to suppress inflammation). The cycloplegic also relieves ciliary spasm, reducing pain. Topical antibiotics are only added if an infective cause is suspected. Beta-blockers are used for IOP control as an adjunct if pressure is elevated.
options: Topical beta-blocker and carbonic anhydrase inhibitor
Topical antihistamine and mast cell stabilizer

questions.question: A patient with facial nerve palsy is unable to fully close the eyelids, resulting in a persistent inferior corneal epithelial defect. Which term describes this corneal condition?
questions.explanation: Exposure keratopathy results from incomplete eyelid closure, or lagophthalmos, leaving the inferior cornea chronically exposed and susceptible to desiccation and epithelial breakdown. Facial nerve palsy is a common cause because it impairs orbicularis oculi function needed for lid closure. This differs from neurotrophic keratopathy, which arises from loss of corneal sensory innervation rather than mechanical exposure.

Cataract is the most common cause of blindness worldwide, accounting for approximately 51% of global blindness according to WHO data. It is particularly prevalent in low-income countries where surgical services are limited. Importantly, cataract blindness is reversible with surgery. Glaucoma is the most common cause of irreversible blindness worldwide.
questions.question: The MOST common cause of irreversible blindness worldwide according to WHO data is:

questions.explanation: The defining hallmark that separates proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR) from non-proliferative (NPDR) is the presence of neovascularization—new blood vessel growth on the disc (NVD) or elsewhere on the retinal surface (NVE), or on the iris (rubeosis iridis). All other features (microaneurysms, hemorrhages, exudates, cotton wool spots, venous changes, IRMAs) can be seen in NPDR. PDR indicates severe retinal ischemia and warrants urgent treatment.
questions.question: Which ocular finding differentiates non-proliferative from proliferative diabetic retinopathy?
options: Cotton wool spots in the posterior pole

questions.explanation: A Pancoast tumour at the lung apex characteristically compresses the second-order sympathetic neuron as it passes near the superior mediastinum on its way to the superior cervical ganglion. This produces the classic triad of Horner's syndrome. Recognising this localisation prompts chest imaging in any new Horner's presentation.
questions.question: A smoker presents with ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis of one side of the face, and imaging reveals an apical lung mass. The lesion is compressing which neuron in the oculosympathetic pathway?

questions.explanation: Myopia results from the eye's refractive power being too strong or the axial length too long, so parallel rays focus anterior to the retina. A concave, or minus, lens diverges incoming rays before they enter the eye, moving the focal point back onto the retina. Convex lenses would worsen the error by adding further convergent power.
questions.question: A young myopic patient's image of a distant object focuses in front of the retina. Which lens type corrects this refractive error?

questions.explanation: Failure to achieve target IOP despite maximum tolerated medical therapy (four or more medications) is a clear indication for surgical management of glaucoma. Trabeculectomy is the most commonly performed procedure. Continuing to add medications provides minimal additional IOP reduction and increases side effects, cost, and non-compliance.
questions.question: When using four or more glaucoma medications without reaching target IOP, the NEXT appropriate management step is:
options: Observe for another 6 months without change

questions.question: The parasympathetic fibres responsible for pupillary constriction reach the eye by travelling from the ciliary ganglion through which nerves?
questions.explanation: Postganglionic parasympathetic fibres synapse in the ciliary ganglion and then travel to the iris sphincter and ciliary muscle via the short ciliary nerves. The long ciliary nerves instead carry sensory and sympathetic fibres. Knowing this pathway clarifies why ciliary ganglion lesions produce a tonic, poorly reactive pupil.

questions.question: At an arteriovenous crossing, a hypertensive patient's fundus shows the underlying vein appearing to taper and disappear beneath a thickened arteriole. This finding, called Gunn's sign, results from
options: lipid deposition within the vein wall
new vessel growth at the crossing point
retinal detachment at the crossing site
arteriolar wall thickening compressing the underlying vein
questions.explanation: Gunn's sign, or arteriovenous nicking, occurs when a sclerotic, thickened arteriole shares a common adventitial sheath with the vein at their crossing point and compresses it, producing the appearance of venous tapering. This is a mechanical compressive effect rather than true occlusion or thrombosis. It is a classic sign of chronic hypertensive vascular change.

questions.question: The term 'buphthalmos' refers to which condition?
questions.explanation: Buphthalmos (Greek: 'ox eye') describes the enlarged globe in congenital glaucoma. In infants, the distensible ocular coats (sclera and cornea) expand under elevated IOP, causing progressive globe enlargement. This is pathognomonic of infantile glaucoma and does not occur in adult-onset glaucoma.
options: Globe enlargement due to congenital glaucoma

questions.question: The aqueous humor is primarily drained through which structure to maintain normal intraocular pressure?
questions.explanation: The conventional drainage pathway for aqueous humor involves the trabecular meshwork located at the anterior chamber angle, followed by Schlemm's canal, then episcleral veins. Imbalance between production and drainage raises IOP, a key risk factor for glaucoma.

When vitreous hemorrhage prevents a direct view of the retina, B-scan ultrasound can still assess retinal attachment status and detect associated tractional detachment. Fundus photography and slit-lamp examination are limited by the same media opacity that obscures direct visualisation. This information guides the timing and type of surgical intervention needed.
questions.question: A diabetic patient develops a sudden vitreous hemorrhage obscuring the fundus view. The MOST appropriate imaging modality to assess the retina in this situation is

questions.explanation: Pars plana vitrectomy allows controlled access to the posterior segment to retrieve a foreign body while preserving an intact, clear lens. Cataract extraction is unnecessary and would risk lens damage if the lens is not already involved. This approach minimises additional trauma to uninjured structures.
questions.question: A surgeon plans to remove a posterior segment intraocular foreign body while the crystalline lens remains clear and intact. The preferred surgical approach is

questions.explanation: Acetazolamide inhibits carbonic anhydrase within the ciliary epithelium, reducing bicarbonate-dependent aqueous humour secretion and thereby lowering intraocular pressure. This mechanism is distinct from beta-blockers, which act through a different secretory pathway, or prostaglandins, which enhance outflow. Its systemic use is generally reserved for pressures not controlled by topical therapy alone.
options: blocking beta-adrenergic receptors in the ciliary body
inhibiting carbonic anhydrase to reduce aqueous formation
questions.question: A patient with glaucoma is started on acetazolamide tablets in addition to topical drops. This oral agent lowers intraocular pressure by

questions.explanation: Adenoviral conjunctivitis is highly contagious, spreading readily among close contacts, and classically presents with watery discharge and tender preauricular lymphadenopathy. It is typically self-limiting but hygiene measures are essential to prevent spread. Epidemic keratoconjunctivitis is a more severe adenoviral variant with corneal involvement.
questions.question: A patient presents with a red eye, watery discharge, and a highly contagious presentation spreading through a household. Preauricular lymphadenopathy is present. What is the likely cause?

questions.explanation: Thin corneas require less force to flatten, underestimating true IOP, while thick corneas require more force, overestimating true IOP on Goldmann tonometry. CCT is an independent risk factor for glaucoma conversion — thin corneas indicate higher glaucoma risk. CCT measurement is now routine in glaucoma assessment.
questions.question: Regarding central corneal thickness (CCT) and tonometry, which statement is CORRECT?
options: Thick corneas cause underestimation of IOP
Thin corneas cause overestimation of IOP
IOP readings are always corrected by adding measured corneal thickness
Thin corneas cause underestimation and thick corneas cause overestimation of IOP
CCT has no effect on Goldmann readings

questions.question: In acute PACG, the IOP elevation can reach:
questions.explanation: During acute PACG, IOP can rise dramatically to 40–80 mmHg or higher as aqueous is completely unable to drain through the closed angle. Such extreme IOP elevation causes ischaemia of the iris (glaukomflecken), corneal endothelial decompensation, optic nerve ischaemia, and intense pain. This constitutes a true ophthalmic emergency.

questions.question: The Snellen chart largest first-line letter subtends a visual angle of 1 minute of arc for a normal eye at which distance?
questions.explanation: The largest letter on the Snellen chart (top line, 60 m line) subtends a visual angle of 1 minute of arc at 60 meters for a person with normal visual acuity. Subsequent lines represent 36 m, 24 m, 18 m, 12 m, 9 m, and 6 m. This is why the 6-meter line corresponds to normal 6/6 vision.

questions.question: A patient reads only the top line of the Snellen chart at 6 metres, a line normally read at 60 metres. How is this visual acuity recorded?
questions.explanation: The Snellen fraction numerator represents the testing distance and the denominator represents the distance at which a normal eye reads that line. Reading only the largest line at 6 metres, normally legible at 60 metres, is recorded as 6/60. This reflects markedly reduced visual acuity requiring further refractive or pathological assessment.

CRAO presents with sudden, painless, severe monocular visual loss (often hand movements or light perception only). The fundus shows diffuse retinal oedema (pale, white), cherry-red foveal spot (intact choroidal circulation visible through thin fovea), and a relative APD. It is an ophthalmic emergency with a narrow therapeutic window.
questions.question: Central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO) presents characteristically with:
options: Gradual bilateral progressive visual loss over years
Sudden painless profound monocular visual loss with cherry-red spot at fovea
Acute painful red eye with raised IOP
Gradual loss of peripheral field in a classic nasal step pattern

questions.explanation: Cataract surgery in diabetic patients carries an increased risk of worsening pre-existing diabetic macular oedema and accelerated progression of diabetic retinopathy postoperatively. Careful preoperative retinal assessment and optimisation of glycaemic control are recommended before elective surgery. Close postoperative monitoring for macular oedema is important to preserve visual outcomes in these patients.
questions.question: A patient with diabetes is scheduled for cataract surgery. The surgical team notes that diabetic patients face increased risk of which specific postoperative complication?

questions.explanation: Preservatives in multi-dose ophthalmic preparations (e.g., benzalkonium chloride) are essential to prevent microbial contamination during the in-use period, as repeated opening of the container introduces risk of contamination. High-risk microbial contaminants include Pseudomonas aeruginosa, which can cause devastating ocular infections. Preservative-free formulations are available for patients with hypersensitivity.
options: Prevent microbial contamination during use of multi-dose containers
Increase shelf life by preventing oxidation in most clinical presentations
Enhance drug penetration across the cornea under standard examination conditions
