questions.question: Ophthalmic preparations containing antimicrobial preservatives are required PRIMARILY to:

questions.explanation: In congenital or long-standing Horner's syndrome, loss of sympathetic trophic influence on melanocytes can leave the affected iris paler than the fellow eye, termed hypochromia iridis. This finding supports a chronic rather than acute sympathetic lesion. It helps date the onset of the underlying condition.
options: congenital hypochromia iridis from sympathetic denervation
questions.question: A patient with anisocoria has a smaller pupil that dilates poorly in dim light, along with mild ptosis and lighter iris colour on that side since birth. The lighter iris colour is best explained by
A patient with Graves' ophthalmopathy has visual acuity dropping from 6/6 to 6/24 with an afferent pupillary defect. This presentation suggests:
questions.explanation: Dysthyroid optic neuropathy (DON) occurs when enlarged fibrotic extraocular muscles at the orbital apex compress the optic nerve, reducing visual acuity and producing a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD). It is a vision-threatening complication of severe Graves' ophthalmopathy requiring urgent systemic steroids and/or orbital decompression. Color vision loss (desaturation) often precedes acuity loss and is an early warning sign.
options: Macular edema from thyroid-related choroidal changes as commonly encountered in practice
Compressive optic neuropathy from enlarged extraocular muscles
Retinal detachment from orbital congestion during routine ophthalmic assessment

questions.question: Primary congenital glaucoma most commonly presents within:
options: Young adulthood between 18 and 25 years of age
First 3 years of life, with 86% within the first year
questions.explanation: Primary congenital glaucoma (PCG) typically presents within the first year of life in 86% of cases — 40% at birth, 34% between birth and 6 months. The annual incidence is approximately 1 in 10,000 live births. It results from developmental abnormality of the anterior chamber angle causing obstructed aqueous outflow.

options: It removes the entire trabecular meshwork
It always requires general anaesthesia only
It cannot be combined with cataract surgery
It avoids the need for a surgical iridectomy
It eliminates any risk of hypotony completely
questions.question: A patient with glaucoma requiring surgery is offered a smaller, non-valved implanted device placed under a scleral flap rather than traditional excisional surgery. What is a key difference of this technique?
questions.explanation: The mini glaucoma shunt device is inserted under a scleral flap to regulate aqueous outflow into the subconjunctival space, similar in concept to trabeculectomy but without the need for a surgical iridectomy. It can often be combined with cataract surgery in a single procedure. It aims to provide more predictable pressure control with a potentially faster recovery.

Senile (involutional) ectropion occurs due to age-related horizontal laxity of the lower lid tissues, including the canthal tendons and orbicularis muscle. This allows the lid margin to sag outward (evert), causing epiphora and conjunctival exposure. Cicatricial ectropion involves scarring, paralytic ectropion involves CN VII palsy.
questions.question: Senile ectropion causes the lid margin to turn outward. The primary mechanism in this form is:
options: Cicatricial traction from anterior lamellar scarring
Paralytic weakness of the facial nerve
Involutional laxity of lower lid tissues with aging
Mechanical pressure from lower lid tumor

questions.explanation: Leber's hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON) is a mitochondrial inherited disease predominantly affecting young males (male:female = 4:1). It causes bilateral sequential or simultaneous painless visual loss with cecocentral scotoma. The mitochondrial DNA mutations at positions 11778, 3460, and 14484 account for 95% of cases. Males are more severely affected due to unknown modifying factors. There is no proven effective treatment.
questions.question: The MOST common hereditary optic neuropathy with bilateral painless visual loss in young males is:
A child at birth has an estimated visual acuity of approximately:
questions.explanation: At birth, the estimated normal visual acuity is 3/60. By 1 year of age, it improves to approximately 6/12, and by 1–6 years, it reaches 6/6 or better. This corresponds to the increasing hypermetropia (normal in infancy) resolving with eye growth. VA assessment in infants requires behavioral testing methods.

options: Elevated IOP alone without structural or functional changes
Optic neuropathy with characteristic visual field loss and structural disc damage
Elevated IOP with corneal edema and anterior chamber cells
Optic nerve pallor with preserved visual field and normal IOP
Painful red eye with markedly elevated IOP only
questions.question: Glaucoma is characteristically defined by which combination of features?
questions.explanation: Glaucoma is defined as a progressive optic neuropathy with characteristic visual field defects (arcuate scotoma, nasal step, altitudinal defect) and structural optic disc changes (enlarged cup, RNFL thinning, neuroretinal rim notching). Elevated IOP is a major risk factor but is neither necessary nor sufficient for the diagnosis. Normal tension glaucoma has IOP within normal range.

options: Fluorescein staining with cobalt-blue filter illumination
B-scan ultrasonography of the posterior segment
questions.explanation: Corneal abrasion (breach of corneal epithelium) is diagnosed by instilling fluorescein dye and examining under cobalt-blue filter illumination. Abraded epithelium stains bright yellow-green. Linear patterns suggest foreign body under the upper lid. Management includes antibiotic prophylaxis and topical cycloplegia for pain relief.
questions.question: Corneal abrasion is best clinically diagnosed using:

questions.explanation: Episcleritis involves only the superficial episcleral vessels and is generally self-limiting, distinguishing it from the deeper, more painful, and potentially sight-threatening scleritis. The blanching response to phenylephrine reflects the superficial location of the inflamed vessels. This distinction avoids unnecessary systemic work-up for a benign, self-resolving condition.
questions.question: A patient is told that their red, mildly tender eye is self-limiting, blanches with phenylephrine, and requires only lubrication. Compared with scleritis, this presentation of episcleritis is
options: milder and confined to the superficial episcleral vessels

questions.question: Laser photocoagulation treatment in diabetic maculopathy is specifically aimed at which pathological change?
questions.explanation: Focal/grid laser photocoagulation for diabetic maculopathy is specifically indicated for clinically significant macular oedema (CSMO), defined by thickening or hard exudates within 500 microns of the fovea. Laser coagulates leaking microaneurysms and creates a diffuse grid pattern to reduce oedema. Intravitreal anti-VEGF injections are now preferred for centre-involving DMO affecting the fovea.
options: Destroying new vessels at the disc to prevent vitreous hemorrhage
Treating clinically significant macular oedema (CSMO) to preserve vision
Inducing choroidal neovascularization to supplement retinal oxygenation
Sealing peripheral retinal breaks in tractional retinal detachment
Reducing IOP by creating drainage through the posterior segment

questions.question: Neuroretinal rim loss in glaucoma follows the ISNT rule, meaning which pole is FIRST affected?
questions.explanation: Glaucomatous neuroretinal rim loss begins at the inferior and superior poles of the optic disc, corresponding to the dense arcuate nerve fibre bundles entering the disc at these locations. The ISNT rule (Inferior > Superior > Nasal > Temporal) defines normal rim tissue distribution; glaucoma violates this by preferentially thinning the inferior and superior rims.

Punctate epithelial erosions (PEE) are small superficial fluorescein-staining defects scattered across the corneal epithelium. They are a non-specific sign of epithelial distress with multiple causes: dry eye, blepharitis, trichiasis, contact lens overwear, topical drug toxicity, UV exposure (arc eye/welder's flash), and viral conjunctivitis. The distribution pattern helps identify the cause.
questions.question: A patient presents with photophobia, tearing, and a foreign body sensation. Slit lamp reveals multiple small epithelial erosions staining with fluorescein scattered across the cornea. This pattern is termed:

questions.explanation: Vernal keratoconjunctivitis is an allergic condition marked by intense itching and characteristic giant papillae giving a cobblestone appearance on the upper tarsal conjunctiva. It typically occurs in atopic children and adolescents, often seasonally. Recognising this pattern avoids mistaking it for an infective conjunctivitis requiring antibiotics.
questions.question: A young patient with intense itching, giant cobblestone papillae on the upper tarsal conjunctiva, and a history of atopy is BEST diagnosed with
The drug of choice for mass drug administration (MDA) against trachoma at the community level is:
questions.explanation: Single-dose oral azithromycin (1 g in adults, 20 mg/kg in children) is the WHO-recommended drug for mass drug administration against trachoma. It achieves high tissue concentrations, has a long half-life, and single-dose regimen ensures compliance. Community-wide MDA programmes reduce trachoma prevalence significantly.

Electrical injuries to the eye can cause corneal burns at the entry point, cataracts (typically anterior subcapsular forming tree-like 'lightning' pattern), vitreous haemorrhage, retinal damage, and optic nerve injury from electrical current. However, permanent globe enlargement does not occur — the sclera is a firm, non-distensible structure in adults that does not expand from electrical injury.
questions.question: Electrical injury to the eye may cause all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Cataract formation, usually anterior subcapsular in type
Permanent enlargement of the globe from electrical expansion

questions.question: The FIRST-LINE conservative management for a chalazion includes:
questions.explanation: Conservative management of chalazia begins with warm compresses and lid massage to soften the retained meibomian secretion and promote drainage. More than 50% of chalazia resolve with conservative treatment. Intralesional steroid or 5-fluorouracil injection is used for moderate-sized lesions, and surgical incision/curettage for larger ones.

questions.question: A patient with refractory glaucoma despite previous trabeculectomy is being considered for a tube-shunt device. In which situation is this device typically preferred over repeat trabeculectomy?
questions.explanation: Glaucoma drainage devices are particularly useful in eyes with extensive conjunctival scarring from previous surgeries, where standard trabeculectomy is more likely to fail due to poor bleb formation. They provide a reliable, tube-mediated drainage pathway independent of conjunctival healing at the immediate surgical site. Long-term studies support their use in complex or refractory glaucoma cases.
options: Eyes with extensive conjunctival scarring from prior surgery
Eyes undergoing their first glaucoma surgery
Mild glaucoma with early field loss
Patients with no previous ocular surgery
Pupillary block caused by progressive lens enlargement
Posterior synechiae formation from chronic recurrent uveitis
Anteriorly rotated ciliary processes pushing peripheral iris into the angle
Pupillary block from a thick lens
questions.question: Plateau iris configuration predisposes to angle closure by which mechanism?
questions.explanation: In plateau iris syndrome, anteriorly rotated ciliary processes mechanically push the peripheral iris into the angle even after laser iridotomy (which eliminates pupillary block). This distinct mechanism means iridotomy alone does not fully prevent angle closure. Argon laser peripheral iridoplasty or surgery targeting the ciliary processes may be required.

In chronic papilledema (from longstanding raised ICP), optociliary shunt vessels (collateral vessels between the central retinal and choroidal circulations at the disc) may develop, and progressive optic nerve axonal death leads to secondary (consecutive) optic atrophy—where the disc appears pale despite ongoing swelling ('atrophic papilledema'). These features indicate long-standing elevated ICP with established axonal damage and represent a different stage from acute papilledema.
questions.question: The 'sandwich' pattern of optic disc change in chronic papilledema versus acute papilledema is characterized by which feature seen only in chronic cases?
options: Blurred disc margins superiorly and inferiorly in most clinical presentations
Optociliary shunt vessels and secondary optic atrophy
Cotton wool spots surrounding the disc under standard examination conditions

questions.explanation: Bell's phenomenon rotates the cornea upward and under the protective upper lid during forceful eyelid closure, reducing the chance of direct corneal trauma or desiccation. This reflex is a protective mechanism rather than one related to visual acuity or tear production. Its absence, as in some facial nerve palsies, increases corneal exposure risk.
questions.question: The protective blink and Bell's phenomenon, in which the eye rotates upward during forced lid closure, PRIMARILY serve to
options: shield the cornea from direct injury
Bilateral disc swelling with preserved visual acuity from raised intracranial pressure
Presence of visual loss and color desaturation in one eye only
Unilateral disc pallor from chronic optic nerve compression
Flame-shaped hemorrhages limited to one quadrant around the disc
Marked disc elevation with hard exudates at the macula (macular star)
questions.explanation: Papilloedema is specifically bilateral optic disc swelling from raised intracranial pressure. Visual acuity is typically preserved until late, distinguishing it from optic neuritis (where VA is markedly reduced). It is caused by meningitis, cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, idiopathic intracranial hypertension, and space-occupying lesions. Urgent neuroimaging and lumbar puncture are required.
questions.question: Papilloedema is distinguished from other causes of disc swelling by which key feature?
Fundus fluorescein angiography is performed in a diabetic patient primarily to
questions.explanation: Fluorescein angiography highlights areas of vascular leakage and capillary non-perfusion by tracking dye movement through the retinal circulation, information not obtainable from routine fundus photography alone. It plays no role in measuring pressure, corneal thickness, or axial length. This detailed vascular map guides decisions about laser treatment location.
options: identify areas of capillary leakage and retinal non-perfusion
measure axial length of the eye

questions.question: Sebaceous (meibomian) gland carcinoma of the eyelid masquerades as which common benign condition?
questions.explanation: Sebaceous gland carcinoma (SGC) is a rare but malignant eyelid tumour that frequently masquerades as a recurrent or refractory chalazion (meibomian gland blockage) or unilateral blepharitis. This masquerade syndrome leads to delayed diagnosis. Any recurrent chalazion or unilateral blepharitis that does not respond to standard treatment should be biopsied to exclude SGC.

questions.question: Venous drainage of the orbit flows primarily through which sinus, making orbital infections potentially life-threatening?
questions.explanation: The superior and inferior ophthalmic veins drain into the cavernous sinus. Orbital infections can spread through this route to cause cavernous sinus thrombosis, a life-threatening complication with fever, proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, and meningeal signs. This is why orbital cellulitis requires urgent IV antibiotics.

options: Peptic ulcer disease in most clinical presentations
Chronic kidney disease under standard examination conditions
questions.explanation: Systemic corticosteroid use (as in asthma, rheumatoid arthritis, and organ transplant patients) is a well-recognized cause of posterior subcapsular cataract. The PMH is specifically designed to identify such risk factors and potential drug interactions affecting ocular health. Hypertension is a risk factor for hypertensive retinopathy, not directly for cataract.
questions.question: Which systemic disease in the past medical history (PMH) is MOST directly associated with increased risk of posterior subcapsular cataract?

questions.explanation: In primary congenital glaucoma, the distensible infant sclera and cornea expand under elevated IOP, increasing corneal diameter beyond normal (<12 mm). Measurement of corneal diameter is used to confirm the diagnosis and monitor treatment response. Haab's striae (horizontal breaks in Descemet's membrane) also appear from stretching.
questions.question: Corneal diameter measurement is diagnostically important in congenital glaucoma because:
options: It closely correlates with lens thickness in neonates
It determines visual acuity in infants
It helps measure anterior chamber depth accurately in infants
An enlarged cornea (>12 mm) indicates raised IOP and globe distension in infants
It predicts surgical outcome of goniotomy

questions.question: A hypermetropic child accommodates excessively to see clearly at both distance and near. Which ocular misalignment commonly develops as a consequence?
questions.explanation: Accommodation and convergence are neurologically linked, so excessive accommodative effort in uncorrected hypermetropia drives excessive convergence. This can produce an accommodative convergent squint, particularly in early childhood. Correcting the hypermetropic refractive error often reduces or eliminates the squint.

Vernier acuity, or hyperacuity, measures the smallest detectable offset of a line, with a threshold of 3–5 seconds of arc. This is finer than Snellen acuity (1 minute of arc) because it relies on relative position comparison across photoreceptors rather than absolute resolution. It is measured using square wave gratings.
questions.question: Vernier acuity (hyperacuity) detects smaller offsets than Snellen acuity because it measures:
options: Minimal angle of cone resolution at the fovea
Threshold of rod stimulation under scotopic conditions
Smallest detectable offset of a line (3–5 seconds of arc)
Minimum wavelength discrimination by short-wave cones

questions.explanation: The normal range of visual acuity is 6/5 to 6/18 based on WHO classification. Visual acuity of 6/5 is better than normal (common in young adults), while 6/18 is the lower limit of normal. Category 1 visual impairment begins at less than 6/18 to 6/60, representing mild-to-moderate impairment.
questions.question: Normal range of visual acuity is considered to be between:

options: Liquefactive necrosis in most clinical presentations
Fat necrosis under standard examination conditions
Coagulative necrosis forming a protective barrier
questions.question: Acid chemical burns to the eye cause which type of tissue necrosis that limits damage?
questions.explanation: Acid chemical burns cause coagulative necrosis of the ocular tissues, denaturing proteins to form a coagulum that acts as a physical barrier, limiting further acid penetration into deeper structures. This self-limiting mechanism gives acid burns a relatively better prognosis than alkali burns. However, concentrated acids can still cause severe damage and require the same emergency irrigation protocol.

Preseptal (periorbital) cellulitis is confined anterior to the orbital septum, presenting with lid oedema and erythema only — no proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, or VA change. Orbital cellulitis extends behind the septum, causing proptosis, restricted motility, pain on movement, reduced VA, and risk of cavernous sinus thrombosis, brain abscess, and blindness.
questions.question: Orbital cellulitis is distinguished from preseptal cellulitis by all of the following EXCEPT:
Susac syndrome (retinocochleocerebral vasculopathy) is characterised by the triad of:
questions.explanation: Susac syndrome is a rare autoimmune endotheliopathy affecting small vessels of the retina, cochlea, and brain. The classic triad is branch retinal artery occlusions (causing visual field defects), sensorineural hearing loss, and encephalopathy (cognitive changes, psychiatric symptoms, headache). It predominantly affects young women. Immunosuppression is the treatment.
options: Optic disc swelling, retinal whitening, and choroidal folds
Angioid streaks, vitreous haemorrhage, and choroidal neovascularisation
Optic atrophy, nystagmus, and macular degeneration
Proptosis, dry eye, and restricted eye movements
Branch retinal artery occlusions, sensorineural hearing loss, and encephalopathy

questions.explanation: The major therapeutic objective following thermal eye burns is to relieve discomfort and prevent secondary complications including corneal inflammation, ulceration, perforation from infection, and exposure. Treatment includes intensive topical antibiotics, steroids (with caution), lubricants, and bandage contact lenses to protect the healing epithelium. Grafting may be required for severe cases but is not the immediate priority.
questions.question: In thermal burns to the eye, the primary objective of therapy is to:
options: Prevent secondary corneal inflammation, ulceration, and infection
Dilate the pupil to reduce iris damage

questions.explanation: Cytomegalovirus retinitis occurs almost exclusively in severely immunocompromised patients, particularly those with advanced HIV and low CD4 counts, producing a characteristic pattern of haemorrhage and granular retinal whitening following the vascular arcades, often described as a pizza-pie appearance. It causes progressive painless visual loss if untreated. Immune reconstitution with antiretroviral therapy alongside antiviral treatment is central to management.
questions.question: An immunocompromised patient with advanced HIV develops painless progressive visual loss with a fundus showing haemorrhages and granular white retinal opacification following blood vessels. Which infection is most likely?

questions.explanation: Onchocerciasis, caused by the filarial worm Onchocerca volvulus transmitted by blackfly bites, produces subcutaneous nodules containing adult worms. Migrating microfilariae in ocular tissues incite chronic inflammation, leading to progressive peripheral visual field loss and eventual blindness. Mass ivermectin distribution is central to control programmes.
questions.question: A patient from an endemic rural area presents with subcutaneous nodules and progressive visual field constriction. Which organism is responsible for this blinding disease?

questions.explanation: The E-chart (tumbling/illiterate E-chart) or Landolt's C is most appropriate for non-literate adults who cannot identify letters. The patient indicates the direction of the letter 'E' without needing to know the alphabet. Pictorial tests (like Kay's) are used for young children, while letter-matching tests are for children over 2 years.
questions.question: Which visual acuity test is MOST appropriate for a non-literate adult patient?

questions.explanation: High-dose oral corticosteroids (1–2 mg/kg/day, typically prednisolone) are the first-line treatment for VKH, targeting the autoimmune inflammatory mechanism against melanocytes. Steroid-sparing immunosuppression (azathioprine, mycophenolate, cyclosporine) is added for chronic disease or steroid intolerance. Early and aggressive treatment prevents chronic recurrent VKH and 'sunset glow' fundus.
options: Oral acyclovir for presumed viral etiology
questions.question: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada disease causes bilateral exudative retinal detachments. The FIRST-LINE systemic treatment is:
A routine well-child check includes shining a light into both eyes to look for a normal, symmetric reddish-orange reflection. This red reflex test is MOST valuable for detecting
questions.explanation: The red reflex test screens for any opacity or mass in the visual axis, such as retinoblastoma or congenital cataract, both of which disrupt the normal uniform red-orange reflection. It is not designed to detect refractive error, iris colour variation, or lid position. Early detection through this simple test can be sight- and life-saving in retinoblastoma.
options: leucocoria from retinoblastoma or congenital cataract
Diffuse retinal haemorrhages with disc involvement
Sub-retinal neovascular membrane at the macula
Peripheral white retinal lesions without any vitreous reaction present
Fluffy white retinal infiltrates with no prior scar
White active chorioretinal lesion (satellite) adjacent to an old pigmented scar
questions.question: Ocular toxoplasmosis characteristically presents as:
questions.explanation: Ocular toxoplasmosis presents with an active white chorioretinal satellite lesion adjacent to an old hyperpigmented chorioretinal scar — the 'headlight in the fog' appearance. Overlying vitreous haze is typical. It is the most common cause of posterior uveitis in immunocompetent patients. Pyrimethamine-sulphadiazine or clindamycin are used for treatment.

options: Irreversible optic nerve damage, extensive retinal damage, or severe endophthalmitis
Anterior segment injury exclusively without posterior involvement
questions.question: The 'no light perception' (NLP) vision after an open globe injury that has been primarily repaired is MOST likely due to:
questions.explanation: NLP vision after primary repair of an open globe injury most often reflects irreversible damage to the optic nerve (either from direct injury, avulsion, or indirect compressive haemorrhage), extensive retinal destruction, or fulminant endophthalmitis with retinal necrosis. NLP is the most important negative prognostic indicator after open globe injury, though some centres still attempt repair for cosmesis and pain prevention. SUBTOPIC 6: OCULAR MANIFESTATIONS OF SYSTEMIC DISEASES

questions.question: The optic cup-to-disc (C/D) ratio in a normal adult is typically:
questions.explanation: A normal optic C/D ratio is typically 0.3 or less. Ratios greater than 0.5, asymmetry of >0.2 between eyes, or progressive cup enlargement are suspicious for glaucoma. The neuroretinal rim normally follows the ISNT rule (Inferior > Superior > Nasal > Temporal) in healthy optic discs.

Choroidal detachment typically appears as a smooth, dome-shaped elevation on ultrasonography that does not extend to the ora serrata and lacks the characteristic folds of a retinal detachment. It often results from hypotony following trauma or surgery. Management focuses on treating the underlying cause and monitoring resolution.
questions.question: A patient presents with reduced vision after trauma and B-scan ultrasonography shows a smooth, dome-shaped elevation that does not reach the ora serrata, without visible tears. What is this most consistent with?

questions.explanation: Long duration of diabetes combined with poor blood sugar control (reflected by elevated HbA1c) is the strongest risk factor for developing and progressing diabetic retinopathy. After 20 years of Type 1 diabetes, up to 99% of patients develop some degree of retinopathy. Good glycemic control (HbA1c 6-7%) significantly delays onset and reduces progression of DR.
questions.question: Which risk factor is MOST strongly associated with the development and progression of diabetic retinopathy?
options: Short duration of diabetes with good control in the majority of documented cases
Type 2 diabetes exclusively based on typical clinical findings
Long duration of diabetes with poor glycemic control

questions.explanation: Phacomorphic glaucoma occurs when a swollen (intumescent) or mature cataract enlarges the lens volume, pushing the iris-lens diaphragm forward and physically closing the anterior chamber angle. This causes acute angle-closure glaucoma with severe pain, IOP elevation, and corneal edema. Treatment is urgent IOP reduction followed by prompt lens extraction (cataract surgery) to relieve the angle closure.
questions.question: A patient with mature cataract presents with acute onset severe eye pain, reduced vision, and elevated IOP. This complication is MOST likely:
options: Posterior vitreous detachment with retinal tear
Phacomorphic glaucoma from lens-induced angle closure

questions.explanation: The orbital floor is the thinnest and weakest wall and fractures most readily under blunt trauma, producing a blowout fracture. Herniation of orbital contents into the maxillary sinus causes enophthalmos, while entrapment of the inferior rectus limits upward gaze. Diplopia worsens on attempted upgaze due to muscle tethering.
questions.question: A patient sustains blunt orbital trauma and develops enophthalmos with diplopia on upward gaze. Which orbital wall was most likely fractured?

questions.explanation: The fundus encompasses the retina, optic nerve head, macula, and retinal vessels — all visible on ophthalmoscopy. The trabecular meshwork is located at the anterior chamber angle and is examined by gonioscopy, not ophthalmoscopy. It is part of the aqueous drainage pathway.
questions.question: The fundus visible on ophthalmoscopy does NOT include which of the following structures?
A patient presents with a chronic red, irritated eye and crusting eyelid margins with collarettes at the lash base. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Staphylococcal blepharitis is a chronic bacterial colonisation of the eyelid margins producing scaling, crusting, and collarette formation around the lash base. It causes chronic irritation, redness, and recurrent styes. Management includes lid hygiene and, in refractory cases, topical antibiotics.

Scleritis presents with severe, deep, boring eye pain (often waking the patient at night), sectoral redness involving the deep episcleral and scleral vessels that does NOT blanch with topical phenylephrine, and photophobia. It is strongly associated with systemic autoimmune diseases, particularly rheumatoid arthritis. Episcleritis involves only the superficial episcleral vessels and typically blanches with phenylephrine.
questions.question: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis presents with a deep, boring eye pain, sectoral redness that does not blanch with phenylephrine, and photophobia. The MOST likely diagnosis is:
Povidone-iodine in ophthalmic use serves PRIMARILY as:
questions.explanation: Povidone-iodine is a broad-spectrum antiseptic used in ophthalmology for preoperative conjunctival preparation, treatment of conjunctivitis, and neonatal ocular prophylaxis (Ophthalmia neonatorum). A 5% solution is more effective and better tolerated than 2% silver nitrate for neonatal prophylaxis. It is not a therapeutic drug for IOP reduction or inflammation.

options: Chemical reaction to silver nitrate prophylaxis (first 24 hours)
questions.question: In neonatal conjunctivitis (ophthalmia neonatorum), infection presenting with profuse purulent discharge 2–5 days after birth is MOST likely caused by:
questions.explanation: The timing of neonatal conjunctivitis helps identify the cause: chemical (silver nitrate) occurs within 24 hours; gonococcal occurs at 2–5 days with hyperacute profuse purulent discharge; chlamydial occurs at 5–14 days with mucopurulent discharge. Gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum requires urgent systemic treatment to prevent corneal perforation.

questions.question: The MOST common presenting complaint of a patient with early POAG is:
options: Coloured haloes around lights at night
Sudden loss of central visual acuity
questions.explanation: POAG is classically asymptomatic in its early stages because visual field loss begins peripherally and patients are unaware of the defect due to binocular filling-in by the contralateral eye. Central vision is often preserved until very late disease. This asymptomatic nature is why glaucoma is called the 'silent thief of sight.'

questions.question: A patient reads fine print easily under bright light but struggles at dusk, with preserved colour vision. Which photoreceptor is primarily deficient?
questions.explanation: Rods mediate scotopic vision and function best in dim light, unlike cones which need brighter illumination and mediate colour discrimination. Preserved colour vision with poor night vision points to rod dysfunction rather than cone loss. This pattern is classic for conditions such as retinitis pigmentosa.

questions.question: The hallmark histological findings of glaucomatous optic nerve damage are:
questions.explanation: Glaucoma is characterized by progressive loss of retinal ganglion cells and their axons, resulting in a specific pattern of optic atrophy—cupping of the optic disc (increased cup-to-disc ratio) with loss of the neuroretinal rim. This is accompanied by characteristic visual field defects (arcuate scotomas, nasal steps). The diagnosis is based on optic nerve appearance plus visual field changes, not IOP alone.
options: Retinal microaneurysms and hard exudates in the majority of documented cases in most clinical presentations
Flame-shaped hemorrhages at the disc based on typical clinical findings under standard examination conditions
Progressive cupping of the optic disc and loss of retinal ganglion cells

questions.question: The VISION 2020 initiative defines 'avoidable blindness' as blindness that is:
questions.explanation: Avoidable blindness is defined as blindness that could either be prevented or treated by known, cost-effective means. Up to 80% of global blindness is avoidable. This concept underpins the VISION 2020 mission and the prioritization of cost-effective interventions (cataract surgery, trachoma control, vitamin A supplementation) in blindness prevention programs.
options: Due exclusively to trauma and injuries as commonly encountered in practice
Untreatable by any currently known means during routine ophthalmic assessment
Preventable or treatable by known, cost-effective interventions
Caused by uncorrected refractive errors only

questions.explanation: Selective laser trabeculoplasty uses a specific wavelength that targets melanin-containing trabecular meshwork cells selectively, minimising thermal damage to surrounding non-pigmented tissue compared with older argon laser techniques. This allows the procedure to be repeated more safely if needed. It improves aqueous outflow, lowering intraocular pressure with a favourable side-effect profile.
questions.question: A patient with open-angle glaucoma undergoes a newer laser procedure targeting pigmented trabecular meshwork cells selectively while sparing surrounding tissue. What technique is this?

questions.explanation: Trachoma is hyperendemic in Asia, parts of Africa (especially sub-Saharan and North Africa), and the Middle East, predominantly affecting poor communities with limited access to water and sanitation. Western Europe has virtually eliminated trachoma through improvements in living standards and sanitation. The disease strikes the most vulnerable—women and children in resource-poor communities.
questions.question: Trachoma is hyperendemic in all of the following regions EXCEPT:

options: Acids cannot ever damage ocular tissue
Alkalis are always more dilute in concentration
Acids penetrate more deeply than alkalis
Alkalis are less commonly encountered in industry
Alkalis cause liquefactive necrosis allowing deep penetration
questions.explanation: Alkaline substances cause liquefactive necrosis, breaking down cell membranes and allowing continued penetration deep into ocular tissues including the anterior chamber. Acids typically cause coagulative necrosis, which forms a barrier limiting further penetration. This explains the generally worse prognosis associated with alkali injuries.
questions.question: A patient sustains an alkali splash to the eye. Why are alkali burns generally more severe than acid burns?

questions.explanation: The arcuate (Bjerrum) scotoma follows the arcuate nerve fibre bundle from the blind spot, arcing above or below fixation to the horizontal nasal midline (nasal step). This pattern is pathognomonic of glaucoma and corresponds to damage at the superior or inferior optic disc poles where nerve fibres are most densely packed.
questions.question: The most characteristic and pathognomonic glaucomatous visual field defect is:
In sickle cell haemoglobinopathy, 'black sunburst' lesions on fundoscopy are formed by:
options: Haemorrhage into the retina followed by pigment migration and RPE hyperplasia
Proliferative sickle cell retinopathy with sea-fan vessels
questions.explanation: Black sunburst lesions are circumscribed, black stellate/spiculated lesions in the peripheral retina of sickle cell patients. They result from haemorrhage into or beneath the retina, which organises and undergoes pigment migration and RPE hyperplasia. They represent healed peripheral haemorrhage and are a marker of past peripheral microvascular occlusion.

questions.question: The uveal tract is composed of three structures. Which is the CORRECT order from anterior to posterior?
questions.explanation: The uveal tract comprises three continuous vascular structures from anterior to posterior: the iris, ciliary body, and choroid. Together they form the middle (vascular) coat of the eye. The choroid provides the blood supply to the outer retina. Understanding uveal anatomy is essential for classifying uveitis anatomically.

Papilledema (optic disc swelling from raised intracranial pressure) produces blurring and indistinctness of the disc margins beginning superiorly and inferiorly, followed by congestion of the disc with dilated veins, loss of the spontaneous venous pulse, obliteration of the physiological cup, and eventually flame-shaped hemorrhages around the disc. It is bilateral and does not typically cause early vision loss (unlike anterior ischemic optic neuropathy which causes sudden visual loss).
questions.question: In fundoscopy, the optic disc margins in papilledema are described as:
options: Blurred, congested, and indistinct with obliteration of the cup
Sharp and well-defined with a normal cup in the majority of documented cases
Pale with loss of the neuroretinal rim based on typical clinical findings
Fully excavated to the disc margin

questions.question: In severe NPDR, the '4-2-1 rule' refers to criteria for classification. Which feature if present in ALL FOUR quadrants of the fundus mandates this diagnosis?
options: Cotton wool spots in all 4 quadrants
questions.explanation: The '4-2-1 rule' classifies severe NPDR when any one of the following is present: intraretinal hemorrhages in ALL FOUR quadrants, venous beading in TWO or more quadrants, or prominent IRMAs in ONE or more quadrants. The presence of any of these features indicates a high risk (50% within 1 year) of progression to proliferative retinopathy and warrants close follow-up or consideration of early treatment.

questions.question: Panophthalmitis differs from endophthalmitis in that panophthalmitis involves:
options: The globe plus extension through the sclera to Tenon's capsule and orbital tissues
Fungal infection confined exclusively to the vitreous cavity
Only the uveal tract and vitreous
questions.explanation: Endophthalmitis is infection confined within the globe (vitreous cavity, uveal tract). Panophthalmitis is extension of infection through the sclera to involve Tenon's capsule and orbital tissues, causing proptosis, restricted movements, orbital cellulitis, and systemic sepsis. Panophthalmitis is more severe and life-threatening than endophthalmitis.

questions.question: In Sturge-Weber syndrome, the mechanism of associated glaucoma is:
options: Angle closure from anteriorly rotated and swollen ciliary processes
Pupillary block by a thick iris
Elevated episcleral venous pressure from ipsilateral vascular malformation
questions.explanation: Glaucoma in Sturge-Weber syndrome results from elevated episcleral venous pressure from the ipsilateral choroidal haemangioma and diffuse vascular malformation, reducing aqueous outflow by raising downstream venous pressure. Glaucoma develops ipsilateral to the port-wine stain and occurs in approximately 30% of cases.

Automated perimetry (visual field testing, e.g., Humphrey Visual Field Analyser) maps the spatial extent of vision and detects characteristic glaucomatous defects including arcuate scotomas, nasal steps, and paracentral scotomas. It is the gold standard for detecting and monitoring functional glaucomatous damage.
questions.question: In glaucoma evaluation, the functional assessment of the visual field is performed using:
The OHTS (Ocular Hypertension Treatment Study) established which important principle?
options: Surgery is superior to medical treatment in all POAG patients
Race is irrelevant as a POAG risk factor
Normal corneal thickness provides complete protection against POAG
IOP lowering reduces conversion from ocular hypertension to POAG
questions.explanation: The OHTS demonstrated that topical medication reducing IOP by approximately 20% significantly reduces the rate of conversion from ocular hypertension to POAG (from 9.5% to 4.4% over 5 years). It also identified thin central corneal thickness, large C/D ratio, high IOP, older age, and African ancestry as risk factors for conversion to POAG.

Target IOP is individualised in POAG — based on baseline IOP, degree of optic nerve damage, rate of progression, and life expectancy. A 20–30% reduction from untreated baseline is commonly used. More advanced disease requires lower targets. Regular follow-up perimetry and OCT assess whether the target provides adequate neuroprotection.
options: Always below 10 mmHg for all patients
Fixed at a 10% reduction from baseline always
Individualised based on baseline IOP, damage severity, and progression rate
Determined solely by a single corneal pachymetry measurement reading
questions.question: Target IOP in managing POAG is best described as:

questions.explanation: Adnexal causes of red eye include conditions of the eyelids and lacrimal system: blepharitis, trichiasis (misdirected eyelashes), stye (external hordeolum), chalazion, and dacryocystitis. These are structural causes that can produce secondary conjunctival or corneal irritation. Correctly classifying the anatomical source of redness guides targeted management.
options: Conjunctiva based on typical clinical findings
Anterior chamber in the majority of documented cases
questions.question: The classification of red eye by anatomical location that would include blepharitis, chalazion, and trichiasis is:
A patient with a hyphema following trauma develops sudden severe pain and blood staining of the cornea. What does corneal blood staining indicate?
questions.explanation: Corneal blood staining occurs when prolonged elevated intraocular pressure combined with a large hyphema forces red blood cell breakdown products into the corneal stroma. This can cause long-term visual impairment even after the hyphema clears. Early recognition and pressure control reduce the risk of this complication.
options: A normal expected finding after any hyphema
Prolonged high pressure driving blood into the stroma
17p13 (TP53 gene) as commonly encountered in practice
questions.question: The 'two-hit' hypothesis for retinoblastoma was proposed by Knudson in 1971 based on statistical analysis. The gene implicated in retinoblastoma is located at:
questions.explanation: Retinoblastoma results from biallelic inactivation of the RB1 tumour suppressor gene located at chromosome 13q14. The RB1 protein (pRb) normally regulates the cell cycle by binding and inhibiting the E2F transcription factor. Loss of both copies of RB1 removes this inhibition, allowing uncontrolled retinal cell proliferation. RB1 was the first tumour suppressor gene identified in humans, and Knudson's 'two-hit' model became foundational to cancer genetics.

questions.question: The Macular star in Grade IV hypertensive retinopathy forms because:
options: VEGF drives neovascularization in a radial pattern around the fovea as commonly encountered in practice
Macular photoreceptors degenerate in a starfish pattern
Hard exudates accumulate in the outer plexiform layer radiating from the fovea
Nerve fiber layer infarcts create a star-shaped scar during routine ophthalmic assessment
Choroidal hemorrhage dissects under the macula symmetrically
questions.explanation: A macular star forms when hard exudates (lipid deposits) accumulate in the outer plexiform (Henle's fiber) layer of the retina. In this layer, photoreceptor axons radiate in a fan-like pattern from the fovea, causing exudates to track along these fibers and arrange in a characteristic star or fan pattern around the fovea. This is a classic sign of Grade IV hypertensive retinopathy and severe diabetic maculopathy.

questions.question: A patient with sickle cell disease has an area of superficial pink-orange preretinal hemorrhage that later evolves into a spot with a scalloped, refractile appearance. These lesions are known respectively as
options: microaneurysm evolving into a macular star
salmon patch hemorrhage evolving into a black sunburst
Elschnig spot evolving into a Gunn sign
cotton wool spot evolving into a hard exudate
questions.explanation: In sickle cell retinopathy, an intraretinal or preretinal hemorrhage initially appears as a salmon-coloured patch, which over time can evolve into a darker, pigmented lesion with a refractile, scalloped border called a black sunburst. These findings represent non-proliferative features of the disease. Recognising them helps stage the retinopathy even before proliferative changes develop.

Miotics such as pilocarpine are parasympathomimetic agents that constrict the pupil (miosis) and contract the ciliary muscle, which opens the trabecular meshwork and increases aqueous outflow from the anterior chamber. They are used in open-angle and acute angle-closure glaucoma management. Beta-blockers and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors reduce aqueous production rather than enhancing outflow.
questions.question: Which class of ophthalmic drug works by constricting the pupil AND contracting the ciliary muscle to increase aqueous drainage from the anterior chamber?

questions.explanation: Blunt trauma causes rapid globe deformation, generating vitreoretinal traction that can tear the peripheral retina at points of firm vitreous attachment. This can lead to recurrent vitreous haemorrhage and risk of subsequent retinal detachment. Prompt identification and laser or cryotherapy treatment of the tear is important.
options: Vitreous traction on a weakened peripheral retina
questions.question: A patient sustains blunt trauma and later develops recurrent vitreous haemorrhage with a peripheral horseshoe-shaped retinal tear. What is the underlying mechanism of tear formation?

options: Contracting the ciliary muscle to open trabecular meshwork spaces
Reducing aqueous production via beta-adrenergic receptors
Directly stimulating beta-adrenergic receptors on the iris
questions.explanation: Pilocarpine is a direct-acting cholinergic (miotic) agent that contracts the ciliary muscle, which pulls on the scleral spur and mechanically opens the trabecular meshwork, reducing resistance to aqueous outflow. It also causes pupillary miosis, which can relieve pupil-block in angle-closure glaucoma.
questions.question: Pilocarpine lowers IOP primarily by:

questions.explanation: Vitamin A (retinol) is an essential component of rhodopsin (visual purple), the photopigment in rod photoreceptors responsible for scotopic (dim light/night) vision. Deficiency causes night blindness (nyctalopia) as the earliest symptom, reflecting insufficient rhodopsin regeneration. While Vitamin A also supports epithelial integrity, its most direct role in vision is in the rod phototransduction cycle.
questions.question: Vitamin A (retinol) is classified as a fat-soluble vitamin. Its role in vision is MOST specifically related to:
options: Color vision in bright light (photopic) in the majority of documented cases
Control of intraocular pressure based on typical clinical findings
Scotopic vision as a component of rhodopsin

questions.explanation: Topical corticosteroids reduce the inflammatory reaction of iridocyclitis, while cycloplegics relieve ciliary spasm and reduce the risk of posterior synechiae. Antibiotics and antifungals treat infective rather than primarily inflammatory disease and would not address the underlying process. This combination remains the standard first-line approach.
questions.question: In managing acute iridocyclitis, the combination MOST appropriate to control inflammation and prevent complications is
options: topical steroid with a cycloplegic agent
topical antiviral with a mydriatic alone

questions.explanation: A focal area of retinal whitening with overlying vascular attenuation, sometimes likened to a 'headlight in fog' appearance, reflects localised ischaemia from occlusion of a branch retinal artery supplying that segment of retina. This contrasts with the diffuse pale retina of a central retinal artery occlusion, which affects the entire territory supplied by the vessel. Investigation for embolic sources and hypercoagulable states is warranted in young patients presenting this way.
questions.question: A patient develops a focal, well-demarcated white retinal lesion with overlying vascular sheathing following an acute vascular event in a young adult with a hypercoagulable tendency. This finding is sometimes described using an automotive fog analogy. Which vascular event does this represent?
A patient with known herpes simplex keratitis starts topical steroid drops without antiviral cover. The MOST likely complication is:
questions.explanation: Topical steroids are CONTRAINDICATED in active epithelial HSV keratitis (dendritic ulcer stage) because they enhance viral replication by suppressing local immunity, worsening the epithelial keratitis. Steroids are indicated only for immune-mediated stromal disease (disciform keratitis) with antiviral prophylactic cover. This principle is a critical clinical concept in managing HSK.
options: Corneal thinning from collagen cross-linking inhibition
Worsening of active epithelial keratitis with dendritic spread

questions.question: Among global causes of blindness, the single condition that is both most common and most amenable to a single curative procedure is
questions.explanation: Cataract remains the leading cause of blindness worldwide, and unlike glaucoma or diabetic retinopathy, it can be effectively cured with a single surgical procedure restoring vision. This makes cataract surgery one of the most cost-effective interventions in eliminating avoidable blindness. Programmes therefore prioritise cataract surgical coverage as a key public health target.

questions.question: The MOST common type of age-related cataract in individuals under 65 years in the tropics is:
questions.explanation: Posterior subcapsular cataract (PSC) is the most visually disabling type and the most common in younger individuals in tropical regions. It causes severe glare and reduced vision in bright light (due to pupil constriction directing light through the opacity). It is also associated with steroids, diabetes, high myopia, and radiation. Nuclear sclerotic cataract predominates in elderly individuals over 65.

options: Reassure the parents and review in a year
Start topical antibiotics for suspected conjunctivitis
Patch the eye to reduce tearing
Measure intraocular pressure and corneal diameter urgently
Refer only if squint develops later
questions.question: A child is noted to have an enlarged, hazy cornea with excessive tearing and light sensitivity shortly after birth. What is the priority action?
questions.explanation: These features suggest primary congenital glaucoma, an ophthalmic emergency requiring prompt assessment of intraocular pressure and corneal diameter. Delay in diagnosis risks permanent corneal scarring, amblyopia, and optic nerve damage. Early surgical intervention offers the best visual prognosis.

Having a first-degree relative (parent or sibling) with POAG increases an individual's risk by approximately 4–9 times compared to the general population. This reflects a strong genetic predisposition. First-degree relatives of POAG patients should be screened regularly, particularly after age 35 in West African populations.
questions.question: Family history in a first-degree relative increases POAG risk by approximately:
Panretinal photocoagulation (PRP) is the treatment for proliferative diabetic retinopathy. It works by:
options: Destroying ischaemic peripheral retina to reduce VEGF production
Coagulating new vessels directly to stop bleeding
Increasing retinal oxygenation by creating laser-induced vascular channels
Reducing macular oedema by tightening the posterior hyaloid face
Stimulating collateral vessel formation via laser-induced angiogenesis
questions.explanation: PRP destroys the ischaemic peripheral retinal tissue, which is the source of VEGF (the driver of retinal neovascularization). By ablating oxygen-deprived retina, VEGF production is reduced, causing regression of new vessels. The remaining central retina with better oxygenation survives. PRP is also used in CRVO-related neovascularization and retinal ischaemia from sickle cell disease.

questions.question: Which brainstem structure does the oculomotor nerve pass through after leaving the Edinger-Westphal nucleus?
options: Red nucleus and ipsilateral corticospinal tract
Dorsal raphe nucleus in the majority of documented cases
Inferior olivary nucleus based on typical clinical findings
questions.explanation: As CN III courses ventrally from the midbrain, it passes through the red nucleus and the ipsilateral corticospinal tract before emerging from the ventral surface of the midbrain. Lesions in this path can cause 'Weber's syndrome' (CN III palsy with contralateral hemiplegia). This anatomical course is critical for neurological localization of CN III palsies.

questions.question: A patient with a shallow anterior chamber is examined using oblique torchlight, and a crescentic shadow falls on the nasal iris. This positive Eclipse sign should raise concern for
questions.explanation: A positive Eclipse sign indicates a shallow anterior chamber where the peripheral iris is closer to the cornea than normal. This anatomical configuration predisposes to pupillary block and acute angle-closure glaucoma. Recognising it prompts closer angle assessment before dilating the pupil.

questions.question: A patient with temporal headache, jaw pain on chewing, and sudden profound visual loss is found to have a pale, swollen optic disc. What underlying condition must be urgently excluded?
questions.explanation: Arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy is caused by giant cell arteritis, an inflammatory vasculitis affecting medium and large arteries including the posterior ciliary arteries supplying the optic nerve head. Associated symptoms include jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, and systemic malaise. Urgent high-dose corticosteroid treatment is required to prevent bilateral blindness.

Topical ophthalmic steroids carry the highest risk of steroid-induced IOP elevation by directly affecting trabecular meshwork cells, reducing their phagocytic activity and causing accumulation of glycosaminoglycans that obstruct outflow. Potent steroids like dexamethasone carry higher risk than fluorometholone. Risk is dose- and duration-dependent.
questions.question: Steroidal glaucoma is MOST likely to occur with which route of steroid administration?

questions.explanation: Plateau iris configuration causes angle narrowing due to an anteriorly positioned ciliary body pushing the peripheral iris into the angle, independent of pupillary block. This explains why some patients continue to have angle-closure risk even after a patent iridotomy has relieved pupillary block. Additional treatments such as laser iridoplasty may be required to manage this anatomical variant.
questions.question: A patient with recurrent acute angle-closure symptoms despite a patent laser iridotomy is found to have a flat, anteriorly positioned iris root pushing into the angle. What condition explains this persistent narrowing?

questions.explanation: Rigid, sickled erythrocytes obstruct the narrow peripheral retinal capillaries, causing localised ischemia that drives the characteristic non-proliferative and proliferative changes of sickle cell retinopathy. This vaso-occlusive mechanism is distinct from processes affecting the lens, aqueous production, or the optic nerve directly. Understanding this mechanism explains why peripheral retina is preferentially affected.
questions.question: Sickle cell retinopathy develops primarily because sickled red blood cells cause
options: occlusion of small peripheral retinal vessels
direct toxic damage to the optic nerve
primary degeneration of the retinal pigment epithelium

questions.explanation: Bacillus cereus endophthalmitis following vegetative/agricultural trauma is among the most devastating of all endophthalmitis types. It presents explosively within 12–24 hours with extreme pain, lid oedema, chemosis, a ring corneal abscess, and profound visual loss — often to no light perception. Despite aggressive treatment, most eyes have very poor visual outcomes.
questions.question: A patient with penetrating ocular trauma in an agricultural setting who develops severe pain, ring abscess, and rapid visual loss within 24 hours MOST likely has:

questions.explanation: Viral conjunctivitis is characterized by clear watery discharge (not purulent), mononuclear cell infiltrate (not polymorphonuclear leukocytes), and preauricular lymphadenopathy — due to viral lymph node drainage. Bacterial conjunctivitis has purulent discharge and PMN cells. Allergic conjunctivitis has mucoid/ropy discharge with eosinophils and intense itching.
questions.question: In differentiating acute conjunctivitis causes, which combination of findings BEST suggests viral etiology?
options: Purulent discharge, moderate lid edema, no lymphadenopathy
Ropy mucoid discharge, eosinophils, no lymph node involvement
Clear watery discharge, mononuclear cells, preauricular lymphadenopathy
Mucopurulent discharge, polymorphonuclear cells, minimal chemosis
Papillary hypertrophy with yellow crusting on lashes
Evaluate retinal health, blood flow, and identify areas of neovascularization and capillary non-perfusion
Grade nuclear sclerosis of the lens as commonly encountered in practice as commonly encountered in practice
Detect intraocular foreign bodies during routine ophthalmic assessment during routine ophthalmic assessment
questions.explanation: Fundus fluorescein angiography (FFA) involves intravenous injection of sodium fluorescein dye and sequential imaging to evaluate retinal blood flow, vascular integrity, neovascularization, microaneurysm leakage, and areas of capillary non-perfusion (ischemia). It guides laser photocoagulation planning and helps diagnose macular ischemia vs. macular edema. OCT has largely replaced FFA for routine macular edema monitoring.
questions.question: Fundus Fluorescein Angiography (FFA) in diabetic retinopathy is used to:

options: G-protein → rhodopsin activation → cGMP degradation → channel closure
Light → rhodopsin → transducin activation → phosphodiesterase → cGMP degradation → Na channel closure → hyperpolarization
Light → cone activation → L-type calcium influx → glutamate release → bipolar depolarization
All-trans retinal → opsin binding → guanylate cyclase activation → cGMP production
Light → Na+ influx → K+ efflux → depolarization → glutamate cessation
questions.question: The correct sequence of photoreceptor signal transduction in the visual cycle begins with:
questions.explanation: The visual transduction cascade: Light isomerizes 11-cis-retinal to all-trans-retinal in rhodopsin → activated rhodopsin (metarhodopsin II) activates transducin (a G-protein) → transducin activates phosphodiesterase → PDE degrades cGMP → cGMP-gated Na+ channels close → cell hyperpolarizes → reduced glutamate release → signal to bipolar cells. This is the fundamental mechanism of phototransduction.

Corticosteroids are the primary treatment for non-infectious uveitis due to their potent anti-inflammatory effects. They are available in topical, injectable (subconjunctival/intravitreal), and systemic forms. The choice of formulation depends on the anatomical location of the uveitis (anterior vs posterior). Antihistamines are used for allergic conditions, not uveitis.
questions.question: A patient is being treated for active uveitis. Which ophthalmic preparation is the MOST appropriate?
Pars planitis (intermediate uveitis) in a young adult should prompt screening for which systemic association?
questions.explanation: Pars planitis (intermediate uveitis) is associated with multiple sclerosis (MS) in approximately 15–20% of cases, and sarcoidosis in another 10%. All young patients with intermediate uveitis should undergo MRI brain to screen for MS demyelinating plaques. Sarcoidosis requires chest X-ray and serum ACE. Most cases of pars planitis are idiopathic.

questions.question: A patient with chronic anterior uveitis on long-term topical steroids develops raised intraocular pressure. Which mechanism, among several possible in uveitic glaucoma, is directly attributable to the steroid rather than the inflammation itself?
questions.explanation: Corticosteroids can increase outflow resistance through biochemical changes in the trabecular meshwork independent of the underlying uveitis, contributing to steroid-induced ocular hypertension. This differs from mechanisms directly caused by inflammation, such as trabeculitis, synechiae formation, or pupillary block. Distinguishing steroid-induced pressure rise from inflammation-driven glaucoma guides whether to taper steroids or intensify anti-inflammatory treatment.

Trabeculectomy creates a partial-thickness scleral flap under which a full-thickness sclerostomy (fistula) allows aqueous from the anterior chamber to drain into a subconjunctival filtration bleb. The scleral flap acts as a 'guard' controlling drainage rate and preventing hypotony. Antimetabolites (MMC, 5-FU) prevent bleb scarring.
questions.question: Trabeculectomy (guarded filtration surgery) creates IOP reduction by:
options: Creating a full-thickness sclerostomy without a guarding flap
Performing a goniotomy to open trabecular spaces
Ablating the ciliary body to reduce aqueous production
Removing the cataractous lens to open the angle
Creating a guarded fistula under a scleral flap for controlled aqueous drainage into a bleb

questions.question: Treatment of gonococcal conjunctivitis requires BOTH topical AND systemic antibiotics because:
options: Systemic treatment prevents concurrent genital gonococcal infection and corneal involvement
Topical antibiotic penetration to the cornea is insufficient alone
N. gonorrhoeae has intrinsic resistance to topical antibiotics
Topical treatment prevents complications while systemic treats the conjunctiva
Standard antibiotic dosing from systemic route alone is adequate
questions.explanation: Gonococcal conjunctivitis requires both topical quinolones/bacitracin (for local ocular control) AND IV/IM cefotaxime or cefoxitin (for concurrent systemic gonococcal infection — urogenital or disseminated). Copious irrigation removes exudate. Systemic treatment is essential because gonococcal conjunctivitis is a manifestation of systemic infection. Sexual contacts should also be treated.

options: Engorgement of veins distal to AV crossings as commonly encountered in practice
Deflection of the vein at an AV crossing due to arteriolar rigidity
Presence of silver wiring in arterioles during routine ophthalmic assessment
questions.explanation: Salus' sign describes the deflection or bending of the retinal vein at an arteriovenous crossing, caused by the rigidity and adventitial thickening of the arteriosclerotic arteriole. The vein appears deflected at an angle away from its usual course at the crossing point. It is an early sign of arteriosclerosis in hypertensive retinopathy, accompanying other AV crossing changes such as Gunn's sign and Bonnet's sign.
questions.question: Salus' sign in hypertensive retinopathy refers to:

questions.explanation: The Na-K+ pump in the crystalline lens maintains a relatively dehydrated state, which is essential for lens transparency. Loss of this pump function leads to water imbibition, causing opacification (cataract). This mechanism is analogous to the bicarbonate pump in the corneal endothelium.
options: Produces the inner mucous tear layer
Provides nutrition to the corneal stroma
questions.question: The Na-K+ pump of the crystalline lens serves which primary function?

options: Assess colour vision defects in the central macula
Differentiate refractive error from ocular pathology
questions.explanation: The pin-hole eliminates peripheral light rays, allowing only paraxial rays to reach the retina. If VA improves with a pin-hole, the reduction in acuity is due to a refractive error (correctable). If VA does not improve, an ocular pathology or neurological cause is likely. Pin-hole testing is a critical first step in VA assessment.
questions.question: The pin-hole test in visual acuity assessment is primarily used to:

options: new vessel growth from the disc
lipid and lipoprotein deposition rather than ischemic infarction
areas of localised nerve fibre layer infarction
calcified scar tissue from old trauma
an area of active retinal bleeding
questions.explanation: Hard exudates form from leakage and deposition of lipids and lipoproteins from damaged capillaries, giving them sharp, well-defined margins compared with the fluffy, indistinct edges of cotton wool spots caused by nerve fibre layer ischemia. This distinction helps identify the underlying pathological process on fundus examination. Recognising hard exudates near the macula also flags a risk for macular edema.
questions.question: On fundoscopy, yellow-white deposits with sharply defined margins are noted in the macula of a diabetic patient. These hard exudates are distinguished from cotton wool spots because they represent
A patient with sickle cell retinopathy at Goldberg Stage III sea-fan neovascularization is monitored closely because untreated progression MOST often leads next to
options: spontaneous complete regression in most cases
vitreous hemorrhage from fragile new vessels
improvement in visual acuity without treatment
questions.explanation: The fragile new vessels characteristic of Stage III sea-fan neovascularization are prone to spontaneous bleeding into the vitreous cavity, representing the natural progression toward Stage IV and V disease if left untreated. Spontaneous regression can occur in some cases, but progression to haemorrhage remains the more clinically significant risk requiring monitoring. This is why timely laser treatment is considered once sea-fans are identified.

questions.question: Visual contrast sensitivity is MOST impaired in which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation: Contrast sensitivity, the ability to perceive slight luminance differences, is impaired in refractive errors, glaucoma, cataract, and optic nerve disease. It results in mild fogginess of vision even when Snellen acuity is preserved. It is often the first visual function affected in these diseases.
options: Isolated ptosis blocking the visual axis
Band keratopathy limited to the periphery
Optic nerve disease, refractive error, glaucoma

questions.question: Damage to the superior oblique muscle would most significantly impair which eye movement?
questions.explanation: The superior oblique muscle, innervated by CN IV (trochlear), produces intorsion, depression, and abduction when the eye is adducted. CN IV palsy causes vertical diplopia and a characteristic head tilt. It has the longest intracranial course making it vulnerable to head trauma.
options: Elevation and abduction of the globe superiorly
Pure adduction of the eyeball medially
Intorsion, depression, and abduction of the eyeball
Elevation in adduction of the eyeball
Abduction and extorsion of the eyeball

questions.question: A patient with raised intracranial pressure and bilateral papilloedema threatening vision despite maximal medical therapy is considered for a specific ophthalmic surgical procedure. What is this procedure called?
questions.explanation: Optic nerve sheath fenestration creates a window in the optic nerve sheath, allowing cerebrospinal fluid to decompress locally and protecting the optic nerve from further pressure-related damage. It is considered when papilloedema threatens vision despite maximal medical management of the underlying intracranial pressure. Systemic treatment of the underlying cause remains essential alongside this local procedure.

Cytomegalovirus retinitis typically occurs in severely immunocompromised patients, particularly those with very low CD4 counts, and produces characteristic full-thickness retinal necrosis with haemorrhage along vessels, often described as a pizza-pie appearance. It progresses relentlessly without antiviral treatment. Immune reconstitution is also important in overall management.
questions.question: An HIV-positive patient with a low CD4 count presents with painless progressive retinal whitening and haemorrhages along vascular arcades. What is the likely cause?
A patient has misdirected eyelashes arising from an abnormal accessory row of lash follicles rather than the normal lash line. Which condition is this?
questions.explanation: Distichiasis refers to an accessory row of eyelashes emerging from the meibomian gland orifices, a congenital or acquired anomaly distinct from normal lash follicles. Trichiasis, by contrast, involves normally positioned follicles producing misdirected lashes due to lid margin disease. Both conditions can cause corneal irritation but differ in their follicular origin.

Phlytenular keratoconjunctivitis is a delayed hypersensitivity (type IV) reaction to microbial antigens — most commonly staphylococcal proteins from blepharitis or tuberculoprotein from Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It presents as a small grey-white nodule at the limbus that migrates centrally, leaving a vascularised scar. Treatment targets the underlying sensitising organism.
questions.question: Phlytenular conjunctivitis is a hypersensitivity reaction MOST commonly associated with:
options: Viral antigens resulting from adenoviral conjunctival infection
Staphylococcal blepharitis antigens or Mycobacterium tuberculosis proteins

questions.explanation: Onchocerciasis causes blindness primarily through sclerosing (punctate) keratitis — an inflammatory response to dying microfilariae in the corneal stroma. Repeated inflammatory episodes lead to progressive corneal scarring and vascularisation. Posterior segment involvement (chorioretinitis, optic atrophy) also contributes to visual loss in endemic communities.
options: Sclerosing keratitis from inflammatory response to dying microfilariae in the cornea
Retinal detachment resulting from chronic vitreous inflammation
Direct optic nerve invasion by adult worms
questions.question: Onchocerciasis ('river blindness') causes blindness primarily through:

A patient is diagnosed with glaucoma only after combining intraocular pressure measurement, optic disc assessment, and visual field testing. This reflects the modern principle that glaucoma diagnosis requires
questions.explanation: Modern glaucoma practice recognises that intraocular pressure alone is neither sensitive nor specific, since some patients have normal-tension glaucoma while others tolerate higher pressures without damage. Combining optic disc appearance and visual field function with pressure gives a more accurate diagnosis. This integrated approach avoids both over- and under-diagnosis based on a single measurement.
options: a combination of structural and functional findings rather than pressure alone

questions.question: Retinal detachment characteristically presents with which symptom complex?
questions.explanation: Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment classically presents with a sudden onset of new floaters (vitreous haemorrhage/pigment), photopsia (flashing lights from vitreoretinal traction), and then a peripheral field defect described as a 'curtain' or 'shadow' advancing centrally. Visual acuity is severely reduced if the macula detaches. Urgent surgical repair is required.
options: Gradually worsening central vision over years
Bilateral simultaneous visual loss over hours
Haloes around lights with moderate discomfort
Severe eye pain and acute redness with new floaters present
Sudden onset of floaters, flashes (photopsia), and a 'curtain' shadow in the visual field

questions.question: A patient with newly diagnosed POAG is started on brimonidine but develops drowsiness. Which patient group should avoid this drug?
questions.explanation: Brimonidine, an alpha-2 agonist, readily crosses the immature blood-brain barrier in infants and young children. This can cause profound central nervous system depression, apnoea, and hypotension. It is therefore contraindicated in this age group.

questions.question: Aspirin has been studied for a possible protective effect against cataract formation, thought to act through its
options: antibacterial effect on the lens capsule
questions.explanation: Aspirin is proposed to reduce oxidative stress and non-enzymatic glycation of lens proteins, both implicated in cataract formation, offering a theoretical protective effect. It has no direct surgical or pressure-lowering action on the lens. This remains an area of ongoing research rather than an established clinical intervention.

questions.question: A 55-year-old presents with hazy vision after cataract surgery. Slit lamp shows corneal oedema with folds in Descemet's membrane. Which structure was most likely damaged intraoperatively?
questions.explanation: The endothelium actively pumps fluid out of the stroma to keep the cornea deturgesced. Surgical trauma to endothelial cells reduces pump function below the critical density needed for clarity. This produces stromal oedema and Descemet folds seen on slit lamp.

questions.question: In ophthalmic history taking, quantifying alcohol and smoking consumption is specifically required under:
questions.explanation: Social history, which is part of the family and social history (FSH) section, requires quantification of alcohol and tobacco use since both are modifiable risk factors for various ocular conditions including cataract, optic neuropathy, and retinal vascular disease. If a patient declines, the clinician must ask if they were ever used and when they were discontinued.

questions.question: A patient presents with a penetrating corneal wound and a dark tissue prolapsing through the defect. What is the significance of this tissue prolapse?
questions.explanation: Incarcerated iris tissue within a corneal wound can act as a wick, allowing surface organisms direct access into the eye and increasing the risk of endophthalmitis. Careful surgical repositioning or excision of prolapsed tissue during repair reduces this risk. Prompt surgical closure is important to restore the globe's integrity.
options: Risk of infection tracking along the incarcerated iris
It indicates the wound has already healed
It confirms there is no infection risk
It means surgery is no longer needed
It always resolves without any treatment

questions.question: Iris melanoma presenting as a discrete sector of iris darkening with distortion of the pupil is classified as:
options: Iris melanoma — typically the most BENIGN uveal melanoma type
Ciliary body melanoma requiring enucleation only
Diffuse iris melanoma — requiring immediate enucleation
Iris nevus requiring no treatment regardless of size
questions.explanation: Iris melanoma is the most benign form of uveal melanoma, with a much lower metastatic rate than ciliary body or choroidal melanoma. It presents as a pigmented discrete iris lesion with a distorted pupil, sentinel vessels, and progressive growth. Management ranges from observation (for small lesions) to local resection or plaque radiotherapy for growing lesions.

questions.question: In Graves' orbitopathy, which clinical feature occurs in the HIGHEST percentage of affected patients?
questions.explanation: Eyelid retraction is the most common clinical feature of Graves' orbitopathy/TED, occurring in more than 90% of patients. This creates the characteristic staring appearance. Exophthalmos occurs in approximately 60%, restrictive ophthalmopathy in 40%, and optic neuropathy in 6%. Only about 5% have all classic signs.

questions.question: A patient develops bilateral panuveitis with vitiligo, poliosis, and hearing disturbance following a viral-like prodrome. Which condition best fits this presentation?
questions.explanation: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada syndrome is a bilateral granulomatous panuveitis with systemic features including vitiligo, poliosis, alopecia, and auditory or meningeal symptoms, reflecting autoimmune attack on melanocyte-containing tissues. The condition typically follows a prodromal phase resembling meningitis before ocular symptoms appear. Recognising these systemic associations is key to distinguishing it from other panuveitic conditions.

questions.question: Congenital ptosis causing deprivation amblyopia in a child requires:
options: Urgent surgical correction to prevent amblyopia from visual axis obstruction
Observation until school age for spontaneous resolution
Patching of the fellow eye without surgery until age 8
Spectacle correction for hypermetropia first, then surgery
Botulinum toxin injection into levator to rest the muscle
questions.explanation: Congenital ptosis that covers the visual axis (severe ptosis) causes deprivation amblyopia through obstruction of form vision to the developing visual cortex. This requires urgent surgical correction (sling or levator resection) to restore the visual axis, followed by amblyopia treatment. Delay beyond the critical period of visual development leads to permanent amblyopia.

questions.question: Radiation-induced cataracts from X-ray, gamma ray, or neutron exposure characteristically affect which part of the lens?
questions.explanation: Radiation-induced cataracts characteristically affect the posterior subcapsular region of the lens. The lens epithelium is the most radiosensitive part; radiation damages equatorial lens epithelial cells, causing abnormal fibre migration that forms posterior subcapsular opacity. There is typically a latent period of months to years between radiation exposure and cataract formation.

options: avoid the need for any sedation
obtain images faster than CT allows
avoid ionising radiation exposure that raises secondary cancer risk
achieve better bone detail than CT
questions.question: A child with a germline RB1 mutation undergoing surveillance imaging is preferentially imaged with MRI rather than CT of the orbits mainly to
questions.explanation: Children with germline RB1 mutations are already at increased risk of radiation-induced secondary malignancies, so repeated CT scans using ionising radiation are avoided in favour of MRI, which provides comparable soft tissue detail without this risk.
