CT remains superior for bone detail but this is not the priority in retinoblastoma surveillance. This imaging choice reflects long-term cancer prevention rather than convenience.

questions.question: Glaucoma causes 'tunnel vision' as a late manifestation because:
questions.explanation: Glaucomatous field loss characteristically begins peripherally (arcuate and nasal step defects) while central visual acuity is preserved until very late disease. The progressive narrowing of the peripheral field creates characteristic tunnel vision in advanced glaucoma. Central vision loss represents near end-stage disease with minimal remaining functional field.
options: Glaucoma damages central macular fibres first
Optic nerve damage in glaucoma begins at the central papillomacular bundle
Retinal detachment extends from the periphery centrally
Progressive peripheral field loss spares central vision until end stage
The lens develops a central opacity blocking central vision

questions.question: Trachoma remains hyperendemic in resource-limited communities primarily where there is
questions.explanation: Trachoma transmission thrives in settings with poor facial cleanliness, crowding, and limited water access, which facilitate spread of the causative organism through contact and flies. Communities with good hygiene and water access have markedly lower transmission. This environmental link underlies the facial cleanliness and environmental components of the SAFE strategy.
options: poor facial hygiene and limited access to clean water
high consumption of vitamin A rich foods
low population density in urban centres

questions.explanation: Thyroid eye disease (Graves' ophthalmopathy) is associated with hyperthyroidism in approximately 90% of cases. About 6% of patients are euthyroid at presentation. It is the most common cause of both unilateral and bilateral proptosis in adults. The disease may progress and remit independently of thyroid function, which complicates management.
questions.question: Graves' ophthalmopathy (thyroid eye disease) is MOST commonly associated with which thyroid condition?

questions.explanation: Fungal keratitis in West Africa and tropical regions is most frequently preceded by vegetative (plant) trauma introducing fungi (Fusarium, Aspergillus). The cornea develops a dry, raised, feathery infiltrate with satellite lesions and hypopyon. Diagnosis is by corneal scraping for KOH preparation and culture. Natamycin and voriconazole are first-line treatments.
questions.question: Fungal keratitis (keratomycosis) in West Africa is MOST commonly preceded by:
options: Vegetative (plant) trauma — injury with sticks, leaves, or agricultural material
Contact lens wear in young otherwise healthy adults

questions.explanation: The LogMAR chart standardises the number of optotypes per line and uses a logarithmic size progression between lines, unlike the Snellen chart's uneven spacing. This design produces more consistent and reproducible acuity measurements, particularly useful in research and low-vision assessment. It has largely replaced the Snellen chart in clinical trials.
questions.question: An optometrist explains that a newer chart uses equal numbers of letters per line and geometric size progression, improving test-retest reliability. Which chart is being described?

options: Inhibiting ciliary body carbonic anhydrase to reduce aqueous production
Reducing the episcleral venous pressure at the angle
Significantly increasing the uveoscleral outflow pathway
questions.question: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (e.g., acetazolamide) reduce IOP by:
questions.explanation: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors reduce aqueous humour production by blocking carbonic anhydrase II in ciliary body epithelium. This enzyme catalyses the hydration of CO2 essential for bicarbonate-driven active aqueous secretion. Both systemic (acetazolamide) and topical (dorzolamide, brinzolamide) forms are available.

questions.question: On fundoscopy, small red dots representing focal outpouching of retinal capillary walls are seen scattered in the posterior pole. These earliest lesions of diabetic retinopathy are called
questions.explanation: Microaneurysms represent focal dilatations of the capillary wall and are typically the earliest visible sign of diabetic retinopathy on fundus examination. Cotton wool spots and hard exudates appear at later stages, and neovascularization signifies advanced proliferative disease. Identifying microaneurysms prompts closer monitoring even in an otherwise asymptomatic patient.

options: Accommodation of the lens in most clinical presentations in most clinical presentations
Pupillary dilation and elevation of upper lid via Muller's muscle
Aqueous humor production only under standard examination conditions under standard examination conditions
questions.explanation: The sympathetic nervous system controls pupillary dilation (via the dilator pupillae) and the superior tarsal muscle (Muller's muscle), which assists in elevating the upper eyelid. Disruption causes the characteristic miosis and ptosis of Horner's syndrome. Accommodation and pupillary constriction are parasympathetic functions mediated by CN III.
questions.question: Sympathetic innervation controls which of the following in the eye?

questions.explanation: People of African ancestry have significantly higher risk of POAG, present at younger ages, have higher IOP at diagnosis, and progress to blindness more rapidly than other races. In West Africa, POAG is the second most common cause of blindness after cataract. This racial predisposition underlies Nigeria's high glaucoma blindness burden.
questions.question: Which racial group has the HIGHEST risk and most severe course of POAG?

questions.explanation: Weber's syndrome results from a midbrain lesion affecting the exiting third nerve fascicles together with the adjacent corticospinal tract, producing ipsilateral third nerve palsy with contralateral hemiparesis. This crossed pattern is a hallmark of brainstem, rather than purely peripheral, third nerve lesions. Localising to the midbrain guides urgent neuroimaging.
questions.question: A patient with Weber's syndrome has an ipsilateral third nerve palsy together with contralateral limb weakness. This combination localises the lesion to the

options: Multiple hard exudate rings around the fovea
Disciform scar at the fovea with surrounding subretinal haemorrhage
White fluffy vitreal opacities at the posterior pole
Outer retinal atrophy from the disc to the periphery
Concentric rings of pigmentation surrounding the fovea with a central spared foveal island
questions.explanation: Bull's-eye maculopathy is characterised by a ring of RPE atrophy and depigmentation surrounding a relatively preserved central foveal island, creating a 'target' or 'bull's-eye' appearance. It is most classically associated with hydroxychloroquine/chloroquine toxicity but also occurs in Stargardt's disease, cone-rod dystrophies, and benign concentric annular macular dystrophy.
questions.question: Bull's-eye maculopathy is characterised by which fundoscopic pattern?

options: topical corticosteroid with a cycloplegic agent
questions.explanation: Corticosteroids control the inflammatory response in anterior uveitis, while cycloplegics such as cyclopentolate relax the ciliary muscle and dilate the pupil to prevent painful spasm and posterior synechiae formation. Antibiotics and antivirals do not address a primarily inflammatory, non-infective process. This combination remains standard first-line therapy.
questions.question: A patient with active anterior uveitis requires a combination that reduces inflammation while preventing painful ciliary spasm and posterior synechiae. The MOST appropriate regimen is

questions.explanation: Normal diurnal IOP variation is 2–6 mmHg over 24 hours, with IOP highest in the early morning and lowest at night. Glaucoma patients may have wider diurnal fluctuations exceeding 6 mmHg. Measurement of IOP at different times of day (phased tonometry) is diagnostically useful in patients with suspected glaucoma and borderline single readings.
questions.question: The diurnal variation of IOP over 24 hours in a normal individual is approximately:
The MOST common peripheral corneal opacity associated with physiological aging in adults is:
questions.explanation: Arcus senilis is the most common peripheral corneal opacity, occurring with normal aging. It appears as a circumferential grey-white lipid ring at the corneal periphery, separated from the limbus by a clear zone. In patients under 40 years, arcus senilis (arcus juvenilis) may indicate hyperlipidemia. It does not impair vision as it is peripheral and not on the visual axis.

options: Trabeculectomy to reduce CSF via the optic nerve sheath
Optic nerve sheath fenestration (ONSF) in cases of visual deterioration
Bilateral laser photocoagulation of the disc
Topical IOP-lowering drops to reduce CSF pressure
questions.question: In the management of a patient with raised ICP and bilateral papilloedema, which ophthalmic procedure provides the MOST definitive relief of the disc swelling?
questions.explanation: Optic nerve sheath fenestration (ONSF) is the ophthalmic surgical procedure for progressive visual loss from papilloedema/raised ICP, creating a window in the optic nerve sheath to allow CSF to decompress around the optic nerve. It primarily protects vision on the operated side. Neurosurgical CSF diversion (ventriculoperitoneal shunt or lumboperitoneal shunt) addresses the underlying ICP elevation systemically.

questions.question: The Sheridan-Gardiner test uses which subset of letters for visual acuity testing in children?
questions.explanation: The Sheridan-Gardiner test uses the letters HOTVX (letters first recognized by children) plus A and U, giving HOTVXAU. The child matches letters shown at 6 m to a key card held nearby. This matching format avoids the need to name letters, making it suitable for children approximately 2–5 years of age. SUBTOPIC 3: DISEASES OF EYELIDS, ORBIT AND LACRIMAL APPARATUS
options: E, H, O, T, V, X (HOTVX) plus A and U
Full 26-letter alphabet on a tumbling format
HOTV with A and U added (HOTVXAU)

questions.explanation: Cotton-wool spots represent localised infarction of the retinal nerve fibre layer due to microvascular occlusion, causing accumulation of axoplasmic debris. They appear as fluffy white patches with indistinct borders, distinguishing them from the sharper hard exudates. Their presence indicates significant retinal ischaemia.
options: New vessel growth on the disc
questions.question: A diabetic patient's fundus shows fluffy white patches with ill-defined margins overlying retinal vessels. What do these represent?

options: A wound with both entry and exit wounds
Any injury involving an intraocular foreign body
A full-thickness wound with only one entry point (no exit)
Full-thickness wound from blunt force only
questions.question: According to BETT classification, a penetrating injury is defined as:
questions.explanation: The Birmingham Eye Trauma Terminology (BETT) defines a penetrating injury as a full-thickness wound of the globe wall with ONE entry point and NO exit wound. A perforating injury has both entry and exit wounds. A rupture is a full-thickness wound from blunt force. Accurate BETT classification guides surgical planning and prognostication.

questions.question: In alkali burns, the indicator of SEVERE prognosis is:
questions.explanation: In chemical (alkali) burns, limbal ischaemia is the most critical prognostic indicator. The limbus contains the corneal stem cells (limbal stem cells); their destruction leads to persistent epithelial defects, corneal vascularisation, conjunctivalisation, and ultimately corneal opacification. More than 50% limbal ischaemia (Roper-Hall Grade IV) portends very poor visual prognosis.
options: Peripheral fluorescein staining of the cornea
Corneal epithelial defect with clear stroma
Mild conjunctival hyperaemia without any limbal ischaemia present
Limbal whitening (ischaemia) involving more than 50% of the limbus

questions.question: Preseptal (periorbital) cellulitis differs from orbital cellulitis in that:
questions.explanation: Preseptal (periorbital) cellulitis involves tissues anterior to the orbital septum — eyelid and periorbital tissues — without proptosis, restricted eye movements, or visual loss. Orbital cellulitis involves post-septal tissues, causing proptosis, painful restricted eye movements, chemosis, and potentially visual loss from optic nerve compression. This distinction determines management urgency.
options: Preseptal cellulitis requires immediate surgical drainage
Preseptal cellulitis involves tissues anterior to the orbital septum with no proptosis or restricted movements
Preseptal cellulitis always causes visual loss
Orbital cellulitis never causes restricted eye movements
Orbital cellulitis is always caused by viral infection

questions.question: Barkan's membrane, incised during goniotomy, is located:
questions.explanation: In primary congenital glaucoma, an abnormal membrane (Barkan's membrane) is believed to cover the trabecular meshwork, obstructing aqueous outflow. Goniotomy incises this membrane under direct gonioscopic visualisation, restoring trabecular access. Success rates are 80–90% when cornea is clear enough for adequate angle visualisation.
options: Diffusely covering the entire optic disc surface
Overlying the trabecular meshwork at the anterior chamber angle
Located within the posterior vitreous face region

questions.explanation: Diabetic macular edema results from breakdown of the blood-retinal barrier, allowing fluid to accumulate and thicken the central macula, producing the gradual blurring commonly reported by patients. It can occur at any stage of retinopathy severity, unlike proliferative changes which specifically involve new vessel growth. It remains the most common cause of visual impairment in diabetic patients.
questions.question: A diabetic patient reports gradually blurred central vision, and examination reveals retinal thickening centred on the macula from leaking capillaries. This is BEST described as
options: proliferative diabetic retinopathy without macular involvement
It prevents pupillary block from developing
It is a normal finding in young patients with elastic iris tissue present
It plugs the wound temporarily but risks endophthalmitis and sympathetic ophthalmia
It indicates the injury is superficial and self-limiting
questions.explanation: Iris prolapse into a corneal wound is a serious sign of an open globe. While the uveal tissue may temporarily tamponade the wound, it creates a portal for bacterial entry (endophthalmitis risk) and exposes uveal tissue, triggering an autoimmune response (sympathetic ophthalmia risk). Surgical closure is mandatory; viable iris is repositioned, contaminated iris is excised.
questions.question: Iris incarceration in a penetrating corneal wound is clinically important because:

options: Whether diplopia is monocular or binocular
questions.question: In evaluating a third nerve palsy, the FIRST clinical determination to make is:
questions.explanation: Pupillary involvement is the single most important initial determination in a CN III palsy because it distinguishes compressive (surgical) from ischemic (medical) causes. A dilated, unreactive pupil suggests aneurysmal compression requiring urgent imaging. A pupil-sparing palsy in an older patient with vascular risk factors is more likely ischemic in origin.

questions.question: A patient presents with an eyelid laceration involving the area near the nose. Why is careful assessment of this specific region particularly important?
questions.explanation: Lacerations near the medial canthus carry a risk of injury to the canalicular lacrimal drainage system, which if unrepaired can cause chronic epiphora. Careful exploration and, if necessary, stenting of the canaliculi during repair preserves normal tear drainage function. Missed canalicular injury is a common cause of poor outcomes after eyelid trauma.
options: Increased risk of orbital fracture only
Higher chance of globe rupture only
Greater risk of eyebrow loss only
Possible involvement of the lacrimal drainage system
Higher likelihood of corneal abrasion only
Laser peripheral iridotomy or surgical iridectomy
Continued topical medication indefinitely without surgery
questions.explanation: After IOP is acutely lowered, the definitive treatment for pupil-block PACG is laser peripheral iridotomy (LPI) or surgical iridectomy. LPI creates a small opening in the peripheral iris, bypassing the pupillary block, equalising pressure between posterior and anterior chambers, and preventing further attacks. Prophylactic LPI is also performed on the fellow eye.
questions.question: The DEFINITIVE surgical treatment for pupil-block acute PACG is:

options: Progressive stromal thinning with corneal ectasia
questions.explanation: Keratoconus results from progressive thinning and weakening of the corneal stroma, causing the cornea to bulge forward into a cone shape, termed ectasia. This produces irregular astigmatism and reduced vision that worsens over time. Contact lenses, corneal cross-linking, or transplantation are used depending on disease severity.
questions.question: A patient with keratoconus is noted to have progressive corneal thinning and irregular astigmatism. What is the underlying structural change causing this?

questions.explanation: Peripheral scatter laser photocoagulation targets the ischemic retina driving neovascularization, reducing the risk of vitreous hemorrhage from fragile sea-fan vessels in sickle cell retinopathy. Systemic steroids and antibiotics have no established role in halting this ischemia-driven neovascular process. Early laser treatment at this stage can prevent progression to more severe haemorrhagic complications.
questions.question: A patient with sickle cell disease has peripheral sea-fan neovascularization confirmed on examination. The MOST appropriate treatment to reduce the risk of vitreous hemorrhage is
A sexually active adult presents with severe hyperacute purulent conjunctivitis threatening corneal perforation. Which organism must be urgently excluded?
questions.explanation: Adult gonococcal conjunctivitis presents hyperacutely with copious purulent discharge and can rapidly cause corneal ulceration and perforation if untreated. It requires urgent systemic antibiotic therapy alongside topical treatment and same-day ophthalmology referral. Sexual partners should also be treated to prevent reinfection.

questions.question: Which investigation is recommended for all patients over 40 years with diabetes to assess for diabetic retinopathy, even without visual symptoms?
options: Dilated fundus examination with slit-lamp biomicroscopy and/or fundus photography
Schirmer's test for tear production as commonly encountered in practice
Automated perimetry (visual field test) during routine ophthalmic assessment
questions.explanation: All patients above 40 years with diabetes—even without visual symptoms—require dilated fundus examination with slit-lamp biomicroscopy and/or fundus photography to screen for diabetic retinopathy. This is because significant retinopathy (including CSME) can exist without symptoms. The internist/endocrinologist plays a critical role by performing initial fundoscopy and referring early to ophthalmology. Screening coverage of at least 80% is required for effective population-level impact.

questions.question: Ocular sarcoidosis characteristically produces which type of uveitis?
questions.explanation: Sarcoidosis characteristically causes granulomatous uveitis — large 'mutton-fat' keratic precipitates (KPs) on the corneal endothelium, iris nodules (Koeppe and Busacca nodules), trabecular meshwork granulomas, posterior uveitis with periphlebitis ('candle-wax drippings'), disc granulomas, and choroidal nodules. Systemic sarcoidosis evaluation and ACE level, chest imaging are essential.
options: Granulomatous uveitis with mutton-fat keratic precipitates, iris nodules, and posterior segment involvement
Posterior vitritis occurring without any anterior chamber inflammation
Anterior uveitis with hypopyon and fibrin

questions.question: A patient with visual acuity of less than 3/60 but greater than or equal to 1/60 falls into which WHO visual handicap category?
questions.explanation: WHO visual handicap Category 3 corresponds to VA less than 3/60 to 1/60 (counting fingers at 1 meter). Categories 3, 4, and 5 together constitute legal blindness (VA less than 3/60 to no light perception). Category 2 is severe visual impairment (less than 6/60 to 3/60).

Band-shaped keratopathy involves deposition of calcium hydroxyapatite in the Bowman's membrane and anterior superficial stroma. It appears as a horizontal grey-white band across the interpalpebral zone with clear areas corresponding to corneal nerve canal perforations. Causes include chronic iridocyclitis, hypercalcemia, phthisis bulbi, and idiopathic degeneration.
options: Corneal stroma at all levels uniformly
Posterior stroma immediately adjacent to Descemet's membrane
Bowman's membrane and anterior stroma (subepithelial region)
questions.question: Band-shaped keratopathy is characterized by calcium salt deposition in which corneal layer?

questions.explanation: Onchocerciasis causes visual loss through inflammatory corneal opacity (sclerosing keratitis) and optic atrophy resulting from the death of Onchocerca volvulus microfilariae within the eye and their associated inflammatory reaction. It is endemic in West, Central, and East Africa. The Onchocerciasis Control Programme (OCP) using ivermectin has significantly reduced the burden of river blindness.
options: Corneal opacity and optic nerve atrophy from Onchocerca volvulus microfilariae
Macular degeneration from photoreceptor damage in most clinical presentations as commonly encountered in practice
Congenital lens opacities under standard examination conditions during routine ophthalmic assessment
questions.question: Onchocerciasis (river blindness) causes visual loss primarily through:
POAG most commonly affects adults over the age of:
questions.explanation: POAG most commonly affects adults over 35 years of age. Its prevalence increases with age, affecting 1–3% of persons over 40 years. In West Africa, POAG tends to present at an earlier age and with more aggressive progression than in Caucasian populations. Screening from age 35 is recommended for Africans.

The corneal stroma comprises about ninety percent of total corneal thickness and consists of regularly arranged collagen lamellae interspersed with keratocytes, giving the cornea its strength and transparency. This regular collagen architecture is essential for maintaining optical clarity. Disruption of stromal collagen organisation, as in scarring or oedema, leads to loss of corneal transparency.
questions.question: A corneal biopsy shows the thickest layer of the cornea composed of organised collagen lamellae and keratocytes, providing most of the tensile strength. Which layer is this?

options: within the first week of life
only if discharge is already present
within the first month of life
questions.question: To prevent ophthalmia neonatorum, ocular prophylaxis should be instilled into a newborn's eyes within which timeframe after delivery?
questions.explanation: Prompt instillation of prophylactic ocular agents within the first hour after birth aims to prevent colonisation and infection before pathogens acquired during passage through the birth canal can establish disease. Delaying prophylaxis reduces its preventive effectiveness. This timing is a key component of standard newborn care protocols in preventing ophthalmia neonatorum.

Orbital compartment syndrome (OCS), most commonly from retrobulbar haemorrhage after trauma, causes rapid pressure rise within the rigid bony orbit. Optic nerve compression and vascular compromise cause rapid, irreversible visual loss within minutes to hours. It presents with proptosis, increasing periorbital tightness, and vision loss. Immediate lateral canthotomy/cantholysis is the emergency treatment.
questions.question: Orbital compartment syndrome presents as an ophthalmic emergency because:
options: It only affects the eyelid tissues superficially
It causes chronic corneal scarring over time
It always causes bilateral proptosis requiring no treatment
Rapidly increasing orbital pressure compresses the optic nerve, threatening irreversible visual loss
It is caused by a slow-growing orbital tumour

questions.explanation: Rubeosis iridis (new vessels on the iris) occurs when severe retinal ischemia triggers VEGF production, which diffuses anteriorly to stimulate neovascularization on the iris and trabecular meshwork. This leads to neovascular glaucoma—a devastating complication with markedly elevated IOP due to angle occlusion by fibrovascular tissue. Neovascular glaucoma is extremely difficult to treat and often results in blindness.
questions.question: Rubeosis iridis (iris neovascularization) in advanced diabetic eye disease indicates which serious complication?
options: Background retinopathy only during routine ophthalmic assessment
Benign iris pigmentation change as commonly encountered in practice
Neovascular glaucoma from anterior segment ischemia
B-scan ultrasonography to assess the retina behind the hemorrhage
Fundus fluorescein angiography through the hemorrhage based on typical clinical findings
Visual field testing to localize the hemorrhage in the majority of documented cases
questions.explanation: B-scan ultrasonography (contact ultrasound of the eye) is the primary investigation when media opacity (vitreous hemorrhage, dense cataract) prevents direct visualization of the posterior segment. It can detect retinal detachment, vitreous organization, intraocular masses, and foreign bodies behind opaque media. This is critical in diabetic patients as tractional retinal detachment requiring urgent vitrectomy may be present behind the hemorrhage.
questions.question: A patient with diabetes and a vitreous hemorrhage obscuring the fundus view is BEST evaluated using:

questions.explanation: Leucocoria (white pupil reflex or 'cat's eye reflex') is the most common presenting feature of retinoblastoma, resulting from the white intraocular tumor visible through the pupil. It is detectable on the red reflex test, which is an important neonatal and infant screening tool. Squint is the second most common presentation. Early detection through leucocoria recognition is lifesaving.
questions.question: Retinoblastoma (RB) most commonly presents with which clinical sign?
The procedure of choice for primary congenital glaucoma is:
questions.explanation: Primary congenital glaucoma is primarily a surgical disease. Goniotomy (incision of trabecular meshwork under gonioscopic visualisation) and trabeculotomy ab externo (external cannulation and tearing of the trabecular meshwork) are the procedures of choice. Medical therapy with CAIs or beta-blockers serves only as a temporising measure.
options: Oral carbonic anhydrase inhibitors as adjunct therapy

questions.question: Combined mechanism glaucoma occurs when a patient has:
options: Both primary and secondary glaucoma causes
Both POAG and congenital glaucoma occurring in the same eye
Bilateral PACG in both eyes simultaneously
Glaucoma in both eyes by different mechanisms
Features of both open-angle and angle-closure mechanisms in the same eye
questions.explanation: Combined mechanism glaucoma occurs when both trabecular (open-angle) and appositional/synechial (angle-closure) mechanisms contribute to elevated IOP in the same eye. For example, a patient with POAG may develop partial angle closure, or a patient with treated PACG may have underlying trabecular dysfunction. Management must address both components.

questions.question: A patient undergoes pterygium excision and is counselled about recurrence risk. Which adjunctive measure is NOT used to reduce recurrence?
questions.explanation: Recurrence after pterygium excision is reduced by adjunctive measures such as conjunctival autografting, mitomycin C, beta irradiation, or amniotic membrane grafting, all of which target the local fibrovascular proliferation. Systemic corticosteroids are not used for this purpose since the recurrence process is localised to the surgical site. Bare sclera excision alone carries the highest recurrence rate.

questions.question: For optimal fundoscopy with 1/3 fundal view, the pupil-dilating agent of choice and recommended waiting time are:
questions.explanation: Tropicamide 1% is the standard mydriatic for fundoscopy, with adequate dilation occurring within 15 minutes. It has a shorter duration of action compared to atropine or cyclopentolate, reducing patient inconvenience. Pilocarpine is a miotic agent and would constrict rather than dilate the pupil.

questions.question: A patient recovering from measles infection develops bilateral corneal ulceration and perforation in a malnourished setting. What combined deficiency worsens this outcome?
questions.explanation: Measles infection can precipitate acute vitamin A deficiency in malnourished children, severely compromising corneal epithelial integrity. This combination markedly increases the risk of corneal ulceration, melting, and perforation, a condition known as keratomalacia. Vitamin A supplementation during measles outbreaks significantly reduces this blinding complication.

options: Only arteriolar narrowing and AV nipping as commonly encountered in practice
Disc pallor from previous optic neuritis during routine ophthalmic assessment
Macular star, papilledema, flame hemorrhages, cotton wool spots, and hard exudates
questions.explanation: Grade IV (malignant) hypertensive retinopathy demonstrates the full spectrum of hypertensive fundus changes: papilledema (swollen optic disc), macular star (hard exudates radiating around the fovea in a star pattern), flame-shaped hemorrhages, cotton wool spots, and hard exudates. This complete picture correlates with diastolic BP =130 mmHg and represents severe end-organ damage requiring urgent treatment.
questions.question: Fundoscopy in a patient with grade IV hypertensive retinopathy would MOST likely reveal:

questions.explanation: Mutations in CYP1B1 (cytochrome P450 family 1B member 1, locus GLC3A) are the most common cause of autosomal recessive PCG. CYP1B1 is involved in the metabolism of substances important for anterior segment development. Mutations result in abnormal angle development and obstructed aqueous outflow causing congenital glaucoma.
questions.question: The gene MOST commonly mutated in autosomal recessive primary congenital glaucoma is:
The primary mechanism of visual loss in Branch Retinal Vein Occlusion (BRVO) is:
questions.explanation: In branch retinal vein occlusion, compression of the vein at an arteriovenous crossing causes venous obstruction, leading to retinal hemorrhages, macular edema, and macular ischemia in the affected sector. Macular edema is the primary driver of visual loss in BRVO. Anti-VEGF therapy and laser photocoagulation are used for macular edema management. Neovascularization may develop as a secondary complication.
options: Macular edema and macular ischemia secondary to venous occlusion
Lens opacification from venous stasis during routine ophthalmic assessment
Neovascular glaucoma as the initial event as commonly encountered in practice

questions.question: A patient with a retinal detachment caused by a single superior retinal break is treated with an intraocular gas bubble combined with laser. What is this minimally invasive technique called?
questions.explanation: Pneumatic retinopexy involves injecting an expansile gas bubble into the vitreous cavity, positioned to tamponade a superior retinal break while laser or cryotherapy seals the tear. Careful patient positioning after the procedure is essential to keep the bubble over the break. It is best suited to selected cases with a single, superiorly located break.

questions.question: A neonate born prematurely at 28 weeks gestation is at highest risk for which blinding condition?
questions.explanation: Retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) is the major ocular risk for preterm neonates, especially those born before 32 weeks gestation or with birth weight below 1500 g requiring supplemental oxygen. The immature retinal vasculature is susceptible to oxygen-induced dysregulation. All high-risk premature neonates require retinal screening by indirect ophthalmoscopy starting at 4–6 weeks of age. ROP is now a leading cause of childhood blindness in middle-income countries with improving neonatal care.

Ocular toxoplasmosis characteristically presents as a focal necrotising retinochoroiditis adjacent to an old pigmented scar, representing reactivation of congenital or previously acquired infection. Cat exposure is a relevant epidemiological clue due to the parasite's feline definitive host. Treatment is reserved for sight-threatening or macula-involving lesions.
questions.question: A patient with a history of cat exposure presents with a focal, yellow-white retinochoroiditis lesion adjacent to an old pigmented scar. What is the diagnosis?

questions.explanation: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a common and particularly aggressive cause of contact lens-associated bacterial keratitis, capable of rapid stromal destruction if untreated. It classically produces a greenish-tinged mucopurulent discharge and can lead to corneal melting and perforation within days. Empirical fortified antipseudomonal antibiotic therapy is started immediately while awaiting culture confirmation.
questions.question: A contact lens wearer develops a rapidly progressive corneal ulcer with a greenish stromal infiltrate and mucopurulent discharge. Which organism should be treated empirically as the leading concern?

options: Ciliary muscle spasm causing reversible accommodation loss
Posterior synechiae leading to pupil block glaucoma
Keratic precipitate deposits on the corneal endothelium
Low IOP from reduced ciliary body secretion
Iris discolouration from altered melanocyte pigmentation
questions.explanation: Posterior synechiae forming silently in chronic or recurrent anterior uveitis can lead to iris bombé and acute pupil-block glaucoma — a sudden severe IOP elevation that permanently damages the optic nerve if untreated. This can progress unnoticed in low-grade uveitis. Cycloplegia prevents synechiae, and monitoring IOP at every visit is critical in uveitis management.
questions.question: In anterior uveitis, the MOST immediate complication that can permanently damage vision without causing symptoms is:

questions.explanation: Malignant (aqueous misdirection) glaucoma is a rare complication often following intraocular surgery. Aqueous is misdirected posteriorly into the vitreous, causing anterior displacement of the lens-iris diaphragm and shallowing of the ENTIRE anterior chamber (both central and peripheral). It does not respond to miotics and requires vitreous drainage.
questions.question: Malignant glaucoma (aqueous misdirection) is characterised by:
options: Congenital angle dysgenesis causing high IOP
Angle closure from pupillary block exclusively
Aqueous misdirection posteriorly into vitreous with shallowing of the entire anterior chamber
Open angle glaucoma with very high IOP and vitreous haemorrhage present

questions.explanation: Post-operative endophthalmitis following cataract surgery is most commonly caused by Staphylococcus epidermidis (coagulase-negative staphylococci), part of normal conjunctival flora. The Endophthalmitis Vitrectomy Study showed that intravitreal antibiotics (vancomycin + ceftazidime/amikacin) with or without vitrectomy are the treatment standard.
options: Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection of the cornea
questions.question: Post-operative endophthalmitis after cataract surgery is MOST commonly caused by:

questions.explanation: Postoperative endophthalmitis requires urgent vitreous and aqueous sampling for microbiological analysis combined with immediate empirical intravitreal antibiotic injection to control the infection rapidly. Delayed treatment significantly worsens visual outcomes due to the rapid destructive potential of intraocular infection. Vitrectomy may be added in severe cases with poor initial vision.
questions.question: A patient develops sudden severe pain, hypopyon, and marked visual loss several days after uncomplicated cataract surgery. What is the recommended emergency treatment approach?
options: Immediate vitreous sampling with intravitreal antibiotic injection

questions.explanation: Hyperopic (farsighted) eyes are too short, requiring converging (plus) lenses to bring the fundus into focus during direct ophthalmoscopy. The green dial numbers correspond to plus-powered lenses. Minus (red) numbers are used for myopic patients, whose eyes are too long and require diverging lenses for clear fundal visualization.
questions.question: A hyperopic patient undergoing fundoscopy will require the ophthalmoscope dial to be adjusted to:
A patient presents with red eye, watery discharge, pre-auricular lymphadenopathy, and a recent upper respiratory tract infection. The MOST likely causative agent is:
questions.explanation: Viral conjunctivitis caused by adenovirus typically presents with watery (not purulent) discharge, conjunctival hyperemia, and pre-auricular lymphadenopathy, often accompanying or following an upper respiratory tract infection. It is bilateral and highly contagious. The pre-auricular node is a key differentiating feature from bacterial conjunctivitis, which usually lacks lymphadenopathy.

questions.question: In managing thyroid eye disease, which systemic treatment is first-line for the active inflammatory phase?
options: Radioactive iodine treatment as sole therapy
questions.explanation: High-dose systemic corticosteroids (typically IV methylprednisolone pulse therapy) are the first-line treatment for active, moderate-to-severe Graves' ophthalmopathy. They reduce orbital inflammation, improve soft tissue changes, and may partially reduce proptosis. Orbital decompression, radiotherapy, and surgical correction of eyelid retraction/strabismus are deferred until the active phase has resolved and disease has been stable for at least 6 months.

options: Destroying ciliary body epithelium to permanently reduce aqueous production
Creating a filtering bleb for controlled aqueous drainage
questions.question: Cycloablation (cyclodiode laser) as a glaucoma treatment works by:
questions.explanation: Cycloablation (cyclodiode laser or cryotherapy) reduces IOP by destroying ciliary body epithelium, thereby permanently reducing aqueous production. It is used in refractory glaucoma where other surgeries have failed, in end-stage glaucoma with poor visual potential, or in blind painful eyes. Risk of hypotony and phthisis bulbi must be carefully considered.

questions.question: A patient with sickle haemoglobin C genotype presents with peripheral fan-shaped new vessels on the retina. Which genotype is most associated with this proliferative complication?
questions.explanation: Although haemoglobin SS disease causes more severe systemic complications, haemoglobin SC disease is paradoxically associated with a higher rate of proliferative sickle retinopathy with sea-fan neovascularisation. This is thought to relate to relatively preserved blood viscosity allowing more localised peripheral vaso-occlusion. Regular retinal screening is important in SC patients.

questions.question: A patient presents with a suspected intraocular foreign body but has an intact-looking cornea on examination. Why should imaging still be pursued?
options: Imaging is never necessary if the cornea looks intact
Small entry wounds can self-seal and be easily missed
Foreign bodies always cause obvious external wounds
Ultrasound is contraindicated in trauma cases
Self-sealing wounds exclude foreign body risk
questions.explanation: Small, high-velocity foreign bodies can create tiny self-sealing corneal or scleral wounds that are easily overlooked on routine examination. A high index of suspicion based on injury mechanism should prompt imaging even when the globe appears externally intact. Missing a retained foreign body risks later infection or toxic retinal damage.

Early POAG field loss typically occurs in the paracentral area and the arcuate (Bjerrum) zone, corresponding to the dense nerve fibre bundles entering at the superior and inferior optic disc poles. Nasal steps, arcuate scotomas, and paracentral defects are characteristic early automated perimetry findings.
questions.question: Visual field defects in POAG typically begin in which region?
A patient with dry eyes and joint pains is found to have deficient tear production on Schirmer's testing. What underlying condition should be considered?
questions.explanation: Sjögren's syndrome is an autoimmune condition causing lymphocytic infiltration of the lacrimal and salivary glands, leading to reduced tear and saliva production. This produces keratoconjunctivitis sicca alongside dry mouth and joint symptoms. Diagnosis is supported by reduced Schirmer's test values and specific autoantibody testing.

questions.question: A pingueculum differs from a pterygium in which critical characteristic?
options: Pingueculum is more common temporally; pterygium is more common nasally
Pingueculum remains on the conjunctiva and does NOT invade the cornea
Pingueculum always requires surgical excision for definitive treatment
Pterygium has elastotic degeneration while pingueculum has fibrovascular tissue only
Pingueculum arises from meibomian gland secretions while pterygium is vascular
questions.explanation: The critical distinction is that a pingueculum is a conjunctival degenerative lesion in the interpalpebral zone that does NOT invade the cornea, while a pterygium is a fibrovascular tissue that has invaded the superficial cornea. Pingueculum appears as a yellowish-white subconjunctival deposit, usually nasally. Both involve elastotic collagen degeneration from UV exposure.

Goniotomy involves a direct incision into the abnormal trabecular meshwork tissue under gonioscopic visualisation, relieving the developmental obstruction to aqueous outflow characteristic of primary congenital glaucoma. Adequate corneal clarity is essential for good visualisation during the procedure. It is considered the primary surgical treatment for this condition when the cornea remains sufficiently clear.
questions.question: A child with primary congenital glaucoma undergoes an incisional procedure opening the abnormal tissue obstructing aqueous outflow under direct visualisation. What is this procedure called?
A patient with chronic anterior uveitis develops adhesions between the iris and the anterior lens capsule, causing an irregular pupil. What are these adhesions called?
questions.explanation: Posterior synechiae refer to adhesions between the iris and the anterior lens capsule that develop during inflammation, distorting the pupil shape and impeding its normal dilation. These adhesions can obstruct aqueous flow through the pupil, raising intraocular pressure if extensive. This differs from peripheral anterior synechiae, which involve adhesion between the iris and the trabecular meshwork or cornea.

questions.question: A patient with a dermatomal vesicular rash extending to the tip of the nose develops keratitis. Which sign predicts a high likelihood of ocular involvement?
questions.explanation: Hutchinson's sign refers to vesicular lesions on the tip or side of the nose, indicating involvement of the nasociliary branch of the trigeminal nerve which also supplies the eye. Its presence strongly predicts ocular complications in herpes zoster ophthalmicus. Recognising this sign prompts closer ophthalmic monitoring even before overt eye symptoms develop.

questions.question: A patient has a painless, slowly enlarging nodule on the eyelid that developed from a previously tender swelling. Which condition has this evolved from?
questions.explanation: An internal hordeolum results from acute infection of a meibomian gland and can resolve into a chronic, painless granulomatous nodule known as a chalazion. The lesion loses its acute inflammatory tenderness as it becomes a lipogranulomatous reaction to retained secretions. This differs from an external hordeolum, which arises from glands of Zeis or Moll near the lash line.

Third nerve palsy causes pupillary dilation (mydriasis) because the parasympathetic fibers that constrict the pupil are disrupted. These fibers run on the outer surface of CN III and are particularly vulnerable to compressive lesions. Miosis would instead result from a Horner's syndrome (sympathetic disruption).
questions.question: Third nerve palsy produces which of the following characteristic pupillary change?
options: Miosis with loss of the light reflex

questions.question: A patient develops iris atrophy, corectopia, and secondary glaucoma following a viral illness affecting the corneal endothelium. What syndrome should be suspected?
questions.explanation: Iridocorneal endothelial (ICE) syndrome is characterised by abnormal proliferation of corneal endothelial cells, which migrate onto the iris causing atrophy, corectopia, and peripheral anterior synechiae. This mechanically obstructs the angle, leading to secondary glaucoma. It typically affects one eye in middle-aged women.

questions.question: WHO Category 2 (severe visual impairment) is defined by a best corrected VA in the better eye of:
questions.explanation: WHO visual handicap Category 2 (severe visual impairment) is defined by a best corrected VA of less than 6/60 to 3/60 (counting fingers at 3 meters) in the better eye. Category 1 is visual impairment (less than 6/18 to 6/60), and Categories 3–5 constitute legal blindness. These categories guide resource allocation in eye care programs.
options: Less than 1/60 to light perception only

questions.question: Among infective causes of ophthalmia neonatorum worldwide, the MOST common organism identified is
questions.explanation: Chlamydia trachomatis is globally the most frequently identified cause of ophthalmia neonatorum, typically producing a more indolent presentation than the more dramatic but less common gonococcal infection. Recognising chlamydia as the leading cause supports routine screening and appropriate systemic therapy. Gonococcal infection, while less common, is more rapidly sight-threatening and must not be missed.

questions.question: Congenital cataract causing deprivation amblyopia must be treated within what timeframe for optimal visual outcome?
questions.explanation: Dense unilateral congenital cataract must be surgically removed within the first 6–10 weeks of life to prevent severe deprivation amblyopia, as the critical period of visual cortical development is most active in early infancy. After surgery, optical rehabilitation (contact lens or glasses for aphakia) and amblyopia patching of the fellow eye are essential. Delayed surgery leads to permanent visual loss.
options: Within the first 3 years of life
Anytime before puberty for adequate cortical plasticity
After the age of 2 when surgery risk is reduced
Within the first 10 weeks of life for dense unilateral cataracts
Reducing aqueous production from the ciliary body in the majority of documented cases
Widening the trabecular meshwork drainage angle directly based on typical clinical findings
Creating a direct communication between posterior and anterior chambers to relieve pupillary block
questions.explanation: Laser peripheral iridotomy creates a small full-thickness hole in the peripheral iris, allowing aqueous humor to pass directly from the posterior to anterior chamber, bypassing the pupillary block that is the mechanism of acute angle-closure glaucoma. This equalizes pressure across the iris, opens the angle, and prevents future attacks. Prophylactic iridotomy in the contralateral eye is also recommended.
questions.question: Laser peripheral iridotomy in acute angle-closure glaucoma works by:

options: Congenital rubella syndrome causing retinal vascular inflammation
Prematurity (less than 32 weeks) and low birth weight (less than 1500 g)
questions.explanation: The most important risk factors for ROP are prematurity (especially less than 28 weeks) and low birth weight (less than 1250–1500 g). Supplemental oxygen therapy disrupts normal retinal vascular development by causing hyperoxia-induced vessel obliteration followed by hypoxia-driven pathological neovascularization. Screening and laser ablation of avascular retina prevent progression to retinal detachment.
questions.question: Retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) is caused by oxygen-induced retinal vascular abnormality. The MOST important risk factor is:
Diabetic papillopathy is a condition of optic disc swelling in diabetics that:
options: Requires immediate laser treatment of the disc
Usually resolves spontaneously with good visual recovery
Is associated with rapidly progressive retinopathy
questions.explanation: Diabetic papillopathy is a self-limiting optic disc swelling occurring in type 1 and type 2 diabetics, often in younger patients with relatively good glycaemic control. It presents with disc oedema, dilated disc capillaries, and mildly reduced vision or asymptomatic. Most cases resolve over months with good final visual acuity, distinguishing it from the poor prognosis of anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy.

options: The aqueous humor component of the tear film
questions.explanation: The aqueous component of the tear film is produced by the main lacrimal gland and accessory glands — NOT by the conjunctiva. The conjunctival goblet cells produce the mucin (inner) layer. The conjunctiva contributes to ocular protection through MALT, lymphoid follicles, and mechanical protection during ocular movement.
questions.question: The bulbar conjunctiva does NOT produce which of the following?
The weakest wall of the bony orbit, most susceptible to fracture in blunt trauma, is the:
questions.explanation: The orbital floor is the weakest wall of the bony orbit and is most commonly fractured in blunt trauma (blowout fracture). The medial wall, though thin (lamina papyracea), is not the weakest. Blowout fracture typically causes enophthalmos and diplopia.

questions.question: A patient with myasthenia gravis has a levator function measured at 3 mm on assessment. What does this level of levator action indicate?
questions.explanation: Levator palpebrae superioris action is graded by the excursion of the upper lid from extreme downgaze to extreme upgaze. An excursion below 4 mm indicates poor levator function and typically requires a frontalis sling procedure rather than levator resection. Grading levator function guides the choice of surgical correction for ptosis.

Ischemic third nerve palsy from microvascular disease preferentially affects the centrally located motor fibres while sparing the peripheral parasympathetic fibres responsible for pupil constriction. This pupil-sparing pattern differs from compressive lesions, where the pupil is typically involved early. Diabetes is a classic risk factor for this ischemic pattern.
questions.question: A diabetic patient develops sudden ptosis and diplopia with full extraocular movements limited except sparing pupil size and reactivity. This pattern is MOST consistent with
Kayser-Fleischer rings are copper deposits in Descemet's membrane. Their presence is pathognomonic of:
questions.explanation: Kayser-Fleischer rings are golden-brown or greenish deposits of copper in the peripheral Descemet's membrane, pathognomonic of Wilson's disease (hepatolenticular degeneration) when accompanied by neurological or hepatic features. They are best seen on slit-lamp examination or gonioscopy. Treatment with copper chelation (penicillamine) can cause them to fade.
options: Alkaptonuria with ochronosis of corneal collagen
Fabry's disease with glycolipid deposits in the cornea
Cystinosis with crystalline deposits in the stroma

questions.question: Corneal graft rejection is most commonly of which type and involves which layer primarily?
questions.explanation: Endothelial rejection is the most clinically significant form of corneal graft rejection, characterized by the Khodadoust line (a line of keratic precipitates on the donor endothelium advancing across the graft). It threatens graft survival because endothelial cells cannot regenerate. Epithelial rejection is the most common type but rarely threatens graft clarity. Urgent topical steroids are required.
options: Epithelial rejection — most common — white rejection line across epithelium
Stromal rejection — most common — stromal vascularization and haze
Bowman's rejection — earliest — anterior lamellae opacification
Endothelial rejection — most serious — Khodadoust line of KPs across endothelium
Descemet's rejection — white ring deposit on Descemet's membrane

questions.explanation: For two points to be resolved as distinct, their retinal images must fall on two stimulated cones separated by at least one unstimulated cone. This anatomical spacing sets the limit of visual resolving power at the fovea. Reduced cone density or photoreceptor damage raises this threshold and worsens acuity.
questions.question: A patient with a visual acuity of 6/60 can only resolve two points that a normal eye separates at 6 metres. What minimum retinal requirement allows two points to be seen as separate?

questions.explanation: The WHO-recommended short-term prophylaxis for children aged 12–59 months at risk of Vitamin A deficiency is 200,000 IU of Vitamin A orally every 4–6 months (6-monthly supplementation). Infants aged 6–11 months receive 100,000 IU. This periodic supplementation approach is used in endemic areas alongside food fortification (medium-term) and nutritional education (long-term) strategies.
questions.question: In the short-term approach to xerophthalmia prevention, the WHO-recommended Vitamin A supplementation schedule for children aged 12–59 months is:
Gonorrhoeal keratoconjunctivitis in adults is characterised by:
questions.explanation: Gonococcal (gonorrhoeal) conjunctivitis in adults presents as a hyperacute, severely purulent conjunctivitis with copious discharge, marked lid oedema, and chemosis. Crucially, the organism can penetrate intact corneal epithelium, causing rapid ulceration, perforation, and endophthalmitis within hours if untreated. Systemic ceftriaxone and urgent ophthalmology review are mandatory.
options: Hyperacute onset, profuse purulent discharge, chemosis, and risk of rapid corneal perforation
Follicular conjunctivitis with tender preauricular lymphadenopathy present
Membranous conjunctivitis with bilateral eye involvement noted
Mild chronic follicular conjunctivitis over weeks
Circular lesion at the fovea with drusen
Red lesion with hard exudates in the macula
Flame-shaped haemorrhages present along the vascular arcades
Crescent-shaped white subretinal streak concentric to the optic disc
questions.question: Choroidal rupture following blunt ocular trauma typically appears on fundoscopy as:
questions.explanation: Choroidal rupture appears as a white or yellowish crescent-shaped subretinal streak concentric to the optic disc (because the choroid is most tightly adherent at the optic disc and ruptures concentrically around it). Subretinal haemorrhage initially obscures the streak. Late complications include choroidal neovascularisation at the rupture site, threatening central vision.

Elevated IOP is the only modifiable risk factor proven by randomised controlled trials (OHTS, AGIS, EMGT) to slow POAG progression when reduced. IOP lowering remains the cornerstone of glaucoma management. Non-modifiable risk factors (age, race, genetics) cannot be altered but inform screening and treatment thresholds.
questions.question: The MOST important reversible risk factor targeted in POAG treatment is:

questions.explanation: Electrical injury can cause direct thermal damage to lens epithelial cells, leading to characteristic cataract formation that may develop over subsequent weeks to months. This is a recognised delayed complication of significant electrical injury to the head and face. Regular follow-up after such injuries allows early detection of this complication.
questions.question: A patient with an electrical injury to the face develops cataract weeks later. What is the likely explanation for this delayed lens change?
options: Direct thermal or electrical damage to lens fibres
Corneal infection spreading to the lens
Normal postoperative change after any injury

questions.explanation: Medial eyelid lymphatics drain to the submandibular lymph nodes, while the lateral eyelid drains to the preauricular nodes. There are no lymph nodes within the orbit itself. Lymph node involvement in eyelid tumors indicates metastatic spread.
questions.question: The lymphatics of the eyelids drain into which nodes when located at the medial aspect?

questions.explanation: The SAFE strategy bundles Surgery for trichiasis, Antibiotics for active infection, Facial cleanliness, and Environmental improvement to interrupt both individual disease progression and community transmission of trachoma. Other listed terms refer to unrelated classification systems in trauma, retinal disease, or oncology. This integrated strategy remains the global standard for trachoma elimination programmes.
questions.question: A national trachoma control programme implements surgery for trichiasis, antibiotics for active infection, facial cleanliness, and environmental improvement. This combined approach is known as the

questions.explanation: Sensation to the cornea, conjunctiva, lids, upper face, and sides of the nose is provided by CN V1 (ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve), specifically the nasociliary, frontal, and lacrimal branches. Loss of corneal sensation (e.g., in herpes simplex) predisposes to neurotrophic keratopathy.
questions.question: Which sensory nerve provides sensation to the cornea and conjunctiva?

options: Congenital cataract and ROP based on typical clinical findings
Trauma from road traffic accidents in the majority of documented cases
Vitamin A deficiency, measles, and ophthalmia neonatorum
questions.explanation: In very low-income countries, corneal scarring causing childhood blindness is predominantly due to preventable infectious and nutritional causes: Vitamin A deficiency (xerophthalmia/keratomalacia), measles-related keratitis, and ophthalmia neonatorum (untreated gonococcal or chlamydial). These can be largely prevented through vaccination, Vitamin A supplementation, neonatal prophylaxis, and improved nutrition—making them a priority for public health intervention.
questions.question: Childhood blindness from corneal scarring in low-income countries is MOST commonly caused by:
A patient with facial cellulitis around the eye develops proptosis, restricted eye movement, and reduced vision. What distinguishes this from simple eyelid infection?
questions.explanation: Orbital cellulitis involves infection spreading posterior to the orbital septum, affecting orbital fat and muscles, unlike preseptal cellulitis which remains anterior. This produces proptosis, painful restricted eye movements, and potential visual loss from optic nerve compression. It requires urgent imaging and intravenous antibiotics due to risk of intracranial spread.
options: Redness confined only to the eyelid skin
Absence of any fever or systemic signs
Involvement of orbital soft tissue behind the septum

questions.explanation: Keratoconus is an ectatic disorder (corneal ectasia) classified among the corneal dystrophies. It involves progressive thinning and conical protrusion of the central or paracentral cornea, leading to irregular myopic astigmatism. It presents with recurrent corneal erosion syndrome or progressive visual impairment. It is associated with eye rubbing, Down syndrome, atopy, and connective tissue disorders.
questions.question: Keratoconus is best classified as which type of corneal disorder?

options: Disruption of the zonular fibres supporting the lens
Normal lens position after any trauma
Complete lens dislocation into the vitreous
questions.question: A patient presents following blunt trauma with a tremulous, wobbling lens visible on examination. What does this finding indicate?
questions.explanation: Phacodonesis describes a tremulous movement of the lens seen after blunt trauma, resulting from partial disruption of the zonular fibres that normally anchor it in place. This can progress to partial or complete lens dislocation if zonular damage is extensive. Careful monitoring for progression and cataract formation is required.

Contusion (blunt) injuries transmit force through closed eyelids and cause structural damage including hyphema, traumatic iridocyclitis, subconjunctival hemorrhage, vitreous hemorrhage, and lens subluxation. A corneal laceration requiring sutures implies a penetrating (open globe) injury—not a contusion. This distinction is critical as open globe injuries require different and more urgent surgical management.
questions.question: Contusion injuries to the eye can produce all the following EXCEPT:
options: Traumatic iridocyclitis in the majority of documented cases
Subconjunctival hemorrhage based on typical clinical findings

questions.explanation: The oculocardiac reflex (OCR) is triggered by pressure on the globe or traction on the extraocular muscles, particularly the medial rectus. Afferent fibres travel via the trigeminal nerve (ophthalmic branch/ciliary ganglion) and efferent fibres via the vagus nerve, causing bradycardia, ventricular arrhythmias, and potentially asystole. It is clinically important during strabismus surgery and retinal surgery.
questions.question: The oculocardiac reflex, triggered by pressure on the globe or traction on the extraocular muscles, can cause:

questions.explanation: Sickle cell disease and autoimmune conditions (e.g., HLA-B27-associated spondyloarthropathies, sarcoidosis, Behcet's disease) are systemic conditions strongly associated with anterior uveitis. Identifying these links guides both the investigation and systemic management of the patient. Surgical history and hypertension are less directly relevant to uveitis.
options: Hypertension treated with beta-blockers in most clinical presentations
Previous inguinal hernia repair under standard examination conditions
History of sickle cell disease or autoimmune conditions
questions.question: A patient with anterior uveitis is being assessed. Which past medical history item is MOST clinically relevant to document?

options: Lacrimal gland and accessory glands of Krause/Wolfring
Moll sweat glands at the anterior lid margin
Zeis sebaceous glands of the lashes
questions.explanation: The aqueous (middle) layer of the tear film is produced by the main lacrimal gland (orbital/palpebral lobes) and the accessory lacrimal glands of Krause and Wolfring. The goblet cells produce the mucin layer, and the meibomian glands produce the lipid layer. Lacrimal gland dysfunction (Sjogren's syndrome) causes aqueous tear deficiency.
questions.question: In the lacrimal secretory system, the aqueous component of the tear film is produced by the:

questions.explanation: Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) provides high-resolution, quantitative cross-sectional imaging of the retinal nerve fibre layer (RNFL), optic nerve head, and ganglion cell complex. It detects structural damage years before functional field loss is measurable and is essential for monitoring early glaucomatous progression.
questions.question: Which glaucoma investigation provides the BEST quantitative structural measure of the retinal nerve fibre layer?

questions.explanation: Optic nerve gliomas are associated with neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1/von Recklinghausen disease) in 25–50% of cases. In NF1, optic gliomas are typically low-grade pilocytic astrocytomas. NF1 is also associated with Lisch nodules (iris hamartomas), café-au-lait spots, and cutaneous neurofibromas. NF1 gliomas tend to be more benign than sporadic cases.
questions.question: An optic nerve glioma is most commonly occurs in association with which systemic condition?

A patient with a chronic, non-healing corneal ulcer despite maximal antimicrobial therapy is considered for a surgical procedure to remove infected tissue and preserve globe integrity. What is this urgent procedure known as?
questions.explanation: Therapeutic keratoplasty involves surgical removal of infected or necrotic corneal tissue in cases of severe, progressive keratitis unresponsive to medical therapy, helping to control infection and preserve the structural integrity of the eye. It differs from optical keratoplasty, which aims primarily to restore vision. It may be combined with later optical grafting once infection is controlled.

options: Associated with systemic autoimmune disease and does not blanch
Superficial, typically benign, and blanches with topical phenylephrine
Always bilateral and causes corneal perforation
questions.explanation: Episcleritis involves only the superficial episcleral vessels and is typically benign, self-limiting, and mildly painful. Topical phenylephrine causes blanching of the episcleral vessels—a key differentiating test from scleritis. Episcleritis may be associated with systemic disease in a minority, unlike scleritis where systemic association is stronger and the condition is more severe.
questions.question: Episcleritis differs from scleritis in that episcleritis is:
Ecchymosis ('black eye') following blunt periorbital trauma results from:
options: Bleeding into loose subcutaneous tissue of the eyelid
Corneal oedema spreading to the periorbital skin
Ruptured choroidal vessels under the conjunctiva
questions.explanation: Periorbital ecchymosis (black eye) is caused by haemorrhage into the loose subcutaneous periorbital tissue following blunt trauma. Blood tracks along tissue planes. Bilateral periorbital ecchymosis (raccoon eyes / panda sign) in the context of head trauma should raise suspicion of a basal skull fracture.

Exudative (secondary) retinal detachment results from fluid accumulation under the retina without a retinal break — caused by systemic diseases (VKH, posterior scleritis, hypertensive retinopathy, malignant HTN). Unlike rhegmatogenous detachment (which requires surgical repair of retinal breaks), exudative detachment requires identification and treatment of the underlying systemic cause. Treating the cause resolves the detachment.
options: Both require scleral buckling as first-line treatment
Exudative detachment requires identifying and treating the underlying cause
Both are managed by gas tamponade injections
Exudative detachment requires vitrectomy and laser
Rhegmatogenous detachment requires medical management only
questions.question: The surgical management of exudative retinal detachment DIFFERS from rhegmatogenous detachment in that:
Thyroid-associated ophthalmopathy (Graves' orbitopathy) is characterised by:
options: Proptosis, lid retraction, restricted eye movements, and potentially optic neuropathy
Anterior uveitis resulting from autoimmune inflammatory activation
questions.explanation: Graves' ophthalmopathy results from autoimmune inflammation of orbital contents, predominantly extraocular muscles and fat. Features include bilateral (often asymmetric) proptosis (exophthalmos), upper eyelid retraction, lid lag on downgaze, restricted eye movements, exposure keratopathy, and compressive optic neuropathy (dysthyroid optic neuropathy) requiring urgent treatment.

questions.question: Dry eye disease (keratoconjunctivitis sicca) in Sjögren's syndrome is caused primarily by:
questions.explanation: In Sjögren's syndrome, T-cell–mediated autoimmune destruction of the lacrimal glands reduces aqueous tear production, causing aqueous-deficient dry eye. This is the primary mechanism in primary and secondary Sjögren's. Histology shows lymphocytic infiltration of lacrimal gland acini. Management includes artificial tears, punctal plugs, cyclosporine A drops, and systemic hydroxychloroquine.
options: Decreased blink rate from neurological damage
Autoimmune destruction of lacrimal glands reducing aqueous tear production
Increased tear evaporation from meibomian gland dysfunction disease

questions.question: Epidemic keratoconjunctivitis (EKC) caused by adenovirus presents with subconjunctival hemorrhages and pseudomembranes when:
questions.explanation: Adenoviral EKC usually presents with acute watery discharge, follicular conjunctivitis, and preauricular adenopathy. Subconjunctival hemorrhages and pseudomembranes indicate severe disease. EKC is caused by adenovirus serotypes 8, 11, and 19 most commonly. Treatment is symptomatic (cold compresses, vasoconstrictors); antiviral preparations are not routinely useful.
options: The infection is mild and self-limited
The patient is immunocompetent with primary infection
The infection is caused by serotype 3 primarily
The patient uses contact lens concurrently

questions.explanation: Meibomian gland dysfunction (MGD) is a common cause of evaporative dry eye. Features include lid margin redness, foam in the tear meniscus, rapid tear break-up time, and recurrent chalazia. Risk factors include rosacea and oral retinoids. Management involves warm compresses, lid scrubs, and systemic tetracyclines for inflammatory cases.
questions.question: A 45-year-old woman has redness, lid margin irritation, and foam in her tear meniscus with a rapid tear break-up time. The MOST likely diagnosis is:
Intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy (e.g., ranibizumab, bevacizumab) is MOST indicated for which retinal condition?
questions.explanation: Intravitreal anti-VEGF agents work by blocking VEGF-A, reducing abnormal vascular permeability and neovascularization. They are first-line for: wet AMD (active CNV), centre-involving diabetic macular oedema (DMO), and macular oedema from CRVO/BRVO. They have transformed the prognosis of wet AMD. Treatment requires repeated injections (monthly initially, then as-needed/treat-and-extend protocols).
options: Non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy without macular oedema
Retinitis pigmentosa with progressive rod degeneration
Wet AMD with active choroidal neovascularization and centre-involving DMO

questions.question: A farmer presents with a grey-white corneal ulcer with indistinct feathery margins and hypopyon after a twig injury. The MOST likely causative organism is:
questions.explanation: Filamentous fungal keratitis (Aspergillus, Fusarium) classically occurs after vegetable matter/twig injury in agrarian communities. The greyish-white ulcer with indistinct feathery margins, satellite lesions, and finger-like stromal infiltrations is characteristic. Hypopyon may be present. Treatment requires broad-spectrum antifungals (econazole, natamycin, imidazole) for 6 weeks. Candida presents differently (white suppurative ulcer).

Aqueous flare is the Tyndall phenomenon — scattering of the slit-lamp beam by protein molecules (primarily albumin) that have leaked into the aqueous humor through a disrupted blood-aqueous barrier from uveitis. It is graded 0–4+. Flare persists after cells resolve as the blood-aqueous barrier remains compromised. It is an objective measure of uveitis activity.
questions.question: A flare in the anterior chamber of the eye in uveitis represents:
options: Red blood cells in the aqueous from rubeosis iridis
Inflammatory cells floating in the vitreous cavity
Scattering of slit-lamp beam from protein leakage through a disrupted blood-aqueous barrier
Calcium deposits in the anterior lens capsule
Posterior vitreous detachment with protein condensation debris
Spherical concave lens for all meridians
Cylindrical lens with power in one meridian
Prism to deviate light from both axes
Spherical convex lens for highest meridian
questions.question: The specific corrective lens used for astigmatism targets:
questions.explanation: Astigmatism is corrected with a cylindrical lens, which has refractive power in only one meridian. The two principal meridians with different refractive power are identified, and the cylindrical lens neutralizes the difference between them. Simple spherical lenses cannot correct astigmatism because they affect all meridians equally.

Immediate and copious irrigation is the most critical first step in chemical eye injuries, diluting and removing the offending agent before further tissue damage occurs. Delaying irrigation for examination or other assessment can significantly worsen the outcome. Irrigation should continue until pH normalises before detailed examination proceeds.
options: Copious irrigation of the eye with water
questions.question: A patient presents after a chemical splash to the eye. What is the single most important immediate action before any other assessment?

questions.explanation: When a retinoblastoma has extensively replaced the globe with no realistic chance of preserving vision, enucleation removes the tumour-bearing eye and reduces the risk of extraocular spread. Laser or topical therapy alone would be inadequate for such advanced local disease. This decision balances eye preservation against the greater priority of preventing life-threatening tumour spread.
questions.question: A child with an advanced retinoblastoma filling most of the globe with no useful vision remaining is BEST managed by

A patient with chronic atopic dermatitis has conjunctival scarring, lower lid involvement, and corneal vascularisation persisting into adulthood, unlike a related paediatric allergic condition. Which condition is this?
questions.explanation: Atopic keratoconjunctivitis typically affects an older age group than vernal keratoconjunctivitis and tends to involve the lower palpebral conjunctiva with a chronic course leading to scarring and corneal vascularisation. It is associated with atopic dermatitis and persists beyond childhood, unlike vernal disease which often resolves after puberty. Both conditions share allergic mechanisms but differ in age distribution and chronicity.

questions.question: A young adult male presents with recurrent branch retinal vein occlusions, vitreous haemorrhage, and peripheral neovascularisation in both eyes without significant systemic vascular risk factors. Which condition should be considered?
questions.explanation: Eales disease is an idiopathic retinal vasculitis predominantly affecting young adult males, causing peripheral venous occlusions, neovascularisation, and recurrent vitreous haemorrhage in the absence of significant systemic vascular disease. Its exact cause remains uncertain, though associations with tuberculosis hypersensitivity have been proposed. Management includes laser photocoagulation of ischaemic retina and control of intraocular inflammation.

questions.question: Corneal sensitivity is reduced in which systemic condition, predisposing to neurotrophic keratopathy?
questions.explanation: Diabetic autonomic and peripheral neuropathy reduces corneal sensitivity by affecting the sensory nerve supply (trigeminal V1). Reduced corneal sensation impairs the protective blink reflex, reduces tear production stimulation, and delays epithelial healing after injury—predisposing to neurotrophic keratopathy and recurrent corneal erosions. Corneal examination including sensitivity testing is part of the ocular assessment in diabetic patients.

questions.question: A patient with severe red eye, severe lid swelling, proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, and fever is MOST likely to have:
questions.explanation: Orbital cellulitis is a potentially life-threatening condition presenting with lid edema and redness, conjunctival injection, proptosis, restricted extraocular movements (ophthalmoplegia), and systemic features like fever. It requires urgent IV antibiotics and imaging. Allergic or vernal conjunctivitis lacks proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, and fever.

Cyanoacrylate tissue glue is applied to small corneal perforations (under 1 mm) to temporarily seal the perforation, restore the anterior chamber, and prevent aqueous loss. It provides a bridge until definitive keratoplasty can be arranged. It is not a permanent repair. Other measures for impending perforation include collagenase inhibitors (tetracycline, doxycycline).
options: Permanent structural repair equivalent to keratoplasty
Temporary sealing of active perforation to restore anterior chamber and IOP
Antifungal effect against filamentous organisms at the ulcer base
Stimulation of corneal re-epithelialization by growth factors
Reduction of corneal vascularization in stromal keratitis
questions.question: Cyanoacrylate (tissue glue) is applied to a perforating corneal ulcer to achieve which specific outcome?

questions.explanation: Topical beta-blockers such as timolol reduce IOP by blocking beta-2 adrenergic receptors in ciliary body epithelium, decreasing aqueous production by approximately 20–50%. Systemic absorption through the nasolacrimal mucosa can cause bradycardia and bronchospasm. They are widely used first-line agents.
questions.question: Topical beta-adrenergic blockers (e.g., timolol) reduce IOP by:
options: Reducing aqueous production by ciliary body epithelium
Directly opening trabecular meshwork outflow spaces

questions.explanation: HbA1c reflects the average blood glucose concentration over the preceding 2–3 months (the lifespan of red blood cells) and is the gold standard for assessing long-term glycemic control. It directly predicts the risk of developing and progressing diabetic retinopathy, nephropathy, and neuropathy. A target HbA1c of 6–7% significantly reduces retinopathy risk compared to poorly controlled levels above 9%.
questions.question: The most useful biochemical marker for assessing long-term blood glucose control relevant to diabetic retinopathy risk is:
Chlamydial ophthalmia neonatorum is treated with systemic erythromycin because:
options: Topical treatment alone eliminates conjunctival infection
Chlamydia may also cause systemic infection
IV ceftriaxone is ineffective against Chlamydia
questions.explanation: Systemic erythromycin (50 mg/kg/day for 2 weeks) is essential because Chlamydia trachomatis can cause systemic disease in neonates, including chlamydial pneumonia and otitis media. Topical treatment alone fails to eradicate the nasopharyngeal reservoir that enables systemic spread. Systemic treatment treats both the ocular and systemic components of the infection.

Proliferative diabetic retinopathy (neovascular bleed) and posterior vitreous detachment with associated retinal tear (which bleeds from the retinal vessel at the tear site) are the most common causes of vitreous haemorrhage in adults. Both present with sudden onset floaters and visual blurring. B-scan ultrasound is essential when the fundus cannot be examined due to the haemorrhage.
questions.question: The MOST common cause of vitreous haemorrhage in adults is:
options: Anticoagulant therapy causing spontaneous retinal haemorrhage
Age-related macular degeneration with sub-retinal haemorrhage
Proliferative diabetic retinopathy or posterior vitreous detachment with tear

questions.question: Uveitis in a child with positive ANA and oligoarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) is MOST commonly:
questions.explanation: Uveitis in JIA is characteristically a chronic, asymptomatic (white eye) anterior uveitis discovered only on routine slit-lamp screening. The absence of symptoms makes regular screening mandatory because untreated disease leads to band keratopathy, cataract, glaucoma, and blindness.
