ANA-positive, oligoarticular JIA in girls aged under 6 years carries the highest uveitis risk.
options: Symptomatic with acute red eye and pain
Posterior granulomatous panuveitis with disc swelling
Chronic asymptomatic anterior uveitis discovered on routine screening
Intermediate uveitis with snowballs and pars plana exudates

questions.question: Corneal Foreign Body (FB) causing red eye is BEST identified by:
questions.explanation: Slit-lamp examination provides magnified illumination of the corneal surface, making it ideal for identifying and locating foreign bodies. Fluorescein staining highlights associated corneal epithelial defects around the FB. Imaging (X-ray, CT) is reserved for suspected intraocular or intraorbital foreign bodies. Direct focal illumination with a pen torch is an initial bedside assessment.
options: CT orbits only in most clinical presentations
Visual field testing under standard examination conditions
Flame-shaped hemorrhages at the disc margin based on typical clinical findings
Areas of retinal pigment epithelial detachment
Small black spots surrounded by yellow halos representing focal choroidal infarcts
Cotton wool spots in the nerve fiber layer in the majority of documented cases
questions.explanation: Elschnig spots are small black spots surrounded by yellow halos that represent focal areas of choroidal ischemia and infarction (choroidal infarcts) seen in hypertensive choroidopathy. They occur as a result of an acute hypertensive crisis, particularly in young adults. Hypertensive choroidopathy is rare compared to hypertensive retinopathy but is an important sign of severe, acute hypertension.
questions.question: Elschnig spots in hypertensive choroidopathy are described as:

options: The acute leukocyte inflammatory reaction in the corneal stroma
Collagen synthesis during corneal healing in the majority of documented cases
Corneal neovascularization after day 7 based on typical clinical findings
questions.explanation: In the first week after chemical burns, intense topical steroids inhibit the acute inflammatory response (leukocyte infiltration), which is responsible for stromal collagen dissolution and ulceration. After the third week, steroids may be resumed as the secondary stromal reaction resumes. Steroids are AVOIDED in the 2nd to 3rd week as they may impair collagen synthesis needed for healing.
questions.question: In the management of chemical burns, intense topical steroid therapy is recommended in the FIRST week because it inhibits:

questions.explanation: POAG involves increased resistance to aqueous outflow at the trabecular meshwork (juxtacanalicular tissue), raising IOP. The anterior chamber angle is anatomically open (unlike angle-closure glaucoma). The mechanism involves trabecular meshwork cell loss, ECM accumulation, and reduced pore size. Medical treatment targets aqueous production (beta-blockers, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors) or outflow (prostaglandins, miotics).
options: Anatomical pupil block from enlarged lens pushing iris forward
Increased aqueous production by the ciliary body
Closure of the anterior chamber angle by peripheral iris
Elevated episcleral venous pressure from cavernous sinus thrombosis
Increased outflow resistance at the trabecular meshwork
questions.question: The pathophysiology of primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) involves elevated IOP through which mechanism?
In the WHO grading of xerophthalmia, corneal xerosis (grade X2) typically begins in which part of the cornea?
questions.explanation: Corneal xerosis in vitamin A deficiency characteristically begins in the inferior corneal quadrant, likely related to relative exposure and drying in this area, before potentially progressing centrally if untreated. Recognising this early localisation allows detection before central visual axis involvement threatens vision. This staged progression underlies the WHO grading system used to monitor disease severity.

questions.question: A patient with advanced glaucoma reports frequently bumping into objects on either side despite good central vision. What visual field pattern explains this?
options: Severe peripheral constriction sparing central vision
questions.explanation: Advanced glaucoma classically spares central vision until very late while progressively constricting the peripheral visual field. This produces a tunnel-like field of vision, impairing navigation and awareness of objects to the sides. Patients may still read well despite significant disability in mobility.

questions.question: A patient develops chronic follicular conjunctivitis with small pearly, umbilicated eyelid lesions shedding infectious material into the tear film. What is the cause?
questions.explanation: Molluscum contagiosum produces small, pearly, umbilicated papules on the eyelid margin that continuously shed infectious viral particles into the tear film. This chronic antigenic exposure causes a persistent follicular conjunctivitis. Removal or destruction of the eyelid lesion resolves the associated conjunctivitis.

options: Application of topical steroids to reduce inflammation
Patching the affected eye and referring next day
Cycloplegics to dilate the pupil and break the block
Rapid medical lowering of IOP as an emergency
Immediate surgical iridectomy in the operating room
questions.question: The FIRST priority in managing a patient with acute PACG is:
questions.explanation: The immediate priority in acute PACG is rapid medical IOP lowering to relieve pain, reduce ischaemia, and clear corneal oedema to allow subsequent laser treatment. IV acetazolamide, topical beta-blockers, topical pilocarpine (once IOP is reduced sufficiently), and hyperosmotic agents (IV mannitol) are used urgently before definitive laser iridotomy.

options: Optic nerve infiltration by chronic inflammatory cells
Peripheral retinal vasculitis with neovascularisation and recurrent vitreous haemorrhage
questions.explanation: Eales disease is an idiopathic obliterative peripheral retinal vasculitis predominantly affecting young South Asian (Indian subcontinent) males. It causes peripheral retinal vasculitis, perivasculitis, neovascularisation, and recurrent vitreous haemorrhage from rupture of new vessels. Peripheral scatter laser photocoagulation treats neovascularisation, and vitrectomy addresses persistent vitreous haemorrhage.
questions.question: Eales disease, common in young South Asian males, primarily affects the eye through:
A hypertensive patient's fundus shows small, round, yellow-white lesions at the level of the retinal pigment epithelium, called Elschnig spots. These are best understood as
options: focal areas of choroidal ischemia and infarction
lipid deposits within the vitreous cavity
questions.explanation: Elschnig spots represent focal infarcts of the choriocapillaris secondary to severe hypertensive choroidopathy, later appearing as pigmented spots at the level of the retinal pigment epithelium. They reflect choroidal rather than retinal vascular pathology, distinguishing hypertensive choroidopathy from hypertensive retinopathy proper. Their presence signals a more severe, often accelerated hypertensive process.

options: Ipsilateral facial drooping without other signs as commonly encountered in practice
Contralateral hemiplegia due to corticospinal tract involvement
Horner's syndrome on the same side during routine ophthalmic assessment
questions.question: Compared to other types of third nerve palsy, a palsy due to brainstem pathology (e.g., Weber's syndrome) is MOST likely to also present with:
questions.explanation: Weber's syndrome results from a midbrain lesion involving CN III as it passes through the ipsilateral red nucleus and corticospinal tract. Patients present with ipsilateral CN III palsy and contralateral hemiplegia (the 'crossed' pattern). This anatomical localization is a classic teaching point in neuro-ophthalmology.

The uveoscleral pathway is the unconventional (secondary) route where aqueous passes through the ciliary muscle interstitium and supraciliary/suprachoroidal spaces. The conventional pathway consists of trabecular meshwork → Schlemm's canal → collector channels → episcleral veins. Prostaglandin analogues primarily enhance the uveoscleral route.
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT part of the conventional aqueous outflow pathway?

options: Inhibiting ciliary body carbonic anhydrase to reduce aqueous production
Reducing episcleral venous pressure levels significantly
Mechanically opening the trabecular meshwork drainage spaces
Causing miosis to reduce angle crowding
questions.question: Oral acetazolamide lowers IOP by which primary mechanism?
questions.explanation: Acetazolamide (systemic carbonic anhydrase inhibitor) reduces aqueous humour production by inhibiting carbonic anhydrase II in the ciliary body, thus reducing bicarbonate-driven fluid secretion. It is used acutely in angle-closure crises or as short-term adjunctive therapy. Side effects include paraesthesias, metabolic acidosis, renal calculi, and hyponatraemia.

options: a blow-out fracture of the orbital floor
questions.explanation: Blunt trauma can fracture the thin orbital floor, entrapping the inferior rectus or surrounding tissue and restricting upward gaze along with possible enophthalmos. Superficial injuries like abrasions or subconjunctival hemorrhage do not cause restricted motility. Imaging confirms the fracture and guides the decision for surgical repair.
questions.question: A football player is struck in the eye and develops restricted upward gaze with entrapment suspected on imaging. This presentation is MOST consistent with
The MOST common cause of posterior segment endophthalmitis after cataract surgery is:
questions.explanation: Post-cataract endophthalmitis is most commonly caused by coagulase-negative Staphylococcus (primarily Staphylococcus epidermidis), which colonizes the normal ocular surface and lid margins and is introduced intraoperatively. It presents with progressive pain, visual loss, and hypopyon, typically 4–7 days post-surgery. Treatment is intravitreal antibiotics (vancomycin + ceftazidime/amikacin); vitrectomy is needed for severe cases.
options: Staphylococcus epidermidis (coagulase-negative) from ocular surface flora
Streptococcus pneumoniae from the upper respiratory tract flora

questions.explanation: Neck masses (lymphadenopathy, tumors, or surgical trauma) that compress the sympathetic chain between the superior cervical ganglion and T1 represent preganglionic (second-order neuron) causes of Horner's syndrome. Carotid artery dissection typically affects the third-order (postganglionic) neuron. Correct localization has important implications for underlying pathology and investigation.
options: Internal carotid artery dissection as commonly encountered in practice
Orbital apex syndrome during routine ophthalmic assessment
Neck lymph node mass compressing the sympathetic chain
questions.question: Which of the following is a preganglionic cause of Horner's syndrome?

questions.explanation: Immediate copious irrigation at the site of the chemical injury—before any other intervention—is the single most important treatment for chemical eye burns. This dilutes and removes the chemical, limiting penetration and tissue damage. Alkali injuries are particularly severe because they cause liquefactive necrosis that allows continued penetration into the eye. Irrigation should be maintained until the patient reaches an ophthalmologist.
options: Refer urgently to a tertiary ophthalmology center as commonly encountered in practice
Immediate and copious irrigation with water or normal saline at the scene
Apply a pressure patch and observe during routine ophthalmic assessment
questions.question: A patient presents with a red, painful eye following an alkali splash. The FIRST and MOST critical management step is:
A contact lens wearer develops a corneal ulcer. The clinician explains that the central cornea receives most of its oxygen from which source when lenses are removed?
questions.explanation: The avascular central cornea depends mainly on oxygen dissolved in the tear film from the atmosphere, supplemented by limited diffusion from the aqueous humour. Contact lens wear reduces this atmospheric oxygen supply and predisposes to hypoxic epithelial compromise. This increases susceptibility to infection when lens hygiene is poor.

questions.question: The MOST common postoperative complication of extracapsular cataract extraction (ECCE) is:
questions.explanation: Posterior capsule opacification (PCO), caused by proliferation and migration of residual lens epithelial cells across the posterior capsule, is the most common long-term complication of ECCE, occurring in up to 50% of patients within 5 years. It causes progressive visual blurring similar to the original cataract. Treatment is Nd:YAG laser posterior capsulotomy, which is safe, quick, and definitive.

questions.question: A patient with suspected infective conjunctivitis undergoes conjunctival swab and culture. This investigation is MOST useful for
questions.explanation: Culture and sensitivity of conjunctival swabs identify the causative organism and its antibiotic sensitivity, helping distinguish bacterial infection requiring antibiotics from viral infection that does not. It has no role in pressure, curvature, or lens assessment. This targeted use makes it valuable mainly in atypical or non-resolving cases.

questions.question: A patient develops ptosis, miosis, and facial anhidrosis after a stroke affecting the lateral medulla. This localises the lesion to which order of sympathetic neuron?
questions.explanation: The first-order sympathetic neuron runs from the hypothalamus through the brainstem to the ciliospinal centre of Budge, and brainstem strokes such as lateral medullary syndrome interrupt this segment. Second and third-order lesions occur outside the brainstem. Localising the neuron order narrows the list of causative lesions.

Topical anaesthetics such as proxymetacaine or tetracaine block sodium channels in corneal sensory nerve endings, providing rapid surface anaesthesia for minor procedures. They are not used for repeated home use because of epithelial toxicity with prolonged exposure. Their action is purely sensory and does not affect pupil size.
questions.question: Before performing minor corneal foreign body removal at the slit lamp, the clinician instils a topical agent to numb the ocular surface. This drug class is a
An examiner tests a patient's ability to identify a break in a ring rotated in different positions, requiring finer discrimination than letter recognition. Which chart uses this principle?
questions.explanation: The Landolt C chart presents a ring with a gap in varying orientations, and the patient identifies the position of the gap. This optotype avoids reliance on letter recognition and provides a precise measure of the minimum angle of resolution. It is often used as a reference standard in visual acuity research.

questions.question: Which of the following laser procedures is used to treat narrow angles BEFORE an acute attack occurs?
questions.explanation: Prophylactic laser peripheral iridotomy (LPI) is performed in eyes with anatomically narrow angles (identified on gonioscopy or anterior segment OCT) to eliminate relative pupillary block before an acute attack occurs. It is also indicated in the contralateral eye after an acute attack. By creating an iris opening, it equalises pressure between anterior and posterior chambers and opens the angle.

Nuclear sclerotic cataract is the most common type of age-related cataract encountered in tropical regions, often presenting at a younger age than in temperate populations, possibly related to increased ultraviolet exposure. It produces a brownish discolouration of the lens nucleus and gradual painless visual decline. This differs from posterior subcapsular cataracts, which are more strongly linked to steroid use or diabetes.
questions.question: A patient under 65 years in a tropical region presents with progressive painless visual loss and a brownish nuclear lens opacity. Which type of cataract is most likely?

options: Malignant transformation of normal conjunctival epithelium
Benign hyperplasia of conjunctival goblet cells
Normal tissue elements in an abnormal location (ectopic tissue)
Vascular hamartomas of choroidal origin extending anteriorly
Reactive proliferation from chronic UV-induced damage
questions.explanation: Conjunctival dermoids and dermolipomas are choristomas — normal tissues (skin elements: keratin, hair, sebaceous glands, fibrous/fatty tissue) located in an abnormal position. They are the most common epibulbar tumor in children, most often at the inferotemporal limbus. They are congenital hamartomas representing displaced embryonal tissue. Treatment is surgical if visually significant.
questions.question: Conjunctival dermoid tumors in children are classified as choristomas because they represent:

questions.explanation: Trichiasis involves normally positioned lash follicles whose lashes are curved or misdirected posteriorly toward the cornea, often from subtle cicatricial entropion (trachoma, pemphigoid, Stevens-Johnson). Distichiasis is a congenital or acquired extra row of lashes arising from meibomian gland ducts. Both cause corneal abrasion and ulceration.
options: An extra row of lashes from the meibomian gland ducts
Congenitally absent lashes from alopecia areata
Normal lashes misdirected backward toward the cornea
Lash follicles replaced by fibrous tissue from burns
Excessive lash growth from chronic blepharitis
questions.question: Trichiasis differs from distichiasis in that trichiasis involves:

questions.explanation: Optic neuritis typically presents in young adults, more often women, with subacute painful unilateral visual loss, an afferent pupillary defect, and impaired colour vision, frequently as a first presentation of multiple sclerosis. Pain on eye movement is a distinguishing feature from ischaemic optic neuropathy, which is usually painless and occurs in an older age group. MRI evidence of demyelination supports the diagnosis and helps assess the risk of future multiple sclerosis.
questions.question: A young woman develops sudden unilateral painful visual loss with an afferent pupillary defect, and MRI shows demyelinating lesions. Which diagnosis is most likely?
A patient presents with sudden red eye, purulent discharge, and a grey membrane that bleeds when peeled from the conjunctival surface. What organism is classically implicated?
questions.explanation: A true membrane that bleeds on removal, as opposed to a pseudomembrane, is characteristically associated with severe streptococcal or diphtherial conjunctivitis. This reflects deeper tissue involvement with fibrin adherent to the epithelium. Prompt antibiotic treatment prevents scarring complications.

options: Infrared light in the 800–840 nm wavelength range
Low-frequency ultrasound waves under standard examination conditions
Visible blue light at 488 nm in most clinical presentations
questions.question: Ocular Coherence Tomography (OCT) uses which type of energy for retinal imaging?
questions.explanation: OCT uses near-infrared light in the 800–840 nm wavelength range to provide real-time, non-invasive, high-resolution (micron-level) cross-sectional imaging of the retina and other ocular structures. It is analogous to ultrasound but uses light instead of sound waves, allowing far greater resolution. It is non-contact, does not require dye injection, and is non-ionizing—making it safe for repeated use.

questions.question: In addition to pupil dilation, third nerve palsy results in paralysis of all the following extraocular muscles EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The lateral rectus is supplied by CN VI (abducens), not CN III. Third nerve palsy paralyzes the medial, superior, and inferior recti and the inferior oblique muscle, resulting in a characteristic 'down and out' eye position. Sparing of the lateral rectus explains the outward deviation seen in complete CN III palsy.

In a Snellen fraction (e.g., 6/24), the numerator is the test distance and the denominator is the distance at which a person with normal visual acuity should be able to read that line. Each letter is designed so that its features subtend 1 minute of arc at the denominator distance. This is the principle incorporated in Snellen test types.
options: The patient's testing distance in meters
The number of lines read correctly by the patient overall
The visual angle in minutes of arc at 6 meters
The dioptric power of the correcting lens
The distance at which letters subtend 1 min of arc for a normal eye
questions.question: The denominator in the Snellen fraction denotes:
'Sea-fan' neovascularization in sickle cell retinopathy represents which Goldberg stage?
questions.explanation: Goldberg Stage III of proliferative sickle cell retinopathy is characterized by 'sea-fan' neovascularization—named for its resemblance to the marine organism Gorgonia. These frond-like networks of new vessels arise from peripheral arteriovenous anastomoses (Stage II) at areas of retinal ischemia. Sea-fan lesions may auto-infarct in 20–60% of cases without treatment but carry a risk of vitreous hemorrhage (Stage IV) if they bleed.

options: Elderly females with watery discharge and forniceal follicles
Adult men with unilateral tarsal scarring and trichiasis
Newborns with hyperacute purulent discharge within 24 hours
Middle-aged adults with chronic granulomatous eyelid inflammation
Male children in warm climates with intense itching and mucoid discharge
questions.explanation: VKC typically affects children and young adults, is more common in males, and is more prevalent in warm climates. The hallmark is intense itching with mucoid discharge and lacrimation. It is frequently associated with atopy (asthma, hay fever, dermatitis) and is recurrent/seasonal. Cobblestone papillae on the upper tarsal conjunctiva are characteristic.
questions.question: Vernal keratoconjunctivitis (VKC) is MOST characteristic of which demographic and presentation?
Gonococcal keratoconjunctivitis is classified as hyperacute because of which distinctive feature?
questions.explanation: Gonococcal keratoconjunctivitis is termed 'hyperacute' because of its sudden onset, acute profuse purulent discharge, marked chemosis, and hyperaemia. The critical concern is that N. gonorrhoeae can penetrate intact corneal epithelium, leading to rapid corneal ulceration, perforation, and endophthalmitis if untreated. Treatment requires topical and systemic antibiotics plus copious irrigation.
options: Gradual onset over weeks with superior pannus
Bilateral watery discharge without corneal involvement
Chronic follicular conjunctivitis with tarsal conjunctival scarring
Papillary hypertrophy with mucoid ropy discharge
Acute profuse purulent discharge with potential for corneal perforation

questions.explanation: HLA-B27-associated AAU (ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis) is characteristically: unilateral, alternating between eyes (rarely simultaneous bilateral), acute onset with pain, photophobia, and red eye, and non-granulomatous with fine KPs and flare. It responds well to topical steroids and cycloplegics. Recurrent episodes are common; systemic disease screening is essential.
questions.question: Acute anterior uveitis (AAU) associated with ankylosing spondylitis is classically:
options: Bilateral, chronic, granulomatous with mutton-fat KPs
Posterior segment only — no anterior chamber involvement
Bilateral synchronous with vitritis and snowballs
Constricts the pupil to open the angle
Reduces aqueous production and increases uveoscleral outflow as an alpha-2 agonist
Selectively inhibits carbonic anhydrase enzymes within the ciliary body epithelium
questions.question: Brimonidine lowers IOP through which mechanism?
questions.explanation: Brimonidine is a selective alpha-2 adrenergic agonist that reduces IOP by both decreasing aqueous production and increasing uveoscleral outflow. It also has potential neuroprotective properties by activating alpha-2 receptors on retinal ganglion cells. It is used as monotherapy or adjunctive therapy in open-angle glaucoma.

Fuchs' heterochromic cyclitis is a chronic, unilateral, low-grade anterior uveitis characterized by: heterochromia (lighter iris on the affected side), fine diffuse stellate KPs, lack of synechiae or significant flare despite long duration, and complications of cataract and glaucoma. It is often asymptomatic for years. The etiology is unclear; rubella virus has been implicated.
questions.question: Fuchs' heterochromic cyclitis is a chronic low-grade anterior uveitis distinguishable from other forms by which combination of features?
options: Bilateral, large mutton-fat KPs, severe anterior chamber flare, posterior synechiae
Unilateral, painful red eye, hypopyon, fibrinous exudate in the AC
Unilateral, heterochromia, fine stellate KPs, no synechiae, no flare, associated cataract
Bilateral, retinal perivasculitis, vitreous opacities, disc swelling
Unilateral, iris nodules, band keratopathy, secondary glaucoma

questions.question: During near focusing, a patient's ciliary muscle contracts and the lens becomes more spherical. What happens to zonular tension during this process?
questions.explanation: Ciliary muscle contraction moves the ciliary body forward and inward, reducing the diameter of the ciliary ring. This slackens the zonular fibres attached to the lens capsule, allowing the elastic lens to assume a more rounded shape for near focus. This is the accommodation reflex.

questions.question: A patient with longstanding thyroid eye disease in the inactive fibrotic phase has persistent diplopia despite normal thyroid function. The MOST appropriate next step to correct the diplopia is
options: urgent orbital decompression regardless of vision
strabismus surgery once the disease is stable
questions.explanation: Once thyroid eye disease has stabilised in the inactive phase, residual restrictive strabismus causing diplopia is best addressed surgically rather than with further immunosuppression, which is more effective during the active inflammatory phase. Decompression is reserved for compressive optic neuropathy rather than isolated diplopia. Timing surgery after disease stabilisation gives more predictable and lasting results.

Salmon patch haemorrhages are bright red to orange-pink, round superficial or preretinal haemorrhages at the peripheral retina in sickle cell disease, resulting from arteriolar occlusion with haemorrhage. They may resolve, leaving iridescent spots (retinoschisis cavities) or pigmented lesions (black sunburst). They are early signs of peripheral retinal ischaemia.
options: The peripheral retina at the equator
The posterior pole of the fundus
questions.question: 'Salmon patch' haemorrhages in sickle cell retinopathy occur at:

questions.explanation: Immediate, copious irrigation with any available non-toxic fluid (water, saline) is the single most important first step in chemical eye burns, beginning within seconds of exposure and continuing for at least 20–30 minutes for acids and 30–60 minutes for alkalis. Delaying irrigation to check vision or identify the agent significantly worsens prognosis.
options: Instilling topical anaesthetic drops before starting irrigation
Immediate, copious, prolonged irrigation with water or saline
questions.question: The FIRST and MOST important step in managing any chemical eye burn is:

options: Thin fovea allowing the underlying choroid to show through
Active new vessel growth at the fovea
Pigment epithelial detachment at the fovea
Vitreous blood pooling over the fovea
questions.question: A patient presents with sudden painless visual loss, a pale retina, and a bright red spot at the centre of the macula. What causes the bright red appearance at this location?
questions.explanation: In central retinal artery occlusion, the surrounding retina becomes pale and oedematous due to ischaemia, while the thin fovea, lacking the same ganglion cell layer thickness, allows the normal red colour of the underlying choroid to show through by contrast. This produces the classic cherry-red spot appearance. The finding reflects the sudden and severe nature of the ischaemic insult.

questions.question: A young adult presents with floaters and mild blurred vision. Examination shows vitreous cellular infiltration concentrated over the pars plana with snowbank formation. Which uveitis subtype is this?
questions.explanation: Intermediate uveitis, or pars planitis, predominantly affects the vitreous and peripheral retina, producing vitreous cellular infiltration and characteristic snowbank exudates over the pars plana. It typically presents with floaters and mild blurring rather than the pain and redness seen in anterior uveitis. It is associated with systemic conditions such as multiple sclerosis in some patients.

The infraorbital nerve runs along the orbital floor and is commonly injured in blowout fractures, producing numbness of the cheek, upper lip, and lateral nose. Combined with inferior rectus entrapment causing restricted upgaze, this creates the classic triad of a floor fracture. Recognising this sensory pattern helps localise the fracture site clinically.
questions.question: A patient with an orbital floor blowout fracture presents with double vision, numbness of the cheek, and inability to look upward. Which nerve territory explains the numbness?

questions.explanation: Bilateral retinoblastoma with positive family history and early age of onset is characteristic of the hereditary (germline) form, where the first RB1 gene mutation is inherited through the germline and present in all body cells. All bilateral cases and 15% of unilateral cases are hereditary. These patients are also predisposed to second non-ocular tumors (osteosarcoma, other sarcomas) and should be enrolled in long-term cancer surveillance.
questions.question: A child presenting with bilateral leucocoria, family history of retinoblastoma, and early age of onset most likely has which form of retinoblastoma?

questions.explanation: A disc haemorrhage (splinter haemorrhage at the optic disc margin) in a POAG patient signifies active ongoing optic nerve damage and is an independent risk factor for glaucomatous progression. It frequently corresponds to rim notching and nerve fibre layer loss. It carries a poor prognosis and warrants treatment intensification.
questions.question: A disc haemorrhage (Drance haemorrhage) at the optic disc margin in a POAG patient indicates:
options: Accelerated glaucomatous optic nerve damage with poor prognosis
Normal anatomical variation requiring no further clinical intervention

questions.explanation: The Sheridan-Gardiner test uses a limited set of letters that the child matches on a key card rather than naming aloud, making it suitable for young children with limited verbal skills. This matching format reduces the literacy and communication demands of standard letter charts. It remains a practical option in preschool vision screening.
questions.question: A child aged 3 years is unable to name letters but can match shapes. Which visual acuity test would be most appropriate?
For two separate points to be discriminated by the retina, what anatomical requirement must be met?
options: Three consecutive cones must be stimulated
Two adjacent cones must be simultaneously stimulated
One cone must be doubly stimulated
Two cones stimulated with one unstimulated cone between them
One rod and one cone must be co-stimulated
questions.explanation: For spatial resolution, two points of light must stimulate two separate cones with at least one unstimulated cone between them. The average diameter of a foveal cone is 0.004 mm, which equals the minimum retinal image size required for discrimination. This is the anatomical basis for minimum angle of resolution (MAR).

questions.question: The Imbert-Fick principle, on which Goldmann applanation tonometry is based, states that pressure inside a sphere equals:
options: The refractive index multiplied by corneal curvature
The force applied to flatten a given area divided by that area
The weight of the sphere divided by its volume
The square root of corneal thickness divided by radius
The product of aqueous flow rate and outflow resistance
questions.explanation: The Imbert-Fick principle states that for a dry, thin, flexible sphere, internal pressure equals force applied to flatten it divided by the flattened area (P = F/A). Goldmann tonometry uses a fixed 3.06 mm diameter area, so IOP is directly proportional to the applied force. Corneal thickness deviations cause measurement error.

options: Macular disease in the affected eye
Bilateral lens opacity gradually reducing the afferent pupillary light signal
Raised IOP in both eyes simultaneously
Asymmetric optic nerve damage with reduced afferent input from the more affected eye
questions.explanation: An afferent pupillary defect (Marcus Gunn pupil) in POAG indicates asymmetry in optic nerve function between the two eyes, with significantly more damage in the eye with the APD. It is tested by the swinging flashlight test. It reflects decreased retinal ganglion cell output from the more damaged optic nerve.
questions.question: An afferent pupillary defect (APD) detected in a POAG patient indicates:

questions.explanation: The type of discharge is the key differentiating feature: bacterial conjunctivitis typically produces mucopurulent (thick, yellow-green) discharge, while viral conjunctivitis produces watery or serous discharge. Both conditions can be bilateral and cause conjunctival hyperemia. Pre-auricular lymphadenopathy is characteristic of viral (especially adenoviral) conjunctivitis.
questions.question: Bacterial conjunctivitis is BEST distinguished from viral conjunctivitis by:
options: Type of discharge: mucopurulent vs watery
Presence of conjunctival hyperemia based on typical clinical findings
Duration longer than 2 weeks in the majority of documented cases
The high density of mast cells and IgE-binding capacity in conjunctival tissue
Greater thickness of the conjunctival mucosa compared to skin
Reduced lactoferrin concentration in conjunctival tears
Higher ambient temperature at the conjunctival surface
Absence of keratin layer allowing direct allergen-cell contact
questions.question: The conjunctiva is ten times more sensitive than skin to allergens. This is due to:
questions.explanation: The conjunctiva is exquisitely sensitive to allergens because of the high density of mast cells and their IgE-mediated degranulation capability in the subepithelial tissue. IgE-sensitized mast cells degranulate when allergens cross-link two IgE molecules, releasing histamine and other mediators. This accounts for the immediate hypersensitivity response in allergic conjunctivitis.

Dim lighting causes physiological pupillary dilatation, which in an eye with a narrow anterior chamber angle can precipitate pupillary block. This obstructs aqueous outflow, causing a sudden painful rise in intraocular pressure. Immediate treatment is required to prevent optic nerve damage.
questions.question: A patient presents with a red, painful eye, fixed mid-dilated pupil, and hazy cornea after watching a film in a dark cinema. What triggered this?
options: Reflex miosis narrowing the angle further
Increased aqueous outflow through Schlemm's canal

questions.question: A diabetic patient with extensive peripheral retinal ischaemia and early new vessel formation is scheduled for treatment. What is the goal of the recommended laser therapy?
questions.explanation: Panretinal photocoagulation destroys areas of ischaemic peripheral retina, reducing the release of vascular endothelial growth factor that drives neovascularisation. This causes regression of new vessels and reduces the risk of vitreous haemorrhage and tractional detachment. Central vision is usually preserved as peripheral, not central, retina is treated.
options: Directly seal all leaking new vessels
Reduce ischaemic drive for new vessel growth

questions.question: Toxocara canis infection causing posterior uveitis in children occurs through:
options: Ingestion of embryonated eggs from dog feces (visceral larva migrans)
Direct person-to-person transmission of larvae via contact
Inhalation of Toxocara ova from contaminated soil during play
Transmission from infected mosquitoes in endemic regions
Transplacental transmission from affected mother to fetus
questions.explanation: Toxocara canis infection in children (ocular toxocariasis / visceral larva migrans) occurs by ingestion of embryonated Toxocara eggs from soil contaminated with dog feces. The larvae migrate to the eye causing a severe inflammatory reaction — peripheral granuloma, endophthalmitis, or posterior pole granuloma. It classically affects young children and may present as strabismus or leukocoria.

questions.question: A child presents with a white raised fundal mass, eosinophilia, and positive ELISA for Toxocara. The ocular diagnosis is:
options: Ocular toxocariasis with posterior pole granuloma
questions.explanation: Ocular toxocariasis presents with a white raised peripheral or posterior pole granuloma from Toxocara larval migration. It causes a leukocoria-like appearance mimicking retinoblastoma. Eosinophilia and ELISA for Toxocara IgG antibodies help confirm the diagnosis. Unlike retinoblastoma, it is typically unilateral in an older child (3–11 years) and may be associated with a history of geophagia or dog exposure.

options: Has live virus actively replicating in the ulcer base
Stains with rose bengal but NOT fluorescein
Represents an epithelial defect without live virus — damaged basement membrane
Has branching dendritic edges with terminal bulb swellings
Responds promptly to topical trifluridine drops
questions.explanation: Metaherpetic (trophic) ulcer is an epithelial defect in the absence of live virus — the result of damaged basement membrane after prior herpetic infection. The ulcer bed stains with fluorescein but NOT rose bengal (opposite to active epithelial disease which stains with both). Treatment focuses on protecting the damaged basement membrane with lubrication and bandage contact lens, not antivirals.
questions.question: Metaherpetic (trophic) ulcer differs from active herpetic dendritic ulcer because it:

questions.explanation: Glaucoma drainage devices are used in refractory glaucoma where trabeculectomy has failed or carries high failure risk — aphakic/pseudophakic patients, neovascular glaucoma, conjunctival scarring from prior surgery, and some paediatric glaucomas. A silicone tube drains aqueous to an equatorial plate sutured to the sclera.
options: Eyes with uncontrolled IOP where trabeculectomy has failed or is high risk
Prophylactic surgery performed in ocular hypertension cases
questions.question: Glaucoma drainage device (tube-shunt) implantation (Ahmed, Molteno, Baerveldt) is primarily indicated for:

questions.explanation: Microaneurysms (tiny saccular outpouchings of capillary walls from pericyte loss) are pathognomonic of diabetic retinopathy and are NOT a feature of hypertensive retinopathy. Both conditions can produce cotton wool spots, flame-shaped hemorrhages, and hard exudates. Arteriovenous nipping (Gunn's sign) is specific to hypertensive arteriosclerotic retinopathy. The presence of microaneurysms on fundoscopy is the earliest specific sign of diabetic retinopathy.
questions.question: In comparing retinal vascular changes between diabetic and hypertensive retinopathy, which feature is EXCLUSIVELY seen in diabetic retinopathy?

questions.explanation: Trachoma is caused by Chlamydia trachomatis serovars A, B, Ba, and C. Repeated infections cause tarsal conjunctival scarring, cicatricial entropion, trichiasis, corneal abrasion, and blindness. The WHO SAFE strategy (Surgery, Antibiotics, Facial cleanliness, Environmental hygiene) is used for trachoma control.
options: Chlamydia trachomatis serovars A, B, Ba, and C
questions.question: Trachoma, the leading infectious cause of preventable blindness, is caused by:

questions.explanation: Blood pressure control and smoking cessation are the two modifiable factors most strongly linked to preventing or slowing hypertensive retinal vascular damage. Age and sex, while associated with risk, cannot be modified through intervention. Targeting these two factors forms the cornerstone of preventing progression of hypertensive retinopathy.
options: elevated blood pressure and cigarette smoking
questions.question: The two MOST important modifiable risk factors for the development and progression of hypertensive retinopathy are

questions.explanation: The internal limiting membrane is the innermost layer of the retina, directly adjacent to the vitreous. The layer of rods and cones (photoreceptors) is more peripheral/outer. Understanding retinal layer anatomy is critical for interpreting OCT findings in macular diseases.
questions.question: The retina's innermost layer that lines the vitreous cavity is the:
Purtscher's retinopathy, which may complicate crush injuries or acute pancreatitis, appears as:
questions.explanation: Purtscher's retinopathy presents with multiple white, polygonal patches (Purtscher flecken — retinal infarcts from complement-activated leucocyte aggregation in retinal arterioles) and haemorrhages clustered around the optic disc. It occurs after severe compressive trauma, pancreatitis, childbirth, or connective tissue disease. Visual prognosis is variable.
options: Multiple white patches (infarcts) around the optic disc and haemorrhages — Purtscher flecken
Cherry-red spot at the fovea only
Diffuse dot-blot haemorrhages present in all four fundus quadrants

questions.question: An adult develops progressive ptosis over several weeks with variable severity throughout the day and associated double vision. Which underlying cause should be excluded first?
questions.explanation: Fluctuating ptosis that worsens with fatigue and improves with rest, especially when accompanied by diplopia, is characteristic of myasthenia gravis due to impaired neuromuscular transmission. This variability distinguishes it from static causes such as congenital or mechanical ptosis. Diagnostic confirmation may involve the ice pack test or acetylcholine receptor antibody testing.

questions.question: The Keith-Wagener-Barker (KWB) classification of hypertensive retinopathy is based on:
options: Severity of macular changes only based on typical clinical findings
IOP levels and optic nerve cupping in the majority of documented cases
Combination of retinal vascular changes and systemic cardiovascular risk
questions.explanation: The Keith-Wagener-Barker classification combines retinal vascular changes (arteriolar narrowing, AV nicking, hemorrhages, exudates, papilledema) with assessment of overall cardiovascular risk. Patients with higher grades have progressively increased risk of stroke, myocardial infarction, and renal disease. It remains a clinically useful system despite being supplemented by more detailed classifications.

Acid burns to the eye produce coagulative necrosis, which creates a protein coagulum that acts as a barrier limiting further penetration of the acid. Alkali burns cause liquefactive necrosis, allowing continued deep tissue penetration even after initial exposure has ended—hence alkali burns have a worse prognosis overall. However, both require immediate and copious irrigation.
questions.question: Which chemical injury has a BETTER prognosis: acid or alkali burns?
options: Alkali burns, because they are less painful
Alkali burns heal faster with steroids

questions.question: A patient with hyperthyroidism develops eyelid retraction, proptosis, and restricted eye movement. This ocular condition is MOST commonly associated with
questions.explanation: Graves' disease is the autoimmune hyperthyroid condition most strongly associated with thyroid eye disease, producing the characteristic combination of lid retraction, proptosis, and restrictive myopathy from autoimmune infiltration of orbital tissues. Other thyroid conditions listed are far less commonly linked to this ocular presentation. Recognising Graves' disease as the underlying cause guides coordinated endocrine and ophthalmic management.

questions.question: A hypertensive patient's fundus shows arterioles that appear as thin white lines without visible blood column, indicating severe wall sclerosis. This advanced sign is known as
questions.explanation: Silver wiring represents advanced sclerotic thickening of the arteriolar wall so severe that the vessel appears as a thin white line with no visible blood column. This is a more advanced finding than copper wiring and reflects long-standing, severe hypertensive vascular disease. It is one of the chronic structural changes that does not reverse even after blood pressure control.

questions.question: The MOST appropriate initial management of a large central corneal laceration with iris prolapse is:
options: Rigid eye shield, nil by mouth, systemic antibiotics, urgent surgical repair
Watchful waiting with frequent IOP measurement
Cycloplegic eye drops combined with oral antibiotics
questions.explanation: A corneal laceration with iris prolapse constitutes an open globe emergency. Management: rigid shield application without pressure, systemic antibiotics (cefuroxime IV), antiemetics, nil by mouth for anaesthesia, and urgent surgical exploration and primary repair. Topical drops, irrigation, or any pressure on the eye must be strictly avoided.

options: Less than 6/6 in the better eye in most clinical presentations as commonly encountered in practice as commonly encountered in practice
Less than 6/18 but equal to or better than 3/60 in the better eye with best correction
Less than 6/60 in the worse eye under standard examination conditions during routine ophthalmic assessment during routine ophthalmic assessment
questions.question: The term 'low vision' as used in the VISION 2020 framework is defined as visual acuity of:
questions.explanation: Low vision is defined as visual acuity less than 6/18 but equal to or better than 3/60 in the better eye with best correction, or a central visual field of less than 20 degrees. This distinguishes it from blindness (VA <3/60) and from mild impairment. Low vision rehabilitation (optical aids, training) allows individuals to maximize functional vision and independence despite impairment.

questions.question: The Seidel test is performed to:
options: Detect aqueous humour leakage from a corneal wound using fluorescein
Diagnose retinal detachment using transillumination testing
Assess visual field loss in glaucoma
Measure intraocular pressure with a tonometer
questions.explanation: The Seidel test detects aqueous leakage through a corneal wound. Concentrated fluorescein is applied to the wound site; if aqueous leaks, it dilutes the fluorescein, producing a bright green flow against an orange background under cobalt-blue illumination. A positive Seidel test confirms open globe requiring immediate surgical repair.

questions.question: A young patient presents with sudden hearing loss, confusion, and multiple branch retinal artery occlusions. What rare condition should be considered?
questions.explanation: Susac syndrome is a rare autoimmune endotheliopathy affecting the brain, retina, and inner ear, producing the classic triad of encephalopathy, branch retinal artery occlusions, and sensorineural hearing loss. Fundoscopy showing multiple, sometimes asymptomatic, retinal artery occlusions is an important diagnostic clue. Early immunosuppressive treatment can improve outcomes.

A pterygium is a wing-shaped fibrovascular growth of bulbar conjunctiva that invades the cornea, typically related to chronic ultraviolet exposure in outdoor workers. Its encroachment onto the cornea can induce astigmatism and threaten vision if it approaches the visual axis. This distinguishes it from a pinguecula, which remains confined to the conjunctiva without corneal invasion.
questions.question: A 60-year-old outdoor labourer has a fleshy triangular growth of conjunctival tissue extending onto the cornea, causing induced astigmatism. Which lesion is this?

questions.explanation: Vernal keratoconjunctivitis typically affects young boys with an atopic background and shows seasonal exacerbation, giant cobblestone papillae on the upper tarsal conjunctiva, and characteristic ropy mucoid discharge. This distinguishes it from atopic keratoconjunctivitis, which tends to affect an older age group with perennial symptoms and lower lid involvement. Severe cases can threaten vision through corneal shield ulcers.
questions.question: A young boy with a history of atopy presents with intense itching, giant papillae on the upper tarsal conjunctiva, and thick ropy discharge, worse in warm seasons. Which condition is most likely?

questions.explanation: APMPPE is an acute inflammatory condition of the retinal pigment epithelium and choriocapillaris, typically affecting young adults (20–40 years), often following a viral prodrome. Multiple bilateral creamy-white placoid lesions at the RPE level in the posterior pole cause rapid visual blurring. Most cases self-resolve over weeks with excellent visual recovery, though a minority have persistent central scotomas. SUBTOPIC 7: OCULAR EMERGENCIES AND SURGICAL MANAGEMENT
questions.question: Acute posterior multifocal placoid pigment epitheliopathy (APMPPE) is characterised by:
options: Gradual bilateral progressive visual loss over years
Choroidal neovascularisation with rapid central visual loss
Multiple creamy-white placoid lesions at the RPE/choriocapillaris level, often post-viral

questions.question: The SAFE strategy for trachoma prevention stands for:
questions.explanation: The WHO SAFE strategy for trachoma elimination consists of: Surgery (for trichiasis), Antibiotics (azithromycin for active infection), Facial cleanliness (reducing transmission), and Environmental improvement (water, sanitation, hygiene). It is the global strategy to eliminate trachoma as a public health problem. Surgery and antibiotics address existing disease while the last two prevent new cases.
options: Sterilization, Antifungal drugs, Face washing, Education
Surgery, Antibiotics, Facial Cleanliness, Environmental Improvement
Sight restoration, Ablation, Fluoroquinolones, Eye drops

questions.explanation: In ocular onchocerciasis, punctate keratitis results from a host inflammatory response to microfilariae dying within the cornea rather than from direct mechanical damage by living larvae. Repeated cycles of microfilarial death and inflammation over years lead to progressive corneal scarring, or sclerosing keratitis, and eventual blindness. This mechanism underlies the rationale for antiparasitic treatment to reduce microfilarial load and limit further inflammatory damage.
questions.question: A patient from an onchocerciasis-endemic region develops chronic keratitis and eventual blindness related to microfilarial death in the cornea. What is the initial mechanism of corneal damage?
options: Autoimmune reaction unrelated to the parasite
Direct larval migration through Descemet's membrane
Haematogenous spread from an underlying septicaemia
questions.explanation: Orbital cellulitis most commonly arises from contiguous spread of bacterial sinusitis, particularly ethmoid sinusitis, because the ethmoid sinus shares a thin bony wall (lamina papyracea) with the medial orbit. Common organisms include Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus, and H. influenzae. It requires urgent IV antibiotics and otolaryngology assessment.
questions.question: Orbital cellulitis is MOST commonly caused by spread of infection from:
Non-arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy (NAION) classically presents with:
questions.explanation: Non-arteritic AION (NAION) classically presents with painless, sudden unilateral visual loss (often noticed on waking) with an inferior altitudinal field defect and disc oedema (swollen optic disc). It affects patients over 50 with cardiovascular risk factors and small 'disc at risk' (small cup-to-disc ratio). No proven treatment exists; visual recovery is variable.
options: Painful visual loss with a swollen disc
Gradual visual loss over weeks in young patients
Painless unilateral visual loss with altitudinal field defect and disc oedema on waking
Progressive visual loss with an entirely normal disc appearance

questions.explanation: Lidocaine is commonly used by injection for retrobulbar or peribulbar blocks because it provides deeper and longer anaesthesia than topical agents allow. Topical anaesthetics only numb the surface and cannot block the deeper orbital structures moved during intraocular surgery. Its rapid onset also suits time-limited surgical procedures.
questions.question: A patient requires retrobulbar anaesthesia before intraocular surgery, and the surgeon selects an injectable local anaesthetic rather than a topical drop. The agent typically used is

questions.explanation: The Mantoux (tuberculin skin) test combined with chest X-ray is the most important initial investigation to screen for tuberculosis in posterior uveitis. Choroidal tubercles, periphlebitis, and Dalen-Fuchs nodules are ocular features of TB uveitis. QuantiFERON-Gold test is more specific. TB is a major cause of posterior uveitis in endemic regions including Nigeria and sub-Saharan Africa.
questions.question: The MOST important investigation to exclude tuberculosis as a cause of posterior uveitis is:

options: Topical steroids target anterior segment inflammation more directly and rapidly
NSAIDs do not penetrate the blood-aqueous barrier
NSAIDs increase IOP while topical steroids reduce it
NSAIDs cause corneal melting when used with ocular inflammation
Topical steroids are proton-pump inhibitors protecting the gastric mucosa
questions.explanation: Topical corticosteroids (prednisolone acetate, dexamethasone) are the first-line treatment for anterior uveitis because they deliver high drug concentrations directly to the anterior segment inflammation quickly. NSAIDs are used systemically for the underlying spondyloarthropathy to reduce systemic disease activity and frequency of uveitis recurrence, but do not replace topical steroids for acute episodes.
questions.question: Aspirin and NSAIDs are used systemically for HLA-B27-associated anterior uveitis as part of spondylarthropathy management. They are NOT a substitute for topical steroids because:

options: Optic nerve head and peripapillary retina
Vitreous, pars plana, and peripheral retina
questions.explanation: Intermediate uveitis involves the vitreous, pars plana, and peripheral retina/choroid. It presents with floaters and gradual visual loss from vitreous cells and snowball/snowbank opacities over the pars plana. Multiple sclerosis and sarcoidosis are important associations. Cystoid macular oedema is the most common cause of visual loss. Treatment uses periocular or systemic steroids.
questions.question: Intermediate uveitis (pars planitis) predominantly affects the:

questions.explanation: Diabetic retinopathy is the most common and clinically significant ocular complication of diabetes mellitus, and the leading cause of blindness in working-age adults in developed countries. It results from retinal microvascular damage. DR is classified as non-proliferative (NPDR) or proliferative (PDR), with diabetic maculopathy the main cause of visual loss.
questions.question: The MOST common and clinically significant ocular complication of diabetes mellitus is:

questions.explanation: Elevated intraocular pressure is the most dangerous acute complication of hyphema because blood in the anterior chamber can obstruct the trabecular drainage meshwork. Persistent elevated IOP can lead to irreversible optic nerve damage (glaucoma) and corneal bloodstaining. Daily IOP monitoring is mandatory, and anti-glaucoma medications may be required.
questions.question: The MOST important complication of hyphema that must be closely monitored is:
options: Corneal scarring from ulceration as commonly encountered in practice
Formation of corneal neovascularization during routine ophthalmic assessment
Elevated intraocular pressure leading to optic nerve damage

questions.explanation: The orbicularis oculi is innervated by CN VII (facial nerve). Facial nerve palsy results in inability to close the eyelid (lagophthalmos), exposing the cornea to desiccation and ulceration. This is why facial nerve palsy requires urgent eye protection with lubricants or tarsorrhaphy.
questions.question: Which nerve innervates the orbicularis oculi muscle?

questions.explanation: Subconjunctival haemorrhage from a ruptured conjunctival vessel following straining, coughing, or minor trauma is a benign, self-limiting condition that resolves without treatment. Reassurance and observation are sufficient in most cases, with resolution typically within two weeks. Investigation for a bleeding tendency or blood pressure check may be warranted if episodes recur without clear precipitating cause.
questions.question: A patient develops a painless area of bright red blood beneath the conjunctiva after a coughing fit, with no other ocular symptoms. What is the most appropriate initial management?

questions.explanation: Leber hereditary optic neuropathy is a mitochondrial disorder that predominantly affects young males and causes painless, sequential, bilateral central visual loss due to maternal inheritance of mitochondrial DNA mutations. This inheritance pattern distinguishes it from dominant optic atrophy, which follows autosomal dominant transmission. There is currently no definitive cure, though some gene therapies are under investigation.
questions.question: A young male presents with painless bilateral sequential visual loss and a central scotoma, with a family history suggesting maternal inheritance. Which condition is most likely?
A patient has absent corneal reflex on the left. The most likely cause involves a lesion in which nerve?
questions.explanation: The afferent limb of the corneal reflex is provided by CN V1 (ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve), while the efferent limb is CN VII (facial nerve). An absent corneal reflex with loss of sensation on the left suggests a lesion of the left CN V1. Testing both direct and consensual responses localizes the defect.

questions.question: A patient presents with a red, painful eye, nausea, vomiting, a hazy cornea, and a mid-dilated pupil that does not react to light. This presentation is MOST consistent with
questions.explanation: The combination of severe pain, systemic symptoms, corneal haze from oedema, and a fixed mid-dilated pupil is classic for a sudden rise in intraocular pressure seen in acute angle closure. Conjunctivitis and episcleritis do not typically cause such severe pain or pupillary abnormality. Recognising this pattern demands urgent pressure-lowering treatment.

questions.question: Which characteristic does NOT apply to primary open-angle glaucoma?
questions.explanation: POAG is chronic, slowly progressive, bilateral (though asymmetric), and has an insidious onset WITHOUT pain. Acute painful presentation with corneal oedema is characteristic of acute primary angle-closure glaucoma. Confusion between the two is dangerous, as their management differs fundamentally.
options: Progressive optic nerve damage over time
Painful acute onset with corneal oedema

questions.question: Optical coherence tomography (OCT) is MOST useful in diabetic retinopathy for:
questions.explanation: OCT provides high-resolution cross-sectional imaging of the retina, allowing precise measurement of retinal thickness and direct visualization of macular edema—essential for managing diabetic macular edema (DMO). It can detect subtle intraretinal fluid (IRF) and subretinal fluid before they are visible clinically. OCT has largely supplanted fluorescein angiography as the primary tool for monitoring macular disease.
options: Measuring retinal thickness and detecting macular edema with precision
Assessing the optic disc for glaucomatous cupping as commonly encountered in practice
Localizing intraocular foreign bodies during routine ophthalmic assessment

questions.explanation: Blunt orbital trauma can cause a blow-out fracture of the thin orbital floor, leading to herniation of orbital contents (including the inferior rectus muscle) into the maxillary sinus. This produces restricted upgaze, vertical diplopia, enophthalmos, and periorbital emphysema. Immediate imaging (CT orbits) confirms the diagnosis. Surgical repair is required if diplopia or enophthalmos is significant.
questions.question: A football player sustains blunt trauma to the right eye and develops restricted ocular movement on upgaze, periorbital edema, and enophthalmos. The MOST likely diagnosis is:
options: Traumatic optic neuropathy during routine ophthalmic assessment
Hyphema with IOP elevation as commonly encountered in practice
Orbital floor fracture with inferior rectus entrapment

questions.explanation: Proliferative sickle cell retinopathy (PSR) with sea fan neovascularisation is paradoxically most common in HbSC disease (and HbS-beta thalassaemia) compared to HbSS disease. HbSC patients have higher haematocrit, causing more frequent microvascular occlusion at the peripheral retina, while HbSS patients have lower haematocrit and more collateral circulation.
questions.question: Proliferative sickle cell retinopathy ('sea fan' neovascularisation) is MOST common in which sickle haemoglobin genotype?

options: Provides ipsilateral monocular visual field representation
Compensates for the blind spot of each eye
Enhances contrast sensitivity in dim light
questions.question: Temporal retinal fibers at the optic chiasm do NOT cross over. What is the functional significance of this arrangement?
questions.explanation: Nasal fibers cross at the chiasm while temporal fibers remain ipsilateral. This arrangement ensures each visual cortex receives input from both eyes, allowing comparison of slightly different images from each eye, which forms the basis of stereopsis (depth perception).

options: Face washing under standard examination conditions
Vitamin A supplementation in most clinical presentations
questions.question: The SAFE strategy for trachoma control includes Surgery, Antibiotics, Face washing, and Environmental improvement. Which component directly treats established trichiasis?
questions.explanation: Surgery in the SAFE strategy specifically refers to surgical correction of trichiasis (entropion surgery) to prevent further corneal abrasion from inward-turning eyelashes. This is the only direct treatment for established trichiasis and late-stage trachoma. Antibiotics treat active infection, face washing interrupts transmission, and environmental improvement reduces the fly vector and contaminated water.

In sickle cell patients with hyphema, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors can promote further red cell sickling within the anterior chamber, worsening pressure elevation and optic nerve damage. Careful pressure control avoiding these agents, along with close monitoring, is essential. Rebleeding risk is also higher in this population.
options: Immediate surgical evacuation in all cases
Avoiding carbonic anhydrase inhibitors that worsen sickling
Patching both eyes for two weeks
Avoiding all forms of pain relief
questions.question: A patient presents with sudden loss of vision after a blow to the eye, with blood layering in the anterior chamber. What immediate precaution is important in a sickle cell patient?

options: Abnormal vascularisation from oxygen therapy exposure
questions.question: A premature infant born at very low birth weight develops abnormal peripheral retinal vessel growth on screening. What is the underlying cause?
questions.explanation: Retinopathy of prematurity results from disrupted normal retinal vascular development, often related to supplemental oxygen exposure in preterm infants with immature retinal vasculature. This can lead to abnormal fibrovascular proliferation at the vascular-avascular junction. Screening and timely laser treatment prevent progression to retinal detachment.

questions.question: Peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS) in uveitis refers to adhesions between the iris and:
options: Posterior lens capsule causing posterior chamber obstruction
Anterior lens capsule causing pupil block and iris bombé
Trabecular meshwork or peripheral cornea causing secondary glaucoma
questions.explanation: Peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS) are adhesions between the peripheral iris and the trabecular meshwork or peripheral cornea (angle structures). They mechanically obstruct aqueous outflow, causing secondary angle-closure glaucoma. PAS are a serious complication of chronic anterior uveitis, angle neovascularization, or prolonged flat anterior chamber post-surgery. They are best assessed by gonioscopy.

options: Cotton-wool spots from nerve fibre infarction
Vitreous haemorrhage or traction retinal detachment from rupture of new vessels
Gradual central vision loss from chronic macular ischaemia
questions.explanation: Sea fan neovascularisation in proliferative sickle cell retinopathy is fragile new vessel growth at the peripheral retina (stage V = PSR). These vessels can rupture, causing vitreous haemorrhage, or undergo fibrous proliferation causing traction retinal detachment — both potentially vision-threatening. Auto-infarction (spontaneous regression) occurs in some cases. Laser photocoagulation of feeding arterioles is the treatment.
questions.question: The 'sea fan' neovascularisation in sickle cell retinopathy is MOST likely to cause:
Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes on histology of retinoblastoma are significant because they:
options: Indicate complete necrosis of the tumor as commonly encountered in practice
Represent true photoreceptor differentiation and are specific to retinoblastoma
Are seen only in bilateral cases during routine ophthalmic assessment
questions.explanation: Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes (with a central lumen) are a histological hallmark of retinoblastoma, representing differentiation toward photoreceptors (likely cones). Homer Wright rosettes (with a neurofibrillary tangle) are less specific and seen in other neuroblastic tumors. The presence of Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes confirms the diagnosis and indicates a degree of tumor differentiation. They originate from neuroblastic precursors of the sensory retina.

options: Night blindness and bone spicule pigmentation
Sudden painless visual loss with floaters
Eye pain and headache from accommodative strain
questions.explanation: Hypermetropic patients must constantly accommodate to see both far and near objects, unlike emmetropes who only accommodate for near. This sustained ciliary muscle effort causes eye strain symptoms including eye pain, headache, and brow ache. These symptoms worsen toward the end of the day or with prolonged near work.
questions.question: Hypermetropic patients who use accommodation for both near AND distance vision most commonly present with:

questions.explanation: The central retinal artery is an end-artery supplying the inner retina, and its occlusion causes acute ischaemic whitening of the retina. The fovea appears red because it is thin and overlies the intact choroidal circulation, producing the cherry-red spot. Sudden painless visual loss without warning is characteristic of arterial rather than venous occlusion.
questions.question: A patient develops sudden painless monocular vision loss described as 'a curtain falling'. Fundoscopy shows a pale, oedematous retina with a cherry-red spot. Which vessel is occluded?
In Graves' ophthalmopathy, which is the MOST common clinical sign on examination?
questions.explanation: Eyelid retraction is the MOST common sign of Graves' ophthalmopathy, present in up to 90% of patients with thyroid eye disease. It results from sympathetic overstimulation of Muller's muscle (superior tarsal muscle) from hyperthyroidism AND from fibrosis and inflammation of the levator palpebrae and inferior retractor muscles. Proptosis (exophthalmos) is the second most common sign and the most common cause of adult proptosis.

options: Direct glycosylation damage to iris endothelial cells
Elevated IOP damaging the iris sphincter
VEGF release from ischaemic retina stimulating new vessel growth on the iris
Trauma to the iris from vitreous prolapse
questions.explanation: Rubeosis iridis (neovascularisation of the iris) results from VEGF produced by extensively ischaemic retina in advanced proliferative diabetic retinopathy. New, abnormal blood vessels grow on the iris surface and angle. Angle neovascularisation leads to secondary closed-angle (neovascular) glaucoma. Anti-VEGF injection and panretinal photocoagulation are used to regress rubeosis.
questions.question: Rubeosis iridis (iris neovascularisation) in diabetes is caused by:

options: reducing oxygen demand of ischemic peripheral retina to limit VEGF drive
questions.explanation: Panretinal photocoagulation ablates areas of ischemic peripheral retina, reducing their oxygen demand and thereby lowering the drive for vascular endothelial growth factor production that fuels neovascularization. It does not directly treat macular edema or mechanically remove blood. Its benefit lies in halting further progression of proliferative disease rather than reversing existing new vessels instantly.
questions.question: A patient with proliferative diabetic retinopathy undergoes panretinal laser photocoagulation. This treatment works PRIMARILY by
A patient has a red eye with a corneal ulcer and organisms cultured that are capable of penetrating an intact corneal epithelium, unlike most bacteria. Which organisms fit this description?
questions.explanation: Most bacteria require a break in corneal epithelial integrity to establish infection, but Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Neisseria meningitidis, and Corynebacterium diphtheriae possess the ability to invade an intact epithelium. This unique virulence explains why gonococcal keratoconjunctivitis can rapidly progress to corneal perforation even without prior trauma. Recognising these organisms is important for anticipating aggressive corneal involvement.

Dense congenital cataracts must be removed within the first few weeks of life, ideally by six to eight weeks, because the visual system is highly sensitive to form deprivation during this critical period. Delay beyond this window significantly worsens the prognosis for useful vision due to irreversible amblyopia. Unilateral cases are particularly urgent since the fellow eye's clear vision accelerates suppression of the affected eye.
options: Within the first month only if bilateral
questions.question: An infant is diagnosed with a dense congenital cataract in one eye. To achieve the best visual outcome and prevent deprivation amblyopia, surgery should be performed within which timeframe?

questions.explanation: Epidemic keratoconjunctivitis caused by adenovirus classically presents with subconjunctival haemorrhage, watery discharge, and highly contagious spread within households or clinics. Corneal subepithelial infiltrates typically develop after the acute phase and can cause prolonged visual blurring. Strict hygiene measures are essential to limit transmission during outbreaks.
questions.question: An outbreak of conjunctivitis with subconjunctival haemorrhages, watery discharge, and later corneal subepithelial infiltrates affects several members of a household. Which virus is most likely responsible?

questions.explanation: Aspirin has been investigated as a protective factor against age-related cataract primarily due to its anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties, which may prevent oxidative damage to lens proteins. Oxidative stress is a major pathogenic mechanism in lens opacification. However, the evidence remains inconclusive, and aspirin is not routinely recommended as cataract prophylaxis.
options: Miotic effect reducing UV light exposure
questions.question: The protection offered by aspirin against cataract formation is thought to be through its:
The sex predilection for POAG differs from that of PACG in that:
questions.explanation: POAG has an approximately equal sex distribution. PACG affects women approximately 4 times more commonly than men due to women's anatomically smaller eyes, shallower anterior chambers, and more anteriorly placed lenses. This important epidemiological difference has implications for screening targeted at women aged 40 and over.
options: POAG affects men and women equally; PACG affects women 4 times more
POAG affects women twice as commonly
POAG and PACG affect women equally
POAG affects only men; PACG affects only women exclusively

questions.explanation: An inflamed pterygium that is encroaching on the visual axis requires surgical excision to prevent corneal scarring and visual loss. Lubricants and topical steroids may reduce inflammation temporarily but do not remove the pterygium. Surgical excision with or without adjunctive antimetabolite therapy (e.g., mitomycin C) reduces recurrence rates.
questions.question: A pterygium causing red eye that is inflamed and growing toward the visual axis should be managed by:

questions.explanation: Intermittent (subacute) angle closure presents with repeated, self-limited episodes of blurred vision, haloes around lights (corneal oedema), and mild eye discomfort, triggered by dim light or emotional stress causing pupil dilation. The angle reopens spontaneously on pupil constriction. Without treatment, it may progress to acute PACG.
questions.question: Intermittent angle closure typically presents with:
options: Fixed dilated pupil that never recovers
Permanent corneal clouding resulting from repeated acute attacks
Constant severe and unremitting eye pain
Episodic blurred vision with haloes in dim light, resolving spontaneously

questions.explanation: Retinal vein occlusion in sickle cell disease occurs because the low-flow, relatively hypoxic venous circulation is particularly prone to sickling of red cells, causing increased blood viscosity, cellular adhesion to endothelium, and vascular stasis that leads to thrombotic occlusion. This is compounded by the activation of the inflammatory cascade triggered by sickled cells interacting with endothelial von Willebrand factor and thrombospondin.
questions.question: Retinal vein occlusion in a young patient with sickle cell disease occurs because:
options: Sickling in the slow-flow venous circulation causes thrombosis and vascular obstruction
Elevated IOP compresses retinal veins at the optic disc in the majority of documented cases
Autoimmune vasculitis targets retinal veins selectively
Vitreous traction on venous bifurcations at AV crossings based on typical clinical findings

questions.question: A patient has chronic conjunctival scarring with progressive entropion and trichiasis after repeated infections in childhood, now causing corneal scarring and blindness. Which infectious agent is responsible for this sequence?
questions.explanation: Trachoma results from repeated conjunctival infection with Chlamydia trachomatis serotypes A to C, producing chronic follicular conjunctivitis that progresses to conjunctival scarring, entropion, and trichiasis. The resulting inward-turning lashes abrade the cornea, causing opacification and blindness over years. This progression underlies the WHO grading system used to assess trachoma severity.

options: The treated eye always requires re-enucleation within 5 years
Anti-VEGF therapy must be maintained indefinitely
There is increased lifetime risk of second non-ocular malignancies
Retinoblastoma spreads to the contralateral eye after 10 years in all hereditary cases
All hereditary RB patients require annual brain MRI only
questions.question: Long-term follow-up of patients with retinoblastoma who have the hereditary form is necessary PRIMARILY because:
questions.explanation: Hereditary retinoblastoma patients carry the RB1 tumour suppressor gene mutation in every cell and have a significantly elevated lifetime risk of developing second non-ocular malignancies, including osteosarcoma (most common), pinealoblastoma, soft tissue sarcomas, and melanomas—particularly in previously irradiated fields. Long-term multidisciplinary cancer surveillance is therefore essential for all germline RB1 mutation carriers throughout their lives.

questions.question: A patient develops sudden central visual distortion with straight lines appearing wavy, and is found to have fluid beneath the macula without haemorrhage. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Central serous chorioretinopathy is characterised by localised serous detachment of the neurosensory retina, typically at the macula, causing visual distortion and a relative central scotoma without haemorrhage. It is more common in young to middle-aged men, often associated with stress or corticosteroid use. Most cases resolve spontaneously, though persistent or recurrent cases may need treatment.

questions.question: A capillary hemangioma in a child's orbit causing amblyopia. The CURRENT preferred systemic treatment is:
questions.explanation: Current first-line treatment for capillary hemangioma causing complications (amblyopia, proptosis, cosmetic deformity) is systemic oral propranolol, a beta-blocker that promotes involution of the hemangioma. It has largely replaced intralesional steroids. Radiation is avoided due to risks of cataract and malignancy. Amblyopia therapy is also essential.

questions.question: A young woman presents with mild unilateral anterior uveitis, heterochromia, and diffuse fine keratic precipitates without posterior synechiae despite a chronic course. Which diagnosis fits best?
questions.explanation: Fuchs' heterochromic cyclitis is a chronic, low-grade anterior uveitis characterised by iris heterochromia, fine stellate keratic precipitates, and a notable absence of posterior synechiae despite chronicity. This distinguishes it from other forms of anterior uveitis that typically cause synechiae formation. Cataract and secondary glaucoma are recognised long-term complications.

Classifying red eye causes by anatomical location groups conditions affecting the lids and lacrimal drainage system separately from those affecting the conjunctiva, cornea, or deeper globe. Blepharitis, chalazion, and dacryocystitis all originate from adnexal rather than intraocular structures. This classification helps direct examination toward the correct anatomical region first.
options: involvement of the eyelids or lacrimal apparatus
questions.question: Conditions such as blepharitis, chalazion, and dacryocystitis are grouped together in red eye classification because they share which anatomical feature?
When performing Crede's method of neonatal prophylaxis, which solution was classically used?
questions.explanation: Crede's method (introduced in 1880) involved instillation of 2% silver nitrate (later reduced to 1%) into the conjunctival sac of the neonate at birth to prevent gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum. While highly effective against Neisseria gonorrhoeae, it causes chemical conjunctivitis in up to 90% of neonates, is ineffective against Chlamydia, and is no longer the recommended agent. 0.5% erythromycin and 1% tetracycline are now preferred.

Molluscum contagiosum is a DNA poxvirus spread by direct contact, characterized by umbilicated lesions on the eyelid.
