questions.answerText:
A(i) Definition: meningitis is inflammation of the meninges (layers of tissue covering the brain and spinal cord) and the fluid-filled subarachnoid space; encephalitis is inflammation of the brain parenchyma, a pathologic diagnosis used to describe a clinical syndrome of brain inflammation.
A(ii) Aetiology: meningitis may be viral, bacterial or fungal; bacterial organisms gain access to the subarachnoid space through bacteraemia, contiguous spread from dental/sinus infection, traumatic/congenital communications, or neurosurgical procedures, with causative organisms varying by age (S. agalactiae, E. coli, L. monocytogenes in the first week of life, replaced by S. pneumoniae and N. meningitidis by the sixth week). Encephalitis has infectious (viral, bacterial, parasitic), post-infectious and non-infectious (metabolic, toxic, autoimmune, paraneoplastic) causes, with HSV-1 the most common cause of sporadic viral encephalitis.
A(iii) Classification: meningitis types are viral, fungal and bacterial; encephalitis presentation correlates with the brain region involved (temporal lobe with HSV, basal ganglia/thalamus with West Nile/Eastern equine viruses, brainstem encephalitis).
A(iv) Clinical features: meningitis presents with the classic triad of fever, neck stiffness/nuchal rigidity and altered mental status (present in only a minority), plus nausea/vomiting, cranial nerve abnormalities, rash and seizure, with infants showing non-specific lethargy and irritability; Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs may be positive. Encephalitis presents according to the region affected - HSV encephalitis (temporal lobes) with personality change, psychosis, hallucinations; frontal/temporal involvement with visual field deficits, memory problems, hemiparesis or aphasia; basal ganglia/thalamus involvement with tremors; brainstem involvement with autonomic dysfunction.
B. Clinical basis for vulnerability in children: the most common predisposing conditions in children are sinus or middle ear infection, leading to transient bacteraemia and haematogenous seeding of the CNS. Infants under 90 days present a particular challenge because many febrile infants of this age have no obvious infection focus yet about 10% have an underlying serious bacterial infection; infants younger than 28 days have an even greater risk (11-25% prevalence), so a lumbar puncture is generally recommended in all such cases.
C. Distinction: meningitis primarily involves the meninges/subarachnoid space with neck stiffness and altered mental status but no focal neurologic findings; encephalitis involves the brain parenchyma and is distinguished by focal neurologic findings or seizures. The first step in suspected CNS infection is to determine if bacterial meningitis requires emergent antibiotics; encephalitis is considered when there is additional evidence of parenchymal involvement.
questions.question:
A(i) Define meningitis and encephalitis.
A(ii) State their aetiology.
A(iii) Classify each condition.
A(iv) Describe their clinical features.
B. Explain the clinical basis for why children are particularly vulnerable to these CNS infections.
C. Distinguish between meningitis and encephalitis.

questions.answerText:
(i) Description: in the neonatal period the infant adjusts to the extra-uterine environment, maintains a physiological flexion position, has no anti-gravity control except lifting/rotating the head, with the centre of gravity high in the thoracic spine. By 3 months, physiological flexion decreases, head raising reaches 90°, and head lag when pulled to sit begins disappearing. By 6 months there is good head control, greater trunk mobility, and sitting using hands for support. By 8 months, equilibrium reactions develop and crawling becomes the main means of mobility, with pulling into kneeling and standing beginning. By 11-12 months, equilibrium reactions are established in all positions except standing, and the child attempts to walk with a toe-walking, high-guard pattern. Development proceeds cephalo-caudally, proximal to distal, and from gross to fine movement, and involves differentiation from reflexive mass forms to elaborate, specific responses; head control is an important motor prerequisite for all functions.
(ii) Relation to paediatric pathologies: normal motor development depends primarily on maturation of the nervous system and occurs in the same sequence for all children, though the rate varies. Growth and development of the nervous system, and consequently motor development, may be hindered by diseases, trauma or developmental abnormalities before, during or after birth, as in cerebral palsy.
(iii) Secondary impairment/functional deficit: in cerebral palsy, poor head control, low trunk tone, persistence of primary reflexes, and incomplete development of righting reflexes and equilibrium reactions mean that key milestones such as independent sitting, standing and walking are delayed or not attained, with limbs often maintained in midrange and stereotypical, slow, laborious movements, creating a high risk of musculoskeletal adaptations and deformities.
questions.question:
(i) Describe the sequence of normal motor development from the neonatal period to 12 months.
(ii) State how this sequence relates to common paediatric pathologies.
(iii) Explain how disruption of this sequence leads to secondary impairment/functional deficit.

A(i) State the principles of Neurodevelopmental Treatment (NDT).
A(ii) State its indications.
A(iii) Describe the procedure/focus of NDT.
A(iv) State the positioning focus.
B. State the safe/age-appropriate application.
C. Explain the rationale for the expected outcome.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Principles: NDT uses guided or facilitated movements to ensure correlation of input from tactile, vestibular and somatosensory receptors. It is an interactive, problem-solving approach focused on continuing reassessment, individual goals, working hypotheses and objective measures; it is goal-orientated and task-specific, aiming to organise the internal (proprioceptive) and external (exteroceptive) environment of the nervous system for efficient functioning.
A(ii) Indications: conditions with abnormal tone and movement such as Patau syndrome and cerebral palsy (Bobath's approach being a school of thought in CP management).
A(iii) Procedure: repeated experience in movement during treatment ensures a particular pattern becomes readily accessible for motor performance. NDT focuses on encouragement of normal movement patterns, quality of movement, normalisation of tone to facilitate active movement, and discouragement of compensatory movements.
A(iv) Positioning: attention to positioning and posture in lying, sitting and standing is a specific focus.
B. Safe/age-appropriate application: tone can be reduced through mobilisation of muscles and stiff joints, muscle stretch, practice of more normal movement patterns, more efficient performance of functional tasks, and weight-bearing, applied according to the individual child's needs and developmental stage.
C. Rationale: benefits of NDT include normalising tone, regaining motor control, making movements easier to achieve that are precise and goal-directed, improving posture, lengthening tight muscles to decrease spasticity and reduce contractures, improving ability with everyday activities, increasing independence, and helping the child achieve maximum potential.

(i) Diagnosis: Pes planus (pes planovalgus), or flat foot.
(ii) Pathophysiological basis: pes planus is an excessive valgus alignment of the heel (hindfoot) with loss or flattening of the medial longitudinal arch; the forefoot is abducted outward but often rotated inward (supinated) relative to the hindfoot; it may be congenital or acquired, and flexible or rigid. The medial longitudinal arch normally develops by age 5 or 6 years as the fat pad in babies is gradually absorbed, balance improves and skilled movements are acquired; in some children the arch fails to develop because of tightness in the calf muscles or laxity in the Achilles tendon. Flat foot is termed developmental when observed in infants/toddlers as part of normal development; if it persists to ages 8-10 it may be considered a true flat foot.
(iii) Assessment findings/problem list: flexible flat foot shows longitudinal arches present on heel elevation (tiptoe standing) and non-weight-bearing, but the arches disappear with full weight bearing; in many cases there are no signs or symptoms, but when present, clinical features include cramps in the leg, muscle pain (aching/fatigue) in the foot or leg, pain in the arch/ankle/heel/outside of the foot, and pain when walking.
(iv) Physiotherapy goals: relieve pain and inflammation; improve flexibility and mobility; stretch and strengthen tight tendons and muscles.
(v) Treatment plan: nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs; rest and ice to ease inflammation and pain; exercises to stretch/strengthen tight tendons/muscles and improve flexibility/mobility; supportive devices such as foot orthotics, foot/leg braces and custom-made shoes; specific exercises include heel stretches, tennis/golf ball rolls, arch lifts, calf raises, stair arch raises, towel curls and toe raises.

A child presents with fever, headache, sore throat and muscle pain that progresses over days to asymmetric muscle weakness and paralysis of a limb, with preserved sensation.

(i) Identify the developmental level/abnormality shown.
(ii) State the motor domains/body structures affected.
(iii) State the differential conditions to consider.
(iv) Give the clinical reasoning for physiotherapy intervention.
questions.answerText:
(i) Identification: this presentation is consistent with poliomyelitis, a contagious disease caused by poliovirus that can cause permanent disability, paralysis and death. The virus enters through the mouth or nose, multiplies in the throat and intestines, and travels to the nervous system via the bloodstream and lymphatic channels, with an incubation period of 5 to 35 days.
(ii) Motor domains/body structures affected: symptoms include fever, fatigue, headache, vomiting, diarrhoea/constipation, sore throat, muscle pain, weakness or paralysis, photophobia, and difficulty breathing or swallowing; the paralysis reflects lower motor neurone involvement leading to muscle weakness and, characteristically, asymmetric limb weakness.
(iii) Differential conditions: poliomyelitis is part of the acute flaccid paralysis group of conditions alongside sciatica and Guillain-Barre syndrome. The poliovirus spreads by the faecal-oral route; wild poliovirus type 2 was declared eradicated in 2015 and type 3 in 2019, leaving only type 1, while circulating vaccine-derived poliovirus (cVDPV) outbreaks can occur in communities with low immunisation rates and poor sanitation.
(iv) Clinical reasoning for intervention: management includes a sustained immunisation programme and rehabilitation; physiotherapy prescribes orthotics such as ring-top callipers and ankle-foot orthotic devices and back slabs; gait re-education works on hand-to-knee gait; postural education addresses correction of deformity and post-surgical intervention; ambulation aids include axillary and elbow crutches; surgery such as tendon transfer and release of contractures may be needed; children should usually receive 4 doses of polio vaccine at ages 2 months, 4 months, 6-18 months and 4-6 years as prevention.

(i) Description: at birth only about 15% (15-20%) of brain growth/CNS maturation has occurred; only a few nerve fibres are myelinated at birth - myelinated fibres include ascending afferent fibres of the spinal cord (e.g. spinothalamic tract) and all cranial nerves except the olfactory nerve (optic nerve only partially myelinated); unmyelinated fibres include descending corticospinal fibres, cerebral/cerebellar white matter, and the olfactory tract. The cerebral cortex is only half its eventual adult thickness at birth, with minimal cortical connections because dendrites are rudimentary. By 6 months most spinal cord tracts are well myelinated and the optic nerve is completely myelinated; by 2 years all nerve fibres in the spinal cord, brain stem and cerebellum are myelinated. Myelination starts near the cell body and spreads along the fibre, and nerve fibres become functional at approximately the same time as they become myelinated.
(ii) Relation to paediatric pathologies: there is a correlation between maturation of the nervous system, especially myelination, and motor development. Growth and development of the nervous system, and consequently a child's motor development, may be hindered by diseases, trauma or developmental abnormalities occurring before, during or after birth, as seen in cerebral palsy and intellectual disability.
(iii) Secondary impairment/functional deficit: in children with cerebral palsy or intellectual disability, serious limitations in adapting movement to functional purposes occur even with very good opportunities to interact with the environment, because CNS maturation is the major force driving child development, showing that disruption to nervous system maturation directly translates into a functional motor deficit regardless of environmental enrichment.
questions.question:
(i) Describe CNS maturation and myelination at birth and in infancy.
(ii) State how this relates to common paediatric pathologies.
(iii) Explain how disrupted maturation leads to secondary impairment/functional deficit.

A 6-week-old infant is brought in with the head persistently tilted toward the right shoulder and the chin rotated toward the left. The mother reports the baby prefers to look to one side and has difficulty feeding on that side. On examination there is a firm palpable mass within the right sternocleidomastoid muscle and reduced neck rotation to the right and lateral flexion to the left.

(i) State the most likely diagnosis.
(ii) State the predisposing factors and pathophysiology.
(iii) Outline the physiotherapy management.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Congenital muscular torticollis (CMT) - a non-progressive unilateral contracture of the sternocleidomastoid muscle.
(ii) Predisposing factors/pathophysiology: cited theories include ischaemia, trauma during childbirth, and intrauterine malposition (pelvic/breech position); the current theory favoured is intrauterine or perinatal compartment syndrome. The most common explanation involves birth trauma to the sternocleidomastoid resulting in fibrosis, or intrauterine malpositioning causing unilateral shortening of the muscle, with possible hematoma formation followed by muscular contracture. Incidence has increased with the "back to sleep" programme. If untreated it may lead to plagiocephaly (misshapen head).
(iii) Physiotherapy management: controlled manual stretching in two parts - lateral flexion (stabilise the shoulder girdle on the involved side to prevent elevation, use an open flat hand avoiding the ear to move the head into lateral flexion to the opposite side) and rotation (stabilise the shoulder on the opposite side to prevent elevation/protraction, turn the head toward the involved side). A home exercise programme trains caregivers in this controlled manual stretching with instructions on duration, repetitions and frequency. Environmental changes include arranging the crib/changing table to promote turning the head toward caregivers and stimulate active head turning to toys/sounds; towel rolls or soft collars prevent the head falling passively into the shortened direction; placing the infant prone on the elbows over a small towel roll on the caregiver's chest encourages symmetrical head lifting from prone. The child should be screened for developmental dysplasia of the hip because of its close association with CMT, and more serious causes (posterior fossa tumour, Sandifer syndrome, craniosynostosis) must first be ruled out. Helmet therapy is a second-line treatment for moderate-to-severe persisting asymmetry. Most babies improve with position changes and stretching (which may take up to 6 months or longer); muscle-release surgery may be offered if stretching does not help.

questions.question:
A 5-year-old boy is brought to the clinic because his mother has noticed frequent falls, difficulty keeping up with peers while playing, and that he uses his hands to push up on his thighs to stand from the floor. On examination there is enlargement of both calves.

(i) State the most likely diagnosis.
(ii) Explain the pathophysiological/developmental basis.
(iii) State the assessment findings and problem list.
(iv) State the physiotherapy goals.
(v) Outline the treatment plan.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Duchenne's Muscular Dystrophy (DMD), the most common X-linked disorder (incidence 1 in 3500 live male births).
(ii) Pathophysiological basis: progressive loss of muscle contractility from destruction of myofibrils, caused by a missing/defective gene (Xp21) resulting in absent dystrophin, which normally reinforces the sarcolemma and protects fibres during contraction. Hypothesised mechanisms for myofibril damage include mechanical weakening of the sarcolemma, inappropriate calcium influx, increased oxidative stress and recurrent muscle ischaemia. Pseudohypertrophy of the calf occurs from fatty/connective tissue infiltration; initial weakness affects neck flexor, abdominal, inter-scapular and hip extensor muscles.
(iii) Assessment findings/problem list: Gower's sign (using the arms to push on the thighs to attain standing) present after repeated trials of standing from the floor; clumsiness and frequent falling; inability to keep up with peers; slight gait abnormality with increased lateral trunk sway; gradual loss of ability to run or jump. Problem list: early proximal hip/shoulder girdle weakness, calf pseudohypertrophy, and emerging gait changes that will progress to waddling gait, lumbar lordosis, forward abdominal thrust, scapular winging and toe-walking.
(iv) Physiotherapy goals: prolong independent ambulation; maximise functional ability; prevent complications of inactivity; improve emotional well-being.
(v) Treatment plan: family counselling and education; sub-maximal exercise programmes in safety (long-distance walk, cycling, swimming, ball throwing/kicking) rather than resistance exercise, since overexertion and immobilisation are both detrimental; moderate resistance exercises using gravity for key muscle groups (abdominal trunk curls not sit-ups, hip extensors/abductors, knee extensors); breathing exercises (inflating balloons, blow-bottles, blowing cotton wool) to slow loss of vital capacity; passive movements to maintain/increase ROM especially hips, knees and ankles; gentle passive stretching of gastrocnemius-soleus and tensor fasciae latae; exercise home programme teaching caregivers passive movements and stretching; continuation of standing/walking using orthoses (AFOs, KAFOs) to delay wheelchair use; once in a wheelchair, shift emphasis to active-assisted upper limb exercises.

A(i) Principles: controlled manual stretching for congenital muscular torticollis has two parts - lateral flexion and rotation of the head - aimed at lengthening the shortened sternocleidomastoid muscle and improving range of motion.
A(ii) Indications: congenital muscular torticollis, a non-progressive unilateral contracture of the sternocleidomastoid muscle causing the head to be held in lateral flexion toward the involved side with rotation to the opposite side and limited range of motion.
A(iii) Procedure: for lateral flexion, the shoulder girdle on the involved side is stabilised to prevent elevation, and an open flat hand (avoiding the ear) is used to move the child's head into lateral flexion to the opposite side; for rotation, the shoulder on the opposite side is stabilised to prevent elevation/protraction, and an open flat hand (avoiding the ear) is used to turn the child's head toward the involved side.
A(iv) Positioning: the infant may also be placed prone on the elbows over a small towel roll on the caregiver's chest, encouraged to look up at the caregiver to achieve symmetrical head lifting from prone.
A(v) Precautions: other more serious conditions that can manifest as torticollis must be ruled out first - a posterior fossa tumour, Sandifer syndrome (where placing the child in prone can increase reflux/irritability and reinforce the apparent torticollis posture), and craniosynostosis; the child should also be screened for developmental dysplasia of the hip because of its close association with congenital muscular torticollis.
B. Safe/age-appropriate application: a home exercise programme trains caregivers in the controlled manual stretching with specific instructions on the duration of each stretch, repetitions per session, and frequency per day, making the technique deliverable safely and consistently by caregivers between clinic visits.
C. Rationale: most babies with torticollis improve through position changes and stretching, which work best when started at 3-6 months of age and may take up to 6 months or longer to fully resolve; combined with environmental changes (crib/changing table arrangement, towel rolls or soft collars), controlled stretching addresses the underlying muscle shortening directly and helps prevent progression to plagiocephaly; if stretching does not improve the condition, muscle-release surgery may be considered.
questions.question:
A(i) State the principles of controlled manual stretching for congenital muscular torticollis.
A(ii) State its indications.
A(iii) Describe the procedure.
A(iv) State the positioning used.
A(v) State the precautions.
B. State the safe/age-appropriate application.
C. Explain the rationale for the expected outcome/prevention of deformity.

A newborn is found to have a sac protruding from the lower back through an opening in the vertebrae, exposing tissue and nerves, with observed weakness and reduced sensation in both lower limbs.

(i) State the most likely diagnosis.
(ii) Name the assessment tool/technique used.
(iii) Describe the key findings expected at different lesion levels.
(iv) State the precautions to be observed.
(v) Outline the parent/caregiver education and home programme.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Myelomeningocele, the most severe form of spina bifida, in which the spine and spinal canal fail to close before birth so the spinal canal is open along several back vertebrae; the membranes and spinal nerves push through the opening at birth forming a sac and exposing tissues and nerves, resulting in paralysis, loss of sensation, and urinary/faecal incontinence; 75% of cases occur at the lumbar/lumbosacral levels; Arnold-Chiari malformation and hydrocephalus are present in over 90% of cases.
(ii) Assessment tool/technique: physiotherapy assessment includes history taking (including incontinence history), observation of the back incision, head size, posture and joint alignment, physical examination of sensation (tactile), muscle power, muscle tone, and motor function assessed as age- and lesion-level-appropriate (sitting balance, kneeling, standing with support); head circumference is measured at every visit.
(iii) Key findings by lesion level: above L3 - complete paraplegia, dermatomal para-anaesthesia, bladder incontinence, non-ambulatory. L4 and L5 - paraplegia with preservation of hip flexors, hip adductors and knee extensors, dermatomal para-anaesthesia, bladder incontinence, ambulatory with walking aids/braces. S1 and S2 - same deficits as L4/L5 plus preservation of dorsiflexors of the feet and partial preservation of hip extensors/knee flexors, bladder incontinence, ambulatory with minimal aids. S3 and below - normal lower extremity motor function, saddle anaesthesia, variable bladder-rectal incontinence.
(iv) Precautions: protection of insensate feet against injury; monitoring of head size for early detection of hydrocephalus; care during passive movements because of possible muscle tightness and contractures.
(v) Parent/caregiver education and home programme: education on the condition for acceptance, protection of foot care against injury, monitoring of head size for early detection of hydrocephalus, and the importance of regular passive movements; muscle strengthening of the upper limbs, trunk and residual innervated lower limb muscles; training in age-appropriate motor function - head control in prone/supine, sitting, sitting balance, standing with support, standing balance, and transfers; for likely ambulatory children, fitting with light, well-padded orthotic devices; for non-ambulatory children, appropriate wheelchair provision and community-level wheelchair mobility training.

questions.question:
A 4-year-old child is brought for evaluation of knock-knees. On standing with the knees together there is a visible 3-inch gap between the ankles, and the parents report an altered gait with occasional knee pain.

(i) State the most likely diagnosis.
(ii) Explain the pathophysiological/developmental basis.
(iii) State the assessment findings and problem list.
(iv) State the physiotherapy goals.
(v) Outline the treatment plan.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Genu valgum (knock-knee deformity).
(ii) Pathophysiological basis: in genu valgum the knees are tilted toward the midline so the legs curve inward and the knees are closer together than normal; it can result from injury or septic destruction of the lateral half of the lower femoral epiphyseal plate leading to arrested growth of the lateral condyle of the femur. It is almost always a benign variation in a child's growth that runs in families and affects more than 20 percent of 3-year-olds, with most cases naturally correcting. Most patients present between ages 3 and 5 years, with the distal femur the most common site. Bilateral causes include physiologic genu valgum, skeletal dysplasias, metabolic bone diseases and lysosomal storage diseases; unilateral causes include trauma, tumours or infection; other causes include rickets, other bone diseases, obesity, and knee arthritis; a proximal metaphyseal tibial fracture can also predispose to a valgus posture.
(iii) Assessment findings/problem list: the typical gait pattern is circumduction, requiring the individual to swing each leg outward to take a step without striking the planted limb; with significant angular deformity, anterior and medial knee pain occur from patellofemoral extensor mechanism strain; other symptoms include a limp, pain in the feet/hips/ankles, stiff joints and lack of balance when standing. The degree of genu valgum is clinically estimated by the Q angle (normal about 12° in men and 17° in women); on radiography the hip-knee-ankle angle quantifies the deformity.
(iv) Physiotherapy goals: realign and stabilise the knees; relieve symptoms; correct gait.
(v) Treatment plan: developmental/idiopathic genu valgum is usually self-limiting; genu valgum from nutritional rickets is treated with adequate sun exposure, a calcium-rich diet, and calcium/vitamin D supplementation. If the deformity persists with gait impairment, surgery (guided growth or osteotomy) may be offered. Physiotherapy management includes braces, insole orthotics, stretching exercises, strengthening exercises for the leg/hip/thigh muscles (e.g. leg raises progressing with leg weights), EMS and frictional massage; a heel insert can correct unequal leg length; post-operatively, gradual knee mobilisation, heat modalities, strengthening of quadriceps/hamstrings/gluteus muscles, and correct training for standing, balancing, weight transferring and walking are given.

questions.question:
A 10-month-old infant remains unable to sit independently and still shows a strong startle (Moro-type) response to sudden movement, with movements described as coarse and jerky and a marked head lag on pulling to sit.

(i) Identify the developmental level/abnormality shown.
(ii) State the motor domains/body structures affected.
(iii) State the differential conditions to consider.
(iv) Give the clinical reasoning for physiotherapy intervention.
questions.answerText:
(i) Identification: this picture suggests delayed motor development at the primary reflex level rather than the expected righting reflex level for age, since righting reflexes normally emerge at about 3 months and become prominent between 6 and 9 months, while primary/infant reflexes are naturally expected to gradually integrate between age 3-6 months. Persistence of infant reflexes beyond age six months hinders the child's brain development and can be a major contributor to physical, intellectual, emotional, behavioural and social problems.
(ii) Motor domains/body structures affected: in children with developmental delay, persisting reflexes can keep a body part in a particular position, leading to musculoskeletal adaptation and deformities, and further delaying motor development. A baby whose reflex development does not go beyond the primary reflex level remains an apedal (lying) creature for life; a baby whose reflex development does not go beyond the righting reflex level remains a quadrupedal creature, able to sit, crawl and cruise round furniture but unable to stand or walk independently; only children whose reflex development reaches the equilibrium reaction and protective response level become bipedal.
(iii) Differential conditions: this pattern of retained primary reflexes and delayed righting/equilibrium development is seen in neuromotor conditions such as cerebral palsy, where persistence of primary reflexes and incomplete development of righting reflexes, equilibrium reactions and protective responses is a recognised major problem.
(iv) Clinical reasoning for intervention: knowledge of reflex development in early childhood is desirable for identification of abnormal reflexes in children and for correcting poor handling by caregivers that may stimulate abnormal reflexes; however, current physiotherapy approach to neuromotor disorders focuses on motor functions rather than reflexes themselves, so intervention should be directed at facilitating age-appropriate motor function and functional movement rather than reflex integration alone.

(i) Diagnosis: Klumpke's palsy, a lower brachial plexus injury involving the C8 and T1 nerve roots.
(ii) Predisposing factors/pathophysiology: obstetric causes include shoulder dystocia during vaginal delivery, macrosomia, prolonged/difficult labour, and use of forceps. The condition primarily affects the forearm and hand, causing weakness/paralysis of the intrinsic hand muscles (lumbricals, interossei) with weak grip and poor fine motor control, and may involve the wrist and finger flexors. Sensory loss occurs along the medial forearm and hand; Horner's syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis on the affected side of the face) may accompany it. The claw hand deformity results from hyperextension at the MCP joints and flexion at the IP joints, most prominent in the 4th and 5th fingers.
(iii) Physiotherapy management: electrotherapy modalities such as TENS for pain relief and functional electrical stimulation to assist functional tasks (grasping, lifting) and aid motor re-education in partial recoveries; cryotherapy in the acute phase to reduce inflammation/pain, and thermotherapy in the subacute/chronic stage to improve blood flow and reduce stiffness (with caution over denervated skin); manual therapy including passive range of motion to prevent joint stiffness/contractures, and soft tissue mobilisation; therapeutic exercise including isometric and active/active-assisted exercises; splinting/orthotics using dynamic or static splints to prevent contractures and maintain limb alignment; biofeedback and mirror therapy to promote neuroplasticity; phased management from pain relief/immobilisation in the acute stage, through passive/active-assisted ROM and electrical stimulation in the subacute stage, to functional training, strengthening and assistive devices in rehabilitation, and compensatory strategies or vocational rehabilitation in the chronic phase if full recovery is not achieved.
questions.question:
A newborn delivered after a difficult breech delivery is noted to have a claw-like posture of the hand with hyperextension at the metacarpophalangeal joints and flexion at the interphalangeal joints, most marked in the 4th and 5th fingers, with drooping of the eyelid and a constricted pupil on the same side.

(i) State the most likely diagnosis.
(ii) State the predisposing factors and pathophysiology.
(iii) Outline the physiotherapy management.

A(i) State the principles of serial casting.
A(ii) State its indications.
A(iii) Describe the procedure.
A(iv) State the positioning aim.
A(v) State the precautions.
B. State the safe/age-appropriate application.
C. Explain the rationale for the expected outcome.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Principles: conservative treatment is always attempted before surgical correction in congenital talipes equinovarus; serial casting gradually corrects the components of the deformity through repeated gentle correction.
A(ii) Indications: congenital talipes equinovarus (clubfoot), which occurs in a 2:1 male:female ratio and is bilateral in 50% of cases, with varying rigidity of the foot, calf atrophy, and mild hypoplasia of the tibia, fibula and foot bones.
A(iii) Procedure: treatment begins with passive movements and gentle passive stretching, followed by serial casting; improvement should occur within 4-6 weeks; tape strapping is particularly useful for preterm babies.
A(iv) Positioning: casting aims to correct the components of the deformity - inversion, forefoot adduction and ankle plantarflexion.
A(v) Precautions: reconstruction surgery is indicated when correction by conservative treatment is not sufficient to permit functional use of the leg, so correction adequacy must be monitored.
B. Safe/age-appropriate application: serial casting is applied from early infancy since most cases are congenital and present at birth; tape strapping is specifically useful for preterm babies, showing an age/maturity-adapted approach.
C. Rationale: gentle passive stretching and serial casting gradually correct the rigid clubfoot deformity while the infant's tissues and bones are still highly malleable, achieving improvement within 4-6 weeks without the risks of surgery; at a later stage, fitting an appropriate orthosis sustains the correction achieved and facilitates weight-bearing and walking, preventing recurrence of the deformity.

(i) Risk factors: JIA is an idiopathic (unclear-cause) arthritis.
(ii) Complications/secondary impairments: joints are painful, swollen, warm and inflamed; inflammation can lead to capsular hypertrophy, irregular bone growth, osteoporosis and small stature; prolonged inflammation and swelling can stretch surrounding ligaments and lead to chronic joint instability when the swelling subsides; painful inflammation of muscles/tendons can cause the child to move less or adopt an abnormal movement pattern, and decreased motion over time can lead to joint contractures. These changes alter normal skeletal alignment and cause further destructive forces on the body. Inflammation can change the growth rate of bones - inflammatory hyperaemia can stimulate adjacent growth plates causing overgrowth or early epiphyseal closure, and if only one side of a growth plate is affected, limb shortening occurs, with asymmetric bone growth causing angular postural deformities and limb length discrepancy. Leg length discrepancy is a common complication of oligoarthritis due to disease of the knee; foot deformities are prevalent; subluxation or ankylosing of the cervical spine can limit neck extension range of motion; temporomandibular joint disease is also more prevalent than in typical youth.
(iii) Management options and justification: goals of management are pain relief, prevention of range of motion limitation or restoration of range of motion, restoration of muscular strength, prevention or correction of deformity, and maintenance or improvement of functional abilities. Early physiotherapy intervention aimed at maintaining or restoring range of motion is the justified priority in this case because the pathway from painful inflammation to reduced motion, joint contracture, altered skeletal alignment and leg length discrepancy means that addressing the movement limitation early is key to preventing the secondary deformities and functional losses that JIA can otherwise cause.
questions.question:
A 7-year-old girl presents with a painful, swollen and warm knee joint of several weeks' duration, with reduced motion and reluctance to bear weight, and on examination one leg appears longer than the other.

(i) State the risk factors relevant to this presentation.
(ii) State the complications/secondary impairments.
(iii) State the physiotherapy management options and justify the one you would prioritise.

A(i) Define Edwards' syndrome and Patau syndrome.
A(ii) State their aetiology.
A(iii) Classify each condition.
A(iv) Describe their clinical features.
B. Explain the clinical basis for the severity seen in these conditions.
C. Distinguish between Edwards' syndrome and Patau syndrome.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Definition: Edwards' syndrome (Trisomy 18) is an autosomal chromosomal disorder due to an extra copy of chromosome 18; Patau syndrome (Trisomy 13) is caused by extra genetic material from chromosome 13 in some or all body cells.
A(ii) Aetiology: both can arise from meiotic nondisjunction (Edwards' more frequent with advancing maternal age; Patau's more frequent in mothers over 35), unbalanced Robertsonian translocation, or mosaicism (a mitotic nondisjunction error unrelated to maternal age, associated with a better prognosis in both).
A(iii) Classification: Edwards' syndrome types are full/complete Trisomy 18 (about 95%), mosaic Trisomy 18 (about 5%), and partial Trisomy 18 (less than 1%); Patau syndrome types are full Trisomy 13 (about 95%), mosaic Trisomy 13 (about 5%), and partial Trisomy 13 (less than 1%).
A(iv) Clinical features: Edwards' syndrome features include club feet, clenched fists with overlapping fingers, defects of the lungs/kidneys/stomach or intestine, feeding problems, heart defects, chest deformity and microcephaly. Patau syndrome features include heart defects, brain/spinal cord abnormalities, cleft lip/palate, extra fingers and toes, vision/hearing problems, seizures and hypotonia, severe mental deficiency and holoprosencephaly; both cause significant intellectual disability, usually severe, in survivors.
B. Clinical basis for severity: in both conditions the extra chromosomal material disrupts normal embryonic development from a very early stage, causing multiple complex organ defects across the heart, brain, face and limbs, which is why survivors have significant intellectual disability and why most affected pregnancies (about 95% in Edwards' syndrome) do not result in a live birth, with approximately 90% of Patau syndrome infants dying within the first year of life.
C. Distinction: Edwards' syndrome is caused by an extra chromosome 18, features clenched fists with overlapping fingers and microcephaly, has a live birth prevalence of 1 in 3600-10,000 and is more prevalent in females (3:2); Patau syndrome is caused by an extra chromosome 13, features extra fingers/toes, cleft lip/palate and holoprosencephaly, and occurs in about 1 per 5000 total births, a frequency similar to Edwards' syndrome but less common than Down syndrome (1 per 700 births).

questions.question:
(i) Describe motor development milestones from 7 to 10 months.
(ii) State how this relates to common paediatric pathologies.
(iii) Explain how delayed attainment leads to secondary impairment/functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
(i) Description: at 7 months, prone position is very stable, allowing dissociated upper/lower extremity movement patterns during play, and the child may play in side lying, requiring strongly balanced postural mechanisms. There is good stability and balance in sitting, with the child playing in sitting using both hands, head steady and back straight, beginning to shift weight laterally when reaching for dropped toys, and beginning to assume a quadruped position. At 8 months, equilibrium reactions (lateral protective responses) develop, allowing greater ease of movement in sitting, which becomes the baby's functional position, with more developed pelvic mobility/stability, and crawling becomes the main means of mobility while the child begins to pull into kneeling and standing. At 9-10 months, sitting is the child's most functional position and crawling the major means of independent mobility, with greater control of mobility and trunk allowing rapid change from one position to another and increased mobility of the hip and pelvis.
(ii) Relation to paediatric pathologies: developmental dysplasia of the hip can interfere with motor milestone acquisition, impeding ambulation and other upright activities because of the unstable hip joint, limited hip abduction and poor weight-bearing surface; in cerebral palsy, many children (especially those with spastic quadriplegia) fail to attain independent sitting.
(iii) Secondary impairment/functional deficit: failure to progress through sitting and crawling milestones on schedule can be an early clinical clue prompting assessment for hip pathology or neuromotor disorders, and once identified, physiotherapy goals for such milestones are set within an appropriate developmental context so that intervention (e.g. training in sitting balance, standing with support) directly targets the specific milestone that is delayed, reducing the risk of further secondary impairment such as increased energy expenditure in ambulation or degenerative joint changes.

questions.question:
A(i) Define Legg-Calve-Perthes syndrome and Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis.
A(ii) State their aetiology.
A(iii) Classify each condition.
A(iv) Describe their clinical features.
B. Explain the clinical basis for occurrence of each condition in its typical age group.
C. Distinguish between Legg-Calve-Perthes syndrome and Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Definition: Legg-Calve-Perthes (LCP) syndrome is a bone abnormality resulting in avascular necrosis of the femoral head; Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis (SCFE) is a posterior sliding of the femoral epiphysis in relation to the femoral neck.
A(ii) Aetiology: LCP is believed to be multifactorial, resulting from interruption of blood flow (suspected medial femoral circumflex artery) leading to aseptic avascular necrosis of the femoral head and bone reabsorption; heavy maternal smoking during pregnancy and second-hand smoke exposure are linked to increased risk. SCFE's increased incidence has been attributed to the growing paediatric obesity rate.
A(iii) Classification: LCP hips are categorised by the Salter-Thompson classification into group A (less than 50% of the femoral head involved, relatively good prognosis) and group B (more than 50% involved, relatively poor prognosis); SCFE has no classification system stated beyond noting it can affect one or both hips.
A(iv) Clinical features: LCP predominantly affects boys' hips (4:1 male:female ratio) between 4 and 8 years, with boys typically of shorter stature and active/athletic; children present with an insidious limp with a pelvic drop of the swinging leg and trunk leaning toward the stance side, often with little complaint of pain unless prompted, pain aggravated by activity and relieved by rest, sometimes referred to the anteromedial thigh or knee. SCFE occurs more in adolescent males aged 12-14 years, presenting with mild to moderate hip/anterior thigh pain with activity, a limp, and range of motion limited in flexion, abduction and internal rotation, with the hip falling into external rotation on passive flexion.
B. Clinical basis: LCP occurs between 4 and 8 years, an age when the proximal femur's blood supply (extracapsular arterial ring, ascending cervical vessels, vessel of the ligamentum teres) is particularly vulnerable to interruption; SCFE occurs at 12-14 years, coinciding with the adolescent growth spurt when the capital femoral epiphysis is most susceptible to posterior slippage, compounded by the mechanical stress of obesity.
C. Distinction: LCP occurs in younger children (4-8 years) from avascular necrosis of the femoral head with an insidious, often painless-to-mild limp, managed conservatively (observation, ROM exercises, traction, Petrie casts) in milder cases; SCFE occurs in adolescents (12-14 years) from posterior slippage of the femoral epiphysis with hip/thigh pain and characteristic limitation of flexion, abduction and internal rotation, generally requiring urgent surgical screw fixation.

questions.question:
A(i) State the principles of splinting/orthotic management.
A(ii) State its indications.
A(iii) Describe the procedure.
A(iv) State the positioning considerations.
A(v) State the precautions.
B. State the safe/age-appropriate application.
C. Explain the rationale for the expected outcome/prevention of deformity.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Principles: splints, orthoses and other assistive devices are used to immobilise a bleeding or painful joint, prevent deformity, improve range of motion and function, or support an unstable or weak joint (haemophilia); in arthrogryposis, splinting and total body positioning decrease the degree of joint contracture and improve/maintain postural alignment; braces are used for adaptive equipment selection in osteogenesis imperfecta.
A(ii) Indications: arthrogryposis multiplex congenita (joint stiffness/contracture), haemophilia (target joints prone to recurrent bleeding such as the knee, elbow, ankle, hip and shoulder), and osteogenesis imperfecta (fragile bones prone to fracture).
A(iii) Procedure: in arthrogryposis, gentle stretching, splinting and total body positioning are combined with appropriate range of motion and resistance exercises, with the child benefiting from a standing frame, braces or crutches, and a wheelchair/adaptive devices for mobility.
A(iv) Positioning: total body positioning is used in arthrogryposis to maintain postural alignment; in haemophilia, splints support an unstable or weak joint in a protective position during a bleed.
A(v) Precautions: in osteogenesis imperfecta, rough house play and contact sports should be avoided to prevent recurrent fractures; in haemophilia, recombinant clotting factor should be given as a prophylactic measure or to treat an acute bleed, with splinting used alongside this rather than as a substitute.
B. Safe/age-appropriate application: caregivers should be trained in some exercises as home assignments; for young children developing crawling/walking skills, protective equipment such as knee pads and a helmet along with environmental modifications (baby gates, padded furniture edges) should be used, while accepting that some minor bleeding/injury during infancy and toddlerhood is unavoidable, so as not to over-restrict gross motor, cognitive and emotional development.
C. Rationale: appropriately fitted splints and orthotic devices protect vulnerable joints and bones from further damage while allowing continued, safe exercise, range of motion work and weight-bearing, together preventing the joint contractures, postural deformities and recurrent fractures that would otherwise result from unprotected activity or, conversely, from excessive immobilisation.

questions.question:
(i) Describe equilibrium reactions and protective responses.
(ii) State how they relate to common paediatric pathologies.
(iii) Explain how their incomplete development leads to secondary impairment/functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
(i) Description: equilibrium reactions and protective responses (ERPR) are the second and ultimate set of reflexes to develop after birth, stimulated by changes in body position. They occur as "twin" reactions - for example, in sitting, the arm moving toward the head is a protective response while the raised arm is an equilibrium reaction. They start to emerge by 6 months and are retained throughout life.
(ii) Relation to paediatric pathologies: only children whose reflex development reaches the equilibrium reaction/protective response level become bipedal, that is, independent in standing and walking. In children with cerebral palsy there is incomplete development of righting reflexes, equilibrium reactions and protective responses, recognised as a major problem across spastic, dyskinetic and ataxic types.
(iii) Secondary impairment/functional deficit: incomplete development of equilibrium reactions and protective responses contributes to poor balance, fear of movement, high risk of falls, and failure to attain independent sitting, standing or walking in many children (especially those with spastic quadriplegia). In ataxic cerebral palsy specifically, poorly coordinated righting reflexes, equilibrium reactions and protective responses contribute to dysmetria and poor co-contraction/sustained holding of postures, further limiting safe, independent mobility.

A(i) Definition: spina bifida is a birth defect falling under the category of neural tube defects; the neural tube is the embryonic structure that develops into the baby's brain, spinal cord and their enclosing tissues.
A(ii) Aetiology: normally the neural tube forms early in pregnancy and closes by the fourth week; in spina bifida a portion fails to develop or close properly. The exact cause is unknown but may involve genetic and environmental factors. Risk factors include family history, female gender, having neural tube defects, folic acid deficiency during pregnancy, certain medications (e.g. anti-seizure drugs), maternal obesity, maternal diabetes, radiation exposure, and increased body temperature in early pregnancy (e.g. saunas).
A(iii) Classification: spina bifida occulta (mildest, small gap in one or more vertebrae, no opening/sac, usually normal spinal nerves); meningocele (rare, fluid-filled sac protruding through the vertebral opening, not containing the spinal cord); myelomeningocele (most severe, spinal canal open along several vertebrae, spinal cord/nerves protrude, forming a sac).
A(iv) Clinical features: spina bifida occulta typically has no signs/symptoms, though there may be an abnormal tuft of hair, a small dimple or birthmark on the back; meningocele may result in minor disabilities since nerve damage is less likely; myelomeningocele results in moderate to severe disabilities such as loss of sensation in the legs/feet, with complications including bowel/bladder problems, urinary tract infections, leg paralysis, orthopaedic complications, scoliosis, hydrocephalus, meningitis and learning/speech difficulties.
B. Clinical basis: spina bifida results from a defect during early embryonic development, specifically failure of the neural tube to close by the fourth week of pregnancy, so the defect and its consequences are present from birth, reflecting the fetus's vulnerability to genetic and environmental factors (including folic acid deficiency) during this critical early period.
C. Distinction: in meningocele the sac is fluid-filled but does not contain the spinal cord, so nerve damage is less likely and only minor disabilities may result; in myelomeningocele the membranes and spinal nerves push through the opening, exposing tissue and nerves and making the baby prone to life-threatening infection, resulting in moderate to severe disabilities such as loss of sensation in the legs or feet.
questions.question:
A(i) Define spina bifida.
A(ii) State its aetiology.
A(iii) Classify the types of spina bifida.
A(iv) Describe the clinical features of each type.
B. Explain the clinical basis for why spina bifida particularly affects children from early development.
C. Distinguish between meningocele and myelomeningocele.

A 6-year-old falls onto an outstretched hand and presents with forearm pain and deformity; an X-ray shows the bone bent and partially broken on one side (cortex) with the other side of the cortex still intact.

(i) State the most likely diagnosis.
(ii) State the predisposing factors and pathophysiology.
(iii) Outline the physiotherapy/medical management.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Greenstick fracture, an atypical/incomplete fracture pattern in which the bone doesn't break completely.
(ii) Predisposing factors/pathophysiology: a fracture is a break in the continuity of bone that occurs when the stress placed on the bone is greater than the bone can absorb; causes include blunt trauma, road traffic accidents, pedestrian events, falls, direct blows, forced flexion and hyperextension, twisting forces, industrial heavy equipment, penetrating objects, gunshot, blast, pathological conditions, violent muscle contraction and crush injury. After the injury, a haematoma forms at the fracture site within 48-72 hours because bone has a rich blood supply; within about a week a callus develops and can be seen on X-ray; as healing continues, osteoclasts resorb necrotic bone while osteoblasts build new bone in a process called remodelling; young healthy bone can heal completely within 6 weeks, though remodelling can take up to a year.
(iii) Management: general goals of fracture management are reduction (realigning the fractured bone fragments), stabilisation (holding the reduced fragments in place), facilitating healing through immobilisation and rehabilitation, preventing complications like infection, malunion or non-union, and promoting optimal recovery. For simple/closed fractures, management focuses on closed reduction and immobilisation using a cuff and collar sling for upper limb fractures, strapping for fractures such as a clavicle or rib fracture, and plaster of Paris slabs for temporary support; rest allows the bone to heal without undue stress; pharmacological management includes NSAIDs for pain and inflammation; internal fixation with K-wires, intramedullary nails, or plates and screws may be used for select unstable or complex fractures.

questions.question:
A newborn presents with multiple joints held stiffly, the upper limbs internally rotated and the lower limbs externally rotated, with clubfeet and cylindrical-appearing, ankylosed elbows and knees.

(i) State the risk factors/predisposing factors.
(ii) State the complications/secondary impairments.
(iii) State the physiotherapy management options and justify the one you would prioritise.
questions.answerText:
(i) Risk factors/predisposing factors: arthrogryposis is a hereditary disorder of fibrous tissues; arthrogryposis multiplex congenita usually occurs independently of other anomalies but may be associated with arachnodactyly and/or premature union of the skull bones; it is associated with hypoplasia of the attached muscles and results from incomplete fibrous ankylosis; it appears sporadically, yet familial cases have been seen.
(ii) Complications/secondary impairments: dislocation of the hips and other joints is common; upper limbs are usually internally rotated and lower extremities externally rotated; elbows and knees appear cylindrical and are usually ankylosed in extension, though fixation of the knees in flexion may occur; wrists and fingers are flexed; clubfeet are usually present; there may be groups of muscles that are absent or undeveloped; skin may appear thickened; pathologic changes include thick, inelastic articular capsules and atrophic muscle fibres with fibrosis and fatty infiltration; functional limitations include difficulty with mobility, ambulation and activities of daily living, including developmental delay from decreased mobility.
(iii) Management options and justification: correction of major joint anomalies is by orthopaedic surgery, while physiotherapy focuses on reduction of impairments and functional limitations through gentle stretching, splinting and total body positioning to decrease joint contracture and improve/maintain postural alignment; appropriate range of motion and resistance exercises to improve/maintain muscle strength and joint flexibility, with caregivers trained in some exercises as home assignments; use of a standing frame, braces or crutches; a wheelchair and other adaptive devices for mobility; and teaching of compensatory movement strategies. Gentle stretching and positioning is the justified priority in the newborn period because early, regular stretching directly addresses the joint stiffness and contracture that is the primary impairment and helps prevent fixed deformities from worsening before surgery is considered.

questions.question:
A(i) Define muscular dystrophy.
A(ii) State its aetiology/pathophysiology.
A(iii) Classify the forms of childhood muscular dystrophy.
A(iv) Describe its clinical features.
B. Explain the clinical basis for why Duchenne's muscular dystrophy affects boys and progresses so severely.
C. Distinguish between Duchenne's and Becker's muscular dystrophy.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Definition: muscular dystrophy (MD) is a broad term describing a genetic (inherited) disorder of the muscles that causes the muscles to become very weak; the muscles break down and are replaced with fatty deposits over time.
A(ii) Aetiology/pathophysiology: pathophysiology is progressive loss of muscle contractility from destruction of myofibrils. The genetic defect in Duchenne's is a missing protein called dystrophin, caused by a missing/defective gene at Xp21 (also implicated in Becker's); in other forms, dystrophin-associated proteins are defective. Dystrophin normally reinforces the sarcolemma and protects muscle fibres during contraction; DAPs act as a pathway for trans-membrane signalling, so their absence causes faulty cell membrane mechanics.
A(iii) Classification: Duchenne's (onset 1-4 years, X-linked, rapidly progressive, loss of walking by 9-10 years, death in late teens); Becker's (onset 5-10 years, X-linked, slowly progressive, walking maintained past early teens, lifespan into 3rd decade); Congenital (birth onset, recessive, slow but variable, shortened lifespan); Congenital myotonic (birth onset, dominant, slow, significant intellectual impairment); Childhood-onset facioscapulohumeral (first decade, dominant/recessive, slow loss of walking later in life); Emery-Dreifuss (childhood to early teens, X-linked, slow, cardiac abnormality, normal lifespan).
A(iv) Clinical features: at age 4-5 years, pseudohypertrophy of the calf (fatty/connective tissue infiltration) and initial weakness of neck flexor, abdominal, inter-scapular and hip extensor muscles; as disease progresses, tightness of gastrocnemius-soleus and tensor fasciae latae, increased lordosis, mild scapular winging, Gower's sign, waddling gait and eventual loss of ambulation.
B. Clinical basis: Duchenne's is the most common X-linked disorder (incidence 1 in 3500 live male births); being X-linked, boys with only one X chromosome have no normal copy to compensate for the defective dystrophin gene, whereas carrier girls usually have a normal copy on the other X chromosome. Because dystrophin is completely absent in Duchenne's, muscle damage and disease progression are far more rapid and severe than in Becker's, where dystrophin is present but abnormal/reduced.
C. Distinction: Duchenne's has earlier onset (1-4 years) and is rapidly progressive with loss of walking by 9-10 years and death in late teens; Becker's has later onset (5-10 years) and is slowly progressive, with walking maintained past early teens and survival into the third decade. Dystrophin is essentially absent in Duchenne's but present in reduced/abnormal form in Becker's.

(i) Diagnosis: Sickle cell disease (SCD), specifically an acute pain event/vaso-occlusive crisis.
(ii) Pathophysiological basis: SCD is a group of inherited red blood cell disorders caused by mutations in HBB, the gene encoding a haemoglobin subunit; it leads to production of abnormal haemoglobin (HbS) that causes red blood cells to become rigid and sickle-shaped. Healthy red blood cells are normally round and move through small blood vessels to carry oxygen to all parts of the body, but sickle cells die early, causing a constant shortage of red blood cells, and when they travel through small vessels they get stuck and clog blood flow, causing severe pain and problems such as infection, acute chest syndrome and stroke. It is inherited when a child receives two sickle cell genes, one from each parent; HbSS disease (sickle cell anaemia) is usually the most severe form.
(iii) Assessment findings/problem list: common acute complications are acute pain events, acute chest syndrome and stroke; chronic complications, including chronic kidney disease, can damage all organs. Organ damage can include sickle cell nephropathy, acute chest syndrome, heart murmurs/enlargement, liver damage and gallstones, avascular necrosis and dactylitis (painful swelling) in bones/joints, retinopathy, splenic sequestration, and chronic haemolytic anaemia. Other complications include priapism, increased susceptibility to infection, leg ulcers, pulmonary hypertension and sleep-disordered breathing.
(iv) Physiotherapy goals: the general aim is to reduce the severity of the disease and its complications.
(v) Treatment plan: hydroxycarbamide, blood transfusions and haematopoietic stem cell transplantation can reduce the severity of the disease; a bone marrow or stem cell transplant takes healthy blood-forming cells from a donor (ideally a sibling) and puts them into someone whose bone marrow is not working properly; although potentially curative for severe disease in children with minimal organ damage, this is a high-risk procedure with serious side effects, including death. Early diagnosis (through routine newborn blood test screening) and treatment are important because children with SCD are at increased risk of infection and other health problems.
questions.question:
A 6-year-old known to have a blood disorder presents with acute severe pain in the limbs and back, and the mother reports the child has had similar painful episodes before along with occasional swelling of the hands.

questions.answerText:
(i) Description: at 9-10 months the child frequently pulls up to standing and cruises, permitting lifting of weight from one leg and lateral weight shift, approximating ambulation, and may begin to climb; use of the index finger develops at 9 months and a pincer grip at 10 months. At 11-12 months equilibrium reactions are established in all positions except standing, the child uses half-kneeling to get to standing, and attempts to walk using a toe-walking, high-guard posture (arms raised for stability), falling frequently but recovering skilfully; by 12 months better equilibrium in standing develops, with increased stability and control in walking. At 18 months equilibrium reactions in standing are established, standing erect reduces lumbar lordosis, the child plays in squatting, climbs more, can run, and gait is characterised by a flat-footed posture.
(ii) Relation to paediatric pathologies: developmental dysplasia of the hip can interfere with motor milestone acquisition, impeding ambulation and other upright activities; many children with cerebral palsy, especially spastic quadriplegia, fail to attain independent walking; in Duchenne muscular dystrophy, toe-walking (initially a compensation for weakness of the abdominal and hip extensor muscles) results in lordosis and forward shift of the body's centre of mass, later due to contracture of the posterior calf muscles.
(iii) Secondary impairment/functional deficit: delayed or abnormal attainment of standing and walking milestones can result in leg length inequality requiring increased energy expenditure in ambulation, or in progressive gait deviations such as the waddling gait, increased lateral trunk sway (compensated Trendelenburg), toe-walking, shoulder retraction and loss of arm swinging that develop in Duchenne muscular dystrophy as weakness progresses, ultimately contributing to loss of the ability to walk in adolescence.

A newborn presents with clenched fists with overlapping fingers that are difficult to straighten, club feet, a small head, and severe developmental delay, with feeding problems and a heart defect noted on examination.

(i) Identify the developmental level/abnormality shown.
(ii) State the motor domains/body structures affected.
(iii) State the differential conditions to consider.
(iv) Give the clinical reasoning for physiotherapy intervention.
questions.answerText:
(i) Identification: the features are consistent with Edwards' syndrome (Trisomy 18), an autosomal chromosomal disorder due to an extra copy of chromosome 18; all babies who survive with Trisomy 18 have significant intellectual disability, usually in the severe range.
(ii) Motor domains/body structures affected: physiotherapy in Edwards syndrome addresses delayed developmental milestones, balance issues, decreased strength, reduced levels of physical activity, and reduced mental health and emotional well-being; associated signs include club feet, clenched fists with overlapping fingers, defects of the lungs/kidneys/stomach or intestine, feeding problems, heart defects (atrial or ventricular septal defect), chest deformity and microcephaly.
(iii) Differential conditions: causes include meiotic nondisjunction of chromosome 18, unbalanced Robertsonian translocation, and mosaicism (unrelated to maternal age); types are full/complete Trisomy 18 (about 95%), mosaic Trisomy 18 (about 5%) and partial Trisomy 18 (less than 1%). Differential diagnoses with overlapping features include Patau's syndrome (Trisomy 13), Pena-Shokeir syndrome/fetal akinesia sequence, and CHARGE syndrome.
(iv) Clinical reasoning for intervention: the physiotherapy plan aims to improve functionality, improve balance and coordination, increase muscle strength, increase hand dexterity, improve posture and alignment, reduce risk of secondary complications, and prevent further deformity. Means include "tummy time" to develop strength, balance and motor skills against gravity and promote earlier achievement of motor milestones such as rolling, sitting and crawling; advice about supportive devices (wheelchair, orthotic devices); hydrotherapy to relax stiff muscles/joints and maximise mobility in water; cardiovascular activity such as swimming or cycling; range of movement exercises; strengthening exercises; gentle mobilisation techniques; provision of splints; corrective positioning; and stability exercises.

A(i) Principles: correcting foot drop and gait abnormality (foot dragging or a high-stepping gait) is achieved by fitting the child with an ankle-foot orthosis; gait re-education works on retraining a functional walking pattern.
A(ii) Indications: poliomyelitis (where physiotherapy prescribes orthotics such as ring-top callipers, ankle-foot orthotic devices and back slabs) and sciatic nerve palsy/sciatic nerve injection injury (where foot drop and abnormal gait result from paralysis of the dorsiflexors).
A(iii) Procedure: in poliomyelitis, management includes a sustained immunisation programme, rehabilitation, prescription of orthotics, gait re-education working on hand-to-knee gait, postural education for correction of deformity and post-surgical intervention, and ambulation with axillary or elbow crutches, with surgery (tendon transfer, release of contractures) considered when needed; in sciatic nerve palsy, physiotherapy corrects the deformity and gait abnormality by fitting an ankle-foot orthosis, alongside electrical stimulation to maintain/facilitate weak muscle contraction and progressively resisted exercises once contractions are established.
A(iv) Precautions: in sciatic nerve injury, surgical intervention (neurolysis, or resection and anastomosis) is considered when there is poor recovery after a period of conservative management, indicating orthotic/gait management is the first-line, safer approach before surgery.
B. Safe/age-appropriate application: ambulation training in poliomyelitis progresses through assistive devices such as axillary and elbow crutches, appropriate to the child's stage of recovery and level of residual weakness, while orthotic devices such as callipers and ankle-foot orthoses compensate for persisting weakness and maintain safe, functional walking.
C. Rationale: fitting an ankle-foot orthosis corrects the biomechanical foot drop directly, preventing abnormal compensatory gait patterns (dragging or high-stepping) and reducing the risk of secondary contractures (such as Achilles tendon tightening described in sciatic nerve injection injury) that would otherwise develop from prolonged abnormal positioning and reduced weight-bearing.

A 1-year-6-month-old male child is brought to the physiotherapy clinic by his mother because he is unable to use his left hand and cannot stand or walk unaided. He was delivered through spontaneous vaginal delivery and the birth was uneventful. At about 4 months of age the mother noticed the left hand was kept straight without bending the elbow, with the palm facing backwards. A doctor applied a POP cast at 6 months for two months without improvement before he was referred for physiotherapy.

(i) State the most likely diagnosis.
(ii) Explain the developmental/pathophysiological basis of this condition.
(iii) State the assessment findings and problem list you would expect.
(iv) State the physiotherapy goals for this child.
(v) Outline the physiotherapy treatment plan.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Erb's palsy, a form of obstetric brachial plexus palsy; a lesion of the upper brachial plexus (C5 and C6 nerve roots).
(ii) Pathophysiological basis: injury to the brachial plexus at birth causing stretching, rupture or avulsion of the nerve roots from the spinal cord. Affected nerves are the axillary, musculocutaneous and suprascapular nerves; the axillary nerve supplies the shoulder joint, teres minor and deltoid; the musculocutaneous nerve supplies the anterior arm muscles and skin of the lateral forearm; the suprascapular nerve supplies supraspinatus, infraspinatus and the shoulder joint. This produces the classical "waiter's tip" posture from loss of the lateral rotators of the shoulder, arm flexors and hand extensor muscles.
(iii) Assessment findings/problem list: left PROM full and painfree; grip strength poor on the left; left wrist extensors, elbow flexors and shoulder abductors graded 1/5 (right side 5/5); left elbow extensors, shoulder adductors and forearm pronators 4/5; left forearm supinators 1/5; lower limb PROM full and painfree bilaterally with good gross motor power; good neck control and trunk strength; child can sit and crawl unaided and stand with support. Problem list: does not use the left hand properly; cannot stand unsupported; cannot walk.
(iv) Physiotherapy goals: encourage normal development of milestones; strengthen weak muscles; teach standing and walking; teach functional activities.
(v) Treatment plan: stretching (passive ROM) exercises to prevent deformity; tactile stimulation; proper positioning; electrical stimulation; facilitation of normal movement patterns while inhibiting substitutions; home programme; on follow-up, passive movement to the left upper limb joints, play therapy (e.g. with a soccer ball), weight-bearing exercises to the left upper limb, and re-emphasis of the home programme.

(i) Diagnosis: Congenital talipes equinovarus (clubfoot).
(ii) Predisposing factors/pathophysiology: most cases are congenital; 75% occur without other congenital abnormalities; there are varying degrees of rigidity of the foot, calf atrophy, and mild hypoplasia of the tibia, fibula and bones of the foot; occurs in a 2:1 male to female ratio and is bilateral in 50% of cases.
(iii) Physiotherapy management: conservative treatment is always attempted before surgical correction - passive movements and gentle passive stretching; serial casting, with improvement expected within 4-6 weeks; tape strapping, particularly useful for preterm babies. If conservative correction is insufficient for functional use of the leg, surgical reconstruction corrects all components of the deformity. At a later stage, fit the child with an appropriate orthosis to sustain correction and facilitate weight-bearing and walking, with strengthening of muscles, gait training, and functional training - walking within parallel bars, with a walking frame, crutches or cane, climbing/descending stairs, standing on one leg, and ball kicking for weight-bearing training.
questions.question:
A newborn is noted at birth to have the foot fixed in a position of inversion, adduction of the forefoot and plantarflexion at the ankle, with calf atrophy of the affected leg and no other congenital abnormality.

(i) State the most likely diagnosis.
(ii) State the predisposing factors and pathophysiology.
(iii) Outline the physiotherapy management.

questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Acute Disseminated Encephalomyelitis (ADEM), a rare, immune-mediated inflammatory demyelinating disorder of the CNS typically involving the brain and spinal cord, most commonly seen in children and young adults and often following a viral infection.
(ii) Assessment framework: diagnosis follows the International Pediatric MS Study Group criteria (especially in children).
(iii) Key diagnostic findings: the criteria require a first polyfocal CNS event with presumed inflammatory demyelination, presence of encephalopathy (altered consciousness or behavioural change) unexplained by fever, brain MRI showing diffuse, large, poorly demarcated lesions predominantly in the white matter (which can include grey matter), and no new clinical or MRI findings after 3 months of onset. Investigations include MRI showing multiple, bilateral, asymmetric white matter lesions, CSF analysis showing mild lymphocytic pleocytosis and elevated protein, blood tests to rule out infection/autoimmune markers, and EEG which may show diffuse slowing in encephalopathy; seizures may occur in up to 20-35% of cases, more commonly in children.
(iv) Precautions: the general focus in the acute phase is on preventing complications.
(v) Phased physiotherapy programme: in the acute phase (hospital/ICU), focus is on preventing complications through passive ROM exercises to maintain joint mobility, positioning to prevent pressure sores and contractures, chest physiotherapy if respiratory function is compromised, and sensory stimulation for unconscious or severely impaired patients; in the chronic phase (outpatient or home-based), focus shifts to maximising independence through task-specific training (dressing, climbing stairs), advanced gait training (treadmill, obstacle courses), coordination exercises (ball catching, fine motor tasks), occupational therapy collaboration for activities of daily living, and neurocognitive rehabilitation if cognitive deficits are present.
questions.question:
A 7-year-old develops confusion, behavioural change and weakness of one side of the body two weeks after recovering from chickenpox, with a recent seizure noted by the parents.

(i) State the most likely diagnosis.
(ii) Name the diagnostic criteria/assessment framework used.
(iii) Describe the key diagnostic findings expected.
(iv) State the precautions to be observed.
(v) Outline the phased physiotherapy programme.

questions.answerText:
(i) Risk factors: injections given outside the upper outer quadrant of the buttock (dorso-gluteal region) rather than the ventro-gluteal site or anterior thigh; inappropriate needle length (appropriate length is ≤2.5cm) and angle (appropriate angle is 90° to the body); wrong patient position during injection, e.g. side lying, standing or forward leaning (correct position for children is prone); use of neurotoxic agents such as antimalarials (quinine, chloroquine), certain antibiotics, analgesics, antiemetics, vitamin K, local anaesthetics, vaccines, steroids, phenobarbital and paraldehyde; incidence is higher in economically poorer countries such as Nigeria, India and Pakistan due to injections given by inadequately trained staff; the peroneal division of the sciatic nerve is more frequently injured than the tibial division because of its more lateral position and reduced protective connective tissue.
(ii) Complications/secondary impairments: early stage - neuropathic pain in the buttock and back of the leg, spasm of the posterior leg muscles (knee kept bent), refusal to bear weight, foot drop; later stage - contracture of the Achilles tendon and reduced ankle ROM, atrophy of paralysed muscles, atrophy of the quadriceps from compromised anti-gravity function and reduced weight bearing; neurological sequelae can range from minor transient sensory disturbance to severe sensory disturbance and paralysis with poor recovery.
(iii) Management options and justification: fit an ankle-foot orthosis to correct the foot drop and gait abnormality (foot dragging or high-stepping gait); maintain physiological properties of weak muscles by electrical stimulation with interrupted direct current; facilitate contractions of weak muscles through electrical and tactile stimulation; strengthen weak muscles once contractions are established using resisted exercises (gravity, manual resistance, thera-band, sandbag); train relevant age-appropriate functions such as gait training, ball kicking and skipping. Ankle-foot orthosis fitting is the priority justified choice at this stage because the child already has established foot drop and gait deviation, and correcting this biomechanical deformity protects the limb and supports safe weight-bearing while nerve recovery is awaited.
questions.question:
A 2-year-old child received an intramuscular injection of an anti-malarial drug in the buttock at a rural clinic. Shortly afterward the child developed pain in the buttock and back of the leg, kept the knee bent, refused to bear weight on the leg, and now shows a foot drop.

(i) State the risk factors relevant to this presentation.
(ii) State the complications/secondary impairments that may develop.
(iii) State the physiotherapy management options and justify the one you would prioritise.

questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Blount disease (tibia vara).
(ii) Predisposing factors/pathophysiology: Blount disease is a varus or bowing deformity of the tibia due to mechanical stress; excess weight from obesity repeatedly overloads immature bones, causing abnormal growth slowing at the medial aspect of the proximal tibia (bowlegs). It can have an infantile or juvenile onset; obese children who walk before 1 year of age are most likely to have the infantile type. Children normally have some degree of bowlegs until age 2 years, so persistence beyond age 3 suggests Blount disease; juvenile/late-onset Blount disease occurs primarily in obese teenage boys.
(iii) Management: a knee-ankle-foot orthosis worn during ambulation can be prescribed to attempt correction of the angulation in children under age 3 years; late-onset disease requires surgical correction through a tibial osteotomy or progressive realignment by an external fixation device; counselling on lifestyle choices (addressing obesity) should be part of best practice care.
questions.question:
An obese 2-year-old boy who began walking before 1 year of age is noted to have persistent bowing of both lower legs beyond the degree normally expected for his age.

(i) State the most likely diagnosis.
