A female infant, first-born, was delivered in breech presentation. At the six-week check the mother reports asymmetry of the gluteal/thigh skin folds and that one hip abducts less than the other.

(i) State the risk factors relevant to this presentation.
(ii) State the complications/secondary impairments that may develop if untreated.
(iii) State the physiotherapy management options and justify the one you would prioritise.
questions.answerText:
(i) Risk factors: female sex (girls have more ligament laxity than boys); breech presentation; first-born child (uterus not previously stretched); family history of congenital hip dislocation; positive family history occurs in 20% of infants with DDH; higher incidence in Native Americans and Arabs, lower in Chinese and Africans; generalised ligamentous laxity from maternal oestrogen and pelvic relaxation hormones of pregnancy; oligohydramnios; neuromuscular conditions such as myelomeningocele; association with congenital muscular torticollis (14-20%) and metatarsus adductus (1-10%).
(ii) Complications/secondary impairments: delayed gross motor development; unequal leg length; hip pain; loose or unstable hip joint; waddling gait pattern; poor hip socket development; apparent leg length discrepancy; painful degenerative changes over time; compression of the circumflex artery by the muscles around the joint, reducing blood flow to the femoral head.
(iii) Management options and justification: a Pavlik harness is used in children less than 6 months to hold the hip in the correct position, and over 90% of children treated with it recover fully; a Frejka pillow splint abducts and flexes the femur; strengthening exercises for the hip stabilisers (gluteus maximus and medius) support the joint and help prevent future dislocation; stretching and flexibility exercises are also used. The Pavlik harness is the justified first choice in this young infant because it is the least invasive option, has the highest success rate for this age group, and allows continued normal growth and development of the acetabulum while achieving reduction.

A(i) Definition: Acute Disseminated Encephalomyelitis (ADEM) is a rare, immune-mediated inflammatory demyelinating disorder of the CNS, typically involving the brain and spinal cord; Neuromyelitis Optica (NMO)/NMOSD, also known as Devic's disease, is a rare autoimmune disorder of the CNS characterised by inflammatory attacks and demyelination in the spinal cord and optic nerve.
A(ii) Aetiology: ADEM often follows an antecedent infection (commonly viral, e.g. measles, varicella, influenza, Epstein-Barr virus) or, rarely, vaccination, typically appearing 1-3 weeks after the infection, from an immune response mistakenly targeting CNS myelin through molecular mimicry. NMO's hallmark is autoantibodies against aquaporin-4 (AQP4), a water channel protein on astrocytes, with the immune system mistakenly producing AQP4-IgG antibodies that bind to astrocytes and trigger complement activation, though some patients are AQP4-negative but anti-MOG antibody-positive.
A(iii) Classification: ADEM is typically described as monophasic; NMO is classified as AQP4-antibody positive (most common), MOG-antibody positive (less common), or double-antibody negative.
A(iv) Clinical features: ADEM presents with encephalopathy (behavioural change, confusion or decreased consciousness), seizures (up to 20-35% of cases, more common in children), often asymmetric weakness, fever, headache, vomiting, optic neuritis, ataxia and hemiparesis. NMO presents with sudden loss of vision (often with eye pain, from optic neuritis), sudden onset of limb weakness or paralysis usually beginning in both legs with tingling/numbness (from transverse myelitis), and severe, persistent nausea, vomiting or hiccups (from area postrema involvement), with brainstem symptoms and excessive daytime sleepiness less common at onset.
B. Clinical basis: ADEM is most commonly seen in children and young adults, often following a viral illness or vaccination, most common in children typically aged 5-8 years, reflecting children's higher exposure to and immune response against common viral triggers (measles, varicella, EBV, influenza); NMO is more common in females (up to 9 times more than men) and post-infectious autoimmune responses are suspected triggers in some cases.
C. Distinction: ADEM is typically a monophasic illness following infection/vaccination, with diffuse, poorly demarcated white matter lesions on MRI and no new findings after 3 months, whereas NMO is an episodic disease with attacks lasting days to months, diagnosed through core clinical characteristics plus a positive AQP4-IgG antibody test and MRI lesions that are longitudinally extensive (spanning ≥3 vertebral segments).

questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Bacterial meningitis - inflammation of the meninges and the subarachnoid space.
(ii) Pathophysiological basis: organisms gain access to the subarachnoid space through bacteraemia (usually from an upper airway source), contiguous spread from dental/sinus infections, traumatic/congenital communications, or a neurosurgical procedure; causative organisms vary with age, with S. agalactiae, E. coli and L. monocytogenes in the first week of life replaced by S. pneumoniae and N. meningitidis by the sixth week. Severe inflammation causes oedema of the brain/meninges, increasing intracranial pressure, and can be severe once compensatory mechanisms for CSF displacement are overwhelmed; mortality ranges from 13-27%.
(iii) Assessment findings/problem list: infants can present with non-specific lethargy and irritability, temperature instability, apnoea/bradycardia spells and feeding difficulty; beyond 48 hours of age, infants more often present with seizures, a bulging anterior fontanelle, extensor posturing, focal cerebral signs or cranial nerve palsies. The classic triad of fever, neck stiffness and altered mental status is present in only a minority; Kernig's sign (pain on knee extension with the neck flexed, at an angle less than 135°) and Brudzinski's sign (hip/knee flexion on passive neck flexion in supine) may be positive but their absence does not rule out meningitis.
(iv) Physiotherapy goals: minimise secondary impairments; address muscle weakness, poor balance and coordination, stiff neck and reduced range of motion; promote functional mobility.
(v) Treatment plan: early intervention as soon as safely possible; strengthening exercises (sit-to-stand, walking); balance exercises (standing with eyes closed or on a wobble board); stretching exercises for neck stiffness; range of motion exercises to prevent contractures; neurodevelopmental techniques to retrain motor skills/coordination; positioning to prevent pressure sores and contractures; sensory stimulation; equipment such as walkers, braces or orthotics; home exercise programmes; multidisciplinary work with occupational and speech therapists; close monitoring of vital signs, with progressive advancement of the programme as the patient improves.

A 13-year-old obese boy presents with a limp and mild anterior thigh pain that worsens with activity. On examination the hip falls into external rotation when passively flexed, and range of motion is limited in flexion, abduction and internal rotation.

(i) State the most likely diagnosis.
(ii) Name the assessment technique used.
(iii) Describe the key findings expected.
(iv) State the precautions to be observed.
(v) Outline the parent/caregiver education and home programme.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis (SCFE), a posterior sliding of the femoral epiphysis in relation to the femoral neck.
(ii) Assessment technique: clinical examination of hip range of motion in flexion, abduction and internal rotation, and observation for obligate external rotation of the hip on passive flexion.
(iii) Key findings: SCFE occurs in both sexes but is more common in adolescent males, with children aged 12-14 years most at risk; increased incidence has been attributed to the growing paediatric obesity rate. Clinical features are mild to moderate hip or anterior thigh pain with activity, a limp, and range of motion frequently limited in flexion, abduction and internal rotation; when the hip is passively flexed it tends to fall into an externally rotated position; SCFE can affect one or both hips, and if suspected the child should see an orthopaedic surgeon immediately because progression can lead to permanent deformation and disability.
(iv) Precautions: following surgical screw fixation the child will likely have weight-bearing restrictions; because of the high incidence of bilateral disease, prophylactic pinning of the uninvolved hip may be performed in girls younger than 10 and boys younger than 12.
(v) Parent/caregiver education and home programme: after surgery, physiotherapy includes crutch walking instruction and instructions in hip range of motion and strengthening exercises; because the hip is very sore, gravity-eliminated exercises in bed are often the first step, including quad sets, ankle pumps (dorsiflexion/plantarflexion), hip abduction/adduction by sliding the leg across the bed, and knee flexion by sliding the heel up the bed.

questions.question:
An 18-month-old boy presents with stiff muscles, exaggerated reflexes and increased tone predominantly affecting both lower limbs more than the upper limbs. He has not yet attained independent standing, shows persistence of some early reflexes, and demonstrates poor trunk stability alongside limb stiffness.

(i) Identify the developmental level/abnormality shown.
(ii) State the motor domains/body structures affected.
(iii) State the differential conditions to consider.
(iv) Give the clinical reasoning for physiotherapy intervention.
questions.answerText:
(i) Identification: this picture is consistent with spastic cerebral palsy (a diplegic distribution pattern) - a disorder of movement and posture due to a non-progressive lesion of the immature brain. Increased tone, stiff muscles and jerky/awkward movement affecting the lower limbs more than the upper limbs match the spastic type, the most common form, affecting about 80% of individuals with cerebral palsy.
(ii) Motor domains/body structures affected: spasticity in limb musculature; low tone in trunk musculature causing poor trunk stability and control; poor head control; persistence of primary reflexes; incomplete development of righting reflexes, equilibrium reactions and protective (postural) responses; limbs often maintained in midrange; stereotypical, slow, laborious movements; high risk of musculoskeletal adaptations and deformities; may fail to attain independent sitting or walking.
(iii) Differential conditions: dyskinetic (athetoid) cerebral palsy with involuntary movements and fluctuating tone from basal ganglia/thalamus damage; ataxic cerebral palsy with balance/coordination problems from cerebellar damage; hypotonic presentations with poverty of movement, poor head/trunk control and joint hypermobility; classification can also be topographical (hemiplegia, diplegia, quadriplegia) or by GMFCS E&R level.
(iv) Clinical reasoning for intervention: management follows schools of thought such as Bobath's Neuro-Developmental Treatment, which encourages normal movement patterns, focuses on quality of movement, normalises tone to facilitate active movement, addresses positioning/posture in lying, sitting and standing, discourages compensatory movements, and promotes maximum functional recovery; Rood's approach uses sensory stimulation (fast brushing, light touch, joint compression) to normalise tone; PNF and a multidisciplinary team (paediatrician, occupational therapist, speech therapist, clinical psychologist, physiotherapist) support functional independence.

questions.question:
A(i) State the principles of hydrotherapy/aquatic therapy.
A(ii) State its indications.
A(iii) Describe the procedure.
A(iv) State the precautions.
B. State the safe/age-appropriate application.
C. Explain the rationale for the expected outcome/prevention of deformity.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Principles: hydrotherapy uses water to relax stiff muscles and joints, maximise mobility, strengthen muscles and increase circulation; aquatic exercises are described as a great resource for range of motion and muscle strengthening.
A(ii) Indications: Edward syndrome (to relax stiff muscles/joints and maximise mobility) and Legg-Calve-Perthes syndrome (aquatic exercises for range of motion and strengthening, and as part of pain relief).
A(iii) Procedure: in Edward syndrome, hydrotherapy treatment is combined with cardiovascular activity such as swimming or cycling; in LCP, aquatic exercises are used alongside ultrasound, pulsed electromagnetic energy, heat or electro-analgesic current (e.g. TENS) for pain relief, and crutch walking instruction to reduce weight bearing in severe pain while keeping the child active.
A(iv) Precautions: in LCP, activities likely to increase pain such as distance running and football should be avoided, with patient/caregiver education about activity choices provided.
B. Safe/age-appropriate application: hydrotherapy is applied as part of a broader physiotherapy plan that also includes range of movement exercises, strengthening exercises, gentle mobilisation techniques, splints, corrective positioning and stability exercises, making it one component of an individualised, progressively applied programme.
C. Rationale: the buoyancy and support of water allow muscles and joints to move and be strengthened with reduced weight-bearing stress, which in LCP helps maintain hip abduction and external rotation range without aggravating pain, optimising containment of the femoral head within the acetabulum and encouraging remodelling back into a spherical shape, thereby helping prevent further flattening and deformity.

(i) Diagnosis: Neuromyelitis Optica Spectrum Disorder (NMOSD/Devic's disease), a rare autoimmune disorder of the CNS characterised by inflammatory attacks and demyelination in the spinal cord and optic nerve; the sudden vision loss is from optic neuritis, the limb weakness from transverse myelitis, and the persistent hiccups/nausea from involvement of the area postrema in the brainstem.
(ii) Assessment tool/technique: diagnosis is based on a combination of clinical symptoms, MRI findings, and antibody testing, especially detection of Aquaporin-4 antibodies (AQP4-IgG).
(iii) Key diagnostic findings: to diagnose NMOSD with AQP4-IgG positivity, all of the following must be met - at least one core clinical characteristic (optic neuritis, acute myelitis, area postrema syndrome, acute brainstem syndrome, symptomatic narcolepsy/diencephalic syndrome, or symptomatic cerebral syndrome with NMO-typical MRI lesions), a positive serum AQP4-IgG antibody test, and MRI findings consistent with NMO with exclusion of alternative diagnoses; lesions on spinal MRI are usually longitudinally extensive, spanning ≥3 vertebral segments.
(iv) Precautions: avoid aggressive exercise during active infections or untreated spasticity; steroid myopathy requires dose-adjusted strengthening; coordinate with neurology for immunotherapy timing (e.g. avoid exercise 24 hours post-rituximab); resume physiotherapy after plasmapheresis only after 6 hours if the patient is haemodynamically stable.
(v) Phased management/caregiver education: acute phase (days 0-14) focuses on preventing complications through bed mobility/positioning every 2 hours to prevent pressure injuries, tilt-table use for orthostatic intolerance, and monitoring vital capacity in cervical myelitis; recovery phase (2 weeks-3 months) includes progressive resistance training for paretic limbs, static/dynamic balance training, gait training with orthotics (e.g. KAFO for foot drop), daily stretching for spasticity management, and modified constraint-induced movement therapy for the affected upper limb; maintenance/preventive phase (>3 months) includes a tailored home exercise programme for strength/balance, fatigue management through energy conservation and pacing, fall prevention through home hazard modification, and patient/family education about infection prevention (vaccination, avoiding contact with sick individuals) since infections can trigger relapses.
questions.question:
A 15-year-old presents with sudden loss of vision in one eye with pain on eye movement, followed within days by weakness of both legs with tingling and numbness, and persistent hiccups and nausea that are initially misdiagnosed as a digestive problem.

(i) State the most likely diagnosis.
(ii) Name the assessment tool/technique used.
(iii) Describe the key diagnostic findings required.
(iv) State the precautions to be observed.
(v) Outline the phased management and caregiver education programme.

A(i) State the principles of traction and hip spica casting.
A(ii) State their indications.
A(iii) Describe the procedure.
A(iv) State the positioning achieved.
A(v) State the precautions.
B. State the safe/age-appropriate application.
C. Explain the rationale for the expected outcome/prevention of deformity.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Principles: traction is the application of force to stretch the tissues around the femoral head to move it back toward the acetabulum, used before surgical reduction to avoid avascular necrosis; a hip spica cast holds the hip in flexion and abduction following reduction.
A(ii) Indications: developmental dysplasia of the hip diagnosed at 6-18 months of age, where surgical closed hip reduction may be needed followed by a hip spica cast; also used in DDH generally as traction for approximately 10-14 days; used in Legg-Calve-Perthes syndrome as bilateral long leg casts with a fixed abduction bar (Petrie casts).
A(iii) Procedure: for DDH at 6-18 months, surgical reduction is preceded by 2-3 weeks of traction to avoid avascular necrosis; the hip spica cast places the hip in flexion and abduction and may allow weight-bearing/ambulation; if closed reduction fails, open reduction and containment may be needed.
A(iv) Positioning: the hip is held in flexion and abduction, similar to the reduction position achieved with the Pavlik harness.
A(v) Precautions: diagnosis at 6-18 months carries a poorer prognosis than diagnosis at less than 1 month of age; traction before surgery specifically avoids the complication of avascular necrosis.
B. Safe/age-appropriate application: traction and hip spica casting are applied at the 6-18 month age range where the Pavlik harness is less effective and surgical management becomes more likely, reflecting the age-dependent shift in treatment strategy as the hip's capacity to remodel decreases with age.
C. Rationale: pre-reduction traction gently stretches the tissues around the femoral head so it can be repositioned into the acetabulum without abrupt force that could compromise its blood supply and cause avascular necrosis, while the subsequent cast maintains the reduced, congruent position needed for continued normal acetabular development.

(i) Diagnosis: Haemophilic joint bleed (haemarthrosis) in a child with haemophilia, a chronic X-linked bleeding disorder in which the body fails to produce one or more clotting proteins, resulting in excessive internal and external bleeding; the knee is one of the most frequent "target joints" along with the elbow, ankle, hip and shoulder.
(ii) Assessment tool/technique: assessment of the joint for swelling, warmth, pain and range of motion; specific physiotherapy guidelines exist for joint bleeds, iliopsoas bleeds, cryotherapy and muscle bleeds.
(iii) Key findings with recurrent bleeds: flexion deformity with quadriceps atrophy, posterior subluxation, valgus and external rotation of the tibia, hypertrophy of the medial femoral condyle, squaring of the patella, and widening of the intra-condylar notch; recurrent bleeding into joints generally causes thickening of the synovial tissue, breakdown of joint cartilage with narrowing of the joint space, and contractures of the surrounding muscles.
(iv) Precautions: recombinant clotting factor is used as a prophylactic measure or to treat an acute bleeding episode before physiotherapy proceeds; splints, orthoses and other assistive devices are often needed to immobilise a bleeding or painful joint, prevent deformity, improve range of motion and function, or support an unstable/weak joint.
(v) Parent/caregiver education and home programme: educate parents on promoting physical health and development while balancing injury risk minimisation with the child's opportunity to develop new skills - for example fitting a crawling/walking child with knee pads and a helmet, installing baby gates, and padding sharp edges of furniture; parents should understand that some bleeding during infancy and toddler years is unavoidable, and that over-protecting a child may limit gross motor, cognitive and emotional development.
questions.question:
A 4-year-old boy with a known bleeding disorder presents with a swollen, warm and painful knee following a minor fall, with reduced knee range of motion.

(i) State the most likely diagnosis.
(ii) Name the assessment tool/technique used.
(iii) Describe the key findings expected with recurrent joint bleeds.
(iv) State the precautions to be observed.
(v) Outline the parent/caregiver education and home programme.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Definition: congenital talipes equinovarus is a foot deformity present at birth involving inversion, adduction and plantarflexion of the foot; metatarsus adductus is a deformity in which the forefoot is adducted relative to the hindfoot.
A(ii) Aetiology: most cases of talipes equinovarus are congenital, and 75% occur without other congenital abnormalities; the exact cause of metatarsus adductus is not known, but it is thought to be a "packaging" disorder or a result of positioning inside the uterus.
A(iii) Classification: talipes equinovarus varies in degree of rigidity of the foot, calf atrophy and mild hypoplasia of the tibia, fibula and foot bones; metatarsus adductus has 3 classifications of forefoot flexibility (from Type I flexible up to Type III rigid), with treatment recommended according to severity.
A(iv) Clinical features: talipes equinovarus occurs in a 2:1 male:female ratio and is bilateral in 50% of cases; metatarsus adductus is usually noted soon after birth but can present at any age, and in Type I deformity the foot is flexible and can be actively positioned into abduction, elicited by stimulating the peroneal musculature by stroking the lateral border of the foot.
B. Clinical basis for occurrence in infancy: both conditions are thought to relate to intrauterine positioning/packaging during fetal development, which is why they present at or soon after birth and why conservative treatments (passive stretching, serial casting) started early, while the infant's tissues and bones are still highly malleable, are effective in achieving correction.
C. Distinction: talipes equinovarus involves inversion, forefoot adduction and ankle plantarflexion, with possible calf atrophy and bone hypoplasia, managed with passive stretching and serial casting (improvement within 4-6 weeks); metatarsus adductus involves adduction confined to the forefoot relative to the hindfoot, classified by flexibility, with a flexible Type I deformity needing no treatment while a rigid Type III deformity requires serial casting changed at 1-2 week intervals, started before 8 months of age.
questions.question:
A(i) Define talipes equinovarus and metatarsus adductus.
A(ii) State their aetiology.
A(iii) Classify each condition.
A(iv) Describe their clinical features.
B. Explain the clinical basis for their occurrence in infancy.
C. Distinguish between talipes equinovarus and metatarsus adductus.

A(i) State the principles of the Pavlik harness.
A(ii) State its indications.
A(iii) Describe the procedure of its use.
A(iv) State the positioning it achieves.
A(v) State the precautions to observe.
B. State the safe/age-appropriate application of the harness.
C. Explain the rationale for the expected outcome/prevention of deformity.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Principles: the Pavlik harness places the hips in about 100° of flexion and about 30° of abduction; this induces femoral head growth toward the acetabulum and maintains reduction of the femoral head while allowing tightening of the ligaments and stimulation of normal acetabular development.
A(ii) Indications: developmental dysplasia of the hip (dysplastic, subluxated or dislocated hips) in infants aged 1-6 months.
A(iii) Procedure: the harness holds the hips continuously in flexion and abduction; spontaneous relocation of the femoral head is usually accomplished in 3 to 4 weeks; positioning is continued for 3-9 months once hip stability is achieved.
A(iv) Positioning: approximately 100° of hip flexion and 30° of abduction.
A(v) Precautions: the harness should not place the hip in more than 100° of flexion, because at 120° of hip flexion the vascular supply to the femoral head may be compromised and lead to avascular necrosis.
B. Safe/age-appropriate application: indicated specifically for infants aged 1-6 months, in whom it is approximately 95% successful in dysplastic/subluxated hips and about 80% effective in true dislocations, because the infant hip and acetabulum still have substantial capacity to remodel; treatment continues until there is clinical stability of the hip and normal radiographic findings.
C. Rationale: keeping the femoral head flexed and abducted directs it toward the acetabulum, stimulating normal acetabular development while allowing the surrounding ligaments to tighten and restore stability. Respecting the 100-degree flexion limit prevents compromise of the blood supply through the circumflex vessels, thereby preventing avascular necrosis of the femoral head that could result from over-flexion.

questions.question:
A child with a known congenital heart condition suddenly develops weakness down one side of the body, with the mother reporting the child cannot use the right hand and the right side of the mouth appears to droop.

(i) State the risk factors relevant to this presentation.
(ii) State the complications/secondary impairments.
(iii) State the physiotherapy management options and justify the one you would prioritise.
questions.answerText:
(i) Risk factors: hypertension, raised cholesterol, atherosclerosis, diabetes mellitus, cardiac disease, smoking, excessive alcohol consumption, physical inactivity and obesity.
(ii) Complications/secondary impairments: stroke results in hemiplegia (contralateral), with the most common deficit being motor; other neurological deficits are visual, perceptual, sensory, communication and swallowing (dysphagia). Medical complications include venous thromboembolism, pneumonia, dysphagia, ventilatory dysfunction, cardiac disease, seizure, central post-stroke pain syndrome, spasticity, bladder dysfunction, bowel dysfunction, pressure ulcers, malnutrition and dehydration, depression, falls and injuries, shoulder pain and dysfunction, and recurrent stroke.
(iii) Management options and justification: goals of stroke rehabilitation are to prevent, recognise and manage comorbid medical conditions, maximise functional independence, optimise psychosocial adaptation of patients and families, facilitate resumption of prior life roles and community reintegration, and enhance quality of life. Acute phase rehabilitation involves range of motion/stretching exercises, frequent position changes, sitting in an upright position to improve orthostatic tolerance, psychological counselling, patient/family education, training in personal care skills, mobility and ambulation training, bladder/bowel management, evaluation of swallowing function, and identification/treatment of depression; interventions across levels of care include functional skills training, mobility activities, therapeutic exercises for flexibility/strength/coordination/fitness, spasticity management, and aphasia treatment. Early range of motion/stretching combined with mobility and ambulation training is the justified priority in the acute phase because it directly targets the contralateral hemiplegia and motor deficit while guarding against complications such as contracture, pressure ulcers and loss of orthostatic tolerance.

questions.question:
A 19-year-old primiparous woman presents 10 days after a prolonged, obstructed home delivery of a macrosomic infant. She complains of continuous passage of faeces and flatus per vaginam and has no perineum on inspection. She is febrile and the area is infected.
(i) What is the diagnosis? Classify the perineal injury and state what structures are involved.
(ii) Describe the causes/aetiology of this injury.
(iii) Given that the repair is discovered more than 12 hours after delivery and there is local infection, outline the full management plan including the timing of repair.
(iv) Describe the operative technique for primary repair of a complete perineal tear when performed within the optimal window.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Complete (third-degree) perineal tear, likely with rectovaginal involvement (4th degree involvement as the rectal wall is breached, causing passage of faeces per vaginam).
Classification: First degree — involves perineal skin, minor part of perineal body, related posterior wall of vagina. Second degree — involves perineal body up to but not including the anal sphincter; corresponding tear in vagina. Third degree (complete tear) — includes the anal sphincter; extends 2 cm or more up the anal canal; associated with incontinence of flatus and loose stool. Fourth-degree perineal tear — involvement of the rectal mucosa. These patients have no perineum.
Structures involved: vaginal mucosa, perineal skin, perineal body and muscles, anal sphincter, and rectal wall/mucosa.
(ii) Aetiology: during delivery (commonest cause); big babies (greater than 4 kg); forceps delivery; persistent occipito-posterior position; badly supervised delivery; rape; falling astride a sharp object.
(iii) Management when repair is delayed (more than 12 hours) or infected:
Primary repair more than 12 hours after delivery is seldom successful — defer for 6–8 weeks. Primary repairs that break down, like lacerations seen too late for primary suture, should be deferred for 6–8 weeks after all local sepsis has subsided and the tissues have returned to normal.
Pre-operative preparation for delayed repair: 3 days pre-op — empty bowel, low residue/fluid diet, nightly aperient, reduce bacterial activity by giving sulphonamide. Few hours pre-op — saline rectal enema (may be difficult with large high RVF). Bowel prep — preliminary colostomy is not necessary for repair of complete perineal tears. More dissection is required to identify and mobilise layers; scar tissue may need to be excised from the edges of the rectal defect.
Post-operative: confine bowel for at least 6–7 days; continue low residue diet; avoid digital examination ± liquid paraffin; antibiotics; twice-daily sitz baths; effective analgesia.
(iv) Operative technique for primary repair within the optimal window: Anaesthesia — GA, spinal, or caudal. Position — lithotomy. Repair layer by layer: identify apex, start above it; close entire length of defect in rectal wall in layers that evert the raw edges towards the lumen of the rectum. Identify torn, retracted edges of external anal sphincter with tissue forceps; carefully unite in front of the reconstructed anal canal. Repair posterior vaginal wall as far as the fourchette. Reconstruct perineal body by drawing the levator ani between the rectal and vaginal repair line. Close perineal skin with interrupted non-absorbable sutures because of the likelihood of local infection.

questions.question:
A 15-year-old girl is brought to a gynaecological clinic by her parents requesting female genital mutilation (FGM) as a cultural rite of passage.

(i) How is FGM classified within international reproductive health frameworks?
(ii) State the immediate and long-term reproductive health complications associated with FGM.
(iii) Does parental consent legitimise the procedure? Explain the ethical basis of your answer.
(iv) Identify two other harmful traditional practices classified alongside FGM in the reproductive health framework.
(v) State the reproductive rights principle that underpins the rejection of this request.
questions.answerText:
(i) FGM is explicitly classified within reproductive health frameworks as a harmful traditional practice that must be eliminated.

(ii) Immediate complications: haemorrhage, infection. Long-term complications: dyspareunia, obstetric complications, and genital fistula.

(iii) No. Parental consent does not legitimise procedures that cause harm to a minor and violate her bodily integrity and reproductive rights. The individual-centred framing of reproductive rights is a deliberate departure from policies that prioritised others' goals over personal autonomy.

(iv) Premature marriage and domestic and sexual violence against women are classified alongside FGM as harmful traditional practices to be eliminated.

(v) Reproductive rights affirm the right of individuals to make decisions about reproduction free from coercion, discrimination, and violence. The reproductive health framework upholds voluntary participation in all reproductive health services as a fundamental human right.

(i) Laparoscopic sterilisation offers better intraperitoneal visualisation through a camera, performed through very small (5-10 mm) incisions, resulting in faster recovery and less postoperative pain compared to mini-laparotomy. The failure rates are comparable between approaches for the same tubal occlusion technique.

(ii) Extensive previous abdominal surgery (three caesarean sections) is a relative contraindication because of likely pelvic and abdominal adhesions that may obscure anatomy, increase the risk of bowel or bladder injury on trocar insertion, and prevent adequate visualisation. Obesity and cardiopulmonary conditions precluding Trendelenburg positioning and pneumoperitoneum are also relative contraindications.

(iii) Interval mini-laparotomy sterilisation is performed through a small (2-5 cm) suprapubic vertical incision. Postpartum mini-laparotomy uses an infraumbilical incision because after delivery the uterus is still enlarged and the tubes are accessible near the umbilicus. At interval surgery, the uterus has returned to its normal size and the tubes are best reached through a suprapubic incision.

(iv) The Pomeroy technique offers the highest probability of successful reversal because it removes only 3-4 cm from the mid-isthmic region, often leaving adequate tube on both sides for microsurgical reanastomosis. A minimum of 4 cm of combined remaining tube is generally required. Bilateral salpingectomy and hysteroscopic occlusion have virtually no prospect of reversal.

(v) After vasectomy, alternative contraception must be continued until azoospermia is confirmed on two consecutive semen analyses, typically at 8-12 weeks and 16 weeks post-procedure (or after 20+ ejaculations), because residual sperm in the vas deferens remain viable and can cause pregnancy.
questions.question:
A 38-year-old woman (G4P4) with three previous caesarean sections requests interval surgical sterilisation. She is counselled about laparoscopic versus mini-laparotomy approaches.

(i) State the primary advantage laparoscopic sterilisation offers over mini-laparotomy.
(ii) State the relative contraindications to laparoscopy in this patient's context and explain why they affect the approach.
(iii) Describe the incision used for interval mini-laparotomy sterilisation and explain why the site differs from postpartum mini-laparotomy.
(iv) Name the technique with the best probability of successful reversal, state the minimum total tubal length required, and name two techniques with virtually no reversal potential.
(v) If her partner undergoes vasectomy instead, state when alternative contraception may be discontinued and what must be confirmed first.

A 28-year-old woman presents to a sexual health clinic with a 5-day history of frothy offensive vaginal discharge and lower abdominal discomfort. On speculum examination, mucopurulent cervical discharge is noted and the cervix appears inflamed with multiple shallow ulcers around the introitus. She is sexually active with two partners. High vaginal swab shows motile flagellated organisms on wet preparation. A second swab grows Chlamydia trachomatis on tissue culture.

(i) What is the spot diagnosis for each infection, and how does the pathogen of Chlamydia differ biologically from the gonococcus?
(ii) What are the full clinical manifestations of Chlamydial infection in women, men, and neonates?
(iii) What are the complications of Chlamydial infection in women and men?
(iv) What is the treatment regimen for Chlamydial infection?
(v) What is the relationship of Chlamydia trachomatis to lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV), and how does LGV differ clinically and in treatment from uncomplicated Chlamydial urethritis?
questions.answerText:
(i) First infection: trichomoniasis—Trichomonas vaginalis (protozoan); microscopy of vaginal secretions reveals the flagellae. Second infection: non-specific urethritis/Chlamydial infection—Chlamydia trachomatis (chlamydiae); weakly gram-negative intracellular parasite, unlike Neisseria gonorrhoeae which is a gram-negative intracellular diplococci that is oxidase positive. Chlamydia is diagnosed by tissue culture, serology (ELISA, polymerase chain reaction, direct fluorescent antibody test) rather than simple microscopy or standard culture media.
(ii) Clinical manifestations of Chlamydial infection in women: mucopurulent cervicitis; salpingitis; urethral syndrome. In men: non-gonococcal urethritis. In both: inflammation of throat and rectum. Neonatal infection: conjunctivitis; otitis media; pneumonia. Majority of infected women are asymptomatic. Higher prevalence among female adolescents. Chlamydia is a common cause of PID.
(iii) Complications in women: chronic/recurrent PID; pelvic abscess; ectopic pregnancy; infertility; chronic pelvic pain. Complications in men: chronic genital tract infection; infertility. Complications in children: pneumonia; conjunctivitis. Tubal blockage accounts for 60–80% of female infertility; gonorrhoea and Chlamydia are the greatest culprits.
(iv) Treatment of Chlamydial infection: tetracycline 500mg four times daily for 7–14 days; doxycycline 200mg start then 100mg twice daily for 21 days; erythromycin 500mg twice daily for 14 days; others include floxacin and erythromycin.
(v) LGV is caused by L1, L2, L3 serotypes of Chlamydia trachomatis (specifically serovars L1–L3). Clinical features of LGV: shallow painless ulcer of the vestibule and labia; painful adenopathy in inguinal and peri-rectal areas which if untreated eventually suppurates; nodes become matted together and adhere to overlying skin; sinuses and fistulae ensue; elephantiasis; stenosis of the anal canal and rectum. LGV differs from uncomplicated Chlamydial infection in that it produces bubo formation and fistulae. Investigations for LGV: culture of aspirates; monoclonal antibody test; complement fixation antibody (Frei test). Treatment of LGV: tetracycline; erythromycin group; sulphonamides; doxycycline; surgery—vulvectomy; manual dilatation of strictures. Uncomplicated Chlamydial infection is treated with tetracycline 500mg four times daily for 7–14 days, doxycycline, or erythromycin for shorter courses.

questions.question:
A) Describe the management of benign ovarian tumours under the following headings:
A(i) Indications for laparotomy, the combination of features at laparotomy that indicate higher risk of malignancy (listing all seven), and when a frozen section should be requested
A(ii) How the choice of surgical procedure is determined by age, parity and reproductive wishes, including what should be done about the contralateral ovary

B) Explain the clinical basis of:
B(i) Why ovarian cancer screening is not currently recommended for the general population of low or moderate risk, citing the specific problems with current screening methods stated in the lectures
B(ii) What the screening strategy involves for high-risk women, what percentage of high-risk women may opt for prophylactic oophorectomy, and when this is usually done

C) State the management of ovarian cysts in pregnancy — the indications for emergency surgery, the risks of elective surgery to the fetus, and how to manage the case where a cyst is discovered after 14 weeks of gestation.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Indication for laparotomy: any ovarian swelling greater than 5 cm in diameter, particularly if it is continuing to enlarge.
Seven features at laparotomy indicating higher risk of malignancy:
1. The tumour is totally or partly solid
2. Bilateral tumours
3. Fungation through the capsule (not merely papillary growths)
4. Large vessels on the tumour surface
5. Blood-stained ascites
6. Invasion of or adhesion to surrounding structures
7. Metastatic deposits
A frozen section should be requested if there is real doubt about the nature of the tumour at the time of surgery.

A(ii) Choice of surgical procedure by age/parity/reproductive wishes:
- Young women wishing to conserve reproductive capacity: enucleation of the cyst (cystectomy) is carried out; large cysts may demand removal of the ovary.
- Women past child-bearing age: it is customary to remove both ovaries and the uterus.
- If the cyst is unilateral: consider biopsy of the other ovary to exclude an occult tumour.
In young women with Stage Ia disease and no ascites: unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy may be justifiable after careful exploration to exclude metastatic disease and curettage of the uterine cavity to exclude a synchronous endometrial tumour.

B(i) Problems with current screening methods:
- Despite a relatively high sensitivity and specificity, the low prevalence of the disease means that the positive predictive value is only 10% — 10 women would require laparoscopy or laparotomy for every one cancer detected.
- Interval cancers occur as frequently as those detected; therefore screening would need to be carried out at least yearly.
- There is no evidence that screening reduces mortality, probably because it cannot detect the cancer early enough.
- Ultrasound is not suitable as a primary screening tool because it is too expensive and has a high false-positive rate.
On current evidence there is no justification for screening women at low or moderate risk.

B(ii) Screening for high-risk women: best available strategy combines vaginal examination, vaginal ultrasound (carried out by experienced personnel) and serum CA-125 levels. Some opt for prophylactic oophorectomy with HRT around the age of 40 years (high-risk women with strong family history or carrying BRCA1/BRCA2 gene). The protective effects of oral contraceptive use should also be borne in mind when counselling young women at high risk.

C) Management of ovarian cysts in pregnancy:
Indications for emergency surgery: acute pain (torsion, haemorrhage); possibility of appendicitis; rapidly enlarging cyst.
Risks of elective surgery to the fetus: no urgent operation should be postponed solely because of the pregnancy; cover the operation with tocolytics and perform in a centre with intensive neonatal care when possible.
Management after 14 weeks: if asymptomatic, prudent to wait until after 14 weeks gestation to avoid removal of a corpus luteal cyst; management may be conservative or surgical; risk to mother and fetus of elective procedure must be balanced against chance of cyst accident, unexpected malignancy or spontaneous resolution. Ovarian cancer is uncommon in pregnancy (less than 3% of cysts). A cyst with features suggestive of malignancy on ultrasound, or one that is growing, should be removed surgically. CA-125 is not useful in pregnancy since elevated levels occur frequently as an apparently physiological change.

A(i) Mons and labia:
Mons pubis: hair-bearing skin overlying a cushion of adipose tissue.
Labia majora: hair-bearing skin; contain the termination of the round ligaments of the uterus; sebaceous glands and sweat glands are present.
Labia minora: hairless skin folds; lack a bed of adipose tissue; form the prepuce and frenulum of the clitoris.
Clitoris: erectile structure; has crura.
Vestibule: the space enclosed by the labia minora.
A(ii) Glands of the vulva: labial sebaceous glands; sweat glands (in labia majora); Bartholin's glands (vestibular glands).
A(iii) Contents of the superficial perineal pouch (space between subcutaneous tissues and the perineal membrane):
- Clitoris (crura)
- Vestibular bulb/Bartholin's glands
- Ischiocavernosus muscle (from ischial tuberosity)
- Bulbospongiosus muscle (from perineal body)
- Superficial transverse perineal muscle
B. Clinical importance of Bartholin's glands: located within the superficial perineal pouch. Infection (Bartholin's abscess) commonly arises from gonococci, chlamydia, or other organisms, producing an acutely painful swelling at the posterior introitus. Chronic infection leads to Bartholin's cyst. Their location at the base of the labia minora and relation to the vaginal introitus means that they may be mistaken for other perineal swellings.
C. Distinction between superficial and deep compartments:
Superficial perineal pouch: space between subcutaneous tissues and the perineal membrane; contains the clitoris (crura), vestibular bulb, Bartholin's glands, ischiocavernosus, bulbospongiosus, and superficial transverse perineal muscles.
Deep compartment: lies above (deep to) the perineal membrane. The perineal membrane itself is described as a triangular sheet of dense fibromuscular tissue (previously called the urogenital diaphragm) arising from the ischiopubic rami; it is a complete sheet in males. It supports the pelvic floor, counteracts raised intra-abdominal pressure and gravity, and limits downward descent of pelvic structures through its attachments to the urethra, vagina, and perineal body. The deep perineal pouch's exact contents (deep transverse perineal muscle, external urethral sphincter) are less consistently distinguished separately, beyond the perineal membrane description.

questions.answerText:
A(i) STIs and their complications are amongst the top 5 disease categories for which people seek healthcare. STIs (as well as HIV/AIDS) have major demographic, economic, social, and political impacts particularly in sub-Saharan Africa. They have been reported to be the second most common cause of healthy life lost in women after maternal morbidity and mortality. STIs enhance sexual transmission of HIV; untreated STDs increase the risk of HIV acquisition/transmission by a factor of 10; improved STI management can reduce HIV infection by 40%. Untreated STI may result in various sequelae such as pelvic inflammatory disease, infertility, ectopic pregnancies, urethral stricture, congenital infections, cancers, and premature death. Bacterial STIs are more common in developing countries.
A(ii) Risk groups: urban residents; adolescents and young adults (highest incidence rates of STIs occur among adolescent women aged 15–19 years and males aged 20–24 years; in developing countries such as Nigeria, highest rates among those aged 20–24 and 25–29 years); young females; undergraduates and street hawkers; commercial sex workers; migrant workers; highly mobile people such as long-distance truck drivers; refugees. Risk factors specific to adolescents: inadequate or incorrect information about how to prevent STIs; less likely to seek proper information or treatment due to fear, ignorance, shyness, or inexperience; early initiation of sexual activity among males; unprotected sex (without condoms); sex with multiple partners; having a partner with other sex partners; having a partner with STI symptoms; sex with a new partner or more than one partner in the last three months; sex with strangers or sex in exchange for money; vulnerability to sexual violence, coercion, and abuse; use of vaginal drying agents; a history of STIs or PID; the myth that sex with a virgin is a cure for STIs.
B(i) Women are biologically more susceptible to STIs because: the vagina acts as a receptacle where sperm is retained and the female urethra is short; the surface of the vagina is larger and more vulnerable than the skin-covered penis; the amount of ejaculate deposited in the vagina during intercourse is greater than the amount of cervical and vaginal secretions to which a man is exposed; young women often have cervical ectopy in which the cells that line the inside of the cervix extend to the outer surface of the cervix—these cells are more vulnerable to infections such as Chlamydia; early sexual experience can result in trauma to vaginal tissue; young women are less likely than men to experience symptoms so some STIs go undiagnosed until a major health problem develops.
B(ii) Long-term health consequences of untreated STIs in women: pelvic inflammatory disease; infertility (tubal blockage accounts for 60–80% of female infertility; gonorrhoea and Chlamydia are the greatest culprits); ectopic pregnancy (incompletely blocked tubes predispose to ectopic pregnancy; most tubes removed at salpingectomy have evidence of previous PID); spontaneous abortion; once they have an STI, young women are at greater risk of reproductive cancers; other health problems include chronic liver disease, cirrhosis, chronic pelvic pain, cervical carcinoma, and neurological problems.
C(i) Major sequelae in women: cancers (cervical, vulval, vaginal, anal, liver, T-cell leukaemia, Kaposi's sarcoma); pelvic inflammatory disease, infertility, ectopic pregnancy, spontaneous abortion; preterm delivery, premature rupture of membranes, puerperal sepsis, postpartum infection; neurosyphilis; chronic liver disease, cirrhosis. Major sequelae in men: penile cancer, anal cancer, liver cancer, T-cell leukaemia, Kaposi's sarcoma; epididymitis, prostatitis, infertility; neurosyphilis; chronic liver disease, cirrhosis. Major sequelae in infants: stillbirth, low birth weight, pneumonia, neonatal sepsis, congenital abnormalities; neurological problems (cytomegalovirus, neurosyphilis); blindness from neonatal eye infections; chronic liver disease, cirrhosis.
C(ii) The ABCDE of HIV prevention: A—Abstinence from sexual intercourse; B—Be faithful to one uninfected sexual partner (mutual fidelity); C—Correct and consistent use of condoms; D—Desist from sharing needles and syringes, contaminated blood; E—Encourage voluntary counselling and testing. Follow-up of STIs/HIV/AIDS: contact tracing; screen and give appropriate treatment.

Describe the gross anatomy of the ovary, state how its zones relate to common pathologies, and explain why ovarian failure may cause distant functional deficit at the pituitary level.

A(i) Describe the ovary under the headings: embryological origin, normal position in the pelvis, and relation to the fallopian tube.
A(ii) State the gonadal finding in Turner's syndrome (45,X) and in Swyer's syndrome (46,XY), and relate each finding to its specific pathological consequence and management.
B(i) Explain why ovarian failure in Turner's syndrome produces markedly elevated FSH and LH, naming the hormones involved in normal negative feedback.
B(ii) State the proportion of true hermaphroditism cases associated with 46,XX karyotype, and distinguish ovotestes (true hermaphroditism) from pseudohermaphroditism.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Embryological origin: the ovaries develop from the gonadal ridge (genital ridge) of the intermediate mesoderm — they are NOT derived from the Mullerian ducts. Normal position: in the ovarian fossa on the lateral pelvic wall, adjacent to the fimbriated end of the fallopian tube. Relation to fallopian tube: the fimbriae of the infundibulum sweep over the ovarian surface to capture the oocyte at ovulation.

A(ii) Turner's syndrome (45,X): bilateral streak gonads — fibrous connective tissue containing no oocytes. Consequence: primary ovarian failure, no oestrogen production, failure of secondary sexual development, primary amenorrhoea, and infertility. Management: oestrogen replacement for puberty induction; fertility only through oocyte donation and embryo transfer.
Swyer's syndrome (46,XY pure gonadal dysgenesis): bilateral streak gonads with high risk of gonadoblastoma and dysgerminoma. Consequence: uterus is present (no AMH from dysgenetic gonads so Mullerian structures persist); primary amenorrhoea. Management: prophylactic gonadectomy after diagnosis; pregnancy achievable through oocyte donation and embryo transfer.

B(i) The streak gonads of Turner's syndrome produce no oestrogen and no inhibin. Oestrogen and inhibin normally exert negative feedback on the pituitary, suppressing FSH and LH release. In the absence of this feedback, FSH and LH are markedly elevated — a hypergonadotrophic state. This markedly elevated gonadotrophin level is the biochemical signature of primary ovarian failure.

B(ii) True hermaphroditism is associated with 46,XX in 71% of cases, 46,XX/46,XY chimerism in 20%, and 46,XY in 7%. True hermaphroditism requires both ovarian and testicular tissue (ovotestes, or a separate ovary and testis). Pseudohermaphroditism has only one type of gonadal tissue present — either ovaries (female pseudohermaphrodite) or testes (male pseudohermaphrodite) — but the external phenotype does not match the gonads.

A(i) Transdermal patch (Ortho Evra): contains norelgestromin/ethinyl oestradiol (progestin/oestrogen); applied on skin of trunk, abdomen, upper arm, or buttocks—avoid breast; maintains a steady level of hormone in the bloodstream; changed once a week; worn continuously; worn for 3 weeks per month; effectiveness 99%; similar effectiveness and mode of action as oral contraceptives. Patch contains 6 mg norelgestromin and 0.75 mg ethinyl oestradiol; delivers continuous systemic doses of 150 mcg norelgestromin (NGMN) and 20 mcg ethinyl oestradiol (EE) per day.
A(ii) Levonorgestrel-releasing vaginal ring: contains 5 mg LNG; releases 20 mcg/day; worn continuously for 90 days; associated with irregular bleeding when used as combined preparation; not as effective as combined oral pills.
A(iii) Etonogestrel–ethinyl oestradiol vaginal ring (NuvaRing): contains progestin/oestrogen; self-inserted; remains in place for 3 weeks then removed for the fourth week; menstruation begins a few days into week 4; new ring inserted one week after removing old one (same time of day); NuvaRing releases 15 mcg of ethinyl oestradiol and 120 mcg of etonogestrel daily; worn for 3 out of 4 weeks; self-insertion and removal; pregnancy rate 0.65 per 100 woman-years.
B(i) Mirena (levonorgestrel intrauterine system): releases 20 mcg of levonorgestrel per 24 hours; duration 5 years; packaged with sterile inserter; high efficacy with Pearl Index of 0.1. Mechanism of action of hormonal IUDs: contraceptive mechanisms are mediated locally and not associated with systemic effects; the progestin is released continuously, causing development of progestational or decidual endometrium which is incompatible with implantation of the blastocyst; affects the quality of cervical mucus, interfering with sperm transport; reduces menstrual loss; amenorrhoea present in many women due to endometrial atrophy.
B(ii) Male contraception: development of male hormonal contraception is very challenging; several candidates have been tried; none has proven suitable.
C(i) Biodegradable implants: Annuelle—contains norethindrone enanthate (35 mg), effective for 1 year; Capronor II—contains 18 mg levonorgestrel (single caprolactone capsule), effective for 1 year; Capronor III—contains 32 mg levonorgestrel, effective for 1 year; capsule biodegrades to CO2 and water after one year. Non-biodegradable implants do not biodegrade and must be surgically removed; they include Norplant (6 rods, 5 years), Jadelle (2 rods, 5 years), Uniplant (1 rod, 1 year), and Implanon (1 rod, 3 years).
C(ii) Implants as a group: provide contraceptive protection for a set duration (1–5 years); require only a minor surgical procedure for insertion under the skin of a woman's upper arm; protection commences within hours of insertion; normal fertility rapidly returns following removal; no daily compliance required (unlike oral pills or patches); most side effects are not serious and the commonest is a change in menstrual bleeding pattern. Most suitable patient profile: women seeking continuous contraception; long-term birth spacing; method unrelated to intercourse; alternative to sterilisation; those requiring an oestrogen-free method; women with contraindications to combined hormonal methods.

questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix. Stage IIb: the tumour involves the cervix, extends to the vagina (except the lower third), with obvious parametrial involvement.
(ii) Lymphatic spread: to the parametrium, internal iliac, obturator, external iliac, sacral, common iliac, inguinal, and para-aortic lymph nodes.
Direct spread: to the vagina, parametrium, pelvic side walls, bladder, and rectum.
Blood-borne metastasis: to the liver, lungs, bones, and brain.
(iii) Definitive treatment for Stage IIb: Radiotherapy (advanced disease Stage IIb–IV is treated with radiotherapy; Stage IV receives palliative treatment). Stage Ib may be treated with radical surgery or radiotherapy; Stage IIa with radiotherapy or radical surgery.
(iv) Aetiological factors: (i) Sexual behaviour — age at first coitus, age at first pregnancy, multiple sexual partners; (ii) Race and socio-economic status, including social status of spouse; (iii) Smoking (more than 20 sticks/day); (iv) Vitamin deficiency — Vitamin A and folic acid; (v) Oral contraceptive pills; (vi) Infectious agents — Human Papilloma Virus (types 6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 35, 39, 45, 51, 52, 56, 58), which produces oncoproteins that initiate malignant transformation; male factor — higher risk in wives of long-distance drivers and wives of men with prostatic/penile cancers.
(v) 5-year survival rates: Overall 55%; Stage I — 78.1%; Stage II — 57.0%; Stage III — 31.0%; Stage IV — 7.8%. Prognosis depends on age, histological type, vascular invasion, tumour volume, and pelvic lymph node involvement (type, number, unilateral or bilateral).

A 17-year-old girl is brought to clinic with primary amenorrhoea and cyclical lower abdominal pain that has been worsening over several months. On examination, a bulging bluish membrane is visible at the introitus.

(i) State the most likely diagnosis.
(ii) Name the predisposing embryological factor that leads to this condition.
(iii) Explain the pathophysiological mechanism that produces the abdominal pain and the introital bulge.
(iv) Describe the definitive management.
(v) State two other Mullerian anomalies that may also present with primary amenorrhoea and contrast them with this diagnosis.
questions.answerText:
(i) Imperforate hymen with haematocolpos.

(ii) Failure of perforation/canalisation of the hymen, which is derived from the urogenital sinus, during embryological development.

(iii) The imperforate hymen creates outflow obstruction; menstrual blood accumulates in the vagina (haematocolpos) and possibly the uterus (haematometra). The increasing volume generates cyclical pressure-related pain coinciding with expected menstruation. The accumulated blood distends the vagina, producing the characteristic bluish bulging membrane visible at the introitus due to vascularity beneath the stretched hymen.

(iv) Cruciate incision of the hymen, which is curative, allowing drainage of accumulated menstrual blood.

(v) MRKH syndrome (Mullerian aplasia): 46,XX female with agenesis or hypoplasia of the vagina and uterus and normal ovarian function; presents with primary amenorrhoea but NO cyclical pain because there is no functional endometrium. Complete androgen insensitivity syndrome (CAIS): 46,XY with intra-abdominal testes; AMH causes Mullerian regression so no uterus; presents with primary amenorrhoea and no cyclical pain because no functional endometrium is present.

A(i) Cell of origin: totipotential germ cells; results from differentiation into embryonic tissues. Accounts for around 40% of all ovarian neoplasms; most common benign germ cell tumour. Most common in young women (median age 30 years). Bilateral in 11%.

A(ii) Gross: usually unilocular cyst less than 15 cm in diameter; ectodermal elements predominate. Microscopic: lined with epithelium like the epidermis; contains skin appendages — hair, sebaceous material, sebaceous and sweat glands, teeth. Also contains: nervous tissue, cartilage. Endodermal derivatives — thyroid, bronchial, and intestine. Mesodermal derivatives — bone, cartilage, smooth muscle.

B(i) Torsion is more common in pregnancy due to external pressure from the expanding gravid uterus or trauma during delivery. 2% of dermoid cysts contain a malignant component, usually squamous carcinoma, occurring in women over 40 years.

B(ii) The contents of dermoid cysts (sebaceous material) are extremely irritant and therefore may cause severe symptoms on rupture. Acute rupture causes sudden onset with acute abdomen and chemical peritonitis. Slow/chronic rupture causes chronic granulomatous peritonitis. Intra-operative spillage must be avoided; if it occurs, thorough peritoneal lavage is required.

C) Dermoid cyst: contains elements of all three germ layers as described above; only 5–6% of struma ovarii produce sufficient thyroid hormone to cause hyperthyroidism. Monodermal teratoma (struma ovarii): reserved for tumours composed predominantly of thyroid tissue (only 1.4% of cystic teratomas); only 5–6% of struma ovarii produce sufficient thyroid hormone to cause hyperthyroidism; 5–10% of struma ovarii develop into carcinoma.

A 34-year-old multiparous woman presents at a district hospital following a prolonged, obstructed labour. She delivered a stillbirth after more than 24 hours of labour with inadequate progress. Eight days later she notices continuous, uncontrollable passage of urine per vaginam. She has an ammoniacal odour and footdrop. On examination she appears short-statured and malnourished with obvious urinary wetness.
(i) What is the most likely diagnosis?
(ii) Explain the pathological basis by which obstructed labour produces this condition, including the tissues involved and the timeline of tissue breakdown.
(iii) Outline the essential investigations required before definitive repair.
(iv) Describe the definitive surgical management, including post-operative care and instructions for future pregnancies.
questions.answerText:
(i) Vesicovaginal fistula (VVF) — an abnormal communication between two epithelial surfaces (bladder and vagina), resulting from neglected obstructed labour.
(ii) Pathological basis: Obstructed labour = failure of descent of the presenting part through the pelvis for mechanical reasons in the presence of strong uterine contractions. The main thrust of pressure is directed to the back of the symphysis pubis, causing ischaemic sloughing of the compressed tissues, compounded by infection. Tissue breakdown (pressure necrosis) produces symptoms approximately 10–14 days later (or as early as 3 days). The cervix or distal ureters may also be involved, and the result is typically total incontinence or dribbling. Other sequelae include gynatresia, secondary amenorrhoea, haematometra, and obstructive uropathy.
(iii) Investigations: FBC + PCV, urea and electrolytes, USS, IVU, midstream urine for M/C/S, grouping and crossmatching of blood. Pre-operative EUA and dye test to determine location, site, number of fistulae, and best position for repair; digital examination and Sim's speculum ± three-swab test.
(iv) Definitive surgical management: Dissect, isolate and freshen the edges of the fistula(e). Repair the bladder in two layers, then repair the vaginal wall. Insert an indwelling catheter (Foley or whistle-tip) for continuous bladder drainage.
Post-operative care: Free drainage ×14 days; hourly intake/output chart (if hourly output <50 cc, inform the doctor); 2-hourly turning of patient side to side; monitor vital signs; analgesics; parenteral antibiotics; twice-weekly CSU for M/C/S. Remove catheter on 14th day and institute bladder drill. No sexual intercourse for 3 months post-repair. All future deliveries by elective LSCS. First attempt carries >80% success rate.

(i) Most likely diagnosis: Mayer-Rokitansky-Kuster-Hauser syndrome (congenital absence of the vagina). Features: blindly ending shallow vagina; absence of upper vagina; partial or complete absence of uterus; patient may have skeletal or urological abnormalities but is otherwise normal; relatively uncommon; presents after puberty with amenorrhoea and difficulty with coitus. Goal of treatment: to achieve adequate coitus.

(ii) Embryological and anatomical factors: background knowledge of basic embryology is essential; the female genital tract is formed by the fusion of the paramesonephric (Mullerian) ducts and sino-vaginal bulbs; congenital gynaetresia results from failure of canalization of the paramesonephric duct and sino-vaginal bulbs; in Mayer-Rokitansky-Kuster-Hauser syndrome, there is failure of canalization of variable portions of the Mullerian ducts resulting in a shallow vagina, absence of upper vagina, and partial or complete absence of uterus; the hymen arises from the urogenital sinus (separate origin from the vagina); Mullerian duct failure explains the absent uterus and upper vagina while the lower vagina and external genitalia (derived from urogenital sinus) are present.

(iii) Investigations: general principles of evaluation — rectal examination to palpate cervix and fundus; serum testosterone (post-pubertal); pelvic ultrasound (post-pubertal) to assess uterus and ovaries; chromosomal studies (pre-pubertal children) and karyotyping; laparoscopy when USS is inconclusive; IVU (association with urological anomalies); hormonal profile (as patients mostly present with primary amenorrhoea); renal function tests. Differentials to exclude: androgen insensitivity syndrome (46XY karyotype — XY will be excluded by karyotype; testosterone levels elevated; shallow vagina, no uterus, but ovaries absent); low-lying transverse vaginal septum (vaginal exam and imaging); imperforate hymen (purplish/bluish bulging membrane on inspection of vulva; rectal examination shows large tense cystic swelling in pelvis).

(iv) Management options: non-surgical — Frank's procedure (use of graduated glass dilators on introitus; gentle pressure 10–20 minutes twice daily; takes 8–10 weeks to achieve satisfactory result; success rate 90% with good patient selection; for congenital stenosis only). Surgical — McIndoe-Reed's vaginoplasty: creation of cavity between bladder and bowel lined with a split-thickness skin graft from thigh, placed on a plastic mould; may contract unless intercourse is regular or dilator is worn; normal sexual function in 80–90% of patients; reconstruction can also be done with sigmoid colon; postoperative vaginal dilation essential. William's vulvovaginoplasty: edges of posterior parts of labia majora are sutured together in the midline to form a perineal pouch — vulvovaginoplasty; external pouch created by suturing labia majora to form horizontal 'vagina'; advantages: good clitoral stimulation; disadvantages: shortness, awkward angle for penetration, abnormal-looking genitalia, pressure on rectum during sex. Timing: in congenital type — when patient is emotionally mature; in acquired — when intercourse is feasible. Crucial issues: correct diagnosis; evaluate for associated congenital anomalies; careful psychological preparation; non-surgical management preferred first.

(v) Complications of vaginoplasty: infection; lack of skin graft take; fistulae (vesicovaginal); stress incontinence; vaginal stricture; McIndoe vaginoplasty may contract except if intercourse is regular or dilator is worn. Contraindications to vaginoplasty: post-menopausal women (symptoms less); vesico-vaginal fistula; dense scar tissue; in pregnant women (excessive bleeding); in the puerperium (extent of damage unknown); after severe obstetric trauma (little vaginal tissue remaining); after successful closure of extensive vesicovaginal fistulae.
questions.question:
A 25-year-old woman with primary amenorrhoea and no history of menstruation presents. She has normal secondary sexual characteristics but no uterus or upper vagina on examination. There is a blind vaginal pouch of 3 cm on gentle digital examination. Her karyotype is 46XX.
(i) What is the most likely diagnosis and what syndrome does it represent?
(ii) What are the predisposing anatomical and embryological factors that lead to this condition?
(iii) What investigations should be performed, and what differentials must be excluded?
(iv) What are the surgical and non-surgical management options?
(v) What are the complications of vaginoplasty?

A 38-year-old multiparous woman with a history of vaginal delivery of large babies presents with a 2-year history of involuntary urine loss each time she laughs, coughs, or lifts heavy objects. She denies urgency or urge incontinence. Pad weighing test shows 15 g loss in one hour. Cystometry shows no detrusor contractions during filling.
(i) What is the most likely diagnosis, and what does the cystometry finding confirm?
(ii) Explain the pathophysiological basis of this condition including the structures damaged.
(iii) Outline the conservative management options with a brief explanation of each.
(iv) List the surgical operations available for this condition and name the operation of choice, giving its goals.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Genuine stress incontinence (GSI). Cystometry confirms: no detrusor contractions during the filling phase — confirming that the involuntary urine loss is not due to detrusor instability. Definition: involuntary loss of urine when intravesical pressure exceeds the maximum urethral closure pressure in the absence of detrusor activity. Commonest cause of urinary incontinence. Pad test: more than 1 g in 1 hour is diagnostic.
(ii) Pathophysiological basis: GSI results from damage to the pelvic floor and/or pubourethral ligaments, causing descent of the proximal urethra (normally an intra-abdominal organ) out of its intra-abdominal position. When intra-abdominal pressure rises (coughing, laughing), it is transmitted to the bladder but not equally to the descended proximal urethra, so intravesical pressure exceeds urethral closure pressure and urine leaks. Causes include: pelvic floor weakness (prolapse, childbirth, pelvic surgery, menopause), urethral scarring (surgery, recurrent UTI, radiotherapy), and raised intra-abdominal pressure (pregnancy, chronic cough, abdominal/pelvic mass, obesity).
(iii) Conservative management: Indications — mild incontinence, patient unfit for surgery, declines surgery, or pending surgery.
- Pelvic floor exercises: strengthen the levator ani and extrinsic sphincter mechanism.
- Vaginal cones: same shape and size with increasing weight (20–90 g); retained in vagina to exercise pelvic floor.
- Electrical stimulation: stimulates pelvic floor musculature.
- Oestrogens: address postmenopausal atrophy contributing to urethral weakness.
- Vaginal/urethral devices: mechanical support.
(iv) Surgical operations: anterior colporrhaphy (vaginal); injectables; Marshall-Marchetti-Krantz procedure (abdominal); Burch colposuspension (abdominal); laparoscopic colposuspension; sling (organic/inorganic materials — combined vaginal/abdominal); endoscopic bladder neck suspension (Stamey, Raz); artificial sphincter; urinary diversion.
Operation of choice: Burch colposuspension.
Goals: elevation of the bladder neck and proximal urethra into an intra-abdominal position; support of the bladder neck; and increase in outflow resistance.

(i) Most likely diagnosis: Ruptured corpus luteum (luteal cyst) with intraperitoneal haemorrhage. The key differential diagnosis that must be excluded is ectopic pregnancy — haemorrhage from even a normal corpus luteum can mimic ectopic pregnancy closely, and the positive home pregnancy test must be evaluated urgently.

(ii) Predisposing factors: Luteal cysts are more likely to rupture especially on days 20–26 (corresponding to this patient's presentation on day 22); they are more likely to present with intraperitoneal bleeding especially on the right side. Anatomical basis for right-sided predominance: increased intraluminal pressure secondary to ovarian vein anatomy — the right ovarian vein drains directly into the inferior vena cava, while the left drains into the left renal vein; this asymmetry in venous pressure accounts for the right-sided predominance.
Distinction from ruptured dermoid cyst: dermoid cyst rupture causes intense chemical peritonitis due to the extremely irritant sebaceous contents, causing more severe symptoms; it can rupture suddenly (acute abdomen with chemical peritonitis) or slowly (chronic granulomatous peritonitis); luteal cyst rupture causes haemorrhagic peritonism without the same chemical irritation.

(iii) Resuscitative measures: IV access with large-bore cannula; IV fluid resuscitation; blood group and crossmatch; FBC and coagulation screen; monitor pulse, blood pressure and urine output; analgesia; nil by mouth; serum/urine beta-hCG to exclude ectopic pregnancy.

(iv) Investigations: Ultrasound to confirm free fluid and characterize the cyst; serum beta-hCG (to exclude ectopic pregnancy); haemoglobin/haematocrit; coagulation screen. If haemodynamically unstable or ectopic pregnancy cannot be excluded: laparotomy/laparoscopy is indicated. Definitive treatment: at laparoscopy or laparotomy, haemostasis is achieved; the cyst is evacuated and the ovary conserved if possible.
questions.question:
A 30-year-old woman on the 22nd day of her menstrual cycle presents with sudden onset of right-sided lower abdominal pain and signs of peritoneal irritation. She had a positive urine pregnancy test performed at home the previous week. On examination the abdomen is guarded and she is mildly hypotensive.

(i) What is the most likely diagnosis, and what is the key differential diagnosis that must be excluded?
(ii) State the predisposing factors for this complication, the anatomical basis for its side predominance, and distinguish it from the presentation of a ruptured dermoid cyst.
(iii) What immediate resuscitative measures are required?
(iv) What investigations confirm the diagnosis, and what is the definitive treatment?

questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: complete hydatidiform mole with complications (pre-eclampsia and bilateral theca-lutein cysts). Clinical features of hydatidiform mole: abnormal uterine bleeding (90%); passage of molar vesicles; hyperemesis gravidarum (25%); excessive uterine size (50%) — uterus larger than dates in 50%, less in 25%, appropriate in 25%; pre-eclampsia (10–12%) — suspected in cases occurring before 20 weeks; hyperthyroidism (10%) — due to non-specificity of thyroid receptors (TSH has same alpha-subunit as hCG); multiple theca-lutein cysts (15–30%) — due to hCG stimulation; respiratory distress (2%); trophoblastic embolization; absent fetal heart tones (complete moles); quickening does not occur; amenorrhoea; breast changes.

(ii) Complications present in this patient: pre-eclampsia (hypertension 160/110 mmHg) occurring before 20 weeks — a characteristic complication of hydatidiform mole; bilateral theca-lutein cysts (bilateral adnexal enlargement) — ovarian enlargement due to effect of hCG; the markedly elevated hCG (280,000 mIU/ml) — molar pregnancy characterised by beta-hCG greater than 100,000 mIU/L; respiratory distress may be impending due to trophoblastic embolization; the patient is at high risk of malignant sequelae as hCG level is greater than 100,000 mIU/ml and there is excessive uterine enlargement and theca-lutein cysts greater than 6 cm.

(iii) Pre-treatment investigations: serum hCG level; pelvic ultrasound — diffuse mixed echogenic pattern, snowstorm appearance, absent fetus; FBC; serum electrolytes, urea and creatinine (E&U); liver function tests; clotting profile; renal function; chest X-ray (to exclude pulmonary metastases and assess for respiratory complications); serum T3 and T4 assays (hyperthyroidism); blood group and crossmatch; pre-treatment evaluation: full blood count, serum biochemistry; CSF hCG if CNS involvement suspected (plasma-CSF ratio greater than 60:1 suggests CNS disease); CT/MRI of brain, chest, abdomen-pelvis for pre-evacuation staging.

(iv) Procedure of choice: suction curettage (suction evacuation) under general anaesthesia — this is the treatment of choice; lower risk of metastasis than with dilatation and curettage; uterine stimulation with oxytocin (pitocin) — commence oxytocin drip prior to suction evacuation, or uterine stimulation by pitocin; must empty the uterus as trophoblast cells continue to secrete hCG; ensure histological examination of evacuated material. Intraoperative complications: uterine perforation; haemorrhage; infection; pulmonary complications (trophoblastic embolization); laparotomy set-up required as surgical intervention may be necessary; hysterectomy is an alternative for patients with complete families — reduces malignant sequelae to less than 5%.

(v) Follow-up: serum hCG weekly after treatment until normal for 3 consecutive assays, then monthly for a year (mostly normal by 14 weeks); pelvic examination — uterine size, presence of adnexal masses and metastases, one week post-treatment, if normal then 4-weekly; CXRs if metastases seen in baseline film — 4-weekly till remission, then 3-monthly; contraception throughout entire follow-up — sterilisation and barrier methods are safest; IUCDs not used before hCG is normal because of risk of perforation; avoid pregnancy for at least one year. Criteria for active therapy: hCG constant for 3 consecutive weeks; rising hCG after normal levels; post-evacuation haemorrhage; high hCG levels at 4 weeks post-evacuation (urinary hCG greater than 20,000 or serum hCG greater than 30,000 IU/ml); histological evidence of choriocarcinoma; trophoblastic activity 1 month after normal pregnancy or non-molar abortion.
questions.question:
A 19-year-old nulliparous girl is brought to the emergency department with a 6-hour history of severe lower abdominal pain and amenorrhoea of 3 months duration. She has a history of passage of vesicles per vaginam 2 weeks ago. Her uterus is 14 weeks in size, there is marked bilateral adnexal enlargement, and her blood pressure is 160/110 mmHg. Serum hCG is 280,000 mIU/ml.
(i) What is the diagnosis, and what are the complete mole's most important clinical features?
(ii) What complications are present in this patient at this time?
(iii) What pre-treatment investigations are required before uterine evacuation?
(iv) Describe the procedure of choice for uterine evacuation and intraoperative complications.
(v) What follow-up is required and what criteria trigger active treatment?

Describe the benign and malignant conditions of the vulva under the following structured headings.
A(i) Define the anatomy of the vulva, listing all constituent structures.
A(ii) Describe Paget's disease of the vulva: histological appearance, clinical features, associated risk, and treatment.
B(i) Describe pruritus vulvae: clinical importance, all causes, and the diagnostic approach.
B(ii) Explain the principles of treatment of pruritus vulvae and vulvodynia.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Anatomy of the vulva: the vulva consists of the labia majora, labia minora, mons pubis, clitoris, perineum, and vestibule.
