Mons pubis — fibro-fatty cushion covered with coarse skin, anterior and superior to the symphysis pubis. Labia majora — fibro-fatty folds extending from the mons to the perineum, covered with coarse skin containing hair follicles, sebaceous glands, and sweat glands. Labia minora — flaps of soft skin within the labia majora, bordering the vaginal orifice, devoid of hair, contain sebaceous and sweat glands, vascular and nerve endings; anteriorly — prepuce and frenulum of clitoris; posteriorly — fourchette. Clitoris — vascular plexus (erectile tissue) with glans, prepuce, body, and two crura. Vestibule — area enclosed by the labia minora containing the urethra, vagina, Bartholin's ducts, and Skene's ducts.

A(ii) Paget's disease of the vulva: a variant of Paget's disease of the breast; histologically typical 'Paget's cells' are present; common in postmenopausal women presenting with pruritus; lesions are scaly-erythematous; underlying adenocarcinoma is found in 25% of cases; treatment — wide excision only.

B(i) Pruritus vulvae — clinical importance: distressful; prolonged scratching predisposes to cancer. Causes include: dermatoses (lichen sclerosus, psoriasis, seborrhoea, eczema, intertrigo, contact/irritant dermatitis); dystrophies (squamous cell hyperplasia); infections — bacterial (syphilis, bartholinitis, perifoliculitis), viral (genital warts — HPV, herpes simplex type 2), fungal (Candida albicans, tinea cruris), parasitic (Trichomonas vaginalis, pediculosis, threadworms, amoebiasis, schistosomiasis, filariasis); pre-malignant and malignant disease (VIN, carcinoma vulva, Paget's disease); medical disorders (diabetes, liver failure/jaundice, uraemia); poor hygiene; psychogenic. Diagnostic approach: history — duration, site, intensity; physical examination — inspect skin for dermatological disorder, metabolic disturbance; inspect vulva, vagina, and cervix; investigations — microbiology and serology, cytology, colposcopy and biopsy, renal/liver/thyroid function tests, FBC, glucose tolerance test.

B(ii) Treatment of pruritus vulvae: treat the underlying cause; avoid allergic/irritant materials; topical corticosteroid; specialist consultation. Treatment of vulvodynia (chronic vulval pain): feeling of vulval burning, usually no itching; chronic vulval discomfort — burning, irritation, rawness; aetiology uncertain and no specific cause is usually identifiable; treatment is often unsatisfactory.

questions.question:
A 26-year-old woman who is 8 weeks postpartum and exclusively breastfeeding presents seeking contraception. She has not yet resumed menses and is keen to avoid hormonal methods due to concerns about her infant. She wishes to use lactational amenorrhoea method (LAM) but asks how to strengthen its effect and when she must switch to another method.

(i) What is the physiological basis of LAM, and what is its failure rate when conditions are met?
(ii) What three conditions must be met for LAM to be effective, and what is its maximum recommended duration?
(iii) What are the advantages of LAM, including its non-contraceptive health benefits for the infant?
(iv) What are the disadvantages and cautions related to LAM?
(v) When she transitions away from LAM, what is the most appropriate contraceptive method for her, and what is the management if her return to fertility is delayed beyond expected?
questions.answerText:
(i) Physiological basis of LAM: ovulation is delayed after delivery due to nursing-induced hypothalamic suppression of ovulation; however, the duration of this suppression is variable—about 50–60% of women begin ovulation between 6–12 months postpartum even while nursing; therefore 15–55% can get pregnant without additional contraception. When conditions are met, the failure rate of LAM is as low as 2%.
(ii) Three conditions (ways of strengthening contraceptive effect of LAM): exclusive breastfeeding on demand; should only be used when the woman has not yet seen her period (has not resumed menses); should only be used for a maximum of 6 months.
(iii) Advantages of LAM: effectively prevents pregnancy for at least 6 months and maybe longer if a woman keeps breastfeeding often, day and night; encourages the best breastfeeding patterns; can be used immediately after childbirth; no need to do anything at time of sexual intercourse; no direct cost for family planning or for feeding the baby; no supplies or procedures needed to prevent pregnancy; no hormonal side effects; counselling for LAM encourages starting a follow-on method at the proper time. Non-contraceptive health benefits for infant: provides the healthiest food for the baby; protects the baby from life-threatening diarrhoea; helps protect the baby from life-threatening diseases such as measles and pneumonia by passing the mother's immunities to the baby; helps develop close relationship between mother and baby.
(iv) Disadvantages and cautions: effectiveness after 6 months is not certain; frequent breastfeeding may be inconvenient or difficult for some women, especially working mothers; no protection against STDs including HIV/AIDS. Cautions: HIV infection in the mother (there is a small chance that breast milk will pass HIV to the baby); condition of the woman postpartum; medication use during nursing.
(v) Most appropriate method after LAM: progestin-only injectable (DMPA 150mg every 3 months or NET-EN 200mg every 2 months) or progestin-only pills, since she is still breastfeeding and these do not contain oestrogen; indications for progestogen-only contraceptives include lactating women. If return to fertility is delayed after stopping DMPA: the return to fertility is delayed by about 4 months longer than other methods and may be up to 1 year; the client should be counselled about this delay; she should be reassured that less than 10% of women on DMPA experience regular monthly bleeding during use, and that this is an expected effect.

questions.question:
Describe the female sexual response cycle and the clinical basis of sexual dysfunction in women.

A(i) The four phases of the female sexual response cycle as described by Masters and Johnson
A(ii) The physiological characteristics of the excitement phase and the stage of orgasm
B(i) The definition and types of sexual orientation
B(ii) The definition and clinical features of inhibited sexual desire (ISD) and female sexual arousal disorder (FSAD)
B(iii) The causes of inhibited sexual desire in women, including hormonal factors
C(i) The definition, types, and causes of dyspareunia, distinguishing superficial from deep
C(ii) The contributory factors to sexual dysfunction, classified under psychological, biological, interpersonal, and environmental domains
questions.answerText:
A(i) Masters and Johnson described four phases of the sexual response: Excitement or Seduction Phase; the Plateau Phase; the Orgasmic Phase; and the Stage of Resolution. In the modified Kaplan model the stages are: Desire; Arousal; and Orgasm—these phases overlap.
A(ii) Excitement phase: most of the response is due to stimulation of the parasympathetic fibres of the autonomous nervous system. Characteristics: deep breathing; increased pulse; warmth and erotic feelings; increased tension; generalised vasocongestion; skin flush; breast engorgement; nipple erection; engorgement of the labia and clitoris; vaginal transudation; uterine tenting. Stage of orgasm: release of sexual tension built up in the entire body; generalised myotonic contractions; contractions of perivaginal muscles and anal sphincter; uterine contractions. Muscle contractions occur 2 to 4 seconds after the woman begins to experience orgasm and repeat at 0.8-second intervals. Plateau phase: culmination of the excitement phase; marked degree of vasocongestion throughout the body; breasts and their areola are markedly enlarged; labia and lower third of the vagina are markedly enlarged; clitoris retracts tightly against the pubic symphysis; vagina lengthens with dilatation of the upper two-thirds. Resolution phase: return of the woman's physiologic state to pre-excitement level; no refractory period (unlike in the male) so new sexual cycles may be stimulated at any time after orgasm; woman generally experiences a feeling of personal satisfaction and well-being.
B(i) Types of sexual orientation: Bisexuality—sexual orientation characterised by romantic love or sexual desire for members of either or both genders. Heterosexuality—characterised by aesthetic attraction, romantic love, and sexual desire exclusively or almost exclusively for members of the opposite sex. Homosexuality—characterised by sexual and emotional interest in members of the same sex. Asexuality—people who lack feelings of sexual attraction and/or sexual desire; debate exists as to whether this is a sexual dysfunction or an actual sexual orientation. Pederasty—erotic love between adolescents and adult men. Paedophilia—psychosexual disorder in which there is preference for sexual activity with prepubertal children; almost always males; children typically 13 years of age or younger. Celibacy—abstinence from sexual intercourse, especially by reason of religious vows; voluntary refusal to enter the married state with abstinence from sexual activity.
B(ii) ISD—persistent loss of desire that disrupts sexual relationships; characterised by diminished sexual attraction, decreased sexual activity, few or no sexual dreams or fantasies, and diminished attention to erotic material by one or both partners; most common presenting sexual dysfunction in women; less commonly reported in men. Female sexual arousal disorder (FSAD)—persistent or recurrent inability to achieve or maintain an adequate lubrication-swelling response; a woman with FSAD may or may not find enjoyment in physical contact.
B(iii) Causes of ISD in women: contributing factors include hormone deficiencies, depression, alcoholism, liver or kidney disease, chronic illness, and side effects of drugs (e.g., antihypertensives and antidepressants); psychological factors include stress, relationship problems, sexual trauma, major life changes, and pairing of negative memories with sexual interactions. Testosterone plays a vital role in women's sexual desire; reduction in testosterone (e.g., due to removal of ovaries, chemotherapy, menopause) can be treated through supplementation. Life events affecting hormonal patterns include premenstrual tension, childbirth, pregnancy, and menopause.
C(i) Dyspareunia is a condition in women characterised by recurrent genital pain with sexual activity. Pain usually occurs with penetration but can also occur during nonpenetrative genital stimulation. Superficial dyspareunia (at the vaginal opening): caused by vulvovaginitis, genital herpes, atrophic vulvitis, urethral problems, episiotomy, radiation vaginitis, sexual trauma, inadequate lubrication, or topical irritants such as spermicides or latex; symptoms include burning, itching, stinging, or inflammation in any area of the perineum. Deep pelvic dyspareunia: caused by thrusting by the partner hitting an ovary, PID, pelvic or abdominal surgery, postoperative adhesions, endometriosis, genital or pelvic tumours, irritable bowel syndrome, urinary tract infection, and ovarian cysts; can also have psychological causes.
C(ii) Contributory factors to sexual dysfunction: Psychological/emotional—stress, negative body image, performance anxiety, expectation of failure, fear of pregnancy, memory of negative sexual experiences, fear of acquiring or transmitting a sexually transmitted disease. Biological/physiological—changes related to aging, certain medical conditions (arthritis, reproductive cancers, diabetes, cardiac disease, hypertension), physical injury (spinal cord injuries), effects of hormonal contraceptive methods, pregnancy, and substance abuse. Interpersonal/social—peer pressure, poor communication with a partner, sexual abuse, attitudes toward sexual orientation, uncertainty of how to behave, and conflicts with one's partner. Environmental—cultural influences, gender dynamics, availability of partners (partner ratio), and physical setting (lack of privacy).

questions.question:
A. Describe the perineal body under the following headings:
A(i) Nature, synonyms, and location
A(ii) Structures attached to it
B. Explain why failure to repair a deep perineal laceration involving the perineal body increases the risk of subsequent pelvic organ prolapse.
C. Distinguish between the perineal membrane and the perineal body in terms of their nature, location, attachments, and functions.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Nature, synonyms, and location: The perineal body is a fibromuscular mass; synonym — central tendon of the perineum. Located between the vagina and the anus, at the junction of the anterior and posterior perineum.
A(ii) Structures attached to it: the perineal membrane; superficial and deep transverse perineal muscles; bulbospongiosus; levator ani; and the coccyx (via the external anal sphincter).
B. Clinical basis: Deep laceration involving the perineal body that is not sutured or does not heal increases the possibility of subsequent utero-vaginal prolapse. The perineal body anchors the levator ani and the bulbospongiosus and limits downward descent of pelvic structures. Damage to these attachments removes a critical component of pelvic floor support; the three components responsible for support (ligaments and fascia, levator ani, and the posterior angulation of the vagina) are all compromised when the perineal body is disrupted.
C. Distinction between the perineal membrane and the perineal body:
Perineal membrane: triangular sheet in the anterior half of the pelvic outlet; composed of dense fibromuscular tissue; previously called the urogenital diaphragm; arises from the ischiopubic rami. Complete sheet in males. Attachments: urethra, vagina, and perineal body. Functions: supports the pelvic floor, counteracts the effects of raised intra-abdominal pressure, and counteracts the effects of gravity; limits downward descent.
Perineal body: fibromuscular mass (central tendon of the perineum); located between vagina and anus at the junction of anterior and posterior perineum. Attachments: perineal membrane; superficial and deep transverse perineal muscles; bulbospongiosus; levator ani; coccyx via external anal sphincter. It is a convergence point for multiple perineal muscles rather than a sheet-like structure.

questions.question:
A) Describe the pre-operative assessment of a gynaecological patient under the following headings:
A(i) History taking — the specific items of special attention, including the timing of the last menstrual period and drugs to be noted
A(ii) Physical examination — systems to be examined, and what baseline investigations are required specifying the minimum acceptable haemoglobin level for major and minor surgery

B) Explain the clinical basis of:
B(i) The principles of valid informed consent — who can sign consent, the age threshold, and special considerations for sterilisation and for girls under 16 requesting termination of pregnancy
B(ii) Why thromboembolism is a specific risk in gynaecological surgery, listing the four predisposing causes of phlebothrombosis and the measures used to prevent thrombosis and embolism

C) State the post-operative complications that must be monitored in the first 12 hours, and distinguish between primary, delayed and secondary haemorrhage as defined in the lectures.
questions.answerText:
A(i) History: complete history with special attention to any recent illness. The date of the last period should be noted — some surgeons try to avoid major operations in the premenstrual phase when pelvic organs are more vascular. The possibility of pregnancy should not be ignored. Drugs and medications recently taken should be noted — these include hormones (especially oral contraceptives), antibiotics and tranquillisers.

A(ii) Physical examination: general examination (teeth — exclude septic lesions in mouth or throat; heart and lungs examined; blood pressure measured; abdomen and pelvis examined; legs inspected for varicosities).
Baseline investigations: haemoglobin/PCV — minimum for major surgery: haematocrit 10.5 g/dl (33%), or PCV 30% (which is accepted for both major and minor surgeries in the local environment); minimum for minor surgery: 10 g/dl (PCV 30%). Test for haemoglobinopathies if suspected. Blood group and Rhesus factor; urine tested for albumin and sugar; cervical smear if not done recently; mid-stream urine if urinary infection suspected; renal function tests for major surgeries; chest X-ray if indicated; ECG if heart disease suspected.

B(i) Valid consent must be given in writing by the patient herself, clearly and legibly countersigned by a doctor who has explained the operation and its possible sequelae. Girls aged 16 or over sign consent on their own behalf; for those under that age, consent of a parent or legal guardian is usually necessary except in an emergency. For a married woman, her husband's consent is not legally necessary in the UK for operations leading to sterility, but counselling of the couple is important. For sterilisation or vasectomy: the operation should be considered irreversible, though failures occur; this must be recorded in case notes.

B(ii) Predisposing causes of phlebothrombosis: trauma; anaemia; stasis; high oestrogen levels. Prevention measures: pneumatic boots and leggings during surgery; elasticated stockings before, during and after operation; early movement; avoidance of anaemia; prompt treatment of infection; prophylactic low-dose heparin before and just after surgery; the contraceptive pill should be stopped six weeks before major elective surgery.

C) Post-operative complications in the first 12 hours: respiratory failure or obstruction to the airways; shock; haemorrhage; cardiac failure.
Types of haemorrhage:
- Primary haemorrhage: occurring during the operation, requiring immediate transfusion.
- Delayed haemorrhage: occurring during the immediate post-operative period, generally due to a slipped ligature or bleeding vessel in the vagina or cervix; blood transfusion given and patient returned to theatre.
- Secondary haemorrhage: occurring up to 14 days after the operation, generally from the vagina or cervix, occasionally from the abdominal wound; infection is commonly associated; suturing and transfusion may be needed.

questions.question:
A 16-year-old male presents with a painless ulcer on the glans penis. He reports unprotected sexual intercourse 3 weeks ago. On examination, there is a single well-defined painless ulcer (chancre) with firm borders and a clean base. Regional lymph nodes are enlarged but painless. Three weeks later he returns with a widespread skin rash over his palms and soles.

(i) What is the spot diagnosis with the causative organism and its microscopic characteristics?
(ii) Describe the progression of this disease through all its stages.
(iii) What are the investigations used to diagnose this condition, distinguishing screening from specific tests?
(iv) What is the treatment, including for the congenital form?
(v) What are the prevention strategies and the implications of this diagnosis for his sexual contacts?
questions.answerText:
(i) Spot diagnosis: syphilis. Causative organism: Treponema pallidum—a spirochaete; not stainable by Gram's method. Identified by: darkfield microscopy of specimens; silver staining of specimen.
(ii) Stages of syphilis: Primary syphilis—painless genital sore (chancre) and painless lymphadenopathy. Secondary syphilis—bilateral and symmetrical squamo-papular eruptions (the rash over palms and soles); condyloma acuminata; lymphadenopathy. Tertiary syphilis—neurosyphilis; alopecia; arthritis.
(iii) Investigations: Identification of organism—darkfield microscopy of specimens; silver staining. Serological tests: non-specific (screening)—Kahn test, Wasserman Reaction test, VDRL, Hinton and Kleine tests. Specific tests—Fluorescent treponema antibody absorption test; micro-haemagglutination assay; haemagglutination treponemal tests for syphilis. The gonococcal complement fixation test may be useful in diagnosing chronic infections in females and for suspected complications such as salpingitis or arthritis (relevant for co-infection).
(iv) Treatment: Procaine penicillin 600,000 units daily for 14 days; benzathine penicillin 2.4 million units i.m.; erythromycin if allergic to penicillin. Congenital syphilis: benzyl penicillin 6–50,000 units/kg; erythromycin if allergic to penicillin.
(v) Prevention strategies: health education; modification of risk behaviour; barrier method of contraception (condom); prompt and early treatment; contact tracing. Implications for sexual contacts: all sexual contacts must be traced, screened, and given appropriate treatment. The ulceration associated with syphilis compromises the skin's physical barrier to infection, increasing susceptibility to HIV; contact tracing is therefore also important for HIV prevention.

questions.question:
Describe the gross anatomy of the uterus and relate its zones and layers to the pathological basis of the two main types of endometrial carcinoma. Then explain how the lymphatic drainage of the uterus determines the lymph node groups at risk in advanced endometrial cancer.
A(i) Describe the histological types and grading system of endometrial carcinoma and the clinical significance of each histological subtype.
A(ii) Describe the two pathogenetic types of endometrial carcinoma (Type 1 and Type 2) and how they differ in phenotypic characteristics, tumour biology, and prognosis.
B(i) Explain the surgical staging system of endometrial carcinoma and how the depth of myometrial invasion relates to risk of lymph node involvement and prognosis.
B(ii) Explain why leiomyosarcoma and mixed mesodermal tumours are distinct from endometrial carcinoma and describe their presentation and prognosis.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Histological types and grading of endometrial carcinoma: endometrioid adenocarcinoma — the most common histopathological subtype; the grade of the adenomatous component affects prognosis; papillary serous and clear cell histotypes — confer a poor prognosis; fortunately uncommon; secretory carcinomas — least frequently occurring; good prognosis; adenocarcinoma with squamous component — benign squamous component (adenoacanthoma) or malignant (adenosquamous); squamous component does not affect prognosis, but malignant squamous component (adenosquamous carcinoma) may be associated with a poorer outcome. Grading (degree of differentiation): G1 — nonsquamous or nonmorular solid growth pattern of 5% or less; G2 — nonsquamous or nonmorular solid growth pattern of 6–50%; G3 — nonsquamous or nonmorular solid growth pattern of more than 50%.

A(ii) Two pathogenetic types: Type 1 (classic category) — most women in this category; tend to be white, nulliparous; obese, hyperlipidaemia, signs of hyperestrogenism, uterine bleeding, infertility, late onset of menopause; may have hyperplasia of the ovary and endometrial stroma; well-differentiated, superficially invasive cancers sensitive to progesterone; very favourable prognosis; extrauterine disease is unusual. Type 2 — have none of the disease states in the classic presentation; tend to be thin, multiparous, and African American; tend to have poorly differentiated tumours, deep myometrial invasion; high degree of metastasis to lymph nodes and other sites; decreased sensitivity to progestins; poor prognosis.

B(i) FIGO surgical staging and myometrial invasion: Stage IA — tumour limited to endometrium; Stage IB — invasion to less than half of myometrium; Stage IC — invasion to more than half of myometrium; Stage IIA — endocervical glandular involvement only; Stage IIB — cervical stromal invasion; Stage IIIA — tumour invades serosa and/or adnexa and/or positive peritoneal cytology; Stage IIIB — vaginal metastasis; Stage IIIC — metastases to pelvic and/or para-aortic lymph nodes; Stage IVA — tumour invasion of bladder and/or bowel mucosa; Stage IVB — distant metastases including intra-abdominal and/or inguinal lymph nodes. Clinical implication: radiotherapy is added if invasion is more than the inner half of the myometrium (Stage IC) — this is because deeper invasion correlates with higher risk of lymph node spread and distant metastasis; in Stage II, radical hysterectomy and bilateral pelvic lymphadenectomy with para-aortic node sampling are performed; lymphadenectomy in staging laparotomy includes pelvic and para-aortic dissection; increased bleeding may develop with lymphadenectomy.

B(ii) Leiomyosarcoma: may arise de novo in the uterine muscle or from transformation of a benign fibroid (rare, less than 0.2%); may also arise in the endometrial stroma (endometrial stromal sarcoma). Presentation: uterine bleeding; rapid growth of the tumour with increasing pains, especially after menopause (when fibroids normally remain unchanged or shrink); these tumours grow more rapidly and are softer than fibromyomata. Naked eye inspection: tumour may be seen to have invaded the uterine wall or the capsule of the fibromyomata; cut surface shows small haemorrhages and areas of degenerative softening. Treatment: TAH, BSO followed by radiotherapy; prognosis is poor except for leiomyosarcoma arising in a fibromyomata. Mixed mesodermal tumours: tumours with heterologous mesenchymal elements; occasionally follow uterine irradiation; presentation — bleeding from the uterus, sometimes pain; histology — some elements resembling sarcoma and others resembling carcinoma, together with bizarre components (e.g. cartilage, striped muscle); prognosis is poor; metastasis via the bloodstream is common as is local recurrence after removal. Sarcoma botryoides (embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma): a variety seen in infants and young children; presentation — blood-stained watery discharge; grape-like masses of soft growth arising from the cervix; among the myxomatous cells are primitive striped muscle cells (rhabdomyoblasts); treatment — external irradiation and chemotherapy; prognosis with conventional treatment is very poor in children.

(i) Diagnosis: hydatidiform mole. Two types: complete mole — chromosomes are entirely paternal, mainly 46XX karyotype (90%) from fertilization by a haploid sperm which duplicates its chromosome, occasionally from dispermic fertilization 46XX or 46XY (10%); features include oedema of virtually all chorionic villi, hydrops villi 1–3 cm in diameter, no fetal tissue or amniotic membrane, marked trophoblastic proliferation. Partial mole — often triploid karyotype (occasionally tetraploid) with maternal genetic contribution retained; features include identifiable fetal tissue or amniotic membrane, placenta has normal and hydropic villi, focal mild trophoblastic hyperplasia, scalloping of hydropic villi, trophoblastic inclusions in stroma, fetal vessels and nucleated fetal erythrocytes; ratio of complete to partial mole is 1:1.

(ii) Risk factors: age less than 20 or over 40 years; low socioeconomic status; malnutrition; previous spontaneous abortion; nutritional deficiency of protein or animal fat, carotene, and folic acid; higher incidence among Asians; previous hydatidiform mole (incidence of repeat molar pregnancy is 4–5 times higher); ABO blood group — group A women with group O husbands, poor prognosis in group AB; incidence of mole is 1 in 1500–2000 in the US and 1 in 667 deliveries in Ibadan.

(iii) Complications: persistent disease — complete moles may persist after evacuation as local uterine invasion in 15% or metastases in 4%; progression to choriocarcinoma; pulmonary complications; uterine perforation; haemorrhage; infection. High-risk women (most likely to develop malignant sequelae) have features of marked trophoblastic proliferation: hCG level greater than 100,000 mIU/ml; excessive uterine enlargement; theca-lutein cysts greater than 6 cm; urine hCG greater than 100,000 IU per 24 hours; serum hCG greater than 40,000 mIU/ml. Non-metastatic persistence in 4% of partial moles.

(iv) Primary management: suction curettage followed by sharp curettage — treatment of choice; laparotomy set-up as intervention may be required; hysterectomy is an alternative for patients with complete families (malignant sequelae less than 5%). Follow-up: serum hCG weekly until normal for 3 consecutive assays, then monthly for a year; mostly normal by 14 weeks; pelvic examination one week post-treatment, then 4-weekly; CXRs if metastases seen at baseline; contraception throughout entire follow-up period. Criteria for active therapy: hCG constant for 3 consecutive weeks; rising hCG after normal levels; post-evacuation haemorrhage; high hCG levels at 4 weeks post-evacuation (urinary hCG greater than 20,000 or serum hCG greater than 30,000 IU/ml); histological evidence of choriocarcinoma; trophoblastic activity 1 month after normal pregnancy or non-molar abortion.

(v) For persistent GTD without wish to retain fertility: hysterectomy plus adjuvant chemotherapy. Chemotherapy — single agent for low-risk: Methotrexate (4 doses on alternate days with folinic acid) or Actinomycin-D (5-day regimen); combination for high-risk: EMA-CO (Etoposide, Methotrexate, Actinomycin-D, Cyclophosphamide, Vincristine) — most successful and least toxic; salvage regimens: MAC, MAC-III; second-line: cisplatin with MTX and vincristine. Surgical options: wide local excision of vaginal metastases; arteriographic embolization of hypogastric arteries; pulmonary segmental resection; hepatic resection; hepatic artery embolization or ligation; craniotomy. Whole-liver or whole-brain irradiation for liver and brain metastases respectively. Prognosis: 100% of low-risk can be completely cured; greater than 90% in high-risk with EMA-CO.
questions.question:
A 28-year-old woman is referred because of a 6-week history of lower abdominal pain, amenorrhoea of 10 weeks, and passage of grape-like vesicles per vaginam. On examination the uterus is large for the gestational age and no fetal heart is heard. Serum beta-hCG is markedly elevated.
(i) What is the diagnosis, and what are the two distinct types of this condition and their cytogenetic differences?
(ii) What risk factors predispose to this condition?
(iii) What are the complications that may arise, and which patients are at highest risk of malignant sequelae?
(iv) Describe the primary management including the procedure of choice, follow-up protocol, and criteria for initiating active therapy.
(v) What definitive treatments, including surgical options and chemotherapy regimens, are available for persistent or malignant disease?

questions.answerText:
(i) First patient (beefy-red granulomatous perineal ulcer): Granuloma inguinale—caused by Klebsiella granulomatis. Second patient (genital warts): Human papilloma virus (HPV) infection.
(ii) Clinical features of granuloma inguinale: discrete vulval papules; beefy-red painful vulval ulcers and perineum; lymphoedema; elephantiasis. Investigations: biopsy of affected areas; crush preparations of affected areas.
(iii) Treatment of granuloma inguinale: tetracycline group.
(iv) HPV subtypes: the majority of genital warts are caused by HPV types 6 and 11, which have little oncogenic potential. The subtypes 16 and 18 may cause flat warts and have been linked with the development of cervical carcinoma. Carcinoma of the cervix is the commonest female malignancy in this environment and is believed to be a sexually transmitted disease.
(v) Treatment of genital warts: podophyllin in spirit (10–25%)—dangerous in pregnancy; electrocautery; cryosurgery; surgery. Prevention strategy for oncogenic HPV: regular Pap smear; vaccination against oncogenic serotypes of HPV (latest strategy).
questions.question:
A 38-year-old woman presents to your gynaecology outpatient clinic with a 3-month history of painful vulval lesions and a painless, slowly enlarging ulcer on the perineum with beefy-red granulomatous appearance. She comes from a rural area and reports no history of prior treatment. A biopsy is taken. Additionally, a 26-year-old woman in the next clinic is noted to have genital warts—multiple papular lesions on the vulva.

(i) What is the spot diagnosis for each patient, with the causative organisms?
(ii) What are the clinical features and investigations for granuloma inguinale?
(iii) What is the treatment for granuloma inguinale?
(iv) For the second patient, what HPV subtypes cause genital warts versus those with oncogenic potential, and what is the link to cervical carcinoma?
(v) What are the treatment options for genital warts, and what is the recommended prevention strategy for oncogenic HPV?

questions.answerText:
(i) Pre-operative preparations: the patient should be weighed on admission or in the out-patient clinic; anaemia must be corrected — it is unlikely to carry out major surgery with a haematocrit level below 10.5 g/dl (33%), though a level of 30% is accepted for both major and minor surgeries in this environment; crossmatch blood as transfusion may be needed; treat co-morbid conditions including hypertension; the lower bowel should be emptied by a suitable laxative; perioperative antibiotics may be given before elective surgery; a physiotherapist should visit every patient before the operation to teach breathing and leg movements; written informed consent must be obtained; the oral contraceptive pill should ideally be stopped 6 weeks before major elective surgery; in postmenopausal women, pre-operative treatment with oestrogen is helpful (by mouth or vaginal cream); the patient should take a bath and put on a clean operation gown; nothing should be taken by mouth for at least four hours before the operation; valid written consent must be given, clearly countersigned by a doctor.

(ii) Baseline and specific investigations: haemoglobin/PCV (minimum level of 30%); FBC; blood group and Rhesus factor determination, serum saved in blood bank; crossmatching of necessary quantity of blood; test for haemoglobinopathies; urine tested for albumin and sugar; mid-stream urine for bacteriology if urinary infection suspected; renal function tests (serum electrolytes, urea, and creatinine) — advisable for major surgeries; chest X-ray if indicated; ECG — advisable in patients with any suggestion of heart disease; IVU before operations when ureters may be involved (Wertheim's hysterectomy) to exclude double ureters and other variations; cervical smear if not done recently; coagulation profile; liver function tests; barium enema if bowel involvement suspected.

(iii) Complications to anticipate in first 12 hours: respiratory failure or obstruction to the airways; shock; haemorrhage; cardiac failure. Monitoring: the patient must be nursed in a recovery unit until she has recovered consciousness, then returned to a general ward; pulse rate and blood pressure should be taken and charted every 15 minutes for the first 2 hours, then every few hours for the first 12 hours and longer if there is any anxiety; level of consciousness; continuation of intra-operative management (blood transfusion/IV fluid); monitor urine output hourly; post-operative sedation and analgesia; pain must be relieved by adequate doses of analgesics such as morphine, pethidine, or pentazocine; patient-controlled analgesia is useful; addition of promethazine or chlorpromazine increases the effect of analgesics and helps prevent post-operative vomiting; post-operative physiotherapy (chest and mobilization).

(iv) Venous thrombosis — prevention and treatment: two types — phlebothrombosis (primary venous thrombosis beginning in deep veins of calf; predisposing causes: trauma, anaemia, stasis, high oestrogen levels) and thrombophlebitis (caused by infection, generally in pelvic veins initially, spreading to iliac veins). Prevention: pneumatic boots and leggings during surgery; elasticated stockings worn before, during, and after operation; early movement; avoidance of anaemia; prompt treatment of infection; prophylactic low-dose heparin before and just after surgery; low molecular weight heparin (e.g. clexane) is now available as prophylaxis. Treatment of established thrombosis: heparin given initially intravenously in a continuous dose of 1000–1500 IU per hour or by separate intravenous injection of 10,000 IU every 6 or 8 hours; calcium heparin can be given subcutaneously; dindevan (phenindione) given by mouth — initial dose 200 mg, then 100 mg, then 50 mg daily; warfarin: 30–50 mg on first day, dose adjusted according to INR; prothrombin time should be kept at 20–30% of normal; pulmonary embolism can follow thrombosis and if massive is rapidly fatal; small emboli cause pulmonary infarction.

(v) Post-operative urinary complications: retention of urine — complete retention often occurs after hysterectomy or repair of prolapse; treatment is by immediate catheterisation, usually emptying the bladder once; if repeated, an indwelling catheter for a few days; some surgeons prefer suprapubic catheterisation; partial retention — catheter should be passed for residual urine 5 days after operation; catheter drainage continues until residual urine is below 200 mls; cystitis and pyelonephritis — very common after gynaecological operations; catheter specimen or mid-stream specimen should be examined for evidence of infection after all major operations; suppression of urine — due to obstruction of ureters which may be accidentally injured, ligated, or obstructed by a haematoma, or reflex blockage; warning given by unilateral loin ache and slight temperature; very serious complication; must be dealt with urgently, if necessary with relieving surgery by a urologist; urinary fistulae — vesico-vaginal or uretero-vaginal; caused by trauma at operation, haematoma formation, or difficult obstetric delivery; uretero-vaginal fistula may follow operations especially Wertheim's hysterectomy where ureters are extensively dissected; incontinence of urine after catheterisation in elderly women — usually transient; persistent incontinence suggests a fistula.
questions.question:
A 45-year-old woman is scheduled for elective total abdominal hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy for multiple symptomatic fibroids. She is hypertensive and takes amlodipine. Pre-operative haemoglobin is 9.8 g/dl.
(i) What are the pre-operative preparations specifically required for this patient?
(ii) What baseline and specific investigations must be completed before the operation?
(iii) What are the complications to be anticipated in the first 12 hours after surgery, and how are they monitored?
(iv) Describe the management of post-operative venous thrombosis, including prevention and treatment.
(v) What post-operative urinary complications may arise after this procedure?

questions.answerText:
A(i) Definition and prevalence: Prolapse is protrusion of an organ or structure beyond its normal confines. It affects 12–30% of multiparous women and 2% of nulliparous women. In the UK and USA, women have an 11% lifetime risk of having an operation for prolapse.
A(ii) Types by compartment:
Anterior vaginal wall prolapse: urethrocele (urethral descent); cystocele (bladder descent); cysto-urethrocele (descent of both bladder and urethra).
Posterior vaginal wall prolapse: rectocele (rectal descent); enterocele (small bowel descent).
Apical vaginal prolapse: utero-vaginal — uterine descent with inversion of the vaginal apex; vault — post-hysterectomy inversion of the vaginal apex.
Three degrees: 1st degree — slight descent of the uterus, cervix remains within the vagina; 2nd degree — cervix projects to or through the introitus; 3rd degree (complete/procidentia) — entire uterus prolapses outside the introitus, whole vaginal/anterior wall is inverted.
B. The most dependent portion of the prolapse is assessed while the patient is straining. In utero-vaginal prolapse, the most dependent portion is the cervix — this determines the type and degree of prolapse observed.
C. Vault prolapse after hysterectomy: poor attention to vaginal vault support at the time of hysterectomy leads to vault prolapse in 1% of cases. Mechanical displacement due to gynaecological surgery (e.g. colposuspension) may lead to development of rectocele or enterocele.
Surgical treatments for vault prolapse:
Sacrocolpopexy: the inverted vaginal vault tissue is attached to the sacrum using a mesh, and the pouch of Douglas is closed.
Colpocleisis: obliteration of the vaginal canal (used when preservation of coital function is not required).
questions.question:
A. Describe the gross anatomy and classification of genital prolapse under the following headings:
A(i) Definition and prevalence
A(ii) Types of prolapse by compartment (anterior wall, posterior wall, apical), with examples of each
B. Explain how the most dependent portion of the prolapse determines the type of compartment involved, and which specific structure defines the dependent portion in utero-vaginal prolapse.
C. Describe how vault prolapse can develop after hysterectomy, and outline the surgical treatments available for vault prolapse.

A 22-year-old woman presents with painful vesicles and shallow ulcers on her labia and introitus, associated with fever and myalgia. She had a similar episode 6 months ago that resolved spontaneously. On examination, there are multiple painful superficial ulcers with an erythematous base.

(i) What is the spot diagnosis, what is the causative virus, and how does it differ from the cause of oral infection?
(ii) What are the full clinical features and potential systemic complications of this infection?
(iii) How is the diagnosis confirmed in the laboratory?
(iv) What is the management of this episode?
(v) How does this infection interact with HIV, and what are the strategies for preventing further episodes and transmission?
questions.answerText:
(i) Spot diagnosis: genital herpes. Most genital herpes infections are caused by Herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV2). Oral infections are caused by HSV1. Spread by contact. Genital herpes infection causes painful shallow genital ulcers.
(ii) Clinical features: painful vesicles; painful ulcers; herpes pharyngitis from oral sex; autonomic nervous dysfunction; recurrent infection. Systemic symptoms include fever and myalgia. Systemic complications: meningitis (viral); encephalitis.
(iii) Laboratory diagnosis: viral culture; indirect immuno-peroxidase test; direct immuno-fluorescent test.
(iv) Management: analgesics; sitz bath; acyclovir.
(v) Interaction with HIV: the ulceration associated with herpes simplex compromises the skin's physical barrier to infection and provides the infectious agent easier access to the bloodstream. STIs (including HSV) cause recruitment of target cells—lymphocytes and macrophages—to the genital mucosa, making them accessible to HIV infection. These infected cells can cross back into the bloodstream and disseminate the infection. STIs increase levels of HIV virus present in genital secretions. Prevention strategies: health education; modification of risk behaviour; consistent and correct use of condoms (barrier contraception); prompt and adequate treatment; contact tracing; abstinence from sexual intercourse (A—abstinence); being faithful to one uninfected partner (B—be faithful); correct and consistent use of condoms (C); desisting from sharing needles and syringes or contaminated blood (D); encouraging voluntary counselling and testing (E).

questions.question:
A 63-year-old woman presents with vague indigestion, weight loss, and a sensation of abdominal fullness. On abdominal examination there is a firm irregular mass arising from the pelvis with dullness on percussion in the flanks. A chest X-ray shows a right pleural effusion. Tumour markers show CA-125 of 480 u/ml. CT scan confirms bilateral ovarian masses with omental deposits and right pleural fluid.

(i) Identify the likely ovarian tumour type and sub-type based on all the imaging and examination findings; justify your reasoning using the clinical features of malignancy stated in the lectures.
(ii) What structures are compressed or involved as the tumour spreads through the peritoneal cavity, giving rise to each symptom described?
(iii) List the differential pathologies that must be excluded before a final diagnosis is made, and what specific investigations distinguish each.
(iv) Outline the clinico-anatomical reasoning for why pleural effusion in this case requires cytological analysis before Stage IV is assigned, and what this means for surgical eligibility.
questions.answerText:
(i) Most likely tumour type: Serous cystadenocarcinoma (malignant epithelial ovarian cancer). Justification using clinical features of malignancy: bilateral tumours (75% of malignant tumours are bilateral vs 15% of benign); solid, nodular, irregular growth; ascites (shifting dullness — usually a sign of peritoneal metastasis, especially if blood-stained); CA-125 480 u/ml (greatly elevated above the 35 u/ml threshold; >100 u/ml strongly suggests ovarian malignancy); omental deposits on CT; pleural effusion consistent with Stage IV or Meigs syndrome must be distinguished. The insidious onset with vague gastrointestinal upset (indigestion) is characteristic — ovarian tumours rarely give rise to specific symptoms early.

(ii) Structures compressed/involved causing each symptom:
- Indigestion and sensation of fullness: the enlarging omental deposits and tumour mass press on the stomach and small bowel, causing early satiety and GI symptoms.
- Weight loss: from cancer cachexia and impaired GI absorption due to peritoneal involvement.
- Abdominal fullness and distension: malignant ascites from peritoneal metastases causing fluid accumulation; the omentum and peritoneal surfaces are involved.
- Pleural effusion: peritoneal fluid flows through diaphragmatic lymphatics to the pleural cavity, causing a transudative or exudative effusion.

(iii) Differential pathologies:
- Krukenberg tumour (secondary ovarian metastasis from GI primary, especially stomach): bilateral adnexal masses; requires barium meal/endoscopy and gastroscopy to exclude gastric primary.
- Primary peritoneal carcinoma: indistinguishable from ovarian cancer; confirmed at histology.
- Metastatic breast cancer to ovaries: requires mammography, breast examination.
- Colonic carcinoma with ovarian metastases: requires barium enema or colonoscopy; also useful to assess bowel involvement from the ovarian tumour itself.
- Lymphoma: requires lymph node biopsy, chest CT.
- Meigs syndrome (benign fibroma with ascites and pleural effusion): resolved by histological analysis of the ovarian tumour at laparotomy.

(iv) Clinico-anatomical reasoning for pleural effusion and Stage IV:
The presence of a pleural effusion is insufficient to assign Stage IV status unless malignant cells are found on cytological examination of the pleural fluid. Peritoneal fluid flowing through diaphragmatic lymphatics can produce a benign reactive pleural effusion even in Stage III disease. If cytology is negative, the disease remains Stage III, and the patient may still be eligible for primary debulking surgery with curative intent. If cytology is positive, the disease is Stage IV, which means curative surgery is unlikely and management focuses on palliation and chemotherapy; a vertical incision is still required at any laparotomy for adequate exploration of the upper abdomen.

questions.question:
A 15-year-old girl presents with primary amenorrhoea, monthly cyclical lower abdominal pain, and acute urinary retention. On inspection of the vulva, a bluish-purple bulging membrane is seen at the introitus. Rectal examination reveals a large, tense, cystic swelling filling the pelvis.

(i) What is the diagnosis? Name the embryological structure from which the hymen arises, and state what would have been the presentation in infancy.
(ii) List the differential diagnoses of this condition.
(iii) What are the principles of evaluation in this condition, and why is vaginal examination specifically contraindicated?
(iv) State the definitive treatment, the specific technique used, and the measures required to prevent infection.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Imperforate hymen with haematocolpos (blood accumulated in the vagina). The hymen arises from the urogenital sinus (not the Müllerian duct). In infancy/before puberty: the presentation would be mucocolpos or hydrocolpos — accumulated cervical secretion causing a palpable abdominal mass in the newborn (this may present in the newborn period).

(ii) Differential diagnoses of cryptomenorrhoea:
- Pregnancy
- Pelvic tuberculosis
- Acute/sub-acute appendicitis
- Ovarian cyst
- Pelvic kidney
- Transverse vaginal septum
- Low-lying transverse vaginal septum
- Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser syndrome
- Androgen insensitivity syndrome

(iii) Principles of evaluation:
- History: cyclic abdominal pain, primary amenorrhoea, urinary symptoms
- Examination: inspection of the vulva only — the purplish/bluish bulging membrane is visible at the introitus; rectal examination — reveals large, tense, cystic cylindrical swelling filling the pelvis; palpate cervix and fundus through rectal wall
- Vaginal examination must be avoided: it risks introducing infection into the collected blood (haematocolpos), rupturing the membrane prematurely, or precipitating septicaemia. Haematosalpinx may cause aseptic inflammation of tubes leading to blockage.

(iv) Definitive treatment: Excision of the membrane to aid drainage. Technique: cruciate incision over the membrane — or complete excision of the imperforate hymen. This must be performed over a period of approximately one week to allow gradual drainage.
Measures to prevent infection: meticulous aseptic technique is essential; prophylactic antibiotics must be given; prompt action prevents spillage of infected blood into the peritoneal cavity (which can cause adhesions, endometriosis and infertility).

questions.question:
Describe the origin, classification, and mechanism of action of barrier contraceptive methods under the following headings.

A(i) Definition of barrier methods of contraception and their overall advantages and disadvantages as a group
A(ii) Prescription versus non-prescription barrier methods: classification
B(i) The diaphragm: description, types, mechanism of fitting, and post-prescription instructions
B(ii) Contraindications to the diaphragm use
C(i) The female condom: material, design, insertion technique, advantages, and disadvantages
C(ii) The male condom: types by material, advantages of latex versus polyurethane condoms, and failure rates of the male and female condom
questions.answerText:
A(i) Barrier methods of contraception are those that prevent the entry of spermatozoa into the uterus either by chemical action or mechanical obstruction. Overall advantages: preferred by many who have occasional intercourse; useful alternatives for those who want to avoid hormonal side effects; some methods available without prescription; some methods offer protection against sexually transmitted disease. Overall disadvantages: not as effective as hormonal methods in preventing pregnancy; efficacy is highly dependent on consistent and correct use; some methods require fitting by healthcare provider; all female barrier methods require vaginal insertion and removal by the patient that may be difficult or unacceptable; all methods require concomitant use of spermicide; all prescription barrier methods are associated with an increased risk of urinary tract infections and toxic shock syndrome.
A(ii) Prescription methods: diaphragm; cervical cap. Non-prescription methods: female condom; male condom; spermicides; sponge.
B(i) Diaphragm: dome-shaped rubber cup with a flexible rim, inserted into the vagina so the posterior rim rests in the posterior fornix and the anterior rim fits behind the pubic bone; the dome covers the cervix; best used with spermicidal cream poured inside the dome. Types: arching spring; flat spring; coil spring; wide seal spring. Fitting: perform pelvic examination to exclude contraindications; identify posterior fornix with middle and index fingers; mark the point of index finger under the pubic bone; the distance between this mark and the tip of the middle finger is the diameter of the suitable diaphragm; add 5mm to account for vaginal expansion during sexual intercourse. Post-prescription instructions: insert diaphragm before initial act of intercourse; always check for proper placement; leave diaphragm in place for 6 hours after the act of intercourse; use additional spermicide with each subsequent act of intercourse; after removal wash with clean water, soap, and unscented powder; do not use lubricants like vaseline or other petroleum products; re-check diaphragm size every year, after pregnancy, after abortion, after pelvic operation, and after noticeable weight gain or loss.
B(ii) Contraindications to diaphragm: history of allergy or sensitivity to rubber or spermicide; history of repeated UTI; anatomical abnormalities including cystocoele, rectocoele, uterine prolapse, fistulae, and vaginal septum.
C(i) Female condom: sheath of soft polyurethane; has two flexible rings—a removable ring at the closed end to aid insertion and a fixed ring at the open end to rest on the vulva and hold the condom in place. Insertion technique: can be inserted anytime before sexual intercourse; squeeze the inner ring between thumb, index and middle fingers; with the other hand separate the labia; insert the squeezed ring into the vagina and push in the rest of the condom until the inner ring reaches the end of the vagina; the larger flexible ring is smoothened over the vulva; to remove, hold onto the outer ring and twist it so semen does not spill out; do not reuse. Advantages: does not require medical prescription; provides some protection against STIs including HIV; can be inserted well before intercourse; can be used by those with latex allergies; very few side effects; promotes partner participation; usage is controlled by the woman. Disadvantages: may not be as effective against pregnancy as the male condom; available in only one size; can only be used for one act of intercourse; may be noisy and uncomfortable; outer ring may be visually unappealing; relatively expensive; failure rate 210 per 1000 women per year.
C(ii) Male condom types: latex; polyurethane; sheep membrane. Latex advantages: highly effective against most sexually transmitted disease transmission including HIV; more resistant to breakage than polyurethane condoms. Latex disadvantages: cannot be used in growing population of people with latex allergies; should not be used with oil-based lubricants; can be degraded by heat, light, and oxidation. Polyurethane advantages: safe for those with latex allergy; thinner; odourless, colourless, nonallergenic; greater resistance to heat and oxidation; may increase sensation of body heat; can be used with any type of lubricant. Polyurethane disadvantages: may not be as effective in protecting against sexually transmitted disease; higher rate of breakage; nearly double the price of latex condoms. Sheep membrane: provides less protection than latex and polyurethane. Failure rate of male condom: 150 per 1000 women per year.

questions.question:
A 27-year-old woman undergoes a vaginal hysterectomy and pelvic floor repair for symptomatic second-degree utero-vaginal prolapse. Post-operatively she develops right-sided loin pain, haematuria, and a rising serum creatinine.
(i) What post-operative complication has most likely occurred, and what is the anatomical reason it can occur during hysterectomy?
(ii) Name the specific structure injured and its relationship to the cardinal ligament.
(iii) Describe the classification of urinary fistulae based on their anatomical relation to the bladder and urethra.
(iv) In the context of surgical (iatrogenic) urinary fistula, state when repair should be carried out and describe the post-operative management after surgical repair.
questions.answerText:
(i) Post-operative complication: Ureteric injury (most likely ureterovaginal fistula or ureteric ligation/transection). During hysterectomy, the ureter is at risk because it runs in close proximity to the cardinal ligament and the uterine artery before entering the bladder. In Nigeria (and other developing countries), 5% of urinary fistulae are iatrogenic — following total abdominal hysterectomy, vaginal hysterectomy, LSCS, anterior colporrhaphy, and vaginoplasty.
(ii) Specific structure: The ureter. Its relationship to the cardinal ligament: the ureter runs in the upper part of the cardinal ligament (Mackenrodt's ligament). Similarly, in cervical leiomyoma repair, caution is required regarding the ureters and bladder.
(iii) Classification of urinary fistulae (by anatomical relation):
- Juxta-cervical: high VVF in the anterior fornix
- Mid-vaginal: lower site, no involvement of the trigone
- Juxta-urethral: involves the bladder neck; may lead to incontinence post-closure
- Circumferential: loss of the full circumference of the bladder neck and urethra
- Compound: massive VVF; loss of trigone and intramural terminal ureters
- Vesico-uterine: no communication with the vagina; leakage through the portio vaginalis of the cervix
- Urethrovaginal: isolated VVF secondary to surgical injury
(iv) Timing and post-operative management of surgical repair:
For operative injury — repair immediately when symptoms appear immediately; for ischaemic necrosis — delay repair 2–3 months, when effects of trauma and superadded infection have subsided.
Post-operative management: free drainage for 14 days; hourly intake/output chart (if hourly output less than 50 cc, inform the doctor); 2-hourly turning of patient side to side; monitor vital signs; analgesics; parenteral antibiotics; twice-weekly CSU for M/C/S. Remove catheter on 14th day and institute bladder drill; no sexual intercourse for 3 months post-repair; all future deliveries by elective LSCS.

questions.question:
Describe the origin, course, and embryological significance of the Mullerian ducts; explain the clinical basis for why Mullerian anomalies present differently from gonadal dysgenesis; and distinguish between two related anomalies of septate uterus and uterus didelphys.

A(i) Describe the normal development of the Mullerian (paramesonephric) ducts, listing all structures they contribute to and noting what they do NOT form. State the approximate incidence of Mullerian duct anomalies and the proportion that are asymptomatic.
A(ii) Explain the clinical basis for why MRKH syndrome presents without cyclical pain, and contrast the presentation with imperforate hymen.
B(i) Distinguish between septate uterus and uterus didelphys under the headings: fusion event, external uterine contour, cervices, vaginal findings, and best diagnostic approach.
B(ii) State the investigation most essential for confirming Mullerian duct anomalies and explain how it differentiates anomalies when combined with laparoscopy.
questions.answerText:
A(i) The Mullerian ducts fuse in the midline to form the uterus, cervix, and upper two-thirds of the vagina. The lateral unfused portions remain patent as the fallopian tubes. The ovaries are NOT derived from the Mullerian ducts; they develop from the gonadal ridge (genital ridge) of the intermediate mesoderm. In females, the Wolffian ducts regress passively in the absence of androgens. Mullerian duct anomalies occur in approximately 0.5% of the general female population. Approximately 75% of cases are asymptomatic and discovered incidentally; 25% present with primary amenorrhoea, dysmenorrhoea, pelvic mass, or obstetric complications.

A(ii) In MRKH there is agenesis or hypoplasia of the vagina and uterus, so no functional endometrium exists; therefore no cyclical pain occurs despite primary amenorrhoea. Normal secondary sexual characteristics and normal ovarian function are present (46,XX karyotype). By contrast, imperforate hymen produces cyclical pain because a functional endometrium is present; menstrual blood accumulates (haematocolpos) causing pressure-related cyclical pain and a visible bluish introital bulge.

B(i) Septate uterus: incomplete resorption of the fused midline septum after Mullerian duct fusion; external uterine contour is NORMAL; single cervix; no vaginal septum. Uterus didelphys: complete failure of Mullerian duct fusion; two completely separate uteri; two cervices; often a longitudinal vaginal septum; associated with dyspareunia from vaginal septum.

B(ii) Hysterosalpingography (HSG) is the primary imaging investigation, delineating the uterine cavity and tubal patency. Combined with laparoscopy (which shows the external uterine contour), it differentiates septate uterus (normal external contour with internal septum) from bicornuate uterus (bifid external contour). MRI is increasingly used as a non-invasive alternative providing excellent soft tissue detail of both internal and external anatomy.

(i) Most likely diagnosis: Dysgerminoma. Macroscopic: solid tumours with a smooth or nodular, bosselated external surface; soft or rubbery in consistency depending on the proportion of fibrous tissue; may reach considerable size (mean diameter 15 cm). Microscopic: the female counterpart of testicular seminoma; spread mainly by lymphatics; approximately 10% are bilateral — alone among malignant germ tumours in having a significant incidence of bilaterality.

(ii) Dysgerminomas account for 2–5% of all primary malignant ovarian tumours. Nearly all occur in women less than 30 years old. Risk factors from the lectures: karyotype 45,XO increases the risk of dysgerminoma and gonadoblastoma. Elements of immature teratoma, yolk sac tumour or choriocarcinoma are found in about 10% of dysgerminomas; the presence of these more malignant cell elements indicates a worse prognosis.

(iii) Pre-operative management: IV access, fluid resuscitation if needed; full blood count, serum urea, electrolytes and creatinine, liver function tests, blood group and crossmatch. Specific investigations required before treatment: chest X-ray, CT scan, serum AFP and beta-hCG must be assayed to exclude the ominous presence of elements of choriocarcinoma, endodermal sinus tumour or teratoma. LDH is also produced by ovarian germ cell tumours and may be elevated.

(iv) Definitive treatment: Pure dysgerminomas have a good prognosis; 75% are Stage I (most being Stage Ia). For a young woman wishing to preserve fertility: conservative surgery — unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy is appropriate for Stage Ia disease. Biopsy of the contralateral ovary may be considered.
Radiotherapy: dysgerminoma is radiosensitive, and radiotherapy has historically been effective; however, it impairs fertility.
Chemotherapy: for Stage I malignant dysgerminomas and other germ cell tumours, close follow-up may be appropriate without further treatment. For remaining stages, chemotherapy (BEP — cisplatin, bleomycin and etoposide) has replaced radiotherapy, particularly when there is a wish to preserve fertility; short courses of BEP are curative in 90% of patients without adverse features.
questions.question:
A 19-year-old woman presents with a three-month history of right lower abdominal discomfort and increasing abdominal girth. Ultrasound confirms a large, solid right ovarian mass. Serum AFP is normal; serum beta-hCG is mildly elevated. Her karyotype is 46,XX.

(i) What is the most likely diagnosis? Describe the macroscopic and microscopic appearance of this tumour.
(ii) State the risk factors and aetiological associations for dysgerminoma, and what percentage of all primary malignant ovarian tumours it accounts for.
(iii) What is the resuscitative and pre-operative management required, and what investigations must be performed prior to treatment?
(iv) What is the definitive treatment for a young woman wishing to preserve fertility, and what is the role of radiotherapy versus chemotherapy?

questions.answerText:
(i) Most likely diagnosis: gonorrhoea (pelvic inflammatory disease secondary to Neisseria gonorrhoeae). Causative organism: Neisseria gonorrhoea—gram negative intracellular diplococci, oxidase positive. Swabs from: urethral, endocervix, anal canal, and pharynx. Microscopy: intracellular gram negative diplococcus. Culture: Thayer-Martin or Stuart medium. Non-specific (chlamydial) infection should also be sought by tissue culture, serology (ELISA, polymerase chain reaction, direct fluorescent antibody test).
(ii) Complications of gonorrhoea in women: PID; infertility; ectopic pregnancy; chronic pelvic pain; urethral stricture. Disseminated complications: arthritis; endocarditis; meningitis; perihepatitis (Fitz-Hugh Curtis Syndrome). In children exposed during delivery: conjunctivitis, corneal ulceration, opacification, and blindness.
(iii) Treatment approach—single dose therapy options: Cap Amoxycillin 3g stat; Cap Ampicillin 3.5g stat + oral Probenecid 1gm given 30 minutes earlier; Procain penicillin 4.8 million units i.m. given at two sites; i.m. ceftriaxone 250mg + Cap tetracycline 500mg qds for 7 days or doxycycline 100mg twice daily for 7 days; Spectinomycin (Togamycin) 2g stat; Erythromycin in penicillin allergy.
(iv) Drug resistance is a major barrier to effective treatment. Resistance exists to: penicillin; spectinomycin; tetracycline; third-generation cephalosporins; quinolones. There is a need for constant drug susceptibility tests and constant monitoring. This makes single-agent empirical treatment less reliable and may necessitate combination regimens.
(v) Prevention strategies: health education; modification of risk behaviour; use of barrier contraception (condom)—provides greater protection against STDs than any other method of contraception; prompt and adequate treatment; contact tracing—screen and give appropriate treatment to all sexual partners.
questions.question:
A 25-year-old nulliparous woman presents with a 3-day history of purulent vaginal discharge, dysuria, and lower abdominal pain. She has had two sexual partners in the last 3 months. Examination reveals Bartholinitis and cervical excitation tenderness. High vaginal and endocervical swabs are taken.

(i) What is the most likely diagnosis, and which organisms should be sought on microscopy and culture?
(ii) What are the complications of this infection in women if left untreated?
(iii) What is the single-dose treatment approach for the most likely causative bacterial STI?
(iv) How does this infection contribute to the problem of drug resistance, and what are the implications for management?
(v) What is the definitive strategy to prevent transmission to partners and the community?

questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Complete hydatidiform mole.
Predisposing factors: girls <20 or women >40 years of age; low socioeconomic status; malnutrition; previous spontaneous abortion; previous hydatidiform mole (incidence of repeat molar pregnancy is 4–5 times higher); nutritional deficiencies of protein or animal fat, carotene and folic acid; ABO blood group — group A women with group O husbands, poor prognosis in group AB.

(ii) Complete vs Partial mole:
- Karyotype: Complete mole mainly 46XX (90%), occasionally 46XX or 46XY from dispermic fertilisation (10%). Partial mole usually triploid (XXX 40%, XXY 58%, XYY 2%).
- Trophoblastic hyperplasia: Complete — marked, significant hyperplasia/anaplasia; Partial — minimal to moderate.
- Fetal tissue: Complete — no cord, amnion or fetus; Partial — fetal parts seen.
- Malignant potential: Complete — 15–20%, forms 2–3% choriocarcinoma; Partial — minimal.

(iii) Management:
Evacuation: Suction curettage under GA (treatment of choice); oxytocin drip commenced prior to evacuation; laparotomy set-up as intervention may be required; hysterectomy is an alternative for patients with complete families (malignant sequelae <5%).
Post-evacuation baseline: CXR, FBC, clotting profile, LFTs, renal function, HCG assay, pelvic examination.
Follow-up: Serial weekly then monthly serum hCG; pelvic examination at every visit; CXR if metastases seen.
Contraception required throughout follow-up; avoid pregnancy for at least one year after disappearance of signs/symptoms.
Criteria for active therapy (chemotherapy): Rising or plateauing hCG for 3 consecutive weeks; histological evidence of choriocarcinoma; trophoblastic activity 1 month after normal pregnancy or non-molar abortion; urinary hCG >20,000 or serum hCG >30,000 IU/ml at 4 weeks post-evacuation.
questions.question:
A 22-year-old woman, 14 weeks by dates, presents with abnormal vaginal bleeding, severe hyperemesis and a uterus that is much larger than expected for dates. Her blood pressure is 150/100 mmHg. Ultrasound shows a diffuse mixed echogenic pattern with no fetal parts visible. Serum beta-hCG is markedly elevated.

(i) What is the diagnosis? State the predisposing factors for this condition as described in the lectures.
(ii) Describe the pathophysiology of this condition, distinguishing complete from partial forms under the headings of karyotype, trophoblastic hyperplasia, presence of fetal tissue, and malignant potential.
(iii) Outline the complete management of this patient from evacuation to follow-up, including the criteria that mandate active (chemotherapy) treatment.

A(i) Ovarian artery: the arterial supply is directly from the abdominal aorta; the ovarian arteries arise from the abdominal aorta and supply the ovaries via the infundibulo-pelvic ligament (suspensory ligament of the ovary), reaching the ovary through the mesovarium at the hilum; the ovarian artery also anastomoses with the uterine artery through the ovarian branch. Clinical significance: the high origin from the aorta means the infundibulopelvic ligament contains the ovarian vessels; these vessels are ligated during oophorectomy or salpingo-oophorectomy; the proximity of the ureter (which lies posterior to the ovary in the ovarian fossa) means care must be taken not to injure it during surgery.

A(ii) Venous drainage: the right ovarian vein drains into the inferior vena cava; the left ovarian vein drains into the left renal vein. Luteal cysts are less common than follicular cysts and are more likely to present with intraperitoneal bleeding especially on the right side, due to increased intraluminal pressure secondary to ovarian vein anatomy; the right ovarian vein's more direct and shorter course into the IVC (compared with the left draining at right angles into the left renal vein) results in higher intraluminal pressure on the right side, predisposing to rupture of right-sided luteal cysts and intraperitoneal bleeding. Corpora lutea are not called luteal cysts unless they are more than 3 cm in diameter; may also rupture especially on days 20–26 of the cycle.

B(i) Follicular cyst: pathogenesis — due to enlargement of one or more follicles which fail to rupture, or failure of atresia in non-dominant follicles; can persist for several menstrual cycles; may achieve a diameter of up to 10 cm; lined by granulosa cells. Associations: anovulatory cycles; fertility drugs (including clomiphene — seldom more than 5 cm in diameter except when due to overdosage with clomiphene or HMG); polycystic ovary syndrome; may continue to produce oestrogen, causing menstrual disturbance and endometrial hyperplasia. Clinical features: majority are asymptomatic; pain (usually mild but sometimes severe) is due to rupture or haemorrhage into the cyst; if unilateral pain is accompanied by slight menstrual disturbance, ectopic pregnancy must be excluded. Management: if ovarian enlargement estimated at 4–6 cm — perform pelvic ultrasound; if presumed diagnosis is 'cystic ovary' rather than neoplasm, no immediate action is necessary; re-examine in 2 weeks — a follicular cyst will usually have disappeared; if unchanged or larger, further investigation (e.g. laparoscopy) is warranted; if discovered or confirmed by laparoscopy, the cysts can be aspirated — laparotomy is not necessary; send fluid for cytology; treat any underlying condition; smaller cysts are more likely to resolve; follow-up with 6-monthly ultrasound and CA-125.

B(ii) Theca-lutein cyst: pathogenesis — corpus luteum becomes cystic and persists in a functional state for longer than normal, or the granulosa and theca cells of a follicular cyst become luteinised; may also result from atretic ovarian follicles stimulated by abnormally high levels of hCG. Associations: characteristically associated with trophoblastic tumours (hydatidiform mole, choriocarcinoma) due to hCG stimulation; may also occur in pregnancies complicated by hyperplacentosis (multiple pregnancy); theca-lutein cysts greater than 6 cm are a marker for high-risk hydatidiform mole. Clinical features: characteristically, short periods of amenorrhoea are followed by heavier than usual uterine bleeding; the endometrium is secretory; multiple and sometimes moderately large theca-lutein cysts; complications include haemorrhage and torsion. Management: usually conservative as cysts regress when hCG levels fall after treatment of the underlying condition. Distinction from a simple corpus luteum cyst: a corpus luteum is not called a luteal cyst unless it is more than 3 cm in diameter; theca-lutein cysts are specifically associated with abnormally high hCG levels (GTD) and are typically bilateral and multiple, whereas a simple luteal cyst results from failure of the corpus luteum to regress after 14 days and is typically unilateral.

questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Torsion of an ovarian cyst. The cyst rotates on its pedicle causing occlusion of venous return and eventually arterial supply, leading to ischaemia, infarction and the acute pain.

(ii) The commonest cyst undergoing torsion in young women is the dermoid cyst (mature cystic teratoma), a germ cell tumour arising from totipotential germ cells and containing elements of all three germ layers — ectodermal elements predominate (lined by stratified squamous epithelium with hair, sebaceous and sweat glands, teeth, neural tissue, cartilage). It is bilateral in 10% of cases.

(iii) Resuscitative measures:
- Intravenous access and fluid resuscitation
- Adequate analgesia (e.g. morphine, pethidine or pentazocine)
- Nil by mouth in preparation for surgery
- Blood group and crossmatch, full blood count, urea and electrolytes
- Monitor pulse, blood pressure and urine output

(iv) Definitive treatment is laparotomy. If the ovary is viable, the cyst is untwisted and cystectomy performed. If the ovary is infarcted, oophorectomy is necessary. The decision to conserve depends on the viability of the ovarian tissue at the time of surgery.
questions.question:
A 28-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with sudden severe right iliac fossa pain of one hour's duration, accompanied by mild nausea and vomiting. On examination she is in mild distress; the lower abdomen is tender with guarding, and bimanual examination reveals a tender adnexal mass on the right. Ultrasound confirms an ovarian cyst.

(i) What is the most likely diagnosis, and what pathological process underlies it?
(ii) Describe the embryological/tissue origin of the most common type of ovarian cyst that undergoes this complication in young women, and state its bilateral incidence.
(iii) What immediate resuscitative measures should be instituted?
(iv) What is the definitive treatment, and what determines whether the ovary can be conserved?

questions.answerText:
A(i) Genetic risk factors: Family history is present in 5–10% of women with epithelial ovarian cancers (usually serous adenocarcinomas). A woman with one affected relative has a lifetime risk of 2.5%, which is twice the general population risk. With two affected relatives, lifetime risk increases to 30–40%. Most of these families also have breast or colorectal cancer. The defective gene most commonly is the tumour suppressor gene BRCA1 (81%), on chromosome 17; BRCA2 is defective in about 14%, on chromosome 13. These mutations are inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion. BRCA1 mutations increase risk of ovarian cancer to 40% and breast cancer risk to 80%.

A(ii) Non-genetic factors: nulliparity; early menarche; late age at menopause; a long estimated number of years of ovulation (incessant ovulation theory); unopposed oestrogen HRT; infertility treatment; high social class (excess mortality class I over V); asbestos/talc exposure (unproven); high-fat diet.
Protective factors: oral contraceptive use reduces risk four-fold (greatest reduction with 4–6 years use, persists after discontinuation); pregnancy (each pregnancy provides 10–15% additional risk reduction); breastfeeding; tubal ligation (50–70% risk reduction).

B(i) Ovarian cancer presents late because it is hidden within the pelvis, gives vague or no symptoms early in its course, and is often attributed to 'indigestion' or 'middle age spread'. They are often found accidentally; if malignant, disease has commonly spread outside the ovary before diagnosis. The two most common presenting complaints are: (1) abdominal pain or discomfort (commonest); (2) distension or feeling a lump (next most frequent).

B(ii) Bimanual examination findings suggesting malignancy: hard, fixed, irregular pelvic mass; bilateral tumours (75% of malignant tumours are bilateral vs 15% of benign); presence of ascites (usually sign of peritoneal metastasis, especially if blood-stained); nodularity in the pouch of Douglas; oedema of legs and vulva suggesting venous obstruction.

C) FIGO staging:
Stage I — Growth limited to the ovaries: Ia: one ovary, no ascites, capsule intact, no surface tumour. Ib: both ovaries, no ascites, capsule intact. Ic: Ia or Ib plus surface tumour, ruptured capsule, or ascites with malignant cells.
Stage II — Extension to the pelvis: IIa: uterus or fallopian tubes; IIb: other pelvic tissues; IIc: IIa or IIb plus findings as in Ic.
Stage III — Peritoneal implants outside pelvis or retroperitoneal/inguinal nodes: IIIa: microscopic metastasis on abdominal peritoneal surfaces; IIIb: tumour metastasis <2 cm; IIIc: tumour metastasis >2 cm or metastatic disease in pelvic, para-aortic or inguinal nodes.
Stage IV — Distant metastatic disease: malignant pleural effusion (must have positive cytology), pulmonary parenchymal metastasis, liver or splenic parenchymal metastasis (not surface implant), metastasis to supraclavicular lymph nodes or skin.

A(i) Genetic risk factors including BRCA1 and BRCA2, stating the chromosomal locations, mode of inheritance, and the specific lifetime risk figures for one and two first-degree relatives
A(ii) Non-genetic aetiological factors associated with epithelial ovarian cancer, and the factors that are protective
