Describe the origin, course, relations, and clinical significance of the endometrial vascular supply; state the pharmacological approach that safely interrupts haemostasis; and explain the anatomical basis of the menstrual disturbance that follows disruption of normal haemostatic mechanisms.

A(i) Describe the vascular supply to the endometrium, naming the arteries, the unique feature of the spiral arterioles, and their hormonal control.
A(ii) Describe the two-phase haemostatic mechanism that arrests bleeding in the spiral arterioles during menstruation, and explain how each phase may fail to produce menorrhagia.
B(i) Explain the role of prostaglandins in normal and abnormal menstruation: state which prostaglandin mediates vasoconstriction at menstruation and how prostaglandin imbalance in DUB worsens menorrhagia.
B(ii) State the objective test used in research to measure total menstrual blood loss, describe its methodology, and state the upper limit of normal MBL it helped establish.
questions.answerText:
A(i) The endometrium is supplied by branches of the uterine artery (a branch of the internal iliac artery). The basalis is supplied by basal arterioles that are not shed. The functionalis is supplied by spiral arterioles, which are unique to the functionalis layer and are under direct hormonal control — oestrogen promotes their development during the proliferative phase and progesterone maintains their structure in the secretory phase. Withdrawal of hormonal support at the end of the luteal phase triggers vasoconstriction of the spiral arterioles leading to endometrial shedding.

A(ii) Phase 1 (primary haemostasis): within the first 24 hours of menstruation, plugs of aggregated platelets and fibrin form to temporarily arrest blood flow in the spiral arterioles. Phase 2 (secondary haemostasis/vascular closure): vasoconstriction of the spiral arterioles with swelling of endothelial cells completely occludes the vessels for more durable haemostasis. Failure of Phase 1 (platelet dysfunction) produces menorrhagia from impaired primary haemostasis. Failure of Phase 2 (abnormal vasoreactivity) produces menorrhagia from inadequate vasoconstriction.

B(i) PGF2a (prostaglandin F2 alpha) mediates vasoconstriction of spiral arterioles initiating menstruation. In DUB, endometrial eicosanoid imbalance produces excess PGE2/prostacyclin relative to PGF2a/thromboxane; PGE2 promotes vasodilatation and inhibits platelet aggregation, worsening menorrhagia. This prostaglandin imbalance is a primary disturbance in endometrial eicosanoid metabolism forming part of the aetiopathogenesis of DUB.

B(ii) The alkaline haematin test is the reference standard for objectively measuring menstrual blood loss in research settings. Methodology: all sanitary products (pads, tampons) used during a menstrual period are collected; haemoglobin extracted from these products is converted to alkaline haematin and measured spectrophotometrically to calculate total MBL. This method confirmed the upper limit of normal MBL as 79 mls per cycle (Hallberg et al., 1966); menorrhagia is defined as MBL exceeding 80 mls per cycle.

(i) Risk factors for STIs and pelvic complications: multiple sexual partners, history of ectopic pregnancy, previous pelvic infection. Contraindications to combined oral contraceptives: she smokes more than 15 cigarettes per day, is over 30, and has a history of hypertension and cardiovascular risk, which are contraindications related to an increased risk of circulatory-system disease, particularly venous thrombosis, ischaemic heart disease, cerebrovascular disorders, and hypertension. History of ectopic pregnancy is a relative contraindication to IUCD.
(ii) The most appropriate emergency contraceptive method is insertion of a copper-containing IUCD (not Mirena). An IUD can be inserted as a form of emergency contraception as late as five days after the unprotected episode of sex. The success rate is variable and is not 100 per cent. Mirena cannot be used for post-coital contraception; only standard IUDs are suitable.
(iii) Complications to warn about: PAINS danger signs—Period late (pregnancy) or abnormal spotting/bleeding; Abdominal pain or pain during intercourse; Infection or abnormal vaginal discharge; Not feeling well, fever or chills; String missing, shorter, or longer. Specific risks include an increased risk of PID within the first 3 months of insertion (may be related to transfer of vaginal flora into the uterine cavity); women who become pregnant with an IUCD in place have a higher risk of spontaneous abortion; women who become pregnant while using an IUCD are at a greater risk of having a tubal (ectopic) pregnancy.
(iv) Long-term options available: progestin-only injectable (DMPA 150mg every 3 months or NET-EN 200mg every 2 months), progestin-only oral pills (minipills), or contraceptive implants. Progestin-only methods are most suitable for her because the contraindications to combined oral contraceptives (smoking, hypertension, age over 35) do not apply to progestogen-only contraceptives, which contain no oestrogen. Most criteria restricting use of oral contraceptives do not apply to progestogen-only contraceptives.

questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia Grade 3 (CIN 3) — severe dysplasia/carcinoma-in-situ. Under the Bethesda classification this falls under High-Grade Squamous Intraepithelial Lesion (HSIL), which encompasses CIN 2 and CIN 3.
(ii) Aetiological factors: (i) Sexual behaviour — age at first coitus, age at first pregnancy, multiple sexual partners; in prostitutes, STD clinic attendees, women in prison, and multiparas; rare in nuns; (ii) Race and socio-economic status — commoner in lower socio-economic groups; (iii) Smoking — more than 20 sticks per day; (iv) Vitamin deficiency — Vitamin A and folic acid; (v) Oral contraceptives; (vi) Infectious agents — Human Papilloma Virus (types 6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 35, 39, 45, 51, 52, 56, 58); HPV produces oncoproteins which initiate malignant transformation; (vii) Male factor — higher risk in wives of long-distance drivers; increased risk in wives of men with prostatic/penile cancers.
(iii) Pathological features of CIN 3/severe dysplasia: Nuclei are enlarged and darkly staining; loss of polarity; abnormal cells in the upper, middle, and lower thirds of the epithelium. Carcinoma-in-situ: all or most of the epithelium shows cellular features of carcinoma without invasion of the underlying stroma; orderly stratification is lacking; the lesion involves the glands. Mitoses (both normal and abnormal) are seen; disparity in cytoplasm ratio; keratinisation may be found.
Natural history if untreated: 18% progress to invasion over 10 years; 36% progress to invasion over 20 years. Immediate treatment is recommended for CIN 3.
(iv) Management:
Colposcopy mandatory for all patients with abnormal smears.
If no colposcopy available — cone biopsy is mandatory.
If transformation zone cannot be fully visualised at colposcopy — excisional cone biopsy.
Treatment modalities:
- Cryotherapy: destroys by freezing; depth of destruction 3–4 mm; healing in 6–8 weeks; minimal discomfort as outpatient; complications rare. Success = three consecutive negative smears at 3-monthly intervals.
- Electrocautery: destroys by heat; depth 2–3 mm; requires regional or general anaesthesia; complications — excessive bleeding, cervical stenosis, acute pelvic infection.
- Electrodiathermy: destroys by heat; depth up to 1.5 cm; similar complications.
- Cold coagulator: thermal probe at 100°C for approximately 20 seconds.
- Laser therapy: no anaesthesia required; healing rapid (10–12 days); depth of destruction 5–7 mm.
- Cone biopsy: tissue available for histological examination; colposcopically directed reduces complications.
- Hysterectomy: recurrence of intraepithelial or invasive neoplasia less than 1%.
Residual and recurrence rates are at least 5% for all methods except hysterectomy.
Follow-up: 3-monthly intervals following treatment; three consecutive negative smears = cure. After treatment: 6 weeks, then 3-monthly for 2 years, then 6-monthly for 2 years, then yearly for life.
questions.question:

She is sexually active with multiple partners, smokes 25 cigarettes per day, and uses the oral contraceptive pill. She has no symptoms. Colposcopy reveals an acetowhite lesion with abnormal vascular patterns at the transformation zone.
(i) What is the diagnosis, and how does the Bethesda classification apply to this finding?
(ii) List all the aetiological factors for CIN, including the role of HPV subtypes.
(iii) Describe the pathological features (microscopy) of severe dysplasia/CIN 3, and the natural history if untreated.
(iv) Outline the full management of an abnormal Pap smear and CIN 3, including all treatment modalities with their depths of destruction and follow-up criteria.

questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Mucinous cystadenocarcinoma with pseudomyxoma peritonei. Mucinous cystadenocarcinoma accounts for 10–20% of epithelial ovarian tumours and 10% of the malignant tumours of the ovary. It is bilateral in only 10% of cases (usually unilateral). It is notably large — average size 16–17 cm; some may reach up to 150 lbs (enormous dimensions; cyst diameter of 25 cm is quite common). Usually multilocular, thin-walled cysts with a smooth external surface containing mucinous fluid.

(ii) Anatomical structures affected: local peritoneal spread to the omentum, surfaces of small and large bowels, parietal peritoneum throughout the abdominal cavity, and on the surface of the diaphragm. Lymphatic spread to pelvic and para-aortic nodes. Pseudomyxoma peritonei: follows rupture of a mucinous tumour of the ovary; the tumour continues to secrete mucin into the peritoneal cavity even after removal of the primary; mucin continues to accumulate. It significantly increases mortality (mortality 50%).

(iii) Surgical staging procedure: a vertical incision (midline or paramedian) is required for adequate exploration of the upper abdomen. Procedure: sample of ascitic fluid or peritoneal washings for cytology; full pelvic and abdominal exploration; total abdominal hysterectomy; bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy; infracolic omentectomy; appendicectomy (particularly important as the appendix may be a source of mucinous tumour or may be involved); peritoneal biopsies; pelvic and para-aortic lymph node biopsies; remove all visible tumour deposits (optimal debulking surgery).

(iv) Post-operative treatment: adjuvant chemotherapy for Stage II–IV disease; platinum drugs (cisplatin or carboplatin) are the most effective drugs in general use; paclitaxel is part of standard treatment given in combination with cisplatin or carboplatin; given for five or six cycles at three- to four-weekly intervals. Five-year survival for mucinous tumours specifically at Stage III is not well defined; the overall 5-year survival for Stage III epithelial ovarian cancer is 23–41%.
questions.question:

(i) What is the diagnosis? Name the tumour type, state its frequency among malignant ovarian tumours, its typical size, and whether it is usually unilateral or bilateral.
(ii) Describe the anatomical structures affected by the spread of this tumour and explain why pseudomyxoma peritonei occurs and what it does to mortality.
(iii) What is the procedure for surgical staging, including the specific incision type and the structures that must be removed or sampled?
(iv) What post-operative treatment is given, and what is the five-year survival for this tumour type at Stage III?

questions.answerText:
A(i) Epithelial tumours: derive from the surface epithelium (coelomic epithelium/mesothelium) overlying the embryonic gonadal ridge; they are essentially mesothelial in nature; may develop along endocervical pathways (mucinous cystadenomata), endometrial pathways (endometrioid cystadenomata), tubal pathways (serous cystadenomata), or uroepithelial lines (Brenner's tumour); most common group of tumours — 85–95% of ovarian cancers; predominantly affect post-menopausal women; mainly affects women between 40 and 60 years; average age at diagnosis approximately 50; CA-125 is the main marker (elevated in 80% of non-mucinous epithelial tumours, cut-off 35 u/ml); CA 19-9 also expressed by most mucinous ovarian tumours; CEA expressed by malignant mucinous tumour (100%); PLAP (serous and endometrioid tumours); alpha amylase (serous and endometrioid tumours); MCSF (along with CA-125 helps in early diagnosis of epithelial tumours); TATS (in mucinous carcinoma); GAT (used to differentiate from endometriosis). Management: staging laparotomy, TAH, BSO, infracolic omentectomy, platinum-based chemotherapy.

A(ii) Germ cell tumours: arise from totipotential germ cells; tend to occur in the second and third decades; produce biological tumour markers (AFP and hCG). Dysgerminoma: female counterpart of seminoma; 2–5% of all primary malignant ovarian tumours; nearly all in women less than 30 years; mainly unilateral (85–90%); rubbery, smooth, rounded with thin capsule; markers: hCG (±), LDH, PLAP; radiosensitive; treatment — unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy in young women; BEP chemotherapy. Endodermal sinus tumour (yolk sac tumour): 10–20% of germ cell tumours; extremely rapid growth; mainly unilateral; marker: AFP (elevated) — widely used in diagnosis, monitoring, and follow-up; treatment — oophorectomy plus BEP (curative in 90%). Immature teratoma: unilateral in almost all cases; solid masses; marker: AFP (±); degree of malignancy related to maturity of component tissues; treatment — oophorectomy in young women; BEP chemotherapy. Choriocarcinoma (ovarian, non-gestational): rare; marker: hCG; lower hCG levels than gestational; may cause precocious puberty, uterine bleeding, or amenorrhoea. Embryonal carcinoma: very rare in pure form; marker: hCG (±). Mixed germ cell: AFP (±) and hCG (±). Management priority for germ cell tumours: conservative surgery preferred in young women to preserve fertility; specialist referral because of rarity and sensitivity to intensive chemotherapy.

B(i) Sex cord stromal tumours: stromal cells retain potential for differentiation into cells arising from gonadal mesenchyme — granulosa, theca, Leydig, and Sertoli cells; these rare tumours may therefore secrete any or all of the ovarian steroids; occur at any age from pre-pubertal children to elderly postmenopausal women. Feminising (oestrogen-producing) tumours — granulosa-theca cell group: cause precocious puberty before the menarche; cystic glandular hyperplasia in menstruating women; postmenopausal bleeding in older women; granulosa cell tumours usually secrete inhibin (used to monitor effects of treatment); thecoma — usually benign; fibroma — benign but noted for Meigs syndrome (ascites and pleural effusion). Virilising (androgen-producing) tumours — Sertoli-Leydig cell group: initially defeminisation including secondary amenorrhoea, then hirsuitism, enlargement of the clitoris, and deepening of the voice; half of Sertoli-Leydig cell neoplasms produce male hormones causing virilisation. Management: surgical treatment is the same as for epithelial tumours — TAH, BSO in older women; unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy may be justifiable in young women with localised disease; granulosa cell tumours can recur up to 20 years after initial diagnosis; 5-year survival around 80% overall; chemotherapy in advanced or recurrent cases; radiotherapy largely replaced by chemotherapy.

B(ii) Distinction between primary and secondary (metastatic) ovarian tumours: secondary ovarian tumours account for up to 25% of all ovarian malignancies; they mimic primary ovarian cancer; usually present as bilateral adnexal masses, smooth, bosselated, solid, and mobile; Krukenberg tumours — carcinomas of the stomach metastasising to both ovaries (or other GIT cancers); other primaries that metastasise to the ovary: breast, colon, endometrium, lymphoma. Distinguishing features of Krukenberg tumours: bilateral; smooth, bosselated, solid, and mobile; the primary is in the stomach or other GIT organ; represent up to 25% of all ovarian malignancies; features mimicking primary ovarian cancer. Primary ovarian tumours are usually unilateral initially (bilaterality in only 15% of benign and 75% of malignant primary tumours); histological examination is the definitive distinguishing method — Krukenberg tumours show signet-ring cells on histology; management requires addressing the primary tumour as well as the ovarian metastases.
questions.question:
Describe the classification of ovarian tumours according to cell of origin and relate each class to the age group most commonly affected, the specific tumour markers produced, and the management priorities.
A(i) Epithelial tumours: derivation, predominant age group, and markers.
A(ii) Germ cell tumours: derivation, predominant age group, tumour markers for each type, and management priorities.
B(i) Sex cord stromal tumours: derivation, hormones produced, clinical effects (feminising versus virilising), and management.
B(ii) Distinguish between primary and secondary (metastatic) ovarian tumours, giving examples of primaries that metastasise to the ovary and the distinguishing features of Krukenberg tumours.

A 50-year-old perimenopausal multiparous woman presents with a chronic, heavy offensive vaginal discharge and intermenstrual bleeding. On speculum examination a bright red, velvety area is seen around the external os, and pap smear shows Grade II (infections/inflammation). Colposcopy shows the lesion to be aceto-negative and well-defined at the transformation zone.
(i) What is the most likely diagnosis, and how does it differ pathologically from CIN?
(ii) Describe the clinical and pathological features of benign cervical diseases that can produce similar-appearing lesions on the cervix (cervical ectropion, cervical erosion, cervicitis).
(iii) What investigation algorithm should be followed for this woman?
(iv) Outline the management of each benign cervical lesion: acute cervicitis, chronic cervicitis, cervical erosion, and cervical ectropion.
questions.answerText:
(i) Most likely diagnosis: Cervical ectropion (eversion of columnar epithelium onto the ectocervix) or cervical erosion. This is benign and differs from CIN in that there are no dysplastic cellular changes — the acetowhite test is negative, colposcopy shows a regular vascular pattern, and biopsy would not show nuclear atypia or loss of polarity. CIN involves: nuclei that are enlarged, irregular, and darkly stained; loss of polarity; mitoses (both normal and abnormal); keratinisation; disparity in cytoplasm ratio; replacement of varying thicknesses of the epithelium by atypical cells.
(ii) Benign cervical lesions:
Cervical erosion: replacement of ectocervical stratified squamous epithelium by endocervical columnar epithelium (eversion). Seen at birth, puberty, in patients on OCP, during pregnancy, and puerperium. Features: often no symptoms; mucoid discharge; brown intermenstrual discharge or slight post-coital bleeding. Investigation: cervical cytology; colposcopy and biopsy.
Cervical ectropion: eversion of the cervical lips following bilateral lacerations. Features: often no symptoms; mucoid discharge; cervical incompetence — mid-trimester abortion, premature delivery.
Acute cervicitis: originating organisms — gonococci, chlamydia, herpes simplex, HPV; predisposing factors: childbirth, sexual intercourse, surgery. Features: vaginal discharge, pruritus, cervical and pelvic discomfort, dyspareunia; reddening and swelling of the cervix with discharge from the os.
Chronic cervicitis: organisms mostly from the vagina following damage. Features: persistent leucorrhoea (thick, viscid, whitish or mucopurulent); post-coital bleeding; lower abdominal discomfort; dyspareunia.
(iii) Investigation algorithm: Cervical cytology (Pap smear); colposcopy (with 3–5% acetic acid and/or Lugol's iodine); colposcopically directed biopsy if an abnormal area is identified; bacteriological examination; and M/C/S of discharge.
(iv) Management:
Acute cervicitis: culture; Pap smear; local cream/suppositories; oral/parenteral antibiotics.
Chronic cervicitis: antibiotics (especially in infertility cases); cryotherapy; thermal cauterisation; laser ablation. Complications of treatment: haemorrhage, infection, cervical fibrosis/stenosis.
Cervical erosion: nil treatment if asymptomatic; remove cause (e.g. stop OCP if applicable); thermal cauterisation; cryosurgery; laser ablation.
Cervical ectropion: Trachelorrhaphy.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old married woman presents to the family planning clinic requesting a long-term reversible contraceptive. She has two children, is currently breastfeeding her 4-month-old infant, and has a history of hypertension and valvular heart disease. On examination, she is well, BP 145/92 mmHg, with no pelvic tenderness.

(i) What is the most appropriate contraceptive method for this woman, and what is the embryologic/pharmacologic basis for its contraceptive action?
(ii) What specific contraindications must be considered before prescribing this method in her case?
(iii) Describe the steps involved in inserting this device.
(iv) What are the danger signs she should be counselled to watch for during use?
(v) What is the definitive management if she develops acute pelvic inflammatory disease with this device in situ?
questions.answerText:
(i) An IUCD (specifically a copper-containing device such as the Copper T380A) is appropriate. The anti-fertility effects originate within the uterus and include: local sterile foreign body reaction interfering with decidualization, production of embryotoxic substances (mobilisation of polymorphonuclear leukocytes and macrophages forming a barrier preventing implantation), retardation of sperm transport, increased motility of the ovum in the fallopian tube, and prevention of implantation/disruption of the implanted blastocyst. Copper accentuates the foreign body reaction, releases cytolytic enzymes acting directly on the pre-implanted blastocyst, may be spermicidal, and may interfere with oestrogen uptake making the endometrium unresponsive to the blastocyst.
(ii) Absolute contraindications: acute, sub-acute or recurrent PID and known or suspected pregnancy. Relative contraindications applicable to her: valvular heart disease, history of hypertension (impaired response to infections), abnormal uterine bleeding, and cervical stenosis.
(iii) Insertion steps: take a proper history and perform full physical examination; insert Cusco's speculum; clean cervix with antiseptic solution; apply tenaculum to upper lip of cervix with gentle traction to align cervical canal with uterine cavity; introduce uterine sound slowly and gently to determine length of cervical canal and uterine cavity, confirm position of uterus, and determine intra-uterine position of inserter barrel; load IUCD into inserter barrel (pre-loading technique); insert IUCD by the withdrawal technique—retract inserter barrel over the inner plunger; ensure correct fundal placement; advise client on how to feel the strings.
(iv) Danger signs (PAINS): Period late (pregnancy), abnormal spotting or bleeding; Abdominal pain or pain during intercourse; Infection or abnormal vaginal discharge; Not feeling well, fever or chills; String missing, shorter, or longer.
(v) If acute PID occurs with the IUCD in situ, it may be severe and difficult to treat and is a strong indication for removal of the IUCD, followed by appropriate antibiotic therapy.

(i) Dyspareunia is a condition in women characterised by recurrent genital pain with sexual activity. Pain usually occurs with penetration but can occur during nonpenetrative genital stimulation as well. She exhibits: superficial dyspareunia—pain at the vaginal opening (burning, itching, stinging, or inflammation in any area of the perineum); and deep dyspareunia—deep pain inside the vagina, associated with deep pelvic thrusting.
(ii) Main causes of superficial dyspareunia: vulvovaginitis, genital herpes, atrophic vulvitis, urethral problems, episiotomy, radiation vaginitis (relevant given her cancer treatment history), and sexual trauma, as well as inadequate lubrication or topical irritants such as spermicides or latex. Main causes of deep pelvic pain: thrusting by the partner that hits an ovary during sexual intercourse, pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), pelvic or abdominal surgery, postoperative adhesions, endometriosis, genital or pelvic tumours, irritable bowel syndrome, urinary tract infection, and ovarian cysts.
(iii) Pathophysiology linking PID to deep pelvic pain: incompletely treated PID leads to chronic pelvic infection and formation of postoperative adhesions. Most tubes removed at salpingectomy have evidence of previous PID. Repeated episodes of PID can lead to chronic pelvic abscess, peritoneal adhesions, and chronic pelvic pain. Ectopic pregnancy resulting from incompletely blocked tubes is also a consequence of previous PID. Repeated pain creates a negative cycle leading to avoidance of sexual activity, lack of arousal, anorgasmia, and inhibited sexual desire (ISD).
(iv) Vaginismus is a distinct entity not addressed further here, but dyspareunia can lead to avoidance of sexual activity, lack of arousal, anorgasmia, and ISD through a negative pain cycle. Management approach: determine if there are relationship, situational, physical, or psychological issues contributing; treat or refer the client to a sex therapist, urologist, or other appropriate specialist on the basis of the underlying cause, where possible.
(v) Sexual dysfunction is the persistent or recurrent inability to react emotionally or physically to sexual stimulation in a way expected of the average healthy person or according to one's own standards of acceptable sexual response. Sexual dysfunction can occur during the desire, excitement, plateau, or orgasm stage of the sexual response cycle. Contributing factors: psychological/emotional (stress, negative body image, performance anxiety, fear of pregnancy, memory of negative sexual experiences); biological/physiological (certain medical conditions, reproductive cancers, effects of hormonal contraceptive methods); interpersonal/social (poor communication, sexual abuse). Dyspareunia is classified under physical/organic causes of sexual dysfunction affecting the excitement and desire stages.

(i) What are the two types of dyspareunia she is exhibiting, and what is the clinical definition of this condition?

(iv) What is the diagnosis and management approach for vaginismus if it develops secondarily?

questions.answerText:
A(i) Components: The external anal sphincter has a superficial portion and a deep portion; it is voluntary striated muscle. The internal anal sphincter is a thickening of the circular smooth muscle of the anal wall; it is involuntary.
A(ii) Importance in perineal repair: The anal sphincter is important during repair of third (and fourth) degree perineal laceration. During primary repair: torn edges of the retracted external anal sphincter are identified with tissue forceps and carefully united in front of the reconstructed anal canal using interrupted sutures. Interrupted non-absorbable sutures are used for the perineal skin because of the likelihood of local infection. The layers of repair proceed from the rectal wall (inner sutures tied inside the bowel lumen), anal sphincter, posterior vaginal wall, perineal body, and perineal skin.
B. Anatomical basis of partial continence: Not all lesions produce total incontinence. Women with an unhealed complete perineal tear or a low recto-vaginal fistula learn to kink the rectum forwards by contracting the pubo-coccygeus portions of the levator ani — this provides continence of formed faeces but not of flatus or liquid stools. A high RVF — where the aperture is above the pelvic floor — cannot be controlled, because the pubo-coccygeus cannot kink the rectum above its own level.
C. Primary (immediate) vs delayed repair:
Primary repair: performed within 12 hours of discovery; requires experienced surgeon, properly equipped theatre, GA or epidural; gives very good results if done soon after delivery. Pre-op — no bowel preparation for primary repair; anaesthesia: GA, spinal, or caudal; lithotomy position; repair layer by layer (rectal wall, anal sphincter, vaginal wall, perineal body, perineal skin with interrupted non-absorbable sutures).
Delayed repair: primary repair more than 12 hours is seldom successful; defer 6–8 weeks for all local sepsis to subside and tissues to return to normal. Pre-op: 3 days — empty bowel, low residue/fluid diet, nightly aperient, reduce bacterial activity with sulphonamide; hours before — saline rectal enema; more dissection required; scar tissue may need excision.
Post-op for both: confine bowel for at least 6–7 days; continue low residue diet; avoid digital examination ± liquid paraffin; antibiotics; twice-daily sitz baths; effective analgesia; remove sutures on 5th day; regular sitz baths. Future deliveries: vaginal delivery allowed with generous episiotomy (small, low RVF); all future confinements must be hospital supervised; large RVF — elective caesarean section preferred.

questions.answerText:
(i) First patient (painful vulval ulcers + matted nodes): Chancroid, caused by Haemophilus ducreyi—a gram-negative bacillus; features include multiple small shallow painful vulval ulcers and localised lymphadenopathy with suppuration. Second patient (painless sore + painless lymphadenopathy): Primary syphilis, caused by Treponema pallidum—a spirochaete, not stainable by Gram's method.
(ii) Chancroid investigations: culture on a specialised medium obtained by direct inoculation from patient. Chancroid treatment: sulfonamide group; streptomycin in resistant cases. Syphilis investigations: darkfield microscopy of specimens; silver staining; serological tests including Kahn test, Wasserman Reaction test, VDRL, Hinton and Kleine tests; more specific tests include fluorescent treponema antibody absorption test, micro-haemagglutination assay, and haemagglutination treponemal tests for syphilis. Syphilis treatment: penicillin group; erythromycin. Congenital syphilis: benzyl penicillin 6–50,000 units/kg; erythromycin if allergic to penicillin.
(iii) Long-term complications if chancroid remains untreated: localised lymphadenopathy with suppuration leading to bubo formation; rupture of bubo leads to fistula formation. (Bubo formation and fistula formation are specifically associated with LGV; chancroid instead typically causes localised lymphadenopathy and suppuration.)
(iv) Stages of syphilis: Primary syphilis—painless genital sore (chancre) and painless lymphadenopathy. Secondary syphilis—bilateral and symmetrical squamo-papular eruptions; condyloma acuminata; lymphadenopathy. Tertiary syphilis—neurosyphilis; alopecia; arthritis. Investigations confirmed by: dark field microscopy of specimens; silver staining; serological tests (Kahn test, Wasserman Reaction test, VDRL, Hinton and Kleine tests); specific tests (fluorescent treponema antibody absorption test, micro-haemagglutination assay, haemagglutination treponemal tests for syphilis).
(v) Prevention strategies common to both conditions: health education; modification of risk behaviour; barrier method of contraception (condom)—male condom provides greater protection against STDs than any other method of contraception; prompt and early treatment; contact tracing.
questions.question:

On examination, the ulcers are irregular and the lymph nodes are matted and adherent to the overlying skin. A second student from the same class presents with a painless genital sore and painless lymphadenopathy.

(ii) Compare the investigation and treatment for each condition.

A 48-year-old woman attends with a 12-month history of increasingly heavy menstrual periods with cycle lengths of 20 days and flow lasting 9 days. Bimanual examination reveals a slightly enlarged, tender uterus. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an endometrial thickness of 12 mm.

(i) Classify this woman's bleeding using correct menstrual terminology, stating the cycle-length and flow-duration abnormalities.
(ii) State the FIGO PALM-COEIN structural cause most likely to produce a tender enlarged uterus and define this condition.
(iii) Using Treloar's established cycle-length values, state whether a 20-day cycle and a 9-day flow duration fall outside normal ranges.
(iv) State what the endometrial thickness of 12 mm indicates and what investigation must follow.
(v) State the first-line pharmacological management for heavy menstrual bleeding in a woman who does not desire future fertility and wishes to avoid surgery, giving the percentage reduction in MBL it achieves.
questions.answerText:
(i) A cycle length of 20 days is less than 21 days (the lower limit for normal cycle frequency), classifying this as polymenorrhoea. A flow duration of 9 days exceeds the normal maximum of 7 days, constituting menorrhagia. The combined classification is polymenorrhoea with menorrhagia.

(ii) The PALM structural cause most likely to produce a tender enlarged uterus is Adenomyosis — endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium. Adenomyosis is a structural cause of heavy menstrual bleeding classified under the 'A' in FIGO PALM-COEIN.

(iii) Treloar et al. established a mean cycle length of 29.6 days, with the 5th centile at 23 days and the 95th centile at 39.4 days. A 20-day cycle falls below the 5th centile (23 days) and is therefore outside the normal range. A flow duration of 9 days exceeds the accepted normal maximum of 7 days and is abnormal.

(iv) An endometrial thickness of 12 mm in a perimenopausal woman with abnormal bleeding exceeds the 4 mm threshold (some guidelines 5 mm) above which endometrial sampling is mandatory. Endometrial biopsy or hysteroscopy with directed biopsy must follow to exclude endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma before attributing bleeding to a functional cause.

(v) The levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system (LNG-IUS, Mirena) is considered first-line for managing menorrhagia, achieving 80-95% reduction in menstrual blood loss through local progestogenic effects causing endometrial atrophy and decidualisation. Its efficacy is comparable to endometrial ablation, superior to oral progestogens and tranexamic acid, avoids systemic side effects, and provides concurrent contraception.

questions.question:
Describe the origin, course, relations, branches and distribution of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis as it pertains to the menstrual cycle; state the safe approach to pharmacological interruption; and explain the physiological basis of anovulation and its endometrial consequences.

A(i) Describe the HPO axis: origin of GnRH neurons, the significance of pulse frequency on FSH vs LH secretion, and the sequence of events from GnRH pulse to ovulation.
A(ii) State the normal mean menstrual cycle length and the 5th and 95th centile values established by Treloar, and state the upper limit of normal menstrual blood loss.
B(i) Explain what happens to endometrial histology in anovulatory DUB, name the endometrial finding most common overall, the most common abnormal pathological finding, and describe how irregular shedding is diagnosed on biopsy.
B(ii) State the safe pharmacological approach for ovulation induction in a young woman with anovulatory DUB who desires fertility, naming the first-line and second-line agents.
questions.answerText:
A(i) GnRH neurons originate from the olfactory placode and migrate to the hypothalamus during embryological development (failure of this migration causes Kallmann's syndrome with hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism and anosmia). GnRH is released in pulses: high-frequency pulses stimulate predominantly FSH secretion, whereas low-frequency pulses favour LH secretion. This allows independent control of FSH and LH. Rising follicular oestrogen triggers a positive feedback LH surge, causing ovulation. After ovulation, the corpus luteum produces progesterone, converting the endometrium to secretory type.

A(ii) Treloar et al. established a mean cycle length of 29.6 days, with the 5th centile at 23 days and the 95th centile at 39.4 days. The upper limit of normal menstrual blood loss is 79 mls per cycle (Hallberg et al., 1966); menorrhagia is defined as MBL exceeding 80 mls per cycle.

B(i) Normal endometrium is found in approximately 60% of DUB cases — the most common overall finding — indicating biochemical or local vascular abnormalities rather than structural change. Endometrial hyperplasia accounts for approximately 30% of cases and is the most common abnormal pathological finding. Irregular shedding (caused by prolonged corpus luteum activity) is diagnosed by performing endometrial biopsy on the 4th-5th day of menstruation, when the biopsy reveals secretory endometrium mixed with early proliferative endometrium, indicating shedding is still occurring while the new cycle has begun.

B(ii) The pharmacological approach is ovulation induction. Clomiphene citrate is the first-line agent; gonadotrophins are reserved for clomiphene-resistant cases. This approach addresses both the menstrual disorder and the underlying fertility problem simultaneously.

(i) Spot diagnosis: lichen sclerosus. This is a non-neoplastic epithelial disorder of the vulval skin and mucosa (chronic epithelial dystrophy); characterised by white crinkly plaques with shrinkage; presenting features of vulval disease include pruritus, pain, burning or stinging, superficial dyspareunia, discharge, or lesions that are white, red, pigmented, raised, or ulcerated.

(ii) Predisposing factors and aetiology: aetiology is uncertain/unknown; associated with auto-immune disorders; lichen sclerosus is common in elderly women; thickened, leathery skin may result from constant rubbing (lichenification); aetiology is unknown for squamous cell hyperplasia and also for lichen sclerosus. Pruritus vulvae is associated with several vulval/vaginal conditions and may predispose to cancer if prolonged scratching occurs. Causes of pruritus vulvae that may accompany lichen sclerosus: dermatoses (including lichen sclerosus itself); dystrophies; medical disorders (diabetes, liver failure, uraemia); poor hygiene; psychogenic.

(iii) Pathophysiology: lichen sclerosus causes atrophy and shrinkage of the vulval epithelium with loss of normal architecture; it is classified as a non-neoplastic epithelial disorder (chronic epithelial dystrophy); it can cause loss of the labia minora and clitoral hood and narrowing of the introitus leading to dyspareunia. Important association to exclude: vulval intraepithelial neoplasia (VIN) — VIN includes carcinoma-in-situ and Bowen's disease; risk of progression to invasive carcinoma is uncertain but increases in older age; all atypical epithelium should be suspected and biopsied; carcinoma of the vulva is associated with HPV infection, smoking, immunosuppression, advanced age, and history of cervical neoplasia; 90% of vulval cancers are squamous cell carcinomas; investigations include colposcopy and biopsy of any suspicious area.

(iv) Management and risk: treatment of lichen sclerosus — betamethasone (topical corticosteroid); topical corticosteroids in general are used for vulval conditions; specialist consultation is recommended; avoid allergic or irritant materials. Risk of progression: the risk of VIN progressing to invasive carcinoma is uncertain but increases in older age and with immunosuppression; all atypical epithelium should be suspected and biopsied; regular biopsies and follow-up are recommended for VIN; wide excision for Paget's disease which is another vulval condition with 25% association with underlying adenocarcinoma; there is no universally agreed specific percentage risk of lichen sclerosus progressing to squamous cell carcinoma.

(i) What is the spot diagnosis?
