A) Describe human chorionic gonadotrophin (HCG) under the following headings:
A(i) Cell of production, molecular nature, molecular weight, half-life, and the fractions that comprise it
A(ii) The kinetics of HCG rise in normal pregnancy and the timing of its detection after implantation, ovulation and LH surge

B) Explain the clinical basis of:
B(i) How HCG doubling time distinguishes viable intrauterine pregnancy from ectopic pregnancy, citing the exact percentage values that create diagnostic uncertainty
B(ii) The HCG levels that indicate hydatidiform mole and those that predict choriocarcinoma development

C) Distinguish between the uses of HCG in monitoring choriocarcinoma during methotrexate treatment, stating the criteria for administering a second course and the definition of adequate response.
questions.answerText:
A(i) HCG is selectively produced by the syncytiotrophoblast. It is a glycoprotein with a molecular weight of 36,000 to 40,000 and a half-life of 32 to 37 hours. Normal titre is 20 to 30 mIU/ml. It has two fractions: alpha and beta. There is immunological and biological similarity between the alpha fraction and pituitary gonadotrophins. The beta fraction of HCG is specific, measured by immunological and biological methods, RIA and enzyme immunoassay.

A(ii) HCG can be detected in pregnancy one day after implantation, 8 days after ovulation and 9 days after LH surge. Concentration rises exponentially until 9 to 10 weeks of gestation with a doubling time of 1.3 to 2 days. It reaches its peak of around 10⁵ IU/ml after 60 to 90 days of gestation. It then decreases to a plateau value of 10,000 to 20,000 IU/ml maintained for the remainder of pregnancy. HCG returns to non-pregnant level of less than 5 mIU/ml 21 to 24 days after delivery.

B(i) A 66% rise in HCG level over 48 hours represents the lower limit of normal for viable intrauterine pregnancy. However, in 15% of cases of viable intrauterine pregnancy the rise may be less than 66% in 48 hours; and in 15% of cases of ectopic pregnancy the rise may be more than 66% in 48 hours. This overlap of 15% in both groups creates diagnostic uncertainty.

B(ii) Hydatidiform mole is very much suggested if: urine in dilution of 1 in 200 to 1 in 500 is positive for HCG beyond 100 days of gestation; or HCG in urine in 24 hours is around 0.3 to 3 million IU during similar period of amenorrhoea. Patients more prone to develop choriocarcinoma if: excreting HCG >100,000 IU per 24 hours in urine; or serum level of HCG is >40,000 mIU/ml.

C) During methotrexate treatment, serum HCG is measured at weekly intervals. A second course of chemotherapy is required if: HCG level plateaus for more than 3 consecutive weeks or begins to rise again; or the HCG level does not decline by one log within 18 days of completion of the first course. An adequate response is defined as serum HCG falling by one log. If response to two consecutive courses is inadequate, the patient is considered resistant to methotrexate-folic acid and Actinomycin-D is given.

(i) Diagnosis: Choriocarcinoma with pulmonary metastases developing from a complete molar pregnancy.
Risk factors for progression to choriocarcinoma after molar pregnancy:
- hCG >100,000 IU per 24 hours in urine, or serum HCG >40,000 mIU/ml after evacuation
- Excessive uterine enlargement
- Theca-lutein cysts >6 cm
- High-risk features from the FIGO/WHO scoring: age >39; antecedent pregnancy being a term gestation; interval from antecedent pregnancy to diagnosis >6 months; ABO blood groups O×AB; large tumour >5 cm; certain metastatic sites; previous chemotherapy

(ii) Complications by site and investigations:
- Pulmonary (80%): chest pain, cough, haemoptysis, dyspnoea, respiratory failure; CXR shows coin lesion (or cannon-ball opacities), alveolar pattern, discrete rounded densities, pleural effusion, embolic pattern from arterial occlusion; CT chest.
- Vaginal (30%): bleeding, purulent discharge; colposcopy/examination.
- Cerebral (10%): epilepsy, psychosis, acute focal neurological deficits; CT/MRI brain; CSF hCG (plasma-CSF ratio >60:1 suggests CNS involvement).
- Hepatic (10%): RUQ pain, rupture, haemorrhage, jaundice; CT/MRI abdomen; liver function tests.

(iii) Chemotherapy:
Low-risk (score <5): single agent — Methotrexate (4 doses on alternate days with folinic acid) or Actinomycin-D (5-day regimen); given in 14-day cycles.
Medium-risk (score 5–7): combination chemotherapy.
High-risk (score >7): intensive combination chemotherapy — EMA-CO (Etoposide, Methotrexate, Actinomycin-D, Cyclophosphamide, Vincristine) is the most successful and least toxic regimen. Give cycles until complete remission (3 consecutive normal hCG levels); then at least one complete course after first negative hCG titre. If resistant: MAC (Methotrexate, Actinomycin-D, Cyclophosphamide) or salvage MAC-III; second-line: cisplatin with MTX and vincristine.

(iv) Surgical options when chemotherapy is insufficient: Hysterectomy (uncontrollable haemorrhage, tumour perforation, septicaemia, resistance to chemotherapy); wide local excision of vaginal metastases; pulmonary segmental resection; arteriographic embolisation of hypogastric arteries; hepatic resection or hepatic artery embolisation or ligation; craniotomy for brain metastases.
Follow-up after treatment: hCG every 1–2 weeks for first 3 months; every 2–4 weeks for next 3 months; every 1–2 months to complete first year; every 6 months indefinitely. Avoid pregnancy for 1 year after remission.
questions.question:
A 30-year-old woman underwent suction evacuation for a complete hydatidiform mole six weeks ago. She now returns with persistent vaginal bleeding and a rising serum beta-hCG titre over three consecutive weekly measurements. Chest X-ray shows bilateral coin-shaped opacities in the lung fields.

(i) What is the diagnosis, and state all the risk factors for this patient developing this complication from the lectures?
(ii) Describe the complications of the disease, including pulmonary, vaginal, cerebral and hepatic manifestations and the investigations needed to identify each.
(iii) Outline the chemotherapy management, distinguishing treatment for low-risk versus high-risk disease, and name the specific drug regimens used.
(iv) What surgical options exist when chemotherapy alone is insufficient, and what follow-up schedule is used after treatment?

A. Describe the gross anatomy of the female bladder and urethra, including their anatomical relationships, epithelium, and sphincter mechanisms.
B. Explain how the zones of the lower urinary tract (bladder dome, bladder neck, urethra) relate to the pathology of genuine stress incontinence and detrusor instability.
C. Explain why damage to the pelvic floor and pubourethral ligaments during childbirth can cause urine loss with coughing or lifting, using the anatomical and physiological basis.
questions.answerText:
A. Gross anatomy of bladder: hollow muscular organ; located behind the pubic symphysis; covered anteriorly and superiorly by peritoneum; bladder muscle is the detrusor (smooth muscle); contraction reduces the bladder in all diameters; urothelium consists of two or three layers of transitional cells; the trigone is the portion between the ureteric and urethral openings.
Female urethra: located under the pubic symphysis; 3–5 cm long; hollow tubular structure joining the bladder to the exterior; proximal half lined by pseudostratified transitional epithelium; distal half by non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium.
Sphincter mechanism: external (intrinsic) sphincter = rhabdosphincter urethrae (striated muscle), located in the middle third of the urethra, responsible for urethral closure at rest. Extrinsic sphincter = periurethral muscle (levator ani, striated), located at the junction of middle and lower thirds, not directly connected with the urethra, adding additional closure force at times of physical effort. Combined effect: greater pressure within the urethra than in the bladder.
B. Zone–pathology relationships: Genuine stress incontinence involves involuntary loss of urine when intravesical pressure exceeds maximum urethral closure pressure in the absence of detrusor activity; it is the commonest cause and results from damage to the pelvic floor and/or pubourethral ligaments causing descent of the proximal urethra (normally an intra-abdominal organ). Detrusor instability is the presence of spontaneous or provoked detrusor contractions during the filling phase when the patient attempts to inhibit micturition; it is the second commonest cause and is commoner in the elderly; the detrusor is innervated by parasympathetic nerves S2–4, adrenergic receptors at the dome, bladder neck, and urethra, with sympathetic outflow T10–L2.
C. Anatomical basis of stress incontinence: During normal filling, intravesical pressure remains low and maximum urethral pressure exceeds bladder pressure. At times of physical effort (coughing, lifting), the extrinsic sphincter (levator ani) adds additional closure force. Damage to the pelvic floor or pubourethral ligaments allows descent of the proximal urethra out of its normal intra-abdominal position; rises in intra-abdominal pressure are therefore no longer transmitted equally to the bladder and urethra, and intravesical pressure exceeds urethral closure pressure, causing leakage. Causes of pelvic floor damage include childbirth, pelvic surgery, menopause (oestrogen deficiency), and raised intra-abdominal pressure (pregnancy, chronic cough, obesity, pelvic mass).

questions.question:
A 7-year-old girl presents with breast enlargement, pubic hair growth, and vaginal bleeding. On examination a right-sided adnexal mass is palpated. Ultrasound confirms a solid ovarian tumour.

(i) What is the most likely diagnosis? State its risk factors and what percentage of ovarian neoplasms it constitutes.
(ii) What hormonal product does this tumour produce, and what are the complications of excess hormone production at this age group and in postmenopausal women?
(iii) Outline the management options, the surgical treatment, and state the five-year survival rate and the important feature of its long-term behaviour.
(iv) What tumour marker can be used to monitor treatment response for this tumour?
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Granulosa cell tumour (sex cord stromal tumour). Granulosa cell tumours account for 1–2% of ovarian neoplasms. They may be malignant but are usually low-grade. They occur at all ages, including pre-pubertal children.

(ii) Granulosa cell tumours produce oestrogen. In pre-pubertal girls: precocious puberty (before the menarche) — breast development, pubic hair, vaginal bleeding as seen in this patient. In menstruating women: cystic glandular hyperplasia, menorrhagia. In postmenopausal women: postmenopausal bleeding due to endometrial stimulation.

(iii) Management: The surgical treatment is the same as for epithelial ovarian tumours — total abdominal hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy. In young women who wish to conserve fertility, conservative surgery (unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy) may be considered. Radiotherapy has been largely replaced by chemotherapy in advanced or recurrent cases. The effect of adjuvant therapy is difficult to assess as granulosa cell tumours can recur up to 20 years after initial diagnosis. The five-year survival is around 80% overall, but recurrence is associated with a high mortality.

(iv) Granulosa cell tumours usually secrete inhibin. This can be used to monitor the effects of treatment and detect recurrence.

questions.question:
Describe sexually transmitted infections (STIs) under the following headings.

A(i) Definition and routes of transmission of STIs
A(ii) Classification of causative organisms with examples for each class
B(i) Epidemiology: populations most vulnerable to STIs and the reasons adolescent females are particularly susceptible
B(ii) Complications and sequelae of STIs in women, men, and infants
C(i) Why STIs are important from a public health perspective, including their relationship to HIV infection
C(ii) The effect of STIs and HIV/AIDS on fertility in women and men
questions.answerText:
A(i) STIs are infections transmitted principally through sexual contact with mucous membranes and/or skin surfaces (infections whose primary route of transmission is through sexual contact). They may also be acquired through transplacental spread, during the perinatal period, through oral sex, oral intercourse, and kissing. STIs are caused mainly by bacteria, viruses, or protozoa; bacterial STIs are more common in developing countries.
A(ii) Classification of organisms: Bacterial—Neisseria gonorrhoea, Syphilis (Treponema pallidum), Gardnerella vaginalis, Haemophilus ducreyi, Calymmatobacterium granulomatis; Protozoal—Trichomonas vaginalis; Chlamydial—Lymphogranuloma venereum; Viral—Hepatitis, Human papilloma virus, Herpes simplex Types I and II, Cytomegalovirus, Human immunodeficiency virus; Fungal—Candida; Others—Scabies, Pubic louse.
B(i) Highest incidence rates of STIs occur among adolescent women aged 15–19 years and males aged 20–24 years in developed countries; in developing countries such as Nigeria, highest rates occur among those aged 20–24 and 25–29 years. Adolescent females are more susceptible because: they have immature cervices; early sexual experience can cause trauma to vaginal tissue increasing vulnerability; the risk of acquiring Chlamydia, genital herpes, or HPV is greater at first exposure; young women often have cervical ectopy in which cells lining the inside of the cervix extend to the outer surface making them more vulnerable to infections such as Chlamydia; the amount of ejaculate deposited in the vagina is greater than cervical and vaginal secretions to which a man is exposed; young women are less likely to experience symptoms so STIs go undiagnosed.
B(ii) Complications in women: cancers (cervical, vulval, vaginal, anal, liver, T-cell leukaemia, Kaposi's sarcoma); pelvic inflammatory disease, infertility, ectopic pregnancy, spontaneous abortion, chronic pelvic pain; preterm delivery, premature rupture of membranes, puerperal sepsis, postpartum infection; neurosyphilis; chronic liver disease, cirrhosis. Complications in men: penile cancer, anal cancer, liver cancer, T-cell leukaemia, Kaposi's sarcoma; epididymitis, prostatitis, infertility; neurosyphilis; chronic liver disease, cirrhosis. Complications in infants: stillbirth, low birth weight, pneumonia, neonatal sepsis, congenital abnormalities, neurological problems including cytomegalovirus and neurosyphilis; blindness from neonatal eye infections.
C(i) STIs (as well as HIV/AIDS) have major demographic, economic, social, and political impacts particularly in sub-Saharan Africa. They are the second most common cause of healthy life lost in women after maternal morbidity and mortality. STIs enhance sexual transmission of HIV; untreated STDs increase the risk of HIV acquisition/transmission by a factor of 10; improved STI management can reduce HIV infection by 40%. STI-related ulceration (HSV, syphilis, chancroid) compromises the skin's physical barrier, providing easier access to the bloodstream; STIs have immuno-suppressive effects increasing susceptibility to HIV; STIs cause recruitment of target cells (lymphocytes and macrophages) to the genital mucosa, making them accessible to HIV infection; STIs increase the levels of HIV virus present in genital secretions.
C(ii) Effects of STIs/HIV/AIDS on fertility in women: pelvic inflammatory disease; infertility (tubal blockage accounts for 60–80% of female infertility; gonorrhoea and Chlamydia are the greatest culprits); ectopic pregnancy (incompletely blocked tubes predispose to ectopic pregnancy; most tubes removed at salpingectomy have evidence of previous PID); spontaneous abortion; IUGR and low birth weight. Effects in men: epididymitis, prostatitis, infertility. Carcinoma of the cervix is the commonest female malignancy in this environment and is believed to be a sexually transmitted disease; strategies for prevention include regular Pap smear and vaccination against oncogenic serotypes of HPV.

(i) Both ovaries are involved with tumour on the surface, and malignant ascites is present. Tumour type: Serous cystadenocarcinoma. It is the most common malignant ovarian tumour, accounting for 35–50% of all epithelial tumours. It is bilateral in 50% of cases. Histological hallmarks: usually unilocular with a smooth surface and internal papillae; cuboidal/low columnar lining cells; psammoma bodies (calcospherules) are often present in well-differentiated tumours.

(ii) FIGO Stage: Stage IIIa. Justification: growth involves both ovaries (tumour on ovarian surface — meets Ic criteria); however, metastatic deposits are present on the abdominal peritoneal surface which extends beyond the pelvis. Microscopic implants on abdominal peritoneal surfaces with no implants exceeding 2 cm = Stage IIIa. Malignant ascites upgrades from Ib to Ic; peritoneal spread beyond pelvis = Stage III; microscopic only with deposits <2 cm = IIIa.

(iii) Surgical procedure: A vertical (midline or paramedian) incision is required for adequate exploration of the upper abdomen. Sample of ascitic fluid or peritoneal washings for cytology. Full exploration of pelvis and abdomen to identify metastatic disease. Total abdominal hysterectomy (TAH), bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (BSO), infracolic omentectomy, appendicectomy (in some centres), peritoneal biopsies, lymph node biopsies. The objective is removal of all tumour — optimal debulking surgery.

(iv) Adjuvant chemotherapy: platinum drugs (cisplatin and carboplatin) are the most effective. Cisplatin causes severe nausea/vomiting, permanent renal damage unless given with adequate IV hydration, peripheral neuropathy and hearing loss with cumulative doses. Carboplatin: as effective as cisplatin, less nausea, no significant renal toxicity, neurotoxicity rare, hearing loss subclinical; dose calculated on glomerular filtration rate. Paclitaxel (Taxol) derived from Pacific yew tree bark, combined with cisplatin or carboplatin; causes sensory neuropathy and neutropenia in high doses, total hair loss, mild nausea/vomiting. Chemotherapy is given for five or six cycles at three- to four-weekly intervals. Five-year survival for Stage III: 23–41%.
questions.question:
A 55-year-old woman undergoes laparotomy for a large ovarian mass. At surgery, tumour is found on the surface of both ovaries, malignant ascites is present, and microscopic deposits are seen on the abdominal peritoneal surface but no deposits exceed 2 cm in size. Biopsy confirms serous cystadenocarcinoma.

(i) Identify the ovarian structures involved and name the tumour type; state its frequency among malignant ovarian tumours, whether it is commonly bilateral, and its histological hallmarks.
(ii) Using the FIGO staging system described in the lectures, assign the correct stage to this patient and justify each criterion applied.
(iii) Describe the complete surgical procedure required for this patient's primary management, including the incision type and why it is necessary.
(iv) Outline the adjuvant chemotherapy regimen, naming the specific drugs considered most effective and their toxicity profiles, and state the five-year survival expected for this stage.

A 58-year-old postmenopausal woman presents with gradual abdominal distension and progressive dyspnoea. Ultrasound confirms a right-sided solid ovarian mass and significant right pleural effusion. CA-125 is mildly elevated. On examination, abdominal percussion reveals shifting dullness.

(i) Identify the ovarian structure most likely responsible for this combination of findings; state its histological type and what it looks like macroscopically; name the syndrome it produces.
(ii) What are the conditions in the differential diagnosis that must be distinguished from this benign tumour, based on the clinical features described in the lectures?
(iii) What investigations are required, and how does the CA-125 result influence management?
(iv) Outline the definitive management appropriate for this postmenopausal woman, including the surgical approach and the extent of surgery required.
questions.answerText:
(i) Most likely ovarian structure: Fibroma (a benign sex cord stromal tumour / solid epithelial tumour). Histologically it is a solid tumour with a smooth surface resembling a fibroid. It may rarely undergo the same degenerative changes found in a fibroid. The syndrome it produces is Meigs syndrome: defined as the presence of ascites plus hydrothorax (pleural effusion, usually right-sided) associated with a fibroma. The fluid transudes through the capsule from intermittent torsion or compromised venous/lymphatic drainage.

(ii) Differential diagnosis:
- Malignant ovarian tumour (serous cystadenocarcinoma) — the most important differential given ascites and pleural effusion; bilateral tumours, solid nodular irregular growth, fixation, blood-stained ascites suggest malignancy.
- Pseudomyxoma peritonei from a ruptured mucinous cystadenoma.
- Other causes of ascites: hepatic disease, heart failure, tuberculosis, peritoneal carcinomatosis.
- The presence of a right pleural effusion must also raise the possibility of pulmonary metastases from malignancy.

(iii) Investigations: ultrasound (TAS and TVS) to characterise the mass as solid/cystic, assess for bilateral involvement, free fluid; CA-125 (already mildly elevated — elevated in 5% of benign gynaecological disorders including benign ovarian tumours; not diagnostic nor pathognomonic); chest X-ray (pleural effusion); full blood count, urea and electrolytes, liver function tests; IVP if ureteric involvement suspected; CT/MRI scan; barium meal/enema to exclude GI primary. The mildly elevated CA-125 does not exclude malignancy but does not confirm it either; it influences the decision to proceed to surgical staging.

(iv) Definitive management for a postmenopausal woman: Laparotomy is mandatory. In postmenopausal/perimenopausal women with ovarian swelling greater than 5 cm, it is customary to remove both ovaries and the uterus (total abdominal hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy). If frozen section confirms benign fibroma, no further surgery is required. If doubt exists regarding malignancy, a frozen section should be requested. Ascites is sampled for cytology at the time of laparotomy.

A(i) Layers: the endometrium comprises the functionalis (shed at menstruation) and the basalis (regenerative layer retained at menstruation). Vascular supply: spiral arterioles supply the functionalis layer and are under direct hormonal control; the basalis is supplied by basal arterioles that are not shed. Proliferative phase: oestrogen produced in the follicular phase drives proliferation of endometrial glands, stroma, and spiral arterioles. Secretory phase: progesterone from the corpus luteum after ovulation converts the oestrogen-primed endometrium to secretory type characterised by tortuous glands, glycogen-rich secretions, and oedematous stroma. Menstruation initiation: when progesterone and oestrogen fall at the end of the luteal phase, PGF2a and endothelin are released, causing vasoconstriction of spiral arterioles, ischaemia and necrosis of the functionalis, and shedding.

A(ii) Menstrual blood does not normally clot because fibrinolytic substances (particularly plasmin and fibrin degradation products) are present in the menstrual discharge, lysing clots as they form. When blood loss exceeds the capacity of these fibrinolytics, clots form — a clinical indicator of menorrhagia. Approximately 75% of menstrual discharge is blood; the remainder is endometrial tissue and cervical mucus.

B(i) In adolescence, the HPO axis is immature and fails to generate the positive feedback LH surge in response to rising oestrogen, so anovulatory cycles predominate. In the perimenopausal period, declining ovarian follicular reserve with increased resistance of remaining follicles to gonadotrophins leads to failure of folliculogenesis and anovulation. In both situations, no corpus luteum forms, no progesterone is produced, and unopposed oestrogen drives irregular endometrial bleeding.

B(ii) Irregular shedding: caused by prolonged corpus luteum activity with continued progesterone secretion beyond the normal luteal phase; biopsy performed on day 4-5 of menstruation; histology shows secretory endometrium mixed with early proliferative endometrium; presents as prolonged menstrual bleeding with intermenstrual spotting. Irregular ripening (luteal phase deficiency): caused by corpus luteum insufficiency — deficient progesterone production during the luteal phase; biopsy in the second half of the cycle shows endometrium 'out of phase' with the expected cycle day; associated with infertility and recurrent miscarriage rather than heavy bleeding.
questions.question:
Describe the structure of the endometrium under relevant headings, explain the clinical basis for why anovulatory cycles are commoner at the extremes of reproductive life, and distinguish between two related endometrial conditions — irregular shedding and irregular ripening.

A(i) Describe the endometrium under the headings: layers, vascular supply (spiral arterioles), hormonal control of proliferative and secretory phases, and the mechanism by which menstruation is initiated.
A(ii) Explain why menstrual blood does not normally clot, and state the composition of menstrual discharge.
B(i) Explain the clinical basis for why anovulatory DUB is commoner in adolescence and again in the perimenopausal period compared with the mid-reproductive years.
B(ii) Distinguish between irregular shedding and irregular ripening: cause, timing of diagnostic biopsy, histological finding, and clinical presentation.

Describe the types and mechanism of action of contraceptive implants, and explain their clinical pharmacology.

A(i) Types of contraceptive implants with their composition, rod numbers, and duration of action
A(ii) The mechanism of action of contraceptive implants
B(i) The pharmacokinetics of levonorgestrel release from Jadelle compared to Norplant
B(ii) Efficacy of Jadelle and Norplant, and the clinical basis of return to fertility after removal
B(iii) Side effects of contraceptive implants: those related to bleeding pattern and other method-related complaints
C(i) Indications and contraindications for contraceptive implants
C(ii) The clinical basis of choosing implants over combined oral contraceptives for certain categories of women
questions.answerText:
A(i) Types—Biodegradable: Annuelle (effective for 1 year); Non-biodegradable: Norplant (6 soft plastic rods each containing 36 mg levonorgestrel, effective for 5 years); Jadelle (2 silicon rods containing 75 mg levonorgestrel, improved version of Norplant, effective for 5 years); Uniplant (1 rod containing normogestrel acetate, effective for 1 year); Implanon (1 rod containing progestin 3-ketodesogestrel, effective for 3 years).
A(ii) Mechanism of action—Pregnancy is prevented through a combination of mechanisms: inhibition of ovulation; thickening of the cervical mucus; thinning atrophic endometrium resulting in inadequate development of secretory endometrium incompatible with implantation. Norplant provides slow, constant release of progestin into the bloodstream (30 mcg/24 hours), maintaining effective hormone levels. Implanon contains etonorgestrel—the active metabolite of desogestrel—and avoids first-pass effect.
B(i) Jadelle release rate: 100 mcg/day at 1 month; 40 mcg/day at 1 year; 30 mcg/day at 3 years; 25 mcg/day at 5 years. Norplant release rate: 85 mcg/day at 1 month; 50 mcg/day at 9 months; 30 mcg/day at 5 years. Serum levonorgestrel concentrations—Jadelle: maximum 772 pg/mL within 1–2 days, declining to 270 pg/mL at 5 years. Norplant: maximum 1600 pg/mL on first day, declining to 260 pg/mL at 5 years. The two rods of Jadelle release more levonorgestrel per unit area, so two 4.3 cm rods deliver the same daily dose as the six 3.4 cm capsules of Norplant.
B(ii) Efficacy—Jadelle: annual 0.2/100 women, 5-year cumulative 1.1/100 women. Norplant: annual 0.26/100 women, 5-year cumulative 1.1/100 women. Return to fertility: there is no evidence that prolonged use of levonorgestrel implants impairs subsequent fecundity; life-table pregnancy rates compare favourably with those of women not previously using contraceptive methods who wish to become pregnant; a blood level of levonorgestrel sufficient to prevent conception is reached within a few hours after placement and is maintained at an effective level for at least five years.
B(iii) Bleeding pattern side effects: prolonged bleeding during first months of use; bleeding or spotting between periods; no bleeding for several months; combination of patterns—the kind of bleeding pattern a woman will have cannot be predicted. Other method-related complaints: headache, nervousness, nausea, dizziness, dermatitis, acne, change in appetite, weight gain, mastalgia, hirsutism or hair loss. Complaints that may or may not be method-related: breast discharge, cervicitis, mood change, depression, general malaise, weight loss, pruritus, hypertension.
C(i) Indications: continuous contraception; long-term birth spacing; method unrelated to intercourse; alternative to sterilisation; oestrogen-free method. Absolute contraindications: acute liver disease; jaundice; unexplained vaginal bleeding; history of thrombophlebitis, pulmonary embolism, coronary artery disease, or cerebrovascular disease. Use with precautions in: breast nodules or fibrocystic disease, abnormal breast x-ray/mammogram, diabetes, elevated cholesterol/triglycerides, high blood pressure, migraine or other headaches, epilepsy, gallbladder, heart, or kidney disease.
C(ii) Combined oral contraceptives contain oestrogen, which is absolutely contraindicated in women with cardiovascular disease, hypertension, venous thrombosis, liver disease, and breastfeeding women (less than 6 months postpartum). Contraceptive implants are progestin-only (oestrogen-free) and do not carry these risks; there is no increased risk of venous thrombosis, cardiovascular infarction or stroke, or diabetes with Jadelle or Norplant. They are therefore preferred for: lactating women, older women, and women with contraindications to oestrogen-containing contraceptives.

(i) Organ/structure: The bladder descends through the anterior vaginal wall — this is a cystocele (or cysto-urethrocele if the urethra also descends). The anatomical layer responsible for its support is the pubocervical fascia, which extends between the cardinal ligament and the pubis, lateral to the bladder, and is significant in the repair operation for cystocele (anterior colporrhaphy).
(ii) Structures compressed/affected: The prolapsed bladder creates a dependent pouch in which urine pools (residual urine), causing chronic cystitis, frequency, and dysuria. The patient may need to manually replace the prolapsed bladder to complete voiding. Urethral kinking with a cystourethrocele may lead to voiding difficulty and, rarely, urinary retention.
(iii) Differential diagnoses of anterior wall prolapse (as stated): congenital or inclusion dermoid vaginal cyst; urethral diverticulum. Diverticulum of the urethra can be mistaken for urethrocele and cystocele. Vaginal and peri-urethral cysts simulate cystocele and/or rectocele but cannot be reduced.
(iv) Clinico-anatomical reasoning: In genuine stress incontinence, the proximal urethra (normally an intra-abdominal organ) descends; rises in intra-abdominal pressure are no longer transmitted equally to the bladder and urethra, so intravesical pressure exceeds urethral closure pressure, causing leakage during stress. In urinary retention/kinking, a large cystourethrocele obstructs the urethral outlet mechanically — urethral kinking leads to voiding difficulty. The same anatomical displacement (descent of the bladder neck and proximal urethra) thus produces either incontinence (when closure pressure is lost) or obstruction (when the descent is large enough to kink the urethra), depending on the degree and configuration of the prolapse.
questions.question:
A 52-year-old postmenopausal woman presents with recurrent urinary tract infections, difficulty completing voiding (relieved by pressing on the vaginal wall), and a sensation of incomplete bladder emptying. Speculum examination reveals anterior vaginal wall prolapse. Urodynamic studies show a large residual volume of urine.
(i) Identify the organ/structure causing the anterior vaginal wall bulge and the anatomical layer responsible for its support.
(ii) Describe the structures compressed or affected by this prolapse, explaining the urinary symptoms.
(iii) List the differential diagnoses of anterior wall prolapse.
(iv) Using the relevant clinico-anatomical information, explain why a cystourethrocele may also cause urinary stress incontinence in some patients and urinary retention/kinking in others.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Anatomy of the ovary: pinkish-white oval structure measuring 3x2x1 cm in the adult female; lies posterio-lateral to the uterus and attached to it by the ovarian ligament; attached to pelvic side wall by the infundibulo-pelvic (suspensory) ligaments; not covered by peritoneum; has a surface (germinal epithelium), cortex, and medulla; hilum is the entry point for vessels through the mesovarium; mean volume 6.8 cc (premenopausal) and 3.0 cc (postmenopausal). Arterial supply: directly from the abdominal aorta. Venous drainage: right ovarian vein drains into the inferior vena cava; left ovarian vein drains into the left renal vein. Close relations: uterus; ureter (directly posterior to the ovary in the ovarian fossa); external iliac vein; obturator nerve; fallopian tube.

A(ii) Embryological origin: derived from the coelomic epithelium of the posterior abdominal wall; triple origin — coelomic epithelium (mesothelium), mesoderm, and germ cells; coelomic epithelium gives rise to sex cord cells (granulosa, stroma — theca and luteal cells). Three main cell lines giving rise to primary ovarian tumours: surface epithelium (mesothelium/coelomic epithelium) — gives rise to epithelial tumours (serous, mucinous, endometrioid, clear cell, Brenner, undifferentiated); germ cells — give rise to germ cell tumours (dysgerminoma, teratoma, endodermal sinus tumour, choriocarcinoma, embryonal carcinoma, gonadoblastoma); gonadal stroma (sex cord stromal/mesenchyme) — gives rise to granulosa cell tumours, thecoma, fibroma, and Sertoli-Leydig cell tumours; these may sometimes be mixed.

B(i) Routes of metastatic spread: transperitoneal locoregional dissemination is the dominant pattern — unusual to present with visceral metastatic disease initially; peritoneum and other pelvic organs become involved by direct spread; peritoneal fluid flowing to lymphatic channels on the undersurface of the diaphragm carries malignant cells to the omentum, liver, peritoneal surface of small and large bowels, parietal peritoneal surface throughout the abdominal cavity, and surface of diaphragm; metastasis on the undersurface of the diaphragm may be found in what otherwise seems to be Stage I–II disease. Lymphatic spread: pelvic and para-aortic nodes; may also occur to nodes in the neck or inguinal region. Haematogenic spread: usually occurs late in the course; main areas involved are liver and lungs; bone and brain sometimes. Locoregional spread also: invades vagina, fallopian tube, and other pelvic structures.

B(ii) Ovarian cancer presents late because it rarely gives rise to specific symptoms early in its course; commonest presenting features are vague gastrointestinal upset (usually dyspepsia) or increasing abdominal girth; tumours are often found accidentally; the hidden location of the ovaries means women tend to present late; even if malignant, disease has commonly spread outside the ovary before the diagnosis is made; less than 25% of women with ovarian cancer are alive after 5 years; 70%+ of epithelial ovarian cancer patients present with advanced disease (Stages III/IV); unlike cervical and colorectal cancer there are no defined anatomical steps in early tumour progression to allow screening for preneoplastic or preinvasive stages; ovarian cancer screening strategies have not been proven to be effective in detecting early stage disease. Structures involved in advanced disease: omentum; liver (peritoneal surface and eventually parenchyma at Stage IV); small and large bowel peritoneal surfaces; diaphragmatic surface; pelvic organs; para-aortic and pelvic nodes; supraclavicular nodes; pouch of Douglas (irregular deposits felt on bimanual examination); ascites (usually a sign of peritoneal metastasis, especially if blood-stained); pleural effusion (malignant — Stage IV).
questions.question:
Describe the gross anatomy of the ovary and relate its embryological origin to the derivation of the main categories of ovarian tumours. Then explain the patterns of metastatic spread of ovarian cancer and the pathological basis for the disease commonly presenting at an advanced stage.
A(i) Anatomy of the ovary: size, surface, attachments, blood supply, venous drainage, and close relations.
A(ii) Embryological origin of the ovary and the three main cell lines that give rise to the majority of primary ovarian tumours.
B(i) Routes and patterns of metastatic spread of ovarian cancer.
B(ii) Explain why ovarian cancer so frequently presents at Stage III or IV and what structures and organs are involved in advanced disease.

A. Describe the exfoliative cytology of the cervix (Pap smear) under the following headings:
A(i) History and purpose of the test
A(ii) Target population and screening frequency
A(iii) Technique of smear-taking and fixation
B. Describe colposcopy — its principle, magnification used, what is applied to the cervix, and what findings it identifies.
C. Explain the grading system used for Pap smear results, and state the indications for diagnostic cone biopsy.
questions.answerText:
A(i) History and purpose: Exfoliative cytology of the cervix was introduced in 1943 by Papanicolaou and Traut. It reduces morbidity and mortality from cervical cancer. Its prominent application is screening for CIN and cervical cancer. CIN is usually asymptomatic and is easily identifiable through the Pap smear; treatment prevents progression to cervical cancer.
A(ii) Target population and screening: Ideally, screen all women aged 20–65 every 3–5 years. Better to concentrate on high-risk groups and screen more women at least once than to repeatedly screen previously screened women. New WHO approach — screen at least once at the age of 45 years. Following a negative smear, repeat one year after. Screening methods: national programme or opportunistic.
A(iii) Technique: Smear obtained by spatula (e.g. Ayre's spatula) from the squamo-columnar junction and from the endocervical canal using a special brush (cytobrush). Rapidly spread thinly on a glass slide. Immediately fix with 95% ethyl alcohol. Liquid media are now available as an alternative.
B. Colposcopy: endoscopic device; provides visualisation of the cervix with a magnification of ×10–40 (stated range: 3, 10, 40, 100–200, and more than 300). Three to five percent acetic acid solution is applied — it causes columnar cells to swell and opacifies metaplastic and dysplastic squamous epithelium by denaturing the protein in them (acetowhite epithelium). Colposcopy assesses vascular patterns, degree of acetowhite epithelium, and surface pattern of the lesion; it permits colposcopically directed biopsy. Schiller's iodine (0.3%) or Lugol's iodine (5%) may also be applied; iodine-negative areas are biopsied.
C. Pap smear grading:
- Grade I: Normal
- Grade II: Infections
- Grade III: Mild dysplasia
- Grade IV: Moderate to severe dysplasia
- Grade V: Carcinoma
Indications for diagnostic cone biopsy: (1) squamo-columnar junction not visualised at colposcopy; (2) lesion extends into the endocervical canal and upper limits are not seen; (3) smear, colposcopy, and biopsy reports are contradictory; (4) suspicion of micro-invasion. Also mandatory when colposcopy is not available and all patients with abnormal smears must be investigated.

A(i) Most common histopathological subtype: endometrioid adenocarcinoma; the grade of the adenoid component affects prognosis. Poor prognosis histotypes: papillary serous and clear cell — fortunately uncommon. Secretory carcinomas: least frequently occurring; good prognosis. Adenoacanthoma: has a benign squamous component; does not affect prognosis. Adenosquamous carcinoma: has a malignant squamous component; may be associated with a poorer outcome.

A(ii) Grading system:
- Class G1: non-squamous or non-morular solid growth pattern of 5% or less
- Class G2: non-squamous or non-morular solid growth pattern of 6–50%
- Class G3: non-squamous or non-morular solid growth pattern of more than 50%

B(i) Hereditary non-polyposis colon cancer (HNPCC) is associated with a combination of familial colon cancer and increased rates of ovarian, endometrial and breast cancers. Individuals with HNPCC have a markedly increased risk for developing endometrial cancer. Screening should be offered with an endometrial biopsy by age 35 years.

B(ii) First type (classic): well-differentiated, superficially invasive cancers that are sensitive to progesterone; favourable prognosis; extra-uterine disease unusual. Second type: poorly differentiated tumours, deep myometrial invasion, high degree of metastasis to lymph nodes and other sites, decreased sensitivity to progestins, poor prognosis.

C) Stage III sub-stages:
- IIIA: tumour invades serosa and/or adnexa and/or positive peritoneal cytology
- IIIB: vaginal metastasis
- IIIC: metastases to pelvic and/or para-aortic lymph nodes
The finding of malignant peritoneal cytology is significant even in an otherwise Stage I tumour because it upstages the patient from Stage I to Stage IIIA, indicating occult peritoneal spread, which changes management to include adjuvant therapy (chemotherapy or radiotherapy) and worsens prognosis.
questions.question:

A(i) The most common histopathological subtype, the two histotypes that confer poor prognosis, and what the secretory and adenoacanthoma subtypes signify
A(ii) The grading system (G1, G2, G3) used for endometrial carcinoma as stated in the lectures

B) Explain the clinical basis of:
