questions.answerText:
(i) Swyer's syndrome (46,XY pure gonadal dysgenesis).

(ii) The dysgenetic streak gonads produce no Anti-Mullerian hormone (AMH); therefore, the Mullerian (paramesonephric) ducts are not suppressed and persist, forming the uterus, cervix, and upper vagina. This contrasts with CAIS, where functional testes produce AMH causing Mullerian regression and an absent uterus.

(iii) The bilateral streak gonads carry a high risk of gonadal malignancy — specifically gonadoblastoma and dysgerminoma. This risk arises because dysgenetic gonadal tissue containing a Y chromosome is prone to neoplastic transformation.

(iv) Prophylactic gonadectomy is required after diagnosis to prevent malignant transformation. This is performed as soon as practicably possible after the diagnosis is confirmed to eliminate the malignancy risk from the streak gonads.

(v) Fertility can be achieved through oocyte donation and embryo transfer, because the uterus is present and functionally capable of carrying a pregnancy after hormonal preparation. Comparison with CAIS: CAIS has functional testes (not streak gonads) producing testosterone and AMH; AMH causes Mullerian regression so no uterus is present; the testes carry malignant transformation risk requiring gonadectomy but differ from Swyer's in that they are functional and produce hormones, while Swyer's streak gonads are non-functional fibrous tissue.
questions.question:
A 17-year-old girl with 46,XY karyotype is found to have bilateral streak gonads during laparoscopy for primary amenorrhoea. She has a uterus and normal female external genitalia. Secondary sexual development is absent.

(i) State the diagnosis.
(ii) Explain the embryological basis for the presence of a uterus in this 46,XY individual.
(iii) State the pathological risk associated with the streak gonads and the reason for this risk.
(iv) Describe the immediate surgical management required and the timing of this intervention.
(v) State how fertility may be achieved in this patient after management, and compare the gonadal finding with that of CAIS.

A 45-year-old multiparous postmenopausal woman attends clinic complaining of a lump protruding from her vagina, worse on standing and at the end of the day, and disappearing when she lies down. She also reports a dragging pelvic discomfort and low backache. On Sim's speculum examination in the left lateral position while she strains, the cervix projects to and through the introitus.
(i) What is the diagnosis, and what degree/grade does this represent?
(ii) List the predisposing (aetiological) factors for this condition.
(iii) Describe the pathophysiology, including the three components responsible for normal support and what happens when they are damaged.
(iv) List the complications of this condition.
(v) Outline the full management, covering conservative, medical, and surgical options.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Utero-vaginal prolapse — second degree (the cervix projects to or through the introitus). Grading: 1st degree — slight descent, cervix remains within the vagina; 2nd degree — cervix projects to or through the introitus; 3rd degree (complete/procidentia) — entire uterus prolapses outside the introitus with inversion of the whole vaginal wall.
(ii) Predisposing (aetiological) factors: Connective tissue, levator ani, and intact nerve supply are vital. Factors include pregnancy, childbirth, and ageing; congenital connective tissue defects (2% of symptomatic prolapse in nulliparous women; relatively rare in Afro-Caribbean women suggesting genetic differences); vaginal delivery (single major factor); parity (associated with increasing prolapse); raised intra-abdominal pressure; post-menopausal oestrogen deficiency causing loss of collagen and weakness of fascia; post-operative poor attention to vaginal vault support (vault prolapse in 1% after hysterectomy); and mechanical displacement from gynaecological surgery.
(iii) Pathophysiology: Three components responsible for support — (1) ligaments and fascia, by suspension from the pelvic side walls; (2) levator ani muscles, by constricting and maintaining organ position; (3) posterior angulation of the vagina, enhanced by rises in abdominal pressure causing closure of the flap valve. Endopelvic fascia (derived from paramesonephric ducts) forms a continuous sheet attaching laterally to the arcus tendineus fascia and levator ani, extending from the symphysis pubis to the ischial spine; in parts it thickens to form ligaments (uterosacral/cardinal complex — probably most important). The pubocervical fascia supports the bladder; the recto-vaginal fascia prevents anterior rectal protrusion. Damage to any of these mechanisms contributes to prolapse.
(iv) Complications: Keratinisation of the vagina; decubital ulceration; hypertrophy of the cervix; obstructive lesions of the urinary tract (large cystocele or 3rd degree prolapse); urinary tract infection; incarceration of the prolapse.
(v) Management: Prior to definitive treatment — correct obesity, chronic cough, and constipation; if prolapse is ulcerated, apply 7-day topical oestrogen. Conservative: ring pessaries (silicon rubber-based, inserted like a contraceptive diaphragm, replaced annually); shelf pessaries for those who cannot retain ring pessaries. Indications for pessary: patient's wish, therapeutic test, childbearing not completed, medically unfit, during/after pregnancy awaiting involution, awaiting surgery. Surgical: aim to restore anatomy and function. Cystourethrocele — anterior colporrhaphy; rectocele — posterior repair; enterocele — ligation of the sac; utero-vaginal prolapse (fertility not desired) — vaginal hysterectomy and pelvic floor repair; fertility desired — Manchester (Fothergill's) operation (partial amputation of cervix, approximation of cardinal ligaments, combined with ant and post repair) or sacrohysteropexy; vault prolapse — sacrocolpopexy (inverted vault attached to sacrum with mesh, Douglas obliterated) or colpocleisis.

A(i) Neural control: Parasympathetic: nerves S2–4 (pelvic nerves) to the detrusor — responsible for detrusor contraction during voiding. Sympathetic: outflow T10–L2; adrenergic receptors at the dome, bladder neck, and urethra — promote bladder filling by relaxing detrusor and contracting the bladder neck. Urethra: rhabdosphincter urethrae innervated by S2–4 (sacral root); levator ani by S2–4 via the pudendal nerve.
A(ii) CNS control: complex; the sacral spinal reflex arc is controlled by the cerebral cortex (voluntary control), cerebellum, and sub-cortical areas (basal ganglia — provide initial inhibition). Proprioceptive impulses from bladder stretch receptors travel via pelvic nerves to sacral roots S2–4; initial inhibition is mediated by the basal ganglia; desire to void is appreciated at half bladder capacity; cortical inhibition then takes over; conscious inhibition continues with further bladder fill; at full bladder capacity, urethral closure is aided by voluntary pelvic floor contraction.
A(iii) Sequence during micturition: When a suitable time is reached, cortical inhibition is released → relaxation of pelvic floor → relaxation of intrinsic striated muscle of the urethra → fall in urethral pressure → parasympathetic discharge → detrusor contraction → intravesical pressure rises to 50–60 cm H₂O → urethra opens from above downward. After voiding: pelvic floor/intrinsic striated muscle of urethra contract → urethra closes from below upward → urine is milked into the bladder → subconscious inhibition of sacral reflex arc is re-instituted → bladder storage phase starts.
B. Filling phase physiology: During filling, intravesical pressure is not normally greater than 10 cm H₂O to 300 mL, and not normally greater than 15 cm H₂O to 500 mL. Continence is maintained because intravesical pressure remains low and maximum urethral pressure is greater than bladder pressure. Bladder filling occurs at 0.5–5 mL/min; sensation of filling begins at 150–250 mL; bladder capacity is 400–600 mL. The low compliance of the filling phase is maintained by the sympathetic outflow that relaxes the detrusor dome and contracts the bladder neck.
C. Urinary retention with overflow vs detrusor instability:
Urinary retention with overflow: mechanism — failure of detrusor to contract (lower/upper motor neuron lesion, atonic detrusor due to overdistension), or failure of urethral sphincteric mechanism to open (post-surgical spasm/oedema, urethral stenosis/stricture, pelvic floor spasm, pelvic mass). Clinical: dribbling of urine, voiding small amounts frequently, stress incontinence, recurrent UTI. Investigation: distended bladder; residual urine greater than 50% of bladder capacity; post-micturition ultrasound; catheterisation. Management: urine culture; swabs; IVU; X-ray lumbosacral spine; treat underlying cause; continuous bladder drainage.
Detrusor instability: mechanism — presence of spontaneous or provoked detrusor contractions during the filling phase when the patient is attempting to inhibit micturition; causes: idiopathic (most), emotional/psychosomatic, upper motor neuron lesions (multiple sclerosis). Clinical: urgency, urge incontinence, stress incontinence, enuresis, frequency/nocturia, incontinence during sexual intercourse. Urodynamic investigation: cystometry (pressure–volume relationship) shows uninhibited detrusor contractions during the filling phase; uroflowmetry; video-cysto-urethrography (most informative); cystourethroscopy; micturition cystography; IVU; ultrasound.
questions.question:
A. Describe the control of micturition under the following headings:
A(i) Neural control — parasympathetic and sympathetic innervation of the bladder and urethra
A(ii) CNS control — role of the cortex, cerebellum, basal ganglia, and sacral reflex arc
A(iii) The sequence of events during normal micturition
B. Explain the physiological basis of why intravesical pressure remains low during the filling phase despite increasing bladder volume.
C. Distinguish between the mechanisms and investigation of urinary retention with overflow incontinence and detrusor instability, including the urodynamic features of each.

A 24-year-old woman presents with frothy yellow-green vaginal discharge, vulval irritation, and punctate haemorrhages on her cervix (strawberry cervix) on speculum examination. She is 18 weeks pregnant.

(i) What is the spot diagnosis, and what is the causative organism?
(ii) What are the predisposing factors and the epidemiological setting for this infection?
(iii) How is the diagnosis confirmed in the laboratory?
(iv) What is the treatment, and what are the pregnancy complications associated with this infection?
(v) How does this organism relate to the risk of HIV acquisition?
questions.answerText:
(i) Spot diagnosis: trichomoniasis. Causative organism: Trichomonas vaginalis—a protozoan. Clinical features include frothy vaginal discharge, irritation, vaginal bleeding, and punctate haemorrhages on the cervix (strawberry cervix).
(ii) Trichomoniasis is the most common STI. Predisposing epidemiological factors: urhan residents, adolescents and young adults (15–35 years), unmarried individuals, multiple sexual partners, unprotected sex; prevalence in pregnancy in Africa is 9.9%–41.4%.
(iii) Diagnosis confirmed by: wet preparation (microscopy of vaginal secretions reveals the flagellae); culture of swabs taken in a specific medium such as Fineberg–Whittington medium.
(iv) Treatment: Metronidazole is the drug of choice; others include Arsphenamine pessaries and Cotrimazole. Partner treatment (contact tracing) is essential for prevention. Pregnancy complications associated with trichomoniasis: associated with adverse pregnancy outcomes including premature delivery, premature rupture of membranes (PROM), and low birth weight (LBW).
(v) Trichomoniasis is associated with increased HIV infection. STIs enhance sexual transmission of HIV; untreated STDs increase the risk of HIV acquisition and transmission by a factor of 10. The genital inflammation and disruption of mucosal integrity associated with trichomoniasis facilitates HIV entry. STIs cause recruitment of HIV target cells (lymphocytes and macrophages) to the genital mucosa, making them accessible to HIV infection.

questions.question:
Describe the non-neoplastic epithelial disorders of the vulva, vulval intraepithelial neoplasia (VIN), and carcinoma of the vulva, covering their pathology, clinical features, staging, and management.
A(i) Non-neoplastic disorders: list all categories, give the aetiology and treatment of lichen sclerosus and squamous cell hyperplasia.
A(ii) Vulval intraepithelial neoplasia: grading, associations, malignant potential, diagnosis, and treatment.
B(i) Carcinoma of the vulva: epidemiology, histological types, associations, patterns of spread, and FIGO staging.
B(ii) Principles of surgical and adjuvant management of vulval cancer.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Non-neoplastic disorders: epithelial disorders of the skin and mucosa (chronic epithelial dystrophy): lichen sclerosus — white crinkly plaques with shrinkage; aetiology uncertain; associated with auto-immune disorders; treatment is betamethasone; squamous cell hyperplasia — formerly known as dystrophy; aetiology unknown; associated with pruritus; histology shows squamous cell hyperplasia; treatment involves topical corticosteroid and specialist consultation. Other dermatoses: psoriasis, eczema, lichen simplex chronicus, contact dermatitis (irritant and allergic), seborrhoeic dermatitis, intertrigo (more commonly affects obese women in interlabial/crural folds — related to moisture, warmth, and chafing). Vulval ulceration: Behcet's syndrome, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, pemphigoid. Infections: fungal (Candida albicans — pruritus; tinea cruris); viral (genital warts — HPV, 60 subtypes, sexually transmitted, treatment includes 2% trichloroacetic acid, podophyllin, cryotherapy, electrocautery, CO2 laser; herpes simplex virus type 2 — incubation 7 days, treatment acyclovir 200 mg five times); bacterial (bartholinitis; perifoliculitis/impetigo — Staphylococcus aureus; syphilis — Treponema pallidum, indurated painless vulval ulcer with painless inguinal nodes, treatment bicillin/doxycycline/erythromycin; chancroid — Haemophilus ducreyi; granuloma inguinale/donovanosis; LGV — Chlamydia trachomatis, suppurative ulceration and fibrosis, treatment doxycycline).

A(ii) Vulval intraepithelial neoplasia: cause unknown; includes carcinoma-in-situ and Bowen's disease; age incidence 14–80, mean 40–45 years; presents with pruritus or no symptoms; white, red, or brown lesions; graded as for CIN — VIN I, VIN II, VIN III; VIN III is equivalent to carcinoma-in-situ; VIN has lower malignant potential than CIN; risk of progression to invasive carcinoma is uncertain but increases in older age and with immunosuppression; associated with cervical and vaginal neoplasia; diagnosis by colposcopy and biopsy; treatment: not usually recommended in younger people; options include excision biopsy, skinning vulvectomy, laser destruction (laser vaporization), regular biopsies, and observation.

B(i) Carcinoma of the vulva: uncommon with an incidence of 0.5–2 per 100,000 women per year; rises with age — peak incidence in the seventh decade (over 75 years). Histological types: squamous cancers 90% (5% of all female genital cancers); other malignancies — verrucous and basal cell carcinoma, malignant melanoma, Bartholin's carcinoma, Adenocarcinoma, metastases from cervix, kidney, and endometrium. Associations: HPV infection, smoking, immunosuppression, advanced age, history of cervical neoplasia; two aetiological pathways — de novo in the elderly and associated with VIN (particularly multifocal HPV-linked disease). Spread: local invasion and by lymphatics; invades vagina, perineum, anal canal, urethra, clitoris, and in late disease bone; lymphatics to superficial inguinal nodes, then to deep inguino-femoral nodes; central structures drain bilaterally; lateral ones drain ipsilaterally primarily; late presentation still common. FIGO staging: Stage I — limited to vulva and/or perineum, 2 cm or less in diameter, no groin node metastasis; Stage II — limited to vulva and/or perineum, greater than 2 cm, no groin nodes; Stage III — extends beyond vulva to vagina, lower urethra, or anus, or unilateral regional node metastasis; Stage IVa — involves mucosa of rectum/bladder, upper urethra, or pelvic bone, and/or bilateral regional node metastases; Stage IVb — any distant metastasis including pelvic lymph node.

B(ii) Management: planning based on stage, site, spread, and size (tumour thickness and capillary lymphatic space involvement). Objectives: remove the cancer and reduce risk of local recurrence; preserve as much function as possible. Wide local excision (10 mm perimeter of normal epithelium) for T1 and T2 tumours; radical vulvectomy for multifocal tumours using triple incision for better cosmetic outcome; involvement of central structures warrants preoperative radiotherapy; all atypical epithelium should be biopsied. Groin node assessment: biopsy suspicious nodes; formal groin node dissection still required even if FNAB is negative; if positive, preoperative radiotherapy. Radiotherapy and chemotherapy: squamous vulval cancers are sensitive to radiotherapy especially basal cell carcinoma; also useful for treatment of involved nodes if 1–2 are positive after groin dissection (external beam megavoltage); treatment of primary tumour to preserve function; complications include erythema, moist desquamation, rarely bone necrosis and fistula formation; chemotherapy is less used but can be combined with radiotherapy. Prognosis: related to size of tumour — good prognosis if less than 2 cm; poor prognosis with nodal involvement.

questions.question:
Describe the anatomy and physiology of human sexuality, including definitions of key terms used in the study of sexual health.

A(i) WHO definition of sexual health and its components
A(ii) Definitions of sex, gender identity, gender role, and how they differ from sexual orientation
B(i) Anatomy of the female external genitalia, naming each structure and its function
B(ii) Anatomy of the female internal genitalia relevant to sexual function, including the G-spot
C(i) Conditions that affect sexual function in females, listing specific causes
C(ii) Stages of sexual development from birth through adolescence, with approximate age milestones
questions.answerText:
A(i) WHO definition of sexual health: the integration of the physical, emotional, intellectual and social aspects of sexual being in ways that are positively enriching and that enhance personality, communication, and love; every person has a right to receive sexual information and to consider sexual relationships for pleasure as well as for procreation (WHO Technical Report Series #572). Sexual health is also defined as the ability to express one's sexuality free from the risk of STIs, unwanted pregnancy, coercion, violence, and discrimination; it means being able to have an informed, enjoyable, and safe sex life based on a positive approach to sexual expression and mutual respect. It is positively enriching, includes pleasure, and enhances self-determination, communication, and relationships.
A(ii) Sex: one's biological characteristics—anatomical (breasts, vagina; penis, testicles), physiological (menstrual cycle; spermatogenesis), and genetic (XX; XY)—as a female or as a male. Gender identity (sexual identity): the personal, private conviction each individual has about being 'feminine' or 'masculine'. Gender role: the set of socially or culturally defined attitudes, behaviours, expectations, and responsibilities considered appropriate for women (feminine) and men (masculine); gender roles may vary according to culture, class, and ethnicity. Sexual orientation: the erotic or romantic attraction (or 'preference') for sharing sexual expression with members of the opposite sex (heterosexuality), one's own sex (homosexuality), or both sexes (bisexuality). Human sexuality is different from gender identity: gender refers to the socially constructed roles of females and males within a given culture; gender attitudes and behaviour are learnt and can change.
B(i) Female external genitalia: Mons pubis—a pad of fatty tissue over the pubic bone, becomes covered with hair during puberty, protects internal sexual and reproductive organs. Clitoris—an erectile, hooded organ at the upper joining of the labia that contains a high concentration of nerve endings, very sensitive to stimulation, the only anatomical organ whose sole function is providing sexual pleasure. Labia majora—two spongy folds of skin, one on either side of the vaginal opening, that cover and protect the genital structures. Labia minora—two erectile folds of skin between the labia majora that extend from the clitoris on both sides of the urethral and vaginal openings; the area covered by the labia minora (including vaginal, urethral, Bartholin's, and Skene's gland openings) is called the vestibule. Perineum—a network of muscles located between and surrounding the vagina and anus that support the pelvic cavity and help keep pelvic organs in place.
B(ii) The Grafenberg spot (G-spot): a small area (about 1–2 cm) on the front wall of the vagina (closest to the bladder and urethra), about halfway between the pelvic bone and the cervix, especially sensitive to sexual stimulation in some women and may be the source of a small amount of fluid ejaculated at orgasm; if stimulated this area becomes engorged; has no known function except as a source of sexual stimulation. Others: vagina; cervix; uterus; uterine tubes; ovaries.
C(i) Conditions affecting sexual function in females: Female genital mutilation—various types; hysterectomy; mastectomy; medical conditions; age/menopause. Also: reproductive cancers; diabetes; cardiac disease; hypertension; physical injury such as spinal cord injuries; effects of hormonal contraceptive methods; substance abuse; psychological conditions (stress, negative body image, performance anxiety, fear of pregnancy, sexual trauma, depression).
C(ii) Sexual development milestones: Before birth—male fetus achieves erections in utero; female sexual response cycle also functional before birth. Ages 6 months to 1 year—genital self-exploration and masturbation occur for both sexes. By 2 years—children are aware of their biological sex and show an understanding of sexual identity. Ages 3–5 years—children begin to conform to society's messages about how females and males should act (understanding of gender roles); begin asking where babies come from. Ages 5–12 years—children begin to show romantic interest; first signs of sexual orientation. Ages 8–13 years—first physical signs of puberty; girls between ages 9 and 16 experience first menstruation; boys between ages 11 and 18 see onset of sperm production. Ages 10–15—young people begin to engage in romantic activity (depends heavily on cultural factors).

questions.question:
A 56-year-old postmenopausal woman has a routine ultrasound showing a simple 4 cm unilateral ovarian cyst. She is asymptomatic. CA-125 is 18 u/ml.
(i) What is the clinical approach to this finding, and what are the features that allow conservative management?
(ii) What screening strategies for ovarian cancer are, and what are their limitations?
(iii) What are the non-surgical and surgical prevention strategies for ovarian cancer?
(iv) How does the risk of malignancy differ between premenopausal and postmenopausal ovarian cysts, and what surgical threshold applies?
questions.answerText:
(i) Clinical approach and features allowing conservative management: amongst those ovarian tumours that require surgery, 45% are malignant in postmenopausal women (compared with 13% in premenopausal women); however, to avoid unnecessary surgery in this older age group, evaluate the cyst with tumour markers, ultrasound, colour flow Doppler studies, and careful follow-up; simple unilateral cysts less than 6 cm in diameter with CA-125 less than 35 u/ml and normal vascular resistance patterns are likely to be benign and may safely be managed conservatively; this patient meets these criteria (4 cm, CA-125 18 u/ml, unilateral, simple); laparotomy is mandatory for any ovarian swelling greater than 5 cm, particularly if it is continuing to enlarge — this cyst is below this threshold; postmenopausal women over 50 have little to gain from conservative management of a pelvic mass more than 5 cm; physiological cysts are unlikely in a postmenopausal woman; follow-up with 6-monthly ultrasound and CA-125 is appropriate; re-examine; if cyst is unchanged or larger, further investigation (laparoscopy) is warranted.

(ii) Ovarian cancer screening strategies and limitations: best available screening strategy combines vaginal examination, vaginal ultrasound (carried out by experienced personnel), and serum CA-125 levels; problems with current screening: despite relatively high sensitivity and specificity, the low prevalence of disease means the positive predictive value is only 10% — 10 women would require laparoscopy or laparotomy for every one cancer detected; interval cancers occur as frequently as those detected — screening would need to be carried out at least yearly; there is no evidence that screening reduces mortality, probably because it cannot detect the cancer early enough; ultrasound is not suitable as a primary screening tool because it is too expensive and has a high false-positive rate; no tumour marker has become truly specific and suitable for early detection; no justification for screening women at low or even moderate risk; screening is probably justified in women with a strong family history; on current evidence, screening the general population is neither useful nor safe. Screening components for high-risk groups: annual ultrasound; serum CA-125; family pedigree and karyotyping; bimanual examination.

(iii) Prevention strategies: non-surgical — pregnancy (single pregnancy reduces risk by 20–40%; each additional pregnancy reduces relative risk by 10–15%); oral contraceptives (40% risk reduction; greatest reduction with 4–6 years of use; persists several years after discontinuation; relevant for both low- and high-risk individuals; oral contraceptive use is protective, reducing risk by 50% with greater than 5 years use); aspirin (25% reduction for women taking at least weekly for greater than 6 months); acetaminophen (40–60% reduced risk); breastfeeding; OCP — the protective effects should be borne in mind when counselling young women at high risk; some opt for prophylactic oophorectomy with HRT around age 40. Surgical — tubal ligation (50–70% risk reduction; benefits observed in both low- and high-risk populations); incidental oophorectomy in association with any abdominal/pelvic surgery in a postmenopausal woman; bilateral prophylactic oophorectomy in high-risk (family history/genetic) women — 90% reduced risk (less than 10-year follow-up); chemoprophylaxis with OCP; prophylactic oophorectomy.

(iv) Risk of malignancy and surgical thresholds: in childhood, tumours are frequently malignant; in older women, the risk of malignancy is proportional to age — 45% of tumours removed from women aged 45 years or over are malignant; 13% are malignant in premenopausal women; physiological cysts are unlikely in postmenopausal women; amongst ovarian tumours: in infancy/childhood 10% are malignant; in reproductive years most are functional/non-neoplastic; at menopause, half of all ovarian tumours are malignant. Surgical threshold: laparotomy is mandatory for any ovarian swelling greater than 5 cm, particularly if continuing to enlarge; in premenopausal women, a clear unilocular cyst of 3–10 cm should be re-examined 12 weeks later; in postmenopausal women, they have little to gain from conservative management of a pelvic mass more than 5 cm; women over 50 are far more likely to have a malignancy; in women past child-bearing age, it is customary to remove both ovaries and the uterus.

(i) Predisposing factors (aetiology): Exact aetiology not known. Oestrogen receptors are present in fibroids. Associated factors: negroid race, nulliparity, excessive oestrogen, pelvic inflammatory disease, and infertility.
(ii) Degenerative changes/complications:
- Atrophy
- Hyaline degeneration: softening, contains hyaline tissue
- Fatty degeneration
- Red degeneration (necrobiosis): due to infarction; flesh-like changes; associated with OCP use and pregnancy
- Calcification
- Malignant/sarcomatous change (in less than 0.2%)
- Torsion
- Haemorrhage
- Infection
(iii) Effects of fibroids on pregnancy: increase in symphysio-fundal height, abortion, malpresentation, obstructed labour, fetal parts difficult to feel, premature labour, postpartum haemorrhage, and subinvolution. Classical caesarean section may be required when fibroids are in the lower segment. Myomectomy during pregnancy is dangerous; pedunculated fibroids are easier to manage.
(iv) Medical options: Progestogens, prostaglandin synthetase inhibitors, oral contraceptives, Danazol, Gestrinone, LHRH analogues.
Surgical options: Uterine artery ablation, polypectomy, vaginal myomectomy, abdominal myomectomy, abdominal hysterectomy, vaginal hysterectomy, laparoscopic and hysteroscopic myomectomy, hysterectomy.
Most appropriate option: Abdominal myomectomy — justified because the patient desires fertility; myomectomy preserves the uterus while removing the fibroids, unlike hysterectomy. Treatment is affected by associated symptoms, age, and reproductive status.
questions.question:
A 28-year-old nulliparous woman is found at routine pelvic examination to have an irregular, enlarged uterus approximately 16 weeks in size. She reports heavy, prolonged menstrual periods, increasing abdominal swelling, and pelvic pressure symptoms. Pelvic ultrasound confirms multiple uterine fibroids. She is married, desires fertility, and her haemoglobin is 8.5 g/dL.
(i) List the predisposing factors (aetiology) associated with uterine fibroids.
(ii) State the degenerative changes and complications that may occur in fibroids.
(iii) Outline the complications that fibroids may cause during pregnancy.
(iv) List the available medical and surgical treatment options. Justify the single most appropriate surgical option for this patient.

questions.answerText:
(i) Contraindications precluding COCs in this woman: breastfeeding less than 6 months postpartum (absolute contraindication); migraines with focal neurological symptoms (absolute contraindication). If she were also a smoker over 35, those would apply, but they do not here. Liver disease, breast cancer, cardiovascular disease, and pregnancy are also absolute contraindications but are not present.
(ii) Appropriate alternative: progestogen-only contraceptives. Types: progestogen-only pills (minipills)—contain ½ to 1/10th the progestin in combined oral contraceptives, 30–75 mcg; less effective than COCs; progestogen-only injectables—DMPA (150mg every 3 months), NET-EN (200mg every 2 months); subdermal implants—Norplant, Jadelle, Uniplant, Implanon. Mechanism of action of progestogen-only methods: inhibits ovulation in half of women; thickens cervical mucus preventing sperm transport (principal mode of action); reduces tubal mobility; for injectables: also causes endometrial suppression. Most of the criteria restricting use of oral contraceptives do not apply to progestogen-only contraceptives—no oestrogen.
(iii) Ideal contraceptive from provider's perspective: effective and safe with no side effects; independent of the act of coitus; long-lasting and easily administered; reversible and not costly. Women's perspectives on the most ideal method: should be highly effective; should have prolonged duration of action and still be rapidly reversible; should not have any side effects and complications; should be easily accessible and provide privacy of use; offer protection against HIV/AIDS and STIs.
(iv) Non-contraceptive benefits of progestogen-only methods (specifically injectables/implants): no systemic oestrogen side effects; can be used by breastfeeding mothers; can be used by women with contraindications to oestrogen; useful in older women or women with reduced fertility. For hormonal IUDs (Mirena): reduces menstrual loss; amenorrhoea present in many women due to endometrial atrophy; useful in older women with menstrual irregularities; highly effective.
(v) Factors to reassess before prescribing COCs at 12 months: confirm cessation of breastfeeding (breastfeeding <6 months is an absolute contraindication); reassess migraine pattern—if migraines with focal neurological symptoms persist, COCs remain absolutely contraindicated; screen for other absolute contraindications: liver disease, breast cancer, diabetes with complications, hypertension, cardiovascular disease; enquire about smoking (significant risk if ≥35 years); take careful history and thorough physical examination to exclude absolute contraindications; where relative contraindications are encountered, client should be assessed by a physician; a Pap smear should be taken; all clients should be allowed to make a voluntary informed choice after counselling.
questions.question:
A 32-year-old woman presents requesting combined oral contraceptives (COCs). She is 6 weeks postpartum and exclusively breastfeeding. She has a personal history of migraines with focal neurological symptoms. Her BMI is 22 and she does not smoke.

(i) What are all the contraindications that preclude the use of COCs in this woman?
(ii) What alternative hormonal contraceptive category is appropriate, and what are its types and mechanisms of action?
(iii) What is the clinical definition of the ideal contraceptive from both the provider's and the woman's perspectives?
(iv) What are the non-contraceptive benefits of the category of hormonal method chosen?
(v) When she stops breastfeeding at 12 months, what factors must be reassessed before prescribing COCs?

A 47-year-old woman presents with a 6-month history of increasingly irregular and heavy menstrual bleeding. She has no pelvic mass on examination and her cervical smear is normal.

(i) State the most likely underlying physiological diagnosis.
(ii) Explain the pathophysiological mechanism that produces this bleeding pattern at this age.
(iii) State why this presentation always requires investigation before attributing it to a functional cause, and name the investigation most sensitive for detecting endometrial polyps.
(iv) Classify this woman's bleeding using the FIGO PALM-COEIN system, identifying the relevant PALM and COEIN components.
(v) State the first-line pharmacological management for acute heavy anovulatory uterine bleeding requiring hospital admission.
questions.answerText:
(i) Perimenopausal anovulatory dysfunctional uterine bleeding (DUB).

(ii) In the perimenopausal period, declining ovarian follicular reserve combined with increased resistance of remaining follicles to gonadotrophin stimulation leads to anovulatory cycles. No corpus luteum forms, so no progesterone is produced. The resulting unopposed oestrogen causes endometrial hyperplasia and heavy irregular menstrual bleeding. Unlike adolescent anovulation, perimenopausal anovulation requires investigation to exclude malignancy.

(iii) Unlike adolescent anovulatory DUB which typically resolves spontaneously, perimenopausal bleeding requires investigation to exclude malignancy before attributing it to a functional cause. The most sensitive investigation for detecting endometrial polyps is saline infusion sonohysterography (SIS) or office hysteroscopy; SIS has sensitivity of 90%+ and hysteroscopy approaches 100%, compared to only 60-70% for standard TVUS.

(iv) PALM component: Adenomyosis or Malignancy/hyperplasia must be excluded (structural causes). COEIN component: Ovulatory dysfunction (anovulation) is the relevant non-structural cause.

(v) High-dose intravenous conjugated oestrogens (25 mg every 4-6 hours) or high-dose combined oral contraceptive pills, to rapidly promote endometrial proliferation and stabilisation, arresting the bleeding. Once bleeding is controlled, progestogen is added or the OCP is tapered to prevent rebound. Surgical curettage is reserved for failure of medical treatment.

questions.question:
A. Describe the gross anatomy and pathology of uterine fibroids under the following headings:
A(i) Macroscopic appearance and microscopy
A(ii) Sites (anatomical locations)
B. Explain how the site of a fibroid determines the clinical features (symptoms and signs) it produces.
C. Explain why a submucous fibroid can cause infertility and how it can be confused with a uterine polyp on clinical examination.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Macroscopic appearance and microscopy: Fibroids range from microscopic (single cell) to large sizes. On gross examination they are pale, firm, fibrous, and round masses enclosed in a false capsule. The cut surface shows a glistening white, whorled pattern. On microscopy: closely set smooth muscle cells with concentric nuclei; fibrous tissue is present in the outer part. Also known as fibromyoma, myoma, fibroleiomyoma, and leiomyoma.
A(ii) Sites: subserous (also polypoidal), interstitial, submucous (also pedunculated), cervical, intraligamentary, and parasitic.
B. Site determines clinical features:
- Submucous fibroids: most likely to cause abnormal uterine bleeding (heavy, prolonged periods) and infertility because they distort the uterine cavity; pedunculated submucous fibroids may prolapse through the cervix.
- Interstitial (intramural) fibroids: produce abdominal swelling, an enlarged irregular uterus on examination, and may cause dysmenorrhoea and pressure symptoms.
- Subserous fibroids: predominantly cause abdominal swelling; may become pedunculated (polypoidal) or parasitic; pressure symptoms on bladder, rectum, pelvic veins, and nerves depend on size and direction.
- Cervical fibroids: may cause pressure symptoms and obstructed labour; caution is required regarding ureters and bladder.
Clinical features depend on size, site, and number.
C. Submucous fibroid and infertility: fibroids are associated with infertility; a submucous fibroid distorts the uterine cavity, interfering with implantation and causing recurrent abortion. Leiomyomas are listed under the differential diagnosis of ovarian tumours and other pelvic masses. A pedunculated submucous fibroid prolapsing through the cervix may resemble a large cervical polyp (endocervical polyp) or a large uterine polyp on examination; the differential diagnosis of utero-vaginal prolapse includes large cervical polyps and polypoid tumours projecting through the introitus on straining.

questions.question:
A. Describe the cardinal ligament (Mackenrodt's ligament) and uterosacral ligament under the following headings:
A(i) Composition, attachments, and relationship to adjacent structures
A(ii) Their combined role in uterine support
B. Explain how damage to or weakness of these ligaments produces the dragging pelvic discomfort and low backache characteristic of utero-vaginal prolapse.
C. Describe the Manchester (Fothergill's) operation, stating the anatomical steps performed and why it is chosen when fertility is desired.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Cardinal ligament (Transverse cervical/Mackenrodt's ligament): Attaches the lateral cervix and upper vagina to the pelvic side wall. Composed of connective tissue and involuntary muscle. The ureter runs in its upper part. It is probably the most important component of the supporting structure of the uterus.
Uterosacral ligament: provides postero-lateral attachment of the lateral vaginal fornix, cervix, and isthmus to the sacro-iliac joint and third piece of the sacrum.
A(ii) Combined role: The uterosacral and cardinal complex constitute the principal suspensory and lateral support of the uterus and upper vagina. The endopelvic fascia (continuous sheet attaching laterally to the arcus tendineus fascia and levator ani, extending from the symphysis pubis to the ischial spine) thickens in parts to form these ligaments. Together with levator ani, ligaments and fascia by suspension from the pelvic side walls, and the posterior angulation of the vagina (flap valve mechanism), they maintain the uterus in its normal position.
B. When these ligaments are stretched or attenuated, prolapse occurs. The dragging pelvic discomfort and low backache in prolapse are due to stretching of the supporting ligaments — mainly the uterosacral and cardinal ligaments. This pain is typically worse when the patient is on her feet and disappears on lying down, because gravitational load is removed.
C. Manchester (Fothergill's) operation — steps: (1) Partial amputation of the cervix; (2) Approximation of the cardinal ligaments below the retained (amputated) cervix; (3) Combined with anterior colporrhaphy and posterior colpo-perineorrhaphy.
Reason chosen when fertility is desired: the uterus is preserved (unlike vaginal hysterectomy); the cardinal ligaments are shortened and re-attached below the retained cervix, restoring support without removing the uterus. The alternative when fertility is desired is sacrohysteropexy (abdominal procedure — attachment of a synthetic mesh from the uterocervical junction to the anterior longitudinal ligament of the sacrum, with closure of the pouch of Douglas).

A(i) Epidemiology: extremely rare, accounting for 0.3% of gynaecological malignancies; usually unilateral; mean age at diagnosis — 56 years. Associated factors: nulliparity (45% of patients); infertility (71% of patients). Secondary tumours to the fallopian tubes also occur — most from ovarian cancer; others from breast and GIT.

A(ii) Pathology: tumour usually distends the lumen of the tube and may protrude through the fimbrial end; the tube may be retort-shaped, resembling a hydrosalpinx. Histologically: similar to ovarian serous adenocarcinoma. Tumour spread: identical to ovarian cancer; metastasis to pelvic and para-aortic nodes is common. Staging: FIGO clinical staging is similar to that of ovarian cancer.

B(i) Clinical presentation and diagnosis: diagnosis is seldom considered pre-operatively; most cases are diagnosed at laparotomy; usual presenting symptoms — postmenopausal bleeding; watery discharge; lower abdominal pain. Unexplained postmenopausal bleeding or abnormal cervical cytology without obvious cause demands a careful bimanual examination and pelvic ultrasound; laparoscopy in doubtful cases.

B(ii) Management and prognosis: management is similar to carcinoma of the ovary; surgery to remove gross tumour — total abdominal hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (TAH, BSO); post-operative chemotherapy (platinum-based combination) for all but the earliest cases. Prognosis: overall 5-year survival approximately 35%; prognosis improved if tumour is detected early; 5-year survival by stage — Stage Ia: 70%; Stage IIb–IIIc: 25–30%; best results with platinum agents.

questions.answerText:
(i) Most likely acute complication: torsion of the dermoid cyst (mature cystic teratoma). Acute or subacute pain may be accompanied by mild shock; lower abdomen is tender with guarding and rigidity; pelvic examination reveals a tender adnexal mass; laparotomy is indicated and removal of the ovary is usually necessary. Torsion is the commonest complication: 3.5–10% of dermoid cysts undergo torsion; torsion causes sharp, constant pain due to ischaemia of the cyst and areas become infarcted.

(ii) Predisposing factors and pathophysiology: dermoid cysts account for about 40% of all ovarian neoplasms; they are the commonest ovarian tumour in young women (median age 30 years); they arise from totipotential germ cells through differentiation into embryonic tissues; they contain all three germ layers; bilateral in 10–11% of cases. Macroscopic features: usually unilocular cyst, less than 15 cm in diameter, in which ectodermal elements are predominant; lined with epithelium like the epidermis and contains skin appendages, teeth, sebaceous material, hair, and nervous tissue; endodermal derivatives include thyroid, bronchial, and intestinal tissue; mesodermal derivatives include bone, cartilage, and smooth muscle. Microscopic features: lined by stratified squamous epithelium with usual cutaneous elements — hair, sebaceous and sweat glands, teeth, neural tissue, cartilage, alimentary and respiratory epithelium, and even active thyroid tissue (struma ovarii); solid teratomas may be benign but are usually malignant; 2% of dermoid cysts contain a malignant component, usually squamous carcinoma, in women over 40 years.

(iii) Investigations: pelvic ultrasound — reveals cystic ovarian mass with possible solid elements; may show disruption of blood flow in torsion; abdominal X-ray — may show calcification suggesting a benign teratoma; serum tumour markers — CA-125, beta-hCG, AFP, LDH; FBC — white cell count increased suggests infection; laparoscopy may be performed in doubtful cases. In this case: ultrasound likely shows the right ovarian cystic mass with characteristic features of dermoid (hyperechoic foci, shadowing from teeth or calcification), evidence of torsion including lack of Doppler flow.

(iv) Immediate management of torsion: laparotomy is indicated; removal of the ovary (oophorectomy) is usually necessary because of ischaemic damage; in a young woman where the ovary may be viable, detorsion and conservation may be considered, but removal is usually necessary; avoid rupture of the cyst intraoperatively; if rupture occurs, thorough peritoneal lavage is required; in pregnancy, prompt removal should not be postponed solely because of pregnancy; cover with tocolytics and perform in a centre with intensive neonatal care when possible.

(v) Other acute complications of ovarian cysts and their distinction: Rupture — signs and symptoms vary; contents of chocolate (endometriotic) and dermoid cysts are extremely irritant and may cause severe symptoms — acute abdomen with chemical peritonitis (sudden rupture) or chronic granulomatous peritonitis (slow leak); during pregnancy, rupture is more common due to external pressure from expanding gravid uterus or trauma during delivery. Haemorrhage into or from cyst — signs and symptoms vary according to degree of haemorrhage; haemorrhage (intraperitoneal bleeding) due to rupture of the tumour may mimic ectopic pregnancy; happens most frequently with a luteal cyst. Infection — not a common complication of ovarian tumours. Torsion is distinguished by the sudden onset of pain, absence of fever initially, and a palpable tender adnexal mass; rupture produces signs of peritoneal irritation; haemorrhage may mimic ectopic pregnancy with peritoneal signs.

questions.answerText:
A(i) The first visible sign of puberty in the female is breast budding (thelarche), occurring under the influence of rising oestrogen levels as the HPO axis activates. Pubic and axillary hair development (adrenarche) typically follows, driven by DHEA (dihydroepiandrosterone) synthesised by the adrenal glands; DHEA levels rise before visible signs of puberty appear and girls achieve higher DHEA concentrations at a similar bone age than boys. Adrenarche is independent of the gonadal axis and can precede gonadarche by 1-2 years. The growth spurt precedes menarche. Menarche usually occurs 2-3 years after thelarche. A critical body weight of approximately 48 kg has been proposed as necessary for onset of menarche, reflecting the relationship between body fat, leptin signalling, and activation of the HPO axis; this explains delayed menarche in female athletes and girls with anorexia nervosa.

A(ii) Delayed puberty: absence of thelarche by 14 years, or absence of menarche by 17 years. Hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism: low GnRH, low FSH and LH, low oestrogen — the problem is at or above the pituitary, with the gonads not being adequately stimulated. Hypergonadotrophic hypogonadism: markedly elevated FSH and LH, low oestrogen — primary gonadal failure with no negative feedback from the gonads.

B(i) Kallmann's syndrome results from failed migration of GnRH neurons and olfactory neurons from the olfactory placode to the hypothalamus during embryological development. Biochemistry: low FSH and LH with low oestrogen, normal karyotype. MRI: absent or hypoplastic olfactory bulbs. Additional characteristic feature: anosmia (absent sense of smell). This combination of absent/delayed puberty with anosmia is pathognomonic.

B(ii) Turner's syndrome (45,X) produces primary amenorrhoea because of bilateral streak gonads — fibrous connective tissue containing no oocytes — resulting in primary ovarian failure. The absence of ovarian function means no oestrogen production, leading to failure of secondary sexual development. Characteristic clinical features: short stature, webbed neck, and shield chest. Fertility can only be achieved through oocyte donation and embryo transfer.
questions.question:
Describe the structure of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis as it relates to puberty, explain the clinical basis for why delayed puberty from a hypothalamic cause differs from gonadal-level disease, and distinguish between Kallmann's syndrome and Turner's syndrome.

A(i) Describe the normal sequence of pubertal events in the female from earliest to latest, naming the first visible sign and the hormone responsible; include the role of DHEA in adrenarche and the critical body weight proposed for menarche onset.
A(ii) Define delayed puberty in the female and state the age thresholds. State the key biochemical findings that distinguish hypogonadotrophic from hypergonadotrophic hypogonadism.
B(i) Explain the embryological basis of Kallmann's syndrome, state the diagnostic findings on MRI and biochemistry, and state its additional characteristic feature.
B(ii) Explain why Turner's syndrome (45,X) produces primary amenorrhoea, state the gonadal finding and its characteristic clinical features, and state the only means by which fertility can be achieved.

questions.answerText:
A(i) The female genital tract forms from fusion of the paramesonephric (Müllerian) ducts and the sino-vaginal bulbs. Congenital gynaetresia results from failure of canalization of the paramesonephric ducts and sino-vaginal bulbs.

A(ii) Types of congenital gynaetresia:
- Absence of vagina (MRKH Syndrome): blindly ending shallow vagina, absence of upper vagina, partial/complete absence of uterus. Relatively uncommon. May have skeletal or urological abnormalities; otherwise normal. Presents after puberty with primary amenorrhoea or difficulty with coitus. Goal of treatment: achieve adequate coitus — by repeated pressure with glass dilators or surgery.
- Septate vagina: transverse septum may mimic congenital absence of vagina/uterus. Perforate septum: normal menses but difficulty with coitus or at delivery. Imperforate septum: retention of blood after menarche. Longitudinal septum associated with double vagina (rarely double cervix/uterus).
- Imperforate hymen: arises from urogenital sinus. Before puberty: mucocolpos or hydrocolpos (accumulated cervical secretion). After puberty: cryptomenorrhoea; cyclic lower abdominal pain; haematocolpos/haematometra/haematosalpinx.

B(i) Imperforate hymen: before puberty may present with mucocolpos in the newborn. After puberty: cryptomenorrhoea — distinct from amenorrhoea; large amount of blood accumulates causing haematocolpos, haematometra, haematosalpinx; presents with amenorrhoea, abdominal mass, urinary retention from displaced bladder or elongated urethra. Transverse vaginal septum: if perforate — normal menses; if imperforate — retention of blood, same as imperforate hymen.

B(ii) Vaginal examination should be avoided in cryptomenorrhoea. The correct examination technique is: inspection of the vulva only — the purplish/bluish bulging membrane is visible; rectal examination — reveals a large, tense and cystic cylindrical swelling filling the pelvis; this allows assessment without disrupting the obstruction or introducing infection.

C) McIndoe-Reed's vaginoplasty: creation of a cavity between the bladder and bowel, lined with a split-thickness skin graft from the thigh on a plastic mould; may contract unless intercourse is regular or a dilator is worn; normal sexual function in 80–90% of patients; reconstruction can also be done with sigmoid colon.
William's vulvovaginoplasty: an external pouch is created by suturing the edges of the posterior parts of the labia majora together in the midline to form a perineal pouch (horizontal 'vagina'); advantage: good clitoral stimulation; disadvantages: shortness, awkward angle for penetration, abnormal-looking genitalia, pressure on rectum during sex.
questions.question:
A) Describe congenital gynaetresia (narrowing of the lower female genital tract) under the following headings:
A(i) Embryological basis, naming the structures whose failure of canalization produces congenital gynaetresia
A(ii) The types of congenital gynaetresia, including Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser (MRKH) syndrome — its features, associated anomalies, presentation and goal of treatment

B) Explain the clinical basis of:
B(i) Why imperforate hymen and transverse vaginal septum differ in clinical presentation before and after puberty, including the distinction between cryptomenorrhoea and amenorrhoea
B(ii) Why vaginal examination should be avoided in a pre-pubertal girl with suspected cryptomenorrhoea, and what the correct examination technique is

C) Distinguish between William's vulvovaginoplasty and McIndoe-Reed's vaginoplasty — their surgical technique, advantages and disadvantages.

questions.answerText:
(i) Complete androgen insensitivity syndrome (CAIS).

(ii) Target tissues are completely unable to respond to androgens (testosterone) because of a defective androgen receptor. Without androgen action on the external genitalia (which require dihydrotestosterone/DHT for virilisation), development proceeds in the default female direction despite 46,XY karyotype and functional testes.

(iii) The testes produce Anti-Mullerian hormone (AMH), which causes Mullerian regression; therefore the uterus, cervix, and upper vagina are absent. However, testosterone cannot virilise external genitalia because of androgen receptor deficiency.

(iv) The intra-abdominal or inguinal testes carry a risk of malignant transformation; prophylactic gonadectomy is required after diagnosis. It is typically deferred until after puberty to allow oestrogen-mediated pubertal development from peripheral aromatisation of androgens, after which gonadectomy is performed.

(v) Swyer's syndrome (46,XY pure gonadal dysgenesis) vs CAIS:
Karyotype: both 46,XY.
Gonads: Swyer's — bilateral streak gonads (fibrous non-functional tissue); CAIS — functional testes in inguinal canal or abdomen.
Uterus: Swyer's — uterus IS present (dysgenetic gonads produce no AMH so Mullerian structures persist); CAIS — uterus is absent (functional testes produce AMH causing Mullerian regression).
Malignancy risk: Swyer's — high risk of gonadoblastoma and dysgerminoma in streak gonads, requiring prophylactic gonadectomy; CAIS — malignant transformation risk in retained testes, also requiring gonadectomy.
questions.question:
A 28-year-old woman with known 46,XY karyotype presents to a genetic clinic. She has complete female external genitalia, absent uterus, and bilateral gonads identified in the inguinal canals. She has never menstruated.

(i) State the most likely diagnosis.

(iv) State the management of the gonads and the reason for this management.
(v) Compare this diagnosis with Swyer's syndrome under the headings: karyotype, gonads, uterus, and malignancy risk.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Position: the cervix projects into the upper vagina, creating the anterior, posterior, and lateral fornices. The transformation zone (squamocolumnar junction) is where columnar endocervical epithelium meets squamous ectocervical epithelium; this is the most common site for cervical dysplasia and carcinoma. Ectropion: eversion of columnar endocervical epithelium onto the ectocervix, appearing as a red raw-looking area around the cervical os; it is a normal variant especially in pregnancy and OCP users, and is a cause of post-coital bleeding and discharge.

A(ii) Cervical smear examination is performed with the patient in the dorsal lithotomy position (supine with hips and knees flexed and legs in stirrups or held apart), which provides optimal access to the cervix for speculum insertion and sampling. The left lateral (Sims') position may be used when dorsal lithotomy is not feasible (e.g. disabled patients). Standardised positioning ensures consistency of examination findings and sampling adequacy.

B(i) Cervical carcinoma classically presents with post-coital bleeding because the tumour is vascular and friable; mechanical trauma from intercourse disrupts the tumour surface causing bleeding. The first-line investigation is cervical smear and speculum examination. If an abnormal cervix is found or the smear is abnormal, the next steps are colposcopy and directed biopsy for histological diagnosis.

B(ii) Gillick competence (Fraser guidelines) is the ethical and legal framework. A young person under 16 can consent independently to examination and treatment if they have sufficient maturity and intelligence to understand the proposed treatment. Clinicians must assess competence individually rather than assuming parental consent is always required. This is particularly relevant in gynaecological practice involving contraception, sexual health, and STI management.
questions.question:
Describe the gross anatomy of the cervix, state how its anatomical zones relate to common pathologies, and explain why disease of the cervix may cause distant functional effects relevant to gynaecological examination.

A(i) Describe the cervix under the headings: position within the vagina, the transformation zone (squamocolumnar junction), and the clinical significance of ectropion.
A(ii) State the correct patient position for performing a cervical smear and explain why standardised positioning is important.
B(i) Explain why post-coital bleeding is the classical presenting symptom of cervical carcinoma, and state the first-line investigation and next steps if an abnormal cervix or abnormal smear is found.
B(ii) State the ethical and legal framework governing consent for gynaecological examination in an adolescent under 16, name the principle, and state the clinician's assessment duty.

A 62-year-old obese nulliparous woman presents with a three-month history of postmenopausal bleeding. She has a history of late menopause at age 54 and type 2 diabetes mellitus. Examination reveals a normal-sized uterus; no cervical or vaginal lesion is seen.

(i) What is the most likely diagnosis, and state all the risk factors present in this patient and those described in the lectures for this condition.
(ii) Describe the two phenotypic categories of patients with this cancer, contrasting their clinical and pathological characteristics.
(iii) What complications arise from surgical staging, and what co-morbidities increase peri-operative risk?
(iv) Outline the surgical options according to stage of disease, and justify the choice of operation for Stage I disease.
questions.answerText:
(i) Most likely diagnosis: Carcinoma of the body of the uterus (endometrial carcinoma). 75% of cases are postmenopausal and the most common symptom is postmenopausal bleeding.
Risk factors present in this patient: obesity (conversion of androstenedione to oestrogen at a higher rate in adipose tissue), nulliparity, late menopause (aged >52 years), diabetes (postmenopausal diabetic women have increased oestrogen levels).
Additional risk factors from the lectures: unopposed oestrogen (from HRT, granulosa cell tumour, polycystic ovarian disease, anovulation), family history (breast/colon/ovarian cancers), hereditary non-polyposis colon cancer (HNPCC), use of tamoxifen.

(ii) First type (classic): tends to be white, nulliparous; obese, hyperlipidaemia, signs of hypoestrogenism, uterine bleeding, infertility, late onset menopause; well-differentiated, superficially invasive, sensitive to progesterone; favourable prognosis; extra-uterine disease unusual.
Second type: tends to be thin, multiparous, African American; poorly differentiated tumours, deep myometrial invasion; high metastasis to lymph nodes and other sites; decreased sensitivity to progestins; poor prognosis.

(iii) Surgical complications: increased bleeding with lymphadenectomy. Post-operative complications related to co-morbidities of hypertension, obesity, diabetes and increased age. Thromboembolism is a risk because of cancer, obesity and older age; prophylaxis with external pneumatic compression or low-dose heparin is recommended.

(iv) Stage I: treatment of choice is total abdominal hysterectomy (TAH) and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (BSO). Radiotherapy is added if invasion extends beyond the inner half of the myometrium. Stage II (surgically fit patient): radical hysterectomy and bilateral pelvic lymphadenectomy with para-aortic node sampling; if unfit, radiotherapy alone. Stage III/IV: treatment is individualised; surgery is not usually first line; radiotherapy followed by occasional surgical intervention for residual disease.

A(i) Normal epithelium: The ectocervix (portio vaginalis) is covered by stratified squamous epithelium. The endocervical canal is lined by columnar epithelium. Dysplasia occurs in either the squamous epithelium of the portio, or in metaplastic epithelium of the endocervical mucosa or in the cervical glands.
A(ii) Transformation zone and squamo-columnar junction: The squamo-columnar junction is the site where squamous epithelium replaces columnar epithelium (metaplasia). As the squamo-columnar junction descends, columnar epithelium changes to squamous epithelium. The site of this metaplasia is called the transformation zone. It is the site where CIN originates; it must be fully visualised at colposcopy, and if it cannot be seen, cone biopsy is mandatory. The Pap smear samples the squamo-columnar junction using a spatula (e.g. Ayre's spatula) and the endocervical canal using a cytobrush.
B. Pathogenesis: The transformation zone is a dynamic area of active cell turnover; it is the site where HPV (especially types 16, 18) infects metaplastic cells, producing oncoproteins that initiate malignant transformation. CIN (pre-malignant condition) shares similar epidemiological characteristics with invasive cervical cancer and is easily identifiable through Pap smear. CIN 1 — mild dysplasia (lower third); CIN 2 — moderate; CIN 3 — severe/carcinoma-in-situ (all thirds). Without treatment, 18% progress to invasion at 10 years and 36% at 20 years.
C. Stage IIIb and hydronephrosis: Stage IIIb — extension on to the pelvic side wall and/or hydronephrosis or a non-functioning kidney not due to other causes. Direct extension of cervical carcinoma to the parametrium and pelvic side walls compresses or encases the ureter at or above the pelvic brim, causing ureteric obstruction, hydronephrosis, and ultimately renal failure (uraemia). A bullous oedema of the bladder does not constitute Stage IV disease.
Causes of death in advanced cervical carcinoma: haemorrhage; infections; and renal failure.

A(i) Normal epithelium — ectocervix and endocervix
