questions.answerText:
A(i) Origin: the mesonephric (Wolffian) ducts develop from the intermediate mesoderm as part of the embryonic urogenital system. Fate in the male: testosterone from fetal Leydig cells stimulates Wolffian duct development into the epididymis, vas deferens, and seminal vesicles. Fate in the female: the Wolffian ducts regress passively in the absence of androgens — not because of active hormonal suppression. This concept of default female differentiation occurs in the absence of androgens rather than requiring active feminising hormones.

A(ii) 5-alpha reductase converts testosterone to dihydrotestosterone (DHT), which is required for virilisation of the external genitalia. Without DHT, despite 46,XY karyotype and functional testes, the external genitalia develop in the default female direction (female or ambiguous at birth) because testosterone alone is insufficient to virilise external genitalia.

B(i) At puberty, the surge in testosterone (which does not require conversion to DHT for its anabolic effects on muscle, voice, and secondary sexual characteristics) causes significant virilisation of the external genitalia — clitoral enlargement, deepening voice, and increased muscle mass. This biological masculinisation at puberty drives gender identity reassessment; 60-80% of affected individuals raised as female undergo gender change to male — a remarkable example of biological and social interaction in gender identity.

B(ii) True hermaphroditism: gonads — both ovarian and testicular tissue present (ovotestes, or one ovary and one testis); karyotype — 46,XX in 71%, 46,XX/46,XY chimerism in 20%, 46,XY in 7%; external genitalia — ambiguous; mechanism — presence of both Y-chromosome-bearing and XX gonadal tissue.
Female pseudohermaphroditism (CAH): gonads — bilateral ovaries; karyotype — 46,XX; external genitalia — virilised/ambiguous; mechanism — excess adrenal androgens in utero causing virilisation of the external genitalia despite normal 46,XX karyotype and normal ovaries.
questions.question:
Describe the origin, course, relations, and significance of the mesonephric (Wolffian) ducts in both sexes; state the approach to managing patients with disorders of sexual development affecting these ducts; and explain the anatomical basis of the deformity in 5-alpha reductase deficiency.

A(i) Describe the mesonephric duct: embryological origin, fate in the male (structures formed), and fate in the female (passive regression).
A(ii) State the role of DHT in external genital development and describe the external genitalia in 5-alpha reductase deficiency at birth and at puberty.
B(i) Explain the anatomical basis for why 60-80% of individuals with 5-alpha reductase deficiency raised as female undergo gender change to male at puberty.
B(ii) Distinguish between true hermaphroditism and female pseudohermaphroditism (CAH) under the headings: gonads, karyotype, external genitalia, and mechanism of virilisation.

A 30-year-old nulliparous woman presents with a 4-year history of pelvic pain, secondary dysmenorrhoea, and progressive infertility. Diagnostic laparoscopy shows bilateral chocolate cysts of the ovaries, adhesions, and powder-burn lesions on the peritoneum. The disease is confirmed as endometriosis.
(i) Describe the pathology of endometriosis, covering both the adenomyotic (internal) and external forms.
(ii) List all the clinical features including history and examination findings.
(iii) What investigations are required?
(iv) Outline the complete treatment protocol, including the medical treatment, its rationale, the role of combined therapy, and the follow-up plan.
questions.answerText:
(i) Pathology:
Adenomyosis (internal): symmetrical enlargement of the uterus; firm walls, coarse, no definite capsule; islands of haemorrhagic cysts; nodes of hyperplastic smooth muscle; involves the inner two-thirds; contains endometrial tissue components with muscular hypertrophy/hyperplasia.
External endometriosis: cysts — young lesions contain altered blood and have thin walls; old lesions contain chocolate-coloured fluid with thick fibrous walls; adhesions. Histologically: endometrial tissue (new), fibrous tissue and siderophages (old). Squamous metaplasia may be seen.
(ii) Clinical features:
Symptoms: may be asymptomatic. Pelvic symptoms: secondary (acquired) dysmenorrhoea beginning 1–2 days before onset of menses; deep dyspareunia; abnormal uterine bleeding; rectal or bladder bleeding and/or pain; infertility; and acute abdomen.
Examination: tenderness; masses or nodules; fixed retroversion of the uterus. Superficial endometriosis: vulva, vagina, cervix, perineum, anterior abdominal wall, umbilicus.
(iii) Investigations: following history and examination — USS; laparoscopy/biopsy (definitive); cystoscopy; colonoscopy; pulmonary tomography; MRI; laparotomy/biopsy.
(iv) Treatment protocol:
Determined by: extent of disease, presence of symptoms, age, parity, and reproductive intentions of the patient/couple.
Conservative (watchful waiting).
Medical: Stilboestrol; combined oral contraceptive (6 months continuous or intermittent); progestogens (MPA, Primolut) continuously for 9 months; Danazol (gold standard) 200–800 mg twice daily for 6 months — relieves symptoms in 70%, pregnancy rate 50%; methyltestosterone; gestrinone; GnRH agonists; gossypol.
Surgical: Conservative surgery (excision/ablation of lesions, drainage of cysts, adhesiolysis); radical surgery (total hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy for completed family).
Combined therapy: pre-operative 6–8 weeks or post-operative hormonal therapy.
IVF and ET. Radiation (rarely).
Follow-up: physical examination 3–12 monthly for 5 years; laparoscopy if symptoms recur; document recurrence.

questions.question:
A 40-year-old woman presents with secondary amenorrhoea of 6 months, gradually deepening voice, facial hair, and clitoral enlargement. Bimanual examination reveals a 4 cm left adnexal solid mass.
(i) What is the spot diagnosis?
(ii) What are the predisposing factors and pathophysiology of sex cord stromal tumours that produce androgens?
(iii) What hormonal and imaging investigations should be performed?
(iv) What is the management, including the surgical approach and follow-up?
questions.answerText:
(i) Spot diagnosis: Sertoli-Leydig cell tumour (androblastoma/arrhenoblastoma) producing androgens, causing virilisation. Masculinising (androgen-producing) tumours initially result in defeminisation — including secondary amenorrhoea — then hirsuitism, enlargement of the clitoris, and deepening of the voice.

(ii) Predisposing factors and pathophysiology: sex cord stromal tumours — the stromal cells retain a potential for differentiation into any of the cells or tissues arising from the mesenchyme of the gonad (granulosa, theca, Leydig, and Sertoli cells); these rare tumours may therefore secrete any or all of the ovarian steroids; Sertoli-Leydig cell group may secrete androgens; Sertoli-Leydig cell tumours (androblastoma/arrhenoblastoma) — rare tumour; half of these neoplasms produce male hormones causing virilisation; rarely, oestrogens are secreted; sex cord stromal tumours represent only 4% of benign ovarian tumours; they occur at any age from pre-pubertal children to elderly postmenopausal women; many secrete hormones and present with the result of inappropriate hormone effects. Granulosa cell tumours (feminising) produce oestrogen; Sertoli-Leydig cell tumours produce androgens.

(iii) Investigations: serum androgen levels (testosterone, androstenedione) — increased in Sertoli-Leydig tumours; oestradiol levels may be elevated in some ovarian tumours; ultrasound (TAS or TVS) — solid ovarian masses are more likely to be malignant than cystic counterparts; CT scan or MRI; CA-125; FBC, LFTs, RFTs; laparoscopy in doubtful cases; serum markers including inhibin (secreted by granulosa cell tumours); beta-hCG and AFP to exclude germ cell components; abdominal X-ray.

(iv) Management: surgical treatment is the same as for epithelial tumours — TAH, BSO in older women; in young women with localised disease, unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy may be justifiable; prognosis for the majority with localised disease is good; Sertoli-Leydig cell tumours that are well-differentiated have a good prognosis; adjuvant therapy assessment is difficult; radiotherapy has been largely replaced by chemotherapy in advanced or recurrent cases; treatment is the same as for granulosa cell tumours; follow-up with serial androgen and oestrogen levels; reassessment of virilisation after surgical removal; fertility may be preserved in younger women with Stage I disease.

questions.question:
A. Describe the ischio-rectal fossa under the following headings:
A(i) Boundaries — lateral, medial, posterior, anterior, and floor
A(ii) Contents
B. Explain the clinical significance of the ischio-rectal fossa in relation to the pudendal nerve during perineal surgery and delivery.
C. Distinguish between the anterior perineum (urogenital triangle) and the posterior perineum (anal triangle) in terms of boundaries, division, and principal contents.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Boundaries of the ischio-rectal fossa:
- Lateral: pudendal vessels and nerve within the pudendal canal
- Medial: fascial covering of the levator ani and external anal sphincter
- Posterior: sacrotuberous ligament
- Anterior: urogenital perineum
- Floor: skin and subcutaneous fat
A(ii) Contents: the pudendal nerve and vessels (within the pudendal canal on the lateral wall), fat filling the fossa, and branches of the inferior rectal nerve/vessels crossing to the anal sphincter.
B. Clinical significance: the pudendal nerve (S2–S4) runs within the pudendal canal on the lateral wall of the ischio-rectal fossa, in close proximity to the ischial spine. This is the anatomical basis for the pudendal nerve block used in obstetric analgesia. The nerve supplies the external anal sphincter (via the inferior rectal branch) and the perineal muscles (via the perineal branch — the largest branch — and the clitoral branch). Injury to the pudendal nerve during delivery or perineal repair can cause denervation of the levator ani and external anal sphincter, contributing to pelvic floor weakness and faecal incontinence. Studies show evidence of nerve and mechanical damage in women with prolapse, compared with those without, occurring as a result of vaginal delivery.
C. Anterior vs posterior perineum:
The perineum is bounded anteriorly by the ischiopubic rami, posteriorly by the coccyx and sacrotuberous ligament. Division is by a line between the ischial tuberosities.
Anterior perineum (urogenital triangle): contains the structures of the vulva (mons, labia, clitoris, vestibule, erectile structures), the superficial perineal pouch (ischiocavernosus, bulbospongiosus, superficial transverse perineal muscle, vestibular bulb, Bartholin's glands), the perineal membrane (triangular dense fibromuscular sheet, previously urogenital diaphragm), and the perineal body.
Posterior perineum (anal triangle): contains the anus, anal sphincter (external and internal), levator ani, and ischio-rectal fossa.

questions.question:
A 56-year-old nulliparous woman presents with postmenopausal bleeding, watery vaginal discharge and intermittent lower abdominal pain. She has a history of infertility. Laparotomy reveals a retort-shaped mass arising from the left fallopian tube.

(i) What is the diagnosis? State the mean age at diagnosis, the percentage of patients with nulliparity and infertility, and whether it is typically unilateral or bilateral.
(ii) Describe the pathological features including the histological type, how the tumour spreads, and how it is staged.
(iii) Outline the initial resuscitation and pre-operative assessment required before surgery.
(iv) State the definitive surgical procedure and the post-operative adjuvant treatment, including the survival figures by stage.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Cancer of the fallopian tube. Mean age at diagnosis: 56 years. Nulliparity is present in 45% of patients. Infertility is present in 71% of patients. Usually unilateral.

(ii) Pathological features: The tumour usually distends the lumen of the tube and may protrude through the fimbrial end. The tube may be retort-shaped, resembling a hydrosalpinx. Histologically, the tumour is similar to ovarian serous adenocarcinoma. Tumour spread is identical to ovarian cancer; metastasis to pelvic and para-aortic nodes is common. Staging: FIGO clinical staging is similar to that of ovarian cancer.

(iii) Pre-operative assessment: full history and physical examination; investigations — full blood count (haemoglobin/haematocrit minimum 30%), blood group and crossmatch, serum urea, electrolytes and creatinine, liver function tests, ECG and chest X-ray. Ultrasound of pelvis and abdomen. Assessment of fitness for surgery.

(iv) Definitive treatment: Surgery to remove gross tumour — total abdominal hysterectomy (TAH) and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (BSO). Post-operative chemotherapy (platinum-based combination) for all but the earliest cases. Survival results: overall 5-year survival approximately 35%; prognosis improved if tumour detected early. Stage 1a: 70% 5-year survival. Stage 2b–3c: 25–30% 5-year survival. Best results with platinum agents.

questions.question:
A) Describe the post-operative urinary tract complications of gynaecological surgery under the following headings:
A(i) Types of urinary retention — complete and partial — their causes and treatment including catheter management
A(ii) Urinary fistulae — types, causes, and the specific operation after which uretero-vaginal fistula most commonly occurs and why

B) Explain the clinical basis of:
B(i) The difference between phlebothrombosis and thrombophlebitis, including their sites of origin, predisposing causes and how pulmonary embolism arises from each
B(ii) The anticoagulation regimen for established thrombosis — naming the drugs, doses and monitoring parameters specified in the lectures

C) Describe the post-operative respiratory complications that can arise from general anaesthesia and state how pulmonary embolism is distinguished from simple chest complications.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Urinary retention:
Complete retention: common after hysterectomy or repair of prolapse; hysterical retention may rarely occur after minor operations such as dilatation and curettage. Treatment: immediate catheterisation, usually emptying the bladder once; if must be repeated, an indwelling catheter for a few days; some surgeons prefer suprapubic catheterisation.
Partial retention: common after operations for prolapse; a catheter should be passed to check for residual urine 5 days after operation; catheter drainage should continue until residual urine is below 200 mls.

A(ii) Urinary fistulae:
Types: vesico-vaginal fistula (VVF) and uretero-vaginal fistula.
Causes: trauma at operation, haematoma formation, difficult obstetric delivery, malignant disease.
Uretero-vaginal fistula most commonly follows Wertheim's hysterectomy, where the ureters are extensively dissected so that their blood supply is imperilled and they become devascularised. Warning is often given by unilateral loin ache and a slight temperature.

B(i) Phlebothrombosis: primary venous thrombosis; generally begins in the deep veins of the calf. Predisposing causes: trauma; anaemia; stasis; high oestrogen levels. Thrombophlebitis: caused by infection, generally in the pelvic veins initially, spreading to involve the iliac veins. Pulmonary embolism can follow either type of thrombosis; if massive, it is rapidly fatal; small emboli cause pulmonary infarction. Chest symptoms after the first week sometimes indicate pulmonary embolism.

B(ii) Anticoagulation for established thrombosis: Heparin initially — continuous intravenous infusion at 1000–1500 IU per hour, or by separate intravenous injection of 10,000 IU every 6–8 hours; calcium heparin can be given subcutaneously. Dindevan (phenindione): initial dose 200 mg, then 100 mg, then 50 mg daily, depending on prothrombin time, which should be kept at 20–30% of normal. Warfarin: 30–50 mg on first day, none on second day, then adjusted according to the International Normalised Ratio (INR). Low molecular weight heparin (e.g. clexane) now available as prophylaxis.

C) Respiratory complications from general anaesthesia: sore throat, tracheitis, bronchitis, bronchopneumonia, massive collapse of the lungs. Treatment: breathing exercises post-anaesthesia; antibiotics for pulmonary infection. Pulmonary embolism is distinguished from simple chest complications by: later onset (after the first week); symptoms of pleuritic pain, haemoptysis, dyspnoea, and signs of hypoxia; these are different from the early onset of simple atelectasis and bronchopneumonia.

questions.question:
A 22-year-old woman presents with primary infertility. Bimanual examination reveals a fixed, tender adnexal mass with restricted uterine mobility. Hysterosalpingography shows bilateral tubal occlusion. Laparoscopy is planned.

(i) State the most likely underlying diagnosis based on the clinical and investigative findings.
(ii) Explain the pathophysiological mechanism by which this condition causes tubal factor infertility.
(iii) State the specific examination finding that palpates the posterior pelvis for deep infiltrating disease of this type.
(iv) State the nerve and ligament structures at risk during extensive pelvic dissection in this area.
(v) State the sonographic finding that most sensitively detects endometrial polyps (an alternative cause of infertility), giving its sensitivity compared to standard TVUS.
questions.answerText:
(i) Endometriosis with pelvic adhesions and bilateral tubal occlusion causing tubal factor infertility. A fixed, tender adnexal mass with restricted uterine mobility suggests pelvic adhesions or endometrioma from endometriosis or previous pelvic inflammatory disease.

(ii) Endometriosis or PID causes peritubal adhesions and tubal occlusion. The adhesions may surround and kink the fallopian tubes, preventing normal sperm-egg transport and embryo passage. Tubal occlusion detected on HSG confirms blocked transport pathways.

(iii) Recto-vaginal examination is performed to palpate the posterior cul-de-sac (pouch of Douglas), uterosacral ligaments, and rectovaginal septum for nodularity — characteristic of deep infiltrating endometriosis. This provides information about the posterior pelvic compartment not accessible on bimanual examination alone.

(iv) The uterosacral ligaments (which contain autonomic nerve fibres) and the ureter are at risk during extensive pelvic dissection. Recto-vaginal examination specifically palpates the uterosacral ligaments for nodularity of deep infiltrating endometriosis.

(v) Saline infusion sonohysterography (SIS) or office hysteroscopy. SIS has sensitivity of 90%+ for polyps; hysteroscopy approaches 100%. Standard TVUS has sensitivity of only 60-70% because polyps may not distort the endometrial outline without cavity distension. Hysteroscopy also allows simultaneous therapeutic polypectomy.

questions.question:
A 55-year-old postmenopausal woman presents with post-coital bleeding, an offensive purulent vaginal discharge, pelvic pain, and lower limb oedema. Pelvic examination reveals an ulcerated, friable lesion replacing most of the cervix. Biopsy shows squamous cell carcinoma. Staging reveals extension to the pelvic side walls and non-functioning right kidney (not due to other causes).
(i) What FIGO stage does this represent, and what are the staging criteria from Stage I to Stage IV?
(ii) Describe all histological types of cervical carcinoma.
(iii) Outline the management of this patient, including the treatment appropriate for her stage and follow-up.
(iv) State the complications that can necessitate ultraradical surgery, and name the procedures involved.
questions.answerText:
(i) FIGO Stage IIIb: extension on to the pelvic side wall and/or hydronephrosis or non-functioning kidney not due to other causes.
Full staging criteria:
Stage I — confined to the cervix (disregard extension to the corpus).
Ia — microinvasive carcinoma (early stromal invasion).
Ib — all other cases of Stage I.
Stage II — involves the cervix and vagina (except the lower third).
IIa — no obvious parametrial involvement.
IIb — obvious parametrial involvement.
Stage III — involves the lower third of the vagina.
IIIa — no extension on to the pelvic side wall.
IIIb — extension on to the pelvic side wall and/or hydronephrosis or non-functioning kidney.
Stage IV — has extended beyond the true pelvis or involved the mucosa of the bladder or rectum. A bullous oedema does not constitute Stage IV.
IVa — involvement of adjacent organs.
IVb — spread to distant organs.
(ii) Histological types: Squamous cell carcinoma — percentage variously quoted as 65–70% or 90%. Adenocarcinoma — approximately 10%, predominantly endocervical in origin; varieties: mucinous, capillary, endometrioid, and clear-cell forms; thought to be of worse prognosis than squamous carcinoma. Adenocarcinoma-in-situ — unlike CIN, does not seem to relate to sexual activity or socio-economic class. Clear cell adenocarcinoma — like the corresponding vaginal tumour, is related to exposure in utero to DES.
(iii) Management for Stage IIIb: Radiotherapy. Advanced disease (Stage IIb–III) is treated with radiotherapy; Stage IV receives palliative treatment. Follow-up: 6 weeks post-treatment; then 3-monthly for 2 years; 6-monthly for 2 years; then yearly for life. During each visit: history, full clinical examination, smear, chest X-ray, IVU, renal function tests, FBC, and treatment of recurrent or persistent disease.
(iv) Ultraradical surgery: Pelvic exenteration (anterior, posterior, or total); urinary diversion; and faecal diversion. Causes of death in advanced cervical carcinoma: haemorrhage, infections, and renal failure.

questions.question:
A) Describe placental site trophoblastic tumour (PSTT) under the following headings:
A(i) Cell of origin, relative rarity, and what markers it produces (distinguishing it from other GTD types)
A(ii) Pathological features — gross and microscopic appearance, and what it may be mistaken for

B) Explain the clinical basis of:
B(i) Why PSTT responds poorly to chemotherapy, and what the preferred treatment is
B(ii) Why the FIGO classification system requires PSTT to be reported separately

C) Distinguish between the clinical behaviour of PSTT and that of choriocarcinoma, under the headings of hCG levels, response to chemotherapy, degree of local invasiveness, and prognosis.
questions.answerText:
A(i) PSTT is the rarest form of GTD — approximately 1% of GTD. It derives from a monomorphic population of implantation-site intermediate trophoblast. It can arise from any pregnancy, mostly from hydatidiform mole. It is locally invasive; invasion to the adnexa is rare. Unlike other GTD types, it produces low levels of hCG, but is more likely to produce human placental lactogen (hPL).

A(ii) Pathological features: Gross — microscopic, polypoidal or nodular lesions with haemorrhage and necrosis. Microscopic — intermediate trophoblast with no chorionic villi. Malignant variants show high mitotic index, extreme cellularity, extensive necrosis, local spread and widespread metastases. It may be mistaken for sarcoma because of its microscopic appearance with no villi.

B(i) PSTT has poor response to chemotherapy. The preferred treatment is total abdominal hysterectomy (TAH), which is the best option for definitive treatment. This is because the tumour arises from implantation-site intermediate trophoblast and lacks the chemosensitivity of choriocarcinoma.

B(ii) FIGO requires PSTT to be reported separately because: its behaviour and treatment differ fundamentally from other GTD; it produces low hCG (unlike choriocarcinoma which produces very high hCG); it is resistant to chemotherapy; and surgical resection is the primary treatment. Including it with other GTD would distort treatment response statistics.

C) PSTT vs Choriocarcinoma:
- hCG levels: PSTT — low hCG level (but high hPL); Choriocarcinoma — extremely high hCG (a single tumour cell produces 5×10⁻⁵ to 5×10⁻⁶ IU hCG/24 hours).
- Response to chemotherapy: PSTT — poor response, resistant; Choriocarcinoma — highly responsive to single agent (methotrexate, actinomycin D) or combination (EMA-CO) chemotherapy.
- Local invasiveness: PSTT — locally invasive, invasion to adnexa rare, rarely metastasises; Choriocarcinoma — rapidly invades myometrium and blood vessels, haematogenous spread to lungs (80%), vagina, brain, liver.
- Prognosis: PSTT — may be self-limiting but can be highly aggressive; Choriocarcinoma — 100% cure in non-metastatic disease, >90% in high-risk with EMA-CO.

questions.question:
Describe the population dynamics of Nigeria and the indices used in measuring population growth.

A(i) Definition of population dynamics and the factors that determine the size and pattern of growth of a population
A(ii) Definition and formulae for crude birth rate, crude death rate, crude rate of natural increase, and net migration rate
B(i) Specific rates used in measuring population: infant mortality rate, neonatal mortality rate, stillbirth rate, perinatal mortality rate, maternal mortality ratio, and fertility rate
B(ii) Sources of health statistics and vital statistics, with examples
C(i) Nigeria's demographic profile, highlighting key indices from available data
C(ii) The significance of crude rates of population increase, with examples of doubling time, and the implications of rapid population growth for national development
questions.answerText:
A(i) Population dynamics is the study of the size, composition, and growth of populations. The size of a population and its pattern of growth depend on the balance between: births; deaths; and migration—either increasing population if there is immigration or decreasing if there is emigration.
A(ii) Crude Birth Rate (CBR): (Births Per Year / Total Population mid-year) × 1,000 = births per 1,000 population per year. Crude Death Rate (CDR): (Deaths Per Year / Total Population mid-year) × 1,000 = deaths per 1,000 population per year. Crude Rate of Natural Increase: Crude Birth Rate (CBR) minus Crude Death Rate (CDR). Net Migration Rate (NMR): (Number of Immigrants − Number of Emigrants) / Total Population (mid-year) × 1,000 = net migration per 1,000 population per year; may be positive or negative. Crude Rate of Population Increase: Crude Birth Rate − Crude Death Rate + Net Migration Rate. These rates are called 'crude' because they do not relate the events (births, deaths, or migration) to the true population at risk; e.g., births can only occur to women of reproductive age, but CBR relates births to the total population which includes children, the elderly, and men.
B(i) Infant Mortality Rate: (No. of deaths in infants < 1 year / No. of live births during the year) × 1,000. Neonatal Mortality Rate: (No. of deaths in infants < 1 month / No. of live births during the year) × 1,000. Stillbirth Rate: (No. of fetal deaths after 28 weeks of pregnancy / No. of births during the year) × 1,000. Perinatal Mortality Rate: (No. of stillbirths and deaths in infants ≤ 1 month / No. of births during the year) × 1,000. Maternal Mortality Ratio: (No. of maternal deaths due to pregnancy / No. of births during the year) × 100,000. Fertility Rate: (No. of births in a year / No. of women between 15–49) × 1,000.
B(ii) Vital statistics are records of certain vital events, e.g., births, deaths, marriages. Sources of health statistics include: notification of diseases; institutional records; epidemiological surveys; demographic surveys (e.g., NDHS, Fertility Surveys); data collected for determination of population—census; data collected for other purposes, e.g., school health, utilisation of medical services, insurance.
C(i) Nigeria's demographic profile: land area 923,768 sq km; arable land 285,912; forest land 140,600; total population 88,500,000 (estimated 2003: 126,000,000); crude population density 96/sq m (varies from 27 persons/sq km in Taraba State to 1,712 persons in Lagos State); critical population density 310. In the past three decades Nigeria has made very bold efforts to achieve rapid economic development; however, rapid population growth has affected the quality of life and made achievement of socio-economic development goals difficult.
C(ii) Significance of crude rates of population increase: if the crude rate of population increase is 1% per year, the population will double in approximately 69 years; if the crude rate of population increase is 3% per year, the population will double in approximately 23 years (69 divided by 3). Despite positive gains, 123 million women around the world, mostly in developing countries, are not using contraception despite an expressed desire to space or limit the number of births. Contraceptive use is still low and the need high in some of the world's poorest and most populous places. Rapid population growth makes achievement of socio-economic development goals difficult; family planning can save lives by: delaying motherhood; avoiding too many children; avoiding closely-spaced children; preventing pregnancy under stress; avoiding unsafe abortion.

questions.question:
A 33-year-old woman presents with persistent vaginal bleeding after evacuation of a molar pregnancy 6 weeks ago. Serum hCG is 60,000 mIU/ml and rising. Pelvic ultrasound shows an irregular heterogeneous uterine mass. Chest X-ray shows multiple rounded opacities in both lung fields.
(i) What is the diagnosis and what is the differential between invasive mole and choriocarcinoma in this presentation?
(ii) Using the FIGO/WHO risk factor scoring system, classify this patient's risk level and justify.
(iii) What pre-chemotherapy workup must be completed?
(iv) Describe the chemotherapy options for low-risk versus high-risk gestational trophoblastic neoplasia, including specific drugs and regimens.
(v) What are the surgical options available and when are they used?
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: persistent/malignant gestational trophoblastic neoplasia, most likely choriocarcinoma. Distinction: invasive mole — confined to the uterus (or rarely to vagina and lungs), invades myometrium and pelvic blood vessels; chorionic villi present (small villi); most often a D&C would have been performed; TAH is beneficial; locally invasive, rarely metastasises late; occurs after hydatidiform mole. Choriocarcinoma — purely epithelial, no chorionic villi; sheets of anaplastic cells consisting of intermingled syncytio- and cytotrophoblastic elements; extensive necrosis and haemorrhage; rapidly invades myometrium and vessels — haematogeneous embolization to lungs (80%), vagina, pelvis, liver, brain (10%); 50% follow molar pregnancy; clinical features: great imitator — metastases reported in virtually every part of the body, most commonly lungs, vagina, liver, brain; pulmonary metastases on CXR as coin lesion or cannonball opacities.

(ii) Risk classification using FIGO/WHO scoring: Age (greater than 39 years) — scores 0 if less than 39; Antecedent pregnancy (molar) — scores 0; Interval from antecedent pregnancy 6 weeks (less than 4 months) — scores 0; Pre-treatment hCG (60,000 mIU/ml = 10^4–10^5) — scores 2; Largest tumour (including uterine, assuming greater than 5 cm from imaging) — scores 2; Site of metastases (lungs) — scores 0; Number of metastases (multiple bilateral — more than 8 possible) — scores 3; Previous chemotherapy — none, scores 0. Total score approximately 7 — medium risk (5–7) or high risk depending on exact interpretation; if score greater than 7, high risk. High-risk criteria: liver or brain metastasis; interval greater than 4 months; serum beta-hCG titre greater than 40,000 IU/ml (this patient has 60,000 — exceeds threshold); initial titre greater than 100,000 IU per 24-hour urine; previous chemotherapy failure; choriocarcinoma following normal term gestation. This patient meets high-risk criteria due to hCG greater than 40,000 IU/ml and pulmonary metastases with multiple lesions.

(iii) Pre-chemotherapy workup: serum hCG level; FBC (PCV greater than 30%, WBC greater than 3,000/mm^3, platelets greater than 100,000/mm^3); LFTs; RFTs; chest X-ray; CT/MRI of brain, chest, abdomen-pelvis; pelvic USS; CSF hCG (plasma-CSF ratio greater than 60:1 indicates CNS disease); coagulation profile; blood group and crossmatch; serum electrolytes; histological diagnosis where available (not required for treatment initiation in GTD).

(iv) Chemotherapy options: low-risk (score less than 5): single agent — Methotrexate (4 doses on alternate days with folinic acid to limit systemic toxicity) or Actinomycin-D (5-day regimen); given in 14-day cycles or as soon as toxicity permits; if resistant to single agent, switch to combination chemotherapy. Medium risk (score 5–7): combination chemotherapy. High-risk (score greater than 7/8): intensive combination chemotherapy — EMA-CO (Etoposide, Methotrexate, Actinomycin-D, Cyclophosphamide, Vincristine) — most successful and least toxic; salvage regimens: MAC, MAC-III (Methotrexate, Actinomycin-D, Cyclophosphamide); second-line: cisplatin with MTX and vincristine; repeat cycles until complete remission (3 consecutive normal hCG levels); then commence surveillance; 2–3 more courses after remission. Prognosis: 100% remission non-metastatic; 70–80% for metastatic (high-risk with EMA-CO).

(v) Surgical options and indications: hysterectomy — for invasive mole, uncontrollable haemorrhage, tumour perforation, septicaemia, resistance to chemotherapy, patients with complete families (reduces malignant sequelae to less than 5%); adjuvant chemotherapy given with hysterectomy to reduce likelihood of disseminating viable tumour cells at surgery, maintain cytotoxic levels in bloodstream and tissue, and treat occult metastases. Other surgical options: wide local excision of vaginal metastases; arteriographic embolization of hypogastric arteries; pulmonary segmental resection; hepatic resection; hepatic artery embolization or ligation; craniotomy; role of surgery in GTD also includes control of bleeding from vaginal/vulval secondaries; occasional haemostatic dose of irradiation to abort a heavy bleeding episode. Resistant or Stage IV disease should be referred to centres with special expertise.

A(i) Physiological cysts: large versions of cysts that form during the normal ovarian cycle. Follicular cysts arise from failure of the dominant follicle to rupture or failure of atresia in non-dominant follicles; they may produce oestrogen and cause menstrual disturbance and endometrial hyperplasia; they can persist for several menstrual cycles and may reach 10 cm. Luteal (corpus luteum) cysts are less common, more likely to present with intraperitoneal bleeding especially on the right, and rupture most frequently on days 20–26. Theca-lutein cysts are associated with GTD and high hCG stimulation. Most functional cysts regress spontaneously.

A(ii) Neoplastic benign ovarian tumours by cell of origin:
- Epithelial tumours: serous cystadenoma, mucinous cystadenoma, endometrioid, clear cell, Brenner tumour
- Germ cell tumours: dermoid cyst (mature cystic teratoma), monodermal teratomas (struma ovarii, carcinoid)
- Sex cord stromal tumours: granulosa cell tumour, thecoma, fibroma, Sertoli-Leydig cell tumour

B(i) The risk of malignancy is proportional to age because malignant tumours increase from the age of 50 onwards. 45% of tumours removed from women aged 45 years or over are malignant.

B(ii) Most benign ovarian tumours are cystic. The finding of solid elements makes malignancy most likely, because malignant transformation alters tumour architecture from cystic to solid or mixed.

C) Serous cystadenoma: consists of clear watery fluid; may be unilocular with finger-like papillary excrescences; can be bilateral. Mucinous cystadenoma: can attain huge size, usually multi-locular; content is clear, thick and viscid; rupture can cause pseudomyxoma peritonei where tumour continues to secrete mucin into the peritoneal cavity.
questions.question:
A) Describe benign ovarian tumours under the following headings:
A(i) Physiological (functional) types — their pathogenesis and clinical behaviour
A(ii) Histological classification of neoplastic benign ovarian tumours by cell of origin, giving examples under each class

B) Explain the clinical basis of the following:
B(i) Why the risk of malignancy in an ovarian tumour is proportional to age, and what percentage of tumours removed from women aged 45 years or over are malignant
B(ii) Why solid elements in an ovarian mass are particularly significant

C) Distinguish between a serous cystadenoma and a mucinous cystadenoma with regard to size, laterality, content and association with complications.

questions.answerText:
A(i) GnRH pulse frequency: high-frequency GnRH pulses stimulate predominantly FSH secretion; low-frequency pulses favour LH secretion, allowing independent control. Proliferative phase: rising oestrogen from the growing follicle drives endometrial proliferation and spiral arteriole development. Secretory phase: progesterone from the corpus luteum after ovulation converts the oestrogen-primed endometrium to secretory type — tortuous glands, glycogen-rich secretions, oedematous stroma. Leading to menstruation: when progesterone and oestrogen fall at end of the luteal phase, PGF2a and endothelin are released causing vasoconstriction of spiral arterioles, ischaemia, and shedding of the functionalis.

A(ii) The aetiopathogenesis of DUB involves primary disturbances in endometrial eicosanoid (prostaglandin and thromboxane) metabolism and in lysosomal and fibrinolytic enzyme systems regulating endometrial haemostasis and shedding. Prostaglandin imbalance — excess PGE2/prostacyclin relative to PGF2a/thromboxane — promotes vasodilatation and inhibits platelet aggregation, worsening menorrhagia. These disturbances may originate primarily in the endometrium or secondarily from endocrine changes at the ovarian, pituitary, or hypothalamic level.

B(i) The LNG-IUS (Mirena) reduces menstrual blood loss by 80-95% through local progestogenic effects on the endometrium, causing endometrial atrophy and decidualisation. This efficacy is superior to oral progestogens and tranexamic acid, comparable to endometrial ablation, and is associated with high patient satisfaction. It avoids systemic hormonal side effects and provides concurrent contraception.

B(ii) PALM (structural causes): Polyps, Adenomyosis, Leiomyoma, Malignancy/hyperplasia. Examples: adenomyosis (endometrial glands within myometrium); endometrial polyps detected on SIS/hysteroscopy. COEIN (non-structural causes): Coagulopathy, Ovulatory dysfunction, Endometrial, Iatrogenic, Not yet classified. Examples: anovulatory cycles (ovulatory dysfunction); coagulopathy. Adenomyosis falls under PALM (the 'A' in PALM).
questions.question:
Describe the structure of the HPO axis components relevant to menstrual control, explain the clinical basis for why DUB from primary endometrial disturbances produces different management than DUB from ovulatory causes, and distinguish between the PALM and COEIN components of abnormal uterine bleeding.

A(i) Describe the HPO axis: GnRH pulse frequency and differential FSH/LH effects; the role of oestrogen; the role of progesterone; and the hormonal events leading to menstruation.
A(ii) Describe the two endometrial systems involved in the aetiopathogenesis of DUB and state how prostaglandin imbalance worsens menorrhagia.
B(i) Explain the clinical basis for why the LNG-IUS is considered first-line management of menorrhagia, state the percentage reduction in MBL it achieves, and compare its efficacy with endometrial ablation.
B(ii) Distinguish between the PALM and COEIN components of the FIGO classification, giving two examples for each, and state which component adenomyosis falls under.

A) Describe the CA-125 tumour marker under the following headings:
A(i) Nature, molecular weight, and the monoclonal antibody used to identify it
A(ii) Tissues and tumours that express it, the cut-off level used clinically, and the method of detection in serum

B) Explain the clinical basis of the following:
B(i) Why CA-125 is more useful for monitoring than for primary screening, using the positive and negative predictive values stated in the lectures
B(ii) How CA-125 levels behave in endometriosis across different disease severities, and what specificity and sensitivity values apply

C) Distinguish between the role of CA-125 used alone and in combination with ultrasound for the early detection of epithelial ovarian cancer.
questions.answerText:
A(i) CA-125 is a Mullerian differentiated antigen identified by a monoclonal antibody OC 125. It is a mucin-like glycoprotein with a molecular weight greater than 200 KDA.

A(ii) It is expressed by 80% of non-mucinous ovarian tumours including serous, endometrioid, clear cell and undifferentiated ovarian tumours, and by endometriosis. It can also be positive in 0.2% of healthy blood donors, 1% of normal healthy women, 5% of benign gynaecological disorders, 16% of women in the first trimester of pregnancy, 25% of non-gynaecological conditions such as GI tract cancers and breast cancer. High levels are also detected in advanced cases of adenocarcinoma of the cervix, endometrium and fallopian tube. The cut-off level is 35 u/ml. It is detected in serum by RIA.

B(i) The predictive value of a positive test is 100% — when the level was >35 u/ml, disease was always detected during second-look surgery. The predictive value of a negative test is only 56% — when the level was <35 u/ml, disease was still detected in 44% during second-look surgery. Persistently high levels after chemotherapy indicate resistant clones of tumour tissue. Therefore it is better as a monitor than as a diagnostic screening tool.

B(ii) In normal persons without endometriosis: 8–22 u/ml (non-menstrual phase). In minimal to mild endometriosis: 14–31 u/ml. In moderate to severe endometriosis: 13–95 u/ml. Specificity in endometriosis is about 80%; sensitivity is around 66%. If the ratio during menstrual phase to follicular phase is more than 1.5, it is a better sensitive marker.

C) CA-125 alone has a sensitivity of 50% for Stage I and 60% for Stage II ovarian cancer. Its specificity increases when combined with ultrasound or measured over a period of time. The most promising screening approach combines CA-125 with ultrasound for women with persistently raised values. At present, screening the general population is neither useful nor safe.

questions.question:
Describe the acquired causes of gynaetresia, their pathogenesis, clinical presentation, management principles, and prevention.
A(i) List all the acquired causes of gynaetresia/vaginal stenosis, categorising them by mechanism.
A(ii) Describe the clinical features and symptoms of acquired gynaetresia, and the complications of female genital mutilation specifically.
B(i) Describe the surgical and non-surgical management of acquired gynaetresia including vaginoplasty techniques, postoperative care, and contraindications.
B(ii) State the prevention measures for acquired gynaetresia.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Acquired causes of gynaetresia/vaginal stenosis by mechanism: chemical and traumatic — insertion of herbal concoctions or corrosive properties (alum, potassium permanganate, crude potash mixed with palm oil in southwest Nigeria, rock salt in Middle Eastern countries, special leaves in Southern Nigeria, herbal pessary and soap); traditional vulvo-vaginal incisions (Gishiri cut, angurya cuts); caustic/toxic materials cause irritation, chemical burns, and necrosis. Obstetric — prolonged obstructed labour; pressure necrosis/sloughing of vaginal wall; difficult labour (Gishiri cut, episiotomy, birth injuries); abortion complications. Surgical — repair of vesicovaginal fistula especially for large defects; colporrhaphy (too much vaginal tissue excised); anterior and posterior vaginal wall repairs. Infectious/inflammatory — following healing of ulcers of lymphogranuloma venereum (Chlamydia trachomatis); vaginitis from diphtheria or measles causing vaginitis and atresia. Radiotherapy — post-intracavitary radiotherapy; post-caesium therapy for cancer of cervix. Senile — senile vaginitis (oestrogen deficiency). Iatrogenic — female genital mutilation/cutting (FGM/FGC); circumcision (Type III — infibulation especially). Malignancies. In Ibadan: chemical vaginitis is the commonest cause; accounts for 7 in 1000 admissions; peak age 20–30 years.

A(ii) Clinical features and symptoms: continuous dribbling incontinence; dyspareunia; apareunia (most common presenting complaints); urethral coitus; dysmenorrhoea/amenorrhoea/cryptomenorrhoea; haematocolpos; haematometra; pyometra; monthly acute retention of urine/difficulty in initiating micturition; infertility; dystocia; clitoral retention cysts; fistulae. Age at presentation: neonate — congenital; 3–18 months — labial agglutination, circumcision; peripubertal — circumcision; childbearing age — chemical vaginitis, obstructed labour, colporrhaphy, birth traumas; peri- and postmenopausal — LGV, brachytherapy. Complications of FGM specifically — common presentations: urinary splashing; dyspareunia; apareunia; cryptomenorrhoea; infertility; obstructed labour. WHO classification of FGM: Type 1 — excision of prepuce and clitoris; Type 2 — excision of prepuce and clitoris with partial or total excision of labia minora; Type 3 — excision of part or all of external genitalia and stitching/narrowing of vaginal opening (infibulation); Type 4 (unclassified) — pricking, piercing, incision, stretching, cauterization by burning, angurya/gishiri cuts, introduction of corrosive substances.

B(i) Non-surgical management: Frank's procedure — use of graduated glass dilators on introitus; gentle pressure 10–20 minutes twice daily; takes 8–10 weeks to achieve satisfactory result; success rate 90% with good patient selection; for congenital stenosis only. Surgical management: separation of labia under GA with daily application of lubricant; vaginoplasty — more difficult in acquired gynaetresia; methods: division of stricture and simple suture (defects less than 1 cm thick); dissection and reconstruction (per vaginam or per abdomen with opening made in the uterus); McIndoe-Reed's vaginoplasty — creation of cavity between bladder and bowel lined with split-thickness skin graft from thigh on a plastic mould; may be one-stage or two-stage (first stage: dissection with antiseptic gauze pack; second stage 2–7 days later: apply graft using mould of Stent's dental composition with central hole, remove after 21 days); William's vulvovaginoplasty — edges of posterior parts of labia majora are sutured together in midline to form a perineal pouch; laparoscopic vaginoplasty; other options: pedicle grafts from labia; reconstruction with sigmoid colon/ileum (Baldwin's operation — now obsolete); hysterectomy for reproductive-age group with extensive lesion. Postoperative care: passage of dilators for at least 6 months; encouragement of sexual intercourse; normal sexual function in 80–90% after McIndoe. Contraindications to vaginoplasty: pregnant women (excessive bleeding); in the puerperium (extent of damage unknown); peri- or postmenopausal women (symptoms less); following severe obstetric trauma (little vaginal tissue); after successful closure of extensive vesicovaginal fistulae; vesico-vaginal fistula; dense scar tissue.

B(ii) Prevention: laws against female circumcision — operative in Egypt and Sudan; adequate obstetric care and medical services; vigorous treatment of acute cases of insertion of chemical irritants — hospitalisation; removal of the irritant if necessary under GA; bland antiseptic douches given twice daily with a rubber catheter; systemic antibiotics; cortisone pack; insertion of skin graft on a large mould as soon as the vaginal cavity is clean; health education — against harmful traditional practices (circumcision, insertion of pessaries, Gishiri cut); antenatal, intrapartum, and postpartum care; screening for genital tract malignancies.

(i) Diagnosis: cryptomenorrhoea due to imperforate hymen. Accumulated pathology: large amounts of blood accumulate; haematocolpos (blood accumulated in the vagina); haematometra (blood accumulated in the uterus); haematosalpinx (blood accumulated in the fallopian tubes). Haematosalpinx may cause aseptic inflammation of the tubes leading to blockage; spillage into peritoneal cavity may lead to adhesions, endometriosis, and infertility.

(ii) Embryological origin: the hymen arises from the urogenital sinus — this is distinct from the vagina, which is formed by the fusion and canalization of the paramesonephric (Mullerian) ducts and the sino-vaginal bulbs; imperforate hymen is therefore different from a transverse vaginal septum; the hymen's different embryological origin (urogenital sinus vs. Mullerian duct) explains why imperforate hymen can occur as an isolated anomaly while the vagina and uterus above remain normal.

(iii) Clinical findings on examination: examination should avoid vaginal examination; vulva inspection only — reveals a purplish or bluish bulging membrane; rectal examination reveals a large, tense, and cystic cylindrical swelling filling the pelvis (haematocolpos/haematometra); abdominal examination may show an abdominal mass (displaced bladder or elongated urethra leading to urinary retention); before puberty may present with mucocolpos or hydrocolpos (accumulated cervical secretion, which may present in the newborn).

(iv) Definitive management: excise the membrane over one week to aid drainage; ensure meticulous aseptic technique; ensure prophylactic antibiotics are given; adequate drainage must be achieved; cruciate incision over the membrane, or excision of the membrane is the surgical treatment; menstrual suppression with progestogens may be used before surgery to reduce blood volume.

(v) If left untreated: infertility (due to tubal blockage from haematosalpinx or adhesions/endometriosis); endometriosis (spillage of blood into peritoneal cavity causes adhesions and endometriosis); pelvic adhesions; infection and pyocolpos if secondary infection occurs; acute urinary retention (displaced bladder from haematocolpos); amenorrhoea persists; recurrent cyclical abdominal pain; the large haematocolpos may cause urinary retention by displacing the bladder and elongating the urethra.
questions.question:
A 24-year-old woman presents with a 2-year history of primary infertility, and is found on examination to have an imperforate hymen. She has a history of cyclic lower abdominal pain and urinary retention during her expected menstrual periods but has never bled per vaginam.
(i) What is the diagnosis and what accumulated pathology has likely developed?
(ii) What is the embryological origin of the hymen, and how does this differ from the origin of the vagina?
(iii) What are the characteristic clinical findings on examination?
(iv) What is the definitive management of this condition?
(v) What are the potential consequences if this condition is left untreated?

Describe the classification and epidemiology of gestational trophoblastic disease (GTD), the role of beta-hCG as a tumour marker, and the principles of its use in monitoring treatment.
A(i) Modified WHO classification of GTD: list all entities under molar and non-molar categories.
A(ii) Epidemiology: state the incidence of hydatidiform mole and choriocarcinoma in different regions.
B(i) Beta-hCG: biochemical nature, secreting cell, normal values, and kinetics in pregnancy.
B(ii) Explain how hCG is used to distinguish viable intrauterine pregnancy from ectopic pregnancy, to diagnose and monitor hydatidiform mole, and to guide chemotherapy in choriocarcinoma.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Modified WHO classification: Molar lesions — hydatidiform mole (complete and partial); invasive mole. Non-molar lesions — choriocarcinoma; placental-site trophoblastic tumour; epithelioid trophoblastic tumour. Miscellaneous trophoblastic lesions — exaggerated placental site (exuberant infiltration of myometrium by implantation-site intermediate trophoblast; no increased risk of persistent GTD when not associated with hydatidiform mole); placental site nodule (benign counterpart of epithelioid tumour; small well-circumscribed nodular aggregates of chorionic-type intermediate trophoblastic cells embedded in hyaline; usually removed completely by the surgical procedure that discovered them — no local recurrence or persistent disease).

A(ii) Incidence of hydatidiform mole: 1 in 82 (Taiwan); 1 in 522 (Japan); 1 in 1000 (UK); 1 in 1500–2000 (USA); 1 in 1560 (Sweden); 1 in 667 deliveries in Ibadan; 1 in 125 pregnancies in Mexico and Taiwan; 1 in 500 in Japan. Choriocarcinoma: rarer, 2.5% of all GTD; 1 in 2500 (Ibadan) to 1 in 40,000 (USA); occurs in 1 in 20,000–40,000 pregnancies generally; 50% after molar pregnancy, 25% after abortion or ectopic pregnancy, 25% after normal pregnancy or term gestation.

B(i) Beta-hCG: a glycoprotein with molecular weight 36,000–40,000, half-life 32–37 hours; selectively produced by syncytiotrophoblast; normal titre 20–30 mIU/ml; has two fractions — alpha and beta; alpha fraction has immunological and biological similarity to pituitary gonadotrophins; beta fraction is specific and is measured by immunological and biological methods, RIA and enzyme immunoassay. In pregnancy: can be detected one day after implantation, 8 days after ovulation, and 9 days after LH surge; concentration rises exponentially until 9–10 weeks of gestation with a doubling time of 1.3–2 days; reaches its peak of around 10^5 IU/ml after 60–90 days of gestation; decreases to a plateau of 10,000–20,000 IU/ml maintained for the remainder of pregnancy; returns to non-pregnant level of less than 5 mU/ml 21–24 days after delivery.

B(ii) Distinguishing viable IUP from ectopic: a 66% rise in hCG level over 48 hours represents the lower limit of normal for viable intrauterine pregnancy; however, in 15% of cases of viable IUP, rise may be less than 66% in 48 hours; in 15% of ectopic pregnancies, rise may be more than 66% in 48 hours. Diagnosing hydatidiform mole: suggestive if urine in dilution of 1 in 200 to 1 in 500 is positive for hCG beyond 100 days of gestation; or if hCG in 24-hour urine is around 0.3–3 million IU during similar period of amenorrhoea. High risk of choriocarcinoma if excreting hCG greater than 100,000 IU/24-hour urine or serum hCG greater than 40,000 mIU/ml. In choriocarcinoma monitoring: one tumour cell produces 5x10^-5 to 5x10^-4 IU/24 hours; if patient excretes 10^6 IU/24 hours, this indicates 10^11 viable tumour cells; serum hCG measured at weekly intervals; hCG regression curve indicates need for a second course of chemotherapy; second course indicated if hCG level plateaus for more than 3 consecutive weeks or begins to rise again, or if hCG level does not decline by one log within 18 days of completion of first course; adequate response is when serum hCG falls by one log; remission is 3 consecutive weekly negative hCG levels.

A(i) Embryological derivation and histological character: The endopelvic fascia is derived from the paramesonephric ducts. It is histologically distinct from the fascia investing the pelvic musculature.
A(ii) Extent and attachments: It is a continuous sheet that attaches laterally to the arcus tendineus fascia and the levator ani muscle; it extends from the symphysis pubis to the ischial spine. In parts it thickens to form ligaments, e.g. the uterosacral/cardinal complex (probably the most important component of the structure).
A(iii) Named segments: The pubocervical fascia is the segment of fascia that supports the bladder and lies between the bladder and the vagina; it is significant in the repair operation for cystocele (anterior colporrhaphy) and extends between the cardinal ligament and the pubis, lateral to the bladder. The recto-vaginal fascia prevents anterior rectal protrusion. Together these named segments form part of the pelvic support system.
B. Aetiology: Congenital connective tissue defects appear to be the most important factor in the aetiology of prolapse and urinary stress incontinence. Evidence: 2% of symptomatic prolapse occurs in nulliparous women, implying a congenital weakness of connective tissue; prolapse is relatively rare in Afro-Caribbean women, suggesting genetic differences. Additionally, the process of ageing results in loss of collagen and weakness of fascia and connective tissue, noted particularly during the post-menopause as a consequence of oestrogen deficiency.
C. Anatomical basis of anterior colporrhaphy: Anterior colporrhaphy (anterior repair) corrects a cystocele (anterior vaginal wall prolapse due to descent of the bladder). The fascial layer being repaired is the pubocervical fascia — the segment lying between the bladder and the vagina, extending between the cardinal ligament and the pubis. Caution required: during repair, care must be taken to protect the ureters (which run in the upper part of the cardinal ligament) and the bladder from injury. The aim is to restore anatomy and function.
questions.question:
A. Describe the endopelvic fascia under the following headings:
A(i) Embryological derivation and histological character
A(ii) Extent, lateral attachment, and ligamentous condensations it forms
A(iii) Named fascial segments and their functional roles
B. Explain why defects in the endopelvic fascia are the most important factor in the aetiology of prolapse and urinary stress incontinence.
C. Describe the anatomical basis of an anterior colporrhaphy (anterior repair), stating which fascial layer is being repaired, what condition it corrects, and the caution required.

Describe all the gynaecological tumour markers, under the following headings for each marker: chemical nature, normal levels, conditions in which it is elevated (gynaecological and non-gynaecological), clinical uses, and limitations.
A(i) CA-125: full description including its sensitivity and specificity in ovarian cancer and endometriosis.
A(ii) AFP (alpha-fetoprotein): physiological production, pathological elevations, and its role in germ cell tumour monitoring.
B(i) CEA, CA 19-9, PLAP, SCCA, and CA 15-3: one distinguishing point for each.
B(ii) State the classification of tumour markers (Classes 1, 2, and 3) and the criteria for an ideal tumour marker. Explain why no ideal tumour marker currently exists.
questions.answerText:
A(i) CA-125: a Mullerian differentiated antigen identified by monoclonal antibody OC-125; a mucin-like glycoprotein with molecular weight greater than 200 kDa; detected in serum by RIA; cut-off level is 35 u/ml. Expressed by: 80% of non-mucinous ovarian tumours including serous, endometrioid, clear cell, and undifferentiated; endometriosis. Can also be positive in: 0.2% of healthy blood donors; 1% of normal healthy women; 5% of benign gynaecological disorders (endometriosis and PID); 16% of women in first trimester of pregnancy; 25% of non-gynaecological conditions (GI tract cancers and breast cancer); advanced adenocarcinoma of cervix, endometrium, and fallopian tube. Use in ovarian cancer: useful for screening along with bimanual examination and USS in high-risk groups; sensitivity — detects ovarian cancer in 50% of Stage I and 60% of Stage II; specificity increases if combined with USS or measured over time; predictive value of a positive test is 100% (disease always detected during second-look surgery when level greater than 35 u/ml); predictive value of a negative test is only 56% (disease still detected in 44% at second-look surgery when level less than 35 u/ml); persistently high levels after chemotherapy indicates resistant clones. Use in endometriosis: in minimal to mild endometriosis — level is normal (14–31 u/ml in non-menstrual phase); in moderate to severe — level rises (13–95 u/ml); sensitivity approximately 66%; specificity about 80%; ratio during menstrual to follicular phase greater than 1.5 is a better sensitive marker.

A(ii) Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP): a major foetal serum protein resembling albumin; exists in a number of isoforms separable by differential binding to lectins; physiologically produced by the yolk sac of the human foetus older than 4 weeks, and later by the liver and GI tract; attains peak values of 4 mg/ml at 34 weeks of gestation; after birth falls within 8–12 months to a very low concentration of 10 mcg/ml and persists at this low level throughout life. Role in prenatal diagnosis: measurement of maternal serum and amniotic fluid levels important in screening for foetal neural tube defects and chromosomal abnormalities including Down's syndrome; most measurements at 16 weeks of gestation; must be used in combination with other modalities. Elevated maternal AFP: NTD, GI obstruction, liver necrosis, abdominal wall defects, sacrococcygeal tumour, cystic hygroma, IUGR, multiple pregnancies, renal anomalies. Low maternal AFP: chromosomal trisomies, GTD, IUD, placental defects, foetal distress, hydrops foetalis. Pathological elevations in non-pregnant state: hepatocellular carcinoma, germ cell tumour, hereditary persistence of AFP, viral hepatitis, cirrhosis. Germ cell tumour monitoring: AFP elevated in endodermal sinus tumour/yolk sac tumour (positive); immature teratoma (positive/negative); mixed germ cell tumour (positive/negative); dysgerminoma (negative); choriocarcinoma (negative); widely used in diagnosis, therapeutic monitoring, and follow-up of germ cell tumours.

B(i) CEA: glycoprotein of molecular weight 200 kDa; expressed by malignant mucinous tumour (100%), 100% of atypical hyperplasia of endometrium, 60% of endometrial carcinoma, 50–80% of squamous cell carcinoma of cervix, 75–100% of adenocarcinoma of cervix; also produced in pneumonia, hypothyroidism, and pancreatic tumours. CA 19-9: carbohydrate determinant 19-9; mainly expressed by colonic carcinoma; also expressed by most mucinous ovarian tumours and a significant proportion of serous and other non-mucinous ovarian tumours; used in combination with CA-125 for clinical monitoring. PLAP (placental alkaline phosphatase): normally produced by the placenta; also expressed by serous and endometrioid tumours of the ovary as well as by the germ cell tumour dysgerminoma. SCCA (squamous cell carcinoma antigen): a sub-fraction of glycoprotein TA-4; produced mainly by squamous cell carcinoma of cervix, vagina, and vulva; used as a marker for monitoring squamous cell and adenosquamous cell carcinoma; levels become highest if there is metastasis. CA 15-3: a circulating breast cancer-associated antigen identified by two distinct monoclonal antibodies; present in a variety of adenocarcinomas of breast, colon, lung, ovary, pancreas; sensitive and specific marker for monitoring breast cancer; raised levels also in chronic hepatitis, liver cirrhosis, sarcoidosis, TB, SLE.

B(ii) Classification of tumour markers: Class 1 — antigens unique to a neoplasm not shared by other tumours of the same histological type; Class 2 — antigens expressed by many or most tumours of a specific histological type and of other histological types, but not expressed by normal adult tissue; Class 3 — antigens expressed by both cancer and normal adult tissue. Criteria for an ideal tumour marker: specific (should not be present in any other condition); sensitive; concentration should be proportionate to the amount of malignant tissue present; could be used for screening, diagnosis, and monitoring of disease progression; the method of assay must be cheap and easy. Why no ideal tumour marker currently exists: a large number of tumour markers have been found to be associated with gynaecological malignancies; however, most of them have low and variable specificity; the methods of their detection and estimation are difficult, costly, and not widely available; despite relatively high sensitivity and specificity, the low prevalence of disease means the positive predictive value for CA-125 is only 10% in the general population; interval cancers occur as frequently as those detected; no marker has become truly specific and suitable for early detection of epithelial tumours.

(i) The most appropriate method is a progestogen-only injectable preparation (e.g., DMPA 150mg every 3 months). Pharmacologic basis: ovulation inhibition; cervical mucus thickening; endometrial suppression. Efficacy: 0.3 per 100 woman-years. Progestogen-only methods are appropriate because smoking and age ≥35 years are absolute contraindications to combined oral contraceptives due to significantly increased risk of circulatory-system disease; progestogen-only contraceptives contain no oestrogen and most of the criteria restricting use of oral contraceptives do not apply to them.
(ii) Risk factors relevant to contraceptive choice: age ≥35 years (increases cardiovascular risk with oestrogen); smoking (>15 cigarettes/day is a significant cardiovascular risk with COCs; she smokes 10, which is still a relative contraindication); BMI 32 (associated with thrombo-embolic risk with oestrogen-containing preparations; also, efficacy of Norplant is slightly higher in women >70 kg); high parity (3 deliveries); irregular menstrual cycles (makes cycle-dependent methods unreliable); perimenopausal symptoms (oestrogen-containing methods may influence perimenopausal transition).
(iii) Options within progestogen-only injectables: DMPA (150mg every 3 months); NET-EN/Noristerat (200mg every 2 months). Combined once-a-month injectables (e.g., Cyclofem—DMPA 25mg + oestradiol cypionate 5mg; Mesigyna—NET-EN 50mg + oestradiol valerate 5mg) provide improvement in bleeding patterns but contain oestrogen and are contraindicated here. Progestogen-only pills (minipills) are also an option. Subdermal implants (Norplant, Jadelle, Implanon) are progestogen-only but involve a device; she declined this.
(iv) Side effects to counsel: irregular bleeding (spotting/heavy bleeding); amenorrhoea (80% of women); weight gain; less than 10% of women experience regular monthly bleed. Return to fertility: delayed return of about 4 months longer than other methods and may be up to 1 year.
(v) If she develops irregular heavy bleeding after 3 months: treatment for heavy bleeding with IUCDs and progestogen-only methods includes expectant management with reassurance; prostaglandin synthetase inhibitors or antifibrinolytic agents if profuse; if excessive, consider changing the contraceptive method. She should be reassured that this is a known and expected side effect of progestogen-only injectables and amenorrhoea is very common at 80% of users.

She currently has irregular menstrual cycles and complains of perimenopausal symptoms. She does not wish to use a device or barrier method.
