questions.answerText:
A(i) WHO (1994): Reproductive Health is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being in all matters relating to the reproductive system. Four principal implications: (1) the ability to have a satisfying and safe sex life; (2) the freedom to decide if, when, and how to reproduce; (3) access to safe, effective, and affordable family planning methods; (4) the right to health-care services enabling safe pregnancy and childbirth. UN (1994) extension: sexual health, defined as enhancing life and personal relations, extends the definition beyond fertility regulation and STI counselling to encompass the quality of sexual relationships and individual wellbeing.

A(ii) Sixty-one per cent of all maternal deaths occur in just 10 countries. The supermarket approach provides a range of reproductive health services — including STI management, family planning, and maternal and child health (MCH) — at one point of contact in a combined, coordinated manner.

B(i) Integrated care reduces unmet need because clients often have multiple overlapping reproductive health needs that single-service vertical programmes fail to address simultaneously. The quality of integrated services depends heavily on adequate management policy, trained staff, and sufficient infrastructure.

B(ii) The three evidence-based elements are: (1) Skilled attendance for every woman in labour — addresses the proximate cause of death from unmanaged obstetric complications; (2) An effective referral system linking primary to tertiary facilities — addresses delay in reaching definitive care, ensuring complications identified at primary level can be treated at higher-level facilities; (3) Prevention of unwanted pregnancies — addresses the distal cause of maternal death from unsafe abortion and unintended high-parity pregnancies. Without skilled attendance and functioning referral systems, even the best-equipped facilities cannot reduce maternal mortality at population level.
questions.question:
Describe the components of the reproductive health care framework, explain the clinical basis for why integrated service delivery reduces maternal mortality more effectively than vertical programmes, and distinguish between the three evidence-based interventions identified at the Safe Motherhood Initiative anniversary meeting.

A(i) State the WHO (1994) definition of Reproductive Health and list its four principal implications. State the UN (1994) component that extends the definition beyond fertility regulation.
A(ii) Give the percentage of maternal deaths that occur in the 10 highest-burden countries. Describe the supermarket approach to integrated reproductive health care, naming the services combined.
B(i) Explain the clinical basis for why integrated care reduces unmet need, and state what the quality of integrated services depends on.
B(ii) State and distinguish the three evidence-based elements identified at the 10th Anniversary Safe Motherhood Initiative meeting in Colombo, Sri Lanka, explaining how each addresses a proximate or distal cause of maternal death.

questions.answerText:
(i) Most likely diagnosis: benign ovarian cyst (likely serous cystadenoma), belonging to the benign epithelial category of ovarian tumours arising from the surface epithelium. 90% of ovarian tumours are benign. Most benign ovarian tumours are cystic; the finding of solid elements makes malignancy most likely.

(ii) Aetiological/predisposing factors: nulliparity; social class (mortality in class I is twice that in class V); association with breast cancer; association with endometrial cancer; incessant ovulation; use of fertility drugs; BRCA1 and BRCA2 gene mutations; two or more first- or second-degree relatives affected (lifetime risk up to 50%); Lynch 2 syndrome / HNPCC; age (incidence rises after 40); asbestos; diet; blood group A; mumps; oral contraceptive use is protective (reduces risk by 50% with >5 years use).

(iii) Investigations: pelvic ultrasound (TAS or TVS); serum CA-125 (cut-off 35 u/ml); beta-hCG (to exclude ectopic pregnancy and trophoblastic tumour); alpha-fetoprotein; oestradiol; androgen levels (Sertoli-Leydig tumours); LDH; FBC; chest X-ray; abdominal X-ray; IVU; CT/MRI (seldom indicated for benign); colour flow Doppler studies; laparoscopy in doubtful cases.

(iv) Laparotomy is mandatory when ovarian swelling is >5 cm diameter, particularly if continuing to enlarge. Features at laparotomy suggesting malignancy: totally or partly solid tumour; bilateral tumours; fungation through the capsule; large vessels on tumour surface; blood-stained ascites; invasion of or adhesion to surrounding structures; metastatic deposits. In young women wishing to conserve reproductive capacity, enucleation of the cyst (cystectomy) is carried out. In women past child-bearing age, it is customary to remove both ovaries and the uterus. If the cyst is unilateral, consider biopsy of the other ovary to exclude an occult tumour. Guiding principle: type of tumour / age / desire for future childbearing.

(v) Torsion: acute or subacute pain with mild shock; lower abdomen tender with guarding and rigidity; tender adnexal mass on pelvic examination; laparotomy indicated and removal of the ovary usually necessary. Rupture: signs and symptoms vary; contents of chocolate (endometriotic) and dermoid cysts are extremely irritant and may cause severe symptoms. Haemorrhage into or from cyst: signs and symptoms vary according to degree of haemorrhage. Infection: not a common complication of ovarian tumours. Malignant change: occurs mostly in serous and mucinous cystadenoma; no new symptoms are produced.
questions.question:
A 38-year-old nulliparous woman presents to the gynaecology clinic with vague abdominal discomfort and mild dyspepsia for three months. On bimanual examination, a smooth right adnexal mass of approximately 7 cm is felt, with the uterus of normal size. An ultrasound reveals a unilocular cystic mass with no solid elements or ascites. Serum CA-125 is 18 u/ml.
(i) What is the most likely diagnosis, and what pathological category does it belong to?
(ii) What are the predisposing and aetiological factors associated with ovarian tumours?
(iii) What investigations, including tumour markers, are indicated before any surgical intervention?
(iv) What are the indications for laparotomy and the guiding principles of surgical management?
(v) What complications of ovarian cysts must be anticipated, and how is each managed?

questions.answerText:
(i) Breakthrough bleeding is a known side effect of COCs. Its pharmacological explanation: combined oral contraceptives contain low doses of synthetic oestrogen and progestogen; missing 3 consecutive pills results in withdrawal of the hormonal support to the endometrium, causing breakthrough bleeding; the endometrium thins and becomes atrophic during COC use and is therefore unreceptive to the blastocyst—sudden interruption of hormone delivery causes endometrial instability and irregular bleeding.
(ii) Management of missing 3 pills in a row: stop taking pills and use another method; consider changing the contraceptive method. If she misses 1 or more inactive (brown/reminder) pills: throw the missed pill away and take the rest of the brown pills as usual, then start a new packet as due.
(iii) Side effects of COCs: in the first 3 months of use—nausea, flatulence, vomiting (minor). Major side effects: breakthrough bleeding; myocardial infarction; cerebrovascular accidents; hypertension (not common with low-dose pills currently in circulation). Longer-term side effects: increases risk for thrombo-embolism; increases risk for stroke in smokers; weight gain; increases blood pressure; adverse effects on cholesterol/lipid levels.
(iv) ACHES warning signs: A = Abdominal pain (severe)—suggests mesenteric thrombosis or liver disease; C = Chest pain (severe)—suggests pulmonary embolism or myocardial infarction; H = Headache (severe)—suggests stroke or hypertension; E = Eye problems, blurring of vision—suggests stroke or hypertension; S = Severe calf pain—suggests deep vein thrombosis. Client should report to clinic immediately if she experiences any of these.
(v) Available hormonal alternatives not requiring daily compliance: Progestogen-only injectables—DMPA 150mg every 3 months; NET-EN (Noristerat) 200mg every 2 months. Combined once-a-month injectables—Cyclofem (DMPA 25mg + oestradiol cypionate 5mg) monthly; Mesigyna (NET-EN 50mg + oestradiol valerate 5mg) monthly. Subdermal implants—Norplant (5 years); Jadelle (5 years); Uniplant (1 year); Implanon (3 years); Annuelle (1 year). Transdermal patch—changed once a week, worn for 3 weeks per month. Vaginal ring (NuvaRing/etonogestrel-ethinyl oestradiol)—remains in place for 3 weeks, removed for the fourth week; pregnancy rate 0.65 per 100 woman-years. Hormonal IUD (Mirena)—releases 20 mcg levonorgestrel per 24 hours, effective for 5 years.
questions.question:
A 29-year-old woman who has been using combined oral contraceptives for 6 months presents with complaints of irregular breakthrough bleeding, nausea, and weight gain. On enquiry, she admits she missed 3 consecutive pills in the third week of her current pack.

(i) What is the spot diagnosis for her current irregular bleeding, and what is its pharmacological explanation?
(ii) What is the correct management of missing 3 consecutive pills in the third week of the pack?
(iii) What are all the side effects of combined oral contraceptives she should be counselled about?
(iv) What are the ACHES warning signs, and what clinical conditions do they each represent?
(v) If she wishes to switch to a method that does not require daily compliance, what are the available hormonal alternatives and their respective durations of action?

A 55-year-old postmenopausal woman presents with irregular vaginal bleeding of 3 months' duration. She is obese, hypertensive, and nulliparous. Pelvic examination reveals a slightly enlarged uterus but no cervical or vaginal abnormality. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an endometrial thickness of 16 mm.
(i) What is the most likely diagnosis?
(ii) What are the aetiological and risk factors for this condition?
(iii) What investigations, including imaging, endometrial sampling, and histological grading, are required?
(iv) Describe the FIGO surgical staging system for this condition.
(v) What is the definitive treatment at each stage, and what is the prognosis?
questions.answerText:
(i) Most likely diagnosis: endometrial carcinoma (adenocarcinoma of the body of the uterus/endometrioid adenocarcinoma). Most common symptom is postmenopausal bleeding or a postmenopausal blood-stained discharge; 75% of cases are postmenopausal.

(ii) Aetiological and risk factors: obesity — conversion of androstenedione to oestrogen compounds at a much higher rate; nulliparity; late menopause (aged over 52 years); unopposed oestrogen — replacement therapy or endogenously produced (e.g. granulosa cell tumour, polycystic ovarian disease, anovulation); diabetes — increased oestrogen levels in postmenopausal women; hereditary nonpolyposis colon cancer (HNPCC) — markedly increased risk; breast cancer — 2- to 3-fold increased risk; family history of endometrial cancer; classic phenotypic characteristic — obese, nulliparous, hyperlipidaemia, signs of hyperestrogenism, uterine bleeding, infertility, late onset of menopause; second type — poorly differentiated tumours, tend to be thin, multiparous, African American, deep myometrial invasion, decreased sensitivity to progestins, poor prognosis. Protective factors: combined oral contraceptives reduce risk; continues for at least 10 years after OC use; cigarette smoking decreases the risk.

(iii) Investigations: transvaginal ultrasound for endometrial thickness; hydroultrasonography (instilling saline into endometrial cavity); outpatient endometrial biopsy using instruments such as a pipelle sampler — office procedure, quick, well tolerated, and quite sensitive; hysteroscopically directed biopsy; dilatation and curettage — current role very limited; chest X-ray; CT abdomen/pelvis; MRI; surgical staging by exploratory laparotomy. Histological grading (degree of differentiation): G1 — nonsquamous or nonmorular solid growth pattern of 5% or less; G2 — nonsquamous or nonmorular solid growth pattern of 6–50%; G3 — nonsquamous or nonmorular solid growth pattern of more than 50%. Histological subtypes: endometrioid adenocarcinoma — most common; papillary serous and clear cell — poor prognosis; secretory carcinomas — best prognosis; adenocanthoma (benign squamous component) or adenosquamous (malignant squamous component) — latter may be associated with poorer outcome.

(iv) FIGO surgical staging: Stage I — tumour confined to the corpus: IA — tumour limited to endometrium; IB — invasion to less than half of myometrium; IC — invasion to more than half of myometrium. Stage II — tumour has involved corpus and cervix but not extended outside uterus: IIA — endocervical glandular involvement only; IIB — cervical stromal invasion. Stage III — tumour extended outside uterus but not outside true pelvis: IIIA — tumour invades serosa and/or adnexa and/or positive peritoneal cytology; IIIB — vaginal metastasis; IIIC — metastases to pelvic and/or para-aortic lymph nodes. Stage IV — tumour extended outside the true pelvis or obviously involves mucosa of bladder or rectum: IVA — tumour invasion of bladder and/or bowel mucosa; IVB — distant metastases including intra-abdominal and/or inguinal lymph nodes. Note: a bullous oedema does not permit a case to be allotted to Stage IV.

(v) Treatment and prognosis: Stage I — treatment of choice is TAH, BSO; radiotherapy if invasion is more than the inner half of myometrium. Stage II — in a surgically fit patient, radical hysterectomy and bilateral pelvic lymphadenectomy with para-aortic node sampling; if surgically unfit, radiotherapy. Stage III — if nodes suggest spread, adjuvant radiotherapy necessary. Stages III and IV — treatment is individualised; surgery is not usually the first line; radiotherapy then occasionally surgical intervention for residual disease. Progestogens — no randomised study to suggest benefit; some belief they are helpful in preventing recurrence after treatment of early stage disease. Prognosis is related to stage, including grade of disease, myometrial invasion, and lymph node involvement; other factors such as age and body morphology; squamous metaplasia does not imply worse prognosis but malignant squamous component may be associated with poorer outcome.

A(i) Choriocarcinoma: purely epithelial, no chorionic villi; sheets of anaplastic cells consisting of intermingled syncytio- and cytotrophoblastic elements; extensive necrosis and haemorrhage; rapidly invades myometrium and vessels — haematogeneous embolization to lungs (80%), vagina, pelvis, liver and brain (10%); 50% follow molar pregnancy (85% complete, 15% partial), 25% follow abortion or ectopic pregnancy, 25% follow normal pregnancy or term gestation. Macroscopy: red, haemorrhagic, necrotic appearance, focal or diffuse lesions. Microscopy: uncontrolled growth of cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast in sheets and columns; chorionic villi are absent. Sites of metastasis: lungs (80%), vagina (30%), brain (10%), liver (10%), kidneys, small intestine, spleen, bone.

A(ii) FIGO Revised Staging (2000): Stage I — confined to uterus; Stage II — extending outside uterus but limited to genital structures (adnexa, vagina, broad ligament); Stage III — extending to lungs with or without known genital tract involvement; Stage IV — other metastatic sites. Substage: A — no risk factors; B — one risk factor; C — two risk factors. Risk factors for substaging: hCG greater than 100,000 mIU/ml; duration from antecedent pregnancy to diagnosis greater than 6 months. Prognostic scoring system (low risk less than 4, high risk greater than 8): Age: less than 39 scores 0, greater than 39 scores 1; Antecedent pregnancy: mole scores 0, abortion/ectopic scores 1, term scores 2; Interval (months): 4 scores 0, 4–6 scores 1, 7–12 scores 2, greater than 12 scores 3; Pre-treatment hCG (IU/L): less than 10^3 scores 0, 10^3–10^4 scores 1, 10^4–10^5 scores 2, greater than 10^5 scores 3; Largest tumour including uterine: 3–5 cm scores 1, greater than 5 cm scores 2; Site of metastases: lungs scores 0, spleen/kidneys scores 1, GIT/liver scores 2, brain scores 3; Number of metastases: 1–4 scores 1, 4–8 scores 2, greater than 8 scores 3; Previous chemotherapy (failed): single drug scores 2, 2 or more drugs scores 3.

B(i) Clinical classification: benign TD — hydatidiform mole; malignant TD — hydatidiform mole persistent after evacuation, invasive mole, choriocarcinoma; non-metastatic TD; metastatic TD — good prognosis, poor prognosis. High-risk criteria: liver or brain metastasis; interval from antecedent pregnancy greater than 4 months; serum beta-hCG titre greater than 40,000 IU/ml; initial titre greater than 100,000 IU per 24-hour urine collection; previous chemotherapy (resistance to previous single agent chemotherapy); choriocarcinoma following normal term gestation.

B(ii) Follow-up post evacuation: hCG weekly, then monthly; at every visit ask for symptoms, thorough clinical examination, assessment of uterine size/theca-lutein cysts, hCG assay. Baseline at discharge: bimanual pelvic examination — size of bilateral theca-lutein cysts, size of uterus, vaginal secondaries; CXR to exclude secondaries; hCG assay or pregnancy test in serial dilution. Avoid pregnancy for at least one year after disappearance of signs/symptoms. Follow-up after chemotherapy: hCG 1–2 weeks for first 3 months; 2–4 weeks for next 3 months; 1–2 months to complete first year of surveillance; then 6-monthly indefinitely. Change drugs if titre does not drop by 25% or more after a cycle, or if toxicity does not permit adequate dose or frequency. In subsequent pregnancies: early ultrasound to confirm normal pregnancy; histological examination of placenta or products of conception; hCG level 6–8 weeks after termination of pregnancy.
questions.question:
Describe the spectrum of gestational trophoblastic disease in terms of pathology, clinical features, staging, and prognostic scoring.
A(i) Describe the pathological features of choriocarcinoma including macroscopic and microscopic appearance, cell types, and common sites of metastasis.
A(ii) Describe the FIGO revised staging (2000) and the risk factor scoring system for GTD, listing all risk factors and their weighted scores.
B(i) State the clinical classification of GTD (benign TD and malignant TD including non-metastatic and metastatic subtypes) and the criteria for high-risk disease.
B(ii) Describe the follow-up protocol after evacuation of hydatidiform mole and after chemotherapy for malignant GTD.

questions.answerText:
A(i) VIN — Aetiology: cause unknown; includes carcinoma-in-situ and Bowen's disease. Age incidence: 14–80 years, mean 40–45 years. Presenting symptoms: pruritus, or no symptoms. Lesions are white, red or brown; a white lesion may also be a non-neoplastic epithelial disorder. All atypical epithelium should be suspect and biopsied.

A(ii) VIN is graded as for cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN): VIN I, VIN II, VIN III. VIN III is equivalent to carcinoma-in-situ. VIN is associated with cervical and vaginal neoplasia. Risk of progressing to invasive carcinoma is uncertain but increases with older age. VIN also occurs in an HPV-linked multifocal form, particularly in younger women.

B(i) Lichen sclerosus presents as white crinkly plaques with shrinkage of the vulval skin (chronic epithelial dystrophy). Aetiology is unknown. Treatment is with betamethasone (β-methasone) topical cream.

B(ii) Colposcopy is used to evaluate the extent and nature of VIN lesions. The diagnosis is confirmed by biopsy — excision biopsy of suspicious areas. Biopsy is mandatory before any ablative treatment to exclude invasive disease.

C) Treatment options for VIN:
- Excision biopsy: used for isolated suspicious lesions; provides tissue for histological diagnosis; required before ablative treatment to confirm absence of invasion; for small discrete lesions.
- Skinning vulvectomy: removal of the skin of the vulva, with skin grafting; used for multifocal or extensive VIN, particularly when non-surgical options have failed; not usually recommended for younger people.
- Laser destruction: CO₂ laser vaporisation; used for extensive or multifocal VIN, particularly in younger women where preservation of vulval anatomy is important; cannot provide tissue for histology, so biopsy must precede this.
Post-treatment: regular biopsies are required for surveillance regardless of treatment method, because of the risk of recurrence and progression.
questions.question:
A) Describe vulval intraepithelial neoplasia (VIN) under the following headings:
A(i) Aetiology, age range, presenting symptoms and the types of lesions visible
A(ii) Grading system for VIN, and the relationship between VIN III and invasive carcinoma, including the risk increase with age

B) Explain the clinical basis of the following:
B(i) Why lichen sclerosus predisposes to vulval disease and what treatment is used
B(ii) The role of colposcopy in the evaluation of VIN and how the diagnosis is confirmed

C) Distinguish between the treatment options for VIN — stating for each (excision biopsy, skinning vulvectomy, laser destruction) when each is used and what the post-treatment surveillance requirement is.

A 25-year-old female graduate student presents with a 3-year history of progressively worsening secondary dysmenorrhoea beginning 1–2 days before her period, deep dyspareunia, and infertility. Examination reveals a fixed, retroverted uterus with tender nodules felt in the posterior fornix. Diagnostic laparoscopy confirms the diagnosis.
(i) State the diagnosis and list all the aetiological theories.
(ii) List the complications of this condition.
(iii) List all the differential diagnoses.
(iv) Outline the available medical and surgical treatment options. Justify the role of Danazol and state its expected outcomes.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Endometriosis — functional endometrial tissue outside the uterine cavity.
Aetiological theories: Metaplasia (embryonic coelomic epithelium); transplantation; direct spread (adenomyosis); lymphatic spread; haematogenous spread; retrograde menstruation; and inoculation.
(ii) Complications:
- Ureteric obstruction
- Cyst accidents
- Adhesions
- Gastrointestinal complications
- Malignant change
(iii) Differential diagnoses: Pelvic inflammatory disease; ovarian malignancy and cyst accidents; gastrointestinal malignancy; uterine fibroids; acute appendicitis; diverticular disease; abdominal tuberculosis; ruptured ectopic pregnancy; pelvic/abdominal malignancy; and psychosomatic pelvic pain.
(iv) Treatment options:
Conservative: Watchful waiting determined by the extent of disease, presence of symptoms, age, parity, and reproductive intentions.
Medical: Stilboestrol; combined oral contraceptive (6 months continuous or intermittent); progestogens (MPA, Primolut) continuously for 9 months; Danazol (gold standard); methyltestosterone; gestrinone; GnRH agonists; gossypol.
Surgical: Conservative surgery; radical surgery. Combined therapy: pre-operative 6–8 weeks or post-operative hormonal therapy. IVF and ET. Radiation.
Role of Danazol: Danazol is described as the gold standard medical treatment; the dose is 200–800 mg twice daily for six months. Outcomes: relief of symptoms in 70% of patients; pregnancy rate of 50%.

questions.question:
Describe the pathogenesis, clinical features, investigations, and management of acquired vaginal stenosis due to chemical vaginitis, the commonest cause of gynaetresia in this clinical setting.
A(i) Describe the types of chemicals and the mechanism by which they cause vaginal stenosis.
A(ii) Describe the epidemiology of acquired gynaetresia and chemical vaginitis.
B(i) Describe the clinical features, including the spectrum from complete to incomplete stenosis, and the complications.
B(ii) Describe the acute management of chemical vaginitis and the long-term surgical correction of the resulting stenosis.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Types of chemicals and mechanism: caustic/toxic materials cause irritation, chemical burns, and necrosis; insertion of lumps of rock salt (Middle Eastern countries, 2nd–15th day post-partum); special leaves (Southern Nigeria); herbal pessary and soap from crude potash mixed with palm oil (Southwest Nigeria); alum and potassium permanganate (presumed treatment of fibroids or to narrow vagina for enhanced sexual performance); various reasons given include hygiene, contraction of vagina, amenorrhoea, and infertility; caustic/toxic materials cause irritation — chemical burns leading to necrosis, followed by scarring during healing; any inflammatory or ulcerating insult to the normally opposed anterior and posterior vaginal walls is likely to cause atresia/stenosis during healing; the proximity of the vaginal walls means that once necrosis occurs, fibrous healing obliterates the vaginal lumen.

A(ii) Epidemiology: in Ibadan, gynaetresia accounts for 7 in 1000 admissions; peak age 20–30 years; chemical vaginitis is the commonest cause of acquired gynaetresia in this environment; acquired gynaetresia is more common than congenital; FGM and chemical vaginitis are among the most common acquired causes.

B(i) Clinical features: complete acquired vaginal stenosis — involves the whole vaginal canal replaced by fibrosis; incomplete — diameter of the vagina reduced throughout its length; hourglass contracture. Symptoms: apareunia (most common); dyspareunia; amenorrhoea/cryptomenorrhoea; infertility; obstructed labour; difficulty in initiating micturition; menstrual disturbances. Complications: haematocolpos; haematometra; pyometra; fistulae; clitoral retention cysts; continuous dribbling incontinence; urethral coitus; dystocia; monthly acute retention of urine.

B(ii) Acute management of chemical vaginitis: hospitalisation; removal of the irritant, if necessary under GA; bland antiseptic douches given twice daily with a rubber catheter; systemic antibiotics; cortisone pack; insertion of skin graft on a large mould as soon as the vaginal cavity is clean. Long-term surgical correction (vaginoplasty): simpler procedure in congenital than acquired gynaetresia; may be one-stage or two-stage vaginoplasty; McIndoe-Reed's vaginoplasty — creation of cavity between bladder and bowel lined with split-thickness skin graft from thigh on a plastic mould; may contract except if intercourse is regular or dilator is worn; normal sexual function in 80–90% of patients; two-stage procedure — first stage (dissection with antiseptic gauze pack), second stage 2–7 days later (apply graft on Stent's dental composition mould with central hole, remove after 21 days); William's vulvovaginoplasty as an alternative; postoperative care — passage of dilators for at least 6 months; encouragement of sexual intercourse; prognosis in Ibadan: 68% successful repair; 28% residual stenosis; 4% complete stenosis.

questions.question:
Describe the classification and pharmacology of hormonal contraceptives under the following headings.

A(i) Classification of hormonal contraceptive methods
A(ii) Types of oral contraceptive pills and their hormonal constituents
B(i) Mechanism of action of combined oral contraceptives (COCs)
B(ii) Effectiveness of COCs with typical use versus perfect use
B(iii) Absolute contraindications to COCs, with physiological explanation for the greatest risks
C(i) Mechanism of action of progestogen-only pills and their principal mode of action
C(ii) Indications for progestogen-only contraceptives
C(iii) The clinical distinction between combined injectables and progestogen-only injectables, including specific preparations for each
questions.answerText:
A(i) Classification: Oral Contraceptive Pills (Combined Oral Contraceptive Pills—COCs; Progestin-only Pills—POPs or Minipills; Emergency Contraceptive Pills—ECPs); Vaginal Contraceptive Pills (Intermittent VCPs; Continuous VCPs); Injectable Contraceptives (Progestin-only Injectables; Combined Injectables); Implants (Biodegradable; Non-biodegradable); Hormonal Intrauterine Devices; Hormonal Vaginal Rings.
A(ii) COCs: mixture of synthetic oestrogen (ethinyl oestradiol) and progestogen—a C-19 steroid (norethindrone, norethisterone); taken daily for 21 days; low-dose preparation (≤30 mcg ethinyl oestradiol); third-generation progestogens (desogestrel, gestodene, norgestimate) produced to minimise androgenic side effects but associated with thrombo-embolic phenomenon. Progestin-only pills (minipills): contain ½ to 1/10th the progestin (norethindrone/levonorgestrel) in combined oral contraceptives, 30–75 mcg; less effective than COCs.
B(i) Mechanism of action of COCs: inhibition of ovulation by preventing follicular maturation and blocking production and release of FSH and LH, and blocking the LH surge; thickens the cervical mucus, impeding transport and decreasing ability of spermatozoa to penetrate the cervical mucus; prevents implantation as the endometrium is thin and atrophic and therefore unreceptive to the blastocyst.
B(ii) Effectiveness as commonly used: 6–8 pregnancies per 100 women in first year of use. Very effective when used correctly and consistently: 0.1 pregnancies per 100 women in first year of use.
B(iii) Absolute contraindications: women who smoke and are ≥35 years; liver disease; breast cancer; diabetes with complications; hypertension; breastfeeding; cardiovascular disease; pregnancy; gallbladder disease. The greatest danger associated with pill use is an increased risk of circulatory-system disease, particularly in clients with previous history of venous thrombosis, ischaemic heart disease, cerebrovascular disorders, and hypertension; risks are significantly increased in those over 35 especially if they also smoke heavily (over 15 cigarettes per day).
C(i) Mechanism of action of progestogen-only pills: inhibits ovulation in half of women; thickens cervical mucus, preventing sperm transport—this is the principal mode of action; reduces tubal mobility.
C(ii) Indications for progestogen-only contraceptives: women with reduced fertility; lactating women; older women; women with contraindications to OCs.
C(iii) Progestogen-only injectables: DMPA (150mg every 3 months), NET-EN/Noristerat (200mg every 2 months); mode of action—ovulation inhibition, cervical mucus thickening, endometrial suppression; efficacy 0.3 per 100 woman-years; side effects include irregular bleeding, amenorrhoea (80%), and weight gain; delayed return to fertility of about 4 months longer than other methods. Combined once-a-month injectables: Cyclofem (DMPA 25mg + oestradiol cypionate 5mg) and Mesigyna (NET-EN 50mg + oestradiol valerate 5mg); provides improvement in bleeding patterns—50–70% users experience regular monthly bleed; equally effective as progestogen-only preparation; better accepted.

questions.question:
Describe the histological classification of benign ovarian tumours under the following headings: cell of origin, benign examples, and key distinguishing microscopic and macroscopic features.
A(i) Physiological (non-neoplastic) cysts: types and pathogenesis.
A(ii) Benign epithelial tumours: derivation, types, and characteristic features of each.
B(i) Benign germ cell tumours: derivation and features of the dermoid cyst.
B(ii) Benign sex cord stromal tumours: cell types, hormones produced, and clinical effects.
Explain why most ovarian tumours present late and why the peak age for epithelial versus germ cell tumours differs.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Physiological (non-neoplastic) cysts: these are distension cysts that are physiological in nature. Types include: follicular cysts — due to enlargement of one or more follicles that fail to rupture, seldom more than 5 cm in diameter, often associated with anovulatory cycles, fertility drugs, and PCOS; theca-lutein cysts — corpus luteum becomes cystic and persists in a functional state, short periods of amenorrhoea followed by heavier than usual uterine bleeding, multiple and sometimes moderately large theca-lutein cysts are associated with trophoblastic tumours due to hCG stimulation; luteal cysts — less common than follicular cysts, more likely to present with intraperitoneal bleeding especially on right side.

A(ii) Benign epithelial tumours derive from the surface epithelium (coelomic epithelium/mesothelium) overlying the embryonic gonadal ridge, which may differentiate along tubal pathways (serous cystadenoma), endocervical pathways (mucinous cystadenoma), endometrial pathways (endometrioid), or uroepithelial lines (Brenner tumour). Serous cystadenoma: account for about 10% of ovarian neoplasms, bilateral in about 50% of cases. Mucinous cystadenoma: form 30–40% of ovarian neoplasms, often large, unilateral, multilocular cysts. Brenner tumour: unilateral and usually benign; vaginal bleeding is a common feature; endometrial hyperplasia occasionally present. Fibroma: bilateral in about 10% of cases; associated with Meigs syndrome (ascites and pleural effusion, usually right-sided). Clear cell (mesonephroid) tumour: classified separately.

B(i) Benign germ cell tumours arise from totipotential germ cells (embryonic structures). Dermoid cyst (mature cystic teratoma): the only common benign germ cell tumour; accounts for about 40% of all ovarian neoplasms; commonest ovarian tumour in young women; median age 30 years; bilateral in 10–11% of cases; seldom larger than 12–15 cm; lined by stratified squamous epithelium with cutaneous elements — hair, sebaceous and sweat glands, teeth, neural tissue, cartilage, alimentary and respiratory epithelium; may contain active thyroid tissue (struma ovarii); 60% asymptomatic; 3.5–10% undergo torsion; 1–4% spontaneous rupture; 2% contain a malignant component, usually squamous carcinoma, in women over 40 years.

B(ii) Benign sex cord stromal tumours: stromal cells retain potential for differentiation into any cells arising from gonadal mesenchyme — granulosa, theca, Leydig, and Sertoli cells. These rare tumours may therefore secrete any or all of the ovarian steroids. Granulosa–theca cell group may produce oestrogen: granulosa cell tumour (not infrequently malignant but usually low grade); thecoma–fibroma. Feminising (oestrogen-producing) tumours cause: precocious puberty before the menarche; cystic glandular hyperplasia in menstruating women; postmenopausal bleeding in older women. Sertoli–Leydig cell group may secrete androgens (androblastoma/arrhenoblastoma). Masculinising tumours cause defeminisation, secondary amenorrhoea, hirsuitism, enlargement of the clitoris, and deepening of the voice.

Most ovarian tumours present late because they rarely give rise to specific symptoms early in their course; commonest presenting features are vague gastrointestinal upset (dyspepsia) or increasing abdominal girth; if malignant, disease has commonly spread outside the ovary before diagnosis is made. Epithelial tumours peak between 40 and 60 years; germ cell tumours (teratomas) and gonadal stromal tumours occur at any age, including young women.

questions.question:
Describe natural family planning methods under the following headings.

A(i) Definition of natural family planning methods and why they are classified separately from other contraceptives
A(ii) Methods available under natural family planning
B(i) Periodic abstinence (rhythm method): the physiological basis, assessment tools for ovulation, and how basal body temperature is used
B(ii) Effectiveness of periodic abstinence, and its advantages and disadvantages
C(i) Coitus interruptus: definition, effectiveness, mechanism of failure, and disadvantages
C(ii) Lactational amenorrhoea method (LAM): physiological basis, conditions for use, failure rate, and cautions
questions.answerText:
A(i) Natural family planning methods are physiologically based methods that do not require the use of either chemical or mechanical barriers. They are mostly promoted by deep religious or philosophical reasons, e.g., Catholics. These are the least effective methods of contraception and are not advised if pregnancy prevention is a high priority.
A(ii) Methods available: periodic abstinence; coitus interruptus; lactational amenorrhoea.
B(i) Periodic abstinence (also called rhythm method) emphasises fertility awareness and abstinence shortly before and after the estimated ovulation period. The woman needs to understand the physiology of menstruation and conception, and how to assess ovulation with: kits; basal body temperature (BBT); menstrual cycle tracking; cervical mucus evaluation. BBT: the woman must take her body temperature in the same way (orally, rectally, or vaginally) at the same time each morning before she gets out of bed and must record her temperature on a special graph; the woman's temperature rises 0.2°–0.5°C (0.4°–1.0°F) around the time of ovulation; the couple avoids sex, uses a barrier method, or uses withdrawal from the first day of menstrual bleeding until the woman's temperature has risen above her regular temperature and stayed up for 3 full days (meaning ovulation has occurred and passed); after this, the couple can have unprotected sex over the next 10 to 12 days until her next menstrual bleeding period begins.
B(ii) Effectiveness: only about 55–80% effective. Advantages: once learned, can be used to avoid pregnancy or to become pregnant; no physical side effects; very little or no cost; can be used by most couples if committed; effective if used correctly and consistently; can be learned from trained volunteers without medical personnel; immediately reversible; acceptable to some religious groups that reject or discourage use of other methods; no effect on breastfeeding or breast milk; no hormonal side effects; involves men in family planning; educates people about women's fertility cycles. Disadvantages: usually only somewhat effective; takes up to 2 or 3 cycles to learn to identify fertile time accurately; requires long periods without vaginal intercourse—8 to 16 days each menstrual cycle; requires continuing cooperation and commitment of both partners; can become unreliable if the woman has fever, vaginal infection, is breastfeeding, or has any other condition that changes body temperature, cervical mucus, or menstrual cycle length; calendar method may not be effective for women with irregular menstrual cycles; most methods require careful daily records; does not protect against STDs including HIV/AIDS; requires motivation, some degree of literacy, and regular cycles.
C(i) Coitus interruptus: withdrawal of penis before ejaculation; oldest method of contraception. Effectiveness: 15%–25%. Mechanism of failure: failure is due to pre-ejaculation before orgasm (presence of sperm in pre-ejaculatory fluid). Disadvantages: high failure rate; need for sufficient self-control to withdraw the penis before ejaculation.
C(ii) LAM: ovulation is delayed after delivery due to nursing-induced hypothalamic suppression of ovulation; duration of suppression is variable; about 50%–60% of women begin ovulation between 6–12 months postpartum even while nursing; therefore 15%–55% can get pregnant. Conditions for use (to strengthen contraceptive effect): exclusive breastfeeding on demand; should only be used when the woman has not yet seen her period; should only be used for a maximum of 6 months; failure rate as low as 2% when these conditions are met. Cautions: HIV infection in the mother (small chance breast milk will pass HIV to the baby); condition of the woman postpartum; medication use during nursing.

questions.question:
A 21-year-old presents with primary amenorrhoea, cyclical pelvic pain, and a lower abdominal mass. Ultrasound shows a large fluid-filled vaginal collection and a further fluid collection in the uterine cavity.

(i) Identify the obstructed structures causing the vaginal and uterine collections and name these collections.
(ii) State the embryological structure from which the obstructing membrane originates.
(iii) List the differential diagnoses for primary amenorrhoea with cyclical pain and pelvic mass.
(iv) Explain the clinico-anatomical reasoning that distinguishes this presentation from MRKH syndrome and from CAIS.
(v) State the definitive management and describe the appearance of the obstructing lesion on speculum examination.
questions.answerText:
(i) The vaginal collection is haematocolpos (blood accumulation in the vagina); the uterine collection is haematometra (blood accumulation in the uterus). Both result from outflow obstruction preventing menstrual blood from escaping.

(ii) The obstructing membrane (imperforate hymen) is derived from the urogenital sinus (endodermal origin), which contributes to the lower one-third of the vagina and the hymen.

(iii) Differential diagnoses for primary amenorrhoea with cyclical pain and pelvic mass: imperforate hymen with haematocolpos/haematometra; transverse vaginal septum with haematocolpos; cervical stenosis with haematometra.

(iv) MRKH syndrome (46,XX): agenesis or hypoplasia of the vagina and uterus; no functional endometrium therefore no cyclical pain; no pelvic mass from blood accumulation; normal secondary sexual characteristics. CAIS (46,XY): absent uterus (AMH causes Mullerian regression) and absent functional endometrium; no cyclical pain; testes in abdomen or inguinal canals; primary amenorrhoea with normal female phenotype. In this vignette, cyclical pain plus haematocolpos and haematometra confirms a functional endometrium with outflow obstruction, which excludes MRKH and CAIS.

(v) Definitive management: cruciate incision of the hymen, which is curative, allowing drainage of accumulated blood. On speculum examination, the classic finding is a bulging bluish membrane at the introitus due to blood under pressure behind the imperforate hymen producing characteristic discolouration from vascularity beneath the stretched membrane.

questions.question:
Describe the gross anatomy of the uterine tubes and ovaries as an integrated functional unit, state how their anatomical relationship relates to common pathologies, and explain why disease originating at the ovarian level may spread to cause a distant functional deficit at the pituitary level.

A(i) Describe the integrated anatomy of the ovary and fallopian tube relevant to oocyte capture and transport, naming the relevant portions and their embryological origins.
A(ii) Describe how the Pomeroy and Parkland tubal ligation techniques interrupt tubal function, and explain why the Parkland method has a lower failure rate.
B(i) Explain how primary ovarian failure (e.g. from Turner's streak gonads) causes a distant functional effect at the pituitary level, naming the hormones involved and the direction of change.
B(ii) Distinguish between hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism (Kallmann's) and hypergonadotrophic hypogonadism (Turner's) under the headings: site of lesion, GnRH, FSH/LH levels, oestrogen level, and gonadal finding.
questions.answerText:
A(i) The ovary develops from the gonadal ridge (intermediate mesoderm) and lies in the ovarian fossa on the lateral pelvic wall. The fallopian tube develops from the lateral unfused portions of the Mullerian (paramesonephric) ducts. The fimbriated infundibulum of the tube sweeps over the ovarian surface at ovulation to capture the released oocyte. The oocyte is transported through the ampulla (where fertilisation normally occurs) then the isthmus and intramural portion into the uterine cavity. Any disruption along this pathway causes tubal factor infertility.

A(ii) Pomeroy technique: grasps a mid-tube loop, ligates with absorbable suture (plain catgut), excises the elevated loop removing approximately 3-4 cm; as suture dissolves the stumps separate, preventing reanastomosis. Parkland method: ligates and excises two separate segments of the tube, making a window in the mesosalpinx, creating a gap between ends with a bridge of mesosalpinx. The Parkland method has a lower failure rate because the separated ends with interposed mesosalpinx provide better assurance against spontaneous reanastomosis than Pomeroy stumps alone.

B(i) Turner's streak gonads produce no oestrogen and no inhibin. Both oestrogen and inhibin normally provide negative feedback to the pituitary, suppressing FSH and LH release. Without this feedback, the pituitary releases FSH and LH at markedly elevated levels — a hypergonadotrophic state. This represents ovarian disease causing dramatic distant hormonal change at the pituitary level.

B(ii) Kallmann's syndrome (hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism): site of lesion — hypothalamus (failed GnRH neuron migration from olfactory placode); GnRH — absent or very low; FSH/LH — low; oestrogen — low; gonadal finding — ovaries present but unstimulated; additional feature — anosmia, absent/hypoplastic olfactory bulbs on MRI.
Turner's syndrome (hypergonadotrophic hypogonadism): site of lesion — ovary (streak gonads from 45,X karyotype); GnRH — elevated (no negative feedback); FSH/LH — markedly elevated; oestrogen — very low; gonadal finding — bilateral streak gonads containing no oocytes; additional features — short stature, webbed neck, shield chest.

(i) The ovary is identified as the source: the mass arises from the pelvis (felt on bimanual examination); nodules in the pouch of Douglas indicate peritoneal metastases; the irregular, fixed, pelvic mass with ascites (central dullness, flanks tympanitic — shifting dullness) and markedly elevated CA-125 (890 u/ml, well above the cut-off of 35 u/ml) are highly consistent with malignant ovarian tumour; a hard abdominal mass arising from the pelvis is highly suggestive, especially in the presence of ascites; a fixed, hard, irregular pelvic mass is usually felt best by combined vaginal and rectal examination; the pouch of Douglas may contain irregular deposits which can be felt on bimanual examination — this is a sign of advanced ovarian malignancy; 75% of malignant tumours are bilateral; solid, nodular, irregular growths are more likely to be malignant; fixation is suggestive of malignancy; ascites is usually a sign of peritoneal metastasis, especially if blood-stained; the majority of patients with ovarian cancer present with advanced disease.

(ii) Compressed or affected structures explaining each symptom: urinary frequency — the large pelvic mass exerts pressure on the bladder (GIT and urinary symptoms may result from pressure effects); constipation — pressure on the rectum and large bowel from the pelvic mass and peritoneal deposits (GIT symptoms result from pressure effects; extreme cases can cause oedema of legs, varicose veins, haemorrhoids, and uterine prolapse); early satiety — peritoneal metastases on the surface of the small and large bowel and omentum impair bowel motility and reduce gastric capacity; vague GIT disturbance including dyspepsia is the commonest presenting feature; the peritoneal fluid flowing to lymphatic channels on the undersurface of the diaphragm carries malignant cells to the omentum causing omental disease which impairs gastric emptying; pleural effusion — peritoneal fluid flowing to lymphatic channels on the undersurface of the diaphragm carries malignant cells there; metastasis on the undersurface of the diaphragm is found in what otherwise seems to be Stage I–II disease; if pleural effusion is present, there must be positive cytology to allot a case to Stage IV.

(iii) Differential pathologies and clinico-anatomical distinction: malignant ovarian tumour — most likely given the features; bilateral adnexal mass, ascites, nodules in pouch of Douglas, elevated CA-125, pleural effusion; secondary (metastatic) ovarian tumour — Krukenberg tumour from stomach, colon, breast, endometrium, or lymphoma — would present similarly with bilateral smooth bosselated solid masses; primary GIT malignancy with ovarian metastasis — barium studies or colonoscopy differentiate; ovarian cancer and colonic tumour distinction aided by barium enema or colonoscopy; uterine malignancy — would have uterine enlargement and abnormal uterine bleeding as predominant features; tubo-ovarian mass from PID — typically in younger women with fever and elevated WBC; would not cause CA-125 as high as 890 u/ml in most cases; ovarian cyst with malignant ascites — ultrasound distinguishes cystic from solid; pelvic tuberculosis — may cause ascites and pelvic mass but different clinical context; peritoneal carcinomatosis from GIT primary — requires endoscopy and biopsy.

(iv) FIGO stage: this patient has Stage III disease at minimum, and possibly Stage IV. Evidence for Stage III: peritoneal implants outside the pelvis (nodules in pouch of Douglas represent pelvic peritoneal disease but the central dullness/ascites and early satiety suggest abdominal peritoneal involvement); Stage IIIc — abdominal peritoneal implants greater than 2 cm in size (likely given the extent of disease) or metastatic disease in pelvic, para-aortic, or inguinal nodes. Evidence possibly supporting Stage IV: the right-sided pleural effusion — if pleural effusion is present, there must be positive cytology to allot a case to Stage IV; until cytology of the pleural fluid confirms malignant cells, the patient cannot formally be staged IV; if cytology of pleural effusion is positive for malignant cells — Stage IV; parenchymal liver metastasis equals Stage IV (peritoneal deposits on the liver surface do not make Stage IV — the parenchyma must be involved). Currently: minimum Stage IIIc with possible Stage IV pending pleural fluid cytology.

(v) Clinico-anatomical reasoning for late presentation and peritoneal spread: ovarian cancer rarely gives rise to specific symptoms early in its course; the ovaries are located deeply in the pelvis and are not covered by peritoneum — this hidden location means tumours can grow to considerable size before causing symptoms; the commonest presenting features are vague gastrointestinal upset (usually dyspepsia) or increasing abdominal girth, which patients and medical attendants often ascribe to 'middle age spread'; abdominal swelling may be present but ignored; menstrual function is not usually affected (except by rare gonadal stromal tumours); tumours are often found accidentally. Peritoneal fluid dynamics facilitating spread: the dominant pattern of metastasis is transperitoneal locoregional dissemination; peritoneal fluid flowing to lymphatic channels on the undersurface of the diaphragm carries malignant cells to the omentum, liver (peritoneal surface), peritoneal surface of small and large bowels, parietal peritoneal surface throughout the abdominal cavity, and surface of diaphragm; metastasis on the undersurface of the diaphragm may be found in what otherwise appears to be Stage I–II disease; unlike cervical and colorectal cancer there are no defined anatomical steps in early tumour progression to allow screening for preneoplastic or preinvasive stages; ovarian cancer screening strategies have not been proven to be effective in detecting early stage disease; 70%+ of epithelial ovarian cancer patients present with advanced disease (Stages III/IV).
questions.question:
A 48-year-old woman presents with progressive abdominal distension, early satiety, urinary frequency, and constipation over 4 months. On examination the abdomen is distended with a large central dull area and flanks that are tympanitic. A firm, irregular pelvic mass is felt on bimanual examination and nodules are felt in the pouch of Douglas. Chest X-ray shows a right-sided pleural effusion. CA-125 is 890 u/ml.
(i) What organ or structure is identified as the source of this mass, and what do the clinical and imaging clues indicate about the extent of disease?
(ii) What compressed or affected adjacent structures account for each symptom — urinary frequency, constipation, early satiety, and pleural effusion?
(iii) What are the differential pathologies that could produce this clinical picture, and how are they distinguished clinico-anatomically?
(iv) What is the FIGO stage of this patient's disease based on the findings, and justify using the FIGO staging criteria?
(v) What clinico-anatomical reasoning explains why ovarian cancer so frequently presents at an advanced stage and how the peritoneal fluid dynamics facilitate spread?

questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: mucinous cystadenoma. Management approach in a young woman desiring fertility: laparotomy is mandatory for any ovarian swelling greater than 5 cm diameter, particularly if it is continuing to enlarge; in young women who wish to conserve reproductive capacity, enucleation of the cyst (cystectomy) is carried out; large cysts may demand removal of the ovary; ovarian cyst in young women — ovarian cystectomy is the standard management; if the cyst is unilateral, consider biopsy of the other ovary to exclude an occult tumour; guiding principle: type of tumour/age/desire for future childbearing; in doubtful cases, a frozen section should be asked for.

(ii) Risk factors for malignant change in mucinous tumours: malignant change occurs mostly in serous and mucinous cystadenoma; new symptoms are not produced by malignant change; it is commonly assumed that all malignant ovarian tumours develop from benign cysts, though there is little evidence this happens frequently; specific risk factors for ovarian cancer: nulliparity; incessant ovulation; age over 40; BRCA1/BRCA2 gene mutations; family history; unopposed oestrogen; the finding of solid elements makes malignancy most likely; malignant mucinous tumours are bilateral in only 10% of cases; mucinous cystadenocarcinoma causes pseudomyxoma peritonei if it ruptures.

(iii) Surgical procedure: ovarian cystectomy (enucleation of the cyst) is carried out in young women wishing to conserve reproductive capacity; the procedure conserves the remaining ovarian tissue and the contralateral ovary; the fallopian tube on the same side is usually preserved; cystectomy is the standard management for dermoid cysts and benign cysts in young women; a frozen section should be requested if there is real doubt about the nature of the cyst; biopsy of the contralateral ovary to exclude an occult tumour if the cyst is unilateral.

(iv) Intraoperative findings suggesting malignancy: the tumour is totally or partly solid; bilateral tumours; there is fungation through the capsule (not merely papillary growths); large vessels on the tumour surface; blood-stained ascites; invasion of or adhesion to surrounding structures; metastatic deposits. If these features are found, a frozen section should be requested; if malignancy is confirmed, the surgical approach changes to staging laparotomy with TAH, BSO, infracolic omentectomy, pelvic and para-aortic lymph node biopsies, and peritoneal cytology.

(v) Risk of recurrence and follow-up: ovarian tumours are common and mostly benign; there is no proper screening method for the disease; follow-up with tumour markers (CA-125) and ultrasound; a simple unilateral cyst less than 6 cm with CA-125 less than 35 u/ml and normal vascular resistance patterns is likely to be benign and may be managed conservatively; if the cyst is unchanged or larger at follow-up, further investigation (laparoscopy) is warranted; recurrence after cystectomy is possible, particularly if cyst wall is not completely excised; regular pelvic ultrasound; bilateral nature of mucinous cystadenoma in only 10–15% of cases; contraception has a protective effect against future ovarian tumours.

Describe the Intrauterine Contraceptive Device under the following headings, and explain why certain complications arise from its use.

A(i) Definition and classification of IUCDs
A(ii) Non-medicated IUCDs: examples and clinical significance
A(iii) Medicated IUCDs: types, active agents, and duration of use
B(i) Mode of action generic to any IUCD foreign body
B(ii) Contraceptive mechanism specific to copper-containing IUCDs and hormone-containing IUCDs
B(iii) Contraceptive effectiveness of the Copper T380A, Multiload, and Mirena
C(i) The anatomical and physiological basis of the side effect of bleeding with IUCD use, and its management
C(ii) The anatomical basis of uterine perforation and its management
questions.answerText:
A(i) Intrauterine devices (IUDs) are small flexible devices made of metal and/or plastic that prevent pregnancy when inserted into a woman's uterus through her vagina. Classified as: Non-medicated (first generation) IUCDs, e.g., Lippes loop, Dalkon Shield; and Medicated (second generation) IUCDs which serve as carriers or vehicles for pharmacologically active anti-fertility agents, e.g., Copper T380A, Multiload (MLCu-375), Nova T (which contains copper and silver), Mirena (which contains levonorgestrel).
A(ii) Non-medicated IUCDs: the Lippes loop was commonly used at UCH and in Africa, packed as sterile units or as less expensive packages of 100 loops sterilisable with antiseptic solution, comes in sizes A (smallest) to D (largest, suitable for highly parous women). The Dalkon Shield was withdrawn from the world market in 1974 because of a high incidence of PID, attributed to its multifilament tail whose wicking properties facilitated ascent of bacteria from the vagina into the uterus.
A(iii) Medicated IUCDs: each device is impregnated with a pharmacologically active agent gradually dissolved when placed in the uterus; unlike non-medicated IUCDs, these can only be used for a limited length of time. Types: copper-containing (Copper T-200, Copper 7, Copper T-380A); copper and silver (Nova T); hormone-containing (Mirena, releasing levonorgestrel). The rate of release depends on type, quantity, and surface area of the active agent.
B(i) Anti-fertility effects of non-medicated IUCDs: originate within the uterus; become active promptly following insertion; disappear when IUCD leaves the uterine cavity; are not negated by menstruation; do not influence the oestrogen-progesterone balance. Main effects: local sterile foreign body reaction interfering with decidualization making the uterine environment unsuitable for nidation; production of embryotoxic substances through localised mobilisation of polymorphonuclear leukocytes and macrophages; retardation of sperm transport due to altered intrauterine environment; increased motility of ovum in the fallopian tube via increased prostaglandin release; prevention of implantation/disruption of implanted blastocyst mediated by increased IgG levels counteracting the immunological response that permits nidation.
B(ii) Effect of copper: accentuates foreign-body reaction; releases cytolytic enzymes acting directly on pre-implanted blastocyst; copper may be spermicidal; may interfere with oestrogen uptake making endometrium unresponsive to blastocyst. Competition of copper with zinc causes inhibition of carbonic anhydrase and alkaline phosphatase activity, resulting in altered biochemical environment. Effect of progestin (Mirena): contraceptive mechanisms are mediated locally without systemic effects; continuous release of progestin promotes development of progestational or decidual endometrium incompatible with implantation; affects quality of cervical mucus, interfering with sperm transport.
B(iii) Copper T380A (TCu-380A): widely available, lasts at least 10 years; effectiveness is 0.8 pregnancies per 100 women in first year. Multiload (MLCu-375): lasts for 5 years; effectiveness close to that of TCu-380A. Mirena: highly effective; first year failure rate of 0.1% and five-year cumulative failure rate of 0.7%; lasts for 5 years.
C(i) Bleeding—most frequent side effect, occurring in about 15% of women; also the commonest reason for discontinuation; can be heavy, prolonged or inter-menstrual. Mechanism not clearly understood but may be due to: abrasive effect of the IUCD or pressure necrosis; IUCD causing increased vascularity and congestion of the endometrium; the anti-fertility agent impregnated on IUCD, e.g., copper. Management: expectant unless bleeding is profuse—assure the client; if profuse, use prostaglandin synthetase inhibitors or antifibrinolytic agents; if excessive, remove IUCD and give haematinics.
C(ii) Perforation: may be fundal or cervical; commonest initiating factor is faulty IUCD placement; influenced by size and shape of IUCD and skills of the inserter. Suspected when sharp pain occurs coincidentally with insertion, tails cannot be visualised, or an intrauterine pregnancy occurs. Diagnosis: ultrasonography; or insert a tracer IUCD into the uterus and perform antero-posterior and lateral x-rays. Management: remove the IUCD by laparoscopy or small laparotomy incision.

questions.question:
A. Describe the levator ani muscle under the following headings:
A(i) Constituent parts and origin
A(ii) Insertion
A(iii) Functions and what it constitutes
B. Explain the clinical significance of damage to the levator ani and the pelvic floor in women.
C. Distinguish between the cardinal ligament and the uterosacral ligament, including their attachments and clinical relevance.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Constituent parts and origin: The levator ani is the most important muscle of the pelvic floor. It consists of: pubo-coccygeus, pubo-vaginalis, pubo-rectalis, ilio-coccygeus, and coccygeus. Origin: posterior aspect of the pubic bone, fascia of the pelvic side wall, and the ischial spine.
A(ii) Insertion: perineal body, anal sphincter, and coccyx. The pubo-rectal and pubo-coccygeal components are the most medial. The pelvic diaphragm forms a U-shaped layer of muscle; the open end of the U is directed anteriorly (urogenital sinus), transmitting the urethra, vagina, and rectum. Both surfaces are covered by fascia.
A(iii) Functions and what it constitutes: Together with the coccygeus, the levator ani constitutes the pelvic diaphragm. It supports pelvic structures, meets the demands of upright posture, assists passage of the fetus, and provides openings for waste elimination.
B. Clinical significance: Damage, weakness or denervation of the levator ani and the pelvic floor contributes to prolapse of pelvic structures. Connective tissue, levator ani, and intact nerve supply are vital for maintenance of the position of pelvic structures. Deep laceration involving the perineal body that is not sutured or does not heal increases the possibility of subsequent utero-vaginal prolapse. Studies of the levator ani and fascia have shown evidence of nerve and mechanical damage in women with prolapse, compared with those without, occurring as a result of vaginal delivery.
C. Cardinal ligament (Transverse cervical/Mackenrodt's ligament): attaches the lateral cervix and upper vagina to the pelvic side wall; composed of connective tissue and involuntary muscle; the ureter runs in its upper part. It is probably the most important component of the supporting structure.
Uterosacral ligament: provides postero-lateral attachment of the lateral vaginal fornix, cervix, and isthmus to the sacro-iliac joint and third piece of the sacrum. Together the uterosacral and cardinal complex form the principal ligamentous support of the uterus, and their stretching causes the dragging pelvic discomfort and low backache that characterise prolapse.

questions.question:
Describe the gross anatomy and embryological derivation of the vagina, explain the clinical basis of why anomalies of the lower vagina differ from those of the upper vagina, and distinguish between two related congenital obstructive lesions.

A(i) Describe the embryological origin of the vagina stating which structure contributes to the upper two-thirds and which to the lower one-third. State the anatomical features of the vagina relevant to clinical examination: position, axis, fornices, and Chadwick's sign.
A(ii) Explain why imperforate hymen presents differently from transverse vaginal septum in terms of location, symptom onset, and examination findings.
B(i) State the investigation most essential for confirming Mullerian duct anomalies and explain how it differentiates septate from bicornuate uterus when combined with laparoscopy.
B(ii) State the incidence of MRKH syndrome, the proportion with associated renal anomalies, and the primary management for creating a functional vagina.
questions.answerText:
A(i) The upper two-thirds of the vagina is derived from the Mullerian (paramesonephric) ducts. The lower one-third is derived from the urogenital sinus (endodermal origin). The vagina runs posterosuperiorly from the introitus to the cervix. The cervix projects into the upper vagina, creating the anterior, posterior, and lateral fornices; the posterior fornix is deepest and overlies the pouch of Douglas. Chadwick's sign: a bluish-purple discolouration of the vaginal walls and cervix in an amenorrhoeic woman due to increased vascularity in early pregnancy, visible from 6-8 weeks; combined with amenorrhoea, it is highly suggestive of pregnancy.

A(ii) Imperforate hymen affects the most distal part of the urogenital sinus contribution (at the introitus); presents at menarche with cyclical pain, primary amenorrhoea, and a visible bluish bulging introital membrane (haematocolpos). A transverse vaginal septum is at the junction of Mullerian and urogenital sinus contributions; also causes haematocolpos and cyclical pain at menarche but the obstructing membrane is higher in the vagina and not visible at the introitus.

B(i) Hysterosalpingography (HSG) is the primary imaging investigation, delineating the uterine cavity and tubal patency. Combined with laparoscopy (which shows the external uterine contour), it differentiates septate uterus (normal external contour with an internal septum) from bicornuate uterus (bifid external contour indicating incomplete fusion). MRI is increasingly used as a non-invasive alternative providing excellent soft tissue detail.

B(ii) Incidence of MRKH is 1 in 4,000 to 6,000 females. Thirty to 40% have associated renal anomalies requiring renal tract imaging. Primary management focuses on creating a functional vagina through gradual self-dilation therapy or surgical vaginoplasty.

questions.question:
A 40-year-old woman with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus and a history of previous pelvic inflammatory disease presents requesting contraception. She currently has two children and is in a stable relationship. She reports heavy, irregular menses and her last Pap smear showed cervical dysplasia. She declines any injectable or surgical method.

(i) Given her history, which contraceptive methods are absolutely contraindicated, and which require precaution?
(ii) What is the most appropriate single method for her, and what is the complete mechanism of action?
(iii) What risks related to her underlying condition must be discussed with her before insertion?
(iv) Describe the complete insertion procedure for this method.
(v) What are the danger signs she must be counselled to recognise and return for immediately?
questions.answerText:
(i) Absolutely contraindicated: combined oral contraceptives (diabetes with complications is an absolute contraindication; also heavy irregular menses/undiagnosed abnormal uterine bleeding is an absolute contraindication; cervical dysplasia is a relative contraindication to COCs). Injectable methods declined by patient. Relative contraindications to IUCD: impaired response to infections (diabetes mellitus), history of relative infertility from previous PID, abnormal uterine bleeding, history of ectopic pregnancy (if applicable), multiple sexual partners (if applicable), previous pelvic surgery.
(ii) Most appropriate method: a copper-containing IUCD (Copper T380A). Complete mechanism of action: (1) foreign body reaction—most important effect; causes local sterile foreign body reaction which interferes with decidualization, making the uterine environment unsuitable for nidation and embryo development; (2) production of embryotoxic substances—prompt localised mobilisation of polymorphonuclear leukocytes preventing embryo development; coating of macrophages in the endometrium forms a barrier preventing implantation; (3) retardation of sperm transport due to altered intrauterine environment; (4) increased motility of ovum in the fallopian tube via increased prostaglandin release altering tubal motility; (5) prevention of implantation/disruption of blastocyst—increased IgG levels counteract immunological response permitting nidation; (6) effect of copper: accentuates foreign-body reaction; releases cytolytic enzymes acting directly on pre-implanted blastocyst; copper may be spermicidal; may interfere with oestrogen uptake making endometrium unresponsive to blastocyst.
(iii) Risks to discuss given her conditions: diabetes mellitus causes impaired response to infections, increasing risk of PID following IUCD insertion; the risk of PID is slightly increased within the first 3 months of insertion (may be related to transfer of vaginal flora into the uterine cavity; after three months, the risk is reduced); heavy menses may worsen since bleeding is the most frequent side effect of IUCD, occurring in about 15% of women and being the commonest reason for discontinuation; risk of ectopic pregnancy—women who become pregnant while using an IUCD are at a greater risk of having a tubal pregnancy; risk of uterine perforation influenced by skills of the inserter.
(iv) Insertion procedure: take proper history; perform full physical examination; conduct pelvic examination to determine size, position, mobility of uterus, pelvic tenderness, and incidental adnexal mass. Major instruments: Cusco's speculum, tenaculum, sponge holding forceps, uterine sound. Steps: insert Cusco's speculum; clean cervix with antiseptic solution; apply tenaculum to upper lip of cervix with gentle traction (to put the cervical canal in line with the uterine cavity); introduce uterine sound slowly and gently to determine combined length of cervical canal and uterine cavity, confirm position of uterus, and determine intra-uterine position of inserter barrel; load IUCD into the inserter barrel (pre-loading technique—if done too early the IUCD may lose memory); insert IUCD by the withdrawal technique (retract inserter barrel over inner plunger); ensure correct fundal placement; advise client on how to feel the strings.
(v) Danger signs (PAINS): P—Period late (pregnancy), abnormal spotting or bleeding; A—Abdominal pain, pain during intercourse; I—Infection, abnormal vaginal discharge; N—Not feeling well, fever or chills; S—String missing, gets shorter or longer. Advise client to return if she has any symptoms of pregnancy, infection, or missing IUCD.

A(i) Transperitoneal spread: the peritoneum and other pelvic organs become involved by direct spread. The peritoneal fluid, flowing to lymphatic channels on the undersurface of the diaphragm, carries malignant cells to: the omentum and the liver; peritoneal surface of small and large bowels; the parietal peritoneal surface throughout the abdominal cavity and on the surface of the diaphragm. Metastasis on the undersurface of the diaphragm may be found in what otherwise seems to be Stage I–II disease. In most ovarian carcinomas the dominant pattern is transperitoneal locoregional dissemination; it is unusual to present with visceral metastatic disease.

A(ii) Lymphatic spread: commonly involves the pelvic and para-aortic nodes; may also occur to nodes in the neck or inguinal region. Lymph node involvement is relatively common.
Haematogenous spread: usually occurs late in the course of the disease. Main areas involved: liver and lungs; bone and brain (sometimes).

B(i) Peritoneal deposits on the surface of the liver equal Stage III (not Stage IV) — the parenchyma of the liver must be involved to constitute Stage IV. Similarly, the presence of a pleural effusion is insufficient to put the patient in Stage IV status unless malignant cells are found on cytological examination of the pleural fluid (positive cytology is required to allot a case to Stage IV).

B(ii) Krukenberg tumours: carcinomas of the stomach metastasising to both ovaries (or other GIT cancers — breast, colon, endometrium, lymphoma). Secondary (metastatic) ovarian tumours constitute up to 25% of all ovarian malignancies. They mimic primary ovarian cancer. Usually present as bilateral adnexal masses, smooth, bosselated, solid and mobile.

C) Interval debulking surgery: defined as a second laparotomy performed when bulky disease remains after initial surgery, in those who respond after 2 to 4 courses of chemotherapy. The chemotherapy is then resumed as soon as possible after the second operation. Indication: bulky residual disease after primary surgery. Improvement in survival: interval debulking may improve survival at 3 years from 10 to 20 per cent.
questions.question:
A) Describe the routes of metastatic spread of malignant ovarian cancer under the following headings:
A(i) Transperitoneal (locoregional) spread — the peritoneal surfaces and organs involved, and how peritoneal fluid facilitates spread to the undersurface of the diaphragm
A(ii) Lymphatic and haematogenous spread — the lymph node groups involved and the main organs affected by blood-borne spread

B) Explain the clinical basis of:
B(i) Why peritoneal deposits on the surface of the liver do not constitute Stage IV disease, and what finding does constitute Stage IV, with the same reasoning for pleural effusion
B(ii) What Krukenberg tumours are, which primary tumours give rise to them, and how they present clinically

questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Carcinoma of the vulva (squamous cell type — 90% of vulval cancers are squamous).
Aetiological associations: HPV infection, smoking, immunosuppression, advanced age, history of cervical neoplasia, vulval intraepithelial neoplasia (VIN), lichen sclerosus. Two types exist: de novo in the elderly, and associated with VIN, particularly multifocal HPV-linked disease.

(ii) Surgical procedure: Radical vulvectomy (for multifocal tumours) or wide local excision with 10mm perimeter of normal epithelium for T1 and T2 lesions.
Lymphatic spread: From lateral vulval lesions, lymphatics drain ipsilaterally primarily — to superficial inguinal nodes then to deep inguino-femoral nodes. Central structures (clitoris, urethra) drain bilaterally.

(iii) The femoral vessels and femoral nerve are at risk during deep inguino-femoral node dissection. Formal groin node dissection is required even if fine needle aspiration biopsy is negative. If nodes are positive, pre-operative radiotherapy is added.

(iv) Management principles: Wide local excision for T1 and T2 tumours. Radical vulvectomy using triple incision for multifocal tumours (better cosmetic outcome). Involvement of central structures necessitates pre-operative radiotherapy.
Radiotherapy: Squamous vulval cancers are sensitive to radiotherapy; also useful for treatment of involved nodes if 1–2 are positive after groin dissection (external beam megavoltage). Complications include erythema, moist desquamation, rarely bone necrosis and fistula formation. Chemotherapy can be combined with radiotherapy.
Staging: FIGO staging — Stage I: limited to vulva/perineum ≤2 cm, no groin nodes; Stage II: >2 cm, no groin nodes; Stage III: extends to vagina, lower urethra, anus, or unilateral regional node metastasis; Stage IVa: mucosa of rectum/bladder, upper urethra, or pelvic bone, or bilateral node metastases; Stage IVb: any distant metastasis.
questions.question:

questions.answerText:
A(i) Length, location, and epithelium: The female urethra is located under the pubic symphysis; it is 3–5 cm long; a hollow tubular structure joining the bladder to the exterior. The proximal half is lined by pseudostratified transitional epithelium; the distal half by non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium.
A(ii) External (intrinsic) sphincter: rhabdosphincter urethrae (striated muscle); located in the middle third of the urethra; responsible for urethral closure at rest. Innervated by sacral roots S2–4.
A(iii) Extrinsic sphincter: periurethral muscle (levator ani, striated); not directly connected with the urethra; located at the junction of the middle and lower thirds of the urethra (S2–4 via pudendal nerve); adds additional closure force at times of physical effort. Combined effect: greater pressure within the urethra than in the bladder ensures continence.
B. Anatomical basis for Burch colposuspension: the goals of surgical management of genuine stress incontinence are — elevation of the bladder neck and proximal urethra into an intra-abdominal position, support of the bladder neck, and increase in outflow resistance. The Burch colposuspension (abdominal approach) achieves all three goals by suturing the paravaginal fascia to Cooper's (pectineal) ligament, thereby elevating and supporting the bladder neck back into its intra-abdominal position where rises in intra-abdominal pressure are transmitted equally to bladder and urethra. It is listed as the operation of choice.
C. Genuine stress incontinence vs detrusor instability:
Definition: GSI — involuntary loss of urine when intravesical pressure exceeds maximum urethral closure pressure in the absence of detrusor activity. DI — presence of spontaneous or provoked detrusor contractions during the filling phase when the patient is attempting to inhibit micturition.
Cause: GSI — damage to pelvic floor and/or pubourethral ligaments, descent of proximal urethra; DI — idiopathic in most cases, emotional/psychosomatic problems, upper motor neuron lesions (multiple sclerosis). DI is the second commonest cause; commoner in the elderly.
Treatment: GSI — conservative (pelvic floor exercises, vaginal cones, electrical stimulation, oestrogens, vaginal/urethral devices) and surgical (Burch colposuspension as operation of choice). DI — conservative (psychotherapy, bladder drill, biofeedback, acupuncture), drug treatment (anticholinergic agents — oxybutynin, tricyclic antidepressants — imipramine, desmopressin, oestrogens), and surgical (clam ileo-cystoplasty — operation of choice).
