questions.answerText:
A(i) The sponge is a soft disposable polyurethane foam device impregnated with spermicides; it fits over the cervix; traps and absorbs spermatozoa to augment the effects of spermicides; the spermicides disable the spermatozoa; effects can last up to 12 hours.
A(ii) Advantages of sponge and spermicides: does not contain steroids or any hormone; can be used by breastfeeding mothers; can be used by women who smoke; spermicide may provide added lubrication. Disadvantages: does not protect against STIs; contraindicated in people with allergy to spermicide; requires insertion technique; sponge can cause vaginitis; product use is time-dependent; sponge can cause toxic shock syndrome. Failure rate of sponge and spermicides: 160–320 per 1000 women per year.
B(i) Spermicides contain chemicals that disable spermatozoa. Available forms: creams; jellies; tablets; suppositories; foams; films. Spermicides should be used with another form of contraception.
B(ii) Cervical cap: barrier contraception used with spermicide; thimble-shaped silicone cap; positioned in the vagina over the cervix before sexual intercourse. Distinction from diaphragm: the diaphragm is a dome-shaped rubber cup with a flexible rim that covers the cervix from the posterior fornix to behind the pubic bone; the cervical cap is smaller and thimble-shaped, fitting directly over the cervix, without requiring the rim placement across the vagina. Both require spermicide.
C(i) Danger signs during use of sponge and spermicides requiring evaluation: fever for unknown reason; profuse, foul-smelling vaginal discharge; unusual lower abdominal pain. Also: fever; fainting spell/dizziness; rash; diarrhoea (as listed for diaphragm users).
C(ii) Microbicides: compounds that can be applied inside the vagina or rectum to protect against sexually transmitted infections (STIs) including HIV (main objective); some may have spermicidal activity (contraceptive effect); they can be formulated as gels, creams, films, or suppositories; may offer an alternative to condoms as the most feasible method for primary prevention of HIV but not necessarily as a method of contraception; have the advantage that women can easily control and do not require the cooperation, consent, or even knowledge of the partner. Current status: at present, an effective microbicide is not available.
questions.question:
Describe the sponge and spermicides as barrier contraceptive methods, and explain new developments in barrier contraception.

A(i) The sponge: composition, mechanism of action, and duration of effect
A(ii) Advantages and disadvantages of the sponge and spermicides as a combined group, including failure rates
B(i) Spermicides: available forms and the principle of their action
B(ii) The cervical cap: description and its distinction from the diaphragm
C(i) Danger signs during use of the sponge and spermicides requiring clinical evaluation
C(ii) Microbicides: definition, formulations, advantages, and current status of availability

Describe the gross anatomy of the uterus under the following headings, state how its anatomical zones relate to common pathologies, and explain why disease arising in the uterus may cause distant functional effects.

A(i) Describe the uterus under the headings: position and supports; layers of the uterine wall; the endometrium including the proliferative and secretory phases.
A(ii) State how the zones of the uterus relate to common pathologies encountered in gynaecological practice, naming at least four specific conditions.
B(i) Explain why anovulatory disease of the endometrium causes unopposed oestrogen effect and what functional consequence follows at the endometrial level, including the proportion of DUB cases where normal endometrium is found.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Position and supports: the uterus is normally anteverted and anteflexed; a retroverted uterus is a normal variant present in approximately 20% of women and requires no treatment unless fixed. A fixed retroverted uterus suggests pathological adhesions from endometriosis or PID. The uterus is supported by the broad, round, cardinal, and uterosacral ligaments.
Layers: perimetrium (outer peritoneal covering), myometrium (smooth muscle), and endometrium (inner glandular lining).
Endometrium: comprises the functionalis (shed at menstruation) and the basalis (regenerative layer). Oestrogen drives proliferation of the functionalis. After ovulation, progesterone from the corpus luteum converts the oestrogen-primed proliferative endometrium to secretory type, characterised by tortuous glands, glycogen-rich secretions, and oedematous stroma.

A(ii) Endometrial hyperplasia (30% of DUB) results from unopposed oestrogen. Normal endometrium is found in approximately 60% of DUB cases, indicating biochemical/local vascular abnormalities. Adenomyosis is endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium (PALM structural cause of AUB). Endometrial polyps are focal overgrowths detected by SIS or hysteroscopy (sensitivity 90%+). Postmenopausal endometrial atrophy produces large fragile dilated venules that rupture spontaneously. Endometrial thickness of >=4 mm in a postmenopausal woman with bleeding has approximately 96% sensitivity for endometrial carcinoma.

B(i) In anovulation (approximately 90% of DUB), no corpus luteum forms and no progesterone is produced. The endometrium is exposed to unopposed oestrogen, causing irregular proliferation, hyperplasia, and ultimately anovulatory bleeding. Normally, withdrawal of progesterone triggers vasoconstriction of spiral arterioles leading to orderly menstruation; without progesterone, this orderly shedding does not occur, producing heavy or irregular bleeding. Normal endometrium is found in approximately 60% of DUB cases.

questions.question:
A 52-year-old woman presents with vague abdominal distension and increasing abdominal girth for 4 months. She has a family history of breast cancer. On examination there is a hard, fixed, irregular pelvic mass and clinical ascites. CA-125 is 320 u/ml.
(i) What is the most likely diagnosis, and what are the imaging and laparotomy findings that confirm malignancy?
(ii) What are the specific risk factors and genetic factors for malignant ovarian tumours?
(iii) Classify the disease using the FIGO staging system.
(iv) What surgical procedure is performed at staging laparotomy, and what is the role of debulking surgery?
(v) What adjuvant chemotherapy agents are recommended, and what are the toxicities of the most important drugs?
questions.answerText:
(i) Most likely diagnosis: malignant epithelial ovarian tumour (serous cystadenocarcinoma most likely given age and CA-125). Features at laparotomy confirming malignancy: tumour totally or partly solid; bilateral tumours; fungation through the capsule; large vessels on tumour surface; blood-stained ascites; invasion of or adhesion to surrounding structures; metastatic deposits. Investigations: ultrasound (TAS and TVS); chest X-ray; IVU; CT scan/MRI; barium studies; endoscopy; FBC, RFTs, LFTs; laparoscopy/laparotomy for histological diagnosis.

(ii) Risk factors: nulliparity; incessant ovulation; early menarche; late age at menopause; infertility treatment increases risk; PCOS — 2.5-fold increased risk; social class (excess mortality of class I over V); asbestos/talc exposure; unopposed oestrogen HRT; high-fat diet; age (rises after 40 years). Genetic factors: family history in 5–10% of women with epithelial ovarian cancers; one affected first-degree relative — lifetime risk 2.5–5%, twice the general population risk; two affected first-degree relatives — lifetime risk 30–50%; BRCA1 mutations (chromosome 17) — increase risk of ovarian cancer to 40%, increase breast cancer risk to 80%; BRCA2 is defective in about 14%; Lynch 2 syndrome/HNPCC — combination of familial colon cancer and increased rate of ovarian, endometrial, and breast cancers; mutations inherited in autosomal dominant fashion; Turner's syndrome 45XO associated with increased dysgerminoma and gonadoblastoma.

(iii) FIGO staging: Stage I — growth limited to ovaries (Ia: one ovary, capsule intact, no ascites; Ib: both ovaries, capsule intact, no ascites; Ic: Ia or Ib with ovarian surface tumour, ruptured capsule, malignant ascites, or positive peritoneal cytology). Stage II — extension to pelvis (IIa: uterus or fallopian tube; IIb: other pelvic tissues; IIc: IIa or IIb with findings as in Ic). Stage III — peritoneal implants in abdominal cavity (IIIa: microscopic metastases on abdominal peritoneal surfaces; IIIb: tumour metastases less than 2 cm; IIIc: metastases greater than 2 cm or metastatic disease in pelvic, para-aortic, or inguinal nodes). Stage IV — distant metastatic disease (malignant pleural effusion, pulmonary parenchymal metastases, liver or splenic parenchymal metastases, metastasis to supraclavicular nodes or skin). Note: peritoneal deposits on the surface of the liver do not make Stage IV; parenchyma must be involved.

(iv) Surgical staging laparotomy: requires a vertical (midline or paramedian) incision; aspiration of ascitic fluid/peritoneal washings for cytology; full abdominal exploration; total abdominal hysterectomy; bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy; infracolic omentectomy; appendicectomy; peritoneal biopsies; pelvic and para-aortic lymph node biopsies; removal of all visible masses (optimal debulking — less than 2 cm maximum diameter residual disease). In Stage Ia disease in young women desiring fertility: unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy may be justifiable after careful exploration to exclude metastatic disease and curettage of uterine cavity to exclude synchronous endometrial tumour. Interval debulking surgery: when bulky disease remains, a second laparotomy may be performed after 2–4 courses of chemotherapy; may improve 3-year survival from 10 to 20%.

(v) Chemotherapy agents: platinum drugs (cisplatin and carboplatin) are the most effective — cause cross-linkage of DNA strands similar to alkylating agents; given alone or in combination; paclitaxel (derived from bark of Pacific yew tree — taxus brevifolia) is now part of standard treatment in combination with cisplatin or carboplatin. Others: cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin/adriamycin, etoposide, bleomycin, vincristine. Toxicities: cisplatin — severe nausea and vomiting, permanent renal damage unless given with adequate intravenous hydration, peripheral neuropathy and hearing loss with increasing cumulative doses; carboplatin — less nausea and vomiting, no significant renal toxicity, neurotoxicity rare, hearing loss subclinical; paclitaxel — sensory neuropathy and neutropenia in high doses, total loss of body hair irrespective of dose, mild nausea and vomiting. Chemotherapy complications generally include: alopecia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, nephrotoxicity, neurotoxicity, emesis, joint pain syndrome.

(i) Informed consent must explicitly address: (1) the permanence of the procedure; (2) the small but real failure rate including risk of ectopic pregnancy; (3) available reversible and irreversible alternatives and the risks and benefits of the specific technique.

(ii) Young age at sterilisation, particularly under 30 years, is most strongly associated with regret; regret rates approach 20% in this group vs less than 5% in women over 40. This 26-year-old woman is under 30 and is undergoing sterilisation at the time of caesarean section — both factors known to be associated with elevated regret risk.

(iii) Haemodynamic instability or active postpartum haemorrhage is an absolute contraindication to postpartum tubal ligation because surgery in this context increases mortality risk and adds unnecessary blood loss.

(iv) Ectopic pregnancy following failed tubal ligation is characteristically isthmic, occurring in the proximal isthmic stump because partial occlusion allows sperm passage but impedes normal embryo transport. Isthmic ectopic pregnancies rupture earlier and more catastrophically than ampullary ectopics because the isthmus has less distensibility.

(v) Filshie clips and other mechanical occlusion devices have higher failure rates compared to excision techniques because they rely on complete occlusion without removing tubal tissue. Clip failures may result from incomplete application, clip migration, or spontaneous reanastomosis of the tubal ends.
questions.question:
A 26-year-old woman requests surgical sterilisation during her fourth caesarean section. She states she is certain she does not want more children.

(i) State the three elements that informed consent for surgical sterilisation must explicitly address according to medicolegal standards.
(ii) Identify the patient characteristic most strongly associated with regret after sterilisation and explain why this woman is at elevated risk.
(iii) State the absolute contraindication to performing postpartum tubal ligation that would prevent proceeding at this time.
(iv) Name the complication characteristically associated with failed tubal ligation and explain why it is more catastrophic at the isthmic site.
(v) State the technique of sterilisation with the highest failure rate and explain the mechanism of failure.

Describe the components of the surgical sterilisation procedures, explain the clinical basis for why the reversal potential differs between techniques, and distinguish between two related sterilisation approaches — laparoscopic versus mini-laparotomy.

A(i) Describe the Pomeroy technique and Parkland method under the headings: site of interruption, suture material, length of tube removed/occluded, and mechanism of permanent contraception.
A(ii) Describe non-scalpel vasectomy (NSV) and state how it differs from conventional vasectomy in terms of complications and efficacy.
B(i) Explain the clinical basis for why the Pomeroy technique has the highest reversal potential, stating the minimum tubal length required for reanastomosis and which techniques have virtually no reversal potential.
B(ii) Distinguish between laparoscopic sterilisation and mini-laparotomy under the headings: incision, visualisation, recovery, and contraindications.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Pomeroy technique: mid-isthmic portion of the tube; absorbable suture (plain catgut); approximately 3-4 cm of tube removed; as absorbable suture dissolves the two stumps separate, reducing the chance of spontaneous reanastomosis. Parkland method: two separate segments of the tube are ligated and excised (making a window in the mesosalpinx); leaves a gap between ligated ends with a bridge of mesosalpinx; very low failure rate because the separated ends with interposed mesosalpinx provide better assurance against spontaneous reanastomosis.

A(ii) NSV uses a small pointed haemostat to puncture and stretch scrotal skin rather than a scalpel incision, producing fewer haematomas, infections, and other complications, with faster procedure time and quicker return to normal activity. The contraceptive efficacy is equivalent to conventional vasectomy. Like all vasectomy techniques, NSV should be considered permanent. NSV has become the preferred technique globally due to its superior safety profile.

B(i) Successful reversal depends primarily on the length and health of remaining tube after reanastomosis; a minimum of 4 cm of combined remaining tube is generally required. The Pomeroy technique removes only 3-4 cm from the mid-isthmic region, often leaving adequate tube on both sides for microsurgical reanastomosis. Bilateral salpingectomy and hysteroscopic occlusion have virtually no prospect of reversal; electrocoagulation destroys tubal architecture and leaves little viable tissue for anastomosis.

B(ii) Laparoscopy: 5-10 mm incisions; camera provides better intraperitoneal visualisation; faster recovery and less postoperative pain; relatively contraindicated in extensive previous abdominal surgery (adhesions), obesity, or cardiopulmonary conditions precluding Trendelenburg positioning and pneumoperitoneum. Mini-laparotomy: 2-5 cm suprapubic (interval) or infraumbilical (postpartum) incision; direct visualisation without camera; more accessible in resource-limited settings; failure rates comparable to laparoscopy for the same technique.

A(i) Pre-operative management components: psychological preparation — counselling; choice and cost of procedure; benefits and expectations; tour of facilities; admission at least 48 hours before; talking to patients with similar experiences; benefits include patient satisfaction, reduced analgesic requirement, and increased cooperation. Physical assessment: correct diagnosis; detailed history with special attention to recent illness, date of last period (surgeons may avoid major operations in the premenstrual phase), drugs and medications (including hormones, antibiotics, tranquillisers), and possibility of pregnancy; physical examination — general examination, teeth inspection, mouth and throat for septic lesions, heart and lungs, blood pressure, abdomen and pelvis, legs for varicosities; re-evaluation of cardiovascular, respiratory, gastrointestinal, genitourinary, and central nervous systems. Investigations: baseline (urinalysis for protein/sugar, haemoglobin/haematocrit minimum 30%, FBC, serum electrolytes and urea, blood group); specific (ECG, chest X-ray, coagulation profile, LFTs, IVU, barium enema); crossmatch blood if transfusion likely; haemoglobinopathy testing; mid-stream urine if infection suspected; cervical smear if not done recently. Skin preparation: shaving now generally abandoned for minor cases; elaborate skin preparation considered unnecessary; septic lesions should be noted and treated; patient to take bath. Bowel preparation: lower bowel emptied by suitable laxative; NPO from midnight; enemas and ritual purgation now little used; bowel prepared with succinyl sulphathiazole or neomycin if operation may involve intestine or rectum. Physiotherapist should visit every patient before operation to teach breathing and leg movements.

A(ii) Consent: written consent is probably best obtained before the day of operation in the out-patient or pre-operative assessment clinic; a responsible person should accompany the patient to her home after day-case surgery; valid consent must be given in writing for the operation by the patient herself, clearly countersigned by a doctor who should have explained the operation and its possible sequelae; girls aged 16 or over sign consents on their own behalf; for those under 16 years, consent of a parent or legal guardian is usually necessary except in emergency; difficulty may arise in the case of a girl under 16 requesting termination of pregnancy and insisting parents are not to be informed — doctor must exercise discretion and act in the girl's best interest. Consent for sterilisation: in the case of a married woman, husband's consent is not legally necessary in the UK for operations leading to sterility such as hysterectomy or sterilisation, but counselling of the couple is important; it should be made clear that sterilisation should be considered irreversible; it must be emphasised that a few failures occur with sterilisations; this advice should be recorded in the case notes. Counselling in general is important as many women do not understand pelvic anatomy and have unnecessary fears about effects of operations on sexual function.

B(i) Post-operative complications in first 24 hours: respiratory failure or obstruction to the airways; shock; haemorrhage; cardiac failure. Monitoring parameters: nurse in recovery unit until fully conscious; pulse rate and blood pressure charted every 15 minutes for first 2 hours, then every few hours for 12 hours; level of consciousness; continuation of intra-operative management (blood transfusion/IV fluid); monitor urine output hourly/daily; monitor fluid input; presence of bowel sounds; post-operative temperature, pulse, BP, respiratory rate observation chart; pain management with adequate analgesics; post-operative antibiotics (prophylactic or therapeutic); post-operative physiotherapy.

B(ii) Three types of haemorrhage: Primary haemorrhage — occurring during the operation; requires immediate transfusion; managed intraoperatively. Delayed (reactionary) haemorrhage — occurring during the immediate post-operative period; generally due to a slipped ligature or a bleeding vessel in the vagina or cervix; blood transfusion is given and the patient returned to the operating theatre to deal with the haemorrhage. Secondary haemorrhage — occurring up to 14 days after the operation; generally from the vagina or cervix, but occasionally from the abdominal wound; infection is commonly associated; suturing of the bleeding area and blood transfusion may be needed in all but the slightest cases; after cauterisation of the cervix there is generally some bleeding about the 10th and 12th day and the patient should be warned to expect this; anaemia is common after gynaecological operations and should be prevented with adequate diet.
questions.question:
Describe the principles of pre-operative and post-operative management of gynaecological patients, covering all major components.
A(i) Pre-operative management: list all components including psychological preparation, physical assessment, investigations, consent, and bowel/skin preparation.
A(ii) Consent: outline the requirements for written consent, the legal age for consent, and consent in the context of sterilisation or hysterectomy.
B(i) Post-operative complications in the first 24 hours: list all and describe the monitoring parameters.
B(ii) Haemorrhage after gynaecological surgery: describe the three types, their timing, causes, and management.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Embryological origin: the fallopian tubes develop from the lateral, unfused portions of the Mullerian (paramesonephric) ducts. Parts medial to lateral: intramural (interstitial) portion passing through the myometrium; isthmus (narrow, thick-walled medial segment); ampulla (widest, most tortuous portion where fertilisation normally occurs); infundibulum (funnel-shaped, bearing fimbriae that sweep over the ovary). Fertilisation normally occurs in the ampulla.

A(ii) Pomeroy technique: grasps a loop of mid-tube, ligates with absorbable suture (plain catgut), excises the elevated loop removing approximately 3-4 cm; stumps separate as suture dissolves. Parkland method: ligates and excises two separate segments, leaving a gap with a bridge of mesosalpinx between ends; very low failure rate. Filshie clip/silastic band: mechanical occlusion of the isthmic portion without excision; higher failure rates because they rely on complete occlusion without removing tubal tissue. Electrocoagulation (bipolar): destroys a segment by thermal injury; low failure rate. Bilateral salpingectomy: removes tubes entirely; no reversal possible. Highest reversal probability: Pomeroy technique, because it removes only 3-4 cm from the mid-isthmic region, often leaving adequate tube for microsurgical reanastomosis; minimum 4 cm of combined remaining tube required.

B(i) Following failed tubal ligation (particularly electrocoagulation or clip failure), ectopic pregnancies tend to occur in the proximal isthmic stump because partial occlusion allows sperm passage but impedes normal embryo transport. The isthmus has less distensibility than the ampulla; therefore isthmic ectopic pregnancies rupture earlier and more catastrophically than ampullary ectopics.

B(ii) The cumulative 10-year failure rate of PBTL is approximately 1.85%. Successful reversal depends primarily on the length and health of remaining tube after reanastomosis; a minimum of 4 cm of combined remaining tube is generally required. Bilateral salpingectomy and hysteroscopic occlusion have virtually no prospect of reversal.
questions.question:
Describe the gross anatomy of the fallopian tube, state how its parts relate to common pathologies, and explain why disease originating in the tube may cause a distant functional complication.

A(i) Describe the fallopian tube under the headings: embryological origin, parts from medial to lateral, and the segment where fertilisation normally occurs.
A(ii) State the techniques of tubal ligation in common use, specifying the segment excised or occluded in each, and state which technique has the highest probability of successful reversal and why.
B(i) Explain why failed tubal ligation is characteristically associated with isthmic ectopic pregnancy rather than ampullary ectopic, and what clinical consequence follows from the anatomical differences between these sites.
B(ii) State the cumulative 10-year failure rate of postpartum bilateral tubal ligation and the key factor determining success of reversal.

A) Describe the gross anatomy and histology of choriocarcinoma under the following headings:
A(i) Macroscopic appearance and tissue of origin
A(ii) Microscopic features and vascular behaviour that explain its pattern of spread

B) State how the site of metastases relates to common presenting features, listing the four most frequent sites of spread and the specific symptoms arising at each site.
B(i) Why does choriocarcinoma produce false-positive HCG tests, and under what drug or clinical circumstances can false positives occur?

C) Explain, using the WHO/FIGO risk factor scoring system described in the lectures, why choriocarcinoma following term gestation carries a worse prognosis than that following a molar pregnancy, and name the chemotherapy regimen used for high-risk disease.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Macroscopic appearance: red, haemorrhagic, necrotic appearance of the uterus; focal or diffuse lesions. Tissue of origin: trophoblastic tissue of the placenta — it is purely epithelial with no chorionic villi. 50% follow molar pregnancy (85% complete, 15% partial), 25% follow abortion or ectopic pregnancy, 25% follow normal term pregnancy.

A(ii) Microscopic features: uncontrolled growth of cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast in sheets and columns; chorionic villi are absent; extensive necrosis and haemorrhage. Vascular behaviour: rapidly invades the myometrium and blood vessels — this leads to haematogenous embolisation to lungs (80%), vagina, pelvis, liver and brain (10%). This vascular invasion explains why haematogenous spread is the dominant pattern.

B) Sites and presenting symptoms:
- Lungs (80%): chest pain, cough, haemoptysis, dyspnoea, respiratory failure; CXR shows coin lesion or cannon ball opacities.
- Vagina (30%): bleeding, purulent discharge.
- Brain (10%): epilepsy, psychosis, acute focal neurological deficits.
- Liver (10%): right upper quadrant pain, rupture, haemorrhage, jaundice.

B(i) False-positive HCG tests can occur when a patient is taking drugs such as phenothiazines, antidepressants and antiepileptics, or in proteinuria/proteinaemia, menopause, or pelvic TB associated with amenorrhoea.

C) In the WHO/FIGO scoring system, antecedent pregnancy from term gestation scores 2 points, whereas mole scores 0. This immediately raises the risk score. Additionally, the interval from antecedent pregnancy to diagnosis scores 3 if greater than 12 months. Choriocarcinoma following term gestation is therefore more likely to be high-risk. High-risk disease (score >7 or >8 depending on classification) requires intensive combination chemotherapy; the EMA-CO regimen (Etoposide, Methotrexate, Actinomycin D, Cyclophosphamide, Vincristine) is the most successful and least toxic combination for high-risk disease.

questions.question:
Describe the gross anatomy, histological classification, and clinical staging of malignant tumours of the ovary. Under each heading, relate the anatomical or pathological feature to an important clinical or management implication.
A(i) Describe the histological classification of primary malignant ovarian tumours with one distinguishing pathological feature of each major type.
A(ii) Describe the FIGO staging of ovarian cancer in full, and state the 5-year survival rates corresponding to each stage.
B(i) Explain the pathological basis and clinical significance of serous versus mucinous cystadenocarcinoma, including their bilaterality, macroscopic appearance, and association with peritoneal complications.
B(ii) Describe the pathological features, tumour markers produced, and treatment principles for germ cell malignancies of the ovary (dysgerminoma, endodermal sinus tumour, and immature teratoma).
questions.answerText:
A(i) Histological classification of primary malignant ovarian tumours: Epithelial tumours (85–95%): serous cystadenocarcinoma — most common malignant ovarian tumour, 35–50% of all epithelial tumours, bilateral in 50%, psammoma bodies often present; mucinous cystadenocarcinoma — 10–20% of epithelial tumours, bilateral in only 10%, notably large (up to 150 lbs), multilocular cysts filled with mucin, causes pseudomyxoma peritonei; endometrioid carcinoma — bilateral in 30–50%, may coexist with uterine endometrial carcinoma; clear cell (mesonephroid) carcinoma — 5–10% of epithelial cancers, solid/cystic, aggressive, may cause hypercalcaemia and pyrexia; undifferentiated carcinoma — less than 10% of epithelial neoplasms, no distinguishing features; Brenner — poor prognosis. Germ cell tumours: dysgerminoma — female counterpart of seminoma, mainly unilateral (85–90%), rubbery smooth rounded with thin capsule; endodermal sinus tumour (yolk sac) — extremely rapid growth, friable, necrotic and haemorrhagic, secretes AFP; immature teratoma — usually unilateral solid masses; choriocarcinoma (non-gestational) — rare, unrelated to pregnancy, lower hCG levels. Sex cord stromal tumours: granulosa cell tumour — may produce oestrogen causing precocious puberty or postmenopausal bleeding; Sertoli-Leydig cell tumour — rare, virilizing, half produce male hormones; gynandroblastoma — mixed elements. Metastatic tumours (secondary ovarian): Krukenberg tumours — carcinomas of the stomach metastasizing to both ovaries; also from breast, colon, endometrium, lymphoma.

A(ii) FIGO staging and 5-year survival: Stage I — growth limited to the ovaries: Ia (one ovary, capsule intact, no ascites); Ib (both ovaries, capsule intact, no ascites); Ic (Ia or Ib with ovarian surface tumour, ruptured capsule, malignant ascites, or positive peritoneal cytology). Stage II — extension to the pelvis: IIa (extension to uterus or fallopian tube); IIb (extension to other pelvic tissues); IIc (IIa or IIb with findings as in Ic). Stage III — extension to abdominal cavity: IIIa (microscopic metastases on abdominal peritoneal surfaces); IIIb (tumour metastases less than 2 cm); IIIc (tumour metastases greater than 2 cm or metastatic disease in pelvic, para-aortic, or inguinal nodes). Stage IV — distant metastatic disease (malignant pleural effusion, pulmonary parenchymal metastases, liver or splenic parenchymal metastases — not surface implants, metastasis to supraclavicular nodes or skin). 5-year survival: Stage I — 75–93% (other sources cite 90%); Stage II — 60–74% (other sources cite 65%); Stage III — 23–41% (other sources cite 30%); Stage IV — 11%.

B(i) Serous cystadenocarcinoma: bilateral in 50% of cases; both solid and cystic elements usually present; well-differentiated tumours have a papillary pattern with stromal invasion; psammoma bodies (calcospherules) are often present; may occasionally have glandular structures enabling diagnosis of adenocarcinoma. Mucinous cystadenocarcinoma: bilateral in only 10% of cases; usually multilocular, thin-walled cysts with smooth external surface containing mucinous fluid; among the largest tumours of the ovary — a cyst diameter of 25 cm is quite common; causes pseudomyxoma peritonei — follows rupture of mucinous tumour of ovary; tumour continues to secrete mucin; mortality 50%; 15-year survival for Stage III mucinous tumours is only 44%. Clinical implication: the higher bilaterality of serous tumours means the contralateral ovary must always be examined; pseudomyxoma peritonei from mucinous tumours is a life-threatening peritoneal complication requiring aggressive surgical management.

B(ii) Dysgerminoma: accounts for 2–5% of all primary malignant ovarian tumours; nearly all occur in women less than 30 years; spread by lymphatics; pathology — solid tumours with smooth or nodular bosselated external surface; soft or rubbery; mean diameter 15 cm; 10% are bilateral (alone among malignant germ tumours with significant bilaterality); tumour marker: hCG (±), LDH, PLAP; pure dysgerminomas have a good prognosis — 75% are Stage I (mostly Stage Ia); treatment: unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy in young women; radiosensitive and responds to chemotherapy. Endodermal sinus tumour (yolk sac): second most common malignant germ cell tumour, 10–20% of germ cell tumours; extremely rapid growth; may present as acute abdomen due to rupture following necrosis and haemorrhage; tumour marker: AFP (elevated); treatment: oophorectomy plus BEP chemotherapy (bleomycin, etoposide, cisplatin) — curative in 90% without adverse features. Immature teratoma: comprises about 1% of all ovarian teratomas; unilateral in almost all cases; appears as solid masses with smooth bosselated surfaces; degree of malignancy and prognosis related to maturity of component tissues; tumour marker: AFP (±); treatment: oophorectomy in young women with Stage I disease; short courses of BEP chemotherapy; stage I malignant teratomas may be followed up without further treatment.

questions.question:
Describe the HIV/AIDS epidemic, its pathogenesis, clinical manifestations, and its relationship to STIs.

A(i) Definition of HIV and AIDS, and the distinction between the two conditions
A(ii) Global and Nigerian epidemiology of HIV/AIDS, including distribution by age and region
B(i) Routes of transmission of HIV and populations at high risk
B(ii) Pathogenesis of HIV infection: how HIV causes AIDS, including the role of CD4 cells
C(i) AIDS-defining illnesses and clinical manifestations of advanced HIV disease by organ system
C(ii) Investigations and treatment of HIV/AIDS
C(iii) The ABCDE of HIV prevention
questions.answerText:
A(i) HIV: acronym for Human Immunodeficiency Virus—a virus that infects human beings and lowers the immune system of the body, consequently exposing the body to infections. It is a retrovirus; genetic code is in a single strand of RNA; types 1 and 2. AIDS: Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome—a viral disease caused by HIV; AIDS destroys the body defence system so that anyone infected develops various illnesses; at present AIDS has no cure. Distinction: anyone infected with HIV may look healthy for many years while the virus progressively destroys the immune system (asymptomatic stage—virus is easily transmitted at this stage); an AIDS patient is a person infected with HIV who has developed opportunistic infections because the immune system has been destroyed; an HIV-infected person may eventually develop AIDS, whereas AIDS cannot be contracted without first being infected by HIV.
A(ii) Global: an estimated 40.3 million people are living with HIV; 4.9 million newly infected and more than 3.1 million lost to AIDS in 2005. The second leading cause of death worldwide among those 15–29 years (number 1 cause in Sub-Saharan Africa). Africa: 25.8 million adults and children living with HIV; estimated 3.2 million newly infected; 2.4 million adults and children died of AIDS; Africa alone accounted for about 67% of global infections in 2005. Nigerian: first reported in Nigeria in 1986; prevalence increased from 1.8% in 1991 to 5.8% in 2001; decreased from 5.0% in 2003 to 4.4% in 2005; North Central Zone highest prevalence (7%), followed by South-South and North-East (both 5.8%); Cross Rivers recorded highest state-level prevalence; Osun State recorded least prevalence in 2003. 54% of seropositive individuals develop AIDS within 10 years; 12-week window period.
B(i) Routes of transmission: unprotected sexual intercourse (heterosexual 80% or homosexual); blood or blood products; donated semen or organs; mother-to-child transmission (MTCT/vertical transmission)—90% of infections in children result from MTCT; seroprevalence 4.4%. HIV is NOT transmitted through: hugging and handshaking; coughing and sneezing; eating together; using public toilets; sharing cups, dishes and cutleries; mosquito bites. High-risk groups: adolescents and young people; people with multiple sexual partners; people sharing needles, syringes, contaminated razors and other sharp objects; sex workers; soldiers, sailors, police officers; long-distance truck drivers and their wives; rapists.
B(ii) Pathogenesis: HIV attacks the cells of the immune system known as CD4 (T-helper) cells; seroconversion takes place about four weeks after the virus enters the body; there is gradual replication of the virus—at this stage the individual may show no signs and symptoms (asymptomatic stage) lasting 6 months to 15 years during which CD4 cells are destroyed; immunity is suppressed as a result of destruction of CD4 cells; immune suppression gives way to opportunistic infections (symptomatic stage); any one infected by more than one of the illnesses (syndrome) is said to have AIDS.
C(i) AIDS-defining illnesses: Pulmonary—Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia, tuberculosis. Neurological—cerebral toxoplasmosis, cryptococcal meningitis, AIDS dementia. Gastrointestinal—diarrhoea and wasting syndrome, oesophageal candidiasis. Ophthalmic—CMV retinitis. Malignancies—Kaposi sarcoma, non-Hodgkin's lymphoma. Systemic—Mycobacterium Avium intracellular Complex (MAC) infection. Other symptoms: severe weight loss (up to 10% of body weight), fever lasting more than one month, chronic diarrhoea lasting more than one month, constant cough, night sweat, swollen glands, mouth thrush, herpes simplex (cold sores) or herpes zoster (shingles), constant fatigue.
C(ii) Investigations: serology using ELISA test; agglutination assays; Western blot technique. Treatment: counselling and behavioural change; nutritional support; antiretroviral drugs.
C(iii) The ABCDE of HIV prevention: A—Abstinence from sexual intercourse; B—Be faithful to one uninfected sexual partner (mutual fidelity); C—Correct and consistent use of condoms; D—Desist from sharing needles and syringes, contaminated blood; E—Encourage voluntary counselling and testing.

(i) Complication: Red degeneration (necrobiosis) of a uterine fibroid during pregnancy.
Pathological basis: Red degeneration occurs due to infarction of the fibroid. The expanding uterus causes the fibroid to outgrow its blood supply; thrombosis of the venous outflow at the periphery of the fibroid leads to venous infarction, producing the characteristic flesh-like (red) appearance. This change is particularly associated with pregnancy and OCP use.
(ii) Degenerative changes in fibroids:
- Atrophy
- Hyaline degeneration: softening, contains hyaline tissue
- Fatty degeneration
- Red degeneration (necrobiosis): due to infarction; flesh-like changes; associated with OCP use and pregnancy
- Calcification
- Malignant/sarcomatous change (in less than 0.2%)
- Torsion
- Haemorrhage
- Infection
(iii) Immediate management: This is a medical complication. Treatment is conservative (analgesics and supportive care). Myomectomy during pregnancy is dangerous. Conservative treatment is appropriate when the fibroid is less than 12 weeks' size, the patient is pregnant, or the condition is managed expectantly. Surgical intervention (myomectomy) during pregnancy carries high risk; pedunculated fibroids are easier to manage if surgery is required.
(iv) Effects of fibroids on pregnancy: increase in symphysio-fundal height; abortion; malpresentation; obstructed labour; fetal parts difficult to feel; premature labour; postpartum haemorrhage; subinvolution. Classical caesarean section may be required when fibroids are in the lower segment.
questions.question:
A 32-year-old gravida 3 para 2 woman at 28 weeks gestation presents with sudden onset severe abdominal pain localised to the right side. Examination reveals a tender, enlarged uterus with an irregular outline; one of the fibroid masses feels particularly tender and boggy. Temperature is 37.9°C.
(i) What complication of uterine fibroids has most likely occurred, and what is the pathological basis for this complication in pregnancy?
(ii) List all the degenerative changes that can occur in fibroids.
(iii) Outline the immediate management of this complication.
(iv) What are the effects of fibroids on the progress and outcome of pregnancy?

questions.answerText:
(i) Dysfunctional uterine bleeding (DUB) due to immaturity of the hypothalamic-pituitary axis. The immature HPO axis fails to produce the positive feedback LH surge in response to rising oestrogen, resulting in anovulatory cycles without corpus luteum formation and therefore no progesterone production. Unopposed oestrogen causes irregular endometrial proliferation and heavy irregular bleeding.

(ii) Approximately 90% of DUB results from anovulation.

(iii) Adolescent DUB typically resolves spontaneously within 2-5 years as the HPO axis matures. Expectant management is appropriate unless bleeding is severe.

(iv) For a young woman who desires fertility: ovulation induction is the appropriate primary management, with clomiphene citrate as first-line and gonadotrophins for clomiphene-resistant cases. For acute heavy anovulatory bleeding requiring hospital admission: high-dose intravenous conjugated oestrogens or high-dose combined oral contraceptive pills to promote endometrial stabilisation; progestogen is added once bleeding is controlled. Surgical curettage is reserved if medical treatment fails.

(v) Polymenorrhoea: menstrual cycles with an interval of less than 21 days between cycle onset. Oligomenorrhoea: cycles with an interval of greater than 35 days. Normal cycle length ranges from 21-35 days (Treloar 5th-95th centile: 23-39.4 days).
questions.question:
A 16-year-old girl presents with heavy irregular bleeding 8 months after menarche. Examination is normal; no organic pathology is found.

(i) State the most likely diagnosis and the physiological reason for this presentation.
(ii) What proportion of all DUB results from anovulation?
(iii) Explain why adolescent DUB typically resolves spontaneously and over what timeframe.
(iv) State the management for a young woman with this condition who desires fertility, versus one with acute severe bleeding requiring hospital admission.
(v) Using correct menstrual terminology, define polymenorrhoea and oligomenorrhoea with their cycle-length thresholds.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Origin and constituents: The pudendal nerve arises from the sacral plexus (S2–S4). It carries both sensory and motor fibres.
A(ii) Relations within the ischio-rectal fossa: The ischio-rectal fossa boundaries are — lateral: pudendal vessels and nerve within the pudendal canal; medial: fascial covering of the levator ani and external anal sphincter; posterior: sacrotuberous ligament; anterior: urogenital perineum; floor: skin and subcutaneous fat.
A(iii) Branches and distribution: The pudendal nerve gives rise to — (1) clitoral branch, (2) perineal branch (the largest branch, supplying muscles and skin), and (3) inferior rectal branch. The corresponding artery is the anterior division of the internal iliac artery, with similar named branches.
B. Safe site for pudendal nerve block: The pudendal nerve runs within the pudendal canal on the lateral wall of the ischio-rectal fossa, in close relation to the ischial spine; this is the anatomical landmark used in clinical practice for pudendal nerve block.
C. Anatomical basis of footdrop in obstetric fistula: VVF patients characteristically present with footdrop due to obstetric neuropraxia. This is caused by prolonged pressure from the impacted fetal head against the pelvic side wall during obstructed labour, damaging the lumbosacral nerve trunks or branches of the sacral plexus, producing motor weakness of dorsiflexion (footdrop). The main thrust of pressure is directed to the back of the symphysis pubis, and the same ischaemic mechanism that creates the fistula also injures adjacent neural structures.
questions.question:
A. Describe the pudendal nerve under the following headings:
A(i) Origin and constituents
A(ii) Relations within the ischio-rectal fossa
A(iii) Branches and their distribution
B. State the safest site for a nerve block of the pudendal nerve in obstetric practice, explaining the anatomical basis for this approach.
C. Describe the anatomical basis of footdrop seen in women with prolonged obstructed labour and obstetric fistula.

A) Describe alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) under the following headings:
A(i) Nature, physiological sites of production in the fetus, and the peak values attained during gestation
A(ii) What happens to AFP levels after birth, and what conditions in the non-pregnant adult are associated with unexplained persistent elevation

B) Explain the clinical basis of:
B(i) The foetal conditions associated with elevated and low maternal serum AFP levels, naming specific conditions under each category
B(ii) Why AFP must be used in combination with other modalities for neural tube defect screening, not as a standalone test

C) State the pattern of AFP and HCG production in each of the six germ cell tumour types listed in the lectures, distinguishing which produce AFP, which produce HCG, and which produce neither.
questions.answerText:
A(i) AFP is a major foetal serum protein that resembles albumin. It is physiologically produced by: the yolk sac of the human foetus more than 4 weeks old, and later by the liver and GI tract. AFP attains peak values of 4 mg/ml at 34 weeks of gestation.

A(ii) After birth, AFP usually falls within 8 to 12 months of delivery to a very low concentration of 10 mcg/ml and persists at this low level throughout life. Unexplained and persistent elevation in the non-pregnant state may be due to: hepatocellular carcinoma, germ cell tumour, hereditary persistence of AFP, viral hepatitis and cirrhosis.

B(i) Elevated maternal serum AFP: neural tube defects (NTD), GI obstruction, liver necrosis, abdominal wall defects (omphalocele, gastroschisis), sacrococcygeal tumour, cystic hygroma, IUGR, multiple pregnancies, renal anomalies.
Low maternal serum AFP: chromosomal trisomies (Down's syndrome), gestational trophoblastic disease, IUD, placental defects, gestational age underestimated, foetal distress, hydrops foetalis, TOF, cyclopia.

B(ii) Raised maternal serum AFP levels are not specific for neural tube defects. It must be used in combination with other modalities such as ultrasound, amniotic fluid AFP and acetylcholinesterase. Most measurements are done at 16 weeks of gestation.

C) Germ cell tumour AFP and HCG production:
1. Dysgerminoma: AFP negative, HCG positive/negative (±)
2. Endodermal sinus tumour/yolk sac tumour: AFP positive (+), HCG negative (--)
3. Immature teratoma: AFP positive/negative (±), HCG negative (--)
4. Mixed germ cell tumour: AFP positive/negative (±), HCG positive/negative (±)
5. Choriocarcinoma: AFP negative (--), HCG positive (+)
6. Embryonal carcinoma: AFP negative (--), HCG positive (+)

(i) Chadwick's sign: bluish-purple discolouration of the vaginal walls and cervix due to increased vascularity and venous congestion of the pelvic organs in early pregnancy. It is typically visible from 6-8 weeks gestation.

(ii) TVUS can visualise the gestational sac as early as 4-5 weeks gestation and fetal cardiac activity by 5-6 weeks gestation, approximately 1 week earlier than transabdominal scanning. TVUS provides superior near-field resolution because the probe is closer to pelvic organs without the intervening body wall and bowel.

(iii) The most diagnostic finding is a discrete extrauterine gestational sac with an echogenic ring (tubal ring sign) containing a yolk sac or fetal pole with or without fetal cardiac activity. Absence of an intrauterine sac alone is not diagnostic; free fluid in the pouch of Douglas alone is also not diagnostic.

(iv) Absent end-diastolic flow (AEDF) in the umbilical artery reflects severely elevated resistance within the placental vasculature, indicating loss of more than 70% of the placental vascular cross-section and significant uteroplacental insufficiency. This is a pre-terminal sign associated with high perinatal mortality and is typically an indication for delivery in a preterm fetus once steroids have been administered. Reversed end-diastolic flow (REDF) is an even more ominous finding indicating imminent fetal death.

(v) In postmenopausal women not on HRT, normal endometrial thickness is less than 4 mm. An endometrial thickness of 4 mm or greater in a postmenopausal woman with vaginal bleeding has a sensitivity of approximately 96% for detecting endometrial carcinoma; women with thickness above this threshold require endometrial sampling for histological diagnosis.
questions.question:
A 32-year-old woman with secondary infertility presents for evaluation. Speculum examination reveals a bluish-purple cervix; bimanual examination shows a soft, mobile, slightly enlarged uterus. A urine pregnancy test is positive. Transvaginal ultrasound (TVUS) is performed.

(i) Name the sign present on speculum examination and state its physiological basis and the gestational age at which it is visible.
(ii) State the earliest gestational age at which a gestational sac and fetal cardiac activity can be visualised on TVUS, and compare with transabdominal scanning.
(iii) State the most diagnostic sonographic finding for ectopic pregnancy when a positive pregnancy test is present.
(iv) State what absent end-diastolic flow (AEDF) in the umbilical artery reflects and its clinical management implication.
(v) State the role of TVUS in assessing endometrial thickness postmenopausally and the action required when thickness exceeds the normal threshold.

Describe the classification, epidemiology, mode of action, effectiveness, and non-contraceptive benefits of combined oral contraceptives (COCs).

A(i) Classification of COCs: types of pill packets, hormone constituents, and preparations
A(ii) When to initiate COCs and indications for use
B(i) Absolute and relative contraindications to COCs, with the physiological basis of the greatest risks
B(ii) Instructions for use: what to do when pills are missed, including the ACHES warning signs
C(i) Side effects and advantages of COCs
C(ii) Why COCs do not protect against STIs, and what additional protection is required, with the non-contraceptive benefits of COCs on the reproductive system
questions.answerText:
A(i) Combined oral contraceptives: women swallow a pill each day to prevent pregnancy; also called combined pills, COCs, OCs, the Pill, and birth control pills. Two types of pill packets: 28-pill packets (21 active pills containing hormones followed by 7 remainder pills of a different colour that do not contain hormones); 21-pill packets (only 21 active pills). COCs contain low doses of synthetic oestrogen (ethinyl oestradiol) and progestogen (a C-19 steroid such as norethindrone, norethisterone). Third-generation progestogens (desogestrel, gestodene, norgestimate) were produced to minimise androgenic side effects; they are more potent ovulation inhibitors but are associated with thrombo-embolic phenomenon. Preparations: monophasic (commoner) and triphasic (sequential).
A(ii) When to initiate: pills can be given anytime during the menstrual cycle when one is reasonably sure the woman is not pregnant, but preferably during the first 7 days of the cycle. If after 5 days, use back-up method for 7 days. Indications: healthy women in their early reproductive years who desire effective reversible contraception e.g., adolescents, nulliparous women; postpartum women (3 weeks if not breastfeeding; after 6 months if breastfeeding); immediate post-abortion.
B(i) Absolute contraindications: women who smoke and are ≥35 years; liver disease; breast cancer; diabetes with complications; hypertension; breastfeeding; cardiovascular disease; pregnancy; gallbladder disease; undiagnosed abnormal uterine bleeding; migraines with focal neurological symptoms; malignancies of the breast or reproductive system. The greatest danger associated with pill use is increased risk of circulatory-system disease, particularly in clients with previous history of venous thrombosis, ischaemic heart disease, cerebrovascular disorders, and hypertension; risks significantly increased in those over 35 who also smoke heavily (over 15 cigarettes per day). Relative contraindications: migraine headaches; cervical dysplasia; smoking; diabetes mellitus without kidney, eye or valvular disease; gallbladder disease; uterine fibroids; benign breast disease; endometritis; epilepsy; asthma; cardiac disease.
B(ii) Instructions for missed pills: miss 1 pill—take the forgotten pill as soon as you remember and take today's pill at the usual time. Miss 2 pills in a row—take 2 pills as soon as you remember and take 2 pills the next day. Miss 3 pills in a row—stop taking pills and use another method; consider changing the contraceptive method. Miss 1 or more inactive pills—throw the missed pill away and take the rest of the brown pills as usual, then start a new packet as due. Warning signs (ACHES): A = Abdominal pain (severe); C = Chest pain (severe); H = Headache (severe); E = Eye problems, blurring of vision; S = Severe calf pain. Client should report to clinic immediately if she experiences any of these.
C(i) Side effects in first 3 months: nausea, flatulence, vomiting (minor). Major side effects: breakthrough bleeding; myocardial infarction; cerebrovascular accidents; hypertension (not common with low-dose pills currently in circulation). Advantages: highly effective if used correctly; client can discontinue independently; suitable for all reproductive age groups and parity; use is not related to intercourse; relieves dysmenorrhoea; reduces menstrual flow in heavy bleeders; regularises irregular cycles; offers some protection against cancer of the uterus, ovary, and also PID; does not delay return to fertility.
C(ii) COCs do not protect against STIs and HIV; condom should be used for protection against STIs and HIV. Non-contraceptive benefits of COCs: reduces risk of ovarian and endometrial cancer; regulates menstrual cycle; relieves dysmenorrhoea; relieves perimenopausal symptoms.

(i) Cervical smear and speculum examination. Post-coital bleeding requires urgent cervical assessment to exclude cervical carcinoma, which classically presents with this symptom. The cervix may show an obvious lesion (polyp, ectropion, or malignant lesion) visible on speculum examination. Colposcopy and biopsy follow if an abnormal cervix is found or if smear is abnormal. Cervical evaluation takes priority over endometrial assessment given the most common serious cause.

(ii) The correct sequence for abdominal examination is: Inspection (looking for distension, visible masses, surgical scars, and asymmetry) → Palpation (light then deep, to assess tenderness and masses) → Percussion (to define organ boundaries, detect ascites, characterise masses) → Auscultation (bowel sounds). Pelvic assessment then proceeds with speculum examination followed by bimanual examination assessing uterine size, position, consistency, mobility, cervical motion tenderness, adnexal masses, and fornicial tenderness.

(iii) Post-coital bleeding is bleeding occurring after sexual intercourse. It most commonly signals cervical pathology — classically cervical carcinoma, but also cervical ectropion and polyps — and warrants urgent cervical smear and speculum examination.

(iv) Superficial dyspareunia (pain at the introitus during attempted penetration) is associated with vulvovaginal conditions such as vaginismus, vestibulitis, atrophic vaginitis, or hymenal abnormalities. Deep dyspareunia (pain during deep penetration) most commonly indicates pelvic pathology such as endometriosis or pelvic inflammatory disease causing adhesions, retroverted fixed uterus, or involvement of the uterosacral ligaments, and requires pelvic examination and often imaging or laparoscopy.

(v) Recto-vaginal examination is performed to palpate the posterior cul-de-sac (pouch of Douglas), uterosacral ligaments, and rectovaginal septum for nodularity — characteristic of deep infiltrating endometriosis. It also allows better assessment of a retroverted uterus, adnexal masses in the posterior pelvis, and involvement of pelvic organs in malignancy.
questions.question:
A 35-year-old woman attends for routine gynaecological assessment. She reports irregular intermenstrual bleeding and post-coital bleeding for 3 months. Speculum examination reveals a visible lesion on the cervix.

(i) State the most important first investigation and justify its priority over other investigations.
(ii) Describe the correct sequence of gynaecological examination steps.
(iii) Define post-coital bleeding and state the pelvic pathology it most commonly signals.
(iv) Distinguish between superficial and deep dyspareunia and state what each most commonly suggests.
(v) State the purpose of recto-vaginal examination and what it specifically palpates.

questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Recto-vaginal fistula (RVF) — low (in the lower half of the vagina, below the levator ani). Classification: RVF may be high or low; the type is determined by its relation to the levator ani. A low RVF is below the levator ani; a high RVF is above the levator ani in the posterior fornix, inaccessible from below, requiring abdominal repair.
(ii) Aetiology:
- Tissue necrosis following obstructed labour (prolonged pressure necrosis — sloughing — fistulous connection; commonest cause)
- Incompletely repaired third-degree perineal tear (breaks down at apex, leaving an RVF just above the perineal body)
- Rectal injury during pelvic procedures (e.g. vaginal hysterectomy and pelvic floor repair, or abdominal hysterectomy complicated by scarring from pelvic sepsis or endometriosis)
- Radiation therapy for carcinoma of the cervix
- Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV)
- Gynaecological operations (Manchester repair, vaginal hysterectomy)
- Complete tear of the perineum and recto-vaginal septum in which the lower part has healed but a defect remains higher up (in countries with inadequate obstetric services)
(iii) Pre-operative management for vaginal repair:
Defer repair for at least 2 months after the causative labour or previous attempt at repair.
Low residue diet from 5 days pre-operatively. Sterilise the bowel by giving antibiotics (e.g. neomycin). On the day of surgery: rectal washout. If a preliminary colostomy is in situ: parenteral antibiotics are more effective than oral (oral preparation may not reach the large bowel); descending colon and rectum are cleaned by daily washouts through the distal loop of the colostomy. Preliminary colostomy unnecessary if RVF is in the lower half of the vagina; a wise precaution for high fistula greater than 1 cm in diameter. Transverse colostomy preferred to iliac colostomy (leaves abdominal wall below the umbilicus clear for pelvic approach; an iliac colostomy tethers the pelvic colon to the anterior abdominal wall, making ureteric transplantation difficult if needed).
(iv) Management with co-existing VVF: RVF of obstetric origin usually co-exists with VVF. The bladder (VVF) lesion should be dealt with first, because borrowing tissues to fill in vaginal defects opposite each other produces tension, favouring breakdown; and if a second attempt at VVF repair is required, scarring from the posterior wall repair would interfere with access. Good policy: tackle VVF first, then repair the rectal defect 3 weeks later when examination shows the anterior wall fistula is soundly healed. Post-op after RVF repair: instil dye in the distal loop with a clean swab in the vagina, after repair of the RVF but before closure of the colostomy, to confirm successful repair.
questions.question:
A 29-year-old woman presents at the gynaecology clinic with a history of passage of faeces per vaginam since a difficult forceps delivery one year ago. She also has infertility. On Sim's speculum examination, a small opening is seen in the posterior vaginal wall in the lower half of the vagina.
(i) What is the diagnosis and what is its anatomical classification based on relation to the pelvic floor?
(ii) List the full aetiology of this condition.
(iii) Outline the pre-operative management before vaginal repair, including bowel preparation.
(iv) Describe the management strategy where a co-existing vesicovaginal fistula is also present, including which fistula is repaired first and why.

questions.answerText:
(i) Mayer-Rokitansky-Kuster-Hauser (MRKH) syndrome: agenesis or hypoplasia of the vagina and uterus in a phenotypic female with a 46,XX karyotype.

(ii) Incidence is 1 in 4,000 to 6,000 females. Thirty to 40% of cases have associated renal anomalies requiring renal tract imaging.

(iii) MRKH results from failure of Mullerian (paramesonephric) duct development (agenesis or hypoplasia). The ovaries are normal and functioning because they develop from the gonadal ridge (genital ridge) of the intermediate mesoderm — a separate embryological origin from the Mullerian ducts. Therefore, normal secondary sexual characteristics (thelarche, pubic hair) develop from normal ovarian oestrogen and adrenal androgen production, but no uterus or upper vagina forms because the Mullerian ducts did not develop.

(iv) Primary management focuses on creating a functional vagina through gradual self-dilation therapy (using progressively larger dilators to stretch the vaginal dimple) or surgical vaginoplasty.

(v) The renal anomaly reflects that the mesonephric (Wolffian) duct plays a role in ureteric bud development; anomalies of the intermediate mesoderm (from which both Mullerian and Wolffian structures derive) can produce co-existing renal and Mullerian duct anomalies at the same developmental stage. Two other anomaly categories commonly associated with this syndrome: renal tract anomalies (unilateral renal agenesis, ectopic kidney) and skeletal/vertebral anomalies.
questions.question:
A 19-year-old presents with primary amenorrhoea. She has normal breast development and pubic hair but MRI shows absent uterus and upper vagina. Karyotype is 46,XX. Renal ultrasound shows a unilateral absent kidney.

(i) State the diagnosis.
(ii) State the incidence of this condition and the proportion with associated renal anomalies.
(iii) Describe the embryological basis for the absent uterus and upper vagina, and explain why the ovaries are normal and functioning.
(iv) Describe the primary management aimed at creating a functional vagina.
(v) State the embryological explanation for the associated renal finding, and name two other anomaly categories commonly associated with this syndrome.

Describe the origin, course, and clinical significance of the approach to voluntary surgical contraception (VSC) and the principles of family planning programme planning.

A(i) Types of voluntary surgical contraception available for women and men
A(ii) Definition of contraception and fecundity; the Pearl Index and its role in comparing contraceptive methods
B(i) The ideal contraceptive method from a woman's perspective
B(ii) The three reasons given in support of modern family planning methods
B(iii) Types of family planning methods available in Nigeria
C(i) The epidemiology of contraceptive use in Nigeria, including the gap between knowledge and practice
C(ii) How family planning can prevent maternal and infant deaths
questions.answerText:
A(i) Voluntary Surgical Contraception for women—Bilateral Tubal Occlusion: tubal ligation; electrocoagulation; use of clips (Filschie) and rings (Falope); use of chemicals. For men—Vasectomy: conventional vasectomy; no-scalpel vasectomy. Recently introduced method for female sterilisation: Essure.
A(ii) Contraception is the use of a substance or device to prevent conception. Modern techniques seek to interrupt the process of conception by impacting on the ovum, the sperm, the meeting of the sperm and ovum, and implantation. Fecundity is the biological capacity to procreate, which remains unchanged. Pearl Index: Pearl Index = (Number of events × 1200) / (Number of months of exposure); expressed as a rate per 100 woman-years; still valid (assumes constant risk of events) for reporting contraceptive efficacy; useful in comparing methods and events (an event = anything medical e.g., pregnancy, or non-medical e.g., no further need for contraception).
B(i) Women's perspectives on the most ideal method: should be highly effective; should have prolonged duration of action and still be rapidly reversible; should not have any side effects and complications; should be easily accessible and provide privacy of use; offer protection against HIV/AIDS and STIs.
B(ii) Three reasons in support of modern family planning methods: to improve individual rights and welfare of women; to combat population explosion secondary to uncontrolled fertility; to tailor population growth to available resources, improving societal welfare.
B(iii) Types of family planning methods available in Nigeria: hormonal methods; intrauterine contraceptive devices; barrier methods; natural family planning; voluntary surgical contraception; immunological methods; male methods.
C(i) Knowledge of Nigerians and attitude towards family planning has improved in the last two decades; contraceptive use is generally poor; there is a wide gap between the north and the south; accessibility to FP services is very poor—in rural areas only 30% of married women are within 6 km of service delivery points; Nigeria has a large population of adolescent and eligible women of reproductive age (approximately 18 million); the NDHS of 2003 showed that 75% of Nigerian women of childbearing age are in union; Nigerians marry early, have the first pregnancy early, have a high fertility rate (5.7/woman), and desire many children.
C(ii) Family planning can prevent maternal and infant deaths by: delaying motherhood; avoiding too many children; avoiding closely-spaced children; preventing pregnancy under stress; avoiding unsafe abortion. Direct obstetric causes are responsible for most maternal deaths in Nigeria, and FP can save lives. FP is a primary health strategy with important benefits for both maternal and child health and an important component of strategies adopted to combat rising maternal mortality at the Safe Motherhood Conference.

questions.question:
A 55-year-old postmenopausal woman presents with vaginal bleeding. She is not on hormone replacement therapy. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an endometrial thickness of 6 mm.

(i) State the most appropriate first-line investigation and justify it.
(ii) State the endometrial thickness threshold above which endometrial sampling is mandatory in a postmenopausal woman with bleeding, and give the sensitivity of this threshold for endometrial carcinoma.
(iii) Describe the mechanism by which endometrial atrophy — the most common cause of postmenopausal bleeding — produces bleeding.
(iv) State the most sensitive investigation for detecting endometrial polyps and give its sensitivity compared with standard TVUS.
(v) State what constitutes normal endometrial thickness on TVUS in a postmenopausal woman not on HRT.
questions.answerText:
(i) Hysteroscopy with directed endometrial biopsy (or transvaginal ultrasound followed by biopsy if endometrial thickness >4 mm). This is the first-line investigation because postmenopausal bleeding requires exclusion of endometrial carcinoma as the priority; endometrial carcinoma is present in approximately 10% of women with postmenopausal bleeding.

(ii) An endometrial thickness of 4 mm or greater in a postmenopausal woman with vaginal bleeding requires endometrial sampling; this threshold has a sensitivity of approximately 96% for detecting endometrial carcinoma.

(iii) Endometrial atrophy in postmenopausal women is associated with the development of large, fragile dilated venules lying superficially under the thin atrophic endometrium. These venules are prone to spontaneous rupture, producing unpredictable light to moderate postmenopausal bleeding. Despite being the most common cause of postmenopausal bleeding, atrophy can only be diagnosed after exclusion of endometrial malignancy through appropriate biopsy.

(iv) Saline infusion sonohysterography (SIS) or office hysteroscopy. SIS has sensitivity of 90%+ for polyps; hysteroscopy approaches 100%. Standard TVUS has sensitivity of only 60-70% because polyps may not distort the endometrial outline without cavity distension. Hysteroscopy also allows simultaneous therapeutic polypectomy.

(v) Normal endometrial thickness in a postmenopausal woman not on HRT is less than 4 mm (some guidelines use less than 5 mm as the threshold).

questions.question:
A 24-year-old woman from southwest Nigeria presents with inability to have sexual intercourse (apareunia), secondary amenorrhoea and inability to conceive for two years after inserting herbal soap made from crude potash mixed with palm oil into her vagina. Examination under anaesthesia reveals near-complete fibrosis of the vaginal canal.

(i) What is the diagnosis? Name the types of this condition by cause, listing the specific local agents in Nigeria mentioned in the lectures.
(ii) Name the surgical procedure required, and describe its technique (specifically the McIndoe operation), including the source of the graft and the type of mould used.
(iii) What structures are at risk during the surgical dissection, and what are the contraindications to this operation?
(iv) State the post-operative care required and the outcomes reported in Ibadan.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Acquired gynaetresia (acquired vaginal stenosis) due to chemical vaginitis.
Local agents causing acquired gynaetresia in Nigeria:
- Special leaves (Southern Nigeria)
- Herbal pessary and soap from crude potash mixed with palm oil (Southwest Nigeria)
- Rock salt lumps (Middle East countries, 2nd–15th day post-partum)
Other causes include: prolonged obstructed labour (pressure necrosis of vaginal wall), repair of VVF, colporrhaphy (too much vaginal tissue excised), post-caesium radiotherapy for cancer of cervix, lymphogranuloma venereum, post-vaginal fistula repair for large defects.

(ii) Surgical procedure: Vaginoplasty — McIndoe operation (McIndoe-Reed's vaginoplasty).
Technique: Dissection of a space between the bladder/urethra anteriorly and the rectum posteriorly. A split-thickness skin graft is taken from the thigh. The graft is placed on a mould made of Stent's dental composition with a central hole. Two stages in acquired variety: First stage — dissection, pack with lubricated antiseptic gauze. Second stage (two to seven days later) — apply graft using mould; remove after 21 days.

(iii) Structures at risk during dissection: bladder and urethra anteriorly; rectum posteriorly; risk of fistula formation if planes are incorrect.
Contraindications to vaginoplasty: pregnant women (excessive bleeding); in the puerperium (extent of damage unknown); peri- or post-menopausal women (symptoms less); following severe obstetric trauma (little vaginal tissue remaining); after successful closure of extensive vesicovaginal fistulae; dense scar tissue; vesico-vaginal fistula.

(iv) Post-operative care: passage of dilators for at least six months; encouragement of sexual intercourse.
Outcomes in Ibadan: 68% successful repair; 28% residual stenosis; 4% complete stenosis.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the origin, types, and functions of cells found in connective tissue under the following headings: cells of fixed (resident) population and cells of wandering (transient) population.
A(ii) State where the mesenchymal stem-like cells persist in adults and state their clinical significance.
B(i) Explain the anatomical and histological basis of why connective tissue of the head region differs in embryological origin from the rest of the body, and state the clinical implication.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Fixed (resident) cells: Mesenchyme cells — embryonic source of all connective tissue cells; only found in embryos, but some mesenchyme-like cells persist in adult connective tissue. Fibroblasts — most common cell type in connective tissue; elongated, spindle-shaped cells with many cell processes; have oval, pale-staining, regular nuclei with prominent nucleoli; abundant rough endoplasmic reticulum and active Golgi bodies; synthesize collagen, reticular and elastic fibers, and amorphous extracellular substance. Fibrocytes — quiescent fibroblasts; smaller, darker nucleus; less rough ER. Chondroblasts/osteoblasts — synthesize cartilage and bone matrices. Adipocytes — energy storage, thermal insulation. Wandering (transient) cells: Macrophages — ingestion by phagocytosis; antigen presentation; secretion of enzymes and cytokines; long-lived (several months); originate from monocytes in bone marrow. Plasma cells — defense and immune function. Lymphocytes — immune function. Neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils — immune function. Mast cells — immune function. All connective tissue cells are derived from mesenchymal cells.
A(ii) Mesenchyme-like cells (pericytes) persist in adult connective tissue, including that of tooth pulp and some adipose tissue. These mesenchyme-like cells retain their capacity to differentiate into other connective tissue cells in response to injury (e.g., pericytes — perivascular cells of blood capillaries). They are being investigated as possible sources of stem cells for therapeutic repair and organ regeneration. Some multipotent stem cells potentially useful in regenerative medicine after grafting to replace damaged tissue in certain patients.
B(i) All connective tissue cells are derived from mesenchymal cells; mesenchyme cells are for the most part derived from the mesoderm. However, several of the connective tissues of the head region are derived from the neural crest cells (ectodermal origin). Endothelial cells lining blood vessels are derived from mesenchyme. The clinical implication is that connective tissue tumors or developmental disorders in the head may follow patterns distinct from those in the rest of the body due to this different embryological derivation.

A(i) The oesophageal hiatus is an oval opening in the muscular right crus of the diaphragm at the level of the T10 vertebra; it transmits the oesophagus, the anterior and posterior vagal trunks, oesophageal branches of the left gastric vessels, and lymphatic vessels. Fibres of the right crus decussate inferior to the hiatus, forming a muscular sling that constricts the oesophagus when the diaphragm contracts.
A(ii) The aortic hiatus lies posterior to the diaphragm, between the two crura, at the level of the lower border of the T12 vertebra; it transmits the aorta, the thoracic duct and sometimes the azygos and hemiazygos veins. Because the aorta does not pierce the diaphragm itself, movements of the diaphragm during respiration do not affect blood flow through it.
A(iii) The caval opening lies in the central tendon of the diaphragm at the level of T8; it transmits the inferior vena cava, terminal branches of the right phrenic nerve, and a few hepatic lymphatic vessels. The inferior vena cava is adherent to the margin of this opening, so diaphragmatic contraction during inspiration widens the opening and dilates the inferior vena cava, aiding venous return to the heart.
B(i) The right and left crura arise from the bodies of the L1-L3 vertebrae, the anterior longitudinal ligament and the intervertebral discs; the oesophageal hiatus lies within the right crus, to the left of the midline, superior to and to the left of the aortic hiatus. Diaphragmatic hernia (sliding and paraoesophageal types) and diaphragmatic rupture are clinical considerations related to weakness or defects around these openings.
In most individuals, about 70%, both margins of the oesophageal hiatus are formed by muscular bundles of the right crus; in others the left crus contributes to the right margin, and such variation can affect the sphincter-like action around the oesophagus.
C(i) The oesophageal hiatus is a muscular opening in the right crus at the level of T10 that actively constricts around the oesophagus with diaphragmatic contraction, contributing to prevention of reflux.
The aortic hiatus is a non-muscular, fibrous opening bounded by the crura and the median arcuate ligament at the lower border of T12, so diaphragmatic contraction does not compress or affect flow through the aorta.
The oesophageal hiatus transmits the oesophagus and vagal trunks, whereas the aortic hiatus transmits the aorta and thoracic duct, reflecting their different anatomical roles.

questions.answerText:
(i) The diagnosis is varicosity and thrombosis of the great saphenous vein (GSV). The GSV is the longest vein in the body. It is formed by the union of the dorsal vein of the great toe and the dorsal venous arch of the foot. It ascends anterior to the medial malleolus, passes posterior to the medial condyle of the femur (about a hand's breadth posterior to the medial border of the patella), traverses the saphenous opening in the fascia lata, and empties into the femoral vein.
(ii) Anatomical risk factors include the length of the vein (it is the longest vein in the body and has 10–12 valves), valve incompetence (valves are usually located just inferior to perforating veins), and the presence of perforating veins connecting superficial to deep systems whose valves may also fail. The vein traverses the saphenous opening, a potential site of external compression. Standing occupations increase venous pressure.
(iii) If the thrombus propagates into the femoral vein (deep vein thrombosis), complications include pulmonary embolism (thrombus travels through the femoral vein to the heart and lungs), post-thrombotic syndrome with chronic venous insufficiency, leg oedema, skin changes, and venous ulceration.
(iv) Management options: conservative (compression stockings, elevation, anticoagulation with low-molecular-weight heparin or direct oral anticoagulants). Definitive surgical options include great saphenous vein ligation at the saphenofemoral junction combined with stripping or endovenous thermal ablation (laser or radiofrequency). Anticoagulation is justified as the definitive treatment here because thrombus is already extending to the saphenofemoral junction, and anticoagulation prevents propagation into the femoral vein and reduces the risk of pulmonary embolism, while simultaneously treating the underlying thrombosis.
questions.question:

(i) State the diagnosis and name the affected vein fully.
(ii) What are the anatomical risk factors for this condition?
(iii) What are the complications if the thrombus propagates into the femoral vein?
(iv) Describe the management options, justifying one definitive treatment.
