A(i) Three regions of the male urethra:
1. Prostatic urethra (2.5 cm): located within the prostate.
2. Intermediate part of the urethra (membranous urethra) (2 cm): passes through the urogenital diaphragm from the prostate to the beginning of the penis.
3. Spongy urethra (15 cm): passes through the penis and opens via the external urethral orifice.
The male urethra carries both semen and urine.
A(ii) Two sphincters:
- Internal urethral sphincter: involuntary (smooth muscle) at the bladder-urethra junction; contracts to open (its contraction, paradoxically, opens the sphincter as described — 'contracts to open').
- External urethral sphincter: voluntary (skeletal muscle) surrounding the urethra as it passes through the pelvic floor.
B(i) Female urethra:
- Length: 3–4 cm.
- Relations: tightly bound to the anterior vaginal wall.
- External urethral orifice: anterior to the vaginal opening and posterior to the clitoris.
B(ii) Layers of the urinary bladder wall visible :
- Peritoneum, rugae, detrusor (muscle), adventitia, ureteric orifices, trigone of bladder, bladder neck, internal urethral sphincter.

questions.answerText:
A(i) The cubital fossa is a triangular space, a shallow depression on the anterior surface of the elbow region, located anterior to the elbow joint, formed between two forearm muscles (brachioradialis and pronator teres).
A(ii) Boundaries: base (superior) — an imaginary horizontal line connecting the medial and lateral epicondyles; medial (ulnar) wall — lateral border of pronator teres; lateral (radial) wall — medial border of brachioradialis; apex — directed inferiorly, where the medial and lateral boundaries meet; floor — brachialis and supinator; roof — continuity of brachial and antebrachial (deep) fascia, reinforced by the bicipital aponeurosis, superficial fascia and skin.
A(iii) The major contents, from medial to lateral, are the median nerve, the brachial artery (which bifurcates near the apex into the radial and ulnar arteries), deep accompanying veins of the arteries, and the tendon of biceps brachii.
B. The median cubital vein, cephalic vein and basilic vein are present in the area but are usually considered superficial to the cubital fossa and not part of its contents.
During blood pressure measurement the stethoscope is placed over the brachial artery in the cubital fossa, and the fossa is also used to palpate the brachial pulse.
The area just superficial to the cubital fossa is often used for venous access (phlebotomy), since it is superficial and accessible.
The bicipital aponeurosis forms the roof of the fossa and was historically called the "grace of God" tendon because it protected the brachial artery and median nerve during blood-letting.
C. The radial nerve is in the vicinity of the cubital fossa, located between brachialis and brachioradialis, but is often, though not always, considered part of the cubital fossa's contents.
This differs from the median nerve and brachial artery, which are consistently listed as major contents of the fossa.
The superficial veins similarly lie in the roof/superficial region and are related to, rather than contained within, the fossa proper.
Venipuncture therefore uses the superficial veins overlying the fossa, while palpation of the brachial pulse and auscultation for blood pressure use the deeper true content, the brachial artery.
This distinction between superficial and deep structures is the basis for choosing the correct site for a given clinical procedure at the elbow.

questions.answerText:
A(i) The notochord is a cellular rod developed from the notochordal process; it defines the primordial axis of the embryo, gives it rigidity, serves as the basis for development of the axial skeleton, indicates the future site of the vertebral bodies, and functions as the primary inductor in the early embryo.
A(ii) Neurulation occurs in four stages: thickening of ectoderm (neural plate); shaping of the neural plate (lengthening, narrowing, thickening, wedging); bending of the neural plate (hinge joints, neural fold formation); and fusion of the neural folds. The hinge points are areas of neural plate attachment to adjacent tissue: one median hinge point (attached to the notochord) and two dorsolateral hinge points (attached to adjacent epidermal ectoderm); at these points the neuroepithelial cells become wedge-shaped and the neural plate undergoes furrowing.
A(iii) Neural crest cells emigrate from the elevating/converging neural folds, contributing to the PNS (cranial, spinal and autonomic ganglia) and other tissues: connective tissue/bones of the face and skull, cranial nerve ganglia, C cells of the thyroid, the conotruncal septum of the heart, odontoblasts, dermis of face and neck, spinal (dorsal root) ganglia, sympathetic/preaortic ganglia, parasympathetic ganglia of the gut, adrenal medulla, Schwann cells, glial cells, leptomeninges, and melanocytes.
B) The major abnormalities of neurulation occur from failure of closure of the neuropores and associated mesodermally derived structures, collectively called Neural Tube Defects, occurring in about 1 in 1,000 births; anterior neuropore defects give meningocoele, meningoencephalocoele and anencephaly, while posterior neuropore defects give spina bifida (occulta and cystica) and myeloschisis.
C) Primary neurulation forms the neural tube by folding and fusion of the neural plate, whereas secondary neurulation forms the neural tube by condensation of mesenchyme into a rod, which undergoes epithelial transition and cavitation; both can occur in the same animal, commonly in the tail.

questions.answerText:
(i) The heart has four chambers, the right and left atria (receiving chambers) and the right and left ventricles (discharging chambers), enclosed in the double-walled pericardial sac, and rests on its diaphragmatic (inferior) surface.
It has an apex, formed by the inferolateral part of the left ventricle and lying posterior to the 5th intercostal space where the apex beat is felt, a base, formed mainly by the left atrium and part of the right atrium, four borders and three surfaces.
The right border is formed mainly by the right atrium; the left border by the left ventricle and left auricle; the inferior border by the right ventricle mainly and the left ventricle; the superior border by both atria, auricles and the great vessels.
The anterior (sternocostal) surface consists chiefly of the right ventricle; the inferior (diaphragmatic) surface consists chiefly of the left ventricle and a small part of the right ventricle; the left (pulmonary) surface is formed mainly by the left ventricle.
The right atrium receives venous blood from the SVC, IVC and coronary sinus, has a smooth sinus venarum and a rough muscular wall with pectinate muscles, and communicates with the right ventricle via the right atrioventricular (tricuspid) orifice.
The left atrium receives the four pulmonary veins and communicates with the left ventricle via the left atrioventricular (mitral) orifice; the right ventricle has a tricuspid valve and leads to the pulmonary trunk via the conus arteriosus, while the left ventricle, with twice the wall thickness, has the mitral valve and leads to the aorta via the aortic vestibule and aortic valve.
(ii) Valvular insufficiency results from valve leaflets not completely sealing when a valve is closed, so regurgitation of blood occurs into the proximal chamber, generating a characteristic heart murmur.
Positional and septal anomalies include dextrocardia, atrial septal defects and ventricular septal defects.
Aortic dissection, a tear in the inner wall of the aorta associated with high blood pressure, and aortic aneurysm, dilation of an artery greater than 50% of its normal diameter, are documented pathologies of the great vessel arising from the left ventricle.
(iii) The conducting system, the SA node in the posterior wall of the right atrium, the AV node in the floor of the right atrium, the AV bundle and Purkinje fibres, initiates and coordinates the heartbeat; damage to a coronary artery supplying these nodes can disturb heart rhythm.
Cardiac afferent fibres carrying pain from ischaemic myocardium travel via sympathetic afferents in the cardiac plexus to spinal cord segments T1-T5 shared with dermatomes of the chest wall and upper limb, so the central nervous system perceives cardiac pain as coming from the body wall.
This explains why myocardial ischaemia is felt as pain in the mid or left chest that radiates to the left jaw and left arm, a distant somatic sensation produced by a cardiac (visceral) problem.

A(i) Describe the autonomic nerve supply to the salivary glands, including which division of the autonomic nervous system produces each type of secretory response and what type of saliva each produces.
A(ii) Describe the full immunological secretory mechanism of the large salivary glands, identifying the cell type that secretes IgA and the cell types that synthesise the secretory component.
B(i) The parotid gland resembles pancreatic tissue but can be distinguished from it. State the distinguishing features described for each gland.
B(ii) Classify all minor salivary glands by location and secretion type, and state what proportion of total saliva volume and mucus the minor glands produce.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Autonomic nerve supply:
- Vessels and nerves enter the large salivary glands at the hilum and gradually branch into the lobules; a rich vascular and nerve plexus surrounds the secretory and ductal components of each lobule.
- The capillaries surrounding the secretory end pieces are important for saliva secretion, stimulated by the autonomic nervous system.
- Parasympathetic stimulation (usually through smell or taste of food): promotes vasodilation and a copious watery secretion.
- Sympathetic stimulation: produces small amounts of viscous saliva, rich in organic material. NOTE: dry mouth sensation in stressful situations (sympathetic predominance).
A(ii) Immunological secretory mechanism:
- Plasma cells (in the connective tissue around the glands) secrete IgA.
- IgA forms a complex with a secretory component synthesized by the serous acinar cells, intercalated duct cells, and striated duct cells.
- The IgA-rich secretory complex released into the saliva is resistant to enzymatic digestion and constitutes an immunological defense mechanism against pathogens in the oral cavity.
B(i) Parotid vs pancreatic tissue:
- Both resemble each other histologically.
- Parotid gland: has adipocytes (fat cells) in its parenchyma.
- Pancreatic tissue: has islets of Langerhans (endocrine clusters) and centroacinar cells.
B(ii) Minor salivary glands by location and secretion:
- von Ebner's glands of tongue (posterior dorsal and lateral): serous acini only.
- Palate, base and lateral border of tongue: predominantly mucous acini.
- Lip, cheek, apex of tongue: mixed serous and mucous acini.
- Minor glands secrete 10% of the total volume of saliva but account for approximately 70% of the mucus secreted.

questions.question:
A. Describe the gross anatomy of the pterygopalatine fossa under the following headings: description/location, boundaries, and contents.
B. State the communications of the pterygopalatine fossa and relate these to how disease may spread from this region.
C. Explain why disease or infection arising near the pterygopalatine fossa can spread to distant structures such as the orbit, the nasal cavity, the middle cranial fossa or the pharynx, and the functional deficit that could result.
questions.answerText:
A. The pterygopalatine fossa is an inverted pyramidal-shaped, fat-filled space located on the lateral side of the skull, between the infratemporal fossa and the nasopharynx; it is antero-posteriorly between the maxilla/palatine bone and the pterygoid process, and laterally between the infratemporal fossa and nasopharynx. Its boundaries are: anterior - posterior surface of maxilla below the floor of the orbit; posterior - lateral pterygoid plate and part of the medial plate; medial - perpendicular plate of the palatine bone; lateral - pterygomaxillary fissure; superior - undersurface of the greater wing of the sphenoid; inferior - absent (the posterior wall meets the anterior wall, and between them is the greater palatine canal). Its contents are the terminal (third/pterygoid) part of the maxillary artery and the initial parts of its branches, the maxillary vein, the maxillary nerve, and the pterygopalatine ganglion (a parasympathetic ganglion, one of four parasympathetic ganglia of the head and neck, the others being the submandibular, otic and ciliary ganglia).
B. The pterygopalatine fossa is described as a major neurovascular crossroad between the orbit, the nasal cavity, the nasopharynx, the oral cavity, the infratemporal fossa and the cranial fossa. Its communications are: laterally with the infratemporal fossa through the pterygomaxillary fissure; medially with the nasal cavity through the sphenopalatine foramen; anterosuperiorly with the orbit through the inferior orbital fissure; posterosuperiorly with the middle cranial fossa through the foramen rotundum and pterygoid canal; with the palate through the greater and lesser palatine canals and foramina; and with the pharynx through the pterygoid canal and palatovaginal canal - in general, vascular structures enter the fossa through its lateral wall, while nerve structures enter through its posterior wall.
C. Because the pterygopalatine fossa communicates directly with the orbit (via the inferior orbital fissure), the nasal cavity (via the sphenopalatine foramen), the middle cranial fossa (via the foramen rotundum and pterygoid canal), and the pharynx (via the pterygoid canal and palatovaginal canal), disease or infection arising in or near the fossa has multiple direct anatomical routes by which it can spread to these distant sites; clinical correlates noted for this region include hay fever affecting the ganglion here (the pterygopalatine ganglion is also known as the hay fever ganglion), and maxillary nerve block is performed in relation to this fossa.

questions.question:
Describe the gross anatomy of the proximal carpal row/wrist region:
A(i) Bones forming the proximal row and their articulation with the radius
A(ii) The scaphoid's distinguishing feature
B. State how the scaphoid and lunate each relate to common wrist pathologies.
C. Explain how pathology at the lunate spreads to affect a distant structure, causing a functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
A(i) The wrist (radiocarpal) joint is formed distally by the proximal row of carpal bones — the scaphoid, lunate and triquetrum, excluding the pisiform — and proximally by the distal end of the radius and the articular disk; the ulna is not part of the wrist joint, being prevented from articulating with the carpal bones by this fibrocartilaginous articular disk, and instead articulates with the radius at the distal radioulnar joint.
A(ii) The scaphoid has a unique blood supply that runs from distal to proximal, unlike most bones.
B. The scaphoid is the carpal bone most commonly fractured, more so in the younger population, typically from a blow to the wrist such as falling on an outstretched hand, when it takes most of the force.
Because of its distal-to-proximal blood supply, a scaphoid fracture can disrupt supply to the proximal fragment; this is considered an emergency, and failure to revascularise can lead to avascular necrosis and future arthritis.
The lunate is prone to anterior dislocation, which is uncommon but can occur by falling on a dorsiflexed wrist, forcing the lunate anteriorly.
The lunate can also undergo avascular necrosis, so it too requires immediate clinical attention when injured.
C. Anterior dislocation of the lunate compresses the carpal tunnel, since the lunate lies immediately related to the floor of this tunnel region.
This compression of the carpal tunnel affects the median nerve, which lies within it.
The resulting clinical picture manifests as paraesthesia in the sensory distribution of the median nerve.
There is also weakness of the thenar muscles, which are supplied by the median nerve's recurrent branch.
This produces the symptoms of carpal tunnel syndrome, even though the primary pathology (lunate dislocation) is a distinct injury from the usual causes of carpal tunnel syndrome.
This illustrates how a purely skeletal injury at the wrist can spread to compromise an adjacent soft-tissue structure, producing a functional/sensorimotor deficit in the hand.

A(i) The space between two ribs; with 12 ribs on each side there are 11 intercostal spaces; each space contains intercostal muscles, the intercostal neurovascular bundle and lymphatics.
A(ii) Three muscles (external, internal, innermost; transversus thoracis, subcostalis and levator costarum are also listed), supplied by the corresponding intercostal nerves, that pull the ribs nearer to each other and strengthen the space. External intercostal: most superficial, fibres downward and forward, origin lower border of the rib above, insertion upper border of the rib below, from the rib tubercle behind to the costochondral junction in front, replaced anteriorly by the anterior intercostal membrane.
A(ii) Internal intercostal: intermediate layer, fibres downward and backward, origin subcostal groove of the rib above, insertion upper border of the rib below, from the sternum in front to the angle of the rib behind, replaced posteriorly by the posterior intercostal membrane.
A(iii) Innermost intercostal: deepest, incomplete layer divided into 3 portions, its fibres cross more than one space; related externally to the intercostal nerve and vessels and internally to the endothoracic fascia. Endothoracic fascia: extrapleural fascia lining the chest wall between the muscles and bones and the parietal pleura, extending over the pleural apex as the suprapleural membrane and forming a thin layer between diaphragm and pleura.
A(iv) The neurovascular bundle lies between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles, high in the space in relation to the subcostal groove of the rib above; strict order from above downwards: vein, artery, nerve (VAN); because the innermost layer is incomplete it is generally covered on the inside by endothoracic fascia.
A(v) Each space has a single posterior and 2 anterior intercostal arteries, giving branches to muscles, skin, parietal pleura and breast. Posterior: upper 2 spaces from the superior intercostal artery (costocervical trunk of the subclavian artery), lower 9 spaces from the thoracic aorta. Anterior: upper 6 spaces from the internal thoracic artery, lower 5 from the musculophrenic artery; they anastomose with the posterior arteries.
A(vi) Veins accompany the arteries and nerves (11 posterior intercostal and 1 subcostal vein); valves direct blood posteriorly. Right side: 1st space to the brachiocephalic vein, the rest to the azygos vein. Left side: upper 3 spaces to the left brachiocephalic vein, the rest to the hemiazygos and accessory hemiazygos veins, which drain to the azygos vein. Anterior veins: upper 6 spaces to the internal thoracic vein, lower 5 to the musculophrenic vein.
A(vii) 12 pairs, the anterior primary rami of the thoracic spinal nerves and mixed nerves; nerves 1-6 are distributed in the intercostal spaces, 7-11 supply the anterior abdominal wall, and the 12th runs forward in the abdomen as the subcostal nerve; they supply skin, muscles of the space and abdomen, parietal pleura and parietal peritoneum. Branches: rami communicantes, collateral (muscular), lateral cutaneous, anterior cutaneous, pleural and peritoneal (7th-11th).
A(viii) Deep lymphatics follow the arteries: anteriorly they drain into the anterior intercostal (parasternal) nodes along the internal thoracic artery; posteriorly they drain into the posterior intercostal nodes in the posterior mediastinum.
B(i) A needle or drain is passed immediately above the upper border of the rib to avoid the neurovascular bundle (vein, artery, nerve from above downwards) running under the rib above in the subcostal groove.
B(i) Intercostal spaces are access points for surgical procedures (e.g. resection of part of the lung), for percussion and auscultation of the heart and lung, and for sampling pleural fluid or draining pus or blood from the pleural cavity; disease in the thorax may cause pain in the anterior abdominal wall because the intercostal nerves supply both the thoracic and abdominal wall and the parietal pleura.
C(i) Typical nerves are T3-6. T1 is atypical: no anterior cutaneous branch, joined to the brachial plexus by a large branch corresponding to the lateral cutaneous branch. T2 is atypical: its lateral cutaneous branch is the intercostobrachial nerve, which joins the medial cutaneous nerve of the arm through the brachial plexus.

questions.answerText:
(i) Haemorrhage or thrombosis of the striate artery around the posterior fibres (posterior limb) of the internal capsule, causing paralysis of the opposite skeletal muscles; the fibres of Broca's speech are affected on the left side.
(ii) Internal capsule: the most prominent projection fibre bundle; afferent fibres from thalamic nuclei and efferent fibres travelling through the cerebral peduncle of the midbrain; separated from the lateral ventricle by the caudate nucleus; the globus pallidus of the lentiform nucleus indents its lateral edge.
- Parts: anterior limb, genu, posterior limb, retrolentiform and sublentiform parts.
- Posterior limb: between the thalamus (medially) and the lentiform nucleus (laterally); anterior 2/3 carries corticospinal fibres from cortical cell bodies to the anterior horn cells of the spinal cord; posterior 1/3 carries thalamocortical fibres to the sensory cortex.
- The corticospinal fibres pass through the brainstem to the lower medulla, where most decussate to form the lateral corticospinal tract (hence paralysis on the opposite side).
- Anterior limb (between head of caudate and lentiform nucleus): frontopontine fibres; genu: corticonuclear fibres to the motor nuclei of cranial nerves; retrolentiform: corticopontine fibres and optic radiations; sublentiform: auditory radiations from the MG
B.

A. Describe the gross anatomy of the gallbladder and the extrahepatic bile ducts under the following headings:
A(i) Location, shape, dimensions and parts;
A(ii) The ducts and course of the common bile duct;
A(iii) Blood and nerve supply.
B(i) State how the neck relates to gallstones.
B(ii) State how Calot's triangle and its lymph node relate to surgery and inflammation.
B(iii) State how the sphincters relate to biliary dyskinesia.
C(i) Explain why gallbladder inflammation may cause pain at the right shoulder tip and a positive Murphy's sign.
questions.answerText:
A(i) A pear-shaped fibromuscular sac that stores and concentrates bile, in the gallbladder fossa on the inferior surface of the right lobe of the liver, 7 to 10 cm long, 3 cm broad and 30 to 50 ml in capacity.
A(i) Fundus: projects beyond the inferior border of the liver, covered by peritoneum on all sides. Body: superior surface adherent to the liver and devoid of peritoneum. Neck: upper narrow part ending in the cystic duct, with a spiral fold.
A(i) The fundus is related to the anterior abdominal wall and transverse colon; the body's inferior surface to the transverse colon and the 1st and 2nd parts of the duodenum.
A(ii) Right and left hepatic ducts emerge at the porta hepatis; the common hepatic duct (3 to 4 cm) is joined by the cystic duct (3 to 4 cm, spiral folds of Heister) to form the common bile duct.
A(ii) The common bile duct (about 8 cm, 6 mm wide) has supraduodenal, retroduodenal, infraduodenal and intraduodenal parts, joining the main pancreatic duct at the hepatopancreatic ampulla.
A(iii) Cystic artery (from the right hepatic artery) is the chief supply, with the cystic vein to the portal vein; the posterior superior pancreaticoduodenal branches supply the lower bile duct.
A(iii) Sympathetic nerves come from the celiac plexus and parasympathetic from the vagus.
B(i) The posteromedial wall of the neck may dilate as Hartmann's pouch, where gallstones may lodge.
B(ii) Calot's triangle (liver inferior surface, common hepatic duct, cystic duct) locates the cystic artery in laparoscopic cholecystectomy; Lund's node enlarges in cholecystitis or cholangitis and may be removed.
B(iii) Gallbladder muscle and the sphincter of Oddi have reciprocal innervation (gallbladder contracts, sphincter relaxes); disruption is biliary dyskinesia.
C(i) Inflammation irritates the subdiaphragmatic parietal peritoneum supplied by the phrenic nerve (C3, 4, 5), referred to the right shoulder tip supplied by the supraclavicular nerve (C3, C4).
C(i) In Murphy's sign the inflamed gallbladder descends on deep inspiration and contacts the palpating hand at the right costal margin, causing pain and a caught breath.

A(i) Path of blood flow:
Aorta → Renal artery → Segmental artery → Interlobar artery → Arcuate artery → Cortical radiate artery → Afferent arteriole → Glomerulus (capillaries) → Efferent arteriole → Peritubular capillaries (cortical nephrons) or Vasa recta (juxtamedullary nephrons) → Cortical radiate vein → Arcuate vein → Interlobar vein → Renal vein → Inferior vena cava.
Renal arteries deliver approximately one-quarter (1,200 ml) of cardiac output to the kidneys each minute.
A(ii) Nerve supply is via sympathetic fibers from the renal plexus.
B(i)
- Cortical nephrons (85% of nephrons): efferent arteriole supplies peritubular capillaries — low-pressure, porous capillaries adapted for absorption of water and solutes; they cling to adjacent renal tubules in the cortex and empty into venules.
- Juxtamedullary nephrons: efferent arteriole supplies vasa recta — long, thin-walled vessels parallel to the long nephron loops; important in formation of concentrated urine.
B(ii) Blood pressure in the glomerulus is high because:
- Afferent arterioles are larger in diameter than efferent arterioles.
- Arterioles are high-resistance vessels.
The glomerulus is fed and drained by arterioles (not venules), which maintains the high filtration pressure. The glomerulus is also specialized for filtration, with fenestrated endothelium that is highly porous, allowing filtrate formation.

A(i) It has cervical, thoracic and abdominal parts and is not a straight structure: it lies to the left in the neck, returns to the midline at the thoracic inlet, lies to the left in the superior mediastinum, returns to the midline in the posterior mediastinum and deviates to the left as it pierces the diaphragm at T10.
A(ii) Cervical part lies in front of the prevertebral fascia, behind the trachea; the thoracic part is crossed on the right by the azygos vein and on the left by the aorta; in the posterior mediastinum it lies behind the left main bronchus and left pulmonary artery and in front of the thoracic duct; it is the most posterior tube of the superior mediastinum and the most anterior structure of the posterior mediastinum, with the vagus nerves around it, the azygos vein behind and to the right and the descending aorta behind and to the left.
A(iii) Four constrictions: at its origin (C6), 15 cm from the incisor teeth; where the arch of the aorta lies in front of it, 22 cm; where the left main bronchus lies in front of it (tracheal bifurcation), 27 cm; at the diaphragm (T10), 38-40 cm.
A(iv) Arteries: inferior thyroid artery, oesophageal branches of the descending thoracic aorta, and the left gastric artery.
A(iv) Veins: upper part to the brachiocephalic vein, middle part to the azygos vein, lower part to the portal vein.
A(iv) Lymphatics: upper part to deep cervical nodes, middle part to tracheobronchial nodes, lower part to preaortic nodes.
A(iv) Nerves: upper third is striated, supplied by the recurrent laryngeal branch of the vagus, with sympathetics from the middle cervical ganglion; lower two-thirds is smooth, receiving sympathetics from the sympathetic trunk and greater splanchnic nerve, and parasympathetic secretomotor fibres from the vagus to the oesophageal glands.
B(i) Upper part: inferior thyroid artery, brachiocephalic vein, deep cervical nodes, striated muscle with recurrent laryngeal supply, related to the trachea and prevertebral fascia in the neck.
B(i) Middle and lower parts: middle drains to the azygos vein and tracheobronchial nodes and is crossed by the azygos vein, arch of the aorta and left main bronchus; lower part has aortic and left gastric arteries, portal venous drainage, preaortic nodes and smooth muscle, and passes through the diaphragm at T10.
C(i) Venous routes: upper part to the brachiocephalic vein, middle part to the azygos vein (which empties into the SVC and forms a communication between the SVC and IVC), lower part to the portal vein.
C(i) Lymphatic routes: upper part to deep cervical nodes, middle part to tracheobronchial nodes, lower part to preaortic nodes.
C(i) How disease spreads along these routes and the functional deficit that follows: not covered.

questions.answerText:

questions.question:

questions.answerText:
(i) Reticular formation: loosely arranged network of neurons throughout the brainstem wherever there are no specific tracts or nuclei; the core of the brainstem through the midbrain, pons and medulla.
- Three groups: median (raphe/paramedian) column; medial column (magnocellular, large cells with long ascending and descending fibres); lateral column (parvocellular, small cells close to the motor nuclei of cranial nerves, modulating their functions).
- Ascending reticular activating system: connects to thalamus, hypothalamus and cortex; responsible for the sleep-wake cycle and levels of alertness; critical for the conscious state, attention and sleep.
- Descending system: connects to the cerebellum and sensory nerves; posture, equilibrium and autonomic activity; tone, balance and posture via the reticulospinal tract; PPRF most essential for maintenance of equilibrium.
- Gaze: median pontine RF controls horizontal gaze, midbrain RF vertical gaze, medullary RF head movement and gaze holding.
- Autonomic and other functions: heart rate, breathing and digestion via the cardiac and vasomotor centres of the medulla; pain modulation; habituation.

(ii) Predisposing factors/causes include birth injury (undue separation of the head from the shoulder during difficult labour), a fall on the shoulder, or occurrence during anaesthesia.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Collagen fibers: protein fibers that form the bulk of connective tissue fibers. Major types and distribution: Type I collagen — fibril-forming; found in bone, dermis, tendon, ligaments, and cornea; produced by fibroblasts, osteoblasts, odontoblasts. Type II collagen — fibril-forming; found in cartilage and vitreous body of the eye; produced by chondrocytes and retinal cells. Type III collagen — fibril-forming; found in loose connective tissue and reticular fibers in lungs, liver, and spleen; produced by fibroblasts and reticular cells. Type IV collagen — network-forming; found in basement membranes; produced by epithelial and endothelial cells. Type XI collagen — fibrillar; found in cartilage. Elastic fibers: present in elastic connective tissue; provide elasticity. Reticular fibers: fine fibers present in reticular connective tissue; form reticular (meshwork) framework of organs.
A(ii) Dense regular connective tissue is present in tendons and ligaments because it is organized to withstand forces from specific directions; the regular parallel arrangement of collagen type I fibers allows maximum tensile strength along the axis of the tendon or ligament.
B(i) The regenerative capacity of connective tissue is clearly observed in organs damaged by ischemia, inflammation, or traumatic injury. Spaces left after such injuries, especially in tissues whose cells divide poorly or not at all (e.g., cardiac muscle), are filled by connective tissue, forming dense irregular scar tissue. The healing of surgical incisions and other wounds depends on the reparative capacity of connective tissue and the activity of fibroblasts. Fibroblasts synthesize collagen, reticular and elastic fibers, and the amorphous extracellular substance. In some rapidly closing wounds, a cell called the myofibroblast (with features of both fibroblasts and smooth muscle cells) is observed. Myofibroblasts have most of the morphologic characteristics of fibroblasts but contain increased amounts of actin microfilaments and myosin and behave like smooth muscle cells. Their activity is responsible for wound contraction (wound closure after tissue injury).

- Ascending and descending fibres pass through: corticospinal (motor), posterior column (fine touch, vibration sense, proprioception) and spinothalamic (crude touch, temperature, pain); cranial nerve nuclei 3-12 lie in the brainstem (midbrain 3, 4; pons 5, 6, 7; medulla 9, 10, 11, 12; CN 8 at the pontomedullary junction).
- The pons contains the respiratory centre; the medulla contains centres for reflex activities (coughing, swallowing, vomiting) and for the control of respiratory, cardiac and motor function.

(ii) Midbrain: superior cerebellar and posterior cerebral arteries; pons: basilar, superior cerebellar and anterior inferior cerebellar arteries; medulla: as above.

A(i) Describe the dura mater: the meaning of its name and its general features.
A(ii) Describe its layers and histology.
A(iii) Describe the four projections of its inner layer, with their attachments and the venous sinus each houses.
B(i) Explain where the dura is most firmly adherent to the skull and where its layers separate.
C(i) Distinguish between the cranial and the spinal dura mater in their layers, spaces and termination.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Latin for 'tough mother' (pachymeninges): a thick, dense, inelastic membrane, continuous over the brain and spinal cord but with different composition; serves as the periosteum of the cranium and protects the brain.
A(ii) Two layers: outer endosteal layer, tough and fibrous, closely adherent to the inner surface of the cranial bone, carrying vessels for the cranium and continuous with the periosteum at the foramen magnum.
- Inner meningeal layer: thin and smooth, lined by a single endothelial layer; a thin space between the layers is wider at the dural sinuses; histologically white fibrous tissue and elastic fibres in flattened lamina separated by lacunae filled with blood vessels.
A(iii) Falx cerebri: sickle-shaped process dividing the two hemispheres, from the crista galli to the internal occipital protuberance; the upper margin houses the superior sagittal sinus and the free lower margin the inferior sagittal sinus.
- Tentorium cerebelli: attached posteriorly to the transverse ridge of the occipital bone (transverse sinus) and laterally to the superior angle of the petrous temporal bone; the falx cerebri meets its superior surface (straight sinus); a large central U-shaped opening transmits the brainstem.
- Falx cerebelli: small triangular fold between the two posterior cranial fossae, from the internal occipital protuberance to the posterior margin of the foramen magnum; houses the small occipital sinus.
- Diaphragma sellae: small circular horizontal fold roofing the sella turcica; its central opening transmits the infundibulum connecting to the hypophysis.
B(i) Adherence is most prominent around the skull base and sutures; the layers separate at the dural sinuses.
C(i) Cranial dura has two layers (endosteal and meningeal) and serves as the periosteum of the cranium; the spinal dura is formed only by the continuation of the meningeal layer, with the same histology.
- Spaces: cranial dura has the venous sinuses between its layers; spinal dura has the epidural space outside it (loose areolar tissue and venous plexuses) and the subdural cavity (thin film of fluid) separating it from the arachnoid.
- Termination: the spinal dura covers the filum terminale beyond the level of S2 and forms a tubular prolongation around the spinal nerves.

A(i) Quadriceps femoris forms the main bulk of the anterior thigh muscles; it collectively constitutes the largest and one of the most powerful muscles of the body. It covers almost all the anterior aspect and sides of the femur. It is the great extensor of the leg. It consists of 4 muscles: rectus femoris, vastus lateralis, vastus medialis, and vastus intermedius. The tendons of the four parts unite in the distal portion of the thigh to form a single, strong, broad tendon — the quadriceps tendon; this continues as the patellar ligament (in which the patella is embedded) and is attached to the tibial tuberosity.
A(ii) Rectus femoris — origin: anterior inferior iliac spine and ilium superior to acetabulum; insertion: via common quadriceps tendon and patellar ligament to tibial tuberosity; innervation: femoral nerve (L2, L3, L4); action: extends leg at knee joint, steadies hip joint, and helps iliopsoas flex thigh. It is the only part of the quadriceps that crosses the hip joint, named because it runs straight down the thigh. Vastus lateralis — origin: greater trochanter and lateral lip of linea aspera of femur; same insertion and innervation; action: extends leg at knee joint; it is the largest component. Vastus medialis — origin: intertrochanteric line and medial lip of linea aspera of femur; same insertion and innervation; action: extends leg at knee joint; inferior fibres are particularly important in stabilising the knee joint. Vastus intermedius — origin: anterior and lateral surfaces of shaft of femur; same insertion and innervation; action: extends leg at knee joint; lies deep to rectus femoris between the vastus medialis and lateralis.
B(i) The quadriceps is the primary extensor of the knee — the most important movement for standing, walking, climbing stairs, and rising from a chair. Stability of the knee joint depends on the strength and action of surrounding muscles and tendons; the quadriceps femoris is most important in stabilising the knee joint. Paralysis means the patient cannot extend the knee or control descent on stairs, rendering them unable to walk safely without a brace.
B(ii) All four components of the quadriceps are innervated by the femoral nerve (L2, L3, L4). The femoral nerve also supplies the hip joint via intermediate and cutaneous branches and the skin of the front and medial side of the thigh (Hilton's law). Loss of knee extension eliminates the ability to straighten or stabilise the knee against gravity — the most critical functional deficit for bipedal locomotion.
C(i) Quadriceps femoris: origin from femur and ilium; action — extends the knee (and rectus femoris also flexes the hip); nerve supply — femoral nerve (L2, L3, L4). Hamstrings (semitendinosus, semimembranosus, biceps femoris): origin from ischial tuberosity (long head of biceps femoris and both semi-muscles) and linea aspera (short head of biceps femoris); action — extend the thigh, flex the leg, and rotate it (semitendinosus and semimembranosus medially, biceps femoris laterally); nerve supply — tibial division of sciatic nerve for semitendinosus, semimembranosus, and long head of biceps femoris; common fibular division of sciatic nerve for short head of biceps femoris. The quadriceps is 3 times stronger than its antagonist muscle group (the hamstrings).

questions.answerText:
A(i) The great saphenous vein (GSV) is the longest vein in the body. It is formed by the union of the dorsal vein of the great toe and the dorsal venous arch of the foot. It ascends anterior to the medial malleolus, passes posterior to the medial condyle of the femur (about a hand's breadth posterior to the medial border of the patella), anastomoses freely with the small saphenous vein, traverses the saphenous opening in the fascia lata, and empties into the femoral vein.
A(ii) The GSV has 10–12 valves, which are more numerous in the leg than in the thigh; these valves are usually located just inferior to the perforating veins. Perforating veins also have their own valves. Tributaries in the anterior and lateral part of the thighs converge to form the accessory saphenous vein (ASV), which communicates the GSV with the small saphenous vein. Just before emptying into the femoral vein, the GSV receives tributaries from the superficial circumflex iliac, superficial epigastric, and external pudendal veins.
B(i) The small saphenous vein (SSV) arises on the lateral side of the foot from the union of the dorsal vein of the little toe with the dorsal venous arch. It ascends posterior to the lateral malleolus as a continuation of the lateral marginal vein, passes along the lateral border of the calcaneal tendon, inclines to the midline of the fibula and penetrates the deep fascia, ascends between the heads of the gastrocnemius muscle, and empties into the popliteal vein in the popliteal fossa.
B(ii) There are four main pulse points in the lower limb: femoral (palpated midway between the anterior superior iliac spine and pubic symphysis — the mid-inguinal point); popliteal (deep in the popliteal fossa, requires deep palpation, best with slight knee flexion); dorsalis pedis (on the dorsum of the foot, just lateral to extensor hallucis longus tendon); and posterior tibial (inferoposteriorly to the medial malleolus). The GSV anterior to the medial malleolus is the classic site for venous cut-down; the GSV at the medial condyle of the femur is another accessible site.
C(i) Superficial veins (GSV and SSV) are unaccompanied, lie in the superficial fascia, and their varicosity is visible. Deep veins of the lower limb accompany the arteries (read-up). Deep vein thrombosis involves the deep system and poses a risk of pulmonary embolism because the deep veins drain directly into the popliteal, femoral, and iliac veins and thence to the inferior vena cava. Superficial varicosity alone rarely embolises unless thrombosis extends through a perforating vein into the deep system.

questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Sickle cell disease requiring haematopoietic stem cell transplantation. Classification by potency: Totipotent — all somatic cell types, germ cells, and placenta (includes zygotes; fertilization creates a single totipotent cell). Pluripotent — all somatic cell types and germ cells; embryonic stem cells from the blastocyst's inner cell mass are pluripotent, not totipotent. Multipotent — lineage-restricted cell types (e.g., haematopoietic stem cell, mesenchymal stem cell, neural stem cell). Unipotent — single cell type (e.g., epidermal stem cell, germ line stem cell).
(ii) Indications and sources: The transplantation of haematopoietic stem cells can cure congenital or acquired diseases including some leukaemias. Sources: haematopoietic stem cells can be collected from living donors as bone marrow, from peripheral blood, or as cord blood drawn from the placenta during or after delivery. Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) can be created using genetic reprogramming techniques from adult body tissues.
(iii) Complications of defective apoptosis: Excessive apoptosis causes atrophy, such as in ischemic damage. Insufficient apoptosis results in uncontrolled cell proliferation such as cancer. Defective apoptotic processes have been implicated in an extensive variety of diseases. Cell immortality (transformation) may be a first step in transforming a normal cell into a cancer cell.
(iv) Other clinical applications: A corneal graft can restore sight in corneal blindness. The transplantation of a human heart valve often constitutes the best replacement situation, and recipient patients do not require long-term anti-coagulation therapy.
(v) Justification: Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation can cure congenital or acquired diseases including some leukaemias and sickle cell disease. It directly replaces the defective haematopoietic cells with healthy ones, addressing the root cause of the disease.

(i)
- Plicae circulares (valves of Kirkring): permanent circular or semilunar folds composed of the mucosa and submucosa layers; the core projects as a narrow shelf from the main layer of the submucosa and is covered by the mucosa.
- Villi: finger-like or leaf-like projections of the mucosa; consist of an epithelial covering and an underlying lamina propria (mucosa only — they do not contain submucosa in their core).
(ii) The central lymphatic vessel is the lacteal.
- Function: lacteals are especially important for lipid absorption. When absorption is taking place after a meal, the lacteals are dilated and prominent; at other times they are collapsed and not prominent.
(iii) Core of a villus (loose connective tissue from lamina propria) contains:
- Fibroblasts
- Lymphocytes and plasma cells
- Smooth muscle fibers
- Fenestrated capillaries
- A lacteal (central lymphatic)
(iv) Plicae circulares:
- Best developed in the jejunum.
- Best seen in longitudinal section of the small intestine because of their generally circular arrangement.
(v) Villus shape: in the duodenum they are leaf-shaped, but gradually assume finger-like shapes moving towards the ileum.
Goblet cells: less abundant in the duodenum and more numerous in the ileum.

A. Describe the gross anatomy of the tongue under the following headings: division into anterior and posterior parts, and the intrinsic and extrinsic muscles.
B. State how the different regions of the tongue relate to common developmental and pathological conditions.
C. Explain why disease affecting one region of the tongue can produce a functional deficit at a distant site, based on its lymphatic drainage pattern.
questions.answerText:
A. A V-shaped groove, the sulcus terminalis, demarcates the anterior two-thirds of the tongue from the posterior one-third. The intrinsic muscles of the tongue are the superior longitudinal, inferior longitudinal, transverse, and vertical muscles. The extrinsic muscles are the genioglossus, styloglossus, palatoglossus, and hyoglossus. The mucosa of the anterior two-thirds is formed into papillae (filiform, fungiform, circumvallate, foliate), which contain taste buds.
B. Clinical correlates involving the tongue include loss of taste sensation, bifid tongue, tongue tie (ankyloglossia), microglossia/macroglossia, and lingual carcinoma. Nerve supply differs by region: in the anterior two-thirds, motor supply to the muscles is via CN XII (except palatoglossus, supplied by the pharyngeal plexus of the vagus nerve), sensory supply to the mucous membrane is via the lingual nerve (a branch of CN V3), and special (taste) sensory supply is via the chorda tympani nerve (a branch of CN VII); in the posterior one-third, motor supply is via CN XII, and sensory supply (general and special) is via the lingual branch of CN IX and the internal laryngeal nerve (a branch of CN X).
C. Lymphatic drainage of the tongue takes 4 routes: the posterior third drains to the superior deep cervical lymph nodes; the medial part of the anterior two-thirds drains to the inferior deep cervical lymph nodes; the lateral parts of the anterior two-thirds drain to the submandibular lymph nodes; and the apex of the tongue drains to the submental lymph nodes - with the posterior third and the area near the midline draining bilaterally. Because disease (such as lingual carcinoma) arising in a particular region of the tongue follows that region's specific lymphatic drainage route, it can spread to produce nodal or functional deficits at lymph node groups that are anatomically distant from the primary site, with the pattern of spread differing depending on which part of the tongue is affected, and bilateral drainage from the posterior third and midline region meaning disease there can involve lymph nodes on both sides of the neck.

A(i) The liver appears in the 4th week as a ventral bud (hepatic diverticulum) from the caudal part of the foregut, growing into the septum transversum; it develops in the ventral mesentery.
A(i) The bud divides into a larger cranial part (liver primordium) and a smaller caudal part (gall bladder and cystic duct).
A(i) The liver grows rapidly and fills much of the abdominal cavity in weeks 5 to 10; by the 9th week it forms about 10% of body weight; the right lobe later grows larger than the left.
A(ii) Hepatic cords and the epithelial lining of the intrahepatic biliary system are endoderm; fibrous and haematopoietic tissue and Kupffer cells derive from mesenchyme of the septum transversum; the sinusoids derive from vitelline veins.
A(ii) Haematopoiesis begins in the 6th week; hepatic cells begin to form bile in the 12th week.
A(iii) The stalk of the diverticulum forms the cystic duct; the stalk connecting hepatic and cystic ducts to the duodenum becomes the bile duct, opening ventrally, then dorsally after duodenal rotation; the ducts are initially occluded and later canalized.
A(iii) The origins of the liver and pancreatic buds are just proximal to the junction of the foregut and midgut parts of the duodenum.
B(i) Anomalies of the liver are rare, but variations in hepatic, cystic and bile ducts are common and clinically significant.
B(i) Extrahepatic biliary atresia is the most common serious anomaly.
C(i) Jaundice develops soon after birth in extrahepatic biliary atresia; if uncorrected surgically it leads to death.
C(i) After the 13th week, bile entering the duodenum gives a dark green colour to the intestinal contents (meconium).

A(i) The popliteal fossa is a diamond-shaped depression in the posterior aspect of the knee. Superolateral border: biceps femoris. Superomedial border: semimembranosus and semitendinosus. Inferolateral border: lateral head of gastrocnemius. Inferomedial border: medial head of gastrocnemius.
A(ii) Roof (posteriorly): skin and fascia — the popliteal fascia is a strong sheet of deep fascia continuous superiorly with the fascia lata and inferiorly with the deep fascia of the leg. Floor (anteriorly): popliteal surface of femur, capsule of knee joint, oblique popliteal ligament, and popliteal fascia over popliteus.
B(i) From superficial to deep: posterior cutaneous nerve of thigh; tibial nerve (most superficial of the neurovascular bundle); popliteal vein; popliteal artery (deepest structure in the fossa, running close to the articular capsule of the knee joint); popliteal lymph nodes and lymphatic vessels. The small saphenous vein and three cutaneous nerves (posterior cutaneous nerve of thigh, medial sural cutaneous nerve, lateral sural cutaneous nerve) lie in the superficial fascia.
B(ii) The popliteal artery is the deepest structure and lies in close proximity to the tibial nerve. An aneurysm (dilation of the artery beyond 50% of its normal diameter) causes compression of the tibial nerve. The tibial nerve is particularly susceptible to this compression; the major features include weakened or absent plantarflexion, paraesthesia of the foot and posterolateral leg, and paralysis of flexor muscles in the leg and intrinsic muscles of the sole.
C(i) The tibial nerve is the medial and larger branch of the sciatic nerve; it bisects the fossa passing from the superior to the inferior angle and gives muscular branches to soleus, gastrocnemius, plantaris, and popliteus, and the medial sural cutaneous nerve. The common fibular nerve is the lateral, smaller terminal branch; it begins at the superior angle, closely follows the medial border of biceps femoris, exits the fossa by passing superficial to the lateral head of gastrocnemius, then winds around the neck of fibula where it divides into terminal branches. Injury to the tibial nerve causes inability to plantarflex the ankle or flex the toes and loss of sensation on the sole of the foot.

(i) The diagnosis is acute proximal hamstring avulsion from the ischial tuberosity. The hamstrings are: semitendinosus (origin — ischial tuberosity), semimembranosus (origin — ischial tuberosity), and the long head of biceps femoris (origin — ischial tuberosity). All three originate from the ischial tuberosity and their tendons are avulsed at this point.
(ii) The ischial tuberosity is a traction epiphysis. Traction epiphyses are pulled by muscles (e.g., greater trochanter — traction epiphysis for gluteus medius; lesser trochanter — traction epiphysis for iliopsoas). The ischial tuberosity is a secondary centre of ossification that fuses at 20–25 years of age. In adolescents the apophysis (secondary centre) is not yet fully fused; the apophyseal cartilage is weaker than the tendon, so sudden forceful contraction of the hamstrings (as in sprinting) avulses the apophysis rather than tearing the tendon itself.
(iii) The sciatic nerve (L4, 5; S1, 2, 3) is at risk. The sciatic nerve curves downward midway between the tuber ischii and the greater trochanter. Haematoma from the avulsion can compress the sciatic nerve directly at this site. The inferior gluteal artery is also present in this region (the cruciate anastomosis is situated at the level of the lesser trochanter, involving the inferior gluteal artery, medial femoral circumflex artery, lateral femoral circumflex artery, and 1st perforating branch of profunda femoris). Posterior cutaneous nerve of the thigh also traverses the region and may be contused.
(iv) Conservative management (for partial avulsions with less than 2 cm displacement): rest, ice, compression, elevation, analgesia, and gradual rehabilitation with physiotherapy — progressing from gentle stretching to eccentric hamstring loading. Surgical management (for complete avulsions with greater than 2 cm displacement, or in high-level athletes): open repair of the avulsed tendons back to the ischial tuberosity using suture anchors, to restore full hamstring function and prevent chronic weakness and sciatic nerve tethering by scar tissue.

(i) Describe the origin, course, branches and distribution of the right and left coronary arteries.
(ii) State which artery gives off the posterior interventricular artery in most individuals (arterial dominance).
(iii) Explain the anatomical basis for the pattern of myocardial damage that follows occlusion of a particular coronary artery.
questions.answerText:
(i) The right and left coronary arteries are the first branches of the aorta, arising from the corresponding right and left aortic sinuses at the proximal ascending aorta.
The right coronary artery runs in the atrioventricular (coronary) groove and gives off the SA nodal branch, right marginal branch, AV nodal branch, and posterior interventricular branch, which anastomoses with the anterior interventricular branch of the left coronary artery.
The right coronary artery typically supplies the right atrium, most of the right ventricle, part of the left ventricle, the posterior third of the AV septum, the SA node in 60% of people and the AV node in 80% of people.
The left coronary artery arises from the left aortic sinus, runs in the AV groove, and divides into the circumflex and anterior interventricular branches.
The left coronary artery typically supplies the left atrium, most of the left ventricle, part of the right ventricle, most of the interventricular septum and the SA node in 40% of people.
Venous drainage is mainly through the coronary sinus, which receives the great, middle and small cardiac veins and the left posterior ventricular and left marginal veins.
(ii) Arterial dominance is defined by which artery gives rise to the posterior interventricular artery; right dominance is typical, the left is dominant in about 10% of people, and co-dominance occurs in about 15% of people.
(iii) Because the right coronary artery mainly supplies the right atrium, right ventricle and, in most people, the SA and AV nodes, its occlusion can damage right-sided myocardium and disturb the conduction system.
Because the left coronary artery mainly supplies the left atrium, left ventricle and interventricular septum, its occlusion tends to damage the left ventricle, which performs more work than the right, and the septum.
Damage to the region supplying the SA or AV node can disturb the heart's conducting system, since the SA and AV nodes are the pacesetters of the heart.
Tissue damage from reduced blood flow in the territory of the affected artery causes the chest pain of ischaemia/infarction, which can radiate as referred pain to the jaw and left arm.
Not covered : specific data on infarct size relative to the vessel occluded.

(i) M (microfold) cells — specialised epithelial cells for transport of particles and microorganisms. Located in the ileum overlying the lymphoid follicles of Peyer's patches.
(ii) Function: M cells are important in the defense provided by mucosal immunity; they transport particles and microorganisms.
(iii) Lymphoid aggregates: Peyer's patches.
- In the mucosa: throughout the small intestine, the mucosa contains isolated nodules of lymphatic tissue; in the distal part (especially the ileum) there are aggregates of nodules called Peyer's patches.
- In the submucosa: in the ileum, both the lamina propria and submucosa contain the lymphoid nodule aggregates known as Peyer's patches, an important component of the mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT).
(iv) Mucosal immune system:
- The abundant free immune cells and lymphoid nodules in the mucosa and submucosal layers constitute the Mucosa-Associated Lymphoid Tissue (MALT).
- The lamina propria is rich in macrophages and lymphocytes, some of which actively produce antibodies — mainly immunoglobulin A (IgA).
- These antibodies undergo transcytosis into the intestinal lumen bound to the secretory protein produced by the epithelial cells; this complex protects against viral and bacterial pathogens.
- IgA is resistant to proteolytic enzymes and can therefore coexist with the proteases present in the lumen.
(v) Paneth cells:
- Location: in the basal portion of the intestinal crypts, below the stem cells.
- Ultrastructural features: large eosinophilic secretory granules; numerous RER, well-developed Golgi apparatus, and numerous secretory granules (typical of protein-secreting cells).
- Products released (by exocytosis): lysozymes, phospholipase A2, and defensins — which bind and break down membranes of microorganisms and bacterial cell walls.
- Functions: innate immunity; regulate the microenvironment of the intestinal crypts.

A(i) Describe the segmental (cervical, thoracic, lumbar, sacral) differences in spinal cord cross-sectional anatomy.
A(ii) Describe the Rexed lamina organization of the gray matter.
B) How do specific zones/laminae relate to particular functions?

questions.answerText:
A(i) The cervical segment is a large, oval-shaped structure with relatively larger white matter; the posterior horn is smaller than the anterior, enlarged from C5 downwards, with a posterior intermediate septum dividing gracilis from cuneatus. The thoracic segment has gray matter relatively smaller than white matter, with a lateral horn at the base of the anterior horn (preganglionic sympathetic efferents) and the dorsal nucleus of Clarke (most obvious T10-T12). The lumbar segment is almost circular, with white matter proportionally less than gray matter and a stout anterior horn; the dorsal nucleus of Clarke is found at L1-L2. The sacral segment is small and cylindrical, with gray matter relatively more than white matter, a thickened gray commissure, and a small lateral horn for preganglionic parasympathetic cells.
A(ii) In 1952, Rexed found that cell clusters are arranged into 10 zones/laminae: Laminae I-IV (exteroceptive sensations), Laminae V-VI (proprioceptive), Lamina VII (relay between midbrain and cerebellum), Lamina VIII (modulates motor activity), Lamina IX (main motor area, somatotopically organized), and Lamina X (surrounds the central canal).
B) The intermediolateral horn (T1-L2) contains preganglionic sympathetic neurons; the sacral lateral horn contains preganglionic parasympathetic cells.
C) Onuf's nucleus, located in Lamina IX of segments S1-4, controls the anal and urethral sphincters.

(i) Although protected by the 9th to 12th ribs, the spleen is the most frequently injured organ in the abdomen; severe blows to the left side may fracture ribs, producing sharp fragments that lacerate the spleen. Blunt trauma elsewhere that suddenly and markedly raises intra-abdominal pressure can also rupture the spleen because its capsule is thin and its parenchyma (pulp) is soft and pulpy.
(ii) A ruptured spleen bleeds profusely, causing severe intraperitoneal haemorrhage and shock.
(iii) Management is splenectomy or subtotal (partial) splenectomy, removing one or more segments, to prevent the patient bleeding to death. Subtotal splenectomy is justified because the terminal branches of the splenic artery do not anastomose with each other, so each supplies an independent vascular segment of the spleen, allowing removal of a damaged segment without affecting the blood supply of the rest of the organ. Even total splenectomy usually does not produce serious side effects in adults because most splenic functions are assumed by other reticuloendothelial organs such as the liver and bone marrow, though the patient becomes more susceptible to certain bacterial infections.

A(i) Fixation: to achieve a permanent section, tissues must be fixed to preserve the structure and molecular composition; fixation prevents autolysis (self-digestion by enzymes present in the cells) and destruction by bacteria. Dehydration and clearing: tissues are progressed in graded steps to 100% alcohol to remove water; after the solvent replaces the alcohol, the tissue becomes transparent in xylene (clearing). Embedding: once the tissue is impregnated with the solvent, it is placed in a hard medium (e.g., wax); heat causes the solvent to evaporate, and the spaces within the tissue are filled by the embedding medium. Sectioning: tissues are sectioned by the microtome's steel or glass blade; this method allows stained sections to be prepared rapidly for study of specimens. Mounting: sections are mounted on a supportive structure (e.g., slide) that can be placed on a microscope stage. Staining: stains are applied to differentiate tissue components.
A(ii) The most commonly used stains are hematoxylin and eosin (H & E). Hematoxylin stains basic (acidic) structures — the most acidic components are DNA and RNA; therefore, the nucleus and cytoplasmic RNA stain blue/purple (basophilic). Eosin stains acidophilic (basic) structures — many cytoplasmic constituents stain pinkish (eosinophilic/acidophilic). Reason: differential staining is based on the acid-base chemistry of cell components; acidic cell components bind basic dyes (hematoxylin) and basic components bind acidic dyes (eosin).
B(i) Light microscopy: the standard technique; produces images of tissue sections examined by transmitted light; maximum resolving power is 0.2 micrometers (two marks 0.2 micrometers apart can be seen as two distinct entities). Types include brightfield, phase contrast, differential interference contrast (DIC), fluorescence, and confocal. Preferred for: routine tissue examination, diagnosis of pathology, overview of cell and tissue structure. Electron microscopy: has extended the detail at which subcellular structures can be studied; reveals ultrastructural details such as organelles, myelin sheaths, and synapse morphology. Preferred for: study of subcellular structures, ultrastructural detail, and molecular architecture of cell membranes.

A(i) The orbit is shaped like a pear or quadrilateral pyramid, with its base in the plane of the orbital rim and its pyramidal cavity base in front and apex behind; it protects, supports and maximises the function of the eye, and seven bones conjoin to form the orbital structure. The average dimensions of the orbit are: height of orbital margin 40 mm, width of orbital margin 35 mm, depth of orbit 40-50 mm, interorbital distance 25 mm, and volume of orbit 30 cm3; 20% of this space is occupied by the eyeball, and about one-sixth of the eye is exposed, the remainder being protected by the walls of the orbit.
A(ii) The major nerves and vessels to the orbit and globe enter through 3 openings. The superior orbital fissure, bounded by the lesser and greater wings of the sphenoid, transmits cranial nerves III, IV and VI, the lacrimal nerve, frontal nerve, nasociliary nerve, orbital branch of the middle meningeal artery, recurrent branch of the lacrimal artery, superior orbital vein and superior ophthalmic vein. The inferior orbital fissure, bounded by the greater wing of the sphenoid, the maxilla and the palatine bones, transmits the infraorbital nerve, zygomatic nerve, parasympathetics to the lacrimal gland, infraorbital artery, infraorbital vein, and the inferior ophthalmic vein branch to the pterygoid plexus. The optic canal, at the apex of the orbit within the sphenoid bone, transmits the optic nerve, ophthalmic artery, and central retinal vein. The connective tissue boundaries of the orbit are divided into 4 main units: the bulbar (Tenon) fascia, surrounding and protecting the globe and providing a barrier between the globe and retrobulbar fat; multiple connective tissue septa extending from the globe to the periorbita like spokes on a wheel; the individual connective tissue sheath of each extraocular muscle, which fuses to form a confluent muscle sheath and the medial and lateral check ligaments; and the periosteal lining of the orbit, which can be elevated in surgery to expose the bony orbit.
B. Clinical correlates of the orbit include eye trauma with blow-out fracture, due to blunt trauma, which displaces the orbital walls; paralysis of the extraocular muscles results in double vision. Obstruction of the flow of aqueous humor results in a rise in intraocular pressure called glaucoma, leading to degenerative changes in the retina with consequent blindness.
C. The superior orbital fissure transmits cranial nerves III, IV and VI, the lacrimal, frontal and nasociliary nerves, the orbital branch of the middle meningeal artery, the recurrent branch of the lacrimal artery, and the superior orbital and superior ophthalmic veins. The inferior orbital fissure, in contrast, transmits the infraorbital nerve, the zygomatic nerve, parasympathetics to the lacrimal gland, the infraorbital artery and vein, and the inferior ophthalmic vein branch to the pterygoid plexus.

(i) The radial nerve is affected. In the posterior compartment of the arm it winds around the spiral (radial) groove of the humerus, accompanied by the profunda brachii artery.
(ii) The nerve supplies muscular twigs to triceps brachii and anconeus in the arm, and via its deep branch (posterior interosseous nerve) supplies the extensor muscles of the forearm and brachioradialis; its superficial branch supplies cutaneous sensation to the dorsal aspect of the hand and the dorsal aspect of the lateral three and a half digits. Compression/fracture at the spiral groove therefore affects these muscular and posterior interosseous branches, producing "wrist drop."
(iii) Radial nerve injury can occur at any level: axilla, spiral groove, radial tunnel, posterior interosseous nerve, or superficial radial nerve. Injury may result from fracture of the body (shaft) of the humerus, or from "Saturday Night Palsy" — compression of the nerve in the axilla, e.g. from using improperly adjusted crutches.
(iv) Because the radial nerve winds directly around the humeral shaft in the spiral groove, closely applied to bone, a mid-shaft (transverse) fracture, which frequently results from a direct blow to the arm, places the nerve at direct risk of injury, explaining the resulting wrist drop.
questions.question:

An elderly woman presents with a jaw that has become locked open after a wide yawn. Separately, another patient presents with a longstanding inability to open the jaw, with a history of forceps delivery at birth.
(i) What risk factors predispose to each of these presentations?
(ii) What complications can result from the second condition described?
questions.answerText:
(i) Dislocation of the TMJ is common in aged persons and females, due to wearing and resorption of the articular eminence and reducing muscle tone with advancing age. Ankylosis of the TMJ can result from spasm of masticatory muscles due to infection/injury, intrauterine fetal abnormality, forceps deliveries, malunion of condylar fractures, metastatic malignancies, rheumatoid arthritis, and inflammation of the joint (e.g. otitis media). Developmental disturbances of the TMJ include aplasia, hypoplasia and hyperplasia of the condyle (the latter from chronic mild inflammation).
(ii) Ankylosis results in inability to open the jaw; other clinical correlates of the TMJ include arthritis, myofascial pain dysfunction syndrome (MPD - pain, muscle tenderness, clicking/popping noise, limitation of jaw motion, mainly involving the lateral pterygoid, and possibly related to stress), fracture of the articular fossa, structural changes (loss of posterior teeth, separation between collagen bundles), and trauma (cartilage/new bone may develop in marrow spaces and the periphery of the condyle).

questions.question:
A patient develops a boil on the upper lip, which becomes infected. Some days later, the patient develops swelling around the eyes with tenderness along the side of the nose extending to the inner corner of the eye.
(i) What is the diagnosis, and what facial region/mechanism accounts for its spread?
(ii) What is the anatomical basis of this spread?
questions.answerText:
(i) The presentation is thrombophlebitis of the facial vein, with spread occurring through the "danger triangle" of the face.
(ii) The facial vein drains the forehead, eyelids, anterior cheek, lips and chin. Boundaries of the danger triangle of the face are marked by vessels including the supraorbital vein, supratrochlear vein, superior and central retinal veins, superior palpebral vein and the ophthalmic vein. The superior and inferior ophthalmic veins communicate with the cavernous sinus, and the skin of the periorbital region drains to the angular vein and to the superior ophthalmic vein; so there is a direct communication between the skin of the face and the cavernous sinus, which is the basis of the danger triangle.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the gross anatomy of epithelial tissue under the following headings: general characteristics, morphological classification (by cell shape and number of layers), and the basement membrane.
A(ii) Relate specific epithelial types to their common locations in the body, giving one example each of simple squamous, simple cuboidal, simple columnar, ciliated columnar, stratified squamous, and transitional epithelium.
B(i) Explain why epithelial tissue is avascular, how it receives nutrients, and state the clinical consequence when the basement membrane is disrupted in disease.
questions.answerText:
A(i) General characteristics: epithelial tissue consists of closely packed cells arranged in one or more layers; these cells are specialized and fill roles such as protection, secretion, and absorption; the cells are tightly packed together with very little extracellular matrix and almost no intercellular substance; they rest on a basement membrane (a basal lamina containing the glycoprotein laminin). Morphological classification by cell shape: squamous (flat), cuboidal (square or cube-like), columnar (tall and thin). By number of layers: simple epithelium (one cell thick) — can be simple squamous, simple cuboidal, or simple columnar; stratified epithelium (multiple layers — described as heterogeneous); pseudostratified epithelium — appears stratified but all cells contact the basal lamina. Transitional epithelium: recognized by its appearance — when the bladder is empty (relaxed), the epithelium appears thicker and has more layers than when the bladder is full. Basement membrane: contains the glycoprotein laminin; the border between epithelia and the underlying connective tissue is sharp and distinct.
A(ii) Simple squamous epithelium: lines blood vessels (endothelium) and body cavities. Simple cuboidal epithelium: lines many small ducts in the body. Simple columnar epithelium: lines the gallbladder, larger ducts near the urinary papilla; also found in the jejunum (with goblet cells). Ciliated columnar epithelium: found in the respiratory tract and fallopian tubes; goblet cells (glandular epithelium) are present, making it heterogeneous. Stratified squamous epithelium (keratinized): forms the outer layer of skin; contains the protective protein keratin; a keratinized (dry) epithelium. Transitional epithelium: lines the urinary bladder.
B(i) Epithelial tissue is avascular (contains no blood vessels); the lamina propria (underlying connective tissue) supplies the necessary nutrients and metabolites, which are transported to and from epithelial cells by diffusion through the basement membrane. If the basement membrane is disrupted (e.g., in cancer invasion or severe inflammation), the barrier between epithelium and connective tissue is lost, allowing unrestricted cell invasion into the underlying stroma; epithelial cells in contact with the environment are constantly subjected to mechanical damage and must show many dividing cells (mitoses) to replace lost cells; disruption of this repair mechanism contributes to disease progression.

questions.question:
(i) Describe the gross anatomy of the spleen - measurements, external features (ends, borders, surfaces, hilum) and peritoneal ligaments.
(ii) Relate the surfaces/impressions of the spleen to organs it may affect in disease.
(iii) Explain why splenic rupture produces a distant, life-threatening functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
(i) The spleen is an ovoid, highly vascular, reddish-purple organ, on average about 12 cm long, 7 cm broad, 3 cm thick and weighing about 150 g, related to the 9th to 11th ribs on the left side.
It has two ends, an expanded anterior end and a rounded posterior end resting on the upper pole of the left kidney, three borders (superior, inferior and intermediate), and two surfaces (diaphragmatic and visceral).
The diaphragmatic surface is convex and related to the diaphragm, left lung and pleura, and the 9th-11th ribs; the visceral surface is concave and bears gastric, renal, colic and pancreatic impressions.
The hilum lies on the inferomedial part of the gastric impression and transmits the splenic vessels and nerves, giving attachment to the gastrosplenic and splenorenal ligaments; the phrenicocolic ligament supports, but is not attached to, the anterior end of the spleen.
(ii) The gastric impression, related to the fundus of the stomach, is the largest impression; the renal impression relates to the left kidney and sometimes the suprarenal gland; the colic impression relates to the splenic flexure of the colon; the pancreatic impression relates to the tail of the pancreas.
The gastrosplenic ligament contains the short gastric vessels supplying the stomach, and the splenorenal ligament contains the tail of the pancreas and splenic vessels, so disease or surgery at the spleen can affect the stomach, kidney, colon or pancreas through these relations.
(iii) Although protected by the 9th to 12th ribs, the spleen is the most frequently injured organ in the abdomen.
Severe blows to the left side may fracture ribs, producing sharp fragments that lacerate the spleen, and blunt trauma elsewhere that raises intra-abdominal pressure can also rupture it because its capsule is thin and the pulp soft.
If ruptured, the spleen bleeds profusely because it is a highly vascular organ receiving the splenic artery, the largest branch of the coeliac trunk.
This produces severe intraperitoneal haemorrhage and shock, a systemic and distant functional deficit in circulation arising from a local splenic injury.
Repair of a ruptured spleen is difficult, so splenectomy or subtotal splenectomy is often performed to prevent the patient from bleeding to death.
Even after total splenectomy, most splenic functions are assumed by other reticuloendothelial organs such as the liver and bone marrow, though susceptibility to certain bacterial infections increases.

questions.answerText:
(i) The diagnosis is peripheral arterial disease (intermittent claudication) due to atherosclerotic occlusion of the femoral artery at the adductor hiatus. The adductor hiatus is the opening between the aponeurotic distal attachment of the adductor part of adductor magnus and the tendinous distal attachment of its hamstring part; it transmits the femoral artery and vein from the adductor canal in the thigh to the popliteal fossa posterior to the knee. The femoral artery divides to give the profunda femoris 5 cm below the inguinal ligament.
(ii) Risk factors: smoking (which promotes atherosclerosis and vasoconstriction), hypertension (endothelial injury), type 2 diabetes (accelerated atherosclerosis), advanced age, and male sex. Pathophysiology: atherosclerotic plaque formation narrows the vessel lumen, reducing blood supply to the muscles of the leg during exercise; pain results from ischaemic metabolites accumulating in muscle and is relieved by rest when demand falls.
(iii) The adductor hiatus is located just lateral and superior to the adductor tubercle of the femur. It is the anatomical transition point where the femoral artery becomes the popliteal artery; it is also the termination of the adductor canal. Surgically, it marks the site where a distal femoral or proximal popliteal bypass graft is anastomosed. Profunda femoris branches form collateral circuits and the superior muscular branches of the popliteal artery anastomose with the terminal part of the profunda femoris and gluteal arteries.
(iv) Conservative management: smoking cessation, supervised exercise rehabilitation, antiplatelet therapy, statin, and blood pressure control. Endovascular management: percutaneous transluminal angioplasty ± stenting of the occluded segment. Open surgical bypass: femoral–popliteal bypass graft using the great saphenous vein (the preferred conduit because it is autologous, long, and readily available). Surgical bypass is justified here because the ABPI of 0.5 indicates critical ischaemia and an occlusion at the adductor hiatus is a well-defined anatomical segment amenable to bypass, with the GSV as the ideal conduit given its length and availability.

(i) Lumbar puncture (LP): CSF within the lumbar cistern is tapped.
- Lumbar cistern: subarachnoid dilatation lying after the end of the spinal cord (L2); the spinal arachnoid widens below to invest the cauda equina.
(ii) Epidural space: outside the spinal dura in the vertebral canal, containing loose areolar tissue and venous plexuses.
