questions.question:
A child has a heart defect involving the atrial septum.
(i) State the embryologic basis and the causes of the defect.
(ii) State the complications of premature closure of the foramen ovale.
(iii) State the management options and justify one.
questions.answerText:
(i) Atrial septal defects (ASDs) are heart defects involving the atrial septum; a foramen secundum defect is caused by excessive resorption of the septum primum, the septum secundum, or both.
(i) Normally the septum primum grows at the end of the 4th week; the ostium primum closes when it fuses with the AV septum; perforations coalesce to form the ostium secundum.
(i) The septum secundum appears at the beginning of the 5th week and never forms a complete partition; the opening it leaves is the oval foramen, with the remnant of the septum primum forming its valve (right to left flow only).
(ii) Premature closure of the foramen ovale during prenatal life results in hypertrophy of the right side of the heart and underdevelopment of the left side.
(ii) Normally, most blood in the right atrium flows into the left atrium through the foramen ovale; after birth the rising left atrial pressure presses the valve against the septum secundum.
(iii) Management options and their justification are not covered.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the location and coverings of the spinal cord.
A(ii) Describe its external features.
A(iii) Describe its internal structure (gray and white matter).
B) Explain the clinical basis for choosing the lower lumbar region as the safe site for lumbar puncture.
C) Distinguish between the gracile and cuneate fasciculi.
questions.answerText:
A(i) The spinal cord is located in the vertebral canal, covered by the meninges: the dura mater (tough, outer sheath), the arachnoid (thin and transparent), and the pia mater (closely applied to the spinal cord). The epidural space contains a venous plexus, and the subarachnoid space contains the CSF.
A(ii) It measures about 42-45cm in the adult, extends from the foramen magnum to the conus medullaris, and is continuous cranially with the medulla. Cervical and lumbar dilatations represent increased cellular and fibre content for the upper and lower limbs. A condensation of pia mater extends beyond the conus medullaris as the filum terminale; the lumbosacral nerve roots (cauda equina) descend almost parallel to it, and spinal nerve roots become more oblique from above downwards. The anterior median fissure is deep while the posterior median septum is shallow, with posterolateral sulci (exit of posterior root) and anterolateral sulci (exit of anterior root).
A(iii) The internal structure consists of H-shaped gray matter (cellular aggregates) within cylindrical white matter (myelinated fibres); the bridge of the H incorporates the central canal. Dorsal limbs form the posterior horn; anterior horns lie farther from the surface. White matter bounded by the limbs of the H is grouped into anterior, posterior and lateral white columns.
B) The lumbosacral nerve roots (cauda equina) descend almost parallel to the filum terminale below the conus medullaris; this lumbosacral nerve root lengthening is functionally useful for the LP tap, since the cord has ended and the nerve roots lie free in CSF at this level.
C) The gracile and cuneate fasciculi are separated by the posterior intermediate septum, with sacral fibres most medial (gracile) and cervical fibres most lateral (cuneate) within the posterior column system.

questions.question:
Describe the lateral compartment muscles of the leg under the following headings, explain the anatomical basis of their action, and distinguish the consequences of superficial fibular nerve injury from deep fibular nerve injury.
A(i) Name both muscles, giving full OCIANA (origin, course, insertion, action, nerve, artery) for each
A(ii) The superficial fibular nerve — its origin, course in the lateral compartment, and cutaneous distribution
B(i) The mechanical basis of eversion and plantarflexion — how fibularis longus and brevis produce their actions based on their insertions
B(ii) The role of fibularis longus in maintaining the transverse arch of the foot
C(i) Distinguish the clinical effects of superficial fibular nerve injury from those of deep fibular nerve injury at the fibular neck, and state which movements are lost in each
questions.answerText:
A(i) Fibularis longus: origin — head and superior 2/3 of lateral surface of fibula; insertion — base of 1st metatarsal and medial cuneiform; innervation — superficial fibular nerve (L5, S1, S2); action — everts foot and weakly plantarflexes ankle. Fibularis brevis: origin — inferior 2/3 of lateral surface of fibula; insertion — dorsal surface of tuberosity on lateral side of base of 5th metatarsal; innervation — superficial fibular nerve (L5, S1, S2); action — everts foot and weakly plantarflexes ankle. Arterial supply: not covered — both are supplied by the fibular (peroneal) artery.
A(ii) The common fibular nerve is the lateral, smaller terminal branch of the sciatic nerve; it begins at the superior angle of the popliteal fossa, closely follows the medial border of biceps femoris and its tendon, exits the fossa by passing superficial to the lateral head of gastrocnemius, then over the posterior aspect of the head of fibula, winds around the neck of fibula, and divides into the superficial fibular nerve (to the lateral compartment) and the deep fibular nerve (to the anterior compartment). The superficial fibular nerve runs in the lateral compartment to supply fibularis longus and brevis; its cutaneous distribution supplies the dorsum of the foot (lateral side of leg and ankle, as the sural nerve — formed by medial sural cutaneous nerve joined by the sural communicating branch of the common fibular nerve — supplies the lateral side of leg and ankle).
B(i) Fibularis longus inserts onto the base of the 1st metatarsal and medial cuneiform on the plantar aspect of the foot — it therefore acts as a stirrup, pulling the medial forefoot downward and laterally, producing eversion and weak plantarflexion. Fibularis brevis inserts onto the tuberosity of the base of the 5th metatarsal on the lateral side of the foot — it abducts the forefoot and everts the foot. The lateral longitudinal arch (made of calcaneus, cuboid, and 4th and 5th metatarsals) is supported by peroneus longus and brevis; muscles of the lateral arch include peroneus longus and brevis, flexor digitorum longus, and short muscles of the little toe.
B(ii) The transverse arch muscles include peroneus longus and brevis, transverse head of adductor hallucis, and slips of tibialis posterior. Fibularis longus, by crossing under the foot from the lateral side to insert medially at the base of the 1st metatarsal, acts as a dynamic tie-beam, pulling the medial and lateral borders of the foot together and maintaining the curvature of the transverse arch; adductor hallucis transverse head also assists by pulling metatarsals medially.
C(i) Superficial fibular nerve injury (at fibular neck): loss of eversion of the foot (fibularis longus and brevis paralysed); weakness of plantarflexion; sensory loss on dorsum of foot. Deep fibular nerve injury (at fibular neck): loss of dorsiflexion (tibialis anterior paralysed) and toe extension (extensor digitorum longus, extensor hallucis longus paralysed); loss of eversion contribution of fibularis tertius; result is foot drop with the foot held in plantarflexion and inversion; sensory loss is limited to the 1st web space (between 1st and 2nd toes). Injury to the common fibular nerve at the fibular neck produces both effects combined — foot drop with loss of both dorsiflexion and eversion.

A(i) The glenohumeral (shoulder) joint is a multiaxial synovial joint of the ball-and-socket variety, formed by articulation between the head of the humerus and the glenoid cavity of the scapula; due to the very limited interface between humerus and scapula, it is the most mobile joint in the human body.
A(ii) The joint capsule is a fibrous sheath enclosing the joint structures; it is thin and lax to allow a wide range of movement (particularly abduction), is strengthened by muscles and ligaments, but is weakest inferiorly, placing it at risk of dislocation in that direction. It is lined by synovial membrane and forms a tubular sheath around the tendon of the long head of biceps, and a number of bursae aid mobility.
A(iii) Factors contributing to mobility are the ball-and-socket joint type, the shallow glenoid cavity against the large humeral head (a 1:4 disproportion, likened to a golf ball and tee), and laxity of the joint capsule.
Factors contributing to stability are the rotator cuff muscles, whose resting tone pulls the humeral head into the glenoid cavity, the glenoid labrum, which deepens the cavity and reduces dislocation risk, and the ligaments, which reinforce the capsule and form the coraco-acromial arch.
B. The glenohumeral joint is the most commonly dislocated joint in the body, accounting for approximately 95% of all shoulder dislocations, and anterior dislocations are the most prevalent.
An anterior dislocation is usually caused by excessive extension and lateral rotation of the humerus, which forces the humeral head anteriorly and inferiorly into the weakest (inferior) part of the joint capsule.
Tearing of the joint capsule during dislocation is associated with an increased risk of future (recurrent) dislocations.
C. The axillary nerve runs in close proximity to the shoulder joint and can be damaged during dislocation.
Injury to the axillary nerve causes paralysis of the deltoid muscle, with loss of sensation over the "regimental badge" area of skin overlying the deltoid.
A dislocation can also stretch the radial nerve, since it is tightly bound within the radial (spiral) groove of the humerus.
These nerve injuries represent the spread of the joint pathology to distant neurological structures.
The resulting functional deficits include loss of shoulder abduction and sensory loss from axillary nerve injury, reflecting how a purely mechanical joint injury can produce a distinct neurological deficit at a distance from the joint itself.

questions.answerText:
A(i) The deep cervical fascia consists of areolar tissue that supports the muscles, vessels and viscera of the neck; it is condensed to form well-defined fibrous sheets, labelled as: (1) the investing layer (superficial), (2) the pretracheal fascia, (3) the prevertebral fascia, (4) the carotid sheath, and (5) the axillary fascia. More generally, deep fascia is the membranous investment of structures deep to the superficial fascia, containing cells (fibroblasts), fibres (collagen, elastic) and matrix; being subjected to tensile strains, the collagen forms parallel fibre bundles, with the cells flattened. Deep fascia is best marked in the limbs and neck, where it is wrapped around the muscles, veins and nerves like a bandage, the fibres being mainly circularly arranged; around the thorax and abdomen, which require to expand and contract, there is merely a film of areolar tissue but no true deep fascia.
A(ii) The pretracheal fascia is found only in the anterior region; superiorly it is attached to the thyroid and cricoid cartilage, and inferiorly it extends into the thorax to blend with the fibrous pericardium; laterally it blends with the carotid sheath and with the investing layer of the deep cervical fascia beneath sternocleidomastoid. The prevertebral fascia is attached superiorly to the base of the skull, and inferiorly enters the thorax and blends with the anterior longitudinal ligament of the vertebral column; it covers the prevertebral muscles (longus capitis and longus cervicis), passes round the neck, attaches to the ligamentum nuchae, and in the posterior triangle forms the fascial floor, covering the muscles scalenus anterior, scalenus medius, scalenus posterior, levator scapulae and splenius capitis.
B. Penetration of the fascia during instrumentation of the pretracheal fascia can lead to collection of infectious substances (pus) in the retropharyngeal space (the space between the pharynx and the prevertebral fascia); whiplash injury of the neck can cause quadriplegia, stabbing injury of the neck can cause vascular/nervous injury, and a tumour blocking the airway may necessitate insertion of a tracheostomy tube. The deep cervical fascia will necessarily be pierced during tracheostomy.
C. The pretracheal fascia surrounds the thyroid gland completely, forming a sheath for it, binds the thyroid gland to the larynx, encloses the parathyroid gland, invests the infrahyoid muscles, and encloses the visceral components of the neck (larynx and trachea, pharynx and oesophagus, and the thyroid and parathyroid glands). The prevertebral fascia, in contrast, surrounds the vertebral column and its associated muscles, extending from the base of the skull to approximately the T3 vertebra, and extends laterally as the axillary sheaths.

(iv) Resuscitation, management and definitive treatment are not covered.
questions.question:
An infant, whose pregnancy was complicated by accumulation of excess fluid in the amniotic sac, has oesophageal atresia with or without a tracheo-oesophageal fistula.
(i) Give the diagnosis and the term for the excess amniotic fluid with its mechanism.
(ii) Explain the embryologic basis, including the normal separation of the oesophagus from the trachea.
(iii) State the associated anomalies.
(iv) State the resuscitation, management and definitive treatment.

questions.answerText:
A(i) A strong, incomplete fibrous compartment of the rectus abdominis and pyramidalis, formed by the aponeuroses of the three flat muscles.
A(i) The linea alba separates the right and left rectus abdominis; the linea semilunaris marks the lateral border; tendinous intersections and linea alba give the 'six packs'.
A(ii) It has an anterior and posterior wall for most of its length: anterior wall from the aponeuroses of external oblique and half of internal oblique; posterior wall from the aponeuroses of half of internal oblique and transversus abdominis.
A(iii) Superior and inferior epigastric arteries and veins, lymphatic vessels and the distal portions of the thoracoabdominal nerves (anterior rami of T7 to T12).
A(iii) Superior epigastric: terminal branch of internal thoracic, descends posterior to the muscle, anastomoses with inferior epigastric; inferior epigastric: from external iliac, enters the sheath at the arcuate line.
A(iv) A strong expandable support; protects viscera from injury such as a low blow in boxing; compresses the abdominal contents; maintains or increases intra-abdominal pressure; moves the trunk and maintains posture.
B(i) In anterior cutaneous nerve entrapment syndrome (ACNES), 12 of 95 adolescents with chronic abdominal pain had it; the Carnett sign was positive at the lateral border of rectus abdominis in all 12.
B(i) Altered skin sensation was present in 11 of 12; the distal thoracoabdominal nerves run in the rectus sheath.
B(i) After treatment (1 to 3 injections, n = 5; neurectomy, n = 7) pain was absent in 11; the conclusion was that ACNES is present in 1 of 8 such adolescents.
C(i) Rectus abdominis: long paired muscle split by the linea alba, origin pubic crest, insertion xiphoid process and costal cartilages of ribs 5 to 7, nerve T7 to T11, stabilises the pelvis in walking and depresses the ribs.
C(i) Pyramidalis: small triangular muscle superficial to rectus, base on the pubis and apex on the linea alba, origin pubic crest and symphysis, insertion linea alba, tenses the linea alba;
C(i) Nerve supply is the subcostal nerve (T12).

questions.question:
A patient develops sudden colicky pain in the flank referred to the ipsilateral lower abdominal wall and groin, attributed to a stone lodged in the ureter and confirmed on contrast imaging.
(i) Identify the structure involved and, from imaging, the points along its course where a stone would most likely be seen impacted.
(ii) What structures does this structure's course relate to that could be affected by the obstruction?
(iii) What differential levels of obstruction should be considered based on the sites of constriction?
(iv) Provide the clinico-anatomical reasoning for the pattern of referred pain in this patient.
questions.answerText:
(i) The ureter is the structure involved; on contrast-enhanced radiographic images the ureters are normally constricted at three places: the pelviureteric junction, where they cross the brim of the pelvic inlet, and their intravesical (intramural) course - a ureteric stone typically impacts at one of these constricted areas.
(ii) The abdominal ureters lie on the psoas major muscle and are related anteriorly, on the right, to the duodenum, terminal ileum, right colic and ileocolic vessels and the root of the mesentery, and on the left to the sigmoid colon, sigmoid mesocolon and left colic vessels; they are crossed anteriorly by the gonadal vessels and posteriorly relate to the bifurcation of the common iliac artery.
(iii) The differential levels to consider are obstruction at the pelviureteric junction, at the pelvic brim where the ureter crosses the common iliac vessels, or at the intramural/intravesical segment near the bladder.
(iv) Ureteric pain is mediated by sympathetic afferent fibres that arise from the T11-T12 segments of the spinal cord, so ureteric pain is usually referred to the ipsilateral lower quadrant of the anterior abdominal wall and especially to the groin, reflecting the shared segmental innervation of the ureter and these somatic regions.

(i) Disrupted structures:
The filtration slits between the podocyte foot processes allow filtrate to pass into the capsular space. When foot processes are effaced (fused), these filtration slits are lost, allowing proteins that would normally be retained to leak through.
(ii) Filtration barrier (from blood to capsular space):
1. Fenestrated endothelium of the glomerulus (highly porous — allows filtrate formation).
2. Basement membrane.
3. Podocyte foot processes (visceral layer of the glomerular capsule) with filtration slits between them.
(iii) Two layers of the glomerular capsule:
- Parietal layer: simple squamous epithelium.
- Visceral layer: branching epithelial podocytes; their extensions terminate in foot processes that cling to the basement membrane; filtration slits between foot processes allow filtrate to pass into the capsular space.
(iv) Cortical nephrons (85%): almost entirely in the cortex; short nephron loop; efferent arteriole supplies peritubular capillaries (absorption of water and solutes in cortex). Juxtamedullary nephrons: long nephron loops deeply invading the medulla; efferent arteriole supplies vasa recta. Juxtamedullary nephrons with their vasa recta are important in the production of concentrated urine.
(v) Seven renal functions that would be compromised:
1. Regulating total water volume and total solute concentration in water.
2. Regulating ECF ion concentrations.
3. Ensuring long-term acid-base balance.
4. Removal of metabolic wastes, toxins, and drugs.
5. Endocrine functions (renin — blood pressure; erythropoietin — RBC production).
6. Activation of vitamin D.
7. Gluconeogenesis during prolonged fasting.
questions.question:
A 35-year-old man with a history of recurrent sore throats develops puffiness around the eyes and ankles and frothy urine. Urinalysis shows heavy proteinuria. Renal biopsy shows effacement of podocyte foot processes.
(i)considering the filtration apparatus, explain which specific structures are disrupted to allow protein to leak into the filtrate.
(ii) Describe the full filtration barrier across the glomerulus, naming each component in sequence from blood to capsular space.
(iii) Distinguish between the parietal and visceral layers of the glomerular capsule, including cell type and structural features.
(iv) Describe the difference between cortical and juxtamedullary nephrons in terms of where they are located and the capillary beds they use, and explain which is more important for producing concentrated urine.
(v) State the full list of functions of the kidney that would be compromised if filtration fails completely.

A pregnant woman has antepartum bleeding; imaging shows the placenta implanted so that it covers the external os, and in another patient the placenta is noted to be abnormally attached into the myometrium.
(i) State the diagnoses.
(ii) Explain the embryologic/pathologic basis of each.
questions.answerText:
(i) Placenta previa (complete) for the first patient, and placenta accreta for the second.
(ii) These are listed among the clinical correlates of the placenta and fetal membranes, alongside placenta percreta, erythroblastosis fetalis and fetal hydrops.
Based on the labelled layers of the uterine wall shown (endometrium, myometrium, perimetrium, with the external os of the uterus and vagina below), placenta accreta corresponds to abnormal placental attachment extending into the myometrium, and placenta percreta corresponds to attachment penetrating through to the perimetrium, while placenta previa (complete) corresponds to the placenta lying over the external os, in contrast to the normal placental attachment site.

(i) The diagnosis is posterior dislocation of the right hip joint. The hip is held in flexion, adduction, and internal rotation with shortening — this is the classic position of posterior dislocation, because the femoral head has been driven posteriorly out of the acetabulum and the capsule.
(ii) Anatomical basis: posteriorly, the obturator internus, the gemelli, and the quadratus femoris muscle separate the joint from the sciatic nerve; superiorly lie the piriformis and gluteus minimus. The ischiofemoral ligament reinforces the posterior aspect of the capsule; it is attached medially to the ischium just posteroinferior to the acetabulum and laterally to the greater trochanter. When the femoral head dislocates posteriorly, the iliofemoral ligament (which is the strongest ligament and prevents overextension anteriorly) is relatively spared, but the posterior capsule and ischiofemoral ligament rupture. The femoral head lying posteriorly pulls the thigh into flexion, adduction, and internal rotation — the position of maximum capsular laxity posteriorly.
(iii) The sciatic nerve (L4, 5; S1, 2, 3) is the nerve at risk. It curves downward midway between the tuber ischii and the greater trochanter. The posteriorly displaced femoral head can compress or stretch the sciatic nerve as it lies posterior to the hip joint separated only by the quadratus femoris, the gemelli, and the obturator internus. The nerve has a side of danger and a side of safety in the gluteal region.
(iv) Resuscitation: ABCDE approach; analgesics; IV access and fluids; assess for associated fractures (acetabular fracture) and neurovascular status (sciatic nerve — check sensation on sole of foot, plantarflexion, and ankle jerks). Definitive management: urgent closed reduction under general anaesthesia (Allis manoeuvre — flexing the hip to 90° and applying upward traction along the femoral axis with internal then external rotation) within 6 hours to minimise risk of avascular necrosis of the femoral head. If closed reduction fails or there is an associated acetabular fracture, open reduction and internal fixation is required. Post-reduction, monitor for avascular necrosis of the head of femur (the main long-term complication).
questions.question:
A 25-year-old man presents after being thrown from a motorbike. He has severe pain in the right hip, which is held in flexion, adduction, and internal rotation, and the leg appears shortened. X-ray confirms posterior dislocation of the hip.
(i) State the diagnosis and identify the direction of dislocation from the clinical position.
(ii) What is the anatomical basis for the typical position of the limb in posterior dislocation?
(iii) Which nerve is at risk, and explain its anatomical relationship to the hip joint posteriorly?
(iv) Describe the resuscitation and the definitive management.

A patient with chronic hepatitis C presents with vomiting of blood and a distended abdomen with radiating veins on the abdominal wall. Ultrasound examination reveals a mass in the right lobe of the liver.
(i) What is the most likely diagnosis?
(ii) What predisposing factor for this condition is present in this patient?
(iii) Explain the pathophysiology linking the patient's chronic liver disease to the abdominal wall findings and the vomiting of blood.
(iv) What imaging approach was used to identify the hepatic mass?
questions.answerText:
(i) Hepatoma (a mass in the liver) arising in a background of chronic liver disease.
(ii) Chronic hepatitis C is the predisposing factor present in this patient; cirrhosis, the most common cause of portal hypertension, frequently develops in chronic alcoholics and provides a similar background for hepatic mass formation.
(iii) Chronic liver disease leads to destruction of hepatocytes with replacement by fibrous tissue, which impedes blood circulation through the liver and produces portal hypertension. This opens up portal-systemic anastomoses, producing distended (radiating) veins around the abdominal wall (paraumbilical anastomosis) and varices at the lower oesophagus, which bleed to cause haematemesis (vomiting of blood).
(iv) Ultrasound examination was used, which revealed the mass in the right lobe of the liver.

questions.question:
A(i) Define the pleura and describe its parts.
A(ii) Describe the parietal pleura and its parts.
A(iii) Describe the visceral pleura and the pleural cavity.
A(iv) Describe the lines of pleural reflection with their surface markings.
A(v) Describe the pleural recesses.
A(vi) Describe the blood supply, nerve supply and lymphatic drainage of the pleura.
B(i) Explain why the cervical pleura and the lower pleural margin are vulnerable to injury.
B(ii) Explain why the costodiaphragmatic recess is the clinically more important recess.
C(i) Distinguish between the parietal and the visceral pleura.
questions.answerText:
A(i) A thin, double-layered serous membrane that envelops each lung and lines the thoracic cavity, made of visceral and parietal layers with the intervening pleural cavity; the two pleural cavities are totally separate.
A(ii) Thicker outer layer lining the thoracic wall, mediastinum, diaphragm and neck, and can be stripped; 4 parts: costal (ribs, costal cartilages, intercostal spaces, sides of vertebral bodies, back of sternum, separated from them by endothoracic fascia), diaphragmatic, mediastinal (encloses the hilum structures, continuous with visceral pleura at the hilum, and below the hilum forms the pulmonary ligament) and cervical (cupola, 2.5-4 cm above the medial third of the clavicle, attached to the suprapleural membrane).
A(iii) Visceral pleura: closely adherent to the lung including its fissures, cannot be stripped, smooth and slippery, continuous with the parietal pleura at the hilum; the pleural cavity is a potential space with a small amount of lubricating pleural fluid that reduces friction and helps prevent lung collapse.
A(iv) Sternal (costal to mediastinal anteriorly): from behind the sternoclavicular joints to the midline at the 2nd costal cartilage, then the right edge passes vertically to the 6th costal cartilage while the left arches laterally at the 4th costal cartilage (because of the heart) to the 6th. Costal (costal to diaphragmatic): crosses the 8th rib in the midclavicular line, the 10th rib in the midaxillary line and the 12th rib at the lateral border of erector spinae. Vertebral: rounded reflections in the paravertebral planes from T1 to T12.
A(v) Recesses are spaces not occupied by lung that lung enters only on forced deep respiration: costodiaphragmatic (between costal and diaphragmatic pleura, shallow in inspiration and deeper in expiration) and costomediastinal (behind the sternum where costal pleura becomes mediastinal pleura, more conspicuous on the left near the heart).
A(vi) Blood supply: visceral pleura from bronchial and pulmonary arteries, veins to the pulmonary vein; parietal pleura from the vessels of the structures covered - cervical and costal from intercostal vessels, diaphragmatic outer part from intercostal and inner part from pericardiophrenic vessels, mediastinal from pericardiophrenic vessels.
A(vi) Nerve supply: costal pleura by intercostal nerves; diaphragmatic pleura by phrenic nerves centrally and intercostal nerves peripherally; mediastinal pleura by the phrenic nerve; the visceral pleura is described as having no nerve supply and as receiving vasomotor supply from autonomic nerves (pulmonary plexuses).
A(vi) Lymph: visceral to the pulmonary plexus in interlobar and peribronchial spaces; parietal costal, mediastinal and cervical to the internal thoracic (anterior) and intercostal (posterior) chains; diaphragmatic to retrosternal, mediastinal and sometimes coeliac nodes.
B(i) The cervical pleura reaches about 1 inch (2.5 cm) above the clavicle because of the oblique slope of the first rib, so it can be wounded (pneumothorax) by a stab wound, a surgeon's knife or an anaesthetist's needle above the clavicle; the lower edge descends just below the 12th rib medially (below the 11th if the 12th is short), so it may be opened in a loin incision.
B(ii) The costodiaphragmatic recess is the larger recess and the clinically more important one, providing the space where fluid collects in disease (pneumothorax with air, haemothorax with blood, empyema with pus, effusion); fluid is drained with a needle just above a rib, or through the space between the 7th costal cartilage and the xiphoid process.
C(i) Parietal: thicker, outer, lines wall, diaphragm, mediastinum and neck, named regionally, can be stripped, supplied by intercostal and phrenic nerves (so pleural irritation refers pain along the thoracic and anterior abdominal wall, and to the shoulder from the central diaphragm).
C(i) Visceral: inner layer closely adherent to the lung surface and fissures, cannot be stripped, smooth and slippery so the lung moves freely, supplied by bronchial and pulmonary vessels; pleurisy is inflammation of the pleura, usually with pneumonia or other lung infection.

(i) The four major stages of neurulation are: transformation of the general ectoderm into a thickened neural plate; shaping of the plate so it becomes narrower and longer; lateral folding of the neural plate; and fusion of the two most lateral apical surfaces of the neural folds.
Neurulation is induced by the notochord and begins in the 3rd week of intrauterine life.
(ii) The hinge points are areas of neural plate attachment to adjacent tissues: one median hinge point (MHP), attached to the notochord, and paired dorsolateral hinge points (DLHP), attached to the adjacent epidermal ectoderm.
At the hinge points, the neuroepithelial cells become wedge-shaped and the neural plate undergoes furrowing.
(iii) The neural tube so formed has two openings, the cranial (anterior) neuropore and the caudal (posterior) neuropore.
The cranial neuropore closes on day 25, while the caudal neuropore closes on day 27, preceding development of the CNS.
Clinical basis: failure of the neuropores to close results in neural tube defects (NTDs); failure of closure of the cranial neuropore causes anencephaly, while failure of closure of the caudal neuropore, with a bifid vertebral arch, causes spina bifida.
Because the two neuropores are the last points of the tube to seal and close on different days, a defect can selectively affect the cranial end, the caudal end, or in principle both, producing these different patterns of NTD.
Distinguishing the neural tube: it is formed by fusion of the neural folds and is the precursor of the CNS and most of the PNS; neurohistiogenesis derives neurons, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes and ependymal cells from its neuroepithelial wall.
Distinguishing the neural crest: as the neural tube forms, cells of the neural fold proliferate and, once the tube detaches from the surface ectoderm, migrate dorsolaterally on each side of the tube to form the neural crest.
The neural crest gives rise to the ganglia of the PNS (cranial, spinal and autonomic) and to other tissues such as Schwann cells, melanocytes, the adrenal medulla, facial dermis, connective tissue and bones of the skull, and the leptomeninges.
Thus the neural tube gives rise mainly to the central nervous system and its own histological cell types, while the neural crest is a separate population that emigrates from the folds to form the peripheral ganglia and a wide range of non-neural derivatives.
questions.question:
Describe the neural tube under the following headings:
(i) The four stages of its formation
(ii) The hinge points
(iii) Closure of the neuropores.
Explain the clinical basis for why failure of closure at the two ends of the neural tube produces different defects.
Distinguish between the neural tube and the neural crest.

A neonate is found to have a large tumour in the sacrococcygeal region, arising from tissue that normally regresses by the end of the 4th week of development.
(i) State the diagnosis.
(ii) Explain the pathophysiology.
questions.answerText:
(i) Sacrococcygeal teratoma.
(ii) The primitive streak continues to produce mesoderm until the early 4th week, when it regresses and becomes an insignificant structure in the sacrococcygeal region of the embryo, normally degenerating and disappearing by the end of the 4th week.
Persistence of the primitive streak, instead of this normal regression, results in a large tumour called a sacrococcygeal teratoma.

questions.question:
A patient presents with vertigo and deafness; occlusion of a small branch artery of the basilar system supplying the ear is suspected.
(i) Identify the vessel/structure responsible.
(ii) What structure does it supply, and what other artery does it often arise from?
(iii) What differential vascular territory could also be considered given its origin?
(iv) Explain the clinico-anatomical reasoning for the presentation.
questions.answerText:
(i) The internal auditory artery.
(ii) It supplies the ear; occlusion causes vertigo and deafness. It often arises from the anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA).
(iii) Because it often arises from the AICA, a lesion of the anterior inferior cerebellar artery territory (which supplies the anterior part of the inferior cerebellar surface and the lower part of the pons) could also be considered.
(iv) The internal auditory artery supplies the ear; its occlusion therefore produces vertigo and deafness, as its stated clinical effect.

A(i) Astrocytes are large stellate cells with processes/footplates attaching to capillaries, pia mater and neurons, regulating the neuronal microenvironment, forming the inner layer of the blood-brain barrier, and proliferating to aid repair after injury; fibrous astrocytes occur mainly in white matter, and protoplasmic astrocytes relate closely to cell bodies (satellite cells). Oligodendrocytes are smaller with fewer processes, producing the myelin sheath around CNS axons (done by Schwann cells in the PNS), with intervening nodes of Ranvier for faster conduction. Microglia are the smallest, of mesenchymal origin, are the phagocytes of the nervous system, and are involved in immune defence and inflammation. Ependymal cells are cylindrical cells lining the ventricles and central canal, playing a role in production, transport and circulation of CSF, and forming a filter regulating exchange between CSF and the CNS.
A(ii) Nerve cells are secretory cells whose secretory zone (axon terminal) is far from the production site (cell body); proteins are transported to the axon terminal by axoplasmic flow/axonal transport, using microfilaments and microtubules; nutrients for axonal integrity come from the cell body, so Wallerian degeneration occurs in the distal part of a cut axon.
B) Myelin sheaths insulate axons and make conduction faster, maintaining axonal integrity and neuron-to-cell communication; loss of the myelin sheath (demyelination) has serious effects on neuron function. Multiple sclerosis is a chronic, degenerating disease that progressively destroys oligodendrocyte cells in the CNS, producing symptoms from loss of myelination.
C) Astrocytes are large, star-shaped cells with processes attaching to capillaries/pia mater/neurons and form the blood-brain barrier, whereas oligodendrocytes are smaller, with fewer processes, and function to produce the myelin sheath enveloping CNS axons.
questions.question:
A(i) List the four types of neuroglial cells and describe each under origin, morphology and function.
A(ii) Describe axonal transport and its relevance to neuronal integrity.
B) Explain the clinical basis for why loss of a specific glial cell type is clinically significant.
C) Distinguish between astrocytes and oligodendrocytes.

A patient has a pathological lesion involving the lateral part of the tuber cinereum, resulting in loss of appetite.
(i) Give the diagnosis and identify the region and nuclear group affected.
(ii) Explain the anatomical basis: position, parts, nuclear groups with their functions, and the afferent and efferent connections of the region.
questions.answerText:
(i) Pathology of the lateral group of hypothalamic nuclei, located on the lateral part of the tuber cinereum, resulting in loss of appetite.
(ii) The hypothalamus lies below the thalamus, forming the lower lateral wall and floor of the 3rd ventricle (separated from the thalamus by the hypothalamic sulcus); it consists of the mammillary bodies, tuber cinereum, infundibulum and optic chiasma.
- Anterior group: paraventricular and supraoptic nuclei; rich blood supply; connected to the neurohypophysis via the pituitary stalk; control production of oxytocin and ADH.
- Middle group: ventromedial and dorsomedial nuclei; control appetite. Posterior group: medial and lateral mammillary nuclei; control memory and learning.
- Tuber cinereum: median eminence rostral to the mammillary bodies; centre for control of sleep. Median eminence: behind the infundibulum, cells that control the anterior pituitary, no BBB; with the infundibular stalk and posterior pituitary forms the neurohypophysis.
- Afferents: thalamus, fornix, stria terminalis, lentiform nucleus and tegmentum of the midbrain; efferent tracts connect the neurohypophysis, tegmentum and thalamus.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the muscularis and serosa of the small intestine, naming the layers of the muscularis, the nerve plexus between them, and the covering of the serosa.
A(ii) Describe the lamina propria of the small intestine, including its composition, its role in each intestinal villus, and the role of smooth muscle fibers within the villi.
B(i) Describe the submucosa of the small intestine, giving particular attention to the Brunner (duodenal) glands — location, type of gland, product, pH, and all three functions —.
B(ii) Describe the lacteals of the small intestine: what they are, where they begin, their course, their function, and how they change in appearance depending on the absorptive state of the intestine.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Muscularis and serosa:
- Muscularis: composed of an internal circular layer and an external longitudinal layer; between these muscle layers is the myenteric (Auerbach) nerve plexus, which produces peristalsis.
- Serosa: the small intestine is covered by a thin serosa.
A(ii) Lamina propria of the small intestine:
- Composed of loose connective tissue containing extensive blood and lymph microvasculature, nerve fibers, smooth muscle cells, and lymphoid tissue.
- It penetrates the core of each intestinal villus, bringing microvasculature, lymphatics, and nerves into each villus.
- Smooth muscle fibers inside the villi are responsible for rhythmic movements important for efficient absorption.
- Contractions of the muscularis mucosae also produce local movements of the plicae circulares that help propel lymph from the lacteals into submucosal and mesenteric lymphatics.
B(i) Submucosa — Brunner (duodenal) glands:
- Location: present in the proximal part of the duodenum; large clusters of branched tubular mucous glands with small excretory ducts opening among the intestinal crypts.
- Type: branched tubular mucous glands.
- Product: mucus, which is alkaline (pH 8.1–9.3).
- Three functions:
 1. Protects the mucous membrane.
 2. Brings the intestinal contents to the optimum pH for pancreatic enzyme action.
 3. Neutralises chyme entering the duodenum from the pylorus.
B(ii) Lacteals:
- Lymph vessels of the intestine beginning as closed tubes in the cores of villi.
- They run to the region of the lamina propria above the muscularis mucosae, where they form a plexus.
- From there they are directed to the submucosa, where they surround lymphoid nodules; they anastomose repeatedly and leave the intestine along with blood vessels.
- Function: especially important for lipid absorption.
- Absorptive state: when absorption is taking place after a meal, the lacteals are dilated and prominent; at other times they are collapsed and not prominent.

questions.question:
A tissue section from a patient shows the following features under the light microscope: cells with prominent intercalated discs, branching short cells with central nuclei, cross-striations, and a high cytoplasm-to-nucleus ratio. The patient presented following a sudden reduction in blood supply to the heart.
(i) Identify the diagnosis and name the tissue type seen.
(ii) Describe the detailed structure of intercalated discs, naming the three main junctional specializations within them.
(iii) State the anatomical basis of how cardiac muscle contraction is coordinated throughout the heart.
(iv) Identify the structure at risk when coronary arteries are occluded and explain the histological consequence.
(v) State the embryologic origin of cardiac muscle cells and the significance of their limited regenerative capacity.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Myocardial infarction (sudden reduction in blood supply to the heart causing necrosis). Tissue type: cardiac muscle (myocardium).
(ii) Intercalated discs contain adherent junctions for electrical excitation between cells and synchronous muscle contraction. Intercalated discs may appear as straight lines or exhibit a steplike pattern. Two regions can be distinguished in the steplike junctions: a transverse portion which runs across the fibers. Three main junctional specializations: fasciae adherentes (the most prominent membrane, representing hemi-Z bands), maculae adherentes (desmosomes — also present in the transverse portion, binding cardiac muscle under constant contractile activity), and gap junctions (provide ionic continuity between adjacent cells, allowing cardiac muscle cells to act as a syncytium so that the signal to contract passes throughout the organ).
(iii) Myocardial activity is coordinated by an intrinsic conducting system (the Purkinje system) and is modulated by neural inputs and hormonal regulation. Cardiac muscle cells act as a syncytium, allowing the signal to contract to pass throughout the organ.
(iv) The blood supply to the heart is through the three main coronary arteries, which are prone to atheroma. Acute coronary arterial occlusion involving nearly the entire area at risk causes necrosis of the myocardium. Histological consequence: cardiac muscle cells may undergo necrosis.
(v) Muscle cells are of mesodermal origin. Cardiac muscle has limited regenerative capacity; spaces left after injury in tissues whose cells divide poorly or not at all (e.g., cardiac muscle) are filled by connective tissue, forming dense irregular scar tissue.

questions.question:
A patient presents with facial paralysis on one side of the face.
(i) What is the diagnosis?
(ii) What are the predisposing factors and pathophysiology?
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Bell's palsy.
(ii) Predisposing factors: not covered. Pathophysiology: Bell's palsy is facial paralysis ipsilateral to a facial nerve lesion. The facial nerve carries special visceral efferent (SVE) fibres supplying the muscles of facial expression, so a lesion of the nerve paralyses these muscles on the same side as the lesion.

questions.question:
A patient is found to have a congenital defect of the diaphragm through which abdominal contents pass into the chest.
(i) State the diagnosis and the sites at which such herniae occur, naming the eponymous ones and the commoner side.
(ii) Explain the embryologic basis, naming the four developmental components of the diaphragm and the failure that produces the commonest type.
(iii) Explain why the phrenic nerve has a long course.
questions.answerText:
(i) Congenital diaphragmatic hernia, from incomplete fusion of the septum transversum, the dorsal mesentery and the pleuroperitoneal membranes from the body wall. Sites: (a) the pleuroperitoneal canal (foramen of Bochdalek, lying posteriorly; more common on the left); (b) the opening between the xiphoid and costal origins (foramen of Morgagni, anteriorly); (c) a congenitally large oesophageal hiatus (hiatal hernia); (d) deficiency of the whole central tendon (occasionally traumatic in origin).
(ii) The diaphragm is entirely mesodermal and develops from 4 sources: the septum transversum (central tendon), the right and left pleuroperitoneal membranes (close the fetal communication between pleural and peritoneal cavities), the dorsal mesentery of the oesophagus and the mesoderm of the body wall (peripheral rim); the Bochdalek type is caused by failure of fusion of the septum transversum with the pleuroperitoneal membrane.
(iii) The septum transversum lies in front of the head end of the embryo and, with folding of the head, is carried ventrally and caudally to the anterior part of the diaphragm; the cervical myotomes and nerves contribute muscle and nerve supply, so the phrenic nerve (C3, 4, 5) runs a long course from the neck; despite this complex development, congenital abnormalities are unusual.

Origin/identity: the nerve of the second pharyngeal arch is the 7th cranial nerve (facial nerve).
Distribution: it supplies the muscles that develop from the second arch, which include stapedius, stylohyoid, the posterior belly of digastric, the auricular muscles, the muscles of facial expression, occipitofrontalis, and platysma.
The skeletal elements of the same arch (Reichert's cartilage) form the stapes, the styloid process of the temporal bone, the stylohyoid ligament, the lesser horn of the hyoid bone, and the upper part of the body of the hyoid bone, which lie in relation to this nerve's territory.
Course: not covered beyond its arch of origin.
Safe site for a procedure: not covered.
Anatomical basis of the deformity after injury: not covered.
What can be stated is only the identity of the nerve and the list of muscles it supplies as the motor nerve of the second arch.
No detail of its intracranial or extracranial course, its branching pattern, or the consequence of damage to it is given.
The muscles listed (including the muscles of facial expression, occipitofrontalis and platysma) indicate the breadth of its distribution over the face, scalp and neck.
This distribution is consistent with it being grouped, in the same source, with the second-arch skeletal and muscular derivatives rather than described as an isolated nerve.
No further course or injury-related information beyond this is provided.
These additional details would need to be sourced elsewhere.
questions.question:
Describe the origin and distribution of the nerve of the second pharyngeal arch.
State the safe site for a procedure on this nerve.
Explain the anatomical basis of the deformity following injury to this nerve.

questions.answerText:
(i) Organ: the eye/retina. Two photoreceptor types: rods — more sensitive to light and are the receptors primarily used in dim light. Cones — require more intense lighting; conical in shape.
(ii) Three major neuron types in the inner nuclear layer: horizontal cells, bipolar cells, and amacrine cells. The rod and cone cells project their processes into the outer plexiform layer and synapse with these cells. The retinal ganglion cell layer receives processed signals. Supporting Müller glia cells are also present in the inner nuclear layer. In general: bipolar cells relay signals from photoreceptors; horizontal and amacrine cells modulate signals between photoreceptors and bipolar cells and between bipolar and ganglion cells.
(iii) Structures affected by blood-retina barrier damage: tight junctions between the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells establish the blood-retina barrier; disruption allows uncontrolled passage of substances into the neural retina, damaging photoreceptor function and causing visual disturbance. The outermost layer, the RPE, is close to the choriocapillaris; Bruch's membrane is located between the choroid and the RPE.
(iv) Differential pathology: when the lens becomes opaque, the condition is termed cataract, which may also be caused by excessive exposure to ultraviolet radiation. Histological change: the lens fibers become less transparent (opacification), impairing light transmission to the retina.
(v) The optic nerve arises in the embryo as an outgrowth of the diencephalon (forebrain); it is therefore part of the CNS, not a true peripheral nerve. Its myelin is produced by oligodendrocytes (not Schwann cells), and it lacks neurilemma; therefore it does not regenerate after injury (unlike peripheral cranial nerves). It is also associated with multiple sclerosis, a demyelinating disease of the CNS — unlike other cranial nerves which are peripheral and can regenerate via neurilemma.
questions.question:
A histology slide of the retina shows ten distinct layers from the outermost (closest to the choroid) to the innermost (facing the vitreous body). Among these layers, two photoreceptor types are identified: one is more sensitive to dim light and the other requires more intense lighting. Tight junctions between the outermost cell layer establish a blood-retina barrier.
(i) Identify the organ and name the two photoreceptor types.
(ii) Describe the three major neuron types of the retina found in the inner nuclear layer and state their roles.
(iii) State which structures are affected and what functional deficit results from damage to the blood-retina barrier.
(iv) Identify the differential pathology caused by excessive ultraviolet radiation on the lens, and describe the histological change.
(v) Apply clinico-anatomical reasoning to explain why lesions of the optic nerve behave differently from lesions of other cranial nerves.

questions.answerText:
(i) Tissue: Hyaline cartilage. It is the most common and best studied of the three forms of cartilage. Fresh hyaline cartilage is bluish-white and translucent.
(ii) Predisposing factors/sites: In the embryo, hyaline cartilage serves as a temporary skeleton until it is gradually replaced by bone, forming models for immature bones. It forms epiphyseal cartilage on long bones. It gives shape to nose, trachea, and bronchi; forms the ventral ends of ribs where they articulate with the sternum; and covers the mating surfaces of bones in synovial joints. It is resilient and shock absorbing. Collagen type II is the primary fiber; chondroitin is the major component of ground substance.
(iii) Pathophysiology of calcification: Hyaline cartilage is more susceptible to degenerative aging processes. Calcification of the matrix is preceded by an increase in the size and volume of the chondrocytes, followed by their death. Cartilage cells can give rise to benign (chondroma) or malignant (chondrosarcoma) tumors.
(iv) Management: Stem cell therapy, particularly mesenchymal stem cells, is a strong promise in treatment of cartilage defects and osteoarthritis. It is hoped that the whole cartilage can be repaired, not just focal defects. Various options have been made available over the years; new techniques have merits and demerits.
questions.question:
A section of tissue viewed under the light microscope shows sparse cells embedded in a large amount of firm characteristic matrix; the cells are located within cavities called lacunae; the matrix contains collagen type II as the primary fiber along with chondroitin as the major ground substance component; no blood vessels are visible within the tissue; it has a bluish-white, translucent appearance on fresh examination; a perichondrium is present at the periphery.
(i) Identify the tissue and state its specific type.
(ii) State the predisposing factors and sites where this tissue is found in the body.
(iii) Describe the pathophysiology of cartilage matrix calcification.
(iv) Outline the management approach including cell-based therapy.

questions.answerText:
(i) Acute appendicitis (right iliac fossa pain may also arise from caecum or a right ovarian cyst).
(ii) Appendicectomy; McBurney's point, one-third lateral along the line joining the ASIS to the umbilicus, is roughly the point of making a transverse incision.
(iii) McBurney's point represents the base of the vermiform appendix and is the point of maximal tenderness.
(iii) The umbilicus is the site of first pain; its dermatome (T10) is the same root as the visceral supply to the appendix, so referred pain is felt there.
(iv) The ilioinguinal, iliohypogastric and inferior thoracic nerves are prone to injury because they spread across the abdominal wall; injury causes muscle weakness of the wall.
(iv) The inferior epigastric vessels, covered by the lateral umbilical folds, bleed if cut; the appendicular artery runs in the free margin of the mesoappendix.
(v) The appendix is a midgut derivative supplied by the superior mesenteric artery (appendicular branch of the ileocolic artery); midgut nerve supply is sympathetic lesser splanchnic (T10, T11) plus vagus.
(v) Variant: retrocaecal appendix; inflammation causes spasm of psoas major so the patient keeps the right thigh flexed and medially rotated, the basis of the psoas test.
questions.question:
A patient has pain first felt around the umbilicus and later maximal tenderness at a point one-third of the way along the line from the anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus; in another form of the condition the patient keeps the right thigh flexed and medially rotated.
(i) Give the diagnosis.
(ii) Name the procedure and the surface landmark on which its incision is based.
(iii) State the anatomical landmarks that explain the first site of pain and the location of the organ.
(iv) State the nerves and vessels at risk in the abdominal wall and in the organ's mesentery.
(v) Explain the embryologic basis of its supply and the positional variant with its test.

questions.answerText:
(i) The diagnosis is an orbital blow-out fracture.
(ii) Eye trauma from blunt trauma displaces the orbital walls, producing the blow-out fracture.
(iii) Paralysis of the extraocular muscles results in double vision; each orbit contains 6 extraocular muscles (4 rectus muscles - superior, inferior, lateral, medial - and 2 oblique muscles - superior, inferior) that function together to move the eye, with the medial rectus producing adduction, lateral rectus abduction, superior rectus elevation/adduction/intorsion, inferior rectus depression/adduction/extorsion, inferior oblique extorsion/elevation/abduction, and superior oblique intorsion/depression/abduction; displacement of the orbital walls and/or entrapment or paralysis affecting these muscles disrupts their coordinated action, producing double vision.

questions.answerText:
A(i) At the end of the 4th week a sickle-shaped crest grows from the roof of the common atrium, the first portion of the septum primum; its two limbs extend toward the endocardial cushions in the AV canal.
A(i) The opening between the lower rim of the septum primum and the endocardial cushions is the ostium primum; it is obliterated when the septum primum fuses with the AV septum.
A(ii) The dorsal and ventral AV cushions fuse to form the AV septum, dividing the AV canal into right and left canals.
A(ii) Before closure is complete, cell death perforates the upper septum primum; coalescence of the perforations forms the ostium secundum, ensuring free blood flow from right to left atrium.
A(iii) At the beginning of the 5th week a new crescent-shaped fold, the septum secundum, appears to the right of the septum primum; its anterior limb extends downward to the septum in the AV canal.
A(iii) The opening left by the septum secundum is the oval foramen; the remaining septum primum (its upper part gradually disappears) becomes the valve of the oval foramen, allowing flow from right to left but not left to right.
A(iv) After birth, when lung circulation begins and left atrial pressure increases, the valve is pressed against the septum secundum, obliterating the oval foramen and separating the right and left atria.
B(i) Atrial septal defects are heart defects involving the atrial septum; a foramen secundum defect is caused by excessive resorption of the septum primum, the septum secundum, or both.
B(i) Premature closure of the foramen ovale in prenatal life results in hypertrophy of the right side of the heart and underdevelopment of the left side.
C(i) Septum primum: first, sickle-shaped, from the roof of the atrium; perforated to form the ostium secundum; its upper part disappears and the remainder forms the valve of the oval foramen.
C(i) Septum secundum: appears in the 5th week to the right of the septum primum; crescent-shaped; never a complete partition; the opening it leaves is the oval foramen.
C(i) The ostium primum closes on fusion of the septum primum with the AV septum, whereas the ostium secundum ensures right-to-left flow.

(i) The frontal sinuses are contained within the frontal bone; their posterosuperior wall lies adjacent to the frontal lobe of the brain, and their floor abuts the ethmoid cells, the roof of the nasal fossa, and the orbit; the ethmoid sinuses similarly lie on each side of the cribriform plate and are related above to the frontal lobes of the brain.
(ii) The close relation of the frontal sinus to the frontal lobe of the brain explains how infection of this sinus may result in the development of a frontal lobe abscess. A fracture involving the sinus, severe enough to tear the dura and pia-arachnoid, will place the subarachnoid space in communication with the nasal cavity, so CSF may be detected trickling through the nostril (CSF rhinorrhoea), usually on the affected side, though a contralateral leak can occur since these sinuses may communicate. Infection of the ethmoid sinuses (ethmoiditis) may similarly result in a frontal cerebral abscess, and an ethmoidal fracture may cause CSF leakage into the nasal cavity.
(iii) Not covered for the frontal/ethmoid sinuses specifically. For the related maxillary sinus, antral puncture using a trocar and cannula through the nasal cavity, or the Caldwell-Luc operation (fenestrating the antrum in the gingivolabial fold), are the management options given; however, specific management options for frontal sinusitis or ethmoiditis complications are not covered.
questions.question:
A patient with a history of recurrent sinus infection develops severe frontal headache, followed by fever, drowsiness and neurological signs.

questions.answerText:
(i) The diagnosis is an acute lateral ankle sprain — tear of the lateral ligaments of the ankle, which can be quite severe.
(ii) The ankle (talocrural) joint is more stable during dorsiflexion than plantarflexion. The mortise of the ankle joint is formed by the roof (inferior surface of tibia), walls (lateral malleolar surface from the fibula, medial malleolar surface from tibia), and floor (superior surface of talus). In plantarflexion the narrower posterior part of the talus sits in the mortise, reducing bony congruence and making the joint mechanically vulnerable. In dorsiflexion, the wider anterior articular surface of the talus is gripped by the mortise, providing bony stability.
(iii) The lateral ligaments at risk include the anterior talofibular ligament (the most commonly injured), calcaneofibular ligament, and posterior talofibular ligament. The medial ligament is the deltoid ligament. The tibiofibular ligament and interosseous membrane also stabilise the joint. Complications of a severe sprain include chronic lateral ankle instability, recurrent sprains, peroneal tendon damage, osteochondral lesions of the talus, and functional instability leading to impaired locomotion. The talus articulates with the calcaneus inferiorly, the navicular anteriorly, the tibia superiorly, and the malleoli laterally and medially.
(iv) Management follows RICE (rest, ice, compression, elevation) in the acute phase. Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for analgesia. Early controlled mobilisation with physiotherapy and proprioceptive rehabilitation. Surgical ligament reconstruction (Brostrom procedure) is reserved for cases with chronic instability that fails conservative management.
questions.question:
A 19-year-old female gymnast presents after landing awkwardly. She has marked swelling and ecchymosis around the ankle, pain on weight-bearing, and the ankle is held in plantarflexion and inversion. Examination shows tenderness over the anterior talofibular ligament. X-ray shows no bony fracture.
(i) State the diagnosis.
(ii) What is the embryologic and anatomical basis of why plantarflexion is the position of maximum instability of the ankle?
(iii) What structures are at risk and what are the complications?
(iv) Describe the management.

A 45-year-old seamstress presents with numbness and tingling in the lateral three and a half fingers of the palmar hand, weakness of fine thumb movements, and thenar muscle wasting, worse at night.
(i) What is the diagnosis?
(ii) What surgical procedure may be used to manage this condition?
(iii) What are the anatomical landmarks/attachments relevant to this procedure?
(iv) Which nerve/structure is at risk during this procedure, and why is the palm spared of sensory symptoms?
questions.answerText:
(i) Carpal tunnel syndrome.
(ii) Management may involve incision of the flexor retinaculum — carpal tunnel (CT) release.
(iii) The flexor retinaculum is attached medially to the pisiform and the hook of the hamate, and laterally to the tubercle of the scaphoid and the ridge of the trapezium; it converts the concave carpal sulcus into the carpal tunnel.
(iv) The median nerve is at risk, as it lies anterior to the tendons of flexor digitorum superficialis, deep to the flexor retinaculum, within the tunnel; its recurrent branch, supplying the thenar muscles (flexor pollicis brevis, abductor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis), arises in the hand and is also at risk. The skin of the palm is not affected because the palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve arises in the forearm and does not traverse the carpal tunnel.

(i) Occlusion of one posterior cerebral artery (PCA) results in contralateral loss of vision - homonymous hemianopia - with sparing of macular vision, due to collateral circulation from the middle cerebral artery.
(ii) The posterior cerebral artery can be compressed by herniation of the uncus; this is associated with increased intracranial pressure, whereby the circulation of the visual cortex is impaired, resulting in cortical blindness.
(iii) Other clinical correlates of PCA territory lesions include prosopagnosia (can't recognise faces), palinopsia (abnormal recurring visual imagery), alexia (can't read), and transcortical sensory aphasia (loss of power to comprehend written or spoken words). Structures supplied by the interpeduncular branch (cranial nerves III and IV) give rise to syndromes such as oculomotor palsy with contralateral hemiplegia (Weber's syndrome) and trochlear nerve palsy.
(iv) Because the PCA supplies the occipital lobe/visual cortex, with the macula typically also perfused via collateral middle cerebral artery supply, occlusion or compression (as by uncal herniation raising intracranial pressure and impairing visual cortex circulation) of the PCA territory characteristically spares macular vision while affecting the rest of the corresponding visual field, and can additionally produce the higher cortical visual deficits (prosopagnosia, palinopsia, alexia) and language deficits (transcortical sensory aphasia) associated with this territory.
questions.question:
A patient presents with loss of vision in the same half of the visual field in both eyes, but with the very centre of vision preserved. On further assessment there is also difficulty recognising familiar faces.

questions.answerText:
(i) Positive Murphy's sign, seen in acute cholecystitis.
(i) It is elicited by firmly placing a hand at the costal margin in the right upper abdominal quadrant and asking the patient to inspire deeply.
(ii) Gallstones may lodge in Hartmann's pouch, the outward dilation of the posteromedial wall of the neck of the gallbladder. Other predisposing factors are not covered.
(iii) If the gallbladder is inflamed it descends on inspiration and contacts the palpating hand, so the patient has pain and catches the breath.
(iii) Inflammation irritates the subdiaphragmatic parietal peritoneum, supplied by the phrenic nerve (C3, 4, 5); pain is referred to the skin over the tip of the right shoulder, supplied by the supraclavicular nerve (C3, C4).
(iv) Cholecystectomy: Calot's (cystohepatic) triangle is the landmark for locating the cystic artery during laparoscopic cholecystectomy.
(iv) Boundaries: superiorly the inferior surface of the liver, left the common hepatic duct, right the cystic duct; Lund's node in the triangle may be removed with the gallbladder. Non-surgical management is not covered.
questions.question:
A patient with an inflamed gallbladder feels pain and catches the breath when a hand is placed firmly at the right costal margin in the right upper abdominal quadrant during deep inspiration, and also has pain at the tip of the right shoulder.
(i) Name the sign and the diagnosis.

questions.answerText:
A. Most of the muscles of the larynx receive their innervation via the recurrent laryngeal branch of the vagus nerve; the exception is the cricothyroid muscle, which receives its innervation via the external laryngeal nerve. Motor supply to the muscles is from the nucleus ambiguus via the cranial accessory: to the cricothyroid via the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve, and to all other laryngeal muscles, including the upper oesophagus and cricopharyngeus, via the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
B. Sensory innervation of the larynx is via branches of the vagus nerve: above the vocal folds it is via the internal laryngeal nerve, and below the vocal folds it is by way of branches of the recurrent laryngeal nerve; parasympathetic innervation of the larynx is mainly by way of branches of the vagus nerve. Lymphatic drainage similarly follows this division: above the cords to the upper deep cervical nodes, and below the cords to the lower deep cervical nodes.
C. Not covered beyond the statement that the cricothyroid is the only muscle that tightens the vocal cords, is the only intrinsic laryngeal muscle supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve rather than the recurrent laryngeal nerve, and is the only intrinsic muscle of the larynx situated on the outside of the larynx - so that injury confined to the external laryngeal nerve would be expected to spare all laryngeal muscles except cricothyroid, while the recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies all the other laryngeal muscles; the specific voice change resulting from each injury is not covered.
questions.question:
A. Describe the nerve supply of the larynx, including the origin and distribution of the recurrent laryngeal nerve and the exception to its motor supply.
B. State how the sensory innervation of the larynx is divided in relation to the vocal folds.
C. Explain the anatomical basis of the voice change/deformity that follows injury to the recurrent laryngeal nerve, as distinguished from injury to the external laryngeal nerve.

A. Describe the course of the maxillary nerve, from its origin to its continuation on the face, and list its branches.
B. State the clinically relevant procedure and the region associated with this nerve.
C. Explain the anatomical basis of the sensory deficit that would follow injury/block of this nerve, based on its distribution.
questions.answerText:
A. The maxillary nerve passes through the pterygopalatine fossa, where it is one of the contents (along with the terminal part of the maxillary artery, the maxillary vein, and the pterygopalatine ganglion); nerve structures enter the fossa through its posterior wall. Its branches include the superior alveolar nerves (anterior, posterior and middle), the middle meningeal nerve, the infraorbital nerve, the zygomatic nerve, the inferior palpebral nerve, the superior labial nerve, the pharyngeal nerve, the greater and lesser palatine nerves, and the nasopalatine nerve. The infraorbital nerve continues from the maxillary nerve onto the face via the infraorbital groove and canal, situated on the floor of the orbit in the orbital plate of the maxilla, and via the infraorbital foramen.
B. Clinical correlates of this region include maxillary nerve block, and the pterygopalatine ganglion is also referred to as the "hay fever ganglion".
C. Not covered beyond the listing of the nerve's branches (superior alveolar, infraorbital, zygomatic, palatine, nasopalatine, pharyngeal, middle meningeal) and their general regions of distribution; the specific sensory deficit pattern following injury or block is not covered.

questions.question:
A patient has progressive difficulty swallowing, with failure of the lower oesophagus to relax normally so that food accumulates and the oesophagus above becomes dilated.
(i) What is the diagnosis?
(ii) What is the pathologic/embryologic basis of this condition?
questions.answerText:
(i) Achalasia cardia - inability of the oesophagus to dilate due to poor neuromuscular coordination, causing accumulation of food in the oesophagus.
(ii) It may be due to congenital absence of nerves in the oesophageal wall, so the lower oesophagus fails to relax and food backs up with dilation of the oesophagus above the block.

questions.question:
Describe the gross anatomy of the clavicle:
A(i) Shape and articulations
A(ii) Surface features
A(iii) Functions
B. State how a particular part of the clavicle relates to a common fracture pattern.
C. Explain how injury at this region may involve a distant structure, causing a functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
A(i) The clavicle forms the anterior portion of the shoulder girdle; it is curved like the italic letter "f" and lies nearly horizontally at the upper and anterior part of the thorax, immediately above the first rib. It articulates medially with the manubrium sterni and laterally with the acromion of the scapula.
A(ii) The upper surface is flat, rough, and marked by impressions for the attachment of deltoid in front and trapezius behind; the bone has no medullary cavity.
A(iii) Its functions are to transmit forces from the upper limb to the axial skeleton, to act as a strut holding the arm free from the trunk (supported principally by trapezius), and to provide attachment for muscles.
B. The weakest point along the clavicle is the junction of the middle and outer thirds.
Transmission of forces to the axial skeleton in falls on the shoulder or hand may exceed the strength of the bone at this site, and this indirect force commonly results in fracture there.
Clavicle fracture is caused by landing on the hand from a fall with the arm rigidly outstretched, or by a direct blow.
C. The clavicle has important deep relations that make it clinically significant beyond the bone itself.
The third parts of the subclavian vessels and the trunks of the brachial plexus pass behind the medial third of the shaft of the clavicle, separated only by the thin subclavius muscle.
At the sternal end, behind the sternoclavicular joints, lie the common carotid artery on the left and the bifurcation of the brachiocephalic artery on the right, with the internal jugular vein lying a little more laterally; these vessels are separated from the bone only by the strap muscles (sternohyoid and sternothyroid).
Because these major vessels and the brachial plexus trunks lie in such close proximity to the clavicle, deep or displaced injury involving the bone can threaten them.
Compromise of the subclavian vessels can produce vascular insufficiency of the upper limb, while injury to the brachial plexus trunks passing behind the medial clavicle can produce motor and sensory deficits in the limb.
This illustrates how a skeletal injury at the clavicle can spread to affect distant neurovascular structures, producing a functional deficit beyond the fracture site itself.

(i) Diagnosis: a cavernous sinus lesion/syndrome affecting the cranial nerves closely related to the cavernous sinus.
(ii) Anatomical landmark: because of their close relationship to the cavernous sinus, certain cranial nerves are susceptible to compression or injury related to pathologies of the sinus, such as infections and thrombophlebitis.
(iii) Nerves at risk: CN III, CN IV, CN V1 (ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve) and especially CN VI.
questions.question:
A patient presents with combined ophthalmoplegia and facial sensory loss attributed to a lesion related to the cavernous sinus (e.g. infection or thrombophlebitis).
(i) What is the diagnosis?
(ii) What anatomical landmark explains the pattern of nerve involvement?
(iii) Which nerves/structures are at risk?

A 25-year-old footballer sustains a tackle from the side with his foot planted. He hears a 'pop', develops immediate medial knee swelling, and has medial joint-line tenderness. On examination, the anterior drawer test is negative but the valgus stress test is markedly positive. MRI reveals rupture of the tibial collateral ligament and a tear of the medial meniscus.
(i) State the diagnosis and explain the imaging findings.
(ii) What predisposes these two structures to combined injury?
(iii) What are the complications of an untreated medial meniscus tear?
(iv) Describe the surgical and conservative management options, justifying your choice.
questions.answerText:
(i) The diagnosis is combined rupture of the tibial (medial) collateral ligament and medial meniscus tear — the 'unhappy triad' variant. The tibial collateral ligament is a strong flat band extending from the medial epicondyle of the femur to the medial condyle and superior part of the tibia; it is firmly attached at its midpoint to the medial meniscus. Positive valgus stress test indicates disruption of the medial stabilisers. The anterior drawer test is negative, indicating the ACL is intact.
(ii) At its midpoint the tibial collateral ligament is firmly attached to the medial meniscus; thus any valgus force that tears the ligament simultaneously tears the medial meniscus to which it adheres. The medial meniscus is C-shaped, broader posteriorly, and less mobile than the lateral meniscus, making it more vulnerable to rotational and valgus forces. Compared with the fibular collateral ligament, the tibial collateral ligament is weaker and more often damaged.
(iii) Complications of untreated medial meniscus tear include persistent knee pain, locking and giving way of the knee, chronic synovitis, and accelerated osteoarthritis from loss of the shock-absorbing function of the meniscus. Osteoarthritis accelerates the degenerative wear and tear of the menisci, and may progress to genu varum (tibia diverted medially) or genu valgum (tibia diverted laterally).
(iv) Conservative management includes rest, ice, elevation, physiotherapy, and quadriceps strengthening — the quadriceps femoris is the most important muscle in stabilizing the knee joint, particularly the inferior fibres of vastus medialis and lateralis. Surgical management includes arthroscopic partial meniscectomy or meniscal repair for the meniscal tear, and ligament reconstruction for complete collateral rupture. In a young active athlete, surgical repair/reconstruction is preferred to restore full stability and reduce the risk of long-term osteoarthritis.

questions.question:
A patient presents with sudden onset of loss of coordination on one side of the body, difficulty swallowing, a hoarse voice, and drooping of one eyelid with a small pupil on the same side.
(i) What is the diagnosis, and which vessel territory is implicated?
(ii) What is the pathological basis of this presentation?
questions.answerText:
(i) The diagnosis is Wallenberg's syndrome (lateral medullary syndrome), a stroke affecting the medulla.
(ii) A stroke is a sudden onset of neurological deficits due to a cerebrovascular accident; cerebrovascular disease (CVD) may be ischaemic, due to blockage of vessels by a thrombus or embolus, or haemorrhagic, due to rupture of an artery or aneurysm from high blood pressure. Main causes of CVA include thrombosis (obstruction of a blood vessel by a locally forming clot), embolism (obstruction by an embolus formed elsewhere), hypoperfusion (lack of blood supply due to systemically low blood pressure, e.g. shock), and haemorrhage (accumulation of blood within the cranial cavity). Medullary involvement produces Wallenberg's syndrome, characterised by ataxia on the same side of the body as the injury, inability to swallow, hoarse voice, and Horner's syndrome (a sympathetic nervous system deficit), with contralateral and ipsilateral consequences.

questions.question:
(i) Describe the origin, course, branches and distribution of the renal artery.
(ii) State why the segmental arteries of the kidney are described as end arteries.
(iii) Explain the anatomical basis of the consequence of injury or occlusion of a segmental renal artery.
questions.answerText:
(i) The renal arteries arise from the aorta at the level of the L1/L2 intervertebral disc; the right renal artery passes posterior to the inferior vena cava.
Each renal artery divides at the hilum into anterior and posterior branches; these give rise to segmental arteries.
Four segmental arteries, apical, anterosuperior, anteroinferior and inferior, arise from the anterior branch, and the posterior branch itself constitutes the posterior segmental artery.
Each segmental artery further gives lobar arteries, one for each renal pyramid, which give two or three interlobar arteries running toward the cortex on each side of the pyramid.
Interlobar arteries give arcuate arteries at the corticomedullary junction, which give several interlobular arteries, from which afferent glomerular arterioles arise.
The renal veins lie anterior to their respective arteries; each renal vein drains into the inferior vena cava, and the left renal vein additionally receives the left suprarenal and left gonadal veins before crossing anterior to the aorta.
(ii) The segmental arteries of the kidney are described as end arteries, meaning they do not anastomose with one another.
Because each segmental artery supplies its own renal segment without collateral supply from adjacent segmental arteries, the renal parenchyma is divided into distinct vascular segments.
(iii) Since the segmental arteries are end arteries, occlusion or injury of one segmental artery cuts off blood supply to its corresponding renal segment.
This lack of anastomosis means the affected segment cannot receive compensatory blood flow from neighbouring segments.
