Lymphatic drainage of the kidney is to the right and left lumbar lymph nodes, and nerve supply is via the renal plexus (vagus and abdominopelvic splanchnic nerves), so a segmental vascular injury is an isolated event within the kidney rather than one shared with adjacent segments.
Not covered : the specific clinical outcome, such as extent of infarction, following segmental artery occlusion.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the five functions of the epithelial lining of the digestive tract.
A(ii) Describe the submucosal (Meissner) plexus and the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus together as the local enteric nervous system: name the layers of the GIT wall each is found in, state the ganglia they are composed of, what the number of ganglia depends on, and what system they function independently of.
B(i) Describe the muscularis mucosae: its composition, its location, and the two functions attributed to it.
B(ii) Explain the immunological backup to the thin epithelial barrier of the GIT, and identify what the digestive tract normally contains that makes this backup essential.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Five functions of the epithelial lining:
1. Provide a selectively permeable barrier between the contents of the tract and the tissues of the body.
2. Facilitate the transport and digestion of food.
3. Promote the absorption of the products of digestion.
4. Produce hormones that affect the activity of the digestive system.
5. Produce mucus for lubrication and protection.
A(ii) Local enteric nervous system:
- The submucosal (Meissner) plexus is located in the submucosa; the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus is located in the connective tissue between the circular and longitudinal muscle sublayers of the muscularis.
- Together they constitute the local enteric nervous system of the digestive tract.
- This system functions independently of the CNS.
- Both plexuses are composed mainly of nerve cell aggregates forming small parasympathetic ganglia.
- The number of ganglia along the digestive tract is variable — numerous in the regions of greatest motility.
B(i) Muscularis mucosae:
- Composition: thin layer of smooth muscle.
- Location: usually separates the mucosa from the submucosa.
- Functions: (1) allows local movements of the mucosa independent of other movements of the digestive tract, helping to increase contact of the lining with food; (2) its contractions contribute to mixing and propelling food (the plexuses coordinate the contractions of the muscularis to mix and propel food).
B(ii) Immunological backup:
- The mucosa-associated immune defense system (MALT) provides an essential backup to the thin physical barrier of the epithelial lining.
- The lamina propria (just below the epithelium) is a zone rich in macrophages and lymphocytes, some of which actively produce IgA antibodies.
- The digestive tract normally contains thousands of microbial species, including both useful gut inhabitants and potential pathogens ingested with food and drink, making this immune backup essential.

A(i) The articular surfaces of the TMJ are the condyle of the mandible (inferior) and the articular tubercle/mandibular fossa of the temporal bone (squamous part). The articular capsule is loose and fibrous, attaching to the margins of the articular area on the temporal bone and around the neck of the mandible. The superior synovial membrane lines the fibrous capsule superior to the articular disc, and the inferior synovial membrane lines the capsule inferior to the disc; the joint is divided into two compartments (superior and inferior) by an articular disc of fibrocartilage.
A(ii) The ligaments of the TMJ are divided into an intrinsic ligament and extrinsic ligaments. The intrinsic ligament, also known as the lateral ligament, is the thick part of the articular capsule, strengthens the TMJ laterally, and prevents posterior dislocation of the TMJ. The extrinsic ligaments are the sphenomandibular ligament, which runs from the spine of the sphenoid to the lingula of the mandible and is the primary passive support of the mandible, and the stylomandibular ligament, a thickening of the fibrous capsule of the parotid gland, extending from the styloid process of the temporal bone to the angle of the mandible, which does not contribute significantly to the strength of the joint.
B. Dislocation of the TMJ is common in aged persons and females, due to wearing and resorption of the articular eminence and reducing muscle tone with advancing age.
C. The intrinsic (lateral) ligament is the thick part of the articular capsule, strengthens the joint laterally and prevents posterior dislocation. The sphenomandibular ligament, by contrast, runs from the spine of the sphenoid to the lingula of the mandible and is the primary passive support of the mandible, while the stylomandibular ligament is a thickening of the fibrous capsule of the parotid gland, running from the styloid process to the angle of the mandible, and does not contribute significantly to the strength of the joint.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the temporomandibular joint (TMJ) under the following headings: articular surfaces, articular capsule, and synovial membranes/compartments.
A(ii) Describe the ligaments of the TMJ.
B. Explain the clinical basis for why TMJ dislocation is commoner in the aged and in females.
C. Distinguish between the intrinsic (lateral) ligament and the extrinsic ligaments (sphenomandibular and stylomandibular) of the TMJ.

A patient who had parotid gland surgery some months previously now complains of sweating, warmth and redness over the cheek whenever he smells or tastes food.
(i) What is the diagnosis?
(ii) What predisposing event/injury accounts for this condition?
(iii) What is the pathophysiological basis of the presentation?
(iv) How is this condition also known?
questions.answerText:
(i) The diagnosis is Frey's syndrome, also known as gustatory sweating or auriculo-temporal nerve syndrome.
(ii) Frey's syndrome commonly occurs after parotid surgery or trauma, involving injury of the auriculo-temporal nerve and great auricular nerve.
(iii) During healing, the secreto-motor fibres of the auriculo-temporal nerve join with the great auricular nerve and reach the sweat glands of the facial skin; it is characterised by sweating, warmth and redness of the face, as a result of salivary stimulation by the smell or taste of food.
(iv) It is also known as gustatory sweating or auriculo-temporal nerve syndrome.

A(i) Molecular composition: The cell membrane consists of amphipathic phospholipids arranged so that the hydrophobic tails face inward (away from water) and the more hydrophilic head regions associate with the cytosolic and extracellular environments, forming a spherical lipid bilayer. The phospholipid bilayer was proposed by Gorter and Grendel in 1925. It also includes integral membrane proteins and peripheral membrane proteins (almost half of the total mass of the membrane), a network of tiny microfilaments of the cytoskeleton, and the lipid molecule cholesterol, which stabilizes and makes the cell membrane more rigid. Functions: structural support; semi-permeable membrane (controls what molecules enter and leave the cell); establishes and maintains an electrochemical gradient; contains receptors that recognize and respond to molecular signals; supports cell adhesion and cell communication. Membrane transport mechanisms: passive (osmosis, diffusion, simple diffusion), facilitated transport, active transport (primary and secondary), and vesicular transport (endocytosis: pinocytosis and phagocytosis; exocytosis).
A(ii) Several diseases have been implicated with defective membrane receptors. Pseudohypoparathyroidism is associated with defective parathyroid and growth hormone receptors. In these conditions, the glands produce the respective hormones, but the target cells do not respond because they lack normal receptors. Signal transduction can be hindered and cause diseases when mutations occur in the genes that encode and regulate receptor proteins.
B(i) Integral membrane proteins: are directly incorporated within the lipid bilayer; most are transmembrane proteins passing through the entire membrane; inserted into the lipid bilayer. Functions: transport, signal transduction, structural support. Peripheral membrane proteins: exhibit a looser association with the membrane; bound to the membrane indirectly by protein-protein interactions; located on the cytosolic face. Plasma membrane contains proteins called integrins that are linked to cytoplasmic molecules; through these linkages there is a connection between the extracellular matrix and cytoplasm, mediating cell adhesion and cell communication.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the histology of the cell membrane (plasma membrane) under the following headings: molecular composition (phospholipid bilayer and proteins), functions, and membrane transport mechanisms.
A(ii) Explain the clinical basis of diseases caused by defective membrane receptors, giving a named example from the documents.
B(i) Distinguish between integral (transmembrane) membrane proteins and peripheral membrane proteins, stating the function of each.

questions.answerText:
A(i) The duodenum is the first, shortest (about 25 cm) and widest part of the small intestine; it is C-shaped and mostly retroperitoneal, made up of four parts - superior (5 cm), descending (7.5-8 cm), horizontal (6-10 cm) and ascending (2.5 cm).
A(ii) The proximal 2.5 cm of the superior part is movable and intraperitoneal, attached to the lesser omentum above and greater omentum below; the rest of the duodenum is retroperitoneal, covered by peritoneum only on its anterior aspect.
A(iii) The superior part is anteriorly related to the quadrate lobe of the liver and gallbladder, and posteriorly to the gastroduodenal artery, bile duct, portal vein and inferior vena cava; the descending part is related medially to the head of pancreas and bile duct, laterally to the right colic flexure, and rests on the right kidney, ureter, psoas major and renal vessels, and receives the major duodenal papilla; the horizontal part crosses the inferior vena cava, aorta and L3 vertebra and is crossed anteriorly by the superior mesenteric vessels; the ascending part rises to the duodenojejunal flexure.
B(i) The proximal (superior) part of the duodenum is the most common site of duodenal ulcer.
B(ii) The duodenojejunal flexure is fixed by the suspensory muscle of the duodenum (ligament of Treitz), which passes posterior to the pancreas and splenic vein and anterior to the left renal vein; a weakness near this fixed flexure is the anatomical basis for a paraduodenal hernia.
C(i) The jejunum lies mainly in the left upper (infracolic) quadrant, has thicker, more vascular walls and a wider, often empty lumen, with long and few vasa recta, one or two layers of arterial arcades, numerous circular mucosal folds, and large, thick, abundant villi.
The ileum lies predominantly in the right lower quadrant and pelvis, has thinner, less vascular walls and a narrower, often loaded lumen, with short and numerous vasa recta and multiple layers of arterial arcades.
The ileum has smaller and sparser circular mucosal folds and shorter, thinner villi than the jejunum, but the terminal ileum has numerous Peyer's patches and more numerous solitary lymphatic follicles, which are absent or scanty in the jejunum.
The jejunum has mesenteric windows and less abundant mesenteric fat, whereas the ileum has no windows and more abundant mesenteric fat.
questions.question:
(A) Describe the duodenum under the headings: A(i) parts and dimensions A(ii) peritoneal relations A(iii) visceral relations.
(B) Explain the clinical basis for the duodenum's common site of ulceration and for paraduodenal hernia.
(C) Distinguish between the jejunum and the ileum.

questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Glenohumeral (shoulder) joint dislocation. It is a synovial joint.
(ii) Structures in the joint (anteroposterior and superoinferior): skin, subcutaneous tissue, glenohumeral ligaments, posterior capsule, rotator cuff muscles, deltoid nerve (nerve to deltoid), glenoid labrum, articular cartilage, joint space/cavity, synovial membrane, scapula.
(iii) Joint cartilage is hyaline cartilage (connective tissue of mesenchymal origin); the synovial membrane is a connective tissue lining; ligaments and capsule are dense regular connective tissue (collagen type I fibers, fibroblasts).
(iv) Immediate management: pain relief was administered at the University Health Center; shoulder X-ray was performed to confirm diagnosis.
(v) Predisposing factor: shallow glenoid labrum leads to instability and may lead to recurrent dislocation.
questions.question:
A 19-year-old undergraduate handball player suddenly became unable to lift his upper limb during a match. His shoulder sagged and he had severe pain in the axilla. He was taken to the University Health Center where pain was relieved and a diagnosis of glenohumeral joint dislocation was made following urgent shoulder X-ray.
(i) Identify the diagnosis and state the type of joint involved.
(ii) List all the structures found in the glenohumeral joint anteroposteriorly and superoinferiorly.
(iii) State the embryologic/tissue basis of the joint structures.
(iv) Describe the immediate management of the patient's pain and instability.
(v) State the factor that predisposes this joint to recurrent dislocation and the definitive clinical implication.

A dental student examining a cadaver notes that one of the major salivary glands located below the jaw is a branched tubuloacinar gland with 90% serous acini, 10% mucous tubules with serous demilunes, and easily observed striated ducts.
(i) Identify this gland and state where its duct opens in the oral cavity.
(ii) Describe the cells that form the demilunes in this gland, including what enzyme they secrete and its function.
(iii) Explain the immunological secretory mechanism of the salivary glands, including the type of antibody, the complex it forms, and why this complex is resistant to digestion.
(iv) Compare this gland with the sublingual gland under the following headings: predominant cell type, status of intralobular ducts, and demilunes.
(v) Describe what sialorrhea is and the conditions associated with it.
questions.answerText:
(i) Submandibular (submaxillary) gland. Its duct (submandibular duct) opens at the sublingual caruncle in the floor of the mouth.
(ii) The cells that form the demilunes in the submandibular gland secrete the enzyme lysozyme, whose main activity is to hydrolyze the walls of certain bacteria (bactericidal function).
(iii) Immunological secretory mechanism:
- Plasma cells secrete IgA, which forms a complex with a secretory component synthesized by the serous acinar, intercalated duct, and striated duct cells.
- The IgA-rich secretory complex released into the saliva is resistant to enzymatic digestion and constitutes an immunological defense mechanism against pathogens in the oral cavity.
(iv) Comparison:
- Submandibular gland: serous cells predominate (90% serous acinar, 10% mucous tubules with demilunes); striated ducts easily observed; intercalated ducts very short.
- Sublingual gland: mucous cells predominate; serous cells present almost exclusively on demilunes of mucous tubules; intralobular ducts are not as well developed as in other major salivary glands.
(v) Sialorrhea: excessive saliva production; associated with the autonomic activity of nausea, inflammation within the oral cavity, and rabies viral infection.

(i) The spleen receives its arterial supply from the splenic artery, the largest branch of the coeliac trunk.
The splenic artery runs laterally along the superior aspect of the pancreas, within the splenorenal ligament.
As it reaches the spleen it branches into about five vessels, each supplying a different vascular segment of the spleen.
Along its course it also gives off the short gastric and left gastroepiploic arteries to the stomach, and pancreatic branches to the pancreas.
Venous drainage is through the splenic vein, which combines with the superior mesenteric vein to form the hepatic portal vein.
(ii) The terminal arterial branches of the splenic artery do not anastomose with one another, so each supplies an independent vascular segment of the spleen.
This segmental (end-arterial) arrangement allows a surgeon to remove one diseased or injured segment (subtotal splenectomy) without compromising the blood supply of the remaining segments.
(iii) The tail of the pancreas lies within the splenorenal ligament, close to the splenic vessels at the hilum, and may be injured during splenectomy, producing a pancreatic fistula.
The spleen is the most frequently injured organ in the abdomen despite protection by the 9th to 12th ribs.
Severe blows to the left side may fracture ribs, producing sharp fragments that lacerate the spleen.
Blunt trauma elsewhere that suddenly raises intra-abdominal pressure can also rupture the spleen because its capsule is thin and its pulp is soft and pulpy.
A ruptured spleen bleeds profusely, causing severe intraperitoneal haemorrhage and shock, so splenectomy or subtotal splenectomy is often required to prevent the patient from bleeding to death.
questions.question:
(i) Describe the origin, course, branches and distribution of the splenic artery.
(ii) State the anatomical basis that makes subtotal (partial) splenectomy a safe surgical option.
(iii) Explain the anatomical basis of the complications that can follow injury to the spleen and its vasculature.

A newborn has cataract, cardiac defects and deafness; the mother had German (three-day) measles in early pregnancy.
(i) Give the diagnosis.
(ii) State the predisposing factors.
(iii) Explain the pathophysiology.
(iv) State the management.
questions.answerText:
(i) Congenital rubella syndrome (CRS), features being cataract, cardiac defects and deafness.
(i) Other observed abnormalities: mental deficiencies, microphthalmia, tooth defects, chorioretinitis and glaucoma.
(ii) Congenital anomalies are observed if the disease occurs during the first 4 to 5 weeks after fertilization; the earlier the maternal infection, the greater the danger of malformation.
(ii) The risk of anomalies is low in the 2nd and 3rd trimesters, but functional defects of the CNS and internal ear (hearing loss) may result.
(iii) The virus is an infective teratogen; the placenta is an imperfect barrier and large viral particles such as rubella cross by special mechanisms.
(iii) Congenital cataracts result from genetic reasons or rubella infection between the 4th and 7th week of gestation.
(iv) Management is not covered.

A(i) The greater sac is the main larger part; the lesser sac (omental bursa) lies posterior to the stomach, adjoining structures and lesser omentum; an incision through the anterolateral wall enters the greater sac; the sacs communicate through the epiploic foramen.
A(ii) The transverse mesocolon divides the cavity into supracolic and infracolic compartments; the infracolic lies posterior to the greater omentum and is divided by the mesentery of the small intestine into right and left infracolic spaces.
A(ii) Right space: triangular, between the root of the mesentery, ascending colon and right two-thirds of transverse colon; left: between the root, descending colon and left one-third of transverse colon, widening below into the pelvis.
A(iii) Right paracolic gutter lies lateral to the ascending colon and communicates with the hepatorenal recess and pelvic cavity; the left, lateral to the descending colon, is separated from the splenic area by the phrenicocolic ligament.
A(iv) Lesser sac: superior wall peritoneum over the caudate lobe and diaphragm; anterior lesser omentum, peritoneum of the posterior stomach and anterior two layers of greater omentum; posterior the posterior two layers, transverse colon and mesocolon, peritoneum over pancreas, left kidney and suprarenal gland.
A(iv) Omental foramen (of Winslow), behind the hepatoduodenal ligament, admits 2 fingers: liver superiorly, first part of duodenum inferiorly, hepatoduodenal ligament anteriorly, IVC and right crus posteriorly.
B(i) Median umbilical fold covers the urachal remnant, medial folds the obliterated umbilical arteries, lateral folds the inferior epigastric vessels; the supravesical fossa is a site for external supravesical hernia, the medial inguinal fossa for the less common direct hernia, the lateral inguinal fossa for the most common indirect hernia.
B(ii) Blockage of the uterine tubes (hysterosalpingography), peritonitis, ascites, paracentesis and intraperitoneal injection, flow of exudates in the paracolic gutters, and adhesions with adhesiotomy in intestinal obstruction.
C(i) The right paracolic gutter provides a route for spread of infection between the pelvic and upper abdominal regions, and the supracolic and infracolic compartments communicate freely through the gutters.
C(i) In the female the cavity communicates with the exterior via the uterine tubes, uterus and vagina.
C(i) Parietal peritoneum is supplied by the nerves of the adjacent body wall and diaphragm; visceral peritoneum by sympathetic nerves of the underlying viscus.
C(i) Receptors respond to overdistension, traction on mesenteries, spasm of smooth muscle and ischaemia.

(i) The first is an internal haemorrhoid (above Hilton's line, between mucosa and internal sphincter, generally painless); the second an external haemorrhoid (below Hilton's line, between perianal skin and external sphincter, generally painful).
(ii) Internal: tributary of the superior rectal vein (portal system); radicles and columns of superior rectal veins in the anal columns (6 to 10 folds of Morgagni); primary internal piles at 3 o'clock (left lateral), 7 o'clock (right posterior), 11 o'clock (right anterior).
(ii) External: tributary of the inferior rectal vein (via internal pudendal vein, systemic); the middle rectal vein drains to the internal iliac vein.
(iii) The submucosal veins are normally dilated (varicose in appearance) even in newborns; when the mucosa containing them prolapses they form haemorrhoids.
(iii) Above the pectinate line the nerve supply is autonomic and stretch-sensitive, so painless; below it the inferior rectal (pudendal) nerve is sensitive to pain and touch, so painful.
(iii) Superior rectal vein drains to inferior mesenteric vein then portal vein, forming a portal-systemic anastomosis with middle and inferior rectal veins.
(iv) Management is not covered.
questions.question:
A patient has a painless swelling of prolapsed mucosa containing veins above the line of the anal valves, while another has a painful swelling around the anus below the white line of Hilton.
(i) Give the diagnosis of each.
(ii) State the predisposing anatomical factors and the veins and positions involved.
(iii) Explain the pathophysiology and the difference in pain.
(iv) State the management.

A patient with reduced blood flow and oxygen to the heart muscle (cardiac ischaemia) presents with chest pain that radiates to the left side of the jaw and into the left arm.
(i) Identify the vessels whose territory is affected to explain reduced perfusion in this condition.
(ii) What is the basis for the pain being felt in the chest wall, jaw and arm rather than only over the heart?
(iii) Provide the clinico-anatomical reasoning for why the central nervous system misinterprets the source of this pain.
questions.answerText:
(i) Ischaemia/myocardial infarction results from decreased blood flow and oxygen to the heart muscle through the coronary arteries; occlusion of a coronary artery reduces perfusion of the territory it supplies. The right coronary artery supplies the right atrium, most of the right ventricle, part of the left ventricle and, in most people, the SA and AV nodes; the left coronary artery supplies the left atrium, most of the left ventricle, part of the right ventricle and most of the interventricular septum.
(ii) Cardiac afferent fibres carry pain sensations from the heart to the central nervous system via sympathetic afferents that form part of the cardiac plexus.
(iii) The dermatomes of the chest wall and upper limb in this region (T1-T5) have their neuronal cell bodies in the same dorsal root ganglia and synapse on the same second-order neurons in the spinal cord segments (T1-T5) as the general visceral afferent fibres from the heart. The central nervous system cannot clearly discern whether the pain is coming from the body wall or the viscera, so it perceives the pain as coming from the body wall - substernal pain, left arm/hand pain and jaw pain.

(i) The bleeding point described corresponds to the Kiesselbach plexus, or Little's area, in the anteroinferior third of the nasal septum.
(ii) This region represents where all 3 of the chief blood supplies to the internal nose converge: branches of the sphenopalatine artery (a lateral nasal branch to the conchae, a posterior septal branch to the septum), the greater and lesser palatine arteries (to the hard and soft palates), the superior labial artery (entering from the face), and branches of the anterior and posterior ethmoid arteries (from the ophthalmic artery), which also supply the septum, together with contribution of the superior labial artery anteriorly and the greater palatine artery posteriorly.
(iii) Venous blood leaves the region in veins that course alongside the arteries and drain into the facial, ophthalmic and sphenopalatine veins; these veins are significant for their direct communication with the cavernous sinus and for their lack of valves, features that potentiate the intracranial spread of infection - so the cavernous sinus can become involved.
(iv) Because the Kiesselbach plexus/Little's area is the single site in the anteroinferior nasal septum where all three chief nasal blood supplies converge, it is the most richly vascularised and superficial site in the nasal mucosa, making it the common source of nosebleeds (epistaxis), and because its draining veins communicate directly and without valves with the cavernous sinus, infection at this site has a direct anatomical route for intracranial spread.
questions.question:
A child presents with recurrent bleeding from the front of the nose, with the bleeding point visualised in the lower front part of the nasal septum.
(i) What structure/region is implicated by this site of bleeding?
(ii) What structures converge at this site to account for its vulnerability?
(iii) What distant structure can become involved if infection tracks along the venous drainage of this region, and why?
(iv) Give the clinico-anatomical reasoning for why this site is the common source of nosebleeds.

A newborn infant is born with a light gray shiny mass, the size of an orange, protruding from the umbilical region and covered by a thin transparent membrane.
(i) Name the congenital anomaly and the origin of the covering membrane.
(ii) State the composition of the mass and the embryologic basis of the protrusion.
(iii) Describe the normal development of the midgut that explains the anomaly.
(iv) State the associated anomalies and the definitive management.
questions.answerText:
(i) Omphalocele: herniation of abdominal viscera through a large umbilical ring defect (a defect of lateral plate mesoderm).
(i) The viscera are covered by peritoneal and amniotic membrane.
(ii) The mass is abdominal viscera (bowel) that failed to return to the body cavity.
(ii) Basis: failure of the bowel to return to the body cavity from its physiological herniation during the 6th to 10th week.
(iii) Midgut derivatives: small intestine including the duodenum distal to the opening of the bile duct, caecum, appendix, ascending colon and right half to two-thirds of the transverse colon, supplied by the superior mesenteric artery.
(iii) The elongating midgut forms a U-shaped loop projecting into the umbilical cord (physiological umbilical herniation, beginning of the 6th week); it rotates 90° counterclockwise around the axis of the SMA (cranial limb to the right, caudal limb to the left).
(iii) During the 10th week the intestines return: small intestine first, then the large intestine, which rotates a further 180° counterclockwise and occupies the right side; retraction is helped by regression of the mesonephric kidney, reduced growth of the liver and expansion of the abdominal cavity.
(iv) About 50% have other serious congenital or chromosomal abnormalities; associated defects include cardiac anomalies and neural tube defects.
(iv) Definitive management is not covered.

questions.question:
Describe the femoral triangle and adductor canal under the following headings, state how they relate to common pathologies, and explain the anatomical basis of referred pain to the knee from the hip.
A(i) Boundaries, roof, and floor of the femoral triangle; contents from lateral to medial
A(ii) Femoral artery — branches within the femoral triangle, including the profunda femoris and its branches
B(i) Adductor canal — boundaries, contents, and where it terminates
B(ii) Clinical basis: femoral hernia, femoral pulse palpation, and profunda femoris in femoral artery occlusion
C(i) Explain why hip joint disease causes referred pain at the knee, based on the nerve supply of both joints
questions.answerText:
A(i) Boundaries: superiorly — inguinal ligament; medially — medial border of adductor longus; laterally — medial border of sartorius; apex — where adductor longus and sartorius cross. Roof: fascia lata (deep fascia) pierced by the great saphenous vein at the saphenous opening (fossa ovalis). Floor: formed by iliopsoas laterally and pectineus medially. Contents from lateral to medial: femoral nerve, femoral artery, femoral vein (the mnemonic 'NAVY' — from lateral: Nerve, Artery, Vein, Y-fronts/lymphatics). The femoral pulse can be palpated as it enters the femoral triangle, midway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis — the mid-inguinal point.
A(ii) The femoral artery divides to give the profunda femoris 5 cm below the inguinal ligament. Branches of the femoral artery (mnemonic: 'Does She Scream During Poking Sessions?'): Deep external pudendal arteries, Superficial epigastric, Superficial external pudendal, Descending genicular artery, Profunda femoris artery, Superficial circumflex iliac. Profunda femoris arises from the posterolateral aspect of the femoral artery; it gives: (1) Perforating branches — 3 or 4 arteries that perforate adductor magnus, contributing to medial and posterior thigh. (2) Lateral femoral circumflex artery — wraps around anterior and lateral side of femur, supplying muscles on lateral aspect of thigh. (3) Medial femoral circumflex artery — wraps around posterior side of femur, supplying its neck and head; in a fracture of the femoral neck this artery can easily be damaged and avascular necrosis of the femoral head can occur.
B(i) The adductor canal is a passageway in the medial thigh. The adductor hiatus is an opening between the aponeurotic distal attachment of the adductor part of adductor magnus and the tendinous distal attachment of the hamstring part. The hiatus transmits the femoral artery and vein from the adductor canal in the thigh to the popliteal fossa posterior to the knee. It is located just lateral and superior to the adductor tubercle of the femur.
B(ii) Femoral hernia: not covered. Femoral pulse: palpated at mid-inguinal point (midway between ASIS and pubic symphysis). In femoral artery occlusion, the profunda femoris artery is the main collateral channel because the superior muscular branches of the popliteal artery have clinically important anastomoses with the terminal part of the profunda femoris and gluteal arteries, maintaining perfusion to the leg.
C(i) The posterior division of the obturator nerve supplies both the hip and the knee joint; therefore, pain from hip pathology is referred along this common nerve pathway to present as knee pain. This is the basis of Hilton's law applied to the hip: 'the nerve supplying the joint also supplies the muscles moving the joint and the skin covering the insertion of these muscles.' The femoral nerve also supplies the hip joint via intermediate and cutaneous branches and the knee via branches of obturator and femoral nerves.

(i) Cell type: Fibroblast. It is the most common cell type found in connective tissue. The mature quiescent form is the fibrocyte, which shows less active synthetic activity.
(ii) Products synthesized: Fibroblasts synthesize collagen, reticular and elastic fibers, and the amorphous extracellular substance including glycosaminoglycans and glycoproteins. Fibroblasts are also involved in the production of growth factors that influence cell growth and differentiation.
(iii) Histological differences: Active fibroblast — elongated, spindle-shaped cells with many cell processes; oval, pale-staining, regular nuclei with prominent nucleoli; abundant rough endoplasmic reticulum and active Golgi bodies. Quiescent fibrocyte — smaller than the active fibroblast and tends to be spindle-shaped; fewer processes; smaller, darker, elongated nucleus; acidophilic cytoplasm; small amount of rough endoplasmic reticulum.
(iv) Myofibroblast: has features of both fibroblasts and smooth muscle cells. Myofibroblasts have most of the morphological characteristics of fibroblasts but contain increased amounts of actin microfilaments and myosin and behave like smooth muscle cells. Their activity is responsible for wound closure after tissue injury (wound contraction).
(v) The regenerative capacity of connective tissue is clearly observed in organs damaged by ischemia, inflammation, or traumatic injury. Spaces left after such injuries, especially in tissues whose cells divide poorly or not at all (e.g., cardiac muscle), are filled by connective tissue, forming dense irregular scar tissue. In adults, fibroblasts in connective tissue rarely undergo division; mitoses are observed only when the organism requires additional fibroblasts. The healing depends on the reparative capacity of connective tissue, particularly the activity and growth of fibroblasts.
questions.question:
A pathology specimen from a surgical biopsy shows a tissue section with the following features: elongated spindle-shaped cells with many cell processes, oval pale-staining regular nuclei with prominent nucleoli, abundant rough endoplasmic reticulum and active Golgi bodies in the cytoplasm, and active synthesis of extracellular matrix components including glycosaminoglycans and glycoproteins.
(i) Identify the cell type and state its mature (quiescent) counterpart.
(ii) List all the products synthesized by this cell type.
(iii) Describe the histological differences between the active and quiescent forms.
(iv) Identify the differential cell type involved in wound healing that has features of both this cell and smooth muscle, and describe its role.
(v) Apply clinico-anatomical reasoning to explain how this cell participates in organ repair after ischemia.

questions.answerText:
(i) The pericardial cavity, the potential space between the parietal and visceral layers of serous pericardium that normally contains a thin film of fluid, is affected; the diagnosis is cardiac tamponade due to pericardial effusion.
(ii) The heart's ventricles are compressed and prevented from expanding fully.
(iii) Pericarditis, inflammation of the pericardium, has many causes, including bacterial infection and myocardial infarction, and its main symptom is chest pain; it can cause acute cardiac tamponade due to fluid accumulation in the pericardial cavity.
(iv) The fibrous pericardium is relatively inextensible; while this property normally prevents the heart from increasing in size too rapidly, placing a physical limit on cardiac enlargement, the same inextensibility means that when fluid accumulates within the enclosed pericardial cavity, it cannot expand to accommodate the extra volume, so pressure builds up on the heart instead, impairing ventricular filling.
questions.question:
A patient develops accumulation of fluid within the pericardial cavity, presenting with chest pain; the relatively inextensible fibrous pericardium places extreme pressure on the heart, preventing the ventricles from expanding fully.
(i) Identify the space/structure primarily affected and, from the clinical picture described, the diagnosis.
(ii) What structures are compressed as a result of this fluid accumulation?
(iii) What is a documented differential cause of this presentation?
(iv) Provide the clinico-anatomical reasoning for why the fibrous pericardium worsens this condition rather than protecting against it.

questions.answerText:
(i) Tissue: Epithelial tissue. Criteria for classification: the histological appearance describing the various epithelia is that seen in vertical sections; epithelial cells are described as squamous (flat), cuboidal (more square or cube-like), or columnar (tall and thin). It is also classified by number of layers: simple (one cell thick) or stratified (multiple layers). Transitional epithelium can also be recognised. Nuclear shape corresponds roughly to cell shape: tall cells have elongated nuclei; squamous cells have flat nuclei; cuboidal or pyramidal cells have more spherical nuclei.
(ii) Embryologic origin: epithelial tissue is derived from all three germ layers — ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm. Endoderm forms the inner layer (interior stomach lining, gastrointestinal tract, lungs); mesoderm forms the middle layer (muscle, bone, blood, urogenital tissues); ectoderm forms the outer layer (skin and neuroectoderm).
(iii) Functional specializations on the free surface: microvilli, stereocilia, cilia, and a brush border.
(iv) Cell junctions: tight junctions (occluding junctions) — seal cells together in an epithelium, enabling the organism to maintain paracellular transport control. Adherens junctions (zonula adherens) — protein complexes at cell-cell junctions, usually more basal than tight junctions, providing attachment. Desmosomes (maculae adherentes) — anchor cells; appear in ribbon-like patterns. Gap junctions — provide ionic continuity between adjacent cells. Junctional complexes are especially abundant in epithelial tissues.
(v) Epithelial cells are constantly subjected to mechanical damage and show many dividing cells (mitoses) in order to replace lost cells. In wounds, the epithelia need to cover the lesion as rapidly as possible, repair the lining tissue, and prevent damage to the underlying tissues. The basement membrane (containing the glycoprotein laminin) supports epithelial regeneration.
questions.question:
A 25-year-old student in a histology practical identifies a tissue section showing cells arranged in sheets with almost no intercellular material, cells packed tightly together with very little extracellular matrix, a prominent basement membrane, and cells showing mitoses at the basal layer. The lecturer asks the student to identify the tissue and answer the following:
(i) Identify the tissue type and state the general criteria for classifying it.
(ii) State the embryologic origin of all epithelial types.
(iii) List the functional specializations found on the free surface of epithelial cells.
(iv) Describe the types of cell junctions found in epithelial tissue and their function.
(v) Explain the significance of epithelial cells showing many mitoses at the basal layer.

Describe the brachial artery:
A(i) Origin and termination
A(ii) Course
A(iii) Branches
B. State the safe site associated with clinical use of the brachial artery.
C. Explain the anatomical basis of the deformity/complication (Volkmann's ischaemic contracture) that can follow injury to this artery.
questions.answerText:
A(i) The brachial artery provides the main arterial supply to the arm and is the continuation of the axillary artery; it begins at the inferior border of teres major and ends in the cubital fossa opposite the neck of the radius.
A(ii) Under cover of the bicipital aponeurosis, it divides into the radial and ulnar arteries.
A(iii) Its branches include the deep brachial (profunda brachii) artery, which accompanies the radial nerve, the superior ulnar collateral artery, which accompanies the ulnar nerve, and the inferior ulnar collateral artery.
B. During blood pressure measurement, the stethoscope is placed over the brachial artery in the cubital fossa, and the cubital fossa is the site used to palpate the brachial pulse.
C. Volkmann's ischaemic contracture is a deformity of the hand, fingers and wrist caused by injury to the muscles of the forearm.
The classical presentation is a supracondylar fracture of the humerus, although fracture of the arm or elbow may also result in this deformity; the artery involved is the brachial artery.
The contracture occurs when there is a lack of blood flow (ischaemia) to the forearm, usually from increased pressure resulting from swelling (compartment syndrome).
Because there is very little room within each fascial compartment of the arm and forearm, haemorrhage or oedema following injury to the brachial artery can cause secondary vascular compression: veins are affected first, and later the arteries, resulting in ischaemia of the affected part.
The classical presentation of the resulting acute compartment syndrome is remembered by "the five P's": pulselessness, paraesthesia, poikilothermia, paralysis and pallor.
There are three levels of severity of the resulting Volkmann's contracture: the mildest involves flexion contracture of only two or three fingers with no or limited loss of sensation; a more severe form involves all fingers flexed with the thumb stuck in the palm and some sensory loss.
The most severe form involves all the muscles in the forearm that flex and extend the wrist and fingers, producing a severely disabling condition.
This progression illustrates how injury to the brachial artery at the elbow can produce a graded functional deficit distally in the hand and fingers.

A(i) Definition: The cell cycle, or cell-division cycle, is the series of events that takes place in a cell leading to its division and duplication (replication). In cells with a nucleus (eukaryotes), the cell cycle can be divided into two brief periods: interphase (during which the cell grows, accumulates nutrients needed for mitosis and duplicates its DNA) and the mitosis (M) phase (during which the cell splits itself into two distinct cells, often called daughter cells). Phases: G1 (Gap 1) — cell grows; S phase (synthesis) — chromosomes are replicated; G2 (Gap 2) — cell grows more and prepares for mitosis; M phase (mitosis and cytokinesis) — cell division. Cells that have temporarily or reversibly stopped dividing are said to have entered the G0 phase (quiescence). Two key regulatory molecules: cyclins and cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs), which determine a cell's progress through the cell cycle.
A(ii) In non-disjunction, a chromosome may fail to separate during anaphase: one daughter cell will receive both sister chromosomes (leading to trisomy — three copies) and the other will receive none (leading to monosomy — one copy). These cells are considered aneuploid, a condition often associated with cancer. Other chromosomal abnormalities: deletion — an arm of the chromosome may be broken and the fragment lost. Translocation — the fragment incorrectly reattaches to another, non-homologous chromosome. Inversion — the fragment reattaches to the original chromosome in reverse orientation. The effect may range from no noticeable effect to cancer induction or organism death.
B(i) Apoptosis (programmed cell death): biochemical events lead to characteristic cell changes including blebbing, loss of cell membrane asymmetry and attachment, cell shrinkage, nuclear fragmentation, chromatin condensation, and chromosomal DNA fragmentation. Apoptosis differs from necrosis in that the cellular debris does not damage the organism. Necrosis: a form of traumatic cell death that results from acute cellular injury; cellular debris can damage the organism. Clinical consequences: excessive apoptosis causes atrophy (e.g., ischemic damage); insufficient apoptosis results in uncontrolled cell proliferation such as cancer.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the cell cycle under the following headings: definition, phases (G1, S, G2, M), and the two key regulatory molecules that control progression through the cycle.
A(ii) Explain the clinical consequences of errors in mitosis, naming three chromosomal abnormalities that can result.
B(i) Distinguish between apoptosis and necrosis, giving the distinguishing morphological changes and clinical consequences of each.

questions.answerText:
A(i) The cloaca is divided by the urorectal septum (mesoderm) into the urogenital sinus and the anal canal; the tip of the septum forms the perineal body.
A(i) The urogenital sinus has three parts: a vesical part forming most of the bladder and continuous with the allantois; a pelvic part forming the urethra in the neck of the bladder, the prostatic and membranous urethra in males and the entire urethra in females; and a phallic part growing toward the genital tubercle.
A(ii) The bladder develops mainly from the vesical part; the trigone derives from the caudal ends of the mesonephric ducts.
A(ii) The whole bladder epithelium is derived from the endoderm of the vesical part; the other layers of the wall develop from adjacent splanchnic mesenchyme.
A(iii) At first the bladder is continuous with the allantois, which constricts into a thick fibrous cord, the urachus, extending from the apex of the bladder to the umbilicus; in adults it becomes the median umbilical ligament.
A(iii) The urachus remains when the lumen of the allantois is obliterated.
A(iv) The epithelium of most of the male urethra and the entire female urethra is derived from the endoderm of the urogenital sinus.
A(iv) In males the distal urethra in the glans derives from a solid cord of ectodermal cells growing inward from the tip of the glans; the connective tissue and smooth muscle of the urethra in both sexes come from splanchnic mesenchyme.
B(i) Urachal cyst, fistula and sinus are listed anomalies; exstrophy of the bladder is a ventral body wall defect with exposed bladder mucosa (2 per 100,000 live births) from failure of formation of the anterior bladder and part of the anterior abdominal wall.
B(i) Duplication of the ureter gives an ectopic opening into the urethra or vagina.
C(i) Exstrophy of the cloaca is a more severe ventral body wall defect in which mesoderm migration to the midline is inhibited and the tail fold fails to progress (1 in 30,000), associated with early amniotic rupture.
C(i) It includes exstrophy of the bladder, spinal defects with or without meningomyelocele, and imperforate anus.

(i) Ruptured spleen from trauma, causing severe intraperitoneal haemorrhage and shock.
(ii) The splenorenal (lienorenal) ligament, extending from the hilum of the spleen to the anterior surface of the left kidney, must be mobilised; the hilum lies on the inferomedial part of the gastric impression and transmits the splenic vessels and nerves, and gives attachment to the gastrosplenic and splenorenal ligaments.
(iii) The tail of the pancreas lies within the splenorenal ligament and may be injured during splenectomy, producing a pancreatic fistula.
(iv) The terminal branches of the splenic artery do not anastomose with each other, giving rise to independent vascular segments of the spleen; this segmental arrangement enables a surgeon to remove one segment (subtotal splenectomy) without affecting the blood supply of the others.
questions.question:
A patient with a ruptured spleen from blunt abdominal trauma is scheduled for splenectomy.
(i) What is the diagnosis necessitating surgery?
(ii) Name the ligament that must be mobilised, and the anatomical landmark through which the splenic vessels enter/exit.
(iii) Identify a nearby structure at risk of injury during this procedure.
(iv) Describe the anatomical (vascular segmentation) basis that allows a variant of this operation to preserve part of the spleen.

A(i) Describe the histology of the eye under the following headings: three tunics (layers) of the eyeball, contents of each layer, and the photoreceptor cell types in the retina.
A(ii) Explain the clinical basis of cataract and state the histological changes in the lens.
B(i) Distinguish between the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and the neural retina, stating the function of each and their embryological origin.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Three tunics: The eye has three layers. Outer tunic: the sclera and cornea; the sclera serves primarily as a structural support for the optic apparatus. Middle layer (vascular layer, uvea): the choroid, ciliary body, and iris. The iris functions as a contractile diaphragm (the aperture of the eye). Inner tunic: the retina — a double-layered epithelium consisting of an outer pigmented layer and an inner neural retina; it is subdivided into 10 recognizable layers. The outermost layer (closest to the choriocapillaris) contains the photoreceptors whose outer segments are in close contact with pigmented epithelial cells. Contents: the vitreous body fills the space between the lens and retina; the aqueous humor is in the anterior and posterior chambers; the lens is a transparent biconvex structure that, along with the cornea, focuses light on the retina. Photoreceptors: rods — more sensitive to light, primarily used in dim light. Cones — require more intense lighting; conical in shape. There are also bipolar cells, horizontal cells, amacrine cells, and Müller glia cells, and a retinal ganglion cell layer.
A(ii) Cataract: when the lens becomes opaque, the condition is termed cataract, which may also be caused by excessive exposure to ultraviolet radiation. Histological changes: the lens has three principal components — lens capsule (corresponds to a thick, elastic basal lamina), subcapsular epithelium, and lens fibers. Opacification of the lens fibers makes them less transparent; this is the basis of cataract. A myopic (short-sighted) eye can be corrected by wearing glasses with concave lenses; a hyperopic eye with convex lenses.
B(i) Retinal pigment epithelium (RPE): the outer cell layer is pigmented; it lies between the choroid and the neural retina; Bruch's membrane is located between the choroid and the RPE. Tight junctions between RPE cells establish a blood-retina barrier. Neural retina: the inner cell layer; it is a multi-layered structure containing photoreceptors (rods and cones), neurons, and glial cells. The optic nerve (and the retina) arises in the embryo as an outgrowth of the diencephalon (forebrain); thus the optic nerve is not a true peripheral nerve — its myelin is produced by oligodendrocytes (not Schwann cells), and it is associated with multiple sclerosis.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the gross and microscopic structure of the large salivary glands under the following headings: capsule and septa; parenchyma (secretory end pieces); cell types in the secretory end pieces; the duct system in sequence from secretory unit to oral cavity.
A(ii) State the type of secretion produced by each of the three pairs of major salivary glands and by the minor glands.
B(i) Distinguish between striated ducts and intercalated ducts, including location, epithelium, and function.
B(ii) Explain how saliva is modified as it passes through the duct system.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Structure:
- Capsule and septa: a capsule of connective tissue rich in collagen fibers surrounds the large salivary glands; septa of connective tissue originate from the capsule and divide the glands into lobules; each lobule contains numerous secretory units (acini).
- Parenchyma: consists of secretory end pieces and a branching duct system arranged in lobules separated by septae of connective tissue from the capsule. Vessels and nerves enter at the hilum and gradually branch into the lobules.
- Cell types in secretory end pieces: serous cells (polarized protein-secreting cells, pyramidal in shape, round nuclei, well-stained RER, apical secretory granules; joined apically by tight and adherent junctions; form a spherical unit called an acinus with a very small central lumen; secrete enzymes and other proteins); mucous cells; and nonsecretory myoepithelial cells.
- Duct system in sequence: secretory end pieces → intercalated ducts (lined by simple low cuboidal epithelium, surrounded by myoepithelial cells) → striated ducts (intralobular) → interlobular (excretory/striated ducts drain into these) → interlobar ducts → main duct (opens into the oral cavity, lined with nonkeratinized-stratified squamous epithelium).
A(ii) Secretion types:
- Parotid gland: serous and watery.
- Submandibular and sublingual glands: seromucous secretion.
- Minor glands: mostly mucous.
- Type depends on content of glycoprotein mucin: serous, seromucous, or mucous.
B(i)
- Intercalated ducts: several short intercalated ducts join to form striated ducts; they are lined by cuboidal epithelial cells that have the ability to divide and differentiate into secretory or ductal cells; also called intralobular ducts.
- Striated ducts: characterized by radial striations that extend from the bases of the cells to the level of the central nuclei; striations consist of infoldings of the basal plasma membrane with numerous elongated mitochondria aligned parallel to the infolded membranes (characteristic of ion-transporting cells); they have a folded basal membrane enabling active transport; also called intralobular ducts.
B(ii) Saliva is modified by the cells of the duct system draining the secretory units: much Na+ and Cl- is reabsorbed while certain growth factors and digestive enzymes are added. Water resorption and ion secretion in the striated ducts make saliva hypotonic (reduced Na and Cl ions; increased carbonate and potassium ions).

(i) Meckel's (ileal) diverticulum: persistence of the proximal part of the vitelline duct, in 2% of normal individuals, 2 feet from the ileocaecal valve and 2 inches long.
(i) Variants: vitelline fistula (meconium oozes out of the umbilicus); vitelline cyst (part of the duct not obliterated); vitelline cord or ligament (attaches ileum to umbilicus); combinations may occur.
(i) Normally the tip of the midgut loop connected to the yolk sac by the vitelline duct persists until the end of the 10th week.
(ii) A persistent vitelline duct of any degree may contain ectopic gastric mucosa and pancreatic acini, causing intestinal ulceration and bleeding.
(iii) Management options and justification are not covered.
questions.question:
An individual has a persistent proximal part of the vitelline duct (vitello-intestinal duct) containing ectopic gastric mucosa and pancreatic acini.
(i) Give the diagnosis, its frequency and the embryologic variants of persistence.
(ii) State the complications.
(iii) State the management options and justify one.

A patient presents with a drooping eyelid and an eye that cannot move normally on one side, with weakness of the limbs on the opposite side of the body.
(i) What is the diagnosis, and what is the site of the lesion?
(ii) What is the pathological basis of this presentation?
questions.answerText:
(i) The diagnosis is Weber's syndrome, a midbrain stroke; it is described as occulomotor palsy with contralateral hemiplegia.
(ii) A stroke is a sudden onset of neurological deficits due to a cerebrovascular accident; cerebrovascular disease may be ischaemic (due to blockage of vessels by a thrombus or embolus) or haemorrhagic (due to rupture of an artery or aneurysm from high blood pressure). Structures supplied by the interpeduncular branch include CN III and CN IV, and syndromes arising here include oculomotor palsy with contralateral hemiplegia (Weber's syndrome) and trochlear nerve palsy; the Circle of Willis is the anastomotic channel between the internal carotid and vertebrobasilar systems, sited around the infundibulum of the pituitary and optic chiasma, and provides blood when major arteries become occluded.

A(i) In the middle of the 4th week a fusiform dilatation appears in the caudal foregut; from the 4th to 8th week it grows in all directions into a sac-like structure, the dorsal border growing faster than the ventral to give the greater and lesser curvatures; it acquires its characteristic shape by the 8th week.
A(i) The ventral border moves to the right and the dorsal border to the left; the original left side becomes ventral and the right side dorsal (90° clockwise rotation), so the left vagus supplies the anterior wall and the right vagus the posterior wall.
A(ii) Endoderm gives gastric pits and glands; splanchnic mesoderm gives connective tissue, smooth muscle and blood vessels; neural crest gives the submucosal and myenteric autonomic plexuses.
A(ii) Rugae, pits and smooth muscle appear by 8 weeks; chief and parietal cells at 10 to 20 weeks; glands become functional and secrete HCl and enzymes at 8 to 9 months.
A(iii) Descent: the cardiac end descends from C2 at 4 weeks to T11 at 12 weeks because of rapid elongation of the oesophagus; tilting: vertical at 4 weeks to oblique by 8 weeks due to faster growth of the greater curvature.
A(iii) Rotation: 90° around a vertical axis, the cranial end moving left and slightly inferior and the caudal end right and superior, so the long axis is almost transverse; the dorsal mesentery and stomach shift to the left.
A(iv) The stomach is suspended by double-layered mesenteries (mesogastria); rotation pulls the dorsal mesogastrium to the left, forming the omental bursa, a pouch of peritoneal cavity behind the stomach that communicates with the peritoneal cavity on the right.
B(i) Pyloric stenosis is hypertrophy of the stomach musculature in the region of the pylorus with extreme narrowing of the lumen; it is one of the most common stomach abnormalities in infants and is believed to develop during fetal life.
B(i) It presents with forceful (projectile) non-bilious vomiting about 1 hour after feeding; the hypertrophied sphincter can be palpated as a spherical nodule; it is due to overproliferation, not a recanalization error, and is more common in males, probably with a genetic basis.
C(i) Dorsal mesogastrium: connects the stomach to the dorsal body wall; the spleen develops in it; it forms the greater omentum, lienorenal ligament and gastrosplenic ligament.
C(i) Ventral mesogastrium: attaches the gut tube to the anterior abdominal wall; the liver develops in it; it forms the lesser omentum, visceral peritoneum of the liver and falciform ligament.
C(i) With rotation, the greater curvature with its dorsal mesogastrium becomes the greater omentum, and the ventral mesogastrium between the lesser curvature and the liver becomes the lesser omentum.

(i) The thymus and the parathyroid glands, the derivatives of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches.
(ii) DiGeorge sequence (the 3rd and 4th pouch syndrome) is listed alongside other craniofacial defects arising from anomalies of the pharyngeal arches: Treacher Collins syndrome (mandibulofacial dysostosis, with deformities of the ears, eyes, cheekbones and chin, and possible breathing problems, visual problems, cleft palate and hearing loss), Pierre Robin sequence (the 1st arch sequence, with micrognathia, glossoptosis and airway obstruction), and Goldenhar syndrome (oculo-auriculo-vertebral).
(iii) The thymus arises from the endoderm of the ventral part of the third pouch, the inferior parathyroid also arises from the third pouch and descends with the thymus into the thorax, and the superior parathyroid arises from the fourth pouch along with the thyroid gland in the neck.
Because the thymus and inferior parathyroid share a third-pouch origin, and the superior parathyroid shares a fourth-pouch origin, a defect of third and fourth pouch development affects the thymus and parathyroid glands together, distinguishing DiGeorge sequence from the other, differently-derived craniofacial defects listed (Treacher Collins arising from neural crest craniofacial defects, Pierre Robin from the first arch, and Goldenhar from oculo-auriculo-vertebral structures).
questions.question:
Examination of an infant with craniofacial abnormalities raises concern for a pouch-derived syndrome; imaging is requested to assess the neck and mediastinum.
(i) Identify the organs/structures likely to be affected.
(ii) State the differential pathologies to consider.
(iii) Give the clinico-anatomical reasoning linking these findings.

In a histology practical, a student examines a section of the inner ear and notes the following: a membranous labyrinth housed within a bony labyrinth; a cochlear duct containing endolymph; a basilar membrane; scala vestibuli and scala tympani containing perilymph; and specialized receptor cells.
(i) Identify the part of the ear being examined and state its overall function.
(ii) Describe the three divisions of the ear, listing the structures found in each division.
(iii) Name the three ossicles in the middle ear, the joints between them, and the two muscles that insert into them.
(iv) State the nerve at risk in middle ear infections and name the communication between the middle ear and the nasopharynx.
(v) Explain the embryologic significance of the auditory tube and its clinical implication in children.
questions.answerText:
(i) The inner ear (internal ear) is being examined. Functions: the vestibulocochlear apparatus serves two functions related to equilibrium and hearing.
(ii) Three divisions: External ear — includes the pinna (visible ear) and external auditory canal; the canal contains specialized ceruminous (ear-wax) glands; the eardrum (tympanic membrane) is a thin membrane separating the external and middle ears; the tympanic membrane is covered externally with squamous epithelium. Middle ear (tympanic cavity) — an irregular space lined by simple cuboidal epithelium; contains the three middle ear ossicles (malleus, incus, and stapes); contains two small muscles (tensor tympani and stapedius); communicates anteriorly with the oropharynx via the auditory (eustachian) tube and posteriorly. Inner ear — the membranous labyrinth is completely within the temporal bone; the bony labyrinth houses the smaller membranous labyrinth (epithelium-lined tubes and chambers); contains scala vestibuli (perilymph), cochlear duct (endolymph), and scala tympani (perilymph); the vestibular organ maintains equilibrium.
(iii) Ossicles: malleus (hammer), incus (anvil), and stapes (stirrup). These bones are articulated by synovial joints and are covered with simple cuboidal epithelium. Two muscles: tensor tympani (inserts into the malleus) and stapedius (inserts into the stapes).
(iv) Chorda tympani nerve passes through the middle ear and is at risk in middle ear infections. The auditory (eustachian) tube communicates the middle ear anteriorly with the oropharynx/nasopharynx.
(v) The middle ear may show upper respiratory tract infections via the auditory tubes. In children, the short auditory tubes make children more susceptible to middle ear infections (otitis media) because the short tube allows pathogens to travel more easily from the nasopharynx into the middle ear.

questions.question:
Describe the muscles of the posterior compartment of the leg under the following headings and explain why disease of tibialis posterior leads to collapse of the medial longitudinal arch.
A(i) Classify muscles into superficial and deep groups; give origin, insertion, innervation, and action of each
A(ii) The calcaneal (Achilles) tendon — formation, course, and clinical significance
B(i) The tibial nerve — course in the posterior compartment, branches, safe site for tarsal tunnel block
B(ii) How tibialis posterior supports the medial longitudinal arch and why its dysfunction causes pes planus
C(i) Distinguish the actions of gastrocnemius from soleus, explaining the anatomical basis of their different clinical testing
questions.answerText:
A(i) Superficial group (3 muscles): Gastrocnemius — lateral head from lateral aspect of lateral condyle of femur; medial head (specific origin not detailed here); insertion: posterior surface of calcaneus via calcaneal tendon; innervation: tibial nerve (S1, S2); action: plantarflexes ankle when knee is extended, raises heel during walking, flexes leg at knee joint. Soleus — posterior aspect of head and superior quarter of posterior surface of fibula; soleal line and middle third of medial border of tibia; tendinous arch; insertion: posterior surface of calcaneus via calcaneal tendon; innervation: tibial nerve (S1, S2); action: plantarflexes ankle independent of position of knee, steadies leg on foot. Plantaris — inferior end of lateral supracondylar line of femur, oblique popliteal ligament; insertion: posterior surface of calcaneus via calcaneal tendon; innervation: tibial nerve (S1, S2); action: weakly assists gastrocnemius in plantarflexing ankle. Deep group (4 muscles): Popliteus — lateral surface of lateral condyle of femur and lateral meniscus; posterior surface of tibia superior to soleal line; tibial nerve (L4, L5, S1); weakly flexes knee, unlocks it by rotating femur 5° on fixed tibia, and medially rotates tibia of unplanted limb. Flexor hallucis longus — inferior 2/3 of posterior surface of fibula; base of distal phalanx of great toe; tibial nerve (S2, S3); flexes great toe at all joints, weakly plantarflexes ankle, supports medial longitudinal arch. Flexor digitorum longus — medial part of posterior surface of tibia inferior to soleal line; bases of distal phalanges of lateral 4 digits; tibial nerve (S2, S3); flexes lateral 4 digits, plantarflexes ankle, supports longitudinal arches. Tibialis posterior — interosseous membrane, posterior tibia inferior to soleal line, posterior fibula; tuberosity of navicular, cuneiform, cuboid, sustentaculum tali of calcaneus, bases of 2nd, 3rd, and 4th metatarsals; tibial nerve (L4, L5); plantarflexes ankle and inverts foot.
A(ii) The calcaneal tendon is formed by the union of the tendons of gastrocnemius, soleus, and plantaris; it inserts into the posterior surface of the calcaneus. It is the largest and strongest tendon in the body. Clinical significance: rupture of the Achilles tendon (commonly felt as a 'pop' and tested by Thompson's squeeze test) results in inability to plantarflex the foot. Not covered in further detail.
B(i) The posterior tibial artery enters the sole of the foot through the tarsal tunnel, accompanying the tibial nerve. The tibial nerve enters the sole of the foot via the tarsal tunnel and then splits into the lateral and medial plantar arteries. For a tarsal tunnel block, the posterior tibial pulse can be palpated inferoposteriorly to the medial malleolus, where the artery turns to enter the foot — the tibial nerve lies adjacent.
B(ii) Tibialis posterior inserts into the tuberosity of the navicular, cuneiform, cuboid, sustentaculum tali of calcaneus, and the bases of the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th metatarsals — the very bones that form the medial longitudinal arch. It plantarflexes the ankle and inverts the foot; by pulling the navicular and cuneiforms downward and inward it actively maintains the height of the medial longitudinal arch. Dysfunction (e.g., from tenosynovitis or rupture) leads to eversion of the calcaneus, slipping down of the talus and navicular, and pes planus — collapse of the medial longitudinal arch.
C(i) Gastrocnemius spans the knee joint (arising from the femoral condyle) and the ankle joint; it plantarflexes the ankle only when the knee is extended and also flexes the knee. It is tested with the knee extended. Soleus arises entirely from the tibia and fibula (below the knee) and plantarflexes the ankle independent of the position of the knee. It is tested by single-leg heel raise with the knee flexed to 90°, which eliminates gastrocnemius from the movement and isolates soleus.

(i) Three cell populations and their locations:
- Macula densa: tall, closely packed cells of the ascending limb (distal portion) of the nephron loop.
- Granular cells (juxtaglomerular / JG cells): enlarged smooth muscle cells of the afferent (and sometimes efferent) arteriole.
- Extraglomerular mesangial cells: located between the arteriole and the tubule cells.
(ii) Functions of each population:
- Macula densa: chemoreceptors — they sense the NaCl content of the filtrate.
- Granular cells: mechanoreceptors — they sense blood pressure in the afferent arteriole; their secretory granules contain the enzyme renin.
- Extraglomerular mesangial cells: interconnected by gap junctions; they may pass signals between the macula densa and granular cells.
(iii) The granular cells (JG cells) contain secretory granules with renin. They are enlarged smooth muscle cells of the arteriole (i.e., modified vascular smooth muscle cells).
(iv) The extraglomerular mesangial cells are interconnected with gap junctions and may pass signals between the macula densa and the granular cells, thereby coordinating the response to changes in filtrate NaCl content and arterial blood pressure.
(v) The JGC is important in:
- Regulation of the rate of filtrate formation.
- Regulation of blood pressure.
questions.question:
A 55-year-old hypertensive man is found to have elevated plasma renin activity. Investigations point to the juxtaglomerular apparatus as the site of renin release.
(i) Name the three cell populations of the juxtaglomerular complex (JGC) and state the precise anatomical location of each.
(ii) For each cell population, state its specific function or sensing role.
(iii) Which cell type contains secretory granules with renin, and what type of cell is it derived from?
(iv) Describe how the extraglomerular mesangial cells may participate in the JGC function.
(v) State the two broad roles of the JGC.

questions.answerText:
A(i) A fibroserous sac that encloses the heart and the roots of the great vessels; it lies behind the body of the sternum and the 2nd-6th costal cartilages and in front of the T5-T8 vertebrae; it is attached to the central tendon of the diaphragm (pericardiophrenic ligament).
A(ii) The outer fibrous tissue layer, enclosing the heart and the roots of the great vessels (the IVC excepted, as stated); its base is attached to the central tendon of the diaphragm.
A(iii) Thin, elastic tissue lining the fibrous pericardium, made of a parietal layer (lines and fuses with the fibrous pericardium) and a visceral layer (forms the epicardium of the heart and encloses the aorta and pulmonary trunk); between them lies the pericardial cavity containing pericardial fluid.
A(iv) Transverse sinus: formed by a tear in the dorsal mesocardium; lies behind the aorta and pulmonary trunk, in front of the SVC on the right and the left atrium on the left.
A(v) Oblique sinus: a blind sac (cul-de-sac) formed as a result of the entrance of the 4 pulmonary veins and the IVC into the heart; lies behind the 2 left pulmonary veins and in front of the 2 right pulmonary veins and the IVC.
A(vi) Blood supply: fibrous pericardium from the pericardiophrenic and musculophrenic arteries; serous pericardium from the coronary arteries; veins drain to the azygos system, and the pericardiophrenic vein drains to the internal thoracic vein.
A(vi) Nerve supply: the fibrous and parietal pericardium by the phrenic nerve; the visceral pericardium by autonomic nerves.
B(i) Draining of pericardial fluid is done between the 7th costal cartilage and the xiphoid process.
B(i) In pulmonary embolectomy a temporary ligature is passed through the transverse sinus to occlude the aorta and pulmonary trunk; the oblique sinus allows for pulsation of the left atrium.
B(ii) Pain from irritation of the pleura or pericardium covering the central part of the diaphragm may be referred to the shoulder, because the phrenic nerve (C3,4,5) supplies the central diaphragm and the pericardium, and the supraclavicular nerve (C3,4) supplies the shoulder skin; pericarditis may also cause hiccup.
C(i) The transverse sinus is a passage formed by a tear in the dorsal mesocardium, lying behind the great arteries and used for the ligature; the oblique sinus is a blind sac formed by the entry of the pulmonary veins and IVC, allowing pulsation of the left atrium.
C(i) The fibrous pericardium is the outer fibrous layer with phrenic nerve and pericardiophrenic/musculophrenic arterial supply; the serous pericardium is thin and elastic, with a parietal layer fused to the fibrous layer and a visceral layer forming the epicardium, supplied by coronary arteries and autonomic nerves.

(ii) The diaphragm is formed from four components: the septum transversum, the pleuroperitoneal membranes, the dorsal mesentery of the esophagus, and muscular ingrowth from the lateral body walls.
During the 6th week these components fuse to form a complete partition between the thoracic and abdominal cavities, closing the pericardioperitoneal openings.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Protective coverings: the nervous system contains very little collagen or fibrous tissue; it is relatively soft and easily damaged by injuries affecting the cranium or vertebral bones. It is covered by three connective tissue layers — the meninges: dura mater (thickest and toughest layer, contains sinuses to collect venous blood), arachnoid membrane (middle web-like covering; cerebrospinal fluid flows in the web-like spaces), and pia mater (thin delicate layer that follows the contour of the brain and spinal cord). Gray matter and white matter: myelinated fibers make up the white matter in the CNS; cell bodies and unmyelinated fibers make the gray matter. Glial cells in CNS: Oligodendrocytes — produce myelin in CNS. Microglia — part of the MPS (CNS macrophages). Astrocytes and other glial cells — support, nourish, and protect neurons; they are far more numerous than neurons; unlike neurons, they are capable of mitosis.
A(ii) Dura mater — thickest and toughest layer; contains sinuses to collect venous blood. Arachnoid membrane — middle web-like covering; cerebrospinal fluid flows in the web-like (subarachnoid) spaces. Pia mater — thin delicate layer that follows the contour of brain and spinal cord. CSF flows within the subarachnoid spaces of the arachnoid.
B(i) The optic nerve and retina arise in the embryo as an outgrowth of the diencephalon (forebrain); the optic nerve is therefore not a true peripheral nerve like the other cranial nerves. Its myelin is produced by oligodendrocytes (not by Schwann cells). Because the optic nerve is part of the CNS (produced by oligodendrocytes and without neurilemma), it is associated with multiple sclerosis — a demyelinating disease. Demyelination of the optic nerve disrupts the action potential transmission from the retinal ganglion cells, causing visual symptoms. The retinal ganglion cells communicate with the cerebrum through the optic nerve and extend into the brain.

questions.answerText:
(i) Fiber type: myelinated peripheral nerve fiber (the myelin is produced by Schwann cells, and a neurilemma is present). Peripheral nerve anatomy: endoneurium surrounds the myelin sheath; perineurium (composed of perineural epithelioid cells) surrounds bundles; epineurium surrounds the whole nerve. Diagnosis: nerve injury with foot drop (unable to dorsiflex foot).
(ii) Predisposing structural feature for regeneration: the presence of the neurilemma (the cytoplasm, nucleus, and outer cell membrane of the Schwann cell forming a tight covering around the myelin and around the axon at the nodes of Ranvier). The neurilemma plays an important role in the regeneration of nerve fibers.
(iii) Pathophysiology of nerve impulse: neurons respond to stimuli by altering the ionic gradient (electrical potential) across their plasma membranes. This causes membrane depolarization (reversal of ionic gradient) that spreads from the stimulus site and is propagated across the neuron's entire plasma membrane. This propagation, called the action potential, depolarization wave, or nerve impulse, is capable of traveling long distances along neuronal processes. In the injured area, disruption of the axon prevents conduction. Most local anesthetics bind to voltage-gated sodium channels of the axolemma, interfering with sodium ion influx and inhibiting the action potential.
(iv) Management principle: peripheral nerve fibers may regenerate because they have a neurilemma. Neurons do not divide, though neuroglia can divide. The neurilemma guides regeneration of peripheral nerve fibers.
(v) In the CNS, oligodendrocytes produce myelin, but there is no neurilemma. Because the neurilemma is absent in the CNS, fibers within the CNS do not regenerate after injury. In the PNS, the neurilemma is present around myelinated fibers, enabling regeneration of peripheral nerve fibers.

A clinician needs to obtain hepatic tissue for diagnostic purposes and also considers where pathological fluid would collect first in a bedridden patient with intra-abdominal bleeding or ascites.
