(ii) State the anatomical landmark (site) used for this procedure and the positioning manoeuvre required.
(iii) Identify the structure(s) at risk during this procedure that the positioning manoeuvre is designed to protect.
(iv) Name the anatomical recess where abdominal fluid is most likely to collect in a supine (bedridden) patient, and its boundaries.
questions.answerText:
(i) Liver biopsy.
(ii) The needle puncture is commonly made through the right 10th intercostal space in the midaxillary line; before the biopsy, the patient is asked to hold their breath in full expiration.
(iii) Full expiration reduces the costodiaphragmatic recess, lessening the possibility of damaging the lung and contaminating the pleural cavity.
(iv) Morison's pouch, a potential space between the visceral surface of the liver and the right kidney, is the deepest part of the peritoneal cavity when a patient is supine, so pathological abdominal fluid such as blood or ascites is most likely to collect there in a bedridden patient.

questions.question:
An infant is diagnosed with a cardiac malformation involving the membranous portion of the interventricular septum, occurring as an isolated condition in about 12 per 10,000 births.
(i) State the surgical/management options, and justify one.
questions.answerText:
(i) Not covered.
Diagnosis for reference: ventricular septal defect (VSD) involving the membranous portion of the septum, described as the most common congenital cardiac malformation, occurring as an isolated condition in about 12/10,000 births.
Embryologic basis: the membranous interventricular septum normally forms by fusion of three components — the right bulbar ridge, the left bulbar ridge, and the atrioventricular (AV) cushions — and this fusion closes the interventricular foramen; a VSD of the membranous type results when this fusion is incomplete.

A(i) The parotid gland is the largest salivary gland (para = around, otic = ear); it is situated below the external acoustic meatus, in front of the sternomastoid, and also projects forward onto the surface of masseter. It is pyramidal in shape with the apex pointing downward, has 4 surfaces (superior/base, lateral/superficial, anteromedial, posteromedial) separated by 3 borders (anterior, posterior, medial), and has 1 main lobe and 1 accessory lobe (a small detached part called the accessory parotid gland or Socia Parotidis, lying on masseter between the zygomatic arch and the parotid duct). The capsule has a false capsule, formed by the investing layer of deep cervical fascia, and a true capsule, formed by condensation of the stroma.
A(ii) The parotid duct is about 5 cm long, arises from the anterior border of the gland, runs on masseter, and at the anterior border of masseter runs medially to pierce buccinator and the mucosa, opening into the vestibule of the mouth opposite the crown of the upper 2nd molar tooth; its surface anatomy corresponds to the middle third of a line from the lower border of the tragus to a point midway between the nasal ala and the upper labial margin. From superficial to deep within the substance of the gland are: the facial nerve and its branches; the retromandibular vein and its two divisions (maxillary vein, superficial temporal vein); and the external carotid artery and its two terminal branches. Other structures within the gland are the auriculotemporal nerve, the posterior auricular artery, and the preauricular lymph nodes.
B. Within the gland, the facial nerve radiates like a goose's foot (Pes Anserinus) through the anterior border of the gland into its branches (temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular, cervical); because the facial nerve runs through the substance of the gland, it is at risk during parotid surgery or trauma. Frey's syndrome (also known as gustatory sweating or auriculo-temporal nerve syndrome) commonly occurs after parotid surgery or trauma, from injury of the auriculotemporal and great auricular nerves; during healing, secretomotor fibres of the auriculotemporal nerve join with the great auricular nerve and reach the sweat glands of facial skin, so that sweating, warmth and redness of the face occur as a result of salivary stimulation by the smell or taste of food.
C. The parotid gland's duct is not given an eponymous name here by eponym in this section, but its secretomotor (parasympathetic) supply is via the auriculotemporal nerve, producing a watery secretion, with sympathetic supply producing a mucous-rich, sticky secretion derived from the plexus around the external carotid artery. In contrast, the submandibular gland's duct is the submandibular duct (Wharton's duct), and its nerve supply is via branches from the submandibular ganglion, through which it receives parasympathetic fibres from the chorda tympani, sensory fibres from the lingual branch of the mandibular nerve, and sympathetic fibres from the plexus on the facial artery.

A(i) Describe the basic architectural components of the liver, including the capsule, parenchyma, and the spaces between liver cells.
A(ii) There are three different ways to represent the microscopic organisation of the liver parenchyma. Name and describe each model, stating the geometric shape used and the central and peripheral reference points for each.
B(i) Describe the three zones of the hepatic acinus (acinus of Rappaport), stating what distinguishes each zone.
B(ii) Describe the complete pathway of bile flow from bile canaliculi to the duodenum.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Basic architecture:
- Capsule: the outer surface of the liver is composed of a fibrous/connective tissue capsule (Glisson's capsule); the outermost surface is covered by a thin layer of mesothelial cells that arise from the peritoneum.
- Parenchyma: the capsule surrounds the liver parenchyma, composed of hepatocytes — large polygonal cells with eosinophilic (pink) cytoplasm, round nuclei, and prominent nucleoli.
- Bile canaliculi: spaces present between the plasma membranes of adjacent liver cells.
- Perisinusoidal space of Disse: separates the surface of the liver cell from the endothelial lining of the sinusoid.
A(ii) Three models:
1. Classic (hepatic) lobule: based on blood flow; organised as hexagons, with the central vein (CV) in the centre and portal tracts (PTs) at the periphery (corners of the hexagon). Each PT consists of hepatic artery (HA), portal vein (PV), and bile duct (BD).
2. Portal lobule: based on bile flow; organised as triangles, with a portal tract at the centre and central veins at the periphery (corners of the triangle). Flow of bile is in the opposite direction to blood flow.
3. Hepatic acinus (acinus of Rappaport): based on blood perfusion; organised as a diamond, with portal tracts at the corners of the short axis and central veins at the corners of the long axis.
B(i) Zones of the hepatic acinus:
- Zone 1: receives the most oxygenated blood and nutrients.
- Zone 2: intermediate oxygenation and nutrient supply.
- Zone 3: receives the least oxygenated blood and nutrients.
B(ii) Bile flow pathway:
Bile canaliculi → Canals of Hering → Bile ductules → Interlobular bile ducts → Intrahepatic ducts → Right and left hepatic ducts → Common hepatic duct → joins with cystic duct to form the common bile duct → Duodenum.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the gross histology of the three types of muscle tissue (skeletal, smooth, and cardiac) as seen in longitudinal section and cross-section under the light microscope.
A(ii) Relate the structural differences of each muscle type to their specific pathological conditions.
B(i) Explain how the histological organization of cardiac muscle facilitates rapid spread of the signal to contract, and state why blockage of the coronary arteries leads to widespread myocardial damage.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Skeletal muscle — longitudinal section: cross-striations of alternating dark (A bands, anisotropic) and light (I bands, isotropic) bands; each I band bisected by a dark transverse Z disc; multinucleated fibers at periphery. Cross-section: peripheral nuclei; high cytoplasm-to-nucleus ratio. Smooth muscle — longitudinal section: meshwork appearance; no striations; elongated spindle-shaped cells; elongated and central nuclei. Cross-section: central nuclei; low cytoplasm-to-nucleus ratio. Cardiac muscle — longitudinal section: striations; branching cells; intercalated discs. Cross-section: central nuclei; high cytoplasm-to-nucleus ratio.
A(ii) Skeletal muscle: troponin subunits (troponin I and troponin T) are integral to muscle contraction; mutations in cardiac troponin subunits can result in cardiomyopathies. Smooth muscle: smooth muscle cells are able to undergo cell division (unlike cardiac and skeletal muscle). Cardiac muscle: atrial myocytes secrete atrial natriuretic peptide; kidneys respond to this to cause sodium and water loss (natriuresis and diuresis); when natriuretic peptide levels fall, kidneys result in sodium and water conservation.
B(i) Cardiac muscle cells act as a syncytium through gap junctions in intercalated discs, which provide ionic continuity between adjacent cells, allowing the signal to contract to pass throughout the organ. The blood supply to the heart is through three main coronary arteries prone to atheroma. Acute coronary arterial occlusion involving nearly the entire area at risk causes necrosis of the myocardium. Because the cardiac muscle acts as a syncytium and is continuously active, obstruction of coronary blood flow rapidly leads to widespread ischemia and necrosis of the myocardium.

questions.question:
An infant, born to parents who had waited a long time for a child, presents with a distended abdomen, and an ultrasound examination reveals a distended colon.
(i) Name the anomaly, the organs likely affected and the likely sex of the infant.
(ii) State the predisposing (genetic) factors and the frequency.
(iii) Explain the embryologic pathophysiology and the resulting features.
(iv) State the management.
questions.answerText:
(i) Hirschsprung disease (aganglionic megacolon; congenital megacolon).
(i) It affects mostly the rectum and sigmoid colon (80% involve sigmoid colon and rectum; 3% involve the whole colon); males are more affected, so the infant is most likely male.
(ii) It may be due to a genetic mutation of the RET gene, a tyrosine kinase receptor involved in neural crest cell migration; it is a dominantly inherited multigenic disorder.
(ii) It occurs in 1 in 5000 live births and is the most common cause of neonatal colonic obstruction.
(iii) Neural crest cells fail to migrate into the wall of the colon, so parasympathetic ganglion cells fail to develop in the Auerbach and Meissner plexuses in the sigmoid colon and rectum during the 5th to 7th week of gestation.
(iii) The resulting lack of innervation causes loss of peristalsis, faecal retention and abdominal distension.
(iv) Management is not covered.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the origin and course of the internal carotid artery and its terminal branches.
A(ii) Describe the branches and distribution of the anterior and middle cerebral arteries.
C. Explain the anatomical basis of the deficits seen after occlusion of these vessels.
questions.answerText:
A(i) The internal carotid, vertebral and basilar systems form the main blood supply of the CNS. The internal carotid system consists of the anterior and middle cerebral arteries, the anterior choroidal artery and posterior communicating artery. The internal carotid artery proceeds superiorly alongside the optic chiasma and bifurcates into the middle and anterior cerebral arteries, after giving off the anterior choroidal artery (a long, thin, clinically significant vessel frequently involved in CVAs, supplying the optic tract, lateral geniculate body, optic radiation, uncus, amygdala, hippocampus, internal capsule, lentiform nucleus and thalamus) and the posterior communicating artery (joining the posterior cerebral artery, part of the circle of Willis).
A(ii) The anterior cerebral artery runs superiorly and medially to the optic nerve into the longitudinal fissure, is joined to its fellow by the anterior communicating artery, and runs posteriorly along the corpus callosum, dividing into pericallosal and callosomarginal branches, supplying the medial frontal/parietal surfaces and the paracentral lobule. The middle cerebral artery runs laterally into the lateral sulcus, supplies the insula and temporal pole, and gives numerous branches (including lenticulostriate arteries) to the lateral cerebral surface and deep telencephalic/diencephalic structures.
C. Occlusion of the anterior cerebral artery causes a restricted contralateral motor and somatosensory deficit (paracentral lobule); occlusion of the middle cerebral artery causes major motor and somatosensory deficits, with language deficits if the left hemisphere is involved; the anterior choroidal artery is frequently involved in CVAs owing to its long, thin course.

(i) Portal hypertension; portasystemic shunts reduce pressure by diverting blood from the portal to the systemic venous system.
(ii) Splenectomy with joining of the splenic vein to the left renal vein.
(iii) Gastrosplenic ligament: fundus of the stomach to hilum of the spleen. Splenorenal ligament: hilum of the spleen to the anterior aspect of the left kidney. Also the phrenicosplenic and splenocolic ligaments.
(iv) Gastrosplenic ligament contains the short gastric and left gastroepiploic vessels; the splenorenal ligament contains the splenic vessels and the tail of the pancreas.
(iv) The splenic artery, largest branch of the celiac trunk, runs tortuously to the left along the superior border of the pancreas in the splenorenal ligament, giving numerous small branches to the neck, body and tail of the pancreas.
(v) The spleen develops in relation to the foregut region, which is supplied by the celiac trunk.
(v) Short gastric arteries pass through the gastrosplenic ligament to the fundus; the left gastro-omental artery runs along the greater curvature to anastomose with the right gastro-omental artery.

An infant with nonrotation or malrotation of the gut presents with bilious vomiting.
(i) State the embryologic basis and the risk factors for the condition.
(ii) State the complications.
(iii) State the management options and justify one.
questions.answerText:
(i) Malrotation is incomplete rotation and/or fixation of the intestines; nonrotation or malrotation can lead to catastrophic twisting of the midgut (midgut volvulus).
(i) Failure of rotation may result in a left-sided caecum, appendix and ascending colon; incomplete rotation gives a subhepatic caecum and appendix.
(i) Infants with malrotation are prone to volvulus and present with bilious emesis (vomiting bile).
(ii) Volvulus is a rotation of an intestinal loop around a branch of the superior mesenteric artery; it may cause intestinal obstruction or even gangrene.
(ii) Midgut volvulus may obstruct the SMA, resulting in infarction and gangrene of the intestines it supplies.
(ii) Some cases of malrotation are asymptomatic but may cause diagnostic problems in appendicitis in later life.
(iii) Some cases correct spontaneously, but surgical intervention is usually performed.
(iii) Justification: because of the risk of obstruction, infarction and gangrene, surgery is the usual choice; the type of operation is not covered.

(ii) An allantoic cyst is a cystic mass in the umbilical cord that may represent the remains of the extra-embryonic part of the allantois.

questions.answerText:
(i) Cell type: Macrophage. Origin: Macrophages originate from monocytes (precursor cells in bone marrow), which migrate to connective tissue and differentiate into tissue macrophages.
(ii) Members of the Mononuclear Phagocyte System (MPS): Kupffer cells of the liver, alveolar macrophages of the lung, osteoclasts in bone, microglia in CNS, Langerhans cells in skin, tissue macrophages in connective tissues, and dendritic cells in lymph nodes.
(iii) Functions of macrophages: (a) Ingestion by phagocytosis of microorganisms (bacteria, viruses, fungi), parasites, particulate matter such as dust, and participation in the breakdown of aged cells including erythrocytes. The intracellular digestion occurs as a result of fusion of lysosomes with the phagosome (ingested body). (b) Macrophages are normally long-lived and survive in tissues for several months. (c) Defense elements: they phagocytose cell debris, abnormal extracellular matrix elements, neoplastic cells, bacteria, and inert elements that penetrate the organism. (d) Antigen-presenting cells: they participate in partial digestion and presentation of antigen to other cells; a typical example is the Langerhans cell in skin epidermis. (e) Secretory cells: produce enzymes (e.g., collagenase) and cytokines that participate in defensive and reparative functions; they exhibit increased tumor cell-killing capacity. (f) Cell-mediated resistance to infection by bacteria, viruses, protozoans, fungi, and metazoans.
(iv) Predisposing condition for multinucleate giant cells: when a foreign body (such as a small splinter) has penetrated the inner tissues, several macrophages may fuse together to form multinuclear foreign body giant cells. These large cells accumulate at sites of invasion of the foreign body and sites of inflammation. Clinical significance: foreign body giant cell reaction is a sign of chronic inflammation around a foreign material.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Medial longitudinal arch: formed by calcaneus, talus (keystone — its superior articular facet is the summit), navicular, 3 cuneiform bones, and 1st, 2nd, and 3rd metatarsals; found on medial aspect of foot; larger, with greatest height, higher, more mobile, and more resilient. Lateral longitudinal arch: formed by calcaneus, cuboid, and the 4th and 5th metatarsals; summit is the subtalar articulation; flat, contains relatively fewer bones, hence more rigid; bears body weight before the medial arch comes into play. Transverse arch: formed proximally by 3 cuneiforms and cuboid, and distally by the bases of 5 metatarsals; it is a partial arch (each foot represents a half dome); the intermediate and lateral cuneiforms are wedge-shaped (bony factor).
A(ii) Medial longitudinal arch: Ligaments — spring ligament, deltoid ligament, plantar aponeurosis, interosseous ligaments, long and short plantar ligaments. Muscles — tibialis posterior, tibialis anterior, flexor hallucis longus, flexor digitorum longus, and short muscles of the big toe. Bony factor — the shape and constitution of the bones. Lateral longitudinal arch: Ligaments — plantar aponeurosis, interosseous ligaments, long and short plantar ligaments. Muscles — peroneus longus and brevis, flexor digitorum longus, and short muscles of the little toe. Bony factor — shape and constitution of the bones. Transverse arch: Bony factor — intermediate and lateral cuneiforms are wedge-shaped. Ligaments — deep transverse ligament and interosseous ligaments (dorsal and plantar). Muscles — peroneus longus and brevis, transverse head of adductor hallucis, and slips of tibialis posterior.
B(i) The human foot supports the body weight and serves as a lever to propel the body forward during locomotion. Functions carried out by arches: (1) Foot acts as a segmented lever with multiple joints and adapts to uneven surfaces. (2) Long flexors and intrinsic muscles assist propulsive action of gastrocnemius and soleus. (3) Arches are springs that absorb shock and store energy — elastic arches present between weight-bearing points can flatten and recoil back to normal.
B(ii) Pes planus (flat foot): rotation of the calcaneus, eversion of the plantar surface, slipping down of the talus and navicular, lengthening of the medial longitudinal arch, and abduction of the forefoot; caused by excess weight on medial side, relaxation of ligaments, or muscular imbalance. Pes cavus (high-arched foot): exaggeration of the longitudinal arch; toes dorsiflexed at metatarsophalangeal joints and plantarflexed at interphalangeal joints — claw foot. Talipes equinovarus: plantar flexion, inversion, and adduction of the foot (clubfoot). Talipes calcaneovalgus: dorsiflexion, eversion, and abduction of the foot.
C(i) The medial longitudinal arch is higher, more mobile, and more resilient — it is dynamic, changes most during movement, and requires active muscular support (particularly tibialis posterior, flexor hallucis longus, and the spring ligament). The lateral longitudinal arch is lower, more stable, built to transmit weight to the ground, makes more contact with the ground, has limited mobility, and depends more on bony and ligamentous rather than muscular support. The medial arch is therefore more clinically vulnerable to collapse (pes planus) when muscles weaken or ligaments stretch.

questions.answerText:

(ii) Nerves such as the ilioinguinal, iliohypogastric and inferior thoracic are prone to injury because they spread across the abdominal wall; the distal thoracoabdominal nerves (T7 to T12) lie in the rectus sheath. Other risk factors and complications are not covered.

questions.question:
A patient presents with a restricted contralateral motor and somatosensory deficit following a cerebrovascular event; anterior cerebral artery occlusion is suspected on clinico-anatomical grounds.
(i) Identify the structure/organ primarily affected.
(ii) What other structures are related to this artery's course and branches?
(iii) How would this presentation differ from a middle cerebral artery occlusion?
(iv) Explain the clinico-anatomical reasoning linking the artery to the deficit.
questions.answerText:
(i) The anterior cerebral artery supplies the paracentral lobule (the medial aspects of the precentral and postcentral gyri); its occlusion causes a restricted contralateral motor and somatosensory deficit.
(ii) The anterior cerebral artery runs superiorly and medially to the optic nerve to enter the longitudinal fissure, is connected to its fellow by the anterior communicating artery, and runs posteriorly along the corpus callosum supplying the medial surfaces of the frontal and parietal lobes rostral to the parieto-occipital sulcus; it divides into the pericallosal artery (adjacent to the corpus callosum) and the callosomarginal artery (following the cingulate sulcus).
(iii) By contrast, middle cerebral artery occlusion causes major motor and somatosensory deficits (not merely restricted ones), and language deficits are almost invariably found if the left hemisphere is involved.
(iv) Because the anterior cerebral artery supplies only the paracentral lobule (a limited area) compared with the extensive lateral cerebral surface supplied by the middle cerebral artery, its occlusion produces a more restricted contralateral deficit.

(i) Retina → optic tract → lateral geniculate body (oval elevation on the posterior end of the pulvinar; receives the optic tract and projects to the visual cortex) → optic radiations (retrolentiform part of the internal capsule) → visual area 17 (medial surface of the occipital lobe, posterior lip of the calcarine sulcus to the occipital pole); areas 18 and 19 are association visual areas.
- Midbrain: the superior colliculus of the tectum has inputs from the retina; the pretectal nucleus at the junction of midbrain and diencephalon subserves the pupillary light reflexes; the Edinger-Westphal nucleus lies in the midbrain.
(ii) The optic chiasma forms the anterior end of the floor of the 3rd ventricle; the optic radiation is related to the lateral wall of the posterior horn of the lateral ventricle.
- Arterial supply: the internal carotid artery supplies the optic nerve, orbital contents including retina, optic tract and LGB; the posterior cerebral artery (posterior circulation) supplies the occipital lobe.
(iii) Efferent fibres of the superior colliculus travel in the tectospinal and tectobulbar tracts for general light (and sound) reflexes; the pretectal nucleus subserves the pupillary light reflex; the resulting visual deficits are not covered.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Vertebral arteries usually arise from the subclavian artery; the basilar artery is formed by the union of the two vertebral arteries.
A(ii) The vertebral artery ascends through the cervical vertebrae and enters the cranium through the foramen magnum.
- The basilar artery runs in the midline pontine groove and terminates by dividing into the two posterior cerebral arteries.

A(iii) Vertebral branches: posterior spinal, anterior spinal, lateral medullary and posterior inferior cerebellar arteries.

A(iv) The vertebrobasilar and posterior cerebral arteries supply the brainstem, cerebellum, occipital lobe etc. (posterior circulation).
- Midbrain: superior cerebellar and posterior cerebral arteries; pons: basilar, superior cerebellar and anterior inferior cerebellar arteries; medulla: anterior spinal branch of the vertebral and posterior inferior cerebellar arteries.

(i) Diagnosis: Osteoarthritis (result from breakdown of joint cartilage). Risk factors: participation in certain sports that involve torsional loading, fast acceleration and deceleration, repetitive high impact, and high level of participation increase risk of osteoarthritis.
(ii) Histological basis of limited healing: Cartilage is avascular and is nourished only by diffusion of nutrients from capillaries in adjacent connective tissue (perichondrium) or by synovial fluid from joint cavities. It has no lymphatic vessels or nerves. Chondrocytes exhibit low metabolic activity. Cartilage cells can also give rise to benign (chondroma) or malignant (chondrosarcoma) tumors, and hyaline cartilage is more susceptible to degenerative aging processes including calcification of the matrix, preceded by an increase in the size and volume of the chondrocytes and followed by their death.
(iii) Complications: progressive cartilage destruction, pain, and functional loss; osteoarthritis.
(iv) Various options have been made available to address cartilage repair. A biological approach is challenging due to cartilage's inherent limited healing potential. Stem cell therapy (particularly mesenchymal stem cells) is a strong promise in the treatment of cartilage defects and osteoarthritis and is expected to revolutionize the treatment for cartilage defects and osteoarthritis in the near future. The justification is that it is hoped that the whole cartilage can be repaired, not just focal defects, using stem cells.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Shortest part of the brainstem (about 2 cm); ventrally V-shaped crura converge on the superior surface of the pons; dorsally the superior and inferior colliculi form two pairs of round elevations; divisible ventro-dorsally into base, tegmentum and tectum.
- The superior cerebellar peduncle connects the cerebellum to the dorsal midbrain caudal to the inferior colliculus; the MGB and LGB lie lateral to the superior colliculus; the pineal gland and pulvinar are superiorly related.
A(ii) CN III emerges ventrally on the medial side of the cerebral peduncle; CN IV emerges dorsally inferior to the inferior colliculus and courses ventrally; both run between the superior cerebellar and posterior cerebral arteries.
A(iii) Superior colliculus level: oculomotor nucleus near the midline with the Edinger-Westphal nucleus cranial to it; red nucleus lateral and ventral to CN III, receiving input from the contralateral dentate nucleus via the superior cerebellar peduncle.
- Inferior colliculus level: trochlear nucleus ventral to the aqueduct, its fibres running dorsally and decussating dorsal to the aqueduct.
- Substantia nigra forms the boundary between crus and tegmentum; mesencephalic nucleus of CN V in the central grey; spinal and medial lemnisci in the lateral tegmentum; reticular formation between the medial lemniscus and central grey.
- Crura: corticospinal and corticonuclear fibres in the middle 2/3, frontopontine and temporopontine fibres in the medial and lateral 1/6; tectum: colliculi with inputs from retina and cochlea, tectospinal and tectobulbar efferents for light and sound reflexes.
A(iv) Supplied by the superior cerebellar and posterior cerebral arteries (perforating branches of the posterior cerebral artery supply the cerebral peduncle, mamillary bodies and midbrain).
B(i) Substantia nigra: gives rise to nigrostriatal fibres projecting to the other basal ganglia nuclei; loss of fibres explains Parkinsonism.
- The pretectal nucleus at the midbrain-diencephalon junction subserves the pupillary light reflex; other pathologies of the midbrain are not covered.
C(i) Because the nigral fibres project to the other basal ganglia nuclei, their loss deprives these distant nuclei and explains Parkinsonism.
- The detailed mechanism and deficits beyond this statement are not covered.

A(i) The vertebral arteries run alongside the medulla and fuse at the pontomedullary junction to form the basilar artery. Before this union, each gives three branches: the posterior spinal artery (runs along the dorsolateral aspect of the spinal cord, supplying the dorsal one-third); the anterior spinal artery (the two join to form a single vessel running on the antero-medial cord surface, supplying the ventral two-thirds, needing caudal reinforcement); and the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PIC
A., which supplies the inferior cerebellar surface, the choroid plexus of the 4th ventricle and much of the lateral medulla.
A(ii) The basilar artery runs in the pontine groove and bifurcates at midbrain level into the two posterior cerebral arteries. It also gives rise to the anterior inferior cerebellar artery (supplies the anterior inferior cerebellar surface and lower pons), the superior cerebellar artery (supplies the upper pons, superior cerebellum and caudal midbrain), the internal auditory artery (supplies the ear; often from AIC
A., and numerous unnamed pontine arteries. The posterior cerebral artery supplies the medial occipital and temporal lobes, the upper midbrain and lower diencephalon, and gives posterior choroidal arteries.
C. Occlusion of the internal auditory artery causes vertigo and deafness; since the primary visual cortex lies in the occipital lobe, occlusion of the posterior cerebral artery can cause visual loss among other symptoms.

questions.question:
Describe the gross anatomy of the brachial plexus:
A(i) Formation (roots)
A(ii) Trunks, divisions, cords
A(iii) Five main terminal branches
B. State how injury at each level (trunk/cord) of the plexus relates to a specific clinical pathology.
C. Explain how injury at the level of a trunk or cord spreads to affect distant structures (individual peripheral nerves), causing specific functional deficits.
questions.answerText:
A(i) The brachial plexus is formed by the union of the C5, C6, C7 and C8 ventral rami and the greater part of the 1st thoracic ventral ramus, with contribution sometimes from C4 (giving a "prefixed" plexus) or T2 (giving a "postfixed" plexus); the roots emerge from the transverse processes of the cervical vertebrae, immediately posterior to the vertebral artery, and lie between the scalene muscles.
A(ii) C5 and C6 unite to form the upper trunk, C7 continues as the middle trunk, and C8 and T1 unite to form the lower trunk, lying in the posterior triangle of the neck; each trunk bifurcates behind the clavicle into an anterior and a posterior division. The anterior divisions of the upper and middle trunks unite to form the lateral cord; the anterior division of the lower trunk continues as the medial cord; the posterior divisions of all three trunks unite to form the posterior cord, lying in the axilla below pectoralis minor.
A(iii) The five main terminal branches are the musculocutaneous nerve and the lateral root of the median nerve (from the lateral cord), the ulnar nerve and the medial root of the median nerve (from the medial cord), and the axillary and radial nerves (from the posterior cord).
B. Injury to the upper trunk (C5, C6), at "Erb's point," produces Erb's paralysis, from causes such as birth injury, a fall on the shoulder, or during anaesthesia, affecting the axillary, musculocutaneous and suprascapular nerves.
Injury to the lower trunk (C8, T1), from causes such as undue abduction of the arm, produces Klumpke's paralysis, with paralysis of the intrinsic hand muscles and ulnar wrist/finger flexors, and possible Horner's syndrome from associated sympathetic fibre injury.
C. Erb's paralysis paralyses biceps, deltoid, brachialis, brachioradialis, supraspinatus, infraspinatus and supinator, producing the "Policeman's/Porter's tip hand": the arm hangs adducted and medially rotated, the forearm extended and pronated, with loss of abduction/lateral rotation of the shoulder and flexion/supination of the forearm.
Klumpke's paralysis produces a claw hand from unopposed long flexors/extensors, plus cutaneous anaesthesia along the ulnar border of the limb.
Injury to the lateral cord (e.g. from dislocation of the humerus) involves the musculocutaneous nerve and the lateral root of the median nerve, paralysing biceps, coracobrachialis and the median-supplied forearm muscles, producing a midprone forearm with loss of elbow and wrist flexion and sensory loss on the radial side of the forearm.
Injury to the medial cord (e.g. from subcoracoid dislocation of the humerus) involves the ulnar nerve and the medial root of the median nerve, producing claw hand with sensory loss on the ulnar side of the forearm and hand.
Injury to the posterior cord involves the upper and lower subscapular nerves, the thoracodorsal nerve, the axillary nerve, and the radial nerve (the largest and most frequently injured branch of the plexus).
This weakens elbow, wrist and metacarpophalangeal joint extension via the radial nerve, and shoulder abduction via the axillary nerve.
In this way, a single lesion at the level of a trunk or cord of the brachial plexus spreads its effect along the several peripheral nerves derived from it, each producing its own characteristic and distant functional deficit in the arm, forearm or hand.

A(i) Lies between the anterior surface of the cerebellum and the posterior surface of the pons and medulla (pons and upper medulla ventrally, cerebellum dorsally); diamond-shaped floor, tent-like roof, triangular in sagittal section; communicates with the 3rd ventricle via the aqueduct and continues caudally with the central canal.
A(ii) Cranial roof: superior medullary velum, a thin stretch of white matter connecting the two superior cerebellar peduncles; caudal roof: pia and ependyma, indented by a T-shaped choroid plexus.
A(iii) Floor: median sulcus connects the aqueduct to the central canal; cranial part divided into a medial pontine part and a lateral vestibular part overlying the vestibular nuclei; facial colliculus adjacent to the median sulcus; medullary striae at the widest part.
- Lateral boundary: cranially the superior cerebellar peduncle; caudally the gracile and cuneate tubercles with the inferior cerebellar peduncle superimposed on them.
- Medullary part divided by a faint groove into the medial hypoglossal trigone (over the hypoglossal nucleus) and the lateral vagal trigone (over the dorsal nucleus of the vagus).
A(iv) Foramina: the median foramen of Magendie (caudal roof) and the two lateral foramina of Luschka (narrow lateral recess); they communicate with the subarachnoid space; the T-shaped choroid plexus is in the posterior part of the roof.
B(i) Hydrocephaly: due to overproduction or obstruction to CSF flow and absorption; CSF exits via the foramina of Magendie and Luschka into the subarachnoid space, or flows into the central canal.
- Clinically significant taps: lumbar, cisternal and ventricular; the CSF within the lumbar cistern is tapped via LP.
- CSF is reabsorbed via arachnoid granulations into the venous system, flowing around the superior sagittal sinus.
C(i) Foramen of Magendie: single, midline, central opening of the caudal roof; communicates with the cerebellomedullary cistern.
C(ii) Foramina of Luschka: paired, in the narrow lateral recesses; communicate with the pontine cistern.
C(iii) Both carry CSF from the 4th ventricle into the subarachnoid space, from which it is reabsorbed into venous sinus blood via arachnoid villi.

(i) The diagnoses are pes planus (flat foot) and hallux valgus (lateral deviation of the great toe). In pes planus: rotation of the calcaneus, eversion of the plantar surface, slipping down of the talus and navicular, lengthening of the medial longitudinal arch, and abduction of the forefoot occur. The medial longitudinal arch is formed by the calcaneus, talus, navicular, 3 cuneiform bones, and 1st, 2nd, and 3rd metatarsals; it is higher, more mobile, and more resilient than the lateral arch.
(ii) Predisposing factors: excess weight on the medial side of the foot due to misalignment of bones, relaxation of ligaments, or muscular imbalance. Chronic synovitis in rheumatoid arthritis destroys ligamentous and capsular supports. The 1st metatarsal is the shortest and thickest, bears most weight, is important in propulsion, and has two sesamoid bones at its head; when medial structures fail, the forefoot deviates laterally. Adductor hallucis (whose transverse head assists in maintaining the transverse arch by pulling metatarsals medially) becomes dysfunctional with joint destruction.
(iii) Structures maintaining the medial longitudinal arch: Ligaments — spring ligament (plantar calcaneonavicular), deltoid ligament, plantar aponeurosis, interosseous ligaments, and long and short plantar ligaments. Muscles — tibialis posterior, tibialis anterior, flexor hallucis longus, flexor digitorum longus, and short muscles of the big toe. Bony factor — the shape and constitution of the bones. In this patient, ligaments and tibialis posterior are deficient due to rheumatoid destruction.
(iv) Conservative: orthotic insoles to support the medial arch, physiotherapy, and anti-inflammatory medication for the underlying arthritis. Surgical options include soft-tissue reconstruction of the spring ligament, tibialis posterior tendon transfer, and corrective osteotomy or arthrodesis. For advanced pes planus with arthritis, hindfoot fusion (subtalar arthrodesis) is justified as it corrects alignment, relieves pain, and stabilises the collapsed arch permanently in a patient with systemic joint disease.

(iii) Within the gland, the facial nerve radiates through the anterior border of the gland like a goose's foot, the Pes Anserinus; other structures within the gland (auriculotemporal nerve, posterior auricular artery, preauricular lymph nodes) provide further landmarks.
(iv) The facial nerve gives off the temporal branch, the zygomatic branch, the buccal branch, the marginal mandibular branch, and the cervical branch; not covered is the specific functional deficit resulting from injury to each individual branch.
(v) The accessory parotid gland (Socia Parotidis) is a small detached part of the gland lying on the surface of masseter between the zygomatic arch and the parotid duct; its specific embryologic basis is not detailed here.

questions.question:
A. Describe the course, relations and branches of the facial nerve within the parotid gland, and its termination pattern.
B. State the structures/procedures for which knowledge of the facial nerve's branching is clinically important.
C. Explain the anatomical/functional basis of the deformity that results when this nerve is injured.
questions.answerText:
A. Within the substance of the parotid gland, from superficial to deep are found the facial nerve and its branches, the retromandibular vein and its two divisions, and the external carotid artery and its two terminal branches. The facial nerve radiates through the anterior border of the gland like a goose's foot, termed the Pes Anserinus, giving off the temporal branch, the zygomatic branch, the buccal branch, the marginal mandibular branch, and the cervical branch.
B. Frey's syndrome commonly occurs after parotid surgery or trauma, from injury of the auriculo-temporal nerve and great auricular nerve; the facial nerve's course through the parotid gland is therefore clinically important in parotid surgery, where the nerve and its branches are structures to be identified and preserved.
C. Bell's palsy is associated with drooping of the mouth, reflecting facial nerve dysfunction; facial laceration is also noted as a clinical correlate involving this nerve's territory. Because the facial nerve, once it has divided within the parotid gland into its temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular and cervical branches, supplies the muscles of facial expression, injury to the trunk or a branch of the nerve produces the drooping and loss of movement seen in facial nerve palsy.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the gross anatomy of the cerebral hemisphere: its general features, lobes and main sulci.
A(ii) Describe its superolateral, medial and inferior surfaces.
A(iii) Describe its white matter.
B(i) State how its cortical areas relate to common pathologies.
C(i) Explain why haemorrhage of a deep artery may cause paralysis of the opposite side and a speech deficit.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Forebrain (telencephalon derivative) sitting in the anterior and middle cranial fossae and on the tentorium cerebelli; two hemispheres of unequal size (the dominant slightly larger) separated by the longitudinal fissure; four lobes named after adjoining cranial bones.
- Central sulcus (Rolando) separates frontal from parietal lobe, with the precentral gyrus in front and postcentral gyrus behind; lateral sulcus (Sylvius) separates frontal from temporal lobe; the parieto-occipital sulcus and the line to the preoccipital notch demarcate the occipital lobe; the insula lies hidden in the lateral sulcus.
A(ii) Superolateral surface: frontal lobe divided into superior, middle and inferior frontal gyri (inferior: orbital, triangular, opercular parts) and temporal lobe similarly; supramarginal gyrus caps the posterior end of the lateral sulcus; angular gyrus caps the superior temporal sulcus.
- Medial surface: corpus callosum with the cingulate gyrus above it; paracentral lobule caps the medial end of the central sulcus; calcarine and parieto-occipital sulci form a Y-shaped furrow with precuneus above, cuneus between the arms and lingual gyrus below.
- Inferior surface (irregular, conforming to the cranial floor): rectus gyrus, olfactory tract/bulb and orbital gyri and sulci from medial to lateral; parahippocampal gyrus ends in the uncus; the brain stem is the other major structure.
A(iii) White matter: commissural fibres (corpus callosum with rostrum, genu, body and splenium; anterior and posterior commissures), association fibres and projection fibres (internal capsule).
- Corpus callosum: forceps minor (genu fibres) connects the frontal cortex and forceps major (splenium fibres) the occipital cortex; the remaining fibres form the roof and lateral walls of the lateral ventricles.
B(i) Broca's area (inferior frontal gyrus, areas 44, 45) lesions cause expressive aphasia; Wernicke's area lesions cause receptive aphasia; prefrontal lesions change personality; premotor ablation causes apraxia.
- The effects of lesions of the primary motor, sensory, visual and auditory areas are not covered.
C(i) The internal capsule is the most prominent projection bundle; its posterior limb lies between the thalamus and lentiform nucleus, with corticospinal fibres in the anterior 2/3 and thalamocortical fibres in the posterior 1/3.
- Haemorrhage or thrombosis of the striate artery around the posterior fibres causes paralysis of the opposite skeletal muscles, because the corticospinal fibres decussate in the lower medulla (lateral corticospinal tract).
- Fibres of Broca's speech are affected on the left side; other parts carry frontopontine (anterior limb), corticonuclear (genu), optic radiation (retrolentiform) and auditory radiation (sublentiform) fibres.

A(i) The ear develops from three distinct parts: the external ear (auricle, external auditory meatus, external layer of the tympanic membrane); the middle ear (three bony ossicles connecting the eardrum to the oval window, and the auditory tube); and the internal ear (the vestibulocochlear organ for hearing and balance).
A(ii) Pharyngeal arch features include the arch itself; the groove/cleft (externally separates each arch; only the first pair persists as the external auditory meatus); the pouch (internally separates each arch, pockets from the pharynx); and the membrane (ectoderm-endoderm contact region; only the first pair persists as the tympanic membrane).
A(iii) The internal ear develops from the otic placode (day 22), which invaginates to form the otic vesicle; its ventral part forms the saccule and cochlear duct, and its dorsal part forms the utricle, semicircular canals and endolymphatic duct, together forming the membranous labyrinth. The cochlear duct forms the organ of Corti; the middle ear's tubotympanic recess derives from the first pharyngeal pouch, with the malleus and incus from first arch cartilage and the stapes from the second arch.
B) The first two ossicles (malleus and incus) are derived from the cartilage of the first pharyngeal arch, and the third (stapes) from the second arch; the auricle develops from six mesenchymal proliferations (auricular hillocks) at the dorsal ends of the first and second pharyngeal arches surrounding the first pharyngeal cleft, which explains why pathology of these arches affects the ossicles and auricle.
C) The utricle and semicircular canals (dorsal otic vesicle derivatives) are concerned with equilibrium/angular acceleration, while the saccule and cochlear duct (ventral otic vesicle derivatives) are concerned with linear acceleration and hearing.

(iii) Benign: liver cyst, haemangiomas, focal nodular hyperplasia, adenoma. Malignant: hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and metastasis.
(iv) CT provides accurate anatomical localisation and characterisation of mass contents such as fluid, fat or calcification.

A(i) Describe the immunological defence system of the gastrointestinal tract, including: the name of the tissue system; the layers of the GIT wall it occupies; the cell types it contains; and the antibody it produces.
A(ii) Explain the complete mechanism by which IgA protects the lumen of the GIT from pathogens, including the role of the secretory protein and the property that makes IgA effective.
B(i) State which regions of the GIT are lined by stratified squamous epithelium rather than the simple thin vulnerable epithelium lining the rest of the tract, and explain the significance of this difference in the context of microbial defense.
B(ii) Explain the clinical and anatomical basis for the well-known effects of emotional stress on the stomach and other regions of the GIT.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Immunological defense system:
- Name: Mucosa-Associated Lymphoid Tissue (MALT).
- Layers occupied: the mucosa (especially the lamina propria located just below the epithelium) and the submucosal layers.
- Cell types: macrophages and lymphocytes (some of which actively produce antibodies); also free immune cells and lymphoid nodules.
- Antibody produced: mainly immunoglobulin A (IgA).
A(ii) IgA protection mechanism:
- IgA antibodies undergo transcytosis into the intestinal lumen, bound to the secretory protein produced by epithelial cells.
- This complex (secretory IgA) protects against viral and bacterial pathogens.
- IgA is resistant to proteolytic enzymes and can therefore coexist with the proteases present in the lumen, making it effective even in the enzyme-rich intestinal environment.
B(i) Stratified squamous epithelium lines the oral cavity, esophagus, and anal canal (not vulnerable simple columnar). The rest of the GIT (except these three regions) is lined by a simple thin vulnerable epithelium. Because the rest of the GIT is lined by this vulnerable epithelium and normally contains thousands of microbial species (including potential pathogens), the MALT provides an essential backup to the thin physical barrier.
B(ii) The enteric nervous system (submucosal/Meissner and myenteric/Auerbach plexuses) provides an anatomic basis for the well-known actions of emotional stress on the stomach and other regions of the GIT. These plexuses are interconnected with the autonomic nervous system and CNS, which is why the enteric nervous system is considered the anatomic basis for these effects; the precise neural pathways by which stress modulates GIT function are not further detailed.

questions.question:
Describe the origin and fate (course and distribution) of the aortic arch arteries numbered I to VI.
State the safe site for a procedure on these vessels.
Explain the anatomical basis of the deformity following injury to one of these vessels.
questions.answerText:
Origin: each pharyngeal arch contains an arterial (aortic) arch, in addition to its skeletal element, striated muscles and nerve.
Fate/distribution of arch I and II: these form the carotid arteries.
Fate/distribution of arch IV: on the left, this forms the arch of the aorta.
Fate of arch V: this arch disappears.
Fate/distribution of arch VI: this forms the pulmonary arteries; the left is connected to the aorta through the ductus arteriosus during fetal life.
Related anomalies of great-vessel septation described alongside these arches include persistent truncus arteriosus and complete D-transposition of the great vessels.
The aorticopulmonary (AP) septum, which divides the truncus arteriosus into the aorta and pulmonary trunk, is formed by pairs of opposing truncal and bulbar ridges that grow and fuse in a spiral (not straight) fashion.
Safe site for a procedure: not covered.
Anatomical basis of the deformity after injury: not covered.
What is stated is limited to the fate of each numbered arch artery and the general description of AP septum formation.
No course, relations or branches of the resulting adult vessels are described beyond their fate as listed above.
No account of the consequence of injury to any of these vessels after development is given.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the gross anatomy of the organ of Corti and the first part of the auditory pathway.
A(ii) Describe the relay stations/nuclei along this pathway up to the cortex.
B) How does pathology near the origin of this pathway (e.g. a tumor) relate to a specific structure?
C) Explain the functional deficit this produces.
questions.answerText:
A(i) The organ of Corti consists of hair cells (the sensory cells of the auditory system) formed from the outer ridge of the cochlear duct epithelium, covered by the tectorial membrane. Ganglion cells of CN VIII migrate along the cochlear duct coils to form the spiral ganglion; peripheral processes extend to the organ of Corti's hair cells, while central processes form the cochlear nerve. First order neurones (bipolar, in the spiral ganglion) send peripheral processes to the hair cells and central processes forming the cochlear nerve, terminating in the dorsal and ventral cochlear nuclei in the pons.
A(ii) Second order neurone axons from the cochlear nucleus form the trapezoid body, crossing the midline to the contralateral superior olivary nucleus (other crossing fibres form the dorsal and intermediate acoustic striae). Third order neurones from the olivary nucleus form the lateral lemniscus, ascending to the inferior colliculus (some fibres synapsing at the nucleus of the lateral lemniscus); fibres then ascend via the inferior quadrigeminal brachium to the medial geniculate body, and from there to the auditory cortex in the temporal lobe via the acoustic radiation (sublenticular part of the internal capsule).
B) An acoustic neuroma is a tumor of the eighth cranial nerve, which lies close to the spiral ganglion/cochlear nerve origin of this pathway.
C) An acoustic neuroma is characterized by deafness and vertigo, reflecting its effect on the eighth cranial nerve (auditory and vestibular components).

A(i) The quadrangular cartilaginous septum extends from the nasal bones in the midline above to the bony septum in the midline posteriorly, then down along the bony floor. Its upper half is flanked by two triangular-to-trapezoidal cartilages, the upper lateral cartilages, which are fused to the dorsal septum in the midline and attached to the bony margin of the pyriform aperture laterally by loose ligaments; the inferior ends of the upper lateral cartilages are free. Beneath the upper lateral cartilages lie the lower lateral cartilages; the paired lower lateral cartilages swing out from medial attachments to the caudal septum in the midline (the medial crura), through an intermediate crus area, finally flaring out superolaterally as the lateral crura; these cartilages are frequently mobile, in contradistinction to the upper lateral cartilages. The internal area or angle formed by the septum and upper lateral cartilage constitutes the internal valve.
A(ii) The nasal septum is supplied from the sphenopalatine artery (posterior septal branch) and the anterior and posterior ethmoid arteries, with contribution of the superior labial artery (anteriorly) and the greater palatine artery (posteriorly).
B. The Kiesselbach plexus, or Little's area, represents a region in the anteroinferior third of the nasal septum where all 3 of the chief blood supplies to the internal nose converge, which is the clinical basis for this being a common site of nosebleeds; venous blood leaving the region drains into the facial, ophthalmic and sphenopalatine veins, and these veins are significant for their direct communication with the cavernous sinus and for their lack of valves, features that potentiate the intracranial spread of infection.
C. The upper lateral cartilages are fused to the dorsal septum in the midline and attached to the bony margin of the pyriform aperture laterally by loose ligaments, with their inferior ends free; they are relatively fixed. The lower lateral (alar) cartilages, by contrast, swing out from medial attachments to the caudal septum (the medial crura) to flare out superolaterally as the lateral crura, and are frequently mobile, unlike the upper lateral cartilages.

A patient was found to have a permanent cell line derived from cervical cancer cells. On investigation, the pathologist reports that the cells have been immortalized, can grow indefinitely in culture, and are called HeLa cells. Separately, the patient's biopsy shows cells undergoing defective apoptosis with uncontrolled proliferation.
(i) Identify the process by which HeLa cells became immortalized and explain its relationship to cancer.
(ii) List the risk factors (cellular processes) that predispose normal cells to become immortalized.
(iii) State the complications that arise when apoptosis is insufficient versus excessive.
(iv) Name two types of transplantable human cells or tissues that can save lives, and justify the use of one.
questions.answerText:
(i) Immortalization: certain changes can promote cell immortality — a process called transformation, which may be a first step in transforming a normal cell into a cancer cell. HeLa cells are the oldest and most commonly used human cell line, derived from cervical cancer cells taken on February 8, 1951 from Henrietta Lacks, who eventually died of her cancer on October 4, 1951. Most cells obtained from normal tissues have a finite, genetically programmed life span.
(ii) Risk factors predisposing to immortalization: transformation (a cellular change that promotes cell immortality); improvements in culture technology; most cell types can now be maintained in the laboratory indefinitely because of transformation and other improvements.
(iii) Complications: Excessive apoptosis causes atrophy, such as in ischemic damage. Insufficient apoptosis results in uncontrolled cell proliferation, such as cancer. Between 50 and 70 billion cells die each day due to apoptosis in the average human adult; for an average child between the ages of 8 and 14, approximately 20 billion to 30 billion cells die per day. Defective apoptotic processes have been implicated in an extensive variety of diseases.
(iv) Transplantable cells/tissues: (a) A corneal graft can restore sight in corneal blindness. (b) The transplantation of haematopoietic stem cells can cure congenital or acquired diseases including some leukaemias; these cells can be collected from living donors either as bone marrow or from peripheral blood, or as cord blood drawn from the placenta during or after delivery. Justification for haematopoietic stem cell transplantation: it can cure sickle cell disease and some leukaemias, addressing life-threatening conditions. The transplantation of a human heart valve often constitutes the best replacement situation and recipient patients do not require long-term anti-coagulation therapy.

questions.question:
A 40-year-old woman presents with pain along the medial side of the arm, a palpable lump in the upper outer quadrant of the breast and enlarged axillary lymph nodes.
(i) State the most likely diagnosis and the quadrant of the breast in which it most commonly arises.
(ii) Describe the lymphatic routes by which the disease spreads (with the proportion drained to each nodal group), the involvement of the opposite breast, the axillary node groups and the skin change that may result.
(iii) State the surgical options for the breast lesion and justify the option of choice in localised disease.
questions.answerText:
(i) Carcinoma of the breast, a common surgical condition; about 60% of breast carcinomas occur in the upper lateral (outer) quadrant.
(ii) About 75% of lymph drains to the axillary nodes: central and lateral parts to the pectoral group, upper part to the apical group; lymphatics pass around the edge of pectoralis major to the pectoral nodes, or through or between the pectoral muscles directly to the apical nodes. About 20% drains to the internal thoracic (parasternal) nodes, mainly from the medial part, along vessels passing through pectoralis major; the lower quadrants drain to the inferior phrenic (abdominal) nodes, and some lymphatics reach the rectus sheath and the subperitoneal and subhepatic plexuses. Lymphatics from the medial part cross the front of the sternum to anastomose with the opposite side, so cancer of one breast can involve the other breast and the opposite axillary nodes; nodes above and below the clavicle, and the axillary and cervical nodes, communicate freely. Axillary nodes lie in 5 groups: pectoral (anterior), subscapular (posterior), brachial (lateral), central and apical; newer levels: low (1), middle (2), upper/apical (3), with Rotter's nodes between pectoralis minor and major; the subclavian lymph trunk from the apical efferents opens into the subclavian vein (usually into the thoracic duct on the left). Infiltration of the ligaments of Cooper by the cancer shortens them and gives the peau d'orange appearance of the breast. Arm pain: the lateral cutaneous branch of T2 (intercostobrachial nerve) is joined to the medial cutaneous nerve of the arm; the explanation of the pain by compression from enlarged nodes is not covered.
(iii) Options named: lumpectomy, simple mastectomy, radical mastectomy and sentinel lymph node biopsy (mammography and lymphoscintigraphy are named as investigations). Option of choice: in localised cancer of the breast, simple mastectomy followed by radiotherapy to the axillary lymph nodes is the treatment of choice; any further justification is not covered. Because the lactiferous ducts are arranged radially from the nipple, an incision of the gland should be made in a radial direction to avoid cutting through the ducts.

(i) Allen's test (the Allen test), a medical sign used in physical examination of arterial blood flow to the hands.
(ii) One hand is examined at a time: the hand is elevated and the patient is asked to clench the fist for about 30 seconds; pressure is then applied over both the ulnar and radial arteries to occlude them; the hand is opened while still elevated, and should appear blanched; ulnar pressure is then released while radial pressure is maintained, and the colour should return within 5 to 15 seconds. If colour returns as described, the test is "positive"/normal; if colour fails to return, the test is "negative"/abnormal.
(iii) The radial and ulnar arteries at the wrist, which together form two interconnected vascular arches in the palm — the superficial palmar arch (mainly from the ulnar artery, with a superficial palmar branch of the radial artery) and the deep palmar arch (mainly from the radial artery, with a deep palmar branch of the ulnar artery).
(iv) The hand is at risk. A negative/abnormal Allen's test suggests that the ulnar artery supply to the hand is not sufficient, indicating that it may not be safe to cannulate or needle the radial artery, since a complication of the radial artery could then compromise the blood supply to the hand.

questions.answerText:
A(i) The internal lining of the larynx is endoderm; the muscle and cartilages come from the 4th and 6th pharyngeal arches.
A(i) The laryngeal orifice is initially a sagittal slit, becoming T-shaped as mesenchyme proliferates; the mesenchyme gives the thyroid, cricoid and arytenoid cartilages.
A(ii) Because the muscles derive from the 4th-6th arches they are supplied by the vagus nerve (CN X).
A(ii) The vagus gives two branches to the larynx: the superior laryngeal nerve supplies derivatives of the 4th arch and the recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies structures derived from the 6th arch.
A(iii) 4th arch: cricothyroid, levator palatini and constrictors of the pharynx.
A(iii) 6th arch: intrinsic muscles of the larynx and laryngeal cartilages (thyroid, cricoid, arytenoid, corniculate, cuneiform).
A(iv) The epithelium proliferates rapidly, temporarily occluding the lumen; vacuolization and recanalization later produce a pair of lateral recesses, the laryngeal ventricles.
A(iv) The recesses are bounded by folds that differentiate into the false and true vocal cords; through the laryngeal orifice the respiratory primordium communicates with the pharynx.
B(i) The safe site for a procedure on these nerves is not covered.
C(i) The anatomical basis of a deficit after injury to these nerves is not covered.
C(i) The vagus nerves also serve as markers of stomach rotation: the left vagus becomes ventral (anterior wall) and the right vagus dorsal (posterior wall).
C(i) The vagus supplies the derivatives of the 4th and 6th arches through its two laryngeal branches, as listed above.

A(i) Each intercostal space has a single posterior and two anterior intercostal arteries.
A(i) In the upper two spaces the posterior intercostal arteries arise from the superior intercostal artery (branch of the costocervical trunk of the subclavian artery); in the lower nine spaces they arise from the thoracic aorta (9 pairs, plus 1 pair of subcostal arteries from the posterior surface of the descending thoracic aorta).
A(ii) Course and branching follow the intercostal nerves: each artery runs forward in the subcostal groove, high in the space between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles, in the order vein, artery, nerve from above downwards, and anastomoses with the anterior intercostal artery.
A(iii) Branches go to adjacent muscles, skin, parietal pleura, spinal cord and breast (branches in the 3rd and 4th spaces supply the breast); the 3rd right posterior intercostal artery gives the right bronchial artery.
A(iii) Distribution: the posterior and lateral parts of the intercostal spaces.
A(iii) Veins accompany the arteries and contain valves that direct blood posteriorly; on the right the 1st space drains to the brachiocephalic vein and the rest to the azygos vein; on the left the upper 3 spaces drain to the left brachiocephalic vein and the rest to the hemiazygos and accessory hemiazygos veins, which drain to the azygos vein.
A(iii) Lymphatics: deep lymphatics follow the arteries; posteriorly they drain to the posterior intercostal nodes in the posterior mediastinum.
B(i) Safe site: a needle or drain is passed immediately above the upper border of a rib; it is dangerous to pass it immediately below a rib.
B(i) Basis: the intercostal vessels lie immediately below their corresponding ribs (vein above artery) in the subcostal groove, so a needle just above the lower rib avoids the neurovascular bundle; in thoracotomy the periosteum over a segment of the 5th or 6th rib is elevated, protecting the bundle.
C(i) In coarctation of the aorta the intercostal arteries derived from the aorta receive blood from the superior intercostals, from the anterior intercostal branches of the internal thoracic artery and from arteries anastomosing around the scapula.
C(i) Together with the communication between the internal thoracic and inferior epigastric arteries, these are the principal collaterals between the aorta above and below the block.
C(i) The intercostal arteries dilate and become tortuous and erode the lower borders of the corresponding ribs, giving the characteristic irregular notching of the ribs that helps radiographic confirmation.

questions.answerText:
(i) The liver has two surfaces - a convex diaphragmatic surface (anterior, superior, posterior and right lateral) and a relatively flat, posteroinferior visceral surface.
It is divided into a large right lobe and a smaller left lobe by the falciform ligament, with the caudate and quadrate lobes arising from the right lobe on the visceral surface.
Two sagittally oriented fissures (for the ligamentum teres and ligamentum venosum on the left, and the gallbladder fossa and IVC groove on the right) are linked by the transverse porta hepatis, forming an H on the visceral surface.
Ligaments include the falciform ligament, the coronary ligament with the right and left triangular ligaments, and the lesser omentum (hepatogastric and hepatoduodenal ligaments).
The porta hepatis transmits the hepatic ducts, hepatic artery and portal vein branches, and hepatic nerves and lymph nodes.
(ii) The bare area of the diaphragmatic surface has no peritoneal covering, so infection there can track through the diaphragm to posterior mediastinal lymph nodes.
The subphrenic and subhepatic spaces, and Morison's pouch between the liver and right kidney, are recesses where pathological fluid such as pus, blood or ascites collects.
Liver fissures serve as surgical landmarks, such as Cantlie's line, which divides the liver into functional right and left lobes along the middle hepatic vein.
Because the liver is large, fixed in position and friable, it is vulnerable to rupture, often from a fractured rib perforating the diaphragm, causing haemorrhage and right upper quadrant pain.
(iii) In cirrhosis, hepatocytes are destroyed and replaced by fibrous tissue that impedes blood flow through the liver, causing portal hypertension.
This opens portal-systemic anastomoses at the lower oesophagus, anal canal, paraumbilical region, retroperitoneum and intrahepatic sites, producing distant complications such as bleeding oesophageal varices.
Distension of Glisson's capsule from an enlarged liver produces sharp, well-localised pain via the lower intercostal nerves, illustrating how a hepatic process produces a distant sensory effect.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Spider-web appearance (leptomeninges together with the pia mater); a thin layer between the dura and pia; the subarachnoid space between it and the pia is filled with CSF.
A(ii) Cranial part: thin over the superior surface and thick at the base of the skull; invests the brain loosely and does not project into sulci and fissures except the longitudinal fissure.
- Spinal part: thin, delicate tube-like loose investment of the cord, continuous above with the cranial part and widening below to invest the cauda equina; also forms a tubular investment of cranial and spinal nerves; outer white fibrous and elastic fibres, inner low cuboidal mesothelium; nervous plexus from CN 5, 7 and 11.
A(iii) Subarachnoid cavity: thin over the summit of gyri, widening over the sulci, widest at the skull base where the cisterns lie; communicates freely with the ventricular system via the foramen of Magendie and the two lateral foramina of Luschka; terminates at S2; contains CSF.
- Cisterns: cisterna magna (largest; between cerebellum, medulla and occipital bone), medullary, pontis (basis pontis and clivus), interpeduncular, suprasellar (dorsal to sella turcica), quadrigeminal (dorsal to midbrain) and lumbar (after the end of the spinal cord).
A(iv) Evaginations of the arachnoid protruding into the dura; seen from the 3rd year of life, increasing in number with age from the 7th year; they pit the inner surface of the cranium and communicate with the venous sinuses.
B(i) The lumbar cistern lies after the end of the spinal cord (L2) and the subarachnoid cavity ends at S2, so CSF within it is tapped via lumbar puncture; cisternal and ventricular taps are also listed.
- CSF is reabsorbed through arachnoid villi/granulations by a valvular mechanism without back-flow of blood; hydrocephaly results from obstruction to CSF flow and absorption.
C(i) Arachnoid: thin, spider-web-like, loosely invests the brain and does not dip into the sulci; pia: delicate, closely applied to the brain surface, dipping into the sulci and cerebellar laminae.
C(ii) Pia is a vascular membrane of blood vessels held by fine areolar tissue, with fibrous tissue covered externally by a sheet of impermeable flat cells; it invaginates into the ventricles forming the tela choroidea and choroid plexus.
C(iii) Spinal pia is thicker, in two layers closely adherent to the cord, and forms the filum terminale below the conus medullaris, blending with the dura at S2.
- Both are leptomeninges with the CSF-filled subarachnoid space between them; both form sheaths around cranial and spinal nerves.

(i) The 'double bubble' sign of duodenal atresia or stenosis (bilious vomiting in infants; double bubble on X-ray or ultrasound).
(ii) Atresia: complete occlusion of the lumen involving the 2nd and 3rd parts of the duodenum; stenosis: incomplete recanalization involving the 3rd and 4th parts.
(ii) Most cases of atresia result from incomplete recanalization of the lumen distal to the duodenal papilla; the lumen is obliterated by rapid cell proliferation in the 2nd month and recanalized by apoptosis soon after.
(ii) About 25% of cases are associated with Down syndrome; it is relieved by resection of the obstructed segment.
(iii) Pyloric stenosis: forceful (projectile) non-bilious vomiting about 1 hour after feeding, hypertrophied sphincter palpable as a spherical nodule; due to overproliferation, not an error of recanalization; more common in males.
(iii) Midgut volvulus in malrotation: bilious emesis, may obstruct the SMA.
(iii) Atresias of the jejunum, ileum or colon: arterial occlusion rather than failed recanalization; present as intestinal obstruction a few days after birth.
(iv) The presence of bile indicates a post-duodenal blockage; the duodenum has a dual origin (caudal foregut and cranial midgut) and dual blood supply (coeliac trunk and SMA), the opening of the bile duct separating the two parts.

questions.answerText:
(i) The diagnosis is severe osteoarthritis of the right hip joint. The waddling gait (Trendelenburg gait) results from weakness of the hip abductors — gluteus medius and gluteus minimus — on the affected side; the pelvis drops on the contralateral side when the affected limb is weight-bearing.
(ii) Gluteus medius: origin from external surface of ilium between anterior and posterior gluteal lines; insertion to lateral surface of greater trochanter; innervation by superior gluteal nerve (L5, S1); action — abducts and medially rotates the thigh, keeps the pelvis level when the ipsilateral limb is weight-bearing, and advances the opposite side during its swing phase. Gluteus minimus: origin from external surface of ilium between anterior and inferior gluteal lines; insertion to anterior surface of greater trochanter; superior gluteal nerve (L5, S1); same actions. When these muscles are weakened by pain and disuse from hip OA, they cannot maintain a level pelvis during the stance phase, causing the contralateral hip to drop — the characteristic Trendelenburg sign and waddling gait.
(iii) In osteoarthritis, the following hip joint structures are destroyed: hyaline articular cartilage covering the lunate surface of the acetabulum and the head of femur; the synovial membrane (which becomes inflamed and thickened); the joint capsule (which becomes fibrotic); and the ligaments (iliofemoral, pubofemoral, ischiofemoral) become contracted. Subchondral bone undergoes sclerosis and osteophytes form at joint margins.
(iv) Conservative: physiotherapy, walking aids, analgesia, and NSAIDs. Surgical options: core decompression (early avascular necrosis), osteotomy (to redistribute load), and total hip replacement (THR). THR is justified here because the patient has end-stage joint destruction (loss of joint space, osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis), functional limitation (unable to walk more than half a mile, difficulty rising), and systemic inflammatory disease that makes conservative management unlikely to succeed. THR replaces the articular surfaces with prosthetic components cemented to the ends of the bones, reliably restoring mobility and eliminating pain.

A. Describe the course and distribution of the lingual nerve, including its relationship to the submandibular duct.

C. Explain the functional deficit that would be anticipated from injury to the lingual nerve, based on the sensory territory it supplies.
questions.answerText:
A. The lingual nerve is a branch of the mandibular nerve (CN V3). It provides sensory supply to the mucous membrane of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue. In its course, the submandibular duct (Wharton's duct) runs forwards on hyoglossus, between the lingual and hypoglossal nerves.
B. At the anterior border of hyoglossus, the submandibular duct is crossed by the lingual nerve; this crossing relationship is anatomically relevant, since a stone in the submandibular duct can be felt bimanually in the floor of the mouth, and surgery/removal in this region places the lingual nerve at risk, along with the hypoglossal nerve, given their close relationship to the duct on hyoglossus.
C. Sensory supply to the mucous membrane of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is via the lingual nerve (a branch of CN V3), while special (taste) sensory supply to the same region is via the chorda tympani nerve (a branch of CN VII); injury to the lingual nerve would therefore be expected to impair general sensation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, distinct from a taste deficit, which would instead follow injury to the chorda tympani.

A(i) The eye is formed by three germ layers: neuroectoderm, surface ectoderm and mesoderm.
A(ii) In the 4th week optic vesicles (outpocketings of the forebrain) touch the surface ectoderm and induce a lens placode; the vesicle invaginates to form a double-walled optic cup that stays attached to the brain by the optic stalk.
A(ii) The lens placode invaginates to a lens vesicle and then a solid lens; posterior wall cells elongate anteriorly and primary lens fibres reach the anterior wall by the 7th week.
A(iii) Optic cup: outer layer forms the pigmented layer of the retina and inner layer the neural layer; the posterior 4/5 (pars optica retinae) has rods and cones and nuclear layers, with nerve cells forming the optic nerve.
A(iii) The anterior 1/5 (pars caeca) divides into pars iridica (inner layer of iris) and pars ciliaris (ciliary body); mesenchyme forms the sphincter and dilator pupillae.
A(iv) 5th week: inner layer to choroid and outer layer to sclera (continuous with the dura around the optic nerve); vacuolization of mesenchyme forms the anterior chamber, and the iridopupillary membrane disappears; hyaloid vessels supply the lens and vitreous fills the network.
A(iv) The choroid fissure closes in the 7th week and the optic stalk becomes the optic nerve; eyelid buds form at 6 weeks, fuse at 8 weeks and separate in the 5th month; ciliary muscles derive from lateral plate mesoderm and extraocular muscles from somitomeres.
B(i) Coloboma (choroid fissure fails to close); persistent pupillary membrane; persistent hyaloid artery (cord or cyst); microphthalmia (too small, from intrauterine infections); anophthalmia; congenital aphakia; aniridia; blue sclera; albinism.
B(i) Cyclopia (single eye) and synophthalmia (fusion of the eyes) are invariably associated with cranial defects in which the cerebral hemispheres merge into a single telencephalic vesicle.
C(i) Congenital cataracts result from genetic reasons or rubella (German measles) infection between the 4th and 7th week of gestation.
C(i) Congenital rubella syndrome features cataract, cardiac defects and deafness, with microphthalmia and glaucoma also observed; the earlier the maternal infection, the greater the danger.
C(i) Thalidomide taken 24-36 days into gestation produces ocular anomaly among its other defects (limb, ear, renal, cardiac).

(i) The maxillary sinus, or antrum, may become infected either from the nasal cavity or from caries of the upper molar teeth; the infra-orbital nerve lies in a groove bulging into the roof of the sinus, while the floor of the sinus bears the impressions of the upper premolar and molar roots, these roots being separated from the sinus only by a thin layer of bone, which may in fact be deficient so that uncovered dental roots project into the sinus.
(ii) Because the medial wall of the maxillary sinus bears the opening (ostium) into the middle meatus above the inferior concha, and drainage channels are narrow and easily occluded, adequate drainage of an infected sinus can be difficult to achieve by the natural ostium alone.
(iii) Antral puncture can be carried out using a trocar and cannula passed through the nasal cavity in an outward and backward direction below the inferior concha; more adequate drainage may require removing a portion of the medial wall of the sinus below the inferior concha, or fenestrating the antrum in the gingivolabial fold (the Caldwell-Luc operation). Justification: since antral puncture alone may not provide adequate drainage, the Caldwell-Luc operation (fenestrating the antrum in the gingivolabial fold) is the option indicated when more adequate, definitive drainage is required.

A female patient develops infection of the peritoneal cavity that appears to have entered from the exterior, and inflammatory exudate later collects in the pelvis and the upper abdomen.

questions.answerText:
(i) Peritonitis (spread of infection within the peritoneal cavity).
(ii) In the female the cavity communicates with the exterior through the uterine tubes, uterus and vagina, a potential pathway of infection; in males it is a closed sac.
(ii) The right paracolic gutter, lateral to the ascending colon, communicates with the hepatorenal recess and the pelvic cavity and provides a route for spread between the pelvic and upper abdominal regions.
(ii) The left paracolic gutter, lateral to the descending colon, is separated from the area around the spleen by the phrenicocolic ligament; free communication exists between supracolic and infracolic compartments through the gutters.
(iii) Peritoneal fluid contains leukocytes and antibodies that resist infection and is absorbed by lymphatics on the inferior surface of the diaphragm; the peritoneum has phagocytic cells.
(iii) The greater omentum can wrap around an inflamed organ such as the appendix, walling it off and protecting other viscera (the 'abdominal policeman').
(iv) Management and definitive treatment are not covered.
