A. The larynx is demarcated by the vestibular fold (containing fibrous tissue, forming the false vocal cord on each side) and the vocal fold (the true vocal cord, containing the vocal ligament) into 3 zones: the supraglottic compartment (vestibule), above the false cords; the glottic compartment, between the false and true cords; and the subglottic compartment, between the true cords and the first ring of the trachea. The space between the vocal cords is the rima glottidis.
B. The mucosa is firmly adherent to the vocal ligament without any intervening submucosa, which accounts for the pearly white, avascular appearance of the vocal cords as seen on laryngoscopy; regulation of vocal cord tension (and therefore pitch of the voice) is accomplished primarily by pivoting the thyroid cartilage forward or backward at the cricothyroid joint, via the cricothyroid muscle, which is the only laryngeal muscle that tightens the cords, is supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (not the recurrent laryngeal nerve), and is the only intrinsic laryngeal muscle situated on the outside of the larynx.
C. Sensory innervation is via the internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve above the cords and via the recurrent laryngeal nerve below the cords; motor supply to the muscles is from the nucleus ambiguus via the cranial accessory, with the cricothyroid supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve and all other laryngeal muscles (including the upper oesophagus and cricopharyngeus) supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve. Lymphatic drainage above the cords is to the upper deep cervical nodes and below the cords to the lower deep cervical nodes; a disease process at either level can therefore spread along its corresponding drainage route to functionally distant lymph node groups. Movements which close off the entrance to the larynx during swallowing involve the epiglottis being pulled down and the arytenoid cartilages being pulled forward toward the epiglottis; the larynx is also raised, along with the pharynx, by contraction of the longitudinal muscles of the pharynx, and the epiglottis acts partly as a passive barrier, so disordered laryngeal muscle action compromises this protective closure mechanism.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Adductor longus: origin — anterior surface of body of pubis, inferior to pubic crest and lateral to pubic symphysis; insertion — middle third of medial lip of linea aspera of femur; innervation — obturator nerve, anterior division (L2, L3, L4); action — adducts thigh. It is the most anteriorly placed muscle of the adductor group, large and fan-shaped. Adductor brevis: origin — body and inferior ramus of pubis; insertion — pectineal line and proximal part of linea aspera of femur; innervation — obturator nerve, anterior division (L2, L3, L4); action — adducts thigh and to an extent flexes it; it is short and lies deep to pectineus and adductor longus. Adductor magnus: largest, most powerful, most posterior muscle in the group; has an adductor part and a hamstring part. Origin — adductor part from inferior ramus of pubis and ramus of ischium; hamstring part from ischial tuberosity. Insertion — adductor part to gluteal tuberosity, linea aspera, medial supracondylar line; hamstring part to adductor tubercle of femur. Innervation — adductor part: obturator nerve (L2, L3, L4); hamstring part: tibial nerve. Action — adducts thigh; adductor part flexes, hamstring part extends. Gracilis: origin — body and inferior ramus of pubis; insertion — superior part of medial surface of tibia; innervation — obturator nerve (L2, L3); action — adducts thigh, flexes leg, helps rotate leg medially. Obturator externus: origin — margins of obturator foramen and obturator membrane; insertion — trochanteric fossa of femur; innervation — obturator nerve (L2, L3); action — laterally rotates thigh, steadies head of femur in acetabulum.
A(ii) All adductor muscles are supplied by the obturator nerve except the hamstring part of adductor magnus and part of pectineus. The hamstring part of adductor magnus is supplied by the tibial nerve — because embryologically the hamstring part shares the same developmental origin as the true hamstrings (which arise from the ischial tuberosity and are all innervated by the tibial division of the sciatic nerve).
B(i) The adductor hiatus is an opening between the aponeurotic distal attachment of the adductor part of adductor magnus and the tendinous distal attachment of the hamstring part. It transmits the femoral artery and vein from the adductor canal in the thigh to the popliteal fossa posterior to the knee. It is located just lateral and superior to the adductor tubercle of the femur.
B(ii) The pes anserinus consists of the conjoined tendons of the sartorius, gracilis, and semitendinosus muscles; they insert into the superior part of the medial surface of the tibia. It acts as a secondary valgus restraint, augmenting the medial supporting structures of the knee. Bursitis of the pes anserinus bursa causes medial knee pain, especially in osteoarthritis.
C(i) Gracilis is unique among the adductor group: it is a long strap-like muscle, the most medial and most superficial of the adductors, and the weakest member; it is the only member of the adductor group to cross both the hip and knee joints. It joins with sartorius (from the anterior compartment, supplied by femoral nerve) and semitendinosus (from the posterior compartment, supplied by tibial nerve) to form the pes anserinus — three muscles from three different compartments with three different nerve supplies share a common insertion.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Three parts of the renal tubule:
1. Proximal convoluted tubule (PCT): cuboidal cells with dense microvilli (brush border — increase surface area); large mitochondria; functions in reabsorption and secretion; confined to the cortex.
2. Nephron loop: descending and ascending limbs; distal descending limb = descending thin limb — simple squamous epithelium; thick ascending limb — cuboidal to columnar cells (thin in some nephrons).
3. Distal convoluted tubule (DCT): cuboidal cells with very few microvilli; functions more in secretion than reabsorption; confined to the cortex.
A(ii) Nephron loop:
- Descending limb: proximal descending limb is continuous with the proximal tubule; distal descending limb (thin limb) is lined by simple squamous epithelium.
- Thick ascending limb: cuboidal to columnar cells; may be thin in some nephrons.
B(i) Renal corpuscle:
- Two components: glomerulus and glomerular (Bowman's) capsule.
- Glomerulus: tuft of capillaries with fenestrated endothelium (highly porous) allowing filtrate formation.
- Glomerular capsule: cup-shaped, hollow structure surrounding the glomerulus; has two layers:
 * Parietal layer: simple squamous epithelium.
 * Visceral layer: branching epithelial podocytes; extensions terminate in foot processes that cling to the basement membrane; filtration slits between foot processes allow filtrate to pass into the capsular space.
B(ii) Structural adaptations of the PCT:
- Dense microvilli (brush border) greatly increase the apical surface area for reabsorption.
- Large mitochondria provide energy (ATP) for active transport processes.
- Highly infolded basolateral membrane increases surface area for solute exchange at the basolateral side.
- These features together support the PCT's role in reabsorption and secretion.

Origin: during the 4th week, the septum transversum lies opposite the 3rd to 5th cervical somites.
During the 5th week, myoblasts from these somites move to the developing diaphragm, bringing their nerve fibres with them; these nerve fibres constitute the phrenic nerve.
Course: as the diaphragm descends with the rapid growth of the body of the embryo, the phrenic nerve accompanies it — by the 6th week the diaphragm (and so the nerve's course) lies at the level of the thoracic somites, and by the end of the 8th week the dorsal end of the diaphragm lies at the level of the first lumbar vertebra.
Distribution: when the four parts of the diaphragm fuse, mesenchymal cells from the septum transversum extend into the other three parts and become myoblasts, so the phrenic nerve supplies all the muscles of the diaphragm.
The phrenic nerve also supplies sensory fibres to the diaphragm, except in the peripheral region.
The peripheral region is derived from the body wall and brings its own nerve supply, the lower intercostal nerves, with it.
Safe site for a surgical procedure: not covered.
Anatomical basis of the deformity after injury: not covered.
What is covered is only the nerve's developmental origin and its motor and sensory distribution as set out above.
The note on the position of the phrenic nerve in the fibrous pericardium (formed from the fused pleuropericardial membranes) is stated but not elaborated further.
No description of a surgical landmark, needle or incision site, or of a post-injury deformity (e.g. of diaphragmatic movement) is given.
These aspects would need to be sourced elsewhere, as they are outside the scope of what is stated here.

A(i) Describe the general features of the lung (shape, appearance, weight, right compared with left) and its apex, base, surfaces and borders.
A(ii) Describe the lobes and fissures and the surface marking of the lower border of the lung.
A(iii) Compare the hilum and roots of the right and left lungs.
A(iv) Describe the bronchopulmonary segments of the right and left lungs and the features of a bronchopulmonary segment.
A(v) Describe the blood supply, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of the lung.
B(i) Relate the parts and segments of the lung to the sites and spread of common pathologies.
C(i) Explain how disease of the lung and pleura may involve distant structures and produce referred pain or a functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Conical, soft, spongy, elastic and pinkish in health (brown in the young, mottled black in adults and dark in city dwellers from deposited dust and carbon particles); right lung about 600 g, left about 550 g; the right is larger, heavier, shorter and wider. Each has an apex, a base, 3 surfaces (costal convex, mediastinal with the hilum, diaphragmatic concave), 3 borders (anterior, posterior, inferior) and a root; the posterior surface lies in the paravertebral gutter.
A(i) Apex: rounded, extends into the root of the neck 2.5-4 cm above the sternal end of the 1st rib, covered by cervical pleura and suprapleural membrane. Base: broad, concave, rests on the diaphragm, which separates the right lung from the right lobe of the liver and the left lung from the left lobe of the liver, stomach and spleen. Anterior border: where costal and mediastinal surfaces meet, with the cardiac notch on the left; posterior border from C7 to T10; inferior border separates the base from the costal and mediastinal surfaces.
A(ii) Right lung: 3 lobes (upper, middle, lower) by oblique and horizontal fissures; left lung: 2 lobes (upper and smaller lower) by the oblique fissure, with the lingula below the cardiac notch; visceral pleura extends into the fissures so the lobes move freely. Lower border (neutral position) crosses the 6th rib in the midclavicular line, the 8th rib in the midaxillary line and reaches the 10th rib posteriorly.
A(iii) Hilum: wedge-shaped area on the mediastinal surface; root lies opposite T5-T7. Right root: in the groove of the arch of the azygos vein; eparterial and hyparterial bronchi, right pulmonary artery, 2 right pulmonary veins, hilar lymph nodes. Left root: in the concavity of the arch of the aorta; left main bronchus, left pulmonary artery, 2 left pulmonary veins, hilar lymph nodes. Both also contain bronchial vessels, nerves and lymphatics enclosed by pleura.
A(iv) Right lung, 10 segments: upper lobe apical, posterior, anterior; middle lobe lateral, medial; lower lobe superior (apical), medial basal, anterior basal, lateral basal, posterior basal. Left lung, 8 segments: upper lobe apicoposterior, anterior, superior lingula, inferior lingula; lower lobe superior (apical), medial basal, anterior basal, lateral basal, posterior basal.
A(iv) Each segment is pyramidal (apex to the hilum, base to the surface), separated from its neighbours by connective tissue septa, with the segmental bronchus, bronchial vessels and a pulmonary artery branch central; little arterial anastomosis between segments; intersegmental pulmonary vein tributaries guide separation; it has its own lymphatics and autonomic supply and is the smallest part that can be removed without affecting adjacent lung.
A(v) Arteries: 2 left bronchial arteries from the descending thoracic aorta and 1 right bronchial artery from the 3rd right posterior intercostal supply the bronchial tree down to the respiratory bronchioles; pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood to the alveoli and anastomose with the bronchial arteries at the precapillary level. Veins: 4 pulmonary veins to the left atrium; right bronchial vein to the azygos vein, left to the accessory hemiazygos vein.
A(v) Lymph: superficial plexus (deep to the visceral pleura) and deep plexus (peribronchial) drain to pulmonary then bronchopulmonary (hilar) nodes, then superior and inferior tracheobronchial nodes, then the bronchomediastinal trunks to the junction of subclavian and internal jugular veins (right trunk may form the right lymphatic duct; left may end in the thoracic duct). Nerves: pulmonary plexuses; vagus is bronchoconstrictor, vasodilator and secretomotor, sympathetic has the opposite actions.
B(i) Connective tissue septa between segments are a natural barrier to the spread of infection, but carcinoma and tuberculosis break through; abscesses are commoner in the posterior segment of the upper lobe and the apical segment of the lower lobe because these are the most dependent segments in the supine position.
B(i) Other pathologies: foreign particles enter the right main bronchus easily (wider, more vertical); pulmonary embolism (pulmonary artery obstructed by air, blood clot, fat, tumour cells or foreign particles); asthma (dyspnoea); fibrosis reduces compliance and emphysema reduces elasticity; lobectomy or pneumonectomy is used in lung cancer.
C(i) Costal pleura is supplied by intercostal nerves, so pleural or lung disease may cause referred pain along the thoracic wall and anterior abdominal wall; irritation over the central diaphragm refers pain to the shoulder through the phrenic nerve (C3-5).
C(i) Lymphatic spread passes from the hilar nodes to the tracheobronchial nodes and bronchomediastinal trunks; a tumour within the chest cavity may compress the phrenic nerve and cause diaphragmatic paralysis with paradoxical movement (functional deficit).

questions.question:
Describe the gross anatomy of the thyroid gland, including its development and final position.
State how its developmental parts/zones relate to the anomalies that can occur.
Explain how disease may spread to affect a distant structure and cause a functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
Gross anatomy: the thyroid is the first endocrine gland to develop, in the 4th week, from the endoderm, as an epithelial proliferation in the floor of the pharynx.
After formation of the arches, the medial ends of the two mandibular arches are separated by the tuberculum impar, behind which lies the foramen caecum; the foramen caecum thickens below the surface to form the thyroglossal duct, which at first connects the developing tongue and thyroid gland.
The tip of the duct becomes bilobed, and proliferating cells in the bifid end form the two lobes of the thyroid gland; the thyroglossal duct later becomes solid and disappears, and the developing gland descends in front of the hyoid bone and laryngeal cartilage.
The gland reaches its final position in the 7th week in the neck, in front of the trachea, with the two lobes connected by an isthmus to the 2nd, 3rd and 4th tracheal rings.
Colloid is formed within the gland by the 11th week, and it becomes functional by the 12th week; the parafollicular (C) cells, derived from the ultimobranchial body, form the C cells of the thyroid gland.
Zones/parts relating to anomalies: thyroglossal cysts and fistulae, and carcinoma of the thyroglossal duct, arise along the course of the duct that normally becomes solid and disappears.
Lingual thyroid and intralingual thyroid represent arrest of descent of the gland near its site of origin at the foramen caecum/tongue.
Ectopic thyroid represents arrest of descent anywhere else along the normal path of migration.
Absence of the isthmus is an anomaly of the paired lobes failing to be connected as normal.
Congenital hypothyroidism is listed among these anomalies.
Spread to a distant structure causing a functional deficit: not covered.
No mechanism of disease spread beyond the gland's own developmental region is described.

questions.question:
A patient in the late stage of Parkinson's disease is to be treated by stimulation of a diencephalic region lying between the midbrain and the thalamus.
(i) Give the diagnosis and the anatomical basis of the disease.
(ii) Name the procedure and the region stimulated.
(iii) State the anatomical landmarks: boundaries, contents, connections and functions of the region.
(iv) State any embryologic variant.
questions.answerText:
(i) Parkinson's disease (Parkinsonism): the substantia nigra forms the boundary between the crus and the tegmentum of the midbrain and gives rise to nigrostriatal fibres that project to the other basal ganglia nuclei; loss of these fibres explains Parkinsonism.
(ii) Stimulation of the subthalamus helps in the late stage of Parkinson's disease.
(iii) The subthalamus lies between the midbrain and the thalamus; the hypothalamus forms its medial boundary and the internal capsule its lateral boundary.
- The red nucleus and the substantia nigra extend into its caudal portion from the midbrain.
- The subthalamic nuclei lie lateral to the red nucleus and substantia nigra, receive afferents from the globus pallidus and form the efferent pathway for the corpus striatum.
- The subthalamus is concerned with control of micturition and generation of rhythmic movement.
(iv) Embryologic variant: not covered (the subthalamus is stated to be present only in mammals).

questions.question:
A young male presents with a unilateral, oval groin swelling that descends downwards, forwards and medially into the scrotum and is reduced by moving it upward, backward and laterally.
(i) Give the diagnosis and the features that distinguish it from the direct type.
(ii) Explain the embryologic basis of the swelling and the relation of its neck to the deep inguinal ring and the inferior epigastric vessels.
(iii) State the coverings of the sac and why males and the right side are commonly affected.
(iv) State the clinical tests used to confirm it and the definitive management.
questions.answerText:
(i) Indirect inguinal hernia, the most common form of hernia.
(i) Indirect: young, unilateral, oval, can reach the scrotum, descends downwards, forwards and medially, reduces upward, backward and laterally, lies lateral to the inferior epigastric artery. Direct: common in old, usually bilateral, hemispherical, never reaches the scrotum, moves forwards, reduces backward, lies medial to the artery.
(ii) It is believed to be congenital in origin; the hernial sac is the remains of the processus vaginalis.
(ii) It enters the inguinal canal through the deep inguinal ring lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels and may extend part of the way along the canal or as far as the superficial inguinal ring.
(ii) If the processus vaginalis has undergone no obliteration, the hernia is complete and extends through the superficial ring into the scrotum or labium majus; the neck of the sac lies at the deep inguinal ring.
(iii) Coverings: skin, superficial fascia, external spermatic fascia, cremasteric muscle and fascia, internal spermatic fascia and extraperitoneal fat.
(iii) It is 20 times more common in young males than females (more common in males because of the larger passage caused by the descent of the testis) and more common on the right because the right testis descends later than the left.
(iv) Superficial ring test: feel an impulse on the tip of the finger. Deep ring test: reduce the hernia, put the thumb over the deep ring and ask the patient to cough; the hernia does not appear.
(iv) A prosthesis can be placed in the retroinguinal space (between parietal peritoneum and transversalis fascia); the iliopubic tract is a landmark in laparoscopic hernia repair. The specific operative steps and resuscitation are not covered.

questions.question:
Laryngoscopy in a patient with fever and difficulty swallowing demonstrates bulging of the posterior pharyngeal wall, obstructing the laryngeal inlet.
(i) What space is implicated in this finding, and what are its boundaries?
(ii) What structure is being compressed/obstructed as a result?
(iii) What iatrogenic cause is described for collections in this space?
(iv) Give the clinico-anatomical reasoning linking the fascial planes of the neck to this presentation.
questions.answerText:
(i) The retropharyngeal space is the space between the pharynx and the prevertebral fascia; the prevertebral layer of the deep cervical fascia is attached superiorly to the base of the skull, and inferiorly enters the thorax and blends with the anterior longitudinal ligament of the vertebral column.
(ii) The image demonstrates bulging of the posterior pharyngeal wall, with the swelling obstructing the laryngeal inlet.
(iii) Penetration of the fascia during instrumentation of the pretracheal fascia can lead to collection of infectious substances (pus) in the retropharyngeal space.
(iv) The deep cervical fascia is condensed into well-defined fibrous sheets, including the investing layer, pretracheal fascia, prevertebral fascia, carotid sheath, and axillary fascia; because the retropharyngeal space lies specifically between the pharynx and the prevertebral fascia, and is anatomically continuous along the length of the neck (from skull base into the thorax), instrumentation-related penetration of the adjacent pretracheal fascia can allow pus to track into this potential space, producing the posterior pharyngeal wall bulging and laryngeal inlet obstruction seen on laryngoscopy; other clinical correlates of the deep neck fascia include whiplash injury causing quadriplegia, and stabbing injury causing vascular/nervous injury.

(i) Klumpke's paralysis (lower brachial plexus palsy).
(ii) It is caused by undue abduction of the arm, as in clutching a tree branch with the hand during a fall from a height, or sometimes as a birth injury.
(iii) The site of injury is the lower trunk of the brachial plexus, with nerve roots T1 and C8 involved. Muscles paralysed are the intrinsic muscles of the hand (T1) and the ulnar flexors of the wrist and fingers (C8), producing a claw hand due to the unopposed action of the long flexors and extensors of the fingers — hyperextension at the metacarpophalangeal joints and flexion at the interphalangeal joints. Cutaneous anaesthesia and analgesia occur in a narrow zone along the ulnar border of the forearm and hand. The eye findings represent Horner's syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhydrosis, enophthalmos and loss of the ciliospinal reflex), which occurs because of injury to sympathetic fibres to the head and neck that leave the spinal cord through the T1 nerve; vasomotor changes (skin warmer from arteriolar dilation, drier from loss of sweating) and, in long-standing cases, trophic changes (dry, scaly skin, nails that crack easily, atrophy of the pulp of the fingers) may also occur.
questions.question:
A 25-year-old man falls from a height while clutching a tree branch with his hand. He is found to have a claw-hand deformity of the affected limb, along with drooping of the eyelid and a constricted pupil on the same side.
(i) What is the diagnosis?
(ii) What are the predisposing factors for this condition?
(iii) What is the pathophysiology, including an explanation for the eye findings?

Describe the blastocyst under the following headings:
(i) The trophoblast and embryoblast
(ii) The blastocystic cavity
(iii) Implantation and repair of the implantation defect.
Explain the clinical basis of the reparation of the implantation defect in the endometrium.
Distinguish between the cytotrophoblast and the syncytiotrophoblast.
questions.answerText:
(i) The morula cells separate into two cell lines: an outer cell layer, the trophoblast, which gives rise to the chorion and finally the fetal part of the placenta, and a group of centrally located cells, the inner cell mass or embryoblast, which gives rise to the embryo.
By day 8, the trophoblast has differentiated into cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast, and the embryoblast into a hypoblast layer and an epiblast layer; spaces occur within the epiblast to form the amniotic cavity.
(ii) Shortly after the morula enters the uterus (day 4), fluid passes from the uterine cavity through the zona pellucida to form a single fluid-filled space, the blastocystic cavity (blastocoele); the blastocyst is enclosed by the zona pellucida and lies free in the uterine cavity.
(iii) Implantation, the penetration of the uterine wall by the blastocyst, begins on day 7 and ends on day 13, occurring through five stages, including attachment of the blastocyst to the endometrial epithelium (mediated by L-selectin on the trophoblast and its receptor on the endometrial epithelium) and invasion of the trophoblast cells into the endometrium.
The third stage is reparation of the implantation defect in the endometrium, in which the defect in the epithelium is filled with a closing plug (operculum), consisting of a blood clot and cellular debris.
By day 9, when the blastocyst is deeply embedded, the defect is described as plugged with fibrin clots.
Clinical basis: as the trophoblast invades the endometrium, it creates a defect in the endometrial epithelium; this is repaired by formation of the operculum (blood clot and cellular debris), and later reinforced by fibrin clots, sealing the implantation site as the blastocyst becomes completely embedded by days 11 and 12.
This reparative plugging allows the blastocyst to become fully embedded within the endometrium while the defect it created is closed over.
Distinguishing feature 1: the cytotrophoblast is the inner, cellular layer of the trophoblast surrounding the embryo.
Distinguishing feature 2: the syncytiotrophoblast is the outer layer; it erodes the uterine glands and blood vessel walls, and mediates placental transfer by diffusion from the lacunae to the embryo.
By day 13, the cytotrophoblast grows outwards into the syncytiotrophoblast in a finger-like manner, forming the primary villi, showing the cytotrophoblast as the proliferative source that the syncytiotrophoblast overlies.
Both layers together constitute the trophoblast, which as a whole gives rise to the chorion and the fetal part of the placenta.

questions.question:
An elderly man with weak abdominal muscles has a usually bilateral, hemispherical groin swelling that never reaches the scrotum, and the neck of its sac is wide.
(i) Give the diagnosis and its frequency.
(ii) Name the type of repair and where the prosthesis may be placed.
(iii) State the anatomical landmarks used in the repair and in locating the sac.
(iv) State the structures at risk during the repair.
(v) Explain the embryologic variant of the condition and contrast it.
questions.answerText:
(i) Direct inguinal hernia; about 15% of all inguinal hernias, common in old men with weak abdominal muscles and rare in women.
(ii) Laparoscopic hernia repair; a prosthesis can be placed in the retroinguinal space between the parietal peritoneum and the transversalis fascia.
(iii) The iliopubic tract (thickened inferior margin of transversalis fascia running deep and parallel to the inguinal ligament) is a landmark in laparoscopic repair.
(iii) The sac bulges forward through the posterior wall of the inguinal canal medial to the inferior epigastric artery, passing directly through the inguinal triangle and possibly disrupting the floor of the canal.
(iv) The inferior epigastric vessels, covered by the lateral umbilical folds, bleed if cut; the ilioinguinal and iliohypogastric nerves are prone to injury across the abdominal wall.
(v) The indirect variant is believed to be congenital: its sac is the remains of the processus vaginalis and it enters through the deep ring lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels, may reach the scrotum, and is unilateral and oval.
(v) Direct hernia coverings are the same as indirect but the conjoint tendon replaces the cremasteric muscle and fascia; the neck of the sac is wide.
(v) Further operative steps are not covered.

questions.question:
Describe the tibia under the following headings, state how its zones relate to common pathologies, and explain why fracture of the middle third is at highest risk of delayed union.
A(i) General features, upper end, shaft, and lower end of the tibia
A(ii) How the upper end of the tibia relates to the knee joint — tibial plateaus, menisci, and intercondylar areas
B(i) Blood supply of the tibia and the significance of nutrient artery direction
B(ii) Common pathologies related to zones of the tibia — proximal, mid-shaft, and distal
C(i) Distinguish tibia from fibula with respect to weight-bearing function, articulations, and nerve–vessel relations at each malleolus
questions.answerText:
A(i) The tibia is the large weight-bearing medial bone of the leg; it articulates with femoral condyles superiorly and the head of fibula laterally. It has an expanded upper end, a shaft, and a smaller lower end. Upper end (see A(ii)). Shaft: triangular in cross-section; 3 borders and 3 surfaces (borders and surfaces are named by opposites); anterior border forms the shin; soleal line on the posterior surface is for soleus. Lower end: expanded; saddle-shaped articular surface for talus; prolonged downwards medially to form the medial malleolus; the medial surface is subcutaneous from the medial malleolus to the medial condyle above.
A(ii) The upper end has tibial plateaus (lateral and medial condyles); the lateral and medial menisci; anterior and posterior intercondylar areas separate the tibial plateaus; the intercondylar eminence; an articular facet for the head of fibula; and a groove on the medial condyle for semimembranosus. The anterior intercondylar area of the tibia is where the ACL attaches (just posterior to attachment of medial meniscus); the posterior intercondylar area is where the PCL attaches.
B(i) The nutrient artery (medullary artery) is the main artery of the diaphysis. It is directed obliquely away from the epiphyseal end. When there is an epiphysis at both ends (tibia is one of the 5 bones unique in having epiphyseal plates at both ends — viz: femur, tibia, fibula, humerus, and radius), the nutrient canal is directed away from the more actively growing end. Hughes: 'to the elbow I go, from the knee I flee'. Fracture of the middle third of the tibia lies in a 'watershed' zone between the nutrient artery (supplying the upper 2/3) and the periosteal vessels (supplying the lower 1/3), making this zone most susceptible to avascular non-union.
B(ii) Proximal tibia: tibial plateau fractures (high-energy trauma), associated with meniscal and ligamentous tears. Mid-shaft tibia: most common site of delayed or non-union, stress fractures (runners), and compartment syndrome (anterior compartment syndrome). Distal tibia (ankle): Pott's fracture involving the malleolus; ankle sprains; avulsion fractures.
C(i) Tibia: large weight-bearing medial bone; articulates with femoral condyles, fibula head, and talus; contributes the roof (inferior surface of tibia) and the medial malleolus (wall) of the ankle mortise; the medial surface is subcutaneous. Fibula: not a weight-bearing bone; does not articulate with the femur or patella at the knee (only serves as attachment for knee joint structures); contributes the lateral malleolus (wall of ankle mortise) from fibula. At the ankle: lateral malleolar wall is from fibula and medial malleolar wall is from tibia.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the gross anatomy of cartilage under the following headings: definition, histogenesis (development from mesenchyme), growth mechanisms, and nutrient supply.
A(ii) Relate the three types of cartilage to their specific locations and collagen types, explaining why each is suited to its location.
B(i) Explain why articular cartilage degenerates with age and state the role of exercise in cartilage health.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Definition: Cartilage is a connective tissue in which the cells are relatively sparse and embedded in a large amount of firm characteristic matrix. It is a specialized form of connective tissue in which the firm consistency of the extracellular matrix allows the tissue to bear mechanical stresses without permanent distortion. Histogenesis: Cartilage is derived from the mesenchyme. The first modification observed is the rounding up of mesenchymal cells, which retract their extensions, multiply rapidly, and form mesenchymal condensations of chondroblasts (cells with ribosome-rich basophilic cytoplasm). Synthesis and deposition of matrix then begin to separate chondroblasts from one another. Differentiation takes place from center outward: central cells have characteristics of chondrocytes, peripheral cells are typical chondroblasts. The superficial mesenchyme develops into the perichondrium. Growth mechanisms: interstitial growth (from mitotic division of preexisting chondrocytes, expanding from within) and appositional growth (from differentiation of perichondrial cells, expanding from the outside). Nutrient supply: Cartilage is avascular; nourished by diffusion of nutrients from capillaries in adjacent connective tissue (perichondrium) or by synovial fluid. It has no lymphatic vessels or nerves. Chondrocytes exhibit low metabolic activity.
A(ii) Hyaline cartilage: most common form; collagen type II is the principal collagen; found in nose, trachea, bronchi, rib-sternal joints, and synovial joints; resilient and shock absorbing. Elastic cartilage: contains abundant elastic fibers in addition to collagen type II; found in auricle of ear, external auditory canals, eustachian tubes, epiglottis, and cuneiform cartilage in larynx; elastic fibers allow flexibility. Fibrocartilage: rich in collagen type I (acidophilic matrix); found in intervertebral disks, attachments of certain ligaments to cartilaginous surfaces, and symphysis pubis; dense collagen provides strength for high-load sites.
B(i) Articular cartilage is devoid of perichondrium and is sustained by diffusion of oxygen and nutrients from synovial fluid; this limited supply combined with low metabolic activity of chondrocytes means repair is slow. Hyaline cartilage is more susceptible to degenerative aging processes; calcification of the matrix, preceded by an increase in size and volume of chondrocytes followed by their death, leads to osteoarthritis. Role of exercise: participation in sports involving torsional loading, fast acceleration/deceleration, repetitive high impact increases risk of osteoarthritis. However, some levels of loading and exercise are beneficial: exercise enhances production of matrix molecules, which can have a positive effect on joint health. Exercise has both beneficial and detrimental effects on cartilage.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the gross anatomy of the pons: position, relations and external features.
A(ii) Describe its internal structure at the upper and lower levels.
A(iii) Describe its blood supply.
B(i) State how its parts relate to common pathologies.
C(i) Explain how its fibre connections link distant structures.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Forms a bridge between the midbrain, medulla and cerebellum; its transversely running fibres coalesce to form the middle cerebellar peduncle; contains the respiratory centre.
- The cerebellum covers its dorsal surface with the pontine part of the 4th ventricle between; the central aqueduct opens into the 4th ventricle; the superior medullary velum (anchored on the SCP) forms the roof; upper and lower pons differ by absence or presence of the opened 4th ventricle.
- Ventrally a midline groove houses the basilar artery and the superior cerebellar artery curves around its boundary with the midbrain; CN V (motor and sensory) emerges lateral to the midline; at the pontomedullary junction CN VI emerges at the midline and CN VII and VIII more laterally.
A(ii) Basis pontis (ventral): pontine nuclei and fibre bundles; tegmentum (dorsal): forms the floor of the 4th ventricle.
- Upper pons: motor nucleus of CN V on the lateral floor with the main sensory nucleus (touch) lateral to it, continuous with the mesencephalic nucleus (proprioception); lateral lemniscus and smaller superior olivary nucleus; bounded by superior cerebellar peduncles.
- Lower pons: CN VI nucleus on the floor near the midline, CN VII nucleus ventral and lateral to it; CN VII fibres course dorsal to the CN VI nucleus raising the facial colliculus; CN VIII nuclei lateral (vestibular part more medial), fibres travel in the inferior cerebellar peduncle.
A(iii) Supplied by the basilar, superior cerebellar and anterior inferior cerebellar arteries.
B(i) The nuclei and vital centres (respiratory centre) make injury to the brainstem present with grave clinical consequences; pathologies of specific pontine parts are not covered.
C(i) The marginal layer of the basal plates expands into a bridge for nerve fibres connecting the cerebral cortex and cerebellar cortex with the spinal cord; pontine nuclei originate in the alar plates of the metencephalon.
- Corticopontine fibres pass through the pontine nuclei; pontine nuclei fibres travel in the middle cerebellar peduncle to all parts of the cerebellum except the nodulus.
- The dorsolateral parts of the alar plates bend medially to form the rhombic lips, which compress to form the cerebellar plate.
- The functional deficit produced when disease spreads along these connections is not covered.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old competitive tennis player presents with shoulder pain, particularly in the middle of the arc of abduction of the arm.
(i) What are the risk factors for this condition?
(ii) What are the pathological changes associated with this condition?
(iii) Explain the anatomical basis for the characteristic "painful arc" in this condition.
questions.answerText:
(i) The rotator cuff muscles control rotation of the shoulder and are put under a great deal of strain, especially in throwing events and racket sports where the arm is repeatedly raised above the head; tendonitis usually results from overuse.
(ii) Over time, tendonitis (inflammation of the muscle tendons) causes degenerative changes in the subacromial bursa and the supraspinatus tendon; this increases friction between the structures of the joint.
(iii) The subacromial bursa is located inferior to the deltoid and acromion, and superior to the supraspinatus tendon and the joint capsule; it is the largest bursa in the body and intervenes between supraspinatus and the coraco-acromial arch, protecting the supraspinatus tendon against friction with the acromion during abduction of the arm. The characteristic "painful arc" is pain in the middle of abduction, where the affected, degenerated area of tendon/bursa comes into contact with the acromion.

(i) Procedure: the lumbar puncture (LP) tap, sampling cerebrospinal fluid from the subarachnoid space.
(ii) Anatomical landmarks: the spinal cord extends from the foramen magnum to the conus medullaris and, in adults, ends at the L1 level (at birth it ends at the lower border of L3, and in the newborn at L2/3). Below this, the lumbosacral nerve roots (cauda equina) descend almost parallel to the filum terminale (a condensation of pia mater extending beyond the conus medullaris); the lengthening of the lumbosacral nerve roots marks the point of the LP tap.
(iii) Structure at risk: the spinal cord itself, if the needle is placed too high (above the conus medullaris); below this level the cauda equina nerve roots lie free in the subarachnoid space, which is functionally useful for the LP tap.
(iv) Embryologic basis: at about the 3rd month of intrauterine life, the spinal cord length equals that of the vertebral column. Differential growth of the vertebral column thereafter outpaces that of the spinal cord, producing an apparent ascent of the spinal cord and increasing obliquity of the spinal nerve roots from above downwards, forming the cauda equina and filum terminale.
questions.question:
A clinician plans to obtain a sample of cerebrospinal fluid by needle puncture of the lumbar subarachnoid space, taking advantage of the fact that the spinal cord ends higher than the vertebral column in the adult.
(i) Identify the region/structure being sampled and the named procedure.
(ii) What are the anatomical landmarks that make this level appropriate?
(iii) What structure is placed at risk if the needle is inserted too high?
(iv) What is the embryologic basis for the disparity between the length of the spinal cord and the vertebral column that permits this safe level?

questions.answerText:
(i) The kidneys are bean-shaped, retroperitoneal organs lying on the posterior abdominal wall from about the T12 to L3 vertebral level, each about 10 cm long, 5 cm wide and 2.5 cm thick, with the right kidney slightly lower due to the liver.
Each kidney has a superior pole bearing the suprarenal gland, an inferior pole, a convex lateral border, and a concave medial border indented by the renal hilum.
Coverings, from within outward, are the fibrous (renal) capsule, perirenal fat, renal fascia, and pararenal fat.
Internally, a dark brown outer cortex surrounds a lighter medulla composed of about a dozen renal pyramids, each with its base toward the cortex and its apex (renal papilla) projecting into a minor calyx; cortex extends between pyramids as renal columns.
At the hilum, the renal vein lies anterior to the renal artery, which lies anterior to the renal pelvis; the hilum leads into the renal sinus, which contains the pelvis, calyces, vessels, nerves and fat.
The renal pelvis, a funnel-shaped expansion of the ureter, receives two or three major calyces, each dividing into two or three minor calyces.
(ii) Renal (kidney) stones are a clinical consideration associated with the kidney and relate to the calyceal and pelvic system where urine collects before draining into the ureter.
The renal pyramids and papillae are the sites from which urine is excreted into the minor calyces, so pathology of the papillae or pyramids affects urine drainage.
(iii) The ureter has three points of constriction - the pelviureteric junction, where it crosses the pelvic brim, and its intramural (intravesical) course - which are potential sites of obstruction by ureteric stones.
Obstruction at any of these constrictions causes back-pressure on the kidney, from the collecting system through the pelvis to the pyramids, producing a functional deficit in urine drainage from that kidney.
Ureteric pain from such obstruction is referred to the ipsilateral lower quadrant of the anterior abdominal wall and especially the groin, showing how a renal or ureteric problem produces a distant clinical effect.
This referred pain reflects the segmental (T11-T12) sympathetic innervation shared by the ureter and the abdominal wall/groin dermatomes.
questions.question:
(i) Describe the gross anatomy of the kidney, including its shape, coverings, and internal structure (cortex, medulla, pyramids, sinus, calyces).
(ii) Relate the parts of the kidney to a common renal pathology.
(iii) Explain how disease/obstruction of the kidney or its drainage system can produce a functional deficit at a distance.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Oculomotor nuclei form a complex in the upper midbrain (superior colliculus level), near the midline, with the Edinger-Westphal nucleus (GVE) cranial to it.
- Trochlear nucleus: lower midbrain (inferior colliculus level), ventral to the aqueduct.
A(ii) CN III emerges from the ventral surface on the medial side of the cerebral peduncle; its axons pass through the red nucleus.
- CN IV fibres run dorsally and decussate dorsal to the aqueduct, emerging on the dorsal surface inferior to the inferior colliculus, then course ventrally; all cranial nerves emerge ventrally except the trochlear.
A(iii) Both nerves run between the superior cerebellar and posterior cerebral arteries, which supply the midbrain; the red nucleus lies lateral and ventral to CN III.
- Fibres from the frontal eye field to the oculomotor nucleus are suspected to pass through the anterior limb of the internal capsule; the midbrain reticular formation controls vertical gaze.
- In development each basal plate of the mesencephalon contains two groups of motor nuclei, represented by the oculomotor and trochlear nerves; the marginal layer forms the crus cerebri.
- Medio-lateral order of nuclear columns: SE, SVE, GVE, GVA, SVA, GSA, SSA (efferents medial to afferents).
C(i) The anatomical basis of the deformity after injury: not covered.
- Only the general statement is given that the nuclei and vital centres of the brainstem make injury to it present with grave clinical consequences.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the nuclei of origin of the oculomotor and trochlear nerves.
A(ii) Describe their emergence from the brainstem and course.
A(iii) Describe their relations.

questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Otitis media (middle ear infection). Predisposing anatomical factor: in children, the short auditory tubes allow pathogens to travel more easily from the nasopharynx into the middle ear, making children more susceptible to middle ear infections.
(ii) Structures of the middle ear involved in sound transmission: the tympanic membrane, the three ossicles (malleus/hammer, incus/anvil, and stapes/stirrup) articulated by synovial joints. These bones transmit mechanical vibrations generated in the tympanic membrane to the internal ear. Two small muscles: tensor tympani (inserts into malleus) and stapedius (inserts into stapes). The oval window and round window in the medial bony wall.
(iii) The middle ear is lined by a simple cuboidal epithelium. The auditory (eustachian) tube communicates the middle ear anteriorly with the oropharynx. In the auditory tube and its interior, the simple epithelium that lines the middle ear gradually transitions into ciliated columnar epithelium. The tympanic membrane is covered externally with squamous epithelium and internally by the simple cuboidal epithelium of the middle ear cavity. The auditory tube is usually collapsed but opens during the process of swallowing or yawning, balancing the pressure in the middle ear with the outside.

Describe the knee joint under the following headings and explain its clinical importance.
A(i) Type, articular surfaces, and articular bones
A(ii) Ligaments — classify as extracapsular or intra-articular; describe each fully
B(i) Movements and muscles responsible
B(ii) Blood supply and nerve supply of the knee joint
C(i) Distinguish the medial from the lateral meniscus, and explain the anatomical basis of why the medial meniscus is more frequently injured
questions.answerText:
A(i) The knee joint is primarily a hinge type of synovial joint. It is the largest and very complex joint in the body. Articulations: femur with tibia (tibiofemoral joint) and femur with patella (patellofemoral joint). Articular bones: (1) Femur — enlarged medial and lateral femoral condyles. (2) Tibia — enlarged medial and lateral tibial condyles (tibial plateaus), which are the receptacles for the femoral condyles; tibia bears most of the weight. (3) Patella — a true sesamoid bone embedded in the quadriceps and patellar tendon; serves as a pulley improving the angle of pull. Fibula is not part of the knee joint and does not articulate with the femur or patella; it only serves as attachment for knee joint structures.
A(ii) Extracapsular ligaments (5): (1) Patellar ligament — distal part of quadriceps tendon; strong, thick fibrous band passing from apex of patella to tibial tuberosity. (2) Fibular (lateral) collateral ligament — strong, rounded, cordlike; extends from lateral epicondyle of femur to head of fibula; tendon of popliteus passes deep to it, separating it from the lateral meniscus. (3) Tibial (medial) collateral ligament — strong flat band from medial epicondyle of femur to medial condyle and superior part of tibia; firmly attached to medial meniscus; weaker and more often damaged than the fibular collateral ligament. (4) Oblique popliteal ligament — expansion of tendon of semimembranosus; strengthens fibrous capsule posteriorly. (5) Arcuate popliteal ligament — arises from posterior aspect of fibular head; passes superomedially over tendon of popliteus; strengthens fibrous capsule posteriorly. Intra-articular ligaments (3): (1) ACL — from anterior intercondylar area of tibia to lateral condyle of femur; weaker; slack when flexed, taut when extended; prevents posterior displacement of femur on tibia and hyperextension. (2) PCL — from posterior intercondylar area of tibia to medial condyle of femur; stronger; taut during flexion; prevents anterior displacement of femur on tibia; main stabilizing factor in weight-bearing flexed knee. (3) Menisci — crescentic plates of fibrocartilage that deepen the surface and act as shock absorbers.
B(i) Flexion — hamstrings. Extension — quadriceps. Medial rotation — popliteus, semitendinosus, semimembranosus. Lateral rotation — biceps femoris. Locking: when fully extended with foot on ground, the knee locks because of medial rotation of femur on tibia. Unlocking: popliteus contracts rotating femur laterally so flexion can occur.
B(ii) Blood supply: genicular branches of femoral artery, popliteal artery, anterior and posterior recurrent branches of anterior tibial recurrent artery, and anterior and posterior branches of circumflex fibular arteries. The middle genicular branches of the popliteal artery penetrate the fibrous capsule and supply the cruciate ligaments, synovial membrane, and peripheral margins of the menisci. Nerve supply: branches of obturator nerve, femoral nerve, tibial nerve, and common fibular nerve.
C(i) Medial meniscus: C-shaped, broader posteriorly; anterior end attaches to anterior intercondylar area of tibia anterior to ACL; posterior end to posterior intercondylar area anterior to PCL; firmly adheres to tibial collateral ligament. Lateral meniscus: almost circular, smaller and more freely movable; tendon of popliteus separates it from fibular collateral ligament; attached posteriorly via the posterior meniscofemoral ligament to PCL and medial femoral condyle. The medial meniscus is more frequently injured because its firm attachment to the tibial collateral ligament makes it immobile and liable to being trapped and torn when the ligament is stressed; the lateral meniscus is protected by its free mobility.

A(i) The phrenic nerve is formed in the neck within the cervical plexus and contains fibres from spinal roots C3, C4 and C5.
A(ii) Its long course from the neck follows the embryological migration of the diaphragm from the cervical region: the septum transversum is carried ventrally and caudally, and the cervical myotomes and nerves contribute the muscle and nerve supply. It passes through the superior and middle mediastinum: the right phrenic descends on the right side of the SVC and heart; the left phrenic descends on the left side of the heart.
A(iii) Both nerves terminate in the diaphragm: terminal branches of the right phrenic pass through the caval opening (T8) in the central tendon, and the left phrenic pierces the left dome.
A(iv) Motor: the sole motor supply of the diaphragm; the right nerve supplies the right half up to the right margin of the oesophageal opening and the left nerve the left half up to the left margin. Sensory: the central part of the diaphragm and the related pleura and peritoneum, and sensory fibres to the pleurae and pericardium (mediastinal pleura, fibrous and parietal pericardium); the peripheral part receives sensory fibres from the lower 6 or 7 intercostal and subcostal nerves.
C(i) Sectioning or injury of a phrenic nerve in the neck causes complete paralysis and eventual atrophy of the muscular part of the corresponding half of the diaphragm, except in persons who have an accessory phrenic nerve. Causes of injury: mechanical trauma (ligation or damage during surgery) and compression by a tumour within the chest cavity; myopathies (e.g. myasthenia gravis) and neuropathies (e.g. diabetic neuropathy) also interrupt the supply. The paralysed half is elevated and shows paradoxical movement: it moves upwards during inspiration (forced up by abdominal viscera) and downwards during expiration; only one half is affected because each dome has a separate nerve supply. Unilateral paralysis is usually asymptomatic and an incidental finding on X-ray; if both sides are paralysed there is poor exercise tolerance, orthopnoea and fatigue, and lung function tests show a restrictive deficit. Irritation of the diaphragmatic pleura or of the peritoneum under the diaphragm (pleurisy, subphrenic pus or blood) refers pain to the shoulder tip, because the central diaphragm sends sensory fibres in the phrenic nerve (C3-5) and the shoulder skin is supplied by the supraclavicular nerve (C3,4).

questions.answerText:
(i) Carcinoid tumour.
(ii) Carcinoids are tumours that arise from enteroendocrine cells. These cells are epithelial cells scattered throughout the gastric mucosa with endocrine or paracrine functions.
(iii) Carcinoids are responsible for clinical symptoms caused by overproduction of serotonin. Serotonin increases gut motility, and chronic high levels of this hormone/neurotransmitter can produce mucosal vasoconstriction and tissue damage.
(iv) Enteroendocrine cell secretions by location:
- In the fundus: these cells secrete principally serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine).
- In the pylorus: G cells produce the peptide gastrin.
(v) Leiomyomas — benign tumours of smooth muscle cells; the most common type of tumour in the stomach and small intestine. Autopsy records suggest that the muscularis of the stomach may include leiomyomas in up to 50% of the population older than 50 years.

A(i) Continuation of the sigmoid colon at S3; ends as the anal canal one inch below and in front of the tip of the coccyx; about 12 to 13 cm (5 inches); lower end dilated as the ampulla; lacks mesentery, taeniae coli, sacculations and appendices epiploicae.
A(i) Two anteroposterior curves (sacral posterior; perineal anterior at puborectalis) and three lateral curves (upper convex to right, middle convex to left and most prominent, lower convex to right).
A(ii) Upper third: front and sides covered; middle third: front only; lower third: none; posterior surface: none. Male: recto-vesical pouch 7.5 cm from anus; female: recto-uterine pouch of Douglas 5.5 cm from anus.
A(iii) Four permanent horizontal Houston's valves (1st and 3rd constant); the 3rd at S5, 5 cm above the anus, if completely encircling forms Nelaton's sphincter, and divides an upper chamber (faeces without reflex to defecate) from a lower sensitive chamber; valves support faecal weight; cannulae/rectal washing are given in left lateral position to avoid injury to the 3rd valve.
A(iv) Wall: serous, muscular (outer longitudinal, inner circular), submucosa, mucosa. Arteries: superior rectal (main, from inferior mesenteric), middle rectal (anterior division of internal iliac), inferior rectal (internal pudendal), median sacral (aorta), inferior gluteal.
B(i) Superior rectal vein drains to inferior mesenteric then portal vein; middle rectal to internal iliac and inferior rectal to internal pudendal (systemic). Internal haemorrhoids (superior rectal tributaries, above Hilton's line, painless); external (inferior rectal, below, painful).
B(ii) Support: puborectal sling, Waldeyer fascia, lateral ligaments, pelvirectal and ischiorectal fat. Upper third lateral: pararectal fossa (sigmoid colon, small intestine); middle third: pelvirectal space; lower third: ischioanal fossa.
B(iii) Sympathetic (L1, L2) is vasomotor, stimulates the internal anal sphincter and inhibits the rest of the musculature; parasympathetic (S2 to S4) is secretomotor, stimulates peristalsis and relaxes sphincters.
C(i) Lymph: upper half via superior rectal to left common iliac and pararectal nodes; middle half to internal iliac nodes; lower part to anal valves to internal iliac nodes; below the anal valves to superficial inguinal nodes.
C(ii) Portal-systemic anastomosis: superior rectal (portal) with middle and inferior rectal veins (systemic); gut lymph follows arteries to pre-aortic nodes.
C(iii) Male: anterior sigmoid colon, small intestine, seminal vesicles, ampulla of vas, posterior bladder and prostate; female: posterior vaginal wall; posterior: sacrum, sacral plexus, coccyx, and piriformis, coccygeus, levator ani.
C(iv) Hindgut origin (endoderm), sympathetic least splanchnic (T12, L1) plus hypogastric (S2 to S4), inferior mesenteric artery (L3); mucosa above the 3rd valve from pre-allantoic hindgut, below from cloaca; muscle from splanchnic mesoderm.

A patient with cancer of the lung confined to one lobe is to undergo lobectomy through a conventional posterolateral thoracotomy.

(iii) State the structure at risk in the incision and how it is protected.
(iv) State the anatomical knowledge of the lung that guides the surgeon.
questions.answerText:
(i) Cancer of the lung (lobectomy or pneumonectomy is often used in its treatment); the procedure is pulmonary lobectomy through a conventional posterolateral thoracotomy.
(ii) The incision is made along the line of the 5th or 6th rib; the periosteum over a segment of the rib is elevated and the rib excised; the lung or mediastinum is reached through the intercostal space, which can be opened out considerably because of the elasticity of the thoracic cage. Oblique fissure (upper and lower lobes): a line from 1 in (2.5 cm) lateral to the spine of T5 obliquely downwards and outwards to the 6th costal cartilage about 1.5 in (4 cm) from the midline; with the shoulder fully abducted it corresponds to the medial border of the scapula. Transverse fissure of the right lung: a horizontal line along the 4th costal cartilage meeting the oblique fissure where it crosses the 5th rib.
(iii) The intercostal neurovascular bundle (vein, artery, nerve from above downwards, under the rib above); elevation of the periosteum protects it.
(iv) Knowledge of the lobes and fissures allows precise targeting of diseased segments while preserving healthy tissue; knowledge of vascular and bronchial structures avoids damage to critical structures; knowledge of pleural reflections and recesses guides access and avoids injury to the pleura; the right lung has 3 lobes and the left 2 (with the lingula), and the visceral pleura extends into the fissures.

A(i) The bony wall is the carpal sulcus, formed by the concavity on the anterior aspect of the carpal bones, forming the base and sides of the tunnel; it is bounded laterally by the scaphoid and trapezium tubercles and medially by the hook of the hamate and the pisiform.
A(ii) The fibrous wall is the flexor retinaculum, a thick connective tissue band that stretches over the carpal sulcus, converting it into the carpal tunnel by bridging the space between the medial and lateral parts of the arch, spanning from the hook of hamate and pisiform medially to the scaphoid and trapezium laterally.
A(iii) Contents: four tendons of flexor digitorum profundus (the deepest structures), four tendons of flexor digitorum superficialis lying anterior to those of profundus (all eight enclosed in a common synovial sheath), the tendon of flexor pollicis longus occupying the lateral angle of the compartment with its own synovial sheath, and the median nerve, which lies anterior to the tendons of flexor digitorum superficialis, deep to the flexor retinaculum.
B. Carpal tunnel syndrome may occur following inflammatory reactions (synovitis) in the synovial sheath of the tendons traversing the tunnel.
Excess fluid, such as follows inflammation of the synovial sheaths, compresses the structures within the confined tunnel.
The median nerve is the structure most adversely affected, since it lies anterior to the crowded flexor tendons, immediately deep to the unyielding flexor retinaculum, leaving it particularly exposed to any rise in pressure within the tunnel.
Compression of the median nerve produces sensory disturbance (hypoesthesia or anaesthesia) in the skin of the lateral three and a half fingers on their palmar aspect.
Weakness or paralysis of the thenar muscles also occurs, because the recurrent branch of the median nerve that supplies these muscles arises in the hand and is also compressed.
C. Within the tunnel, the tendons of flexor digitorum profundus are the deepest structures.
The tendons of flexor digitorum superficialis lie anterior to (more superficial than) those of profundus.
Both sets of four tendons are enclosed together in a single common synovial sheath, whereas the tendon of flexor pollicis longus lies separately at the lateral angle of the compartment, enclosed in its own distinct synovial sheath.
This layered arrangement of tendons deep to the median nerve means the nerve is the most superficial of the tunnel's principal contents, most exposed to the flexor retinaculum's unyielding roof.

questions.answerText:
(i) The diagnosis is a displaced fracture of the patella with disruption of the extensor mechanism. The patella is a sesamoid bone embedded in the quadriceps and patellar tendon. The quadriceps tendon continues as the patellar ligament (in which the patella is embedded) and is attached to the tibial tuberosity. The patellar ligament is the distal part of the quadriceps tendon (anterior ligament of the knee joint) — a strong, thick fibrous band passing from the apex and adjoining margins of the patella to the tibial tuberosity. When the patella is fractured and the extensor retinaculae are disrupted, the proximal pull of quadriceps can no longer be transmitted to the tibia, and knee extension is lost.
(ii) The patella is the largest sesamoid bone in the human body. Sesamoid bones are small nodules of bone found in certain tendons where they rub over bony surfaces. Functions of the patella: (1) increases the angle of pull of the quadriceps on the tibia, improving the ratio of motive to resistive torque by 50%; (2) centralises the divergent tension of quadriceps into a single line of action; (3) provides some protection of the anterior aspect of the knee. It articulates with the femur at the knee joint; it is triangular in shape with the apex inferiorly. Its posterior aspect has paired facets for articulation during extension, slight flexion, flexion, and full flexion. The patella slides within the trochlear groove of the femur.
(iii) Structures at risk include the quadriceps and patellar tendons (extensor retinaculae), the synovial membrane and joint capsule of the knee (which may be breached causing haemarthrosis), and the articular cartilage of the femoral trochlea and posterior patella surface. Complications include failure of extensor mechanism, patellofemoral osteoarthritis (particularly with articular cartilage damage), malunion, and loss of knee extension.
(iv) Surgical management depends on displacement. For displaced fractures with disruption of the extensor mechanism, open reduction and internal fixation (tension band wiring or lag screws) to restore the articular surface and repair the extensor mechanism is indicated. Partial or total patellectomy is reserved for severely comminuted fractures where reconstruction is impossible, accepting some loss of extension strength.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Contains 10-20 billion neurons and is 1.5-4.5 mm thick; only 1/3 of its area is exposed because of sulci.
- Cells: pyramidal (large, multipolar, long axons); stellate (small star-shaped interneurons, short or no axons, extensive dendrites); horizontal cells of Cajal (fusiform, in neonates); cells of Martinotti (multipolar, in deeper lamina).
A(ii) Cells are assembled in a definite pattern along morphological and functional lines; over 90% of the cortex has a 6-layered arrangement.
- Layer I plexiform/molecular (few cells, mostly glia); II external granular (small granular cells); III external pyramidal (pyramidal cells); IV internal granular (medium to large granular cells; external band of Baillarger).
- Layer V internal pyramidal (medium to large pyramidal cells, giant pyramidal cells of Betz; internal band of Baillarger); VI multiform (different cell types, including fusiform and Martinotti cells).
A(iii) Oligodendrocytes are present in each layer to different degrees; astrocytes and microglia are mobilised in pathology.
B(i) The ratio of granular to pyramidal cells in a layer depends on the modality it subserves; areas differ in cortical thickness, layer widths and cell density (functional classification into sensory, motor and association areas; Brodmann's 52 areas).
- Astrocytes and microglia mobilised in pathology; the reason certain regions are more vulnerable to disease is not covered.
C(i) Neocortex: about 90% of the human cortex; laminae I-VI; recent phylogenetic development; formed by successive waves of migrating neuroblasts from the periventricular area (inside-out gradient).
C(ii) Allocortex: phylogenetically older; three layers only (laminae I, V and VI as stated).
- Paleocortex (ancient): insula, primary olfactory and piriform cortex.
- Archicortex (beginning): hippocampal formation (hippocampus proper, dentate gyrus and subiculum, 3-layered).

A(ii) Describe its cortical layers.
A(iii) Describe its glial cells.

questions.answerText:
Gross anatomy: the interatrial septum develops with a septum primum and a septum secundum, an ostium (foramen) secundum, an endocardial cushion, and an interventricular foramen described in relation to the atrioventricular canal.
The septum primum carries venous valves and forms a valve over the oval foramen.
After birth, when lung circulation begins and pressure in the left atrium increases, the valve of the oval foramen is pressed against the septum secundum, obliterating the oval foramen and separating the right and left sides.
Parts relating to ASDs: heart defects involving the atrial septum are called atrial septal defects (ASDs).
A foramen secundum defect is caused by excessive resorption of the septum primum, the septum secundum, or both, so that the opening between the atria is not closed off after birth.
Spread to a distant structure causing a functional deficit: no mechanism of disease spreading from the interatrial septum to another structure, or any downstream haemodynamic or structural effects on distant organs, is described here; the clinical correlate for this structure is limited to the naming of ASDs and the single stated cause (excessive resorption of septum primum/secundum). By contrast, the ventricular septal defect involves the membranous portion of the interventricular septum, a different structure from the interatrial septum.
questions.question:

State how its parts relate to the atrial septal defects that can occur.
Explain how disease may spread to affect a distant structure and cause a functional deficit.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
- Mucosa: consists of an epithelial lining, lamina propria (zone of loose connective tissue rich in blood vessels, lymphatics, lymphocytes, smooth muscle cells, and sometimes small glands), and muscularis mucosae (thin layer of smooth muscle that separates the mucosa from the submucosa and allows local movements of the mucosa).
- Submucosa: denser connective tissue containing larger blood and lymph vessels, the submucosal (Meissner) plexus of autonomic nerves, and possibly glands and lymphoid tissue.
- Muscularis (muscularis externa): thick layer of smooth muscle organized into an internal circular sublayer and an external longitudinal sublayer; connective tissue between them contains blood vessels, lymph vessels, and the myenteric (Auerbach) nerve plexus.
- Serosa: outermost layer; a thin sheet of loose connective tissue covered with mesothelium (simple squamous covering epithelium); rich in blood vessels, lymphatics, and adipose tissue.
A(ii)
- Submucosal (Meissner) plexus: located in the submucosa between the submucosa and the muscularis; together with the myenteric plexus constitutes the local enteric nervous system.
- Myenteric (Auerbach) plexus: located in the connective tissue between the circular and longitudinal muscle sublayers; responsible for local contraction of the muscularis, mixing and propelling the contents of the lumen (peristalsis).
- Both plexuses together form the local enteric nervous system, which functions independently of the CNS; they are composed mainly of nerve cell aggregates forming small parasympathetic ganglia, numerous in regions of greatest motility.
B(i) The esophagus is not suspended in a cavity but is bound directly to adjacent structures, so instead of a serosa it has a thick adventitia. The adventitia consists of connective tissue containing vessels and nerves but lacks mesothelium, whereas the serosa is covered by mesothelium.
B(ii) The serosa of the small and large intestines is continuous with parts of the mesentery. The mesentery is a large fold of adipose connective tissue covered on both sides by mesothelium; it suspends the intestines and is continuous with the peritoneum (the serous membrane lining the abdominal cavity).

questions.answerText:
(i) Acquired hiatus hernia (found usually in middle-aged people); it is either sliding or rolling (paraoesophageal, alongside the oesophagus).
(ii) Predisposing factors: middle age, with weakening and widening (weak musculature) of the oesophageal hiatus; the hiatus is an oval opening in the muscle of the right crus at T10 that transmits the oesophagus, the anterior and posterior vagal trunks, oesophageal branches of the left gastric vessels and a few lymphatics; some fibres of the right crus loop round the oesophagus as a physiological sphincter that prevents reflux.
(iii) Sliding hernia (commoner): the upper stomach and lower oesophagus slide upwards into the chest through the lax hiatus when the patient lies down or bends over; competence of the cardia is often disturbed and peptic juice regurgitates into the gullet, followed by oesophagitis with heartburn, bleeding and eventually stricture formation. Rolling hernia (far less common): the cardia stays in its normal position and the cardio-oesophageal junction is intact, but the fundus of the stomach rolls up through the hiatus in front of the oesophagus; there may be epigastric discomfort, flatulence and even dysphagia, but no regurgitation because the cardiac mechanism is undisturbed.
questions.question:
A middle-aged patient with weakened and widened musculature around the oesophageal opening of the diaphragm complains of heartburn on lying down or bending over.
