A medical student examines a histology slide and identifies a tissue section with the following: concentric lamellae surrounding a central canal containing small blood vessels and nerves; between the lamellae are lacunae each containing one cell with dendritic processes; thin channels (canaliculi) connect the lacunae; outer canals connect these central canals with one another and with the marrow cavity.
(i) Identify the structural unit seen and name the tissue.
(ii) Name all three cell types found in this tissue, state the function of each, and identify which cell type is found in the lacunae.
(iii) Name the outer canals that connect the central canals and state their functional significance.
(iv) State the nerve and structure at risk when this tissue is surgically approached (as in open bone surgery).
(v) Identify the embryologic origin of the cells that produce the organic matrix of this tissue.
questions.answerText:
(i) Structural unit: the osteon (Haversian system). Tissue: compact bone (cortical or dense bone).
(ii) Three cell types: Osteocytes — found in lacunae (cavities within the matrix); maintain calcium and phosphate ion levels in blood fluids; they are essentially stress sensors; are osteoblasts that have been trapped in their own matrix. Osteoblasts — synthesize the organic matrix (osteoid) prior to mineralization. Osteoclasts — multinucleated giant cells involved in resorption and remodeling of bone. Chondrocytes are also listed in the bone healing context.
(iii) Volkmann's canals: canals called Volkmann's canals link the Haversian canals with one another and with the marrow cavity. Functional significance: metabolic exchanges between osteocytes and blood capillaries depend on communication through the canaliculi; Volkmann's canals allow blood vessels and nerves to pass between osteons and connect all parts of bone tissue with the marrow cavity.
(iv) Bone tissue is highly vascularized and metabolically very active; it harbors bone marrow where blood cells are formed. The Haversian canal contains small blood vessels and nerves; these are at risk when bone is surgically drilled or cut. Bone marrow is in the medullary cavity.
(v) Bone is a connective tissue; all connective tissue cells are derived from mesenchymal cells. Mesenchyme cells are for the most part derived from the mesoderm. However, several of the connective tissues of the head region are derived from the neural crest cells (ectodermal origin). Osteoblasts synthesize the organic matrix and are of mesenchymal origin.

A(i) The urinary bladder is a musculomembranous sac composed of a body, which collects urine, and a neck, a funnel-shaped extension passing inferiorly to join the urethra; it is divided into apex, fundus and body, with superior, posterior (base) and two inferolateral surfaces.
The apex points towards the pubic symphysis and continues as the median umbilical ligament, a remnant of the embryonic urachus, up to the umbilicus; the base faces posteroinferiorly, with the two ureters entering at its upper corners and the urethra draining from its lower corner.
A(ii) The trigone is the smooth, posteroinferior triangular area of the bladder wall formed by imaginary lines connecting the two ureteric orifices and the internal urethral orifice; it has four tunics, mucosa, submucosa, muscularis (detrusor muscle) and adventitia.
A(iii) Except for its superior surface, which is covered by peritoneum, the bladder is connected to surrounding structures by fibroareolar tissue (true ligaments): the lateral true ligaments, the puboprostatic or pubovesical ligaments anteriorly, the median umbilical ligament at the apex, and a posterior ligament.
In the male, the upper posterior surface is related to the rectovesical pouch, and the lower part relates to the seminal vesicles and vas deferens; in the female, the posterior surface is related to the anterior wall of the vagina.
B(i) The trigone remains immovable as the bladder fills and empties, and functions as a funnel that directs urine into the urethra as the bladder wall (detrusor) contracts.
B(ii) This fixed relationship of the ureteric and urethral orifices at the trigone is why it is used as a constant anatomical landmark despite the changing size and shape of the rest of the bladder.
C(i) The male urethra is about 20 cm long and is divided into four parts: intramural (preprostatic), prostatic, membranous, and spongy (penile) parts, opening at the end of the penis.
The male urethra passes through the prostate, the deep perineal pouch/urogenital diaphragm as the membranous urethra, and then the length of the penis as the spongy urethra, bending twice along its course.
The female urethra is much shorter, about 3-4 cm long, corresponding to the prostatic part of the male urethra proximal to the prostatic utricle.
The female urethra begins at the internal urethral orifice about 5 cm behind the pubic symphysis, runs downward embedded in the anterior wall of the vagina, traverses the urogenital diaphragm, and ends at the external urethral orifice in the vestibule, receiving the paraurethral (Skene's) glands.
Both sexes have an internal, smooth muscle, involuntary urethral sphincter continuous with the detrusor muscle, and an external, skeletal muscle, voluntary sphincter innervated by the pudendal nerve, located inferior to the prostate in males and at the bladder's distal inferior end in females.
questions.question:
(A) Describe the urinary bladder under the headings: A(i) parts A(ii) trigone A(iii) peritoneal/ligamentous relations.
(B) Explain the clinical basis of why the trigone remains an important fixed landmark during bladder filling.
(C) Distinguish the male urethra from the female urethra.

questions.answerText:
(i) The diagnosis is sciatic nerve compression secondary to L5–S1 disc herniation, with compression of the sciatic nerve (L4, 5; S1, 2, 3) as it exits through the greater sciatic foramen. The sciatic nerve curves downward midway between the tuber ischii and the greater trochanter; it has a side of danger and a side of safety in the gluteal region.
(ii) The greater sciatic foramen (GSF) provides an exit from the pelvis into the gluteal region. 14 structures exit through it: 1 muscle — piriformis (the landmark); 7 nerves — sciatic nerve, posterior cutaneous nerve of the thigh, superior gluteal nerve, inferior gluteal nerve, nerve to obturator internus, nerve to quadratus femoris, pudendal nerve; 6 vessels — superior gluteal arteries and veins, inferior gluteal arteries and veins, and internal pudendal arteries and veins.
(iii) The lesser sciatic foramen (LSF): (1) provides an entrance into the perineum from the gluteal region; (2) enables nerves and vessels that left the pelvis through the GSF above the pelvic floor to enter the perineum below the pelvic floor. 5 structures pass through the LSF: 2 nerves — pudendal nerve and nerve to obturator internus; 2 vessels — internal pudendal artery and vein; 1 tendon — tendon of obturator internus.
(iv) Complications include progressive weakness of muscles supplied by the sciatic nerve (hamstrings, all muscles of the leg and foot), sensory loss in the distribution of the sciatic nerve, and loss of reflexes. Conservative management includes rest, analgesia, physiotherapy, and epidural steroid injection. Definitive surgical management is microdiscectomy to decompress the nerve root where conservative measures fail or where there is progressive neurological deficit.
questions.question:
A 40-year-old bus driver develops progressive posterior thigh pain radiating to the calf, worsened by sitting. On examination, straight leg raise is positive at 40°. MRI shows L5–S1 disc herniation compressing the sciatic nerve in the greater sciatic foramen.
(i) State the diagnosis and identify the exact anatomical level of compression.
(ii) What structures pass through the greater sciatic foramen, and which muscle is the landmark?
(iii) What is the role of the lesser sciatic foramen, and name the structures that pass through it?
(iv) What are the complications and management?

A patient requires an operation on the thymus gland (or, occasionally, for a retrosternal goitre), which needs access to the superior mediastinum through the sternum; the whole sternum is split for surgery on the heart and great vessels.
(i) Name the surgical approach and state when the manubrium alone is split and when the whole sternum is split.
(ii) State the anatomical landmarks (parts of the sternum with their vertebral levels and articulations).
(iii) Describe the superior mediastinum that is entered, including its boundaries and contents from superficial to deep.
(iv) Name the vessels that run close to the lateral border of the sternum.
(v) Describe the developmental features of the sternum relevant to this approach.
questions.answerText:
(i) Splitting of the sternum: the manubrium is split in the midline for operations on the thymus gland and occasionally for retrosternal goitre, to gain access to the superior mediastinum; a complete vertical split of the whole sternum is a standard approach to the heart and great vessels in cardiac surgery. The specific disease (diagnosis) is not covered.
(ii) Suprasternal (jugular) notch at T2/3; the manubrium (opposite T3-4, overlying the aortic arch) articulates with the clavicles and the 1st and upper part of the 2nd costal cartilage; the sternal angle of Louis (manubriosternal joint, T4/5, 2nd costal cartilage) is the landmark for counting ribs; the body (opposite T5-T8, overlying the heart) takes the 2nd-7th costal cartilages; the xiphisternal joint lies at T9.
(iii) Superior mediastinum: bounded above by the thoracic outlet, below by the T4 plane, in front by the manubrium and behind by T1-T4; contents from superficial to deep: thymus, brachiocephalic veins and SVC, arch of the aorta and its branches, vagus and phrenic nerves, trachea, oesophagus, thoracic duct and lymph nodes.
(iii) The thymus extends from the lower pole of the thyroid gland to the 4th costal cartilage; its anterior relations are the pretracheal fascia, sternohyoid and sternothyroid muscles and the upper part of the body of the sternum.
(iv) The internal thoracic (internal mammary) vessels run vertically downwards behind the costal cartilages, half an inch from the lateral border of the sternum; the intercostal vessels lie immediately below their ribs (vein above artery).
(v) The body of the sternum is composed of four sternebrae that fuse between puberty and 25 years of age; the xiphoid process usually remains cartilaginous well into adult life; the manubriosternal joint and the xiphisternal joint may become ossified after the age of 30; any embryologic variant beyond this is not covered.

questions.question:
A patient is found to have a lesion along the pathway that carries auditory information from the cochlea to the auditory cortex.
(i) Identify the structures along the pathway from the cochlea to the cortex.
(ii) Name the structures related to, or affected along, the pathway and the associated reflex pathway.
(iii) Give the clinico-anatomical reasoning.
questions.answerText:
(i) Cochlear fibres from the spiral ganglia of the cochlea reach the cochlear nucleus at the pontomedullary junction (floor of the 4th ventricle, lateral to CN VII) and travel in the inferior cerebellar peduncle.
- Upper pons: lateral lemniscus and the smaller superior olivary nucleus (auditory pathway); midbrain: inferior colliculus (input from the cochlea).
- Medial geniculate body: ventral to the pulvinar and lateral to the midbrain; receives fibres from the lateral lemniscus and inferior colliculus; projects into the temporal lobe.
- Sublentiform part of the internal capsule (below the posterior end of the lentiform nucleus) carries auditory radiations from the MGB to the auditory area of the cortex: areas 41, 42 (floor of the lateral sulcus and superior temporal gyrus); area 22 is the association area.
(ii) Reflex pathway: efferent fibres of the colliculi travel in the tectospinal and tectobulbar tracts for general light and sound reflexes.
- Wernicke's area (comprehension of language) lies in the posterior part of the temporal lobe (area 22).
(iii) Clinico-anatomical reasoning: the clinical effects of lesions at each level of the pathway are not covered.

(i) Diagnosis: anterior spinal artery syndrome.
(ii) Pathologic basis: the anterior spinal artery is formed by the union of two arteries from the vertebral artery and runs on the antero-medial surface of the spinal cord, supplying the ventral two-thirds of the cord; it requires caudal reinforcement. Anterior spinal artery syndrome is listed among the spinal cord injury syndromes, alongside complete transection, hemisection and central cord syndrome.

A patient develops a clinical syndrome attributed to compromise of the vessel supplying the ventral two-thirds of the spinal cord.
(i) What is the diagnosis?
(ii) What is the pathologic basis of this condition?

questions.answerText:
A(i) Oblique, tunnel-shaped passage through the lower part of the anterior abdominal wall just above the medial half of the inguinal ligament, present in both sexes; about 4 cm (1½ inches) long in adults, directed downwards, forwards and medially.
A(ii) It extends from the deep inguinal ring to the superficial inguinal ring; in the newborn the deep ring lies almost directly posterior to the superficial ring.
A(iii) Anterior wall: external oblique aponeurosis, reinforced laterally by internal oblique. Posterior wall: transversalis fascia, reinforced medially by the conjoint tendon.
A(iii) Roof: arching lowest fibres of internal oblique and transversus abdominis with transversalis fascia. Floor: inguinal ligament, reinforced medially by the lacunar ligament.
A(iv) Spermatic cord (male) or round ligament of uterus (female); processus vaginalis remnant; 3 fasciae; 3 arteries (artery to vas, cremasteric, testicular); 3 nerves (ilio-inguinal L1, genital branch of genitofemoral L2, sympathetic); vas, pampiniform plexus, lymphatics.
B(i) It is a potential weakness in the abdominal wall. The posterior wall is weak laterally at the deep ring, but the anterior wall opposite is reinforced by internal oblique, so a hernia through the deep ring must travel along the canal.
B(i) The anterior wall is weak medially at the superficial ring, but the posterior wall opposite is reinforced by the conjoint tendon; weakness there leads to direct hernias.
B(ii) In the male it allows spermatic cord structures to pass to and from the testis (normal spermatogenesis needs the cooler scrotum) while preventing intestine entering the scrotum; in the female the smaller canal carries the round ligament of the uterus to the labium majus.
C(i) Deep ring: oval opening in the transversalis fascia, about ½ inch (1.3 cm) above the inguinal ligament at the midinguinal point, lateral to the inferior epigastric artery; margins give attachment to internal spermatic fascia; entrance of the cord.
C(i) Superficial ring: triangular defect in the external oblique aponeurosis, immediately above and medial to the pubic tubercle;
C(i) Its medial and lateral crura give attachment to the external spermatic fascia;
C(i) It is the exit of the cord from the canal.

questions.question:
A(i) Define the mediastinum and state its extent and boundaries.
A(ii) State its divisions and the plane that separates them.
A(iii) Describe the boundaries and contents of each division.
A(iv) List the structures that occupy more than one division.
B(i) Explain the importance of the level of T4 in relation to the mediastinum.
B(ii) Explain why the mediastinum is vulnerable when the chest wall is severely injured.
C(i) Distinguish between the superior and the inferior mediastinum.
questions.answerText:
A(i) A highly mobile, bulky connective tissue septum (thick movable partition) in the midline between the right and left pleural cavities and their lungs, containing the heart and great vessels, oesophagus, trachea and its bifurcation, thoracic duct, and vagus and phrenic nerves; superior: root of the neck (thoracic outlet: manubrium, 1st rib, T1); inferior: diaphragm; anterior: sternum; posterior: thoracic vertebrae; lateral: lungs and pleurae.
A(ii) A horizontal plane from the sternal angle to the lower border of T4 divides it into the superior mediastinum (above) and the inferior mediastinum (below), the latter subdivided into anterior (in front of the heart), middle (containing the heart) and posterior (behind the heart) parts.
A(iii) Superior: bounded by the thoracic outlet above, the T4 plane below, the manubrium in front and T1-T4 vertebrae behind; contents from superficial to deep: thymus; right and left brachiocephalic veins and SVC; arch of the aorta with brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid and left subclavian arteries; right and left vagus and phrenic nerves; trachea and oesophagus (most posterior); thoracic duct beside the oesophagus; lymph nodes.
A(iii) Anterior: bounded by the T4 plane above, the diaphragm below, the body of the sternum in front and the pericardium/heart behind; contains the thymus, fatty tissue and lymph nodes.
A(iii) Middle: lies between the anterior and posterior mediastina; contains the pericardium and heart, ascending aorta, pulmonary trunk, SVC and IVC, right and left pulmonary veins, main bronchi, part of the phrenic nerves and lymph nodes.
A(iii) Posterior: bounded by the T4 plane above, the heart/middle mediastinum and diaphragm in front, and the T5 (lower border of T4) to T12 vertebrae behind; contains the oesophagus (most anterior), right and left vagus nerves around it, thoracic duct behind it, azygos vein (behind and to the right), descending aorta (behind and to the left), sympathetic trunks and lymph nodes.
A(iv) Six structures lie in more than one division: thoracic duct, oesophagus and vagus nerves (superior and posterior); phrenic nerves and SVC (superior and middle); thymus (superior and anterior); lymph nodes are present in all regions.
B(i) The T4 level marks the sternal angle and the 2nd costal cartilage, the bifurcation of the trachea, the bifurcation of the pulmonary trunk, and the beginning and termination of the arch of the aorta.
B(ii) The mediastinum is highly mobile; in a stove-in chest the loose chest wall segment produces swinging movements of the mediastinum that cause severe shock.
C(i) Superior mediastinum: one part above the T4 plane, bounded in front by the manubrium and behind by T1-T4, containing thymus, great veins, aortic arch and its branches, trachea, oesophagus, thoracic duct, vagus and phrenic nerves.
C(i) Inferior mediastinum: three parts below the T4 plane down to the diaphragm - anterior (thymus and fat, in front of the heart), middle (heart, pericardium, ascending aorta, pulmonary trunk) and posterior (oesophagus, descending aorta, azygos system, thoracic duct, sympathetic trunks).
C(i) Nerves differ by position: the right vagus descends on the right of the trachea, forms the posterior oesophageal plexus and continues as the posterior gastric nerve; the left vagus descends between the left common carotid and left subclavian arteries and forms the anterior oesophageal plexus; the right phrenic descends on the right of the SVC and heart, the left on the left side of the heart.

questions.question:
A patient presents with drooping of the upper eyelid on one side.
(i) What is the diagnosis?
(ii) What are the predisposing factors and pathophysiology?
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: ptosis due to oculomotor nerve palsy.
(ii) Predisposing factors: not covered. Pathophysiology: ptosis is drooping of the upper lid from oculomotor nerve palsy, resulting from paralysis of the levator palpebrae muscle. The oculomotor nerve (CN III) has a general somatic efferent (GSE) component supplying the levator palpebrae (and four extra-ocular muscles) and a general visceral efferent (GVE) component giving parasympathetic innervation to the sphincter pupillae and ciliary muscles.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the gross anatomy of the pancreas, including its nature as a gland, its retroperitoneal position, its capsular covering, and how its parenchyma is organised into lobules.
A(ii) Describe the two functional components of the pancreas — exocrine and endocrine —, including the cell types involved and the products of each.
B(i) Describe the exocrine secretory acini of the pancreas, including the arrangement around the acini and the volume of juice produced.
B(ii) Explain the role of the pancreas in digestion and hormonal regulation, and contrast this with the role of the liver and the gallbladder.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Gross anatomy of the pancreas:
- Nature: a mixed exocrine-endocrine gland that produces both digestive enzymes and hormones.
- Position: retroperitoneally positioned on the posterior wall of the abdominal cavity at the level of the 2nd and 3rd lumbar vertebrae.
- Capsular covering: it has no distinct capsule, but is covered by a thin layer of loose connective tissue, from which septa extend to cover the larger vessels and ducts and to separate the parenchyma into lobules.
A(ii) Two functional components:
- Exocrine: produces digestive enzymes that act in the small intestine; secretory acini produce about 1.6 litres of pancreatic juice every day.
- Endocrine: involves primarily smaller cells similar to enteroendocrine cells located in variously sized clusters called the pancreatic islets (islets of Langerhans); secretes hormones such as insulin and glucagon into the bloodstream, which are very important for the metabolism of absorbed nutrients.
B(i) Exocrine acini:
- The secretory acini are surrounded by a basal lamina that is supported only by a delicate sheath of reticular fibers with a rich capillary network.
- The exocrine part produces about 1.6 litres of pancreatic juice every day.
B(ii)
- Pancreas: produces digestive enzymes that act in the small intestine; secretes insulin and glucagon, both important for metabolism of absorbed nutrients.
- Liver: produces bile, an important fluid in the digestion of fats; plays a major role in lipid, carbohydrate, and protein metabolism; inactivates and metabolizes many toxic substances and drugs; participates in iron metabolism and the synthesis of blood proteins and factors necessary for blood coagulation.
- Gallbladder: absorbs water from bile and stores bile in a concentrated form.

(i) The aorta and pulmonary trunk (the great vessels arising from division of the truncus arteriosus).
(ii) Two related anomalies are grouped together: persistent truncus arteriosus, and complete D-transposition of the great vessels.
A separately described anomaly involving four cardiovascular alterations is also listed: a narrowing of the ventricular outflow region (pulmonary stenosis), a large defect of the ventricular septum, an overriding aorta arising directly above the septal defect, and hypertrophy of the right ventricular wall due to higher pressure on the right side.
(iii) The aorticopulmonary (AP) septum normally divides the truncus arteriosus into the aorta and pulmonary trunk; it is formed by pairs of opposing truncal and bulbar ridges that grow and fuse in a spiral, not straight, fashion.
Persistent truncus arteriosus and D-transposition of the great vessels are both listed as anomalies of this septation process, consistent with a failure of the normal spiral growth and fusion of the truncal and bulbar ridges that would otherwise establish the normal crossing relationship between the aorta and pulmonary trunk.
questions.question:
Echocardiography in a cyanotic neonate shows the great vessels arising from the heart in an abnormal, non-crossing relationship, without the usual spiral winding of one vessel around the other.
(i) Identify the structures affected.
(ii) State the differential pathologies.
(iii) Give the clinico-anatomical reasoning for this finding.

A patient presents with deafness and vertigo and is found to have a tumor of the eighth cranial nerve.
(i) What are the complications?
questions.answerText: (i) Complications: acoustic neuroma is a tumor of the eighth cranial nerve characterized by deafness and vertigo; the intracranial portions of certain cranial nerves are susceptible to compression owing to a tumor or aneurysm.

(i) Umbilical hernia: the intestines return to the abdominal cavity at the 10th week but herniate through an imperfectly closed umbilicus; a common type of hernia.
(ii) Surgery is performed at the age of 3 to 5 years if it persists; the specific operation is not covered.
(iii) Landmark: the fibrous ring at the umbilicus through which it is reduced; herniated contents are usually the greater omentum and small intestine.
(iv) The structure at risk is not covered.
(v) Omphalocele: herniation of viscera through a large umbilical ring defect (lateral plate mesoderm), covered by peritoneal and amniotic membrane; 50% have other serious congenital or chromosomal abnormalities.
(v) Gastroschisis: herniation of viscera through a ruptured abdominal wall defect into the amniotic cavity, to the right of the umbilicus, from abnormal closure of the body wall around the connecting stalk; no covering membranes, so the bowel is bathed in amniotic fluid and may be damaged; less commonly associated with other anomalies.

A. Describe the origin, course, and branches/distribution of the ophthalmic artery.
B. State why the ophthalmic artery and its central retinal branch are of particular functional importance to the orbit.
C. Explain the anatomical basis of the visual deficit that follows occlusion or injury of the central artery of the retina.
questions.answerText:
A. The only artery supplying structures in the orbit is the ophthalmic artery, which is a branch of the internal carotid artery; it enters the orbit with the optic nerve through the optic foramen (canal). Its branches include the lacrimal artery (to the lacrimal gland and upper eyelid), muscular branches to the muscles, long posterior ciliary arteries (to the ciliary body), short posterior ciliary arteries (to the choroid and part of the optic nerve), and medial palpebral arteries (to the eyelids).
B. The ophthalmic artery gives rise to the very important branch, the central artery of the retina; because the ophthalmic artery is the only artery supplying orbital structures, and the central retinal artery is its branch, the retina is dependent on this single arterial source, so the optic nerve is covered by dura, arachnoid and pia from the sclera to the canal, where the dura is continuous with the periosteum of the orbit, and venous drainage (superior and inferior ophthalmic veins) communicates with the cavernous sinus, giving direct communication between the skin of the face and the cavernous sinus (the danger triangle).
C. Not covered beyond the statement that the central artery of the retina is a branch of the ophthalmic artery supplying the retina; the specific visual deficit following its occlusion is not covered.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the origin of the internal carotid artery.
A(ii) Describe its course, entry into the skull and the circle of Willis.
A(iii) Describe its branches.
A(iv) Describe its distribution.
C(i) Explain the anatomical basis of the effects of occlusion of a major cerebral artery.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Arises as the bifurcation of the common carotid artery.
A(ii) Enters the skull through the carotid canal; further details of its intracranial course are not covered.
- Circle of Willis: anastomotic channel between the internal carotid and vertebrobasilar systems, around the infundibulum of the pituitary and the optic chiasma at the base of the brain.
A(iii) The internal carotid artery and its branches, including the anterior cerebral artery (in the interhemispheric fissure) and the middle cerebral artery, supply the anterior 2/3 of the brain (anterior circulation).
- The individual branches and cortical territories of these arteries are not covered.
A(iv) Supplies the optic nerve and orbital contents including the retina; the optic tract, LGB and the posterior limb of the internal capsule (thalamus, cerebral peduncles).
- The vertebrobasilar and posterior cerebral arteries supply the brainstem, cerebellum and occipital lobe (posterior circulation) and join the carotid system in the circle.
C(i) The circle of Willis provides collateral circulation to supply blood when major arteries become occluded.
- The brain receives about 15% of the cardiac output; loss of consciousness occurs if blood supply is interrupted for about 5 seconds.
- Irreversible brain damage occurs if the brain is deprived of blood for more than 4-5 minutes.
- The specific deficit after injury of the internal carotid artery is not covered.

(i) Chronic alcoholism is the risk factor stated; cirrhosis, the most common cause of portal hypertension, frequently develops in chronic alcoholics.
(ii) In cirrhosis, hepatocytes are destroyed and replaced by fibrous tissue that surrounds the intrahepatic blood vessels and biliary ducts, making the liver firm and impeding circulation of blood through it. Obstruction to portal circulation opens up communicating veins (portal-systemic anastomoses) between the left gastric vein and systemic veins at the lower oesophagus, producing bleeding oesophageal varices and upper gastrointestinal haemorrhage (haematemesis). Other anastomotic sites are the anal canal, the paraumbilical region, retroperitoneal tissues, and intrahepatic sites (patent ductus venosus).
(iii) Peptic ulcer disease (gastric and duodenal ulcer) is managed with anti-ulcer drugs (antacids, proton pump inhibitors) and, definitively, with ulcer surgery such as vagotomy and pyloroplasty. Vagotomy is justified because the vagal (parasympathetic) fibres are secretomotor to the gastric glands and motor to the stomach wall, so dividing the vagal trunks reduces the drive to gastric acid secretion responsible for the ulcer. Specific surgical treatment of bleeding oesophageal varices is not covered.
questions.question:

questions.answerText:
A(i) A wide tube about 10 cm long and 2 cm wide, lying in the superior mediastinum and extending from C6 (lower border of the cricoid cartilage) to T4, where it divides into the right and left main bronchi; it has cervical and thoracic parts, the cervical part measuring 5 cm.
A(ii) The cervical part is in contact posteriorly with the oesophagus and anteriorly with the isthmus of the thyroid gland; it is palpable in the suprasternal notch midway between the heads of the clavicles; it ends at the sternal angle (T4/5) just to the right of the midline (at T6 in the erect position in full inspiration).
A(ii) At the bifurcation the azygos vein arches over the right main bronchus (T4) and the left main bronchus lies in front of the oesophagus (27 cm from the incisor teeth); the cardiac plexus lies on the lowest part of the trachea behind the arch of the aorta.
A(iii) Right main bronchus: 2.5 cm long, shorter, wider and vertically oriented; left main bronchus: 5 cm long, longer, narrower and horizontally oriented.
A(iv) Right main bronchus divides into upper (outside the hilum), middle and lower lobar bronchi, giving 10 bronchopulmonary segments; the left divides within the hilum into 2 lobar bronchi, giving 8 segments; segmental (third-order) bronchi supply the segments.
A(iv) The U-shaped cartilage bars of the trachea are replaced by irregular plates in smaller bronchi; the smallest bronchi give bronchioles (under 1 mm), then terminal bronchioles and respiratory bronchioles (about 0.5 mm, with outpouchings where gas exchange occurs), then alveolar ducts, alveolar sacs and alveoli surrounded by capillaries.
A(v) Trachea: lymphatics drain to the deep cervical and paratracheal lymph nodes; the mucous membrane is supplied by the vagus, which also gives the parasympathetic supply. Lung and bronchi: pulmonary plexuses with vagal (bronchoconstrictor, secretomotor) and sympathetic (bronchodilator) fibres.
B(i) The wider, more vertical right main bronchus allows foreign particles to enter it easily; asthma (dyspnoea); pneumonia (bacterial or viral infection of the lung); pulmonary embolism (pulmonary artery obstructed by air, blood clot, fat, tumour cells or foreign particles).
B(i) Abscesses are commoner in the posterior segment of the upper lobe and the apical segment of the lower lobe (most dependent supine); septa between segments limit infection but carcinoma and tuberculosis break through; fibrosis reduces compliance and emphysema reduces elasticity.
C(i) Lymph from lung and bronchi passes to the bronchopulmonary (hilar) nodes, then to the superior and inferior tracheobronchial nodes (above and below the tracheal bifurcation), then to the right and left bronchomediastinal trunks.
C(i) The trunks usually end at the junction of the subclavian and internal jugular veins; the right trunk may join other trunks to form the right lymphatic duct and the left may end in the thoracic duct.
C(i) The functional deficit that follows spread of disease along these routes: not covered.

questions.answerText:
(i) Tissue: Elastic cartilage. It is found in the auricle of the ear.
(ii) Locations: elastic cartilage is found in the auricle of the ear, the walls of the external auditory canals, the auditory (eustachian) tubes, the epiglottis, and the cuneiform cartilage in the larynx.
(iii) Comparison: Hyaline cartilage — most common form; collagen type II is the principal collagen; chondroitin is the major ground substance component; found in nose, trachea, bronchi, ventral ends of ribs, and synovial joints. Elastic cartilage — essentially identical to hyaline cartilage except it contains an abundant network of fine elastic fibers in addition to collagen type II fibrils; fresh elastic cartilage has a yellowish color due to elastin in the elastic fibers. Fibrocartilage — intermediate between dense connective tissue and hyaline cartilage; matrix contains a dense network of coarse collagen type I fibers; matrix is acidophilic because it is rich in collagen type I; chondrocytes are arranged either singly or in isogenous groups in long rows; found in intervertebral disks, attachments of certain ligaments to cartilaginous surface of bones, and symphysis pubis.
(iv) Clinical conditions: Cartilage cells can give rise to benign (chondroma) or malignant (chondrosarcoma) tumors. Hyaline cartilage is more susceptible to degenerative aging processes; calcification of the matrix, preceded by an increase in size and volume of chondrocytes followed by their death. Osteoarthritis results from breakdown of joint cartilage.
(v) Cartilage is avascular and is nourished only by diffusion of nutrients from capillaries in adjacent connective tissue (perichondrium) or by synovial fluid. It has no lymphatic vessels or nerves. Chondrocytes exhibit low metabolic activity. This avascularity and low metabolic activity account for the inherently limited healing potential of cartilage.
questions.question:
A histology slide shows a tissue with the following features: cells embedded in lacunae, matrix containing an abundant network of fine elastic fibers in addition to collagen type II fibrils, yellowish color on fresh specimen, no perichondrium in one region, and presence in the auricle of the external ear.
(i) Identify the organ/tissue and its specific type.

questions.answerText:
A(i) The gluteal region is the region of the buttock. Bony landmarks — surface anatomy: iliac crest, gluteus medius, tip of greater trochanter, gluteus maximus (fold of buttock), ischial tuberosity, tip of coccyx, natal cleft, posterior superior iliac spine (PSIS), sciatic nerve. Bones: os coxae (ilium, ischium, pubis) and femur.
A(ii) Superficial fascia: thick in women; impregnated with large quantities of fat, hence the prominence of the buttock. Deep fascia: continuous with fascia lata of the thigh. The 9 muscles: gluteus maximus, gluteus medius, gluteus minimus, tensor fasciae latae (superficial layer); piriformis, obturator internus, gemellus superior, gemellus inferior, quadratus femoris (deep layer). Deep layer muscles all have distal attachments on or adjacent to the intertrochanteric crest of the femur; they are lateral rotators of the thigh and stabilise the hip joint. Obturator internus, superior gemellus, and inferior gemellus form the triceps coxae of the hip.
B(i) 6 nerves of the gluteal region: sciatic nerve (L4, 5; S1, 2, 3); posterior cutaneous nerve of the thigh; superior gluteal nerve; inferior gluteal nerve; nerve to quadratus femoris; pudendal nerve. (Nerve to obturator internus also exits here.) The sciatic nerve curves downward midway between the tuber ischii and the greater trochanter.
B(ii) 4 arteries: superior gluteal artery (SGA), inferior gluteal artery (IGA), medial femoral circumflex artery (MFCA), lateral femoral circumflex artery (LFCA). Trochanteric anastomosis (TA) — main blood supply to the head of femur: SGA, IGA, MFCA, LFCA. Cruciate anastomosis (CA) — situated at the level of the lesser trochanter: IGA, MFCA, LFCA, and 1st perforating branch of profunda femoris. The CA jointly with the TA provides a connection between the femoral arteries and the internal iliac arteries.
C(i) Sacrotuberous ligament (STL) and sacrospinous ligament (SSL): (1) both stabilise the sacrum and prevent its rotation at the sacroiliac joint by the weight of the vertebral column; (2) in conjunction with bones, they form the greater sciatic foramen (GSF) and lesser sciatic foramen (LSF). Functions of GSF and LSF: GSF provides an exit from the pelvis into the gluteal region. LSF (1) provides an entrance into the perineum from the gluteal region; (2) enables nerves and vessels that left the pelvis through the GSF above the pelvic floor to enter the perineum below the pelvic floor.

questions.answerText:
A(i) The surface marking of the base of the appendix is McBurney's point, at the junction of the lateral one-third and medial two-thirds of a line drawn from the right anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus. The appendix is attached to the cecum below the ileocaecal valve, and the teniae coli of the cecum converge at the root of the appendix.
A(ii) The appendix is one of the intraperitoneal parts of the large intestine, suspended by its own mesentery, the mesoappendix.
A(iii) The appendix opens at the posteromedial aspect of the cecum, about one inch below the ileocaecal junction; its positions include retrocecal, the most common, pelvic, subcecal, preileal, and postileal, the least common.
B(i) Deep tenderness at McBurney's point, McBurney's sign, is the clinical sign used to localise inflammation of the appendix, that is, acute appendicitis.
B(ii) The appendix is described as an intestinal tonsil because of the abundant lymphatic nodules in its lamina propria, which extend into the submucosa and give it an immune function, similar to the tonsils.
C(i) Grossly, the appendix has no teniae coli and shows various shapes and positions, whereas the rest of the colon shows three longitudinal teniae coli, free, mesocolic and omental, which converge at the root of the appendix.
The colon has haustra (sacculations), because the teniae are shorter than the length of the gut wall, appendices epiploicae (fat-filled peritoneal pouches), and semilunar folds; the appendix lacks these features.
Microscopically, the appendix has no villi and its crypts (of Lieberkuhn) are less abundant than in the colon.
The colon's mucosa shows enterocytes with no digestive enzyme production, water and electrolyte reabsorption, deep crypts, a thick mucin layer, and goblet cells that increase in number caudally.
The appendix has prominent lymphatic nodules in the lamina propria extending into the submucosa, which are far less prominent in the general colon.
Both the appendix and colon lack villi, unlike the small intestine, but only the appendix is described as functioning analogously to the tonsils.

A(i) Describe the medulla oblongata: its extent and dorsal features.
A(ii) Describe its ventral features and the emergence of cranial nerves.
A(iii) Describe its internal structure at its three levels.
B(i) State how its parts relate to common pathologies.
C(i) Explain why disease of the medulla may cause distant functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
A(i) The part of the brainstem connecting the pons to the spinal cord, continuous with the cord at the foramen magnum; the upper part is covered dorsally by the cerebellum with the caudal 4th ventricle between, roofed by ependyma and pia mater.
- The caudal dorsal surface has the gracile and cuneate tubercles (from underlying nuclei) medio-laterally.
A(ii) Ventrally the upper part is grooved in the midline; the pyramid (corticospinal fibres) and the olive (inferior olivary nucleus) are elevations lateral to it; the most lateral elevation is the inferior cerebellar peduncle.
- CN VI, VII and VIII emerge at the pontomedullary junction medio-laterally; CN IX, X and XI emerge as rootlets lateral to the olive and CN XII between the pyramid and olive.
A(iii) Three levels: open part, upper closed part and lower closed part; the open part (floor of the 4th ventricle) carries most cranial nerve nuclei: hypoglossal (under the hypoglossal trigone), vagal (vagal trigone), solitary tract nucleus and nucleus ambiguus.
- Inferior olivary nucleus: crenated C-shaped strip of grey matter with its open end facing the opposite cerebellar peduncle (principal, medial and dorsal accessory nuclei).
- Upper closed part: central decussation forming the medial lemniscus (fibres of the gracile and cuneate nuclei); lower closed part: pyramidal decussation.
B(i) Blood supply: anterior spinal branch of the vertebral artery (medial medullary syndrome) and posterior inferior cerebellar artery (lateral medullary syndrome).
- The specific features of these syndromes are not covered.
C(i) Injury to the brainstem has grave consequences because of the nuclei and vital centres: reflex centres for coughing, swallowing and vomiting and centres for respiratory, cardiac and motor function are in the medulla.
- Corticospinal fibres form the pyramids and decussate at the lower medulla, so the motor pathway to the body passes through it.
- The mechanism by which a medullary lesion spreads to distant structures is not covered.

A(i) Stomach mucosa:
- Surface epithelium and gastric pits: consists of a simple columnar epithelium that invaginates into the lamina propria forming gastric pits. Millions of gastric pits each open into the lumen of the stomach; the gastric pits lead into long, branched, tubular glands extending through the thickness of the lamina propria; between each gastric pit and gastric gland is the isthmus (region of stem cells).
- Isthmus and stem cells: the pluripotent stem cells divide asymmetrically producing progenitor cells for all other epithelial cells; they can move upwards to replace surface mucous cells or downwards to replace other secretory cells.
- Lamina propria: highly vascularised; supports pits and glands; contains smooth muscle fibers, capillaries, lymphatics, and lymphoid cells.
- Muscularis mucosae: layer of smooth muscle separating the mucosa from the underlying submucosa.
A(ii) Four secretory cell types of fundic/body glands:
1. Mucous neck cells (MNCs): less columnar than surface mucous cells; irregular in shape with round nucleus and apical secretory granules; secrete acidic fluid containing mucin (less alkaline than surface mucous cells).
2. Parietal (oxyntic) cells: large, rounded or pyramidal cells; one central spherical nucleus; intensely eosinophilic cytoplasm due to high density of mitochondria; secrete hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor.
3. Chief (zymogen) cells: predominate in lower regions; abundant RER and numerous apical secretory granules (characteristics of protein-secreting cells); secrete pepsinogen (converted to pepsin at pH < 5), lipase, and leptin.
4. Enteroendocrine cells: scattered throughout the gastric mucosa; secrete hormones with endocrine or paracrine functions (e.g., serotonin in fundus; gastrin from G cells in pylorus).
B(i)
- Fundus/body: long branched tubular gastric glands (3 to 7 per pit); each gland has an isthmus, neck, and base; contains all four cell types above; secretes acidic gastric juice.
- Cardia/pylorus: tubular glands with long pits, usually branching into coiled secretory portions (cardiac/pyloric glands); lack parietal and chief cells; major secretion is abundant mucus.
B(ii) Rugae are longitudinally directed folds of the mucosa and submucosa of the empty stomach. They flatten when the stomach is full with food.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the mucosa of the stomach under the following headings: surface epithelium and gastric pits; the isthmus and stem cells; the lamina propria; and the muscularis mucosae.
A(ii) Name and describe all four secretory epithelial cell types found in the gastric glands of the fundus and body, including the characteristics of each cell and what it secretes.
B(i) Distinguish between the mucosa of the fundus/body and the mucosa of the cardia/pylorus under the headings: gland type, cell types present, and principal secretion.
B(ii) Explain what rugae are and the physiological condition under which they disappear.

A patient develops acute necrotizing pancreatitis in which proenzymes are prematurely activated and digest pancreatic tissue.
(i) What are the risk factors/possible causes for this condition?
(ii) What are the complications that can result?
(iii) State the mechanism by which the body normally prevents this, and how it is understood to fail in this condition.
questions.answerText:
(i) Possible causes include infection, gallstones, alcoholism, drugs and trauma.
(ii) The activated proenzymes may digest the pancreatic tissues, leading to very serious complications, that is, acute necrotizing pancreatitis; in conditions of extreme malnutrition such as kwashiorkor, pancreatic acinar cells and other active protein-secreting cells atrophy and lose much of their rough endoplasmic reticulum, hindering production of digestive enzymes.
(iii) Normally, the proteases (trypsinogens, chymotrypsinogen, proelastases, protease E, kallikreinogen, procarboxypeptidases) are stored as inactive zymogens in the secretory granules of acinar cells, and only after secretion are trypsinogens cleaved and activated by enterokinase in the lumen of the small intestine, generating trypsins that activate the other proteases in a cascade; production of protease inhibitors by the acinar cells normally prevents the pancreas from digesting itself. In acute necrotizing pancreatitis this protective mechanism fails and the proenzymes are activated within the gland itself.

A(i) Cell body (soma): The neuronal cell body has a nucleus with at least one nucleolus and typical cytoplasmic organelles; it lacks centrioles, consistent with the amitotic nature of neurons. Types of neurons by structure: Unipolar (pseudounipolar) neurons — sensory neurons with only a single process or fiber that divides close to the cell body into two main branches (axon and dendrite); the longer branch extends to a peripheral ending and the other toward the CNS. Multipolar neurons — motor neurons and interneurons with numerous cell processes (an axon and many dendrites). Bipolar neurons — spindle-shaped, with a dendrite at one end and an axon at the other; found in the light-sensitive retina of the eye. Anaxonic neurons — have many dendrites but no true axon; do not produce action potentials, but regulate electrical changes of adjacent neurons. Glial cells (neuroglia): Neuroglia is a special type of connective tissue for the nervous system. Glial cells are nonconductive; they provide a support system for neurons; they support, nourish, and protect neurons. They are far more numerous than neurons and, unlike neurons, are capable of mitosis. Types include oligodendrocytes (produce myelin in CNS), Schwann cells and satellite cells (in PNS), and microglia.
A(ii) Neurons are highly specialized and amitotic: if a neuron is destroyed, it cannot be replaced because neurons do not go through mitosis. This means that neuronal loss (e.g., in injury or disease) is permanent and irreplaceable.
B(i) CNS consists of the brain and spinal cord; it is covered by three connective tissue layers called meninges (dura, arachnoid, and pia maters); it contains very little collagen or fibrous tissue and is relatively soft, easily damaged by injuries affecting the cranium or vertebral bones. The PNS is composed of nerves and ganglia. Functionally, the CNS is the master control unit while the PNS is the body's link to the outside world. Sensory (afferent) and motor (efferent) are the functional categories.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the cell body (soma), types of neurons by structure, and the glial cells of the nervous system under the following headings: cell types, function, and capacity for mitosis.
A(ii) Explain the clinical significance of neurons being amitotic.
B(i) Distinguish between the central nervous system (CNS) and peripheral nervous system (PNS) structurally and functionally.

A patient has poor exercise tolerance, orthopnoea and fatigue, lung function tests show a restrictive deficit, and both halves of the diaphragm are found to be paralysed.
(i) State the diagnosis.
(ii) Explain the pathological and embryologic basis, including the possible sites and causes of the lesion, the paradoxical movement, and why injury to one nerve spares the other half.
(iii) State the initial management.
(iv) State the definitive (symptomatic) treatment.
questions.answerText:
(i) Bilateral diaphragmatic paralysis, due to an interruption of the nervous supply of the diaphragm.
(ii) The interruption may lie in the phrenic nerve, the cervical spinal cord or the brainstem, and is most often a lesion of the phrenic nerve: mechanical trauma (ligation or damage during surgery), compression by a tumour within the chest cavity, myopathies (e.g. myasthenia gravis) or neuropathies (e.g. diabetic neuropathy).
(ii) Embryology: the diaphragm is entirely mesodermal, developing from the septum transversum, the pleuroperitoneal membranes, the dorsal mesentery of the oesophagus and the mesoderm of the body wall; cervical myotomes and nerves contribute the muscle and nerve supply, hence the long course of the phrenic nerve (C3, C4, C5).
(ii) Paralysis produces paradoxical movement: the affected side moves upwards during inspiration and downwards during expiration.
(ii) Each dome has a separate nerve supply, so injury to the motor supply of one phrenic nerve does not affect the other half; unilateral paralysis is usually asymptomatic and an incidental finding on X-ray.
(ii) Sectioning of a phrenic nerve in the neck causes complete paralysis and eventual atrophy of the muscular part of that half of the diaphragm, except in persons who have an accessory phrenic nerve.
(iii) Management is two-fold; firstly the underlying cause must be identified and treated.
(iv) The second part is symptomatic relief, usually by non-invasive ventilation such as a CPAP (continuous positive airway pressure) machine.

questions.question:
A patient's brain is deprived of its blood supply.
(i) State the complications in relation to the duration of interruption of blood flow, and explain why the brain depends so heavily on its blood supply.
(ii) State the sources of the brain's arterial supply and the parts each supplies, name the anastomosis that provides collateral circulation, and state and justify one protective or management option.
questions.answerText:
(i) The constantly active brain needs a rich blood supply; about 15% of the cardiac output reaches the brain.
- Loss of consciousness occurs if the blood supply is interrupted for about 5 seconds.
- Irreversible brain damage occurs if the brain is deprived of blood for more than 4-5 minutes.
(ii) Internal carotid artery and its branches supply the anterior 2/3 of the brain (anterior circulation); it enters through the carotid canal and supplies the optic nerve, orbital contents including retina, optic tract, LGB and posterior limb of the internal capsule.
- Vertebrobasilar and posterior cerebral arteries supply the brainstem, cerebellum, occipital lobe etc. (posterior circulation); the two vertebral arteries join to form the basilar artery, which ends by dividing into the two posterior cerebral arteries.
- Circle of Willis: anastomotic channel between the internal carotid and vertebrobasilar systems, around the infundibulum of the pituitary and the optic chiasma at the base of the brain.
- Surgical or medical management options: not covered.
- Justified option: the circle of Willis, because this collateral circulation provides blood when major arteries become occluded.

questions.question:
A patient who has undergone ablation of part of the frontal lobe lying in front of the primary motor area has difficulty in walking, with no paralysis.
(i) Give the diagnosis and identify the cortical area involved, with its Brodmann area, location and function.
(ii) Explain the pathophysiology, including the related motor areas and the association area of the frontal pole.
questions.answerText:
(i) Apraxia (difficulty in walking with no paralysis) following ablation of the premotor area.
- Premotor area (area 6): frontal lobe, anterior to the primary motor area; concerned with voluntary motor functions dependent on sensory input, e.g. walking.
(ii) Three major cortical areas are involved in motor control: primary motor area (area 4), supplementary motor area and premotor area (area 6).
- Primary motor area (area 4): the contralateral half of the body is represented in a disproportionate order, giving rise to the motor homunculus.
- Supplementary motor area: medial surface anterior to the medial extension of area 4; crucial in sequential performance of multiple movements, e.g. alternating hand movements.
- Frontal eye fields: middle frontal gyrus anterior to the precentral gyrus (area 8).
- Prefrontal area: pole of the frontal lobe (areas 9, 10, 11); role in affective behaviour and judgement; lesions cause change in personality.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the processes of digestion, naming all eight steps in order.
A(ii) Describe the four main functions of the GI tract, distinguishing between the role of the small intestine and the role of the large intestine in absorption.
B(i) Describe the composition and function of the serosa, including the structures it is continuous with and how it differs between organs within the abdominal cavity and the esophagus.
B(ii) Explain why the enteric nervous system provides the anatomical basis for the effects of emotional stress on the GIT, and name the two diseases that demonstrate the clinical consequences of plexus destruction.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Eight processes of digestion (in order):
1. Ingestion
2. Mastication
3. Peristalsis / motility
4. Secretions
5. Hormone release
6. Chemical digestion
7. Absorption
8. Elimination
A(ii) Four main functions of the GI tract:
1. Macromolecules (proteins, complex carbohydrates, nucleic acids, and fat) obtained from ingested food are broken down into smaller subunits for easy absorption through the lining of the small intestine during digestion.
2. These smaller subunits are required for the release of energy, maintenance, and growth.
3. Most of the water and electrolytes are absorbed in the large intestine.
4. The inner layer of the entire GI tract forms an important protective barrier between the contents of the tract and the tissues of the body.
B(i) Serosa:
- Composition: a thin sheet of loose connective tissue covered with mesothelium (a simple squamous covering epithelium); rich in blood vessels, lymphatics, and adipose tissue.
- Function: the outermost covering of GIT organs within the abdominal cavity.
- Continuity: the serosa of the small and large intestines is continuous with parts of the mesentery (a large fold of adipose connective tissue covered on both sides by mesothelium, which suspends the intestines and is continuous with the peritoneum).
- Esophagus: because the esophagus is bound directly to adjacent structures and not suspended in a cavity, it has a thick adventitia instead of a serosa; the adventitia consists of connective tissue containing vessels and nerves, lacking mesothelium.
B(ii) The enteric nervous system (submucosal and myenteric plexuses) functions independently of the CNS; because it is anatomically connected to the autonomic nervous system, it provides the anatomical basis for the well-known actions of emotional stress on the stomach and other regions of the GIT.
Two diseases demonstrating clinical consequences of plexus destruction:
1. Hirschsprung disease (congenital aganglionic megacolon): caused by absence or severely injured plexuses in parts or all of the large intestine; disturbs motility and produces dilation, causing difficulty passing stool.
2. Chagas disease / trypanosomiasis (infection with Trypanosoma cruzi): the protozoan destroys the enteric plexuses, producing similar motility disturbance.

(i) The posterior cerebral artery supplies the medial surfaces of the occipital and temporal lobes; since the primary visual cortex is located in the occipital lobe, this is the structure primarily affected.
(ii) The posterior cerebral artery also sends branches to the upper part of the midbrain and lower part of the diencephalon, and gives rise to several posterior choroidal arteries, which form the choroid plexus of the 3rd ventricle and that of the body of the lateral ventricles.
(iii) Vertigo and deafness instead relate to occlusion of the internal auditory artery (which supplies the ear and often arises from the anterior inferior cerebellar artery), whereas visual loss relates to the posterior cerebral artery because it supplies the occipital lobe containing the primary visual cortex.
(iv) Since the primary visual cortex is located in the occipital lobe, occlusion of the posterior cerebral artery could lead to visual loss among other symptoms.
questions.question:
A patient presents with visual field loss following a cerebrovascular event; posterior cerebral artery occlusion is suspected on clinico-anatomical grounds.
(i) Identify the structure/organ primarily affected.
(ii) What other structures may be affected by compromise of this artery's territory?
(iii) What is the differential basis for visual loss versus vertigo/deafness in vertebrobasilar territory occlusion?

A patient with disease of the thoracic vertebrae has pain referred to the front of the chest or abdomen and a swelling that appears on the chest wall.
(i) State the diagnosis.
(ii) State the predisposing factor.
(iii) Explain the pathophysiology: the pathway of the pus and the anatomical basis of the referred pain.
(iv) State the management.
questions.answerText:
(i) Tuberculous cold abscess tracking forwards from a diseased thoracic vertebra (Pott's disease, tuberculosis of the thoracic vertebrae).
(ii) Predisposing factor: disease (tuberculosis) of the thoracic vertebrae.
(iii) Local irritation of the intercostal nerves by the disease gives pain referred to the front of the chest or abdomen, in the region of the peripheral termination of the nerves; the intercostal nerves are the anterior primary rami of the thoracic spinal nerves, with nerves 7-11 supplying the anterior abdominal wall.
(iii) Pus from the region of the vertebral column tracks around the thorax along the course of the neurovascular bundle (between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles) and points at the three sites of exit of the cutaneous branches of the intercostal nerves: lateral to erector spinae, in the midaxillary line and just lateral to the sternum.
(iv) Management of the abscess: not covered ; only local anaesthesia of an intercostal space by infiltration around the intercostal nerve trunk and its collateral branch (intercostal nerve block) is described.

(i) Small bowel obstruction: central, numerous, over 2.5 to 5.0 cm, small radius of curvature, valvulae conniventes, multiple fluid levels.
(i) The sign is the 'string of beads' on the erect film: small pockets of gas trapped between the valvulae conniventes.
(ii) Large bowel obstruction: tends to be peripheral, few in number, large (above 5.0 cm in diameter), with haustra seen as thick white lines that are widely separated.
(iii) Air inside the bowel: ileus (localised or generalised), bowel obstruction, volvulus (e.g. sigmoid volvulus).
(iii) Air outside the lumen: intraperitoneal air, retroperitoneal air, branching air in the liver, pneumatosis; Chilaiditi syndrome is a loop of large bowel (usually transverse colon) between the diaphragm and liver, asymptomatic form called Chilaiditi's sign.
(iii) Densities: bones/foreign bodies, appendicolith, stones, pancreatic calcification, abdominal aortic aneurysm; also free fluid.
(iv) Abdominal X-ray remains an important initial investigation for intestinal obstruction, perforation of the GI tract and foreign bodies.
(iv) The features that distinguish mechanical obstruction from ileus are not covered.
