A 7-year-old child falls onto an outstretched hand and sustains a fracture near the supracondylar ridges of the humerus. Over the following hours the forearm becomes increasingly painful and pale, and the child develops progressive flexion of the fingers and wrist.
(i) What is the diagnosis of the limb complication that is developing?
(ii) What is the pathologic basis for this complication?
(iii) What important clinical feature should be recognised early?
questions.answerText:
(i) Volkmann's ischaemic contracture, complicating a supracondylar fracture of the humerus.
(ii) It occurs when there is a lack of blood flow (ischaemia) to the forearm, usually caused by increased pressure resulting from swelling (compartment syndrome); the classical presentation is a supracondylar fracture of the humerus, with the brachial artery being the artery involved. There is very little room within each fascial compartment of the arm/forearm, so haemorrhage or oedema can cause secondary vascular compression of blood vessels — veins are affected first, and later the arteries, resulting in ischaemia of the affected part.
(iii) The classical presentation of acute compartment syndrome is remembered by "the five P's": pulselessness, paraesthesia, poikilothermia, paralysis and pallor — though apart from paraesthesia, which may occur earlier, the others are typically late findings. There are three levels of severity of Volkmann's contracture, ranging from flexion contracture of two or three fingers with no or limited sensory loss, to involvement of all fingers with the thumb stuck in the palm and some sensory loss, to the most severe form involving all forearm flexor and extensor muscles.

questions.question:
Describe the anterior compartment muscles of the leg and the dorsum of the foot under the following headings, and explain why injury to the deep fibular nerve causes foot drop.
A(i) Name all 4 muscles of the anterior compartment; give origin, insertion, innervation, and action for each
A(ii) The dorsalis pedis artery — origin, course, and branches
B(i) The deep fibular nerve — its origin, course, and distribution in the anterior compartment and the foot
B(ii) Explain the anatomical basis of foot drop following injury to the deep fibular nerve at the fibular neck
C(i) Distinguish the actions of tibialis anterior and fibularis tertius; state which muscle inverts and which everts the foot, and name the nerve supplying each
questions.answerText:
A(i) Tibialis anterior: origin — lateral condyle and superior half of lateral surface of tibia and interosseous membrane; insertion — medial and inferior surfaces of medial cuneiform and base of 1st metatarsal; innervation — deep fibular nerve (L4, L5); action — dorsiflexes ankle and inverts foot. Extensor digitorum longus: origin — lateral condyle of tibia and superior 3/4 of medial surface of fibula and interosseous membrane; insertion — middle and distal phalanges of lateral 4 digits; innervation — deep fibular nerve (L4, L5); action — extends lateral 4 digits and dorsiflexes ankle. Extensor hallucis longus: origin — middle part of anterior surface of fibula and interosseous membrane; insertion — dorsal aspect of base of distal phalanx of great toe; innervation — deep fibular nerve (L4, L5); action — extends great toe and dorsiflexes ankle. Fibularis tertius: origin — inferior 3rd of anterior surface of fibula and interosseous membrane; insertion — dorsum of base of 5th metatarsal; innervation — deep fibular nerve (L4, L5); action — dorsiflexes ankle and aids in eversion of foot.
A(ii) The dorsalis pedis artery begins as the anterior tibial artery enters the foot. It passes over the dorsal aspect of the tarsal bones, then moves inferiorly towards the sole of the foot. It then anastomoses with the lateral plantar artery to form the deep plantar arch. It supplies the tarsal bones and the dorsal aspect of the metatarsals; via the deep plantar arch, it also contributes to the supply of the toes. The dorsalis pedis pulse is found by palpating on the dorsum of the foot, just lateral to extensor hallucis longus tendon.
B(i) The common fibular nerve is the lateral, smaller terminal branch of the sciatic nerve; it begins at the superior angle of the popliteal fossa, closely follows the medial border of biceps femoris, exits the fossa superficial to the lateral head of gastrocnemius, passes over the posterior aspect of the head of fibula, and winds around the neck of fibula where it divides into its terminal branches — the deep fibular nerve and superficial fibular nerve. The deep fibular nerve supplies all 4 muscles of the anterior compartment (tibialis anterior, extensor digitorum longus, extensor hallucis longus, fibularis tertius) and the foot.
B(ii) At the neck of fibula the common fibular nerve is subcutaneous and directly palpable, making it vulnerable to direct trauma, compression, or traction. Injury here interrupts the deep fibular nerve before it reaches the anterior compartment. All 4 anterior compartment muscles (which perform dorsiflexion and toe extension) are paralysed. The result is foot drop: the foot hangs in plantarflexion and inversion (because the unopposed plantarflexors — gastrocnemius, soleus — and invertor — tibialis posterior — continue to act), and the patient develops a high-stepping gait to clear the dragging toe.
C(i) Tibialis anterior: dorsiflexes the ankle AND inverts the foot; supplied by the deep fibular nerve (L4, L5). Fibularis tertius: dorsiflexes the ankle AND aids eversion of the foot; supplied by the deep fibular nerve (L4, L5). Both share the same nerve supply but perform opposite movements about the subtalar axis (inversion vs. eversion), reflecting their positions on opposite sides of the interosseous membrane.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old competitive cyclist sustains a blow to the lateral aspect of the knee and presents with foot drop. On examination there is weakness of dorsiflexion and eversion of the right foot, with sensory loss on the dorsum and lateral side.
(i) State the diagnosis and name the nerve injured.
(ii) Identify the anatomical landmark at which injury most commonly occurs and explain why.
(iii) What anatomical structures pass through which foramina to explain the nerve's origin and course?
(iv) What is the definitive management?
questions.answerText:
(i) The diagnosis is foot drop due to injury to the common fibular (common peroneal) nerve. The common fibular nerve is the lateral, smaller terminal branch of the sciatic nerve.
(ii) The most common site of injury is where the common fibular nerve winds around the neck of the fibula. After exiting the popliteal fossa by passing superficial to the lateral head of gastrocnemius, it passes over the posterior aspect of the head of fibula and then winds around the neck of the fibula, where it is subcutaneous and directly palpable — making it highly vulnerable to direct trauma, compression (plaster casts, tight bandages), or traction injury at this point. At this level it divides into its terminal branches.
(iii) The sciatic nerve (L4, 5; S1, 2, 3) exits the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen below piriformis (the landmark muscle of the foramen). In the popliteal fossa it divides at its superior angle into the tibial nerve (medial, larger branch) and the common fibular nerve (lateral, smaller branch). The common fibular nerve then closely follows the medial border of biceps femoris and its tendon, exits the fossa superficial to the lateral head of gastrocnemius, passes over the posterior aspect of the fibular head, and winds around the neck of fibula.
(iv) Conservative management for neuropraxia: padded splinting to hold the foot in neutral position, physiotherapy to prevent contracture, and ankle-foot orthosis (foot drop splint) to allow ambulation. Surgical management: decompression, neurolysis, or nerve repair/grafting for axonotmesis or neurotmesis; tendon transfer (tibialis posterior transfer) for permanent palsy not amenable to nerve repair.

(i) The tongue begins development in the 4th week with two lateral lingual swellings, a first median swelling (the tuberculum impar), a second median swelling (the cupola or hypobranchial eminence), and a third median swelling which forms the epiglottis; posterior to the epiglottis lies the laryngeal eminence.
(ii) The anterior two-thirds is formed by fusion of the lingual swellings and the tuberculum impar.
The posterior one-third is formed by the cranial part of the hypobranchial eminence.
The papillae form by epithelial proliferation of tongue cells, and taste buds form by inductive interaction between the epithelial cells and invading gustatory nerve cells from the chorda tympani branch of cranial nerve VII.
Tongue musculature develops from occipital myotomes, and the salivary glands develop as solid epithelial buds from the primordial oral cavity.
(iii) The anterior two-thirds is supplied by the lingual branch of the mandibular nerve, and by the chorda tympani branch of cranial nerve VII for special taste (except the vallate papillae); the posterior one-third is supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve, including taste to the vallate papillae; the epiglottis and most of the posterior part are supplied by the vagus nerve; the musculature is supplied by the hypoglossal nerve, except palatoglossus, which is supplied by the pharyngeal branch of the vagus.
Clinical basis: the thyroid gland develops as an epithelial proliferation at the foramen caecum, which lies at the junction behind the tuberculum impar, between the anterior two-thirds and posterior one-third of the tongue, and normally migrates caudally along the thyroglossal duct to its final pretracheal position.
Arrest of this normal descent leaves thyroid tissue at or near the tongue, which is listed among the anomalies of the tongue as the presence of thyroid tissue, and corresponds to the lingual/intralingual thyroid anomalies described for the thyroid gland.
Distinguishing feature 1: the anterior two-thirds arises from the lingual swellings and tuberculum impar, while the posterior one-third arises from the hypobranchial eminence.
Distinguishing feature 2: general sensation of the anterior two-thirds is via the lingual (mandibular) nerve, while the posterior one-third is via the glossopharyngeal nerve.
Distinguishing feature 3: special taste in the anterior two-thirds is via the chorda tympani (CN VII), except at the vallate papillae; taste in the posterior one-third, including the vallate papillae, is via the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX).
Both parts, however, share hypoglossal nerve supply to their musculature, except for palatoglossus.
questions.question:
Describe the tongue under the following headings:
(i) The swellings from which it develops
(ii) Formation of its anterior two-thirds and posterior one-third
(iii) Its nerve supply.
Explain the clinical basis for why ectopic thyroid tissue can occur in relation to the tongue.
Distinguish between the anterior two-thirds and the posterior one-third of the tongue.

Describe the diaphragm under the following headings:
(i) Its four embryonic components
(ii) The septum transversum
(iii) The pleuroperitoneal membranes and closure of the pericardioperitoneal openings.
Explain the clinical basis for why a posterolateral diaphragmatic defect is more common on the left side.
Distinguish between the septum transversum and the pleuroperitoneal membranes.
questions.answerText:
(i) The diaphragm develops from four embryonic components: the septum transversum, the pleuroperitoneal membranes, the dorsal mesentery of the esophagus, and muscular ingrowth from the lateral body walls.
(ii) The septum transversum is a thick plate of mesodermal tissue lying between the pericardial cavity and the yolk sac, ventral to the foregut and the pleuroperitoneal canals; it grows dorsally from the ventrolateral body wall.
It forms an incomplete partition between the thoracic and abdominal cavities and, on expanding and fusing with the pleuroperitoneal membranes and the mesenchyme ventral to the esophagus, becomes the primordium of the central tendon of the diaphragm.
(iii) The pleuroperitoneal membranes develop from the pleuroperitoneal folds attached dorsolaterally to the body wall, whose free edges project into the caudal part of the pericardioperitoneal canals; they become more prominent and membranous, and are invaded by myoblasts.
During the 6th week they extend ventromedially and fuse with the dorsal mesentery of the esophagus and the septum transversum, closing the pericardioperitoneal openings; the right opening closes slightly earlier than the left.
Clinical basis: because the right pericardioperitoneal opening closes slightly earlier than the left, the left side remains open for a longer period, making a persistent posterolateral defect more likely on the left.
This is the same principle described for the pleuropericardial openings, where the larger right common cardinal vein raises a bigger fold and closes its opening earlier than the left.
Distinguishing feature 1: the septum transversum is a thick mesodermal plate lying centrally, ventral to the foregut, and becomes the central tendon of the diaphragm.
Distinguishing feature 2: the pleuroperitoneal membranes arise from folds attached dorsolaterally to the body wall and, in the fetus, form a large portion of the diaphragm but represent a smaller portion in infants once muscle has grown in from the body wall.
The septum transversum is grown into and fused with by the other three components; the pleuroperitoneal membranes are one of those components that fuse with it and the dorsal mesentery of the esophagus during the 6th week.
Both are among the three basic components that fuse in the 6th week to form a complete thoraco-abdominal partition, together with the mesoesophagus.
Positionally, the septum transversum initially lies opposite the 3rd-5th cervical somites in the 4th week before both sets of components descend together with the diaphragm to the level of the thoracic somites by the 6th week.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the gross anatomy of the kidney, naming its outer and inner regions and the structures visible in a frontal section.
A(ii) State all seven functions of the kidney.
B(i) Compare cortical nephrons and juxtamedullary nephrons under the headings: proportion, loop length, glomerulus position, and capillary bed supplied by the efferent arteriole.
B(ii) Describe the two cell types in the collecting ducts, including their microscopic features and functions, and describe how the collecting ducts contribute to urine delivery.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Gross anatomy of the kidney:
- Renal cortex: granular-appearing superficial region.
- Renal medulla: composed of cone-shaped medullary (renal) pyramids; pyramids are separated by renal columns (inward extensions of cortical tissue).
- Structures in frontal section: renal hilum, renal cortex, renal medulla, major calyx, papilla of pyramid, renal pelvis, minor calyx, ureter, renal pyramid in renal medulla, renal column, fibrous capsule.
A(ii) Seven functions of the kidney:
1. Regulating total water volume and total solute concentration in water.
2. Regulating ECF ion concentrations.
3. Ensuring long-term acid-base balance.
4. Removal of metabolic wastes, toxins, and drugs.
5. Endocrine functions: renin (regulation of blood pressure) and erythropoietin (regulation of RBC production).
6. Activation of vitamin D.
7. Gluconeogenesis during prolonged fasting.
B(i) Comparison of nephron types:
- Cortical nephrons: 85% of nephrons; short nephron loop; glomerulus further from the cortex-medulla junction; efferent arteriole supplies peritubular capillaries.
- Juxtamedullary nephrons: long nephron loops that deeply invade the medulla; glomerulus closer to the cortex-medulla junction; efferent arteriole supplies vasa recta; ascending limbs have thick and thin segments; important in production of concentrated urine.
B(ii) Two collecting duct cell types:
- Principal cells: sparse, short microvilli; maintain water and Na+ balance.
- Intercalated cells (A and B types): cuboidal cells with abundant microvilli; both types help maintain acid-base balance of blood.
Collecting ducts receive filtrate from many nephrons; run through medullary pyramids giving them a striped appearance; fuse together to deliver urine through papillae into minor calyces.

(i) Cleft lip and cleft palate.
(ii) The upper lip is formed in the 6th week by fusion of the medial nasal prominence and the two maxillary prominences; the lower lip and jaw form by fusion of the two mandibular prominences, and the cheeks and maxilla by fusion of the maxillary prominences.
The intermaxillary segment (formed by fusion of the two medial nasal prominences) carries the four incisor teeth, forms the philtrum of the upper lip, and forms the triangular primary palate.
The secondary palate is formed in the 6th week from the palatine shelves derived from the maxillary prominence, which anteriorly fuse with the primary palate to form the incisive foramen, the midline landmark between the primary and secondary palate.
Cleft lip and palate are listed among the anomalies of the face arising in this region; no further mechanistic detail beyond the fusion events described above.
questions.question:
A newborn is noted to have a gap in the upper lip lateral to the philtrum, with failure of union of the tissues that normally form the upper lip and palate.
(i) State the diagnosis.
(ii) Explain the pathophysiology (embryologic basis).

A(i) Describe the thalamus: position, surfaces and features.
A(ii) Describe its limits and relations.
A(iii) Describe its internal medullary lamina and nuclear groups with their connections.
B(i) State the clinical basis for its vulnerability to disease.
C(i) Distinguish between the medial and lateral geniculate bodies.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Forms the lateral wall of the diencephalon; the medial surfaces lie parallel, slightly bulging into the 3rd ventricle; an interthalamic adhesion joins the two thalami in about 60-80% of cases (no exchange of substance); the pulvinar is the posterior end of the medial surface.
- Superior surface tapers anteriorly from the pulvinar to the small anterior pole; its pia covering extends back as far as the pineal gland; the lateral edge is covered by ependyma and forms part of the floor of the lateral ventricle.
A(ii) Anterior limit: the interventricular foramen; posterior limit: the posterior commissure; extends from the 3rd ventricle to the medial side of the posterior limb of the internal capsule (separated by the external medullary lamina).
- The inferior surface is continuous medially with the hypothalamus, separated by the hypothalamic sulcus.
A(iii) A Y-shaped internal medullary lamina divides it into lateral, medial and anterior portions; nuclei are grouped by this lamina and by function.
- Anterior group: afferents from the mammillary body; projects to the cingulate gyrus. Medial group: projects to the frontal cortex.
- Lateral group: anterior to the pulvinar; receives the medial lemniscus, spinothalamic and trigeminal tracts; projects to motor cortex, postcentral gyrus and parietal lobe.
- Posterior group: pulvinar (projects to temporal and parietal lobes), medial geniculate body and lateral geniculate body.
B(i) Clinical basis for vulnerability to disease: not covered.
- Thalamostriate vessels lie between the thalamus and the body of the caudate nucleus; the internal carotid artery supplies the thalamus.
C(i) Medial geniculate body: ventral to the pulvinar and lateral to the midbrain; receives fibres from the lateral lemniscus and inferior colliculus; projects into the temporal lobe (auditory).
C(ii) Lateral geniculate body: oval elevation on the posterior end of the pulvinar; receives fibres from the optic tract; projects to the visual cortex.

questions.question:
A patient presents with a swelling in the groin below the inguinal ligament after pus has accumulated in the region of the vertebral column.
(i) Give the diagnosis.
(ii) Explain the anatomical basis of the route taken by the pus, including the sheath of the muscle involved.
(iii) State the origin, insertion, nerve supply and actions of the muscle.
(iv) State the resuscitation, management and definitive treatment.
questions.answerText:
(i) Psoas abscess: accumulation of pus in the vertebral column region.
(ii) Pus trickles along the psoas muscle within the psoas sheath, passes underneath the inguinal ligament and presents as a swelling in the groin below the ligament.
(ii) The psoas fascia forms a sheath: superiorly thickened as the medial arcuate ligament, laterally fused with the anterior layer of thoracolumbar fascia, medially attached to lumbar vertebral bodies and discs, inferiorly fused with the fascia covering iliacus.
(iii) Psoas major occupies abdomen, false pelvis and upper thigh; origin 14 fleshy strips from the lower border of T12 to the upper border of L5 (discs, adjoining vertebral bodies and 4 fibrous arches); insertion as iliopsoas tendon at the lesser trochanter.
(iii) Nerve supply ventral rami L1 to L4; actions: chief flexor of the thigh at the hip, bilateral action flexes the trunk, medial rotator of the thigh.
(iv) Resuscitation, management and definitive treatment are not covered.

A(i) The basal ganglia consist of the caudate nucleus, lentiform nucleus, amygdaloid body and claustrum. The lentiform nucleus consists of an outer putamen and an inner globus pallidus. The caudate nucleus is a comma-shaped structure with a bulbous head, body and tail attached to the amygdaloid body; its convexity projects into the ventricle, with internal capsule fibres running in its concavity. The lentiform nucleus is biconvex, with the putamen lateral and the smaller globus pallidus medial. The caudate nucleus and putamen are joined by interconnecting fibres running through the anterior part of the internal capsule, forming the corpus striatum. The amygdaloid body lies on the roof of the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle; the claustrum is a saucer-shaped thin lamina of gray matter lateral to the putamen.
A(ii) The corpus striatum is the afferent centre of the basal ganglia, receiving fibres from the cortex, thalamus and substantia nigra. The globus pallidus is the efferent pathway, sending fibres to the thalamus, subthalamic nucleus, substantia nigra, etc. The basal ganglia offer supraspinal control over skeletal muscle movement, modulating its rate, range and coordination, using neurotransmitters such as acetylcholine, dopamine, glutamate and serotonin.
B. Parkinsonism, the most common anomaly of the basal nuclei, involves a decrease in dopamine in the nigrostriatal pathway.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the gross anatomy/components of the basal ganglia.
A(ii) Describe the functional anatomy (afferent and efferent pathways).
B. How do these components relate to a common pathology?

questions.answerText:
A(i) The epidermis derives from surface ectoderm and the dermis from mesenchyme; at 4-5 weeks a single ectodermal layer covers mesoderm, and in the 2nd month it divides into periderm and a basal (germinative) layer, with an intermediate zone forming by the 11th week.
A(i) The periderm is completely replaced by the 21st week; its exfoliated cells form part of the vernix caseosa, protecting the skin from amniotic fluid; the definitive five layers (basalis, spinosum, granulosum, lucidum, corneum) are present by the 4th month.
A(ii) The dermis is dense irregular connective tissue from mesenchyme; in the 3rd-4th month dermal papillae form, containing a capillary or sensory nerve end organ, over a fatty subcorium.
A(ii) The papillary layer forms ridges (fingerprints) and the reticular layer lies beneath; dermal vessels arise from mesenchyme with angiogenesis from the 5th week and major vascular organization is established by the end of the first trimester.
A(iii) Sebaceous glands bud from hair follicle root sheaths; sweat glands begin in the 13th-14th week and mature by week 24 (eccrine functioning shortly after birth; apocrine in axilla, pubic and perineal regions and areolae, secreting at puberty); mammary glands arise from buds in the 6th week.
A(iii) Hair appears in the 9th-12th week (first on eyebrows, upper lip, chin); lanugo appears at the 12th week; arrector pili muscles differentiate from mesenchyme; nail fields appear at the 10th week, fingernails precede toenails by 4 weeks and reach the tips at the 32nd week (toenails 36th week).
B(i) Albinism: generalized, autosomal recessive, melanocytes fail to produce melanin; piebaldism: autosomal dominant, lack of melanin in patches; Waardenburg syndrome; vitiligo (autoimmune loss of melanocytes); ichthyosis (keratinization).
B(i) Hypertrichosis (excessive hair) and atrichia (congenital absence of hair, associated with abnormal teeth and nails); polythelia, athelia, polymastia, amastia, gynecomastia; cavernous angiomas, lymphangiomas (cystic hygromas) and port-wine stain.
C(i) Melanocytes are neural crest derived and migrate into the fetal epidermis by 12 weeks; Langerhans cells appear at 6 weeks (functional at 12-14 weeks) and Merkel cells at 18 weeks.
C(i) Neural crest cells become melanoblasts, migrate to the dermo-epidermal junction and become melanocytes, each associated with 30-40 keratinocytes; melanin content accounts for skin colour and increases with ultraviolet light.
C(i) Deletion of both Eda and Edar causes failure of induction of hair follicles; sweat gland formation depends on epidermal Eda signalling (up-regulating Shh); TGF signalling stimulates hair follicle initiation.
C(i) Wnt, FGF and BMP signalling determine neural versus epidermal fate after gastrulation.

A(i) Four stomach regions:
- Cardia and pylorus are histologically similar: tubular glands with long pits usually branching into coiled secretory portions (cardiac and pyloric glands respectively); pits are longer in the pylorus; lack both parietal and chief cells; major secretion is abundant mucus.
- Fundus and body are histologically identical: simple columnar epithelium invaginates to form gastric pits leading into long, branched, tubular gastric glands; 3 to 7 glands usually open into the bottom of each gastric pit; contain all four secretory cell types; involved in secretion of acidic gastric juice.
A(ii) Structure of fundic/body glands:
- Each gland has three named parts: isthmus, neck, and base.
- Isthmus: the region of stem cells (between the gastric pit and gland); the pluripotent stem cells divide asymmetrically and can move upward or downward to replace epithelial cells.
- Neck: contains mucous neck cells (MNCs) in clusters or singly; also contains parietal cells.
- Base: predominantly chief (zymogen) cells; also contains enteroendocrine cells.
B(i) Mucous neck cells (MNCs):
- Present in clusters or singly in the necks of gastric glands.
- Less columnar than surface mucous cells; irregular in shape with round nucleus and apical secretory granules.
- Their mucous secretion is less alkaline than that of the surface epithelial mucous cells; they secrete acidic fluid containing mucin (not mucus, which implies alkaline content).
B(ii) Intrinsic factor:
- Produced by: parietal (oxyntic) cells.
- Chemical nature: a glycoprotein.
- Function: required for the uptake of vitamin B12 in the small intestine.
- Deficiency and anaemia: if parietal cells are damaged, insufficient quantities of intrinsic factor are secreted; without adequate intrinsic factor, vitamin B12 is not absorbed adequately; low levels of vitamin B12 reduce the proliferation of erythroblasts, resulting in pernicious anaemia.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the histological features of the four stomach regions — cardia, fundus, body, and pylorus — under the headings: surface epithelium, gland type, gastric pit length, and principal secretion.
A(ii) Explain the complete structure and function of the gastric glands of the fundus/body, including the isthmus, neck, and base, and what cells are found in each part.
B(i) Explain the full role of mucous neck cells in the gastric gland, comparing their secretion to that of surface mucous cells.
