questions.answerText:
A(i) The axillary artery is a continuation of the subclavian artery; it begins at the lateral border of the first rib and ends at the lower border of teres major, continuing thereafter as the brachial artery. It is closely related to the cords of the brachial plexus and is enclosed with them in the axillary sheath.
A(ii) Pectoralis minor divides the axillary artery into three parts: the first part extends from the lateral border of the first rib to the upper border of pectoralis minor; the second part lies behind pectoralis minor; the third part extends from the lower border of pectoralis minor to the lower border of teres major.
A(iii) The first part gives one branch, the superior (highest) thoracic artery; the second part gives two branches, the thoracoacromial and lateral thoracic arteries; the third part gives three branches, the subscapular artery and the anterior and posterior circumflex humeral arteries.
B. The inferior part of the axillary artery can be palpated in the inferior part of the lateral wall of the axilla.
This part can be compressed against the humerus to control profuse bleeding.
C. The scapular anastomosis is a system of arteries connecting the subclavian artery and the corresponding axillary artery, forming an anastomosis around the scapula, occurring in the subscapular, supraspinatus and infraspinatus fossae.
It is formed by the suprascapular artery (a branch of the thyrocervical trunk from the subclavian artery), the deep branch of the transverse cervical artery (another branch of the thyrocervical trunk), and the circumflex scapular artery (a branch of the subscapular artery arising from the third part of the axillary artery).
These vessels anastomose the first part of the subclavian artery with the third part of the axillary artery, allowing blood to flow past the shoulder joint regardless of the position of the arm.
A further anastomosis occurs over the acromion process, formed by the acromial branch of the thoracoacromial artery, the acromial branch of the suprascapular artery, and the acromial branch of the posterior circumflex humeral artery, linking the subclavian with the second and third parts of the axillary artery.
The arterial anastomoses around the scapula thus provide a collateral circulation through which blood can continue to flow to the limb when the distal part of the subclavian artery or the proximal part of the axillary artery is blocked or occluded.
This collateral circulation is clinically important because it allows blood to continue circulating to the upper limb even if the main line of supply is obstructed.
This anatomical arrangement explains why proximal occlusion of the axillary or subclavian artery does not necessarily result in complete loss of blood supply to the limb.
questions.question:
Describe the axillary artery:
A(i) Origin, extent and continuation
A(ii) Division into three parts by pectoralis minor
A(iii) Branches of each part
B. State the safe site associated with clinical control of bleeding from the axillary artery.
C. Explain the anatomical basis for the scapular anastomosis providing a collateral circulation if the artery is occluded.

questions.answerText:
(i) The interatrial septum, specifically the region of the septum primum/septum secundum and the oval (foramen ovale) region.
(ii) This group of defects is termed atrial septal defects (ASDs); a distinct entity, the ventricular septal defect (VSD), instead involves the membranous portion of the interventricular septum.
(iii) A foramen secundum defect is caused by excessive resorption of the septum primum, the septum secundum, or both.
Normally, after birth, when lung circulation begins and pressure in the left atrium increases, the valve of the oval foramen (formed by the septum primum) is pressed against the septum secundum, obliterating the oval foramen and separating the right and left sides.
Excessive resorption of the septum primum and/or septum secundum leaves an abnormally large or unclosed opening, so this normal apposition and obliteration cannot occur, resulting in a persistent atrial septal defect.
questions.question:
Echocardiography in an infant shows a defect at the region of the oval fossa in the interatrial septum, with resorption noted of the septum primum, the septum secundum, or both.
(i) Identify the structure/organ affected.
(ii) State the differential pathologies.
(iii) Give the clinico-anatomical reasoning for this finding.

Describe the median nerve:
A(i) Formation (roots)
A(ii) Relations in the cubital fossa and at the wrist
A(iii) Branches
A(iv) Distribution
C. Explain the anatomical basis of the deformity seen after a low (wrist-level) injury to the median nerve.
questions.answerText:
A(i) The median nerve is formed by the union of a lateral root from the lateral cord (C5, C6, C7) and a medial root from the medial cord (C8, T1) of the brachial plexus.
A(ii) In the cubital fossa the median nerve is the most medial of the major vertical contents, lying medial to the brachial artery and the tendon of biceps brachii; at the wrist it lies anterior to the tendons of flexor digitorum superficialis, deep to the flexor retinaculum, within the carpal tunnel.
A(iii) It gives a palmar cutaneous branch that arises in the forearm, proximal to the flexor retinaculum, and a recurrent branch that arises in the hand to supply the thenar muscles.
A(iv) It supplies flexor carpi radialis, palmaris longus, pronator teres, pronator quadratus and the digital flexors, producing thumb flexion and opposition, flexion of digits 2 and 3, wrist flexion and abduction, and forearm pronation; it also supplies sensation to the anterolateral surface of the hand.
C. A low (wrist-level) median nerve injury produces an "ape-like hand."
There is flattening of the thenar eminence because the recurrent branch supplying abductor pollicis brevis and flexor pollicis brevis, which arises in the hand, is affected.
Opposition and abduction of the thumb become impossible, so the pincer-like action of the hand is lost, causing difficulty with fine manual tasks such as buttoning.
Adductor pollicis, being supplied by the ulnar nerve, is unopposed, further contributing to the deformity.
This contrasts with an elbow-level injury, where flexion of the index and middle fingers is lost (flexor digitorum superficialis and the lateral half of profundus are affected), the ring and little fingers weakly flex, and flexion of the distal phalanx of the thumb is lost, while the interosseous muscles are unaffected, being supplied by the ulnar nerve.
The median nerve can be torn partially or fully, or compressed, at the elbow, from fracture, other trauma, or compression from fluid build-up following injury.
The most common site of median nerve injury overall is at the wrist, within the carpal tunnel.

questions.question:
A(i) Define the thoracic duct and state its origin.
A(ii) Describe its course and relations.
A(iii) State its tributaries and termination.
A(iv) Describe the area it drains and compare it with the right lymphatic duct.
questions.answerText:
A(i) The longest lymphatic duct, conveying lymph to the circulatory system. It begins as the upward continuation of the cisterna chyli, a dilated sac formed by the union of the left and right lumbar trunks and the intestinal trunk, in front of L1 (also stated at T12).
A(ii) It enters the thorax through the aortic opening of the diaphragm and ascends in the posterior mediastinum, on the right side of and behind the oesophagus, with the oesophagus lying in front of it. It veers to the left at the level of T5 and ascends in the superior mediastinum to the left of the oesophagus. At the root of the neck it turns laterally, arches forwards and descends to enter the left venous angle.
A(iii) Before termination it receives the left jugular, left subclavian and left bronchomediastinal trunks; it ends in the left brachiocephalic vein. It contains many valves, with no valve at its termination.
A(iv) It drains lymph from the lower limbs, pelvic cavity, abdominal cavity, left half of the thorax and left side of the head, neck and upper limb (all the body except the right side of the head, neck, thorax and upper limb). The right lymphatic duct, formed by the union of the right jugular, subclavian and bronchomediastinal trunks, drains the right half of the head, neck, thorax and upper limb, right lung, right side of the heart and right surface of the liver, and ends in the right brachiocephalic vein. The lymph trunks are the right and left jugular, subclavian, bronchomediastinal and lumbar trunks and the intestinal trunk; the left brachiocephalic vein receives the thoracic duct, the right brachiocephalic vein the right lymphatic duct.

A(i) 12 pairs of intercostal (thoracic) nerves, the anterior primary rami of the thoracic spinal nerves; they are mixed nerves; T3-6 are typical and T1 and T2 are atypical.
A(ii) A typical nerve lies in the neurovascular bundle between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles, high in the space in relation to the subcostal groove of the rib above, below the artery (vein, artery, nerve from above downwards); nerves 1-6 are distributed in the intercostal spaces, 7-11 pass to the anterior abdominal wall, and the anterior ramus of the 12th runs forward in the abdomen as the subcostal nerve.
A(iii) Branches: rami communicantes, collateral (muscular) branches, lateral cutaneous branch, anterior cutaneous branch, muscular branches, pleural branch and peritoneal branches (7th-11th).
A(iv) They supply the skin, the muscles of the intercostal space and abdomen, and the parietal pleura and parietal peritoneum; cutaneous supply of the anterior wall is by supraclavicular nerves (C4) above the sternal angle and by the anterior and lateral cutaneous branches below it; the posterior wall is supplied by the posterior rami of the thoracic spinal nerves.
A(i) Atypical nerves: T1 has no anterior cutaneous branch and is joined to the brachial plexus by a large branch corresponding to the lateral cutaneous branch; the lateral cutaneous branch of T2 is the intercostobrachial nerve, joined to the medial cutaneous nerve of the arm.
B(i) Local anaesthesia of an intercostal space is easily produced by infiltration around the intercostal nerve trunk and its collateral branch (intercostal nerve block).
B(i) A needle or drain is passed immediately above the upper border of a rib, to avoid the neurovascular bundle lying under the rib above.
B(i) In a conventional posterolateral thoracotomy the incision is along the 5th or 6th rib; the periosteum over a segment of the rib is elevated, protecting the neurovascular bundle, and the rib is excised to reach the lung or mediastinum through the intercostal space.
C(i) Local irritation of the intercostal nerves (e.g. by Pott's disease, tuberculosis of the thoracic vertebrae) gives pain referred to the front of the chest or abdomen, in the region of the peripheral termination of the nerves.
C(i) Pus from the region of the vertebral column tracks around the thorax along the neurovascular bundle and points at the three sites of exit of the cutaneous branches: lateral to erector spinae, in the midaxillary line and just lateral to the sternum.
C(i) A rib fracture is extremely painful because the periosteum of the rib is supplied by the intercostal nerves above and below the rib; the parietal pleura is segmentally supplied by the intercostal nerves, so pleural disease refers pain along the thoracic wall and anterior abdominal wall.
C(i) The deformity that follows injury of an intercostal nerve: not covered.
questions.question:
A(i) State the nature and number of the intercostal nerves and distinguish the typical from the atypical nerves.
A(ii) Describe the course and relations of a typical intercostal nerve.
A(iii) State its branches.
A(iv) Describe its distribution, including the cutaneous supply of the thoracic wall.
B(i) State the safe method and site for anaesthetising an intercostal space and for passing a needle or drain.
C(i) Explain the anatomical basis of the effects of irritation or injury of the intercostal nerves, including any deformity that follows injury.

A 3-week-old neonate presents with failure to pass meconium since birth, progressive abdominal distension, and bilious vomiting. The mother reports the baby has never had a normal stool. Rectal examination reveals a tight sphincter and an explosive gush of stool and gas on withdrawal of the finger.
(i) What is the most likely diagnosis?
(ii) What is the histological basis of this condition?
(iii) Which plexuses are absent, and what functional consequence does their absence produce?
(iv) What other disease, caused by a protozoan, produces a similar injury to these plexuses?
(v) What is the nature of the definitive surgical treatment implied?
questions.answerText:
(i) Hirschsprung disease (congenital aganglionic megacolon).
(ii) The condition is caused by absence or severely injured plexuses in parts or all of the large intestine.
(iii) The submucosal (Meissner) plexus and the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus are absent or severely injured. Their absence disturbs the tract's motility and produces dilation in some areas, resulting in difficulty passing stool.
(iv) Chagas disease / trypanosomiasis, caused by the protozoan Trypanosoma cruzi, can also destroy the enteric plexuses.
(v) The definitive treatment is surgical correction by removal of the aganglionic segment; further operative detail is not covered here.

questions.question:
Describe the popliteal artery and its branches, stating the safe site for popliteal pulse palpation, and explain the anatomical basis of the deformity and functional deficit after tibial nerve injury in the popliteal fossa.
A(i) Origin, course, and relations of the popliteal artery
A(ii) All branches of the popliteal artery — genicular and muscular
B(i) Termination and continuation of the popliteal artery into the leg and foot
B(ii) Safe site for popliteal pulse palpation and clinical technique
C(i) Anatomical basis of the deformity and functional deficit after tibial nerve injury in the popliteal fossa
questions.answerText:
A(i) The popliteal artery is the continuation of the femoral artery; it begins when the femoral artery passes through the adductor hiatus. It descends through the fossa, passing inferolaterally and is the deepest structure in the fossa — it runs in close proximity to the articular capsule of the knee joint. It terminates at the inferior border of the popliteus by dividing into the anterior and posterior tibial arteries.
A(ii) Five genicular branches participate in the genicular anastomosis (a network of vessels surrounding the knee providing collateral circulation capable of maintaining blood supply to the leg during full knee flexion): superior lateral genicular artery, superior medial genicular artery, middle genicular artery (penetrates the fibrous capsule and supplies the cruciate ligaments, synovial membrane, and peripheral margins of the menisci), inferior lateral genicular artery, and inferior medial genicular artery. Muscular branches supply the hamstring, gastrocnemius, soleus, and plantaris muscles. The superior muscular branches have clinically important anastomoses with the terminal part of the profunda femoris and gluteal arteries.
B(i) Termination: the popliteal artery divides into the anterior tibial artery and the tibioperoneal trunk; the tibioperoneal trunk divides into the posterior tibial artery and fibular (peroneal) artery. Anterior tibial artery: passes anterior to the interosseous membrane between tibia and fibula; supplies muscles of anterior compartment; continues as the dorsalis pedis artery in the foot, supplying tarsal bones and dorsal metatarsals, and anastomoses with the lateral plantar artery to form the deep plantar arch. Posterior tibial artery: continues inferiorly along surface of deep posterior leg muscles; enters the sole of the foot via the tarsal tunnel; splits into lateral and medial plantar arteries supplying the plantar foot.
B(ii) The popliteal artery is the hardest pulse to find, lying deep in the popliteal fossa; it requires deep palpation. To make it easier, the patient should slightly flex the leg — this relaxes the fascia around the popliteal fossa. An aneurysm of the popliteal artery can be detected by an obvious palpable pulsation in the popliteal fossa; an arterial bruit may be heard on auscultation.
C(i) The tibial nerve is the medial and larger branch of the sciatic nerve and the most superficial of the neurovascular bundle. Injury causes: paralysis of flexor muscles in the leg and intrinsic muscles in the sole of the foot; inability to plantarflex the ankles or flex the toes; and loss of sensation on the sole of the foot. The resulting deformity is a calcaneovalgus posture — unopposed dorsiflexion with loss of plantarflexion, the foot assuming a dorsiflexed position because the antagonist muscles remain intact. Weakened or absent plantarflexion and paraesthesia of the foot and posterolateral leg are the major features of tibial nerve compression.

(i) Receptive aphasia from a lesion of Wernicke's area (area 22 and parieto-occipito-temporal gyrus, area 39), which is concerned with the comprehension of spoken and written language.
(ii) Most components of the language system are in the dominant hemisphere (left in most people); the language areas involve both execution and comprehension of speech.
- Primary auditory area: transverse temporal gyri (areas 41, 42) within the lateral fissure; receives fibres from the medial geniculate body; the surrounding area 22 is the association area.
- Broca's area (motor speech area): inferior frontal gyrus (areas 44, 45) of the dominant hemisphere; receives input from Wernicke's area; lesions cause expressive aphasia.
- Major association cortex: supramarginal and angular gyri of the inferior parietal lobe; connected with all the sensory cortical areas; functions in higher order, complex multisensory perception.
questions.question:
A patient with a lesion in the posterior part of the temporal lobe (area 22) and the parieto-occipito-temporal gyrus (area 39) of the dominant hemisphere has impaired comprehension of spoken and written language.
(i) Give the diagnosis and name the cortical area involved.
(ii) Explain the pathophysiology: the language system, the related cortical areas and the effect of a lesion of the connected motor speech area.

A 19-year-old man falls onto an outstretched hand while playing basketball and now has wrist pain.
(i) What are the risk factors for this injury?
(ii) What are the complications of this injury?
(iii) What management options are available?
(iv) Justify the urgency of management for this fracture.
questions.answerText:
(i) A fractured scaphoid is more common in the younger population; it typically results from a blow to the wrist, such as falling onto an outstretched hand, when the scaphoid takes most of the force.
(ii) The scaphoid has a unique blood supply, which runs distal to proximal; a fracture can disrupt the blood supply to the proximal portion. Failure to revascularise the scaphoid can lead to avascular necrosis and future arthritis for the patient.
(iii) Not covered, beyond the statement that immediate clinical attention to the fracture is needed.
(iv) Because the scaphoid's blood supply runs from distal to proximal, a fracture can cut off supply to the proximal fragment; this is described as an emergency, since failure to revascularise leads to avascular necrosis and subsequent arthritis — justifying urgent attention rather than delay.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the size, shape, position, base, apex, surfaces and borders of the heart.
A(ii) Describe the surface marking of the heart.
A(iii) Describe the chambers and valves of the heart.
A(iv) Describe the conducting system of the heart.
A(v) Describe the blood supply, venous drainage and nerve supply of the heart.
B(i) Relate the arterial supply and structure of the heart to common cardiac pathologies.
C(i) Explain how disease of the heart coverings and neighbouring structures may cause pain or disturbance in a distant structure.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Shape of a clenched fist; base to apex 12 cm in males and 10 cm in females, anteroposterior 6 cm and 5 cm, transverse 9 cm and 8 cm; weight 280-340 g in males and 230-280 g in females; lies behind the body of the sternum, in front of T5-T8, with a base, an apex, 3 surfaces and 4 borders.
A(i) Base: posterior, mostly left atrium, receives the 4 pulmonary veins; ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk emerge from it; separated from the diaphragmatic surface by the coronary sulcus. Apex: inferolateral, mostly left ventricle, behind the 5th left intercostal space. Surfaces: sternocostal (mostly right ventricle), diaphragmatic (concave), pulmonary (left ventricle, fitting the cardiac notch of the left lung). Borders: right (right atrium), left (mostly left ventricle with the left auricle), superior (auricles and upper right ventricle), inferior (right atrium and right ventricle).
A(ii) Right border: 3rd to 6th right costal cartilage; left border: 5th left intercostal space (apex beat, 9 cm from the midline) up to the 2nd costal cartilage; superior border: 2nd left to 3rd right costal cartilage; inferior border: 6th right costal cartilage to the 5th left intercostal space.
A(iii) Four chambers: atria separated by the interatrial septum, ventricles by the interventricular septum, atria from ventricles by the right and left coronary (AV) sulci. Right atrium: forms the right border, lies between SVC and IVC, has the right auricle; rough part (musculi pectinati) and smooth part (from the right horn of the sinus venosus) separated by the sulcus terminalis (crista terminalis); receives SVC, IVC and coronary sinus.
A(iii) Right ventricle: forms the sternocostal and diaphragmatic surfaces and inferior border; trabeculae carneae including the septomarginal trabecula (carries part of the AV bundle) and anterior, posterior and septal papillary muscles joined by chordae tendineae to the tricuspid valve (3 cusps, admits 3 fingertips), the chordae preventing the cusps being driven into the right atrium; pulmonary orifice about 2.5 cm with 3 semilunar cusps (anterior, left, right).
A(iii) Left atrium: posterior, forms the base, receives 4 valveless pulmonary veins; left auricle forms the upper left border; smooth wall except the auricle. Mitral (bicuspid) valve: anterior and posterior cusps, admits 2 fingertips, overlaps the tricuspid and lies slightly higher. Left ventricle: aortic orifice about 2.5 cm at the right upper part with 3 semilunar cusps (posterior, right, left); numerous trabeculae carneae; anterior and posterior papillary muscles with chordae to the mitral valve.
A(iv) SA node: natural pacemaker, first conducting cell, below the opening of the SVC in the right atrium, contains pacemaker P-cells, autonomic supply from the cardiac plexus (sympathetics increase and parasympathetics decrease the rate of impulse generation). AV node: slow conducting tissue in the posterior and inferior interatrial septum, allows complete atrial contraction before ventricular contraction. AV bundle of His: Purkinje fibres in the membranous part of the interventricular septum, the only bridge between atrial and ventricular muscle; right branch to papillary muscles and moderator band, left branch to the left papillary muscles.
A(v) Arteries: right and left coronary arteries from the ascending aorta run in the right and left AV sulci; the right gives posterior interventricular and marginal arteries, the left gives anterior interventricular and circumflex arteries (the circumflex gives a marginal branch). Veins: the coronary sinus (posterior part of the AV sulcus, valve at its opening, empties into the right atrium) receives the great, small and middle cardiac veins, posterior vein of the left ventricle and oblique vein of the left atrium; the anterior cardiac vein opens into the right atrium and venae cordis minimae open into the chambers. Nerve supply: cardiac plexus.
B(i) The heart has a poor anastomotic network, so blockage of one coronary artery (coronary thrombosis) leads to myocardial infarction; the heart wall has 3 layers (epicardium, myocardium, endocardium) and the serous pericardium receives the coronary arteries.
B(i) Angina pectoris: chest pain originating from the heart, caused by insufficient supply of oxygen to the heart muscle.
C(i) Irritation of the pleura or pericardium covering the central part of the diaphragm is referred to the shoulder, because the central diaphragm is supplied by the phrenic nerve (C3-5) and the shoulder skin by the supraclavicular nerve (C3,4); the fibrous and parietal pericardium are supplied by the phrenic nerve.
C(i) Hiccup: involuntary spasmodic contraction of the diaphragm with approximation of the vocal folds and closure of the glottis; it may be due to pleurisy, peritonitis or pericarditis.

questions.question:
A pathology student viewing a histology slide sees hexagonal units of liver tissue with a central lumen and portal tracts at the corners; the portal tracts each contain three tubular structures. Blood flows from the periphery towards the centre.
(i) Identify the lobule model being described, and name and describe the three structures visible in each portal tract.
(ii) Explain the direction of bile flow in relation to blood flow in the classic hepatic lobule model, using the pathway described.
(iii) If the student switched to the portal lobule model, how would the geometric arrangement and the reference points change?
(iv) Using the hepatic acinus model, which zone would be most vulnerable to ischaemic (hypoxic) injury, and why?
(v) Describe the hepatic portal system, tracing the route of nutrient-rich blood from the small intestine to the general circulation.
questions.answerText:
(i) Classic (hepatic) lobule model.
- Arranged as hexagons, with the central vein (CV) in the centre of the lobule and portal tracts (PTs) at the periphery (corners of the hexagon).
- Three structures in each portal tract: hepatic artery (HA), portal vein (PV), and bile duct (BD). Blood enters the liver via the portal vein and hepatic artery, drains into the central vein, and exits the liver via the hepatic vein to the IVC.
(ii) Bile flow is in the opposite direction to blood flow. Blood flows from the portal tracts (periphery) towards the central vein. Bile flows from hepatocytes into bile canaliculi → canals of Hering → bile ductules → interlobular bile ducts → intrahepatic ducts → right and left hepatic ducts → common hepatic duct → joins with cystic duct to form common bile duct → duodenum (i.e., from the centre outward towards the portal tracts, opposite to blood flow).
(iii) Portal lobule model: organised as triangles (not hexagons), with a portal tract at the centre of the lobule and central veins at the periphery (corners of the triangle). The geometric shape is a triangle; the reference points are inverted compared to the classic lobule.
(iv) Zone 3 of the hepatic acinus (acinus of Rappaport) would be most vulnerable to ischaemic injury because it receives the least oxygenated blood and the fewest nutrients, being farthest from the portal tracts (short axis corners).
(v) Hepatic portal system:
1. The small intestine absorbs products of digestion.
2. Nutrient molecules travel in the hepatic portal vein to the liver.
3. The liver monitors blood content.
4. Blood enters general circulation by way of the hepatic vein.

questions.question:
Describe the gross anatomy of the developing external and middle ear, including the tubotympanic recess.
State how its parts relate to the anomalies that can occur in this region.
Explain how disease may spread to affect a distant structure and cause a functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
Gross anatomy: the ventral part of the first pharyngeal pouch obliterates with the formation of the tongue.
The dorsal part of the first pouch receives a contribution from the dorsal part of the second pouch to form the tubotympanic recess.
The recess comes into contact with the epithelium of the first pharyngeal cleft to form the external auditory meatus, and the epithelial lining of the meatus contributes to the formation of the tympanic membrane.
The distal portion of the recess widens to form the tympanic (middle ear) cavity, and the proximal portion narrows to form the Eustachian (auditory) tube; the lining of the tympanic cavity also contributes to the tympanic membrane.
The ventral part of the second pharyngeal pouch forms the palatine tonsil, and its dorsal part joins the dorsal part of the first pouch to form the external auditory meatus.
Only the first of the four clefts of a five-week embryo contributes to a definitive structure: its dorsal part forms the external auditory meatus, while its ventral part disappears.
Zones/parts relating to anomalies: preauricular fistulas are described in the same region as the external auditory meatus, alongside the lateral cervical cysts and fistulas and the internal and external branchial fistulas that arise from persistence of pharyngeal cleft/pouch remnants.
Because the external auditory meatus and tympanic membrane derive jointly from the first pharyngeal cleft and the tubotympanic recess (itself formed from the first and second pouches), anomalies in this region cluster around this shared junction.
Spread to a distant structure causing a functional deficit: not covered.
No mechanism by which disease of the ear region spreads to affect a distant structure is described.
the coverage of this region is limited to the developmental origin of the meatus, tympanic membrane, middle ear cavity and Eustachian tube, and the palatine tonsil from the second pouch.
Beyond naming preauricular fistulas in this region, no further pathological detail is given.

questions.question:
A patient presents with inability to concentrate urine. Investigations show normal glomerular filtration but defective generation of the medullary concentration gradient. A renal biopsy shows that the long loops of Henle and their associated thin-walled blood vessels in the medulla are abnormal.
(i) Identify the type of nephrons and the specific blood vessels that are abnormal in this patient, 's description.
(ii) Describe the vasa recta — their origin, course, and function —.
(iii) Explain the difference between the ascending limbs of cortical and juxtamedullary nephrons.
(iv) Describe the role of the collecting duct in delivering the final urine product, tracing urine from the collecting duct to the ureter.
(v) 's account, identify which renal function would be most directly impaired by failure to concentrate urine, and name the endocrine product of the kidney that indirectly supports water balance via red cell mass.
questions.answerText:
(i) Abnormal structures:
- Juxtamedullary nephrons (with long nephron loops that deeply invade the medulla).
- Vasa recta (long, thin-walled vessels parallel to the long nephron loops of juxtamedullary nephrons).
(ii) Vasa recta:
- Origin: arise from the efferent arterioles serving juxtamedullary nephrons (instead of peritubular capillaries).
- Course: long, thin-walled vessels parallel to the long nephron loops of juxtamedullary nephrons.
- Function: important in the formation of concentrated urine.
(iii) Ascending limbs:
- Cortical nephrons: the thick ascending limb is cuboidal to columnar; may be thin in some nephrons.
- Juxtamedullary nephrons: ascending limbs have both thick and thin segments (unlike cortical nephrons, which may only have a thick ascending limb).
(iv) Route from collecting duct to ureter:
- Collecting ducts receive filtrate from many nephrons.
- They run through medullary pyramids (giving them a striped appearance).
- They fuse together to deliver urine through papillae into minor calyces → major calyces → renal pelvis → ureter.
(v) Failure to concentrate urine most directly impairs the kidney's function of regulating total water volume and total solute concentration in water.
The endocrine product of the kidney that supports water balance indirectly via red cell mass is erythropoietin, which regulates red blood cell production; adequate RBC mass maintains oxygen delivery, supporting overall homeostasis. (The direct mediators of water concentration — ADH/vasopressin and aquaporins — are not further detailed.)

questions.question:
A newborn is noted to have a midline defect over the lower back involving failure of closure of the neural tube at its caudal end.
(i) What is the diagnosis?
(ii) What is the embryologic basis of this condition?
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: a posterior neuropore neural tube defect - spina bifida (occulta or cystica) or myeloschisis.
(ii) Embryologic basis: Neural Tube Defects are the major abnormalities of neurulation, resulting from failure of closure of the neuropores and the associated mesodermally derived structures. Defects of the posterior neuropore give spina bifida (occulta and cystica) and myeloschisis. Neural tube defects occur in about 1 in 1,000 births.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the origin and course of the corticospinal tract.
A(ii) Describe its distribution/termination.
C. Explain the anatomical basis of the deficit seen after injury to this tract.
questions.answerText:
A(i) The corticospinal tract arises majorly from areas 4 and 6 of the cortex (cells of layer V of the motor cortex), passing through the corona radiata and brain stem, with 80% decussating at the pyramidal decussation in the medulla to form the lateral corticospinal tract in the lateral funiculus; uncrossed fibres remain as the anterior corticospinal tract in the anterior funiculus, crossing later in the spinal cord (the tract of Barne's never crosses, about 2%).
A(ii) The tract is for precision and skill of voluntary movements, especially fine finger movements of the extremities; over 50% of fibres synapse with anterior horn cells of the cervical segment, while the lumbosacral region receives about 25%.
C. Lesions of the corticospinal tract result in paralysis, contralateral or ipsilateral, along with upper motor neuron signs: spasticity, hyperactive reflexes, Babinski sign and clonus.

questions.question:
Describe the nerve supply of the fourth and sixth pharyngeal arches, including the named branches involved.
State the safe site for a procedure involving these nerves.
Explain the anatomical basis of the deformity following injury to one of these nerves.
questions.answerText:
Origin: the fourth and sixth pharyngeal arches are supplied by the 10th cranial nerve (vagus).
Distribution: the vagus supplies the fourth arch via the superior laryngeal nerve, and the sixth arch via the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
The skeletal elements of the fourth and sixth arches (cartilages that fuse to form the thyroid, cricoid, arytenoid, corniculate and cuneiform cartilages of the larynx) lie in the territory of these nerves.
The fourth arch muscles supplied include cricothyroid, levator palatini and the constrictor muscles of the pharynx; the sixth arch muscles are the intrinsic muscles of the larynx.
Course: not covered beyond the named branch supplying each arch.
Safe site for a procedure: not covered.
Anatomical basis of the deformity after injury: not covered.
What is stated is limited to which branch of the vagus supplies which arch, and the muscles each arch's derivatives contain.
No description of the relations of these nerves to the great vessels, thyroid gland, or larynx is given.
No account of voice or airway deformity following injury to either nerve is provided.
the coverage of arch 4 and 6 nerves is therefore restricted to naming and to the muscle groups they supply.
Further anatomical or clinical detail on these nerves would need to be sourced elsewhere.

(i) Flail chest (stove-in chest): a whole segment of the thoracic cage is torn free after several ribs fracture in front and behind; injuries involving multiple ribs result in flail chest.
(ii) Ribs may be fractured by direct violence or indirectly by crushing injuries; in a crush injury the rib tends to give way at its weakest part, the angle.
(ii) The flail segment is sucked in during inspiration and pushed out during expiration (paradoxical respiratory movement); the associated swinging movements of the mediastinum produce severe shock.
(ii) The upper two ribs (protected by the clavicle) and the lower two ribs (unattached, so they swing free) are the least commonly injured.
(ii) The chest wall of a child is highly elastic, so rib fractures in children are rare.
(iii) Urgent treatment: insertion of a chest drain with underwater seal.
(iv) Definitive treatment: endotracheal intubation, or tracheostomy, combined with positive pressure respiration.
(v) A fractured rib may penetrate the lung and produce pneumothorax, or may damage upper abdominal organs.
(v) A fractured rib is extremely painful because the periosteum of the rib is supplied by the intercostal nerves above and below the rib.
questions.question:
An adult sustains a severe crush injury to the chest. Several ribs are fractured both in front and behind, a segment of the chest wall is sucked in with each inspiration and blown out with each expiration, and there are swinging movements of the mediastinum with severe shock.
(i) State the diagnosis.
(ii) Explain the pathological basis of this injury, including the part of the rib that tends to give way, the ribs least commonly injured and why, and why rib fractures are rare in children.
(iii) State the immediate (urgent) management.
(iv) State the definitive treatment that follows.
(v) State the other complications that a fractured rib may cause and explain why a rib fracture is extremely painful.

A 28-year-old woman presents with chronic diarrhoea, weight loss, iron-deficiency anaemia, and bloating after eating wheat products. Jejunal biopsy shows blunting and loss of the mucosal projections normally responsible for surface amplification.
(i) What is the diagnosis, and how is this condition described histologically?
(ii) Describe the three levels of surface amplification normally present in the small intestine, including the quantitative contribution of each to total surface area increase.
(iii) Name all five cell types of the intestinal epithelium, and for each state its key function.
(iv) What is the total absorptive area produced by all three surface amplifications working together, and how many microvilli does each absorptive cell carry?
(v) Name the other two conditions affecting the small intestine described and describe each briefly.
questions.answerText:
(i) Celiac disease — a disorder of the small intestine mucosa that causes malabsorption and can lead to damage or destruction of the villi.
(ii) Three levels of surface amplification:
- Plicae circulares (valves of Kirkring): permanent circular or semilunar folds of mucosa and submucosa; best developed in the jejunum; increase the intestinal surface three-fold.
- Villi: finger-like or leaf-like projections of the mucosa (leaf-shaped in the duodenum, becoming finger-like toward the ileum); increase surface 10-fold.
- Microvilli of the striated (brush) border: each absorptive cell has an average of 3,000 microvilli; 1 mm2 of mucosa contains about 200 million microvilli; increase surface 20-fold.
Together these three processes are responsible for a 600-fold increase in intestinal surface.
(iii) Five cell types:
1. Enterocytes/absorptive cells: tall columnar cells; absorb nutrient molecules; also synthesize digestive enzymes located on the membrane of the striated border.
2. Goblet cells: produce glycoprotein mucins hydrated to form mucus — protect and lubricate the lining; more numerous in the ileum.
3. Paneth cells: exocrine cells located in the basal portion of intestinal crypts; release lysozymes, phospholipase A2, and defensins; function in innate immunity and regulate the microenvironment of the intestinal crypts.
4. Enteroendocrine cells: secrete various peptide hormones controlling peristalsis, regulation of secretions for digestion, and sense of satiation.
5. Stem cells: give rise to all other cell types.
(iv) Total absorptive area: 200 m2. Each absorptive cell carries an average of 3,000 microvilli.
(v)
- Leiomyomas: benign tumors of smooth muscle cells; the most common type of tumor in the stomach and small intestine.
- Crohn disease: chronic inflammatory bowel disease occurring most commonly in the ileum or colon; causes excessive lymphocytic activity and inflammation in any or all of the tract, producing pain, localized bleeding, malabsorption, and diarrhoea.

questions.question:
A skull radiograph of an adult over 40 years old shows a calcified, small, conical structure projecting from the posterior wall of the third ventricle, which radiologists use as an indicator of brain symmetry.
(i) Identify the structure and describe its position and attachments.
(ii) Name the neighbouring structures and the group of structures to which it belongs (affected structures).
(iii) Give the clinico-anatomical reasoning, including the function of the structure.
questions.answerText:
(i) Pineal gland: calcification is common after 40 years and is useful to radiologists as an indicator of brain symmetry.
- Small conical body projecting posteriorly from the posterior wall of the 3rd ventricle, above the superior colliculus; its stalk is attached to the posterior and habenular commissures; a pineal recess separates its proximal end.
(ii) The posterior wall of the 3rd ventricle tapers towards the midbrain; the pineal gland and pulvinar are superiorly related to the midbrain; the pia mater covering the superior surface of the thalamus extends as far back as the pineal gland.
- Habenular nuclei (triangular area anterior to the superior colliculus, receiving the stria medullaris), the pineal gland and the posterior commissure (cylindrical band of white matter anterior to the dorsal part of the cerebral aqueduct) constitute the epithalamus.
(iii) The pineal gland secretes melatonin, related to control of circadian rhythm and sleep induction.
- The epithalamus is the smallest and oldest part of the diencephalon, concerned with autonomic (respiratory and cardiovascular), endocrine (thyroid function) and reproductive functions.

A(i) A thin serous membrane lining the walls of the abdominal and pelvic cavities and covering the organs within; two layers: parietal and visceral.
A(ii) The cavity is the potential space between the layers, contains no organs and a thin layer of fluid, and is a closed sac in males; it is divided into greater and lesser sacs that communicate through the epiploic foramen.
A(ii) The fluid lubricates the surfaces so viscera move without friction, contains leukocytes and antibodies, and is absorbed by lymphatics on the inferior surface of the diaphragm.
A(iii) Provides a slippery surface for movement of viscera; phagocytic cells protect viscera; can store large amounts of fat.
A(iii) Mesothelial cells transform into fibroblasts, promoting healing; the mesothelium acts as a semi-permeable membrane.
A(iv) Intraperitoneal organs are completely surrounded (stomach, spleen, small intestine); retroperitoneal organs are covered partially on their anterior surfaces only (kidney, ureter).
B(i) In the female the cavity communicates with the exterior through the uterine tubes, uterus and vagina, a potential pathway of infection.
B(i) Because the mesothelium is semi-permeable, urea can be removed from blood by circulating fluids through the cavity: peritoneal dialysis.
C(i) Parietal: lines the inner surface of abdominal and pelvic walls and lower surface of diaphragm; loosely attached by extraperitoneal connective tissue; pain sensitive; nerve supply same as the overlying body wall.
C(i) Visceral: lines the outer surface of viscera; cannot be stripped; nerve supply is that of the underlying viscera (sympathetic), with receptors sensitive to overdistension, traction on mesenteries, spasm and ischaemia.
C(i) Blood supply: parietal from lumbar vessels, inferior and superior epigastric, musculophrenic and deep circumflex arteries;
C(i) Visceral from the arteries supplying the appropriate viscera.

(i) Portal hypertension: scarring and fibrosis from cirrhosis obstruct the portal vein in the liver, so pressure mounts in the portal vein and its tributaries.
(i) Portal circulation through the liver can be diminished or obstructed by liver disease or pressure from a tumor (intrahepatic or extrahepatic portal venous block).
(ii) Normally portal blood traverses the liver and drains to the IVC via the hepatic veins (direct route); other communications (alternative routes) let blood from the GIT reach the heart through the IVC.
(ii) This is possible because the portal vein and its tributaries have no valves, so blood can flow in a reverse direction; the volume forced through collaterals may be excessive, giving abnormally dilated veins (varices) that can be fatal.
(ii) Sites: lower third of oesophagus (left gastric veins with oesophageal veins to azygos: oesophageal varices); halfway down anal canal (superior rectal with middle and inferior rectal veins: haemorrhoids); anterior abdominal wall (paraumbilical with superficial epigastric veins: caput medusae); colic veins with retroperitoneal renal, lumbar and phrenic veins.
(iii) Portasystemic shunts reduce portal hypertension by diverting blood from the portal to the systemic venous system through a communication between the portal vein and the IVC.
(iii) Options: join the portal vein to the IVC; join the splenic vein to the left renal vein after splenectomy.
(iii) Justification: the splenic vein to left renal vein shunt is the option linked to splenectomy; criteria for choosing between shunts are not covered.
questions.question:
A patient with cirrhosis has scarring and fibrosis that obstruct the portal vein within the liver and pressure is rising in the portal vein and its tributaries.
(i) State the condition and the factors that can diminish or obstruct portal circulation through the liver.
(ii) Explain why blood can still reach the heart and the complications that follow, naming the sites of anastomosis.
(iii) State the surgical options to reduce the pressure and justify one.

Describe the radial nerve:
A(i) Origin and course in the arm
A(ii) Course/division in the cubital fossa and forearm
A(iii) Branches
A(iv) Distribution
C. Explain the anatomical basis of the deformity ("wrist drop") seen after radial nerve injury.
questions.answerText:
A(i) The radial nerve is a terminal branch of the posterior cord of the brachial plexus; it courses posteromedially with the axillary vessels and enters the posterior compartment of the arm under teres major, where it winds around the spiral (radial) groove of the humerus, accompanied by the profunda brachii artery.
A(ii) It pierces the lateral intermuscular septum to enter the anterior compartment of the arm, passes to the forearm at the level of the elbow joint, enters the cubital fossa, and there divides into a superficial and a deep branch.
The superficial branch courses toward the wrist lateral to the radial artery and enters the hand, dividing into dorsal digital cutaneous branches; the deep branch gives off the posterior interosseous nerve, which passes between the heads of supinator to enter the posterior compartment of the forearm and terminates near the wrist joint.
A(iii) Branches include muscular twigs in the arm to triceps brachii and anconeus, the posterior interosseous nerve to the forearm extensors, the superficial (cutaneous) branch, and articular twigs to the elbow and wrist joints.
A(iv) The deep branch/posterior interosseous nerve supplies the extensor muscles in the forearm as well as brachioradialis; the superficial branch supplies cutaneous sensation to the dorsal aspect of the hand, the dorsal aspect of the first to third digits, and the dorsolateral aspect of the fourth finger.
C. Injury to the radial nerve produces "wrist drop."
Because the nerve's deep branch/posterior interosseous nerve supplies the extensor muscles of the forearm, injury interrupts the motor supply to the wrist and finger extensors.
The nerve can be injured at any level — axilla, spiral groove, radial tunnel, posterior interosseous, or superficial radial.
Injury may result from fracture of the body (shaft) of the humerus, where the nerve lies in close contact with the bone in the spiral groove.
"Saturday Night Palsy" describes compression of the nerve in the axilla, such as from using improperly adjusted crutches, which similarly interrupts its motor function.
With the extensors paralysed and unopposed flexor tone at the wrist, the hand falls into flexion at the wrist, producing the characteristic wrist drop.

A(i) The oesophagus has four constrictions: at 15 cm (cricopharyngeus, upper oesophageal sphincter),
at 22.5 cm (crossed by the aortic arch) and 27.5 cm (crossed by the left main bronchus) from the upper incisor teeth,
and at 40 cm, where it passes through the right crus of the diaphragm (oesophageal hiatus).
A(ii) The upper oesophageal sphincter is an anatomical sphincter formed by the cricopharyngeus muscle at the pharyngo-oesophageal junction.
A(iii) The lower oesophageal sphincter is a physiological sphincter at the gastro-oesophageal junction with no true muscular thickening.
It is maintained by the acute angle of entry of the oesophagus into the stomach, compression of the intra-abdominal oesophagus by positive intra-abdominal pressure, prominent mucosal folds at the junction, and the pinch-cock effect of the right crus of the diaphragm.
B(i) The constrictions are clinically important because they are sites where swallowed foreign bodies commonly impact.
They are prone to trauma during instrumentation such as rigid oesophagoscopy.
They are common sites for stricture formation following ingestion of corrosive substances.
They are also common sites of oesophageal carcinoma.
C(i) The upper oesophageal sphincter is a true anatomical (muscular) sphincter formed by the cricopharyngeus, located at 15 cm from the incisor teeth.
The lower oesophageal sphincter is a physiological sphincter maintained by mechanical factors at the gastro-oesophageal junction and prevents gastric reflux, rather than a distinct muscular ring controlling food passage.
questions.question:
(A) Describe the oesophagus under the following headings: A(i) its four constrictions along its length A(ii) the upper oesophageal sphincter A(iii) the lower oesophageal sphincter.
(B) Explain the clinical basis of why the areas of constriction are important.
(C) Distinguish between the upper oesophageal sphincter and the lower oesophageal sphincter.

A 4-week-old male infant presents with projectile vomiting immediately after feeding. Examination reveals a palpable olive-shaped mass in the right upper quadrant. Ultrasound shows a thickened pyloric channel.
(i)considering the muscular layers of the stomach at the pylorus, explain the anatomical basis for this presentation.
(ii) Describe all three muscular layers of the stomach's muscularis, including the arrangement and orientation of each.
(iii) Describe the submucosa of the stomach.
(iv) Describe what happens to the stomach's rugae as the stomach fills, and explain what rugae are composed of.
(v) Describe how the enteroendocrine cells of the stomach pylorus contribute to the control of gastric secretion and motilityconsidering the cells found there and their secretion.
questions.answerText:
(i) At the pylorus, the middle (circular) layer of the stomach muscularis is greatly thickened to form the pyloric sphincter. Hypertrophy of this sphincter causes gastric outlet obstruction, producing projectile non-bilious vomiting in the infant.
(ii) Three muscular layers of the stomach muscularis:
- External layer: longitudinal.
- Middle layer: circular (greatly thickened at the pylorus to form the pyloric sphincter).
- Internal layer: oblique.
The muscularis is composed of three poorly delineated layers of smooth muscle fibers.
(iii) Submucosa of the stomach:
Composed of connective tissue containing large blood and lymph vessels; many lymphoid cells, macrophages, and mast cells.
(iv) Rugae are longitudinally directed folds of the mucosa and submucosa of the empty stomach; they flatten (disappear) when the stomach is full with food.
(v) In the pylorus, G cells (enteroendocrine cells) produce the peptide gastrin. Gastrin acts as one of the stimuli that activate parietal cells — stimulating secretory activity through paracrine release — thereby stimulating gastric acid secretion. Enteroendocrine cells in general, including those in the pylorus, represent part of the widely distributed diffuse neuroendocrine system and may exert paracrine (local) or endocrine effects including control of peristalsis, regulation of secretions necessary for food digestion, and sense of satiation.

A. The nasal sinuses are air-containing sacs lined by ciliated epithelium, communicating with the nasal cavity through narrow, easily occluded channels; they develop as outgrowths from the nasal cavity. There are 4 pairs: the maxillary antrum, sphenoid, frontal and ethmoid sinuses. The maxillary antrum and ethmoid sinuses are present in a rudimentary state at birth, while the rest become evident at about the 7th year of life. The lining of the sinuses is continuous with the nasal mucosa; their function is obscure, but they provide resonance to the voice, shape to the face, and some degree of warmth and humidification to inspired air. The paranasal sinuses are supplied by branches of the ophthalmic and maxillary nerves.
B. The frontal sinuses' posterosuperior wall lies adjacent to the frontal lobe of the brain, and their floor abuts the ethmoid cells, nasal fossa roof and orbit; infection here may cause a frontal lobe abscess, and fracture severe enough to tear the dura and pia-arachnoid causes CSF rhinorrhoea. The maxillary sinus (antrum) may become infected from the nasal cavity or from caries of the upper molar teeth, whose roots are separated from the sinus floor only by a thin, sometimes deficient, layer of bone. The ethmoid sinuses lie on each side of the cribriform plate, related above to the frontal lobes; infection (ethmoiditis) may result in a frontal cerebral abscess, and ethmoidal fracture may cause CSF leakage into the nasal cavity. The sphenoid sinuses lie within the body of the sphenoid and may extend laterally into the greater wing of the sphenoid or backward into the basal part of the occipital bone; each drains into the nasal cavity above the superior concha (the sphenoethmoidal recess).
C. Because the frontal and ethmoid sinuses are directly related anatomically to the frontal lobes of the brain (posterosuperior wall of the frontal sinus, and the region above the cribriform plate for the ethmoid sinuses), infection at either site can spread directly to produce a frontal lobe or frontal cerebral abscess; and because fracture of either sinus, if severe enough to tear the dura and pia-arachnoid, places the subarachnoid space in communication with the nasal cavity, CSF rhinorrhoea (leakage of CSF into the nose) results, sometimes even on the contralateral side since the sinuses may communicate with one another.
questions.question:
A. Describe the gross anatomy of the paranasal sinuses under the following headings: the four pairs of sinuses, their development, and their general function.
B. State how each of the paranasal sinuses relates to a specific clinical complication when infected or fractured.
C. Explain why disease of the paranasal sinuses can spread to produce a functional deficit in a distant structure, namely the brain or the nasal cavity.

questions.answerText:
A(i) The anterior branch of the abdominal aorta supplying the midgut; it arises immediately below the celiac artery, anterior to the lower part of vertebra LI.
A(ii) It is crossed anteriorly by the splenic vein and the neck of the pancreas; posterior to it are the left renal vein, the uncinate process of the pancreas and the inferior part of the duodenum.
A(ii) The middle colic artery arises as it emerges from beneath the pancreas.
A(iii) First branch: inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery, dividing into anterior and posterior branches that anastomose with the superior pancreaticoduodenal arteries.
A(iii) Left side: numerous jejunal and ileal arteries passing between the two layers of the mesentery to form arcades, whose number increases distally.
A(iii) Vasa recta: long, close together and narrow windows in the jejunum; short, far apart and low broad windows in the ileum.
A(iii) Right side: middle colic (transverse mesocolon; anastomoses with left colic), right colic (inconsistent, retroperitoneal) and ileocolic arteries.
A(iii) The ileocolic divides into superior and inferior branches; the inferior gives colic, cecal, appendicular (in the mesoappendix free margin) and ileal branches.
A(iv) Midgut: duodenum below the major papilla, jejunum, ileum, cecum, appendix, ascending colon and right two-thirds of the transverse colon.
A(iv) The midgut ends at the junction of the proximal two-thirds and distal one-third of the transverse colon.
B(i) The safe site for a procedure on it is not covered.
C(i) The deformity after its injury is not covered.

questions.question:
Describe the gross anatomy of the placenta, including its fetal and maternal components.
State how attachment site/depth relates to the placental pathologies that can occur.
Explain how disease of the placenta may spread to affect a distant structure and cause a functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
Gross anatomy: the placenta is the first site of nutrient and gas exchange between the mother and the fetus.
It also transmits maternal antibodies (e.g. IgG) and produces hormones (e.g. progesterone, estriol, somatomammotropin).
It is a fetomaternal organ composed of two components: a fetal portion, from the chorionic sac, called the chorion frondosum, and a maternal portion, from the endometrium, called the decidua basalis.
Attachment relating to pathology: placenta previa (complete) describes the placenta lying over the external os of the uterus, in contrast to the normal placental attachment site.
Placenta accreta describes abnormal attachment extending into the myometrium, while placenta percreta describes attachment penetrating through to the perimetrium, based on the labelled uterine wall layers (endometrium, myometrium, perimetrium).
Other listed clinical correlates of the placenta include placenta as an allograft, the placental barrier, erythroblastosis fetalis and fetal hydrops.
Spread to a distant structure causing a functional deficit: crossing of the placental barrier by diethylstilbestrol caused carcinoma of the vagina and testicular abnormalities in individuals exposed during intrauterine life, the clearest instance of a substance crossing the placenta to affect a distant structure.
Viruses such as rubella, CMV, coxsackie, variola, varicella, measles and poliomyelitis virus, and drugs such as heroin and cocaine, are also listed as crossing the placental barrier, with heroin and cocaine noted to cause habituation in the fetus.
Beyond naming these agents and their stated effects, no further mechanism of spread to a distant fetal structure is described.
Umbilical cord abnormalities are also listed, such as the cord encircling the fetal neck, which is usually not lethal but, if short, can detach the placenta from its attachment.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the gross histology of bone under the following headings: chemical composition and properties, cell types and their functions, and types of bone.
A(ii) State how the Haversian system (osteon) is organised and relate this to bone function.
B(i) Explain how blood calcium levels are regulated through bone, naming the hormones involved and their actions.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Chemical composition and properties: Bone is a connective tissue mineralized by calcium phosphate in the form of crystals very similar to hydroxyapatite. The minerals are both in the type I collagen fibers (which constitute about 95% of the matrix) and in the ground substance. Bone is both resilient and hard. Its resilience is due to the organic matter (collagen); its hardness is due to the inorganic minerals (calcium phosphate, calcium carbonate, calcium fluoride, calcium hydroxide, and citrate). Cell types: Osteocytes — maintain calcium and phosphate ion levels in the blood, are essentially stress sensors, and are osteoblasts that have been trapped in their own matrix in lacunae. Osteoblasts — synthesize the organic matrix (osteoid). Osteoclasts — multinucleated giant cells involved in resorption and remodeling of bone; they are also chondrocytes during bone healing and remodeling. Osteoid is the matrix secreted by osteoblasts and osteocytes prior to mineralization. Types of bone: compact bone (also called dense bone, cortical bone, or lamellar bone) and spongy bone (also called cancellous bone, trabecular bone, and medullary bone).
A(ii) Compact bone is organized into structures called osteons or Haversian systems: concentric lamellae surrounding a central canal called the Haversian canal, which contains blood vessels, nerves, loose connective tissue, and endosteum. Between lamellae are lacunae, each with one osteocyte interconnected by canaliculi containing the cells' dendritic processes. Canals called Volkmann's canals link Haversian canals with one another and with the marrow cavity. Metabolic exchanges between osteocytes and blood capillaries depend on communication through the canaliculi.
B(i) Blood calcium levels are regulated by the hormones parathormone (parathyroid hormone), which raises blood calcium levels by stimulating bone resorption, and calcitonin, which reduces blood calcium by suppressing bone resorption and increasing osteoid calcification.

questions.question:
A child of a mother who consumed alcohol chronically in early pregnancy has pre- and postnatal growth deficiency, microcephaly, short palpebral fissures, a short nose with a low bridge, decreased philtrum and congenital heart disease.
(i) Give the diagnosis.
(ii) State the predisposing factors.
(iii) Explain the pathophysiology.
(iv) State the management.
questions.answerText:
(i) Fetal alcohol syndrome (FAS), defined in 1970 as a combination of malformations.
(i) Other features: mental retardation, maxillary hypoplasia, microphthalmia, narrow upper lip.
(ii) Chronic alcohol consumption during early pregnancy; moderate maternal consumption may produce fetal alcohol effects (FAE), with behavioural and learning difficulties in children.
(iii) The CNS is particularly sensitive to alcohol; the placenta is an imperfect barrier and small non-polar molecules cross easily.
(iii) A teratogen acts during a specific window of development; the principles of teratology include critical periods and a dose-response relationship.
(iv) Management is not covered.

A(i) The most common sites of ulnar nerve entrapment around the elbow are: above the elbow, in the region of the intermuscular septum; the medial epicondylar region; the epicondylar (ulnar) groove; the region of the cubital tunnel; and the point where the nerve exits from flexor carpi ulnaris, where the usual cause of compression is the deep flexor-pronator aponeurosis.
A(ii) Medially, in relation to the elbow joint, the ulnar nerve passes behind the medial epicondyle and crosses the medial collateral ligament of the joint.
B. The medial epicondyle of the humerus bears a groove on its posterior aspect specifically for the ulnar nerve, and the medial epicondyle is the larger of the two epicondyles, extending more distally.
This places the ulnar nerve in a relatively superficial, subcutaneous position as it passes behind the medial epicondyle and through the cubital tunnel region, making it vulnerable to direct trauma and to compression at each of the sites listed above.
Ulnar nerve injuries are recognised as a distinct item of applied anatomy at the elbow, alongside subluxation/dislocation of the radial head, the carrying angle, olecranon bursitis, avulsion of the medial epicondyle, and dislocation with Volkmann's ischaemic contracture.
C. The ulnar nerve's entrapment region at the elbow lies behind the medial epicondyle of the humerus, where it crosses the medial collateral ligament of the elbow joint, and where compression is often caused by the deep flexor-pronator aponeurosis as the nerve exits between the heads of flexor carpi ulnaris.
The median nerve's tunnel at the wrist, the carpal tunnel, differs in that it has a defined bony floor — the carpal sulcus, bounded laterally by the scaphoid and trapezium and medially by the hook of hamate and pisiform — roofed by the fibrous flexor retinaculum.
The carpal tunnel additionally transmits eight flexor tendons and the tendon of flexor pollicis longus alongside the median nerve, whereas other tendons sharing the ulnar nerve's entrapment site at the elbow are not described.
Both regions, however, are sites where a single major nerve is placed in a confined space adjacent to bone, predisposing it to compression.
At the elbow, injury or entrapment of the ulnar nerve is associated with claw hand and sensory/motor deficits in the ulnar nerve distribution of the hand and forearm.
At the wrist, compression of the median nerve within the carpal tunnel produces carpal tunnel syndrome, with sensory disturbance in the lateral three and a half digits and weakness of the thenar muscles.
The comparison illustrates a shared anatomical principle, nerve entrapment at a narrow passage, applied to two different nerves at two different levels of the upper limb.
questions.question:
Describe the region of the ulnar nerve at the elbow:
A(i) Common sites of entrapment
A(ii) Relation to the elbow joint
B. Explain the clinical basis for the ulnar nerve being vulnerable at the elbow.
C. Distinguish between the ulnar nerve's entrapment region at the elbow and the median nerve's carpal tunnel at the wrist.

questions.answerText:
(i) The diagnosis is an intracapsular fracture of the neck of femur. The most critical vascular complication is avascular necrosis of the head of femur (HOF), because the medial femoral circumflex artery (MFCA) wraps around the posterior side of the femur supplying its neck and head and is easily damaged in a fracture of the femoral neck.
(ii) Predisposing factors include osteoporosis (weakened bone), advanced age, and female sex. The femoral neck is intracapsular; the capsule attaches laterally to the intertrochanteric line. The blood supply to the head travels along the neck intracapsularly, primarily from the medial femoral circumflex artery which is a branch of the profunda femoris. Disruption of these retinacular vessels at the time of fracture interrupts the blood supply, leading to ischaemia and avascular necrosis.
(iii) Complications include avascular necrosis of the head, non-union of the fracture, coxa vara (which follows fracture of the neck of femur), deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, pressure sores, and pneumonia from prolonged immobility.
(iv) Surgical options include dynamic hip screw fixation (for undisplaced fractures in younger patients) and hemiarthroplasty or total hip replacement (for displaced fractures in elderly patients). In this elderly osteoporotic patient with a displaced intracapsular fracture, hemiarthroplasty is preferred because the high risk of avascular necrosis and non-union with internal fixation makes joint replacement more reliable, restoring earlier mobilisation and reducing mortality from prolonged immobility.
questions.question:
A 62-year-old man with a history of osteoporosis trips and falls. Radiograph shows a fracture of the femoral neck (intracapsular). On examination the limb is shortened, externally rotated, and abducted.
(i) State the diagnosis and identify the most critical vascular complication.
(ii) What are the predisposing factors and pathophysiological basis of the complication?

Describe the axilla under the following headings:
A(i) Shape and apex
A(ii) Base
A(iii) Walls
A(iv) Contents
B. Explain the clinical basis for the axillary vein being particularly vulnerable to injury in this region.
C. Distinguish between the quadrangular space and the triangular interval found in the posterior wall of the axilla.
questions.answerText:
A(i) The axilla is a pyramid-shaped space between the upper part of the arm and the side of the upper chest; its apex is the cervicoaxillary canal, bounded by the 1st rib, clavicle, and superior edge of the scapula, forming the passageway between the neck and axilla.
A(ii) The base is formed by concave skin, subcutaneous tissue, and the axillary (deep) fascia.
A(iii) Anterior wall: pectoralis major and minor, subclavius, and clavipectoral fascia. Posterior wall: scapula and subscapularis above, teres major and latissimus dorsi below. Medial wall: upper ribs, intercostal muscles, and serratus anterior. Lateral wall: narrow and bony, formed by the intertubercular groove of the humerus.
A(iv) Contents: the axillary artery and its branches, the axillary vein and its tributaries, the infraclavicular part of the brachial plexus, axillary lymph nodes, and loose areolar/adipose tissue, all enclosed with the plexus in the axillary sheath.
B. The axillary vein is large and lies in an exposed, superficial position within the axilla.
Wounds to the axilla therefore often involve the axillary vein because of its large size and exposed position.
A wound to the proximal part of the axillary vein is especially dangerous because of the risk of air entering the vessel (air embolism).
C. The quadrangular space lies in the posterior wall of the axilla and transmits the axillary nerve and the posterior circumflex humeral artery and vein.
The triangular interval also lies in the posterior wall and transmits the radial nerve and the profunda brachii artery.
Both spaces are related to the long head of triceps brachii and the teres major muscle in their boundaries.
The quadrangular space thus carries the nerve/vessels supplying the deltoid and teres minor region, while the triangular interval carries those continuing into the posterior compartment of the arm.
This distinction explains why injury near the surgical neck of the humerus threatens the axillary nerve, whereas injury lower down at the spiral groove threatens the radial nerve instead.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe connective tissue under the following headings: definition and function, major constituent and its components, classification.
A(ii) Explain the clinical basis of edema in connective tissue.
B(i) Distinguish between loose connective tissue and dense connective tissue, giving two examples of each.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Definition and function: Connective tissue derives its name from its function in connecting or binding cells and tissues; it maintains the form of organs throughout the body. Unlike other tissue types (epithelium, muscle, nerve) which consist mainly of cells, the major constituent of connective tissue is the extracellular matrix. The extracellular matrix is composed of protein fibers (collagen, elastic, and reticular fibers), ground substance (a jelly-like, amorphous, anionic, hydrophilic complex of proteoglycans, glycosaminoglycans, and multiadhesive glycoproteins such as laminin and fibronectin), and tissue fluid. Classification: connective tissue is classified as connective tissue proper (loose: areolar, adipose, reticular; dense: regular, irregular, elastic) and specialized connective tissue (blood, cartilage, bone).
A(ii) The amount of tissue fluid (interstitial fluid) is fairly constant and there is an equilibrium between water entering and leaving the intercellular substance. In pathological conditions (traumatic injury and inflammation), fluid may accumulate in the connective tissue, a condition known as edema.
B(i) Loose connective tissue: irregularly arranged tissue with abundant ground substance, capable of withstanding stress from many directions; present in dermis, capsules of joints, and submucosa of the alimentary tract. Examples: areolar tissue, adipose tissue. Dense connective tissue: tissue in which fibers predominate; it is organized to withstand forces in specific directions. Dense regular: present in tendons and ligaments. Dense irregular: present in the dermis of skin and capsules of organs.

(i) Xerostomia (dry mouth): a common condition associated with difficulties in chewing, swallowing, tasting, and speaking, dental caries, and atrophy of the oral mucosa.
(ii) Causes listed :
- Use of certain systemic medications (mostly in the elderly)
- High doses of radiation
- Certain diseases such as Sjögren's syndrome
- Mumps viral infection (listed as affecting the major salivary glands and causing inadequate saliva production)
- Antihistamines (listed as a drug causing dry mouth as a normal side effect)
(iii) Sjögren's syndrome: a chronic autoimmune disorder characterised by lymphocytic infiltration of the exocrine glands, particularly the salivary and lacrimal glands. Clinical features may involve the skin, eyes, oral cavity, and salivary glands, as well as the nervous, musculoskeletal, genitourinary, and vascular systems.
(iv) The main functions of the saliva produced by salivary glands include: wetting and lubricating the oral mucosa and ingested food; initiating digestion of carbohydrates and lipids (by amylase and lingual lipase); secreting germicidal protective substances (IgA, lysozyme, lactoferrin); and forming a protective pellicle on the teeth by means of calcium-binding proline-rich salivary proteins. Saliva also has an important buffering function. When production is inadequate, these protective mechanisms fail, leading to dental caries and mucosal atrophy.
(v) Three major salivary glands: parotid, submandibular (submaxillary), and sublingual glands. Together with the minor salivary glands they produce 0.75–1.50 litres of saliva daily.
questions.question:
A 68-year-old woman receiving radiotherapy to the head and neck region complains of progressive difficulty in chewing, swallowing, and speaking. Oral examination reveals atrophy of the oral mucosa and multiple dental caries.
(i) What is the clinical term for this condition, and how is it defined?
(ii) List all the causes of this condition described.
(iii) Name and describe the autoimmune disease described that can cause this condition, including the organs primarily affected and the range of clinical features.
(iv) Explain how inadequate salivary function causes dental caries and atrophy of the oral mucosaconsidering the functions of saliva.
(v) What are the three major salivary glands, and what volume of saliva do they and the minor glands together produce daily?

A(i) List and describe the seven functional components of cranial nerves, with an example for each.
A(ii) State the general features that distinguish cranial nerves from spinal nerves.
B) Explain the clinical basis for why certain cranial nerves are commoner sites of injury/compression.
C) Distinguish between somatic efferent and special visceral efferent fibres.
questions.answerText:
A(i) The seven functional components are: Somatic Efferent (supplies skeletal muscles of somatic origin); Special Visceral (branchial) Efferent (supplies skeletal muscles derived from the branchial arches); General Visceral Efferent (parasympathetic motor to viscera, i.e. smooth muscle or glands); General Visceral Afferent (general sensation of viscera, e.g. larynx, pharynx, carotid body); Special Visceral Afferent (taste and olfaction); General Somatic Afferent (general sensation); Special Somatic Afferent (vision and hearing).
A(ii) Unlike spinal nerves, cranial nerves are not spaced at regular intervals; they contain brachial and special efferent and special sensory components; some contain only motor or sensory components; sensory and motor axons of mixed nerves enter and exit at the same point on the brainstem; and their points of exit/entry are ventral or ventrolateral, except for cranial nerve IV.
B) Injury to the cranial nerves is a frequent complication of a fracture of the base of the cranium, and may also occur from ischaemia and deep lacerations of the neck; the intracranial portions of certain cranial nerves are also susceptible to compression owing to a tumor or aneurysm. Because of their close relationship to the cavernous sinus, CN III, CN IV, CN V1 and especially CN VI are susceptible to compression or injury related to pathologies of the sinus, e.g. infections and thrombophlebitis.
C) Somatic efferent fibres supply skeletal muscles of somatic origin (e.g. extraocular muscles), whereas special visceral (branchial) efferent fibres supply skeletal muscles derived from the branchial arches (e.g. muscles of facial expression, mastication).

questions.question:
A young man sustains a gunshot wound to the axilla with profuse bleeding.
(i) What is the vascular diagnosis/structure injured?
(ii) What emergency manoeuvre can be used to control the bleeding?
(iii) What are the anatomical landmarks relevant to this manoeuvre?
(iv) What other structure is at risk of injury in this region, and what is the specific danger if it is involved proximally?
questions.answerText:
(i) Injury to the axillary artery.
(ii) The inferior part of the axillary artery can be compressed against the humerus to control profuse bleeding.
(iii) This inferior part of the axillary artery can be palpated in the inferior part of the lateral wall of the axilla, where it can be pressed against the humerus (the lateral wall being narrow and bony, formed by the intertubercular groove of the humerus); the axillary artery is divided by pectoralis minor into three parts.
(iv) The axillary vein is also at risk, because wounds to the axilla often involve it due to its large size and exposed position; a wound to the proximal part of the axillary vein is particularly dangerous because of the risk of air entering the vessel (air embolism).

(i) Scapular winging.
(ii) Not covered, beyond the underlying cause of weak or paralysed serratus anterior.
(iii) Scapular winging is due to weak or paralysed serratus anterior; the serratus anterior is the most powerful protractor of the shoulder girdle, so its weakness or paralysis impairs the muscle's normal role in protraction and in holding the medial border of the scapula against the thoracic wall, causing the medial border to protrude (wing).
