questions.answerText:
(i) The arteries of the stomach are derived from branches of the coeliac artery. The left gastric artery arises from the coeliac artery, passes upward and to the left to reach the oesophagus, then descends along the lesser curvature, supplying the lower third of the oesophagus and the upper right part of the stomach. The right gastric artery arises from the hepatic artery at the upper border of the pylorus and runs left along the lesser curvature, supplying the lower right part of the stomach.
The short gastric arteries arise from the splenic artery at the hilum of the spleen and pass forward in the gastrosplenic omentum to supply the fundus. The left gastro-omental (gastroepiploic) artery arises from the splenic artery at the hilum of the spleen and passes forward in the gastrosplenic omentum to supply the stomach along the upper part of the greater curvature. The right gastro-omental artery arises from the gastroduodenal branch of the hepatic artery and passes left to supply the stomach along the lower part of the greater curvature.
(ii) The left and right gastric veins drain directly into the portal vein.
The short gastric veins and the left gastroepiploic vein join the splenic vein.
The right gastroepiploic vein joins the superior mesenteric vein.
All venous drainage of the stomach therefore ultimately enters the portal circulation, via the portal vein, splenic vein or superior mesenteric vein, before passing through the liver.
This portal route explains why bleeding from portal-systemic anastomoses, such as oesophageal varices, is related to the portal venous system.
Not covered : any additional structure specifically at risk during ligation of these vessels beyond their stated course and relations.
questions.question:

(ii) Explain the anatomical basis of the venous route through which gastric bleeding enters the portal circulation.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Pronephros: 7-10 cell clusters in the cervical region at the beginning of the 4th week, non-functional and gone by the end of the 4th week.
A(i) Mesonephros: late 4th week, glomeruli and tubules draining via the mesonephric duct to the cloaca, functioning briefly and degenerating by the end of the first trimester; metanephros: the permanent kidney, beginning early in the 5th week and functioning about 4 weeks later.
A(ii) Ureteric bud (metanephric diverticulum): outgrowth from the mesonephric duct near its entrance into the cloaca; metanephric blastema: mesenchyme from intermediate mesoderm; the two induce each other.
A(iii) The stalk of the bud becomes the ureter; the bud dilates into the primitive renal pelvis and splits into the future calyces, which subdivide into 12 or more generations of tubules; second-order tubules form the minor calyces and 5th-order and later collecting tubules converge to form the renal pyramid.
A(iii) The ureteric bud gives the ureter, renal pelvis, major and minor calyces and about 1 to 3 million collecting tubules.
A(iv) Each collecting tubule is capped by metanephric tissue whose cells form renal vesicles, then S-shaped tubules; capillaries form glomeruli; the proximal end forms Bowman's capsule, the distal end opens into a collecting tubule, and lengthening forms the proximal convoluted tubule, loop of Henle and distal convoluted tubule.
A(iv) Nephrons form until birth (over 1 million per kidney); the kidneys ascend from the pelvis and reach the adult position by the 9th week, the hilum rotating almost 90° to face anteromedially, and become retroperitoneal.
B(i) Renal agenesis: unilateral in 1/1000 neonates (males, left kidney usually) causes no symptoms as the other kidney hypertrophies; bilateral in 1/3000 births is associated with oligohydramnios, is multifactorial and is incompatible with postnatal life.
B(i) Horseshoe kidney (0.2%): inferior poles fused, U-shaped in the pubic region, held down by the root of the inferior mesenteric artery; usually no symptoms as the collecting system develops normally.
C(i) The ureteric bud gives rise to the collecting system; the metanephric blastema (mesoderm) gives rise to the excretory units (nephrons).
C(i) The definitive kidney becomes functional at about 12 weeks; urine passes into the amniotic cavity, is swallowed and recycled, while the placenta excretes waste.
C(i) Urine production begins soon after differentiation of glomerular capillaries, which start to form by the 10th week.

A(i) Cell body (soma): The neuronal cell body is similar to other cell types; it has a nucleus with at least one nucleolus and many typical cytoplasmic organelles. It lacks centrioles, which is consistent with the amitotic nature of neurons. Dendrites: Dendrites are cytoplasmic extensions that project from the cell body; they are usually short and branching, increasing their surface area to receive signals from other neurons. The number of dendrites varies. They are called afferent processes because they transmit impulses to the neuron cell body. Axon: There is only one axon projecting from each cell body; it is usually elongated and carries impulses away from the cell body, so it is called an efferent process. Axons may have infrequent branches called axon collaterals; these terminate in short branches or telodendria, whose distal ends are slightly enlarged to form synaptic bulbs. Myelin sheath: Many axons are surrounded by a segmented, white, fatty substance called myelin or myelin sheath. Myelinated fibers make up the white matter in the CNS, while cell bodies and unmyelinated fibers make the gray matter. Nodes of Ranvier: The unmyelinated regions between myelin segments are called nodes of Ranvier. Neurilemma: In the peripheral nervous system, myelin is produced by Schwann cells. The cytoplasm, nucleus, and outer cell membrane of the Schwann cell form a tight covering around the myelin and around the axon at the nodes of Ranvier — this covering is the neurilemma, which plays an important role in regeneration of nerve fibers.
A(ii) Most local anesthetics are low-molecular-weight molecules that bind to the voltage-gated sodium channels of the axolemma, interfering with sodium ion influx and, consequently, inhibiting the action potential responsible for the nerve impulse.
B(i) In the CNS, oligodendrocytes produce myelin, but there is no neurilemma. It is the neurilemma that plays an important role in regeneration of nerve fibers; therefore fibers within the CNS do not regenerate because they lack neurilemma.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the origin, structural components, and classification of neurons under the following headings: cell body (soma), dendrites, axon, myelin sheath, nodes of Ranvier, and neurilemma.
A(ii) State the basis of why local anaesthetics block nerve impulse transmission.
B(i) Explain the anatomical basis of why nerve fibers within the CNS do not regenerate after injury, while peripheral nerve fibers may regenerate.

questions.answerText:
A(i) The upper end has a large, rounded head joined to the shaft by a constricted surgical neck, and greater and lesser tubercles.
The tubercles are separated by the intertubercular (bicipital) groove, which lodges the long tendon of biceps brachii and transmits a branch of the anterior humeral circumflex artery to the shoulder joint.
A(ii) The shaft is circular in section above and flattened in its lower part, bears the deltoid tuberosity, and its posterior aspect shows the spiral groove, which demarcates the origins of the medial and lateral heads of triceps and between which the radial nerve and profunda vessels wind.
A(iii) The lower end bears the rounded capitulum laterally, for articulation with the radial head, and the spool-shaped trochlea medially, for articulation with the trochlear notch of the ulna; the medial and lateral epicondyles are extracapsular, the medial being the larger, extending more distally and bearing a groove on its posterior aspect for the ulnar nerve.
B. Fractures of the surgical neck of the humerus are especially common in elderly people with osteoporosis, usually from a minor fall on the hand with the force transmitted up the extended limb.
Transverse fractures of the shaft frequently result from a direct blow to the arm.
Fracture of the distal humerus, near the supracondylar ridges, is a supracondylar fracture.
C. Because the axillary, radial and ulnar nerves are in close contact with the humerus, they may be damaged when the associated part of the bone is fractured.
Fracture at the surgical neck threatens the axillary nerve, producing deltoid paralysis with loss of abduction and sensory loss over the regimental badge area.
Fracture through the radial (spiral) groove of the shaft threatens the radial nerve, producing wrist drop.
Fracture at the medial epicondyle at the lower end threatens the ulnar nerve, while injury at the distal humerus (supracondylar region) threatens the median nerve.
Fractures of the humeral neck, midshaft and lower end are therefore each associated with a characteristic pattern of nerve injury and resultant functional deficit.
questions.question:

A(i) Upper end
A(ii) Shaft
A(iii) Lower end
B. State how different parts of the humerus relate to common fracture patterns.
C. Explain how injury at each of these parts may spread to affect a distant structure, causing a functional deficit.

(i) Diabetes mellitus.
(ii) It results from lack of insulin production by the beta cells of the islets of Langerhans, or from defective insulin receptors on the target cells.
(iii) The endocrine part of the pancreas, made up of the microscopic pancreatic islets of Langerhans, secretes hormones such as insulin and glucagon that are released into the blood; failure of this insulin-secreting/receptor mechanism produces the hyperglycaemic state.
(iv) There are two major forms, type 1 and type 2 diabetes mellitus; type 2 is more common, and the most significant laboratory result indicative of diabetes is elevated blood glucose levels after an overnight fast.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Begins in the 4th week as the respiratory diverticulum (lung bud) from the ventral foregut; its location is controlled by TBX4, upregulated by retinoic acid from adjacent mesoderm, which determines the location, induces the bud and promotes growth.
A(i) The epithelial lining of larynx, trachea, bronchi and lung is endoderm; cartilage, muscle and connective tissue are splanchnic mesoderm; the tracheoesophageal ridges fuse into a septum separating the lung bud from the foregut.
A(i) Larynx: internal lining is endoderm; muscle and cartilages come from the 4th and 6th pharyngeal arches.
A(ii) Two bronchial buds grow in the early 5th week into the right and left main bronchi; secondary bronchi: three on the right and two on the left (3 and 2 lobes); tertiary (segmental) bronchi: ten on the right and eight on the left, establishing the bronchopulmonary segments.
A(iii) Embryonic 3-7 weeks; pseudoglandular 5-16 weeks (terminal bronchioles, no respiratory bronchioles or alveoli); canalicular 16-26 weeks (respiratory bronchioles divide into 3-6 alveolar ducts).
A(iii) Terminal sac 26 weeks to birth (primitive alveoli, capillary contact); alveolar 8 months to childhood (mature alveoli); about 17 generations of subdivisions by the end of the 6th month and six more after birth.
B(i) Related anomalies: oesophageal atresia with or without tracheoesophageal fistula (a VACTERL component), respiratory distress syndrome, ectopic lung lobes arising from the trachea or oesophagus, and congenital lung cysts formed by dilation of terminal or larger bronchi.
B(i) The pleura: visceral layer from splanchnic mesoderm covering the lung, parietal layer from somatic mesoderm covering the body wall; the space between is the pleural cavity.
C(i) By the 7th month the epithelium changes from cuboidal to flat, and thinning of type I cells allows epithelial-endothelial contact to form the blood-air barrier; type II alveolar cells form by the 7th month.
C(i) The lung is fluid-filled at birth but the fluid is eventually resorbed; breathing movements start before birth.
C(i) After birth growth is mainly by increase in respiratory bronchioles and alveoli: 1/6 of the alveoli are present at birth and 5/6 form in the next 10 years.
C(i) The mechanism by which respiratory distress syndrome causes functional deficit is not covered.

questions.question:
A chest radiograph shows irregular notching of the lower borders of several ribs.
(i) Identify the underlying condition and the vessel involved, and describe the vessel.
(ii) State the structures affected and the collateral pathways involved.
(iii) Explain the clinico-anatomical reasoning for the rib changes.
questions.answerText:
(i) Coarctation of the aorta; the irregular notching of the ribs is characteristic and very useful in radiographic confirmation of the lesion. The aorta is the largest artery, arising from the aortic orifice of the left ventricle behind the 3rd left intercostal space; it has ascending, arch, descending thoracic and abdominal parts, the descending thoracic part beginning at T4 and ending at T12; the arch (right to left side of T4) gives brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid and left subclavian arteries.
(ii) The intercostal arteries derived from the aorta receive blood from the superior intercostals (costocervical trunk of the subclavian artery), from the anterior intercostal branches of the internal thoracic artery (from the subclavian artery) and from arteries anastomosing around the scapula. The communication between the internal thoracic and inferior epigastric arteries, with these, provides the principal collaterals between the aorta above and below the block.
(iii) The intercostal vessels lie immediately below their ribs in the subcostal groove (vein above artery); as collaterals the intercostal arteries dilate and become tortuous and erode the lower borders of the corresponding ribs, giving the irregular notching. Posterior intercostal arteries of the lower 9 spaces come from the thoracic aorta and anastomose with the anterior intercostal arteries (from the internal thoracic artery in the upper 6 spaces and the musculophrenic artery in the lower 5), which explains how blood can bypass the block.

A(i) The sacrum is formed by the union of 5 sacral vertebrae (fusion begins at 16 to 18 years, usually complete by 30); wedge-shaped; concave anterior surface with four transverse lines and four pairs of anterior sacral foramina.
A(i) Dorsally a median sacral crest and posterior foramina; the sacral canal is continuous with the vertebral canal; an auricular surface forms the sacroiliac joint; structures emerge at the sacral hiatus.
A(ii) Each hip bone is three bones (ilium, pubis, ischium) separated by cartilage in the newborn and fused at puberty in the acetabulum; the ilium is the largest, with ala, body, crest, spines, greater sciatic notch, iliac fossa, auricular surface and arcuate line.
A(ii) Ischium: body, ramus, spine, lesser sciatic notch and tuberosity; pubis: superior and inferior rami, body, crest, tubercle, iliopectineal line; ischium and pubis surround the obturator foramen.
A(iii) Two hip bones united at the pubic symphysis and with the sacrum at the sacroiliac joints; the girdle moves as a unit and supports and protects lower abdominal and pelvic organs; the pelvic brim divides true and false pelves.
B(i) The female pelvis serves for childbearing and easier delivery; it is bigger and wider, with a large oval brim and a wider outlet.
B(i) The sacral promontory, the superior border of the anterior sacral surface, is an important obstetric landmark for pelvic measurements.
B(i) The sacral index is about 105 in males and 115 in females, and the sacrovertebral angle is more prominent in females.
C(i) Male: smaller, narrower, heavier and thicker bone; deep false pelvis; pubic arch V-shaped and less than 90°; acetabulum larger, facing laterally; coccyx immovable; brim smaller and heart-shaped; outlet narrower.
C(i) Male: narrower greater sciatic notch, round obturator foramen, longer narrower sacrum, more vertical ilium, ischial tuberosities longer, close together and laterally projecting.
C(i) Female: shallow false pelvis; wider pubic arch greater than 90°; acetabulum smaller, facing anteriorly; coccyx movable; large oval brim; wider outlet.
C(i) Female: wider greater sciatic notch, oval obturator foramen, less vertical ilium, ischial tuberosities shorter, farther apart and projecting medially.

(i) The sciatic nerve has been injured. The sciatic nerve (L4, 5; S1, 2, 3) curves downward midway between the tuber ischii and the greater trochanter; it has a side of danger and a side of safety. Injection into the lower medial quadrant places the needle directly in the path of the sciatic nerve.
(ii) The sciatic nerve is the largest nerve in the body and the main nerve of the gluteal region. It exits through the greater sciatic foramen below piriformis and runs close to the bone in the lower medial quadrant. The safe quadrant for intramuscular injection is the upper lateral quadrant, where the nerve is furthest from the needle.
(iii) Immediate management includes stopping any further injections in that site, immobilising the limb, neurological assessment of motor and sensory function in the distribution of the sciatic nerve, and analgesic administration.
(iv) Definitive management depends on the degree of nerve damage. Conservative physiotherapy for a neuropraxia; surgical exploration and decompression if there is evidence of severe axonotmesis or neurotmesis, with physical rehabilitation of the affected muscles including those responsible for dorsiflexion, eversion and toe extension.

(i) What is the most likely diagnosis and which structure has been injured?

Describe the gross anatomy and development of the thymus and the parathyroid glands.
State how their shared developmental origin relates to the anomalies that can occur.
Explain how disease affecting this region may cause a functional deficit in a distant/associated structure.
questions.answerText:
Thymus: develops from the endoderm of the ventral part of the third pharyngeal pouch in the 5th week.
It is large at birth, reaches its full size at puberty, and shrinks in old age.
It has a cranial part in the neck and a caudal part in the thorax, has a lobulated appearance, and is invaded by vascular mesoderm containing lymphoblasts.
Parathyroid glands: four in number, located on the dorsal surface of the thyroid gland, starting development in the 5th week.
The inferior parathyroid develops from the third pouch along with the thymus and descends with it into the thorax.
The superior parathyroid develops from the fourth pouch along with the thyroid gland, remaining in the neck.
Relation to anomalies: DiGeorge sequence is described as the '3rd and 4th pouch syndrome', one of the craniofacial defects listed among anomalies of the pharyngeal arches.
Because the thymus and inferior parathyroid share a third-pouch origin, and the superior parathyroid shares a fourth-pouch origin with the thyroid gland, a defect of third and fourth pouch development affects the thymus and parathyroid glands together.
This shared-pouch relationship is why thymic and parathyroid involvement occur together in this sequence rather than in isolation.
Functional deficit in a distant structure: no mechanism by which disease of the thymus or parathyroid spreads to, or produces a deficit in, another distant structure is described here; the discussion is limited to the pouch of origin, descent, and final location of each gland.

questions.question:
A ventricular tap is to be performed on a patient with an abnormal accumulation of CSF in the ventricular system.
(i) Give the diagnosis.
(ii) Name the procedure and the ventricle entered, with its parts and communications.
(iii) State the anatomical landmarks: the boundaries, floor, roof and medial wall of the parts of the ventricle.
(iv) State the embryologic variant.
questions.answerText:
(i) Hydrocephaly: due to overproduction of CSF or obstruction to CSF flow and absorption.
(ii) Ventricular tap (one of the clinically significant taps, with lumbar and cisternal taps) into the lateral ventricle: a C-shaped continuous cavity within the cerebral hemisphere consisting of anterior, body, posterior and inferior horns; communicates with the 3rd ventricle via the interventricular foramen of Monro.
(iii) Anterior horn: triangular, apex pointing laterally; the forceps minor forms the roof; the floor is indented by the head of the caudate nucleus; the septum pellucidum lies medially.
- Foramen of Monro: just behind the anterior column of the fornix; boundary between anterior horn and body; point of continuation of the choroid plexus of the body and 3rd ventricle.
- Body: floor bulged by the thalamus and body of the caudate (thalamostriate vessels between them); roof formed by the corpus callosum and body of the fornix; choroid plexus invaginates via the medial wall.
- Inferior horn (largest part): floor formed by the hippocampus (medial) and collateral eminence (lateral); roof by the tail of the caudate nucleus; lateral wall by the tapetum.
(iv) Embryologic variant: the existence of the posterior horn is variable; the two bulges on its medial wall (upper bulb and lower calcar avis) can obliterate it.

questions.question:
(i) Describe the gross anatomy of the pancreas - location, shape, and its four parts (head, neck, body, tail) with their relations.
(ii) Relate the parts of the pancreas to pathology (annular pancreas, pancreatitis).
(iii) Explain how pancreatic disease can produce a functional deficit in a distant organ/system.
questions.answerText:
(i) The pancreas is a soft, lobulated, J- or retort-shaped gland lying retroperitoneally, except for the tail, and transversely across the posterior abdominal wall at the level of L1-L2, posterior to the stomach, between the duodenum on the right and the spleen on the left; it is about 15-20 cm long and weighs about 90 g.
The head is disc-shaped, enlarged, and lies within the concavity of the duodenum; the uncinate process projects from its lower part, posterior to the superior mesenteric vessels.
The neck is the constricted portion connecting the head to the body and overlies the superior mesenteric vessels.
The body is centrally located, crossing the midline behind the stomach, with anterior, posterior and inferior surfaces; the posterior surface contacts the aorta, splenic vein, left kidney and vessels, left suprarenal gland, origin of the superior mesenteric artery, and the crura of the diaphragm.
The tail is narrow, lies at the level of T12, ends within the splenic hilum in the splenophrenic ligament, and is the only intraperitoneal part of the pancreas; it may be injured during splenectomy, causing a pancreatic fistula.
The main pancreatic duct, of Wirsung, begins in the tail and runs to the head, usually joining the bile duct to form the hepatopancreatic ampulla, which opens at the major duodenal papilla; the accessory duct, of Santorini, drains the upper head via the minor duodenal papilla.
(ii) Annular pancreas is a rare congenital defect in which the pancreas encircles the duodenum; ectopic pancreatic tissue outside the gastrointestinal tract is a very common anomaly.
Due to its deep retroperitoneal position, the pancreas is not easily accessible for direct clinical examination, so diagnosis of pancreatic disease relies on ultrasound, CT scan, special investigations of the pancreatic and biliary ducts, and biochemical tests.
Acute necrotizing pancreatitis results when proenzymes are prematurely activated and digest pancreatic tissue, from causes including infection, gallstones, alcoholism, drugs and trauma.
(iii) The endocrine part of the pancreas, the islets of Langerhans, secretes insulin and glucagon into the blood; lack of insulin production by the beta cells, or defective insulin receptors, causes diabetes mellitus, a hyperglycaemic metabolic disorder affecting the whole body.
Because the exocrine pancreas secretes digestive enzymes and bicarbonate essential for neutralising gastric acid and digesting food in the duodenum, pancreatic disease impairing exocrine secretion produces a functional deficit in intestinal digestion, a distant effect of pancreatic pathology.
In extreme malnutrition, acinar cell atrophy further reduces digestive enzyme production, compounding this distant digestive deficit.

questions.question:
A radiograph of a patient with paraesthesiae along the ulnar border of the forearm and wasting of the small muscles of the hand shows an additional rib above the first rib, attached to the seventh cervical vertebra.
(i) Identify the structure and describe its attachments and incidence.
(ii) State the structures compressed or affected and the resulting clinical features.
(iii) Name the clinical syndrome and give the differential pathologies.
(iv) Explain the clinico-anatomical reasoning using the boundaries of the thoracic inlet and the relations of the first rib.
questions.answerText:
(i) Cervical rib: attached to the transverse process of the 7th cervical vertebra; it articulates with the 1st (thoracic) rib or, if short, has a free end that usually attaches to the normal first rib by a fibrous strand.
(i) It occurs in 0.5% of subjects and is bilateral in half of these.
(ii) The lowest trunk of the brachial plexus arches over the rib and is stretched; the subclavian vessels may also be compressed.
(ii) Nerve effect: paraesthesiae along the ulnar border of the forearm and wasting of the small muscles of the hand (T1).
(ii) Vascular effect: pressure on the overlying subclavian artery may cause vascular changes, even gangrene; post-stenotic dilatation of the vessel distal to the rib, in which a thrombus forms and throws off emboli.
(iii) Thoracic outlet syndrome (compression of nerves or vessels at the superior aperture of the thorax); other differential pathologies are not covered.
(iv) The thoracic inlet is bounded by the T1 vertebra behind, the medial border of the 1st ribs and their costal cartilages at the sides and the manubrium in front; it is closed on either side by the dense suprapleural membrane.
(iv) On the first rib, scalenus anterior inserts on the tubercle; the subclavian vein crosses in front of the tubercle; the subclavian artery and the lowest trunk of the brachial plexus lie in the subclavian groove behind the tubercle.
(iv) The sympathetic trunk, the superior intercostal artery and the large branch of the first thoracic nerve to the brachial plexus cross the neck of the first rib from medial to lateral.

questions.question:
A 60-year-old woman presents with fatigue, pallor, and a smooth tongue. Blood film shows enlarged red blood cells with hypersegmented neutrophils. She gives a history of previous gastric surgery.
(i) What is the most likely diagnosis based on the histological mechanism described?
(ii) Which specific gastric cell type is damaged in this condition, where is it located in the gastric gland, and what are the two products it normally secretes?
(iii) Explain the full chain of events from cell damage to the haematological abnormality.
(iv) What stimuli normally activate this cell type?
(v) State the additional product secreted by chief cells and its significance.
questions.answerText:
(i) Pernicious anaemia — caused by damage to parietal cells such that insufficient quantities of intrinsic factor are secreted and vitamin B12 is not absorbed adequately.
(ii) Parietal (oxyntic) cells. They are present among the mucous neck cells and throughout the deeper parts of the gastric glands. They normally secrete both hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor.
(iii) Chain of events:
- Parietal cells are damaged → insufficient intrinsic factor is secreted.
- Intrinsic factor is the glycoprotein required for the uptake of vitamin B12 in the small intestine.
- Without adequate intrinsic factor, vitamin B12 is not absorbed adequately.
- Low levels of vitamin B12 reduce the proliferation of erythroblasts, leading to megaloblastic anaemia (pernicious anaemia).
(iv) Secretory activity of parietal cells is stimulated through:
- Cholinergic nerve endings (parasympathetic stimulation)
- Paracrine release of histamine
- Gastrin
(v) Chief (zymogen) cells produce the inactive enzyme pepsinogen, which is converted to the highly active enzyme pepsin in the acidic environment of the stomach. Pepsins are active at pH < 5. In humans, chief cells also produce the enzyme lipase and the hormone leptin.

questions.question:
Describe the hip joint under the following headings and explain its clinical correlates.
A(i) Type and articular surfaces
A(ii) Capsule, ligaments — name, attachments and function of each
B(i) Nerve supply, applying Hilton's law
B(ii) Movements and muscles responsible for each movement
C(i) Explain why referred pain from the hip can present at the knee, and distinguish coxa valga from coxa vara
questions.answerText:
A(i) The hip joint is a multiaxial ball-and-socket type of synovial joint. It is the largest joint in the human body and the 2nd largest weight-bearing joint. Articular surfaces: the lunate surface of the acetabulum (covered by hyaline cartilage except at the fovea) and the spherical head of femur (which forms 2/3 of a sphere, covered by hyaline cartilage except at the fovea capitis). The acetabulum is deepened by the fibrocartilaginous acetabular labrum; it is deficient inferiorly as the acetabular notch, bridged by the transverse acetabular ligament.
A(ii) Capsule: strong and thick; medially attached to margin of acetabulum, transverse acetabular ligament, and adjacent margin of obturator foramen; laterally attached to the intertrochanteric line anteriorly. Ligaments: (1) Iliofemoral ligament (ligament of Bigelow) — one of the strongest in the body, Y-shaped; apex at inferior iliac spine, base to intertrochanteric line; prevents overextension and prevents trunk from falling backwards while standing. (2) Pubofemoral ligament — triangular; attached superiorly to iliopubic eminence and obturator crest, inferiorly merges with capsule; limits extension and abduction. (3) Ischiofemoral ligament — reinforces posterior aspect; medially attached to ischium posteroinferior to acetabulum, laterally to greater trochanter deep to the iliofemoral ligament; limits extension. Fibers of all three spiral so they become taut in extension, stabilizing the joint and reducing muscle energy needed for standing. Ligament teres (round ligament): flat triangular band from fovea to acetabular notch and transverse ligament; ensheathed by synovial membrane; transmits arteries to head of femur.
B(i) By Hilton's law: the nerve supplying the joint also supplies the muscles moving the joint and the skin covering the insertion of those muscles. Nerve supply: femoral nerve, anterior division of obturator nerve, nerve to rectus femoris, nerve to quadratus femoris, sciatic nerve, and superior gluteal nerve. The posterior division of the obturator nerve supplies both the hip and the knee joint.
B(ii) Flexion (120–140°): iliopsoas, sartorius, rectus femoris, tensor fasciae latae. Extension: gluteus maximus, semimembranosus, semitendinosus, biceps femoris. Abduction (60–80°): gluteus medius, minimus, tensor fasciae latae. Adduction: pectineus, adductor longus, brevis, magnus, gracilis. Medial rotation: gluteus medius, minimus, tensor fasciae latae. Lateral rotation: obturator internus and externus, gemellus superior and inferior, quadratus femoris, piriformis, posterior fibres of gluteus medius and minimus, superior fibres of gluteus maximus.
C(i) The posterior division of the obturator nerve supplies both the hip and knee joints; pain from hip pathology is therefore referred along this common nerve pathway to the knee joint. Coxa valga follows congenital dislocation of the head of femur; coxa vara follows fracture of the neck of femur.

(i) Lingual thyroid.
(ii) The foramen caecum, lying behind the tuberculum impar between the medial ends of the two mandibular arches, marks the site of origin of the thyroid primordium; the normal path of descent is in front of the hyoid bone and laryngeal cartilage to a final pretracheal position with the isthmus opposite the 2nd, 3rd and 4th tracheal rings.
(iii) Arrest of the normal descent of the thyroid primordium along the thyroglossal duct, from the foramen caecum to its final pretracheal position, is the embryologic variant responsible, leaving thyroid tissue at the base of the tongue (lingual thyroid) rather than in its normal cervical position.

Describe the deep fascial spaces of the hand:
A(i) Thenar space
A(ii) The list of compartments/fascial spaces of the hand
A(iii) Space of Parona
B. Explain the clinical basis for infection spreading between these compartments.
C. Distinguish between the thenar space and the midpalmar space.
questions.answerText:
A(i) The thenar space lies on the thumb side of the septum that joins the border of the palmar aponeurosis to the palmar border of the third metacarpal bone; it contains the first lumbrical muscle and is overlaid by the flexor tendons to the index finger.
A(ii) The compartments and fascial spaces of the hand include the dorsal spaces, hypothenar space, midpalmar space, thenar space, web spaces and pulp spaces, all bounded by connective tissue.
A(iii) The space of Parona extends from the proximal margin of the carpal tunnel to the mid-forearm; its roof is formed distally by the flexor digitorum profundus tendons and proximally by the belly of flexor digitorum superficialis (whose origin forms the proximal boundary), it is limited medially by flexor carpi ulnaris and laterally by flexor pollicis longus, and its floor is formed by pronator quadratus distally and the interosseous membrane in its proximal two-thirds.
B. These fascial spaces allow mobility of the hand structures but, being bounded by connective tissue, offer little resistance to the spread of infection.
Infection within the thenar space can readily break into the connective tissue canals surrounding the ulnar three lumbricals.
For practical purposes the thenar space may therefore be considered continuous distally with these lumbrical canals, and thus distally communicates with the web spaces.
The thenar space also communicates proximally with the space of Parona.
Infection of these deep spaces, including the space of Parona, can be difficult to diagnose.
C. The thenar space lies on the thumb (radial) side of the septum joining the palmar aponeurosis to the third metacarpal, contains the first lumbrical, and is overlaid by the flexor tendons of the index finger.
The midpalmar space, by contrast, lies on the ulnar side of this septum, related to the tendons for the middle, ring and little fingers and to adductor pollicis, separated from the thenar space by the lateral palmar septum.
The thenar space communicates proximally with the space of Parona and distally with the lumbrical canals/web spaces, reflecting its position along the flexor tendon of the index finger.
This anatomical separation by the lateral palmar septum explains why infection in one compartment tends initially to remain localised to that space before spreading along its own specific communicating pathway.

A(i) The ulnar nerve is an extension of the medial cord of the brachial plexus.
A(ii) The most common sites of ulnar nerve entrapment are: above the elbow in the region of the intermuscular septum; the medial epicondylar region; the epicondylar (ulnar) groove; the region of the cubital tunnel; and the region where the nerve exits from flexor carpi ulnaris, where compression is usually caused by the deep flexor-pronator aponeurosis.
A(iii) In the forearm it supplies flexor carpi ulnaris and the medial (3rd & 4th) part of flexor digitorum profundus.
In the hand it supplies the hypothenar muscles, adductor pollicis, flexor pollicis brevis, the palmar and dorsal interossei, the 3rd and 4th lumbricals, and the muscles of digiti minimi (abductor, opponens, flexor digiti minimi).
A(iv) It provides sensation to the medial surface of the hand and the medial half of the 4th and 5th digits, on both palmar and dorsal aspects, through its superficial branch; its motor functions include finger adduction and abduction other than the thumb, thumb adduction, flexion of digits 4 and 5, and wrist flexion and adduction.
C. Injury to the ulnar nerve, or to the medial cord/lower trunk from which it derives, produces a claw hand deformity.
This deformity arises from the unopposed action of the long flexors and extensors of the fingers once the ulnar-innervated intrinsic muscles (interossei, medial lumbricals) are paralysed.
In a claw hand there is hyperextension at the metacarpophalangeal joints and flexion at the interphalangeal joints.
Where the injury occurs at the level of the medial cord (e.g. from subcoracoid dislocation of the humerus), the ulnar nerve and medial root of median nerve are both involved.
This produces sensory loss on the ulnar side of the forearm and hand, along with vasomotor and trophic changes.
The claw hand deformity, together with the specific pattern of muscle paralysis, thus reflects the level and combination of nerve fibres interrupted along the course of the ulnar nerve or its parent cord/trunk.

A. Describe the gross anatomy of the cranial base under the following headings: the anterior cranial fossa, the middle cranial fossa, and the posterior cranial fossa, and their main foramina and contents.
B. State how fractures involving the different regions of the skull base relate to specific clinical presentations.
C. Explain why disease/infection or trauma involving one region of the skull base can produce a functional deficit at a distant site, such as the nasal cavity or the brain itself.
questions.answerText:
A. In the anterior cranial fossa, the foramen caecum transmits a nasal emissary vein (in 1% of the population), the cribriform foramina in the cribriform plate transmit axons of olfactory cells forming the olfactory nerves, and the anterior and posterior ethmoidal foramina transmit vessels and nerves of the same names. In the middle cranial fossa, the optic canals transmit the optic nerves (CN II) and ophthalmic arteries; the superior orbital fissure transmits ophthalmic veins, the ophthalmic nerve (CN V1), CN III, IV and VI, and sympathetic fibres; the foramen rotundum transmits the maxillary nerve (CN V2); the foramen ovale transmits the mandibular nerve (CN V3), the accessory meningeal artery, the lesser petrosal nerve and an emissary vein; the foramen spinosum transmits the middle meningeal artery and vein and the meningeal branch of CN V3; and the foramen lacerum transmits the deep petrosal nerve and some meningeal arterial branches and small veins. In the posterior cranial fossa, the foramen magnum transmits the medulla and meninges, vertebral arteries, CN XI, dural veins, and the anterior and posterior spinal arteries; the jugular foramen transmits CN IX, X and XI, the superior bulb of the internal jugular vein, the inferior petrosal and sigmoid sinuses, and meningeal branches of the ascending pharyngeal and occipital arteries; the hypoglossal canal transmits the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII); the condylar canal transmits an emissary vein from the sigmoid sinus to the vertebral veins in the neck; and the mastoid foramen transmits a mastoid emissary vein from the sigmoid sinus and a meningeal branch of the occipital artery.
B. Fractures of the calvaria are classified as depressed, linear, comminuted, or basilar fractures; fractures of the maxillae and associated bones are termed Le Fort fractures; and there are also fractures of the mandible.
C. The close relation of the frontal sinus to the frontal lobe of the brain explains how infection of this sinus may result in development of a frontal lobe abscess; a fracture involving the sinus, severe enough to tear the dura and pia-arachnoid, will place the subarachnoid space in communication with the nasal cavity, so that CSF may be detected trickling through the nostril (CSF rhinorrhoea), usually on the affected side, although a contralateral leak can occur since these sinuses may communicate. Similarly, infection of the ethmoid sinuses (ethmoiditis) may result in a frontal cerebral abscess, and an ethmoidal fracture may cause CSF leakage into the nasal cavity, because the ethmoid sinuses lie on each side of the cribriform plate and are related above to the frontal lobes of the brain.

questions.question:
A patient is found to have an abnormal accumulation of cerebrospinal fluid within the ventricular system, attributed either to overproduction of the fluid or to obstruction of its flow and absorption.
(i) Name the condition, list the components of the ventricular system and trace the route of CSF from its site of production to its reabsorption.
(ii) Explain the embryologic and pathologic basis: the origin of the ventricles and of the choroid plexus, the structure and sites of the choroid plexus, and the site and rate of CSF production.
(iii) State the definitive treatment.
questions.answerText:
(i) Hydrocephaly: due to overproduction of CSF or obstruction to CSF flow and absorption.
- Ventricular system: right and left lateral ventricles, 3rd ventricle and 4th ventricle; continuous with the central canal of the spinal cord.
- Circulation: lateral ventricles → foramen of Monro → 3rd ventricle → aqueduct of Sylvius → 4th ventricle → foramina of Magendie and Luschka → subarachnoid space over brain and spinal cord (or straight into the central canal) → reabsorption into venous sinus blood via arachnoid granulations/villi, a valvular mechanism with no back-flow of blood into the CSF.
(ii) The ventricles are a modified derivative of the neural canal.
- Roof plate of the myelencephalon: single layer of ependymal cells covered by vascular mesenchyme (pia mater) = tela choroidea; saclike tuftlike invaginations into the ventricular cavity form the choroid plexus, which produces CSF.
- Choroid plexus: evaginations of pia mater and blood vessels lined by a single layer of ependymal cells joined by tight junctions (blood-CSF barrier).
- Sites: body, atrium and inferior horn of the lateral ventricle, foramen of Monro, roof of the 3rd ventricle and posterior part of the roof of the 4th ventricle.
- Production: about 0.4 mL/min (about 600 mL/day); 70% from the ventricles and 30% from brain capillaries; the lateral ventricle produces most of the CSF.
(iii) Definitive treatment: not covered (only lumbar, cisternal and ventricular taps are listed as clinically significant procedures).

A(i) 3.8 cm long, an anteroposterior slit; anterior wall shorter, posterior longer; begins one inch below and in front of the tip of the coccyx at the recto-anal junction, runs down and backwards, ends at the anus.
A(i) Relations: laterally the ischioanal fossa; posteriorly the anococcygeal raphe; anteriorly the perineal body with bulb of penis and spongy urethra (male), or perineal body and posterior vaginal wall (female).
A(ii) The pectinate (dentate) line is the mucocutaneous junction at the level of the anal valves; Hilton's white line lies at the lower end of the internal sphincter.
A(ii) Upper area 15 mm (columns, valves, papillae, sinuses, glands); intermediate area 15 mm (pecten, stratified squamous without sebaceous or sweat glands); lower area 8 mm (true skin).
A(iii) Internal sphincter: thickened involuntary circular muscle around the upper three-quarters, sympathetic L1, L2 and parasympathetic S2 to S4. External sphincter: striated voluntary, whole length, subcutaneous, superficial and deep parts, supplied by the inferior rectal nerve (pudendal) and perineal branch of S4.
B(i) Internal haemorrhoids: above Hilton's line, tributaries of the superior rectal vein, painless (primary piles at 3, 7 and 11 o'clock); external: below the line, inferior rectal vein, painful.
B(ii) Anal sinuses are recesses above the anal columns where foreign bodies may impact and cause infection; infection of the anal glands in the sinus floors may lead to anal fistula; rupture of an anal valve with a tag is a sentinel pile.
B(iii) Anal columns of Morgagni (6 to 10 folds with superior rectal vein radicles); anal valves of Ball form the pectinate line; anal papillae are remnants of the anal membrane.
C(i) Above: superior rectal artery with drainage by the superior rectal vein (portal); below: inferior rectal artery (internal pudendal) with the middle rectal artery, draining to the internal iliac vein (systemic).
C(ii) Above the pectinate line lymph goes to the internal iliac nodes; below it to the superficial inguinal nodes.
C(iii) Above the line the fibres are autonomic and pain-insensitive to stretch; below, the inferior rectal nerve is sensitive to pain and touch.
C(iv) Above the line is hindgut/endodermal with columnar epithelium; below is cloacal membrane/ectodermal with stratified epithelium; the lower third has somatic supply (inferior rectal nerves).

questions.answerText:
A(i) Formed by the ventral rami of L1, L2, L3 and the upper part of L4; the lower part of L4 joins L5 to form the lumbosacral trunk.
A(i) The rami emerge from the intervertebral foramina, enter psoas, give branches to psoas and quadratus lumborum, then form the plexus within the substance of psoas major.
A(ii) Iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal: L1; genitofemoral: L1, L2; lateral femoral cutaneous: L2, L3 (posterior division).
A(ii) Femoral: L2, L3, L4 (posterior division); obturator: L2, L3, L4 (anterior division); sometimes an accessory obturator L3, L4.
A(iii) From the lateral border of psoas major: iliohypogastric, ilioinguinal, lateral femoral cutaneous, femoral.
A(iii) Through psoas anteriorly: genitofemoral; from the medial border: obturator.
A(iv) It innervates part of the lower abdominal wall but chiefly supplies skin and muscle 'borrowed from the trunk by the lower limb'.
A(iv) The genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve supplies the cremasteric muscle; the ilioinguinal nerve runs in the inguinal canal.
B(i) The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve normally passes deep to the lateral end of the inguinal ligament; sometimes it passes through the substance of the ligament.
B(ii) The safe site for a procedure on the plexus is not covered.
C(i) Entrapment causes pain along its distribution (meralgia paresthetica); deficits from other lumbar plexus injuries are not covered.
C(i) Psoas major is supplied by ventral rami L1 to L4, psoas minor by L1, quadratus lumborum by upper lumbar and subcostal nerves, iliacus by the femoral nerve.

A(i) A double-domed, thin fibromuscular (musculotendinous) partition between the thoracic and abdominal cavities and the main muscle of respiration; convex superior surface faces the thorax (covered by diaphragmatic pleura, lungs fit the domes, fibrous pericardium on the central tendon), concave inferior surface faces the abdomen (parietal peritoneum; liver, kidneys, suprarenals, stomach, spleen); higher on the right because of the liver (in expiration the right dome reaches the 5th rib, the left the 5th intercostal space); level varies with respiration, posture and abdominal distension, and the domes flatten in maximal inspiration.
A(ii) Sternal: 2 slips from the posterior xiphoid process; costal: deep surfaces of the lower 6 ribs and costal cartilages (forms the domes); vertebral: the crura and 3 arcuate ligaments - medial (thickened psoas fascia, from the body of L2 to the tip of the L1 transverse process), lateral (thickened quadratus lumborum fascia, from the L1 transverse process to the lower border of the 12th rib) and median (joins the crura across the front of the aorta). Insertion: trefoil central tendon, no bony attachments, partly fused with the fibrous pericardium (pericardiophrenic ligament).
A(iii) Caval opening (T8; the only opening in the central tendon): IVC, terminal branches of the right phrenic nerve, a few lymphatics. Oesophageal opening (T10; in the right crus): oesophagus, anterior and posterior vagal trunks, oesophageal branches of the left gastric vessels, a few lymphatics. Aortic opening (T12; lowest and most posterior, between the crura): aorta, thoracic duct, sometimes azygos and hemiazygos veins.
A(iii) Smaller openings: greater and lesser splanchnic nerves pierce each crus; hemiazygos vein pierces the left crus; left phrenic nerve pierces the left dome; sympathetic trunks pass behind the diaphragm deep to the medial arcuate ligament; subcostal vessels and nerve pass behind the lateral arcuate ligament; superior epigastric vessels pass between the sternal and costal origins; 7th-11th intercostal neurovascular bundles pass through the costal origin.
A(iv) Arteries: pericardiophrenic and musculophrenic (from the internal thoracic) and superior phrenic (from the thoracic aorta) to the superior surface; inferior phrenic (first branches of the abdominal aorta) to the inferior surface. Veins: pericardiophrenic and musculophrenic to the internal thoracic vein; superior phrenic vein (right) and right inferior phrenic vein to the IVC; the left inferior phrenic vein drains to the IVC and the left suprarenal vein.
A(v) Motor: phrenic nerves (C3-5) only - the right nerve to the right half up to the right margin of the oesophageal opening, the left to the left half. Sensory: central part (with related pleura and peritoneum) via the phrenic nerves; peripheral part via the lower 6 or 7 intercostal and subcostal nerves.
A(v) Lymph: thoracic surface to anterior and posterior diaphragmatic nodes (anterior on to parasternal nodes; posterior to phrenic and posterior mediastinal nodes); abdominal surface to anterior diaphragmatic, phrenic and superior lumbar (caval/aortic) nodes.
B(i) The central diaphragm is supplied sensorily by the phrenic nerve (C3-5) and the shoulder skin by the supraclavicular nerve (C3,4); so pain from irritation of pleura or pericardium over the central diaphragm, or of the peritoneum under it by subphrenic pus or blood, is referred to the shoulder tip.
B(ii) Acquired herniae occur in middle-aged people with weak musculature around the oesophageal opening; they are either sliding or paraoesophageal (rolling, alongside the oesophagus).
B(iii) Hiccup is an involuntary spasmodic contraction of the diaphragm with approximation of the vocal folds and closure of the glottis; common after eating or drinking from gastric irritation of vagus nerve endings; it may be due to pleurisy, peritonitis or pericarditis.
C(i) Right crus: larger and longer, arises from the upper 3 lumbar vertebrae (L1-L3) and their intervertebral discs; some of its fibres pass up to the left and loop round the oesophageal orifice as a physiological sphincter preventing reflux of gastric contents.
C(i) Left crus: smaller, arises from the side of the bodies of the upper 2 (L1-L2) lumbar vertebrae and their discs; each crus is attached to the medial and lateral arcuate ligaments, and the medial borders of the two crura unite in front of T12 as the median arcuate ligament over the aorta.

questions.answerText:
A(i) The vagus is the 10th cranial nerve. The right vagus descends on the right side of the trachea, forms the posterior oesophageal plexus and continues in the abdomen as the posterior gastric nerve. The left vagus descends between the left common carotid and left subclavian arteries, forms the anterior oesophageal plexus and continues in the abdomen as the anterior gastric nerve.
A(ii) The vagus nerves lie in both the superior and the posterior mediastinum; in the posterior mediastinum the right and left vagi lie around the oesophagus and pass through the oesophageal opening of the diaphragm (T10) as the anterior and posterior vagal trunks. The left recurrent laryngeal branch of the vagus winds round the ligamentum arteriosus, which connects the inferior concave surface of the arch of the aorta to the left pulmonary artery.
A(iii) Branches: recurrent laryngeal branches on both sides and superior and inferior cervical cardiac branches (the right has both, the left has the inferior branch) to the cardiac plexus; pulmonary plexuses to the lungs; oesophageal plexuses. Cardiac plexus: the superficial part lies in front of the ligamentum arteriosus (inferior cervical cardiac branch of the left vagus); the deep part lies in front of the left bronchus and at the bifurcation of the pulmonary trunk, behind the arch of the aorta on the lowest part of the trachea; parasympathetic fibres relay in the heart.
A(iv) Heart: through the cardiac plexus to the SA and AV nodes and the AV bundle; parasympathetics decrease the rate of impulse generation, sympathetics increase it. Lungs and visceral pleura (via the pulmonary plexuses): bronchoconstrictor, vasodilator to pulmonary vessels and secretomotor to glands; the vagal efferents mediate the cough reflex that clears secretions and dust. Oesophagus and trachea: recurrent laryngeal branch to the striated upper third of the oesophagus, parasympathetic secretomotor fibres to the oesophageal glands; vagus to the mucous membrane and parasympathetics of the trachea; gastric irritation of vagus nerve endings may cause hiccup.

questions.answerText:
A(i) The eye's structures are formed by three germ layers: neuroectoderm, surface ectoderm and mesoderm. The optic cup differentiates into the retina (an outer pigmented layer, and an inner photoreceptive layer forming the posterior four-fifths, plus the inner layer of the iris and ciliary body); the optic stalk becomes the optic nerve. The choroid (vascularized, pigmented) and sclera (tough outer layer) form from surrounding lateral plate mesoderm. The cornea forms from three sources: an epithelial layer from surface epithelium, the substantia propria (continuous with the sclera), and an epithelial layer over the anterior chamber.
A(ii) Photoreceptive cells (rods and cones) connect via bipolar cells to ganglion cells (optic nerve fibres); at the optic chiasma the medial fibres cross; the optic tract goes to the lateral geniculate body of the same side, then via the optic radiation to the visual cortex (area 17).
B) The sclera is continuous with the dura mater around the optic nerve, similar to the relationship of the pia and dura mater in the brain.
C) Some fibres bypass the lateral geniculate body and synapse in the superior colliculus, forming the basis of the pupillary light reflex (direct and consensual): from the optic tract to the superior colliculus, to the Edinger-Westphal nucleus, with fibres travelling via CN III to the sphincter pupillae; each colliculus projects to both oculomotor nuclei, producing bilateral constriction.

questions.answerText:
(i) The diagnosis is acute limb ischaemia due to occlusion of the popliteal artery (or common femoral bifurcation) given the presence of a femoral pulse with absence of popliteal, dorsalis pedis, and posterior tibial pulses. The popliteal artery is the continuation of the femoral artery; it begins when the femoral artery passes through the adductor hiatus; it terminates at the inferior border of the popliteus by dividing into the anterior and posterior tibial arteries.
(ii) Arterial tree from femoral artery to foot: External iliac artery → Femoral artery (gives off profunda femoris 5 cm below the inguinal ligament) → passes through adductor hiatus → Popliteal artery → divides into Anterior tibial artery and Tibioperoneal trunk → Tibioperoneal trunk divides into Posterior tibial artery and Fibular (peroneal) artery. Anterior tibial artery: passes anterior to interosseous membrane; supplies anterior compartment; continues as Dorsalis pedis artery in foot (supplies tarsal bones and dorsal metatarsals; anastomoses with lateral plantar artery to form deep plantar arch). Posterior tibial artery: enters sole of foot via tarsal tunnel; splits into Lateral and Medial plantar arteries (supply plantar side of foot and contribute to supply of toes via deep plantar arch).
(iii) Structures at risk of ischaemia include the muscles of all compartments of the leg (anterior, lateral, and posterior), peripheral nerves (tibial and common fibular nerves), and the skin. Compartment syndrome results from ischaemia-reperfusion injury after revascularisation: oedema within the fascial compartments raises intracompartmental pressure, further compromising perfusion. The anterior compartment (containing tibialis anterior, extensor digitorum longus, extensor hallucis longus, and fibularis tertius) is at highest risk; injury to the deep fibular nerve causes foot drop.
(iv) Emergency management: anticoagulation with heparin, urgent vascular surgery referral. Surgical options: catheter-directed thrombolysis (if onset within 14 days), or surgical embolectomy via a Fogarty catheter introduced through an arteriotomy in the common femoral artery or popliteal artery. The popliteal artery is approached through the popliteal fossa — it is the deepest structure in the fossa, so the approach requires careful dissection to protect the popliteal vein (which lies in the same fibrous sheath just superficial to the artery) and the tibial nerve (most superficial of the neurovascular bundle). Four-compartment fasciotomy is performed prophylactically after revascularisation to prevent compartment syndrome.
questions.question:
A 48-year-old man with known hypertension and hypercholesterolaemia develops sudden-onset severe pain in the right leg with pallor and paraesthesia. On examination the leg is cold, the femoral pulse is present, but there is no popliteal, dorsalis pedis, or posterior tibial pulse. He is diagnosed with acute limb ischaemia.
(i) State the diagnosis and identify the most likely level of arterial occlusion based on the pulse findings.
(ii) Identify the complete arterial tree from the femoral artery to the foot, naming all main arteries in order.
(iii) What structures are at risk of ischaemia, and what are the compartment syndrome complications?
(iv) Describe the management, including the anatomical basis for the surgical approach.

questions.answerText:
(i) The anterior vagal trunk is formed mainly in the thorax from the left vagus nerve; it enters the abdomen on the anterior surface of the oesophagus and divides into branches that supply the anterior surface of the stomach. A large hepatic branch of the anterior vagal trunk passes up to the liver, and from this a pyloric branch passes down to the pylorus.
The posterior vagal trunk is formed mainly from the right vagus nerve; it enters the abdomen on the posterior surface of the oesophagus and divides into branches supplying mainly the posterior surface of the stomach. A large branch of the posterior vagal trunk passes to the coeliac and superior mesenteric plexuses and is distributed to the intestine as far as the splenic flexure and to the pancreas.
(ii) At the opening in the diaphragm (the oesophageal hiatus), the oesophagus is accompanied by the two vagal trunks, branches of the left gastric vessels, and lymphatic vessels, with fibres of the right crus forming a sling around the oesophagus. Inferior to the root of the lungs, the vagus nerves leave the pulmonary plexus and join sympathetic nerves to form the oesophageal plexus, from which the anterior trunk (left vagus, anterior) and posterior trunk (right vagus, posterior) are derived.
(iii) The vagal (parasympathetic) fibres are secretomotor to the gastric glands and motor to the muscular wall of the stomach, and the pyloric sphincter receives inhibitory fibres from the vagus.
Vagotomy is a recognised surgical option for peptic ulcer disease; division of the vagal trunks reduces the vagal secretomotor drive to the gastric glands, decreasing acid secretion.
Since the hepatic branch arises from the anterior vagal trunk and the coeliac/pancreatic branch from the posterior trunk, a truncal vagotomy also interrupts vagal input to the liver, pancreas and intestine as far as the splenic flexure.
Loss of vagal inhibitory input to the pyloric sphincter can alter pyloric motor function, which is why vagotomy for peptic ulcer disease is often combined with a drainage procedure such as pyloroplasty.
Not covered : further detail on specific effects following selective vagal nerve injury.
questions.question:
(i) Describe the origin, course and distribution of the anterior and posterior vagal trunks in the abdomen.
(ii) State where the vagal trunks lie in relation to the oesophageal hiatus.
(iii) Explain the anatomical basis of the effect of vagal injury (vagotomy) on the stomach and related viscera.

questions.answerText:
(i) Horseshoe kidney, present in 0.2% of the population; usually the inferior poles are fused and the large U-shaped kidney lies in the pubic region.
(ii) Normal ascent is prevented because the kidney is held down by the root of the inferior mesenteric artery.
(ii) Normally the kidneys ascend from the pelvis to the abdomen by the 9th week, rotating medially almost 90° so that the hila face anteromedially; the renal arteries arise first from the common iliac arteries and later from the aorta.
(iii) Unilateral renal agenesis; pelvic kidney; malrotation (hilum facing laterally); crossed renal ectopia (one kidney crossed to the other side and fused); discoid kidney (joined at both poles); rosette kidney (joined at the upper pole); supernumerary kidney (two ureteric buds); bifid ureter; polycystic kidney.
(iv) It usually produces no symptoms because its collecting system develops normally and the ureters enter the bladder.
questions.question:
Imaging shows a large U-shaped kidney lying in the pubic region, with fusion of the inferior poles, in a person with no symptoms.
(i) Identify the anomaly and its frequency.
(ii) State the structure that prevented normal ascent and the structures that remain normal.
(iii) State the differential renal anomalies.
(iv) Give the clinico-anatomical reasoning for the absence of symptoms.

questions.answerText:
Origin/identity: the motor nerve of the first pharyngeal arch is the mandibular division of the 5th cranial nerve (trigeminal); the sensory nerve of the same arch comprises the ophthalmic, maxillary and mandibular divisions of the 5th cranial nerve.
Distribution (motor): the muscles supplied include the muscles of mastication (temporalis, medial and lateral pterygoids), the anterior belly of digastric, mylohyoid, tensor tympani and tensor palatini.
Related skeletal elements: the cartilage of the first arch has a ventral maxillary process and a dorsal mandibular process containing Meckel's cartilage; the mesenchyme surrounding Meckel's cartilage forms the mandible, and Meckel's cartilage also forms the anterior ligament of malleus and the sphenomandibular ligament.
The dorsal part of the maxillary process forms the premaxilla, maxilla, zygomatic bone and part of the temporal bone, all lying within the territory of this arch's nerve.
Course: not covered beyond its arch of origin and the divisions named.
Safe site for a procedure: not covered.
Anatomical basis of the deformity after injury: not covered.
What can be stated is limited to the identity of the motor and sensory nerves of the first arch and the muscles and skeletal derivatives they relate to.
No description of the peripheral course, branching pattern in the face, or consequence of injury (e.g. on mastication or facial sensation) is given.
The muscles named (muscles of mastication, digastric anterior belly, mylohyoid, tensor tympani, tensor palatini) indicate the motor territory of this nerve as described here.
The three sensory divisions named (ophthalmic, maxillary, mandibular) indicate the sensory territory, but without further detail on their individual courses.
Further anatomical or clinical detail on this nerve would need to be sourced elsewhere.

questions.answerText:
A(i) The facial nerve has the following components: special visceral efferent (SVE) fibres, general visceral efferent (GVE) fibres, special visceral afferent (SV
A. Fibres, and general somatic afferent (GS fibres.
A(ii) SVE fibres supply the muscles of facial expression; GVE fibres supply the salivary and lacrimal glands; SVA fibres supply the taste buds of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue; GSA fibres supply the skin of the external ear.
C. Bell's palsy is facial paralysis ipsilateral to a facial nerve lesion; because the SVE component of the facial nerve supplies the muscles of facial expression, a lesion of the nerve paralyses these muscles on the same side as the lesion, producing the deformity.
