questions.answerText:
(i) This is acute nociceptive (somatic) pain arising from the soft tissue injury of the sprain, caused by threat of or actual tissue damage.
(ii) Cold therapy (cryotherapy).
(iii) Indicated for pain relief and inflammation control in acute pain, and for reduction of swelling accompanying pain.
(iv) Physiological effect: control of inflammation and reduction of swelling.
General advice for pain includes rest and activity modification - avoiding activities that worsen pain while staying active as tolerated.
questions.question:
A patient presents with an ankle sprain causing pain.
(i) State the pain type and mechanism involved.
(ii) Name a suitable physiotherapy modality.
(iii) State the application/indication for this modality.
(iv) State the expected physiological effects and patient education.

questions.answerText:
(i) This is acute pain: sudden onset, usually lasting less than 6 months, with easily identified, well localised and defined underlying pathology, associated with tissue damage; stimulation of the autonomic nervous system (mydriasis, tachycardia, tachypnoea, sweating, vasoconstriction) can be observed during this type of pain.
(ii) Cold therapy (cryotherapy).
(iii) Indicated for pain relief and inflammation control in acute pain, and for reduction of swelling accompanying pain.
(iv) Physiological effect: control of inflammation and swelling, which subsides as tissue heals since acute pain subsides with tissue healing.
Patient education: avoid activities that worsen the pain while staying active as tolerated (rest and activity modification).
questions.question:
A patient with a fresh tissue injury shows signs of autonomic nervous system stimulation, including mydriasis, tachycardia, tachypnoea, sweating and vasoconstriction.
(i) State the pain type and mechanism responsible for the autonomic signs.
(ii) Name a suitable physiotherapy modality.
(iii) State the application/indication for this modality.
(iv) State the expected physiological effects and patient education.

questions.answerText:
A) Central sensitisation is caused by continued stimulation of the NMDA (N-methyl-D-aspartate) receptor, which evokes a change in the sensitivity of the post-synaptic cell so it responds more strongly to all its inputs.
C fibres and nociceptors release glutamate, aspartate and substance P as neurotransmitters; the receiving interneurons in the dorsal horn express NMDA and AMPA glutaminergic receptors; high afferent input depolarises the cell, activating AMPA then NMDA receptors, causing a cascade of further depolarisation.
B) In chronic low back pain, the area of the brain's body map representing the lower back can become larger and even take over other body-map areas, so movement of other body parts can be felt as pain in the low back; this is an example of the 'representation' mechanism of chronic pain.
C) The mechanism is self-propagating; positive feedback loops may induce and maintain central sensitisation.
This hyperexcitability state may change genetic expression, influencing long-term changes in cellular function, e.g. development of 'pain memory'.
Clinically this shows as increased response to afferent input (hyperalgesia), expansion of peripheral nociceptor receptive fields (allodynia), increased spontaneous activity, and neuroplasticity/pain memory (e.g. phantom limb pain) if stimulation is prolonged.
Together with emotional factors (low mood, stress, frustration) and poor healthcare (multiple/conflicting diagnoses), these mechanisms maintain persistent pain and its associated functional and psychological deficit.
questions.question:
A) Describe the mechanism of central sensitisation.
B) Relate this mechanism to a common chronic pain condition.
C) Explain why pain associated with this mechanism may become chronic and cause a functional deficit.

questions.answerText:
(i) These are features of chronic pain: extension beyond normal recovery time; activation of dysfunctional neurological or psychological response; history of treatment (Rx) failure; and common side effects of depression, anger, frustration, decreased activity level and decreased sleep.
(ii) Expectations, cognition and emotions affect the experience of pain; anxiety, depression and catastrophising predict reactions to pain and ability to cope; how much pain a person expects influences processing in the cingulate cortex, anterior insula and thalamus.
Negative emotions and stress increase pain by augmenting somatosensory attention to pain, intensifying muscle tension, decreasing role performance, diminishing social participation, and inhibiting neural inhibition in pain pathways.
(iii) This should be differentiated from acute pain, which has a clear description of location, pattern, quality, frequency and duration and functions as a warning enforcing rest of healing tissue; here the pain no longer serves that biological function.
(iv) Management must address the '3 D's' of chronic pain - distress, disuse, disability - which requires a multidimensional approach combining psychological interventions (relaxation, biofeedback, imagery, cognitive-behavioural therapy) with appropriate physiotherapy modality selection.
questions.question:
A patient with long-standing pain has had a history of treatment failure and now shows depression, anger, frustration, decreased activity level and decreased sleep.
(i) Interpret these assessment findings.
(ii) State the structures/pathways/processes involved.
(iii) State the differential considerations for this presentation.
(iv) State the clinical reasoning for progressing management of this patient.

questions.answerText:
(i) This is neuropathic pain - pain caused by a primary lesion or dysfunction in the nervous system, which can be peripheral (e.g. diabetic neuropathy, trigeminal neuralgia, post-herpetic zoster pain) or central (e.g. thalamic pain syndrome) in origin.
(ii) Pathophysiology: it can arise from inflammation of the nerves (e.g. temporal neuritis); injury to the nerve/nerve endings with scar formation (e.g. surgical damage or disc prolapse); nerve invasion by cancer (e.g. brachial plexopathy); injury to structures of the spinal cord, thalamus or cortical areas that process pain, causing de-afferentation (e.g. spinal trauma); or abnormal activity in nerve circuits perceived as pain (e.g. phantom pain with cortical re-organisation).
Such pain becomes independent of the initial injury or damage and sustains a chronic pain state.
(iii) Physiotherapy management: electro-analgesic currents (TENS and Interferential Current), which are indicated for neuropathic pain.
questions.question:
A patient presents with pain described as burning, electric shock or lightning bolt in nature, consistent with conditions such as diabetic neuropathy, trigeminal neuralgia, post-herpetic zoster pain or thalamic pain syndrome.
(i) State the diagnosis/pain condition.
(ii) State the predisposing factors/pathophysiology of this pain.
(iii) State the physiotherapy management for this patient.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Locus of control; anxiety and depression; age; cultural differences; gender; cognitions and incentives; chronic stress.
A(ii) Negative emotions and stress increase pain by augmenting somatosensory attention to pain, intensifying muscle tension, decreasing role performance, diminishing social participation, and inhibiting neural inhibition in pain pathways; distraction reduces pain awareness, while isolation and inactivity increase it and foster self-preoccupation.
B) Expectations, cognition and emotions affect the experience of pain; anxiety, depression and catastrophising predict reactions to pain and ability to cope; how much pain a person expects influences processing in the cingulate cortex, anterior insula and thalamus - so patients with these traits process and experience pain differently and are more vulnerable to chronic pain.
Chronic stress increases both the perception of pain and disability, further predisposing such patients to persistent pain.
C) Pain is composed of both protective sensation and the emotional response to this sensation; it is difficult to measure because it has an emotional/psychological component as well as a physical component.
Some people express extreme discomfort from relatively small injuries while others show little or no pain even after severe injury; sometimes pain is present even though no injury is apparent, or pain lingers long after an injury appears to have healed.
The physical component relates to actual/potential tissue damage detected by nociceptors, while the psychological/emotional component relates to how sensory information is integrated with memories, expectations, emotions and thoughts to form the complete perceptual experience of pain.
questions.question:
A(i) List the psychological factors that affect pain perception.
A(ii) State how negative emotions and stress affect pain.
B) Explain the clinical basis for why some patients are more vulnerable to persistent/chronic pain than others.
C) Distinguish between the physical and psychological/emotional components of pain.

A(i) Define the terms allodynia, hyperalgesia and hyperpathia.
A(ii) Define the terms hypoalgesia and hypoesthesia.
A(iii) Define neuralgia, neuritis and nociceptor.
B) Explain the clinical basis for using precise pain terminology in assessment.
C) Distinguish between allodynia and hyperalgesia.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Allodynia: pain evoked by stimuli that are usually not painful. Hyperalgesia: an increased response to a stimulus that is normally painful. Hyperpathia: a painful syndrome characterised by an abnormally painful reaction to a stimulus (especially repetitive) and an increased threshold.
A(ii) Hypoalgesia: diminished pain in response to a normally painful stimulus (raised threshold). Hypoesthesia: decreased sensitivity to stimulation, excluding the special senses.
A(iii) Neuralgia: pain in the distribution of a nerve or nerves. Neuritis: inflammation of a nerve or nerves. Nociceptor: a receptor preferentially sensitive to a noxious stimulus, or to a stimulus which would become noxious if prolonged.
B) Precise and systematic pain assessment is required to make the correct diagnosis and to determine the most efficacious treatment plan for patients presenting with pain, since pain is a highly subjective experience but its management necessitates an objective standard of care.
C) Allodynia is pain evoked by a stimulus that is usually not painful (e.g. a feather touch on a burn), reflecting a decreased threshold for nociceptor activation.
Hyperalgesia is an increased/exaggerated response to a stimulus that is normally painful (e.g. a slap on a sun-burnt back), reflecting a leftward shift of the nociceptor's stimulus-response curve.
Both arise from the 'chemical soup' of algesic substances sensitising nociceptors after tissue injury, but allodynia concerns a non-painful stimulus becoming painful, while hyperalgesia concerns a painful stimulus becoming more painful.

questions.question:
A) Describe the components of the Gate Control Theory of pain.
B) State how the components of this theory relate to a common pain-relieving action and to a clinical device developed from it.
C) Explain, using this theory and related mechanisms, why pain may become chronic.
questions.answerText:
A) Proposed by Melzack and Wall in 1965, the theory states that transmission of information across the synapse between Aδ and C nerve fibres (which carry noxious information from the periphery) and cells in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord can be diminished or blocked.
Information from first-order low-threshold mechanical afferents and first-order nociceptive afferents converges onto the same second-order neurons; the balance of activity in these afferents determines the pattern of signals the second-order neurons transmit.
Activation of large myelinated Aβ fibres (low-threshold mechanoreceptors) stimulates an inhibitory nerve in the spinal cord that inhibits synaptic transmission, so the perception of the painful stimulus is diminished or not felt at all.
B) This explains why rubbing an injured area reduces pain sensation, and it was the clinical basis for the development of Transcutaneous Electrical Nerve Stimulation (TENS).
C) Pain may become chronic through central sensitisation: continued stimulation of the NMDA receptor changes the sensitivity of the post-synaptic cell so it responds more strongly to all inputs, and this mechanism is self-propagating through positive feedback loops.
This hyperexcitability can change genetic expression, influencing long-term cellular function and the development of 'pain memory'.
Clinically this appears as hyperalgesia, allodynia, spontaneous pain, and neuroplastic pain memory (e.g. phantom limb pain) even after the initial stimulus is gone.

questions.question:
A patient who had surgical damage to a nerve reports burning, electric-shock-type pain in the distribution of that nerve.
(i) State the type/classification of this pain.
(ii) Explain the underlying mechanism of this pain.
(iii) Outline the physiotherapy assessment for this patient.
(iv) Outline the physiotherapy management for this patient.
questions.answerText:
(i) This is neuropathic pain (neuralgia - pain in the distribution of a nerve), of peripheral origin, caused by a primary lesion/dysfunction in the nervous system, often described as burning or electric shock/lightning bolt in nature.
(ii) Mechanism: injury to the nerve and nerve endings with scar formation, e.g. surgical damage, is one of the causes by which pain sensations arise in neuropathic pain; such pain becomes independent of the initial injury and sustains a chronic pain state.
(iii) Subjective assessment: determine the quality of pain (e.g. burning, electric shock), location/distribution along the nerve, and chronicity.
Outcome measures: pain scales (visual analogue, numerical, verbal rating scale).
(iv) Management: electro-analgesic currents (TENS/Interferential Current), indicated for neuropathic pain; anticonvulsants and antidepressants are noted to prevent abnormal axon-generated action potentials at the periphery level of antinociception, decreasing pain.

questions.question:
A patient with chronic non-cancer pain, having both nociceptive and neuropathic features, has been on long-term NSAID therapy.
(i) State the contributing/risk factors relevant to this patient's pain presentation.
(ii) State the complications/chronicity risks associated with the current drug therapy.
(iii) State and justify one physiotherapy (non-pharmacological) treatment option for this patient.
questions.answerText:
(i) Pharmacological treatment for chronic non-cancer pain may be complicated because there are both nociceptive and neuropathic features present in this group.
(ii) It is important to consider the potential side effects of long-term administration of medications, e.g. NSAIMs; in general, strong opioids should be avoided in chronic non-cancer pain.
(iii) Non-pharmacological treatments are usually very important for chronic non-cancer pain; tricyclic antidepressants and anticonvulsants may be helpful for the neuropathic features, and physiotherapy modalities selected according to whether the pain is nociceptive or neuropathic (e.g. electro-analgesic currents for the neuropathic component) are justified.

questions.question:
A) Describe the principles and application of therapeutic exercise and mobilization as physiotherapy modalities for pain.
B) State the step-by-step recommended method for selecting a physiotherapy modality for a patient in pain.
C) Explain the basis on which chronic pain may fail to respond to treatment.
questions.answerText:
A) Therapeutic exercises include specific exercises for correction of body mal-alignment, and mobilization techniques for correction of body mal-alignment and increase of range of motion; elastic band exercises have been noted to reduce pain.
B) Step 1: identify the type of pain - nociceptive or neuropathic; acute, subacute or chronic; cancer or non-cancer pain.
Step 2: analyse underlying factors and presenting symptoms - inflammation, muscle spasm, soft tissue tightness, slight mal-alignment, loss of range of motion and function.
Step 3: decide on the appropriate modality (e.g. cold/heat therapy, electro-analgesic currents, or therapeutic exercise) based on the above analysis.
C) In chronic pain, if tissue damage is continuing there is no biological benefit to the pain, unlike acute pain which functions as a warning and enforces rest for healing.
Chronic pain is maintained by sensitisation of nociceptive pathways, brain 'memory' of pain, enlarged cortical 'representation', negative emotion/stress, and poor healthcare with multiple/conflicting diagnoses - factors not resolved by exercise alone.

questions.question:
A) Describe the classification of pain according to temporal, etiologic and physiological factors.
B) Relate this classification to common chronic pain conditions.
C) Explain why chronic pain persists rather than resolving, in comparison with acute pain.
questions.answerText:
A) Temporal classification: acute pain (up to 3 months) or chronic pain (3 months or more).
Etiologic classification: malignant (of cancer origin) or non-malignant (not of cancer origin).
Physiological classification: nociceptive (somatic - from skin/deeper tissues, usually localised; or visceral - from internal organs, usually diffuse, poorly localised and often referred) or neuropathic (caused by a lesion/dysfunction in the nervous system, peripheral or central).
B) Examples of chronic pain given include low back pain, arthritis, fibromyalgia, migraine, sickle cell disease pain, malignant pain, and neuropathic pain such as trigeminal neuralgia, diabetic neuropathy, phantom limb pain, and post-herpetic neuralgia.
C) Acute pain is caused by threat of or actual tissue damage and functions as a warning, enforcing rest of the healing tissue; it has a clear description of location, pattern, quality, frequency and duration.
Chronic pain is caused by continuing tissue damage and sensitisation of nociceptive pathways, has a vague description, and if tissue damage is continuing has no biological benefit, though it may have social or psychological benefit.
Chronic pain persistence is further explained by sensitivity (nerve hyper-sensitivity), memory (stored pain), representation (enlarged cortical map), emotion (mood/stress), and poor healthcare (conflicting diagnoses).

A(i) The WHO Ladder for cancer pain: Step 1 (mild pain) - use simple analgesics; Step 2 (moderate pain) - continue simple analgesics, add codeine or tramadol (mild opioid); Step 3 (severe pain) - continue simple analgesics, add a strong opioid, usually morphine; the ladder emphasises regular, oral administration of medications.
A(ii) The Reverse WHO Ladder for nociceptive pain: Step 1 (severe pain) - use a strong opioid such as morphine, also use simple analgesics; Step 2 (moderate pain) - continue simple analgesics, use a mild opioid e.g. codeine or tramadol; Step 3 (mild pain) - continue simple analgesics.
B) The WHO Ladder was developed for pain that is getting worse over time as the cancer progresses, allowing stepwise escalation of analgesia matched to increasing severity; additional medications may be required, e.g. strong opioids and NSAIMs for acute-on-chronic bone pain, or tricyclic antidepressants/anticonvulsants for neuropathic pain.
C) The WHO Ladder starts from mild pain and escalates upward through moderate to severe pain as cancer pain worsens over time.
The Reverse WHO Ladder starts from severe pain and steps downward through moderate to mild pain, matching the pattern of nociceptive pain (e.g. acute pain that is initially severe and settles as healing occurs).
Both retain simple analgesics as a continuing base at every step, with opioids (mild or strong) added or reduced according to the direction of the ladder.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the steps of the WHO Analgesic Ladder.
A(ii) Describe the steps of the Reverse WHO Ladder.
B) Explain the clinical basis for using a ladder approach in cancer pain management.
C) Distinguish between the WHO Ladder and the Reverse WHO Ladder.

A patient over 30 years old who is overweight, and whose occupation requires frequent heavy lifting and bending, presents with low back pain.
(i) State the contributing/risk factors present in this patient.
(ii) State the complications or chronicity risks for this patient.
(iii) State and justify one physiotherapy treatment option for this patient.
questions.answerText:
(i) Age: people over 30 are more likely to experience back pain as vertebral disks wear away with age, causing pain and stiffness.
Weight: people who are overweight are more likely to have back pain, as excess weight puts pressure on joints and disks.
Occupation and hobbies: jobs and activities requiring heavy lifting or frequent bending increase the risk of back injury.
(ii) Complications: reduced mobility (difficulty bending, lifting or walking); chronic pain; mental health issues (stress, anxiety, depression); loss of productivity; increased healthcare costs; and reduced quality of life.
(iii) Physical therapy exercises to strengthen core muscles and improve posture are justified, alongside correct lifting technique (bend at hips/knees, keep object close, avoid twisting) and mobilisation techniques for correction of mal-alignment and increase of range of motion.

questions.question:
A patient presents with low back pain that has persisted beyond three months.
(i) State the type/classification of this patient's pain.
(ii) Explain the underlying mechanism of this pain.
(iii) Outline the physiotherapy assessment you would carry out, covering subjective, objective and outcome-measure components.
(iv) Outline a physiotherapy management plan for this patient.
questions.answerText:
(i) This is chronic pain, since it persists beyond three months; chronic low back pain is listed among the common examples of chronic pain.
(ii) Mechanism: sensitised nerves become hyper-sensitive so light touch is felt as pain (sensitivity); the brain stores memory of past pain and reproduces it on a previously painful movement (memory); the brain's body map area for the low back can enlarge and take over other body-part areas so movement elsewhere is felt as low back pain (representation); low mood, decreased activity/fitness and increased stress/frustration maintain the pain (emotion); multiple/conflicting diagnoses (poor healthcare) also contribute.
(iii) Subjective: determine chronicity, severity/intensity, quality, contributing/associated (aggravating/alleviating) factors, and location/distribution or etiology.
Objective: consider the anatomy of the spine, noting the lumbar spine bears most of the body's weight and is a common site of low back pain.
Outcome measures: pain scales such as the visual analogue scale, numerical scale, or verbal rating scale.
(iv) Management: practise back hygiene - maintain good posture, use correct lifting technique (bend at hips/knees, keep the object close, avoid twisting), sit with lumbar support, sleep in a supportive position, exercise to strengthen core muscles, and optimise the workstation; physical therapy exercises to strengthen core muscles and improve posture; rest and activity modification while staying active as tolerated.

(i) A noxious thermal stimulus caused tissue/cell damage, which releases 'algesic' substances such as leukotrienes, hydrogen ions, bradykinin, histamine and serotonin; prostaglandin, though not itself algesic, increases the algesic effect of bradykinin and serotonin.
(ii) This chemical soup sensitises nociceptors so they discharge spontaneously (producing soreness), lower their threshold for activation (producing allodynia, e.g. a feather touch on a burn), and shift their stimulus-response curve leftward (producing hyperalgesia, e.g. a slap on a sun-burnt back); massive/prolonged input can also cause wind-up, giving cutaneous hypersensitivity as seen in sunburned skin areas.
(iii) Cold therapy (cryotherapy) is justified: it is indicated for pain relief and inflammation control in acute pain and for reduction of swelling accompanying pain.
questions.question:
A patient develops acute nociceptive pain following a fresh thermal injury such as a sunburn.
(i) State the contributing/risk factors that led to this pain.
(ii) State the complications or chronicity risks this patient may develop.
(iii) State and justify one physiotherapy treatment option for this patient.

A patient who sustained a burn injury reports that a feather-light touch on the area is now painful, and a slap-like contact on the surrounding sun-burnt skin produces an exaggerated painful response.
(i) State the diagnosis/pain conditions present.
(ii) State the predisposing factors and mechanisms for these conditions.
(iii) State the physiotherapy management for this patient.
questions.answerText:
(i) The feather-touch pain is allodynia (pain evoked by a stimulus that is usually not painful), and the exaggerated response to the slap is hyperalgesia (an increased response to a stimulus that is normally painful).
(ii) Predisposing factor: a noxious stimulus caused cell damage and release of 'algesic' substances (leukotrienes, hydrogen ions, bradykinin, histamine, serotonin), with prostaglandin increasing the algesic effects of bradykinin and serotonin.
Mechanism: this chemical soup sensitises the nociceptors so that their threshold for activation is decreased (producing allodynia) and their stimulus-response curves are shifted to the left (producing hyperalgesia); nociceptors may also discharge spontaneously, producing soreness.
(iii) Physiotherapy management: cold therapy, indicated for pain relief and inflammation control in acute pain and for reduction of swelling; counterirritant-level modalities such as superficial heat or TENS act at the dorsal horn level of antinociception.

questions.question:
A) Describe the principles, physiological effects, indications and parameters of electro-analgesic currents (TENS/Interferential Current) as pain-relief modalities.
B) State the safe/recommended method of applying stimulation to achieve endorphin-mediated pain relief.
questions.answerText:
A) Principle: activation of the large myelinated Aβ fibres associated with low-threshold mechanoreceptors stimulates an inhibitory nerve in the spinal cord that inhibits synaptic transmission, so the painfulness of the stimulus is diminished or not felt - the clinical basis for the development of TENS.
Physiological effect: transmission across the synapse between Aδ/C fibres and dorsal horn cells can be diminished or blocked; a low rate frequency and high intensity current is required to activate C fibres.
Indications: electro-analgesic currents (TENS and Interferential Current) are indicated for neuropathic pain, cancer pain, labour pain, and chronic nociceptive pain.
Parameters: stimulation of afferent nerve fibres for endorphin release uses pulsed rhythmical motor stimulation at low frequency of 2-7 hertz for a long duration of 20-40 minutes.
High-frequency, low-intensity TENS is associated with the counterirritant level of antinociception at the dorsal horn; low-frequency TENS has lasting effects.
B) Apply pulsed rhythmical motor stimulation at a low frequency of 2-7 hertz for a long duration of 20-40 minutes so that Aδ fibres stimulate the pituitary gland to release endogenous opiates (endorphins and adrenocorticotropic hormone) into the blood for prolonged pain control.

questions.question:
A woman in labour requests a non-pharmacological method of pain relief.
(i) State the pain type and mechanism relevant to this request.
(ii) Name a suitable modality.
(iii) State the application/parameters for this modality.
(iv) State the expected physiological effects of this modality.
questions.answerText:
(i) This is acute nociceptive pain of labour; transmission can be modulated at the dorsal horn/gate-control level and via the endogenous opioid and descending inhibitory systems.
(ii) Electro-analgesic currents (TENS/Interferential Current).
(iii) Electro-analgesic currents (TENS and Interferential Current) are indicated for labour pain; specific stimulation parameters include high-frequency low-intensity stimulation (counterirritant/gate effect) or low frequency 2-7 hertz for 20-40 minutes (endorphin-mediated).
(iv) Physiological effect: activation of large Aβ mechanoreceptor fibres closes the gate in the dorsal horn, decreasing transmission of nociceptive impulses and diminishing pain perception.

(i) This is chronic pain (some experts prefer the term 'persistent pain'); it can start with an injury or disease but persists after the injury is healed or the disease is cured, and is a key part of the definition of ailments such as low back pain, some headaches, and fibromyalgia.
(ii) Predisposing factors: psychological factors such as cognitions, incentives, chronic stress, anxiety, depression, and catastrophising predict reactions to pain and ability to cope; distraction reduces pain awareness while isolation and inactivity increase it.
Mechanism: sensitivity (hyper-sensitive nerves), memory (stored pain reproduced on movement), representation (enlarged cortical map), emotion (low mood, stress, frustration), and poor healthcare (multiple/conflicting diagnoses) maintain the chronic pain state.
(iii) Management: address the 3D's - distress, disuse, disability - using psychological interventions (relaxation, biofeedback, imagery, cognitive-behavioural therapy) together with the appropriate physiotherapy modality selected via the identify-analyse-decide management steps.
questions.question:
A patient's pain started with an injury but has persisted well after the injury has healed; the patient's presentation is consistent with conditions such as arthritis, low back pain or fibromyalgia.
(i) State the diagnosis/pain condition.
(ii) State the predisposing factors and mechanisms for this pain persisting.
(iii) State the physiotherapy management for this patient.

A) Describe the drugs used for neuropathic pain and their site/mechanism of action.
B) State the recommended approach to using tramadol and strong opioids in neuropathic pain.
C) Explain the basis on which strong opioids may fail to be effective in neuropathic pain.
questions.answerText:
A) Tricyclic antidepressants (amitriptyline, nortriptyline) and anticonvulsants (carbamazepine, sodium valproate, gabapentin, pregabalin) are likely to play an important role in neuropathic pain; simple analgesics may also be helpful.
Mechanism: tricyclic antidepressants increase descending inhibitory signals in the spinal cord; anticonvulsants are 'membrane stabilisers', probably working by reducing abnormal firing of pain nerves.
Tramadol acts weakly on opioid receptors and also increases descending inhibitory signals in the spinal cord.
B) Tramadol may be useful for neuropathic pain because of its action on descending inhibitory pathways.
Occasionally, strong opioids are helpful in acute, severe, neuropathic pain, but their use should be frequently reassessed.
C) Strong opioids may not be particularly effective in neuropathic pain, which is why their use should be frequently reassessed rather than continued by default.
According to the analgesic usefulness table, morphine is rated only moderately effective (++) for acute neuropathic pain, compared with tricyclic antidepressants and anticonvulsants which are also rated moderately effective (++), indicating that opioids alone are not the most reliable option for this pain type.

questions.question:
During assessment, a patient rates pain intensity on a Visual Analogue Scale and describes the pain as diffuse and poorly localised, seeming to arise from an internal organ but felt on the skin surface.
(i) Interpret these assessment findings.
(ii) State the structures/pathways involved.
(iii) State the differential considerations for this presentation.
(iv) State the clinical reasoning for progressing this patient's treatment.
questions.answerText:
(i) The diffuse, poorly localised quality and the perception on the skin at a site distinct from the actual site of origin indicate referred pain, most often referred from visceral tissue to skin.
(ii) Referred pain is explained by convergence and facilitation of nociceptive information from different sources; it occurs when branches of nociceptive fibres from the skin converge on the same second-order neurons in the spinal cord or in the thalamus, and the central neurons become sensitised.
(iii) This should be differentiated from somatic pain (nociceptive pain from skin/deeper tissue, which is usually well localised) since visceral pain is harder to pinpoint than somatic pain; identifying referred pain is important in preventing misdiagnosis.
(iv) A precise and systematic pain assessment (chronicity, severity, quality, contributing/associated factors, location/distribution or etiology, and mechanism of injury) is required to make the correct diagnosis and determine the most efficacious treatment plan, since the Visual Analogue Scale alone measures only the intensity quality of pain.

A) Cold therapy (cryotherapy): used for pain relief and inflammation control in acute pain, for reduction of swelling accompanying pain, and in certain chronic pain.
Heat therapy (thermotherapy): used for chronic pain, for relief of muscle spasm, and for promoting healing of injured soft tissue.
B) Cold therapy is recommended for acute pain (pain relief, inflammation and swelling control) and for certain chronic pain; heat therapy is recommended for chronic pain, muscle spasm relief, and promoting soft-tissue healing.
C) Selection follows the physiotherapy management steps: first identify the type of pain (nociceptive or neuropathic; acute, subacute or chronic; cancer or non-cancer); then analyse underlying factors and presenting symptoms such as inflammation, muscle spasm or soft tissue tightness; then decide on the appropriate modality accordingly.
questions.question:
A) Describe the principles, physiological effects and indications of cold therapy and heat therapy as pain-relief modalities.
B) State the recommended use of each modality according to the type of pain.
C) Explain the basis on which each modality should be selected.

A(i) Define pain.
A(ii) State the three functions of pain as a warning system.
A(iii) State the three bases on which pain is classified.
B) Explain why a course dedicated to pain is considered necessary in physiotherapy.
C) Distinguish between acute pain and chronic pain.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Pain is an unpleasant sensory and emotional experience associated with actual or potential tissue damage, or described in terms of such damage (IASP).
A(ii) It warns of injury; it protects against further injury by causing reflexive withdrawal from the source of injury; it leads to a period of reduced activity, enabling injuries to heal more efficiently.
A(iii) Temporal (acute or chronic); Etiologic (malignant or non-malignant); Physiological (nociceptive - somatic or visceral - or neuropathic).
B) Pain is a prevalent health complaint and a common reason people seek physiotherapy; it often causes disability requiring physiotherapy; it is often undertreated in Nigeria because of cultural beliefs and poor health services.
C) Acute pain is caused by threat of or actual tissue damage; chronic pain is caused by continuing tissue damage and sensitisation of nociceptive pathways.
Acute pain has a clear description of location, pattern, quality, frequency and duration; chronic pain has a vague description.
Acute pain functions as a warning of tissue damage and enforces rest of healing tissue; if tissue damage is continuing, chronic pain has no biological benefit but may have social or psychological benefit.

(i) This is neuropathic pain of central origin, given as an example of abnormal activity in the nerve circuits that is perceived as pain, with cortical re-organisation.
(ii) Mechanism: continued stimulation of the NMDA receptor produces central sensitisation, causing the post-synaptic cell to respond more strongly to inputs; this hyperexcitable state can change genetic expression and influence long-term cellular function, giving rise to neuroplasticity and 'pain memory' - pain in the absence of a stimulus, as in phantom limb pain.
(iii) Subjective assessment: chronicity, severity/intensity, quality (e.g. burning, electric shock, lightning bolt), and contributing factors.
Outcome measures: pain scales such as the visual analogue, numerical, or verbal rating scale.
(iv) Management: electro-analgesic currents (TENS/Interferential Current), which are indicated for neuropathic pain; psychological interventions to decrease activation of the pain system and improve coping skills.
questions.question:
A patient who has undergone limb amputation reports pain that feels as if it is arising from the missing limb.
(i) State the type/classification of this pain.
(ii) Explain the underlying mechanism of this pain.
(iii) Outline the physiotherapy assessment for this patient.
(iv) Outline the physiotherapy management for this patient.

questions.answerText:
A) Psychological interventions decrease activation of the pain system and improve coping skills; they include relaxation (breathing and muscle relaxation), biofeedback, imagery, and cognitive-behavioural therapy.
They are indicated for chronic pain, particularly to address the '3D's' - distress, disuse, disability.
B) Placebo-associated improvement is any genuine psychological or physiologic effect attributable to receiving a substance or undergoing a procedure; the recommended method is speaking positively (yet honestly), providing encouragement and education, and developing trust with the patient.
Placebo antinociception activates the same higher-order cognitive and brainstem structures that are activated by opiate drugs.
C) Chronic pain treatment can fail because of continuing sensitisation of nociceptive pathways, brain memory and cortical representation of pain, negative emotion/stress, and poor healthcare with multiple/conflicting diagnoses.
The patient's psychological state can contribute significantly to complaints of pain and suffering (psychogenic pain); symptoms and their distress are real to the patient regardless of the degree to which psychological factors are involved.
Focusing exclusively on and worrying about pain (an aspect of the cognitive-evaluative component of the pain matrix) can increase distress and hinder resolution.
questions.question:
A) Describe the principles, effects and indications of psychological interventions used in pain management.
B) State the recommended method of delivering placebo-associated improvement.
C) Explain the basis of treatment failure for chronic pain that these interventions aim to address.

questions.answerText:
A) A low rate frequency and high intensity current is required to activate C fibres; modalities listed for this purpose include acupuncture, acupressure, point stimulators, neural probe, and Interx 5000.
Mechanism: all endogenous opioids (endorphins, enkephalins, dynorphin) act by attaching to opiate receptors on the plasma membrane of the afferent neuron, inhibiting release of neurotransmitter and thus blocking transmission of the painful stimulus.
Aδ fibres send messages via the spinothalamic tract to activate the reticular formation and thus the pituitary gland, causing production of endorphins and adrenocorticotropic hormone, which cause pain relief.
B) Stimulation of afferent nerve fibres should have the following characteristics: pulsed rhythmical motor stimulation; low frequency of 2-7 hertz; long duration of 20-40 minutes, for prolonged pain control via endogenous opiate release.
questions.question:
A) Describe the principle and physiological basis of acupuncture/point-stimulation modalities for pain relief.
B) State the parameters and application method for stimulating C-fibre-mediated pain relief.

A) Describe the classification of analgesic drugs used for pain control.
B) State the recommended (WHO Ladder) method of administering analgesics for cancer pain.
C) Explain the basis of treatment failure for chronic non-cancer pain drug therapy.
questions.answerText:
A) Simple analgesics (paracetamol/acetaminophen; NSAIMs such as aspirin, ibuprofen, diclofenac); opioids - mild (codeine, tramadol) and strong (morphine, pethidine, oxycodone); tricyclic antidepressants (amitriptyline, nortriptyline); anticonvulsants (carbamazepine, sodium valproate, gabapentin, pregabalin); local anaesthetics (lignocaine/lidocaine, bupivacaine); and others (ketamine, clonidine).
They act at different sites: paracetamol, opioids and tramadol act in the brain; amitriptyline, tramadol and clonidine act on descending pathways; opioids, local anaesthetics and ketamine act at the spinal cord; local anaesthetics and NSAIMs act at the periphery/site of injury.
B) The WHO Ladder was developed for cancer pain that worsens over time: Step 1 (mild pain) - use simple analgesics; Step 2 (moderate pain) - continue simple analgesics and add codeine or tramadol; Step 3 (severe pain) - continue simple analgesics and add a strong opioid, usually morphine.
The WHO Ladder emphasises regular, oral administration of medications; additional medications may be needed, e.g. strong opioids and NSAIMs for acute-on-chronic bone pain, or tricyclic antidepressants/anticonvulsants for neuropathic pain.
C) For chronic non-cancer pain, treatment may be complicated because there are both nociceptive and neuropathic features; potential side effects of long-term administration of medications (e.g. NSAIMs) must be considered.
In general, strong opioids should be avoided in chronic non-cancer pain; non-pharmacological treatments are usually very important for this group.
The effectiveness of an individual analgesic depends on the type of pain, so combinations of medications are usually required, e.g. paracetamol plus morphine for severe acute nociceptive pain.
