questions.explanation: Neutrophil hypersegmentation, defined as more than 5% of neutrophils having more than five nuclear lobes, is a hallmark of megaloblastic anaemia. This nuclear abnormality reflects impaired DNA synthesis affecting all rapidly dividing cells. Hypersegmented neutrophils may persist for weeks after treatment initiation, indicating their prolonged lifespan.
questions.question: What characteristic neutrophil abnormality appears in megaloblastic anaemia?

questions.explanation: Bronze or slate-gray skin pigmentation results from iron deposition in dermal melanocytes combined with increased melanin production in advanced haemochromatosis. This pigmentation particularly affects sun-exposed areas and earned the historical term "bronzed diabetes" when combined with pancreatic involvement. The pigmentation may partially reverse with treatment.
questions.question: What dermatological finding is characteristic of advanced haemochromatosis?
When is splenectomy indicated in ITP?
questions.explanation: Splenectomy is indicated for patients not responding to corticosteroids or requiring high maintenance doses. Approximately 80% of patients respond to splenectomy. Steroids and platelet transfusion support perioperative period.
options: Non-response to steroids or high-dose requirement

questions.question: For what indication has Oxygent been studied in Phase III clinical trials
questions.explanation: Oxygent underwent Phase III trials for use in cardiac surgery as a CPB prime and hemodilution application. The trials evaluated its effectiveness in reducing allogeneic blood transfusion requirements. This indication represented a controlled environment for blood substitute evaluation.

Beta thalassaemia major symptoms emerge around one year when foetal haemoglobin levels decline physiologically. Initial neonatal period appears normal due to compensatory HbF. Clinical manifestations develop as beta chain requirement increases postnatally.
questions.question: What age marks onset of beta thalassaemia major symptoms
What characterizes the bleeding pattern in platelet disorders?
questions.explanation: Platelet disorders characteristically cause mucocutaneous bleeding (epistaxis, gum bleeding, menorrhagia, GI bleeding) with petechiae and purpura, contrasting with coagulation disorders causing deep tissue bleeding. Bleeding occurs immediately after trauma and is usually mild. Petechiae (pinpoint hemorrhages) are pathognomonic of thrombocytopenia or platelet dysfunction, never occurring in pure coagulation factor deficiencies, providing important clinical diagnostic distinction.

SDS coats protein molecules giving all proteins a constant charge-to-mass ratio masking intrinsic charges. Proteins then migrate according to size in order of increasing molecular weights. This uniform charging enables accurate molecular weight determination.
questions.question: What does SDS do to proteins in SDS-PAGE?

questions.explanation: Blood trafficking of B and T lymphocytes occurs in the marginal zone, facilitating immune cell circulation and surveillance. This trafficking allows lymphocytes to sample blood antigens before entering white pulp. The marginal zone serves as a transitional area between the vascular compartment and lymphoid tissue.
questions.question: What cellular trafficking function occurs in the marginal zone

questions.explanation: The direct antiglobulin test (DAT) using anti-IgG reagent is the most important serologic test for HDFN diagnosis, detecting maternal IgG antibodies coating infant red cells. Positive DAT confirms in vivo antibody binding, though negative results don't exclude HDFN.
questions.question: Which test is most important for diagnosing HDFN in cord blood

questions.explanation: Haemoglobin is measured at 525 nanometers after LH diluent breaks down red blood cells and binds to haemoglobin. This forms a stable complex that is measurable at this specific wavelength using a specialized photometer. The measurement provides accurate haemoglobin concentration for anaemia assessment.
questions.question: What wavelength is used to measure haemoglobin in automated analyzers?
What is the normal PT range in seconds?
questions.explanation: The normal Prothrombin Time range is 11-16 seconds, though some laboratories report 12-14 or 16-18 seconds depending on reagent sensitivity and methodology. Values exceeding this range indicate deficiencies in extrinsic or common pathway factors or presence of inhibitors. PT standardization through INR calculation addresses inter-laboratory variability, making results comparable regardless of thromboplastin reagent used.

questions.question: What combination achieves high resolution typing?
questions.explanation: Combining SSP-PCR with RFLP analysis can achieve high resolution by using complementary strengths of both methods. SSP-PCR provides initial allele group identification while RFLP resolves ambiguities within groups. This combination approach is more comprehensive than either method alone.

2,3-BPG decreases the affinity of hemoglobin for oxygen, helping oxyhemoglobin unload oxygen to tissues. It is formed through the Rapoport-Luebering shunt, a modification of the glycolytic pathway. Storage of blood results in decreased 2,3-BPG, leading to high oxygen affinity hemoglobin and oxygen trapping.
questions.question: What is the role of 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG) in red blood cells?
What accompanies qualitative test results in pattern recognition?
questions.explanation: Pattern recognition involves discerning qualitative plus quantitative test results as normal or abnormal, then establishing disease associations. This integrated approach combines morphological features with numerical parameters. Comprehensive assessment enhances diagnostic accuracy significantly.

questions.question: What immunoglobulin abnormality occurs in CLL?
questions.explanation: Hypogammaglobulinemia develops in CLL as abnormal lymphocytes don't produce functional antibodies. Low immunoglobulin levels increase infection susceptibility. Some patients receive immunoglobulin replacement therapy for recurrent severe infections.

Platelets possess Fc receptors (CD32) allowing them to bind immunoglobulin G antibodies. They also have complement binding molecules including C1q, C2, and C4 receptors. These immune receptors enable platelets to participate in inflammatory and immune responses.
questions.question: What immune receptor is found on platelets?

options: Deep bleeding into muscles or joints
questions.explanation: Deep bleeding into muscles or joints characteristically occurs with coagulation disorders affecting clotting factors. Hemarthrosis and muscle hematomas suggest factor deficiency. Coagulation defects cause deep tissue bleeding.
questions.question: What bleeding pattern suggests coagulation disorders?

questions.explanation: Factor IX is activated by the complex of tissue factor and factor VII in the coagulation cascade. This activation connects extrinsic and intrinsic pathways. Factor IXa then participates in tenase complex formation.
questions.question: What activates factor IX in the intrinsic pathway?
options: Complex of tissue factor and factor VII

questions.question: How do NSAIDs interact with warfarin to increase bleeding risk?
questions.explanation: NSAIDs inhibit platelet aggregation and may displace warfarin from binding sites, increasing bleeding risk. The combined antiplatelet and anticoagulant effects potentiate hemorrhage. This interaction requires careful consideration of bleeding risk.

questions.question: What is the typical white blood cell count range in CML chronic phase?
questions.explanation: White blood cell counts in CML chronic phase typically range from 25,000 to 300×10⁹/L. The count shows marked granulocytosis including all maturation stages from blasts to segmented neutrophils. Predominance of more mature forms from myelocytes to segmented neutrophils is characteristic.

Volume reduction removes ABO-incompatible plasma from platelet products to prevent hemolytic reactions. This is critical when transfusing platelets with significant plasma volume. It also reduces volume load in at-risk patients.
questions.question: When must volume reduction of platelets be considered

questions.explanation: CD8+ T-cells are typically absent from splenic follicles, which are composed primarily of B-cells with fewer follicular dendritic cells and CD4+ T-cells. This selective cell distribution reflects the specialized function of follicles in humoral immunity. The larger lymphocytes at the follicular center are surrounded by a mantle zone of small to medium lymphocytes.
questions.question: Which cell type is typically absent from splenic follicles

questions.explanation: LTT requires specialized equipment (incubators, sterile culture facilities, scintillation counters or flow cytometers) and trained personnel for proper execution and interpretation. This technical complexity limits availability to specialized laboratories, potentially affecting clinical accessibility and implementation.
questions.question: Which technical requirement limits LTT accessibility
options: No equipment beyond basic microscope needed
Any clinic can perform without special training
Results available within 30 minutes of testing
Specialized laboratory equipment and expertise required

questions.explanation: Sodium dithionite (NaSO), also called sodium hydrosulfite, serves as the potent reducing agent. This chemical rapidly removes oxygen from haemoglobin molecules. The strong reducing properties make dithionite ideal for sickling test applications.
questions.question: What is the chemical formula for sodium dithionite

questions.explanation: Standard haemoglobin electrophoresis runs for 30 minutes duration allowing adequate variant separation. This timeframe provides sufficient migration distance for visual distinction. Shorter times produce incomplete separation while longer times offer minimal improvement.
questions.question: What duration is standard for haemoglobin electrophoresis

questions.explanation: Neutrophils are treated with 1% paraformaldehyde for 5 minutes to stabilize cell membranes and prevent nonspecific antibody binding to Fc receptors. This fixation step is critical for reducing background in immunofluorescence assays. Paraformaldehyde maintains membrane antigen integrity while blocking Fc receptors.
questions.question: What pretreatment stabilizes neutrophils for immunofluorescence?

questions.explanation: CLL cells are fragile and break easily when smeared on glass slides, creating characteristic smudge cells. These broken cells appear as bare nuclei or nuclear remnants on peripheral blood films. The cells morphologically resemble normal lymphocytes although slightly larger.
questions.question: What is the characteristic appearance of CLL cells on blood smear?

questions.explanation: Severe B12 deficiency requires at least 2 years to develop following complete cessation of absorption, reflecting the time needed for hepatic stores to deplete at the rate of 1-2μg daily. This contrasts sharply with folate deficiency which develops within 4 months. The prolonged timeframe explains delayed symptom onset after gastrectomy.
questions.question: How long does it take for severe B12 deficiency to develop after complete malabsorption begins?

options: Type I affects only RBCs, Type II affects all cells
questions.explanation: Type I cytochrome b5 reductase deficiency affects only red blood cells, causing cyanosis without other symptoms. Type II affects all cell types, causing severe neurological abnormalities in addition to methemoglobinemia. The different tissue distributions reflect expression of different isoforms from alternative transcription start sites in the same gene.
questions.question: What differentiates Type I from Type II cytochrome b5 reductase deficiency?

questions.explanation: Thalassaemia demonstrates normal or elevated ferritin levels contrasting with low ferritin in iron deficiency anaemia. Iron stores remain adequate or increased despite microcytic anaemia. This distinction proves crucial for differential diagnosis.
questions.question: What iron study pattern distinguishes thalassaemia from iron deficiency

questions.explanation: CDC testing begins with obtaining a buffy coat sample from the patient, which contains the lymphocytes to be tested. These lymphocytes are then exposed to panels of known HLA-specific antibodies. The buffy coat provides concentrated white blood cells necessary for the assay.
questions.question: What sample is used for CDC testing?
What is the normal weight range of an adult spleen
questions.explanation: The normal adult spleen weighs between 70 and 200 grams, with variations depending on individual body size and gender. Weights exceeding 400-500g indicate splenomegaly, while weights over 1000g represent massive splenomegaly. This weight measurement is more accurate than size alone for defining splenic enlargement in pathological conditions.

Pancellular HPFH shows uniform HbF distribution throughout all red blood cells rather than restricted populations. Every erythrocyte contains elevated foetal haemoglobin. This contrasts with heterocellular HPFH where only specific cell populations contain HbF.
questions.question: What distribution pattern defines pancellular HPFH

questions.explanation: Ferritin assessment distinguishes thalassaemia trait from iron deficiency anaemia, both presenting with microcytosis. Thalassaemia maintains normal/elevated stores while iron deficiency depletes them. This differentiation prevents inappropriate iron therapy.
questions.question: Why must ferritin be assessed in microcytic anaemia evaluation
At what age do premature infant APTT values normalize?
questions.explanation: Premature infants have physiologically prolonged APTT values due to immature liver synthesis of contact factors (XII, XI) and vitamin K-dependent factors, normalizing by 6 months as hepatic function matures. Term infants show milder prolongation normalizing earlier. This physiological immaturity doesn't indicate bleeding disorder unless excessive bleeding occurs. Factor levels reach adult values by 6-12 months, explaining why neonatal coagulation testing requires age-specific reference ranges.

Beta-2 microglobulin (β2M) is a non-transmembrane polypeptide that forms the light chain of Class I molecules. Unlike the heavy chain, β2M is non-polymorphic and not encoded by the HLA complex. Its association with the heavy chain is essential for stable expression of Class I molecules on cell surfaces.
questions.question: What is the characteristic of beta-2 microglobulin in Class I molecules?
What shelf life advantage does Hemopure offer
questions.explanation: Hemopure can be stored for 24 months at room temperature, providing exceptional shelf life compared to donated blood's 42 days. This extended stability simplifies inventory management and enables stockpiling for emergencies. The long shelf life is a significant logistical advantage.

questions.question: What granule contents amplify platelet aggregation?
questions.explanation: Platelet granules contain ADP, serotonin, and other substances that amplify the aggregation response when released. This positive feedback mechanism enhances platelet recruitment to growing thrombi. Granule release is a critical amplification step in hemostasis.

questions.question: Which haemoglobin variant contains delta chains in its structure
questions.explanation: Haemoglobin A possesses the molecular structure , making it the only normal adult haemoglobin containing delta chains. This minor component comprises less than 3% of adult erythrocyte haemoglobin content. Elevated HbA levels serve as diagnostic markers for beta thalassaemia trait.
During Hess's test, sphygmomanometer is inflated to 80 mm Hg for 5 minutes to assess capillary fragility. A 5 cm diameter area is marked on antecubital fossa. Normally 3-5 purpuric eruptions appear.
questions.question: How long is the sphygmomanometer inflated during Hess's test?
What explains the difference in DAT positivity between Rh and ABO HDFN
options: Both are consistently positive in all cases
Rh can be negative; ABO always strongly positive
Rh always positive; ABO can be positive or negative
Neither shows reliable DAT positivity patterns
Both are typically negative requiring elution
questions.explanation: Rh HDFN consistently produces positive DAT due to strong IgG anti-D binding to well-developed RhD antigen. ABO HDFN may show positive or negative DAT because of weak foetal ABO antigen expression and low antibody density, despite clinical disease.

One RBC unit increases hemoglobin by approximately 1 g/dL and hematocrit by 3% in average adults. This predictable increment helps guide transfusion therapy. Individual response varies with blood volume, ongoing bleeding, and hemolysis.
questions.question: By approximately how much does one unit of RBCs increase hemoglobin in an average adult
What does gene expression profiling identify in leukemia?
questions.explanation: Gene expression profiling identifies molecular subtypes and provides prognostic information beyond morphology and cytogenetics. This technology measures thousands of gene expression levels simultaneously. Patterns predict treatment response and outcomes guiding personalized therapy.

HPA polymorphisms result from single nucleotide polymorphisms in genes encoding platelet membrane glycoproteins. These SNPs cause amino acid changes that create antigens capable of eliciting antibodies. The polymorphisms are inherited and vary in frequency among different populations.
questions.question: What causes HPA polymorphisms?
What cell type appears elevated in beta thalassaemia major peripheral blood
questions.explanation: Numerous nucleated red blood cells (NRBCs) appear in beta thalassaemia major reflecting premature release from hyperplastic marrow. This leukoerythroblastic picture indicates severe erythroid stress. NRBC presence correlates with disease severity and transfusion dependence.

questions.question: How many G6PD variants have been defined worldwide?
questions.explanation: More than 300 G6PD variants have been defined globally with varying degrees of enzyme deficiency and clinical severity. Five classes of G6PD deficiency exist based on enzyme activity levels ranging from severe deficiency (<10%) to increased enzyme activity. Different variants predominate in different racial groups reflecting geographic distribution patterns.

Duration and severity of vitamin B12 deficiency directly correlate with neuropathy extent and potential for recovery. Severe, long-standing deficiency causes irreversible demyelination and axonal degeneration. Early detection and treatment, particularly before severe neuropathy develops, enables complete or near-complete neurological recovery. Mild cases may recover fully.
questions.question: What factor influences severity of B12 neuropathy?
Which complement components are encoded in Class III region?
questions.explanation: The Class III region encodes complement components C2, C4, and factor B, which are crucial for immune defense. These complement proteins participate in the classical and alternative pathways of complement activation. The region also contains genes for TNF and heat shock proteins.

The density of A or B antigens on platelet surfaces is about 5% of that on erythrocytes. Despite this lower density, ABO antigens can still produce immune conflicts. Some ABO antigens are intrinsic membrane components while others are plasma-derived and adsorbed.
questions.question: What is the density of ABO antigens on platelets?
At what gestational week does the spleen become the principal site for erythropoiesis
questions.explanation: From week 10 to 25 of gestation, the spleen functions as the principal site for erythropoiesis after starting this function at week 9. This period represents a critical phase in fetal hematopoiesis before the bone marrow assumes dominance. After week 25, the bone marrow gradually becomes the primary site of blood cell production.

ITP results from immune destruction of platelets by IgG antibodies, causing accelerated reticuloendothelial system removal. Sensitized platelets have 1-2 day lifespan versus normal 10 days. Spleen is primary destruction site.
questions.question: What is the primary mechanism in idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura?

questions.explanation: Outdated banked blood serves as a primary source of hemoglobin for many HBOCs, utilizing blood that would otherwise be discarded. This approach addresses both supply and waste issues. However, public concerns exist about using outdated blood products.
questions.question: What is the primary source of hemoglobin for first-generation HBOCs

questions.explanation: directly measures fibrinogen-to-fibrin conversion by adding thrombin to plasma, bypassing all upstream coagulation steps in both intrinsic and extrinsic pathways. This test specifically evaluates fibrinogen concentration and function, and detects thrombin inhibitors like heparin or fibrin degradation products. TT is markedly prolonged by heparin contamination, making it useful for detecting heparin in samples.
questions.question: Which test bypasses all prior coagulation steps to measure fibrin formation directly?

questions.explanation: MAIPA requires considerable operator expertise to ensure maximum sensitivity and specificity. The technique involves multiple steps including platelet preparation, antibody incubation, glycoprotein capture, and detection. Proper technique and quality control are essential for reliable results.
questions.question: What does MAIPA require for optimal results?

questions.explanation: Production of immune mediators involved in bacterial clearance includes complement, opsonins, properdin, and tuftsin. These molecules enhance bacterial opsonization and phagocytosis. Tuftsin specifically stimulates phagocyte function and is unique to splenic production.
questions.question: What immune molecule production involves white pulp for bacterial clearance
What effect do third-generation cephalosporins have on warfarin?
questions.explanation: Third-generation cephalosporins potentiate warfarin effect, increasing bleeding risk through multiple mechanisms. Antibiotics reduce vitamin K-producing gut bacteria. Combined effect requires INR monitoring.

options: All A, B, C, DRB1 matched
questions.explanation: An 8 of 8 match means the patient's and donor's HLA markers at A, B, C, and DRB1 all match perfectly. This represents matching at two alleles for each of these four loci. When DQ markers also match, it becomes a 10 of 10 match.
questions.question: What is an 8 of 8 HLA match?
What is the outdate time for deglycerolized RBCs after thawing
questions.explanation: Deglycerolized RBCs must be transfused within 24 hours after thawing and washing. The deglycerolization process opens the system, eliminating sterility assurance. This short outdate necessitates careful planning for frozen RBC use.

questions.question: Why don't all DNA changes affect proteins?
questions.explanation: Some DNA sequence changes are silent mutations that do not alter the amino acid sequence of the resulting protein. Other nucleotide changes may cause amino acid substitutions that don't affect antibody recognition. Not all genetic variation results in functional or immunological differences.

questions.question: What is the incubation temperature for coagulation testing?
questions.explanation: Coagulation testing is performed at 37°C (normal body temperature) to ensure physiological enzyme activity and reaction kinetics. Temperature significantly affects coagulation times: lower temperatures prolong tests by slowing enzymatic reactions, while higher temperatures accelerate reactions. Water baths, heat blocks, or automated analyzers maintain precise 37°C temperature. All reagents, plasma samples, and reaction mixtures must equilibrate to 37°C before testing.

Hemolink is both crosslinked and polymerized using ring-opened raffinose, providing a different chemical approach to hemoglobin stabilization. This technique aims to optimize both molecular stability and circulation time. The raffinose-based modification creates unique product characteristics.
questions.question: What crosslinking agent is used in Hemolink production

questions.explanation: G6PD activity decreases significantly as erythrocytes age, with a half-life of approximately 60 days. Reticulocytes have five times higher G6PD activity than the oldest erythrocyte subpopulation. This explains why hemolytic episodes in G6PD A- deficiency are self-limited, as young RBCs have nearly normal enzyme levels.
questions.question: What is the approximate half-life of G6PD enzyme activity in erythrocytes?

questions.explanation: Cytochrome b5 reductase (previously known as NADH diaphorase or methemoglobin reductase) catalyzes the physiologically important NADH-dependent reduction of methemoglobin. This enzyme contains a noncovalently bound FAD group that acts as electron acceptor, transferring electrons from NADH to cytochrome b5. Type I deficiency affects only red blood cells.
questions.question: Which enzyme catalyzes the physiologically important reduction of methemoglobin?
How is DNA sequencing performed in SBT?
questions.explanation: After PCR amplification, products undergo DNA sequencing using both forward and reverse sequencing primers for bidirectional coverage. This bidirectional approach ensures complete coverage of amplified regions and provides redundancy for accuracy. Both strands are analyzed to confirm sequence determination.

Platelets are small anucleate discoid cells measuring approximately 1-2 micrometers in diameter. They are abundantly present in blood at 150,000-450,000 per microliter during normal health. Their small size allows them to circulate easily and respond quickly to vascular injury.
questions.question: What size are platelets typically?

questions.explanation: ABO HDFN causes delayed bilirubin peak at 1-3 days postpartum, later than Rh disease which presents with higher immediate levels. This delayed peak in ABO disease reflects milder ongoing haemolysis and allows time for phototherapy intervention before dangerous levels develop.
options: ABO peaks at birth; Rh peaks at 3-5 days
ABO peaks at 5-7 days; Rh peaks at 1-3 days
ABO peaks at 1-3 days; Rh peaks immediately at birth
ABO peaks earlier than Rh by 24 hours
questions.question: When does bilirubin peak in ABO HDFN compared to Rh disease

questions.explanation: Platelets are disc-shaped with 2-3 microns diameter, appearing with blue granular core on microscopy. Electron microscopy reveals peripheral and central zones. Size uniformity indicates normal platelet production.
questions.question: What is the normal diameter range of platelets?
Why does the foetus not develop jaundice in utero despite ongoing haemolysis
options: Foetal liver efficiently conjugates all bilirubin produced
Placenta transfers unconjugated bilirubin to maternal circulation
Foetal kidneys excrete bilirubin directly through amniotic fluid
Maternal antibodies prevent bilirubin formation in utero
Foetal macrophages sequester bilirubin in spleen tissue
questions.explanation: During pregnancy, unconjugated bilirubin from foetal red cell destruction crosses the placenta into maternal circulation. The maternal liver then conjugates this bilirubin for excretion, preventing foetal jaundice until birth when placental transfer ceases.

Diphyllobothrium latum (fish tapeworm) infection causes vitamin B12 deficiency by competing for B12 in the intestinal lumen, with the parasite consuming dietary B12 before host absorption. This occurs primarily in regions consuming raw freshwater fish. Parasite eradication with praziquantel combined with B12 replacement resolves the deficiency.
questions.question: What mechanism causes megaloblastic anaemia in fish tapeworm infection?

options: 5 mL packed cells or 10 mL whole blood
10 mL packed cells or 20 mL whole blood
20 mL packed cells or 40 mL whole blood
25 mL packed cells or 50 mL whole blood
15 mL packed cells or 30 mL whole blood
questions.question: How many milliliters of D-positive packed RBCs does full-dose RhIg neutralize
questions.explanation: Standard 300 microgram dose of RhIg is sufficient to neutralize 15 mL D-positive packed red cells, equivalent to 30 mL whole blood. Larger foeto-maternal haemorrhage volumes require additional RhIg doses calculated from Kleihauer-Betke or flow cytometry quantification.

PBF exposes the morphology of peripheral blood cells, ensuring its place in morphologic diagnosis of blood-related diseases. Direct visualization reveals cellular details including size, shape, color, and inclusions. This morphological information is essential for diagnosing conditions that automated analyzers cannot fully characterize.
questions.question: What ensures PBF's place in morphologic diagnosis?
What percentage of enzyme deficiency patients are affected by phosphoglucose isomerase deficiency?
questions.explanation: Phosphoglucose isomerase deficiency accounts for 4% of genetic defects in glycolytic enzymes, while pyruvate kinase deficiency accounts for 95%. The remaining 1% includes various other rare glycolytic enzyme deficiencies. All these defects result in reduced ATP production, compromising cell integrity and causing hemolytic anemia.

questions.question: What is the earliest observable change in complete blood count during folate deficiency?
questions.explanation: Red cell distribution width (RDW) increases earliest during folate deficiency, even before macrocytosis becomes apparent or anaemia develops. This reflects increasing variation in red cell size as the deficiency progresses. RDW elevation precedes changes in MCV and haemoglobin concentration by several weeks.

questions.question: What erythrocyte inclusion has diagnostic significance for hyposplenism
questions.explanation: Howell-Jolly bodies have greater diagnostic significance for hyposplenism than nonspecific changes like leukocytosis or thrombocytosis. These nuclear remnants persist because the spleen normally removes them through pitting. Their presence, along with pitted erythrocytes and target cells, confirms reduced splenic function.

questions.question: What increases in old red blood cells compared to young cells?
questions.explanation: Osmotic fragility increases in old red blood cells while sialic acid, potassium, and enzyme activity decrease. Sodium concentration, IgG binding, cell density, and sphericity increase with aging. These cumulative changes make aging RBCs less flexible, more spherical, and more prone to hemolysis, ultimately leading to removal by the reticuloendothelial system.

questions.question: Faggot cells are characteristic of which AML classification?
questions.explanation: Faggot cells represent bundles of Auer rods and are classical findings in M3 (acute promyelocytic leukaemia). These structures appear as multiple Auer rods clustered together within a single cell. Their presence strongly suggests the diagnosis of acute promyelocytic leukaemia variant.

questions.question: How does heparin enhance anticoagulation?
questions.explanation: Heparin enhances anticoagulation by binding to antithrombin, inducing conformational change that accelerates its inhibition of thrombin and Factor Xa approximately 1000-fold. Unfractionated heparin inhibits both thrombin and Xa (requires longer chain), while low molecular weight heparins preferentially inhibit Xa. This indirect mechanism explains why heparin requires adequate antithrombin levels for effect and why antithrombin deficiency causes heparin resistance.

In PK deficiency, 2,3-DPG levels increase due to metabolic block at the pyruvate kinase step in glycolysis. PK enzymatic activity and ATP levels are usually decreased in the red cell. The elevated 2,3-DPG decreases hemoglobin's oxygen affinity, partially compensating for the anemia by improving oxygen delivery to tissues.
questions.question: What metabolic change occurs in RBCs with pyruvate kinase deficiency?
What is the normal thrombin time range?
questions.explanation: Normal thrombin time ranges from 10 to 20 seconds, measuring fibrinogen conversion to fibrin. Prolongation occurs with fibrinogen deficiency, dysfibrinogenemia, or inhibitors like heparin. TT isolates fibrinogen function assessment.

Blast crisis is defined by presence of more than 30% blasts in blood or bone marrow. This represents transformation to aggressive acute phase with median survival of 3 months or less. The blasts may have myeloid (70-75%) or lymphoid (25-30%) phenotype.
questions.question: What percentage of blasts defines blast crisis in CML?

questions.explanation: Massive splenomegaly may extend far enough to be palpable in the right iliac fossa, crossing the midline. Normal splenomegaly is usually apparent under the left costal margin. The extent of splenic enlargement helps narrow the differential diagnosis.
questions.question: Where can massive splenomegaly be palpated during physical examination
What is the minimum granulocyte count required in apheresis-derived products
questions.explanation: Apheresis granulocytes must contain at least 1 x 10^10 granulocytes per collection. Donor stimulation with G-CSF and corticosteroids can increase yields above 1 x 10^11. Higher doses improve therapeutic efficacy.

Coverslip edges should be sealed with petroleum jelly-paraffin wax mixture or depex preventing oxygen diffusion. This sealing maintains deoxygenated conditions essential for HbS polymerization. Proper sealing prevents false-negative results from oxygen contamination.
questions.question: How should coverslip edges be sealed in sickling test preparations

questions.explanation: Rejuvenation restores 2,3-DPG and ATP to near-fresh levels in stored RBCs. This process improves oxygen delivery capacity. Rejuvenation is typically performed before freezing; units must be washed before transfusion.
questions.question: What is the purpose of red blood cell rejuvenation

questions.explanation: DIC pathophysiology involves widespread coagulation activation causing microthrombi formation (thrombosis) with simultaneous consumption of platelets and coagulation factors, followed by secondary fibrinolysis producing FDPs/D-dimer. This creates paradoxical bleeding despite ongoing thrombosis. Triggering conditions include sepsis, obstetric complications, malignancy, and major trauma. Treatment requires addressing underlying cause while supporting hemostasis with transfusions.
questions.question: What characterizes DIC pathophysiology?
What is TRALI mortality rate?
questions.explanation: The mortality associated with TRALI was 6% in early series. Most patients recover rapidly with 80% showing resolution within 96 hours. However, pulmonary infiltrates can persist for at least 7 days in approximately 17% of cases requiring extended respiratory support.

questions.question: Which deficiency specifically causes subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord?
questions.explanation: uniquely causes subacute combined degeneration affecting posterior columns and lateral corticospinal tracts of the spinal cord. The neuropathy is progressive, symmetrical, and affects lower limbs more than upper limbs. Peripheral sensory nerves are also involved. Folate deficiency does not cause neurological manifestations despite similar haematological changes.

questions.question: What cancer risk increases in long-standing pernicious anaemia?
questions.explanation: Gastric carcinoma and gastric carcinoid tumor risk increases 2-3 fold in pernicious anaemia due to chronic atrophic gastritis, achlorhydria, hypergastrinaemia, and intestinal metaplasia. Endoscopic surveillance is recommended though optimal intervals are debated. Helicobacter pylori infection additionally increases gastric cancer risk requiring eradication when present.

questions.question: What parasitic infection commonly causes iron deficiency in tropical regions?
questions.explanation: Hookworm infestation causes chronic intestinal blood loss through attachment to intestinal mucosa and anticoagulant secretion, making it a leading cause of iron deficiency globally in endemic areas. Schistosomiasis also contributes significantly. Heavy infestations can cause severe iron deficiency requiring both iron replacement and antiparasitic treatment.

Plasma thaws at 30-37 degrees C in approximately 20 minutes, preserving coagulation factor activity. Lower temperatures require excessive time while higher temperatures may denature proteins. Thawed plasma is then refrigerated if not immediately transfused.
questions.question: What temperature range is used for thawing plasma products before transfusion
What age group is primarily affected by Henoch-Schonlein purpura?
questions.explanation: Henoch-Schonlein purpura affects children following streptococcal sore throat, causing IgA-mediated vasculitis. Capillaritis and arteriolitis produce characteristic purpura over extensor surfaces. Most cases resolve spontaneously.

APTT evaluates intrinsic and common pathways, detecting deficiencies or inhibitors of factors I, II, V, VIII, IX, X, XI, XII. Prolonged APTT indicates intrinsic pathway abnormalities. This test monitors heparin therapy.
questions.question: Which coagulation pathway does APTT evaluate?

questions.explanation: Full siblings have a 25% chance of being HLA-identical because each parent contributes one haplotype. Four possible combinations exist: both haplotypes matched, one matched, the other matched, or neither matched. Only one of these four combinations results in complete HLA identity.
questions.question: What percentage of sibling matches have HLA identity?
What is the typical MCV range in beta thalassaemia major
questions.explanation: Beta thalassaemia major demonstrates markedly reduced MCV typically ranging from 50-60 fL reflecting severe microcytosis. This extreme reduction accompanies hypochromia and bizarre poikilocytosis. The low MCV results from insufficient haemoglobin synthesis per developing erythrocyte.

DDAVP stimulates endothelial cells to release stored von Willebrand factor and Factor VIII from Weibel-Palade bodies, temporarily increasing plasma levels 3-5 fold within 30-60 minutes. This makes DDAVP useful in Type I vWD and mild Hemophilia A for minor procedures or bleeding episodes, avoiding need for factor concentrates. DDAVP is ineffective in Type III vWD (no vWF to release) or Type II variants with dysfunctional vWF.
questions.question: What is the mechanism of DDAVP (desmopressin) in treating von Willebrand disease?
options: Replaces missing von Willebrand factor directly
Stimulates vWF and Factor VIII release from storage

questions.question: What is the primary transport protein for delivering B12 to tissues?
questions.explanation: I (TC) is the essential plasma protein for transferring absorbed B12 from enterocytes to bone marrow and other tissues. Although TC carries less than 50ng/L B12, this represents the metabolically active fraction. TC deficiency causes megaloblastic anaemia despite normal serum B12 levels.

questions.question: What distinguishes HbH inclusions from Heinz bodies
questions.explanation: HbH inclusions appear smaller and more evenly distributed throughout cells than Heinz bodies which are larger and peripherally located. The golf ball pattern of multiple small inclusions specifically indicates HbH. Size and distribution differences enable morphologic distinction.

questions.question: What causes vascular purpura in Henoch-Schonlein purpura?
questions.explanation: Henoch-Schonlein purpura involves IgA deposition in capillaries and arterioles causing immune-mediated vasculitis (capillaritis), typically following streptococcal infection in children. The tetrad includes palpable purpura over extensor surfaces (legs, buttocks, arms), arthritis (periarticular swelling), abdominal pain (intestinal vessel involvement), and glomerulonephritis (usually benign, occasionally progresses to chronic renal disease). Platelet counts and coagulation tests remain normal.

questions.question: Which fruit is mentioned as a good folate source?
questions.explanation: Oranges, along with lemons, bananas, strawberries and melons, provide good dietary folate sources among fruits. Vegetables like spinach and lettuce, plus liver, kidney, yeast, mushrooms and peanuts represent other rich sources. Adequate consumption of fresh fruits and vegetables generally prevents nutritional folate deficiency.

options: In conjunction with symptoms, history, and other tests
Definitive proof of clinical drug allergy alone
As false positive requiring no further investigation
Excluding possibility of true drug allergy
questions.question: How should positive LTT results be interpreted clinically
questions.explanation: Positive LTT indicates drug-specific sensitization but must be interpreted alongside clinical symptoms, patient history, and other allergy tests. Sensitization can exist without clinical allergy, so comprehensive evaluation prevents over-diagnosis and unnecessary drug avoidance.

A peripheral blood film represents a snapshot of cells present in blood at sample collection time. This temporal representation captures the current haematological status. The film preserves cellular morphology for detailed microscopic examination and provides permanent documentation.
questions.question: What does a peripheral blood film represent temporally?
What is the primary indication for volume-reduced RBCs in neonates
questions.explanation: Volume reduction removes supernatant containing potassium that leaks from RBCs during storage. Neonates are particularly susceptible to hyperkalemia due to immature renal function. This modification also reduces overall transfusion volume in volume-sensitive patients.

Acidic pH electrophoresis involves interactions between haemoglobin variants and agarose gel components affecting migration. These physicochemical interactions supplement charge-based separation. The dual mechanism enhances resolution of closely migrating variants.
questions.question: What additional factor affects separation at acidic pH besides charge

questions.explanation: Adults typically receive 8-10 cryoprecipitate units pooled together (cryopool). This dose provides adequate fibrinogen replacement for most clinical situations. Pooling occurs just before transfusion to maintain sterility and potency.
questions.question: How many cryoprecipitate units are typically pooled for adult dosing
Which laboratory finding suggests tumor lysis syndrome?
questions.explanation: Tumor lysis syndrome produces hypocalcemia, hyperuricemia, hyperkalemia, and hyperphosphatemia from rapid cell breakdown. This oncologic emergency occurs during initial treatment of high-burden leukemia. Preventive hydration, allopurinol, and rasburicase minimize complications.

Acute leukemias typically present with pancytopenia affecting all normal blood cell lines. Anemia, thrombocytopenia, and neutropenia occur as blast cells crowd out normal hematopoiesis. This bone marrow failure produces multiple cytopenias characteristic of acute leukemia.
questions.question: Which blood cell type is normal in both acute leukemias at diagnosis?
Which antigen is commonly used to assess T-cell memory in LTT
questions.explanation: Tetanus toxoid is commonly used because most individuals have vaccination-induced immunity. Proliferative response to tetanus toxoid indicates functional T-cell memory and intact cell-mediated immunity, making it valuable for assessing immune competence in clinical settings.
options: Keyhole limpet hemocyanin for primary response

questions.explanation: Random donor platelet concentrates have volumes of 40-70ml containing concentrated platelets in residual plasma. This small volume requires pooling multiple units for adult dosing. Each unit derives from one whole blood donation.
questions.question: What is the typical volume of a whole blood-derived platelet concentrate
What is the minimum fibrinogen content required in each unit of cryoprecipitate
questions.explanation: Each cryoprecipitate unit must contain at least 150mg of fibrinogen as its primary component. This concentrated source treats hypofibrinogenemia effectively. The actual fibrinogen content typically exceeds this minimum requirement.

questions.question: What laboratory pattern distinguishes liver disease from vitamin K deficiency?
questions.explanation: Factor V reduction distinguishes liver disease from vitamin K deficiency because Factor V is not vitamin K-dependent but requires hepatic synthesis. Liver disease reduces all factors (except VIII and vWF), while vitamin K deficiency affects only factors II, VII, IX, X. Both prolong PT/APTT, but Factor V assay differentiates: reduced in liver disease, normal in pure vitamin K deficiency.
options: Factor V reduction in liver disease

questions.question: What response pattern is a minor HMS criterion
questions.explanation: Normal cellular and humoral responses to antigenic challenge, including normal phytohemagglutination response, is a minor criterion. This paradoxically normal response contrasts with the abnormal malaria-specific response. The pattern reflects selective rather than global immune dysfunction.

options: Activate cells for subsequent proliferation testing
Add essential nutrients for cell survival
Remove residual density gradient medium and contaminants
questions.explanation: Washing with phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) removes residual Ficoll-Paque or other density gradient medium that could interfere with subsequent culture. Multiple wash-centrifuge-resuspension cycles ensure clean lymphocyte preparation for accurate LTT results.
questions.question: What is the purpose of washing isolated lymphocytes with PBS

questions.explanation: MZ (marginal zone) macrophages specifically perform phagocytosis of circulating microorganisms and immune complexes in the marginal zone. These specialized macrophages are strategically positioned at the interface between blood and lymphoid tissue. Their location enables rapid clearance of blood-borne pathogens before they reach systemic circulation.
questions.question: Which macrophage type performs phagocytosis in the marginal zone
What percentage of splenic blood flow follows the fast pathway through venous sinuses
questions.explanation: Approximately 90% of splenic blood flow follows the fast pathway, flowing directly into adjacent venous sinuses continuous with the marginal zone. The remaining 10% takes the slow pathway through the reticular meshwork of red pulp, allowing more intimate contact with splenic macrophages. This dual circulation pattern enables both rapid transit and thorough filtration functions.

questions.question: Why cannot granulocyte products be leukoreduced
questions.explanation: Leukoreduction would remove the therapeutic granulocytes which are white blood cells. Granulocytes are the intended product, not a contaminant. CMV-seronegative products may be used instead for at-risk patients.

Detection of BCR-ABL rearrangement by cytogenetics, FISH, or molecular testing confirms CML diagnosis. The Philadelphia chromosome t(9:22) or BCR-ABL fusion gene is present in 85-95% of cases. This genetic marker is essential for diagnosis and treatment monitoring.
questions.question: Which genetic analysis is essential for confirming CML diagnosis?
What is the probability of HLA matching between siblings?
questions.explanation: Each brother and sister has a 25%, or 1 in 4, chance of matching a sibling if they have the same biological parents. This is because each parent contributes one HLA haplotype, creating four possible combinations in offspring. Full siblings can be HLA-identical, haploidentical, or completely mismatched.

questions.question: Which marker distinguishes CLL from other B-cell lymphoproliferative disorders?
questions.explanation: Co-expression of CD5 and CD23 with B-cell markers distinguishes CLL from other disorders. This unusual immunophenotype combined with clonal restriction confirms diagnosis. Mantle cell lymphoma expresses CD5 but lacks CD23 helping differentiate these entities.

Transfused platelets in ITP patients are rapidly destroyed (within hours) by the same antiplatelet antibodies destroying autologous platelets, making routine transfusions ineffective. Platelet transfusions are reserved for life-threatening hemorrhage (severe epistaxis, GI bleeding, intracranial hemorrhage) as temporizing measure while other therapies (IVIG, high-dose steroids) take effect. In antibody presence, even massive transfusions provide only brief hemostatic improvement.
questions.question: How long do transfused platelets remain viable in ITP patients?

questions.explanation: Liquid scintillation counting detects beta particles emitted by tritium decay. After cell harvesting, washing, and lysis, the radioactivity in counts per minute (cpm) directly correlates with DNA synthesis amount, providing quantitative measurement of lymphocyte proliferation.
questions.question: How is radioactivity measured after tritiated thymidine incorporation

questions.explanation: Trisomy 8 is frequently observed in AML M1 subtype. This chromosomal abnormality involves an extra copy of chromosome 8 and affects prognosis. Cytogenetic analysis revealing trisomy 8 helps confirm diagnosis and guide treatment decisions for this particular subtype.
questions.question: Which trisomy is frequently seen in AML M1 subtype?
What is the maximum storage life for donor red blood cells
questions.explanation: Donor red blood cells have a relatively short storage life of 42 days, which creates significant logistical challenges for blood banks. This limited shelf life contributes to shortages and wastage of blood products. Blood substitutes with longer shelf lives could address this critical limitation.

questions.question: What advantage does CFSE staining provide over tritiated thymidine
questions.explanation: CFSE uniquely provides division history, showing how many times individual cells divided through progressive fluorescence dilution. Flow cytometry reveals proliferation heterogeneity within populations, offering more detailed information than tritiated thymidine's bulk measurement of total DNA synthesis.
options: Lower cost and faster result availability
No requirement for flow cytometry equipment
Detailed information on division number per cell

questions.question: Why does whole blood lose platelet function during refrigerated storage
questions.explanation: Cold storage (1-6 degrees C) causes irreversible platelet function damage through membrane and cytoskeletal changes. Platelets require room temperature storage (20-24 degrees C). This is why whole blood cannot provide functional platelets.

Hypercoagulable state develops in thalassaemia intermedia patients increasing thromboembolism risk including stroke and pulmonary embolism. Chronic anaemia, abnormal red cells, and splenectomy contribute to hypercoagulability. Thrombosis prevention requires careful monitoring.
questions.question: What hematologic state complicates thalassaemia intermedia

options: Mitogens require specific antigen recognition by receptors
Mitogens induce non-specific proliferation regardless of specificity
Antigens cause proliferation without receptor engagement
Mitogens only activate previously sensitized cells
questions.explanation: Mitogens bypass antigen-specific recognition, causing polyclonal T-cell or B-cell activation regardless of receptor specificity. This non-specific stimulation assesses general immune competence, while antigen-specific stimulation evaluates responses to particular pathogens or allergens.
questions.question: How does mitogen stimulation differ from antigen-specific stimulation
What weight pattern do almost all HMS patients report
questions.explanation: Almost all HMS patients report weight loss as part of their clinical presentation. Despite this, many patients are capable of normal daily activity. The weight loss reflects chronic disease and possible malnutrition.

questions.question: What format is used for SSOP hybridization?
questions.explanation: SSOP uses a dot-blot format where denatured amplified DNA is spotted onto membranes. Allele-specific probes are then applied to detect specific sequences. This membrane-based format allows multiple samples to be tested simultaneously with different probes.

questions.question: What is the typical haemoglobin range in beta thalassaemia minor
questions.explanation: Beta thalassaemia minor typically presents with haemoglobin levels between 10-13 g/dL accompanied by microcytosis. This mild anaemia usually remains asymptomatic under normal physiological conditions. The RBC count typically appears normal or slightly elevated despite reduced haemoglobin.

Plummer-Vinson syndrome (also called Paterson-Kelly syndrome) manifests as postcricoid web formation causing dysphagia in chronic iron deficiency, particularly affecting middle-aged women. The webs are thin mucosal membranes that partially obstruct the esophagus. This condition increases esophageal carcinoma risk and resolves with iron replacement.
questions.question: What syndrome involves pharyngeal webs causing dysphagia in iron deficiency?

questions.explanation: A single warfarin dose effect lasts 4-5 days despite rapid gastrointestinal absorption. This prolonged duration relates to the elimination half-lives of affected clotting factors. Extended action requires careful monitoring and dose adjustments.
questions.question: How long does the effect of a single warfarin dose last?
What cardiovascular complication beyond iron deposition affects thalassaemia patients
questions.explanation: Pericarditis represents an additional cardiovascular complication beyond iron-induced cardiomyopathy affecting thalassaemia patients. Inflammatory processes and metabolic disturbances contribute to pericardial involvement. Multiple mechanisms converge causing cardiovascular morbidity.

The BCR-ABL fusion gene produces P210 protein which acts as an oncogene in CML. This protein has constitutive tyrosine kinase activity causing uncontrolled myeloid cell proliferation. P210 distinguishes CML from Philadelphia-positive ALL which produces P190 protein instead.
questions.question: Which protein functions as the oncogene in CML pathophysiology?

questions.explanation: Approximately 20% of plasma vitamin B12 is bound to transcobalamin II (TC), representing the metabolically active fraction delivered to tissues. Although haptocorrin carries 80% of plasma B12, this fraction is functionally inactive. TC deficiency causes megaloblastic anaemia despite normal total serum B12 levels.
questions.question: What percentage of vitamin B12 is bound to functionally active transcobalamin?
What is the minimum platelet count required in apheresis platelet products
questions.explanation: Apheresis platelets must contain at least 3.0 x 10^11 platelets in 75% of tested units. This single-donor product equals 6-8 random donor units. Apheresis collection uses automated devices to harvest platelets efficiently.

questions.question: What is the most common congenital bleeding disorder?
questions.explanation: Von Willebrand disease is the most common congenital bleeding disorder with estimated prevalence of 0.8-2% (likely underestimated due to mild cases). It results from quantitative or qualitative defects in von Willebrand factor, affecting both platelet function (adhesion) and coagulation (Factor VIII carrier). The autosomal dominant inheritance (Types I and II) allows it to affect both sexes, unlike X-linked hemophilias.

Glycophorins comprise only 2% of RBC membrane proteins but are rich in sialic acid, contributing significantly to the negative charge. They consist of three domains: cytoplasmic (COOH-terminal), transmembrane (single spanning alpha helix), and extracellular (NH2-terminal glycosylated). Glycophorins serve as receptors for infectious agents including Plasmodium falciparum.
questions.question: What percentage of RBC membrane proteins do glycophorins comprise?

questions.explanation: Platelets play roles in inflammation, innate and adaptive immunity, and diseases such as heart disease and cancer. They possess features of classical inflammatory cells including chemotaxis and mediator release. Platelets interact with neutrophils and contain complement receptors and Fc receptors.
questions.question: What role do platelets play beyond hemostasis?
Which antibody type is highly specific for pernicious anaemia?
questions.explanation: Anti-intrinsic factor antibodies (type I blocking and type II binding) are highly specific for pernicious anaemia diagnosis, though sensitivity is only 50-70%. Type I antibodies prevent B12 binding to intrinsic factor while type II antibodies block ileal receptor binding. Their presence confirms autoimmune gastritis with pernicious anaemia.

questions.question: Which translocation is associated with L3 morphology?
questions.explanation: The t(8:14) translocation is characteristic of L3 morphology and Burkitt-type leukaemia. This translocation involves the MYC oncogene on chromosome 8 and immunoglobulin heavy chain locus on chromosome 14. The resulting dysregulation leads to aggressive lymphoproliferation characteristic of Burkitt leukaemia.

Tissue plasminogen activator (t-PA) is formed in vascular endothelium, converting plasminogen to plasmin. t-PA preferentially activates fibrin-bound plasminogen. Endothelial t-PA release maintains local fibrinolysis.
questions.question: Which plasminogen activator is formed in vascular endothelium?
What distinguishes D-dimer from total FDPs?
questions.explanation: D-dimer specifically measures cross-linked fibrin degradation (indicating thrombin has generated fibrin that was then lysed), while total FDPs measure both fibrinogen and fibrin degradation products. D-dimer elevation confirms actual clot formation and lysis occurred, making it more specific for thrombotic processes (DVT, PE, DIC) than total FDPs, which can elevate from primary fibrinolysis without prior clot formation.

questions.question: What early clinical feature suggests beta thalassaemia major in infants
questions.explanation: Infants with beta thalassaemia major fail to thrive demonstrating poor growth and developmental delays. Severe anaemia impairs tissue oxygenation affecting growth. Additional features include pallor, jaundice, and hepatosplenomegaly.

Reversed phase columns analyze individual globin chains following haemoglobin denaturation and chain separation. These columns separate based on hydrophobicity differences. The reversed phase approach enables detailed chain characterization.
questions.question: What column type analyzes globin chains by HPLC

questions.explanation: Haemoglobin reaches 97% saturation when departing the lungs, allowing efficient oxygen delivery to peripheral tissues. This high saturation level ensures adequate oxygen supply for cellular metabolism and aerobic respiration. The remaining 3% unsaturated capacity provides a safety margin for varying physiological demands.
questions.question: What percentage of oxygen saturation does haemoglobin achieve upon leaving the lungs
In the modern concept of coagulation, how many main pathways converge to form fibrin?
questions.explanation: The modern concept describes two separate pathways (intrinsic and extrinsic) that converge into a common pathway for fibrinogen-to-fibrin conversion. The extrinsic pathway initiated by tissue factor provides rapid response, while the intrinsic pathway amplifies the coagulation response. Both pathways converge at Factor X activation, leading through the common pathway to thrombin generation and fibrin formation.

Reticulocyte counts in thalassaemia typically elevate proportionally to anaemia severity reflecting attempted compensation. The elevation varies from mild in trait to more significant in major disease. However, ineffective erythropoiesis in severe forms produces inappropriately low reticulocyte responses.
questions.question: What reticulocyte response characterizes compensated thalassaemia
What allows sensors to count cells in flow cytometry?
questions.explanation: Sensors detect cells using laser light that interacts with cells passing through the flow cell aperture. The scattered and fluorescent light signals are captured by detectors, enabling cell identification and counting. This optical detection system provides rapid, accurate analysis of thousands of cells per second.

Alemtuzumab targets CD52 antigen expressed on CLL cells. It is typically reserved for patients with refractory disease not responding to other treatments. This monoclonal antibody can effectively treat bone marrow-based disease resistant to conventional chemotherapy.
questions.question: What is the target of alemtuzumab in CLL therapy?
Which test is essential for confirming ALL diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Bone marrow aspiration is essential for ALL diagnosis, showing hypercellular marrow with greater than 30% lymphoblasts. Microscopic examination confirms lymphoblast morphology and distinguishes ALL from AML. The aspirate allows cytochemical staining, immunophenotyping, and cytogenetic analysis for complete characterization.

Glanzmann's thrombasthenia is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by deficient or dysfunctional GP-IIb/IIIa complex (fibrinogen receptor), preventing platelet aggregation despite normal adhesion. Platelets fail to aggregate with all agonists (ADP, epinephrine, collagen) except ristocetin (tests vWF-GP-Ib interaction). Bleeding can be severe despite normal platelet counts, requiring platelet transfusions for hemorrhage.
questions.question: What characterizes Glanzmann's thrombasthenia?
What does electrophoresis separate molecules based on fundamentally?
questions.explanation: Electrophoresis separates proteins and nucleic acids based on their size and charge characteristics. Charged molecules migrate through gel matrices in electric fields toward opposite electrodes. The separation depends on molecular physical properties and experimental conditions.

questions.question: What is the most serious complication of NAITP?
questions.explanation: Intracranial hemorrhage is the most serious complication of NAITP and can occur in utero or postnatally. It may present as ventriculomegaly, cerebral cysts, or hydrocephalus on ultrasound. ICH can result in permanent neurological damage or death.

questions.question: Which coagulation factor has the shortest half-life?
questions.explanation: Factor VII has the shortest half-life (4-6 hours) among coagulation factors, explaining why PT/INR responds quickly (within 24 hours) to warfarin therapy initiation or vitamin K administration. Other vitamin K-dependent factors have longer half-lives: IX (24 hours), X (40 hours), II (60 hours). Factor VII's short half-life makes PT/INR sensitive for detecting early vitamin K deficiency or warfarin effect.

questions.question: What percentage of CLL patients eventually require treatment?
questions.explanation: Although some patients with slowly progressive disease may never need treatment, most eventually require intervention. The decision to start treatment depends on disease progression markers, symptom development, and deteriorating blood counts. Treatment timing balances disease control with quality of life considerations.

questions.question: Which protein blocks apoptosis in most CLL cases?
questions.explanation: BCL-2 protein is elevated in approximately 90% of CLL cases, blocking normal apoptosis. This anti-apoptotic protein prevents programmed cell death, allowing abnormal lymphocytes to accumulate progressively. The accumulation occurs primarily in blood, bone marrow, lymph nodes, spleen, and liver.

questions.question: What is the normal INR range for individuals not on anticoagulants?
questions.explanation: The normal INR range for healthy individuals not on anticoagulant therapy is 0.8-1.1, indicating normal PT relative to standardized controls. An INR of 1.0 means the patient's PT exactly matches the control mean. INR values above 1.1 suggest prolonged clotting times from factor deficiencies or anticoagulants, while therapeutic warfarin targets INR 2.0-3.0 for most indications.

Platelet factor-3 is released during platelet aggregation, initiating blood coagulation cascade. This phospholipid surface supports coagulation factor assembly. Platelet factor 3 links primary and secondary hemostasis.
questions.question: What platelet factor initiates blood coagulation?

questions.explanation: Asymptomatic patients with severe thrombocytopenia (<10,000/muL) typically receive prophylactic platelets to prevent spontaneous bleeding. Higher thresholds apply for bleeding patients or surgical procedures. Clinical judgment considers individual risk factors.
questions.question: What platelet count threshold generally requires prophylactic transfusion in asymptomatic patients

questions.explanation: Clinical severity in compound heterozygotes depends primarily on the inherited beta thalassaemia mutation severity. Mutations completely preventing beta chain synthesis produce more severe phenotypes. Partial beta chain production from thalassaemia alleles ameliorates sickling manifestations.
questions.question: What determines clinical severity in beta thalassaemia with HbS
Where do inclusion bodies form in beta thalassaemia
questions.explanation: Free alpha globin chains precipitate in red cell precursors within bone marrow, forming characteristic inclusion bodies. These precipitates cannot form viable tetramers due to absent beta chain partners. The inclusions cause mechanical damage to developing erythroblasts before peripheral circulation entry.

questions.question: What is another name for Factor X?
questions.explanation: Factor X is called Stuart-Prower factor after the two patients (Stuart and Prower) in whom the deficiency was first identified. Factor X deficiency is rare, inherited as autosomal recessive, presenting with variable bleeding severity. As a common pathway factor, Factor X deficiency prolongs both PT and APTT. Treatment requires fresh frozen plasma or prothrombin complex concentrates containing Factor X.

The FCGR3B gene encoding HNA-1 antigens is located on chromosome 1. This location is distinct from the HLA complex on chromosome 6. The genetic basis of HNA-1 involves copy number variation and allelic polymorphisms.
questions.question: What chromosome contains the HNA-1 gene?
Where do proteins migrate when pH is below their pI?
questions.explanation: When pH is below pI, proteins become protonated (positively charged) and move toward the negative cathode. Basic groups accept protons at low pH values. This directional migration focuses proteins to their respective pI values.

questions.question: What cardiovascular symptom results from severe anaemia-induced hypoxia?
questions.explanation: Severe anaemia causes tissue hypoxia triggering compensatory tachycardia, increased cardiac output, and palpitations; in susceptible individuals this precipitates angina pectoris even without coronary disease. Headache, lightheadedness, and dyspnea accompany these cardiovascular responses. Symptoms correlate with anaemia severity and rapidity of onset.

Class II molecules present antigens to helper T-cells, which are CD4+ T cells. These TH-cells then activate B-cells to produce antibodies or coordinate other immune responses. The presentation of exogenous antigens by Class II is crucial for humoral immunity development.

questions.explanation: Proliferation in MLC is measured using radioactive thymidine incorporation during the last 6-18 hours of culture. The amount of radioactive thymidine incorporated into DNA is proportional to the degree of HLA disparity. Alternative proliferation markers may also be used in modern assays.
questions.question: What measures proliferation in MLC?
What are the three main components of normal hemostasis?
questions.explanation: Normal hemostasis depends on interaction between vessel wall, platelets, and coagulation factors working synergistically. Each component contributes specific functions to prevent hemorrhage. Defects in any component cause bleeding disorders.

questions.question: What activates protein C in the coagulation system?
questions.explanation: Activated protein C is generated when thrombin binds to thrombomodulin, an endothelial receptor. This activation converts procoagulant thrombin into anticoagulant activator. Activated protein C destroys factors V and VIII.

questions.question: Why does ABO HDFN typically occur in first pregnancies
questions.explanation: Group O mothers possess naturally occurring IgG anti-A,B antibodies from environmental exposure before pregnancy. Unlike Rh sensitization requiring prior foetal cell exposure, these pre-existing antibodies can affect the first ABO-incompatible pregnancy, though disease is usually mild.
options: Naturally occurring anti-A,B present before pregnancy
ABO antibodies develop only during first pregnancy
Foetal ABO antigens strongest in primigravidas
Maternal immune system most reactive initially
Placental transfer highest in first gestations

questions.question: What skeletal complication affects thalassaemia patients
questions.explanation: Thalassaemia patients develop osteoporosis, osteopenia, and other bone diseases from multiple factors including marrow expansion, endocrine dysfunction, and iron deposition. Bone mineral density decreases increasing fracture risk. Calcium and vitamin D supplementation provides partial protection.

The RBC membrane structure consists of 49% membrane proteins, 43% lipid bilayer, and 8% carbohydrate. This protein-rich composition provides the structural framework and functional capabilities of the membrane. The proteins include both integral proteins penetrating the lipid bilayer and peripheral proteins forming a meshwork beneath it.
questions.question: What percentage of RBC membrane composition is protein?
Which organ enlargement commonly occurs in chronic leukemias?
questions.explanation: Splenomegaly commonly occurs in chronic leukemias from leukemic cell infiltration. The enlarged spleen may cause left upper quadrant fullness and early satiety. Massive splenomegaly can cause cytopenias through hypersplenism requiring intervention.

Myeloperoxidase staining is positive in most AML cases with at least 3% blast positivity. This stain helps differentiate AML from ALL where it remains negative. Sudan Black staining shows similar patterns and is often used alongside myeloperoxidase for confirmation.
questions.question: Which cytochemical stain is positive in most AML cases but negative in ALL?

questions.explanation: FDP levels exceeding 600 mg/mL indicate severe DIC with extensive fibrin formation and degradation, correlating with worse prognosis and increased bleeding/thrombotic complications. Normal FDP is <10 mcg/mL, with elevations occurring in DIC, thromboembolic disease (DVT, PE), and postoperatively. Very high levels (>600 mg/mL) are relatively specific for severe DIC, reflecting massive fibrin turnover from widespread intravascular coagulation.
questions.question: What D-dimer level suggests severe DIC?

questions.explanation: MAIPA stands for Monoclonal Antibody Immobilization of Platelet Antigens. This widely used assay captures specific glycoproteins using monoclonal antibodies. It can analyze complex mixtures of platelet antibodies and identify their glycoprotein specificity.
questions.question: What does MAIPA stand for?
What future direction is being explored for plasma expanders
questions.explanation: Future directions include combining plasma expanders with oxygen carriers to provide both volume support and oxygen delivery simultaneously. This combination approach addresses multiple aspects of blood function. Integration of these technologies could optimize resuscitation strategies.

questions.question: What inhibits tissue plasminogen activator?
questions.explanation: Tissue plasminogen activator is inactivated by plasminogen activator inhibitor I (PAI-1), regulating fibrinolysis. PAI-1 prevents excessive fibrinolysis maintaining hemostatic balance. Elevated PAI-1 levels increase thrombotic risk.

questions.question: In which direction does the hemoglobin-oxygen dissociation curve shift in 2,3-BPG deficiency?
questions.explanation: Decreased 2,3-BPG shifts the hemoglobin-oxygen dissociation curve to the left, increasing hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen. This left shift means hemoglobin binds oxygen more tightly and releases it less readily to tissues. The resulting tissue hypoxia triggers compensatory erythropoietin release and secondary polycythemia.

questions.question: How long should coagulation samples be tested after collection ideally?
questions.explanation: Coagulation samples should ideally be tested within 4 hours of collection to preserve labile coagulation factors, particularly Factors V and VIII. Longer storage may cause factor degradation affecting test accuracy. Factor assay samples should be stored at 4°C, while screening test samples and Factor VII assays should be maintained at room temperature to avoid cold activation artifacts.

questions.question: What PaO2/FIO2 ratio indicates TRALI?
questions.explanation: TRALI criteria include hypoxemia with PaO2/FIO2 ratio <=300 mmHg or oxygen saturation <=90% on room air. This degree of hypoxemia indicates significant pulmonary dysfunction. The ratio measures severity of oxygenation impairment.

questions.question: Why is whole blood generally not stocked in modern blood banks
questions.explanation: Component therapy allows precise treatment of specific deficiencies with each element stored under optimal conditions. Whole blood loses platelet function during refrigeration and coagulation factors deteriorate. Modern transfusion medicine prioritizes targeted, efficient therapy over whole blood use.
options: Component therapy better targets specific patient needs
Whole blood expires faster than components

questions.explanation: Cryoprecipitate thaws at 30-37 degrees C to preserve factor activity while ensuring complete thawing. Lower temperatures require excessive time while higher temperatures risk protein denaturation. Proper thawing maintains therapeutic efficacy.

questions.explanation: Hepatosplenomegaly consistently appears in beta thalassaemia major from extramedullary haematopoiesis and haemosiderosis. Massive splenomegaly may cause hypersplenism and increased transfusion requirements. Organ enlargement reflects disease chronicity and severity.
questions.question: What physical examination finding indicates beta thalassaemia major

questions.explanation: Selection of appropriate screening cells is critical for MAIPA assay sensitivity. Panel selection requires careful consideration of antigen expression levels.

questions.question: When can haemochromatosis patients donate blood to blood banks?

options: Males have only one X chromosome
questions.explanation: Males are more commonly and severely affected by G6PD deficiency because they have only one X chromosome (hemizygous). A single defective G6PD gene on their X chromosome results in enzyme deficiency. Females require two defective genes (homozygous) for full expression, though heterozygous females can be variably affected due to lyonization (random X-inactivation).
questions.question: Why are males more commonly affected by G6PD deficiency?
What effect does hyperthyroidism have on warfarin therapy?
questions.explanation: Hyperthyroidism potentiates warfarin effect through increased metabolic rate and faster clotting factor turnover. Enhanced catabolism increases anticoagulant sensitivity. Lower warfarin doses achieve therapeutic anticoagulation.

questions.question: What is the critical timeframe for postpartum RhIg administration
options: Within 72 hours of delivering D-positive infant
questions.explanation: Postpartum RhIg must be administered within 72 hours of delivering an RhD-positive infant for optimal immune response suppression. Although some efficacy remains up to 28 days, maximum protection occurs when given promptly after delivery.

The metabolic block at the PK step affects RBCs of all ages, but young cells are paradoxically more affected because they have higher metabolic demands and ATP requirements for maintaining shape and deformability. options: Metabolic block affects all ages equally
questions.question: Why are young RBCs more affected in PK deficiency?

questions.explanation: Phosphofructokinase deficiency is associated with mild hemolysis and myopathy due to enzyme involvement in muscle glycolysis. This demonstrates that some RBC enzymopathies have non-hematological manifestations. Similarly, triosephosphate isomerase deficiency causes severe neuropathy in addition to hemolytic anemia, reflecting the enzyme's importance in multiple tissues.
questions.question: What clinical feature is associated with phosphofructokinase deficiency?

What activates the intrinsic fibrinolytic pathway?
questions.explanation: Factor XIIa activates the intrinsic fibrinolytic pathway through Factor XI, kallikrein, and high molecular weight kininogen, linking contact activation to both coagulation and fibrinolysis. Extrinsic fibrinolytic activation involves tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) from endothelium and urokinase from kidney. This dual activation ensures fibrinolysis accompanies coagulation, preventing excessive clot accumulation and maintaining vascular patency.

questions.question: What allows assessment of cell size, shape, and color?
questions.explanation: Examination of well-prepared and properly stained blood smears allows assessment of RBC, WBC, and platelet morphology. Staining reveals cellular details including size, shape, and color variations. Proper preparation and staining are critical for accurate morphological interpretation.

Acellular hemoglobin has a lower P50 value, meaning increased oxygen affinity that makes oxygen release to tissues more difficult. This altered oxygen affinity represents a significant physiological challenge in blood substitute development. Modifications are required to achieve appropriate oxygen delivery characteristics.
questions.question: What is the primary functional challenge with acellular hemoglobin regarding oxygen affinity
What happens to RBCs during haemoglobin measurement in analyzers?
questions.explanation: RBCs are lysed by LH diluent during haemoglobin measurement, releasing haemoglobin which then forms a measurable complex. This complete lysis ensures all haemoglobin is converted to the stable colored compound. The lysate's absorbance at 525nm directly correlates with haemoglobin concentration.

questions.question: How many satellite bags are attached in a quadruple bag system
questions.explanation: Quadruple bag systems have one primary collection bag with three attached satellite bags. This enables preparation of red cells, plasma, platelets, and plasma factors. The closed system maintains sterility throughout processing.
