questions.question: Which phase follows chronic phase in CML progression?
What characteristic inclusions appear with supravital staining in HbH disease
questions.explanation: Brilliant cresyl blue supravital staining precipitates HbH creating multiple small discrete inclusions throughout cells. This "golf ball" appearance distinguishes HbH inclusions from larger, peripheral Heinz bodies. The distribution and size characteristics aid HbH disease diagnosis.

Blood folate levels rise within 15-20 minutes after ingestion and peak at 1-2 hours, demonstrating rapid and efficient absorption from the upper small intestine. This contrasts with the slower, more complex B12 absorption requiring multiple binding proteins. The rapid absorption reflects direct monoglutamate uptake by enterocytes.
questions.question: What is the peak blood folate level timing after ingestion?
What major advantage do PFCs have regarding chemical properties
questions.explanation: PFCs are completely inert, meaning they do not participate in chemical reactions and cause minimal biological responses. This chemical inertness significantly reduces toxicity risks compared to hemoglobin-based products. The inert nature contributes to the safety profile of PFC emulsions.

questions.question: What is the maximum time allowed for cryoprecipitate transfusion after pooling in an open system
questions.explanation: Pooled cryoprecipitate in an open system must be transfused within 4 hours due to loss of sterility. Closed system pooling extends this to 6 hours. Rapid transfusion ensures optimal factor activity and prevents bacterial growth.

Acute iron poisoning, mainly occurring in children, presents with severe gastrointestinal symptoms including nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and diarrhea. Free iron in plasma exerts direct toxic effects that can be life-threatening. Urgent chelation therapy may be required in severe cases to prevent systemic toxicity.
questions.question: Which symptom is characteristic of acute iron poisoning in children?

questions.explanation: Platelet adhesion to exposed subendothelial collagen and von Willebrand factor occurs within approximately 3 seconds of vessel injury, representing the most rapid phase of hemostasis. This immediate response involves GP-Ib binding to von Willebrand factor and GP-Ia binding to collagen under high shear stress conditions. The rapid adhesion prevents excessive blood loss and provides the foundation for subsequent platelet activation and aggregation.
questions.question: What is the normal time frame for platelet adhesion to occur after vessel injury?
What is the primary function of Band 3 protein in the RBC membrane?
questions.explanation: Band 3 is the major integral protein that forms the anion transporter, exchanging bicarbonate for chloride ions. It comprises three distinct domains: cytoplasmic, transmembrane, and C-terminal domains. Band 3 also provides linkage of the lipid bilayer to underlying membrane skeleton proteins through interaction with ankyrin and protein 4.2.

Daily oral iron therapy of 100-200mg elemental iron (one 200mg ferrous sulphate tablet contains 67mg elemental iron; 2-3 tablets daily) is sufficient for treating iron deficiency. Higher doses increase gastrointestinal side effects without improving absorption. Doses should be spaced at least 6 hours apart and taken on an empty stomach for optimal absorption.
questions.question: What daily iron dose is typically sufficient for treating iron deficiency?

questions.explanation: Protein S von Willebrand factor serves dual critical roles: mediating platelet adhesion and serving as the carrier protein that stabilizes Factor VIII, protecting it from premature proteolytic degradation. Without von Willebrand factor, Factor VIII has a markedly shortened half-life, explaining why von Willebrand disease presents with both platelet dysfunction (prolonged bleeding time) and reduced Factor VIII levels (prolonged APTT).
questions.question: Which protein is essential for stabilizing Factor VIII in circulation?

questions.explanation: Acellular hemoglobin scavenges nitric oxide, which is essential for vasodilation and blood pressure regulation, leading to hypertension and vasoconstriction. questions.question: What critical molecule does acellular hemoglobin inappropriately scavenge, causing complications

questions.explanation: Patients with sickle disease who develop HMS remain functionally asplenic and don't appear to benefit from enlarged spleen expansion. This contrasts with sickle trait that provides protection. The autoinfarction prevents functional splenic tissue despite enlargement.
questions.question: What protection pattern is observed in sickle cell disease patients with HMS
What is the alternative name for the haemoglobin sickling test
questions.explanation: The sickling test is alternatively known as the dithionite solubility test utilizing sodium dithionite as reducing agent. This nomenclature reflects the chemical mechanism inducing deoxygenation. The test exploits HbS polymerization properties under reduced oxygen conditions.

HPA-1a has a phenotype frequency of 97.9% in most populations, making it a high-frequency antigen. This means HPA-1b homozygotes are relatively rare, occurring in approximately 2-3% of Caucasians. The high frequency of HPA-1a explains why anti-HPA-1a is the most common clinically significant antibody.
questions.question: What is the frequency of HPA-1a in populations?

What was one of the earliest protein separation methods?
questions.explanation: Starch gel electrophoresis was one of the earliest methods for protein separation using starch matrices. It provided a porous medium for protein migration under electric fields. Though historically important, it has largely been replaced by higher-resolution methods.

The liver synthesizes most coagulation factors except Factor VIII (endothelium/sinusoidal cells) and von Willebrand factor (endothelium/megakaryocytes), explaining why severe liver disease causes complex coagulopathy with multiple factor deficiencies. Liver disease prolongs PT and APTT due to decreased synthesis of factors II, V, VII, IX, X, XI, and fibrinogen. Unlike vitamin K deficiency, Factor V is also reduced in liver disease.

What percentage of NAITP cases occur in first pregnancy?
questions.explanation: Approximately 30% of neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia cases occur in the first pregnancy. This contrasts with hemolytic disease of the newborn which rarely affects first pregnancies. The early occurrence in NAITP reflects different immunological mechanisms of platelet versus red cell alloimmunization.

Red cells contain 35% solids with hemoglobin being the chief protein component. The remaining 65% consists of water and other fluid components. This composition is essential for maintaining the cell's flexibility and function in oxygen transport.

At what stored blood age do viable platelets become minimal?
questions.explanation: Stored blood loses viable platelets within 48 hours of collection, as platelets have limited viability without temperature and agitation control used in platelet concentrate storage. Massive transfusion of stored blood (multiple blood volumes rapidly) causes dilutional thrombocytopenia by replacing patient's blood with platelet-poor stored blood. Hyposplenism increases the risk of severe bloodstream infections, particularly from encapsulated bacteria. The impaired filtering and immune function removes crucial defense against pneumococcus, meningococcus, and Haemophilus. This susceptibility necessitates vaccination and antibiotic prophylaxis.

questions.explanation: Veganism, particularly in Hindu Indian populations, causes severe B12 deficiency through complete dietary exclusion of animal products containing the vitamin. Unlike vegetarians who consume dairy products, vegans lack all B12 sources. Dietary deficiency develops more rapidly than malabsorptive causes in young vegans with minimal stores.
questions.question: What dietary practice most commonly causes severe B12 deficiency in Western countries?
What are the most common causes of splenomegaly in developed countries
questions.explanation: In developed countries, infectious mononucleosis, hematological malignancy, and portal hypertension are the most common causes of splenomegaly. This contrasts with developing countries where infectious and hereditary causes predominate. The geographic variation in etiology reflects disease prevalence patterns.

Good correction in mixing studies (50:50 patient:normal plasma) indicates factor deficiency because normal plasma supplies the missing factor(s), normalizing the coagulation time. For example, if APTT is 60 seconds and corrects to 42 seconds with mixing, this suggests factor deficiency rather than inhibitor. Failure to correct (remaining prolonged) suggests an inhibitor that affects both patient and normal plasma factors.
questions.question: What does good correction in mixing studies indicate?

questions.explanation: Coagulation factor disorders cause deep tissue bleeding (hematomas in muscles like psoas), joint bleeding (hemarthrosis, particularly knees, elbows, ankles), and delayed bleeding (1-2 days post-trauma/surgery) that's often severe. Petechiae never occur in pure coagulation disorders. The deep, delayed bleeding pattern reflects inadequate fibrin formation to stabilize platelet plugs under tissue pressure, distinguishing factor deficiencies from platelet disorders.
questions.question: What characterizes bleeding in coagulation factor disorders?
What information does flow cytometry provide for cell analysis?
questions.explanation: Flow cytometry provides forward light scatter (cell size), side scatter (internal complexity), and side fluorescence (specific markers) for comprehensive cell analysis. These parameters allow identification of different cell populations, immature cells, and abnormal morphologies. The multi-parameter approach enhances diagnostic accuracy significantly.

questions.question: What serum IgM elevation defines HMS in major criteria
questions.explanation: Elevated serum IgM level 2 standard deviations or more above the local mean is a major diagnostic criterion. This marked elevation reflects polyclonal B-cell activation. Local population norms must be used since baseline levels vary geographically.

questions.question: What is the target Factor VIII level needed for major surgery in hemophilia A?
questions.explanation: For major surgery in hemophilia A patients, Factor VIII levels should be raised to at least 50% (0.5 IU/mL) and maintained above 30% during the perioperative period to ensure adequate hemostasis. Minor surgery may be managed with 30-50% levels. Severe hemophilia A (<1% Factor VIII) requires significant replacement therapy to achieve these therapeutic targets, usually using recombinant Factor VIII concentrates.

Gross splenomegaly of 10 cm or more below the costal margin in adults for which no other cause can be found is a major criterion. This substantial enlargement distinguishes HMS from mild splenomegaly. The measurement must be carefully documented.
questions.question: What is the minimum splenomegaly measurement in HMS major criteria

questions.explanation: Serum ferritin above 300mg/L in postmenopausal females (and males) suggests iron overload warranting further investigation for haemochromatosis. Premenopausal females have a lower threshold of 200mg/L due to physiological iron losses through menstruation. However, elevated ferritin alone does not exclude or confirm HFE genotype.
questions.question: What serum ferritin level indicates iron overload in postmenopausal females?

questions.explanation: Hypersplenism appears as a minor diagnostic criterion, reflecting sequestration and destruction of blood cells. The cytopenias result from splenic function augmentation. Bone marrow typically shows compensatory hyperplasia.
questions.question: What hematologic manifestation appears as a minor HMS criterion
Which complication should be monitored throughout ALL treatment?
questions.explanation: Serious infections are major complications during ALL treatment due to neutropenia and immunosuppression. Normal infection-fighting white blood cells are reduced, making patients vulnerable to bacterial, viral, and fungal infections. Close monitoring and prompt treatment with antimicrobials are essential throughout therapy.

questions.question: What is the pathophysiology of scurvy-related bleeding?
questions.explanation: Scurvy (vitamin C deficiency) causes bleeding through defective collagen synthesis, as vitamin C is essential cofactor for proline and lysine hydroxylation in collagen formation. Defective perivascular collagen support causes capillary fragility manifesting as petechiae, ecchymoses, and bleeding gums despite normal platelet counts and coagulation tests. Vitamin C supplementation corrects the bleeding tendency by restoring collagen synthesis.

DNA typing focuses on analyzing the most polymorphic regions of HLA genes, particularly HLA-B and HLA-DRB1 loci. These regions show the highest degree of genetic variation among populations. Examining actual genetic sequences provides superior resolution compared to serological approaches.
questions.question: What regions do DNA typing methods primarily analyze?

questions.explanation: Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) amplifies specific DNA sequences enabling mutation detection from minimal sample quantities. This powerful technique revolutionized molecular diagnostics through exponential target amplification. PCR forms the basis for numerous mutation detection strategies.
questions.question: What DNA technique amplifies specific gene sequences

questions.explanation: Pulse magnitudes are directly proportional to the size of particles in the electrical field during impedance counting. Larger particles displace more electrolyte, creating bigger disturbances in electrical current. This proportional relationship allows accurate size distribution analysis of cell populations.
questions.question: What is the relationship between pulse magnitude and particle characteristics?

questions.explanation: Total gastrectomy causes vitamin B12 deficiency through complete loss of intrinsic factor production from removed parietal cells, making B12 absorption impossible through the normal intrinsic factor-dependent pathway. Deficiency develops over 2-5 years as hepatic stores deplete. Lifelong parenteral B12 replacement is mandatory after gastrectomy.
questions.question: What mechanism explains B12 deficiency after total gastrectomy?
What is the mean molecular weight of low molecular weight heparins?
questions.explanation: Low molecular weight heparins have a mean molecular weight of 5,000 Daltons, approximately one-third the size of unfractionated heparin. This smaller size provides more predictable pharmacokinetics and bioavailability. LMWHs are produced by controlled depolymerization of standard heparin.

Patients with HMS have high levels of antibody for Plasmodium falciparum, Plasmodium vivax, or Plasmodium ovale. The antibody response is polyclonal and not species-specific. These antibody patterns reflect exposure history in endemic regions where multiple species may circulate.
questions.question: What is the predominant Plasmodium species associated with HMS based on antibody levels
What is the relationship between RBC deformability and capillary transit?
options: Deformability must be high for capillary passage
questions.explanation: RBCs must squeeze through tight spots in microcirculation, requiring easy and reversible deformability. The biconcave shape provides optimum surface-to-volume ratio essential for deformability and respiratory exchange. Loss of deformability due to ATP depletion, membrane defects, or cytoplasmic viscosity changes prevents capillary passage, leading to splenic sequestration and hemolysis.

Pancreatic iron deposition causes fibrotic damage leading to diabetes mellitus, historically termed "bronzed diabetes" when combined with skin pigmentation. The iron accumulation destroys insulin-producing beta cells and impairs glucose metabolism. This represents one of the classical clinical presentations of advanced haemochromatosis.
questions.question: Which clinical syndrome results from pancreatic iron deposition in haemochromatosis?
What defective immunoregulatory mechanism contributes to HMS
questions.explanation: Defective immunoregulatory control of B lymphocytes by suppressor or cytotoxic T lymphocytes causes the increase in B lymphocytes in HMS. This loss of immune regulation permits uncontrolled B-cell proliferation. T-cell infiltration of hepatic and splenic sinusoids accompanies this process.

options: Prevent transfusion-associated graft versus host disease
questions.question: Why must all granulocyte products be irradiated
questions.explanation: Granulocyte products contain viable lymphocytes capable of causing transfusion-associated GVHD in immunocompromised recipients. Irradiation inactivates these lymphocytes while preserving granulocyte function. This modification is mandatory for all granulocyte products.

options: Fresh whole blood less than 24 hours old
Platelet-rich plasma with high factor content
Irradiated packed cells with standard haematocrit
questions.question: What blood component characteristic is essential for intrauterine transfusion
questions.explanation: Intrauterine transfusion requires frozen deglycerolized red cells with 75-80% haematocrit, providing maximal oxygen-carrying capacity in minimal volume. These cells are group O negative, HbS negative, CMV negative (or leukoreduced), and irradiated to prevent graft-versus-host disease.

HLA genes are highly polymorphic with many different alleles that modify the adaptive immune system. This polymorphism helps the body distinguish its own proteins from foreign invaders like viruses and bacteria. The extensive variation in HLA genes among individuals is crucial for population-level immunity against diverse pathogens.
questions.question: Why are HLA genes highly polymorphic?
What reticulocyte percentage typically appears in beta thalassaemia major
questions.explanation: Beta thalassaemia major paradoxically shows low reticulocyte counts (2-8%) despite severe anaemia reflecting ineffective erythropoiesis. Most erythroid precursors undergo intramedullary death before maturation. The inappropriate reticulocyte response distinguishes thalassaemia from haemolytic anaemias with effective erythropoiesis.

The formula (60 - hematocrit)/100 x 4.5 calculates the blood volume in ml to add to 0.5 ml of 0.109M citrate, adjusting for hematocrit to maintain proper anticoagulant-to-plasma ratio. This adjustment is critical because high hematocrit reduces plasma volume, causing relative citrate excess that prolongs coagulation times artificially. Low hematocrit has opposite effects, requiring more blood to achieve proper ratio.
questions.question: What formula calculates blood volume to add to citrate based on hematocrit?

questions.explanation: Bead arrays can detect lower levels of antibodies that might not be sufficient to cause complement-mediated cytotoxicity in traditional CDC. This higher sensitivity allows earlier detection of alloimmunization. The technology provides semi-quantitative results through fluorescence intensity measurements.
questions.question: What advantage do bead arrays offer over traditional CDC?

questions.explanation: Arthritis develops in haemochromatosis affecting metacarpophalangeal joints, wrists, hips, and knees due to iron and calcium pyrophosphate deposition in synovium and cartilage. Joint pain and stiffness are common presenting symptoms. Unlike other manifestations, arthropathy may not improve with iron removal and can progress despite treatment.
questions.question: What musculoskeletal manifestation occurs in haemochromatosis?

questions.explanation: Hemopure is indicated for situations of low hemoglobin where oxygen carrying capacity needs augmentation. This indication addresses anemia and acute blood loss scenarios. The product provides temporary oxygen delivery support while hemoglobin levels recover.
questions.question: What clinical indication for Hemopure relates to inadequate hemoglobin levels

questions.explanation: Congenital asplenia occurs in rare cases, representing a developmental anomaly. It may be isolated or associated with other congenital abnormalities such as cardiac defects. These patients require lifelong infection prophylaxis similar to those who undergo splenectomy.
questions.question: When can congenital asplenia occur

questions.explanation: The buffy coat method begins with a heavy spin to separate RBCs and plasma, leaving the buffy coat. Subsequently, a light spin separates platelets from residual WBCs. This reverses the traditional PRP method sequence.
questions.question: In the buffy coat method, what type of spin is performed first on whole blood

options: At 20 weeks gestation for all negative women
Immediately after positive antibody screen detection
At 36 weeks gestation before expected delivery
At conception when paternal type confirmed positive
At 28 weeks gestation to D-negative women
questions.explanation: Antepartum RhIg is administered at 28 weeks gestation to RhD-negative women with negative antibody screens. This timing prevents late pregnancy sensitization from small foeto-maternal bleeds, providing protection until postpartum RhIg administration after delivery of RhD-positive infant.
questions.question: When is antepartum RhIg prophylaxis routinely administered

questions.explanation: Severe hemophilia A is defined as Factor VIII <1 IU/dL (<1%), causing spontaneous bleeding into joints and muscles without trauma. Moderate hemophilia (1-5 IU/dL) bleeds with minor trauma, while mild hemophilia (5-40 IU/dL) bleeds only with significant trauma or surgery. Severity classification guides treatment intensity: severe requires prophylactic factor replacement, moderate needs treatment for minor trauma, mild may need treatment only for surgery.
questions.question: What Factor VIII level defines severe hemophilia A?
Which substance synthesized by endothelium opposes thromboxane A2 action?
questions.explanation: synthesized in vascular endothelium opposes thromboxane A2 by inhibiting platelet aggregation and promoting vasodilation through increased cyclic AMP levels. This creates a critical balance preventing inappropriate platelet activation on normal vessel walls while allowing hemostatic plug formation at injury sites. The prostacyclin-thromboxane balance represents an important regulatory mechanism preventing pathological thrombosis while maintaining hemostatic capability.

questions.question: Where are the most efficient macrophages located for removing old RBCs?
questions.explanation: Aging RBCs are removed by the reticuloendothelial system (RES), a system of fixed macrophages located throughout the body. However, macrophages in the spleen are the most efficient at removing old RBCs due to the unique filtering function of splenic sinusoids. These cells recognize and phagocytose senescent RBCs based on surface changes.

It is unthinkable to practice haematology without support from an expert morphologist for complete diagnostic assessment. Morphological expertise complements automated data providing comprehensive patient evaluation. This integration ensures optimal diagnostic accuracy and patient care.
questions.question: What makes practicing haematology without morphology unthinkable today?

questions.explanation: Flow cytometric crossmatching can detect both complement-fixing and non-complement-fixing antibodies, providing more comprehensive immunological assessment. Donor lymphocytes are incubated with recipient serum, then fluorescently labeled antibodies detect binding. This method is more sensitive than traditional CDC testing.
questions.question: What does flow cytometric crossmatching detect?
At what wavelength can absorbance interference occur in Anti-Xa assay?
questions.explanation: Substances that interfere with absorbance of 405nm light can produce spurious Anti-Xa results. Bilirubin, hemolysis, and triglycerides affect this wavelength. Grossly lipemic samples require increased centrifugation.

questions.question: Which cells release immunoglobulins from the marginal zone following antigenic challenge
questions.explanation: Splenic B lymphocytes in the marginal zone release immunoglobulins upon antigenic challenge, providing rapid humoral immunity. These B-cells are specialized for responses to thymus-independent antigens. Their positioning in the marginal zone allows immediate response to blood-borne pathogens.

questions.question: What does thrombin hydrolyze from fibrinogen?
questions.explanation: Thrombin hydrolyzes fibrinopeptides A and B from fibrinogen, enabling fibrin polymerization. This enzymatic cleavage exposes polymerization sites. Fibrin monomers spontaneously polymerize into strands.

questions.question: What is the treatment goal for essential thrombocythemia?
questions.explanation: Treatment goals in essential thrombocythemia focus on reducing thrombotic and bleeding risk rather than normalizing platelet counts, as patients remain asymptomatic at moderately elevated counts. Aspirin reduces thrombotic risk (particularly erythromelalgia, digital ischemia). Cytoreductive therapy (hydroxyurea, anagrelide, interferon-alpha) targets high-risk patients (age >60, prior thrombosis, platelets >1,500,000/mm3) to reduce counts below 400,000-600,000/mm3.

questions.question: Why is warfarin contraindicated during pregnancy?
questions.explanation: Warfarin is contraindicated in pregnancy because it crosses the placental barrier causing teratogenicity in first trimester. It can also induce intracranial hemorrhage in the baby during delivery. Heparin is the anticoagulant of choice in pregnant women.

Special bags designed for frozen blood storage withstand temperatures as low as -70 to -90 degrees C. These bags prevent brittleness and cracking during freezing. Standard bags would rupture at these extreme temperatures.
questions.question: What specialized blood bags allow extended frozen storage
At what dilution is patient plasma typically tested in factor assays?
questions.explanation: Patient plasma is typically tested at 1:10, 1:20, and 1:40 dilutions in one-stage factor assays to ensure at least one dilution falls within the linear range of the standard curve (usually 5-100% factor activity). Multiple dilutions verify linearity, detect inhibitors (non-parallel curves), and ensure accurate quantification. Plastic tubes are used for Factor VIII assays to prevent contact activation, and samples are kept on ice until testing.

questions.question: What is the primary mechanism by which anticoagulants prevent thrombosis?
questions.explanation: Anticoagulants work by reducing the body's ability to form clots through blocking certain clotting factors or platelets in the blood. This mechanism prevents blood clot formation or stops existing clots from enlarging. The mode of action does not involve increasing platelet production or enhancing vasoconstriction.
options: Increasing platelet production in bone marrow
Reducing the body's ability to form blood clots

questions.question: What characterizes the G6PD Mediterranean variant compared to A-?
questions.explanation: G6PD Mediterranean variant causes more severe enzyme deficiency (<10% activity) compared to G6PD A- (10-60% activity). Mediterranean variant is common in Sicilians, Greeks, Sephardic Jews, and Arabs. The more severe deficiency affects younger RBCs as well, causing more prolonged and severe hemolytic episodes that are not self-limited.

Alternative therapies for severe methemoglobinemia include hyperbaric oxygen therapy (increasing dissolved oxygen in plasma) and exchange transfusions (replacing methemoglobin-containing RBCs with normal cells). These are reserved for life-threatening situations where methylene blue is contraindicated or ineffective. Ascorbic acid works slowly and is used for mild cases or as adjunctive therapy.
questions.question: What alternative therapy can be used for severe methemoglobinemia besides methylene blue?

options: Foetal middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity
Liley graph zone determination through ultrasound
questions.explanation: MCA-PSV measurement uses Doppler ultrasound to detect increased blood flow velocity resulting from reduced viscosity in anaemic foetuses. Readings exceeding 1.5 multiples of the mean sensitively predict significant foetal anaemia, performed every 2 weeks without invasive risk.
questions.question: Which non-invasive technique predicts significant foetal anaemia most reliably

options: Isolate the specific factor being measured
questions.explanation: Factor-deficient substrate plasma contains all coagulation factors except the one being assayed (either from congenitally deficient patients or immunodepleted commercial preparations), isolating the specific factor's contribution to clotting time. When patient plasma is added, only the measured factor affects clotting time, allowing quantification by comparing to standard plasma dilutions. This principle applies to all one-stage factor assays based on PT or APTT.
questions.question: What is the purpose of using Factor-deficient substrate plasma in factor assays?

questions.explanation: Granulocytes store at room temperature (20-24 degrees C) without agitation to maintain function. Unlike platelets, granulocytes should not be agitated. Storage at cold temperatures damages granulocyte function, similar to platelets but should be transfused as soon as possible.
questions.question: At what temperature are granulocytes stored after collection

questions.explanation: Class II molecules consist of two different transmembrane polypeptides: an alpha chain and a beta chain. The beta chain is much more polymorphic compared to the alpha chain. Current HLA typing focuses on beta chain polymorphisms including HLA-DRB1, DQB1, and DPB1.
questions.question: How many transmembrane polypeptides form Class II molecules?
What compensatory marrow response indicates effective erythropoiesis in HMS
questions.explanation: The reticulocyte count is increased and reflects erythroid hyperplasia compensating for anemia. This response confirms adequate marrow function. The elevation distinguishes HMS from primary marrow disorders.

questions.question: What is the predominant haemoglobin type in beta thalassaemia major
questions.explanation: Beta thalassaemia major shows predominant HbF (foetal haemoglobin) comprising most measurable haemoglobin with minimal HbA. The inability to produce beta chains prevents HbA formation. Compensatory gamma chain production maintains HbF synthesis throughout life.

questions.question: What protein carrier binds free hemoglobin released during intravascular hemolysis?
questions.explanation: Free hemoglobin and alpha-beta dimers released into the bloodstream during intravascular hemolysis are picked up by haptoglobin. The haptoglobin-hemoglobin complex is large and cannot be excreted in urine, being carried to the liver for breakdown. When intravascular destruction increases, haptoglobin is depleted and free hemoglobin appears in urine (hemoglobinuria).

options: Red cells, plasma, platelets, and cryoprecipitate
questions.question: What components can be prepared from a double bag collection system
questions.explanation: Double bag systems allow separation of red cells and plasma only. One bag collects blood while the satellite receives separated plasma. Triple bags add platelet preparation capability.

Foetal haematocrit below 30% indicates severe anaemia requiring intrauterine transfusion to prevent cardiac failure and hydrops. This threshold is determined through cordocentesis, providing direct measurement of foetal blood parameters and guiding timing of therapeutic intervention.
questions.question: At what foetal haematocrit level is intrauterine transfusion indicated
What is the primary advantage of closed blood bag systems
questions.explanation: Closed systems maintain sterility throughout component preparation, extending product shelf life. Opening the system significantly shortens expiration dates. Modern component therapy relies on closed system technology.
options: Maintained sterility with extended shelf life

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of lymphocyte transformation tests
questions.explanation: LTT measures lymphocyte proliferative capacity when exposed to specific antigens or non-specific mitogens. This in vitro assay evaluates immune system functionality by quantifying cell division and transformation, critical for diagnosing immune disorders and drug hypersensitivity.
options: Measure antibody production by plasma cells directly
Assess lymphocyte proliferation response to antigens or mitogens
Quantify total lymphocyte count in peripheral blood
Determine natural killer cell cytotoxic activity

questions.question: What component does Oxygent contain to stabilize the product in aqueous solutions
questions.explanation: Oxygent contains egg yolk lecithin as an emulsifier to stabilize perfluorocarbon in aqueous solutions, allowing uniform distribution. This phospholipid stabilization is essential for maintaining PFC emulsion stability. The lecithin component enables clinical administration of the hydrophobic PFC.

Tissue thromboplastin with calcium chloride solution (0.025M) is incorporated in PT reagent for testing. Calcium is essential for coagulation cascade activation. The reagent tests the extrinsic pathway function.
questions.question: What reagent component is incorporated with tissue thromboplastin for PT testing?

options: NADH fluorescence increases with normal PK
NADPH fluorescence increases with normal PK
FAD fluorescence decreases with normal PK
NADH fluorescence decreases with normal PK
NAD fluorescence increases with normal PK
questions.explanation: The fluorescent screening test measures NADH oxidation to NAD by lactate dehydrogenase, which is limited by PK levels. Normal samples show time-dependent loss of fluorescence as NADH is oxidized to NAD within 15 minutes. In PK deficiency, fluorescence fails to disappear even after 45-60 minutes of incubation.
questions.question: What is the fluorescent screening principle for pyruvate kinase deficiency?
What is the normal prothrombin time range?
questions.explanation: Normal prothrombin time ranges from 16 to 18 seconds, testing extrinsic pathway function. PT measures factors VII, X, V, prothrombin, and fibrinogen. Prolongation indicates deficiency in these factors.

questions.question: What specific gravity range characterizes red blood cells
questions.explanation: Red blood cells have specific gravity of 1.08-1.09, making them the densest blood component. This density difference enables centrifugal separation. Platelets (1.023) and plasma (1.03-1.04) are progressively lighter.

options: Present antigenic peptides to T lymphocytes
questions.question: What is the primary function of HLA molecules?
questions.explanation: HLA molecules function primarily to present protein chains of antigens to T lymphocytes, thereby initiating specific immune responses. This presentation process is essential for both adaptive and innate immunity, allowing the immune system to distinguish self from non-self proteins. The HLA system represents the human version of the Major Histocompatibility Complex with critical roles in immune surveillance.

Chromogen substrate binds excess factor Xa producing a colour change measured spectrophotometrically. The colour change is directly proportional to unbound Xa amount. Heparin functional activity is inversely proportional to colour intensity.
questions.question: What is measured spectrophotometrically in the Anti-Xa assay?
What happens when antimalarial prophylaxis is withdrawn in HMS patients
questions.explanation: Withdrawal of prophylaxis in patients from malaria-endemic regions has been associated with relapse anywhere from 2-18 months after initial diagnosis. This relapse pattern necessitates prolonged treatment. Lifelong prophylaxis may be required for endemic area residents.

questions.question: What test monitors treatment response in leukemia?
questions.explanation: Bone marrow examination monitors treatment response by assessing blast percentage and cellularity. Serial marrows during and after treatment determine remission status. Cytogenetics and molecular tests on marrow samples detect minimal residual disease.

questions.question: How does elevated 2,3-DPG partially compensate in PK deficiency?
questions.explanation: Elevated 2,3-DPG in PK deficiency shifts the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve to the right, decreasing hemoglobin's oxygen affinity and improving oxygen delivery to tissues. This partially compensates for the anemia by making the available hemoglobin more efficient at releasing oxygen. However, this compensation comes at the cost of reduced ATP production.

questions.question: What does granulocyte agglutination assay detect?
questions.explanation: The granulocyte agglutination assay detects antibodies that cause neutrophils to actively agglutinate or clump together. Cells and serum are incubated for 4-6 hours at 30°C. This assay is very reliable but less sensitive than immunofluorescence methods.

questions.question: Where are HNA-1 antigens located?
questions.explanation: HNA-1 antigens are located on human neutrophil Fc-gamma receptor IIIb (CD16) encoded by the FCGR3B gene. This receptor is found only on neutrophils making HNA-1 antigens neutrophil-specific. Soluble forms of FcγRIIIb expressing HNA-1 are present in plasma.

Standard whole blood collection uses 63ml of anticoagulant-preservative solution mixed with 450ml of blood. This ratio ensures adequate anticoagulation and metabolic support throughout storage. The mixture creates a final product with hematocrit of 36-44%.
questions.question: What volume of anticoagulant solution is typically used with 450ml of whole blood collection

questions.explanation: Scurvy (vitamin C deficiency) impairs collagen synthesis because vitamin C is essential cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase enzymes modifying procollagen. Defective collagen weakens perivascular connective tissue support, causing capillary fragility manifesting as petechiae, ecchymoses, gum bleeding, and poor wound healing. Platelet counts and coagulation tests remain normal. Vitamin C supplementation (100-200 mg daily) rapidly corrects the deficiency, with clinical improvement within days to weeks.
questions.question: What hemostatic component deficiency causes scurvy?

questions.explanation: Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) is elevated in CML reflecting increased cell turnover and tissue damage. LDH is a tissue enzyme released when cells break down. Uric acid is also elevated due to rapid cell proliferation and breakdown.
questions.question: Which enzyme is elevated in CML due to increased cell turnover?

questions.explanation: Pyruvate kinase deficiency is the most common cause of hereditary chronic nonspherocytic hemolytic anemia (HNSHA). The term "nonspherocytic" distinguishes it from hereditary spherocytosis, which has a different membrane defect. Clinical presentation includes anemia, jaundice, splenomegaly, and gallstones with widely variable severity.
questions.question: What is the most common presentation of pyruvate kinase deficiency?

questions.explanation: PT evaluates Factors I (fibrinogen), II (prothrombin), V, VII, and X - comprising the extrinsic pathway (Factor VII) and common pathway (Factors X, V, II, I). Factor VII is unique to the extrinsic pathway, making PT specific for detecting Factor VII deficiency. PT is particularly useful for monitoring warfarin therapy since vitamin K-dependent factors (II, VII, IX, X) are affected by warfarin.
options: Factors I, II, V, VII, X
questions.question: Which factors are evaluated by the Prothrombin Time test?
What does the HLA Class III region encode?
questions.explanation: The Class III region does not encode HLA molecules but contains genes for complement components including C2, C4, and factor B. It also encodes 21-hydroxylase, tumor necrosis factors, and other immune-related proteins. These products differ structurally and functionally from Class I and II molecules.

The haem group specifically binds ferrous iron (Fe) rather than ferric iron (Fe) for functional oxygen transport. This reduced iron state is essential for reversible oxygen binding and release. Oxidation to Fe produces methaemoglobin, which cannot transport oxygen effectively.
questions.question: Which ion does the haem group bind to enable oxygen transport

questions.explanation: Vitamin B12 deficiency must be excluded before folate therapy because folate administration partially corrects the anaemia while allowing B12 neuropathy to progress irreversibly. If both deficiencies coexist or cannot be distinguished, both vitamins should be administered simultaneously. Never treat suspected megaloblastic anaemia with folate alone without assessing B12 status.
questions.question: What critical precaution must occur before initiating folate therapy?
Which ions' content determines RBC volume and water content?
questions.explanation: RBCs control volume and H2O content primarily through control of sodium and potassium content via ATP-dependent cation pumps. Maintenance of proper Na+ and K+ gradients is essential for cell volume regulation and osmotic stability. Failure of these pumps due to ATP depletion leads to cell swelling and eventual hemolysis.

CLL survival varies widely from 5 years to more than 25 years depending on multiple factors. Prognostic markers including cytogenetics, mutation status, and staging help predict individual outcomes. Some patients with favorable features live for decades without requiring treatment.
questions.question: What is the typical prognosis range for CLL patients?

questions.explanation: Cell coincidence occurs when two or more cells pass through the impedance counting aperture at the same time. This causes two cells to be counted as one voltage pulse, resulting in falsely low counts. Modern analyzers minimize this problem through hydrodynamic focusing techniques that ensure single-file cell passage.
questions.question: Which problem occurs when multiple cells pass through the aperture simultaneously?
Which red cell index is characteristically reduced in iron deficiency anaemia?
questions.explanation: Mean corpuscular volume (MCV) is characteristically reduced in iron deficiency anaemia, typically falling below 79fl, creating microcytic red cells. This reduction reflects decreased haemoglobin synthesis resulting in smaller red blood cells. MCH and MCHC also decrease, producing the hypochromic microcytic picture typical of iron deficiency.

Each cryoprecipitate unit contains approximately 15ml, making it a concentrated product. This small volume allows large doses of fibrinogen without volume overload. Multiple units are typically pooled for adult transfusion.
questions.question: What is the typical volume of one unit of cryoprecipitate
Which mechanism best explains RhIg's prevention of anti-D formation
questions.explanation: RhIg coats D antigen sites on foetal RBCs, preventing maternal B-cell recognition and activation. Additionally, antibody-antigen complexes inhibit BCR cross-linking and trigger FcRII inhibitory signals while promoting macrophage clearance of D-positive cells before immune response initiation.
options: Coating D antigens inhibiting B-cell response
Activation of natural killer cell function

questions.question: Which zone of follicles surrounds the larger lymphocytes at the follicular center
questions.explanation: The follicular center with larger lymphocytes is surrounded by a mantle zone or corona composed of small to medium lymphocytes. This arrangement reflects different stages of B-cell maturation. The mantle zone contains naive B-cells while the center has activated cells.

Platelet counts below 10,000/mm3 significantly increase spontaneous bleeding risk, particularly intracranial hemorrhage, warranting prophylactic platelet transfusion even without active bleeding. Counts 10,000-20,000/mm3 may need transfusion before invasive procedures. Counts 20,000-50,000/mm3 rarely cause spontaneous bleeding but increase surgical bleeding risk. Transfusion thresholds are higher for bleeding patients, surgery, or platelet dysfunction coexisting with thrombocytopenia.
questions.question: What is the platelet transfusion threshold for spontaneous bleeding risk?
How is the Mean Cell Lifespan (MCL) determined on a linear graph?
questions.explanation: On a linear graph, when plotting percentage radioactivity against time, if a straight line is obtained, it is extended to the time axis. Where the line reaches the time axis represents the Mean Cell Lifespan (MCL). Alternatively, on a semi-log plot, the MCL is determined by finding where 37% radioactivity intersects the curve.
options: Where the extended line reaches the time axis

questions.explanation: ITP diagnosis classically involves three negative findings: absence of fever (distinguishes from infectious causes), absence of lymphadenopathy or marked splenomegaly (spleen may be barely palpable in 10%), and normal ESR/serology (excludes systemic disease). These criteria help distinguish ITP from thrombocytopenia secondary to leukemia, lymphoma, infections, or other systemic diseases presenting with additional clinical features.
questions.question: What are the three negative findings defining ITP diagnosis?
options: Absence of fever, lymphadenopathy, marked splenomegaly
Absence of infection, malignancy, drug exposure
Absence of thrombosis, factor deficiency, inhibitors

questions.explanation: Light transmission aggregometry (LTA) is considered the gold standard for measuring platelet aggregation with high sensitivity. It detects turbidity changes as platelets aggregate in platelet-rich plasma. LTA remains the reference method against which newer techniques are validated.
questions.question: What is considered the gold standard for platelet aggregation measurement?
What glycoprotein contains HPA-1 polymorphism?
questions.explanation: The HPA-1a/1b polymorphism is located on GPIIIa, the β3 subunit of the αIIbβ3 integrin. It results from a single amino acid substitution: Leu33 for HPA-1a versus Pro33 for HPA-1b. A rare third alloantigen, HPA-1c with Val33, has also been identified.

questions.question: Which glycoprotein binds Von Willebrand factor on platelet membrane?
questions.explanation: Glycoprotein Ib (GP-Ib) binds to Von Willebrand factor which then adheres to collagen. This indirect binding mechanism is crucial for platelet adhesion. GP-Ib deficiency causes Bernard-Soulier disease.

questions.question: What determines need for ongoing phlebotomy after initial haemochromatosis treatment?
questions.explanation: Persistent iron reaccumulation necessitates lifelong maintenance phlebotomy (typically 3-4 sessions annually) because the genetic defect causing increased intestinal absorption persists despite depleting excess stores. Maintenance frequency depends on individual absorption rates, dietary intake, and blood loss. Monitoring ferritin guides phlebotomy scheduling.

AML M6 requires 50% or more nucleated marrow cells to be erythroid precursors. Additionally, 30% or more of remaining non-erythroid cells must be myeloblasts for diagnosis. If myeloblasts are less than 30%, the condition is classified as myelodysplasia rather than acute erythroleukaemia.
questions.question: What percentage of erythroid precursors is required for AML M6 diagnosis?

questions.explanation: AML M1 (acute myeloblastic leukaemia without maturation) represents 15-20% of all AML cases. It features 30% or more myeloblasts among non-erythroid marrow cells with less than 10% promyelocytes. The blasts show positive staining for myeloperoxidase or Sudan Black in at least 3%.
questions.question: What percentage of AML cases does M1 subtype represent?

questions.explanation: Untreated cardiac haemochromatosis progresses to restrictive and dilated cardiomyopathy with heart failure and arrhythmias, representing a major cause of mortality in young homozygotes. Iron deposits in myocardium impair contractility and conduction. Aggressive early venesection or chelation prevents cardiac complications. Established cardiomyopathy shows poor response to iron removal.
questions.question: What cardiac outcome results from untreated severe haemochromatosis?

questions.explanation: Approximately 30% of hemophilia patients develop antibodies (inhibitors) against the factor they receive for treatment, representing a major complication. These inhibitors neutralize infused factor, making standard replacement ineffective. Management involves high-dose recombinant Factor VIIa to bypass the inhibited factor or immune tolerance induction using high-dose Factor VIII/IX to eradicate inhibitors gradually over months to years.
questions.question: What percentage of hemophilia patients develop inhibitors to replacement therapy?

questions.explanation: Folate monoglutamates are absorbed most efficiently by duodenal and jejunal enterocytes, requiring no further digestion before transport across the intestinal epithelium. Dietary polyglutamates must be enzymatically cleaved to monoglutamates before absorption. The small intestine possesses tremendous capacity for absorbing monoglutamate forms.
questions.question: Which form of folate is absorbed most efficiently by enterocytes?

questions.explanation: Gray platelet syndrome results from failure of alpha granule packaging, causing platelets to appear gray on blood smears due to absence of alpha granule contents (normally give purplish hue). Patients cannot release alpha granule proteins (fibrinogen, Factor V, vWF, platelet factor 4) during activation, causing mild-moderate bleeding from defective platelet secretion despite normal aggregation capability.
questions.question: What characterizes gray platelet syndrome?

questions.explanation: Agonist binding to platelet receptors triggers intracellular signaling pathways leading to activation responses. These cascades involve calcium mobilization, protein phosphorylation, and cytoskeletal rearrangement. The signaling pathways coordinate the complex process of platelet activation.
questions.question: What does agonist binding to platelet receptors trigger?

questions.explanation: Infections, pregnancy, or oxidative drug exposure may trigger acute hemolytic crises in otherwise stable HbH disease. These stressors exacerbate HbH instability causing accelerated red cell destruction. Patients normally maintain compensated anaemia but require monitoring during illness.
questions.question: What condition triggers hemolytic crisis in HbH disease

questions.explanation: 2,3-DPG levels decline linearly toward zero during the first two weeks of RBC storage. This increases oxygen affinity and reduces oxygen delivery. Rejuvenation can restore 2,3-DPG levels.
options: Fall linearly toward zero in first 2 weeks
questions.question: What happens to 2,3-DPG levels in stored red blood cells

questions.explanation: The Clauss technique measures functional fibrinogen by adding strong thrombin solution to diluted plasma and measuring clotting time, which is inversely proportional to fibrinogen concentration. Plasma dilution minimizes inhibitor effects (heparin, FDPs), while strong thrombin ensures clotting time depends on fibrinogen level rather than thrombin concentration. A calibration curve using known fibrinogen standards allows quantification.
options: Clotting time with diluted plasma and strong thrombin
questions.question: What is the principle of the Clauss fibrinogen assay?

questions.explanation: IEF is widely used in soil science to identify organic fertilizer matrices and assess soil organic matter stabilization. The technique provides insights into soil health and nutrient management for agriculture. IEF also analyzes proteins in oilseeds and cereals for nutritional enhancement.
questions.question: What field uses IEF for soil organic matter assessment?

questions.explanation: Thrombocytopenia is generally mild because platelets are trapped but not destroyed in the spleen. This contrasts with red cells that undergo destruction. The mild degree rarely causes bleeding complications.
questions.question: Why is thrombocytopenia generally mild in HMS

questions.explanation: Anticonvulsants, particularly phenytoin, phenobarbital, and primidone, interfere with folate metabolism through multiple mechanisms including impaired absorption and increased metabolism. Long-term therapy often requires folate supplementation. Sulfasalazine similarly impairs folate status by inhibiting intestinal folate conjugase and increasing urinary excretion.
questions.question: What medication class commonly causes folate deficiency?

questions.explanation: Long-term survivors face risks including infertility, growth problems, secondary cancers, and organ dysfunction. These late effects result from intensive chemotherapy and radiation exposure. Regular surveillance throughout life detects complications early enabling intervention.
questions.question: What late effect concerns children treated for acute leukemia?
Which immunoglobulin is deposited in Henoch-Schonlein purpura?
questions.explanation: IgA deposition characterizes Henoch-Schonlein purpura, causing capillaritis and arteriolitis with immune complex formation. IgA immune complexes damage vessel walls triggering inflammation. Renal involvement shows IgA nephropathy.

questions.question: Which staging system is commonly used for CLL management?
questions.explanation: The Rai staging system (stages 0-4) is commonly used alongside Binet classification for CLL management. Staging considers lymphocyte counts, lymph node enlargement, splenomegaly, hepatomegaly, anemia, and thrombocytopenia. This helps determine prognosis and guide treatment timing decisions.

questions.question: What does MLC testing measure?
questions.explanation: Mixed lymphocyte culture measures the proliferative response of lymphocytes when exposed to foreign HLA antigens. This functional assay assesses biological significance of HLA differences through actual cellular immune responses. Proliferation is measured using radioactive thymidine incorporation or other markers.

questions.question: What volume ratio is typically used in PT testing?
questions.explanation: PT testing typically uses 100 μL plasma with 200 μL thromboplastin reagent (containing tissue factor and calcium), providing excess thromboplastin to ensure extrinsic pathway saturation. This 1:2 ratio standardizes the test, making results dependent on plasma factor levels rather than thromboplastin concentration. The large thromboplastin excess ensures sensitivity to factor deficiencies while minimizing reagent variability effects.

In ischemic areas where RBCs become less deformable and stiffen, small PFC particles can penetrate more easily to deliver oxygen. This advantage is crucial for reperfusion of compromised tissue. The superior flow characteristics improve outcomes in ischemic conditions.
questions.question: What advantage do PFCs have in areas of tissue ischemia
What is the primary site of plasminogen synthesis?
questions.explanation: Plasminogen is synthesized primarily in the liver and circulates as inactive zymogen awaiting conversion to plasmin by plasminogen activators (tPA, urokinase). The liver also synthesizes most coagulation factors and inhibitors, making it central to hemostatic balance. Severe liver disease causes complex coagulopathy affecting procoagulant factors, anticoagulant proteins, and fibrinolytic components. Plasminogen deficiency causes thrombotic tendency from impaired fibrinolysis.

The hexose monophosphate shunt metabolizes 5-10% of glucose with NADPH as the end product. This pathway protects the RBC from oxidative injury by maintaining glutathione in its reduced state. The most common defect in this pathway is glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G-6PD) deficiency.
questions.question: What percentage of glucose is metabolized through the hexose monophosphate shunt?

questions.explanation: Rh HDFN frequently required exchange transfusion historically due to severe anaemia and hyperbilirubinaemia. ABO HDFN infrequently needs exchange transfusion as phototherapy usually suffices for slowly rising bilirubin, with severe disease occurring in less than 1% of cases.
questions.question: How does exchange transfusion frequency compare between ABO and Rh HDFN
options: ABO requires frequent exchange; Rh requires infrequent exchange
Both require exchange with equal frequency
Neither requires exchange with modern phototherapy
ABO requires more exchanges in premature infants
Rh requires frequent exchange; ABO requires infrequent exchange

questions.question: Which molecules provide essential costimulatory signals for T-cell activation
options: CD4 on helper cells and MHC class I
CD8 on cytotoxic cells and MHC class II
TCR on T cells and peptide alone
CD28 on T cells and B7 molecules on APCs
LFA-1 on T cells and fibronectin on APCs
questions.explanation: CD28 on T cells interacts with B7 molecules (CD80/CD86) on antigen-presenting cells, providing crucial costimulatory signals beyond TCR-MHC-peptide binding. Without costimulation, T cells may become anergic (non-responsive), so both signals are essential for activation.

During deoxygenation, some oxygen leaves as a superoxide (O2-) radical, leaving iron in the ferric state forming methemoglobin. During oxygenation, one electron is partially transferred from iron to bound oxygen, forming a ferric-superoxide complex. This explains the continuous low-level methemoglobin formation that must be reduced by cytochrome b5 reductase.
questions.question: What forms during hemoglobin deoxygenation that can lead to methemoglobin?

questions.explanation: The greatest source of variation in the Ivy bleeding time method is difficulty performing standardized punctures, as manual lancet technique produces variable depth and length incisions. This variability usually leads to erroneously low (shortened) results when incisions are too shallow. The Simplate/Surgicutt method addressed this limitation by mechanically standardizing incision dimensions, dramatically improving test reproducibility.
questions.question: What is the most significant source of variation in the Ivy bleeding time method?
What is the half-life of Oxygent in circulation
questions.explanation: Oxygent has a circulation half-life of approximately 13 hours, providing relatively short-term oxygen carrying support. This short half-life necessitates repeated dosing for prolonged support. The clearance rate is faster than many hemoglobin-based alternatives.

FNAIT stands for fetal/neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia, also called fetomaternal alloimmune thrombocytopenia. It results from maternal immunization against fetal platelet antigens inherited from the father. Maternal IgG antibodies cross the placenta causing immune destruction of fetal platelets.
questions.question: What does FNAIT stand for?

questions.explanation: The normal prothrombin time reference range is 11 to 13.5 seconds, representing normal extrinsic pathway function. PT measures factors VII, X, V, prothrombin, and fibrinogen activity. Prolongation beyond this range suggests coagulation factor deficiency or anticoagulant effect.
questions.question: What is the normal reference range for prothrombin time?

options: Hydrophobic heads outside, hydrophilic tails inside
Hydrophobic tails inside, hydrophilic heads outside
questions.explanation: Lipids in the RBC membrane form a bilayer with hydrophobic tails on the inside and hydrophilic polar head groups facing either the extracellular or cytoplasmic surface. This arrangement provides a permeability barrier between the external environment and red cell cytoplasm. The lipid bilayer is essential for membrane fluidity and selective permeability.
questions.question: How are lipids arranged in the RBC membrane bilayer?

questions.explanation: Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia develops in approximately 10-15% of CLL patients. The abnormal lymphocytes produce antibodies against red blood cells causing premature destruction. This autoimmune phenomenon adds to anemia caused by bone marrow infiltration.
questions.question: Which complication occurs in 10-15% of CLL patients?

questions.explanation: Ferrous sulphate is the preferred oral iron preparation due to its low cost, good absorption, and 67mg elemental iron per 200mg tablet. It should be administered on an empty stomach at intervals of at least 6 hours for optimal absorption. Gastrointestinal side effects can be minimized by starting with lower doses.
questions.question: What medication is the best oral preparation for treating iron deficiency?

questions.explanation: Patients must rest 30-60 minutes after venesection and avoid strenuous work for 24 hours to prevent syncope and cardiovascular complications. Drinking 500ml fluid within 1 hour beforehand maintains blood volume. The procedure takes approximately 30 minutes. Age and comorbidities determine individual tolerance requiring informed consent.
questions.question: What precaution is necessary after venesection therapy?

questions.explanation: The liver contains the largest folate store in the body, accounting for a significant portion of the total 10-12mg body folate. This hepatic storage provides a reserve that can sustain folate requirements for approximately 4 months. Unlike vitamin B12 stores, folate reserves deplete relatively rapidly during deficiency states.
questions.question: Which organ contains the largest store of folate in the adult body?

options: Requires high FiO2 for adequate oxygen delivery
questions.explanation: PFCs require supplemental oxygen administration (high FiO2) to achieve adequate oxygen carrying capacity, limiting their use in certain settings. This oxygen dependency makes them less versatile than hemoglobin-based carriers. The requirement for supplemental oxygen restricts some clinical applications.
questions.question: What is a major disadvantage requiring supplemental oxygen with PFC use

questions.explanation: Whole blood storage at 1-6 degrees C preserves red cell viability while slowing metabolic processes. However, this cold temperature irreversibly damages platelet function. Coagulation factors, particularly factors V and VIII, also deteriorate progressively during refrigerated storage.
questions.question: At what temperature range must whole blood be stored
Which immune mediators are produced by white pulp for bacterial clearance
questions.explanation: The white pulp produces complement, opsonins, properdin, and tuftsin as immune mediators involved in bacterial clearance. These molecules enhance phagocytosis and complement activation against pathogens. The production of these specific mediators reflects the spleen's specialized role in defense against encapsulated bacteria.

G-CSF (granulocyte colony-stimulating factor) and corticosteroids mobilize granulocytes into peripheral blood, increasing collection yields. Combined use can increase yields above 1 x 10^11 granulocytes. Donor safety requires careful monitoring.
questions.question: What medications are used to stimulate donors for improved granulocyte collection
Which condition is characterized by spoon-shaped nails?
questions.explanation: Koilonychia (spoon-shaped nails) is a classic clinical feature of severe iron deficiency anaemia, resulting from decreased iron-containing enzymes in epithelial tissues. The nails become brittle, ridged, and develop a concave shape resembling spoons. This manifestation occurs only in chronic, severe iron deficiency states.

Retinal hemorrhages and exudates develop in severely anemic patients, particularly when hemoglobin falls below 5g/dL, due to hypoxic damage to retinal vessels and increased blood flow. Cotton-wool spots may also appear. These findings indicate severe, prolonged anaemia requiring urgent treatment to prevent permanent visual damage.
questions.question: What ophthalmological finding occurs in severe anaemia?

questions.explanation: Antithrombin III (ATIII) binding is a necessary requirement for heparin's anticoagulant activity through conformational change acceleration. Heparin accelerates ATIII-mediated inactivation of clotting enzymes by 1000-fold. Without ATIII binding, heparin cannot exert anticoagulant effects.
questions.question: Which protein must heparin bind to for anticoagulant activity?
What is unconjugated bilirubin transported by in the blood?
questions.explanation: The protoporphyrin ring from heme is converted to biliverdin, then to unconjugated bilirubin, which is carried to the liver by albumin. In the liver, bilirubin is conjugated and excreted into the intestine where flora convert it to urobilinogen. Most urobilinogen is excreted in stool, with some reabsorbed and excreted in urine.

questions.question: What charge does haemoglobin carry at alkaline pH
questions.explanation: Haemoglobin becomes negatively charged at alkaline pH values migrating toward the positive anode. The alkaline conditions deprotonate amino acid residues creating net negative charge. This predictable behavior enables systematic variant separation.

An elevated reticulocyte count indicates the compensatory increase in red cell production responding to hemolytic anemia in hypersplenism. This marrow hyperplasia attempts to compensate for accelerated red cell destruction. The reticulocytosis confirms appropriate marrow response to anemia.
questions.question: What compensatory mechanism indicates increased red cell production in hypersplenism

questions.explanation: Platelet distribution width increases in megaloblastic anaemia reflecting greater variation in platelet size due to abnormal megakaryocyte development. Platelets are often reduced in number and may be larger than normal with abnormal morphology. Thrombocytopenia results from ineffective megakaryocytopoiesis similar to dyserythropoiesis.
questions.question: What happens to platelet distribution width (PDW) in megaloblastic anaemia?
What method detects specific DNA sequence variations
questions.explanation: Restriction enzyme digestion detects specific mutations by cutting DNA at recognition sequences altered by mutations. The resulting fragment patterns change with mutation presence. This technique, called restriction fragment length polymorphism (RFLP), enables mutation identification.

Intravenous heparin has an onset of action within few minutes, providing immediate anticoagulation. This rapid effect is crucial for acute thrombotic emergencies. Subcutaneous administration has delayed onset of 1-2 hours.
questions.question: What is the onset of action for intravenous heparin?
Which coagulation factors are included in prothrombin complex concentrates
questions.explanation: Prothrombin complex contains the vitamin K-dependent factors II, VII, IX, and X. These factors are grouped together in fractionation processes. The concentrate treats multiple factor deficiencies or warfarin reversal.

Clinical manifestations of beta thalassaemia major typically emerge around one year of age when foetal haemoglobin levels decline. Infants initially appear normal due to persistent HbF compensating for absent HbA. Symptoms develop as gamma chain production decreases and beta chain requirement increases.
questions.question: At what age do symptoms typically manifest in beta thalassaemia major

questions.explanation: Spectrin is composed of alpha and beta chains that join to form a matrix strengthening the membrane against shear force and controlling biconcave shape. It forms the primary structural component of the cytoskeleton beneath the lipid bilayer. Ankyrin serves as the binding site for spectrin to attach to the membrane.
questions.question: Which protein forms the major structural matrix that strengthens the RBC membrane against shear force?

questions.explanation: Minimal tissue damage must be ensured during blood sampling to prevent cellular activation and morphological artifacts. Traumatic collection causes platelet clumping and white cell activation. Clean venipuncture technique maintains sample integrity for accurate morphological assessment.
questions.question: What must be minimized during blood sampling for PBF?

questions.explanation: Iron overload causes multiple endocrine dysfunctions including diabetes mellitus, hypogonadism, hypothyroidism, and growth hormone deficiency. Siderosis damages hormone-producing glands impairing function. Endocrine complications significantly affect quality of life.
questions.question: What endocrine complication commonly affects thalassaemia major patients

questions.explanation: Lupus anticoagulant causes poor correction in mixing studies because these antibodies interfere with phospholipid-dependent coagulation tests regardless of factor levels present. Even when normal plasma (with all factors) is mixed with patient plasma, the antibodies inhibit the coagulation reaction, keeping the APTT prolonged. This distinguishes lupus anticoagulant from factor deficiencies, which correct with normal plasma addition.
questions.question: Which condition would show poor correction in APTT mixing studies?

questions.explanation: FFP must be frozen within 6-8 hours of collection to preserve labile coagulation factors. This rapid processing maintains optimal factor V and VIII levels. Longer delays result in FP24 classification with reduced labile factor content.
questions.question: What is the maximum time allowed between collection and freezing for fresh frozen plasma
How many minimum HLA markers are reviewed for matching?
questions.explanation: Health teams review at least 8 HLA markers: two A markers, two B markers, two C markers, and two DRB1 markers. Some transplant centers also match DQ markers for additional compatibility. This minimum matching requirement balances practical feasibility with transplant success rates.

questions.question: What is the primary clinical indication for granulocyte transfusion
questions.explanation: Granulocytes treat profound persistent neutropenia (WBCs <500/muL) with life-threatening sepsis unresponsive to antibiotics. This is a last-resort therapy. Improved antibiotics and G-CSF have made granulocyte transfusions rare.
options: Treatment of neutropenia with life-threatening infection unresponsive to antibiotics

questions.question: Which condition is NOT a typical indication for anticoagulant therapy?
questions.explanation: Anticoagulants are prescribed for conditions with high risk of thromboembolic events including atrial fibrillation, deep vein thrombosis, mechanical heart valves, and stroke history. Essential hypertension alone does not require anticoagulation unless complicated by other thrombotic risk factors. The primary concern in these conditions is prevention of clot formation.

HMS has been documented in immunocompromised patients from malaria-endemic regions who have HIV infection and lung carcinoma. Other entities like EBV, CMV, or lymphoproliferative disorders must be excluded. The combination complicates diagnosis and management.
questions.question: In which immunocompromised patients has HMS been documented

questions.explanation: Lead can induce pyrimidine 5' nucleotidase deficiency resulting in hemolytic anemia and characteristic basophilic stippling on peripheral smear. This is treatable with chelation therapy and stopping lead exposure. Pyrimidine 5' nucleotidase deficiency is one of the less common but clinically significant RBC enzymopathies.
questions.question: What toxin can induce pyrimidine 5' nucleotidase deficiency?
What electrolyte abnormality can occur with unfractionated heparin therapy?
questions.explanation: Hyperkalemia rarely occurs with unfractionated heparin attributed to inhibition of aldosterone secretion. It occurs with both low and high-dose therapy within a week. Diabetic and renal failure patients face higher risk.

questions.question: Which method does the Caveron Alpha analyzer primarily use?
questions.explanation: The Caveron Alpha analyzer operates on photometric measurement principles, detecting turbidity changes caused by fibrin fiber formation during coagulation (clotting methods) or absorbance changes in chromogenic assays. For immunological methods, it detects absorbance changes during antigen-antibody complex formation. The analyzer performs routine coagulation tests (PT, APTT, TT, fibrinogen) and specialized assays using clotting, chromogenic, and turbidimetric methodologies with automated result calculation.

questions.question: How many distinct structures exist on platelet membranes?
questions.explanation: There are about 45 distinct structures on the platelet membrane categorized into 5 groups: adhesion molecules, immune molecules, blood group antigens, receptors, and other molecules. These structures include integrins like CD41 and CD61, MHC class I molecules, Fc receptors, and various receptor types. The complexity reflects platelets' diverse functions beyond hemostasis.

Potassium, magnesium, and zinc concentrations in red cells are much higher than in plasma. RBCs control volume and water content primarily through control of sodium and potassium content via cation pumps. This electrolyte gradient is maintained by energy-dependent Na+/K+ ATPase pumps in the membrane requiring ATP from glycolysis.
questions.question: Which electrolyte concentration is higher in RBCs than plasma?

questions.explanation: Compound heterozygotes with one C282Y and one H63D mutation may develop haemochromatosis, though risk and severity are substantially lower than C282Y homozygotes. Most remain asymptomatic. Penetrance is highly variable. Monitoring ferritin and transferrin saturation guides need for intervention. Environmental factors influence phenotypic expression.
questions.question: What percentage of HH risk does C282Y/H63D compound heterozygosity confer?
Which cell lineage is most commonly affected in ALL?
questions.explanation: B-lymphocyte precursors account for 80-85% of ALL cases. T-cell precursors comprise 15-20% of cases, while rarely the lineage remains unclear. This distinction is important for treatment planning and prognosis determination using WHO classification system.

questions.question: On which chromosome are the alpha-like globin genes located
questions.explanation: Alpha-like globin genes, including  and  chains, are encoded on chromosome 16. This chromosomal location is distinct from beta-like genes which reside on chromosome 11. The separation of alpha and beta gene clusters allows independent regulation of globin chain synthesis.

questions.question: What effect does hypothyroidism have on warfarin requirements?
questions.explanation: Hypothyroidism increases warfarin requirements because reduced metabolic rate decreases clotting factor turnover. Slower factor synthesis reduces anticoagulant sensitivity. Thyroid status influences warfarin dosing requirements.

questions.question: What intravenous iron preparation is considered safest?
questions.explanation: Ferric hydroxide-sucrose (Venofer(R)) is considered the safest intravenous iron preparation with lowest risk of anaphylactic reactions, administered by slow intravenous injection or infusion, usually 200mg iron per session. Parenteral iron is indicated when oral iron fails due to intolerance, malabsorption, or inadequate response. Total dose required is calculated based on haemoglobin deficit and body weight.

A trained haemomorphologist must be a laboratory scientist or physician, especially for slides with significant pathology. Skilled interpretation requires extensive training in recognizing normal and abnormal cellular features. Expertise ensures accurate diagnosis of complex haematological conditions.
questions.question: Who must interpret slides with significant pathology?
What skin manifestation indicates leukemic infiltration?
questions.explanation: Leukemia cutis results from direct skin infiltration by leukemic cells. This uncommon manifestation appears as papules, nodules, or plaques. It occurs more frequently in monocytic leukemias (M4, M5) than other subtypes.

The Philadelphia chromosome is detected in approximately 15-20% of adult ALL cases. This genetic abnormality significantly impacts treatment decisions and prognosis. Patients with Philadelphia chromosome-positive ALL often require tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy in addition to standard chemotherapy.
questions.question: What percentage of ALL cases feature the BCR-ABL fusion gene?
How long should labeled blood circulate before taking the Day 0 sample in patients with circulatory issues?
questions.explanation: For patients with cardiovascular or circulatory issues, 60 minutes should be allowed for circulation before taking the Day 0 sample instead of the standard 10 minutes. This ensures complete mixing and equilibration of the labeled RBCs throughout the circulation. The Day 0 sample establishes the baseline radioactivity for comparison with subsequent samples.

options: Insufficient protection for any bleeding volume
Cost-effectiveness not superior to full dose
Adverse reactions more common with mini-dose
Full dose now recommended for all indications
Availability issues limit widespread clinical use
questions.question: Why is mini-dose RhIg rarely used in current practice
questions.explanation: Mini-dose (50 g) RhIg for first-trimester events is rarely used because full-dose administration is now recommended for all potential sensitizing events. This approach ensures adequate protection regardless of actual bleed volume, eliminating underdosing risk from volume estimation errors.

questions.question: Which G6PD variant is most clinically significant among US Black populations?
questions.explanation: G6PD A- is the most clinically significant variant among US Black populations, affecting 11% of Black men. It has the same electrophoretic mobility as G6PD A but is unstable, resulting in enzyme loss with older RBCs having only 5-15% enzyme activity. G6PD B is the normal variant found in all populations.

questions.question: What is the median age at CML diagnosis?
questions.explanation: CML median age at diagnosis is 50-60 years, though it can occur at all ages. The disease is rare in children and shows slight male predominance. CML represents approximately 20% of all leukemias in the United States.

questions.question: Which route should be avoided for heparin administration?
questions.explanation: Intramuscular injection should be avoided as it produces hematoma formation at injection sites. Heparin's anticoagulant effect causes bleeding into muscle tissue. Intravenous or subcutaneous routes are preferred for safe administration.

questions.question: What blood finding suggests bone marrow recovery after chemotherapy?
questions.explanation: Rising reticulocyte count indicates bone marrow recovery with renewed red cell production. Increasing neutrophils and platelets also signal engraftment. These changes typically occur 2-4 weeks after intensive chemotherapy completion.

options: When DAT is strongly positive requiring identification
For all ABO incompatibility cases routinely
In blocked Rh cases with false-negative DAT
When maternal sample is readily available
Only when exchange transfusion is planned
