This dual pattern distinguishes vWD from pure platelet disorders (only mucocutaneous) or pure coagulation disorders (only deep tissue). Severity varies by type: Type I (mild), Type II (variable), Type III (severe).

questions.question: How many major HLA antigen groups exist?
questions.explanation: There are six major groups of HLA antigens: HLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-C, HLA-DR, HLA-DQ, and HLA-DP. These groups are divided into classes representing different types of HLA molecules with distinct functions. Class I includes HLA-A, B, and C, while Class II includes HLA-DR, DQ, and DP.

questions.question: What characteristic finding appears in thalassaemia CBC compared to haemoglobin decrease
questions.explanation: Thalassaemias demonstrate disproportionately decreased MCV compared to haemoglobin reduction, creating marked microcytosis. This distinguishing feature helps differentiate thalassaemia from other anaemias. The MCV reduction exceeds expectations based on haemoglobin levels alone.

HLA types are inherited, so the best chance of finding suitable donors may be with someone of similar racial or ethnic background. Some HLA types are more common in certain populations than others. This population distribution affects the probability of finding compatible donors.
questions.question: Why is ethnic background important in matching?
Which genes encode HLA Class II proteins?
questions.explanation: HLA Class II proteins are encoded by the genes HLA-DR, HLA-DQ, and HLA-DP, located in the MHC region. These molecules have more restricted tissue distribution compared to Class I molecules. Class II genes are also highly polymorphic, particularly in the beta chain regions.

International Normalized Ratio (INR) is the standard test for monitoring warfarin therapy effectiveness and adjusting dosage accordingly. Initially monitored daily, frequency reduces to every few weeks once therapeutic range is achieved. INR standardizes prothrombin time results across different laboratories.
questions.question: Which laboratory parameter is primarily used to monitor warfarin therapy?
How many recognized HPA biallelic systems exist?
questions.explanation: The HPA nomenclature recognizes 21 biallelic systems although some other unpopular ones exist. The most clinically significant include HPA-1 through HPA-6 and HPA-15. Each system represents a different glycoprotein polymorphism with clinical importance.

questions.question: Which enzyme deficiency accounts for 95% of genetic defects in glycolytic enzymes?
questions.explanation: Pyruvate kinase deficiency accounts for 95% of cases of genetic defects in glycolytic enzymes. The remaining 4% is caused by phosphoglucose isomerase deficiency. These defects result in reduced glycolysis rate, depriving RBCs of energy and causing hemolytic anemia as cells cannot maintain their biconcave flexible shape.

questions.question: What finding suggests CML transformation to acute phase?
questions.explanation: Increasing blast percentage in blood or bone marrow suggests transformation to accelerated phase or blast crisis. Additional abnormal chromosome changes may develop with disease progression. Patients may experience worsening symptoms unresponsive to previous therapy.

Phosphatidylcholine (PC) and sphingomyelin (SM) are predominantly located on the outer leaflet of the RBC membrane bilayer. Phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) and phosphatidylserine (PS) are predominantly on the inner leaflet. This asymmetric distribution is actively maintained and is important for membrane function and recognition of aging cells.
questions.question: Which phospholipid is predominantly located on the outer leaflet of the RBC membrane?
What serological pattern may occur with HMS causing diagnostic confusion
questions.explanation: Serologies for CMV, toxoplasmosis, EBV, HH6, parvovirus B19, and schistosomiasis may be false-positive due to polyclonal B-cell activation. This pattern can lead to diagnostic confusion. The false positivity results from non-specific antibody production.

questions.question: What is the recommended platelet concentrate transfusion dose?
questions.explanation: The recommended platelet concentrate dose is 2 units per 10 kg body weight, expected to increase platelet count by approximately 30,000-50,000/mm3 in non-refractory patients. One platelet concentrate unit (from single whole blood donation) or one apheresis unit (from single donor by apheresis) provides approximately 5.5 x 1010 platelets. Transfusions should occur within 5-6 hours of collection for optimal viability and function.

Febrile reactions can be prevented by transfusing leukocyte-reduced red blood cell and platelet components. Originally buffy-coat removal was used, but modern leukocyte reduction filters are more effective. This intervention significantly reduces both frequency and severity of febrile reactions.
questions.question: How are febrile reactions prevented?

questions.explanation: Polyacrylamide gel pore size can be altered easily and controllably by changing monomer concentrations. This adjustability allows customization for specific separation requirements. The controllability makes PAGE extremely versatile for various applications.
questions.question: What can be controlled in polyacrylamide gels easily?

questions.explanation: The GP-IIb/IIIa complex functions as the fibrinogen receptor, essential for platelet aggregation by forming bridges between activated platelets. This complex undergoes conformational changes upon platelet activation, increasing its affinity for fibrinogen. Absence or dysfunction of GP-IIb/IIIa characterizes Glanzmann's thrombasthenia, resulting in severe bleeding despite normal platelet counts due to inability to aggregate.
questions.question: What is the primary function of GP-IIb/IIIa complex on platelets?

questions.explanation: HMS is associated with high mortality in untreated individuals; overwhelming infections are the leading cause of death. The impaired immune function despite B-cell expansion creates susceptibility. Encapsulated bacteria pose particular risk.
questions.question: What organism causes the leading cause of death in untreated HMS
What characterizes non-thrombocytopenic purpura?
questions.explanation: Non-thrombocytopenic purpura features easy bruising with normal platelet count and bleeding time. Bleeding occurs from vascular defects rather than platelet abnormalities. Diagnosis requires excluding thrombocytopenia.

questions.question: Which technique isolates lymphocytes from whole blood most effectively
options: Differential sedimentation based on size only
questions.explanation: Density gradient centrifugation using Ficoll-Paque or Lymphoprep separates blood components by density. Lymphocytes and mononuclear cells form a distinct layer at the plasma-medium interface, allowing clean isolation from erythrocytes, granulocytes, and platelets.

Clinicians may request peripheral blood films based on clinical suspicion of haematological disorders. Laboratory medical scientists also prepare films following abnormal automated count findings. This dual indication system ensures appropriate utilization of microscopic examination resources.
questions.question: Who may request a peripheral blood film examination?
What baseline test is essential before anthracycline chemotherapy?
questions.explanation: Cardiac function assessment including echocardiogram or MUGA scan precedes anthracycline therapy due to cardiotoxicity risk. These agents cause cumulative dose-dependent cardiac damage. Baseline evaluation identifies pre-existing dysfunction and guides safe dosing.

questions.question: What can IEF detect in purified proteins?
questions.explanation: IEF's exceptional resolving power makes it ideal for detecting microheterogeneity in purified proteins from post-translational modifications. Subtle charge differences from glycosylation or phosphorylation are revealed. This sensitivity identifies protein variants otherwise appearing homogeneous.

HbS disease manifests significantly faster sickling (immediate or near-immediate) compared to HbS trait requiring extended incubation. Higher HbS concentrations in disease accelerate polymerization kinetics. Trait carriers may require prolonged observation for definitive sickling.
questions.question: What distinguishes HbS disease from HbS trait in sickling test timing

questions.explanation: A specialized photometer called a haemoglobinometer measures haemoglobin concentration after RBC lysis and complex formation. This instrument detects light absorbance at the specific wavelength where the haemoglobin complex absorbs maximally. The photometric measurement provides accurate haemoglobin values essential for anaemia diagnosis.
questions.question: Which component measures haemoglobin concentration in analyzers?

questions.explanation: LMWH is given at fixed doses once to twice daily by subcutaneous route due to favorable pharmacokinetics. The predictable dose-response relationship eliminates need for monitoring. Convenient dosing improves patient compliance.
questions.question: How frequently can LMWH be administered subcutaneously?
What does the term "myeloid" indicate in leukemia classification?
questions.explanation: "Myeloid" indicates the abnormal cells originated from myeloid stem cells. These produce granulocytes, monocytes, erythrocytes, and platelets normally. Myeloid leukemias include AML and CML with non-lymphoid cell characteristics.

questions.question: What is antithrombin's primary target?
questions.explanation: Antithrombin is a serine protease inhibitor (serpin) primarily targeting thrombin (IIa) and Factor Xa, forming irreversible 1:1 complexes that neutralize their enzymatic activity. Antithrombin also inhibits Factors IXa, XIa, XIIa, and kallikrein. Congenital antithrombin deficiency causes severe thrombophilia with high venous thromboembolism risk. Acquired deficiency occurs in DIC (consumption), liver disease (decreased synthesis), and nephrotic syndrome (urinary loss).

Acellular hemoglobin causes elevation of oncotic pressure, potentially leading to fluid shifts and circulatory complications. This increased oncotic pressure can affect tissue perfusion and cardiovascular function. Managing oncotic effects is crucial in blood substitute formulation.
questions.question: What circulatory problem does acellular hemoglobin cause through oncotic pressure

questions.explanation: Complete cytogenetic response requires absence of Philadelphia chromosome on conventional cytogenetics examining 20 metaphases. This milestone indicates excellent treatment response and improved long-term outcomes. However, molecular testing may still detect low-level BCR-ABL transcripts.
questions.question: What finding indicates complete cytogenetic response in CML?

questions.explanation: HBOCs are not as efficient as intact RBCs in oxygen delivery and regulation due to altered oxygen binding characteristics and lack of 2,3-DPG regulation. This reduced efficiency limits their effectiveness in some clinical situations. The regulatory mechanisms present in natural RBCs are difficult to replicate.
options: Not as efficient in oxygen delivery and regulation
questions.question: What is a major efficiency disadvantage of HBOCs compared to RBCs

questions.explanation: Starch gel electrophoresis has lower resolution compared to polyacrylamide gels, limiting discrimination between similar proteins. It identified only six Listeria types while PAGE identified seventeen types. This inferior discriminatory power led to its replacement in most laboratories.
questions.question: What is the major disadvantage of starch gel electrophoresis?

questions.explanation: Bromodeoxyuridine (BrdU) is a thymidine analog incorporating into DNA during replication. After incubation, anti-BrdU antibodies with colorimetric or fluorescent labels detect incorporated BrdU, providing specific quantification of DNA synthesis without radioactive hazards.
questions.question: How does BrdU incorporation detect lymphocyte proliferation
options: Thymidine analog detected by anti-BrdU antibodies

questions.explanation: Peak areas serve as primary quantitative measurements in HPLC haemoglobin analysis providing proportional concentration information. Area integration offers more reliable quantification than peak height. Though peak height sometimes yields equivalent results, area remains preferred.
questions.question: What measurement parameter typically quantifies haemoglobin in HPLC
Which lymphatic vessel type is notably absent in the spleen
questions.explanation: The spleen lacks afferent lymphatic vessels, possessing only efferent vessels through which lymphocytes migrate to splenic lymph nodes. This unique feature distinguishes the spleen from lymph nodes and reflects its role as a blood filter rather than a lymph filter. The efferent vessels are located within the trabeculae alongside blood vessels and nerves.

Periconceptional folate supplementation of 400-800μg daily, starting before conception and continuing through the first trimester, reduces neural tube defect risk by 50-70%. Women with previous NTD-affected pregnancy require higher doses (4-5mg daily). Universal flour fortification with folate has significantly reduced NTD incidence in implementing countries.
questions.question: What folate dose prevents neural tube defects periconceptionally?
What concern exists regarding the lipid component of PFC emulsions
options: Introduction of large amounts of lipids to circulation
questions.explanation: PFC emulsions require phospholipids that introduce many grams of lipids into circulation during transfusion, similar to adding cholesterol. This large lipid load raises concerns about metabolic effects and lipid-related complications. The lipid burden is a significant limitation of PFC technology.

Cryoprecipitate stores at -18 degrees C or colder for up to one year. This frozen storage maintains coagulation factor stability. Thawing at 30-37 degrees C takes approximately 15-20 minutes before transfusion.
questions.question: What is the storage temperature and maximum shelf life for cryoprecipitate
At what temperature does agarose gel form?
questions.explanation: Agarose remains liquid until temperature is lowered to about 40°C, at which point it gels. The temperature-dependent gelation allows easy gel preparation and casting. This property makes agarose convenient for routine laboratory use.

High-dose intravenous immunoglobulin (400 mg/kg/day for 5 days) produces rapid but transient platelet rise by blocking Fc receptors on splenic macrophages, preventing phagocytosis of antibody-coated platelets. This effect lasts 2-6 weeks, making IVIG useful for acute hemorrhage or preparing chronic ITP patients for surgery. IVIG doesn't address underlying antibody production, explaining its transient effect.
questions.question: How does intravenous immunoglobulin work in acute ITP bleeding?
What bone marrow finding is characteristic of ITP?
questions.explanation: ITP bone marrow shows abundant megakaryocytes (4-8 fold increase) without excessive budding due to rapid release. Normal granulopoiesis and erythropoiesis exclude other disorders. Megakaryocyte reduction rules out ITP.

questions.question: What is the approximate normal fibrinogen concentration range?
questions.explanation: Normal fibrinogen concentration ranges approximately 1.8-3.6 g/L (or 150-400 mg%), essential for adequate fibrin clot formation during hemostasis. Fibrinogen increases physiologically during pregnancy and postoperatively as an acute phase reactant. Decreased levels occur in congenital hypofibrinogenemia/afibrinogenemia, DIC (consumption), and severe liver disease (decreased synthesis), each causing bleeding tendency from inadequate clot formation.

questions.question: What inheritance pattern characterizes sickle cell disease
questions.explanation: Sickle cell disease follows autosomal recessive inheritance, requiring two mutated genes for clinical manifestation. Heterozygotes (carriers) possess sickle cell trait without severe symptoms. Both parents must carry the mutation for offspring to develop full disease expression.

PFA-100 measures platelet function under high shear conditions mimicking small arteries and capillaries. Blood passes through membranes coated with collagen/epinephrine or collagen/ADP. The closure time reflects platelet adhesion and aggregation under physiological shear stress.
questions.question: What does PFA-100 measure under specific conditions?
Which AML subtype is most frequently associated with gum infiltration?
questions.explanation: AML M5 (acute monocytic leukaemia) commonly presents with infiltration into gums and skin. Patients typically experience weakness, bleeding, and diffuse erythematous skin rash as presenting features. The monocytic cells have particular propensity for extramedullary infiltration compared to other AML subtypes.

questions.question: What does impedance aggregometry measure in whole blood?
questions.explanation: Whole blood impedance aggregometry measures electrical impedance changes as platelets adhere to electrodes after agonist stimulation. Impedance increases as platelet aggregates form on electrode surfaces. This method maintains more physiological conditions than PRP-based methods.

Mesothelial cells compose the outermost layer of the splenic capsule, though they may not always be evident on histologic sections. Beneath this layer lies dense fibrous tissue, elastic fibers, and smooth muscle that form the main capsular structure. The capsule provides structural support and allows for splenic contraction during increased demand.
questions.question: Which cells form the outermost layer of the splenic capsule

questions.explanation: Negatively charged haemoglobin at alkaline pH migrates toward the positive anode following electrostatic attraction principles. The directional migration creates characteristic separation patterns. Different variants migrate at different rates based on charge magnitude.
questions.question: What direction does haemoglobin migrate at alkaline pH
What is the maximum time FFP can be stored after thawing before it becomes classified as thawed plasma
questions.explanation: Once thawed, FFP must be transfused within 24 hours or reclassified as thawed plasma. This timeframe balances clinical utility with maintaining adequate factor levels. After 24 hours, labile factors decline significantly.

questions.question: What is warfarin's plasma protein binding characteristic?
questions.explanation: Warfarin demonstrates powerful plasma protein binding exceeding 99%, affecting drug interactions and metabolism. High protein binding creates reservoir effect prolonging action. Drugs displacing warfarin increase free fraction and bleeding risk.

SSP-PCR is typically performed using 96-well plate formats, with each well containing primers specific for different alleles. This allows high-throughput testing and comprehensive allele coverage. Multiple reactions can be performed simultaneously on each sample.
questions.question: What format is typically used for SSP-PCR?
What wavelength is used for spectrophotometric enzyme assays?
questions.explanation: Spectrophotometric techniques for RBC enzyme activity assays depend on absorption of light by reduced pyridine nucleotides (NADPH or NADH) at 340 nm. Reduction results in formation of NADPH or NADH with increased absorbance, while oxidation decreases absorbance. The change in absorbance is used to calculate enzyme activity levels.

questions.question: What surgical procedure predisposes to folate deficiency?
questions.explanation: Partial gastrectomy may contribute to folate deficiency by reducing stomach acid production necessary for optimal folate absorption, though it is rarely the sole cause. Extensive jejunal resection more significantly impairs folate absorption since the upper small intestine is the primary absorption site. Crohn's disease affecting jejunum similarly reduces absorption.

Lead poisoning produces basophilic stippling (accumulation of denatured RNA) in red cells due to inhibition of pyrimidine 5'-nucleotidase, distinguishing it from iron deficiency. Lead also inhibits multiple steps in heme and globin synthesis causing microcytic anaemia. Elevated zinc protoporphyrin and blood lead levels confirm diagnosis.
questions.question: What distinguishes lead poisoning blood film from iron deficiency?
What does IEF analyze regarding MHC molecules?
questions.explanation: Isoelectric focusing is used for analyzing polymorphism of the major histocompatibility complex showing allelic variants. Different MHC alleles have distinct charge properties creating characteristic IEF patterns. This aids in tissue typing and immunogenetic studies.

options: Prolonged bleeding time, APTT, and reduced Factor VIII
questions.explanation: Von Willebrand disease characteristically shows prolonged bleeding time (platelet dysfunction from defective vWF-mediated adhesion), prolonged APTT (reduced Factor VIII which vWF normally carries/protects), and abnormal ristocetin cofactor activity. This combination of platelet and coagulation abnormalities distinguishes vWD from pure hemophilia (normal bleeding time) or pure platelet disorders (normal APTT, Factor VIII).
questions.question: Which laboratory findings characterize von Willebrand disease?
What is the inheritance pattern of pyruvate kinase deficiency?
questions.explanation: Pyruvate kinase deficiency is an autosomal recessive disorder requiring homozygosity for full trait expression. It is the most common cause of hereditary chronic non-spherocytic hemolytic anemia. The estimated prevalence is approximately 1:20,000 in White populations with worldwide distribution and highly variable phenotypic expression.

Haemoglobin S results from GAG to GTG point mutation in codon 6 of the beta-globin gene. This single nucleotide substitution causes glutamic acid replacement with valine at position 6. The altered amino acid properties induce structural changes promoting haemoglobin polymerization under deoxygenated conditions.
questions.question: What genetic mutation pattern causes haemoglobin S formation

questions.explanation: Richter's transformation describes development of high-grade non-Hodgkin lymphoma in CLL patients. This aggressive transformation occurs in approximately 5% of cases. It can also manifest as prolymphocytic leukaemia, Hodgkin disease, or acute leukaemia.
questions.question: What transformation can occur in approximately 5% of CLL cases?
What mechanism causes drug-induced immune thrombocytopenia?
questions.explanation: Drug-induced immune thrombocytopenia occurs through drug-antibody immune complex formation or antigenic drug-platelet complex binding, with antibodies targeting the drug-platelet complex causing platelet destruction. Common culprits include quinine, quinidine, penicillin, sulfonamides, thiazides, and heparin (HIT). Thrombocytopenia resolves within days to weeks after drug discontinuation as drug-antibody complexes clear and platelet production normalizes.

Only about 20% of low molecular weight heparin chains contain the unique antithrombin III-binding pentasaccharide sequence. This is less than the 33% found in unfractionated heparin preparations. The pentasaccharide presence determines anticoagulant activity potential.
questions.question: What percentage of LMWH molecules contain the ATIII-binding pentasaccharide?
What finding on bone marrow biopsy suggests M7 diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Marked bone marrow fibrosis in M7 often prevents successful aspiration requiring trephine biopsy. The fibrosis results from cytokines released by megakaryocytes stimulating fibroblast proliferation. Excess megakaryoblasts confirmed by immunohistochemistry establish diagnosis.

Portal hypertension, along with infectious mononucleosis and hematological malignancy, is a common splenomegaly cause in developed countries. The elevated portal pressure causes congestive splenomegaly. Cirrhosis is the most common underlying cause.
questions.question: What portal-related condition causes splenomegaly in developed countries

questions.explanation: FISH uses fluorescent probes detecting specific DNA sequences revealing cryptic abnormalities invisible to standard karyotyping. This technique identifies translocations, deletions, and amplifications at higher resolution. FISH provides rapid results without requiring dividing cells.
questions.question: Which technique replaced standard cytogenetics for detecting cryptic abnormalities?
What facilitates the environment for erythrocytes to eliminate solid waste in the spleen
questions.explanation: The red pulp architecture facilitates an environment wherein erythrocytes rid themselves of solid waste material through a process called pitting. The slow transit through splenic cords allows macrophages to remove inclusions without destroying the entire cell. This unique function preserves red cell mass while removing damaged components.

The linear oxygen dissociation curve of PFCs provides an improved driving gradient that facilitates oxygen delivery to tissues across a wider range of partial pressures. This characteristic enhances oxygen unloading in hypoxic areas. The favorable gradient improves tissue oxygenation efficiency.
questions.question: What advantage does the PFC oxygen dissociation curve provide
options: Improved driving gradient for oxygen delivery

questions.explanation: SSP-PCR includes amplification controls to ensure negative results are due to genuine absence of target alleles rather than PCR failure. These internal controls verify that the PCR reaction worked properly in each well. Control amplification is essential for reliable interpretation of negative results.
questions.question: What controls ensure valid SSP-PCR results?
What cells are associated with splenic cords besides macrophages
questions.explanation: Associated with splenic cords are lymphocytes and hematopoietic cells as well as plasma cells and plasmablasts migrating from follicles and outer PALS. This cellular diversity supports multiple splenic functions. The hematopoietic cells enable extramedullary blood production when needed.

Therapeutic venesection removes 400-500mls of blood per session, though some patients tolerate less depending on age and comorbidities. Venesections continue every 1-2 weeks until serum ferritin decreases to 50-100ng/ml. Maintenance therapy typically requires 3-4 venesections annually to prevent iron reaccumulation.
questions.question: What volume of blood is typically removed during therapeutic venesection for haemochromatosis?
What immune complication develops from repeated transfusions
questions.explanation: Repeated transfusions stimulate alloantibody formation against minor red cell antigens complicating future compatibility. Alloimmunization increases transfusion reaction risks and blood procurement difficulties. Extended phenotype matching reduces but doesn't eliminate alloimmunization.

questions.question: Which scenario correctly differentiates ABO from Rh HDFN regarding stillbirth risk
questions.explanation: Rh HDFN historically caused frequent stillbirths from severe hydrops foetalis and cardiac failure before prophylaxis and intrauterine transfusion. ABO HDFN rarely causes stillbirth due to milder disease from weak foetal antigen expression and tissue antigen neutralization.
options: ABO causes frequent stillbirths; Rh causes rare stillbirths
Both cause equal stillbirth rates approximately
Neither causes stillbirth in modern obstetric care
ABO causes more stillbirths in African populations
Rh causes frequent stillbirths; ABO causes rare stillbirths

questions.question: What regions does SBT typically sequence?
questions.explanation: SBT typically focuses on sequencing the most polymorphic exon regions of HLA genes. Forward and reverse PCR primers flank these regions of interest for amplification. Sequencing these critical regions provides high-resolution allele identification while remaining practically feasible.

questions.question: When should donors be tested for leukocyte antibodies?
questions.explanation: Donors should be tested for leukocyte antibodies only after a determination that the transfusion was responsible for a reaction. Testing all implicated donors would be impractical and unnecessary. The purpose is identifying donors whose components are at high risk for causing reactions.

options: Low, normal, or high with lymphoblasts present
questions.question: What is the typical white blood cell count finding in ALL at diagnosis?
questions.explanation: White blood cell count in ALL may be low, normal, or high at diagnosis. However, lymphoblasts are characteristically present regardless of total count. The total white cell count can be misleading as it may be elevated due to lymphoblasts while functional neutrophils remain depleted.

Thalassaemia trait shows disproportionately elevated red blood cell count relative to the degree of microcytosis and mild anaemia, unlike iron deficiency where RBC count is appropriately reduced. The Mentzer index (MCV/RBC) below 13 suggests thalassaemia while above 13 suggests iron deficiency. RDW is typically normal in thalassaemia but elevated in iron deficiency.
options: RBC count proportionately higher in thalassaemia
MCV more severely reduced in IDA
questions.question: What distinguishes thalassaemia trait from iron deficiency on red cell indices?

options: Antibody secretion by differentiated plasma cells
Cytotoxic killing of target cells specifically
Proliferation and clonal expansion of lymphocytes
Complement activation and membrane attack complex
questions.question: Which immunological process is directly measured in lymphocyte transformation
questions.explanation: LTT directly measures lymphocyte proliferation through cell division and clonal expansion following antigen or mitogen stimulation. This proliferation reflects immune competence, with increased division indicating functional immune response capability essential for pathogen elimination.

questions.question: What is the approximate thickness of the glycocalyx around RBCs?
questions.explanation: The glycocalyx is a negatively charged barrier approximately 10 Å thick around the RBC membrane formed by carbohydrates. The negative charge is due to sialic acid residues and prevents spontaneous aggregation of circulating RBCs and adhesion to endothelium. It also protects against microbial invasion.

questions.question: What donors commonly have TRALI-associated antibodies?
questions.explanation: Lymphocytotoxic antibodies were found in 72% of TRALI-associated donors, with many being multiparous women. Pregnancy exposure to fetal antigens leads to HLA alloimmunization. Many blood services now preferentially collect plasma from male donors to reduce TRALI risk.

Platelet aggregation is primarily mediated by interaction of platelets with specific agonists like ADP or collagen. These agonists bind respective receptors triggering intracellular signaling pathways. The agonist-receptor interaction initiates the cascade leading to platelet clumping.
questions.question: What primarily mediates platelet aggregation initiation?
Which structures compose the three-dimensional meshwork of red pulp
questions.explanation: The red pulp consists of a three-dimensional meshwork of splenic cords (reticular fibers, reticular cells, and associated macrophages) and venous sinuses. Within the spaces between cords are blood cells including erythrocytes, granulocytes, mononuclear cells, and platelets. This architecture enables effective filtration and sequestration of blood cells.

Major spontaneous bleeding in ITP typically occurs only with severe thrombocytopenia below 10,000/mm3, though individual bleeding risk varies. Platelet counts 20,000-50,000/mm3 cause bleeding with minor trauma, while counts above 50,000/mm3 rarely cause significant bleeding. Mucosal bleeding (epistaxis, menorrhagia) and petechiae/purpura occur below 50,000/mm3, while intracranial hemorrhage risk becomes significant below 10,000/mm3.
questions.question: At what platelet count does spontaneous bleeding typically occur in ITP?

questions.explanation: NADPH from the hexose monophosphate shunt is essential for keeping glutathione in the reduced state. Reduced glutathione plays a crucial role in protecting RBCs from oxidative damage to membranes and proteins. Without adequate NADPH, intracellular oxidants cannot be neutralized, leading to globin denaturation and hemolysis.
questions.question: What is the primary function of NADPH produced by the hexose monophosphate shunt?

questions.explanation: Thalassaemias arise from reduced synthesis rates of one or more globin chains rather than structural abnormalities. This quantitative deficiency creates imbalanced globin chain production. The resulting excess unmatched chains precipitate within erythrocytes, causing premature cell destruction.
questions.question: What fundamental defect characterizes thalassaemia syndromes
What forms at sites of vascular injury?
questions.explanation: Platelets clump together forming a platelet plug that helps seal damaged blood vessels at injury sites. This temporary plug provides immediate hemostasis while coagulation cascade proceeds. The platelet plug is the primary hemostatic mechanism for small vessel injuries.

IEF is extensively used for diagnosing genetically transmitted disorders by identifying abnormal proteins associated with conditions. Hemoglobinopathies and enzyme deficiencies show characteristic IEF patterns. This application enables accurate molecular diagnosis.
questions.question: What does IEF identify in genetic disorders?

questions.explanation: Most enlarged spleens in hypersplenism have a smooth surface, soft consistency, and sharp border. Approximately one-third may be tender on palpation. These characteristics help distinguish splenic enlargement from other abdominal masses during physical examination.
questions.question: What structural characteristic describes most enlarged spleens in hypersplenism
What is the estimated carrier frequency for sickle cell mutation in West African populations
questions.explanation: West African populations demonstrate sickle cell gene carrier frequency of approximately 1:5 individuals. This high prevalence reflects evolutionary selection favoring heterozygotes with malaria resistance. Geographic distribution correlates strongly with historical malaria endemicity patterns.

Factor V Leiden mutation affects 3-8% of Caucasians, making it the most common inherited thrombophilia. The mutation (G1691A) causes Factor V resistance to inactivation by activated protein C, prolonging its procoagulant activity. Heterozygotes have 5-10 fold increased VTE risk, homozygotes 50-100 fold. The mutation is rare in African and Asian populations, explaining ethnic variation in thrombotic risk.
questions.question: Which thrombophilia is most common in Caucasians?
What percentage of bone marrow blasts is typically required to diagnose AML?
questions.explanation: Most AML subtypes demonstrate more than 30% blasts in blood or bone marrow for diagnosis. This threshold distinguishes acute leukaemia from myelodysplastic syndromes which have less than 20% blasts. The presence of adequate blast percentage combined with cytochemical staining confirms the diagnosis of acute myeloid leukaemia.

questions.question: What staining technique distinguishes pancellular from heterocellular HPFH
questions.explanation: Acid elution staining differentiates pancellular HPFH (uniform HbF in all cells) from heterocellular HPFH (HbF in scattered cells). The distribution pattern reveals whether HbF expression is universal or restricted. This distinction aids genetic counseling and diagnosis.

questions.question: What disease transmission advantage do HBOCs provide
questions.explanation: HBOCs carry no risk of disease transmission from blood-borne pathogens, eliminating concerns about viral, bacterial, and prion infections. This safety advantage is particularly important given historical transfusion-transmitted diseases. The absence of infectious risk improves patient safety significantly.

Bone marrow aspiration with morphologic, cytochemical, immunophenotypic, and cytogenetic analysis definitively diagnoses leukemia type. Peripheral blood may suggest diagnosis but marrow examination provides complete characterization. Accurate classification guides appropriate therapy selection.
questions.question: Which test definitively diagnoses leukemia type?

questions.explanation: Von Willebrand factor is associated with factor VIII, functioning to stabilize it and prevent premature destruction. It also promotes platelet-endothelial interactions during adhesion. VWF deficiency causes combined platelet and coagulation defects.
questions.question: What is the role of Von Willebrand factor with factor VIII?

questions.explanation: Approximately 13μg of folate is lost daily through combined urinary, sweat, and fecal excretion, establishing minimum daily replacement requirements. This exceeds the typical absorption from food during inadequate intake. When combined with increased utilization during pregnancy or haemolysis, rapid folate depletion occurs.
questions.question: How much folate is lost daily through urine, sweat, and feces?
Which medication class inhibits hepatic P450 enzymes and potentiates warfarin?
questions.explanation: Cimetidine and co-trimoxazole inhibit hepatic P450 enzymes, reducing warfarin metabolism and potentiating anticoagulant effects. This interaction increases bleeding risk requiring INR monitoring. Dose adjustment prevents excessive anticoagulation.

questions.question: What platelet count characterizes essential thrombocythemia?
questions.explanation: Essential thrombocythemia typically shows platelet counts above 600,000/mm3 as a clonal myeloproliferative disorder. Abnormal platelet function paradoxically causes both thrombotic and bleeding manifestations. Multilineage stem cell abnormality drives overproduction.

questions.question: What is the typical lymph node finding in HMS
questions.explanation: Lymphadenopathy is absent in HMS, helping distinguish it from lymphoproliferative disorders. However, bilateral parotid swelling has been described. The absence of lymphadenopathy is an important diagnostic clue.

questions.question: What is the normal plasma fibrinogen level?
questions.explanation: Normal plasma fibrinogen level ranges from 150 to 400 mg%, essential for clot formation. Fibrinogen increases in pregnancy and postoperatively. Decreased levels occur in DIC and congenital hypofibrinogenemia.

Iron deficiency anaemia produces decreased serum iron with compensatory increased total iron-binding capacity (TIBC), resulting in transferrin saturation below 10%. This pattern reflects depleted iron stores and increased production of transferrin attempting to maximize iron uptake. The combination distinguishes iron deficiency from anaemia of chronic disease.
questions.question: What is the typical serum iron pattern in iron deficiency anaemia?

questions.explanation: Thawed plasma stores for up to 5 days at 1-6 degrees C with acceptable factor levels except factor VIII. Factor VIII decreases approximately 30% during this period. TP provides cost-effective plasma availability for emergency situations.
questions.question: How long can thawed plasma be stored at 1-6 degrees C
What monitoring parameter assesses treatment response in iron deficiency?
questions.explanation: Reticulocyte count increases within days of starting iron therapy, peaking at 5-10 days, confirming effective treatment and compliance. Haemoglobin rises approximately 1g/dL every 7-10 days, normalizing over 2-3 months. MCV gradually normalizes. Failure to respond suggests incorrect diagnosis, ongoing bleeding, malabsorption, non-compliance, or concurrent disease.

Nucleated RBCs may erroneously increase the total WBC count reported by automated analyzers. These immature cells are counted as leucocytes by impedance methods. Microscopic examination allows correction using specific mathematical formulas.
questions.question: What may nucleated RBCs cause in automated analyzers?
What happens to proteins when pH exceeds their pI?
questions.explanation: When pH exceeds pI, proteins become negatively charged as acidic groups lose protons. Negatively charged proteins migrate toward the positive anode in electric fields. This pH-dependent charging is fundamental to IEF separation.

options: Measures protein expressed in proliferating cells only
Detects thymidine analog incorporation during S phase
Quantifies metabolic activity through enzyme reduction
Tracks fluorescent dye dilution during division
Identifies apoptotic cells with nuclear fragmentation
questions.explanation: Ki-67 is a nuclear protein expressed in proliferating cells (G1, S, G2, M phases) but absent in quiescent G0 cells. Anti-Ki-67 antibodies detected by flow cytometry identify actively cycling cells, providing proliferation status without requiring incorporation assays.
questions.question: How does Ki-67 staining assess lymphocyte proliferation
Which test is used to monitor unfractionated heparin therapy?
questions.explanation: Activated Partial Thromboplastin Time (aPTT) monitors unfractionated heparin therapy effectiveness by assessing intrinsic pathway function. Increased aPTT levels reflect heparin's anticlotting effect and guide dose adjustments. Testing is performed regularly, usually daily, to maintain therapeutic ranges.

questions.question: What storage advantage do HBOCs have over donated blood
questions.explanation: Many HBOCs are stable at room temperature for extended periods, eliminating refrigeration requirements and simplifying storage logistics. This stability is particularly valuable in resource-limited settings. Room temperature storage enables rapid deployment in emergencies.

One platelet unit increases count by approximately 10,000/muL in average adults. This predictable increment guides transfusion dosing. Individual responses vary with splenomegaly, fever, or alloimmunization.
questions.question: By approximately how much does one platelet concentrate unit increase the platelet count
Which membrane component is responsible for the negative charge on RBCs?
questions.explanation: The negative charge on RBCs is due to sialic acid residues present in the glycocalyx. This negative charge prevents spontaneous aggregation of circulating RBCs and adhesion to endothelium. The glycocalyx forms a negatively charged barrier approximately 10 Å thick around the RBC membrane.

D-dimer elevates in any condition involving fibrin formation and subsequent fibrinolysis: DIC, intravascular thrombosis (MI, stroke, DVT, PE), postoperative period, trauma, pregnancy, malignancy, and inflammation. This lack of specificity limits D-dimer's positive predictive value but high negative predictive value makes it useful for excluding thromboembolism. Normal D-dimer effectively rules out acute DVT/PE in low-probability patients.
questions.question: When are D-dimer levels elevated?

questions.explanation: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia is a life-threatening immune reaction occurring in up to 3% of patients on 5-14 days therapy. It induces platelet activation with paradoxical thrombosis despite thrombocytopenia. Immediate heparin discontinuation is mandatory.
questions.question: What is heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT)?
Which modification prevents febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reactions most effectively
questions.explanation: Leukoreduction removes white blood cells that release pyrogenic cytokines causing febrile reactions. Modern filters remove >=99.99% of WBCs. This modification also prevents HLA alloimmunization and CMV transmission.

Foetal red cells express ABO antigens weakly compared to adult levels, reducing antibody binding and haemolysis. Additionally, A and B antigens present in foetal tissues and secretions neutralize some maternal antibodies, further limiting red cell destruction.
options: Enhanced placental clearance of ABO antibodies
Poor development of ABO antigens on foetal RBCs
questions.question: Which factor most contributes to mild ABO HDFN compared to Rh disease
What SI value is generally considered positive in classical LTT
questions.explanation: SI >= 2.0 is generally considered positive, indicating stimulated proliferation is at least twice background levels. However, some drugs like beta-lactams may use SI >= 3.0 threshold to improve specificity, reflecting inherent variability in LTT interpretation.

questions.question: What medium is commonly used for haemoglobin electrophoresis
questions.explanation: Agarose serves as the common medium for haemoglobin electrophoresis providing consistent separation characteristics. This polysaccharide gel offers appropriate pore size for protein migration. Cellulose acetate represents an alternative medium for specific applications.

Platelet Immunofluorescence Test is non-specific and cannot distinguish between HPA and HLA class I antibodies. Despite this limitation, when analyzed by flow cytometry it remains one of the most sensitive assays available. Confirmation with specific assays like MAIPA is usually necessary.
questions.question: What does PIFT detect non-specifically?
What happens to oxygen binding in familial 2,3-BPG deficiency?
questions.explanation: In familial 2,3-BPG deficiency due to bisphosphoglyceromutase deficiency, decreased 2,3-BPG levels increase hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen. This shifts the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve to the left, resulting in decreased oxygen delivery to peripheral tissues. The tissue hypoxia triggers compensatory polycythemia through erythropoietin release.

Rapid B12 replacement in severe deficiency causes hypokalemia due to massive cellular uptake of potassium during brisk reticulocytosis and DNA synthesis. Cardiac arrhythmias may result if uncorrected. Potassium supplementation is necessary during initial treatment of severe megaloblastic anaemia. Regular monitoring prevents life-threatening hypokalaemia.
questions.question: What complication results from rapid B12 replacement in severe deficiency?
What class of G6PD deficiency has enzyme levels less than 10%?
questions.explanation: Five classes of G6PD deficiency exist: Class 1 (enzyme deficiency with chronic nonspherocytic hemolytic anemia), Class 2 (severe enzyme deficiency <10%), Class 3 (moderate-to-mild enzyme deficiency 10-60%), Class 4 (very mild-to-no enzyme deficiency >60%), and Class 5 (increased enzyme activity). Classification helps predict clinical severity.

Hemopure uses bovine hemoglobin from cow blood, which is polymerized similarly to Polyheme but from an animal source. Bovine hemoglobin offers advantages in supply availability. However, concerns exist about using animal-derived products in human medicine.
questions.question: What is the source of hemoglobin in Hemopure

questions.explanation: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia represents approximately 85% of childhood acute leukaemias, making it the most common childhood malignancy. The highest incidence occurs between ages 1-5 years with slight male predominance. About 6 in 10 ALL cases occur in children with peak incidence between one and four years.
questions.question: What is the most common malignancy in childhood?

questions.explanation: Leukocyte Alkaline Phosphatase (LAP) score is markedly decreased in CML due to lack of gene transcription. This helps differentiate CML from leukemoid reactions where LAP is elevated. The low LAP score is a useful diagnostic tool despite the high white cell count.
questions.question: What is the characteristic LAP score finding in CML?
What confirmatory test is used for M7 when bone marrow aspiration is unobtainable?
questions.explanation: When marrow fibrosis prevents aspiration in M7, diagnosis relies on platelet peroxidase positivity confirmed by electron microscopy. Monoclonal antibodies to von Willebrand factor or glycoproteins can also confirm megakaryoblast origin. The presence of circulating megakaryoblasts supports the diagnosis when combined with these confirmatory tests.

Bart's hydrops fetalis syndrome involves complete absence of functional alpha genes (--/--), proving incompatible with postnatal survival. No alpha chain production occurs, preventing HbA or HbF formation. Affected fetuses produce only non-functional gamma and beta tetramers.
questions.question: How many functional alpha genes exist in Bart's hydrops fetalis
What RDW pattern typically characterizes thalassaemia trait
questions.explanation: Thalassaemia trait typically maintains normal red cell distribution width (RDW) despite microcytosis reflecting uniform cell size. This contrasts with iron deficiency showing elevated RDW from anisocytosis. The normal RDW helps distinguish thalassaemia from other microcytic anaemias.

questions.question: Which organ system is NOT typically affected by iron deposition in haemochromatosis?
questions.explanation: Kidneys are not primary sites of pathological iron deposition in haemochromatosis, unlike the liver, pancreas, heart, skin, gonads, joints and adrenal glands. The disease preferentially affects parenchymal organs where excess iron accumulates in cells. Renal involvement occurs rarely and usually represents secondary damage from other affected organs.

Fresh frozen plasma is a blood component, not a derivative, because it's prepared by simple freezing without fractionation. Plasma derivatives undergo pharmaceutical manufacturing processes. FFP contains all plasma proteins in their native concentrations.
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a plasma derivative
What advantage does MAIGA offer over other methods?
questions.explanation: MAIGA permits recognition of antibodies to specific neutrophil glycoproteins even when antibodies to HLA antigens are simultaneously present. This specificity is crucial for identifying the clinical significance of antibodies. The assay can distinguish between different neutrophil antigen systems.

Chronic abdominal swelling is the most common presenting symptom, occurring in 64% of HMS patients. This swelling may wax and wane over time. Pressure on abdominal contents may lead to hernias and leg swelling.
questions.question: What is the most common presenting symptom of HMS
Which inheritance pattern characterizes Hemophilia C (Factor XI deficiency)?
questions.explanation: Hemophilia C (Factor XI deficiency) follows autosomal recessive inheritance, unlike Hemophilias A and B which are X-linked, allowing Factor XI deficiency to affect both males and females equally. It's particularly common in Ashkenazi Jewish populations (8% carrier rate in Israel). Clinical bleeding is typically mild, often manifest only with surgery or trauma, distinguishing it from severe bleeding in Hemophilias A and B.

questions.question: What morphologic change may appear in red cells during hypersplenism
questions.explanation: Spherocytes may be present in hypersplenism due to metabolic conditioning of red cells during slow transit through the red pulp. This membrane change occurs as cells lose surface area while passing through the spleen. The presence of spherocytes can mimic hereditary spherocytosis but is distinguished by the underlying cause.
FP24 has slightly lower factors V and VIII than FFP due to the 8-24 hour freezing delay. This reduction is rarely clinically significant. Both products are used interchangeably in most situations.
questions.question: How do factor V and VIII levels change in plasma stored as FP24 compared to FFP

questions.explanation: Reticulocyte response peaking at day 6 post-therapy confirms effective treatment of megaloblastic anaemia, provided only low-dose vitamin replacement was administered. This brisk reticulocytosis reflects correction of ineffective erythropoiesis. Haemoglobin rises gradually over weeks. Inadequate iron stores may blunt the reticulocyte response despite B12/folate repletion.
questions.question: What response confirms effective treatment of megaloblastic anaemia?

options: Measures maternal antibody titre levels accurately
Assesses foetal haematocrit through plasma analysis
Determines foetal RHD and KEL genotypes non-invasively
Predicts disease severity from DNA concentration
questions.explanation: Cell-free foetal DNA isolated from maternal plasma allows non-invasive determination of foetal RHD, KEL, and other blood group genotypes. This technology avoids invasive procedures like amniocentesis or chorionic villous sampling while providing critical information for risk assessment.
questions.question: How is cell-free foetal DNA utilized in HDFN diagnosis
Which hepatic enzyme system metabolizes warfarin?
questions.explanation: Warfarin is metabolized by hepatic Cytochrome P450 enzymes with 40-hour half-life. P450 inducers or inhibitors significantly affect warfarin levels. Drug interactions through this system require careful monitoring.

questions.question: What converts the temporary platelet plug into a definitive hemostatic plug?
questions.explanation: The temporary platelet plug is converted into a definitive (secondary) hemostatic plug through blood coagulation, which deposits fibrin strands that mechanically reinforce the platelet aggregate. This creates a tight, unyielding seal capable of withstanding physiological blood pressure and shear forces. The fibrin mesh interweaves with platelets and undergoes cross-linking by Factor XIII, forming a stable hemostatic plug that prevents rebleeding.

HMS may develop years after returning home in expatriates and visitors who previously resided in endemic areas. This delayed presentation reflects cumulative immune dysregulation. Extensive travel history including distant past is essential.
questions.question: How long after returning from endemic areas can HMS develop in expatriates

questions.explanation: Vitamin K in parenteral nutrition can inhibit warfarin effect by providing alternative vitamin K source. Intravenous vitamin K bypasses intestinal absorption. Nutritional vitamin K requires monitoring and dose adjustment.
questions.question: What vitamin K source can inhibit warfarin effect?

questions.explanation: Splenectomy is indicated when hypersplenic cytopenias are severe enough to demand intervention or when the enlarged spleen causes pain and discomfort. Either partial or total splenectomy may be performed depending on the situation. The decision balances cytopenia severity against post-splenectomy infection risks.
questions.question: When is splenectomy indicated for hypersplenism management

questions.explanation: The IEF profile of a monoclonal antibody is sometimes referred to as the spectrotype for identification purposes. This characteristic pattern serves as a molecular fingerprint. Spectrotyping helps verify antibody identity and detect contamination.
questions.question: What is an antibody's IEF profile sometimes called?
What modification technique is used in Hemassist
questions.explanation: Hemassist uses diaspirin crosslinking between alpha-chains to stabilize the hemoglobin tetramer and reduce renal toxicity. This intramolecular crosslinking prevents hemoglobin dissociation. The crosslinking technology was an important early modification strategy.

questions.question: What is the primary clinical indication for cryoprecipitate transfusion
questions.explanation: Fibrinogen replacement is the primary indication for cryoprecipitate use. It effectively treats hypofibrinogenemia in various conditions including DIC and massive transfusion. Specific factor concentrates now treat most other deficiencies previously managed with cryoprecipitate.

options: Remove foetal haemoglobin and replace with adult
Correct metabolic acidosis from tissue hypoxia
Replace antibody-coated RBCs and remove maternal antibody
Provide platelets and clotting factors primarily
questions.explanation: Exchange transfusion simultaneously removes antibody-coated red cells, passively transferred maternal antibody, and accumulated bilirubin while replacing with compatible red cells. This procedure treats anaemia and prevents kernicterus, though now rarely needed with modern interventions.
questions.question: What is the primary purpose of exchange transfusion in HDFN

questions.explanation: Glycosylation and phosphorylation affect protein isoelectric points by adding charged groups modifying net charge. These post-translational modifications create protein variants with different pI values. IEF reveals this heterogeneity invisible to other techniques.
questions.question: What affects protein isoelectric points significantly?

questions.explanation: DNA analysis serves primarily for prenatal diagnosis and resolving complex diagnostic cases rather than routine screening. Molecular methods definitively identify mutations enabling accurate genetic counseling. Prenatal applications allow informed reproductive decisions.
questions.question: When is DNA analysis primarily employed in haemoglobinopathy diagnosis

questions.explanation: Long-standing subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord becomes irreversible despite B12 replacement due to permanent demyelination and axonal loss. Early neurological symptoms may improve or stabilize with aggressive therapy. This emphasizes the importance of recognizing B12 neuropathy before irreversible damage occurs. Neurological deterioration may paradoxically worsen initially with treatment.
questions.question: What neurological complication is irreversible despite B12 replacement?

questions.explanation: Platelet transfusion refractoriness is defined as an inadequate increase in platelet count following transfusion of ABO-identical donor platelets. This can result from immune causes like HPA or HLA antibodies, or non-immune factors. Refractoriness increases bleeding risk and requires alternative management strategies.
questions.question: What characterizes platelet transfusion refractoriness?

questions.explanation: Recent RBC transfusion can cause false negative results in PK screening tests because transfused normal RBCs contain adequate PK enzyme. Patients with reticulocytosis may also have normal screening tests since young RBCs have higher enzyme levels. For definitive diagnosis, quantitative enzyme assays and DNA analysis should be performed when transfusion history exists.
questions.question: What can cause false negative results in PK screening tests?

questions.explanation: Flow cytometry assesses platelet activation by measuring surface expression of activation markers like P-selectin (CD62P). Fluorescently labeled antibodies detect marker expression changes after agonist exposure. This method provides sensitive detection of platelet activation states.
questions.question: What does flow cytometry assess regarding platelet activation?

questions.explanation: Peripheral blood film maintains an important diagnostic role in haematological disorders despite automated analyzer advances. It provides morphological details that automated systems cannot fully assess. The PBF remains invaluable for characterizing various clinical diseases and validating automated results.
questions.question: What role does peripheral blood film maintain despite analyzer advancement?
Why does LMWH have a longer half-life than unfractionated heparin?
questions.explanation: Reduced binding of LMWH to cell surfaces explains its longer half-life compared to standard heparin. Less cellular binding means slower clearance from circulation. This pharmacokinetic advantage provides more stable anticoagulation.

Additive solutions extend RBC storage from 35 days (CPDA-1) to 42 days through optimized nutrient provision. These solutions contain dextrose, adenine, and sodium chloride with varying additional components. The extended shelf life improves inventory management and reduces outdates.
questions.question: What shelf life extension do additive solutions like AS-1, AS-3, and AS-5 provide for red blood cells
What minimum haemoglobin level defines beta thalassaemia intermedia without transfusions
questions.explanation: Beta thalassaemia intermedia patients maintain minimum haemoglobin of 7 g/dL or greater without regular transfusions. This intermediate severity falls between minor and major disease expressions. Patients manage compensated anaemia but may require transfusions during stress.

Cholestyramine reduces gastrointestinal absorption of warfarin, decreasing anticoagulant effect through bile acid binding. Separating administration times minimizes interaction. Reduced absorption requires dose adjustment.
questions.question: How does cholestyramine affect warfarin?

questions.explanation: The normal bleeding time range using general interpretation standards is 1-9 minutes, though specific methods have narrower ranges (Duke <3 minutes, Ivy <8 minutes, Simplate 3.65+/-1.22 minutes). Times between 9-15 minutes suggest platelet dysfunction, while times exceeding 15 minutes are critical and require test discontinuation with pressure application.
questions.question: What is the normal bleeding time range using the general interpretation?
What minimum percentage of monocytic elements in blood is required for M4 diagnosis?
questions.explanation: AML M4 requires at least 5×10⁹/L monocytic elements in blood combined with specific bone marrow criteria. Additionally, either 20% monocytic lineage cells in bone marrow or serum lysozyme three times normal is needed. These criteria help distinguish M4 from other AML subtypes with monocytic features.

questions.question: Where are Class II molecules primarily found?
questions.explanation: Class II molecules are found only on antigen-presenting cells including B-cells, macrophages, and dendritic cells. This restricted distribution contrasts with the ubiquitous expression of Class I molecules. Class II expression can be induced on other cell types through activation or inflammatory cytokines.

Flow cytometry parameters including light scatter and fluorescence enable detection of immature granulocytes and other abnormal cells. These measurements identify cells based on size, complexity, and specific staining characteristics. The analyzer generates flags alerting laboratory staff to review abnormal findings.
questions.question: What enables automated analyzers to detect immature granulocytes?

questions.explanation: Rifampicin and barbiturates induce hepatic P450 enzymes, accelerating warfarin metabolism and reducing anticoagulant effect. Increased clearance necessitates higher warfarin doses for therapeutic effect. This interaction requires careful monitoring.
questions.question: Which drugs induce hepatic P450 enzymes and reduce warfarin effectiveness?
What unusual symptom may occur in iron deficiency anaemia?
questions.explanation: Pica, characterized by unusual dietary cravings for non-nutritive substances like ice, clay, or starch, occurs in iron deficiency anaemia. The mechanism remains unclear but resolves with iron replacement. Other specific features include koilonychia, angular stomatitis, and Paterson-Kelly syndrome (pharyngeal webs causing dysphagia).

questions.question: What MHC molecules do platelets express?
questions.explanation: Platelet membranes contain MHC class I molecules (HLA-A, B, C) but not class II molecules. This class I expression makes platelets targets for HLA alloimmunization. The presence of both HLA and HPA antigens complicates platelet transfusion immunology.

questions.question: What is the minimum final hematocrit required for whole blood after collection
questions.explanation: Whole blood must have a final hematocrit of at least 38% to ensure adequate oxygen-carrying capacity. This requirement balances the need for sufficient red cell mass with fluid volume. The standard collection of 450ml blood with 63ml anticoagulant typically achieves this.

questions.question: What test measures RBC susceptibility to osmotic stress?
questions.explanation: The osmotic fragility test measures RBC susceptibility to hypotonic stress by exposing cells to varying salt concentrations. Spherocytes and metabolically compromised cells have reduced surface-to-volume ratio, making them more fragile and prone to lysis in hypotonic solutions. This test helps diagnose hereditary spherocytosis and other membrane defects.

questions.question: Which receptor facilitates vitamin B12 absorption in the terminal ileum?
questions.explanation: Cubilin serves as the specific surface receptor for the intrinsic factor-B12 complex in terminal ileum enterocytes, facilitating B12 absorption through receptor-mediated endocytosis. After internalization, B12 is released and binds to transcobalamin II for delivery to tissues. Genetic cubilin defects cause congenital B12 malabsorption.

questions.question: What is the primary genetic mutation associated with hereditary haemochromatosis in Irish patients?
questions.explanation: Homozygosity for the C282Y mutation confers the greatest risk of developing hereditary haemochromatosis, accounting for 98% of Irish HH genotypes. This mutation involves substitution of tyrosine for cysteine in the HFE protein. However, the disease demonstrates incomplete penetrance with only 20-30% developing clinical complications.

questions.question: Why must blood be fresh (less than 6 hours old) for optimal component preparation
questions.explanation: Fresh blood (<6 hours) preserves platelet function and labile coagulation factors for component manufacturing. Delays compromise these temperature-sensitive components. Platelet concentrates particularly require fresh starting material.

questions.question: What determines life expectancy in treated hereditary haemochromatosis?
questions.explanation: Patients diagnosed and treated before developing cirrhosis have normal life expectancy. Those with established cirrhosis face significantly reduced survival due to persistent hepatocellular carcinoma risk, hepatic decompensation, and complications despite adequate iron removal. Early diagnosis through screening programs dramatically improves outcomes by enabling pre-cirrhotic intervention.

Aspirin irreversibly acetylates and inhibits cyclooxygenase (COX), preventing conversion of arachidonic acid to prostaglandin H2 and subsequently thromboxane A2. Since platelets lack nuclei and cannot synthesize new enzymes, this inhibition persists for the platelet's lifespan (7-10 days). This mechanism explains why aspirin must be discontinued 7-10 days before bleeding time testing or surgery to normalize platelet function.
questions.question: Which enzyme in platelets is irreversibly inhibited by aspirin?

questions.explanation: Enzyme conversion treatment leaves fewer than 2000 antigenic sites per RBC without affecting membrane deformability, gas exchange, or expression of Rh, MNS, Lewis, Kell, Lutheran, Duffy, and Kidd blood group systems. Their antigenicity does not depend on terminal galactose residues removed during conversion. This represents a significant reduction from millions of antigens normally present.
questions.question: How many antigenic sites remain per RBC after enzyme conversion of B antigen?

questions.explanation: Traditional serological typing using CDC represents the lowest resolution method available. It can typically distinguish broad HLA groups but cannot differentiate between closely related alleles within serological groups. CDC was the standard before molecular methods became available.
questions.question: What resolution does traditional CDC provide?
What blood film finding suggests concurrent iron and folate deficiency?
questions.explanation: A dimorphic blood film shows two distinct red cell populations: one macrocytic (from folate/B12 deficiency) and one microcytic hypochromic (from iron deficiency). This occurs when iron deficiency coexists with severe folate or B12 deficiency, partially masking the expected macrocytosis. The MCV may appear deceptively normal.

Normal whole blood clotting time is 5 to 10 minutes, providing crude coagulation assessment. Normal result excludes gross deficiency but misses minor abnormalities. This simple bedside test has limited sensitivity.
questions.question: What is the normal whole blood clotting time?

questions.explanation: Normal Factor VII assay range is 50-150 IU/dL (or IU/mL), with levels below 40% considered abnormal. Factor VII has the shortest half-life (4-6 hours) among coagulation factors, making it the first to decrease in vitamin K deficiency or warfarin therapy and the first to recover with vitamin K administration. Isolated Factor VII deficiency is rare, inherited as autosomal recessive, causing variable bleeding severity correlating with residual factor levels.
questions.question: What is the normal Factor VII assay range?
What is the recommended centrifugation speed for obtaining platelet-poor plasma?
questions.explanation: Platelet-poor plasma is obtained by centrifuging citrated blood at minimum 1700 rpm for at least 10 minutes, preferably at 4°C in a refrigerated centrifuge. Alternative acceptable parameters include 2500 rpm for 15 minutes. Insufficient centrifugation leaves excessive platelets that provide phospholipid, potentially shortening coagulation times and causing erroneous results, particularly in lupus anticoagulant testing.

questions.question: What bilirubin fraction elevates in thalassaemia major
questions.explanation: Indirect (unconjugated) bilirubin elevates in thalassaemia major and intermedia reflecting chronic haemolysis. Red cell destruction releases haem requiring hepatic conjugation. The elevation indicates ongoing erythrocyte breakdown.

options: Young RBCs have nearly normal enzyme
questions.question: Why is hemolytic anemia self-limited in G6PD A- deficiency?
questions.explanation: In G6PD A- deficiency, hemolytic anemia is self-limited because young RBCs produced in response to hemolysis have nearly normal enzyme levels. As reticulocytes and young erythrocytes replace the destroyed older cells with very low enzyme activity, hemolysis stops even with continued exposure to the oxidant trigger. This distinguishes A- from Mediterranean variants with more severe deficiency.

IEF has better resolution and quantitation than standard gel electrophoresis due to the focusing mechanism. Even proteins with very similar pI values can be separated. This superior resolution makes IEF valuable for detecting protein microheterogeneity.
questions.question: What advantage does IEF offer over standard gel electrophoresis?
What physical finding is the hallmark of HMS
questions.explanation: Moderate-to-massive splenomegaly is the hallmark of HMS on physical examination. The enlarged spleen may be visible protruding against the abdominal wall. Despite massive size, splenic rupture is rare.

Liver biopsy with quantitative hepatic iron concentration measurement provides definitive diagnosis of iron overload, particularly when combined with calculation of hepatic iron index. Prussian blue staining demonstrates iron distribution in hepatocytes versus Kupffer cells. However, MRI now increasingly replaces biopsy for hepatic iron quantification.
questions.question: What finding on liver biopsy confirms hepatic iron overload?

questions.explanation: PFC administration may cause flu-like symptoms, representing a tolerability issue though generally less severe than hemoglobin-based product complications. These symptoms are typically transient and manageable. The side effects are related to the lipid emulsion components rather than PFC itself.
questions.question: What side effect may occur with PFC administration

options: Only detects IgE-mediated type I reactions
Limited to antibody-mediated type II reactions
Detects T-cell-mediated types I through IV reactions
Exclusively identifies immune complex type III reactions
questions.explanation: LTT detects T-cell involvement across hypersensitivity types I-IV because T cells participate in most allergic mechanisms. Memory T cells respond to drug re-exposure in vitro regardless of clinical phenotype, making LTT applicable to diverse drug-induced hypersensitivity reactions.
questions.question: Why can LTT detect various hypersensitivity reaction types
What major complication occurred during the first clinical trials of hemoglobin-based oxygen carriers in 1978
questions.explanation: The first clinical trials in 1978 demonstrated significant systemic toxicity, revealing that free hemoglobin outside red blood cells posed serious safety challenges. This toxicity highlighted the need for extensive modifications to create safer products. The findings led to decades of research focused on reducing hemoglobin toxicity.

questions.question: What is the principle of the fluorescent screening test for enzyme deficiencies?
questions.explanation: The fluorescent screening test principle is that reduced pyridine nucleotide (NADH) fluoresces when illuminated with long-wave UV light, while oxidized NAD+ does not fluoresce. In enzyme-deficient samples, NADH consumption is reduced, so fluorescence persists. Normal samples show disappearance of fluorescence as NADH is oxidized to NAD+.

questions.question: Which dental procedures require antibiotic coverage in asplenic patients
questions.explanation: Tooth extraction and other invasive dental procedures should be covered with broad-spectrum antibiotics such as clindamycin or amoxicillin in asplenic patients. These procedures create bacteremia risk from oral flora. The impaired splenic clearance cannot handle transient bacteremia that normal individuals tolerate.

questions.question: Which syndrome can CML transform into during blast crisis?
questions.explanation: CML blast crisis resembles acute leukemia with aggressive behavior and poor prognosis. The disease transforms into either myeloid (70-75%) or lymphoid (25-30%) blast crisis. This terminal phase shows rapid progression with median survival of 3 months despite treatment.

Patients with cytochrome b5 reductase deficiency can tolerate methemoglobin levels as high as 40% through physiological adaptations including polycythemia (increased RBC mass), changes in 2,3-DPG concentration and pH (altered oxygen affinity), and synthesis of globin chains. These compensatory mechanisms maintain adequate tissue oxygenation despite reduced functional hemoglobin.
questions.question: What allows patients to tolerate methemoglobin levels up to 40%?

questions.explanation: Volume-reduced platelets prevent hemolytic reactions by removing ABO-incompatible plasma. This also prevents volume overload in at-risk patients. The procedure concentrates platelets while removing most supernatant plasma.
questions.question: What is the primary indication for volume-reduced platelets
What receptor facilitates platelet bridging during aggregation?
questions.explanation: Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptors bind fibrinogen, which acts as a bridge between adjacent platelets facilitating clumping. Receptor activation is essential for stable aggregate formation. This bridging mechanism creates cohesive platelet plugs at injury sites.

T lymphocytes are the responding cells in MLC that recognize alloantigens expressed by stimulator cells. B cells and monocytes serve as antigen-presenting stimulator cells. The T cell proliferation indicates recognition of foreign HLA class II antigens.
questions.question: What cell types are responding cells in MLC?

questions.explanation: Haemoglobin electrophoresis typically operates at 50 volts providing optimal separation without excessive heat generation. This voltage balances migration speed against gel integrity maintenance. Higher voltages risk heat-induced denaturation and evaporation.
questions.question: What voltage is typically used for haemoglobin electrophoresis

questions.explanation: Deletion of chromosome 13q (del 13q) is most common, occurring in approximately 50% of CLL patients. This abnormality confers the best prognosis with many patients living decades without treatment. The deletion affects genes producing small inhibitory RNA molecules regulating cell death.
questions.question: Which genetic abnormality confers the best prognosis in CLL?

questions.explanation: Deficiency of bisphosphoglycerate mutase results in decreased 2,3-BPG levels, shifting the hemoglobin-oxygen dissociation curve to the left. This increases hemoglobin affinity for oxygen, resulting in decreased oxygen delivery to peripheral tissues. Compensatory polycythemia develops due to erythropoietin release in response to tissue hypoxia.
questions.question: What is the primary cause of polycythemia in bisphosphoglycerate mutase deficiency?

questions.explanation: Iron deficiency anemia commonly causes reactive thrombocytosis through increased thrombopoietin production and platelet release as part of the bone marrow's compensatory response. Other reactive causes include inflammatory diseases (rheumatoid arthritis, ulcerative colitis), acute trauma, infections (tuberculosis, osteomyelitis), blood loss, hemolytic anemia, splenectomy, malignancy, and postoperative states. Reactive thrombocytosis rarely causes thrombotic or bleeding complications unlike primary thrombocythemia.
questions.question: Which condition is associated with reactive thrombocytosis?
Which hemophilia is known as "Christmas Disease"?
questions.explanation: is called "Christmas Disease" after Stephen Christmas, the first patient identified with Factor IX deficiency in 1952. It accounts for 10-15% of hemophilias with prevalence 1:30,000 males. Clinically indistinguishable from Hemophilia A, requiring specific factor assays for differentiation. Treatment uses Factor IX concentrates or prothrombin complex concentrates. Like Hemophilia A, it's X-linked recessive affecting primarily males.

Each mutation requires its own specific probes or primers for detection reflecting genetic heterogeneity. Different thalassaemia mutations necessitate customized detection strategies. This specificity ensures accurate genotype determination.
questions.question: What requires mutation-specific detection in DNA analysis
What parasitic infection causes massive splenomegaly besides malaria
questions.explanation: Leishmaniasis, along with malaria and schistosomiasis, can cause massive splenomegaly in endemic regions. Visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar) produces marked splenic enlargement. The diagnosis requires demonstration of parasites in splenic or bone marrow aspirates.

questions.question: What does MLC assess functionally?
questions.explanation: Mixed lymphocyte culture measures the proliferative response of lymphocytes when exposed to foreign HLA antigens. This functional assay assesses the biological significance of HLA differences through actual cellular immune responses. MLC provides information about cellular compatibility beyond molecular typing.

Megaloblastic anaemia demonstrates nuclear-cytoplasmic asynchrony where nuclear maturation is delayed relative to normal cytoplasmic development and haemoglobinization. Defective DNA synthesis causes this dissociation, producing large cells with immature nuclear chromatin pattern but adequate haemoglobin content. This characteristic finding defines megaloblastic erythropoiesis.
questions.question: What characterizes the nuclear-cytoplasmic asynchrony in megaloblastic anaemia?

questions.explanation: Blood transfusions are associated with higher frequencies of surgical infections, delayed wound healing, and progression of malignant disease through immunological effects. These complications represent significant clinical concerns beyond infectious disease transmission. The immunomodulatory effects of transfusion can compromise patient outcomes.
