questions.question: Life, with the exception of viruses, is characterized by which of the following structural units as the basic organizational level?
options: Membrane-bound compartments interacting with each other and surroundings
Tissues — collections of cells with similar function

questions.explanation: The diencephalon consists of roof plate and 2 alar plates; basal and floor plates are absent. The roof plate forms choroid plexus. The alar plates differentiate into thalamus and hypothalamus.
questions.question: The diencephalon consists of which plates?

options: The organ of Corti with hair cells
Spiral ganglion housing CN VIII auditory neuron cell bodies
The stapes footplate in the oval window
The endolymphatic sac in the temporal bone
questions.explanation: The modiolus is the conical bony core around which the cochlea spirals and it contains the spiral ganglion housing the cell bodies of bipolar primary auditory neurons. The central processes of these neurons form the cochlear nerve which is a branch of cranial nerve VIII traveling to the cochlear nuclei in the brainstem. The modiolus also transmits blood vessels to the cochlea and is targeted during cochlear implant electrode array insertion.
questions.question: The bony core of the cochlea called the modiolus contains which structure of critical auditory importance?

questions.explanation: The metencephalon is the cranial portion of the rhombencephalon formed by differential growth. It has well-defined basal and alar plates. The pontine flexure separates it from the myelencephalon.
questions.question: The metencephalon is the cranial portion of which vesicle?
The hippocampus is formed from which region?
questions.explanation: Just beyond the choroid plexus bearing region, neuroblast proliferation forms the slightly thickened hippocampus. This portion gets buried within the enlarging cortex. It bulges into the cavity of the lateral ventricle.

Three disc-like flattened outpocketings develop from the utricular portion of the otic vesicle to form the semicircular canals. The central portions of these outpocketings oppose and fuse, then disappear, leaving the peripheral unfused parts. These peripheral portions become the semicircular ducts housed within the semicircular canals.
questions.question: The semicircular canals develop from which portion of the otic vesicle?

options: Multipolar motor neurons with ventral horn characteristics
Large pseudounipolar neurons with satellite glia in a connective tissue capsule
Bipolar neurons identical to retinal bipolar cells
Interneurons connecting ascending sensory and descending motor pathways
Oligodendrocytes that exclusively produce myelin in the CNS
questions.explanation: Dorsal root ganglia contain large pseudounipolar sensory neurons whose single T-shaped process divides into a peripheral branch to sensory receptors and a central branch entering the spinal cord. Each neuron is surrounded by satellite cells which are glial cells that regulate the local ionic environment around the neuron cell body. The entire ganglion is enclosed in dense connective tissue continuous with the epineurium of the nerve.
questions.question: A section through the dorsal root ganglion would show which cell types?
The lateral ventricles develop from which embryonic structure?
questions.explanation: The lateral ventricles develop from the cavity of the telencephalon. The third ventricle develops from the diencephalon cavity, the cerebral aqueduct from the mesencephalon cavity, and the fourth ventricle from the rhombencephalon cavity (metencephalon and myelencephalon).

The pronephros is represented by 7-10 solid cell groups in the cervical region at the beginning of the fourth week. These form vestigial excretory units called nephrotomes. By the end of the fourth week, all indications of the pronephric system have disappeared.
questions.question: The pronephros is typically represented by how many solid cell groups?
Embryonic induction is involved in development of all EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Embryonic induction is involved in development of many organs including eyes (lens, optic cup), ears, limbs, kidney, teeth, hair, salivary glands, and pancreas. Blood cell development (hematopoiesis) occurs through intrinsic differentiation programs rather than classical tissue-to-tissue induction.

The anterior spinal artery supplies the medial medulla, including the pyramids, medial lemniscus, and hypoglossal nucleus. Occlusion causes medial medullary syndrome with contralateral hemiplegia (pyramid damage), contralateral loss of fine touch and proprioception (medial lemniscus), and ipsilateral tongue paralysis with deviation toward the lesion side (hypoglossal nucleus). This contrasts with lateral medullary syndrome caused by PICA occlusion, demonstrating the distinct vascular territories of the medulla.
questions.question: The anterior spinal artery supplies which region of the medulla?

questions.explanation: Parietal (oxyntic) cells are large, rounded or pyramidal cells with intensely eosinophilic cytoplasm due to abundant mitochondria. They secrete both hydrochloric acid, which creates the acidic environment for protein digestion, and intrinsic factor, which is essential for vitamin B12 absorption. Deficiency of intrinsic factor causes pernicious anemia.
questions.question: Which cells in the gastric mucosa secrete hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor?
The uncinate fasciculus connects which lobes?
questions.explanation: The uncinate fasciculus connects the orbital and inferior frontal cortex with the anterior temporal lobe, hooking around the lateral sulcus. This association bundle is involved in memory retrieval, emotion processing, and social cognition, connecting limbic temporal structures with frontal executive regions. Damage can cause emotional dysregulation, memory deficits, and impaired social judgment. The uncinate fasciculus has been implicated in various psychiatric and neurological disorders including frontotemporal dementia and schizophrenia.

Nasal placodes appear around day 30 as thickenings on the right and left of the anteroinferior portion of the frontal prominence. They are located above the stomodeum and below the forebrain. These placodes appear after optic and otic placodes and after the neural tube has completely closed.
questions.question: The nasal placodes appear on approximately which day of development?
Closure of the cranial neuropore occurs on day 25. Failure causes which anomaly?
questions.explanation: Failure of anterior neuropore closure (day 25) causes anencephaly. This results in absence of brain and cranial vault. It is incompatible with life. Posterior neuropore failure causes spina bifida.

options: All five types present in equal proportions of 20% each
Neutrophils 90% with all others less than 2%
questions.question: The normal white blood cell differential count in percentage terms is approximately which of the following?
questions.explanation: Normal adult peripheral blood differential shows neutrophils as the largest proportion at 60 to 70% as first responders; lymphocytes as second most common at 20 to 30%; monocytes at 5 to 8%; eosinophils at 2 to 4%; and basophils at 0 to 1% as the rarest type. Neutrophilia indicates bacterial infection, lymphocytosis indicates viral infection, and eosinophilia indicates allergy or parasitic infection. Left shift with immature neutrophils indicates severe bacterial infection.

questions.question: Hair cells of the organ of Corti develop from which embryonic ridge?
questions.explanation: The outer ridge of epithelial cells in the cochlear duct forms rows of hair cells, which are the sensory cells of the auditory system. These hair cells are covered by the tectorial membrane. The inner ridge forms other supporting structures of the organ of Corti.

questions.question: Kupffer cells in the liver sinusoids are the most numerous tissue macrophages in the body. They perform which primary functions?
options: Synthesizing albumin for plasma oncotic pressure
Storing vitamin A in lipid droplets which is the function of hepatic stellate cells
Phagocytosing aged erythrocytes and bacteria from portal blood; antigen presentation
questions.explanation: Kupffer cells are liver-resident macrophages lining the hepatic sinusoids representing approximately 80 to 90% of all fixed tissue macrophages in the body. They phagocytose aged RBCs contributing to heme and bilirubin metabolism, bacteria from portal blood as first defense against gut-derived pathogens, endotoxin or LPS, immune complexes, and cellular debris. They are part of the MPS and contribute to liver inflammation in alcoholic hepatitis and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease.

The basal plate forms most of the ventral portion of the nervous system including the motor portion of the spinal cord and brainstem. The alar plate forms the dorsal portions, devoted mainly to sensory processing. This patterning is established by signals including Sonic hedgehog (SHH) and bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs).
questions.question: The basal plate of the neural tube forms which functional component?

questions.explanation: The plicae circulares (valves of Kerckring) and intestinal villi are tallest and most densely packed in the jejunum, where surface area for absorption reaches its maximum. They are well-developed in the duodenum but become progressively shorter and less frequent in the ileum. This maximizes jejunal surface area for absorption of carbohydrates, proteins, fats, and water-soluble vitamins. Vitamin B12 and bile salts are specifically absorbed in the terminal ileum.
questions.question: The jejunum is considered the primary site of nutrient absorption. Which feature is MOST developed in the jejunum compared to the duodenum and ileum?

questions.explanation: The tensor tympani muscle is derived from the first pharyngeal arch and is innervated by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V3). It attaches to the malleus and dampens sound. The tensor veli palatini (also first arch) is also innervated by CN V3.
questions.question: The tensor tympani muscle is innervated by which division of the trigeminal nerve?

questions.explanation: The urachus, which connects the apex of the bladder to the umbilicus, becomes the median umbilical ligament in adults. Initially, the bladder is continuous with the allantois, which constricts to form the urachus. In some cases, the urachus may persist as a patent canal, leading to urachal abnormalities.
questions.question: The urachus in adults becomes which structure?
The accessory pancreatic duct (of Santorini) opens at:
questions.explanation: The accessory pancreatic duct (of Santorini), when present, opens at the minor duodenal papilla, located approximately 2 cm proximal to the major papilla. It represents the proximal part of the dorsal pancreatic bud duct. The main pancreatic duct (of Wirsung) opens at the major duodenal papilla along with the common bile duct.

questions.question: The lens develops from which tissue?
questions.explanation: Surface epithelium of frontonasal prominence is induced by optic vesicles to form lens placodes. Placodes invaginate to form lens vesicles which develop lens fibers. The lens is entirely ectodermal.

Six levels are implicated in movement: motor units, spinal cord, brainstem nuclei, basal ganglia, cerebellum, and motor/association cortex. Commands cascade down through levels. It is a parallel hierarchical system.
questions.question: How many levels are in the motor system hierarchy?
The cingulum is best described as:
questions.explanation: The cingulum is a major association fiber bundle running within the cingulate gyrus, connecting frontal, parietal, and temporal lobes along the medial hemispheric surface. It carries fibers from the entorhinal cortex to the hippocampus and connects components of the limbic system. The cingulum curves around the splenium of the corpus callosum to reach the parahippocampal gyrus and hippocampus. Damage can cause memory impairment and emotional dysregulation, reflecting its role in the limbic system.

The proximal part of the notochordal canal forms the neurenteric canal, which provides temporary communication between the amniotic cavity and the yolk sac. The neural plate, groove, and tube are bathed in amniotic fluid that reaches them through the neurenteric canal. This canal is a transient structure.
questions.question: The neurenteric canal forms a temporary communication between which two cavities?

questions.explanation: The choroid is a highly vascularized layer between the sclera and retinal pigment epithelium that provides the sole blood supply to the outer one-third of the retina including photoreceptors and RPE. The inner two-thirds of the retina receive blood from the central retinal artery. Choroidal blood flow is the highest per gram of tissue in the body reflecting the extremely high metabolic demand of photoreceptors. Age-related macular degeneration involves abnormal choroidal neovascularization.
questions.question: The choroid layer of the uveal tract primarily serves which function for the retina?
options: Regulating light entry through pupil diameter changes
Producing vitreous humor for the posterior chamber
Focusing light on the retina through refractive power
Providing oxygen and nutrients to the outer retinal layers including photoreceptors
Converting light energy to neural impulses in the photoreceptor layer

questions.question: Down syndrome is most commonly caused by which chromosomal abnormality?
questions.explanation: Down syndrome is most commonly caused by trisomy 21, where there are three copies of chromosome 21 instead of the normal two copies. This usually results from nondisjunction during meiosis, producing a gamete with an extra chromosome 21. The risk increases with maternal age.

Tooth development requires reciprocal inductive interactions between mesenchyme (neural crest-derived) and epithelium (ectodermal). The epithelium induces the mesenchyme to form dental papilla and dental follicle, while the mesenchyme induces the epithelium to form enamel organ. Both tissues are required.
questions.question: Tooth development requires inductive stimuli from which tissue?

options: To cool the lens and prevent heat damage
To increase the depth of focus significantly
To stain the specimen more uniformly
To increase the numerical aperture and resolving power
To reduce the total magnification produced
questions.explanation: Immersion oil has a refractive index similar to glass, preventing light refraction at the interface between the coverslip and objective lens, thereby increasing numerical aperture. Higher numerical aperture directly improves the resolving power of the objective. This allows visualization of structures at very fine resolution approaching 0.2 micrometers.
questions.question: In a compound microscope, the objective lens magnifying 100× is usually used together with immersion oil primarily for which of the following reasons?

questions.explanation: In membranous nephropathy, subepithelial immune complex deposits cause the GBM to appear diffusely thickened on light microscopy. With silver methenamine staining, the GBM shows characteristic 'spike and dome' or 'spike' formation — projections of GBM material growing up between and around the subepithelial deposits. Immunofluorescence shows granular IgG and C3 deposits in a peripheral (capillary wall) pattern. This is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults.
options: No visible changes on light microscopy
questions.question: In membranous nephropathy, immune complexes deposit on the subepithelial aspect of the GBM (between the GBM and podocyte foot processes). On light microscopy, the GBM shows:

questions.explanation: In anaphylactic shock, mast cell degranulation releases preformed histamine which rapidly causes bronchospasm and increased vascular permeability causing hypotension and urticaria. Newly synthesized leukotrienes LTC4 and LTD4 (slow-reacting substances of anaphylaxis) sustain bronchoconstriction more potently than histamine. Platelet activating factor contributes to hypotension. Treatment with epinephrine reverses bronchospasm through beta-2 receptor stimulation and hypotension through alpha-1 vasoconstriction.
options: IgE directly causing smooth muscle contraction
Complement C5a causing mast cell activation
questions.question: A patient presents with anaphylactic shock after a bee sting. The life-threatening bronchospasm and hypotension are primarily mediated by which substances released from mast cells?
The mamillary body is formed from which region?
questions.explanation: A ventral thickening of the neuroepithelium results in formation of the mamillary body. It is functionally related to the hypothalamus. The mamillary bodies are involved in memory and emotional responses.

The alar plate cells are divided into dorsal thalamus and ventral hypothalamus by the hypothalamic sulcus. Thalamic cells proliferate rapidly causing inward bulging. The hypothalamus regulates homeostatic functions.
questions.question: Which structure divides the thalamus from the hypothalamus?

questions.explanation: The eponychium (cuticle) is formed from the stratum corneum of the epithelium of the proximal nail fold. Initially, this band covers the developing nail completely, but later degenerates and persists only at the nail base. The eponychium protects the nail matrix from infection.
questions.question: The eponychium (cuticle) is formed from:

questions.explanation: Dysmetria is impaired distance or range judgment in voluntary movements, manifesting as overshooting (hypermetria) or undershooting (hypometria) when reaching for targets. It reflects the cerebellum's role in calibrating movement amplitude and direction. Dysmetria is tested by finger-nose-finger and heel-shin tests where patients overshoot or undershoot the target. This deficit results from impaired internal models of movement dynamics and inability to use sensory feedback effectively to correct ongoing movements, seen with cerebellar hemisphere lesions.
questions.question: Dysmetria is best defined as:
An osteoblast that becomes completely surrounded by the bone matrix it has secreted is henceforth called which of the following?
questions.explanation: When an active osteoblast secreting matrix becomes entrapped in the matrix it has produced, it transforms into an osteocyte. Osteocytes reside in lacunae and maintain the surrounding matrix through limited secretion and resorption. They extend cytoplasmic processes through canaliculi, connecting to neighboring osteocytes and to vascular channels, functioning as the primary mechanosensory cells of bone that regulate remodeling in response to mechanical loading.

options: Increased LH receptor expression on theca cells
questions.question: Atresia is the process by which most ovarian follicles are destroyed. It can occur at any stage of follicular development. Which characteristic histological change marks follicular atresia?
questions.explanation: Follicular atresia is characterized histologically by: apoptosis and pyknosis of granulosa cells, shrinkage of the oocyte, thickening and eventual hyalinization of the zona pellucida, and invasion by macrophages. The theca interna cells may persist temporarily as interstitial cells. Atresia affects the vast majority of follicles — of the approximately 2 million primordial follicles at birth, only 400 will be ovulated during a woman's reproductive lifetime.

questions.question: Potter facies is characterized by all EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Potter facies is characterized by low-set ears, prominent epicanthal folds, flattened nose, and receding chin, but NOT hypertelorism (widely-spaced eyes). Instead, there is often hypotelorism (closely-spaced eyes). These facial features result from oligohydramnios and compression. The term "Potter sequence" encompasses the full spectrum of oligohydramnios effects including pulmonary hypoplasia and limb deformities.

questions.question: Anorectal malformations most commonly result from abnormal development of:
questions.explanation: Anorectal malformations most commonly result from abnormal development of the urorectal septum, causing incomplete separation of the cloaca into urogenital and anorectal portions. This can lead to various types of fistulas between the rectum and urogenital structures, as well as imperforate anus and rectal atresia.

The primary fissure is the deepest fissure on the cerebellar surface, separating the anterior lobe (paleocerebellum) from the larger posterior lobe (neocerebellum). The anterior lobe receives proprioceptive input from the spinal cord and controls muscle tone. The posterior lobe receives input from the contralateral cerebral cortex via pontocerebellar pathways and is concerned with coordination of voluntary motor function.
questions.question: What is the primary fissure that separates the anterior from the posterior lobe of the cerebellum?
Ureteropelvic junction obstruction most commonly results from:
questions.explanation: Ureteropelvic (UPJ) obstruction in children most commonly results from intrinsic narrowing or a crossing vessel (accessory lower pole renal artery) compressing the ureter. UPJ obstruction is the most common cause of hydronephrosis detected on prenatal ultrasound. Treatment (pyeloplasty) is indicated for symptoms, progressive hydronephrosis, or declining renal function.

questions.question: The heart and blood vessels are derived from which germ layer?
questions.explanation: The heart and all blood vessels are mesodermal in origin. The mesoderm constitutes the cardiogenic field or area, which is closely related to the pericardial cavity and heart tube. This cardiogenic mesoderm differentiates to form the endocardium, myocardium, and epicardium.

questions.question: The secondary oocyte is released at ovulation and arrested at which stage of meiosis?
questions.explanation: At ovulation, the secondary oocyte is arrested at metaphase II of meiosis. The first meiotic division is completed just before ovulation, expelling the first polar body. Meiosis II is only completed if fertilization occurs, when the sperm's penetration provides the activating signal. The second polar body is then expelled. If not fertilized, the secondary oocyte degenerates without completing meiosis. This arrest mechanism prevents parthenogenetic activation.

Germinal centers form in secondary lymphoid follicles when antigen-activated B cells with T cell help undergo rapid clonal expansion. Within germinal centers, activation-induced cytidine deaminase causes somatic hypermutation of immunoglobulin variable regions; selection retains high-affinity mutants in affinity maturation; class switch recombination changes immunoglobulin isotype from IgM to IgG, IgA, or IgE; selected cells differentiate into long-lived plasma cells or memory B cells.
questions.question: The germinal center within a lymph node secondary follicle is the site of which critical immunological process?
options: T cell positive selection on MHC molecules
Plasmacytoid dendritic cell production of type I interferons
B cell clonal expansion, hypermutation, affinity maturation, and class switching
Mast cell IgE production following allergen exposure

questions.question: The nasal placodes are formed by inductive influence of which structure?
questions.explanation: On both sides of the frontonasal prominence, the ectoderm shows localized thickening called nasal or olfactory placodes. These are formed by the inductive influence of the ventral part of the forebrain. The placodes develop into nasal pits, which are primordia of the anterior nares and nasal cavities.

questions.question: The nasal cavity is lined by olfactory epithelium in its superior portion. This epithelium is correctly classified as:
questions.explanation: The olfactory epithelium is a specialized pseudostratified columnar epithelium containing three cell types: olfactory receptor neurons (bipolar neurons with cilia bearing odorant receptors), supporting (sustentacular) cells, and basal cells (stem cells). It is one of the few sites in the adult nervous system with neuronal regeneration from basal cells. Olfactory neurons project axons to the olfactory bulb via the cribriform plate.

questions.question: The female ovary contains follicles at various stages of development. Primordial follicles consist of:
questions.explanation: Primordial follicles consist of a primary oocyte arrested in prophase I of meiosis, surrounded by a single layer of flattened (squamous) follicular cells. These are the smallest and most numerous follicles in the ovary and represent the ovarian reserve. Activation of primordial follicles triggers their transition to primary follicles, where follicular cells become cuboidal and begin proliferating.
options: A primary oocyte arrested in meiosis I surrounded by a single layer of flattened follicular
A primary oocyte surrounded by several layers of granulosa cells with a zona pellucida
A secondary oocyte with a fully formed antrum
A secondary oocyte surrounded by cumulus oophorus
A mature egg with zona pellucida and corona radiata only

questions.question: The corona radiata is continuous with which structure inferiorly?
questions.explanation: The corona radiata is the fan-shaped array of projection fibers that radiates from the internal capsule to reach all parts of the cerebral cortex. These fibers converge as they descend to form the internal capsule, which then continues as the cerebral peduncle in the midbrain. The corona radiata contains both ascending fibers (thalamocortical) and descending fibers (corticospinal, corticobulbar, corticopontine). Strokes affecting the corona radiata can produce deficits similar to internal capsule strokes but may be more variable depending on the specific fiber involvement.

questions.question: The orbital gyri are located on which brain surface?
questions.explanation: The orbital gyri are located on the inferior (orbital) surface of the frontal lobe, resting on the orbital plate of the frontal bone and forming the roof of the orbit. These gyri are highly variable and irregular, separated by an H-shaped orbital sulcus. The orbital cortex is part of the prefrontal cortex involved in emotion regulation, decision-making, and inhibitory control. Damage to orbital frontal cortex (as in frontal lobe syndrome) causes disinhibition, impulsivity, personality changes, and impaired social judgment.

The extracellular matrix (ECM) is the dominant component of connective tissue, distinguishing it from other tissue types where cells predominate. The ECM consists of protein fibers (collagen, elastic, reticular) and ground substance, providing structural support, hydration, and signaling scaffold. This ECM dominance is the defining histological characteristic of connective tissue.
questions.question: The major constituent that distinguishes connective tissue from all other tissue types (epithelium, muscle, nerve) is which of the following?
options: The abundance of specialized secretory cells
The presence of gap junctions between all cells
The extracellular matrix, which dominates the tissue composition
The high mitotic rate of its cells
The presence of myofilaments in all connective tissue cells

questions.question: Weibel-Palade bodies are found exclusively in endothelial cells. These organelles are used as a definitive immunohistochemical marker of endothelial cell origin using antibodies against:
questions.explanation: Von Willebrand factor (vWF, also known as Factor VIII-related antigen) stored in Weibel-Palade bodies is the most specific immunohistochemical marker of endothelial cell origin. It is routinely used in surgical pathology to confirm vascular tumors (hemangiomas, angiosarcomas) and to identify endothelial cells in tissue sections. CD31 (PECAM-1) is another highly sensitive endothelial marker. CD68 marks macrophages; smooth muscle actin marks smooth muscle cells.

questions.question: Polyhydramnios may be associated with which fetal condition?
questions.explanation: Polyhydramnios (excessive amniotic fluid, usually >2000 ml) may be associated with esophageal atresia or other conditions that prevent the fetus from swallowing amniotic fluid. It can also occur with anencephaly, where there is excessive CSF production. Oligohydramnios (too little fluid) is associated with renal agenesis.

options: The site of aldosterone synthesis switching to cortisol production
A watershed zone with the lowest blood supply
The location of the adrenal capsule blood vessels
A region containing only adipocytes with no endocrine cells
Boundary between mesodermal cortex and neural crest-derived chromaffin medulla
questions.question: The corticomedullary junction of the adrenal gland is significant histologically because it represents which of the following?
questions.explanation: The corticomedullary junction represents the meeting point between the adrenal cortex derived from mesodermal coelomic epithelium and the adrenal medulla derived from neural crest cells that migrated and became encapsulated by the cortex. Histologically the boundary shows the transition from cortical zona reticularis cells to larger medullary chromaffin cells with their prominent eosinophilic granules. This dual developmental origin explains why cortical and medullary function is regulated by entirely different signaling systems.

questions.question: The internal auditory artery supplies which structure?
questions.explanation: The internal auditory artery supplies the middle ear; its occlusion causes vertigo and deafness. It often arises from AICA. It travels through the internal auditory meatus.

questions.question: The coronary arteries supply the myocardium. They arise from the aortic sinuses (sinuses of Valsalva) just above the aortic valve. These sinuses serve which function during diastole?
questions.explanation: During diastole, when the aortic valve closes, the aortic sinuses (sinuses of Valsalva) fill with blood and create eddy currents that flow backward toward the valve. This prevents the valve cusps from apposing the aortic wall (which would obstruct the coronary ostia) and simultaneously fills the coronary ostia with blood, driving coronary perfusion during diastole. This is why the majority of coronary perfusion occurs during diastole, not systole.
options: Preventing regurgitation of blood into the ventricle
Acting as pressure reservoirs for the coronary circulation
Storing oxygenated blood for direct myocardial diffusion
Creating eddy currents that fill the coronary ostia with blood

questions.question: Bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs) during neurulation are neutralized by which molecules?
questions.explanation: Three main neural inducers present in the notochord and primitive node are noggin, chordin, and follistatin. These molecules are secreted and bind to bone morphogenetic proteins (especially BMP-4), thus neutralizing them. This neutralization is essential for neural induction to occur.

questions.question: The cavernous sinus drains primarily into which structure?
questions.explanation: The cavernous sinus drains primarily into the superior and inferior petrosal sinuses, with the inferior petrosal sinus providing the main outflow to the internal jugular vein. The superior petrosal sinus drains into the transverse sinus. The cavernous sinus also has connections to facial veins through the superior and inferior ophthalmic veins, providing a route for facial infections to spread intracranially. Cavernous sinus thrombosis can result from facial infections, causing ophthalmoplegia, orbital edema, and potential bilateral involvement.

questions.question: Undescended testis (cryptorchidism) most commonly involves:
questions.explanation: Cryptorchidism most commonly involves retention in the inguinal canal (70% of cases). Abdominal retention accounts for about 20%, and other locations 10%. The condition may be bilateral or unilateral (right side more common). Orchiopexy (surgical placement into scrotum) is recommended by 12-18 months to preserve fertility and reduce malignancy risk.

options: Large pale erythrocytes with hypersegmented neutrophils
Target cells with a central dense area surrounded by a pale ring
Small pale (microcytic hypochromic) red cells with increased central pallor
questions.explanation: Iron deficiency anemia results in microcytic hypochromic erythrocytes because insufficient iron limits hemoglobin synthesis causing smaller RBCs with less hemoglobin per cell. The peripheral smear shows: microcytosis with MCV less than 80 fL; hypochromia with increased central pallor occupying more than one-third of the cell diameter; and anisocytosis and poikilocytosis with variable size and shape. Large hyperchromic macrocytic cells with hypersegmented neutrophils indicate B12 or folate deficiency megaloblastic anemia instead.
questions.question: The peripheral blood smear of a patient with iron deficiency anemia would show erythrocytes with which morphological abnormalities?
The spinoreticulothalamic pathway comprises what percentage of anterolateral fibers?
questions.explanation: About 90% of anterolateral tract fibers synapse with reticular formation rather than going directly to thalamus. They connect to thalamus via interneurons forming the spinoreticulothalamic pathway. This mediates arousal and affective pain components. ## CRANIAL NERVES

questions.question: The head fold causes the septum transversum to move to which region?
questions.explanation: As a result of growth of the brain and cephalic folding of the embryo, the buccopharyngeal membrane is pulled forward while the heart and pericardial cavity move first to the cervical region. Eventually, these structures move to their final position in the thorax. The septum transversum develops into the central tendon of the diaphragm.

questions.question: Membrane phospholipids in one leaflet can flip to the other leaflet of the bilayer by a process requiring which of the following?
questions.explanation: Transleaflet flip-flop of phospholipids is thermodynamically unfavorable because the polar headgroup must pass through the hydrophobic core. Specific enzymes catalyze this movement: flippases (P4-ATPases) move phosphatidylserine from outer to inner leaflet, floppases move lipids outward, and scramblases non-selectively equilibrate both leaflets. The asymmetric distribution of phospholipids (PS on inner leaflet) is physiologically important, e.g., PS exposure on apoptotic cells signals for phagocytosis.
options: Specific enzymes that catalyze phospholipid transleaflet movement
Spontaneous random thermal diffusion without any enzyme
Lysosomal hydrolysis of the phospholipid headgroup

questions.explanation: The intrinsic muscles of the larynx are derived from the sixth pharyngeal arch. The fourth arch gives rise to the cricothyroid, levator palatini, and constrictor muscles of the pharynx. Both fourth and sixth arches contribute to formation of laryngeal cartilages.
questions.question: Intrinsic muscles of the larynx are derived from which pharyngeal arch?
The definitive kidney begins functioning at approximately:
questions.explanation: The definitive metanephric kidney begins functioning at approximately 12 weeks gestation when glomerular filtration commences. Before this, the mesonephros serves as the interim kidney. Although the metanephric kidney is functional by 12 weeks, it doesn't perform true excretory function during fetal life - the placenta handles waste removal. The fetal kidneys primarily regulate amniotic fluid volume.

Type II collagen is the principal collagen of cartilage (both hyaline and elastic types) and the vitreous body of the eye. Its fibrils are finer than type I collagen and are embedded in the proteoglycan-rich cartilage matrix. Chondrocytes are the cell type that synthesizes type II collagen. Autoimmune destruction of type II collagen characterizes relapsing polychondritis and contributes to joint cartilage loss in rheumatoid arthritis.
options: Hyaline cartilage, elastic cartilage, and vitreous body
questions.question: Type II collagen is specifically found in which of the following tissue locations?
The classic hepatic lobule is described as hexagonal. Which structure is located at the CENTER of this lobule?
questions.explanation: The classic hepatic lobule is centered on the central vein (terminal hepatic venule). Portal tracts — containing branches of the hepatic artery, portal vein, and bile duct — are located at the periphery (corners of the hexagon). Blood flows from the portal tracts centripetally through sinusoids toward the central vein, while bile flows in the opposite direction toward the bile ducts in the portal tracts.
The choroid fissure is a ventral invagination of optic stalk into which hyaloid vessels grow. Nerve fibers from neural retina converge to the optic stalk. The fissure normally closes completely.
questions.question: The choroid fissure allows entry of which structure?
In a histology practical, a GIT segment is identified by its LACK of muscularis mucosae. This feature is characteristic of which structure?
questions.explanation: The gallbladder notably lacks a muscularis mucosae layer — one of its key histological distinguishing features from other GIT structures. Its wall consists of mucosa (epithelium + lamina propria), a fibromuscular layer, perimuscular connective tissue, and serosa/adventitia. The absence of muscularis mucosae is paired with the absence of a submucosa, making the gallbladder structurally unique among tubular digestive organs.

The infundibular recess extends from the floor of the third ventricle into the infundibulum (pituitary stalk), projecting toward the pituitary gland. This recess is bounded anteriorly by the optic chiasma and posteriorly by the mammillary bodies. The close relationship between the third ventricle and hypothalamus is evident in these recesses, which project into hypothalamic structures. Tumors in this region (craniopharyngiomas, pituitary adenomas) may obstruct CSF flow or cause endocrine dysfunction.
questions.question: Which recess of the third ventricle extends into the pituitary stalk?
In the ileum, specialized cells overlie Peyer's patches and sample luminal antigens. These are the:
questions.explanation: M cells (microfold cells) overlie the dome epithelium of Peyer's patches in the ileum. They lack a brush border, have an irregular apical surface with short microfolds, and contain a basolateral pocket housing lymphocytes and macrophages. M cells transcytose luminal antigens, bacteria, and viruses to the underlying lymphoid tissue for immune processing. Pathogens such as Salmonella, Yersinia, and poliovirus exploit M cells as entry points into the body.

The lesser omentum is derived from the ventral mesogastrium, not the dorsal mesogastrium. The dorsal mesogastrium gives rise to the greater omentum, gastrosplenic ligament, and lienorenal ligament. The ventral mesogastrium also forms the visceral peritoneum of the liver and falciform ligament.
questions.question: The dorsal mesogastrium gives rise to all EXCEPT:
The median umbilical ligament in adults represents:
questions.explanation: The median umbilical ligament in adults represents the obliterated urachus, which connected the apex of the bladder to the umbilicus during fetal life. The medial umbilical ligaments represent the obliterated umbilical arteries. The ligamentum teres represents the obliterated umbilical vein. These structures are useful anatomical landmarks during surgery.

questions.question: The outer longitudinal smooth muscle layer of the GIT is continuous throughout EXCEPT at which region where it forms three longitudinal bands?
questions.explanation: In the colon (large intestine), the outer longitudinal smooth muscle of the muscularis externa is not a complete circumferential sheet but is condensed into three distinct longitudinal bands — the teniae coli (taenia libera, taenia mesocolica, and taenia omentalis). This unique arrangement is a defining histological and anatomical feature of the colon. The teniae converge at the base of the appendix, which has a complete longitudinal layer.

questions.question: Gastroschisis differs from omphalocele by having:
questions.explanation: Gastroschisis differs from omphalocele by having no covering membranes; the viscera are bathed directly in amniotic fluid. The defect occurs to the right of the umbilicus through a ruptured abdominal wall defect. It is less commonly associated with other anomalies compared to omphalocele.

questions.question: Primary oocytes are arrested in which stage of meiosis until puberty?
questions.explanation: Primary oocytes begin meiosis I during fetal life but are arrested in prophase I (specifically diplotene stage) until puberty. At puberty, with each ovarian cycle, one or more primary oocytes complete meiosis I to form secondary oocytes, which are then arrested in metaphase II.

questions.question: The secondary palate develops from which structures?
questions.explanation: The secondary palate is formed in the 6th week from the palatine shelves derived from the maxillary prominences. Anteriorly, the palatine shelves fuse with the primary palate. The incisive foramen marks the midline landmark between the primary and secondary palate.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes the structural and functional difference between myelin in the PNS versus CNS?
questions.explanation: PNS myelin is produced by Schwann cells where one Schwann cell myelinates one internode of one axon, and the Schwann cell cytoplasm and basal lamina form the neurilemma tube that guides axon regeneration. CNS myelin is produced by oligodendrocytes where one oligodendrocyte myelinates segments of multiple axons through cytoplasmic processes, without forming a cellular tube, and CNS environment contains inhibitory factors preventing regeneration. PNS myelin contains P0 protein as the major structural protein while CNS myelin contains MBP and PLP.
options: PNS myelin is thicker but has fewer lamellae than CNS myelin
CNS myelin contains more cholesterol than PNS myelin
PNS myelin has identical protein composition to CNS myelin
Both CNS and PNS myelin are produced by identical Schwann cells
PNS Schwann cell myelin enables regeneration; CNS oligodendrocyte myelin does not

questions.question: Most tissues require slicing into thin sections before microscopic examination primarily because of which of the following reasons?
questions.explanation: Light microscopy requires transmitted light to pass through specimens, but intact tissues or organs are too thick to allow adequate light transmission. Thin sections, typically 3–10 micrometers, are mounted on glass slides to achieve the translucency required for microscopic examination. This is the fundamental reason for the sectioning step in histological preparation.
options: To prevent contamination of the specimen
To allow staining solutions to penetrate faster
They are too thick for transmitted light to pass through
To reduce the size of the specimen on the slide
To improve resolution of the electron microscope

questions.explanation: Maternal blood enters the intervillous spaces through spiral arteries, which become less convoluted and increase in diameter during pregnancy. This increases maternal blood flow to the placenta for gaseous exchange. Deoxygenated maternal blood flows back through endometrial veins.
questions.question: Maternal blood enters the intervillous spaces through which vessels?

questions.explanation: The alar plates of the myelencephalon contain three groups of sensory nuclei. Similarly, the basal plates contain three groups of motor neurons which form cranial nerve nuclei in the medulla. These nuclei are arranged in distinct columns.
questions.question: The alar plates of the myelencephalon contain how many groups of sensory nuclei?
On day 8, the trophoblast differentiates into which two layers?
questions.explanation: On day 8, the trophoblast differentiates into two layers: an inner cellular layer called cytotrophoblast and an outer multinucleated layer called syncytiotrophoblast. The syncytiotrophoblast is highly invasive and erodes maternal tissues to establish uteroplacental circulation.

questions.question: The maximum resolving power of a standard compound light microscope is closest to which of the following values?
questions.explanation: Resolving power refers to the minimum distance between two points that can be distinguished as separate. The compound light microscope achieves approximately 0.2 micrometers, compared to normal human eye resolution of ~100 micrometers. This limit is governed by the wavelength of visible light and the numerical aperture of the objective lens.

questions.question: The olfactory epithelium is derived from which embryonic structure?
questions.explanation: The stratified placodal base of the invaginating olfactory pits forms the olfactory epithelium containing neurosensory cells. The lateral walls around the pits become the surface ectodermal covering of nasal cavities. Placodal cells differentiate into neurosensory cells that give rise to olfactory nerve fibers.

questions.question: Mesonephric ridges, which indicate sites of future kidneys, appear during which week?
questions.explanation: Mesonephric ridges appear during the 5th week of development and indicate the sites of the developing kidneys. During this week, the brain grows rapidly, the face contacts the heart prominence, the hyoid (2nd) arch overgrows the 3rd and 4th arches forming the cervical sinus, and upper limbs show elbows and hand plates.

questions.question: The first indication of respiratory system development is:
questions.explanation: The first indication of respiratory system development is the respiratory diverticulum (lung bud), which appears during the 4th week as an outgrowth from the ventral wall of the foregut. This location is determined by transcription factor TBX4. The diverticulum subsequently elongates and divides to form the respiratory tree.

The calcarine sulcus on the medial occipital surface contains the primary visual cortex (area 17, striate cortex) along its banks. The upper and lower lips of the sulcus represent the inferior and superior visual fields respectively, with macular (central) vision represented posteriorly near the occipital pole. The stria of Gennari, a prominent myelinated fiber layer, gives the name \"striate cortex\" and is visible grossly. Posterior cerebral artery strokes affecting this region cause contralateral homonymous hemianopia with characteristic macular sparing.
questions.question: The calcarine sulcus contains which functional area?

options: 4× lens used for scanning wide fields
100× lens used with immersion oil for highest magnification
40× lens used for most detailed cellular work
60× lens standard in all compound microscopes
questions.explanation: The 100× objective lens is the oil immersion lens, requiring immersion oil between the lens and coverslip to prevent light refraction. It provides the highest magnification and best resolving power of the objective lenses in the standard set (4×, 10×, 40×, 100×). Without oil, light bends at the air-glass interface, drastically reducing resolution and brightness.
questions.question: Which objective lens is designated as the 'oil immersion' lens in a compound microscope and at what magnification?
The collateral eminence in the lateral ventricle is caused by indentation from which structure?
questions.explanation: The collateral eminence is a bulge on the floor of the posterior and inferior horns of the lateral ventricle caused by the indentation of the collateral sulcus from the inferior surface of the temporal lobe. This eminence runs longitudinally along the floor lateral to the hippocampus in the inferior horn. The collateral sulcus on the brain's inferior surface creates this inward bulge into the ventricular cavity.

The glycocalyx is a fuzzy extracellular coat composed of carbohydrate chains covalently attached to membrane proteins (glycoproteins) and lipids (glycolipids). It plays roles in cell recognition, adhesion, and protection from mechanical damage. Its presence is detectable in electron micrographs as an electron-dense coating on the outer surface of the plasma membrane.
questions.question: The glycocalyx, which surrounds the cell membrane, is composed primarily of which of the following?

questions.explanation: The cingulate gyrus is located above the corpus callosum on the medial surface of the cerebral hemisphere, separated from superior structures by the cingulate sulcus. This gyrus forms part of the limbic system and extends from the region of the genu to behind the splenium of the corpus callosum. The paracentral lobule caps the medial end of the central sulcus, while the precuneus lies in the superior parietal region.
questions.question: On the medial cerebral surface, which gyrus lies immediately above the corpus callosum?
The periderm (epitrichium) is typically replaced completely by which gestational week?
questions.explanation: The periderm, which is the outermost layer of early fetal skin, is completely replaced by the 21st week of gestation. Peridermal cells continually undergo keratinization and desquamation, being replaced by cells from the basal layer. Exfoliated peridermal cells contribute to the formation of vernix caseosa.

All decidua (decidua basalis, decidua capsularis, and decidua parietalis) are shed at birth along with the placenta and fetal membranes. The decidua is the modified endometrium of pregnancy. After delivery, the endometrium regenerates from the basal layer.
questions.question: All decidual layers are shed at which time?

questions.explanation: The stomach body (and fundus) is characterized by simple columnar epithelium with gastric pits and glands (invaginations into the lamina propria), absence of villi, and a uniquely three-layered muscularis externa (oblique, circular, longitudinal). The colon also lacks villi but has only two distinct muscularis layers arranged as teniae coli. The three-layered muscularis is the key distinguishing feature pointing to the stomach.
questions.question: A section of GIT stained with H&E shows mucosa with simple columnar epithelium invaginating into the lamina propria, NO villi, and a thick muscularis externa with three distinct layers. Which region is MOST likely depicted?
The cerebellar cortex follows which organizational principle?
questions.explanation: The cerebellar cortex is organized into parasagittal zones and microzones with specific input-output relationships, despite its uniform histological appearance. Purkinje cells are arranged in parasagittal bands that project to specific regions of deep nuclei, and these zones receive climbing fiber input from specific olivary subdivisions. Within zones, smaller microzones (\~1mm wide) may represent functional units. This modular organization allows different cerebellar regions to control specific body parts and motor functions independently.

questions.question: At birth, the spinal cord ends at which vertebral level?
questions.explanation: At birth, the spinal cord ends at the lower border of L3, while in adulthood it ends at L2/L3 boundary. At 3 months of intrauterine life, it extends the entire length of the vertebral column. This differential growth creates the cauda equina.

questions.question: The middle cerebellar peduncle primarily contains fibers from which nuclei?
questions.explanation: The middle cerebellar peduncle contains fibers originating from the pontine nuclei that project to all parts of the cerebellum except the nodulus. These pontocerebellar fibers carry information from the cerebral cortex via corticopontine pathways, forming an important link in cortical control of cerebellar function. The middle cerebellar peduncle is the largest of the three cerebellar peduncles and consists entirely of afferent fibers to the cerebellum.

Volkmann's canals (perforating canals) run perpendicular or oblique to the long axis of bone, connecting adjacent Haversian canals to each other and to the periosteum and marrow cavity. They are the primary route by which blood vessels from the marrow cavity reach the Haversian canals of individual osteons. Unlike Haversian canals, Volkmann's canals are NOT surrounded by concentric lamellae.
options: Volkmann's canals contain larger blood vessels and no nerves
Volkmann's canals run parallel to the long axis of the bone
Volkmann's canals run perpendicular to the long axis of bone
Volkmann's canals are absent in mature bone and present only during development
Volkmann's canals are only found in spongy bone trabeculae
questions.question: Volkmann's canals in compact bone differ from Haversian canals primarily in which of the following ways?

questions.explanation: The inferior longitudinal fasciculus connects the occipital and temporal lobes, running along the lateral wall of the inferior and posterior horns of the lateral ventricle. It carries visual information from occipital cortex to temporal lobe structures involved in object recognition (ventral visual stream---the \"what\" pathway). Damage to this pathway can contribute to visual agnosia (inability to recognize objects) and prosopagnosia (face recognition deficit), particularly when bilateral. This fasciculus is crucial for linking visual perception with memory.
questions.question: The inferior longitudinal fasciculus connects which lobes?

questions.explanation: The angular gyrus (Brodmann area 39) in the inferior parietal lobule is crucial for reading, integrating visual word recognition with language comprehension. It caps the posterior end of the superior temporal sulcus and serves as a multimodal association area connecting visual, auditory, and somatosensory information. Dominant hemisphere lesions cause alexia (inability to read) and agraphia (inability to write), as well as Gerstmann syndrome (acalculia, finger agnosia, left-right disorientation, agraphia). The angular gyrus is unique to humans and great apes, correlating with language capabilities.
questions.question: The angular gyrus is involved primarily in which function?

questions.explanation: A rectovesical fistula is an abnormal communication between the rectum and urinary bladder. This results from incomplete separation of the cloaca by the urorectal septum. Boys with high anorectal malformations may have rectovesical or rectourethral fistulas. These require surgical correction to separate the systems.
questions.question: A rectovesical fistula connects the rectum to:
The pineal body develops from which structure?
questions.explanation: A caudal neuroepithelial thickening on the dorsal surface evaginates around the 7th week to form the pineal body. It sits on the mesencephalon. The pineal gland secretes melatonin and regulates circadian rhythms.

questions.question: Neurotransmitters are transported to axon terminus by which structures?
questions.explanation: Neurotransmitter molecules are transported to axon terminus by microfilaments and microtubules. This is called axoplasmic flow or axonal transport. The transport can be anterograde or retrograde.

questions.question: Which fissure on the cerebral hemisphere separates the frontal lobe from the temporal lobe?
questions.explanation: The lateral sulcus (fissure of Sylvius) separates the frontal lobe from the temporal lobe on the superolateral surface of the cerebrum. Its anterior end penetrates the inferior frontal gyrus with ascending and anterior rami, dividing it into orbital, triangular, and opercular parts. The depth of the lateral sulcus contains the insular cortex, which is covered by the frontal, parietal, and temporal opercula.

questions.question: The corpus callosum develops from which embryonic structure?
questions.explanation: The corpus callosum develops from the lamina terminalis, which thickens to form commissural pathways connecting the cerebral hemispheres. Development proceeds from anterior to posterior, with the genu and body forming before the splenium. The anterior commissure and hippocampal commissure also develop from the lamina terminalis. Developmental abnormalities can cause partial or complete agenesis of the corpus callosum, sometimes compensated by enlargement of the anterior commissure. The lamina terminalis represents the rostral-most end of the neural tube.

Peyer's patches are large aggregates of lymphoid follicles located predominantly in the distal ileum, where they can extend from the lamina propria into the submucosa. They are part of the gut-associated lymphoid tissue (GALT) and play a crucial role in immune surveillance of intestinal contents. Isolated lymphoid nodules are distributed throughout the small intestine but aggregated patches characterize the ileum.
questions.question: Peyer's patches are aggregated lymphoid nodules found predominantly in which segment of the small intestine?

questions.explanation: Neurulation is the process involved in formation of the neural plate, neural groove, neural folds, and fusion of the folds to form the neural tube. The process is completed by the end of the 4th week with closure of the neural tube. The neural tube is the primordium of the central nervous system.
questions.question: Neurulation is completed by the end of which week with closure of the neural tube?

questions.explanation: Unilateral renal agenesis is often associated with ipsilateral genital anomalies (absent vas deferens in males, uterine anomalies in females) because both systems develop from adjacent mesoderm and share inductive interactions. The condition results from failure of ureteric bud formation or degeneration of the metanephric blastema. Most cases are compatible with normal life if the contralateral kidney is normal.
questions.question: Unilateral renal agenesis is often associated with:
Most neurons in the CNS are which type?
questions.explanation: Most neurons in the CNS are multipolar with many dendrites and one axon. This includes Purkinje cells, pyramidal cells and motor neurons. Bipolar neurons are found in special sensory organs.

Carnegie stage 22 corresponds to the 8th week when webbed digits of the hand are present. This is the final week of the embryonic period. At this stage, notches are also present between digits of the foot, the tail is still present, and the scalp vascular plexus is visible.
questions.question: Which Carnegie stage corresponds to the appearance of webbed digits of the hand?

questions.explanation: The large intestine has no villi and is lined by simple columnar epithelium with numerous crypts (tubular glands). Goblet cells are the predominant secretory cell type in the colonic mucosa and are far more numerous than in the small intestine. The abundant mucus they produce lubricates the passage of increasingly solid fecal matter. Paneth cells are rare or absent in the adult colon.
questions.question: The large intestine lacks villi but retains crypts of Lieberkühn. What is the predominant cell type in these colonic crypts?
The trapezoid body is formed by axons crossing from which nuclei?
questions.explanation: Axons of second-order neurons from cochlear nucleus form trapezoid body as they cross midline to contralateral superior olivary nucleus. Other crossing fibers form dorsal and intermediate acoustic striae. This allows bilateral hearing.

questions.question: The amygdala is located at the tip of which structure?
questions.explanation: The amygdala consists of groups of neurons connected to the tip of the tail of the caudate nucleus, lying on the roof of the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle anterior to the hippocampus. This almond-shaped complex modulates the association between different sensory modalities and exerts emotional control over sensory input. The amygdala is involved in fear conditioning, emotional memory, and social behavior; bilateral damage causes Klüver-Bucy syndrome with emotional blunting and hypersexuality.

The cecal swelling (diverticulum) in the caudal limb of the midgut loop marks the primordium of both the cecum and appendix. This swelling appears during the 6th week. The appendix initially arises from the distal end of the cecum but shifts to the medial side with unequal cecal wall growth.
questions.question: The cecal swelling marks the future:

questions.explanation: Granule cells in the cerebellar cortex use glutamate as their excitatory neurotransmitter, consistent with their role in relaying mossy fiber input to Purkinje cells. These small neurons (5-8 μm in diameter) are the most numerous neurons in the brain. Their unmyelinated axons ascend to the molecular layer where they bifurcate to form parallel fibers that run perpendicular to Purkinje cell dendritic trees, creating numerous synaptic contacts.
questions.question: Which neurotransmitter is utilized by granule cells in the cerebellar cortex?

questions.explanation: The central nervous system (brain and spinal cord) is concerned with integration, analysis and response to information. The peripheral nervous system receives sensory information and delivers responses. Together they form the complete nervous system.
questions.question: The central nervous system is concerned with which functions?
The mesonephric tubules in males contribute to formation of:
questions.explanation: In males, some caudal mesonephric tubules persist to form the efferent ductules connecting the testis to the epididymis. The mesonephric duct itself becomes the ductus deferens, epididymis, and ejaculatory duct. In females, mesonephric structures largely degenerate, with only vestigial remnants (epoophoron, paroophoron) persisting.

The mammillary nuclei (medial and lateral) belong to the posterior hypothalamic group and are visible as paired prominences on the inferior surface of the hypothalamus. These nuclei receive input from the hippocampus via the fornix and project to the anterior thalamic nuclei via the mammillothalamic tract, forming a key link in the Papez circuit. The mammillary nuclei are involved in memory processing and learning; their damage (as in Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome) causes severe memory impairment.
questions.question: The mammillary nuclei are part of which hypothalamic group?

options: It is produced continuously and drains like aqueous humor
It is a free-flowing liquid with no gel structure
It contains photoreceptors embedded within its matrix
It is replaced by fresh fluid every few hours
Stable gelatinous gel not replaced throughout life, stabilizing the eyeball
questions.explanation: Vitreous humor is a stable transparent gel of 98% water with 2% type II collagen and hyaluronic acid filling the vitreous chamber. Unlike aqueous humor which continuously circulates, vitreous is not replaced and the same gel present in infancy persists throughout adult life. It maintains the spherical shape of the eyeball supports the lens anteriorly and keeps the retina pressed against the choroid. Liquefaction with aging contributes to floaters and increased risk of retinal detachment.
questions.question: The vitreous humor fills the space between the lens and retina. It differs from aqueous humor in which of the following ways?
A sickle-shaped projection of meningeal dura dividing cerebral hemispheres houses which venous sinus in its upper margin?
questions.explanation: The falx cerebri is the sickle-shaped projection extending from the crista galli to the internal occipital protuberance, dividing the two cerebral hemispheres. Its upper convex margin is attached to the cranial vault and contains the superior sagittal sinus. The free crescentic lower margin houses the inferior sagittal sinus, while the straight sinus is located at its posterior junction with the tentorium cerebelli.
Microglia are smallest neuroglia with few processes, of mesodermal origin. They are the phagocytes of the nervous system. They clear pathogens and debris.
questions.question: Microglia are derived from which tissue?

questions.explanation: The neuron consists of a cell body (soma) with cytoplasmic extensions and organelles. The soma is the trophic center of the cell. It contains the nucleus and most organelles.
questions.question: The cell body of a neuron is also called which term?

questions.explanation: Club cells (formerly Clara cells) in bronchioles secrete a surfactant-like lipoprotein that reduces surface tension in smaller airways. They also contain cytochrome P450 enzymes for detoxification of inhaled xenobiotics. Additionally, they serve as progenitor cells for bronchiolar epithelium. Their dome-shaped apical surface protrudes into the airway lumen — a useful histological feature for identification.
questions.question: Clara cells (club cells) are non-ciliated secretory cells found primarily in terminal and respiratory bronchioles. Their secretion performs which function?
options: Production of mucus for airway lubrication
Production of IgA for mucosal immunity
Secretion of HCl to maintain airway pH
Production of lysozyme for antibacterial defense

questions.question: The serosa of the GIT is derived from which embryological structure?
questions.explanation: The serosa is derived from splanchnic mesoderm and is equivalent to the visceral peritoneum. It consists of a mesothelial cell layer over a thin layer of connective tissue. In retroperitoneal organs, this covering is replaced by the adventitia — a connective tissue layer without mesothelium.

questions.question: Eosinophils are most characteristically elevated in which clinical conditions?
questions.explanation: Eosinophils are classically elevated in IgE-mediated allergic diseases including asthma atopic dermatitis and food allergy, and in parasitic helminth infections. Their bilobed nucleus and prominent orange-red granules containing major basic protein and eosinophil peroxidase allow cytotoxic killing of parasites too large to phagocytose. Eosinophil recruitment is directed by IL-5 from T helper 2 cells and eotaxin from tissue cells.

The pupillary light reflex develops during 30-34 weeks as the nervous system matures. At this stage, the upper and lower limbs have a chubby appearance, the skin is pink and smooth, and infants born at 32 weeks usually survive with proper medical care.
questions.question: The pupillary light reflex develops during which weeks?

questions.explanation: Birth normally occurs 266 days or 38 weeks after fertilization (280 days or 40 weeks after the last normal menstrual period). The fetus is considered full term at this point. Gestational age is usually calculated from the last menstrual period rather than fertilization.
questions.question: Birth normally occurs how many days after fertilization?
The double bubble sign on imaging indicates:
questions.explanation: The "double bubble" sign indicates distension of both the stomach and the duodenum proximal to an obstruction, typically duodenal atresia. One bubble represents the air-filled stomach, and the second represents the dilated duodenal segment. The pyloric canal appears as an air-free space between the two bubbles.

The cerebral aqueduct (aqueduct of Sylvius) connects the third ventricle to the fourth ventricle, allowing CSF to flow between these cavities. This narrow channel runs through the midbrain dorsal to the cerebral peduncles and ventral to the tectum. Obstruction of the cerebral aqueduct, whether congenital or acquired, causes obstructive hydrocephalus with dilation of the lateral and third ventricles while the fourth ventricle remains normal or small.
questions.question: Through which structure does CSF flow from the third to the fourth ventricle?

questions.explanation: Physiological umbilical herniation of the midgut loop occurs at the beginning of the 6th week due to rapid intestinal elongation and liver enlargement. The abdominal cavity becomes relatively too small to accommodate the growing intestines. The intestines return to the abdomen during the 10th week.
questions.question: The midgut loop herniates into the umbilical cord during which week?
The vestibular nerve synapses in which brainstem nuclei?
questions.explanation: The vestibular nerve synapses in the vestibular nuclei in the pons. There are four vestibular nuclei: superior, inferior, medial and lateral. These project to multiple targets for balance and eye movement control.

questions.question: The fibrous pericardium is the outermost covering of the heart. It is composed of which tissue and serves which primary function?
questions.explanation: The fibrous pericardium is a tough, inextensible sac of dense irregular fibrous (collagenous) connective tissue that encloses the heart. It is anchored to the central tendon of the diaphragm, the sternum, and the great vessels. Its primary functions are: anchoring the heart in the mediastinum, preventing cardiac overdistension (cardiac tamponade physiology), and providing a barrier against infection. The serous pericardium (inner layer) secretes pericardial fluid for lubrication.
options: Elastic tissue providing compliance during cardiac filling
Serous tissue secreting lubricating pericardial fluid
Dense irregular fibrous connective tissue anchoring the heart

questions.question: The esophagus is lined by which type of epithelium that provides protection against mechanical abrasion?
questions.explanation: Wait — the correct answer: The esophagus is lined by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium, appropriate for a food-conducting passage exposed to mechanical trauma. Keratinization occurs in truly exposed skin surfaces like the skin. Option C is correct. Answer: C (non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium).

questions.question: Lymph nodes filter lymph and contain B cell follicles and T cell zones. The germinal center of a lymphoid follicle represents:
questions.explanation: Germinal centers are specialized microenvironments within secondary lymphoid follicles where antigen-activated B cells undergo rapid clonal expansion (centroblasts → centrocytes), somatic hypermutation of immunoglobulin genes (affinity maturation), and class-switch recombination. The resulting high-affinity antibody-secreting plasma cells and long-lived memory B cells are the products of the germinal center reaction. Abnormal germinal centers are the origin of most B-cell lymphomas.
options: The primary B cell zone in a non-stimulated lymph node
The T cell-rich area around the follicle
A site of active B cell proliferation, somatic hypermutation,
The site of T cell receptor gene rearrangement

questions.explanation: The liver develops from the hepatic diverticulum of the foregut, not from the primitive pharynx. The primitive pharynx gives rise to the thyroid gland, parathyroid glands, thymus gland, tympanic cavity, and contributes to trachea and lung development. These structures develop from pharyngeal pouches and floor of the pharynx.
questions.question: The primitive pharynx gives rise to all EXCEPT:

questions.explanation: Lung elastic recoil during passive expiration is provided by: (1) elastic fibers (elastin) in alveolar walls, which store energy during inspiration and recoil during expiration; (2) surface tension at the alveolar air-liquid interface, which tends to collapse alveoli (opposing inspiration). Surfactant reduces this surface tension, making inflation easier and preventing alveolar collapse at end-expiration. Loss of elastic fibers (emphysema) or surfactant deficiency profoundly impairs lung mechanics.
questions.question: During expiration, the lung recoils due to elastic properties. The elastic recoil of the lung is primarily provided by which two structural components?
options: Hyaline cartilage in bronchi and smooth muscle in bronchioles
Tight junctions between Type I pneumocytes
The bronchial smooth muscle and pleural fluid tension

questions.explanation: Renal tubules of the kidney develop through reciprocal induction between ureteric bud (from mesonephric duct) and metanephric mesenchyme. The ureteric bud induces the mesenchyme to form nephrons, while the mesenchyme induces branching of the ureteric bud to form collecting system.
questions.question: The developing kidney is an example of which type of induction?

questions.explanation: A urachal cyst results from partial persistence of the urachus, with the central portion remaining patent while the ends close. This creates a fluid-filled cyst between the bladder and umbilicus. Urachal cysts may become infected and require surgical excision. Complete patency results in a urachal fistula, while persistence at the bladder end causes a urachal sinus.
questions.question: A urachal cyst results from:

questions.explanation: Permissive induction occurs when the responding cell is already committed to a certain fate and requires the inducing signals to proceed in the developmental pathway. An example is pancreas development, which depends on associated mesoderm to permit the endoderm to develop into pancreatic tissue.
questions.question: Permissive induction occurs when the responding cell is already committed to which state?

questions.explanation: There are three natural constrictions of the ureter where ureteric stones commonly lodge: (1) ureteropelvic junction (UPJ); (2) as the ureter crosses the common iliac vessels at the pelvic brim; (3) ureterovesical junction (UVJ) — the narrowest point. The UVJ is the most common site for stone impaction because the ureter passes obliquely through the bladder wall (antireflux mechanism), creating the narrowest luminal diameter. Stones >5mm at the UVJ are unlikely to pass spontaneously.
questions.question: The ureter descends retroperitoneally and crosses anterior to the common iliac artery. At which anatomical location does the ureter have the narrowest caliber, making it a common site for ureteral stone impaction?
options: At the ureterovesical junction (UVJ) as it enters the bladder
At the pelvic brim crossing anterior to iliac vessels

questions.question: Thalamic proliferation results in which phenomenon?
questions.explanation: Cells of the thalamus proliferate rapidly resulting in inward bulging that obliterates the cavity. This creates the interthalamic adhesion across the third ventricle. The thalamus serves as a relay station for sensory information.

questions.question: The collecting system of the kidney (collecting tubules and ducts) is derived from which embryological structure, distinct from the nephrons?
questions.explanation: Kidney development involves two distinct embryological components: (1) the ureteric bud (metanephric diverticulum), which branches from the mesonephric (Wolffian) duct and gives rise to the collecting system — collecting tubules, papillary ducts, calyces, renal pelvis, and ureter; (2) the metanephric mesenchyme (blastema), which is induced by the ureteric bud to undergo mesenchymal-to-epithelial transition, forming the nephrons (glomeruli, proximal tubules, loop of Henle, distal tubules). Failure of ureteric bud induction causes renal agenesis.

questions.question: The right main bronchus gives rise to how many secondary bronchi?
questions.explanation: The right main bronchus gives rise to three secondary bronchi, corresponding to the three lobes of the right lung. The left main bronchus forms two secondary bronchi for the two lobes of the left lung. These appear as lateral outpocketings during the early 5th week.

questions.question: Glomerular filtration rate in newborns is approximately what fraction of adult values?
questions.explanation: Glomerular filtration rate (GFR) in term newborns is approximately 1/3 of adult values when corrected for body surface area. GFR increases rapidly during the first two weeks, doubles by 2-3 months, and reaches adult values (per unit surface area) by 1-2 years. The low neonatal GFR reflects immature nephrons, low renal blood flow, and high renal vascular resistance. This affects drug dosing and fluid management in neonates.

options: The need for axonal transport to deliver organelles from cell body to distant terminals
The necessity for multiple nuclei to support such a long cell
The requirement for lysosomes at each node of Ranvier
The generation of a large number of synaptic vesicles in the cell body only
The need for peroxisomes to oxidize myelin along the axon length
questions.question: A neuron with an axon 1 meter long (e.g., motor neuron to the foot) demonstrates which cellular challenge most dramatically?
questions.explanation: Motor neurons with meter-long axons cannot rely on diffusion to supply synaptic terminals with neurotransmitters, organelles, and trophic factors synthesized in the cell body. Fast anterograde axonal transport (via kinesin on microtubule tracks at ~400 mm/day) and retrograde transport (via dynein at ~200 mm/day) are essential for neuronal survival and function. Disruption of axonal transport underlies several neurodegenerative diseases.

The superior colliculus in the tectum receives direct input from the retina and is involved in visual reflexes, particularly controlling rapid eye movements and orienting responses to visual stimuli. The superior colliculus also receives input from visual cortex and projects through tectospinal and tectobulbar tracts. The inferior colliculus receives auditory input from the cochlea and is involved in auditory reflexes and sound localization.
questions.question: Which midbrain structure receives direct input from the retina for visual reflexes?
Broca's area is located in which lobe?
questions.explanation: Broca's area is located in the inferior frontal gyrus of the dominant (usually left) frontal lobe. It controls speech production. Lesions cause expressive aphasia. Patients understand but cannot speak fluently.

questions.question: The ampulla of Vater marks the boundary between:
questions.explanation: The ampulla of Vater (where the common bile duct opens into the duodenum) marks the boundary between foregut and midgut. This anatomical landmark corresponds to the junction between celiac artery and superior mesenteric artery blood supply. The foregut extends from the oral cavity to this point.

The placenta produces hormones including progesterone, estrogens (especially estriol), human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), and human placental lactogen (somatomammotropin). It does not produce follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), which is secreted by the anterior pituitary gland.
questions.question: The placenta produces all of the following hormones EXCEPT:

questions.explanation: The canal of the neural tube in the rhombencephalon forms the fourth ventricle. Both metencephalon and myelencephalon contribute to it. It has a characteristic diamond shape due to the pontine flexure.
questions.question: The fourth ventricle is derived from which embryonic structure?

questions.explanation: I cells are enteroendocrine cells of the duodenum and jejunum that release cholecystokinin (CCK) in response to dietary fat and protein. CCK stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion, gallbladder contraction, and relaxation of the sphincter of Oddi. S cells release secretin in response to acid; K cells release GIP (glucose-dependent insulinotropic peptide); G cells release gastrin; L cells release GLP-1 and GLP-2. This is a frequently tested aspect of GIT endocrinology.
questions.question: The enteroendocrine cell type in the small intestine that releases cholecystokinin (CCK) in response to fat and protein is the:
The ureteric bud arises from which structure?
questions.explanation: The ureteric bud (metanephric diverticulum) sprouts from the distal end of the mesonephric duct at about 5 weeks.
