questions.explanation: The roof plate consists of ependymal lining which forms choroid plexus with surrounding vascular mesenchyme. Posterior choroidal arteries supply this plexus. The third ventricle choroid plexus produces cerebrospinal fluid.
questions.question: The choroid plexus of the third ventricle is formed from which components?

questions.explanation: The JGA has three components: (1) juxtaglomerular (granular) cells — modified smooth muscle of the afferent arteriole that secrete renin; (2) macula densa — specialized DCT cells that sense NaCl concentration and signal to JG cells; (3) extraglomerular mesangial cells (lacis cells) — mediators between macula densa and JG cells. Together they regulate renin release and hence blood pressure via the RAAS.
questions.question: The juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA) is a specialized structure that regulates blood pressure and filtration. Which three components make up the JGA?
options: Podocytes, mesangial cells, and parietal cells
Collecting duct cells, juxtaglomerular cells, and podocytes
Macula densa, vasa recta, and PCT cells
Distal tubule cells, podocytes, and parietal epithelium

questions.question: The median eminence of the hypothalamus is significant because it lacks what feature?
questions.explanation: The median eminence lacks a blood-brain barrier, allowing hypothalamic releasing and inhibiting hormones to enter the hypophyseal portal system and reach the anterior pituitary. This region is located on the floor of the third ventricle just behind the infundibulum and contains neurosecretory terminals that release hormones directly into fenestrated capillaries. This anatomical arrangement enables the hypothalamus to control anterior pituitary hormone secretion through hormonal rather than direct neural connections.

The pars opercularis (opercular part) of the inferior frontal gyrus, along with the pars triangularis, comprises Broca's motor speech area (Brodmann areas 44 and 45) in the dominant hemisphere. The pars opercularis is the posterior portion, bounded posteriorly by the precentral sulcus and anteriorly by the ascending ramus of the lateral sulcus. Damage causes expressive (Broca's) aphasia with non-fluent, effortful speech, agrammatism, and relatively preserved comprehension. In the non-dominant hemisphere, this region may be involved in prosody (emotional tone of speech).
questions.question: The pars opercularis of the inferior frontal gyrus corresponds to which area?
Epispadias is characterized by:
questions.explanation: Epispadias is characterized by the urethral opening on the dorsal (upper) surface of the penis due to faulty positioning of the genital tubercle and inadequate ectodermal ingrowth. It is much less common than hypospadias and is often associated with bladder exstrophy. The penis is typically short, broad, and curves dorsally. Surgical reconstruction is required.

questions.question: Lenticulostriate arteries supply which structures?
questions.explanation: Anterolateral (lenticulostriate) arteries supply internal capsule, globus pallidus, putamen, head of caudate, claustrum and external capsule. They are end arteries prone to hemorrhage. Occlusion causes contralateral hemiplegia.
options: Internal capsule, globus pallidus, putamen, caudate

questions.explanation: The urorectal septum divides the cloaca into the ventral urogenital sinus and the dorsal rectum/cranial anal canal. This septum grows from mesoderm at the junction between the connecting stalk and yolk sac. By the 7th week, it fuses with the cloacal membrane, dividing it into anal and urogenital membranes.
questions.question: The urorectal septum divides the cloaca into:

questions.explanation: Erythropoietin is produced predominantly by peritubular interstitial cells (EPO-producing cells, which resemble fibroblasts) in the renal cortex and outer medulla in response to hypoxia via HIF-2α activation. A smaller amount is produced in the liver. Renal failure causes EPO deficiency and normochromic, normocytic anemia. Recombinant EPO is used therapeutically in renal anemia.
questions.question: Erythropoietin (EPO) is produced primarily by which kidney cell type in response to hypoxia?
options: Principal cells of the collecting duct

questions.explanation: The external capsule is a thin layer of white matter separating the claustrum laterally from the putamen (lateral portion of lentiform nucleus) medially. It contains association fibers and some projection fibers connecting cortical regions. The external capsule lies between the more lateral extreme capsule and the more medial internal capsule. These white matter layers interdigitate with gray matter structures (insula, claustrum, lentiform nucleus) forming the complex architecture of the basal forebrain region.
questions.question: The external capsule separates which structures?

questions.explanation: Cerebrospinal fluid is produced at approximately 0.4 mL/min, totaling about 600 mL per day. With a total CSF volume of about 150 mL, this results in complete CSF turnover 3-4 times daily. This constant production and absorption maintains stable intracranial pressure and ensures continuous waste removal and nutrient delivery. Production rate is relatively constant and independent of intracranial pressure, while absorption rate varies with pressure, providing a homeostatic mechanism.
questions.question: What is the approximate production rate of cerebrospinal fluid?

questions.explanation: The flocculonodular lobe constitutes the archicerebellum and is phylogenetically the oldest part of the cerebellum, closely related to vestibular function. It consists of the nodulus (vermis) and paired flocculi (hemispheres), separated from the rest of the cerebellum by the posterolateral fissure. This lobe receives input from vestibular nuclei and is essential for maintaining balance and equilibrium; damage results in truncal ataxia and nystagmus.
questions.question: Which cerebellar lobule is phylogenetically the oldest and related to vestibular function?
The neocerebellum is primarily concerned with which function?
questions.explanation: The neocerebellum (posterior lobe hemispheres and dentate nucleus) is primarily concerned with planning, timing, and coordination of voluntary skilled movements, particularly fine finger movements. It receives cortical input via pontocerebellar fibers and projects back to motor and premotor cortex via the thalamus. This cerebrocerebellar loop is most developed in humans and non-human primates, correlating with manual dexterity. The neocerebellum is involved in motor learning, predicting sensory consequences of movements, and internal models of movement dynamics.

Plasma cell nuclei display a distinctive 'clock-face' or 'cartwheel' pattern in which heterochromatin is arranged in clumps around the periphery of the nucleus, alternating with pale euchromatin regions. This pattern results from the heavy ribosome production needed for antibody synthesis. Plasma cells also have eccentrically placed nuclei and basophilic cytoplasm due to abundant rough ER.
questions.question: Which of the following best describes the characteristic appearance of plasma cell nuclei in histological sections, making them easily identifiable?
options: Clock-face or cartwheel pattern of heterochromatin
Multiple prominent nucleoli in a clear nucleus
Lobulated multilobed nucleus with fine chromatin
Pyknotic condensed nucleus against cell membrane

questions.question: The enteric nervous system (ENS) is called the 'second brain'. What is the total approximate number of neurons in the ENS?
questions.explanation: The ENS contains approximately 100 million (10^8) neurons — more than the spinal cord — organized into the myenteric and submucosal plexuses. This vast neuronal network enables autonomous regulation of GIT motility, secretion, and blood flow, earning the ENS its designation as the 'second brain.' The ENS communicates bidirectionally with the CNS via the vagus nerve and sympathetic pathways.

questions.question: The tonsils of Waldeyer's ring encircle the entrances to the respiratory and digestive tracts. The palatine tonsils are covered by which epithelium?
options: Stratified squamous non-keratinized epithelium in the lateral oropharynx
Pseudostratified ciliated epithelium with goblet cells
Simple columnar epithelium with goblet cells
Transitional urothelial epithelium of the bladder
questions.explanation: Palatine tonsils are located in the lateral walls of the oropharynx and are covered by stratified squamous non-keratinized epithelium continuous with the oral cavity lining. Their deep crypts lined by this epithelium increase surface area for antigen sampling. Pharyngeal tonsils or adenoids are covered by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium reflecting their nasopharyngeal location. This epithelial difference is histologically diagnostic between the two tonsil types.
Internal ear development starts around day 22 with otic placode thickening beside the myelencephalon. This invaginates to form otic vesicles. The placode is surface ectoderm.
questions.question: The otic placode first appears on which day of intrauterine life?
The gustatory cortex is located in which region?
questions.explanation: The gustatory (taste) cortex is located in the inferior part of the postcentral gyrus and adjacent opercular region (Brodmann area 43), near the somatosensory representation of the tongue. This area receives taste information from the ventral posteromedial nucleus of the thalamus, which in turn receives input from the nucleus solitarius via the gustatory pathway. The gustatory cortex processes taste quality, intensity, and affective components of taste perception.

questions.question: S-shaped tubules in kidney development give rise to:
questions.explanation: S-shaped tubules formed from metanephric vesicles give rise to the nephrons (excretory units). One end develops into Bowman's capsule around a developing glomerulus, while the other end connects to a collecting tubule. The middle portion elongates to form the proximal convoluted tubule, loop of Henle, and distal convoluted tubule. Each kidney contains over 1 million nephrons.

questions.question: Enteroendocrine cells in the stomach are best characterized by which feature?
questions.explanation: Enteroendocrine cells (also called APUD cells or diffuse neuroendocrine cells) are scattered throughout the GIT epithelium and release hormones and peptides — such as gastrin, somatostatin, and secretin — into the lamina propria vasculature. They are characterized by basal granules visible on electron microscopy. They constitute the largest endocrine system in the body.
options: They are the most numerous cells lining gastric pits
They release hormones into the bloodstream
They produce HCl and intrinsic factor
They are exclusively found in the pyloric glands
They stain intensely with PAS reagent for mucus

questions.question: Which foramen allows CSF to exit the fourth ventricle into the subarachnoid space?
questions.explanation: The fourth ventricle communicates with the subarachnoid space through three openings: the midline foramen of Magendie and the two lateral foramina of Luschka. The foramen of Magendie opens into the cerebellomedullary cistern (cisterna magna), while the foramina of Luschka open into the pontine cistern at the cerebellopontine angles. These openings are critical for CSF circulation; their obstruction causes internal hydrocephalus with dilated ventricles.

Esophageal cardiac glands are small clusters of mucus-secreting glands found in the mucosa of the upper esophagus and near the gastroesophageal junction. They closely resemble the cardiac glands of the stomach in histological appearance — both are simple tubular mucous glands. They should be distinguished from the esophageal glands proper (submucosal compound mucous glands found throughout the esophagus).
questions.question: Esophageal cardiac glands are located in the mucosa near the gastroesophageal junction. They are so named because they resemble which gastric glands?
Cardiac muscle is unique among the three muscle types in possessing which structural feature?
options: Multiple peripheral nuclei, identical to typical skeletal muscle fibers
Uniform smooth histological appearance without visible cross-striations
Intercalated discs with gap junctions for coupling and desmosomes for cohesion
Satellite cells providing regeneration after myocardial infarction
Voluntary motor control through upper alpha motor neurons
questions.explanation: Intercalated discs are the unique structural feature of cardiac muscle at the junctions between cardiomyocytes. They contain gap junctions that electrically couple adjacent cells allowing rapid action potential propagation throughout the myocardium creating a functional syncytium; desmosomes providing mechanical cohesion during vigorous contraction; and fascia adherens for myofibril anchoring. This organization enables the coordinated, rhythmic heart contractions.

options: Isolated renal failure without other effects
questions.explanation: Bilateral renal agenesis (Potter syndrome) prevents fetal urine production, causing oligohydramnios (markedly reduced amniotic fluid). This leads to the Potter sequence: pulmonary hypoplasia (lack of fluid for lung expansion), limb contractures (restricted movement), and characteristic Potter facies (flattened nose, low-set ears, epicanthal folds, recessed chin from oligohydramnios compression). It is invariably lethal due to pulmonary insufficiency. Amniotic fluid is essential for normal fetal lung development.
questions.question: The fetal kidney produces urine, which becomes the primary source of amniotic fluid from the second trimester. Bilateral renal agenesis causes which condition?

questions.explanation: The glycocalyx's carbohydrate chains serve as recognition molecules for cell-cell adhesion, immune recognition (self vs. non-self), and receptor-ligand interactions including microbial adhesion to host cells. Blood group antigens (ABO system) are glycocalyx components. The unique carbohydrate sequences on different cell types allow specific cellular recognition and communication.
options: Cell recognition, adhesion, and immune self/non-self identification
Generating the membrane potential across the bilayer
Regulating gene expression in the nucleus
questions.question: The plasma membrane's glycocalyx performs which of the following functions that most directly relates to cell-to-cell recognition?

options: Beta cells (~70%) centrally; alpha cells (~20%) peripherally; delta cells also present
Alpha cells are central and beta cells are peripheral in all islets
Only two cell types exist in equal proportions
All islet cells produce identical hormone mixtures without specialization
Alpha cells produce insulin and beta cells produce glucagon opposite to the traditional teaching
questions.explanation: Pancreatic islets contain beta cells at approximately 70% concentrated in the islet center producing insulin that lowers blood glucose; alpha cells at approximately 20% in the islet periphery producing glucagon that raises blood glucose; and delta cells at approximately 10% producing somatostatin that paracrine inhibits both alpha and beta cells. This architectural arrangement facilitates paracrine signaling between cell types. Type 1 diabetes involves autoimmune destruction of beta cells.
questions.question: The islets of Langerhans in the pancreas contain alpha cells producing glucagon and beta cells producing insulin. Which of the following correctly describes their arrangement?
The most common site for Meckel's diverticulum is:
questions.explanation: Meckel's diverticulum is typically located approximately two feet (60 cm) from the ileocecal valve on the antimesenteric border of the ileum. It follows the "rule of 2s": 2% prevalence, 2 feet from ileocecal valve, 2 inches long, and may contain 2 types of ectopic tissue (gastric mucosa and pancreatic acini).

questions.question: The Nissl substance visible in neuronal cell bodies corresponds to which ultrastructural organelle and what does its dissolution (chromatolysis) indicate?
options: Mitochondria with chromatolysis indicating increased ATP demand
Golgi apparatus with chromatolysis indicating secretory cell activation
Lipofuscin granules with chromatolysis indicating cellular aging
Rough ER with ribosomes; chromatolysis indicates neuronal injury after axonal damage
Melanin granules with chromatolysis indicating decreased dopamine production
questions.explanation: Nissl bodies are stacks of rough ER visible with basic dyes in neuronal cell bodies reflecting the neuron's high capacity for protein synthesis. Chromatolysis is the dissolution of Nissl substance occurring as the histological hallmark of the axonal reaction after peripheral axon injury, characterized by cell body swelling, nuclear eccentricity, and dispersal of Nissl substance as the neuron redirects synthetic activity toward axon regeneration proteins.

Connective tissue derives its name from its fundamental function of connecting or binding cells and tissues together throughout the body. It maintains the form of organs and serves as a structural framework for other tissue types. Unlike epithelium, muscle, and nerve (which consist mainly of cells), connective tissue's dominant component is the extracellular matrix.
questions.question: Connective tissue derives its name from which of the following primary functional characteristics?
options: It forms the outer covering of all organs
It generates electrical impulses through gap junctions
It absorbs and secretes fluids in body cavities
It provides contractile force for body movement
It connects and binds cells and tissues together

questions.question: In a postmenopausal woman, the endometrium typically becomes thin and atrophic due to estrogen deficiency. Histologically, the postmenopausal endometrium shows:
questions.explanation: After menopause, estrogen withdrawal causes progressive endometrial atrophy. The postmenopausal endometrium becomes very thin (< 4mm on ultrasound), composed of a small amount of fibrous stroma with widely spaced, small, straight, inactive glands lined by low cuboidal cells with no mitoses. This atrophic endometrium is the expected finding. Unexpected endometrial thickening (> 4mm on TVUS) in a postmenopausal woman warrants investigation to exclude endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma.
options: Thin mucosa with small, straight, inactive glands

questions.question: The allantois first appears around which day of development?
questions.explanation: The allantois first appears around day 16 as a small diverticulum projecting from the caudal end of the yolk sac into the connecting stalk. In humans, the allantois is vestigial and contributes to bladder development and formation of the urachus. In other species, it plays important roles in waste storage and gas exchange.

The pectinate line marks the junction between endodermal and ectodermal portions of the anal canal. Above this line, the anal canal is endodermal (from hindgut), while below it is ectodermal (from proctodeum). This junction has clinical significance regarding blood supply, innervation, lymphatic drainage, and epithelial type.
questions.question: The pectinate line in the anal canal marks the junction between:
Pancreatic acinar cells synthesize and store digestive enzymes as inactive zymogens to prevent autodigestion. Trypsinogen is the key precursor enzyme activated in the duodenal lumen by which enzyme?
questions.explanation: Trypsinogen, secreted by pancreatic acinar cells, is activated in the duodenal lumen by enterokinase (enteropeptidase) — a specific protease anchored to the duodenal brush border epithelium. Active trypsin then activates all other pancreatic zymogens (chymotrypsinogen, proelastase, procarboxypeptidase) in a cascade. In acute pancreatitis, premature intrapancreatic activation of trypsinogen (by cathepsin B or other triggers) initiates this destructive cascade within the pancreas itself.

questions.question: Which paranasal sinuses develop before birth?
questions.explanation: The maxillary and sphenoidal sinuses develop before birth as diverticula from the nasal cavity. The frontal and ethmoid sinuses develop after birth. Enlargement of all sinuses is associated with overall facial skeleton growth, providing space for jaw development and teeth eruption.

Mast cells function as tissue sentinels, strategically positioned near blood vessels and mucosal surfaces to detect antigens and pathogens. When activated (especially through IgE-antigen crosslinking), they rapidly release preformed mediators (histamine, heparin, tryptase) from their granules and synthesize new mediators (prostaglandins, leukotrienes). This response mediates both protective immunity and allergic/hypersensitivity reactions.
questions.question: Which of the following most accurately describes the primary function of mast cells in connective tissue?
options: Microbial sentinels mediating hypersensitivity via granule mediator release
Presenting antigens to T lymphocytes directly
Storing neutral fats and releasing them during fasting
Producing antibodies of the IgG class

questions.question: Invasion of trophoblast cells into the endometrium is mediated by which molecules?
questions.explanation: The second stage of implantation involves invasion of trophoblast cells into the endometrium. This invasion is mediated by adhesion molecules including integrins, laminin, and fibronectin. These molecules allow the trophoblast to penetrate the endometrial stroma.

questions.question: Which structure serves as the primary inducer during primary embryonic induction?
questions.explanation: During primary embryonic induction, the mesoderm (particularly the notochord and prechordal mesoderm) serves as the primary inducer of neural tissue. These structures secrete factors like noggin, chordin, and follistatin that induce the overlying ectoderm to form neural tissue.

Pulmonary edema is characterized histologically by widening of the alveolar septa (interstitial edema from fluid accumulation) and flooding of the alveolar spaces with a pale, homogeneous eosinophilic proteinaceous fluid (alveolar edema). In cardiogenic pulmonary edema, hemosiderin-laden macrophages ('heart failure cells') may be present from previous episodes. Severe acute pulmonary edema manifests as intra-alveolar hyaline membranes (as in ARDS).
questions.question: The interstitium of the lung between alveolar septa and bronchioles is normally very thin. Accumulation of edema fluid in this space (pulmonary edema) manifests histologically as:
options: Replacement of alveoli by fibrous tissue
Collapse of alveoli with no fluid
Widening of alveolar septa with pale

questions.explanation: M cells are specialized epithelial cells overlying Peyer's patches that lack a conventional brush border and instead have an irregular apical surface. They transcytose antigens, bacteria, and macromolecules from the intestinal lumen to the underlying lymphoid tissue for immune processing. This makes them critical portals for mucosal immunity but also pathogen entry points.
questions.question: M cells (microfold cells) in the small intestinal epithelium overlie Peyer's patches. Their primary function is:
At the end of the 4th week, how many mesenchymal prominences surround the stomodeum?
questions.explanation: At the end of the 4th week, five mesenchymal prominences can be recognized surrounding the stomodeum: one frontonasal prominence, two mandibular prominences, and two maxillary prominences. These prominences are derived from neural crest cells and play crucial roles in facial development.

questions.question: Which vein connects the superficial and deep venous systems?
questions.explanation: The basal vein of Rosenthal serves as an important connection between superficial and deep venous systems, receiving tributaries from superficial structures like the insula and temporal lobe while draining into the deep system via the great vein of Galen. The superficial middle cerebral vein also provides connections, draining superficial lateral structures into either the cavernous sinus or deep system. These connections allow alternative drainage pathways if one system becomes thrombosed.
Voluntary movements require the entire motor system from cortex to muscles. Simple rhythms need only spinal circuits. Complex movements need multiple levels of hierarchy.
questions.question: Voluntary movements require which system?

questions.explanation: The allantois plays a significant role in development of the urinary bladder through the urachus, which later becomes the median umbilical ligament. The urachus connects the apex of the bladder to the umbilicus. Persistence of the urachal lumen can result in urachal cysts or fistulas.
questions.question: The urachus later becomes which adult structure?
At 12 weeks, the cerebellum consists of which parts?
questions.explanation: At 12 weeks, a central vermis and 2 lateral dilated cerebellar hemispheres are identified. A transverse fissure separates upper and lower parts. The cerebellum continues developing postnatally.

The definitive urinary bladder develops from the urogenital sinus (part of the cloaca). The allantois contributes to formation of the urachus (median umbilical ligament). The trigone of the bladder is derived from incorporated portions of the mesonephric ducts.
questions.question: The definitive urinary bladder develops from which embryonic structure?
Bipolar neurons with a dendrite at one end and an axon at the other are found predominantly in which locations?
options: Motor neurons of the spinal cord ventral horn
Retinal, cochlear, and olfactory epithelium sensory neurons
questions.explanation: Bipolar neurons are spindle-shaped with a single dendrite at one pole and a single axon at the opposite pole. They are specialized sensory neurons found in the retina as bipolar cells, in the cochlear spiral ganglion as first-order auditory neurons, in the vestibular ganglion, and in the olfactory epithelium. Their simple two-process form reflects their specialized role as first-order sensory transducer cells.

questions.question: The zona glomerulosa, fasciculata, and reticularis are the three zones of the adrenal cortex. Which zone primarily produces mineralocorticoids (aldosterone)?
questions.explanation: The zona glomerulosa is the outermost zone of the adrenal cortex and is the exclusive site of aldosterone synthesis (it uniquely expresses aldosterone synthase/CYP11B2). Aldosterone regulates sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion in the renal collecting duct. The zona fasciculata (middle, largest zone) produces cortisol (glucocorticoids), and the zona reticularis (innermost) produces weak androgens (DHEA). The adrenal medulla secretes catecholamines (epinephrine, norepinephrine).

questions.question: The stomach rotates approximately how many degrees around its longitudinal axis?
questions.explanation: The stomach rotates approximately 90 degrees clockwise around its longitudinal axis (when viewed from above). This rotation causes the original left side to become the ventral (anterior) surface and the original right side to become the dorsal (posterior) surface. This explains the innervation pattern by vagus nerves.

Folding of the embryo occurs in both the median (longitudinal) and horizontal (transverse) planes. Median plane folding includes the head fold and tail fold, which result from differential growth of the embryonic structures. This folding converts the flat embryonic disc into a cylindrical embryo.
questions.question: Longitudinal folding of the embryo occurs in which plane?

questions.explanation: Varicose veins show irregular remodeling of the vein wall: areas of smooth muscle hypertrophy alternating with atrophy and fibrosis in the media, intimal thickening, adventitial fibrosis, and calcification. Valve leaflets are thickened and fibrotic (incompetent). The irregular contraction of the remodeled smooth muscle makes varicose veins tortuous. These changes result from chronic venous hypertension due to gravitational stress and valve failure.
questions.question: Varicose veins are dilated, tortuous superficial veins caused by incompetent venous valves. Histologically, varicose veins show which changes compared to normal veins?
options: Thinning of all vessel wall layers with normal valve architecture
Replacement of venous wall by arterial tissue
Cartilaginous metaplasia of the vein wall

questions.question: The juxtaglomerular apparatus develops from:
questions.explanation: The juxtaglomerular apparatus develops from specialized cells in the distal convoluted tubule (macula densa) and the afferent arteriole (juxtaglomerular cells). This structure regulates renal blood flow and glomerular filtration rate through the renin-angiotensin system. It forms during late fetal development and continues maturing postnatally. The JGA is important for blood pressure regulation and fluid homeostasis.

questions.question: Vesicoureteral reflux is graded from I-V based on:
questions.explanation: Vesicoureteral reflux is graded I-V based on the extent of reflux and degree of system dilation: Grade I (ureter only), Grade II (ureter and pelvis, no dilation), Grade III (mild dilation), Grade IV (moderate dilation with blunted calyces), Grade V (severe dilation with tortuous ureter). Higher grades have greater risk of renal scarring and may require surgical correction. Lower grades often resolve spontaneously.
options: Extent of reflux and system dilation

questions.explanation: Lamina IX is the main motor area containing alpha motor neurons somatotopically organized. Medial groups innervate axial muscles. Lateral groups innervate limb muscles.
questions.question: Lamina IX contains which neurons?

options: A central nutrient foramen surrounded by randomly arranged trabecular bone
Concentric lamellae surrounding a central Haversian canal with blood vessels and nerves
A solid block of mineralized matrix with no canal system
Interconnecting trabeculae with red marrow in all spaces
A single osteocyte surrounded by ground substance only
questions.explanation: Each osteon (Haversian system) is the basic structural unit of compact bone, consisting of 5–20 concentric lamellae of mineralized matrix (with alternating collagen fiber orientations) surrounding a central Haversian canal containing small arterioles, venules, nerves, and loose connective tissue. Osteocytes reside in lacunae between lamellae and communicate via canaliculi that penetrate all lamellae to reach the central canal.
questions.question: Compact (cortical) bone is organized into cylindrical structures called osteons (Haversian systems), each of which consists of which of the following?
The reticular formation's role in consciousness is primarily mediated through which system?
questions.explanation: The ascending reticular activating system (ARAS) connects reticular formation neurons to the thalamus, hypothalamus, and cortex, mediating consciousness, attention, and the sleep-wake cycle. The ARAS integrates sensory input from multiple modalities and maintains cortical arousal. Damage to the ARAS in the brainstem can cause coma or persistent vegetative state, while functional changes contribute to sleep disorders and alterations in consciousness.

options: Naïve lymphocyte homing from blood into
questions.question: High endothelial venules (HEVs) are specialized post-capillary venules found in lymphoid organs. Their distinctive tall, cuboidal endothelial cells facilitate which process?
questions.explanation: High endothelial venules in lymph nodes (and other peripheral lymphoid organs) have tall, cuboidal endothelial cells that express specialized adhesion molecules (peripheral node addressins/MAdCAM-1, PNAd) and chemokines (CCL21/CCL19). Naïve lymphocytes expressing L-selectin and CCR7 adhere to and migrate through these HEVs into the lymph node parenchyma for immune surveillance — lymphocyte homing. HEVs are the primary route of lymphocyte recruitment to lymph nodes under steady-state conditions.

Follicular fluid in the antrum is a plasma transudate enriched with hormones (estradiol, FSH, LH), growth factors, and metabolites. It creates a specialized microenvironment (follicular niche) that supports oocyte maturation and the growth of granulosa cells. At ovulation, the surge in LH causes follicular rupture and release of the oocyte with its surrounding cumulus oophorus and zona pellucida into the peritoneal cavity.
questions.question: A Graafian (mature preovulatory) follicle contains a fluid-filled antrum. The primary function of follicular fluid in the antrum is:
options: To nourish the oocyte with oxygen directly
To transport the oocyte to the fallopian tube
To provide a niche of hormones, growth factors,
To suppress GnRH release via negative feedback

questions.question: Which of the following characteristics makes hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining the most commonly used technique in routine histology?
questions.explanation: H&E staining is the standard general-purpose histological stain because hematoxylin colors nuclei blue-purple (basophilic structures) while eosin stains cytoplasm, collagen, and other acidophilic structures pink. This combination provides the clearest overview of tissue architecture and cell types. It remains the cornerstone of diagnostic pathology worldwide.
options: It visualizes only collagen fibers selectively
It stains nuclei blue-purple and cytoplasm/collagen pink
It specifically marks reticular fibers black
It detects polysaccharides by turning them red
It requires no prior fixation of the tissue

questions.question: The inner hair cells of the organ of Corti differ from outer hair cells in which functionally critical way?
options: Inner hair cells are electromotile through prestin protein
Inner hair cells provide cochlear amplification
Inner hair cells are more sensitive to ototoxic drugs
Inner hair cells are the primary transducers; outer hair cells amplify via electromotility
Inner hair cells detect low-frequency sounds while outer hair cells detect high-frequency sounds
questions.explanation: Inner hair cells numbering approximately 3,500 are the primary auditory sensory transducers with approximately 90 to 95% of all afferent cochlear nerve fibers providing the neural output to the brain. Outer hair cells numbering approximately 12,000 express prestin and are primarily electromotile amplifiers that enhance basilar membrane vibration up to 1,000-fold improving hearing sensitivity and frequency discrimination. Noise-induced hearing loss primarily destroys outer hair cells while sensorineural hearing loss causing deafness typically destroys inner hair cells.

Electron microscopy requires ultra-thin sections (50–100 nm) because electrons cannot penetrate thicker tissue. Specimens are fixed with glutaraldehyde and osmium tetroxide, embedded in epoxy resin (not paraffin), cut on an ultramicrotome, and contrast-stained with heavy metals (uranium, lead) that scatter electrons differentially. These differences from light microscopy preparation are fundamental.
questions.question: The preparation of tissue sections for electron microscopy differs from light microscopy preparation in requiring which of the following?
options: Ultra-thin sections stained with heavy metal salts
Routine H&E staining and glass slides

questions.question: Multiple sclerosis is characterized by which pathology?
questions.explanation: Multiple sclerosis is characterized by demyelination in CNS (oligodendrocyte damage). It causes varied neurological symptoms. It is an autoimmune disease. Plaques form in white matter.

questions.question: Smooth muscle cells differ from skeletal and cardiac muscle cells structurally in which of the following ways?
questions.explanation: Smooth muscle cells are fusiform spindle-shaped, mononucleated with a central nucleus, and lack the organized sarcomere structure responsible for striation in skeletal and cardiac muscle. They contain actin and myosin filaments but arranged in a non-parallel diagonal network rather than aligned sarcomeres. Contraction is slow and sustained, regulated by autonomic nerves and hormones, and they form the walls of blood vessels, GI tract, airways, and glands.
options: Smooth muscle has the most organized sarcomere structure of all three types
Lacks sarcomeres and striations; has a single central nucleus and fusiform cell shape
Smooth muscle has more mitochondria than cardiac muscle
Smooth muscle contracts faster than skeletal muscle
Smooth muscle is derived from the neuroectoderm rather than mesoderm

questions.explanation: The metanephric blastema (metanephric mesenchyme) is induced by the ureteric bud. Reciprocal induction between these two tissues is essential for kidney development. The ureteric bud induces the blastema to form nephrons (excretory units), while the blastema induces the ureteric bud to branch and form the collecting system.
questions.question: The metanephric blastema is induced by:
The liver produces the majority of serum proteins. Which protein, synthesized exclusively by hepatocytes, is the most abundant in plasma and maintains oncotic pressure?
questions.explanation: Albumin is synthesized exclusively by hepatocytes (approximately 12g/day) and is the most abundant plasma protein (35–50 g/L). It maintains plasma oncotic pressure (preventing edema), transports fatty acids, bilirubin, hormones, and drugs, and acts as a buffer. In chronic liver failure, reduced albumin synthesis causes hypoalbuminemia, leading to peripheral edema and ascites. Serum albumin level is a sensitive marker of synthetic function in chronic liver disease.

The lamina propria frequently contains small glands which open into the lumen, forming part of the secretory apparatus of the GIT. These are region-specific — gastric glands in the stomach, intestinal crypts in the intestines. Brunner's glands are specific to the duodenal submucosa, not the lamina propria.
questions.question: A student observes glands within the lamina propria on a GIT slide. These glands most likely represent:
Alveoli at birth are approximately what fraction of the adult number?
questions.explanation: At birth, alveoli number approximately 1/6th of the adult number. The remaining 5/6ths develop postnatally, primarily during the first 10 years of life. This continued alveolar development explains why lung function continues to improve during childhood. Factors affecting early lung development can have lifelong consequences.

questions.question: In which layer of the GIT would you find lymphoid tissue such as isolated nodules or Peyer's patches?
questions.explanation: Lymphoid tissue including isolated nodules may extend from the lamina propria into the submucosa, but Peyer's patches are particularly notable in the distal ileum and can extend into the submucosa. The lamina propria is the primary site of diffuse lymphoid tissue. Option D is most accurate: both mucosa and submucosa can contain lymphoid tissue.

The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) is the nerve of the third pharyngeal arch. It provides both motor and sensory innervation to structures derived from this arch, including the stylopharyngeus muscle and portions of the tongue (posterior one-third).
questions.question: The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) supplies which pharyngeal arch?

questions.explanation: Rathke's pouch is an ectodermal outpocketing from the roof of the primitive oral cavity. It meets the downward extension of the diencephalon (infundibulum). Together they form the anterior and posterior lobes of the pituitary respectively.
questions.question: Rathke's pouch originates from which structure?

questions.explanation: Skene's glands (para-urethral glands) in females are the embryological homologs of the prostate gland in males, both derived from the urogenital sinus (endoderm). Like the prostate, Skene's glands express prostate-specific antigen (PSA). They open on either side of the urethral meatus and secrete a small amount of fluid. They are relevant clinically as a site of infection (causing paraurethral cysts or abscess) and as the glandular origin of female prostate cancer.
questions.question: The female urethra has para-urethral glands (Skene's glands) on its posterior wall. These glands are homologous to which male structure?
Rosenthal fibers and Mallory bodies are cytoplasmic inclusions of hepatocytes. The Mallory body (Mallory-Denk body) is characteristically associated with:
questions.explanation: Mallory-Denk bodies (Mallory bodies) are eosinophilic, irregular cytoplasmic inclusions within hepatocytes composed of aggregated cytokeratin intermediate filaments. They are characteristically seen in alcoholic hepatitis and non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH). Their presence indicates hepatocyte injury with cytoskeletal disruption. They can also be seen less commonly in Wilson's disease and primary biliary cholangitis.

questions.question: The GI tract develops primarily from which germ layer?
questions.explanation: The GI tract develops primarily from the endodermal germ layer, which forms the epithelial lining of the digestive tube. The endoderm covers the ventral surface of the embryo and forms the roof of the yolk sac. The connective tissue, smooth muscle, and blood vessels are mesodermal derivatives.

The basilar artery runs in pontine groove and bifurcates at midbrain level into 2 posterior cerebral arteries. It also gives rise to cerebellar and pontine branches. It is the main arterial supply to the posterior fossa.
questions.question: The basilar artery bifurcates into which arteries?

questions.explanation: The three concentric tunics of the eye are: the outer fibrous tunic consisting of the sclera which is white and protective and the cornea which is transparent and refractive; the middle vascular tunic or uvea consisting of the choroid for nutrition, the ciliary body for accommodation and aqueous humor production, and the iris for pupil control; and the inner nervous tunic which is the retina containing photoreceptors and neurons for vision.
questions.question: The eye is composed of three concentric layers. From outside to inside these are correctly named as which of the following?
options: Uveal tract → Fibrous tunic → Nervous tunic
Fibrous (sclera/cornea), vascular uvea, and nervous tunic (retina)

questions.question: Bladder extrophy is associated with which other anomaly?
questions.explanation: Bladder exstrophy is almost always associated with epispadias (urethral opening on dorsal surface of penis). Both result from defective development of the anterior abdominal wall. The bladder mucosa is exposed, the pubic bones are separated, and the external genitalia are abnormal. The condition requires staged surgical reconstruction.

questions.question: Processes of digestion include ingestion, mastication, peristalsis, secretion, hormone release, and absorption. Which additional process completes this list?
questions.explanation: The complete processes of GIT digestion include: ingestion, mastication, peristalsis/motility, secretions, hormone release, chemical digestion, absorption, and elimination. Elimination is the final step involving the expulsion of undigested materials as feces. Gluconeogenesis is a hepatic metabolic process, not a digestive process.

questions.question: The neck is formed by elongation of the region between which two structures?
questions.explanation: The neck is formed by elongation of the region between the stomodeum and pericardium. This elongation is caused by descent of the developing heart and appearance of the pharyngeal (branchial) arches in the 4th and 5th weeks of development. The developing brain is separated from the future thorax by the stomodeum.

questions.question: Fingerprints and footprints result from the arrangement of:
questions.explanation: Fingerprints and footprints result from the microscopic ridge structures formed by the papillary layer of the dermis. These ridges create unique patterns that remain constant throughout life unless disrupted. The patterns are genetically determined and established during intrauterine development.

Brown fat (brown adipose tissue) forms during 17-20 weeks and is an important site of heat production in the newborn. It is located primarily in the neck, between the scapulae, around the kidneys, and around the adrenal glands. Brown fat helps maintain body temperature after birth.
questions.question: Brown fat, which is important for heat production, forms during which period?

questions.explanation: The zona pellucida first becomes visible as follicular cells proliferate from a single to multiple layers (multilaminar primary/early secondary follicle stage). It is a thick, acidophilic, PAS-positive glycoprotein layer secreted jointly by the oocyte and granulosa cells. The zona pellucida contains ZP3 (sperm receptor) and plays critical roles in sperm binding and the block to polyspermy.
questions.question: The zona pellucida is a glycoprotein coat surrounding the oocyte. It first becomes visible at which stage of follicular development?

questions.explanation: The facial (VII) and vestibulocochlear (VIII) nerves emerge from the cerebellopontine angle at the pontomedullary junction, along with the nervus intermedius. This anatomical region is clinically significant because cerebellopontine angle tumors (usually vestibular schwannomas/acoustic neuromas) compress these nerves, causing hearing loss, tinnitus, vertigo, and facial weakness. The abducens nerve (VI) also emerges near this area but more medially at the pontomedullary junction.
questions.question: Which cranial nerves emerge from the cerebellopontine angle?

questions.explanation: Tongue musculature develops from occipital myotomes (somites). These myoblasts migrate into the developing tongue, bringing their nerve supply (hypoglossal nerve, CN XII) with them. This is why the hypoglossal nerve innervates all intrinsic and most extrinsic tongue muscles.
questions.question: The musculature of the tongue develops from which embryonic structure?

options: Dense mucin granules in the cytoplasm
High content of rough ER for protein
questions.question: Zymogenic (chief) cells contain abundant basophilic rough endoplasmic reticulum and produce pepsinogen. The basophilia of these cells reflects which feature?
questions.explanation: Chief (zymogenic) cells are basophilic because they contain an extensive rough endoplasmic reticulum (rER) for the high-volume synthesis and processing of the zymogen pepsinogen. The rER contains RNA, which stains basophilically with hematoxylin. Apical acidophilic zymogen granules are also present. This combination of basal basophilia with apical granules is the hallmark of zymogenic/serous cells throughout the body.

The trigone of the bladder has mesodermal origin, derived from the caudal ends of the mesonephric ducts. The remainder of the bladder epithelium is endodermal, derived from the urogenital sinus. This dual origin explains the different epithelial characteristics: the trigone has unique smooth muscle and different innervation patterns.
questions.question: The trigone of the bladder has which embryological origin?
Desmin intermediate filaments in muscle primarily serve which function?
questions.explanation: Desmin intermediate filaments form a three-dimensional cytoskeletal lattice that encircles Z discs and connects adjacent sarcomeres to each other and to the sarcolemma and nuclear envelope. This maintains the lateral register of sarcomeres ensuring all contract synchronously and transmits contractile force to the ECM. Desmin mutations cause desminopathies including cardiomyopathies and skeletal muscle diseases with Z disc disruption.
options: Forming the thick filaments that generate force during contraction
Providing the elasticity that returns the sarcomere to its resting length
Connecting Z discs to the sarcolemma, maintaining sarcomere alignment during contraction
Anchoring the motor end plate to the sarcolemma
Transporting calcium from the SR to the troponin complex

questions.question: The neuroepithelial cells lining the neural tube are of which type?
questions.explanation: The neuroepithelial cells lining the neural tube are of simple columnar type initially. These cells undergo increased cellular proliferation after tube closure. They give rise to neuroblasts and eventually all neural and glial cells.

Spontaneous orientation to light and grasp reflex develop during 35-38 weeks. The nervous system is mature enough for integrative functions at this stage. The skin is bluish-pink, and the fetus is considered full term by 38 weeks.
questions.question: Spontaneous orientation to light develops during which weeks?
Surfactant secretion by type II pneumocytes begins during which weeks?
questions.explanation: Secretion of surfactant (a surface-active lipid) begins during 21-25 weeks. Surfactant maintains the patency of developing alveoli of the lungs and prevents collapse. Adequate surfactant production is essential for survival of premature infants; deficiency causes respiratory distress syndrome.

Widened vestibular aqueduct is characteristic of Pendred syndrome, not Treacher Collins syndrome. Treacher Collins syndrome results from abnormal development of first and second pharyngeal arch derivatives. It includes malformed auricles, external auditory canal atresia, middle and inner ear anomalies, micrognathia, and facial bone hypoplasia.
questions.question: Treacher Collins syndrome is characterized by all of the following EXCEPT:

questions.explanation: Horseshoe kidney, present in 0.2% of the population, usually results from fusion of the inferior poles of the kidneys. The fused kidney typically lies in the hypogastric region because normal ascent is prevented by the root of the inferior mesenteric artery. Most cases are asymptomatic as the collecting system develops normally.
questions.question: A horseshoe kidney results from fusion of the kidneys at which pole?

questions.explanation: The vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct connects the midgut loop to the yolk sac and persists until the end of the 10th week. Normally, this duct completely obliterates. Incomplete obliteration can result in Meckel's diverticulum, vitelline cyst, vitelline fistula, or fibrous cord connecting ileum to umbilicus.
questions.question: The vitelline duct connects the midgut loop to:
The frontonasal prominence gives rise to which facial structures?
questions.explanation: The frontonasal prominence forms the forehead, dorsum (bridge) and apex (tip) of the nose. It also contributes to formation of the medial nasal prominences and the nasal septum. The lateral aspects of the nose develop from the lateral nasal prominences.

questions.question: The cochlear duct completes how many coils?
questions.explanation: By the 6th week, the saccule develops a tubular outpocketing that coils 2.5 times in the mesenchyme forming the cochlear duct. The duct is filled with endolymph. Surrounding mesenchyme forms the bony labyrinth.

Karyotyping is performed on metaphase chromosomes because they are maximally condensed and individually distinguishable at this stage. Cells are arrested in metaphase, chromosomes are stained, photographed, and arranged by size and banding pattern to identify abnormalities.
questions.question: Karyotyping is performed during which phase of the cell cycle?
Muscles of mastication are derived from which pharyngeal arch?
questions.explanation: Muscles of the first pharyngeal arch include the muscles of mastication (temporalis, medial and lateral pterygoids), anterior belly of digastric, mylohyoid, tensor tympani, and tensor palatini muscles. These muscles are innervated by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V).

options: Cerebral veins to dural sinuses to internal jugular
questions.question: The principal route of venous drainage is through which system?
questions.explanation: The principal venous drainage route is through cerebral veins into dural venous sinuses and ultimately internal jugular vein. Emissary veins connect extracranial veins with dural sinuses. A basilar plexus also exists.

The general visceral efferent (GVE) column includes the Edinger-Westphal nucleus (midbrain), superior and inferior salivatory nuclei (pons and medulla), and dorsal vagal nucleus (medulla). These parasympathetic nuclei control smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, and glandular secretions. The GVE column lies lateral to somatic efferent nuclei but medial to afferent components in the brainstem's functional organization, providing autonomic control via cranial nerves III, VII, IX, and X.
questions.question: Which cranial nerve nuclei represent the general visceral efferent column?
Neurofilaments provide which function?
questions.explanation: Neurofilaments (neurofibrils) provide structural rigidity to neurons. They are part of the cytoskeleton. Microtubules facilitate axonal transport of materials.

Glial cells are produced by the neuroepithelial cells following the production of neurons. They differentiate into astrocytes in the mantle layer and oligodendrocytes in the marginal layer. This temporal sequence ensures proper nervous system organization.
questions.question: Glial cells are produced after the production of which cells?

questions.explanation: This is a Type I immediate hypersensitivity reaction. Prior peanut exposure sensitized the patient with plasma cells producing peanut-specific IgE that coated tissue mast cells via high-affinity FcεRI receptors. Re-exposure causes IgE crosslinking on mast cells triggering rapid degranulation within minutes. Released histamine causes urticaria, vasodilation, and bronchoconstriction while leukotrienes sustain bronchospasm. Systemic mast cell activation causes the full anaphylaxis syndrome.
questions.question: A 30-year-old patient develops urticaria and bronchoconstriction within minutes of eating peanuts. This reaction is mediated by which mechanism?
options: Peanut allergens crosslink mast cell IgE, triggering degranulation and mediator release
T cell-mediated cytotoxicity against peanut-sensitized cells
Complement activation by IgM antibodies against peanut proteins
Neutrophil-mediated release of reactive oxygen species
B cell direct recognition of peanut antigen causing plasma cell activation

questions.explanation: Parietal cells produce both HCl and intrinsic factor. Intrinsic factor is essential for the absorption of vitamin B12 (cobalamin) in the terminal ileum. Destruction of parietal cells leads to intrinsic factor deficiency, preventing B12 absorption and causing megaloblastic anemia — termed pernicious anemia. This is one of the most important clinical correlates of gastric histology.
questions.question: A patient with pernicious anemia is found to have autoantibodies destroying parietal cells. Which essential substance becomes deficient as a direct consequence?

options: Mesenchyme (via direct differentiation of mesenchymal cells)
Neural crest cells exclusively in all cartilage types
Endoderm of the primitive gut tube
Lateral plate mesoderm only for limb cartilage
questions.explanation: Cartilage histogenesis begins with mesenchymal condensation and subsequent differentiation of mesenchymal cells into chondroblasts. These cells have ribosome-rich basophilic cytoplasm reflecting active matrix synthesis. As they become surrounded by matrix, they mature into chondrocytes residing in lacunae. Neural crest cells contribute to some craniofacial cartilages, but most cartilage derives from mesenchyme.
questions.question: Chondroblasts, the cells that actively produce cartilage matrix, are derived from which embryonic tissue?
Damage to the paracentral lobule would primarily affect:
questions.explanation: The paracentral lobule on the medial surface of the hemisphere contains the motor and sensory representations for the lower limb and perineum, straddling the medial continuation of the central sulcus. Lesions cause contralateral leg weakness and sensory loss, potentially with bladder dysfunction if the representation for the perineum is affected. Anterior cerebral artery strokes affecting this region produce characteristic lower limb deficits with relative sparing of arm and face, distinguishing them from middle cerebral artery strokes.

questions.question: Gastric acid secretion is stimulated by three pathways. Which neurotransmitter/hormone is released by nerve terminals in the stomach to directly stimulate parietal cells?
questions.explanation: Parietal cell acid secretion is stimulated by three pathways: (1) acetylcholine — released by vagal (parasympathetic) nerve terminals acting on M3 muscarinic receptors; (2) gastrin — from G cells acting on CCK-B receptors; (3) histamine — from ECL cells acting on H2 receptors. All three pathways converge on the H+/K+-ATPase. This explains why H2 blockers and PPIs are effective in treating peptic ulcers regardless of the primary trigger.

questions.question: The vagus nerve wanders as far as which structure?
questions.explanation: The vagus nerve (X) wanders as far as the transverse colon providing parasympathetic innervation. It has SVE (pharynx, larynx), GVE (thoracic/abdominal viscera), GVA, GSA and SVA components. It is the main parasympathetic nerve.

questions.question: The anterior limb of the internal capsule lies between which two structures?
questions.explanation: The anterior limb of the internal capsule is positioned between the head of the caudate nucleus medially and the lentiform nucleus laterally. It contains frontopontine fibers traveling from the frontal cortex to pontine nuclei, which then relay to the cerebellum. These fibers pass through the thalamus and occupy the medial part of the cerebral peduncle base, playing a role in corticopontocerebellar pathways.

The notochord degenerates and disappears as the bodies of the vertebrae form during development. However, it persists as the nucleus pulposus of each intervertebral disc. The notochord initially defines the primordial axis of the embryo and indicates the future site of vertebral bodies.
questions.question: The notochord ultimately persists as which adult structure?

questions.explanation: Ciliated columnar cells are the most numerous cells in the respiratory epithelium of the conducting airways. Each cell bears approximately 300 cilia on its apical surface. Coordinated ciliary beating propels the mucus blanket (produced by goblet cells) with trapped particles toward the pharynx — the mucociliary escalator. Dysfunction of cilia (as in primary ciliary dyskinesia) leads to chronic respiratory infections.
questions.question: Respiratory epithelium (pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium) lines most of the conducting airways. Which cell type in this epithelium is most numerous?

questions.explanation: Broca's motor speech area is located in the inferior frontal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere, specifically in the pars triangularis and pars opercularis (Brodmann areas 44 and 45). This region controls the motor aspects of speech production and is critical for articulation. Damage to this area results in expressive or motor aphasia, where patients understand language but struggle to produce coherent speech.
questions.question: Broca's motor speech area corresponds to which anatomical region in the dominant hemisphere?
The organ of Corti converts sound waves into which signals?
questions.explanation: The organ of Corti converts sound waves into nerve impulses by depolarization of hair cell membranes. These impulses are picked and propagated by the cochlear nerve. The cochlea is tonotopically organized.

The fatty streak is the earliest atherosclerotic lesion, appearing in the aorta in children and adolescents. Histologically, it consists of accumulations of foam cells — macrophages that have ingested oxidized LDL via scavenger receptors — in the subintimal space. Foam cells appear as large pale cells with foamy cytoplasm (lipid-filled vacuoles). Fatty streaks are reversible and their progression to advanced plaques depends on continued oxidative stress, inflammation, and endothelial injury.
questions.question: Atherosclerosis begins with endothelial dysfunction and subendothelial lipid deposition. The 'fatty streak' — the earliest macroscopic lesion — is composed histologically of:
Nephrons are formed until:
questions.explanation: Nephrons continue to form until birth, with over 1 million nephrons eventually present in each kidney. After birth, no new nephrons are formed, though existing ones continue to mature. Kidney maturation continues postnatally, but nephrogenesis (formation of new nephrons) is complete before birth.

The substantia nigra degenerates in Parkinson disease causing dopamine depletion. This leads to tremor, rigidity, and bradykinesia. The nigrostriatal pathway is affected. Lewy bodies are pathological hallmarks.
questions.question: The substantia nigra degenerates primarily in which disease?

questions.explanation: The ventricular myocardium of the heart is composed of cardiac muscle not smooth muscle. Cardiac muscle is a striated involuntary muscle type restricted to the heart and great vessel roots. Smooth muscle forms the walls of hollow viscera including GI tract, bladder, and uterus, the tunica media of blood vessel walls, airways, and the iris and ciliary body of the eye.
options: The wall of the heart ventricular myocardium
The iris and ciliary body of the eye
questions.question: The prominent locations of smooth muscle in the body include all of the following EXCEPT which of the following?

options: Filtering blood directly in place of the glomerulus
Producing erythropoietin to stimulate red blood cell production
Secreting aldosterone in direct response to angiotensin II stimulation
Secretes renin in response to low perfusion, low sodium, and sympathetic activation
Phagocytosing damaged and apoptotic glomerular mesangial cells
questions.explanation: Juxtaglomerular cells are modified smooth muscle cells in the wall of the afferent arteriole at the vascular pole of the glomerulus. They contain renin stored in secretory granules and release it in response to: decreased stretch from low blood pressure sensed by baroreceptors in the afferent arteriole; decreased sodium delivery sensed by macula densa cells; and sympathetic beta-1 adrenergic stimulation. Renin cleaves angiotensinogen to angiotensin I initiating the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone axis.
questions.question: The juxtaglomerular apparatus of the kidney consists of juxtaglomerular cells macula densa cells and extraglomerular mesangial cells. The juxtaglomerular cells perform which function?

A biopsy from the gastroesophageal junction shows simple columnar epithelium with occasional goblet cells — features NOT expected in normal esophageal tissue. This histological finding is diagnostic of:
questions.explanation: Barrett's esophagus is defined histologically by the presence of specialized intestinal metaplasia — simple columnar epithelium with goblet cells — replacing the normal non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium of the esophagus. The goblet cells (staining blue/purple with alcian blue stain) are the pathognomonic feature. Barrett's esophagus is a premalignant condition increasing the risk of esophageal adenocarcinoma approximately 30- to 125-fold.

The mesonephros functions as an interim kidney for approximately 4 weeks (from weeks 6-10 of development). It appears late in the 4th week and degenerates toward the end of the first trimester. In males, some caudal tubules persist to form parts of the reproductive system, but in females, the mesonephros disappears almost completely.
questions.question: The mesonephros functions for approximately how many weeks?

questions.explanation: The chorion is histologically composed of four layers: cellular layer, dense reticulum, pseudo-basement membrane, and outer trophoblast. The chorion is the outer membrane of the fetal membranes, is in contact with the uterine wall, and is attached to the margins of the placenta.
questions.question: The chorion is histologically composed of how many layers?
The inferior parathyroid gland develops from which pharyngeal pouch?
questions.explanation: The inferior parathyroid gland develops from the dorsal part of the third pharyngeal pouch in the 5th week. It develops along with the thymus and descends with it into the thorax. There are four parathyroid glands total, with the superior pair developing from the fourth pouch.

The GBM has a trilaminar ultrastructure on electron microscopy: (1) Lamina rara interna — adjacent to the endothelium, contains heparan sulfate (charge barrier); (2) Lamina densa — central electron-dense layer of type IV collagen and laminin (size barrier); (3) Lamina rara externa — adjacent to podocyte foot processes, also contains heparan sulfate. Goodpasture syndrome involves autoantibodies targeting type IV collagen (alpha-3 chain) in the lamina densa.
questions.question: The glomerular basement membrane (GBM) has a trilaminar structure on electron microscopy. The three layers from Bowman's space inward are:
options: Lamina rara externa → Lamina densa → Lamina rara interna
Lamina densa → Lamina rara externa → Lamina rara interna
Lamina rara interna → Lamina densa → Lamina rara externa
Only two layers — lamina rara and lamina densa
The GBM is a single homogeneous layer

questions.question: At what spinal level does the spinal cord typically end in adults?
questions.explanation: The spinal cord typically ends at the L1-L2 vertebral level in adults (at the conus medullaris), though this varies individually from T12 to L3. During fetal development, the cord extends the full length of the vertebral canal, but differential growth of the vertebral column causes the cord to \"ascend\" relatively. The subarachnoid space continues to S2, creating the lumbar cistern containing the cauda equina, which provides a safe location for lumbar puncture below the cord termination.

questions.question: The endocervix is lined by which epithelium, while the ectocervix is lined by what type?
options: Both by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium
Endocervix by transitional epithelium; ectocervix by simple columnar
Endocervix by simple columnar mucus-secreting epithelium
Endocervix by pseudostratified ciliated columnar; ectocervix by keratinized squamous
questions.explanation: The endocervix (canal) is lined by simple columnar mucus-secreting epithelium with endocervical glands (Nabothian follicles when obstructed). The ectocervix (visible portion) is lined by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium continuous with the vagina. The squamocolumnar junction (SCJ/transformation zone) is where these two epithelia meet, and is the critical zone where most cervical intraepithelial neoplasias (CIN) and invasive cervical cancers originate, particularly after HPV infection.

questions.question: The nucleus of a neuron contains which structure prominently?
questions.explanation: The nucleus is large, pale staining with a prominent nucleolus (RNA store). It is surrounded by a double-layered membrane. The nucleolus produces ribosomal RNA.
The spinal cord measures about 42-45 cm in adults and 1.5 cm in diameter. It is enclosed within the vertebral canal covered by meninges. It extends from foramen magnum to conus medullaris.
questions.question: The spinal cord measures approximately what length in adults?

questions.explanation: The ileocecal valve (Bauhin's valve) is a mucosal fold reinforced by thickened circular muscle that controls the flow of ileal content into the cecum and prevents reflux of the heavily colonized large intestinal content into the relatively sterile small intestine. This barrier function is critical for preventing small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO). Surgical removal or incompetence of the ileocecal valve predisposes to SIBO.
options: Prevention of reflux of colonic bacterial
Production of mucus for fecal lubrication
questions.question: The ileocecal valve is a mucosal fold at the junction of the ileum and cecum. Its primary histological function is:

questions.explanation: The basilar artery is formed by the union of the two vertebral arteries at the pontomedullary junction. It ascends along the ventral surface of the pons in the pontine groove (basilar sulcus) and terminates by dividing into the two posterior cerebral arteries at the upper border of the pons. The basilar artery gives off pontine arteries, anterior inferior cerebellar artery, labyrinthine artery, and superior cerebellar arteries, supplying the pons, cerebellum, and inner ear.
questions.question: The basilar artery is formed by union of which vessels?
The two main categories of nervous system cells are which?
questions.explanation: The cells of nervous system are divided into neurons (excitable cells transmitting signals) and neuroglia (supporting cells). Neurons together with neuroglia make up nervous tissue. Each cell type has specialized functions.

questions.question: The palatine tonsil develops from which pharyngeal pouch?
questions.explanation: The ventral part of the second pharyngeal pouch forms the palatine tonsil. The dorsal part of the second pouch joins the dorsal part of the first pouch to contribute to formation of the external auditory meatus. The palatine tonsil is a lymphoid organ of the oropharynx.

The loop of Henle is part of the excretory unit (nephron), which is derived from the metanephric blastema. Each nephron consists of Bowman's capsule, proximal convoluted tubule, loop of Henle, and distal convoluted tubule. The distal tubule connects to a collecting tubule (derived from the ureteric bud).
questions.question: The loop of Henle is part of:

questions.explanation: The cricothyroid membrane is the preferred emergency access point for securing the airway when conventional intubation fails (can't intubate, can't oxygenate — CICO scenario). It is accessible, avascular in its midline, and located below the vocal cords. Needle cricothyroidotomy provides temporary oxygenation, while surgical cricothyrotomy creates a definitive emergency airway. Knowledge of the cricothyroid membrane and its histological composition (fibrous/elastic tissue) is essential for airway management.
questions.question: The cricothyroid membrane connects the cricoid and thyroid cartilages of the larynx. In emergency airway obstruction, which procedure uses this membrane?

A histological section shows a blood vessel with three distinct tunics, a prominent internal elastic lamina, and a media consisting of 8–10 layers of smooth muscle cells. The lumen diameter is approximately 0.5mm. This is most consistent with:
questions.explanation: A muscular (distributing) artery has: a well-defined tunica intima with a prominent internal elastic lamina, a tunica media of 10–40 layers of smooth muscle (the number shown here suggests a medium-caliber muscular artery), an external elastic lamina, and tunica adventitia. Diameter of 0.5mm is within the range of medium muscular arteries. Large elastic arteries have predominantly elastic lamellae in the media. Arterioles have only 1–3 smooth muscle layers and lumen < 0.3mm.

questions.question: Bipolar neurons in dorsal root ganglia send processes to which locations?
questions.explanation: The medial process of bipolar dorsal root ganglion neurons enters the marginal layer of the alar plate. It ends in the dorsal horn or ascends to higher centers. The peripheral process extends to sensory receptors in the body.

questions.question: Interstitial cells of the renal medulla produce prostaglandins. These prostaglandins act on the kidney to produce which effect?
questions.explanation: Renal medullary interstitial cells produce prostaglandins (primarily PGE2 and PGI2) that have local vasodilatory effects on renal vasculature, counteracting excessive renal vasoconstriction. They also inhibit tubular sodium reabsorption, promoting natriuresis. NSAIDs, by inhibiting prostaglandin synthesis, can cause renal vasoconstriction and sodium retention — particularly dangerous in states of reduced renal perfusion.
options: Increase urea reabsorption in collecting ducts

questions.explanation: Intercalated discs are specialized junctional complexes unique to cardiac muscle. They contain fascia adherens (anchoring myofibrils), desmosomes (mechanical coupling), and gap junctions (electrical coupling via connexins). Gap junctions allow rapid propagation of action potentials, making the heart function as an electrical syncytium. Skeletal muscle lacks intercalated discs; its cells are multinucleate with peripheral nuclei, unlike the central single nucleus of cardiomyocytes.
questions.question: Cardiac muscle cells differ from skeletal muscle cells in several ways. Which feature is UNIQUE to cardiac muscle?
options: Presence of actin and myosin filaments
Striated pattern due to sarcomere arrangement
Dependence on oxygen for sustained function

questions.question: Lacunae appear in the syncytiotrophoblast on which day?
questions.explanation: On day 9, the blastocyst is deeply embedded in the endometrium and the defect is plugged with a fibrin clot. Spaces called lacunae appear within the syncytiotrophoblast. These lacunae will later fill with maternal blood to establish uteroplacental circulation.

questions.question: Limb development involves induction from which signaling center?
questions.explanation: Limb development involves reciprocal induction between the apical ectodermal ridge (AER) and underlying mesenchyme. The AER secretes FGFs that maintain proliferation of underlying mesenchyme, while the mesenchyme signals maintain the AER. Both are required for proper limb outgrowth.

questions.question: Which glial cell type acts as the macrophage of the CNS performing phagocytic functions?
questions.explanation: Microglia are the resident immune and phagocytic cells of the CNS derived from bone marrow monocyte precursors not neuroectoderm. They continuously survey the CNS parenchyma and respond to injury or infection by proliferating, migrating to the site, phagocytosing debris and pathogens, and presenting antigens. They are the CNS equivalent of the peripheral tissue macrophage within the Mononuclear Phagocyte System.

Blood flow to glomeruli follows: renal artery → segmental arteries → interlobar arteries → arcuate arteries → interlobular (cortical radiate) arteries → afferent arterioles → glomerular capillaries. After filtration, blood exits via efferent arterioles into peritubular capillaries (cortex) or vasa recta (medulla). This unique portal-like arrangement with two capillary beds allows independent regulation of filtration and tubular blood flow.
questions.question: The arcuate arteries of the kidney run along the boundary between cortex and medulla. From these arteries, which vessels supply blood directly to the glomeruli?
The optic recess of the third ventricle is located above which structure?
questions.explanation: The optic recess is located above the optic chiasma at the anterior floor of the third ventricle. This recess marks the junction between the lamina terminalis (anterior wall) and the floor of the third ventricle. Tumors arising from or near the optic chiasma (craniopharyngiomas, pituitary adenomas, suprasellar meningiomas) may compress this recess, potentially obstructing CSF flow and causing hydrocephalus, in addition to producing visual field defects from chiasmal compression.

The epiploic foramen (of Winslow) provides communication between the greater peritoneal sac and the lesser sac (omental bursa). Its boundaries are: anteriorly - hepatoduodenal ligament (free edge of lesser omentum); posteriorly - inferior vena cava; superiorly - caudate lobe of liver; inferiorly - first part of duodenum. Understanding this anatomy is important for surgical access to the lesser sac.
questions.question: The epiploic foramen (of Winslow) provides communication between:

questions.explanation: In Hirschsprung's disease, absence of ganglion cells (aganglionosis) in the myenteric and submucosal plexuses of the affected bowel segment means it cannot relax — it remains in a state of tonic contraction, creating a functional obstruction. The proximal bowel dilates massively (megacolon) due to retained feces and gas. Diagnosis requires rectal biopsy showing absence of ganglion cells. Treatment is surgical resection of the aganglionic segment.
questions.question: Hirschsprung's disease results from absence of the myenteric and submucosal plexuses in a segment of colon. This leads to which functional consequence?
options: Functional obstruction with failure of relaxation

questions.question: The telencephalon develops from which primary brain vesicle?
questions.explanation: The prosencephalon (forebrain) divides into telencephalon and diencephalon. The telencephalon gives rise to the cerebral hemispheres (cortex, white matter, and basal nuclei), while the diencephalon forms the thalamus and hypothalamus. This subdivision occurs during formation of secondary brain vesicles.

The granular appearance of the renal cortex results from the presence of numerous renal corpuscles (glomeruli enclosed in Bowman's capsule) and convoluted tubules (proximal and distal). These structures give the cortex its characteristic granular texture on gross and histological examination. The medullary pyramids, in contrast, contain straight tubules (loops of Henle, collecting ducts) giving them a striated appearance.
questions.question: The renal cortex contains granular-appearing regions because of which structures concentrated there?
The lesser omentum extends between:
questions.explanation: The lesser omentum extends between the liver and stomach (lesser curvature), connecting the lesser curvature of the stomach to the inferior surface of the liver. It develops from the ventral mesogastrium. The lesser omentum contains the hepatic artery, portal vein, and bile duct in its free edge.

The external auditory meatus develops from the dorsal portion of the first pharyngeal cleft, forming the meatal plug. Initially, the epithelium proliferates and fills the meatus temporarily. Later recanalization occurs to establish the patent external auditory canal.
questions.question: The external auditory meatus develops from which pharyngeal structure?

questions.explanation: The female urethra (approximately 4cm long) transitions from transitional epithelium near the bladder to non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium near the external urethral orifice, with patches of pseudostratified or stratified columnar epithelium in between. This epithelial variability makes the female urethra susceptible to ascending infections, contributing to the higher incidence of UTIs in women compared to men.
questions.question: The urethra in females is shorter than in males. The female urethra is lined by which epithelium in its middle portion?
The morula enters the uterine cavity on approximately which day?
questions.explanation: The morula (16-32 cell stage) enters the uterine cavity on day 4. Cleavage takes place partly in the uterine tube (during the first three days) and partly in the uterus (from day 4 to 6). Shortly after entering the uterus, the morula transforms into a blastocyst.

options: Type III collagen (encoded by COL3A1 gene)
Type I collagen (most abundant fibrillar collagen)
questions.explanation: Ehlers-Danlos syndrome vascular type (EDS-IV) results from autosomal dominant mutations in COL3A1, which encodes type III procollagen — the main collagen of reticular fibers in arterial walls and intestines.
