Treatment is whole-lung lavage.
options: Deficiency of surfactant proteins A and D
Excess production of type I collagen
Loss of ciliary function in bronchioles

questions.question: Which nucleus in the medulla is responsible for motor control of the larynx and pharynx?
questions.explanation: The nucleus ambiguus lies laterally in the medulla and contains motor cell bodies that innervate skeletal muscles of the larynx, soft palate, pharynx, and upper esophagus via cranial nerves IX, X, and XI. This nucleus is crucial for swallowing, phonation, and maintaining airway patency. Lesions affecting the nucleus ambiguus result in dysphagia, dysphonia, and potential aspiration due to impaired swallowing coordination.

questions.question: Marfan syndrome results from mutations in which gene, affecting which structural protein of the elastic fiber system?
options: COL3A1 gene encoding type III collagen
COL1A1 gene encoding type I collagen
FBN1 mutation affecting fibrillin-1, the elastin scaffolding protein
questions.explanation: Marfan syndrome results from autosomal dominant mutations in the FBN1 gene encoding fibrillin-1, a glycoprotein that forms the microfibrillar scaffold essential for elastin deposition and elastic fiber integrity. Without functional fibrillin-1, elastic fibers lack mechanical resistance, causing aortic aneurysm/dissection, lens dislocation, and skeletal abnormalities (tall stature, arachnodactyly). Aortic rupture is the major life-threatening complication.

questions.question: Vernix caseosa is formed from which substances?
options: Fatty secretions and dead epithelial cells
questions.explanation: Vernix caseosa is formed from fatty secretions from fetal sebaceous glands and dead epithelial cells. It covers the fetal skin during 17-20 weeks and protects the skin from abrasions, chapping, and hardening that could result from exposure to amniotic fluid. It is a white, cheese-like substance.

questions.question: The primary visual cortex located in the occipital lobe receives input from the retina through which relay station?
options: The superior colliculus directly without any relay
Lateral geniculate nucleus projecting to the occipital visual cortex
The medial geniculate nucleus of the thalamus
The inferior colliculus which processes visual information
questions.explanation: The main visual pathway from retina to cortex: retinal ganglion cell axons form the optic nerve, partially decussate at the optic chiasm where nasal fibers cross, form the optic tract, and synapse in the lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus. Geniculocalcarine fibers project through the optic radiation to the primary visual cortex in area 17 of the occipital lobe. The superior colliculus receives a separate projection involved in eye movement control. The medial geniculate nucleus handles auditory information.

The trigone of the bladder is derived from the caudal ends of the mesonephric ducts, which become incorporated into the bladder wall. Although the trigone has mesodermal origin, the rest of the bladder epithelium is endodermal from the urogenital sinus. The trigone is the triangular area between the ureteric and urethral openings.
questions.question: The trigone of the bladder is derived from:
Surface mucous cells lining the gastric pit produce alkaline mucus. This mucus is chemically distinguished from the mucus of the mucous neck cells in that it is:
questions.explanation: Surface mucous cells produce thick, alkaline, insoluble mucus (containing MUC5AC mucin) that forms the protective gel-like layer adherent to the gastric epithelium. This alkaline mucus traps bicarbonate ions, creating a pH gradient from ~7 at the mucosa surface to ~2 in the gastric lumen. Mucous neck cells secrete soluble, less alkaline (slightly acidic) mucus (MUC6) that lubricates the gland lumen and acts as a precursor to surface mucous cells.
Laminae I-IV are concerned with exteroceptive sensations (pain, temperature, touch). Laminae V-VI process proprioceptive information. This dorsoventral organization reflects functional specificity.
questions.question: Laminae I-IV are concerned with which sensations?
Amniocentesis for genetic testing is typically performed after which week?
questions.explanation: Amniocentesis is typically performed after 14 weeks when there is about 200 ml of amniotic fluid, and 20-30 ml can be safely withdrawn. The procedure is performed under ultrasound guidance. The risk of inducing an abortion is approximately 0.5%.

questions.question: During return to the abdomen, which intestinal segment returns first?
questions.explanation: During return of herniated intestines (10th week), the small intestine loops (cranial limb) return first and are situated to the right of the dorsal mesentery. The large intestine follows, with the cecum being the last to return. This sequence is important for proper intestinal positioning.

questions.question: In eukaryotic cells, the phase during which the cell grows, accumulates nutrients, and duplicates its DNA before mitosis is specifically called which of the following?
questions.explanation: Interphase is the preparatory phase preceding mitosis during which the cell grows (G1 and G2 phases) and replicates its DNA (S phase). Nutrients are accumulated and the cell size increases substantially. Interphase occupies the majority of the cell cycle duration in most dividing cells.

Meckel's diverticulum can result from persistence of the vitelline duct (yolk stalk). This is the most common congenital malformation of the gastrointestinal tract, occurring in about 2% of the population. It is typically located about 2 feet from the ileocecal valve on the ileum.
questions.question: Meckel's diverticulum represents persistence of which embryonic structure?

options: They produce antibodies against bacterial antigens
They present antigens to T lymphocytes at infection sites
Rapidly recruited phagocytes killing bacteria via oxidative burst
They release histamine causing vascular dilation
They transform into macrophages at infection sites
questions.question: Neutrophils are the first responders to bacterial infection primarily because of which of the following?
questions.explanation: Neutrophils are the dominant acute inflammatory cells and first responders to bacterial infection. They migrate rapidly via chemotaxis to infection sites within hours, phagocytose bacteria, and kill them through: oxidative burst where NADPH oxidase generates reactive oxygen species; azurophilic granule enzymes including myeloperoxidase and elastase; and defensins and lactoferrin. Their short lifespan of 1 to 2 days in tissues and abundant bone marrow production support rapid response.

The total cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) volume in an adult is approximately 150 mL, with about 30 mL in the ventricles and 120 mL in the subarachnoid space. CSF is produced at a rate of approximately 0.4 mL/min (about 600 mL/day), resulting in a complete turnover 3-4 times daily. This continuous production and reabsorption maintains constant intracranial pressure and provides metabolic support to the brain.
questions.question: What is the approximate total volume of cerebrospinal fluid in an adult?
The optic cup differentiates into which structures?
questions.explanation: The optic cup differentiates into retina (outer pigmented layer, inner neural layer), inner iris layer, and ciliary body. The optic stalk becomes the optic nerve. The cup maintains attachment to brain.

options: Finger-like mucosal projections into the lumen
Lymphoid follicles scattered in the lamina propria
Goblet cell clusters in the epithelium
questions.question: The crypts of Lieberkühn in the small intestine are structurally defined as:
questions.explanation: Intestinal glands — the crypts of Lieberkühn — are simple tubular glands that extend through the full thickness of the mucosal lamina propria. They open at the base of the villi and contain stem cells, goblet cells, Paneth cells, and enteroendocrine cells. They are the proliferative compartment of the intestinal epithelium, constantly renewing the villous epithelium.

The cephalic flexure topographically makes the connection between infundibulum and Rathke's pouch possible. This flexure bends the developing brain ventrally. It creates the characteristic angle of the developing forebrain.
questions.question: Which flexure enables the pituitary connection with oral cavity?

questions.explanation: The transverse sinuses drain from the confluence of sinuses at the internal occipital protuberance, where multiple venous channels meet. The right transverse sinus is typically a continuation of the superior sagittal sinus, while the left continues from the straight sinus. These large sinuses pass laterally along the margin of the tentorium cerebelli before turning downward and medially to become the sigmoid sinus and eventually drain into the internal jugular vein.
questions.question: At which anatomical landmark do the right and left transverse sinuses typically originate?
Which organ system does NOT primarily develop through epithelial-mesenchymal interactions?
questions.explanation: Most inductive processes during embryonic development involve epithelial-mesenchymal interactions, including development of kidneys, gastrointestinal derivatives, respiratory system, and skin appendages. Skeletal muscles develop primarily from somitic mesoderm through intrinsic differentiation programs rather than epithelial-mesenchymal induction.

questions.question: The parietal layer of Bowman's capsule is lined by which type of epithelium?
questions.explanation: The parietal layer of Bowman's capsule is lined by simple squamous epithelium. This thin, flat epithelium forms the outer boundary of the urinary space (Bowman's space) between the parietal and visceral (podocyte) layers. In rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, parietal epithelial cells proliferate to form crescents, a pathological hallmark of severe glomerular injury.

questions.question: The canalicular period is characterized by formation of:
questions.explanation: The canalicular period (16-26 weeks) is characterized by division of terminal bronchioles into respiratory bronchioles, which then divide into alveolar ducts. Primitive alveoli begin forming, and capillaries establish close contact with developing air spaces. Fetuses born at the end of this period may survive with intensive care.

questions.question: Compaction of blastomeres occurs at which cell stage?
questions.explanation: At the 2- and 4-cell stages, blastomeres are loosely bound. With the third division producing 8 cells, compaction occurs, producing tightly bound cells. This compaction maximizes cell-to-cell contact and is essential for subsequent differentiation into inner cell mass and trophoblast.

questions.question: Cortical neurons migrate in which pattern?
questions.explanation: Cortical neurons migrate in an inside-out pattern with earlier-born neurons in deeper layers. Later neurons migrate past them to superficial layers. This establishes six-layered cortex. Radial glia guide migration.

questions.question: The submucosal Meissner's plexus and myenteric Auerbach's plexus together constitute which nervous system component?
questions.explanation: The enteric nervous system is a complex intrinsic neural network within the GI wall containing approximately 500 million neurons organized into Meissner's submucosal plexus which regulates secretion and blood flow and Auerbach's myenteric plexus between circular and longitudinal muscle layers which controls motility. The ENS can function autonomously without input from the CNS and is often called the second brain. It is derived from neural crest cells and contains as many neurons as the spinal cord.
options: Intrinsic GI nervous system with independent control of motility and secretion
The sympathetic chain ganglia innervating the intestine
The somatic motor system controlling intestinal smooth muscle
The central nervous system extension into the gut wall
The lymphatic plexus draining intestinal villi

questions.question: The upper third of the esophagus contains which type of muscle in its muscularis externa?
questions.explanation: The upper third of the esophagus contains skeletal muscle (for voluntary swallowing), the middle third contains mixed skeletal and smooth muscle, and the lower third contains smooth muscle only. This gradation reflects the transition from voluntary to involuntary control of swallowing. This is a classic and frequently tested histological feature of the esophagus.

questions.question: Vesicoureteral reflux predisposes to:
questions.explanation: Vesicoureteral reflux (VUR) predisposes to renal scarring (reflux nephropathy) from recurrent urinary tract infections, as bacteria can ascend from bladder to kidneys. Primary VUR results from inadequate length of intramural ureter or lateral positioning of ureteric orifice. High-grade reflux may require surgical reimplantation to prevent progressive renal damage and chronic kidney disease.

options: To kill microorganisms on the tissue surface
Thin slices allowing transmitted light to pass through the  tissue
To increase the density of the specimen
To remove blood from the tissue before viewing
questions.question: When examining slides with the light microscope, the preparation of tissue sections primarily serves which of the following purposes?
questions.explanation: The primary purpose of sectioning is to produce thin, translucent slices that permit transmitted light to pass through the tissue for microscopic examination. Intact tissues are opaque and cannot be visualized with a transmitted-light microscope. Sections are typically 3–10 μm thick to achieve adequate translucency.

Wait — Chief cells secrete pepsinogen (converted to pepsin by HCl) and gastric lipase. Gastrin is secreted by G-cells (enteroendocrine cells). The correct answer is C: Chief (zymogen) cells are basophilic cells in the base of gastric glands that produce pepsinogen and gastric lipase. Answer: C.
questions.question: Chief (zymogen) cells of the gastric glands are characterized by which secretory product?

questions.explanation: Brunner's glands (duodenal glands) are compound tubulo-alveolar mucous glands located in the submucosa of the duodenum — a unique feature not found in the jejunum or ileum. They secrete alkaline (bicarbonate-rich) mucus in response to acid, secretin, and vagal stimulation, neutralizing the highly acidic chyme entering from the stomach. Their presence in histological sections is the single most reliable criterion for identifying duodenal tissue.
questions.question: Which segment of the small intestine is identified histologically by the presence of Brunner's glands in the submucosa?

questions.explanation: Patau syndrome results from trisomy 13 (47,XX,+13 or 47,XY,+13). Features include holoprosencephaly, cleft lip and palate, polydactyly, cardiac defects, and severe intellectual disability. Like trisomy 18, most affected infants die within the first year of life.
questions.question: Patau syndrome results from trisomy of which chromosome?
Recanalization of the esophageal lumen normally occurs by:
questions.explanation: Recanalization of the esophageal lumen normally occurs by the end of the embryonic period (8th week). During the 4th-7th weeks, epithelial proliferation partly or completely obliterates the lumen temporarily. Failure of proper recanalization leads to esophageal stenosis or atresia. This process of obliteration and recanalization occurs throughout the GI tract.

Basket cells are inhibitory interneurons in the molecular layer that synapse on Purkinje cell bodies (soma) and initial axon segments, forming basket-like networks around them. These GABAergic interneurons are activated by parallel fibers and provide lateral inhibition, sharpening the spatial pattern of Purkinje cell activity. This inhibition enhances contrast between active and inactive Purkinje cells, improving the precision of cerebellar output. Basket cells help define which Purkinje cells are active in response to specific inputs.
questions.question: Basket cells in the cerebellar cortex primarily synapse on which structure?

questions.explanation: The common hepatic duct (formed by the union of right and left hepatic ducts) joins the cystic duct of the gallbladder to form the common bile duct (choledochus). The common bile duct descends through the pancreatic head to join the main pancreatic duct at the ampulla of Vater. Obstruction of the common bile duct (by gallstones, carcinoma) causes obstructive jaundice with conjugated hyperbilirubinemia.
questions.question: The common hepatic duct is formed by the union of the right and left hepatic ducts at the porta hepatis. It then joins the cystic duct from the gallbladder to form the:

questions.explanation: Rough ER derives its name from the ribosomes attached to its cytoplasmic surface, which synthesize proteins destined for secretion, membrane insertion, or lysosomal targeting. These proteins are co-translationally threaded into the ER lumen for subsequent folding, modification, and transport. Its basophilic appearance in H&E-stained sections (due to ribosome RNA) is a key histological feature of secretory cells.
questions.question: Rough endoplasmic reticulum (RER) is characterized by which of the following distinguishing features?
options: Absence of associated ribosomes on its cytoplasmic surface
Role in lipid synthesis and detoxification
Ribosomes-studded membrane for secretory and membrane protein synthesis
Located only in the cell periphery near the plasma membrane
Serves as the primary site of ATP production

questions.question: A patient with Hashimoto's thyroiditis has autoimmune destruction of thyroid follicles. The histological features expected include which of the following?
options: Absence of inflammatory cells with intact follicular architecture
Replacement of all thyroid tissue by adipose cells
Lymphocytic infiltration, germinal centers, follicular atrophy, Hürthle cell change
Proliferation of C cells producing excessive calcitonin
questions.explanation: Hashimoto's thyroiditis shows characteristic histological features: dense lymphocytic infiltration with germinal center formation reflecting autoimmune T and B cell responses; follicular atrophy and destruction; oxyphilic Hürthle cell metaplasia of follicular cells reflecting mitochondrial hyperplasia as a cellular response to injury; and fibrosis in chronic cases. The autoantibodies against thyroid peroxidase and thyroglobulin are diagnostic markers. The result is hypothyroidism due to follicular destruction.

options: Direct absorption of digested nutrients in the stomach
Supply of substrates for HCl synthesis
questions.explanation: The rich vascularity of the gastric lamina propria serves multiple critical functions: it delivers CO2, water, and substrates needed for acid production; it transports oxygen to support the high metabolic activity of parietal and chief cells; it carries regulatory hormones and neural signals to epithelial cells; and it rapidly clears absorbed substances and waste products. Any disruption of this blood supply (as in mucosal ischemia) quickly compromises the gastric mucosal barrier.
questions.question: A researcher studying the stomach notices that the lamina propria is highly vascularized to support gastric pits and glands. This rich vascularity is essential for which function?

questions.explanation: The precentral sulcus runs parallel and anterior to the central sulcus, separating the precentral gyrus (primary motor cortex) from the more anterior frontal cortex. Between the precentral sulcus and superior and inferior frontal sulci lie the superior, middle, and inferior frontal gyri. The precentral sulcus is variable in configuration but generally follows the orientation of the central sulcus. This sulcus helps identify the precentral gyrus containing the primary motor cortex (Brodmann area 4).
questions.question: The precentral sulcus runs parallel to which major sulcus?
First-order auditory neurons are located in which structure?
questions.explanation: First-order neurons of auditory pathway are in spiral ganglion close to cochlea. They are bipolar neurons with peripheral processes reaching organ of Corti hair cells. Central processes form cochlear nerve terminating in cochlear nuclei.

questions.question: Which artery supplies the medial surface of the cerebral hemispheres?
questions.explanation: The anterior cerebral artery supplies the medial surface of the cerebral hemispheres, including the paracentral lobule (containing motor and sensory areas for the lower limb), as well as the medial portions of the frontal and parietal lobes. It also supplies a strip of the lateral surface along the superior border. Occlusion causes contralateral lower limb weakness and sensory loss, with relative sparing of the upper limb and face. The anterior cerebral arteries are connected by the anterior communicating artery.

questions.question: The urinary bladder wall contains the detrusor muscle, which is composed of which type of muscle and how is it arranged?
options: Smooth muscle in three interwoven layers
Cardiac muscle in a single layer
Two layers of smooth muscle (circular only)
Mixed skeletal and smooth muscle in two layers
questions.explanation: The detrusor muscle of the bladder is composed of three interwoven layers of smooth muscle: inner longitudinal, middle circular, and outer longitudinal. Unlike the GIT where layers are distinct, the bladder muscle layers are less clearly defined and fibers run in multiple directions, giving the bladder its unique distensibility. The internal urethral sphincter at the bladder neck is a thickening of the circular smooth muscle.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes the five zones of the epiphyseal growth plate from the epiphyseal to the diaphyseal side?
questions.explanation: The epiphyseal plate from epiphyseal to diaphyseal side has five zones: resting zone with quiescent hyaline cartilage chondrocytes; proliferative zone with rapidly dividing chondrocytes in longitudinal columns; hypertrophic zone with enlarged chondrocytes accumulating glycogen; calcified cartilage zone where matrix calcifies as chondrocytes die; and ossification zone where endochondral bone tissue appears as blood vessels and osteoblasts invade. This progression drives longitudinal bone growth.
options: Resting → proliferative → hypertrophic → calcified cartilage → ossification
Ossification zone then calcified zone then hypertrophic zone then proliferative zone then resting zone
Only three zones exist: proliferative hypertrophic and ossification
Calcified zone is immediately adjacent to the resting zone
The proliferative zone is closest to the diaphysis

questions.question: The anterolateral system decussates at which level?
questions.explanation: Anterolateral system fibers ascend 1-2 segments after entry before decussating ventral to central canal. This creates a small ipsilateral zone. Decussation is more oblique cervically, transverse lumbosacral.

The Edinger-Westphal nucleus provides parasympathetic (GVE) innervation to the sphincter pupillae muscle (causing pupillary constriction) and ciliary muscle (controlling lens accommodation) via the oculomotor nerve. These preganglionic fibers synapse in the ciliary ganglion, with postganglionic fibers reaching the eyeball. Damage to the Edinger-Westphal nucleus or oculomotor nerve causes a dilated pupil that doesn't constrict to light (due to unopposed sympathetic activity) and impaired accommodation.
questions.question: The Edinger-Westphal nucleus provides parasympathetic innervation to which structures?

options: It contains large quantities of type I collagen fibers
It forms protective sheaths around peripheral nerves
It produces antibodies in response to infection
Adipocytes derived from mesenchyme and classified within connective tissue
It replaces bone marrow in adults
questions.question: In the classification of connective tissue, adipose tissue is considered a specialized connective tissue because of which of the following?
questions.explanation: Adipose tissue is classified as a specialized connective tissue because adipocytes are mesenchymally derived (like all connective tissue cells) and are embedded in a connective tissue framework of reticular fibers. The specialization lies in the extreme adaptation of adipocytes for lipid storage and metabolic signaling. Like other connective tissues, it has an ECM (though sparse) and derives from the same mesodermal origin.

Malrotation of the midgut can lead to volvulus, which is rotation of an intestinal loop around a branch of the superior mesenteric artery. This can cause intestinal obstruction or even gangrene. Volvulus requires emergency surgical intervention to prevent bowel ischemia and necrosis.
questions.question: Malrotation of the midgut can lead to:

questions.explanation: The spinal dura mater extends beyond the conus medullaris and covers the filum terminale, blending with the dura at the level of the second sacral vertebra (S2). Beyond this point, the filum terminale continues as the coccygeal ligament attached to the coccyx. The subdural cavity separates the dura from the arachnoid mater and is filled with a thin film of fluid.
questions.question: At what vertebral level does the spinal dura mater covering the filum terminale blend with other structures?

questions.explanation: The vestibular apparatus detects two types of motion through distinct receptor organs: the maculae of the utricle and saccule contain hair cells with overlying otolithic membranes carrying calcium carbonate crystals called otoliths that respond to linear acceleration and gravity; and the cristae ampullares in the three semicircular ducts oriented in the three planes of space detect angular acceleration and rotation. Together these five receptor organs provide complete three-dimensional vestibular sensing.
questions.question: The vestibular apparatus of the inner ear detects which types of motion through its specialized sensory receptor structures?
options: Sound vibrations converted to nerve impulses
Macular otolith organs (linear) and semicircular cristae (angular acceleration)
Only static head position without any dynamic movement detection

questions.explanation: Appendices epiploicae are small peritoneal pouches filled with adipose tissue attached to the outer surface of the colon along the teniae coli. They are a distinctive anatomical feature of the large intestine absent in the small intestine and rectum. Torsion or infarction of appendices epiploicae can mimic acute appendicitis or diverticulitis clinically.
questions.question: Appendices epiploicae are small fat-filled peritoneal pouches on the surface of the colon. Their histological composition is:

questions.explanation: Hassall's corpuscles are spherical structures in the thymic medulla composed of concentrically arranged keratinized medullary epithelial cells forming onion-skin-like whorls. They appear in increasing numbers with age and thymic involution. Recent evidence shows they produce thymic stromal lymphopoietin that activates medullary dendritic cells to induce regulatory T cells contributing to self-tolerance. They are pathognomonic for thymic tissue identification in histological sections.
questions.question: The Hassall's corpuscles found exclusively in the thymic medulla are composed of which of the following?
options: Clusters of mature T lymphocytes expressing CD8
Keratinized epithelial whorls involved in regulatory T cell induction
Macrophages that have phagocytosed dying thymocytes
Type IV collagen deposits forming the blood-thymus barrier

questions.question: Crossed fused renal ectopia most commonly involves:
questions.explanation: In crossed fused renal ectopia, both kidneys are most commonly on the left side (though right-sided can occur). One kidney crosses the midline during development and fuses with the other. The ureters still insert normally in the bladder on their respective sides. The fused kidneys typically function normally. Various fusion patterns exist (inferior, sigmoid, lump, disc). The condition is usually discovered incidentally.

questions.question: Cholangiocytes are the epithelial cells lining the bile ducts. What type of epithelium lines the large intrahepatic bile ducts?
questions.explanation: Intrahepatic bile ducts are lined by cholangiocytes — simple cuboidal epithelium in smaller ducts transitioning to simple columnar epithelium in larger ducts. These cells regulate bile composition through secretion and reabsorption. Cholangiocytes are targets of autoimmune destruction in primary biliary cholangitis and primary sclerosing cholangitis, causing progressive biliary cirrhosis.

questions.question: Which of the following features best distinguishes the 10× eyepiece lens from a 10× objective lens in terms of function within a compound microscope?
options: The eyepiece magnifies the actual specimen while the objective produces a virtual image
The objective creates an enlarged real image; the eyepiece further magnifies it
Both lenses function identically with only placement differing
The eyepiece lens improves resolving power; the objective only magnifies
The objective is adjusted by the coarse focus; the eyepiece by the fine focus
questions.explanation: The objective lens creates an enlarged real, inverted intermediate image of the specimen based on its proximity to the object. The eyepiece then acts as a magnifying glass to further enlarge this intermediate image for the observer's eye. Only the objective lens determines resolving power; the eyepiece simply increases perceived magnification without improving resolution.

The nasopharynx is a respiratory passageway lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar (respiratory) epithelium with goblet cells, continuous with the nasal cavity epithelium. The oropharynx and laryngopharynx are food-conducting passages that transition to non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium to withstand mechanical abrasion during swallowing. This epithelial transition at the pharyngeal isthmus is clinically relevant in nasopharyngeal carcinoma.
questions.question: Which structural feature distinguishes the oropharynx histologically from the nasopharynx?
options: Oropharynx has pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium; nasopharynx has stratified squamous
Both have identical pseudostratified columnar epithelium
Oropharynx has non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium
Oropharynx has transitional epithelium; nasopharynx has simple columnar
Both have non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium

questions.explanation: Contraction of muscles depends on pattern and rate of firing of spinal motor neurons. These are bombarded by an array of pathways. Motor neurons are the final common pathway.
questions.question: Muscle contraction depends on the firing pattern of which cells?

questions.explanation: The upper lip is formed in the 6th week by fusion of the medial nasal prominence and the two maxillary prominences. The lower lip and jaw are formed by fusion of the two mandibular prominences in the midline. The cheeks and maxilla are formed by fusion of the maxillary prominences.
questions.question: The upper lip is formed by fusion of which structures?
options: Medial nasal and two maxillary prominences

questions.explanation: Arachnoid villi are evaginations of the arachnoid mater that protrude into the dura mater and are visible from the third year of life. Their number increases proportionately with age from the seventh year onward, eventually pitting the inner surface of the cranium. These structures communicate with the venous sinuses and are crucial for cerebrospinal fluid absorption into the venous system.
questions.question: The arachnoid villi begin to appear and increase with age. From which year of life do they become consistently visible?
Which component of the GIT wall forms an important physical barrier between luminal contents and the body's deeper tissues?
questions.explanation: The inner epithelial lining of the mucosa acts as the primary barrier separating the potentially harmful luminal environment from underlying tissues. This epithelium is also the interface for absorption and secretion. The lamina propria, submucosa, and other layers provide structural support but are not the primary barrier.

options: Nasopharynx equalizing pressure between middle ear and atmosphere
The inner ear labyrinth and cochlea directly
questions.question: The Eustachian tube connects the middle ear cavity to which structure allowing pressure equalization?
questions.explanation: The Eustachian or auditory tube connects the middle ear tympanic cavity to the nasopharynx, equalizing atmospheric pressure on both sides of the tympanic membrane. Swallowing and yawning open the tube momentarily allowing air exchange. Obstruction from upper respiratory infection or adenoid hypertrophy prevents pressure equalization causing negative middle ear pressure, tympanic membrane retraction, and fluid accumulation known as otitis media with effusion.

Polycystic kidney disease is characterized by multiple cysts throughout the kidney parenchyma that can lead to renal failure. There are autosomal dominant (adult) and autosomal recessive (infantile) forms. The cysts result from abnormal development of collecting tubules and nephrons. Childhood or adulthood onset depends on the genetic form.
questions.question: Polycystic kidney disease is characterized by:
During the pseudoglandular period (5-16 weeks), which structures are absent?
questions.explanation: During the pseudoglandular period (5-16 weeks), branching continues to form terminal bronchioles, but respiratory bronchioles and alveoli are not yet present. The lung resembles a gland histologically during this period. Respiration is not possible if a fetus is born during this stage.

questions.question: The 'cytosol' is distinguished from the 'cytoplasm' in that the cytosol specifically refers to which of the following?
options: All contents of the cell including the nucleus
Only the membrane-bound organelles within the cell
The soluble aqueous phase of the cytoplasm, excluding organelles
The gel-like material found only within the nucleus
The extracellular fluid immediately surrounding the cell
questions.explanation: The cytosol is the soluble, aqueous phase of the cytoplasm in which organelles are suspended; it excludes membrane-bound organelles, cytoskeletal elements, and inclusions. The cytoplasm encompasses everything between the plasma membrane and nuclear envelope, including both the cytosol and all organelles. The distinction matters when discussing metabolic reactions that occur 'in the cytosol' (glycolysis) versus 'in the cytoplasm' more broadly.

Ankyloglossia (tongue-tie) is characterized by an unusually short, thick lingual frenulum that may decrease tongue mobility. It is a congenital oral anomaly that can affect speech and feeding. Severe cases may require surgical intervention (frenulotomy) to improve tongue movement.
questions.question: Ankyloglossia results from:
The intermediate horn is limited to which spinal segments?
questions.explanation: The intermediate horn is limited to the region of T1 to T12 and L2-L3 spinal segments. Neuroblast aggregation between basal and alar plates forms this structure. It contains neurons of the sympathetic portion of the autonomic nervous system.

questions.question: Which cellular deterioration process occurring after tissue removal involves self-digestion by the cell's own enzymes?
questions.explanation: Autolysis is self-digestion resulting from release of lysosomal enzymes within dying cells, which hydrolyze cellular components. It is a key reason why tissues must be fixed immediately after removal. Necrosis is a broader term for cell death, while apoptosis is programmed cell death distinct from autolysis.

questions.question: Vernix caseosa is composed of:
questions.explanation: Vernix caseosa is a white, greasy substance composed of sebum (from sebaceous glands) and desquamated peridermal cells. It covers fetal skin and protects against constant exposure to amniotic fluid with its high urine content. Vernix also facilitates birth by providing lubrication.

Megaureter refers to a dilated ureter, which may result from obstruction (obstructive megaureter), reflux (refluxing megaureter), or aperistaltic segment (primary megaureter). Congenital causes include posterior urethral valves, ureteropelvic junction obstruction, or vesicoureteral reflux. Chronic dilation can lead to progressive loss of ureteral function and renal damage.
questions.question: Megaureter refers to:
Astrocytes serve as which intermediary?
questions.explanation: Astrocytes are large stellate cells serving as metabolic intermediaries for neurons. Their processes attach to capillaries and neurons. They form the inner layer of blood-brain barrier.

The substantia nigra forms a boundary between the crus cerebri (basis pedunculi) ventrally and the tegmentum dorsally in the midbrain. Its cells contain melanin, giving it a dark appearance, and it projects nigrostriatal fibers to the basal ganglia. Loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra leads to Parkinson's disease, characterized by tremor, rigidity, and bradykinesia.
questions.question: The substantia nigra separates which two parts of the midbrain?
The intrinsic muscles of the larynx are supplied by:
questions.explanation: The intrinsic muscles of the larynx, derived from the 6th pharyngeal arch, are supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve. The cricothyroid muscle (4th arch derivative) is supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve. Both are branches of the vagus nerve (CN X).

Hematopoiesis begins in the liver during the 6th week, giving the organ a dark red color. The liver serves as the major hematopoietic organ during fetal life. By the 9th week, the rapidly growing liver comprises about 10% of total body weight.
questions.question: Hematopoiesis in the liver begins during which week?

questions.explanation: Langerhans cells are specialized antigen-presenting macrophages resident in the skin epidermis, named after Paul Langerhans who also described the pancreatic islets. They capture antigens entering through the skin and migrate to draining lymph nodes to present antigens to T lymphocytes, initiating adaptive immune responses. They are part of the MPS and contain characteristic tennis racket-shaped cytoplasmic Birbeck granules.
questions.question: Which connective tissue cell type acts as an antigen-presenting cell (APC) in the skin epidermis and is specifically named after the scientist who described it?

questions.explanation: The inferior colliculus, located in the tectum of the lower midbrain, is part of the auditory pathway. It receives input from the lateral lemniscus and projects to the medial geniculate body of the thalamus, which then projects to the auditory cortex.
questions.question: The inferior colliculus is associated with which sensory system?

questions.explanation: Complete cord transection causes total paralysis and sensory loss below lesion level. Initially there is spinal shock. Later upper motor neuron signs develop. Autonomic dysfunction occurs.
options: Total paralysis and sensory loss below lesion
questions.question: Complete spinal cord transection causes which clinical picture?
The renal corpuscle consists of the glomerular tuft and Bowman's capsule. The urinary space (Bowman's space) is located between which two structures?
questions.explanation: Bowman's space (urinary space) is the crescent-shaped cavity between the visceral epithelium (podocytes) covering the glomerular capillaries and the parietal epithelium (simple squamous cells) lining the outer wall of Bowman's capsule. Ultrafiltrate crosses the filtration barrier into this space, then flows into the proximal convoluted tubule. In glomerulonephritis with crescents, proliferating parietal epithelial cells and infiltrating macrophages fill Bowman's space, compressing the glomerular tuft.
options: Between the endothelium and the GBM
Between the GBM and podocyte foot processes

questions.explanation: The stapedius muscle (smallest skeletal muscle in the body) is derived from the second pharyngeal arch and is innervated by the facial nerve (CN VII). It attaches to the stapes and dampens excessive vibrations of the ossicles. Other second arch muscles include stylohyoid and posterior belly of digastric.
questions.question: The stapedius muscle is derived from which pharyngeal arch?

questions.explanation: The superior parathyroid gland develops from the fourth pharyngeal pouch in the 5th week, along with contributions to thyroid gland formation. It remains in the neck region along with the thyroid gland. The inferior parathyroid from the third pouch descends with the thymus.
questions.question: The superior parathyroid gland develops from which pharyngeal pouch?
Reciprocal induction involves which type of interaction?
questions.explanation: Reciprocal induction involves interactions between different tissues in which cells in one tissue express a set of inductive signals to which cells in the other tissue respond. The responding cells then express signals that affect the inducing tissue. Many organs develop through reciprocal induction.

Duplicated collecting system (duplicated ureter and renal pelvis) is the most common congenital anomaly of the urinary system, occurring in about 1% of the population. It results from premature division of the ureteric bud or development of two separate buds. Most cases are asymptomatic, though they may predispose to urinary tract infections.
questions.question: The most common congenital anomaly of the urinary system is:
Renal columns (of Bertin) are composed of:
questions.explanation: Renal columns (of Bertin) are composed of cortical tissue that extends between the pyramids down to the renal sinus. They contain cortical nephrons and interlobular vessels. Prominent columns are normal variants but can be mistaken for masses on imaging. The columns represent the cortical tissue separating adjacent renal pyramids.

The postcentral sulcus runs parallel and posterior to the central sulcus, separating the postcentral gyrus (primary somatosensory cortex) from the superior and inferior parietal lobules posteriorly. This sulcus marks the posterior boundary of the primary somatosensory cortex (areas 3, 1, 2). The region between the postcentral and central sulci contains the postcentral gyrus, which has a somatotopic organization (sensory homunculus) similar to the motor homunculus of the precentral gyrus.
questions.question: The postcentral sulcus runs parallel to which structure?

questions.explanation: The superior longitudinal fasciculus is a major association fiber system connecting the frontal, parietal, occipital, and temporal lobes within the same hemisphere. It arches over the insula deep to the lateral surface and includes several components: SLF I (superior parietal-frontal connections), SLF II (inferior parietal-frontal), and SLF III (supramarginal gyrus-frontal). The arcuate fasciculus, connecting Wernicke's and Broca's areas, is sometimes considered part of SLF. Damage can cause conduction aphasia and visuospatial deficits.
questions.question: The superior longitudinal fasciculus connects which regions?

questions.explanation: Third-order neurons from superior olivary nucleus form lateral lemniscus ascending the brainstem to inferior colliculus. Some fibers synapse with nucleus of lateral lemniscus. The lateral lemniscus is a major ascending auditory pathway.
questions.question: The lateral lemniscus is formed by neurons from which nucleus?

questions.explanation: Colloids are formed within the thyroid gland by the 11th week of development. The thyroid gland becomes functional by the 12th week of development. This timing is important for normal fetal development as thyroid hormones are essential for brain development.
questions.question: Colloid formation in the thyroid gland occurs by which week?

questions.explanation: The trigeminal sensory nuclei (main sensory, spinal, and mesencephalic nuclei) represent the general somatic afferent (GSA) column, receiving pain, temperature, touch, and proprioception from the face and head via cranial nerve V. The GSA column is lateral to visceral afferent components in the brainstem organization. The spinal trigeminal nucleus extends from the pons through the medulla to the upper cervical spinal cord, while the main sensory nucleus processes discriminative touch and the mesencephalic nucleus handles proprioception.
questions.question: Which nucleus represents the general somatic afferent column in the brainstem?
The kidneys ascend from the pelvis to the abdomen primarily due to:
questions.explanation: The kidneys "ascend" from the pelvis to the abdomen primarily due to disproportionate growth in the caudal region of the embryo. As the lumbar and sacral regions grow, the kidneys appear to move cranially. They attain their adult position by the 9th week and simultaneously rotate medially approximately 90 degrees.

A fresh cut section of the spleen shows easily distinguishable red pulp which appears dark red due to its massive blood content in sinuses and cords, and white pulp which appears as white or gray nodular areas along the branches of the splenic artery. The white pulp lymphoid nodules were originally described as Malpighian bodies or corpuscles in the unfixed spleen where this macroscopic distinction is most visible. Processing changes these appearances.
questions.question: Which of the following describes the histological appearance of the spleen when the organ is freshly sectioned, without tissue processing?
options: Entirely white throughout with no distinction between areas
Entirely red pulp throughout without white pulp areas
Yellow-gray coloration throughout due to extensive adipose tissue infiltration
Uniformly brown from bile pigment and hemosiderin accumulation
Dark red pulp from blood cells and white-gray nodules of white pulp

questions.explanation: The mantle layer, formed by neuroblasts, differentiates into the gray matter of the CNS. It is the second layer formed in the developing neural tube. The neurons in this layer will form the functional cellular components.
questions.question: The mantle layer differentiates into which tissue?
The rectum differs from the sigmoid colon histologically in that the rectum:
questions.explanation: The rectum differs from the rest of the large intestine in that the teniae coli spread out into a complete longitudinal muscle layer (no longer forming three bands), and haustra are absent — giving the rectum a smooth, non-sacculated outline. This smooth muscle coat contributes to the rectal reservoir function. The rectum is lined by simple columnar epithelium with goblet cells, transitioning to stratified squamous in the anal canal.
options: Is lined by stratified squamous epithelium
Has no teniae coli, as the longitudinal muscle is
Contains Brunner's glands in its submucosa
Has three distinct layers of muscularis externa

questions.question: Secondary neurulation involves formation of neural tube by which mechanism?
questions.explanation: Secondary neurulation involves mesenchyme condensing to form a rod which undergoes epithelial transition and cavitation. This is common in tail formation. It differs from primary neurulation's folding mechanism.

The right and left main bronchi appear during the early 5th week as lateral outpocketings of the lung bud. The right bronchus subsequently divides to form three secondary bronchi, while the left forms two. This asymmetric branching establishes the foundation for the three-lobed right lung and two-lobed left lung.
questions.question: The right and left main bronchi appear during which week?

questions.explanation: The subarachnoid cavity communicates with the fourth ventricle through the central foramen of Magendie and the two lateral foramina of Luschka. This communication allows cerebrospinal fluid to flow from the ventricular system into the subarachnoid space surrounding the brain and spinal cord. The subarachnoid cavity terminates at the level of S2 and contains cerebrospinal fluid throughout its extent.
questions.question: Through which foramina does the subarachnoid cavity communicate with the ventricular system?
Which dural venous sinus is formed by the union of the great cerebral vein and inferior sagittal sinus?
questions.explanation: The straight sinus is formed by the union of the great cerebral vein (of Galen) with the inferior sagittal sinus. It runs posteriorly along the junction of the falx cerebri and tentorium cerebelli, continuing mainly with the left transverse sinus. This sinus is a major drainage pathway for deep cerebral structures and plays a crucial role in venous return from the brain.

The solitary nucleus receives both general visceral afferent (GVA) and special visceral afferent (SVA) components via cranial nerves VII, IX, and X. The GVA component carries visceral sensory information from thoracoabdominal organs, carotid sinus baroreceptors, and chemoreceptors. The SVA component, located in the rostral nucleus, receives taste (gustatory) information. This combined sensory nucleus integrates taste and visceral sensation, coordinating reflex responses including salivation, swallowing, and cardiovascular regulation.
questions.question: The solitary nucleus receives which two functional components?

questions.explanation: The periosteum has an outer fibrous layer (dense irregular connective tissue with fibroblasts providing mechanical protection) and an inner osteogenic (cambium) layer containing osteoprogenitor cells that differentiate into osteoblasts. The inner layer is essential for appositional bone growth (increasing bone diameter), fracture repair, and endochondral ossification during development. Bones stripped of periosteum heal poorly due to loss of this progenitor cell reservoir.
questions.question: The periosteum, which surrounds bone, has two layers; the inner layer is specifically responsible for which of the following?
options: Attaching tendons and ligaments to bone through Sharpey's fibers
Providing nutrition to cortical bone through nutrient arteries
Acting as the outer fibrous layer with typical fibroblasts
Forming the epiphyseal plate for longitudinal growth
Contains osteoprogenitor cells giving rise to osteoblasts for appositional growth

questions.question: Respiratory distress syndrome in premature infants primarily results from:
questions.explanation: Respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) in premature infants primarily results from insufficient surfactant production by immature type II pneumocytes. Without adequate surfactant, alveoli collapse during expiration, requiring greater effort for breathing. Treatment includes surfactant replacement therapy and respiratory support.

Fibers from the cervical region travel with fasciculus cuneatus to form the cuneocerebellar tract. They exit through the inferior cerebellar peduncle. This pathway conveys upper limb proprioceptive information.
questions.question: The cuneocerebellar tract carries information from which region?

questions.explanation: The palatal component of the intermaxillary segment forms the triangular primary palate. Cranially, the intermaxillary segment is continuous with the rostral part of the nasal septum formed by the frontonasal prominence. The primary palate forms only a small part of the adult hard palate.
questions.question: The primary palate is formed from which component of the intermaxillary segment?

questions.explanation: After 90-degree clockwise rotation (viewed from above), the stomach's original dorsal border becomes the left surface and forms the greater curvature. The original ventral border becomes the right surface and forms the lesser curvature. The original left surface becomes anterior, and the original right surface becomes posterior. This rotation explains the vagal nerve distribution.
questions.question: The stomach's original dorsal border becomes which surface after rotation?
Proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) cells have numerous apical microvilli (brush border) and extensive basolateral infoldings. These adaptations are designed for:
questions.explanation: The PCT reabsorbs approximately 65% of the glomerular filtrate — including virtually all glucose and amino acids, most sodium, water, potassium, and bicarbonate. The brush border greatly increases the apical surface area, while basolateral infoldings and abundant mitochondria support the energy-intensive Na+/K+-ATPase-driven active transport. PCT cells are the most metabolically active cells in the kidney.

Vitamin D deficiency impairs intestinal calcium absorption and bone mineralization. Without adequate calcium and phosphate, osteoblasts continue to produce osteoid but it cannot be mineralized, accumulating as wide seams of unmineralized matrix. In children, the epiphyseal plate also fails to mineralize properly causing characteristic bowing of weight-bearing bones and epiphyseal widening in rickets. In adults the same osteoid accumulation causes bone pain and stress fractures of osteomalacia. The tetracycline labeling distance is reduced in osteomalacia.
questions.question: Vitamin D deficiency in children causes rickets while in adults it causes osteomalacia. The underlying histological defect common to both is which of the following?
options: Decreased osteoclast activity causing excessive bone density
Increased osteoblast apoptosis reducing bone formation
Inflammatory destruction of bone collagen matrix
Unmineralized osteoid accumulation from impaired bone mineralization
Complete absence of osteoid synthesis by osteoblasts

questions.explanation: Principal cells (most numerous in collecting duct) have aldosterone-regulated ENaC channels for Na+ reabsorption and ROMK channels for K+ secretion; ADH-regulated aquaporin-2 insertion mediates water reabsorption. Intercalated cells manage acid-base balance: Type A intercalated cells secrete H+ (via H+/K+-ATPase and H+-ATPase) and reabsorb HCO3- for acid excretion. Type B intercalated cells secrete HCO3- and reabsorb H+ for base excretion. This functional specialization is critical for renal acid-base regulation.
options: Principal cells reabsorb H+; intercalated cells reabsorb Na+
Both cell types perform identical functions
Principal cells secrete aldosterone; intercalated cells secrete ADH
Principal cells are responsible for potassium reabsorption only
questions.question: Principal cells and intercalated cells are the two main cell types of the collecting duct. Which statement correctly distinguishes their functions?
Multicystic dysplastic kidney is characterized by:
questions.explanation: Multicystic dysplastic kidney (MCDK) is characterized by multiple non-communicating cysts of varying sizes completely replacing normal kidney tissue. It is usually unilateral and non-functional. MCDK results from early ureteric bud obstruction or failure of induction between ureteric bud and metanephric blastema. The contralateral kidney undergoes compensatory hypertrophy. Bilateral MCDK is incompatible with life.

questions.question: Which cranial nerves have nuclei in the mesencephalon basal plate?
questions.explanation: The somatic efferent nuclei in the basal plate are CN3 and CN4, which supply extraocular muscles. CN3 also contains the Edinger-Westphal nucleus. These motor nuclei are medially placed in the tegmentum.

questions.question: The inferior petrosal sinus runs in which anatomical location?
questions.explanation: The inferior petrosal sinus runs in the petrooccipital fissure at the junction of the petrous temporal bone and basilar occipital bone in the posterior cranial fossa. It drains the cavernous sinus into the internal jugular vein at the jugular foramen. This sinus is clinically important as a route for catheter sampling of pituitary hormones (for diagnosing Cushing's disease) and as a potential pathway for infection spread from the middle ear or mastoid to the cavernous sinus.

Myelination is a function of Schwann cells in axons outside the spinal cord. The portion within the SC is myelinated by oligodendrocytes. This division of labor distinguishes peripheral from central myelination.
questions.question: Schwann cells myelinate axons in which location?
The septum primum grows from the roof of the common atrium toward which structure?
questions.explanation: At the end of the fourth week, a sickle-shaped crest (septum primum) grows from the roof of the common atrium into the lumen. The two limbs of this septum extend toward the endocardial cushions in the atrioventricular canal. The opening between the septum primum and endocardial cushions is called the ostium primum.

questions.question: Rexez's laminae number how many zones?
questions.explanation: Rexed found that spinal cord cell clusters are arranged into 10 zones or laminae (I-X). This replaced the older nuclear terminology. Each lamina has specific functions and connections.

If splitting of monozygotic twins occurs at the 2-cell stage, they will have separate placentas, separate amniotic cavities, and separate chorionic cavities. If splitting occurs at the early blastocyst stage, they have a common placenta and common chorionic cavity but separate amniotic cavities.
questions.question: Monozygotic twins with separate placentas result from splitting at which stage?

questions.explanation: Red bone marrow fills the spaces of cancellous bone and is the site of hematopoiesis — the continuous production of all formed elements of blood: erythrocytes, leukocytes, and megakaryocytes which produce platelets. Yellow marrow (fat-filled) predominates in adult long bone shafts but can revert to active red marrow during increased demand such as severe anemia or hemorrhage.
options: Mineral storage exclusively without any cellular function
Hematopoiesis — production of erythrocytes, leukocytes, and platelets
Synthesis of cortical bone matrix as the primary source
Production of cartilage matrix for endochondral ossification
Secretion of parathyroid hormone to regulate blood calcium
questions.question: The bone marrow housed in cancellous bone serves which of the following essential functions?

questions.explanation: Wait — G-cells are enteroendocrine cells that secrete gastrin. Secretin is produced by S-cells in the duodenum. Gastrin stimulates parietal cells to secrete HCl and promotes gastric motility. This is a key distinction in GIT endocrinology. Answer: D (Gastrin).
questions.question: G-cells of the stomach primarily secrete which hormone that stimulates gastric acid production?
On day 8, the embryoblast differentiates into which two layers?
questions.explanation: On day 8, the embryoblast differentiates into a hypoblast layer (adjacent to the blastocystic cavity) and an epiblast layer (adjacent to the amniotic cavity). The epiblast will give rise to all three germ layers of the embryo, while the hypoblast contributes to extraembryonic structures.

The posterior cerebral artery runs around midbrain supplying medial surfaces of occipital and temporal lobes. It also sends branches to upper midbrain and lower diencephalon. Occlusion can cause visual field defects.
questions.question: The posterior cerebral artery supplies which brain lobes?

options: Skeletal (striated, voluntary), Cardiac (striated, involuntary), Smooth (non-striated, involuntary)
Skeletal (smooth, voluntary), Cardiac (striated, voluntary), Smooth (striated, involuntary)
All three types are striated and voluntary
Cardiac (smooth, voluntary), Skeletal (striated, involuntary), Smooth (striated, voluntary)
questions.question: The three main types of muscle tissue are classified functionally as voluntary or involuntary and structurally as striated or smooth. Which of the following correctly pairs each type with its characteristics?
questions.explanation: The three muscle types are: skeletal muscle which is striated and voluntary with quick forceful contractions under conscious control; cardiac muscle which is striated and involuntary with vigorous rhythmic contractions; and smooth muscle which is non-striated and involuntary with slow sustained contractions in visceral organs. This classification reflects both the structural organization of myofilaments and the neural control systems involved.

questions.question: Ventral motor roots form approximately in which week?
questions.explanation: The axons of the basal plate neurons coalesce and exit through the marginal layer to form the ventral motor root about the 4th week. These roots carry motor impulses to skeletal muscles. They combine with dorsal sensory roots to form spinal nerves.

questions.question: Which cranial nerves emerge from the medulla?
questions.explanation: The glossopharyngeal (IX), vagus (X), accessory (XI), and hypoglossal (XII) cranial nerves emerge from the medulla oblongata. The hypoglossal nerve emerges between the pyramid and olive, while IX, X, and XI emerge posterior to the olive.

Some vestibular fibers project to cerebellum via inferior cerebellar peduncle to the flocculonodular lobe. This is important for balance and coordination. The cerebellum integrates vestibular information.
questions.question: Vestibular fibers reach the cerebellum via which peduncle?

questions.explanation: Visual stimuli are represented on retina in reverse. At optic chiasma, medial (nasal retina) fibers cross to the contralateral side. This allows each hemisphere to process the opposite visual field.
questions.question: In the visual pathway, fibers from the nasal retina project to which side?

questions.explanation: Bone has three distinct cell types with complementary roles: osteoblasts are active matrix-synthesizing cells that produce osteoid (unmineralized matrix); osteocytes are mature osteoblasts entrapped in lacunae that maintain the matrix and act as mechanosensors; and osteoclasts are large multinucleated cells (monocyte-derived) that resorb bone through acid and lysosomal enzyme secretion. The balance between osteoblast and osteoclast activity determines bone mass.
questions.question: The three cell types found in bone tissue and their respective primary functions are best described by which of the following?
options: Osteoblasts (synthesize osteoid), osteocytes (maintain matrix), and osteoclasts (resorb bone)
Fibroblasts, macrophages, and adipocytes performing structural roles
Osteoblasts and osteocytes performing identical functions with no resorption cells

questions.explanation: Elastic arteries (conducting arteries like the aorta, pulmonary trunk, and common carotid) have a tunica media composed of 40–70 concentric layers of fenestrated elastic lamellae with smooth muscle cells and collagen between them. This elastic composition allows the artery to expand during systole and recoil during diastole — the 'Windkessel' effect that maintains diastolic blood pressure. Muscular arteries have predominantly smooth muscle in the media.
questions.question: Elastic arteries (e.g., the aorta) are distinguished from muscular arteries by the composition of their tunica media, which contains:
Hematopoiesis first occurs in which embryonic location?
questions.explanation: Hematopoiesis (blood cell formation) first occurs in the yolk sac wall and allantois during the third week. It later shifts to the liver (6 weeks), then to the spleen (12 weeks), and finally to the bone marrow (which becomes the primary site by 28 weeks and throughout life).

questions.question: The choroid plexus extends into which parts of the lateral ventricle?
questions.explanation: The choroid plexus of the lateral ventricle extends through the body, trigone (atrium), and inferior horn, but is absent from the anterior and posterior horns. It enters through the choroid fissure, the cleft between the fornix and thalamus where pia mater invaginates into the ventricle. The choroid plexus is continuous with that of the third ventricle through the interventricular foramen. In the inferior horn, the choroid plexus lies in the choroid fissure between the fimbria and the stria terminalis.

questions.question: At what gestational week does the lens vesicle separate from the surface ectoderm?
questions.explanation: By the 5th week of development, the lens vesicle has completely separated from the surface ectoderm and lies free within the rim of the optic cup. This separation allows the lens vesicle to develop independently while maintaining its position. The lens vesicle then undergoes further differentiation to form the definitive lens structure.

A vitelline fistula represents complete persistence of the vitelline duct, creating a communication between the ileum and umbilicus. Meconium (intestinal contents) oozes out of the umbilicus. This requires surgical repair to close the fistula and restore intestinal continuity. It differs from a urachal fistula, which would drain urine.
questions.question: A vitelline fistula is characterized by:

questions.explanation: RET gene mutations are associated with Hirschsprung disease. RET is a tyrosine kinase receptor involved in neural crest cell migration. Mutations impair the migration of neural crest cells into the distal colon, resulting in absence of ganglia. Genetic testing can help diagnose and counsel families about recurrence risks.
questions.question: The RET gene mutation is associated with:
The extreme capsule is located between which structures?
questions.explanation: The extreme capsule is a thin layer of white matter located between the insula medially and the claustrum laterally. It contains association fibers connecting different cortical regions, particularly frontal and temporal areas. The extreme capsule, along with the external capsule and internal capsule, comprises the white matter system surrounding the basal ganglia. Lateral to the claustrum lies the external capsule, separating the claustrum from the putamen. These capsular systems contain various association and projection fibers.

options: They secrete hormones into the bloodstream
They store glycogen like endocrine cells
They secrete bile into the bile canaliculi,
questions.question: The liver is described as a modified exocrine gland. This classification reflects which feature of hepatocytes?
questions.explanation: Hepatocytes function as exocrine secretory cells by producing bile — approximately 600–1000 mL daily — which they secrete into bile canaliculi. Bile drains through the intrahepatic and extrahepatic biliary tree into the duodenum where it aids fat digestion. This secretory product (bile) traveling through a duct system to a body surface (duodenum) is the defining characteristic of an exocrine gland. Hepatocytes also have endocrine functions (producing plasma proteins, clotting factors) making the liver a uniquely multifunctional organ.

Brush cells (tuft cells) are solitary chemosensory cells found in the respiratory epithelium, including the trachea and bronchi. They have a characteristic tuft of blunt microvilli on their apical surface and express taste receptor proteins (T2R bitter taste receptors). When activated by bitter compounds (bacterial metabolites, irritants), they trigger rapid cholinergic reflexes causing bronchoconstriction and mucus secretion as a defense mechanism.
questions.question: The tracheal epithelium contains Basal cells, goblet cells, and ciliated cells. Which additional specialized cell type is found in the tracheal epithelium that monitors airway chemicals?

questions.explanation: Inductive forces from pigmented outer optic cup layer cause surrounding lateral plate mesoderm to form choroid (vascularized, pigmented) and sclera (tough outer layer). Sclera is continuous with dura around optic nerve.
questions.question: The choroid and sclera are formed from which tissue?

questions.explanation: The reticular formation consists of more than 100,000 brainstem nuclei. These nuclei are divided into three subgroups: paramedian nuclear group, central/medial column group (magnocellular), and lateral group (parvocellular column). They acquire different names in different parts of the brainstem.
questions.question: The reticular formation consists of approximately how many nuclei?

questions.explanation: The paraxial mesoderm gives rise to all voluntary muscles of the craniofacial region, the floor of the brain case, a small portion of the occipital region, dermis and connective tissues in the dorsal head region, and meninges caudal to the prosencephalon.
questions.question: The paraxial mesoderm gives rise to which head structure?
The inferior salivatory nucleus provides parasympathetic innervation to which gland?
questions.explanation: The inferior salivatory nucleus provides parasympathetic innervation exclusively to the parotid gland via the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX). Preganglionic fibers travel in the tympanic nerve (Jacobson's nerve), then as the lesser petrosal nerve, synapsing in the otic ganglion. Postganglionic fibers join the auriculotemporal nerve to reach the parotid gland. Parasympathetic stimulation increases parotid secretion, producing watery saliva rich in enzymes.

DNA replication occurs during the S (synthesis) phase of interphase; if replication is incomplete or damaged, checkpoint mechanisms arrest the cell in S phase or at the S/G2 boundary. Checkpoints prevent progression to mitosis until DNA integrity is confirmed. Arrest in S phase occurs when replication forks stall or when DNA damage is detected during replication.
questions.question: During cell cycle arrest, a cell accumulates in which phase if it fails to complete DNA replication?
The accessory nerve has which two roots?
questions.explanation: The accessory nerve (XI) has cranial (from medulla) and spinal (from C1-C5) roots both with SVE fibers. Spinal root supplies trapezius and sternocleidomastoid. Cranial root joins vagus.

Filtration slits between podocyte foot processes are bridged by thin protein structures called slit diaphragms, composed primarily of nephrin and podocin. The slit diaphragm acts as the final filtration barrier, preventing proteins above 8nm from passing into Bowman's space. Mutations in nephrin (NPHS1 gene) cause congenital nephrotic syndrome with complete loss of slit diaphragms.
questions.question: Podocytes are specialized cells of the visceral epithelium of Bowman's capsule. The spaces between their foot processes are called filtration slits, which are bridged by:

questions.explanation: Distinct basal and alar plates, representing motor and sensory areas respectively, are found on each side of the midline in the rhombencephalon and mesencephalon, separated by the sulcus limitans. The basal plate is ventral (motor), and the alar plate is dorsal (sensory).
questions.question: The sulcus limitans in the brainstem separates which two functional areas?
The Golgi apparatus is primarily responsible for which of the following cellular functions?
questions.explanation: The Golgi apparatus receives proteins from the rough ER, modifies them (glycosylation, phosphorylation, proteolytic cleavage), sorts them, and packages them into vesicles directed to the cell surface (secretion), lysosomes, or other organelles. It functions as the cell's postal sorting and processing center. The 'cis' face receives from the ER while the 'trans' face dispatches vesicles.
options: Sorting, modifying, and packaging proteins for secretion
Generating cellular energy through oxidative phosphorylation
Detoxification of drugs and metabolic byproducts
Rostral to notochord and ventral to prosencephalon
questions.explanation: Face development depends on inductive influences from two organizing centers. The prosencephalic organizing center (POC) is located rostral to the notochord and ventral to the prosencephalon. The rhombencephalic organizing center (ROC) is located ventral to the rhombencephalon.
questions.question: The prosencephalic organizing center (POC) is located in which position?
The circle of Willis provides which benefit?
questions.explanation: The circle of Willis provides collateral circulation if one vessel is occluded. It connects anterior and posterior circulations. Anatomical variations are common. Complete circles occur in only about 50% of people.

questions.question: The yolk sac is connected to the midgut by which structure?
questions.explanation: The yolk sac is connected to the midgut by a narrow yolk stalk (also called the vitelline duct). The yolk sac is a pear-shaped remnant of about 5 mm in diameter by 20 weeks, after which it is very small and usually not visible. It can persist as Meckel's diverticulum.

questions.question: The most common cell type in the brain is which?
questions.explanation: Astrocytes are the most common cells in the brain, outnumbering neurons 10:1. They provide metabolic support, form blood-brain barrier, and regulate extracellular environment. They are essential for neuronal function.

Parallel fibers are the unmyelinated axons of granule cells that ascend to the molecular layer and bifurcate, running parallel to the cerebellar folia (perpendicular to Purkinje cell dendritic trees). Each parallel fiber synapses with hundreds of Purkinje cells along its length, while each Purkinje cell receives input from approximately 200,000 parallel fibers. This arrangement allows widespread distribution of mossy fiber input and enables the cerebellum to integrate diverse information for motor coordination.
questions.question: Parallel fibers in the cerebellar cortex are formed by axons of which cells?
The first two ossicles (malleus and incus) derive from which arch?
questions.explanation: The first two ossicles (malleus and incus) derive from cartilage of 1st pharyngeal arch. The stapes is from the 2nd arch. The tympanic cavity gradually envelopes these ossicles.

The pars orbitalis (orbital part) is the most anterior portion of the inferior frontal gyrus, located anterior to the anterior horizontal ramus of the lateral sulcus and above the orbital surface of the frontal lobe. While the pars opercularis and triangularis comprise Broca's area, the pars orbitalis is more involved in cognitive and emotional processing as part of the orbitofrontal cortex. This region participates in decision-making, impulse control, and processing reward-related information.
questions.question: The pars orbitalis is the most anterior part of which gyrus?
The thyroid gland reaches its final position in the neck during which week?
questions.explanation: The thyroid gland reaches its final position in the 7th week in the neck, anterior to the trachea. The two lobes become connected by an isthmus attached to the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th tracheal rings. The thyroglossal duct becomes solid and normally disappears as the gland descends.

questions.question: A 45-year-old develops Barrett's esophagus. Histologically, this condition is characterized by replacement of normal esophageal epithelium with:
options: Intestinal-type columnar epithelium with goblet cells
questions.explanation: Barrett's esophagus is a metaplastic condition where the normal non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium of the esophagus is replaced by intestinal-type simple columnar epithelium with goblet cells (specialized intestinal metaplasia). This occurs due to chronic gastroesophageal acid reflux and carries a risk of progression to esophageal adenocarcinoma.

Kupffer cells are fixed macrophages lining the hepatic sinusoids. Their strategic position allows them to phagocytose particulate matter, old red blood cells, bacteria, and endotoxins arriving via the portal circulation from the intestine. They are the largest pool of fixed macrophages in the body, playing a critical role in immune surveillance and iron recycling from hemoglobin breakdown.
questions.question: Kupffer cells are resident macrophages of the liver. Their location within hepatic sinusoids allows them to perform which primary function?
Which cortical area is responsible for understanding written language?
questions.explanation: The angular gyrus (Brodmann area 39) in the inferior parietal lobe is crucial for reading and understanding written language, integrating visual word recognition with language comprehension. It connects visual cortex (recognizing letter shapes) with Wernicke's area (language comprehension). Lesions of the angular gyrus in the dominant hemisphere cause alexia (inability to read) and agraphia (inability to write), as well as elements of Gerstmann syndrome including acalculia and left-right disorientation.

questions.question: A cell produces large quantities of steroid hormones. Which organelle is most likely most abundant in this cell's cytoplasm?
questions.explanation: Smooth ER (SER) is the primary site of lipid synthesis, steroid hormone biosynthesis, and detoxification. Steroid-secreting cells (adrenocortical cells, Leydig cells, luteal cells) are therefore rich in SER. Unlike rough ER, SER lacks ribosomes and appears smooth in electron micrographs. The agranular appearance reflects its functional specialization for lipid metabolism rather than protein synthesis.

The facial colliculus is formed by the facial nerve (CN VII) wrapping around the abducens nucleus (CN VI) before exiting the brainstem. This occurs at the level of the lower pons. The facial nucleus is located in the ventrolateral pontine tegmentum.
questions.question: The facial colliculus in the floor of the fourth ventricle is formed by which nerve?
During which weeks do primary ossification centers appear in the skeleton?
questions.explanation: Primary ossification centers appear in the skeleton (skull and long bones) during 9-12 weeks. During this period, there is also rapid growth in body length, decrease in relative head growth compared to earlier stages, and beginning of erythropoiesis by the liver and spleen.

Genomic imprinting is an epigenetic phenomenon where certain genes are expressed in a parent-of-origin-specific manner. Some genes are only expressed from the maternal allele, others only from the paternal allele. Abnormalities in imprinting can cause disorders like Prader-Willi and Angelman syndromes.
questions.question: Genomic imprinting refers to which phenomenon?

questions.explanation: Chorionic villus sampling (CVS) has a risk of fetal loss of approximately 1%. Trophoblast cells are obtained by needle through the mother's abdominal and uterine wall under ultrasound guidance. There is also a risk of limb defects if the procedure is performed too early (before 10 weeks).
questions.question: Chorionic villus sampling (CVS) has what risk of fetal loss?

questions.explanation: Several neurotransmitters are involved in different basal ganglia pathways including acetylcholine, dopamine, glutamate, and serotonin. This chemical complexity allows fine motor control. Neurotransmitter imbalances cause movement disorders.
questions.question: Which neurotransmitters are involved in basal ganglia pathways?
Upper motor neuron signs include which features?
questions.explanation: Upper motor neuron signs include spastic paralysis, hyperreflexia, Babinski sign and clonus. Lower motor neuron signs include flaccid paralysis and hyporeflexia. This distinction aids localization. UMN lesions are above anterior horn.

Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) is caused by mutations in PKD1 (encoding polycystin-1, chromosome 16 — 85% of cases) or PKD2 (encoding polycystin-2, chromosome 4 — 15% of cases).
