Polycystins are membrane proteins involved in mechanosensation, cell-cell and cell-matrix interactions, and fluid flow sensing. Their dysfunction causes collecting duct cells to proliferate and form cysts. ADPKD is the most common hereditary kidney disease, causing end-stage renal disease in 50% of patients by age 60.
questions.question: Polycystic kidney disease (PKD) causes progressive replacement of renal parenchyma by cysts. The autosomal dominant form (ADPKD) involves mutations in which genes?

questions.explanation: The caudal limb of the midgut loop gives rise to the lower portion of the ileum, cecum, appendix, ascending colon, and proximal 2/3 of the transverse colon. The cranial limb forms the distal duodenum, jejunum, and upper ileum. The hindgut forms the distal 1/3 of transverse colon through the upper anal canal.
questions.question: The caudal limb of the midgut loop gives rise to:
The anterior cerebral artery supplies which brain surfaces?
questions.explanation: The anterior cerebral artery supplies medial surfaces of frontal and parietal lobes rostral to parieto-occipital sulcus. It divides into pericallosal and callosomarginal arteries. Occlusion causes restricted motor/sensory deficits.
options: Medial surfaces of frontal and parietal lobes

questions.explanation: Fracture healing proceeds through: (1) hematoma and inflammatory phase, (2) soft callus phase where periosteal cells produce fibrocartilage bridging the gap via endochondral ossification, (3) hard callus phase where cartilage is replaced by woven bone, and (4) remodeling phase where woven bone is replaced by lamellar bone. Cells involved include osteocytes, osteoblasts, osteoclasts, and fibroblasts.
questions.question: A fracture that heals correctly undergoes a sequence that includes which stage where fibrocartilage temporarily bridges the fracture gap?
options: Inflammatory phase with neutrophil predominance only
Hard callus phase with lamellar bone formation only
Remodeling phase where osteoclasts remove excess bone
Primary bone healing without any cartilage formation
Fibrocartilage callus later replaced by woven bone via endochondral ossification

questions.explanation: Extraocular muscles form from the first three somitomeres (pre-otic head mesoderm). Each somitomere contributes specific muscles. They are innervated by cranial nerves III, IV, and VI.
questions.question: Extraocular muscles develop from which embryonic structures?
Failure of recanalization of the anal membrane results in:
questions.explanation: Failure of recanalization of the anal membrane, which normally occurs during the 9th week, results in imperforate anus. The anal membrane forms at the junction of the proctodeum (ectoderm) and hindgut (endoderm). Temporary occlusion by epithelial proliferation is normal, but failure of subsequent recanalization causes this anomaly.

questions.question: The thymus develops from which pharyngeal pouch?
questions.explanation: The thymus develops from the endoderm of the ventral part of the third pharyngeal pouch in the 5th week. It is large at birth, reaches full size at puberty, and shrinks in old age. It has both cranial (neck) and caudal (thorax) parts and is invaded by vascular mesoderm containing lymphoblasts.

questions.question: The processus vaginalis normally:
questions.explanation: The processus vaginalis, an evagination of peritoneum that precedes testicular descent through the inguinal canal, normally obliterates after testicular descent (except for portion covering testis = tunica vaginalis). Patent processus vaginalis allows communication between peritoneal cavity and scrotum, predisposing to indirect inguinal hernia or hydrocele. Obliteration usually occurs shortly before or after birth.

Congenital lung cysts are formed by dilation of terminal or larger bronchi. These cysts may be single or multiple and can cause respiratory compromise if large. They result from abnormal branching morphogenesis or obstruction during development. Large cysts may require surgical resection.
questions.question: Congenital lung cysts are formed by:

questions.explanation: Mammary glands are modified and highly specialized apocrine sweat glands. They develop from mammary buds that appear during the 6th week as solid downgrowths of epidermis. These buds give rise to secondary mammary buds that become lactiferous ducts and their branches.
questions.question: Mammary glands are modified forms of:
The vestibulocochlear nerve divisions are both which component?
questions.explanation: Both cochlear and vestibular divisions of CN VIII are special somatic afferent for hearing and balance. They carry information from inner ear receptors. The nerve enters at the cerebellopontine angle.

The hippocampal commissure (psalterium or commissure of the fornix) is a thin sheet of transverse fibers connecting the two crura of the fornix inferior to the splenium of the corpus callosum. While called the hippocampal commissure, it actually connects the fornices and may exchange some fibers between hippocampi. It is a small commissure compared to the corpus callosum and anterior commissure. The hippocampal commissure is part of the complex white matter architecture of the limbic system beneath the splenium.
questions.question: The hippocampal commissure (psalterium) connects which structures?
How many functional components can cranial nerve fibers belong to?
questions.explanation: There are seven functional components: somatic efferent, special visceral efferent, general visceral efferent, general visceral afferent, special visceral afferent, general somatic afferent, special somatic afferent. Each has specific nuclei.

After the 13th week, bile entering the duodenum gives meconium its characteristic dark green color. Bile formation by hepatic cells begins around the 12th week. Meconium accumulates in the fetal intestines throughout gestation and is normally passed within the first 24-48 hours after birth. Delayed passage may indicate intestinal obstruction.
questions.question: Bile entering the duodenum gives meconium its characteristic color around:
The seminal vesicles prostate gland and bulbourethral glands are male accessory sex glands. Their primary contribution to semen is which of the following?
options: Producing spermatozoa as an additional sperm source
Filtering sperm removing abnormal cells before ejaculation
Providing oxygen for sperm metabolism during ejaculation
questions.explanation: Male accessory sex glands contribute secretions forming semen: seminal vesicles provide approximately 60% of semen volume containing fructose as sperm energy source, prostaglandins that stimulate female reproductive tract contractions, and coagulation proteins; the prostate contributes approximately 30% with zinc for sperm motility, PSA protease that liquefies semen, and acid phosphatase; bulbourethral glands secrete mucus neutralizing urethral acidity and providing pre-ejaculatory lubrication.

questions.question: Tetralogy of Fallot includes all of the following features EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Tetralogy of Fallot consists of four cardiovascular alterations: pulmonary stenosis (narrow ventricle outflow region), large ventricular septal defect, overriding aorta that arises directly above the septal defect, and right ventricular hypertrophy. Atrial septal defect is not part of this tetralogy.

options: Simple columnar with tall cells; lacks submucosa
questions.question: The gallbladder wall is lined by which type of epithelium and is notable for lacking which layer present in other parts of the GIT?
questions.explanation: The gallbladder mucosa is lined by simple columnar epithelium with tall cells specialized for water absorption (concentrating bile). Importantly, the gallbladder lacks a muscularis mucosae — bile contents are directly adjacent to the lamina propria without this thin muscle layer. It also lacks a submucosa. Rokitansky-Aschoff sinuses are mucosal herniations into the muscularis seen in chronic cholecystitis.

The kidneys "ascend" from the pelvis to the abdomen primarily between weeks 6-9, reaching their final position by the 9th week. This apparent ascent occurs through disproportionate growth of the embryo, particularly in the lumbar and sacral regions. During ascent, the kidneys rotate 90 degrees medially and acquire new blood supply from progressively higher aortic branches.
questions.question: The kidneys ascend from the pelvis primarily between which weeks?
The spiral ganglion of the cochlea is formed by migration of cells from:
questions.explanation: Ganglion cells of cranial nerve VIII migrate along the coils of the membranous cochlea to form the spiral ganglion. Peripheral processes from this ganglion extend to the organ of Corti and terminate on hair cells. Central processes form the cochlear nerve that transmits auditory information to the brain.

Prune belly syndrome (Eagle-Barrett syndrome) is characterized by deficiency of abdominal wall muscles, giving the abdomen a wrinkled, prune-like appearance. It is associated with urinary tract abnormalities including megacystis, hydroureter, and cryptorchidism. The condition occurs almost exclusively in males and has a complex, poorly understood etiology.
questions.question: Prune belly syndrome is associated with:

questions.explanation: Juxtamedullary nephrons (approximately 15% of nephrons) have long loops of Henle that penetrate deep into the medulla. Their long ascending limbs actively transport more NaCl, creating a deeper and steeper medullary osmotic gradient. This allows the formation of highly concentrated urine when ADH is present. The vasa recta, which run alongside these loops, maintain this gradient via countercurrent exchange.
questions.question: The kidney has cortical and juxtamedullary nephrons. Juxtamedullary nephrons have longer loops of Henle that extend deeper into the medulla. Their primary functional advantage is:
The ratio of granular to pyramidal cells in any cortical layer primarily depends on what factor?
questions.explanation: The ratio of granular to pyramidal cells in any cortical layer depends on the functional modality it subserves, distinguishing sensory from motor cortices. Primary sensory cortices (visual, auditory, somatosensory) have abundant granule cells in layer IV for receiving thalamic input (granular cortex). Primary motor cortex has few granule cells but many pyramidal cells in layer V for output functions (agranular cortex). Association cortices have intermediate characteristics, with balanced populations of both cell types.

options: Stimulating thyroid hormone production by follicular cells
Raising blood calcium by stimulating osteoclasts
Regulating sodium reabsorption in the kidney
Mediating the stress response through cortisol release
Suppresses bone resorption and increases calcification, lowering blood calcium
questions.question: Parafollicular C cells of the thyroid gland produce calcitonin which has which physiological action?
questions.explanation: Parafollicular C cells scattered between thyroid follicles produce calcitonin which lowers blood calcium by inhibiting osteoclast activity reducing bone resorption and promoting calcium deposition in bone. It opposes parathyroid hormone action. While important pharmacologically for treating Paget's disease and hypercalcemia, calcitonin's physiological role in human calcium homeostasis is less critical than that of PTH.

questions.question: Which artery typically gives rise to the posterior spinal arteries?
questions.explanation: The vertebral artery, which typically arises from the subclavian artery, gives rise to several branches including the posterior spinal arteries. Other branches include the anterior spinal artery, lateral medullary artery, and posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA). The two vertebral arteries ascend through the cervical vertebrae and unite at the pontomedullary junction to form the basilar artery.
The spinal cord develops from neural tube caudal to 4th pair of somites. Neuroepithelial cells line the wall giving rise to neurons and macroglial cells. The rostral neural tube becomes the brain.
questions.question: The spinal cord develops from neural tube caudal to which somite pair?
Neural systems serve how many general functions?
questions.explanation: Neural systems serve three general functions: sensory systems, motor systems, and association systems. Sensory systems gather information. Motor systems produce responses. Association systems integrate and process. ## NEURULATION AND ANOMALIES

The internal elastic lamina is most prominent in muscular (distributing) arteries such as the femoral, radial, and coronary arteries. It appears as a wavy, bright eosinophilic band on H&E staining and stains black with Verhoeff elastic stain. Muscular arteries also have an external elastic lamina separating the media from the adventitia. These landmarks help distinguish muscular arteries from elastic arteries in histological sections.
questions.question: The internal elastic lamina is a prominent layer separating the tunica intima from the tunica media. It is best developed in which type of artery?

questions.explanation: Renal columns (columns of Bertin) are inward projections of cortical tissue that separate adjacent medullary pyramids. They contain interlobar arteries and veins, as well as cortical nephrons extending into the columns. Prominent renal columns can be mistaken for renal masses on imaging — an important radiological consideration. They represent the normal infolding of cortex between the lobes of the kidney.
questions.question: The renal medulla is organized into pyramids separated by renal columns. Renal columns (columns of Bertin) are composed of:
options: Medullary tissue extending toward the cortex
Inward extensions of cortical tissue between
Mucus layer secreted by surface mucous cells
Bicarbonate secreted beneath the mucous layer
Tight junctions between surface epithelial cells
questions.question: The mucosa of the stomach is protected from self-digestion by a gastric mucosal barrier. Which component is NOT part of this barrier?
questions.explanation: The gastric mucosal barrier consists of: mucus layer (traps bicarbonate), bicarbonate secretion (creates alkaline microenvironment at mucosa surface), tight junctions (prevent acid backflow), rapid cell renewal (replaces damaged cells), and rich blood supply. Pepsinogen granules in chief cells are precursors to the digestive enzyme pepsin — they are part of the digestive mechanism, not the protective barrier. NSAIDs disrupt the barrier by inhibiting prostaglandin synthesis.

Each horn of the sinus venosus receives three veins: one vitelline vein (from the yolk sac), one umbilical vein (from the placenta), and one common cardinal vein (from the body wall). The sinus venosus is the first area of the heart to receive venous blood.
questions.question: How many veins join each horn of the sinus venosus?

questions.explanation: Corticopontine fibers arise from cortex passing through internal capsule: frontopontine through anterior limb. Others pass through retrolentiform part. They synapse with pontine nuclei in the crus
questions.question: Frontopontinecorticospinal fibers pass through which part of internal capsule?

questions.explanation: The adrenal medulla is derived from neural crest cells, specifically from sympathetic ganglion precursors. These cells migrate to the developing adrenal gland and differentiate into chromaffin cells that secrete epinephrine and norepinephrine. The adrenal cortex is derived from mesoderm.
questions.question: The adrenal medulla is derived from which embryonic source?
Gastrulation converts the bilaminar disc into a trilaminar disc during which week of development?
questions.explanation: Gastrulation is the process whereby the bilaminar germ disc is converted into a trilaminar germ disc during the 3rd week of development. This process begins with formation of the primitive streak and results in the differentiation of the three germ layers: ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm.

Congenital diaphragmatic hernia commonly occurs through a posterolateral defect in the diaphragm, most frequently on the left side. This defect results from incomplete fusion of the pleuroperitoneal membranes with other diaphragmatic components. The herniation causes the left lung to show hypoplasia due to compression by abdominal viscera.
questions.question: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia most commonly occurs through which defect?

questions.explanation: The mesentery of the small intestine acquires its final attachment line running obliquely from the duodenojejunal junction (left of L2 vertebra) to the ileocecal junction (right sacroiliac joint). This fan-shaped mesentery allows mobility of the jejunum and ileum. The attachment line changes during fixation as the ascending and descending colons become retroperitoneal.
questions.question: The mesentery of the small intestine acquires its final attachment line between:

questions.explanation: Volvulus (twisting) of the midgut can result from malrotation, which creates a narrow mesenteric base predisposing to twisting around the superior mesenteric artery. This can cause intestinal obstruction and ischemia. Midgut volvulus is a surgical emergency requiring prompt intervention to prevent bowel necrosis. It typically presents with bilious vomiting in infants.
questions.question: Volvulus of the midgut can result from:

questions.explanation: Renal hypoplasia is defined as a small kidney with reduced nephron number but otherwise normal architecture and function. It differs from a small kidney secondary to chronic disease (where architecture is abnormal). True hypoplasia results from reduced branching of the ureteric bud or inadequate metanephric mesenchyme. Bilateral hypoplasia can cause chronic kidney disease. Unilateral hypoplasia with contralateral compensatory hypertrophy is usually asymptomatic.
questions.question: Renal hypoplasia is defined as:

questions.explanation: The lienorenal (splenorenal) ligament connects the spleen to the left kidney and is derived from the dorsal mesogastrium. It contains the splenic vessels and the tail of the pancreas. Together with the gastrosplenic ligament, it forms the lateral boundary of the lesser sac. These ligaments must be divided during splenectomy.
questions.question: The lienorenal ligament connects:
Spina bifida results from failure of closure of which structure?
questions.explanation: Spina bifida results from failure of closure of the posterior (caudal) neuropore along with failure of the vertebral arches to fuse. Failure of the anterior (cranial) neuropore to close results in anencephaly. These conditions are collectively known as neural tube defects (NTDs).

questions.question: A student views a specimen and finds it cannot be examined directly because of its thickness. Which instrument is most appropriate to produce thin translucent sections?
questions.explanation: A microtome is the specialized instrument used to cut tissue blocks into thin sections (typically 3–10 μm) that allow light transmission for microscopy. The cryostat is a variant used for frozen sections. A centrifuge separates components and an autoclave sterilizes, neither producing histological sections.

Bronchopulmonary segments are established by the formation of tertiary (segmental) bronchi. There are ten on the right and eight on the left. Each segment represents a functional unit of lung tissue supplied by a segmental bronchus and its branches.
questions.question: Bronchopulmonary segments are established by formation of:

questions.explanation: The duodenum uniquely has Brunner's glands located in its submucosa. These glands secrete alkaline mucus to neutralize the acidic chyme entering from the stomach. The esophagus also has glands in its submucosa (esophageal glands proper), but Brunner's glands are the most clinically significant submucosal glands in the GIT.
questions.question: A histological preparation shows a GIT wall segment where the submucosa contains glands. This is a unique feature of which region?
A tissue section examined under polarized light shows alternating bright and dark layers corresponding to perpendicular collagen fiber orientation. This is most characteristic of which structure?
options: Reticular fiber networks in lymph nodes
questions.explanation: In bone osteons, collagen fibers within adjacent lamellae are oriented at right angles to one another, creating anisotropy detectable with polarized light. Lamellae with fibers parallel to the polarizer appear dark (extinct) while those with perpendicular fibers appear bright, producing the characteristic alternating pattern. This structural arrangement gives bone its mechanical strength and resistance to multidirectional stress.

Merkel cells are sensitive mechanoreceptors essential for light touch sensation and discrimination of shapes and textures. They appear in human fetal skin at 18 weeks of gestation. These cells are joined by desmosomes to keratinocytes and contact sensory nerve fibers at their basolateral surfaces.
questions.question: Merkel cells are primarily associated with:
The primitive streak first appears at which location on the embryonic disc?
questions.explanation: At the beginning of the 3rd week, epiblast cells proliferate and migrate to the median plane of the germ disc, forming the primitive streak. As the primitive streak elongates, its cranial part forms the primitive node. The primitive groove appears in the streak and is continuous with the primitive pit.

questions.question: Ependymal cells are the final derivative of which cells?
questions.explanation: Ependymal cells are the final derivative of neuroepithelial cells and line the ventricles and central canal. They are cuboidal and low columnar in shape. These cells play a role in CSF production and circulation.

A compound microscope employs both an eyepiece (ocular) lens and an objective lens to produce a magnified image. The eyepiece typically provides 10× magnification, while objective lenses vary from 4× to 100×. This two-lens system distinguishes it from a simple single-lens microscope.
questions.question: A light microscope that uses two sets of lenses — an eyepiece and an objective — to magnify specimens is correctly described as which of the following?
Myoglobin in skeletal muscle primarily serves which of the following functions?
questions.explanation: Myoglobin is a single-chain oxygen-binding heme protein in muscle cells that stores oxygen and facilitates its diffusion from the sarcolemma to mitochondria. This oxygen reserve allows continued aerobic metabolism during brief periods of reduced blood flow during contraction. Type I slow oxidative muscle fibers are rich in myoglobin appearing red while type II fast glycolytic fibers have less myoglobin appearing white.
options: Synthesizing ATP directly through oxidative phosphorylation
Regulating calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Storing and diffusing oxygen within muscle cells to support aerobic metabolism
Acting as a structural protein anchoring actin to the Z disc
Catalyzing the breakdown of glycogen for anaerobic glycolysis

questions.question: Which cerebellar peduncle contains the major efferent pathway from deep cerebellar nuclei?
questions.explanation: The superior cerebellar peduncle is the major efferent pathway from the cerebellum, carrying fibers primarily from the dentate and interposed nuclei to the contralateral red nucleus and thalamus. These fibers decussate in the lower midbrain at the level of the inferior colliculus. The superior cerebellar peduncle also contains some afferent fibers from the ventral spinocerebellar tract and trigeminal mesencephalic nucleus.

The epithelium of most of the male urethra is derived from endoderm of the urogenital sinus. Only the terminal part in the glans penis is derived from a solid cord of ectodermal cells that grows inward. The connective tissue and smooth muscle are derived from splanchnic mesenchyme.
questions.question: The epithelium of most of the male urethra is derived from:

questions.explanation: Normal ascent of horseshoe kidney is prevented by the root of the inferior mesenteric artery, which acts as a mechanical barrier to the fused kidneys. The kidneys typically lie in the lower lumbar region with the isthmus (fusion point) at or near the level of the IMA origin. Despite their low position, horseshoe kidneys usually function normally.
questions.question: Horseshoe kidney ascent is prevented by:

questions.explanation: Lingual tonsils located in the lamina propria at the root of the tongue are covered by stratified squamous epithelium reflecting their location within the oral cavity where mechanical abrasion from food necessitates a protective stratified squamous surface. This is the same epithelial type as palatine tonsils. In contrast pharyngeal tonsils have respiratory pseudostratified ciliated epithelium reflecting their nasopharyngeal location.
options: Glandular columnar epithelium with goblet cells
questions.question: Lingual tonsils located at the base of the tongue are covered by which epithelium?

questions.explanation: The ECM is the non-cellular material of connective tissue consisting of protein fiber networks (collagen for tensile strength, elastic for extensibility, reticular for support scaffolding) and ground substance (proteoglycans providing hydration and compressive resistance, adhesive glycoproteins like fibronectin and laminin). The composition varies among connective tissue types to fulfill specific mechanical and functional requirements.
questions.question: The extracellular matrix (ECM) of connective tissue is composed of which of the following?
options: Protein fibers (collagen, elastic, reticular) and ground substance
Cellular debris and metabolic waste products
Blood plasma proteins and immunoglobulins only
Basement membrane only with no other components

questions.question: Microfilaments of actin within the cytoskeleton primarily enable cells to perform which of the following functions?
questions.explanation: Actin microfilaments (7 nm diameter) are the thinnest cytoskeletal filaments and generate the forces necessary for cell shape changes, movement, and cell division through dynamic polymerization and depolymerization. They are concentrated beneath the plasma membrane forming the cell cortex. They work with myosin motors in muscle contraction and in non-muscle cell motility.
options: Give the cell rigid structural support
Act as tracks for organelle movement

questions.question: Bowman's capsule develops from:
questions.explanation: Bowman's capsule develops from metanephric vesicles, which form from the metanephric blastema. These vesicles elongate to form S-shaped tubules. One end of the tubule invaginates to form Bowman's capsule around a developing glomerulus. The other end connects to a collecting tubule, establishing continuity of the nephron.

If splitting occurs at the bilaminar disc stage (after formation of the amniotic cavity), monozygotic twins will share a common placenta, common chorionic cavity, and common amniotic cavity. This is the rarest and most dangerous type, with risk of cord entanglement and twin-to-twin transfusion.
questions.question: Monozygotic twins sharing both amniotic and chorionic cavities result from splitting at which stage?
The fourth ventricle is bounded laterally by which structures?
questions.explanation: The fourth ventricle is bounded laterally by the cerebellar peduncles (superior, middle, and inferior), which form its walls as they course between the brainstem and cerebellum. The superior cerebellar peduncles form the upper lateral boundaries, while the inferior peduncles (with the gracile and cuneate tubercles) form the lower lateral boundaries. The floor is the rhomboid fossa formed by the posterior pons and medulla, while the roof is formed by the superior medullary velum and inferior medullary velum with cerebellum.

Collecting tubules are derived from the ureteric bud through repeated branching (approximately 15 generations). The ureteric bud gives rise to the entire collecting system: ureter, renal pelvis, major and minor calyces, and collecting tubules. The metanephric blastema forms the nephrons (glomeruli and tubules from Bowman's capsule to distal convoluted tubule).
questions.question: Collecting tubules are derived from:
The cerebellum contains approximately what percentage of the brain's total neurons?
questions.explanation: The cerebellum, despite representing only about 10% of brain volume, contains approximately 50% or more of the brain's total neurons, primarily due to the enormous number of tiny granule cells. This massive neural substrate supports the cerebellum's computational functions in motor coordination, timing, and learning. The highly regular, repetitive architecture allows uniform processing across the cerebellar cortex, with local circuits repeated millions of times. This computational capacity underlies the cerebellum's roles in motor control, cognitive functions, and motor learning.

questions.question: Which type of cortical neuron is characterized by extensive dendritic trees in a single plane?
questions.explanation: Pyramidal cells, the principal neurons of the cerebral cortex, are characterized by pyramid-shaped cell bodies and extensive dendritic trees that spread in a cone shape, primarily in planes perpendicular to the cortical surface. Their apical dendrites extend toward the cortical surface, while basal dendrites spread laterally. Pyramidal cells have long axons projecting to other cortical areas, subcortical structures, or spinal cord, making them the main output neurons of the cortex.

questions.question: Cristae ampullae are specialized receptors for which function?
questions.explanation: Localized dilatations (ampullae) develop at one end of each semicircular duct where cristae ampullae differentiate. These are specialized receptor areas for equilibrium. They are also present in utricle and saccule.

questions.question: Which type of pancreatic duct cell is stimulated by secretin to produce the bicarbonate-rich component of pancreatic juice?
questions.explanation: Secretin, released from S-cells in the duodenum in response to acid, stimulates centroacinar cells and small pancreatic duct cells to secrete large volumes of water and bicarbonate. This alkaline fluid (pH ~8) neutralizes gastric acid in the duodenum and creates the optimal pH for pancreatic enzyme activity. In cystic fibrosis, CFTR mutations impair this bicarbonate secretion.

questions.question: The oviduct (fallopian tube) is lined by which type of epithelium that facilitates the transport of the oocyte?
questions.explanation: The oviduct is lined by simple columnar epithelium containing two cell types: ciliated cells (whose cilia beat toward the uterus, propelling the oocyte) and secretory (peg) cells (which produce nutrient secretions to support the oocyte and early embryo). The mucosa of the ampulla (site of fertilization) is especially complex with elaborate mucosal folds. Loss of ciliary function impairs oocyte transport and increases ectopic pregnancy risk.

The occipital sinus is located at the posterior attachment of the falx cerebelli in the midline, extending from the internal occipital protuberance to the posterior margin of foramen magnum. It is the smallest of the major dural sinuses and drains into the confluence of sinuses above or the marginal sinus around the foramen magnum. The occipital sinus lies between the two layers of the falx cerebelli and receives small veins from the cerebellar hemispheres.
questions.question: Which sinus is located at the attachment of the falx cerebelli?

questions.explanation: The confluence of sinuses (torcular Herophili) is located at the internal occipital protuberance where the superior sagittal sinus, straight sinus, occipital sinus, and transverse sinuses meet. This is a major venous confluence point, though the exact pattern of communication varies individually. Typically, the superior sagittal sinus continues primarily into the right transverse sinus, while the straight sinus continues into the left transverse sinus, though significant anatomical variation exists.
questions.question: The confluence of sinuses is located at which anatomical landmark?
Acute inflammation differs from chronic inflammation histologically primarily in which of the following?
options: Only chronic inflammation involves vascular changes
Acute inflammation always leads to tissue fibrosis
Chronic inflammation lacks any cellular component
Acute: neutrophil-dominated; chronic: lymphocytes, macrophages, fibrosis
questions.explanation: Acute inflammation is characterized by vascular changes and neutrophil (PMN) infiltration as the dominant cellular response, typically resolving within days. Chronic inflammation (lasting weeks to months) features a mononuclear cell infiltrate (lymphocytes, macrophages, plasma cells), tissue destruction, and attempts at healing/fibrosis. The temporal and cellular differences reflect distinct immunological mechanisms and different tissue repair outcomes.

The axons of the mantle layer neurons coalesce in the outermost layer forming the marginal layer. This layer eventually becomes the white matter of the CNS. The myelination of these axons gives it the white appearance.
questions.question: The marginal layer is formed by which components?

questions.explanation: The stomach uniquely possesses three smooth muscle sublayers: inner oblique, middle circular, and outer longitudinal. This arrangement allows the mechanical churning and mixing of food necessary for gastric digestion. All other GIT regions have only two layers (inner circular and outer longitudinal) in the muscularis externa.
questions.question: On a histological slide, three distinct smooth muscle sublayers are seen in the muscularis of one GIT region. This finding is characteristic of which region?

options: Two-thirds of total refractive power; primary refraction site
All refractive power without the lens
Only 10 percent of total refractive power
Equal contribution to the lens of 50 percent each
questions.explanation: The cornea provides approximately two-thirds of the total refractive power of the eye at about 43 diopters of the approximately 58 total, making it the primary refractive surface. The lens provides the remaining one-third and fine-tunes focus through accommodation. The cornea's refractive power is fixed while the lens changes shape. Corneal transparency depends on its regular collagen fiber arrangement, avascularity, and the endothelial fluid pump.
questions.question: The cornea as part of the eye's optical apparatus provides approximately what proportion of the eye's total refractive power?

questions.explanation: The fetal period begins at 9 weeks after fertilization and ends at birth. It is characterized by rapid body growth and differentiation of tissues and organs that were established during the embryonic period. The major events are maturation and growth rather than organogenesis.
questions.question: The fetal period begins at which week after fertilization?
The respiratory diverticulum appears during which week?
questions.explanation: The respiratory diverticulum (lung bud) appears during the 4th week as an outgrowth from the ventral wall of the foregut. This location is controlled by transcription factor TBX4, upregulated by retinoic acid from adjacent mesoderm. The bud induces formation and promotes growth and differentiation of the lungs.

questions.question: Neural induction occurs by preventing ectoderm from forming which tissue?
questions.explanation: Neural induction occurs by preventing ectoderm from forming epidermis through neutralization of BMPs. Neural inducers (noggin, chordin, follistatin) bind BMPs. This allows default neural fate.

questions.question: The histological appearance of the liver lobule shows hepatocytes arranged in radiating cords from the central vein to the portal tracts. Blood flows from which direction through the hepatic sinusoids?
questions.explanation: In the classic hepatic lobule, blood flows from the portal triads at the periphery which contain branches of the portal vein, hepatic artery, and bile duct, through the sinusoids between hepatocyte cords toward the central vein at the lobule center, which then drains into hepatic veins and the inferior vena cava. This centripetal blood flow exposes hepatocytes to portal blood first at the periportal zone accounting for zone 1 being most vulnerable to toxins in portal blood.
options: From the central vein outward toward portal tracts
From portal tracts (hepatic artery and portal vein) toward the central vein
Bidirectionally through hepatic sinusoids without directional preference
From hepatic veins retrograde toward portal tracts
Only from hepatic artery branches without any portal venous component

questions.question: In skeletal muscle, which structure represents the functional unit for calcium release that triggers contraction?
questions.explanation: The triad is the functional calcium-release unit of skeletal muscle excitation-contraction coupling, consisting of one transverse tubule, which is an invagination of the sarcolemma that rapidly propagates the action potential, flanked by two terminal cisternae of the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Voltage sensors called dihydropyridine receptors in the T-tubule mechanically open ryanodine receptors in the SR, releasing calcium into the cytoplasm to trigger contraction.
options: The M line of the sarcomere
The sarcolemma and its overlying myelin sheath
The Z line and attached titin proteins
One T-tubule flanked by two SR terminal cisternae

questions.question: The small intestine renews its epithelium approximately every 3–5 days. This rapid renewal protects against environmental damage but also makes the intestinal epithelium particularly vulnerable to:
questions.explanation: The high proliferative rate of intestinal stem cells makes the intestinal epithelium one of the most sensitive targets of cytotoxic chemotherapy and radiation therapy, which preferentially damage rapidly dividing cells. This accounts for the GI toxicity (mucositis, diarrhea, nausea, vomiting) seen with these treatments. Intestinal stem cells in the crypts are the primary target, and their loss leads to villous atrophy and malabsorption.

questions.question: Which Brodmann areas constitute the primary somatosensory cortex?
questions.explanation: Brodmann areas 3, 1, and 2 in the postcentral gyrus constitute the primary somatosensory cortex, processing touch, proprioception, and vibration from the contralateral body. Area 3 receives the main thalamic input, while areas 1 and 2 process this information further. These areas maintain somatotopic organization (sensory homunculus) with disproportionate representation of hands and face. Lesions cause contralateral sensory loss, particularly affecting fine discriminative touch and position sense.

Hypospadias results from incomplete fusion of the urethral folds on the ventral surface of the penis, leaving the urethral opening on the underside rather than at the tip. Severity varies from glandular (near tip) to penoscrotal. It is one of the most common congenital anomalies in males. Associated chordee (ventral curvature) often requires surgical correction.
questions.question: Hypospadias results from:
The anterior spinocerebellar tract exits to cerebellum via which peduncle?
questions.explanation: Anterior spinocerebellar fibers decussate and lie on the cord's margin, exiting via superior cerebellar peduncle. They synapse with posterior horn cells in lower lumbar and sacral segments. They do not synapse with thoracic nuclei.

Histology, also called microanatomy, is the study of the microscopic structure of cells, tissues, and organs. It is dependent on microscopes and molecular methods because cells and tissue components are too small to visualize with the naked eye. Gross anatomy by contrast examines structures visible to the unaided eye.
questions.question: The science of microanatomy, which studies the microscopic organization of cells, tissues, and organs, is most accurately referred to as which of the following?
Bile formation by hepatic cells begins around:
questions.explanation: Bile formation by hepatic cells begins around the 12th week of development. After the 13th week, bile entering the duodenum gives a dark green color to intestinal contents (meconium). This meconium accumulates in the fetal intestines and is normally passed shortly after birth.

While the amygdala regulates aspects of emotional behavior and influences autonomic and endocrine function through connections with the hypothalamus, it is actually the hypothalamus (part of the diencephalon involved in limbic function) that directly regulates endocrine and autonomic functions. The amygdala sends efferents to hypothalamic nuclei that control heart rate, respiration, blood pressure, feeding, and sexual behavior, serving as a link between emotional processing and physiological responses.
questions.question: Which nucleus in the limbic system directly regulates endocrine and autonomic functions?

questions.explanation: Cajal-Retzius cells are horizontally lying cells of the molecular layer that produce reelin. Reelin is important for the process of myelination and neuronal migration. These cells are almost non-existent at birth.
questions.question: Cajal-Retzius cells produce which important substance?

questions.explanation: Primordial germ cells appear in the endodermal lining of the yolk sac wall. These cells later migrate to the developing gonads to form oogonia and spermatogonia. The yolk sac also functions in early blood development and contributes endoderm to various organs.
questions.question: Primordial germ cells appear in the endodermal lining of which structure?

options: Sensory interneurons receiving and relaying dorsal root input
Autonomic preganglionic neurons of the lateral horn
Astrocytes providing structural support in the gray matter framework
Large multipolar alpha motor neurons with axons exiting via ventral roots
Pseudounipolar sensory neurons with peripheral and central branches
questions.explanation: The ventral horns of the spinal cord gray matter contain large multipolar alpha motor neurons whose axons exit through ventral nerve roots and travel in peripheral nerves to innervate skeletal muscle at neuromuscular junctions. These are the lower motor neurons of the corticospinal motor system. The dorsal horns contain sensory interneurons receiving input from dorsal root ganglion sensory neurons. The lateral horn present only at thoracic and upper lumbar levels contains autonomic preganglionic neurons.
questions.question: The spinal cord gray matter in cross-section shows a butterfly or H-shape. The ventral horns of this gray matter primarily contain which of the following?

options: Subepithelial immune deposits on electron microscopy
questions.question: Interstitial nephritis is inflammation of the renal interstitium. The characteristic histological finding of acute interstitial nephritis (typically drug-induced) is:
questions.explanation: Acute interstitial nephritis (AIN) is characterized histologically by edema and dense inflammatory infiltrate in the renal interstitium — predominantly lymphocytes, plasma cells, monocytes, and characteristically eosinophils (suggesting drug-induced type). Tubular injury (tubulitis — inflammatory cells invading the tubular epithelium) is a key feature. Glomeruli are typically normal or show minor changes. NSAIDs, beta-lactam antibiotics, and PPIs are common causes. AIN is an important reversible cause of acute kidney injury.

The submucosal (Meissner) plexus is located within the submucosa of the GIT wall. It regulates glandular secretion and local blood flow. This is distinct from the myenteric plexus found between the muscle layers of the muscularis externa.
questions.question: Which layer of the gastrointestinal tract wall contains the Meissner plexus of autonomic nerves?

questions.explanation: Tracheoesophageal fistulas are components of the VACTERL association (Vertebral anomalies, Anal atresia, Cardiac defects, Tracheoesophageal fistula, Esophageal atresia, Renal anomalies, and Limb defects). This is a collection of defects of unknown causation that tend to occur together.
questions.question: Tracheoesophageal fistulas are components of which association?
Neural crest cells migrate to which position relative to the neural tube?
questions.explanation: As the neural tube detaches from surface ectoderm, neural crest cells migrate dorsolaterally on each side of the neural tube to form the neural crest. The neural crest then separates into right and left parts lying on the dorsolateral aspect of the neural tube, giving rise to dorsal root ganglia.

CNS white matter appears white due to the high lipid content of myelin sheaths wrapping the axons running through it. The lipid-rich myelin is white-appearing in fresh tissue and provides electrical insulation for saltatory conduction. Gray matter contains neuronal cell bodies, dendrites, unmyelinated axons, and most synapses, and appears gray due to the absence of myelin and the presence of many nuclei and neuropil.
questions.question: The white matter of the CNS appears white because it consists predominantly of which of the following?
options: Cell bodies of neurons containing pale cytoplasm
Myelinated axons with high lipid content appearing white
Blood vessels with whitish tunica adventitia
Collagen fibers providing structural support to the CNS

questions.explanation: The cauda equina consists of lumbosacral nerve roots that descend almost parallel to the filum terminale. This results from the differential growth of the vertebral column and spinal cord. The obliquity of spinal nerves increases caudally.
questions.question: The cauda equina is formed by which structures?

questions.explanation: Prune belly syndrome is characterized by abdominal muscle deficiency (wrinkled skin), cryptorchidism, and urinary tract abnormalities (megacystis, hydroureter, hydronephrosis), but NOT renal agenesis. The kidneys are present but often dysplastic. The syndrome occurs almost exclusively in males. The exact cause is unknown but may relate to early urethral obstruction.
questions.question: Prune belly syndrome is characterized by all EXCEPT:
The superior cerebellar peduncle decussates at which level?
questions.explanation: The superior cerebellar peduncle decussates in the lower midbrain at the level of the inferior colliculus. After decussation, fibers continue to the contralateral red nucleus and thalamus (ventrolateral nucleus). This decussation explains why cerebellar lesions cause ipsilateral deficits---the cerebellum influences the contralateral motor cortex, which then sends crossed corticospinal fibers back to the ipsilateral side. The decussating fibers are visible in cross-sections of the lower midbrain.

questions.question: The myelencephalon forms which adult structure?
questions.explanation: The myelencephalon is the caudal portion of rhombencephalon that forms the medulla oblongata. The dorso-lateral wall is opened up. Basal and alar plates are separated by sulcus limitans.

Oligohydramnios can cause club foot and other limb deformities due to compression and restricted fetal movement. It also causes pulmonary hypoplasia (most serious complication), characteristic facial features (Potter facies), and growth restriction. Oligohydramnios results from decreased fetal urine production (renal anomalies), chronic amniotic fluid leak, or placental insufficiency.
questions.question: Oligohydramnios can cause which fetal deformity?

options: A single central nucleus and faint cross-striations
A single peripheral nucleus without cross-striations
questions.explanation: Skeletal muscle fibers can be identified histologically by their multiple peripheral nuclei (pushed to the periphery by myofibrils), prominent cross-striations (due to regular sarcomere arrangement), and large diameter. Smooth muscle cells have a single central nucleus, no cross-striations, and are spindle-shaped. Cardiac muscle has central nuclei, cross-striations, and intercalated discs. These features allow confident identification of muscle type in the esophageal wall.
questions.question: The tunica muscularis of the esophagus in its middle third contains both skeletal and smooth muscle. These two muscle types can be distinguished histologically because skeletal muscle has:

questions.explanation: Neural plate formation is induced by the underlying notochord and adjacent mesoderm. The notochord secretes neural inducing factors that cause the overlying ectoderm to thicken and form the neural plate. This induction is the first step in formation of the central nervous system.
questions.question: Which structure induces formation of the neural plate?

questions.explanation: Bilateral renal agenesis shows oligohydramnios (decreased amniotic fluid) on ultrasound because the fetus cannot produce urine. Unilateral renal agenesis typically shows normal amniotic fluid because the contralateral kidney produces adequate urine. Other ultrasound findings in bilateral renal agenesis include non-visualization of kidneys and bladder. Oligohydramnios impairs ultrasound visualization and causes Potter sequence.
questions.question: Renal agenesis on ultrasound may show which associated finding?

questions.explanation: The first urine is produced around 12 weeks when the metanephric kidney becomes functional and glomerular filtration begins. Urine is excreted into the amniotic cavity and becomes a major component of amniotic fluid in the second half of pregnancy. Fetal urine is hypotonic compared to fetal plasma. The placenta handles waste excretion; the kidneys primarily regulate fluid balance.
questions.question: The first urine is produced around:

questions.explanation: Special visceral efferent continues cranially as a motor column with CN11, CN10, CN9. They supply striated muscles of soft palate, larynx, pharynx, heart and gut. These are branchial arch derivatives.
questions.question: Which cranial nerves form a special visceral efferent column?

questions.explanation: Erythroblastosis fetalis (hemolytic disease of the newborn) results from Rh incompatibility between mother and fetus, typically when an Rh-negative mother carries an Rh-positive fetus. Maternal antibodies cross the placenta and destroy fetal red blood cells, causing anemia, jaundice, and potentially fetal hydrops.
questions.question: Erythroblastosis fetalis results from which mechanism?

options: Type I pneumocyte → capillary endothelium → basement membrane
Type I pneumocyte → fused basement membrane → capillary endothelium
Type II pneumocyte → basement membrane → capillary endothelium
questions.explanation: The blood-air barrier consists of: (1) the thin cytoplasm of Type I pneumocytes, (2) a fused basement membrane shared between the pneumocyte and endothelial cells (the thinnest part of the barrier), and (3) the thin cytoplasm of the capillary endothelium. The total thickness is approximately 0.2–0.5 μm. This minimal diffusion distance allows rapid O2/CO2 exchange by passive diffusion.
questions.question: The blood-air barrier across which gas exchange occurs in the lung consists of which three layers in correct sequence from alveolar air to capillary blood?

options: Fenestrated endothelium → glomerular basement membrane → podocyte foot
Podocyte cell body → basement membrane → mesangial cell
Continuous endothelium → thick basement membrane → parietal epithelium
questions.question: The glomerulus is a tuft of capillaries enclosed within Bowman's capsule. The filtration barrier between blood and Bowman's space consists of which three layers?
questions.explanation: The glomerular filtration barrier has three layers: (1) fenestrated glomerular capillary endothelium (without diaphragms) — provides size selectivity; (2) glomerular basement membrane (GBM) — provides charge and size selectivity; (3) podocyte foot processes with filtration slit diaphragms — provides the final size selectivity. Disruption of any layer (e.g., podocyte effacement in nephrotic syndrome) leads to proteinuria.

The muscularis mucosae of the esophagus begins as a single longitudinal layer in the upper esophagus and develops into two layers (inner circular + outer longitudinal) in the lower esophagus. This is an important histological feature distinguishing the esophagus from the stomach, where the muscularis mucosae has two layers throughout. This developmental variation in the esophageal muscularis mucosae is a reliable landmark for esophageal identification.
questions.question: The esophageal muscularis mucosae is noteworthy because it consists of:
options: Two layers from the start of the esophagus
No muscularis mucosae in the esophagus
A single longitudinal layer in the upper

questions.question: Canaliculi in bone serve which of the following critical physiological functions?
questions.explanation: Canaliculi are minute tunnels radiating from each osteocyte lacuna, containing cytoplasmic processes of osteocytes that form gap junctions with adjacent osteocytes. Since metabolites cannot diffuse through calcified matrix, this canalicular network creates a 'bucket brigade' relay system for nutrients, oxygen, hormones, and waste products between blood vessels in Haversian canals and the most distant osteocytes. Osteocytes also sense mechanical strain through canalicular fluid flow.
options: Allow osteoclasts to migrate between different bone surfaces
Store calcium phosphate reserves for blood calcium regulation
Serve as channels for osteoblast migration during bone remodeling
Provide direct routes for nerve fibers to reach osteocytes
Allow osteocytes to exchange nutrients with blood vessels via gap junctions

questions.explanation: Brown-Séquard syndrome results from hemisection of spinal cord. It causes ipsilateral motor loss and proprioception loss, contralateral pain/temperature loss. It demonstrates crossed pathways. Pure forms are rare.
questions.question: Brown-Séquard syndrome results from which lesion?

questions.explanation: Surface mucous cells of the stomach are among the most rapidly renewed cells in the body, with a turnover rate of approximately 3–7 days. This rapid replacement is driven by the pluripotent stem cells in the isthmus of gastric glands, which continuously produce new cells that migrate upward to the surface. This rapid renewal is essential for maintaining mucosal integrity against the highly acidic and proteolytic gastric environment.
questions.question: The gastric mucosa undergoes rapid renewal. Surface mucous cells of the stomach are replaced approximately every:

A tissue section shows a gland composed of spherical follicles filled with homogeneous pink material lined by a single layer of cuboidal cells. This histological picture is most consistent with which of the following organs?
questions.explanation: The thyroid gland has a pathognomonic histological appearance of spherical follicles filled with eosinophilic homogeneous colloid which is iodinated thyroglobulin, lined by a single layer of follicular cells. The height of the follicular epithelium reflects activity: flat squamous cells in inactive thyroid and tall columnar cells in hyperstimulated thyroid. No other endocrine gland has this follicular colloid-filled architecture, making thyroid histology immediately recognizable.
options: Colloid-filled follicles lined by follicular epithelium
Parathyroid gland with chief cell cords
Pituitary gland with acidophils and basophils

questions.question: The external ear develops from which pharyngeal structures?
questions.explanation: The external ear (auricle) develops from six auricular hillocks (3 on each side) at dorsal ends of 1st and 2nd pharyngeal arches. These surround the 1st pharyngeal cleft. The hillocks later fuse.

questions.question: The genu of the corpus callosum primarily connects which regions?
questions.explanation: The genu (anterior bend) of the corpus callosum primarily connects the frontal poles and prefrontal cortex bilaterally. The forceps minor, formed by fibers radiating anteriorly from the genu, connects the orbital and medial frontal cortices. The genu is important for bilateral coordination of executive functions, emotional processing, and social cognition. Damage to the genu may contribute to executive dysfunction, emotional dysregulation, and impaired interhemispheric transfer of prefrontal information. The genu is the first portion of the corpus callosum to show thinning in normal aging.

Cochlear nerve terminates in dorsal and ventral cochlear nuclei in pons containing second-order neurons. Their axons form trapezoid body and acoustic striae. Most fibers cross to contralateral superior olivary nucleus.
questions.question: Second-order auditory neurons are located in which nuclei?

questions.explanation: The uncrossed fibers remain as anterior corticospinal tract and decussate in upper thoracic region. They run in the spinal cord adjacent to anterior median fissure. Most motor control is contralateral.
questions.question: The uncrossed corticospinal fibers eventually decussate at which level?
The larynx contains true and false vocal cords. The TRUE vocal cords (vocal folds) are covered by which epithelium, reflecting their vibratory function?
questions.explanation: The true vocal cords (vocal folds) are covered by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium, which can withstand the mechanical trauma of rapid vibration during phonation. The false vocal cords and most of the larynx above the vocal folds are covered by respiratory epithelium (pseudostratified ciliated columnar). This sharp epithelial transition at the vocal folds is the basis for the distinction between supraglottic, glottic, and subglottic laryngeal carcinomas.

Uniparental disomy occurs when both homologs of a chromosome pair are inherited from one parent with no contribution from the other parent. This can result in abnormalities if the genes are subject to genomic imprinting, where expression depends on parent of origin.
questions.question: Uniparental disomy refers to which situation?
Non-rotation of the gut results in:
questions.explanation: Non-rotation or incomplete rotation of the gut may result in a left-sided cecum, appendix, and ascending colon. While some cases are asymptomatic, they may cause diagnostic confusion in cases of appendicitis. Incomplete rotation also predisposes to midgut volvulus due to narrow mesenteric attachment.

options: Provide the contractile force for muscle contraction
Generate cell surface projections like microvilli
Provide rigidity and tracks for organelle movement
questions.explanation: Microtubules (25 nm diameter, hollow cylinders of tubulin dimers) provide structural rigidity to maintain cell shape and serve as tracks for motor proteins (kinesins and dyneins) carrying organelles and vesicles throughout the cell. They also form the mitotic spindle during cell division. Their dynamic instability allows rapid reorganization in response to cellular needs.
questions.question: Microtubules within the cytoskeleton serve which of the following primary functions?

A cell type in connective tissue that is the most abundant fixed cell and is responsible for synthesizing extracellular matrix components including collagen and ground substance is which of the following?
questions.explanation: Fibroblasts are the most numerous and principal cells of connective tissue proper, responsible for synthesizing and secreting all components of the extracellular matrix — collagen, elastic fibers, reticular fibers, proteoglycans, and glycoproteins. They are spindle-shaped cells with elongated nuclei that align with collagen fibers. Fibroblast dysfunction underlies excessive scarring (keloid, fibrosis) and wound healing defects.

options: Lateral nasal and medial nasal prominences
questions.explanation: By the 3rd month, mesenchyme between the sensory epithelium and olfactory bulb forms the cartilaginous lamina cribrosa of the ethmoid. This structure later ossifies to form the cribriform plate through which olfactory nerves pass. The cribriform plate has numerous perforations for olfactory nerve fascicles.
questions.question: The cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone forms from mesenchyme located between:

questions.explanation: All three muscle types are of mesodermal origin, differentiating from mesodermal precursor cells during embryogenesis. Skeletal muscle derives from paraxial mesoderm in somites; cardiac muscle from splanchnic lateral plate mesoderm; and smooth muscle from lateral plate mesoderm and splanchnic mesoderm. Neural crest cells contribute to smooth muscle of head and neck blood vessels but the primary origin of muscle is mesodermal.
questions.question: Muscle cells are described as being of mesodermal origin. This means all three muscle types derive from which embryonic germ layer?
options: Neural crest cells for all muscle types

questions.explanation: The gallbladder develops from the smaller caudal part of the hepatic diverticulum. The larger cranial part forms the liver parenchyma. The stalk of the diverticulum connecting these parts becomes the cystic duct. The bile duct forms from the stalk connecting to the duodenum. These structures undergo temporary occlusion and recanalization.
questions.question: The gallbladder develops from which part of the hepatic diverticulum?

questions.explanation: Podocytes extend major processes that branch into smaller foot processes or pedicels that interdigitate with those of adjacent podocytes. Between adjacent foot processes are filtration slits of 25 to 60 nm bridged by the slit diaphragm composed primarily of nephrin protein. The slit diaphragm is the final and most selective barrier to protein filtration. Nephrin mutations cause congenital nephrotic syndrome. In minimal change disease and focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, foot process effacement is the pathological hallmark causing nephrotic syndrome.
questions.question: The podocytes or visceral epithelial cells of the Bowman's capsule in the kidney have specialized foot processes. What is the functional significance of these foot processes?
options: Phagocytosing protein that leaks through the glomerular basement membrane
Secreting components of the glomerular basement membrane
Podocyte filtration slits with slit diaphragms as the final filtration barrier
Actively pumping water across the glomerular filtration barrier
Producing renin for blood pressure regulation

questions.explanation: Wait — proteins are broken down into amino acids and small peptides (di- and tripeptides) that are transported across the brush border of enterocytes. Disaccharides are intermediate products of carbohydrate digestion, not protein. Monoglycerides and fatty acids are products of fat digestion. Answer: C (Amino acids and small peptides).
questions.question: The GIT processes macromolecules into absorbable subunits. Proteins are ultimately broken down into which absorbable units?

questions.explanation: The facial motor nucleus innervates all muscles of facial expression, including orbicularis oculi, orbicularis oris, buccinator, frontalis, and platysma, plus the stapedius, stylohyoid, and posterior belly of digastric. These muscles derive from the second branchial arch (SVE component). The nucleus is located in the lower pons, with its axons looping around the abducens nucleus before exiting the brainstem. Upper motor neuron lesions spare forehead muscles due to bilateral innervation, while lower motor neuron lesions cause complete hemifacial paralysis.
questions.question: The facial motor nucleus innervates which group of muscles?

questions.explanation: The special visceral efferent nuclei are CN5 and CN7 for the 1st and 2nd pharyngeal arches respectively. CN5 supplies muscles of mastication. CN7 supplies muscles of facial expression.
questions.question: Which cranial nerves supply the 1st and 2nd pharyngeal arches?
The third ventricle is derived from the cavity of which vesicle?
questions.explanation: The canal of the neural tube differentiates to form various ventricles including the third ventricle from diencephalon. Lateral ventricles derive from telencephalon. The fourth ventricle originates from the rhombencephalon.

The sliding filament model explains contraction through cross-bridge cycling: calcium binds troponin exposing myosin-binding sites on actin; myosin heads attach to actin; the power stroke pivots the head pulling actin toward the M line; ATP binding causes myosin head release; and ATP hydrolysis re-cocks the head. Repeated cycling slides actin over myosin, shortening the sarcomere without changing the length of individual filaments.
questions.question: In the sliding filament model of muscle contraction, shortening of the sarcomere is produced by which molecular events?
options: Shortening of individual myosin and actin filaments
Enzymatic degradation of titin elastic proteins
Disassembly of Z line proteins releasing actin filaments
Cross-bridge cycling: myosin heads bind actin, pivot, release, and re-cock
Calcium directly shortening thick filaments through conformational change

questions.explanation: Polar bodies are small cells with minimal cytoplasm that result from asymmetric division during oogenesis. They contain genetic material but lack the cytoplasm and organelles needed for development. Polar bodies are nonfunctional cells that degenerate and serve to discard excess chromosomes.
questions.question: Polar bodies are characterized by which feature?
The vermis of the cerebellum projects to which deep nucleus?
questions.explanation: The vermis (midline cerebellum) projects to the fastigial nucleus, the most medial deep cerebellar nucleus. The fastigial nucleus then projects to the vestibular nuclei, reticular formation, and contralateral motor cortex, influencing proximal limb muscles, trunk, and posture. This medial cerebellar system (vermis-fastigial-vestibulospinal/reticulospinal) controls balance, posture, and axial movements. Vermal lesions cause truncal ataxia with difficulty sitting and standing, wide-based gait, and titubation (rhythmic head tremor).

questions.question: Cerebellar hemispheres project to which deep nucleus?
questions.explanation: The cerebellar hemispheres (lateral zone) project to the dentate nucleus, the largest and most lateral deep cerebellar nucleus. This pathway represents the neocerebellum, phylogenetically newest and most developed in humans. The dentate nucleus projects to the contralateral motor and premotor cortex via the thalamus, participating in motor planning, timing, and learning of skilled voluntary movements. Hemispheric lesions cause appendicular ataxia with dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia, intention tremor, and impaired motor learning on the ipsilateral side.

The buccopharyngeal membrane, an ectodermal-endodermal membrane at the cranial end of the foregut, ruptures during the 4th week. This establishes an open connection between the oral cavity and the primitive gut. Before rupture, the membrane temporarily bounds the foregut anteriorly.
questions.question: The buccopharyngeal membrane ruptures during which week?

questions.explanation: The anterior communicating artery is the most common site for berry (saccular) aneurysm formation, accounting for approximately 30-35% of intracranial aneurysms. Other common sites include the posterior communicating artery junction with internal carotid and middle cerebral artery bifurcation. These aneurysms form at arterial bifurcations where hemodynamic stress is greatest and the vessel wall lacks normal medial layer support. Rupture causes subarachnoid hemorrhage with sudden severe headache (\"thunderclap headache\"), meningismus, and potential complications.
questions.question: Which artery is most commonly involved in berry aneurysm formation?

questions.explanation: Rods number approximately 120 million and contain rhodopsin, are extremely sensitive to low light, provide monochromatic peripheral vision, and are distributed throughout the retina except the fovea. Cones number approximately 6 to 7 million and come in three types for trichromatic color vision concentrated at the fovea centralis for maximum visual acuity. Cone-dominated foveal vision requires bright light.
questions.question: The retina's rods and cones differ in which of the following ways?
options: Rods provide color vision and cones detect low light and movement
Both rods and cones function identically in all light conditions
Rods detect dim light and provide achromatic vision; cones detect color and high-acuity vision
Rods are concentrated at the fovea centralis and cones are in the peripheral retina
Only cones are present in humans as rods are vestigial structures

questions.explanation: Skeletal muscle has classic triads with one T-tubule flanked by two SR terminal cisternae. Cardiac muscle has dyads with one T-tubule and one SR cistern. Additionally, skeletal muscle excitation-contraction coupling is entirely SR-dependent through mechanical linkage via dihydropyridine-ryanodine receptor interaction, while cardiac muscle requires calcium-induced calcium release from SR triggered by calcium entry through L-type channels. This difference explains why cardiac muscle is affected by extracellular calcium concentration while skeletal is not.
questions.question: The triad of excitation-contraction coupling in skeletal muscle differs from the dyad in cardiac muscle in which of the following ways?
options: Skeletal muscle uses dyads while cardiac muscle uses triads
Both cardiac and skeletal muscle use identical triads
Cardiac muscle has no T-tubules unlike skeletal muscle
Skeletal muscle does not require calcium release from SR for contraction
Skeletal: two SR cisternae per T-tubule (triads); cardiac: one SR cisterna (dyads)

questions.question: The straight gyrus (gyrus rectus) is located where?
questions.explanation: The straight gyrus (gyrus rectus) is located on the inferior medial frontal surface, medial to the olfactory sulcus and lateral to the interhemispheric fissure. It is a straight, narrow gyrus running anteroposteriorly along the medial inferior frontal lobe. The olfactory bulb and tract lie lateral to it in the olfactory sulcus. The gyrus rectus is part of the orbitofrontal cortex and involved in decision-making and impulse control; damage can contribute to frontal lobe syndrome.

In females, the mesonephric duct may persist as Gartner's duct, a vestigial structure in the lateral vaginal wall. The epoophoron and paroophoron in the broad ligament also represent mesonephric remnants. These structures are usually clinically insignificant but may occasionally form cysts. In males, the mesonephric duct becomes the ductus deferens and related structures.
questions.question: In females, the mesonephric duct remnant may persist as:

options: It eliminates the need for tissue fixation
It achieves greater magnification than electron microscopy
It stains all nuclei uniformly without antibodies
It visualizes tissue sections in real time without preparation
Fluorescent-labeled antibodies localize specific antigens with high specificity
questions.question: Which of the following fluorescence microscopy properties makes it particularly useful for localizing specific proteins or antibodies in tissues?
questions.explanation: Immunofluorescence uses antibodies conjugated to fluorescent dyes to bind specific tissue antigens, allowing precise localization of target molecules with high sensitivity. When excited by specific wavelengths of light, the fluorescent labels emit distinguishable colors pinpointing the molecule's location. This technique is invaluable in diagnostic pathology and research for identifying specific cell types and disease markers.

questions.question: Sebaceous glands develop from:
questions.explanation: Sebaceous glands develop from buds of the epidermal root sheaths of hair follicles. The glandular buds grow into surrounding connective tissue and branch to form alveoli and ducts. Central cells of the alveoli break down to form the oily secretion called sebum.

questions.question: The middle cerebral artery supplies which functional area critical for motor control?
questions.explanation: The middle cerebral artery supplies the primary motor cortex in the precentral gyrus, the primary somatosensory cortex in the postcentral gyrus, and large portions of the frontal, parietal, and temporal lobes. It also supplies the internal capsule through its lenticulostriate branches. Occlusion of this artery results in severe contralateral motor and sensory deficits, often with aphasia if the dominant hemisphere is affected.

Dizygotic (fraternal) twins result from fertilization of two separate ova by two different spermatozoa. These twins have separate amnions, chorions, and placentas (though placentas may be fused). They are genetically no more similar than any siblings and may be of different sexes.
questions.question: Dizygotic twins result from fertilization of how many ova?

options: Osteomalacia involves osteoclast hyperactivity; osteitis fibrosa involves mineralization failure
They both result from identical biochemical defects in collagen synthesis
Osteomalacia involves excessive mineralization; osteitis fibrosa involves matrix dissolution
Osteomalacia involves impaired mineralization; osteitis fibrosa involves excess osteoclast activity
They are the same disease at different ages
questions.explanation: Osteomalacia involves vitamin D deficiency leading to failure of osteoid mineralization, with accumulation of unmineralized osteoid seams and soft, painful bones. Osteitis fibrosa cystica (von Recklinghausen disease of bone) results from hyperparathyroidism causing excessive osteoclast activity, which removes both mineral and organic matrix and replaces it with fibrous tissue and cysts. Tetracycline labeling diagnostically distinguishes these opposite metabolic bone disorders.
questions.question: Osteomalacia (adult) and osteitis fibrosa cystica represent opposite extremes of bone pathology because of which of the following?

questions.explanation: Emphysema is defined histologically by permanent, abnormal enlargement of airspaces distal to the terminal bronchioles, accompanied by destruction of alveolar walls without significant fibrosis. This destroys the elastic recoil of the lung and the blood-air barrier for gas exchange. Smoking activates alveolar macrophages and neutrophils that release elastases and proteases, overwhelming the lung's protective alpha-1-antitrypsin. The result is dynamic airway collapse and air trapping during expiration.
questions.question: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) encompasses emphysema and chronic bronchitis. Histologically, emphysema involves permanent abnormal enlargement of airspaces distal to the terminal bronchioles with:
options: Fibrosis and collagen deposition in alveolar walls
Destruction of alveolar walls without significant fibrosis
Excessive goblet cell metaplasia in alveoli

questions.question: The lamina propria of the GIT mucosa characteristically contains all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The lamina propria is composed of loose connective tissue — not dense fibrous collagen. It contains blood vessels, lymphatics, lymphocytes, plasma cells, smooth muscle cells, and small glands. Dense connective tissue is a feature of the submucosa, not the lamina propria.

The muscles of facial expression are derived from the second pharyngeal arch and are innervated by the facial nerve (CN VII). This includes muscles like orbicularis oculi, orbicularis oris, buccinator, platysma, and the occipitofrontalis. Paralysis of CN VII results in facial weakness (Bell's palsy).
questions.question: The muscles of facial expression are innervated by which cranial nerve?

questions.explanation: The lateral geniculate body (nucleus), part of the posterior thalamic group, receives fibers from the optic tract and projects via the optic radiations to the primary visual cortex (area 17) along the calcarine sulcus. This six-layered nucleus maintains retinotopic organization and is the principal relay station for visual information from the retina to the cortex. Each layer receives input from either the ipsilateral or contralateral eye, forming the basis for binocular vision.
questions.question: Which structure receives projections from the lateral geniculate body?

questions.explanation: The pharyngeal wall contains circular constrictor muscles (superior, middle, and inferior pharyngeal constrictors) and longitudinal elevator muscles (stylopharyngeus, palatopharyngeus, salpingopharyngeus). This arrangement allows coordinated constriction and elevation during swallowing. The pharynx is also notable for having skeletal muscle throughout — unlike the esophagus which transitions to smooth muscle.
questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes the arrangement of smooth muscle in the pharyngeal wall?
options: Exclusively inner circular and outer longitudinal layers
Three layers — oblique, circular, and longitudinal
Circular constrictors and longitudinal elevator muscles

questions.explanation: The cloacal membrane is located on the caudal end of the primitive streak and develops into the future anus. Neural tube growing over the cloacal membrane causes tail folding and turns part of the yolk sac into the embryo as hindgut. The connecting stalk turns to the ventral surface during this process.
questions.question: The cloacal membrane is located at the caudal end of which embryonic structure?

options: Only a single layer of simple squamous epithelium
Two layers of keratinized squamous epithelium enclosing air
Three layers: outer keratinized skin, middle fibrous layer, inner simple squamous epithelium
Stratified columnar epithelium with goblet cells identical to respiratory mucosa
Fibrocartilage identical to the ear pinna
questions.explanation: The tympanic membrane has three layers: an outer lateral layer continuous with the skin of the external auditory canal with thin keratinized stratified squamous epithelium; a middle fibrous layer of radially and circularly arranged collagen and elastic fibers providing structural integrity; and an inner medial layer of simple squamous to low cuboidal epithelium continuous with the middle ear mucosa. The tympanic membrane vibrates in response to sound waves transmitting them to the malleus handle attached to its inner surface.
questions.question: The tympanic membrane or eardrum consists of which layers and performs which function?
The Circle of Willis provides anastomosis between which major arterial systems?
questions.explanation: The Circle of Willis provides important anastomotic connections between the internal carotid (anterior circulation) and vertebrobasilar (posterior circulation) systems. It consists of the anterior communicating artery connecting the anterior cerebral arteries, the posterior communicating arteries connecting the internal carotid to the posterior cerebral arteries, and the posterior cerebral arteries themselves. This arrangement allows collateral blood flow when one major vessel is occluded, though anatomical variations and incomplete circles are common.

options: Granulomatous destruction of interlobular bile ducts
Periportal fibrosis with plasma cell infiltrate
