questions.explanation: The three layers from innermost outward are: (1) fibrous (true) capsule — tightly adherent to renal parenchyma; (2) adipose (perinephric fat) capsule — layer of perinephric fat providing cushioning; (3) renal (Gerota's) fascia — outer fibrous layer anchoring the kidney to surrounding structures. This fat layer acts as a protective shock absorber. In thin patients, loss of perinephric fat contributes to renal ptosis (nephroptosis).

Collagen fibers derive their tensile strength from the triple-helical structure of collagen protein and the cross-linking between fibrils. Elastic fibers are composed of elastin (a cross-linked rubber-like protein providing extensibility) surrounded by fibrillin-containing microfibrils (providing structural scaffolding). The distinct molecular architectures of collagen versus elastin-fibrillin directly determine the different mechanical properties.
questions.question: Collagen fibers possess greater tensile strength than elastic fibers, while elastic fibers possess superior elasticity. These structural differences primarily reflect differences in which of the following?
options: Their staining affinity with H&E staining
Their cellular origin (fibroblasts vs. mast cells)
Their presence in specific organs only
The diameter of their constituent fibrils

questions.explanation: Vertebral arteries run alongside medulla and fuse at pontomedullary junction to form basilar artery. Before fusion they give off three branches. The basilar artery supplies the brainstem and cerebellum.
questions.question: The vertebral arteries fuse to form which artery?
A section of compact bone stained with hematoxylin and eosin shows concentric lamellae, lacunae, canaliculi, and a central canal. The entire cylindrical structure is called which of the following?
questions.explanation: The osteon or Haversian system is the basic structural unit of compact bone consisting of a central Haversian canal containing blood vessels and nerves surrounded by 5 to 20 concentric lamellae of mineralized matrix. Osteocytes reside in lacunae between lamellae connected by canaliculi extending to the central canal and adjacent osteocytes. Osteons run parallel to the bone long axis and are the result of bone remodeling where osteoclasts create tunnels subsequently filled by osteoblasts depositing concentric lamellar bone.

questions.question: Lymph nodes function as filters for lymph and sites of adaptive immune responses. Swollen lymph nodes at a site of infection indicate which of the following?
questions.explanation: Lymph node enlargement reflects massive lymphocyte proliferation in response to antigens drained from the infected tissue and trapped in the node. B cells proliferate in germinal centers producing antibodies while T cells proliferate in the paracortex. Germinal center reaction produces plasma cells and memory B cells. Persistent lymphadenopathy requires investigation to exclude malignancy or systemic infection.
options: Permanent destruction of lymph node structure
Lymphocyte proliferation and germinal center formation
Viral infection of macrophages causing their enlargement

questions.question: In the classification of epithelium, the urinary bladder epithelium that can change from columnar to squamous depending on distension is specifically called which of the following?
questions.explanation: Transitional epithelium or urothelium is the specialized epithelium lining the renal pelvis, ureters, bladder, and proximal urethra. When the bladder is empty it appears stratified cuboidal to columnar with large rounded umbrella cells at the surface; when distended it stretches to appear much thinner and more squamous. The umbrella cells are joined by tight junctions forming an impermeable barrier and have specialized cytoplasmic plaques containing uroplakin proteins resistant to urine.

options: Forms thick parallel bundles like type I collagen
Organizes into reticular fibers staining with silver salts
Forms non-fibrillar sheet-like networks rather than fibrillar bundles
Is produced exclusively by chondrocytes in cartilage
Contains no triple helical domains unlike other collagens
questions.explanation: Type IV collagen forms a non-fibrillar sheet-like or meshwork structure rather than fibrillar bundles. Type IV collagen molecules assemble into polygonal networks through end-to-end and lateral associations, forming the structural scaffolding of all basement membranes. Basement membranes also contain laminin, perlecan, nidogen, and other non-collagenous components. Goodpasture syndrome involves autoantibodies against type IV collagen in glomerular and alveolar basement membranes.
questions.question: Collagen type IV found in basement membranes has which of the following structural characteristics that distinguish it from fibrillar collagens?
Betz cells are characteristic of which cortical layer?
questions.explanation: Giant pyramidal cells of Betz are characteristic of layer V (internal pyramidal layer) specifically in the primary motor cortex. These are among the largest neurons in the central nervous system, with cell bodies up to 100 μm in diameter. Betz cells send their axons down the corticospinal tract, directly influencing spinal motor neurons. Although Betz cells are a hallmark of the primary motor cortex, they represent only about 3% of corticospinal neurons, with most coming from smaller layer V pyramidal cells.

Spermiogenesis is the structural modification of spermatids (which have already completed meiosis) into spermatozoa. It involves cytoplasm shedding, nucleus condensation, formation of neck, middle piece and tail, and acrosome formation. Meiotic division occurs earlier during conversion of spermatocytes to spermatids.
questions.question: Spermiogenesis involves all of the following EXCEPT:

questions.explanation: The blood-brain barrier is formed primarily by astrocyte foot processes inducing tight junctions in endothelial cells. It protects brain from toxins. It restricts drug delivery. Some areas lack this barrier.
questions.question: The blood-brain barrier is formed primarily by which cells?
The claustrum is shaped like which structure?
questions.explanation: The claustrum is a saucer-shaped thin lamina of gray matter lateral to putamen. It is separated from the putamen by external capsule. Its function remains somewhat unclear.

Sinusoidal capillaries (sinusoids) have large, tortuous lumens, fenestrated endothelium without diaphragms, large gaps between cells, and a discontinuous or absent basement membrane. This structure permits passage of blood cells, large proteins, and even entire cells between blood and tissue. They are found in the liver (hepatic sinusoids), spleen (splenic sinusoids), and bone marrow, all sites of cell production or destruction.
questions.question: Sinusoidal (discontinuous) capillaries are found in which organs where maximum exchange of cells and large molecules with blood is required?

questions.explanation: Extrahepatic biliary atresia typically presents with jaundice developing soon after birth due to obstruction of bile flow. This is the most common serious anomaly of the biliary system. If uncorrected surgically, it leads to progressive liver damage and death. Early diagnosis and surgical intervention (Kasai procedure) are critical.
questions.question: Extrahepatic biliary atresia typically presents with:

options: The molecular weight of the antigen only
The carbohydrate component of the antigen exclusively
The overall three-dimensional shape of the entire antigen molecule
The specific epitope (antigenic determinant) on the antigen
The foreign origin of the antigen regardless of its structure
questions.explanation: Each antibody recognizes a specific epitope (the precise molecular shape of a small region of the antigen) rather than the entire antigen or its molecular weight. Antibodies raised against one epitope will react with any molecule displaying that same or similar epitope (cross-reactivity). This exquisite epitope-specificity is the molecular basis of immunological specificity and is exploited in diagnostic tests and therapeutic antibodies.
questions.question: An antibody produced by a plasma cell is specific for which of the following characteristics of the antigen that stimulated its production?
Meckel's cartilage is found in which pharyngeal arch?
questions.explanation: Meckel's cartilage is the cartilage of the first pharyngeal arch, specifically in the mandibular process (dorsal part). The mesenchyme surrounding Meckel's cartilage forms the mandible. Meckel's cartilage itself forms the anterior ligament of malleus and the sphenomandibular ligament.

questions.question: The neuromuscular junction uses which neurotransmitter binding to which receptor type on the skeletal muscle fiber?
options: Norepinephrine binding to beta-adrenergic smooth muscle receptors
Acetylcholine on nicotinic motor end plate receptors causing Na⁺ influx
Glutamate binding to ionotropic postsynaptic NMDA receptors
Substance P binding to NK1 pain receptors
Dopamine binding to postsynaptic D2 dopamine receptors
questions.explanation: At the neuromuscular junction, motor neurons release acetylcholine from synaptic vesicles into the synaptic cleft. Acetylcholine binds nicotinic ACh receptors which are ligand-gated ion channels on the muscle fiber's motor end plate, causing sodium influx and depolarization that triggers the action potential propagating along T-tubules to initiate excitation-contraction coupling. Acetylcholinesterase rapidly hydrolyzes ACh to terminate the signal.

questions.question: The large intestine contains bacteria (microbiome) that produce vitamin K and certain B vitamins. These vitamins are primarily absorbed in which colonic segment?
questions.explanation: The ascending colon and proximal colon (cecum and ascending colon) are the primary sites of bacterial fermentation and vitamin K / B-vitamin production and absorption. These regions also absorb the majority of the remaining water and electrolytes. Fermentation in the proximal colon produces short-chain fatty acids (butyrate, acetate, propionate) that are absorbed and serve as major energy sources for colonocytes.

questions.question: The periosteum surrounding bone differs from the perichondrium surrounding cartilage primarily in which fundamental way?
options: Both have identical inner layers containing the same stem cells
Periosteum contains only fibroblasts without any progenitor function
Periosteum inner layer with osteoprogenitor cells capable of producing osteoblasts
The perichondrium is more vascularized than the periosteum
They are structurally identical with the same cellular composition
questions.explanation: Both periosteum (over bone) and perichondrium (over cartilage) have an outer fibrous and an inner cellular layer, but their inner layers contain different progenitor cells. The periosteal inner layer contains osteoprogenitor cells giving rise to osteoblasts, while the perichondrial inner layer contains chondroprogenitor cells giving rise to chondroblasts. This distinction is critical for understanding bone and cartilage repair mechanisms.

options: The vascular channels in Haversian systems
The osteocyte network in lacunae and canaliculi
The non-collagenous proteins like osteocalcin and osteopontin only
The inorganic mineral component hydroxyapatite alone
Organic type I collagen provides resilience; mineral phase provides hardness
questions.question: The structural resilience of bone — its ability to resist fracture — is attributed primarily to which of its components?
questions.explanation: Bone's unique mechanical properties result from its composite structure: the mineral phase (hydroxyapatite ~50% dry weight) provides compressive hardness and rigidity, while the organic matrix (type I collagen ~35% dry weight) provides tensile strength and resilience. Demineralized bone is flexible and tough like rubber; deproteinized bone is brittle and shatters easily. The combination creates the optimal structural material found nowhere else in nature.

questions.question: The insula is covered by opercula from which lobes?
questions.explanation: The insula (island of Reil) is buried in the depth of the lateral sulcus and covered by opercula (lips) from the frontal, parietal, and temporal lobes. These overlying cortical regions must be retracted to visualize the insular cortex. The insula is divided into anterior and posterior portions by the central insular sulcus and is involved in interoception, emotion, autonomic control, taste processing, and possibly pain perception. Insular strokes can cause subtle deficits including ageusia, autonomic dysfunction, and sometimes pure motor or sensory deficits.

questions.question: The double bubble sign on ultrasound is characteristic of which condition?
questions.explanation: The "double bubble sign" on prenatal ultrasound or postnatal X-ray is characteristic of duodenal atresia. The two bubbles represent the distended stomach and proximal duodenum, with absence of gas distally due to the obstruction. This condition is associated with Down syndrome in about 30% of cases.

options: Bile ductules → Canals of Hering → common bile duct → duodenum
Interlobular ducts → Canals of Hering → bile ductules → common hepatic duct
Bile canaliculi → sinusoids → central vein → hepatic vein
Canals of Hering → bile ductules → interlobular bile ducts → intrahepatic ducts →
Bile canaliculi → space of Disse → portal vein → duodenum
questions.question: Bile canaliculi are spaces between adjacent hepatocyte plasma membranes. Bile flows from canaliculi in which sequential pathway toward the duodenum?
questions.explanation: Bile flows from bile canaliculi (between hepatocytes) to Canals of Hering (transitional channels at the periphery of lobules), then to bile ductules, interlobular bile ducts, intrahepatic ducts, right and left hepatic ducts, common hepatic duct, and finally joins the cystic duct to form the common bile duct which empties into the duodenum at the ampulla of Vater.

Cogwheel rigidity is a feature of Parkinson's disease (basal ganglia dysfunction), not cerebellar ataxia. Cerebellar ataxia includes intention tremor (tremor increasing during goal-directed movement), dysmetria (overshooting or undershooting targets), dysdiadochokinesia (inability to perform rapid alternating movements), past-pointing (missing targets), decomposition of movement (breaking complex movements into components), scanning dysarthria, and hypotonia. These deficits reflect impaired motor coordination, timing, and motor learning rather than the rigidity seen in basal ganglia disorders.
questions.question: Cerebellar ataxia is characterized by all EXCEPT:
Sphincter and dilator pupillae muscles develop from which tissue?
questions.explanation: Sphincter and dilator pupillae muscles are unique smooth muscles formed from neuroectoderm of optic cup. Ciliary muscles form from lateral plate mesoderm. This dual origin reflects the complex iris development.

The functional unit of the kidney is the nephron, consisting of the renal corpuscle (glomerulus plus Bowman's capsule) and renal tubule (proximal convoluted tubule, loop of Henle, distal convoluted tubule). Each kidney contains over 1 million nephrons. The collecting duct, while essential for urine concentration, is not part of the nephron proper as it derives from the ureteric bud rather than metanephric mesenchyme. Together, nephrons and collecting system enable filtration, reabsorption, and excretion.
questions.question: The functional unit of the kidney is the:

questions.explanation: The I band consists only of thin actin filaments without any overlapping thick myosin filaments. Each I band is bisected by a Z disc to which the thin filaments are anchored. During contraction, actin filaments slide deeper into the A band, narrowing the I band and H zone but not the A band. The degree of I band narrowing reflects the degree of muscle shortening.
questions.question: The I band of a sarcomere which appears light under polarized microscopy contains which of the following?
options: Only thick myosin filaments with no actin
Both thick and thin filaments in maximum overlap
The M line with myomesin cross-linking thick filaments
Only titin spanning from M line to Z disc
Thin actin filaments only, bisected by the Z disc; no myosin overlap

questions.explanation: The pineal gland secretes melatonin which regulates circadian rhythms. It develops from the diencephalon roof plate. Light inhibits melatonin secretion. It influences sleep-wake cycles.
questions.question: The pineal gland secretes which hormone?

questions.explanation: The laryngeal muscles are derived from the 4th and 6th pharyngeal arches. The cricothyroid muscle (4th arch) is innervated by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve. The intrinsic laryngeal muscles (6th arch) are innervated by the recurrent laryngeal nerve. Both nerves are branches of the vagus.
questions.question: The laryngeal muscles are derived from which pharyngeal arches?
Chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla secrete which hormones in response to sympathetic nerve stimulation?
questions.explanation: Adrenal medullary chromaffin cells are modified postganglionic sympathetic neurons that upon preganglionic sympathetic stimulation via acetylcholine release catecholamines predominantly epinephrine at 80% and norepinephrine at 20% directly into the bloodstream. This hormonal output mediates the systemic fight-or-flight response including increased heart rate, blood pressure, blood glucose through glycogenolysis, and bronchodilation.

The general visceral efferent nucleus of Edinger-Westphal supplies the sphincter pupillary muscle. It is laterally placed relative to the somatic motor nuclei. This parasympathetic nucleus controls pupillary constriction.
questions.question: The Edinger-Westphal nucleus supplies which muscle?

questions.explanation: Hepatic stellate cells (Ito cells) normally store vitamin A as retinyl esters in lipid droplets within the space of Disse. Upon activation by cytokines released during liver injury, they transform into myofibroblasts, proliferate, and deposit collagen type I and III in the space of Disse. This is the central mechanism of hepatic fibrosis and cirrhosis, which is a major cause of liver failure worldwide.
options: Synthesis of albumin to compensate for liver failure
questions.question: Hepatic stellate cells (Ito cells) are pericytes of the liver sinusoids. When activated in response to liver injury, their primary pathological role is:
High anorectal malformations are characterized by:
questions.explanation: High anorectal malformations are characterized by the rectum ending above the levator ani muscle, often with a fistula to the urinary tract (males) or vagina (females). Low malformations involve the rectum ending below the levator ani. This classification is important for surgical planning, as high malformations require more extensive reconstruction.

After birth, when lung circulation begins and pressure in the left atrium increases, the valve of the foramen ovale is pressed against the septum secundum, functionally closing the foramen ovale. This separates the right and left atria and establishes separate pulmonary and systemic circulations.
questions.question: The foramen ovale functionally closes due to increased pressure in which chamber?
Myelin sheaths in the axon serve which function?
questions.explanation: Myelin sheaths make excellent insulators which help impulse conduction through saltatory conduction. They are formed by oligodendrocytes in CNS and Schwann cells in PNS. Nodes of Ranvier are gaps between myelin segments.

questions.question: The membranous urethra in males is derived from:
questions.explanation: The membranous urethra in males is derived from the pelvic part of the urogenital sinus, along with the prostatic urethra. This is the shortest and least distensible portion of the male urethra, passing through the urogenital diaphragm. It contains the external urethral sphincter (voluntary muscle from surrounding mesenchyme).

questions.question: The kidneys initially receive blood supply from:
questions.explanation: The kidneys initially receive blood supply from the common iliac arteries when they are pelvic organs. As the kidneys ascend, they receive new arterial branches successively from higher levels of the aorta. Eventually, they receive their definitive blood supply from the renal arteries arising from the abdominal aorta. Accessory renal arteries represent persistence of embryonic vessels.

questions.question: Which venous structure drains the deep white matter of the cerebral hemispheres?
questions.explanation: The internal cerebral veins drain deep structures including the thalamus, basal ganglia, and deep white matter of the cerebral hemispheres. These paired veins run posteriorly in the roof of the third ventricle and unite beneath the splenium of the corpus callosum to form the great vein of Galen. The great vein then drains into the straight sinus. Thrombosis of deep cerebral veins is less common than superficial thrombosis but can cause hemorrhagic infarction of deep structures.
There are 12 pairs of cranial nerves numbered I-XII from their cranio-caudal arrangement. Three are purely sensory, five purely motor, four mixed. They differ from spinal nerves in several features.
questions.question: How many pairs of cranial nerves exist?

options: Absence of fibroblasts in the cartilage matrix
Immune suppression preventing any cellular activity
Type II collagen being unable to be synthesized by mature chondrocytes
Avascular with few cells and no perichondrium, severely limiting regenerative capacity
Synovial fluid preventing cell migration to damage sites
questions.explanation: Articular hyaline cartilage lacks blood vessels nerves and lymphatics and has no perichondrium. Its sparse chondrocytes cannot migrate being trapped in lacunae and have minimal proliferative capacity. Damage cannot be repaired through the usual healing cascade requiring vascular invasion. Fibrocartilage rather than hyaline cartilage forms any repair tissue which has inferior mechanical properties explaining the progressive joint destruction in rheumatoid and osteoarthritis.
questions.question: A 45-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis has destruction of articular cartilage. The inability of this cartilage to repair itself is primarily explained by which of the following?
The ventral pancreatic bud gives rise to:
options: Uncinate process and part of head
questions.explanation: The ventral pancreatic bud gives rise to the uncinate process and part of the head of the pancreas. The dorsal bud forms most of the pancreas including the body, tail, and remainder of the head. The two buds fuse as the duodenum rotates, bringing the ventral bud dorsally.

MUC2 is the predominant mucin glycoprotein secreted by goblet cells throughout the intestine (both small and large intestine). It forms the structural backbone of the intestinal mucus gel layer. MUC5AC is the primary gastric surface mucous cell mucin; MUC6 is produced by gastric mucous neck cells and Brunner's glands. Deficiency of MUC2 (in MUC2 knockout mice) leads to spontaneous colitis, demonstrating its essential protective role.
questions.question: The small intestine has specialized mucus produced by goblet cells. Which mucin glycoprotein predominates in the small intestinal goblet cells?

questions.explanation: The hepatic diverticulum appears as a ventral bud from the caudal part of the foregut during the 4th week. This diverticulum grows into the septum transversum and divides into a larger cranial part (liver primordium) and smaller caudal part (gallbladder and cystic duct).
questions.question: The hepatic diverticulum appears during which week?

options: Bile pigment processing and bilirubin conjugation only
Lipid synthesis and detoxification of drugs
Urea cycle and albumin synthesis equally in all zones
questions.explanation: Zone 1 (periportal) hepatocytes receive well-oxygenated blood rich in nutrients and are therefore specialized for oxygen-dependent processes: oxidative phosphorylation, fatty acid oxidation, gluconeogenesis, and amino acid metabolism (including urea synthesis). Zone 3 (centrilobular) hepatocytes, receiving less oxygen, are specialized for glycolysis, lipogenesis, and drug biotransformation (high CYP450). This metabolic zonation explains why different liver diseases affect different zones.
questions.question: Hepatocytes in Zone 1 (periportal) of the hepatic acinus are specialized for which metabolic function?
At which vertebral level is lumbar puncture typically performed to access CSF safely?
questions.explanation: Lumbar puncture is typically performed at the L3-L4 or L4-L5 interspace, below the termination of the spinal cord at L1-L2 in adults. This allows access to the lumbar cistern, which contains CSF and the cauda equina (nerve roots), without risking direct injury to the spinal cord. The subarachnoid space extends to S2, providing a safe window for CSF sampling and measurement of opening pressure.
Medial reticulospinal tract from pontine reticular system runs in anterior white column inhibiting anterior horn cells. Lateral tract facilitates them. Together they modulate motor neuron activity.
questions.question: Medial reticulospinal tract has which effect on anterior horn cells?
The facial nerve supplies which pharyngeal arch derivatives?
questions.explanation: The facial nerve (VII) SVE fibers supply 2nd pharyngeal arch derivatives (muscles of facial expression, stapedius, stylohyoid, posterior digastric). It also has GVE, SVA and GSA components. It exits at pontomedullary junction.

The cisterna magna (cerebellomedullary cistern) is the largest subarachnoid cistern, located between the cerebellum, medulla, and occipital bone. It receives CSF from the fourth ventricle via the foramen of Magendie and serves as a major reservoir in the subarachnoid space. The lumbar cistern is also significant, extending from L2 (where the spinal cord ends) to S2 (where the dural sac terminates), containing the cauda equina and serving as the site for lumbar puncture.
questions.question: Which cistern is the largest subarachnoid CSF reservoir?
The cell membrane consists of a phospholipid bilayer in which the hydrophilic heads face outward and hydrophobic tails face inward. This arrangement primarily serves which of the following functions?
options: To allow free passage of all water-soluble molecules
To provide binding sites for all hormones
To form a selectively permeable barrier controlling molecular entry and exit
To anchor cells permanently to the extracellular matrix
To generate electrical potential differences across the membrane
questions.explanation: The phospholipid bilayer arrangement with polar (hydrophilic) heads facing the aqueous environments (cytoplasm and extracellular fluid) and nonpolar (hydrophobic) tails forming the interior creates a selectively permeable barrier. This barrier controls which molecules can enter or exit the cell based on size, charge, and lipid solubility. Specialized transport proteins embedded in the bilayer mediate the passage of ions and polar molecules.

The hinge points are areas where the neural plate attaches to adjacent tissues during neurulation. The median hinge point is attached to the notochord, while paired dorsolateral hinge points are attached to adjacent epidermal ectoderm. At these points, neuroepithelial cells become wedge-shaped and the neural plate undergoes furrowing.
questions.question: The hinge points during neurulation are areas of neural plate attachment to which structures?

questions.explanation: The cloacal membrane disappears during the 7th week, after the urorectal septum has divided it into anal and urogenital membranes. This breakdown exposes a ventral urogenital opening and a dorsal anal opening. The tip of the urorectal septum forms the perineal body.
questions.question: The cloacal membrane disappears during which week?
Dense irregular connective tissue, found in the dermis of skin and organ capsules, differs from dense regular connective tissue in which of the following ways?
questions.explanation: Dense irregular connective tissue has collagen fiber bundles oriented randomly in multiple planes, conferring tensile strength resistant to forces from all directions rather than a single direction. This is optimal for skin dermis, organ capsules, joint capsules, and the tunica albuginea, which must withstand multidirectional mechanical stresses. The irregular arrangement distinguishes it functionally and structurally from the unidirectional dense regular type.
options: Collagen bundles arranged randomly to resist tearing from all directions
It contains only elastic fibers arranged haphazardly
It is composed entirely of reticular fibers
It has a much lower collagen content than loose connective tissue
Its fiber bundles run parallel like those of tendons

questions.question: The pars triangularis is bounded by which structures?
options: Ascending and anterior rami of lateral sulcus
questions.explanation: The pars triangularis (triangular part) of the inferior frontal gyrus is bounded by the ascending and anterior horizontal rami of the lateral sulcus, forming a triangular region. Along with the pars opercularis, it forms Broca's area in the dominant hemisphere. This region is involved in phonological and syntactic processing in language production. The triangular configuration created by the diverging rami of the lateral sulcus makes this gyrus readily identifiable on lateral brain views.

Before closure of the ostium primum is complete, programmed cell death produces perforations in the upper portion of the septum primum. Coalescence of these perforations forms the ostium secundum. This allows continued right-to-left shunting of blood in the fetal circulation.
questions.question: The ostium secundum forms in the septum primum by which process?
Kidneys attain their adult position by which week?
questions.explanation: The kidneys attain their adult position in the abdomen by the 9th week of development. This "ascent" occurs through disproportionate growth of the lumbar and sacral regions. During ascent, the kidneys rotate medially approximately 90 degrees, bringing their hila to face anteromedially. Blood supply changes from iliac to aortic branches.

questions.question: The series of events in a cell leading to its division and duplication is collectively called which of the following?
questions.explanation: The cell cycle is the complete series of events from cell growth through DNA duplication to division into daughter cells. It encompasses both interphase (growth and DNA replication) and the mitotic (M) phase. The term mitogenesis describes factors stimulating cell division, not the cycle itself.

questions.question: Patent urachus is characterized by:
questions.explanation: Patent urachus is characterized by persistent communication between the bladder and umbilicus, resulting in urine drainage from the umbilicus. This represents complete failure of urachus obliteration. The condition is evident at birth and requires surgical repair to prevent infection and establish normal urinary drainage.

questions.question: Layer IV of the cerebral cortex is particularly well-developed in which type of cortex?
questions.explanation: Layer IV (internal granular layer) is particularly well-developed in primary sensory cortices, which receive abundant thalamocortical inputs. This layer is especially thick in the primary visual cortex (striate cortex), where it is subdivided and contains the stria of Gennari. In contrast, the primary motor cortex has a poorly developed layer IV but prominent layer V containing Betz cells. The relative thickness of layers IV and V distinguishes granular (sensory) from agranular (motor) cortex.

Mature mammalian erythrocytes are anucleate and lack all membrane-bound organelles including mitochondria, lost during terminal erythroid differentiation to maximize intracellular space for hemoglobin. They rely entirely on anaerobic glycolysis for ATP. Their biconcave disc shape maximizes surface area for gas exchange and provides flexibility to traverse capillaries smaller than their diameter. The 120-day lifespan underlies the use of HbA1c as a 3-month glucose control marker.
options: The capacity to maintain ionic gradients
A nucleus and all membrane-bound organelles
questions.question: Mature human erythrocytes are unique among blood cells in that they lack which of the following?

questions.explanation: Ventricular septal defect involving the membranous portion of the septum is the most common congenital cardiac malformation, occurring as an isolated condition in 12 per 10,000 births. It results from incomplete fusion of the components that form the membranous interventricular septum.
questions.question: Ventricular septal defect (VSD) most commonly involves which portion of the interventricular septum?

questions.explanation: Initially 2 longitudinal elevations form, then a transverse furrow separates them creating 4 colliculi. These are inferior and superior colliculi on both sides of median sulcus. They serve as relay centers for auditory and visual impulses.
questions.question: How many colliculi are formed in the mesencephalon?

options: Filtration of blood plasma through slit diaphragms
Structural support of capillary loops, phagocytosis
questions.explanation: Mesangial cells are specialized pericyte-like cells within the mesangium (matrix between glomerular capillary loops). Their functions include: structural support and anchoring of glomerular capillaries; phagocytosis and removal of immune complexes, macromolecules, and cellular debris; contraction/relaxation to regulate capillary surface area available for filtration; and secretion of cytokines. In IgA nephropathy, mesangial IgA immune complex deposition causes mesangial cell proliferation and matrix expansion.
questions.question: The mesangium is the supporting tissue of the glomerulus between and within the glomerular capillary loops. Mesangial cells perform which functions?

questions.explanation: Superior sagittal sinus thrombosis typically presents with bilateral leg weakness (and possibly paraplegia) because the parasagittal cortex containing leg motor and sensory areas drains into this sinus. Venous infarction of these areas causes bilateral lower extremity deficits. Additional features include headache, seizures, papilledema from elevated intracranial pressure, and potential hemorrhagic infarction. The presentation may be subacute, distinguishing it from arterial stroke, and requires imaging showing the absence of flow in the sinus.
questions.question: Thrombosis of the superior sagittal sinus typically presents with what finding?

questions.explanation: Oligohydramnios (amniotic fluid volume <500 ml) is most commonly associated with renal agenesis or other urinary tract abnormalities that prevent fetal urine production. This can result in Potter sequence: pulmonary hypoplasia, limb deformities, and characteristic facial features. Polyhydramnios is associated with esophageal atresia and anencephaly.
questions.question: Oligohydramnios (too little amniotic fluid) is most commonly associated with which condition?
The inferior mesenteric artery supplies derivatives of which embryonic gut?
questions.explanation: The inferior mesenteric artery (IMA) supplies derivatives of the hindgut, including the left 1/3 to 1/2 of the transverse colon, descending colon, sigmoid colon, rectum, and superior part of the anal canal. The foregut is supplied by the celiac artery, and the midgut by the superior mesenteric artery.

questions.question: Melanocytes originate from which embryonic source?
questions.explanation: Melanocytes are neural crest derivatives that migrate into the embryonic epidermis during the first three months of development. They migrate to the dermo-epidermal junction where they differentiate from melanoblasts. One melanocyte typically associates with 30-40 keratinocytes, forming an epidermal-melanin unit.

Shortly after the morula enters the uterus on day 4, fluid from the uterine cavity passes through the zona pellucida to form a single fluid-filled space called the blastocystic cavity, primitive chorionic cavity, or blastocoele. This transforms the morula into a blastocyst.
questions.question: The blastocystic cavity is also known as which structure?

options: Spiral ganglion neurons secreting potassium into the scala media
Basilar membrane vibration generating piezoelectric potentials
Stria vascularis maintaining high-K+ endolymph and the positive endocochlear potential
Outer hair cells through their electromotile activity
The round window membrane oscillating against the tectorial membrane
questions.explanation: The stria vascularis is a specialized epithelium on the lateral wall of the cochlear duct containing marginal cells, intermediate cells, and basal cells with extensive ion transport machinery including Na-K-ATPases and KCNJ10 potassium channels. It maintains the endolymph composition of high potassium and low sodium and generates the endocochlear potential of approximately +80 mV. This large potential difference drives potassium through mechanosensitive channels in hair cell stereocilia amplifying the transduction current.
questions.question: The endocochlear potential of approximately +80 mV in the scala media endolymph is generated by which structure and serves which function?

options: Hyaluronic acid and heparan sulfate predominantly
Type II collagen and aggrecan proteoglycan
questions.question: Ground substance of bone matrix contains which important non-collagenous proteins that participate in mineralization regulation?
questions.explanation: Bone matrix non-collagenous proteins include osteocalcin which binds calcium and regulates mineral crystal growth, osteopontin which mediates osteoclast attachment and cell signaling, and bone sialoprotein which nucleates hydroxyapatite crystallization. These proteins are synthesized by osteoblasts and regulate mineralization. Osteocalcin is also used as a serum marker of bone formation activity in metabolic bone disease assessment.

Histology derives from the Greek 'histos' meaning web or tissue, and 'logia' meaning the study of a science. It specifically focuses on the microscopic anatomy of cells and tissues. Understanding this etymology distinguishes histology from gross anatomy, cytology, and biochemistry.
questions.question: Which of the following correctly defines histology in terms of its Greek etymological roots?
options: Study of living organisms using electron beams
Study of tissues derived from 'histos' and 'logia'
Study of cells using biochemical markers only
Anatomical study limited to the gross level
Study of body fluids and their components

questions.explanation: On day 13, new cells from the hypoblast migrate to the inner part of Heuser's membrane. Spaces develop within these cells to form the definitive (secondary) yolk sac, which is smaller than the primitive yolk sac. The primitive yolk sac is pushed aside and eventually degenerates.
questions.question: The definitive (secondary) yolk sac forms on which day?
The sinoatrial (SA) node is located in the wall of the right atrium. The artery supplying the SA node arises from which coronary artery in most individuals?
questions.explanation: The sinoatrial nodal artery supplies the SA node and arises from the right coronary artery (RCA) in approximately 55–60% of individuals and from the left circumflex artery in the remaining 40–45%. This is clinically important because RCA territory myocardial infarctions (inferior MI) can cause sinus node dysfunction (bradycardia, sick sinus syndrome). Understanding coronary artery anatomy and conduction system blood supply is essential for interpreting ECG changes in MI.

Unlike spermatogenesis which is continuous, oogenesis is cyclic and limited only to the period of sexual maturity (from puberty to menopause). Only about 400 ova are ovulated during a woman's reproductive life. No new oogonia are formed after birth.
questions.question: In females, oogenesis is characterized as which type of process?

questions.explanation: Pontine nuclei are formed from the alar region of the rhombencephalon and migrate into the pons. They migrate through the marginal layer during development. These nuclei relay information from cortex to cerebellum.
questions.question: Pontine nuclei originate from which region?
A reciprocal translocation involves which process?
questions.explanation: A reciprocal translocation involves exchange of segments between two non-homologous chromosomes. This is a balanced rearrangement if no genetic material is lost or gained. However, carriers may produce unbalanced gametes, leading to miscarriages or offspring with developmental abnormalities.

questions.question: A nerve is defined as which structure?
questions.explanation: A nerve is a bundle of many nerve fibers (axons and dendrites of neurons). A neuron is a single nerve cell. This distinction is important for anatomical understanding.

questions.question: The adrenal gland's zona glomerulosa produces aldosterone regulated by the renin-angiotensin system. Which stimulus directly acts on zona glomerulosa cells to stimulate aldosterone production?
questions.explanation: Zona glomerulosa aldosterone synthesis is regulated by two primary stimuli: angiotensin II generated by the renin-angiotensin system in response to decreased renal perfusion, decreased sodium, or sympathetic activation; and elevated serum potassium which directly depolarizes zona glomerulosa cells opening calcium channels. While ACTH provides permissive support for aldosterone production in stress, the principal regulators are angiotensin II and potassium. Aldosterone increases renal sodium reabsorption and potassium excretion.
options: ACTH from the anterior pituitary exclusively
Low serum sodium without any other stimulus
Cortisol feedback through negative feedback mechanism
Angiotensin II and elevated potassium stimulating zona glomerulosa cells

questions.question: Onuf's nucleus is located in which lamina and segments?
questions.explanation: Onuf's nucleus is located in lamina IX of S1-4 segments supplying anal and urethral sphincters. It is sexually dimorphic and resists degeneration in motor neuron disease. It provides somatic control of sphincters.

questions.question: Which commissure connects the olfactory areas of both cerebral hemispheres?
questions.explanation: The anterior commissure connects the olfactory areas and temporal lobes of both cerebral hemispheres, crossing anterior to the columns of the fornix at the anterior wall of the third ventricle. It consists of two parts: a smaller anterior portion connecting the olfactory bulbs and tracts, and a larger posterior portion connecting the temporal lobes. The anterior commissure is phylogenetically older than the corpus callosum and remains important for interhemispheric olfactory and temporal lobe communication.

options: Superior cerebellum, upper pons, caudal midbrain
questions.explanation: The superior cerebellar artery forms just before basilar bifurcation, supplies upper pons, superior cerebellar surface and caudal midbrain. It runs below the tentorium cerebelli. Occlusion causes cerebellar and sensory deficits.
questions.question: The superior cerebellar artery supplies which structures?

questions.explanation: Each primary oocyte produces only one ovum. During meiosis I, the primary oocyte produces one secondary oocyte and one first polar body. During meiosis II, the secondary oocyte produces one mature ovum and one second polar body. The polar bodies are nonfunctional and degenerate.
questions.question: In females, how many ova result from each primary oocyte?
Which structure induces the formation of the neural plate?
questions.explanation: The notochord induces the overlying ectoderm to form the neural plate through inductive signals. It serves as the primary inductor in the early embryo and defines the primordial axis. The notochord produces neural inducers that neutralize bone morphogenetic proteins, allowing neural differentiation.

Skeletal muscle fibers develop embryologically by fusion of numerous mononucleated myoblasts, mesodermal precursors, into a single elongated syncytium with hundreds of peripherally placed nuclei. This multinucleated state reflects the syncytial origin. Satellite cells, positioned between the sarcolemma and basal lamina, serve as the adult muscle stem cell pool for regeneration after injury but do not fuse to form the original fiber during embryogenesis.
questions.question: Skeletal muscle fibers are multinucleated. This multinuclearity arises during development from which of the following processes?
options: Polyploidy of a single myoblast nucleus through repeated karyokinesis without cytokinesis
Invasion of fibroblasts into the muscle fiber
Fusion of multiple myoblasts into a single multinucleated fiber
Amitotic replication unique to skeletal muscle cells
Satellite cell proliferation within adult muscle fibers

questions.explanation: The tympanic membrane consists of three layers: ectodermal lining at bottom of auditory meatus, endodermal lining of tympanic cavity, and intermediate connective tissue layer. It separates external from middle ear.
questions.question: The tympanic membrane is composed of how many layers?

questions.explanation: In the late secretory phase, falling progesterone (and estrogen) levels trigger intense vasospasm of the spiral arteries of the stratum functionalis. This ischemia causes breakdown of the functionalis. The subsequent reperfusion causes lysis of the ischemic tissue, which sloughs as menstrual flow. Prostaglandins (particularly PGF2α) mediate this spiral artery vasospasm. Excessive prostaglandin production causes dysmenorrhea; NSAIDs treat dysmenorrhea by inhibiting prostaglandin synthesis.
questions.question: In the late secretory phase of the endometrial cycle (days 25–28), just before menstruation, the endometrium shows which specific vascular change?

questions.explanation: The celiac trunk supplies the abdominal foregut derivatives, including the abdominal esophagus, stomach, proximal duodenum (to the ampulla of Vater), liver, gallbladder, and pancreas. The superior mesenteric artery supplies the midgut, and the inferior mesenteric artery supplies the hindgut.
questions.question: The celiac trunk supplies which embryonic gut division?

questions.explanation: The medial longitudinal fasciculus connects vestibular nuclei with extraocular motor nuclei (CN3, 4, 6). It coordinates eye and head movements. It also connects to spinal cord. It mediates vestibulo-ocular reflex.
questions.question: The medial longitudinal fasciculus connects which nuclei?

questions.explanation: Replacement of normal fundic gland epithelium (with parietal and chief cells) by mucous glands resembling pyloric glands (pseudo-pyloric metaplasia) or intestinal-type epithelium with goblet cells (intestinal metaplasia) is a form of metaplasia representing an adaptive response to chronic injury (H. pylori, autoimmune gastritis). Intestinal metaplasia is a precancerous lesion, increasing the risk of gastric adenocarcinoma.
questions.question: A patient undergoing endoscopy has a biopsy taken from the stomach body. The section shows loss of parietal and chief cells with replacement by mucous glands resembling the pyloric or intestinal type. This process is called:

questions.explanation: Endothelial cells produce nitric oxide (NO, via eNOS stimulated by shear stress) and prostacyclin (PGI2), both of which cause vasodilation and inhibit platelet aggregation, maintaining vascular homeostasis. In contrast, damaged endothelium produces less NO/PGI2 and releases endothelin-1 (vasoconstrictor), PAI-1 (pro-thrombotic), and von Willebrand factor (platelet adhesion). This balance between vasodilatory and vasoconstrictive endothelial products underlies the pathogenesis of atherosclerosis and hypertension.
questions.question: The endothelium lining blood vessels is metabolically active and produces multiple vasoactive substances. Which endothelial product causes vasodilation and inhibits platelet aggregation?
Potter sequence is characterized by all EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Potter sequence is characterized by oligohydramnios (not polyhydramnios), which leads to pulmonary hypoplasia, limb deformities, and characteristic facial features (low-set ears, epicanthal folds, flattened nose). The sequence results from bilateral renal agenesis or severe bilateral renal dysplasia. The condition is lethal due to pulmonary hypoplasia preventing adequate breathing after birth.

The muscular interventricular septum develops in the floor of the ventricle and grows toward the AV cushions but stops short, leaving the interventricular foramen. The membranous IV septum later forms by fusion of three components: right bulbar ridge, left bulbar ridge, and AV cushions, closing this foramen.
questions.question: The muscular interventricular septum develops in the floor of the ventricle and grows toward which structure?

questions.explanation: Plasma cells are terminally differentiated B lymphocytes that have undergone antigen activation, B cell receptor signaling, and somatic hypermutation, resulting in high-affinity antibody-secreting cells. They are the primary humoral immune effector cells, producing thousands of antibody molecules per second. Their unique morphology (eccentric clock-face nucleus, basophilic cytoplasm) reflects extreme adaptation for protein secretion.
questions.question: Plasma cells are responsible for antibody production and are derived from which precursor cell type?
options: B lymphocytes following antigen activation and maturation

questions.explanation: The cephalic flexure is a ventral flexure that forms in the midbrain region. The cervical flexure (also ventral) forms at the junction of the hindbrain and spinal cord. The pontine flexure (dorsal) forms later and is responsible for the diamond shape of the fourth ventricle.
questions.question: The cephalic flexure forms in which brain region?

options: Two ureteric buds on same side
questions.question: Supernumerary kidney results from:
questions.explanation: Supernumerary kidney results from development of two separate ureteric buds on the same side, each inducing separate metanephric tissue. This is extremely rare and differs from duplicated collecting system (bifid ureter), where a single ureteric bud branches early. Each supernumerary kidney has its own blood supply, ureter, and collecting system.

Triploidy (69 chromosomes, three complete sets) is a lethal condition usually resulting from fertilization of an egg by two sperm (dispermy) or failure of meiotic division. Most triploid conceptuses are spontaneously aborted. Tetraploidy (92 chromosomes) is even rarer and also lethal.
questions.question: A person with 69 chromosomes has which condition?
Myeloschisis is characterized by which feature?
questions.explanation: Myeloschisis is the most severe form with exposed unfused neural plate. The spinal cord is open and exposed. It causes severe neurological impairment. Immediate surgical coverage is needed.

questions.question: The process of erythropoiesis involves a series of precursor stages. Which of the following correctly sequences erythroid development from earliest to most mature in bone marrow?
questions.explanation: Erythropoiesis progresses: proerythroblast (large cell with prominent nucleolus basophilic cytoplasm) to basophilic erythroblast (active ribosome synthesis) to polychromatic erythroblast (hemoglobin accumulation mixed colors) to orthochromatic erythroblast (pyknotic nucleus pink cytoplasm) where the nucleus is extruded to form a reticulocyte (still contains ribosomes staining with supravital dyes) which matures into an erythrocyte. This 5 to 7 day process is driven by erythropoietin from the kidney.
options: Proerythroblast → basophilic → polychromatic → orthochromatic erythroblast → reticulocyte → erythrocyte
Myeloblast then promyelocyte then myelocyte then metamyelocyte then erythrocyte
Lymphoblast then prolymphocyte then lymphocyte then erythrocyte
Stem cell directly producing mature erythrocytes without intermediate stages

questions.question: The only viable human monosomy is which condition?
questions.explanation: Monosomy X (Turner syndrome, 45,X) is the only viable human monosomy. All autosomal monosomies are lethal and result in early miscarriage. Even monosomy X has a high rate of spontaneous abortion; about 99% of 45,X conceptuses are lost during pregnancy.

questions.question: The red nucleus is located in which part of the midbrain?
questions.explanation: The red nucleus is located in the tegmentum of the upper midbrain. It receives input from the cerebellum and cerebral cortex and gives rise to the rubrospinal tract. It is involved in motor coordination. It appears reddish due to high vascularity and iron content.

Intention tremor increases as the limb approaches its target during goal-directed voluntary movement, particularly near the end of movement. It is absent or minimal at rest and with supported posture, distinguishing it from Parkinsonian resting tremor (which decreases with voluntary movement). Intention tremor reflects impaired cerebellar correction of ongoing movements---as the limb approaches the target, increasing precision is required, and cerebellar inability to make fine adjustments becomes apparent. Lesions of the dentate nucleus and superior cerebellar peduncle typically cause pronounced intention tremor.
questions.question: Intention tremor differs from resting tremor in that it:
Esophageal glands proper are located in which layer of the esophageal wall?
questions.explanation: Esophageal glands proper are small mucous glands located in the submucosa throughout the esophagus. They produce mucus that lubricates the passage of food boluses. In contrast, esophageal cardiac glands are found in the mucosa near the gastroesophageal junction. This submucosal location is a useful histological landmark for identifying esophageal tissue.

As a result of further deepening of the pontine flexure, the rhombic lips compress cephalocaudally and form the cerebellar plate. This plate differentiates into the cerebellum, with an external granular layer, cortex (with Purkinje cells), and deep nuclei.
questions.question: The cerebellar plate forms due to compression of which structures?
Which cranial nerve nucleus is continuous from the pons through the medulla to the spinal cord?
questions.explanation: The spinal trigeminal nucleus extends continuously from the pons through the medulla to approximately C2-C3 of the spinal cord, where it merges with the substantia gelatinosa. This long rostrocaudal extent allows somatotopic organization, with different regions processing pain and temperature from different facial areas (onion-skin distribution). The rostral portions process perioral sensation while caudal portions process more peripheral facial regions, explaining the pattern of sensory loss in lesions at different levels.

questions.question: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) is absorbed in which specific region of the intestine after binding to intrinsic factor?
questions.explanation: Vitamin B12 bound to intrinsic factor (IF, produced by gastric parietal cells) is specifically absorbed in the terminal ileum via cubilin receptors on enterocyte surfaces. This is a critical location because surgical resection or Crohn's disease affecting the terminal ileum will cause B12 malabsorption and megaloblastic anemia. The terminal ileum also specifically absorbs bile salts (enterohepatic circulation) — their malabsorption leads to bile salt-induced diarrhea.

Cholangiocytes are reliably identified by immunostaining for cytokeratin 7 (CK7) — a type II intermediate filament characteristic of biliary epithelial cells and some hepatic progenitor cells. CK7 positivity differentiates bile duct cells from hepatocytes (which are negative for CK7 but express albumin). CK7 immunostaining is used in liver biopsies to identify ductular reactions, bile duct proliferation, and metastatic carcinomas of biliary origin.
questions.question: The interlobular bile ducts in the portal tracts are lined by cuboidal to low columnar epithelial cells called cholangiocytes. Which immunohistochemical marker is most useful for identifying these cells?

questions.explanation: The foregut extends from the oral cavity to the ampulla of Vater (opening of the bile duct into the duodenum). This division is based on arterial supply, with the celiac trunk supplying foregut derivatives. The midgut extends from the ampulla of Vater to the proximal 2/3 of the transverse colon.
questions.question: The foregut extends from the oral cavity to:

options: Two lateral swellings and tuberculum impar
questions.question: The anterior 2/3 of the tongue develops from which pharyngeal arch structures?
questions.explanation: The anterior 2/3 (oral part) of the tongue develops from two lateral lingual swellings and the tuberculum impar, all from the 1st pharyngeal arch. The posterior 1/3 (pharyngeal part) develops from the copula (hypobranchial eminence) of the 3rd pharyngeal arch. These parts are separated by the linguo-gingival swelling.

questions.question: Perilymph-filled spaces include which structures?
questions.explanation: Mesenchyme around cochlear duct becomes cartilage which undergoes vacuolization giving 2 perilymph-filled spaces. These are scala vestibuli and scala tympani separated from cochlear duct. The duct contains endolymph.

options: Changing the curvature of the cornea through ciliary muscle contraction
Rotating the eyeball to shift the angle of refraction
Adjusting aqueous humor volume in the anterior chamber
Ciliary muscle contraction reduces zonular tension, allowing the lens to round up
Pupil constriction reducing spherical aberration for near objects
questions.question: The lens of the eye achieves accommodation for near vision by which mechanism?
questions.explanation: Accommodation for near vision involves ciliary muscle contraction which relaxes the circular zonular fibers attached to the lens, allowing the elastic lens to recoil into a more spherical shape with greater refractive power to focus near objects on the retina. For far vision, ciliary muscle relaxes causing zonular fibers to tighten and flatten the lens. The lens loses elasticity with age causing presbyopia with reduced near vision accommodation.

questions.question: Horizontal folding of the embryo results in incorporation of which structure into the midgut?
questions.explanation: Lateral (horizontal) folding rolls the sides of the embryonic disc and turns part of the yolk sac into the embryo as midgut. The rest is left outside as the yolk stalk and is incorporated into the umbilical cord. This folding brings the ventral body wall together and establishes the tubular gut.

options: Regeneration of the stratum functionale after menstruation
Production of progesterone during the luteal phase
Formation of the decidua basalis only in pregnancy
questions.explanation: The stratum basale contains the stems cells and gland bases that regenerate the entire stratum functionale after it is shed during menstruation. It is not shed because it receives blood from the straight (basal) arteries, which do not undergo the vasoconstriction that precipitates menstruation. The stratum functionale, supplied by spiral arteries (responsive to progesterone withdrawal), is the layer that proliferates, secretes, and is shed cyclically.
questions.question: The endometrium undergoes cyclical changes under hormonal control. The stratum functionale is shed during menstruation, while the stratum basale remains. The stratum basale is responsible for:
Which nuclei lie lateral to the red nucleus in the subthalamus?
questions.explanation: The subthalamic nuclei lie lateral to the red nucleus and substantia nigra in the subthalamus, which is located between the midbrain and thalamus. These lens-shaped nuclei receive afferent input from the globus pallidus and form part of the efferent pathway for the corpus striatum. The subthalamic nuclei are involved in motor control; their damage or dysfunction (as in hemiballismus) causes violent, involuntary flinging movements of the contralateral limbs.

Mitochondria contain their own circular DNA (mtDNA), 70S ribosomes, and double membrane — features consistent with endosymbiotic origin from an ancient alpha-proteobacterium engulfed by a proto-eukaryotic cell. Mitochondrial ribosomes are sensitive to the same antibiotics that inhibit bacterial ribosomes. mtDNA is inherited maternally in most species and is used for phylogenetic and forensic analysis.
questions.question: Which cellular organelle is correctly described as having its own DNA and ribosomes, and is thought to have originated from endosymbiosis with an ancient bacterium?
At the level of the superior colliculus, which nucleus is located close to the midline?
questions.explanation: The oculomotor nucleus is located close to the midline ventral to the cerebral aqueduct at the level of the superior colliculus. The Edinger-Westphal nucleus (parasympathetic component) lies cranial to the main oculomotor nucleus. The oculomotor nerve fibers pass through the red nucleus, which lies lateral and ventral to the nucleus, before emerging from the medial aspect of the cerebral peduncle.

questions.question: The lesser omentum contains which structures in its free edge?
questions.explanation: The lesser omentum contains the portal triad (hepatic artery, portal vein, and bile duct) in its free right edge, known as the hepatoduodenal ligament. This free edge forms the anterior boundary of the epiploic foramen (of Winslow). The hepatogastric ligament is the portion extending between liver and lesser curvature of stomach.

Three disc-like diverticuli develop at the utricular part of otic vesicle. Their central parts fuse and disappear leaving peripheral unfused parts as three semicircular ducts. They detect angular acceleration.
questions.question: How many semicircular ducts develop from the utricle?

questions.explanation: On days 11-12, new cells appear between the cytotrophoblast and Heuser's membrane to form extraembryonic mesoderm. Spaces appear in this mesoderm to form the chorionic cavity (extraembryonic coelom), which will eventually surround the amnion and yolk sac.
questions.question: Extraembryonic mesoderm appears between which two structures?
Which thalamic nuclei group projects to the cingulate gyrus?
questions.explanation: The anterior nuclei group of the thalamus receives afferents from the mammillary bodies via the mammillothalamic tract and projects to the cingulate gyrus, forming part of the Papez circuit involved in emotion and memory. These nuclei are separated from other thalamic groups by the anterior limbs of the internal medullary lamina. The anterior nuclei are part of the limbic system and play a role in regulating emotional tone and recent memory.

In portal hypertension (e.g., from liver cirrhosis), increased pressure in the portal venous system is transmitted to the submucosal venous plexus of the lower esophagus via portosystemic anastomoses. This causes dilation of these submucosal veins into esophageal varices. Variceal rupture during vomiting or Valsalva can cause massive, life-threatening upper GI hemorrhage. Endoscopic band ligation or sclerotherapy is used to obliterate these vessels.
questions.question: The esophageal wall contains a rich submucosal venous plexus. In which pathological condition does this plexus become clinically life-threatening?

questions.explanation: Meningomyelocele is a cystic form of spina bifida where both meninges and spinal cord tissue protrude through the vertebral defect. Other forms include spina bifida occulta (hidden, minimal defect) and meningocele (only meninges protrude). These result from failure of posterior neuropore closure.
questions.question: Meningomyelocele is a type of which congenital anomaly?

questions.explanation: The dorsal septum is formed by enlargement of the alar plate. The ventral fissure forms from basal plate enlargement. These landmarks divide the white matter into funiculi.
questions.question: The dorsal septum is formed by enlargement of which plate?
The lenticulostriate arteries are branches of which vessel?
questions.explanation: The lenticulostriate arteries (lateral striate arteries) are small perforating branches of the middle cerebral artery that supply the basal ganglia and internal capsule. These vessels are particularly vulnerable to hypertensive damage and are common sites of intracerebral hemorrhage (\"hemorrhagic stroke\"). Occlusion or rupture of these arteries causes contralateral hemiplegia due to internal capsule involvement, often with severe permanent deficits. They are sometimes called \"arteries of stroke\" due to their clinical significance.

In Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, excessive gastrin from a gastrinoma (often in the duodenal wall or pancreas) continuously stimulates parietal cell HCl secretion and promotes mucosal growth. This causes hypertrophy and hyperplasia of fundic glands, particularly parietal and chief cells, with markedly thickened, prominent rugae. Patients develop severe, refractory peptic ulcers. This is the opposite of gastric atrophy seen in pernicious anemia.
options: Replacement of gastric epithelium by intestinal metaplasia
Infiltration of the mucosa by goblet cells
questions.question: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome is caused by a gastrin-secreting tumor (gastrinoma). Histologically, the gastric mucosa in this condition would show:

options: Acinar cells are pale-staining with irregular nuclei
Acinar cells are large cells with central nuclei and clear cytoplasm
Acinar cells are pyramidal with basophilic cytoplasm and apical zymogen granules
Acinar cells are arranged in cords surrounded by fenestrated capillaries
questions.explanation: Pancreatic acinar cells are pyramidal or triangular cells with intensely basophilic basal cytoplasm (due to abundant rough ER for enzyme synthesis) and acidophilic apical zymogen granules (containing inactive digestive enzymes). They are arranged in rounded secretory units (acini). Islet cells (of Langerhans), in contrast, are paler-staining, spherical cells arranged in cords with rich capillary networks.
questions.question: The pancreatic acinar cells produce digestive enzymes. Which morphological feature distinguishes them from islet cells?

options: Woven bone is more mineralized than lamellar bone
Lamellar bone forms faster than woven bone
Woven bone contains more osteocytes per unit volume
Regularly organized collagen lamellae providing superior mechanical strength
They are mechanically identical with only age-related differences
questions.explanation: Woven bone is the primary bone type formed rapidly during fetal development and fracture healing, with randomly arranged collagen fibers and more osteocytes per unit volume, providing structural support quickly but with inferior mechanical strength. It is subsequently replaced by lamellar bone through remodeling, which has precisely organized parallel collagen lamellae in alternating orientations conferring superior mechanical properties. Pathological persistence of woven bone occurs in Paget's disease and osteosarcoma.
questions.question: The transition from woven bone to lamellar bone during development and fracture healing is important because of which difference between the two bone types?

questions.explanation: The gracile fasciculus (medial) carries discriminative touch and proprioception from lower limb and trunk. The cuneate fasciculus (lateral) carries similar information from upper limb. They ascend in posterior columns.
questions.question: The gracile fasciculus carries information from which body region?

questions.explanation: The appendix is characterized histologically by the presence of numerous lymphoid follicles that may extend from the mucosa into the submucosa. This prominent lymphoid tissue has led to the appendix being called a gut tonsil or abdominal tonsil. It is thought to function in immune surveillance. In chronic inflammation, this lymphoid tissue may atrophy in elderly individuals.
questions.question: The appendix is a blind-ended tubular appendage of the cecum. Its histological hallmark that distinguishes it from the rest of the large intestine is:
The superior mesenteric artery supplies:
questions.explanation: The superior mesenteric artery supplies all midgut derivatives, from the distal duodenum (past the ampulla of Vater) to the proximal 2/3 of the transverse colon. The celiac artery supplies foregut derivatives, and the inferior mesenteric artery supplies hindgut derivatives. These three unpaired ventral branches of the aorta define the three divisions of the gut.

questions.question: Lateral reticulospinal tract originates from which structure?
questions.explanation: Lateral reticulospinal tract originates from medullary reticular system. Fibers run in lateral white column facilitating anterior horn cells. It helps control posture and movement.
The metencephalon is the point of formation of both the pons and cerebellum. Pontine nuclei migrate into the developing pons. The rhombic lips differentiate into cerebellar plates.
questions.question: Which structures develop from the metencephalon?
The decidua capsularis initially covers which structure?
questions.explanation: The decidua capsularis overlies the developing fetus and separates the fetus from the uterine lumen, forming a capsule around the fetus. As the embryo grows, the decidua capsularis expands to meet the decidua parietalis, eventually fusing together and obliterating the uterine cavity.

questions.question: The autonomic nervous system is distinguished from the somatic nervous system primarily by which of the following?
questions.explanation: The ANS is the visceral motor division controlling involuntary functions including heart rate, digestion, glandular secretion, smooth muscle tone, and pupil size. It uses a two-neuron chain where a preganglionic neuron in the CNS synapses in an autonomic ganglion on a postganglionic neuron that innervates the target organ, unlike the somatic motor system using a single motor neuron. The ANS subdivides into sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions.
options: The ANS uses myelinated fibers exclusively
The ANS controls voluntary skeletal muscle contractions
The ANS is located only in the brain without peripheral components
The ANS uses only a single neuron between CNS and target
Two-neuron chains controlling involuntary visceral functions below conscious awareness

questions.explanation: Cardiomyocytes are mononucleated and occasionally binucleated cells with centrally placed nuclei, in contrast to skeletal muscle fibers with multiple peripheral nuclei reflecting their syncytial origin from myoblast fusion. The central nuclear position in cardiac muscle reflects that cardiomyocytes are individual cells joined at intercalated discs rather than true syncytia. This distinction is diagnostically useful in differentiating cardiac from skeletal muscle in tissue sections.
options: One or two centrally placed nuclei
Multiple peripherally placed nuclei like skeletal muscle
A single very large lobulated nucleus
Multiple nuclei arranged only at the intercalated disc
questions.question: Cardiac muscle cells have which of the following nuclear arrangement that distinguishes them from skeletal muscle fibers?

options: The resting zone is where chondrocytes rapidly divide in columns
The proliferative zone shows hypertrophied chondrocytes accumulating glycogen
The hypertrophic zone is where cartilage matrix becomes calcified
Resting zone: quiescent hyaline chondrocytes with no morphological changes
The ossification zone consists only of dying chondrocytes with no bone formation
questions.explanation: The resting (reserve) zone consists of typical hyaline cartilage with small, quiescent chondrocytes showing no morphological changes — it acts as a reservoir of cells for the proliferative zone. Moving toward the diaphysis: proliferative zone (rapid division in columns), hypertrophic zone (large cells accumulating glycogen), calcified cartilage zone (matrix calcification, chondrocyte death), and ossification zone (endochondral bone deposition by invading osteoblasts).
questions.question: The epiphyseal (growth) plate allows long bones to grow in length. This process involves five histological zones; which zone is correctly described?

questions.explanation: Neurulation involves four major stages: transformation of general ectoderm into a thickened neural plate, shaping the plate so it becomes narrower and longer, lateral folding of the neural plate, and fusion of the two most lateral apical surfaces of the neural folds.
questions.question: Neural tube formation involves how many major stages?
A section through the ileum shows dome-shaped protrusions overlying lymphoid aggregates with follicle-associated epithelium containing M cells. This structure corresponds to which of the following?
options: Thymic lobule with cortex and medulla
Lymph node germinal center with B cells
Peyer's patches: ileal submucosal aggregates of lymphoid follicles
questions.explanation: Peyer's patches are identified histologically as submucosal lymphoid aggregates underlying the intestinal epithelium in the ileum. Their characteristic features include multiple secondary follicles with germinal centers, a dome-shaped villus-free follicle-associated epithelium overlying each aggregate, M cells interspersed in the FAE, and an interfollicular zone containing T lymphocytes. These features distinguish Peyer's patches from solitary intestinal lymphoid nodules and other GALT structures.

questions.question: The parietal cell cytoplasm appears intensely eosinophilic in H&E staining. The organelle responsible for this staining property is:
questions.explanation: Parietal cells are intensely eosinophilic because they contain an exceptionally high density of mitochondria required for the energy-intensive process of HCl secretion via proton pumps. This is a distinctive feature that aids histological identification. Chief cells, by contrast, are basophilic due to abundant rough ER for protein synthesis.
Reflexes are mediated by local spinal circuitry. Rhythmic movements use multisegmental spinal circuitry. Postural adjustments involve brainstem and spinal cord.
questions.question: Local spinal circuitry mediates which movements?

options: It can rapidly change its membrane electrical potential in response to stimuli
It is easily damaged by mechanical force
It secretes large quantities of hormones in response to signals
It undergoes rapid division when stimulated
It migrates toward the source of a chemical signal
questions.question: When a cell is described as 'excitable' or 'irritable' in the context of membrane physiology, this specifically means which of the following?
questions.explanation: Excitable cells (neurons, muscle cells, some gland cells) are capable of responding to stimuli by rapidly reversing their membrane potential (action potential/depolarization). All cells maintain an electrical potential across their membrane, but only excitable cells can rapidly and significantly change this potential to propagate a signal. This property is the basis of nerve impulse transmission and muscle contraction.

The terminal sac period extends from 26 weeks to birth, during which terminal sacs (primitive alveoli) form and capillaries establish close contact with the epithelium. The epithelium thins from cuboidal to squamous, creating the blood-air barrier. Surfactant production by type II pneumocytes begins during this period.
questions.question: The terminal sac period of lung development extends from:

questions.explanation: Addison's disease destroys all cortical zones causing: cortisol deficiency from zona fasciculata destruction producing weakness fatigue hypoglycemia and impaired stress response; aldosterone deficiency from zona glomerulosa destruction causing salt wasting hyponatremia hyperkalemia hypotension and salt craving; and adrenal androgen deficiency from zona reticularis destruction. Loss of negative feedback causes excess ACTH and MSH from the anterior pituitary producing the characteristic bronzed hyperpigmentation especially in sun-exposed areas and pressure points.
options: Excess aldosterone and cortisol causing hypertension
Cortisol deficiency, aldosterone deficiency, and ACTH-driven hyperpigmentation
Deficiency of epinephrine causing bradycardia only
Isolated aldosterone deficiency without cortisol effects
questions.question: A patient with Addison's disease has primary adrenal insufficiency destroying the entire adrenal cortex. Which combination of hormonal deficiencies and clinical features would result?
TBX4 is a transcription factor that:
questions.explanation: TBX4 is a transcription factor that determines the location of the lung bud along the gut tube and induces its formation. It is upregulated by retinoic acid produced by adjacent mesoderm. TBX4 also promotes growth and differentiation of the developing lung. Mutations in TBX4 can cause lung hypoplasia.

questions.question: The filum terminale is formed from which tissue?
questions.explanation: The filum terminale is a condensation of pia mater extending from the conus medullaris. It anchors the spinal cord to the coccyx. This structure is important anatomically for lumbar puncture procedures.

Lactobacillus species (dominant members of the normal vaginal microbiome) metabolize glycogen stored in vaginal epithelial cells to lactic acid. This maintains vaginal pH at approximately 3.8–4.5 — an acidic environment that inhibits colonization by pathogenic bacteria and fungi. Estrogen promotes glycogen deposition in vaginal epithelium; postmenopausal women have reduced estrogen, less glycogen, and higher vaginal pH, predisposing to atrophic vaginitis and bacterial vaginosis.
questions.question: The vagina is lined by stratified squamous epithelium that is not keratinized. The glycogen content of vaginal epithelial cells is metabolized by Lactobacillus species to lactic acid, maintaining the vaginal pH at:

questions.explanation: The nuclear envelope consists of inner and outer lipid membranes separated by the perinuclear space (continuous with ER lumen). Nuclear pore complexes (~120 nm diameter) perforate both membranes and mediate selective bidirectional traffic: mRNAs and ribosome subunits exit to cytoplasm while transcription factors, histones, and polymerases enter. The outer nuclear membrane is continuous with rough ER.
questions.question: Which of the following describes the structure and function of the nuclear envelope?
options: A single lipid membrane with no pores that completely isolates nuclear contents
A double membrane perforated by nuclear pores regulating nucleocytoplasmic exchange
A rigid structure composed entirely of intermediate filaments
A membrane identical in composition to the plasma membrane
A structure that only allows RNA to exit while blocking all proteins from entering

questions.question: Which germ layer gives rise to the epithelial lining of the respiratory tract?
questions.explanation: The endoderm gives rise to the epithelial lining of the respiratory tract (pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi, and lungs).
