Osteomeatal complex (OMC): the functional unit comprising the natural ostia of the anterior sinuses (maxillary, anterior ethmoid, frontal) and the infundibulum; obstruction here is the primary pathophysiological mechanism for most rhinosinusitis and is the target of FESS.

B)
Maxillary sinus: its natural ostium opens at the roof of the sinus; keeping the head upright allows secretions to pool at the floor away from the ostium, potentially improving drainage transiently, but positional change causes pain due to pressure changes — keeping the head upright worsens maxillary sinusitis symptoms, while lying supine improves them. Frontal sinusitis: the fronto-nasal duct drainage is impaired in the supine position; keeping the head upright improves frontal drainage.

C)
Standard X-ray views: Waters' (occipitomental) — best for maxillary sinus; Caldwell (occipitofrontal) — best for ethmoid and frontal sinuses; Lateral — for sphenoid, frontal, and maxillary; Submentovertical ("bucket-handle") — for ethmoid sinuses (fluid in maxillary sinus layers out here too).

(i)
Temporal bone fracture. The presentation of SNHL and vertigo is most consistent with a transverse fracture, which commonly involves the bony labyrinth.

(ii)
Longitudinal fractures: most common (up to 80%); take the path of least resistance; may involve the ossicular chain and the perigeniculate ganglion region; otic capsule involvement is rare; facial nerve injury in 10–20%. Transverse fractures: less common but higher-impact injuries caused by anterior-posterior force; commonly involve the bony labyrinth leading to SNHL and vertigo; facial nerve injury quoted in up to 50%; associated with jugular foramen or foramen magnum to middle cranial fossa fracture lines. Mixed fractures: most fractures in reality are mixed type.

(iii)
Investigations: nasal exam for rhinorrhoea; facial nerve examination; extraocular movement examination for nystagmus or diplopia; tuning fork exam; audiometric testing; high-resolution CT is the gold standard; MRI is used for cranial nerve injury; MRA or angiogram for vascular injury.

(iv)
Facial nerve injury occurs in 7% of all temporal bone fractures, with 25% of these being permanent. Delayed onset paralysis has complete recovery in 94%. Immediate onset has complete recovery in 50–75%. The most common site of injury is the perigeniculate (tympanic segment) in 80–90% of cases, followed by the labyrinthine and meatal segments. Electrodiagnostic criteria for surgery: EMG showing voluntary activity indicates a good prognosis; operate when ENOG shows 90% degeneration; Wallerian degeneration is not evident on electrodiagnostic testing for 3 to 5 days after neurotmesis, so surgical intervention is delayed until several days after degeneration. Indications for surgical exploration: 90% degeneration on ENOG; immediate onset paralysis with sharp drop over three days; CN VII transection.

(v)
CSF otorrhoea occurs in 15–20% of all temporal bone fractures and is usually associated with longitudinal fractures involving the tegmen; leaks from otic capsule disruption are less likely to heal spontaneously. Conservative management: head of bed elevation >30 degrees; lumbar drain; stool softeners; no nose-blowing or coughing. Outcome: 95/122 (78%) of leaks resolve with conservative measures within 7 days; 17% between 7–14 days; 4% persist beyond 2 weeks. Antibiotics: meta-analysis shows difference of 8% vs 2% for antibiotics versus no antibiotics; no consensus on routine prophylaxis. Surgical indications: persistent leak beyond 2 weeks; otic capsule disruption; multi-layer technique (muscle, fascia, fat, cartilage, Duragen, bone paste, hydroxyapatite cement) has a significantly higher success rate than single-layer closure; refractory cases require closure of the EAC and obliteration.
questions.question:
A 25-year-old man presents to the emergency department following a road traffic accident. He is unconscious. On examination, there is haemotympanum, postauricular ecchymosis (Battle's sign), and bleeding from the ear canal. Audiological testing reveals sensorineural hearing loss and vertigo.
(i) State the diagnosis and classify the fracture type most likely responsible for this presentation.
(ii) Describe the two classical types of temporal bone fracture, their incidence, and the typical neurovascular structures each type injures.
(iii) Outline the immediate investigations required, including the gold standard imaging modality.
(iv) Describe the management of facial nerve injury associated with temporal bone fracture, including electrodiagnostic criteria for surgery.
(v) Describe the management of CSF otorrhoea following temporal bone fracture, including conservative measures and surgical indications.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Carcinoma of the larynx: squamous cell carcinoma is the commonest type and the commonest head and neck cancer in the western world, representing approximately 1% of all malignancies in men. It is about 5 times commoner in males than females. The peak age of presentation is the seventh decade (incidence increases with age).

A(ii)
Predisposing factors: persons who smoke tobacco and drink alcohol; the cause is not known but these are the strongest recognised factors; the tumour is very rare in non-smokers. Alcohol is highly synergistic with cigarette smoking.

A(iii)
The male-to-female ratio is changing with the increase in social habit change in females (implying greater female uptake of smoking and alcohol, narrowing the traditional male predominance).

B)
Follow-up schedule after curative treatment: monthly for the first 6 months; then every 2 months for 6 months; then every 3 months for 12 months; then 6-monthly for the next 3 years. At each follow-up: examine for signs of primary recurrence, neck node spread and distant metastases; record weight at each outpatient visit.

C)
The subglottis has a rich lymphatic drainage; subglottic tumours spread to cervical lymph nodes AND additionally drain to paratracheal and mediastinal nodes. The glottis, in contrast, virtually has no lymphatic drainage; thus early glottic tumours (T1, T2 confined to the cords) rarely spread to cervical lymph nodes, and metastases from the glottis usually only occur when the tumour has extended to involve the supraglottis and subglottis (transglottic spread), which grants access to richer lymphatic networks.
questions.question:
A) Describe the epidemiology and predisposing factors for carcinoma of the larynx under the following headings:
A(i) Sex ratio, peak age of presentation, and approximate percentage of all malignancies in men.
A(ii) The specific predisposing factors and the relationship between smoking and alcohol.
A(iii) The change in the male-to-female ratio over time and the reason given.
B) Describe the follow-up schedule for patients who have had potentially curative treatment for laryngeal carcinoma, including frequency and duration of review visits.
C) Explain anatomically why subglottic tumours have both cervical and mediastinal nodal involvement, whereas early glottic tumours rarely metastasise to lymph nodes.

questions.answerText:
(i)
Tracheostomy is a surgical opening made into the anterior wall of the trachea and maintained with a special tube. It is a life-saving surgical procedure. Alexandra the Great is credited as the first person to perform a tracheotomy, done on the war field.

(ii)
The four indications for tracheostomy are:
• Relief of upper airway obstruction
• Protection of the lower airway
• Ventilatory support in respiratory insufficiency
• Tracheo-bronchial toileting.

(iii)
Classification by level of tracheal incision: High — between the 1st and 2nd tracheal rings; Normal — between the 3rd and 4th tracheal rings; Low — below the 4th tracheal ring. Classification by duration: temporary or permanent/end tracheostomy. Classification by timing: elective or emergency.

(iv)
The two main types of tracheostomy tubes are:
• Metallic tracheostomy tube
• Plastic tracheostomy tube.
questions.question:
A 20-year-old man presents to the ENT outpatient clinic after being told by a doctor that he needs a tracheostomy. He asks for a full explanation.
(i) Define tracheostomy and state who is credited as the first to perform it and in what setting.
(ii) List all four indications for tracheostomy.
(iii) Classify tracheostomy by the level of tracheal incision (stating exact anatomical levels), by duration, and by timing.
(iv) State the two main types of tracheostomy tubes.

A) Describe the gross anatomy of the larynx under the following headings:
A(i) The three named anatomical regions of the larynx and their boundaries.
A(ii) The subglottis and its lymphatic drainage pattern, naming all groups of nodes.
A(iii) The glottis and the basis for its very different metastatic behaviour compared to the other regions.
B) Explain how the TNM staging of glottic carcinoma reflects the anatomical progression of disease, giving the T-stage descriptors (T1a through T4).
C) Explain anatomically why a transglottic tumour behaves differently in terms of lymph node spread, and name the structure from which such tumours are said to arise.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Three regions:
• Supraglottis: includes the epiglottis (laryngeal surface, tip and lingual surface), aryepiglottic folds and associated structures.
• Glottis: comprises the vocal cords and the anterior and posterior commissures.
• Subglottis: extends from the inferior border of the glottis to the lower border of the cricoid cartilage.

A(ii)
Subglottic lymphatic drainage: subglottis has a rich lymphatic drainage and a high proportion of tumours spread to cervical lymph nodes; additionally, subglottis drains to paratracheal and mediastinal nodes in addition to the cervical lymph nodes.

A(iii)
The glottis virtually has no lymphatic drainage; thus metastases usually only occur when the tumour has spread to involve the supraglottis and subglottis (transglottic tumour). This explains why early glottic tumours rarely metastasise.

B)
Glottic T-stage descriptors:
• T1(a): tumour limited to one vocal cord.
• T1(b): involved both vocal cords.
• T2: tumour extends to supraglottis and/or subglottis, or impaired cord mobility.
• T3: confined to the larynx with a fixed vocal cord, or invades postcricoid area, pre-epiglottic tissues, base of tongue.
• T4: extends beyond the larynx.

C)
Transglottic tumours arise from the laryngeal ventricle (some authorities maintain). Because the transglottic tumour involves both supraglottis and subglottis, it gains access to both the rich supraglottic lymphatics (draining to deep cervical nodes bilaterally) and the subglottic lymphatics (draining to paratracheal and mediastinal nodes), explaining why such tumours have a worse nodal metastatic pattern.

A(i)
WHO classification: Type 1 — keratinizing SCC, 10% (radioresistant; <5% in South-East Asia); Type 2 — non-keratinizing SCC, 20%; Type 3 — undifferentiated carcinoma (lymphoepithelioma), 70%.

A(ii)
T staging: T1 — confined to nasopharynx; T2 — extended to soft tissue of oropharynx and/or nasal fossa (T2a without, T2b with parapharyngeal extension); T3 — invades bony structures and/or paranasal sinuses; T4 — intracranial extension and/or involvement of cranial nerves, infratemporal fossa, hypopharynx, or orbit. N staging: Nx — cannot be assessed; N0 — no regional LN metastasis; N1 — unilateral metastasis, LN ≤6 cm, above supraclavicular fossa; N2 — bilateral metastasis, LN ≤6 cm, above supraclavicular fossa; N3a — LN >6 cm diameter; N3b — LN in supraclavicular fossa.

A(iii)
Stage I — T1 N0 M0; Stage IIa — T2a N0 M0; Stage IIb — T1/T2, N1, M0; T2b N0/N1 M0; Stage III — T1/T2a/T2b N2 M0; T3 N0/N1/N2 M0; Stage IVa — T4 N0/N1/N2 M0; Stage IVb — Any T, N3, M0; Stage IVc — Any T, Any N, M1.

B.
Radiotherapy: treatment of choice at 65–75 Gy minimum to the site bilaterally; WHO Type 1 is radioresistant. Chemoradiation (Al-Saraaf et al 1998) for advanced NPC (WHO Types II and III): cisplatin 100 mg/m² + 5-FU 1 g/m² for 4 weeks x 3 cycles; overall survival at 3 years — 75% vs 46%; at 5 years — 67% vs 37%. Chemotherapy agents include: cisplatin, 5-FU, doxorubicin, epirubicin, bleomycin, mitoxantrone, methotrexate, vincristine alkaloids. For persistent or recurrent NPC: re-irradiation (only 15–23% achieve disease-free survival); nasopharyngectomy for salvage; radical neck dissection for regional failure (local control rate up to 66%).

C.
Surgical indications for nasopharyngectomy: limited to rT1, rT2, rT3. Contraindications: involvement of cavernous sinus, cranial nerves, or carotid artery. Surgical approaches: Fee — transpalatal; transmaxillary (pterygomaxillary space); transcervical (lateral nasopharyngeal wall); Fisch — infratemporal approach; Gross and Panje — lateral temporal approach; Wie et al (1995) — maxillary swing (facial translocation), local control rate 42% at 3.5 years; Biller and Krespi — transcervico-mandibulo-palatal, local control rate 67% at 2 years. Complications of radiotherapy: brain — pituitary dysfunction, brainstem damage, encephalopathy, temporal lobe necrosis, cranial nerve palsy; ear — SNHL, OME, ETD; eye — dry eye syndrome, ischaemic retinopathy; thyroid — hypothyroidism; GIT — severe mucositis, xerostomia, nausea, vomiting, dysphagia, oesophageal stricture; MSS — fibrosis, trismus, radiation myelitis, osteoradionecrosis; vascular — carotid artery stenosis. Complications of surgery: poor wound healing; palatal fistula; nasopharyngeal wound infection; osteonecrosis; osteomyelitis of cervical vertebrae or skull base; malunion or non-union of osteotomy sites; wound necrosis.
questions.question:
A. Describe the classification system and treatment principles for nasopharyngeal carcinoma under the following headings:
A(i) WHO histological classification with frequency of each type
A(ii) AJCC-UICC TNM staging 2002: T and N classifications
A(iii) Stage groupings I through IV
B. Describe the primary treatment modalities for NPC (radiotherapy and chemoradiation), including radiation dose, agents used, and outcome data for advanced disease.
C. State the surgical indications and contraindications for nasopharyngectomy, describe the principal surgical approaches, and list the complications due to both radiotherapy and surgery.

A 60-year-old male smoker who drinks alcohol heavily presents with progressive hoarseness of 3 months, recent onset of dyspnoea and stridor, and right-sided neck swelling. Indirect laryngoscopy reveals a fixed right vocal cord with a mass extending across both cords.
(i) State the diagnosis and the two strongest predisposing factors, including the relationship between them.
(ii) State the sub-site of origin inferred from the symptom of early hoarseness and the fixed cord, and classify the T-stage.
(iii) What does the neck swelling most likely represent, and what proportion of patients with no palpable nodes actually have histological nodal invasion?
(iv) List all the investigations for staging this tumour.
(v) Outline the curative and palliative treatment options, distinguishing small from large tumours.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Carcinoma of the larynx (squamous cell carcinoma — the commonest histological type and the commonest head and neck cancer in the western world, representing approximately 1% of all malignancies in men; approximately 5 times commoner in males than females). The two strongest predisposing factors: smoking tobacco and alcohol; alcohol is highly synergistic with cigarette smoking. The tumour is very rare in non-smokers.

(ii)
Early hoarseness indicates glottic origin (vocal cords); fixed cord indicates transglottic or advanced glottic involvement (T3 or T4). A fixed vocal cord at T3 stage: tumour confined to the larynx with a fixed vocal cord. Extension beyond the larynx = T4.

(iii)
Neck swelling most likely represents lymph node metastasis (lymphadenopathy in the deep cervical nodes). One third of patients with no palpable lymph nodes have histologically invaded nodes; a similar number of palpable nodes are not invaded by tumour. Presence of palpable lymph nodes is the most important factor in determining prognosis, but assessment of lymphadenopathy is subjective.

(iv)
Investigations for staging:
• CXR, FBC, serum analysis (baseline)
• LFT (liver metastases or hypoproteinaemia)
• MRI or CT scan (distant metastases)
• Ultrasound scan (liver)
• Direct laryngoscopy under GA (tissue diagnosis, extent of disease)
• Pan-endoscopy including bronchoscopy
• General examination (distant metastases and overall physical status)
• Indirect laryngoscopy (primary tumour site, size, vocal cord mobility)

(v)
Curative treatment: small tumours (Stages 1 and 2) — surgery or radiotherapy or both; large tumours (Stages 3 and 4) — surgery followed by radiotherapy; primary surgery usually with post-operative radiotherapy. Preservation laryngeal surgery is also an option with small tumours. Palliative treatment: pain relief, tracheostomy, insertion of percutaneous gastrostomy, palliative radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and occasionally surgery; early involvement of the palliative care team.

A(i)
History taking is a process of obtaining informed, guided information from a patient or an informant regarding the patient's presenting complaint(s)/symptom(s), with the aim of arriving at a provisional diagnosis and the subsequent management (or treatment) plan of the patient. A very good history can contribute about 80% of the diagnosis. A diagnosis is arrived at only after the history, examination, and investigations.

A(ii)
Using deafness as an example: Onset — sudden or gradual. Duration — present since birth may be due to genetic causes; of recent origin could be due to traumatic, inflammatory, neoplastic, vascular, or metabolic causes. Nature of deafness — a patient may hear better in a noisy surrounding (paracusis willisi, characteristic of otosclerosis); in cochlear lesions, patients do not hear at conversational intensity but get irritated by loud sounds (recruitment). Fluctuant deafness occurs in secretory otitis media and Menière's disease.

B(i)
Drug history — to exclude ototoxicity. Occupation — people working in a noisy environment are at risk of noise-induced hearing impairment (acoustic trauma). Family history — e.g. otosclerosis has a familial predisposition.

B(ii)
Other otological symptoms to be taken along the same line include: tinnitus; vertigo or syncopal attacks or giddiness; ear discharge (otorrhoea); and ear-ache (otalgia). Principles of clinical examination: in ENT, as in any other specialty of medicine, examination follows the same principles of inspection, palpation, percussion, and auscultation; usually palpation is done using instruments and percussion in most cases, as sites of lesions are not readily accessible to the hands of the examiner.
questions.question:
Describe history-taking in ENT, using deafness (hearing impairment) as an illustrative example, and outline the principles of clinical examination.
A(i) Define history-taking and state what proportion of the diagnosis a very good history can contribute.
A(ii) Using deafness as an example, describe all the specific points to be noted in the history of an otological symptom, covering onset, duration, nature, and specific subtypes.
B(i) Explain the significance of drug history, occupation, and family history in hearing impairment.
B(ii) State what other otological symptoms should be taken along the line of the deafness history, and describe the principles of clinical examination in ENT.

A 55-year-old male smoker who works in the leather industry presents with progressive left-sided nasal obstruction, epistaxis, left cheek swelling, loose upper teeth and diplopia. CT scan of the paranasal sinuses reveals a destructive soft-tissue mass occupying the left maxillary antrum with erosion of the medial and superior walls.
(i) State the most likely diagnosis and justify it based on the site of origin, percentage occupancy, and risk factors.
(ii) Name the structures compressed or invaded that account for each symptom (loose teeth, diplopia, cheek swelling).
(iii) List the lymphatic drainage pathway of the paranasal sinuses, explaining why palpable cervical lymphadenopathy is only present in 15% of cases.
(iv) List the differential diagnoses for a destructive antral mass.
(v) Outline the investigations and the surgical treatment options for this tumour.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Malignant sinonasal tumour — most likely squamous cell carcinoma of the maxillary antrum (squamous cell carcinoma is the commonest, accounting for 80%). Antrum (maxillary sinus) is the commonest site: 60% of sinonasal tumours. Risk factors: leather/shoe/dye industry exposure to nickel/chromate (Ni/CrO3) causing squamous cell carcinoma; wood dust causing adenocarcinoma; chronic sinusitis; smoking (cigarette); Human Papilloma Virus (papilloma/squamous cell carcinoma).

(ii)
Loose upper teeth: erosion of alveolar process/floor of antrum with involvement of upper dental roots. Diplopia: erosion of the superior wall of the antrum (orbital floor), compressing extraocular muscles or orbital contents, causing restricted eye movement. Cheek swelling: direct erosion and extension through anterior antral wall into soft tissues of the cheek.

(iii)
Lymphatic drainage: paranasal sinuses drain first to retropharyngeal nodes, then to the deep cervical chain. Because the first echelon nodes (retropharyngeal) are not palpable in the neck, palpable cervical lymphadenopathy is only present in 15% of cases.

(iv)
Differential diagnoses for destructive antral mass: squamous cell carcinoma, anaplastic carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, adenocystic carcinoma; sarcomas (osteogenic sarcoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, chondrosarcoma); malignant lymphoma/Burkitt lymphoma; esthesioneuroblastoma; plasmacytoma; malignant melanoma; inverted papilloma (benign but locally destructive).

(v)
Investigations: FBC, U/E; X-rays of sinuses and chest; CT scan sinuses; MRI sinuses; nasoendoscopy; examination under anaesthesia and biopsy (for histological diagnosis). Surgical treatment: medial maxillectomy; total maxillectomy; extended maxillectomy; palatal resection; combination with radiotherapy and/or chemotherapy.

A(i)
The luminal surface of the tonsils is covered by deeply invaginated clefts of stratified squamous epithelium. These clefts (crypts) are lined by specialised squamous epithelium that transports antigens by M-type cells to be presented and processed by antigen-presenting cells. The tonsil parenchyma can vary in its extent, sometimes extending into the nasopharynx causing nasal obstruction, and sometimes inferiorly causing extreme dysphagia.

A(ii)
Immune cell zones: the extrafollicular area has abundant T-lymphocytes which aid in the differentiation of B-lymphocytes. The lymphoid follicle is encased by the mantle zone where mature B-lymphocytes reside. At the core of the lymphoid follicle is the germinal centre where B-lymphocytes produce antigen-specific immunoglobulin. Transported antigens are presented and processed by antigen-presenting cells and then transported to the extrafollicular area before reaching the mantle zone and germinal centre.

A(iii)
The adenoid produces antibodies locally: IgA locally; the tonsils and adenoids together produce IgG and IgM systemically. Stromal cells are mostly fibroblasts showing intensive immunostaining for vimentin; myofibroblasts may occur focally in fibrotic areas.

B.
Peritonsillar abscess: extension of tonsillitis beyond the tonsillar capsule into the peritonsillar space (bounded medially by the tonsillar capsule, laterally by the superior pharyngeal constrictor); infection tracks into the loose connective tissue, forming a pus collection. Lemierre's syndrome: internal jugular bacterial thrombophlebitis is a complication of GABHS pharyngitis; the infection spreads via the peritonsillar veins to the internal jugular vein, causing septic thrombophlebitis with bacteraemia, septic pulmonary emboli, and metastatic abscesses; it is a named complication of GABHS pharyngitis. Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis: a non-suppurative complication of GABHS (Group A beta-haemolytic Streptococcus) pharyngitis; occurs due to immune complex deposition in the glomeruli following streptococcal infection; it is a listed complication of GABHS pharyngitis.

C.
Differential diagnosis of exudative tonsillitis: mononucleosis (Epstein-Barr virus, detected by monospot test; CBC typically shows lymphocytosis); scarlet fever (GABHS with erythrotoxin, produces a diffuse erythematous rash); diphtheria (grey pseudo-membrane, Corynebacterium diphtheriae, may require swab and culture); tularaemia; toxoplasmosis; lymphoma; leukaemia; carcinoma. Investigations to differentiate: rapid Strep test and throat culture (to confirm GABHS); CBC (higher WBC and granulocyte shift in bacterial vs viral; lymphocytosis in mononucleosis); monospot test (for mononucleosis); blood culture; electrolytes and urea; serological tests; 24-hour ambulatory pH (for GERD-associated pharyngitis); radiological investigations. GABHS is differentiated from viral tonsillitis by: fever >38.5°C, positive GABHS culture, tender cervical lymphadenopathy >2 cm, and erythematous or exudative tonsils; patients with viral pharyngitis have lower-grade fever and less tonsillar exudate.
questions.question:
A. Describe the anatomy and immunology of the palatine tonsil under the following headings:
A(i) The luminal surface, crypt structure, and specialised epithelium in antigen transport
A(ii) The immune cell zones within the tonsil parenchyma (extrafollicular area, mantle zone, germinal centre) and the function of each
A(iii) The normal immunological products of the tonsil and adenoid (immunoglobulin classes produced)
B. Explain the pathophysiology by which recurrent tonsillitis leads to the following complications: peritonsillar abscess, Lemierre's syndrome, and post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.
C. Describe the differential diagnosis of exudative tonsillitis, distinguishing the infectious causes that must be excluded before attributing the condition to bacterial tonsillitis, and state the investigations that help differentiate them.

questions.answerText:
(i)
Laryngotracheobronchitis (Croup). Causative organism: Parainfluenza virus (preceded by a cold). Typical age group: 6 months to 2 years.

(ii)
Grading of croup according to severity of obstruction:
• Grade 1: inspiratory obstruction present; no expiratory obstruction; no pulsus paradoxus.
• Grade 2: inspiratory obstruction present; passive expiratory obstruction; no pulsus paradoxus.
• Grade 3: inspiratory obstruction present; active expiratory obstruction; pulsus paradoxus present.
• Grade 4: as Grade 3 plus apathy and cyanosis (most severe — implies impending respiratory failure).

(iii)
Management: adrenaline inhalations; steroids; avoid crying (which worsens obstruction); if the above measures fail — airway management: intubation, then tracheostomy if intubation fails or prolonged airway support is needed.

(iv)
Distinguishing croup from epiglottitis:
• Croup: age 6 months–2 years; preceded by a cold (parainfluenza virus); stridor; normal voice; barking cough; gradual onset; no drooling; no pyrexia stated.
• Epiglottitis (H. influenzae type B): acute onset; drooling; pyrexia; posture (child sits forward in sniffing position); no barking cough; voice may be muffled; older children typically; airway management and antibiotics are the primary management priorities.
questions.question:
A child aged 18 months is brought to the casualty department with sudden onset of noisy breathing, barking cough, inspiratory stridor and a normal voice. The mother reports that the symptoms were preceded by a cold. Severity grading shows Grade 2 obstruction with passive expiratory obstruction but no pulsus paradoxus.
(i) State the diagnosis, causative organism and age group typically affected.
(ii) Describe the grading system for this condition according to severity, and state what Grade 4 represents.
(iii) Outline the management of this child from immediate treatment to airway intervention.
(iv) Distinguish this condition from epiglottitis (supraglottitis), listing the differentiating clinical features for each.

questions.answerText:
(i)
Diagnosis: Foreign body aspiration causing complete airway obstruction. Sites of arrest: bronchi — 80–90% (commonest site); trachea; larynx (larger objects, irregular edges or conforming objects). The right mainstem bronchus is the commonest specific site because it has a less divergent angle and a greater diameter than the left.

(ii)
Physical examination findings: Larynx/cervical trachea — inspiratory or biphasic stridor. Intrathoracic trachea — prolonged expiratory wheeze. Bronchi — unequal breath sounds; the diagnostic triad (present in less than 50%) of unilateral wheeze, cough, and ipsilateral diminished breath sounds. Fiberoptic laryngoscopy may also be performed.

(iii)
Radiographic investigation includes PA and lateral views of chest and neck X-rays taken in inspiration and expiration, lateral decubitus views, and airway fluoroscopy. Twenty-five percent of patients have a normal radiograph.

(iv)
For complete airway obstruction (inability to speak or cough, respiratory distress): in a child under one year — back blows; in a child over one year — gentle abdominal thrusts while supine; in older children and adults — Heimlich manoeuvre. Note: back blows and probing of the hypopharynx are not recommended in children over one year or adults. Endoscopy is usually not a dire emergency and awaits preparation of instruments and trained personnel.
questions.question:
A 2-year-old child is brought to the emergency department with sudden onset of respiratory distress, inability to speak, and cyanosis developing over 20 minutes. There is no fever. The parents report the child was playing with small toy parts.
(i) What is the diagnosis? State the three sites where foreign bodies are most likely to arrest in the airway (with percentages) and the anatomical reason for the commonest site.
(ii) Describe the physical examination findings on the larynx/cervical trachea, intrathoracic trachea, and bronchi.
(iii) What are the radiographic findings in foreign body aspiration, and what percentage of patients have a normal radiograph?
(iv) What action should be taken immediately for complete airway obstruction in a child under one year, and in one over one year, before definitive endoscopy?

questions.answerText:
A(i)
The four main steps in speech production are:
• Respiration — provides the main driving force by which phonation is made possible
• Phonation — produces the initial sound waves, which are then modulated
• Articulation and resonance — modulate the sound waves through the vocal tract
• Co-ordination and language formulation — the sounds are fluently co-ordinated into an appropriate pattern, then formulated to convey appropriate symbols of language concept.

A(ii)
The four groups of speech disorders:
• Voice — related to respiration, phonation, and resonance
• Articulation — related to articulatory processes in the vocal tract
• Fluency — related to co-ordination
• Language — related to proper adequate symbolization in the brain.

B(i)
Fluency disorders include stuttering or stammering. Clinical features are involuntary repetitions, prolongations, and hesitations in speaking. Aetiology: physiological problems; laryngeal dysfunction, as has been suggested.

B(ii)
Language disorders may involve reception and comprehension; formation of spoken or written symbols may be difficult. Developmental language disorder occurs often in children and may result from: emotional disturbance or neurological impairment. An example is aphasia — an impairment or nearly total loss in the reception, manipulation, and sometimes the use of words as symbols of ideas, caused by lesions in the cerebral cortex and association paths of the dominant hemisphere. Learning-disabled children exhibit impaired language acquisition without impairment of specific sensory, motor, intellectual, or emotional functions.
questions.question:
Describe the process of making speech, classify all speech disorders under their four groups, and explain the full pathophysiology of fluency disorders and language disorders.
A(i) Describe the four main steps in speech production, in the correct order, stating the role of each step.
A(ii) List all four groups of speech disorders with their relation to the speech process.
B(i) Describe fluency disorders, their clinical features, and their aetiology.
B(ii) Describe language disorders, their subtypes, and the conditions that produce developmental language disorder in children.

questions.answerText:
(i)
Retropharyngeal abscess. Fifty per cent occur in patients 6–12 months of age; 96% occur before 6 years of age. In children, the cause is a suppurative process in lymph nodes draining the nose, adenoids, nasopharynx, and sinuses. In adults, the cause is trauma, instrumentation, or extension from an adjoining deep neck space.

(ii)
Retropharyngeal space: posterior to the pharynx and oesophagus; anterior to the alar layer of deep fascia; extends from skull base to T1–T2. Danger space: anterior border is the alar layer of deep fascia; posterior border is the prevertebral layer; extends from skull base to the diaphragm. Prevertebral space: anterior border is the prevertebral fascia; posterior border is the vertebral bodies and deep neck muscles; extends along the entire length of the vertebral column.

(iii)
Transoral drainage is performed under general anaesthesia after confirming vessel positions on preoperative CT. A cruciate mucosal incision is made at the point of maximum bulge, followed by blunt spreading through the superior pharyngeal constrictor to enter the abscess. Anatomical precaution: great vessels must be identified on CT before the procedure to determine their proximity to the abscess; the lateral incision risks entry into the parapharyngeal space.

(iv)
During transoral drainage, the structures at risk include the internal carotid artery and the cranial nerves in the poststyloid compartment. The poststyloid compartment of the parapharyngeal space contains the carotid sheath and cranial nerves IX, X, and XII.

(v)
In recurrent deep neck space infection at the same site in a child, a congenital abnormality must be considered. The most common is a second branchial cleft cyst. Others include first, third, and fourth branchial cleft cysts, lymphangiomas, thyroglossal duct cysts, and cervical thymic cysts.
questions.question:
A 6-year-old child is brought to the ENT clinic with a 3-week history of fever, irritability, refusal to eat, drooling, and stridor. On examination, there is a lateral posterior oropharyngeal wall bulge and torticollis. Lateral neck radiograph shows widening of the retropharyngeal space.
(i) State the diagnosis, the age group predominantly affected, and the cause in children versus adults.
(ii) Describe the anatomical boundaries of the retropharyngeal space, the danger space, and the prevertebral space.
(iii) Name the surgical drainage procedure of choice and describe its technique, including the anatomical precaution regarding vessels.
(iv) Identify the structures at risk during transoral drainage and state the nerve and vessel findings in the poststyloid compartment of the parapharyngeal space.
(v) State the most common congenital cause to suspect in a child with a recurrent deep neck space infection at the same site.

A. Describe the parapharyngeal space under the following headings:
A(i) Boundaries (superior, inferior, anterior, posterior, medial, lateral)
A(ii) Contents of the prestyloid and poststyloid compartments
A(iii) Spaces communicating with or adjacent to the parapharyngeal space
B. Explain the anatomical basis for each clinical feature observed when an infection fills the parapharyngeal space (fever, trismus, medial wall bulge, dysphagia).
C. Distinguish between the clinical presentation and complications of retropharyngeal abscess and danger space infection, and explain why the danger space is of particular clinical importance.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Parapharyngeal space boundaries: superior — skull base; inferior — hyoid; anterior — pterygomandibular raphe; posterior — prevertebral fascia; medial — buccopharyngeal fascia; lateral — superficial layer of deep fascia.

A(ii)
Prestyloid compartment: medial — tonsillar fossa; lateral — medial pterygoid; contains fat, connective tissue, and nodes. Poststyloid compartment: contains the carotid sheath and cranial nerves IX, X, and XII.

A(iii)
Spaces that communicate with or are adjacent to the parapharyngeal space: peritonsillar space (medial — capsule of palatine tonsil; lateral — superior pharyngeal constrictor; superior — anterior tonsil pillar; inferior — posterior tonsil pillar); retropharyngeal space; prevertebral space; danger space; masticator space; parotid space; and infratemporal fossa.

B.
Fever: extension of infection from adjacent spaces (pharynx, tonsil, adenoids, dentition, parotid, mastoid, or suppurative lymphadenitis) causes systemic inflammatory response. Trismus: infection infiltrates or causes spasm of the medial pterygoid muscle, which forms the lateral boundary of the prestyloid compartment. Medial wall bulge: pus accumulating in the parapharyngeal space pushes the lateral pharyngeal wall medially, producing the visible bulge. Dysphagia: parapharyngeal swelling and inflammation impair the normal pharyngeal constrictor function and may compress the oropharynx.

C.
Retropharyngeal abscess presents in children with fever, irritability, lymphadenopathy, torticollis, poor oral intake, sore throat, and drooling; in adults with pain, dysphagia, anorexia, snoring, nasal obstruction, and nasal regurgitation; change in voice, dyspnoea, and stridor may occur; lateral posterior oropharyngeal wall bulge is seen on examination. Danger space: its presentation and examination findings are nearly identical to retropharyngeal space infection; its cause is extension from the retropharyngeal, prevertebral, or parapharyngeal space. The danger space is clinically critical because it extends from the skull base to the diaphragm, providing a direct pathway for descending mediastinitis; mediastinitis carries a mortality of 40% and requires aggressive IV antibiotic therapy and early surgical drainage (transcervical approach, chest tube, or thoracotomy).

questions.question:
A) Describe the microscopic anatomy of the nasal mucosa under the following headings:
A(i) Types of epithelial cells lining the nasal cavity and sinuses, with their distribution and function.
A(ii) The mucous blanket — its two layers and the function of each.
A(iii) Goblet cells: their secretory product and how autonomic innervation controls secretion viscosity.
B) Explain the physiological role of mucociliary transport, stating the direction of flow and what happens when normal ostium drainage is bypassed by surgery.
C) List the seven functions of the paranasal sinuses.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Epithelial cell types:
• Ciliated columnar cells: predominant; beat in a coordinated direction to transport mucus toward the choanae; contact inhibition is a recognised feature.
• Non-ciliated columnar cells: present throughout; specific function not fully detailed.
• Basal cells: present in the epithelium.
• Goblet cells: produce glycoproteins contributing to mucus viscosity and elasticity.

A(ii)
Mucous blanket — two layers:
• Superficial (gel) layer: traps bacteria, particulate matter, enzymes, antibodies and immune cells.
• Sol layer (deeper, periciliary): allows ciliary movement; cilia beat within this layer to propel the overlying gel layer.

A(iii)
Goblet cells secrete glycoproteins that determine viscosity and elasticity of mucus. Autonomic innervation: parasympathetic stimulation produces thick mucus; sympathetic stimulation produces thin mucus.

B)
Mucociliary transport: directional flow of mucus is toward the choanae. Regarding ostium drainage — Hilding demonstrated that even after surgery creating new openings, mucus continues to flow toward the natural ostium first before reaching any surgically created opening ("a stubborn beast"); contact inhibition and Haller's cells can disrupt normal flow.

C)
Seven functions of the paranasal sinuses:
• Humidifying and warming inspired air.
• Regulation of intranasal pressure.
• Increasing surface area for olfaction.
• Lightening the skull.
• Resonance (contributing to voice quality).
• Absorbing shock.
• Contributing to facial growth.

questions.question:
Describe the radiological investigation of the ear, nose, and paranasal sinuses, stating the information provided by each standard view.
A(i) Name and describe the four main standard plain radiographic views for the ear, including what each view demonstrates.
A(ii) Name and describe the four standard views for the nose and paranasal sinuses, stating the structures shown by each.
B(i) Describe the plain radiographic features of disease in the paranasal sinuses (fluid level and malignancy).
B(ii) Compare CT scan and MRI in ENT radiology under the following headings: dimensionality of image, tissue differentiation, vascular demonstration, metallic implant considerations, and main clinical value.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Standard ear views: (A) 22–25° fronto-occipital (Towne's) view — shows both mastoid bones, the external and internal auditory meati on the same film; useful for detecting pathology in the internal auditory canal such as acoustic neuroma; also shows the superior semicircular canal, middle ear, and ossicles. (B) Lateral oblique (Law's/Stockholm B) view — shows the mastoid antrum and periantral cells, e.g. cells of the sino-dural angle, squamous cells, and apical cells. (C) Stenver's view (postero-anterior oblique) — demonstrates the mastoid bone tip, the whole length of the petrous bone, and the superior and horizontal semicircular canals. (D) Owen's view — good for assessing the ossicles, e.g. malleus and incus. (E) Submento-vertical (full axial) view — shows the middle ear, bony eustachian tube, mastoid antrum, and petrous apex.

A(ii)
Nose/paranasal sinus views: (A) Lateral view — shows antero-posterior depth of the frontal sinuses, sphenoid sinuses, jaws, and facial bones. (B) Occipito-mental view (Water's view) — shows the maxillary antrum, orbital margins, and malar bones. (C) Occipito-frontal view (Caldwell view) — shows the petrous temporal bone ridge, ethmoidal sinus, frontal sinus, and nasal septum. (D) Submento-vertical view — shows ethmoidal and sphenoidal sinuses from below.

B(i)
Radiological signs of paranasal sinus disease: fluid level in the sinuses; malignancy destroys the bone.

B(ii)
CT scan vs MRI: CT gives a 2-D image; MRI gives a 3-D image in any plane. CT: air, bone, and calcification are well differentiated; cannot demonstrate arteries and veins without contrast; no problem with metallic implants; most valuable for lesions of the external, middle, and inner ear; faster and more economical. MRI: best for soft tissue shadows; can demonstrate arteries and veins without contrast; cannot be done with implants such as cochlear implants, aneurysm clips, or pacemakers; most valuable for cerebral/cerebellar and other brain lesions and inner ear lesions; post-contrast MRI can differentiate between scar tissue and recurrence of a tumour; no signal from cortical bone and calcification.

questions.question:
Describe allergy as an ENT condition, its familial basis, systemic associations, and surgical management options.
A(i) Explain why history-taking is described as the most diagnostic tool in allergy, and list the family and personal conditions that should be specifically asked about.
A(ii) Describe the nasal examination findings in allergic rhinitis, and explain why they are unreliable as a diagnostic criterion.
B(i) List environmental and precipitating factors that should be sought in the history, including household, occupational, and hormonal factors.
B(ii) State the surgical procedures available for allergic ENT conditions, and list the four components of medical management.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
History-taking is described as the most diagnostic tool in allergy because the paroxysmal nature of the complaint makes clinical findings difficult to capture at the time of examination. In the family history, the following conditions should be asked about: (a) asthma, (b) eczema, (c) urticaria, (d) migraine, chronic sinusitis or chronic rhinosinusitis, and gastrointestinal disorder. The patient should also be asked whether they personally suffer from any of the conditions mentioned above.

A(ii)
On nasal examination, the presence of enlarged turbinates with a blue hue has been thought to be diagnostic of the allergic nose. However, actually there are no typical allergic nasal findings; the paroxysmal nature of the complaint makes it more difficult to find specific signs at the time of examination.

B(i)
Environmental and precipitating factors: whether the pillow material is feather or synthetic; presence of flowers or plants around the patient in the house; use of medicated or scented soaps; whether the patient has any animals at home or at work; whether onset was associated with any change in the nature of jobs; whether onset was associated with pregnancy or menopause; and history of endogenous precipitating factors such as injured tissue from recent injuries.

B(ii)
Surgical procedures: removal of allergic polyps; submucous resection (SMR) of deviated nasal septum; sinus drainage if necessary. Medical management:
• avoidance of precipitating factors (prevention is better than cure)
• oestrogen or steroids
• cromoglycate, available as powder insufflation or aqueous spray
• appropriate treatment of associated infections (antibiotics).

questions.question:
A. Describe the course of the facial nerve from the facial nucleus to the extracranial branches under the following headings:
A(i) Intracranial and intracanalicular course, including the geniculate ganglion and its branches at that level
A(ii) Tympanic and mastoid segments, including relationships to the ossicular chain and the oval window
A(iii) Extracranial course from the stylomastoid foramen through the parotid gland and terminal branches
B. State the classification of facial nerve injuries (Seddon 1943 and Sunderland 1978) and describe the histopathological changes in each grade.
C. Describe the anatomical basis of Wallerian degeneration and nerve misdirection after severe injury, and explain how these underlie the complications of hemifacial spasm and synkinesis.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The facial nucleus is intracranial (15–17 mm). The nerve enters the internal auditory meatus (meatal segment 10 mm) where the nervus intermedius accompanies the main trunk. At the geniculate ganglion (5th week of embryologic development), the greater superficial petrosal nerve (GSPN) branches off, carrying parasympathetic fibres to the lacrimal gland and taste fibres from the soft palate.

A(ii)
Tympanic segment (11 mm): runs above the oval window; the ossicular chain (incus long process) lies in close relation; the most common anomaly (dehiscence of the facial canal) occurs most often here and at the geniculate ganglion, making the nerve susceptible to injury during otologic surgery. Mastoid segment (13 mm): descends vertically; the chorda tympani branches off to join CN V3, carrying taste from anterior two-thirds of the tongue and parasympathetic fibres to submandibular and sublingual glands.

A(iii)
The nerve exits the stylomastoid foramen and travels 15–20 mm through the parotid gland to bifurcate. Terminal branches (from superior to inferior): temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular, and cervical — supplying the scalp, face, auricula, buccinator, platysma, stylohyoid, and posterior belly of the digastric. The stapedius branch arises in the mastoid segment.

B.
Seddon 1943 classification: neuropraxia (reversible conduction block); axonotmesis (loss of structural continuity of axon with intact endoneurial sheath); neurotmesis (complete disruption of the nerve). Sunderland 1978 (5 grades): 1st degree — neuropraxia, transient block of axoplasmic flow, no neural atrophy; 2nd degree — axonotmesis, damage to nerve axon with preservation of epineurium (regrowth possible); 3rd degree — loss of continuity of axons and endoneurial sheaths; 4th degree — loss of continuity of axons, sheaths, and funiculus; 5th degree — complete loss of nerve continuity.

C.
In 4th and 5th degree injuries, Wallerian degeneration occurs distal to the site of injury: the axon and myelin degenerate, creating an empty endoneurial tube. Regenerating axons from the proximal stump may grow into incorrect endoneurial tubes (simple misdirection) or into multiple incorrect tubes (complex misdirection). Synkinesis arises when regenerating axons innervate incorrect muscle groups, causing involuntary co-contraction (e.g., eye closure on smiling). Hemifacial spasm results from abnormal electrical activity in misdirected or partially regenerated nerve fibres; treatment is botulinum toxin injection. Blepharospasm may require orbital muscle decompression.

A(i)
Lateral view — soft tissue neck: visualises the nasopharynx, retropharyngeal airway, laryngeal surface of the epiglottis and trachea, the laryngeal cartilages, hyoid bone, prevertebral space, and the cervical spine. Specific use: post-nasal space — assesses the nasopharyngeal airway, e.g. in adenoid hyperplasia.

A(ii)
AP (A-P) view: assesses the tissue details of the hypopharynx, larynx, trachea, and the surrounding soft tissue.

B(i)
Barium swallow is a simple and easy means of examination for lesions below the cricopharyngeus which cannot be assessed with a laryngeal mirror. Indications: demonstration of tumours of the pharynx — which are well outlined by a coating of barium — and masses within the pyriform sinuses; demonstration of features of growths in the pharynx or oesophagus.

B(ii)
Radiological distinction: P/lateral views are used to demonstrate radio-opaque foreign bodies in the larynx/oesophagus. A coin in the larynx shows the edge on the AP view and the flat surface on the lateral view. A coin in the oesophagus shows the flat surface on the AP view and the edge on the lateral view. For non-radio-opaque (radiolucent) foreign bodies in the oesophagus: a trapped air column above the FB may be visible, or barium (using wisps of cotton wool) can be used to demonstrate it.
questions.question:
Describe the radiological investigation of the oropharynx, hypopharynx, larynx, and salivary glands; include the indications for barium swallow and sialography, and explain how foreign bodies are distinguished radiologically depending on their location and radiopacity.
A(i) Describe the lateral soft-tissue neck view: what it visualises and its specific use in assessing the post-nasal space.
A(ii) Describe the AP view of the hypopharynx and larynx.
B(i) State the indications for barium swallow in ENT practice and what lesions it can demonstrate.
B(ii) Describe the radiological distinction between a coin in the larynx and a coin in the oesophagus on AP and lateral views, and state how non-radio-opaque foreign bodies in the oesophagus are demonstrated.

A 5-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department after she is witnessed to have swallowed a coin. She has drooling, dysphagia, and refuses feeds. On soft tissue neck X-ray, the coin shows its flat surface on the anteroposterior view and its edge on the lateral view.
(i) What is the diagnosis, and state the most common type of foreign body in children and the common locations where foreign bodies may be found in the food passage.
(ii) List the risk factors that predispose toddlers to foreign body ingestion.
(iii) State the indications for endoscopy in the management of foreign body ingestion.
(iv) Describe the endoscopic procedure, and outline the postoperative monitoring for complications.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Diagnosis: Foreign body (coin) in the oesophagus. The coin shows the flat surface on AP view and the edge on lateral view when in the oesophagus — in contrast to a coin in the larynx which shows the edge on AP view and flat surface on lateral. The commonest type in children is coins (75%). Common locations: Oropharynx — base of tongue, tonsillar fossa/tissue, posterior wall; Hypopharynx — pyriform fossae, posterior wall; Oesophagus — cricopharyngeus, aorta/left mainstem bronchus, gastroesophageal junction.

(ii)
Risk factors in toddlers: oral exploration; lack of posterior dentition; easy distractibility; cognitive development (inability to judge whether an object is edible).

(iii)
Indications for endoscopy: complete obstruction; airway compromise; impacted foreign body; caustic foreign bodies (e.g. disc batteries — emergency; NaOH, KOH, mercury — which cause mucosal damage at 1 hour, muscular layer damage at 2–4 hours, and perforation at 8–12 hours).

(iv)
Procedure: Oropharyngeal FB removal under visualization using local anaesthesia (spray). Difficult cases or oesophageal FB: removal under general anaesthesia via ET intubation, then pharyngoscopy/oesophagoscopy. Examine for ulceration/perforation if the FB is a disc battery or caustic agent. If FB is not visible for removal, observe for gastric location for 4–7 days; laparotomy for bowel perforation. Postoperative management: NPO for 4–12 hours; monitoring of vital signs for signs of perforation — tachycardia, tachypnea, fever, and chest pain.

questions.question:
A) Describe the orbital complications of rhinosinusitis under the following headings:
A(i) The five stages (A–E) of orbital complication, with the defining clinical feature of each.
A(ii) The two anatomical routes by which infection can spread from the sinuses to the orbit.
A(iii) The bacteriology of orbital complications, listing the specific organisms most commonly involved and those that occur when the sphenoid sinus is the primary source.
B) Explain the anatomical basis for retrograde thrombophlebitis as a route of intracranial spread from the frontal sinus.
C) State the most common sinus source of intracranial complication, the frequency of intracranial complications in admitted frontal sinusitis patients , and list all the intracranial complications.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Five stages of orbital complication:
• A (Preseptal/periorbital cellulitis): inflammatory oedema of the eyelid only.
• B (Orbital cellulitis): inflammation and oedema of orbital contents; proptosis, chemosis, decreased extraocular movement; may progress to orbital abscess and blindness.
• C (Subperiosteal abscess): collection of pus between periorbita and bony orbital wall; proptosis with displacement of the globe, decreased extraocular movement and vision.
• D (Orbital abscess): collection of pus in the orbit; ophthalmoplegia, proptosis, and visual loss.
• E (Cavernous sinus thrombosis): spread of infection to the cavernous sinus; proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, and visual loss, with development of contralateral ocular signs and signs of meningitis.

A(ii)
Two routes of spread from sinuses to orbit:
• Direct extension: through congenital bony dehiscences, open suture lines or foramina, or by erosion of the bony barrier, especially of the lamina papyracea.
• Retrograde thrombophlebitis: through the rich network of valveless veins providing free communication between the face, nasal cavity, sinuses and the orbit.

A(iii)
Bacteriology: most common — Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis, Streptococcus pyogenes; less often — Staphylococcus aureus and anaerobes. When the sphenoid sinus is involved: S. aureus and S. pneumoniae. Bacteraemia can occur and is more common in the paediatric population.

B)
Frontal sinus retrograde thrombophlebitis: the dural and cortical veins both drain into the sagittal sinus; there is a direct pathway for propagation of septic thrombi from the frontal sinuses to the brain parenchyma via the valveless diploic veins (Breschet's veins), which provide free communication between the sinuses and the veins of dural, orbital, and cranial periosteum.

C)
Most common sinus source of intracranial complication: frontal sinus; followed by ethmoid, sphenoid, and maxillary sinuses. Ten percent of patients with frontal sinusitis admitted to hospital eventually developed intracranial complications. Intracranial complications: osteomyelitis; epidural abscess; subdural empyema; intracerebral (brain) abscess; superior sagittal sinus thrombosis (SSST); cavernous sinus thrombosis (CST); meningitis.

questions.question:
A 19-year-old male is admitted in respiratory distress following blunt trauma to the lower face in a road traffic accident. There is trismus, an anterior open bite deformity, dish-face appearance and bilateral periorbital swelling. Cervical spine radiograph is clear.
(i) State the specific type of fracture and classify it according to the LeFort system.
(ii) List the associated injuries for maxillary LeFort fractures, including the ocular injuries, specifying the percentage of patients with some ocular injury.
(iii) Describe the anatomical landmarks of the midfacial buttress system (vertical and horizontal buttresses).
(iv) State the structures at risk requiring examination or imaging, and the sequence of treatment priorities before addressing the facial fracture.
(v) Describe the post-operative care following open reduction and internal fixation, including the timing of follow-up appointments.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Midfacial (maxillary) fractures — LeFort II (pyramidal fracture): fracture of the maxilla across the nasal root and through the infraorbital rim — explains periorbital swelling. The dish-face appearance and bilateral periorbital swelling with anterior open bite also suggest a LeFort III component (craniofacial separation). The common factor of all LeFort fractures is fracture of the pterygoid plates.

(ii)
Associated injuries for maxillary fractures:
• Lacerations and abrasions; orthopedic injury; other facial fractures; neurological injury; pulmonary, abdominal and cardiac injuries; ocular injury.
• 90.6% of patients had some ocular injury: 63% minor or transient; 16% moderately severe; 12% severe (angle recession, retinal or vitreous injury, optic nerve damage); loss of vision in the affected eye.
• Zygoma fractures: lacerations; orthopedic injuries; additional facial fractures; neurological injury; pulmonary.
• MVA-related: 59% had intracranial injury; fall/beating: 10% had intracranial injury.

(iii)
Midfacial buttress system:
• Vertical buttresses: nasomaxillary, zygomaticomaxillary, and pterygomaxillary.
• Horizontal buttresses: frontal bar, orbital rims, zygomatic processes of temporal bone, maxillary alveolus and palate, and serrated edges of the greater wing of the sphenoid.

(iv)
Structures at risk: airway (addressed first); intracranial structures (mental status changes, loss of consciousness); cervical spine; orbits and vision; ocular structures (ophthalmology consultation for orbit/globe involvement). Sequence: stabilise patient, address airway, treat intracranial and cervical spine injuries, then address facial fracture.

(v)
Post-operative care: light pressure dressing — if dry, remove after 2–5 days; prophylactic antibiotics covering gram-positive and anaerobic organisms for 5–10 days; observe overnight for bleeding, airway problems and vomiting; diet limited to pureed or liquid intake. Follow-up: at 5–7 days (skin sutures removed); at 2–4 weeks; then at 3–8 weeks for removal of maxillo-mandibular fixation (MMF); longer-term follow-up for complications or deformity.

questions.question:
A) Describe the anatomy relevant to tracheostomy and upper airway management, under the following headings:
A(i) The structures of the upper airway in order from nose to extrathoracic trachea.
A(ii) The clinical signs that indicate severity of upper airway obstruction.
A(iii) The relationship between the noise of breathing (stridor/wheeze) and the degree of airway obstruction.
B) For each named condition causing upper airway obstruction in children, state the exact site of obstruction, causative organism or mechanism, and management — covering: laryngomalacia, epiglottitis, croup, congenital subglottic stenosis, and bacterial tracheitis.
C) Explain why the worst obstruction is said to be silent.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Structures of the upper airway in order: nose → nasopharynx → oropharynx → larynx (supraglottis, subglottis) → trachea (extrathoracic).

A(ii)
Clinical signs of severity of obstruction:
• Recession (sternal, lower costal margin)
• Tachypnoea
• Tachycardia
• Expiratory difficulty (abdominal muscles contract)
• Depressed consciousness
• Cyanosis
• Noise soft or absent

A(iii)
Noise decreases as obstruction worsens; noise is NOT indicative of degree of obstruction. Therefore, THE WORST OBSTRUCTION IS SILENT.

B)
Conditions causing obstruction:
• Laryngomalacia: site — larynx; mechanism — flaccidity of the larynx; age — newborn infant; presents with stridor; improves in prone position and with age at age 2; voice normal; paroxysmal attacks of breathing difficulty.
• Epiglottitis: site — supraglottis; causative organism — H. influenzae type B; acute onset; drooling, pyrexia, posture; management — airway first, then antibiotics.
• Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis): site — subglottis; causative organism — parainfluenza virus; age 6 months–2 years; preceded by a cold; stridor, normal voice, barking cough; management — adrenaline inhalations, steroids, avoid crying, airway (intubation, tracheostomy if needed).
• Congenital subglottic stenosis: site — subglottis; mechanism — congenital narrowing ± history of intubation; age <6 months; no preceding infection; diagnosed by endoscopy; management — tracheostomy.
• Bacterial tracheitis: site — trachea; causative organism — Staphylococcus aureus; older child (<2 years); toxic, erythematous rash, thick secretions; management — airway (tracheostomy), antibiotics.

C)
As obstruction worsens, airflow through the narrowed segment decreases to the point where turbulence generating sound diminishes; a silent chest indicates near-complete obstruction and is therefore the most dangerous sign — the noise of stridor or wheeze is generated by turbulent airflow, and when airflow is critically reduced, noise disappears.

questions.question:
A) Describe the LeFort classification of midfacial fractures under the following headings:
A(i) LeFort I — the fracture line and the defining common factor shared by all three LeFort fractures.
A(ii) LeFort II (pyramidal fracture) — the fracture pattern and characteristic facial deformity.
A(iii) LeFort III (craniofacial separation) — the extent of fracture and the defining involvement of bones.
B) Explain the epidemiology of midfacial fractures: the sex ratio, age group predominantly affected, and percentage of all facial fractures they account for.
C) Describe the initial management priorities for a patient with a LeFort III fracture, listing the methods of airway management and haemostasis.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
LeFort I: a transverse fracture across the maxilla just above the maxillary tooth apices and through the nasal pyramid. The common factor of all three LeFort fractures is fracture of the pterygoid plates.

A(ii)
LeFort II (pyramidal fracture): fracture of the maxilla across the nasal root and through the infraorbital rim. Characteristic deformity: periorbital swelling and "dish-face or pan-face deformity" may occur; anterior open bite deformity may be present.

A(iii)
LeFort III (craniofacial separation): the most severe; complete mid-face separation from the skull including both zygomas; the LeFort III involves complete detachment of the facial skeleton from the cranial base including both zygomatic arches.

B)
Epidemiology of midfacial fractures: predominantly affect young males aged 20–40 years; male-to-female ratio is 7.6:1; account for approximately 6–25% of all facial fractures. Common mechanisms: assault, MVA, gunshot wounds, sports, falls, and industrial accidents.

C)
Initial management priorities for LeFort III:
• Stabilise the patient first.
• Treat serious insults to the airway, neurological system, cervical spine, chest and abdomen prior to definitive facial fracture management.
• Airway management: orotracheal intubation; manual disimpaction or with large disimpaction forceps; emergent tracheotomy or cricothyrotomy may be necessary.
• Haemostasis: combination of pressure, packing, cauterisation, and suturing for severe bleeding.
• Anti-tetanus prophylaxis; antibiotics; analgesics and anxiolytics.
• High-energy trauma should raise concern about intracranial injury; history of mental status changes or loss of consciousness requires neurological assessment.

(i)
Ethmoidal nasal polyps (nasal polyposis). Two most strongly associated conditions: chronic rhinosinusitis (both allergic and non-allergic forms) and asthma (about 7% of polyp patients have asthma).

(ii)
Associated conditions and percentages:
• Aspirin intolerance: 36% (Samter's triad)
• Allergic fungal rhinosinusitis (AFS): almost all cases (85% of patients with AFS have polyps)
• Cystic fibrosis: 20%
• Kartagener syndrome: 30%

(iii)
In long-standing cases, broadening of nasal bridge with increased intercanthal distance occurs; unremoved polyps can extend intracranially and into the orbital vaults, altering the craniofacial skeleton.

(iv)
Surgical options: Functional Endoscopic Sinus Surgery (FESS) – current practice and treatment of choice; nasal polypectomy; ethmoidectomy (intranasal, extranasal, or transantral approach). FESS is justified because polyp recurrence was 28% following endoscopic sinus surgery compared with 35% following intranasal polypectomy. Specific risk of inadvertent trauma to the skull base during ESS: cerebrospinal fluid leakage; also loss of vision and damage to the internal carotid artery are recognised serious complications.
questions.question:
A 40-year-old man presents with a 4-month history of bilateral nasal obstruction, sneezing, watery rhinorrhoea, reduced sense of smell and snoring. Anterior rhinoscopy reveals bilateral, pale, multiple polypoid masses that are insensitive to probing and do not bleed on touch.
(i) State the diagnosis, and identify two conditions most strongly associated with this presentation.
(ii) List four risk factors or associated conditions for this condition, including the specific percentage associations.
(iii) What are the potential complications if the masses remain unremoved for a prolonged period?
(iv) Describe the surgical treatment options and justify the treatment of choice, naming the specific risk of inadvertent skull-base trauma during this procedure.

questions.answerText:
(i)
Differential diagnosis of pulsatile tinnitus: benign intracranial hypertension (pseudotumor cerebri); glomus tumours (glomus jugulare or tympanicum); arteriovenous malformations; venous hum; palatomyoclonus; idiopathic stapedial muscle spasm. The most likely diagnosis in this overweight young woman with a bluish-red pulsatile retrotympanic mass is a glomus tympanicum (vascular neoplasm).

(ii)
Objective (para-auditory) tinnitus: audible to the physician or observer; includes all para-auditory causes; pulsatile or non-pulsatile; sources are vascular abnormalities (neoplasm, AVM, arterial bruit, venous hums) and palatomyoclonus; less prevalent. Subjective (sensorineural) tinnitus: originates within the auditory system; more prevalent; physiological mechanism involves hyperactive hair cells or nerve fibres, chemical imbalance, or reduced suppressive influence of the CNS; prevalence increases with age with equal sex distribution.

(iii)
Investigations: ENT examination; otoscopy (examine for retrotympanic mass); auscultation of the external auditory canal, orbit, mastoid, skull, and neck; audiogram. For suspected vascular neoplasm: CT scan to identify the mass in the middle ear; arteriography; MRI; check head and neck for masses; cranial nerve and cerebellar function assessment. Radiograph must be performed before myringotomy because the bluish/reddish pulsatile mass could be a glomus tumour or dehiscent jugular bulb — inadvertent myringotomy could cause catastrophic haemorrhage.

(iv)
Management of glomus tympanicum: bruit is not altered by neck pressure, head position, posture, or Valsalva; confirm with CT and arteriography; treatment is usually surgical after arteriography and MRI; embolization may precede surgery.

(v)
Subjective tinnitus treatments: avoid loud noise and wear ear protection; avoid caffeinated beverages and stimulants (coffee, tea, colas, chocolate); stop smoking; counselling. Medications: avoid aspirin, aminoglycoside antibiotics, NSAIDs, heterocycline antidepressants; lidocaine (IV) is beneficial but has short half-life and poor side effects; oral analogues (tocainide, flecainide) show no benefit; benzodiazepines (clonazepam, oxazepam, alprazolam) may help especially with concurrent depression — alprazolam reduced loudness in 76% versus 5% placebo. Device-based: environmental masking (broad-band noise at home, particularly useful at night); hearing aids (amplify background noise, mask tinnitus, improve speech); commercial tinnitus maskers. Electrical stimulation: DC to round window or promontory; external stimulation pre-/post-auricular; intracochlear stimulation via cochlear implant. Surgery: effective for conditions where tinnitus is a symptom (otosclerosis, acoustic neuroma, glomus jugulare); cochlear neurectomy and microvascular decompression produce inconsistent results.
questions.question:
A 30-year-old woman presents with complaints of tinnitus in her right ear that she describes as a pulsatile, rushing sound synchronous with her heartbeat. She is overweight with a BMI of 34. On examination, otoscopy reveals a bluish-red pulsatile mass behind the right tympanic membrane.
(i) List the differential diagnosis for pulsatile tinnitus and identify the most likely diagnosis in this patient.
(ii) Describe the two types of tinnitus (objective and subjective) and state their relative prevalence, sources, and clinical features.
(iii) Outline the investigations needed for this patient, including what must be performed before myringotomy and why.
(iv) Describe the management of objective pulsatile tinnitus due to vascular neoplasm.
(v) For subjective (sensorineural) tinnitus, outline the full range of treatments including medical, device-based, and surgical options.

A 45-year-old man who smokes 30 cigarettes daily and drinks two bottles of alcohol per week presents with a 4-month history of progressive sore throat, difficulty swallowing, and a sensation of a foreign body in the throat. He has also noticed a lump in the right side of his neck. Examination with indirect laryngoscopy and fiberoptic nasopharyngoscopy reveals an ulcerative lesion of the right palatine tonsil extending to the posterior tonsillar pillar. The right jugulodigastric node is enlarged and firm.
(i) State the diagnosis, the most common histological type at this site, and explain why this patient's age is significant.
(ii) List the risk factors for this malignancy and explain the role of each.
(iii) Describe the natural history of this tumour with respect to lymphatic spread from the tonsil, and state the incidence of cervical metastasis from tonsillar cancer.
(iv) Outline the investigations required including the role of diagnostic endoscopy.
(v) Describe the definitive surgical treatment options for the primary tumour and cervical metastasis, including the justification for postoperative radiotherapy.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Oropharyngeal carcinoma of the right palatine tonsil. The most common histological type is squamous cell carcinoma (SCCa). Age is significant because many cases are now being diagnosed in the fifth or sixth decades of life rather than at an elderly age, affecting younger patients than traditionally expected.

(ii)
Risk factors: tobacco use — associated with oropharyngeal cancer; alcohol consumption — a risk factor both by itself and when combined with tobacco use (synergistic effect). Males have a higher incidence than females, but the number of cases in women is rising.

(iii)
SCCa of the head and neck spreads by local extension and regional lymphatics long before distant metastases. The first drainage is to the upper deep cervical chain. The rate of cervical metastasis from the palatine tonsil is about 60% for tonsillar cancer. Retropharyngeal nodes (not palpable on examination) also drain oropharyngeal sites. Distant metastases occur to the lung and liver (most common sites). Contralateral metastases are prone to occur in cases where the tumour crosses the midline.

(iv)
Investigations: thorough head and neck and complete general physical examination; indirect laryngoscopy and fiberoptic nasopharyngoscopy; toluidine blue application to mucosal surface to enhance detection of suspicious areas; palpation for submucosal extension; check for serous otitis media (skull base involvement); CT scanning (useful); MRI (complementary, especially in parapharyngeal space); Pantomogram (bony mandible involvement); contrast videofluoroscopic examination to rule out second primaries and GERD; liver function studies; CBC; electrolytes; ECG; chest x-ray; diagnostic endoscopy to stage, map, and biopsy the tumour and uncover second primaries.

(v)
Surgery and radiation therapy, alone or combined, are the mainstays of treatment. For advanced lesions, surgery is the primary treatment with decision for postoperative radiation therapy after histopathological examination. Surgical approaches: transoral (for small, superficial stage I lesions, carcinoma in situ, exophytic tumours, soft palate, tonsil, upper posterior pharyngeal wall); lateral mandibular osteotomy and pharyngotomy (for tonsillar cancers — most direct approach, widest exposure; disadvantage: anesthesia of ipsilateral lower lip due to mandibular nerve transection); mandibular swing approach (good for tumours involving the parapharyngeal space). Treatment for cervical metastasis: surgery, radiation, or both; external approaches combined with neck dissection; an advantage of elective neck dissection is pathologic staging. Indications for postoperative radiotherapy: primary — large size (T3, T4), deeply infiltrating, positive or close surgical margins; cervical — >2 positive nodes, any positive node >3 cm, extracapsular spread, field cancerization.

(i)
The choice between radical and palliative treatment depends on: spread (loco-regional/metastatic spread); radiosensitivity/chemosensitivity; histology (including differentiation); clearance of surgical resection margins; age and general condition (physical and mental); morbidity and mortality; function and cosmetics; reliability of follow-up after treatment; preference of patient; and technical expertise.

(ii)
Radiosensitivity categories: Highly sensitive — lymphoma, seminoma, myeloma, Ewing's tumour. Moderately sensitive — small cell lung cancer, breast cancer, basal cell carcinoma, medulloblastoma, teratoma, ovarian cancer. Relatively resistant — squamous cell carcinoma of the lung, rectal carcinoma, soft tissue sarcoma. Highly resistant — pancreatic carcinoma.

(iii)
A multidisciplinary approach is preferred in cancer management because: it enables correct decisions to be taken, especially when cure is the goal, since inappropriate initial treatment may compromise both the quantity and quality of survival; it ensures collaborative spirit among specialists; timing of different modalities is properly synchronized; patients have access to advice from different specialists; and patients are more reassured that all treatment options have been considered before embarking on the chosen course. Also, it provides a basis for audit of treatment.

(iv)
A Consultant Radiotherapist and Oncologist is both a physician and a technical specialist; hence clinical and technical factors must be balanced to adequately plan radiotherapy. Note: discussion about treatment is made by specialists and the primary physician without the patient in attendance to prevent the patient from being intimidated.
questions.question:
A 45-year-old man presents with hoarseness lasting 8 weeks. Indirect laryngoscopy reveals a mass on the vocal cord. He is referred for radiotherapy assessment.
(i) State the factors that determine whether a patient is treated with radical or palliative intent in the radiotherapy assessment.
(ii) List the radiosensitivity categories of tumours, giving two examples in each category.
(iii) Explain the multidisciplinary approach to cancer management and state the five benefits of this approach in the radiotherapy assessment.
(iv) State the clinical assessment considerations that must be balanced by a Consultant Radiotherapist when planning treatment.

A) Describe the classification of nasal polyps under the following headings:
A(i) The two major varieties of nasal polyp — their site of origin, laterality, and sex/age incidence.
A(ii) The pathogenesis of ethmoidal polyp formation at the level of the middle meatus, citing the role of oedema, cellular infiltration and the effect of gravity.
A(iii) The macroscopic and histological features of ethmoidal polyps.
B) Explain the clinical and rhinoscopic features that distinguish ethmoidal nasal polyps from antrochoanal polyps in terms of laterality, appearance, and posterior rhinoscopy findings.
C) State all differential diagnoses for nasal polyposis, and state the specific clinical feature that should always prompt histological examination of any nasal polyp.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Two major varieties:
• Ethmoidal polyps: arise from mucosa of ethmoidal air cells; usually multiple and bilateral; pearly white, grape-like appearance; commoner in adults; no sex predilection.
• Antrochoanal (Killian's) polyps: arise from mucosa of maxillary sinus, near the accessory ostium; extend to the choana towards the nasopharynx; usually single and unilateral; commoner in children; said to affect males more.

A(ii)
Pathogenesis of ethmoidal polyp: oedema — collection of extracellular fluid in the nasal mucosa especially in the region of the middle turbinate and meatus. Cellular infiltration — eosinophils and round cells. The oedematous swelling is initially sessile but becomes pedunculated due to gravity and sneezing.

A(iii)
Macroscopic features: pale, soft, smooth masses; sometimes opaque and fleshy; appear as smooth, glistening, pale, grape-like masses; insensitive to probing; do not bleed on touch. Histological features: epithelium may be ciliated columnar or may have undergone squamous or transitional metaplasia; submucosa shows large intercellular spaces filled with serous fluid; scanty blood vessels and nerve fibres; eosinophils and round cells are seen.

B)
Distinguishing features:
• Ethmoidal polyp: nasal obstruction usually bilateral; sneezing and watery rhinorrhoea; anosmia or hyposmia; broadening of nasal bridge in long-standing cases. Anterior rhinoscopy: bilateral, pale, multiple, grape-like masses, insensitive, do not bleed.
• Antrochoanal polyp: nasal obstruction usually unilateral; nasal discharge unilateral, mucopurulent and occasionally blood-tinged; posterior nasal drip; hyponasality (thick, dull voice). On rhinoscopy: may be missed on anterior rhinoscopy if grown posteriorly; posterior rhinoscopy reveals a globular mass filling the choana or nasopharynx — smooth, greyish, covered with nasal discharge, not sensitive to probe, does not bleed.

C)
