Differential diagnoses: hypertrophied turbinate; angiofibromas (septal or nasopharyngeal); glioma; encephalocele or meningoencephalocele; transitional or squamous papilloma; rhinosporidiosis; hamartoma; nasal malignancies (neuroblastoma, neurofibromatosis, rhabdomyosarcoma, Burkitt lymphoma, sarcoma, chordoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, inverting papilloma, haemangioma). Clinical feature that must prompt histological examination: any unilateral nasal polyp requires histological examination (nasal smear) to exclude malignancy; also any polyp that is red and fleshy, friable and has a granular surface, especially in older patients, must be submitted to histology as it may masquerade malignancy.

questions.question:
Describe the classification of deep neck spaces and explain the anatomical basis for the spread of infection between them, with particular attention to the prevertebral space and the visceral vascular space.
A(i) Name the four deep neck spaces that run the entire length of the neck.
A(ii) Describe the boundaries and extent of the prevertebral space, and explain why infection in this space tends to stay somewhat localised.
B(i) Describe the visceral vascular space: its content, extent, and why it can be secondarily involved by infection from any other deep neck space.
B(ii) List the potential sources of parapharyngeal space infection and explain why etiology cannot be defined in nearly half of parapharyngeal abscess cases; state two specific infection pathways involving the mastoid.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The four deep neck spaces that run the entire length of the neck are: the retropharyngeal space, the danger space, the prevertebral space, and the visceral vascular space.

A(ii)
The prevertebral space is limited anteriorly by the prevertebral fascia, laterally by the attachment of this fascia to the transverse processes, and posteriorly by the anterior longitudinal ligament, the vertebral bodies, and the deep musculature. It extends the entire length of the vertebral column. Infection in this space tends to stay somewhat localised due to the dense fibrous attachments between the fascia and the deep muscles.

B(i)
The visceral vascular space is the potential space within the carotid sheath. Like the prevertebral space, the visceral vascular space is quite compact, contains little areolar tissue, and is resistant to the spread of infection. It extends from the base of the skull into the mediastinum and because it receives contributions from all three layers of deep fascia it can become secondarily involved by infection in any other deep neck space by direct spread.

B(ii)
Parapharyngeal space abscess may follow infection in the pharynx, tonsils, adenoids, teeth, parotid, or lymph node chains. Middle ear infections or mastoiditis may involve the parapharyngeal space after rupture of a Bezold's abscess on the inner aspect of the mastoid tip along the digastric ridge. More commonly, the parapharyngeal space becomes involved from extension of infection from the peritonsillar space, submandibular space, retropharyngeal space, or masticator space. Despite the multitude of potential sources, in nearly half of cases the aetiology cannot be defined.

questions.question:
A 6-year-old child presents with fever, neck stiffness, and decreased appetite. The neck is swollen. The parents cannot recall any specific causative event.
(i) What is the most likely diagnosis? State the symptoms of retropharyngeal abscess specifically in children older than 1 year, and separately in infants.
(ii) List the physical signs specific to children, distinguishing features from adults.
(iii) State what antibiotic regimen is reasonable to begin, and describe the criteria for deciding between medical and surgical management.
(iv) Describe image-guided aspiration as an alternative to open drainage, including which patients are most likely to respond.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Diagnosis: Retropharyngeal abscess. Symptoms in children older than 1 year: sore throat, fever, neck stiffness, odynophagia, decreased appetite, chills, malaise. Symptoms in infants: fever (100%), neck swelling (84%), anorexia (58%), decreased appetite (22%), irritability (11%).

(ii)
Physical signs specific to children: tender cervical lymphadenopathy; posterior pharyngeal bulge — do not palpate in children; fever; stridor; torticollis; drooling. Difference from adults: adults may also present with nuchal rigidity, posterior pharyngeal oedema, and drooling, but torticollis is more characteristic in children; the posterior pharyngeal bulge should not be palpated in children.

(iii)
A reasonable initial regimen is a beta-lactamase resistant penicillin, likely in combination with metronidazole to improve anaerobic coverage; third-generation cephalosporins are an alternative. Medical management criteria: patients with CT evidence of cellulitis rather than abscess can be managed with intravenous antibiotic therapy; the majority will improve. If clinical improvement does not occur within 24 to 48 hours of medical therapy, re-imaging and possibly surgery are indicated.

(iv)
Image-guided aspiration or catheter insertion is an alternative to open drainage. The successful use of these methods is most dependent upon proper patient selection. Those patients with smaller, more isolated, and uniloculated abscesses are more likely to respond favourably. The use of image guidance — whether CT or ultrasound — helps to ensure that the needle or catheter is placed appropriately in the affected space while vital structures are avoided.

(i)
Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC). Serological significance: NPC cells express EBV proteins; plasma antibodies to viral capsid antigen (VCA) and to early antigens (EA) are seen. Elevated EA titres are a predictor of tumour relapse after radiotherapy. HLA pattern AW19-B17 is associated with short-term survival, mostly young-onset cases (<30 years) with high VCA and EA titres; A2-BW46 with intermediate-term survival; A2 without BW46 or B17 with long-term survival and low VCA/EA titres.

(ii)
Aetiology: NPC is thought to result from both genetic susceptibility and environmental factors. Genetic factors: association with HLA-A2 and HLA-B Sin2 (rare in blacks and whites); chromosomal abnormalities in multiple chromosomes (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 11, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 22, and X). Viral: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV). Environmental factors: cooking habits; occupation; religious practices; diet; drugs; and others. Sex: male:female = 3:1. Age: bimodal peaks at 30–40 and 50–60 years.

(iii)
Nasal obstruction: the primary tumour fills the nasopharynx, obstructing the posterior choanae. Epistaxis: the tumour may be exophytic, ulcerative, or infiltrative, eroding mucosal vasculature. Tinnitus: tumour at or near the Eustachian tube orifice (fossa of Rosenmuller, lateral wall) obstructs the tube, causing middle ear pressure changes. Unilateral conductive hearing loss: Eustachian tube blockage results in otitis media with effusion, causing conductive hearing loss.

(iv)
Advanced NPC with intracranial extension involves cranial nerves producing: diplopia and extraocular movement palsy (CN III, IV, VI); facial numbness (CN V); and general cranial neuropathy. Cervical metastasis is evident in 44–57% and likely in 60–85%; the metastatic nodes are referred to as HO (supraclavicular fossa metastasis).

(v)
Imaging investigations: MRI with gadolinium contrast (primary modality for local extent and intracranial involvement); CT scan of chest; CT scan of abdomen; PET scan; spectral MRI. Diagnostic procedures: transnasal biopsy of the nasopharyngeal mass with multiple biopsy samples; FNA of the neck mass; laboratory tests — FBC, LFT (to rule out distant metastases). Distant metastases sites in order of frequency: lung > bone > liver; occurring in 18–35% of cases; treatment at this stage is palliative — chemotherapy, pain relief, and symptom control.
questions.question:
A 55-year-old male smoker (30 pack-years) presents to the ENT clinic with a 3-month history of nasal obstruction, unilateral epistaxis, tinnitus, and progressive unilateral conductive hearing loss. He is from the Southern Chinese community. Examination reveals a mass in the nasopharynx. Serology shows elevated viral capsid antigen (VCA) and early antigen (EA) titres.
(i) State the most likely diagnosis and explain the significance of the serological findings.
(ii) Describe the aetiology of this condition, covering genetic factors, viral factors, environmental factors, and the sex and age distribution.
(iii) Identify the anatomical structures compressed or obstructed by a primary nasopharyngeal tumour that account for each of the presenting symptoms (nasal obstruction, epistaxis, tinnitus, conductive hearing loss).
(iv) In advanced disease, name the cranial nerves involved and state the specific deficits produced by each.
(v) Describe the imaging investigations required, and outline the staging workup for distant metastasis with the most common metastatic sites in order of frequency.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Incidence in children (United States): overall incidence in children is 0.1%; incidence in children with cystic fibrosis is 6–48%.

A(ii)
IL-5 is significantly raised in nasal polyp tissue compared with healthy controls; the concentration of IL-5 is independent of the atopic status of the patient. IL-5 prolongs eosinophil survival and activation; eosinophils are the most common inflammatory cells in nasal polyps (found in 85%). Studies showed that total and specific IgE and allergic-type histologic features of polyps are unrelated to positive skin prick tests but did correlate with levels of eosinophils — suggesting local allergic mechanisms rather than systemic atopy may be relevant.

A(iii)
In cystic fibrosis, patients have a defective small chloride conductance channel regulated by cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP), causing abnormal chloride transport across the apical cell membrane of epithelial cells; the pathogenesis of nasal polyposis in cystic fibrosis could be associated with this defect.

B)
Bernstein's theory: inflammatory changes first occur in the lateral nasal wall or sinus mucosa as a result of viral-bacterial host interactions or secondary to turbulent airflow. Polyps originate from contact areas of the middle meatus, especially narrow clefts in the anterior ethmoid region that create turbulent airflow. Ulceration or prolapse of the submucosa can occur, with re-epithelialization and new gland formation. The heightened inflammatory process from epithelial cells, vascular endothelial cells, and fibroblasts affects the bioelectric integrity of sodium channels at the luminal surface of the respiratory epithelial cell; this increases sodium absorption, leading to water retention and polyp formation.

C)
Three scenarios requiring heightened suspicion in children with apparent nasal polyp:
• A simple polyp in a child may be a glioma, encephalocele or meningoencephalocele — it should always be aspirated and the fluid examined for CSF; careless removal would result in CSF rhinorrhoea and meningitis.
• Multiple nasal polyps in children may be associated with mucoviscidosis (cystic fibrosis).
• If a polyp is red and fleshy, friable and has a granular surface, especially in older patients, malignancy must be excluded; epistaxis and orbital symptoms associated with a polyp should always arouse suspicion of malignancy.
questions.question:
A) Describe nasal polyposis in children and its associated conditions, under the following headings:
A(i) Incidence of nasal polyps in children in the United States (overall) and in children with cystic fibrosis.
A(ii) The role of interleukin-5 (IL-5) in the pathogenesis of nasal polyps and its relationship to eosinophils and atopic status.
A(iii) The pathogenesis of nasal polyps in cystic fibrosis, specifically the cellular defect involved.
B) Explain Bernstein's theory of nasal polyp pathogenesis and how it accounts for polyp formation at the middle meatus.
C) State the three scenarios that should prompt heightened suspicion of a more serious diagnosis when evaluating nasal polyps in children.

A 50-year-old man presents with a 6-month history of progressive dysphagia, worse for solid foods. He reports gurgling noises on swallowing, occasional regurgitation of undigested food, and an unintentional weight loss of 6 kg. Indirect laryngoscopy reveals frothy secretions pooling in the hypopharynx and piriform sinus.
(i) List the most likely structural diagnoses that should be considered in this patient, based on his presenting features.
(ii) Describe the phases of swallowing and the cranial nerves involved in each phase.
(iii) Select the single investigation most appropriate to this patient's symptoms and justify your choice.
(iv) Outline the full classification of causes of dysphagia.
(v) Describe the systemic and autoimmune disorders associated with dysphagia, and state the initial management approach when no organic cause is found.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Given progressive dysphagia worse for solids, gurgling, regurgitation of undigested food, pooling in the piriform sinus and hypopharynx, and weight loss, the structural differentials are: Zenker's diverticulum (pharyngeal pouch); oesophageal carcinoma (squamous cell carcinoma); cricopharyngeal achalasia; oesophageal stricture or ring; gastroesophageal reflux disease with stricture.

(ii)
Swallowing involves three phases, taking 8–10 seconds. Oral preparatory phase: food is manipulated and masticated; CN I (smell), V (mandibular movement), VII (elevation of hyoid and tongue base), XI (tongue), XII (intrinsic and extrinsic tongue muscles). Oral phase: tongue propels food posteriorly to trigger pharyngeal swallow; CN V (soft palate elevation), VII (elevation of tongue base), accessory (soft palate and tongue), hypoglossal. Pharyngeal phase: bolus moves through the pharynx; CN V (elevation of larynx), VII (elevation of hyoid), X (pharyngeal constrictors, cricopharyngeus, vocal folds), XI (pharynx), XII (hyoid and larynx). Oesophageal phase: peristalsis carries the bolus through the cervical and thoracic oesophagus into the stomach.

(iii)
Modified barium swallow or barium oesophagram is most appropriate: it gives good anatomic detail, evaluates all phases of swallowing, and is specifically suited for structural disorders such as dysphagia worse for solids; it can also demonstrate a pharyngeal pouch (Zenker's diverticulum) and strictures. Videofluoroscopy (the most frequently used technique) would also evaluate dynamic disorders and aspiration. Manometry would be reserved if achalasia or oesophageal spasm is suspected and intraluminal pressures must be measured.

(iv)
Classification of causes of dysphagia: Structural — oral, pharyngeal, laryngeal, oesophageal; including congenital (cleft lip/palate, laryngeal cleft, tracheo-oesophageal fistula), acquired inflammatory (pharyngitis, oesophagitis), traumatic (ill-fitting dentures, foreign body), neoplastic (squamous carcinoma), and other (GERD, pharyngeal pouches). Neurological — congenital; acquired with expected recovery (CVA/TIA, closed head trauma, cervical spinal cord injury, post surgery, poliomyelitis, Guillain-Barré, CP, dysautonomia); neurodegenerative (Parkinson's, Alzheimer's, ALS, post-polio syndrome, MS, myasthenia gravis, muscular dystrophy, dystonia, dermatomyositis). Medication (NSAIDs, anticholinergics, sympathomimetics). Environmental (dislike of food, distractions). Psychological (psychosomatic dysphagia, globus sensation).

(v)
Systemic disorders: stroke (present in up to 47%); amyotrophic lateral sclerosis; Parkinson's disease; multiple sclerosis; muscular dystrophy; myasthenia gravis. Autoimmune disorders: systemic sclerosis; systemic lupus erythematosus; dermatomyositis; mixed connective tissue disease; mucosal pemphigoid; epidermolysis bullosa; Sjögren's syndrome (xerostomia); rheumatoid arthritis (cricoarytenoid joint fixation). Initial management when no organic cause is found: exclude malignancy first; if no organic cause is identified, try a proton pump inhibitor (PPI), speech therapy, and reassure the patient.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old male presents to the emergency department with profuse bleeding from the right nostril following a road traffic accident. He is anxious, with BP 90/60 mmHg, pulse 120/min. Blood is seen draining both anteriorly from the nostril and posteriorly into the pharynx.
(i) Classify the type of epistaxis and state the likely source, named anatomical plexus and the vessels forming it.
(ii) Outline the resuscitation steps in order.
(iii) Describe the steps to stop the bleeding, listing all types of nasal packing materials.
(iv) If packing fails, list all surgical and interventional radiology options, and state the indication for arterial ligation.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Posterior epistaxis (blood draining both anteriorly and posteriorly). Likely source: Woodruff's plexus, located at the lateral wall of the inferior turbinate posteriorly; formed by posterior nasal arteries, sphenopalatine artery, and ascending pharyngeal arteries — all branches of the internal maxillary artery (external carotid).

(ii)
Resuscitation steps (in order):
• Assess severity — check PR/BP.
• Modified Trotter's technique (ice pack, sitting up).
• Establish IV line and fluids.
• Blood taken for investigations (FBC, blood film, U/E, bleeding/clotting time, group and cross-match).
• Blood transfusion if indicated.
• Sedative (IV Diazepam) for anxiety and blood pressure control.

(iii)
Steps to stop bleeding: Modified Trotter's technique; nasal packing — anterior, posterior, or both. Packing materials: Vaseline gauze; BIPP; Foley's catheter; nasal balloons (Simpson, Brighton, Bivona T3L); postnasal pack; Kaltostat (calcium-sodium alginate); Expandacell nasal packs; Epifast; gel foam; Merocel; fibrin glue; Surgicel. Cauterization: chemicals (AgNO3, chromic acid, trichloracetic acid); electrocautery; cryotherapy; laser; endoscopic cautery and ligation.

(iv)
Surgical and interventional options: arterial ligation (anterior/posterior ethmoidal arteries, internal maxillary artery, external carotid artery); angiography and embolization using polyvinyl alcohol, gel foam, or coiled springs; septodermoplasty/laser ablation; rhinoplasty; tumour excision if tumour is the cause. Indication for arterial ligation: persistent or recurrent epistaxis uncontrolled by packing and cauterization.

questions.question:
A 40-year-old woman presents with a 5-month history of progressive dysphagia for solids and liquids, hoarseness, nasal regurgitation, and choking episodes. She also reports an unintentional 8 kg weight loss. On examination, there is a right lower cranial nerve palsy with deviation of the uvula to the left, absence of the right gag reflex, right vocal cord palsy, and tongue deviation to the right.
(i) Identify the anatomical structure most likely affected and the specific lesion site, based on the pattern of cranial nerve involvement.
(ii) Describe the pharyngeal phase of swallowing and the cranial nerves responsible for each component of this phase, and explain why their injury causes aspiration.
(iii) List the neurological causes of dysphagia that may produce this presentation, categorised by those with expected recovery and those that are neurodegenerative.
(iv) Describe the full investigation protocol for dysphagia in this patient, including why the modified barium swallow is preferred over plain barium oesophagram in this case.
(v) Outline the treatment approach for neurological dysphagia from this cause, and describe the special considerations for dysphagia in children.
questions.answerText:
(i)
The pattern of right-sided IX (absent gag reflex, uvula deviation to left), X (right vocal cord palsy, hoarseness, nasal regurgitation), and XII (tongue deviation to the right — to the side of the lesion) palsy points to a lesion at the right jugular foramen and hypoglossal canal area, consistent with a skull base or high cervical lesion (e.g., jugular foramen syndrome/Vernet's syndrome), or a deep neck space mass compressing these nerves. The poststyloid compartment of the parapharyngeal space contains the carotid sheath and cranial nerves IX, X, and XII, so a lesion here would produce this combination.

(ii)
Pharyngeal phase: the pharyngeal swallow is triggered and the bolus moves through the pharynx; this phase involves: CN V (elevation of larynx); CN VII (elevation of hyoid); CN X (pharyngeal constrictors, cricopharyngeus, and vocal folds); CN XI (pharynx); CN XII (hyoid and larynx). Injury to these nerves impairs laryngeal elevation and closure, cricopharyngeal relaxation, and vocal fold adduction — resulting in the bolus entering the larynx and trachea (aspiration) rather than being directed into the oesophagus.

(iii)
Neurological causes of dysphagia with expected recovery: CVA/TIA (present in up to 47% of stroke patients); closed head trauma; cervical spinal cord injury; post-surgery; poliomyelitis; Guillain-Barré; cerebral palsy; dysautonomia. Neurodegenerative: Parkinson's disease; Alzheimer's; dementia; ALS; post-polio syndrome; multiple sclerosis; myasthenia gravis; muscular dystrophy; dystonia; dermatomyositis.

(iv)
Investigations: history (duration, dietary changes, weight loss, odynophagia, whether solids or liquids, level of sensation of dysphagia, past head and neck surgery, associated symptoms including GERD, voice changes, nasal leakage, otalgia, medications); review of systems; physical examination (cranial nerves, tongue and palate strength/symmetry, full ENT examination including nasoendoscopy/indirect laryngoscopy with assessment of pooled secretions, vocal fold movement, inter-arytenoid area, ears, nose, oropharynx). Modified barium swallow is preferred over plain barium oesophagram in neurological dysphagia because it evaluates all phases of swallowing, detects dynamic (neuromuscular) disorders and aspiration, and provides good anatomic detail; the plain barium oesophagram cannot detect dynamic swallowing disorders. FEES (fiberoptic endoscopic evaluation) allows assessment of sensation and can be used for biofeedback training; is portable. Exclude malignancy before attributing dysphagia to a neurological cause.

(v)
Treatment of neurological dysphagia: exclude malignancy first; if no organic cause — try PPI, speech therapy, and reassure; for organic/neurological cause, treat the specific lesion. Dysphagia in children: nasal obstruction; oral lesions (clefts, ranulas, mucoceles); laryngomalacia, laryngeal clefts, tracheo-oesophageal fistula; vascular rings; foregut malformations; tumours (haemangiomas, lymphangiomas, papillomas, leiomyomas, neurofibromas). General approach: thorough examination; appropriate primary treatment; early specialist referral; regular review of status.

questions.question:
A 4-year-old boy is brought to the ENT clinic with a 12-hour history of drooling, stridor, fever, and refusal to eat. His neck is swollen and he holds his neck in extension. On examination, there is a posterior pharyngeal bulge and tender cervical lymphadenopathy. Torticollis is noted.
(i) What is the most likely diagnosis, and state two features of his age and sex that predispose him to this condition.
(ii) Describe the pathophysiologic basis of this condition in children of his age group.
(iii) State the three keys to successful management of this condition, and outline the steps for initial airway care.
(iv) Describe the two main surgical approaches available for definitive drainage, including the incision used in each.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Diagnosis: Retropharyngeal abscess. Predisposing features: (a) Age — nearly one-half of retropharyngeal abscesses affect patients between 6 and 12 months, and 96% occur prior to 6 years; mean age is 3–4 years. (b) Sex — a higher incidence of deep neck infections has been noted in boys, although no sex predilection has been formally described.

(ii)
In children, retropharyngeal abscess is usually caused by an infection that spreads to the retropharyngeal lymph nodes, with subsequent cellulitis and abscess formation. By the time the child is aged 6 years, fibrosis and atrophy of these nodes have regressed completely. In older patients, infection of the retropharyngeal space usually occurs from penetrating trauma or direct spread from an adjacent space.

(iii)
The three keys are: protection and control of the airway, antibiotic therapy, and surgical drainage. Initial airway care: apply supplemental oxygen; in young children this can be done by letting the parent direct blow-by oxygen at the child's face. Endotracheal intubation may be required if there are signs of upper airway obstruction, though it may be difficult due to upper airway swelling. Cricothyrotomy (surgical or needle) may be required in the patient with upper airway obstruction who cannot be intubated. Tracheostomy may be required for definitive airway management. Intravenous fluids are required if the patient is dehydrated due to fever and difficulty swallowing.

(iv)
Transoral (intraoral) approach: a cruciate incision is made through the mucosa followed by blunt dissection through the constrictor muscle; it is limited to isolated retropharyngeal abscesses and is safe only if the great vessels can be definitively identified on preoperative imaging. External anterior approach: an incision paralleling the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid, dissection along the anterior border of the muscle, lateral retraction of the carotid sheath, medial retraction of the larynx, trachea and thyroid, and exposure of the abscess cavity at the hypopharynx. External posterior approach: an incision behind the sternocleidomastoid, medial and anterior retraction of the muscle and carotid sheath, and opening into the abscess from posterior to the great vessels.

questions.question:
A. Describe the anatomy of the nasal fracture and the mid-face fracture complex under the following headings:
A(i) Nasal fracture: mechanism, clinical signs, vascular anatomy, and timing of treatment
A(ii) LeFort I, II, and III fractures: defining features and common fracture factor
A(iii) Frontal sinus fractures: table involvement, the role of the naso-frontal duct, and long-term complication if untreated
B. Describe the naso-ethmoid fracture: mechanism, diagnostic sign, and surgical repair.
C. Outline the initial evaluation sequence for a patient with maxillofacial trauma, covering airway management, haemorrhage control, and clinical evaluation, and state the cervical spine precaution that must be maintained throughout.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Nasal fractures are the most common facial fractures, seen most often with direct nasal trauma. Clinical signs: periorbital ecchymosis, nasal congestion, oedema, and epistaxis. The diagnosis is made clinically, though radiographic evaluation may support it. The vascular supply to the nose is extensive via both external and internal carotid artery systems; most nasal fracture patients present with brisk epistaxis. Treatment: delayed until approximately 5 days post-injury when nasal swelling has diminished, allowing anatomically precise closed reduction under local anaesthesia.

A(ii)
LeFort fractures were described by the French physician LeFort who studied fractures in cadaver skulls. LeFort I: a transverse fracture across the maxilla just above the maxillary tooth apices and through the nasal pyramid. LeFort II (pyramidal fracture): fracture of the maxilla across the nasal root and through the infraorbital rim. LeFort III (craniofacial separation): the most severe — complete mid-face separation from the skull including both zygomas. Common factor: all three fractures involve fracture of the pterygoid plates. These fractures are associated with significant bleeding and swelling and often present with upper airway obstruction; many require urgent airway intervention with intubation and/or tracheotomy. Signs: airway obstruction, severe mid-face swelling and ecchymosis, epistaxis, CSF rhinorrhoea, high incidence of orbital complications, mid-face movement relative to the skull; if untreated, all three create a "dish face deformity."

A(iii)
The anterior wall of the frontal sinus is made up of very thick strong bone. Fractures may involve the inner or outer table or the naso-frontal duct area. Non-displaced fractures not involving the naso-frontal duct require no therapy. Any displaced fracture or posterior table fracture must be explored and reduced. Long-term complication if untreated: formation of a mucocele of the frontal sinus, which over many years creates pressure necrosis of the frontal bone and may present late with brain abscesses, subdural abscesses, or Pott's Puffy Tumor (frontal bone osteomyelitis). Treatment when displaced: removal of the sinus mucosa and fat obliteration with plugging of the naso-frontal ducts.

B.
Naso-ethmoid fractures involve displacement of the nasal bones and ethmoid complex medially, and are often associated with frontal sinus or mid-face fractures. The medial canthal tendons are frequently disrupted. The most common presenting sign is rounding of the medial canthus and traumatic telecanthus. Diagnostic sign: the bow-string sign — tugging laterally on the lateral canthus of the eye; absence of the typical bow-string feel of the intact medial canthal tendon confirms disruption. Surgical repair: via coronal scalp flap or Lynch incisions; fractures are most commonly plated with facial micro-plates; the medial canthal tendons must be reattached to avoid cosmetic deformity.

C.
Initial evaluation sequence:
• Airway management — clear obstruction by suction or digital removal of loose teeth, dentures, blood or vomitus; pull mandible forward with towel clip; insert nasopharyngeal airway; nasal or oral intubation; cricothyrotomy or tracheotomy. Cervical spine injury must be kept in mind throughout.
• Haemorrhage control — digital pressure (effective most of the time); occasionally haemostat application; anterior and posterior nasal packing; external carotid artery ligation (rarely needed); if patient is in shock, look for another bleeding source.
• Clinical evaluation — inspect face for asymmetry or paralysis; examine orbital rims, malar eminence, frontal bones, and zygomatic arches for tenderness, irregularity, or depression; check for hypesthesia of branches of 2nd and 3rd division of CN V; ocular examination (subconjunctival haemorrhage, telecanthus, widened palpebral fissure, extraocular motion, diplopia, visual acuity); nasal examination (bones for deviation or depression, septal deviation, CSF leak, dishpan deformity, mobile maxilla); mandible (abnormal motion, tenderness, intraoral lacerations, trismus); ear (ear canal laceration, haemotympanum, ecchymosis behind the pinna); neck (tenderness, ecchymosis, subcutaneous air, larynx palpation).

questions.question:
A) Describe the gross anatomy of the esophagus as a passage at risk from corrosive ingestion, under the following headings:
A(i) The Fatti, Marchand and Crawshaw grading system for corrosive strictures — describe all four grades.
A(ii) The clinical features that distinguish each phase of corrosive injury.
B) Explain how the pathological changes of the cicatrization phase permanently alter esophageal physiology.
C) Explain why the long-term risk of esophageal carcinoma is raised in survivors, quantify this risk, and describe the prognosis for stricture management.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Fatti, Marchand and Crawshaw grades of stricture:
• Grade 1: fibrosis circumscribed, confined to less than total circumference; short segment; "shelf stricture" — never causes significant luminal narrowing.
• Grade 2: localized annular stricture less than 0.5 inch in length; fibrosis does not penetrate beyond submucosa; narrowing never pronounced; treatment not usually difficult.
• Grade 3: dense stricture less than 0.5 inch; fibrosis extends through outer muscular coats; lumen may be reduced to thread-like size; lined by epithelium.
• Grade 4: tubular stricture with dense fibrotic walls, periesophageal adhesions, marked luminal narrowing; epithelium cannot rebridge the gap; lumen lined by fibrous and granulation tissue; always difficult to treat.

A(ii)
Clinical features by phase: Acute phase (day 1–4) — burning sensation of lips/mouth/pharynx, pain beneath sternum, abundant salivation, pale and anxious appearance, thready rapid pulse, dysphagia, odynophagia, haematemesis, respiratory distress. Ulcerative/granulation phase (day 3–12) — features of ulceration; reparative processes begin. Cicatrization phase (week 3 onward) — progressive dysphagia worsening as stricture tightens; signs of progressive esophageal narrowing.

B)
The collagenous connective tissue formed in the cicatrization phase contracts, causing narrowing. Degeneration of both muscle and nerve tissue occurs after inflammation subsides; the submucosa and muscularis are replaced by dense fibrous tissue, permanently altering peristaltic movements and secretory activity — the physiological behaviour of the esophagus is permanently altered with decreased peristalsis.

C)
Long-term (average onset 40 years after injury): carcinoma of the esophagus is a major hazard; the risk is 1000 to 3000 times the expected risk. Prognosis for stricture: caustic substances are difficult and hazardous to treat by peroral dilatation; about half of patients require esophageal resection.

questions.question:
A) Describe the medical treatment of nasal polyposis under the following headings:
A(i) The drugs used, their mechanism of action relevant to nasal polyps, and the specific cell types and cytokines they target.
A(ii) The roles of saline douching, antihistamines, and leukotriene receptor antagonists.
A(iii) The corticosteroid formulations available, their routes, and the preferred method of delivery to the middle meatus.
B) Describe the surgical treatment of nasal polyposis: list all three intraoperative techniques used in FESS for polyp removal, and state the serious complications the patient must be counselled about pre-operatively.
C) Explain why recurrence after surgical treatment of nasal polyps is particularly high in patients with asthma, quantifying the increased likelihood, and state the overall recurrence rate for severe disease after ESS.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Corticosteroids are the mainstay of conservative therapy. Mechanism of action: anti-inflammatory effects and ability to reduce airway eosinophilic infiltration by preventing increased viability and activation of eosinophils. Both topical and systemic glucocorticoids may affect eosinophil function by directly reducing eosinophil viability and function, or indirectly reducing secretion of chemotactic cytokines by nasal mucosa and polyp epithelial cells.

A(ii)
Saline nasal douching: improves nasal mucociliary clearance (measured by the saccharine test) and cleanses the nose prior to topical medications. Antihistamines: can have significant reduction in symptoms in simple nasal polyp. Leukotriene receptor antagonists: recently shown to be effective but larger-scale trials are required to prove efficacy. Topical capsaicin: also shown effective. Antibiotics: not effective in medical management of uncomplicated nasal polyp; mucolytics can be used as adjuncts in acute sinusitis to reduce viscosity of sinus secretions.

A(iii)
Corticosteroid formulations: topical (nasal drops or sprays — fluticasone propionate); systemic (oral/parenteral for short courses). Preferred delivery to middle meatus: nasal drops (deliver a higher dose of medication to the middle meatus); the lying, head-back position is both comfortable and effective. Intranasal aqueous nasal spray is used for long-term maintenance once symptoms have resolved.

B)
Three intraoperative techniques in FESS:
• Traditional snare polypectomy
• Cold steel instruments
• Micro-debridement (rotating blade in combination with suction and irrigation). Pre-operative counselling for serious complications: loss of vision; damage to the internal carotid artery; cerebrospinal fluid leakage after inadvertent trauma to the skull base.

C)
Recurrences are common, particularly in patients with asthma who are twice as likely to develop recurrence compared with non-asthmatics. Overall recurrence rate for severe disease after ESS: severe disease recurring in around 5–10% of patients. Post-operative care to prevent recurrence: regular saline nasal douching to prevent crusting and adhesions; topical intranasal steroids as a routine part of after-surgery care.

(i)
Oesophageal foreign body.

(ii)
The aortic arch (second physiological constriction).

(iii)
Clinical features of oesophageal foreign body: dysphagia (difficulty swallowing); odynophagia (pain on swallowing); chest pain; drooling/excessive salivation; noisy breathing if the foreign body compresses the trachea; regurgitation or vomiting.

(iv)
Investigations: upper GI endoscopy (gold standard); plain radiograph of chest and abdomen; barium swallow studies; CT scan. Management: airway assessment first; endoscopic removal (rigid or flexible oesophagoscopy); surgical intervention if endoscopic removal fails or if perforation has occurred (oesophageal perforation requires broad-spectrum antibiotics and surgical repair).
questions.question:
A 6-year-old child presents with noisy breathing and intermittent dysphagia. The mother states that 4 days ago the child appeared to swallow something whilst playing with toy parts. Anterior rhinoscopy is normal. A plain X-ray of the neck and chest shows a radio-opaque object in the mid-oesophagus at the level of the aortic arch.
(i) State the diagnosis.
(ii) State which level is demonstrated radiologically.
(iii) Describe the clinical features of an oesophageal foreign body.
(iv) Outline the investigations and complete management.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
MRI is an imaging modality that produces cross-sectional images of the body in any plane without exposing the body to ionising radiation. Advantages: three-dimensional images in any plane; non-invasive; greater potential for soft tissue differentiation — white and grey matter of the brain and blood vessels can be differentiated; post-contrast MRI can differentiate between scar tissue and recurrence of a tumour; can demonstrate arteries and veins without contrast.

A(ii)
Disadvantages of MRI: the best for soft tissue shadows (which is also a relative disadvantage if bony detail is needed); no signal from cortical bone and calcification; costly and time-consuming; cannot be done with implants such as cochlear implants, aneurysm clips, or pacemakers.

B(i)
MRI is most valuable for: cerebral/cerebellar and other brain lesions; inner ear lesions.

B(ii)
CT scan features: gives a 2-D image; air, bone, and calcification are well differentiated; cannot demonstrate arteries and veins without contrast; no problem with metallic implants; most valuable for lesions of the external, middle, and inner ear; faster and more economical; minimum exposure to radiation; better visualization of bony details; advantages of accuracy. MRI complements CT because: MRI gives superior soft tissue contrast and 3-D imaging in any plane and can show blood vessels without contrast, while CT excels at bony detail, is faster, is widely available, and can be used in patients with metallic implants — together they provide complementary anatomical and tissue-specific information.
questions.question:
Describe the MRI as an imaging modality in ENT radiology: its advantages, disadvantages, and specific applications; then describe how CT and MRI complement each other in clinical practice.
A(i) Define MRI, state its plane capabilities and its relation to ionising radiation, and list its advantages.
A(ii) List the disadvantages of MRI and state the specific contraindications related to implants.
B(i) State the specific ENT lesions for which MRI is most valuable.
B(ii) Describe the key CT features (dimensionality, tissue differentiation, vascular and bony imaging, cost and availability) and compare them with MRI to explain why the two modalities complement each other.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Sialography is a radio-opaque medium study of the salivary glands. A radio-opaque medium is injected through the duct for sialogram and detection of cysts. It is useful in sialolithiasis (salivary gland stones) and in cases of foreign body or stricture in the duct or the gland itself.

A(ii)
CT scanning is an accurate and non-invasive 2-dimensional method in radiology. It can be conventional or high-resolution CT, which combines the use of thinly collimated CT slices that are 1 to 1.5 to 2 mm in thickness.

B(i)
Advantages of CT scan: accuracy; minimum exposure to radiation; better visualisation of bony details. Disadvantages: high cost; non-availability at all centres.

B(ii)
Ultrasound is an imaging modality gaining popularity in assessing deep neck abscesses. It is safer than CT scan because it is portable and does not use radiation; it is also less traumatic to children, requiring less frequent use of sedation. In experienced hands, ultrasound can help determine the presence and location of an abscess and can allow the clinician to distinguish an abscess from cellulitis with some accuracy. However, CT with IV contrast remains more definitive, showing RPA as a hypodense lesion with peripheral ring enhancement, and is very useful in diagnosis and management.
questions.question:
Describe the nature and purpose of sialography and CT scanning in ENT radiology, and explain how imaging is used in assessing the salivary glands and neck masses, including the clinical relevance of each modality.
A(i) Describe sialography: what it is, how it is performed, and for which conditions it is indicated.
A(ii) Describe CT scanning in ENT radiology: state whether it is invasive, how it produces images, what types are available, and their slice thickness.
B(i) List all the advantages and disadvantages of CT scanning.
B(ii) Describe the role of ultrasound in assessing deep neck abscesses, including its safety advantages, what it can determine, and its limitations compared to CT.

A) Describe the management principles for acute rhinosinusitis under the following headings:
A(i) First-line and second-line antibiotic choices for community-acquired acute rhinosinusitis, including specific drug names and dosing regimens.
A(ii) Minimum duration of antibiotic treatment and when prophylactic antibiotics are added.
A(iii) The role, mechanism of action, duration of safe use, and risk of overuse for topical nasal decongestants.
B) Describe the surgical treatment options for acute rhinosinusitis, including the specific contraindications to antral washout and the indication for frontal sinus trephination.
C) Distinguish between the use of oral decongestants and topical nasal steroids in acute rhinosinusitis: state the mechanism of each and the specific cautions for each drug group.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Recommended first-line antibiotic choices: amoxicillin or trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole as first-line agents. Additional acceptable first-line choices: trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole double-strength (bid); lorcarbacef (400 mg bid); amoxicillin/clavulanate (500/125 mg tid); cefuroxime axetil (250 mg tid); clarithromycin (500 mg bid). Young children with mild to moderate ARS: amoxicillin at normal or high dose. Amoxicillin-allergic patients: cephalosporin; severe allergy — macrolide. Non-responders or high-risk for resistant Strep: high-dose amoxicillin/clavulanate. Second-line (adults): respiratory quinolones — ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, gatifloxacin, moxifloxacin. Backup: clarithromycin and azithromycin (excellent mucosal levels but increasing pneumococcal resistance — approximately 10–20%); clindamycin reserved for culture-documented resistant S. pneumoniae.

A(ii)
Minimum antibiotic duration: 2 weeks minimum; may continue for 1 month if symptoms not completely resolved. For therapy longer than 2 weeks: encourage diet including lactobacillus acidophilus (yogurt or pill) to prevent diarrhoea from depletion of normal intestinal flora. Rapid recurrence after previous treatment: add a 3- to 6-week course of once-daily prophylactic antibiotic therapy. Paediatric duration: usually 10–21 days or until symptoms resolve plus 10 days; parenteral ceftriaxone for children not tolerating oral medications.

A(iii)
Topical nasal decongestants (phenylephrine and oxymetazoline): vasoconstriction of dilated mucosal blood vessels (α-adrenergic agonists). Safe duration of use: first 3–5 days only (for immediate symptomatic relief and to speed sinus drainage). Risk of overuse: rhinitis medicamentosa (rebound vasodilation) — occurs after 10 days to 2 weeks of use.

B)
Surgical treatment of acute rhinosinusitis:
• Antral washout: was the mainstay procedure in the past; now limited to severe cases with abscess formation; sinus puncture and irrigation removes thick purulent secretions. Contraindications: children under 3 years of age; undeveloped maxillary sinus; trauma to the orbital floor; acute febrile maxillary sinusitis untreated with antibiotics.
• External frontoethmoidectomy: limited to complications of acute ethmoiditis (orbital cellulitis/abscess); allows decompression and drainage; can now be done endoscopically.
• Frontal sinus trephination: traditional approach to acute frontal sinusitis (empyema) that fails to respond to conservative treatment; endoscopic restoration of integrity of the nasofrontal duct using FESS is the ideal alternative.

C)
Oral decongestants (phenylpropanolamine or pseudoephedrine): α-adrenergic agonists that vasoconstrict nasal vascular bed, limiting blood flow and reducing mucosal oedema. Caution: prostatic hypertrophy or prostatitis — urinary retention may be exacerbated.
Topical nasal steroids: not beneficial in early stages because mucosal penetration is lessened by tissue oedema and mechanism of action is slow; initiation after several days of therapy hasten resolution through anti-inflammatory action. Not recommended during early phases of varicella or measles as they may exacerbate the infection. Oral steroids rarely required but may be needed in recalcitrant cases especially with reactive airway disease.

questions.question:
A child is diagnosed with cerebral palsy from birth. The parents are concerned about his speech and communication.
(i) Define cerebral palsy and describe the possible spectrum of speech involvement in this condition.
(ii) Define dysarthria and list the six aspects of speech production it involves.
(iii) Describe developmental language disorder, give an example, and define aphasia including its anatomical basis and what it impairs.
(iv) Distinguish learning-disabled children from those with aphasia in terms of their specific language deficits.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Cerebral palsy is an impairment of neurological function starting from birth day or early infancy. It shows no clinical evidence of progression. Speech involvement ranges widely: speech may not be affected at all; on the other hand, it may be so severely affected that even non-verbal communication is impossible.

(ii)
Dysarthria is a motor speech disorder resulting from a neurological lesion. It involves respiration, phonation, articulation, resonance, fluency, and both voluntary and involuntary movement.

(iii)
Developmental language disorder occurs often in children and may result from: emotional disturbance or neurological impairment. An example of a developmental language disorder is aphasia. Aphasia is an impairment or nearly total loss in the reception, manipulation, and sometimes in the use of words as symbols of ideas. It is caused by lesions in the cerebral cortex and association paths of the dominant hemisphere.

(iv)
Learning-disabled children exhibit impaired language acquisition function without impairment of specific sensory, motor, intellectual, or emotional functions. This distinguishes them from children with aphasia, in whom there is an impairment or nearly total loss in the reception, manipulation, and use of words as symbols of ideas caused by lesions in the cerebral cortex.

A(i)
The nasopharynx is a cuboidal space postero-superior to the soft palate. Its boundaries: inferior border — palate; anterior border — junction between the hard and soft palate; roof and posterior wall — basisphenoid bone; inferior border posteriorly — base of skull; lateral walls — eustachian tube orifices/fossa of Rosenmüller.

A(ii)
Histologic types: squamous cell carcinoma; undifferentiated carcinoma; lympho-epithelioma; connective tissue tumours. 90% of tumours arise from the epithelium, subdivided into well differentiated and undifferentiated.

B(i)
Clinical features: neck nodes — 80%; difficulty in breathing; cranial nerve involvement — at the base of skull: cranial nerves IX, X, XI, XII; at the roof through the foramen lacerum: cranial nerves III, IV, VII.

B(ii)
Treatment volume with generous margin is necessary. Boundaries of treatment volume: declivity of the sphenoid; posterior portion of the orbit; posterior half of the nasal fossa; just below the level of the angle of the jaw to enclose retropharyngeal nodes. Two opposed lateral fields plus an anterior field to the neck are used. Doses: large field — 50 Gy; reduced field (with cord off) — 50 Gy + 15 Gy = 65 Gy total. Vital structures protected using the shrinking field technique include: hypothalamus, pituitary, brain stem, spinal cord, optic nerve, and optic chiasma. Reported changes in the optic nerve and hypothalamus occur in 5% of patients; middle ear changes also occur.

questions.answerText:
(i)
Nasal polyposis (ethmoidal). The specific triad is Samter's Triad: polyposis, asthma, and aspirin hypersensitivity — makes up almost 10% of cases of nasal polyps.

(ii)
Lund-Mackay CT staging system: scores each sinus system on a scale of 0–2 (0 = no opacification; 1 = partial opacification; 2 = complete opacification). The osteomeatal complex is also scored (0 or 2). Maximum score is 12 per side (24 total). The system has been validated, but the correlation between CT score and symptoms is poor and is not a good indicator of outcome.

(iii)
Medical treatment sequence:
• Simple saline nasal douching first to cleanse the nose prior to topical medications; improves mucociliary clearance.
• Topical nasal steroids (first-line): fluticasone propionate drops or spray; nasal drops deliver higher dose to middle meatus; lying head-back position is comfortable and effective. Corticosteroids may also be given systemically for short courses.
• Additional agents: antihistamines (significant reduction in symptoms in simple nasal polyp); leukotriene receptor antagonists (recently shown effective); topical capsaicin (shown effective); antibiotics not effective in uncomplicated nasal polyp; mucolytics as adjunct in acute sinusitis only.
• Corticosteroids with caution in: diabetes, uncontrolled hypertension, peptic ulcer disease.
• Adverse effects of short-term steroids: glucose intolerance, hypertension, adrenal suppression, gastrointestinal bleeding, altered mental state.
• Allergic fungal rhinosinusitis: treated with topical and systemic antimycotics as adjunct to sinus surgery.

(iv)
FESS is justified because polyp recurrence following endoscopic sinus surgery was 28% compared with 35% following intranasal polypectomy (National Health Service Research and Development Health Technology Assessment Programme Evaluation). FESS restores sinus drainage by careful removal of nasal polyps or other soft tissue obstructing natural sinus ostia, using traditional snare polypectomy, cold steel instruments, or micro-debridement (rotating blade with suction and irrigation). The micro-debrider enables accurate removal whilst preserving normal anatomical structures such as the turbinates.
questions.question:

He has a known history of aspirin hypersensitivity and bronchial asthma. CT scan of the paranasal sinuses shows complete opacification of the bilateral ethmoid sinuses and partial opacification of both maxillary sinuses with a Lund-Mackay score of 18/24.

(iv) Justify the choice of FESS over intranasal polypectomy, using the recurrence rates.

questions.answerText:
(i)
Diagnosis: Foreign body aspiration. Commonest type: vegetable matter (70–80%), with peanuts and other nuts accounting for 35%. Commonest site: the bronchi (80–90%), with the right mainstem bronchus being most common; this is because the right mainstem bronchus has a less divergent angle and a greater diameter than the left.

(ii)
The diagnostic triad is: unilateral wheeze, cough, and ipsilateral diminished breath sounds. It is present in less than 50% of affected patients.

(iii)
In a child older than one year with complete airway obstruction: use gentle abdominal thrusts while the child is supine. In older children and adults: use the Heimlich manoeuvre. In infants under one year: back blows are used. Note: back blows and probing of the hypopharynx are not recommended as first-line measures in children over one year or adults.

(iv)
Goal of treatment: prompt endoscopic removal under conditions of maximal safety and minimal trauma. Endoscopy is usually not a dire emergency. The procedure requires trained personnel with instruments assembled and checked; await emptying of the stomach; find a duplicate foreign body to test instruments and techniques. Procedure: general anaesthesia; spontaneous ventilation; laryngoscopy; bronchoscopy; suction; forceps; rod-lens telescopes. Alternative — endoscopy by short apnoeic technique: be ready to assume the airway during induction; laryngoscopy; examination of the upper airway; atraumatic insertion of bronchoscope; topical anaesthesia; bronchoscopy.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
The two parent vessels are: the internal carotid artery (via ophthalmic artery) and the external carotid artery (via the maxillary artery and facial artery).

A(ii)
Lateral nasal wall supply: anterior ethmoidal artery and posterior ethmoidal artery (from ophthalmic artery/internal carotid); sphenopalatine artery (from internal maxillary artery/external carotid).

A(iii)
Medial wall (septal) supply: anterior and posterior ethmoidal arteries (internal carotid), sphenopalatine artery (external carotid), greater palatine artery (external carotid), septal branch of superior labial artery (facial artery/external carotid); these anastomose to form Kiesselbach's plexus at Little's area.

B(i)
Safe site for sphenopalatine artery ligation: transnasal sphenopalatine ligation (endoscopic approach); the sphenopalatine foramen at the posterior end of the middle meatus is the landmark.

B(ii)
Arterial ligation options: external carotid artery ligation; transmaxillary IMA (internal maxillary artery) ligation; transnasal sphenopalatine ligation; anterior and posterior ethmoidal artery ligation.

C)
Division of the anterior ethmoidal artery during sinus surgery causes loss of blood supply to the anterosuperior nasal septum and roof; it also removes the artery's contribution to Kiesselbach's plexus. The anterior ethmoidal artery is a branch of the ophthalmic artery (internal carotid); inadvertent injury within the orbit can cause orbital haematoma and loss of vision by compression of the optic nerve — a serious, recognised complication of endoscopic sinus surgery.
questions.question:
A) Describe the arterial supply of the nose under the following headings:
A(i) Origin of the two parent vessels from which the nasal arterial supply is derived.
A(ii) Named branches from each parent vessel that supply the lateral nasal wall.
A(iii) Named branches that supply the medial wall (septum).
B) In a patient requiring cauterisation for a posterior nasal bleed, state:
B(i) The anatomical safe site for sphenopalatine artery ligation.

A. Describe the anatomy of the palatine tonsil and its relationship to adjacent structures that are relevant during tonsillectomy under the following headings:
A(i) The superior constrictor muscle as the surgical bed and the relationship of the internal carotid artery to the tonsillar fossa
A(ii) The anterior and posterior pillars and the plica triangularis
A(iii) The blood supply and the vessels most at risk during tonsillectomy
B. Describe the technique of tonsillectomy with respect to anatomical landmarks, and state the safe lateral limit of dissection.
C. Classify and describe all complications of tonsillectomy by timing and mechanism, and distinguish reactionary haemorrhage from secondary haemorrhage.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The superior constrictor muscle makes up the bed of the tonsillar fossa. The internal carotid artery lies just two centimetres posterolateral to the deep surface of the tonsil; in 1% of the population, it is found just deep to the superior constrictor muscle, making it particularly vulnerable to injury during deep dissection.

A(ii)
The anterior pillar is the palatoglossus muscle; the posterior pillar is the palatopharyngeus muscle. The base of the tonsil is separated from the underlying muscles by a dense collagenous hemi-capsule. The tonsil is continuous with the lymphoid tissue at the base of the lingual tonsils; the point of attachment is the plica triangularis, which must be transected during tonsillectomy to fully mobilise the tonsil.

A(iii)
The majority of blood supply arises from the tonsillar branch of the facial artery. Additional supply from the ascending pharyngeal artery, the descending palatine artery, and the dorsal lingual branch of the lingual artery. The most dangerous vessel at risk during tonsillectomy is the internal carotid artery (lying 2 cm posterolateral to the tonsil deep surface, or superficially in 1% of cases) and the tonsillar branch of the facial artery, which is the primary blood supply.

B.
Tonsillectomy technique and landmarks: dissection proceeds within the peritonsillar plane, between the tonsil capsule and the superior constrictor muscle; the anterior pillar (palatoglossus) is incised superiorly; the tonsil is dissected from superior to inferior pole in the avascular plane between the hemi-capsule and the superior constrictor; the plica triangularis at the inferior pole must be transected; the safe lateral limit of dissection is the medial surface of the superior pharyngeal constrictor — the dissection must not breach this muscle, as the internal carotid artery and carotid sheath structures lie just beyond.

C.
Complications by timing: Immediate — haemorrhage (reactionary, within 24 hours, due to primary haemostasis failure); anaesthetic complications (airway, laryngospasm); soft palate damage; dislocation of the cervical spine. Intermediate (within days to weeks) — secondary haemorrhage (usually day 5–10, due to sloughing of the tonsillar bed eschar and underlying infection); haematoma and oedema of the uvula; infection; pulmonary complications (aspiration, pneumonia). Late — subacute bacterial endocarditis; eustachian tube stenosis; hypernasal speech (rhinolalia aperta, due to temporary velopharyngeal incompetence); persistence of symptoms; tonsillar remnants; postoperative scarring. Reactionary haemorrhage: occurs within 24 hours of surgery; due to failure of primary haemostasis (inadequate ligation of vessels or slippage of ligature); requires return to theatre for control. Secondary haemorrhage: occurs 5–10 days postoperatively; caused by separation of the postoperative slough from an underlying infected wound; may be managed with antibiotics and local measures if mild, or return to theatre if severe. The incidence of postoperative haemorrhage is 0.1–8.1%; transfusion is required in 0.04%; mortality from haemorrhage occurs in 0.002%.

questions.question:
A 6-year-old child presents with a 2-week history of fever, nasal obstruction, rhinorrhoea, mouth breathing, excessive sneezing, and difficulty sleeping at night due to noisy breathing and snoring. Parents report she stops breathing for brief periods during sleep and wakes gasping. On examination, the tonsils are grade 3 (50–75% obstruction of the oropharynx).
(i) State the diagnosis and classify the type of sleep-disordered breathing using the criteria given.
(ii) Describe the pathophysiology by which bacterial biofilms in adenotonsillar tissue contribute to recurrent upper respiratory tract and ear disease.
(iii) List all the most common bacteria isolated from adenotonsillar infections, and identify which three are the most important pathogens in otitis and rhinosinusitis in children.
(iv) Describe the medical management with specific antibiotic options and the rationale for treating beta-lactamase-producing organisms.
(v) Outline the indications and contraindications for adenotonsillectomy in this child, and state the mortality rate and incidence of postoperative haemorrhage from the procedure.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Diagnosis: obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) due to adenotonsillar hyperplasia. Sleep-disordered breathing classification using PSG: OSA is diagnosed as RDI >5 and SpO2 <90%; upper airway resistance syndrome as RDI <5 and SpO2 >90%; primary snoring when RDI <1 and SpO2 >90%. In children, an adequate and convincing history combined with physical evidence of adenotonsillar hypertrophy is relied upon in lieu of a sleep study; PSG is reserved for children in whom the diagnosis is unclear or who have an unusual surgical risk.

(ii)
Pathophysiology: bacterial biofilms play an integral role in harbouring chronic infection in tonsil and adenoid tissue, contributing to recurrent sinusitis and recurrent or persistent ear disease. After repeated or chronic infections, the ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelium of the adenoid thins, resulting in stasis of secretions and impaired mucociliary clearance; the increased antigen exposure from mucus stasis leads to an increased inflammatory response within the adenoid. Enlarged adenoids and tonsils may obstruct the Eustachian tube, producing otitis media with effusion and recurrent acute otitis media.

(iii)
Most common bacteria isolated: Haemophilus influenzae; group A beta-haemolytic Streptococcus; Staphylococcus aureus; Moraxella catarrhalis; Streptococcus pneumoniae. The three most important pathogens in otitis and rhinosinusitis in children suffering from these diseases are: Haemophilus influenzae; Moraxella catarrhalis; and Streptococcus pneumoniae.

(iv)
Medical management: GABHS is exquisitely sensitive to penicillin (traditionally a 10-day regimen); cephalosporins demonstrate greater eradication rates; for co-colonising beta-lactamase-producing organisms (Staphylococcus aureus, M. catarrhalis, H. influenzae, and anaerobes), antibiotics with high potency against GABHS that are beta-lactamase stable — such as Augmentin, clindamycin, or cefdinir — are superior to penicillin; macrolides for proven penicillin allergy (erythromycin and clarithromycin for 10 days; azithromycin 12 mg/kg/day for 5 days); adenoid hyperplasia may also respond to a 6–8 week course of intranasal steroids.

(v)
Indications for adenotonsillectomy: the only absolute indication for adenoidectomy is airway obstruction with secondary cardiopulmonary complications and failure to thrive; relative indications include recurrent acute adenotonsillitis, chronic nasal obstruction with rhinorrhoea or recurrent sinusitis, recurrent otitis media with effusion, sleep apnoea, speech and swallowing abnormalities, suspected neoplasia; absolute indications for tonsillectomy include severe dysphagia, failure to thrive, and cor pulmonale. Contraindications: cleft deformities and velopharyngeal insufficiency (for adenoidectomy); recent URTI; haematological disorders (for tonsillectomy). Mortality rate for adenotonsillectomy: 1 in 16,000 to 35,000, mostly from anaesthetic complications and haemorrhage. Incidence of postoperative haemorrhage: 0.1–8.1%; transfusion required in 0.04% of bleeding patients; mortality from haemorrhage occurs in 0.002%.

A(i)
Waldeyer's ring consists of: nasopharyngeal tonsils (adenoids); palatine tonsils; tubal tonsils; lingual tonsils; and posterior pharyngeal wall lymphoid follicles.

A(ii)
The luminal surface of the tonsils is covered by deeply invaginated clefts of stratified squamous epithelium lined by specialised squamous epithelium which transports antigens by M-type cells to antigen-presenting cells. These are transported to the extrafollicular area which has abundant T-lymphocytes that aid differentiation of B-lymphocytes. The lymphoid follicle is encased by the mantle zone where mature B-lymphocytes reside. At the core of the lymphoid follicle is the germinal centre where B-lymphocytes produce antigen-specific immunoglobulin.

A(iii)
The tonsil lies within a bed of three muscles: the palatoglossus (anterior pillar), palatopharyngeus (posterior pillar), and superior constrictor (bed of fossa). It is separated from lateral pharyngeal walls by a connective tissue capsule. Blood supply: mainly the tonsillar branch of the facial artery; also ascending pharyngeal, descending palatine, and dorsal lingual branch of the lingual artery. The internal carotid artery lies just two centimetres posterolateral to the deep surface of the tonsil; in 1% of the population it is found just deep to the superior constrictor muscle. Nerve supply: ninth cranial nerve and descending branches from the lesser palatine nerves; the tympanic branch of CN IX explains referred ear pain in tonsillitis. Lymphatic drainage: efferent lymph drains through the upper cervical nodes, especially the jugulodigastric group.

B.
Adenoids develop from a subepithelial infiltration of lymphocytes after the 16th week of embryonic life. Enlargement begins after birth and continues until aged 5 to 7 years; symptomatic enlargement between 18 to 24 months is not uncommon. Pathologically, bacterial biofilms play an integral role in harbouring chronic infection in tonsil and adenoid tissue, contributing to recurrent sinusitis and otitis media. Enlarged adenoids and tonsils may obstruct breathing, causing sleep apnoea. The most common bacteria isolated are Haemophilus influenzae, group A beta-haemolytic Streptococcus, Staphylococcus aureus, Moraxella catarrhalis, and Streptococcus pneumoniae.

C.
The adenoids have deep folds and few crypts, and their surface is covered by ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelium that plays an important role in mucociliary clearance. The palatine tonsils have deeply invaginated clefts (crypts) of stratified squamous epithelium. After repeated or chronic infections of the adenoid, the ciliated epithelial layer thins, resulting in stasis of secretions and impaired mucociliary clearance; the increased antigen exposure from mucus stasis leads to an increased inflammatory response within the adenoid.

Describe the ENT clinical examination process, including instruments, the approach to examining the ear, and the technique for nasal and throat examination.
A(i) State the principles of ENT examination that apply as in any specialty of medicine.
A(ii) Describe the process of otoscopic examination of the ear, including the direction of pull and the structures to be identified and recorded.
B(i) Describe the nasal examination procedure, including the use of the Thudicum speculum and assessment of airflow, and state what additional areas must be examined.
B(ii) Describe the examination of the oral cavity and oropharynx, including the number of tongue depressors to use, the surfaces to examine, and the structures to assess bimanually.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
In ENT, as in any other specialty of medicine, examination follows the same principles: inspection, palpation, percussion, and auscultation. Usually palpation is done using instruments as well as percussion in most cases, as sites of lesions are not readily accessible to the hands of the examiner.

A(ii)
Otoscopic examination: pull the pinna upwards, outwards, and backwards. Look for any cavity; assess all quadrants; look for the malleus and incus. Record all abnormalities. Structures identified include the long process of the incus and the handle of the malleus; also look for central or marginal perforations. Tuning fork tests and simple free-field tests are also used.

B(i)
Nasal examination: look at the skin and scars; look at the vestibules by lifting the tip. Palpation/inspection: occlude each nostril in turn and assess air entry; look at misting of a tongue depressor. Anterior rhinoscopy: use the Thudicum speculum and hold it properly. Also examine the neck and oral cavity; check the post-nasal space. Ear disease may suggest nasal pathology.

B(ii)
Oral cavity and oropharynx examination: use two tongue depressors; examine every mucosal surface; look at salivary orifices; perform bimanual palpation. Examine the larynx by asking the patient to swallow and protrude the tongue, to breathe deeply, and to count to ten; adequate exposure is needed. Indirect or direct laryngoscopy is to be learned in the OPD. Neck examination: from in front then mainly from behind; examine the submandibular area, both triangles, and the supraclavicular area; listen for bruit; examine the thyroid and carotid. Indirect or direct laryngoscopy includes visualisation of the arytenoid cartilage.

(i)
The left maxillary sinus is the most likely affected structure, as maxillary sinus carcinoma is the commonest paranasal sinus malignancy (80%). The occipito-mental (Water's view) is the most useful standard view for the maxillary antrum; it shows the maxillary antrum, orbital margins, and malar bones. The radiographic sign of malignancy in this region is bone destruction — malignancy destroys the bone.

(ii)
Nasal and paranasal sinus cancers constitute 3% of head and neck cancers. They are usually diagnosed late because their symptoms overlap with those of upper respiratory tract infections.

(iii)
Occipito-mental (Water's) view shows: maxillary antrum, orbital margins, and malar bones. Occipito-frontal (Caldwell) view shows: petrous temporal bone ridge, ethmoidal sinus, frontal sinus, and nasal septum. Submento-vertical view shows: ethmoidal and sphenoidal sinuses from below.

(iv)
CT scanning is an accurate and non-invasive 2-dimensional method that provides better visualisation of bony details; it can identify bone destruction, extent of soft tissue involvement, and orbital or cranial base invasion that plain radiographs cannot show. MRI provides greater potential for soft tissue differentiation — in any plane, without ionising radiation — and post-contrast MRI can differentiate between scar tissue and tumour recurrence. Together, CT (for bony detail and extent of destruction) and MRI (for soft tissue spread and intracranial extension) provide complementary information essential for staging and radiotherapy planning in paranasal sinus malignancy.
questions.question:
A 14-year-old boy presents with 3 weeks of left-sided nasal obstruction, unilateral blood-stained nasal discharge, and facial swelling. A plain X-ray of the sinuses is taken.
