A 55-year-old woman with known HIV infection presents with neck pain, severe odynophagia, and back pain on swallowing. She has no history of pharyngeal trauma.
(i) Name the most common cause of prevertebral abscess historically, and list the other causes.
(ii) List all conditions that increase the risk of retropharyngeal abscess in the immunocompromised.
(iii) Describe the symptoms of retropharyngeal abscess in adults (at least eight symptoms).
(iv) Describe the physical signs in adults, and explain what specific vascular examination must be performed and why.
questions.answerText:
(i)
The most common cause of prevertebral abscess historically was the extension of a tuberculous infection of a vertebral body — a Pott's abscess. Other sources of prevertebral abscess include trauma, postoperative infection, anterior spread of cervical osteomyelitis, or posterior spread from the retropharyngeal space.

(ii)
Conditions that increase the risk in immunocompromised patients: immunocompromised state; chronic illness; diabetes; cancer; alcoholism; AIDS. Pharyngeal trauma from endotracheal intubation, endoscopy, or foreign body ingestion also predisposes.

(iii)
Symptoms in adults: sore throat; fever; chills; malaise; dysphagia; odynophagia; neck pain; dyspnoea; muffled voice; jaw stiffness; sensation of a lump in the throat; and pain in the back and shoulders upon swallowing.

(iv)
Physical signs in adults: posterior pharyngeal oedema; nuchal rigidity; tender cervical lymphadenopathy; fever; drooling; stridor. Associated signs may include tonsillitis, peritonsillitis, pharyngitis, and otitis media. The 'tracheal rock sign' elicits pain while gently moving the larynx and trachea from side to side; patients preferring to lie supine with necks extended suggests potential airway compromise — sitting up or flexing their necks worsens respiratory distress. Vascular examination is essential: jugular vein thrombophlebitis may manifest as tender induration at the anterior sternocleidomastoid border, vocal cord paralysis, or sepsis of unknown source; carotid artery rupture can be heralded by sentinel bleeding from the ear, nose, or mouth; ecchymosis may be detected in the lateral neck.

(i)
Two urgent diagnoses:
• Septal haematoma — fluctuant bilateral swelling on the nasal septum requires urgent drainage to prevent avascular necrosis of septal cartilage and subsequent saddle deformity.
• CSF rhinorrhoea — blood-stained nasal fluid may represent a CSF leak, indicating skull base fracture. Investigation to exclude CSF leak: CSF rhinorrhoea must be ruled out on examination; clinically, fluid dripping from the nose with a head injury is suggestive.

(ii)
Variables determining type and severity of nasal fracture:
• The patient's age (tissue flexibility)
• The amount of force applied
• The direction of the force
• The nature of the striking object

(iii)
Early complications and management:
• Septal haematoma: urgent drainage; antibiotic prophylaxis.
• Infections: antibiotic prophylaxis.
• Epistaxis: cautery, packing, or ligation.
• CSF rhinorrhoea: must be excluded; neurosurgical management.
• Emphysema of the face and neck: conservative; avoid nose-blowing.
Late complications: organization of haematomas causing airway obstruction; synechia (divide if symptomatic); obstruction of nasal vestibule; residual osteitis; malunion; naso-facial disproportion.

(iv)
Timing of reduction: less than 3–6 hours — immediate reduction; less than 2–3 weeks — closed reduction; more than 3 weeks — delayed 3–6 months. Method: closed reduction of mild unilateral fractures; on rare occasions open reduction in an operating room is necessary. Post-operative care: silastic splints (removed at 10 days); intranasal packing (removed at 2–3 days); external splint application (removed when fracture stable).
questions.question:
A 25-year-old male sustains direct nasal trauma following an assault. He presents 6 hours after injury with nasal deviation to the left, ecchymosis, lid oedema, and a fluctuant swelling on the nasal septum bilaterally. There is also blood-stained fluid dripping from the nose.
(i) State the two urgent diagnoses that must be made, and the investigation required to exclude cerebrospinal fluid leak.
(ii) List the risk factors — specifically the variables that determine the type and severity of nasal fracture.
(iii) Describe the early complications of nasal fractures, and state the management of each.
(iv) Describe the timing and method of fracture reduction, and outline the post-operative care.

A patient with a sphenoid sinus tumour is planned for surgical resection.
(i) State the diagnosis category, and list the surgical approaches for sphenoid tumours.
(ii) Describe the anatomical relations of the sphenoid sinus, including its relation to the sella turcica and optic structures.
(iii) What is the named embryological/anatomical variant of the posterior ethmoid cells that directly relates to the sphenoid sinus, and what is its clinical significance?
(iv) Name the two structures within or immediately adjacent to the sphenoid sinus walls that are at greatest risk during sphenoid sinus surgery.
(v) Describe how the degree of pneumatization of the sphenoid sinus (sellar versus postsellar) affects surgical risk.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Sphenoid sinus tumours (rare; frontal and sphenoid sinuses are the least common sites). Surgical approaches: lateral rhinotomy and craniotomy.

(ii)
The sphenoid sinus arises within the nasal capsule (no pouch); begins to pneumatize at age 3. It is positioned within the sphenoid bone; its sellar and postsellar relationships are key — it relates to the sella turcica, and variable pneumatization affects proximity to critical neurovascular structures. The ostium size is 0.5–4 mm; ostium location may be on the sinus floor, anterior nasal floor, anterior sinus wall, superior turbinate, or cribriform plate.

(iii)
The Onodi cell: a posterior ethmoidal cell that has pneumatized laterally and posteriorly into the region of the sphenoid sinus, placing the optic nerve at risk during posterior ethmoid surgery. Its clinical significance is that surgeons must be aware of it to avoid optic nerve injury.

(iv)
Two structures at greatest risk: the internal carotid artery (runs in the lateral wall of the sphenoid sinus) and the optic nerve (superior lateral wall, especially in association with Onodi cells). Bony dehiscence of the sinus wall increases risk.

(v)
Sellar pneumatization (sinus extends beneath the sella) increases proximity to the internal carotid artery and optic nerve, making surgery more hazardous. Presellar (conchal) pneumatization leaves a thick bony barrier between the sinus and the sella, reducing risk. Surgeon must assess CT for degree of pneumatization before operating.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old female presents to the emergency department with sudden onset of severe frontal headache, high fever, periorbital swelling, and proptosis of the right eye. She gives a 10-day history of right-sided purulent nasal discharge and nasal obstruction. On examination there is periorbital oedema, restricted right extraocular movements and chemosis.
(i) State the two most likely diagnoses in order of severity (according to the staging of orbital complications) and the source sinus.
(ii) Explain the two anatomical pathways by which the sinusitis has spread to the orbit.
(iii) Outline the investigations required to stage the orbital involvement and to guide treatment.
(iv) Describe the medical and surgical management, including the specific indication for external frontoethmoidectomy.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Two most likely diagnoses (in order of staging):
• Orbital cellulitis (Stage B): inflammation and oedema of orbital contents causing proptosis, chemosis, and decreased extraocular movement.
• If globe is displaced and vision impaired: subperiosteal abscess (Stage C). The source sinus in this presentation is most likely the ethmoid sinus (ethmoid sinusitis characteristically causes medial canthal pressure, periorbital swelling, and headache).

(ii)
Two anatomical pathways:
• Direct extension: through congenital bony dehiscences, open suture lines, foramina, or by erosion of the lamina papyracea (thin medial orbital wall separating the ethmoid from the orbit).
• Retrograde thrombophlebitis: through the rich network of valveless veins providing free communication between the nasal cavity, sinuses, and orbit.

(iii)
Investigations: CT scan (axial and coronal) to stage orbital involvement — shows whether there is preseptal, intraconal, or subperiosteal collection; MRI for soft tissue detail and intracranial extension; FBC (leukocytosis); blood cultures (bacteraemia documented in paediatric patients); endoscopy-guided middle meatus swab for culture; ophthalmology assessment of visual acuity and extraocular movements.

(iv)
Medical management: broad-spectrum antibiotics (organisms: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis, S. pyogenes; parenteral antibiotics for severe cases). Surgical management: external frontoethmoidectomy — indicated for complications of acute ethmoiditis such as orbital cellulitis or abscess; allows decompression and drainage of involved sinuses including subperiosteal and retro-orbital abscess; can now be accompanied endoscopically in most patients. FESS can be used for milder cases; frontal sinus trephine for frontal empyema unresponsive to conservative treatment.

A(i)
Classification by duration:
• Acute rhinosinusitis: sudden onset, lasting up to 4 weeks; symptoms resolve after treatment.
• Subacute rhinosinusitis: persisting more than 4 weeks but less than 12 weeks; symptoms eventually may be less severe but still resolve with treatment.
• Chronic rhinosinusitis: 12 weeks or more of signs and symptoms (alternatively defined as more than 3 months).
• Recurrent acute rhinosinusitis: 4 or more episodes per year, with resolution of symptoms between attacks (episodes lasting 1–4 weeks).

A(ii)
Pain by anatomical site:
• Maxillary sinusitis: pain/pressure over cheek, toothache, temporal headache; worsens with head upright, improves lying supine.
• Frontal sinusitis: severe frontal headache, tenderness above medial canthus; worst supine, improved upright.
• Ethmoid sinusitis: medial canthal pressure, pain/tenderness between/behind eyes, periorbital headache; coughing/straining/lying supine exacerbates; head upright may improve.
• Sphenoid sinusitis: diffuse headache (may refer to occiput or any skull focus); worsened by lying supine, bending forward, or Valsalva; improved upright.

A(iii)
Acute rhinosinusitis organisms: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis, anaerobes (Peptococcus, Peptostreptococcus, Fusobacterium). Chronic rhinosinusitis aerobes: Staph aureus, Strep pneumoniae, Staph epidermidis, Strep pyogenes, alpha-haemolytic streptococcus; Gram-negative: Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenza, E. coli. Anaerobes: Bacteroides spp, anaerobic gram-positive cocci, Fusobacterium spp, Veillonella, Corynebacterium spp.

B)
Pathophysiology: ostia obstruction creates an increasingly hypoxic environment within the sinus; retention of secretions results in inflammation and bacterial infection; secretions stagnate, obstruction increases, cilia and epithelial damage become more pronounced. The most common inciting event is viral upper respiratory infection causing mucosal oedema of the osteomeatal complex.

C)
Diagnostic criteria: Major factors: facial pain/pressure, facial congestion/fullness, nasal obstruction/blockage, nasal discharge (anterior or posterior), hyposmia/anosmia, cough. Minor factors: headache, fever, halitosis, fatigue, dental pain, ear pain/pressure/fullness. Strongly suspected: two or more major criteria, OR one major and two minor criteria, OR more than three minor criteria. Suggested: one major factor or two or more minor criteria.
questions.question:
A) Describe the classification of rhinosinusitis under the following headings:
A(i) Classification by duration — define all four categories with their time boundaries.
A(ii) Classification by anatomical site — name each sinus and its characteristic pain location and aggravating or relieving posture.
A(iii) Classification by microbiology — list the most common causative organisms in acute rhinosinusitis and in chronic rhinosinusitis (both aerobic and anaerobic).
B) Explain the pathophysiology of acute rhinosinusitis centred on the osteomeatal complex.
C) Distinguish between the clinical diagnostic criteria for acute rhinosinusitis: define major and minor factors, and state the number of criteria needed for a diagnosis to be strongly suspected versus suggested.

questions.answerText:
(i)
Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma (JNA). It occurs exclusively in males; females diagnosed with JNA should undergo genetic testing.

(ii)
Etiological theories include: hormonal theory (occurrence in adolescent males); desmoplastic response of the nasopharyngeal periosteum; embryonic fibrocartilage between the basiocciput and basisphenoid; harmatomas; nest cells (undifferentiated epitheloid cells); and vestiges of the atrophied stapedial artery. The lesion originates adjacent to the posterior attachment of the middle turbinate, near the superior border of the sphenopalatine foramen.

(iii)
Anterior growth: occurs under the nasopharyngeal mucous membrane, displacing it anteriorly and inferiorly; the nasal cavity fills on one side and the septum deviates. Superior growth: directed toward the sphenoid sinus, which may be eroded; the cavernous sinus may be invaded if the tumor advances further. Lateral growth: toward the pterygopalatine fossa, bowing the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus; the infratemporal fossa is invaded; the greater wing of the sphenoid may be eroded, exposing the middle fossa dura; proptosis and optic nerve atrophy result if orbital fissures are encroached upon.

(iv)
Investigations: plain x-ray (bowing of the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus is very suggestive); CT scan (demonstrates extension to the sphenoid sinus, erosion of the greater sphenoidal wing, invasion of pterygomaxillary and infratemporal fossae); MRI (to delineate intracranial involvement); angiography (confirms hypervascularity; external carotid system is the primary feeder in 94%, mainly the internal maxillary artery; unnamed branches from the internal carotid may contribute rarely); CBC, E/U/C, ESR, clotting profile, ECG, CXR; biopsy at EUA is no longer justified due to risk of severe haemorrhage.

(v)
Definitive surgical treatment is complete excision, performed under hypotensive anaesthesia, with preoperative selective arterial embolization (using reabsorbable microparticulate substances e.g. Gelfoam, polyvinyl alcohol, or nonabsorbable microparticulates e.g. Ivalon, Terbal) and adequate preoperative donated autologous blood. Approach by stage: lateral rhinotomy, transpalatal, transmaxillary or sphenoethmoidal for small tumours (Fisch stage I or II); infratemporal fossa approach for large lateral extension; midfacial degloving with or without LeFort osteotomy improves posterior access; facial translocation combined with Weber-Ferguson incision and coronal extension for frontotemporal craniotomy with midface osteotomies; intranasal endoscopic surgery reserved for tumours limited to the nasal cavity and paranasal sinuses. Surgical complications: excessive bleeding; malignant transformation; transient blindness from embolization; osteoradionecrosis/blindness from radiotherapy; fistula of the palate at junction of soft and hard palate with transpalatal approach; anaesthesia of the cheek with Weber-Ferguson incision.
questions.question:
A 14-year-old male presents with a 3-month history of progressive unilateral nasal obstruction and recurrent severe unilateral nosebleeds that have required hospital visits. Examination reveals a nasal mass and plain x-ray shows bowing of the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus.
(i) What is the most likely diagnosis, and what demographic feature is essential to its recognition?
(ii) State the predisposing/etiological theories given for this lesion, and identify the exact site of origin.
(iii) Describe how the lesion spreads in each direction (anterior, superior, lateral), and state which structures are at risk with each direction of spread.
(iv) Outline the investigations required before definitive treatment, including the role of angiography.
(v) Describe the definitive surgical treatment, including preoperative preparation, choice of surgical approach based on stage, and complications of surgery.

Describe the retropharyngeal space under the following headings, and explain the clinical significance of each boundary or relation.
A(i) Define the retropharyngeal space (its alternative names and general position).
A(ii) Describe its anterior wall, posterior wall, and lateral boundary, and state the vertical extent of the space.
B(i) Explain why infection in the adjacent danger space spreads so readily, stating what lies between these two spaces.
B(ii) Explain why the retropharyngeal abscess typically presents as a lateral rather than a midline bulge, and which space presents midline masses.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The retropharyngeal space is also known as the posterior visceral space, the retrovisceral space, and the retroesophageal space. It occupies the space posterior to the pharynx and esophagus.

A(ii)
Its anterior wall is made up of the buccopharyngeal fascia superiorly and the visceral division of the middle fascia inferiorly. The posterior wall is the alar layer of the deep fascia. The lateral boundary is the carotid sheath. The space extends from the base of the skull to the level of the first and second thoracic vertebra, where the fascial layers making up its walls join together.

B(i)
Posterior to the retropharyngeal space lies the danger space, so named because it contains loose areolar tissue and offers little resistance to the spread of infection. It is the space between the alar layer and prevertebral layer of the deep fascia and runs from the skull base to the diaphragm. Because the loose areolar tissue provides minimal resistance, infection spreads rapidly within this space.

B(ii)
The retropharyngeal abscess is not midline due to the presence of the raphe in the retropharyngeal space caused by the superior constrictor muscle. Midline masses are usually in the prevertebral space.

(i)
Benign positional vertigo (BPV). The most common cause is head trauma or other damage to the ear, such as infections; this patient's bicycle fall (head trauma 3 months ago) is the most likely precipitant. Pathophysiology: results from the free movement of dislodged utricle particulate debris — calcium carbonate crystals (otoliths/otoconia) — that have been displaced into the posterior semicircular canal; movement of the head to a provocative position causes the crystals to shift within the canal, generating an abnormal endolymph current that stimulates the cupula, producing vertigo and nystagmus.

(ii)
Dix-Hallpike test: the examiner uses positional testing with the head-hanging technique; the patient is moved from sitting to a supine position with the head turned 45 degrees to the side being tested and hanging over the edge of the examination couch. Positive result: patients with BPV show a burst of nystagmus after a latency of 5 to 10 seconds; the nystagmus lasts about 30 seconds. The test is never subtly positive — when the test is positive, the nystagmus and vertigo are clear and unmistakable; a faint, equivocal, or borderline response does not constitute a positive test for BPV.

(iii)
Epley manoeuvre: the patient's head is systematically rotated through a sequence of positions to move the loose calcium carbonate crystal particles out of the posterior semicircular canal back into the utricle, where they no longer cause abnormal cupular deflection with positional change. The rationale is mechanical repositioning of the displaced otoliths using gravity to guide them through the canal and back into the utricular saccule.

(iv)
Peripheral versus central vertigo (all five features): Frequency — peripheral: episodic; central: prolonged. Otological findings — peripheral: may have hearing loss; central: may have neurological lesion. Nature of nystagmus — peripheral: horizontal or horizontorotatory; central: nystagmus in any direction including vertical. Position dependence — peripheral: vertigo may depend on position of the head; central: vertigo not related to movement of the head. Nystagmus and visual fixation — peripheral: nystagmus and vertigo suppressible by visual fixation; central: vertigo or nystagmus not suppressible by visual fixation. Ratio: peripheral vertigo to central vertigo in acute vertigo is 99:100 (peripheral accounts for the vast majority).

(v)
Vertigo of central origin investigation: look for diagnostic clues such as vascular risk factors and focal neurological findings; diagnostic tests — MRI brain scan; MRI angiography. Treatment of central vertigo: aspirin 325 mg per day (for vascular/ischaemic causes).
questions.question:
An 18-year-old male presents with recurrent episodes of sudden, severe rotatory vertigo lasting 20–30 seconds, always triggered when he lies down to sleep or rolls over in bed. Each episode is associated with nystagmus but no hearing loss or tinnitus. He has had no ear infections but fell off his bicycle 3 months ago and hit his head.
(i) State the most likely diagnosis, identify the most common precipitating cause, and describe the pathophysiology including the specific structure and material involved.
(ii) Describe the Dix-Hallpike test: how it is performed, what constitutes a positive result, and why the test is described as "never subtly positive."
(iii) Describe the Epley manoeuvre as the definitive treatment, including its rationale.
(iv) Distinguish peripheral from central vertigo under all five features, and state the ratio of peripheral to central vertigo in acute vertigo.
(v) Describe the investigation and treatment of vertigo of central origin.

A. Describe the pathophysiology and clinical features of dysphagia arising at each of the following levels:
A(i) Oral and pharyngeal structural disorders
A(ii) Oesophageal structural disorders (congenital and acquired)
A(iii) Neurological causes: disorders with expected recovery and neurodegenerative disorders
B. Describe the physiological basis of swallowing impairment in aging, and list the medications known to cause or worsen dysphagia.
C. Describe the advantages, disadvantages, and specific indications for each of the following investigations in a patient with dysphagia: plain film, barium oesophagram, manometry, modified barium swallow, and fiberoptic endoscopic evaluation of swallowing (FEES).
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Oral structural disorders: poor dentition (ill-fitting dentures, foreign body); cleft lip/palate (congenital, impairs oral phase). Pharyngeal structural disorders: pharyngitis and oesophagitis (inflammatory); neoplastic (squamous cell carcinoma producing dysphagia, odynophagia, and obstruction); pharyngeal pouches (Zenker's diverticulum — gurgling on swallowing, regurgitation of undigested food, pooling of secretions in the piriform sinus); cricopharyngeal achalasia (failure of the cricopharyngeus to relax, treated by cricopharyngeal myotomy).

A(ii)
Oesophageal structural disorders — congenital: tracheo-oesophageal fistula; laryngeal cleft. Acquired: gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD); achalasia (absence of peristalsis and failure of lower oesophageal sphincter relaxation); diffuse oesophageal spasm; oesophageal webs and rings; strictures from caustic ingestion; cancer. Zenker's diverticulum presents with gurgling noises on swallowing and regurgitation of undigested food.

A(iii)
Neurological causes with expected recovery: CVA/TIA (dysphagia present in up to 47% of stroke patients); closed head trauma; cervical spinal cord injury; post-surgery; poliomyelitis; Guillain-Barré syndrome; cerebral palsy; dysautonomia. Neurodegenerative disorders: Parkinson's disease; Alzheimer's; dementia; ALS (amyotrophic lateral sclerosis); post-polio syndrome; multiple sclerosis; myasthenia gravis; muscular dystrophy; dystonia; dermatomyositis.

B.
Dysphagia in aging: present in 2% of those over 65; poor dentition; loss of tongue connective tissue; increased pharyngeal transit time. Medications that cause or worsen dysphagia: NSAIDs; anticholinergics; sympathomimetics; antihistamines; antidepressants; antihypertensives.

C.
Plain film: uses — suspected infectious cause of dysphagia with gross displacement of structures; advantages — cheap and fast; disadvantages — radiation exposure, poor anatomic detail, no assessment of swallow. Barium oesophagram: uses — structural disorders, dysphagia for solid foods (can use air contrast); advantages — good anatomic detail; disadvantages — radiation, logistics in bedridden patients, cannot detect dynamic disorders. Manometry: uses — disorders requiring intraluminal pressure measurement (achalasia, oesophageal spasm); advantages — only test of pressure wave physiology; disadvantages — cannot diagnose visible lesions, unpleasant for patient, technically demanding. Modified barium swallow: uses — excellent for evaluating dynamic (neuromuscular, aspiration) swallow disorders; advantages — good anatomic detail, evaluates all phases of swallowing; disadvantages — radiation, does not directly test sensitivity, logistics. FEES (fiberoptic endoscopic evaluation of swallowing): uses — mobile tool, biofeedback training; advantages — portable, allows assessment of sensation, cheap, can be used for patient teaching, no radiation; disadvantages — blind spot, cannot directly evaluate cricopharyngeus, cannot evaluate the oesophagus.

questions.question:
A 7-year-old boy is brought in by his parents with a history of snoring, mouth breathing, nasal blockage, and difficulty feeding as an infant. The mother notes that he always breathes with his mouth open. On examination, he has underdeveloped thin nostrils, a short upper lip, prominent upper teeth, a narrow upper alveolus, and a high-arched palate.
(i) Name this clinical syndrome and state its specific cause.
(ii) List all the clinical features of adenoid hypertrophy that this child is likely to have, including its effects on the ear.
(iii) Describe the pathophysiology by which enlarged adenoids produce each of the following: nasal obstruction, otitis media with effusion, sleep apnoea, and adenoid facies.
(iv) State the investigations needed to assess this child, including how the gold standard for sleep-disordered breathing is defined and what alternative is used in children.
(v) Outline the medical and surgical management, including indications and contraindications for adenoidectomy, and its complications.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Adenoid facies (also called "long face syndrome"). It is caused by obstructive adenoid hyperplasia producing chronic mouth breathing.

(ii)
Clinical features of adenoid hypertrophy: nasal blockage; nasal discharge and postnasal drip or catarrh (due to secondary chronic rhinitis and sinusitis); mouth breathing; noisy breathing; snoring; daytime hypersomnolence; obstructive sleep apnoea; excessive sneezing; fever; earache and deafness due to recurrent bouts of acute otitis media and otitis media with effusion (glue ear) caused by Eustachian tube obstruction.

(iii)
Nasal obstruction: enlarged adenoids physically block the nasopharynx, leading to mouth breathing and hyponasal speech; infants may have difficulty feeding because they have to stop sucking intermittently to take a breath. Otitis media with effusion: Eustachian tube obstruction by the enlarged adenoid impairs middle ear drainage and ventilation, resulting in glue ear. Sleep apnoea: enlarged adenoids and tonsils obstruct the upper airway during sleep, causing apnoeic episodes, choking or gasping, frequent awakenings, restless sleep, nocturnal enuresis, and behavioural disturbances; the most seriously affected patients may present with heart failure and failure to thrive. Adenoid facies: chronic mouth breathing due to nasal obstruction leads to underdeveloped thin nostrils, short upper lip, prominent upper incisors, narrow upper alveolus, high-arched palate, and hypoplastic maxilla.

(iv)
Investigations: fibreoptic endoscopy (if tolerated by the child); postnasal mirror examination; lateral neck x-ray; audiometric testing; the gold standard for OSA diagnosis is polysomnography (PSG), which diagnoses OSA as an RDI >5 and SpO2 <90%; upper airway resistance syndrome is diagnosed as RDI <5 and SpO2 >90%; primary snoring when RDI <1 and SpO2 >90%. In children, an adequate history combined with physical evidence of adenotonsillar hypertrophy is relied upon in lieu of a sleep study; PSG is reserved for children in whom the diagnosis is unclear or who have unusual surgical risk.

(v)
Medical: topical and systemic decongestants; antihistamines; antibiotics; anti-inflammatory agents; intranasal steroids for adenoid hyperplasia (6–8 week course); a one-month antibiotic course against BLPO can reduce adenotonsillar size in 10–15% of children. Surgical: adenoidectomy. Indications: nasal obstruction; otitis media with effusion; recurrent acute otitis media; sleep apnoea. Contraindications: recent URTI; bleeding diathesis; cleft palate; velopharyngeal insufficiency. Complications: haemorrhage; injury to soft palate and Eustachian tubes; temporomandibular joint dislocation; postoperative scarring; hypernasal speech (temporary); persistent symptoms; Eustachian tube stenosis (late).

questions.question:
A 20-year-old medical student notices that a classmate has progressive bilateral proptosis, epistaxis and a palpable right cheek mass. A CT scan shows a heterogeneous mass occupying 60% of the right maxillary antrum with erosion of the posterior antral wall; the mass has fluid-attenuating areas within it suggesting internal vascularity.
(i) From the site incidence, state what percentage of sinonasal tumours occur in the antrum and what this makes the antrum.
(ii) List the structures that may be compressed or invaded, accounting for each symptom (proptosis, epistaxis, cheek mass).
(iii) Describe the lymphatic drainage of the paranasal sinuses and explain the clinical relevance to staging.
(iv) List the benign and malignant histological types of sinonasal tumour in full.
(v) Outline the staged surgical approach for antral tumours, and state the role of radiotherapy and chemotherapy.
questions.answerText:
(i)
The antrum (maxillary sinus) is the commonest site of sinonasal tumours: 60% occur in the antrum; nasal cavity accounts for 30%; ethmoid for 10%; frontal and sphenoid sinuses are rare.

(ii)
Structures compressed or invaded:
• Proptosis: superior wall of the antrum (orbital floor) is eroded, allowing direct invasion of the orbit or compression of orbital contents causing forward displacement of the globe.
• Epistaxis: tumour infiltrates the medial wall of the antrum (lateral nasal wall), eroding blood vessels; also direct nasal cavity invasion.
• Cheek mass: anterior antral wall erosion allows tumour extension into soft tissues of the cheek, causing visible and palpable swelling; facial pain and paraesthesia due to infraorbital nerve involvement.

(iii)
Lymphatic drainage: paranasal sinuses drain first to retropharyngeal nodes, then to the deep cervical chain. The first echelon (retropharyngeal) nodes are not palpable in the neck; therefore, palpable cervical lymphadenopathy is only present in 15% of cases — this means a clinically node-negative neck may harbour occult nodal disease, which is relevant to staging and elective neck dissection decisions.

(iv)
Benign tumours: papilloma (inverted, everted, transitional), adenoma, haemangioma, fibroma, chondroma, osteoma, neurofibroma, rhabdomyoma. Malignant tumours: squamous cell carcinoma (commonest, 80%), anaplastic carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, haemangiosarcoma, fibrosarcoma, chondrosarcoma, osteosarcoma, neurofibrosarcoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, esthesioneuroblastoma, plasmacytoma, lymphoma, salivary gland tumours, adenoid-cystic carcinoma, malignant melanoma.

(v)
Surgical approaches for antral tumours: medial maxillectomy; total maxillectomy; extended maxillectomy; palatal resection. Radiotherapy: used as primary treatment for small tumours, or as post-operative adjunct for large tumours; curative treatment may involve radiotherapy, surgery, or a combination. Chemotherapy: included in combination treatment; chemoradiation is an option. Rehabilitation is required post-maxillectomy (prosthetics, dental rehabilitation).

questions.question:
A 45-year-old woman, who is overweight, presents with recurrent bilateral headaches, intermittent pulsatile tinnitus in her right ear, and transient blurring of vision. On examination, fundoscopy shows bilateral papilloedema. Pressing on her right jugular vein relieves the tinnitus. Otoscopy is normal.
(i) State the most likely diagnosis and its diagnostic criteria.
(ii) Describe the clinical features that help confirm this diagnosis at the bedside and on examination, distinguishing them from features of a glomus tumour.
(iii) List the risk factors and categories of patients typically affected.
(iv) Describe the medical and surgical management of this condition in order of escalating intervention.
(v) Classify all causes of objective pulsatile tinnitus and describe how each category is investigated.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Benign intracranial hypertension (pseudotumor cerebri) syndrome. Diagnostic criteria: increased intracranial pressure with no focal neurological deficit except occasionally 6th or 7th nerve palsy; head imaging must rule out an intracranial lesion.

(ii)
Clinical features at the bedside: pulsatile tinnitus relieved by ipsilateral internal jugular vein digital pressure; possible blurred vision and light-headedness/disequilibrium; bilateral papilloedema on fundoscopy; no retrotympanic mass on otoscopy. Distinction from glomus tumour: in a glomus tympanicum, the bruit is NOT altered by neck pressure, head position, posture, or Valsalva; otoscopy reveals a bluish or reddish pulsatile mass that pales with positive pressure; CT shows a mass in the middle ear. In BIH, otoscopy is normal and jugular compression relieves the tinnitus.

(iii)
Risk factors and typical patients: females aged 20–50 years who are overweight; increased cardiac output states such as anaemia, thyrotoxicosis, and pregnancy are associated with venous hum (a related entity); in venous hum, gentle anterior neck pressure may relieve the tinnitus; head toward the uninvolved side decreases it, deep breathing and Valsalva increase it.

(iv)
Management in order of escalating intervention: weight loss; acetazolamide; furosemide; subarachnoid-peritoneal shunt; occasionally gastric bypass for weight reduction.

(v)
All causes of objective pulsatile tinnitus: vascular neoplasms — glomus jugulare and tympanicum (diagnosis: CT, arteriography, MRI; treatment usually surgical); arteriovenous malformations — developmental abnormalities, often larger than symptoms suggest, may enlarge rapidly and recur; posterior fossa occipital artery and transverse sinus AVM most common; carotid artery/cavernous sinus fistula from trauma (pulsatile tinnitus, papilloedema, bruit with thrill; heart rate slows with compression; treatment surgical, preceded by angiography with embolization; max benefit if surgery follows within 72 hours of embolization); venous hum — eddy currents in IJV, normal in children and young women, attributed to increased cardiac output; treated by reassurance and correcting the underlying cause; palatomyoclonus — irregular clicking sound 20–400 bpm, palatal musculature and Eustachian tube mucous membrane, diagnosed with Toynbee tube in ear canal, tympanogram movement synchronous with contraction; treatment — clonazepam, diazepam, or botulinum toxin for severe cases; idiopathic stapedial muscle spasm — rough rumbling sound triggered by external noises, variable intensity tympanometry to induce spasm, acoustic reflex shows prolonged increased impedance; treatment — clonazepam, diazepam, or surgical division of tendon as last resort.

questions.question:
A. Describe the gross anatomy of the tonsil under the following headings:
A(i) Position, muscles forming the tonsillar fossa, and its capsular attachment
A(ii) Blood supply — all arteries contributing to tonsillar vasculature
A(iii) Nerve supply and explain the basis of referred otalgia in tonsillitis
A(iv) Lymphatic drainage
B. Describe the classification of tonsillitis (by type and chronicity) and the criteria used to establish recurrent acute tonsillitis as an indication for surgery.
C. State the absolute and relative indications for tonsillectomy, its contraindications, and classify all its complications by timing, giving one example of each.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The palatine tonsil lies within a bed of three muscles: the palatoglossus (anterior pillar), the palatopharyngeus (posterior pillar), and the superior constrictor muscle (bed of the fossa). A dense collagenous hemi-capsule (the base) separates the tonsil from the underlying muscles. A capsule of connective tissue also separates the tonsil from the lateral pharyngeal walls. The point of attachment to the lingual tonsils is the plica triangularis, which must be transected during tonsillectomy.

A(ii)
Blood supply: the majority arises from the tonsillar branch of the facial artery; additional contributions from the ascending pharyngeal artery, the descending palatine artery, and the dorsal lingual branch of the lingual artery. The internal carotid artery lies just two centimetres posterolateral to the deep surface of the tonsil; in 1% of the population, it is found just deep to the superior constrictor muscle.

A(iii)
Nerve supply: from the ninth cranial nerve and descending branches from the lesser palatine nerves. The tympanic branch of CN IX (Jacobson's nerve) is thought to account for referred ear pain in tonsillitis, because CN IX has a branch to the middle ear (Jacobson's plexus).

A(iv)
Lymphatic drainage: the tonsils have no afferent lymphatic vessels; their efferent lymph drains through the upper cervical nodes, especially to the jugulodigastric group.

B.
Classification of tonsillitis: acute — parenchymatous, follicular, and membranous; recurrent acute; chronic (persistent); obstructive tonsillar hyperplasia. Criteria for establishing recurrent acute tonsillitis: 4–7 episodes of acute tonsillitis in one year; five episodes per year for two years; or three episodes per year in three consecutive years. The severity of infections and associated complications, as well as lost productivity or school absences, must also be considered.

C.
Absolute indications for tonsillectomy: severe dysphagia; failure to thrive; cor pulmonale. Relative indications: recurrent acute tonsillitis; chronic tonsillitis; obstructive sleep apnoea; peritonsillar abscess; suspected neoplasia; halitosis; elongated styloid process surgery; glossopharyngeal neurectomy; uvulopalatopharyngoplasty; unilateral tonsillar enlargement. Contraindications: recent URTI; haematological disorders. Complications by timing: immediate — haemorrhage, anaesthetic complications; intermediate — haemorrhage, haematoma and oedema of uvula, infection, pulmonary complications; late — subacute bacterial endocarditis, post-operative scarring, tonsillar remnants, eustachian tube stenosis, hypernasal speech (rhinolalia aperta), persistence of symptoms.

questions.question:
A. Describe the facial nerve (CN VII) under the following headings:
A(i) Embryological development
A(ii) Surgical anatomy: segments and their lengths from the facial nucleus to the extracranial portion
A(iii) Fibre types and their specific functions and distributions
A(iv) Anomalous course and its clinical significance
B. State the anatomical basis for the approach used to surgically explore the facial nerve, and identify the indications for surgical intervention.
C. Describe the anatomical basis for the deformity and dysfunction that follow complete infranuclear facial nerve paralysis, and explain why the eye is particularly at risk.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The facial nerve develops from the facioacoustic primordium. The chorda tympani and main trunk appear at the 4th week. At the 5th week the geniculate ganglion, nervus intermedius, and greater superficial petrosal nerve develop. Branching occurs extensively by the 11th week. The nerve is fully developed by the 3rd month.

A(ii)
Segments and lengths: facial nucleus (intracranial) 15–17 mm; meatal segment 10 mm; labyrinthine segment 2–4 mm; tympanic segment 11 mm; mastoid segment 13 mm; extracranial segment 15–20 mm from the stylomastoid foramen to the parotid.

A(iii)
The facial nerve contains motor, autonomic, and sensory fibres. Motor fibres supply: scalp, face, and auricula; buccinator muscle; platysma muscle; stapedius muscle; stylohyoid muscle; posterior belly of the digastric muscle. Autonomic motor fibres supply: vasodilatation and secretion of salivary glands (submaxillary gland, sublingual gland). Sensory fibres carry: taste for the anterior two-thirds of the tongue; sensation to the ear canal and behind the ear.

A(iv)
The most common anomaly is dehiscence of the facial canal. Common sites are the oval window and the geniculate ganglion. The exposed nerve is more susceptible to injury during otologic surgery.

B.
Surgical approach options are transmastoid, labyrinthine, or middle fossa. Indications for surgical exploration of the infranuclear nerve: EEM showing 25% or a sharp drop over three days with progression of paralysis; malignant otitis externa; iatrogenic or external trauma; CSOM with cholesteatoma; CN VII transection.

C.
Complete infranuclear paralysis produces: facial asymmetry; eyebrow droop and Bell's phenomenon; loss of forehead and nasolabial folds; drooping of the corner of the mouth; uncontrolled tearing; inability to close the eye; inability to hold the lips tightly together causing difficulty keeping food in the mouth; and late facial muscle atrophy. The eye is particularly at risk because the inability to close the eye (lagophthalmos) is caused by loss of the orbicularis oculi, which is supplied by CN VII. Once the nerve is transected it never attains normal function and produces permanent weakness or dysfunction. Surgical eye care indications are the BAD syndrome, and options include temporary tarsorrhaphy, spring or gold implant in the upper eyelid, and lower eyelid tightening procedures.

questions.question:
A 2-year-old child is brought with coughing, gagging, and wheezing after a meal. Chest X-ray in expiration shows mediastinal shift. The clinical team prepares for bronchoscopy.
(i) Describe the historical development of bronchoscopic removal of foreign bodies from the 19th century.
(ii) List the commonest types of foreign bodies aspirated in order, with their respective percentages.
(iii) What is the goal of endoscopic treatment, and list in full the preparations required before endoscopy is performed?
(iv) Describe the endoscopic technique including anaesthesia, ventilation mode, and instruments used; also describe the alternative short apnoeic technique.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Historical development:
• Prior to the 20th century, foreign body aspiration frequently resulted in death
• Gross advocated 'bronchotomy in all cases'
• Killian in 1897 performed the first bronchoscopic removal of a foreign body
• In the early 1900s, distal illumination was introduced
• Jackson revolutionised the field of bronchoesophagology
• In the 1970s, rod-lens telescopes were introduced.

(ii)
Commonest types of foreign bodies aspirated:
• Vegetable matter — 70–80%
• Peanuts and other nuts — 35%
• Carrot pieces, beans, sunflower and watermelon seeds
• Metallic objects
• Plastic objects.

(iii)
Goal of treatment: prompt endoscopic removal under conditions of maximal safety and minimal trauma. Preparations required: endoscopy is usually not a dire emergency; trained personnel must be present; instruments must be assembled and checked; await emptying of the stomach; find a duplicate foreign body to test instruments and techniques.

(iv)
Standard endoscopic procedure:
• General anaesthesia
• Spontaneous ventilation
• Laryngoscopy
• Bronchoscopy
• Suction
• Forceps
• Rod-lens telescopes.
Short apnoeic technique:
• Be ready to assume airway during induction
• Laryngoscopy
• Examination of the upper airway
• Atraumatic insertion of bronchoscope
• Topical anaesthesia
• Bronchoscopy.

questions.question:
A. Describe the aetiology of nasopharyngeal carcinoma under the following headings:
A(i) Genetic susceptibility factors, including HLA associations and chromosomal abnormalities
A(ii) Viral factors and the significance of EBV antibody titres
A(iii) Environmental factors and the epidemiology by geographic region, sex, and age
B. Describe the clinical features of NPC in terms of how lesion morphology (exophytic, ulcerative, infiltrative) produces the four presenting syndromes (rhinological, neuro-ophthalmological, otological, and cervical).
C. Describe the management of persistent and recurrent NPC after primary radiotherapy, covering options for the nasopharynx, neck, and distant metastases, including outcomes data.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Genetic factors: association of NPC with HLA-A2 and HLA-B Sin2 (rare in blacks and whites); chromosomal abnormalities of multiple chromosomes including 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 11, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 22, and X. HLA pattern and prognosis: AW19-B17 — short-term survival, mostly young-onset <30 years, high VCA/EA titres; A2-BW46 — intermediate-term survival; A2 without BW46 or B17 — long-term survival, low VCA/EA titres.

A(ii)
NPC cells express two species of EBV proteins. Plasma antibodies to viral capsid antigen (VCA) and to early antigens (EA) are seen; EA titres are a predictor of tumour relapse after radiotherapy.

A(iii)
Environmental factors: cooking habits; occupation; religious practices; diet; drugs; and others. Epidemiology: prevalent in South-East Asia, especially of Cantonese origin (boat people of Southern Hong Kong and Guangdong district of Singapore); age-standardized rate per 100,000 — males 29.4, females 10.8; also high in Malaysia, Taiwan, Eskimos in Alaska and Greenland, and Tunisians. Sex: male:female = 3:1. Age: bimodal peaks at 30–40 and 50–60 years.

B.
As defined by the lesion morphology (exophytic, ulcerative, or infiltrative), NPC presents in four ways: rhinological — nasal obstruction (most frequent, 80–90%), epistaxis (45–60%, mostly unilateral and recurrent; severe epistaxis necessitating medical attention warrants ruling out NPC in adolescent males), headache (25%, especially if paranasal sinuses are blocked), facial swelling (10–18%), unilateral rhinorrhoea, anosmia, hyposmia, rhinolalia. Otological — tinnitus, ear fullness, unilateral conductive hearing loss, otalgia; due to Eustachian tube blockage producing serous otitis media. Neuro-ophthalmological — in advanced cases: diplopia ± numbness of the face due to cranial nerve involvement; proptosis and optic nerve atrophy if orbital fissures are encroached upon; decreasing vision due to optic nerve tenting. Cervical — neck swelling (cervical metastasis evident in 44–57%, likely in 60–85%); HO denotes supraclavicular fossa involvement.

C.
Persistent or recurrent NPC: locoregional failure rate up to 15.6–58% (median 34%). Nasopharynx (failure rate 18–58%): re-irradiation options — brachytherapy, stereotactic radiotherapy; only 15–23% achieve disease-free survival; salvage nasopharyngectomy. Neck (regional failure 8–34%): re-irradiation local control rate 28–33%; radical neck dissection — local control rate up to 66%. Distant metastases (18–35%, lung > bone > liver): palliative chemotherapy, pain relief, symptom control, prolongation of life.

(i)
This is a lower motor neurone (infranuclear) facial nerve palsy. The term Bell's palsy denotes cases of lower motor neurone facial nerve paralysis for which no specific cause is identified. In upper motor neurone lesions (supranuclear), the forehead is spared because it has bilateral cortical representation; in infranuclear lesions all ipsilateral facial muscles including the forehead are paralysed. Supranuclear lesion sites: cortex and internal capsule (opercular syndrome, extrapyramidal, midbrain, or pontine nucleus). Infranuclear lesion sites: cerebellopontine angle, skull base, transtemporal (geniculate ganglion, tympanomastoid), and extracranial.

(ii)
Bell's palsy is idiopathic lower motor neurone facial nerve paralysis. Pathophysiology: the nerve is devastated both cosmetically and functionally; once transected it never attains normal function; it produces permanent weakness or dysfunction. Seddon classification (1943): neuropraxia (reversible conduction block); axonotmesis (loss of axon continuity with intact endoneurial sheath, allowing regrowth); neurotmesis (complete disruption). House-Brackmann grading: Grade I — normal; Grade II — slight; Grade III — moderate; Grade IV — moderately severe; Grade V — severe; Grade VI — complete.

(iii)
Clinical signs of complete infranuclear paralysis: facial asymmetry; eyebrow droop and Bell's phenomenon; loss of forehead and nasolabial folds; drooping of the corner of the mouth; uncontrolled tearing; inability to close the eye (lagophthalmos); inability to hold the lips tightly together causing difficulty keeping food in the mouth; late facial muscle atrophy.

(iv)
Investigations: electrophysiological tests (EMG and ENOG — ENOG requires the normal side for comparison; operate when ENOG shows 90% degeneration; EMG shows voluntary activity if prognosis is good; fibrillation potentials appear if nerve is out at 2 weeks); topognostic tests — Schirmer's test (lacrimal function, GSPN level), stapedial reflex (stapedius branch, mastoid segment), taste testing (chorda tympani level), salivary flow/pH (chorda tympani level); audiometry; E/U/A and muscle biopsy; radiological tests; general — FBC, ESR, FBS, E/U/C, serological tests, ear swabs.

(v)
Conservative treatment: physiotherapy — heat massage, facial exercise; psychophysical therapy; medications — steroids, antidepressants, antiviral agents, antibiotics. Eye care: voluntary intermittent eye closure; eye ointment/drops; eye moisture chamber; artificial tears; surgical eye care (indication — BAD syndrome) — temporary tarsorrhaphy; spring or gold implant in the upper eyelid; lower eyelid tightening procedure. Surgical correction of mouth deviation: reanimation procedures — fascia lata loop around the paralysed side; masseter muscle transposition plus fascia lata sling. Surgical management of infranuclear paralysis: indications — EEM 25% or sharp drop over three days with progression; malignant otitis externa; iatrogenic/external trauma; CSOM with cholesteatoma; CN VII transection; approaches — transmastoid, labyrinthine, middle fossa; method of repair — approximation (rule of 10), graft from greater auricular or sural nerve, re-routing, facial animation. Complications and treatment: hemifacial spasm and synkinesis — botulinum toxin; blepharospasm — orbital muscle decompression; extrusion of gold weight.
questions.question:
A 28-year-old man presents to the emergency department with facial asymmetry noticed on waking. He has complete inability to close his right eye, loss of the right nasolabial fold, drooping of the right corner of the mouth, and loss of the right forehead wrinkle. There is no history of trauma, otitis media, or parotid disease. He reports mild pain behind the right ear.

questions.answerText:
(i)
Diagnosis: Retropharyngeal abscess. Lateral neck X-ray features: widening of the retropharyngeal soft tissues was observed in 88% of patients, defined as more than 7 mm at C2 and more than 14 mm at C6; the anteroposterior diameter of the prevertebral soft tissue space in children should not exceed that of the contiguous vertebral bodies. The lateral neck X-ray may also rarely show a gas–fluid level, gas in the tissues, or a foreign body.

(ii)
CT scan: RPA appears as a hypodense lesion in the retropharyngeal space with peripheral ring enhancement. A CT scan of the neck with IV contrast is very useful in diagnosis and management. A chest X-ray is indicated to look for aspiration pneumonia and mediastinitis.

(iii)
The mean WBC count was 17,000, with a range of 3,100–45,900. WBC counts in 18% of patients were less than 8,000; thus, a normal WBC count does not rule out the diagnosis of RPA. Blood cultures are indicated before administration of IV antibiotics but may be negative. A culture of pus aspirated at the time of surgical drainage can grow out one or more organisms in 91% of cases.

(iv)
Complications include: atlantooccipital dislocation; adult respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS); erosion of the second and third cervical vertebrae; cranial nerve deficits (cranial nerves IX–XII are contained in the cervical fascia); septic thrombosis of the jugular vein or haemorrhage secondary to erosion into the carotid artery. Jugular vein thrombophlebitis may manifest as tender induration at the anterior sternocleidomastoid border, vocal cord paralysis, or sepsis of unknown source. Carotid artery rupture can be heralded by sentinel bleeding from the ear, nose, or mouth, and ecchymosis may be detected in the lateral neck.
questions.question:
A 10-year-old child presents with a posterior pharyngeal bulge, high fever, neck stiffness, and odynophagia. A lateral soft tissue neck X-ray is taken and a CT scan with IV contrast is requested.

questions.answerText:
(i)
The voice disorder described is dysphonia, defined as a functional overadduction of the vocal cords giving rise to a harsh strident voice.

(ii)
The four main categories of speech disorders are:
• Voice — related to respiration, phonation, and resonance; this includes disorders of pitch (too high or too low for age or sex), loudness (habitually loud or soft), and quality.
• Articulation — related to articulatory processes in the vocal tract; may present as inconsistent error of one speech sound, and may be due to structural anomalies or neurological impairment as in cerebral palsy.
• Fluency — related to co-ordination; includes stuttering or stammering with involuntary repetitions, prolongations, and hesitations, due to physiological problems or laryngeal dysfunction.
• Language — related to proper adequate symbolization in the brain; involves reception and comprehension, and may result from emotional disturbance, neurological impairment, or developmental causes. The two specific aphonia-producing conditions under quality/phonation are: (I) completely abducted vocal folds; (II) previous total laryngectomy — in which case the speech therapist needs to teach the patient oesophageal voice.

(iii)
Hypernasality (rhinolalia aperta): occurs with poor velopharyngeal closure, as in some cases of submucosal cleft after adenoidectomy or in obvious cleft palate with or without adenoid removal. Hyponasality (rhinolalia clausa): the nasal cavity may be blocked anteriorly or posteriorly.

(iv)
Management: take a good history and perform clinical examination to elucidate the possible causes of the various types of voice disorders. Perform indirect laryngoscopy looking for polyps, nodes, degree of approximation of vocal cords, and other abnormalities. Examine other areas of ear, nose, and throat for other pathologies. Assess neurological status. Order appropriate investigations. Treat any organic cause. If there is no improvement, or if the need arises, send the patient to a speech therapist or pathologist.
questions.question:

A 15-year-old female presents with a 9-month history of progressive left-sided nasal obstruction and unilateral, mucopurulent nasal discharge that is occasionally blood-tinged. CT scan reveals a single soft-tissue-density polypoidal lesion extending from the left maxillary sinus through the left nasal cavity towards the ipsilateral posterior choana.
(i) State the specific diagnosis, and describe its three anatomical parts.
(ii) List the proposed aetiological theories for this condition.
(iii) Describe the macroscopic and histological appearances.
(iv) Outline the management, distinguishing medical from surgical treatment.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Antrochoanal (Killian's) polyp. Three anatomical parts (trilobed): antral part (within the maxillary sinus), nasal part (within the nasal cavity), and choanal part (extending to the choana/nasopharynx).

(ii)
Proposed aetiological theories: infective aetiology, allergic aetiology, mixed aetiology, Bernoulli phenomenon, polysaccharide changes of ground substance, vasomotor imbalance.

(iii)
Macroscopic: single unilateral lesion, similar in appearance to ethmoidal polyp but mass may be grey-coloured and covered with mucous nasal discharge. Histology: essentially similar to ethmoidal polyp — ciliated columnar or squamous/transitional metaplastic epithelium; submucosa with large intercellular spaces filled with serous fluid; scanty blood vessels and nerve fibres; eosinophils and round cells.

(iv)
Medical: in early stages — antihistamines, decongestants with or without antibiotics; corticosteroids for patients intolerant of antihistamines or those with associated asthma; control of allergy where necessary. Surgical: FESS (functional endoscopic sinus surgery) is current practice and treatment of choice; nasal polypectomy; ethmoidectomy (intranasal, extranasal, or transantral approach). Note: the polyp may be missed on anterior rhinoscopy if it has grown posteriorly; posterior rhinoscopy is required.

(i)
Corrosive esophagitis. In children, ingestion is most frequently accidental, particularly in those from families with low income.

(ii)
Three phases:
• Acute necrotic phase (day 1–4): cell death by coagulation of intracellular protein; intense inflammatory reaction, thrombosis, bacterial and haemorrhagic infiltration.
• Ulcerative granulation phase (day 3–5 onward): necrotic tissue sloughs, ulcerated inflamed base remains; new blood vessels and fibroblasts appear; collagenous connective tissue develops from day 10–12.
• Cicatrization and stricture formation (week 3–4 onward): collagenous tissue contracts causing narrowing; degeneration of muscle and nerve tissue; re-epithelialization at 4 weeks to 3 months; greatest clinical vigilance required for stricture signs during this period.

(iii)
Acute management: assess and treat dyspnoea, dysphagia, bleeding, ulceration, necrosis and perforation; nasogastric suction; broad-spectrum antibiotics to reduce infective complications; close observation for perforation signs; plain chest and abdominal radiograph to rule out pneumomediastinum or pneumoperitoneum; upper GI endoscopy (gold standard).

(iv)
Primary treatment is esophageal dilatation. Esophagectomy with colonic interposition is required for patients with severe strictures (Grade 4: tubular stricture with dense fibrotic walls, periesophageal adhesions and marked luminal narrowing; epithelium cannot rebridge the gap).

(v)
In the long term (average onset 40 years after injury), carcinoma of the esophagus is a major hazard; the risk is 1000 to 3000 times the expected risk.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
The endolarynx and hypopharynx are subdivided into: pyriform sinus; pharyngeal wall; post-cricoid region.

A(ii)
Factors considered in radical vs. palliative treatment: spread (loco-regional/metastatic spread); radiosensitivity/chemosensitivity; histology (including differentiation); clearance of surgical resection margins; age and general condition (physical and mental); morbidity and mortality; function and cosmetics; reliability of follow-up after treatment; preference of patient; and technical expertise.

B(i)
Hyperfractionated radiotherapy and chemo-radiotherapy are advanced techniques used in ENT malignancies, particularly for tumours with certain radiosensitivity profiles.

B(ii)
A Consultant Radiotherapist and Oncologist is both a physician and a technical specialist; hence clinical and technical factors must be balanced to adequately plan radiotherapy. Discussion about treatment is made by specialists and the primary physician without the patient in attendance, to prevent the patient from being intimidated. The multidisciplinary approach also ensures that the timing of different modalities is properly synchronized, that patients have access to advice from different specialists, and that the patient is more reassured that all treatment options have been considered.
questions.question:
Describe how the endolarynx and hypopharynx are subdivided in the context of radiotherapy planning, and explain the factors considered in radical versus palliative treatment decisions; then outline special techniques used in radiotherapy.
A(i) State how the endolarynx and hypopharynx are subdivided in ENT oncology.
A(ii) State the factors considered in the choice between radical and palliative radiotherapy treatment in clinical assessment.
B(i) Define hyperfractionated radiotherapy and chemo-radiotherapy as advanced techniques.
