Fecal fat excretion greater than 7 grams per day defines steatorrhea indicating significant fat malabsorption. This threshold represents pathological fat excretion requiring clinical evaluation. Values this high usually cause noticeable symptoms.
questions.question: Steatorrhea is defined as fecal fat excretion exceeding what amount?

options: The highest dose not producing toxic signs
The dose achieving peak plasma levels
questions.question: Maximum tolerated dose (MTD) in drug safety assessment indicates:
questions.explanation: MTD (also called highest non-toxic dose or minimum toxic dose) represents the largest dose tolerated without producing signs of toxicity, defining the upper boundary of the therapeutic window. The ratio MTD/MED indicates therapeutic window width. Narrow windows require careful dose titration.

questions.question: Where does bacterial conversion of conjugated bilirubin to urobilinogen occur
questions.explanation: Bacterial enzymes in the terminal ileum hydrolyze conjugated bilirubin to stercobilinogen and reduce it to urobilinogen. Some urobilinogen undergoes enterohepatic circulation while the remainder is excreted in feces as stercobilin or absorbed and excreted in urine. This process gives stool its characteristic brown color.

questions.question: What clinical sign presents as cracks at the corners of the mouth?
questions.explanation: Cheilosis (angular cheilitis) appears as painful fissures and cracks at the mouth corners in riboflavin deficiency. The condition results from impaired epithelial cell renewal and secondary bacterial or fungal infection. Associated features include red, inflamed lips and seborrheic dermatitis around the nose.

questions.question: What determines whether porphyria presents with neurological versus cutaneous symptoms?
questions.explanation: The location of the enzyme defect in the heme synthesis pathway determines clinical presentation: early defects cause precursor accumulation with neurotoxicity, while late defects cause porphyrin accumulation with photosensitivity. Some defects (Hereditary Coproporphyria, Variegate Porphyria) occur at intermediate positions, producing both neurological and cutaneous manifestations. The biochemical pattern directly determines the clinical syndrome.

Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) is synthesized in the supraoptic nucleus of the hypothalamus and transported along neuronal axons for storage in the posterior pituitary. Upon appropriate stimulation, ADH is released directly into the bloodstream from posterior pituitary nerve terminals. This neurohormone then acts on distal renal tubules to regulate water reabsorption and maintain plasma osmolality within normal limits.
questions.question: Where is antidiuretic hormone synthesized before posterior pituitary storage?
What reagent oxidizes cyanide in the spectrophotometric color reaction?
questions.explanation: Chloramine-T is added along with pyridine and barbituric acid to generate the red color complex in spectrophotometric cyanide determination. This oxidizing agent facilitates the reaction between cyanide and the other reagents. The sequence and timing of reagent additions critically affect color development and sensitivity.

Exercise-induced cramping in myopathy reflects insufficient energy production needed for muscle relaxation, as ATP is required for both contraction and relaxation. When energy production mechanisms fail, muscles cannot properly relax after contraction leading to cramping. This symptom is particularly prominent in metabolic myopathies affecting energy metabolism.
questions.question: Muscle cramping during exercise in myopathy primarily indicates dysfunction in which process?

questions.explanation: Urobilinogen is the colorless tetrapyrrole compound formed when intestinal bacteria reduce unconjugated bilirubin. This reduction occurs primarily in the colon where anaerobic bacteria are abundant. Urobilinogen undergoes further reduction to stercobilinogen and mesobilinogen or may be reabsorbed for enterohepatic circulation.
questions.question: What colorless compound is formed from intestinal bilirubin reduction?
Why are heme biosynthetic enzyme assays challenging?
questions.explanation: Heme biosynthetic enzyme assays pose unique challenges due to substrate instability, fluorescence of both substrate and product, and enzyme distribution between cytoplasm and mitochondria. Porphyrin precursors spontaneously oxidize, requiring careful handling and storage. Mitochondrial enzymes require tissue biopsies rather than blood samples, limiting clinical applicability.

questions.question: What distinguishes hyperpituitarism from hypopituitarism?
questions.explanation: Hyperpituitarism involves hormone overproduction, contrasting with hypopituitarism's hormone deficiencies. Overproduction typically results from pituitary adenomas secreting excess hormones. Clinical manifestations depend on which hormone is overproduced.

The ampulla of Vater is alternatively called the hepatopancreatic ampulla reflecting its role in delivering both hepatic and pancreatic secretions. This confluence point is regulated by the sphincter of Oddi. The anatomical arrangement optimizes digestive secretion coordination.
questions.question: The ampulla of Vater is also known by which alternative name?
Life-threatening hyperkalemia can progress to which fatal cardiac arrhythmia?
questions.explanation: Severe hyperkalemia depolarizes cardiac cell membranes, predisposing to ventricular fibrillation and cardiac arrest. Progressive ECG changes culminate in sine wave patterns that degenerate into ventricular fibrillation requiring immediate defibrillation. The narrow margin between asymptomatic hyperkalemia and fatal arrhythmias mandates urgent treatment at potassium levels exceeding 6.5 mmol/L.

Bacterial enzymes in the terminal ileum deconjugate and dehydroxylate conjugated bilirubin, converting it to urobilinogen and stercobilinogen. Some urobilinogen undergoes enterohepatic circulation while the remainder is excreted. This bacterial action is essential for bilirubin metabolism completion.
questions.question: What is the primary site of conjugated bilirubin deconjugation

questions.explanation: Ketolactic acidosis and hypoglycemia develop in severe biotin deficiency from impaired gluconeogenesis and carboxylation reactions. Reduced pyruvate carboxylase activity prevents glucose synthesis from pyruvate and lactate. Accumulation of organic acids causes metabolic acidosis requiring urgent biotin replacement.
questions.question: What metabolic crisis can occur in severe biotin deficiency?
What role do bile acids play in gallstone prevention?
questions.explanation: Bile acids solubilize cholesterol in bile by forming mixed micelles with phospholipids and cholesterol. When the ratio of cholesterol to bile acids exceeds solubilizing capacity, cholesterol precipitates. Adequate bile acid concentration prevents stone formation by maintaining cholesterol in solution.

questions.question: The protein deficient in Duchenne dystrophy primarily functions to perform which role?
questions.explanation: Dystrophin attaches the contractile apparatus to the muscle membrane, providing structural integrity during contraction. Without this anchoring protein, muscle contractions cause progressive membrane damage and fiber death. The attachment function is critical for maintaining muscle fiber integrity.

Vitamin K prophylaxis at birth prevents hemorrhagic disease of the newborn from physiological deficiency. Neonates have minimal vitamin K stores, no intestinal bacterial synthesis initially, and low breast milk content. The single intramuscular injection provides adequate vitamin K for coagulation factor production.
questions.question: Which vitamin is given to all newborns to prevent hemorrhagic disease?
Through which receptor mechanism do barbiturates exert their central nervous system effects?
questions.explanation: Barbiturates function by enhancing the action of gammα-aminobutyric acid (GABA) through binding to specific sites on the GABA A receptor/chloride channel complex. This mechanism is shared with benzodiazepines, though the binding sites differ between the two drug classes. The enhancement of GABAergic transmission produces the characteristic central nervous system depressant effects ranging from mild sedation to general anesthesia.

Drugs excreted in bile enter the intestinal lumen where bacterial enzymes may deconjugate them, enabling reabsorption and return to the liver via portal circulation, creating a recycling loop. This process significantly prolongs elimination half-life and drug effects. Oral adsorbents like cholestyramine can interrupt this cycle to enhance elimination.
questions.question: Enterohepatic recirculation prolongs drug presence in the body by:

questions.question: Methanol-induced blindness results from specific toxicity to which anatomical structure?
questions.explanation: Formic acid causes optic neuropathy through direct toxicity to optic nerve tissue, potentially resulting in permanent blindness even with survival. questions.question: What organs are primarily affected in liver forms of glycogen storage diseases?
questions.explanation: Liver forms (Types I, III, IV, VI) present with hepatomegaly and symptomatic hypoglycemia. There is increased glucagon response and decreased insulin response. These forms affect glucose homeostasis and liver function.

questions.question: Renal impairment necessitates dose adjustment primarily because of compromised:
questions.explanation: Reduced glomerular filtration and tubular function in renal disease impairs drug elimination, causing accumulation of renally cleared drugs and active metabolites with increased toxicity risk. Dose reduction or interval extension maintains therapeutic levels while preventing toxic accumulation. Creatinine clearance guides adjustment magnitude.

questions.question: What happens to ALT levels with weight loss in fatty liver disease
questions.explanation: ALT levels decline with weight loss in non-alcoholic fatty liver disease as hepatic steatosis improves. Both ALT and AST are elevated in obese patients with fatty liver infiltration. Weight reduction through diet and exercise improves hepatocellular injury markers.

Once normal osmolality is achieved, the sensation of thirst is removed, preventing excessive water intake and maintaining precise homeostatic control.

questions.question: What compounds result from heat-alkali hydrolysis of long-acting barbiturates?
questions.explanation: Long- and intermediate-acting barbiturates undergo hydrolytic breakdown in hot alkaline conditions to yield malonic acid and urea as degradation products. The extent of hydrolysis, measured by decreased UV absorbance, serves as a classification tool in barbiturate analysis.

questions.question: What percentage of resting cardiac output does the liver receive
questions.explanation: The liver receives approximately 25% of resting cardiac output, similar to the kidneys, reflecting its high metabolic activity. questions.question: Why are newborns particularly susceptible to kernicterus?
questions.explanation: Newborns have immature hepatic glucuronyl transferase systems that cannot adequately conjugate bilirubin, leading to unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia. Premature infants are especially vulnerable due to even less enzyme development. When unconjugated bilirubin exceeds albumin binding capacity, free bilirubin crosses the blood-brain barrier causing kernicterus.

questions.question:
A patient after major abdominal surgery on the ward is receiving PCA morphine and a thoracic epidural infusion.
(a) Describe the assessment of this patient.
(b) State the expected complications and their signs.
(c) Outline the nursing care and monitoring plan.
(d) State the level-of-care considerations and handover.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Pain scores are documented on a numerical or visual analogue scale at rest and on movement (WILDA: words, intensity, location, duration, aggravating/alleviating factors); assess sedation, nausea and vomiting and the height of the epidural block; most pain is self-limiting with analgesic requirements falling by 48 hours, even after major surgery.
(b)
Opioid effects: respiratory depression, sedation and cough suppression, nausea and vomiting, reduced peristalsis (constipation, ileus, urinary retention); epidural: hypotension, weakness, urinary retention; onset of severe weakness and back pain may indicate epidural haematoma or abscess and needs urgent investigation (MRI); unrelieved pain can cause low lung volumes, retained secretions, pneumonia and increased DVT risk.
(c)
• PCA gives a patient-pressed bolus of morphine (nurse-controlled analgesia when the patient cannot use the handset); epidural infusion contains LA (e.g. bupivacaine) and opioid (e.g. fentanyl); multimodal opioid-sparing analgesia with regular rather than as-required doses.
• Monitor pulse, blood pressure and respiratory rate plus sedation (excess opioid), nausea and vomiting, leg weakness and block height, using hospital scoring systems; high pain scores need intervention and reassessment; antiemetics are combined (prochlorperazine, ondansetron, dexamethasone); an early warning score of 3 triggers senior review.
(d)
• Patients need an environment where appropriate observation and intervention can be done: elderly patients with a thoracic epidural infusion may require level 1 care (high dependency); levels run 0 ward, 1 HDU, 2 and 3 ICU.
• Handover includes the analgesia given, regional or nerve blocks and use of local anaesthetic infiltration, antiemetics, antibiotics and thromboprophylaxis; heparin timing is balanced against postoperative bleeding risk, especially if an epidural is in situ.

questions.question:
A patient is scheduled for surgery below the level of the umbilicus under spinal anaesthesia.
(a) Describe the anaesthetic technique, the needle and the drug preparation used.
(b) State the monitoring, equipment and set-up required.
(c) Outline the nursing responsibilities and the positioning of the patient.
(d) Explain how complications of the technique are prevented and recognised.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Central blockade gives anaesthesia for surgery below the umbilicus (T10); the spinal needle is introduced at or below the L2/L3 interspace (Tuffier's line, L4/5, is a landmark); narrow-gauge (25 or 27G) blunt pencil-point needles separate the dural fibres and reduce CSF-leak headache; LA ampoules often contain dextrose so the solution is heavy (hyperbaric) and sinks, while plain LA is hypobaric.
(b)
Full aseptic technique with gloves, gown, mask and cap; IV access is needed (no IV access is a contraindication); ECG, pulse oximeter and non-invasive blood pressure are applied before induction and continued until recovery; all anaesthetic and monitoring equipment is checked before use and alarm limits set with audible alarms enabled.
(c)
• The anaesthetic nurse must be present and care for the patient throughout and record a summary of monitoring information on the anaesthetic record; the patient sits or lies on their side with the back curled forward to widen the intervertebral spaces; with the patient on their side, heavy LA affects the dependent side more.
• The affected extremity is positioned in proper alignment with pressure points padded to decrease the possibility of compression injury.
(d)
• Repeated syringe aspiration on injecting LA prevents inadvertent intravenous injection; contraindications are screened: patient refusal, no IV access, severe CVS disease, hypovolaemia, sepsis, LA allergy, coagulopathy (INR below 1.5).
• Side effects to watch for: hypotension (sympathetic block), nausea and vomiting, lower limb motor block, post dural puncture headache (reduced by pencil-point needles), high block affecting upper limb power and respiration (C3-5), loss of consciousness (total spinal) and rare nerve damage, which should be discussed with the patient.
• Maternal hypotension after regional anaesthesia is managed by elevating the legs and turning the mother to a side-lying position.

(a)
• ALS is a continuum of BLS and a standardised approach to cardiac arrest management, enabling treatment without protracted discussion so each team member can predict and prepare for the next stage; it emphasises good CPR and early defibrillation.
• Steps: check for danger; check response (hand on forehead, shake shoulders, shout); shout for help; check breathing and pulse for 10 seconds; start CPR 30:2, swapping rescuers every 2 minutes; when help arrives a senior takes control while CPR continues and the defibrillator is prepared.
• Pads: white lead under the right clavicle, red lead at the apex; the defibrillator in shock-advisory mode analyses the rhythm; if shockable warn everyone to stand clear and shock, then do CPR for another two minutes regardless of the outcome and repeat the analysis.
(b)
• Shockable rhythms are VF and pulseless VT; non-shockable are asystole (no electrical activity) and PEA (organised electrical activity without palpable pulses); the principal difference is the attempt at defibrillation in VF/VT.
• Shockable: first shock 150 to 200 J biphasic and 150 to 360 J subsequent (monophasic 360 J), CPR 30:2 for 2 minutes between shocks, after the third shock adrenaline 1 mg IV and amiodarone 300 mg IV, further adrenaline after alternate shocks (every 3 to 5 minutes), with an additional 150 mg amiodarone possible.
• Non-shockable: CPR 30:2, adrenaline 1 mg IV/IO as soon as access is achieved and every 3 to 5 minutes, recheck rhythm every 2 minutes (change to the shockable side if VF/VT); in asystole check for P waves because pacing may help ventricular standstill.
(c)
• Minimise interruptions, give 100% oxygen, obtain IV or IO access, consider airway adjuncts without stopping CPR for more than five seconds, use waveform capnography to confirm airway placement and monitor CPR adequacy, with compressions at least 5 cm deep at 100 to 120 per minute.
• Adrenaline causes alpha-mediated vasoconstriction directing output to myocardium and brain; amiodarone is an antiarrhythmic; vasopressin is a vasopressor; there is no evidence that routinely giving other drugs (buffers, aminophylline, atropine, calcium, magnesium) increases survival.
(d)
• Reversible causes: hypoxia, hypovolaemia, electrolyte disturbances (hyperkalaemia 5.5 mmol/L or more, hypokalaemia under 3.5), hypothermia (severe below 32 deg C), tension pneumothorax, cardiac tamponade, drug toxicity and thromboembolism.
• Signs of life include gasping or normal breathing, pupillary response and movements during CPR.
• Post-resuscitation care after ROSC: ABCDE re-evaluation, 12-lead ECG and chest X-ray, assess perfusion and consider reperfusion therapy, confirm oxygenation and ventilation (advanced airway may be needed), targeted temperature management and investigate reversible causes.
• Survival after asystole or PEA is unlikely unless a reversible cause is treated quickly.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Local anaesthetics are weak bases divided by the linkage between an aromatic ring and an amine group: esters (cocaine, procaine, amethocaine) - allergy common, metabolized by plasma and liver cholinesterase; amides (bupivacaine, lidocaine, prilocaine, ropivacaine) - allergy rare, metabolized by the liver.
(b)
They reversibly inhibit action potential transmission by blocking sodium channels of nerve cell membranes and preventing sodium influx; only the non-polar form crosses the membrane and the polar form inside blocks the channel; sensory fibres are blocked before motor; onset relates to the unionized fraction (pKa), so lidocaine (7.9) acts faster than bupivacaine (8.1) and bicarbonate speeds onset; protein-bound LAs last longer, vasoconstrictors (epinephrine, felypressin) prolong action, and potency relates to lipid solubility.
(c)
Uses: local infiltration, topical to mucous membranes, spinal and epidural, minor and major nerve blocks, IV regional anaesthesia (Bier's block with prilocaine or lidocaine), lidocaine for ventricular tachycardia, EMLA to skin, and reducing discomfort of propofol injection.
(d)
• Allergy is common with esters (especially procaine, via para-aminobenzoic acid), very rare with amides (more likely due to additives); excess prilocaine causes methaemoglobinaemia (treated with methylene blue).
• Toxicity arises from membrane stabilization of CNS and heart through excess dose or a wrong route: circumoral tingling, feeling of impending doom, dysrhythmias, CVS collapse, loss of consciousness, convulsions and cardiac arrest.
(e)
• Maximum safe dose of lidocaine is 3 mg/kg (7 mg/kg with epinephrine; bupivacaine is unchanged); mepivacaine adult maximum 400 mg (500 mg with epinephrine), paediatric 5 to 6 mg/kg; LA with a vasoconstrictor is never used in areas with terminal arterial supply (digits, penis) because necrosis can result.
• Administer slowly in small incremental doses with frequent aspiration before and during injection; absorption rate is mucous membranes > intercostals > major nerve block > infiltration; chloroprocaine ampoules are inspected (no discoloured or particulate solution), not heated or autoclaved, used immediately once opened and the unused portion discarded.
• Assess allergies, hepatic and renal impairment and baseline vital signs; lidocaine IV push is 25 mg/minute, used with caution in hepatic disease (effect prolonged), and not used in severe heart block, Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome, Stokes-Adam syndrome or allergy; no eating or drinking for 1 hour after oral lidocaine.
• Procaine doses are reduced in elderly, debilitated, cardiac and liver disease; it is contraindicated with hypersensitivity to ester LAs or PABA and for spinal use in septicaemia and CSF diseases such as syphilis and meningitis.
(f)
• Consciousness is monitored after each injection because restlessness, anxiety, tinnitus, dizziness, blurred vision, tremors, depression or drowsiness are early warnings of CNS toxicity; if a patient on lidocaine appears upset or agitated consider toxicity (therapeutic level 1.5 to 5 mcg/ml; stopping the infusion drops levels in 10 to 20 minutes); overdose signs include nervousness, double vision, tremors and confusion.
• BP, cardiac monitor, neurological and respiratory status are monitored; airway and ventilation equipment is prepared, and temperature and jaw spasm or rigidity are monitored for malignant hyperthermia with dantrolene on standby.
(g)
Treatment is supportive: airway maintenance or tracheal intubation, IV fluids and vasopressors (e.g. epinephrine), seizure control with benzodiazepines, thiopental or propofol, and CPR if cardiac arrest occurs; intravenous lipid emulsion (Intralipid 20%, 1.5 mL/kg) is recommended for LA toxicity or cardiovascular collapse; recovery can take more than an hour so CPR may be prolonged.
questions.question:
Discuss local anaesthetic drugs.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Defibrillation is the administration of electric shocks to the heart to reset normal rhythm in persons in cardiac arrest or whose heart function is endangered by severe arrhythmia; a defibrillator is a device that uses electricity to re-start the heart or shock it back into a normal rhythm and checks the heart rhythm to decide whether a shock is needed.
(b)
• Automated external defibrillators (AEDs): electrode pads detect irregularities, identify ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia and shock to restore pulse; used at home, schools and public places, lightweight and portable, without a prescription.
• Advanced life support defibrillators: heavy-duty machines used by medical professionals and paramedics (older models used paddles), often in ambulances, that also monitor blood pressure and carbon monoxide levels.
• Implantable cardioverter-defibrillators (ICDs): implanted beneath the collarbone with wires to the heart, shock if an irregular heartbeat is detected, newer models also pace, for patients with recurring irregularities or heart failure.
• Manual external defibrillators: used by technicians with extensive training, connected to an ECG, the user selects the shock and time; wearable defibrillators (WCDs): vests worn under clothes, sensors detect ventricular arrhythmia and shock automatically, the external removable version of an ICD for patients needing support for a shorter period.
(c)
• Check breathing and pulse; if none, call emergency help (one person calls 112 while the other prepares the AED; if alone call first); turn on the AED and follow voice instructions for pad position on the bare chest.
• The AED measures the rhythm and, if a shock is needed, tells the user to stand back and push the button (it will not shock if not needed); begin CPR after the shock if still needed and repeat until emergency crews take over.
(d)
• Nursing responsibilities: hand hygiene; confirm identity with at least two patient identifiers; gloves and standard precautions; assess that the patient is unresponsive and not breathing (or only gasping); monitor vital signs especially blood pressure, heart rate and rhythm.
• Ensure paddles do not touch the patient's clothing or bed linen; maintain safety of the caregiver since electric current can be conducted from one patient to another individual; ensure the defibrillator is not in synchronized mode; do not charge the device until ready to shock; administer emergency medication as indicated.
• In ALS practice pads go below the right clavicle (white lead) and at the apex (red lead), everyone is warned to stand clear before the shock, and CPR continues for two minutes after a shock; biphasic default initial energy is 200 J and monophasic 360 J.
(e)
• An AED detects the rhythm and decides whether a shock is needed, with step-by-step voice instructions, so it can be used in public places; a manual external defibrillator requires the user to select the shock and administer it at their own designated time and does not automatically detect the heartbeat or select the voltage.
• Manual machines are usually connected to an ECG that gives a more accurate, timely view of heart activity than AEDs and allow the shock to be customised, making them a good option for babies in cardiac arrest.
questions.question:
Discuss the defibrillator.
(a) Define defibrillation and defibrillator.
(b) Describe the five main types of defibrillator.
(c) State the steps in using an automated external defibrillator.
(d) List the nursing responsibilities in the use of a defibrillator and the safety points for shock delivery.

A patient who had major upper abdominal surgery and is receiving postoperative opioids has a low oxygen saturation on room air in the postoperative period.
(a) Describe the assessment in the recovery unit.
(b) State the expected complications and their signs.
(c) Outline the nursing care and monitoring plan.
(d) State the level-of-care and discharge considerations and handover.
questions.answerText:
(a)
After sedation, patients breathing room air have varying hypoxaemia because raised arterial CO2 lowers alveolar O2; the effect is short lived for peripheral surgery (under 30 minutes) but more prolonged (over 3 days) after major upper abdominal or thoracic surgery, especially with postoperative opioids (e.g. PCA); assess saturation, and use an early warning score (CNS, respiratory rate, heart rate, systolic BP, temperature, SaO2, urine output).
(b)
Hazards of hypoxaemia: CNS (cerebral ischaemia, confusion, postoperative cognitive dysfunction); CVS (myocardial ischaemia and infarction, arrhythmias); reduced wound healing and increased postoperative infection; opioids cause apnoea, respiratory depression and sedation; unrelieved pain leads to low lung volumes, retained secretions, lung collapse and pneumonia.
(c)
• Oxygen therapy is not required if saturations are normal on air; fixed-performance devices (Venturi) supply a known concentration and must match peak inspiratory flow (over 30 L/min); variable-performance devices (simple face masks, nasal prongs) give an unknown concentration.
• A score of 3 (or 3 in a single category) triggers senior review and repeat scoring assesses interventions; multimodal regular analgesia with sedation monitoring; IV fluids until the patient can drink (maintenance about 2.5 L/day), with a 250 mL colloid fluid challenge if urine output is low or the patient hypotensive.
(d)
Level of care: 0 ward, 1 HDU (at risk of deterioration), 2 ICU (single failing organ system), 3 ICU (ventilation or two organ systems); unplanned ICU admission may follow major blood loss, sepsis or an exacerbation such as MI; recovery discharge needs airway reflexes, no or minimal pain, nausea and bleeding, and normothermia, with handover of technique, analgesia, blocks, antiemetics, antibiotics and thromboprophylaxis.

questions.question:
A pregnant woman at term is scheduled for a lower segment Caesarean section (LSCS).
(a) Describe the preoperative assessment and the risks identified.
(b) State the nursing problems or nursing diagnoses that arise.
(c) Outline the preoperative preparation and nursing interventions, giving the rationale for each.
(d) Explain the patient education, consent and safety checks required.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• About 20% of deliveries need LSCS; pregnancy changes include increased cardiac output and workload, risk of aortocaval compression, difficult tracheal intubation (e.g. upper airway oedema), reduced FRC with tendency to hypoxia, dilutional anaemia, hypercoagulability and risk of oesophageal reflux; the position of the placenta should be known because low-lying anterior placentae may cause massive blood loss.
• Leading obstetric risks include sepsis, thrombosis and thromboembolism, pre-eclampsia and eclampsia, haemorrhage and amniotic fluid embolism; a GA carries much greater risk in late pregnancy (difficult or failed intubation, hypoxia, aspiration).
(b)
Problems identified: risk of aspiration, aortocaval compression with hypotension, risk of massive haemorrhage and difficult or failed intubation if GA is needed.
(c)
• Full blood count and group and save, with O negative blood on hand for urgent resuscitation; antacid prophylaxis (usually H2 antagonists and 30 mL 0.3 M sodium citrate); left lateral tilt or wedge to minimise aortocaval compression.
• Regional anaesthesia is preferred as safer for mother and baby: an indwelling epidural can be topped up (about 20 minutes to become effective) or a single-shot spinal used (lasts 1 to 1.5 hours); if GA is required: skilled assistance, tipping table, good suction, one or two peripheral cannulae, preoxygenation, full monitoring, rapid sequence induction with cricoid pressure, and a variety of airway devices including a cricothyroidotomy set at hand.
(d)
• Benefits of regional anaesthesia explained: avoids risks of GA (failed intubation, aspiration, neonatal depression, awareness), good immediate postoperative analgesia, possible reduced blood loss and pulmonary thromboembolism, and usually a positive experience for mother and partner.
• Consent includes discussion of side effects and is obtained before any sedating premedication; contraindications to regional (patient refusal, no IV access, amide allergy, sepsis, coagulopathy, hypovolaemia, severe cardiac disease) are checked; WHO checklist sign-in before anaesthesia.

questions.question:
A patient is to have general anaesthesia induced intravenously with propofol.
(a) Describe the technique of intravenous induction and the agent involved.
(b) State the monitoring and equipment to be prepared.
(c) Outline the nursing responsibilities and the positioning of the patient.
(d) Explain how intraoperative complications are prevented.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• The IV route is the most common method of induction: a bolus to the brain gives rapid loss of consciousness, is more acceptable than inhalational induction and minimises the excitement phase; advantages are rapid onset, titratable dose, early LMA insertion, and anti-emetic and anti-convulsive properties; disadvantages are venous access, hypotension, apnoea, loss of airway control and anaphylaxis.
• Propofol (Diprivan) is a non-barbiturate sedative that enhances GABA; induction 2 to 2.5 mg/kg IV at 40 mg every 10 seconds until onset, maintenance 6 to 12 mg/kg/hour; used for short procedures with rapid clearance, less hangover and quick recovery; it has no analgesic property so an analgesic must be given with it.
(b)
Minimum monitoring (ECG, SpO2, NIBP, capnography) is attached before induction and continued until recovery, with an oxygen analyser; IV access is established; propofol and emergency airway supplies such as a laryngeal mask airway must be readily available and functioning; equipment is checked and alarm limits set before use.
(c)
• Ensure informed consent has been provided; assess vital signs, airway status and level of consciousness; calculate the dose accurately by weight, medical condition and urgency; administer slowly, titrate to the desired level while monitoring the response, with proper dilution and technique to avoid medication errors; manage the airway and support ventilation; the anaesthetic nurse stays with the patient throughout.
• GA can be administered without moving the patient from the supine position; every surgical position carries some risk that is magnified under anaesthesia because the patient cannot make position changes, so positioning is a team task needing timing and communication.
(d)
• Reduce the dose by 20 to 30% in elderly, debilitated or hypovolaemic patients; premedication with benzodiazepines can reduce the dosage; do not give to patients allergic to soybean oil or egg phosphatide; maximum 5 mg/kg/hr (higher doses associated with propofol syndrome); infusion over 24 hours is not recommended under 18 years.
• Observe for hypotension and myocardial depression, bradycardia (treated with atropine), apnoea (use only with mechanical ventilation or during conscious procedural sedation), arrhythmias, anaphylaxis, excitatory phenomena and propofol syndrome (metabolic acidosis, elevated lactate, hypotension, cardiogenic shock, hyperkalaemia, rhabdomyolysis, lipaemia, renal failure); prompt recognition and intervention are essential.

(a)
• Assess nausea and vomiting together with pain score, sedation and pulse, BP and respiratory rate; overall PONV incidence is about 30% but can be as high as 80%; patient risk factors: female (ratio 2.5:1 to male), anxiety, previous PONV, history of motion sickness, non-smoker, pain, gastric contents.
• Anaesthetic factors: volatile agents, nitrous oxide, opioids, intravenous anaesthetics (ketamine, etomidate), neostigmine, stomach insufflation, spinal anaesthetic with hypotension; surgical factors: ENT (middle ear, adenoids, tonsillectomy), squint, gynaecological, gastrointestinal and laparoscopic surgery.
(b)
• Complications: aspiration of gastric contents (especially in recovery before protective airway reflexes have fully returned), dehydration and electrolyte disturbance, increased intraocular and intracranial pressure in susceptible patients, delayed discharge and increased anxiety for subsequent anaesthetics; vomiting is active whereas regurgitation is passive and more likely when conscious level is reduced.
• Opioid effects: apnoea, respiratory depression, sedation and cough suppression; reduced peristalsis causing constipation, ileus and urinary retention.
(c)
• Antiemetics are prescribed and combined (e.g. phenothiazine prochlorperazine, 5-HT3 antagonist ondansetron, dexamethasone); combination therapy acting at different receptors is more effective than one drug; dopamine antagonists can cause extrapyramidal effects (oculogyric crisis, dystonia, slurred speech) and ondansetron causes dizziness, headache and constipation.
• Perioperative IV fluids reduce PONV and time to first oral intake; hypotension is avoided, especially after spinal anaesthesia; P6 acupuncture stimulation reduces PONV; sedation, nausea and vomiting are scored, pain scores documented at rest and on movement, and multimodal opioid-sparing analgesia used.
(d)
• Patients stay in recovery until awake with airway reflexes under complete control, pain free, with no or minimal nausea and vomiting, no or minimal bleeding and normothermic.
• Handover includes name and age, operation details, blood loss, anaesthetic technique with analgesia given, regional blocks, antiemetics given, antibiotics, local anaesthetic infiltration and thromboprophylaxis.
questions.question:
A patient recovering from general anaesthesia in the recovery unit is receiving opioid analgesia and develops nausea and vomiting.
(a) Describe the assessment of this patient, including factors that increase risk.
(b) State the expected complications and their signs.
(c) Outline the nursing care and monitoring plan.
(d) State the discharge criteria and the handover.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Ventilation is the process of the lungs obtaining air by exchanging contents with the environment; the two main types are pulmonary ventilation (breathing, driven by pressure gradients involving intrapleural, atmospheric and interalveolar pressures) and mechanical ventilation (gas exchange assisted by an external device, the ventilator).
• Mechanical ventilation continues gas exchange, reduces the effort of respiring, helps with anaesthesia and muscle relaxation, and aids lung expansion and stabilisation of the thoracic wall.
(b)
• Types: high-frequency ventilators (oscillatory and jet), continuous flow ventilators, and positive-pressure ventilators (pressure cycling, flow cycling or a mixture).
• Hook-up: connect the breathing system hose to the rebreathing bag connection, attach the airway pressure sensing tee to the inhalation side, close the pop-off valve, plug in and hook up scavengers; use a leak-free anaesthetic machine and check for leaks first.
• Four controls: Rate and Volume set ventilation, one sets the maximum pressure limit and one pauses cycling.
• Alarms: maximum working pressure limit (10 to 60 cm H2O, ends inspiration, yellow light and short tone) and low breathing system pressure alarm (less than 5 cm H2O at end of inspiration, e.g. disconnection or running out of oxygen).
(c)
• Set VOLUME to minimum before switching on, set the maximum working pressure limit, then the RATE before adjusting volume; tidal volume 10 to 20 ml/kg; peak inspiratory pressure 15 to 20 cm H2O; never make gross adjustments with the patient connected.
• The flush button must not be used in the inspiratory phase and never with the patient connected (danger of rupturing a lung); change bellows by weight (under 30 lbs small 300 ml bellows) based on lean body weight; clean externally with a damp cloth and the bellows with water and mild detergent only, no alcohol.
(d)
• Mechanical ventilation is an indispensable life support for patients under GA or in respiratory failure; intensive monitoring identifies early worsening and minimises iatrogenic harm; a ventilator failure or disconnection alarm should be in continuous operation and automatically activated.
• Ventilation rate is tidal volume multiplied by respiratory rate (adult at rest about 6 L/min); pulse oximetry, capnography and the alarms ensure appropriate ventilation; mechanical ventilation decreases urine volume and sodium excretion through raised intrathoracic pressure.
(e)
• Similarities: both aim at gas exchange, both rely on the natural respiratory system and on elastic recoil of the lungs.
• Differences: in mechanical ventilation gas exchange is facilitated by the ventilator and isolated from the atmosphere, at a set rate; in pulmonary ventilation exchange occurs directly between lungs and atmosphere and speeds up or slows down with the environment.
questions.question:
Discuss mechanical ventilation and the ventilator.
(a) Define ventilation and state its types.
(b) Describe the types of ventilator, the hook-up, controls and alarms.
(c) State the steps in using a ventilator.
(d) Explain the nursing importance of mechanical ventilation and its monitoring.
(e) Distinguish between mechanical (artificial) ventilation and pulmonary (natural) ventilation.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Intubation (tracheal or endotracheal) is performed in a hospital in an emergency or before surgery: a laryngoscope guides an endotracheal tube through the mouth or nose into the trachea to keep it open, and the tube can connect to a machine delivering air or oxygen.
• Indications: airway obstruction, cardiac arrest, injury or trauma to the neck, abdomen or chest affecting the airway, loss or low level of consciousness, respiratory failure or apnoea; contraindicated in severe airway trauma or an obstruction blocking safe tube placement.
(b)
• Steps 1 to 4: insert an IV needle in the arm; give anaesthetics through the IV to put the patient to sleep; place an oxygen mask over the nose and mouth for extra oxygen; remove the mask.
• Steps 5 to 8: tilt the head back and insert the laryngoscope (handle, light, blade) into the mouth avoiding the teeth; move toward the back of the mouth; raise the epiglottis; advance into the larynx and then the trachea.
• Steps 9 to 12: inflate the cuff so the tube stays in place and air reaches the lungs; remove the laryngoscope; tape or strap the tube; confirm position by X-ray or by squeezing air through a bag and listening for breath sounds (capnography also confirms tracheal intubation).
(c)
• Preparation includes reviewing the history and pathology, a multi-faceted airway examination and assembling equipment, with a primary plan and backup plans.
• Predictors of difficulty include small mouth opening, short thyromental distance, prominent incisors, reduced mandibular protrusion, short neck, limited neck extension, Mallampati 3 or 4 and obesity.
• Nurses assist with intubation and, in failed intubation, maintain oxygenation (bag-mask, supplemental oxygen), monitor vital signs and capnography continuously, call for assistance, communicate with the team and the family, and document the entire event.
(d)
• Complications: failed intubation; aspiration of vomit, blood or fluids; endobronchial (mainstem) intubation; oesophageal intubation, which can cause brain damage or death if not recognised soon enough.
• Infections such as sinus infections; injury to the mouth, teeth, tongue, vocal cords or airway with bleeding or swelling; problems coming out of anaesthesia; tension pneumothorax.
• Prevention: verify intubation visually, with capnography and an oesophageal detector ('if in doubt, take it out'), and limit laryngoscopy attempts (maximum 3 + 1).
• They matter because failed intubation occurs in about 1 in 390 patients and maternal mortality is four times higher; poor judgement and suboptimal preparation cause negative outcomes.
questions.question:
Discuss endotracheal intubation as a nursing process.
(a) Define intubation and state its indications and contraindications.
(b) List the steps of intubation.
(c) List the nursing responsibilities and preparation.
(d) Explain the complications, how they are prevented and why they matter.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Children are not miniature adults and differences are most marked in neonates; induction may be intravenous (if access is present) or inhalational (sevoflurane and nitrous oxide in oxygen is potent, rapid and smooth); maintenance is almost always inhalational because IV techniques such as propofol are not licensed in young children; spontaneous breathing suits older children or short procedures but infants usually need artificial ventilation; neuromuscular blockade is reversed as in adults.
• After inhalational induction the airway must not be instrumented until venous access is secured (laryngospasm may result); a Guedel airway may be inserted and, if laryngeal spasm occurs without venous access, suxamethonium can be given i.m.
(b)
• Establish rapport with the child and parents and invite a parent to the anaesthetic room; note weight and age including prematurity (weight = (age in years + 4) x 2), past illnesses, medication, allergies and teeth; upper respiratory tract infection increases risk and a child with a productive cough, chest signs or temperature should not have elective surgery; tests are seldom required.
• Fasting is typically 2 hours for clear fluids, 6 hours for solids and 4 hours for milk (some advocate 3 hours for breast milk); premedication is usually topical local anaesthetic for venous access; tracheal tube length = (age/2) + 12 cm and internal diameter = (age/4) + 4 mm for children over 2 years.
(c)
• Higher oxygen consumption per kg, reduced lung compliance, neonates at risk of apnoea; a high surface area to weight ratio causes rapid heat loss and poor thermoregulation, so hypothermia is a risk; the narrowest part of the airway is just below the cords and a tube with no audible leak may cause post-extubation oedema and stridor.
• Hypotonic fluids (e.g. 0.4% dextrose, 0.18% saline) may cause hyponatraemia and cerebral oedema; neonates show increased opioid and neuromuscular sensitivity and increased volume of distribution of suxamethonium; intramuscular opioids are best avoided.
(d)
• Discuss the anaesthetic plan with the parents: method of induction, postoperative analgesia (including suppositories) and what to expect such as IV cannulae, infusions and nasogastric tubes; warm the theatre and IV fluids with temperature monitoring; give 0.9% saline or Hartmann's solution (glucose only for babies and those with hypoglycaemia) using the 4-2-1 rule (0 to 10 kg 4 mL/kg/h).
• Pain control assessment is fundamental postoperatively: paracetamol loading dose then regular doses, rectal diclofenac after parental consent, PCA in older children or nurse-controlled analgesia in younger children; caudals and nerve blocks are less common outside specialist centres.
questions.question:
A healthy child is scheduled for a minor operation under general anaesthesia.
(a) Describe the anaesthetic approach and technique suitable for the child.
(b) Outline the nursing preparation and assistance, including preoperative assessment and fasting.
(c) State the risks and side effects specific to children.
(d) Describe patient care, teaching and evaluation for the child and parents.

During induction of general anaesthesia in an adult, tracheal intubation is unsuccessful after repeated attempts.
(a) Describe how failed intubation is recognised and what increases the risk.
(b) State the immediate nursing actions and how help is escalated.
(c) Outline the management, equipment and algorithm used.
(d) Describe the documentation and follow-up.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Failed tracheal intubation is failure to intubate in a maximum of three attempts regardless of technique; it is difficult if more than one attempt at optimised laryngoscopy is made, a more experienced worker is needed or a change of technique or device is made.
• Causes: mouth opening under 4 cm, thyromental distance under 6 cm, Mallampati III or higher, limited neck mobility, inability to sublux the mandible, blood and secretions, subglottic oedema; risk factors: emergency surgery, pregnant patients needing emergency GA, trauma with cervical spine injury, morbid obesity and previous head and neck cancer treatment.
(b)
Call for help or a rapid response team; maintain oxygenation with bag-mask ventilation or advanced airway devices and supplemental oxygen; monitor vital signs and capnography continuously; re-evaluate the airway (obstruction, repositioning of head and neck); a maximum of 3 + 1 attempts, since more than three by the same clinician is unlikely to succeed and risks trauma.
(c)
• DAS algorithm: Plan A effective mask ventilation and intubation (reposition, paralytic drug, external laryngeal manipulation, remove cricoid pressure, bougie); Plan B supraglottic airway (second-generation recommended); Plan C reattempt mask ventilation with paralysis using a two-person technique; Plan D emergency front of neck access (open scalpel cricothyrotomy).
• Prepare a cricothyrotomy kit, oxygen, suction and monitoring devices; consider bronchoscopy and specialists (anaesthesiologist, otolaryngologist); cricothyrotomy is a last resort (complications: bleeding, infection, damage to surrounding structures, vocal cord injury, pneumothorax).
(d)
Document the entire event, including interventions, responses and communication with the healthcare team; communicate clearly with the team, the patient and the family and offer psychological support; an airway history from previous anaesthetics helps airway assessment.

questions.question:
Discuss inhalational induction of anaesthesia.
(a) State the objective of induction, define MAC and describe the uptake of inhaled agents.
(b) State the advantages and disadvantages of inhalational induction.
(c) Explain the nursing importance and clinical basis of the technique.
(d) Distinguish inhalational induction from intravenous induction.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• The objective of modern anaesthesia is rapid unconsciousness, maintenance of that state and rapid recovery; MAC is the concentration of agent that prevents reflex response to skin incision in 50% of a population, an easily defined measure of depth of anaesthesia.
• Sufficient concentration must reach the CNS through uptake by the lungs and distribution to the brain.
• Uptake depends on inspired concentration, alveolar ventilation, diffusion, blood/gas partition coefficient and removal by the pulmonary circulation, in delivery, pulmonary and circulatory phases (cardiac output, cerebral blood flow, tissue distribution).
• Agents include desflurane, enflurane, halothane, isoflurane, sevoflurane, nitrous oxide, xenon and ethyl chloride; cooperative patients may take a vital capacity breath of isoflurane or sevoflurane but most need gradual introduction.
(b)
• Advantages: avoids venepuncture, respiration is maintained, slow loss of protective reflexes, end-tidal concentration can be measured, rapid recovery if induction is abandoned, upper oesophageal sphincter tone is maintained.
• Disadvantages: slow process, potential excitement phase, irritant and unpleasant (may induce coughing), pollution, may raise ICP/IOP.
(c)
• Airway control is maintained: if ventilation ceases through respiratory depression or obstruction the induction process is reversed; it suits patients with a great fear of needles; slow absorption across mucous membranes may offer some immunological protection.
• Inspired and expired concentrations should be monitored; MAC guides the concentration required and falls with age.
• In children sevoflurane with nitrous oxide in oxygen is potent, rapid and smooth, and the airway must not be instrumented until venous access is secured, because laryngospasm may result.
(d)
• Intravenous induction is the most common method: a bolus gives rapid loss of consciousness, is more acceptable to patients and minimises the excitement phase; disadvantages are venous access, risk of hypotension, common apnoea, loss of airway control and anaphylaxis.
• Inhalational induction is slow but keeps the airway and respiration and needs no needle.
• IV induction is rapid but needs venous access and carries risks of apnoea, hypotension, respiratory depression and loss of airway control, with adverse reactions likely to be more severe by the IV route.

(a)
NSAIDs decrease pain by inhibiting cyclo-oxygenase (COX), the rate-limiting enzyme in prostaglandin production from traumatized or inflamed tissues (prostaglandins increase the sensitivity of pain receptors); they are very helpful in arthritic diseases, may be especially powerful in cancer-related bone pain, are combined with opioids for postoperative and other severe pain, and with paracetamol are the simple analgesics at the first step of the WHO ladder; examples are ibuprofen, diclofenac and celecoxib.
(b)
• Diclofenac: phenylacetic acid derivative, potent COX inhibitor; oral tablets (enteric coated, sustained release, dispersible), syrup, IM/IV; oral 75 to 150 mg/day in 2 to 3 divided doses (children 1 to 3 mg/kg/day), rectal maximum daily dose 150 mg, deep IM 75 mg once or twice daily, IV infusion 75 mg 6-hourly.
• Ibuprofen: propionic acid derivative, COX inhibitor; oral tablets (coated or slow release), capsule, syrup; adults 1.2 to 1.8 g/day in 3 to 4 divided doses, children 20 mg/kg in divided doses.
• Paracetamol (acetaminophen, a hydroxyphenylactamide): oral tablet, suspension, suppository, IM/IV; oral 500 mg to 1 g 4 to 6 hourly; IM/IV child 10 to 50 kg 15 mg/kg 4 to 6 hourly, child under 10 kg 7.5 mg/kg 4 to 6 hourly.
(c)
• Diclofenac: dizziness, vertigo, peptic ulceration; adverse renal impairment. Ibuprofen: nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea; adverse renal insufficiency, hypersensitivity reactions, toxic amblyopia. Paracetamol: nausea, vomiting; adverse hepatic cell damage with overdosage or prolonged use.
• Postoperatively NSAID problems include bleeding (especially gastrointestinal), gastrointestinal perforation, asthma, renal failure and myocardial and cerebral thrombosis; paracetamol overdose causes liver dysfunction.
(d)
• Diclofenac: monitor closely for signs of peptic ulcer and use with an antacid in prolonged use; in children diclofenac per rectum is given under general anaesthesia after obtaining parental consent.
• Ibuprofen: not recommended in children under 7 kg and not to be given to asthmatic patients or patients with a history of peptic ulcer.
• Paracetamol: use with caution in hepatic impairment and infuse IV over 15 minutes; in children a loading dose is often given on the ward followed by regular doses, taking care another dose is not inadvertently given.
(e)
• Patients are monitored for peptic ulcer signs because NSAIDs cause peptic ulceration and gastrointestinal bleeding, and renal function is a concern because NSAIDs cause renal impairment; liver damage is the concern with paracetamol overdose or prolonged use.
• Regular rather than as-required prescribing gives better pain control, and multimodal analgesia with NSAIDs and paracetamol reduces opioid requirements and adverse effects.
questions.question:
Discuss the non-opioid analgesic drugs (NSAIDs and paracetamol).
(a) State how NSAIDs act and their uses.
(b) Describe diclofenac, ibuprofen and paracetamol (class, presentation, doses).
(c) State their side effects and adverse effects.
(d) State the safe-practice precautions and nursing responsibilities for each drug.
(e) Explain the rationale for monitoring and the management of adverse effects.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• This is an anaphylactic reaction: an immediate-type hypersensitivity reaction from interaction of antigens with specific IgE antibodies bound to mast cells and basophils, releasing histamine, leukotrienes and eosinophil chemotactic factor; it occurs in sensitised individuals, while anaphylactoid reactions are clinically indistinguishable but follow no prior exposure (IgG-mediated complement activation); reactions are likely to be more severe when drugs are given intravenously.
• Clinical features: cardiovascular collapse 88%, bronchospasm 36%, swelling of the face 24%, generalized swelling 7%, erythema 45%, urticaria 9%, rash 3%.
(b)
Stop administration of all agents likely to have caused the reaction; call for help; maintain the airway, give 100% oxygen and lie the patient flat with legs elevated.
(c)
• Epinephrine: IM 0.5 to 1 mg repeated every 10 minutes as required according to arterial pressure and pulse; IV 50 to 100 micrograms over 1 minute, repeated as required; never give undiluted 1:1000 IV; for cardiovascular collapse 0.5 to 1 mg (5 to 10 ml of 1:10,000) IV in divided doses by titration at 0.1 mg per minute, stopping when a response is obtained.
• Paediatric IM epinephrine 1:1000: over 12 years 500 micrograms (0.5 ml); 6 to 12 years 250 micrograms (0.25 ml); over 6 months to 6 years 120 micrograms (0.12 ml); under 6 months 50 micrograms (0.05 ml).
• Secondary therapy: antihistamines (chlorpheniramine 10 to 20 mg by slow IV infusion), corticosteroids (hydrocortisone 100 to 500 mg slowly IV), bronchodilators for persistent bronchospasm; rapid IV infusion of colloids or crystalloids (adults may need 2 to 4 litres of crystalloid).
(d)
• After a suspected drug reaction the patient should be counselled and investigated; no tests until the resuscitation period is completed; 10 ml venous blood in a plain glass tube is taken immediately after resuscitation and at 1 hour and 6 to 24 hours for serum tryptase (serum separated and stored at -20 deg C), elevation indicating mast cell degranulation.
• EDTA tubes are useful for complement assays and haematology, disappearance of basophils indicating a type I anaphylactic reaction.
questions.question:
During anaesthesia, after intravenous drugs are given, a patient develops cardiovascular collapse, bronchospasm, facial swelling and erythema.
(a) Identify the problem and state how it is recognised.
(b) State the immediate nursing actions and how help is escalated.
(c) Outline the management, drugs and fluids to be prepared.
(d) Describe the documentation and follow-up required afterwards.

A patient under general anaesthesia is to be positioned prone for spinal surgery.
(a) Describe the anaesthetic technique and the reason for the position.
(b) State the monitoring and set-up required.
(c) Outline the nursing responsibilities and positioning.
(d) Explain how intraoperative complications related to position are prevented.
questions.answerText:
(a)
GA is induced and maintained with a combination of intravenous and inhaled agents; the patient is unarousable, amnesic and cannot maintain airway or ventilation; the prone position provides optimal exposure for spine, certain orthopaedic and some rectal procedures and has been advocated for intracranial procedures because of lower risk of venous air embolism than the sitting position.
(b)
ECG, pulse oximeter and NIBP with capnography are applied before induction and continued until recovery; continuous core temperature monitoring; the anaesthesia provider continually monitors the physiologic changes, which depend on the position, its duration, the padding and positioning devices, the type of anaesthesia and the procedure.
(c)
• Positioning is a group endeavour requiring teamwork, timing, communication and knowledge of measures protecting against injury; the goal is optimal surgical access while minimising risk; anaesthesia providers coordinate and direct positioning; every position carries risk magnified by anaesthesia because the patient cannot make position changes.
• Pressure points and the extremities are positioned in proper alignment and padded to decrease the possibility of compression injury; skin, eyes, breast and genitalia are vulnerable areas.
(d)
• Cardiac output and BP generally fall under GA with blood pooling in dependent areas, reducing preload and stroke volume; changes are minimal in supine and lateral but often decreased in sitting, prone and flexed lateral positions; postural change alters compliance, lung volumes and ventilation/perfusion, more evident in prone and lateral positions (sitting is most favourable).
• Other positions: supine (most frequent), Trendelenburg (increases venous return in hypotension), reverse Trendelenburg (head above heart reduces cerebral perfusion and is monitored closely), lithotomy and lateral decubitus.

questions.question:
Discuss intravenous induction agents (etomidate, ketamine and diazepam).
(a) State the general features and classes of intravenous agents.
(b) Describe etomidate and ketamine (class, dose, mode of action, effects).
(c) Describe diazepam and the side effects of all three.
(d) State the safe-practice precautions and nursing responsibilities.
(e) Explain the rationale for monitoring and the management of adverse effects.
questions.answerText:
(a)
IV agents transfer rapidly from blood to brain, giving brief anaesthesia with rapid recovery; adverse reactions range from minimal to serious and no ideal agent exists; examples: barbiturates (thiopental), ketamine, etomidate, propofol and benzodiazepines (diazepam, lorazepam).
(b)
• Etomidate: general anaesthetic and cortisol synthesis inhibitor, given IV; depresses the reticular activating system and enhances GABA; induction 0.3 mg/kg (0.2 to 0.6) over 30 to 60 seconds.
• Cardiovascular stability is its main advantage (cardiac output and heart rate minimally affected, MAP maintained), useful in poor ejection fraction, coronary artery disease or severe aortic stenosis.
• Etomidate also causes cerebral vasoconstriction, less ventilatory depression than other IV agents and suppression of adrenocortical cortisol production.
• Ketamine: phencyclidine derivative, IV 1 to 4.5 mg/kg or IM 4 to 13 mg/kg, an NMDA antagonist causing 'dissociative anaesthesia' with loss of consciousness and profound analgesia, with abuse potential.
(c)
• Diazepam: 1,4-benzodiazepine, oral, IM or IV, IV bolus 0.1 to 0.3 mg/kg; side effects respiratory depression and decreased cardiac output.
• Etomidate: pain at injection site, myoclonus, seizure activation, nausea, vomiting, hiccup; ketamine: increased heart rate, nausea and vomiting, bronchodilation, with rashes, hallucination and delirium as adverse effects.
(d)
• Etomidate: recognise adrenal suppression (especially adrenal insufficiency or chronic steroid therapy), monitor for adrenal insufficiency, minimise injection pain by dilution, larger veins or local anaesthetics, reassure patients with myoclonus and consider benzodiazepine or opioid premedication, monitor neurological status in intracranial pathology or head injury, and monitor vital signs continuously.
• Ketamine: monitor closely for delirium and hallucinations; diazepam: use with caution with cimetidine because it reduces clearance; contraindicated in etomidate hypersensitivity.
(e)
• The dose needed for unconsciousness gives a plasma concentration that depresses the CNS and affects other systems, especially the cardiovascular system.
• Common effects are hypotension, respiratory depression and rapid loss of airway control, so the dose and rate are individualised and premedication with benzodiazepines can reduce the dose.

(a)
Central blockade is the introduction of drugs into the CSF within the subarachnoid space (spinal) or into the surrounding epidural space (epidural); it provides anaesthesia for surgery below the level of the umbilicus (T10).
(b)
• The spinal cord ends at the lower border of L1 or upper border of L2, so the spinal needle is introduced at or below the L2/L3 interspace; Tuffier's line (between the iliac crests, level L4/5) is a landmark.
• Needles are narrow gauge (25 or 27G) and the commonest has a blunt pencil-point tip that separates dural fibres and reduces CSF-leak headache; the patient sits or lies on their side with the back curled forward to widen the intervertebral spaces.
(c)
A catheter is placed in the epidural space for continuous or intermittent drug administration: a Tuohy needle is advanced with pressure on a saline-filled syringe, there is a sudden loss of resistance as the ligamentum flavum is breached, the catheter is threaded down the needle and the needle removed; positioning is as for spinal; used for labour analgesia, surgery and postoperative analgesia.
(d)
• Advantages: avoids GA in at-risk patients (severe respiratory disease, difficult intubation, diabetic, myopathies, pregnant, malignant hyperthermia), good postoperative analgesia, avoids sedation and nausea from morphine, reduced pulmonary thromboembolism, reduced blood loss and reduced stress response.
• Side effects: hypotension (sympathetic block), nausea and vomiting, lower limb motor block, post dural puncture headache (more likely with a large needle, non-pencil-point tip, inadvertent Tuohy puncture of dura, young age), high block affecting upper limb power and respiration (C3-5), total spinal with loss of consciousness, rare nerve damage.
• Contraindications: patient refusal, no IV access, severe CVS disease, hypovolaemia, sepsis, LA allergy, coagulopathy (INR needs to be below 1.5); caution with previous major spinal surgery or ongoing CNS disease.
(e)
A full aseptic technique with gloves, gown, mask and cap must be used; repeated syringe aspiration on injecting LA prevents inadvertent intravenous injection; nerve damage is rare but must be discussed with the patient; IV access is required because lack of it is a contraindication.
(f)
Spinal LA ampoules often contain dextrose to increase baricity relative to CSF; the heavy LA sinks, giving a denser block on the dependent side when lying on the side, whereas plain LA is hypobaric and affects the non-dependent (lower) side more.
(g)
• Spinal: single shot into the CSF so it cannot be topped up, rapid onset, small needle, used for LSCS, instrumental delivery and retained placenta, missed segments rare.
• Epidural: catheter inserted so it can be topped up, slow onset, large needle, used for labour analgesia, LSCS and instrumental delivery, may get missed segments.
(h)
Combined spinal-epidural gives rapid onset (spinal) and the ability to supplement with the epidural as the spinal wears off (e.g. postoperative analgesia or prolonged surgery).
questions.question:
Discuss central neuraxial (spinal and epidural) blockade.
(a) Define central blockade and state the level of surgery for which it provides anaesthesia.
(b) Describe spinal anaesthesia: needle level, landmark, needle type and patient positioning.
(c) Describe epidural block: needle, catheter placement, positioning and uses.
(d) State the advantages, side effects and contraindications of central blockade.
(e) Explain the nursing importance of aseptic technique, aspiration on injection and IV access.
(f) Explain the clinical basis for adding dextrose to spinal local anaesthetic.
(g) Distinguish between spinal and epidural anaesthesia.
(h) State the advantage of the combined spinal-epidural technique.

Discuss neuromuscular blocking agents.
(a) Classify the types of blockade with examples.
(b) Describe suxamethonium and pancuronium (class, presentation, dose, mode of action).
(c) State their side effects and adverse effects.
(d) State the safe-practice precautions and nursing responsibilities.
(e) Explain the rationale for monitoring neuromuscular blockade and the management of adverse effects.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Neuromuscular blockade prevents transmission of neuronal impulses to skeletal muscles and is assessed by clinical observation and by response to electrical stimulus.
• Types: prevention of acetylcholine synthesis (hemicholiniums); prevention of release (botulinum toxin, local anaesthetics, magnesium ions); depletion of stores (tetanus toxin); receptor blockade - depolarising (nicotine, suxamethonium) and non-depolarising (pancuronium, vecuronium).
(b)
• Suxamethonium (succinylcholine): dicholine ester of acetylcholine, clear colourless aqueous solution; acts by rapidly depolarizing the neuromuscular junction; IV bolus 0.3 to 1.1 mg/kg, children 1 to 2 mg/kg, infusion 0.1% solution at 2 to 15 mg/min; effective within 30 seconds and lasts several minutes.
• Pancuronium bromide: bisquaternary aminosteroid, clear colourless aqueous solution (4 mg in 2 ml); IV bolus 0.05 to 0.1 mg/kg, initial dose lasts 45 to 60 minutes.
(c)
• Suxamethonium: muscle pains, malignant hypertension, hyperkalaemia; adverse paralysis of respiratory muscle, increased blood pressure and IOP; it produces fasciculations that raise intragastric pressure, which may overcome lower oesophageal sphincter tone and allow reflux.
• Pancuronium: respiratory muscle paralysis, bronchodilatation, increased heart rate and cardiac output; adverse increase in lower oesophageal sphincter pressure and increased prothrombin time and partial thromboplastin time.
(d)
• Suxamethonium should not be given to patients suspected to have malignant hyperthermia or burns; aspiration risk should not necessarily preclude it, since body habitus, technical difficulty of intubation, NPO status and comorbidities determine the risk; it is avoided in ophthalmic surgery to control extraocular muscle tone.
• Pancuronium: monitor vital signs periodically and ensure the clotting time is checked before administering the drug.
(e)
• Quantitative neuromuscular monitoring is available for every patient in whom blockade is induced and used when extubation is considered after non-depolarising blockade.
• The adductor pollicis response to ulnar nerve stimulation at the wrist is ideal (facial or posterior tibial nerves if not possible); it is applied after induction but before blockade and used throughout.
• A train-of-four ratio above 0.9 must be demonstrated and documented before awakening and extubation.
• A simple stimulator is only qualitative, grip strength or lifting a body part is a crude clinical test, and clinical and autonomic signs cannot distinguish an awake paralysed patient from an anaesthetised one.

(a)
Pulse oximetry is a noninvasive monitor giving continuous real-time estimates of arterial haemoglobin saturation with oxygen (SpO2); it warns of significant hypoxaemia, is essentially risk free and monitors oxygen at the arterial level, confirming that the lungs transfer oxygen from alveoli to blood.
(b)
• Its principles are optical plethysmography (pulsatile volume change at the probe site detected optically) and spectrophotometry (proportion of haemoglobin saturated with oxygen in pulsatile arterial blood), an application of the Beer-Lambert law.
• The probe has two light emitting diodes and a photodetector opposite each other across the arterial bed; the LEDs emit light at 660 nm and 940 nm because deoxyhaemoglobin absorbs maximally at 600 to 750 nm (red) and oxyhaemoglobin at 850 to 1000 nm (infrared).
• They switch on and off hundreds of times per second and an empiric algorithm relates the ratio of absorptions (R) to SpO2.
(c)
• The most common probe sites are the fingers, toes, ear lobes and nasal ala (usually a fingertip or ear lobe).
• ASA Standard II requires a quantitative method of assessing oxygenation such as pulse oximetry during all anaesthetics; the variable pitch pulse tone and low threshold alarm must be audible to the anaesthesia team, and adequate illumination and exposure of the patient are needed to assess colour.
(d)
• It ensures timely detection of hypoxia, playing a crucial role in patient safety throughout the perioperative period, and can reduce the need for invasive monitoring and frequent arterial blood gas measurements.
• Minimum monitoring (ECG, SpO2, NIBP, capnography) is checked for correct function and begun before induction and continued through transfer to the recovery unit; alarm limits are set to patient-specific values and audible alarms enabled.
• Limitation: it does not guarantee that adequate oxygen is delivered to, and used by, body tissues.
(e)
• Pulse oximetry measures oxygen saturation of arterial haemoglobin (oxygenation) using light absorption, whereas capnography measures carbon dioxide concentration in exhaled breath (ventilation) and displays it against time or volume using infrared absorption spectroscopy.
• Capnography confirms tracheal intubation, respiratory rate and adequacy of ventilation and indicates breathing circuit disconnection, sudden circulatory collapse, air embolism and malignant hyperthermia; normal end-tidal CO2 is 35 to 45 mm Hg (about 5%); it is used for every patient under GA and immediately available for sedation.
• They work alongside each other to give a comprehensive picture of respiratory status; poor ventilation and hypercarbia can lead to respiratory acidosis and cardiovascular collapse that pulse oximetry may not detect until very late when supplemental oxygen is given.
questions.question:
Discuss pulse oximetry as a monitoring technique.
(a) Define pulse oximetry and state what it measures.
(b) Describe its principles of operation and the components of the probe.
(c) State the usual probe sites and the ASA requirements for its use.
(d) Explain the nursing importance of pulse oximetry and its limitations.
(e) Distinguish between pulse oximetry and capnography.

An elderly patient with arthritis, a sensory deficit and poor cognition is listed for surgery under anaesthesia.
(a) Describe the preoperative assessment and the risks that should be identified.
(b) State the nursing problems or nursing diagnoses that arise.
(c) Outline the preparation and nursing interventions, giving the rationale for each.
(d) Explain the consent process and the safety checks required.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Elderly patients have declining physiological reserve that may not be apparent and is not always easy to test (exercise tolerance may be limited by arthritis rather than cardiorespiratory reserve); all patients have serum electrolytes, glucose, full blood count and ECG, with further tests as dictated by findings and severity of surgery (e.g. echocardiography, pharmacological stress testing, cardiopulmonary exercise testing, chest X-ray, arterial blood gases) and a neurological assessment such as the Mini-mental State Examination, which also helps assess ability to consent.
• Drug handling changes: opioids and IV anaesthetics last longer and reduced protein binding gives a greater free (active) fraction, risking inadvertent overdose; markedly increased arm-brain circulation time can lead to excess induction agent or sedative; MAC of inhalational agents falls with age; response to beta agonists is reduced.
• Other risks: slow arm-brain circulation with poor vasopressor response may cause profound hypotension; maintaining the airway after loss of consciousness may be difficult (soft tissues lose tone, edentulous patients, arthritic neck and jaw); the elderly are more likely to become hypothermic; for emergency admissions a fall may be due to confusion (chest or urinary infection) or a cardiac dysrhythmia.
(b)
Problems identified: reduced physiological reserve, risk of overdose and profound hypotension, difficult airway, hypothermia, a very small therapeutic window for fluids, and difficulty understanding consent because of sensory deficit or poor cognition.
(c)
• Large-bore IV access is required; fluids have a very small therapeutic window (excess causes ventricular failure and oedema, too little causes poor cardiac output, hypotension and renal impairment), and because pulse, BP, urine output and capillary refill may be inadequate guides, central venous pressure and flow measurements (e.g. oesophageal Doppler) are frequently used.
• Temperature maintenance is crucial: warm IV fluids and use a warming mattress and forced-air warmers; hypothermia reduces drug metabolism, increases vascular resistance, causes muscle weakness and coagulopathy, and shivering increases oxygen consumption.
(d)
• Check that the patient has understood the procedure and the alternatives, recognising concerns from sensory deficit or poor cognition, and involve family members and friends if required; a separate form (Consent Form 4) is needed for patients who lack capacity when the procedure is in their best interests; consent is obtained before any sedating premedication and documented.
• WHO checklist sign-in before anaesthesia confirms identity, site, procedure and consent, site marking, allergy, difficult airway or aspiration risk and expected blood loss.

questions.question:
A woman in labour requests epidural pain relief.
(a) Describe the technique, the solution used and why it is chosen.
(b) Outline the nursing preparation and assistance, including positioning and the contraindications checked.
(c) State the risks and side effects and how they are recognised or managed.
(d) Describe patient care, teaching and evaluation after the epidural is sited.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Epidural is the most common type of pain control for labour and delivery: a catheter is placed in the epidural space (Tuohy needle with loss of resistance to a saline-filled syringe, catheter threaded down the needle) for continuous or intermittent drug administration; it gives excellent segmental analgesia and allows the mother to be awake and able to push.
• Bupivacaine is the only LA used because it is long acting with low transfer to the fetus; adding an opioid (commonly fentanyl) reduces leg weakness and enhances analgesia (the mobile epidural).
(b)
Positioning is as for a spinal (sitting or on the side with the back curled forward); full aseptic technique with gloves, gown, mask and cap; IV access is mandatory; contraindications checked: patient refusal, no IV access, allergy to amide local anaesthetics, sepsis, coagulopathy, hypovolaemia and severe cardiac disease (e.g. stenotic valvular disease), major spinal surgery (e.g. spinal rods); the catheter is sited only in the absence of coagulopathy and infection.
(c)
Risks: hypotension from sympathetic block; weakness (much less with mobile mixtures); urinary retention; headache from accidental dural puncture (about 0.6%) from CSF leak, often needing a blood patch; catheter misplacement into the CSF (total spinal with paralysis and loss of consciousness) or intravenously (arrhythmias, l-bupivacaine being safer); neurological damage (very rare, under 1 in 10,000); longer labour; regional techniques do not cause backache.
(d)
• Maternal hypotension is managed by elevating the legs and turning the mother to a side-lying position; fetal heart rate is monitored continuously and electronic fetal monitoring is highly advisable; consciousness is monitored for CNS toxicity (anxiety, dizziness, restlessness, tremors, blurred vision).
• With epidural infusions pulse, BP and respiratory rate are monitored plus sedation, nausea and vomiting, leg weakness and height of the block; severe weakness and back pain may indicate epidural haematoma or abscess and need urgent investigation (MRI); pain scores are documented at rest and on movement.
• Patients or caregivers are advised to seek immediate attention for pale, grey or blue skin, headache, rapid heart rate, shortness of breath, lightheadedness or fatigue.

questions.question:
Discuss inhaled anaesthetic gases and vapours.
(a) State their general features and uptake.
(b) Describe isoflurane, halothane and nitrous oxide (actions, side effects, adverse effects).
(c) State the safe-practice precautions.
(d) Explain the rationale for monitoring their use and the management of adverse effects.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Gases and vapours are volatile liquids with low boiling point and high saturated vapour pressure, so they evaporate easily; most have a characteristic smell.
• They are inhaled and enter the circulation through the pulmonary alveolar capillaries; examples: desflurane, enflurane, halothane, isoflurane, sevoflurane, nitrous oxide, xenon and ethyl chloride.
• Uptake occurs in delivery, pulmonary and circulatory phases (pulmonary factors include inhaled concentration, alveolar ventilation, blood/gas partition coefficient, concentration effect and second gas effect); MAC is the guide to the concentration required.
(b)
• Isoflurane: halogenated ether, colourless liquid in a brown glass bottle with keyed filling collar and no additive; anaesthetic effect, not analgesia or muscle relaxant; lowers blood pressure and systemic vascular resistance; adverse increased bronchial secretions and raised intracranial pressure.
• Halothane: halogenated alkane, clear liquid in a brown bottle with 0.1% thymol; anaesthetic effect only; reduces metabolic rate, oxygen consumption and CO2 production.
• Reduces myocardial contractility and heart rate (vagal); adverse decreased coronary perfusion, reduced GI motility and uterine tone, and raised secretion of vasopressin, thyroxine, growth hormone and corticosteroids.
