• Nitrous oxide: a vapour rather than a gas, given in oxygen as Entonox; suppresses spinal impulses; prolonged use interferes with vitamin B12; adverse decreased tidal volume and increased vascular tone.
(c)
• Nitrous oxide is 30 times more soluble than nitrogen and diffuses into gas-containing cavities faster than nitrogen leaves, distending the bowel; it expands gas-filled spaces (avoided in eye surgery with intraocular gas) and is thought to cause PONV, so it is avoided in at-risk patients.
• Volatile agents depress GI activity (small intestine recovers first, stomach in about 24 hours, colon in 30 to 40 hours); rapid rises in desflurane cause greater sympathetic activation; inhalational agents generally decrease glomerular filtration and urine output (mitigated by preoperative hydration); pollution is a disadvantage.
(d)
• Anaesthesia depresses ventilatory drive, alters lung compliance, impairs airway reflexes (aspiration risk) and causes atelectasis, so monitoring is essential.
• Inspired and expired concentrations and age-adjusted MAC are monitored, with an oxygen analyser and capnography (infrared absorption spectroscopy measures CO2 and anaesthetic gases).

(a)
• History and examination cover cardiac disease (e.g. angina, hypertension), respiratory, GI, renal, CNS and musculoskeletal disease, endocrine disease (e.g. diabetes), medication (including non-prescription drugs and herbal remedies), allergies, and tobacco, alcohol and recreational drugs; the airway is assessed, past anaesthetic history is taken and family history of malignant hyperthermia is asked.
• Risk is judged from the patient and from the proposed surgery (cardiac risk is the major area studied) and can be graded with the ASA scale; patients with ischaemic heart disease or insulin-dependent diabetes are at risk of gastric aspiration even after fasting.
• Common tests: full blood count, electrolytes and urea, coagulation screen, ECG and chest X-ray, with urinalysis for all patients; at-risk patients or major surgery may need liver function tests, arterial blood gases, respiratory function tests and echocardiography.
(b)
Problems identified: risk of perioperative cardiac events, risk of aspiration, risk of thromboembolism if coagulation drugs are stopped versus bleeding if continued, and the need for glycaemic control in an insulin-dependent diabetic.
(c)
• Fasting: elective surgery should not proceed unless more than 2 hours since clear fluid, more than 4 hours since milk and more than 6 hours since food, to prevent gastric acid pneumonitis and airway obstruction by particulate matter.
• Medication is generally continued except drugs that affect coagulation (warfarin, heparin, aspirin, clopidogrel), hypoglycaemics and ACE inhibitors (stopped only on the day of surgery); for coagulation drugs the risk of stopping (thromboembolism) is weighed against continuing (perioperative bleeding), sometimes switching to low-molecular-weight heparin.
• Long-acting insulin is generally discontinued and a sliding scale of short-acting IV insulin started; some drugs (beta blockers, ACE inhibitors, statins) may be commenced to reduce risk; ward staff prepare the patient (DVT prophylaxis, MRSA testing, pre-assessment paperwork collated) and the anaesthetist should see the patient on the ward.
(d)
• Consent requires capacity (ability to understand and retain information, weigh it up and make a free choice), voluntariness and enough relevant information; the patient is told of common (e.g. PONV), rare (e.g. nerve damage after spinal or epidural) and patient-specific risks; consent must be obtained before any sedating premedication and the information discussed documented.
• WHO checklist sign-in before anaesthesia: patient confirms identity, site, procedure and consent; site marked; anaesthesia safety check; pulse oximeter on patient; known allergy; difficult airway or aspiration risk; risk of more than 500 mL blood loss.
questions.question:
A patient listed for elective major surgery has a history of angina and hypertension, is an insulin-dependent diabetic and takes drugs that affect coagulation.
(a) Describe the preoperative assessment of this patient and the risks that should be identified.
(b) State the nursing problems or nursing diagnoses that arise from this assessment.
(c) Outline the preoperative preparation and nursing interventions, giving the rationale for each.
(d) Explain the patient education, consent and safety checks required before the patient goes to theatre.

Discuss opioid analgesic drugs.
(a) Define opioid and opiate and state how opioids are classified.
(b) Describe morphine, codeine and tramadol (class, presentation, doses).
(c) State the uses, side effects and adverse effects of opioids.
(d) State the nursing considerations and safe-practice precautions.
(e) Explain the rationale for monitoring patients on opioids and the management of adverse effects.
questions.answerText:
(a)
An opioid is a natural (morphine), semisynthetic (diamorphine) or synthetic (pethidine) compound acting at opioid receptors; opiate describes drugs derived from the opium poppy (Papaver somniferum); opioids are classified by chemical structure, production, receptor activity and receptor subtype affinity; they bind opioid receptors, can be given by oral, IV, subcutaneous, intraspinal, intranasal, rectal and transdermal routes and are addictive controlled substances (e.g. morphine, oxycodone, buprenorphine).
(b)
• Morphine: a phenanthrene, principal alkaloid of opium; oral tablets, modified-release tablets, suppositories, IV ampoules; SC/IM 0.1 to 0.3 mg/kg (peak 30 min, duration 3 to 4 h), rectal 15 to 30 mg 4-hourly, intrathecal 0.2 to 1 mg, IV 0.05 to 0.1 mg/kg, epidural 2.5 to 10 mg.
• Codeine: a morphine analogue (3-methyl morphine), principal alkaloid of opium; oral (tablet, syrup), IM, IV; oral/IM 30 to 60 mg 4 to 6 hourly.
• Tramadol: phenylpiperidine analogue of codeine, weak agonist at all opioid receptor types that also blocks noradrenaline and serotonin reuptake; oral, IM, IV; PO 50 to 100 mg 4-hourly, slow IV/IM 50 to 100 mg 4-hourly (100 mg initially then 50 mg increments to maximum 250 mg), maximum 600 mg/day; half-life 4 to 6 hours, extensively metabolised in the liver.
(c)
• Uses: tramadol for moderate to severe pain with little respiratory depression; on the WHO analgesic ladder mild opioids (codeine, tramadol) precede strong opioids (morphine); morphine is given by PCA, and opioids are combined with NSAIDs for postoperative and other severe pain, but pain of neurologic origin is difficult to treat with opioids.
• Morphine: nausea, vomiting, drowsiness, euphoria; adverse: respiratory and circulatory depression, delayed gastric emptying, histamine release, urticaria. Codeine: respiratory depression, low euphoria, constipation, mild nausea and vomiting. Tramadol: nausea, vomiting, respiratory distress, dizziness, dry mouth; adverse: increased risk of CNS toxicity.
• General opioid effects: apnoea, respiratory depression, sedation, cough suppression (aspiration, respiratory infection); nausea and vomiting (electrolyte imbalance, dehydration, wound dehiscence, delayed discharge); reduced peristalsis (constipation, ileus, urinary retention, slow return of GI function).
(d)
• Patients need close monitoring because morphine is easily addicted to; tramadol is used with caution with tricyclic antidepressants and benzodiazepines; multimodal analgesia aims to minimise opioids ('opioid sparing') to reduce adverse effects; regular prescribing for 48 to 72 hours optimises drug levels; analgesia is best given when pain is first felt, so less medication is needed.
• In the elderly opioids have a longer duration and reduced protein binding gives more free drug, risking inadvertent overdose; in children intramuscular opioids are best avoided, and PCA (older child) or nurse-controlled analgesia (younger child) is used.
(e)
• Monitoring includes pulse, BP and respiratory rate plus sedation, which may reflect excess opioid administration, and nausea and vomiting; pain scores are documented at rest and on movement, high scores require intervention and its effect is reassessed.
• Nausea and vomiting are treated with prescribed combined antiemetics (e.g. prochlorperazine, ondansetron, dexamethasone); for suspected opioid overdose naloxone is given if available and protocols allow.

questions.question:
A patient is transferred to the post-anaesthesia care unit after a surgical procedure under anaesthesia.
(a) Describe the initial assessment of the patient on admission to the recovery unit.
(b) State the complications to be expected and the areas assessed to detect them.
(c) Outline the nursing care and monitoring plan.
(d) State the discharge criteria and the content of the handover.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Before transfer the recovery staff are notified and equipment needed (e.g. ventilator, nebulizer, invasive monitoring, infusions, capnograph) is ready; the anaesthesia provider and recovery nurse collaborate on admission; the immediate priority is evaluation of respiratory and circulatory adequacy, identifying any signs of inadequate oxygenation or ventilation and their cause.
• The assessment determines physiologic status on admission, allows periodic re-examination so trends are obvious, establishes the baseline, assesses the surgical site, assesses recovery from anaesthesia and residual effects, prevents or treats complications and provides a safe environment for the impaired patient.
(b)
Ongoing assessment covers respiratory function (obstruction, hypoxaemia, hypercarbia), cardiovascular function (hypotension, hypertension, dysrhythmias), neuromuscular function (inadequate reversal of blockade), mental status (delayed awakening, emergence delirium), pain, temperature (hypothermia), nausea and vomiting, fluids, and urine output and voiding.
(c)
• The anaesthesia provider gives a standardized verbal handoff and the nurse may ask questions; further analgesia is given if needed (including epidural management) along with antiemetics and fluids; all patients receive supplemental oxygen during transfer, but oxygen is not required if saturations are normal on air.
• Multimodal analgesia (paracetamol, NSAIDs, local anaesthetics, opioids) is used with regular rather than as-required dosing; an early warning score is used and a score of 3 triggers review by senior staff, with repeat scoring to assess interventions.
(d)
• Patients stay in recovery until awake and in complete control of airway reflexes, pain free, with no or minimal nausea and vomiting, no or minimal bleeding from the surgical site and normothermic; they should be oriented enough to assess their condition and summon help, with airway reflexes and motor function adequate to prevent aspiration and acceptable ventilation and oxygenation.
• Discharge may be to home, an ambulatory surgical unit, an inpatient unit or ICU depending on need and resources; handover gives name and age, operation details, blood loss, anaesthetic technique (analgesia given, regional blocks, antiemetics, antibiotics, local anaesthetic infiltration, thromboprophylaxis), the surgical and anaesthetic course, preoperative conditions and the recovery treatment plan.

(a)
Cataract surgery needs anaesthesia of the conjunctiva and a quiet eye (no rise in intraocular pressure; some surgeons also want akinesia); most are done under LA with a hospital stay of only a couple of hours; techniques: topical alone (e.g. oxybuprocaine), sub-Tenon's block (blunt needle after a small conjunctival incision), peribulbar block (25 mm 25G needle outside the muscle cone, inferotemporal) and retrobulbar block (almost obsolete, within the cone, often with facial nerve block).
(b)
IV access, pulse oximetry and ECG are often used for the blocks; occasionally sedation with small increments of midazolam 1 mg; contraindications are patient refusal, inability to lie flat or still, and INR over 2.5 for techniques 2 to 4; normal IOP is 10 to 20 mmHg and rises are prevented by avoiding coughing, keeping the head up with unobstructed neck veins, avoiding facemask pressure and avoiding large LA volumes.
(c)
Complications of sharp-needle techniques: retrobulbar haemorrhage; globe penetration (more likely in a myopic eye with axial length over 26 mm, causing vitreous haemorrhage and blindness); injection into muscle (paresis) or optic nerve (blindness) or spread causing total spinal (apnoea and loss of consciousness); intravenous injection; topical alone gives no akinesia.
(d)
• Day-surgery discharge criteria: pain free; has taken oral fluids (preferred but not essential); passed urine; carer at home for the first 24 hours; given and understands oral and written instructions; contact number and access to a telephone; adequate oral analgesia; told not to drive, operate machinery or cook for 24 hours.
• Local anaesthetic cases such as cataract removal bypass the recovery room and go to stage 2 recovery in the day surgery unit; elderly patients' consent understanding and sensory or cognitive deficits are checked.
questions.question:
An elderly patient is to have cataract surgery as a day case under local anaesthesia.
(a) Describe the technique or approach.
(b) Outline the nursing preparation and assistance.
(c) State the risks and side effects.
(d) Describe patient care, teaching and evaluation including discharge.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• BLS is a level of medical care for life-threatening illness or injury until full care by ALS providers; it includes recognising sudden cardiac arrest, heart attack, stroke and foreign body airway obstruction, plus CPR and AED defibrillation.
• It can be given by first responders, healthcare providers or any individual. A collapsed patient suddenly loses postural tone, not necessarily with loss of consciousness.
• Causes: simple fainting, heart problems such as heart attack, seizures, poisoning, pulmonary embolism, stroke and injury; signs include loss of consciousness, weakness, shortness of breath, chest pain, dizziness, paleness or cyanosis, confusion, slurred speech, nausea or vomiting and a sudden weak pulse.
(b)
• Verify scene safety; check responsiveness (tap, shout 'Are you OK?'); shout for help, activate the emergency response system and get an AED; check breathing by watching the chest for 5 to 10 seconds and the carotid pulse for at least 5 but no more than 10 seconds.
• Pulse and normal breathing: monitor, recovery position (lower arm in front of body); pulse but abnormal breathing: one breath every 5 to 6 seconds (10 to 12 per minute), check pulse every 2 minutes, naloxone if opioid overdose is suspected and protocols allow.
• No pulse within 10 seconds: begin CPR with compressions (CAB, not ABC) at 100 to 120 per minute, depth 2 inches, ratio 30:2, head tilt-chin lift, each breath over 1 second with visible chest rise; with an advanced airway in 2-person CPR give 1 breath every 6 to 8 seconds without pausing compressions.
• Apply the AED as soon as available and follow prompts; if shockable, clear the patient, shock and resume CPR immediately with compressions for 2 minutes; if non-shockable resume CPR for 2 minutes; compressions are not stopped for more than 10 seconds until ALS providers take over or the victim breathes, moves or reacts.
(c)
• Assess the situation (ABC; check the mouth and throat; roll on side if foreign material), activate emergency services without leaving the patient, administer medications if trained and authorised (e.g. anaesthetic anaphylaxis, cardiac arrest), maintain oxygenation, monitor vital signs and provide emotional support to bystanders and family.
• Barrier devices (face shields, face masks) may be used for rescue breaths, and foreign-body obstruction is relieved by finger sweep, back slaps, abdominal thrusts, chest thrusts or suction devices.
(d)
• Failure to manage a collapse can cause aspiration, airway obstruction, oxygen deprivation, skin ulcerations, anoxic brain injuries, organ failure and loss of life.
• Excessive ventilation causes gastric inflation, regurgitation and aspiration, raises intrathoracic pressure, decreases venous return and cardiac output and reduces survival, so rescuers avoid too many breaths or too large a volume (the primary purpose is oxygenation, the secondary is CO2 elimination).
• About 70% of cardiac arrests occur out of hospital and early bystander CPR improves outcome; CPR is not harmful, inaction is, and quality is critical: compress hard and fast, allow full recoil and minimise interruptions.
questions.question:
Discuss basic life support (BLS) and the algorithm for managing a collapsed adult.
(a) Define BLS and a collapsed patient and state the causes and signs of collapse.
(b) List the steps of the BLS algorithm.
(c) List the nursing responsibilities in managing a collapsed patient.
(d) Explain the complications of poor technique or no action, how they are prevented and why they matter.

A patient is scheduled for major emergency abdominal surgery for peritonitis with dehydration.
(a) Describe the preoperative assessment and the risks identified.
(b) State the nursing problems or nursing diagnoses that arise.
(c) Outline the preoperative preparation and nursing interventions, giving the rationale for each.
(d) Explain the patient education, consent and safety checks required.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Surgery is classed by NCEPOD as immediate, urgent, expedited or elective; morbidity and mortality are much higher in major emergency surgery when preoperative resuscitation is incomplete; any significant intra-abdominal pathology (e.g. peritonitis) means the patient is treated as having a full stomach, so the airway is protected with a cuffed tracheal tube.
• Usual history and examination; investigations include haemoglobin, U&E, blood clotting and group and save (or cross match), with arterial blood gases for base excess and lactate considered; a poorly resuscitated patient may be drowsy, and haemoglobin may look normal or high due to haemoconcentration with anaemia unmasked after resuscitation.
• Base excess of -5 mmol/L is a moderate and -10 mmol/L a severe acidosis (probably needing ICU postoperatively); lactate over 2 mmol/L implies significant anaerobic metabolism; CVP (normal 4 to 8 mmHg) guides fluid replacement.
(b)
Problems identified: dehydration and fluid or blood loss, incomplete resuscitation, full stomach with risk of aspiration, and possible postoperative deterioration.
(c)
• Correct fluid and blood loss first (the major focus), with venous access for IV fluids including blood and blood products; some patients need CVP monitoring and blood transfusion; many GI emergencies need nasogastric tubes; the aim is adequate blood pressure and heart rate before surgery; epidural analgesia may be contraindicated in this scenario.
• For the sickest patients induction in theatre rather than the anaesthetic room may be appropriate; patients may deteriorate postoperatively needing ventilation, inotropic support or renal replacement, so the appropriate level of care (ICU or high dependency) is arranged.
(d)
• The risks of surgery are discussed with the patient and/or family; in an emergency where consent cannot be obtained because of the patient's condition it is reasonable to proceed without it to save life; fasting is required before anaesthesia unless it is an emergency.
• WHO checklist sign-in before anaesthesia: identity, site, procedure, consent, site marking, allergy, difficult airway or aspiration risk, risk of more than 500 mL blood loss with adequate IV access and fluids planned.

(a)
Pain is an unpleasant sensory and emotional experience associated with actual or potential tissue damage; it is subjective, and nociception is the neural process of encoding noxious stimuli; sources: somatic (cutaneous and deep), visceral, thalamic, neuropathic, psychosomatic, referred and phantom pain; types: acute, chronic, neuropathic, nociceptive and radicular.
(b)
• Transduction: tissue-damaging stimuli (mechanical, heat, chemical) activate nerve endings; transmission: A-delta fibres carry fast pain and C fibres carry slower dull, burning pain through the dorsal horn, with the spinothalamic pathway carrying impulses to the thalamus.
• Modulation: descending control from the periaqueductal gray using endorphins and enkephalins inhibits transmission (gate control theory: large fibres close the gate); perception: subjective awareness that varies with anxiety, past experience and expectations.
• Sensitization: peripheral (inflammatory molecules such as histamine and prostaglandins lower nociceptor thresholds) and central; hyperalgesia and allodynia are its clinical markers.
(c)
• The nurse administers pharmacologic and nonpharmacologic interventions, assesses their effectiveness, monitors adverse effects, advocates for the patient and educates the patient and family.
• Assessment uses WILDA (Words, Intensity, Location, Duration, Aggravating/alleviating factors), with the Wong-Baker faces scale for paediatric and elderly patients and those with language barriers.
• Analgesia is best given when pain is first felt because repeated C-fibre input causes hyperalgesia.
• Unrelieved pain causes endocrine catabolism, sympathetic activation (hypercoagulation, increased heart rate, blood pressure and oxygen demand), ileus and immune suppression, so pain is managed with multimodal analgesia (opioids, NSAIDs, tricyclic antidepressants or anticonvulsants, local anaesthetic techniques) and non-drug methods (cutaneous stimulation, massage, TENS, distraction, relaxation, hypnosis).
(d)
• Acute pain is short in duration (minutes to about three months, sometimes up to six), tends to relate to soft-tissue injury or temporary illness and subsides when the injury heals; it can evolve into chronic pain if the injury does not heal correctly or pain signals malfunction.
• Chronic pain is longer in duration, constant or intermittent (e.g. headaches continuing over months or years), often due to a condition such as arthritis, fibromyalgia or a spine condition.
(e)
• Nociceptive pain is caused by damage to body tissue and is sharp, achy or throbbing, often from external injury, felt in joints, muscles, skin, tendons and bones, and can be acute or chronic.
• Neuropathic pain is due to damage to nerves or other parts of the nervous system, described as shooting, stabbing or burning with pins and needles, affects sensitivity to touch, and is a common type of chronic pain.
questions.question:
Discuss pain.
(a) Define pain and state its sources and types.
(b) Describe the four processes in the physiology of pain.
(c) Explain the nursing importance of pain assessment and management, including the effects of unrelieved pain.
(d) Distinguish between acute pain and chronic pain.
(e) Distinguish between nociceptive pain and neuropathic pain.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Informed consent is a crucial ethical and legal principle ensuring patients have the right to make autonomous decisions about healthcare; it is a process involving communication and understanding, not just a signature on a form, and is the permission given by the patient to proceed with an intervention such as treatment, tests or examination.
(b)
• Key elements: disclosure of information (diagnosis, treatment options including none, risks and benefits, prognosis); comprehension; decision-making capacity (a surrogate may be involved if lacking).
• Voluntary consent free from coercion; documentation (usually a signed form, verbal assent may be valid in some situations). Capacity means understanding the nature of the proposed treatment, anticipating effects and consequences of refusal.
• Types: verbal consent (usually low or no risk procedures), implied consent (co-operating with instructions for routine procedures, e.g. extending an arm for a blood pressure reading), written consent (signed for treatment or procedure carrying complex or significant risk).
(c)
• The nurse first identifies the correct person to consent; patients have the right to consent or refuse when competent and at least 18 years old, parents or guardians consent for minors, and in an emergency where consent is impossible it is reasonable to proceed to save life.
• Consent is documented with date and time once satisfied it is voluntary and understood; the teach-back method is used and the patient given the chance to ask questions; if the patient remains confused the nurse, as advocate, explains again or involves the primary physician.
(d)
• Nurses assist with patient comprehension, facilitating documentation, addressing anxiety and identifying the appropriate decision maker.
• Barriers include language barriers or insufficient information about the condition; nurses must ensure patients are informed of the treatment and its risks and agree before starting, since care without consent is unlawful.
• Nurses' responsibilities (RNs and nurse anaesthetists): maintain competence, follow protocols and procedures, advocate for patient safety (questioning orders that seem wrong), and document accurately and thoroughly.
(e)
• Negligence occurs when a healthcare professional deviates from the accepted standard of care and the deviation causes harm.
• Forms: medication errors (wrong medication, dose or route, e.g. intrathecal instead of intravenous), monitoring failures (e.g. missing awareness under anaesthesia), equipment problems (improper maintenance or use of machines), communication breakdowns, and human judgement errors.
• Prevention is through competence, following protocols, advocacy, accurate documentation and reporting concerns about potential negligence to the appropriate authorities in the facility and professional organisation; each case depends on various factors.
questions.question:
Discuss informed consent and negligence as legal aspects of anaesthetic nursing.
(a) Define informed consent.
(b) State the principles or key elements of informed consent and the types of consent.
(c) Describe the nurse's role and the steps in practice when obtaining consent.
(d) State the nurse's responsibilities and potential liabilities.
(e) Define negligence in anaesthesia, state its forms, how it is prevented and why it matters.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• CPR is a lifesaving technique used when breathing or heartbeat has stopped (e.g. heart attack); untrained rescuers give hands-only CPR (uninterrupted compressions of 100 to 120 a minute until paramedics arrive) while trained rescuers check pulse and breathing, begin compressions if none within 10 seconds, and give 30 compressions before two rescue breaths.
• Before starting check that the environment is safe and whether the person is conscious (tap or shake the shoulder and ask loudly "Are you OK?"); if help is present one person calls the emergency number and gets the AED while the other begins CPR; if alone with a phone, call first and get the AED.
(b)
• CPR adopts a C-A-B approach (compression, airway, breathing): person on their back on a firm surface, heel of the hand on the centre of the chest between the nipples with the other hand on top, elbows straight and shoulders above hands; push at least 5 cm (2 inches) but no more than 6 cm (2.4 inches) at 100 to 120 compressions a minute, letting the chest spring back.
• Airway: head-tilt, chin-lift; breathing: mouth-to-mouth (or mouth-to-nose), pinch the nostrils and seal, give a one-second breath and watch the chest rise (if it does not rise repeat head-tilt, chin-lift before the second breath); 30 compressions and two breaths is one cycle; apply an AED as soon as available, give one shock then compressions for two more minutes before a second shock, and continue until signs of movement or medical personnel take over.
(c)
• Nurses check vitals, place ECG leads, have the resuscitation cart at the bedside, insert an IV cannula, document, check pulses, apply defibrillator pads and obtain blood for analysis.
• Nurses also monitor (ICU monitoring, ventilation required, oxygenation status), assess mental status and neurovitals, check arterial blood gases and labs, check eyes for reaction to light, measure ins and outs, insert a Foley catheter and keep the patient warm.
(d)
• Child: if alone and the collapse was not seen, compress for about two minutes before calling (if seen, call first); one or two hands on the lower half of the breastbone, press about 5 cm (not more than 6 cm) at 100 to 120 a minute; with two rescuers change every two minutes and give one to two breaths every 15 compressions; use pediatric pads for children older than 4 weeks up to age 8, otherwise adult pads.
• Baby (4 weeks or older; not newborns): arrest is usually due to lack of oxygen such as choking; two fingers just below the nipple line, compress about 1.5 inches (4 cm) at 100 to 120 a minute; cover the baby's mouth and nose and give gentle puffs using the cheeks over one second; two breaths after every 30 compressions, or one to two after every 15 with two rescuers.
(e)
• Excessive ventilation is unnecessary and harmful: it causes gastric inflation with regurgitation and aspiration, and raises intrathoracic pressure, decreasing venous return, cardiac output and survival; too many breaths or too large a volume should be avoided.
• The most common cause of ventilation difficulty is an improperly opened airway, so if the chest does not rise reposition with head-tilt, chin-lift; a regular (not deep) breath prevents rescuer dizziness and overinflation of the victim's lungs.
• Compressions should not be discontinued for more than 10 seconds, interruptions are minimised and complete chest recoil allowed, because the quality of CPR is critical; inaction is harmful and CPR can be lifesaving.
• Dangers of not managing a collapse: aspiration, airway obstruction, oxygen deprivation, skin ulcerations, anoxic brain injuries, organ failure and ultimately loss of life.
questions.question:
Discuss cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) as a nursing process.
(a) Define CPR and state what is checked before starting.
(b) Describe the C-A-B procedure for an adult.
(c) List the nursing responsibilities during CPR.
(d) State how CPR differs for a child and for a baby.
(e) Explain the complications of poor CPR technique (e.g. excessive ventilation, interruptions), how they are prevented and why they matter.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Monitoring is observing and checking progress and quality over a period of time, including clinical observation and measurement and recording of relevant variables; it is used to titrate anaesthetic medication, detect physiologic changes so intervention occurs before harm, and detect and correct equipment malfunction; it cannot prevent all incidents but reduces risk by detecting the consequences of errors and giving early warning of deterioration.
(b)
Standard I: qualified anaesthesia personnel are present in the room throughout all general anaesthetics, regional anaesthetics and monitored anaesthesia care; Standard II: oxygenation, ventilation, circulation and temperature are continually evaluated during all anaesthetics.
(c)
• The anaesthetic nurse must be present and care for the patient throughout the anaesthetic; minimum monitoring devices are attached before induction and used until the patient has recovered; a summary of all monitoring information is recorded on the anaesthetic record (automated electronic records recommended).
• The nurse checks all anaesthetic and monitoring equipment before use, sets alarm limits appropriately with audible alarms enabled, notes the reason in the record if an essential monitor must be omitted, provides additional monitoring as judged appropriate and uses monitoring during transfer of anaesthetised patients.
(d)
• Oxygenation: oxygen analyser with low-oxygen alarm (FiO2, sampled downstream of the inspiratory unidirectional valve), pulse oximetry (fingers, toes, ear lobes, nasal ala), and clinical observation of mucosal colour, pupil size, lacrimation and chest movement, with a stethoscope available.
• Ventilation: breathing system disconnection or ventilator failure alarm and a carbon dioxide monitor (capnography); normal end-tidal CO2 is 35 to 45 mm Hg, above 45 indicates hypoventilation and below 35 hyperventilation; it also confirms tracheal intubation and indicates circuit disconnection, circulatory collapse, air embolism and malignant hyperthermia.
• Circulation: ECG, intermittent non-invasive BP, continuous invasive BP through an intra-arterial line, echocardiography, cardiac output monitors (pulmonary artery catheter most accurate), capillary blood glucose (target 6 to 10 mmol/l, at least hourly in diabetes on medication) and capillary ketone monitoring.
• Temperature: continuous core temperature for GA using an infrared tympanic thermometer, nasopharyngeal or oesophageal thermistor, pulmonary artery thermistor or liquid crystal forehead strip (hypothermia 35.9 deg C or less, normal 36.0 to 37.2, hyperthermia 37.3 or more); neuromuscular function with a quantitative peripheral nerve stimulator (ulnar nerve, train-of-four ratio above 0.9 before awakening and extubation); brain activity with EEG/BIS (0 to 100, lower values deeper anaesthesia).
(e)
• A hypoxic gas mixture can be delivered through hypoxic gas in the oxygen pipeline, failure of the fail-safe or nitrous oxide-oxygen proportioning system, leaks or low-flow anaesthesia with inadequate oxygen; it is prevented by a calibrated oxygen analyser with the low-oxygen alarm set.
• Poor ventilation and hypercarbia can cause respiratory acidosis and cardiovascular collapse not detected by pulse oximetry until very late on supplemental oxygen, so capnography is used; the pulse oximeter does not guarantee oxygen is delivered to and used by tissues.
• Patients under anaesthesia lose heat by radiation, convection, evaporation and conduction and severe hypothermia can delay recovery, so temperature is monitored throughout and whenever warming devices are used, to avoid over-warming.
• In a paralysed patient awareness cannot be detected clinically, so the isolated forearm technique and quantitative neuromuscular monitoring are used; monitoring all body systems prevents complications during surgery and avoids delayed recovery post operation.
questions.question:
Discuss the role of the anaesthetic nurse in patient monitoring during anaesthesia.
(a) Define monitoring and state why it is essential in anaesthesia.
(b) State the two ASA standards for basic anaesthetic monitoring.
(c) List the minimum standards and responsibilities of the anaesthetic nurse.
(d) List the monitoring techniques for oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, temperature, neuromuscular function and brain activity.
(e) Explain the complications that arise from inadequate monitoring, how they are prevented and why they matter.

Discuss antiemetic drugs used for postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV).
(a) Classify antiemetic drug groups with examples and state their actions.
(b) State their uses and side effects.
(c) State the safe-practice precautions in preventing PONV.
(d) Explain the rationale for monitoring and the management of adverse effects.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Afferents from the GI tract supply the chemoreceptor trigger zone (area postrema, outside the blood-brain barrier), which interacts with the vomiting centre in the medulla.
• Groups: antihistamines (cyclizine), anticholinergics (atropine, hyoscine), dopamine antagonists (phenothiazines such as prochlorperazine, butyrophenones such as droperidol and haloperidol, benzamides such as metoclopramide), steroids (dexamethasone), 5-HT3 antagonists (ondansetron, granisetron), benzodiazepines (lorazepam, temazepam), cannabinoids (nabilone) and ginger.
• Antihistamines act on central H1 receptors (cyclizine also has anticholinergic action); anticholinergics are non-polar, cross the blood-brain barrier, act on muscarinic receptors in the vomiting centre and GI tract, reduce secretions and tone and counteract motion and opiate-induced nausea.
• Phenothiazines act on D2 receptors; butyrophenones by central D2 antagonism; metoclopramide has D2, H1 and 5-HT3 antagonism and speeds gastric emptying; 5-HT3 antagonists act in the area postrema and GI tract; the mechanism of dexamethasone is unclear.
(b)
• Benzodiazepines are used more commonly for chemotherapy prophylaxis, cannabinoids are not used routinely for PONV (a place in chemotherapy nausea), ginger results are mixed (also used for motion sickness); P6 acupuncture stimulation preoperatively reduces PONV.
• Side effects: anticholinergics cause dry mouth and blurred vision; all dopamine antagonists can cause extrapyramidal effects (oculogyric crisis, dystonia, slurred speech); 5-HT3 antagonists cause dizziness, headache and constipation.
(c)
• Combination (multimodal) therapy acting at different sites is more effective than monotherapy (e.g. prochlorperazine, ondansetron and dexamethasone).
• At risk: female (2.5:1), previous PONV, motion sickness, non-smokers, with volatile agents, nitrous oxide, opioids, ketamine, etomidate and neostigmine adding risk.
• Prevention: ensure 6 hours' starvation from solids; in full-stomach patients give antacids and prokinetics (sodium citrate, metoclopramide); avoid nitrous oxide in at-risk patients.
• TIVA with propofol avoids nitrous oxide and volatiles; avoid hypotension (especially with spinal anaesthesia); perioperative IV fluids reduce PONV.
(d)
PONV occurs in about 30% (up to 80%) and causes aspiration (before protective reflexes return), dehydration and electrolyte disturbance, raised IOP and ICP, delayed discharge and anxiety; vomiting is active whereas regurgitation is passive and more likely when conscious level is reduced.

questions.question:
A patient at high risk of awareness is to receive general anaesthesia with a non-depolarising neuromuscular blocking drug.
(a) Describe the anaesthetic technique and the agents involved.
(b) State the monitoring and equipment set-up.
(c) Outline the nursing responsibilities and positioning of the patient.
(d) Explain how intraoperative complications such as awareness and hypothermia are prevented.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• GA is induced and maintained with a combination of intravenous and inhaled agents; the patient is unarousable to painful stimuli, amnesic and cannot maintain airway or spontaneous ventilation; when a neuromuscular blocking drug is used the capacity to respond is lost whatever the level of consciousness.
• In the isolated forearm technique a tourniquet on one upper limb is inflated above arterial pressure before the blocker is given in a vein elsewhere, so the hand can still move and the nurse can observe reflex movements or responses to command; a positive response is termed wakefulness.
(b)
• ECG, SpO2, NIBP and capnography are applied and checked before induction and continued to recovery; oxygen analyser with low-oxygen alarm; core temperature monitoring; quantitative nerve stimulator activated after induction but before blockade (ulnar nerve), with EEG or BIS monitoring (0 to 100) when clinically indicated for high awareness risk.
• IFT set-up: IV cannula in left forearm, BP cuff on right upper arm, padded tourniquet on right forearm, nerve-stimulating electrodes on ulnar and/or median nerves at right elbow; the tourniquet is deflated after 20 minutes and re-inflated for top-up doses.
(c)
• The anaesthetic nurse is present throughout, checks equipment, sets alarm limits with audible alarms enabled and records a summary of monitoring information; positioning is a team task needing timing and communication, with the goal of optimal surgical access while minimising risk, and every position carries risk magnified under anaesthesia.
• Cardiac output and BP fall under GA with blood pooling in dependent areas, especially in sitting, prone and flexed lateral positions; reverse Trendelenburg lowers brain perfusion pressure and is monitored closely; skin, eyes, breast and genitalia are vulnerable areas.
(d)
Autonomic signs are unreliable indicators of consciousness in a paralysed patient, so a hypnotic dose sufficient to prevent recall, a processed EEG or the IFT is used; train-of-four above 0.9 is demonstrated before awakening and extubation; temperature is monitored throughout, since heat is lost by radiation, convection, evaporation and conduction and severe hypothermia delays recovery.

(a)
• These are the signs of malignant hyperthermia: muscle rigidity (especially masseter muscles noticed on intubation), tachycardia, cardiovascular instability, hypercapnia (progressively increasing CO2 capnograph reading), acidosis, hyperkalaemia, cyanosis and hyperthermia or sweating; capnography monitoring gives an indication of it.
• Family history of malignant hyperthermia is asked about at assessment; suxamethonium should not be given to patients suspected to have it, and mepivacaine may potentially trigger it.
(b)
Call for help and stop surgery if possible; always ensure senior help is sought early; stop the trigger and change the anaesthetic breathing circuit; the mnemonic COVER ABCD is an aide-memoire to work through during an acute event (it accounts for about 95% of critical incidents).
(c)
Give 100% oxygen, hyperventilate, apply active cooling and give dantrolene IV; treat complications as they arise (renal failure and hyperkalaemia, coagulopathy, cardiovascular complications); temperature is monitored and life-support equipment and IV dantrolene kept readily available.
(d)
General principle: a summary of monitoring information is recorded on the anaesthetic record by the anaesthetic nurse.
questions.question:
During general anaesthesia an adult develops muscle rigidity (especially of the jaw), tachycardia, a progressively rising end-tidal CO2 and sweating.
(a) Describe how the problem is recognised.
(b) State the immediate nursing actions and how help is escalated.
(c) Outline the management, drugs and equipment prepared.
(d) Describe the documentation and follow-up.

questions.answerText:
(a)
A BP cuff is applied to the upper arm after a cannula is placed in the hand; the limb is exsanguinated by elevation or a compression bandage and the cuff inflated to 100 mmHg above systolic BP; prilocaine (preferred, or lidocaine) is injected IV and cannot spread beyond the cuff, acting within the confined area; it gives good analgesia for distal limb procedures such as fracture manipulation.
(b)
A second cannula must always be sited in the other arm for emergency use; full resuscitation facilities, including drugs and equipment for tracheal intubation, are available whenever a nerve block is performed; check allergies, inspect the ampoule, and establish baseline vital signs and monitoring (ECG, pulse oximetry).
(c)
• The cuff is let down only after at least 20 minutes so the LA can spread into adjacent tissues and prevent toxic plasma levels after systemic absorption; toxicity features: circumoral tingling, feeling of impending doom, dysrhythmias, CVS collapse, loss of consciousness, convulsions and cardiac arrest.
• Treatment is supportive (airway, IV fluids, vasopressors, seizure control, CPR if arrest) with IV lipid emulsion (Intralipid 20% 1.5 mL/kg); excess prilocaine can cause methaemoglobinaemia, treated with methylene blue.
(d)
• Monitor consciousness after injection for CNS toxicity (anxiety, dizziness, restlessness, tremors, blurred vision); monitor pulse, temperature and capillary refill every 15 minutes in the first hour, every 30 minutes in the next hour and hourly for the next four hours; position the limb in alignment, pad pressure points and restrict movement until fully recovered.
• Teach the patient about the drug, what to expect and side effects; patients without GA or sedation bypass the recovery room and go to stage 2 recovery in the day surgery unit; transfer to the ward when stable; day-surgery discharge criteria and 24-hour instructions apply.
questions.question:
A patient requires manipulation of a forearm fracture under intravenous regional anaesthesia (Bier's block).
(a) Describe the technique and agent used.
(b) Outline the nursing preparation and assistance.
(c) State the risks and side effects and how they are managed.
(d) Describe patient care, teaching and evaluation.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Invasive procedures require general anaesthesia and invasive surgeries; non-invasive procedures offer treatment without surgery or invasive techniques; the choice depends on the type of surgery, patient preference and overall health status.
• Non-invasive procedures aim at effective pain management and less discomfort while avoiding invasive risks: TENS, ultrasound guidance, topical anaesthesia, inhalational anaesthetics (nitrous oxide, sevoflurane, desflurane) and non-invasive monitoring (pulse oximetry, capnography, blood pressure).
(b)
• TENS uses low-voltage electrical currents applied to the skin to stimulate nerves and block pain signals, operating on the gate control theory (non-painful input closes the neural gates to painful input); a battery-operated unit produces tingling, vibrating or buzzing sensation.
• Components: electrodes placed over the painful area, and a pulse generator controlling frequency, intensity and duration, which patients can adjust for comfort.
• Applications: acute and chronic pain (musculoskeletal, postoperative, osteoarthritis, arthritis, back pain, headaches), physical therapy and rehabilitation, and labour pain (efficacy variable, some women benefit in early labour).
(c)
• TENS is generally safe but patient selection is crucial and it may not suit people with certain medical conditions; proper electrode placement, parameter adjustment and following guidelines are essential, and patient education on correct use is paramount.
• Ultrasound guidance gives real-time imaging for accurate nerve localisation, improves the safety of nerve blocks and vascular access, reduces complications such as nerve damage and minimises accidental injection into blood vessels.
(d)
• Non-invasive advantages: lower infection risk, faster recovery, fewer side effects, greater comfort and less anxiety, improved ambulation and potentially lower cost.
• Disadvantages: limited pain control (may need conversion to GA), unpredictable depth, need for patient cooperation, possible discomfort and limited availability.
• Invasive advantages: broader and more predictable pain control, greater haemodynamic stability, muscle relaxation, amnesia and secure airway management (e.g. endotracheal intubation).
• Invasive disadvantages: increased infection risk, longer recovery, more frequent and severe side effects, discomfort (e.g. sore throat after intubation) and potential complications such as nerve damage, bleeding or allergic reactions.
• Invasive examples: peripheral nerve blocks, epidurals and conscious sedation (e.g. midazolam, fentanyl).
questions.question:
Discuss non-invasive procedures in anaesthesia with emphasis on transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS).
(a) Define invasive and non-invasive procedures and list the non-invasive procedures.
(b) Describe TENS (principle, components, clinical applications).
(c) Explain the nursing importance of TENS and ultrasound guidance.
(d) Distinguish between invasive and non-invasive procedures (advantages and disadvantages).

During induction of general anaesthesia, a patient at risk of aspiration regurgitates gastric contents.
(a) Describe how the problem is recognised and which patients are at risk.
(b) State the immediate nursing actions and how help is escalated.
(c) Outline the management and the equipment prepared.
(d) Describe the documentation and follow-up.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Regurgitation can happen in any patient without fully functioning upper airway protective reflexes; risk factors: inadequate preoperative starvation, delayed gastric emptying (opiates, pain, bowel obstruction, pregnancy at term), insufficient or no cricoid pressure at induction, and early extubation in an at-risk patient.
• Signs: gastric contents visible within the breathing circuit or airway adjunct (e.g. LMA), changes in SaO2 and airway pressure, wheeze or stridor and tachycardia.
• Patients at risk of aspiration even after fasting include those with increased age, cerebrovascular disease, opioid use, heart failure, ischaemic heart disease, insulin-dependent diabetes, renal impairment or dialysis, hiatus hernia, acute abdomen with raised intra-abdominal pressure, gastrointestinal obstruction, pregnancy (2nd and 3rd trimester) and severe trauma.
(b)
Give 100% oxygen, call for help and place the patient in a head-down position to prevent or limit aspiration.
(c)
• Oropharyngeal suction and tracheal intubation if needed, including tracheal suctioning; some advocate antibiotics and steroids.
• Prevention: delay surgery until starvation (more than 6 hours for solids); in patients who may have a full stomach give antacids and prokinetics (e.g. sodium citrate and metoclopramide); at-risk patients need early tracheal intubation to protect the airway; succinylcholine raises intragastric pressure enough to overcome lower oesophageal sphincter tone but its use depends on body habitus, difficulty of intubation, NPO status and comorbidities.
(d)
Postoperatively the patient receives physiotherapy and oxygen.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the parts and the course of the oesophagus.
A(ii) Describe its relations.
A(iii) State its constrictions and their distances from the incisor teeth.
A(iv) Describe its arterial supply, venous drainage, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply.
B(i) Relate the upper, middle and lower parts of the oesophagus to their differing supply and relations.
C(i) Explain how disease may spread from the oesophagus to distant structures through its venous and lymphatic drainage.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
It has cervical, thoracic and abdominal parts and is not a straight structure: it lies to the left in the neck, returns to the midline at the thoracic inlet, lies to the left in the superior mediastinum, returns to the midline in the posterior mediastinum and deviates to the left as it pierces the diaphragm at T10.
A(ii)
Cervical part lies in front of the prevertebral fascia, behind the trachea; the thoracic part is crossed on the right by the azygos vein and on the left by the aorta; in the posterior mediastinum it lies behind the left main bronchus and left pulmonary artery and in front of the thoracic duct; it is the most posterior tube of the superior mediastinum and the most anterior structure of the posterior mediastinum, with the vagus nerves around it, the azygos vein behind and to the right and the descending aorta behind and to the left.
A(iii)
Four constrictions: at its origin (C6), 15 cm from the incisor teeth; where the arch of the aorta lies in front of it, 22 cm; where the left main bronchus lies in front of it (tracheal bifurcation), 27 cm; at the diaphragm (T10), 38-40 cm.
A(iv)
• Arteries: inferior thyroid artery, oesophageal branches of the descending thoracic aorta, and the left gastric artery.
• Veins: upper part to the brachiocephalic vein, middle part to the azygos vein, lower part to the portal vein.
• Lymphatics: upper part to deep cervical nodes, middle part to tracheobronchial nodes, lower part to preaortic nodes.
• Nerves: upper third is striated, supplied by the recurrent laryngeal branch of the vagus, with sympathetics from the middle cervical ganglion; lower two-thirds is smooth, receiving sympathetics from the sympathetic trunk and greater splanchnic nerve, and parasympathetic secretomotor fibres from the vagus to the oesophageal glands.
B(i)
• Upper part: inferior thyroid artery, brachiocephalic vein, deep cervical nodes, striated muscle with recurrent laryngeal supply, related to the trachea and prevertebral fascia in the neck.
• Middle and lower parts: middle drains to the azygos vein and tracheobronchial nodes and is crossed by the azygos vein, arch of the aorta and left main bronchus; lower part has aortic and left gastric arteries, portal venous drainage, preaortic nodes and smooth muscle, and passes through the diaphragm at T10.
C(i)
• Venous routes: upper part to the brachiocephalic vein, middle part to the azygos vein (which empties into the SVC and forms a communication between the SVC and IVC), lower part to the portal vein.
• Lymphatic routes: upper part to deep cervical nodes, middle part to tracheobronchial nodes, lower part to preaortic nodes.

A(i)
Adductor longus: origin — anterior surface of body of pubis, inferior to pubic crest and lateral to pubic symphysis; insertion — middle third of medial lip of linea aspera of femur; innervation — obturator nerve, anterior division (L2, L3, L4); action — adducts thigh. It is the most anteriorly placed muscle of the adductor group, large and fan-shaped. Adductor brevis: origin — body and inferior ramus of pubis; insertion — pectineal line and proximal part of linea aspera of femur; innervation — obturator nerve, anterior division (L2, L3, L4); action — adducts thigh and to an extent flexes it; it is short and lies deep to pectineus and adductor longus. Adductor magnus: largest, most powerful, most posterior muscle in the group; has an adductor part and a hamstring part. Origin — adductor part from inferior ramus of pubis and ramus of ischium; hamstring part from ischial tuberosity. Insertion — adductor part to gluteal tuberosity, linea aspera, medial supracondylar line; hamstring part to adductor tubercle of femur. Innervation — adductor part: obturator nerve (L2, L3, L4); hamstring part: tibial nerve. Action — adducts thigh; adductor part flexes, hamstring part extends. Gracilis: origin — body and inferior ramus of pubis; insertion — superior part of medial surface of tibia; innervation — obturator nerve (L2, L3); action — adducts thigh, flexes leg, helps rotate leg medially. Obturator externus: origin — margins of obturator foramen and obturator membrane; insertion — trochanteric fossa of femur; innervation — obturator nerve (L2, L3); action — laterally rotates thigh, steadies head of femur in acetabulum.
A(ii)
All adductor muscles are supplied by the obturator nerve except the hamstring part of adductor magnus and part of pectineus. The hamstring part of adductor magnus is supplied by the tibial nerve — because embryologically the hamstring part shares the same developmental origin as the true hamstrings (which arise from the ischial tuberosity and are all innervated by the tibial division of the sciatic nerve).
B(i)
The adductor hiatus is an opening between the aponeurotic distal attachment of the adductor part of adductor magnus and the tendinous distal attachment of the hamstring part. It transmits the femoral artery and vein from the adductor canal in the thigh to the popliteal fossa posterior to the knee. It is located just lateral and superior to the adductor tubercle of the femur.
B(ii)
The pes anserinus consists of the conjoined tendons of the sartorius, gracilis, and semitendinosus muscles; they insert into the superior part of the medial surface of the tibia. It acts as a secondary valgus restraint, augmenting the medial supporting structures of the knee. Bursitis of the pes anserinus bursa causes medial knee pain, especially in osteoarthritis.
C(i)
Gracilis is unique among the adductor group: it is a long strap-like muscle, the most medial and most superficial of the adductors, and the weakest member; it is the only member of the adductor group to cross both the hip and knee joints. It joins with sartorius (from the anterior compartment, supplied by femoral nerve) and semitendinosus (from the posterior compartment, supplied by tibial nerve) to form the pes anserinus — three muscles from three different compartments with three different nerve supplies share a common insertion.

A(i) Describe the origin, course, and distribution of the three types of muscle tissue under the following headings: structural features at the light microscope level, connective tissue organization (endomysium, perimysium, epimysium), and characteristic distinguishing feature of each type.
A(ii) State the safe structural basis of how skeletal muscle contraction is transmitted to produce movement.
B(i) Explain the anatomical and histological basis of why cardiac muscle does not fatigue and cannot be replaced after infarction.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Skeletal muscle: contains bundles of very long, multinucleated cells with cross-striations; contraction is quick, forceful, and usually under voluntary control. Connective tissue: endomysium surrounds individual muscle fibers (nerve fibers and capillaries form a rich network in the endomysium); perimysium surrounds fascicles; epimysium (deep fascia) surrounds the whole muscle belly and connects to tendons. Distinguishing feature: cross-striations; multinucleated; sarcomeres extending from Z disc to Z disc (~2.5 µm long in resting muscle). The A bands are anisotropic (dark); I bands are isotropic (light); each I band is bisected by the Z disc. Smooth muscle: consists of collections of fusiform cells that lack striations and have slow, involuntary contractions; elongated and spindle-shaped; single nucleus at the widest point; contain actin and myosin filaments but lack sarcomeres. Prominent locations: wall of GI tract, walls of arteries and veins, around glands. Distinguishing feature: no striations; slow, sustained contractions; non-voluntary. Cardiac muscle: cross-striations; composed of elongated, often branched cells; bound by intercalated discs unique to cardiac muscle; contraction is involuntary, vigorous, and rhythmic. Central nuclei; high cytoplasm-to-nucleus ratio. Distinguishing feature: intercalated discs; branching cells; involuntary continuous rhythmic contraction.
A(ii)
Skeletal muscle fibers show cross-striations of alternating light and dark bands. The sarcomere extends from Z disc to Z disc. During contraction, shortening of myofibrils (shortening of sarcomeres) is transmitted through the connective tissue (endomysium, perimysium, epimysium) and via tendons to bone, producing bodily movements.
B(i)
Cardiac muscle cells contain numerous mitochondria; a large proportion of cell volume is occupied by mitochondria. Fatty acids, transported by lipoproteins, are stored as triglycerides in numerous lipid droplets in cardiac muscle cells — this supports the extremely rich capillary network and strong continuous activity. Cardiac muscle has limited regenerative capacity; spaces left after infarction are filled by connective tissue forming dense irregular scar tissue, because cardiac muscle cells do not go through mitosis.

A(i)
Fibularis longus: origin — head and superior 2/3 of lateral surface of fibula; insertion — base of 1st metatarsal and medial cuneiform; innervation — superficial fibular nerve (L5, S1, S2); action — everts foot and weakly plantarflexes ankle. Fibularis brevis: origin — inferior 2/3 of lateral surface of fibula; insertion — dorsal surface of tuberosity on lateral side of base of 5th metatarsal; innervation — superficial fibular nerve (L5, S1, S2); action — everts foot and weakly plantarflexes ankle. Arterial supply: both are supplied by the fibular (peroneal) artery.
A(ii)
The common fibular nerve is the lateral, smaller terminal branch of the sciatic nerve; it begins at the superior angle of the popliteal fossa, closely follows the medial border of biceps femoris and its tendon, exits the fossa by passing superficial to the lateral head of gastrocnemius, then over the posterior aspect of the head of fibula, winds around the neck of fibula, and divides into the superficial fibular nerve (to the lateral compartment) and the deep fibular nerve (to the anterior compartment). The superficial fibular nerve runs in the lateral compartment to supply fibularis longus and brevis; its cutaneous distribution supplies the dorsum of the foot (lateral side of leg and ankle, as the sural nerve — formed by medial sural cutaneous nerve joined by the sural communicating branch of the common fibular nerve — supplies the lateral side of leg and ankle).
B(i)
Fibularis longus inserts onto the base of the 1st metatarsal and medial cuneiform on the plantar aspect of the foot — it therefore acts as a stirrup, pulling the medial forefoot downward and laterally, producing eversion and weak plantarflexion. Fibularis brevis inserts onto the tuberosity of the base of the 5th metatarsal on the lateral side of the foot — it abducts the forefoot and everts the foot. The lateral longitudinal arch (made of calcaneus, cuboid, and 4th and 5th metatarsals) is supported by peroneus longus and brevis; muscles of the lateral arch include peroneus longus and brevis, flexor digitorum longus, and short muscles of the little toe.
B(ii)
The transverse arch muscles include peroneus longus and brevis, transverse head of adductor hallucis, and slips of tibialis posterior. Fibularis longus, by crossing under the foot from the lateral side to insert medially at the base of the 1st metatarsal, acts as a dynamic tie-beam, pulling the medial and lateral borders of the foot together and maintaining the curvature of the transverse arch; adductor hallucis transverse head also assists by pulling metatarsals medially.
C(i)
Superficial fibular nerve injury (at fibular neck): loss of eversion of the foot (fibularis longus and brevis paralysed); weakness of plantarflexion; sensory loss on dorsum of foot. Deep fibular nerve injury (at fibular neck): loss of dorsiflexion (tibialis anterior paralysed) and toe extension (extensor digitorum longus, extensor hallucis longus paralysed); loss of eversion contribution of fibularis tertius; result is foot drop with the foot held in plantarflexion and inversion; sensory loss is limited to the 1st web space (between 1st and 2nd toes). Injury to the common fibular nerve at the fibular neck produces both effects combined — foot drop with loss of both dorsiflexion and eversion.

(i) Describe the gross anatomy of the liver under the headings: surfaces, lobes, fissures and peritoneal ligaments.
(ii) Relate the lobes/fissures of the liver to common hepatic pathology.
(iii) Explain how liver disease can spread its effects to a distant structure, producing a functional deficit there.
questions.answerText:
(i)
• The liver has two surfaces - a convex diaphragmatic surface (anterior, superior, posterior and right lateral) and a relatively flat, posteroinferior visceral surface.
• It is divided into a large right lobe and a smaller left lobe by the falciform ligament, with the caudate and quadrate lobes arising from the right lobe on the visceral surface.
• Two sagittally oriented fissures (for the ligamentum teres and ligamentum venosum on the left, and the gallbladder fossa and IVC groove on the right) are linked by the transverse porta hepatis, forming an H on the visceral surface.
• Ligaments include the falciform ligament, the coronary ligament with the right and left triangular ligaments, and the lesser omentum (hepatogastric and hepatoduodenal ligaments).
• The porta hepatis transmits the hepatic ducts, hepatic artery and portal vein branches, and hepatic nerves and lymph nodes.
(ii)
• The bare area of the diaphragmatic surface has no peritoneal covering, so infection there can track through the diaphragm to posterior mediastinal lymph nodes.
• The subphrenic and subhepatic spaces, and Morison's pouch between the liver and right kidney, are recesses where pathological fluid such as pus, blood or ascites collects.
• Liver fissures serve as surgical landmarks, such as Cantlie's line, which divides the liver into functional right and left lobes along the middle hepatic vein.
• Because the liver is large, fixed in position and friable, it is vulnerable to rupture, often from a fractured rib perforating the diaphragm, causing haemorrhage and right upper quadrant pain.
(iii)
• In cirrhosis, hepatocytes are destroyed and replaced by fibrous tissue that impedes blood flow through the liver, causing portal hypertension.
• This opens portal-systemic anastomoses at the lower oesophagus, anal canal, paraumbilical region, retroperitoneum and intrahepatic sites, producing distant complications such as bleeding oesophageal varices.
• Distension of Glisson's capsule from an enlarged liver produces sharp, well-localised pain via the lower intercostal nerves, illustrating how a hepatic process produces a distant sensory effect.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the origin, structural components, and classification of neurons under the following headings: cell body (soma), dendrites, axon, myelin sheath, nodes of Ranvier, and neurilemma.
A(ii) State the basis of why local anaesthetics block nerve impulse transmission.
B(i) Explain the anatomical basis of why nerve fibers within the CNS do not regenerate after injury, while peripheral nerve fibers may regenerate.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Cell body (soma): The neuronal cell body is similar to other cell types; it has a nucleus with at least one nucleolus and many typical cytoplasmic organelles. It lacks centrioles, which is consistent with the amitotic nature of neurons. Dendrites: Dendrites are cytoplasmic extensions that project from the cell body; they are usually short and branching, increasing their surface area to receive signals from other neurons. The number of dendrites varies. They are called afferent processes because they transmit impulses to the neuron cell body. Axon: There is only one axon projecting from each cell body; it is usually elongated and carries impulses away from the cell body, so it is called an efferent process. Axons may have infrequent branches called axon collaterals; these terminate in short branches or telodendria, whose distal ends are slightly enlarged to form synaptic bulbs. Myelin sheath: Many axons are surrounded by a segmented, white, fatty substance called myelin or myelin sheath. Myelinated fibers make up the white matter in the CNS, while cell bodies and unmyelinated fibers make the gray matter. Nodes of Ranvier: The unmyelinated regions between myelin segments are called nodes of Ranvier. Neurilemma: In the peripheral nervous system, myelin is produced by Schwann cells. The cytoplasm, nucleus, and outer cell membrane of the Schwann cell form a tight covering around the myelin and around the axon at the nodes of Ranvier — this covering is the neurilemma, which plays an important role in regeneration of nerve fibers.
A(ii)
Most local anesthetics are low-molecular-weight molecules that bind to the voltage-gated sodium channels of the axolemma, interfering with sodium ion influx and, consequently, inhibiting the action potential responsible for the nerve impulse.
B(i)
In the CNS, oligodendrocytes produce myelin, but there is no neurilemma. It is the neurilemma that plays an important role in regeneration of nerve fibers; therefore fibers within the CNS do not regenerate because they lack neurilemma.

A(i)
The ulnar nerve is an extension of the medial cord of the brachial plexus.
A(ii)
The most common sites of ulnar nerve entrapment are: above the elbow in the region of the intermuscular septum; the medial epicondylar region; the epicondylar (ulnar) groove; the region of the cubital tunnel; and the region where the nerve exits from flexor carpi ulnaris, where compression is usually caused by the deep flexor-pronator aponeurosis.
A(iii)
• In the forearm it supplies flexor carpi ulnaris and the medial (3rd & 4th) part of flexor digitorum profundus.
• In the hand it supplies the hypothenar muscles, adductor pollicis, flexor pollicis brevis, the palmar and dorsal interossei, the 3rd and 4th lumbricals, and the muscles of digiti minimi (abductor, opponens, flexor digiti minimi).
A(iv)
It provides sensation to the medial surface of the hand and the medial half of the 4th and 5th digits, on both palmar and dorsal aspects, through its superficial branch; its motor functions include finger adduction and abduction other than the thumb, thumb adduction, flexion of digits 4 and 5, and wrist flexion and adduction.
C
• Injury to the ulnar nerve, or to the medial cord/lower trunk from which it derives, produces a claw hand deformity.
• This deformity arises from the unopposed action of the long flexors and extensors of the fingers once the ulnar-innervated intrinsic muscles (interossei, medial lumbricals) are paralysed.
• In a claw hand there is hyperextension at the metacarpophalangeal joints and flexion at the interphalangeal joints.
• Where the injury occurs at the level of the medial cord (e.g. from subcoracoid dislocation of the humerus), the ulnar nerve and medial root of median nerve are both involved.
• This produces sensory loss on the ulnar side of the forearm and hand, along with vasomotor and trophic changes.
• The claw hand deformity, together with the specific pattern of muscle paralysis, thus reflects the level and combination of nerve fibres interrupted along the course of the ulnar nerve or its parent cord/trunk.
questions.question:
Describe the ulnar nerve:
A(i) Origin
A(ii) Course and common entrapment sites
A(iii) Muscles innervated (forearm and hand)
A(iv) Sensory distribution

questions.answerText:
A(i)
The duodenum is the first, shortest (about 25 cm) and widest part of the small intestine; it is C-shaped and mostly retroperitoneal, made up of four parts - superior (5 cm), descending (7.5-8 cm), horizontal (6-10 cm) and ascending (2.5 cm).
A(ii)
The proximal 2.5 cm of the superior part is movable and intraperitoneal, attached to the lesser omentum above and greater omentum below; the rest of the duodenum is retroperitoneal, covered by peritoneum only on its anterior aspect.
A(iii)
The superior part is anteriorly related to the quadrate lobe of the liver and gallbladder, and posteriorly to the gastroduodenal artery, bile duct, portal vein and inferior vena cava; the descending part is related medially to the head of pancreas and bile duct, laterally to the right colic flexure, and rests on the right kidney, ureter, psoas major and renal vessels, and receives the major duodenal papilla; the horizontal part crosses the inferior vena cava, aorta and L3 vertebra and is crossed anteriorly by the superior mesenteric vessels; the ascending part rises to the duodenojejunal flexure.
B
• The proximal (superior) part of the duodenum is the most common site of duodenal ulcer.
• The duodenojejunal flexure is fixed by the suspensory muscle of the duodenum (ligament of Treitz), which passes posterior to the pancreas and splenic vein and anterior to the left renal vein; a weakness near this fixed flexure is the anatomical basis for a paraduodenal hernia.
C
• The jejunum lies mainly in the left upper (infracolic) quadrant, has thicker, more vascular walls and a wider, often empty lumen, with long and few vasa recta, one or two layers of arterial arcades, numerous circular mucosal folds, and large, thick, abundant villi.
• The ileum lies predominantly in the right lower quadrant and pelvis, has thinner, less vascular walls and a narrower, often loaded lumen, with short and numerous vasa recta and multiple layers of arterial arcades.
• The ileum has smaller and sparser circular mucosal folds and shorter, thinner villi than the jejunum, but the terminal ileum has numerous Peyer's patches and more numerous solitary lymphatic follicles, which are absent or scanty in the jejunum.
• The jejunum has mesenteric windows and less abundant mesenteric fat, whereas the ileum has no windows and more abundant mesenteric fat.
questions.question:
(A) Describe the duodenum under the headings: A(i) parts and dimensions A(ii) peritoneal relations A(iii) visceral relations.
(B) Explain the clinical basis for the duodenum's common site of ulceration and for paraduodenal hernia.
(C) Distinguish between the jejunum and the ileum.

A(i) Describe the temporomandibular joint (TMJ) under the following headings: articular surfaces, articular capsule, and synovial membranes/compartments.
A(ii) Describe the ligaments of the TMJ.
B. Explain the clinical basis for why TMJ dislocation is commoner in the aged and in females.
C. Distinguish between the intrinsic (lateral) ligament and the extrinsic ligaments (sphenomandibular and stylomandibular) of the TMJ.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The articular surfaces of the TMJ are the condyle of the mandible (inferior) and the articular tubercle/mandibular fossa of the temporal bone (squamous part). The articular capsule is loose and fibrous, attaching to the margins of the articular area on the temporal bone and around the neck of the mandible. The superior synovial membrane lines the fibrous capsule superior to the articular disc, and the inferior synovial membrane lines the capsule inferior to the disc; the joint is divided into two compartments (superior and inferior) by an articular disc of fibrocartilage.
A(ii)
The ligaments of the TMJ are divided into an intrinsic ligament and extrinsic ligaments. The intrinsic ligament, also known as the lateral ligament, is the thick part of the articular capsule, strengthens the TMJ laterally, and prevents posterior dislocation of the TMJ. The extrinsic ligaments are the sphenomandibular ligament, which runs from the spine of the sphenoid to the lingula of the mandible and is the primary passive support of the mandible, and the stylomandibular ligament, a thickening of the fibrous capsule of the parotid gland, extending from the styloid process of the temporal bone to the angle of the mandible, which does not contribute significantly to the strength of the joint.
B
Dislocation of the TMJ is common in aged persons and females, due to wearing and resorption of the articular eminence and reducing muscle tone with advancing age.
C
The intrinsic (lateral) ligament is the thick part of the articular capsule, strengthens the joint laterally and prevents posterior dislocation. The sphenomandibular ligament, by contrast, runs from the spine of the sphenoid to the lingula of the mandible and is the primary passive support of the mandible, while the stylomandibular ligament is a thickening of the fibrous capsule of the parotid gland, running from the styloid process to the angle of the mandible, and does not contribute significantly to the strength of the joint.

A(i)
Quadriceps femoris forms the main bulk of the anterior thigh muscles; it collectively constitutes the largest and one of the most powerful muscles of the body. It covers almost all the anterior aspect and sides of the femur. It is the great extensor of the leg. It consists of 4 muscles: rectus femoris, vastus lateralis, vastus medialis, and vastus intermedius. The tendons of the four parts unite in the distal portion of the thigh to form a single, strong, broad tendon — the quadriceps tendon; this continues as the patellar ligament (in which the patella is embedded) and is attached to the tibial tuberosity.
A(ii)
Rectus femoris — origin: anterior inferior iliac spine and ilium superior to acetabulum; insertion: via common quadriceps tendon and patellar ligament to tibial tuberosity; innervation: femoral nerve (L2, L3, L4); action: extends leg at knee joint, steadies hip joint, and helps iliopsoas flex thigh. It is the only part of the quadriceps that crosses the hip joint, named because it runs straight down the thigh. Vastus lateralis — origin: greater trochanter and lateral lip of linea aspera of femur; same insertion and innervation; action: extends leg at knee joint; it is the largest component. Vastus medialis — origin: intertrochanteric line and medial lip of linea aspera of femur; same insertion and innervation; action: extends leg at knee joint; inferior fibres are particularly important in stabilising the knee joint. Vastus intermedius — origin: anterior and lateral surfaces of shaft of femur; same insertion and innervation; action: extends leg at knee joint; lies deep to rectus femoris between the vastus medialis and lateralis.
B(i)
The quadriceps is the primary extensor of the knee — the most important movement for standing, walking, climbing stairs, and rising from a chair. Stability of the knee joint depends on the strength and action of surrounding muscles and tendons; the quadriceps femoris is most important in stabilising the knee joint. Paralysis means the patient cannot extend the knee or control descent on stairs, rendering them unable to walk safely without a brace.
B(ii)
All four components of the quadriceps are innervated by the femoral nerve (L2, L3, L4). The femoral nerve also supplies the hip joint via intermediate and cutaneous branches and the skin of the front and medial side of the thigh (Hilton's law). Loss of knee extension eliminates the ability to straighten or stabilise the knee against gravity — the most critical functional deficit for bipedal locomotion.
C(i)
Quadriceps femoris: origin from femur and ilium; action — extends the knee (and rectus femoris also flexes the hip); nerve supply — femoral nerve (L2, L3, L4). Hamstrings (semitendinosus, semimembranosus, biceps femoris): origin from ischial tuberosity (long head of biceps femoris and both semi-muscles) and linea aspera (short head of biceps femoris); action — extend the thigh, flex the leg, and rotate it (semitendinosus and semimembranosus medially, biceps femoris laterally); nerve supply — tibial division of sciatic nerve for semitendinosus, semimembranosus, and long head of biceps femoris; common fibular division of sciatic nerve for short head of biceps femoris. The quadriceps is 3 times stronger than its antagonist muscle group (the hamstrings).
questions.question:

A(ii) Origin, insertion, innervation, and action of each component
B(i) Why paralysis of the quadriceps femoris produces more functional disability than paralysis of the hamstrings
B(ii) The femoral nerve — its role in supplying the quadriceps and why knee extension is the most critical movement lost
