A(i) Describe the immunological defence system of the gastrointestinal tract, including: the name of the tissue system; the layers of the GIT wall it occupies; the cell types it contains; and the antibody it produces.
A(ii) Explain the complete mechanism by which IgA protects the lumen of the GIT from pathogens, including the role of the secretory protein and the property that makes IgA effective.
B(i) State which regions of the GIT are lined by stratified squamous epithelium rather than the simple thin vulnerable epithelium lining the rest of the tract, and explain the significance of this difference in the context of microbial defense.
B(ii) Explain the clinical and anatomical basis for the well-known effects of emotional stress on the stomach and other regions of the GIT.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Immunological defense system:
• Name: Mucosa-Associated Lymphoid Tissue (MALT).
• Layers occupied: the mucosa (especially the lamina propria located just below the epithelium) and the submucosal layers.
• Cell types: macrophages and lymphocytes (some of which actively produce antibodies); also free immune cells and lymphoid nodules.
• Antibody produced: mainly immunoglobulin A (IgA).
A(ii)
IgA protection mechanism:
• IgA antibodies undergo transcytosis into the intestinal lumen, bound to the secretory protein produced by epithelial cells.
• This complex (secretory IgA) protects against viral and bacterial pathogens.
• IgA is resistant to proteolytic enzymes and can therefore coexist with the proteases present in the lumen, making it effective even in the enzyme-rich intestinal environment.
B(i)
Stratified squamous epithelium lines the oral cavity, esophagus, and anal canal (not vulnerable simple columnar). The rest of the GIT (except these three regions) is lined by a simple thin vulnerable epithelium. Because the rest of the GIT is lined by this vulnerable epithelium and normally contains thousands of microbial species (including potential pathogens), the MALT provides an essential backup to the thin physical barrier.
B(ii)
The enteric nervous system (submucosal/Meissner and myenteric/Auerbach plexuses) provides an anatomic basis for the well-known actions of emotional stress on the stomach and other regions of the GIT. These plexuses are interconnected with the autonomic nervous system and CNS.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the three parts of the renal tubule, including the cell type lining each part, distinguishing microscopic features, and the primary function (reabsorption vs. secretion) attributed to each part.
A(ii) Describe the two parts of the nephron loop, including the type of epithelium lining each limb and any variation across nephron types.
B(i) Describe the renal corpuscle, naming its two components, the two layers of the glomerular capsule, and the specialised features of the visceral layer.
B(ii) For the proximal convoluted tubule, explain how its structure is adapted for its function.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Three parts of the renal tubule:
• Proximal convoluted tubule (PCT): cuboidal cells with dense microvilli (brush border — increase surface area); large mitochondria; functions in reabsorption and secretion; confined to the cortex.
• Nephron loop: descending and ascending limbs; distal descending limb = descending thin limb — simple squamous epithelium; thick ascending limb — cuboidal to columnar cells (thin in some nephrons).
• Distal convoluted tubule (DCT): cuboidal cells with very few microvilli; functions more in secretion than reabsorption; confined to the cortex.
A(ii)
Nephron loop:
• Descending limb: proximal descending limb is continuous with the proximal tubule; distal descending limb (thin limb) is lined by simple squamous epithelium.
• Thick ascending limb: cuboidal to columnar cells; may be thin in some nephrons.
B(i)
Renal corpuscle:
• Two components: glomerulus and glomerular (Bowman's) capsule.
• Glomerulus: tuft of capillaries with fenestrated endothelium (highly porous) allowing filtrate formation.
Glomerular capsule: cup-shaped, hollow structure surrounding the glomerulus; has two layers:
• Parietal layer: simple squamous epithelium.
• Visceral layer: branching epithelial podocytes; extensions terminate in foot processes that cling to the basement membrane; filtration slits between foot processes allow filtrate to pass into the capsular space.
B(ii)
Structural adaptations of the PCT:
• Dense microvilli (brush border) greatly increase the apical surface area for reabsorption.
• Large mitochondria provide energy (ATP) for active transport processes.
• Highly infolded basolateral membrane increases surface area for solute exchange at the basolateral side.
• These features together support the PCT's role in reabsorption and secretion.

questions.question:
A. Describe the course and distribution of the lingual nerve, including its relationship to the submandibular duct.
B. State the site at which the lingual nerve crosses the submandibular duct, which is relevant to procedures in this region.
C. Explain the functional deficit that would be anticipated from injury to the lingual nerve, based on the sensory territory it supplies.
questions.answerText:
A
The lingual nerve is a branch of the mandibular nerve (CN V3). It provides sensory supply to the mucous membrane of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue. In its course, the submandibular duct (Wharton's duct) runs forwards on hyoglossus, between the lingual and hypoglossal nerves.
B
At the anterior border of hyoglossus, the submandibular duct is crossed by the lingual nerve; this crossing relationship is anatomically relevant, since a stone in the submandibular duct can be felt bimanually in the floor of the mouth, and surgery/removal in this region places the lingual nerve at risk, along with the hypoglossal nerve, given their close relationship to the duct on hyoglossus.
C
Sensory supply to the mucous membrane of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is via the lingual nerve (a branch of CN V3), while special (taste) sensory supply to the same region is via the chorda tympani nerve (a branch of CN VII); injury to the lingual nerve would therefore be expected to impair general sensation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, distinct from a taste deficit, which would instead follow injury to the chorda tympani.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the cell cycle under the following headings: definition, phases (G1, S, G2, M), and the two key regulatory molecules that control progression through the cycle.
A(ii) Explain the clinical consequences of errors in mitosis, naming three chromosomal abnormalities that can result.
B(i) Distinguish between apoptosis and necrosis, giving the distinguishing morphological changes and clinical consequences of each.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Definition: The cell cycle, or cell-division cycle, is the series of events that takes place in a cell leading to its division and duplication (replication). In cells with a nucleus (eukaryotes), the cell cycle can be divided into two brief periods: interphase (during which the cell grows, accumulates nutrients needed for mitosis and duplicates its DNA) and the mitosis (M) phase (during which the cell splits itself into two distinct cells, often called daughter cells). Phases: G1 (Gap 1) — cell grows; S phase (synthesis) — chromosomes are replicated; G2 (Gap 2) — cell grows more and prepares for mitosis; M phase (mitosis and cytokinesis) — cell division. Cells that have temporarily or reversibly stopped dividing are said to have entered the G0 phase (quiescence). Two key regulatory molecules: cyclins and cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs), which determine a cell's progress through the cell cycle.
A(ii)
In non-disjunction, a chromosome may fail to separate during anaphase: one daughter cell will receive both sister chromosomes (leading to trisomy — three copies) and the other will receive none (leading to monosomy — one copy). These cells are considered aneuploid, a condition often associated with cancer. Other chromosomal abnormalities: deletion — an arm of the chromosome may be broken and the fragment lost. Translocation — the fragment incorrectly reattaches to another, non-homologous chromosome. Inversion — the fragment reattaches to the original chromosome in reverse orientation. The effect may range from no noticeable effect to cancer induction or organism death.
B(i)
Apoptosis (programmed cell death): biochemical events lead to characteristic cell changes including blebbing, loss of cell membrane asymmetry and attachment, cell shrinkage, nuclear fragmentation, chromatin condensation, and chromosomal DNA fragmentation. Apoptosis differs from necrosis in that the cellular debris does not damage the organism. Necrosis: a form of traumatic cell death that results from acute cellular injury; cellular debris can damage the organism. Clinical consequences: excessive apoptosis causes atrophy (e.g., ischemic damage); insufficient apoptosis results in uncontrolled cell proliferation such as cancer.

A(i)
The most common sites of ulnar nerve entrapment around the elbow are: above the elbow, in the region of the intermuscular septum; the medial epicondylar region; the epicondylar (ulnar) groove; the region of the cubital tunnel; and the point where the nerve exits from flexor carpi ulnaris, where the usual cause of compression is the deep flexor-pronator aponeurosis.
A(ii)
Medially, in relation to the elbow joint, the ulnar nerve passes behind the medial epicondyle and crosses the medial collateral ligament of the joint.
B
• The medial epicondyle of the humerus bears a groove on its posterior aspect specifically for the ulnar nerve, and the medial epicondyle is the larger of the two epicondyles, extending more distally.
• This places the ulnar nerve in a relatively superficial, subcutaneous position as it passes behind the medial epicondyle and through the cubital tunnel region, making it vulnerable to direct trauma and to compression at each of the sites listed above.
• Ulnar nerve injuries are recognised as a distinct item of applied anatomy at the elbow, alongside subluxation/dislocation of the radial head, the carrying angle, olecranon bursitis, avulsion of the medial epicondyle, and dislocation with Volkmann's ischaemic contracture.
C
• The ulnar nerve's entrapment region at the elbow lies behind the medial epicondyle of the humerus, where it crosses the medial collateral ligament of the elbow joint, and where compression is often caused by the deep flexor-pronator aponeurosis as the nerve exits between the heads of flexor carpi ulnaris.
• The median nerve's tunnel at the wrist, the carpal tunnel, differs in that it has a defined bony floor — the carpal sulcus, bounded laterally by the scaphoid and trapezium and medially by the hook of hamate and pisiform — roofed by the fibrous flexor retinaculum.
• The carpal tunnel additionally transmits eight flexor tendons and the tendon of flexor pollicis longus alongside the median nerve, whereas other tendons sharing the ulnar nerve's entrapment site at the elbow are not described.
• Both regions, however, are sites where a single major nerve is placed in a confined space adjacent to bone, predisposing it to compression.
• At the elbow, injury or entrapment of the ulnar nerve is associated with claw hand and sensory/motor deficits in the ulnar nerve distribution of the hand and forearm.
• At the wrist, compression of the median nerve within the carpal tunnel produces carpal tunnel syndrome, with sensory disturbance in the lateral three and a half digits and weakness of the thenar muscles.
• The comparison illustrates a shared anatomical principle, nerve entrapment at a narrow passage, applied to two different nerves at two different levels of the upper limb.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
The gluteal region is the region of the buttock. Bony landmarks — surface anatomy: iliac crest, gluteus medius, tip of greater trochanter, gluteus maximus (fold of buttock), ischial tuberosity, tip of coccyx, natal cleft, posterior superior iliac spine (PSIS), sciatic nerve. Bones: os coxae (ilium, ischium, pubis) and femur.
A(ii)
Superficial fascia: thick in women; impregnated with large quantities of fat, hence the prominence of the buttock. Deep fascia: continuous with fascia lata of the thigh. The 9 muscles: gluteus maximus, gluteus medius, gluteus minimus, tensor fasciae latae (superficial layer); piriformis, obturator internus, gemellus superior, gemellus inferior, quadratus femoris (deep layer). Deep layer muscles all have distal attachments on or adjacent to the intertrochanteric crest of the femur; they are lateral rotators of the thigh and stabilise the hip joint. Obturator internus, superior gemellus, and inferior gemellus form the triceps coxae of the hip.
B(i)
6 nerves of the gluteal region: sciatic nerve (L4, 5; S1, 2, 3); posterior cutaneous nerve of the thigh; superior gluteal nerve; inferior gluteal nerve; nerve to quadratus femoris; pudendal nerve. (Nerve to obturator internus also exits here.) The sciatic nerve curves downward midway between the tuber ischii and the greater trochanter.
B(ii)
4 arteries: superior gluteal artery (SGA), inferior gluteal artery (IGA), medial femoral circumflex artery (MFCA), lateral femoral circumflex artery (LFCA). Trochanteric anastomosis (TA) — main blood supply to the head of femur: SGA, IGA, MFCA, LFCA. Cruciate anastomosis (CA) — situated at the level of the lesser trochanter: IGA, MFCA, LFCA, and 1st perforating branch of profunda femoris. The CA jointly with the TA provides a connection between the femoral arteries and the internal iliac arteries.
C(i)
Sacrotuberous ligament (STL) and sacrospinous ligament (SSL): (1) both stabilise the sacrum and prevent its rotation at the sacroiliac joint by the weight of the vertebral column; (2) in conjunction with bones, they form the greater sciatic foramen (GSF) and lesser sciatic foramen (LSF). Functions of GSF and LSF: GSF provides an exit from the pelvis into the gluteal region. LSF (1) provides an entrance into the perineum from the gluteal region; (2) enables nerves and vessels that left the pelvis through the GSF above the pelvic floor to enter the perineum below the pelvic floor.

A(i) Describe the orbit under the following headings: shape, the bones forming it, and its average dimensions.
A(ii) Describe the three openings into the orbital cavity and the structures transmitted through each, and describe the connective tissue planes of the orbit.
B. Explain the clinical basis for why orbital trauma can result in double vision and in a rise of intraocular pressure.
C. Distinguish between the superior orbital fissure and the inferior orbital fissure in terms of the structures each transmits.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The orbit is shaped like a pear or quadrilateral pyramid, with its base in the plane of the orbital rim and its pyramidal cavity base in front and apex behind; it protects, supports and maximises the function of the eye, and seven bones conjoin to form the orbital structure. The average dimensions of the orbit are: height of orbital margin 40 mm, width of orbital margin 35 mm, depth of orbit 40-50 mm, interorbital distance 25 mm, and volume of orbit 30 cm³; 20% of this space is occupied by the eyeball, and about one-sixth of the eye is exposed, the remainder being protected by the walls of the orbit.
A(ii)
The major nerves and vessels to the orbit and globe enter through 3 openings. The superior orbital fissure, bounded by the lesser and greater wings of the sphenoid, transmits cranial nerves III, IV and VI, the lacrimal nerve, frontal nerve, nasociliary nerve, orbital branch of the middle meningeal artery, recurrent branch of the lacrimal artery, superior orbital vein and superior ophthalmic vein. The inferior orbital fissure, bounded by the greater wing of the sphenoid, the maxilla and the palatine bones, transmits the infraorbital nerve, zygomatic nerve, parasympathetics to the lacrimal gland, infraorbital artery, infraorbital vein, and the inferior ophthalmic vein branch to the pterygoid plexus. The optic canal, at the apex of the orbit within the sphenoid bone, transmits the optic nerve, ophthalmic artery, and central retinal vein. The connective tissue boundaries of the orbit are divided into 4 main units: the bulbar (Tenon) fascia, surrounding and protecting the globe and providing a barrier between the globe and retrobulbar fat; multiple connective tissue septa extending from the globe to the periorbita like spokes on a wheel; the individual connective tissue sheath of each extraocular muscle, which fuses to form a confluent muscle sheath and the medial and lateral check ligaments; and the periosteal lining of the orbit, which can be elevated in surgery to expose the bony orbit.
B
Clinical correlates of the orbit include eye trauma with blow-out fracture, due to blunt trauma, which displaces the orbital walls; paralysis of the extraocular muscles results in double vision. Obstruction of the flow of aqueous humor results in a rise in intraocular pressure called glaucoma, leading to degenerative changes in the retina with consequent blindness.
C
The superior orbital fissure transmits cranial nerves III, IV and VI, the lacrimal, frontal and nasociliary nerves, the orbital branch of the middle meningeal artery, the recurrent branch of the lacrimal artery, and the superior orbital and superior ophthalmic veins. The inferior orbital fissure, in contrast, transmits the infraorbital nerve, the zygomatic nerve, parasympathetics to the lacrimal gland, the infraorbital artery and vein, and the inferior ophthalmic vein branch to the pterygoid plexus.

A(i)
• Formed by the ventral rami of L1, L2, L3 and the upper part of L4; the lower part of L4 joins L5 to form the lumbosacral trunk.
• The rami emerge from the intervertebral foramina, enter psoas, give branches to psoas and quadratus lumborum, then form the plexus within the substance of psoas major.
A(ii)
• Iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal: L1; genitofemoral: L1, L2; lateral femoral cutaneous: L2, L3 (posterior division).
• Femoral: L2, L3, L4 (posterior division); obturator: L2, L3, L4 (anterior division); sometimes an accessory obturator L3, L4.
A(iii)
• From the lateral border of psoas major: iliohypogastric, ilioinguinal, lateral femoral cutaneous, femoral.
• Through psoas anteriorly: genitofemoral; from the medial border: obturator.
A(iv)
• It innervates part of the lower abdominal wall but chiefly supplies skin and muscle 'borrowed from the trunk by the lower limb'.
• The genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve supplies the cremasteric muscle; the ilioinguinal nerve runs in the inguinal canal.
B(i)
The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve normally passes deep to the lateral end of the inguinal ligament; sometimes it passes through the substance of the ligament.
C(i)
• Entrapment causes pain along its distribution (meralgia paresthetica).
• Psoas major is supplied by ventral rami L1 to L4, psoas minor by L1, quadratus lumborum by upper lumbar and subcostal nerves, iliacus by the femoral nerve.

A(i)
Oblique, tunnel-shaped passage through the lower part of the anterior abdominal wall just above the medial half of the inguinal ligament, present in both sexes; about 4 cm (1½ inches) long in adults, directed downwards, forwards and medially.
A(ii)
It extends from the deep inguinal ring to the superficial inguinal ring; in the newborn the deep ring lies almost directly posterior to the superficial ring.
A(iii)
• Anterior wall: external oblique aponeurosis, reinforced laterally by internal oblique. Posterior wall: transversalis fascia, reinforced medially by the conjoint tendon.
• Roof: arching lowest fibres of internal oblique and transversus abdominis with transversalis fascia. Floor: inguinal ligament, reinforced medially by the lacunar ligament.
A(iv)
Spermatic cord (male) or round ligament of uterus (female); processus vaginalis remnant; 3 fasciae; 3 arteries (artery to vas, cremasteric, testicular); 3 nerves (ilio-inguinal L1, genital branch of genitofemoral L2, sympathetic); vas, pampiniform plexus, lymphatics.
B(i)
• It is a potential weakness in the abdominal wall. The posterior wall is weak laterally at the deep ring, but the anterior wall opposite is reinforced by internal oblique, so a hernia through the deep ring must travel along the canal.
• The anterior wall is weak medially at the superficial ring, but the posterior wall opposite is reinforced by the conjoint tendon; weakness there leads to direct hernias.
B(ii)
In the male it allows spermatic cord structures to pass to and from the testis (normal spermatogenesis needs the cooler scrotum) while preventing intestine entering the scrotum; in the female the smaller canal carries the round ligament of the uterus to the labium majus.
C(i)
• Deep ring: oval opening in the transversalis fascia, about ½ inch (1.3 cm) above the inguinal ligament at the midinguinal point, lateral to the inferior epigastric artery; margins give attachment to internal spermatic fascia; entrance of the cord.
• Superficial ring: triangular defect in the external oblique aponeurosis, immediately above and medial to the pubic tubercle; its medial and lateral crura give attachment to the external spermatic fascia; it is the exit of the cord from the canal.

A(i)
• The sacrum is formed by the union of 5 sacral vertebrae (fusion begins at 16 to 18 years, usually complete by 30); wedge-shaped; concave anterior surface with four transverse lines and four pairs of anterior sacral foramina.
• Dorsally a median sacral crest and posterior foramina; the sacral canal is continuous with the vertebral canal; an auricular surface forms the sacroiliac joint; structures emerge at the sacral hiatus.
A(ii)
• Each hip bone is three bones (ilium, pubis, ischium) separated by cartilage in the newborn and fused at puberty in the acetabulum; the ilium is the largest, with ala, body, crest, spines, greater sciatic notch, iliac fossa, auricular surface and arcuate line.
• Ischium: body, ramus, spine, lesser sciatic notch and tuberosity; pubis: superior and inferior rami, body, crest, tubercle, iliopectineal line; ischium and pubis surround the obturator foramen.
A(iii)
Two hip bones united at the pubic symphysis and with the sacrum at the sacroiliac joints; the girdle moves as a unit and supports and protects lower abdominal and pelvic organs; the pelvic brim divides true and false pelves.
B(i)
• The female pelvis serves for childbearing and easier delivery; it is bigger and wider, with a large oval brim and a wider outlet.
• The sacral promontory, the superior border of the anterior sacral surface, is an important obstetric landmark for pelvic measurements.
• The sacral index is about 105 in males and 115 in females, and the sacrovertebral angle is more prominent in females.
C(i)
• Male: smaller, narrower, heavier and thicker bone; deep false pelvis; pubic arch V-shaped and less than 90°; acetabulum larger, facing laterally; coccyx immovable; brim smaller and heart-shaped; outlet narrower.
• Male: narrower greater sciatic notch, round obturator foramen, longer narrower sacrum, more vertical ilium, ischial tuberosities longer, close together and laterally projecting.
• Female: shallow false pelvis; wider pubic arch greater than 90°; acetabulum smaller, facing anteriorly; coccyx movable; large oval brim; wider outlet.
• Female: wider greater sciatic notch, oval obturator foramen, less vertical ilium, ischial tuberosities shorter, farther apart and projecting medially.

A(i)
• The longest lymphatic duct, conveying lymph to the circulatory system.
• It begins as the upward continuation of the cisterna chyli, a dilated sac formed by the union of the left and right lumbar trunks and the intestinal trunk, in front of L1 (also stated at T12).
A(ii)
• It enters the thorax through the aortic opening of the diaphragm and ascends in the posterior mediastinum, on the right side of and behind the oesophagus, with the oesophagus lying in front of it.
• It veers to the left at the level of T5 and ascends in the superior mediastinum to the left of the oesophagus.
• At the root of the neck it turns laterally, arches forwards and descends to enter the left venous angle.
A(iii)
• Before termination it receives the left jugular, left subclavian and left bronchomediastinal trunks; it ends in the left brachiocephalic vein.
• It contains many valves, with no valve at its termination.
A(iv)
• It drains lymph from the lower limbs, pelvic cavity, abdominal cavity, left half of the thorax and left side of the head, neck and upper limb (all the body except the right side of the head, neck, thorax and upper limb).
• The right lymphatic duct, formed by the union of the right jugular, subclavian and bronchomediastinal trunks, drains the right half of the head, neck, thorax and upper limb, right lung, right side of the heart and right surface of the liver, and ends in the right brachiocephalic vein.
• The lymph trunks are the right and left jugular, subclavian, bronchomediastinal and lumbar trunks and the intestinal trunk; the left brachiocephalic vein receives the thoracic duct, the right brachiocephalic vein the right lymphatic duct.

A(i) Describe the origin, types, and functions of cells found in connective tissue under the following headings: cells of fixed (resident) population and cells of wandering (transient) population.
A(ii) State where the mesenchymal stem-like cells persist in adults and state their clinical significance.
B(i) Explain the anatomical and histological basis of why connective tissue of the head region differs in embryological origin from the rest of the body, and state the clinical implication.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Fixed (resident) cells: Mesenchyme cells — embryonic source of all connective tissue cells; only found in embryos, but some mesenchyme-like cells persist in adult connective tissue. Fibroblasts — most common cell type in connective tissue; elongated, spindle-shaped cells with many cell processes; have oval, pale-staining, regular nuclei with prominent nucleoli; abundant rough endoplasmic reticulum and active Golgi bodies; synthesize collagen, reticular and elastic fibers, and amorphous extracellular substance. Fibrocytes — quiescent fibroblasts; smaller, darker nucleus; less rough ER. Chondroblasts/osteoblasts — synthesize cartilage and bone matrices. Adipocytes — energy storage, thermal insulation. Wandering (transient) cells: Macrophages — ingestion by phagocytosis; antigen presentation; secretion of enzymes and cytokines; long-lived (several months); originate from monocytes in bone marrow. Plasma cells — defense and immune function. Lymphocytes — immune function. Neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils — immune function. Mast cells — immune function. All connective tissue cells are derived from mesenchymal cells.
A(ii)
Mesenchyme-like cells (pericytes) persist in adult connective tissue, including that of tooth pulp and some adipose tissue. These mesenchyme-like cells retain their capacity to differentiate into other connective tissue cells in response to injury (e.g., pericytes — perivascular cells of blood capillaries). They are being investigated as possible sources of stem cells for therapeutic repair and organ regeneration. Some multipotent stem cells potentially useful in regenerative medicine after grafting to replace damaged tissue in certain patients.
B(i)
All connective tissue cells are derived from mesenchymal cells; mesenchyme cells are for the most part derived from the mesoderm. However, several of the connective tissues of the head region are derived from the neural crest cells (ectodermal origin). Endothelial cells lining blood vessels are derived from mesenchyme. The clinical implication is that connective tissue tumors or developmental disorders in the head may follow patterns distinct from those in the rest of the body due to this different embryological derivation.

questions.question:
(i) Describe the origin, course, branches and distribution of the right and left coronary arteries.
(ii) State which artery gives off the posterior interventricular artery in most individuals (arterial dominance).
(iii) Explain the anatomical basis for the pattern of myocardial damage that follows occlusion of a particular coronary artery.
questions.answerText:
(i)
• The right and left coronary arteries are the first branches of the aorta, arising from the corresponding right and left aortic sinuses at the proximal ascending aorta.
• The right coronary artery runs in the atrioventricular (coronary) groove and gives off the SA nodal branch, right marginal branch, AV nodal branch, and posterior interventricular branch, which anastomoses with the anterior interventricular branch of the left coronary artery.
• The right coronary artery typically supplies the right atrium, most of the right ventricle, part of the left ventricle, the posterior third of the AV septum, the SA node in 60% of people and the AV node in 80% of people.
• The left coronary artery arises from the left aortic sinus, runs in the AV groove, and divides into the circumflex and anterior interventricular branches.
• The left coronary artery typically supplies the left atrium, most of the left ventricle, part of the right ventricle, most of the interventricular septum and the SA node in 40% of people.
• Venous drainage is mainly through the coronary sinus, which receives the great, middle and small cardiac veins and the left posterior ventricular and left marginal veins.
(ii)
Arterial dominance is defined by which artery gives rise to the posterior interventricular artery; right dominance is typical, the left is dominant in about 10% of people, and co-dominance occurs in about 15% of people.
(iii)
• Because the right coronary artery mainly supplies the right atrium, right ventricle and, in most people, the SA and AV nodes, its occlusion can damage right-sided myocardium and disturb the conduction system.
• Because the left coronary artery mainly supplies the left atrium, left ventricle and interventricular septum, its occlusion tends to damage the left ventricle, which performs more work than the right, and the septum.
• Damage to the region supplying the SA or AV node can disturb the heart's conducting system, since the SA and AV nodes are the pacesetters of the heart.
• Tissue damage from reduced blood flow in the territory of the affected artery causes the chest pain of ischaemia/infarction, which can radiate as referred pain to the jaw and left arm.

A(i)
• A strong, incomplete fibrous compartment of the rectus abdominis and pyramidalis, formed by the aponeuroses of the three flat muscles.
• The linea alba separates the right and left rectus abdominis; the linea semilunaris marks the lateral border; tendinous intersections and linea alba give the 'six packs'.
A(ii)
It has an anterior and posterior wall for most of its length: anterior wall from the aponeuroses of external oblique and half of internal oblique; posterior wall from the aponeuroses of half of internal oblique and transversus abdominis.
A(iii)
• Superior and inferior epigastric arteries and veins, lymphatic vessels and the distal portions of the thoracoabdominal nerves (anterior rami of T7 to T12).
• Superior epigastric: terminal branch of internal thoracic, descends posterior to the muscle, anastomoses with inferior epigastric; inferior epigastric: from external iliac, enters the sheath at the arcuate line.
A(iv)
A strong expandable support; protects viscera from injury such as a low blow in boxing; compresses the abdominal contents; maintains or increases intra-abdominal pressure; moves the trunk and maintains posture.
B(i)
• In anterior cutaneous nerve entrapment syndrome (ACNES), 12 of 95 adolescents with chronic abdominal pain had it; the Carnett sign was positive at the lateral border of rectus abdominis in all 12.
• Altered skin sensation was present in 11 of 12; the distal thoracoabdominal nerves run in the rectus sheath.
• After treatment (1 to 3 injections, n = 5; neurectomy, n = 7) pain was absent in 11; the conclusion was that ACNES is present in 1 of 8 such adolescents.
C(i)
• Rectus abdominis: long paired muscle split by the linea alba, origin pubic crest, insertion xiphoid process and costal cartilages of ribs 5 to 7, nerve T7 to T11, stabilises the pelvis in walking and depresses the ribs.
• Pyramidalis: small triangular muscle superficial to rectus, base on the pubis and apex on the linea alba, origin pubic crest and symphysis, insertion linea alba, tenses the linea alba; nerve supply is the subcostal nerve (T12).

A(i)
• Continuation of the sigmoid colon at S3; ends as the anal canal one inch below and in front of the tip of the coccyx; about 12 to 13 cm (5 inches); lower end dilated as the ampulla; lacks mesentery, taeniae coli, sacculations and appendices epiploicae.
• Two anteroposterior curves (sacral posterior; perineal anterior at puborectalis) and three lateral curves (upper convex to right, middle convex to left and most prominent, lower convex to right).
A(ii)
Upper third: front and sides covered; middle third: front only; lower third: none; posterior surface: none. Male: recto-vesical pouch 7.5 cm from anus; female: recto-uterine pouch of Douglas 5.5 cm from anus.
A(iii)
Four permanent horizontal Houston's valves (1st and 3rd constant); the 3rd at S5, 5 cm above the anus, if completely encircling forms Nelaton's sphincter, and divides an upper chamber (faeces without reflex to defecate) from a lower sensitive chamber; valves support faecal weight; cannulae/rectal washing are given in left lateral position to avoid injury to the 3rd valve.
A(iv)
Wall: serous, muscular (outer longitudinal, inner circular), submucosa, mucosa. Arteries: superior rectal (main, from inferior mesenteric), middle rectal (anterior division of internal iliac), inferior rectal (internal pudendal), median sacral (aorta), inferior gluteal.
B(i)
Superior rectal vein drains to inferior mesenteric then portal vein; middle rectal to internal iliac and inferior rectal to internal pudendal (systemic). Internal haemorrhoids (superior rectal tributaries, above Hilton's line, painless); external (inferior rectal, below, painful).
B(ii)
Support: puborectal sling, Waldeyer fascia, lateral ligaments, pelvirectal and ischiorectal fat. Upper third lateral: pararectal fossa (sigmoid colon, small intestine); middle third: pelvirectal space; lower third: ischioanal fossa.
B(iii)
Sympathetic (L1, L2) is vasomotor, stimulates the internal anal sphincter and inhibits the rest of the musculature; parasympathetic (S2 to S4) is secretomotor, stimulates peristalsis and relaxes sphincters.
C(i)
Lymph: upper half via superior rectal to left common iliac and pararectal nodes; middle half to internal iliac nodes; lower part to anal valves to internal iliac nodes; below the anal valves to superficial inguinal nodes.
C(ii)
Portal-systemic anastomosis: superior rectal (portal) with middle and inferior rectal veins (systemic); gut lymph follows arteries to pre-aortic nodes.
C(iii)
Male: anterior sigmoid colon, small intestine, seminal vesicles, ampulla of vas, posterior bladder and prostate; female: posterior vaginal wall; posterior: sacrum, sacral plexus, coccyx, and piriformis, coccygeus, levator ani.
C(iv)
Hindgut origin (endoderm), sympathetic least splanchnic (T12, L1) plus hypogastric (S2 to S4), inferior mesenteric artery (L3); mucosa above the 3rd valve from pre-allantoic hindgut, below from cloaca; muscle from splanchnic mesoderm.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
• A modified sweat gland of ectodermal origin, non-capsulated, present in both sexes (rudimentary in males), starting to develop at puberty in females with most development in late pregnancy and lactation; lies in the superficial fascia; shape and size vary with genetics, race, diet, age, parity and menopausal status (hemispherical, conical, pendulous, piriform, flattened).
• Base extends vertically from the 2nd to the 6th rib and transversely from the sternal edge to the midaxillary line; two-thirds of the base lie on pectoralis major and the inferolateral third on serratus anterior and external oblique; the axillary tail (of Spence) passes into the axilla; the retromammary space (loose areolar tissue) separates it from the deep fascia.
A(ii)
Nipple: at the greatest prominence, opposite the 4th intercostal space (about 10 cm from the midline in men and young nulliparous women); carries 15-20 pores of the lactiferous ducts; circular and radial smooth muscle causes erection with cold, tactile or emotional stimuli; devoid of fat, hair and sweat glands. Areola: pigmented skin (22-60 mm) with sebaceous glands and glands of Montgomery; darkening in the 2nd month of pregnancy is permanent.
A(iii)
Glandular tissue (15-20 lobes made of lobules of alveoli/acini and alveolar ducts converging on 15-20 lactiferous ducts, each with a lactiferous sinus deep to the areola), stroma (fibrous strands, the suspensory ligaments of Astley Cooper, connecting the skin with the deep fascia of pectoralis major) and adipose tissue (determines form and size).
A(iv)
Arteries: internal thoracic (medial mammary and perforating branches of the 2nd-4th spaces, the 2nd largest; about 60% of flow, mainly medial), lateral thoracic and thoraco-acromial pectoral branch (axillary), lateral mammary branches of posterior intercostal arteries, anterior intercostal branches. Veins correspond, with a circular venous plexus at the base of the nipple draining to the axillary and internal thoracic veins. Nerves: anterior and lateral cutaneous branches of the 4th-6th intercostal nerves (sensory to skin, sympathetic to vessels and the smooth muscle of skin and nipple).
B(i)
Cancer of the breast is a common surgical condition, about 60% arising in the upper lateral quadrant; the lactiferous ducts are radial, so incisions are made radially; infiltration of the ligaments of Cooper shortens them and gives peau d'orange; fibroadenoma is also listed.
B(ii)
Polymastia, polythelia and amastia; the mammary ridge extends from the axilla to the inguinal region and disappears in humans except in the pectoral region, so accessory breasts or nipples can occur along it (axillary and inguinal); the male breast stays rudimentary (small ducts without lobules or alveoli).
C(i)
• About 75% of lymph drains to the axillary nodes (central and lateral parts to the pectoral group, upper part to the apical group), about 20% (medial part) to the internal thoracic (parasternal) chain, and the lower quadrants to the inferior phrenic (abdominal) nodes.
• Axillary nodes lie in 5 groups: pectoral (anterior), subscapular (posterior), brachial (lateral), central and apical; levels 1-3 and Rotter's nodes between pectoralis minor and major; the subclavian lymph trunk from the apical group opens into the subclavian vein (left side usually the thoracic duct).
• Other routes: lymphatics follow vessels through pectoralis major to parasternal nodes, cross the median plane to the opposite breast, and reach the sheath of rectus abdominis and the subperitoneal and subhepatic plexuses.
• Nodes below and above the clavicle, and axillary and cervical nodes, communicate freely; cancer of one breast can affect the other breast and the opposite axillary nodes through the anastomosing lymphatics.

A(i) Describe the origin, composition, and classification of connective tissue fibers under the following headings: collagen fibers (types and tissue distribution), elastic fibers, and reticular fibers.
A(ii) State the safe structural principle that makes collagen type I dominant in tendons and ligaments.
B(i) Explain the anatomical basis of scar formation after organ injury, with specific reference to fibroblasts and myofibroblasts.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Collagen fibers: protein fibers that form the bulk of connective tissue fibers. Major types and distribution: Type I collagen — fibril-forming; found in bone, dermis, tendon, ligaments, and cornea; produced by fibroblasts, osteoblasts, odontoblasts. Type II collagen — fibril-forming; found in cartilage and vitreous body of the eye; produced by chondrocytes and retinal cells. Type III collagen — fibril-forming; found in loose connective tissue and reticular fibers in lungs, liver, and spleen; produced by fibroblasts and reticular cells. Type IV collagen — network-forming; found in basement membranes; produced by epithelial and endothelial cells. Type XI collagen — fibrillar; found in cartilage. Elastic fibers: present in elastic connective tissue; provide elasticity. Reticular fibers: fine fibers present in reticular connective tissue; form reticular (meshwork) framework of organs.
A(ii)
Dense regular connective tissue is present in tendons and ligaments because it is organized to withstand forces from specific directions; the regular parallel arrangement of collagen type I fibers allows maximum tensile strength along the axis of the tendon or ligament.
B(i)
The regenerative capacity of connective tissue is clearly observed in organs damaged by ischemia, inflammation, or traumatic injury. Spaces left after such injuries, especially in tissues whose cells divide poorly or not at all (e.g., cardiac muscle), are filled by connective tissue, forming dense irregular scar tissue. The healing of surgical incisions and other wounds depends on the reparative capacity of connective tissue and the activity of fibroblasts. Fibroblasts synthesize collagen, reticular and elastic fibers, and the amorphous extracellular substance. In some rapidly closing wounds, a cell called the myofibroblast (with features of both fibroblasts and smooth muscle cells) is observed. Myofibroblasts have most of the morphologic characteristics of fibroblasts but contain increased amounts of actin microfilaments and myosin and behave like smooth muscle cells. Their activity is responsible for wound contraction (wound closure after tissue injury).

• 3.8 cm long, an anteroposterior slit; anterior wall shorter, posterior longer; begins one inch below and in front of the tip of the coccyx at the recto-anal junction, runs down and backwards, ends at the anus.
• Relations: laterally the ischioanal fossa; posteriorly the anococcygeal raphe; anteriorly the perineal body with bulb of penis and spongy urethra (male), or perineal body and posterior vaginal wall (female).
A(ii)

A(iii)
Internal sphincter: thickened involuntary circular muscle around the upper three-quarters, sympathetic L1, L2 and parasympathetic S2 to S4. External sphincter: striated voluntary, whole length, subcutaneous, superficial and deep parts, supplied by the inferior rectal nerve (pudendal) and perineal branch of S4.
B(i)
Internal haemorrhoids: above Hilton's line, tributaries of the superior rectal vein, painless (primary piles at 3, 7 and 11 o'clock); external: below the line, inferior rectal vein, painful.

Anal sinuses are recesses above the anal columns where foreign bodies may impact and cause infection; infection of the anal glands in the sinus floors may lead to anal fistula; rupture of an anal valve with a tag is a sentinel pile.

Anal columns of Morgagni (6 to 10 folds with superior rectal vein radicles); anal valves of Ball form the pectinate line; anal papillae are remnants of the anal membrane.

Above: superior rectal artery with drainage by the superior rectal vein (portal); below: inferior rectal artery (internal pudendal) with the middle rectal artery, draining to the internal iliac vein (systemic).
C(ii)
Above the pectinate line lymph goes to the internal iliac nodes; below it to the superficial inguinal nodes.
C(iii)
Above the line the fibres are autonomic and pain-insensitive to stretch; below, the inferior rectal nerve is sensitive to pain and touch.
C(iv)
Above the line is hindgut/endodermal with columnar epithelium; below is cloacal membrane/ectodermal with stratified epithelium; the lower third has somatic supply (inferior rectal nerves).

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Gross anatomy of the kidney:
• Renal cortex: granular-appearing superficial region.
• Renal medulla: composed of cone-shaped medullary (renal) pyramids; pyramids are separated by renal columns (inward extensions of cortical tissue).
• Structures in frontal section: renal hilum, renal cortex, renal medulla, major calyx, papilla of pyramid, renal pelvis, minor calyx, ureter, renal pyramid in renal medulla, renal column, fibrous capsule.
A(ii)
Seven functions of the kidney:
• Regulating total water volume and total solute concentration in water.
• Regulating ECF ion concentrations.
• Ensuring long-term acid-base balance.
• Removal of metabolic wastes, toxins, and drugs.
• Endocrine functions: renin (regulation of blood pressure) and erythropoietin (regulation of RBC production).
• Activation of vitamin D.
• Gluconeogenesis during prolonged fasting.
B(i)
Comparison of nephron types:
• Cortical nephrons: 85% of nephrons; short nephron loop; glomerulus further from the cortex-medulla junction; efferent arteriole supplies peritubular capillaries.
• Juxtamedullary nephrons: long nephron loops that deeply invade the medulla; glomerulus closer to the cortex-medulla junction; efferent arteriole supplies vasa recta; ascending limbs have thick and thin segments; important in production of concentrated urine.
B(ii)
Two collecting duct cell types:
• Principal cells: sparse, short microvilli; maintain water and Na+ balance.
• Intercalated cells (A and B types): cuboidal cells with abundant microvilli; both types help maintain acid-base balance of blood.
• Collecting ducts receive filtrate from many nephrons; run through medullary pyramids giving them a striped appearance; fuse together to deliver urine through papillae into minor calyces.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Three regions of the male urethra:
• Prostatic urethra (2.5 cm): located within the prostate.
• Intermediate part of the urethra (membranous urethra) (2 cm): passes through the urogenital diaphragm from the prostate to the beginning of the penis.
• Spongy urethra (15 cm): passes through the penis and opens via the external urethral orifice.
• The male urethra carries both semen and urine.
A(ii)
Two sphincters:
• Internal urethral sphincter: involuntary (smooth muscle) at the bladder-urethra junction; contracts to open (its contraction, paradoxically, opens the sphincter as described — 'contracts to open').
• External urethral sphincter: voluntary (skeletal muscle) surrounding the urethra as it passes through the pelvic floor.
B(i)
Female urethra:
• Length: 3–4 cm.
• Relations: tightly bound to the anterior vaginal wall.
• External urethral orifice: anterior to the vaginal opening and posterior to the clitoris.
B(ii)
Layers of the urinary bladder wall:
• Peritoneum, rugae, detrusor (muscle), adventitia, ureteric orifices, trigone of bladder, bladder neck, internal urethral sphincter.

A(i) Define the mediastinum and state its extent and boundaries.
A(ii) State its divisions and the plane that separates them.
A(iii) Describe the boundaries and contents of each division.
A(iv) List the structures that occupy more than one division.
B(i) Explain the importance of the level of T4 in relation to the mediastinum.
B(ii) Explain why the mediastinum is vulnerable when the chest wall is severely injured.
C(i) Distinguish between the superior and the inferior mediastinum.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
A highly mobile, bulky connective tissue septum (thick movable partition) in the midline between the right and left pleural cavities and their lungs, containing the heart and great vessels, oesophagus, trachea and its bifurcation, thoracic duct, and vagus and phrenic nerves; superior: root of the neck (thoracic outlet: manubrium, 1st rib, T1); inferior: diaphragm; anterior: sternum; posterior: thoracic vertebrae; lateral: lungs and pleurae.
A(ii)
A horizontal plane from the sternal angle to the lower border of T4 divides it into the superior mediastinum (above) and the inferior mediastinum (below), the latter subdivided into anterior (in front of the heart), middle (containing the heart) and posterior (behind the heart) parts.
A(iii)
• Superior: bounded by the thoracic outlet above, the T4 plane below, the manubrium in front and T1-T4 vertebrae behind; contents from superficial to deep: thymus; right and left brachiocephalic veins and SVC; arch of the aorta with brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid and left subclavian arteries; right and left vagus and phrenic nerves; trachea and oesophagus (most posterior); thoracic duct beside the oesophagus; lymph nodes.
• Anterior: bounded by the T4 plane above, the diaphragm below, the body of the sternum in front and the pericardium/heart behind; contains the thymus, fatty tissue and lymph nodes.
• Middle: lies between the anterior and posterior mediastina; contains the pericardium and heart, ascending aorta, pulmonary trunk, SVC and IVC, right and left pulmonary veins, main bronchi, part of the phrenic nerves and lymph nodes.
• Posterior: bounded by the T4 plane above, the heart/middle mediastinum and diaphragm in front, and the T5 (lower border of T4) to T12 vertebrae behind; contains the oesophagus (most anterior), right and left vagus nerves around it, thoracic duct behind it, azygos vein (behind and to the right), descending aorta (behind and to the left), sympathetic trunks and lymph nodes.
A(iv)
Six structures lie in more than one division: thoracic duct, oesophagus and vagus nerves (superior and posterior); phrenic nerves and SVC (superior and middle); thymus (superior and anterior); lymph nodes are present in all regions.
B(i)
The T4 level marks the sternal angle and the 2nd costal cartilage, the bifurcation of the trachea, the bifurcation of the pulmonary trunk, and the beginning and termination of the arch of the aorta.
B(ii)
The mediastinum is highly mobile; in a stove-in chest the loose chest wall segment produces swinging movements of the mediastinum that cause severe shock.
C(i)
• Superior mediastinum: one part above the T4 plane, bounded in front by the manubrium and behind by T1-T4, containing thymus, great veins, aortic arch and its branches, trachea, oesophagus, thoracic duct, vagus and phrenic nerves.
• Inferior mediastinum: three parts below the T4 plane down to the diaphragm - anterior (thymus and fat, in front of the heart), middle (heart, pericardium, ascending aorta, pulmonary trunk) and posterior (oesophagus, descending aorta, azygos system, thoracic duct, sympathetic trunks).
• Nerves differ by position: the right vagus descends on the right of the trachea, forms the posterior oesophageal plexus and continues as the posterior gastric nerve; the left vagus descends between the left common carotid and left subclavian arteries and forms the anterior oesophageal plexus; the right phrenic descends on the right of the SVC and heart, the left on the left side of the heart.

questions.question:
Describe the knee joint under the following headings and explain its clinical importance.
A(i) Type, articular surfaces, and articular bones
A(ii) Ligaments — classify as extracapsular or intra-articular; describe each fully
B(i) Movements and muscles responsible
B(ii) Blood supply and nerve supply of the knee joint
C(i) Distinguish the medial from the lateral meniscus, and explain the anatomical basis of why the medial meniscus is more frequently injured
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The knee joint is primarily a hinge type of synovial joint. It is the largest and very complex joint in the body. Articulations: femur with tibia (tibiofemoral joint) and femur with patella (patellofemoral joint). Articular bones: (1) Femur — enlarged medial and lateral femoral condyles. (2) Tibia — enlarged medial and lateral tibial condyles (tibial plateaus), which are the receptacles for the femoral condyles; tibia bears most of the weight. (3) Patella — a true sesamoid bone embedded in the quadriceps and patellar tendon; serves as a pulley improving the angle of pull. Fibula is not part of the knee joint and does not articulate with the femur or patella; it only serves as attachment for knee joint structures.
A(ii)
Extracapsular ligaments (5): (1) Patellar ligament — distal part of quadriceps tendon; strong, thick fibrous band passing from apex of patella to tibial tuberosity. (2) Fibular (lateral) collateral ligament — strong, rounded, cordlike; extends from lateral epicondyle of femur to head of fibula; tendon of popliteus passes deep to it, separating it from the lateral meniscus. (3) Tibial (medial) collateral ligament — strong flat band from medial epicondyle of femur to medial condyle and superior part of tibia; firmly attached to medial meniscus; weaker and more often damaged than the fibular collateral ligament. (4) Oblique popliteal ligament — expansion of tendon of semimembranosus; strengthens fibrous capsule posteriorly. (5) Arcuate popliteal ligament — arises from posterior aspect of fibular head; passes superomedially over tendon of popliteus; strengthens fibrous capsule posteriorly. Intra-articular ligaments (3): (1) ACL — from anterior intercondylar area of tibia to lateral condyle of femur; weaker; slack when flexed, taut when extended; prevents posterior displacement of femur on tibia and hyperextension. (2) PCL — from posterior intercondylar area of tibia to medial condyle of femur; stronger; taut during flexion; prevents anterior displacement of femur on tibia; main stabilizing factor in weight-bearing flexed knee. (3) Menisci — crescentic plates of fibrocartilage that deepen the surface and act as shock absorbers.
B(i)
Flexion — hamstrings. Extension — quadriceps. Medial rotation — popliteus, semitendinosus, semimembranosus. Lateral rotation — biceps femoris. Locking: when fully extended with foot on ground, the knee locks because of medial rotation of femur on tibia. Unlocking: popliteus contracts rotating femur laterally so flexion can occur.
B(ii)
Blood supply: genicular branches of femoral artery, popliteal artery, anterior and posterior recurrent branches of anterior tibial recurrent artery, and anterior and posterior branches of circumflex fibular arteries. The middle genicular branches of the popliteal artery penetrate the fibrous capsule and supply the cruciate ligaments, synovial membrane, and peripheral margins of the menisci. Nerve supply: branches of obturator nerve, femoral nerve, tibial nerve, and common fibular nerve.
C(i)
Medial meniscus: C-shaped, broader posteriorly; anterior end attaches to anterior intercondylar area of tibia anterior to ACL; posterior end to posterior intercondylar area anterior to PCL; firmly adheres to tibial collateral ligament. Lateral meniscus: almost circular, smaller and more freely movable; tendon of popliteus separates it from fibular collateral ligament; attached posteriorly via the posterior meniscofemoral ligament to PCL and medial femoral condyle. The medial meniscus is more frequently injured because its firm attachment to the tibial collateral ligament makes it immobile and liable to being trapped and torn when the ligament is stressed; the lateral meniscus is protected by its free mobility.

A
In the anterior cranial fossa, the foramen caecum transmits a nasal emissary vein (in 1% of the population), the cribriform foramina in the cribriform plate transmit axons of olfactory cells forming the olfactory nerves, and the anterior and posterior ethmoidal foramina transmit vessels and nerves of the same names. In the middle cranial fossa, the optic canals transmit the optic nerves (CN II) and ophthalmic arteries; the superior orbital fissure transmits ophthalmic veins, the ophthalmic nerve (CN V1), CN III, IV and VI, and sympathetic fibres; the foramen rotundum transmits the maxillary nerve (CN V2); the foramen ovale transmits the mandibular nerve (CN V3), the accessory meningeal artery, the lesser petrosal nerve and an emissary vein; the foramen spinosum transmits the middle meningeal artery and vein and the meningeal branch of CN V3; and the foramen lacerum transmits the deep petrosal nerve and some meningeal arterial branches and small veins. In the posterior cranial fossa, the foramen magnum transmits the medulla and meninges, vertebral arteries, CN XI, dural veins, and the anterior and posterior spinal arteries; the jugular foramen transmits CN IX, X and XI, the superior bulb of the internal jugular vein, the inferior petrosal and sigmoid sinuses, and meningeal branches of the ascending pharyngeal and occipital arteries; the hypoglossal canal transmits the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII); the condylar canal transmits an emissary vein from the sigmoid sinus to the vertebral veins in the neck; and the mastoid foramen transmits a mastoid emissary vein from the sigmoid sinus and a meningeal branch of the occipital artery.
B
Fractures of the calvaria are classified as depressed, linear, comminuted, or basilar fractures; fractures of the maxillae and associated bones are termed Le Fort fractures; and there are also fractures of the mandible.
C
The close relation of the frontal sinus to the frontal lobe of the brain explains how infection of this sinus may result in development of a frontal lobe abscess; a fracture involving the sinus, severe enough to tear the dura and pia-arachnoid, will place the subarachnoid space in communication with the nasal cavity, so that CSF may be detected trickling through the nostril (CSF rhinorrhoea), usually on the affected side, although a contralateral leak can occur since these sinuses may communicate. Similarly, infection of the ethmoid sinuses (ethmoiditis) may result in a frontal cerebral abscess, and an ethmoidal fracture may cause CSF leakage into the nasal cavity, because the ethmoid sinuses lie on each side of the cribriform plate and are related above to the frontal lobes of the brain.
