questions.answerText:
A(i)
• The thoracoabdominal nerves are the abdominal portions of the anterior rami of T7 to T12 (T7 to T11 thoracoabdominal, T12 subcostal); their distal portions lie in the rectus sheath.
• External oblique: T7 to T11 and T12; internal oblique and transversus abdominis: T7 to T11, T12 and branches of the lumbar plexus; rectus abdominis: T7 to T11; pyramidalis: subcostal T12.
A(ii)
• The lumbar plexus (ventral rami L1 to L4, formed within psoas major) innervates part of the lower abdominal wall.
• The iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves (L1) emerge from the lateral border of psoas major.
A(iii)
• The umbilicus is the segmental landmark with dermatome T10, the same root that innervates the appendix, so appendicular referred pain is felt there.
• The segmental innervation applies to both the anterior abdominal skin and musculature.
B(i)
• The TAP block is a peripheral nerve block that anaesthetises the nerves of the abdominal wall.
• It is performed by injecting anaesthetic into the fascial plane between transversus abdominis and internal oblique muscles.
C(i)
• The ilioinguinal, iliohypogastric and inferior thoracic nerves are spread across the abdominal wall and so are prone to injury.
• Their injury results in muscle weakness of the abdominal wall.
• In entrapment (ACNES) the Carnett sign is positive at the lateral border of the rectus abdominis, with altered skin sensation.

questions.question:
A(i) State the nature and number of the intercostal nerves and distinguish the typical from the atypical nerves.
A(ii) Describe the course and relations of a typical intercostal nerve.
A(iii) State its branches.
A(iv) Describe its distribution, including the cutaneous supply of the thoracic wall.
B(i) State the safe method and site for anaesthetising an intercostal space and for passing a needle or drain.
C(i) Explain the anatomical basis of the effects of irritation or injury of the intercostal nerves.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
• 12 pairs of intercostal (thoracic) nerves, the anterior primary rami of the thoracic spinal nerves; they are mixed nerves; T3-6 are typical and T1 and T2 are atypical.
• Atypical nerves: T1 has no anterior cutaneous branch and is joined to the brachial plexus by a large branch corresponding to the lateral cutaneous branch; the lateral cutaneous branch of T2 is the intercostobrachial nerve, joined to the medial cutaneous nerve of the arm.
A(ii)
A typical nerve lies in the neurovascular bundle between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles, high in the space in relation to the subcostal groove of the rib above, below the artery (vein, artery, nerve from above downwards); nerves 1-6 are distributed in the intercostal spaces, 7-11 pass to the anterior abdominal wall, and the anterior ramus of the 12th runs forward in the abdomen as the subcostal nerve.
A(iii)
Branches: rami communicantes, collateral (muscular) branches, lateral cutaneous branch, anterior cutaneous branch, muscular branches, pleural branch and peritoneal branches (7th-11th).
A(iv)
They supply the skin, the muscles of the intercostal space and abdomen, and the parietal pleura and parietal peritoneum; cutaneous supply of the anterior wall is by supraclavicular nerves (C4) above the sternal angle and by the anterior and lateral cutaneous branches below it; the posterior wall is supplied by the posterior rami of the thoracic spinal nerves.
B(i)
• Local anaesthesia of an intercostal space is easily produced by infiltration around the intercostal nerve trunk and its collateral branch (intercostal nerve block).
• A needle or drain is passed immediately above the upper border of a rib, to avoid the neurovascular bundle lying under the rib above.
• In a conventional posterolateral thoracotomy the incision is along the 5th or 6th rib; the periosteum over a segment of the rib is elevated, protecting the neurovascular bundle, and the rib is excised to reach the lung or mediastinum through the intercostal space.
C(i)
• Local irritation of the intercostal nerves (e.g. by Pott's disease, tuberculosis of the thoracic vertebrae) gives pain referred to the front of the chest or abdomen, in the region of the peripheral termination of the nerves.
• Pus from the region of the vertebral column tracks around the thorax along the neurovascular bundle and points at the three sites of exit of the cutaneous branches: lateral to erector spinae, in the midaxillary line and just lateral to the sternum.
• A rib fracture is extremely painful because the periosteum of the rib is supplied by the intercostal nerves above and below the rib; the parietal pleura is segmentally supplied by the intercostal nerves, so pleural disease refers pain along the thoracic wall and anterior abdominal wall.

questions.question:
Describe the gross anatomy of the proximal carpal row/wrist region:
A(i) Bones forming the proximal row and their articulation with the radius
A(ii) The scaphoid's distinguishing feature
B. State how the scaphoid and lunate each relate to common wrist pathologies.
C. Explain how pathology at the lunate spreads to affect a distant structure, causing a functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The wrist (radiocarpal) joint is formed distally by the proximal row of carpal bones — the scaphoid, lunate and triquetrum, excluding the pisiform — and proximally by the distal end of the radius and the articular disk; the ulna is not part of the wrist joint, being prevented from articulating with the carpal bones by this fibrocartilaginous articular disk, and instead articulates with the radius at the distal radioulnar joint.
A(ii)
The scaphoid has a unique blood supply that runs from distal to proximal, unlike most bones.
B
• The scaphoid is the carpal bone most commonly fractured, more so in the younger population, typically from a blow to the wrist such as falling on an outstretched hand, when it takes most of the force.
• Because of its distal-to-proximal blood supply, a scaphoid fracture can disrupt supply to the proximal fragment; this is considered an emergency, and failure to revascularise can lead to avascular necrosis and future arthritis.
• The lunate is prone to anterior dislocation, which is uncommon but can occur by falling on a dorsiflexed wrist, forcing the lunate anteriorly.
• The lunate can also undergo avascular necrosis, so it too requires immediate clinical attention when injured.
C
• Anterior dislocation of the lunate compresses the carpal tunnel, since the lunate lies immediately related to the floor of this tunnel region.
• This compression of the carpal tunnel affects the median nerve, which lies within it.
• The resulting clinical picture manifests as paraesthesia in the sensory distribution of the median nerve.
• There is also weakness of the thenar muscles, which are supplied by the median nerve's recurrent branch.
• This produces the symptoms of carpal tunnel syndrome, even though the primary pathology (lunate dislocation) is a distinct injury from the usual causes of carpal tunnel syndrome.
• This illustrates how a purely skeletal injury at the wrist can spread to compromise an adjacent soft-tissue structure, producing a functional/sensorimotor deficit in the hand.

questions.question:
Describe the gross anatomy of the brachial plexus:
A(i) Formation (roots)
A(ii) Trunks, divisions, cords
A(iii) Five main terminal branches
B. State how injury at each level (trunk/cord) of the plexus relates to a specific clinical pathology.
C. Explain how injury at the level of a trunk or cord spreads to affect distant structures (individual peripheral nerves), causing specific functional deficits.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The brachial plexus is formed by the union of the C5, C6, C7 and C8 ventral rami and the greater part of the 1st thoracic ventral ramus, with contribution sometimes from C4 (giving a "prefixed" plexus) or T2 (giving a "postfixed" plexus); the roots emerge from the transverse processes of the cervical vertebrae, immediately posterior to the vertebral artery, and lie between the scalene muscles.
A(ii)
C5 and C6 unite to form the upper trunk, C7 continues as the middle trunk, and C8 and T1 unite to form the lower trunk, lying in the posterior triangle of the neck; each trunk bifurcates behind the clavicle into an anterior and a posterior division. The anterior divisions of the upper and middle trunks unite to form the lateral cord; the anterior division of the lower trunk continues as the medial cord; the posterior divisions of all three trunks unite to form the posterior cord, lying in the axilla below pectoralis minor.
A(iii)
The five main terminal branches are the musculocutaneous nerve and the lateral root of the median nerve (from the lateral cord), the ulnar nerve and the medial root of the median nerve (from the medial cord), and the axillary and radial nerves (from the posterior cord).
B
• Injury to the upper trunk (C5, C6), at "Erb's point," produces Erb's paralysis, from causes such as birth injury, a fall on the shoulder, or during anaesthesia, affecting the axillary, musculocutaneous and suprascapular nerves.
• Injury to the lower trunk (C8, T1), from causes such as undue abduction of the arm, produces Klumpke's paralysis, with paralysis of the intrinsic hand muscles and ulnar wrist/finger flexors, and possible Horner's syndrome from associated sympathetic fibre injury.
C
• Erb's paralysis paralyses biceps, deltoid, brachialis, brachioradialis, supraspinatus, infraspinatus and supinator, producing the "Policeman's/Porter's tip hand": the arm hangs adducted and medially rotated, the forearm extended and pronated, with loss of abduction/lateral rotation of the shoulder and flexion/supination of the forearm.
• Klumpke's paralysis produces a claw hand from unopposed long flexors/extensors, plus cutaneous anaesthesia along the ulnar border of the limb.
• Injury to the lateral cord (e.g. from dislocation of the humerus) involves the musculocutaneous nerve and the lateral root of the median nerve, paralysing biceps, coracobrachialis and the median-supplied forearm muscles, producing a midprone forearm with loss of elbow and wrist flexion and sensory loss on the radial side of the forearm.
• Injury to the medial cord (e.g. from subcoracoid dislocation of the humerus) involves the ulnar nerve and the medial root of the median nerve, producing claw hand with sensory loss on the ulnar side of the forearm and hand.
• Injury to the posterior cord involves the upper and lower subscapular nerves, the thoracodorsal nerve, the axillary nerve, and the radial nerve (the largest and most frequently injured branch of the plexus).
• This weakens elbow, wrist and metacarpophalangeal joint extension via the radial nerve, and shoulder abduction via the axillary nerve.
• In this way, a single lesion at the level of a trunk or cord of the brachial plexus spreads its effect along the several peripheral nerves derived from it, each producing its own characteristic and distant functional deficit in the arm, forearm or hand.

questions.question:
(i) Describe the origin, course, branches and distribution of the splenic artery.
(ii) State the anatomical basis that makes subtotal (partial) splenectomy a safe surgical option.
(iii) Explain the anatomical basis of the complications that can follow injury to the spleen and its vasculature.
questions.answerText:
(i)
• The spleen receives its arterial supply from the splenic artery, the largest branch of the coeliac trunk.
• The splenic artery runs laterally along the superior aspect of the pancreas, within the splenorenal ligament.
• As it reaches the spleen it branches into about five vessels, each supplying a different vascular segment of the spleen.
• Along its course it also gives off the short gastric and left gastroepiploic arteries to the stomach, and pancreatic branches to the pancreas.
• Venous drainage is through the splenic vein, which combines with the superior mesenteric vein to form the hepatic portal vein.
(ii)
• The terminal arterial branches of the splenic artery do not anastomose with one another, so each supplies an independent vascular segment of the spleen.
• This segmental (end-arterial) arrangement allows a surgeon to remove one diseased or injured segment (subtotal splenectomy) without compromising the blood supply of the remaining segments.
(iii)
• The tail of the pancreas lies within the splenorenal ligament, close to the splenic vessels at the hilum, and may be injured during splenectomy, producing a pancreatic fistula.
• The spleen is the most frequently injured organ in the abdomen despite protection by the 9th to 12th ribs.
• Severe blows to the left side may fracture ribs, producing sharp fragments that lacerate the spleen.
• Blunt trauma elsewhere that suddenly raises intra-abdominal pressure can also rupture the spleen because its capsule is thin and its pulp is soft and pulpy.
• A ruptured spleen bleeds profusely, causing severe intraperitoneal haemorrhage and shock, so splenectomy or subtotal splenectomy is often required to prevent the patient from bleeding to death.

A(i)
Muscularis and serosa:
• Muscularis: composed of an internal circular layer and an external longitudinal layer; between these muscle layers is the myenteric (Auerbach) nerve plexus, which produces peristalsis.
• Serosa: the small intestine is covered by a thin serosa.
A(ii)
Lamina propria of the small intestine:
• Composed of loose connective tissue containing extensive blood and lymph microvasculature, nerve fibers, smooth muscle cells, and lymphoid tissue.
• It penetrates the core of each intestinal villus, bringing microvasculature, lymphatics, and nerves into each villus.
• Smooth muscle fibers inside the villi are responsible for rhythmic movements important for efficient absorption.
• Contractions of the muscularis mucosae also produce local movements of the plicae circulares that help propel lymph from the lacteals into submucosal and mesenteric lymphatics.
B(i)
Submucosa — Brunner (duodenal) glands:
• Location: present in the proximal part of the duodenum; large clusters of branched tubular mucous glands with small excretory ducts opening among the intestinal crypts.
• Type: branched tubular mucous glands.
• Product: mucus, which is alkaline (pH 8.1–9.3).
Three functions:
• Protects the mucous membrane.
• Brings the intestinal contents to the optimum pH for pancreatic enzyme action.
• Neutralises chyme entering the duodenum from the pylorus.
B(ii)
Lacteals:
• Lymph vessels of the intestine beginning as closed tubes in the cores of villi.
• They run to the region of the lamina propria above the muscularis mucosae, where they form a plexus.
• From there they are directed to the submucosa, where they surround lymphoid nodules; they anastomose repeatedly and leave the intestine along with blood vessels.
• Function: especially important for lipid absorption.
• Absorptive state: when absorption is taking place after a meal, the lacteals are dilated and prominent; at other times they are collapsed and not prominent.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the muscularis and serosa of the small intestine, naming the layers of the muscularis, the nerve plexus between them, and the covering of the serosa.
A(ii) Describe the lamina propria of the small intestine, including its composition, its role in each intestinal villus, and the role of smooth muscle fibers within the villi.
B(i) Describe the submucosa of the small intestine, giving particular attention to the Brunner (duodenal) glands: location, type of gland, product, pH, and all three functions.
B(ii) Describe the lacteals of the small intestine: what they are, where they begin, their course, their function, and how they change in appearance depending on the absorptive state of the intestine.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Skeletal muscle — longitudinal section: cross-striations of alternating dark (A bands, anisotropic) and light (I bands, isotropic) bands; each I band bisected by a dark transverse Z disc; multinucleated fibers at periphery. Cross-section: peripheral nuclei; high cytoplasm-to-nucleus ratio. Smooth muscle — longitudinal section: meshwork appearance; no striations; elongated spindle-shaped cells; elongated and central nuclei. Cross-section: central nuclei; low cytoplasm-to-nucleus ratio. Cardiac muscle — longitudinal section: striations; branching cells; intercalated discs. Cross-section: central nuclei; high cytoplasm-to-nucleus ratio.
A(ii)
Skeletal muscle: troponin subunits (troponin I and troponin T) are integral to muscle contraction; mutations in cardiac troponin subunits can result in cardiomyopathies. Smooth muscle: smooth muscle cells are able to undergo cell division (unlike cardiac and skeletal muscle). Cardiac muscle: atrial myocytes secrete atrial natriuretic peptide; kidneys respond to this to cause sodium and water loss (natriuresis and diuresis); when natriuretic peptide levels fall, kidneys result in sodium and water conservation.
B(i)
Cardiac muscle cells act as a syncytium through gap junctions in intercalated discs, which provide ionic continuity between adjacent cells, allowing the signal to contract to pass throughout the organ. The blood supply to the heart is through three main coronary arteries prone to atheroma. Acute coronary arterial occlusion involving nearly the entire area at risk causes necrosis of the myocardium. Because the cardiac muscle acts as a syncytium and is continuously active, obstruction of coronary blood flow rapidly leads to widespread ischemia and necrosis of the myocardium.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the gross histology of the three types of muscle tissue (skeletal, smooth, and cardiac) as seen in longitudinal section and cross-section under the light microscope.
A(ii) Relate the structural differences of each muscle type to their specific pathological conditions.
B(i) Explain how the histological organization of cardiac muscle facilitates rapid spread of the signal to contract, and state why blockage of the coronary arteries leads to widespread myocardial damage.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
The deep cervical fascia consists of areolar tissue that supports the muscles, vessels and viscera of the neck; it is condensed to form well-defined fibrous sheets, labelled as: (1) the investing layer (superficial), (2) the pretracheal fascia, (3) the prevertebral fascia, (4) the carotid sheath, and (5) the axillary fascia. More generally, deep fascia is the membranous investment of structures deep to the superficial fascia, containing cells (fibroblasts), fibres (collagen, elastic) and matrix; being subjected to tensile strains, the collagen forms parallel fibre bundles, with the cells flattened. Deep fascia is best marked in the limbs and neck, where it is wrapped around the muscles, veins and nerves like a bandage, the fibres being mainly circularly arranged; around the thorax and abdomen, which require to expand and contract, there is merely a film of areolar tissue but no true deep fascia.
A(ii)
The pretracheal fascia is found only in the anterior region; superiorly it is attached to the thyroid and cricoid cartilage, and inferiorly it extends into the thorax to blend with the fibrous pericardium; laterally it blends with the carotid sheath and with the investing layer of the deep cervical fascia beneath sternocleidomastoid. The prevertebral fascia is attached superiorly to the base of the skull, and inferiorly enters the thorax and blends with the anterior longitudinal ligament of the vertebral column; it covers the prevertebral muscles (longus capitis and longus cervicis), passes round the neck, attaches to the ligamentum nuchae, and in the posterior triangle forms the fascial floor, covering the muscles scalenus anterior, scalenus medius, scalenus posterior, levator scapulae and splenius capitis.
B
Penetration of the fascia during instrumentation of the pretracheal fascia can lead to collection of infectious substances (pus) in the retropharyngeal space (the space between the pharynx and the prevertebral fascia); whiplash injury of the neck can cause quadriplegia, stabbing injury of the neck can cause vascular/nervous injury, and a tumour blocking the airway may necessitate insertion of a tracheostomy tube. The deep cervical fascia will necessarily be pierced during tracheostomy.
C
The pretracheal fascia surrounds the thyroid gland completely, forming a sheath for it, binds the thyroid gland to the larynx, encloses the parathyroid gland, invests the infrahyoid muscles, and encloses the visceral components of the neck (larynx and trachea, pharynx and oesophagus, and the thyroid and parathyroid glands). The prevertebral fascia, in contrast, surrounds the vertebral column and its associated muscles, extending from the base of the skull to approximately the T3 vertebra, and extends laterally as the axillary sheaths.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the deep cervical fascia under the following headings: composition, and the named fibrous sheets into which it is condensed.
A(ii) Describe the attachments of the pretracheal fascia and the prevertebral fascia.
B. Explain the clinical basis for why infection can spread within specific fascial planes/spaces of the neck.
C. Distinguish between the pretracheal fascia and the prevertebral fascia in terms of what each surrounds/encloses.

A(i) Define the pericardium and state its position and relations.
A(ii) Describe the fibrous pericardium.
A(iii) Describe the serous pericardium and the pericardial cavity.
A(iv) Describe the transverse sinus.
A(v) Describe the oblique sinus.
A(vi) Describe the blood supply, venous drainage and nerve supply of the pericardium.
B(i) Explain the clinical importance of the pericardial sinuses and of the site for draining pericardial fluid.
B(ii) Explain why pericardial irritation may cause pain or disturbance in a distant structure.
C(i) Distinguish between the transverse and the oblique sinus, and between the fibrous and the serous pericardium.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
A fibroserous sac that encloses the heart and the roots of the great vessels; it lies behind the body of the sternum and the 2nd-6th costal cartilages and in front of the T5-T8 vertebrae; it is attached to the central tendon of the diaphragm (pericardiophrenic ligament).
A(ii)
The outer fibrous tissue layer, enclosing the heart and the roots of the great vessels (the IVC excepted, as stated); its base is attached to the central tendon of the diaphragm.
A(iii)
Thin, elastic tissue lining the fibrous pericardium, made of a parietal layer (lines and fuses with the fibrous pericardium) and a visceral layer (forms the epicardium of the heart and encloses the aorta and pulmonary trunk); between them lies the pericardial cavity containing pericardial fluid.
A(iv)
Transverse sinus: formed by a tear in the dorsal mesocardium; lies behind the aorta and pulmonary trunk, in front of the SVC on the right and the left atrium on the left.
A(v)
Oblique sinus: a blind sac (cul-de-sac) formed as a result of the entrance of the 4 pulmonary veins and the IVC into the heart; lies behind the 2 left pulmonary veins and in front of the 2 right pulmonary veins and the IVC.
A(vi)
• Blood supply: fibrous pericardium from the pericardiophrenic and musculophrenic arteries; serous pericardium from the coronary arteries; veins drain to the azygos system, and the pericardiophrenic vein drains to the internal thoracic vein.
• Nerve supply: the fibrous and parietal pericardium by the phrenic nerve; the visceral pericardium by autonomic nerves.
B(i)
• Draining of pericardial fluid is done between the 7th costal cartilage and the xiphoid process.
• In pulmonary embolectomy a temporary ligature is passed through the transverse sinus to occlude the aorta and pulmonary trunk; the oblique sinus allows for pulsation of the left atrium.
B(ii)
Pain from irritation of the pleura or pericardium covering the central part of the diaphragm may be referred to the shoulder, because the phrenic nerve (C3,4,5) supplies the central diaphragm and the pericardium, and the supraclavicular nerve (C3,4) supplies the shoulder skin; pericarditis may also cause hiccup.
C(i)
• The transverse sinus is a passage formed by a tear in the dorsal mesocardium, lying behind the great arteries and used for the ligature; the oblique sinus is a blind sac formed by the entry of the pulmonary veins and IVC, allowing pulsation of the left atrium.
• The fibrous pericardium is the outer fibrous layer with phrenic nerve and pericardiophrenic/musculophrenic arterial supply; the serous pericardium is thin and elastic, with a parietal layer fused to the fibrous layer and a visceral layer forming the epicardium, supplied by coronary arteries and autonomic nerves.

questions.question:
Describe the arches of the foot under the following headings and explain their clinical relevance.
A(i) Name and constituent bones of each arch, identifying the keystone of each
A(ii) Factors maintaining the arches — ligaments, muscles, and bony factor for each arch
B(i) Functions of the foot arches in weight-bearing and locomotion
B(ii) Deformities of the foot — name and define pes planus, pes cavus, talipes equinovarus, and talipes calcaneovalgus
C(i) Explain why the medial longitudinal arch is more dynamic and more clinically vulnerable than the lateral longitudinal arch
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Medial longitudinal arch: formed by calcaneus, talus (keystone — its superior articular facet is the summit), navicular, 3 cuneiform bones, and 1st, 2nd, and 3rd metatarsals; found on medial aspect of foot; larger, with greatest height, higher, more mobile, and more resilient. Lateral longitudinal arch: formed by calcaneus, cuboid, and the 4th and 5th metatarsals; summit is the subtalar articulation; flat, contains relatively fewer bones, hence more rigid; bears body weight before the medial arch comes into play. Transverse arch: formed proximally by 3 cuneiforms and cuboid, and distally by the bases of 5 metatarsals; it is a partial arch (each foot represents a half dome); the intermediate and lateral cuneiforms are wedge-shaped (bony factor).
A(ii)
Medial longitudinal arch: Ligaments — spring ligament, deltoid ligament, plantar aponeurosis, interosseous ligaments, long and short plantar ligaments. Muscles — tibialis posterior, tibialis anterior, flexor hallucis longus, flexor digitorum longus, and short muscles of the big toe. Bony factor — the shape and constitution of the bones. Lateral longitudinal arch: Ligaments — plantar aponeurosis, interosseous ligaments, long and short plantar ligaments. Muscles — peroneus longus and brevis, flexor digitorum longus, and short muscles of the little toe. Bony factor — shape and constitution of the bones. Transverse arch: Bony factor — intermediate and lateral cuneiforms are wedge-shaped. Ligaments — deep transverse ligament and interosseous ligaments (dorsal and plantar). Muscles — peroneus longus and brevis, transverse head of adductor hallucis, and slips of tibialis posterior.
B(i)
The human foot supports the body weight and serves as a lever to propel the body forward during locomotion. Functions carried out by arches: (1) Foot acts as a segmented lever with multiple joints and adapts to uneven surfaces. (2) Long flexors and intrinsic muscles assist propulsive action of gastrocnemius and soleus. (3) Arches are springs that absorb shock and store energy — elastic arches present between weight-bearing points can flatten and recoil back to normal.
B(ii)
Pes planus (flat foot): rotation of the calcaneus, eversion of the plantar surface, slipping down of the talus and navicular, lengthening of the medial longitudinal arch, and abduction of the forefoot; caused by excess weight on medial side, relaxation of ligaments, or muscular imbalance. Pes cavus (high-arched foot): exaggeration of the longitudinal arch; toes dorsiflexed at metatarsophalangeal joints and plantarflexed at interphalangeal joints — claw foot. Talipes equinovarus: plantar flexion, inversion, and adduction of the foot (clubfoot). Talipes calcaneovalgus: dorsiflexion, eversion, and abduction of the foot.
C(i)
The medial longitudinal arch is higher, more mobile, and more resilient — it is dynamic, changes most during movement, and requires active muscular support (particularly tibialis posterior, flexor hallucis longus, and the spring ligament). The lateral longitudinal arch is lower, more stable, built to transmit weight to the ground, makes more contact with the ground, has limited mobility, and depends more on bony and ligamentous rather than muscular support. The medial arch is therefore more clinically vulnerable to collapse (pes planus) when muscles weaken or ligaments stretch.

questions.question:
A. Describe the gross anatomy of the tongue under the following headings: division into anterior and posterior parts, and the intrinsic and extrinsic muscles.
B. State how the different regions of the tongue relate to common developmental and pathological conditions.
C. Explain why disease affecting one region of the tongue can produce a functional deficit at a distant site, based on its lymphatic drainage pattern.
questions.answerText:
A
A V-shaped groove, the sulcus terminalis, demarcates the anterior two-thirds of the tongue from the posterior one-third. The intrinsic muscles of the tongue are the superior longitudinal, inferior longitudinal, transverse, and vertical muscles. The extrinsic muscles are the genioglossus, styloglossus, palatoglossus, and hyoglossus. The mucosa of the anterior two-thirds is formed into papillae (filiform, fungiform, circumvallate, foliate), which contain taste buds.
B
Clinical correlates involving the tongue include loss of taste sensation, bifid tongue, tongue tie (ankyloglossia), microglossia/macroglossia, and lingual carcinoma. Nerve supply differs by region: in the anterior two-thirds, motor supply to the muscles is via CN XII (except palatoglossus, supplied by the pharyngeal plexus of the vagus nerve), sensory supply to the mucous membrane is via the lingual nerve (a branch of CN V3), and special (taste) sensory supply is via the chorda tympani nerve (a branch of CN VII); in the posterior one-third, motor supply is via CN XII, and sensory supply (general and special) is via the lingual branch of CN IX and the internal laryngeal nerve (a branch of CN X).
C
Lymphatic drainage of the tongue takes 4 routes: the posterior third drains to the superior deep cervical lymph nodes; the medial part of the anterior two-thirds drains to the inferior deep cervical lymph nodes; the lateral parts of the anterior two-thirds drain to the submandibular lymph nodes; and the apex of the tongue drains to the submental lymph nodes - with the posterior third and the area near the midline draining bilaterally. Because disease (such as lingual carcinoma) arising in a particular region of the tongue follows that region's specific lymphatic drainage route, it can spread to produce nodal or functional deficits at lymph node groups that are anatomically distant from the primary site, with the pattern of spread differing depending on which part of the tongue is affected, and bilateral drainage from the posterior third and midline region meaning disease there can involve lymph nodes on both sides of the neck.

A(i)
Chemical composition and properties: Bone is a connective tissue mineralized by calcium phosphate in the form of crystals very similar to hydroxyapatite. The minerals are both in the type I collagen fibers (which constitute about 95% of the matrix) and in the ground substance. Bone is both resilient and hard. Its resilience is due to the organic matter (collagen); its hardness is due to the inorganic minerals (calcium phosphate, calcium carbonate, calcium fluoride, calcium hydroxide, and citrate). Cell types: Osteocytes — maintain calcium and phosphate ion levels in the blood, are essentially stress sensors, and are osteoblasts that have been trapped in their own matrix in lacunae. Osteoblasts — synthesize the organic matrix (osteoid). Osteoclasts — multinucleated giant cells involved in resorption and remodeling of bone; they are also chondrocytes during bone healing and remodeling. Osteoid is the matrix secreted by osteoblasts and osteocytes prior to mineralization. Types of bone: compact bone (also called dense bone, cortical bone, or lamellar bone) and spongy bone (also called cancellous bone, trabecular bone, and medullary bone).
A(ii)
Compact bone is organized into structures called osteons or Haversian systems: concentric lamellae surrounding a central canal called the Haversian canal, which contains blood vessels, nerves, loose connective tissue, and endosteum. Between lamellae are lacunae, each with one osteocyte interconnected by canaliculi containing the cells' dendritic processes. Canals called Volkmann's canals link Haversian canals with one another and with the marrow cavity. Metabolic exchanges between osteocytes and blood capillaries depend on communication through the canaliculi.
B(i)
Blood calcium levels are regulated by the hormones parathormone (parathyroid hormone), which raises blood calcium levels by stimulating bone resorption, and calcitonin, which reduces blood calcium by suppressing bone resorption and increasing osteoid calcification.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the gross histology of bone under the following headings: chemical composition and properties, cell types and their functions, and types of bone.
A(ii) State how the Haversian system (osteon) is organised and relate this to bone function.
B(i) Explain how blood calcium levels are regulated through bone, naming the hormones involved and their actions.

A(i) Describe the five functions of the epithelial lining of the digestive tract.
A(ii) Describe the submucosal (Meissner) plexus and the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus together as the local enteric nervous system: name the layers of the GIT wall each is found in, state the ganglia they are composed of, what the number of ganglia depends on, and what system they function independently of.
B(i) Describe the muscularis mucosae: its composition, its location, and the two functions attributed to it.
B(ii) Explain the immunological backup to the thin epithelial barrier of the GIT, and identify what the digestive tract normally contains that makes this backup essential.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Five functions of the epithelial lining:
• Provide a selectively permeable barrier between the contents of the tract and the tissues of the body.
• Facilitate the transport and digestion of food.
• Promote the absorption of the products of digestion.
• Produce hormones that affect the activity of the digestive system.
• Produce mucus for lubrication and protection.
A(ii)
Local enteric nervous system:
• The submucosal (Meissner) plexus is located in the submucosa; the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus is located in the connective tissue between the circular and longitudinal muscle sublayers of the muscularis.
• Together they constitute the local enteric nervous system of the digestive tract.
• This system functions independently of the CNS.
• Both plexuses are composed mainly of nerve cell aggregates forming small parasympathetic ganglia.
• The number of ganglia along the digestive tract is variable — numerous in the regions of greatest motility.
B(i)
Muscularis mucosae:
• Composition: thin layer of smooth muscle.
• Location: usually separates the mucosa from the submucosa.
• Functions: (1) allows local movements of the mucosa independent of other movements of the digestive tract, helping to increase contact of the lining with food; (2) its contractions contribute to mixing and propelling food (the plexuses coordinate the contractions of the muscularis to mix and propel food).
B(ii)
Immunological backup:
• The mucosa-associated immune defense system (MALT) provides an essential backup to the thin physical barrier of the epithelial lining.
• The lamina propria (just below the epithelium) is a zone rich in macrophages and lymphocytes, some of which actively produce IgA antibodies.
• The digestive tract normally contains thousands of microbial species, including both useful gut inhabitants and potential pathogens ingested with food and drink, making this immune backup essential.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the mucosa of the stomach under the following headings: surface epithelium and gastric pits; the isthmus and stem cells; the lamina propria; and the muscularis mucosae.
A(ii) Name and describe all four secretory epithelial cell types found in the gastric glands of the fundus and body, including the characteristics of each cell and what it secretes.
B(i) Distinguish between the mucosa of the fundus/body and the mucosa of the cardia/pylorus under the headings: gland type, cell types present, and principal secretion.
B(ii) Explain what rugae are and the physiological condition under which they disappear.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Stomach mucosa:
• Surface epithelium and gastric pits: consists of a simple columnar epithelium that invaginates into the lamina propria forming gastric pits. Millions of gastric pits each open into the lumen of the stomach; the gastric pits lead into long, branched, tubular glands extending through the thickness of the lamina propria; between each gastric pit and gastric gland is the isthmus (region of stem cells).
• Isthmus and stem cells: the pluripotent stem cells divide asymmetrically producing progenitor cells for all other epithelial cells; they can move upwards to replace surface mucous cells or downwards to replace other secretory cells.
• Lamina propria: highly vascularised; supports pits and glands; contains smooth muscle fibers, capillaries, lymphatics, and lymphoid cells.
• Muscularis mucosae: layer of smooth muscle separating the mucosa from the underlying submucosa.
A(ii)
Four secretory cell types of fundic/body glands:
• Mucous neck cells (MNCs): less columnar than surface mucous cells; irregular in shape with round nucleus and apical secretory granules; secrete acidic fluid containing mucin (less alkaline than surface mucous cells).
• Parietal (oxyntic) cells: large, rounded or pyramidal cells; one central spherical nucleus; intensely eosinophilic cytoplasm due to high density of mitochondria; secrete hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor.
• Chief (zymogen) cells: predominate in lower regions; abundant RER and numerous apical secretory granules (characteristics of protein-secreting cells); secrete pepsinogen (converted to pepsin at pH < 5), lipase, and leptin.
• Enteroendocrine cells: scattered throughout the gastric mucosa; secrete hormones with endocrine or paracrine functions (e.g., serotonin in fundus; gastrin from G cells in pylorus).
B(i)
• Fundus/body: long branched tubular gastric glands (3 to 7 per pit); each gland has an isthmus, neck, and base; contains all four cell types above; secretes acidic gastric juice.
• Cardia/pylorus: tubular glands with long pits, usually branching into coiled secretory portions (cardiac/pyloric glands); lack parietal and chief cells; major secretion is abundant mucus.
B(ii)
Rugae are longitudinally directed folds of the mucosa and submucosa of the empty stomach. They flatten when the stomach is full with food.

(i)
• The pancreas is a soft, lobulated, J- or retort-shaped gland lying retroperitoneally, except for the tail, and transversely across the posterior abdominal wall at the level of L1-L2, posterior to the stomach, between the duodenum on the right and the spleen on the left; it is about 15-20 cm long and weighs about 90 g.
• The head is disc-shaped, enlarged, and lies within the concavity of the duodenum; the uncinate process projects from its lower part, posterior to the superior mesenteric vessels.
• The neck is the constricted portion connecting the head to the body and overlies the superior mesenteric vessels.
• The body is centrally located, crossing the midline behind the stomach, with anterior, posterior and inferior surfaces; the posterior surface contacts the aorta, splenic vein, left kidney and vessels, left suprarenal gland, origin of the superior mesenteric artery, and the crura of the diaphragm.
• The tail is narrow, lies at the level of T12, ends within the splenic hilum in the splenophrenic ligament, and is the only intraperitoneal part of the pancreas; it may be injured during splenectomy, causing a pancreatic fistula.
• The main pancreatic duct, of Wirsung, begins in the tail and runs to the head, usually joining the bile duct to form the hepatopancreatic ampulla, which opens at the major duodenal papilla; the accessory duct, of Santorini, drains the upper head via the minor duodenal papilla.
(ii)
• Annular pancreas is a rare congenital defect in which the pancreas encircles the duodenum; ectopic pancreatic tissue outside the gastrointestinal tract is a very common anomaly.
• Due to its deep retroperitoneal position, the pancreas is not easily accessible for direct clinical examination, so diagnosis of pancreatic disease relies on ultrasound, CT scan, special investigations of the pancreatic and biliary ducts, and biochemical tests.
• Acute necrotizing pancreatitis results when proenzymes are prematurely activated and digest pancreatic tissue, from causes including infection, gallstones, alcoholism, drugs and trauma.
(iii)
• The endocrine part of the pancreas, the islets of Langerhans, secretes insulin and glucagon into the blood; lack of insulin production by the beta cells, or defective insulin receptors, causes diabetes mellitus, a hyperglycaemic metabolic disorder affecting the whole body.
• Because the exocrine pancreas secretes digestive enzymes and bicarbonate essential for neutralising gastric acid and digesting food in the duodenum, pancreatic disease impairing exocrine secretion produces a functional deficit in intestinal digestion, a distant effect of pancreatic pathology.
• In extreme malnutrition, acinar cell atrophy further reduces digestive enzyme production, compounding this distant digestive deficit.
questions.question:
(i) Describe the gross anatomy of the pancreas - location, shape, and its four parts (head, neck, body, tail) with their relations.
(ii) Relate the parts of the pancreas to pathology (annular pancreas, pancreatitis).
(iii) Explain how pancreatic disease can produce a functional deficit in a distant organ/system.

A(i) Describe the complete path of blood flow through the renal blood vessels, from the aorta to the peritubular capillaries or vasa recta.
A(ii) State the nerve supply to the kidneys and name the source.
B(i) Distinguish between the capillary beds associated with cortical nephrons and those associated with juxtamedullary nephrons.
B(ii) Explain the anatomical basis for high blood pressure in the glomerulus.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Path of blood flow:
• Aorta → Renal artery → Segmental artery → Interlobar artery → Arcuate artery → Cortical radiate artery → Afferent arteriole → Glomerulus (capillaries) → Efferent arteriole → Peritubular capillaries (cortical nephrons) or Vasa recta (juxtamedullary nephrons) → Cortical radiate vein → Arcuate vein → Interlobar vein → Renal vein → Inferior vena cava.
• Renal arteries deliver approximately one-quarter (1,200 ml) of cardiac output to the kidneys each minute.
A(ii)
Nerve supply is via sympathetic fibers from the renal plexus.
B(i)
• Cortical nephrons (85% of nephrons): efferent arteriole supplies peritubular capillaries — low-pressure, porous capillaries adapted for absorption of water and solutes; they cling to adjacent renal tubules in the cortex and empty into venules.
• Juxtamedullary nephrons: efferent arteriole supplies vasa recta — long, thin-walled vessels parallel to the long nephron loops; important in formation of concentrated urine.
B(ii)
Blood pressure in the glomerulus is high because:
• Afferent arterioles are larger in diameter than efferent arterioles.
• Arterioles are high-resistance vessels.
• The glomerulus is fed and drained by arterioles (not venules), which maintains the high filtration pressure. The glomerulus is also specialized for filtration, with fenestrated endothelium that is highly porous, allowing filtrate formation.

questions.question:
Describe the femur under the following headings and explain how its zones relate to common pathologies.
A(i) General features, parts, and gross anatomy of the femur
A(ii) The neck of femur — angles of inclination and torsion, and why fracture here causes coxa vara
B(i) Blood supply of the head of femur and why avascular necrosis occurs after intracapsular fracture
B(ii) The linea aspera — muscular and bony attachments, and clinical significance
C(i) Distinguish pressure epiphysis from traction epiphysis with examples from the femur, and explain why the nutrient canal direction matters surgically
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The femur is the long bone of the thigh; the longest and strongest bone in the body (Latin: femur = thigh); it accounts for approximately one-quarter of a person's total height and averages 45 cm. It has a shaft (body) and 2 expanded ends. Parts: (1) proximal end — consisting of head, neck, and the trochanters; (2) shaft; (3) distal end — consisting of the femoral condyles. It articulates superiorly with the acetabulum to form the hip joint, and inferiorly with the patella and tibia to form the knee joint.
A(ii)
The neck is the curved upper end of the shaft; it connects the head to the shaft and passes downward, backward, and laterally, obliquely placed to the long axis of the shaft. The angle of inclination (neck–shaft angle) is approximately 135 degrees; reduction of this angle is coxa vara and follows fracture of the neck of femur. The angle of anteversion (torsion) — the forward relationship of head and neck — is normally 12–15 degrees; wide variation in anteversion of the femoral neck means that during total hip arthroplasty, orientation of the femoral neck osteotomy in correct anteversion must be assessed after hip dislocation with reference to the shaft of femur with knee flexed at 90 degrees, or an inaccurate cut and malposition of the prosthesis may result.
B(i)
The fovea capitis on the head of femur transmits blood from the obturator artery via the ligament of the head of femur (ligamentum teres). The main blood supply travels retinacularly along the intracapsular neck from the medial femoral circumflex artery (which wraps around the posterior side of the femur supplying its neck and head). In an intracapsular fracture, these retinacular vessels are disrupted; the obturator artery contribution via ligamentum teres is insufficient to sustain the head, and avascular necrosis results.
B(ii)
The linea aspera is a posterior ridge on the shaft of femur; it diverges superiorly and inferiorly. The inferior divergence ends as the medial supracondylar ridge to the adductor tubercle and the lateral supracondylar ridge. The linea aspera gives origin to many muscles: adductor longus inserts into the middle third of its medial lip; adductor magnus into the gluteal tuberosity, linea aspera, and medial supracondylar line; the vastus lateralis arises from its lateral lip.
C(i)
Pressure epiphyses are formed at joints and bear compressive forces (e.g., head of femur — a pressure epiphysis; femoral condyles). Traction epiphyses are pulled by muscles (e.g., greater trochanter — traction epiphysis for gluteus medius which draws it upward, medially, and backward; lesser trochanter — traction epiphysis for iliopsoas, the great flexor of the hip joint). The nutrient artery is directed obliquely away from the epiphyseal end; when there is an epiphysis at both ends, the nutrient canal is directed away from the more actively growing end (as per Hughes's rule: 'to the elbow I go, from the knee I flee'). Surgically, the nutrient canal direction matters during intramedullary nail insertion, as the nail must not block the nutrient foramen.

A(i)
Three tunics: The eye has three layers. Outer tunic: the sclera and cornea; the sclera serves primarily as a structural support for the optic apparatus. Middle layer (vascular layer, uvea): the choroid, ciliary body, and iris. The iris functions as a contractile diaphragm (the aperture of the eye). Inner tunic: the retina — a double-layered epithelium consisting of an outer pigmented layer and an inner neural retina; it is subdivided into 10 recognizable layers. The outermost layer (closest to the choriocapillaris) contains the photoreceptors whose outer segments are in close contact with pigmented epithelial cells. Contents: the vitreous body fills the space between the lens and retina; the aqueous humor is in the anterior and posterior chambers; the lens is a transparent biconvex structure that, along with the cornea, focuses light on the retina. Photoreceptors: rods — more sensitive to light, primarily used in dim light. Cones — require more intense lighting; conical in shape. There are also bipolar cells, horizontal cells, amacrine cells, and Müller glia cells, and a retinal ganglion cell layer.
A(ii)
Cataract: when the lens becomes opaque, the condition is termed cataract, which may also be caused by excessive exposure to ultraviolet radiation. Histological changes: the lens has three principal components — lens capsule (corresponds to a thick, elastic basal lamina), subcapsular epithelium, and lens fibers. Opacification of the lens fibers makes them less transparent; this is the basis of cataract. A myopic (short-sighted) eye can be corrected by wearing glasses with concave lenses; a hyperopic eye with convex lenses.
B(i)
Retinal pigment epithelium (RPE): the outer cell layer is pigmented; it lies between the choroid and the neural retina; Bruch's membrane is located between the choroid and the RPE. Tight junctions between RPE cells establish a blood-retina barrier. Neural retina: the inner cell layer; it is a multi-layered structure containing photoreceptors (rods and cones), neurons, and glial cells. The optic nerve (and the retina) arises in the embryo as an outgrowth of the diencephalon (forebrain); thus the optic nerve is not a true peripheral nerve — its myelin is produced by oligodendrocytes (not Schwann cells), and it is associated with multiple sclerosis.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the histology of the eye under the following headings: three tunics (layers) of the eyeball, contents of each layer, and the photoreceptor cell types in the retina.
A(ii) Explain the clinical basis of cataract and state the histological changes in the lens.
B(i) Distinguish between the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and the neural retina, stating the function of each and their embryological origin.

A(i) State the origin and root value of the phrenic nerve.
A(ii) Describe its course, relations and embryological basis of its long course on the right and left.
A(iii) Describe its termination and the points at which it reaches the diaphragm.
A(iv) Describe its distribution (motor and sensory).
C(i) Explain the anatomical basis of the deformity and other consequences after injury or section of the nerve.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The phrenic nerve is formed in the neck within the cervical plexus and contains fibres from spinal roots C3, C4 and C5.
A(ii)
• Its long course from the neck follows the embryological migration of the diaphragm from the cervical region: the septum transversum is carried ventrally and caudally, and the cervical myotomes and nerves contribute the muscle and nerve supply.
• It passes through the superior and middle mediastinum: the right phrenic descends on the right side of the SVC and heart; the left phrenic descends on the left side of the heart.
A(iii)
Both nerves terminate in the diaphragm: terminal branches of the right phrenic pass through the caval opening (T8) in the central tendon, and the left phrenic pierces the left dome.
A(iv)
• Motor: the sole motor supply of the diaphragm; the right nerve supplies the right half up to the right margin of the oesophageal opening and the left nerve the left half up to the left margin.
• Sensory: the central part of the diaphragm and the related pleura and peritoneum, and sensory fibres to the pleurae and pericardium (mediastinal pleura, fibrous and parietal pericardium); the peripheral part receives sensory fibres from the lower 6 or 7 intercostal and subcostal nerves.
C(i)
• Sectioning or injury of a phrenic nerve in the neck causes complete paralysis and eventual atrophy of the muscular part of the corresponding half of the diaphragm, except in persons who have an accessory phrenic nerve.
• Causes of injury: mechanical trauma (ligation or damage during surgery) and compression by a tumour within the chest cavity; myopathies (e.g. myasthenia gravis) and neuropathies (e.g. diabetic neuropathy) also interrupt the supply.
• The paralysed half is elevated and shows paradoxical movement: it moves upwards during inspiration (forced up by abdominal viscera) and downwards during expiration; only one half is affected because each dome has a separate nerve supply.
• Unilateral paralysis is usually asymptomatic and an incidental finding on X-ray; if both sides are paralysed there is poor exercise tolerance, orthopnoea and fatigue, and lung function tests show a restrictive deficit.
• Irritation of the diaphragmatic pleura or of the peritoneum under the diaphragm (pleurisy, subphrenic pus or blood) refers pain to the shoulder tip, because the central diaphragm sends sensory fibres in the phrenic nerve (C3-5) and the shoulder skin is supplied by the supraclavicular nerve (C3,4).

questions.question:
A(i) State the origin of the posterior intercostal arteries.
A(ii) Describe their course and relations in the intercostal space.
A(iii) State their branches, distribution and venous and lymphatic companions.
B(i) State the safe site and the danger site for passing a needle or drain through an intercostal space and the anatomical basis.
C(i) Explain the anatomical basis of the rib deformity seen on radiographs in coarctation of the aorta.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
• Each intercostal space has a single posterior and two anterior intercostal arteries.
• In the upper two spaces the posterior intercostal arteries arise from the superior intercostal artery (branch of the costocervical trunk of the subclavian artery); in the lower nine spaces they arise from the thoracic aorta (9 pairs, plus 1 pair of subcostal arteries from the posterior surface of the descending thoracic aorta).
A(ii)
Course and branching follow the intercostal nerves: each artery runs forward in the subcostal groove, high in the space between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles, in the order vein, artery, nerve from above downwards, and anastomoses with the anterior intercostal artery.
A(iii)
• Branches go to adjacent muscles, skin, parietal pleura, spinal cord and breast (branches in the 3rd and 4th spaces supply the breast); the 3rd right posterior intercostal artery gives the right bronchial artery.
• Distribution: the posterior and lateral parts of the intercostal spaces.
• Veins accompany the arteries and contain valves that direct blood posteriorly; on the right the 1st space drains to the brachiocephalic vein and the rest to the azygos vein; on the left the upper 3 spaces drain to the left brachiocephalic vein and the rest to the hemiazygos and accessory hemiazygos veins, which drain to the azygos vein.
• Lymphatics: deep lymphatics follow the arteries; posteriorly they drain to the posterior intercostal nodes in the posterior mediastinum.
B(i)
• Safe site: a needle or drain is passed immediately above the upper border of a rib; it is dangerous to pass it immediately below a rib.
• Basis: the intercostal vessels lie immediately below their corresponding ribs (vein above artery) in the subcostal groove, so a needle just above the lower rib avoids the neurovascular bundle; in thoracotomy the periosteum over a segment of the 5th or 6th rib is elevated, protecting the bundle.
C(i)
• In coarctation of the aorta the intercostal arteries derived from the aorta receive blood from the superior intercostals, from the anterior intercostal branches of the internal thoracic artery and from arteries anastomosing around the scapula.
• Together with the communication between the internal thoracic and inferior epigastric arteries, these are the principal collaterals between the aorta above and below the block.
• The intercostal arteries dilate and become tortuous and erode the lower borders of the corresponding ribs, giving the characteristic irregular notching of the ribs that helps radiographic confirmation.

A(i)
Boundaries: superiorly — inguinal ligament; medially — medial border of adductor longus; laterally — medial border of sartorius; apex — where adductor longus and sartorius cross. Roof: fascia lata (deep fascia) pierced by the great saphenous vein at the saphenous opening (fossa ovalis). Floor: formed by iliopsoas laterally and pectineus medially. Contents from lateral to medial: femoral nerve, femoral artery, femoral vein (the mnemonic 'NAVY' — from lateral: Nerve, Artery, Vein, Y-fronts/lymphatics). The femoral pulse can be palpated as it enters the femoral triangle, midway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis — the mid-inguinal point.
A(ii)
The femoral artery divides to give the profunda femoris 5 cm below the inguinal ligament. Branches of the femoral artery (mnemonic: 'Does She Scream During Poking Sessions?'): Deep external pudendal arteries, Superficial epigastric, Superficial external pudendal, Descending genicular artery, Profunda femoris artery, Superficial circumflex iliac. Profunda femoris arises from the posterolateral aspect of the femoral artery; it gives: (1) Perforating branches — 3 or 4 arteries that perforate adductor magnus, contributing to medial and posterior thigh. (2) Lateral femoral circumflex artery — wraps around anterior and lateral side of femur, supplying muscles on lateral aspect of thigh. (3) Medial femoral circumflex artery — wraps around posterior side of femur, supplying its neck and head; in a fracture of the femoral neck this artery can easily be damaged and avascular necrosis of the femoral head can occur.
B(i)
The adductor canal is a passageway in the medial thigh. The adductor hiatus is an opening between the aponeurotic distal attachment of the adductor part of adductor magnus and the tendinous distal attachment of the hamstring part. The hiatus transmits the femoral artery and vein from the adductor canal in the thigh to the popliteal fossa posterior to the knee. It is located just lateral and superior to the adductor tubercle of the femur.
B(ii)
Femoral pulse: palpated at mid-inguinal point (midway between ASIS and pubic symphysis). In femoral artery occlusion, the profunda femoris artery is the main collateral channel because the superior muscular branches of the popliteal artery have clinically important anastomoses with the terminal part of the profunda femoris and gluteal arteries, maintaining perfusion to the leg.
C(i)
The posterior division of the obturator nerve supplies both the hip and the knee joint; therefore, pain from hip pathology is referred along this common nerve pathway to present as knee pain. This is the basis of Hilton's law applied to the hip: 'the nerve supplying the joint also supplies the muscles moving the joint and the skin covering the insertion of these muscles.' The femoral nerve also supplies the hip joint via intermediate and cutaneous branches and the knee via branches of obturator and femoral nerves.
questions.question:
Describe the femoral triangle and adductor canal under the following headings, state how they relate to common pathologies, and explain the anatomical basis of referred pain to the knee from the hip.
A(i) Boundaries, roof, and floor of the femoral triangle; contents from lateral to medial
A(ii) Femoral artery — branches within the femoral triangle, including the profunda femoris and its branches
B(i) Adductor canal — boundaries, contents, and where it terminates
B(ii) Clinical basis: femoral pulse palpation and profunda femoris in femoral artery occlusion
C(i) Explain why hip joint disease causes referred pain at the knee, based on the nerve supply of both joints

questions.answerText:
A(i)
• The vagus is the 10th cranial nerve.
• The right vagus descends on the right side of the trachea, forms the posterior oesophageal plexus and continues in the abdomen as the posterior gastric nerve.
• The left vagus descends between the left common carotid and left subclavian arteries, forms the anterior oesophageal plexus and continues in the abdomen as the anterior gastric nerve.
A(ii)
• The vagus nerves lie in both the superior and the posterior mediastinum; in the posterior mediastinum the right and left vagi lie around the oesophagus and pass through the oesophageal opening of the diaphragm (T10) as the anterior and posterior vagal trunks.
• The left recurrent laryngeal branch of the vagus winds round the ligamentum arteriosus, which connects the inferior concave surface of the arch of the aorta to the left pulmonary artery.
A(iii)
• Branches: recurrent laryngeal branches on both sides and superior and inferior cervical cardiac branches (the right has both, the left has the inferior branch) to the cardiac plexus; pulmonary plexuses to the lungs; oesophageal plexuses.
• Cardiac plexus: the superficial part lies in front of the ligamentum arteriosus (inferior cervical cardiac branch of the left vagus); the deep part lies in front of the left bronchus and at the bifurcation of the pulmonary trunk, behind the arch of the aorta on the lowest part of the trachea; parasympathetic fibres relay in the heart.
A(iv)
• Heart: through the cardiac plexus to the SA and AV nodes and the AV bundle; parasympathetics decrease the rate of impulse generation, sympathetics increase it.
• Lungs and visceral pleura (via the pulmonary plexuses): bronchoconstrictor, vasodilator to pulmonary vessels and secretomotor to glands; the vagal efferents mediate the cough reflex that clears secretions and dust.
• Oesophagus and trachea: recurrent laryngeal branch to the striated upper third of the oesophagus, parasympathetic secretomotor fibres to the oesophageal glands; vagus to the mucous membrane and parasympathetics of the trachea; gastric irritation of vagus nerve endings may cause hiccup.
questions.question:
A(i) State the nature of the vagus nerve and describe its course in the thorax on the right and left.
A(ii) Describe its relations in the mediastinum.
A(iii) State its branches and plexuses in the thorax.
A(iv) Describe its distribution to thoracic structures.

A(i) Describe the four main layers of the gastrointestinal tract wall, giving the composition of each layer.
A(ii) For the muscularis layer, name the two nerve plexuses associated with it, state where each is located, and explain the function of each.
B(i) Explain why the esophagus has an adventitia instead of a serosa, and state the structural difference between these two outermost coverings.
B(ii) Distinguish between the serosa and the mesentery, naming the structures each is continuous with.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
• Mucosa: consists of an epithelial lining, lamina propria (zone of loose connective tissue rich in blood vessels, lymphatics, lymphocytes, smooth muscle cells, and sometimes small glands), and muscularis mucosae (thin layer of smooth muscle that separates the mucosa from the submucosa and allows local movements of the mucosa).
• Submucosa: denser connective tissue containing larger blood and lymph vessels, the submucosal (Meissner) plexus of autonomic nerves, and possibly glands and lymphoid tissue.
• Muscularis (muscularis externa): thick layer of smooth muscle organized into an internal circular sublayer and an external longitudinal sublayer; connective tissue between them contains blood vessels, lymph vessels, and the myenteric (Auerbach) nerve plexus.
• Serosa: outermost layer; a thin sheet of loose connective tissue covered with mesothelium (simple squamous covering epithelium); rich in blood vessels, lymphatics, and adipose tissue.
A(ii)
• Submucosal (Meissner) plexus: located in the submucosa between the submucosa and the muscularis; together with the myenteric plexus constitutes the local enteric nervous system.
• Myenteric (Auerbach) plexus: located in the connective tissue between the circular and longitudinal muscle sublayers; responsible for local contraction of the muscularis, mixing and propelling the contents of the lumen (peristalsis).
• Both plexuses together form the local enteric nervous system, which functions independently of the CNS; they are composed mainly of nerve cell aggregates forming small parasympathetic ganglia, numerous in regions of greatest motility.
B(i)
The esophagus is not suspended in a cavity but is bound directly to adjacent structures, so instead of a serosa it has a thick adventitia. The adventitia consists of connective tissue containing vessels and nerves but lacks mesothelium, whereas the serosa is covered by mesothelium.
B(ii)
The serosa of the small and large intestines is continuous with parts of the mesentery. The mesentery is a large fold of adipose connective tissue covered on both sides by mesothelium; it suspends the intestines and is continuous with the peritoneum (the serous membrane lining the abdominal cavity).

questions.question:
(i) Describe the gross anatomy of the kidney, including its shape, coverings, and internal structure (cortex, medulla, pyramids, sinus, calyces).
(ii) Relate the parts of the kidney to a common renal pathology.
(iii) Explain how disease/obstruction of the kidney or its drainage system can produce a functional deficit at a distance.
questions.answerText:
(i)
• The kidneys are bean-shaped, retroperitoneal organs lying on the posterior abdominal wall from about the T12 to L3 vertebral level, each about 10 cm long, 5 cm wide and 2.5 cm thick, with the right kidney slightly lower due to the liver.
• Each kidney has a superior pole bearing the suprarenal gland, an inferior pole, a convex lateral border, and a concave medial border indented by the renal hilum.
• Coverings, from within outward, are the fibrous (renal) capsule, perirenal fat, renal fascia, and pararenal fat.
• Internally, a dark brown outer cortex surrounds a lighter medulla composed of about a dozen renal pyramids, each with its base toward the cortex and its apex (renal papilla) projecting into a minor calyx; cortex extends between pyramids as renal columns.
• At the hilum, the renal vein lies anterior to the renal artery, which lies anterior to the renal pelvis; the hilum leads into the renal sinus, which contains the pelvis, calyces, vessels, nerves and fat.
• The renal pelvis, a funnel-shaped expansion of the ureter, receives two or three major calyces, each dividing into two or three minor calyces.
(ii)
• Renal (kidney) stones are a clinical consideration associated with the kidney and relate to the calyceal and pelvic system where urine collects before draining into the ureter.
• The renal pyramids and papillae are the sites from which urine is excreted into the minor calyces, so pathology of the papillae or pyramids affects urine drainage.
(iii)
• The ureter has three points of constriction - the pelviureteric junction, where it crosses the pelvic brim, and its intramural (intravesical) course - which are potential sites of obstruction by ureteric stones.
• Obstruction at any of these constrictions causes back-pressure on the kidney, from the collecting system through the pelvis to the pyramids, producing a functional deficit in urine drainage from that kidney.
• Ureteric pain from such obstruction is referred to the ipsilateral lower quadrant of the anterior abdominal wall and especially the groin, showing how a renal or ureteric problem produces a distant clinical effect.
• This referred pain reflects the segmental (T11-T12) sympathetic innervation shared by the ureter and the abdominal wall/groin dermatomes.

questions.question:
A. Describe the gross anatomy of the paranasal sinuses under the following headings: the four pairs of sinuses, their development, and their general function.
B. State how each of the paranasal sinuses relates to a specific clinical complication when infected or fractured.
C. Explain why disease of the paranasal sinuses can spread to produce a functional deficit in a distant structure, namely the brain or the nasal cavity.
questions.answerText:
A
The nasal sinuses are air-containing sacs lined by ciliated epithelium, communicating with the nasal cavity through narrow, easily occluded channels; they develop as outgrowths from the nasal cavity. There are 4 pairs: the maxillary antrum, sphenoid, frontal and ethmoid sinuses. The maxillary antrum and ethmoid sinuses are present in a rudimentary state at birth, while the rest become evident at about the 7th year of life. The lining of the sinuses is continuous with the nasal mucosa; their function is obscure, but they provide resonance to the voice, shape to the face, and some degree of warmth and humidification to inspired air. The paranasal sinuses are supplied by branches of the ophthalmic and maxillary nerves.
B
The frontal sinuses' posterosuperior wall lies adjacent to the frontal lobe of the brain, and their floor abuts the ethmoid cells, nasal fossa roof and orbit; infection here may cause a frontal lobe abscess, and fracture severe enough to tear the dura and pia-arachnoid causes CSF rhinorrhoea. The maxillary sinus (antrum) may become infected from the nasal cavity or from caries of the upper molar teeth, whose roots are separated from the sinus floor only by a thin, sometimes deficient, layer of bone. The ethmoid sinuses lie on each side of the cribriform plate, related above to the frontal lobes; infection (ethmoiditis) may result in a frontal cerebral abscess, and ethmoidal fracture may cause CSF leakage into the nasal cavity. The sphenoid sinuses lie within the body of the sphenoid and may extend laterally into the greater wing of the sphenoid or backward into the basal part of the occipital bone; each drains into the nasal cavity above the superior concha (the sphenoethmoidal recess).
C
Because the frontal and ethmoid sinuses are directly related anatomically to the frontal lobes of the brain (posterosuperior wall of the frontal sinus, and the region above the cribriform plate for the ethmoid sinuses), infection at either site can spread directly to produce a frontal lobe or frontal cerebral abscess; and because fracture of either sinus, if severe enough to tear the dura and pia-arachnoid, places the subarachnoid space in communication with the nasal cavity, CSF rhinorrhoea (leakage of CSF into the nose) results, sometimes even on the contralateral side since the sinuses may communicate with one another.

questions.question:
(i) Describe the origin, course, branches and distribution of the renal artery.
(ii) State why the segmental arteries of the kidney are described as end arteries.
(iii) Explain the anatomical basis of the consequence of injury or occlusion of a segmental renal artery.
questions.answerText:
(i)
• The renal arteries arise from the aorta at the level of the L1/L2 intervertebral disc; the right renal artery passes posterior to the inferior vena cava.
• Each renal artery divides at the hilum into anterior and posterior branches; these give rise to segmental arteries.
• Four segmental arteries, apical, anterosuperior, anteroinferior and inferior, arise from the anterior branch, and the posterior branch itself constitutes the posterior segmental artery.
• Each segmental artery further gives lobar arteries, one for each renal pyramid, which give two or three interlobar arteries running toward the cortex on each side of the pyramid.
• Interlobar arteries give arcuate arteries at the corticomedullary junction, which give several interlobular arteries, from which afferent glomerular arterioles arise.
• The renal veins lie anterior to their respective arteries; each renal vein drains into the inferior vena cava, and the left renal vein additionally receives the left suprarenal and left gonadal veins before crossing anterior to the aorta.
(ii)
• The segmental arteries of the kidney are described as end arteries, meaning they do not anastomose with one another.
• Because each segmental artery supplies its own renal segment without collateral supply from adjacent segmental arteries, the renal parenchyma is divided into distinct vascular segments.
(iii)
• Since the segmental arteries are end arteries, occlusion or injury of one segmental artery cuts off blood supply to its corresponding renal segment.
• This lack of anastomosis means the affected segment cannot receive compensatory blood flow from neighbouring segments.
• Lymphatic drainage of the kidney is to the right and left lumbar lymph nodes, and nerve supply is via the renal plexus (vagus and abdominopelvic splanchnic nerves), so a segmental vascular injury is an isolated event within the kidney rather than one shared with adjacent segments.

A(i)
• Conical, soft, spongy, elastic and pinkish in health (brown in the young, mottled black in adults and dark in city dwellers from deposited dust and carbon particles); right lung about 600 g, left about 550 g; the right is larger, heavier, shorter and wider. Each has an apex, a base, 3 surfaces (costal convex, mediastinal with the hilum, diaphragmatic concave), 3 borders (anterior, posterior, inferior) and a root; the posterior surface lies in the paravertebral gutter.
• Apex: rounded, extends into the root of the neck 2.5-4 cm above the sternal end of the 1st rib, covered by cervical pleura and suprapleural membrane. Base: broad, concave, rests on the diaphragm, which separates the right lung from the right lobe of the liver and the left lung from the left lobe of the liver, stomach and spleen. Anterior border: where costal and mediastinal surfaces meet, with the cardiac notch on the left; posterior border from C7 to T10; inferior border separates the base from the costal and mediastinal surfaces.
A(ii)
Right lung: 3 lobes (upper, middle, lower) by oblique and horizontal fissures; left lung: 2 lobes (upper and smaller lower) by the oblique fissure, with the lingula below the cardiac notch; visceral pleura extends into the fissures so the lobes move freely. Lower border (neutral position) crosses the 6th rib in the midclavicular line, the 8th rib in the midaxillary line and reaches the 10th rib posteriorly.
A(iii)
Hilum: wedge-shaped area on the mediastinal surface; root lies opposite T5-T7. Right root: in the groove of the arch of the azygos vein; eparterial and hyparterial bronchi, right pulmonary artery, 2 right pulmonary veins, hilar lymph nodes. Left root: in the concavity of the arch of the aorta; left main bronchus, left pulmonary artery, 2 left pulmonary veins, hilar lymph nodes. Both also contain bronchial vessels, nerves and lymphatics enclosed by pleura.
A(iv)
• Right lung, 10 segments: upper lobe apical, posterior, anterior; middle lobe lateral, medial; lower lobe superior (apical), medial basal, anterior basal, lateral basal, posterior basal. Left lung, 8 segments: upper lobe apicoposterior, anterior, superior lingula, inferior lingula; lower lobe superior (apical), medial basal, anterior basal, lateral basal, posterior basal.
• Each segment is pyramidal (apex to the hilum, base to the surface), separated from its neighbours by connective tissue septa, with the segmental bronchus, bronchial vessels and a pulmonary artery branch central; little arterial anastomosis between segments; intersegmental pulmonary vein tributaries guide separation; it has its own lymphatics and autonomic supply and is the smallest part that can be removed without affecting adjacent lung.
A(v)
• Arteries: 2 left bronchial arteries from the descending thoracic aorta and 1 right bronchial artery from the 3rd right posterior intercostal supply the bronchial tree down to the respiratory bronchioles; pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood to the alveoli and anastomose with the bronchial arteries at the precapillary level. Veins: 4 pulmonary veins to the left atrium; right bronchial vein to the azygos vein, left to the accessory hemiazygos vein.
• Lymph: superficial plexus (deep to the visceral pleura) and deep plexus (peribronchial) drain to pulmonary then bronchopulmonary (hilar) nodes, then superior and inferior tracheobronchial nodes, then the bronchomediastinal trunks to the junction of subclavian and internal jugular veins (right trunk may form the right lymphatic duct; left may end in the thoracic duct). Nerves: pulmonary plexuses; vagus is bronchoconstrictor, vasodilator and secretomotor, sympathetic has the opposite actions.
B(i)
• Connective tissue septa between segments are a natural barrier to the spread of infection, but carcinoma and tuberculosis break through; abscesses are commoner in the posterior segment of the upper lobe and the apical segment of the lower lobe because these are the most dependent segments in the supine position.
• Other pathologies: foreign particles enter the right main bronchus easily (wider, more vertical); pulmonary embolism (pulmonary artery obstructed by air, blood clot, fat, tumour cells or foreign particles); asthma (dyspnoea); fibrosis reduces compliance and emphysema reduces elasticity; lobectomy or pneumonectomy is used in lung cancer.
C(i)
• Costal pleura is supplied by intercostal nerves, so pleural or lung disease may cause referred pain along the thoracic wall and anterior abdominal wall; irritation over the central diaphragm refers pain to the shoulder through the phrenic nerve (C3-5).
• Lymphatic spread passes from the hilar nodes to the tracheobronchial nodes and bronchomediastinal trunks; a tumour within the chest cavity may compress the phrenic nerve and cause diaphragmatic paralysis with paradoxical movement (functional deficit).
