questions.answerText:
(i)
• The spleen is an ovoid, highly vascular, reddish-purple organ, on average about 12 cm long, 7 cm broad, 3 cm thick and weighing about 150 g, related to the 9th to 11th ribs on the left side.
• It has two ends, an expanded anterior end and a rounded posterior end resting on the upper pole of the left kidney, three borders (superior, inferior and intermediate), and two surfaces (diaphragmatic and visceral).
• The diaphragmatic surface is convex and related to the diaphragm, left lung and pleura, and the 9th-11th ribs; the visceral surface is concave and bears gastric, renal, colic and pancreatic impressions.
• The hilum lies on the inferomedial part of the gastric impression and transmits the splenic vessels and nerves, giving attachment to the gastrosplenic and splenorenal ligaments; the phrenicocolic ligament supports, but is not attached to, the anterior end of the spleen.
(ii)
• The gastric impression, related to the fundus of the stomach, is the largest impression; the renal impression relates to the left kidney and sometimes the suprarenal gland; the colic impression relates to the splenic flexure of the colon; the pancreatic impression relates to the tail of the pancreas.
• The gastrosplenic ligament contains the short gastric vessels supplying the stomach, and the splenorenal ligament contains the tail of the pancreas and splenic vessels, so disease or surgery at the spleen can affect the stomach, kidney, colon or pancreas through these relations.
(iii)
• Although protected by the 9th to 12th ribs, the spleen is the most frequently injured organ in the abdomen.
• Severe blows to the left side may fracture ribs, producing sharp fragments that lacerate the spleen, and blunt trauma elsewhere that raises intra-abdominal pressure can also rupture it because its capsule is thin and the pulp soft.
• If ruptured, the spleen bleeds profusely because it is a highly vascular organ receiving the splenic artery, the largest branch of the coeliac trunk.
• This produces severe intraperitoneal haemorrhage and shock, a systemic and distant functional deficit in circulation arising from a local splenic injury.
• Repair of a ruptured spleen is difficult, so splenectomy or subtotal splenectomy is often performed to prevent the patient from bleeding to death.
• Even after total splenectomy, most splenic functions are assumed by other reticuloendothelial organs such as the liver and bone marrow, though susceptibility to certain bacterial infections increases.
questions.question:

(ii) Relate the surfaces/impressions of the spleen to organs it may affect in disease.

(i) Describe the origin, course, branches and distribution of the arteries supplying the stomach.
(iii) Explain the anatomical basis of the venous route through which gastric bleeding enters the portal circulation.
questions.answerText:
(i)
• The arteries of the stomach are derived from branches of the coeliac artery. The left gastric artery arises from the coeliac artery, passes upward and to the left to reach the oesophagus, then descends along the lesser curvature, supplying the lower third of the oesophagus and the upper right part of the stomach. The right gastric artery arises from the hepatic artery at the upper border of the pylorus and runs left along the lesser curvature, supplying the lower right part of the stomach.
• The short gastric arteries arise from the splenic artery at the hilum of the spleen and pass forward in the gastrosplenic omentum to supply the fundus. The left gastro-omental (gastroepiploic) artery arises from the splenic artery at the hilum of the spleen and passes forward in the gastrosplenic omentum to supply the stomach along the upper part of the greater curvature. The right gastro-omental artery arises from the gastroduodenal branch of the hepatic artery and passes left to supply the stomach along the lower part of the greater curvature.
(iii)
• The left and right gastric veins drain directly into the portal vein.
• The short gastric veins and the left gastroepiploic vein join the splenic vein.
• The right gastroepiploic vein joins the superior mesenteric vein.
• All venous drainage of the stomach therefore ultimately enters the portal circulation, via the portal vein, splenic vein or superior mesenteric vein, before passing through the liver.
• This portal route explains why bleeding from portal-systemic anastomoses, such as oesophageal varices, is related to the portal venous system.

questions.question:
(A) Describe the oesophagus under the following headings: A(i) its four constrictions along its length A(ii) the upper oesophageal sphincter A(iii) the lower oesophageal sphincter.
(B) Explain the clinical basis of why the areas of constriction are important.
(C) Distinguish between the upper oesophageal sphincter and the lower oesophageal sphincter.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The oesophagus has four constrictions: at 15 cm (cricopharyngeus, upper oesophageal sphincter), at 22.5 cm (crossed by the aortic arch) and 27.5 cm (crossed by the left main bronchus) from the upper incisor teeth, and at 40 cm, where it passes through the right crus of the diaphragm (oesophageal hiatus).
A(ii)
The upper oesophageal sphincter is an anatomical sphincter formed by the cricopharyngeus muscle at the pharyngo-oesophageal junction.
A(iii)
• The lower oesophageal sphincter is a physiological sphincter at the gastro-oesophageal junction with no true muscular thickening.
• It is maintained by the acute angle of entry of the oesophagus into the stomach, compression of the intra-abdominal oesophagus by positive intra-abdominal pressure, prominent mucosal folds at the junction, and the pinch-cock effect of the right crus of the diaphragm.
B
• The constrictions are clinically important because they are sites where swallowed foreign bodies commonly impact.
• They are prone to trauma during instrumentation such as rigid oesophagoscopy.
• They are common sites for stricture formation following ingestion of corrosive substances.
• They are also common sites of oesophageal carcinoma.
C
• The upper oesophageal sphincter is a true anatomical (muscular) sphincter formed by the cricopharyngeus, located at 15 cm from the incisor teeth.
• The lower oesophageal sphincter is a physiological sphincter maintained by mechanical factors at the gastro-oesophageal junction and prevents gastric reflux, rather than a distinct muscular ring controlling food passage.

A
Most of the muscles of the larynx receive their innervation via the recurrent laryngeal branch of the vagus nerve; the exception is the cricothyroid muscle, which receives its innervation via the external laryngeal nerve. Motor supply to the muscles is from the nucleus ambiguus via the cranial accessory: to the cricothyroid via the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve, and to all other laryngeal muscles, including the upper oesophagus and cricopharyngeus, via the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
B
Sensory innervation of the larynx is via branches of the vagus nerve: above the vocal folds it is via the internal laryngeal nerve, and below the vocal folds it is by way of branches of the recurrent laryngeal nerve; parasympathetic innervation of the larynx is mainly by way of branches of the vagus nerve. Lymphatic drainage similarly follows this division: above the cords to the upper deep cervical nodes, and below the cords to the lower deep cervical nodes.
questions.question:
A. Describe the nerve supply of the larynx, including the origin and distribution of the recurrent laryngeal nerve and the exception to its motor supply.
B. State how the sensory innervation of the larynx is divided in relation to the vocal folds.

Describe the brachial artery:
A(i) Origin and termination
A(ii) Course
A(iii) Branches
B. State the safe site associated with clinical use of the brachial artery.
C. Explain the anatomical basis of the deformity/complication (Volkmann's ischaemic contracture) that can follow injury to this artery.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The brachial artery provides the main arterial supply to the arm and is the continuation of the axillary artery; it begins at the inferior border of teres major and ends in the cubital fossa opposite the neck of the radius.
A(ii)
Under cover of the bicipital aponeurosis, it divides into the radial and ulnar arteries.
A(iii)
Its branches include the deep brachial (profunda brachii) artery, which accompanies the radial nerve, the superior ulnar collateral artery, which accompanies the ulnar nerve, and the inferior ulnar collateral artery.
B
During blood pressure measurement, the stethoscope is placed over the brachial artery in the cubital fossa, and the cubital fossa is the site used to palpate the brachial pulse.
C
• Volkmann's ischaemic contracture is a deformity of the hand, fingers and wrist caused by injury to the muscles of the forearm.
• The classical presentation is a supracondylar fracture of the humerus, although fracture of the arm or elbow may also result in this deformity; the artery involved is the brachial artery.
• The contracture occurs when there is a lack of blood flow (ischaemia) to the forearm, usually from increased pressure resulting from swelling (compartment syndrome).
• Because there is very little room within each fascial compartment of the arm and forearm, haemorrhage or oedema following injury to the brachial artery can cause secondary vascular compression: veins are affected first, and later the arteries, resulting in ischaemia of the affected part.
• The classical presentation of the resulting acute compartment syndrome is remembered by "the five P's": pulselessness, paraesthesia, poikilothermia, paralysis and pallor.
• There are three levels of severity of the resulting Volkmann's contracture: the mildest involves flexion contracture of only two or three fingers with no or limited loss of sensation; a more severe form involves all fingers flexed with the thumb stuck in the palm and some sensory loss.
• The most severe form involves all the muscles in the forearm that flex and extend the wrist and fingers, producing a severely disabling condition.
• This progression illustrates how injury to the brachial artery at the elbow can produce a graded functional deficit distally in the hand and fingers.

questions.question:
Describe the deep fascial spaces of the hand:
A(i) Thenar space
A(ii) The list of compartments/fascial spaces of the hand
A(iii) Space of Parona
B. Explain the clinical basis for infection spreading between these compartments.
C. Distinguish between the thenar space and the midpalmar space.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The thenar space lies on the thumb side of the septum that joins the border of the palmar aponeurosis to the palmar border of the third metacarpal bone; it contains the first lumbrical muscle and is overlaid by the flexor tendons to the index finger.
A(ii)
The compartments and fascial spaces of the hand include the dorsal spaces, hypothenar space, midpalmar space, thenar space, web spaces and pulp spaces, all bounded by connective tissue.
A(iii)
The space of Parona extends from the proximal margin of the carpal tunnel to the mid-forearm; its roof is formed distally by the flexor digitorum profundus tendons and proximally by the belly of flexor digitorum superficialis (whose origin forms the proximal boundary), it is limited medially by flexor carpi ulnaris and laterally by flexor pollicis longus, and its floor is formed by pronator quadratus distally and the interosseous membrane in its proximal two-thirds.
B
• These fascial spaces allow mobility of the hand structures but, being bounded by connective tissue, offer little resistance to the spread of infection.
• Infection within the thenar space can readily break into the connective tissue canals surrounding the ulnar three lumbricals.
• For practical purposes the thenar space may therefore be considered continuous distally with these lumbrical canals, and thus distally communicates with the web spaces.
• The thenar space also communicates proximally with the space of Parona.
• Infection of these deep spaces, including the space of Parona, can be difficult to diagnose.
C
• The thenar space lies on the thumb (radial) side of the septum joining the palmar aponeurosis to the third metacarpal, contains the first lumbrical, and is overlaid by the flexor tendons of the index finger.
• The midpalmar space, by contrast, lies on the ulnar side of this septum, related to the tendons for the middle, ring and little fingers and to adductor pollicis, separated from the thenar space by the lateral palmar septum.
• The thenar space communicates proximally with the space of Parona and distally with the lumbrical canals/web spaces, reflecting its position along the flexor tendon of the index finger.
• This anatomical separation by the lateral palmar septum explains why infection in one compartment tends initially to remain localised to that space before spreading along its own specific communicating pathway.

questions.question:
A(i) Define the pleura and describe its parts.
A(ii) Describe the parietal pleura and its parts.
A(iii) Describe the visceral pleura and the pleural cavity.
A(iv) Describe the lines of pleural reflection with their surface markings.
A(v) Describe the pleural recesses.
A(vi) Describe the blood supply, nerve supply and lymphatic drainage of the pleura.
B(i) Explain why the cervical pleura and the lower pleural margin are vulnerable to injury.
B(ii) Explain why the costodiaphragmatic recess is the clinically more important recess.
C(i) Distinguish between the parietal and the visceral pleura.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
A thin, double-layered serous membrane that envelops each lung and lines the thoracic cavity, made of visceral and parietal layers with the intervening pleural cavity; the two pleural cavities are totally separate.
A(ii)
Thicker outer layer lining the thoracic wall, mediastinum, diaphragm and neck, and can be stripped; 4 parts: costal (ribs, costal cartilages, intercostal spaces, sides of vertebral bodies, back of sternum, separated from them by endothoracic fascia), diaphragmatic, mediastinal (encloses the hilum structures, continuous with visceral pleura at the hilum, and below the hilum forms the pulmonary ligament) and cervical (cupola, 2.5-4 cm above the medial third of the clavicle, attached to the suprapleural membrane).
A(iii)
Visceral pleura: closely adherent to the lung including its fissures, cannot be stripped, smooth and slippery, continuous with the parietal pleura at the hilum; the pleural cavity is a potential space with a small amount of lubricating pleural fluid that reduces friction and helps prevent lung collapse.
A(iv)
Sternal (costal to mediastinal anteriorly): from behind the sternoclavicular joints to the midline at the 2nd costal cartilage, then the right edge passes vertically to the 6th costal cartilage while the left arches laterally at the 4th costal cartilage (because of the heart) to the 6th. Costal (costal to diaphragmatic): crosses the 8th rib in the midclavicular line, the 10th rib in the midaxillary line and the 12th rib at the lateral border of erector spinae. Vertebral: rounded reflections in the paravertebral planes from T1 to T12.
A(v)
Recesses are spaces not occupied by lung that lung enters only on forced deep respiration: costodiaphragmatic (between costal and diaphragmatic pleura, shallow in inspiration and deeper in expiration) and costomediastinal (behind the sternum where costal pleura becomes mediastinal pleura, more conspicuous on the left near the heart).
A(vi)
• Blood supply: visceral pleura from bronchial and pulmonary arteries, veins to the pulmonary vein; parietal pleura from the vessels of the structures covered - cervical and costal from intercostal vessels, diaphragmatic outer part from intercostal and inner part from pericardiophrenic vessels, mediastinal from pericardiophrenic vessels.
• Nerve supply: costal pleura by intercostal nerves; diaphragmatic pleura by phrenic nerves centrally and intercostal nerves peripherally; mediastinal pleura by the phrenic nerve; the visceral pleura is described as having no nerve supply and as receiving vasomotor supply from autonomic nerves (pulmonary plexuses).
• Lymph: visceral to the pulmonary plexus in interlobar and peribronchial spaces; parietal costal, mediastinal and cervical to the internal thoracic (anterior) and intercostal (posterior) chains; diaphragmatic to retrosternal, mediastinal and sometimes coeliac nodes.
B(i)
The cervical pleura reaches about 1 inch (2.5 cm) above the clavicle because of the oblique slope of the first rib, so it can be wounded (pneumothorax) by a stab wound, a surgeon's knife or an anaesthetist's needle above the clavicle; the lower edge descends just below the 12th rib medially (below the 11th if the 12th is short), so it may be opened in a loin incision.
B(ii)
The costodiaphragmatic recess is the larger recess and the clinically more important one, providing the space where fluid collects in disease (pneumothorax with air, haemothorax with blood, empyema with pus, effusion); fluid is drained with a needle just above a rib, or through the space between the 7th costal cartilage and the xiphoid process.
C(i)
• Parietal: thicker, outer, lines wall, diaphragm, mediastinum and neck, named regionally, can be stripped, supplied by intercostal and phrenic nerves (so pleural irritation refers pain along the thoracic and anterior abdominal wall, and to the shoulder from the central diaphragm).
• Visceral: inner layer closely adherent to the lung surface and fissures, cannot be stripped, smooth and slippery so the lung moves freely, supplied by bronchial and pulmonary vessels; pleurisy is inflammation of the pleura, usually with pneumonia or other lung infection.

A(i)
A thin serous membrane lining the walls of the abdominal and pelvic cavities and covering the organs within; two layers: parietal and visceral.
A(ii)
• The cavity is the potential space between the layers, contains no organs and a thin layer of fluid, and is a closed sac in males; it is divided into greater and lesser sacs that communicate through the epiploic foramen.
• The fluid lubricates the surfaces so viscera move without friction, contains leukocytes and antibodies, and is absorbed by lymphatics on the inferior surface of the diaphragm.
A(iii)
• Provides a slippery surface for movement of viscera; phagocytic cells protect viscera; can store large amounts of fat.
• Mesothelial cells transform into fibroblasts, promoting healing; the mesothelium acts as a semi-permeable membrane.
A(iv)
Intraperitoneal organs are completely surrounded (stomach, spleen, small intestine); retroperitoneal organs are covered partially on their anterior surfaces only (kidney, ureter).
B(i)
• In the female the cavity communicates with the exterior through the uterine tubes, uterus and vagina, a potential pathway of infection.
• Because the mesothelium is semi-permeable, urea can be removed from blood by circulating fluids through the cavity: peritoneal dialysis.
C(i)
• Parietal: lines the inner surface of abdominal and pelvic walls and lower surface of diaphragm; loosely attached by extraperitoneal connective tissue; pain sensitive; nerve supply same as the overlying body wall.
• Visceral: lines the outer surface of viscera; cannot be stripped; nerve supply is that of the underlying viscera (sympathetic), with receptors sensitive to overdistension, traction on mesenteries, spasm and ischaemia.
• Blood supply: parietal from lumbar vessels, inferior and superior epigastric, musculophrenic and deep circumflex arteries; visceral from the arteries supplying the appropriate viscera.

A(i)
The parotid gland is the largest salivary gland (para = around, otic = ear); it is situated below the external acoustic meatus, in front of the sternomastoid, and also projects forward onto the surface of masseter. It is pyramidal in shape with the apex pointing downward, has 4 surfaces (superior/base, lateral/superficial, anteromedial, posteromedial) separated by 3 borders (anterior, posterior, medial), and has 1 main lobe and 1 accessory lobe (a small detached part called the accessory parotid gland or Socia Parotidis, lying on masseter between the zygomatic arch and the parotid duct). The capsule has a false capsule, formed by the investing layer of deep cervical fascia, and a true capsule, formed by condensation of the stroma.
A(ii)
The parotid duct is about 5 cm long, arises from the anterior border of the gland, runs on masseter, and at the anterior border of masseter runs medially to pierce buccinator and the mucosa, opening into the vestibule of the mouth opposite the crown of the upper 2nd molar tooth; its surface anatomy corresponds to the middle third of a line from the lower border of the tragus to a point midway between the nasal ala and the upper labial margin. From superficial to deep within the substance of the gland are: the facial nerve and its branches; the retromandibular vein and its two divisions (maxillary vein, superficial temporal vein); and the external carotid artery and its two terminal branches. Other structures within the gland are the auriculotemporal nerve, the posterior auricular artery, and the preauricular lymph nodes.
B
Within the gland, the facial nerve radiates like a goose's foot (Pes Anserinus) through the anterior border of the gland into its branches (temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular, cervical); because the facial nerve runs through the substance of the gland, it is at risk during parotid surgery or trauma. Frey's syndrome (also known as gustatory sweating or auriculo-temporal nerve syndrome) commonly occurs after parotid surgery or trauma, from injury of the auriculotemporal and great auricular nerves; during healing, secretomotor fibres of the auriculotemporal nerve join with the great auricular nerve and reach the sweat glands of facial skin, so that sweating, warmth and redness of the face occur as a result of salivary stimulation by the smell or taste of food.
C
The parotid gland's secretomotor (parasympathetic) supply is via the auriculotemporal nerve, producing a watery secretion, with sympathetic supply producing a mucous-rich, sticky secretion derived from the plexus around the external carotid artery. In contrast, the submandibular gland's duct is the submandibular duct (Wharton's duct), and its nerve supply is via branches from the submandibular ganglion, through which it receives parasympathetic fibres from the chorda tympani, sensory fibres from the lingual branch of the mandibular nerve, and sympathetic fibres from the plexus on the facial artery.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the parotid gland under the following headings: location, external features, and capsule.
A(ii) Describe the parotid duct, and list the structures within the substance of the gland from superficial to deep, and the other structures found within the gland.
B. Explain the clinical basis for why the parotid gland is particularly vulnerable to nerve injury during surgery, and describe the syndrome that can follow such injury.
C. Distinguish between the parotid gland and the submandibular gland in terms of their ducts and ganglia associated with their secretomotor supply.

questions.answerText:
(i)
• The heart has four chambers, the right and left atria (receiving chambers) and the right and left ventricles (discharging chambers), enclosed in the double-walled pericardial sac, and rests on its diaphragmatic (inferior) surface.
• It has an apex, formed by the inferolateral part of the left ventricle and lying posterior to the 5th intercostal space where the apex beat is felt, a base, formed mainly by the left atrium and part of the right atrium, four borders and three surfaces.
• The right border is formed mainly by the right atrium; the left border by the left ventricle and left auricle; the inferior border by the right ventricle mainly and the left ventricle; the superior border by both atria, auricles and the great vessels.
• The anterior (sternocostal) surface consists chiefly of the right ventricle; the inferior (diaphragmatic) surface consists chiefly of the left ventricle and a small part of the right ventricle; the left (pulmonary) surface is formed mainly by the left ventricle.
• The right atrium receives venous blood from the SVC, IVC and coronary sinus, has a smooth sinus venarum and a rough muscular wall with pectinate muscles, and communicates with the right ventricle via the right atrioventricular (tricuspid) orifice.
• The left atrium receives the four pulmonary veins and communicates with the left ventricle via the left atrioventricular (mitral) orifice; the right ventricle has a tricuspid valve and leads to the pulmonary trunk via the conus arteriosus, while the left ventricle, with twice the wall thickness, has the mitral valve and leads to the aorta via the aortic vestibule and aortic valve.
(ii)
• Valvular insufficiency results from valve leaflets not completely sealing when a valve is closed, so regurgitation of blood occurs into the proximal chamber, generating a characteristic heart murmur.
• Positional and septal anomalies include dextrocardia, atrial septal defects and ventricular septal defects.
• Aortic dissection, a tear in the inner wall of the aorta associated with high blood pressure, and aortic aneurysm, dilation of an artery greater than 50% of its normal diameter, are pathologies of the great vessel arising from the left ventricle.
(iii)
• The conducting system, the SA node in the posterior wall of the right atrium, the AV node in the floor of the right atrium, the AV bundle and Purkinje fibres, initiates and coordinates the heartbeat; damage to a coronary artery supplying these nodes can disturb heart rhythm.
• Cardiac afferent fibres carrying pain from ischaemic myocardium travel via sympathetic afferents in the cardiac plexus to spinal cord segments T1-T5 shared with dermatomes of the chest wall and upper limb, so the central nervous system perceives cardiac pain as coming from the body wall.
• This explains why myocardial ischaemia is felt as pain in the mid or left chest that radiates to the left jaw and left arm, a distant somatic sensation produced by a cardiac (visceral) problem.
questions.question:
(i) Describe the gross anatomy of the heart under the headings: chambers, borders and surfaces.
(ii) Relate the chambers/valves of the heart to a recognised pathology.
(iii) Explain how a cardiac problem can produce a functional deficit or sensation felt at a distant site.

questions.answerText:
A
The pterygopalatine fossa is an inverted pyramidal-shaped, fat-filled space located on the lateral side of the skull, between the infratemporal fossa and the nasopharynx; it is antero-posteriorly between the maxilla/palatine bone and the pterygoid process, and laterally between the infratemporal fossa and nasopharynx. Its boundaries are: anterior - posterior surface of maxilla below the floor of the orbit; posterior - lateral pterygoid plate and part of the medial plate; medial - perpendicular plate of the palatine bone; lateral - pterygomaxillary fissure; superior - undersurface of the greater wing of the sphenoid; inferior - absent (the posterior wall meets the anterior wall, and between them is the greater palatine canal). Its contents are the terminal (third/pterygoid) part of the maxillary artery and the initial parts of its branches, the maxillary vein, the maxillary nerve, and the pterygopalatine ganglion (a parasympathetic ganglion, one of four parasympathetic ganglia of the head and neck, the others being the submandibular, otic and ciliary ganglia).
B
The pterygopalatine fossa is described as a major neurovascular crossroad between the orbit, the nasal cavity, the nasopharynx, the oral cavity, the infratemporal fossa and the cranial fossa. Its communications are: laterally with the infratemporal fossa through the pterygomaxillary fissure; medially with the nasal cavity through the sphenopalatine foramen; anterosuperiorly with the orbit through the inferior orbital fissure; posterosuperiorly with the middle cranial fossa through the foramen rotundum and pterygoid canal; with the palate through the greater and lesser palatine canals and foramina; and with the pharynx through the pterygoid canal and palatovaginal canal - in general, vascular structures enter the fossa through its lateral wall, while nerve structures enter through its posterior wall.
C
Because the pterygopalatine fossa communicates directly with the orbit (via the inferior orbital fissure), the nasal cavity (via the sphenopalatine foramen), the middle cranial fossa (via the foramen rotundum and pterygoid canal), and the pharynx (via the pterygoid canal and palatovaginal canal), disease or infection arising in or near the fossa has multiple direct anatomical routes by which it can spread to these distant sites; clinical correlates noted for this region include hay fever affecting the ganglion here (the pterygopalatine ganglion is also known as the hay fever ganglion), and maxillary nerve block is performed in relation to this fossa.
questions.question:
A. Describe the gross anatomy of the pterygopalatine fossa under the following headings: description/location, boundaries, and contents.
B. State the communications of the pterygopalatine fossa and relate these to how disease may spread from this region.
C. Explain why disease or infection arising near the pterygopalatine fossa can spread to distant structures such as the orbit, the nasal cavity, the middle cranial fossa or the pharynx, and the functional deficit that could result.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
The clavicle forms the anterior portion of the shoulder girdle; it is curved like the italic letter "f" and lies nearly horizontally at the upper and anterior part of the thorax, immediately above the first rib. It articulates medially with the manubrium sterni and laterally with the acromion of the scapula.
A(ii)
The upper surface is flat, rough, and marked by impressions for the attachment of deltoid in front and trapezius behind; the bone has no medullary cavity.
A(iii)
Its functions are to transmit forces from the upper limb to the axial skeleton, to act as a strut holding the arm free from the trunk (supported principally by trapezius), and to provide attachment for muscles.
B
• The weakest point along the clavicle is the junction of the middle and outer thirds.
• Transmission of forces to the axial skeleton in falls on the shoulder or hand may exceed the strength of the bone at this site, and this indirect force commonly results in fracture there.
• Clavicle fracture is caused by landing on the hand from a fall with the arm rigidly outstretched, or by a direct blow.
C
• The clavicle has important deep relations that make it clinically significant beyond the bone itself.
• The third parts of the subclavian vessels and the trunks of the brachial plexus pass behind the medial third of the shaft of the clavicle, separated only by the thin subclavius muscle.
• At the sternal end, behind the sternoclavicular joints, lie the common carotid artery on the left and the bifurcation of the brachiocephalic artery on the right, with the internal jugular vein lying a little more laterally; these vessels are separated from the bone only by the strap muscles (sternohyoid and sternothyroid).
• Because these major vessels and the brachial plexus trunks lie in such close proximity to the clavicle, deep or displaced injury involving the bone can threaten them.
• Compromise of the subclavian vessels can produce vascular insufficiency of the upper limb, while injury to the brachial plexus trunks passing behind the medial clavicle can produce motor and sensory deficits in the limb.
• This illustrates how a skeletal injury at the clavicle can spread to affect distant neurovascular structures, producing a functional deficit beyond the fracture site itself.
questions.question:
Describe the gross anatomy of the clavicle:
A(i) Shape and articulations
A(ii) Surface features
A(iii) Functions
B. State how a particular part of the clavicle relates to a common fracture pattern.
C. Explain how injury at this region may involve a distant structure, causing a functional deficit.

Describe the carpal tunnel:
A(i) Bony wall (carpal arch/sulcus)
A(ii) Fibrous wall (flexor retinaculum)
A(iii) Contents
B. Explain the clinical basis for the median nerve being the structure most adversely affected in carpal tunnel syndrome.
C. Distinguish between the tendons of flexor digitorum profundus and flexor digitorum superficialis as they lie within the tunnel.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The bony wall is the carpal sulcus, formed by the concavity on the anterior aspect of the carpal bones, forming the base and sides of the tunnel; it is bounded laterally by the scaphoid and trapezium tubercles and medially by the hook of the hamate and the pisiform.
A(ii)
The fibrous wall is the flexor retinaculum, a thick connective tissue band that stretches over the carpal sulcus, converting it into the carpal tunnel by bridging the space between the medial and lateral parts of the arch, spanning from the hook of hamate and pisiform medially to the scaphoid and trapezium laterally.
A(iii)
Contents: four tendons of flexor digitorum profundus (the deepest structures), four tendons of flexor digitorum superficialis lying anterior to those of profundus (all eight enclosed in a common synovial sheath), the tendon of flexor pollicis longus occupying the lateral angle of the compartment with its own synovial sheath, and the median nerve, which lies anterior to the tendons of flexor digitorum superficialis, deep to the flexor retinaculum.
B
• Carpal tunnel syndrome may occur following inflammatory reactions (synovitis) in the synovial sheath of the tendons traversing the tunnel.
• Excess fluid, such as follows inflammation of the synovial sheaths, compresses the structures within the confined tunnel.
• The median nerve is the structure most adversely affected, since it lies anterior to the crowded flexor tendons, immediately deep to the unyielding flexor retinaculum, leaving it particularly exposed to any rise in pressure within the tunnel.
• Compression of the median nerve produces sensory disturbance (hypoesthesia or anaesthesia) in the skin of the lateral three and a half fingers on their palmar aspect.
• Weakness or paralysis of the thenar muscles also occurs, because the recurrent branch of the median nerve that supplies these muscles arises in the hand and is also compressed.
C
• Within the tunnel, the tendons of flexor digitorum profundus are the deepest structures.
• The tendons of flexor digitorum superficialis lie anterior to (more superficial than) those of profundus.
• Both sets of four tendons are enclosed together in a single common synovial sheath, whereas the tendon of flexor pollicis longus lies separately at the lateral angle of the compartment, enclosed in its own distinct synovial sheath.
• This layered arrangement of tendons deep to the median nerve means the nerve is the most superficial of the tunnel's principal contents, most exposed to the flexor retinaculum's unyielding roof.

A(i)
The popliteal fossa is a diamond-shaped depression in the posterior aspect of the knee. Superolateral border: biceps femoris. Superomedial border: semimembranosus and semitendinosus. Inferolateral border: lateral head of gastrocnemius. Inferomedial border: medial head of gastrocnemius.
A(ii)
Roof (posteriorly): skin and fascia — the popliteal fascia is a strong sheet of deep fascia continuous superiorly with the fascia lata and inferiorly with the deep fascia of the leg. Floor (anteriorly): popliteal surface of femur, capsule of knee joint, oblique popliteal ligament, and popliteal fascia over popliteus.
B(i)
From superficial to deep: posterior cutaneous nerve of thigh; tibial nerve (most superficial of the neurovascular bundle); popliteal vein; popliteal artery (deepest structure in the fossa, running close to the articular capsule of the knee joint); popliteal lymph nodes and lymphatic vessels. The small saphenous vein and three cutaneous nerves (posterior cutaneous nerve of thigh, medial sural cutaneous nerve, lateral sural cutaneous nerve) lie in the superficial fascia.
B(ii)
The popliteal artery is the deepest structure and lies in close proximity to the tibial nerve. An aneurysm (dilation of the artery beyond 50% of its normal diameter) causes compression of the tibial nerve. The tibial nerve is particularly susceptible to this compression; the major features include weakened or absent plantarflexion, paraesthesia of the foot and posterolateral leg, and paralysis of flexor muscles in the leg and intrinsic muscles of the sole.
C(i)
The tibial nerve is the medial and larger branch of the sciatic nerve; it bisects the fossa passing from the superior to the inferior angle and gives muscular branches to soleus, gastrocnemius, plantaris, and popliteus, and the medial sural cutaneous nerve. The common fibular nerve is the lateral, smaller terminal branch; it begins at the superior angle, closely follows the medial border of biceps femoris, exits the fossa by passing superficial to the lateral head of gastrocnemius, then winds around the neck of fibula where it divides into terminal branches. Injury to the tibial nerve causes inability to plantarflex the ankle or flex the toes and loss of sensation on the sole of the foot.

A(i) Describe the histological features of the four stomach regions — cardia, fundus, body, and pylorus — under the headings: surface epithelium, gland type, gastric pit length, and principal secretion.
A(ii) Explain the complete structure and function of the gastric glands of the fundus/body, including the isthmus, neck, and base, and what cells are found in each part.
B(i) Explain the full role of mucous neck cells in the gastric gland, comparing their secretion to that of surface mucous cells.
B(ii) Describe where intrinsic factor is produced, what it is chemically, what it does, and how its deficiency leads to anaemia.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Four stomach regions:
• Cardia and pylorus are histologically similar: tubular glands with long pits usually branching into coiled secretory portions (cardiac and pyloric glands respectively); pits are longer in the pylorus; lack both parietal and chief cells; major secretion is abundant mucus.
• Fundus and body are histologically identical: simple columnar epithelium invaginates to form gastric pits leading into long, branched, tubular gastric glands; 3 to 7 glands usually open into the bottom of each gastric pit; contain all four secretory cell types; involved in secretion of acidic gastric juice.
A(ii)
Structure of fundic/body glands:
• Each gland has three named parts: isthmus, neck, and base.
• Isthmus: the region of stem cells (between the gastric pit and gland); the pluripotent stem cells divide asymmetrically and can move upward or downward to replace epithelial cells.
• Neck: contains mucous neck cells (MNCs) in clusters or singly; also contains parietal cells.
• Base: predominantly chief (zymogen) cells; also contains enteroendocrine cells.
B(i)
Mucous neck cells (MNCs):
• Present in clusters or singly in the necks of gastric glands.
• Less columnar than surface mucous cells; irregular in shape with round nucleus and apical secretory granules.
• Their mucous secretion is less alkaline than that of the surface epithelial mucous cells; they secrete acidic fluid containing mucin (not mucus, which implies alkaline content).
B(ii)
Intrinsic factor:
• Produced by: parietal (oxyntic) cells.
• Chemical nature: a glycoprotein.
• Function: required for the uptake of vitamin B12 in the small intestine.
• Deficiency and anaemia: if parietal cells are damaged, insufficient quantities of intrinsic factor are secreted; without adequate intrinsic factor, vitamin B12 is not absorbed adequately; low levels of vitamin B12 reduce the proliferation of erythroblasts, resulting in pernicious anaemia.

A(i)
Definition: Cartilage is a connective tissue in which the cells are relatively sparse and embedded in a large amount of firm characteristic matrix. It is a specialized form of connective tissue in which the firm consistency of the extracellular matrix allows the tissue to bear mechanical stresses without permanent distortion. Histogenesis: Cartilage is derived from the mesenchyme. The first modification observed is the rounding up of mesenchymal cells, which retract their extensions, multiply rapidly, and form mesenchymal condensations of chondroblasts (cells with ribosome-rich basophilic cytoplasm). Synthesis and deposition of matrix then begin to separate chondroblasts from one another. Differentiation takes place from center outward: central cells have characteristics of chondrocytes, peripheral cells are typical chondroblasts. The superficial mesenchyme develops into the perichondrium. Growth mechanisms: interstitial growth (from mitotic division of preexisting chondrocytes, expanding from within) and appositional growth (from differentiation of perichondrial cells, expanding from the outside). Nutrient supply: Cartilage is avascular; nourished by diffusion of nutrients from capillaries in adjacent connective tissue (perichondrium) or by synovial fluid. It has no lymphatic vessels or nerves. Chondrocytes exhibit low metabolic activity.
A(ii)
Hyaline cartilage: most common form; collagen type II is the principal collagen; found in nose, trachea, bronchi, rib-sternal joints, and synovial joints; resilient and shock absorbing. Elastic cartilage: contains abundant elastic fibers in addition to collagen type II; found in auricle of ear, external auditory canals, eustachian tubes, epiglottis, and cuneiform cartilage in larynx; elastic fibers allow flexibility. Fibrocartilage: rich in collagen type I (acidophilic matrix); found in intervertebral disks, attachments of certain ligaments to cartilaginous surfaces, and symphysis pubis; dense collagen provides strength for high-load sites.
B(i)
Articular cartilage is devoid of perichondrium and is sustained by diffusion of oxygen and nutrients from synovial fluid; this limited supply combined with low metabolic activity of chondrocytes means repair is slow. Hyaline cartilage is more susceptible to degenerative aging processes; calcification of the matrix, preceded by an increase in size and volume of chondrocytes followed by their death, leads to osteoarthritis. Role of exercise: participation in sports involving torsional loading, fast acceleration/deceleration, repetitive high impact increases risk of osteoarthritis. However, some levels of loading and exercise are beneficial: exercise enhances production of matrix molecules, which can have a positive effect on joint health. Exercise has both beneficial and detrimental effects on cartilage.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the gross anatomy of cartilage under the following headings: definition, histogenesis (development from mesenchyme), growth mechanisms, and nutrient supply.
A(ii) Relate the three types of cartilage to their specific locations and collagen types, explaining why each is suited to its location.
B(i) Explain why articular cartilage degenerates with age and state the role of exercise in cartilage health.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Protective coverings: the nervous system contains very little collagen or fibrous tissue; it is relatively soft and easily damaged by injuries affecting the cranium or vertebral bones. It is covered by three connective tissue layers — the meninges: dura mater (thickest and toughest layer, contains sinuses to collect venous blood), arachnoid membrane (middle web-like covering; cerebrospinal fluid flows in the web-like spaces), and pia mater (thin delicate layer that follows the contour of the brain and spinal cord). Gray matter and white matter: myelinated fibers make up the white matter in the CNS; cell bodies and unmyelinated fibers make the gray matter. Glial cells in CNS: Oligodendrocytes — produce myelin in CNS. Microglia — part of the MPS (CNS macrophages). Astrocytes and other glial cells — support, nourish, and protect neurons; they are far more numerous than neurons; unlike neurons, they are capable of mitosis.
A(ii)
Dura mater — thickest and toughest layer; contains sinuses to collect venous blood. Arachnoid membrane — middle web-like covering; cerebrospinal fluid flows in the web-like (subarachnoid) spaces. Pia mater — thin delicate layer that follows the contour of brain and spinal cord. CSF flows within the subarachnoid spaces of the arachnoid.
B(i)
The optic nerve and retina arise in the embryo as an outgrowth of the diencephalon (forebrain); the optic nerve is therefore not a true peripheral nerve like the other cranial nerves. Its myelin is produced by oligodendrocytes (not by Schwann cells). Because the optic nerve is part of the CNS (produced by oligodendrocytes and without neurilemma), it is associated with multiple sclerosis — a demyelinating disease. Demyelination of the optic nerve disrupts the action potential transmission from the retinal ganglion cells, causing visual symptoms. The retinal ganglion cells communicate with the cerebrum through the optic nerve and extend into the brain.

A(ii) Relate the three meningeal layers to their specific functions and state how cerebrospinal fluid flows.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Gross anatomy of the pancreas:
• Nature: a mixed exocrine-endocrine gland that produces both digestive enzymes and hormones.
• Position: retroperitoneally positioned on the posterior wall of the abdominal cavity at the level of the 2nd and 3rd lumbar vertebrae.
• Capsular covering: it has no distinct capsule, but is covered by a thin layer of loose connective tissue, from which septa extend to cover the larger vessels and ducts and to separate the parenchyma into lobules.
A(ii)
Two functional components:
• Exocrine: produces digestive enzymes that act in the small intestine; secretory acini produce about 1.6 litres of pancreatic juice every day.
• Endocrine: involves primarily smaller cells similar to enteroendocrine cells located in variously sized clusters called the pancreatic islets (islets of Langerhans); secretes hormones such as insulin and glucagon into the bloodstream, which are very important for the metabolism of absorbed nutrients.
B(i)
Exocrine acini:
• The secretory acini are surrounded by a basal lamina that is supported only by a delicate sheath of reticular fibers with a rich capillary network.
• The exocrine part produces about 1.6 litres of pancreatic juice every day.
B(ii)
• Pancreas: produces digestive enzymes that act in the small intestine; secretes insulin and glucagon, both important for metabolism of absorbed nutrients.
• Liver: produces bile, an important fluid in the digestion of fats; plays a major role in lipid, carbohydrate, and protein metabolism; inactivates and metabolizes many toxic substances and drugs; participates in iron metabolism and the synthesis of blood proteins and factors necessary for blood coagulation.
• Gallbladder: absorbs water from bile and stores bile in a concentrated form.
questions.question:

A(ii) Describe the two functional components of the pancreas (exocrine and endocrine), including the cell types involved and the products of each.
B(i) Describe the exocrine secretory acini of the pancreas, including the arrangement around the acini and the volume of juice produced.
B(ii) Explain the role of the pancreas in digestion and hormonal regulation, and contrast this with the role of the liver and the gallbladder.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Superficial group (3 muscles): Gastrocnemius — lateral head from lateral aspect of lateral condyle of femur; insertion: posterior surface of calcaneus via calcaneal tendon; innervation: tibial nerve (S1, S2); action: plantarflexes ankle when knee is extended, raises heel during walking, flexes leg at knee joint. Soleus — posterior aspect of head and superior quarter of posterior surface of fibula; soleal line and middle third of medial border of tibia; tendinous arch; insertion: posterior surface of calcaneus via calcaneal tendon; innervation: tibial nerve (S1, S2); action: plantarflexes ankle independent of position of knee, steadies leg on foot. Plantaris — inferior end of lateral supracondylar line of femur, oblique popliteal ligament; insertion: posterior surface of calcaneus via calcaneal tendon; innervation: tibial nerve (S1, S2); action: weakly assists gastrocnemius in plantarflexing ankle. Deep group (4 muscles): Popliteus — lateral surface of lateral condyle of femur and lateral meniscus; posterior surface of tibia superior to soleal line; tibial nerve (L4, L5, S1); weakly flexes knee, unlocks it by rotating femur 5° on fixed tibia, and medially rotates tibia of unplanted limb. Flexor hallucis longus — inferior 2/3 of posterior surface of fibula; base of distal phalanx of great toe; tibial nerve (S2, S3); flexes great toe at all joints, weakly plantarflexes ankle, supports medial longitudinal arch. Flexor digitorum longus — medial part of posterior surface of tibia inferior to soleal line; bases of distal phalanges of lateral 4 digits; tibial nerve (S2, S3); flexes lateral 4 digits, plantarflexes ankle, supports longitudinal arches. Tibialis posterior — interosseous membrane, posterior tibia inferior to soleal line, posterior fibula; tuberosity of navicular, cuneiform, cuboid, sustentaculum tali of calcaneus, bases of 2nd, 3rd, and 4th metatarsals; tibial nerve (L4, L5); plantarflexes ankle and inverts foot.
A(ii)
The calcaneal tendon is formed by the union of the tendons of gastrocnemius, soleus, and plantaris; it inserts into the posterior surface of the calcaneus. It is the largest and strongest tendon in the body. Clinical significance: rupture of the Achilles tendon (commonly felt as a 'pop' and tested by Thompson's squeeze test) results in inability to plantarflex the foot.
B(i)
The posterior tibial artery enters the sole of the foot through the tarsal tunnel, accompanying the tibial nerve. The tibial nerve enters the sole of the foot via the tarsal tunnel and then splits into the lateral and medial plantar arteries. For a tarsal tunnel block, the posterior tibial pulse can be palpated inferoposteriorly to the medial malleolus, where the artery turns to enter the foot — the tibial nerve lies adjacent.
B(ii)
Tibialis posterior inserts into the tuberosity of the navicular, cuneiform, cuboid, sustentaculum tali of calcaneus, and the bases of the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th metatarsals — the very bones that form the medial longitudinal arch. It plantarflexes the ankle and inverts the foot; by pulling the navicular and cuneiforms downward and inward it actively maintains the height of the medial longitudinal arch. Dysfunction (e.g., from tenosynovitis or rupture) leads to eversion of the calcaneus, slipping down of the talus and navicular, and pes planus — collapse of the medial longitudinal arch.
C(i)
Gastrocnemius spans the knee joint (arising from the femoral condyle) and the ankle joint; it plantarflexes the ankle only when the knee is extended and also flexes the knee. It is tested with the knee extended. Soleus arises entirely from the tibia and fibula (below the knee) and plantarflexes the ankle independent of the position of the knee. It is tested by single-leg heel raise with the knee flexed to 90°, which eliminates gastrocnemius from the movement and isolates soleus.

A. Describe the origin, course, and branches/distribution of the ophthalmic artery.
B. State why the ophthalmic artery and its central retinal branch are of particular functional importance to the orbit.
questions.answerText:
A
The only artery supplying structures in the orbit is the ophthalmic artery, which is a branch of the internal carotid artery; it enters the orbit with the optic nerve through the optic foramen (canal). Its branches include the lacrimal artery (to the lacrimal gland and upper eyelid), muscular branches to the muscles, long posterior ciliary arteries (to the ciliary body), short posterior ciliary arteries (to the choroid and part of the optic nerve), and medial palpebral arteries (to the eyelids).
B
The ophthalmic artery gives rise to the very important branch, the central artery of the retina; because the ophthalmic artery is the only artery supplying orbital structures, and the central retinal artery is its branch, the retina is dependent on this single arterial source, so the optic nerve is covered by dura, arachnoid and pia from the sclera to the canal, where the dura is continuous with the periosteum of the orbit, and venous drainage (superior and inferior ophthalmic veins) communicates with the cavernous sinus, giving direct communication between the skin of the face and the cavernous sinus (the danger triangle).

A(i)
A wide tube about 10 cm long and 2 cm wide, lying in the superior mediastinum and extending from C6 (lower border of the cricoid cartilage) to T4, where it divides into the right and left main bronchi; it has cervical and thoracic parts, the cervical part measuring 5 cm.
A(ii)
• The cervical part is in contact posteriorly with the oesophagus and anteriorly with the isthmus of the thyroid gland; it is palpable in the suprasternal notch midway between the heads of the clavicles; it ends at the sternal angle (T4/5) just to the right of the midline (at T6 in the erect position in full inspiration).
• At the bifurcation the azygos vein arches over the right main bronchus (T4) and the left main bronchus lies in front of the oesophagus (27 cm from the incisor teeth); the cardiac plexus lies on the lowest part of the trachea behind the arch of the aorta.
A(iii)
Right main bronchus: 2.5 cm long, shorter, wider and vertically oriented; left main bronchus: 5 cm long, longer, narrower and horizontally oriented.
A(iv)
• Right main bronchus divides into upper (outside the hilum), middle and lower lobar bronchi, giving 10 bronchopulmonary segments; the left divides within the hilum into 2 lobar bronchi, giving 8 segments; segmental (third-order) bronchi supply the segments.
• The U-shaped cartilage bars of the trachea are replaced by irregular plates in smaller bronchi; the smallest bronchi give bronchioles (under 1 mm), then terminal bronchioles and respiratory bronchioles (about 0.5 mm, with outpouchings where gas exchange occurs), then alveolar ducts, alveolar sacs and alveoli surrounded by capillaries.
A(v)
Trachea: lymphatics drain to the deep cervical and paratracheal lymph nodes; the mucous membrane is supplied by the vagus, which also gives the parasympathetic supply. Lung and bronchi: pulmonary plexuses with vagal (bronchoconstrictor, secretomotor) and sympathetic (bronchodilator) fibres.
B(i)
• The wider, more vertical right main bronchus allows foreign particles to enter it easily; asthma (dyspnoea); pneumonia (bacterial or viral infection of the lung); pulmonary embolism (pulmonary artery obstructed by air, blood clot, fat, tumour cells or foreign particles).
• Abscesses are commoner in the posterior segment of the upper lobe and the apical segment of the lower lobe (most dependent supine); septa between segments limit infection but carcinoma and tuberculosis break through; fibrosis reduces compliance and emphysema reduces elasticity.
C(i)
• Lymph from lung and bronchi passes to the bronchopulmonary (hilar) nodes, then to the superior and inferior tracheobronchial nodes (above and below the tracheal bifurcation), then to the right and left bronchomediastinal trunks.
• The trunks usually end at the junction of the subclavian and internal jugular veins; the right trunk may join other trunks to form the right lymphatic duct and the left may end in the thoracic duct.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
A double-domed, thin fibromuscular (musculotendinous) partition between the thoracic and abdominal cavities and the main muscle of respiration; convex superior surface faces the thorax (covered by diaphragmatic pleura, lungs fit the domes, fibrous pericardium on the central tendon), concave inferior surface faces the abdomen (parietal peritoneum; liver, kidneys, suprarenals, stomach, spleen); higher on the right because of the liver (in expiration the right dome reaches the 5th rib, the left the 5th intercostal space); level varies with respiration, posture and abdominal distension, and the domes flatten in maximal inspiration.
A(ii)
Sternal: 2 slips from the posterior xiphoid process; costal: deep surfaces of the lower 6 ribs and costal cartilages (forms the domes); vertebral: the crura and 3 arcuate ligaments - medial (thickened psoas fascia, from the body of L2 to the tip of the L1 transverse process), lateral (thickened quadratus lumborum fascia, from the L1 transverse process to the lower border of the 12th rib) and median (joins the crura across the front of the aorta). Insertion: trefoil central tendon, no bony attachments, partly fused with the fibrous pericardium (pericardiophrenic ligament).
A(iii)
• Caval opening (T8; the only opening in the central tendon): IVC, terminal branches of the right phrenic nerve, a few lymphatics. Oesophageal opening (T10; in the right crus): oesophagus, anterior and posterior vagal trunks, oesophageal branches of the left gastric vessels, a few lymphatics. Aortic opening (T12; lowest and most posterior, between the crura): aorta, thoracic duct, sometimes azygos and hemiazygos veins.
• Smaller openings: greater and lesser splanchnic nerves pierce each crus; hemiazygos vein pierces the left crus; left phrenic nerve pierces the left dome; sympathetic trunks pass behind the diaphragm deep to the medial arcuate ligament; subcostal vessels and nerve pass behind the lateral arcuate ligament; superior epigastric vessels pass between the sternal and costal origins; 7th-11th intercostal neurovascular bundles pass through the costal origin.
A(iv)
Arteries: pericardiophrenic and musculophrenic (from the internal thoracic) and superior phrenic (from the thoracic aorta) to the superior surface; inferior phrenic (first branches of the abdominal aorta) to the inferior surface. Veins: pericardiophrenic and musculophrenic to the internal thoracic vein; superior phrenic vein (right) and right inferior phrenic vein to the IVC; the left inferior phrenic vein drains to the IVC and the left suprarenal vein.
A(v)
• Motor: phrenic nerves (C3-5) only - the right nerve to the right half up to the right margin of the oesophageal opening, the left to the left half. Sensory: central part (with related pleura and peritoneum) via the phrenic nerves; peripheral part via the lower 6 or 7 intercostal and subcostal nerves.
• Lymph: thoracic surface to anterior and posterior diaphragmatic nodes (anterior on to parasternal nodes; posterior to phrenic and posterior mediastinal nodes); abdominal surface to anterior diaphragmatic, phrenic and superior lumbar (caval/aortic) nodes.
B(i)
The central diaphragm is supplied sensorily by the phrenic nerve (C3-5) and the shoulder skin by the supraclavicular nerve (C3,4); so pain from irritation of pleura or pericardium over the central diaphragm, or of the peritoneum under it by subphrenic pus or blood, is referred to the shoulder tip.
B(ii)
Acquired herniae occur in middle-aged people with weak musculature around the oesophageal opening; they are either sliding or paraoesophageal (rolling, alongside the oesophagus).
B(iii)
Hiccup is an involuntary spasmodic contraction of the diaphragm with approximation of the vocal folds and closure of the glottis; common after eating or drinking from gastric irritation of vagus nerve endings; it may be due to pleurisy, peritonitis or pericarditis.
C(i)
• Right crus: larger and longer, arises from the upper 3 lumbar vertebrae (L1-L3) and their intervertebral discs; some of its fibres pass up to the left and loop round the oesophageal orifice as a physiological sphincter preventing reflux of gastric contents.
• Left crus: smaller, arises from the side of the bodies of the upper 2 (L1-L2) lumbar vertebrae and their discs; each crus is attached to the medial and lateral arcuate ligaments, and the medial borders of the two crura unite in front of T12 as the median arcuate ligament over the aorta.
