questions.answerText:
A(i)
The great saphenous vein (GSV) is the longest vein in the body. It is formed by the union of the dorsal vein of the great toe and the dorsal venous arch of the foot. It ascends anterior to the medial malleolus, passes posterior to the medial condyle of the femur (about a hand's breadth posterior to the medial border of the patella), anastomoses freely with the small saphenous vein, traverses the saphenous opening in the fascia lata, and empties into the femoral vein.
A(ii)
The GSV has 10–12 valves, which are more numerous in the leg than in the thigh; these valves are usually located just inferior to the perforating veins. Perforating veins also have their own valves. Tributaries in the anterior and lateral part of the thighs converge to form the accessory saphenous vein (ASV), which communicates the GSV with the small saphenous vein. Just before emptying into the femoral vein, the GSV receives tributaries from the superficial circumflex iliac, superficial epigastric, and external pudendal veins.
B(i)
The small saphenous vein (SSV) arises on the lateral side of the foot from the union of the dorsal vein of the little toe with the dorsal venous arch. It ascends posterior to the lateral malleolus as a continuation of the lateral marginal vein, passes along the lateral border of the calcaneal tendon, inclines to the midline of the fibula and penetrates the deep fascia, ascends between the heads of the gastrocnemius muscle, and empties into the popliteal vein in the popliteal fossa.
B(ii)
There are four main pulse points in the lower limb: femoral (palpated midway between the anterior superior iliac spine and pubic symphysis — the mid-inguinal point); popliteal (deep in the popliteal fossa, requires deep palpation, best with slight knee flexion); dorsalis pedis (on the dorsum of the foot, just lateral to extensor hallucis longus tendon); and posterior tibial (inferoposteriorly to the medial malleolus). The GSV anterior to the medial malleolus is the classic site for venous cut-down; the GSV at the medial condyle of the femur is another accessible site.
C(i)
Superficial veins (GSV and SSV) are unaccompanied, lie in the superficial fascia, and their varicosity is visible. Deep veins of the lower limb accompany the arteries (read-up). Deep vein thrombosis involves the deep system and poses a risk of pulmonary embolism because the deep veins drain directly into the popliteal, femoral, and iliac veins and thence to the inferior vena cava. Superficial varicosity alone rarely embolises unless thrombosis extends through a perforating vein into the deep system.
questions.question:
Describe the great saphenous vein and small saphenous vein under the following headings, and explain the clinical basis of their use in surgery.
A(i) Origin, course, and termination of the great saphenous vein
A(ii) Tributaries and valves of the great saphenous vein
B(i) Origin, course, and termination of the small saphenous vein
B(ii) Clinical basis: pulse points of the lower limb and sites of venepuncture or cut-down
C(i) Distinguish varicosity from deep vein thrombosis based on the anatomical differences between the superficial and deep venous systems

questions.answerText:
A(i)
The greater sac is the main larger part; the lesser sac (omental bursa) lies posterior to the stomach, adjoining structures and lesser omentum; an incision through the anterolateral wall enters the greater sac; the sacs communicate through the epiploic foramen.
A(ii)
• The transverse mesocolon divides the cavity into supracolic and infracolic compartments; the infracolic lies posterior to the greater omentum and is divided by the mesentery of the small intestine into right and left infracolic spaces.
• Right space: triangular, between the root of the mesentery, ascending colon and right two-thirds of transverse colon; left: between the root, descending colon and left one-third of transverse colon, widening below into the pelvis.
A(iii)
Right paracolic gutter lies lateral to the ascending colon and communicates with the hepatorenal recess and pelvic cavity; the left, lateral to the descending colon, is separated from the splenic area by the phrenicocolic ligament.
A(iv)
• Lesser sac: superior wall peritoneum over the caudate lobe and diaphragm; anterior lesser omentum, peritoneum of the posterior stomach and anterior two layers of greater omentum; posterior the posterior two layers, transverse colon and mesocolon, peritoneum over pancreas, left kidney and suprarenal gland.
• Omental foramen (of Winslow), behind the hepatoduodenal ligament, admits 2 fingers: liver superiorly, first part of duodenum inferiorly, hepatoduodenal ligament anteriorly, IVC and right crus posteriorly.
B(i)
Median umbilical fold covers the urachal remnant, medial folds the obliterated umbilical arteries, lateral folds the inferior epigastric vessels; the supravesical fossa is a site for external supravesical hernia, the medial inguinal fossa for the less common direct hernia, the lateral inguinal fossa for the most common indirect hernia.
B(ii)
Blockage of the uterine tubes (hysterosalpingography), peritonitis, ascites, paracentesis and intraperitoneal injection, flow of exudates in the paracolic gutters, and adhesions with adhesiotomy in intestinal obstruction.
C(i)
• The right paracolic gutter provides a route for spread of infection between the pelvic and upper abdominal regions, and the supracolic and infracolic compartments communicate freely through the gutters.
• In the female the cavity communicates with the exterior via the uterine tubes, uterus and vagina.
• Parietal peritoneum is supplied by the nerves of the adjacent body wall and diaphragm; visceral peritoneum by sympathetic nerves of the underlying viscus.
• Receptors respond to overdistension, traction on mesenteries, spasm of smooth muscle and ischaemia.

A(i)
Formed behind the neck of the pancreas by the union of the superior mesenteric and splenic veins.
A(ii)
• Large but short, about 5 cm; in front of the opening of the lesser sac it passes to the porta hepatis where it divides into right and left terminal branches.
• At the porta hepatis the order from behind forwards is portal vein branches, proper hepatic artery, hepatic ducts; in the hepatoduodenal ligament it lies with the hepatic artery and bile duct.
A(iii)
Drains poorly oxygenated but nutrient-rich blood from the GI tract (lower oesophagus to upper anal canal), pancreas, gallbladder, bile ducts and spleen to the liver.
A(iv)
Direct route: through the liver to the IVC via the hepatic veins; alternative routes exist and the portal vein and its tributaries have no valves.
B(i)
Portasystemic shunts join the portal vein to the IVC or join the splenic vein to the left renal vein after splenectomy.
C(i)
• Portal hypertension: cirrhosis scarring and fibrosis obstruct the portal vein, pressure mounts, and blood forced through collaterals dilates veins into varices, potentially fatal.
• Lower third of oesophagus: left gastric branches with oesophageal veins to the azygos: oesophageal varices.
• Anal canal: superior rectal with middle and inferior rectal veins: haemorrhoids (mucosa with normally dilated submucosal veins prolapses).
• Anterior abdominal wall: paraumbilical with superficial epigastric veins: caput medusae, veins radiating like small snakes from the umbilicus.
• Retroperitoneal: colic twig veins of ascending and descending colon, duodenum, pancreas and liver with renal, lumbar and phrenic veins.

questions.question:
Describe the axilla under the following headings:
A(i) Shape and apex
A(ii) Base
A(iii) Walls
A(iv) Contents
B. Explain the clinical basis for the axillary vein being particularly vulnerable to injury in this region.
C. Distinguish between the quadrangular space and the triangular interval found in the posterior wall of the axilla.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The axilla is a pyramid-shaped space between the upper part of the arm and the side of the upper chest; its apex is the cervicoaxillary canal, bounded by the 1st rib, clavicle, and superior edge of the scapula, forming the passageway between the neck and axilla.
A(ii)
The base is formed by concave skin, subcutaneous tissue, and the axillary (deep) fascia.
A(iii)
Anterior wall: pectoralis major and minor, subclavius, and clavipectoral fascia. Posterior wall: scapula and subscapularis above, teres major and latissimus dorsi below. Medial wall: upper ribs, intercostal muscles, and serratus anterior. Lateral wall: narrow and bony, formed by the intertubercular groove of the humerus.
A(iv)
Contents: the axillary artery and its branches, the axillary vein and its tributaries, the infraclavicular part of the brachial plexus, axillary lymph nodes, and loose areolar/adipose tissue, all enclosed with the plexus in the axillary sheath.
B
• The axillary vein is large and lies in an exposed, superficial position within the axilla.
• Wounds to the axilla therefore often involve the axillary vein because of its large size and exposed position.
• A wound to the proximal part of the axillary vein is especially dangerous because of the risk of air entering the vessel (air embolism).
C
• The quadrangular space lies in the posterior wall of the axilla and transmits the axillary nerve and the posterior circumflex humeral artery and vein.
• The triangular interval also lies in the posterior wall and transmits the radial nerve and the profunda brachii artery.
• Both spaces are related to the long head of triceps brachii and the teres major muscle in their boundaries.
• The quadrangular space thus carries the nerve/vessels supplying the deltoid and teres minor region, while the triangular interval carries those continuing into the posterior compartment of the arm.
• This distinction explains why injury near the surgical neck of the humerus threatens the axillary nerve, whereas injury lower down at the spiral groove threatens the radial nerve instead.

A(i)
Autonomic nerve supply:
• Vessels and nerves enter the large salivary glands at the hilum and gradually branch into the lobules; a rich vascular and nerve plexus surrounds the secretory and ductal components of each lobule.
• The capillaries surrounding the secretory end pieces are important for saliva secretion, stimulated by the autonomic nervous system.
• Parasympathetic stimulation (usually through smell or taste of food): promotes vasodilation and a copious watery secretion.
• Sympathetic stimulation: produces small amounts of viscous saliva, rich in organic material. NOTE: dry mouth sensation in stressful situations (sympathetic predominance).
A(ii)
Immunological secretory mechanism:
• Plasma cells (in the connective tissue around the glands) secrete IgA.
• IgA forms a complex with a secretory component synthesized by the serous acinar cells, intercalated duct cells, and striated duct cells.
• The IgA-rich secretory complex released into the saliva is resistant to enzymatic digestion and constitutes an immunological defense mechanism against pathogens in the oral cavity.
B(i)
Parotid vs pancreatic tissue:
• Both resemble each other histologically.
• Parotid gland: has adipocytes (fat cells) in its parenchyma.
• Pancreatic tissue: has islets of Langerhans (endocrine clusters) and centroacinar cells.
B(ii)
• Minor salivary glands by location and secretion: von Ebner's glands of tongue (posterior dorsal and lateral): serous acini only.
• Palate, base and lateral border of tongue: predominantly mucous acini.
• Lip, cheek, apex of tongue: mixed serous and mucous acini.
• Minor glands secrete 10% of the total volume of saliva but account for approximately 70% of the mucus secreted.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the autonomic nerve supply to the salivary glands, including which division of the autonomic nervous system produces each type of secretory response and what type of saliva each produces.
A(ii) Describe the full immunological secretory mechanism of the large salivary glands, identifying the cell type that secretes IgA and the cell types that synthesise the secretory component.
B(i) The parotid gland resembles pancreatic tissue but can be distinguished from it. State the distinguishing features of each gland.
B(ii) Classify all minor salivary glands by location and secretion type, and state what proportion of total saliva volume and mucus the minor glands produce.

Describe the popliteal artery and its branches, stating the safe site for popliteal pulse palpation, and explain the anatomical basis of the deformity and functional deficit after tibial nerve injury in the popliteal fossa.
A(i) Origin, course, and relations of the popliteal artery
A(ii) All branches of the popliteal artery — genicular and muscular
B(i) Termination and continuation of the popliteal artery into the leg and foot
B(ii) Safe site for popliteal pulse palpation and clinical technique
C(i) Anatomical basis of the deformity and functional deficit after tibial nerve injury in the popliteal fossa
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The popliteal artery is the continuation of the femoral artery; it begins when the femoral artery passes through the adductor hiatus. It descends through the fossa, passing inferolaterally and is the deepest structure in the fossa — it runs in close proximity to the articular capsule of the knee joint. It terminates at the inferior border of the popliteus by dividing into the anterior and posterior tibial arteries.
A(ii)
Five genicular branches participate in the genicular anastomosis (a network of vessels surrounding the knee providing collateral circulation capable of maintaining blood supply to the leg during full knee flexion): superior lateral genicular artery, superior medial genicular artery, middle genicular artery (penetrates the fibrous capsule and supplies the cruciate ligaments, synovial membrane, and peripheral margins of the menisci), inferior lateral genicular artery, and inferior medial genicular artery. Muscular branches supply the hamstring, gastrocnemius, soleus, and plantaris muscles. The superior muscular branches have clinically important anastomoses with the terminal part of the profunda femoris and gluteal arteries.
B(i)
Termination: the popliteal artery divides into the anterior tibial artery and the tibioperoneal trunk; the tibioperoneal trunk divides into the posterior tibial artery and fibular (peroneal) artery. Anterior tibial artery: passes anterior to the interosseous membrane between tibia and fibula; supplies muscles of anterior compartment; continues as the dorsalis pedis artery in the foot, supplying tarsal bones and dorsal metatarsals, and anastomoses with the lateral plantar artery to form the deep plantar arch. Posterior tibial artery: continues inferiorly along surface of deep posterior leg muscles; enters the sole of the foot via the tarsal tunnel; splits into lateral and medial plantar arteries supplying the plantar foot.
B(ii)
The popliteal artery is the hardest pulse to find, lying deep in the popliteal fossa; it requires deep palpation. To make it easier, the patient should slightly flex the leg — this relaxes the fascia around the popliteal fossa. An aneurysm of the popliteal artery can be detected by an obvious palpable pulsation in the popliteal fossa; an arterial bruit may be heard on auscultation.
C(i)
The tibial nerve is the medial and larger branch of the sciatic nerve and the most superficial of the neurovascular bundle. Injury causes: paralysis of flexor muscles in the leg and intrinsic muscles in the sole of the foot; inability to plantarflex the ankles or flex the toes; and loss of sensation on the sole of the foot. The resulting deformity is a calcaneovalgus posture — unopposed dorsiflexion with loss of plantarflexion, the foot assuming a dorsiflexed position because the antagonist muscles remain intact. Weakened or absent plantarflexion and paraesthesia of the foot and posterolateral leg are the major features of tibial nerve compression.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the gross and microscopic structure of the large salivary glands under the following headings: capsule and septa; parenchyma (secretory end pieces); cell types in the secretory end pieces; the duct system in sequence from secretory unit to oral cavity.
A(ii) State the type of secretion produced by each of the three pairs of major salivary glands and by the minor glands.
B(i) Distinguish between striated ducts and intercalated ducts, including location, epithelium, and function.
B(ii) Explain how saliva is modified as it passes through the duct system.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Structure:
• Capsule and septa: a capsule of connective tissue rich in collagen fibers surrounds the large salivary glands; septa of connective tissue originate from the capsule and divide the glands into lobules; each lobule contains numerous secretory units (acini).
• Parenchyma: consists of secretory end pieces and a branching duct system arranged in lobules separated by septae of connective tissue from the capsule. Vessels and nerves enter at the hilum and gradually branch into the lobules.
• Cell types in secretory end pieces: serous cells (polarized protein-secreting cells, pyramidal in shape, round nuclei, well-stained RER, apical secretory granules; joined apically by tight and adherent junctions; form a spherical unit called an acinus with a very small central lumen; secrete enzymes and other proteins); mucous cells; and nonsecretory myoepithelial cells.
• Duct system in sequence: secretory end pieces → intercalated ducts (lined by simple low cuboidal epithelium, surrounded by myoepithelial cells) → striated ducts (intralobular) → interlobular (excretory/striated ducts drain into these) → interlobar ducts → main duct (opens into the oral cavity, lined with nonkeratinized-stratified squamous epithelium).
A(ii)
Secretion types:
• Parotid gland: serous and watery.
• Submandibular and sublingual glands: seromucous secretion.
• Minor glands: mostly mucous.
• Type depends on content of glycoprotein mucin: serous, seromucous, or mucous.
B(i)
• Intercalated ducts: several short intercalated ducts join to form striated ducts; they are lined by cuboidal epithelial cells that have the ability to divide and differentiate into secretory or ductal cells; also called intralobular ducts.
• Striated ducts: characterized by radial striations that extend from the bases of the cells to the level of the central nuclei; striations consist of infoldings of the basal plasma membrane with numerous elongated mitochondria aligned parallel to the infolded membranes (characteristic of ion-transporting cells); they have a folded basal membrane enabling active transport; also called intralobular ducts.
B(ii)
Saliva is modified by the cells of the duct system draining the secretory units: much Na+ and Cl- is reabsorbed while certain growth factors and digestive enzymes are added. Water resorption and ion secretion in the striated ducts make saliva hypotonic (reduced Na and Cl ions; increased carbonate and potassium ions).

A(i)
An omentum is a double-layered extension or fold passing from the stomach and proximal duodenum to adjacent organs or to the abdominal wall; there are two types, lesser and greater.
A(ii)
The lesser omentum is a two-layered fold connecting the lesser curvature of the stomach and proximal duodenum to the liver; the hepatoduodenal ligament is its thickened free edge, conducting the portal vein, hepatic artery and bile duct.
A(iii)
The greater omentum hangs like an apron from the greater curvature of the stomach and proximal duodenum, folds back after descending and attaches to the anterior surface of the transverse colon and its mesocolon.
A(iv)
• Liver: falciform ligament (anterior wall), gastrohepatic ligament (stomach), hepatoduodenal ligament (duodenum). Stomach: gastrophrenic, gastrosplenic, gastrocolic, gastrohepatic, gastropancreatic.
• Spleen: gastrosplenic (short gastric and left gastroepiploic vessels), splenorenal (splenic vessels and tail of pancreas), phrenicosplenic, splenocolic.
B(i)
• It is large and fat laden and prevents the visceral peritoneum adhering to the parietal peritoneum lining the anterolateral wall.
• It is mobile, moving with peristalsis, and can wrap itself around an inflamed organ such as the appendix, walling it off and protecting other viscera.
• It also cushions the abdominal organs against injury and forms insulation against loss of body heat.
C(i)
• Lesser: from liver to lesser curvature and proximal duodenum, containing the hepatoduodenal ligament; greater: hangs from the greater curvature and attaches to the transverse colon.
• The anterior and posterior layers of the lesser omentum extend from the liver to the lesser curvature; the anterior layer continues as the first layer of the greater omentum, the posterior layer forms its second and third layers.
• The lesser omentum forms part of the anterior wall of the lesser sac together with the peritoneum of the posterior wall of the stomach and the anterior two layers of the greater omentum.
• The hepatoduodenal ligament forms the anterior boundary of the omental foramen.

A(i)
Five lumbar vertebrae (1 to 4 typical, 5 atypical); largest and strongest of the column because supported weight increases inferiorly; superior facets face medially, inferior facets laterally; thick broad spines.
A(ii)
• Large kidney-shaped body, deeper anteriorly; triangular foramen (larger than thoracic, smaller than cervical); short strong pedicles; short thick broad laminae; spine a vertical quadrilateral plate.
• Transverse processes thin and tapering (accessory process); superior articular facets concave facing medially and backwards with the mammillary process; inferior facets convex facing laterally and forwards.
A(iii)
L5: thick short pyramidal transverse processes; largest body, anterior deeper than posterior, creating the sharp lumbosacral angle; small short rounded spine; inferior articular distance equal to or more than the superior.
A(iv)
Joints: intervertebral discs (symphysis) between bodies; synovial joints between arches. Ligaments: anterior and posterior longitudinal, ligamentum flavum, interspinous, supraspinous; iliolumbar ligaments strengthen the L5 to S1 lumbosacral joint.
B(i)
• A lumbar vertebra ossifies from three primary centres (body and each half of the neural arch) appearing in the third month of fetal life; the halves of the arch fuse posteriorly in the first year.
• Failure of fusion of the two halves of the neural arch results in spina bifida; if one primary centre of the body fails, hemivertebra.
B(ii)
• Lumbar spinal stenosis: thought hereditary, a narrow vertebral foramen in one or several vertebrae.
• Excessive lumbar lordosis: abnormal anterior curvature with anterior tilting of the pelvis.
C(i)
• The canal formed by L1 and L2 contains the conus medullaris; the lower three contain the cauda equina; all contain the spinal meninges.
• Stenosis can compress the spinal cord and exiting nerves; the pedicles are related above and below to spinal nerves.
• The right crus of the diaphragm attaches to the upper three lumbar vertebrae and the left crus to the upper two; psoas major arises from the vertebral borders.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the nasal septum and the cartilages of the external nose under the following headings: the quadrangular cartilage, the upper lateral cartilages, and the lower lateral (alar) cartilages.
A(ii) Describe the blood supply to the nasal septum.
B. Explain the clinical basis for why the anteroinferior third of the nasal septum is the commonest site of nosebleeds (epistaxis).
C. Distinguish between the upper lateral cartilages and the lower lateral (alar) cartilages of the nose.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The quadrangular cartilaginous septum extends from the nasal bones in the midline above to the bony septum in the midline posteriorly, then down along the bony floor. Its upper half is flanked by two triangular-to-trapezoidal cartilages, the upper lateral cartilages, which are fused to the dorsal septum in the midline and attached to the bony margin of the pyriform aperture laterally by loose ligaments; the inferior ends of the upper lateral cartilages are free. Beneath the upper lateral cartilages lie the lower lateral cartilages; the paired lower lateral cartilages swing out from medial attachments to the caudal septum in the midline (the medial crura), through an intermediate crus area, finally flaring out superolaterally as the lateral crura; these cartilages are frequently mobile, in contradistinction to the upper lateral cartilages. The internal area or angle formed by the septum and upper lateral cartilage constitutes the internal valve.
A(ii)
The nasal septum is supplied from the sphenopalatine artery (posterior septal branch) and the anterior and posterior ethmoid arteries, with contribution of the superior labial artery (anteriorly) and the greater palatine artery (posteriorly).
B
The Kiesselbach plexus, or Little's area, represents a region in the anteroinferior third of the nasal septum where all 3 of the chief blood supplies to the internal nose converge, which is the clinical basis for this being a common site of nosebleeds; venous blood leaving the region drains into the facial, ophthalmic and sphenopalatine veins, and these veins are significant for their direct communication with the cavernous sinus and for their lack of valves, features that potentiate the intracranial spread of infection.
C
The upper lateral cartilages are fused to the dorsal septum in the midline and attached to the bony margin of the pyriform aperture laterally by loose ligaments, with their inferior ends free; they are relatively fixed. The lower lateral (alar) cartilages, by contrast, swing out from medial attachments to the caudal septum (the medial crura) to flare out superolaterally as the lateral crura, and are frequently mobile, unlike the upper lateral cartilages.

questions.question:
A. Describe the course, relations and branches of the facial nerve within the parotid gland, and its termination pattern.
B. State the structures/procedures for which knowledge of the facial nerve's branching is clinically important.
C. Explain the anatomical/functional basis of the deformity that results when this nerve is injured.
questions.answerText:
A
Within the substance of the parotid gland, from superficial to deep are found the facial nerve and its branches, the retromandibular vein and its two divisions, and the external carotid artery and its two terminal branches. The facial nerve radiates through the anterior border of the gland like a goose's foot, termed the Pes Anserinus, giving off the temporal branch, the zygomatic branch, the buccal branch, the marginal mandibular branch, and the cervical branch.
B
Frey's syndrome commonly occurs after parotid surgery or trauma, from injury of the auriculo-temporal nerve and great auricular nerve; the facial nerve's course through the parotid gland is therefore clinically important in parotid surgery, where the nerve and its branches are structures to be identified and preserved.
C
Bell's palsy is associated with drooping of the mouth, reflecting facial nerve dysfunction; facial laceration is also noted as a clinical correlate involving this nerve's territory. Because the facial nerve, once it has divided within the parotid gland into its temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular and cervical branches, supplies the muscles of facial expression, injury to the trunk or a branch of the nerve produces the drooping and loss of movement seen in facial nerve palsy.

questions.question:
A. Describe the gross anatomy of the larynx under the following headings: the three zones/compartments and the folds that demarcate them.
B. State how the zones of the larynx and the vocal folds relate to laryngeal function and clinical assessment (e.g. on laryngoscopy).
C. Explain how disease/infection at a site distant from the larynx can spread to compromise laryngeal or lower respiratory function, and the functional deficit that results from disordered laryngeal muscle action.
questions.answerText:
A
The larynx is demarcated by the vestibular fold (containing fibrous tissue, forming the false vocal cord on each side) and the vocal fold (the true vocal cord, containing the vocal ligament) into 3 zones: the supraglottic compartment (vestibule), above the false cords; the glottic compartment, between the false and true cords; and the subglottic compartment, between the true cords and the first ring of the trachea. The space between the vocal cords is the rima glottidis.
B
The mucosa is firmly adherent to the vocal ligament without any intervening submucosa, which accounts for the pearly white, avascular appearance of the vocal cords as seen on laryngoscopy; regulation of vocal cord tension (and therefore pitch of the voice) is accomplished primarily by pivoting the thyroid cartilage forward or backward at the cricothyroid joint, via the cricothyroid muscle, which is the only laryngeal muscle that tightens the cords, is supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (not the recurrent laryngeal nerve), and is the only intrinsic laryngeal muscle situated on the outside of the larynx.
C
Sensory innervation is via the internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve above the cords and via the recurrent laryngeal nerve below the cords; motor supply to the muscles is from the nucleus ambiguus via the cranial accessory, with the cricothyroid supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve and all other laryngeal muscles (including the upper oesophagus and cricopharyngeus) supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve. Lymphatic drainage above the cords is to the upper deep cervical nodes and below the cords to the lower deep cervical nodes; a disease process at either level can therefore spread along its corresponding drainage route to functionally distant lymph node groups. Movements which close off the entrance to the larynx during swallowing involve the epiglottis being pulled down and the arytenoid cartilages being pulled forward toward the epiglottis; the larynx is also raised, along with the pharynx, by contraction of the longitudinal muscles of the pharynx, and the epiglottis acts partly as a passive barrier, so disordered laryngeal muscle action compromises this protective closure mechanism.

A(i)
• Shape of a clenched fist; base to apex 12 cm in males and 10 cm in females, anteroposterior 6 cm and 5 cm, transverse 9 cm and 8 cm; weight 280-340 g in males and 230-280 g in females; lies behind the body of the sternum, in front of T5-T8, with a base, an apex, 3 surfaces and 4 borders.
• Base: posterior, mostly left atrium, receives the 4 pulmonary veins; ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk emerge from it; separated from the diaphragmatic surface by the coronary sulcus. Apex: inferolateral, mostly left ventricle, behind the 5th left intercostal space. Surfaces: sternocostal (mostly right ventricle), diaphragmatic (concave), pulmonary (left ventricle, fitting the cardiac notch of the left lung). Borders: right (right atrium), left (mostly left ventricle with the left auricle), superior (auricles and upper right ventricle), inferior (right atrium and right ventricle).
A(ii)
Right border: 3rd to 6th right costal cartilage; left border: 5th left intercostal space (apex beat, 9 cm from the midline) up to the 2nd costal cartilage; superior border: 2nd left to 3rd right costal cartilage; inferior border: 6th right costal cartilage to the 5th left intercostal space.
A(iii)
• Four chambers: atria separated by the interatrial septum, ventricles by the interventricular septum, atria from ventricles by the right and left coronary (AV) sulci. Right atrium: forms the right border, lies between SVC and IVC, has the right auricle; rough part (musculi pectinati) and smooth part (from the right horn of the sinus venosus) separated by the sulcus terminalis (crista terminalis); receives SVC, IVC and coronary sinus.
• Right ventricle: forms the sternocostal and diaphragmatic surfaces and inferior border; trabeculae carneae including the septomarginal trabecula (carries part of the AV bundle) and anterior, posterior and septal papillary muscles joined by chordae tendineae to the tricuspid valve (3 cusps, admits 3 fingertips), the chordae preventing the cusps being driven into the right atrium; pulmonary orifice about 2.5 cm with 3 semilunar cusps (anterior, left, right).
• Left atrium: posterior, forms the base, receives 4 valveless pulmonary veins; left auricle forms the upper left border; smooth wall except the auricle. Mitral (bicuspid) valve: anterior and posterior cusps, admits 2 fingertips, overlaps the tricuspid and lies slightly higher. Left ventricle: aortic orifice about 2.5 cm at the right upper part with 3 semilunar cusps (posterior, right, left); numerous trabeculae carneae; anterior and posterior papillary muscles with chordae to the mitral valve.
A(iv)
SA node: natural pacemaker, first conducting cell, below the opening of the SVC in the right atrium, contains pacemaker P-cells, autonomic supply from the cardiac plexus (sympathetics increase and parasympathetics decrease the rate of impulse generation). AV node: slow conducting tissue in the posterior and inferior interatrial septum, allows complete atrial contraction before ventricular contraction. AV bundle of His: Purkinje fibres in the membranous part of the interventricular septum, the only bridge between atrial and ventricular muscle; right branch to papillary muscles and moderator band, left branch to the left papillary muscles.
A(v)
Arteries: right and left coronary arteries from the ascending aorta run in the right and left AV sulci; the right gives posterior interventricular and marginal arteries, the left gives anterior interventricular and circumflex arteries (the circumflex gives a marginal branch). Veins: the coronary sinus (posterior part of the AV sulcus, valve at its opening, empties into the right atrium) receives the great, small and middle cardiac veins, posterior vein of the left ventricle and oblique vein of the left atrium; the anterior cardiac vein opens into the right atrium and venae cordis minimae open into the chambers. Nerve supply: cardiac plexus.
B(i)
• The heart has a poor anastomotic network, so blockage of one coronary artery (coronary thrombosis) leads to myocardial infarction; the heart wall has 3 layers (epicardium, myocardium, endocardium) and the serous pericardium receives the coronary arteries.
• Angina pectoris: chest pain originating from the heart, caused by insufficient supply of oxygen to the heart muscle.
C(i)
• Irritation of the pleura or pericardium covering the central part of the diaphragm is referred to the shoulder, because the central diaphragm is supplied by the phrenic nerve (C3-5) and the shoulder skin by the supraclavicular nerve (C3,4); the fibrous and parietal pericardium are supplied by the phrenic nerve.
• Hiccup: involuntary spasmodic contraction of the diaphragm with approximation of the vocal folds and closure of the glottis; it may be due to pleurisy, peritonitis or pericarditis.

A(ii) Describe the surface marking of the heart.
A(iii) Describe the chambers and valves of the heart.
A(iv) Describe the conducting system of the heart.
A(v) Describe the blood supply, venous drainage and nerve supply of the heart.

Describe the gross anatomy of the humerus:
A(i) Upper end
A(ii) Shaft
A(iii) Lower end
B. State how different parts of the humerus relate to common fracture patterns.
C. Explain how injury at each of these parts may spread to affect a distant structure, causing a functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
• The upper end has a large, rounded head joined to the shaft by a constricted surgical neck, and greater and lesser tubercles.
• The tubercles are separated by the intertubercular (bicipital) groove, which lodges the long tendon of biceps brachii and transmits a branch of the anterior humeral circumflex artery to the shoulder joint.
A(ii)
The shaft is circular in section above and flattened in its lower part, bears the deltoid tuberosity, and its posterior aspect shows the spiral groove, which demarcates the origins of the medial and lateral heads of triceps and between which the radial nerve and profunda vessels wind.
A(iii)
The lower end bears the rounded capitulum laterally, for articulation with the radial head, and the spool-shaped trochlea medially, for articulation with the trochlear notch of the ulna; the medial and lateral epicondyles are extracapsular, the medial being the larger, extending more distally and bearing a groove on its posterior aspect for the ulnar nerve.
B
• Fractures of the surgical neck of the humerus are especially common in elderly people with osteoporosis, usually from a minor fall on the hand with the force transmitted up the extended limb.
• Transverse fractures of the shaft frequently result from a direct blow to the arm.
• Fracture of the distal humerus, near the supracondylar ridges, is a supracondylar fracture.
C
• Because the axillary, radial and ulnar nerves are in close contact with the humerus, they may be damaged when the associated part of the bone is fractured.
• Fracture at the surgical neck threatens the axillary nerve, producing deltoid paralysis with loss of abduction and sensory loss over the regimental badge area.
• Fracture through the radial (spiral) groove of the shaft threatens the radial nerve, producing wrist drop.
• Fracture at the medial epicondyle at the lower end threatens the ulnar nerve, while injury at the distal humerus (supracondylar region) threatens the median nerve.
• Fractures of the humeral neck, midshaft and lower end are therefore each associated with a characteristic pattern of nerve injury and resultant functional deficit.

questions.question:
(A) Describe the three main openings of the diaphragm - A(i) oesophageal hiatus A(ii) aortic hiatus A(iii) caval opening - including their vertebral levels and the structures each transmits.
(B) Explain the clinical basis of diaphragmatic (hiatus) hernia.
(C) Distinguish between the oesophageal hiatus and the aortic hiatus.
questions.answerText:
A(ii)
The aortic hiatus lies posterior to the diaphragm, between the two crura, at the level of the lower border of the T12 vertebra; it transmits the aorta, the thoracic duct and sometimes the azygos and hemiazygos veins. Because the aorta does not pierce the diaphragm itself, movements of the diaphragm during respiration do not affect blood flow through it.
A(iii)
The caval opening lies in the central tendon of the diaphragm at the level of T8; it transmits the inferior vena cava, terminal branches of the right phrenic nerve, and a few hepatic lymphatic vessels. The inferior vena cava is adherent to the margin of this opening, so diaphragmatic contraction during inspiration widens the opening and dilates the inferior vena cava, aiding venous return to the heart.
B
• The right and left crura arise from the bodies of the L1-L3 vertebrae, the anterior longitudinal ligament and the intervertebral discs; the oesophageal hiatus lies within the right crus, to the left of the midline, superior to and to the left of the aortic hiatus. Diaphragmatic hernia (sliding and paraoesophageal types) and diaphragmatic rupture are clinical considerations related to weakness or defects around these openings.
• In most individuals, about 70%, both margins of the oesophageal hiatus are formed by muscular bundles of the right crus; in others the left crus contributes to the right margin, and such variation can affect the sphincter-like action around the oesophagus.
C
• The oesophageal hiatus is a muscular opening in the right crus at the level of T10 that actively constricts around the oesophagus with diaphragmatic contraction, contributing to prevention of reflux.
• The aortic hiatus is a non-muscular, fibrous opening bounded by the crura and the median arcuate ligament at the lower border of T12, so diaphragmatic contraction does not compress or affect flow through the aorta.
• The oesophageal hiatus transmits the oesophagus and vagal trunks, whereas the aortic hiatus transmits the aorta and thoracic duct, reflecting their different anatomical roles.

A(i)
The median nerve is formed by the union of a lateral root from the lateral cord (C5, C6, C7) and a medial root from the medial cord (C8, T1) of the brachial plexus.
A(ii)
In the cubital fossa the median nerve is the most medial of the major vertical contents, lying medial to the brachial artery and the tendon of biceps brachii; at the wrist it lies anterior to the tendons of flexor digitorum superficialis, deep to the flexor retinaculum, within the carpal tunnel.
A(iii)
It gives a palmar cutaneous branch that arises in the forearm, proximal to the flexor retinaculum, and a recurrent branch that arises in the hand to supply the thenar muscles.
A(iv)
It supplies flexor carpi radialis, palmaris longus, pronator teres, pronator quadratus and the digital flexors, producing thumb flexion and opposition, flexion of digits 2 and 3, wrist flexion and abduction, and forearm pronation; it also supplies sensation to the anterolateral surface of the hand.
C
• A low (wrist-level) median nerve injury produces an "ape-like hand."
• There is flattening of the thenar eminence because the recurrent branch supplying abductor pollicis brevis and flexor pollicis brevis, which arises in the hand, is affected.
• Opposition and abduction of the thumb become impossible, so the pincer-like action of the hand is lost, causing difficulty with fine manual tasks such as buttoning.
• Adductor pollicis, being supplied by the ulnar nerve, is unopposed, further contributing to the deformity.
• This contrasts with an elbow-level injury, where flexion of the index and middle fingers is lost (flexor digitorum superficialis and the lateral half of profundus are affected), the ring and little fingers weakly flex, and flexion of the distal phalanx of the thumb is lost, while the interosseous muscles are unaffected, being supplied by the ulnar nerve.
• The median nerve can be torn partially or fully, or compressed, at the elbow, from fracture, other trauma, or compression from fluid build-up following injury.
• The most common site of median nerve injury overall is at the wrist, within the carpal tunnel.
questions.question:
Describe the median nerve:
A(i) Formation (roots)
A(ii) Relations in the cubital fossa and at the wrist
A(iii) Branches
A(iv) Distribution
C. Explain the anatomical basis of the deformity seen after a low (wrist-level) injury to the median nerve.

Describe the radial nerve:
A(i) Origin and course in the arm
A(ii) Course/division in the cubital fossa and forearm
A(iii) Branches
A(iv) Distribution
C. Explain the anatomical basis of the deformity ("wrist drop") seen after radial nerve injury.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The radial nerve is a terminal branch of the posterior cord of the brachial plexus; it courses posteromedially with the axillary vessels and enters the posterior compartment of the arm under teres major, where it winds around the spiral (radial) groove of the humerus, accompanied by the profunda brachii artery.
A(ii)
• It pierces the lateral intermuscular septum to enter the anterior compartment of the arm, passes to the forearm at the level of the elbow joint, enters the cubital fossa, and there divides into a superficial and a deep branch.
• The superficial branch courses toward the wrist lateral to the radial artery and enters the hand, dividing into dorsal digital cutaneous branches; the deep branch gives off the posterior interosseous nerve, which passes between the heads of supinator to enter the posterior compartment of the forearm and terminates near the wrist joint.
A(iii)
Branches include muscular twigs in the arm to triceps brachii and anconeus, the posterior interosseous nerve to the forearm extensors, the superficial (cutaneous) branch, and articular twigs to the elbow and wrist joints.
A(iv)
The deep branch/posterior interosseous nerve supplies the extensor muscles in the forearm as well as brachioradialis; the superficial branch supplies cutaneous sensation to the dorsal aspect of the hand, the dorsal aspect of the first to third digits, and the dorsolateral aspect of the fourth finger.
C
• Injury to the radial nerve produces "wrist drop."
• Because the nerve's deep branch/posterior interosseous nerve supplies the extensor muscles of the forearm, injury interrupts the motor supply to the wrist and finger extensors.
• The nerve can be injured at any level — axilla, spiral groove, radial tunnel, posterior interosseous, or superficial radial.
• Injury may result from fracture of the body (shaft) of the humerus, where the nerve lies in close contact with the bone in the spiral groove.
• "Saturday Night Palsy" describes compression of the nerve in the axilla, such as from using improperly adjusted crutches, which similarly interrupts its motor function.
• With the extensors paralysed and unopposed flexor tone at the wrist, the hand falls into flexion at the wrist, producing the characteristic wrist drop.

questions.question:
Describe the tibia under the following headings, state how its zones relate to common pathologies, and explain why fracture of the middle third is at highest risk of delayed union.
A(i) General features, upper end, shaft, and lower end of the tibia
A(ii) How the upper end of the tibia relates to the knee joint — tibial plateaus, menisci, and intercondylar areas
B(i) Blood supply of the tibia and the significance of nutrient artery direction
B(ii) Common pathologies related to zones of the tibia — proximal, mid-shaft, and distal
C(i) Distinguish tibia from fibula with respect to weight-bearing function, articulations, and nerve–vessel relations at each malleolus
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The tibia is the large weight-bearing medial bone of the leg; it articulates with femoral condyles superiorly and the head of fibula laterally. It has an expanded upper end, a shaft, and a smaller lower end. Upper end (see A(ii)). Shaft: triangular in cross-section; 3 borders and 3 surfaces (borders and surfaces are named by opposites); anterior border forms the shin; soleal line on the posterior surface is for soleus. Lower end: expanded; saddle-shaped articular surface for talus; prolonged downwards medially to form the medial malleolus; the medial surface is subcutaneous from the medial malleolus to the medial condyle above.
A(ii)
The upper end has tibial plateaus (lateral and medial condyles); the lateral and medial menisci; anterior and posterior intercondylar areas separate the tibial plateaus; the intercondylar eminence; an articular facet for the head of fibula; and a groove on the medial condyle for semimembranosus. The anterior intercondylar area of the tibia is where the ACL attaches (just posterior to attachment of medial meniscus); the posterior intercondylar area is where the PCL attaches.
B(i)
The nutrient artery (medullary artery) is the main artery of the diaphysis. It is directed obliquely away from the epiphyseal end. When there is an epiphysis at both ends (tibia is one of the 5 bones unique in having epiphyseal plates at both ends — viz: femur, tibia, fibula, humerus, and radius), the nutrient canal is directed away from the more actively growing end. Hughes: 'to the elbow I go, from the knee I flee'. Fracture of the middle third of the tibia lies in a 'watershed' zone between the nutrient artery (supplying the upper 2/3) and the periosteal vessels (supplying the lower 1/3), making this zone most susceptible to avascular non-union.
B(ii)
Proximal tibia: tibial plateau fractures (high-energy trauma), associated with meniscal and ligamentous tears. Mid-shaft tibia: most common site of delayed or non-union, stress fractures (runners), and compartment syndrome (anterior compartment syndrome). Distal tibia (ankle): Pott's fracture involving the malleolus; ankle sprains; avulsion fractures.
C(i)
Tibia: large weight-bearing medial bone; articulates with femoral condyles, fibula head, and talus; contributes the roof (inferior surface of tibia) and the medial malleolus (wall) of the ankle mortise; the medial surface is subcutaneous. Fibula: not a weight-bearing bone; does not articulate with the femur or patella at the knee (only serves as attachment for knee joint structures); contributes the lateral malleolus (wall of ankle mortise) from fibula. At the ankle: lateral malleolar wall is from fibula and medial malleolar wall is from tibia.

A(i)
General characteristics: epithelial tissue consists of closely packed cells arranged in one or more layers; these cells are specialized and fill roles such as protection, secretion, and absorption; the cells are tightly packed together with very little extracellular matrix and almost no intercellular substance; they rest on a basement membrane (a basal lamina containing the glycoprotein laminin). Morphological classification by cell shape: squamous (flat), cuboidal (square or cube-like), columnar (tall and thin). By number of layers: simple epithelium (one cell thick) — can be simple squamous, simple cuboidal, or simple columnar; stratified epithelium (multiple layers — described as heterogeneous); pseudostratified epithelium — appears stratified but all cells contact the basal lamina. Transitional epithelium: recognized by its appearance — when the bladder is empty (relaxed), the epithelium appears thicker and has more layers than when the bladder is full. Basement membrane: contains the glycoprotein laminin; the border between epithelia and the underlying connective tissue is sharp and distinct.
A(ii)
Simple squamous epithelium: lines blood vessels (endothelium) and body cavities. Simple cuboidal epithelium: lines many small ducts in the body. Simple columnar epithelium: lines the gallbladder, larger ducts near the urinary papilla; also found in the jejunum (with goblet cells). Ciliated columnar epithelium: found in the respiratory tract and fallopian tubes; goblet cells (glandular epithelium) are present, making it heterogeneous. Stratified squamous epithelium (keratinized): forms the outer layer of skin; contains the protective protein keratin; a keratinized (dry) epithelium. Transitional epithelium: lines the urinary bladder.
B(i)
Epithelial tissue is avascular (contains no blood vessels); the lamina propria (underlying connective tissue) supplies the necessary nutrients and metabolites, which are transported to and from epithelial cells by diffusion through the basement membrane. If the basement membrane is disrupted (e.g., in cancer invasion or severe inflammation), the barrier between epithelium and connective tissue is lost, allowing unrestricted cell invasion into the underlying stroma; epithelial cells in contact with the environment are constantly subjected to mechanical damage and must show many dividing cells (mitoses) to replace lost cells; disruption of this repair mechanism contributes to disease progression.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the gross anatomy of epithelial tissue under the following headings: general characteristics, morphological classification (by cell shape and number of layers), and the basement membrane.
A(ii) Relate specific epithelial types to their common locations in the body, giving one example each of simple squamous, simple cuboidal, simple columnar, ciliated columnar, stratified squamous, and transitional epithelium.
B(i) Explain why epithelial tissue is avascular, how it receives nutrients, and state the clinical consequence when the basement membrane is disrupted in disease.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Definition and function: Connective tissue derives its name from its function in connecting or binding cells and tissues; it maintains the form of organs throughout the body. Unlike other tissue types (epithelium, muscle, nerve) which consist mainly of cells, the major constituent of connective tissue is the extracellular matrix. The extracellular matrix is composed of protein fibers (collagen, elastic, and reticular fibers), ground substance (a jelly-like, amorphous, anionic, hydrophilic complex of proteoglycans, glycosaminoglycans, and multiadhesive glycoproteins such as laminin and fibronectin), and tissue fluid. Classification: connective tissue is classified as connective tissue proper (loose: areolar, adipose, reticular; dense: regular, irregular, elastic) and specialized connective tissue (blood, cartilage, bone).
A(ii)
The amount of tissue fluid (interstitial fluid) is fairly constant and there is an equilibrium between water entering and leaving the intercellular substance. In pathological conditions (traumatic injury and inflammation), fluid may accumulate in the connective tissue, a condition known as edema.
B(i)
Loose connective tissue: irregularly arranged tissue with abundant ground substance, capable of withstanding stress from many directions; present in dermis, capsules of joints, and submucosa of the alimentary tract. Examples: areolar tissue, adipose tissue. Dense connective tissue: tissue in which fibers predominate; it is organized to withstand forces in specific directions. Dense regular: present in tendons and ligaments. Dense irregular: present in the dermis of skin and capsules of organs.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe connective tissue under the following headings: definition and function, major constituent and its components, classification.
A(ii) Explain the clinical basis of edema in connective tissue.
B(i) Distinguish between loose connective tissue and dense connective tissue, giving two examples of each.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
The hip joint is a multiaxial ball-and-socket type of synovial joint. It is the largest joint in the human body and the 2nd largest weight-bearing joint. Articular surfaces: the lunate surface of the acetabulum (covered by hyaline cartilage except at the fovea) and the spherical head of femur (which forms 2/3 of a sphere, covered by hyaline cartilage except at the fovea capitis). The acetabulum is deepened by the fibrocartilaginous acetabular labrum; it is deficient inferiorly as the acetabular notch, bridged by the transverse acetabular ligament.
A(ii)
Capsule: strong and thick; medially attached to margin of acetabulum, transverse acetabular ligament, and adjacent margin of obturator foramen; laterally attached to the intertrochanteric line anteriorly. Ligaments: (1) Iliofemoral ligament (ligament of Bigelow) — one of the strongest in the body, Y-shaped; apex at inferior iliac spine, base to intertrochanteric line; prevents overextension and prevents trunk from falling backwards while standing. (2) Pubofemoral ligament — triangular; attached superiorly to iliopubic eminence and obturator crest, inferiorly merges with capsule; limits extension and abduction. (3) Ischiofemoral ligament — reinforces posterior aspect; medially attached to ischium posteroinferior to acetabulum, laterally to greater trochanter deep to the iliofemoral ligament; limits extension. Fibers of all three spiral so they become taut in extension, stabilizing the joint and reducing muscle energy needed for standing. Ligament teres (round ligament): flat triangular band from fovea to acetabular notch and transverse ligament; ensheathed by synovial membrane; transmits arteries to head of femur.
B(i)
By Hilton's law: the nerve supplying the joint also supplies the muscles moving the joint and the skin covering the insertion of those muscles. Nerve supply: femoral nerve, anterior division of obturator nerve, nerve to rectus femoris, nerve to quadratus femoris, sciatic nerve, and superior gluteal nerve. The posterior division of the obturator nerve supplies both the hip and the knee joint.
B(ii)
Flexion (120–140°): iliopsoas, sartorius, rectus femoris, tensor fasciae latae. Extension: gluteus maximus, semimembranosus, semitendinosus, biceps femoris. Abduction (60–80°): gluteus medius, minimus, tensor fasciae latae. Adduction: pectineus, adductor longus, brevis, magnus, gracilis. Medial rotation: gluteus medius, minimus, tensor fasciae latae. Lateral rotation: obturator internus and externus, gemellus superior and inferior, quadratus femoris, piriformis, posterior fibres of gluteus medius and minimus, superior fibres of gluteus maximus.
C(i)
The posterior division of the obturator nerve supplies both the hip and knee joints; pain from hip pathology is therefore referred along this common nerve pathway to the knee joint. Coxa valga follows congenital dislocation of the head of femur; coxa vara follows fracture of the neck of femur.
questions.question:
Describe the hip joint under the following headings and explain its clinical correlates.
A(i) Type and articular surfaces
A(ii) Capsule, ligaments — name, attachments and function of each
B(i) Nerve supply, applying Hilton's law
B(ii) Movements and muscles responsible for each movement
C(i) Explain why referred pain from the hip can present at the knee, and distinguish coxa valga from coxa vara

A(i) Define the intercostal space and state the number of spaces and their contents.
A(ii) Describe the intercostal muscles, including the fibre direction, attachments and extent of the external and internal intercostals.
A(iii) Describe the innermost intercostal muscle and the endothoracic fascia.
A(iv) Describe the intercostal neurovascular bundle and the order of its components.
A(v) Describe the arteries of the intercostal space.
A(vi) Describe the veins of the intercostal space.
A(vii) Describe the intercostal nerves and their branches.
A(viii) Describe the lymphatic drainage of the intercostal space.
B(i) Explain why a needle or drain is passed immediately above the upper border of a rib and state the other clinical uses of the intercostal spaces.
C(i) Distinguish between a typical and an atypical intercostal nerve.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The space between two ribs; with 12 ribs on each side there are 11 intercostal spaces; each space contains intercostal muscles, the intercostal neurovascular bundle and lymphatics.
A(ii)
• Three muscles (external, internal, innermost; transversus thoracis, subcostalis and levator costarum are also listed), supplied by the corresponding intercostal nerves, that pull the ribs nearer to each other and strengthen the space. External intercostal: most superficial, fibres downward and forward, origin lower border of the rib above, insertion upper border of the rib below, from the rib tubercle behind to the costochondral junction in front, replaced anteriorly by the anterior intercostal membrane.
• Internal intercostal: intermediate layer, fibres downward and backward, origin subcostal groove of the rib above, insertion upper border of the rib below, from the sternum in front to the angle of the rib behind, replaced posteriorly by the posterior intercostal membrane.
A(iii)
Innermost intercostal: deepest, incomplete layer divided into 3 portions, its fibres cross more than one space; related externally to the intercostal nerve and vessels and internally to the endothoracic fascia. Endothoracic fascia: extrapleural fascia lining the chest wall between the muscles and bones and the parietal pleura, extending over the pleural apex as the suprapleural membrane and forming a thin layer between diaphragm and pleura.
A(iv)
The neurovascular bundle lies between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles, high in the space in relation to the subcostal groove of the rib above; strict order from above downwards: vein, artery, nerve (VAN); because the innermost layer is incomplete it is generally covered on the inside by endothoracic fascia.
A(v)
Each space has a single posterior and 2 anterior intercostal arteries, giving branches to muscles, skin, parietal pleura and breast. Posterior: upper 2 spaces from the superior intercostal artery (costocervical trunk of the subclavian artery), lower 9 spaces from the thoracic aorta. Anterior: upper 6 spaces from the internal thoracic artery, lower 5 from the musculophrenic artery; they anastomose with the posterior arteries.
A(vi)
Veins accompany the arteries and nerves (11 posterior intercostal and 1 subcostal vein); valves direct blood posteriorly. Right side: 1st space to the brachiocephalic vein, the rest to the azygos vein. Left side: upper 3 spaces to the left brachiocephalic vein, the rest to the hemiazygos and accessory hemiazygos veins, which drain to the azygos vein. Anterior veins: upper 6 spaces to the internal thoracic vein, lower 5 to the musculophrenic vein.
A(vii)
12 pairs, the anterior primary rami of the thoracic spinal nerves and mixed nerves; nerves 1-6 are distributed in the intercostal spaces, 7-11 supply the anterior abdominal wall, and the 12th runs forward in the abdomen as the subcostal nerve; they supply skin, muscles of the space and abdomen, parietal pleura and parietal peritoneum. Branches: rami communicantes, collateral (muscular), lateral cutaneous, anterior cutaneous, pleural and peritoneal (7th-11th).
A(viii)
Deep lymphatics follow the arteries: anteriorly they drain into the anterior intercostal (parasternal) nodes along the internal thoracic artery; posteriorly they drain into the posterior intercostal nodes in the posterior mediastinum.
B(i)
• A needle or drain is passed immediately above the upper border of the rib to avoid the neurovascular bundle (vein, artery, nerve from above downwards) running under the rib above in the subcostal groove.
• Intercostal spaces are access points for surgical procedures (e.g. resection of part of the lung), for percussion and auscultation of the heart and lung, and for sampling pleural fluid or draining pus or blood from the pleural cavity; disease in the thorax may cause pain in the anterior abdominal wall because the intercostal nerves supply both the thoracic and abdominal wall and the parietal pleura.
C(i)
Typical nerves are T3-6. T1 is atypical: no anterior cutaneous branch, joined to the brachial plexus by a large branch corresponding to the lateral cutaneous branch. T2 is atypical: its lateral cutaneous branch is the intercostobrachial nerve, which joins the medial cutaneous nerve of the arm through the brachial plexus.

A(i)
Eight processes of digestion (in order):
• Ingestion
• Mastication
• Peristalsis / motility
• Secretions
• Hormone release
• Chemical digestion
• Absorption
• Elimination
A(ii)
Four main functions of the GI tract:
• Macromolecules (proteins, complex carbohydrates, nucleic acids, and fat) obtained from ingested food are broken down into smaller subunits for easy absorption through the lining of the small intestine during digestion.
• These smaller subunits are required for the release of energy, maintenance, and growth.
• Most of the water and electrolytes are absorbed in the large intestine.
• The inner layer of the entire GI tract forms an important protective barrier between the contents of the tract and the tissues of the body.
B(i)
Serosa:
• Composition: a thin sheet of loose connective tissue covered with mesothelium (a simple squamous covering epithelium); rich in blood vessels, lymphatics, and adipose tissue.
• Function: the outermost covering of GIT organs within the abdominal cavity.
• Continuity: the serosa of the small and large intestines is continuous with parts of the mesentery (a large fold of adipose connective tissue covered on both sides by mesothelium, which suspends the intestines and is continuous with the peritoneum).
• Esophagus: because the esophagus is bound directly to adjacent structures and not suspended in a cavity, it has a thick adventitia instead of a serosa; the adventitia consists of connective tissue containing vessels and nerves, lacking mesothelium.
B(ii)
• The enteric nervous system (submucosal and myenteric plexuses) functions independently of the CNS; because it is anatomically connected to the autonomic nervous system, it provides the anatomical basis for the well-known actions of emotional stress on the stomach and other regions of the GIT.
Two diseases demonstrating clinical consequences of plexus destruction:
• Hirschsprung disease (congenital aganglionic megacolon): caused by absence or severely injured plexuses in parts or all of the large intestine; disturbs motility and produces dilation, causing difficulty passing stool.
• Chagas disease / trypanosomiasis (infection with Trypanosoma cruzi): the protozoan destroys the enteric plexuses, producing similar motility disturbance.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the processes of digestion, naming all eight steps in order.
A(ii) Describe the four main functions of the GI tract, distinguishing between the role of the small intestine and the role of the large intestine in absorption.
B(i) Describe the composition and function of the serosa, including the structures it is continuous with and how it differs between organs within the abdominal cavity and the esophagus.
B(ii) Explain why the enteric nervous system provides the anatomical basis for the effects of emotional stress on the GIT, and name the two diseases that demonstrate the clinical consequences of plexus destruction.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
The cubital fossa is a triangular space, a shallow depression on the anterior surface of the elbow region, located anterior to the elbow joint, formed between two forearm muscles (brachioradialis and pronator teres).
A(ii)
Boundaries: base (superior) — an imaginary horizontal line connecting the medial and lateral epicondyles; medial (ulnar) wall — lateral border of pronator teres; lateral (radial) wall — medial border of brachioradialis; apex — directed inferiorly, where the medial and lateral boundaries meet; floor — brachialis and supinator; roof — continuity of brachial and antebrachial (deep) fascia, reinforced by the bicipital aponeurosis, superficial fascia and skin.
A(iii)
The major contents, from medial to lateral, are the median nerve, the brachial artery (which bifurcates near the apex into the radial and ulnar arteries), deep accompanying veins of the arteries, and the tendon of biceps brachii.
B
• The median cubital vein, cephalic vein and basilic vein are present in the area but are usually considered superficial to the cubital fossa and not part of its contents.
• During blood pressure measurement the stethoscope is placed over the brachial artery in the cubital fossa, and the fossa is also used to palpate the brachial pulse.
• The area just superficial to the cubital fossa is often used for venous access (phlebotomy), since it is superficial and accessible.
• The bicipital aponeurosis forms the roof of the fossa and was historically called the "grace of God" tendon because it protected the brachial artery and median nerve during blood-letting.
C
• The radial nerve is in the vicinity of the cubital fossa, located between brachialis and brachioradialis, but is often, though not always, considered part of the cubital fossa's contents.
• This differs from the median nerve and brachial artery, which are consistently listed as major contents of the fossa.
• The superficial veins similarly lie in the roof/superficial region and are related to, rather than contained within, the fossa proper.
• Venipuncture therefore uses the superficial veins overlying the fossa, while palpation of the brachial pulse and auscultation for blood pressure use the deeper true content, the brachial artery.
• This distinction between superficial and deep structures is the basis for choosing the correct site for a given clinical procedure at the elbow.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Tibialis anterior: origin — lateral condyle and superior half of lateral surface of tibia and interosseous membrane; insertion — medial and inferior surfaces of medial cuneiform and base of 1st metatarsal; innervation — deep fibular nerve (L4, L5); action — dorsiflexes ankle and inverts foot. Extensor digitorum longus: origin — lateral condyle of tibia and superior 3/4 of medial surface of fibula and interosseous membrane; insertion — middle and distal phalanges of lateral 4 digits; innervation — deep fibular nerve (L4, L5); action — extends lateral 4 digits and dorsiflexes ankle. Extensor hallucis longus: origin — middle part of anterior surface of fibula and interosseous membrane; insertion — dorsal aspect of base of distal phalanx of great toe; innervation — deep fibular nerve (L4, L5); action — extends great toe and dorsiflexes ankle. Fibularis tertius: origin — inferior 3rd of anterior surface of fibula and interosseous membrane; insertion — dorsum of base of 5th metatarsal; innervation — deep fibular nerve (L4, L5); action — dorsiflexes ankle and aids in eversion of foot.
A(ii)
The dorsalis pedis artery begins as the anterior tibial artery enters the foot. It passes over the dorsal aspect of the tarsal bones, then moves inferiorly towards the sole of the foot. It then anastomoses with the lateral plantar artery to form the deep plantar arch. It supplies the tarsal bones and the dorsal aspect of the metatarsals; via the deep plantar arch, it also contributes to the supply of the toes. The dorsalis pedis pulse is found by palpating on the dorsum of the foot, just lateral to extensor hallucis longus tendon.
B(i)
The common fibular nerve is the lateral, smaller terminal branch of the sciatic nerve; it begins at the superior angle of the popliteal fossa, closely follows the medial border of biceps femoris, exits the fossa superficial to the lateral head of gastrocnemius, passes over the posterior aspect of the head of fibula, and winds around the neck of fibula where it divides into its terminal branches — the deep fibular nerve and superficial fibular nerve. The deep fibular nerve supplies all 4 muscles of the anterior compartment (tibialis anterior, extensor digitorum longus, extensor hallucis longus, fibularis tertius) and the foot.
B(ii)
At the neck of fibula the common fibular nerve is subcutaneous and directly palpable, making it vulnerable to direct trauma, compression, or traction. Injury here interrupts the deep fibular nerve before it reaches the anterior compartment. All 4 anterior compartment muscles (which perform dorsiflexion and toe extension) are paralysed. The result is foot drop: the foot hangs in plantarflexion and inversion (because the unopposed plantarflexors — gastrocnemius, soleus — and invertor — tibialis posterior — continue to act), and the patient develops a high-stepping gait to clear the dragging toe.
C(i)
Tibialis anterior: dorsiflexes the ankle AND inverts the foot; supplied by the deep fibular nerve (L4, L5). Fibularis tertius: dorsiflexes the ankle AND aids eversion of the foot; supplied by the deep fibular nerve (L4, L5). Both share the same nerve supply but perform opposite movements about the subtalar axis (inversion vs. eversion), reflecting their positions on opposite sides of the interosseous membrane.

A(i) Describe the tissue preparation process used in histology under the following headings: fixation, dehydration and clearing, embedding, sectioning, and staining.
A(ii) State the most commonly used stain in histology, explain what structures it stains and the colors produced, and give the reason for the differential staining.
B(i) Distinguish between light microscopy and electron microscopy in histology, stating what each reveals and an example of when each is preferred.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Fixation: to achieve a permanent section, tissues must be fixed to preserve the structure and molecular composition; fixation prevents autolysis (self-digestion by enzymes present in the cells) and destruction by bacteria. Dehydration and clearing: tissues are progressed in graded steps to 100% alcohol to remove water; after the solvent replaces the alcohol, the tissue becomes transparent in xylene (clearing). Embedding: once the tissue is impregnated with the solvent, it is placed in a hard medium (e.g., wax); heat causes the solvent to evaporate, and the spaces within the tissue are filled by the embedding medium. Sectioning: tissues are sectioned by the microtome's steel or glass blade; this method allows stained sections to be prepared rapidly for study of specimens. Mounting: sections are mounted on a supportive structure (e.g., slide) that can be placed on a microscope stage. Staining: stains are applied to differentiate tissue components.
A(ii)
The most commonly used stains are hematoxylin and eosin (H & E). Hematoxylin stains basic (acidic) structures — the most acidic components are DNA and RNA; therefore, the nucleus and cytoplasmic RNA stain blue/purple (basophilic). Eosin stains acidophilic (basic) structures — many cytoplasmic constituents stain pinkish (eosinophilic/acidophilic). Reason: differential staining is based on the acid-base chemistry of cell components; acidic cell components bind basic dyes (hematoxylin) and basic components bind acidic dyes (eosin).
B(i)
Light microscopy: the standard technique; produces images of tissue sections examined by transmitted light; maximum resolving power is 0.2 micrometers (two marks 0.2 micrometers apart can be seen as two distinct entities). Types include brightfield, phase contrast, differential interference contrast (DIC), fluorescence, and confocal. Preferred for: routine tissue examination, diagnosis of pathology, overview of cell and tissue structure. Electron microscopy: has extended the detail at which subcellular structures can be studied; reveals ultrastructural details such as organelles, myelin sheaths, and synapse morphology. Preferred for: study of subcellular structures, ultrastructural detail, and molecular architecture of cell membranes.

questions.question:
Describe the gross anatomy of the glenohumeral (shoulder) joint:
A(i) Articular surfaces and classification
A(ii) Capsule
A(iii) Factors contributing to its mobility and stability
B. State how a part of the joint capsule relates to the common direction of shoulder dislocation.
C. Explain how shoulder dislocation may spread to affect a distant structure (nerve), causing a functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The glenohumeral (shoulder) joint is a multiaxial synovial joint of the ball-and-socket variety, formed by articulation between the head of the humerus and the glenoid cavity of the scapula; due to the very limited interface between humerus and scapula, it is the most mobile joint in the human body.
A(ii)
The joint capsule is a fibrous sheath enclosing the joint structures; it is thin and lax to allow a wide range of movement (particularly abduction), is strengthened by muscles and ligaments, but is weakest inferiorly, placing it at risk of dislocation in that direction. It is lined by synovial membrane and forms a tubular sheath around the tendon of the long head of biceps, and a number of bursae aid mobility.
A(iii)
• Factors contributing to mobility are the ball-and-socket joint type, the shallow glenoid cavity against the large humeral head (a 1:4 disproportion, likened to a golf ball and tee), and laxity of the joint capsule.
• Factors contributing to stability are the rotator cuff muscles, whose resting tone pulls the humeral head into the glenoid cavity, the glenoid labrum, which deepens the cavity and reduces dislocation risk, and the ligaments, which reinforce the capsule and form the coraco-acromial arch.
B
• The glenohumeral joint is the most commonly dislocated joint in the body, accounting for approximately 95% of all shoulder dislocations, and anterior dislocations are the most prevalent.
• An anterior dislocation is usually caused by excessive extension and lateral rotation of the humerus, which forces the humeral head anteriorly and inferiorly into the weakest (inferior) part of the joint capsule.
• Tearing of the joint capsule during dislocation is associated with an increased risk of future (recurrent) dislocations.
C
• The axillary nerve runs in close proximity to the shoulder joint and can be damaged during dislocation.
• Injury to the axillary nerve causes paralysis of the deltoid muscle, with loss of sensation over the "regimental badge" area of skin overlying the deltoid.
• A dislocation can also stretch the radial nerve, since it is tightly bound within the radial (spiral) groove of the humerus.
• These nerve injuries represent the spread of the joint pathology to distant neurological structures.
• The resulting functional deficits include loss of shoulder abduction and sensory loss from axillary nerve injury, reflecting how a purely mechanical joint injury can produce a distinct neurological deficit at a distance from the joint itself.

A(i)
Molecular composition: The cell membrane consists of amphipathic phospholipids arranged so that the hydrophobic tails face inward (away from water) and the more hydrophilic head regions associate with the cytosolic and extracellular environments, forming a spherical lipid bilayer. The phospholipid bilayer was proposed by Gorter and Grendel in 1925. It also includes integral membrane proteins and peripheral membrane proteins (almost half of the total mass of the membrane), a network of tiny microfilaments of the cytoskeleton, and the lipid molecule cholesterol, which stabilizes and makes the cell membrane more rigid. Functions: structural support; semi-permeable membrane (controls what molecules enter and leave the cell); establishes and maintains an electrochemical gradient; contains receptors that recognize and respond to molecular signals; supports cell adhesion and cell communication. Membrane transport mechanisms: passive (osmosis, diffusion, simple diffusion), facilitated transport, active transport (primary and secondary), and vesicular transport (endocytosis: pinocytosis and phagocytosis; exocytosis).
A(ii)
Several diseases have been implicated with defective membrane receptors. Pseudohypoparathyroidism is associated with defective parathyroid and growth hormone receptors. In these conditions, the glands produce the respective hormones, but the target cells do not respond because they lack normal receptors. Signal transduction can be hindered and cause diseases when mutations occur in the genes that encode and regulate receptor proteins.
B(i)
Integral membrane proteins: are directly incorporated within the lipid bilayer; most are transmembrane proteins passing through the entire membrane; inserted into the lipid bilayer. Functions: transport, signal transduction, structural support. Peripheral membrane proteins: exhibit a looser association with the membrane; bound to the membrane indirectly by protein-protein interactions; located on the cytosolic face. Plasma membrane contains proteins called integrins that are linked to cytoplasmic molecules; through these linkages there is a connection between the extracellular matrix and cytoplasm, mediating cell adhesion and cell communication.

A(ii) Explain the clinical basis of diseases caused by defective membrane receptors.
