It is an autoimmune process in which synovial hyperplasia—driven by T-cell mediated immune dysregulation—is the primary pathological event. Pannus formation distinguishes RA from OA.
questions.question: Rheumatoid arthritis causes articular cartilage loss through a process called 'pannus'. This is BEST defined as:
options: Neutrophil infiltration of cartilage releasing lysozymes
Hyperplastic synovium creeping over and destroying articular cartilage
Periosteal new bone encroaching on the joint space
Calcium pyrophosphate crystals eroding the cartilage surface
Auto-antibody-mediated complement activation at the chondrocyte surface

questions.explanation: Prune belly (Eagle-Barrett) syndrome is characterized by the classic triad of: absent or severely deficient abdominal musculature (giving the prune-like appearance), bilateral undescended testes, and urinary tract anomalies (typically massively dilated ureters and bladder with renal dysplasia). It occurs almost exclusively in males. Management involves urological reconstruction and orchidopexy.
questions.question: Prune belly (triad) syndrome is a congenital anterior abdominal wall condition associated with:

questions.explanation: The standard chemotherapy agents for nephroblastoma are Actinomycin D (dactinomycin) and Vincristine, often combined with Adriamycin (doxorubicin) for advanced stages. Cyclophosphamide is used in some protocols. These agents constitute the VAC (vincristine, actinomycin D, cyclophosphamide) regimen. Cisplatin and carboplatin are used in neuroblastoma and other solid tumours.
questions.question: Chemotherapy agents used in the treatment of nephroblastoma include:

questions.explanation: The rule of twos describes Meckel's diverticulum as occurring in approximately 2 percent of the population, located within 2 feet of the ileocaecal valve, typically around 2 inches in length, and most commonly symptomatic before the age of 2 years, providing a helpful mnemonic for its classical features.
questions.question: Which rule of thumb is classically used to describe the epidemiological and anatomical features of Meckel's diverticulum?

questions.explanation: The seminal vesicles contribute the majority of the seminal fluid volume, and their dysfunction, obstruction, or congenital absence typically presents with markedly reduced ejaculate volume despite normal sperm concentration. This differs from primary testicular pathology, which would more typically affect sperm count and quality rather than volume alone. Transrectal ultrasound can help identify obstruction or agenesis of the seminal vesicles.
questions.question: A man undergoing infertility evaluation produces an ejaculate with a low volume of only 0.8 mL, with sperm otherwise present in normal concentration. This low-volume ejaculate most likely reflects dysfunction of which structure?
Which of the following is a direct function of bone as a connective tissue?
questions.explanation: Bone serves multiple functions beyond the structural: it protects vital organs, supports soft tissues, transmits muscular force, mediates locomotion, acts as a mineral reservoir (calcium, phosphate, and toxic metals like lead), and is a haematopoietic organ—producing red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets within the red bone marrow. These combined structural and metabolic roles make bone unique among connective tissues.
options: Production of blood cells (haematopoiesis) within the marrow
Synthesis of insulin in response to glucose loading
Regulation of serum thyroid hormone levels
Secretion of bile salts for fat digestion

questions.question: A physiotherapist performs specialised gentle skin-stretching massage techniques designed to stimulate lymphatic flow in a patient with lymphoedema. This technique is known as:
questions.explanation: Manual lymph drainage is a specialised, light, rhythmic massage technique performed by trained therapists to stimulate residual lymphatic vessels and redirect fluid toward functioning lymphatic territories. It forms a core component of complete decongestive therapy alongside compression bandaging and skin care. Unlike deep tissue massage, the pressure used is deliberately very light to avoid collapsing superficial lymphatic vessels.

options: Reduced bone marrow content in children
Greater elasticity of paediatric bone and ribs
questions.question: A child with suspected long bone fracture has no visible external bruising over the abdomen but has evidence of internal organ injury on imaging. Which bone characteristic explains this discrepancy?
questions.explanation: Paediatric bones and ribs are more elastic and pliable than adult bone, allowing them to bend and absorb energy without fracturing. This means significant force can be transmitted to underlying organs without an overlying rib fracture being visible. Clinicians must maintain suspicion for internal injury even when bony signs are absent.

options: Reduce the metabolic demands of wound healing
questions.question: Conservative leg ulcer treatment includes maintaining normal weight primarily to:
questions.explanation: Maintaining normal weight is a conservative measure for leg ulcer management because obesity increases venous and lymphatic stasis, venous hypertension, and tissue hypoxia, all of which impair ulcer healing and promote recurrence. Exercise is also encouraged as it activates the calf muscle pump, improving venous and lymphatic drainage.

In septic arthritis of the hip, the joint adopts a position of flexion (which maximizes intra-articular volume and reduces capsular pressure) with all movements grossly restricted or abolished due to pain and muscle spasm. The joint is warm. Differentiating it from transient synovitis is important—septic arthritis has fever, raised CRP/ESR, and toxic appearance.
questions.question: The classic position adopted by a hip joint affected by septic arthritis is:

questions.explanation: Age at the time of Kasai portoenterostomy is the most important prognostic factor, with surgery performed before 8 weeks of age associated with significantly better rates of bile drainage and native liver survival compared to later intervention, as progressive fibrosis reduces the chance of success with delay.
options: Age at surgery, with earlier intervention giving better outcomes
questions.question: Which factor is the most important determinant of successful long-term bile drainage following the Kasai portoenterostomy for biliary atresia?
What is the minimum recommended daily fluid intake to reduce risk of catheter encrustation and stone formation around the catheter tip?
questions.explanation: Patients with indwelling catheters should be encouraged to maintain an oral fluid intake of at least 3 litres per day to maintain a high urine flow, which dilutes crystalloids and reduces the risk of encrustation forming on the catheter tip within the bladder. Inadequate fluid intake allows stagnant concentrated urine to deposit minerals around the catheter, potentially forming a bladder stone and making catheter removal impossible even after balloon deflation.

questions.question: A 4-year-old presents with a firm, non-tender midline swelling just below the umbilicus with intermittent urine leakage from the umbilical region. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.explanation: A patent urachus results from failure of the embryonic urachus, which normally connects the fetal bladder to the allantois, to obliterate completely after birth, allowing urine to leak intermittently from the umbilicus. This is confirmed by demonstrating a patent tract connecting the bladder to the umbilicus.

questions.question: Urologic evaluation before renal transplantation includes bladder and pelvic ultrasound and voiding cystourethrogram. What specific lower tract condition does the VCUG primarily assess?
questions.explanation: Voiding cystourethrogram (VCUG) in the pretransplant evaluation assesses for vesicoureteric reflux, bladder trabeculation indicating outlet obstruction, urethral stricture, and bladder neck obstruction. Reflux into a defunctioned native ureter post-transplant can cause recurrent pyelonephritis. Identifying and treating lower tract pathology before transplantation protects the transplanted kidney from ascending infection and high-pressure reflux.
options: Bladder wall thickness as a marker of detrusor hypertrophy only
Renal artery stenosis and cortical thickness
Vesicoureteric reflux and bladder outlet obstruction pattern
Upper tract hydronephrosis and calyceal morphology
Pelvic lymphadenopathy and iliac vessel anatomy

questions.explanation: The standard initial regimen for tuberculosis, including spinal tuberculosis, combines rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol during the intensive phase. This four-drug combination reduces the risk of resistance developing during treatment. A continuation phase with a reduced drug combination typically follows the initial intensive phase.
questions.question: A patient with confirmed spinal tuberculosis is being started on treatment. Which drug combination forms the standard initial four-drug regimen?

questions.explanation: Urethroplasty is indicated when simpler, less invasive treatments such as dilatation or internal urethrotomy have failed to achieve durable results, since repeated minimally invasive procedures often lead to progressively worsening scarring. Formal surgical reconstruction addresses the diseased segment directly, offering higher long-term success rates. This stepwise escalation reflects the reconstruction ladder principle applied to urethral stricture disease.
questions.question: A patient with a recurrent urethral stricture has already failed repeated dilatation and internal urethrotomy. The next appropriate step in management is:

A 7-year-old presents with recurrent chest infections localised to the left lower lobe. CT chest reveals an area of abnormal lung tissue with a systemic arterial supply from the aorta and no communication with the bronchial tree. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.explanation: Pulmonary sequestration, particularly the intralobar type, commonly presents in older children with recurrent localised chest infections due to poor drainage of the abnormal lung tissue, and the finding of a systemic arterial supply without bronchial communication on imaging confirms the diagnosis, guiding surgical resection as definitive treatment.

questions.question: The MOST important pre-operative requirement before performing any major orthopaedic reconstructive procedure involving large bone defects is:
questions.explanation: Pre-operative planning for bone reconstruction requires comprehensive clinical evaluation, characterisation of the defect size and location by imaging (plain radiograph, CT, MRI), assessment of the surrounding soft tissues and vascularity, and selection of the appropriate reconstruction strategy. Without thorough planning, inadequate graft type selection or insufficient resection leads to poor outcomes, non-union, or tumour recurrence.
options: Inserting a vena cava filter to prevent embolism
Pre-operative physiotherapy to strengthen the limb
Thorough clinical evaluation, imaging for defect characterisation, and surgical planning for reconstruction type
Prescribing a 2-week course of broad-spectrum antibiotics

questions.question: According to the Gustillo–Anderson system, an open fracture with a laceration less than 2 cm and no comminution is classified as:
questions.explanation: Gustillo–Anderson Type I open fractures are characterized by a wound of 2 cm or less with minimal soft-tissue injury and no comminution of the fracture. The wound is usually clean and caused by the bone fragment penetrating from within. Types II and III involve progressively larger wounds, more comminution, and greater soft-tissue damage.

Plain radiography of the affected bone is the first and most essential investigation for a suspected bone tumour. It demonstrates lesion location, size, matrix mineralisation (osteoid vs. cartilaginous), zone of transition (aggressive vs. benign), cortical involvement, periosteal reaction, and soft-tissue extension. Subsequent investigations (CT, MRI, bone scan) are guided by plain film findings.
options: Bone scan to detect skip lesions
Plain radiograph of the affected bone
questions.question: The most important initial investigation when evaluating a suspected bone tumour is:
Avascular necrosis of the femoral head after hip dislocation is directly related to which factor?
questions.explanation: The longer the interval between dislocation and reduction, the greater the risk of avascular necrosis due to sustained interruption of the retinacular blood vessels. Reduction should occur within 6 hours to minimise this risk. Open reduction is indicated when closed reduction fails to restore femoral head perfusion.

An isograft is tissue transferred between genetically identical individuals, such as monozygotic twins, and behaves immunologically like an autograft because there is no antigenic disparity. Allografts, by contrast, are transferred between genetically different individuals of the same species and undergo eventual rejection. Xenografts are transferred between different species.
questions.question: Identical twins undergo skin grafting between one another following a burn injury in one twin. This type of graft is correctly classified as:

questions.explanation: The reconstruction ladder begins with the simplest option (dressings alone) and progresses to more complex options: dressings, direct closure, skin grafts, local flaps, regional flaps, and finally free flaps. The surgeon should use the simplest technique adequate to achieve healing, while considering function and aesthetics.
questions.question: The reconstruction ladder in plastic surgery begins with the SIMPLEST option which is:

questions.explanation: Post-operative management after manual reduction without bowel resection includes nasogastric decompression, IV rehydration, and IV antibiotics for 48 hours followed by oral antibiotics briefly. Long-term prophylactic antibiotics are not required as intussusception is not a chronic infective condition. Overnight monitoring for recurrence and gradual reintroduction of feeds complete the postoperative care.
options: Resumption of feeds after clinical improvement
questions.question: Post-operative management following manual reduction of intussusception without bowel resection includes all EXCEPT:

questions.explanation: Renal transplantation is generally offered across a broad age range, from young children through to selected older adults, with individualised assessment of comorbidity and expected benefit rather than a strict fixed age cut-off determining eligibility. This reflects a shift toward physiological rather than purely chronological assessment of transplant candidacy. Careful case-by-case evaluation is particularly important at the extremes of age.
options: A broad range spanning young children through to selected older adults
Only patients over 70 years of age
Only patients aged exactly 18 to 40 years
No upper or lower age limit is ever applied
Only patients under 10 years of age
questions.question: A transplant centre reviews its recipient selection criteria regarding age. Based on generally accepted published criteria, which age range is considered acceptable for renal transplant recipients?

questions.explanation: Acute tubular necrosis is an EARLY complication of renal trauma. Late complications specifically include delayed bleeding, arteriovenous fistula, urinary fistula, hydronephrosis, PUJ obstruction from perinephric fibrosis, renovascular hypertension, and renal atrophy. Distinguishing early from late complications guides timing of investigation and intervention.
questions.question: Late complications of renal trauma include all of the following EXCEPT:

questions.explanation: Persistent post-operative hiccough (intractable singultus) may be a sign of subphrenic abscess causing diaphragmatic irritation, in addition to uraemia, electrolyte disturbances, and central causes. Subphrenic abscess is a serious post-operative complication following abdominal surgery presenting with fever, raised right hemidiaphragm, and basal pleural effusion. Ultrasound or CT-guided drainage is required.
questions.question: Post-operative hiccough (singultus) that is persistent and intractable may indicate which specific intra-abdominal pathology?

questions.explanation: The visible paradoxical movement is less dangerous than the underlying lung contusion that usually accompanies flail chest. Hypoxia develops from impaired gas exchange in the injured lung parenchyma. Management focuses on oxygenation, analgesia, and ventilatory support rather than the chest wall itself.
options: Underlying pulmonary contusion impairing gas exchange
questions.question: A patient with multiple injuries is found to have a flail chest segment with paradoxical movement. What is the PRIMARY concern with this injury?

questions.explanation: Congenital absence of union between the vas deferens and epididymis results in obstructive azoospermia, as sperm produced in the testis cannot travel to the ejaculate despite normal spermatogenesis. FSH levels are typically normal in such men because spermatogenesis is unimpaired. Treatment involves surgical reconstruction or sperm retrieval for assisted reproduction.
questions.question: Failure of union between the vas deferens and epididymis is a recognized cause of which condition?

A 28-year-old woman presents with pain and swelling around the knee. Imaging shows a lytic, eccentric lesion extending to the subchondral bone of the epiphysis, without periosteal reaction. This presentation is MOST characteristic of:
questions.explanation: Giant cell tumour of bone characteristically presents in skeletally mature young adults as a lytic, eccentric lesion extending to the subchondral bone of the epiphysis, typically around the knee, without an aggressive periosteal reaction, reflecting its typically locally aggressive but usually benign behaviour. Although histologically benign in most cases, giant cell tumour has a notable tendency for local recurrence after curettage and, rarely, malignant transformation or pulmonary metastasis despite benign histology. This distinctive epiphyseal, eccentric location in a skeletally mature patient helps distinguish it from other bone tumours that typically favour the metaphysis or diaphysis.

questions.question: Which variant of oesophageal atresia, involving a proximal blind pouch and a fistula between the distal oesophageal segment and the trachea, accounts for the majority of cases?
options: Type A (pure oesophageal atresia without fistula)
Type C (proximal atresia with distal tracheoesophageal fistula)
Type B (proximal fistula with distal atresia)
Type D (fistula at both proximal and distal segments)
questions.explanation: Type C oesophageal atresia, featuring a blind proximal oesophageal pouch with a fistula connecting the distal oesophageal segment to the trachea, accounts for the vast majority of cases, around 85 percent. This anatomical configuration determines the surgical approach for repair and fistula ligation.

questions.question: Gas gangrene following an open fracture is caused by:
questions.explanation: Gas gangrene is a rapidly progressing, life-threatening infection caused by Clostridium welchii (perfringens) and related anaerobic clostridia. The organism produces gas from tissue fermentation, visible on radiographs as gas in soft tissues, and releases toxins causing extensive myonecrosis and systemic toxaemia. Treatment is aggressive surgical debridement, high-dose penicillin, and hyperbaric oxygen.

questions.question: A newborn boy has a urethral opening located on the dorsal (upper) aspect of the penis rather than the ventral surface. This congenital anomaly is termed:
questions.explanation: Epispadias describes a congenital urethral opening on the dorsal surface of the penis, in contrast to hypospadias, where the opening is displaced ventrally. It is frequently associated with the exstrophy-epispadias complex and disorders of pubic symphysis development. Reconstructive surgery aims to correct both the urethral position and any associated continence issues.

questions.question: A 2-year-old presents with a firm, painless swelling over the anterior fontanelle region present since birth, which does not transilluminate and is separate from the underlying skull on imaging. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.explanation: A dermoid cyst presents as a firm, well-defined, non-transilluminating subcutaneous swelling along embryonic fusion lines such as the anterior fontanelle, resulting from entrapment of ectodermal tissue during development, and is distinct from an encephalocele, which communicates with the intracranial cavity and requires careful imaging before any surgical excision to exclude such a connection.

options: The colour of the wound margins
The speed of the penetrating object
The size of the entry wound
questions.explanation: Wounds are classified by the velocity of the inflicting object because kinetic energy transfer determines the zone of tissue damage. High-velocity missiles cause extensive cavitation and devitalised tissue well beyond the visible tract. This classification guides the extent of surgical debridement required.
questions.question: A gunshot wound to the thigh is assessed in the emergency department. Its classification as a high-velocity missile injury is based primarily on:
Ladd's bands in malrotation cause obstruction by:
options: Twisting the entire midgut around the SMA
Causing intussusception of the proximal jejunum
Compresses duodenum from caecum to right wall
questions.explanation: Ladd's bands are peritoneal folds extending from the abnormally positioned caecum (in the right upper quadrant in malrotation) across the duodenum to the right lateral abdominal wall. They compress the second part of the duodenum from without, causing extrinsic duodenal obstruction. Their division is the first step in Ladd's procedure, immediately relieving the duodenal obstruction.

A junctional naevus contains naevus cells located strictly at the dermo-epidermal junction, typically appearing flat and evenly pigmented. As naevi mature, cells may migrate into the dermis, producing compound then intradermal naevi. Junctional naevi are generally considered to carry a relatively higher potential for change compared with purely intradermal lesions.
questions.question: A congenital pigmented lesion on a child's back is examined and shows naevus cells confined to the dermo-epidermal junction. This is best classified as a:

questions.explanation: Nitric oxide activates guanylate cyclase, increasing cGMP levels that relax cavernosal trabecular smooth muscle, allowing blood to fill the sinusoidal spaces of the corpora cavernosa. This relaxation is the central physiological event initiating penile erection. Impairment of nitric oxide signalling is a common final pathway in many causes of erectile dysfunction.
questions.question: During sexual stimulation, nitric oxide is released from cavernosal nerve endings and endothelium. This mediator produces erection primarily by relaxing which structure?

questions.explanation: A contaminated wound includes fresh traumatic wounds with devitalised tissue, those involving a break in aseptic technique, or wounds containing a foreign body. Clean wounds involve no infection risk and follow elective procedures. Clean-contaminated wounds involve controlled entry into body cavities with minor spillage.
questions.question: A wound classified as 'contaminated' would MOST likely be:

questions.explanation: Tessier's classification of craniofacial clefts numbers them 0-14 based on anatomical location, with clefts 0-7 being facial (below the orbit) and clefts 8-14 being cranial (above the orbit). This system provides a comprehensive map of all possible craniofacial cleft positions and guides surgical planning. The American Cleft Palate Association classification is simpler and more clinically used.
questions.question: The Tessier classification of craniofacial clefts is based on:

questions.explanation: Gastroschisis bowel, damaged by amniotic fluid exposure, has severely impaired motility and function postoperatively. The time to establishment of enteral feeding averages approximately 26 days after primary closure. TPN provides essential nutrition during this prolonged period of gut adaptation. Long-term TPN complications (line infection, liver disease) are therefore important management considerations.
options: Surgery cannot be performed without TPN
TPN reduces the size of the bowel
Delayed bowel function needs nutritional support
TPN prevents infection of the exposed bowel
questions.question: Total parenteral nutrition (TPN) in the management of gastroschisis is important because:

questions.explanation: The non-touch technique specifically refers to handling the catheter using its packaging or sterile instruments so that the portion destined to enter the urethra is never directly touched by the operator's gloved hands, minimising the introduction of contaminants. This is distinct from broader aseptic principles such as skin cleaning or sterile draping, though it complements them. Consistent use of this technique reduces catheter-associated urinary tract infection rates.
options: Avoiding direct hand contact with the catheter segment that will enter the urethra
Never touching the patient during the procedure
Avoiding the use of any lubricant
questions.question: A urology trainee is taught the 'non-touch technique' during catheter insertion. This specific practice refers to:

questions.explanation: The lethal triad of hypothermia, acidosis, and coagulopathy each worsens the others in a self-perpetuating cycle that increases mortality in severe trauma. Damage control resuscitation actively addresses all three simultaneously alongside early haemorrhage control. Correcting this triad is considered as important as surgical control of bleeding itself.
questions.question: A patient in haemorrhagic shock is being resuscitated with damage control principles prior to definitive surgical haemostasis. Which triad of derangements does damage control resuscitation specifically aim to correct?

questions.explanation: Gynaecomastia in the presence of a firm testicular mass raises concern for a hormonally active testicular tumour, such as a Leydig or Sertoli cell tumour, secreting oestrogenic hormones. This warrants urgent scrotal ultrasound and tumour marker assessment rather than reassurance as a benign finding. Recognising this association prevents delay in diagnosing an underlying testicular malignancy.
questions.question: A man with primary infertility undergoes examination and is noted to have gynaecomastia along with a firm testicular mass. This combination should raise suspicion for:

options: Ligation of the thyroglossal tract at the hyoid bone
Cyst, hyoid bone, and tract excised
questions.explanation: The Sistrunk operation (1920) is the standard surgical treatment for thyroglossal duct cyst and involves excision of the cyst, the central portion of the hyoid bone (to ensure complete tract removal), and the tract up to the foramen caecum at the base of the tongue. Simple cystectomy has a recurrence rate of up to 50%; Sistrunk's operation reduces this to less than 5%.
questions.question: The Sistrunk operation for thyroglossal duct cyst involves:

questions.explanation: The Gibson incision provides an extraperitoneal approach to the iliac fossa, enabling vascular anastomosis of the donor renal vein to the external iliac vein (EIV) and the donor renal artery to the internal or external iliac artery, followed by ureteroneocystostomy. The extraperitoneal approach minimizes the risk of intraperitoneal complications. The transplanted kidney is placed in the iliac fossa rather than its native retroperitoneal position.
options: Retroperitoneal flank for native nephrectomy before transplant
Transperitoneal midline for multiple organ retrieval
Inguinal approach for spermatic cord preservation in male recipients
Pfannenstiel incision for pelvic lymphocele drainage
Extraperitoneal iliac fossa for vascular anastomosis and ureteroneocystostomy
questions.question: The Gibson incision is used for renal transplant recipient surgery. What does this incision approach?

questions.explanation: Gillies' approach involves elevating a depressed zygomatic complex through a temporal hairline incision, introducing a periosteal elevator deep to the temporalis fascia to lever the zygoma back into position. It is minimally invasive and cosmetically superior. Inadequate reduction may require additional transosseous wiring or bone plates.
options: Bone plate fixation via temporal incision
questions.question: Which approach is used for SURGICAL REDUCTION of a depressed zygomatic complex fracture via a temporal hairline incision?

questions.explanation: Sodium is the primary extracellular cation responsible for plasma osmolarity. Hypertonic saline (3% or 7.5%) raises serum sodium and osmolarity, creating an osmotic gradient that draws water from the intracellular and interstitial compartments (including cerebral oedema) into the vascular space. This reduces intracranial pressure while simultaneously expanding intravascular volume — a dual benefit in TBI with haemorrhagic shock.
questions.question: Which electrolyte is specifically responsible for the osmotic movement of water OUT of cells in hypertonic saline resuscitation for traumatic brain injury?

questions.explanation: Rhabdomyosarcoma is the commonest soft tissue sarcoma of childhood and can arise in the orbit, presenting with rapidly progressive proptosis. Histology showing small round blue cells with cross-striations reflects the skeletal muscle differentiation characteristic of this tumour, distinguishing it from other small round blue cell tumours of childhood.
questions.question: A 6-year-old presents with a rapidly growing mass in the orbit causing proptosis. Biopsy reveals small round blue cells with cross-striations. Which diagnosis is most likely?
Which general complication of fractures is DEFINED as obstruction of the microcirculation by abnormal red cells in a patient with sickle cell disease after a pelvic injury?
questions.explanation: In sickle cell disease, trauma-induced hypoxia, dehydration, and acidosis trigger sickling of red blood cells, causing vaso-occlusive crises with obstruction of the microcirculation, bone infarction, and pain. This is distinct from fat embolism (fat globules from marrow) and crush syndrome (myoglobin-induced renal failure from rhabdomyolysis).

Prolonged positioning of the knee in flexion after a transtibial amputation, such as with a pillow constantly placed under the stump, risks the development of a knee flexion contracture, which can significantly compromise subsequent prosthetic fitting and gait, since an adequate range of knee extension is important for normal prosthetic limb function. Patients are therefore advised on appropriate positioning and encouraged to perform regular extension exercises as part of early rehabilitation. This is a preventable complication addressed through patient education and structured physiotherapy input from early in the postoperative period.
questions.question: A patient recovering from a transtibial (below-knee) amputation is educated on avoiding prolonged periods of the knee in a flexed position, such as with a pillow constantly under the stump. This advice is given PRIMARILY to prevent:

questions.explanation: Jejunoileal atresia is attributed to intrauterine vascular accidents causing ischaemic necrosis and subsequent resorption of the affected bowel segment. In contrast, duodenal atresia results from failure of vacuolization and recanalization. This vascular theory explains the associated mesenteric defects and distal bowel shortening seen in jejunoileal atresia.
questions.question: The vascular accident theory best explains the aetiology of which intestinal anomaly?

questions.explanation: Bone acts as a mineral reservoir not only for essential ions like calcium and phosphate but also sequesters toxic heavy metals, most notably lead. Bone incorporates lead in place of calcium within the hydroxyapatite crystal lattice, storing it long-term. Lead can be slowly released during bone resorption, particularly during pregnancy, lactation, or osteoporosis, contributing to chronic lead toxicity even years after initial exposure.
questions.question: Bone serves as a reservoir for dangerous ions as well as essential minerals. The dangerous ion specifically mentioned is:
Which clinical sign, elicited by passive extension of the right hip while the patient lies on their left side, suggests retrocaecal appendicitis with irritation of the psoas muscle?
questions.explanation: The psoas sign is elicited by passive extension of the hip while the patient lies on the contralateral side, causing pain due to irritation of the inflamed psoas muscle by an adjacent retrocaecal appendix. This clinical finding helps support the diagnosis of appendicitis, particularly when the appendix lies in a retrocaecal position.

questions.question: Which diagnostic imaging is the FIRST-LINE modality for an haemodynamically unstable trauma patient with suspected abdominal injury?
questions.explanation: FAST ultrasound is the first-line bedside tool in unstable trauma patients, rapidly detecting free peritoneal fluid suggestive of haemoperitoneum. It is non-invasive, portable, and can be performed alongside resuscitation without delay. CT scan is reserved for haemodynamically stable patients requiring detailed anatomical delineation.

options: Jaundice, abdominal pain, and abdominal mass
Jaundice, acholic stools, and failure to thrive
questions.question: The classical clinical triad of choledochal cyst in older children consists of:
questions.explanation: In older children, choledochal cyst classically presents with the triad of jaundice, abdominal pain, and abdominal mass. In infants aged 1-3 months, it presents with obstructive jaundice, acholic stools, and hepatomegaly without the pain or mass component. This age-dependent difference in presentation reflects the evolving nature of the cyst.

questions.question: A patient requires prolonged oral antibiotic therapy for osteomyelitis after an initial intravenous course. A key pharmacological property required of the chosen oral antibiotic is:
questions.explanation: A key pharmacological requirement for antibiotics used to treat osteomyelitis, whether given intravenously or orally, is good penetration into bone tissue, since bone has a relatively poor blood supply compared with soft tissue, and achieving adequate drug concentrations at the site of infection is essential for successful eradication of the causative organism. Antibiotics with poor bone penetration, even if effective against the organism in vitro, may fail clinically despite apparently adequate systemic dosing. This pharmacokinetic consideration, alongside organism susceptibility, guides antibiotic selection for the prolonged treatment courses typically required in osteomyelitis.

questions.question: The most common congenital abnormality of the orofacial structures is:
questions.explanation: Cleft lip and palate is the most common congenital abnormality of the orofacial structures. The incidence varies by ethnicity: 1:2000 in Africa, 1:1000 in Caucasians, 1:500 in Oriental populations, and 1:276 in some Indian tribes. Males are more commonly affected by cleft lip with or without palate, while isolated cleft palate is more common in females.

questions.question: Apligraf (human skin equivalent) for chronic wound management is classified as:
questions.explanation: Apligraf is a bioengineered, bilayer living skin equivalent containing a bovine collagen dermis seeded with human neonatal fibroblasts, covered by a layer of human neonatal keratinocytes. It is used for chronic venous and diabetic ulcers that have not responded to conventional treatment. Unlike split-thickness grafts, it contains living cells that produce growth factors.

questions.question: Which surgical approach is used to ACCESS Zone I neck vascular injuries involving the subclavian vessels and aortic arch?
questions.explanation: Zone I vascular injuries involving the subclavian vessels, brachiocephalic vessels, or aortic arch require median sternotomy for adequate exposure and proximal vascular control. Clavicular extension or supraclavicular incisions may be combined for distal control. Zone I injuries are the most surgically challenging neck injuries with the highest perioperative mortality.

Clear surgical margins are associated with good prognosis (better local control and survival) and do NOT negatively affect prognosis. Negative prognostic factors for squamous cell carcinoma include poor differentiation, deep tumour invasion, perineural invasion, recurrence, tumour size greater than 2cm, and immunosuppression. Clear margins reduce the risk of local recurrence.
questions.question: The prognosis of SCC is NEGATIVELY affected by all EXCEPT:

questions.explanation: Ladd's procedure involves counter-clockwise detorsion of the volvulus if present, division of peritoneal Ladd's bands compressing the duodenum, widening of the mesenteric base, and an incidental appendicectomy, collectively reducing the risk of recurrent volvulus by broadening the narrow mesenteric pedicle.
questions.question: Which surgical procedure is performed to correct malrotation and reduce the risk of recurrent volvulus?
Which sickle cell crisis is the presenting manifestation of SCA most commonly seen in EARLY CHILDHOOD?
questions.explanation: Infectious crisis is the major presenting manifestation of sickle cell anaemia in early childhood, reflecting increased susceptibility to infection from early functional asplenia, reduced IgM, defective alternate complement pathway, and deficiency of phagocytosis-promoting peptides. Early vaccination and prophylactic penicillin are therefore instituted in all children with confirmed SCA.

questions.question: A fair-skinned outdoor labourer has a rough, scaly, erythematous patch on the forearm that has not ulcerated. This lesion is best regarded as a precursor of which malignancy?
questions.explanation: Actinic keratosis is a premalignant lesion caused by cumulative ultraviolet exposure and carries a risk of progression to invasive squamous cell carcinoma if untreated. The scaly, erythematous appearance reflects dysplastic keratinocytes confined to the epidermis. Early treatment reduces the risk of invasive transformation.

Permissive hypotension involves deliberately targeting a lower than normal blood pressure during initial resuscitation of a trauma patient with uncontrolled internal haemorrhage, aiming to maintain adequate but not excessive perfusion pressure, reducing the risk of disrupting early, fragile clot formation at the bleeding site that could occur with aggressive fluid resuscitation and normalisation of blood pressure before definitive surgical or interventional haemostasis is achieved. This strategy is generally avoided in patients with traumatic brain injury, where adequate cerebral perfusion pressure must be maintained. Once definitive haemorrhage control has been achieved, more standard resuscitation targets are then pursued.
questions.question: A trauma patient with uncontrolled internal haemorrhage, awaiting definitive surgical control, is managed with a strategy of 'permissive hypotension', targeting a lower than normal blood pressure. This strategy is used PRIMARILY to:

questions.explanation: Blunt renal trauma accounts for over 90% of all renal injuries, with the majority being minor and managed conservatively without surgery. Penetrating injuries, while less common at under 10%, are more likely to require immediate operative exploration because over 70% are major. Less than 5% of blunt renal injuries are classified as major, requiring surgical intervention.
questions.question: Blunt renal trauma accounts for what percentage of all renal injuries?
In amputations for tumour, exsanguination before tourniquet inflation is specifically avoided to prevent:
questions.explanation: In amputations for malignant or locally expanding tumours, exsanguination (using an Esmarch rubber bandage wrapping) prior to tourniquet inflation is strictly avoided because the mechanical squeezing action could force tumour cells or emboli into the venous circulation, potentially promoting haematogenous metastasis. The tourniquet is applied and inflated without exsanguination in all tumour and infected-limb cases.
options: Haemolysis of red blood cells causing renal failure
Fat embolism from bone marrow manipulation
Nerve ischaemia from prolonged tourniquet time
Dissemination of tumour cells proximally via the venous system

questions.question: A patient with a large open wound following trauma is noted to have significantly increased nitrogen loss in urine despite adequate protein intake. What is the PRIMARY mechanism driving this nitrogen loss?
questions.explanation: The catabolic stress response accelerates skeletal muscle protein breakdown to supply amino acids for wound healing, immune function, and gluconeogenesis. This results in a substantial negative nitrogen balance despite adequate nutritional intake. Prolonged bed rest can further exacerbate this muscle protein loss.
options: Reduced hepatic protein synthesis capacity alone
A Penrose drain left in situ for 2 weeks
Repeated needle aspiration under sterile conditions
Corrugated or suction drain removed at 48–72 hours
No drain; compression dressing alone is sufficient
questions.question: The preferred surgical technique for draining a stump post-amputation to prevent haematoma uses:
questions.explanation: A corrugated or suction drain is placed in the stump at the time of closure and removed at 48–72 hours post-operatively. This prevents haematoma accumulation (a risk factor for infection and flap necrosis) while allowing the wound to be inspected. Leaving the drain too long increases infection risk. After drain removal, sutures remain for approximately 2 weeks.

The early cellulitic phase of acute osteomyelitis presents with acute inflammation characterised by neutrophil accumulation, oedema, and exudate within the metaphyseal marrow. The patient is systemically unwell with fever and raised inflammatory markers. Without intervention, this progresses to the suppurative phase (abscess), then bone necrosis and new bone formation (involucrum).
questions.question: A 5-year-old child presents with fever, severe localized bone pain, and overlying soft-tissue swelling. Blood cultures and ESR are elevated. This MOST likely represents which phase of acute osteomyelitis?
options: Cellulitic phase with early acute inflammation
Septic arthritis of the adjacent joint

questions.question: Haematogenous osteomyelitis in neonates is clinically distinctive because:
questions.explanation: In neonates, osteomyelitis has distinctive features: symptoms may be subtle or entirely absent (making diagnosis difficult), and the metaphyseal vessels cross the growth plate in neonates (unlike older children), allowing infection to spread directly to the epiphysis and adjacent joint. This explains the high rate of septic arthritis complicating neonatal osteomyelitis and the potential for significant growth plate damage leading to deformity.
options: It preferentially affects the metaphysis exclusively
Salmonella is the causative organism in 90% of neonatal cases
It exclusively causes pan-osteomyelitis affecting all bones simultaneously
Symptoms may be mild or absent and the infection may spread directly to the epiphysis
Neonatal osteomyelitis always presents with a sinus and discharge

questions.explanation: Tall, peaked T waves are characteristically one of the earliest ECG changes seen in significant hyperkalaemia, reflecting the effect of elevated extracellular potassium on cardiac myocyte repolarisation, and should prompt urgent treatment even before more advanced changes such as widening of the QRS complex, loss of P waves, or a sine-wave pattern develop, which indicate more severe, life-threatening hyperkalaemia. Crush injury with rhabdomyolysis is a recognised cause of severe hyperkalaemia due to massive release of intracellular potassium from damaged muscle cells. Prompt recognition and treatment of hyperkalaemia is critical to prevent life-threatening cardiac arrhythmia.
questions.question: A trauma patient with crush injury and rhabdomyolysis develops hyperkalaemia. Which ECG change is characteristically an EARLY finding of significant hyperkalaemia?

questions.explanation: In reverse rotation, the midgut rotates clockwise instead of counterclockwise. This results in the transverse colon lying posterior to the SMA, which can obstruct the transverse colon when the SMA compresses it. Surgical correction involves transecting the posteriorly positioned transverse colon and reanastomosing it anterior to the SMA.
questions.question: In reverse rotation malrotation, the clinical consequence is:
A patient's abdominal wound is left open for five days after a contaminated laparotomy before the surgeon sutures the edges together. This technique is best described as:
questions.explanation: Delayed primary closure allows the inflammatory phase to reduce bacterial load before edges are approximated. It combines the safety of an open wound with the speed of primary healing. This is favoured in contaminated wounds at high infection risk.

Wound dehiscence with evisceration classically occurs around the seventh to tenth post-operative day, often related to increased intra-abdominal pressure or wound infection at the time healing strength is still developing. Early recognition and emergency surgical repair prevent further complications. Risk factors include poor nutrition, infection, and increased abdominal pressure.
questions.question: A patient several days after abdominal surgery develops wound breakdown with protrusion of abdominal contents through the incision. Around which post-operative day does this complication classically occur?

questions.explanation: The 'duodenal triangle' is a plain X-ray finding in malrotation located in the right upper quadrant, formed by the triangle of air within the dilated duodenum underneath the liver edge. It reflects the obstructed, air-filled duodenum trapped under the right hepatic lobe in malrotation with Ladd's bands. This subtle sign should prompt urgent upper GI contrast study.
questions.question: The 'duodenal triangle' on plain abdominal X-ray in malrotation is located in:
Bone infection resulting from contiguous spread from an adjacent soft-tissue abscess is classified as:
questions.explanation: Contiguous-focus osteomyelitis arises from spread of infection from adjacent soft tissue, as seen in pressure sores overlying the sacrum or greater trochanter, diabetic foot infections, or direct spread from an adjacent infected wound. It differs from haematogenous osteomyelitis (bloodborne) and direct inoculation (post-traumatic or post-operative). It often involves multiple organisms.

questions.question: A child with confirmed acute haematogenous osteomyelitis responds well to intravenous antibiotics with clinical and laboratory improvement. The typical MINIMUM total duration of antibiotic therapy (intravenous plus oral) recommended is approximately:
questions.explanation: Acute haematogenous osteomyelitis in children typically requires a minimum total duration of antibiotic therapy of approximately 4-6 weeks, combining an initial intravenous course with a subsequent oral course once clinical improvement is established, to ensure adequate eradication of infection from bone tissue with its relatively poor antibiotic penetration compared with soft tissue. Shorter courses risk relapse or progression to chronic osteomyelitis, while unnecessarily prolonged courses increase the risk of drug toxicity and antimicrobial resistance without added benefit. Duration may be extended in more severe, complicated, or chronic cases based on clinical response.

Transcutaneous oxygen pressure measurement provides an objective, non-invasive assessment of local tissue perfusion adequacy at a proposed amputation level, helping predict the likelihood of adequate wound healing at that level in patients with peripheral vascular disease, where clinical assessment alone can be unreliable. Values below a certain threshold suggest an increased risk of poor healing at that level, prompting consideration of a more proximal amputation level with better perfusion, or further attempts at revascularisation. This objective measurement complements clinical assessment and other vascular investigations in guiding the difficult decision regarding optimal amputation level.
questions.question: A patient with peripheral vascular disease is being assessed to determine the most appropriate level for a lower limb amputation. Transcutaneous oxygen pressure measurement at the proposed amputation site is used to assess:

questions.explanation: Immunosuppression is most intense during the first 3 months post-transplantation, corresponding to the period of highest acute rejection risk, and is then gradually reduced to maintenance levels for the remainder of the recipient's life. This initial high-intensity phase also carries the highest infection and PTLD risk. The gradual reduction principle balances the competing risks of rejection and infection.
questions.question: Post-transplant immunosuppression is at its highest intensity during which specific period?
options: The first two weeks during induction only
The first three months following transplantation
The entire first year without reduction
Indefinitely at the same dose throughout life

questions.question: A patient with severe facial trauma has bilateral periorbital ecchymosis without direct periorbital impact, along with epistaxis. What underlying injury does this pattern suggest?
questions.explanation: Bilateral periorbital ecchymosis unrelated to direct local trauma, so-called racoon eyes, is a classic indirect sign of basilar skull fracture. Its presence should prompt evaluation for associated CSF leak and intracranial injury. Nasal precautions such as avoiding nasal tubes then become important.

options: Before any other procedure as the first investigation in theatre
After stabilisation, to define the injury
Immediately after the accident in the emergency department
Only after 6 weeks when the haematoma has resolved
Concurrently with cystostomy insertion during the same procedure
questions.question: A patient with pelvic fracture undergoes suprapubic cystostomy after failed urethral catheterization. A retrograde urethrogram is then planned. What is the CORRECT timing for this investigation?
questions.explanation: Retrograde urethrogram is performed after suprapubic urinary diversion has secured drainage and the patient has been haemodynamically stabilized. Performing a retrograde urethrogram before drainage is secured or during acute haemodynamic instability is inappropriate. Timing allows the perineal haematoma to partially organize, improving urethral imaging clarity. The urethrogram defines injury extent and guides planning for delayed urethroplasty, typically performed 3-6 months after initial injury.

questions.question: Rigid post-amputation dressings are left in place for at least how long before the first planned change?
questions.explanation: Rigid post-amputation dressings (plaster of Paris or thermoplastic socket) are left undisturbed for at least 2 weeks unless there are clinical signs of infection, haematoma, or excessive pain necessitating earlier inspection. The rigid dressing controls oedema, protects the wound, reduces pain, and allows the stump to begin maturing into a shape suitable for early prosthetic fitting—faster than soft dressings achieve.

questions.question: A composite graft consists of:
questions.explanation: A composite graft consists of skin and some underlying tissue, such as skin and cartilage (as used in nasal tip and ear reconstruction) or skin and fat. Unlike simple skin grafts, composite grafts include multiple tissue types for reconstruction of complex three-dimensional structures. They require excellent recipient site vascularity for survival.

questions.question: A patient with an indwelling rubber catheter for 6 weeks presents with inability to deflate the balloon. The best INITIAL management is:
questions.explanation: The very first manoeuvre when a balloon fails to deflate is to apply a syringe to the inflation port and attempt aspiration of the balloon fluid, as a simple valve blockage or luminal narrowing may be overcome by suction. Only if this fails should progressive escalation to cutting the channel, probing the inner channel, or ultrasound-guided suprapubic balloon puncture be attempted. Forcible traction is never appropriate as it risks urethral rupture.
options: Cut the inflation channel at its base to release the balloon fluid
Attempt aspiration of balloon contents via the inflation port first
Apply forcible traction to burst the balloon within the bladder
Immediate cystoscopy to visualize and puncture the balloon
Suprapubic puncture of the balloon under ultrasound guidance directly

questions.question: Diffuse lower abdominal tenderness with lack of sensation of bladder fullness following trauma suggests which specific injury?
questions.explanation: Intraperitoneal bladder rupture allows urine to extravasate freely into the peritoneal cavity, causing chemical peritonitis manifest as diffuse lower abdominal tenderness. Loss of sensation of bladder fullness occurs because urine escapes the bladder before stretch receptors signal fullness. Urine absorption leads to pseudo-renal failure with elevated serum creatinine and urea. This requires urgent surgical exploration and repair.
options: Extraperitoneal bladder rupture contained in the pelvis
Posterior urethral disruption at the prostate
Upper ureteral avulsion with retroperitoneal urinoma
Intraperitoneal bladder rupture with urinary peritonitis

questions.explanation: Approximately 15% of nephroblastoma cases are associated with other congenital anomalies including aniridia, hemihypertrophy of the body, and genitourinary anomalies. Children with aniridia have a 30% risk of developing Wilms' tumour, justifying surveillance. The WAGR syndrome (Wilms', Aniridia, Genitourinary anomalies, mental Retardation) represents a specific chromosomal deletion at 11p13 encompassing these features.
questions.question: Nephroblastoma is associated with which 15% rate of concurrent anomalies?
options: Renal agenesis, duplex systems, and prune belly syndrome
Cardiac defects, vertebral anomalies, and limb defects
Down syndrome, Turner syndrome, and Prader-Willi syndrome

questions.explanation: CT imaging provides superior three-dimensional detail for complex or comminuted mandibular fractures that plain radiographs may not fully characterise. It is considered desirable rather than essential because straightforward fractures can often be managed using the panoramic view alone. The additional detail aids surgical planning in more complicated cases.
questions.question: A patient with facial trauma has a CT scan requested to assess a suspected complex mandibular fracture in addition to the panoramic view. Why is this additional imaging considered DESIRABLE rather than essential?
options: It better defines complex fracture patterns and displacement
It is cheaper than plain radiographs
It avoids the need for any treatment
It is required for all simple fractures

questions.question: Chronic osteomyelitis on plain radiograph characteristically shows all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Chronic osteomyelitis radiographically shows: generalised sclerosis with loss of corticomedullary differentiation, bone-in-bone appearance (from new bone formation), irregular expansion of the cortex, sequestrum (dead bone) visible as a dense fragment, and cloacae (channels for pus drainage). Uniform cortical thinning is not a feature; in fact, cortex typically scleroses and thickens in chronic infection.
options: Uniform cortical thinning of the diaphysis
Generalised sclerosis with irregular bone expansion

questions.question: A fracture through abnormal bone weakened by a metastatic deposit is classified as:
questions.explanation: A pathological fracture occurs through bone that has been structurally weakened by an underlying disease process, most commonly metastatic carcinoma, primary bone tumours, osteoporosis, Paget's disease, or infection. It can occur with minimal or no trauma. Metastatic deposits from breast, lung, kidney, thyroid, and prostate are the commonest causes.

Bilious (green) vomiting distinguishes malrotation/volvulus from pyloric stenosis, in which vomiting is always non-bilious (projectile). The presence of bile in vomitus indicates obstruction at or below the ampulla of Vater. Any neonate with bilious vomiting must be treated as having a surgical emergency (malrotation with volvulus) until proven otherwise.
options: Bilious vomiting in malrotation, absent in stenosis
Abdominal distension is absent in malrotation
Malrotation only presents in the neonatal period
questions.question: Which of the following differentiates malrotation from pyloric stenosis on clinical assessment?

options: A 3–4 stage procedure using open cancellous bone grafting rather than bone cement
Use of a single-stage approach with immediate bone grafting
Use of vascularised fibular graft as the primary reconstruction method
Use of systemic antibiotics without any surgical debridement
questions.question: Compared to the Belfast procedure, the Papineau technique for chronic osteomyelitis is distinguished by:
questions.explanation: The Papineau technique is a 3–4 stage procedure for chronic osteomyelitis that employs open cancellous bone grafting instead of bone cement as a biological spacer. Open grafts are packed into the debrided cavity and allowed to granulate, providing osteoinductive scaffolding. This avoids the foreign body effect of bone cement but requires more stages and wound care.

Buruli ulcer is caused by Mycobacterium ulcerans, which produces the toxin mycolactone that causes extensive, painless tissue necrosis and characteristically undermined ulcer edges. It is classified among the specific infective causes of chronic leg ulceration in endemic tropical regions. Management often requires prolonged antibiotic therapy combined with surgical debridement and skin grafting of the resulting defect.
questions.question: A tropical ulcer specialist evaluates a patient with a chronic, painless, undermined skin ulcer on the limb, caused by a mycobacterial organism producing a tissue-destroying toxin. This condition is known as:

questions.explanation: Normal testicular volume with normal FSH and testosterone in the setting of azoospermia points toward an intact spermatogenic and endocrine axis with a mechanical obstruction preventing sperm delivery. This contrasts with primary testicular failure, where FSH is elevated due to loss of tubular feedback. Identifying the obstruction site guides surgical reconstruction options such as vasoepididymostomy.
questions.question: A man with azoospermia has normal testicular volume, normal FSH, and normal testosterone. Vasography confirms an obstruction. This clinical and hormonal pattern is most consistent with:

questions.explanation: Consolidation with productive cough and fever presenting around five to seven days after surgery is characteristic of post-operative pneumonia, often following aspiration or prolonged reduced ventilation. This differs from early atelectasis, which typically presents within hours of surgery. Appropriate antibiotics and respiratory physiotherapy are central to management.
questions.question: A patient develops fever with a productive cough five to seven days after major abdominal surgery, and the chest radiograph shows lobar consolidation. What is the MOST likely diagnosis?

questions.explanation: Osteoblasts are plump, cuboidal, mononuclear cells derived from mesenchymal stem cells that line the surface of forming bone, actively synthesising and secreting osteoid, the unmineralised organic bone matrix, which is subsequently mineralised to form mature bone. As osteoblasts become surrounded and embedded within the matrix they produce, some differentiate into osteocytes, the mature, quiescent bone cells that maintain the bone matrix and sense mechanical loading. This osteoblast-driven bone formation is balanced against osteoclast-mediated bone resorption in the continuous process of bone remodelling.
questions.question: A histology slide shows plump, cuboidal cells lining the surface of newly forming bone, actively synthesising osteoid (unmineralised bone matrix). These cells are:

questions.explanation: Positive V/Q scanning or pulmonary arteriography provides definitive confirmation of pulmonary embolism. D-dimer has high sensitivity but low specificity and is useful as a rule-out rather than rule-in test. ECG and CXR are important but non-specific investigations that support clinical suspicion without confirming the diagnosis.
questions.question: Which investigation is MOST RELIABLE for confirming the diagnosis of pulmonary embolism?
Which of the following amputation levels preserves the ankle joint and is therefore considered the most distal major lower limb amputation?
questions.explanation: Syme amputation is an ankle disarticulation that removes the foot while preserving the full length of the tibia and fibula. It preserves end-bearing capability on the heel pad, allowing the patient to walk short distances without a prosthesis. Although more distal amputations (transmetatarsal, Lisfranc, Chopart) exist, Syme is the most distal named major amputation providing functional end-bearing weight transmission.

questions.question: Arteriogenic erectile dysfunction in an older patient is considered a component of which systemic condition?
questions.explanation: Arteriogenic erectile dysfunction in older men reflects diffuse penile arterial insufficiency as part of generalized atherosclerosis, and these men are at elevated risk for concurrent coronary artery disease, cerebrovascular disease, and peripheral vascular disease. Therefore, new-onset erectile dysfunction in a middle-aged or older man warrants cardiovascular risk assessment. The penile arteries are small caliber vessels where atherosclerosis manifests early.
options: Generalized atherosclerosis including coronary artery disease
Isolated penile vascular disease without systemic involvement
Peripheral neuropathy from diabetes mellitus only

questions.explanation: Syndactyly is classified as complex, or type II, when there is bony fusion between adjacent digits, in contrast to simple syndactyly where only skin and soft tissue are joined. This distinction affects surgical planning, since bony fusion requires osteotomy in addition to soft tissue separation. Complex syndactyly is often associated with syndromic conditions such as Apert syndrome.
questions.question: Two adjacent fingers are fused with associated bony fusion of the underlying phalanges, rather than simple skin webbing. This is classified as which type of syndactyly?

questions.explanation: Anorectal manometry demonstrating absence of the recto-anal inhibitory reflex (RAIR) has virtually 100% diagnostic accuracy for Hirschsprung's disease. It is particularly valuable for ultrashort segment HD where biopsy findings may be equivocal. Rectal biopsy has 95% accuracy and is used for histological confirmation. Barium enema has only 80% accuracy.
questions.question: In Hirschsprung's disease, which investigation has the highest diagnostic accuracy?

questions.explanation: Burns of the vocal cords are an absolute indication for immediate intubation to secure the airway. Other absolute indications include burns of the palate, tongue, and pharynx, and oedema of the posterior pharynx and upper glottis. Hoarseness, facial burns, and sooty sputum are relative indications requiring close monitoring.
questions.question: An absolute indication for endotracheal intubation in a burn patient is:
Which bone sustains the MOST fractures overall, as the commonest fractured bone encountered clinically?
questions.explanation: Colles' fracture of the distal radius is described as the commonest of all fractures, particularly in middle-aged and elderly women who fall on an outstretched hand. Osteoporosis significantly increases susceptibility. The clavicle is the commonest fracture in children, but overall across all age groups, the distal radius predominates in fracture incidence.

Discitis, infection or inflammation of the intervertebral disc space, characteristically presents in young children with refusal to sit, stand, or walk, back pain, and localised spinal tenderness, with imaging showing disc space narrowing and adjacent vertebral endplate changes, reflecting the disc's relatively good blood supply in young children that later diminishes with age. This age-related vascular pattern explains why discitis is more common in young children than adults, in whom vertebral osteomyelitis is more typical. Management typically involves antibiotics, with surgery reserved for cases with abscess formation or neurological compromise.
questions.question: A young child presents with refusal to sit or walk, back pain, and localised spinal tenderness, with imaging showing narrowing of an intervertebral disc space and adjacent vertebral endplate changes. This presentation is characteristic of:

questions.explanation: Regional nodal involvement in prostate cancer staging is confirmed histologically by identifying metastatic tumour deposits within resected pelvic lymph nodes, rather than by PSA level, Gleason score, or bone scan findings alone, which reflect different aspects of disease. Nodal involvement upstages the cancer and has significant prognostic and treatment implications, often prompting consideration of adjuvant systemic therapy. Pelvic lymphadenectomy at the time of prostatectomy allows this pathological staging to be performed accurately.
questions.question: A patient's prostate cancer is being staged using pathological criteria after radical prostatectomy. Lymph node involvement identified at the time of surgery would upstage the disease. Which specific finding indicates regional nodal involvement in prostate cancer staging?
options: Metastatic tumour deposits within pelvic lymph nodes
A high Gleason score in the primary tumour alone
Bone scan uptake in the pelvis
Elevated PSA alone without tissue confirmation

questions.explanation: Pathological femoral shaft fractures most frequently result from metastatic bone deposits, especially from carcinomas of the breast, lung, kidney, thyroid, and prostate. Importantly, closed femoral fractures can account for 0.5–1 litre of blood loss into the thigh soft tissues, which contributes significantly to hypovolaemic shock.
options: Blood loss into tissues is typically negligible
Pathological fractures of the femur mostly arise from secondary deposits
Open fractures of the femur are commoner than closed
All femoral shaft fractures require immediate fasciotomy
Femoral fractures are excluded when only AP pelvic radiographs are taken
questions.question: Which of the following statements about a fracture of the shaft of the femur is CORRECT?
The MCU (micturating cystourethrogram) finding characteristic of posterior urethral valves is:
questions.explanation: MCU in posterior urethral valves classically shows posterior urethral dilatation above the valves, narrow bladder neck, bladder trabeculation and sacculation, vesicoureteric reflux (in 50%), and a thickened bladder wall. The dilated posterior urethra contrasting with the narrowed anterior urethra (distal to the valves) is the hallmark finding. MCU also demonstrates the severity of reflux and bladder anatomy.

Thiazide diuretics and beta-blockers are the antihypertensive agents most consistently associated with erectile dysfunction, likely through reduction of penile blood flow and depression of libido respectively. In contrast, ACE inhibitors and calcium channel blockers are considered relatively neutral or even favorable regarding erectile function. Switching to a less implicated agent often improves erectile function.
options: Calcium channel blockers and alpha-1 blockers
ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers
Direct vasodilators and centrally acting agents
questions.question: An older hypertensive man develops erectile dysfunction while on antihypertensive therapy. Which drug class is most commonly implicated?
The distal convoluted tubule of the kidney reabsorbs sodium via which specific transporter?
questions.explanation: The distal convoluted tubule reabsorbs sodium via the Na+,Cl- co-transporter (NCC, also called the thiazide-sensitive co-transporter because thiazide diuretics block it). ENaC (epithelial sodium channel) is expressed in the cortical collecting duct principal cells and is regulated by aldosterone. NKCC2 is in the thick ascending limb. SGLT1 is in the small intestine and proximal tubule. NHE3 is in the proximal tubule.

options: Crush bruise plus raised intratracheal pressure against closed glottis
questions.question: A clothesline tackle to the neck causes tracheal injury through which specific mechanism?
questions.explanation: A clothesline tackle creates sudden anterior compression of the trachea while glottic closure creates a trapped air column; the resulting pressure surge ruptures the tracheal wall or cricotracheal junction. This mechanism also occurs from improper seatbelt wearing. Early recognition is vital as progressive oedema can occlude the airway.

questions.question: Early stabilisation of long bone fractures within 24 hours of injury is thought to reduce the incidence of fat embolism syndrome PRIMARILY by:
questions.explanation: Early stabilisation of long bone fractures is thought to reduce the incidence and severity of fat embolism syndrome primarily by limiting ongoing movement at the fracture site, which reduces continued release of marrow fat globules into the venous circulation from the unstable fracture ends. Prolonged instability and repeated manipulation of an unfixed fracture are believed to increase this risk. This is one of several recognised benefits of early definitive fracture fixation in polytrauma patients, alongside earlier mobilisation and reduced pulmonary complications.

Hyperplastic mesenteric lymphadenitis (enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes) is the most common intraoperative finding in idiopathic intussusception, confirming the role of reactive lymphoid hypertrophy (from viral infections) as the precipitating factor. This finding does not itself serve as a fixed lead point but reflects the lymphoid hyperplasia that initiates the peristaltic imbalance.
questions.question: The MOST common intraoperative finding in aetiology of idiopathic intussusception is:
A patient develops increasing airway resistance and desaturation shortly after intubation, with reduced breath sounds on the right and hyper-resonance. What is the LIKELY cause?
questions.explanation: Unilateral reduced breath sounds with hyper-resonance after intubation suggests either the tube has advanced into the right mainstem bronchus or a pneumothorax has developed. Tube position should be checked and withdrawn if too deep, and chest decompression considered if pneumothorax is confirmed. Rapid reassessment prevents ongoing hypoxia.
options: Right mainstem bronchus intubation or pneumothorax

questions.question: Which type of burn is caused by moist heat?
questions.explanation: A scald is a burn caused by moist heat, such as hot water, steam, or hot cooking oil. Scalds are among the most common types of burns, particularly in children and the elderly. The depth of injury depends on the temperature of the liquid and the duration of contact with the skin.

questions.question: A burns patient develops progressive tissue death in a wound zone that was initially viable but poorly perfused, following inadequate resuscitation. Which zone of burn injury is responsible for this extension?
questions.explanation: The zone of stasis surrounds the central zone of coagulation and contains tissue with compromised but potentially salvageable perfusion. Hypotension, infection, or oedema can convert this zone to irreversible necrosis. Adequate early resuscitation aims to preserve this zone.

questions.question: Which acid-base and electrolyte abnormality is classically expected in an infant with prolonged vomiting from hypertrophic pyloric stenosis?
questions.explanation: Persistent vomiting of gastric contents in pyloric stenosis leads to loss of hydrogen and chloride ions, producing a hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis as the kidneys initially compensate by excreting potassium to conserve hydrogen ions. This must be corrected before proceeding to surgery to reduce anaesthetic risk.

Serum testosterone is included in the mandatory work-up of erectile dysfunction specifically to identify hypogonadism as a treatable endocrine cause. Additional tests such as prolactin and thyroid function may be added if the testosterone result or clinical picture suggests a broader endocrine abnormality. Identifying an endocrine cause allows for targeted hormonal therapy rather than symptomatic treatment alone.
questions.question: As part of the mandatory laboratory evaluation of erectile dysfunction, a fasting hormone panel is requested. Which specific test is included primarily to screen for an endocrinological cause?

questions.explanation: Following skin grafts on the reconstruction ladder, the next step is local flaps, then regional flaps (pedicle flaps), and finally free flaps (microsurgical reconstruction). The principle is to use the simplest reliable technique to achieve the goals of reconstruction. Each level is chosen when the simpler option is not feasible or would give an inferior outcome.
questions.question: The reconstruction ladder progresses from simplest to most complex; what comes IMMEDIATELY after skin grafts?
For non-operative management of renal trauma, which imaging is recommended for follow-up at 48 to 72 hours?
questions.explanation: Follow-up imaging at 48 to 72 hours for conservatively managed renal trauma includes repeat USS to detect developing urinoma, perinephric haematoma, or abscesses. CT provides more detailed information when USS is equivocal. Serial monitoring of haematocrit and haematuria is performed concurrently.
options: Repeat CT or USS for fluid collections and haematoma

questions.explanation: Annular pancreas results from abnormal fusion of the ventral and dorsal pancreatic buds during embryogenesis, forming a ring of pancreatic tissue that encircles and can partially or completely obstruct the second part of the duodenum, often presenting similarly to duodenal atresia with bilious vomiting and requiring surgical bypass rather than resection of the pancreatic tissue itself.
questions.question: A neonate presents with bilious vomiting and is found on contrast study to have a ring of pancreatic tissue completely encircling the second part of the duodenum, causing partial obstruction. Which diagnosis is most likely?

questions.explanation: Failure of chest rise during bag-mask ventilation most often results from airway obstruction or poor head positioning rather than equipment further downstream. Repositioning the head and clearing the airway usually restores effective ventilation. Only after this is confirmed should other causes be sought.
questions.question: An unconscious patient is being bag-mask ventilated before intubation. The chest is not rising despite adequate seal and ventilation attempts. What should be checked FIRST?

questions.explanation: Circumferential chest eschar can act like a rigid corset that restricts thoracic expansion and impairs ventilation independent of airway patency. Escharotomy incisions along the chest wall release this constriction and allow adequate respiratory excursion. This differs from airway-directed interventions, which do not relieve mechanical restriction.
questions.question: A patient with deep circumferential burns of the chest wall develops worsening ventilation despite a patent airway. Which procedure directly addresses restricted chest wall movement in this scenario?

questions.explanation: Intravenous antibiotics should be administered as soon as possible after an open fracture injury, ideally within the first hour, since early antibiotic administration has been shown to significantly reduce the risk of subsequent infection, and this timing is more important than waiting for debridement or definitive fixation to be performed. Antibiotic choice and duration are guided by the severity of the wound according to classification systems such as Gustilo-Anderson. Delaying antibiotics until signs of infection appear represents a reactive rather than preventive approach and significantly worsens outcomes.
questions.question: A patient presents with an open fracture of the tibia following a road traffic accident. According to standard trauma protocols, intravenous antibiotics should be administered:

questions.explanation: Total body water constitutes approximately 60% of lean body mass in young adult males. This value is lower in young women and older men (approximately 50%), and lowest in older women (approximately 45%), reflecting the higher fat content in these groups since adipose tissue contains less water than muscle. This baseline understanding is essential for calculating fluid deficits and replacement volumes in trauma.
questions.question: Total body water constitutes approximately what percentage of lean body mass in young adult males?
A crush injury from industrial machinery presents with ragged, devitalised tissue margins and heavy contamination. According to Rank and Wakefield, this wound is best classified as:
questions.explanation: Untidy wounds result from crushing, tearing, or blast mechanisms and contain devitalised, contaminated tissue with irregular margins. They require thorough debridement before any definitive closure is attempted. Immediate primary repair in such wounds risks infection and failure.

options: The neuroma is entrapped by scar tissue with local pressure stimulation
The nerve stump is too long and folds back on itself
The neuroma secretes nociceptive cytokines into the bloodstream
The neuroma invades adjacent bone causing osteomyelitis
The disorganised nerve fascicles compress the adjacent artery
questions.question: A neuroma complication after amputation causes pain specifically because:
questions.explanation: Post-amputation neuromas form at all nerve stumps when axons attempt to regenerate; they become symptomatic when the neuroma is entrapped within scar tissue and subjected to local mechanical pressure during prosthesis use. Prevention requires drawing the nerve gently distally, cutting it cleanly at least 2 cm proximal to the bone section, and ligating large nerve vessels before allowing the nerve to retract proximally.

Injectable calcium phosphate cements (e.g., carbonated apatite preparations) are used to fill osteoporotic metaphyseal cavities commonly seen in elderly patients with distal radius fractures, vertebral compression fractures, and tibial plateau fractures.
